*Patrologiae Cursus Completus*, or Universal Library … of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III … FIRST SERIES,

## Volume LXIII of the Patrology

ENNODIUS / POPE HORMISDA / THE PRIEST TRIFOLIUS / ELPIS / BOETHIUS.

## Front matter of the volume

### Title page of the series

## COMPLETE COURSE OF THE PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL LIBRARY

Complete, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprint of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the utmost diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions issued during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of every page and indicating the subject treated below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by others possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers have commented on the individual books of Scripture, and in which passages of their works they have done so.

The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others when the following matters are weighed: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, and the modest price; above all, this collection is a single, systematic, chronological gathering of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but assembled for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

FIRST SERIES, containing the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of complete courses in the various branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# In the Year of Our Lord 521, Magnus Felix Ennodius, Bishop of Ticinum

[Col. 0009]

## Prologue

*(From Gallandius.)*

[Col. 0009A] **I.** Magnus Felix Ennodius testifies that he was of Gallic, and indeed very illustrious, descent [**Note: [Col. 0009D] Ennodius, Book I, Letter 2**], and that he was born at Arles [**Note: [Col. 0009D] The same, Book VII, Letter 8**]. This is the opinion of those learned men to whom we owe the literary history of Gaul [**Note: [Col. 0009D] *Literary History of France*, vol. III, p. 96**], although Sirmondus [**Note: [Col. 0009D] Sirmondus, *Life of Ennodius*, prefixed to his works**], Sollerius [**Note: [Col. 0009D] Sollerius, *Acts of the Saints*, vol. IV, August, p. 271, no. 5**], and others appear to have doubts on this point.

His birth must be assigned to the year A.D. 473, since he died in 521 at the age of forty-eight, as will become clear below. As a boy he was first educated at Milan in the humanities [**Note: [Col. 0009D] Ennodius, *Eucharisticus*, below, p. 159, col. c]; later he professes that he even came to detest the very names of the liberal studies [**Note: [Col. 0009D] The same, Book IX, Letter 1**]. Then, in the year 489, at the age of sixteen, deprived of the support of the aunt who had raised him, he married a woman of the noblest and wealthiest family [Col. 0009B] [**Note: [Col. 0009D] The same, *Eucharisticus*, p. 160, cols. e, a].

A few years later, renouncing the world, he entered the ecclesiastical service. He was ordained deacon by Epiphanius, bishop of Ticinum [**Note: [Col. 0009D] The same, *Life of Epiphanius*, p. 196, col. b], and also had as his companion in the religious life the wife whom he had married [**Note: [Col. 0009D] The same, *Eucharisticus*, p. 160, col. d]. Having attached himself to the clergy, he placed himself under Servilion as his teacher, and was instructed by him in sacred disciplines [**Note: [Col. 0010D] The same, Book V, Letter 14]. For this reason Sollerius judged less correctly [**Note: [Col. 0010D] Sollerius, cited work, p. 272, no. 2] that Ennodius had studied the liberal disciplines under Servilion.

Meanwhile, Ennodius is reported to have accompanied his bishop Epiphanius as a member of the Burgundian embassy that took place in 494 [**Note: [Col. 0010D] Ennodius, *Life of Epiphanius*, p. 153, col. e], and indeed while he was serving as a deacon. That he remained in this rank for a long time is suggested by the fact that in 513 he composed, while still a deacon, his excellent *Apologeticus* in defense of the Palmary synod. On this matter, I would have you consult Pagius [**Note: [Col. 0010D] Pagius, under the year 502, §§ 3 and 4**].

Indeed, he may perhaps not have advanced beyond that rank until the year 510 or 511, when, after the death of Maximus II, the successor of Epiphanius, he was elevated to the episcopate of the Church of Ticinum. He accomplished many distinguished deeds while occupying the cathedral see. Above all, his proven virtue and learning shone forth in the two embassies to the emperor Anastasius, which he undertook under Pope Hormisda on behalf of the orthodox faith in the years 515 and 517. Although both missions were rendered fruitless by the stratagems of that crafty ruler, this is clear from the ecclesiastical *Annals* of Baronius.

After returning to his Church, the blessed bishop survived for only a short time [Col. 0010A]. For from his epitaph, reported by Sirmondus [**Note: [Col. 0010D] Sirmondus, *Life of Ennodius*] and others, we understand that he departed this life for heaven on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, during the consulship of Valerius, a man of senatorial rank. On that day his memory is annually commemorated in the records of the Church. Thus he died in the year of our Lord 521, at the age of forty-eight.

This chronological calculation is derived from the fact that the holy bishop was approximately sixteen years old, as he himself testifies [**Note: [Col. 0010D] Ennodius, *Eucharisticus*, p. 160, col. e], when Theoderic entered Italy—that is, in the year 489. If this year of his age is reconciled with the consulship of Valerius, during which he is described as having been laid to rest, Ennodius’s final year must have been his forty-eighth, A.D. 521, as Sirmondus correctly argues [**Note: [Col. 0010D] Sirmondus, on Ennodius’s *Eucharisticus*, cited passage].

[Col. 0010B] **II.** The learned and careful writers of the *Literary History of France* make many excellent observations about the literary remains of this holy bishop of Ticinum [**Note: [Col. 0010D] *Literary History of France*, vol. III, pp. 100 ff.]; it will therefore be worthwhile to consult them. Yet, lest we appear entirely to neglect our duty, we wish to bring forward here the judgment of the most learned Sirmondus concerning the same works [**Note: [Col. 0010D] Sirmondus, letter prefixed to Ennodius’s works]:

> “If Ennodius’s age sprinkled some mud upon him, that is no reason why we should not love the flowing spring of genius and eloquence in his writings; nor, because the verse in his poems sometimes limps, should we fail to embrace the sound judgment and acumen found everywhere in them. What of that knowledge and illumination of the times for which even authors of the lowest rank are commonly sought? Who, reading the letters of Ennodius, would not gladly recognize Symmachuses, Hormisdas, Caesariuses, Faustuses, Boethiuses, [Col. 0010C] Liberiuses, Aratores, Elpises, and the other luminaries of his age? Or whom would not the recollection of the varied events that took place in Italy, Gaul, Germany, and Greece during that century, whether in Theoderic’s single *Panegyric* or in the single *Life of Epiphanius of Ticinum*, affect? I pass over his expressions and declamations, which, in my judgment, are such that, although they appear to be the latest-born among Latin compositions, they may be compared with the earliest and middle periods, and, like roses blooming out of season, ought to be more highly prized.”

And elsewhere [**Note: [Col. 0010D] The same, *Life of Ennodius*]:

> “Ennodius flourished with such a reputation for genius and learning that not only were the things he wrote of his own accord held in high esteem, but, at the request of friends whom he cherished most devotedly, he was also compelled to devote constant labor to dictating speeches, letters, epitaphs, and epigrams on various subjects in the name of others. In this field many things were indeed illustrious enough to add glory to Ennodius; but nothing was more illustrious than the *Apologeticus* and the *Panegyric*: in the latter he publicly praised King Theoderic; in the former he defended the cause of Pope Symmachus and the Roman synod with such approval that the entire synod honored him with the most distinguished commendation and decree.”

Thus far the distinguished man.

**III.** Having touched briefly on the excellence of Ennodius’s minor works, it is especially important to observe [Col. 0011B] that there was someone bold enough to associate Saint Ennodius, when he discussed grace and free will, with Faustus of Riez and the Massilians [**Note: [Col. 0011D] Du Pin, *Bibliotheca*, vol. VI, p. 27]. But learned men have solidly repelled this unjust accusation [**Note: [Col. 0011D] Sollerius, cited work, p. 275, nos. 13–14].

> “Certainly,” says the learned editor of Sirmondus [**Note: [Col. 0011D] Baunius, preface to vol. I of Sirmondus, § 12], “the opinion of a most learned and holy bishop, distinguished by immense services to the Church, who vigorously defended the orthodox faith both in the West and in the East, whom the Roman synod honored with an illustrious eulogy and decree [**Note: [Col. 0011D] Councils, vol. V, p. 501, Venetian-Labbé edition], whom the supreme pontiffs Hormisda [**Note: [Col. 0011D] Hormisda, letter to the emperor Anastasius], Nicholas I [**Note: [Col. 0011D] Nicholas I, Letter 8 to the emperor Michael], John VIII [**Note: [Col. 0012D] John VIII, letter to Abbot Bercar], and Gregory VII [**Note: [Col. 0012D] Gregory VII, *Dictatus*] extolled with great praises, and whom the Church, enrolled among her holy confessors, honors with annual worship [Col. 0011C]—the opinion, I say, of so great a bishop concerning free will cannot fail to carry great weight with all Catholics. It is therefore astonishing, indeed utterly unjust and intolerable, that in our own age some should banish Ennodius to the Semipelagians and even to the Pelagians.

> “As though the following words were Pelagian or Semipelagian rather than directly opposed to those errors [**Note: [Col. 0012D] Ennodius, Book II, Letter 19]:

> ‘No one doubts, no one condemns, that, when grace supplies the author, a path to righteousness is opened even to human beings. For grace is the guide and forerunner of good things. Therefore we owe it to grace that we are called, and that, unless we resist, the savor of life is infused into us by hidden paths.’

> “How explicitly the necessity of grace, and indeed of interior grace, is asserted there! … Yet this great man is branded by some [Col. 0011D] as a defender of heretical doctrine, whereas for that very reason he ought to be commended by right of precedence to all orthodox believers: he refuted the deadly dogma by which the foundations of all religion and moral discipline are overthrown.”

Thus far that writer [Col. 0012A].

Here it may be worthwhile to add, after the testimonies of the ancient pontiffs concerning Ennodius, which Baunius has briefly reviewed and which were first collected in Sirmondus’s works, the following notable testimony from the same Baunius. It is that of Florianus, from the Roman monastery, writing approximately in the middle of the sixth century to Nicetius, bishop of Trier. It reads as follows:

> “See, therefore, how many helpers you employ when you begin to entreat on my behalf the lord Ennodius, bishop of the Church of Ticinum, a man of holy memory. He advanced the nobility of his noble blood to glory through humility, so that he might become a senator in the senate of the heavenly homeland and there remain a senator. His incomparable eloquence in learning is attested not only by the West, but also admired by the instructed East. The thunderbolt against Nestorius and destroyer of Eutyches, he taught with apostolic authority concerning my glorious and inviolate lady Mary, Christ-bearer and God-bearer (*Christotocon* and *Theotocon*). He, therefore, is my father from the baptismal font, whom I believe to intercede for his son before the eternal Father through the Son.”

**IV.** Various editions of Ennodius’s writings are in circulation. The first of them was produced in 1569 by the Basel *Orthodoxographa*; yet learned men judge that nothing more corrupted or polluted than it ever appeared in print. To pass over those editions that were later incorporated into the libraries of the Fathers at Cologne, Paris, and Lyons, two editions of Ennodius appeared at the beginning of the previous century, in the same year, 1611 [Col. 0012C]. One was produced at Tournai under the direction of Andreas Schottus; the other at Paris, where Jacobus Sirmondus carefully examined two exemplars of recognized authority, the Vatican manuscript and that of Nicolas Fabrius. With their aid he endeavored to fill the many and very extensive lacunae, to restore to their proper places passages that had been wrongly distorted and transposed, and finally to arrange all the works, rescued from their former confusion, into orderly divisions and something like classes. As we learn from Sirmondus himself, he also illustrated them with exacting notes.

On these two editions, consult the learned men mentioned above [**Note: [Col. 0012D] *Literary History of France*, vol. III, p. 101, note 1]. We have therefore entrusted this excellent edition of Sirmondus to the press. To the notes of the distinguished man we have appended the observations of Bartholomew, which Baunius extracted from his *Adversaria* and placed at the end of the first volume of Sirmondus’s works [Col. 0012D]. We have also added an appendix from the new Martenian *Thesaurus of Anecdotes* [**Note: [Col. 0012D] Martenian *Thesaurus of Anecdotes*, vol. V, p. 61], namely Ennodius’s *Discourse on the Birthday of Laurence, Bishop of Milan*, together with his letter addressed to a certain Venantius.

[Col. 0013]

**[Note: [Col. 0013C] Magnus Felix Ennodius.]** These three names of Ennodius are found in ancient copies—not at the beginning of the work, nor throughout all the titles, but only in the title prefixed to the *Life of Blessed Antony*. In the other passages the scribes were content, after omitting the first names, to record the third, which was the author’s true and proper name.

Proper, I say. For even in Ennodius’s age there persisted the custom that had once prevailed among the peoples of the Latin-speaking world, and ultimately in the City itself after the overthrow of the republic: although the nobility commonly used three or even four names, one name nevertheless belonged properly to each person; this they always placed last, after the others, and by this single name, if they wished to dispense with the rest, they designated each individual.

For example, in *M. Juniani Justini*—for this is how the Vatican codex calls the abbreviator of Trogus Pompeius—the proper name was Justinus. Likewise, in *Fabii Laurentii Marii Victorini*, the name of the celebrated rhetorician who wrote on Cicero’s books *On Rhetorical Art*, the proper name was likewise the final one. We shall demonstrate the same point in its proper places concerning Avienus, Liberius, Symmachus, and the others to whom Ennodius writes.

In the same way, in all the titles of books, on marbles, and in other monuments of those times, whenever several names of one person occur, there can be no doubt that the true and proper name is the one placed last. For now, it is enough to have made this brief observation, since, God willing, we are reserving a full dissertation on the subject elsewhere [**Note: [Col. 0014D] It may be found in the edition of Sidonius, after the preface**].

# The Nine Books of Letters of Magnus Felix Ennodius

(C, S)

## Book One

### Letter One. Ennodius to John

[Col. 0013A]

While you seek the open sea with words arranged like ships in harbor, and describe the uncertain transparency of the fluid element in tranquil speech; while, a careful helmsman, you restrain the boat of discourse amid the reefs of conversation, and, having fashioned an artful course, weigh its progress with a navigator’s judgment—you have displayed before my eyes the sea which you had represented as water: the sea of eloquence.

Good heavens [**Note: [Col. 0014C] “Into how many uses”**]. Read: “into how many appearances.” For he says that the things described are set, as it were, before the eyes; this is entirely required by what follows. **Barthius, *Adversaria*, p. 945.**

Into how many uses a rich tongue disperses itself! When it wishes, it rages like a beast, runs like a river, and heaves like the deep; and whatever appearance it paints with the colored images of words, it represents through the support of truth.

You suggest that you fear writing, as though you were tender at the outset, while your assertion, fleeing the pomp of declamations [Col. 0013B], demands praise; and it becomes greedy for glory while pretending, out of respect for modesty, to spare it. I give and owe you thanks, because you have consecrated the noble beginnings of your eloquence to the praises of a friend whom you esteem [**Note: [Col. 0014D] “How great the esteem”**]. Read: “whom he esteems.” The same, in the same place.

Although I do not acknowledge as mine the qualities you describe, I nevertheless embrace the piety of the speaker and praise the diligence of your heart, which you have dedicated to the light of grace shining through clear weather.

This torch is held out before you, which a flattering speaker kindles in my estimation. I do not flee the night of my conscience, though I do not escape it; nevertheless, I know how to assess it [**Note: [Col. 0014D] “Nevertheless, I know how to estimate”**]. What stands in the old edition is *extimare*, as though meaning “to separate from excessive praise,” lest he seem to think himself greater than he is. **The same, in the same place.**

Credulity entrusted to another’s favor suffers grievous breaches, although every charge passes away when one wishes to deceive a trusting person.

Yet you have filled my joys with the gifts of friendly correspondence, while you display novelty of thought through the serenity of your speech and surpass the ancestral ornaments of your noble lineage by the freshness of your new conversation.

It would have been enough to satisfy the wishes of your parents for you to rival the older adornments of your family. To be able to surpass them—just as no one believed this possible, so no one desired it.

Do you see how conversation polished to the fingernail adds value to a good birth? The brilliance supplied by blood has been surpassed by the diligence of the one who refines it.

I believed that the sum of your vows would be exhausted if you restored yourself to your ancestry, without considering what a companion would infuse into your distinction [**Note: [Col. 0014D] “Perhaps in the estimation”**]. The reading of the older editions, *extimatione*, meaning “separation,” ought not to have been changed. I think it should be read: “Perhaps, I endure, in the separation of my judgment,” and so forth. **The same, in the same place.**

Perhaps my knowledge has been defrauded in the estimation of my judgment. I believed that no one could reach Olybrius; you will join him as a swift pursuer, treading close upon his heels, and will surely make him blessed if you surpass him.

I pray God that in you youth may strengthen the seeds of good fruit, which reveal perfection in their beginnings.

At home you have examples from which to draw living models for my exhortation. May your father produce you as his equal in calmness of character, and your father-in-law as his equal in eloquence.

If the heavenly realms deign to hold me accountable for my prayer, I ask only one thing: that you may deign to remember me, lest you strive to equal, even in forgetfulness, the man whose perfection you contemplate amid the images of eloquence.

But I shall return to the manner of a letter, which your affection has extended at length. Farewell, my lord, and honor your loving friend with frequent services of letters, lest your declaration of love be thought to have existed toward you only as a preliminary speech, as commonly happens among some [**Note: [Col. 0014D] “May it be thought preliminary toward you”**]. Read: “preliminary, without substance.” **The same, in the same place.**

### Letter Two. Ennodius to Florus

I know that I have undertaken a difficult commission and am lifting a heavy burden upon weak shoulders, since, as far as I am concerned, I have roused your sublimity with the goads of words.

Thus a feeble whelp provokes beasts with threatening teeth; and while it challenges things greater than its strength, it considers what it hopes will happen to be a spectacle, not a battle.

Thus a mind unfamiliar with conflict must be stirred toward combat before the danger.

I judge the rage of a lion and the beast that Libya nourishes to be gentler in tongue than you. What ignorance drove me headlong? What fervor of spirit led me, a stranger to knowledge of you, onto a wrong path, so that I did not know what the man provoked by an attack ought to do—though he always begins insults first, and has never deserved to be placed last in the gymnasia of abuse?

Certainly he is the most practiced of the clergy’s revilers. He has always displayed against them the bites of a young and sharp tooth, a life polished to the fingernail having failed to escape him; all learning has yielded to him, and, as though fleeing a comet, the entire community of the religious has fled from him.

This man, then, I—shameless and weak in the face—have roused. With such confidence I might have challenged the winds to blow, rivers to run, my Faustus to eloquence, by which I, sparing of speech, have stirred you to chatter with iron-shod kicks of words.

Forgive me, I beg you, and, since you regard silence in others as a fault, disregard the silence of one who loves you. Refrain from replying; condemn the provocateur by contempt.

Let one drawn from the very midst of the curia’s boundaries contend with you; when it comes to Gallic ancestry, fall silent. If you prevail, let us be soothed by the retaliation of your silence.

Beware, my lord, lest by provoking one inferior in loquacity you begin to be judged humble. For what labor is it to overcome someone lying on that side, and to celebrate a triumph over one who confesses himself unequal before the conflict?

Nevertheless, let me be, with Lord Faustus, the clasp of your love, if you are striving to evade my complaints, however narrow and rustic they may be.

### Letter Three. Ennodius to Faustus

**[Note: [Col. 0015D] “To Faustus.”]** No name occurs more frequently in Ennodius’s works than that of Faustus. In various places he mentions his consulship, quaestorship, prefecture, and patriciate. This is the ex-consul Faustus whom Anastasius identifies as having supported Pope Symmachus during the Laurentian schism and as having fought bravely against Festus and Albinus, also ex-consuls, who favored Laurentius.

At this time, however, there were two consular men named Faustus. One held the consulship without a colleague in the year A.D. 483. He is called Aginantus Faustus in the tomb of Mandrosa. The other was Flavius Faustus the Younger. This may be the man concerned here, who was consul with Longinus in the seventh year after the former.

#### To Faustus

The cause of my desire was advanced through the benefit of complaints; shamelessness achieved what courtesy denied. I drew out the diligence of your holy heart, which artful silence concealed; I brought to an end the silence that had been prepared to nourish my ardor. By prolonging my worthless pages, I received the reward of one who prevails.

Thus the earth returns interest to the cultivator by means of the plowed clods, and the soil gives birth to noble fruit from its singular shoots. Thus, at the voice of one man, the hidden places of the mountains reply; and while a narrow cry is overcome, the elements reveal their strength.

By such an act I have obeyed the evangelical oracles (Luke 11:9), and have obtained fruit from the truth of the command, whose teaching declares that God often rises for the one who knocks and grants what is asked, if not because of merit, at least because of persistence.

Let the ill-considered discussion of the faithless now depart [Col. 0015D]. I offer myself as a competent witness to the integrity of the judgment in the face of present dangers. By frequent prayer I obtained what I desired; what was denied to examination was granted to the persistence of supplication.

My complaints owe you friendship, and I shall love them even more because you give effect to my wishes. Even if their origin came from a just grief, after you have granted my request I shall frequently begin them again with you, even when unharmed.

Embracing the soothing argument of epistolary eloquence, I give and owe thanks that you did not wish me to remain for so long a participant in sorrow. Perhaps you did this from the intention and diligence of one who gives counsel.

Yet I attribute to my own sins the fact that, while you moderated your speech, I was tossed into greater anxieties. Things prepared for adversity befall me alone, while I always regard as more serious the things that remain unspoken, because I believe that words are often exchanged concerning moderate illnesses, whereas the nearness of death commands that silences be broken quickly.

Thanks be to God, who in his mercy turns things thought harsh toward a good outcome, and causes what we have gathered as destined to come upon us according to our merits to be diverted through his compassion.

Nevertheless, I would have wished that your graciousness had held such affection toward my smallness that, having often admitted me as a companion in your joys, you would also have chosen to share adversity with me.

Or do you think that I shall regard such a benefit as received if I am excluded from the heats of your heart like an unfaithful servant? As I see it, no consideration of me has been governed by your counsels.

I think that I am losing your favor unless you nourish it through the communication of all things with me. Cease, I beg you, to give me counsel in this matter, since I greatly desire your words.

If the speech I long for is denied me, I shall wither, like earth upon which nothing is liquefied from heaven and which does not fill its veins with the sap of moistening fluid, from which it might provide nourishment to its native stalks and bring pregnant ears of grain to the sickle.

As a fish, drawn from the water and deprived of the living garments of its body, dies, so I am being killed when the streams of your conversation are withdrawn.

Let others seek what delights them; I demand things that concern the soul. Your words do not so much produce pleasures for me as salvation.

I confess the matter without disguise, without the falsehoods of clouds painted over it, because I am not an artificer of deception. I judged that something had been torn from my life while you remained silent.

You wrongly call yourselves faithful friends if the troubles generally to be mourned are conveyed to my ears through you—as though a Christian could be ignorant of the evil to which Rome is succumbing [**Note: [Col. 0016D] “The evil to which Rome succumbs.”**] That is, because of the faction of the Laurentian schism and the grave disputes, battles, and killings that arose from it. The same Anastasius discusses these matters in the *Life of Symmachus*, and Ennodius himself in the *Apologeticus*.

I infer that barbarian nations, separated from our frontier by almost the whole world, groan over these events in continual lamentation and lend us their tears as consolation.

Your greatness avoids acting as an informer in this matter, so that devilish wishes may, under the assurance of false reports, deceive me to my destruction; so that I may have no one to whom I can return for truth after the stories, nor anyone to sustain my spirit by demonstrating the truth.

Take care, my lord. With you my matter is different: the law of the forum is one thing, that of the dining room another [Col. 0016D]. Let the one whom you learned to be in public conversation hear you disclose the affairs of the household.

Nourish the minds of your subjects, and those faithful hearts which you believe them to possess, with the food of your reports, lest the hungry hearts of friends die unfed by such dishes.

### Letter Four. Ennodius to Faustus

[Col. 0017A]

**[Note: [Col. 0017D] “Anagnosticus.”]** Your letter. In Book VIII, Letter 5, also to Faustus, he expresses disgust at the prolixity of an *anagnosticus*. Among the Greeks, *anagnosticus* (ἀναγνωστικόν) is anything that is read or recited, just as *acroama* (ἀκρόαμα) and *akousma* (ἄκουσμα) refer to something heard. Thus, just as the Latins also used *acroama* for a saying or anything else received by the ears, so *anagnosticus* may mean a letter or any written work. It could also be called an *anagnosma*.

Following the reliability of the *anagnosticus*, and provoked by the sweetness of its eloquence, I almost believed that a fault was a virtue [**Note: [Col. 0017D] “I believed the matter”**]. All the manuscripts read incorrectly, “I may have believed.”]; and while I believed that the diadems of speech were worth more than conscience, I incurred a guilt which my mind did not acknowledge.

A hunter, flattering with artful ambushes, does not mock servants with a whistle [**Note: [Col. 0018D] “Servants.”**] Or should it read “deer”?; nor does the skilled hand arrange nets voluntarily sought by pretending fear with the varied coloring of wings. In no other way did the words of your greatness hold me captive, as I was caught and willingly presenting my mouth to the halters.

Ignorant of the matter at issue, while you attacked me, I long sought to discover whether I was innocent. I thought one thing about your letter and another about my own intention.

Who, I ask, was so attractive an accomplice in the perpetration of a crime as to believe that he could be acquitted if he confessed that he was carrying out another person’s command in his own crime, when no one can justly believe a crime to belong to another person when the accused has confessed it himself?

But I suppose the person was unacquainted with law and statutes, and had been fashioned by cunning alone. To him practice might even grant the appearance of another’s truth in writing, while the seductions of shame joined to it a semblance of individuality.

I do not wish to attack anyone by name, nor to assume the role of an accuser against my conscience. It is enough that I have stationed my modesty at its post. Let others boast of the uncertainties of the winds.

Yet even if the goads of armed reading were driving me to command such things, I would defend myself by imitating the patriarchs.

Jacob, by theft, defeated his brother’s priority in age (Genesis 27), and through that advantage obtained the primacy that nature had not granted him.

David, while he explored the wildernesses (1 Samuel 21:6), drove away hunger with the bread of the Presence by the urgency of his flight and the narrowness of the lands; and, in opposition to the prohibitions of the Law—which have fewer barbs—he escaped bodily hunger.

I had to endure with my failing entrails the hunger that my unfed soul had conceived from the divine books, until the disease conceived within me reached the hidden vital organs.

The prophet Daniel stole divine teachings from the royal chambers; the modest and exemplary thief added them to his own instruction.

Why go through individual examples, when one of the persons just mentioned is sufficient to protect a conscience under attack? Yet that conscience first took care, through a necessary petition, of its own modesty and, so to speak, natural weakness.

For even if, after denial, I am the one who made myself guilty, consider the matter.

You assert that the Libyan teacher [Col. 0017D] lamented the pears he had stolen [**Note: [Col. 0017D] “Pears.”**] This is restored in place of *peripoma*, which was also read in the ancient books. The authority for the correction is Augustine himself, the subject of this discussion, whom he calls the Libyan teacher. In Book II of the *Confessions*, chapter 4, he writes: “There was a pear tree near our vineyard, laden with fruit attractive neither in appearance nor in taste. To shake it and carry the fruit away, we wicked young men went out at dead of night.]; what the belly acquires at the cost of modesty must rightly be expiated with lamentation.

Perhaps what he took was cheap, or destined to perish through neglect, use, or the weather. Nevertheless, according to the Apostle (Romans 2:21), the thief was not free from guilt: he loved the flesh more than the soul.

The prophet Tobias confronts such offenders and testifies with a divine utterance, saying: “It is not permitted for us to eat anything stolen” (Tobit 2:21).

When he said “to eat,” he did not say, “It is not permitted for us to read anything stolen.”

As the history relates (2 Kings 22:11), a stolen papyrus instructed Josiah.

I, a mere little man, would not do this—though you spur me with words to love knowledge beyond the powers of my intellect?

But I return to the excellent man whom I mentioned as the perpetrator of the crime about which you write. By violating trust in both directions, he granted neither you security [Col. 0018B] nor me the completeness of the deed, if I wrote it.

May it be granted to me, without offense to your greatness, when this great man is placed before me according to the commands of God, to punish his back as my spirit sees fit.

### Letter Five. Ennodius to Faustus
[Note: [Col. 0018D] “Abundant.”] He congratulates both himself and Faustus on the consulship of Avienus, his son. Faustus is congratulated because the fasces are continued in his family through his son; Ennodius himself because, through the same man, they are restored to his family after an interruption. Avienus’s mother was related to Ennodius; therefore Avienus appeared to belong to the house of Ennodius. The succession of consuls in Faustus’s family had not, therefore, been interrupted. Faustus himself had held the consulship, as has been said, and before him his father Gennadius Avienus, colleague of the emperor Valentinian in the year of Christ 450; before Avienus, others had held it in an unbroken succession. In Ennodius’s family, however, the succession had been interrupted and broken off; perhaps no one had been consul after Magnus Ennodius—who, according to our conjecture, was his great-uncle—who had Apollonius as his colleague in 460.]

Having prayed for the abundant mercy of God, I commend the auspices of this happy year to Him; and, now that you have been raised to the consular rank by His gifts, I approach you almost as an equal. Until now, foreign adornments had lent our family the splendor of the consular robe and high boots, and we took pride in belonging by affinity rather than by descent to the man who gave his name to the year. It was an unmerited favor that, among the possessors of the curule offices, we were added to the tales of their admirers. How often did the tongue that exalted you make us dependent upon you, so that the insignia of our nobility were owed to the services of others, while our own position was reversed? But now let envy depart: a new consul, restorer of the ancient fasces, has shone forth, and a powerful opener has unlocked the decayed doors of our dignities. The thresholds of the hinges, trembling and withering, grow young again toward renewed strength; and, with God as their guide, I believe they will never again have to be closed by barriers. For my Avienus’s consulship is not merely one among others, but the first. He has gone before, leading the bands that will bear the eagles of his lineage, and has shown the path of courage to the highest service.

If there is any reverence for worldly dignities, if it is honorable for a man to live beyond the grave, if the ingenuity of the ancients devised anything by which mature years might be conquered by human beings, then such men are rightly thought to have discovered these arrangements, whose longevity both defies old age and rejects an end. Good God! How great is the labor expended on a single man’s name [Note: [Col. 0019D] “In drawing up laws.”] Since edicts and constitutions without a date and consul lack authority, according to book 1 of the Theodosian Code.] in drafting laws—whether it can establish that labor or bring it to an end! Well done, young man distinguished by eminent virtues: you have brought the living axes of honor along the path of your mother’s forgotten family line, and with them you have cut away the ancient obstacles of the splendid road, lest they hold back your descendants.

Let the praises of the ancients yield to you—those praises for which the inventions of learned writers produced nobility, and which, with the pomposity of ornamented language, purchase merit from the narrator. For the poverty of the subject must be enlarged by the resources of the storyteller, so that what is not found in the material itself may be inserted through the progress of style. To say nothing of the fact that the Fabii, Torquati, Camilli, and Decii have been surpassed, I think that you yourself, my lord, who have surpassed them all, have gladly yielded to this beginning of yours.

You have walked already, more mature, along the hardened path of your great-grandfathers and grandfathers [Note: [Col. 0019D] “Of the Scipios.”] Of the consular scepters and eagles. Thus, in the panegyric, plowlands produced Serranus through the Scipios; and in the *Paraenesis*, the recitation before the Scipios and the consular robes is pompous. The reason I do not interpret this as referring to the family of the Scipios, as the great man thought, is supplied by Sidonius, who traces the origin of Gennadius Avienus—whom we have shown to have been Faustus’s father—not to the family of the Scipios but to that of the Corvini, in book 1, letter 9.] You have advanced among the connected ranks of those who went before, almost walking shoulder to shoulder with them, so that you proceeded beneath an uninterrupted union of good fortune.

It belongs to the virtues of my still youthful Avienus both to continue the fasces in your family and to restore them to ours. I give thanks for an intention destined to benefit us all: through it, by God’s favor, the splendor of a good birth, hitherto shut away, has shone forth again; through it, a radiant lineage has recognized its own day.

How I would have wished, standing before you, to behold the fulfillment of my prayers, if the greatness of my sins had not denied to my eyes the heavenly gift that it could not deny to my desires, and if it were not wrong for a human being to obtain all his wishes at one and the same time! Nevertheless, I believe this should be counted among the greatest rewards of our Redeemer: that my consul, still at the threshold of happy childhood, has entered upon his office with the dignity of an old man.

But I foresee what is being prepared for his labors, when such things are displayed at the beginning. Unpromising beginnings will bring him the increase of advancement whom we see beginning with the fasces. It is less than this that ancient fame, in the praises of former men, boasts for itself from the outcome of prosperity. What a head of hair worn down by dust, what a life spent beneath the fasces scarcely earned, what an aged man, never certain of obtaining it, desired—this heavenly gift has bestowed upon my young man more often than can be told.

Moreover, because he was trained in the best disciplines at the beginning of his life, he appears to have deserved what he has obtained; nor does he attribute everything to fortune in himself, since still more can be granted to virtue. Having attained schools and literary studies to the glory of his nature, and emulating his father’s perfection, he has made himself by his industry such a son as another could scarcely have read about.

Whatever is outstanding in the Attic language, whatever is outstanding in the Roman, he has learned: he has weighed the gold of Demosthenes and the steel of Cicero, and, as a Latin speaker, has filled out both modes of expression. He has embraced the restraints of grammatical instruction and those legal narrow limits of speech in the name of freedom. By pursuing oratorical splendor, he has led equal contestants into the struggle with the arms of vigorous diction.

But I recognize where the progress of my affection, which rejects an ending, is carrying me: divided between my purpose and my ability, I address an educated consul, though unequal to him in intellect. I return to you, with whom I share joy, desire, and supplication alike. Let us pray to God—for our prayers reject all measure—that He make permanent what He has granted, and never set an end to His gifts toward us, since He does not feel loss when He gives.

Yet rejoice in your exceptionally great blessing, you who are permitted, after wearing the consular robes yourselves, to have a son in attendance upon you as consul. If, however, heavenly power operates in my judgment, and the whole mind, though inclined toward human sins, is not subject to them, then the dignity obtained for your offspring is the recompense of your faithful prayers. One household has enough suppliants to suffice for the city.

Happy mother, mistress of so many emperors: this brave matron raises you before God by her prayers. Through so many people the heavenly kingdom suffers a forceful assault, since by their merits what is asked is exacted from divine clemency. For we remember the Lord’s words to His disciples: “If two or three of you agree, whatever you ask, you will obtain” (Matt. 18:19).

I believe that, seeing the scarcity of the just, the Redeemer said that two would suffice to ask for the salvation of the world; though one may reasonably wonder whether anything could be denied to three asking for the benefit of their own. Encouraged, then, by these hopes and exalted by kinship with the just, I trust that through heavenly kindness I too shall attain the abundance of the grace I desire.

If Lot is counted among the throngs of the holy on account of Abraham’s merits (Gen. 12); if those who lacked virtues of their own have deserved to be led to lofty things by the virtues of their relatives; this year will produce dignities for your family. For if I am dear to you, I shall easily be led to heavenly grace through the fulfillment of my desire.

My lord, having discharged the reverence due in greeting, I ask pardon for the length of my speech, since it is difficult for one who is greatly rejoicing to be content with saying little.

## LETTER VI. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

Good God, how nothing is difficult for those who care for great things, and with what tranquility divine minds describe what they have seen! What endowments adorn places that a rich tongue and an experienced speaker have observed, if a religious man may recount them without compromising his confession and purpose!

God, the creator of the world, has bestowed upon certain provinces blessings through the wondrous abundance of His hidden resources: in some He has ordered wine to flow more abundantly, in others better; to others He has granted the joy of wheat-bearing crops; many He has endowed with a variety or usefulness of fruits. To those to whom the merits of a resistant nature have not given these things, He has made them illustrious through a narrator.

There is no reason for soil barren with rocks to despair, nor for fields that do not answer their cultivator to remain subject to him. The merits of lands are attributed to the genius of their languages; and in whatever manner a person has been able to speak, in that manner he raises up the subject of which he has spoken.

Provinces, you grow through the cultivation of speech: whatever has astonished the reader in you belongs to the mouth of the speaker. Fertile soil, and you, rich land boasting of your vine-shoots, which through modest furrows feed the farmer who scratches your back, which at the very beginning of plowing open your rich veins, which return the seeds entrusted to you multiplied in harvest—you have nothing in common with the greatest lands if the lord Faustus, the serene eloquence of the Roman state, has not approached you.

[Note: [Col. 0021C] “Behold Comus.”] Comus—called *Como* by others, and τὸ Κῶμον (*to Kōmon*) by the Greeks—is a well-known city of the plain of Liguria, beside Lake Larius, through which the river Addua, descending from the Alps, flows in such a way that the distinction between the waters is visible. Faustus had written its praises. Ennodius, in contrast, asserts that it is inferior to his own praises. But in truth he is joking. For the beauty of the territory and city of Como was so great that it seemed to have been established for pleasure; Cassiodorus praises Como among other things in book 11, letter 14, where he describes it at greater length and includes several details relevant to Ennodius.]

Behold Comus, once a lowly condition almost consigned to silence, which until now had boasted neither any advantage nor, as they say, any beauty: how greatly does it rejoice in the privilege of talent! Through precipitous valleys and the open clefts of joined mountains, it knows how to present a miserable harmony of summer snows; and along the perilous slopes of overhanging cliffs, where the cultivator’s road runs, it must sow the earth before it can sow seeds.

Its misfortune is that it has adorned the shores of Larius with white groves, so that, smiling beneath a seductive appearance, it falsely promises fertility to its rulers with a flattering face and nurtures a beauty execrable because it brings its possessor to destruction. There, as soon as the revenues assigned to the masters are consumed on their villas, they strive with frugal economy to repair the gaps in ancient structures and to shore up collapsing roofs at the expense of their patrimony.

The abundance of native inhabitants is preserved for this one purpose: that there should be no shortage of people exceeding even the demands of the public tax-assessor [Note: [Col. 0021D] “Tax equalizer.”] A moderator of taxes, *exisōtēs* (ἐξισωτής). The expression is known from the oration of Gregory the Theologian, *Against Julian the Tax Equalizer* (εἰς Ἰουλιανὸν ἐξισωτὴν), that is, “against the equalizer.” The office itself is called *peraequatio* in Novel 16 of Theodosius; titles belonging to this kind of office occur in both codes. There were also equalizers in other matters, such as equalizers of food supplies in Cassiodorus, *Formula of the Mastership of Offices*.]

It nourishes populations of fish, not for pleasure but for horror; through them we learn what praise the taste of fish caught elsewhere deserves. There the air is perpetually rainy, the sky threatening, and life is passed in a kind of existence without complete daylight. Sweet waters flow before the eyes of those crossing Larius, inviting swimmers whom they may destroy.

Who could endure a beautiful whirlpool deceiving under such a delusion? What shall I say of the island made habitable by the account of its narrator? Who would not marvel at this? On it, life is preserved only by being loved less; in it, escape from danger was itself a portion of good fortune; around it, human food is supplied to fish in the form of corpses. For no dead person except in the waters of Larius has earned a burial there.

You praised the seas, the river [Note: [Col. 0021D] “And the Addua.”] Pliny records this among the marvels of waters in book 2, chapter 103: “Some sweet waters, moreover, flow over others, as in Lake Fucinus, where a river is carried into it; in Larius, the Addua; in Verbano, the Ticinus; in Benacus, the Mincius; in Sevino, the Ollius; in Lemanus, the Rhodanus. Here, across the Alps, the upper waters carry forth in Italy, over many thousands of miles, only their own waters, no greater than those which they brought in.”]

—and the Addua—which, through its confused channels, displays the difference of the swollen lake; waters that could never be recognized in it except through their turbid currents. It was as great a feat to display the riches of eloquence in things lacking any claim to praise as all these natural blessings would have been, had nature herself bestowed them.

Nevertheless, may the Lord of heaven, who granted you the ability to do this, preserve His gifts in perpetual protection. I did not write these things because I regard them as different from you, but so that the reader may recognize from them that Como is better read through your style than seen with the eyes.

## LETTER VII. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

How great is the burden of envy, how easy the path to doing harm, whenever someone attacked is already weighed down by a prior reputation! No one, as I see it, considers what was done or what was not done; the matter proposed is summoned only as a witness to give credibility to the attack.

May almighty God turn the altered fortunes of ranks toward better things, and bathe in the brightness of a golden age the condition of affairs that has grown stale through the stain of time or the clouds of our merits. When have the most obscene crimes of human beings not been covered by the shelter of an innocent office, and whatever descended from the cloud of morals not been excused by the serenity of heavenly service?

But now the clerical office of a credulous interpreter is dragged into a snare, and what it was unseemly to have committed before a religious profession was undertaken, this, after we renounced our faults through the ecclesiastical title, we are believed to perform without any regard for propriety. In what storm did you compel me to go to the famous office amid the tempest of monstrous sins? In that office where all branches of error are accustomed to be cut down with the teaching axe of life, you make a crime be believed of me by everyone who deceives.

A man mourned that his slaves had been taken from him by me, and thought that royal protection ought to be invoked against the power of an ecclesiastical soldier. I ask: what storyteller would put this on the stage? What poet would construct a little tale with similar disguises or imaginary characters? The Lord knows—may He rise as my defender with a strong hand in your aid—that I am wholly ignorant of any such scheme.

Some time ago two boys, who asserted that violence was being inflicted upon them by the aforesaid man, [Note: [Col. 0022C] “For the aid of the Church.”] It is clear from this that slaves were accustomed to flee to churches not only to avoid punishment, if they had committed some offense, but also to obtain justice if they were suffering violence. The Church therefore interceded for them; nor was it lawful for them to be taken away before their masters had given security by oath concerning their immunity or justice. After the oath had been given, the slaves were ordered to return to service, as provided in canon 5 of the First Council of Orléans, so that they would not appear to be retained through fraud against their masters. This remedy was not applied only to slaves but to all the unfortunate and afflicted who, oppressed by the injuries of more powerful people, had fled to the aid of the Church. This is taught by letter 38 of Gregory the Great, book 8, to Januarius, bishop of Caralis. In this matter one scarcely knows whether to admire more the piety combined with the equity of the ancient Church, or the faith and reverence of our ancestors toward the Church. Such interventions were called *intercessions*. Ennodius writes in the *Life of Epiphanius*: “He took such care upon himself for intercessions that he believed he was himself inflicting trouble upon the wretched whenever, through negligence, he allowed it to be inflicted by anyone.” He also speaks of these matters somewhat earlier, in connection with Epiphanius’s diaconate.]

took refuge with the aid of the Church under a public appeal. I remember having offered prayers so that what the deceased had wished might be preserved concerning them; he promised that he would listen to their deceptive and flattering enticements. I urged them, in the presence of your holy father the bishop, who was providing them assistance, and with the city informed, to return to the service to which they had been assigned.

What happened afterward I did not know, until I received the name of a wicked retainer [Note: [Col. 0023D] “Retainer.”] That is, of another person’s slaves, as in the law of Valentinian in the Theodosian Code, under *On Grain Supply and Taxes*, concerning those who retain runaway slaves in their possession; though *retainer* is also used of anyone who retains another’s property. Code, same title, law 12, concerning those who may surrender their property under the Julian law; and in Ennodius’s *Life of Epiphanius* and *Panegyric*. Likewise in Cassiodorus, book 1, letter 22.] by the testimony of my accuser. Nevertheless, I give him thanks, because under any pretext he extracted letters that I desired—letters that caused me much grief through your command’s uncertainty.

For I see that a decision has been made concerning me, if I recognize that you are uncertain whether I hear what you command. Yet no guilt from this side will ever affect either me or your greatness before God, because I immediately compelled the aforesaid men to go into the service of that good man, without weighing any hearing.

My lord, offering you the most generous greeting, I wish that, if you do not deny pages to these matters, you would either settle my accusers yourself or—what is more familiar—make frequent mistakes!

## LETTER VIII. [Note: [Col. 0023D] “To Firminus.”] Book 2, letter 8.] ENNODIUS TO FIRMINUS

Pleasant are exchanges of letters conceived by a learned author: those in which the splendor of polished speech shines forth to perfection, where rich language is restrained by the reins of expertise. When an industrious explorer has brought an abundant vein of eloquence into the light, then the services of the recipient advance, destined to satisfy his desires.

But when rough speech reveals the narrowness of a poor intellect, and the writer does not insert a night of effort in the ordering of his conception and in the arrangement of expression, and, through the ambiguity of a clouded narrative, generates a kind of blindness concerning the explanation itself, who would not, even if such a person were placed in the citadel of eloquence, despise his affection?

The love of an unlearned person burdens the conscience of the perfected. Yet the force of inward affection, strengthened by the bonds of intimate connection, cannot be borne. A person whom charity drives on with its goads does not know how to test what he is capable of.

Nevertheless, the perfected are accustomed to judge worthy of pardon those whose uncertain footsteps have deserted them amid the paths of correspondence. You are accustomed to attend to what we wished to say whenever our wishes are not expressed in words. Yet I have burdened the journey of a suitable bearer; and what could have presented me to the living through spoken addresses, I have brought through the company of a letter, trusting that there is less danger for us if, under the intercession of a good advocate, I have committed an offense in presenting myself.

Farewell, therefore, my lord, and cherish your devoted admirer with special favors. Thus may divine favor raise your high dignity, if there is still any height to which it can rise.

## LETTER IX. [Note: [Col. 0023D] “To Olybrius.”] The most eloquent advocate of that age, concerning whom see letter 1, written to John, Olybrius’s son-in-law: “I believed that no one could reach Olybrius.” His eloquence is also celebrated in book 2, letters 9 and 13, and especially in poem 8; Cassiodorus calls Olybrius “the great” in book 8, letter 19.] ENNODIUS TO OLYBRIUS

While you speak honeycombs and arrange the honey of eloquence, flowing with the nectar of a liquefied element, through waxen houses, you have poured an exotic flavor of a rich feast into my lips, mentioning the contest of Hercules and the triumphal misfortunes of Antaeus.

Thus, indeed, when they are clarified by the palaestrae of literary training [Note: [Col. 0024D] “The palaestrae are clarified.”] The Basel edition has *dilucidat*, “clarifies”; this was evidently required by usage and by the origin of the word *palaestra* (παλαίστρα). But Ennodius used τὰ *palaestra* as a plural also in book 2, in the letter to Pomerium, and in the preface addressed to Arator. He frequently uses similar grammatical changes, as when he says τὸ *aether* and τὸ *epitoma*, and *haec lampada*, *thoraca*, and many other expressions of the same kind.] so the limbs of the mouth submit themselves to the arts of speech, moistened with the oil of study.

But I would not, I confess, have wished to be wounded by the mention of that contest, as they say. The ancient tale of Antaeus tells that, when he began not to fall, he lost the solace of his mother, lest he should win by being thrown down. He is said to have been overcome by the stratagem of a clever enemy while standing, and to have surrendered his life upon the breast of his opponent.

The matter is certainly worthy of remembrance, but unworthy of the purpose of friendship. I remember, of course, that we undertook contests bound by a pact, but contests in which we strive to surpass one another through the services of mutual affection, so that in these struggles both of us may wish both to be defeated and to conquer.

We ought rather to live through the shared secrets of our sins than to die through them, joined together by the aid of Mother Church, who, to speak truly, nourishes us both at her breast with the milk of faith. Let the old women’s tales of poets cease; let ancient fables be rejected; let an innocent state never be mingled with another’s downfall.

If we wish to recall the examples of our ancestors for a new use, it is more fitting for us to remember Pylades and Orestes, Nisus and Euryalus, Pollux and Castor—provided that the obscenity of clandestine acts removes nothing from these examples—in gratitude or faith. Such equality of minds bound them together in harmony that, in two cases, a desired death benefited them together with their friends, while in the other one man brought life to his friend at the price of his own death.

These are worthy of remembrance whenever, amid new bonds of concord, noble growth is joined and wedded—as I might say—in the moist book of our souls, through strong clods of earth. Those minds promise the blessings of concord that recognize what labor is required in cultivation.

Nevertheless, I rejoice that we are now joined in character by an indissoluble partnership, and that from the doorway of affection we weigh the growth of charity on the balance of judgment.

## LETTER X. ENNODIUS TO JOHN

I would return the favor, were restored praise not to burden the diligence of a friend’s heart—lest, while we seem to scratch one another in mutual panegyric, affection be stained by suspicion of flattery, and love run into vice while we improperly thrust upon ourselves what we ought to do for others.

The adornments of lovers ought to be retained within the pages shared by friends, not spoken aloud, lest by an empty recounting of praise we honor our consciences only with empty sensations. There are matters in which, although I remain silent about your virtues before you because of affection, I can celebrate them among others.

In what I perceive concerning your progress, I owe you only a religious silence. I could indeed, following the vices of the age, now disclose your praises in inexhaustible proclamation and color the whole page with painted flatteries. But may this be far from my purpose and absent from my character: I wish the man whom I hold in my mind to be content only with this kind of reward.

To you I owe not soothing speech but the voice of one who corrects. Not mocking you with the painted artifices of words, but holding you wholly in the depths of my mind, I could say: “You have reached the citadel of knowledge without the disadvantage of tender age; you have attained the summit of perfection; no care should distract you, but you should adorn yourself with your virtues as a wealthy possessor.”

But these things, as I said, are foreign to me. With the mouth of a parent I spur you; I say: however great may be the things you promise in the gray flower of eloquence, I do not rejoice except in the harvest, like the avaricious farmer who does not measure the abundance of the year except in his granaries.

Already, even if I do not see ears of grain heavy with seed in you, I nevertheless see them swollen with abundant milk. Your hopes are already approaching the threshing floor. But the more our desires are kindled by near hope, the more we must fear.

Work at your studies; love the light in conversation; devote yourself steadily to reading, so that the fruits of eloquence may be cleansed by the winnowing of many authors. What you write is beautiful, but I love what is stronger; it is crowned with flowers, but I love fruit more.

Farewell, my lord, and embrace these words with the sincerity with which I have presented them; weigh my love in the faithfulness of my admonition. Know that I do not withhold your letters from any learned men, so that whatever escapes me through ignorance may be corrected by those who are learned to perfection. Therefore prepare yourself with much sweat for the cultivation of writing, so that the hopes I have conceived concerning you out of love for the merits of your revered father may, under the effort of your brilliance, reach fulfillment.

## LETTER XI. ENNODIUS TO CASTOR AND FLORUS

You ought to relieve one who loves you through the favor of conversation and to reveal your friendly diligence by the testimony of speech, because silent affection almost assumes the role of ingratitude, and the force of love is intercepted by abstinence from letters.

Only the offering of letters heals the minds of the absent; through a certain art of the mind it paints in writing what it says. We think it superfluous to assert this to you, whom noble training sharpens, to whom birth, learning, and companionship are present. There is nothing in the liberal arts that you could fail to know without blame for negligence, since Faustus, the glory of the Romans, trained you after the splendor of your birth.

Therefore it must rather be confessed that I do not deserve what I ask than that you do not know what you ought to offer.

My lords, [Note: [Col. 0025D] The edition of Schott has “my.”] discharging the duties of greeting with the greatest humility, I beg you finally, mindful of my admonition and of our bond, to write back. You ought not to be sluggish in this matter, since neither holy consciousness can be absent from your conduct nor abundant speech from your conversations.

## LETTER XII. ENNODIUS [Note: [Col. 0025D] “To Avienus.”] Faustus’s son, whose consulship we saw mentioned in letter 5. In the fourth Roman synod of Symmachus, and in the letters of King Theoderic to that same synod, he is called Rufius Magnus Faustus Avienus under all his names. Those are mistaken who think that the names of two consuls are given there, since they are all names of one Avienus, who received the cognomen Faustus from his father and Magnus from his maternal relatives. To this same man, I believe, who was then first among the senators, the doctrinal letter of Pope John II was written many years later; its heading reads: “John, bishop of Rome, to the illustrious and magnificent men Avienus the Senator, Liberius, Severinus, Fidelis, Avitus, Opilio, John, Silverius, Clementinus, and Ampelius.”] TO AVIENUS

If you ask why my lavish brow of modesty does not keep silent, though punished by your silence, and why affection is called shamelessness through misinterpretation; if you say that my loquacity ought to have been restrained when its fruit failed to appear: I address you, most illustrious of men, with that sincerity which is customary in your household; I embrace our pledged promise as a hostage of the mind.

I do grieve over the causes of the prolonged silence you have arranged, since both affection and relationship are neglected. But because your love claims me entirely for itself, I still believe that what you have done can be excused, and I judge that there are reasons for your defense in this matter—though I cannot find them.

I have always heard that you live in good health and possess the fulfillment of your wishes. Often, through the light of your correspondence, you have wiped away your sweat in the adornment of your family. Nothing but contempt is shown whenever silence has no necessity.

Nevertheless, always taking hope from a reply, I wrote and dictated words to be read in a kind of presence of your brilliance. While I spoke, it seemed to me that my page had restored you to me, that you were thinking, and that you were adding words painted with your own images.

Consider carefully, I ask, what sweetness your letter would contain if I were granted the opportunity to receive it, since, although they proceed from us, we nevertheless embrace the words that come to you.

Now I ask you to raise yourself toward the affection of writing and pour your flowing conversation into my dryness, so that I may learn what my service can obtain from God, if I receive your letters as rivals of your father’s perfection.

Do not fear that I speak of him, whom the most learned rightly dread, and bring him before your eyes as an example of expression. It is the custom of skilled physicians to detect the strength of bodies in their veins and to question the fingers concerning a person’s progress. Likewise, the talents of beginners cannot otherwise be known: those who ought not yet to demand robust declamations from tender age may rejoice, by inquiring into their future abundance and revealing the harvest of skill in the root.

My lord, as above, with the honor of greeting and customary reverence, I hope that, even if your merit does not show that you remember me, at least my importunity—which is indefatigable—will make it clear.

## LETTER XIII. ENNODIUS [Note: [Col. 0026D] “To Agapitus.”] An illustrious man. After the Ravennate palatine honor—which Ennodius congratulates him on here, and which is mentioned again in book 4, letter 6—he was also appointed prefect of the City by King Theoderic, as several of his letters preserved by Cassiodorus show in book 1; afterward he held the patriciate and an embassy to the East, probably around the year 510, concerning which see Cassiodorus, book 2, letter 6. Finally, he held the ordinary consulship in 517, witnessed not only by the *Fasti* but also by the Council of Epaon, which ancient copies state was convened under the consulship of Agapitus.] TO AGAPITUS

I am troubled in spirit because your greatness—so scrupulously attentive to what is right and so faithful to friendships—has turned toward such neglect of my being forgotten that, unmindful of your diligence, the good things that have come to you through the advancement of your honors were announced by rumor rather than by a fortunate letter.

Where are those venerable inner chambers of your holy conscience in your conduct? When could a mind anxious for the happiness of one who loves you have found things more worthy of being reported?

But I ask whether some malicious person may have released the south wind upon the springs, or a wanton animal among the rose gardens. For a prosperous outcome is never hidden from friends without offense; disturbance causes those who live far away to keep silent about what gives them joy.

May the obscenity of malice depart far from your character. I suppose I deserved not to know your good fortune. By what frequency of speech can such silence be balanced? No cultivation of affection can soothe a friend who has turned away from his desires.

However greatly, my lord, you may paint these things with the noble images of your learned words, wrongs are rarely healed by conversation, and the pain that has descended from you cannot be cured by speech. You will scarcely be able, by writing, to erase what you disdained to write.

But I return to my purpose, from which, if divinity has compassion, one must never depart. I owe God this: while you arranged your silence, I was the first in Liguria to learn of your prosperity. You have lost the fruit of your studied silence; the world’s tongue celebrates the happiness of the good. What has been added to the highest cannot remain unknown.

In honors, those things that are restored are especially to be embraced. A man is raised badly to the fasces if, amid the stars of the senate house, his mind does not recognize the votes of light in his titles. A dignity white with age, late but deserved, has come to you. The tongue that follows it summoned it; the innocence that you once possessed together with age demanded it.

But now I return to the grace of familiar conversation, even after the offense. Farewell, my lord, and restore through an abundance of speech what you neglected at the cost of a pledged friendship.

## LETTER XIV. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

I would not, I confess, disclose the causes of the delay, lest my spirit, brought back late into peace with joy, be disturbed again by a mournful account, and I should have in my narration a renewed beginning of sadness. For a person who does not refuse to reread what has passed almost owes his own troubles to himself.

Who would repair his anxieties, brought to their end, through the necessity of an untimely speech? But with you and with the purpose of our affairs I have a bond of trust, and sincerity is owed in recounting them whatever the cause.

I willingly endure the goads of recalled grief, provided that nothing is lost to truth; and, lest through the fault of a tender mind I dishonor the page with falsehood, I freely bear what I report.

The life of your holy father was brought almost into doubt, and this held me fast. Although the whole Church wept over his illness, a special grief afflicted me, since I owe him more love. I saw the peace of the city, pressed by urgent discord, pass beyond the thresholds of our city and slip from our eyes like some uncertain or wandering divinity.

But let a concise account suffice for sad matters. Now, with the holy Father’s good health, the desired and cherished breath of recovery has returned. For when my mind returned to its station, it immediately attended to your commands.

I sent boys who could faithfully inform me of the prosperity of your dignity and of the entire holy household. Again I hang suspended, and am constrained by uncertain judgment between hope and fear, since one must be anxious for the prosperity of another parent.

Who can stretch himself out toward my cares? Who could equal the heat of one so torn apart by such division? But these matters are more justly referred to God, whose mercy it is to overcome the prayers of those who supplicate and to prepare a harbor for wavering desires.

Meanwhile I return to the customary use of complaints. I suggest that I ought immediately to have followed your pages and, for my consolation—or because of your recent request—to have extended my letters, lest my mind should have hung in uncertainty upon hearing of your departure. But I believe this fault of writing can be corrected by frequency.

It remains for divinity to cause you to indicate those things that it is helpful to know. My lord, offering an abundant greeting with reverence for you, I beg that what I have entrusted to be conveyed may reach fulfillment.

## LETTER XV. ENNODIUS [Note: [Col. 0027] “To Florianus.”] A man of rank, if indeed he is the one to whom King Theoderic writes in Cassiodorus, book 1, letter 5.] TO FLORIANUS
The same thing is to fail to keep within the bounds of arrogance as to overstep them in humility. It is an affectation of haughtiness to be more submissive than is right. It is characteristic of those who gape solemnly to invent new forms of flattery; and it is a grand cothurnus, in eloquence, to feign fear or to dread an ordeal while secure of praise. I, however, would have devoted care to my purpose if I did not owe it to my family. I received your letter, enriched with Roman refinement and displaying a more Latinate style from the very beginning. My affection compelled me to answer it, though ignorance opposed my hands. For a long time the hope of keeping silent had dulled in me the desire to write, and silence had been counted in place of glory. But if I had not replied, you would not have known that you had been caught: that, with the artificer’s eloquence, you had toyed with less carefully fashioned talents, and with the juice of Romulean cleverness.

A polished blade is not equally fit for cutting as one that rust has possessed; nor can practice and sluggishness enter an equal contest. Now, content with the brevity of my letter, I turn to the duties of greeting. What I could not repay in eloquence, I shall balance by goodwill, returning friendship for the design and pomp of your words. Behold, I have written swiftly, taking from my occupations as much time as I could. May God grant that, if you desire a reply, you find your breast, battered by cares, empty of them.

## Letter XVI. Ennodius to Florianus

[Col. 0028D]

Your fraternity could have bestowed upon my affection that which, with true generosity, would have advanced both the giver’s advantage and my sense of propriety: namely, that once you held letters declaring my eagerness, you would release yourself from the burden of writing. Does anyone paint his forehead with deceitful attractions and weaken his reputation by vigorous attack, while, not content with an obvious excuse, he thinks that what his poorly trusting conscience has acknowledged is still insufficient? He who irritates the throats of greedy friends with the varied flavor of conversation, so that while he supplies pleasant things he alters settled arrangements.

For after I had written that I loved silence, I obtained longer pages, as though in reply to my allegation, and perhaps drew forth, after my refusal, a rich outpouring of eloquence long kept in reserve. What would you have done if I had promised contests, if, incautiously touching the ardor of your studies with any tooth, I had not been a competent assessor of myself and had not kept my inner chambers secure? I believe that against me would have been brought the profound depth of Tully’s gulf, the precision of Chrysippus, and the elegance of Varro. I would have found no support anywhere, since even this did not help me: I neither escaped contests in writing nor, when provoked, escaped them by remaining silent.

Although awareness of my skill and vigor in speaking might raise me up, after the various hazards of writers I would fear the praise that you seek with so much toil. Added to this is the fact that you said I possessed rhetorical cunning, although it has long been the case that affection has cut the oratorical structure away from my speech, and I cannot occupy myself with the flowers of words when the cry of duty summons me to groans and prayers.

Therefore restrain your soothing and ill-advised conversations. If what you write is fabricated and adorned with the brush of falsehood, change your purpose, or do so after you see that what you have done has become known. If it is true and descends from the scales of judgment, enclose it in the deep secrecy of your breast, so that, while preserving the matter intact for a friend, you may show respect for careful conduct. Guard an unchanging heart toward me, and charm others with your conversations.

Behold, while wishing to answer your extended pages, I have exceeded the proper length of a letter. But an offense should not be punished with a special penalty when it has its author among those who err. My lord, returning the greeting that I owe, I beg that, if you insert yourself as a swift investigator into the desires which I have conceived concerning the love of silence, you will at least forgive the occupations by which we are hindered.

## Letter XVII. Ennodius to Faustus

If the mind of a loving person abstains from its customary attentions, it considers the very cessation an unfavorable omen. For he is himself the cause of sorrow who does not always judge that what he loves dwells nearby. Can anyone be considered to have departed into distant places if he is touched by the mind? For if spirit is something divine in a human being, one whom the mind can reach cannot feel the losses caused by vast distances of land.

I have stated the reason that makes me send a written message. I offer the attentions of greeting, for which letters are sent, praying to God that, through the dispensation of heavenly favor, my words may reach your greatness while you are dwelling in good health. But the bearer who provided the opportunity for this conversation is commended by me in return.

## Letter XVIII. Ennodius to Avienus

[Col. 0030A]

How well you imitate what you modestly refuse! And while you seek to be encouraged by difficult examples suited to your greatness, you have shown the pomp of narration which, as a competent advocate, you avoid. I embrace the pleasing argument of fear, which the vein of your rich talent commends in you. I do not want you to fear that the father who ought to be honored for his merits has been placed in the examples of your exhortation; these things you say come from him himself.

I know what earth produces gold more nobly, and whose soil nourishes metals so that they shine more brightly. Often, when I have searched diligently, fruitful labor has shown me the nourishing backs of the yellow element. I know what shells enclose gems proud in price, and from what source comes the stone that will confer distinction upon rulers. Do not attribute what I have done to lack of skill or to error.

The offspring of a brave man recognizes the appearance of weapons in the embrace of its father; and while obeying nature, it learns to love terror.
