Maro, the root of learned men and the fashioner of your eloquence, so presents a son animated by his father’s words that he says: “Learn virtue from me, boy”; and elsewhere, “And father Aeneas.” Was he already rising with strong arms for contests, or was he thought capable, with manly strength, of waging the wars that threatened? Rather, virtue, animated by recent examples more than by admonitions, awaited the bodily growth to come.

Those who know the nature of things say that eagles carry their young, at the very threshold of life, when they are stripped of their egg-shell coverings, to place them in the rays of the sun and to make them recognize the light of their own offspring through the exposure to its immense splendor. Is there impiety in strict testing, when the judgment of the decision in the selection is right? They do not wish any of their offspring to perish, but they do not acknowledge as their own those who withdraw.

Rightly, then, that elevation among birds is thought to be the mother of conquerors. Now, therefore, my dear one, pursue what you have begun well; and, with God’s favor, return the grandfather in name, and the father in learning.

[Note: [Col. 0029D] “Grandfather in name, father in learning.” Avienus’s grandfather was Gennadius Avienus, the father of Faustus, whom we noted to have been consul in 450; Sidonius discusses him in Book I, Letter 9. Ennodius seemed to refer to both father and grandfather by the name Avienus, since Faustus was called Faustus Avienus. But because, as we have shown, each man’s one true and proper name was the final one, he therefore assigned the name Avienus only to the grandfather.]

Do not think that what I say is burdensome. And because I regard you as descended from a distinguished stock, do not fear your beginnings. He too who is feared was once a beginner; and whenever water is drawn through dust by a finger scraping the earth, everything that is first flows turbid.

For the rest, farewell, my lord, and honor your lover with frequent offices of letters. In these pursuits, if you remember me, it is not fitting for you to be sluggish.

## Letter XIX. Ennodius to Deuterius

[Note: [Col. 0029D] Deuterius is described in the heading as “a distinguished grammarian,” as in the epigraph of Poem 2. This is why Ennodius calls him an excellent teacher and, in the epigrams, a master. He had been a student of the Roman rhetorician Felix. He seems to be the man mentioned in Martianus Capella’s Parmese manuscript in these words:]

[“Securus Memor Felix, a man of distinction, companion of the consistory, rhetorician of the city of Rome.” I was correcting this from extremely corrupt copies, while Deuterius, a schoolmaster and my pupil, read against me at Rome by the Porta Rapena, in the consulship of Paulinus, a man of distinction, on the Nones of March, with Christ’s help.]

[Note: [Col. 0029D] Petrus Burmannus, in his commentary on Henri Valois’s Book I *On Criticism*, p. 181, believes that the correction proposed by Petrus Nannius in *Miscellanea*, Book X, chapter 4, ought to be accepted. From the traces of the old abbreviated script of the manuscript of the Egmond library, in which Nannius says he found this same title prefixed to Martianus, he conjectures that it should be read: “Felix Asper, companion of the consistory, rhetorician of the city of Rome,” contrary to the reading “Eleutherius.” The highly learned Fontanini also correctly gives it in this form in Book I, chapter 3, p. 231, of *On the Antiquities of Horta*: “Securus Melior Felix Asper,” whereas Sirmondus incorrectly presents: “Securus Memor Felix, V. S.,” as though *Vir spectabilis*.]

DEUTERIUS.

[Col. 0030D]

How I wish often to omit the duty of visiting, if guilt could offer a sweet reward; and knowingly and deliberately to neglect the judgment of the heavenly command, if opportunity obtained through desire could reconcile what must be claimed! I alone have had it happen that I rejoice in the merit of an offense. Now I have learned to pursue errors for the sake of such a recompense.

What I have been compelled to bring forward, excellent teacher, is not contrary to the religious obligation of friendship. Indeed, because of a confession worthy of your declared state of health, I never wished you to be in doubt of your condition as though I were ungrateful. Rather, as far as I was able, I opposed with the hands of prayer the irregularities that were threatening you.

But behold what a lively state of mind the page reveals—not founded upon the prosperous health of your limbs—in which you have shone with both kinds of light. I ask: are your eyes, whose poems are so bright, dimmed by a cloud of pain? And do you, who speak light, complain of your vision? How I fear that he may find too sparing a praiser of your merits! It is rightly attributed to you to give eyes to all and to illuminate obscure minds with an unfamiliar radiance.

Do you therefore think that what you bestow is not powerful for you? Drive away, I ask, the superfluous cares of your mind, perhaps conceived through anxiety or caution. May God grant that whatever bodily discomfort has been added may be dispelled, in compensation for your soul, by serene radiance shining brightly.

## Letter XX. Ennodius to Faustus

Truly I give thanks to the Trinity, whom we venerate and worship, our God, who under the distinction of persons and marvelous equality has piously commanded us to perceive and adore one substance. He has turned our mourning into joy and changed the tears that accompanied our sorrows into the service of gladness.

Thus I may truly say with the Prophet: “Who will give water to my head and to my eyes a fountain of tears?” (Jeremiah 9:1). Thus, in this devotion, I may respond to the greatness of heavenly benefits: I received heavenly gifts before I asked for them, and first learned what good had happened before I felt what evil my sins threatened.

It is yours, almighty dispenser, that concerning children safe and sound and the inheritance of future innocence I felt no fear in the anxiety that had preceded it. I received the restoration of their health almost stupefied, placed in a state resembling confusion; I scarcely believed that prosperity had occurred which seemed to exceed my merit. Truly the human mind does not know how to measure the riches of heavenly recompense.

Thus the frail are governed in spirit, so that they see their position before they detect the uncertainties of danger. Good God! In what a precipice did we then hang, when heavenly power, so that the testimony of the little ones’ restored health might be complete, had our own condition been shaken more than our merit deserved?

I speak openly, and I do not confine the voice that I owe to my purpose beneath any cloud of falsehood. I mingle my words with sobs, so that under solid thanksgiving my eyes, more abundantly, may overflow into weeping. I often look back upon what I escaped. Where in the world were we? From what ruin did heavenly mercy restore us to human fellowship?

Let us therefore repay the giver of this blessing with the long sighs that we owe him, in more concentrated words. Let us invite him to preserve his gifts, since we have proved that he has brought help in our uncertainties. Let us ask him who surely knows how to preserve what he has granted and to extend the living testimonies of his powers far into the future.

Such are the revered prayers offered concerning you by the community of servants and friends of God established throughout Liguria. The holy household rests upon such intercession; prayers for the children safe and sound are poured forth without ceasing.

The deity who loves truth because it is what he himself is bears witness that I speak the truth: to all who can rely upon innocence and integrity of life, your grief is excessively bitter. But now I return to the business of the letter.

Farewell, my lord, and receive Bassus, a man of distinction, the bearer of this letter, with that favor with which you are accustomed to receive those dear to me. For among all those whose affection is concerned to preserve my friendship for your sake, the man mentioned above has climbed a certain citadel of purity. Therefore assist his requests, so that, receiving the fruit of his expenditures, he may prepare himself for better things.

## Letter XXI. Ennodius to Faustus

For a long time my mind hung in uncertain expectation concerning the arrival of your greatness. But after divine mercy released me from this anxiety, I immediately returned to my customary duties, although I did not suppress the attentions of my pages even when you had departed into distant places.

In these letters, therefore, while informing you of my physical health, I report the sickness of mind that I have contracted from sorrow. I am anxious for the safety of our lights, being stationed in a place to which an awaited messenger arrives only with difficulty. As a consolation, I pray God not to allow his servant to be further tormented by any anxiety, but to come swiftly to the aid of my agitations through the complete restoration of my own people’s prosperity.

Offering the greeting owed in dutiful service, I beg that, once you know the matters over which my mind is tossed by differing judgments, you will diligently come to my aid through the benefit of letters bringing me cheerfulness.

## Letter XXII. Ennodius to Opilio

[Note: [Col. 0031D] Book V, Letter 3.]

Your greatness had begun to raise my littleness through a hope exceeding my prayers, and, in the manner of heavenly discipline, to make your benefits more glorious, since it weighed my merits on no scale of judgment. It even seemed indifferent to censure to give value to gifts which it showed to be undeserved, because affection displayed toward the lowly has no necessity attached to it and reveals its own character in unclouded, radiant splendor.

Long supported by such confidence after God, I did not fear whatever the poisons of slanderers promised. But when your forgetfulness returned me to the ancient dust—a thing that ought to happen to one stripped of a defender as a consolation—I extended letters bearing my complaints, promising myself a reply because of their importunity.

But perhaps the magnitude of the occupations hindering you signifies that you are not coming to these duties. I shall reply that the same condition once belonged to your greatness when it was sending pages. Nevertheless I return to the custom of epistolary writing, lest the length of what has been added create disgust and cause the argument that asked for pages to be denied them all the more.

My lord, I discharge the duty of greeting, and, bound to you in mind, ask about your health, desiring through the evidence of a report to reach the fulfillment of my twofold longing.

## Letter XXIII. Ennodius to Senarius

[Note: [Col. 0033C] Concerning him, see Book III, Letter 11.]

Affection loses the health of silence when weakened by torpor; nor does the course of devotion overflow for its proper use if it is stripped of the fellowship of conversation. Silent love almost presents the appearance of one who does not love, and not declaring what you love through speech is an image of hatred.

I told these things to your greatness when I was present, while you were promising letters as consolation for my absence. But what forgetfulness of me has invaded your mind, that through such long stretches of time I have received no letters indicating your good health? Surely I would not have confronted letters as witnesses to the love between our minds.

Therefore turn your purpose toward one who loves you, in a better direction, and send writings in remembrance of your promised faith. My lord, discharging the greeting owed, I beg that, if a letter reaches you while you remain in your former state of favor toward me, it may deserve a reply. For I think that the two bonds between us—affection and blood—cannot be broken.

## Letter XXIV. Ennodius to Asturius

[Note: [Col. 0033C] He seems different from Asturius, the colleague of Praesidius in the consulship of 494. A memorial of that man’s ancient piety is said still to be preserved at Liège on the ivory cover of a sacred Gospel book, with this inscription: “Flavius Asturius, man of distinction and illustrious, companion and master of both military forces, consul in due order.” Ennodius, however, calls this man only a senator, not a former consul.

But in my judgment those who confuse him with Turcius Rufius Asterius, a man of distinction, ordinary consul, and patrician—who is said to have revised the verses of the poet Sedulius, collected from his writings after Sedulius’s death—are no less mistaken. The following matters seem to belong to that Asterius who was consul with Protegenes in 449: both because these names suit him better and because that date agrees with the death of Sedulius, whom, from the complete copies of Gennadius, we learn to have died during the reigns of Theodosius the Younger, to whom he dedicated his work, and Valentinian.

Finally, all doubt is removed by Asterius’s own epigram, which we read in the Reims manuscript after Sedulius’s letter to the same Macedonius, in these words:]

Take, holy one in merits, the truthful sayings of the poet,

[Note: [Col. 0033D] “Truthful sayings of the poet.” From the very ancient sheet, “the truthful sayings of the poet.” Barth, *Adversaria*, p. 705.]

which have been composed without the fault of fiction,

from which kindly faith and the grace of holy Christ are free,

through which the righteous Sedulius speaks such things.

And bid men always remember your Asterius,

by whose help and care they have been published for the peoples,

[Note: [Col. 0033D] “Published”: *didita*. The same, ibid.]

whom, although the highest annals celebrate him through the ages,

[Note: [Col. 0033D] “They celebrate through the ages.” The very learned Fastus has most clearly published the reading “fastus” in our sheet. If I am not mistaken, the chief of grammarians, Priscian, notes that *fastibus* was said instead of *fastis*. The passage is in Book X, where Caesar speaks: “Nor will my year be conquered by the fasti of Eudoxus.”]

[Note: [Col. 0033D] Moreover, Sedulius’s inscription is conceived in the manuscript as follows: “Sedulius in Christ bids health to his most holy and most blessed father Macedonius, presbyter.” The same, ibid.]

his merit is nevertheless greater if it flourishes upon your lips.

The following note is prefixed to the epigram:

“This work Sedulius left scattered among his papers. Collected and adorned with every elegance, it was published by Turcius Rufius Asterius, a man of distinction, ordinary consul, and patrician.”

ASTURIUS.

What, damn it, is the reason that you are so sparing in goodwill, lavish in complaint, and demand a frequency of letters which you yourself do not grant? You look with viperine eyes upon what another has done wrong, while cutting away none of your own faults with a pruning hook.

It is many years since you chose a dwelling near the Alps, senator and learned man. Where, while you gaze upon the frosty ridges, did the ill-omened snow of old age appear upon your head? Where did you also declare in writing that you were eating acorns? The elegant character of your letters made this credible, when its meaning appeared in the belchings of your swollen breast and in Alpine speech.

Yet I am astonished that among the rivers restrained by the ice of that place and the unbroken cold, the flame of your liver burns more fiercely, and your breast derives no moderation from its dwelling. Age cools toward old age. There is a house that turns waters into metals and, against nature, rules the torrents by its own law. Yet you are said to live among these things as though your fire were stoked by the fuel of frost.

I beg you by the goad of a parent, since I owe both you and my purpose the voice of correction. It is your responsibility, if you choose to receive my letters after this, to rejoice in the admonition. As for me, apart from these matters, I have found nothing that I could write, with a respectful greeting, to people living in the filth of the flesh that you love.

## Letter XXV. Ennodius to Olybrius and Eugenetia

[Col. 0034B]

Desire for your pages has made my forehead lavish in disregard of modesty. And while the tablet promises that a reply has been published, it does not know how to keep an old childishness within the chamber of modesty.

I ought indeed to owe both my family and my purpose of silence a graceful restraint, since my first conversations denied the fruit of my hope. But I do not know whether an intention should be judged perversely stubborn when, without another person’s loss, it multiplies the dangers of anxious experience through love.

Farewell, my lords, and return with me to harmony in writing, lest you act contrary to the Gospel’s admonitions if you deny to importunity what affection may perhaps have justly obtained.

[Note: [Col. 0034D] In Schott’s edition: “my.”]

## Letter XXVI. Ennodius to Faustus

A letter satisfies prayers and desires when, with one who loves you, it performs a service for another’s needs. How I wish, if my purpose did not forbid it, that the quiet of many might often be disturbed, so that, while I give voice to uncertainties, I might discharge the duty of steadfast affection!

My lords, I perform the duty of this present letter at the command of your father, whose mind, while providing for everyone’s security, disregards its own peace under this intention. While he has not yet seen the misfortunes of the Ligurians die with the death of Mauricellus, he is troubled.

[Note: [Col. 0034D] “After the death of Mauricellus.” He had oppressed the province of Liguria with the fiscal administration, through the abuses of the treasury, contrary to the moderation prescribed by his office and the laws. In this matter the instructions of King Theoderic to Marcellus, the fiscal advocate, in Cassiodorus, Book I, Letter 22, are especially pleasing and elegant.]

Our province, suffering from renewed troubles, as though the aforementioned tombs do not contain them, is afflicted by ambushes. While some strive to obtain the fiscal advocacy through unjust men, they reveal, before attaining their wishes, what they are planning in it.

For my part, I did not conceal your greatness’s decision concerning the public good. I maintained that, with God assisting you, you would entrust the aforementioned dignity to no one. But the anxiety of the provincials believes that everything it fears may come to pass.

I received this mission of advocacy from my lord bishop, so that through the service of a letter I might address your conscience, lest someone’s stealthy seizure be brought to fulfillment in this matter. Guard your most faithful promise anxiously with the integrity of your purpose.

As I discharged the duties of greeting, I testified to what I had undertaken to bring forward. Nevertheless, I hope to be informed through the service of letters what has been decided concerning that matter.

# Book Two

## Letter I. Ennodius’s Consolatory Letter to Armenius

[Note: [Col. 0035D] In the old manuscripts this title is written in this form, with the verb omitted. This practice is not uncommon in the headings of letters, in which they also indicated the kind of subject matter. Such is the heading of Sidonius’s poem to Thalia, inserted in Book VIII, Letter 11:

“Much beloved and especially dear,

Phoebus’s memorandum to Thalia.”

In Sidonius’s printed editions these verses are incorrectly joined to what follows, though they ought to be separated, because they form a title resembling that in Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 10: “Sabinus, servant of the Lord Jesus Christ, memorandum to Padu”; and the title of Pope Zosimus: “Zosimus, bishop, memorandum to the presbyters and deacons who are in Ravenna.”]

ENNODIUS’S CONSOLATORY LETTER TO ARMENIUS.

[Col. 0035A]

[Col. 0035B] For a long time, dearest brother, while I sent you a consolatory page with eager prayer, I did not compose words lest I seem either to deprive myself of tears or, amid the losses of lamentation, to make verbal ornaments out of groans and dissipate the proper mourning through figures of speech.

For contrary to the religious obligations of friendship and the bonds of kinship, a hostile conscience would be exposed if, while able to mourn the dead in two ways, you did not do so—that is, if you did not join the service of the mouth to the ministry of the eyes. When the eyes, driven by the goads of grief, shed tears, where are the words of the mourner?

But I, most sincere of men, who owe every service within my power to your grief, wished to attest in writing my sorrow, in which I am your companion. I did so lest, within one generation, the memory of poured-out tears be intercepted, or posterity should think that, at the death of your son, I owed and paid only this much.

On this path I have examples of revered bishops, by whose imitation those whom the shadows of death have enclosed are ennobled. Our Ambrose followed his departing brother with a little book bearing witness to his affliction.

[Note: [Col. 0035D] Book *On the Death of Satyrus*, his brother.]

When the succeeding generation recounts him, it remembers the writer well and joins lamentations to the death of his brother Satyrus. Through Ambrose’s foresight, the recent grief was displayed while he spoke, and before the eyes of readers the limbs of one long dead were continually shown breathing out their spirit. He never allowed the fidelity of the account to grow old, nor the funeral—which passing years could have buried—to become obsolete.

Since these things are so, restrain the rivers of your eyes and, if you please, turn your mind toward the words of one who comes to you as a weeping comforter. The province’s howling shows that you have lost an almost only son, of good character, whom affection for his homeland no less demands, since the whole community, joining its own mourning to the consolation of your groans, bears witness to what it thought of him.

Yet amid these things you are shut in as though oppressed by the death of a uniquely personal evil, not knowing that what has been scattered through many hearts and made common ought to be moderated. Why, then, do you regard as your own anxiety what so many have made their own through their affection for you?

With you, leaving aside your kindred people, the Goth mourns; and you still bend as though you alone were subject to your personal troubles? Let the honors of your ancient forebears instruct you, I ask, and restore you from the inclination of grief to good health.

[Note: [Col. 0035D] “Abraham’s only son.” Commodianus, an ancient writer mentioned by Gennadius in Book II of the *Instructions*, uses the same examples of Abraham and David in the work entitled *Sons Should Not Be Mourned*:

“Are you not ashamed to bewail your children without restraint, like a pagan?

You tear your mouth, beat your breast, and rend your garments.

Nor do you fear the Lord, whose kingdom you desire to see?”

And later:

“Nor did the father, because of grief, lead his son to be sacrificed at the altar;

nor did the prophet, because of grief, mourn his dead son.”]

Abraham, as a devoted father—and what is greater, joyfully—offered his only son to death, and the merciful father prepared the blade for the killing of his son.

You seek him who was transferred by divine judgment as though you were bereaved; and the one whom it would have been sacrilege not to offer, you burden with tears after he has been summoned away.

In this matter let David’s example come before you. He went ahead rejoicing with the bier of his son and giving thanks to God because heavenly favor had called forth from the seed of the revered prophet one whom it might perhaps reward.

If you do not burst into joy as his imitator, at least moderate your grief through some imitation of the example mentioned above.

Perhaps you will reply that such things can scarcely be persuaded to a grieving mind and that counsels have no place in great tribulation; that the bereaved person does not look toward anything that urges him toward life and that the desolate person has only death as a resource.

Add that you lost an upright offspring, one who surpassed his tender age in modest conduct, arguing that your young man had closed his life with a glorious end.

[Note: [Col. 0036D] “With a glorious end.” This refers to the repentance he had performed, discussed shortly afterward and also in Poem 34, where a tablet is described in which angels offered to Christ this son of Armenius, who had done penance. They did not doubt that those who departed purified by the rites of repentance would fly away to blessed life. Hence, just as with the newly baptized, so also with those who died after penance, it was often customary to say that they had “departed to the Lord.”

On a sarcophagus in Rome: “Junius Bassus, man of distinction, who lived forty-one years, two months; while in the prefecture of the city itself, as a neophyte, he went to God on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, during the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius.”

And another inscription at Aix: “Here in peace rests Adjutor, who, after receiving penance, departed to the Lord. He lived sixty-five years, seven months, fifteen days. He was laid to rest on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, during the consulship of Anastasius, a man of distinction.

Furthermore, the opinion of blessed Augustine was that even praised Christians and priests ought not to depart from the body without worthy and fitting penance, as Possidius writes in his *Life* of him.]

He had closed his life with a glorious end, and in the shipwreck of life he had been drawn by that one from the harbor of the soul.

To these consolations for your grief, although sorrowful, I shall oppose the following: he sinned less because he was taken away before maturity. What he preserved in this life, repentance joined to the everlasting life of the better age. The repentance you say he practiced—even if it had found nothing in him to wash away—found something to adorn. Whenever repentance is granted to the innocent, it wins a crown because of the affection of humility.

To this you may reply: “Where shall I turn, brother? Apart from tears, I have nothing in this present light.”

I shall add that a human being can find nearness to God when he does not rejoice in human company, and that in place of a son there can enter a conscience which finds his holy heirs.

I shall therefore show you—not merely one path, if you deign to listen—toward the better life, although your perfection does not need an adviser, nor does one who has been made distinguished by the corrections and adornments of his deeds need a teacher. You need only to weigh carefully the trustworthiness of an exhortation, which you owe to your own counsel and prudence; to recall yourself to affection for heavenly gifts, from which we both receive and love the vital air; and to let us be grateful for the benefit whose author we cultivate and venerate.

These are the things that, grieving, I have woven together in a short discourse, directing a broken declaration, marked by sobs, toward the abundance of style, while I transform lamentations into conversation.

## Letter II. Ennodius to Speciosa

[Note: [Col. 0037D] “To Speciosa,” a religious woman of Ticinum, as the next letter shows. She and her sisters are also mentioned in Book I, Letter 12: “But concerning what you entrusted to me about the religious women Speciosa and her sisters, it weighs heavily upon my mind that I was unable to fulfill it.”]

SPECiosa.

My sorrow demands silence, having suffered to grow while contemplating revenge and the losses of affection. For what else could happen than that, by remaining silent, I should return the favor to one who denied me letters? The contempt shown toward me, which became known through abstinence from revered conversation, was to be struck by an equal blade while I withdrew from conversation.

Perhaps you will say that revenge is contrary to one’s purpose. But I count all errors as obedience to the law whenever you happen to be their authors. Who would think it a fault to do what you have done, or judge it deserving of divine punishment when he knows that it proceeded from you?

Therefore endure with an even mind what I have done wrong, since in this matter you, light of the Church, were the first to wish it so. I preserve the mind that I promised, so that, if I deserve it, I may be an imitator in everything. The truth of this is shown when I remain silent while you are silent and speak when you speak.

I have therefore returned to the duty of writing, after I seemed until now to have kept within the chamber of modesty words that were not loved, intending to offer a similar service in my pages.

Farewell, my lady, splendor of a good conscience without a cloud. Deign to extend your example of holy conduct far into the future and, if I deserve it, to remember me. Forgive the brevity of this letter, which the bearer’s haste has compressed into a narrow space.

## Letter III. Ennodius to Speciosa

How greatly sinners are weighed down by the burden of their deeds! Whatever is offered is removed from their sight, and, so that their desires may not be consigned to oblivion, everything they long for comes near without being permitted to be touched.

I had undertaken a wished-for necessity at the city of Ticinum and had passed through all the difficulties of the journey, thinking that the priest believed this was being done at his command, although it served my own affection. Suddenly, contrary to the limits of my hopes, the fruit already sought with supreme labor escaped from the threshing floor.

Alas! You summon me from an epistolary conversation to tragedy. Because of you I had seen the walls of the revered city after its religious places. I was already preparing grateful words of conversation—though I fear to say what remained—lest by speaking I be compelled to endure again what has passed.

[Note: [Col. 0038D] “The illustrious man Erduic.” I restored the name from the Vatican manuscript, except that it read only *Erdui*, with one letter missing. But he is called Erduic and is counted among the noblest of the Goths in the panegyric. Ennodius had been sent by the bishop of Milan from Ticinum to Erduic and was glad that an opportunity had been offered him to visit Speciosa. Contrary to his hope, however, it happened that he encountered Erduic on the road before he had entered Ticinum and was forced to return home with him, frustrated in his expectation.]

An unforeseen encounter with the illustrious man Erduic, whom you, glory of the Church, had made me desire to see, was thrust upon my eyes. There my companions saw what I was seeking; there the agitation of my mind became known, which I had previously concealed beneath the shadow of the person mentioned above.

I did not know how to conceal, amid the torments of affection, what I desired, nor to color my conscience with any disguise. He who had cut short the grounds for my longer journey brought me home grieving. I confess that I did not welcome this saving of my fatigue.

Behold, I have affirmed the testimony of my diligence and my mind. It is your responsibility, if I have spoken truthfully, to question yourselves and to learn my mind by judging my affection.

My lady, I greet you and beg that you willingly learn through the present bearer what must be reported.

## Letter IV. Ennodius to Olybrius
No prudent person doubts that the faithfulness of a sacred promise is fulfilled, and that a friendship married to fertile kindling rejoices in the nobility of its fruits. I appeal to your conscience, already bound by faithful commitments. As a possessor capable of gathering fruit from a good tree, so I pluck the fruits of mutual affection: let neither party deny that what was intended in the contest of separation has been accomplished. Before God, a vow deserves either punishment or reward.

For my part, considering the religious character of my purpose and the nobility of yours, I judge that what was begun has reached its intended result among us: nor could the exchange of words be denied to young men whose favor was sprouting and whose fruits were bursting into a new light, since he deserves blame who, placed nearby, refused to begin first. Therefore, wishing to avoid the loss of modesty in this matter, I do not wish to escape the reputation of rashness, provided that I show myself to have attained perfection’s goal.

I have burdened the most suitable carrier with the load of an inexperienced speech. In committing this fault through affection, I have done so through one who, when he has sinned, deserves both pardon and favor. Therefore, while discharging the debt of an overflowing greeting, I ask that, if you hold me dear, you show this through the direction of your most abundant conversation. For just as you are an interpreter and lavish advocate of affection, so you do not know how to deceive anyone by the flattering disguise of words.

## LETTER V. ENNODIUS TO LACONIUS

[Note: [Col. 0039D] To Lacon(ius), Book III, Letter 16.]

Among those who love one another, silence is never rightly requited with offense. The novelty of vengeance strikes the one who devised it more heavily than the one who went astray. It is wrong to apply faults as a remedy for faults, while, in the zeal of treatment, the physician himself falls ill.

I wished to imitate the silence that you, forgetful of me, have maintained toward me until now. But, being a weak man among strong spirits, I could not match your contempt. I confess that I was overcome by the frailty of my nature; and what I believe you count among my faults—that I loved silence in writing too much—I have counterbalanced with overflowing talk, and have remedied the pain of prolonged silence with an abundance of words.

Indeed, I was awaiting from you the preliminary gift of a letter. But I did not wish, by remaining silent for so long, to deny myself an answer, judging that I could give form to myself by speaking, and could not do so without speaking. Therefore, my lord, while discharging the duty of the greeting owed to you, receive with your customary graciousness the bearer of this letter, specially sent to you, and restore the use of writing that has been taken away by habit, lest this sparingness of words become a loss to our affection.

## LETTER VI. ENNODIUS TO POMERIUS OF ARLES

[Note: [Col. 0039D] To Pomerius of Arles. Cyprian, in his *Life of Saint Caesarius, Bishop*, writes: “There was then, very familiar to them, a certain Pomerius, a rhetorician by profession and an African by origin; the instruction he had received in grammatical learning made him especially dear to them.” In Gennadius’s catalogue, or appendix, where Pomerius’s minor works are listed, he is called a Moor by nationality and is said to have been ordained a priest in Gaul. Ennodius indicates that Pomerius was learned in Greek and Latin, educated not only in secular letters but also skilled in sacred learning; he calls him a foster-child of the Rhône because he lived at Arles. Two letters of Ruricius to Pomerius, himself an inhabitant of Arles, also survive. For he asks Aeonius, bishop of Arles, to order Pomerius to come to him, Book II, Letter 8. Yet he calls him “abbot,” so that one may now ask whether several men bore this name or whether they were one and the same person; I have readily persuaded myself of the latter.]

How long will absence be permitted to last? How long will a famous reputation, deprived of the intercourse of letters, grow old? I do not wish to escape the reputation of rashness, provided that I may attain complete recognition.

I wish to be the advance courier of these pages, so that the good things of Gaul may migrate to Italy without any loss to their form. Or perhaps you thought that you could hide in whatever place you pleased, when the light of knowledge revealed you to the sight of those who were far away?

And if the report of your household, poor because of its own ignorance, did not confine me in praising you, and if the narrowness of the bearer did not compress the most extensive proclamations of your merits, you have bitten off the greatest portions from both libraries at their clasp of perfection, ensuring that your intellect would grow rich through such nourishment.

I pass over the fullness of the heavenly benefit bestowed upon you, and the fact that you were equipped from above with gifts requiring no human assistance. For it is rightly judged that whatever has no example among human beings comes from the heavenly realm. But I think these matters should be reserved for times to come, with life as our companion.

I come instead to that in which, though separated from me by the greatest distance, you instructed me. As far as I gathered from the testimony of the holy Felix, the bearer of this letter, you examined in my letters, dictated without care, the Roman standard and, as a foster-child of the Rhône, the spring of the Latin stream. As a careful and diligent examiner, I believe, you discovered what the file had polished while you moved through words not fashioned by art.

We do not know what a person has read, or with what intention, when he delivers a judgment after such deliberation—especially since it is written:

> Homer himself, father of poets, prince of Helicon,

has received the severe arrows of a judge’s censure.  
[Note: [Col. 0040D] Claudian, *Epigram to Alethius*.]

I ask: even if Latin shines in its native speakers and in those trained in the arenas of their studies, is it astonishing if it loves outsiders? I ought not to put eloquence’s pomp to the test, nor presume to determine how anyone might be capable of being tested, since it is enough for me, in my profession, to devote myself to simple learning.

Yet if someone had once touched me with such a tooth, while I still rejoiced in the nobility of liberal studies, I would have prepared either something suitable as a defense or something whose accusation would not have shamed me. Farewell now, my lord, and exercise toward me more the support of ecclesiastical discipline.

Write, or send word, about what parents Melchizedek had; explain the ark, the mystery of circumcision, and the matters contained in prophetic mysteries. Let those patterns of secular learning be rejected—occupied with transitory arguments and resembling Penelope’s web.

## LETTER VII. ENNODIUS TO FIRMINUS

[Note: [Col. 0040D] Ennodius calls him his relative. I therefore think he is that Firminus of Arles whom Cyprian likewise praises in his account of Caesarius: “There was then in that city a distinguished man, Firminus, who feared God, and his relative Gregoria, a most distinguished mother of a household; through their zeal, care, and benevolence toward the clergy and monks, toward citizens and the poor, that city was made more distinguished.”]

Although love may demand what perfection cannot fulfill, and affection may obtain, through the boldness of speech, that the hope of remaining silent—which could have adorned it—perish, especially since, as Tully reports, speaking except when necessary is a most foolish condition, still, amid the roads of narration and the paths that must be opened with the sickle of learning, affection reigns, heedless of any consideration of its strength.

Affection, fixed once and for all in the penetrable places of the heart, rules in place of an emperor. It believes that the man who is anxious about the safety of an absent relative is not captivated by the weight or pomp of words, and it does not think that offense can arise from favor. It supposes that this is enough for joy: that the letter announce the desired good health.

But you—whom the scales of expertise will weigh in the balance of eloquence, for whom abundance of language, disciplined speech, a Latin style, and polished expression are established—surely seek in others what you practice; you seek what you love.

We, separated from the gymnasia of the schools, summon certain streams of the ocean from drops of our parched talent, as though we were about to fight with lamps against the sun’s rays.  
[Note: [Col. 0041D] “With lamps against the sun’s rays.” The correction to *lychnis* (“lamps”) in place of *lignis* (“wood”) was easy, since all copies read the word corruptly. *Apology for the Synod*: “Do you not know, fools, that the sun is not helped by torches, nor are lamps lit to support the light of day?”]

The meagerness of my study is plainly evident; and unless loquacity is excused by piety, what I have loved is a loss to my own modesty. The vein of language is indeed drawn from the fountain of one’s lineage, and noble offspring are usually stirred by inborn ardor. I am unequal to my own ancestry: the fullness of your knowledge has not touched me, a stranger, with your gifts. I am able to praise you more than imitate you.

And although mature eloquence has not yet come to flower in me, and I am left without the ability to repay the burden of your favor, I nevertheless entrust my small boat to a calm sea, because silent gratitude differs little from ingratitude.

Hence it happens that the good fortune I learned about you from the bearer’s report is counted among heaven’s benefits for me. And although I ought to return the service of speech, because the negligence of bearers has caused letters sent by you either to be withheld or lost, I have nevertheless led my modesty, dwelling at its post, into uncertainty, and commit my whole self to your judgment as a reader.

Farewell, my lord, and honor your lover through frequent gifts of letters. In such studies it is fitting to be neither lazy nor painstaking nor eloquent.

## LETTER VIII. ENNODIUS TO APOLLINARIS

[Col. 0041C]

For the sake of our own desire, other people’s necessities serve us, whenever we grant compliance to the requests of others for our own joy. Who would not seek for himself, at a price, what on this occasion is provided for another?

The bearers of this letter now owe me my debts; and not only do they not compel me to repayment, but they confess themselves indebted. It is not negligence that causes my writings to be prolonged by rare dispatches: as I now discover, similar circumstances often take away good things.

Therefore, if you love me, let the bearers find the fruit of this benefit. Just as they demanded from me what had to be offered, so, I think, they bring to you, through the exchange of writing, the things you desired.

My lord, while returning the service of a greeting, I pray God that this may reach you in good health, and that the page may promptly be returned—one that seeks my good health and announces yours.

## LETTER IX. ENNODIUS TO OLYBRIUS

At last, scarcely ever, things I had long desired have succeeded according to my wish, so that the thirst I had conceived from the ardor of your letters might be satisfied by the wave of your rich eloquence, and the heats that prolonged expectation had doubled might be quenched by the streams flowing joyfully from your lips.

But why should I claim to have been brought to the summit of my desires, when a greater longing is born from their attainment, as my breast burns from the stream of your words? It is clearly shown to me how ignorant of realities the human mind is: while understanding the value of its own ambition, it grows accustomed to love more dearly what it reaches only after delay; and while it has an abundance of what may delight it in the present, more remains for it to seek.

Now I confess that, as an overcautious evaluator, I was alarmed by the caution displayed in your letter. While the sails of your speech were being carried aloft by favorable success, and everything that breathes was serving your purpose, you say that your conversations lack oars.

When truth’s carefulness has been set aside, the fear portrayed by your words is not permitted. Oars are needed whenever ships are aided by no impulse of the winds. He does not need them for whom a devoted harmony of winds has made the voyage favorable. The sun is not helped by torches, nor have assemblies of lesser stars ever illuminated the brightness of the lunar sphere.

My lord, offering you the honor of a greeting as above, I pray that, through the fruit of my studies, I may not be deprived of your greatness. Since I have not concealed from you what I desire, may you compensate the writing-service you have hitherto extended by the frequency or abundance of your pen.

## LETTER X. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

If the heavenly ruler considered my deserts, I would obtain either scanty blessings or great punishments; and, as one capable of judging my own worth, I would not strive by desire toward what I could not reach through merit. But thanks be to him who cuts back our sins so that we may not become exalted, and thus leads our hope toward greater things.

These prefatory remarks are owed by me to the words of Lord Avienus. Though he had not yet returned to good health, he had loosened the chain of anxiety binding my mind. While anxious hopes still hung between hope and fear, he looked to nature and showed what eloquence it would thunder forth.

I had indeed anticipated these things by judgment, and I recognized in the treasures he had produced the vein that nourishes noble metal. But even in this matter, as a sinner, I scarcely believed that what I did not deserve to attain could come to pass.

I speak the truth, with divine mercy as my witness: if there are any in Liguria capable of judging the genius and splendor of letters, they believed that you had labored over that composition in which a mind already gray with age had been cultivated in a boy, forestalling his years.

But I said these things more with tearful joy to those whom either shed blood enrolled in the white register of the heavenly court or clear confession made illustrious—those who should confirm our beginnings with favorable success.

Greeting you as servants greet their masters, I desire, amid all circumstances, while you relax your mind through these matters, to rejoice in the misfortunes of your adversaries. For there is nothing in which we can feel the losses of our enemies. God has granted us this: that earthly envy cannot take it away.

## LETTER XI. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

What am I to do, when you write that you must write back, and, with heaven obeying you through the good foresight it has granted, you relate whatever the mind of another could investigate? It is clear that it is beyond human power for one person thus to fulfill two roles. But let these things be attributed to him who granted them.

I nevertheless did not promise to return a speech by which ancient Tully would be thrust into the shadows. For I had returned the notebook I had received with greater speed than my talent allowed, while, serving my sense of responsibility, I disregarded what might have contributed to improvement.

Nothing of that revered composition remained with me except what, as I judge, I had snatched from a memory demanding it back, for the benefit of a good reputation. I do not wish to say what the thing was that I unwillingly restored, or what it was that I loved, lest you plainly believe that you had foretold matters to be cited by you without loss to themselves.

Nevertheless, in this matter, the mercy of my lord Avienus, my serene light, although still beginning, yet already approved, came to my aid. He supplied me with a certain little sheet that might have remained with him and bestowed upon me a purple mark of nobility. I have possessed it until now; from it I have both spoken and learned.

But since I have also been ordered to weigh the benefits of another, I shall send it with the bearer who follows. I do not understand this benevolence toward me as being for my sins, so that, in my trusting credulity, I would not deny what fortified the talents of outsiders, knowing that I mingle with human beings through a caution that opposes my purpose.

I speak the truth, with him as witness to whom all things are known: not even tortures can compel me to give to anyone those compositions of yours celebrated by the mouth of the world—which, I believe, is due to my ignorance.

My lord, offering the greeting of my reverence, I affirm that neither negligence attacks my judgment nor flattery my affection.

## LETTER XII. ENNODIUS TO ASTYRIUS

[Col. 0043C]

Your eminence gives heed to prophetic oracles and, through recent events, upholds the authority of ancient ordinances. You took care that a tardy admonition should not remain neglected because health had been withdrawn.

For the worshippers of God have written that the teaching which ought to pass through the ears of the prudent can draw them on by the savor of false speech, alleging that warnings perish when they are offered to persons settled in a different judgment.

I, however, humble in station and poor in speech, had previously granted words only under the goads of kinship; and, as a testimony to my diligence, in my earlier letter I gave a reply under the freedom of blood.  
[Note: [Col. 0043D] “Under the freedom of blood.” Ennodius was related to Astyrius, or perhaps his parent, as he wrote in Book I, Letter 24. In this letter he attempts to soothe Astyrius’s offended mind by appealing to their kinship.]

Now my spirit is troubled because, lacking the fruit of injuries, you perhaps assumed a boastfulness that was false politeness toward yourself, not knowing that weapons return upon the author those which an untrained hand has hurled against another.

Who would regard as an insult something that afflicts only the conscience of the person who sent it? It is the nature of the wicked to feel toward everyone what they themselves deserve, and in evils nowhere to see the consolation of innocence. The torments of a stained life are the inability to believe that others do not share in it.

I have described these things with that state of mind in which, remembering my purpose, I am compelled to owe hatred to crimes. My tooth has touched no one except one who confesses concerning himself: when we attack vices, anger reveals the guilty party.

For I would be unjust if I perceived a plowshare in place of a stylus, or counted as mine writings that, when I reread them, I do not recognize. The Lord knows that, if the letter had not been marked with my name, I would not have known to whom it had been addressed.

Keep your jokes for yourself—or for those with whom, without the duty of open speech, you raise a clamor over actions through the fellowship of secret intimacy.

Now, while discharging the honor of a greeting, I ask you to pay attention to places, times, and persons when sending letters, lest what I do not count as written to me should perhaps injure another. For I judge that you sent the form of this letter to many people and, merely by changing the names, transmitted it to each without considering their merits.

## LETTER XIII. ENNODIUS TO OLYBRIUS

[Note: [Col. 0043D] “As a certain eminent figure of eloquence says.” Symmachus. I agree with Father Juret, who thinks that this alludes to his Book VII, Letter 9, in which he advises his son concerning the style of a letter in these words: “For just as in the clothing of human beings and in the rest of life’s manner, things suited to place and time are chosen, so variety of talent ought in familiar writings to imitate a certain negligence, but in forensic writings to shake the weapons of eloquence.” Cicero has the same opinion in Book IX, Letter 21 to Paetus, where he writes that he usually composes letters in the everyday words he himself uses. Seneca likewise asserts this about his own letters in Letter 75: “What would my speech be like if we were sitting together or walking? Unlabored and easy. I wish my letters to be like that: containing nothing borrowed, nothing artificial.” Artemon, according to Demetrius of Phalerum, likewise says that a letter ought to be written in the same manner as a dialogue; but Demetrius teaches that it should be elaborated somewhat more than a dialogue.]

As a certain eminent figure of eloquence teaches, negligence is the law of letters, and the craftsman makes himself the author of his genius through carelessness. In this work, what subtracts from grace is that which your witness found through his sweat.

A messenger of good health, and one who seeks the good health of another, does not demand words baked in the furnaces of smiths. It is better, in these exchanges, that we meet with a pure face of expression. Simple adornment in conversation rejects diadems; the fellowship of letters has prevailed whenever it has fled affected elegance.

But the rich and elaborated narrative of your greatness cannot be enclosed within beggarly boundaries, nor can the treasure of your speech be confined by any limits. Like great rivers, it scorns the restraints of banks.

Your abundant tongue has not yet passed beyond the composed veil of official occupation; it shows that it serves only those studies to which it has been led by circumstance. And if we did not know that the administration of the state had been entrusted to you, as a testimony to our leisure, and that whatever is arranged everywhere is the work of your labor; if we had not learned that the care of Italy had entered one breast, we would almost think that you were being worn down solely by the care and constant practice of writing.

These gifts are owed to God, who both bestowed a mind that loves knowledge and did not withhold the file of study from the construction of speech. The reed, swift through the air, does not cleave the air with such force through its taut sinews as the speech of your invention describes.  
[Note: [Col. 0044D] “The reed cleaves the ether.” Not “the ether.” Ennodius sometimes uses *aether* in this way: “empty air” in Book VII, Letter 38, and in *Against the Synod*: “They saw only the ether struck by the arrows they themselves had aimed.”]

It grows sluggish against no barrier and is delayed by no obstacle. Whatever difficulty presents itself becomes passable to it. In a wondrous way, through the skill of the advocate, the nature of cases is transformed: you make it appear that you have a matter you wish to possess; whatever you relate as truth is truth.

Hence cautious judges are not permitted to resist. The most minute investigators of opinion regard it as a gain if they follow wherever authoritative speech drags its captives.

To this tongue, to these riches, I confess that I owe a singular reverence; I was the first to run toward them. And I hope that very many things may be entrusted to me to undertake as a clasp of affection.

But as for what you ordered concerning the religious women Speciosa and her sisters, my spirit is troubled that I could not fulfill it. I now have no remaining intimacy or bond with them, especially since they live in separate cities. Nevertheless, I immediately sent to them the letters addressed to me; their reply was delayed until the time when they might see themselves in relation to those matters.

So that I would not keep your greatness in suspense, I delayed writing. If they have sent anything that you would wish to know, it will soon reach you.

Now, imparting the honor of a greeting, I ask that your eminence entrust me, especially in matters concerning the Church, with whatever there is to be done. For I think I have not concealed from you, in the matter of your female relatives, or of the matron, the diligence of a friend toward you.

## LETTER XIV. TO THE AFRICANS

[Note: [Col. 0045D] To the African bishops in exile, whom Thrasamund, king of the Vandals, banished to Sardinia on account of their faith; they numbered 220. Paul the Deacon, *Miscellaneous History*, Book XV, records that Pope Symmachus was accustomed to provide them with daily support. Here he consoles them in this letter and sends the sacred relics of the martyrs that they had requested. The letter was indeed written by Ennodius, but on behalf of Symmachus; in ancient collections it is also found under Symmachus’s name among his other letters.]

The enemy might perhaps have considered it a gain if, amid the dangers he inflicted upon Christians, he had subdued the minds of believers, and, after the Lord’s flock had been scattered in various directions, not even a few had remained whose persevering faith could trample him down.

He still reigns among you who found his satisfaction not so much in numbers as in devotion. For it is written that Satan was given power to sift the servants of Christ, so that whatever might be found among the wheat could be gathered into the granaries, while whatever was straw could pass to feed the fires.

This was said especially to you: “Do not fear, little flock; it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32).

The sword of the faithless entered among you, cutting away the withered members of the Church and leading the sound ones onward to heavenly glory. The contest shows how many soldiers Christ has; through battles it becomes known who deserve triumph.

Do not fear that they have taken away from you the insignia of the pontifical office. That priest, or victim, is with you who has been accustomed to rejoice not so much in honors as in minds. The rewards of confession are greater than the gifts of named rank. Human favor often leads persons of lesser merit to those; these are granted only by heavenly grace.

For he himself fought and conquered in you—the one whom faith deserves to have joined to it even amid human torments.

There is no need, in lengthy conversations, to kindle the heavenly fervor within you. The fire of divine virtue has its own means of growth. Nor is there need to raise with praises those already placed upon the trophy, who conquered without an instructor. Whatever flattery of proclamation brings burdens the Christian conscience.

What you have done is indeed a work of virtue, but it must be surpassed by the restoration of the highest reward. Nevertheless, what you requested in your letter sent to our son H., the deacon—namely, the blessing of the blessed martyrs Nazarius and Romanus—we do not deny to the faithful.  
[Note: [Col. 0046D] H., the deacon. I think this was Hormisdas, who was a deacon of the Roman Church. Those who interpret this as referring to Ennodius, leaving aside other matters, depart from the monogram.]

Receive the revered protection of unconquered soldiers; and because the emperor has already recognized your faith in battle, happily complete the duties of confession.

God will grant, when it pleases him, the Church’s peace restored, so that he may console with the sweetness of peace the sorrow that adversity imposed.

## LETTER XV. ENNODIUS TO EUPREPIA

[Note: [Col. 0046D] To Euprepia, his sister and mother of Lupicinus. At that time she was traveling in the province of Narbonensis, plainly on ancestral soil, that is, at Arles, as Letter 7 of Book VII will show. Several letters are addressed to Euprepia. Lupicinus will be discussed frequently elsewhere, and especially in *Scholastica*, Discourse 2.]

By the dispensation of a heavenly mystery, at one and the same time a sister’s affection was restored to me and a mother’s to Lupicinus; the double bond of kinship deserved, after its interruption, to receive back your affection that had been away.

Through the favor of your letters, you came back to life among us after the death of affection that you had brought about. We saw love rising, as it were, from a certain tomb.

The messenger of your safety came to our ears under ill omens. We believed that, in contempt of us, you had filled tombs while still alive. We believe that you endured harsh things; but we confess that you inflicted harsher still.

What you endured is shared with the good; what you did, with the cruel.

Where has your maternal care been hiding all this time? Where has what was owed to your brother gone astray? Your mind had gone farther away than your body. If adversity had driven you, as the companion of exile, to the furthest boundaries of the earth, your sister’s faith and a mother’s concern ought to have followed you there.

But near the setting of the sun, where you are said to have been, you had a heart cold toward dutiful affection. You should have imitated the fortunate rebirth of the heavenly star after its decline from the care owed to it, and you should not have carried a mind forever withdrawn from grace.

You adopted the mind of the provincials whom you visited; you changed your region and renounced your purpose of devotion. For, abjuring communion with Italy, you rejected not only your friends but also your inner bonds.

Finally, a change of soul came upon you through the change of land.

How I fear that I am attacking your negligence with lengthy conversations! What will offense do, when you have scorned affection unharmed? You have given just pain to the pursuits of one who does not love; you have supplied reasons that make you innocent.

But this reproach, if considered in itself, is harsh; if its origin is investigated, it is seasoned with the honey of every sweetness. He bears negligence in affection heavily who, as a free person, accuses the silence of a parent.

You can correct your errors through abundant writing, if you cannot do so in person. Therefore, while presenting you with the grace of a greeting, I ask you to remember me, who anticipated your prayers and wishes concerning our common son. Before I recognized what you wanted, I considered what I ought to do.

Appease God through religious devotion, and reconcile him through constant prayers for us; may he regard my intention for the boy’s progress and the secrets of my heart, so that what I promise through labor he may accomplish through his help.

## LETTER XVI. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

It would have been fitting for the service of the illustrious Pamphronius, as he traveled, to be transferred from the ministry of a page to the duties of living speech. Nor should one be burdened with an epistolary packet who has come to know not so much my words as my studies.

But in such services his requests are treated as commands. The investigator of hidden minds requests the assistance of a written page; and therefore, lest any lack of service on my part should be found in him, I have supplied these writings, accommodating them to his commands even if they are not necessary for his recommendation.

For with what words should one address him for whom it is permitted to hope for everything from the favor of your greatness? Thus it will happen that the words of the petitioner are narrower than the merits of the bearer.

What assistance could you provide to one for whom, however much you might ask, he deserves more? Therefore these words are joined to the exercise of the pen, not to the benefit of the traveler. It pleases my mind to remember you on every occasion, even though by mentioning him in writing I contribute nothing to the bearer.

Now, however, because I have been ordered to do so, I append the words of recommendation that are offered to outsiders. Help him, who especially seeks you, strengthening his confidence through your graciousness. Let him find whatever he anticipates in hope, so that, if he is a narrow judge of his own merits, he may refer to me whatever he has obtained.

Offering the service of a greeting, I beg you to consider me one who must be relieved by frequent words. Amid the burdens of sorrow, I can have no support except the consolations of your mouth.

## LETTER XVII. ENNODIUS TO CONSTANTIUS

[Note: [Col. 0047D] He calls him an illustrious man in Book IV, Letter 13. Both his homeland, Milan, and the praise of eloquence and piety that Ennodius attributes to this Constantius suggest the epitaph of Constantius the Milanese in the toga, which is compatible both with the period and with Ennodius’s style. I therefore append it here as it is read in the monuments of ancient sacred inscriptions.]

> Constantius, skilled in talent and in laws, lies here,  
> > Buried beneath the dark lot of death in these tombs.  
> >   
> > Let integrity mourn him here, and saddened honor sigh;  
> > Let friendly faith lament the death of its companion.  
> >   
> > Who so often brought back triumph from the battles  
> > Of the forum concerning law, and struck down savage defendants with his speech?  
> >   
> > Ever a man of the toga, he adorned character  
> > With the splendor of his own eloquence, and eloquence with character.  
> >   
> > Cruel death does not greatly harm the funeral of the just:  
> > Your weapons weigh nothing upon him; the devout man possesses the stars.  

No one condemns expertise because of pompous expression, nor does he say, with modesty, that what follows must be despised. Whoever proclaims the adornment of language through elaborated speeches while renouncing it is his own opponent.

I, however, have always weighed in your letters not the words but the care of your greatness. I have not judged eloquence, an accomplice of malice, to have greater value than simplicity, which, with an unpainted face, reveals the secret of the mind. In holy men I have always both loved and honored this quality.

Now I give thanks, and I possess gratitude, because you visit my smallness with the greeting of a written conversation; and amid the occupations and watches with which Ravenna keeps everyone busy, concern for me is not abandoned.

Therefore I return the duties of an overflowing greeting, hoping that, through the graciousness with which you cherish one who trusts in you, you may make my presence desirable to my masters, who love you.

## LETTER XVIII. ENNODIUS TO JOHN

I have plausible reasons for attacking your unanimity with the bite of my pen, though it is stained with rust—reasons that, since you abound in nature’s gifts and are rich in the capacities of talent, you cannot purge away.

Did I ever believe that news of your return could be brought more quickly to someone else? Did I think that concern for me, amid all your occupations, could exceed that breast consecrated to friends?

Behold, pages are returned to others before my eyes, and friendly expectation is frustrated under every form of my credulity’s contempt. I do not wish to fill the letter with the greater bitterness of reproach. A terse account is enough for the sorrowful.

My mind still remains in the state in which it admonished your greatness when you were departing. It is your responsibility, if you disregard the troubles of the times, to preserve the harmony you promised.

Farewell, my lord, and relieve one who loves you through an exchange of words, so that by writing you may erase the pain that you see has come upon your friend through your abstinence from writing.

## LETTER XIX. ENNODIUS TO CONSTANTIUS
I abound in joy, nor is the faith of my rejoicing halting, because, through diabolical inspiration, certain conflicts have arisen, so that you, who have advanced yourself beyond the correction of all, may be congratulated on the honor of triumph. As I see it, Liguria is not exhausted: even at the end of the age she has not laid aside her nobility in giving birth. Still inimical to vices, she nourishes a fire even among the ashes; in whose embers the avenging flame of crimes does not die, nor is the fire of errors covered over. How I feared that it might cease, as though spent, while I anxiously examined the face of your letter, darkened by the deceptions of others—like an astonished parent who, when he sends a dear child to war, cannot remain confident that his valor has been tested.

He counts his son’s triumphs as additions to his anxieties, not as occasions of rest; he fears more for the happiness he has experienced, to which affection supplies dread. For a mind trained by victories is ignorant of caution; and in battle love of praise is forgetfulness of safety: a taste of the trophy commands affection for life to be renounced. Only those possess a relish for life who have learned nothing of the good that comes from conflicts; what has been taken away from concern for one’s own safety is always joined to glory.

But for the present I must refrain from writing of this kind. [Col. 0049A] The conflicts of our soldier must be proclaimed less than asserted. Where javelins are needed, words contribute nothing. Although, in praising you, I have been publishing my own judgment—and to praise answers is itself a response—nevertheless, having prayed for God’s help, I add words obedient to faith, directing the service of my pen to him who, whenever unhappy earth must be tilled with curved plowshares, promises that he will grant his servants shoots that they may sow, saying: “Do not consider what you are to say; for it is your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20).

May he therefore come to bring the promise to fulfillment; may he himself strengthen the faltering infancy of my speech, so that the composition of our hallucination may appear inhuman. But why do I go on repeating this at length? I ask one thing: let my replies be assessed according to my capacity; and let it not be thought that I am lacking either in reading or in defense because I do not know. Thus, as you testify in your letter, a man has been found who, on this occasion, was sifting the servants of Christ, just as Christ himself promised it would be done, asserting that

[Note: [Col. 0049D] On the freedom of the will]

Under an unmentioned name he refutes someone who asserted that human beings had been given free will only for the worse alternative. As Saint Augustine teaches in his work *On Rebuke and Grace*, we must confess that we possess free will for doing both evil and good. Since Ennodius refutes this heresy most aptly, and since it is refuted by the whole school of theologians, both ancient and modern, who discuss free will, it is enough for me to place before the reader some words of Irenaeus from Book IV, chapter 72, which support Ennodius’s arguments and are not commonly known:

“If by nature some have become bad and others good, neither are the latter praiseworthy for being good—for they were fashioned that way—nor are the former blameworthy for having become so. But since all are of the same nature, and are able both to grasp and to practice what is good, and again able to cast it away and not do it, rightly, among human beings who are well governed, and much more before God, some are praised and receive the testimony due for choosing and persevering in goodness as a whole, while others are blamed and receive the penalty due for abandoning what is good and virtuous.

“And for this reason the prophets exhort human beings to act justly and to accomplish what is good, since such conduct lies within our power, although through great negligence we have fallen into forgetfulness and need a good disposition, which the good God has granted us to recognize through the prophets. For all these things demonstrate the human being’s freedom of choice and God’s counsel: he turns us away from disobeying him, but does not compel us.”

[Col. 0050D] Who, under this pretext, was bringing forward an argument that free will had been granted to human beings only in one direction, the worse one, for choosing? O schismatic proposition, which, according to the Apocalypse, has blasphemies written on its forehead (Revelation 17:5)! What sort of freedom is this, if it is valid, when one is allowed to will only what brings punishment? Or why call it a choice, when he asserts that only one alternative was granted? If this stood by the truth, there would be no place for divine judgments. For what good would our God rightly seek from us, who had removed his own desire from the will? But, according to the Apostle, “Is God unjust? By no means” (Galatians 2:17).

Among human beings, someone who demands from his subjects what he has not granted them the power to do is at odds with the love of justice. Consider with what conscience this might be thought of God. Where is that cry of the Apostle, bearing witness to freedom of choice: “To will is present with me, but to accomplish it I do not find” (Romans 7:18)? What else does this mean than: “I know how to choose the right road; but unless heavenly grace helps the one who enters upon it, I shall grow weary”?

No one doubts, no one condemns, that, when the author of grace provides assistance, the path of equity is itself opened to human beings. For grace is the guide and forerunner of good things, when we are invited to rest from heaven by manifold exhortations; when we are told: “Come, children, listen to me” (Psalm 33:11); “Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you” (Matthew 25:31); “Where I am, there my servant also will be” (John 12:26).

But unless, admonished by such words, both our will—which is free—and our labor render obedience, we descend to danger and Gehenna not by any command but willingly. Thus devotion produces reward, or contempt produces punishment. Otherwise the retribution would not be just, if punishment were imposed upon sinners who sinned by necessity, or if a good reward were offered for a work to which unwilling people were dragged.

Therefore we owe grace the fact that we are called; we owe grace the fact that, unless we resist, the taste of life is infused into us by hidden paths. Yet it belongs to our choice that we follow the benefits shown to us. For the way of crimes is read as not our mistress but our servant, since it is said concerning sins: “Their desire shall be under you” (Genesis 4:7).

What else does the prophet’s entire speech mean, as though adorned with garlands: “Do not be jealous of those who do evil” (Psalm 36:1); “Do not trust in princes” (Psalm 145:3); “Do not become like a horse and a mule” (Psalm 31:9); and the Apostle: “Do not become slaves of human beings” (1 Corinthians 7:23)? So often “Do not” is spoken in heavenly admonition—toward what does it look, if it was not permitted to will something else?

Moreover, although spoken in the person of Christ, the testimony of that same prophet supports our freedom of choice: “To do your will, my God, I have willed” (Psalm 39:9). And elsewhere: “I will sacrifice to you voluntarily.” And: “I will fulfill my vows to the Lord.” And again: “Vow and fulfill.”

But the example of the blessed Apostle, by which he believes himself fortified, works in our favor if he observes what follows, when he said, in opposition to arrogance: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:10). Immediately, so that he would not be thought to have fled from glory so completely that he departed far from the truth, the wise architect added: “I labored more abundantly than all of them, and the grace of God in me was not empty” (ibid.). This is to say: “Christ found in me one whom he might enrich—or enrich abundantly—with gifts.”

For divine grace is not poor; rather, it is thought to be weakened by a certain leanness or thinness of our merits. It is then not judged to flow through its own channels when, from its streams, the vein of our dryness receives nothing.

If only the narrowness of a letter allowed the mysteries of the sacred books to be disclosed! But I fear that someone who, with God’s inspiration, will be unable to find any charge against our faith may bring an accusation concerning the length of the page. What of that passage, and with what intention does he receive it: “Behold, water and fire; stretch out your hand toward whichever you wish” (Ecclesiasticus 15:17)? What of the other passages that you yourself, its copious advocate, repeated?

I believe that, as they say, it passed by him with his ear closed like an asp. I see how far the poisons of the Libyan plague extend themselves: the sandy serpent does not possess only the deadly things that it discloses; what he confesses must be weighed in estimating his hidden crimes. For he wishes to reach the point of saying that no one perishes through his own fault or negligence, if a human being is deprived of the choice of good and evil by the power granted to him.

He boasts that only those could have been saved without any labor, without friendship with the commandments, whom heavenly favor alone rescued while they wandered far from merit. Accordingly, insofar as this is referred back to God, he understands that those perished whom divine grace did not wish to save.

But you, my lord—after the word of greeting [salvedicto; wording uncertain]—ensure, for your own part, that you remain as you are; and if a slave of death cannot be healed, desist from the dispute. Otherwise, while you stand firm, supported by the strong root of faith, that man may, under cover of this controversy, shake the divine seed from the wombs of some before the time of publication.

## LETTER XX. ENNODIUS TO CONSTANTIUS

You will forgive me for replying quickly, because at my age I still owe something to inexperienced haste. Maturity and weight befit you. Therefore encourage one who believes, and withdraw my trifles from public severity; for if our page is a doubtful and uncertain matter, it protects itself by the patronage of your command, since no one disdains what has been ordered. Farewell, then; I commend these things to your reading. It will indeed come about that, having afterward been well received, we shall be urged to obedience by the goading of soothing submission.

[Note: [Col. 0051D] A doubtful and uncertain matter]

Symmachus, Letter 1: “Thus a doubtful and uncertain matter holds me in doubt.” An ancient expression, meaning “doubtful and uncertain.” Thus Martianus Capella, Book I, contrasts it with “clear.” “Do you,” he says, “act foolishly, and, knowing the *ἐγειρομνημεῖον* [memorial] of a very clear work, you understand the *ἐγειρομνημεῖον* [memorial of awakening] as doubtful; nor is it clear that, with Hymenaeus leading the procession, the arranged wedding festivities resound.” Hence they also wish *crepusculum* [twilight] to have been named because it is on the boundary between light and night. Symmachus likewise, Letter 7, to Ausonius: “Before manifest day released the doubtful darkness.”

## LETTER XXI. ENNODIUS TO ALBINUS

[Note: [Col. 0051D] Albinus]

A patrician, as is shown not only by the following letter of Ennodius but also by several letters of Theoderic preserved by Cassiodorus. He was also a former consul. For he had been consul in the year 493, that is, three years after Faustus. Thus Boethius calls Albinus a former consul in Book I of *The Consolation*, when discussing the accusation by which he was falsely charged with treason before Theoderic. From Ennodius’s words we further learn that Albinus was Faustus’s parent—that is, his relative and kinsman.]

I have prolonged my letters to your greatness four times, and still I am accused as though idle: my tongue served my affection, but my persistence has not earned the name of diligence. I believe that I have been brought to this offense by either the negligence or the envy of the messenger.

Nevertheless, behold, I multiply my letters, and, offering signs of my prosperity according to your wish, I desire to rejoice in your happiness. Farewell, my lord, and encourage one who loves you with every mark of your favor; for by your patronage you do something close to God when you sustain one who believes with complete faith and fellowship.

## LETTER XXII. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS
