He spends useless effort on benefits who tries to assist the sun with torches. Fullness of favor needs no addition; nor does anyone require increases in recommendation whom merit has brought to the summit of friendship.

My pen’s attention follows the illustrious and patrician Albinus, your relative. In writing I do not offer him what is necessary but what is voluntarily offered;” and although I add nothing to his advantage, I nevertheless earn his affection by fulfilling the commands of the man mentioned above.

Therefore, offering the venerable lord the service of a greeting, I ask that the said magnificent man receive, with regard to his diligence, what he has shown to me while honoring you. For I know that this most distinguished man will soon be brought into the innermost chambers of your heart, and that his innocent purpose will be strengthened in your eyes by his own qualities.

## LETTER XXIII. ENNODIUS THE DEACON TO HIS LORD FAUSTUS

Those who happen to belong to you are deprived of protection without loss, for paternal assistance is not lacking to those whom you cherish. I speak of Lupicinus, the son of our Euprepia: the general statement above applies to him.

[Note: [Col. 0052D] Our Euprepia]

Ennodius’s sister. See above, Letter 15, and Book III, Letters 15 and 28, among others.]

The eminent man, your worshipful associate, Count Tancila, told me that concerning his property something had been obtained from our lord the king, though it is grievous to relate.

[Note: [Col. 0052D] Count Tancila]

The passage was previously very corrupt. I restored the name Tancila from ancient books and from Cassiodorus. He is Tancila, a distinguished man to whom Theoderic writes in Book II of the *Variae*, Letter 35, concerning the recovery of a bronze statue that had been stolen from the city of Como.]

For he asserted that all the small properties of his mother had been claimed by Torisa or others. I had nothing else that I could provide for the orphan’s misfortune except to inform you and perform the duty of a truthful reporter. It is your responsibility, with God’s inspiration, to provide what may help the wretched child; my responsibility was to report what had been entrusted to me.

[Note: [Col. 0052D] Our lord the king]

Theoderic, and consistently so whenever he names the king or calls him lord of affairs.]

Presenting the services of a greeting to my true lords, I ask, in reliance on divine mercy, that heavenly assistance accompany your labor.

## LETTER XXIV. ENNODIUS THE DEACON TO HIS LORD FAUSTUS

I believe diligence suffers a loss when no hands of travelers are rewarded with the gift of letters—letters that by their reading commonly carry faces even to distant places and present the images of dear ones through the service of speech.

To this is added the opportunity provided by the journey of the highly distinguished Luminosus, who deserves well of both of us and who joins the fruits of his own favor to the merits of your devotion. Who could endure that affection should be regarded with any negligence, if I refrained from pages that your favor demanded, and if the named messenger did not receive them for delivery?

Thanks be to God for what had to be placed at the beginning of the letter, because your happiness is raised by successes corresponding to your prayers, and because the swollen neck of your enemies, not burdened by Christ God, bows down.

Hope had foretold what affection has displayed. For he rightly anticipates the end of a heavenly judgment who knows how to infer its character from the serenity of human actions.

Farewell for a long time, my lord, and encourage one who loves you through the use of his pen, so that whatever distances of land take away, the delivery of letters may make up.

## LETTER XXV. ENNODIUS THE DEACON TO FAUSTUS, QUAESTOR

[Note: [Col. 0053D] To Faustus, the quaestor]

Faustus attained all the highest dignities in due order. For several years earlier he had been master of offices, during the consulship of Albinus; in that office he was sent by King Theoderic as ambassador to Augustus Anastasius, as is clear from Pope Gelasius’s memorandum to Faustus, who was serving at Constantinople in the office of ambassador. He is now serving as quaestor of the sacred palace. After this he obtained the belt of the praetorian prefecture. See Epigram 142 and Book IX, Letter 18, to Stephania, Faustus’s sister: “You are surely the sister of that lord Faustus, during whose prefecture he is found to have established monasteries”; and passim in Cassiodorus’s *Variae*, although in them “Faustus the deputy” is everywhere corruptly written instead of “the praetorian prefect.” Finally, he was adorned with the patriciate, as Ennodius testifies in Book V, Letter 26, to Agapitus. Before all this, however, he had already held the consulship when quite advanced in age, as stated in Letter 5 of Book I.]

In accordance with heaven’s ordering, it was especially fitting that news of my return should be sent by none more fittingly than by a friend hurrying to Ravenna; his faithful report would have been sufficient even without a letter. Yet I could not abstain from the practice, since, if I refrained under any sort of neglect, I would seem to have condemned the frequent writing that I have loved.

Moreover, I could not offer the man mentioned above hands refusing him, since he knows how to demand confidently from those who love him what he knows how faithfully to provide for them out of devotion.

[Note: [Col. 0054D] In Schott’s edition, Ravenna.]

Having therefore departed from Ravenna, which embraces everything sweet that I possess in this present life, I reached Milan in sound bodily health, with Christ accompanying me. I suffered the haste of the return, which winter forced me to desire, perhaps against my wishes. But everything must be referred to God, to whom it belongs to arrange human actions and to change bodily diligence through the savor of eternal love.

Now I turn to the reason for writing, offering humble greeting and commending the messenger. If he rejoices in your serene mind because of your benefits, he recognizes either that he has received what he provided through your generosity, or that he has been encouraged to understand how he ought to love.

If he is unwilling, compel him to return quickly: his presence is necessary both to my affection and—if God establishes his promise—when he himself commands, he is expected to be useful to the undertaking.

## LETTER XXVI. ENNODIUS TO LIBERIUS

[Note: [Col. 0054D] Liberius]

Concerning him, see Letter 1 of Book IV.]

Diligence is either nourished or sustained by writing; epistolary conversation is the handmaid of affection. Silent love presents the likeness of an ungrateful person; friendship that does not burst into speech diminishes its own character.

The secret of the heart is rightly unlocked with the key of speech. I now receive your favor. According to the powers of my talent, I have dedicated these small offerings of written exchange, through which I claim for myself the merit of loving more.

For no one offers his lips to the barrier of silence whom speech does not expose as a traitor-minded person mindful of a broken covenant. I therefore hold the chief place in literary fellowship, and I am worthy of greater cultivation, since I was the first to disclose what I was doing through the testimony of my tongue.

Behold, I have plainly explained the purpose governing the dispatch of this letter. [Col. 0054A] It is your responsibility to cherish in me what you have received, lest the judgments of your high position undergo examination while I lie prostrate. For whoever does not defend what he has chosen reveals the sentence of his own censure.

My lord, paying the reverence due in complete obedience, I pray God to multiply the increase of his benefits toward you; for the only full measure of my advantages is that he has raised your greatness to the heights owed to it.

## LETTER XXVII. ENNODIUS TO HONORATUS

[Note: [Col. 0054D] To Honoratus]

Brother of Decoratus, whom he also succeeded in the office of quaestor in a novel example, as appears in Cassiodorus, Book V, Letters 3 and 4, though that occurred later. At this time he had recently completed the Ravenna guard-duty—that is, some other courtly office.]

You indicated in a recent letter that you were living nearby, adding to the diminution of my joys the news that your health had declined. I do not deny it; I deserve that bitter things should always be joined to sweet ones for me.

Until now, adverse circumstances held you occupied with the Ravenna guard-duty. When it happened that this burden was relaxed, your bodily condition was weakened, so that it would not be possible for you wholly to obtain what you desired.

How harsh is the condition of human affairs: whenever it responds to our wishes with some measure of sweetness, it immediately changes what it has granted at the very threshold.

Nevertheless, I was alarmed by the accusation that you introduced into your letter with oratorical and excessively Daedalian foresight, so that you might make me seem unwilling to undertake what had been imposed for your advantage if I indicated that I had been unable to accomplish it.

O secret of an ingenious mind, which looks more to convenience than it trusts affection! God is my witness that I will not deny you what I can do. Pray to God that he will not allow my undertaking on behalf of these unfortunate letters, which he loves, to be obstructed by calamities.

For there is nothing that I fear more as an obstacle to the task imposed upon me than what I know: that receiving a schoolman earns nothing. Apply your talent rather to the rugged courts, through which whatever a rough tongue demands immediately obtains its due—or, if it does not obtain it, immediately snatches it away.

My lord, offering the grace of a greeting, I hope that you will aid my labor with lavish prayers. For although I do not possess the merit of a learned or educated man, I often sustain in lawsuits the deeds of a perfected man.

## LETTER XXVIII. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

[Note: [Col. 0054D] To Avienus]

There is much in this letter to show that this Avienus is someone other than Faustus’s son, whose consulship was discussed in Book I, Letter 5. Yet Ennodius also calls this man consul. I am therefore led to believe that, of the two Avieni—one consul in A.D. 501 with Pompeius as colleague, the other in 502 with Probus—the former was Faustus’s son, while the latter was this other man discussed here. In the *Fasti* and other records he is called Avienus the Younger, not because of his age but because of the order of his consulship.]

Thanks be to God, who must be placed first, since he made your greatness demand what I had to offer. You gave a value to the loquacity that until now I scarcely kept within the modest inner chamber. I make use of the genius of my pen, which I had harshly recalled from importunate writing; I possess the merit of a compelled voice through unusual talkativeness.

For after you ordered me to send letters, you commended to my mind what I had kept silent. Bravo, long-prodigal forehead: at last it has fallen to me to reach an abundance of affection without cost to yourself.

Let us learn not to hate what helps us. The favor of silence has made it possible for us now to speak freely with you; conversations that were often despised are awaited from us.

I shall not go farther. As I see it, the office of the tongue is asserted through the rarity of speech. In this respect the faith of my rejoicing is not halting; our judgment is supported by the agreement of truth.

Behold, the man who scarcely tasted with his lips the letters of learned men, richly endowed with a great harvest of conversation, does not disdain to receive the stalks of our little tablet.

You have benefited me with double joy, O modesty: when you are steadfast in your position, and when words formerly despised are frequently desired, behold, the judgment of the man we love has become better.

Thus we have provided for ourselves by modesty, and for our consul by correction. But lest the page, going beyond its prescribed limits, continue too long and reveal through much speaking that what we kept silent was not deliberate, farewell, my lord, and honor those who love you with this fellowship. For the lofty summits of your honors receive only such proofs as arise from humility.

# BOOK THREE

## LETTER I. ENNODIUS TO SENATOR, BISHOP

[Note: [Col. 0055C] To Senator, bishop]

It is uncertain of which see he was bishop. For he cannot be understood as the bishop Senator of Milan, to whom Epigram 87 was written. That man was considerably earlier, since after Senator Theodorus governed the Milanese see, and after Theodorus Laurentius governed it, who was flourishing when Ennodius wrote this.

Several men in that age bore the name Senator. Among them the best known, and the most distinguished in writings and honors, was the author of the *Variae*, whom we call Cassiodorus through an established, if one may say so, error. For those who think that “Senator” was used *κατ’ ἐξοχήν*—“by distinction”—as though it had been his proper name, are not to be heeded. His true and proper name was Senator, which he prefixed to all his letters in Books XI and XII of the *Variae*, and which alone he entered in his own *Fasti* in the year 513, when he was conducting his consulship.

Thus this was as truly his name as it had been the true name of the other Senator who was consul in 436 with Flavius Anthemius Isidorus. But an error arose from the opinion just mentioned, as though “Senator” were an epithet rather than a name, so that Cassiodorus is commonly called by what is supposedly his proper name, when in reality it was a surname derived from his father’s name.

For Senator’s father was named Cassiodorus; hence the son was Cassiodorus Senator, and was called by all his names Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator, just as Faustus Avienus was named from his father Faustus.

Here again those must be refuted who believe that the Cassiodorus to whom the patriciate was granted by King Theoderic after the prefecture, and concerning whom much is said in Book I, Letters 3 and 4, is the author of the *Variae*, when everything must be understood of his father; to him also Book III, Letter 28, was written.

For it was not Theoderic but his grandson Athalaric who granted the prefecture and then the patriciate to Senator the son, in Book IX, Letters 24 and 25, where he is called by his correct name, Senator: “We have heaped our benefits, Most Honored Father, upon Senator, rich in virtues, wealthy in character, and made still more abundant by honors.”]

The first action unquestionably suited to a holy purpose is to do willingly for the sake of justice whatever others are accustomed to provide when admonished. But the action next, or nearly next, to honesty is not to be burdened by upright suggestions. In this respect, even if the person admonished does not hold the first place, he nevertheless possesses God’s favor because he does not resist the insinuations of truth.

I shall therefore explain the reason for my preface, lest I too seem to delay my advantage through an excess of words. Some time ago I humbly asked through an intermediary that, from among the slaves whom your people were known to have solicited from my household, the one who remained might be returned to me.

You replied to my prayers with a holy promise: even if the boy himself legally belonged to you, you would nevertheless place favor before advantage. When I returned from Ravenna—shameful to say—your priestly decision could not be put into effect because of my sins. I attribute it to my merits that the man whose mouth condemns falsehood violated his established decision.

Behold, I once again appeal to your conscience. Behold, I present what befits a son, so that through the eminent and magnificent man, Lord Victor, I may bring to your humility whatever might have been granted to me by the authority of secular laws.

See whether I am guilty, since I chose a man whose character accords with that of bishops, one who might even soften the untamed hearts of those resisting justice. I have already promised myself the outcome of my business, since I have demonstrated the merit of my envoy.

Consider whether it befits religion, whether it be worthy of a pontiff, that one who can command rocks should be despised. Two things support me: the sincerity of the case and the status of the petitioner. Whatever opposes these will immediately deserve the judgment of good men.

## LETTER II. ENNODIUS TO EUGENETUS

[Note: [Col. 0056D] To Eugenetus]

Concerning him, see Letter 24 of Book IV. I suspect that the learned brother of Eugenetus, whose death is mourned here, was the great Olybrius, concerning whom Letter 9 of Book I speaks. This may be why Olybrius and Eugenetus are joined together in Letter 25 of the same book and in Athalaric’s letter, Book VIII of the *Variae*, 19; and why thereafter Ennodius makes no mention of Olybrius.]

Although the exchange of letters is more a matter of joy than of sorrow, and although neither the secrecy of the heart nor the diligence of friendship is properly brought into the light by speech halting beneath recent confusion, I shall nevertheless see whether more infrequent speech harms affection. If it is not continued at all, it reveals childishness; divinity gave the tongue the office of bearing witness to grace.

But you may say, my lord, that these things are foreign to one whom I know to be occupied by the greatest griefs: that his heart, pressed by anguish, cannot rise to words of love; that lamentation feels nothing soothing; that what burdens the mind rejects what delights the ear; that the brother who had been the greater part of his soul above has transferred it to the tombs. What can be demanded from one whose half of his well-being the grave has enclosed? In the extremity of affliction, no voice can be sought, being subdued by groans. Let an untimely narrative be spoken in the time of tears.

I shall reply that grief from a similarly bitter calamity has also entered my heart; nor can I be separated from the sorrow of one whom, by similarity of our wishes, joyful occasions have sometimes joined to me.

Yet I often show that speech has been the indication of a more serious evil in mourning, and that conversation has betrayed remedies interrupted by silence. I shall say that one who denies pages to his lamentation wishes to let what he mourns perish within a single lifetime.

The memory of a brother and a learned man does not deserve that what we felt about him should die with us. A mind sparing of a mourning mouth is sparing in grief; remembrance of the beloved, entrusted to tablets, violently penetrates the hearts of dear ones with its sting. A report of death arranged in letters never allows death to grow old.

With this intention, I address your greatness as a weeping comforter, so that, through the benefit of a substitute conversation, the affection promised among us under invocation of God may be nourished, and that the person of eloquence, which does not allow his merits to perish, may revive also through our conversation.

## LETTER III. ENNODIUS TO HIS LORD FAUSTUS

Since both domestic and friendly occasions supply a reason for writing, why should I refrain from pages, as though I lacked a messenger—especially since the diligence of letters often customarily provides me with replies?

To this undertaking was added the request of the honorable man, your worshipful brother Constantius, who desires to subject to my benefits the industry by which he has become known to you as a lord, as befits an effective servant.

He transfers his labor to another’s rights, wishing to owe to letters of recommendation what he deserves. Nevertheless, I yielded to his prayers and, under the pretext of showing humility, prolonged my letter according to his desire, asking God that, with all speed, a messenger might lift me up with news of your health and prosperity.

Let your greatness also accompany the man named above, for my sake, with a double favor, if I am not an unworthy petitioner.

## LETTER IV. ENNODIUS TO ABBOT STEPHANUS

[Note: [Col. 0057D] To Abbot Stephanus]

To whom he writes again in Letter 12.]

What a sweet task your letters have been, since they have offered me a spiritual gift! How welcome is the necessity of messengers, which by seeking its own remedy heals the desires of others!

I confess that, if my purpose did not resist it, I would almost conceive hostile prayers to disturb the security of certain people. Behold, adversity supplies what prosperity does not grant. From where, amid peaceful circumstances, would I, a sinner, receive letters from holy men, which the brilliance of my merits never demanded? Behold how much assistance those have brought me who confess that they obtained it from you.

I regard divine providence as granting these things. I already believe that I have laid down much of the burden of an evil way of life. One who deserves the conversation of holy men is close to innocence.

Therefore, while worldly license possessed me in its uncleanness, I never deserved the letters of so great a man; and afterward, even over long intervals, I never received benefits of this kind.

Great God, what dignity you grant to those who serve you, that once you begin to regard them, you also make them acceptable to your friends! Truly, I have always regarded you with singular devotion; always, with my neck weighed down by sins, I have submitted to your venerable character.

Behold, I am now addressed as though an equal. Long-maintained submission has raised me. Therefore cherish me with your prayers; for your pages show that you do not offer fragile protection.

These men too have been received, who have conferred upon me the benefits in which I take pride. I return to the matter.

That lost cleric was afraid to plead his case before the bishop after he saw that I had defended those to whom you assigned my service. If you command, I suggest that one of them travel to Ravenna with letters of recommendation from you to your son, Lord Faustus, lest a venal judgment, plentiful at Milan, be delivered to those men’s prejudice.

## LETTER V. ENNODIUS TO MAXIMUS

I would suffer great gaps in my letters, raised up by the address of your letters, if awareness of my own ignorance did not restrain me with shame, and if I did not hold the scales of judgment even when I am praised undeservedly.

Your favor has made you forget severity; my purpose compels me to dwell within the modest inner chamber. You raise my writings as lovers do; I must fear those who, looking down on everything with rancid neglect, condemn even what has been trimmed.

Nevertheless, I give thanks that you write that I am judged worthy by Lord Patricius of being what your testimony has made me. This expression of affection is therefore owed to the insinuation, not to the page, which my rough style has marked without the gift of eloquence.

Returning a greeting worthy of your greatness, I give thanks to God, who has brought you, enriched with the successes you desired, back to your own home—although my mind, because of the bond of affection, never regards you as absent.

## LETTER VI. ENNODIUS TO LAURENTIUS

We must yield to the command of love; affection holds me bound. I have granted it words so that I would not be silent about what is owed in a greeting.

The opportunity provided by a household messenger could not pass me by without my sending a letter as a testimony of diligence. Therefore, offering the greeting due in reverence, I ask you to encourage me with a substitute conversation, since I promise myself a reply through the extension of letters.

## LETTER VII. ENNODIUS TO ADEODATUS, PRESBYTER

[Note: [Col. 0057D] To Adeodatus, presbyter]

Of the Roman Church, as is shown by what he writes to the same man in Book VII, Letter 27. He is perhaps the man who subscribes at Symmachus’s first synod in these words: “Adeodatus, presbyter of Saint Martin of the title of Equitius.” I do not affirm this completely because at the fourth synod two presbyters named Adeodatus, of the same name and rank, are listed.]

Who could be forgetful of your affection except an inhuman person? Who would not wish to have the support of a person of complete devotion before God? I above all, who am weighed down by heavy burdens of sins and have obtained your favor—a fact that promises me complete absolution.

Therefore, greeting you reverently and as duty requires, I hope that you will make vows for me at all the holy places. Once I have obtained this, I shall without delay repay God’s benefits, for I have learned that you deserve to be heard.

## LETTER VIII. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

If offense causes the letters of your greatness to be doubled, how I wish that the calm of your serene heart might often be disturbed! And if it did not oppose my purpose, I would supply causes for indignation, since through faults I have obtained what love did not deserve.

Yet I announce that I am free from error in that matter in which, while accusing me of negligence, you bestowed a reward. I sent the boy in confusion; through him I showed nothing other than what was needed.

With an unburdened heart, the tongue is free to perform its duties; a confused mind rejects the grace of greeting. Behold, I give thanks to God for both things, because I am not guilty and you believed me guilty. Your agitation bestowed a benefit upon me that affection would scarcely have given.

I cannot explain what I owe you. Love is poor when speech does not fail in its narration.

My lord, offering the greeting due, I ask God that, whatever your state of mind may be, you may always write.

## LETTER IX. ENNODIUS TO MARCELLIANUS
I know that your greatness abounds in the great benefits of God and preserves the steadfastness promised toward friends. Your spirit does not know how to make uncertain promises, preserving its love without any alteration; and therefore, after God, I entrust and commend myself securely to your hands, nor do I doubt that the benefits of God will come to me through you in whatever affairs. My lord, rendering, as above, the honor due in greeting, I ask that you frequently refresh me with the conversation of your letters: for a supreme gift is granted me by God if I shall have deserved to rejoice in knowledge of your well-being; for faith and integrity make all who fear God acceptable.

## LETTER X. ENNODIUS TO LUMINOSUS

[Note: “To Luminosus,” an old friend and companion from early youth. In the preceding book, Letter 24 to Faustus, Ennodius called him “most exalted.” At the time when the case of Pope Symmachus against the schismatics was being handled at Ravenna, the bishop of Milan, I think, had paid out four hundred solidi in his name, with Ennodius as guarantor. When the bishop demanded their return, Ennodius asked Luminosus to deal with Symmachus so that the money might be refunded. On this matter he writes again to the same Luminosus in Book VI, Letter 16, and in Letter 33 to Hormisdas.]

The bond of friendship and the mature plant of grace between us could suffer no loss from the separation of distant regions, if conversation compensated for what is denied to sight; and though divided by the sluggish burden of our bodies, we could be joined in spirit through that part which we have received from heaven. The tongue would mark, at the bidding of our hearts, the token of pure affection, if the service of the mouth answered the abundance of desire, and if the opened inner chamber of the mind were preserved in letters. Then love would grow old through no neglect; then, polished by the diligent practice of mutual attachment, it would shine, nor would the rough torpor of remembrance injure the memory of you.

But what am I to do, since the clouds of my merits obscure the serenity of one who loves well, and my sins win me oblivion? Let it be far from my purpose to imitate what I grieve has been done, and through silence to exact vengeance for your silence. Thus, driven by twin goads, I have allowed words to flow. I could not deny the exchange of letters, which both necessity and affection demanded.

You know very well what your holy father, the lord bishop, requested from you, through me, and in person: that the expenditure incurred at Ravenna for the needs of the lord pope should be balanced by repayment.

[Note: “Should be balanced by repayment.” In Book VI, Letter 16, concerning this same matter, I promise him repayment. Usually *redhibere* means “to return what one owes,” regardless of the title under which one owes it. Sometimes, however, it is taken more broadly, as in the *redhibitory action* among the jurists, for whom *redhibere* means, as our Glosses interpret it, “to cause the buyer to have what he previously had.” Avitus, bishop of Vienne, uses *redhibere* in this sense when he says in a letter to Apollinaris, his brother in the episcopate: “If, for every idle word that people have spoken, they will be compelled to give an account.” Finally, they used *redhibere* simply (*ἁπλῶς*) for “to return.”]

For certain powerful persons, whose names it is not safe to record in writing, the Lord knows that he paid out more than four hundred gold solidi. He granted these when I gave my word; my standing before him cannot be free of obligation until, through you, as I trust, the promise is fulfilled. For this reason I have sent the bearer of this letter, a man of religion and good faith, so that you may relieve me of the agreement and injury I have mentioned. Therefore, rendering the honor of greeting with complete humility, I ask you—calling as witness the one who regarded the common vows concerning the holy pope—to arrange how I may be relieved of such harassment.

Yet, if you do not think it shameful, tell me, and I shall repay from my own resources whatever is known to have been spent by the holy bishop with me as guarantor; for I have letters from the holy pope in which he ordered that whatever was necessary should be done with the assurance that it would be completed under my security. If I deserve to suffer the burden, it will be your responsibility to consider the matter.

## LETTER XI. ENNODIUS TO SENARIUS

[Note: “To Senarius,” a relative and singular friend; hence, in Book I, Letter 27, he says that he shares with him a double bond, of affection and blood. The letters of Cassiodorus’ *Variae*, Book IV, 3 and 4, show that Theoderic made Senarius *comes patrimonii* in the year 511, although the third letter is incorrectly addressed “To the Count of Private Affairs.” Earlier, as the same letters attest, he had long served in that king’s court among the *exceptores*; Ennodius may perhaps have this office in mind here.]

If your spirit had not stripped itself of the memory of its attentiveness toward me, if your greatness had not compelled it to return to judgment after favor, you would have prolonged your frequent letters. But what am I to do, since undeserved love does not rest on strong roots, and whatever the breeze of favor has stolen away is quickly brought back for examination? I know that I ought to have been loved before I was tested; this was the only fruit I gained from affection—something I had secured, though unknown, by prudent provision.

But it was fitting for you not to withdraw so quickly from one upon whom you had bestowed the name of friend, lest it always return to my fault that the affection promised to me is not maintained. The conscience of one bound by attachment is usually unaware of strictness, and it is necessary that it hold forever whatever a faithful heart has once received.

Therefore, offering the greeting that is due, I hope that, scorning the rancid disdain of the powerful, you will exalt your honor—and the ability granted you by God—with the fasces of humility.

[Note: “With the fasces of humility.” This is Senarius’ particular praise. Cassiodorus, Letter 4: “But humility, which is as rare as it is distinguished, commended him still further. For it is a new thing to preserve modesty under the love of a prince.”]

Let the tongue that interprets hearts confirm the truth of this, and let the love displayed through letters convey faithful testimony to your minds.

## LETTER XII. ENNODIUS TO ABBOT STEPHANUS

God’s gifts are doubled for those who hope, and heavenly grace overflows with a twofold benefit. In generous channels the wave of celestial gifts rushes forth; the streams of gifts that come from Christ pass beyond the capacity of the one who drinks. It is the only vein that knows no wasting and rejects exhaustion, supplying its courses with as much as the thirsty heart deserves to receive.

Consider what hidden savor it instils when water kindles ardor, and when the abundance of a living stream brings dryness to lips under the heat of the burning spirit. Such is the character of your letters: as much satisfaction as they bring to desires, so much increase do they also produce. Their depth is both drunk and desired; and they enrich with so pure a flood that the inward parts are secretly drenched by a fire proceeding from them. In them I see kindred flames and cups, and a diversity of nature joined together in an unfamiliar harmony.

My lord, with God our Lord granting it, offer the earth a long example of the most blessed life; and through the sacred philosophy of religion show, by your contempt for the present age, that one must not hope only for this life.

## LETTER XIII. ENNODIUS TO APOLLINARIS

[Note: “To Apollinaris.” The following six letters were hitherto unpublished and are now brought to light for the first time from manuscripts. Ennodius had already written to Apollinaris in Book I, Letter 8, and will write to him again in Book IV, Letter 19, where, because of affection and age, he calls him his brother.]

My care, which serves your affection through kinship, daily shows that there would be no loss in disregarding travellers, were they not to resort to that one consolation of the absent which heavenly providence has found in letters. But what am I to do, when there is such confusion among those who come that you do not know whom above all to choose, to whom the letters intended for your holy conscience could safely be entrusted?

For inferior men draw into an opportunity for their own advantage whatever we offer to affection; and it is grievous that what the force of love demands should serve greed. Therefore I suspended my mind from writing until the opportunity of a household bearer arose, lest the care scattered among unworthy messengers should grow bitter through another’s importunity, and a fault return to me that did not begin with me.

Thus, briefly explaining the necessity of the silence I arranged, I turn to the use of the page, through which the words awaited in letters grant me the presence of your greatness by the secret paths of our spirits. Farewell, therefore, my lord, and with the serenity that you owe to your family, cherish your lover through frequent conversations; for no gift is so venerable to one who is anxious as this: that I may often recognize you announcing your own well-being and asking after mine.

## LETTER XIV. ENNODIUS TO PROMOTUS

My heart would offer frequent conversations both to relationship and to love, unless the consideration of distant lands, without providing a remedy, withdrew remedies from desire. For whatever is joined by affection, whatever is linked by the chain of blood, scarcely breathes when separated by stretches of country.

What support can there be for one who is frequently denied the opportunity of conversation and written address? By what witness can silent care between absent persons be disclosed? Either the hoped-for opportunity of travelers is withdrawn, or men are found to whom letters intended for loved ones cannot safely be entrusted.

Nevertheless, with anxious prayers I scarcely waited until a household bearer appeared. Through him, while presenting the honor of greeting, I shall disclose to you the desired indications of my prosperity, and I shall promise myself an answer through a letter’s announcement—an answer in which, if your health is secure, it may be opened to embraces and words of affection.

## LETTER XV. ENNODIUS TO EUPREPIA

[Note: “To Euprepia.” He reproaches his sister for writing nothing to her son Lupicinus, especially at a time when peace had been secured between the rulers of the regions—namely, between the rulers of Italy, from which Ennodius was writing, and of the province of Arles, where Euprepia lived—and correspondence was free and without suspicion. By “the rulers of the regions,” I understand Theoderic of Italy and Gundobad, king of the Burgundians, who controlled much of the Second Province, or Alaric, to whom Arles was subject.]

It is rare for love, supported by relationship, to bow its neck to necessity; it scarcely happens that one who is sovereign serves, for affection is always master by its own right. What royal name has ever been hindered by an obstacle from showing care? To whom is free love enslaved in service? No one offers an excuse based on fear except one who has cast away the spirit of attachment.

A mind that serves through devotion is not afraid, even when the commands of rulers are harsh. No commands of peoples are so barbarous that they do not permit a mother to render what is owed to her son. Whatever has been born in the world is not separate from humanity; whatever is generated in the light of the world requires the fruit of the womb and of seed. We share with all animals only this common cause and concern. What can that mind of savagery be judged to be which is found to lag behind irrational creatures in care for offspring?

The foregoing composition concerns your relationship. You, forgetting your only pledge and pity for one deprived, have taken away the happiness of one whose mother survives. Truly, I confess with complete freedom of purpose—especially now, when you deny him even conversation, and when, God being gracious, peace has been firmly rooted between the rulers of our regions—that in savagery you have surpassed a tigress.

When could there be found either something you could love more than a son, or something to fear on account of a son? Concern for possessions ought to have been put second, since an inheritance is never properly sought while the heir is despised.

Behold, I say this: if God had not, through my concern for His servant, opposed malicious persons, the whole stock of your family would have been cut down. Lionesses entrust their cubs to the safe recesses of forests or wilderness, lest their offspring become human prey.

Perhaps you will say that this reproach shows that I bear heavily the burden imposed upon me by the young man. God knows that I endure only this bitterly: that I lack your presence and recognize that, through your silence, you have become forgetful of all affection. Yet, by God’s favor, my paternal diligence toward our boy is not diminished.

He has entered the threshold of nobility, to be instructed in the liberal disciplines. I have also sent you the very composition with which he was commended.

[Note: “The composition with which he was commended.” The preface addressed to Lupicinus, which holds second place among the school compositions.]

In it, recognize not eloquence but my prayers. Farewell, therefore, my lady, and, if it can be done, return yourself to our sight in accordance with God’s ordering.

## LETTER XVI. ENNODIUS TO LACONIUS

[Note: “To Laconius,” counsellor of King Gundobad and, as it were, his quaestor, a noble and pious man. In the *Life of Epiphanius*: “Then Gundobad, after summoning Laconius, to whom he had always safely entrusted the truth of both matters and words—whom both the distinction of his birth and the curule chairs of his ancestors had exalted through the insignia of outstanding virtue—consulted him whenever a pious nobility, such as it is not when joined to vices and not bound to the allurements of luxury, was involved in something he could benevolently accomplish.”]

It has been a long time since my spirit has been tortured by waiting for that by which it was accustomed to be refreshed. You have prolonged your silence, compelled by no necessity. I was not an imitator of this negligence, so as to postpone my own letters; but I remained silent for days, deceived by the hope of a conversation that was soon to come.

Now, however, your mature and extensive silence has overcome my deliberation. The silence that has grown stubbornly strong at a certain root must be torn out.

Thus our letters provide two advantages: I commend to you Benenatus,

[Note: “Benenatus.” He is also mentioned in the following letter, and perhaps in Cassiodorus, Book IV, Letter 15. The name is formed according to the pattern of such names as Seronatus in Sidonius, Citonaius in Gregory the Great, and others found here and there. There is a bilingual epitaph at Rome, in the consulship of Lupicinus and Jovinus, part of which reads:

> ΕΝ ΕΙΡΗΝΗ ΑΝΕΠΑΗ ΒΕΝΕΝΑΤΟϹ  
> ΘΕΟΘΙΛΑ [ΘΕΟΟ.]

[Thus the Sirmond edition. Perhaps it should be restored as ΘΕΟΦ.]

> ΕΠΟΙΗϹΑ ϹΥΜΒΙΩ.

“Benenatus rested in peace. Theophila made this for her husband.”]

a man coming on account of his runaway slaves,

[Note: “Because of his runaways.” That is, slaves who escaped by flight. See Letter 19: “your runaway slave, who fled three years ago.” Honorius the emperor likewise used *fugacem servum* for “a fugitive slave” in the Theodosian Code, Book IX, Title 2, Law 8, concerning jurisdiction; Gregory of Tours does so as well, Book VI, chapter 31.]

and I do not defer the benefits you desire.

Therefore, farewell, my lord, and, recognizing that what concerns me has prospered according to your wish, raise me up with corresponding words, so that both the bearer may rejoice in the benefit and I may be refreshed by your reply.

## LETTER XVII. ENNODIUS TO BISHOP STEPHANUS

[Note: “To Bishop Stephanus.” There is no doubt that this was the bishop of the Church of Lyon, where Laconius also lived, to whom Ennodius wrote concerning the same matter. The people of Lyon therefore owe Ennodius this favor: through this letter they see preserved the memory of their bishop, which had remained faint and obscure among them.]

After your dignity was restored through your merits and the honor demanded by your life was conferred upon you, I have received no letter from your blessedness on account of my sins. Such forgetfulness toward suppliants is foreign both to your purpose and to your character. Let pontifical authority not accuse my boldness: it is scarcely possible for diligence to consider what right it may possess. One who is spurred on by the command of affection never measures himself.

It is added that I could not extend a welcoming hand to the bearer of this letter except in order to bring Benenatus, a man seeking Gaul for certain affairs, to the knowledge of your circle through the service of my words. Commending him with complete humility, I ask that through him I may be relieved by reciprocal conversations.

My lord, rendering the service of greeting with complete devotion, I hope above all that the serenity of your prayers will not omit mention of my person when you supplicate the Divinity without ceasing.

## LETTER XVIII. ENNODIUS TO BISHOP EULALIUS

[Note: “To Bishop Eulalius.” Perhaps he was the bishop of Syracuse, who attended several synods of Pope Symmachus and is praised at length in the *Life of Saint Fulgentius*. It is possible, however, that that age had other bishops of the same name.]

[Col. 0064B]

The narrowness of my circumstances would testify to the height to which the gift of spiritual conversation has raised me, if it could be encompassed by speech. The feebleness of my mind is not adequate to recount it, nor is the poverty of my mouth sufficient. For what else shall I count it than the overcoming of sins, that you have shown yourselves mindful of me? The memory of you has already driven away everything that the obscenity of my actions could provide, and has allowed me, in fair serenity, to look upon the heavenly gift.

My lord, offering the services of greeting with due propriety, I ask God that the soul in which everything God commands overflows may preserve, without any diminution, the favor it has promised toward my smallness. Declare that this comes to me by your will through the testimony of frequent letters.

## LETTER XIX. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

[Col. 0064C]

Thanks be to God, who, in accordance with my desires, makes conversations busy, so that I may never at any time refrain from writing: for what the law of love demands can also be useful. Therefore, my lord, giving you indications of my health, I suspect that I have found your runaway boy, Germanus by name, who fled three years ago; I have sent a small description of him. If he truly belongs to you, I shall learn in due course what steps must be taken.

## LETTER XX. FAUSTUS TO ENNODIUS

The affair of my kinsman Julian, whom I commend to you, is being harassed by the intrigues of Marcellinus. He is prepared only for complaint and distrusts the integrity of the judgment; he avoids the examinations he desires.

For after he is said to have presented some order to Gevica, your aforementioned petitioner immediately hastened to the hearing of the Milanese court and, as was proper, repeatedly presented himself publicly before the judge for thirty or forty days. He warned Gevica himself, who was alleged to have been appointed the instigator,

[Note: “The appointed instigator.” An instigator is one who presses for a dispute to be decided by judgment. Compare Cicero, *On Divination*, on the *moratores*, a class of advocates employed to cause delay.]

to send his client to the courts. He also informed the lord Trasemundus, as you will be able to recognize from his letters. But nothing availed with him, for in this miserable case only hiding places can serve as a remedy.

On his behalf I ask—although with you there is no need of entreaties, wherever the truth becomes known—since he has sent all the documents of this affair, that by your direction he may be freed from such troubles. My lord, offering the services of greeting, I hope that, as is your custom, you will take care to remove from the aforementioned man the harassment that afflicts him, and that you will refresh my anxiety concerning the state of your prosperity by letter.

## LETTER XXI. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

One whom the knowledge of an elder and the testimony of a good reputation commend needs to be asserted in few words. He does not need a lengthy speech who is supported before your greatness by his own qualities. The foregoing composition speaks of the distinguished man Vitalis, whom your mouth has made worthy to rejoice in membership in the sacred college.

Will he, then, be fortified by foreign letters, who enters the curia as no stranger through the benefit of your speech? And will the secrets of your heart be closed to one for whom you have opened the innermost chambers of freedom?

I, however, rejoice in writing at length; for although I offer little to the bearer, I suffer no loss of my own desire. My lord, returning the greeting I owe, I ask that your favor may show itself more closely toward the aforementioned man, and that it may also care for me through the restoration of conversation.

## LETTER XXII. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

Hope deceives me, although it demands frequent letters. Relying upon it, I feed my spirit with unproductive conversations. It has been a long time since, by continually prolonging my letters without interruption, the silence that I believed had been conquered has been strengthened.

But what am I to do, when a heart possessed by devoted love is scarcely brought back to deliberation? It considers as remedies even those things that it has discovered to have helped nothing. Therefore, offering the customary service of greeting with reverence, I commend the bearer of this letter, Constantine himself, whose support is honesty and modesty; although I owe him much through affection, I discharge even greater obligations under compulsion of judgment.

## LETTER XXIII. ENNODIUS TO MARCELLIANUS

Among lovers and those powerful in honor, affection for benefits is readily available; nor does the one accustomed to grant them cheapen prayers by delay. The distinguished man Virgilius, eminent in both blood and honor, greatly laments that a necessity of traveling to Ravenna was imposed upon him by an illustrious man, the *comes* of the sacred affairs. If this had been his desire, his age would have brought welcoming hands.

He employs me as his intercessor with you, so that such a burden may be removed from him. Through frequent reports he informs your instructed authority of what he has done. My lord, offering the honor of greeting, I ask that, out of consideration for me, the requests made as a testimony to diligence may receive effect.

## LETTER XXIV. ENNODIUS TO MASCATOR

Your diligence, unfeigned by any novel affectation, has adorned my heart. I make use of the testimony of a pen that, through the chatter of the learned, displeases those above ignorance. My compelled speech has stolen from an imposed necessity a value that it does not possess through eloquence.

No insult was ever worthy of punishment when it was offered under orders. No one justly condemns an obedient man; the one who provokes an unlearned speaker must blame himself for the injuries inflicted by rustic speech. It is arrogance not to obey those higher than oneself; it is worse if you despise whatever you know to have descended from one who is obeying. The assertion that one does not love what is demanded is considered a declaration of wrongful desire. The person who suspends a censure against one who obeys supports his own judgment. A harsh insistence is wrong when it considers merit in the parent rather than in the act.

He has not expelled modesty from his station who owes what he says to command. Therefore, in us, what is coarse in eloquence is commended by obedience. You will judge what sort of thing it is that you ordered to be offered; I consider that, without loss of face, I have earned from you what you desired to receive.

I am silent here about matters that ought to have been narrated in the chief place: ecclesiastical humility.

[Note: “Ecclesiastical humility.” They judged that rhetorical flowers and figures were entirely unsuitable to it. Book I, Letter 16 to Florianus: “You said that there was rhetorical cunning in me, although it has long been the case that the affection of my speech has cut away from me every oratorical figure, and I cannot occupy myself with gusts of words when the cry of duty calls me to groans and prayers.”]

I have renounced whatever could please, and have not pursued the pomp of speeches, although I love speech; considering my purpose, I flee even what leads to glory; as though it were a fault to avoid whatever raises one up; I regard as blameworthy whatever elevates or exalts; I lose the merit of deserved praise through a desire for favor.

I shall not put forward an excuse for the truth painted with a brush, while I repeat that I have now abandoned whatever concern for liberal studies once provided; that from the bed of a once-abundant river, scarcely a drop of eloquence now flows from its drying channel. I am silent about the fact that another use has blunted the tongue which practice had made nimble: that silence exists in place of eloquence, and that we prefer abasement to the cothurnus.

I return to the point: since I was not permitted to hide within the chamber of modesty or to conceal the weakness of my talent beneath the garment of silence, I shall count this as a complete defense, since I have brought it forward. But provoked by love, I have crossed the limits of letters through inconsiderate loquacity.

Farewell, my lord. By offering you the honor of greeting, I shall discover what you think of my letter, whether through silence or through writing at length.

## LETTER XXV. ENNODIUS TO EUGENETUS

A person whose faith is lame may judge that there is no favor in remaining in your service. Nevertheless, I wish the frequency of letters to be prolonged as a testimony of diligence, lest a spirit anxious about the prosperity of one who loves it, while health remains in the body, be tossed about by suspicions.

Behold, my lord, you have the means by which to recognize the serenity of my heart through the betrayal of my desire. Attend to your own part; and just as the distinction of the favor I have obtained exalts me, so may the grace of the words you have offered raise you up.

Therefore, returning the greeting I owe, I ask you to make clear, beneath whatever cloud of expression, what your desire is accomplishing in me. Farewell.

## LETTER XXVI. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

Your greatness attends to its responsibilities and has asserted the splendor of your blood through the testimony of purity. Devout hearts do not know how to abandon love; a noble spirit guards religious diligence.

Thus I received letters shining with a double light, when what your holy heart discovered was marked by a serene right hand. I pray God to preserve in you, perpetually, this devout disposition, if it loves Rome, and to multiply such attentiveness toward me under the care you promised.

## LETTER XXVII. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

I do not know whether frequent conversations are pleasing to your greatness; nevertheless, I shall always offer what I expect from those who love. I allow others to have other purposes; I must live according to my own custom, so that the fullness of love may be opened with the key of conversation.

I cannot endure silence, grown worm-eaten in affection through the passing away of habit. Now, if equal care belongs to your eminence, let it be shown by the constancy of conversation; let it be revealed by the frequency of letters. But if, hitherto occupied with other pursuits, you now yield to my judgment at the command of diligence, as much as you have submitted of your own right, so much will you possess of my services.

Farewell, therefore, my lord, and accept the little gift I send—not measured by its own cheapness, but by the value assigned to it by the sender.

## LETTER XXVIII. ENNODIUS TO EUPREPIA

[Col. 0067D]

Although I had received the page of your love attended only by customary services, and not corresponding to affection or relationship, circumstances nevertheless demanded that I answer your conversations with reciprocal diligence through the likeness of my pen, lest the service of withheld speech reveal not that I had recognized your cunning, but our own childishness.

I do not want you, sister Euprepia, to complain about the misfortunes of the provinces or, as you said, about the intrusion of men. Wherever you have withdrawn, as the matter itself shows, you do not leave behind a mind prone to believe evil; we do not escape our vices by changing regions.

Toward your relatives you had this disposition: neither to weigh their good deeds with a fair interpretation nor to correct their excesses with merely the condemnation they deserved. But what need is there to make a letter of pain longer? No abundance of eloquence can change your character.

For the rest, farewell, my lady, and arrange the order of your life and spirit as is fitting. Know, however, that I shall spend on Lupicinus not what I owe you, but what is suitable to my own soul; for affection alone, when entrusted without being provoked by any human qualities, deserves a greater recompense from God.

## LETTER XXIX. ENNODIUS TO EUGENETUS

Whenever words serve as pledges of the senses, speech paints for itself on the pages, as in a certain mirror, a friendly image with which it converses in a living voice and rejoices while the sweet likeness attends to its desires.

No abundance of speech can express the conception of a united heart; and although words are easier than deeds, and nothing exists that cannot grow through the ambition of speaking, I testify to a barren childishness in expressing my attentiveness toward you.

Nevertheless, I reproach your unanimity for its silence, because, after being honored with a double letter, you thought of nothing concerning a reciprocal report. Behold, I send pages again, knowing that I am giving what I expect.

Farewell, my lord, and address one who loves you with the brilliance in which you are distinguished; cherish him with the integrity in which you prevail.

## LETTER XXX. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

I am amazed that unpleasant things are joined to the honey of your greatness, and that the serenity of your conscience is stained by the austerity of your words, when you write that I command pages rather than earn them through demanding diligence; thinking that no form of domination is more exalted than that which subjects us to love.

[Note: “Any?” Or should it be read “no kind”?]

There are no heights, lord Avienus, exempt from the yoke of love; whatever freedom exists in the world is not withdrawn from such servitude. Behold, I, unknown to honors and in the place of a humble man, shall command your fasces in such a way that I am content to be subject to them in equal order.

Now farewell, and as much as you have perceived has been granted to you, so much affection, as a faithful restorer, bestow upon me.

## LETTER XXXI. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

Although the quality of letters is composed according to the abilities of their authors, and often serves convention, sometimes bears witness to signs of affection, and is at times dictated by sincerity, it is for the most part an arrangement resembling cosmetics. It makes itself known by the courtesy beneath which it is concealed, imagining the brightness of diligence; once stripped of its fabricated coverings, it is revealed within its veil.

I nevertheless think that the pages are a mirror of the conscience, through which absence scarcely dares to discern friendship. It is clear, however, what simple speech and what artful speech convey in them. The mind, interpreter of the dictation, cuts through the clouds of eloquence; it quickly reaches understanding, opening a path with the sickles of its words.

Therefore, I take great pleasure in those services through which sincerity is disclosed and no opportunity for safe deception inserts itself. Yet I rejoice that I have either reasons for writing or bearers to send, so that through this frequency I may satisfy my desire and burden your modesty, unless what you have received is returned by you.

Hail, my lord, and yield to my judgment under the command of affection. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXII. ENNODIUS TO PASSIVUS

If speech were sufficient to carry out affection, if childishness could explain the whole of love, to whom more than to you would we offer the frequency of our pages? And unless the merit of your heart restrained us, for no one would the service of speech more worthily labor.

Some testify with their mouths to an affection they do not know in their minds, and paint moments of correspondence with the alluring exchanges of letters, when, the innermost chambers being idle, all love is on the tongue, and nothing is brought to the interior except what is supplied in writing.

But my spirit toward you, pressed by the poverty of eloquence, has fallen silent amid the abundance of friendship. For I fear that impoverished conversation may set a limit to favor, and that the same measure may be thought to belong both to speech and to the bond. It is better to leave more to esteem through silence than to display, through letters, the losses of diligence.

Behold, I have given the reasons for our rarer conversation, believing that with you the eloquence demanded by sincerity is placed second. For the rest, farewell, my lord, and, making use of divine benefits, fulfill the heavenly commands as life advances into length. For when kindness has begun from a heap, it finds increase with you. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIII. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

The pages serve the purpose by which commendation is offered to the afflicted. In them the integrity of religion is clear: without flattering the powerful through any disguise, they assert the tears of the humble.

But more on this another time; when you see the bearer, you will recognize the wish of the one dictating. May he obtain with your greatness the outcome of his supplication, so that the plea by which he secured a letter from me may win favor.

The foregoing speech introduces a religious woman, poor and relying upon a good cause. Consider whether words ought to have been withheld from weakness or from justice; whether it was fitting for me either to fail in duty or in character.

Behold, while offering the reverence due in greeting, I have testified to what I owed to my part. Consider what remains for you, since just as the request looks to my person on behalf of the woman mentioned above, so affection will look to yours. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIV. ENNODIUS TO SENARIUS

[Col. 0070B]

There is indeed nothing that is not raised aloft from truth by ambitious eloquence. But, in attending to you, I suffer my own childishness of speech. The tongue has never been equal to love; the service of the mouth has always been subordinate to a good conscience.

For this reason I make use of the security of a monitor. I did not believe that your greatness would remain forgetful of me for so long that you would even abstain from customary conversations, so that those forms of greeting which usually feign affection with an imagined expression would be denied between persons bound by chains of fellowship.

If I could tell these things, I could endure them. Behold, I write again, and I testify by examples that what I assert in words must be followed. You will judge how it is from now on to neglect honorable desires; I, trained by habit to patience in sorrow, shall apply patience. Farewell.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0069]

## LETTER ONE. ENNODIUS TO POPE SYMMACHUS

[Note: “To Pope Symmachus.” Ennodius appears to have been the first to assert the title *papa* as proper and peculiar to the one Roman pontiff. For while nearly all others who lived close to his age usually call all bishops *papas*, as Sidonius, Faustus, and Ruricius do, Ennodius consistently calls the leaders of the other Churches bishops, reserving *pope* for the pontiff of the Roman see. He does so both when writing to him—“to Pope Symmachus” and “to the lord pope”—and when speaking of him to others, as in Book III, Letter 10, Book VI, Letter 33, and elsewhere.

After Ennodius, Cassiodorus used the same distinction in applying this word: while he calls Boniface, Agapetus, and John, the pontiffs of the Roman see, popes, he calls Eustorgius and Datius of Milan, and the leaders of other cities, nothing other than bishops.

Not everyone subsequently followed this example, however; many writers of different nations, especially outside Italy, applied the title *pope* to other bishops as well, down to the time of Gregory VII, who, as Cardinal Baronius observes, first decreed at a Roman synod that the title *pope* should belong to one person alone in the Christian world.]

[Col. 0069C]

It is the mark of a good emperor to encourage the proven courage of a soldier in battle, so that courage, invited by the nourishment of praise, may in later engagements unlearn its attachment to life. Whose strength is not nourished by a leader’s commendation? In what conflicts would even the weaker limbs of a recruit refuse themselves, when by the ruler’s testimony he sees that what he has done is not lost to him? This is the sole path by which zeal for fighting increases: whenever oblivion does not efface deeds well done. Would that the deity, moved by your prayers, might destroy [Note: [Col. 0070D] *The diabolical contest*] the diabolical contest of the schismatic faction of Laurentius, which attacked Symmachus in various ways! Would that it might reveal my devotion in peace, so that concord may commend the service of him whose zeal adversity has disclosed. To [Col. 0070C] [Note: [Col. 0070D] *To Marcellinus, bishop*] Marcellinus, bishop of Aquileia. Laurentius, bishop of Milan, had written to him on Symmachus’s behalf; I think that he is the person meant by Ennodius.] Marcellianus, bishop, your brother sent an equipped embassy; but he himself has written back what it achieved. For the rest, having rendered the offices of greeting, I ask that you heal by medicinal prayer whatever is sick and, amid the hidden recesses of diseases, cut away with the spiritual sword the error reserved for general destruction. Farewell.

## LETTER II. ENNODIUS TO ALICO

The venerable priest Amantius, while seeking pages to send to you, made the business of my devotion the object of his authority. Happy is the necessity that renders service to one’s wishes; free is the command of a superior that submits itself to affection. The man who compelled me owes me thanks for having fulfilled my desire. The writing is propitious that bears a double testimony to love: while it draws a new acquaintance into the rights of friendship and binds the heart of an older friend. Since he is the faithful herald of your greatness, through his endorsement he caused you to be chosen before you were known. Rarely has affection preceded knowledge: who has ever had the good fortune to please before being seen?

Observe what weight the bearer has with me, at whose nod our judgments are bent. We have seen the man whom he has come to know; the man whom he praises, we embrace. Often a mind firmly established yields its own judgment to the scrutiny of a friend. Rightly, then, we esteem those whom an approved man exalts.

Now, if the richness of grace could unfold the poverty of my talent; if childish speech, dried up at the fountain of the covenant, were not wearied by the parchedness of my language; if the quality of a letter—which imposes restraints even upon abundant eloquence—allowed me to proceed at greater length, I would assert how much your nobility owes me, since I was the first to approach an exchange of letters with you and to open the door of friendship with the key of speech. Nevertheless, I ask that the bearer be loved in return for what he has offered. I commend the interests of the Church, because whatever is spent on my hope increases your merit.

My lord, while offering the gift of the most abundant greeting, I ask that, if you are willing to receive my offering as a libation of charity, you open the devotion of a friendly conscience through conversation.

## LETTER III. ENNODIUS TO EULALIUS, BISHOP

Thanks be to the Trinity, our God, who through the vigorous zeal of a strong man sustains before himself the burden of sins by which I, a sinner, am weighed down; who inserts the memory of me into that holy temple of your heart in which Christ rejoices, as a subtle craftsman, so that what I have darkened with the cloud of self-preservation he may wipe away with the bright serenity of conscience.

Now I know that the lamentations of sinners are not poured out ineffectually. In the first place, my prayer and my tears have brought me this: that you should rise as a strong intercessor for me, and that, when my shoulders were giving way, you should substitute your right hand, fortified by heavenly aid. It is true that despair alone destroys the sinner before God.

Behold, our tares, thorns or thistles promise barley, wheat, and vines. Come, chosen one of God, continue for me, a humble man, what you have begun; stand by your charge, while by the constancy of your prayers you wash away in me what I have gathered through the abundance of my faults. Feed me also with frequent conversations, so that you may strengthen a tasteless heart, supported by no stability of virtues, with the salt of admonition.

I return to the duties of greeting and, having passed beyond the epistolary boundary, add one thing like a chatterbox, though importunate because of my needs: help me continually with prayers as much as you strengthen me with conversation. Farewell.

## LETTER IV. MODEL OF A LETTER WHICH HE HIMSELF DICTATED. BROTHER TO SISTER

Although some people may owe at least a summary measure of favor even to wicked offspring, and the benefit bestowed upon posterity ought not to be considered a debt; although a malicious interpreter subordinates the judgment of the heart to the commands of nature, and, removing the savor of devotion, thinks that one ought to live solely by the claim of having begotten; when greater value is given to the name “son” than to obedience, and it is not asked what you advance in the balance of love but what name you set against the judgment of the evaluator as a prejudice; among the prudent we rightly call someone offspring in vain unless he displays what he is called.

For whoever neglects moral judgment in a child shows that he is more pleased with conception than with merit. Let it be banished from posterity that we should think only of what has pleased us. Indeed, the fruit of the womb, unless it answers with uprightness, seems to have arisen more as evidence of wantonness than of favor.

It is right that the faithful fellowship of brotherhood should always be preferred even to children. One may be regarded as sharing the same origin in such a way that consideration of blood is not neglected, while the judgment descending from merit is praised. And therefore, so that words may not proceed at length through winding introductory speeches, and so that what is narrow in substance may expand through expression, I grant to your brotherhood and transfer to your right, with perpetual generosity, that slave belonging to my legal possession, and so forth. Farewell.

## LETTER V. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

The eminent man Dalmatius, a portion of my soul not diminished but complete, to whose prerogative of blood the splendor of character has been added, judged that his business would be advanced if he were assisted by my addresses to your highness. I did not think I ought to neglect this, being aware that, through a certain courtesy, I was attributing to the person what I know you owe to justice.

In Sicily, it is alleged, the estate of the aforesaid man, hitherto possessed under good legal title, has been seized by his co-owners. Whatever I may advance by entreaty is now being devoted to the aid of civic justice.

My lord, while paying the duties of greeting with complete humility, I beg you to protect, in the interests of the noble man mentioned above, modesty, the laws, and the other ornaments of the commonwealth that endure through your conscience. Farewell.

## LETTER VI. ENNODIUS TO AGAPITUS

I believed that, after your greatness had been expended upon the common good, and leisure had passed into glory; after, occupied with the watches of Ravenna, while you neglected your own rest, you strengthened ours with every firmness; and after a private genius had passed into the adornments of the kingdom—when the Palatine splendor had added to itself a new light drawn from domestic chambers, and the master of affairs had rightly measured that the pomp of his kingdom had been narrower when he did not have you—I believed that, because of the proximity of our regions, I ought to be refreshed by frequent conversations.

But my sins have mocked the counsels of my hope with ineffectual designs; no serene mind sends pages as a testimony of devotion. It is grievous if I have not deserved love; more grievous if I have perhaps disturbed one whom I had summoned. Yet I know that these matters must be enclosed beneath clouds of excuses corresponding to the truth. The gifts of letters are found among private persons; such things are not rightly demanded of the occupied.

But I know that a conscience firm in affection, amid every burden and adversity, does not deny its owed obligations to grace. Now I do not wish to be extravagant in complaints. Having paid the reverence of greeting, I ask that you bring to a desired conclusion the request which the bearer of this letter has laid before you.

## LETTER VII. ENNODIUS TO JULIANUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, COUNT OF THE SACRED PATRIMONY

[Note: [Col. 0073D] *To Julianus, V. I. C. P.* That is, to an illustrious man, count of the patrimony. Since the Basilian scribes did not understand this monogram, they addressed it to Julianus the bishop. But the true reading, which I have restored from the Vatican, is the one given here. This is Julianus, count of the patrimony, to whom there is a rescript of King Theoderic in *Book I of the Variae*, letter 15; Ennodius alludes to him when he names his purple. What the office of the *Comitiva sacri patrimonii* was is explained by Cassiodorus in its official formula in *Book VI*, and by our legal Glosses, which make Anastasius Augustus the first author of this dignity. They read as follows: **Πατριμονιάλια· ὅσα ἕκαστος βασιλεὺς ἑαυτῷ κτᾶται· ὑπὸ βασιλέως Ἀναστασίου· αὐτὸς γάρ ἐστιν ὁ ἐξευρὼν καὶ τὴν προσηγορίαν ταύτην, καὶ τὴν ἀρχὴν τοῦ κόμιτος τοῦ πατριμονίου.** — “Patrimonial matters: whatever each emperor acquires for himself; [the office was established] under the emperor Anastasius. For he himself was the one who discovered both this designation and the office of the count of the patrimony.”] JULIANUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, COUNT OF THE PATRIMONY

[Col. 0073A]

I received a letter radiant with a double splendor, in which your purple, joined to your dignity, increased in value. I give thanks to almighty God, who surpasses the meagerness of wishes with the abundance of his gift, so that, when conscious of our merits, we pursue narrowness in our desires, he may not restrain the resources of his rich indulgence.

I thought it enough if you made me eminent by a most ample letter. But you, not content merely to provide what a beggar’s petition possesses, send pages worthy of your speech and enriched with praise: like a great river which, whenever it is invited away from its channels to temper the dryness of the neighboring land, flows wholly into the oblique course, and pours its water over the parched backs of the thirsty earth, drunk with the depth of its life-giving stream.

Yet, preserving the custom appropriate to strong men, may your greatness not abandon what it has begun well toward my insignificance, so that written care may be present as a testimony of devotion and the blandishments of conversation may convey the endorsement of pure love. May the affection which you promised before your exalted rank know no setting. May grace toward me increase as the heights of your dignities remain unconquered, lest power appear to have renounced the friendship which mediocrity nurtured.

For whoever curbs pride in exalted station shows that he has deserved what he has attained. Show by the integrity of your conscience that happiness can submit to the commands of love. While you grant form to those free necks of the nobles, subject them to devotion. Let it be permissible to grow accustomed to you in such a way that the greatest retains in his fellowship the one whom the lesser acquires.

Fortune mocks those to whom it points out the forgetfulness of their own people when it brings them to lofty positions. For one who knows how to recognize good things, recalling them is not a necessity of admonition but an occasion for praise. I know that the tranquility of your talent has been fashioned for good pursuits. I mention this particularly so that I may show that, where affection is solid, honors have no power.

But I have passed beyond the epistolary boundary by lingering too long over my commendation. I return to the duties of written conversation and, announcing that I am well, promptly ask about the favorable state of your prosperity.

## LETTER VIII. ENNODIUS TO SYMMACHUS, POPE

You have advanced me through apostolic favor almost to presumption; the confidence granted became the mother of boldness. [Col. 0073D] But he who thinks me ignorant of humility will prove me obedient if he considers your commands. It is presumption if servants do not follow the benefits of their masters. I think that the obedience I offer in anticipation of compliance should be valued.

Behold, I have stated the reason for writing: I feared that, after your command concerning the care of my pen, I might reject your instructions by remaining silent. Added to this was the fact that, in the case of Marius, of venerable memory, when I was in Rome, you gave hope to my prayers. His affair was settled with your holy Church by a lawful agreement; but his heirs lament that for many years the revenues owed to them have been withheld.

On their behalf I approach as a petitioner conscious of your character, because he whose custom it is continually to do what is pious will not despise what is just; and he who gives what is his own will not withhold what belongs to another. He errs who believes that a conscience close to God is enticed by advantages. It is harmful to a holy will not to bestow a benefit. You consider as profit only what arises for you from generosity, since, while you give riches, you receive them.

The stewardship of holy men is miserly in that, reserving nothing, it turns everything back into its own merit. No gains are more valuable than the benefits that accrue to you from generosity. Therefore, confident in what I have set forth above, I have promised the heirs compensation for their loss through your consideration. Complete my promise by your kindly disposition, and relieve them by your action and me by your conversation.

## LETTER IX. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

Epistolary elegance, whenever it is carried away by favor, is accustomed not to love judgment and to make a benefit more abundant by exalting the undeserving. For the person commended owes more to the writer when, through the writer’s favor, he obtains what his character does not demand; since, aided by none of the gifts of conscience, he rightly credits the advocate with whatever he achieves.

It is one thing, in the person being commended as a noble shoot, to weave foreign virtues into one’s words; it is another to make innate qualities common property. It would be as though you confirmed that rustic livestock was naturally clothed in Tyrian purple, or said that noble dye, which no fleece had absorbed while intoxicated by Abenian [uncertain] dye, was spreading through the fields.

Others dye with the purple of their tongue things upon which no pigment suitable for royal use has been bestowed, and wool that has absorbed only the light of eloquence from shells of the unrecognized sea. Whatever the words of the reporter have colored in a lowly service is made worthy of princely garments.

But both my abilities and my wishes withdraw me from this kind of courtesy. No breath of brilliant embellishment will gleam through me with borrowed splendor. No one will find in my statement about anyone anything that he does not recognize in that person’s actions.

For this reason I extend a hand to my modesty and purpose: I offer the service of my speech in advance to one who comes before your notice through well-accomplished deeds. I speak of Venantius, an illustrious man. For this reason he has obtained from me the service of a written recommendation: that he might draw the eyes of your greatness upon himself and not be overlooked amid the burden of your cares.

He has his own recommendations by which he may deserve to be counted among those whom you have received. He has displayed before you modesty, religion, and innocence, by which he might enter the inner chambers of a tranquil mind accompanied by these virtues.
