Believe me, the distinctions you cherish abound in him. You will not find me to have been his eulogist so much as his witness.

My lord, grant the bearer your favor in the first place, lest a good man be disturbed by novelty. He will clearly attend to his own interests and compensate by the resources of his life for the deficiencies of my words.

## LETTER X. ENNODIUS TO THRASAMUND, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

[Note: [Col. 0075D] *To Thrasamund, an illustrious man.* To the king of the Vandals in Africa. He calls the king an illustrious man because in the Roman Empire no title was more honorable than “illustrious”; for that reason they bestowed it upon kings. Traces of this ancient custom remain today in papal diplomas, in which kings are called illustrious men. Indeed, the kings themselves added this title to their names. For in the ancient decrees and constitutions of our kings nothing is more common than “Childebert, Clotaire, Pippin, Charles, king, illustrious man.”

As for the name of this Vandal king, who succeeded his brother Huneric, it is written in various ways by different authors. He is called **THRASAMUNDUS** in the acrostic of an old epigram published by P. Pithou in Book II. Although it has been corrupted through the fault of antiquarians, I shall not hesitate to reproduce it, both because of its hitherto undetected artistry and because, having been written with the king’s own name and placed beside the baths he built, it seems to indicate more certainly how this name was then written. It is as follows:

> Flow gently, nymphs, from the river’s tranquil source.  
> Here the worthy [reading uncertain] succeeds with blazing wicker; I weep,  
> Where now peaks rise upon lofty rocks,  
> And high-raised baths are matched with heaven in their roofs.  
> Here marbles blaze with great images;  
> The lofty baths surpass the soaring summits.  
> And their outstanding author gives gifts of so great a light,  
> Foreknowing the rewards of unbroken fame for one man.  
> Here the flame shall not harm [reading uncertain]; then learn the song;  
> Learn also how great a water lives beneath the pool.  
> Here he renews the bright Vandal name from its seed,  
> Beneath whose title favor stands by meritorious deeds.]

TRASIMUNDUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

It was not presumption that led me to the service of writing, since every royal scion invites his subject to fellowship with him. Such brilliance is woven into the birth of lords that they raise their subjects by their own favor. You wish to treat servants as though they were equals, so that through love they may owe you even more than their condition itself.

Accordingly, most pious lord, while offering the service that must be rendered to all, I announce that I have sent the bearer of this letter to present certain petitions. Grant the suppliant his request, because I have approached you as a petitioner supported by hope.

## LETTER XI. ENNODIUS TO LUMINOSUS

[Col. 0075B]

He who reveals a friendly conscience through evident signs removes leisure from those to whom he has granted favor. For scarcely can the lips of one accustomed to be heard remain idle, since it is a great loss of modesty to withhold the benefit of words, so that, while we spare the tongue, the forehead labors prodigal of good faith.

You have made me talkative, since you have been accustomed to admit my prayers. But lest I circle around what must be granted and delay the petition by the length of my letter, I return to the matter.

The eminent man Laurentius asserts that revenues owed to him, which the Roman Church promised by an agreement made with its author, are being denied by the lord pope under some unknown objection. In this matter he implores the favor of your protection through me, so that you may appear to offer what you owe by the laws, and that what cannot be denied to equity may increase in affection.

Grant me this matter according to my wishes, so that, whatever advantage comes to the man named, I may confess to have received an equal gift. I therefore offer greetings and hope that, in the duties of letters, neither sincere love will accept leave nor eloquence celebrated by the testimony of the whole world will fall silent.

## LETTER XII. ENNODIUS TO JOHN

It is natural that grief should pass into joy and complaint be changed into praise whenever desired things are granted. I was uncertain what your greatness’s long cessation signified; but when one is allowed to obtain what one desires, I myself search on your behalf for an honorable kind of excuse.

See what the serenity of affection can do. As though everything had flowed for me according to my wish, I have been appeased by a simple gift and have forgiven your errors. You have the means to assume the form of pious love and to borrow examples of constancy toward friendship.

If you follow me, no number of offenses will hold you back from our union, and one benefit from your companion will absolve your faults. Do you attack me, brother, with silence, with forgetfulness? Where was this disposition when not even published conversations deserved a reply, and you did not precede me in the care of commanding the pen? Where was the unrestrained exchange of letters that has not been maintained toward everyone in Liguria?

While many people were traveling far from your desire, you offered them pages as a consolation for their sorrow, yet you prolonged silence toward me and granted them conversation contrary to my wishes. For such is the order of human affairs: that, in place of great kinship, equal devotion should always be present.

Mindful of none of this order, you wished to join certain unskilled matters with letters, thinking that things distant by the whole road could come together in affection. What did your persuasive speech accomplish, fashioned from laboriously polished phrases, when it addressed those ignorant of the liberal arts while leaving the lover behind?

But enough of this for now. I do not wish to reread the multitude of your excesses, since I have been soothed by a brief satisfaction. I had used restraint in recounting them because I thought you knew that, of offenses, what is concealed remains, whereas what bursts into speech is removed.

My lord, I ask you henceforth not to aspire to the things you have learned to treat badly as though you despised correction, but frequently to send me sweet pages, so that the dowry of eloquence may grow while it preserves the pledge of concord.

## LETTER XIII. ENNODIUS TO CONSTANTIUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

Your greatness preserves toward friends and its own secular associates what it joins to itself for glory. For while you consider us worthy of remembrance, you prove yourselves worthy.

For a long time I have received writings as a consolation and sigh over the losses caused by your absence. O skillful knowledge established in heavenly goods! So that prolonged separation may not be permitted to tear anything from affection, you send forth letters presenting a sacred image.

God, the examiner of thoughts, knows that I am consumed by remembrance of your eminence and find no support in the exile of the excellent man. Nevertheless, I return the service of greeting through epistolary care, and, repaying your favor, I also confess that through you my brother John has been restored to me. His silence, which until now said what his forgetfulness of me was doing, has now been transformed by your affection toward me and returns to the abandoned care of the pen.

I nevertheless ask you to hasten your return—or, if a fortunate delay holds you, to reveal your affection through conversation.

## LETTER XIV. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

Whatever is often expended with only moderate gratitude, whenever words are offered to those joined by kinship, let everything that has obeyed favor be devoted to serene affection. He does not falsely portray love through embellished addresses who entrusts writings to be returned to a beloved bearer by the lords.

In commending the eminent and magnificent man Panfronius, my mind dictates a letter while my mouth is at rest. For I do not know to what height I should raise the merits of the man I have mentioned, in whom the poverty of my tongue cannot express what my heart owes.

But even if it were available, I ought to renounce the allurements of eloquence, because poor speech more correctly acknowledges abundant devotion; and if through effusive pages we exalt those whose inner qualities we do not know, then a brief tablet rightly contains what is to be granted to those who love.

Having therefore explained the reason for my restrained speech, I introduce my allied brother in a few words but with many services, so that, aided by your greatness, he may appear at last to have overcome in his business the schemes of those who beset him.

For the rest, offering the service of a subordinate’s greeting, I announce that I am well, if indeed heavenly providence grants me prosperity through sure signs.

## LETTER XV. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

[Col. 0077C]

The path to obtaining a request is easier whenever the humility of a suppliant asks something from a religious man. For one who is moved by the misery of a petitioner offers his affection under compulsion; he whose purpose commands him to hear the afflicted cannot fail to extend his hands in welcome.

The bearer of this letter laments that he has been cast down from his ancestral estate and places what remains of his hope in your judgment, lest the power of his adversary rejoice in gain and security. You are concerned with the oaths of the laws; you are concerned with the defense of the humble. I have fortified my part through recommendation.

Therefore increase the honor of your venerable name by benefits. For while you grant what is just, do not put aside what belongs to mercy. My lord, accept the reverence of my greeting and grant my prayers such effect that, while honesty is upheld, his proper desire may be fulfilled.

## LETTER XVI. ENNODIUS TO AGAPITUS

[Col. 0078A]

A reply would rightly be demanded through many conversations if your greatness’s silence did not testify that my pages had been unwelcome. For your silence cries out that you dislike a chatterbox, and, as I think, seeks a new kind of vengeance, since it sees that what it has kept silent has not advanced.

You practice abstinence from letters so that writings may not be sent to you by the unskilled. Yet the result has been removed: consider what may benefit your foresight. I have become more frequent because I have been despised in writing. But brief speech ought to restrain the one who has suffered great grief.

My brother Paufronius, your devoted servant, is accompanied by the care of a letter addressed to your highness. Whatever favor is granted to him will bind me also in the bonds of what has been done. I have also entrusted him with presenting certain matters concerning the office of vicarius.

Bring my petition to completion, because I am present in my own interests whenever I am compelled to submit testimony before the most upright of men while I offer precise evidence.

## LETTER XVII. ENNODIUS TO DECORATUS

[Note: [Col. 0077D] *To Decoratus.* He was the elder brother of Honoratus, as stated at Letter 28 of Book II: a noble pair of brothers who were advocates and, from advocacy, quaestors. King Theoderic says much about the merits of both in *Book V of the Variae*, letters 3 and 4, to Honoratus. “You, Decoratus,” he says, “are from him; he, Honoratus, is from you.”

Likewise, concerning Decoratus’s quaestorship: “Thus Decoratus advanced under such an omen; he advanced, I say, and, praised by our judgment, entered into the Palatine honors, assuming the dignity which we customarily give to the prudent.” But when Ennodius wrote to him, he was not yet quaestor.

His epitaph testifies that he was buried in a humble tomb. It is read among the Christian monuments in these words:

> Decoratus sought this refuge when the light had been withdrawn,  
> So that he might lay his limbs in a modest place.  
> Hence, O Spoleto, you grieve; hence, traveler, you suffer loss,  
> Seeking in vain who might bring aid.  
> For he granted rest to the weary and relieved the wretched.  
> A worshiper of justice, he was generous and hospitable.  
> Distinguished by the fasces, he was not inferior in the distinction of his lineage.  
> Here he was the light of his fatherland, here its every glory.

By “fasces” he means the quaestorship mentioned above. He recalls the people of Spoleto because he had pleaded cases in their tribunal, as Honoratus later did, according to Cassiodorus, who records the matter there.]

It is rightly believed that the tongue is the revealer of the inner chambers, which summons the secrets of the hidden soul into the light through speech. The love of hearts would be unknown unless a revealer disclosed it. The wisdom of the ancients rightly used letters as keys and made the affection stored within them public.

The mind that has testified to devotion has been drawn into the testimony of writing. It was not permitted to alter the love which, in a page expressing desire, had made a promise. I have devoted myself to this custom—or rather, to this law—asserting through the fidelity of letters what has grown in my thoughts concerning your greatness.

If you meet me with equal care in the binding of our relationship; if faithful friendship, judging itself to be an interpreter, sees the wish of the other, let a reply on a tablet make this known. For my part, while distributing the gifts of greeting, I have not hidden my decision as though I were miserly with words.

## LETTER XVIII. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

In asserting matters to which full honesty does not deny its support, I do not use many addresses, lest lengthy speech appear to have obtained a benefit from one who was about to refuse it. For you are accustomed to place before prayers whatever ought to be requested.

To the eminent and magnificent man Opilio, his parents, residing in Africa, sent a trustworthy person, prompted by devotion. When he returned to his ancestral soil, the aforesaid man entrusted me with this service: that a letter from you might be obtained for the magnificent man [Note: [Col. 0078D] *Agnellus.* King Theoderic to the patrician Festus: “Therefore we decree that the house of the patrician Agnellus, who is departing for Africa and, seeking another kingdom, is about to serve our interests, be protected by your guardianship, with the laws preserved.” *Book I of the Variae*, 15.] Agnellus, in commendation of his family.

You will not deny this matter, as the most upright of men, unwilling that only those situated in Italy should have recognized your benevolence. Now, returning my services in writing, I have indicated the reason for my letter in a few words. Grant the speaker of few words something distinguished.

## LETTER XIX. ENNODIUS TO APOLLINARIS

By prolonging your silence toward one who loves you, you transferred my mind to bodily absence. By withholding your pages, what had previously mattered little—the separation—has grown immeasurably. Through your abstinence from letters, matters have reached the point that the foresight of an earlier age contributes nothing to love.

Love has grown stale, when one who is sparing of words disdains to stir it. Devotion not brought into use through pages lacks cultivation. The frequent use of the pen nourishes the friendship planted in our hearts with living sustenance.

Brother, it would have been easier for you never to grant my desires than often to withdraw what you had granted, because hearts do not know what it is that, as a skillful shepherd, you have stirred with sweet nourishment. For some time, by continuing your writing, you had made me forget your separation, while you inserted your venerable image into peaceful conversation. But now I inspect, as a naked investigator, the empty hands of those who travel to and fro.

Nevertheless, I do not wish to assert the faults of others through my own error, lest I be convicted of having committed what I lament. Therefore, most upright of men, receive the consolations of desire, granted to the absent by heavenly grace, and support the bearers, if you remember me, so that they may not know the hardships of travel, while friendly recommendation has brought the homeland to those named.

When they return, relieve me by reporting your good health.

## LETTER XX. ENNODIUS TO JULIANUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

The good of devotion is exercised through repeated writing, for the secrets of minds are disclosed by the testimony of the tongue. He devotes care through constant speech who exchanges leisure for love. These are the services by which affection, though silent, becomes known.

A familiar bearer, unless he had received pages to return to your highness, would testify that I had forgotten your reverence. For I do not know how to be negligent of love, nor how, by serving quiet, to escape the grace acquired through labor.

I owe many words to our bond, but the letter compels brevity. Farewell, my lord, accepting the honor of my greeting, and preserve toward me a favor that has grown with time. Thus, having been called into the public service for the good, you may rejoice in the lasting duration of your happiness.

## LETTER XXI. ENNODIUS TO CONSTANTIUS, BISHOP

Your subdeacon Vigilius wished to discover how much affection would be returned to me by you. Taking his departure as an opportunity, he attempted to bring our relationship forward and wishes to measure the state of our friendship by its increase in honors, so that the benefit we have stored from the harvest of devotion may return to him.

If I deserve this, bring him to the sacred office of the diaconate, so that the dignity of the man mentioned may advance me toward the hope of requesting greater things. But lest the petition, if refused, be frustrated in its effect, may you hold for long ages the place granted by your merits.

## LETTER XXII. ENNODIUS TO SYMMACHUS, POPE

Although the eminent Laurentius is supported by his own integrity in commending his children, and the prudence of the father pursues the interests of his offspring, nevertheless paternal concern proceeds to greater things and scarcely believes that what he deserves is sufficient for his sons.

He seeks a written endorsement to assist his offspring and, with anxious devotion, strives to share the ardor of parents with all. Consider whether effect could be denied to an excellent man asking what is pious and just. May God grant effect to his prayers and deign to procure for the persons named this favor of your blessedness, so that the mercy of your invoked crown may raise up the little ones and surpass their anxious father's wishes concerning them.

My lord, I hope that the benevolence promised long ago will bear witness in this matter, if he who petitions through me understands that I have bestowed a double favor on those mentioned above.

## LETTER XXIII. ENNODIUS TO DOMINATOR

Your desires, which the plea of your brother Agnellus disclosed, ought indeed to have been disclosed by a letter, and a preliminary discourse ought to have provided the form for drawing forth further conversation. For what you owed could have been restored to you, and, while you were speaking, I could not have defended myself by any pretext for abstaining from writing.

It was within your right to exchange the holidays of our tongue for exercise and to remove the rust of rustic speech through the craftsman’s labors of writing. Just as it is a loss to affection not to devote speech first to one who desires it, so to return silence to writing that has been published is advised neither by the memory of friendship nor by modesty.

Now, however, you have commanded pages from my disposition; and, though testimony is withheld, I never question my strength in love. Let it be banished from liberal minds to believe that the burden imposed by a friend is intolerable. You should embrace only what has been demanded and, checking criticism, lay aside the stale distastes of those who judge.

Far be it from you not to cherish one who has obeyed. Even if he comes from a trivial coinage, he is drawn toward the hope of higher merit because he has devoted to you the service of speech that was imposed upon him.

Therefore farewell, my lord. I do not wish to become prolix in conversations that have not been fashioned with exact precision. Restore the harvest of grace to me according to my confidence, as fertile soil restores it, since henceforth it will be within your discretion, if you wish to receive my letters frequently, to invite me by such gifts.

## LETTER XXIV. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

A troubled mind, just as it cannot endure silence, so renounces the progress of narration. Neither silence nor lengthy conversation suits a protest of grief. The page is compressed, and scarcely can words be granted amid groans.

But why do I assert that the tongue is taking a holiday by speaking more, and promise in chatter to bring a letter, compelled by necessity, to its proper limits? I beseech God to come to the aid of my anxiety through a clear sign of your prosperity. May he admit my tears, to whom closed lips speak; to whom, for a full embassy, the rain of eyes flowing from remorse is sufficient.

I recognize that not only my peace but also my well-being has been shaken by the condition of enemies and the storms of rumors. The divinity is powerful enough to remove the uncertainties of an immense tempest through the goodness of serenity.

If I deserve anything from God, be well. For one who loves you, take care of my conscience through the publication of letters, not through the watches of Ravenna.

## LETTER XXV. ENNODIUS TO BASSUS

[Note: [Col. 0081C] *To Bassus.* He called him a Gaul in Letter 20 of Book I; Bassus had an ancient relationship with the parents of Ennodius.]

BASSUS.

If the former devotion which my parents showed toward your eminence, gathering rich fruits from the harvest of favor, were preserved toward my person in remembrance of their loyalty, the frequency of my letters would demonstrate it, and the speech of a faithful heart would bring our unburied affection to light. But now I feel that you have forgotten me and retain no fellowship with the better age, since no letters are sent that might disclose your concern. Yet I have turned the impatience of my longing into words; for I know that a new friendship has sweetness only if it is preserved through the years, and that what our elders have tested is purer in affection. Knowing that [Note: “If you retain Camillus in your thoughts”] “You who loved the father will not reject the son.” Ennodius’s father, therefore, was Camillus. We now know that Ennodius’s parents were Gauls from the province of Narbonensis, and that almost all his family had its ancestral home there. On these grounds, together with the conjecture suggested by the names of the two Ennodiuses, I am led to suppose that Camillus, his father, was the very man whom Sidonius, in a poem addressed to Felix, calls his most distinguished cousin. For Felix was the son of Magnus, and Camillus, the father of Ennodius, was Magnus’s brother. The same Sidonius, in his description of the Arlesian banquet, Book I, Letter 11, writes: “With Camillus, the son of his brother, reclining behind him”—that is, behind Magnus the former consul—“who, after himself completing two offices, had likewise adorned his father’s proconsulate and his uncle’s consulship.” Thus Felix and Camillus were first cousins, born of brothers. And Camillus’s son, as I conjecture, was our Ennodius, who derived the names Magnus and Felix from his great-uncle and his latter’s son. But this is merely my conjecture.] If you retain Camillus in your thoughts, you will not omit Ennodius. Therefore, performing the duty of greeting with epistolary care, I ask that you deign to receive kindly the bearer of this letter, my cleric, whom his own needs and my command have brought to Gaul. When he returns, mark the occasion with favorable writing from you, so that, if forgetfulness has caused any loss in our affection, epistolary solicitude may restore it.

## LETTER XXVI. ENNODIUS TO EUGENETUS, VIR ILLUSTRIS

[Note: To Eugenetus, vir illustris, quaestor of the palace of King Theoderic. He congratulates him on this office, which he also mentioned in Poem 2, written about Eugenetus himself:

> “The voice of a just quaestor, the substance of the laws,  
> As though Phoebus were sending us poems, plectrums, and lyres.”

He later became master of the offices, as may be seen in Book I of the *Variae*, Letters 12 and 13, where Eugenetus’s learning is celebrated with singular praise together with his eloquence. He is likewise praised there by Ennodius. For among the advocates who were leaders of the Roman forum were Olybrius and Eugenes. Thus Athalaric, writing to the Senate in Cassiodorus, Book VII, Letter 19, concerning Felix’s promotion to the quaestorship, says: “He frequently earned the praise of advocacy among the foremost men of eloquence. He stood against the great Olybrius; he equaled him in the abundance of Eugenetus’s eloquent speech; and he was the equal of those whom Rome knew as outstanding.” Further, *Eugenetus* for *Eugenius* results from an altered declension, through the kind of metaplasm by which in writers of the later age we sometimes encounter *Eutychetem, Diogenetem, Eusebetem,* and *Niciatem* instead of *Eutychem, Diogenem, Eusebem,* and *Niciam*, and very frequently in ancient inscriptions, as in this Roman one:

> D. M. S.  
> TI. CLAUDI  
> EUGENETIS  
> VIX. AN. XI. D. IX.  
> TI. CLAUDIUS  
> ANICETUS  
> PATER. FEC.

“To the spirits of the departed. Of Tiberius Claudius Eugenetus, who lived eleven years and nine days. Tiberius Claudius Anicetus, his father, made this.”

> “O insatiable Hades, why did you suddenly snatch me, a young one?  
> Why do you hurry? Do we not all owe ourselves to you?”  
> [Literally: “Insatiable underworld, why did you suddenly snatch me, a young one? What are you hurrying for? Do we not all owe ourselves to you?” Or perhaps, with a question mark after *all*: “Do we not all owe ourselves to you?” EDITOR.]

To Eugenetus, vir illustris.

May an auspicious omen arriving from heaven strengthen your auspices, and may divine counsels fortify the beginnings of your venerable office. Through you may heavenly favor govern the lord of liberty, so that from the fountain of your breast there may flow to the prince’s ears whatever eternal rain has poured into you. Behold, I have recounted the prayers I owed at the beginning of your career, although in words forced into narrow compass. Remember your promised love and covenant, so that the quaestorship may discharge to me what it owes without the loss caused by change. Preserve toward me [Note: “The disposition of your predecessor”] the disposition of Faustus, I think: we saw him above as quaestor in Book II, Letter 25. Let the promise of your dignity not be broken by a change of persons. My lords, receive my greetings according to the longing of your suppliant, and accept these brief words amid the great proclamation of your benefactions. For such is the practice and nature of the fortunate and the better sort: their eloquence exceeds their deeds and services.

## LETTER XXVII. ENNODIUS TO SENARIUS

The haste of the courier forced this letter into narrow compass; grief made me dictate little concerning great matters. Yet such brevity is no burden to him who, amid the narrow confines of speech, is an interpreter of meanings. I am distressed by the delay of our lord Faustus and by the uncertainty of reports. After God, relieve my anxiety by a swift reply, for it is worse to be tormented by uncertain hope than to recognize from the declaration of one who loves us an open despair. Farewell, my lords, and, mindful of what I desire, make known the conversations that are either wished for or necessary.

## LETTER XXVIII. ENNODIUS TO AGAPITUS

If my days flowed according to my wishes, I would devote myself to pages of business rather than to pages of obedience, nor would I transfer the duty of affection to foreign obligations. But, compelled by circumstances, I exchanged the task for one demanded by necessity. For a lofty and magnificent man is suffering from the treacherous plots of his enemies; through me he seeks the protection of your equity, lest a wicked contrivance be allowed to assail his reputation and the profit of fabricated rumor perhaps prevail. My lord, offering you the fullest greeting, I beg that the vigor known to be in you may rise up, and that what is sought from your fathers through the obedience of my speech may be brought to a fitting accomplishment.

## LETTER XXIX. ENNODIUS TO THE POPE

[Note: Ennodius to Pope Symmachus, whom he consistently designates by the title “pope”; for during Symmachus’s lifetime he wrote all, or nearly all, of his letters.]

Heavenly providence orders the welfare of those who follow it. [Note: “Unprecedented.” He uses *inauspicatum* in an unusual sense, taking it in a favorable way to mean an unforeseen and unexpected blessing, something that happens beyond hope and expectation. Thus in Book I, Letter 5: “Through unforeseen successes, advancement and increase will come to him whom we see to have begun from the fasces.” Likewise in Book IX, to Bishop Caesarius: “Whence this unforeseen exaltation for my parents?” Elsewhere too. Usually *inauspicatum* is said of what is adverse and ill-omened, as in Pliny, Book XXVIII, chapter 2.]

Unforeseen gifts are granted to those who have deserved well of God. Heavenly dispensation also supplies what human humility does not dare to request. The adversaries of your see have recognized who will defeat them when he takes up its defense—something which our Redeemer recently revealed through the person of the Aquileian. And therefore, among the outstanding gifts of God, I ask that your crown not refuse to remember me. For he invites many to serve who, although far away, loves the one who obeys. Farewell.

## LETTER XXX. ENNODIUS TO EUGENETUS, VIR ILLUSTRIS

[Col. 0083B]

After your conversation brought about the fulfillment of my first hope, I loosened a mouth long idle and restored it to the practice of speech. Even one who lacks Latian learning in his conscience is animated by success. When study ceases, joy often makes a man eloquent; cheerfulness drives away the clouds of grief, and presently words, glowing like sunlight through the clearing sky, run freely forth. Thus joy either shows us perfected or adversity makes us infants. This, my lord, is confirmed also by your agreement. Therefore, embracing this time of prosperity, I return the affection owed in greeting, hoping that the noble promise toward me, which took its beginning from the fullness of favor, may, as though lacking increase, be doubled. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXI. ENNODIUS TO AVITUS

[Col. 0083C]

Although the opening words of your greatness’s letter gave us abundant occasion for joy, when speech bearing news of a funeral served the purpose of cheerfulness, our gladness was nevertheless not equal to our tears, nor did the serenity of the conversation wholly dispel the gloom of grief. My mind retains its affliction over the death of so great a [Note: “Bishop.” The Aquileian bishop is meant. Avitus was there, as appears in Book V, Letter 20.] bishop, even after the conversation I had desired; for it is the nature of things that every joy is overcome by the addition of even a little sorrow. But why do we revive matters that have hitherto subdued the mind through hidden agitation? With God’s help I promise to accompany your prayers, provided that, with the safety of our lord the pope preserved, I learn that you have chosen someone whom the man charged with the care of souls will not be ashamed to praise. For it is wrong to lead a believer toward crooked paths and to conduct through uncertainty one whom you have bound to yourselves by affection. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXII. ENNODIUS TO EUGENETUS

I do not think that a matter of obedience can become stale through frequent attention, nor that the cultivation of diligence should be charged with the fault of garrulousness. Those occupied with duties of public utility may perhaps offer an excuse for abstaining from letters; but a man who is free does not deserve pardon if he restrains himself from continual writing. The person who can provide letters, in which the nourishment of affection lies, but does not supply them, clearly confesses negligence of love. It is the error of an idle man if a mind that has understood what is good is weakened by going hungry for conversation during the holidays of the tongue. But just as it is fitting for us, who owe nothing to worldly cares, to foster the reverence of gratitude, so, unless your greatness supports its own responsibilities by proclaiming a reply, you rightly condemn good deeds by keeping silent about them. For if rewards are taken away from virtues, who would not be ashamed to have labored? Behold how much I think I have expressed in brief concerning the purpose of both parties: I confess that my spirit is troubled because, when Montanarius returned, although I had given him pages, I received none. I ask that this debt be restored according to law and doubled through shame. Now farewell, my lord. Seeking news of your welfare and reporting my own, I pray God that, if he remembers me, he may multiply your prosperity.

## LETTER XXXIII. ENNODIUS TO SENARIUS

If love obeyed modesty, if the impatience of affection were held by the law of shame, I would abstain from the duties of writing and, imitating you, adopt the form of silence. I would not be an imprudent judge, inferring that what you withhold from me as a reward is not loved, nor would I more readily advise abstinence from letters than silence. [Note: “Men of comitatensian service.” The office called *comitatensis* is mentioned in the Theodosian Code, Law 38, *On Decurions*. *Comitatenses*, like *Palatini*, sometimes generally designates all who serve in the sacred palace in the prince’s retinue. In this sense Senarius is properly called *comitatensis*, since he is shown to have earned his position among the *exceptores* in the king’s service; see Book III, Letter 11. Sometimes *Palatini* specifically designates those who served in the office of either *comes largitionum*. Of these, as the ancient legal glosses show, those who remained in the palace were called *comitatenses*, while those sent into the provinces were called *mittendarii*. Thus they distinguish them:

> “A Palatine is a palace servant. For all those who served among the officials in the treasuries of the palace were commonly called Palatines; but those who always attended upon the palace were called comitatenses—for *comitatus* is the place in which the king dwells—whereas those sent into the provinces were called mittendarii, for *mitto* means ‘I send.’”]

To men of comitatensian service, through the holidays of the tongue, I would proclaim what they reject. But your greatness is not squared by a craftsman’s lines in such a way that it could escape the eyes of one who loves you beneath any covering. For the mind of a friend sees through every obstacle into the innermost recesses. Let no one suppose that the urbanity, wrought in the furnaces of courtiers, can conceal from loved ones the inward counsels that lie hidden. Yet I believe you will oppose my complaints with the excuse appropriate to your station: “It is not right for the occupied to be asked to perform the duties of the idle; those attached to princely service can scarcely descend to such obligations.” I have often heard such things, but I confess that I have not accepted them, because frequent necessities transcend desires, and fear gives way to affection without interruption. The will is at fault when it defends itself with a contrived excuse.

Behold, my lord, how great is my grief, which I have asserted while performing the duty of greeting. I commend the bearer, dear to us both, for his loyalty and nobility, so that, through the favor of your greatness, the insolence of his enemies may be crushed and lie subjected to its own tricks. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIV. ENNODIUS TO HORMISDA, DEACON

[Note: To Hormisda, deacon. Book VIII, Letter 33.]

After your necessary journey, welcome to me because of the benefit of the proximity I had desired, began to promise fulfillment to my hope, you turned your mind toward more distant matters; and when you were almost touching Liguria with your hand, you consigned your tongue to silence. Your absence was less grievous while long intervals of travel held your holiness away: conversation balanced the loss of sight, and the exchanges of letters, prepared as remedies through careful diligence, supplied compensation. Through these services nothing was lost to affection between those separated by their dwellings. But, I suppose, you choose to grant friends what is more difficult, not thinking it a benefit if, in such great proximity, I am nourished by conversation with you.

And so I sigh over my situation with a changed judgment, lest your blessedness should call to account what you have offered as caresses, assigning what came before to time rather than to love. Let a painted expression depart from our purpose in friendship. No file of earlier efforts fashioned us for this construction: we know how to bring an unadorned concord to a union; among loved ones we reject urbanity as we would poison. Therefore, my lord, accepting my greeting, follow one who loves you especially in this respect: devote the cultivation of loyalty through frequent conversation, and grant unvarnished words from the secrecy of your heart to one who awaits them. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXV. ENNODIUS TO APRONIANUS

[Note: To Apronianus, vir illustris, count of the private revenues. Cassiodorus, Book VIII, final letter: “To Apronianus, illustrious man, count of the private revenues.” But, I think, he had not yet held this office.]

It is customary for men distinguished by the brilliance of their character to nourish the reverence of friendship through the cultivation of conversation, so that, while the shoots of favor are animated by the warmth of talk, the joined alliance may reach its harvest. Through these duties, the wisdom of old wished absence to have no power. Quite rightly, our lord Faustus, the most exemplary of men, gives a unique testimony concerning you. One whom an approved witness raises up can be recognized without a cloud of doubt; nothing concerning him needs to be questioned.

But now, reducing myself to the narrow limits of a letter, I close the praise owed to you within secret recesses, lest what must be done before outsiders become stale through importunity in your presence. Farewell, my lord, accepting my most obedient greeting. I pray God, while prolonging your prosperity into the future, to promise me an increase also through the favorable successes of my friends. Farewell.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0085]

## LETTER I. ENNODIUS TO LIBERIUS, PATRICIAN

[Note: To Liberius the patrician. At the Second Synod of Orange he subscribed under all his names: “Petrus Marcellus Felix Liberius, vir clarissimus and illustris, prefect of the praetorium of Gaul and patrician, have subscribed in agreement.” That age had no one more illustrious than Liberius. First, he loyally supported Odoacer against Theoderic; after Odoacer was defeated, he served under Theoderic, for as long as Theoderic reigned, in the highest civil and military honors, and performed many distinguished deeds with great praise in Italy and Gaul; likewise under Athalaric. He was also chosen as ambassador of King Theodahad to the Emperor Justinian. Finally, Justinian himself placed him in command of military forces against the Goths in Italy and Sicily. Procopius testifies that he was “a man exceptionally noble and good, who knew very well how to attend to truthful speech.” Our authorities for all this are Cassiodorus, Book II of the *Variae*, Letters 11 and 15; Book VIII, Letter 6; and Book XI, Letter 1; Procopius, Books I and III of the *Gothic War*; and Ennodius himself, Book IX, Letters 23 and 29, where there is more about Liberius. This letter, however, as though written under the name of Symmachus, was placed by Ennodius among the letters of Symmachus.]

To Liberius the patrician.

When, in the election of the bishop of Aquileia, you direct words in reverence for a conscience devoted to God, and your tongue, initiated into divine worship, serves the consecration, the bonds of our attention were held by the unknown man whom you praised. For nothing surpasses judgment whenever an approved man has advanced someone. What room is left for the judgment of those who follow, when he obeys justice whose decision is not summoned for examination? You are acting from the goodness of your conscience in a matter that scarcely anyone would deny to your authority.

[Note: “Among the judges of Marcellinus.” Namely, the *honorati*, whose judgment was sought in ancient episcopal elections, together with their testimony. Leo, Letter 89 to the bishops of the province of Vienne: “The votes of the citizens, the testimony of the peoples, would certainly be awaited; the judgment of the honorati and the election of the clergy would be sought—matters which, in the ordinations of priests, those who know the rules of the Fathers customarily ensure are observed.”]

The greatest of men, superior through humility, presented the venerable colleague of Marcellinus among the judges; and, lest favor toward authority be attributed to him through crooked interpreters, he joined to the reward of praise what he had taken away from his own inclination. You made him appear ordinary, so that his exalted praise might not be suspect. The heights are chastened so that the testimony of the most illustrious may gain strength. Happy is the priesthood for which a mind full of light held up a torch. Blessed is the conduct that was brought into examination precisely so that, with so great a man supporting it, it might prevail; it would not have learned the taste of victory had it not been subjected to uncertainty. Adversity has always produced glory for the innocent; a mediocre attack provides the strongest defenders.

But why have I prolonged the limits of the letter through loquacity, exceeding the pages confined by their proper law in human composition? I too, most distinguished lord, join my agreement to your efforts according to the measure of my own smallness, with heaven attending upon you; and, what is regarded as marvelous among men, I am drawn by regard for you to love. An affection inspired through another pleases me, while love remains implanted in the deepest parts of the heart even when the person is far away. May heavenly grace therefore join itself as a companion to your desires; and, while the desired result is granted, may it either find goodness in the episcopate or create it.

([Note: “Farewell.” Omitting what follows, the Symmachian manuscripts conclude the letter in this way: “Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the eighth indiction,” that is, in the year 499, as I have said. From this it is clear that the letters of Ennodius do not retain their original order. Otherwise, those dealing with the election of Marcellinus ought to be placed before the preceding letters.])

Farewell, my lord, and relieve one who loves you through frequent conversation, so that, even if frequent business does not require pages, they may nevertheless be supplied to affection.

## LETTER II. ENNODIUS TO MARCIANUS

[Note: To Marcianus, advocate, son of Asterius.]

While my mind was anxiously tossed between hope and fear in uncertain concern for you, you unlocked solid evidence of your progress with the honey of conversation; for, as the faithful heir of learning, you pursue the eloquence native to your family. As I see, the vein of eloquence has not degenerated, and the succession of skill proceeds by the same right by which inheritances pass. I had thought that the gifts of knowledge belonged only to individual talents, not to families, and that what continuous labor and tireless sweat acquire could not be transmitted through genealogies. But, as appears, eloquence preserves its ranks, and the splendor of speech that overflowed in the elders migrates to their descendants; the course of learning agrees with that of rivers, and the wave of eloquence glides through its accustomed channels.

Learning has come to you together with your father’s estate, and the tombs restore Asterius in the goodness of his offspring. I confess that until now I envied the years of our elders, and I sighed for the age to which he had been granted. I was a careless judge of heavenly gifts when I could despair of the fruits of the civil robe while the substance of the root remained. But heavenly dispensation, in order to give talent to its gifts, makes what it bestows appear unforeseen; and, while surpassing our prayers, it reveals its power through generosity.

Liguria is not barren of good offspring: it nourishes shoots for the forum, which the senate too will gladly embrace. Familiar closeness joins together the advocate and the senator. [Note: “The advocate and the senator.” Access to the curia and senate lay open through offices, while advocacy was the step toward offices. Hence Valentinian, in the novella on pleading, which is number 34 among the Theodosian laws, calls advocacy “the nursery of dignities.” Or because quaestors, consulares, governors, and other learned magistrates were generally made from the foremost advocates—as we have seen in Decoratus and Honoratus—and examples are found throughout Marcellinus and Cassiodorus. I think Ennodius is speaking here in this sense. Or because those who had completed the number of years prescribed by law in advocacy were thereafter adorned with the privileges of various dignities. With this in mind, Sidonius, Book I, Letter 11, said that the dignities of advocates begin when their pleadings end.]

For those who have used the civil robe well, the palm-bearing garment smiles enticingly, opening its folds to receive them. Farewell, dearest, and devote yourself fully to these distinctions. Let honorable studies receive your entire self. Hasten to reach your father’s harvest, cleansing your tongue with the hoe of reading and your character through imitation of good men.

## LETTER III. ENNODIUS TO OPILIO, VIR ILLUSTRIS

[Note: He called him a lofty and magnificent man in Book IV, Letter 18. I think this is the Opilio who, near the end of Theoderic’s reign, held the consulship with Justin in the year 524 and whose name is prefixed to the Council of Carpentras, which is known to have been held in that year. That a certain ignorant antiquarian improperly added Vincomalus as Opilio’s colleague in the consulship there need not seem surprising: he had remembered that another Opilio, whom he thought to be the same man, had been consul with Vincomalus in the year 463. With equal boldness, in the letter of Pope Hormisdas to Possessor, which bears in ancient copies the subscription of Rusticus, consul with Vitalian in the year 520, we see Olybrius substituted in most editions for Rusticus—the Olybrius who had been consul with another Rusticus fifty-six years earlier. But to return to Opilio: distinct from the consul of the same period was Opilio, the informer attacked by Boethius in Book I of the *Consolation*. This was the man whom Athalaric later made count of the sacred largesses in the sixth indiction, that is, in the year 528, as reported by Cassiodorus, Book VIII, Letter 16, three years after his brother Cyprian had been adorned with the same office by Theoderic. Cyprian too was an informer, according to Boethius, against the consul Albinus. Moreover, the father of these brothers was another Opilio, who had likewise been count of the sacred largesses under Odoacer, *Variae*, Book X, 61.]

To Opilio, vir illustris.

I certainly owe replies to our earlier conversations and, in obedience to my purpose—or to modesty, if I do not offend by writing in an uncultivated manner—I owe you a doubling of what I received, lest a superior person’s favor return to regret because of a renunciation born of disdain. For those established at the summit do not, through our fault, lose the memory of their dignity if they suspect that we pursue the wrong kind of behavior and look down upon the humble. Since their own restraint exalts the most eminent, and the fullness of worldly honors permits increase only through this art, we must consider what harm the narrowness of an unmeasured condition causes to the lowly.

Therefore let it suffice for your greatness that, after writing twice, I understand what error I incurred through silence. But I feared, I confess, lest flight from faults should lead me into fault, and lest speech assigned to gratitude, while polished by no skill, should provoke offense. I fled the horror that is generated in the ignorant by the opportunity to obey. Behold, I have asserted that I possessed both the soul of one who acknowledges a deposit and the modesty of one conscious of his resources when restoring it.

It remains, most exemplary of men, that I may learn, by your examination of my plea, whether this too pleases you: that I have not yet returned what I received. Consideration is a faithful indicator of our ability; and, as in all things it is foremost, so, by protecting reputation, it guards the meagerness of the tongue. The gift of eloquent men seems to grow through modesty, and one easily acquires the name of wisdom when childishness itself is made silent by it.

Nevertheless, I expose my brow to the loss demanded by the case you entrusted to me; and, while carrying out your instructions, I send my reputation into uncertainty. Agnellus mocks me with various images drawn from his promises concerning the houses, wishing us to specify the total price. But you have learned that the passion of a wicked man is insatiable and cannot be healed except by contempt for money. My lord, I greet you and ask that the reverence of devoted love and our covenant be preserved toward me.

## LETTER IV. ENNODIUS TO HELISEA

[Note: To Helisea, mother of Avitus and a relative of Ennodius; see Letter 5.]

The outcome long sought by my desires has come to pass: when talent is granted to gifts, they are bestowed after a long wait. Kinship lives in every part of the earth; the chain of blood is not broken by the separation of bodies; affection suffers no loss through the division of regions, since among those separated by habitation love takes the place of presence.

I give thanks to Almighty God because he has made you mindful of piety and caused you to remember your lineage under a religious pretext. God is my witness: after the lady Cynegia explained to me the worth of your character, I sought your presence with a special ardor, if the desired opportunity had granted me access according to my prayers.

My lady, offering you the reverence of a greeting, I promise the service of devotion in the matter indicated in your letters; for the soul receives as much as is offered to holy endeavors. I truly say that I have never loved the man whom you detest, and I feared that your assent might also be inclined toward the advancement of that dreadful man. May God prevent anyone from attaining ecclesiastical dignity who has not been formed on the anvil of good instruction.

## LETTER V. ENNODIUS TO AVITUS

I should like to prolong the account, if I did not burden my purpose, by which I earned the frequent letters of one who loves me. For when you send pages concerned with business, you provide a service to affection. But among the wise and those who understand the heart, brief conversations suffice. I do not know how to be urbane in promises, nor to flatter with a feigned expression those to whom I owe my soul.

Only persist in what you have begun, and, obeying heavenly commands, lead the wicked man of whom you speak away from his desires. It is fitting for me to show more by deeds than to promise in words, because I confidently expect what I give to be restored to me. My lord, offering my fullest greeting, I ask you to give thanks on my behalf to the lady Helisea, our common mother, who has deigned through her letters to show the bonds of kinship.

## LETTER VI. ENNODIUS TO LEONTIUS, ABBOT

[Note: To Leontius, abbot, at whose urging he wrote the life of blessed Antony and dedicated it to him.]

The highest abundance of heavenly favor toward me has grown beyond my deserts, while I, deserving punishment, rejoice after obtaining the rewards of the just. Despair, the mother of danger, drives sinners rashly toward extremes. Let those established in the greatest error be restored to solid hope through my example.

I do not know from what work of mine, or from what innocence, the fruit of your letters has come to me; nor how a soul enriched by the abundance of sin has been satisfied with the honey of heavenly goodness—unless it is because he who took upon himself our wounds and suffered for us, changing the condition of our merits, chastens with gifts those whom he has judged worthy of scourging; and, conversely, while filling the souls of the guilty with prosperity, improves them through shame.

Thus, through the favor of heavenly secrecy, I have drawn forth the fruits of your conversation. He made you anxious about my bodily health because he compels the care of my soul, through spiritual physicians, to return to the condition of health that has been granted. You inquire, through the investigation of religious concern, what condition my bodily members are in, although neglecting the state of the soul, whose whole being is weighed down by the rule of this world.

Make me through prayer such a man as you declare me to be through your flatteries; for the clarity of your purpose, which knows no disguise, announces before the time of innocence the one whom it proclaims to be good and says will soon become so.

I did not refuse my brothers and fellow servants whom you sent whatever comfort I could offer—more capable in intention than in deed. It remains for you, after receiving my services, together with the whole community over which you preside, united through the mercy of Almighty God, to persist in prayers to God on behalf of my smallness, so that one who lacks confidence through his own actions may obtain it through your support.

## LETTER VII. ENNODIUS TO EUPREPIA

Although you had often recognized the meagerness of my talent, you nevertheless wished the fasting of a mouth once tested to be endangered by the haste of your command. But I do not refuse to obey one who is diligent, so that, if eloquence lacks merit, the grace of obedience may take its place.

The forms of heavenly gifts are various, although they proceed from one author. One person is commended by perfection; another is commended by what he wishes to obey without delay. Having scarcely the space of one hour for composition, I composed the epitaph of my lady Cynegia with unpolished speed. Consider the necessity under which I had to explain a woman of such great merits through leaps of language. May the venerable soul pardon my sterility, accepting in place of the form of my diction the effort of a speaker without disguise.

You, my lady, embracing this letter as a substitute for my presence, pray that her spirit may in no way be injured by the roughness of my services.

[Note: “Cynegia’s epitaph.” The wife of Faustus. This is shown by another epitaph of hers, which follows in Letter 29 of Book VII.]

### EPITAPH OF CYNEGIA

Neither sex nor tombs harm me, nor the final threads  
Which the sisters of fate spin with deceptive fingers.  

United with God, the woman lives beyond death through her deeds,  
Bearing manly accomplishments along a woman’s path.  

Blood, honor, talent, integrity, steadfastness, and countenance  
Overcame destruction at so great a price.  

By her character she upheld the lineage of great parents,  
A sign of the family—[Note: “Whose mind was clear.” Thus the ancient books. The Basel manuscripts have *mens tua clara*—“your mind was clear”—which is inept. But they were influenced by the diaeresis and metrical quantity of the little word *cui*, which nevertheless rests on examples from ancient poets, and on Paulinus of Nola in the epithalamium of Julian: “So that he may be a man to whom Christ is the crown.” Nor was it unknown to Gottschalk, the monk of Orbais, whose verses I shall append in the preface to his poem addressed to Ratramnus:

> Come, I ask you, proceed, Clio,  
> Hasten, swift heroine,  
> Turn back, wise offspring,  
> Whose brother is Apollo.  
>  
> Carry, exulting, to your friend Ratramnus,  
> To the lord, father, and teacher,  
> In an unpolished meter from the pen,  
> What I gladly return to him.]

whose mind was clear.

She instructed her children to preserve a tranquil life,  
While always teaching them through her example to love God.

## LETTER VIII. ENNODIUS TO PETRUS

[Note: To Petrus, perhaps the man who later held the ordinary consulship in the year 516, to whom Ennodius is now offering congratulations on attaining some other dignity.]

[Col. 0090D]

After the venerable judgment of the ruler, having tested the character of your greatness, granted you the offspring of honors in return for the harvest of your virtues, you have fostered irreligious silence during the holidays of speech, and have offended both against your eloquence and against my affection. For expression naturally grows, fortified by confidence, whenever it serves as a favorable indication; more abundant eloquence serves the advancement of honors, and the mouths of the learned signify their achievements by corresponding successes. Behold, this unlovable silence has both deprived you of the gift of speech and begrudged me the outcome of my joy.

You may perhaps reply: “You could blame me, my friend, for ignorance if report, entrusted to miscellaneous messengers, had suppressed anything concerning my high position. But I cannot bear to learn the heights attained by those dear to me through rumor, nor to gather clear signs of joy from the uncertainty of opinion.” I knew how a simple report from a learned man had long ago created in me the hope of being bound to you; I believed that I was foolishly entrusting my cheerful spirit to those serene ears from which you did not command me to be cheerful. I thought that this very thing, constructed with the oars of a thousand wings in your writing, could have been overtaken on foot, lest another, snatching away the good things awaited by a lover, should bring them to you first.

Behold, my lord: receiving the honor of your greeting, and having recognized the causes of my sorrows, do not refuse the remedies prepared; for, as far as I presume, neither faithfulness in diligence nor speech polished to perfection deserts you in conversation. Yet, not content with displeasing you in only one kind of discourse, I have added a poem, so that after the feasts of Antenor’s waters, which the baths of Aponus [Note: [Col. 0091D] Baths of Aponus.] —this is a corrupt form of the name of a most celebrated spring, still renowned today in the district of Padua because of its health-giving waters. Martial calls the land of Padua *Apona* from this spring; Ennodius and others call it *Antenorean* from the man whom they regard as the founder of the Trojan colony. Claudian also played upon the waters of Aponus in a poem of his own; and Cassiodorus, in his customary manner, described most skillfully and ingeniously the nature, power, and use of Aponus in a letter dictated in the name of King Theoderic to the architect Aloysius, so that he might restore the buildings of the Paduan baths, *Book II, Letter 39.] constrict the flesh by the law of the body, while water cuts away what is distended by the offspring of the waters, let me also, a new poet who has never touched the streams of Helicon, join in. Accept, then, poems intended to provoke laughter; and, content that you alone have recognized your *glovidenum* [Note: [Col. 0091D] Your *glovidenum*. In the preface to the poem addressed to Faustus: “Yet, to the disgrace of the Muses, whose verses are never without a *glovidenum*, I added these lines.” It is sufficiently clear that Ennodius uses *glovidenum* in the language of his own age with nearly the sense in which Sulpicius Severus uses *gurdonicum*, meaning rustic and inept. “I fear,” he says, “that a somewhat rustic expression may offend your exceedingly urbane ears. Yet you will hear a *gurdonicum* man speaking, one who says nothing with cosmetic embellishment or theatrical grandeur.” It is easy to conjecture that *gurdonicum* is derived from *gurdo*, that is, a slow and useless person, as Isidore explains it; but the origin of *glovidenum* is not similarly apparent.] withdraw me from public severity. For if there is something that perhaps pleases, your judgment is sufficient for me; if there is something deserving a bite, I regard as private whatever you have recognized concerning a friend’s faults. You will also grant pardon, because, oppressed by pain in my eyes, I may perhaps have composed poems that limp. Verses cannot have solid tracks when deprived of the service of light. Read, then, about the hot waters that you are going to visit.

## VERSES

[Note: [Col. 0092D] “The land rises on a sloping elevation.” Claudian, on the baths of Aponus:

“Lower than a lofty hill, yet higher than the little fields,  
the slope gleams gently raised in a conspicuous curve.  
Rich in burning water, whoever pierces its caverns  
is driven back when the liquid encounters the fire.”]

The land rises, supported by a sloping swelling,  
gently upheld by a raised brow.  
It brings its proud head near to no peaks,  
nor, like pressed valleys, seeks the lowest depths.

Here smoking Aponus was everywhere through open veins;  
peaceful fire breathes among mingled waters.  
The wave preserves the hearths; the flame does not swallow the liquid;  
from the fire poured into it, the sacred spring crackles.

Here the drunken heat supplies medicine to all,  
drying bodies with vaporous moisture.

[Col. 0092A] [Note: [Col. 0092D] “Here the pyre [*pyra*] among the waters.” This should be read instead of *pera*, which appears in the ancient copies, through a change of letters; compare *peripoma* for *pyripoma* in Book I, Letter 4. Cassiodorus uses corresponding antitheses when writing about the same matter: “It is pleasant to see the secluded place, its waters exhaling fiery vapors, a friendly warmth unceasingly mingled with the waves, and heat coming from the course of the stream, from which it was ordinarily accustomed to be extinguished.”]

Here a pyre among the waters, the liquid undulates with sparks:  
life is sustained by the fellowship of alternating death.  
Lest he obey, Vulcan is submerged in those nymphs;  
the combative concord of nature has broken its treaties.

## LETTER IX. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

May divinity favor honorable desires; may a happy auspice not be denied to worthy pursuits; may noble intentions gain strength through the fruits of prosperity. He who aspires, with the favor of heaven, to the liberal disciplines has entrusted the pledge of his prayers to integrity. The love of the good arts despises a savage nature; no one strives toward the adornments of eloquence unless formed by good character.

Our Parthenius [Note: [Col. 0092D] Our Parthenius. Concerning him, see Book VI, Letter 1.] —the son of my sister—, urged on by these goads, is hastening to visit Rome, where learning is native; and I, as a father, have promised him the support of your greatness. A petitioner gives your high office occasion to display its generosity, while we ask in prayers for what custom requires—as though someone believed that he could earn the sunrise or a river’s course by entreaty. It is not a favor where due order is observed: custom follows what binds everyone.

Yet I come forward to receive something beyond the course from which you never depart. I have sent a person whose standing may be judged according to my merits. Perhaps an undeserved recommendation helps others; to relatives, whatever we cannot surpass is of lesser value. My lord, presenting the service of a greeting, having briefly stated the bearer’s identity and his business, I have only to learn what the person, the cause, and the relationship deserve.

## LETTER X. ENNODIUS TO POPE SYMMACHUS

[Col. 0092C]

While the care of your crown governs the apostolic see and you rule the summit of heavenly authority, the advancement of your forebears is gratified that what was promised through my services is being fulfilled. [Note: [Col. 0092D] “Through my services.” This refers to what he had done in Symmachus’s cause, both in other matters and especially in the *Apology for the Synod*, upon whose defense Symmachus’s innocence rested.] One who has faithfully served a steadfast man obtains hope without labor. Great is the display of one who grants a reward when what one person has earned is repaid to many. They follow the institutions of their predecessors, through whom a generation receives what an individual has established.

Thus the offenses of the Israelite people did not touch them with punishment because of David, while the integrity of their predecessor came to the aid of the nation; and a man’s faith either rescued the people from error or helped them remain in grace.

Parthenius, therefore, the bearer of this letter and the son of my sister, has been sent to your crown, animated by this confidence; liberal concern compelled him to seek Rome. Sacred are the pursuits of literature, in which, before expertise grows, vices are unlearned. On this journey, gray-haired counsels commonly come to youthful years, since those whom age rejects know how to provide instruction.

Therefore cherish him. [Note: [Col. 0093D] In Schott’s edition: “whose reasons for coming,” and so forth.] You have learned the reasons for his coming through the disclosure of our kinship. You have a pledge in whom the quality of my merits before you may become clearly known. My lord, returning the reverence of a greeting with devoted service, I ask that the bearer of this letter, your servant, may by fortunate destiny receive among you the name of a stranger; for whatever is granted through my prayers adorns your service beyond its own gifts.

## LETTER XI. ENNODIUS TO LUMINOSUS

[Col. 0093B]

I seem to require defense before those among whom many must be defended, since concern for a liberal education urges me on; our common cause has found you as patrons. You are not unaware of how to receive strangers, nor do you fail to encourage those who need instruction. Your hand is frequently applied to experienced necessities, while with an idle mouth you invite those who stumble toward the palm of eloquence. By examples, the powerful person encourages the stranger, and the perfected person encourages the ignorant.

Both aspects apply to Parthenius, the son of my sister, who, as he seeks Rome for the venerable disciplines, finds it sufficient—rather than iron spurs—to see you. If it is not foreign to humanity, keeping your sublimity before his eyes, he is stimulated toward virtue by deeds rather than by admonitions. Ambition for praise is the teacher of labor, especially when it flourishes in one whom you remember to have been subject to a similar fortune.

But if I am dear to you, restore him to the father I have mentioned, so that mutual love may rejoice in reciprocal service; so that whatever labor I once displayed for your greatness may be repaid to me through another. My lord, rendering the service of a greeting, I believed it sufficient for a recommendation that the identity of the bearer should not remain concealed. A person who distrusts obtaining something makes use of a long prayer; it is the mark of one deserving nothing to ask for a long time. May such a thing be far from your character: do not lose the gift of benefactions by prolonging, through lengthy supplication, one who ought to be relieved by a speedy result.

## LETTER XII. ENNODIUS TO THE YOUNGER FAUSTUS

Prefaced by thanks to God, who has wiped away the clouds over my eyes that an inexplicable pain had produced—I rightly refer his benefits to him, who gave and restored the light—I scarcely breathe again, encouraged by the hope of health after countless days.

This also bears upon the judgment of your greatness: the man whose own gift deserted him in his neighborhood saw nothing. But he is powerful who removes the mists of the body and changes sadness through the serenity of circumstances. After stating my necessity, I return to the business that compelled this address. You will, I hope, love the bearer whose cause asserts the reason for his coming.

Parthenius, the son of my sister, wishes to appear a freeborn man through the disciplines of liberal study; if I am not mistaken, he desires to possess the testimony of your personal favor. Therefore may your greatness, mindful of the past, remembering the present, and prudent concerning the future, receive the bearer in consideration of my recommendation; and may he who will be happier through your presence, as he writes, not be made to experience the misfortunes of exile.

My lord, returning the service owed to you, I ask that, even through this opportunity by which Parthenius will be able to send you pages received from there, the form of the conversation we desire may be multiplied.

## LETTER XIII. ENNODIUS TO HORMISDAS

We know that the sacred obligations of a religious purpose are separated from a multitude burdened with sins by innocence and faith, and that the titles of a venerable office are marked more by character than by bodies. Who would seek goodness of conscience among human beings if worldly necessity must be applied to the decrees of pontiffs, if the promise of priests is preserved with vigilant caution? He never possessed constancy of feeling who was not permitted to do something other than what he had promised.

The society of the world is restrained by fear of the laws; God’s servants ought to display what is good not because of fear but because of love. Long ago, while fear pressed upon us and we awaited the pious king’s clemency with uncertain assessment of our merits, we delivered so many camels to the lord pope [Note: [Col. 0093D] “To the lord pope.” Symmachus. This too must therefore be counted among Ennodius’s benefactions toward Symmachus.] under this condition of your reverence: if the animals themselves were not necessary to us, the proper price for them would be sent.

And because your holiness knows very well [Note: [Col. 0093D] “Your holiness.” That is, “Your Beatitude,” as above, Book IV, Letter 34, to the same Hormisdas. This is a rare form of address for a deacon, which was Hormisdas’s rank. It is more properly a form of address for bishops or priests, *προσφώνησις*. [Col. 0094D] Nevertheless, Ennodius also calls the same Hormisdas “most holy” without naming him as a deacon in Book VII, Letter 20, to Maximus: “You have what you may communicate with the most holy deacon concerning moral institutions, in the well-known abundance of your speech.”] that, while we were able, we supported the interests of the holy Roman Church through your representation, now, in return, confer a benefit of truth. We also ask, after offering the customary greeting, that you indicate what your deliberation has determined concerning this matter; for we believe that neither the aforesaid prelate of the apostolic see nor you, who act as intermediaries, are considering anything other than what unquestionably accords both with the purpose and with justice.

## LETTER XIV. ENNODIUS TO SERVILION

[Note: [Col. 0094D] Servilion. Ennodius’s teacher, by whom he had been instructed in ecclesiastical disciplines.]

Disciples are confident of perfection whenever they await the presence of their teachers. The hope of learning is manifest: to enjoy its gift, one must invite the teacher. Those minds are brilliant that are stirred by longing for their instructors; those who have learned under favorable circumstances seek an instructor.

Thus, possessed by affection for your holiness, although I do not dare boast of my learning, I nevertheless await the face of my teacher, lest you believe that you entrusted an ecclesiastical offspring to a degenerate son. For although my memory cannot raise itself to produce a hundredfold fruit, it nevertheless knows how to return multiplied seeds to the cultivator.

Come, then, so that, standing before you, you may inspect your harvest in the role of a good farmer. May God keep envy far away. Thus the plant of ecclesiastical fertility has grown strong beneath your plowshares that no force of a raging storm can overturn it. I do not wish, by prejudging the matter, to burden your conscience with praise of holiness; you will inspect what is declared by the testimony of letters.

It remains, after the greeting has been offered, that you now hasten toward your joys; for divine benefits always approach by degrees, and to those to whom they grant good things, they promise better.

## LETTER XV. ENNODIUS TO SENARIUS

A prayer poured out before God is never stripped of its desired result; with him, joy is obtained through tears, and sorrow passes into happiness. The aid of the Godhead attended my desires, and, under the guidance of grace, restored you—the greater part of my soul—from the distant boundaries of the nations.

[Note: [Col. 0095D] “From the distant boundaries of the nations.” In the following letter, Senarius is said to have been restored from the farthest parts of the earth, evidently from some embassy; for it is frequently clear that he was chosen for the honor of an embassy. Cassiodorus, Book IV, Letter 3, to Senarius: “You have often undertaken the office of a difficult embassy; you stood before kings as an advocate equal to them, compelled to show our justice even to those who could scarcely understand reason through their savage obstinacy. Authority inflamed by disputes did not frighten you; rather, you subjected boldness to truth and, obeying our commands, compelled barbarians to examine their own consciences.”]

Truly I cannot spread this letter over many words, hindered by the tears that joys heaped up have produced. Do this, my lord: do not allow the fullness of the heavenly gift to perish for my smallness. Let us both have one lodging; let no anxiety arise from the narrowness of the walls, since one breast provides a sufficient dwelling for our souls.

## LETTER XVI. ENNODIUS TO PANFRONIUS

[Note: [Col. 0096D] Panfronius. He called him “a sublime and magnificent man” in Book II, Letter 16, and Book VI, Letter 14, in which he commends him to Faustus. He also writes to Agapitus on his behalf in Letter 16, where he suggests something concerning the dignity of the Vicarate, for which he perhaps congratulates him here. He calls him “an illustrious man” in Book VII, Letter 1.]

The sovereignty of joys is great: happiness is not restrained, and it longs to burst forth into speech. The day has come that my desires awaited, and the splendor that I always requested from heavenly mercy, never from my own merits, has been added to your greatness. The summit by which faithful integrity need not fear coming into the light has been restored to your birth and character.

Good God, preserve what has been granted; increase through success what you have given; make the first step around your servant the one that is highest. I anticipate in hope what I pray for: things granted by heaven do not know how to linger at the threshold. One always ascends to the summit through successive increases when heavenly favor provides the beginning.

Who among human beings—or among those who keep their conduct unstained by any cloud—would not rejoice that this had come to him in a single day: that you had entered upon the auspices of honors and that my dear Senarius had been restored from the farthest boundaries of the earth? Only a brief passage of hours intervened: you, born for the palace, entered upon office, and he was restored.

I speak in truth, and confidently promise myself, because of God’s mercy, that aids are being granted to my frailty with heaven’s cooperation. What has been granted to you is promised to me.

My lord, receiving the service of a greeting, I ask that, if you grant anything to my love, you not fail to entreat the lord of my soul, Senarius, to remain with me. If you do not obtain this, you will have taken much away from the abundance of my happiness.

## LETTER XVII. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

[Col. 0096A]

Your greatness acts rightly: while showing due regard for origin and character, it joins correction to error without delay; and what it wisely understands to be a fault, it removes before another can denounce it. Who could believe that one so swift in correction had committed an offense? The follower of transgressions scarcely needs to be summoned when he places his hand in the way of slipping faults.

My lord, guided by your grace, I reply in this manner to what you have deigned to write. Otherwise, the weight of my actions has made me humbler in purpose; scarcely have I remained capable, in my misery, of restoring our conversations.

My lord, presenting the service of a greeting, I ask God to repay your greatness for the fruit of this consideration by which you do not despise one who is humble.

## LETTER XVIII. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

It is scarcely possible for someone intent upon fortunate affairs to foresee adversity. He rejects as an evil omen whatever he perceives, through prior understanding, concerning the severity of the future; certainly, he shudders at the very recognition of troubles, lest bitter things mingle with him at an inopportune time.

I believed that unlovable Ravenna, while it was full of my treasures, was now no distance away; no spring invites a thirsty man, nor any breeze one burning with heat, as that city’s rest invited me, though weary, to itself. But now I think that Rome itself has been transferred farther away, in proportion to the burden of my sins.

Where is that abundance of letters, once thought rare? Where is the frequent sight of you? Where are all those comforts of diligence? I truly speak on my own behalf: I detest a life that is not hated even by those who are in misery.

Your greatness may perhaps claim that, through a heavenly dispensation, what you desired has happened to you. Happiness is not complete when one of our own is afflicted by the misery of harsh separation. Believe God: what I mourn is not feigned; neither the polish of a letter nor the narrowness of speech is sufficient to unfold the tragedy of my heart.

Christ, arbiter of all things, come to the aid of my personal necessity, lest human frailty, unequal to the burden of immeasurable grief, succumb beneath its weight.

My lord, rendering the service of a greeting, I ask that care for written pages concerning me be maintained, so that, by this remedy at least, my mind, situated amid its heats, may breathe again.

## LETTER XIX. ENNODIUS TO PARTHENIUS

[Col. 0096D]

I am not surprised at your abstinence from speech, because one who has composed little produces nothing. Do you believe that under this pretext the substance of your advancement remains hidden? Your silence betrays inexperience, and your unconstructed conversation reveals childishness.
