Until now you had not been without a sense of grace, knowing what diligence and what the concern of one who loves demanded. You became ignorant of good things after we sent you away to obtain what are thought to be the greatest things.

For the rest, farewell; and, accepting the words of your instructor, make it known through the constancy of your writing that you have become a better man.

## LETTER XX. ENNODIUS TO AVITUS

While affection seeks its remedies and longs for the heat of anxiety to be relieved through conversation, the spirit burns more intensely through the benefit of anticipation; from the place where it is believed to be extinguished, a doubled fire of diligence rises.

Often, when seeking an abundance of bearers, I have found myself becoming ill precisely where I thought something beneficial would occur. Behold, the man who hastened to you on account of his own affairs remedies my desires; what is received out of consideration for another’s necessity becomes assistance to my own.

I shall see what Boniface advances through my recommendation. Meanwhile, what he obtained from me through lengthy prayers assists my purposes. A mind that bears witness to his blood indicates that he was born of good parents. The man mentioned above asserts that his own brother is being held captive near the city of Aquileia, and he asks that he be helped by you.

The reputation of your holy household is widespread. You have already given such a life of good deeds as a pledge, from which the man crushed by misfortune may ask what is owed to him.

My lord, receiving the service of a full greeting, allow yourselves to be entreated to do what you are accustomed to do of your own accord, so that one who is your suppliant may not be permitted to be another’s.

## LETTER XXI. ENNODIUS TO AVITUS

[Col. 0097C]

Your greatness asks me, by its entreaty, to support its reputation, as though I were still being fashioned on the fresh anvil of friendship, or as though one who changes his purpose of diligence on every occasion did not deprive himself of his own gift.

May the changing judgment of one who loves be far from Christian character. Whoever has dedicated the service of his mouth to praise is not free to abandon what he has begun, lest he disfigure the honey of his earlier commendation by the worthlessness of what follows.

I shall see who [Note: [Col. 0097D] In Schott’s edition, *ingenuum* (“freeborn” or “noble”).] believes that it is talent to pursue novelty. I choose friends slowly, but once chosen, I persevere in them without change. I am present to myself whenever I have raised your reputation to the stars; for among those who do not know us by our character, we are judged by our companions.

I truly confess that I have poured forth the splendor of your conscience, in place of your reputation, more abundantly. [Note: [Col. 0097D] In Schott’s edition, *effundi* (“to be poured forth”).] Before your greatness arrived, the service of my speech in Liguria made known how highly you were regarded.

Thanks be to God, who has made my judgment agree with the general opinion. [Note: [Col. 0098D] *Generalitatem*: perhaps *generalem*? But I change nothing.] May the poverty of my eloquence not humble me! Your merits are greater than what my tongue can express in praise. Though poor in eloquence, amid every kind of clamor I did not remain silent about whatever could suit your glory.

The demonstration of your character has become a light to my conscience. May divinity keep far away the possibility that my testimony should ever allow weakness hostile to distinguished character to creep in.

I recall no cause of error in you that you have so excellently concealed; and if such a cause had existed in proportion to my merits, it would have been lulled to sleep by the memory of your former goodness.

For the rest, farewell, my lord; and, having accompanied my journey with the kindness of your good wishes, compensate for the losses of my absence by remembering your affection.

## LETTER XXII. ENNODIUS TO VENANTIUS

[Note: [Col. 0097D] Venantius. A most illustrious man, Book IV, Letter 9. Cassiodorus mentions two Venantiuses of this age. One was a *vir spectabilis*, governor of Lucania and Bruttium, Book III, Letters 8 and 46; there is nothing to prevent his being the same man as Ennodius’s Venantius. The other was the son of Liberius, an illustrious man, who, while serving as *comes domesticorum*, was appointed by Theoderic, Book II, Letter 15; he is called the patrician Venantius in Book IV, Letter 36.]

If closeness of blood invites minds to diligence, then, obeying the commands of devoted love, I am eager to have offered myself as the first speaker and, by beginning these pages, to have opened a path to conversation for you to embrace.

For a long time I was worn down by vain expectation while I waited for your pages, and I did not send anything. But affection dug its spurs into my spirit and made me approach the duties of correspondence first.

[Note: [Col. 0098D] In Schott’s edition, *Habeo* (“I have”).]

You possess, if I judge rightly, the privilege of one who loves more: I speak even after the long extension of your silence, and I ought to commend to your modesty what I kept silent about. Yet now, lest the polish of a letter, having crossed its proper limit, disfigure its author, I come forward, by laying down the services of a greeting, to be reconciled to your graciousness, even if I deserve it; for the sublimity of the greater is doubled through fellowship, and favor granted to subjects bears a torch before the most eminent.

## LETTER XXIII. ENNODIUS TO CONSTANTIUS

If it were permitted to contend with your greatness on equal terms; if honors, age, and merit—which have placed a torch before you—did not force us into the shadows, I would rather justly blame your high office for abstaining from letters: ever since you departed for the city of Rome, you have lifted me up with no harvest of remembrance.

But observe, through the providence of circumstances, how cautious the arrangement of elders is, and how full of speech it is: innocence is forestalled by complaints, and, lest it bring its pain into the light, it is accused. It is made guilty so that it may not act.

So these were the promises you gave me when you departed? Was it with such confidence that you raised me up with a kiss, so that I might believe you would become forgetful of me? Or for what other purpose were pages assigned than to reveal the secrets of hearts with the key of the mouth?

But I refrain from a lengthy letter, lest prolonged conversation produce a greater bitterness. I return to the service of greetings, asking that you pour out prayers for me before God’s apostles, so that through their benefits the obscurity of mortal limitation may be overcome, and a serene mind may rejoice on the pure path of the heavenly commandments.

## LETTER XXIV. ENNODIUS TO LACONIUS

The heavenly dispensation has rightly granted effect to your good wishes, and, by fostering brotherly diligence through the occasion of a busy conversation, has made what was thought necessary become desirable.

Hence heavenly care commanded that a suitor for my niece, not altogether a stranger to our blood, should approach, so that, while the opportunity for consultation pressed, nourishment might be provided for holy love. I confess that I could scarcely endure the long silence concerning the undertaking; but I thought that a gentler interpreter should apply to fear what was being withdrawn from affection.

Thanks be to God, who has restored your brotherhood to the use of the pen and to grace. [Note: [Col. 0099D] “Yet by divine laws.” Marriages between relatives were restrained both by divine and by human laws, civil as well as canonical. In the sacred Scriptures among the Hebrews, provision was made concerning a few very close relationships; the prohibition generally went no farther than forbidding a man to marry the daughter of his brother or sister. [Col. 0100D] There is a threefold discussion of this matter in the works of Sirmond. Christian emperors also forbade cousins to marry, as did Theodosius, attributing so much, to use the words of Sextus Victor, to modesty and continence that he prohibited the marriages of cousins as though they were marriages between siblings. Therefore they could not be contracted without the emperor’s permission, as the formula of Cassiodorus declares, by which a cousin becomes a lawful wife. Ecclesiastical laws, which today define incestuous marriages as those within the fourth degree, once extended as far as the seventh degree. In Ennodius’s age, however, the custom was still more indulgent. For the canons concerning this matter generally stopped within the degrees forbidden by the sacred Scriptures and the laws of the emperors, as in the Council of Agde, canon 61; the Council of Epaone, canon 30; and the Third Council of Orléans, canon 10. Thus, whether you interpret “divine laws” here as those contained in the sacred Scriptures, or understand him to call the sacred canons by that name—as the Greeks commonly say *θείους κανόνας* (“divine canons”) and the Latins “divine rules”—the distinction was small at that time.]

Nevertheless, you should know without hesitation that, according to divine laws, a relationship included within the indicated degree may lawfully be joined in marriage. But I am immediately sending my men to the city of Rome to obtain from the venerable pope an answer concerning this matter, so that the authority of a superior command may strengthen your mind.

My lord, receiving a fullest greeting, know also that the holy and common father shares the same opinion. If divine favor permits, I shall send you, through my man, a letter from him together with the chief documents of the apostolic see.

## LETTER XXV. ENNODIUS TO AVITUS

How often the sins of others weigh us down, and what does not arise from us is justly charged to us as an offense! From my own case I have learned that the faithfulness of the ancients does not perish, while the announcement of gray-haired poets is restored through new affairs.

I believe the following was said about me: “The unfortunate man falls through another’s wound” (*Aeneid* 10). The aforesaid polished composition is presented to the son of the memorable man Sabinus. [Note: [Col. 0100D] “The son of Sabinus.” He also writes on behalf of the same man in Letters 13 and 14 of the following book, addressed to the same Avitus.]

Until now he had been held back by the obstacles of illness and had violated an arrangement without fault of his own. I confess that your greatness’s weighty assertion had nearly made my spirit guilty, and I believed the fault to be my own, although my conscience did not possess it.

Behold, as soon as he was restored to good health, he hastened to Milan with the greatest speed. I did not think that anything else needed to be reported to you; for one who commends justice to great men seems to be opposing forgetfulness to equity.

My lord, I offer the gift of a fullest greeting. For the rest, I ask that the state of your favor toward me, although already complete, may nevertheless be compelled to receive further increase.

## LETTER XXVI. ENNODIUS TO AGAPITUS

Sins resist desires, and, so that the condition of the merits of those who offend may become known to them, what is desired is withdrawn from the proximity of the lips. Things granted afflict us more sharply when they perish. Thirst is stronger than the taste of water makes it; benefits denied at the very outset do not burn the memory; who could bear with equanimity the sweetness placed before his eyes and then lost?

Yet these matters are rightly referred to heavenly providence, whose heavenly dispensation of the mystery places its hand against human arrangements for this very reason: that it may bring about the fulfillment of prayers.

Your holy father had willingly promised, on the occasion of my request, that he would obey the command of your greatness; but, as he says, plans arising for the benefit of the Church carried his mind in another direction, as the letter mentioned above and sent to you makes clear.

Nevertheless, concerning the matter specified, he awaits further conversations with your greatness, so that it may be made more evident that I am necessary to the interests of your brother Faustus the patrician, whose favor he considers himself in no way free to diminish.

For the rest, having accepted the humility of my service, I ask that the craftsman who has deigned to pour care for my smallness into your high office [Note: [Col. 0100D] “Into your high office.” I would rather read *culmini vestro* (“into your high office”). But *ἀπέχω* (“I keep away” or “I refrain”).] may himself, through you, arrange what ought to follow.

## LETTER XXVII. ENNODIUS TO EUGENETUS

The tireless efforts of the silence you have brought about trouble me beyond measure. Although my spirit is stationed at its post, the abstinence from speech saddens me; through living images, it reveals the secrecy of the heart with the key of the mouth.

At times I endure the appearance of affection being imitated through the publication of pages; yet I never believe that those who love abstain from such duties. Your greatness may perhaps report that concern with public occupations left no room for familiar letters. But the same condition existed when, in an earlier period, your high office frequently provided conversations; nor was he so burdened by courtly duties [Note: [Col. 0100D] “By palace guards.” The palatine quaestorship, which he held, as stated in the note to Book IV, Letter 26.] that he had no memory of promised love.

Who secretly mixed poison with honey? Who mixed filth with fountains? Or perhaps did you bring before judgment what had been stolen from affection? But I do not delay to seize you through the publication of pages, so that, when the goads of your promised favor have ceased, you may return to your former practice, provoked at least by the fruit of my chatter.

My lord, rendering the service of a greeting with complete humility, I declare that I long to be presented to your sight; if it is nevertheless to be done, write back after considering what I do not doubt is close to your heart.

## BOOK SIX

[Col. 0101]

## LETTER I. ENNODIUS TO PARTHENIUS

[Note: [Col. 0101D] Parthenius. Several letters in the preceding book have taught us that he was the son of Ennodius’s sister; in them Ennodius commended Parthenius as he was setting out for Rome for the sake of study. But he nowhere indicates his sister’s name. That she was not Euprepia is shown by the fact that Euprepia’s only son was called Lupicinus, not Parthenius. Moreover, Euprepia was a widow, whereas Parthenius’s father was still alive, Book VII, Letters 30 and 31.

He celebrates Parthenius’s nobility and favorable beginnings in learning in *Diction* 4 of the *Scholastica*, in which he gave thanks to a grammarian when Parthenius recited well; see also Book VI, Letter 23. These arguments lead me to conjecture that this was the Parthenius who eventually became master of offices and patrician. To him there survives an elegiac poem by Arator, which we shall produce in Book IX; it commemorates his exceptional learning joined with nobility of birth, as well as his various embassies.]

[Col. 0101A]

If I did not love you passionately, and if the solidity of a devout heart did not stand firm with an unchanging root, I could be stirred by the pain of your injuries—either when you behave childishly in anger or when you make arrogant supplication. For I find nothing more arrogant than humility deliberately fabricated. I prefer insults to the services of a feigned expression: simulated sweetness overcomes bitterness. There is no need for entreaties if you understand what chain binds you. Let those whose obedience is free ask pardon for their excesses. The splendor of heavenly judgment has appointed servants for us in such a way that, wherever the mind has turned aside, their necessity is bent toward it. He waits mercifully who, if he wishes, can reject the authority that has been imposed.

[Col. 0101B] The power attributed to me by God will not allow you to stray far from this order. You should pray that the just consideration of your merits may not disfigure the gentleness that you praise in me, and that the multitude of your faults may not cheapen the path of piety. Although, if I am not mistaken, vengeance mercifully accompanies the one who errs, and no patience is better than that which does not open an entrance to vices, nevertheless let my indignation depart from you: for what you have done wrong will be chastised by blows, not by suppressed anger preserved through deceptive favor. Now you will be able to force the wounds inflicted by intemperate speech into a single scar in one way: if liberal study shows you to be a freeborn man through the heights of learning. You will not demand pardon unless expertise comes to your aid; having changed the rule of sparing that you know me to follow, I shall preserve severity toward persistent idleness.

For the rest, I pray God that you may be well and, accompanied by heavenly favor in your verses, increase the hope that you have given.

## LETTER II. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

The arrival of a messenger is the highest of joys when, by the necessities of his own affairs, he ministers to the wishes of others and serves the purposes of diligence. Honesty commends this man, and the modesty of a stranger to the merchant’s profession recommends him; moreover, the fact that he knows your high position has added credibility to his integrity. For as he traveled I was nourished by the fruits of his revered letter. I therefore return the deposit, bound by the law of duty; and the letter that I received in Liguria, according to my modest abilities,

[Col. 0101D] I send onward, accompanied by a written petition, to the highest patronage.

[Col. 0102A] For the rest, we offer your Reverence whatever devotion our humility possesses, praying that, because of the constancy of my letters, I may already deserve to receive a letter from you.

## LETTER III. ENNODIUS TO EUPREPIA

The course of all things is constituted by the service of the body and the rule of souls: heavenly kinship ennobles one thing, while earthly abasement submits another. Nor is it permitted that, wherever the mind bestowed by God the Father has turned, what has been taken from the lowest places should fail to follow; nor is it lawful for a soldier to raise a hand against the decrees of the emperor. Hence Crispus asserted that we share one thing with the gods and another with beasts.

[Note: [Col. 0102D] Sallust, in *Catiline*.]

By reason of this hidden bond we travel with absent persons, and, while our limbs remain healthy, we burn with the fevers of those we love. Through these bonds we are not separated by any interruption of travel; though divided by our dwellings, we come together in our desires. You know, venerable sister—and you have surpassed every sweetness in my regard—the occasion that would have required this preface. Now I shall meet you openly and with a face lavish of modesty.

I could scarcely endure the endearments you had previously sent; after my admonition you poured twice as much honey into your letters, enough to shake the whole secret recesses of the heart and to transfer my captive soul from its bodily dwelling into longing for you. I fear that affection may once again be sent back into uncertainty, and that, when the whole mind has spread the sails of devotion, it may suffer danger after its anchorage has been withdrawn.

You have recognized that my spirit is ignorant of disguise; it cannot assume the shameful urbanity of lovers.

[Col. 0102C] Your sex and nature, on the other hand, promise something different, as the wisest Solomon says: “A soul that is sated plays with honeycombs” (Proverbs 27:7).

[Note: [Col. 0102D] “A soul that is in satiety”] Cassian, *Conferences* 14, chapter 13: “A soul that is in satiety plays with honeycombs.” This is the reading of the interpreters of the Septuagint: **Ψυχὴ ἐν πλησμονῇ οὖσα κηρίοις ἐμπαίζει**—“A soul that is in satiety plays with honeycombs.” The Vulgate differs little: “A sated soul will trample the honeycomb.”]

The witness and judge of my words knows that I have resolved—unless perhaps I am deceived by the treacherous flavor of favor and you withdraw the cups offered to one thirsting after the love he has tasted—to fulfill not a likeness but the very reality of a spiritual marriage. Thus, when it has been established that between us there is one will and one refusal, we may display before the eyes and minds of all either what urges the good to imitation or what afflicts the wicked.

You need only promise, with God between us, that against every assault born of envy you will preserve a firm and unchanging constancy. Therefore, farewell, my lady, and content yourself with this brief admonition concerning matters of the greatest importance. Neither the elegance of a letter permits more, nor ought the reasoning of our inmost thoughts to be entrusted to pages. If you respond in wish and faith to what has been indicated, promise it by the testimony of a letter written in your own hand.

## LETTER IV. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

I did not write to burden you with the bitter indication of my misfortune, but to appeal to your concern so that you might persist in your prayers. A labor imposed upon my eyes before they had recovered their former health has afflicted them; all light has departed from me in your company. It is enough that I have indicated what I suffer. It is your part to ask from God, whom you appease with prayers, my recovery, and to aid me with frequent conversations that open the doors of correspondence. My lord, I ask God to grant that you may indicate to me something that I shall be glad to learn.

[Col. 0103B]

## LETTER V. ENNODIUS TO AURELIANUS

My confidence has not been stripped bare by foreknown outcomes. He is strong in affection whom I have rightly promised, in my mind, to be mindful of devotion. Thanks to you, heavenly dispensation, which grants the fruit of prosperity to human affairs through the occasion of adversity and does not allow sad things to remain in their appointed order.

I do not know what hostile malice has torn from your greatness in the abundance of your patrimony; nevertheless, under the title of the most invincible lord, it has acquired a very rich grace. The loss of property is good if, through it, one finds the recognition of a glorious prince. There is no need to fear a diminution of means if, through him who surpasses all riches,

[Col. 0103C] the love of the supreme Lord is acquired. Moreover, that diminution, since it became the mother of gain and the path to honors, could not retain the substance of the humility imposed upon you. What the enemy took has been restored in such a way that you may still await an accumulation of joys. What remains is held in hope, since it has fallen to your high position already to possess the greatest things.

With heaven as author, let us join to these benefits the blessings of our acquaintance and fellowship. When would it have fallen to me to know so great a man except through the circumstances I have mentioned? But may heaven increase what it bestows, and may divine care lead us to the desires toward which we stretch.

For the rest, farewell, my lord, and nurture one who loves you with frequent conversation. If the elegance of a letter did not have a limit prescribed by rule, my joys would pour themselves out into many words.

## LETTER VI. ENNODIUS TO BOETHIUS

[Note: [Col. 0103D] To Boethius] This is Enodius’s second letter to Boethius; the first appears to be Letter 12 of the following book. Thus what we observed is unquestionably true: the sequence of Enodius’s letters is not everywhere correct. The manuscripts already vary in the spelling of the name. Some write *Boetius*, others *Boethius*; the latter would indeed be more correct if the Greek origin of the word were considered. Usage, however, has prevailed so that we generally say *Boetius*. Even in earlier times inscribed stones varied, as in this one at the suburban church of blessed Agnes in Rome:

> VALENS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, COUNT, DEPOSITED  
>   
> ON THE KALENDS OF JULY, DURING THE CONSULSHIP OF BOETHIUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS.

And differently in the four-columned portico of Saint Laurence outside the walls:

> A NOBLE EUNUCH, DEPOSITED  
>   
> IN PEACE ON THE SEVENTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF OCTOBER, DURING THE CONSULSHIP OF BOETIUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS.]

A single letter would indeed have been enough to answer your greatness plainly; once one has become obligated, one ought not to double one’s conversations. Yet I have come to this not through ignorance but through caution. Of the two letters, one fulfills a duty, while the other is offered to affection. Believe me: I considered it wrong not to return with interest what your revered mind had first bestowed. Good things are sweeter when preceded by an example; nor does the man who enters the path of friendship fruitfully possess only a little strength or talent. He cannot claim grace for himself summarily when form is granted to love; it is shameless not to respond to affection when the outcome reveals the virtue of a good beginning.

I wrote this hurriedly because of the messenger’s speed. Hereafter I shall spread my words more broadly; nor, while I consider your merits, shall I look upon the weakness of my own talent—provided that you grant my wishes the convenience of frequent letters. My lord, offering the service of an abundant greeting, I ask that your uninterrupted conversations make clear that you retain a memory of our closeness.

## LETTER VII. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

It has been a long time since, suspended upon genuine desires, I have been nourished solely by the service of letters. For when I address your greatness, I consider myself not to be absent from the sight I long for. Yet the mind of one who suffers grows sick even from its remedies; and the more nourishment for devotion it finds, the more it wastes away from fasting on the fruit of love.

Truly, my lord—as surely as God preserves your eyes safe—if either the strength of my body had allowed it or my lord’s haste had permitted it, I would have sought Ravenna with all the power of my desire. But, if God wills, with my lord your father and my lady your mother in good health, I shall come after Easter with heavenly assistance, so that, after seeing you, I may recover my strength for life through your help.

[Col. 0104C] My lord, offering you my fullest greeting, I ask that you earnestly arrange for all the saints to pray for me.

## LETTER VIII. ENNODIUS TO SENARIUS

Although, because of my sins, even the consolations of your letters are withdrawn from me, I nevertheless do not omit writing, mindful of the obligation by which, through your favor, you bound me as people mindful of God. I hope, lord Senarius, that you will always heed the God whom you have conceived in me, and that you will frequently grant me the gift of your letters. My lord, I greet you with the utmost respect in the customary manner, and I implore you not to cease praying to God for my affliction in all the basilicas of the saints.

## LETTER IX. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

[Col. 0104D]

Although the innocence of his office stands beside the bishop for his protection, and one who has surpassed humanity by profession has no need of human consolations, nevertheless almighty God knows that I have devoted conversation, at the command of the holy bishop who conveys this letter, after being pressed to do so.

[Col. 0105A] For I resisted for a long time, lest it should seem arrogant,

[Note: [Col. 0105D] “If a minister should address the bishop”] A deacon addressing a bishop. **Diaconus** means “minister.” Thus those whom we now call *deacons* in Greek, they also simply called ministers. Commodianus:

> TO THE MINISTERS.  
>   
> Exercise Christ’s ministry, deacons, chastely.  
>   
> Therefore, ministers, carry out the master’s commands.  
>   
> Do not flee the person of the just judge.  
>   
> Complete your office, instructed in all things.  
>   
> Looking upward, always devoted to the supreme God.  
>   
> Return to God the sacred ministries of the altar, unharmed in every respect.  
>   
> Be ready to give an example in different circumstances.  
>   
> You yourselves bow your heads to the shepherds.  
>   
> Thus you will become approved by Christ’s people.]

—if a minister should address the bishop, and before the most holy conscience should assert himself as scarcely even moderately important. But perfect obedience consists in not refusing whatever the highest authority demands. Therefore, having offered the bishop the service of the greeting due to a superior, I ask you to bring aid for the consolation of one weighed down by many assaults, so that, performing an act of exceptional goodness, you may not allow a deserving priest to remain subject to prolonged sadness.

## LETTER X. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

May God, who has implanted in your mind a love of good works, himself protect the one who serves him in the greatest happiness throughout a long life. For although the innocence that you cherish keeps unceasing watch on your behalf, those bound by your benefits cannot suppress the prayers they owe God for you, since even God constituted in the flesh abhorred failing to return thanks for benefits received.

Would that I were able to contribute as much through words to your affairs as I feel I owe! Nevertheless, I do not omit to suggest what concerns another service owed to you: order that the document you drew up in the case of Laurentianus, registrar of Como, be completed and sent to me; and, concerning that blind woman whom Martinus the lessee is oppressing at Moditia, obtain a letter from the count of the patrimony ordering him to restore without delay the slave whom he took from her. For, with rustic insolence, he scorns to do what he has now been commanded.

[Note: [Col. 0106D] “Of Moditia”] Moditia, that is, Modoetia, a Ligurian town not far from Milan, where the kings of the Lombards and of Italy were once crowned. *Moditia* was written for *Modoetia* with the same freedom allowed by antiquarians, just as *mira* was written for *moera*—that is, **μοῖρα**—in Sidonius, and *metici* for *metoeci*—**μέτοικοι**—in an old panegyric by a Gallic author.]

## LETTER XI. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

[Col. 0105C] When our common lord Faustus, Avienus’s father,

[Note: [Col. 0106D] “Our common lord”] Faustus, Avienus’s father.]

departed from the city of Milan, the only consolations that remained for me were the consolations of letters. For when speech is directed to you, some image of your presence flatters my desires. I ask this also of you, my lords: do it frequently, reflecting that your absence can be endured only through such constancy. Let those who are most fortunate possess the presence they desire; for me, who reflect upon my sins, the care of correspondence will suffice.

My lord, offering my fullest greeting, I ask that you not cease to pour out prayers for me through the saints of the Lord, and give thanks to the Lord, whose benefits toward me are granted even beyond hope.

## LETTER XII. ENNODIUS TO LIBERIUS, EUGENETUS, AGAPITUS, SENARIUS, AND ALBINUS

More ample pages are needed when the messenger’s reliability falters. Through your deacon Stephanus, who lovingly serves me, a brief conversation is sufficient. Passing beyond letters spread out into many words, he prefers what is necessary to what is abundant, since, in condensing a faithful secret,

[Col. 0106A] he does not suppress what must be reported.

For the rest, announcing that I am well, with God’s favor, I inquire into the good state of your affairs and offer the full service of a greeting, praying that the integrity of your favor may not strip my confidence bare.

## LETTER XIII. ENNODIUS TO AVITUS

Another person’s necessity makes me importunate, because I ought to speak on behalf of one who is asking. The law of the purpose of intercession rejects greed; for it is added to the burden on my conscience if I reject a suppliant.

Sabinus’s son, whose memory is to be awaited, came on the appointed day to await the judgment. But he was compelled, for practical reasons, to seek his little estate, because both the guarantor and the executor were absent when the appointed day passed. The bearer of my message impelled me, although I had sworn that I would no longer demean myself in the matter mentioned above, to send him word so that he might appear again; I indicate that I have done so.

Now, offering you the services of my greeting, I leave it to your high position, in the case of the man mentioned, to show what the justice you uphold and the confidence you have given may deserve.

## LETTER XIV. ENNODIUS TO AVITUS

I know that my silences cry out before you, and that nothing happens which is not grasped by a secret interpretation. Nevertheless, I have not ceased writing; nor have I withdrawn from judgment, by contrived ingenuity, the son of Sabinus, a man of exalted memory, who, after suffering violence on his little estate, is said to have continued working with the barbarians until now.

Believe me,

[Col. 0106C] he will appear when the inquiry proceeds and will enter your discussion without any fear. My lord, offering you the reverence of a greeting, I ask that you consider me worthy of being supported by the memory of the affection long implanted in you.

## LETTER XV. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

Heavenly providence arranges matters well: whenever benefits are requested from me, my concern finds messengers eager to fulfill my wishes. Let me cease denying to others what I grant to myself, and restraining through sordid greed what relieves the giver.

The bearer of this letter, Pertinax, a young man of the highest nobility, has attempted to seek Rome, the birthplace and seat of learning. He believed that it would bring him an exceptional advantage if he reached your high position under the guidance of a letter.

I did not wish to withhold what he desired, knowing that it is characteristic of your custom to grant what others accomplish only after being entreated. Now, my lord, accepting the services of my greeting, see to it that the hardships of his journey do not weigh him down; and do not cease to relieve me, through the frequent correspondence I have secured, by sending the pages that you receive as a consolation in affection.

## LETTER XVI. ENNODIUS TO LUMINOSUS

Conversations that love finds as a remedy for itself ought not to be burdensome, nor should the service of religion summon us to necessary transactions. It would be sweet if the duties of letters served concord alone, and if devotion were not diverted into the pursuit of advantage.

But matters have reached the point that, unless the mature affection which took its beginning between us from the very light of life and, through the various strengths of our progress, brought the harvest of grace to the threshing floor, rises under compulsion at the goad of my writing on my behalf, I shall be struck by the barren sterility of great ingratitude and loss.

[Note: [Col. 0107D] See Letter 33 below.]

Your greatness remembers

[Col. 0107B] the conversation you had with me concerning the expenses my bishop had incurred at Ravenna, when I promised to repay him, for the benefit of the apostolic see. You had promised a prompt result regarding their repayment; but, because of my sins, some circumstance intervened. The attention of the bishop mentioned above has now turned toward me, so that he has scarcely granted me a delay for sending someone to the sacred city.

Now the matter rests, after God, with you. You can rescue me from both the offense of my bishop and the losses, so that the duty of loyalty may not appear to have produced misfortune for me alone. My lord, offering the gifts of my greeting, I pray the Lord to move your mind without delay to consider my interests. I could find nothing more to do except to send, together with a clear statement of the case, a messenger faithful to me.

## LETTER XVII. ENNODIUS TO MARCELLINUS, BISHOP

The favor of the magnificent man, your son Stephanion, makes it possible for me to come before your Blessedness to be read. Through his kindness the affection of the journey suffers no loss, and what presence cannot accomplish is compensated for by speech.

Presenting, therefore, the services owed to your apostolate, I ask that you raise me up through the support of your prayers, so that, inserted into your venerable conscience, I may deserve to rejoice in every fruit of your favor. For I do not doubt that your crown will answer the confidence I place in you.

## LETTER XVIII. ENNODIUS TO DOMNICA

Your greatness has done what it owes both to its holy character and to its blood: it has not allowed the memory of kinship to grow weak through the torpor of silence. Wherever in the world kinship lives, relations joined by the chain of parentage are not separated by regions.

Believe me, holy affection does not perish, nor does nature suffer any loss through the roads of separation. You should know that your son-in-law has bestowed such love upon me that no repayment would be adequate in return.

For the rest, my lady, accepting the affection of the greeting due to you, I pray God to grant us an opportunity to see you in mutual happiness,

[Col. 0108A] so that, amid the conversation we desire, our pious longings may be lifted up.

## LETTER XIX. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

After the opportunity to see you slipped away from my desires, my mind turns once again to letters. It is forced to ask for the page-based support it had renounced, and to nourish or sustain a soul established among better resources by an exchange that is, as it were, poorer food.

O how grievous it is whenever fugitive freedom, driven away by various necessities from one who serves, leads him to new arrangements! Hard things are broken by continued endurance; habit cuts away much of the burden’s weight; a woeful condition leads one to hopes that will not endure; the lot of one occupied by continual cares is lighter.

I am more unhappy because of the burden of my sins, since I have tasted the flavor of good things. But more on this elsewhere. Matters that human counsel cannot remedy must be left to God.

Meanwhile, offering you the reverence of a greeting, I have not failed to indicate my return, wishing to be relieved by the equal cheerfulness of your correspondence.

## LETTER XX. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

The flavor of good things is unknown amid prosperity; the quality of a heavenly benefit is scarcely recognized while it is possessed. After departure, what was desired becomes sweet; while the prizes of desire are in our hands, we do not know their value.

I openly confess that, as long as Ravenna possessed you, I thought it an evil omen to consider what I now suffer. Nor, amid favorable circumstances, did I sigh over what might happen through your absence, as though I were a malicious interpreter of my own happiness.

I ought not to have recognized my merits if I were not separated from a human being, nor to have understood that what flatters the pursuer of sins is fleeting. But why does the elegance of a letter exceed the disciplined limit of expression? May he whose command all things obey bring healing to these circumstances.

For my part, I am physically well, on account of which these pages were assigned to me; and through these duties, with God’s help, I await news of your prosperity. Receive, therefore, my services; and if any favorable outcome has brought about something among the matters that you have learned are being handled with me, report it without the obstacle of concealment.

## LETTER XXI. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

On this occasion I seized the opportunity to fulfill my humble duty through a household messenger. What you have arranged effectively in the affairs of others will serve my desires.

I confess that I thought it harsh to deny letters to one who was nearer, since, when placed far away, I was never able to abstain from conversation. For I seemed to myself, occupied with the watches of Ravenna, to have touched your greatness with a certain dexterity of mind.

Therefore I extended my writing for the relief of my desire, so that I might compensate through reading for what was taken from me in living speech. Thus, offering the honor of a greeting, I ask that, whenever opportunity arises, you raise me up with remedies of this kind, in which divine providence has granted absence its one support.

You have recognized what treatment a languishing affection requires; it is your part not to deny healing to sick minds.

## LETTER XXII. ENNODIUS TO EUGENETUS

Diligence is the cause of many pages. It is owed to your Reverence that I do not refrain from writing. A voice that has received the testimony of joy cannot fail, since I received the news of your good health with gladness. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIII. ENNODIUS TO PARTHENIUS

With God’s favor, may the beginnings of your affection grow strong; may he be present to our common desires, through whom studies acquire their strength.

You have declared that, by the light of your writing, you already possess a city friendly to liberal studies. You sent ahead, at the threshold, something that would surpass the greedy hopes of parents. I am not a rigid judge of your expression, nor do I reject the slightness of what is present when what is to follow offers promise.

[Col. 0109B] Whenever we write upon the earth with ploughshares, the spirit is lifted by hope of the coming crop. A friend of reason always understands the wealth of ears of grain among the grasses.

[Note: [Col. 0109D] Perhaps “of sowing.”]

The diligent cultivator, while the blossoms of the apples are still white, already measures out whole orchards. Let adversity depart, and let whatever sins produce withdraw. The course of your little speech, although it is not sustained by the brilliance of eloquence, nevertheless shone with the flavor of the Latin vein. The discourse flowed without discord, though it must still be enlarged by the resources of reading.

But why have I, like a goose after swans, cackled after so great a judge, whose mouth you have signaled that you wished to please with the elegance of your work? Whoever has pleased him enters the examination without fear; the eloquence he has praised is strong enough to demand favor even from enemies.

Work, therefore, so that a fortunate outcome may exalt your good beginning. Devote yourself unceasingly to the service of honorable men. Those who pollute themselves through association with their own kind, while you owe reverence to our admonitions, flee like a cup of poison. Announce to me always, through your pages, that you are advancing, for I desire to know it.

For the rest, farewell, and, aided by every assistance of heavenly favor, repay your household with the harvest of your expertise.

## LETTER XXIV. ENNODIUS TO ARCHOTAMIA

[Note: [Col. 0110D] To Archotamia, a kinswoman at Arles; Book VII, Letter 14.]

Although the right of affection, bound by the law of kinship, does not perish through the length of regions, nor is the chain of ancestry that links souls divided by the separation of lands, nevertheless the nourishment of love is either to see the one whom you love or to address that person through the service of speech. The secrets of minds would not be known if tongues did not reveal them. Antiquity brought these things into use so that what is enclosed in hearts would not remain hidden.

Although I do not see Gaul—which claims all of me on your account—with my eyes, I do not abandon it in affection. Yet thanks are due to the bearer of this letter, who, on the occasion of his own necessity, served my desires, offering the desired service amid the fervors of souls where no messenger was available.

Greeting you with the service due to you, I ask that the bearer receive a return for his kindness, and that the man who assisted my joy may believe that, through me, his wishes have received the fulfillment restored to them.

## LETTER XXV. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

Your greatness knows with what prejudicial honor the followers of liberal studies honor me, asking for the support of my recommendation in writing as though it were something owed to them. It is customary for you to contribute benefits and for me to contribute words, while the magnitude of the matters surpasses the desire of the petitioner.

If I refrain from these duties, while the character of your gifts remains safe, I shall not possess the good will of one who seeks a favor. The bearer of this letter, Pertinax, will be publicly known before you by the modesty of his birth. He intends to make good use of the virtue of modesty in support of his lineage.

Through him, having sent you indications of my health for the sake of your desire, I ask that he receive from the harvest of your favor the rich fruit of his confidence. Whenever the desired course of travelers comes near, send me pages to lift me up, like those that you receive as a consolation in affection.

## LETTER XXVI. ENNODIUS TO EUPREPIA

Silence is owed to necessity, but writing to devotion. Fear demands abstinence from letters, but sometimes affection will yield. The mind of one who loves scarcely gives way to any obstacles; rather, when it is forbidden, it preserves itself for returning the services of gratitude.

Behold, I have explained beforehand the reason that would have kept me from these duties; I leave it to your conscience to determine what will make me serve you. Nevertheless, after praying to God, I indicate that I am in good health and that our Lupicinus is well. I wish to learn from you the things that I have extended through my writing.

Yet I do not want you to burden your concern with the weight of the pledge kept apart. Believe my conscience: I owe him more through devotion than you yourself could have displayed through nature. May heavenly benefits improve his talent!

I speak truly: as you both depart for farther places, the concern of both parents falls upon me, which, while we were together, we were able to share with ambition.

My lady, offering you my fullest greeting, I ask that you grant me as much support of affection and prayer as you have seen me striving toward the fulfillment of my desire for you.

## LETTER XXVII. ENNODIUS TO SENARIUS

May an abundant return, through heavenly dispensation, accompany your conscience; may the Most High repay, in accordance with my smallness, what he recognizes as having been bestowed by you, who have always proved faithful to those who love you.

To have found the devotion of your heart is a sure harbor. You possess this character: you surpass the hope of friends by the bestowal of benefits. I desire a second admonition, so that I may undertake the journey assigned to me.

Give a fortunate hand to my humility and share your prosperity with me. My lord, offering the services of a greeting, I ask that, if the master of affairs is staying happily at Ravenna, you inform me so that I may fulfill your commands without uncertainty.

## LETTER XXVIII. ENNODIUS TO GUDILEVUS

Those to whom happiness and power are granted by God’s ordering customarily console the humble through the service of letters and share their prosperity by making it known in pages. I waited a long time to be raised up by such duties.

But since you have ceased, I considered it necessary not to remain silent, so that what love does not demand may, in accordance with the Gospel reading, be obtained by persistence.

My lord, offering you my fullest greeting, I ask that you cherish me, your old servant, with the affection you once promised. Make me acquainted with your prosperity by sending your pages.

## LETTER XXIX. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

Although I would have entrusted the services of letters to the most exalted and wholly upright man Sabinus,

[Note: [Col. 0111D] S. V. Sabinus] Rome had a prefect of the grain supply of this name a few years later. The following epitaph remains in the basilica at Ostia, though it is engraved very incorrectly:

> HERE RESTS IN PEACE SABINUS, VIR SPECTABILIS,  
> PREFECT OF THE GRAIN SUPPLY, WHO LIVED  
> FIFTY-THREE YEARS AND  
>   
> [Col. 0112D] TWENTY-FOUR DAYS. DEPOSITED ON THE FIFTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF AUGUST, DURING THE CONSULSHIP OF SYMMACHUS  
>   
> AND BOETHIUS, VIR CLARISSIMI.]

as he hastened to Rome, so that a faithful messenger might affirm through letters what needed to be disclosed, nevertheless I owed it to my concern to inform your greatness through two indications, so that the messenger, following the beginning of the letter, might undertake the narrative.

This brief taste in writing is sufficient; I return to the matter for which the letter is being sent. I announce that I am physically well, praying to God that he may restore the condition of my soul through your prosperity.

## LETTER XXX. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

The infancy of my speech cannot express the magnitude of the grief that came to me from that matter, because you refrained from writing when the bearers of these letters were being sent to Liguria. I did not believe that you were unaware of their journey, and I understood the presence of your greatness from the character of the petition; for it is possible to discover the person who handles matters among those who are prepared.

Yet the holidays of your letters burn me, since, even when you were most occupied, you rejected them as a relief for my grief. Now I return to my desires. Farewell,

[Note: [Col. 0112D] “My lords”] Perhaps “my lord,” as often elsewhere.]

my lords, and reveal the heavenly grace around you through frequent conversation. For your actions have produced the result that, in a time of rest, you may rejoice in the harvest of innocence sown amid hardships.

## LETTER XXXI. ENNODIUS TO THE LORD POPE

The ever-watchful care of your Blessedness attends to those who serve you as though they were placed before you, wherever they may be, and, without any interruption, grants the support of favor to those who have experienced it while inviting strangers as well. Indeed, many benefits are gained from the spectacle of another’s labor, because a person learns to work when rewards for sweat and loyalty are rendered before his eyes.

Would that the outcome were equal to my wishes, and that I might be granted the opportunity to fulfill what I have learned for the sake of religion! My lord, presenting the humility of my service and content with a brief expression amid matters of great importance, I leave it to the letter of the aforesaid messenger to disclose what your brother, the lord bishop, thought about the embassy sent to him.

## LETTER XXXII. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

[Col. 0111D]

Although exchanges of letters are always pleasant among those who love one another, and from such services extensive joys arise even when Spartan brevity is employed; although such duties are a remedy for the absent and a desired consolation for the anxious, nevertheless a sick mind is tossed about concerning the prosperity of those upon whom it depends, and breathes again only through this treatment.

When the person who is uncertain about nothing denies this treatment to the anxious, he reveals that he is not held by devotion. The conversations sent by your greatness nourished my mind for a long time and provided food suitable to cheerfulness. Their present absence does not bring sadness alone, but compels me toward destruction.

What previously served affection could have given aid to my health; the religion of love has been renounced when words beneficial to my health are denied me. You have recognized what your silences have done; remedy them by correction. For, if forgetfulness of me does not rule you, they are changed by writing.

My lord, returning the most generous greeting, I pray God that the arrangement of heavenly favor may meet my burning distress and cause you to indicate to me, for the consolation of my sorrows, those things that I shall be glad to learn.

## LETTER XXXIII. ENNODIUS TO HORMISDAS AND DIOSCORUS

[Col. 0112B]

I know that a religious conscience considers it a great gain when an opportunity arises to render a service, especially to those whom it remembers to have been devoted. Therefore, although the primary reason for sending a letter is reverence, and a statement of practical benefit ought to be added to the service, nevertheless an anxious mind often places necessities before affection.

Your fraternity remembers that the lord pope promised to repay the expense that my bishop had incurred at Ravenna for his benefit, with me as guarantor. But circumstances have made it so that he scarcely granted time for someone to be sent to you, and he declares that satisfaction must be made to him from my resources.

Now, since the sum demanded is not large, and since it is the greatest benefit to withdraw me from an ingratitude that appears justified, arrange matters so that heavenly repayment may compensate you.

My lord, returning a most abundant greeting, I ask God to inspire your minds with whatever may be able to raise me up. For my part, I have done my duty: together with an expression of grief, I sent through these pages a most faithful messenger who may receive without diminution what he must bring back to us.

## LETTER XXXIV. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS ALBUS
Although your greatness has, by your prolonged silence, declared that you have forgotten me, and, by abstaining from the duties of correspondence, has cast aside the memory of one who serves you, nevertheless heavenly providence does not permit your favorable circumstances toward my desires to remain concealed; by various indications it discloses the desired success attending you. Yet now my spirit has been drawn to such a degree of attachment that I have sent to you a personal messenger, who, nourished by the sight of your living presence, may bring back to me clear reports of your well-being. Believe me, my lords, that I am bound to you by a great obligation, and that no intervals are granted to my heart in which I do not seek your presence with complete attention. It remains that, when concord has been restored in the Roman Church,

[Note: “The concord of the Church restored”: “The disturbances of the Laurentian schism having been quieted.”]

an opportunity may arise for me to come to you. My lord, offering you the fullest greeting of reverence, I beg you graciously to receive the message of my bearer, my servant, and to inform us, through a returning communication, of your happiness and of the condition of your entire household.

## LETTER XXXV. ENNODIUS TO DOMNINA

Amid the cares and troubles to which I am subjected beneath the burden of sins, I chose this singular support: to send a letter to you, my lady, whose prayers would cause everything to turn out favorably for me and would restore me to the clear skies of joy once the clouds of distress had been removed. The first cause of my sorrow is that, while you live far away, your prosperity can scarcely be learned; from this arises every adversity surrounding me. Come, then, to the aid of your suppliant with your prayers, so that, through the intercessions of God’s saints, a remedy may be granted to my ailing spirit. My lady, offering the service of a greeting, I beg and adjure you by the God whom you worship to commend me continually to the Lord in your prayers and tears, by which the kingdom of heaven suffers violence; for I count this a special gift and place it before every advantage.

## LETTER XXXVI. ENNODIUS TO THE PRIEST ADEODATUS

Heavenly providence never denies fulfillment to religious desires; for what we piously wish, it grants with timely diligence. Since I desired to ask through a letter for the assistance of your prayers, a household messenger has brought forth my request, so that, admonished by the spur of this writing, you may pray for the soul entrusted to me—for the teacher of the nations cries out, “Pray for one another” (James 5:16).

[Note: “The teacher of the nations”: He attributes to Paul what belongs to chapter 5 of the Epistle of the Catholic Apostle James.]

For there is nothing that one who loves God cannot obtain, even for those who have sinned. Therefore labor on behalf of the protections you promised long ago, and procure joys for me through your tears. Let the fruit of innocence, unknown to my merits, come to me. These are the matters about which I have presumed to admonish God’s holy servant. I fear making our conversation lengthy, because a necessary request should be made in concise words. Now, my lord, farewell in Christ, and show by favorable indications that I have felt the gifts of your intercession.

## LETTER XXXVII. ENNODIUS TO JOHN

Is it therefore falsely believed that love is returned for diligence, that souls question one another in silent conversations, and that the feeling of minds attests their faith, so that what we provide may be owed to us in reciprocal communication? The secrets of the mountains return the voice, and mute things serve in obedience to human courtesy. Yet it has happened that your greatness has returned silence for my writing, in contempt of me; and, in agreement with an ingenious talent, by refraining from pages, has suppressed the persistence of loquacity, trampling upon the law of nature. Let it be far from my character to follow what I grieve to have been done, or to relieve faults by imitation. Behold, once again I address one who cherishes a holiday from speech, and I pursue you at greater length, retaining the memory of your promised affection. My lord, offering, as above, the most generous greeting, I beg that importunity may now at least demand the debt of gratitude, while you provide for satisfying the ardor of my desire with lengthy conversation.

## LETTER XXXVIII. ENNODIUS TO FIRMINA

Whenever a desired event suddenly occurs, it derives its value from the very brevity of the time. For heavenly providence, so that the power of its benefaction may increase, makes what it grants sudden, lest the prolonged waiting of those who hope should diminish the mercy of the giver. Who, when suddenly receiving what he desires, would not honor what he has obtained with greater eagerness? Thus, thirsting for a letter from your greatness, I received it at the time of my departure. I grieved, I confess, and was deeply distressed, since there was neither a bearer of my attentions nor anyone departing from whom I could learn the good news of your health. Behold, a favorable turn has granted both: I received at once the desired information that I report, and at the same time I announce that, returning from the Cottian Alps,

[Note: “From the Cottian Alps”: This is the route described in the itinerary of Brigantio. Concerning Firmina’s ring, there is an epigram, no. 93.]

I have undertaken a journey to Ravenna. Pray that, tossed amid various hardships and difficulties, I may be infused with the patience that is a gift of heavenly blessing. But as for me, since the splendor of your eminence urges me to preserve your favor, I more readily believe that the courses of rivers can be turned back in different directions, and that, abandoning the nourishment of their streams, fish can seek the empty air, than that offenses could restore me to forgetfulness of such great obligations. For the rest, farewell, my lady, and ceaselessly pray to our Redeemer on behalf of the person entrusted to me.

# BOOK SEVEN

## LETTER I. ENNODIUS TO JULIAN

[Note: “To Julian”: Count of the Patrimony, Book IV, Letter 7.]

We have fulfilled the service of our devotion in accordance with the commands of your greatness, because one who obeys the admonitions of a just man comes close to equity. The character of the business entrusted to be recognized by a friend of truth equips the mind of an upright judge with caution; your greatness’s consideration would have poured affection into us, had our efforts not already done so.

In the case, therefore, that has arisen between Bauton, a tenant of the royal household, and Epiphanius the chartarius, while the outcome of our dispute hung uncertain and the opposing parties clashed in competing claims, Bauton asserted that he could not return the sixty-four public solidi which he had confessed, by issuing a written acknowledgment, that he owed from the remainder of that indiction, because he had given forty solidi to Epiphanius through the hands of the illustrious Projectus as a contribution for support; yet it was shown that no benefit had followed from this payment. Epiphanius replied that, if he had received anything, he had earned it through his labor, and that Bauton had not given him anything without cause; or, whenever the witness produced was brought forward, he continually exalted his credibility with praise. We therefore decreed that the noble Projectus, the aforementioned man, should declare under oath the nature of the benefit that had been hoped for and whether, if the matter stood as alleged, the benefit had failed to follow.

[Note: “Tenant of the royal household”: Those who rented some fiscal estate were called tenants of the Augustan household. There is a title concerning them in the Code, and a law of Valentinian III states that they enjoyed none of the privileges of military rank or dignity. When emperors ruled, it was called the Augustan household; now, under Theoderic, it is the royal household, and its tenants are called tenants of the royal household. See Cassiodorus, Book V, Letter 39. Their cases belonged to the Count of the Patrimony, an office held by Julian. Theoderic wrote to this same Julian, Count of the Patrimony: “The tenants of Apulia have complained to us in a lamentable petition that their grain was burned by the thefts of enemies, asking that they not be compelled to make full payment, since the profits of their commerce have been diminished,” and so forth.]

[Note: “Epiphanius the chartarius”: A funerary stone at Rome reads, LOCUS VALERIANI CHARTARI. But chartarius here does not mean a maker or merchant of paper, but a chartularius of the Count of the Patrimony. This also seems to be the meaning in Athalaric, Book VIII of the Variae, Letter 22, where he mentions the chartarii of the seat of Burgantinus, Count of the Patrimony.]

When this had been done, Epiphanius was to refund the amount of money he had received. It is now within the power of your eminence, if you approve, to support our decision with your authority.

## LETTER II. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

How much interrupted affliction adds to the burden of sorrow, when, in order to make adversity burn more sharply, it flatters us with a change for the better! What burden has ever been increased by throwing off the load of continuous calamity? Long familiarity with time had prepared me well to endure your absence, while I had learned not even to presume upon what happiness did not possess. Behold, once again a new suffering tears me amid old sorrows and a sharper blow reopens the scar that had formed over them. I had begged mercy from you as you departed, asking that what I was losing from present conversation might be compensated by letters; yet, fasting from every desire, I did not earn even this harvest. Faithful to my custom, I compose a letter amid tears, believing that nothing about my affliction should be indicated more clearly, content with the report of the illustrious Lord Pamphronius. Now, my lord, graciously receive the attentions of your servant and grant the customary remedies to a soul placed in distress.

## LETTER III. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

I would rightly have reviewed the prayers with which I implored your greatness as you departed, had I not wished to avoid inflicting insults upon your memory. For when someone who loves you brings up what has recently happened, he improperly opposes to good men the forgetfulness that must be avoided. It is peculiar to those who are united that, under a certain foreknowledge, they mutually supply what each desires; and, through the effective administration of affection, reconcile by an earlier fulfillment what ought to be requested by prayers. Heavenly providence prompts us to do what must be done if you inquire into whatever love desires.

Added to this is the fact that, while you were undertaking your journey, you came to the aid of my fevered soul with many promises, saying that I would have to be sustained by letters because I would be deprived of my own light through your absence. Behold, the promise too limps in its faithfulness, and, irritated by hope, I burn. Confidence born from the anticipation of a remedy has acted through your coming, so that hardships may be endured with greater difficulty. But now, my lord, having received the honor of a greeting, after I have declared to you what is wrong with my spirit, may a swift cure come to my aid, so that whatever is the condition of your health or the favor of your superior may be disclosed to me through awaited communications.

## LETTER IV. ENNODIUS TO AGNELLUS

The pages that have always served your diligence now demand the disclosure of their own sorrow, and have drawn those that conveyed joys into an utterance of the injury that must be revealed. They were not content to cover the secrets of the heart with the cosmetics of polite concealment, either by silence or by transferring them elsewhere through flattery. I know, indeed, the devices that have been fashioned, but I avoid them; content with simplicity, I meet those who love me with an open and serene countenance.

Where in the world was the bond promised between us, sealed under an appeal to God, if, when you departed, you left me without a greeting, as though I were unknown, and, while remaining behind, I was not granted the opportunity to suggest what was necessary? I believe you took care that, being weak in my eyes, I should lose all light together with you, and that, with closed eyes, I should not behold my day in the presence of a friend. If these things happened through negligence, you will leave it to my judgment what place I occupy with you; but they must be endured more bitterly if they are understood to have occurred by design. Now farewell, my lord, and invite into my spirit—which innocence, origin, and purpose persuade to remain steadfast—the greater share of your favor, in the sincerity that has been evident to you.

## LETTER V. ENNODIUS TO SENARIUS

Although a principal concern binds you, my lord, to itself through the proofs of your unstained fidelity, and the distinction of your character so mixes you with public affairs that being loved by you excludes the taste of quiet, I nevertheless do not believe that the religion of friendship is so subordinated that, while fulfilling the commands of the reigning authority with God’s help, you do not restore what is owed to affection. You know what the court demands and what favor demands. At one and the same time you are not lacking either to the master of affairs or to love, since the integrity of a Christian mind is made firm by being divided among these obligations. By these considerations, then, I believe my anxiety is relieved, through which your venerable custom is preserved in acts of devotion.

The only remaining matter is that your greatness, assisted by the consolations of our God, may rejoice. My lord, offering the service of a greeting, I hope that through some welcome indication in a letter I may be made glad concerning the condition of yourself or of your friend, Lord Faustus.

[Note: “The principal duty binding him”: Either because Senarius was often employed on embassies, or because of the office of secretary which he held at the king’s court; see Book III, Letter 11, and Book V, Letter 15.]

## LETTER VI. ENNODIUS TO FLORUS AND DECORATUS

Until now I permitted your greatness to attack the fickleness of the Ligurians with the polish of urbane disputation, because my origin made me a stranger to it and your promised steadfastness separated you from their faults. But since, by a single fate, I have departed from your eyes and mind, I proclaim in the voice of a herald that no one can condemn what follows, nor, without preserving modesty, can a sinner pass judgment upon excesses. It is permissible for those free from guilt to denounce such conduct; but who can bear with equanimity a teacher who does not avoid by his actions what he destroys with his words?

The sentence of the Gospel says that “whoever does and teaches” may be judged worthy of God’s grace (Matthew 5:19). Your speech is abundant whenever error is reproved, and beneath the negligence of conduct you embrace the purity of words. You have lost the memory of my tears, which the blow of a double sorrow poured forth at your departure. Behold how many days have passed in which, amid such a great number of travelers, I have received no letters either from my lord, your friend, or from you—letters that might report something I desire concerning him.

You have absolved the guilty through imitation—not because, as you say, the Ligurians happened to lose their intention of fidelity, but because you happened to find yourselves their companions in what must be avoided. Nevertheless, after offering the service of a greeting, I ask that at last, as good lords mindful of my prayers, you disclose your prosperity, or that of my lord, your lover, through the duties of correspondence.

## LETTER VII. ENNODIUS TO THE DEACON ELPIDIUS

[Note: “To the deacon Elpidius”: Book VIII, Letter 8. Thus they were already writing long ago, using Elpidius for what is ἐλπίδιος: as in Helpis, Euhelpistus, and other names of that kind. It is therefore plausible that Ennodus likewise wrote it in this form.]

Perfect love suffers no loss from bodily absence, nor is the serene union of souls punished by the separation imposed by journeys. The souls of those whom Christ joins in love come together, and no interposition of lands can separate them. With this hope and confidence, secure in your conscience, I address you as one who loves me, as though you were present in my embraces. Cherish, Lord Elpidius, the one whom you received with God as mediator. Let the world have its own stratagems, and let it condemn and call “wisdom” the urbanity that deceives. Do not mix anything with that sweetness which I have experienced in you except what may lead us step by step toward the goods of perfect love. My lord, returning, as above, the fullest greeting, I ask that you frequently inform me of your prosperity and that of those who love us.

## LETTER VIII. ENNODIUS TO EUPREPIA

How well long familiarity had prepared my spirit to endure the separation of your absence, while prolonged silences produced contempt for the sweetness of their own necessities! The scar that had advanced toward the healing of pious love has been cut open again. I confess, venerable sister, that your letters, sealed with a flavor too well known to me, have recalled me to my former longing. Behold by what art you contend: you allow me neither the satisfaction of your presence nor the oblivion provided by silence. The Most High, who examines minds, knows that, when I read your letters, my soul could not remain within its inner chambers but, compelled by their honey, flew toward your presence through its devotion.

A dwelling at Arles was mine while I was enclosed within the walls of Milan; and while the freedom of my mind hastened toward that sweet abode, the captivity of my body confined me within Italy. O, if only an abundance of speech were available for setting forth what my spirit desires—or if shame did not take away those things to which the tongue is adequate! The love that can be sufficiently revealed by testimony of the mouth is small. Whenever eloquence gives way within it, that is a confession of tepid affection. For the rest, I pray God that you may be well and that you may preserve me, through the goodness of mutual prosperity, for the alleviation of my sorrow, which by your writing you have doubled through an art too skillful.

## LETTER IX. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

You possess the display that you avoid in letters; and your speech is nothing other than the preservation of the distinction of declamations. Nature has accumulated this in you, and so has the unwearied care of learning, the mother of skill. But no consolation can come to my miseries when the things I have deserved are placed before my eyes; and the more unworthy the one set over me has proved, the more openly the sins of those who have overcome me become apparent. Why do you try to raise my spirit, most illustrious of men? What can be reserved for my tribulations in a life that is full of sorrow? For the benefit of heavenly providence’s dispensation, I have resolved upon an end even together with life itself.

Nevertheless, I return inadequate thanks to you, who preserve toward me a diligence that you would not extend even to those most worthy. My lord, returning the reverence of a greeting, I hope that you will not cease to pray for me and will send letters bringing aid and consolation amid my calamities.

## LETTER X. ENNODIUS TO FLORUS AND DECORATUS

[Note: “The office of the compulsor”: An exactor of fiscal burdens, who, being responsible for public assessments, compels payment. See Law 7 of the Code, On Exactors, and Law 4, “That the transfer of a contribution not be demanded”; also Cassiodorus, Book VII, 45; Book IX, 4; Book XII, 8. The Basel edition was also mutilated here. For, in the first part of this letter, it attached another passage that belonged to Letter 13. We have therefore supplied the following three letters—from manuscripts—to Agnellus, Hormisda, and Boethius.]

Having exercised the office of a compulsor, I scarcely compelled an advocate to fulfill his promise, so that he might pay what he owed to the advocates. It is a kind of harsh profession, and, to anticipate what must be said by you, I, a cleric, have bent toward shame. Judge what sort of thing it is by which the most obstinate are softened, and what is meant by one who strips the robbers.

I have entrusted a pound of silver given by Brother Epiphanius to Brother Gaianus, to be brought to you, although the agreements concerning what I received have still been settled with me. It remains for you to indicate whether I ought to deliver it. My lord, offering the fullest greeting, I ask that you first deign to pray for me to the saints. Then return my attentions to our beloved lords with that humility in which you know me to desire them.

## LETTER XI. ENNODIUS TO AGNELLUS

My spirit is troubled that your abundance has granted me nothing from the gifts of your eloquence, and that you lie so heavily upon the riches of speech that to make a portion of them available would be counted sacrilege. The avarice of all things is shameful indeed; yet, if you deny words, the offense becomes still more embarrassing. It often happens that those who write frequently love less; yet no one who remains in perpetual silence has ever gone so far as to reserve something for affection. Ambiguity may arise from the flatteries of correspondence; but it is certain that one who preserves silence is not loved by the one who does so.

These are the words I wrote hastily because of the speed of the bearer, driven on by two goads: the urgency of the carrier and my sorrow. Therefore apply remedies to the weariness of my spirit without delay, so that, although affection has thus far lacked its nourishment, the promised love may nevertheless be known to stand firm. My lord, offering the fullest greeting, I ask that what is sufficient for my expectation not be denied by one most skilled in speech.

## LETTER XII. ENNODIUS TO THE DEACON HORMISDAS

There would be no room for pardon for the unskilled if they spoke at greater length; brevity alone recommends the unlearned. A lengthy account from a rustic is beyond error itself: when something has been wrung from an ignorant man that must be read for a long time, the one who exacts it owes him his resentment. Does anyone wish to proceed at length into what must become tedious, and not have brief limits for things prepared without flavor?

You demanded this, brother, with a Roman and excessively artful subtlety. But simplicity fortifies us against fabricated things, colored by no deceptions. For although you drew me onward with the soothing eloquence of your letter, you did not make me forget myself. I know how to narrow a page, whose value I understand as the one who publishes it. Nevertheless, know that I do not fail in my duties, although both a courtier and a cleric summon me into the midst of things. But why am I extending a page whose narrowness I had promised above? This is my contest with a lover; such is the fruit of letters. My lord, offering the fullest greeting, I pray that, by the mercy of our God, you may frequently announce your well-being to me in the desired words of your communications while you seek mine.

## LETTER XIII. ENNODIUS TO BOETHIUS

If it were permissible to delay what has been commanded, I might still be granted the privilege of not losing the ornaments of silence. For it is the gift of silence that you believed I could speak without inhumanity. See how much talent of speech a restrained voice has contributed. But it is the plight of an empty heart not to hold on to remedies put at risk. Concern for speech acts lest the ignorance of the one who publishes be concealed, whenever the labor of leisure intercepts glory. Behold, I, praised before being tested, am submitted to examination, and I break into my holiday lest I seem worthy of praise. For while humility renders service, we do not possess what has been obtained through silence.

You, most polished of men, deign to praise in me the virtues of one whom diligence made old in youthful years, without prejudice from age; one who, through diligence, fills everything that is required; for whom, at the beginning of life, the constant practice of reading is play and another’s sweat is delight; in whose hands the fire shines with doubled brilliance by which the ancients once blazed. For what scarcely happened to older men at the end of life abounds in you at its threshold.

You have truly given value to my loquacity, since you were the first to approach one who desired conversation. A new thing has happened to a chatterer: he was drawn out so far that his writings demanded a reply. Thanks be to God, who by hidden paths moved you, through the necessary affection of a close companion. Behold, you now hold the two grounds of my complaint: for, after I have become known as a rustic, I presume to call myself your relative.

My lord, offering the service of a greeting, I hope that you will lend frequency to the duties of correspondence; in this work the lover and the eloquent man alike display constancy.

## LETTER XIV. ENNODIUS TO ARCHOTAMIA

[Note: “Archotamia”: A noble widow of Arles, a relative of Ennodus. Her great piety is shown by the fact that she could serve as an example and encouragement to her priestly son, who had withdrawn to the solitude of Lérins out of devotion to religion. Cassiodorus, Book IV, 12, erroneously writes Archotonia. The same woman is discussed there, as we shall show in Book VIII, Letter 35.]

You have advanced so far above the brilliance of your lineage through the light of your character that even those whom kinship does not bind to you submit to the goodness of your deeds.
