For who would not be ready to offer complete reverence to a soul exalted in the worship of God? Whoever does not welcome those who serve God makes himself a stranger to the grace of the Redeemer.

It is an indication of outstanding conduct to love the worshipers of our Christ. One is close to the most upright when one loves those already proved; one gives unquestionable testimony to good merits if one strives to pursue the perfect with due continuity of praise. One becomes close to the saints by proclaiming their holiness without deceit. Whoever you have preferred, urged on by diligence, suffers a loss of honor if you do not follow.

Who, while preserving modesty, could walk among thorns, raise up a purified path, and, seeing the way of salvation, choose the tracks of those who cause harm? It is a profession of blindness to look upon good examples placed before one’s eyes and not retain the means by which one might advance through imitation.

These things, my lady, have been reported about you by fame through trustworthy indications; they have not been cast about by the ignorant mouths of a talkative crowd, whose custom is, in human affairs, to extinguish the enlarged flames of the faithful while it kindles sparks into funeral pyres. This has spread through the report of our relatives, especially through the account of Lady Euprepia, your sister: not only that you are worthy of praise, but that you have established what deserves celebration and have placed before your venerable son, together with the rays of his lineage, the torch of your conduct.

As far as I have learned, the inhabitant of Lérins has something to learn from a holy mother, even one who has not abandoned an urban dwelling. If your piety believes me, it is greater to conquer the world in battle than to avoid it. Flight from the contest reveals fear; there is no hope of virtue when the adversary is shunned before the encounter. Awareness of strength will scarcely consent to concealment; to choose secrecy is to show that one has feared.

I write this without reproving my lord and the radiance of our family, the priest. I do not believe that he lacks battles even there, battles that he will overcome; rather, he seems to have avoided the conflict in that place. For he trampled all the flatteries of the world when neither age, wealth, nor birth could restrain his departure. But to you, to the extent that your sex is weaker, an even greater share of praise is owed for the attainment of victory.

You are almost the guardian even of his purpose: although enduring the evils of widowhood and bereavement, you allow nothing to perish from the merits of your venerable son through the occasion of your own consolation. Behold where a woman, forgetful of her frailty, serves as a fortress and withdraws both man and youth from the enemy’s attack. May you continue as the glorious leader of these deeds and persevere in them throughout this age, until the field of this world receives him, already mature, if circumstances should demand it.

I confess that I would wish, if the arrangement of a letter permitted it, to extend my words at length and to recount, amid an abundance of speech, a few things about the ornaments of your deeds. But let these matters be reserved for writing to others. It is enough for you to know that, although I have never seen you, I know you, and that you have already been held fast in my soul, inserted into records worthy of veneration. It is written—you remember—“Let your neighbors praise you” (Proverbs 27:2).

Truly, I could wish that this alone were a reason for me to seek Gaul: that, together with my lord the priest, we might kiss both your hands and your eyes and make you blessed amid every affliction of time. My lady, for whose sake letters are sent, I inform you that I am well in body and inquire after your prosperity; I also beg and adjure you by God never to deny me the assistance of your prayers.

## LETTER XV. ENNODIUS TO AGNELLUS

Thanks be to God, who, although he has brought forth what was desired concerning your greatness, did not reject it. Indeed, lest the faith of the suppliant falter, desires are delayed, because swift fulfillment diminishes the power of the joy that is to follow. It is clear that you have deserved honors rather than sought them, but the preceding composition expresses the wishes of those who love you. The Almighty, moved both by the brilliance of your lineage and invited by confidence in the favor you promised, has gone before you in your prosperity with whatever you restrain through discipline or reason.

Let concise conversations suffice amid the flowers. Reply to one who is anxious about your prosperity, although he does not doubt your love. My lord, offering the fullest service of a greeting, I commend the bearer of this letter, for I have found him faithful and honorable. I wish that it not remain unspoken among everyone what favor I possess from your graciousness, so that those who hope may feed upon the harvest of our shared favor.

## LETTER XVI. ENNODIUS TO AGNELLUS

The pleasant festivity of speech is accustomed to spread reports of prosperity: whatever good comes to eloquent people travels through the nations in the natural voice of joy. It is easier for the tongue to suppress a fire kindled upon funeral pyres than to preserve silence amid desired circumstances. It is the law of humanity and the command of nature that the happiness of the mind should pour forth through the resources of writing.

For favorable things flow out even when they are confined within chambers. But in your greatness, just as your gray age is mature in the gifts of modesty and knowledge, so you bind your joy with the reins of moderation. Yet should discipline go so far as to damage gratitude, and should it diminish the diligence of friends because that diligence is joined to the adornment of character? Although you possess the currency of Latin eloquence, you cannot discover how to assert that it was rightly done to grant no words to me, who am waiting for them.

Is it therefore fitting that heavenly benefits be announced to lovers only by hearsay, and that one who has already obtained solid cause for rejoicing tremble amid joys? For this reason I have sent a boy who does not request letters but demands them. You know the confidence of simple lovers, especially of those whose hope you retain, strengthened by the promise of your favor. My lord, offering the fullest greeting, I ask that you send frequent letters, not compressed into narrow limits. See the confidence of my spirit: I ask for lengthy pages, though I have received none so far.

## LETTER XVII. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

If you had shown any concern for my smallness, such a long silence would not have remained, especially since the indisposition of my lady, your mother, afflicts me in my absence through various reports without remedy. For I know that the holy woman is weighed down by this burden alone: she displays an excessive piety toward one who does not deserve it.

But why should I extend words bound by chains of sadness? If heavenly favor has restored her good health, hasten to announce it to me by letter. For I expect that prosperity will then be reconciled with me, when I learn that she is well. You have learned the cause of my sorrow; after God, provide its remedy without distinction. My lord, offering the service of a greeting, present worthy service to the Lord on behalf of me, your suppliant.

## LETTER XVIII. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

If a judge of lowly persons is burdened by injuries, I do not know whether he can relieve others of this burden when he himself succumbs to it. A heavy hand of medicine must be applied to serious wounds, lest the disease grow through impunity. The high-ranking man vicarius [sic] extorted these words from me, although they ought to have been owed in consideration of justice; let him himself reveal what he has suffered. I know one thing: unless you come to his aid, a general evil will arise, to which he himself, the guardian of discipline, is exposed.

This is not foreign to Christianity, since I bring the matter forward; for it is impious that the order of affairs should be confused under such an entanglement. My lord, having offered you the honor of a greeting, graciously receive the voice of your suppliant, so that the one who has undertaken so great a burden of labor may recover through the result.

## LETTER XIX. ENNODIUS TO SIMPLICIANUS

[Note: “To Simplicianus”: He is the one mentioned in the letter to Faustus, Book VI, Letter 15: “Simplicianus, bearer of the present letter, a most noble young man, attempting to seek Rome, the ancestral seat of learning”; Ennodus now congratulates him on the happy beginnings of his eloquence. He is also mentioned in Letter 29 of this book.]

May the beginnings of your youth be strengthened by the assistance of divine favor. May the one who bestowed adornments upon your beginnings grant success to your fruits, so that what you have anticipated in the gray flower of youth you may not withhold at the maturity of your fruits. It is the first concern of our purpose, when anxious about the praise of one who is beginning, to send our prayers to God, so that what has been undertaken in the cultivation of good character may mature through heavenly assistance.

May the one who drew forth from the earth the nourishing herb of humanity bring the harvest of your talent into the granaries. May he himself shape into wheat the form pressed from earthly milk, whose face, joined to the soil, is made fertile by rain.

But to you, learned boy, I offer thanks because, although you shone with the brilliance of speech and are praised in that city with the knowledge of letters bearing witness, you also desire the aid of my proclamation. The fruit of my diligence has come to you, even if no ornaments of a rustic testimony are bestowed. Gladly I praise your words together with the most eloquent, joining my judgment to theirs so that I may grow rich through the fellowship of good men. It follows that those who agree in any judgment should not be divided in merit.

There is one man—and he has not wandered far from the citadel of the sublime—who agrees with what they predict of you with no lesser admiration. Yet I return to the honey of your letter and diction, whose preface concerning the present and tender age is so pleasing that it does not conceal the virtue and power of what is to come.

[Note: “The Latin eloquence stood in hollowed places”: All the ancient books read this way; what it means, however, is explained by the following mention of the riverbed.]

Latin eloquence stood in hollowed channels while the stream of Roman eloquence flowed onward through its own riverbed. It is scarcely possible to comprehend toward what things your judgment may extend, since you appear greatest at the threshold. In the morning light you shone with the brilliance of midday. May heavenly grace protect its gift in you, and may Christ our salvation inspire you to honor one who loves you through frequent services of correspondence.

## LETTER XX. ENNODIUS TO MAXIMUS

[Note: “To Maximus”: A man of rank and distinction for whom Ennodus wrote an epithalamium; in these letters, too, he repeatedly alludes playfully to his marriage. He later became ordinary consul in the year 523, that is, two years after Ennodus’s death. A letter of Theoderic to him as consul survives concerning the spectacle of games that he was going to provide; Book V of the Variae, Letter 42.]

While the servants of the winepress were filling the autumn’s bounty and, with hastened foot, breaking open the tender skins of the grapes, I turned both eyes and words toward my eminent kinsman and brother. I judged it right that, while the vineyards pour forth abundant liquor, I should address a sober person with cheerful gaiety. Therefore, release your Pythagorean silence and share with me the riches of your knowledge and eloquence; let conversation take the place of joyful vintage; let the sweet musts of discourse flow. [Col. 0123D]

You have material which you may communicate, with the most holy deacon Hormisdas [Note: [Col. 0124D] “With the most holy deacon”: Hormisdas.], in the familiar abundance of speech concerning moral instruction. For those who, like you, stand firm in ecclesiastical integrity, avoidance of silence is a proper duty. Write with what golden strictness chastity is maintained, by what path shameful avarice is avoided, and by what means the darkness of disgraceful deception is shunned. In short, teach without concealment what you practice. Above all, graciously instruct one eager to know how the bride’s [Col. 0124A] blandishments, or the blandishments of the world, are rejected through the discipline of religion. My lord, presenting the gifts of my greeting as above, I ask you graciously to accept that which, amid the burdens of cares, has demanded the insertion of a little diversion that ought not to be rejected.

## LETTER XXI. ENNODIUS TO MAXIMUS

Where is the loyalty of your radiant conscience, a loyalty which hoary reverence does not abandon even in childish years, which the observance of honor illuminates through the precedent of age, and which, maturing in the deeds of youth, advances into manhood? Was it right that only a few instructions should be returned to the pages of one who loves you, or that the freedom of writing and of a servant should be answered with faith? Did you judge it worthy of approved morals not to follow one urging you toward religious duties, or did you think it wrong to return letters which, amid your excesses, you happened not to receive? Is this, then, your discipline? The integrity once made manifest does not spread such a picture of you.

Yet I strive, with the loquacity for which I am known, to change your hardened silences. Is your tongue unequal to your birth? Or do you not proclaim the testimony of your lineage through the flower of your speech? Will the fertile utterance of your breast abandon its purple? Nothing but malice marks the man who, though able, gives no words to one who longs for them.

Behold, amid belches owed to Lyaeus, what sort of words I compose as another Silenus. Know that your name must be written in the purple of my genius and inserted into my own little books, so that even if you contribute nothing in reply, I may still hold the citadel: I send to learned men, without any trembling, something that can be read. My lord, accept the services of my greeting and return the letters that are owed.

May your virginity remain established through enduring time;

and may nothing perish that blessed life has given.

May nothing stain your maiden limbs with blackness,

and may you not lie there because of a Tartarean face.

May you refresh the one eager for the holy through written words,

and may a stream flow from your brother’s fountains.

## LETTER XXII. ENNODIUS TO MAXIMUS

Broken mountain slopes or secluded forest places receive a voice from you more faithfully. By nature’s institution they give human beings an answer, though mute; the alternation of the echoing solitude returns to mortals; what tongues or woodland clearings have received does not perish as a benefit. Why, then, is this a kind of greatness in your praise and philosophy: to say nothing and maintain the caution of silence amid the uncertainties of declaimers?

You are a man whom nature brought forth neither barren nor unfinished, and whom learning did not leave unformed. But, I believe, you disdain me in conversation; unwilling to give precious words to a crude and uneducated man. [Note: [Col. 0124D] “Unwillingly to the Opici”: All the older books read *obicis* incorrectly. The correction seemed certain to me, so that we should read *opici*, that is, “crude and uneducated,” as the following immediately makes clear. In the same sense Sidonius, Book VIII, Letter 3, speaks of an *opica* translation, a designation derived from the people of the Opici, whose speech was uncultivated and barbarous. The expression ὀπικῶν φωνὴ (“the speech of the Opici”) occurs in Suidas under the entry Γέλα.]

What is more, is it not a sign of a rich man’s eloquence not to withhold the words desired even by the unlearned? The course of rivers is miserly if it is thought to satisfy only the thirst of the noblest; the abundance of rain pours even over rocks that will produce nothing. The order of a liquid reason is this: let the one who fears losses renounce poverty; whatever does not flow forth is meager.

Among the birds, however, I sent you as a gift one which the hawk had caught. For, having advanced to Bromius and the orgies of Bacchus, we waged war among the birds; the social contest of feathers benefited our enterprise. [Note: [Col. 0125C] “We waged war among the birds”: Sidonius likewise writes in his panegyric of Avitus:

> What is the purpose of the birds’ contest, which nature gives  
> to the predatory creatures, almost a kindred multitude? Who more learned than this  
> has taught the various quarrels to be joined beneath the clouds?  
> One bird conquers birds, and with swift beating through the air  
> this claw fights better than any other.

Bird-hunting was therefore common in those times and not unknown even to clerics. Later, however, the canons forbade it to them, as in that very region of Liguria the Synod of Pavia in the year 850, canon 4: “Let the bishop entirely reject all occupations which, in holy conduct, are contrary to the priestly office, and let him not himself practice hunting with dogs, hawks, or *capis*, which the common people call falcons.”]

The contest of winged creatures proved profitable to our undertaking. Remember that we sent only a duck, knowing that God delights in an odd number. Our gift is a lesson: accept it, if you love it, as the doctrine of our jest. Make my joy fruitful. If he imposes upon you the constant practice of chastity, your tongue—which is now exercised in admonitions—will labor in your praises. Farewell, my lord, and, as a learned man, reply to one who loves you, if I deserve it, setting dissimulation aside.

## LETTER XXIII. ENNODIUS TO MAXIMUS

[Note: [Col. 0125D] “Your greatness brings forth”: The seven letters that follow are missing from the manuscripts used by us.]

Your greatness prolongs the wedding festivities over time. While you persist for so long in the undertaking to which you were compelled, your necessity has suddenly become a desire. Would anyone devote himself forever to a task to which he descended unwillingly? Thus you have withdrawn from the care of the blessedness you had guarded, as though you had learned over a long period how the married state should be established.

Thirty happy days have passed, and you still withdraw yourself from the city and from my eyes, wearing me down through prolonged expectation. Truly, do whatever you wish; if I live, I shall not keep silent about what I have woven for you to hear. Yet, having received the honor of your greeting, accept from me, as a brother from a brother, a taste of a few drops. Blush, since you neither inquire after the sick man nor send anything from the delights of marriage that might relieve his weariness.

## LETTER XXIV. ENNODIUS TO STEPHANUS

The exhortation of our common son Marcellus—whom nature gave to you and affection gave to me—requires me to take the lead in the duties of writing and, overcome by love, to offer the consolation of letters, through which antiquity has decreed that absence should have no power. You now owe me a double favor, and, if you return an answer, owe it also because I began first.

The one who offers an example in conversation opens the door of affection; those who return writings preserve the established form. Therefore, with God as author, we send a letter announcing our prosperity. To increase your joy, so that your fatherly heart may rejoice more fully, we add that your son already possesses in his liberal studies the testimony of a free-born nature, and that he conducts himself in this pursuit in such a way as to surpass the grudging hopes of his family.

An honorable beginning in a young man is a promise of perfection; nor is he far from being learned who, at the beginning of goodness, seizes the glory of an established character. Greeting you with the affection I owe, I hope that, when opportunity has been restored, your prosperity will raise me up through the good report of your son.

## LETTER XXV. ENNODIUS TO SYMMACHUS

[Note: [Col. 0125D] “To Symmachus”: Not to the pope, but to the patrician, the father-in-law of Boethius. Boethius honors him with this eulogy in Book II of *The Consolation*: “Yet unharmed there flourishes that most precious glory of the human race, your father-in-law Symmachus; and a man wholly formed from wisdom and virtues, whom you would not have been slow to purchase at the price of life, secure in his own affairs, he laments your injuries.” Likewise in Book I: “Holy Symmachus, and as worthy of reverence as you yourself.” Ennodius says that the Symmachan family possessed ancestral eloquence and nobility—and not without reason, since nearly all its members were learned and distinguished by the highest offices. Since most people confuse the Symmachi who flourished in the time of Ennodius and in the preceding century, I think it useful here to distinguish them individually by their identifying marks, beginning with the father of the orator Symmachus.

1. L. AURELIUS AVIANUS SYMMACHUS, prefect of the city in the year 364. The sequence of his merits and the testimony to his authority, prudence, and eloquence are contained in the inscription on a statue which the emperors ordered to be erected for him twice, at Rome and at Constantinople. Marcellinus calls him a learned and modest man in Book XXVII of his *History*. Only one letter of his to his son Symmachus survives, together with a few epigrams remaining from those he composed for eighty illustrious men of his age.

2. Q. AURELIUS SYMMACHUS, son of L. [Aurelius Avianus], the orator, whose nine books of *Letters* and tenth book of *Reports* he wrote during his urban prefecture; among them is the famous report concerning the Altar of Victory, to which St Ambrose and Prudentius replied. He was proconsul of Africa in 370, prefect of the city in 384, and finally ordinary consul with Tatianus in 391. His wife was Rusticiana, daughter of Orfitus; she was the sister of the consul Acyndinus, whom he consequently calls his maternal uncle. He is the man who debates in Macrobius’ *Saturnalia*, to whom Ausonius sends his *Griphus*, and whom Augustine discusses when he writes that he was sent by Symmachus, *vir clarissimus*, to Milan to teach rhetoric, in Book V, chapter 13, of the *Confessions*. Prosper also mentions him in Book III, chapter 38, of *On the Promises*; so do Sidonius in Letter 1 and elsewhere, Socrates in Book V, chapter 14, and Cassiodorus in Book XI, chapter 2.

3. Q. FLAVIANUS MEMMIUS SYMMACHUS, the orator’s only son, by whom his father’s letters were arranged and published after his death. He too was proconsul of Africa, in 415, and prefect of the city, in 420. His are the *Reports* sent to the emperor Honorius concerning the dispute between Eulalius and Pope Boniface, which were included in the ecclesiastical annals. He had also been quaestor candidate and praetor at the beginning of his career. The frequent mention of the honors of both his sons occurs in Symmachus’ letters; Olympiodorus of Thebes, quoted by Photius, mentions the expenses of his praetorship, counting the Symmachi among the richest men of the city of Rome.

4. Q. AURELIUS SYMMACHUS. This is how he is called in Valentinian’s Novel 4. He was ordinary consul with Aetius III in the year 446. I believe him to have been the grandfather of the widow Galla mentioned in Fulgentius’ letter, since Fulgentius addresses Galla, the daughter of the patrician Symmachus, as follows: “Although, through your grandfather, father, father-in-law, and husband, all of whom were once consuls, you were illustrious among secular persons.”

5. Symmachus the patrician, to whom Ennodius writes here, whom he mentions in Book VIII, Letter 28: Q. AURELIUS MEMMIUS SYMMACHUS, former ordinary consul and patrician, as I remember reading in ancient copies. He was Boethius’ father-in-law, and Boethius dedicates several of his little works to him. He was consul without a colleague under Odoacer in 485, and was among those selected by King Theoderic to judge the case of Basilius and Praetextatus, who were accused of magical practices; see Cassiodorus, Book II, Letter 29. Cassiodorus also preserves other letters from Theoderic to the same Symmachus. Pope Hormisdas mentions him in Letters 28 and 66. Later, after being incited by the wicked accusations of informers against him, Theoderic had him cruelly put to death together with his son-in-law Boethius, as Procopius relates in Book I of the *Gothic War*. Two daughters of his are known: Rusticiana, the wife of Boethius, and Galla, concerning whom, besides Fulgentius, Gregory the Great writes in Book IV, *Dialogues*, chapter 13. He left no son. For the man who follows—

6. Symmachus, Boethius’ colleague in the consulship of 522—was not the son of the patrician Symmachus but his grandson, born of Rusticiana and Boethius, as will be said in the note to Book VIII, Letter 1. From the years assigned above to each of them, it will easily be possible to determine to which Symmachus the imperial rescripts found in both codices should be referred.]

TO SYMMACHUS.

A law written in response to desires is scarcely believed. The devotion that cannot endure a stricter command does not always make what is freely given worthy of blame. The guilty party often becomes more lovable when, through lack of restraint, he acquires a character more pleasing; for his fault commends itself through a certain honey of presumption.

I protect myself by my preface, since I am the first to aspire to letters. It remains in your highness’s power, if you choose to endure a chatterbox, not to be silent, but to nourish me with the ancestral milk of the Symmachan spring. Farewell in our Christ, nobility of the Roman people, and deign to regard me now as your client and servant, in view of the light of your character and nature.

## LETTER XXVI. ENNODIUS TO AGNELLUS

You have produced a letter according to my desire, while you cleanse every matter that had been darkened by cloud. By the most fortunate outcome of your defense, we are present on the side of innocence, and we devote the use of our voice to matters that shine of themselves under a favorable omen.

You easily affirm the light of one who shines, and speech is not lacking that may be lent to those who are acquitted. Thus you proceeded in your words concerning the promised horse, as though you had ever possessed a shameful inclination to lie. Truly, by my soul, I would more easily believe that holy bishops could fall into this pit.

Vices do not know maturity except in those whom they have imbued from earliest youth. Denial does not newly spring up among human beings: whatever exists in our character both follows and preceded us. Therefore, fare well, purple of Latin eloquence, and lovingly return my due response, taking care that, as compensation for the delay, a horse worthy of your gift come to my aid.

## LETTER XXVII. ENNODIUS TO PROBUS

[Note: [Col. 0128C] “To Probus”: An illustrious man whom Ennodius praises among the other nobles of the city in the *Paraenesis*. Likewise in Book VIII, Letter 21, to Beatus: “You had done what a wise man does, when you reread my verses to lord Probus alone, who held the citadel [perhaps *artem*, ‘skill’] among the learned.” This letter also mentions both his poetic talent and his nobility, and an inscription among Christian monuments was published in these words:

> Hope of a noble race, glory of great fathers,  
> skilled in talent, eloquent in learned song;  
> illustrious, wise, humble, moderate, honorable,  
> gracious to all, pious through goodness;  
> bearing a mind and character beyond his years,  
> Probus, more renowned in his homeland for nobility.  
> Death harmed you not: here you live in everlasting praise,  
> and in Christ’s kingdom you remain without end.  
> These things I have sung for you are no false praises:  
> your merit is everywhere attested by fame.]

I choose to suffer the loss of modesty rather than incur the disgrace of one who does not love, knowing that wounds to the brow can more easily be repaired than wounds to loyalty. To be unlearned is a misfortune; to hate the virtues of your family is a crime. We could have been lacking in liberal studies without committing an offense; no one is satisfied with the point from which he has shaken off his character.

Should I not honor, in your greatness, so many goods heaped together and expressed in epistolary speech? Should I not admire that light of your lineage, enlarged by study and integrity? He seems to me not far from honesty who honors the improved, since anyone is believed capable of pursuing what he loves. Therefore, fare well through God’s grace, and, approving my devotion, increase the love I bear you through the gifts of letters.

## LETTER XXVIII. ENNODIUS TO ADEODATUS, THE PRESBYTER

The occasion that serves as the instrument of this writing to you fulfills my desire. For the address both flatters in place of presence and promises itself, through the publication of pages, what it presents: just as highly perfected men consider it a diminishment of their virtues if others are thought to have preceded them in the testimony of diligence, so they regard it as disgraceful to neglect examples.

This fellowship lived among holy men, so that, through the foresight of an intimate friend, earthly separation caused no harm. It is fitting, my lord, that you should follow both my desire and my form. Therefore, greeting you in the first place, I ask that you remember me, so that what is taken from me through negligence may be granted through you by the assistance of divine grace.

I report this without lying: on the third night [Note: [Col. 0128D] “From my departure”: While he was returning from the city. We saw another epitaph of Cynegia in Book V, Letter 7. He wrote that one at the request of her sister Euprepia; he composed this one after being admonished by Cynegia herself in a nocturnal vision and sent it to Rome, so that it might be fixed to the wall beside her tomb.] after my departure, my lady Cynegia appeared to me at the very beginning of daylight, and reproached me severely for hastening my journey, because her tomb had not been honored with any verses.

I did not, indeed, accept this as an image of prophetic truth, nor did I perhaps make an offering through the sweat of my work to nocturnal illusions. But because lovers are easily persuaded, the one who admonished me did not labor to demand the work that was owed. The reverence due to my lady is preserved.

I adjure you, by the day of judgment, to have the verses I sent written at once on the wall above her feet. Know that this will also be pleasing to your son, for he wishes her merits to be celebrated by the mouths of many, but in the manner in which he found them here. Greet on my behalf my lady Stephania, my lady Sabiana, and also my lady Fadilla. Once the verses have been written, reply at once.

Deign to tell the lord pope to arrange something concerning my case through the intercession of Dioscorus. [Note: [Col. 0129D] “Through the intercession of Dioscorus”: Since the manuscripts fail us here, as I have said, and conjecture must be used, I believe it will not be an implausible correction to read *per sanctum Dioscorum* (“through Saint Dioscorus”). Dioscorus is the man to whom Hormisdas also wrote concerning this same matter, to be discussed with the pope, in Book VI, Letter 33.]

As much as I could write in the haste of the courier, I have written. Give my greetings sufficiently to the lord and brother Hormisdas, and tell him to send that key.

## LETTER XXIX. ENNODIUS TO BEATUS

I do not confine my letter within narrow bounds, mindful of Spartan concision; nor do I mock your form through deliberately constrained speech. It is foreign to me to speak little to those who are modest. It is the practice of urban people to withdraw from small things what has been extended, and, without necessity, to shape pages according to the measure required by human minds.

What you may have thought subtle in me concerning what I said above was produced by haste, which is not always friendly to art, and by chance. [Col. 0129B] It is a great thing for me if accidents have given me anything you may admire.

Therefore I explain the reason for my writing, which I commend to you after the preceding greeting. When I had departed far from the city, an admonition from my lady Cynegia met me, asking why I had not honored her tomb with the praise of eloquence formed into verse. Although I did this out of reverence for her husband himself, I undertook it because what shines with the light of merit ought to be celebrated through the abundance of style.

For God does not reject the service of the unskilled; and, content with what he himself has granted, he does not demand verbal diadems from rustic speakers. I have therefore sent verses with which her epitaph should be written.

As for what is thought of it, I adjure you—so may your father live, and so may Rome, with regard to those matters in which it is criticized, not make you its own—that you judge simply and honestly. Do not flatter my ears or my judgment with the cosmetics of a fictitious favor. Do not be embarrassed, and review my page with some people, but especially with my lady Barbara—and rightly especially with her ladyship—since she is staying with you.

Yet I hope that my tablet may be as wise as your hope, which, in its hoary bloom, surpasses both my hopes and those of her parents, however miserly they may be. [Note: [Col. 0130D] “And their hopes”: The phrase seems redundant here.]

Greet on my behalf the lord Cethegus and his sister, my lady Blesilla.

Greet Fidelis, Marcellus, Georgius, Solatius, and Simplicianus on my behalf. [Note: [Col. 0129D] “Fidelis”: The Milanese man. Pope John writes to him among the other senators, as noted in the commentary on Book I, Letter 7. At that time, however, he had already been quaestor under Athalaric. Later he also held the praetorian prefecture, as Procopius testifies in Book I of the *Gothic War*. From Procopius we further learn that Fidelis was originally from Milan and was sent as an envoy by the Romans to summon Belisarius to the city. But all this occurred long after Ennodius; he was a young man at the time. Procopius’ words concerning him are:

> Having sent Fidelis, a man originating from Milan, which lies in Liguria (he had previously served Athalaric—the Romans call this office “quaestor”), they summoned Belisarius to Rome, promising to surrender the city without a fight.]

Say to them: If you care about the discipline of my lady Barbara, cultivate the company of her lord, her father, or her brothers, for she is chaste and free from luxury; whoever does otherwise should not expect to return to me.

## EPITAPH OF CYNEGIA

I have obtained the reward of my vows through Christ’s gift:

the life that was a cross to me has given this to the tombs.

I released the offspring of my flesh without wounding my mind,

because I, blessed in my husband Faustus, die before him.

He scattered my tears with a healing of the heart,

which preserves a faithful marriage-bed through merits.

May every married woman hope for a similar lot.

## LETTER XXX. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

[Col. 0130A]

The hope of young men is solid when the cultivation of great men attends it; if care ceases, the abundance of wheat turns into darnel. Parthenius, the son of my sister, had long been drawn toward diligence in letters by fear of your eminence, as far as his father’s report revealed. But now, released by your absence from the law of venerable fear, he is devising shameful things; that age, more friendly to sins, finds many guides toward error.

His father implores the loyalty I have pledged, and mourns his son as though he had died, though he is still alive. So do those whose confidence in the progress of their own people has found no answer. Nothing remained for me to offer as a remedy, after being overcome by prayers, except to inform your eminence quickly of the excesses of the young man mentioned above.

Provide the healing hand; provide the assistance customary to you, lest the growth of vices cut down everything in him that might have borne some good. Commend what is being done to his friends; inform his teacher; and grant whatever may be able to help. These are the things which, with the greetings already offered, I can provide to my kinsman without concealment, mindful of my calling.

## LETTER XXXI. ENNODIUS TO PARTHENIUS

It would have been fitting that a degenerate silence should be answered with a corresponding silence, so that vengeance might depart by the very road along which error had come. Is it right that, in your excesses, your voice should show what you have done wrong, and not silent grief? Believe me, a cure is near to revealed indignation.

The indignation confined within you ought to have wounded you for a long time, if you have not altogether departed from humanity. What wrong had I done after you had asked pardon in your first letter with fabricated humility? [Note: [Col. 0130D] “In your first letter you asked pardon”: He replied to it in Book VI, Letter 1.] Is this a faithful promise of correction: that, after you have extracted the anger you conceived through soothing speech, you should be ashamed to have committed lesser faults?

As far as I see, after having professed your shame, you avoid only the narrow hardships of your errors. You judge it wrong, in dealing with your parent and foster-father, not to lower your arrogance as much as you ought, in return for so many shared benefits.

Or perhaps you think that childish anger troubles me, or that any necessity could overcome a mature affection? Are blows not welcome to a parent from his children? Are the creators of crawling little ones not also soothed by injuries? [Col. 0130D] Nothing seems bitter to those whose desires have been stirred by something that partly opposes their wishes.

We find thorns and darnel among the wheat-bearing fields; and while we pluck the fruitful grass, barren growths are offered. Is care of cultivation therefore to be rejected, or must one cease from the ploughs if the earth has not entirely satisfied its cultivator?

I pray God to exclude from you what I detest. Yet, if you believe me, I shall never abandon the duty of admonition. I have heard from your father’s report that you have now relaxed your attention to studies, and that, as though you had obtained the citadel of knowledge, you are in no way concerned about instruction through reading.

You know, my son, that the highest level of this matter is held only through excessive diligence. It did not benefit the man who once labored at this work but then abandoned his application to labor: knowledge flees the negligent on swift wings, and whatever is produced through delay and sweat is carried away with speed.

I want you greeted and watchful, so that you may bind the harvest of your progress with the daily chains of reading. Write to me even now, if you are considering anything that becomes you; for, if you believe me, you will never find anywhere in the world a patron of your words like me.

# BOOK EIGHT

[Col. 0131]

## LETTER I. ENNODIUS TO BOETHIUS

[Note: [Col. 0131C] “To Boethius”: The ordinary consul of that year, namely 510. This was certainly ANICIUS MANLIUS SEVERINUS BOETHIUS, philosopher and orator, whose praise needs no herald; but if one were required, no letter of Ennodius could be more illustrious than this one. Onuphrius Panvinius judged that he was again consul with his father-in-law Symmachus in 522. But, to omit other considerations, if Boethius had been consul for the second time in that year, he ought to have been placed before his colleague Symmachus, since in the *Fasti* and on all ancient inscriptions he is placed after him. I am certain that Symmachus and Boethius, the consuls of the year 522, were Boethius’ own sons—those, I mean, concerning whose joint consulship he himself writes in Book II of *The Consolation*:

“When you saw your two sons advance from your house as consuls together, amid the attendance of the senators and the joy of the people.”

And:

“What shall I say of your sons as consuls, whose native talent already shines forth, even while they are still boys, as a likeness of either their father’s or their grandfather’s genius?”

I know that the author of Boethius’ *Life* thought otherwise, making his sons Patricius and Hypatius consuls; they held the consulship together in the year 500. But this is certainly an excessive error. Apart from the fact that it ought to have been remembered that those were Greek and Eastern consuls and had nothing to do with Boethius’ family, the words just quoted could refute the claim. From them it is clear that these sons of his were still boys of consular age when he wrote the *Consolation* of his exile—which could certainly not be said if they had been consuls more than twenty years earlier.

Boethius’ sons, then, were Symmachus and Boethius. He gave one the name of his father-in-law, the son’s grandfather, and the other his own name. Many monuments record their consulship. I shall cite one, which seems noteworthy because of the appended note marking the end of the indiction. We saw it at Rome, in the suburban church of St Pancratius. It reads:

> HERE RESTS MAXIMUS, A LITTLE BOY,  
> WHO LIVED SIX YEARS, SEVEN MONTHS, TEN DAYS.  
> HE WAS LAID HERE ON THE THIRD DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF AUGUST,  
> DURING THE CONSULSHIP OF SYMMACHUS AND BOETHIUS,  
> ILLUSTRIOUS MEN,  
> AT THE END OF THE FIFTEENTH INDICTION.]

TO BOETHIUS.

[Col. 0131A]

[Col. 0131B]

Full of the best hopes, for which I desire a favorable outcome, I aspire to the care of epistolary duty. It is fitting that your fasces should be touched by this preface, and that, amid the purples of men whose splendor grows with that of their possessor, I should not abstain from conversation of whatever kind.

Is love recognized only through the benefits of learning, and should it be thought unlawful for the desires of an uncultivated man to come into the open? Vows are more simply made known when they are veiled by no display of skill. Therefore, our mouth is what our heart is: we cannot change the bitterness of our inmost feelings through soothing words. The modest flatterer is one whose mind suggests, in the arrangement of a compliment, what must be said.

Therefore, thanks be to almighty God, who, while preserving in you the old virtues of your family, multiplies new ones, and—what is more—makes those who are worthy by the pinnacle of dignity worthy of the highest positions. This glory is indeed returned to your ancestry, but, what is clearer, it is obtained by the merit of your person.

Let it have been customary for the men of old to purchase the height of curule office through the sweat of the field, and, by despising the brightness of honors, to shine with the brightness of honors. But another kind of virtue is sought now that Rome has become the prize of victors. Our candidate, after a conspicuous struggle, receives the triumph owed to him although he has never seen a war. He demands the laurel by judgment and considered it unnecessary to engage armed men.

He shone among the swords of Cicero [Col. 0132A] and Demosthenes, and, as though born in the very peace of the arts, gathered the sharp points of both their purposes. Let no one fear discord between Attic perfection and Roman perfection, [Col. 0132B] nor doubt that the principal goods of nations can meet in fellowship. You alone are the one who embraces both. [Note: [Col. 0132D] “Who embraces both”: Greek and Latin learning, as all his works testify, as does also the epitaph at Pavia:

> Most illustrious in Maeonian and Latin speech, and he who  
> was consul, here I, Gerbertus, sent into exile, perished.

Gerbertus likewise writes in Book II of the Pithoean *Epigrams*:

> You, father and light of your country, Severinus Boethius,  
> guide the affairs of state through the office of consul.  
> You pour light into studies and do not yield  
> to the talents of the Greeks.]

You embrace both, and eagerly enclose within yourself, as a possessor of the greatest things, whatever might have been sufficient if distributed separately among individuals. While you imitate the eloquence of the ancients, you surpass it; while you seek a form of expression from the most learned, you grant one to them.

I possess a venerable composition of your letter that bears witness to this. Would that what you send were as frequent as it is pleasing! You might say: “It was fitting to praise a relative who is laboring for the common advancement, since what seems to confer a palm as though upon one individual is not his alone.”

Certainly, a portion of the curule office has come to me. But, if you believe me, I am raised up more by the genius and studies of the exalted man. Sometimes these things have come through circumstances; those other things belong solely to virtue.

The man who boasts only of his parents is brought almost destitute to the task of writing, despite the support of the consulship. In you both are held as possessions: Latin learning and the vein of the purple. Oh, if consideration of the epistolary style did not hold my hand and draw it out at such length! What others dictate through a report, I would set forth raw, even if I explained it with the order confused.

I return to the testimony of the tablets. I announce that I am well and beseech that you are well. Finally, I ask as the height of your favor that your graciousness raise me up through a reciprocal conversation. I also beseech you to grant me, in whatever manner you wish, the house which your abundance and neglect have now almost abandoned in the city of Milan. [Note: [Col. 0133D] “The house in the city of Milan”: See again Letters 30, 38, and 40 of this book.]

For it is just that your parents should have something that has descended from the mass of your patrimony. Believe me, with God as my witness: if I deserve to obtain it without diminishing your property, I shall respond, bound as though by a gift, with greater services. Concerning this matter, may everything happen happily for you; if I am to be secure, send me a full document confirming it.

## LETTER II. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

It was fitting that your greatness should display the wealth of its talent while following the principles of your holy father, and should bring forth the learning acquired through much sweat as a testimony of diligence. A twofold praise comes to you through the composition already mentioned: when, as the devotion of those who receive your writings grows, the palm of speech is brought into the open, the very matter that reveals your affection for us exalts you.

Through one and the same practice, the splendor of the mouth and of faith is multiplied. Those established in peace are thought to bestow upon their subjects the affection they express in words. This, my lord, that most occupied father, set in the high place of human affairs, maintains. The man who lives at leisure yet gives no words displays contempt. I remember reading: “There is no honor in a miserly discourse.”

Now, after offering the services of my greeting, I announce that I am well. It remains for my suggestion to rejoice in the abundance of conversation it has elicited.

## LETTER III. ENNODIUS TO MESSALA

[Note: [Col. 0133D] “To Messala”: A young man, Avienus’ brother and Faustus’ son, as Book IX, Letters 12 and 26, makes clear. He was studying eloquence at Rome. Ennodius therefore praises his style in order to spur him on through this encouragement. Other letters to the same man occur in this book and the next. This Messala also seems to be the man whose consulship, which fell in the year 506, Ennodius treated playfully in an epigram. It was not uncommon in this period for boys to be made consuls.]

[Col. 0133C]

After sending me one letter, compelled by my frequent writings, you persist in continuous silence; and I believe that, from necessity rather than choice, you are practicing the Pythagorean philosophy of saying nothing. [Note: [Col. 0134D] “The philosophy of saying nothing”: Pythagorean ἐχεμυθία, “silence.”] You do not consider the ancients, who, in order to speak better, remained silent for the present, and whose care for silence was the nurse of speech.

You seem to me faithfully to practice the Attic disciplines in their silent aspect, unwilling to make public what you have acquired through silence. [Note: [Col. 0134D] “The Attic disciplines”: The rites of the Eleusinian mysteries, which were celebrated in Attica with the most religious silence. Hence Papinius’ “the silent initiates of Ceres,” and the proverb Ἀττικοὶ ἐλευσίνια, referring to those who conceal their secrets in silence, since it was impious to disclose the mysteries of Ceres to the uninitiated.]

After the holiday of your mouth, show what riches have passed through the road of your ears. You sent me your compositions. Even if they did not contain the sublimity one might have desired, no debased poverty was detected in them. I gave thanks to God because you had now freed yourself from the bond in which negligence had shackled you. I promised a better result in what followed, judging from the beginning.

But you have joined your beginning to an end, at least as far as I am concerned, since you send me nothing. My lord Messala, may it be granted you, through the providence of our God, to keep daily before the eyes of your heart whose son you are. But I do not wish to prolong what is harsh.

Farewell, having received the service of my greeting, and show yourself corrected by my frequent suggestions through a ready abundance of letters.

## LETTER IV. ENNODIUS TO ARATOR

[Note: [Col. 0134D] “To Arator”: Book IX, Letter 1.]

Turning to distant places, you proved forgetful of affection: your pious attentiveness was not permitted to leave the city walls with you. While you are an inhabitant of the city, you guard the blandishments you have fashioned, not without Daedalian skill; but once you have decided that the countryside must be sought, you abandon the memory of your friends as though it were a heavy burden. You sought rustic delights, while we remained behind with you amid the evils of the city walls. The affection that you separated from us as though it were the torment of cares had no root. You may say: “Why such swift reproach? Nor is it fair to prepare the torturer before the offenses.” You promised without hesitation that you would write as soon as you had reached your desired destination; yet, as much as your father always exposed your faults, so far the pages empty of their boy have come from you. I fear that this silence may grow strong through lasting duration, and that shameful neglect may increase into a habit of silence. My lord, I salute you, and I call upon you to remember your promise, so that among gray forests, girded with ivy, you may flourish.

## LETTER V. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

There is no need to commend the craftsmen sent by the holy bishop. A work that is more pleasing through its own inherent character rejects the injury of a commendation by its advocate. When you see the household, you will not be able to doubt that it was sent by the Church and proceeded from her treasures and bosom for this purpose: that, generously treated, it may produce for you a reward in the exchange of the better age. Who will deny that, according to the announcement of the most blessed martyr Laurence, these slaves contain immense riches? For there are women who, although they have lost the lights of the outward person, will shine with the splendor of their minds: whatever is taken away from their bodies’ prosperity increases toward the fruitfulness of their souls. Do not take it amiss that they will be unable either to see or to be seen: beauty that allures by its appearance is far removed from your maturity. If he who ordered his life, as you have done, along this path of innocence feeds such women, he is in heaven. Believe me: although that abundance of tears poured out toward God brings you joy, you will be content to possess them while they continue to weep.

Among the good things I have mentioned, even though they may have cost you great labor and expense, I add what follows. One among them is freeborn, childless, and, I think—something close to the desires of the saints—will remain so. For among Christian people there is a fruitful barrenness, and it is the greatest consolation of this world not to possess the assistance of children. But lest your mind perhaps grow weary at the length of the *anagnostici* [Note: [Col. 0135D] “Anagnostici”: mentioned in Book I, Letter 4.]:” although good things placed at the beginning encourage you, and, according to rhetorical discipline, sweetness set at the outset wipes away every bitterness; nevertheless, lest I suspend your desires through a contrived pretense, I have obtained no proof of any of these matters. The bishop considers it harsh that I should mention the mules; and although the persistence of your servant, your brother Gaianus, had pressed the matter, and his importunity had burdened us beyond measure, we accomplished nothing through joint action. They want only this inserted: that your holy father, invited by your many kindnesses and favor, has looked toward a return of the gift to you. If this kind of evidence pleases you, write back without hesitation, or indicate what form it ought to take. Now I, that man of endangered usefulness, already tested for many years in your service, have expressed in swift leaps of words how much I have done—something that scarcely anyone else could have narrated through the endless losses of paper.

## LETTER VI. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

I believe it belongs to justice that I should be the first to provide what I expect from you. For it is fitting that one who awaits good works should invite them by example. The person who supplies the model of service conquers delay with spurs. Therefore, offering you the duty of a greeting, I declare that I am well after the irregularity I suffered on account of my sins, and I inquire into the state of your prosperity, hoping that you will devote considerable attention to resolving this matter.

## LETTER VII. ENNODIUS TO SENARIO

Among holy consciences, the principal preoccupation does not deny the obligations owed to affection, nor does it drive the fervor of pious love from its court. Whoever does not bury affection in oblivion amid obstacles gives testimony to its solidity. Commend your exalted station to me in writing, which I have importunately earned through my desire: the guardianship of fellowship is an honor belonging to the eminent. Therefore, greeting you with the utmost devotion, I confine my letter to brevity, knowing that extended letters may be dreaded; and I ask you to give thanks to the Lord on my behalf, for he removed the trouble I endured before you could learn of it.

## LETTER VIII. ENNODIUS TO ELPIDIUS THE DEACON

How, and by what art, should I urge your fraternity to write, when you, a man rich in words, preserve a foreign silence toward me? I have chosen to make you speak by speaking myself, and to extend that Attic learning into letters through a different kind of chatter. Was it right for you to withdraw from your promise for so many days and to indicate by no direction of a page how you had arrived? Or do you perhaps think that your usual caution ought to be observed against me? Do you disdain the conversation of those whose favor you sought through so much exertion? Believe me, unless you suspend yourself from this fault with the speed at which you customarily walk, we shall have to transfer our patronage to others who, mindful of their position, will reward affection with service.

Therefore, greeting you, my friend and physician, I inform you that I am suffering from a serious bodily disorder. Unless a page dictated by you, destined to display wit, cures it, I shall make my distended *ranula*—a swelling beneath the tongue—match tall men in its torments.

[Note: [Col. 0135D] Elpidius the Deacon: The final letter indicates that he was a physician. There is therefore no doubt that this is Elpidius, the physician of King Theoderic, whose letter to him survives, likewise addressed to “Helpidius the Deacon,” in Book IV of the *Variae*. In it, while commending his devoted service, Theoderic understands this very service to be medical. Procopius, *Gothic War*, Book I: “Afterward, having recounted to Elpidius the physician all that had happened, he began to lament the crime committed against Symmachus and Boethius.” He is indicated as having been from Milan by Book IX, Letter 21. Some think he is the same as Rusticus Helpidius, *vir clarissimus* and *illustris*, former quaestor, whose poems are read in the *Collection of Sacred Poets*. In any case, this example shows that in those early centuries clerics did not abstain from the practice of medicine. The epitaph of another Dionysius, a deacon and physician who flourished after the Goths captured Rome, likewise testifies to the same point. It appears among the *Christian Monuments* and begins as follows:

“Here lies the Levite Dionysius, who practiced the honorable art  
and also the profession that medicine bestowed.”]

## LETTER IX. ENNODIUS TO MESSALA

If divine favor is already leading you from your purpose of negligence toward the studies you desire, if you attend to wherever that impulse, wherever Lord Faustus, calls you, do not keep your wishes silent in writing. But I fear that, while I desire you to be dutiful, I may endure you as a rustic, and that what I desired may begin to resist my desires. May heavenly riches awaken that sluggishness with the goad of piety, and may heavenly assistance enrich the poverty of your speech. See: provoked by injuries, I write. Therefore, offering you a greeting, I ask that I may learn from the publication of your tablets what is happening around you.

## LETTER X. ENNODIUS TO MAXIMUS, *VIR SPECTABILIS*

May our vows be well ordered by the judgment of heaven. May he himself come to your marriage who, while the first parent still rejoiced in his native immortality, granted him the gift of heavenly blessing. May our Christ ensure that neither the fruit of your guarded integrity nor the gifts of marriage perish for you. May virginity contribute to offspring in such a way that fertility takes nothing away from your chastity; and, through the wondrous mystery of divine dispensation, may you not perish from the world while you are a father, nor from God’s grace while you are chaste. May what Isaac, moved by piety toward his younger son, desired come upon you (Gen. 27:28). May your wife enter your mother-in-law’s house under the same auspices under which the daughter-in-law entered Tobias’s inner chamber (Tob. 6). May the cause of perfect affection be in your wife, and virginity preserved in you. Know that she alone has been appointed for you, she for whom you preserved yourself, as though you were not yourself, from the filth of the world.

See, because I could not come, I am not absent in prayer. My lord, I hope that, having received the honor of my greeting, you will graciously accept what I have sent you.

[Note: [Col. 0136D] “What I have sent you”: I suppose, an epithalamium. In ancient copies, the epithalamium written for Maximus is usually placed before the next letter, to Arator, in which Ennodius exhorts him concerning the same subject. We have rejected it from among the other poems of Ennodius.]

## LETTER XI. ENNODIUS TO ARATOR

I wonder why, through shameful silence, you disfigure the good things of polished conversation that had been cultivated in you for Roman refinement, and why, avoiding riches acquired through much labor, you consume your stewardship through silence. Whatever is bestowed upon worthy people adorns its author while it is in use; whoever confines the elegance of talents diminishes it. There is only one error: to come forth as a rustic and to hide what deserves the honor of praise. Did you have nothing worthy of remembrance, or did I seem to you unworthy of being honored with eloquence? Was there ever a subject so deserving celebration by everyone’s tongues and letters as when a man is led into a nuptial union, a man whose birth is illustrious and whose resources are abundant, but whose discipline and modesty surpass both? He renounced the vices of the flesh and rejected, as a shameful indulgence, whatever the laws granted as a remedy; unwilling to devote his wife’s body to servitude, he thought himself enslaved if he contributed anything to the world at the expense of free chastity.

Even if you do not love these matters, you ought nevertheless to praise them for the display of your talent. We may believe that you are becoming a good man if we hear you proclaiming what is honorable. Now, offering you the most generous greeting, I urge you to write back. Do not judge me by this letter of mine: God is my witness, I dictated it in passing while returning from the basilica.

## LETTER XII. ENNODIUS TO FLORUS

You can infer from the quality of your spirit by what devotion I hold you and with what diligence I embrace you. For it scarcely happens that anyone is loved unless it is established that he has sincerely loved. Heavenly strength brings souls together, and through many utterances reveals their interests to one another; therefore you are preparing to repay me in kind.

[Note: [Col. 0137D] “Urge Lord Faustus”: the praetorian prefect, to whom he writes in Letter 19: “I hope that you will deign, with your customary kindness, to receive my petition, which I have sent through my fellow-servant, your brother Florus.” Nor was his hope disappointed, for he obtained it, as Letters 21 and 22 of Book IX show.]

Urge my lord to order that, if he approves, that suburban property be purchased at the price I have offered—a property which I shall possess happily while I am in Liguria, and which he and his family may possess after my death. Yet, after God, he seems to confer upon me liberty and substance if I obtain this favor through him. But may your daughter live; may you hold from her the sons you desire; may God make your soul equal to those of his saints; and may your brother live—urge him humbly and persistently, so that you bring my petition to fulfillment. Consider God; consider my needs; for there is nothing that his power or his affection toward me could do that would be greater.

## LETTER XIII. ENNODIUS TO AURELIANUS THE PRIEST

I would be lying about my affection if, departing from you, I did not remain with you, and if I did not carry away with me your blessedness, although it had been placed in its station.

[Note: [Col. 0137D] “Departing from you, I remained”: Ruricius, Book II, Letters 1 and 9: “For after I departed from your brotherhood, I feel myself divided and recognize that a part of me remained with you. Nor do I seem to myself to be whole when you are absent; and when I do not find myself in myself, I seek myself among you when I have returned to you. And there I perceive that as much of me as I left with you, so much of you I carried away with me.”]

And because the mind is the ruler of the body in me as in others, it is wholly captive to attention toward you. Therefore, paying the honor of greeting with due humility, I declare that no part of my health has diminished through the exhaustion of the journey. See how, through the care of benevolent devotion, I repay your concern: do what is written, returning what you have received, and let me rejoice at the indication of your prosperity.

## LETTER XIV. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

I would be silent about my troubles if I had not understood that your concern lifts me up. For when you learn how I am wearied by various afflictions of disease, and how I am frequently surrendered to fevers on account of my sins, the strength that seemed to have been restored is broken. Therefore provide your customary remedies and offer that practice of holy fellowship, so that by prayers poured out to our God you may obtain whatever the medicine of mortals is unable to accomplish.

## LETTER XV. ENNODIUS TO EDASIUS

Before friends are tested, their fidelity is hidden; once it has emerged into the light, it binds to itself the minds of those who possess any discernment. Yet the servitude offered to loved ones is a less oppressive form of servitude. I confess to your greatness: before my man’s report, I did not know what taste and grace lay hidden beneath your noble humility. I have learned that you are a man who surpasses hoary blessedness in fidelity, because you bear well the absence of friends. You had indeed promised more as you departed, but you have provided greater things, in accordance with the character of your conscience.

My lord and son, offering you the gift of an overflowing greeting, I give and acknowledge insufficient thanks for what was bestowed upon me at the outset of *potitiae* [Note: [Col. 0138D] *potitiae*: “potitiae” in the manuscripts; the *Faber* edition reads *potentiae* (“power”), and the Basel edition reads *pueritiae* (“childhood”).]. As for what remains, I beg you now to have the remaining slaves held. See the confidence descending from the preceding benefits: the man who before feared to offer prayers to one unknown now does not hesitate to give orders.

## LETTER XVI. ENNODIUS TO BARBARA

I did not, forgetful of what I owed, refrain from my duties; nor, despising what had been established, did I suspend my loquacity from the display of service. But after I returned from the city, various illnesses and everything that calls one toward death immediately seized me. Truly, my lady, may such things happily befall you and yours: for, as a testimony to the ancient mystery, our Christ again called Lazarus from the tomb, although I am a sinner and not like the man who deserved to be called his friend. The event is one despite the difference of persons; and now the greatness of the divine work is greater, because what the other deserved came to me undeservedly.

[Note: [Col. 0138D] Barbara: She is mentioned with praise in Book VII, Letter 29, and Ennodius will write to her again in Letter 27.]

This circumstance recalled me from publishing my duty. Yet once I had been restored to life, I immediately turned to discharging my services to you, asking God to protect you and yours by heavenly aid. I also promise myself and my desires that, when your dignity has been obtained, it will summon you to the watches of the court, together with your prosperity and joy, in a way that satisfies my wishes. Do not, my lady, withdraw yourself from this labor or this burden. Let the provinces of the Roman state see good things, and let those who are scarcely instructed by admonitions be formed by the examples of the good things God has bestowed upon you.

Nevertheless, after offering the reverence of a greeting, I ask you to refresh me with the conversation I so greatly desire. But do not permit anyone else to dictate what you write to me: may your prayer never be driven away from obtaining what it seeks.

## LETTER XVII. ENNODIUS TO STEPHANIA

I believe that you have aided me in my dangers even without knowing it. Or why should I trust that you know nothing, when it happens through God that you foresee everything? For after I returned from the city, the divine mysteries were renewed in me, and what had grown old through time rose again in new examples. Lazarus was once again called from the tomb—not indeed with the equal merit of the man who earned the name “friend of the Redeemer,” but in the diversity of actions the form of the same mystery was fulfilled. Led through manifold illnesses to the tombs, but recalled by a heavenly voice, I turned myself first toward these services now rendered to you, believing that I please God if services are offered in the foremost place to his worshipers through the tongue that he himself restored.

Therefore, having offered the reverence of a greeting, I beg you to arrange that you pray more attentively for me, as I requested, so that through your merit divine clemency may deign to strengthen what it has granted; and often refresh me through the pious publication of your letters. I beg you not to have anyone else dictate, by the soul of my lord Asterius and by your profession. May the support you desire remain with him until the time of completion.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] Stephania: Above, Book VII, Letter 29, she was the sister of Faustus the prefect. In Book IX, Letter 18, she is the wife of Asterius, as the conclusion of the letter seems to suggest, and consequently the mother of Marcianus; for Marcianus was the son of Asterius, Book V, Letter 2.]

## LETTER XVIII. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

The bearer of this letter compelled me toward my studies and almost forcibly extracted what I wanted to do. Thus the one who demanded it conferred a favor. In his affair this man asks for your examination of justice, already tested before the world; nor does he think that the truth of his case can be determined by anyone if you refrain from acting. On his behalf I approach as a petitioner, asking that, while you attend to heavenly commands and investigate the truth with complete attention, you assist the needs of an afflicted man. I also hope, after fulfilling the duty of a greeting, that you will refresh me by informing me of your prosperity, without neglecting the opportunities that frequently present themselves.

## LETTER XIX. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

Although every abundance of letters seems rare to those who are anxious, and foresight does not suffice for one who is suspended in piety, nevertheless the party to whom it is directed, unless it responds, is separated from humanity. Therefore, having first offered the duties of a greeting, I declare that, by God’s gift, things are now going better for me through the intercessions of the saints and your prayers, and that the illness of despair and fevers has grown milder. Now, as for what remains, I hope that you will deign, with your customary kindness, to receive my petition, which I sent through my fellow-servant, your brother Florus. For although the matter presently seems to me to be one of economy, to you, whose concern is more with the future, the greatest advantage will result from it.

## LETTER XX. ENNODIUS TO AGNELLUS

If I had the bodily strength to pursue you, I would abstain from words; but since that is lacking to my health, this takes its place. The examiner of secrets knows that, although separated from you in body, I cannot be absent from you in spirit. Therefore I relieve your concern by announcing my own well-being; and, since epistolary exchange has been granted, I inquire after yours, informing you—after offering the honor of a greeting—that I have sent my boy to receive a horse. The only requirement is that you send one such that it will be clear that you gave it, and that I may rejoice to have received it as the highest mark of honor.

## LETTER XXI. ENNODIUS TO BEATUS

If I could erase my page by writing, I would strive to do so with this repeated effort. But since it is not right for a human being not to err, I, that old man, but your father, beg you never to remember my earlier letter.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] “If I could erase”: In the epitaph of Cynegia, which we saw in the preceding book, Letter 29, Ennodius had shortened the first syllable of *matrona* in the final verse. When Beatus, having been warned about this by Probus, mentioned it along with other matters, the report reached Ennodius. Relying upon Terentianus’s authority, as he thought, and believing that there was no fault in that verse, Ennodius sent an abusive letter to Beatus. Now, having recognized his error, he excuses Beatus and wishes the earlier letter to be erased. This is Letter 29 of the present book. Hence the order here is also reversed, as we have noted above concerning other matters.]

May your father and your homeland receive you as the person whom I proclaim to everyone each day. I trusted writings belonging to others, so that through the untimely haste of my style I might bite you. You had done what a wise man should do: you had reread my verses for Lord Probus, who, among learned men, holds the art’s stronghold.

[Note: [Col. 0140D] “Who holds the art’s stronghold among the learned”: Read, “who holds the stronghold among those who possess the art.” Ennodius likewise says in the *Paraenesis* to Beatus and Ambrosius: “Therefore, hastening toward the stronghold of the disciplines.”]

I, being importunate, should not have believed another, and, as I now see, I was moved in vain. Go, therefore, to Lord Probus—for so may your father live; so may you hear me, whom you have always loved, alive, since I dictated this almost dead—and kiss his knees for me. Tell him that concerning the final verse Terentianus led me astray in that example:

“Thus, weeping, he speaks and gives the reins to the fleet.”  
*The Aeneid*, VI.1.

[Col. 0140D] Yet he had foreseen everything that deserved correction. I greet you with the love I owe you. If I survive, I shall correct the verses themselves and send them in that form. For I received your letters, which you sent through the child Rufinus, in the month of July. Hence it happened that I did not know what had taken place and was moved in this way.

## LETTER XXII. ENNODIUS TO FLORUS

Who could know the indications of my prosperity more justly than one who sincerely and unceasingly desired it? Nor is it fitting that one person should first learn another’s desires. Therefore, having offered the service of a greeting, I announce that, by heavenly favor, I was soon healed once human treatment had ceased. That circumstance restored me to hope of recovery, because the physicians had stopped. Now, learning your joys—as I imagine you will learn mine—join me in praising the bestower of so great a benefit. And if a longer delay still holds you back, inform me by letter how well you are.

## LETTER XXIII. ENNODIUS TO FLORUS

The distinguished man Eleutherius, in his affair—which the vicar had undertaken to have heard by the lord prefect—hoped to receive from me a letter of recommendation to your greatness, believing that, without prejudice to justice, he could obtain complete assistance if he were supported by my conversations with you. Therefore, after offering the honor of a greeting, I ask you, if he is truly suffering contrary to equity, to extend a healing hand to him. For it is wrong that cunning should appear able to help itself, to the detriment of a good cause, by what it is attempting.

## LETTER XXIV. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

Your kindness preserves its customary practice, set above ordinary human beings. Truly, the care of the most holy man is medicine, for a reverent conscience always makes known to God what it seeks. After you had departed, a fiercer heat consumed me, and, as the devil drove me toward utter despair, my sails were spread. A physician came to me and said that he had nothing to do. From this came greater hope for me, once the human agent had ceased. Immediately, with tears, I turned to the aid of the heavenly physician, and armed my entire body—which was already being prepared for the tomb—against the fevers with the oil of Lord Victor.

[Note: [Col. 0141D] “Of Lord Victor”: The Milanese martyr. He will treat this wondrous cure at greater length in the *Eucharisticus* of his life.]

My God knows: immediately the commander of the great soldier was present, and I obtained without delay what I had asked through his reliable witness. Soon that fever, the provider of eternal cold, grew mild, and at the ninth hour it departed, as we read, at my Lord’s command (John 4). I know the times of your prayer; I know that the abundance of your tears also aided the sufferer at that moment. See, I have not kept silent about the signs of the fulfillment of your vows; but the scarcity of messengers suspends our shared desire. For your relief greatly delights me, though you, who rejected joyful things, scarcely desire it.

## LETTER XXV. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

As soon as heavenly grace looked upon me and, granting that it should improve, loosened the soul trembling near the heavenly judgment by allowing it a space of life, I did not keep silent in my letters to your greatness about the divine benefits. Truly, when the physicians ceased, the medicine of him who is purchased by innocence and tears did not fail. Believe me: unless the abandonment by those administering treatment had come to my aid, I would have had no strength. For because I was suffering from the attentions of human beings, I began already to be healed by their negligence. These matters have indeed been communicated in earlier letters, but lest the opportunity pass, I have added them, hoping that, after offering the service of a greeting, you will refresh me by your conversation concerning the prosperity on which I depend.

## LETTER XXVI. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

The person who desires your writings must not remain silent, nor should one who desires conversation set an example of silence. In accordance with the intercessions of your prayers, I now feel myself better, since innocence and devotion make those who possess them acceptable to our God. After offering the honor of a greeting, I desire to learn how well you are; for after health has been recovered, the one consolation is to be uplifted by the good fortune of your prosperity.

## LETTER XXVII. ENNODIUS TO BARBARA

Although I am still placed among the extreme dangers, and because of the weight of my sins the benefits of sleep do not follow me while I deserve to be worn down for a long time, my dependent soul has nevertheless not omitted what it owes to the services of your reverence. It is almost already being summoned to judgment, yet it still looks upon those whom it honored in this light. How true is that saying: holy affection does not perish even through death!

Therefore, my lady, following you with the services of a greeting that I owe you, I ask you, once you have learned what is happening around me, to entreat my lord the apostle and his other brothers—for the excellence in which you surpass everyone, both through the brilliance of your blood and through the radiance of your way of life—so that God’s power, entreated through you, may not restrain the benefits of his mercy, which is not accustomed to be slow.

## LETTER XXVIII. ENNODIUS TO BEATUS

By what repayment, by what care of service, shall I measure the fact that I converse with you in frequent pages and do not object to bringing your office of speech out into public light? Neither your age nor an equal measure of talent with mine can turn me away. I choose to trust the kind more than the learned, so that they may place the goodness of their origin before their studies. That you are faithful is a gift of God; learning belongs to nature; through God prosperity will come. It is necessary that love of integrity offer you everything, since you already possess the distinctions of the foremost ranks.
