Therefore, having received the honor of a greeting, know that, in accordance with your request, I have dictated a letter of admonition to you, although in haste.

[Note: [Col. 0142D] “The letter of admonition to you”: the didactic *Paraenesis* written to Beatus and Ambrosius, which we have included among the miscellaneous short works.]

I arranged to send it to Lord Patricius Symmachus for this reason: so that whatever in it deserves correction might be corrected. But, because of the stealth of negligence, I also furnished you with a copy of it. For this reason, keep the matter to yourself, and take care not to reveal that it was brought to you, once you have encountered the eminent man mentioned above, as though you were asking for something new. For if you learn that it pleased him under his instruction, you will not fear to convey it to the notice of those who are wise.

## LETTER XXIX. ENNODIUS TO BEATUS

Your error did not deceive me, nor did affection turned backward mislead me. You preserved the order of age, nature, and purpose; I was at fault in judging you otherwise than truth required. Those who are captured by misguided diligence come back to this point; therefore I must now speak without circumlocution.

Where did insane presumption lead you, that you should say to the holy priest that, in those verses—although they were composed in a moment of time—it seemed to some that the affection of conjugal grace had not been expressed?

[Note: [Col. 0143D] “To the holy priest”: Adeodatus, in the following letter.]

Or did I wish to defame what I had written? Did the epitaphs demand this, or reason? What ignorant person, what man devoid of sound judgment together with you, said that a poem which Lord Faustus received with the greatest favor should be damaged by you and your companions gnawing at it? Perhaps, concerning the third Phalaecian verse, those who do not know Terentianus found something to say while seeking an occasion in a single syllable.

[Note: [Col. 0143D] “Concerning the third Phalaecian”: that is, “May the matron desire a similar lot,” the verse with which Ennodius had closed Cynegia’s epitaph in Book VII, Letter 29. This, then, is the letter that he retracted shortly afterward, in Letter 21.]

I truly deserved what I suffered, because it is written (Matt. 7:6) that pearls should not be cast before unclean animals. Although I am well aware of the poverty of my diction and learning, I had never before learned that you neither knew anything nor would ever know anything. Farewell, and turn to speak with others to whom you owe speech.

## LETTER XXX. ENNODIUS TO ADEODATUS THE PRIEST

Crushed by the bitter assault of illness and the severe excess of fevers, when our Christ had shown in me, as he had done in Lazarus, the truth of the ancient testimony and had made the faith of the Gospel clear through present examples, I received your letters. He who was able arranged that, on the days when he had restored my life, he should also strengthen and support it through the conversations of his friends.

The foolish judgments concerning the verses, from which he told you that portentous tale, made me laugh. Know that they were held in the highest esteem by my lord, although they had been written under the pressure of time and in passing through the garden. But if you did not write them, do not do so. It is enough for me, since I did it, to have fulfilled my vows. Now I turn myself toward that part which ought especially to be requested from the saints: pray more attentively for a sick man who loves, and, if I deserve it, provide me with frequent conversations both of instruction and consolation.

## LETTER XXXI. ENNODIUS TO BOETIUS

Consideration for your greatness demanded an exchange of letters, but the messenger’s haste brought the letter to a close in brevity. I could not delay the man who was hurrying away, but neither did I send him out empty of these duties, since circumstances required it. I have sent frequent letters concerning the house I requested. If it is possible for what I desire to be granted, now report it, because all its buildings are growing old through neglect. My lord, fulfilling the services of a greeting, I ask you to help the petitioner without expense to yourselves.

## LETTER XXXII. ENNODIUS TO SYMMACHUS, THE POPE

He provides for what is necessary who commends to the father of all those who are bereaved and foreigners; the one path is the consolation of your apostolate, which heals outsiders. It is wrong to call afflicted those who happen to reach you: those whom the care of your crown has received do not seek the homeland of their Creator or riches elsewhere. The bearer of this letter, nobly born, seeks Roman studies that will serve as testimony to his free birth.

Now my petitioning assertion commends him to your blessedness, so that, having graciously accepted the services of a greeting, you may, in consideration of me, redouble what you customarily do.

## LETTER XXXIII. ENNODIUS TO HORMISDAS THE DEACON

Both what you are is adorned by compassion, and what you will be is sought through piety. Through these pursuits you have elevated the diaconate, whose care promises the pontificate. The bearer of this letter, honorable in morals and lofty by nature, deprived of the support of twin consolations, has sought Rome, although he will be a foreigner there, for honorable pursuits. See whether what I have brought forward deserves to be aided by a religious, well-born, wealthy man.

Now, having offered the duty of a greeting, I ask that, if you love me and the good opinion you have acquired, the bearer may grow through the assistance you provide.

[Note: [Col. 0143D] Hormisdas the Deacon: His name appears among the deacons of the Roman Church at the synod of Symmachus, which was convened during the consulship of the younger Avienus. He has already appeared several times in Ennodius; here he is not obscurely foretold the papacy. Again, in Letter 39, Ennodius says: “Be a special guardian; soon you will be guardian of all.” The prophecy was not empty, because Hormisdas succeeded Pope Symmachus.]

## LETTER XXXIV. ENNODIUS TO PORTIANUS, THE ABBOT

It is shown by divine examples that heavenly visitations do not come to human beings except through the grace of God. For what remembrance can sinners possess unless heavenly favor works through hidden paths and, by a way inspired in the mind, removes the forgetfulness that could have stolen in on account of sins?

The confidence of divine mercy already obtained is that it does not fail the minds of God’s worshipers. Therefore I give thanks to our triune God, who required that your reverence visit me through conversation. I accept your obedience; for no small worship is owed to those who obey, since the glory of Christ remains the commander.

Pray for me—you who, while you are still human, have escaped the weakness of human nature; you whom it has happened to be freed from the weights of the flesh before the body has yet been separated from it. And, having received the services of a greeting, grant me the fruit of grace toward me while the cultivation of speech grows.

[Note: [Col. 0144D] Portianus the Abbot: Although the dates do not conflict, I would nevertheless not dare to affirm that this is our Saint Portianus, who was abbot of the monastery of Candidobres in the territory of the Arverni and left his name both to it and to the not insignificant town. We call it Sanportianus. There was also a Porcianus who was bishop in the province and attended the synods of Carpentras and Vaison a few years after Ennodius.]

## LETTER XXXV. ENNODIUS TO AURELIANUS THE PRIEST

[Note: [Col. 0144D] Aurelianus the Priest: Of Arles, as the following passages make clear.]

[Col. 0144D] An opportunity quite unwelcome to my desires has served me, and a necessity scarcely bearable has opened a way to my wishes. I embraced the page that began with flattering words, but I was bewildered by what followed. For the sweet beginning and the honeyed serenity of the conversation are overshadowed by the calamity reported, as though by a garment of night. Truly, what I was reading was placed before your eyes as you spoke. For while the page of a wise man interrupted the happiness of absence, I was compelled to see that Aetheria—

[Note: “[That Aetheria] the daughter-in-law of Archotamia,” about whom see Book VII, Letter 14. But the whole interpretation of this letter must be sought in Cassiodorus, where Theoderic writes to Count Merobaudes about this Aetheria in Book IV, Letter 12:

“Thus the illustrious woman Archotamia, lamenting bitterly, bewailed the misfortune of her grandson in the following complaint, since a grandmother’s concern for her family is always the more tenacious. She asserted that her daughter-in-law Aetheria, having set aside her husband’s affection, had joined herself to a certain Liberius in a marital bond; and, wishing to appear more splendid in her new bridal chamber, had endeavored to ruin the resources of her former husband, alleging that it had been assigned to the despoiling of her sons, for whom it ought rather to have been amassed.”

]—that Aetheria had looked too much toward earthly things, and that guilt had cast her down from the sublimity of her name into Tartarus. I say nothing of what she owed her parents, or modesty; from what household the unhappy woman proceeded into crime; what she followed, abandoning the worshipers of God—a marriage in place of a brothel. Believe me: while committing the crime, she carried out its punishment; and, sunk in a disgraceful union, she found in her husband both the offense and the penalty of the offense. She carried with her the status of an accused person; and, by choosing an unworthy man, [became] a judge’s woman (*judicis mulier*; the sense is uncertain).

I would produce the letters, were I not wishing to bury the memory of that ill-fated woman in oblivion. You will choose that they be expelled so that Gaul may be relieved; we, so that Italy may not be polluted. Let them seek instead the Syrtes of Libya and be separated from the fellowship of humanity. For if they flee Lord Aurelian from there, and Ennodius from here, to what places will they turn?

[Note: “To the Lord Prefect Faustus.”]

To the Lord Prefect I have more fully reported what you ordered; and he—

[Note: “The royal commands.” Those, evidently, contained in the Cassiodorian letter mentioned immediately above, in which Theoderic entrusts Merobaudes with Archotamia’s case against her daughter-in-law Aetheria: “We commit this case to the judgment of Your Sublimity, to be heard according to the laws, so that, with every incivility removed, before the holy Gospels, together with three honorable men chosen by agreement of the parties and capable of knowing the laws, you may pronounce between them whatever the form of ancient law establishes, taking account of the discipline of our own time.” After judgment had been rendered, when Liberius complained of his depraved wife, Theoderic wrote again in Letter 46 that the case should be reheard through arbitrators.]

—immediately carried out the royal commands, through which, we believe, good and friendly men found an opportunity to render assistance. Nevertheless, remove anxiety from your mind, for the heavenly power of judgment will suffice to avenge the wicked.

My lord, presenting the duties of a greeting, I beg you, whenever the opportunity of travelers presents itself, to refresh me frequently with conversations concerning your prosperity.

## LETTER XXXVI. ENNODIUS TO BOETHIUS

The tongue had lost the value of its learning while you remained silent. For while silence enclosed the charm of eloquence, it was believed that what recently burst forth did not exist. You have brought a new radiance of eloquence into the light; and, while you make day in your letter, you are believed to have newly acquired a splendor already mature. I give thanks that the flower of your letter compels me to guard our friendship. But if you were aware of my fidelity, you would have no doubt about matters that are constant. I fear that you may display the ambiguity you imagine; and, while you fear the lukewarmness of one who loves, may grow cold toward affection.

[Note: “My lord, as above.” Thus in Book I, Letter 12, Book II, Letter 9, and elsewhere. In writing letters, it was customary to address each person at the beginning with the titles of his honors and to repeat the same titles at the end. For example, the letter of Volusianus to Saint Augustine begins: “To the truly holy and deservedly venerable father Augustine, Volusianus.” It closes in the same manner: “May the highest Godhead preserve your holiness unharmed, my truly holy and deservedly venerable father.” Again, Augustine’s letter replying to Volusianus begins: “To the illustrious, deservedly distinguished, and most excellent son Volusianus, Augustine.” At the end it says: “May the most merciful omnipotence of God preserve you unharmed and more blessed, my illustrious, deservedly distinguished, and most excellent son.” The same repetition is found in many letters of Augustine and others. To avoid it, copyists used the abbreviation “AS ABOVE,” that is, as it had been written at the beginning of the letter. In Ennodius, however, all the letter-titles have been omitted, leaving only bare names. The same happened with imperial rescripts in the Code and the Novels. Thus expressions such as “Hail, Tatianus, dearest to us,” and “Albinus, dearest parent of the Augusti,” and similar formulas—which according to the custom I mentioned were ordinarily repeated twice—now appear only once, sometimes at the beginning and sometimes at the end, because the rescripts are not preserved in their entirety.]

My lord, having fulfilled the courtesy of a greeting, as above, I hope that you will frequently direct to me an exchange of letters, since in these offices both diligence urges you and excellence requires you to be assiduous.

## LETTER XXXVII. ENNODIUS TO BOETHIUS

Although eloquence arises from a petition with scant success, favorable circumstances both win favor for and enrich eloquence. If these are absent amid however great a profusion of words in a letter, such letters are barren of success: praise is owed more to fortunate letters than to skillful ones. He speaks rightly in words of elevated brilliance who captivates the highest men by the beauty of his speech. Every rhetorical figure is scattered by adverse fortune; for the tongue nourished by benefits grows rich.

Some time ago I directed to your Eminence a conversation produced by whatever audacity I possessed. You so elevated it by the spirit of your reply that I thought I had lost the time of deserved favor in sleep, when a modest effort had attracted the judgment of one who holds the citadel. You had also promised that the house I had requested would not be denied. Raised up by these two successes, I proceeded as though both the expectation of completed agreement and the wealth of the richest resources would increase through expenditure.

But I detest the delay produced by barren offenses. For the man of your rank whom I was awaiting did arrive, and he asserted that nothing had been entrusted to him that could benefit my wishes. Behold the dark dealings of my merits: although they shine against me, they cannot break my trust; yet they demand delay. Far be it from my conscience to distrust your distinction. It would be the mark of an evil mind to think that the memory of a settled decision does not remain. But I ask that, while you affirm the light of your intention, you overcome the darkness of what is owed to me.

Therefore infuse the generosity of your performance with the spirit of speed. My lord, offering the service of a greeting, I add my prayers that I may receive, together with the reply to the petition mentioned above, the consular sportula.

[Note: “The consular sportula.” Since Boethius was consul, see Letter 1 of this book. Sportulae were owed to new friends as a mark of honor. Symmachus, Book IX, final letter: “I owe you the sportula of my consulship, both to our friendship and to your honor.”]

## LETTER XXXVIII. ENNODIUS TO SYMMACHUS, THE POPE

[Col. 0147A]

He makes his request effectively who introduces strangers to the father of all. General protection is owed to the noble, especially before those who bestow benefits without being asked. If your crown graciously receives the blessed and distinguished young man who bears this letter, it adorns a splendid office in accordance with the custom of a bishop. He is one who deserves your favor both by birth and by character; for the worthy, concise praise is sufficient.

Now, having rendered the duties of a greeting, I ask you to refresh me, who love you, by frequently proclaiming your conversation.

## LETTER XXXIX. ENNODIUS TO THE DEACON HORMISDAS

If the favor promised toward me endured, the frequency of your letters would confirm it. The humble are scarcely noticed by those whom prosperous fortune has raised to the summit. It is grievous if the hope of favorable circumstances cuts the bonds of affection; it ought not to prejudice the diligence of one whom it pleases according to his wishes.

If, however, you preserve some favor toward me; if the spark of your promised love lives, I commend to you Beatus, a most noble young man, the bearer of this letter. It is right that, out of consideration for me, your Blessedness should provide him with both a parent and a homeland. Be his special guardian, soon to be everyone’s. My brother and lord, having discharged the humility of a greeting, I ask you to mark by writing how well you are as soon as possible.

## LETTER XL. ENNODIUS TO BOETHIUS

The repetition of prayers accuses a good conscience of forgetfulness. But let it cease to spur one who is already running and to drive a steadfast man to remember his promise. I have touched briefly on what I wrote some time ago to your Eminence, so that I may complete the house whose existence your will has already disclosed through the evidence of your letter. I have entrusted the rest of the letter to the messenger of a greeting, so that, just as health is established among us, heavenly favor may make it known that it also exists in your high position.

## LETTER XLI. ENNODIUS TO AGAPITUS

The absence of those who love one another would be unbearable unless the remedies of letters came to our aid; these nourish the hungry souls of those who long with the food of conversation. For affection skillfully paints for itself, through writing, the likeness of a friend, with whom it may mingle the honey of speech without enduring labor.

For this purpose your greatness, acting as an artist so as not to leave your favor unformed, wrote. I owe you a return, since I have learned that you remember me. Therefore, having offered the honor of a greeting, I ask you not to omit doing continuously what you know to be precious among dear friends and those endowed with affection.

## LETTER XLII. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

The news of your illness has contributed to the increase of my own. For it has always been both the habit and almost the nature of an anxious person scarcely to believe that what he fears has passed; and he sighs over what our Redeemer has accomplished in heavenly kindness as though it were stored away in hidden places.

Truly, Lord Avienus, after the love of God, nothing of the interest yielded by this light remains for me except your affection. When things go better with me, I am such as you left me in despair. It remains that, through your prayers, both forgiveness of sins may be granted and, if it so pleases God, death may come swiftly as a remedy, lest what I live through become more bitter than death.

[Note: “Death in place of a remedy.” One who languishes under a prolonged illness longs for death as a remedy. An old epitaph:

> Thou hast come at last, sweeter than my life, who hast released me  
> from grievous illnesses,  
> from suffering,  
> and from wretched gout.

Aurelius Amphictyon, in his seventieth year.]

My lord, paying the debt of a greeting with complete humility, I ask that through you I may learn what is being reported from Rome concerning your affairs.

## LETTER XLIII. ENNODIUS TO MESSALA

Has anyone who entreated God with confidence ever been deprived of the result? If the mind does not falter in faith, both prayers and an abundance of prayers are joined together. Behold, my silence has accomplished with you what loquacity was unable to obtain for so long. As I see it, your writings deserve nothing except silence: you address those whom you think mute, and you abstain from those who are believed to possess a tongue.

Nevertheless, you have done what was fitting for a lord and, as you yourself say, a parent: you judged me, weighed down by severe illness, worthy of conversation. I ask you to continue doing this. My lord, having discharged the reverence of a greeting, I ask you not to cease imploring all God’s saints on my behalf, so that, restored to life, I may rejoice in the sight of you.

# BOOK NINE

## LETTER I. ENNODIUS TO ARATOR

[Col. 0147D]

I gladly accept the conjecture of the most learned cardinal that this Arator is the man who expounded the Acts of the Apostles in verse. At this time, however, he was still a young man, though already not unknown as a soldier in the camp of the Muses, as the two letters above in the preceding book show.

Athalaric testifies that he was a Ligurian by birth, born of an eloquent father, educated in Liguria itself, and engaged in the profession of an advocate. He also records that Arator honorably undertook an embassy to King Theoderic on behalf of the Dalmatians; see Book VIII of the *Variae*, Letter 12, by which he grants Arator the rank of *comes domesticorum*. An old annotation prefixed to the books of Arator in most copies informs us that he was also adorned with the rank of *comes rerum privatarum*, before he left the court and devoted himself to the Church.

The manner in which he was presented to and received by Vigilius is shown by the following beginning of the copy preserved in the Reims codex of the monks of Saint Remigius:

“With Blessed Peter’s assistance, this book was presented by the illustrious Arator, formerly *comes domesticorum*, formerly *comes rerum privatarum*, truly religious, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, to the holy and apostolic man, Pope Vigilius, and was received by him on the eighth day before the Ides of April,”

and so forth.

Parthenius Ennodius had formerly been Arator’s instructor in composing sacred poetry—that is, in turning the Muses toward divine subjects. Therefore, after Arator had sung the Acts of the Apostles and, as has been said, presented his work to Vigilius, he sent it to Parthenius in Gaul so that it might be published there through his efforts.

On this subject there is an outstanding letter from Arator to Parthenius himself, in elegiac verse, in the same Reims codex. Since it has not yet been published, I trust that, if I insert it here as a foreign ornament, this unusual but not useless digression will not be unwelcome.

### TO ARATOR

[Col. 0147D]

I would like you to favor my work in such a way as to grant pardon to my untrained talent, since it is wrong, in matters of devotion, to despise the lovable desire to learn. For when a gracious person offers something, a harsh interpreter of things destroys it.

He who is not thought capable of matching eloquence should nevertheless be praised for his studies. Among the kindly and the learned, it is uncertain what one should choose, since each side possesses its own value. Therefore trust one who is diligent, and soften bitterness with the seasons of legitimate love.

I do not want you to turn the object of my desire into a necessity, or to draw out into grief the wishes that nature has produced for the human race. One who cannot maintain continence except by desiring marriage is at fault; avoiding the remedy of marital union, he must choose either virtues or crimes.

I beg you to measure yourself, so that you neither undertake a path too great for a human being full of misfortunes nor meditate, while still human, on things deserving punishment. One scarcely commits an offense who does not depart from nature and law.

Therefore, after the camp of the Muses and the empty songs of our age, turn to the care of begetting offspring. Life has become cheap, because among the host of the ignorant it is madness to refuse to become rustic; the wise man delights in being what most people are.

Let philosophy depart from the assemblies known to our people. I wish you to have given yourself to cares whenever one who leads follows unhappy ignorance. Therefore, having received the honor of your greeting, write back to me what my page has done to your mind. For if you ask what my judgment is, I now detest the very names of the liberal studies.

## LETTER II. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

Your Eminence’s conscience knows what I owe, in accordance with his wish and his family, to the distinguished man Faustinius. Therefore, although he believes that what a father has requested for his son ought to be sufficient with you, through me—because he considers his own concern inadequate—he repeats his prayers, hoping that our young man, with God’s favor, may be raised toward mature conduct.

You should give him instructions about what he ought to follow and what he ought to avoid; you should, whenever you deem it necessary, pursue him by writing. I know that your Eminence would do this even if I were silent, but I neither ought nor could fail the prayers of so great a man. Moved by this matter and by the tears I mentioned above, I too, weeping, beseech you by that conscience granted to you by God—for may the holy advocacy of the martyrs commend your petitions to our Savior—that both the Creator may plead with you for his son and Lord Faustinus for Ambrosius.

Set the young man in order, and pray for him, so that Rome may not destroy him either in vices or in character. I know that you prevail greatly among human beings, but even more greatly before God. Therefore I now confidently promise fulfillment to those whom I commend.

Thus, having discharged the reverence of a greeting, I have woven many things into a few words. It is enough that the piety of a man pleasing to God should be instructed; with God’s help, let both the case and the person be arranged through your care.

## LETTER III. ENNODIUS TO MERIBAUDES

Just as though one should help the sun with torches or enrich the sea with a small amount of moisture, so does the man labor with needless expenditure who commends what is pleasing in itself. But it is foolish to let an opportunity for doing good perish when a strong man seeks assistance. The generous man is enriched beyond his resources if he believes in the support offered by a poor man.

A gift becomes royal when the recipient gives it distinguished value. Lord Faustinus, concerned for the advancement of his offspring beyond what paternal care ordinarily requires, has believed that our Ambrosius should be strengthened by this recommendation to you. He considers that his blood, his prudence, and his wealth lie hidden within the narrow confines of Liguria, and that the fame of his noble skill is hemmed in by obstacles. Through another’s support he believes that his distinction will break forth into the Roman light.

Let it be far from my studies to deny testimony that gives greater assistance to the author, for one who asserts the good is himself approved. See what confidence he has in you, to whom he has entrusted everything exceptional that a noble land possesses. I do not want him to think that such a family could be found only among us. It is enough for those eager for honors to surpass many in such a way that they are compared with the best.

The young man’s publicly recognized nobility reveals the modesty of his birth. May the dispensation of the divine will ensure that, through you, his beginnings here may be well established and made firm. Therefore accept the honor of a greeting and respond to my request with the paternal affection that antiquity attributed to teachers.

## LETTER IV. ENNODIUS TO PROBINUS

[Note: “To Probinius,” an illustrious man and patrician, as is evident from Theoderic’s letter to him, *Variae* II.11, and from the author’s *Paraenesis* to Beatus and Ambrosius. This is the same Ambrosius, the son of Faustinus, whom he commends to Probinius.]

### TO PROBINUS

[Col. 0150C]

If my supplication remained present in your memory, it would have been evident through frequent writing, and oblivion would not have buried those whom you used to call your dependents in Liguria. But since we are separated by place and resources, and are not matched by the law of diligence, you offer perfect affection to those beneath you, if they are worthy of conversation. Thus you enter into friendship with this distinction: you are compelled merely to look upon us, while we are compelled to love you.

The condition of the lowly will be proud if they await more from the powerful than words. I have descended to complaint at the command of affection. After the danger you had witnessed, you ought to have thought me worthy of conversation—or at least because the advocacy of a recent mystery commended one who was rising again. I think that those restored from the tombs by the power of our Redeemer are worthy of the favor of the good.

Yet I, although extravagant in boldness and talkative, and not yet trusting in myself, introduce my relatives. The bearer of this letter, the son of Lord Faustinus, sufficiently promises good merits derived from his parent. I beg you to encourage him, because you know well how conspicuous his father, who formed him, is for the brilliance of his character. A man armed with the authority of his life and ancestry ought not to hasten to anyone else except you.

Therefore, my lord, having offered the service of a greeting, I ask that your prosperity be made known through epistolary care.

## LETTER V. ENNODIUS TO THE DEACON HORMISDAS

Heavenly providence joins in affection those whom the benefits of letters have joined. While the length of journeys separates them, affection unites them through the remedy of concern, provided there is care for conversation.

Nevertheless, I greatly wonder at your silence: after laying aside the burdens of illness, you have not refreshed me with any conversation. But since speaking opportunely compels you to speak, respond at least by imitating the talkative. For a matter of desire is both requested and obtained through examples.

Therefore, offering the honor of a greeting, I announce that, by God’s favor, I am now well, and I beg you to bless me by a reciprocal proclamation through your writing.

## LETTER VI. ENNODIUS TO BEATUS

If you had stored away in your heart, for presentation at the proper time, the harvest of learning, the right hands of travelers would not have come away empty from your letters. But since abstinence reveals your negligence and sterility of speech, we must once again rise to cultivate admonition and press furrows into your back, thrown out by barren seeds, so that it may return to fruitfulness.

Where are the counsels you asserted would live on in you? Where is the eagerness for conversation through which both knowledge may be revealed and affection? Your silences cry out that you have not attained what could deserve the judgment of the good. For just as rarity exposes the learned, so continual silence exposes the ignorant.

Therefore be ashamed, and at last break the chains and impediments of speech. Show what you are capable of; show how far you have advanced—if indeed heavenly grace has not abandoned you in accordance with our wishes.

Now accept the honor of a greeting, and, content with this brief letter, recognize that these injunctions have been laid upon your father through lengthy correction.

## LETTER VII. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

I bless the triune unity in majesty of our God, who amid my troubles has raised me up, in place of perfect health, through the gift of your companionship. A report has come to me late, but one according to my wishes. May our Redeemer be present and fulfill what, inclined by supplication, he has granted.

My lord, having discharged the reverence of a greeting, I ask you to complete the substance of your undertaking concerning that suburban estate with your parent, Lord Liberius, with Christ laboring together with you, so that, if an exchange has taken place, it may graciously receive its price. Let us not longer waver in uncertainty about the promise, since you know that there is nothing more you can provide in this humble worldly life of yours.

[Note: “Lord Liberius.” Also a patrician; see Book V, Letter 1. This is a different suburban estate from the one that Faustus earlier requested from Florus in Book VIII, Letter 12.]

## LETTER VIII. ENNODIUS TO VICTOR

While your Eminence prefaces your remarks with an avowal of ignorance, you have revealed the secrets of learning; you refute by perfection what you assert. For while you confirm, without compromising your modesty, that you are unlearned, you have shown what the vigor of nature and the polishing of study have contributed.

Believe me, your Eminence: you have already enriched with your own gifts the one who is to be instructed in the liberal disciplines. If such a tongue commends the son of Brother Paul, eloquent affirmation both recommends and teaches him. There is no need for teachers dwelling far away when one who directs a person to a teacher speaks in a manner worthy of praise.

I am ashamed to have found the person introduced less capable than the report conveyed. I ask God that I may be able, by the strength of my talent, to fulfill what you presume about me through affection.

You, however, having received the honor of a greeting, offer whatever service of conversation you please, provided that the manifold care of your writing answers my concern for your welfare.

[Note: Schott reads “your.”]

## LETTER IX. ENNODIUS TO CAMILLA

[Note: “To Camilla,” a widowed relative in Gaul, that is, at Arles. Below, Letter 29: “My relative Camilla is said to have suffered in Gaul both the misery of widowhood and the misfortunes of a twofold captivity.” He calls her a relative, not a mother, but a woman related by blood, according to an old military and barbarian usage of the word, which had nevertheless become current in Ennodius’s time. For this reason he calls the deacon Patricius, Camilla’s son, not his brother but a little kinsman of his blood.]

### TO CAMILLA

[Col. 0152C]

You have interrupted our plan, I do not know following whom. For your little son, whom the care of the liberal studies ought to have received, you have marked with the titles of religion before the appropriate time for judgment. The form of ecclesiastical service is indeed venerable, but it does not allow one to divide one's mind between two pursuits. The road by which one goes to Christ is single and difficult, and a narrow life does not always receive those occupied in many directions.

The craftsman of salvation does not reject those who hasten to him from secular disciplines; but he does not permit anyone to go from his own brilliance to those disciplines. Now, if you had withdrawn him from the world, do not seek the world’s trappings in him. I am ashamed to adorn with secular ornaments one who professes ecclesiastical service.

I had agreed to what you requested through the deacon Patricius, insofar as he himself asserted it. Why was it necessary to send him to me in any condition other than that in which he was found at that time? If you consult my judgment, I want those who belong to me to be holy by merit rather than by title.

Truly, you have driven my mind from the quiet station of rest into a sea of thoughts. Nevertheless, with God’s favor, I have accepted this *vernula* of my own blood.

[Note: “*Vernulam*.” Nicolas Faber’s book reads *venulam*, a reading that could be accepted, since one might properly say “a vein of blood,” just as Symmachus says “a vein of the family” in Book IX, Letter 65. But other manuscripts prefer *vernulam*, which is more correct; it is confirmed by the gloss in the Basel edition, which we have removed, where *vernula* is explained as “servant-born,” that is, born from a slave. For *vernulae* originally meant those born at home from female slaves.]

Now it remains that heavenly favor smile upon my efforts and, with the abundance of merciful moderation, set right the negligence of human beings.

My lady, saying the greeting due, I ask you now to undertake a twofold concern for both of us and not to cease commending them to our God in constant prayers.

## LETTER X. ENNODIUS TO CELSUS

[Note: “To Celsus of Milan.”]

### TO CELSUS

It is flattery, not the sacrament of grace, when something is offered only to those who are present. The sincerity of friendship does not abandon those who are far away. Let the man who obtains benefits when he ceases to plead understand what true faith can accomplish. I owe it to myself that you, placed beyond Gargara at the station of prayers, have reached me.

You have separated friends and letters from yourself at the same time, by the light of your conscience, pursuing not only distant places but hidden ones, so that no pursuer of alert goodness may find you. Here too you always loved hidden lairs among the hares; but the man who tracks footprints with closed lips has often found your hiding place.

Now, I believe, by a deeper plan, so that you might be more greatly inflamed—

[Note: Schott reads “that you might be more greatly inflamed.”]

—you have withdrawn yourself from human gatherings. Were you therefore indebted only to your childhood to your Milanese friends? They ought to have retained you as a man, those who possessed you as a boy; and you ought to have helped by your counsel those whom you gladdened by your embraces.

But more on this elsewhere. You will owe yourself either the joys or the tears of your arrangements. Meanwhile, having prefaced a greeting and mindful of what I owe, I have sent a gift concerning the boy, considering this with myself: that he should neither overcome by importunity during the time of his distrust nor, while ceasing amid the evils of despair, rejoice.

## LETTER XI. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

[Col. 0153C]

I have received a letter enriched by a manifold wealth of joys and announcing the grace of God toward you, which I already knew. Immediately I made the disclosure known to the witnesses of our Christ, with the tears that joy itself prompted; and, giving thanks for what had been obtained through them, I affirmed it as though I were a new reporter.

Truly, Lord Faustus, in this matter it was plainly shown what merit and what power that holy soul who went before us possessed in prayer. For although our hope is still blind, clothed in the light of the world, she obtained without the labor of our action what she knew to be fitting; when she separated from us the things placed in her hands, she offered them to those who were far away, granting necessities more fortunately than things desired.

Therefore this world possesses some truth—or, if it does not, one is soon snatched from its dominion. The people lied who swore that they would receive benefits if they gave them. Even through heavenly providence, those have been joined from whom we neither received flatteries nor gave them: a firm confidence arising from despair, and something cloudy established from a promise made public.

I would truly say, if this separation caused grief, that Liguria could not have sent such people—not even the one whom you call their nurse, though she is a liar. Which should I accuse first in them: the obscenity of deceit or of stupidity? They have lost two people who, through the intercession of the saints, are joined to one another, and through whom the spark of a family lying long prostrate and forced into shadow might have been restored.

You remember that Lord Avienus said to you in the church that he did not specifically pray to God concerning that girl. Behold the offspring advancing toward the interest of life through holy parents. She understood that she would accomplish more through the parents’ tears than through action.

Thanks to you, almighty God; thanks to you, ruler of the faithful, who, looking upon the prayers of your servant, fulfilled in her the promises of prophecy, which says:

“Her soul shall dwell in good,  
and her offspring shall inherit the earth”  
(Psalm 24:13).

Complete, merciful judge, what remains, and graciously look upon the union with another servant of yours.

[Note: “In the union with another servant of yours.” In the marriage of Avienus, discussed in the following letter to Messala and above in Letter 7, also addressed to Avienus himself. Thus the girl whose death is described here was Avienus’s sister, Faustus’s daughter.]

If the illness that has already seized my vital substance does not leave me to see these things, let a good father see them, and let him receive the name of grandfather and great-grandfather before his passing. Yet heavenly grace does not even now abandon me, though I am a sinner, since I anticipate my desires with caution.

For fear that I should receive the designation of provincial envoy—

[Note: “Provincial envoy.” Of the province of Liguria, as in the phrase “the embassy of a proconsular province”; see Code of Theodosius, Book 12, Law 186, *On Decurions*. There were also envoys of cities, who were sent not by an entire province but by a particular city, as the envoy of the city of Hierapolis, Code, same book, Law 8, *On Census-Takers*, and the Alexandrian embassy, Law 42, *On Bishops*, and so forth. Ennodius therefore hesitates to undertake the embassy offered to Theoderic, lest, because of his close relationship with Faustus, he arouse the king’s suspicion that the matters which ought to be requested in the name of the Ligurians were being requested at Faustus’s instigation.]

—even though with grief, I suspended my wishes. I feared that either the master of affairs, acting through your arrangements, might believe that these things were being demanded from him which necessity compels us to request; and that I might become burdensome in duties and unproductive in action, although I would neither be capable of carrying out the task nor of being equal to what had been imposed.

I ask you to pray to God that he may preserve me, at least until the time of our common wishes, in this uncertain world.

## LETTER XII. ENNODIUS TO MESSALA

I endure the absence of your letters if your silence thus contributes to the increase of my joy. The interruption of writing is not burdensome if rare conversations are joined with splendid expressions. I accept what is presumed concerning God’s grace toward you and concerning your holy parents. You have already recognized through the intercessions of God’s friends who is your father and brother.

Truly, I did not reread your expression without the tears that joy supplied. I do not want to draw out what I think about you through an excess of words. Work to compose with eloquence what you discover, suggested by the vein within your feelings. You lack nothing of Lord Faustus and of my lady mother’s son except what you yourself have deliberately withheld.

[Note: Schott reads “this.”]

May God nevertheless forgive you for believing me forgetful of you while illness prevents me from honoring you through frequent writing. You ought to know that whatever is done through necessity deserves forgiveness.

My lord, conveying a most complete greeting, I declare that I bless God in his works concerning Lord Avienus’s union, and I await from you what his piety promises.

## LETTER XIII. ENNODIUS TO PANFRONIUS

You might think that, with you absent, I was traveling in my native land as though in a foreign country, even if I were well. But since illness presses upon me and the weakness of certain others also persists, what am I to do amid both? Who can endure, at one and the same time, diseases and treacherous people?

Know that in our city nothing that has been promised under God’s mediation is preserved by any precaution or innocence. Everything is attributed to prosperity, nothing to love; favor toward the humble is rare. The best man is the one who is higher.

I sigh over this not for my own sake, since nothing remains for me to hope for, but because I grieve that those whom I love are perishing. One of your men will explain the whole matter to you more fully, including the envy I have incurred because of my devotion to you.

I offer the honor of a greeting and ask you immediately to deliver my writings both to Lord Avienus and to Lord Liberius. And, by him who grants you our Panfronia in good health, I adjure you to inform me what reply they give, since, if a royal engagement prevents their coming, I hasten to come to you, with my God’s assistance, despite whatever weakness may afflict my limbs.

## LETTER XIV. ENNODIUS TO THE DEACON ELPIDIUS

May God pursue your holiness with the distinguishing marks of his mercy and grace. Out of regard for my humility, you make the matter your own, deigning to be concerned for me and promising that you will honor me and mine with special affection.

I know that God, in his favor toward you, has bestowed the grace of the unconquered prince upon you in such a way that ecclesiastical humility did not perish. Truly, Lord Elpidius, if the merciful king deigns to be concerned for his servant, you have done what no friend can repay in kind.

Nevertheless, know that I am afflicted daily by illnesses of various kinds, so that I despair of life. Yet, having received the honor of a greeting, I ask you sincerely, mindful of your soul, to love Lord Faustus and his sons. For my soul’s sake, do not cease praying as much as you are able, since nothing remains for me to hope for in this light.

I also ask you to deign to converse with me frequently, and, if our lord is going to Liguria, to make every effort to inform me.

## LETTER XV. ENNODIUS TO STEPHANIA
[Col. 0155D] It is well with my spirit that you have remembered me, burdened as I am with the weight of sin; and amid those cares of your sacred heart, as the letter sent to Lord Avienus makes clear, there has not arisen any forgetfulness of my person. I give thanks to God, who in his customary mercy comes to the aid of sinners through undeserved clemency, while sustaining them through the intercession of holy souls. I do not believe that the one whom you address in the language of nobility is abandoned amid your prayers. I therefore offer you the salutation proper to my humble station, and ask that you grant him the constant support of your prayers, since you nourish him with the abundance of your remembrance.

## LETTER XVI. ENNODIUS TO ADEODATUS

[Col. 0156A]

Long ago I would have replied to the letter of Your Beatitude, if it had been easy to discover the routes of those traveling to Rome. Ecclesiastical humility is passed by the powerful of this world as though it were something foreign. Nevertheless, as soon as Lord Dioscorus had returned to Rome after fulfilling the duty of his pious labor, I looked toward restoring what was owed, in reverence for you. You wish these sons of yours—Lord Paul and his holy offspring—to return to Rome; we wish them to remain: the differing judgments nevertheless return without error to a single path of affection. Yet may God, the best steward, arrange what he knows to suit their happiness. The prosperity of Lord Faustus and his family delights me in place of their presence. My lord, having discharged the duty of salutation with complete affection, I am sending the book you gave me by your son, Lord the Prefect, on his return; please send me either my own book, or the one you promised. Yet grant me this particular favor: never deprive me of the protection of your prayers, for no wall can be more effective for me against the battering-ram of sin than the defense of those prayers.

## LETTER XVII. ENNODIUS TO APODEMIA

Faith in the ancient opinion is not lame: it maintains that kinship of blood is not defrauded by distance of region. The rights of families remain fixed upon their own foundations; those divided by dwellings are not separated in spirit. An ethereal power traverses wherever kinship of flesh is extended, and that heavenly portion of a single homeland is not confined by narrow limits. Thus you, my lady, sought out Ennodius, dwelling far from your body, by sending a noble gift to satisfy his longing eyes. I received a hood of the kind that ought to be sent to one professing religion. Most holy lady, pray that these gifts may make me worthy of humble garments; and, even if your gifts did not find me worthy, may they nevertheless accomplish this through the nobility of their own merit. My lady, offering you the most abundant greeting, I ask that you frequently refresh me with your venerable conversation.

[Note: [Col. 0155D] “A *laena* and *racanae.”] The Vatican manuscript has this punctuation: the others read, “[Col. 0156D] *Laena metra canas*” [“May the cloak cover your gray hairs”], which comes to the same thing. What kind of garment the *racanae* were is unclear; they seem to belong among footwear, like the *rogae* and [Col. 0156D] *tzangae*. See also book 3 of the Theodosian Code, *On the Dress to Be Used within the City*: “Within the city of Rome no one may use either *reges* or *tzangae.”]

Send me promptly a *laena* and *racanae*, in whatever red or dark color you prefer.

## LETTER XVIII. ENNODIUS TO STEPHANIA

The merit of the bearer would indeed suffice for an exchange of letters, since both his own natural disposition supplies what must be said and pure affection toward me does so as well. But my spirit hastens toward a doubled service; not content with the simple humility demanded by your reverence, it joins a letter to Lord Avienus, who is shown by both his life and his speech to have been born from your stock. Yet I take it hard that you describe rustic voices in language that is excessively urbane and refined. Heavenly grace has not become known in your family in such a way that anyone in it could be unlike his elders either in speech or conduct—unless perhaps the radiance of your holy widowhood shines above the distinction of your ancestors. Surely you are the sister of that Lord Faustus, in whose prefecture it is found that he establishes monasteries, and who is more venerable in conduct than in title. Having offered you the service of my salutation, I ask you never to mingle the unlearned compositions of schoolmen with sacred dictations. It is enough for me to admire in your thoughts what, if I am worthy, I ought to follow.

## LETTER XIX. ENNODIUS TO AGNELLO

For a long time my mind remained uncertain whether, trusting in the affection inspired by knowledge of you, I should boldly knock at the door of writing and enter through this path the heart of an outstanding man, or whether, content with a wandering salutation sent through your people, I should break into the secrets by which I was shut out—for it seemed to me that one whom the foremost of men ignored ought not to be counted among men. And plainly neither character nor nature suggests confidence to one who is concealed in a citadel. This is especially true of you, whom both worlds embrace in a friendly and companionable diversity, and whom the fear of God, strengthened by the graciousness of his favor, has already made generous in bestowing the highest honors and in granting subjects what only the most distinguished scarcely attain for the glory of reputation. The highest offices deserve praise, but they are reached only with the greatest toil. Yet—may it be said auspiciously—among your gifts are eminences of this kind. Therefore, offering a reverent salutation, I conclude the letter briefly, lest praise appear importunate before your gracious response. After your reply, you will read a longer page suited to your character and power, with the world bearing witness alongside me.

## LETTER XX. ENNODIUS TO MASCATOR

It is right for me to hope, and it is fitting for you to agree. For by differing paths the intention moves toward a single end, where it is to be rewarded. You provide consolation in practical matters; from me you await assistance in a slight conversation. Thus it happens that the person whose official position obliges him to provide greater things can scarcely demand anything small. Let the palace official show generosity, since the Church can do nothing more than pray. You know [Note: [Col. 0157D] “For the *ascini*”] from whom the reward comes to the *ascini*, if they are helped. The *asceni*—the Greek ἄσκηνοι, *asceni*—are so called because they live without tents in the open air. He therefore commends these dependents, perhaps forcibly expelled from their homes, to Mascator, so that through his assistance they may be restored to their household by right of return.]

Come to the aid of these men, whom their native land both holds captive, who are objects of envy among the natives, and whose condition among the exiles is pitiable. A Christian and a wise man ought not to be admonished at length, lest an extended petition seem to claim for itself the fruit of another’s labor. I therefore offer the salutation proper to my humble station and beg that you send the men mentioned above back to me with joy.

## LETTER XXI. ENNODIUS TO ELPIDIUS

Although Pontic inhumanity makes you forgetful of me, it is not fitting that I imitate what I criticize. Thus, like Icarus, you flew away from the city of Milan, and did not deem me worthy even of a greeting by messenger. This is what happens to those whom an unexpected companionship joins to the sides of powerful men. It is right that the fly about to die should be invited, if not by nature, then by my example, to achieve this: others may be more useful to you because of their abundant resources, but they cannot be sweeter. Yet I return to consideration of your homeland, to which you owe the forgetfulness of your prosperity and the misery under which you suffer. Now, having offered the honor of my salutation, I have sent your servant for this purpose: to announce to your son, Lord the Prefect, and to you, in Christ’s name, that I have received legitimate documents concerning that suburban estate, so that you may not fail to do, together with your son, Lord Triggua, whatever seems necessary [*sic*].

## LETTER XXII. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

I hope in the Trinity, our God, that through the venerable prayers of the saints he will guard servants placed in whatever location, as the pupil of the eye is guarded, and restore to good health whatever hostile misfortune has broken. I, however, follow you in my duties, even though I cannot do so bodily. For, moved by concern, I have gathered words, begging to be informed how sound you are. [Col. 0158C] Behold, I can scarcely bear even a brief absence, being wearied by a long one; but powerful are the friends of the Lord to whom your holy soul has entrusted you. I continually approach them, reminding them to preserve their deposit. They will be present in their proper places and will preserve without diminution what has been entrusted to them. I add that, by the mercy of almighty God, your servants who had already returned from Venetia [Note: [Col. 0157D] “To have produced documents”] concerning the suburb of Milan that Faustus had granted to Ennodius—see the preceding letter—produced documents confirmed by the laws, and that the formal introduction was immediately completed. Now consider, with the maturity customary to you, whether anything ought to be said by you to your friend.

## LETTER XXIII. ENNODIUS TO LIBERIUS

[Note: [Col. 0157D] This letter competes with Liberius’s praises in his epitaph, which was formerly placed by his father at Rimini in the following words:]

Creative nature gave the human race this law:

that tombs should cover buried limbs.

The offspring of Liberius, surviving mother and father,

performed this sad duty with devoted mind.

Here indeed are the limbs, but the urn does not contain the fame.

[Col. 0158D] For fame, ignorant of death, endures in its inscriptions.

He held the Roman fasces as the years passed,

possessing Gallic laws with equal success.

He purchased these honors not at the price of weakness,

but devoted faith brought them to him at a greater price.

He properly arranged foreign cohorts

for the Ausonian peoples; he established treaties and gave laws.

A father to all in spirit, venerable throughout his whole lifetime,

he fell near the completion of thirty lustrums.

O how much good deeds are worth! When the limbs depart,

fame does not know how to die; a radiant life remains.

Pithoeus first published this epitaph. After him Baronius followed our copy, in which the third verse reads *superstes* [“surviving”], which seems more correct than *sepulcrum* [“tomb”], found in the Pithoean copy, since the epitaph is of only one Liberius.]

The infusion of heavenly mystery has granted me freedom of judgment, even when I am bound by benefits. [Col. 0158D] It is a gift from above that one who is obligated should deliver an independent opinion, and that the force of judgment should not take pleasure in the enormity of favor. It is divine when a person to whom you have given much speaks of you without corruption, and does not place anything unjust in the scales of truth because he is subdued by the wealth of your gifts. For when the subject is men of the highest rank, and words are being shaped for public ears, why should public testimony be overshadowed by private action? I owe your eminence more than the whole world does; but I do not wish to say anything greater than the mouths of the whole world can utter. Content with the narrow confines of a letter, I taste only a small portion of that harvest of merits.

Most fortunate of men, the whole hostility of the world labors with all its strength to make you alone restore what has been scattered throughout the earth. One can judge what sort of man he is whom you serve when fallen, burned-out, ruined things recover upon seeing you. [Note: [Col. 0159D] “Italy was scarcely being fed.”] Italy was scarcely being fed by the costly burden of public taxation when you transformed that burden, without delay, both toward the hope of restoration and toward the payment of tribute. We began gladly, under your administration, to bring into the public treasuries what we had been accustomed to receive with the greatest grief. Your administration has always been our abundance. Heavenly powers aided your venerable counsel. For the public good, you either fostered the revenues or supplied them. Higher than all eminences, you were the first to make royal resources flow without the harmful extortion of private persons.

To you, after God, it is owed that under our most powerful and everywhere victorious lord we can safely acknowledge our wealth; for the prosperity of subjects is secure when it is not in need. [Note: [Col. 0159D] “Schot,” the emperor.] What of the countless [Note: [Col. 0159D] “Gothic hordes”] Gothic hordes? The epitaph says: “He properly arranged allied cohorts for the Ausonian peoples.” Cassiodorus says in the same place: “It is worthwhile to recount how, in the allocation of thirds, he joined the estates and dispositions of Goths and Romans. For since men ordinarily quarrel over neighboring property, the sharing of estates between these people is known to have supplied the cause of concord.” Theoderic ordered a third part of the lands to be assigned to the Goths [Col. 0160D]—that is, a *trithemorion* (τριτημόριον), which Odoacer had previously granted to his own people, as Procopius records at the beginning of the Gothic War.]

You enriched the Gothic hordes by a generous distribution of estates, scarcely noticed by the Romans; for the victors desired nothing more, and the defeated perceived no losses. I say nothing, out of regard for the language of this page, about the honey of your fellowship and favors, established by heavenly commands and ennobled by deeds no less than by words. I turn my speech toward the prayers owed to your eminence, because Gaul agrees with me in this affirmation. [Note: [Col. 0160D] “Gaul.”] He also held the prefecture of the praetorium of Gaul toward the end of Theoderic’s reign, under his successor Athalaric; Cassiodorus preserves a letter to Liberius, prefect of Gaul, in book VIII of the *Variae*, letter 6. Ennodius, however, did not see it. Thus what Ennodius mentions here belongs to an earlier period, when Liberius was first sent to Gaul, where he remained for a long time and held more than one administration. He also commanded military forces, as Jordanes records in his *Getica.]

May Christ our living God ordain that, once those whom you brought into civilized life after the passage of many years [Note: [Col. 0160D] “Perhaps, cycles”]—those who before you had never been able to taste the flavor of Roman freedom—have been properly ordered, you may be brought back to your Italy, both at our request and at their insistence. Thus, a native of both worlds through holy deeds, may you possess your venerable household and illustrious sons, with all Italy looking on, exalted by the gift of your blessed presence. I, having offered the services of my salutation, announce that I am well and await from you whatever may satisfy my desire.

## LETTER XXIV. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

My spirit would have been well if a frequent opportunity for messengers had been supplied for writing, since the foresight of an elder, as a remedy for longing, has provided the gift of letters, in which conversation formed as a substitute for presence offers comfort to those who burn with desire. Although my illness suffers from the very remedies for absence, and the care of anxiety is doubled by the medicine, nevertheless what alone remains must not be abandoned. Therefore, when the boy Valentinus was traveling to Rome, I hastily snatched away as much as I could of what had to be said, briefly indicating that my bodily health had been disturbed. [Col. 0160B] It is enough, however, if the report of your prosperity makes my soul cheerful and I recover. My lord, having discharged the duties of salutation as your reverence requires, I ask that you now raise me up by a letter announcing the fulfillment of my prayers and your welfare.

## LETTER XXV. ENNODIUS TO AGNELLA

It is pleasing to me to proclaim the gifts of letters to your greatness, because this honor is offered not so much to your lineage and conscience as returned to them. It is just that a man of religious purpose should freely venerate a holy and noble widow. I give thanks to my God because the good fragrance of your reputation has reached us. May he grant fruit until the completion of life—he who planted a good root in the conduct of this world. You have acted well, Lady Agnella, in rejecting the allurements of this world; and while pursuing higher things, in not possessing even what might have come through legitimate remedies. You knew how not only to seek pardon but also a crown. Let the sick rejoice in their remedy: the person to whom it is granted happily to unlearn temptations is close to wholeness. Therefore, my lady, having rendered the grace and honor of salutation, I ask that you not cease to pray for me, your friend and relative, at the thresholds of the apostles, so that I may be worthy to keep what I proclaim and not neglect in myself what I praise in others.

## LETTER XXVI. ENNODIUS TO MESSALA

I know indeed that you were taken away from me against my desire; [Col. 0160D] but I had anticipated something else from your concern. For if you had remembered me, I would have learned both how our lord had fared by God’s favor and what the course of your journey had been. But what can I do, when I cannot overcome your negligence even by suggesting the form that affection should take? Therefore, if, by the grant of Christ our God, marital hope should breathe upon you, you will not banish the memory of Ennodius. For never has greater diligence ceased in such a way, nor has devoted love been excluded from your heart, as far as I shall be removed from your eyes. Be well, with your father and brother safe; may God do good to you. Let them recognize what may please the ear, and show toward me whatever purpose you wish. I ask you one thing: having offered the honor of my salutation, deign to offer prayers for me before the lords the apostles, so that they may medicinally cure my miseries and not allow me to wish for anything improper; may they discipline the presumption of mind and body. [Col. 0161B] If you do this, I believe that, for the sake of your innocence and purity, you will be heard on my behalf more effectively than if I were present before you.

## LETTER XXVII. ENNODIUS TO AURELIAN, BISHOP

[Note: [Col. 0161D] “Of which see, the books do not determine. Do not suppose that he was Arelatensis. For the bishop who bore this name at Arles assumed that see at least thirty years after Ennodius’s death. At this time the bishop of Arles was Caesarius. Nevertheless, I would not reject the possibility that this Aurelian was a new bishop of some city, or that he was the Arelatensian presbyter Aurelian to whom Ennodius replied in Letter 35 of Book VIII.”]

I owe my grief a voice, but reverence demands silence. And perhaps mute concealment would better follow the sorrow arising from your refusal to speak. It would have been urbane and subtle if, by the same lines through which offense is inflicted upon me, the offenses of greater men had been struck, so that guilt itself might carry its own punishment. But where shall I turn, when I do not cease pursuing with persistent love one who is forgetful of me and rejects knowledge of the humble? Is not the importunity of one who has been rejected the mother of horror, when the desire to please through persistence demands an opportunity for displeasing? For whatever we flee in our minds we scarcely see when it is thrust before our eyes.

O, if only I were still permitted to contend with Your Beatitude on equal terms! But the privileges of kinship sleep beneath your crown, since you have deserved to become a father. Can any man endure that the rights of kinship should perish through the growth of relationship, and that the bonds both of family and of affection should be dissolved by the addition of sacred dignity? Was it therefore fitting that the advancement of your merit should reach me only through unstable rumor, and that I should remain content to learn of our common joys through hearsay? I was chosen as the one from whom a general good would be concealed, so that, because of the obscurity surrounding me, I alone would not know about a matter belonging to the golden age. A noble life, distinguished by birth, has climbed to the summit of ecclesiastical honor, and scorns to address me. Truly, whether this has occurred by design or negligence, the deed is not approved. Nevertheless, I offer the services of my salutation and, with Italian frankness, openly declare where I have found sadness.

## LETTER XXVIII. ENNODIUS TO AGAPIUS

The duty of an eager spirit has harshly recalled the mind, by remembrance, to memories that must be stirred by recollection of sad things. [Col. 0162A] For forgetfulness is always a remedy for grief: what we cannot bury by reason, we bury through the length of time. It is well that affliction grows old through duration and that consolation for great sorrow is secured through silence. In affairs of this kind, more is accomplished by doing nothing. But what can I do, when reading the letter now tears open the innermost places of a scar already formed and, with bitter force, revives the memory of a premature death that had been buried?

Could I therefore give consolation to a common brother, when, if any humanity is believed to exist in me, I would grieve in the same way? Has a weeping man ever pleased as a consoler? Is medicine therefore expected from the sick? You do not judge me well, Lord Agapius, if, amid the griefs of your brother and the death of your spiritual son, I come forward as an opponent of your opinion. Healthy hearts find a path toward healing; no one frees another from the source of his own suffering. But more on this elsewhere. God is powerful—he alone can meet such things and lighten the burden of our common misfortune.

Nevertheless, offering you the honor of my salutation, I ask that you frequently bestow upon me the gift of correspondence, a practice suited neither to one who is sluggish and unloving nor to one who is eloquent.

## LETTER XXIX. ENNODIUS TO LIBERIUS

If the discipline of the page admitted the spirit of the poets, a hundred mouths and an iron voice would scarcely open, with an abundance of words, what I owe to your eminence. But because, burdened by great obligations, I can scarcely manage a few words, after God’s mercy I have provided someone to repay your favor. For your brother, Lord Faustus, when he declares that he owes the benefit you have bestowed upon me, removes from my weak shoulders the burdens of a heavy load.

These things are shared between two men of the highest rank: you know how both to give one another worthy gifts and to return them. For me, placed beneath the burden of your benefaction, only the confession of obligation remains; overwhelmed by the weight of your favor, which has made me attain what I wished, I am unequal to it. Nevertheless, I perform my part and, while praying, although I am a sinner, I implore God to repay you on my behalf as well. These two things are sufficient: you expect from heaven on my behalf what you remember having provided, and there is an equal person on earth who admits that he is indebted.

Yet I quickly await the completion of your benefaction, so that I may receive the letter I requested through the illustrious man Tranquillinus. [Col. 0162D] Consciously relying on your good character, I shall also offer you another way to show mercy. My mother Camilla, in Gaul, is said to have succumbed both to the misery of widowhood and to the hardships of a double captivity. No one except your eminence can avert such manifold necessities. As patron of my family, may you not deny in Gaul what you have provided to those established in Italy, so that, [Note: [Col. 0162D] “Concerning the little houses.”] as Cassiodorus says in Book VII, Letter 45, through the little houses belonging to her, the burdens of the treasury may, by your arrangement, be diverted from them sufficiently to provide her maintenance. The formula concerns relief of the assessment for one who possesses a single burdened house: when an excessively heavy tax had been imposed on someone, it was reduced by the equalizer. This benefit of relief or equalization was so called. Our glosses read: “Relieved land,” ἀνακεκουφισμένος, “lightened of the public burden.”]

My lord, having rendered the services of salutation, I ask that, with God inspiring you, your eminence order the bearer of this letter, my own man whom I have sent to carry out these matters, to come to me with the result I seek. Should one who knows that he has obtained even what he did not request hesitate over his petitions?

## LETTER XXX. ENNODIUS TO POPE SYMMACHUS

[Note: [Col. 0163D] We have added this title; in its place the ancient copies had written “In the sign of Christ.” But it is clear that the letter is addressed to Pope Symmachus, and was written after the remnants of the schism had been extinguished, when all the members, as Ennodius himself says, had been restored to union with their head through the agency of King Theoderic, whom he therefore praises.]

[Col. 0163B] It is the nature of things that even one who is competent in speech or thought may be blamed for presumption, because every verbal convenience that has gone beyond the limits of humility is trampled underfoot; and just as what is demanded must be regarded as valuable, so what is forced upon others becomes cheap. Importunity, when it strips eloquent men of the nobility of reputation, clothes the unlearned in disgrace.

Yet I sustain myself with this reasoning: it was indeed bold, but it was an affectionate beginning to have offered the preceding speech; and, just as it opens a path close to rashness, so it opens one close to diligence and belonging to charity. Among men of the Churches, is it a fault if those unequal in dignity contend with equal love? Or do those who desire to be made equal to the highest by the support of favor exceed the narrow limits of modest honor? The person who does not measure himself in the duties of affection has no proud conscience. I venture to say that it is the error of subjects when, in this matter, one who ought to follow takes precedence. Behold, I have cleared my part, darkened by the cloud of voluntary conversation.

But I say what concerns the fullest defense. Your son, Lord Rhodanius, compelled me to burst forth into the present use of the pen. Yet I confess that what he ordered was already part of my purpose, since one who compels a willing man does not labor.

Let us render thanks to God in the first place, and throughout the entire composition of the letter, because at last the Roman members have joined themselves to their head. It was just that blessed Peter the apostle should restore to his own see, to the Churches, and to a freer senate the rights assigned to them by the Lord. He is a worthy ruler, worthy of one in whom the highest fulfillment of hopes has coincided with age. For even if happiness destined for posterity continues, he must be celebrated with special praise by those from whom he took his beginning.

You earnestly supplicated God that his power might rescue you—the one whose mercy can preserve you. You have learned the prosperous outcome of one whom you see following victory wherever he directs wars. Little remains except that you should understand the depth of his gentleness of spirit, as though he were ignorant of military campaigns. By God’s favor, neither can his peace be disturbed by uncertainties nor his courage broken by any opposition. Nothing is safer with him than the one who supplicates. The man who prayed alone escaped the battles; the man who offered devoted service overcame the onslaught of arms. What ancient rulers could scarcely obtain through the exertion of their presence, the brief letter of our king has always accomplished.

A fortunate army is directed through its campaigns toward triumph. Who would believe that his soldier, amid labor and completion, possesses the glory of a conqueror while also displaying the restraint of one who has been conquered? When the combats are finished, nothing remains of the inheritance of anger. At one and the same time, those whom their adversaries had seen as destructive find them gentle, paying tribute.

These things are prepared by heavenly favor for this repayment of service, because our faith has a safe harbor with him, even though he himself pursues another course. Wonderful is his patience: while firm in his purpose, he does not obscure another’s glory. For he also grieves when the patrimonies of our Churches decline unless they are increased. Thus it has happened that the wealth of the poor supports their own status, and that those of moderate means recover into the highest abundance. In priests he both cultivates innate virtues and inspires those not found there.

But why should I anticipate Your Beatitude by the prejudgment of an extended speech? Your experience and that spiritual perfection of yours will immediately accuse me of having been meager in praising your son; and since deeds are usually magnified by conversation, it will charge me with being a barren narrator of his harvest of virtues.

Now let the secular dignities—the curule offices, the *trabeae*, and even the patrician honors—be proclaimed, through the testimony of the household bearer, as to how he restores them either to nature or to character. For he makes the ancient endure in the ancient light of their lineage, and he illuminates the new with the splendor of an unexpected brilliance. Under his good administration, public wealth more readily passes into private abundance than the wealth of servants is converted into profits for the palace.

Now, having received the services of my salutation, see to it that Christ our Redeemer preserves through a long age whatever he has bestowed upon those serving him in the aforesaid most merciful king. May he also grant a successor to the kingdom from his offspring, lest the blessings of so great a man grow old in a single age and, antiquated by time, be named only in memory of the golden age.

## LETTER XXXI. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

While, by God’s dispensation, I was still enjoying the pleasant sight of your nearness to my presence, and my ears retained the honey of your charming conversations through a venerable deception, an opportunity for writing was offered me. I confess that for a long time I did not wish to interrupt the remedy for longing while another remedy was being arranged. The sequence of events, flattering my spirit with a pious deception, delighted me; I did not wish, in full awareness, to discover the falsehood that nourished my love.

For deception that attends our desires tastes good to us, and we willingly accept sweet images of messages as true. Whenever pleasant dreams are driven away by wakefulness, we grieve; and that image of death is loved all the more for its peaceful deceptions. Therefore, since I was not permitted to preserve what I have described, I must now carry out what remains.

Does anyone labor under the burden of his sin in this way? I would be afflicted if I did not see you; having reached what I desired, I waste away because what we sought has, by God’s favor, been granted. Has anyone ever gained from an occasion of joy something that torments him? Has a plant of sadness ever grown from a harvest of joys?

Thanks be to the inseparable Trinity, the true God, who sometimes disregards prayers in order to fulfill them. May he therefore look favorably upon your union; may he make one out of two. In the body of the first man, while he still rejoiced in native and undefiled immortality, he formed the two of you. May a wife be joined to you, as Sarah was to Abraham, Rebecca to Isaac, and Rachel to Jacob through heavenly blessing. May you possess both the prior fruit of continence and the sweetness of marriage. May the renunciation of virginity obey God’s law, while what it withdraws from itself it restores in offspring.

May a well-established union not require external diligence from you. May she restore your mother to you in character and way of life; and may you restore her parent to her. Let the exemplary pattern of your ancestors, reborn in you, not be subject to the world, but be embraced. No foreign examples of life, nor anything imported from elsewhere, are required; pursue what has been placed before your eyes.

Behold, I who could not attend your wedding approach you with this prosecution of my prayers. In return, show me frequent conversation. Having rendered the love and reverence of salutation, I ask that, if you do not drive my memory from that abundant recollection, you raise me up through prayers and conversations.

## LETTER XXXII. ENNODIUS TO ADEODATUS, PRESBYTER

How much brighter you are than I in merit and in conduct, the effects of your prayers will reveal.
