Behold, you will retain the greatest part of your son Lord Faustus, taken away from my companionship. I indeed placed no obstacle in the way of holy and lawful desires, but Lord Avienus’s departure, because of my affection for him, struck me so deeply that I followed him with tears as he made his way toward what he desired.

In this matter the differing formation of human affairs became clear. Votive hopes call him forth, with Christ as guide; they wound me. Nearness at his union delights him; separation pierces me. Behold, I am anxious about the fruit of my prayers, and, if anything we requested in this matter may be said in the peace of Christ, I grieve that we have obtained it.

Yet amid these things I am sustained by this remedy of diligent care: we have made Lord Avienus surpassing our hopes. Rome boasts of his origin; Liguria of his advancement. In Rome he was granted to Lord Faustus as a son by the law of nature; here his education has revealed him. It was less remarkable that a man should be born with the general characteristics of humanity than that he should prove to be the offspring of Faustus, something that seemed inimitable.

Let us refer his benefits to God, and give thanks to God himself, from whom we requested what we now possess. Receive the services of my salutation for the purity of your holy heart; and, receiving my book, send it together with the one you promised me.

## LETTER XXXIII. ENNODIUS TO CAESARIUS, BISHOP OF ARLES

[Note: [Col. 0165D] “To Bishop Caesarius.” Caesarius was, as Ennodius rightly calls him, the most distinguished of the bishops of his age, renowned for learning, eloquence, and holiness of life. Accused before Theoderic on a fabricated charge and brought under guard to Ravenna, he so moved the king by the sight of his angelic countenance and the security of his innocence that the king not only received him peacefully and humanely but also honored him with gifts. A similar event had occurred some years earlier, when Arles was still subject to the Visigoths: after being accused before Alaric of false treason, he was later released with honor. Cyprian related both histories—the present passage concerns the first—in Book I of the *Life of Caesarius*. We also saw Book II, which is missing from Surius’s edition, in the monastery of Saint-Martin in Paris. It was composed concerning the miracles and death of Saint Caesarius; among other things, it relates that the patrician Liberius, pierced by a mortal spear wound and nearly lifeless, was cured when Caesarius’s garment was applied. There are also extant various letters of the Roman pontiffs to Caesarius, including the letter of Felix that has exercised learned men in vain because of suspicion concerning its corrupt subscription, as though it were said to have been written by P. C. Boethius, whereas the Arelatensian manuscript from which it was taken clearly reads: “P. C. MABORTI,” or Mavorri. That year was A.D. 528, the second year of Pope Felix IV.]

What I had anticipated, you have indicated in your letter. For after the venerable publication of your conversation, I learned what the heavenly emperor had compelled the lord king to do concerning you; I am the one to whom, once your merit became clear, the happiness of your action was by no means hidden. Who among men, the most noble pontiff in the service of Christ, does not know that earthly dominions are subject to you, and that threatening power over the accused is overcome by the plea of innocence—when imperial purple has despised either the hair shirt or the [Col. 0166B] cloak; when that greatest liberty has believed that, before Christian humility, it was permitted to do what it wished; or when it was ever permitted to wish what would cause harm? But if, amid these examples of gray-haired age, you recall the tyrannical cruelty exercised against the worshipers of God, we know that the followers of our doctrine were killed by those men so that they might never die. Then that perpetual commander, with the sword obedient to him, bestowed life and eternity upon his soldiers. Through the agency of their enemies they lost their original baseness.

You, my lord, were born into an already Christian world through divine law, and were nourished with the milk of the apostolic breast. You surpass all others as the sun’s greatness surpasses the lesser stars. Whoever has looked upon you with the eyes of the inner man has been instructed. For while by your very face you foster purity, you chastise offenders [Col. 0166C] with a silent mouth. Wherever they go, the good find in your conduct examples to imitate; the wicked are shown what they must flee. Blessed are you, to whom God has granted that you teach both by admonitions and by examples; you, ever acting as the guide directed toward the path of piety, have invited others to follow. Who, while you speak, would not wish to learn more than to read?

While you reconcile genius with books through your account, and train teachers, every writer, however great, owes you this: you enlarge him with the gift of eloquence. In you the light of speech and action meet. Whence comes this distinction to the Transalpine peoples? Whence this unanticipated elevation to my parents, that they should have sent forth such a man? But why is a heavenly matter sought among earthly things? Could any arrogance of the palace, then, fail to yield before you? Could it withhold from you what you desired, when only errors make one who is gentle toward sheep combative? [Col. 0166D]

Both your merit and my devotion summon me to speak at greater length, but the law of correspondence confines my loquacity. Accept what remains as the gracious service of my devotion, and commend me to our God through the support of your prayers, frequently informing me about what is being done or has been done among you. I also ask you to make known to me by letter what Rusticus’s petition has achieved among you. For, as I hear, he clothes his fornications in the name of wives and thinks that a criminal matter can be excused by the name of the law.

## LETTER XXXIV. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS

Where are those who say that, when people are separated by residence, devotion does not endure; that the warmth of affection grows cold through the division of lands; and that minds cannot advance farther than the eyes? Behold, the fullness of my love grows hot through the violence of separation, and the remedy of conversation is not confined by the weaker bodily dwelling-place. [Col. 0167B]

Yet I bless God, who has looked favorably upon our prayers concerning you and has bestowed upon you not only a noble wife but, as report announces, one holy in her conduct. Those who worship Christ deserve all things in their perfection; only to them, in marriage, is the splendor of wealth, minds, and bloodline not denied. I myself had been saying that such a woman could be formed as the one whom I hear has now come to you. My judgment cannot measure what I think of that man’s progress, since I hear that he began with the best.

My lord, extending the grace of a greeting, I hope that you will not hesitate to fulfill the petition of your holy bishop, your father, and graciously bestow upon his man—the classicus, as he is called—the favor of your goodwill, of which I am confident. [Col. 0168A]

[Note: Schott: “grace.”] [Col. 0168B]

## LETTER XXXV. ENNODIUS TO MESSALA

Necks of proud minds are commonly softened by unanticipated good fortune, and the brows of a sterner resolve are tempered by a new joy. For whatever complies with wishes sows kindness, and nothing humbles the most powerful more than the elevation they have desired. To have reached the summit is a sign of fellowship and obedience.

After you have been advanced to what you desired, you despise me, though until now I had been unaware of your swelling pride. Forgetting what you should regard in your honey, you scorn your old friends solely because of the wealth of your future wife, not knowing that the burden is coming from the source from which you think the reward is traveling: first, because one who does not cast a shadow upon the radiance of his origin ought not to be fickle; and secondly, because I shall take revenge from the very place from which I am despised.

Therefore return kindly to the use of your promise, lest I seem to have suspected what is obvious. Since until now you have abstained from the duty of writing, I have burst into these words: it is fitting for you either to wash away the deed or to affirm your innocence in noble language. My lord, performing the fullest duties of greeting, I hope that you, who have neglected one who was devoted to you, will at least by some other means make the man who reproves you worthy of your attention.

# THE MISCELLANEOUS OPUSCULA OF MAGNUS FELIX ENNODIUS, BOOK X

[Col. 0167]

[Col. 0167]

## FIRST OPUSCULUM

[Note: Panegyric.]

It is equally uncertain where or when the Panegyric was delivered by Ennodius. This is certain: it was not delivered at Rome, since he addresses Rome as absent. I would believe that it was delivered at Milan or Ravenna. If Milan is preferred, then Theoderic must be understood to have been arriving and to have been received with this laudation, in the manner in which Majorian was received at Lyon by Sidonius with a poetic panegyric. If Ravenna, it was pronounced on some embassy, such as Ennodius perhaps indicates in these words: “Now the Church sends a praiser.”

Concerning its date, this much can be affirmed: it could not have been delivered before the consulship of Cethegus—that is, before the year of Christ 504—since it discusses the recovery of Sirmium, which was recovered during Cethegus’s consulship. There are also other indications that it is later. If there is any order in the sequence of Ennodius’s works as they were arranged in ancient copies, it is easy to conjecture that this panegyric ought to be assigned to the year 507 or 508. [Col. 0168C–D]

### PANEGYRIC DELIVERED TO THE MOST CLEMENT KING

[Note: Theoderic.]

To the King of Italy.

While the Ostrogoths were still dwelling in Pannonia, there were three brother-kings of the Amalian stock: Valamer, Theodemer, and Widemer. This Theoderic was Theodemer’s son by a concubine; he was ordinary consul and master of the soldiers in Thrace under Zeno, and finally king of Italy. Marcellinus Comes, in his Chronicle, gives him the cognomen of Valamer. Malchus the Sophist of Philadelphia, however, in his Byzantine History, incorrectly calls him the son of Valamer, although Jordanes repeatedly asserts in his Gothic History that Theodemer was his father and calls Valamer his paternal uncle.

### TO THEODERIC. (C)

[Col. 0167C]

Let professional skill exclude from your praises the man, venerable prince, whom reflection upon your purpose keeps from your praises; let it repel from your defense anyone whom some duty has withdrawn from your protection. Let the whole community, bound to you by its circumstances, return speech to you, while unequal reciprocity compensates with praise what it has gained from toil. Freedom, subject to your arms, has learned to announce with praises the gladness that is the only thing it can offer.

It is yours, illustrious one, to give a reward to devotion, which you understand cannot exceed the strength of your subjects. It will belong to sacred administration to estimate what you demand from those in whom you recognize that everything they possess serves you. May your Majesty deign to offer literary homage at your own altars; for, lest the renown of your deeds grow old, the exercises of languages must be summoned, and a chain of narrators must bind what you have done, lest antiquity claim it for itself. You will grant repose to the disciplines through which eternity will come to you. [Col. 0168C]

The heavenly dispenser of the secret asks nothing more from human intellects than that they understand from what author comes whatever they know. To recognize among those closest to God the one who has bestowed a benefit is itself to return a benefit. What descends from above may be assessed only by the reward of hymns; the Maker of the world is invited to greater gifts by measured speech. Say whether a tongue does not flatter its maker in place of a reward.

It follows that praise ought to flow principally from the sanctuary of the world’s heart, and that the commemoration of your divinity requires not merely the brilliance of the tongue but the testimony of a good conscience. In divine worship, a serene mind performs sacrifice with a reverent mouth; fortified by the splendor of its deeds, it obeys even in heavenly worship when speechless.

Therefore the title that seemed likely to obstruct me also invites me. Would that my outward profession were purer and in harmony with my secrets, so that the splendor of my heart might not disagree with my body. [Col. 0169B]

Hail now, greatest of kings, under whose rule the vigor of freedom has recognized its own character. Hail, state of the republic; for it would be wrong to narrate separately the blessings joined together in you and to distinguish by a division of words the goods of a single age.

If I count the wars of my king, I find as many as there are triumphs. No enemy has encountered your meeting except one who was to be added to your praises. Whoever resisted your will served your trophies; for the one who submitted always produced glory for your piety, while the one who presumed to take up weapons produced glory for your courage. Whoever saw you in battle was overcome; whoever saw you in peace feared nothing. Your venerable promise never faltered amid prosperity, nor did your vigor suffer delay in battles.

Your path, surrounded by many obstacles, both witnessed daily victories and suffered no losses from the march. It was so closed off by the enemy’s ranks that it denied them access; it was so opened by your assault as though the enemy’s foresight could do nothing harmful. If these things are to be attributed to your good fortune, a prince’s endowment is complete; if to toil, it is narrower than every honor.

With favorable omens you first undertook battles against nature, so that no hope of resistance would remain to the enemy. In your sovereign position you subjected to yourself the various laws of heaven, the defenses of the earth, and the arrogance of rivers. [Note: Some editions read *superba*, “proud things.”] [Col. 0169C]

I am lying if your ardor was ever hindered by arranged obstacles, or your coldness; if the swelling of the waters or the need to drink restrained you; if the peaks of the Alps, joined to the height of the vault of heaven, brought delay to your journeys. [Note: Some editions read “convexi,” “arched,” instead of “connexis,” “joined.”] Those whom you found after the defenses of their regions had been conquered did not know how to resist, because broken barriers make secure those whom they protect, and those who possess safer places live with their minds relaxed in leisure.

Against you no dwelling on the plains produced equals; nor did the inaccessible places that embraced their inhabitants protect them from plunder unless they became suppliants. Placed within your possession, a man indicated his wealth without fear; nor did it help a rebel to be known as poor. No one escaped your indignation except through humility, when the one who asked had advanced into the number of your allies.

The cold of Scythia is not unknown to you. You do not fail to know Meroë or the Cancer panting with heat, as the possessor of another world might. By subduing everything, you learned about places that had scarcely become known to us even by hearsay. These things are greater than man; but one who is being prepared for the governance of the world must necessarily come instructed in all its hinges.

Too quickly I have seized the time of mature praise. As though, at the beginning of its course, the river of my talent did not also weaken like a torrent, so, hungry for narration, I have seized the fruits of your perfected age. The man who is surpassed both by the speed and by the number of your laurel crowns seeks their ranks. More quickly than they can be spoken, the distinctions that we recount have been fulfilled by you, most unconquered one. Who could endure sluggishness in the description of his deeds when he did not endure it in action? [Col. 0170B]

[Note: “Greece educated you”: Constantinople. For when he had been given as a hostage by his father to Emperor Leo Augustus, he was brought up in the emperor’s court after scarcely passing his seventh year of life. According to Jordanes in the same book, he earned the favor of the prince, by whom he was eventually sent back to his father after ten years.] 

Greece educated you in the bosom of civilization, foreseeing what was to come. It instructed you as you entered the threshold of life in such a way that, while it still found the cheerfulness of a child in you, security concerning your guardian soon followed. You were still living in the gray bloom of adolescence, and your tender stalk had not yet produced a harvest of virtues through experience. The pleasing image of youth was still present, and the down enclosing your face had not yet covered it. Then, when the purple of your age and the little flower of the approaching empire promised anxious people fear concerning a change of favor, fury burst forth as a test of your strength and clemency, and subjected minds long disemboweled by inactivity to the nourishment of opportunity.

[Note: “He was driven from the imperial city”: Zeno Augustus, ensnared by the treachery of his mother-in-law Verina, fled to Isauria after leaving Constantinople. Basiliscus possessed the vacant court for approximately two years, while Zeno himself was consul for the second time, in the year of Christ 475. This, therefore, is the man whom Ennodius calls the tyrant. Afterward Zeno gathered an army and, when Basiliscus withdrew, recovered the empire. Theoderic must have assisted Zeno on that expedition, since Ennodius attributes to him the full praise for Zeno’s restoration, although he is not mentioned in this connection either in the excerpts of Candidus preserved by Photius or by the others who wrote about Zeno’s affairs.]

Respect for the imperial city was immediately driven out, and a tyrant entered into empty possession without having been admitted through the shedding of blood. Having gained possession of the court, he decided that, after defeating his enemies through fear, nothing remained for him to do. Then the light of nature moved your spirits without the support of years, so that neither a better cause might lie beneath you when you were present, nor might you fail to return, in a time of necessity, the benefit that you had received in peace.

At the very gates of your encounter the invader yielded, when through you the scepters were restored to the exile who was uncertain of his safety. Let us examine the histories and question the annals: where do they record that sovereignty was restored to an exile whom a king by birth had purchased with his own blood? The glory of the camp is dispersed through the participation of the troops; what came through the contribution of many cannot be referred to one man.

The restraint of ambition is the fruit of singular virtue, especially at a time when you could retain what you had acquired without damage to your reputation. Equal praise, illustrious lord, belongs to you for the diadem that you bestowed and for the one that you defended. If the ruler of those regions did not love you, he governed the republic in terror; if he loved you, he was bound to you. You used the purple-clad man as a witness to the faithfulness of your own merits. [Col. 0170D]

By then the palaces themselves had placed themselves under your authority. No one believed that you could not transfer to whomever you wished what you had restored. But sparing in demanding rewards, as though they were sufficient in return for your deeds, [Col. 0171C]

[Note: “You received the fasces”: Marcellinus Comes says that Theoderic was designated consul by Zeno for the year 484. Theoderic, king of the Goths, nearly reconciled through the generosity of Zeno Augustus and made master of the present army, was also designated consul; for a time he held, with his followers, the part of Ripensis Dacia and Lower Moesia entrusted to him. He was consul of the East, with Venantius as his colleague at Rome. Cassiodorus’s Fasti for that year read: “Our Lord Theoderic and Venantius.”]

you received the fasces—not so that distinction might accrue to you from the curule office, but so that the palm-bearing robe might earn its value from you. Who would believe that this civility could live among your companions with the complete execution of virtue? That year had a consul who protected the republic not so much through vigilance as through reputation. [Col. 0171D]

[Note: “When he was placed in the bands”: For as long as he was consul, he wore the embroidered toga, or palmata consular garment, which was customarily adorned with golden bands. Sidonius, concerning the consulship of Asterius, Book VIII, Letter 6, writes: “Among the resounding bands, he adorned that palmata garment, drunk with Saracen juices, with speech more painted and more golden.” This therefore seems a certain emendation: “bands” in place of “figments,” which all the books read.]

When he was placed in the bands, the weapons taken from the enemy trembled. When did the tested brilliance of kings, from the very infancy of the world, ever grant a lictor such a fate? I do not wish to wander through the accidents of dominions; in your lineage those who were found were proved.

Ploughs gave Serranus to the Scipios; while he entrusted great seeds to the furrows, a harvest of honours arose for him. But I value less the prosperity that takes desperation as its beginning. It has scarcely happened to a few to degenerate nobly, whereas you owe it to the acts of your family nobly to preserve the nobility of your stock.

What can antiquity object to me—rustic limbs adorned with military cloaks? I oppose to you something that surpasses wonder: my prince, adorned in such a way that he cannot be disapproved, acting as though he still sought to be added to the number of emperors.

But what shall I do, when the fertile harvest of your deeds confronts me and surpasses one who chooses among all things? I do not know which ears of grain to bring into the granaries and which to leave behind. Before my eyes stands [Col. 0171D]

[Note: “The Bulgar commander Libertus”: Concerning this war, if I am not mistaken, Athalaric, Book VIII of the *Variae*, Letter 21, to the patrician Cyprian, who had earned distinction in that expedition under Theoderic, says: “Under our grandfather, of divine memory, you were always praised for your watchfulness on both fronts. The Danube, while still pagan, saw you as a warrior. The mass of the Bulgars did not terrify you, although their presumption in battle would have obstructed even our men. It was your special quality both to attack resisting barbarians and to pursue those turned to flight by terror. Thus you aided the victory of the Goths not so much by numbers as by toil.” In the same book, Letter 10, he says that the Bulgars were terrifying throughout the world.]

the Bulgar commander, overthrown while your right hand asserted [Note: Perhaps “liberty.”] liberty. He was neither killed, lest he perish from the records, nor left unharmed, lest he live on in arrogance. In that untamed people, he remained as a domestic witness to the strength of your power. If he had received a wound sufficient for death, you would have overcome the person; because he remained alive, he subjected his origin.

This is the nation in which, before you, everything belonged to whoever wished it. In it, men acquired titles who purchased distinction with the blood of their adversaries; among them, the battlefield was the announcer of birth. For the one whose weapons had grown redder in the struggle was judged, without ambiguity, to be the more exalted. Before your battle, it had never happened to recognize anyone resisting it; for a long time it had completed its wars through raiding alone. [Col. 0172A]

Neither mountain masses, nor the obstruction of rivers, nor the scarcity of denied provisions confined them within the narrow limits imposed by necessity, since they believe it sufficient for luxury to drink the milk of horses. Who could tolerate an adversary who runs and feeds by the aid of a swift animal? What is more, they impose upon those same animals the discipline of deliberate hunger, through which they themselves have learned to avoid starvation. How does it happen that the rider of a famished horse extracts food from its entrails, food that the animal, under the guidance of careful preparation, had taken pains not to store?

Before this, the world was believed to be open to them everywhere. Now they consider only that part of the world closed to them which you protect. I pass over many things rapidly, lest through the fault of a slower star you arrive too late, and lest the torch of the Roman senate-house, long forced into shadow, shine forth too slowly. [Note: Schott: *styli* (“style”).] [Col. 0172B]

Between the apprenticeship of your life and the maturity of your triumphs, heavenly favor poured affection into your sacred heart. By then, through the loss occasioned by long peace, the powerful land had grown old through the baseness of its rulers; unviolated peace had already brought exhaustion to public resources; when, among us, the increase of daily plundering was augmented by successive gains, [Col. 0172C]

[Note: “The internal plunderer”: Odoacer, who soon became a tyrant. He deprived Romulus Augustulus, the last Roman emperor, of his kingdom and drove him into exile in the year 476. He had already reigned almost fourteen years when Theoderic entered Italy, which had been assigned to him by Zeno Augustus so that he might defeat Odoacer. Everything in Ennodius’s words is therefore clear. “The powerful land,” namely Italy, had been worn down by the baseness of its rulers, the last emperors; Theoderic expressed his concern and desire for it before Zeno. Jordanes describes this at length, more fully than the others, in his Gothic History.]

an internal plunderer was needed. He was wasteful of his own people and sought to make the treasury increase not so much through rising taxes as through robbery. [Note: Some editions read: “A poor master, through hateful extravagance, had contracted the raging ambition.”] Through hateful extravagance he had contracted the hatred of a poor master’s raging ambition; yet what diminished wealth was not joined to the concern for exhausted strength. For then the narrowness of the court drove private resources into confinement, and the extinguished spark of the tyrant’s retainers had allowed no flame to shine anywhere.

The army feared its own parentage, since an alien honor reminded it of its origin. He commanded the legions to go and return at his nod, chilled with fear. Obedience is suspect when it serves the unworthy; and whenever the consciousness of an ultimate ancestry confronts those placed above, they fear the very thing they are feared for. [Col. 0172C]

[Note: “The cause of discord was born”: So that Odoacer might not seem to have been attacked unjustly in war, he says that Theoderic was provoked by him and stirred up by the slaughter of his relatives. This means, as I conjecture, the Rugians, whom Odoacer afflicted in war after capturing their king Feletheus and his son Frederic, whom Theoderic openly favored; he defeated them in battle once and again, as Eugippius relates in the *Life of Saint Severinus*.]

The happy cause of discord between you was born when Roman prosperity invited rebellious minds to the slaughter of your relatives. The cause of battle was generated by the weak, and, lest confidence arise even from an enterprise destined to perish, part of the fugitives stirred up the fighting.

Then, after your forces had been summoned far and wide, one people, dispersed among innumerable nations, was gathered together, as you migrated with it toward Ausonia; no one except a kinsman took up the journey. Wagons were taken in place of houses, and everything that would serve necessity flowed into unstable dwellings. Then the weapons of Ceres—stones that loosen grain from the ears—were dragged by oxen. Mothers, heavy with children, among your households forgot their sex and burden as they laboured to prepare food. [Note: Schott: *laborabant* (“they laboured”).] [Col. 0173A]

Then, in the open field, winter and the hair covered with the perpetual whiteness of frost entangled the beard in icicles upon the hair that it possessed. For whatever garment a matron had woven with greater care broke in the continuing freeze so that it might cling to the body. Either unwilling peoples or a wild nation raised in caves supplied food for your armies. [Col. 0173B]

Amid these things, which yielded to you through ice or heat, I wish briefly to touch upon one line of your battles. [Col. 0173D]

[Note: “The Ulca is the river of the Gepids”: At this time Theoderic’s royal residence was the city of Novae in Lower Moesia, as Eugippius and Marcellinus likewise show in their Chronicles. Ptolemy calls it Νούας, “Novas.” From there, having begun his Italian expedition, he proceeded directly toward Sirmium. In the intervening region, the Gepids lived in Dacia under King Gundarith; when they dared to obstruct the march, Theoderic routed them at the river Ulca.]

The Ulca is the river that protects the Gepids. It fortifies the bold in place of ramparts and embraces the side of the province with certain walls, like a range of mountains, walls that no battering ram can frustrate. The rigor of your march brought you to it. There, instead of envoys and a request for favor, a people long unconquered hastened with the intention of resisting, while the necessity of hunger was almost besieging your troops before the enemy.

Tell me, I beg you, most clement lord: what hope remained for a people comparable to sand or stars except you? With the Gepids pressing upon you, with the river and disease confronting you, you flew along the route that a fugitive would have avoided, against swords drawn from their sheaths. No one’s unwitting footsteps clung to the mud; no one, prodigal of life, entered danger unknowingly. The authority of the human mind is conquered by foresight of danger; the confidence of the brave falters whenever things to be feared are brought before their eyes.

Before the untamed youth stood a definite choice concerning death, when no security for survival seemed possible. Why have the ancient monuments exalted Cato, because he led an army through the Libyan Syrtes while making human deaths seem the sport of serpents; or because, without the reward of virtue, he was raised amid the vapors of heaven and experienced the cold of poison? No one sees the chelydri before destruction, while through the monstrous flame and the structure of the body the soul, as souls are accustomed to do, flies out into the air. Nor is the man who is destroyed with the praise of a brave man fortunate if he does not know from where his end has come.

The courage of that soldier cannot be compared with the ranks of your troops, nor is his wisdom equal to that of their commander. Him the frenzy of civil war drove; you were summoned by Rome, mistress of the world, for the restoration of her condition.

But why do I delay over what favorable fortune presented to you? The densely packed ranks of your enemies, whom the farther bank had received, gave way. They were pressed by weapons, while neither abyss nor flood could hold them back. Spears driven by stronger arms pierced the empty cages of their chests. Amid earthly shipwrecks and waves of blood, the unconquered commander appeared, strengthening those who stood near him with this address:

> “Whoever desires a path through the enemy line, let him follow me. Let no one look back who seeks an example for battle. Courage does not require a multitude. Battles go to the few; the fruits of battles go to the many. The army will be judged by me, and in what I accomplish the people triumph. Raise the standards, by which provision is made that I not remain hidden. Let them know whom they are attacking or at whose throats they are to rest. Those who meet my charge shall gain distinction through their death.”

After these words he asked for a cup as an auspice, loosened the reins for battle, and hurled himself forward. Like a torrent through crops, like a lion among herds, you laid waste. No one who met you stood firm, and no one could escape you as you pursued. You were borne through everything; the weapons were already failing, while your anger continued to grow.

At once the condition of the Gepids was reversed. They were seen wandering about, victors by a changed fortune. For you, venerable one, who had undertaken the taste of combat without companions, now advanced surrounded by thousands. The opposing multitude was slain until the approaching night rescued a few, while you proceeded toward wandering granaries filled with the resources of cities, which would not merely satisfy necessity but relieve the disgust that follows the height of luxury.

Thus adversity served your prosperity, and the enemy’s hunger fought against the hunger of your men. The hostile encounter overcame starvation; you would not have recovered your health if the battles had ceased. Let these things, arranged in order from countless deeds, suffice. I pass over the Sarmatians migrating with their encampment and remain silent about the common people numbered among the trophies of your conflicts. [Col. 0174C]

[Note: “I encounter Odoacar for you”: Theoderic’s first clash with Odoacer took place at the river Sontius in the province of Venetia, during the consulship of Probinus and Eusebius, in the year of Christ 489. In that battle Odoacer was routed with all his men, as Cassiodorus notes in his Chronicle. The river mentioned by Ennodius is therefore the Sontius, or, as it is written in Cassiodorus’s Chronicle, the Isontius. It is likewise the Sontius of Jordanes and of Cassiodorus himself, *Variae* I.18, in Theoderic’s words: “After, by God’s favor, we had crossed the waters of the Sontius, where Italy first received us as its ruler.”] 

I meet you, Odoacer, together with my ruler—you who had stirred up every nation against him as though you were the shaker of the world. As many kings had gathered with you for battle as the whole community could scarcely support in soldiers. It became clear that the minds of a massed multitude were various and that hope of victory does not come from number.

The right hands of your men still trembled from their previous disaster, and the weakness of their limbs did not carry through their intended assaults. Yet it is enough for one to will according to his strength, and undivided counsel regarding the enemy brought vengeance in place of strength. Neither camps fortified over a long period nor the depths of the river held you back. The enemy was allowed to build a rampart, not to defend it.

Suddenly the level waters were darkened by the movement of fugitives, across which, as they departed, you ordered them to overcome the domestic storm. Meanwhile your battle lines completed the fighting by their appearance, not by their labor. There fortune opened the gates for you, clearly revealing that those who had yielded in the first place would not remain for a second struggle.

But the unsettled mind again arranged a conflict for its own deception, [Col. 0175A]

[Note: “When at Verona”: Cassiodorus says, “In the same year, Odoacer was defeated in a renewed engagement.” Jordanes says: “Theoderic, meeting that Odoacer in the fields of Verona, destroyed him with a great slaughter.”]

when battle was being prepared at your Verona with loose hands and lavish expenditure. Nothing was stronger than your adversaries before the battle line; but when the trumpets of war sounded, nothing was weaker. Their greatest strength lay in the promise of combat, and, if the tongue had been sufficient in place of the right hand, they had an abundance of words.

A location was chosen that was useful not so much for an encounter as for terror. They took care that even the first withdrawal of the deserters not be attributed to chance, yet the bright fortune of the republic pressed you onward so that you would not abandon what you had begun.

Having measured the distances of your march, you saw the fires of the enemy glittering like stars, so that, if fear had ever been known to you, you would have learned that you were hanging over a precipice. The state of your mind was never lifted up by the swelling of good fortune or content with uncertainty.

The day of battle was approaching, bringing darkness to many. When dawn announced the rising of its golden mane with saffron chariots; when the sun’s flame rose from the waters of the ocean; the hoarse trumpets were already sounding, and the army, forgetful of itself, was already seeking you.

While you enclosed your chest in steel defenses, while you armed yourself with greaves, while the sword that avenged liberty was fastened to your side, your holy mother and venerable sister—who had come to you out of devotion—were present. While feminine anxiety hung between hope and fear, while, stunned by the outcome, they fed their eyes upon the star of your face, you strengthened them with these words:

> “You know, mother—known to every nation through the honour of your offspring—that at my birth you, fruitful in bearing a man, gave birth to a male. Today is the day on which the battlefield will proclaim your son's manhood. We must act with weapons, lest through me the honours of our grandfathers perish. In vain do we rely on our parents’ titles unless our own deeds assist us.
>
> “My father stands before my eyes, one whom Fortune never made a mockery of in battle, who through the demands of necessity himself produced successes for his right hand. It is under such a leader that I must contend. He did not fear all uncertainties; he himself brought about his own prosperity.
>
> “Nevertheless, carry away your elaborately made garments and the strains of the looms. Let the battle line receive me more finely dressed than festivals are wont to do. Let anyone who does not know me by my charge judge me by my brilliance. Let the splendour of my clothing invite greedy eyes; let my more precious appearance offer itself to the blows. Let whoever Fortune gives my throat have consolation for his labour; let those not granted to see me fighting gape at my fallen splendour.”

After these words, a horse restless at the calls of the trumpets received you on its back. But while you indulged in speech, the enemy legions were being pressed by the urgency of your advance. You gave confidence to the inactive by delaying, and I believe this happened through the foresight of the heavenly beings, so that the multitude would not be credited with what you conquered.

Immediately the crowd of the slain announced your arrival to the enemy; the enormity of the slaughter revealed its executioner. But they too were not deprived of their customary remedies. At once they took up the wings that fear had given them, choosing the death of destruction in headlong flight.

Let the man who does not know that I have submitted to truth look upon the waters of the Athesis, which became rich with corpses in your place. While you swelled the waters with blood, the advance of the streams was checked on the other side. Thus, lest your swords prove insufficient, the water too fought for you.

Hail, most splendid of rivers, which washed away most of Italy’s filth, receiving the refuse of the world without loss of purity. Behold, that field, covered with armed men, shone most nobly with the whiteness of human bones. Whenever we are oppressed by the memory of ancient suffering, we have something to look upon. Let the earth protect the most beautiful scene. Let what they suffered remain exalted as long as forgetfulness erases what they did.

Oh, would that it were not permitted to ravenous beasts to carry anything away! A spectacle worthy of desire perishes through what the animals have stolen. [Col. 0176A]

There, Rome, I would wish you to pass by, forgetful of your age. If you came trembling on faltering feet, the years would exchange themselves for joys. Why are you always shut away, immersed in shrines? Here it was accomplished that you should have more consuls than you had previously seen candidates. Recognize the clemency of your lord: he wished you to taste the triumphs whose uncertain battles he chose not to know.

Behold, once again a fitting portion of the enemy hastened to the death owed to its recognized surrender; and when those falling had exceeded the required number, yet ranks equipped with gleaming weapons assembled for service. Your spirit, ever inclined toward mercy, was bent toward leniency. You believed that the lessons of necessity would accustom them to loyalty, though they had never displayed it through zeal to conciliate princes. What preserved you, preeminent among kings, was that you had cast away the safeguard provided by confidence in an oath. We anxiously awaited whether those whom you had received from among your enemies would deserve not to perish.

Thanks be to you, God, arbiter of the world, who drove consciences possessed by the torpor of an ancient error toward avenging swords. I would be ashamed to recount their innate fickleness, were I not to see it obedient to your praises. Why should I conceal what happened? It pleased them, with Tusa as leader and instigator, once again to promise Odoacer’s kingdom to his unarmed outstretched right hand [Note: To promise Odoacer’s kingdom. Tusa was the leader and instigator; when he defected again to Odoacer’s side with the surrendered army, the siege of Pavia followed, where Theoderic had withdrawn. So it is related in the *Life of Epiphanius*.]. The error of their hostile minds was immediately revealed when events brought it to light. You summoned foresight as the companion of your actions; and, lest the license of those roaming about remain unpunished, shaking the standards of vengeance, you made a people already tested a participant in your counsels, in secret. No adversary escaped recognition when the better part of the world was arranging matters with you. A vowed slaughter was commissioned throughout the most widely separated regions. Who but the will above brought this about—that in a single instant the long-accumulated disaster of the Roman name should be poured out, gathered through the wickedness of so many ages?

Here I do not know where to turn. Shall I retrace my steps, having undertaken the office of praiser, or enter upon the path of your praises once begun? The matter has been completed through a prosperous and fateful war: Odoacer’s presumption was cut down after he was denied the assistance of deceit. Why should I recall the scattered ranks of the Heruli? They were led against you for this reason: that here they might learn whom they should fear even in their own homes. Alien fury served the causes of your long peace.

I am silent about the place where lasting peace was imposed upon you, Burgundian [Note: “To you, Burgundian, lasting peace.” This refers to the peace made with Gundobad, king of the Burgundians, and joined to the marriage of Theoderic’s daughter, the Ostrogoth, with Sigismund, Gundobad’s son. Concerning this, the Burgundian king himself wrote to Bishop Epiphanius, Theoderic’s envoy: “May the assent of the Godhead grant that the treaty consolidated between us be preserved through a long age.”]. For you obeyed treaties in such a way that it is attributed to steadfastness, not fear, that you live in repose. Who would allow this also to perish from memory: that, to your good fortune, we saw the weapons of traitors converge upon one another, and that you, occupied elsewhere in a pious engagement, struck down hostile battle-lines? How often did the man who had taken up vows of fighting against you prevail—for you?

Let Frideric speak [Note: Frideric, son of Faeban, king of the Rugians, had first served under Theoderic in this war. Later he broke faith and joined the enemy. Then, when discord arose among the enemy themselves, Frideric was defeated in a battle between the opposing standards. Thus the man who had previously won a triumph for Theoderic over his adversaries provided those same adversaries with a triumph over himself when they overthrew him.], who, after violating his allegiance, accompanied your enemies in their destruction; who brandished weapons against those with whom he had been allied through error, when discord arose among the wicked over the fact that they understood themselves to desire one and the same thing. May the Godhead be present and extend its benefits into eternity: under its direction, disputes arose as votive offerings among the guilty. For Frideric, after winning a triumph for you over your adversaries, provided one over himself.

A great part of your venerable merits draws me toward another subject. I see inspired beauty arising among the ashes of cities, and palaces shining everywhere beneath the full splendor of civilized life [Note: “Palatine buildings everywhere.” Cassiodorus, in his letter to Patricius and Hypatius during their consulship, writes of Theoderic: “Under whose fortunate rule many cities are renewed, strongly fortified castles are built, wondrous palaces rise up, and ancient marvels are surpassed by his great works.” Among the rest of Theoderic’s constructions he likewise praises the restored appearance of Ravenna.]. I see buildings completed before my time being arranged and restored. Rome herself, that mother of cities, grows young again by cutting away the withered limbs of old age. Forgive me, sacred beginnings of the Lupercal spirit: it is greater to drive back decline than to have given beginnings. To this is added the fact that you have veiled the senate-house’s crown with an innumerable flowering. Despair has touched none of those honors whom the goodness of their conscience aided when they petitioned; no one who did not ask, poor in splendid merits, knows how to doubt the outcome of a request.

Either we are good because of our own purpose, or we are shaped by your example. The resources of the state have grown together with the advancement of private persons: nowhere in your court is canvassing for office, while wealth is everywhere diffused; no one departs without a gift, and no one laments the hardships of proscription. Immortal vigor inhabits your embassies; you arrange the order of your instructions before you see the envoys. No contradiction is found in your replies, nor is an easy resolution discovered for objections. The reputation of the ruler keeps watch in place of arms; the concern of a great king guards our leisure. Yet you do not cease extending fortifications, carrying your cares far into the future. You possess both the confidence of a brave man and the caution of one who fears. O double fullness of virtues in a single prince, which discloses the Lord as its author—for among men he has no one from whom he might seem to have learned what he displays!

But behold, after profound repose, we call words back to the battle-lines; once again the trumpet summons eloquence to itself. The city of Sirmium [Note: Sirmium, capital of Lower Pannonia, which was therefore called Sirmian Pannonia, as in *Variae* III.23. At this time Trasaric, king of the Gepids, ruled there. Theoderic defeated him through the count Pitzia because of a secret conspiracy, according to Ennodius, with other Gepids under the leadership of Gunderith, and restored Sirmium to the kingdom of Italy during the consulship of Cethegus, in A.D. 504, as Cassiodorus’s *Chronicle* records. Jordanes, *On the Gothic Deeds*: “He sent his count, chosen among the foremost, to secure the city of Sirmium. After expelling its king Trasaric, son of Trastila, and retaining his mother, he obtained it.” Concerning this expedition and the one that followed, see Athalaric, *Variae* VIII.10. The celebrated count Pitzia is also mentioned by Theoderic, *Variae* V.29.]—once the boundary of Italy—was a place where the old masters kept watch, lest the wounds inflicted there upon neighboring peoples should accumulate and spread into the Roman body. Later, through the negligence of rulers, it passed under Gepid authority; from there came daily insults and the disorderly traffic of embassies. The deceptive flatteries of their contrived schemes burned the prince’s mind, as did Trasaric’s untimely intimacy with the other Gepids, whose leader was Gunderith. You believed that your injury was perishing because Italy had long been permitted to retain possession of the territory while you ruled. Nor was it enough as a consolation that you had not lost it: when the pain was immense, why had its occupant not restored it at the beginning of your rule? You considered an empire diminished when it did not grow.

After Trasaric’s schemes became fully clear, you sent Pitzia, Herduic, the noblest Goths, and young men not yet committed to any battles, so that, if Pitzia accepted the terms offered, he might in a single invasion gain control of those places. But Fortune’s customary service to your success intervened: he fled of his own accord and, without pressure from your army, abandoned what he owed. Immediately Pitzia—who had both gained useful outcomes from you and weighed the decisive moments of your plans—believed that the land had not been acquired but restored; and he did not ravage it as profitable booty, but preserved it through orderly administration as his own.

While these arrangements were being directed there, Greece declared its hostility through the attack upon your federate Mundon [Note: That is, after attacking Mundon, who was allied with Theoderic by treaty. Mundon had gathered a band of robbers and cattle-raiders, occupied the fortress of Herta on the Danube, and from there made raids in every direction in barbarian fashion. When Sabinian, master of the soldiers in Illyricum under the emperor Anastasius, attacked him with Bulgarians whom he had joined to himself, Pitzia brought aid to Mundon, who was already nearly despairing and considering surrender. After annihilating Sabinian’s forces in a great slaughter at the Margus, he rescued Mundon and brought him willingly under King Theoderic. This occurred during the consulship of Sabinian and Theodorus, in A.D. 505, as Marcellinus Comes and Jordanes relate more fully in their works on Gothic affairs.]. It led its Bulgarians with it under its protection and, using them as though they were a fortress amid the fighting, threatened us. Then Mundon, believing that it would be enough for his defense if your cohorts learned what he was suffering, entrusted the credibility of his danger to swift messengers. Before he had learned how to devise a defense, he saw the defender entering the combats on his behalf.

Nevertheless, Pitzia observed the unconquered youth of the Bulgarians and armed the burning impulses of the young men with more powerful fires of speech:

> “You remember, comrades, under whose authority you have come to these places. Let no one suppose that the eyes of our king are absent, for whose fame we must fight. If a rain of spears were to cover the sky, it would not remain hidden who could cast the stronger weapon. Plunge your breasts into the steel, so that from the horror of life the clear hope of victory may arise. I believe that the witness of royal strength is already dead; nor does anyone survive who used to show them whom we have as our lord. Or perhaps they disdain to judge our people by their prince. Let them understand that what we are doing has flowed from him. Let them not be permitted to owe to one person alone what our ruler has transmitted to our origin.”

He changed these words into trumpet-calls. Immediately, as usually happens when a black storm-cloud roars through rumbling roofs with the rushing of tempests, so the people of Mars hurled themselves into the fray. For a long time the uncertain contest wavered in the balance, while equal ferocity in fighting arose on both sides. Two nations charged one another, nations to whom flight had never offered refuge among swords. They marveled to find their own likeness in each other, and that in the human race either a Goth dared to resist, or a Bulgarian.

Meanwhile, while the outcome of the battle was uncertain and winged deaths claimed the air for themselves, the memory of our prince prevailed, as they acted so that the field might assert the merits of each before him. The punished nation was turned to flight, punished all the more severely because it escaped. The earth, shaken by the pounding of hoofed horses, trembled. With immense lamentation they hurried away after realizing that their safety was no longer uncertain. God, ruler of heaven, multiply the gifts you have bestowed. They, never uncertain of triumphs—those whom all the world had looked up to—departed, having lost the standards of war and struck down by their own survival, loudly proclaiming three times blessed those whom it had been their lot to perish.

Why should I review the slaughter of the soldiers and the disgraceful departure of the commander Sabinian, when reason forbids me to recount, after the defenses had been destroyed, what happened to one left undefended? Then, lest Pitzia seem destined to be celebrated through the ages as having fought more for glory than for greed, he left the labor of the field to wild beasts and birds, since he ordered that the hungry soldier should take nothing from the rich corpses.

But with what tongues can these things be explained adequately? By what gift of eloquence can they be unlocked? For a long time you have conquered in all your engagements; now you are beginning to hold the victors in obedience. Meanwhile the Roman realms returned to their own frontier. The Sirmians were given commands in the manner of the ancients: those who until now held our possessions now doubt their own because of your proximity.

How shall I describe the depredations of the Vandals, chastised by winds obedient to you, for whom your friendship is sufficient in place of an annual payment? [Note: Cassiodorus, during the consulship of Olybrius Junior: “Then also the Vandals, having humbly requested peace, ceased their depredation of Sicily. Previously they had continually plundered throughout Sicily and along all the shores of Italy wherever the wind drove them.”] Under the guidance of wisdom, they do not know how to wander beyond what is possible. They deserved to become relatives [Note: Through Amalafrida, Theoderic’s sister, who married Thrasamund, king of the Vandals. Jordanes writes: “And, in order to extend his family fully, he sent his sister Amalafrida, mother of Theodahad, who later became king, to Africa as wife to Thrasamund, king of the Vandals.”], because they do not refuse obedience.

These matters concerning the accumulation of your deeds I have briefly reviewed, with greater desire than eloquence, leaving untouched what deserves better treatment. I shall see who can surpass me in eloquence; no one will be able to surpass my devotion to you. God inspiring you, you possess this gentleness: you believe that you can accomplish more through diligence than through fear. Good qualities of distinction have been inserted into the monuments of your glory, so that while kings fear you, servants love you. For whatever you command to be bestowed, after measuring the resources of your subjects, you believe may be refused. O king composed in complete tranquility, who attributes to our devotion what we expend in your service!

What of the fact that the entire Alamannic people was enclosed by you within the borders of Italy without harm to Roman possession? [Note: The Alamanni, neighbors of the Suebi in Germany, had been subdued by our king Clovis. After losing their king, they fled to Theoderic. Theoderic himself writes to Clovis in Cassiodorus, *Variae* II.41: “You have subjected the Alamannic peoples, brought low by stronger circumstances, with your victorious right hand. But moderate your movements against the exhausted remnants, for those whom you see fleeing to the protection of your parents deserve to escape by right of gratitude. Show mercy to those who, terrified, are concealed within our borders.” Ennodius therefore teaches that Theoderic gave settlements in Italy to the surviving remnants of the defeated Alamannic armies.]. She was granted a king after deserving to lose one. She became a guardian of Latium, though she had always ravaged our lands. It turned out happily for her that she fled her homeland, for thus she acquired the wealth of our soil. You obtained lands that know how to yield to the plow, although they have not escaped the knowledge of losses. Under you we saw the best outcomes arise from adversity and danger become the mother of prosperity. Freed from marshes, she rejoices to inhabit land that until then had been sinking amid collapsing dwellings into a more solid [Note: “A *chaenix*.” Only one manuscript has *scheniem*; from the readings of the others we have reconstructed *chaenicem*.] *chaenix* as a benefit.

It was fitting also that you should spur eloquence with the rewards of praise, lest we lose your honors through silence. No art’s industry is idle. Talent, wherever it lies hidden, is sought out. He who deserves office will obtain it even if he lives far away. The man whom innocence has revealed is never concealed, while the subtle judge is not won over by words but by deeds. The good deeds of our parents who have died are preserved with you. When the loyalty of someone’s devotion to your gentleness has become known, you will soon return to his offspring, by right of inheritance, what you owe to its author. We receive the fruit of our ancestors’ services, and yet we do not fear punishment for their excesses. Your measured anger ends with the man, because your piety seeks a successor for the sake of recompense.

Many things still remain that I could say; but among the many heralds of your deeds, it is fitting that something be reserved untouched. Venerable studies owe you the fact that they speak. Your predecessors loved ignorance, because they never accomplished deeds deserving praise. The most eloquent man was despised among the plowshares, and force denied what skill had granted. The tribunals mourned in silence under a mute authority; no palm was granted to the speaker. The outcome of affairs wavered toward disaster when talent was not given to letters. Everywhere a single grief oppressed genius, because leisure wore down the powers of eloquent men. Devouring negligence possessed the splendor of the elders, and no beginner was kindled by the rivalry to be pursued. Behold the riches of your age: then the courts could scarcely find accomplished men; now the Church directs a praiser.

Let antiquity now go and boast of Alexander in its buskined narratives, to whom the wealth of fame was produced by the gift of speakers, so that through assisting eloquence a mendicant praise may appear to grow along with his deeds. The merits of our king do not require the consolation of one who asserts them. Even though the deeds of the ancients have been enlarged by lies, they are less than his true actions. Poets, you pretended great things; but you must admit that the present lord has accomplished greater ones. The leader of Pella wished the total of his praises to depend upon the favor of Choerilus, lest the multitude detect the desire to deceive and the man employed to support the victory become a witness to shamelessness.

I detract nothing from the elders whom antiquity had held in highest esteem, except what the elevation of the Roman name has bestowed upon you. Error’s mother, ignorance, possessed that man, who knew nothing of true religion. But instruction, life-giving from the very light itself, formed you as a worshiper of the supreme God. You never attach to your labors whatever favorable outcome chance has offered. You know that in you the substance of perfection lies with God’s care. You act so as to deserve prosperity, but, having obtained everything, you ascribe it to the author. By strength, vigilance, and prosperity you display a prince; by gentleness, a priest. Why did our ancestors vainly call those gods and pontiffs to whom scepters had been entrusted? It is something unique to fulfill the holiest title through deeds and not possess the venerable names.

Let my king rightly be called Alamannic; let him be called foreign. Let him live as a god through the fruit of his conscience, and not seek the empty titles of pompous boasting, since in his character the flatteries of his ancestors serve the truth.

I confess that I would like, overcome by the enormity of your deeds, to descend to the end of my speech and, dazed by the light of ancient achievements, pass beyond these new honors. If I had wished to reduce the ornaments of the heavenly axis to a number, including the brilliance of the Bears, and describe the beauty of the sky with an inadequate tongue, mortal obscurity would yield to divine splendor; a humble spark of speech would not suffice for the radiant lamp. This condition declares me unequal to the task, though it has shown me obedient.

For with what mouth should that be celebrated: that you guard the instruments of Gothic strength, taking care that our leisure not be disturbed, and that beneath your eyes you make an unconquered youth practice at war amid the benefits of tranquility? Victorious ranks still remain in the fullness of their strength, and others have already grown. Their muscles are hardened by missiles and fulfill the work of brave men while they play. What is done serves as a spectacle that in the future may be sufficient for courage.

While flexible spear-shafts are whirled by boys’ throwing-straps, while bows direct their daily slaughter at heads, the entire circuit of the City is worn down by an imitation of combat. The figure of battle is enacted so that real danger may not arise with it. Who could believe that one mind could suffice both to conquer in battle through unconquered campaigns and to act through counsel so that there would be no occasion for fighting?

We learn that Rutilius and Manlius, under the direction of the people’s foresight, brought about a gladiatorial contest so that the populace, possessed of prolonged peace within the theatrical enclosures, might recognize what was done in battle. But then, with idle hands, the deaths of allies were needlessly inflicted upon the spectators’ eyes. What proceeds from cruelty can never be a good institution: the minds of men had first to see the destruction of their own people before they were armed against their enemies. Meanwhile, as the outcome taught, that encounter produced not so much an increase in strength as in fear: amid prosperous circumstances, the spirit of the unwar like learned what it should fear.

Observe how different the inventions are, diverging along the full path. In that case, the actual shedding of blood drove their minds away from combat. Here, the vigor of the young men was kindled by the image of a fictitious contest. Their early age taught them to regard as stored up for themselves as many deaths of adversaries as there were arrows [Note: “Not through foreign methods.” All the manuscripts read *non te rexoticus*. From this we have extracted, as I believe, the genuine reading: *non per exoticos discursus*.]. They have not been trained through foreign expedients to squander the resources of their quivers carelessly or hurl manifest destruction into the air; they will demand as many lives as the weapons they have brandished.

But amid the martial successes with which you train everyone and reconcile favorable omens of victory, you reserve nothing for the sweetness of civilized life. Who would believe that your heroes do not reject the fear of strangers, so long as it is peaceful? For law restrains their unconquered spirits amid the battle-lines. After their laurels, they submit their necks to commands; having trampled the enemy wedges before whom arms have yielded, they allow decrees to rule. You alone are endowed with merit and nature, and magnanimous men follow your commands. Birth indeed gave you lordship, but virtue established it. The splendor of your lineage won scepters for you; even had its insignia been absent, judgment itself would have chosen you as prince.

Nor should the beauty of your appearance be counted among lesser matters, since the purple of royal countenance radiates the dignity of imperial crimson. Bring forth, Seres, the garments you dye with precious purple; extend the coverings that drink nobility from more than one bronze vessel. A garland is valued by its variegated gems, and let the stone guarded by the fiercer viper come forward. Whatever ornaments may be brought with the world in attendance will shine more brightly when adorned by the sacred character of your venerable body.

A stature has been established that reveals a ruler by its height. The snow of your cheeks harmonizes with their blush; your eyes bloom with perpetual serenity. Your hands are worthy to assign destruction to rebels and the fulfillment of honors to subjects. Let no one boast of what has been placed there out of season: for what diadems accomplish in other lords, nature accomplished in my king, with God as its craftsman. Those ornaments make others conspicuous through the support of so much wealth; but nature, simple and unchanging, brought forth this man more excellent.

Why should those labor over adornment who seek to acquire foreign beauty? The ruler of Italy unites two utterly different qualities in friendship, so that in anger he is thunderous beyond comparison, while in joy he is beautiful without a cloud. To envoys of nations, his reposeful face either promises peace with a gentle appearance or threatens war with a terrible one. He possesses in himself as many distinguishing marks as would make separate men perfect if distributed among them.

But may the golden blessings of the age increase a purple offspring from you! May the heir of the kingdom play in your arms! May these libations of words that we offer you be demanded from us by a holy little child through the testimony of similar joys. Behold, having paid my debt and fulfilled my duty, I have concluded my speech with a prayer.

[Col. 0183]

## SECOND OPUSCULUM. A BOOKLET AGAINST THOSE WHO PRESUMED TO WRITE AGAINST THE SYNOD

[Note: The synod defended by Ennodius in this booklet is the one that should be numbered fourth among the Roman synods of Pope Symmachus. It was held on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, during the consulship of Rufius Magnus Faustus Avienus, a man of illustrious rank, and was also called the Palmary Synod. When Symmachus had been acquitted there of the charges brought against him by his adversaries, certain schismatics were found who dared to write against it and to give their work the title *Against the Synod of the Inappropriate Acquittal*. Ennodius, by order and authority of the synod, answered them in this Apologetic, carefully and precisely defending the entire case of Symmachus and the synod while refuting each of their arguments. The book was so approved by all the bishops that the later synod, held after Avienus’s consulship, confirmed it by its vote and ordered that it be placed between the fourth and fifth Symmachian synods and possess the force of a decree. Today, however, Ennodius’s booklet is wrongly placed after the synod convened during the younger Avienus’s consulship, although it should follow the other synod held, as I have said, during the consulship of Faustus Avienus. That synod, not the other, was the synod of acquittal, the fourth and Palmary Synod, attacked by Symmachus’s rivals and defended by Ennodius.]

**THOSE WHO PRESUMED TO WRITE AGAINST THE SYNOD.** (C)

## PREFACE

The ardor of the subject usually demands the impulse to speak: if the spirit is greedy for praise and desires to purchase favor through toil, while flattering glory is unaware of the narrator’s cross; or if, shackled by gain, it sells the obedience of the tongue, so that, while the mind is subjected to the desire of possession and considers the advantage already secured, it does not know how to fear the dangers advancing through the exercise of the pen; or if, confined by necessity, it brings forth speech captive, without any polish, and displays a brow ignorant of shame, so that, while it serves its purpose, it renounces the care of elegance.

For the ornaments of speech belong not to business but to leisure; painted words are not the equipment of warfare but of repose. A battlefield demands the brave; profound peace calls for one adorned. Whoever asserts what will be useful despises speech colored by the brush of art.

Since these things stand thus, I introduce the subject of my narrative and commend my compelled voice to religious minds against the barking of the wicked, remembering that it is written, “A time for silence and a time for speaking” (Ecclesiastes 3:8); and recalling, after the authority of a prophetic oracle, the example of a certain orator [Note: “Of a certain orator.” In Cicero’s dialogue *On the Orator* I.1, where Crassus is introduced speaking as follows: “For what is more foolish than to speak about speaking, when speaking itself is never not foolish unless it is necessary?”], who reports that speaking is an exceedingly foolish condition except when it is necessary.

Therefore I entrust the ministry of the mouth to the ability of the priests, against whom the poisons of hissing tongues have poured forth. Although religious patience, protected by the shield of faith, does not fear the rain of missiles, the weapons aimed without the art of warfare return to their author. Those for whom Christ is their breastplate do not fear force; through long endurance they overthrow their enemies.

Would anyone nevertheless suppose that there is fear of battle in this array, in which a contest is brought against God and the pontiffs without measuring their strength? Would anyone see a feeble and harassing enemy and fear a weak adversary because of the causes of war? He who ceases to attack an enemy wounded in conscience deprives himself of victory. He advances to the advantage of his enemy who, in conflicts, considers something else before the causes themselves. Innocence gives strength to missiles, and mutually concordant vows sharpen the sword. We know that the impulse to strike has been given more by just grief than by arms. Hence a multitude did not withstand the weapons of a few.

Therefore, since the prophet says with me, “Those who are with us are more than those who are with them” (2 Kings 6:16), I shall begin this work, which, as I judge, will please the good.

## THE BOOKLET

It would indeed be enough for the schismatics’ ignorance to have been struck down by their own proposition, especially since they carry the answer to the charges against them and the title itself deserves to be condemned with its author without examination of the work. For the significance of the impure work is revealed in its very heading: “Against the Synod of the Inappropriate Acquittal.”

Yet I shall now act as though the proposer of these evils must perish by another’s sword. Can this preface be attributed merely to ignorance, you most deranged of men? Is there anyone besides you who should be counted among diseased and wandering sheep, who could have challenged the great king of shepherds? The prophet says, “I have nourished and exalted children, but they have despised me” (Isaiah 1:2); and the Lord says concerning the apostles, “He who despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16). The prophet testifies that these were bishops when he says concerning Judas, “Let another take his bishopric” (Psalm 108:8). The Apostle Paul likewise proclaims, “Obey your leaders, for they themselves will intercede for you” (Hebrews 13:17).

But let us return to the serious and venerable proposition, not merely “drawn from the wing” (*ex ala productam*) [Note: “Drawn from the wing” (*ex ala productam*). All the manuscripts have this reading, though its sense is not apparent. Ennodius alluded to another passage of Cicero, *Against Piso*: “Consider now, our Epicurean, drawn from the sty, not from the school.” I therefore think that *ex hara productam*—“drawn from the sty”—should be read. “Not merely,” he says, “drawn from the sty, but mystical and divine.” The expression is ironic, and *non solum* means “not merely,” as often elsewhere.], but mystical:

> “Not all the priests,” they say, “were summoned to the council by the authority of the king; nor did all take part in the judgment” [Note: “Nor did all take part in the judgment.” Some bishops had left Rome, wearied by delay, after the first or second meeting of the synod.].

Slaves of Tartarus, and plainly ministers of Satan, you have dragged into the matter, through new bonds and the coils of your actions, all whom the prince’s written order did not summon. I do not wish to say what their intention was or what deliberation governed their departure—what weariness that waiting produced in them, when they saw that the venerable pope had received, contrary to all right, long delays in life. They saw only the heavens being struck by missiles aimed by themselves. To prevent these wretched men from hiding secretly in the consolation of evil deeds, your books strip away their concealment, and through you they are not permitted to have solitude in their shameful act, as the Lord says in the Gospels: “Every wicked person hates the light” (John 3:20).

“After this,” you assert [Note: “It should not have been said that they were adversaries.” The schismatics were displeased that Theoderic had removed Symmachus’s accusers from the number of judges as adversaries. Below: “In the selection of the venerable judges, he himself excluded the accusers from the proceedings and restored the accused to hope.”], “you claim that those who accused the Roman pope by submitting petitions should not have been called his adversaries.”

You acted deceitfully, clearly, because it was not unknown to you that, according to the canonical authority proclaimed in the synodal decrees, bishops who were adversaries and suspect should by no means have been admitted to the accusation. You add, as proof of your assertion, that royal instructions had not summoned them by this name.

O men fashioned with every refinement of art and baked through the furnaces of smiths, who have discovered laboriously gathered testimonies to support your statements! We admire your judgment, reverend men, and, as the saying goes, we follow it on foot. We recognize the errors you identify. Let someone call an accuser an enemy and give a tragic name to a man who has deserved no insult.

Then you gnawed at the appended question with a rhetorical clasp, alleging:

> “The Roman city is witness whether all the bishops, old and feeble, assembled.”

Behold a speech resting upon the sinews of a man and preferable to Cepasius himself in the brilliance of its language [Note: “Preferable to Cepasius himself.” This too is Ciceronian and ironic. There were two brothers named Cepasius, extremely bad and foolish orators. In his speech *For Cluentius*, Cicero reports and mocks certain words of the elder Cepasius.].

Therefore, because they said that they were strong in age but weak in body, they themselves testify that they were inept in judgment, since they said that they were already suffering the loss of their limbs—especially if they presumed to thrust this upon the ears of their most merciful lord. You suppose, expelled from the sight of all God’s people, that according to the custom of your gatherings everywhere you may confuse and relate things indiscriminately, and that before the prince you may speak about a gathering of pontiffs only of those whom the maturity of age made authorities in opening the discussion; men to whom their many years had brought reverence, and who were thought to have been preserved for a long time through the suffrage of good merits. It was fitting, then, that those whom age had required to plead the case should complain of the burdens of advanced years.

“Excellent men,” you added, “you have stated that the reason for the summons was already known from the royal instructions, and that the one governing the affairs of Italy had not acted as though a new matter needed consultation; more was owed to the written document and religious record than to the presence of the ruler.”

Therefore no pretext remained in the matter mentioned that could justify those beginning their investigation in prefacing it with such an opening. “After this, turning aside, you praise the king’s affection for good things and honor with words an innocence of which you are ignorant in your deeds.”

If it is honor at all in your speech—for with a rough plowshare, as though driving a furrow through a trackless place, you tear it open, commending weeds to a withered soil—you will receive, in return for such expenditure, straw with which the fire of Gehenna is kindled to your destruction.

But now, as someone is said to have remarked, “What shall I prefer before what?” [Note: [Col. 0186D] Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, line 371.]

“You say, contrary to the Apostle, that the opponents of the supreme pontiff were not heard, although, mindful of the heavenly command, they withdrew themselves [Note: [Col. 0186D] from communion with the adulterer Symmachus.] This declares plainly enough what the crime was of which he was accused by his adversaries. The same point is intended in the *Decree concerning the Cellulans*, which, recalling the recent example of the Roman pontiff, teaches clerics to avoid suspicion of disgraceful cohabitation; and in this very book, in the impersonation of blessed Paul: ‘You teach,’ he says, ‘that no one is to associate with fornicators—either the adulterer Laurentius or his followers or accomplices.’ Thus, what had happened to Xystus III nearly seventy years earlier—when Bassus, a former consul, attacked him with the infamy of a shameful crime—happened in precisely the same way to Symmachus, chiefly through the instigation of Festus, likewise a former consul and head of the Senate, and with no different outcome. For each was cleared by the sentence of the synod whose judgment they had voluntarily submitted to.”

“I do not here charge you with ignorance; I do not accuse you of having a faulty memory. I do not wish to say that you applied the prophet’s words to the Apostle—though I know that those who were sent are rightly called apostles themselves. David says: ‘You saw a thief, and you ran with him, and you made your portion with adulterers’ (Psalm 49:18).”

“Next, who could extricate himself from that question of yours [Col. 0186C] in which you say: ‘In the charges brought, whatever is not excluded is approved’?” Behold a voice suited to the soldiers of the Roman Church, in which one cannot know whether to praise first its polish or its flavor. Do you suppose that you have heard the law read: “What is just, you shall execute justly” (Deuteronomy 16:20)? Have you heard, if human society ever held you in its bonds, that whatever is not approved according to its proper order is excluded?
