Where is the prophet’s saying: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isaiah 3:14)? And this word spoken of you: “They proclaimed their sin as Sodom; woe to their souls” (ibid., 9)?

But what action is needed, when no remedy comes to the desperate, except to implore the Lord, who promised through the prophet (Isaiah 2:12) that he would come upon every proud and lofty one, and upon every arrogant person, so that he might be humbled? Yet I shall pursue your fetid work along its tracks and, if I can, crush it beneath an iron heel. To speak plainly: fact will contend with fact, case with case, reason with what they imagine to be reason.

You allege that priests spoke against royal commands, and you think it a kind of sacrilege that anything evil should be thought of an earthly lord’s command, since you do not know the heavenly Lord. You ask: “Who ought to have said to the king: [Note: [Col. 0187D] that the pope ought to summon a synod] ‘The pope ought to summon a synod’?” The bishops had raised this very objection to Theoderic of Ravenna, as is especially clear from the synodal acts, when, summoned by his command, they were setting out for Rome to attend the synod. But the schismatics censured this freedom of the bishops as supposedly insulting to the king. Yet it did not seem unjust to Theoderic, who recognized that the bishops’ complaint was not without reason; he even testified that the pope himself had indicated his will in writing concerning the gathering of the synod. Thus, what precedent is more certain in this matter? Especially in the case of one already oppressed by the criminal accusations of many—one for whom to be accused was itself to be condemned, and whose enemies’ denunciation had already taken away the prerogative assigned to him from heaven?”

[Col. 0187B] You were gradually drawn by successive stages of evil deeds into this madness, so that you believe that to attack is the same as to convict. Do hatred and truth have no difference among you—hatred which, usually directed against the merit of the person attacked, composes resolutions obedient to faction rather than reason? Where is the saying: “Before you know the matter, do not judge anyone” (Ecclesiasticus 11:7, according to the Septuagint)? Long ago the flock placed on the left received you as its companions. Among such people, the one who deserved to be brought to examination is believed to have received a sentence in advance; and this is what it means to be guilty: to enter the scales of debate.

Nevertheless, in your opening statement you very aptly introduced a divine example—one so well fitted by its wording that you might think Archisippus himself is holding the line in it. [Note: [Col. 0187D] The Cologne edition reads *Chrysippus* instead of *Archisippus*.] God says to the sinner: “Why do you recount my righteous acts?” [Col. 0187C] (Psalm 49:16). Applying this saying, you turn, as it were, to the priests, since he is regarded as the vicar of the blessed apostle Peter.

“[Note: [Col. 0187D] Perhaps you should read *probetis* (‘you approve’).] You forbid his physician to bring medicine to his body; how, then, will you refuse to provide healing for his soul? I do not know whether this is a great joke at the divine level or the greatest lamentation.”

You seek a cure for another’s fever; you want medicine applied to a failing soul; and, placed near death, you forget yourselves while dealing with another’s salvation. What if this was truly said to you by the prophet: “Is it too little that you trouble human beings, that you also trouble my God?” (Isaiah 7:13). And again: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4:23). But more on this elsewhere.

We know that one who has been declared beyond hope cannot be healed, and that “the wicked, when he comes down into the depths, despises” with astonishing recklessness (Proverbs 18:3). Yet I believe that counsel lives among these men—even in the death of their evil conduct—and that a person may wish for another what he himself has already lost. Now I shall rightly say to you with the prophet: “Everything that this people says is conspiracy; do not fear their fear, and do not be afraid” (Isaiah 8:12).

Let this itching of tongues that is in you be removed from us. The same prophet truly reproves you: “You who write injustice, you have written it” (Isaiah 10:1).

“We do not judge, as you say, that blessed Peter received from the Lord, together with the privileges of the See, or that his successors received, permission to sin.” [Note: [Col. 0187D] He sent to posterity an everlasting endowment of merits.] The synod’s emphatic declaration. Especially since the points we set forth above concerning the authority of the See stood in the way of that interpretation: what its former possessor, blessed Peter, earned was added to the nobility of the possession, and he gives the ancient splendor to the new rulers from Christ’s endowment. Thus these final words should be read. What, therefore, had been said by the synod concerning the authority of the See, Ennodius also transferred to its sanctity. John VIII, in his letter to Abbot Bercarius, and Gregory VII in the *Dictatus*, praise Ennodius’s statement from this passage.]

He sent to posterity an everlasting endowment of merits together with the inheritance of innocence. What was granted to him on account of the splendor of his deeds belongs to those whom a corresponding brilliance of conduct illuminates. For who would doubt that the one whom the summit of so great a dignity elevates is holy? If the good acquired by merit should be lacking in him, are not the gifts bestowed by the predecessor of the See sufficient? Either the See raises men who are distinguished to these heights, or it ennobles those whom it raises. For it knows in advance what is suitable for the foundation of the Churches, upon which the whole structure itself rests.

“But on the basis of your deeds you suppose that heavenly power is supported by your assistance, because, as you say, you lend the blessed apostle your helping right hand for his protection.”

“You are ignorant, fools, that the sun is not helped by torches, nor are lamps kindled to protect the light of day. For it is written: ‘God searches hearts and kidneys’” (Psalm 7:10; Jeremiah 17:10).

But in that part, who would dare answer your arguments, except because truth is spoken without artifice, and faith is stitched onto the lies of your speeches by contrivances?

“Why,” they say, “did you come before the prince, if the accused was not permitted to be heard?”

Thus either the fog of sin or divine terror so befogs you into animal-like stupor [Col. 0188C] that your mind either passes over a modest excuse as a fraud or, pressed down by bestial dullness, fails to recognize it. Or perhaps you think that the statement that he himself ought to summon the synod meant something else—although it was the synod’s duty to do so? That is, so that its pontifical examination might strike you with a sentence, you who, through insane zeal, had cut yourselves off from the structure of your head to the detriment of your salvation.

Afterward you introduced Esau into your work—I do not know whether in words or in barking—[Note: [Col. 0188D] Comparing our bishop with him.] though most of you read “with him”; but the matter requires us to read “our,” as the following words make clear. For the schismatics compared Symmachus with Esau and Laurentius with Jacob, through whom they were attempting to seize the pontificate from Symmachus as though it were a blessing. A little later, in the words “Moreover, then Jacob gave,” Isaac should apparently be read instead. [Note: [Col. 0188D]]

You compared our bishop with Esau, who lost the advantage of his elder nature in exchange for a single meal and forfeited the gray dignity of the firstborn by yielding to his appetite (Genesis 25).

What shall I say in response to these things, when I am hemmed in on every side by the whole range of your accusations? Which of you, I ask, stole Symmachus’s blessing while he was serving his father? To whom was nobility conferred in the place of Jacob, with so many gifts? Which of you came forward to satisfy the desires of a blind parent? Which of you, through your devotion, caused a venerable father, captured by blindness, to suffer no loss of light?

Does not the contrast with your darkness make night itself seem to display a brilliant radiance, and does not every obscurity, when compared with your deeds, assume the beauty of the sun? Moreover, at that time Jacob, although he bestowed a blessing suited to the character of the son, nevertheless conferred the blessing already promised (Genesis 48).

Why do we linger any longer over these matters, when those who have driven their heels against goads cannot be taught? Believe me: what you bring forward is hostile to peace and unfit for attack.

But there follows a bond joined to a riddle, which I do not know by what art of repetition we shall unravel. Having entered the sea of Ciceronian depth, our little boat is carried by the winds of questions through the uncertain waters near the shores. Yet, with Christ holding the helm, I shall enter the harbor and examine all your storms one by one, possessing in this undertaking a capacity derived from those men, not my own.

For they say:

“Your assertion concerning the bishops is true: the bishop of the apostolic See has never been subjected to the judgment of inferiors. Why, then, was he brought under a strict summons to judgment?”

Here our long-standing childishness is sorely at work; we must call upon him who always surpasses the inescapable weight of the proposition brought against us. For I openly cry out with the prophet on behalf of priests: “Will the axe boast against him who cuts with it? Or will the saw exalt itself against him who draws it?” (Isaiah 10:15). So that the divine oracle may support me: “As when the exactor ceased, the tribute ceased; so the Lord broke the rod of the impious” (Isaiah 14:4).

Grant, Lord, that what you foretold may come upon them: that, just as a drunkard wanders and vomits, so the unbeliever who acts faithlessly may perish. Therefore the prophet insults you and cries out: “Hear the word of the Lord, you mocking men” (Isaiah 28:14).

Does anyone determine the outcome of cases in advance of knowing them, and measure out a limit to furious conflicts in such a way that a swift decision, by showing itself older than the inquiry, accuses the judge of partiality?

Now, though unworthy for a little while in speech, deeds, and years, I shall rebuke you with a pontifical voice. We do not wish our statutes to be weighed by you on a single scale. Canons have been issued concerning the character of accusers, and among us it is sacrilege to overstep the ancient decisions of the fathers. It is written in the [Note: [Col. 0189D] Council of Carthage] seventh canon, held in the secretariat of the restored basilica in the consulship of P. C. Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, at which Faustinus, bishop of Potentia in Picenum and legate of Pope Boniface, was also present. It alludes to canon 4 of the council.]

The authority of the apostolic See, through Faustinus the bishop, who had been sent by it and was present, approved the canon of the Council of Carthage [Col. 0189D]: “Accusers coming from the household of an enemy are not to be believed.” In such cases, a neighborhood inflamed by hatred kindles the flame of persecution with dry fuel and, through coordinated expense and machinery, secretly constructs the whole apparatus of deceit. What household could have vomited forth such men? Who could have known, from our collection of materials, unless they had been present? And from what source could they have learned the character of the attack except from the written accusation? In bringing forward a charge while pretending that they themselves had suffered persecution because of the charges, did they not thereby reveal their judgment?

After those statements concerning the accusers, you added:

“[Note: [Col. 0189D] Symmachus’s slaves; below: ‘I ask you, of what condition were these slaves whom you announced in written imperial petitions?’ Also, where he speaks of the Visitor: ‘There he ordered the pope, after being greeted by him, to address him personally, so that he might hand over the slaves to his fellow bishop, not to be subjected to any torture, but to be preserved for the deliberation of the synodal examination.’ For the adversaries had obtained this from Theoderic: that they should be produced and, contrary to what laws and canons forbid, ordered to be interrogated against their master. Therefore they also asked the synod in a written petition that they be handed over.] Why were persons ordered to be produced, persons whom the imperial authority had repeatedly demanded? This belongs to the frustration of the genius of the man who now sits in the apostolic See as though in a kind of fortress.”

Wisdom truly says to you: “A man who is weak and of brief life will not attain understanding; let him labor to know what is acceptable before the Lord” (Wisdom 9:5).

And Proverbs again says: “He hates himself who neglects learning, for death confronts the uneducated” (Proverbs 15:32 and 10:21).

[Note: [Col. 0190D] “He hates himself who neglects learning.” In our Vulgate this is written at Proverbs 15:32: “He who rejects discipline despises his own soul.” Among the Septuagint interpreters it reads: Ὃς ἀπωθεῖται παιδείαν, μισεῖ ἑαυτόν. “He who rejects discipline hates himself.” This is without doubt Ennodius’s first clause. The second appears to have been taken from chapter 10:21, where the Greek reads, Οἱ δὲ ἄφρονες ἐν παιδείᾳ τελευτῶσι, while we read: “But the unlearned die in poverty of heart.”]

Why do you fabricate ignorance descended from viperous knowledge? Why do you employ, with astonishing brigandage, the deceptions of robbery while displaying simplicity on your faces? It has truly been said of you: “He who speaks falsehood speaks from his own” (John 8:44).

You removed from the eyes of our priest, by crafty forethought, that appearance of joy which proceeds from the judgment of courts, so that, though equipped with such defenses against your battle lines and bearing throughout the world the weapons of innocence as testimony, you might drive him from the very sanctuaries of judgment. You took care that the innocent man should neither live without opposition nor, when struck down, have the consolation of an incorruptible examination by judges.

You both granted and begrudged him the examination you had proposed: by one and the same path, he was both forbidden and compelled to face the uncertainties of legal debate; he was summoned to the case by a singular route only to be barred from it, lest he either obtain manifest salvation without being attacked or seize it after being acquitted.

In the days of my youth, I remember reading something said about a certain man: “You order exile upon an exile, but do not grant it.” [Note: [Col. 0190D] Concerning a certain saying.] This is Jason. These are Medea’s words to Jason from Seneca’s *Medea*.]

The prophet’s sentence attacks you: “These are the men who disturbed the earth and shook kingdoms” (Isaiah 14:16). And again: “Their branches shall be cut down with pruning hooks, and what is left shall be cut away” (Isaiah 18:5). And again: “When you do not expect it, your destruction will come, and your multitude will be crushed like a potter’s vessel” (Isaiah 30:14).

The prophet also thundered specifically concerning this case: “The Lord will incline his hand, and he who gives assistance to evil will fall, and he to whom assistance is given will fall; and all will be consumed together” (Isaiah 31:3).

Nevertheless, after the ancient refuges of examples, I return to the recent definitions of the canons. The Council of Carthage cries out elsewhere: “Whatever persons the public laws do not admit to accusation, we likewise remove their permission to attack another”; and: “No accusations are to be heard by ecclesiastical judges which are prohibited by the laws of the world.”

I ask you, men whose perfection has been polished to the fingernail: of what condition were these slaves whom you announced in written imperial petitions? If a servile chain still held them in another’s power, and no traces of their shameful bondage had been loosened into freedom, would the words of those men have carried any credibility even while you were debating the case?

But, I suppose, you will reply that the truth which their voluntarily uttered voice could not possess was extracted from its hiding places by a religious torturer through various torments—so that, while their bodies were released by punishments, the soul, which knew what had happened, would not conceal it.

But I ask you first to turn your faces toward the public laws and then toward the judges. They could speak in their own defense as follows:

“We, whom service to God made freeborn after the rejection of these things; we who either disdain or ridicule the insults of insolent little slaves; we to whom the Apostle wrote concerning servants, ‘Remember that your Master and theirs is in heaven’ (Ephesians 6:9)—are we to be recalled to these evils of the world? Are we to do what we insist it is profane for another to do? What would defile the sight through the ministry of a command and the hand of another—shall it be carried out at our command?”

Do not preserve this attitude toward all the Churches in the manner and nature of ravenous wolves. For after a bloody examination had perhaps stained us according to your desires, it would not achieve in these matters the result toward which you are striving.

But when the prophet says to you, “Let us put a circle in your nostrils and a bridle in your lips, and let us lead you back by the way you came” (Isaiah 37:29; 4 Kings 19:28), you are attacked by the same prophet, who says: “They shall be as though they were not, and the men who oppose you shall perish” (Isaiah 41:11).

You have also introduced this new invention against us: that our Lord and Redeemer himself submitted to the judgments of slaves, and that the maker of heaven voluntarily subjected himself to some small portion of earth, when he testifies and says: “You inhabitant of Jerusalem and man of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard” (Isaiah 5:3). You say that blessed Peter also, and the apostle Paul, did not shrink from this; and you drag your own elegance into the law through a chain of preceding examples, as though in this matter an argument remained for you with one who resisted, and as though what you bring forward were extracted by the strong fingers of your eloquence.

You also say that the wonderful prophet Samuel, in the serenity of his conscience, appealed to the testimony of the people. What did Samuel say? That God knew he had never taken anyone’s property, driven away anyone’s flock, opposed gifts, or—something beyond ordinary human conduct—avoided gifts that came voluntarily. He was taking care, of course, lest he suffer damage to his reputation through prejudicial suspicions.

Finally, under divine testimony, he revealed his innocence, lest he undergo human examination. Our Redeemer, when he desires judgment to take place between himself and his vineyard, is rather calling for it while he observes your wickedness in the present case.

Saint Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, while being attacked by the envy of your associates, recognized that he was being granted an exercise in insults, not a cause for fear. He truly joined to the price of the crown what he submitted from his dignity; and, before the heavenly sentence of acquittal, the good assessor of innocence fulfilled the role of the accused.

Thus the soldiers of Christ, by their own sweat, produce for themselves an increase of honors, while they chastise the heights granted to them through still greater humility. They purchase heaps of praise from the very source at which they moderate the summits they have obtained by sublime restraint.

Although the place of blessed Athanasius appears to show him unequal to the Roman bishop, as far as we can know, they are nevertheless compared by what they did in their cases.

[Note: [Col. 0191D] He was present before the judges.] At the synod convened against him at Tyre. Although, because of the open violence and conspiracy of his adversaries, he hesitated for some time about whether he should come when summoned, as Sozomen writes in Book II, chapter 24, he nevertheless afterward set out, relying on his innocence and not wishing to appear to evade judgment.]

Athanasius was present before the judges; Symmachus, as even you say, summoned them. The former did not flee the examination brought against him, as a servant of God; the latter placed the hope of his triumph in the collection of those who were to examine him.

But why should we linger longer over these comparisons? This man wished for judgments, loved them, drew them toward himself, and entered into them. And, in what might stir faithful hearts with the pricks of righteous grief, he even granted authority against himself to the venerable synod.

[Note: [Col. 0191D] “Authority to the council.”] When Symmachus entered the synod that had assembled at the Basilica of Julius on his account, the synod itself said of him: “He professed that he would submit the authority of correcting the order, as ecclesiastical statutes required, in the presence of all the bishops who had gathered there.” [Col. 0192D]

Who, upon seeing the confidence of this appeal, would not know that he had come to his fellow bishops supported by the testimony of purity? He shrank from what it was less permissible for them to enforce, judging that what an incompetent censor had established ought rather to be shaken by every possible means.

Why did you attack the man with your doglike loquacity? Why do you injure one who does not deserve it? His desire is what you suppose to be your terror. But the venom of the new serpent hisses in you more cunningly than it did in the adversaries of Athanasius.

They did not know what you understand perfectly well: how a triumph could be taken away from the person attacked. They feared that the one who had been summoned might appear, lest he fail to come when he ought to be heard. You, unable to endure the delay that the examinations required, drove Pope Symmachus back with weapons when he was going to the second meeting of the synod, which had been forced to assemble in the Basilica of Sessorianus.

[Note: [Col. 0192D] “You drove him back with weapons as he came.”] When Symmachus was going there, as the acts of the synod relate, he was attacked by the rushing crowds of his rivals and treated so violently that, after the priests who were with him had been beaten, he was scarcely brought back safely by Count Aligernus to the enclosure of blessed Peter, from which he had departed.]

You drove him back with weapons as he came, and exchanged the weariness of a sentence being prepared against you for the assumption of avenging arms. O recollection of evils, which both gives voice and destroys it: while it forces those whom it has driven to cry out, the very gravity of their deed confounds their words.

[Col. 0193A] Who could endure you chattering with an even temper? So, according to your assertion, we do not love the advantages of novelty, while we render obedience to the settled determinations of our elders? Here you hoist all the sails of your ingenuity; here the breath that your backward-bent neck had stored in its breast has belched forth from its retreat.

“For,” they say, “the fasts of Moses and the miracles of Elisha, which he performed when he raised the dead, are condemned by you if you pursue only things that are old.”

What reason can a competent investigator find here? Even if a pale seeker after gold should appear, he could not discover the movement of the hidden veins in your minds, nor could a miner of speech admit light into unfamiliar caverns.

Therefore, do we reject ancient miracles because we do not assent to youthful excesses? If, remembering the Gospel, we subordinate the servant to the Lord and the disciple to the teacher (Matthew 10:24; Luke 6:40; John 13:16 and 15:20), do we neglect whatever might have been useful? There are other things, most wicked of men, which we apply to recent use without injury to antiquity.

Next you disclosed a new charge, one which our investigation had passed over:

“Why did the pope, without the precedent of an established example, summon a synod to investigate the accusations brought against him?”

After this you accuse us of falsehood because we say that what is written in the aforementioned case was requested from the prince.

“Grant, Lord, that we may pass through the winding turns of this labyrinth without error; direct the path which the pliant serpent fashions beside the structure of its own body or mind, so that we may truly say: ‘The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our helper’” (Psalm 45:8).

And with Solomon let us rejoice, who says: “A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but all assistance belongs to the Lord” (Proverbs 21:31).

It is indeed beside the point to answer absurd propositions, since the prophet says: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly” (Proverbs 26:4). But if some contempt should pass unnoticed, I fear that my silence might be regarded as strength because I had not touched upon it.

It is better for us to incur, with blessed Paul, the causes of insult and to testify in a full voice: “I have become a fool; you compelled me” (2 Corinthians 12:11).

Was there, then, no precedent whatever for the pope to summon a council of priests, when the calling together of a synod lay within his discretion? Or were the crimes committed by you, in such great numbers, too insignificant to be condemned?

[Note: [Col. 0193D] “Are these not the direct words of the canons?”] The passage is cited under Symmachus’s name, not Ennodius’s, by Gratian, *Decretum* VIII, question 6. Since Ennodius’s pamphlet was inserted into the Symmachian synods, as noted shortly above, with an equal claim to authority, the statements contained in it began to be regarded as Symmachus’s own decrees or judgments. Those canons struck the schismatics, who, under the pretext of the charges by which they attacked Symmachus, had separated from him before the time of judgment, much less before the time of sentence.]

Are these not the direct words of the canons? [Note: [Col. 0193D] *Distinction* 8, question 4.]

“Any cleric who withdraws from his bishop before the time of sentence on the basis of doubtful suspicion leaves manifest censure standing against himself.”

For this task, an army devoted to God ought to have come forward, so that an army of physicians might assist the wounds of the lost and shattered flock. For whenever the violence of disease advances swiftly toward the hidden places of the soul, salutary counsel cannot bring the hands needed to meet it except through the counsel of many.

Our petition also demanded this from the king: that, once the prejudices against the clerics had been cut away, the supreme authority should judge through human speech concerning the merits of the pope’s accusers.

Let us nevertheless, if it pleases you, reread the clever arguments of your didactic pamphlets.

[Note: [Col. 0193D] “Didactic pamphlets.”] Ironically. For διδασκαλικοὶ λόγοι (*didaskalikoi logoi*) means “didactic arguments,” carefully composed and suitable for teaching. Hence Aristotle joins the expressions together: τὸ ἀκριβέστερον καὶ διδασκαλικώτερον, “the more exact and more suitable for teaching.” [Col. 0194D]

We also have before our eyes the enactments of the fathers, by which the cesspool of your excesses may be weighed. Ecclesiastical law requires that a pontiff accused by others not be abandoned before the charges have been established in the light of day.

But you, who, as I suppose, remember divine law, who despise minor errors and rejoice in the nobility of sin, accused him with additions to his offenses, lest any guilt arising from your abandonment of the priest should fall back upon you.

Your predecessor brought you to this condition, so that, after the pontiff had been deserted and attacked, and without the force of any sentence, you believed that the censure of almost all Italy’s bishops should be rejected. As someone said of your company: “He did not entrust a hurried soul to one death.”

Can an unteachable mind, already enriched by the success of crimes, be halted from a detestable purpose, like a spent beast? That one made you rich in evils whose abundance of pride cast down angelic wealth (Isaiah 14:12), and whose treasure begrudged the divine wealth of harming, in which he overflows.

But mindful of my promise, let us touch upon everything we recall as inserted into their work.

“Pope Symmachus is attacked in the most brilliant style: why, anticipating the assembly, did he enter the examination with gatherings of the people, and afterward, although he had been summoned four times, despise the judgments?” [Note: [Col. 0194D] “Although he had been summoned four times.”] Symmachus entered the synod at the first meeting, held in the Basilica of Julius. He was likewise proceeding to the second, at the Sessorian Basilica, when his adversaries ambushed him on the road and nearly overwhelmed him after beating his companions; both events have already been mentioned above. After that slaughter, when asked whether he wished to go out again to the synodal judgment, he denied that he could lawfully be compelled.]

So far has your affection for truth departed from you that, wrapped in clouds of lies, you think the testimony of the city can be obscured, and you believe that words painted with the fine brush of deceit possess more force than the truth retained by Rome.

Did he, then, either approach the examination unbidden or flee when expected? Did that multitude of a people devoted to God come together not from zeal for the faith, but rather from expectation than from fury?

Does anyone running to inflict violence bring tears as companions and, while seeking to inspire fear, display the face of one who is afraid? That multitude, joined to the priest’s duties, brought us lamentations, not weapons; it came not threatening with missiles but pitiable in its tears. It burdened your intention in only one respect: by displaying, through rivers flowing from abundant eyes, how deeply the condition of the man under attack ought to be mourned because of your harshness; and, through the affliction of its own reverent and sober examination, it commended him whom it could not commend by voice.

But this matter makes clear what fury kindles bile in you. For the man over whom the world weeps came to the judgments almost acquitted; and, while you gather in speech an envy foreign to the facts against the aforesaid man, our long-proud neck briefly submits itself to reverence.

You call it a sacred assembly when you wish to maintain that Symmachus was our destroyer; and with cruel piety you think that our honor is increased because he perished while seated in the citadel of the Churches.

We have not merely failed to feel these things; we feel the opposite. Turn the poisons of your protection elsewhere. He has no defender’s testimony who offers the service of his mouth to one who resists. He loses the grace of the benefit he thinks he has rendered who gives something to an unwilling recipient, for there is no gift except what one wishes to receive.

[Col. 0195B] No lengthy admonition is now needed for men already ruined. We owe hatred to a work whose authors have nothing left that can be condemned.

“You assert that crowds of women came with the aforesaid man to the courts in urban finery; and by that subtlety the sex is revealed which ought to have shown greater affection toward the bishop.”

Most profane of men, I retain the written word: “It is one thing to speak ill, another to accuse.” [Note: [Col. 0195D] “It is one thing to speak ill, another to accuse.” These are Cicero’s words in the speech *For Marcus Caelius*, where he refutes the accusations made against Caelius’s chastity without proof. Ennodius most appropriately applies them to a similar situation, to blunt the unspoken insult of the schismatics, who seized upon the crowd of women accompanying Symmachus in the performance of their duty.] The prophet also says: “You rejected the word; you trusted in slander and tumult, and you are in it. Therefore this iniquity shall be for you like a breach” (Isaiah 30:12).

For the Lord speaks on our behalf: “Those who judge you, I will judge” (Isaiah 49:25). And again he says to his servants: “Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies” (Isaiah 51:7).

And again he cries out to you: “Come here, you offspring of the adulterer and the fornicator: over whom did you make sport? Against whom did you open your mouth wide and thrust out your tongue? Are you not wicked children, a lying offspring?” (Isaiah 57:3).

When you have joined these things together, consider them while saying: “Without a trial, with his defenders abandoned, the pope departed: in the present matter you set before us examples from the forum and from the streets, of which you are hypocrites. It is written for us through the Apostle Paul (Gal. 1:14): ‘For those to whom the world has been crucified, what have they to do with the forum?’ But either you do not know these things or, what is worse, you knowingly despise them.”

[Note: [Col. 0195D] “I believe he requested something foreign and unreasonable.” Symmachus had asked two things of the synod, as is clear from the acts: first, that the visitor should withdraw, about which more will be said later; second, that everything he had lost through the representations of his enemies should be restored to him before the trial. Although this could seem neither improper nor unjust—for ecclesiastical laws require that the dispossessed be restored before all else—when the synod referred the matter to the king, the king decided that Symmachus should undergo trial before restoration. He did not refuse this, in keeping with his modesty.]

“I believe that the pope departed requesting something foreign and separated from reason.” Did he not hope for this, bound by pastoral care for the condition of the tottering Church, when both religious foresight and the order of the case demanded it? For what form of judgment had preceded, so that, when you had hostilely torn things apart and, through your own representations, had also removed the Church’s resources, he who had long been food for the hungry might seem to have been made a slave to famine? [Col. 0195D] While the distributor of provisions himself was in need of food, so that servitude might exist in domination and domination in servitude? [Col. 0196A] What character did the preceding age, brought forward into public memory, give to this matter? What result did he have to expect from a censure in which condemnation preceded the trial? There was no privilege from which one already stripped bare could be despoiled.

You thought that one resource remained for you in the sacred assembly: to join priests to yourselves as companions in defending the enormity of your crimes, so that an outrage might go unpunished through the pollution of many. A censor is never appointed at the appropriate time when he is summoned to a matter that is almost already decided; and even if the criminal deserves it, the accuser removes him, for he wants his own fury to have greater license than the judge.

For the prophet says, attacking you: “This is the portion of those who laid us waste, [Col. 0196B] and the lot of those who plundered us. Go, swift messengers, to the people torn apart and mangled, and to the terrifying nation” (Isa. 17:14; 18:2).

An angel was sent to you, namely through the priests, whose voice and merit receive gifts to be carried to Christ, and, when the Lord has been appeased, grant mortals the petitions they have obtained. Through them gifts of concord, which had been offered to you but rejected, were brought to you. They carried the rewards of love to those deserving punishment; while considering themselves, they showed regard in nothing for what you deserved.

“Who,” they say, “saw him engage in open combat, as they claim, with his accusers?” Most shameless of men, look at the one with whom you wish to contend, and, if any hope of salvation remains in you, consider the places, times, and persons of both parties. And if the wealth of your wickedly accumulated and still perverse heart has not yet subdued you, raise your eyes to God for a little while and, even briefly, disregard the commands of your sinister adviser.

You recognize that you are not protected by the commands of the supreme [Col. 0196D] King.

[Note: [Col. 0196D] “You are not protected by the commands of the King.” Although the schismatics produced many instructions and rescripts from Theoderic that seemed adverse to Symmachus—for example, concerning the visitor and what has just been recounted concerning the withheld restoration, as well as other matters of that kind—all these were nevertheless void and empty. Nor could they ever achieve by these protections what they were attempting, namely, Symmachus’s condemnation. For when the king finally left the matter wholly to the synod, it immediately acquitted him.]

You are not protected by the king’s commands in matters for which you rightly deserve punishment. For although the doctrines of the accused dictate the character of the reply, and a petition, when it precedes events, describes what is to follow, you have never received the reigning prince’s unqualified words in your circumstances; never have imperial letters taken the field for your desires through the snares of cunning. How often has an ineffectual bite, crying out through empty gaping, threatened harm? How often has whatever hope you held concerning the accused escaped you, leaving an empty image, seized by presumption, behind?

Thanks be to God, who implanted this foresight in the one to whom he entrusted the governance of human affairs. Certain hope of peace and perfect wisdom in the ruler are present. A ship whose master has been equipped with the gift of understanding for the management of the helm has a station everywhere and a harbor everywhere amid the waves. The security of the whole community is assured when the state is governed by one trained in noble arts. The heaven-sent providence of our emperor knows how to extend a protecting hand against famous minds skilled in deception.

There is no need for labor before him whom naked truth long ago chose as its defender. Let the impious cease trying, through invented tales, to make simplicity appear fraudulent before him. Whatever moves itself against justice is immediately restrained; nothing is safer with the aforesaid ruler than innocence. He uses a powerful embassy who brings matters consistent with equity to his notice. A charge that is usually serious when directed against princes is not read as such when it comes from the flatteries of the less trustworthy.

But these things are better told to God, from whom the plant of this fruit has sprung.

[Col. 0197A] The unfavorable condition of the work I have undertaken brings me back to you, although until now I wished to devote myself to better kinds of discourse, while imperious necessity demands a captive speech. For you said:

“How were you treating the cause or its character at the outset, when the synod did not yet possess firmness?”

[Note: [Col. 0197D] “When the synod did not yet possess firmness.” The bishops were still uncertain whether Symmachus had approved it. When he confirmed this in their presence, then, as the acts of the synod record, the cause of the sadness that had been troubling the priests’ minds because the council was not yet confirmed was removed. The bishops evidently understood that this council could not be valid without the pontiff’s assent. The schismatics nevertheless opposed this, but in vain.]

O filthy face of your statement, and countenance of your pamphlet, which ignorance alone has not stained. You report and question the subject matter of our treatise. We were, of course, uncertain for this reason: because, according to the way you speak, the synod did not possess firmness. The nature of the case was passing on to those who would hear it, and more still remained in the reverence due to the one who had been summoned than existed in the integrity of our own college.

“Then, as a torment in the questions, you repeat that the venerable bishops Laurence and Peter suspended themselves from communion with the pope, and you turn everything that the prudence of the assembled men provided into a crime against the accused.”

[Note: [Col. 0197D] “Laurence and Peter.” One was from Ravenna, the other from Milan; both were moderators and presidents of the synod. This is shown by the subscriptions of the synod itself and by the instruction of King Theoderic to the synod, which was addressed to Laurence, Marcellianus, Peter, and the remaining bishops. Marcellianus, however, did not attend the Palmary assembly. As for the fact that Laurence and Peter had deliberately refrained from Symmachus’s company before the judicial debate, so that they would not appear to create prejudice, the opponents interpreted this in another direction, as though they themselves had already discovered and established the crimes alleged against Symmachus.]

At any time, while sacred Masses were being celebrated by these men, did they cease mentioning his name? Did the bishops ever offer half-completed sacrifices for your desires, without Catholic ritual and canonical custom? Did it ever happen that, by your head’s account, an offense was committed before God through grace, and that an offering became the nurse of pardon and the mother of sin?

Those whom you mention were separated only in bodily assembly; nevertheless, they did not avoid the presence of their souls. If you think that those whom the clasp of religion, biting with a pious tooth, joins together were separated from mutual fellowship, your passion has carried you far from a Catholic judgment about guilt. The dwelling of the heavenly command either unites or separates us. It makes no difference what distances divide us, if we remain in one chamber of the dwelling above.

From this we truly infer that you are slaves of the belly and the body; and by the baseness of your judgment you reveal that you are slaves of earthly things. For it is written: “The natural man does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit” (1 Cor. 2:14).

After this, with your ranks turned to flight, you added in the manner of a delirious speech:

“Then, because councils of priests, decreed by ecclesiastical laws every few years throughout the provinces, do not have the pope’s presence, have they lost their validity?”

Read, most insane men, whether anything was ever established in them without the sanction of the apostolic summit, and whether, in the case of anything arising for consultation concerning more important matters, it was not reserved to the judgment of the aforesaid see. For the Council of Sardica says this [Col. 0198D]: “If any bishop has been deposed by a provincial judgment, let him appeal again, if he wishes, to the Roman pope; and he himself, if it seems good, may reopen the proceedings in aid of the condemned.”

Behold, it is clear what you prepared as a snare—unless perhaps we are bound there by the tightest knots, and the roads of reopening are not open to us, while a path previously passable is blocked by the fresh growth of thickets.

“For you hold us back with these thorny thickets of speech while we walk on level ground, when you say that the prince was offended because we wished at the outset to withdraw the visitor assigned to Bishop Peter of Altinum, contrary to ecclesiastical rules.”

[Note: [Col. 0198D] “The assigned visitor.” Peter, bishop of Altinum, had been appointed visitor by King Theoderic at the demand of the Roman schismatics, contrary to right and custom. For this reason Symmachus requested that he be removed, as stated above. The acts of the synod say: “Hoping that the visitor, who had been requested by the clerical party or by certain laymen against religion, against the statutes of the ancients, and against the rules of our predecessors, would, through the appointment of the bishops, withdraw at the very outset, as a holy purpose required.” Ennodius not only defends Symmachus’s desire as entirely just, but also tries to excuse Theoderic’s action, as though he had wished the visitor’s presence to benefit Symmachus himself.]

“—and that nothing more should be permitted to this man’s vices, lest the weeds grow hard, lest a profane harvest, before maturity, should lie uncut beneath the sickle of discipline, and lest it should be thought permissible to do what the judges did not forbid.”

Thus it is plainly evident that you are supported by no authority of precedent beyond the excellence of the most devout king, to which you vainly desire to join your guilt. It remains for me to teach him also, in these excesses, what happened for the good of all and was not held against him: for he wished his directive to be not an opportunity for litigation or fuel for quarrels, but a cause of concord. He foresaw, of course, that unless the protection of his simple commands enclosed the matter, your poisons would quickly creep in as food for dissension. For it is written: “The simple man believes every word” (Prov. 14:15).

For this reason he fixed the limit of his command so that no violation could transgress it. He ordered the aforesaid man, once he had been brought immediately to Rome, to meet him at the basilica of blessed Peter, making the king’s command conform to the priest’s wish. For who would not think that the pontiff would voluntarily comply in a matter which the prince did not believe was permissible to him, even if he forbade it?

There he ordered the pope, after being greeted by him, to address him in his own voice, so that he might hand over his fellow bishop’s slaves, not to be subjected to any torture.

[Note: [Col. 0199D] “Not to be subjected to any torture.” Thus they could not harm Symmachus, even if they testified against him. Theoderic knew, as he says shortly afterward, that a servile assertion could not be approved in an impartial inquiry. In this way he also removes, in this respect, the odium attached to the royal command.]

They were, in fact, to be preserved for the discussion of the synodal examination. O purity of the command, which, while holding a torch before the present age, drives antiquity into shadow; which, with the unforeseen brilliance of novelty, snatches light away from former times! Who has enriched the reputation of the lord of these actions with such fabricated praises, when the truth of his deeds leaves him poor?

I do not detract from your writers, through whose service it has happened that the deeds of our ancestors, adorned, have been handed down to us. But I shall not be silent about God’s benefits, because our prince surpasses the embellishments of speeches by his deeds. The venerable examiner of causes looked upon glory exposed to the tongues of men, so that, while a skillful effect was supplied for your petition, he nevertheless guarded ecclesiastical law in everything.

What hearts, however much sharper than others, are sufficient for this judgment? At one time, in one written command, without injury to equity, your wishes are fulfilled, and the same document is directed both to the service of religion and to your joy. For the inquiry of a good prince foresaw that a servile assertion could not be approved by an impartial examination. In the selection of the venerable judges, he himself rejected the accusers from the proceedings; he himself restored the accused to hope.

Let us nevertheless see whether these things were actually done. You were enemies of God, and even enemies of your earthly lord, while with equal recklessness you despised Christ and the king, and one set of crimes led you to both insults.

The bishop who had been appointed was snatched from the boundary of the command he was to fulfill by the coils of your mouths and made an instrument of confusion, although he had come to serve peace. Without seeing the thresholds of the blessed Apostle, he was summoned, now forgetful of himself, for the use of your fury; and what draws the devout from every quarter of the world was passed by, though it lay nearby.

A structure of lesser rank was not permitted to approach the foundation of the churches; separated from the root, it then lost the hope of good fruits.

[Note: [Col. 0199D] “Perhaps you will say.” This distinguished passage is directed against those who today make no distinction concerning sacred places, either for forming vows and prayers or for obtaining heavenly benefits.]

Perhaps you will say that the genius of the Apostle is diminished if it is thought that a citizen of heaven can be confined to earthly places. Yet although blessing is granted everywhere to those who ask, and the faith and devotion of the suppliant require the martyr’s presence, it cannot be denied that more is attributed to the birthplace of devotion, and that places from which one passes to the heights obtain greater affection.

[Col. 0199D] What faith has already been given to this claim by the multitude of healings? We make use of witnesses already healed after the devil’s siege. Although these things are celebrated throughout the world through our Redeemer, that monument has nevertheless acquired no small renown through the crowds who visit it, because through the one who changed a human being into an angel the nature of the earth could be illuminated.

You begrudged this grace to your visitor, thinking that he would cease to be a follower of your errors if he touched the inner sanctuary of the revered Passion. Behold, you have no support in royal authority; behold, after the heavenly upheaval, the censure of both justice and the prince whom you had caused to be despised strikes you.

Let us see whether any defense remains for your regular argument.

“Visitors,” they say, “he himself also gave to other bishops, and it is just that he should be bound by the law of his own action.”

I do not attack you here under this heading of falsehood; I do not charge words that have long clung to lies. Yet I say that the bearer of a legal definition is not enclosed within its limits unless he wishes it; and unless the summit of princely rank restrains it, what he has granted is called a right in vain.

It is the law of character and mind that chastises a living man without a written law. He who does not owe discipline to necessity properly devotes himself to moral conduct.

[Note: [Col. 0200D] “The cases of other men.” Here too there is a distinguished passage concerning the primacy of the supreme pontiff and the prerogative of the apostolic see.]

Perhaps God wished to settle the cases of other men through men; but he reserved this bishop to the judgment of his own master, without question. He wished the successors of the blessed Apostle Peter to owe their innocence to heaven alone and to present an inviolate conscience to the scrutiny of the most exact examiner.

Do not think that those souls whom God reserved above all others for his own examination have no fear of inquisitors. The accused has no support before him from the brilliance of his defense when he uses as witness of his deeds the very one who is their judge.

You might say that the condition of all souls will be the same in that judgment. I shall reply with one saying: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18); and, “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (ibid., 19).

[Col. 0200C] And again, through the voice of the holy pontiffs, the dignity of his see was made venerable throughout the whole world: everything belonging to the faithful is everywhere subjected to him, and he is designated as the head of the entire body. Concerning it, I think it was said through the prophet: “If this is humbled, to whose help will you flee, and where will you leave your glory?” (Isa. 10:3).

What if, although I have unclean lips and have not been washed by any of the burning coal’s water, as was granted to Isaiah, I were permitted to summon the Apostle Peter himself to defend the privileges of his possession, and he were to speak in a human voice what he now does through prayers? If you heard him, he would say this:

“Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood? Know that the Lord has made his holy one wondrous” (Ps. 4:3).

[Col. 0200D] Why do you wish to overthrow foundations established by Christ’s hands? Why do you batter with a ram the hoary guardian spirit of the possession of him who grows young through sins, and, by dividing the ecclesiastical flock, subject me anew to sufferings after the flesh?

It is an unheard-of kind of sacrilege that you disguise with the honor of a falsely professed religion. He dishonors the reverence due to a venerable name who claims to be its helper in matters that he boasts have been committed against God. It is an insult to pretend to be present as a lofty supporter, in the words of the Apostle: “Who are you to judge another’s servant?” (Rom. 14:4).

Why do you mock unlearned ears and make the appearance of vengeance seem heavier than the guilt? If you owe hatred to excesses, cleanse yourselves. Why do you condemn crimes more freely than you avoid them? He is his own assailant who presses adulteries through the duties of fornication and, through the violation of souls, accuses the flesh.

Surely you retain the written words: “All who fornicate away from you are accursed” (Ps. 72:27). The bond with his Lord’s radiant purity is therefore dissolved by the one who performs his duties toward the heavenly statutes with less than pure faith.

As I see it, the splendor of our possession has stirred your envy. You transfer this envy into a pretended indignation against its evil possessor while exhausting your resources. The fortress in which you were conspicuous, shaken by repeated blows, you proposed to bury—unless I resisted—and to display, through its ruin, how great was the structure established in heaven.

Do not await victory from your own disaster. Do not lose the triumph by overcoming, a triumph sought through my labors and my sweat. Whatever leads to the trophy, I have obtained; whatever would make you illustrious, I gathered into the see. This torch, which you think can be extinguished with viper’s venom, has granted you glory.

The one who rages in such a way against the shoots of his own grace that he cuts off the plants is kindling a fire for his own destruction. Anger more unrestrained than justice provokes its author more than others.

If the alleged excesses of Symmachus are what you say they are, I await them patiently. It is wicked not to love the patience of a judge toward one who is sinning. What else does he demand but vengeance who, while himself guilty, complains of delays in punishment against another?

This is the voice owed by me to those efforts, because I hold that God said that man is inclined toward wickedness and that all flesh is friendly to sins. I do not wish the possession to be brought low, and thus to confer distinction upon countless persons on account of one individual—lest, while a man is attacked, divine law be broken.

Believe me: if these things you mention are true, I take them into consideration, because I have examined what might have been the case even in those against whom nothing of the sort was said. He is mistaken who thinks that being deceived by God is near at hand: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay,” says the Lord (Deut. 32:35; Sir. 28:1; Rom. 12:19; Heb. 10:30).

You, rather, once my sons, whose spiritual birth filled my womb, return to the concord you have abjured. May Mother Church receive you into her loving embrace, as she has until now. Correction is never too late. She knows how to await those obtained through excessive labor; she does not know how to despise, as worthless, those purchased at great price.

There are many steps on the return to salvation; no one is excluded except the one who despairs. The fruit of pardon is close to the crown.

Do not help Pope Symmachus through your attacks. If he is guilty, believe me: when the agency of human opposition has ceased, divine judgment will immediately follow. Surely, on the scales of the most splendid examiner, punishment or reward is owed to the one mentioned above?

Do not seek from me syllogisms of speech or rhetorical figures. I still use the ancient net after the man, and I have not abandoned the cymbal mocked by the wise of this age. It sustains me across the straits of the world. The net that you see, proven in the capture of men, enriches me.

Return, then, because flight rescued you before you had become wild. Run to the fold, lest you expose yourselves to the ambushes of wolves; lest, by delay, you lose the grace of those who come voluntarily. For contempt of an invitation is followed by Gehenna.

I have fulfilled whatever sweetness I owed as a father, and whatever severity I owed as a teacher appointed by God. Take care lest, for too long, some corner of my cross be surrounded by a sparse company of Levites; lest a solitude lamentable even to strangers rule for a long time; lest the labor of my womb, instead of bearing fertility, prove to have produced a hostile household, and a numerous offspring display the barrenness of its parent through evil actions.

[Col. 0202A] What I have asserted is little, but judge how much depends upon it. “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. 33:12).

Look toward Rome, which the outpouring of Christ’s blood freed from the slavery of idols without the price of gold or silver, and to whose service he commanded even the death of me, his little servant, to be devoted. For many ages she displayed worship before famous shrines; for a long time she revered images of demons, which the hand of the teacher had implanted by exhausting expense as a terror; she looked up to the power of deities purchased for the price of metals; and a more practiced craftsman’s hand gave birth to loftier gods. The divinity that human beings conferred through manufacture had, among human beings, a form greater than God’s.

Behold, now, with Christ favorable, the images have returned to new furnaces. Behold, now your practice receives something from obsolete superstition in which it may rejoice, while new vessels are deservedly prepared from the ancient Thunderer.

Why do you strive to interrupt this peace? Why do you disturb happiness with empty efforts? This madness has no excuse, if you believe. It makes no difference by what roads one runs to the ruler of the world: whoever deserts holy unity sacrifices fat victims to the devil and saddens the Church.

Reject, then, your empty snares. The affection of peace has a simple defense. He is sufficiently armed who disregards the weapons that the adversary supplies to concord. Naked opposition in faith is enough against every missile of quarrels.

[Note: [Col. 0201D] “The times of Eulalius and Boniface.” A schism arose after the death of Pope Zosimus, when the clergy was divided between these two men. Because factional zeal made it difficult to determine whose election was legitimate, and the dispute was prolonged, Honorius ordered both men to withdraw from the city in the meantime. Thus Boniface withdrew to the basilica of Saint Agnes, while Eulalius went to Antium. The opponents wished this example to be renewed in the case of Symmachus, so that he might be expelled together with Laurence. But the circumstances were different.]

Why do you bring forward the times of Eulalius and Boniface while seeking consolation for your evils? Why do you present ancient contagions as additions to present excesses, and, through an unjust intention, make old age powerless to cover offenses?

The cause of the disagreement was different then. And unless I were compelled, by telling the story, to endure matters already past, I would show you that no consolation arises from comparing deeds. For those whom fervent zeal, obedient to ambition, had raised to the pontifical height, I rejected both; I chose this man, because, as the outcome testified, neither of them pleased me. Of these men, I made one, striving against the rules, a fugitive; the other, legitimately promoted though opposed by the world, I preserved.

You know these things; they are not new. While one was thrust aside, the other was confirmed; your approval served me.

Then why do you injure the priestly council to your own destruction? Why do you tear apart the judgment in which, with Christ inspiring it, heavenly oracles were revealed, and the tongue of the pontiffs stood as interpreter between God and human beings?

Why do you inflict pain upon the universal Church, although the deed was committed in one person, even if in a principal one? For that court of heaven, enriched by the various gifts of its magistrates and adorned with much gold and purple belonging to our Redeemer, did not put itself forward as the author of anything in that discussion; rather, through the ministry of human speech, it served the divine command.

It understood that whatever it decided under compulsion was not its own. It has nothing in that judgment except cause to rejoice over its devotion alone. The style recognized a foreign voice, deriving its only glory from the fact that it preserved and cultivated what had been poured into it.

What calumny have you prepared against these Gospel examples? As it is written of you: “They have gone astray through drunkenness; they do not know the seer; they do not understand judgment” (Isa. 28:7). For while you strike at the men mentioned with profane words, you reveal both ignorance and envy.

Did these men, then, not believe the resurrection of the body that they preached, and so mingle themselves with heretical contagions? Did they pursue in their hearts what they renounced with their tongues?

[Note: [Col. 0203D] “Therefore, because they said this.” Words of the synod: “We admonish and instruct the most illustrious senate that the matters of God must be committed to God’s own judgment, for he is able to kill the body and cast the soul into Gehenna.” Those who were constructing heresy in these words were not insulting blessed Luke, but were impious toward Christ himself, who speaks through Luke.]

Therefore, because they said that the one who can kill the body and cast the soul into Gehenna must be feared, did they for that reason weave a doctrine alien to the faith? Behold your profound ignorance. Here is blessed Luke, by whose testimony you can be convicted, crying out: “Fear him who, after he has killed the body, has power to cast the soul into Gehenna” (Luke 12:5).

Where is the opportunity for error here, when the words of example and history converge in harmony along the same path, and what is put forward does not differ from Catholic understanding or from the readings? One should never seek a knot in a rush. The authors of the proclaimed light do not wrap it in a cloud.

Do they therefore not believe in the resurrection of the flesh because they confess that the body can be killed? Because they say that a sinful soul can be handed over to Gehenna? Your heart is choked by dense thickets, and it strives to attribute its inner vices to others.

[Note: [Col. 0204D] “The writings of the Apostle John are violated.” The synod did not quote John’s exact words so much as its judgment from those words. It says: “Although no one is without sin, as the Apostle John testifies: ‘If I say that I have no sin, I am a liar.’”]

You also claim that the writings of the Apostle John are violated because it was said from his words: “If we say that we have no sin, we are liars, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). I make no complaint about the diversity of manuscripts. Are the Apostle’s exhortations therefore corrupted because they did not join the words? Do we deceive ourselves, and are we liars because they did join them?

He is rightly judged a liar who lacks truth, ignorant not only of divine but also of human reason. Nor is he filled with anything other than falsehood who is known to be empty of integrity.

But these things are not to be addressed to you in the language of speech, but in sighs; nor should words be offered to you so much as tears, because plainly the guilty person is the one who opposes either guilt or accusation to the innocent.

I shall not go back over the remaining heads of your objections; it is better that they be buried in silence, condemned. He gives nobility to crimes who transmits their report to future ears through repeated narration.

The judgment of blessed Paul must be followed; through his disciple he admonishes everyone and cries out: “Avoid empty questions” (2 Tim. 2:23). For there are many things in your propositions that the love of sin embraces with such filthy arms that they are unworthy of mention. Levity dishonors still more, while your words are disemboweled after their weights have been removed, and windy speech is composed about matters of religion, having acquired a seriousness suitable to the ear.

This speech, amid an abundance of chaff, will bring nothing of wheat into the granaries. It gives birth to an abundance of stalks barren of grain and falsely promises farmers hope through the luxuriance of grass. From these things the winnowing fans find no profit; they are owed to the fire and destined to perish in the flames. Concerning them it is written: “The men slept their sleep, and found nothing” (Ps. 75:6).

Nothing, dear ones, is sweeter than peace, provided a heart filled with bitterness does not reject its full flavor. I ought indeed to have given a shorter admonition; but the considerable thought I have given you, and the brow long exercised in your quarrels, produced one that was not brief.

It is common for those who sin greatly not to be corrected by a strict address. Many demand in the words of an admonisher the same outpouring that they displayed in their offenses. It is enough for me that I have complied both with your persistence and with the heavenly commands.

In what follows, I shall leave no place for speeches, because I report this: through your designs Rome, the head of the world, has been overthrown, and the motherly chair of the pontificate has been treated with contempt, as though it were the last seat to be seen.

[Col. 0204C] Blessed Paul heard its voice and thundered with the freedom of speech he always used. He attacked the prince of the apostles for preserving, in minds weakened and ruined, the affection of a parent, and for not coming to the aid of deep-drawn ulcers with the surgeon’s knife, teaching that diseased parts must be cut away and that a healing wound must be applied to manifest desperation.

For while the physician’s hand, out of pity, is held back from cutting corrupt flesh, abstention from the instrument invites death. When the right hand spares the sick, it kills those who ought to be cured. Nor is there a great difference between inflicting death and allowing it: whoever does not prevent death in the ailing, when he can, has inflicted it.

With such words, therefore, he opened the door of his mouth to address them.

[Col. 0204D] “Whoever you are that judge, in judging another you condemn yourself, for you do the same things that you judge. We know that God’s judgment is according to truth against those who do such things” (Rom. 2:1–2). And again: “Blessed is the one who does not judge himself in what he approves” (Rom. 14:22).

What kind of evil reasoning is it for one who steals to preach that no one should steal, and for a prodigal brow to cover itself with the cloud of an attack against another’s shame? No one rightly assumes the role of admonisher except one who condemns errors through his own actions and demonstrates his love of innocence through his conduct.

It is also characteristic of tax collectors to condemn vices in speech, friendly to their own habits, and to punish through the services of their tongue what they love. Is it not a kind of greater excess to give the lips affection for a thing whose contempt you profess in your mind, and to clothe the poison of your character in the honey of conversation?

I act as though, if you possessed modesty, chastity, and beauty of character, it would be permissible for you to accuse your teacher and direct the bite of a jealous mouth against the chosen one. Yet before these things occurred, knowing what was to come, I had warned you in a letter with a full voice: “Who will bring an accusation against God’s chosen? God, who justifies. Who is the one who condemns?” (Rom. 8:33). And again: “O man, who judges those who do such things and does them yourself, do you think that you will escape God’s judgment? Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and forbearance?” (Rom. 2:3–4).

You accuse malice, although filled with iniquity, fornication, greed, wickedness, envy, murder, condemnation, deceit, malignity; proud and arrogant, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, foolish, disorderly, without mercy (Rom. 1:29–31).

You teach that no one should associate with fornicators: either the adulterer Laurence’s followers or his predecessors—those through whom he either brought forth the poisons he possessed or received what he displayed while pouring them out. After that stain of seductive communion and that pestilence execrable throughout the world, you blame the priests of God as though they had been purchased by a worn-out communion. You think those guilty who entered into fellowship without being convicted by any witness, and you follow a man pierced throughout the whole ecclesiastical inscription—not merely by a stylus, but by a sword.

“What is permitted is not permitted, and what is not permitted is permitted.” As Jannes and Jambres resisted the truth, so you also, corrupt in mind, traitors regarding the faith, insolent, inflated, lovers of pleasure rather than of God, having the appearance indeed of piety but denying its power (2 Tim. 3:8; 4).

O force of inward grief, which cannot easily express what it has conceived, but breaks forth with the passion of speech that it has commanded, poured into the depths of its entrails! I shall say nothing more to you. What remains of speech will be supplied by lamentation.

After this, if you grow weaker in the hands of physicians through the treatment, and no consideration of salvation begun brings you back, at least look toward your city, the mother of the world. She herself, mourning after her apostolic defenders, approaches you and addresses you; and if any piety remains, she begins a speech by which she may obtain her request.

Me, whom the temples of the highest God have made conspicuous, after the worship of fanes was rejected and as I rejoice in the brightness of a new light; me, whom, after filthy chapels polluted with much gore of beasts, the outpouring of the Lord’s and the apostles’ blood cleansed from the blood of sacrifices; me, whom restored health after a long illness of fevers caused to despise the sanctuaries; me, whom an offering freed from victims; me, who acquired the peace of Christ through the hostility of idols; me, for whom there were scarcely fewer gifts than gods; me, whom the devout man rendered needy by varied devotion, while want oppressed me as I repeatedly sought benefits from my own gods; me, who sent the Curii, Torquati, Camilli—whom the Church did not regenerate—and the rest of that numerous offspring to Tartarus, while I withered, my womb exhausted and barren of its ill-fated fruit; because the Fabii, though they had preserved their country, did not redeem it, and the glory won by the Decii through great toil profited nothing; the innocence of works without faith was overthrown; Scipio, most observant of justice, was joined to criminals because he did not know Christ.

I would like to carry my pen through the whole matter, if the breast of the bereaved could endure the account of its infancy. But whoever rereads the history of that lamentation seems to desire a season of tears. No one is believed not to hate those whose story does not wound him; whoever, recounting the funerals of his children, preserves a dry face is clearly convicted of cruelty by that sure testimony. That posterity brought more grief when it was lost than joy when it was acquired.

Let us nevertheless recall by what successes these things have been changed. Behold, now in that sanctuary of liberty nothing servile from the worship of idols is found. Behold the crown of honors, the genius of the world, the flower of Rome, now tramples the altars once long venerated in complete holiness. Behold, now my senate is summoned to heaven, praised, and welcomed. Nor can I say that I have lost my offspring after the grace of baptism, when sudden death has taken them away. The supreme King embraces many possessors of the purple or the curule chair without loss to religious worship or dignity. Almost now the munificence of the earthly realm purchases divine favor; and this advances the grace of Christ, that you strive to be honored by the world.

[Col. 0206C] I am lying unless the needy ranks of your consulship await its arrival as aid in their miseries. For your purple, by the generosity of clothing, drives away the cold that steals upon the wretched, while the name of the year makes it a mark of nobility.

[Note: [Col. 0205D] “Almost now again.” The custom of consuls in former times had been to scatter money among the people when they proceeded in public; Marcian had abolished that custom by Book 2 of the Code, *De consulibus*. Therefore, in Ennodius’ time, money was not scattered. But because the consuls of his age commonly distributed much among the poor at the beginning of their term of office, they seemed in a certain way to renew the ancient custom, though with a more fortunate generosity.]

[Col. 0206D] Almost now again the dignity of the official registers has become an aid to the necessities of the poor; and once the old infidelity has been laid aside, in such preparation the expenses of wealth are turned into gains for souls. Behold, now candidates send their wet thresholds to the apostolic confession’s sedan chair, and gifts brought by God’s favor are doubled amid abundant tears of joy.

Who, at a time when we dry breasts with precious offspring, when the eternal mother now receives our race in order to bear it again, when her womb after the first birth is filled with aged offspring—she who, by regenerating it, makes dear to me the offspring that I bore, who makes those coming to her cast off old age and, though broken, return to the beginnings of life—who, I ask, would exchange this happiness? Who, by discord contrived with viperous intent, commands the benefits of my golden age to perish? Who secretly inspires decline in my renewal and, beneath the appearance of a flattering countenance, gains strength for enmity? I do not recognize noble lineage in such a business.

Yet if there are any of the highest rank whom the storm of this base tempest has joined to others, they are stained by participation in the crimes of the perpetrators. The splendor of blood, even if it incurs communion in crime, nevertheless does not know itself to be a guide to sinners. Perhaps it bears guilt for neglected caution; it does not deserve punishment for having led the crimes. He is joined to offenders with a certain shame who is summoned to their mature quarrels; he does not merit the despair reserved for the ruined man in whom only an easily forgiven cruelty is condemned.

You, rather, I see: shoots of the common streets; you I recognize—those in whom the baseness of nature has produced fitting manners; whose nobility ought to have prevented degeneration; who rejoice in impunity for your vices under the false title of religion; whose lips have never been touched either by the taste of honors or by tranquility; who violate every sacred law by obeying your origin; whom the present occasion has brought forth from hiding places and caves. Who recognized what you were before the arrangement of this evil? For a long time you cherished the secrets in which the night of your birth had concealed you.

Return instead to your friendly blindness. Leave us a clear and enduring light. Provide concord to the Church either by absence or by correction. Yet if you wish to be counted among illustrious ancestries, I shall recognize you by the amendment of your actions.

[Col. 0207]

## THIRD LITTLE WORK

[Note: [Col. 0207D] *The Life of the Most Blessed Epiphanius.* In the Basel edition scarcely a third of this Life was included; we have supplied the rest from manuscripts. It was certainly in the public interest that this little work should be made available, since among the works of Ennodius it appears to be both the greatest and the best, and it embraces a varied and multifaceted history of those times.]

## LIFE OF THE MOST BLESSED MAN EPIPHANIUS, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF TICINUM

(C)

[Col. 0207B] Although the uncertain necessity of undertaking this work presses upon me, and the task imposed upon me is neither free from labor nor untouched by the disputes of detractors—wherein the twofold caution of expression must on the one hand expect abundance from talent, while on the other it must impose restraints upon a tongue rich in narration—for if someone should strive to raise, with excessively inflated praise, those persons who are thought to be most eminent in the world, or to confine them within the limits of their deeds through poverty of eloquence, either course will be judged by them ungrateful.

For in praises themselves it is shameful to forge things that the man about whom they are told would not recognize; yet it is considered insulting and grievous to pass over in silence what a truthful account could elevate. Indeed, the well-accomplished deeds of our predecessors acquire from the ability of their reporter the value of virtue in our eyes. For what has been undertaken for explanation by a poor stream of words either loses the knowledge of truth or passes on to posterity in diminished form; and praise that is excessively free, without proper justification, subtracts as much from glory as it adds falsehood.

It commonly happens, moreover, that an accumulation lacking credibility diminishes the worthy deeds of many, and that a narrative which grows through lies is vain—untimely and excessively impoverished if it does not reach its proper end. Therefore, as I am about to narrate the life of the most blessed Epiphanius, bishop of Ticinus, I call upon the Holy Spirit as witness and companion of his deeds, so that with his help I may commit to writings destined to endure in the world the glory of the most serene conscience that he granted to that man, so that an example of virtues may provide a model whose fame never dies.

Yet in this work, if narrowness has not confined me within the fixed rule of eloquence that runs according to a prescribed order, so that I may at least arrange the raw facts of his merits in sequence, I shall find nothing in his labors so ordinary or humble that I need, as many do, enlarge it with the pomp of vivid language.
