For I shall summon witnesses of burning affairs, and display his still-smoking trophies, adorned with the spoils of the Devil’s nakedness.

No one recalls things nearly present and excessively well known before people’s eyes except one who trusts in the truth. Thus, as though conscious of my own shamelessness, I shall bring before the ears of those whom I might perhaps avoid if I were about to tell inventions the things that their own eyes have known.

Accordingly, the distinguished man Epiphanius was by origin a native of the town of Ticinus. He was born of his father Maurus and brought forth by his mother Focaria, who touched the lineage of the holy Mirocletus, confessor and bishop—a family of persons drawn from the pure source of free birth.

[Note: [Col. 0207D] “Saint Mirocletus.” Mirocletus, bishop of Milan, sat as a judge with others in the case of Caecilianus in the time of Constantine, as Optatus relates in Book I. The form *Mirocletis* arose through the corruption of the age in place of *Miroclis*, the form used by Mirocles himself in the epigram that he placed before the predecessor of the blessed bishop Anatoloni and closed with this couplet:

> Here Mirocles restores the inscription and the venerable faces  
> painted on the wall to the kindly faith of Praestitis.

**MIROCLES, BISHOP.**]

But what need is there to unfold the privilege of the blood of those whose family and nobility have their head in this son? Under his predecessor, the most upright man Crispinus,

[Note: [Col. 0208D] “Bishop Crispinus.” Crispinus’ name appears among the other bishops of that province who subscribed the synodical letter of Eusebius, bishop of Milan, to Pope Leo the Great. Ennodius mentions the same man in Poem 9 and attributes to him whatever praise belonged to his disciple and successor Epiphanius.]

as bishop of Ticinus, Epiphanius received the beginning of his heavenly military service. At about eight years of age he undertook the office of ecclesiastical lector, after a sign had first been shown from heaven. When he was still in the rattles of nursing infancy, many saw his cradle shine with a heavenly light, so that a radiance illuminating and preceding him displayed the future brightness of his mind and, by a symbolic light, already marked the splendor that would follow in his character.

He quickly mastered the abbreviations used in writing and the various figures that embrace a multitude of words. Enrolled among the *exceptores*, he distinguished himself, and began already to record things in such a way that he could dictate without provoking the reproaches of the good. Thus, as time and labor advanced, divine favor brought him to his sixteenth year, and he meditated gray-haired counsels in boyhood.

Modesty, the mother of good works, flourished in him above all else. He willingly served the bishop, so that if another performed some task, he would take it grievously as a service stolen from him. He received old men gravely and young men courteously; even then he restrained criminals boldly. He was submissive to his elders, obedient to those above him who enjoined holy duties, gentle and attentive toward his equals, and open to those below him with pure charity.

He preferred no one to himself, although in the devout course of his journey he outstripped everyone along the heavenly path. Free from the love of praise, while praiseworthy qualities grew in him each day, he thought that the fruit and reward of glory would perish if people brought forward what he secretly offered to God alone. In short, remembering the apostolic oracle and rejecting flattery, he applauded himself, with conscience as witness, for the recognition of his good work.

I do not refuse to mention also this point: his bodily beauty was an indication of the light within his soul, and the splendor of his appearance shone so strongly against the force of his devotion that it could not be overthrown even by a strong opponent. His cheeks smiled even when his spirit was numbed by grief. His shining lips commended the twofold sweetness of his speech. Wherever he turned his eyes, his expression announced the serenity of his mind. His brow had the beauty of wax and the whiteness of one that, exposed to the rays of the sun, had drawn its color from the heavens. His nostrils were formed with such natural brilliance that no painter representing bodies in images could imitate them. His hands were smooth, his fingers long—something even a foreigner would be glad to receive from them. His stature was tall in a fitting manner, foreshadowing in his limbs the eminence of the dignity he would attain, yet it did not exceed the proper measure of a most elegantly proportioned height.

[Col. 0209C] But lest some malicious interpreter should claim that mention of the charm of the flesh was introduced at an inappropriate point in a man of such virtues, it is rooted in that ancient foundation of the heavenly commandments that the bodies of priests must be examined with careful scrutiny: lest anything weak or deformed, anything excessive or deficient, be found, or an ugly surface disfigure skin marked by blemishes (Lev. 18:21 ff.); lest a fracture of the hand, a fracture of the foot, or a hump make the bishop unworthy of the altars; and that the teacher of the nations and vessel of election proclaim (Rom. 14:2) that a clean man must attain such an office. This, it is believed, he said not only of the purity of the soul but also of the cleanliness of the body.

The one who commands that the deformed and weak be kept away from his offerings is found willingly to admit those who are acceptable in many ways—especially one in whom the light of his limbs is surpassed by the splendor of his soul, and in whom that earthly beauty is not naturally assisted by any artificial means.

Having thus briefly touched upon what ought not to be omitted, so that the man immeasurable in his works might be made known also by his appearance, I shall pass to those features that are not moderately worthy of praise when narrated of the worshipers of God.

His speech was suited to instruction, fashioned for charm, already practiced in intercession,

[Note: [Col. 0209D] “Already skilled in intercessions.” This refers to the petitions that he regularly made before powerful people on behalf of the poor and oppressed, as stated in Book I, Letter 7, and again and again somewhat later.]

full of authority for reproving individuals, and sweetened by necessary charm for exhorting everyone. His voice was resonant, seasoned with the sap of manly elegance, yet neither rustic nor countrified, nor broken and gradually lowered from masculine firmness. Whoever saw him, although he had not yet entered any threshold of office, believed that he had already passed through all the distinctions that lay ahead.

Such was he when he reached his eighteenth year. In that year, ordained second in rank after the deacons, he was joined as a boy to the councils of elders. Many were astonished, but they were outsiders who joined his character to the immaturity of his age. Those who knew him believed that this dignity had been bestowed late.

But the venerable bishop Crispinus, ignorant of favoritism and holding firmly to discipline with persistent strictness—he never admitted anyone to favor except under the guidance of a good conscience—so softened him in his feelings that he wounded him by his gaze. Beneath the appearance of a stern expression, he secretly nourished affection for his disciple. The father fed upon the desirable companionship of his foster son and delighted his eyes with all his actions.

Yet he remained in the order of subdeacon for no more than two years. Raised by the leaps of his merits, he sprang upward, and his soul, rich in virtue, did not allow itself to be restrained long within the narrow bounds of a modest honor. His conscience hastened toward the dignity of the diaconate, although his desires had never presumed to seek it; his conduct demanded what his desires had wholly ignored.

Near the end and boundary of that office, I would like briefly to touch upon one of his works.

[Note: [Col. 0209D] “The field of Summias.” It was near Ticinus. He skillfully describes the inundations of the Po, concerning which Lucan also writes:

> The land flees those masters; to these farmers  
> the fields draw near, as the Po bestows them.

]

The field called Summias lies in a place where the earthly bank, like a throat, is gnawed by the bite of the Po’s whirlpool; and the winding river, by stealing from one side, generously grants a saving to the other. Thus the misfortune of one neighbor becomes the profit of another.

A certain man named Burco had long been engaged in an ancient dispute with the clergy over the boundaries of this estate. To settle the quarrel, this boy was sent—though the matter was excessively senile and older than one could imagine. He had been chosen because he could both withstand those accusations with strength

[Note: [Col. 0210D] Schott and Bolland read “the accusations brought against him.”]

and temper the accusations that had to be made with mature judgment.

The dispute nevertheless produced what contention usually produces, for as the argument and scandal progressed, Burco himself, who lent sordid encouragement to his own malice, committed the supreme crime without any fear: he struck the holy man with a staff so violently that blood immediately boiled forth.

But Epiphanius, fully prepared, restrained his anger. He did not grow hot when provoked by the hope of revenge; instead, he soothed the disturbed and terrified assailant with the gentlest speech.

At once Capraria, Burco’s mother, appeared, crying out that she was wretched and deprived of her son because of the atrocity of the deed. You would have thought that she was being tossed about in lamentation at the funeral of her own child, with that grief by which all counsel is banished in the deaths of loved ones. The mother, wailing, kissed the feet of the most holy youth and cried, “Spare him,” him whom no force had ever driven to anger.

But Epiphanius prevented her from pleading, lest by asking she arouse hatred against him and burden him with an honor he did not deserve. The city was suddenly thrown into confusion; the minds of all Christians turned to fury. Burco was demanded for destruction, and amid so great a multitude no one was found calm except the man who had suffered the injury.

The distinguished bishop wept, while his disciple rejoiced in his own infirmities and troubles. For he made such satisfaction on behalf of the man who was thought to be his enemy, one person after another, that in sparing him he neither sought glory ostentatiously nor, in taking vengeance, passed over the heavenly commands.

Shortly afterward, raised to the insignia of the diaconate, he entered his twentieth year, his face not yet fully bearded. The man who could already have filled the office of Christian leader was disturbed by the apprenticeship of the honor he had received. Out of modesty he avoided the gaze of individuals, while the entire city watched him as though he were some sign of salvation.

Meanwhile, the bishop mentioned above entrusted to his power the whole substance of ecclesiastical life and the wealth of his poor, wishing to discover before his own episcopate what sort of bishop he was preparing for the future. And although it is scarcely possible for envy to be restrained toward those from whose persons even the slightest suspicion of succession is sown, the holy father believed that, through his favor toward this man, whatever had been displayed less fully was lost to himself.

[Note: [Col. 0211D] “Holy father.” Basilius is called *papa* here. Although this could be tolerated elsewhere, since many commonly gave the name *papa* to any bishop, it does not suit Ennodius, who, as we have shown in the letters, calls only the bishop of the Roman See *papa*. The fact that Epiphanius is also called *papa* later in this work does not alter the matter, since the words there quoted belong to Euricus, not to Ennodius. The same judgment applies to the title of the Life, where Epiphanius is called *papa*, for that seems to be an addition. We have therefore rendered the term here as “father,” as the ancient copies affirm; what follows soon afterward sufficiently confirms this, where he is called “begetter.”]

He wanted some qualities in Epiphanius to be his own and others to be greater. But Epiphanius, advancing daily, had surpassed even the wishes of that most eager father in prayer.

For he was a father whose womb, pregnant through the Gospel with the seed of the heavenly word, had brought him forth. What shall I say of the chastity of my young man? In him chastity had established a home for itself, and continence had fixed its roots deep within. He did not know himself to be a man except through endurance of labor; he did not know himself to possess flesh except when he remembered that he would die.

Yet whenever bodily desire, as I learned from him himself, played with him through images of dreams, he immediately ran with complete eagerness to holy vigils, unbroken fasts, and the necessity of standing for a very long time. His warlike right hand returned his flesh to the soul through its battles, so that afterward it was necessary to assist him according to his need.

Even when his body had been restored, he did not indulge in leisure. He used reading as rest, taking the venerable books as instruments of consolation. What he had once read through, he recited from memory. And lest anyone think that he had flown over the path of the divine Scriptures merely with the speed of words, he painted upon his actions the page that he had read.

If a prophet had been in his hands, you would have seen a prophet speaking, with the reader’s book laid aside. If he had reviewed the volumes of the Old Testament, he walked as a worthy rival of Moses, as though the Israelite ranks were following him through the wilderness. If Scripture had revealed the apostolic milk of words and the honey of the Lord’s Passion seasoning the severity of the Law, immediately words sweeter than honey flowed from his mouth. Finally, whatever the books had taught was marked out in his life.

He governed the household of the Church in such a way that he neither exhausted the provisions entrusted to him through immoderate extravagance nor incurred hatred through begrudging parsimony. Even then he was rehearsing the contests of intercession. Wherever he was sent by the bishop’s command on behalf of remedies for the distressed, he demanded the benefit with such skill in pleading that many felt themselves helped in their cases, although the bishop himself had not come in person.

Popular affection for him increased day by day, and love, descending from judgment, was heaped up through great successes. People desired the priesthood for him, although no one wished for the death of his foster father. Yet not even the scent of this opinion had reached him. He thought it sufficient for his advancement if he always served with a good reputation.

When feeble old age, always complaining of its infirmities, took possession of the venerable bishop Crispinus, Epiphanius supported him with his hands and raised him by leaning upon his embrace. He was the bishop’s foot, eye, and right hand; through his service, whatever Crispinus wished to be done he saw completed before he had given the order. Good minds anticipate the desires of those whom they serve with integrity.

He completed eight years in the diaconate, beginning at the age of twenty. At that time the church of Ticinus flourished with the good fruit of its clergy. There were heavenly men whom Epiphanius, beginning from perfection, loved.

[Note: [Col. 0212D] Bollandus reads “whom he surpassed.”]

At that time Silvester was archdeacon, a man highly approved in the ancient instruction of the disciplines; Bonosus was a priest, as noble in holiness as in blood; a Gaul by ancestry but a citizen of heaven. There were others, more numerous and distinguished in virtue. I mention them for this reason: a man deserves little praise if he is preferred only to the wretched.

Near the end of his life, which the holy bishop foresaw in spirit, Crispinus sought the neighboring city of Milan, where the shoots of noble families had grown up in a harvest of pure nobility. After summoning them for a visit, the man of God addressed them in these words:

> “Behold, sons, age now compels me to depart. Earth is already calling back to its own right the fragment that came from it at my origin. I commend the city; I commend the Church; I commend this man, to whose labor and grace I owe the fact that I have lived until this time, old and infirm.
>
> “His bodily strength and the virtue of his soul bore my weakness without annoyance. I walked with his feet, held things with his hands, saw with his eyes, and arranged matters through his speech. To those who looked upon us, we seemed two, although through concord one was made from two.”

[Note: [Col. 0212D] “To Rusticus I.” It seems to be the Rusticus who had been consul with Olybrius a few years earlier, namely in the year 462. This Rusticus was a Milanese; another Rusticus, living at the same time, was a native of Bordeaux, to whom Sidonius writes in Book II and whom he also mentions in Book VIII, Letter 11: “It is sufficiently witty: look for Rusticus only in the soil and in the name.” But the manuscripts of the highest authority read *Rusticium* here.]

These words sank deeply into the heart of Rusticus, a distinguished man who was highly practiced in every kind of speech. He began as follows:

> “We know, holy Father, we know, and have seen with profound reflection, that this young man ought not to be judged according to the immaturity of his age, nor should tender years be brought forward as an obstacle before men of serious counsel. For a man commendable in the gray maturity of his character deserves a double praise if a childish body obeys the venerable rule of his mind.
>
> “But live, live on—an example and model of good works—and add to him the fruits of a radiant conduct, more abundant still, if they can yet grow.”

After these words he fell silent. The most devout bishop thanked him for his goodwill, because he shared with him the same judgment concerning his disciple. He then said farewell and departed, hastening back to Ticinus as though to a tomb. After several days had passed, he was overcome by jaundice and exchanged the light of our world for the heavenly dwelling.

At once the unanimous consent of all good people was brought to bear in Epiphanius’ favor. Immediately there was a great gathering throughout the city. He was snatched from funeral lamentation to be consecrated bishop amid the joy of the people. He wept immoderately from grief at his father’s death, but the shared joy of the multitude did not permit him to shed the tears that were due.

He resisted as much as he could and loudly declared himself unworthy even of apostolic imitation. But the love of all rose in him all the more because amid the great multitude he alone called himself unworthy.

Why should I now use more words, when I cannot explain everything? The enthusiasm of neighboring cities joined with that of Ticinus, and such a gathering was drawn together as though a bishop for the whole world were about to be ordained. He was led to Milan while still resisting and promising great gifts if he were released, although he would not promise even the smallest thing in order to be made bishop.

He was consecrated with the full celebration of all. The world rejoiced in the insignia of so holy an ordination. The inhabitants of foreign cities displayed themselves in such jubilation as though he had received the priestly insignia for their own particular benefit. Yet envy consumed some inhabitants of the great cities, because the narrow town of Ticinus had deserved to possess so great a bishop, while among them only the bishops of metropolitan cities bore the titles of metropolitan grandeur.

When the day of his ordination had been completed, he returned to Ticinus. After summoning all the priests and ministers, he instructed and encouraged them with this address:

> “Although, dearest brothers, at the beginning I was oppressed by the immaturity of my judgment and by the weight of the dignity I have undertaken, I nevertheless remember how much I owe to your favor, since you have bestowed the greatest things upon me. And although I have had more desire to obey you than to command you, I have changed my role through the office of service, not my disposition.
>
> “Be peaceful; be of one mind. Divide my burden with me. A load becomes easy to carry when many shoulders support it. I promise to preserve communion with you in complete humility, and no one will be able to offend me except together with our God.
>
> “Preserve chastity, the author of all good things. Do not think it insulting that a boy speaks to old men and priests about preserving continence and integrity. Conduct, not years, reveals either youth or old age.
>
> “Examine the inner qualities of my conduct, and if you recognize anything unworthy, restrain me. Let no one fear to admonish the ruler of the Church if he proves to be in error.”

When he had said this, he fell silent. They all rose and, with one voice, as though from a long-standing meditation but nevertheless in a sudden utterance, said:

> “Hail, most approved Father; hail, singular bishop. The election of all has indeed judged you good, but your address also declares you excellent. You grow in holy merits before our conscience, and you are revealed by the light of your works to stand above the opinion that had been formed of you.”

After briefly expressing these sentiments, they all departed, having received their commission.

Soon the blessed bishop dictated with his own mouth the rules by which he could hold himself in check. First, he resolved not to bathe, lest baths, more friendly to dirt, weaken the brightness of his soul and the strength of the inner man. Next, he had decided never to eat lunch; but lest any force from outside violate the judgment of his purpose, and lest he be injured either by the clouds of vainglory or by a reputation for greed, he decreed that he would never eat dinner, so that the change of hours might provide an opportunity to refresh himself once each day.

He ordered that the cheaper foods please him, and that nothing in the preparation of dishes be allowed to offend his nose or taste except what was seasoned with spices. He fed on meals of greens and legumes, but took neither of these to satiety. He drank a little wine, though he took even that small amount in remembrance of the apostolic admonition, to guard against weakness of the stomach.

He judged that everyone should set out early, whatever the weather, so that the bishop, preceding the readers, might present at the church the pattern of the vigils. Once he had reached the boundaries of the altar, he resolved that no necessity should arise by which he could be taken away before the sacred rites were completed. He determined to stand with his feet together until the completion of the mystical work, so that the moisture of his footprints would mark the place and indicate it to those looking from far away.

He imposed upon himself so great a concern for intercession that he believed he was inflicting upon the poor the very trouble that he allowed to be inflicted by anyone through his negligence. He trained his body during leisure to be sufficient for the demands of labor. He proposed this practical rule, or discipline of life, to himself; he undertook it, observed it, and fulfilled it.

Soon the fame of his holy conduct—which, although usually slower to appear in glorious deeds, never remains silent—carried it throughout the world. It also reached the ears of Ricimer, who at that time governed the state under the second authority of the emperor Anthemius.

[Note: [Col. 0213D] “To the ears of Ricimer.” Ricimer married the daughter of the emperor Anthemius in 467, as Sidonius informs us; Sidonius entered Rome near the end of that year to attend the wedding, Book I, Letter 5. Ricimer later attacked his father-in-law Anthemius in civil war and killed him in 472. Therefore the embassy undertaken in Ricimer’s name to Anthemius could have occurred neither later than that year nor earlier than 467. Sigonius and others assign it partly to 471 and partly to the following year, an obvious anachronism. Epiphanius was still a new bishop, recently raised to the chair of Ticinus. Since, as will be said later, his eighth year fell in the time of Nepos, this first embassy must necessarily have occurred around the year 468.]

With the emperor established at Rome, envy—the force that separates rulers, despite their equal dignity—had sown the seed of discord between them. Such rage and dissension had arisen that they were preparing for war against one another. Besides the fact that the origin of their anger supplied its own impulses, the quarrel was nourished by the counsel of those around them. The state of Italy, already in danger, tottered, and it was afflicted even more grievously by the present crises while it awaited future ones.

Meanwhile, at the court of the patrician Ricimer, who at that time resided in Milan, a gathering of the nobility of Liguria took place. Falling to their knees and prostrating themselves on the ground, they begged for peace between the rulers and asked one side to offer opportunities for reconciliation, so that both parties might cease from their scandalous conflict.

Why should I weave a longer account? Ricimer was softened, and, moved by the tears of many, promised that he wished to restore concord.

> “But who,” he said, “will bear the principal burden of this embassy? Whom will the care of so great a task await? Who is able to bring back to the prince the agitated Galatian?”

[Note: [Col. 0215D] “The agitated Galatian.” He soon calls Anthemius a “little Greek.” Sidonius likewise, writing about Arvandus and his letter to Euricus in Book I, Letter 7, says: “This document seemed to be sent to the king of the Goths, discouraging peace with the Greek emperor.” By “Greek emperor” he does not mean Leo, the ruler of the East, who had no dealings with Euricus, but Anthemius, who had recently come from Greece and was ruling at Rome.]

> “For whenever he is asked, he overflows; he does not end his anger through natural moderation.”

Then they all answered with one voice:

> “Let only your assent be inclined toward peace. We have a man recently raised to the priesthood of the city of Ticinus, before whom even rabid beasts submit their necks.
>
> “A benefit should be offered to him before anyone asks for it, since anyone who comes to seek something from him receives it. His face resembles life itself; anyone who is a Catholic and a Roman can venerate him, and certainly the little Greek can love him if he is fortunate enough to see him.
>
> “And if we come to his speech, never could a Thessalian magician, by violent incantations, summon such terrible serpents of words with his fingers as this man can draw the fulfillment of his request from those who would refuse it. Once he begins to speak, the judgment of the hearer hangs upon his will. The right of the man who has decided to offer an excuse also hangs upon it, if he is granted the opportunity to make his case.”

Then the patrician Ricimer replied:

> “Fame has brought to me the man whom you describe, glorious in reputation. What amazes me most is that he has so many praisers and that he reveals none of those enemies whom novelty usually produces in abundance through envy. Go, then, and ask the man of God to come. Add my prayers as well.”

They left the council—or, perhaps, the assembly—and immediately set out for Ticinus. They explained the matter, and the blessed Epiphanius was begged with floods of tears to undertake this labor. He did not wish to diminish the benefit by tormenting his sons with prolonged supplication; therefore he anticipated the desires of those who were asking. Nevertheless, he addressed them as follows:

> “Although the necessity of so great a matter requires the weight of a most approved person, and an inexperienced bearer trembles beneath the heavy burden, I shall not refuse the affection that I owe to my country.”

After briefly relating these matters, Epiphanius—who was sparing in speech—went to the patrician Ricimer. As soon as Ricimer saw him, he chose him.

By the terms of the mission entrusted to him, therefore, he set out for Rome. What hardships he endured on this journey, and what acts of virtue he performed, I pass over in haste as I turn to greater matters. Yet as soon as he entered the gates of the city mentioned above, the reputation that had made him known even in his absence began to point him out with a finger. At once everyone’s eyes turned toward him, and astonished minds marveled that his appearance, an indication of holiness, demanded such reverence. [Note: Schott and Bolland: “Inexpiable.”] Every powerful person confessed himself guilty of an unpardonable offense if he had merely embraced his knees. A cry was raised to heaven. No one counted him among ordinary mortals, for they saw in him every good gift of heavenly grace.

It was reported to the emperor Anthemius [Col. 0216B] that the bishop of Liguria had come to undertake a mission, a man whom no one, however rich in eloquence, could adequately describe. But he said:

“Ricimer is clever, and in his missions he competes with me in craft. He sends men who overcome by supplication those whom he harasses with injuries. Nevertheless, bring the man of God to me. If he asks what is possible, I will grant it; if what is difficult, I will beg him not to consider my refusal an offense. Yet I doubt whether Ricimer will obtain from me what he seeks, for I know that he is immoderate in his desires and keeps no reasonable limit when proposing conditions. But let the bishop who has been sent come and present the countenance so long praised.”

The palace officials went out through the entire city. “Command, you are begged”—the bishop heard.

[Col. 0216C] But the venerable pontiff, approved by all the ages, after he had entered and been granted permission to speak—although the insignia of fleeting power, the purple and shining jewels, had been eclipsed by the radiance of his revered appearance (for, as if the emperor were absent, he had drawn everyone’s eyes upon himself)—opened the door of his mouth with an address that began as follows:

“It has been arranged by the supreme ordinance of the heavenly Lord, revered prince, that whoever has been entrusted with the care of so great a commonwealth should, through the doctrine of the catholic faith, recognize God as both the author and lover of piety. Through him the fury of wars is shattered by the weapons of peace, and concord, treading upon the necks of pride, overcomes what strength cannot prevail against. Thus David’s spirit made him more renowned for sparing his enemy than for intending vengeance. [Col. 0216D] Thus the perfect kings and rulers of the ages have learned, by a heavenly art, to show indulgence to those who supplicate them. For he possesses the likeness of heavenly dominion who exalts his rule through compassion.

“Trusting in this judgment, your Italy—or the patrician Ricimer—has sent my insignificance to you with a request [Note: Schott and Bolland: “to petition.”], confidently reasoning that a Roman offers God the gift which even a barbarian requests. [Note: The same editors: “Lord.”] It will be a triumph especially worthy of appearing in your annals if you conquer without bloodshed. At the same time, I do not know what form of warfare could be stronger than fighting against anger and loading the fiercest Goth with benefits. For the man who has been ashamed until now to supplicate is struck more grievously if he obtains what he requested.

“Then there is the uncertain outcome of war, in which, if sins should prevail in the struggle, your kingdom will be deprived of what both sides have lost. For whatever is safe with Ricimer, if he is your friend, is possessed along with him by you, the Patrician. Consider also that he directs the course of his cause well who first offers peace.”

Thus far the admirable pontiff pursued his speech, and then ended it. The prince raised his eyes and saw himself abandoned by everyone’s gaze, while everyone’s faces were turned toward him in expectation; yet he himself could not cease admiring the bishop. Then, drawing his words out with a deep sigh, he began:

“Although, holy bishop, my cause of grief against Ricimer is indescribable, and although it did no good that he was heaped with the greatest benefits by us—indeed, something that cannot be said without shame for our kingdom and our blood, we joined him to our family line, when, out of love for the commonwealth, we indulged what seemed to tend to hatred of our own—who among the princes of old ever did this, that among the gifts which had to be given to a filthy Goth, a daughter should be offered for the sake of public peace?

[Note: “The daughter of Anthemius who married Ricimer.” The name is uncertain. Some thought that she was called Ascyla, but this is an error. Gregory of Tours, in Book II of his *History*, had written from the old consular records that Theodemer, king of the Franks, was born from Ricimer and Ascyla. They considered these to be one and the same Ricimer, although both the intervals of time and their homelands distinguish them. Gregory was a Frank; this Ricimer was born of a Suevic father and a Gothic mother, as Sidonius testifies.]

“We did not know how to spare our own blood while preserving another’s. Yet let no one think that this was done out of personal fear. In such careful concern for the safety of all, we do not know how to fear for ourselves alone. For we know well that an emperor loses the praise of his valor if he has not earned it by guarding others.

“But to disclose fully to your Reverence the character of his efforts: whenever Ricimer was heaped with greater gifts by us, each time he appeared a more serious enemy. How many wars has he prepared against the commonwealth? How much strength from foreign peoples has his madness acquired? Finally, even when he could not inflict harm, he nevertheless supplied the fuel for doing so. Shall we grant him peace? Shall we endure as an internal enemy beneath the appearance of friendship one whom not even the bonds of kinship held to a pact of concord?

“It is a great safeguard to know the mind of an adversary. Indeed, to recognize an enemy at once is to have overcome him: hatred, once detected, always loses the goads that it had conceived while concealed. But if your Reverence, both as guarantor and mediator, comes forward in all these matters—you who can discover wicked counsels by spiritual insight and correct what you have discovered—I do not dare refuse the peace that you also request.

“Finally, if the cunning of his accustomed craft should deceive even you, let the man already wounded take up the contest. But I commit and commend myself, and the condition of the commonwealth, to your hands; and the favor which I had resolved to deny to Ricimer, though he supplicated and lavished gifts on his own behalf, I first grant through you. For by profound deliberation we consult our own advantage in this matter if, amid the uncertain storms of error, we turn the ship according to the direction of a true pilot. Who, after all, would presume to excuse to you a benefit requested by one to whom it ought to have been offered before he asked?”

Thus spoke the emperor. But the venerable priest said:

“I give thanks to almighty God, who has inserted his peace into the mind of the prince, whom he has willed to be, after the likeness of heavenly dominion, the representative of his power among mortals.”

After briefly recounting these events, and after receiving from Anthemius an oath also for the firm establishment of concord, he departed, hastening to return to Liguria, since the time of the Lord’s resurrection was approaching. Through it, while bodies were worn down by the cross of fasting, a joyful spirit would grow warm again in chilled flesh; while death was conquered by our Redeemer’s dying, and the soul was nourished with the food of faithful hope.

When he left Rome, the twentieth day before the coming Easter lay ahead. Yet he completed the journey with such speed that on the fourteenth day he entered Ticinum unexpectedly and ahead of the report of his arrival, leaving many companions behind on the road because they could endure neither his abstinence nor his exertions. Behold the throng of those awaiting the arrival of so great a bishop, seeing him already at home, although they had not yet learned that he had even left Rome. The rejoicing of the happy city was announced to the astonished Ricimer: everyone proclaimed with one voice that peace had been made.

There was endless exultation throughout the provinces. And, as is human nature, people value more highly what is restored than what never perishes at all. Sweeter was the concord recalled after strife, and the peace that had come when it had nearly been abandoned as hopeless. The revered pontiff was summoned so that he might present himself to the Milanese, who had long awaited the sight of him. But he avoided their visits under a plausible pretext, lest he should seem, by appearing in person, to demand the thanks that were owed him.

Thus, as time and labor passed, the merit of his life increased with each day’s achievement. He had a younger sister, equal to him in religious devotion. [Note: “Honorata.” The people of Ticinum commemorate this virgin devoted to God each year on the third day before the Ides of January.] Her name was Honorata, whose life would take too long to recount according to each category of virtue. Yet it is enough to add to her praise that she was the worthy sister of so great a man.

In the very year in which he returned from his mission, he consecrated her. Yet, as though holy nature alone were not enough to instruct her in heavenly disciplines, he entrusted her to a certain woman named Luminosa [Col. 0218D], of astonishing holiness and singular example. It would perhaps be necessary to investigate the heights of her birth, had her life not been more distinguished than her blood. She was such a woman that even he who entrusted to her the companion of his womb believed that he himself had something to learn from her.

Within a short time the bishop’s sacred charge, deposited with her, blossomed and reached maturity, laden with the fruits of good harvest. Meanwhile the venerable priest advanced rapidly along the path of life he had set before himself [Col. 0219A], devoting himself without hesitation to almsgiving. He commended this gift to those who received it with the gentlest expression and disposition, so that anyone who had received merely the favor of his conversation would never think he had departed without a gift. For it was the highest reward at least to have seen such a bishop. His fame grew day by day through glorious successes and filled almost the entire world through his preaching.

[Note: “After the death of Ricimer or Anthemius.” In the year 472 Ricimer killed Anthemius, after Olybrius had already been created in his place; he himself died forty days later, as Cassiodorus records in the *Fasti*, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September. After this Olybrius died at Rome in the seventh month of his reign, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November. In the following year, 473, Glycerius occupied the vacant court at Ravenna on the third day before the Nones of March. The following year he was deprived of the empire, and Julius Nepos was raised to the imperial office on the eighth day before the Kalends of July.]

Then Ricimer or Anthemius died, and Olybrius succeeded him; but at the very beginning of his reign he ended his days. After him Glycerius was summoned to the government. How much the holy man accomplished for the salvation of many under him I omit for the sake of brevity. For Glycerius granted to the holy man the redress of an injury inflicted upon his mother by men under his authority, since his reverence for the aforesaid priest was even greater than that of his predecessor.

After him Nepos assumed the kingdom. Then disagreement arose between him and the Goths of Toulouse [Note: “The Goths of Toulouse.” Their king at this time was Euric, the father of Alaric. Taking advantage of the frequent changes of Roman emperors, as Jordanes also notes in *On the Gothic Affairs*, he attacked the Arverni and extended the boundary of his kingdom toward the limits of Roman power. Sidonius, Book VII, Letter 6: “Evarix, king of the Goths, because he either protects the boundary of his kingdom by the right of arms, after breaking and dissolving the ancient treaty, or advances it, neither is it permitted for us sinners here to accuse him, nor for you holy men here to examine him.” This, then, was the reason that Nepos Augustus sent Epiphanius as envoy to Euric, so that they might renew the rights of the ancient treaty.]

—the Goths of Toulouse, whom King Euric governed with an iron rule. They did not cease to attack the Italian boundaries of the empire, which extended beyond the Gallic Alps, scorning their novelty; while Nepos, lest misguided presumption become customary, desired more sternly to defend the boundary of the kingdom entrusted to him by God. Thus on both sides the causes of litigation began to rise. And while neither party laid aside its swelling anger in the desire to conquer, the cause of discord grew stronger.

The most blessed man had already completed his eighth year in the priesthood when suddenly love of removing the dissension entered Nepos’s mind, so that, rejecting the poison of hostility, he might preserve affection between the kings—something that arms could scarcely protect. The leading men of Liguria were summoned to a council: men of mature judgment, by whose deliberation the tottering condition of the commonwealth might revive and its desperate stability be restored to its ancient foundation; men of such importance for the discussion that, by the prince’s command, they could be as great as governors.

They began to discuss arranging a mission. Everyone’s minds and eyes turned toward the most blessed man Epiphanius. The opinions of all were formed as though they were expressed by one mouth and one heart. What more need be said? When the soldier of Christ joyfully embraced the opportunity for labor and anticipated success in hope, confident in his assessment of the undertaking, he sought a means of action that might improve its prospects. After seeking the support of heavenly power, he undertook and completed an enterprise that had almost been pronounced impossible and was exceedingly difficult.

I could not set out in order the hardships and necessities of this journey, even if words were poured through my flowing channels in a hundred tongues. For after leaving the town of Ticinum, until he reached the appointed places, he doubled the fatigue of his journey by such a method that, if his companions, considering the exhaustion of the animals, went ahead to the lodging places of the next station, he—apart from the uninterrupted recitation of the psalms and his persistence in reading, neither of which he did except while standing—would choose a retreat enclosed by woodland foliage, where the interlaced arms of the trees would roof a domestic night. The sun alone, driven back by the dark shades, could not discover it, and natural grace spread a bed of green turf.

There, with continual tears poured out in prayer, he watered the rainless earth with the showers of his eyes. Those fields, which could not produce crops, were made fertile by the abundance of prayer. [Col. 0220B]

Wearing himself down by such discipline, he entered the city of Toulouse, where Euric was then residing. Advance reports had already made the Gauls aware of what kind of man he was, especially the priests of that region, whom a profound inquiry into the newcomer’s character kept astonished and concerned.

At that time there was also a certain Leo, moderator and arbiter of the prince’s counsels. [Note: “Named Leo.” Sidonius addresses him in Book VIII, Letter 3, in these words: “Set aside for a little while the most resounding declamations which you compose in place of the royal mouth.” For he was, as it were, Euric’s quaestor. Sidonius also praises him elsewhere for his learning, as in Book IV, Letter 22, and at Narbo:

“Whether to the house of eloquent Leo,

Where, teaching twice six tablets of law,

Appius Claudius would willingly hide,

Darker than the famous man in the decemvirate;

But if he speaks an epic and bends the meter

With rhythmic clauses on his thundering lyre,

He could make biting Flaccus fall silent.”]

He was named Leo, and through the distinction of his eloquence had already won more than one prize for declamation. With the greatest joy he announced the bishop’s arrival to the public. The bishop was summoned at once to be presented to the king. As soon as Euric saw him enter, he greeted him and addressed him:

“Although the fame of your virtue, O astonishing prince of the earth, makes you terrible to the ears of many, and although the swords with which you continually oppress your neighbors with devastation reap a kind of harvest of hostile stock, nevertheless the ambition of warfare does not enrich you with any grace of the heavenly divinity. Nor does iron guard the boundaries of an empire if the heavenly Lord is offended.

“Remember that you are a king, and that you must consider what pleases him who, when he carried the man he had taken up to heaven, commended peace to his disciples repeatedly as the reward of an immense inheritance. We must be guardians of this command, especially since we know that a man cannot be called brave if indignation has conquered him.

“Next, we must weigh the fact that no one guards his own possessions more carefully than one who does not covet what belongs to another. Therefore Nepos, to whom divine ordinance has entrusted the government of Italy, has sent us to obtain these things: that, when minds have been restored to trust, the lands adjoining his may be joined to him by the right of affection. Although he does not fear conflict, he desires concord first.

“You know in common within what ancient boundary the domains of rulers are confined, and with what patience of servitude these regions have endured their governors. Let it be enough that a friend—who has deserved to be called a lord—has chosen, or at least endured, being called one.”

Thus spoke the distinguished Epiphanius.

But Euric, breaking off some barbarian murmur, signaled by the serenity of his face that he had been softened by the bishop’s exhortations. Leo, mentioned above, was so profoundly astonished by the bishop’s speech that he believed minds could be conquered by words of this kind, even—if it may be said—when the request was contrary to justice.

Nevertheless, the king is said to have spoken to his interpreter as follows:

“Although a cuirass scarcely leaves my breast, and a bronze shield continually encloses my hand, while the protection of iron also guards my side, I have nevertheless found a man who can conquer me, though armed, by his words. They are wrong who say that Romans have neither shields nor javelins in their tongues. They know how to repel even the words we send forth, and to direct those they launch themselves into the innermost chambers of slaughter. Therefore, venerable pope, I will do what you ask, because in my eyes the person of the envoy is greater than the power of the one who sent him. Now receive my pledge and promise on behalf of Nepos that he will preserve concord inviolate, since your promise is as good as an oath.”

After these words, and after the bond of the agreement had been established, the revered pontiff took his leave and departed. Immediately a crowd of petitioners was sent to him, asking him to attend the king’s banquet on the following day. But he had already learned that Euric’s priests habitually kept polluted feasts. He excused himself and said that it was not his custom ever to eat at another’s meal. He preferred to depart, and hastened to fulfill what he had resolved. He left Toulouse with so many people accompanying him that, when our pontiff departed, the city appeared almost deserted. For in a short time he had bound so many to himself by sincere affection that they wept as though held captive, since necessity compelled them to remain in their homeland.

On his return from there, however, he visited each of the holy settlements. He went to the Median Islands [Note: “The Stoechades Islands.” I judge this to be the proper reading, not Cyclades, which is what the manuscripts have. Pliny, Book III, chapter 4, and the geographers place the Stoechades on the coast of Massilia and explain that they received this name because of the order in which they lie. They are called *Stoichades* (Στοιχάδες) by Ptolemy. An antiquarian who did not know the Stoechades wrote “Cyclades,” because they were better known; just as in the panegyric they likewise wrote “Cyrillus” for “Cochrillus,” and “Cylindros” for “Chelydros. The Stoechades, as I have said, lie on the Massilian coast, while Lerus and Lerinus lie opposite Antipolis. They were formerly all filled with monasteries and monks’ cells, as Cassian’s *Conferences* testify. Of these, the last seven were sent to the saints who were on the Stoechades Islands; an equal number were sent to Honoratus and Eucherius, one the founder and the other a pupil of the monastery of Lérins.”]—the Stoechades, Lerus, and Lerinus itself, the level island that nurtures the highest mountains.

From each of them he gathered individual blossoms of life, that he might implant in himself the seedbed of good growth and bring the tree, laden with heavenly fruits, to the time of maturity. Meanwhile the light long awaited by the Italians was restored, and as the singular priest returned, a radiant brilliance opened beneath a clear sky. He entered Ticinum, long desired. He informed Nepos of the success of his completed mission; and as the heap of his praises grew, his humility increased in equal measure.

Thus, while the servant of Christ and our God exercised himself in such disciplines and labors, behold that enemy, who knew no rest and perpetrated crimes, joined great increases of sorrow together and sought means by which to harass the blameless man with sufferings. He raised an army against the patrician Orestes. [Note: “Against the patrician Orestes.” In the year 476, the previous year, Orestes had given the empire to his son Augustulus after driving out Nepos. In this year Odovacer took up arms against Orestes and besieged him at Ticinum, as Eunodius records, eventually capturing and killing him along with the city of Placentia.] That clandestine plotter sowed the seeds of discord. He disturbed the minds of the desperate with hope of revolution and lifted Odovacer toward the ambition of kingship. And so that this disaster might occur in the city of Ticinum, he invited Orestes there, trusting in the city’s defenses.

The bishop was found present with all who belonged to him. A tremendous crowd gathered in the city, and the frenzy of plunder blazed up. Everywhere there was mourning, everywhere terror, and everywhere the image of death moved about in countless forms. He was anxiously demanded for punishment, whose wealth the old loyalty of his friendships had made well known. Some placed flames beneath houses about to collapse; others demanded the destruction of the lord for whose safety they had come together to fight.

They ran toward the church’s residence, burning with every fire of plunder, while, because they saw him distributing so much, they suspected that he was hiding immeasurably more. Oh, abomination! Savage barbarism sought on earth the treasures that he had sent into the heavenly storehouses.

His holy sister too was plundered and led away from him separately by the lot of captivity. All the noblewomen were separated from their families. Luminosa, that most glorious woman, was likewise bound by the same condition of necessity.

O sorrow! Both churches were consumed by hostile flames, and the entire city shone like a single funeral pyre. The voices of all who called for the priest could be heard. No one remembered his own danger while a greater share of salvation was being distributed by him. Although the confused crowd raged toward the destruction of each individual, honor was nevertheless shown him even among the swords.

For immediately there were no captives whom he could see: before the fatal light of that day slipped into evening, he rescued his venerable sister. He also freed many citizens through his prayers before they felt the bonds of the harshest condition, especially married women, whose prolonged detention could have lasted more cruelly under those circumstances.

Finally, the condition of the city, which the barbarian multitude was cutting down, rose again, supported by the aid of one most steadfast pillar. An army was not so sufficient for destroying it as the person of one bishop was for restoring it. Yet once Orestes had been removed and killed near Placentia, the onrush of plunder subsided.

[Col. 0223A] After this, when Odovacer was raised to the kingship [Note: “Raised to the kingship of Odovacer.” It says “kingship,” not “empire,” because after Odovacer expelled Augustulus into exile and destroyed the Roman imperial power, he assumed only the name of king, without the purple or insignia, and not the name of Augustus. Content with this, he ruled Italy for approximately fourteen years. The old consular chronicle records that he was raised as king on the tenth day before the Kalends of September, and that Orestes was killed five days later.], he began to honor the distinguished man with such respect that all the services rendered to him by his predecessors were surpassed.

Meanwhile, lest the divine dwellings remain long oppressed by ashes, the glorious bishop resolved to rebuild them before preparing either money or resources. He did not fear to raise buildings of immense cost without a store of money, not unaware of the apostolic admonition that for those who seek the heavenly kingdom an inexhaustible wealth continually overflows, and that he who is not constrained by poverty in his willingness to give always distributes from abundance. He used to say:

“It is scarcely possible for wealth to abandon a rich spirit, and it is exceedingly difficult for abundance to follow a man who is poor in mind.”

By now, the work had reached the summit of completion of the greater church, adorned with its building and the insignia of its dedication. Suddenly, however, the columned wall of another church was thrown down by the force of a cunning serpent. The enemy wished to test whether he could overthrow him by multiplying his afflictions. But the bishop rose with even greater force, lest he yield to his misfortunes, and immediately girded himself with full eagerness to repair it, without any sign of suffering.

The whole community, however, was held by an extraordinary wonder: the builders fell from the roof of the temple together with a huge machine, yet none of them was injured in the leg or mutilated in any part of his body. It became clear to everyone’s understanding that this had happened through the bishop’s prayers: the falling mass supported its own weight, and the stones were suspended from their fall.

Yet, through the astonishing course of his providential arrangements, his labor was directed toward completing the aforementioned work. [Col. 0223C] Once the preparation of the greater church had been completed, he began its restoration; he saw the house of God rise rapidly to the heights of its former soundness, although he had not yet learned that the work had begun. After these works had nevertheless been quickly completed by him, divine favor soon manifested itself through him.

For within the course of that same year, a great host of demons began to cry out from possessed bodies that they were being compelled to flee by whips and excessive torments at the command of the priest Epiphanius. With a brief prayer poured forth amid a little weeping, he sent them to the farthest boundaries of the earth and drove them away by the authority of his merits, although they wailed in various voices. Yet although he continually performed such acts through the grace of Christ, he took nothing for himself from the winds of presumption. For good merit loses its power over those whom confidence in their kindness has brought to arrogance.

[Col. 0224A] Meanwhile, lest he seem to have adorned the city only with the buildings of its churches, he provided for its exhausted inhabitants by useful remedies. Through a formal mission to Odovacer, he obtained a five-year remission of fiscal taxes. [Note: “A five-year remission.” It is the custom of good rulers to aid cities and provinces worn down by war or other calamity through remission or indulgence of fiscal burdens. Thus Constantine once remitted five years’ arrears to the severely afflicted city of Autun. The rhetor Eumenius says: “You have remitted five years of arrears to us, O five-year period happier than every five-year period!” Theoderic likewise relaxed the taxes of the third indiction for the province of the Cottian Alps because an army had passed through it. Cassiodorus, Book IV, Letter 36.]

When these benefits were distributed among individuals, he restrained himself with such integrity that no one received less than the person for whom it had been granted at his request. While these things were taking place, however, the stored-up malice of Pelagius [Note: “Pelagius, who was prefect of the praetorium.” It was the duty of the praetorian prefects to collect taxes everywhere, “to collect the taxes from every region through their subordinate officials,” as Zosimus says in Book IV. There was also another Pelagius, similar to this one in age, a patrician, an outstanding man and distinguished as a poet, whom the emperor Zeno killed in the year 490. Marcellinus Comes records: “In the consulship of Longinus II and Faustus, the emperor Zeno ordered Pelagius’s throat to be broken on the island called Panormus.”]—who was at that time prefect of the praetorium—boiled up against the possessors of Liguria, bringing them to ruin.

For by the enormity of forced purchases he doubled the grievous taxes and imposed a twofold burden that they could not bear even in its single form. Soon a crowd of the oppressed flocked to the holy man. He gladly embraced the opportunity to come to their aid and went energetically on behalf of everyone’s need: he asked, obtained, and succeeded.

But why do I struggle to describe in detail the various forms and appearances of his labors, when what ability cannot explain is anticipated by devotion, and the narrowness of speech sets a limit to what those who imagine more extensive things suppose? Yet these were the desires of the most sacred priest: although he did countless things, he wished either nothing or very little to be touched upon in praise of him. Therefore, if my poor tongue has revealed anything inadequately, I leave it to the judgment of my listeners and readers.

After many embassies to King Odovacer, in which he had prevailed by the force of supplication, King Theoderic came to Italy by the disposition of heavenly rule with an immense multitude of his strength. [Note: “King Theoderic.” In the year 489, during the consulship of Cassiodorus, Probinus, and Eusebius, our most fortunate and powerful lord King Theoderic entered Italy.] The blameless man, already residing at Milan, went out to meet him.

When that greatest of kings had examined him with the eyes of his heart and weighed our priest according to the accustomed scale of his judgment, he found the weight of every virtue to be present in him. He measured his integrity, as if with a craftsman’s ruler, against the plumb line of his mind. He used the following words about him before his own people:

“Behold a man whose equal the whole East does not possess: to have seen him is a reward; to live with him is security. While he remains unharmed, the city of Ticinum is enclosed by a mighty wall, which no force of attackers could overwhelm, and which the flight of a Balearic sling could never penetrate. If some necessity should arise amid the waves of battle, it is safe to entrust a mother of a household to him, and convenient to go out to military campaigns.”

[Col. 0224D] Meanwhile the ambition of change inflamed the rebellious minds of the surrendered army [Col. 0225A], whose leader was Tufa. [Note: “Tufa.” According to some writers, he was the consular governor of Liguria and Aemilia. His defection occurred in the year 490.] He was a man stained by an old and notorious reputation among deserters. He conceived the plan of joining himself, with a great multitude, to the desperate cause. When King Theoderic learned this through the anxious vigilance appropriate to a ruler, he immediately gathered together the entire force that the whole East had scarcely been able to sustain and brought it to the narrow confines of the city of Ticinum.

You would have seen the city teeming with gatherings of families, the roofs of enormous houses cut down into the narrowest huts. You would have seen immense buildings moving from their foundations, while the ground itself could scarcely suffice to receive the density of the inhabitants.

Amid these events, that man, practiced in every good work, in whom greatness of spirit opened access to all, judged that an opportunity had been offered him to spread the sails of his kindness in a full southern wind and reach the harbor of glory by a favorable voyage, through the knowledge of various peoples and the renown of his deeds.

First—and no ancient documents, no annals of books, speak of this concerning anyone, so that the reporter may assert it with amazement and the reader receive it with admiration—although he lived among an exceedingly shrewd people, a people whom no breath of suspicion passed by, and although in doubtful circumstances the fear of danger agitates even gentle hearts against everyone, he proved so faithful to them that he kept their enemies bound to him by complete affection, and among the divided rulers alone enjoyed the peace of both. [Note: “Among the divided rulers: Odoacer and Theoderic.”]

Whatever one gave, he applied to the advantage of the other. Through the respect and sweetness of his own person he so moderated the giver’s disposition that the giver was not at all inflamed if his enemy received some benefit from him through the bishop. He was the man around whom even those who were fighting preserved concord, and whose peace the wars did not disturb.

If we come now to the fact that his daily kindness sustained the raiders themselves and supplied them within the city with the necessities of food, even though outside they had destroyed his estates through continual devastation—when so many thousands of men demanded different things at one and the same time—he refreshed them with kindness, humbled them by his address, and fed them with gifts.

If the children or wife of any man had been seized and held by enemies from one side or another, they were immediately restored to their own people through the price of his supplication, whom an outpouring of gold could not have redeemed. He was most suited to the king and revered above all the holy men, so that whenever permission to wage war had made Romans among his men captives, he immediately restored them to the king, understanding that the king was enriched only by the freedom of others.

Furthermore, I cannot enumerate how many bands of the subjugated he restored to their own soil, or how many burdens he took upon himself so that they would not be harassed. If I were to recount the insolence he endured from his enemies, the attacks with which he struggled, and the storms of the worst men that he despised by his courage, my tongue would not suffice for these things. It is pleasant to select certain definite instances when everything you might report is worthy of admiration. Under such a cross he spent three years, revealing the secrets of his sorrows to God alone, from whom he secretly requested that assistance be supplied to him.

After the Goths had departed [Note: “The city of Ticinum was handed over to the Rugians.” In the year 493.], the city of Ticinum was handed over to the Rugians, men savage beyond all human ferocity, whom the harsh and bitter violence of their spirits urged on to daily crimes. They thought that a day had been lost if, through some chance interruption, it had passed without a crime committed by them.

Yet the most blessed bishop softened them with the honey of his words, so that their savage hearts submitted to the authority of the priest and learned to love those whose breasts, as we know, had always been devoted to hatred. Through his merit their natural perversity was changed, as a foreign root of affection was planted in their dishonorable minds.

Who could believe without profound astonishment that the Rugians loved and feared a bishop—both catholic and Roman—when they scarcely deign to spare kings? Yet he spent almost two full years with them in such a way that they departed from him weeping, even when they were returning to their parents and households.

After the wretched and disastrous war had been brought to an end, and the victor was he whose sword, stripped of its sheath after the triumph, no one saw—he who had ended the presumption of his army together with the battle—the revered bishop immediately began to consider the restoration of his city. In order to fill it as soon as possible with worthy inhabitants, he looked ahead by spiritual deliberation and counsel. Although, through his entreaty, no storm of temporal calamity had driven it into desolation, he nevertheless thought it insufficient if, after the ruin of all the cities of Liguria, Ticinum rejoiced while content only with its native inhabitants. He began to select from the citizens of the neighboring cities every little flower of their population and, like a diligent cultivator, to bring already-tested plants to his own gardens, from which a prudent and capable possessor might gather the most suitable fruits. [Note: Schott and Bolland: “diligent.”]

Meanwhile, the sudden decision of the most excellent King Theoderic occupied his mind: he resolved to grant the right of Roman freedom only to those whom tested loyalty had joined to his party; but those whom some necessity had separated from it he ordered to be deprived of all liberty to make wills and to arrange their affairs and wishes. When this judgment had been promulgated, and the laws had been trampled upon in this manner with regard to very many people, all Italy lay subject to a lamentable form of justice.

[Note: “We return again to him.” This was Epiphanius’s third embassy, in which he had as his colleague Laurentius, bishop of Milan, to Theoderic, concerning the repeal of the law that he had enacted against those who had supported Odoacer’s side.]

They went again to him who was accustomed, with a physician’s hand, to aid public wounds, from whose fountain the heat of sorrows had often been extinguished. Since he said that he alone could not suffice to bear so great a burden, the venerable Laurentius, bishop of Milan, was likewise asked to help. They set out together for Ravenna and arrived there together, having been received with honor. When the way of bringing their case had been opened to them, blessed Laurentius deemed it necessary that the opportunity to plead should first be given to the man whose tracks had been worn down by the laborious path of frequent embassies, and whom the military dust had more than once made rough as he hurried along journeys of this kind. He began the public petitions in words such as these:

“Most invincible prince, if I were to recount in order how divine favor has raised your prosperity through countless successes, you would acknowledge—and remember—that, though sparing in your requests, you have always received from our God greater benefits than you dared to hope for. It is sufficient, however, to relate this one thing, though it is the greatest: that here, before you as prince, we are pleading the causes of your servants, in the very place where your enemy used to rejoice in possession of this throne. You owe very much to Christ our Redeemer; what we ask for these men he himself has bestowed. We must beware lest the author of the gift be offended if we do not love what he has granted.

“For a long time I have held back my confidence. I am pleased to proceed point by point through what I have learned by report and what I have seen added to you by the aid of Divinity. [Note: Schott and Bolland: ‘by divine assistance.’] You know what you promised yourself you would do when you were pressed by the close-packed ranks of your enemies, and when the hostile trumpet resounded around the walls of the little city of Ticinum. [Note: The same authorities: ‘the sound of the hostile trumpet.’] You know how, though they were superior in number, the enemy could not stand against you, since an invisible power from heaven fought beside you alone. He dared to attack you who reckoned your armies by mere estimation; yet the entire apparatus of war was unable to bear the weight of your consolations.

“How often the very air served your interests! If you recall it, the clear skies fought for you, and the vault of heaven poured down rain according to your desire. Who dared resist your right hand when it fought together with heavenly grace? How often did your enemies fall beneath the swords of their own companions? How often did he conquer for you who was fighting to the advantage of your enemies?

“Therefore repay these heavenly gifts with a corresponding devotion toward men. The holocausts of a mystical offering are the tears of suppliants not being despised. Consider especially in what circumstances you succeeded to the kingdom. If, as is evident, wickedness expelled those men, their misfortune must necessarily serve to instruct those who come after them. The ruin of predecessors teaches their descendants; an earlier fall is always a warning for the future. He does not fight without an example who considers for what reason his predecessor was expelled.

“Relying on this, your Liguria, poured forth in supplication together with us, asks that you grant the benefits of your laws to the innocent in such a way that you absolve the guilty. Our God’s mercy is slight if injury does not follow only those who are free from guilt: to forgive sins is heavenly; to punish is earthly.” After this he fell silent.

But the most illustrious king began to speak. As he spoke, fear constricted the astonished hearts of those who awaited his decision:

“Although, venerable bishop, I revere you for the radiance of your merits, and although in the time of confusion you had stored up with me many benefits, which it is fitting for you to enjoy now that tranquility has been restored, nevertheless the necessity of ruling by which we are confined does not everywhere open access to the mercy you recommend. And amid the two concerns of a nascent empire, practical advantage drives out the sweetness of compassion. [Note: Schott and Bolland: ‘harsh matters.’]

“My affection rests upon the testimony of heavenly examples. [Note: The same authority: “assertion.”] We read that a prince offended who did not remove from destruction an enemy appointed by heaven; leniency deserved the punishment that severity could have inflicted; the man who shrinks from exacting vengeance receives vengeance himself. He either diminishes or despises the force of divine judgment who, when he has conquered his enemy, spares him. Those whom it is clear have not followed grace must be restrained by justice. He transmits vices to posterity who forgives present crimes.

“As for what you say about the patience of our Redeemer, that truly embraces those whom the austerity of the law disciplines. No sick person has ever been brought to the fullest cure by a physician except by one who first cut away the rotten limbs with iron and brought out from the innermost recesses of the body the hidden filth. He who allows criminals to pass unpunished encourages the innocent to crime.

“Nevertheless, since earthly powers cannot resist your prayers, to which heavenly powers give their assent, we shall forgive all generally for their error. No one’s head shall be struck down by guilt, since you can also plead before our God that criminal minds may abandon the perversity of their purpose. Yet a few whom I have learned to have been instigators of evil I shall deprive only of residence in their own places, lest perhaps a need arising again should find neighbors to nourish it, and wars, aided by the successes of evil men, should rise again.”

When the most excellent king had said this, he ordered the illustrious Urbicus, Quaestor of the Sacred Palace, to be summoned. [Note: “Quaestor,” or an official equivalent to a quaestor. What Leo was to Euric and Laconius to Gundobad, Urbicus was to Theoderic.] He bore all the burdens of the palace and, through his eminent probity, surpassed Cicero in eloquence and Cato in fairness. [The text has *sustentans*, “supporting,” corrected from the OCR reading *su tentans*.] The king commanded him to publish a general pragmatic sanction of pardon. Urbicus, entirely prepared for every act of kindness, immediately composed it with such brevity and clarity that even those classes of offenses thought to have been reserved were recognized as abolished.

Meanwhile, the most excellent king ordered the venerable priest Epiphanius to be summoned in private and addressed him in these words:

“Understand, glorious bishop, from the very judgment of our decision its weight: although there appear to be so many bishops within the circle of the kingdom, you above all have been chosen in this great matter as though you alone were suitable. Nor does this opinion deceive those who judge such things, diminished as it is by your merit. You alone are rightly thought worthy; by your splendor, as the light of the lesser stars is dimmed by the lunar spheres, the rays of lesser light are darkened by the radiance of your conscience. Who would seek a lamp for the night where the sun’s brilliance shines forth? Who would seek the protection of a candle where the pyre of faith is kindled in unceasing flames?

“Finally, I ought to direct such a man as the recipient will gladly hear. You see that every region of Italy has been deprived of its native cultivators. In my sorrow, the fertile field brings forth thorns and unauthorized plantings instead of crops; and Liguria, that mother of the human harvest, whose numerous offspring of farmers once sustained it, bereft and sterile, displays a barren sod before our eyes.

“The land addresses me wherever I look: its face, fertile with vineyards yet uncombed by plows, makes me sorrowful. O grief! No moisture is poured upon the lips of those whom antiquity called Oenotrians because of their abundance of wine. Although the cruel Burgundian, King Gundobad, inflicted these things by ravaging Liguria, carrying many thousands of captives away to Lyon and leaving the fields almost empty of cultivators, we nevertheless have committed the wrong if we do not correct it. [Note: To redeem these captives, a fourth embassy was entrusted to Epiphanius, at his own request with Victor, bishop of Turin, added as colleague, in 494.] We cease to succor our ravaged homeland, while gold is kept stored up among us? What difference does it make whether we incline the minds of our adversaries by money or by the sword? To offer the enemy what can capture his mind is victory; to conceal it is defeat.

“Take up, therefore, with Christ’s help, the burden of this labor, so that we may share a reward in the heavenly promise. For a new title of praise is added to your distinguished honors: through your hands to triumph without bloodshed over the assaults made upon us. [Note: Schott and Bolland: ‘over our attackers.’]

“Their prince is Gundobad, toward whom long-standing acquaintance has instilled reverence for you, and whom an excessive desire to see you urges forward. Believe me: your appearance will be the price of Italy’s captives. I shall think those whom I desire to be redeemed if such a redeemer comes to those lands. How greatly are the eyes of those to whom we present you overcome by this favor! But why do I delay the hands that are asking for fields? I promise you the restoration of Liguria; I promise joy to the soil, and, after a transalpine journey, returning fertility. The gold is advanced to you for this emergency, in exchange for which such an envoy will act.”

To this the light of the bishops, Epiphanius, replied:

“How greatly, venerable prince, you have filled my heart with joy! If speech could encompass it, I would pour forth uninterrupted and continuous words in proportion to the wealth of your merits. But that my speech is denied its proper outcome is shown by the tears of joy which exultation has now brought forth as daughters of grief. Understand, therefore, that in returning thanks to the king, both on our behalf and on his own, I can feel more than I can express.

“Shall I recall that you have surpassed all former emperors in justice, in the practice of war, or—in what is greater than these—in compassion? You have cause to reproach the rulers of our nation: you redeem those whom they very often either allowed to become captives or themselves made captive.

“We read that David, as an outstanding example of praise, attained such nearness to heaven above all because, when Saul his enemy was delivered into his hands, he spared him and took a fragment of his garment as witness to the power granted him—thereby proving both his opportunity and his purpose. O good God, with what great reward do you receive this deed: the man who, having been exalted by you for the blood of one man whom he spared, now labors for the freedom of so many oppressed people!

“Complete what you have begun without delay, and gladly bring the offering of your prosperity. Spur me on, though I am ready, lest in offering so fragrant a sacrifice I be held back by an obstacle of delay. It will belong to Christ our Redeemer to grant—as we infer from future deeds—that you may truly offer your holocausts through my hands.

“I ask, however, that by your gracious indulgence Victor, bishop of the city of Turin, be added as my companion and fellow participant in this journey. In him there is clearly a summary of every virtue; with such a companion beside me, I confidently answer before our God that no result will be denied to our petitions.”

When he heard this, the most illustrious king gave his assent. The awesome bishop, having said farewell, departed.

At once money to be carried for the redemption was designated and received. Epiphanius set out and came swiftly to Ticinum.
