Although it was still winter, and the month of March imposed icy restraints upon the rivers, while the snow-white ridges of the Alps threatened death to those crossing them, the deadly cold and clods hardened by frost were overcome by the heat of faith: the man whose foundation the rock had made firm never slips upon ice.

Having arranged provisions for his journey, he departed. You would have said that necessity was driving forward everything that could have held him back. He allowed no delay even for taking food. Although the perilous road disturbed each of those who traveled with him, he alone did not know how to fear the dangers, because a sure hope of life accompanied him.

Meanwhile, the report of his coming—always the forerunner of his journey and careful in its preparations—went ahead. It filled the Gauls with such accounts of his distinction that their present circumstances seemed to be thrown into confusion as though a heavenly divinity were arriving. Every age and sex came together; and those whom long distances had separated from the vicinity of his route were brought near by the ardor of their hearts.

Everyone offered whatever precious object he possessed; and if he possessed nothing, he bought something elsewhere. [Note: Bolland: “he bought it for his country.”] Everywhere the homeland poured forth an abundant generosity. [Note: Schott: “everywhere in the homeland, everywhere, and so forth.”] The tables of the travelers were heaped with food that had not been purchased; and foreigners consumed without payment the provisions that the inhabitants themselves could not possess except by buying them. Then, wherever he found needy people, he distributed among them the gifts that had been given. At home and abroad he fed the wretched; and it was impossible for anything brought to him to be withheld from the use of the poor.

With remarkable speed he entered Lyon, where Rusticus then held the episcopal chair. [Note: See Sirmond’s first annotation on Avitus, Letter 24. Rusticus was the successor of Patient, to whom a letter of Sidonius survives, and the predecessor of Stephen, to whom Ennodius wrote in Book III, Letter 17.] He was a man who, even in the prefiguration of a secular title, had always displayed himself as a priest, and who, under the guise of the law court, had acted as governor of the Church. Filled with an abundance of spiritual joy, he came to meet Epiphanius across the Rhône, inquired into the reason for his journey, and explained the king’s intentions.

So that Epiphanius might not be caught unprepared by the subtlety of objections or answers, he rehearsed within the inner chamber of his heart the arguments of the coming contest. When Gundobad, lord of that land, learned that he had arrived, he said to his attendants: “Go and see the man whom, both for his merits and his appearance, I have always associated with the person of the martyr Laurentius. Ask when he wishes to see us, and when he commands, invite him.”

Immediately the entire crowd of Christians attending the prince gathered around him. They were filled with abundant wonder that the fame spread through so many tongues revealed him to be so much smaller in person than it had represented him, although it had been extensive. Yet no poverty of speech could ever suffice for the fame, however much richer than fitting it might be in all other respects.

The day for seeing the king was appointed. When Epiphanius entered, he greeted him, and both rejoiced in seeing each other. He gave the distinguished man Victor permission, if he himself ordered it, to begin the embassy. Victor referred the entire burden to Epiphanius, being, as he was, entirely ready for all humility.

Immediately our bishop, the glory of Italy, began to address the king in these words:

“Your immeasurable love, most excellent prince, imposed upon me long ago the task of undertaking, against nature and season, the battles of this journey and of not fearing the dangers of the crusted mountains. There, when water has been compressed into a metal-like hardness, the coagulated liquid threatens death. I crossed snowy mountain passes during months alien to travel; I set my feet upon paths whose force of cold had bound them in their own places. Finally, I did not fear death, so that I might bring you swiftly the reward of eternal light.

“I have been appointed to give testimony before two excellent kings in heaven, if you mercifully grant what he mercifully requests. Divide the gift of the Lord’s promise on equal scales; when both of you possess more, no one will lament a loss. Contend, unconquered leaders, and surpass one another by carrying out these mystical commands. In this contest the victor will receive the prize in such a way that the defeated will not lose his reward. Follow my counsel, and both of you will stand superior, both equal.

“He wishes to redeem captives; you, without payment, return them to their native soil. Believe me: no one will receive a richer or greater reward in this matter than the one who receives nothing. The reward of one side will be deprived of its profit, and another’s gain will pass to your advantage, if you decide to give as a gift those whom it is glorious to sell.

“How great a loss would be inflicted upon the divine promise by offering gold in this affair, if the captives are released—or how great a poverty would be brought about if the gold is accepted! Disdained money will make your armies rich; acquired money will make them poor.

“Hear the voices of the Italian suppliants and serenely accept the prayers of those who place their hope in you. Hear Italy, which has never been separated from you and which places great confidence in the compassion of your heart. If it could speak with one voice, it would say:

“‘How often, if you remember, did you offer your armored breast for me to my enemies? How often did you fight by strategy so that wars might not creep upon us? [Note: Bolland: “might not steal upon us.”] So that none of them might be led away captive in any part of the world?

“‘Those whom you now hold captive you yourself nourished. Your valor dealt me a deceitful benefit if, having protected some as a guardian from foreigners, it then attacked them. Who, fettered by chains, would not shed more abundant tears before a harsh fate, when his liberator was driving him into such a condition? Who would withdraw when the clash of your weapons was heard, in which they had found the safest refuge in their necessities?

“‘A noble matron, with her hands pressed against her neck, when she was being dragged to chains, promised herself that you would be her avenger. A virgin entrusted her chastity to you, believing that it could displease you if she lost it through the plots of a violator.

“‘In short, they were captured whom no one found fleeing. The laborious stock of farmers, and offspring trained by hard hoes, whom unworked simplicity feeds upon their own land—when their necks were being bound with thongs and their palms were being conquered by tight bonds—cried out nothing else in their defense:

“‘“We know, and clearly recognize it: are you not our Burgundians? See to it that you do not excuse before the merciful king what you are doing, or suppress these crimes in the customary manner of city-dwellers. How often have the hands you presume to bind paid tribute to the common lord?”’ We know that he did not order these things to be done.”’

“The wretched used this authority as their consolation. Yet the confidence they placed in your integrity caused many to be killed when, once captured, they answered too proudly.

“Return the survivors to their homeland; return them to their origin; return them to your glory. The ancient lord loves the province that the present lord also embraces. Release them, even to another’s dominion, so that those who live there may recognize themselves as yours. For we render too little gratitude to the rule of one whose mercy we owe nothing.

“Make fertile again that Liguria, which you know so well, now empty and covered with thorns, and fill it with cultivation. How indebted it is to your gifts it will understand if it ever comes to recognize its own face. It has always been natural to you to show indulgence to suppliants, just as it has been natural to crush the proud. Thus, in both matters, you will gain mighty triumphs: there by the sword, here by restraint.

“Be moved by the tears of our people. [Note: Schott and Bolland read: “to move [you] by the tears of our people.”] May a legitimate heir increase for you in the succession of this kingdom, and may, through the hope of an adult offspring, [Note: The same authorities: “progeny.”] you return to the governance of the Burgundians. Although you attribute this to God, add also that you do not bestow this favor upon foreign men.

“The lord of Italy is already joined to you by the bond of kinship. Let the bride of your son be Latin generosity, the release of captives; let him offer his betrothed a gift that Christ also may accept.”

When he had said this, after reminding his holy colleague Victor, he rose. Weeping, they bowed their heads as far as the royal breast, together with all those standing nearby.

Then the most excellent king, rich in speech as he was, wealthy in the resources of eloquence, and a fluent advocate, replied in words such as these:

“You do not understand the laws of war, persuader of peace, and you disembowel the conditions settled by the sword as though you were an author of concord. The law of combatants is what you call an error; hostility does not know the restraint that you, radiance of Christian light, display. No one attaches moderation to battles, yet you, distinguished governor, raise it by the brilliance of your speech.

“It is established among combatants that whatever is not permitted is then permitted. Perhaps the peace you have described may vindicate these things: he assists his enemy who has not harmed him. Little by little the adversary is cut down from the mass of his kingdom, whose imperial roots are severed by force. [Note: Bolland: “by turns.”]

“I repaid the ruler of those regions for the insult that you think was inflicted. Deceived by the appearance of a treaty, I did nothing more earnestly than recognize open enemies in what was a matter of caution. Nevertheless, may divine assent grant that the treaty established between us be preserved through a long age. Those regions will find in me a constant friend, although they perceived me to be destructive to them while the dispute lasted.

“You, holy men, return without distress to the homes in which you dwell. Once I have examined what it is fitting for me to provide for the benefit of my soul and my kingdom, I shall pronounce my decision.”

When they heard this, the bishops withdrew.

But the king summoned Laconius, to whom he had always safely entrusted the reliability both of matters and of words [Note: Ennodius wrote three letters to him that we have seen.], and whom both the distinction of his birth and the curule offices of his ancestors had exalted through the marks of supreme integrity. He consulted him whenever he contemplated anything pious and religious. Just as nobility is not joined to vices, nor is the luxury of nature bound to seductions, so whenever the king wished to do something gracious, he urged that it be doubled once Laconius had been brought in.

“Go,” said the prince, “Laconius, and spread all the sails of your wishes. The priest and blessed Epiphanius were gladly heard by us; when he spoke before us, the tears that reveal the heart testified that you had been deeply moved by his prayers. Go, and pronounce the judgments I have stated with a full heart, by which you may break through the very hard bonds of that agreement.

“Let all Italians whom fear of our Burgundians made captive—those whom the necessity of hunger brought there, those whom fear of dangers brought there, and finally all whom the consent of their own prince permitted or assigned—be set free by us. Let only a few, whom the heat of battle at that time snatched from the dominion of their adversaries, receive at least some amount of payment for them, so that the detestable circumstances of those battles may not become hateful to the men who, after enduring their dangers, would otherwise feel no profit from them.”

After the revered king’s command, that tireless man unfolded, with verbal dexterity, the various forms and conditions of the pardon, and carried the documents to the distinguished bishop. Epiphanius received them with the devotion he had so greatly desired and warmly embraced the bearer of so great a gift.

When the report became known, such a multitude of these people, now free, suddenly appeared that you would have thought even the countryside of Gaul had been deserted of its inhabitants. I myself am a witness to this, since through my hands the written certificates elicited by the priest’s order showed that four hundred people from the single city of Lyon had been released to return to Italy in one day.

We learned with certainty that the same thing had been done repeatedly throughout the individual cities of Sapaudia [Note: “Throughout the individual cities of Sapaudia.” Sapaudia had long before been granted to the Burgundians after their famous defeat and Aetius’s victory. Prosper Tiro writes in his *Chronicle* that Sapaudia was given to the remnants of the Burgundians to be divided with the native inhabitants. It is now called Savoy and retains only part of the ancient Sapaudia. In earlier times it extended farther, since in the *Notitia Dignitatum* of the Western Empire Ebredunum, chief city of the Maritime Alps, is placed in Sapaudia, as is Cularo of the Allobroges, now Grenoble.] and of the other provinces. Thus more than six thousand souls whom the prayers of the most blessed man alone had freed were restored to their native lands. As for those who were redeemed with gold, I could not ascertain their number exactly, since many of them were also rescued by flight. In this way the opportunity to pass over for the liberation of all the subjugated proved sufficient.

After that mass of money had been spent, the necessities of redemption were immediately supplied by Syagria, who was the treasury of the Church there. [Note: “Her life requires a lengthy narrative; it is enough, however, that from her deeds it may be recognized how far they surpass words.”] The most distinguished man among the Gauls, Avitus, bishop of Vienne, also gave assistance. [Note: Avitus of Vienne, renowned for learning and piety, is called by all his names, Alcimus Ecdicius Avitus, in his own letter dedicating his poems to his brother Apollinaris, bishop of Valence, prefixed to the codex of Saint Victor, in these words: “To the holy lord in Christ, most devout and most blessed bishop Apollinaris, Alcimus Ecdicius Avitus, his brother.” Sirmond later published this letter among the works of Saint Avitus in a somewhat more corrected form.]

“Recently, after a few of my homilies had been gathered into one body, I entered upon the risk of publication at the urging of friends. But now, since you advise me to greater things, I proceed with hardened forehead into the high boots of a more reckless daring. For you command that if anything written according to the law of meter on whatever subjects is found, it should be dedicated to your name under the designation of a little work.

“I recall that I said some things in verse, so that, if they were arranged, the multitude of epigrams could have been compressed into a volume of no small size. While I was considering doing this, preserving the order of subjects and times, almost all of them were scattered by that notorious necessity of confusion. Since it would have been difficult to seek them out individually, or impossible to find them, I cast from my mind those whose arrangement or recovery from dispersion seemed burdensome to me.

“Later I did discover certain little books in the possession of a family friend. Although they correspond to their proper names and titles, they also touch upon other subjects as the opportunity afforded by the material presented itself. Since you command it, these works, obscure though they are, will at least be illuminated by your name. Nevertheless, however severe or learned a man may be, if he does not preserve the style of the proposed religious subject according to the law not less of faith than of meter, he can scarcely be suitable for poetry.

“For the license of lying, which is equally granted to painters and poets, must be driven far away from the sequence of historical matters. In composing a secular work in verse, a man is called more skilled in proportion as he has woven falsehood more elegantly—or, to speak truly, more foolishly.

“I now say nothing of those words or names which we are not permitted to use frequently even in the works of others, let alone write in our own; they are of great value to poets for expressing one thing through another. Therefore, in the judgment of secular people, who will attribute it either to ignorance or to laziness that we do not use the license of poets, we have undertaken a work more arduous than fruitful and have sharply distinguished divine judgment from human estimation. For in affirming any matters, or even in explaining them as far as ability permits, if one must sin in some respect, it is safer—as a cleric says—for pomp not to fulfill the rule than for the rule to be fulfilled at the expense of truth, and safer to stumble in the step of art than in the footprint of truth.

“For freedom of expression is not excused by the commission of sin. If people will be compelled to render an account for every idle word they have spoken, it is readily understood that the more dangerous offense is to injure what, having been treated, pondered, and set before the laws of life, is presumed upon by the law of speech.”

From this letter we learn that homilies were also published by Avitus. Indeed, only one now remains, concerning the Rogations instituted by his predecessor Mamertus. But we saw fragments of several others among the remnants of a very ancient book belonging to Jacques-Auguste de Thou, most illustrious president of the senate. One was preached at the conversion of Lord Sigisricus at Lyon, on the day after his sister had been received back from the Arian heresy; another in the basilica of the Agaunian saints, at the renewal of the monastery itself; a third at the restoration of the baptistery in his own city of Vienne; a fourth in the basilica of Saint Peter, which the holy bishop of Tarentaise founded; a fifth at the dedication of the basilica at Geneva, which enemies had burned; and others whose very inscriptions arouse an extraordinary longing for them and for the remaining works of blessed Avitus, which Isidore and Ado of Vienne enumerate. [Note: The preceding bibliographical material is editorial commentary on Avitus’s homilies.]

In Avitus of Vienne the petition found shelter, as though in the lodging of a bright house. What more need be said? Their gold accomplished for the most part the purpose of preventing the youth of Liguria from remaining longer in servitude among the Gauls.

Nor did the great man confine himself to one place in that region, lest perhaps the ferocity of the masters should prevent those living far away from being reached. He was at Geneva, where Godigisclus, the king’s brother, had established his residence. [Note: All the books write *Godigisclus*, not *Godigisilus*, as the printed editions of Gregory of Tours and others have it.] Following the reputation of his brother’s decision, Godigisclus made himself a partner in Avitus’s good works. [Note: Schott and Bolland: “form.”]

Soon such great ranks of the liberated were sent forth that you could see the roads far and wide alive with marching columns, returning with praise both of God and of the splendid bishop Epiphanius, through whose agency and labor they had been rescued. And lest our light should be deprived of the trophy of so great a gift, or the most beautiful spectacle be taken from their eyes, Epiphanius himself returned with them.

You would have seen a free multitude being led in heavenly triumphs, and the earth being moistened not with the blood of victims but with the tears of those rejoicing, as the leader of these companies mounted Elijah’s chariot and, by a four-horse course worthy of his merit, was carried off toward heaven.

The Macedonian prince Alexander, whom empty praise called the pacifier of the world, did not lead an assembly of captured peoples in this way, as Epiphanius brought these people back. Behold, from this we learn that the minds of armed men were overcome by holiness, and that a prince who had always offered his breast to lances yielded to prayers. From this the reader may recognize how much sharper speech was than the blade of iron: the sermon conquered where swords had withdrawn.

When, therefore, in the third month the bishop was returning to Ticinum with such a trophy, he came to Tarantasia. [Note: Tarantasia was once the name of a town and the chief place of the Graian Alps. So it is called both in the old *Itinerary of Aethicus* and in the homily of Avitus just mentioned. Today Tarantasia is the name not of the town but of the village itself and of the whole district of the Centrones. Thus the opposite happened there from what occurred in many other parts of Gaul: the town gave its name to the region, not the region or city to the town.]

There a certain woman was suffering from a severe affliction by an unclean spirit. Immediately, after receiving his blessing, she departed healed. He himself, however, appeared unexpectedly before his own people, who had not suspected that he was coming. He suddenly became visible, though scarcely anyone had believed that a rumor of his arrival could be heard.

But as soon as he returned, he was troubled by his customary concerns: he feared that those to whom God had granted release through him might be distressed by the possession of their own property, especially because of the consideration due to their noble status. Their calamity could have been more severe among their own people if, upon returning, they had endured an impoverished life and lost the sole consolation of mercy amid the hardships of their exile.

He immediately refused to go in person to the most invincible king Theoderic, lest, when placed before him, he might appear to demand repayment for his labor either in the form of a report of thanks or through the presentation of gifts. For the man who, after carrying out the commands of princes, personally announces what has been done seems to demand a return as though it were owed. This man, foreseeing the matter with all the keenness of his mind, eagerly wished to avoid it.

Nevertheless, he wrote and entrusted what had been done to letters, lest by remaining silent he be judged contemptuous, or by appearing in person he be called presumptuous and intemperate. How much more, then, did your absence accomplish, admirable bishop; how much did discovered humility command! [Note: Bolland reads: “obtained.”] Let those whom you made exceedingly rich from among the exiles say so.

Accordingly, everything that the singular bishop requested in writing from the most devout king on behalf of the wretched, he obtained without hesitation. The serene king supplied resources to the suppliant, believing that whatever benefit the redeemed and the poor received through Epiphanius could suffice as compensation for his labor.

After all who had been recalled had been granted their rights by the indulgence of the foremost prince, the admirable bishop considered himself to have discharged the burden of his troubles—when, before two years had elapsed, he was driven from the lap of the deliberate repose he had chosen, as a boat is driven from harbor by a storm brought upon it by others. For a burden of taxes scarcely bearable by the weakened and tottering shoulders of the Ligurians was being imposed. [Col. 0236B]

Again they hasten to you, comforter of the afflicted. [Note: [Col. 0236D] Same witness: “you are taught.”] You were to teach that it had been useless to restore citizens to their homeland if you were not present when they were endangered on their ancestral soil. And because the one who asked was never wearisome to you, you undertook the causes of the unfortunate and immediately prepared yourself for renewed burdens. You hurried to Ravenna to entreat the king on our behalf—a city you had fled lest anyone there should praise you after your Gallic honors. You overcame the threats of the sky and the perils of storms, as though still in the full vigor of life or fortified by bodily strength. Never did your limbs, however feeble, withdraw themselves from the service of your spirit: cold, rain, the Po, fasting, the voyage, danger, thunder, lodging without shelter on the riverbanks, and harbors scarcely possessing any land, were sweet to your virtue and welcome to its success. [Col. 0236C] [Note: [Col. 0236D] Baronius, from the Vatican manuscript: “consoled.”]

That most eminent king, who eagerly desired to see you, was saddened by your presence. By your arrival you explained our necessities before you spoke, and the tears of those who lived with you showed what had compelled you to come and what dangers you had overcome.

But when he had entered before the prince, he began to speak as follows:

“Understand, venerable king, with the customary tranquillity of your mind, the petitions of your servants. Experience instructs both me to ask for what is necessary and you to grant it. It is your law, unconquered leader, always to show mercy. You have always nourished the hope of intercession for the future, since you do not resist those who are present. The confidence of favors obtained has always opened the way for our supplication to further requests before you.

“Grant your Ligurians what you may bring forth; give what you may store up. Temporal indulgence is gain for the future. [Col. 0236D] It is the custom of a good prince to love fame together with virtue and to order his kingdom as though it were to pass to the descendants of his own stock. Unsteady rulers love only what they receive; the most steadfast prefer what they leave behind. Thus we entrust small seeds to the earth so that we may receive them multiplied: lawful interest, [Col. 0237A] as it were, tripled. The wealth of the possessor is the mark of a good ruler.

“Grant Liguria exemption for the present year—you who have brought back those who were supplicants among foreign peoples. Let your Clemency ask those standing here what an abundant present harvest we have enjoyed. No one lies to one whose servants can prove the truth.”

To this the prince replied:

“Although the weight of immense expenses urges us on, and although for the sake of their peace we continually bestow gifts upon embassies, nevertheless the force of your merits reverently intervenes in our deliberations. Whatever you have ordered must be done; everything you command gives pleasure. For we consider that whatever you yourself have taken away is added to our savings. You, who have from us many things that you may rightly demand, should not ask for anything as though it were incidental. Nevertheless, we shall remit two parts of the present indiction’s fiscal assessment, accepting only the third, lest either the narrowness of our treasury bring greater losses upon the Romans or your anticipated petition fail to carry home the joys of your country.” [Col. 0237B]

In such words the supreme bishop gave thanks to the aforesaid king, from whom he departed after saying farewell.

Alas, grief and lamentation! He hastened eagerly to meet everyone, as though with the devotion of a final service or last visitation. And although his house poured forth crowds of Christian people, he himself visited the innermost chambers of them all. No one dulled by the coarseness of the human mind was touched by so mournful a suspicion: no one understood that the departure of the man whom he saw through spiritual revelation was imminent.

He left Ravenna in snowy weather, such as usually drives people to seek shelter indoors, and traveled swiftly through all the cities of Emilia, as though hastening toward the shelter of the grave. [Col. 0237C] To all the priests stationed along the road he was generous, companionable, approachable, and, as it were, leaving behind an *exagella*, superior to himself.

[Note: [Col. 0237D] “Leaving behind an exagella,” that is, as I interpret it, a standard and example. They seem to have called a balance or weighing-scale an *exagella*, from the same source from which come *agina* and *exagium*. In an ancient inscription containing the edict of Apronianus, a *vir perfectissimus*, *sub exagio pecora vendere* means “to sell sheep by weight.” Zeno likewise, in Sermon 6 to the newly baptized, says: “You have an *agina*; make an *exagium*—weigh as you wish.” To make an *exagium* is to weigh; the balance on which we weigh is an *exagella*.] [Col. 0238D]

But as soon as he entered the city of Parma on that same road, a congealed humor entered his vital organs, which physicians call a catarrh. Penetrating into his very marrow, it served as the ruin of the public.

But why are you afraid, my discourse? Why do you shudder at the ship-wrecking rocks? [Note: [Col. 0238D] Others: “ship-wrecking.”] Whether you wish it or not—and even if only briefly—the death of one whose life has been described must be narrated, since his departure cannot be concealed by any lengthening of the book or by any expansion of published praise. And although the sailing vessel may avoid, with a roar, the jagged dangers that threaten like the dogs of Scylla and the wide jaws of Charybdis, his death does not escape shipwreck. Why do I fear to narrate the tears, which a continuous outpouring must always display? [Col. 0237D]

Thus, as he approached the city of Ticinum, now wretched, he appeared lively and healthy. Yet although he had entered amid every expression of joy at his return [Note: [Col. 0238D] Others: “of all.”], he immediately turned the rejoicing into tears, making it clear that he was ill that very day and more seriously ill on the next. As his sickness appeared greater with each passing day, the incompetence of the physicians contributed to it. [Col. 0238A]

The people stood murmuring and stunned, contemplating in one man the misfortune of the entire province and fearing the funeral of the world. On the seventh day, however, an unforeseen evil, an ineffable calamity, an inexplicable grief arrived.

But when the most blessed bishop saw that, having cast off the burden of the flesh, he would soon fly away to the pure radiance of the ether—for his constant saying had been, “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21)—he repeatedly recited with joyful spirit and serene countenance those verses of David:

“I will sing of your mercies, O Lord, forever; from generation to generation I will proclaim your truth with my mouth” (Ps. 88:1).

And also:

“Into your hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit” (Ps. 30:6).

He added, confident of his perfection:

“My heart is established in the Lord, and my horn is exalted in my God, my Savior” (1 Sam. 2:1). [Col. 0238B]

Thus, resounding in hymns and songs even in death, his heavenly soul returned to its own seat. He carried his fifty-eighth year [Note: [Col. 0238D] “Fifty-eighth.” The blessed Epiphanius died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February in the year 497, before completing his fifty-eighth year of life. He therefore seems to have been born in 439 and made bishop in 467.] to the tomb and completed thirty years in this priestly mode of life—one which, reader, even if you consider it only as sketched in excerpts, is before you.

For I must not pass over in silence the fact that his holy remains, until the third day, when they were known to have been buried with the highest reverence, appeared to the eyes of all clothed in such light and beauty that the radiance of his life seemed to mark the face of the dead man, and it was believed that the glorious vessel, in which the treasure of the great King had truly been enclosed, had already received the glory it had laid aside. What rivers of tears were shed there, what lamentation, I shall leave unspoken, lest after so many years and the passage of time a writer should inflict fresh grief. [Col. 0238C]

Every mother who came there cried out that her son had been delivered by him; every wife, that her husband had been delivered; every sister, that her brother had been delivered; every unmarried man, that he himself had been delivered. Finally, amid that immense multitude and assembly of people, to say it boldly, there was no one in the whole world who did not owe something to his benefactions.

But let us now, I beg, restrain our mourning; let us relax the brow contracted by sorrow. He possesses exalted things with God, for whose death we grieve on earth. But what am I to do, when sobs impede the words of your healer, tears pour from my mouth, and everything I utter resounds with a groan? I understand that a consoler who is himself weeping can never properly come to one who weeps.

[Col. 0238D] I have offered these words to the holy Father and most learned teacher with suitable affection, though not with equal learning, so that I might reread a few flowers from his way of life—as travelers on a long journey customarily greet not everyone they encounter. You, mighty soul before our Redeemer, grant that, free from care and unburdened in heart, I may render you the pure praises that are owed to you, as one who is himself pure.

For the rest, do not abandon one who, after God, has his confidence in you; and make him whom you have marked with the titles of religion a participant in the divine promise. [Col. 0239A]

[Col. 0239]

## FOURTH LITTLE WORK

[Note: [Col. 0239D] On the life of the blessed Antony.]

This blessed man, whom Ennodius was the first of all to celebrate a few years after his death, is rightly claimed by three provinces as their own: Pannonia for his birth, Italy for the greater part of his life, and Gaul for his death and the sacred remains of his body.

He was born in Valeria of Pannonia and was first instructed by the blessed Severinus, an abbot, and afterward by his uncle Constantius, bishop of Lauriacum. From there he went to Italy. In the valley of Tellina, through which the river Adda runs before entering Lake Larius, he spent some time with the presbyter Marius. Then, moving away again, he settled beside Lake Larius, not far from the tomb of Saint Felix, the martyr of Como, and attained a most illustrious fame for his name.

To avoid it, he eventually sought the island of Lérins in our sea and there spent the course of his life for two years among the holiest monks of his age.]

## ON THE LIFE OF THE BLESSED ANTONY, MONK OF LÉRINS

[Note: [Col. 0240D] In the Roman Martyrology, 28 December.] (C)

### PREFACE

[Col. 0239A]

As trumpets rouse combatants, and as the speed of horses is urged toward a faster course by the iron-shod hoof, so the virtue of our ancestors, when it stimulates us, strengthens youthful talents. Whoever rereads the venerable exercises and deeds of the ancients burns with the desire for the fruit of discipline, inflamed by the proposed rewards of praise.

The image of earlier glory is held fast in the chain of languages so that it may reach later generations. Nothing that reading has received as a companion to honorable deeds is permitted to perish through the ages. Thus the endurance of eloquence overcomes the narrowness of mortal nature without the danger of confrontation; through it, the conduct of the best men, though the men themselves pass away, knows no setting.

The body will indeed be restored to its origin, and the spirit assigned by heaven will return to its own author. Yet those whose goodness has been entrusted to books possess a living death.

Perhaps a sterner interpreter will say: “A mind that has completed its course in the world rejects the sweetness of praise, and one released from the bonds of the flesh does not desire that the deeds he performed amid the uncertainties of the world should be recognized.”

But the human prison returned such men to their Maker without loss of freedom. While walking amid defilements, the soul, intent upon our God, doubled its brightness; and, following the lines of the heavenly commandments, it did not perceive the seductive error of this light. [Col. 0239C]

For us, however, let these things come to life again; for us, let them be preserved for our benefit. If we lack the zeal to pursue better things, we ought to receive an example from those who carry before them the torch of their way of life.

But you, venerable abbot Leontius, who imposed this work upon me, help me as I falter through your prayer, and enrich the dryness of my style with the rain of holy prayers. For, as I trust, you will make distinguished by its merits what you yourself commanded me to undertake.

It is easy for your blessedness to enlarge barren eloquence with the fertile dishes of innocence. Believe me: either the fault or the genius of my speech will reflect upon you. Unless you strengthen its substance by religious authority, it will seem that the sound judgment of your decision has chosen as less suitable the man to whom you entrusted the task of venerable labor.

## [LIFE]

[Col. 0239D]

Therefore, as I am about to recount the distinctions of the blessed Antony, I must first invoke the majesty of the Holy Spirit, so that he who made Antony rich in deeds may guide me with the reins of his tongue in explaining them, and may hasten to cleanse the filth of my lips with the burning coal of the prophet. Otherwise, amid the clouds of conscience, I might either make the light of his way of life poor through the most lavish praises or disfigure it through dry childishness. [Col. 0240A]

Blessed be the undivided Trinity, our God, who commanded his servant Antony, so exalted by such a wealth of virtues, to enter through his father Secundinus the gate of this light in the city of Valeria, beside the banks of the Danube.

Although he drew the radiance of his conscience from the splendor of his birth, he overshadowed the brilliance of his lineage with the rays of exceptional character. He surpassed the beauty of his blood by the brightness of his intellect, rising beyond the shining lamp of his family through the serenity of his deeds. [Col. 0240B] He became the victor over his own lineage, by which, through birth, he had surpassed everyone.

While he still hung at his mother’s breast, the grace of God, which had foreknown him, did not abandon him. Nor did the heavenly dispensation allow one whom it approved as full of merits to exist without the support of favor.

So that he would not break the institutions of his holy purpose through the indulgence of his parents, he was deprived of his father’s protection at about eight years of age. Soon, however, his youth, still ignorant of deceit, flew to the illustrious Severinus. As he soothed the boy with kisses, he read in him, as though they had already been accomplished, the good things that were to come. For he was a man for whose merits nothing was hidden.

He everywhere proclaimed with devout voice that Antony would one day be his companion. [Col. 0240C] I believe this was so that the announced hope might strengthen the first stages of the novice’s training.

But after the blessed man had been removed from human affairs, he devoted the beginnings of his life to glorious works while attached to the service of Constantius, at that time a most flourishing bishop. Constantius ordered him to begin his heavenly military service among the ecclesiastical scribes; for he was the uncle of our Antony.

Yet that teacher never softened the rigor of instruction through the law of kinship. Nor did he make the disciple secure through family connection, so that he should cease to fear; he granted him a teacher’s favor only by means of discipline. His care for his follower was as great as the judgments of the latter made necessary. Antony recognized his own merit in the face of his admonisher.

But now the completion of sins threatened destruction for the Pannonians. For the condition of that region, its substance cut off at the root, had declined headlong. Through the incursions of different peoples, the daily harvest of swords was cutting down the harvest of the nobility, and, as wrath ravaged them, was laying waste the fruitful lands of the human race. [Col. 0240D]

The Franks, Heruli, Saxons, and others were already practicing many kinds of cruelty in the manner of beasts. This diversity of nations, enslaved to superstitious rites, believed that their gods were appeased by human slaughter. They never trusted that their deities were favorable unless they had placated them with the blood of their equals. They believed that the anger of the heavenly powers could be halted by the shedding of innocent blood. [Col. 0241A] To return to favor with their gods, they had grown accustomed to offer up the deaths of relatives.

Those whom the title of a religious office identified, however, they sacrificed as more acceptable victims, judging that divine indignation would cease at the throats of the pious and that the place of offense would become an occasion of grace.

Amid these storms of the times, Bishop Constantius, with the land assigned to hostile peoples and therefore possessing no support in the world, was freed from human law. [Note: [Col. 0241D] Schott: “assigned to the enemy.”]

After his death, our Antony’s servants brought him, under Christ’s leadership, to the parts of Italy to which he had been assigned from heaven.

First he entered the valley of Tellina, which received that name. Nature enriches it with beauty, formed by the arms of mountains on either side, and the fertile soil is made abundant by the multitude of streams descending from fruitful peaks. It answers the desires of its cultivators, however greedy and immoderate, though it is not so heavily burdened with grain, so endowed with pastures, so adorned with groves, or so gladdened by rivers that the grace of the arriving person did not contribute more than the varied and distinctive beauty of the place itself. [Col. 0241B]

There he was joined to the presbyter Marius, who held power over unclean spirits. For such is the condition of things: the character of a new man is revealed by the companions he finds. One who is unknown by origin becomes illustrious through the affection of those who resemble him. The hidden mind is detected through associates; and although one is not permitted to assess fully the conscience of a newcomer, one is allowed to discover outsiders through their own companions.

When the blessed Marius examined him with those eyes by which minds are seen, and questioned the beauty of his inner man with hidden glances, he wished to associate him with the fellowship of the clergy and to dedicate him as a person distinguished by merits among ecclesiastical gatherings.

But Antony fled honor as though it were a cup of poison. He had always believed that power was subject to danger and preferred patiently to serve rather than to rule royally.

Yet, so that he might not absorb the contagion of association through prolonged contact with the allurements of human society, he chose a retreat not far from the tomb of the blessed martyr Felix, where the Larius lays aside its threats of Ionian marble. There, lest it wander farther, the restraints of the land resist it with opposing banks.

There a mountain, its summit inserted into the clouds, flashes forth and by its height surpasses the eye. But as it is lofty in size, so it is difficult to climb. For before our monk, no footpath had opened upon it; and across its precipitous rocks it had admitted no footprint of the human race, fear resisting every attempt.

Its sheer cliffs provided the wild beasts with a secure and lengthy dwelling, with no one to frighten them away. It was more pleasing to the beasts in proportion as it threatened the excursions of farmers more terribly.

The servant of God loved this place because the sole reason for its appeal was that it in no way courted the eyes. Taking with him from the world’s benefits nothing more than a small amount of vegetables and a hoe with which to work the soil, he dedicated himself to a path unknown because of the surrounding harshness.

Those peaks lost the law of nature’s wildness when Antony confronted them. After his entrance, opened paths became accessible to those who wished to follow. [Col. 0242A]

There he nevertheless found two old men whom their long habitation among the lairs of beasts had so mingled with the wilderness that no report about them reached the world. I seem to have fully recounted their life and knowledge when I openly described, without clouding it, the dwelling they had sought for fear of God.

Shortly afterward, one of them was taken away. Having laid aside the burden of the earthly prison, his happy soul recovered heavenly vitality. For at the time of his release, a fiery column was presented to the eyes of the blessed Antony, reaching all the way to heaven. I believe this was to show, through a symbolic fire, the faith of the venerable man and that ardor which consumed vices.

Then, while the worshiper of God there loosened the sails of his strength to the whole discipline of heaven and received through the folds of his soul and body the winds that drove out the chaff, I would rightly recount his vigils, fasts, and constant reading if I did not have more important things to remember. [Col. 0242B]

He never took food unless his little body was failing; never did he relax his concern through rest unless the duties of his office had been discharged.

But why should I unfold what instruments of perfection the perfect man possessed, or by what steps he climbed to the heights, when it has been clearly shown that he occupied the sublime? He knew how to pursue the outlines of discipline through varied labors without ever assuming arrogance from his labor. Although everything he did was worthy of praise, he believed that to be praised was a loss of virtue.

Thus the whole of his deeds shone with the light of reputation, yet nothing was offered for display. The discipline of his mind prevailed in his body, and his unpainted face depicted the anger that his soul had taken up against sins. You might have seen stern eyes turned against worldly crimes and Christ’s soldier waging tireless war against the blandishments of the age.

[Col. 0242C] When did that face ever relax its customary seriousness into laughter, or become weakened and broken by the frailty of joy from the rigor of its proper order?

Meanwhile, while he fulfilled the entire duty of a monk in all things as though it were sealed and inviolable, a certain man whom love for his bride had driven to crime, and whom passion and indignation had provoked to the shedding of human blood, believed that he could escape his conscience by changing his country. He thought that the innocence he had lost under the leadership of fury might be found in other parts of the province.

Disguised under an appearance of simplicity, he brought the murderer into the secret places of the wilderness, supposing that among men devoted to the service of God nothing about his actions would be apparent beyond his outward appearance. He feigned humility in his gaze and, through the artifices of a deceitful plan, concealed the filth of his crimes beneath the barriers of fabricated submission. [Col. 0242D]

It is difficult for anyone but God to detect whatever is wrapped in the signs of obedience. Thus abasement conceals wickedness, and crimes rarely burst into the light when their perpetrator has learned to bury himself beneath the disguise of obedience.

Yet the customary revealer immediately appeared and unlocked the hidden secrets of his conscience with the key of the divine voice. He addressed Antony in these words, teaching him to know more than a human being could know, and stripping bare the man who concealed a robber beneath a coarse garment:

“Beware of wishing to join a man guilty of so great a crime to the holy fellowship. Do not, through negligent judgment, attach a wolf to sheep or a viper to lambs. This man drove from its dwelling, by a sword cutting through the throat, a soul entrusted to God’s hands [Col. 0243A], and, binding life with the murderous frenzy of a brother, dissolved it from its dwelling while fastening bonds upon its jaws. Due destruction follows him, nor will one who spared no human blood be free from the yoke of punishment. Severity preserved toward criminals is mercy.

“Therefore, putting an end to sleep, drive away the enemy of the heavenly commandments, lest the spotless way of life of those who dwell with you be stained by the dark contagion of the newcomer.”

Immediately Antony obeyed the divine commands. He summoned the man, convicted him of lying, and, with stern face, pursued in every detail all that the guilty man had done.

[Col. 0243B] The man was terrified when he saw his crimes being recounted by someone who had no human witness to the deeds he had committed. He asked for provisions and tremblingly prepared his flight. Yet the vengeance that followed close behind immediately seized the guilty man and announced the expiation of his crime through the perpetrator’s death. Thus the word of the righteous man could not lack power.

Meanwhile, the holy man became known throughout the neighboring regions through the tongues of fame. To prevent fame from producing boastfulness, remedies were provided before the disease grew. For who, whether aged or weak, did not cross the rough paths of that journey under the guidance of devotion, when even illnesses could not hold back bodies whose desires gave them health?

Terrified by this frequent visitation, the blessed Antony believed that he must flee to the more secluded parts of the wilderness, lest the devotion of individuals become the mother of an unlovely arrogance, and lest the many-sided grace bestowed upon him give rise to the collapse of his stricter purpose.

Soon a retreat commended by a hanging cliff was chosen. There he spent many years alone, and truly as a monk, living without the company of the human race. The mountain solitude provided wild beasts as his companions. [Col. 0243C] The threatening growl and menacing murmuring of the bear and other beasts took the place of the fellowship of gentle conversation.

At that time, a particularly impudent bear, destined to add greater glory to him, entered and utterly destroyed the cabbages of the holy man, which were more luxuriant with tender leaves and seemed to rejoice with a kind of gladness for their master, so that no hope of the simple crop remained anywhere.

Antony struck the beast more sternly with his staff and ordered it to depart. He immediately compelled it to go to the other beasts as a witness to his power and a messenger of its suffering, so that the Lord’s faithful promise might be fulfilled—the promise that his followers would receive the obedience of every kind of poison and of all wild beasts.

Yet as the beast again advanced along the path assigned to him, it presented itself growling. Antony, by a single command, caused the creature’s disturbed passage to open and ordered it to abandon the barriers obstructing the road.

[Col. 0243D] But behold, once again, with swift wings, through the course of its betrayal, fame revealed to the servant of God the place where he lived, with different people forming different opinions about him according to the variety of their judgments.

Then it became plainly evident, through repeated encounters, that nothing obstructed those who wished to come: difficult places became level, fissures were made firm, and hanging precipices were not feared.

But, confronted by more dangerous ambushes, Antony opposed a stronger strategy lest the enemy seize him through arrogance, and lest, now aged, he lose what he had preserved through the virtue of his novitiate. For the devil’s struggle is fiercer against the strong, and he attacks with greater forces those who, having experienced his battles, have subdued him through the sweat of their strength.

[Col. 0244A] After considering everything within himself, Antony strengthened his spirit with a brief address:

“What are we doing, mind still weighed down by the burden of worldly cares, whom the bodily prison has not yet cast forth to your own author? You do not possess certain confidence in perfection while you are still enclosed in bodily frailty. Things that appear most secure are full of dangers. You recognize the allurements of your enemy while you are praised by everyone’s voice.

“See how many snares surround your labors. What we approach cannot remain hidden; hostile persecution reveals our hiding place. Let us seek the army of the saints and search out, with ardent zeal, that cohort of the island of Lérins. The adversary, who until now has attacked only one man, will fear him when he sees him stationed among a multitude hostile to himself.

“That battle-ready line is always vigilant and drives away the attacker pierced by many blows. As many wars as the devil has inflicted upon them, so many triumphs do they count. They do not fear whenever the announcement of Satan’s presence sharpens them for battle, once the trumpet has sounded. Daily combat has always made them learned and strong, just as prolonged peace makes men slack.” [Col. 0244B]

After these words, he left the cell to the brothers whom love for the aforesaid man had gathered there, and appeared unexpectedly at Lérins.

The face of the man, distinguished by the pallor of fasting, announced his remarkable merits. For while splendid emaciation revealed the radiance of his hidden self, his customary herald did not fail him: with abundant words and a rich account, it described the spotless beauty of his way of life.

Mixed with old men and with those eminent in their deeds, he understood that the lamp of his own achievements shone with no lesser fire. He measured the light of his own kindling when he saw that of another.

[Col. 0244C] It was as though, among the ornaments of heaven and the stars shining in full radiance, the brightness of a newly arrived star were added. They compete without envy, doubling their rays and surpassing the beauty of their novelty through an increase of light. One star commends its torch by a longer mane; another by a purer one. A more powerful flame enriches one; a flame purer through the spaces of night ennobles another.

Thus, wherever our Antony changed his place, discipline came with him from Christ.

Yet he took care that in that island, the nurse of saints, he should not appear to be preferred in honor, although he surpassed others in merits. He knew that what is planted in the root of humility rises to a hundredfold fruit.

Gentle toward the young, grave toward the mature, learned among the learned, humble in his conduct toward the simple, he gathered that entire legion of the Lord’s flock—distinguished by conduct and varied in nationality—as though it were one soul united in his affection.

There, for two years, becoming greater than himself, he laid aside the burden of this world. Victorious over the snares prepared by the ancient serpent’s cunning, he exchanged our day and the light of the present age for the acquisition of everlasting light. [Col. 0244D]

I am silent about how the splendor of death marked his life, lest, by arranging everything, I seem less to have narrated the truth than to have lingered upon the praises of the aforesaid man.

It is as though someone were to find a planted grove dense with foliage, then cut away a portion of it with a pruning knife, without removing the spirit of the forest by presuming to take only a little. I have reserved for narration the better deeds of our Antony, which I have not touched upon with my pen.

Perhaps I shall be overcome by the river of eloquence; no one will surpass me in affection for him. Let whoever follows me boast of the harvest of his expertise. No one will take from me the grace of the blessed man, since I was the first to undertake the explanation of his goodness. [Col. 0245A]

[Col. 0245]

## FIFTH LITTLE WORK

[Note: [Col. 0245D] *Eucharisticum*.]

Ennodius, freed from a serious illness, composed this little work to give thanks to God both for the restoration of his health and for the other benefits he had received throughout the rest of his life. Since it had no title—except that in one manuscript it was entitled *An Account of the Course of His Life*—we have given it the name *Eucharisticum*, following the example of Paulinus of Bordeaux, who composed a poem of the same subject and title. [Col. 0246D]

## THANKSGIVING FOR HIS LIFE

(C)

[Col. 0245A]

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

The oracle of the most learned doctor of the nations (2 Cor. 12:9) is that our weakness brings forth power, and that the soul grows strong through the crushing of earthly things: for the virtue that has flowed from the substance of the flesh hastens toward the spirit; and while our collapse shapes the heavenly man and prepares him to be placed in the divine citadel for the fruitfulness of the spirit, when bodies are without cultivation or harvest, it is sweet—and when diminution has come for the sake of increase, it is also sweet: one reaches the rich grace of God through the fasting and barren poverty of the limbs.

Therefore, after God, our weakness is owed to you, because we have risen through devotion to sublime things. The fever that fulfilled my vow, and the burning of my marrow that had to be embraced, taught me both to fear God at the departure of health and to rejoice in its return through him. Now, in our Author, the health of the mind rejoices, restored through sickness. Where is the pride in divine salvation, sought through mockery? Where is the haughtiness by which you believed every gift to be your own possession? Suddenly the strength of your vigor abandoned you, and, subjected to the weight of illness, you lay there with your neck crushed. After your prosperity fled and you conceived a belated repentance, you recognized that the prosperity in which you had prevailed belonged to our God.

Thanks to you, ruler and creator of heaven, who by a subtle dispensation and hidden paths of mercy both fashion our ways out of affliction and restore us to perfect virtue through loving wounds. We cannot come to your medicine except by the aid of a wound: when, as you strike us, we become accustomed to having the hardness of our heart softened, and when, by the noble and sweetest suffering of our troubles, we restrain the prompting of earthly worthlessness.

Behold me, that man who used to applaud myself over the long course of my good cheer; while I enjoyed enduring it, as though it would never be interrupted, I sought to know how death, the payment of sin, might come. For, lifted up by mad successes, I had placed myself among the company of poets, ignorant of the venerable calling. I delighted in songs fashioned from measured pieces and made firm by the ordered variation of feet. A flowing or delicate poem mingled me with the choirs of angels; and if it had happened that I was formed according to the preserved rule of distinguished verses, I saw beneath my feet whatever the vault of heaven covers.

Mortal life long rolled this folly about, and the sure blindness of misery exalted me through the false felicity of speech. How often, because of religion, did the crown of my head swell under the applause of those shouting, and, amid the enticements of that deceitful play of lips, did I believe that I ruled the breasts of those who loved me?

But you who dwell in heaven laughed at me (Ps. 2:4): you whom words do not charm, but purity; before whom we often speak while mute, and remain silent while crying out. Thus, while the charm of excessive ornament in the fields of rhetoric and poetry drove me on, I had departed from true wisdom, following a false one, desiring nothing else except to hunt after the ears of empty praise. There was a distaste for prayer, while I was held by the desire to purchase gain through public speaking.

Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death (Rom. 7:24)? The grace of God, granted through the service of a curable illness. For behold, suddenly pain entered the seat of my terrified soul and fed the secret places of my heart with a hostile fire. Then whatever there is in man grew old beneath continual heat, and the inward cooking revealed itself through the natural passages. For when arrogance was driven from its hiding places, although I still retained something of the superstitious man, I now had no hope of survival. This alone remained of the consciousness of one still alive: that I trusted that I could be healed by you, my God, whom by my error I had provoked to anger.

Yet that destructive teacher of disease did not lie hidden, having been thrust into the chambers of my entrails; nor was it content with concealment, but clothed me entirely in a cloud of livid color, so that whatever physicians seek with their fingers in other illnesses, the populace might see here as an evident sign of its correction.

My lovers were consumed by the long calamity; my enemies were consumed as well. Some were distressed by despair of my death, others by its imminence; the judgment of the whole city was united in the division of its concern. Meanwhile an eating fire ravaged me through its internal work and was nourished by the continuous efforts of those caring for me. For, as though it were feeding the disease, whatever was provided against it only increased it.

Then that philosophy of worldly pomp, crushed by the resources of Hippocrates and Galen, turned toward faithful assistance, at last perceiving that the blandishments of the world fade away and that a human being is not helped by human remedies. By then the pressure of this disaster had subjected me to itself for nearly two months. By then I was awaiting a transition in place of a remedy, and, remembering nothing pleasant about the enjoyment of this light, I desired to break off the delay, even if I had to go bearing the burden of sin.

Consider, readers, what scourges and tortures awaited me here: so that, through fear of present punishments, I might seek the penalties of Gehenna, and so that I might hasten toward the expiations of that immortal furnace and that terrible breathing place.

But the Lord was not lacking to me—he who kills and makes alive, who leads down to the underworld and brings back (1 Sam. 2:6)—he whose promise this is, in his majesty: “While the word is still in your mouth, behold, I am present, says the Lord” (Isa. 52:6; 58:9).

For when one of those who sat beside me, and who each day enriched my inequality by the expenditure of his resources, declared that he was exhausted and that nothing remained to be done, at once the hopelessness of my caregiver brought me hope of life. For the benefits of heavenly assistance are readier there where harmful services to the sick have withdrawn.

Immediately I was carried to the protection of the blessed martyr Victor—

**[Note: “Of blessed Victor.”]** Victor was a martyr of Milan, where Ennodius had his home and see. On this very cure, which he obtained through oil poured in by blessed Victor, see Book VIII, Letter 24. Gregory of Tours, Book I of the *Miracles*, chapter 45, recounts another benefit of the same martyr, different in fact and manner, bestowed contrary to custom upon our Apollinaris.

—whose aid I had often experienced; having prayed for the help of that most powerful man, I entrusted to God through him what had to be pleaded with tears.

It is enough to win his mercy if he always sets before his eyes the place from which he has taken us, and recognizes that we cannot easily pass with speed to the sublimity of his commands. Although through the second, benevolent nature of baptism whatever we have sullied from our parent, the clay, has been washed away, nevertheless, because while the enemy of our salvation disguises destruction under flatteries, he has seasoned vice with a sweet flavor—and while we are drawn onward by itching ears and the pleasure of tasting, “death enters through the windows” (Jer. 9:21)—where must we flee from his anger except to the mercy of the one who restored his returning son and the squanderer of his allotted portion? After an unclean fellowship had enslaved him among the pigs to the shameful food of husks, he recalled him to the white robe, the precious ring, and those riches of his father’s estate, as though he had always kept the commands (Luke 15:12).

I prayed through his chosen one that he would forgive me more of what I owed, so that, once released, I might display greater diligence. And, appealing to him with the handwriting of his promise and a chaste pledge, I asked that he also grant me to run with loving devotion through his commandments: because both what we are called and what we willingly accept when called belong to him, though they are credited to us as if they had arisen from us; he himself prompts both the willing of what is right and its accomplishment, yet, as though liable on account of our devotion, he grants the reward.

I also promised that, if through his grace he granted me an inclination toward more distinguished zeal, this confession would proceed from the hand of my tongue, and that I would sacrifice to him the fat of my little intellect from the gifts he had given it; that never would care for the stylus weary itself in the windy execution of worldly matters; and that I would renounce the remaining deformities with which I was reproached—provided that he himself made me willing to speak what he had inspired.

I begged him to be present in me through his benefits, and not to turn away from one whom he had mercifully cherished when deprived of the protection of his natural support, and whom he had preferred to those who rejoiced in the defense of their parents. And he granted these things not as a return for my innocence, but showed how much the fortunate and learned sinner owed to his grace.

For if, in accordance with mercy, he did not relax the guardianship of what is right, but terrified us as a judge rather than cherished us as a father, nowhere would the way of salvation be open, nowhere would there be a means of escape.

My God, my redemption: what comes to me from the things you have done with me, and what from the things I have done against myself? If these are compared, no moment is empty either of your help or of my fault. From your countless gifts to me, I would like to offer up one, and, passing over the multitudes of your benefactions, touch briefly upon a single one.

At the time when the most desired arrival of King Theoderic restored Italy, when everything was being devastated by his enemies in inexplicable destruction, and whatever survived the swords was being killed by hunger; when want was breaking through the lofty mountain strongholds and the citadels of fortified places, and fiercer poverty besieged those stationed in arms upon the heights—

**[Note: “I was about sixteen years old.”]** From this statement Ennodius’s age must be calculated. For if he was sixteen years old when Theoderic entered Italy, namely in the year 489, it follows that, when Valerius was consul—which was the year of Christ 521 and the last year of Ennodius—he was not more than forty-eight years old. Thus he did not exceed that number. Prudentius, by a similar method, disclosed both his age and the year in which he published his books, naming the consul in whose year he was born in the preface to the *Cathemerinon*, which ancient manuscripts rightly place at the beginning as the prologue to the whole work of Prudentius:

> Gray hairs suddenly crept upon the old man,  
> accusing me of having forgotten ancient Salia,  
> under whom my first day dawned.

Salia was consul with Philippus in the year 348. Add the fifty-seven years that Prudentius had lived; it remains that he wrote these words in the year 405.

I was about sixteen years old when, at that time, I was deprived of the comfort of my aunt who had raised me. I remained alone, poor in resources and deprived of counsel, with adversity alone able to offer me a remedy. So that I would not, among relatives—which is more bitter than the lot of captivity—ask freely for the means of living, you immediately extended your accustomed right hand, my defense; and you compelled a house, exceedingly rich in wealth and religion, not to reject my consolation.

I asked in marriage for the young daughter of a certain most noble person, well known to you. At once, with you arranging that she should come to you—as though this ought to have been expected of me—I was received. He granted me companionship with those pleasing to you, so that I might abound in provisions and, fleeing the dark places of unbelief, advance to your cultivation. Almost before I recognized my desolation, the things that were to be given to me began to be available.

Then, changed for the first time from a beggar into a king, I began to laugh at the evils of the afflicted and, as though prosperity had been owed to me, to neglect its author. Yet the rebellious and stiff-necked spirit was not immediately crushed by swelling against you. You prolonged the time of punishment, so that I might perhaps be pierced by remorse and, once healed, recognize who the giver was.

But because a human being does not correct himself after wrongdoing, and does not easily settle into brightness after stains, I persisted in that disposition by which I would fall, and I overcame your patience through the continuation of my sin. And because, although you are most merciful, you do not always restore justice, deprived of your protection I received that voice which was directed to the ears of our first parent: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3:9).

In my confusion I counted how many treasures of your mercy I had lost, and of what endowment I had been stripped. The value of the things granted by you was then understood, when they were perishing for me. I returned to myself and to my troubles, and wept because of joys that had been prolonged.

Immediately, though by another route, you came to my aid no less effectively. You arranged that, through the ministry of the Levites, I should be compelled to be healed, and that the burden of the honor imposed upon me should remove from me the weight that oppressed me. But after the pressure of the venerable dignity had released me, I had enthusiasm for the title, not a conscience concerned with the purity of action.

O mind drunk with poisonous rigor, instructed neither by examples nor by admonitions! If you lack the teaching of venerable books for your improvement, be formed by punishments; and unless you plunge yourself into the mire of destruction, you can learn from punishment. Yet may he who commanded this accomplish it in us, and, so that we may be equal to his commands, may he himself work with us what he enjoins.

These and many other things, as I have said above, I caused to be made known through the most trustworthy witness, the blessed Victor. No rest or delay slowed the undertaking: he accepted my petition, repeated it, and prevailed.

My advocate won this additional favor beyond what I had asked: that she who had shared with me the equality of marriage—

**[Note: “Religious with me.”]** Faustus of Riez writes that something similar happened to Ruricius in Letter 7: his most faithful Sarah, that is, his wife, was proceeding with him under the one yoke of Christ toward the common crown.

—that she should share with me the honors of a religious way of life and become the female leader of a glorious title.

Would that we followed the fragile sex in the strength of its spirit, and that by noble action we excelled in merit as much as she seemed to follow the appearance of feminine weakness. Through the strength of precious constancy she subdued the desires of the flesh and preserved a devoted chastity, not one imposed by force. While she stubbornly loved the observance of what was right, she compelled it to pass into nature. Would that she not be set before me at the severe hour of judgment, and that, while she proves strong in her weakness, I should prove fragile in natural strength!

Behold, Lord, I have recounted the very things you knew, and in this alone have I been faithful: that I did not seize what you held. Be present, King of glory, be present to the suppliant, and, according to your customary kindness, arrange what is to follow.

**Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.**

[Col. 0249]

# SIXTH OPUSCULUM

**[Note: “Didactic admonition.”]** At the beginning the author himself calls the work a didactic composition, and in Book VIII, Letter 28, an epistle of admonition. It is certainly worthy of being read and followed in the place of a pedagogue by all young men who are being formed in virtue and letters. The blessed Ambrosius and Beatus, to whom it was sent, are known from the letters. For he teaches in Book IX, Letters 2 and 3, that Ambrosius was the son of Faustinus. Although he does not reveal Beatus’s father’s name, he calls him a most noble and distinguished young man in Book VIII, Letters 38 and 39. Several letters of Ennodius are also addressed to him; and under the name of Ambrosius there is Controversy 6, *Against a Gambler*. Ambrosius appears to be the man who later became quaestor of King Athalaric, as Cassiodorus records in Book VIII, Letters 13 and 14. The verses of Adonius, however, are to be referred to Ambrosius and Beatus.

## THE DIDACTIC ADMONITION TO AMBROSIUS AND BEATUS. (C)

[Col. 0249B]

We serve God when we command what accords with his admonitions; for our yielding to your request in the zeal of charity consists of mystical precepts. You repeatedly demanded that a page of didactic composition be fashioned for you. Wishing to submit myself to the rights of many, I complied, because I shall see what kind of scrutiny is applied to my words; it is enough if you praise me in your desire.

Yet at the threshold of my writing I shall not be silent about what gives life. Hold God in the pure chambers of your hearts with the whole intention of your minds, and soothe him concerning yourselves through frequent prayers, never led away from him by any fornications of the soul or by any compromise. Cherish your neighbors, whom natural fellowship makes your companions; and do not rejoice in having done to others what, if done to you, would cause you pain. Whatever is desired is the fruit of this good.

For a long time the uncertainties of deliberation held me anxious: whether I should make my words public to you through a poem or according to the rule of an epistle. I chose to reveal my affection for you by both paths of expression, because strong eloquence suits one who commands, while the care of a gentler style comes to the aid of minds compressed by admonition. Therefore receive with kindness what has been demanded.

## PRAISE OF VERSES

[Col. 0249D]

Although whatever the parent Muse has uttered may be tender with the moisture of honey, and although a poem fashioned with delightful brilliance may captivate the teachable moments of the heart; although virtue does not always suit poetry, whose instructive law loosens its flowing course in obedience to the command of zeal—

yet we follow the manner of Pierian speech only so far as concern permits, as much as talent and the vigor of truth allow. We endure the inborn rigor of Christ’s soldier, avoiding an enervated course.

Therefore, fleeing at times the pleasantness of words, let us celebrate solid subject matter with its own voice, lest the manliness of the work feel the losses inflicted by enfeebled speech. The office of an admonisher does not reject my calling, because correction suits those who go before; and just as it is fitting that a torch of innocence be carried before those left behind, so reason demands that you also show in words the path they should follow. For it is established by the voice of divine exhortation: “Reprove the wise man, and he will love you” (Prov. 9:8). Nor does the secular author conceal the statement that those who wished the holy parent to be their teacher said:

> Let him be regarded, by right, on the brow of affection,  
> whom the kindness of correction asserts more readily  
> than the very nature of blood.  
> For to beget is testimony to desire;  
> to educate is testimony to devotion.

Therefore, hastening toward the citadel of the disciplines, truly love modesty, the mother of good works. From herself she gives birth, fertile yet virgin, to the various forms of the virtues, just as bold and corrupt shamelessness gives birth to the forms of vices. Let this voice exhort you to strive toward her.

## MODESTY

Dye your shining faces with rose-colored purple,  
and reveal the faith of your character in your face.  
By sprinkling spots upon your snowy countenance, become more beautiful,  
when, sweating, you bear your tender necks glistening with dew.  
Let your tongue claim nothing more for itself than the shape of your brow.  
Whatever you wish to love, obtain for yourself from here.

It is wrong to deny a hand to advice so sacred, since even she who speaks, adorned with the endowment of profitable beauty, either increases the goods of nobility or suggests them. Therefore always join chastity, the sister of modesty, to it. Let chastity, tempering the prejudice of age with gray-haired moderation, mingle the chill of foreign restraint with years swelling in ardor; and, having subdued the appetite for error, enticing the flesh with the flavor of holy conduct, let it make diligent attention to what is right appear in you, not compulsion.

This must nevertheless be secured through the chastisement of the belly, and it must not be nourished by the hostile errors of crowded dishes. Feasting, sought at great expense, demands even the loss of good merits, and by the same road come losses both of character and of resources. If this should stretch out its step toward you, it must be made to thunder with the following words.

## CHASTITY

I do not hesitate steadfastly to display an afflicted countenance,  
so long as the marks of chaste beauty shine before me.  
For fat bodies suffocate the subtle sense,  
and badly stuffed entrails trample their own minds.  
But for me the cross is a spear, the cross a shield,  
the cross also a breastplate.

**[Note: “And the cross a breastplate.”]** Instead of *thoraca*, that is, “breastplate,” the Basilean editors had printed *corona* in order to assist the faulty meter. But we preferred to follow the authority of the ancient books rather than appear excessively diligent in correction—especially since Ennodius abounds in examples of this kind: *thoraca*, for *thorax*, just as he uses *lampada* for *lampas*. Moreover, he shortened the first syllable, although it is long in θώραξ (*thōrax*).

With this I shall be covered; with this I shall strike; with this I shall strengthen the treaties of peace. This is my commander in war, by which, victorious, I trample slippery things. I detest the dread honey of poisonous desire.

You who run toward me, set childhood aside by your deeds;

and, young men, take for yourselves my gray-headed life.
