Admit her and adorn her with the fellowship of faith. For just as she holds the first place among reformed morals, so, stripped of her own endowments, she is not retained; nor is it right that what is clearly composed of many things should be occupied as though it were solitary. Noble garlands are not composed except from the spoils of many meadows; a single diadem is usually formed from various gems. The wondrous body of electrum has always been produced from numerous portions of metals.

Therefore, since nothing can precede faith, cherish it, and let it grow together in the harvest of diligence, lest the milky stalk of rich nourishment, cut down by an untimely sickle, perish. Let crippled promises therefore withdraw from your purpose, and let the thing that ought to be followed pass into nature through practice. Yet let this seem to suit you in the following words.

## FAITH

Whoever wishes to join earth to heaven,  
and leave behind the fault of the corrupt parent,  
let him seek me, steadfast honor and crown  
of a lofty gift.

He fears neither the dread tribunal,  
nor flutters among urbane powers;  
conscious of what is right, he holds amid the waves  
the pools of salvation.

Although the barbarian Gelon swells,  
and the Morinus barks in Parthian guise,  
he despises and shuts out  
everything the world’s fury whispers.

He enters the inner chamber of the exalted king;  
he remains secure amid the ruins of the rich.  
He suffers neither the law of the tomb  
nor the evils of life.

Let diligence in liberal studies not be lacking from the virtues already mentioned, through which the goods of divine things are raised up like the light of a precious necklace. For imperfect beauty is not far removed from ugliness; and whoever has not stretched himself sufficiently toward the summit of great things has scarcely left the lowest depths of misery.

These virtues, however, place grammar before the doors as the nurse of the others. Grammar attracts the minds of young men with the flavor of artistic and plain speech and brings them sparks of a heat modeled on Cicero’s warmth. The Campus Martius receives the soldier who has been fashioned there, whom the imitation of feigned combat has animated; and he does not turn his foot away from the trumpet calls, for the blare of trumpets and the implements of war have sounded amid the blandishments of peace.

Through practice virtue grows strong, and endurance of dangers is born from training. Beginnings have seen men of completed strength afraid. It is well if the right hand of rhetoricians and that freedom of tongues receive swords shaped in the furnace of grammarians; frequent practice of striking has been brought together so that they may not yield to visible blows.

In this discipline care is required, so that devotion to art may grow beyond the almost natural license of immature age, and that, through continual instruction by pedagogues and through an imposed necessity, spontaneous care for distinguished work may spring forth. Yet he shows that he is tending toward good will who consents in order to be compelled. He already nearly possesses honesty in study whom the concern of an admonisher does not offend.

Thus she speaks to her followers:

## GRAMMAR

We give flavor to minds while polishing stories.  
We retain a fair judge whenever a little boy goes astray.  
Withholding my hand, I chastise modesty through ear and mouth.  
Whatever the art of speech has that is fearful, art moderates.  
With the little ones we also play amid the very doctrines.  
For the stern master commands that you not terrify them throughout.  
That older age called us the best parents,  
whom we reckon, through favor, to be our children,  
whom which the swelling womb gave as pledges of learned seed,  
and desire did not subjugate the rights of a noble heart.

As you now depart from this discipline, Mars of eloquence summons you with rhetorical trumpets and, like a coat of mail made from hooks, constructs for you a defense from the varied and interlocking particles of causes. For when the knotty limbs of speech have been compressed into a solid and simple form, he paints a single image of discourse, in which diverse things are joined by measured squares in such a way that division does not damage conjunction, nor can partition, when separation is necessary, prevent what must be gathered individually from being separated.

After first offering you the flavor of praise, masculine diction and the Latin loftiness of human taste exhort you as follows:

> “After the summit of divinity, I am that which either changes things if they have been done, or does them. However many shadows of actions may enclose a person, the light I bring through speech is sufficient. I am the one through whom people await guilt from a troubled conscience and innocence from a serene one. Through me a darkened conscience receives brightness; through me what shines with its own light is covered by an alien night—or, if it is ignorant of darkness, there is something in which neither purity takes confidence nor guilt sighs.
>
> “Wherever there is a Roman, he watches over my advantage. Fasces, riches, and honors, if you do not adorn them, are worthless. We govern kingdoms and command those in power to do what is salutary. What of the fact that the delight of our declamations conquers everything that possesses wisdom, and that the reputation we create is eternal? Before scepters and robes comes pompous recitation. Whatever we wish is believed concerning the deeds of brave men; no one evaluates what we keep silent. Noble offspring, poured forth from us, illumine the whole world with the sun of perfection. Poetry, knowledge of law, dialectic, and arithmetic, although they use me as their mother, nevertheless possess value through my assertion.”

Hear also the poem that the play of a foreign office suggests to us.

## RHETORIC

Let him be ours alone; poems bind no one.  
By the aid of art we wipe away the stains of life.  
If someone is established in the snow-white merit of his character,  
with the senate as witness we compel everyone to say that he was born in darkness.  
Both the guilty and the holy arise from our mouth;  
while we speak, judgment is led captive.  
The wool of Tarentum’s city, a jewel, power—  
what are they when joined to our brow?  
Whoever serves our studies soon rules the world.  
Fearing nothing, art has given me kingdoms.

Therefore, dearest sons, strive both to attain these things and to preserve them once attained. But you may reply: “With what teachers shall we pursue these studies? With what instructors shall we use, by whose examples shall we be raised, when favorable fortune keeps Faustus and Avienus—the blessedness of our age and the stream of Latin eloquence—occupied in courtly counsels?” While they remain in official service, they are unknown to the multitude; to attempt to praise them is like asserting the light of the sun and the power of divinity.

But while these men labor for the public good, the patricians Festus and Symmachus do not depart from the most sacred city; they are the materials of every discipline and the enduring form of wisdom.

**[Note: “Festus and Symmachus.”]** In this catalogue of illustrious men he follows the order of their dignities. At this time Festus, as Anastasius notes in his account of Symmachus, was head of the senate and the most senior of the former consuls, from the year 472. Symmachus obtained the same honor in 475; Probinus in 489; Cethegus, the son of Probinus, in 504; Boethius, as we have noted, in 510; Agapitus was not yet consul when Ennodius wrote, but was to become consul in 517; Probus perhaps in 525.

In them is the noble leadership of the senate. To have seen them is to have been educated. Among them there is no talk of amusements, nor any mention of pantomimes, for which forgiveness can scarcely be granted. They do not capture popular favor through the loss of modesty; content to please the upright rather than the multitude, they obtain testimony from an innocent course of action. Although their commands are to be followed in all things, there is in them also the silence that teaches and the pattern of educated quiet.

There is also the patrician Probinus, the tested brilliance of a tranquil stock, upon whom the manners of a family of learned men, polished to the nail, have been bestowed; he drew from both his father’s and his father-in-law’s fountain whatever is pure.

There is the patrician Cethegus, his son, a former consul, who, surpassing gray-haired prudence while still young, possesses, without prejudice of age, both the taste of maturity and the honey of childhood.

There is the patrician Boethius, in whom you scarcely observe the years of learning before understanding that childhood already suffices for teaching. The choice of the refined has judged him.

There is the patrician Agapitus, rich both in integrity and in knowledge.

There is Probus, a man of illustrious rank. If you follow him, you will have Faustus and Avienus, whom I mentioned above, present even when they are absent.

I leave the other distinguished men whom reputation alone has brought to me in silence. Recognize them through yourselves, if maturity is now dear to you, or through those whom I have mentioned. For the friend of good people is evident by clear signs; no person embraces in another any character except what he has formed in himself.

If you enjoy the company of noblewomen, you have the lady Barbara, flower of Roman talent, who reveals through the testimony of her face the light of her blood and refinement. In her you will find both modest confidence and confidence in good action arising from modesty; speech seasoned with natural and cultivated simplicity, so that neither charm disfigures her address nor severity makes the brilliance of women rigid. In her diligence in honesty has so passed into nature that, even if she wished to lie, she could not make a mistake.

Her tongue sounds with chaste sweetness, and no cloudiness of mind is concealed beneath the roof of serene speech. What is in her heart is what is in her words.

Let the crown of women forgive me for presuming, since I envy her tranquility. I would wish her to be set before all the women of Italy as an example, so that those who do not submit to admonitions might be shaped by examples.

There also is Stephania, the most brilliant light of the Catholic Church, whose birth and lineage are so overshadowed by a greater light when you understand her character, as though the eye of the sun were to darken the torch of the world. If you set aside the rays of her inborn conduct, nothing will shine more brightly through her blood.

May the heavenly dispensation join you in service to all those whom I have mentioned. Behold, you have this page as the pledge of my favor; follow it as a pedagogue. May God grant you always both to will and to do what is fitting.

Therefore, if I have not been able to help you through pompous speech, I have helped you through prayer, mindful of my calling.

[Col. 0255A]

> Through you—through the one whose parents made you such—  
> Symmachus, lest a harsh fate remain for our little tablet,  
> extend your hand to the lowly and carry me with you across the waves.  
> It does not accord with good character to deceive one who trusts holy men.  
> I do not delay: behold, I come as a suppliant; have mercy on the petitioner,  
> commending humble words to rich patrons.
>
> Accept, illustrious offspring,  
> the dry words  
> of a parent.  
> Noble is the saying  
> that displays good things.

[Col. 0255]

# SEVENTH OPUSCULUM

## A PRECEPT: WHEN ALL BISHOPS WERE ORDERED TO HAVE CELLULANI

**[Note: “To have cellulani.”]** Ennodius wrote this in the name of his bishop. For when all bishops had been ordered by the pope or by a synod—it is not disclosed which—to have clerical companions as witnesses to their life and actions, so as to remove the slanders of malicious persons by which Symmachus had recently been harassed, the bishops, appropriately following the example, likewise ordered the priests and deacons of their dioceses to do the same, so that they too would not be without the companionship of others. He therefore interprets *cellulani* as *concellanei*, “cell-companions,” συγκέλλους (*synkellous*).

## TO HAVE CELLULANI. (C)

[Col. 0255B] No one can doubt that a man who, as a lover of sacred discipline, has subdued the allurements of carnal desire by the art that teaches how to live, and has cut away with the sickle of the commandments the wandering branches from the root of his conduct, to consign them to the life-giving fire, while fostering fruitful plantings capable of yielding a heavenly return—from which divine commands receive their annual revenues—should be congratulated as much for the integrity of his innocence as for the radiance of his reputation. Nor should one believe that the torch of his good merits can be extinguished by the breath of a slanderer: even if the splendor of his life is touched by the tooth of envy, it shuts out the shadow of poisonous abuse.

Darkness claims as its author the one who prepares it to envelop the brilliance; night poured over the sky does not overwhelm the radiance of the stars. Conflict with obscurity advances the cause of brightness. When day withdraws, the moon’s orb shines more brightly, and delights in its own light while driving away another’s. One who assumes the power to create light, as its author, is not handed over to external jurisdiction.

But how do wicked minds suppose that they are not bound by the judgments of the elders, when they think that the prophets’ injunction—“The mouth of the slanderer shall be eradicated”—grows obsolete with age and loses its force over time? As though fear were owed only to recent statutes, and an ancient law did not hold the guilty to punishment; although God, the maker of the ages, acting through the office of a prophet, both commanded what was ancient and orders what is modern. The one and the same author of good discipline preserves among posterity what he first established among their ancestors.

But let us return to our subject. Holy souls are indeed exercised by the words of their rivals, and whatever an accuser brings against their merit they count as an increase of glory, just as the Apostle to the Gentiles declares that people are exercised by slanders. As trees whose strong roots have reached into the earth’s depths are accustomed to look down upon the blasts of the winds and, animated by their own stability, to disregard the struggles of storms, so these men, rejecting as superstitious whatever darkness of fabrication has been cast against them, display through the clear air the rays of a good way of life. For when one of them confronts accusations with conscience as witness, inwardly he hastens toward the hope of triumph.

[Col. 0256B] Yet we whom pastoral care constrains, to whom the guardianship of souls has been entrusted so that none, whether among the greatest or the least, may perish—especially since the example of evil itself has recently been set before our eyes, when the fury of enemies had savagely assailed the bishop of the Apostolic See, who held the reins of nearly all the Churches, amid the conflagration of a neighboring tumult, and when the rage of certain men rose up to their own ruin without just cause for indignation—we therefore wish to cut away this destructive disease, lest anyone among our people should seize upon negligence as an occasion for an unjust assertion and, supported by a semblance of truth, come forward to attack us.

For, as they say, such men do not fear living human witnesses, while—shameful even to say it—an unwary person is treated as a convicted person, and one is believed to have committed a crime merely because he is reported to have been able to commit it. No one judges that the eyes of God should be feared more than those of human beings. Solitude is believed to foster error and to admit profound wickedness when one is without companions—as though crimes enclosed in the innermost recesses were not revealed to heaven, and evil could not be avenged when man does not see it. They believe that what was deliberate can be attributed to necessity, and that, while one human being is the guardian of another, chastity can be entrusted to fear through another order of slander.

We, indeed, have encountered occasions for criticism from more than one side. Yet, mindful of heavenly discipline, we extend a priestly hand of whatever kind to those who wish to perish, and restrain from the precipice of ruin those driven on by the devil’s goads, so that the talkative may learn, at least after the present decrees, to love religious silence.

[Col. 0256D] We therefore wish no priest who obeys the ancient and modern laws, and no Levite, to remain anywhere without a thoroughly approved companion. If a person’s poverty does not permit him to have a companion, let him himself become another’s co-cellmate. Everything that is done among the religious should be public; clandestine obscurity must be rejected. Let the person who owes innocence to God have many witnesses to his actions.

Let rivals see that the person who calls in witnesses wishes to be proved innocent; a way of life that does not wish to be known should rightly be judged bad. Certainly, even if the mind is conscious of what is right, he is worthy of punishment who becomes the cause of danger to another. By opening an approach to suspicion, he becomes the source of a brother’s peril; and he who supplies fuel for sin himself thrusts the throat toward death, as the divine and blessed herald says: “Do not slander, lest you be eradicated.”

Ambrose the Confessor: “Many did not give room to error, yet they gave room to suspicion. Suspicion is the destruction of the one who suspects, and the person who gives rise to it is not free from sin.”

Therefore, with what has been established by the lasting ordinance of God and our Redeemer, we decree—supported by the authority of the blessed Peter of the Apostolic See and of its presiding bishop, the pope—that the vices which ought to be cut out by the roots must be removed, so that no religious person from the orders mentioned above may dare to conduct himself otherwise than we have stated. Whoever presumes to do so shall suffer the loss of his honors together with the forfeiture of his modesty. Let it be said how great an evil it is for a person consecrated to God not to obey salutary admonitions.

**No one shall have foreign women with him**  
[Note: [Col. 0257A] Women designated by the canons. Gregory the Great, Book VII, Letter 39: “If any bishops live with women, do not tolerate it in any way, except in the case of those whom the judgment of the sacred canons permits: that is, a mother, paternal aunt, sister, and others of this kind, concerning whom no improper suspicion can arise.”]

No one shall have women with him except those designated by the canons, lest by acting in this way, even if his life is innocent, he incur damage to his reputation.

[Col. 0257]

## THE EIGHTH OPUSCULUM

[Note: [Col. 0257C] The petition by which Gerontius was freed.]

Manumissions formerly took place in the Church by the privilege of Constantine the Great. His law to Protogenes, bishop of Sardica, is extant and sets out the formula. *Code*, “Concerning Those Who Are Manumitted in the Church”: “It was long ago determined that in the Catholic Church masters may grant freedom to their servants, if they do so in the presence of the people and of Christian bishops standing by, so that, for the remembrance of the act, some sort of written document may be drawn up in the manner of official records, on which the masters themselves sign in place of witnesses.”

Augustine, in a sermon not yet published [Note: [Col. 0258D] Later published with thirty-nine others by Sirmond himself.], but which Nic. Faber expects shortly to bring to light together with the others: “You bring your slave whom you intend to manumit into the church; a petition is read, or a statement of your wish is made. You say that you are manumitting your slave, who has preserved faith toward you in all things.”

Here we have a splendid example of this ancient custom in Gerontius, a slave whom his master manumits before the bishop. This opusculum, therefore, was written in the name of another by Ennodius—namely Agapitus, whose name I have placed in the title—for in old books it is called *GERONTIUS PUER SS.*, that is, “the aforesaid.” It is appended to the letter to Agapitus, which is Book IV, Letter 6.

**PETITION BY WHICH GERONTIUS, THE SLAVE OF AGAPITUS, WAS FREED.** (C)

[Col. 0257B] God, judge and creator of the universe, dispenses human affairs on such a scale that the faithful receive reward and the rebellious punishment. To the weary services of the devoted he grants strength, coming to their aid through the offering of a gift. A mind bound in earthly prisons loses the memory of its labor whenever it is assisted in return; the one whose necessity is exchanged for the sweetness of grace grows young again in the former ardor of his toil. The punishments of the saints are renounced when a crown is sought.

Who could doubt that no one approaches heaven without confidence in recompense? Mortals, under the guidance of wisdom, ought to imitate those principles by which the eternal order is arranged. The soul will follow in its actions the source from which it arose, when we offer to God, who is served with devotion, what we hope to receive from him. For one who bestows upon his servants such a master as he wishes the author of his salvation to be does not depart from heavenly conduct.

Accordingly, since Gerontius—whose faith, modesty, and integrity I have found proven—both demands freedom and makes himself known by his qualities, through this petition I beseech Your Blessedness that he may enjoy the fellowship of the Roman city. I am not so much the giver of his liberation as its witness. His designated condition would have been worthless unless his character had made it known.

I purchased him some time ago through an intervening exchange. But since no advantage is greater than that which a clear judgment secures, I have chosen the palm of judicial decision rather than a profit from what I had acquired. The just servitude of the man named above has shown me that he is not servile in character. Therefore, in the case of the person named, I desire not so much that freeborn status be granted as that it be restored. I know that he has rightly expelled the vile name, since he deserved to be regarded as freeborn before he was called so.

Accordingly, remitting the service owed to me by him, which he has shown by his conduct to be his own, I restore freedom to him. I beseech Your Crown that he be released from every obligation by the official acts of the Church, so that he may rejoice forever in the fellowship of the city of Rome, with all his property granted to him without any diminution. For it would be wrong to diminish anything from what he has acquired, since I promise to follow this with gifts even more valuable.

[Col. 0257]

## THE NINTH OPUSCULUM

[Note: [Col. 0257D] The blessing of the candle.]

Of these two pieces, the one placed later is now published for the first time. They belong to the ancient and solemn custom in the Church concerning the Paschal candle. The writers of ritual books, Alcuin and Amalarius, attribute its origin to Pope Zosimus. [Note: [Col. 0260D] See, among Sirmond’s own opuscula, the letter to Constantine Cajetanus, abbot of Saint Barontus, concerning the two Amalarii.] Amalarius was not, as he is commonly called, bishop of Trier, but a deacon, nearly the same age as the bishop, who composed that work at the command of the emperor Louis.]

**BLESSING OF THE CANDLE**

[Col. 0257D] **I. It Is Worthy and Just.** It is truly worthy and just that what we have received from you, Lord, we should at least repay through prayer and voice. Although our tongue can in no way respond in fitting speech to the benefits of its author, nevertheless it wishes to have advanced toward the divine mystery by the fact that it has been made.

For while the dull density of darkened senses is found in the other animals, in the work of your providence the nobler creature of humankind flourishes in this respect: it alone can more abundantly perceive its creator. Yet it should rightly be associated with the bowed-down beasts if, ignorant of the heavenly gift, it were to imprison divine benefits within itself, as though without a tongue. For just as the absence of anything to offer in mystical holocausts absolves one from guilt, so withholding what ought to be offered is a matter worthy of expiation. By the same judgment, then, the person who by nature never speaks and the person who does not return to his author what he speaks must be judged alike.

Therefore, Lord, maker of this wondrous element, we believe that some portion of it should be returned to you by our humble satisfaction, although we acknowledge that we owe you the whole. For who besides you, having completed the fabric of the world by the measured execution of a sudden command, established it with a twofold authority? At your first command, the earth was coagulated into the sea by a miracle; then, when the waters had been drawn away, that shipwrecked earth thirsted again.

And by the warmth of whose inscrutable command, except yours, are the seeds it has received nourished? Who generates heat when it is infused? Who lets moisture fall upon the dry? Who but our God joins season to season in succession, so that the fruits of the earth now grow hot with fire, now are tempered by frost, now are enlivened by warmth, and now are sprinkled with drinkable moisture?

Who both made all these things from nothing and, through the gate of light, separated them from the dark density of perpetual night? Who, in his most holy ordering, made them eternally worthy of praise, so that after the brightness of light the returning darkness would not be dreaded through day after day?

Who speaks of you in a worthy or eloquent manner as a praiser, whose completed distribution becomes more pleasing through succeeding variety? At your command, is not the light sweeter when it sometimes comes to an end than if it were to remain forever?

Behold, that night which had until then oppressed the world beneath the yoke of the most cruel bondage released peoples from the bonds of violent servitude and became the nurse of freedom, though it had been the mother of slavery. In the service of this most holy night, Lord, we offer you this candle’s light, by which ancient darkness may be driven away. In it, the form joined together in a threefold fellowship is united by the bond of an almost mystical association. The wax was prepared by virginity fruitful in nectar-bearing offspring; the papyrus was conveyed through water to serve as fuel for the flames; the light is supplied from heaven.

No human voice has anything here that it can consecrate, where heavenly knowledge directs everything.

[Col. 0260A] Here the Son of the saving Virgin recognizes his own fragrance, where whatever is offered is born without sexual union. Here no Panchaean fire is kindled upon incense-burning altars; no lowing ox, struck down for a sorrowful final service, is offered; no offspring of two-year-old sheep has been cut down by the executioner’s sword rather than by the priest’s. For the restoration of lost eternity, it is enough that the Lamb was slain not by us but for us.

Far from here be the Jewish slaughterer, who is accustomed to count as many souls acquired for himself as he wounds, by the scars of their groins. The offerings of our Christ are completed in unadulterated simplicity. The cross, water, and confession complete the dedication of our body.

Therefore, Lord, we ask you: just as in the ancient typological mystery, so may this column lead the ranks that are to be renewed across the floods. May the path prepared through the seas burn for us, and may the dusty road thirst amid the waves. Here nothing differs between ancient and new, or modern and old. You are always the same Lord and priest proclaimed by the prophets.

This is he at whose prayer the waters dry up, so that the Hebrew may cross, the Egyptian be overwhelmed, and, while bodies are submerged in water, only sin may experience shipwreck.

[Col. 0260B] This gift of the chaste worker, Lord, and this offspring of the untouched mother, we commend to you. Through it the earth merits possessing what belongs to heaven. Through waxen houses they store up honey for the divine treasury. Their numerous offspring are due to their having known no marriage, lest, while occupied with the bonds of coupling, they lose the time for labor and wait for their womb to pour forth its offspring—offspring which they can more carefully drive forth with their mouths as the profit of herbs than produce through seed.

In the body of this candle’s light, Lord, we ask that you bestow the gift of heavenly blessing. [Note: [Col. 0259D] “If anyone takes a portion from this.” It was the custom, as the same authors report, that portions were cut from the Paschal candle, which had been consecrated on Holy Saturday through prescribed prayers, and distributed to the people on the Sunday *in albis*, after holy communion. They used them to make incense in their homes or to protect their fields and vineyards against the tricks of demons, or against lightning and thunder. This is also the reference of those words of Ennodius, *Blessing* II: “Make the portion taken from this contend against storms and every attack.” In any case, this custom formerly existed only outside the city. At Rome, instead of the Paschal candle, the archdeacon blessed wax poured over with oil; he then preserved portions molded in the form of lambs, to be distributed similarly to the people on the day mentioned. This practice evidently gave rise to the images of the heavenly Lamb in wax, which later began to be consecrated by the pontiffs themselves in a more solemn rite.]

And if anyone takes a portion from this, let it be, while carrying out your commands, a unique refuge for him against blasts of wind and against storm spirits; let it be a wall protecting the faithful from the enemy.

At the same time we ask you: since you have fitted the season of your passion and resurrection to the face of the budding year, when, after clods have been hardened by winter’s torpor and rivers fettered by ice, a jewel of new foliage climbs upward, and when everything revives for us together with the author of growth—grant abundant fruits upon the earth. Make ours what you display, and, preserving the safety of our priest and of the entire clergy, grant us fertile seasons without adverse weather.

[Col. 0261]

## THE TENTH OPUSCULUM. BLESSING OF THE CANDLE. (C)

[Col. 0261A] **II. It Is Worthy and Just.** It is truly worthy and just that, at the very threshold of blessed night, the doors should be opened as though with a fitting key, by means of the service now at hand; that a noble messenger should attest the advent of life; that what is to follow should be weighed according to the merit of its herald; and that the venerable precursor should lend faith to the sacred mysteries.

It is just that the flame should reveal the nearness of the saving water; that the diversity of the elements should come together in an unfamiliar peace; that the sacred fire should show that the remedies of the waters are at hand; and that it should be recognized that the agreement of water with light is not a work of nature but of redemption.

Let that heavenly maker rejoice in his works when he himself blesses what he has bestowed, when he ennobles by sacrament what he produces from the origin of his hidden being. Let him understand, through the ministry of our tongue, the special distinction that he has granted us. Let whatever he commanded to be more excellent in human beings than in the other animals be subjected to his praises.

For the benefits of the best creator have been made manifest, and anger does not differ from piety when he has both taught us the art of supplication and wishes to be appeased by his own gifts. He himself fashioned humankind to serve as his temple through ingenious provision. He himself opens the innermost recesses of our hearts, excavated for the entrance of the holy one, unless the inner places are obstructed by foul contamination through a deliberate act of freedom.

Thus it is clear from all the secrets of creation that the life-giving structure fashioned by the creator’s wisdom cannot perish except through its own neglect. He both formed us for better things and showed us by what paths salvation should be sought.

When he fashioned the human being from earth, when the earth passed into the form of a living creature, when corrupt soil assumed a new appearance, when the fields were moved by the breath of his spirit beneath his footsteps, and when the earth looked upon its possessor—drawn from its own womb and made eminent by an unexpected gift, possessing what the very thing thought to be his mother had not given him—when it, ennobled through its offspring, rendered glory, it would have been incomplete if he had not ordered the path of actions by his own right.

Yet, Lord, the daily succession of your benefits surpasses the earlier gifts, and later things exceed ancient ones in their estimation. The one destined for eternal life, the one made a citizen of heaven from his parent earth, was thrust back toward his origin by voluntary error. And because, when he was permitted to do so, he refused to pursue better things, he lost the sublimity that he had happily received as a gift from his creator. Led back to his lineage by guilt, he mourned his exile.

Unless your omnipotence, Lord, regenerated this lost one, what you had made could have offered little benefit. And unless a birth fruitful in number and prosperity came to his aid, the first birth, in which error produced death, would not have helped him.

Finally, nothing that earth supplied as material for our formation would have been of use unless water came to our aid. You have granted us the single consolation of this sacrament: the waters wash away the sins of the earth.

Therefore, let the type now withdraw, and let those who announced what was to follow through images fall silent. In truth we possess whatever the colored shadow of the Law had promised. The time has come when our bodies and souls should be dedicated to Christ the Redeemer with a sword made idle; when salvation should no longer be sought through wounds; when the priest’s right hand should reject the work of the slaughterer; when faith, water, and the seal should complete the consecration; when the fountain should restore the human race to the place from which it fell.

[Col. 0262B] In the service of this venerable night, therefore, we dedicate to you, Lord, a torch joined from elements worthy of reverence. In it, the union of three gifts will find favor first because of the odd number. It is not uncertain that what comes freely to God is supplied by its makers: one element, because nourishment for the flames comes from the offspring of rivers; another, because the undefiled fecundity of bees supplies it, among whose offspring virginity suffers no loss; and fire, infused from heaven, is also applied.

For the Redeemer dedicated the waters by his own baptism; he loves the integrity that he also preserved by being born from a mother. He accepted, as the prophet could behold, a body of harmless fire, when the shrub felt no loss although the leaves crackled in the burning bush, and when the dry wood, while the flames licked it, did not become fuel for them.

Therefore, Lord, whatever the service of your servants has prepared in this candle is properly yours. Look upon it with serene eyes: what heaven, waters, and chastity have contributed. You, summoned to bestow the blessing through the ministry of human speech, enter into it.

At the time of your resurrection, when the infancy of the reviving year puts forth new growth, make the portion taken from this candle contend against storms and every attack, so that, with the votive prayers of our priest granted to all and the safety of his entire clergy preserved, you may grant fertility to the earth together with innocence and prosperity in their actions.

[Col. 0263]

# OF MAGNUS FELIX ENNODIUS

[Note: [Col. 0263C] *Dictiones*. A *dictio* is sometimes an oration of any kind, whether true or fictitious. Thus Cicero uses it for a true speech when he writes in the *Brutus* that he would prefer one speech of Lucius Crassus on behalf of Marcus Curius to two Castellan triumphs. Ennodius commonly uses it for a fictitious speech in his letters, when he calls the little declamations of the young Avienus, Messala, and Parthenius *dictiones*. He gives the same name to his own compositions, both true and fictitious. We have collected them into one body and arranged them in four classes. The first two contain true encomia and concern either ecclesiastical matters and persons or the school and lecture hall; hence we have called the former sacred by their subject and the latter scholastic. The third order consists of controversies. The last contains what the Greeks call *ἠθοποιΐαι* and *ἠθικοὶ λόγοι* (“character representations” and “ethical speeches”), which imitate the manners and words of other persons; following our Sidonius, we call them ethical speeches. He writes of Lampridius, the rhetorician of Bordeaux, in Book VIII, Letter 11, among other things: “Once he had undertaken the work, he varied an ethical speech according to the character of the person, the time, and the place.” The common text is faulty here and adds an unnecessary word; this is the certain emendation.]

**SPEECHES.** (C)

## FIRST SPEECH

[Note: [Col. 0264C] On the anniversary of Laurentius, bishop of Milan. “Anniversary” here means not the day of birth but of his accession to the see and episcopate. The bishops celebrated this feast each year, just as emperors celebrated the anniversary or commencement of their empire, according to Book II of the Theodosian Code, *Concerning Festivals*. From this speech of Ennodius we also learn that, just as princes were customarily praised in panegyrical orations on the anniversary of their accession—as is shown by the panegyrics delivered at the five-year and ten-year anniversaries and others—so bishops too were praised on the anniversary of their assumption of the episcopate. This is confirmed by another speech of Ennodius, delivered on the thirtieth anniversary of Bishop Epiphanius, and by the sermon on Bishop Peter, which is number 107 among the Chrysologian sermons.]

**ON THE ANNIVERSARY OF LAURENTIUS, BISHOP OF MILAN**

**FIRST SACRED SPEECH**

[Col. 0263A]

How long shall sluggish distrust keep me hidden within a narrow inner chamber? How long shall excessive caution, overstepping the bounds of honorable modesty, incur the very losses to reputation that it avoids? For human experience shows that, among people, just as much reputation is needlessly diminished through boldness, no less is lost through fear. A person should not be marked as one who greedily appropriates praise, nor should he be charged with a desire to display affected devotion, when he fulfills an obligation compelled by the goads of modesty. For just as the desire for glory, when it is sought in speech, drives glory into the shadows, so failing to render what one knows is owed proclaims the approach of night. To write what is superfluous is a matter of boastfulness; to withhold what is necessary is contempt. Often the concealed praise of a teacher is the source of our own condemnation. [Col. 0263B]

Someone, perhaps wishing to offer advice, may say that the emaciation of an intellect exhausted by the magnitude of its task is drying up, and that loquacity, deprived of the strength to speak, earns failure through its very abundance—as though one were pouring a trickling drop of eloquence into the bed of a great river: the expenditure of liquid would scarcely advance its flow, and what is adapted to the waves would barely produce moisture. But we consider in our minds what is said in relation to the value deserved by the subject of the speech; and a vein naturally parched often begins to flow from the theme: the thinness of eloquence grows rich through its subject. Often what must be said is granted in accordance with the merits of those to whom the speech has devoted itself, especially when the speaker serves through praise with genuine affection. Then affection conveys an abundance of words; then love supplies what talent denies. [Col. 0263C]

I am undertaking to say something good about Saint Laurence, insofar as my modest ability permits: the task I am beginning is indeed full of labor, but also full of charity. Let fear, hostile to a reverent purpose, therefore depart. The mind subjected to terror flees from glory, while the Apostle Paul cries out: “Perfect love casts out fear” (I John 4:18). [Col. 0264A] This is to say, and to demonstrate by a sure indication, that the one who is afraid does not love. A person is overcome without guilt by the immensity of a burden when, although unequal to carrying the load, he nevertheless approaches it with devotion.

Since matters stand thus, why should I not celebrate the festivals of the newborn year with a votive speech? Why should I disgrace the beginnings of the bright anniversary with the ugliness of silence? Joy without speech is defective, and concealing what one rejoices in is an image of sorrow; to have no voice in gladness is an imitation of affliction. Therefore, holy father, shall I, conscious of my duty, give you no words? Yet I would like to draw the opening principles of my speech from the season of your consecration and, with the infancy of the reborn year, bring forth spring in a flowery speech, if I can.

Now, when the sap of the earth runs through the veins of dry shrubs into buds, and the womb of dry tinder, married to moisture, swells; when the leafy crowns of young shoots unfold into gentle light and every interweaving of branches spreads forth, or the beauties of foliage that nature had confined within its sheath are released; when the song of birds is accompanied by melodious sweetness; when the life of crops, buried in winter clods—as though released from the barrier of cold and warmed by heat—is conceived anew. [Col. 0264B]

Now the farmer measures the hope of fruits in the white blossom, when the sunny beauty of the vineyards is woven together by the mutual arms of the vine-shoots, and before the time of ripeness cultivation shapes the fruit-bearing appearance, giving beauty with the taming sickle and restraining barren luxuriance with fruit-producing iron.

When the rage of the deep whirlpool passes into a gentle hiss, and the violence of the winds, weakened by warmth, changes into delights for the sailor; when it is safe to release the boat upon the sea and loosen the bites of the anchors; when the breaking of the storms that until now terrified sailors invites them onward, and permits the helmsman to sleep across the watery expanses of the sea; when the meadows, variegated with doubled color, grow rich with the resources of spring; and when, at the ordination of the supreme pontiff, the elements testify to nature’s joy. [Col. 0264C; Col. 0265A]

Shall I therefore now fail to render to you, bishop, what I have already learned to offer to others—you whom dignity, modesty, chastity, and beauty brought to the summit of the episcopate; you who, with so many gifts gathered together as into a heap, assumed the white-haired dignity of your present office, possessing such adornments of virtues that each one separately would make a priest approved?

I say nothing of the unanimous agreement in your election, nor do I review the concordant judgment of different nations. Let these matters speak in your praise, since the person who lacks anything to proclaim about character may establish them as evidence. For the popular breeze of uncertain favor is often driven about by momentary impulses, and the unexamining crowd of the Quirites, swept along by its enthusiasms, loves people it does not know. In your case, the one who either made himself your companion or your sponsor in your candidacy held the scales. [Col. 0265B]

The inexperienced gathering of the multitude weighed your merit with the balance of perfection. While the variety of your qualities pleased them, as though each person had been appointed the sole heir of an entirely different institution, each individual judged that what he approved was sufficient testimony to your distinction. For it was impossible for all your good qualities to be known to everyone. You had drawn everyone individually to favor your star: to one you showed that you were compassionate, to another that you were strict, to another that you were a distributor of a well-acquired patrimony, and to another that you knew how to preserve what had been rightly obtained.

The whole community took this as its aim: while each person surpassed another in the particular praise proposed, each was nevertheless surpassed by another in the comparison of the more excellent title among your praises. I do not wish to linger over these matters any longer. We must come to the labors of your life, because I, who am not competent to praise you in the greatest matters, do not know how to be content with small ones. [Col. 0265C]

[Note: Schott, “with the small.”] [Col. 0265D]

[Note: “When you were still newly appointed.” Laurence succeeded Bishop Theodore in the see of Milan; Ennodius’ epigram 88 survives concerning Theodore. Soon afterward the city of Milan was plundered and Laurence went into exile, I think by Odoacer, when Tufa, as stated in the Life of Epiphanius, rebelled against Theoderic. After Theoderic had won the victory, Laurence returned to Milan and restored the city after its former disasters.] [Col. 0265D; Col. 0266D]

When you were still taking your first steps in the dignity newly laid upon you, the adversity of inescapable times overtook you; and wars waged against liberty made a novice into a most seasoned soldier of the episcopate. You did not know how to fear the savagery of the plunderer; with the shield of steadfastness you rejected the poisons of flatteries, which are the more dangerous weapon among the malicious. How often did the one who could not defeat you in open contest provoke you with insidious honors? How often did he suppose that, to the detriment of your good reputation, you would accept the fabrications of his service, asking you, by entering into collusion with the enemy, to enclose him within the city walls and hand over the limbs of your sheep to the wolves for dispersal—offering many examples of a deed which it is impious even to mention?

You despised these things as to be avoided and committed them to memory, reserving them for the vengeance of a peaceful time: retaining what was detestable so that it would not pass unpunished through forgetfulness, and owing a greater horror to their excesses while you feared the ruin of others. But, once the obstacles to speech have been removed, let us come to those matters worthy of religious remembrance. [Col. 0265D]

When a hostile invasion was scattering the Christian people in every direction like sheep, you were seized by various kinds of torments on behalf of them all; you endured, with the fatherly compassion of a shepherd, the sufferings of many, as the Apostle says: “Who among you is afflicted, and I am not?” (II Corinthians 11:19). [Col. 0266A] Yet amid these things adversity did not see you broken. The enemy perceived that something was taken away from his triumphs: he had not conquered the spirit of the captured priest. You were still fighting for the release of many, fearing nothing for yourself, and hung in anxious concern over your flock.

I do not wish to dwell longer on sorrowful matters; I do not wish to open the tragedy of that evil time. Gladly I pass over some part of your illustrious preservation, lest by recounting them I compel you once again to endure what you suffered—although the teacher of the nations recalls that he was trained by tribulation, crying out: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (II Corinthians 12:10). I say nothing of hunger, cold, insults, and those additions to your illnesses which the mind of the enemy devised. But, I believe, these were childish things, and your limbs, strengthened by the substance of their ancient vigor, endured them. [Col. 0266B]

Did not your joints, deadened throughout their articulations and long since separated by age from their own natural capacity, endure while your soul alone, incapable of being bent, resisted? With an intention worthy of imitation, it fought against its attackers, fortified by a wall of steadfastness.

After these events, Christ our Redeemer, never disregarding pious prayers, came to meet you in the restored condition of the liberty desired; and, once the broken strength of the Roman name had been solidified by an ingenious remedy, the crushed state returned to saving vigor. When the heavenly ruler looked down from on high with kindly eyes, the light of its own priest was restored to the city of Milan.

Then, when there were few inhabitants; when confusion wandered through houses and across the sweet thresholds of bedrooms; when fear and mourning were everywhere, and the temples of God stood filthy, assigned to the habitation of wild beasts; when neglect, wasting away, had covered the once most splendid halls with the squalor of ancient dampness—you gave joy to others by your return, while you returned to tears. [Col. 0266C]

Then, like birds whose land is covered with snow and whose distress strips some place bare in the hope of food, you saw whatever remnants of the people could remain flowing together, and flocks running from every side, with weary bleating through the groves, to the presence of the good shepherd. You soothed some by your words, supporting them in various ways; you restored others through expenditure; you encouraged others by your example.

Soon afterward the city, which owed you its restoration after God, revived to its ancient condition; and what had not believed that what it had been could be restored began already to rival better things. Then it could be seen that all the uses of life were being invited by successful outcomes toward broader progress. [Col. 0266D]

I run through these matters individually, briefly reporting what requires fuller narration, in order to arrive at the contest of your life and the glory of your supreme purpose.

[Note: “The second captivity in the Roman Church.” Because of the machinations of the schismatics against Symmachus. For this reason Laurence remained for a long time in Rome and presided over the synod of absolution, which he calls the senate of the heavenly curia; he resisted the hatred and fury of the opponents with steadfast courage.] [Col. 0266D]

After a time of uncertainty, a second captivity arose in the Roman Church. It drew you away, as though you had already long been idle and a fugitive from labor, from the lap of prolonged repose, when scarcely had the arms of your labor laid down in hope of peace before they were taken up again.

Silence would indeed have been owed in a sorrowful matter, unless the judgment of your praise dragged me onward, so that the shameful event might perish from memory in a single generation. That senate of the heavenly curia was summoned, where a crowd of bishops flowed together from various provinces, where that assembly brought as many varieties of opinion as it contained kinds of people. [Col. 0267A]

But those who possessed the spiritual taste of understanding held you, through their love, as the leader of the principal deliberation. I cannot explain with what force you subdued the assaults of those who threatened by the honey of flatteries, with what elevation of revered humility you broke proud hearts, or with what root of counsel you established wavering minds. I compel anyone eager to know what happened to learn it by contemplating the deed itself. So many elect men followed you alone, and the leaders of so many cities fell into agreement with your judgment.

The one who departed from you in raw obstinacy is now being cooked in the heat of lamentation; and the one who was divided has nothing for consolation except the tears of calamity. Perhaps someone, a malicious interpreter of events, may ask what decision the present case received from such steadfastness, or inquire what end was reached by your celebrated toil. [Col. 0267B]

Trusting in you, I shall answer him: it was done under your leadership so that foreign fury would not seize priests as its ministers; so that the judgment of pontiffs would not serve bloody indignation; so that people stirred to evil would not turn into practice the possibility of making happen whatever they wished. Finally, let the talkativeness of the wicked fall silent, at least at the consideration of this secret: the fires of hatred, which burned not from the merit of the person attacked but from the fuel of factions, could not be extinguished even by the fountain of holy deliberation.

To you, therefore, is owed the preservation of the venerable canons. To you is owed the fact that whatever wickedness now rages has occurred without an episcopal stain. Through you it became clear what others, while accusing, concealed by clandestine fraud; through you it was discovered that hatred need not be satisfied whenever the one who provokes it abandons faith. But these matters are better reserved for narration at another time. [Col. 0267C]

Hail, star of the Churches, and, as an imitator of Abraham, advance toward a good old age; for it is testimony to probity when a man is preserved for a long time in the ecclesiastical citadel, as it is written: “Men of blood and deceit will not halve their days” (Psalm 64:24). Mature in age and early in religious toil, surpass yourself. By praiseworthy devotion, offer examples of good discipline; restrain the wicked with severity; and, as the clasp of each kind of good work, continue without blemish in the testimony of supreme glory.

## DICTION II

[Note: “A speech sent to Honoratus.” This was written by Ennodius, but for the benefit of Honoratus, bishop of Novara in Insubria, who recited it as his own. Likewise, the speech that follows immediately was composed by Ennodius but delivered by Stephen the vicar. There are several other pieces of this kind, which he composed for different people. Gennadius states in his catalogue that Salvian of Marseille, a presbyter, composed many homilies for bishops in the same way.] [Col. 0267D]

Sent to Honoratus, bishop of Novara, at the dedication of the Basilica of the Apostles, where a temple of idols had stood.

[Col. 0267D]

## SACRED SPEECH II

I believe, dearest brothers, that with your whole mind you venerate the fact that, while the name of a temple remains in this place, its former cult has perished for the sake of religion; that reverence for the shrine has been established after its libations were driven away; that it is rightly called a sanctuary after it has rejected the former sacrifices and, through the transformation of sacrifice by burning, has assumed the name of a divine house; and, finally, that its foundations and roof have passed into another condition without being shaken. Although human labor, scarcely adequate, has been added to its structure, whatever has been renewed continues to endure. [Col. 0268A]

In short, what miracle should be considered greater than this: that, while the structure preserves its proportion, it does not cease to rise, and, established upon ancient foundations, is raised by its growth?

It is certainly necessary to ask who was the author of this work and this renewal: namely, the predecessor of my humble self, Victor the bishop of Novara, the predecessor of Honoratus. [Col. 0268D]

[Note: “Victor the bishop.” The epitaph of Victor was written by Ennodius, epigram 95. In epigram 11, concerning this same matter:

“Gods, to whom this was disclosed, leave the dwellings you possess.

What Victor made, the victor holds everywhere.

His successor rightly added to its worship by merit and deeds—

you, Honoratus, who thereby bear the name of moral excellence.”]

[Note: Schott, “of what was to come.”] [Col. 0268D]

The divinity announced beforehand the innocence that was to come by giving him his name. For when you have learned the name, you recognize the deeds: in the contests undertaken against worldly vices, he approached the predicted outcome as “Victor.” Through spiritual combat, as befitted a victor, he triumphed over crimes; and whatever the sinister portion of mortality inflicts, you need not seek his fall, once you understand that he was named for what he was. [Col. 0268B]

His merits demand a field of speech, if either the poverty of my intellect or the limits of his merit allowed me to advance into wider regions. For it is a certain nobility of deeds to be found worthy of the praise of great men. While following him in the care of the building, our modest ability, with God as its guide, brought its hopes to completion.

No one should think that what I have said is arrogance. It is permissible to join one’s hopes with the person whom one cannot equal in action, because it is an assertion of conscience to follow the better person in every respect. The person who follows the one whom he knows to display the light of life, as we believe, never enters a dark path. [Col. 0268C]

Let us nevertheless unfold more clearly, through the service of speech, the truth of what was done. Here, formerly dedicated to deceptive magic and drenched in the shameful blood of beasts, they worshiped ancient images. Here, in an insult to divinity, at an altar heaped with ill-omened gifts, they offered to demons what was owed to heaven. Here, the entrails of a young bull, still palpitating with half-living movements, sang of the future to a wretched inquirer. From here smoke, spread through many contaminations, polluted the air itself.

Finally, from here the multitude of victims slaughtered by butchers drove away whatever is God, while grain, blood, incense, and vervain were displayed to idols; while an age hostile to Christ did not accept a simple rite and, with its judgment laboring under many forms, purchased heavenly offense through its offerings. [Col. 0268D]

I would go through each matter and unlock with the key of my tongue the secrets of these deadly practices, were it not that we rightly judge it an insult to the mouth to recount filthy things, and that what struck them through action would contaminate us through speech.

For the present, let us explain by what successes these things were changed and with what brilliance the darkness that preceded them was put to flight. Where are the seals of the gods, imagined by those who fashioned them according to their vows, whose faces depended upon the power of the craftsman, and whose value was produced either by the concern of the worker or by the metal? Where are the gods to whom human beings gave power through the glitter of gems? [Col. 0269A]

I see that all these things, as I believe, have fled. Christ has entered. Let us see with what aids he is supported. The rays of heaven came with him, as did the diadems of the apostles, Peter and Paul. For who would be necessary in the restoration of a house except the architect and the rock; the stone and the one building upon it; the foundation and the craftsman?

Why do you tremble at the dangers of mortals? Why do you anxiously prepare flight in your excursion? He is the one from whom no slip can conceal your cunning; though he does not move from his place, he follows you wherever you go.

Come, therefore, most merciful Lord, and enter fully into the consecration of your work. Let these temples, hitherto dedicated to shameful patronage, be cleansed in place of human beings through the baptism of the heart. Establish, Lord, the transformation of sacrifices; and while we heap pure gifts upon holy altars, mingle the presence of your majesty, summoned by the merit of the holy priests, especially that of our chosen father Laurence, bishop of Milan. [Col. 0269B]

[Note: “Our father Laurence.” The Novarians regarded him as their metropolitan and as a father. His praise here illustrates the ancient mutual respect of bishops. Whenever bishops of other sees were present at their assemblies, they customarily interwove some praise of them into their speeches. Examples of this practice are common among Greeks and Latins. A particularly notable one is Peter Chrysologus’ Sermon 136, addressed to Bishop Adelphus.] [Col. 0269D]

Our father Laurence, full of so many gifts that each one separately would have made a supreme pontiff, has grown to the heights of the Church. In him flourish the prince of good works, modesty, the mother of honor, patience, the nurse of holy religion, and piety, ever ready to please God. He has given the members of the Church the institutions of life not merely through speech but through examples; as he walks ahead, he shows every path by which one goes to God, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who reigns with the Father forever and ever. Amen. [Col. 0269C]

## DICTION III

[Note: “A speech delivered to Stephen.” Cresconius and several other ancient collections count this speech among the letters of Pope Symmachus, with the heading as though it had been written to Laurence, bishop of Milan. This is also why it was inserted among Symmachus’ other letters in the recent edition of the Councils—an obvious error, since it is entirely inconsistent with Symmachus and is not a letter but a speech. It cannot be referred to Laurence because it contains an allusion to the name Maximus. It was therefore delivered to Maximus, bishop of Ticinum, successor to Epiphanius in that see, and later succeeded by our Ennodius.] [Col. 0269D; Col. 0270D]

Delivered to Stephen, the most distinguished vicar, to be spoken to Maximus, bishop.

[Note: “The most distinguished vicar.” I have added the designation *vir spectabilis* from the manuscripts. This had formerly been, and still was in Ennodius’ time, the proper title of the vicariate prefecture. Cassiodorus, Book III, Letter 17: “The distinguished man Gemellus, vicar of the prefects, known to us for his loyalty and ability.”] [Col. 0270D]

## SACRED SPEECH III

A mind devoted to the praises of pontiffs reveals the vow of a religious conscience. It is an assertion of talent to devote what we say to those who obey God. In their praises, speech may perhaps reveal the narrowness of an unskilled speaker; yet if it is withheld, it reveals childishness. Who would judge a narrative poor when vows enrich it? Often the speaker’s vein is found poor in the gifts of eloquence, while, conversely, the treasure of the heart shines through poverty of words.

The one who judges in God’s place does not desire embellished conversation but what unpainted brilliance of talent commends, because in the former eloquence flatters even without love, while in the latter naked truth commends its own splendor. Everything dictated by affection is without ornamental trappings; those things are polished to perfection which we wish to possess not so much the appearance of what is right as its likeness.

My speech is addressed to you, venerable Bishop Maximus, whose virtue began with your name as a testimony to your merits: the name “Maximus” speaks of the deed. The prudent diligence of your parents wished you to be chosen before you were tested. Once attached to secular titles, military labor refined you, and the adverse side established you firmly for the governance of the Church, as God speaks through the prophet: “The one who is faithful in little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10). [Col. 0270A]

[Note: “You, judge of the sacred [treasury].” *Comes sacrarum largitionum*, “Count of the Sacred Largesses.” Maximus had been his assessor, as Alypius likewise had been before becoming a bishop. Thus Saint Augustine writes of Alypius in *Confessions* VI.10: “At Rome he was assessor to the count of the Italian largesses”; and in VIII.6: “Alypius was with me, idle from the work of the jurists after his third assessorship, waiting to see to whom he might once again sell his counsel.”] [Col. 0270D]

You, as judge of the sacred treasury, earned both the position of counselor and a share in the work. You were well prepared to be initiated into the venerable altars, and even in lay life you chose what was sacred. You were found to be a guardian of chastity at an age when the law itself serves desires. It is enough for childhood to dread the ambition that license supports. Christ seeks his soldiers among the enemy ranks, so that he may raise them into the person of a commander. [Col. 0270B]

Admitted to the Church, you fulfilled the office of a bishop in your deeds before the time of your dignity. Your kindness was not an outsider, since, rooted in nature, it showed its shoot from white-haired blossom. Everything fabricated is temporary; what matures with age is everlasting. We do not believe that the priesthood happened to you as a gift, but as a reward.

Another person is commended by the popular breeze, with favor as his procurer; in your case, stern discipline toward the guilty won affection. You possess exceptional wisdom. Although it is generally desirable, it is especially necessary in a teacher. The person who cannot assess the weight of the office imposed upon him assumes the role of instructor in vain; unless knowledge makes him preeminent, the one superior in honor must be compared with the most worthless. [Col. 0270C]

Judgment, not favor, gave you the summit. The love worthy of a pontiff is the love won by discipline; grace of character is disfigured when one wishes to please through favor alone. Formed and shaped by these gifts of heaven, you instruct the people more by doing than by speaking.

Those admonitions dig into the conscience of disciples which are offered by example. The person who has not himself pursued innocence invites others to it without shame. Those who plan to sin fear you even in the secrets of their inner chambers, as though you were a witness; fear at the birth of faults, and reverence for you, deny them their effect. You confront vices at their beginning, remove the opportunity for a fall, and cleanse the source of desire.

I have dedicated these remarks briefly to your blessedness as a recommendation through the medium of my speech. If the course of life smiles upon me through your prayers, I shall consecrate myself fully to an account of your deeds, so that what is known to everyone may be preserved in writings that will remain for the future, for the joy of the generations to come. [Col. 0271A]

## DICTION IV

[Note: “A speech sent to Maximus at a dedication.” The same bishop of Ticinum, who attended and signed the synod of Symmachus’ absolution with the others. The preceding speech was addressed to Maximus; this one was delivered by Maximus when the Basilica of Saint John the Baptist was dedicated. In a novel usage, he also calls John an apostle, as a forerunner—one sent before the advent of Christ the Lord. In the *Apologeticus* he likewise said that the prophets could be called apostles, since they too were sent. In fact, that church was dedicated not only under the title of John the Baptist but also under those of Antoninus and Cassianus.] [Col. 0271D; Col. 0272D]

Sent to Maximus, bishop, at the dedication.

## SACRED SPEECH IV

The stream of talent should never be feared as poor when the subject of speech is rich. Whenever our mind serves heavenly worship, it surpasses humanity; and the poverty of a narrative is not confined if the speaker renders service to its maker. For the one who bestowed the gifts of eloquence can adorn the tongue with those gifts and give words the character which we admit he gave to speech. [Col. 0271B]

Long ago he aided the poverty of prophetic eloquence, when the weak infancy of Moses was raised to the perfect eloquence of the teacher and the trumpet of the most powerful admonisher. Moses did not blossom gradually while training in skill, nor did he ascend to the harvest of perfection through knowledge acquired at some particular age. For a long time he bore military service with an unformed intellect; when ordered to undertake the office of commander, he fulfilled it steadfastly because he had modestly refused it.

Thus, as we celebrate the festivals of a dedication, we await grace amid the blessings of spiritual joy while we prepare. Let weak fear be absent; let confidence conceived in vain through study be removed. We neither presume upon nor fear anything from the pattern of human perfection.

Besides, once one has entered the temple of blessed John the prophet, how could anyone hesitate to open even silent lips? His grace was older than nature: before he entered the light, he fulfilled the office of the pious prophet and marked the threshold of this life by his virtue. At one and the same time he made his mother illustrious through fertility and restored the speechless lips of his father to their former use.

After the miracles that preceded the example, no one who names John should suppose that he will retain his former ignorance of speech. After the most holy Zachariah, to whose throat the human power of speech returned through this name after its expulsion, John—an apostle—is rightly believed by all to be the key of words. [Col. 0271C]

In the company of John, Antoninus, the hero of the ancient age, and the joined glory of the most blessed Cassianus make the building a sacrament, the earthly dwelling a heavenly fellowship, and the work of human hands something that no old age can violate. Things offered to God do not feel decay; nor are they sent into trembling old age when supported by devotion. The solidity of the structure remains when Christ enters it; having forgotten its original weakness, it receives strength from its possessor.

Poor roofs are adorned by the nobility of their consecrator, when a perishable object is granted the value of possessing something from the Lord. But you, most holy brother, as the donor of this building, rejoice in the repayment of your reward. Hope cannot falter when the fruit of good action is promised; confidence in rewards descends from the practice of good works, and the person who meditates on what deserves praise does not waver in uncertainty. [Col. 0272A]

## DICTION V

[Note: “A speech of a newly appointed bishop.” It is uncertain whether Ennodius himself used this speech when he was made bishop or whether, as I rather think, he wrote a formula for others to use at the beginning of their episcopates. In any case, Bernardo Sacco’s statement in *Historia Ticinensis*, Book VIII, chapter 1, that Ennodius began to occupy the see in the year 490 does not require lengthy refutation. How could he have been made bishop in that year, when in the preceding year—when Theoderic entered Italy—he was only sixteen years old? Or how could he then have been placed upon the see of Ticinum, which Epiphanius still governed and continued to govern for several years afterward, and which after Epiphanius was held by Maximus, whom we have noted as having attended the Palmary Synod? Certainly, both in the *Apology for the Synod* and in all the letters he wrote throughout Symmachus’ pontificate, Ennodius calls himself no more than a deacon. It therefore seems more certain, as others judge, that he was raised to that dignity in the time of Hormisdas. But although the year of the beginning of his episcopate is uncertain, its end is established by the consul named in Ennodius’ epitaph: it fell in the year 521.] [Col. 0271D; Col. 0272D]

Of a newly appointed bishop.

## SACRED SPEECH V

A teacher beginning is equal to his disciples, and at the beginning of his teaching no teacher is elevated above his hearers by any privilege. Honor is owed to tested talents; those not yet proved scarcely demand ordinary respect. Those are true praises which long labor has drawn out; whenever glory bestowed precedes labor, it is flattery, not judgment. Let any soldier count among his blemishes whatever triumphs he acquires before the field has been examined. [Col. 0272B]

Those who enter the Olympic contests with hurried steps—do they possess hope of the crown before the contest has been completed? The Apostle says: “He is not crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (II Timothy 2:5). Behold: even those from whom praise is rightly demanded after labor do not deserve it before merit.

Our condition is different and separated by a lengthy road. From the fruit of our innocence as much is taken away as is added by favor. For, as we judge when placed in training, the path is full of necessity and danger: one must pursue a praiseworthy life, yet it becomes rich in reproaches if it desires to be praised by human beings. [Col. 0272C]

If our action exalts itself because of its good qualities, it will become foul, as the divine words testify: “Those who praise you deceive you and overturn the paths of your feet” (Isaiah 3:12). Let deeds, not the tongue, testify to the splendor of a pontiff. The glory of this office shines more brightly through the evidence of truth than through speech.

You see how secure is the case of the subordinate and how many dangers accompany that of the superior. You will be able to support my duties more through sighs than through shouting. Let no one believe that what flatters the ears is extraordinary. Our speech, unless it heals the soul, is contemptible. Prefer the one who cleanses the inner person of thorns with a spiritual sickle. [Col. 0273A]

Then the shepherd’s diadem is precious, when the ecclesiastical flock does not resist his exhortation while advancing toward uprightness. The person who follows his instructions loves the adviser without deceit and with an unadorned mouth.

Moreover, our inexperience rightly suffers fear from the very novelty of the office. Recently prepared from the sheepfolds for guardianship, we are becoming accustomed, through necessity, to being suspected by everyone; and the person who scarcely had reliable caution for himself undertakes the office of one who must fear everything.

We know how much more humble he must be toward those who serve who is called to religious authority. It is necessary that he obey even persons of the lowest condition, when he is poised to command in such a way. For the teacher of the nations says: “I have become all things to all people, that I might win all” (I Corinthians 9:22).

May the operation of the Divinity now be present for its office, and may it make worthy of so great a summit the one whom it did not find worthy. [Col. 0273B]

## PRAYER OF THE MASSES

It is worthy and just. Truly it is worthy that, at the beginning of dignity, we should pray to you, Lord of beginnings, who established the infancy of the world itself, coming forth into a new light, with as much power as you initiated it in the hiddenness of your goodness. The tender beginning of the universe stood in wonder at itself and almost staggered, shaken by astonishment at its own beauty; before recognizing order, it had received from its creator substance alone. It was asking by what governance the assigned light should be made to revolve and what end the time of day would meet if it were always reborn through repeated settings; whether night, surrounding the world with dark embraces, would hold the primordial thing forever. [Col. 0273C]

Amid this uncertainty, the will of our God established the law by which confused things might serve defined purposes through the long course of time. Every dispensation enclosed within fixed limits was able to accomplish only as much as its creator granted.

Thus, pious maker, at the beginning of our priestly title, shine upon us with the sun of our conduct. Through the sweat of our merits, let the day of our office shine forth. By no stealth, by no flatteries of the devil, let what we are called to be perish. Let us not be permitted to admit what is unbecoming. Under your command, let devotion to what is right pass into our nature. Let a corresponding activity attend our duties. Let blessed authority grow through ordered service, and let one who is superior in dignity not be subordinate in character. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.

## PRAYER BEFORE THE MASS

God who bestows good things, for whom the result is present in the vow, who consecrated Moses from the midst of the people in the person of a prophet—for when he complained of weakness, he grew strong through your agency—he received the merit of a pontiff while, as a just judge of himself, he cried out that he deserved nothing, and humility won for him the exalted summit of action: grant a grace equal to our beginnings, since by our actions we show that we are more prone to incur offense. [Col. 0273D]

What we ask is not unfamiliar. Your kindness is bound by the testimony of an example. You will be more merciful toward us in the bestowal of good things the more our substance has been made inclined toward the burden of sin. [Col. 0274A]

Grant, good ruler, a virtue worthy of your choice, because under a pious ruler no abject condition disgraces the soldier. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.

## DICTION VI

[Note: “A speech on the heresies of the East.” The heading of this speech is not Ennodius’ own, since in the old books it is without a title, prefixed only by the words “In the name of Christ.” Moreover, nothing in it suggests that it was delivered by Ennodius rather than by some other bishop. Nevertheless, it is entirely worthy of the zeal of any excellent bishop, so that he may draw his people away from the contagion of heresies and keep them within orthodox doctrine adhering to Peter and to the Apostolic See.] [Col. 0273D]

On heretics and the synod.

# SACRED ORATION VI

What we have kept silent for a reason must be discharged for a reason. For, so that it may be clear that both the duties of our tongue and our silence have served their appointed times, urged on by faith we burst forth into the service of speech. To speak needlessly is the same as failing to speak when necessary, since the Apostle says: “Woe is me if I do not evangelize” [Col. 0274B] (1 Cor. 9:16); and elsewhere: “A time to keep silence” (Eccles. 3:7). We especially, whom the burden of obedience urges as those set over others, ought either to exalt those who do good or to restrain those who do evil.

Indeed, to teach you is nothing other than applying spurs to your heels. For what you do deliberately, we would be proud if we believed it owed something to our instruction; but whoever approves good endeavors increases them. You know well how Nestorius and Eutyches, twin manifestations of the devil’s instruction, long corrupted the chaste discipline of the Eastern Churches by the fornication of treachery. In accordance with the Apostle’s judgment, “they did not receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved; and therefore God sent them the working of error, that they should believe the lie” (1 Thess. 2:10). Meanwhile, through the occasion of scandal that stealthily intrudes, that field of contention tests Christ’s soldiers, just as it is written: “There must be conflicts, so that those who are approved may be made manifest” (1 Cor. 9:19).
