Where among the peoples is the venerable memory of the Council of Chalcedon not alive? There Dioscorus, together with his followers, was condemned by the pen of pious severity, and the city of Constantinople received with rejoicing the venerable memorials of Flavian, whose sentence the heavenly decrees had long before confirmed.

[Note: “Where among the peoples is Timothy” — Timothy, surnamed Aelurus, occupant of the see of Alexandria after Proterius had been murdered and he had been installed in the place of Dioscorus. Concerning him, see Liberatus the deacon, chapter 15 of the *Breviary*.]

Where among the peoples is Timothy unknown—he who, in order to undertake the murder of Proterius, whose memory ought to have been received [or: whose memory ought to have been revered], did not shrink from becoming worse than a parricide? For by persecuting the holy bishop he surpassed both the kinds and the names of crimes.

[Note: “Peter is known” — Peter Mongus, successor of Aelurus and the chief instigator and standard-bearer of the Dioscorian faction. After removing the name of Proterius and of the Catholic Timothy from the diptychs, he entered the names of Dioscorus and Aelurus, as the same Liberatus relates in chapter 18.]

Peter is known, as are Cyrus and Timothy, who, while extending a hand to the fallen Dioscorus, fell themselves. From their predecessor they inherited both his pursuits and his ruin.

Therefore, brothers, hold fast the judgment of the fathers, which remains in heaven and adheres to blessed Peter, because we desire the unity of the pure Church, “without spot” (Eph. 5:27). We cannot patiently endure those who pour forth empty and blasphemous utterances against our Christ. We know that he who does not use a harsh remedy on rotting limbs [Col. 0275A] gives assistance to spreading diseases: unless the weakened parts are cut away, they contaminate the rest.

There is a peaceful encounter with those who strive to attack what is right. Who would be turned back by the obstacle of fear from such wars, through which one may rejoice in a life-giving death? Even if the powerful of this world threaten us, we do not believe that we should yield to them, when the one who governs kingdoms commands otherwise. The Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present world are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to come, which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18).

The wavering hearts of churchmen are either troubled or delighted by the things of the present life. Among these was Acacius,

[Note: Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, who at first stood against Peter Mongus in defense of the synod and persuaded Basiliscus to revoke the edict he had issued against it, as Evagrius reports from the rhetor Zacharias in book 3, chapter 7 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. Afterward, as Liberatus notes in chapter 17, he changed his mind for an exceedingly trivial reason and began to favor Peter Mongus, whom he had previously condemned. He became the author of a most serious and troublesome disturbance in the Church, which continued for a very long time even after his death.]

Acacius, who, moved by the dreadful command of the devil away from his own judgment, was ashamed that he had long been a defender of the truth. Abandoning the brilliant honors of the struggle, he destroyed the triumph that he had earned beneath Basiliscus by pious toil [Col. 0275B]. He begrudges his own rewards almost at the moment of obtaining them, cutting down with the sickle of treachery the hope of good fruits. For it is more grievous to trample upon good things after tasting them than to trample upon things never touched. No defense remains for the man who, after savoring the sweetness of justice, returns to the deadly poisons of schisms.

From the matters we have mentioned arose what is recently said to have been committed in the Church of Constantinople. Hence we suffer grief without the use of our voice. For those who do not obey remedies when they are offered had, deservedly, no consolation at the time when they were oppressed.

# DICTIO VII

On the dedication of the lecture hall, when the transfer to the Forum took place.

[Note: “On the dedication of the lecture hall” — This is a speech concerning the lecture hall of the Roman school. He calls the transfer festive, since the school moved from its former seats to the Forum, so that playful exercises might take place there, where serious cases had been pleaded. But he does not explain which Forum it was, although rhetors are once said to have declaimed in various places. One may infer that it was Trajan’s Forum from what Fortunatus writes about poems recited there in his own age, book 3, letter 21.]

# SCHOLASTIC ORATION I

Just as the field excites the soldier, the sea the sailor, the courts the advocate, and uncertainties seize the plunderer, so lecture halls exercise the tongue. What reason for silence would persuade anyone in a place where rewards for speech have been established? Where is the prize of eloquence if here there is favor for silence? The rewards of sweat are well paid where there are temples of victory; servitude is well driven away among the halls of freedom.

Let a captive mind keep its lips bound here: the man who still remains silent as though in retreats does not recognize the Forum of the Roman people or the gymnasium of liberal learning. Let remote shelters perhaps be silent; here nothing is so familiar as the parade of eloquence. The applause of the customary profession encourages genius to offer Fescennine jests at wedding songs. Warriors are raised up by trumpets; the heavy sound of the bugles lifts those weak in courage; friendly incentives have been given to all according to their purposes [Col. 0275D].

What shall I do, excellent teacher, while you are speaking? If I keep unformed words within the modest sanctuary of my heart, you will not recognize me as one formed by your instruction. I shall offend the sacred bond of friendship by my lack of gratitude if I discharge neither the festival of the transfer nor the tribute of praise owed to you.

Hail, therefore, nourisher of progress, torch and splendor of free birth: you make noble shoots recognizable by their fruits, cleansing them with laborious hoes; in the gray blossom of a young generation, you show how much is being prepared for the granaries; from the lairs of wild beasts and the dwellings of owls you call us back to the courts, from which our ancestors had almost departed through long age.

For these places are not open to the learned unless they have received knowledge from the very first lips of instruction. Whose trumpet of eloquence is recognized except that of the person whose childish beginnings in speech have become known? These benefits, therefore, are owed to you: an advocate about to summon a defendant will begin a formidable speech in halls where he has already been tested.

To you must be assigned the sole hope of an honorable profession: nobility, after a brief passage of time, will please through the sweat of liberal study. But where is my affection carrying me, ignorant as I am of your powers? Why does it sweep me into the sea of narration without leaving me suspended? It is enough, amid the friendship of the place and the solemnity of the day, to have borne witness to my wishes.

I turn back to you, to whom, in the affection of a fatherly assembly, I owe the voice of admonition. Restore yourselves by study to your origin; restore yourselves by reading to your birth. Let the light of nature display the radiance of eloquence. Multiply the titles of your parents by the support of knowledge; adorn the distinctions of your ancestors through learning.

The nobility of bright metal is almost dulled by the darkness of its mother ore unless the craftsman’s hand brings it to a fine edge. If it is not beautified by the guiding work of polishing, the exaltation granted by its vein does it no good. The persistence of a teacher is indeed aided by the gifts of purer blood; but unless refined, those things that raise themselves up by the privilege of birth do not shine.

A rustic child empties its mother’s breasts among the furrows; while still hanging from the udder, it becomes accustomed to drive cattle through the pastures. It is joined to its father’s arms while he tires out the young bulls; it grasps the right hand that entrusts great seeds to the earth; and at the very threshold of daylight it practices the sweat of its origin.

What should you do, whose excellent mothers gave birth to you for liberal disciplines? You must journey away from a richer stock unless noble institutions have shown you the way. You have before you a teacher of eloquence and character. Run, urged on by the goads of your ancestry; and when promised rewards have brought you to the contest, deign to remember me, because after heavenly recompense there are forms of support that an encourager may receive from you.

These are the admonitions that I have been permitted to address to you in my own voice. Weigh the diligence of my heart by considering my words. Do not let ornate speech, or merely alluring narrative painted with cosmetics, delight you. Seek from me not what flatters but what is necessary; not what is delightful but what is strong.

Does it help to weave a display for someone about to give instruction? Whoever intends to gain approval not so much by his meaning as by his speech nullifies the purpose of the admonisher. Let the speech of one who corrects be adorned with weight [Col. 0276D]. Let him who longs to be heard hold the scales in his exhortation. Let the instructor of virtue exclude applause: a morally disciplined speech commands what it recommends.

Even if I cannot explain these things with eloquence, I have nevertheless learned to love them through reflection on my purpose and through reading wise counsel. It is a part of integrity to know better things even when one cannot fulfill them. The effect of the work follows upon tested intention. He is nearest to the teacher who loves the ornaments of instruction.

May God, however, join himself as a companion to my prayer; and what I commend to the young shoots as their teacher, may I pluck as fruit from an inherited possession.

# DICTIO VIII

Preface spoken to Lupicinus when he was entrusted to Deuterius in the lecture hall.

[Note: “Preface spoken to Lupicinus” — The letters have taught us that Lupicinus was the son of Euprepia, Ennodius’s sister. Here he reveals both of Lupicinus’s grandfathers, Firminus and Licerius, from whom he customarily took his surnames. For he was called Flavius Licerius Firminus Lupicinus. We learned this from a Vatican manuscript of Julius Caesar’s *Commentaries*, at the end of which was written: “I, Julius Celsus Constantinus, have read this. I, Flavius Licerius Firminus Lupicinus, have read this.”]

# SCHOLASTIC ORATION II

Whenever a little flower of amomum or a harvest of cassia is stripped by the plundering of a wanton finger, and a noble shoot is added to the adornment of human hands, the worth of the plant is indicated by its fragrance, and the genius of nature is testified by its first appearance. A lofty offspring does not permit itself to be hidden; the glory of distinguished blood cannot remain concealed; the voice of noble origin, even in retreats, is always heard.

Yet although things are so, it belongs to humanity not to remain silent about what one longs for. He assumes little burden who commends what he knows to be worthy of love; he does not escape the stain of savagery who does not hasten to assert what he knows will please by its merits. Who would refuse to praise the day? Who would fear to raise the sun’s rays through any night of speech? If speech serves its theme, it receives dignity from the theme itself [Col. 0277C].

Therefore do not be troubled by the meagerness of your own talent, when the poverty of eloquence is raised by the value of the speech undertaken. Lift up your mind, weighed down by the burden of ignorance; you will be relieved by the right hand of the burden imposed upon you.

But why do we become entangled in lengthy matters? The foregoing narrative concerns the young man before us. I promise, supported not by the declarations of augurs but, after God, by hope in your perfection, that he will return to his ancestors. Nor do I doubt that you can restore to his family the splendor that you have bestowed upon others. For he can easily revive the honors of the ancients who is permitted to build new ones.

Do not believe that these are merely incentives to eloquence. To you alone it has been granted either to give or to restore the glory of your ancestors. Before your eyes stand not the ancient monuments of a boy but recent ones. Firminus and Licerius, the stars of their age, address you through this voice.

Receive, most learned of men, a shoot from both families, and attend favorably to the stem from which you may produce heavy ears of grain. Scratch the fertile earth with your hoes; if it is the clasp of our stock, it will surely respond to your labors. Make the married plantings grow by teaching from a book. Apply the fruit of the better shoot to the teeth of the young branch. Let the succession of fruits come, while the more exalted plant is bitten by the tender mouth of the one whom you teach. For unless the farmer has written upon subdued earth three and four times with his mattocks [Col. 0278A], the thorny growth and darnel will overtake the wheat harvest.

Cultivation enriches the Palladian gift and the hoary groves with many berries. India nourishes ebony through the great labor of which it boasts. The Sabaean branch does not prosper if the hand ceases from tending the ground. Industry caused the thickets of Praestana to produce roses; labor draws them from the thorns like stars of the earth.

The persistence of the worker is blessed whenever hands are applied to fertile clods. Then tired arms swell with the juice of poured-out vigor, when productive fields repay the husbandmen in full. The fertility of the soil awakens the desire for toil. One must work with plows so that the autumn’s bounty may overflow through the branches.

No one has ever earned foaming must upon his lips unless he cut back the luxuriance of the vine with a curved sickle; and through different kinds of cultivation he poured forth more liquid than he would have received as wine.

Such is the nature of mortals: the beginnings of children are rightly compared with trees and shrubs. After parental care has plucked them from the root of their mother, it must see to whom, according to its wishes, they should be entrusted as soil. After deliberation, we transfer our rights to teachers.

Then those whom nature has granted to us are formed by your instruction. Then the file of study begins to claim for itself as much as origin can scarcely prevail over. For it is almost no injustice for ancestry to be surpassed by the contribution of learning. A father’s office has luxury as its companion; a teacher’s has diligence. A parent makes one soft through indulgence; an instructor through labor. Origin grants freedom; an admonisher makes one worthy of freedom.

Therefore, what is praised in a person belongs more to you. No one, if the testimony of eloquence is absent, can proclaim what we are born to be. The tongue that you bestow reveals the splendor of the family; the teacher’s gift becomes the herald of the lineage. Uneducated nobility renounces a heavenly gift.

Bind, therefore, the wandering slips of youth with tighter bonds. Punish the branches with iron, leaving them without offspring. Raise up the young plant with the nourishment by which you customarily make everything fruitful.

Our young man has before him whatever he has seen in his family to follow. Believe us: his character will fly forward, urged by so many goads, into whatever sea of knowledge he enters. His lineage will be dug up by spurs; through all its ranks he will find nothing except what invites him to letters.

Behold, our little one stands before you, about to be initiated under happy auspices. Just as the sacrifice of a righteous person calls forth the devotion of a priest, so paternal piety demands that his infancy, established at the threshold of life, be commended by every kind of prayer. He does not demand from his parents what he wants in words; his helplessness reveals it. We are compelled to assist the child in the necessity that fear makes plain.

Promise yourself to your worthy beginnings, young man [Note: Perhaps “worthy”]. We conceive a firm hope from your perfection; we entrust a good talent to the best teacher. Reverence now the beginnings of the sacred college. The stars of the Latin court advance those whom you see revealing the future light through modest sparks.

Let this suffice as what the grandfathers have said. For me there remains a brief personal appeal. I have presented to you a near kinsman, religiously deprived of his parents. You already understand what makes the child dear to me. If kinship is considered, I cannot be free from affection. If friendly piety is joined to my purpose, those who are stripped of their parents’ protection become our children.

One bond, therefore, comes from ancestry; another binds us through duty. Look, venerable teacher, upon so many suppliant hands raised on behalf of this child, and consider both his ancestors and me and yourself in the hope of the boy.

The education of a pupil is a unique source of praise for teachers. Chiron became known through the tongue of Achilles; the achievement of his disciple caused the reputation of the man whose own eloquence perhaps could not have emerged into the light to be loved all the more. Your Maro commended his teachers as greatly as he himself is known; and certainly their fame did not reveal them through their own merits [Col. 0279B]. Our Jerome, unless he had named his teacher Gregory, would have been considered superior to him; but the good qualities of the famous man must be attributed to the one from whom they appear to have received their origin.

In short, as I said, the reputation of the teacher reaches heaven through the perfection of the pupil. I do not bring forgetfulness before one who knows these matters, since I am recalling what is familiar. The prayers of the diligent are eager. I ask God to join his favor as a companion to your studies, so that you may make those whom you received from me for polishing supremely learned. Their education will indeed become your glory, but it will be my service.

# DICTIO IX

Preface spoken when Arator entered the lecture hall.

[Note: “Preface when Arator entered the lecture hall” — This entire piece has now been brought to light for the first time from manuscripts. It was written for Arator when he was entrusted to the instruction of Deuterius the grammarian at Milan. At Milan, I say, because, as was noted concerning the letters, Arator did not study outside Liguria. What is written about Deuterius in various places must be referred to Milan, where he had his school.]

# SCHOLASTIC ORATION III

It is known to all good mortals that leisure from business produces the labor of speaking, and that, once the storms of cares have been driven away, the serene skies of oratory shine more brightly. Talents do not lose their own day unless they are darkened by the clouds of occupation. The radiance of thought looks upon those free from care, and an unburdened mind commends the splendor of declamation.

He who rashly cuts through blind seas with oars entrusts to the helm a breast stripped of anxiety; and he weighs the management of the rudder, which belongs to the master of the ship, by inquiry alone. Then the flaxen reins are released from their bonds into the winds; then the long-free seas are bound by the cords of the rigging, and the man who is about to rule the imperious heaps of waves enters, recognizing the uncertainties of the roads as the stars reveal them.

Then, looking upon Phosphorus, the Pleiades, Cynosura, and whatever indicates the route, he orders the path of man according to the guidance of heaven [Col. 0279D], provided that his mind is not gnawed by the uncertainty of some foreign occupation, nor grief, the teacher of inertia, afflicts his wandering knowledge.

But if the mind, dulled by sluggish torpor, sleeps, or if it is awakened by various goads and drawn along byways, it does not know how to advance wholly toward its purpose. Concern, the trainer of souls, tears its limbs apart. He is always ineffective and is shown to be separated from the strength of his own mass who cannot display his full magnitude in a single form of discourse.

Yet it belongs to a good teacher to examine the source of a stream, which is brought to the very earth by a claw that scrapes it; to estimate what its channel is when collected into one course and what it is where it is born; and to gather the strength of the river not from what it has received but from what it could have received.

If you ask, venerable teacher, why I have prefaced these words—interpreter of freedom, witness to good blood, file of talents, craftsman of understanding—I admit that I have spoken of myself, arranged myself: I, whom various occupations and strong grief, the mother of ignorance, have oppressed amid the infancy of sleeping unknowing; I, who am not allowed to loosen my neck from harsh labors so that the mouths of study may be adorned with a bridle.

The roughness of my speech, which shines with no friction of eloquence, is due to the understanding and practice that I am unlearning. You are urged on by the prize of your ancestral language amid your own exercises. Forgetful of me, proud Delos counts you among its citizens. You advance as the clean possessor of the Castalian stream; while I scarcely pour a dripping drop of sluggish liquid from my parched lips.

Through continuous sweat, interrupted by no distraction, the harvest of learning enriches you as its own cultivator. But for me, a poor man, scarcely a morsel of beans is extended from the granaries of the great. You are happily appointed as the right hand supporting freedom as it is about to fall; but the corner of the Church encloses me, even though I fear the good things of the present age.

Why, I ask, did you recently see fit to direct the distinguished eyes of your eloquence so far toward me? There were others more suitable, whom the ornaments of your diction could have adorned, and to whom the trappings of words acquired through Latin elegance would have offered a name destined to live among posterity [Col. 0280C].

It would have been fitting for me to remain silent, since my affection is unequal to your words and separated from your services. Why do you raise spirits whom another order of life has already subjected to itself? Why do you call back to yourself, across such long intervals, a distant man for whom, just as it is sacrilegious not to have deserved praise, so it is a crime to have been praised?

They are yours, yours—do not doubt it—or theirs, if those who follow can nevertheless be found. Yet I turn my words to the young man whom the auspices of this day have dedicated to your lecture halls, and with whom I share an equal infancy, if you grant me pardon. Although I commend his beginnings in unformed speech, I am excused by the commands of love. One constrained by the necessity of affection is placed beneath its yoke; and while we look after those dear to us, we do not see what is fitting for ourselves.

A paternal speech ought to have accompanied him [Col. 0280D]; nevertheless, the speech I offer is not foreign to a father. It was fitting that both your profession and mine should address you with praise. The happy omen of this name among the learned promises, in name as well as in fact, labor necessary for the cultivation of studies, enriching it with the fruits of knowledge.

Cut open, excellent young man, the backs of rich lands. Press into them the tooth of a plow newly formed upon the anvil. Exercise in the soil of study everything that befits the best farmer. If you have thoroughly searched the hidden secrets of the fields, you will find there Deuterius, who, through the abundance of languages, multiplies shoots for you with many seeds and repays the sweat expended.

Learn now to cut away the luxuriance of words with the sickle of art, so that the young plant may advance under the discipline of iron. Let whatever the barren shade of branches has sent forth be cut back; let your vines extend their branches toward the single hope of grapes.

You must return in such a state to your own genius; you must turn in such a state toward our hopes. When you have adorned yourself with heavy stalks of knowledge, then it will be fitting for you to be called the great Arator.

Therefore, let the hope of reward nourish the ardor of praise in you. I have read that it is no game of fortune [the supplied text reads *Jusus*] if a learned man should at times make progress among filthy herds of the unlearned—of whom I am the first. Do not fear the oppression under which the educated are weighed down. Expertise lying low has more honor than the summits of rustic men. The learned are raised up by their own conscience; and if at times they are opposed by the uncertain winds of the age, they endure evils that must be attributed more to the times than to their merits.

Some say that my continuation, which I composed in praise of Arator in a truly rustic manner, merely flattered the fortunate circumstances of his person, and that affection was obtained for him by a feigned necessity arising from his father’s power. In serving this praise, they say, it serves only the living and the present, and the tongue displays temporal servitude. Whenever it plays in praise of certain people with fabricated images of words, it conceals the thought conceived with stronger purpose.

For sometimes a deeper style grants learned people a hiding place for profounder thoughts, if it has enticed the ears of those who do not deserve such sweet refreshments. But such practices must be kept apart from the purpose of our work. We ought both to know them and to hate them. Prudence avoids what is known more cautiously than what is unexpected.

For me, unless love sends words to the praises of friends—words dictated in the inner chambers of conscience under the instruction of charity—I shall tremble beneath the burden of the task undertaken along the paths of public discourse.

[Note: “To my classmate” — A little below, *classicus* does not mean one who is subject to commands, namely Arator. Ennodius has used *classicus* in a new sense for a scholastic auditor, as though the ranks into which students are divided in schools were already called classes. He uses the same word in book 9, the penultimate letter.]

Therefore, to my classmate, whose native talent has served him without deceit, I have brought expressions that reveal my mind, because friendship between equals is free from suspicion of flattery. The sincere diligence of those who care is approved whenever what one fears does not come from power. My classmate does not command me, whatever he does not impose upon obedience.

Yet some say that a faithful orphan, auspiciously entering the gymnasia of letters, ought rather to have had words presented by a religious person. I called him an orphan because, through the fortunate losses of nature, the common father and bishop became his own personal father.

That man—the consolation of the afflicted, the food of the fasting, the eye of the blind, the foot of the lame, possessing so many forms of piety and so many degrees of mercy—has turned all these toward the advancement of this person. And the genius of Lord Laurentius, which comes to the aid of the needs of the world, is exercised in the service of this little child.

Who would not call such a condition a gracious misfortune? Who would not rejoice to have lost a father, if he is permitted to find such a one in a profitable exchange? I will not rashly profane the distinctions of so great a man, which I cannot fulfill, with worldly words.

He is the one whose authority is sweet—or whose sweetness is terrible—who is a teacher in the church, a teacher in the house, a teacher at table, and a teacher even in play; who never does anything that he would not wish those who follow him to imitate.

His conduct, polished to the finest edge, shows his disciples the heavenly path as he walks. For it is a lesser praise to teach what is good unless you demonstrate through your actions what must be taught.

What could my speech have contributed to the young man entrusted to such a man? A favorable outcome awaits him because of his instructor’s merits, and perfection awaits him because of the prosperity of his orphanhood. The prayers of his patron are sufficient for him; through them he will deserve, imbued with the best instruction, to ‘degenerate’ in an exalted way.

# DICTIO X

Thanks expressed to a grammarian when Parthenius recited well.

[Note: “Thanks expressed to a grammarian when Parthenius…” — Parthenius, the son of another sister of Ennodius, was discussed in its proper place in the letters. Earlier, when he was beginning his studies, Ennodius had addressed him in another speech that is no longer extant. Now he gives thanks to his teacher, Deuterius, as I believe, after Parthenius had demonstrated his progress by declaiming. Thus there are two speeches for Arator: one when he was led to school, the other when he advanced to praise.]

# SCHOLASTIC ORATION IV

When we return thanks owed for benefits, I believe that we renounce boastfulness by rendering the necessary service. For no swelling of arrogance is concealed beneath the garment of honor when words serve not glory but kinship. It is one thing to speak so that you may be praised; it is another to speak so that you may not be criticized.

In the first case, the mind is enslaved to fame and boastfulness; in the second, having preserved proper judgment, it rightly restores to the place of glory whatever has come from the sweat of speech. For both just and excessive declamations are displayed to minds that are distinct, even if they receive equal favor in speech. The praises of a tyrant and those of good rulers are both uttered by the mouth; there is no difference between the praise of one who deserves it and that of one who usurps it—unless the weighty minds of judges examined the grounds of the speeches. The breeze of acclamation, which reaches even the unworthy, would provide no distinction.

The secrets of received speeches are examined by listeners not with the tongue but with the heart. In sum, it is one thing to hear a reciter pleasantly and willingly; it is another to approve the feeling with which you recite.

But now, leaving aside commendations of the theme, let the matter itself speak of our modest ability. Once, excellent teacher, I brought Parthenius, who was hastening to your studies, into your presence through the introduction of my little speech—at the time when he was entering the threshold of the liberal disciplines, when it was uncertain whether he would express the splendor of his ancestry through learning. For no one whose instruction does not reveal his blood has a witness to his nobility.

We therefore addressed him in eloquence at the time when it was not permitted to show through our speech what sort of person he had been born to be. For it is always a stain upon good merits to possess the light of blood but be enclosed in the night of rusticity; to be revealed by the voices of one’s ancestors but to lie hidden beneath the darkness of ignorance.

Gold is nothing unless it is shaped by the craftsman’s hand, and the value of yellow metal is joined to it by the file of the maker [Col. 0283A]. When industry ceases, the brilliance that comes from nature is slight. The earth owes to the studies of the smith what is praised in its birth. By the benefit of the furnace and the hidden dregs of its veins, iron gains the appearance of solidity [Note: Schott: “is bestowed”]. And the savage hearts of human beings, captured by discipline that tames affection, would not provide mortals with a livelihood unless they were exercised.

It is the work of art that man safely enters the liquid element of the sea and, through the powers of intelligence, overcomes the path of death with little danger. The simplicity that teaches farmers, while distinguishing the face of the earth with their arms, arranges vineyards and extracts from the offspring of trees a liquid by which health may be nourished.

The diligence of workers is made clear by many indications: either what origin does not grant is infused, or what nature grants as good is preserved. And if this is the universal condition of things, how greatly, most learned teacher, must your diligence be raised by praise? Through your right hand freedom, already about to fall, is restored; through your skill, young things are formed and the honors of ancestors preserved.

I confess truly: if you did not exist, whatever genius displays would soon succumb. But why am I burdened with great matters when I cannot sustain small ones, and why do I make a general return of thanks when I scarcely suffice for one person?

Before many witnesses, most accomplished of men, I offer you abundant thanks because you have made it possible for me to recognize Parthenius through instruction. You removed from his heart, with the hoe of knowledge, the thorn and darnel; you raised up a wheat harvest to feed his kinsmen. Through a fortunate outcome in him, amid the discord of families, you showed one thing to follow and another to avoid.

O virtue of your genius, worthy of praise above mankind! In one and the same person, with what skill you showed what he should learn and what he should unlearn—both of which descended from his blood.

May God arrange our joys with a happy outcome. May whatever threatens adversity remain far away. You deserve more praise because your pupil knows how to avoid his ancestry than because he strives to imitate it.

Behold Parthenius, descending from both paths of his lineage, happily recognizes some things and happily does not recognize others. I feared that the mixture described above, while discordant through its very diversity, might grant the better part of his life to the claims of what was worse, and that, because of the weakness of the times, the unlearned side might more easily rule in him.

But you have shown me, ornament of your age, that I have obtained more in my kinsman than I asked. You have imitated heavenly abundance in the generosity of your gift, when, through multiplied expenditure, you surpassed the hopes of the one who commended him.

Behold, now little flowers of speech bloom in a wintry breast and cold heart, and the smiling shoots of words adorn the baskets of the one who presents them. Behold, after the murmur of his barbarous speech, words pour from his mouth that signify humanity.

If I do not repay these gifts of yours, consider that you have bestowed them upon one who did not deserve them. For whoever receives better successes from a tongue at leisure shows that he does not love the prosperity that brought them. 

# DICTIO XI

Spoken when the son of Eusebius was entrusted to his studies.

# SCHOLASTIC ORATION V
Although novelty, like interruption, has its fears—and this happens when, [Note: perhaps “by friction” (attritu).] because of the wear caused by public favor, the brow recoils from what it was before it learned, while through the loss of practice in speaking old age is brought back to the infancy from which it had struggled free—yet the horse trained for Olympic contests trusts in the palm of victory; and, if it is not weakened by idleness, believes the victory to be its rightful possession. Hope always promises it a crown with effective flatteries, unless the sluggishness of laziness shakes the prize from its speed.

The javelin-thrower, confident of triumphs, seeks uncertainties; and the man whom glory always meets in battle is overcome by prolonged peace. Constant application, nurse of genius, accompanies the ivy of poets with nobler clusters and verdant beauty. When frequent practice ceases, the mouths of advocates grow silent. The sailor, trained among ships, traverses the liquid sea without fear; but if he directs his duties toward earthly life, he discovers neither routes by the stars nor outcomes by auspices. If a farmer, enticed by urban life, should at some time despise the plow, he will be carried off course while he traces furrows with his oxen. Therefore, just as persistent application is the mother of every art in its own work, negligence is the stepmother of learning.

Such is the condition of our speech, which we bring forth after intervals of time: it bears no familiar form and displays none of the pomp it ought to have purchased with age. Placing all its confidence in the goodwill of its hearers, it believes pardon sufficient in place of favor and pious wishes sufficient in place of merit. Keep far away, weak fear: compassion for orphanhood commends the speech as a religious duty. What can a speech endowed with the splendor of expertise accomplish where the case itself pleases even without the service of an insinuating tongue? The matter has won favor; it is enough that the words deserve affection. Both circumstances have come together under favorable omens for your hearing.

I shall say what remains, since I defraud my praises by as much as I leave unsaid in the present case. The most noble father Eusebius, equal in character as in nature, while pressed by his final hour and wishing by a lasting plan to surpass the human condition that would benefit the future; while, with the strength of his life-giving soul, he trod down the confinement of his earthly prison and, when summoned by God, poured himself into spiritual dwellings; while nothing of the human remained in his mind except his son’s unstained devotion—that which not even forgetfulness erases amid heavenly things—left him to me to cherish, insofar as my strength allowed, as one who was, so to speak, well known to his conscience. The words of the man who was laying everything down were confused with his final sighs.

I shall see what he left to others; under oath before God, he entrusted the heir to me. For him, as he touches the taste of life with his first lips, I pray that an abundance of flavor may be poured in, so that, enticed by the honey of disciplines and the combs of knowledge, he may draw for himself nectar from the waxen houses of the liquefying element.

Venerable teacher, your praise has been brought to its culmination through this boy, so that it may grasp what it deserves. The fullness of your merits does not reject increase from the progress of such pupils, because a pupil’s elegance is the teacher’s spotless vindication—especially that of a teacher whose splendid lineage time demands to adorn with the rays of knowledge, so that the glory of his origin may proceed toward the clearest day, when the radiance of speech shines forth in him.

## DICTIO XII

Delivered to Arator when he was advanced to praise.

### SCHOLASTICA SIXTH

### Theme: Praise of letters

### PREFACE

Let the letter be praised for its own splendid wealth,  
for borrowed adornment contributes nothing to genius.

The fleeces of Seres shine more brightly when dyed;  
Persian gems adorn gleaming necks.

It does no good to arrange limbs with external brilliance:  
natural light ennobles the stars.

### NARRATION

For all things that are esteemed through praises, a commendation corresponding to the power of speech must be offered. What is owed to things radiant with the gift of eloquence must be rendered in letters, because just as a gratuitous gift reveals both the wealth and the spirit of the giver, so to deny what has been received exposes the greed and shamelessness of the one who suppresses it.

Let us taste the divinity of letters, which has flowed from their own altars. However greatly this material may be honored by the riches of praise, however abundantly it may pour forth words, it is fed and satisfied by the fruits of its own possession. For, while amid the green places it has arranged it captivates the eyes with its own beauty, it certainly derives pleasure from its own grasses, but through its mistress the harvests of intellect receive greater increase.

Therefore whoever pays his debt to letters grows richer, since what has been directed toward them is brought back through more hidden channels, as through great riverbeds. Nor will you possess what you have lost drop by drop otherwise than if you had the right to claim the receding Ionian Sea. Who would deny the deposit of knowledge except one who wishes to become a beggar while hoarding it? The fruit of this matter—strange though it is to say—boils over when poured into abundance, while those who cling to it remain hungry.

Therefore, after heavenly help and the aid of favor from above, venerable art, administer the praises which you employ; and rejoice in the excellence of your invention over what has been directed by you. Embrace what has arisen from you in the practice of praise. Nothing remains for us in this matter that deserves either punishment or reward. If, through the faithful service of our mouths, we suggest too little in elevating your merits, you have made it so: we are the pipes of these streams, and we drink nothing from the abundance of the liquid entrusted to us. Flow through us, so that you may satisfy your merits, like the Aegean Sea, like a Pegasean torrent.

Before your eyes are the examples of your character, if you retain them well. Whatever jewels we bring from your treasury to be put out at interest remain safe. Behold, a diadem flashing with your light ennobles my head, and with the varied brilliance of precious stones it grows out of genius while it is suitably displayed.

From you institutions of wisdom take their root; through you what has been formed is brought forth. Without you there is no flavor in the breast, nor freedom in speech. You are the testimony of free birth; you are the material of modesty. Through you the tongue speaks what the heart has dictated well. You provide a road for the pursuit of justice, having cleared the overgrown path by which higher things are sought. You turn wheat-bearing grain from darnel; you make fertile the fields of intellect that were barren; and you carry heavy ears of grain to the storehouses of knowledge, lest the hunger of infancy prevail.

By preserving the purity and brightness of a family, you bathe an ignoble lineage in foreign light. A thing infused with genuine benefit is close to God, since through the courses of transmitted study it is ensured that the best do not degenerate and that the bad do degenerate, while the truth of pedigrees is preserved.

Through you the deeds of the innocent that pertain to the instruction of those who follow do not perish. What has been accomplished is brought into the midst through your chains, and buried things come back to life. You are the instruments of memory; you are the cause of piety. Through your plows the soil of the human breast is described as prepared for fertility. You are the authors of religion; you are the enemies of crimes. Under your leadership, crimes that steal in through practice are unlearned, and through you good things are learned. You either enlarge human beings toward a straight purpose or redirect what is crooked.

Through your testimony exiles are adorned, and you join to heaven those separated from the summits of the world. You refuse entry to evil consciences, or, once they have entered the sanctuary, you consecrate them.

Let there be removed from letters both the changing of what is worthy and the failure to change what is harmful. No instruction clothed in steel withdraws from your wounds. You reach the innermost chambers even of those whom iron has covered. The missiles directed by adversaries are repelled by your bosses, and no latticework of shields can be set against the mirrors of your knowledge.

You raise those placed in affliction; you soothe those set upon the cross of their bodies. Thus you add increase to joys while preserving cheerfulness and its proper measure. If caresses come from you, they become sweet.

It is not permitted, against your command, to weep even for a dead person whom one loves. You are suited to weddings; you are suited to funerals. The study of this knowledge holds the most diverse things together in harmony and embraces both sides with rejoicing. Would that it were permitted to honor you with longer utterances, and that brevity were not owed to your laws, from which an abundance of wishes is supplied!

Through the forms of letters, the voice destined to endure for a long time is safely entrusted and, without diminution, made solid by the reader who revisits it. Before you, humanity lived without knowledge of order, and breasts belching acorns spewed out words without measure. You create distinction among human beings of one nature: knowledge of you makes them like heavenly beings, while ignorance makes them like beasts.

It is evident what the abandoned lineage of mortals was like before this harvest, since, although their arrival into the light is equal to ours, their condition of knowing is not the same because of your discrimination.

Farewell, ornaments of a better age, and possess, as a remedy granted by God, the world that you have educated.

## DICTIO XIII

When Paterius and Severus were handed over to study.

### SCHOLASTICA SEVENTH

If the sailor happily crosses the appointed course over a wet path under favorable winds; if better success leads the warrior to triumph; if, through the fields of rhetoric, the soldier of letters is exalted by the favor of the judge, then today it is our part to rejoice in the theme under equal circumstances.

What have I to do with the publicized and degraded poverty of my own talent? Behold, we grow rich from the pleasant harvest of the speech we have undertaken, when the merit of the subject enlarges the merit of the speaker, and the case commends its advocate.

Where is the fear that, because of our awareness of inexperience, used to subject us to itself? Where is the trembling of the brow, made more fragile by use and exercise? We forget our own merit while we speak of another’s brilliance. Now we learn that others are powerful and that you make them so, when such noble fame supplies so great a subject for praise.

I have nothing to do with uncertainties: the splendor of those who are praised illuminates the praisers, and the sun, if they remember it, opens a way for those immersed in darkness. Yet cheerfulness is again joined to fear, and trembling becomes the companion of exultation. When one is unequal in small matters, will one be sufficient in supreme ones? For whoever does not commend brilliance with the light of style obscures it; and just as small things grow through the talent of eloquent men, so the greatest are disfigured by dryness. Unless you undertake the burden with forces proportionate to what you judge yourself capable of, you will lie beneath it.

Behold, Paterius and Severus, ornaments of the curule offices and ancestral names of the purple, await their inherited learning at the very beginnings of life. They do not disdain to drink deeply, with a relish for light, of the studies with which God’s nature and letters endowed them at an undiscriminating age.

For their sake, why should I suggest to their minds the ancestral honors and ancient insignia of their parents? I shall be relieved of this burden if you, my hearer, question the official records on my behalf. With me is that solemn cry of the public courts; with me both the court and the senate honor Severus and Paterius. Although their family deserved staffs of office and trabeae, they have nevertheless, setting aside for the moment the gift of blood—which knows neither decline through offices nor death after burial—earned distinction through their character.

I would be lying if Paterius were not alive. [Note: Paterius was alive: he was the colleague of Petronius Maximus in the consulship of 442 and prefect of the praetorium before his consulship, as attested by a novella of the emperor Valentinian sent to him.] Ennodius also indicates that a bronze statue was erected for Paterius in honor of his learning, evidently in Trajan’s Forum, where it was customary. Sidonius writes:

> “The Ulpian portico gleams with my bronze.”

Paterius, held in esteem by the learned and fashioned in enduring bronze, presents among experts that image renowned for the palms of eloquence.

Their lineage, still small yet already very great, bearing the jewel-like faces of budding youth, implores the eloquence that it will display, making this request through the silent appeal of its discourse.

Help these children, whom you will soon have as fathers of their country. Supply defenses to its defenders, and fight for the tender young, lest, while fighting on behalf of the commonwealth, we who are more mature in age should succumb.

You know which household labors for the general disaster and to whom sacrifice is owed for the common security; from that household has flowed what keeps civility from wavering among you amid adversity. Our origin owes you this tributary service: that it should always nourish, without interruption, the guardians of its country.

Therefore, if the good qualities of our stock are known to you, suggest what ought to be grafted onto it, so that cultivation may improve what shines in the seed. Let the turf that serves the root bear fruits to give. What we ask is neither foreign nor fugitive.

If a horse judged by its parents is nourished by Eleian and Olympic contests, let us still be fortified by examples of those who have advanced from their creators. Circumstances have provided you with so much service, since the posterity of your defenders is growing and the protection of father and grandfather still does not fail.

Therefore, venerable teacher, receive one who brings you the voices of all, stirred by these incentives; and, elevated by consideration of your merit, make yourself equal to the form of judgment of many. Labor so that our fortification may be made firm while you support it, and, lest the hostile assault of battering rams prevail, join the weapons of study to the walls of your country.

We know whose offspring is entrusted to you, so that industry may strengthen what nature has produced strong. It will be the fault of the leader, not of the origin, if one born from the stock of a brave man has fear amid battles. It is enough that you grow through the sweat of your instruction so as to make the boys of the present attain the form of their ancestors.

But perhaps you will say: although a holier profession urges you, my concern does not regard me as the least important in these matters. I am the one whose mother and whose virgin womb of the sacred font brought forth Paterius as a son. In the second birth or renewal of his soul, I am his father. Therefore the provision of his particular education concerns me, whose father I have been called even among heavenly things.

## DICTIO XIV

Against the legate who betrayed his country to its enemies.

### CONTROVERSY ONE

If the crime is more serious when committed by a person worthy of veneration, then, judges, you have in one man two entirely different statuses: the merit of a traitor and the sacred obligation of a legate.

Yet the voice is overcome at the very beginning by the enormity of the deed. I scarcely believe the crime I accuse. Who would think that complete perfidy had fallen within a title of integrity? We are forced to say that neither would a traitor fear any evil nor would a true legate admit it.

Why do you oppose the name of innocence to my accusation? You could escape your pursuer if you deserved what you are called. No one is more cautiously wicked than the man concealed beneath the name of piety; the practice of iniquity is safe when covered by the garment of honesty.

Let the proposal that rests on trickery rather than on principle be dismissed. The defense is weakened when it relies on bare honor and on testimony that will avail nothing. Your counsels provided you a path by which you could become more harmful to your country. We acted so that you might appear a stronger enemy while we sought a defender. We would not have sensed the weight of the hostility you inflicted upon your country unless it had taken its beginning from the sacred bond of friendship.

We meet external adversaries without difficulty. An unarmed breast finds the man who bursts from the fruit of favor into the affection of an enemy. During the time of the treaty we acted so that the general enemy might not conceal what burdened the country.

For this man, most distinguished of the people, if he had performed the office he undertook more negligently and, through weariness of spirit, had persisted against the interests of his allies, capital punishment would have been deserved. But what sort of crime is it to have disclosed to enemies the inner secrets of the country, for which it was sacrilege not to fight? With what variety of disguises and deadly urbanity is he judged to have been brought to the point that he was thought to be fulfilling the role of a legate?

Virtue that is not innate is usually formed by care and nourishment, and what you have done through a study of falsehood passes into affection. Through the practice of honesty, a strength is acquired by one who feigns goodness over a long period.

You would still have preserved your deceptive goodwill had you not examined the path of harming us, unlocked by the key of your embassy. It is as though a physician came to sick men languishing in the agitation of fever to bring them health, then, under the appearance of medicine, sought to shut their life away in its innermost chambers. Who, I ask, would not disclose to such a man the secrets of his vital organs and announce where strength still remained? An easy opportunity for extinguishing life is supplied by the very man from whom health is requested.

Thus, most impure of men, we armed you against us by revealing our innermost secrets. Now it depends on your judgment, judges, whether one who surpassed everyone in crimes ought also to surpass all in punishments. Cut down crimes that would otherwise arise in the future. From the torture of one, a general correction will result. It is a form of piety to be strict toward an enemy of the country, lest, while you spare the person, you encourage the growth of vices.

## DICTIO XV

Against the stepmother who, unable to persuade her husband to hate his stepson, offered poison to both of them.

### CONTROVERSY TWO

Here is the stepmother, judges, who, to satisfy her hatred, spares no affection. To prevent her stepson from escaping her, she chose to involve in his fate the man she loved. Like the fiercest beasts, she made a lottery out of confused deaths, judging all worthy of death who could be slaughtered together with her enemy.

Once the barriers were broken, her rage found exercise, killing whatever it encountered as though it had been assigned to death. Wishing to be destructive to everyone, her anger would still have grown if her poisons had not run out. The poison she had found was drunk by the two of them; nothing remained to be reserved for the destruction of others.

Alas, how she lamented the shortage of the cup when she saw so few corpses, indignant that the deadly liquid had given more to the dead than it had killed! If she had been able, she would have sought the price of another’s death from the entrails of those already destroyed, so that she might scatter death through many throats and so that a noble poison might possess the innermost chambers of their souls.

Before the trial, the destructive liquid was poured into the cup. It made her recognize what she had lost after, from abundant juices, she had extinguished only a few.

Where among the nations was the spirit of marital devotion? Where was the sacred bond of marriage? The memory of the marriage bed achieved less than the stepson: while she obeyed her savagery, affection for her living husband was driven away. She believed that the substance of her stepson could remain in anyone who lived.

She wished to confuse the light through sacrilege and to have the harvest of the human race cut down as the world collapsed. Hurling whatever could go toward sunset into ruin, she wished, under the ancient laws of Erebus, to subject our day to darkness, so that the hated man might not see her even after the underworld.

By how many stages, and through what progress of crimes, did she descend to poison? She long delayed the destruction which she eventually inflicted upon one already subjected to torments, as though it were a benefit. First she afflicted the hostile body with whips, hunger, and cold; the execution of death is the final stage of stepmotherly indignation.

I would linger longer over the accusation, judges, unless a more extended tongue would delay the punishment of the criminal. We do not want to grant her the pauses you allow the speaker at the end, so that she might deserve an adjournment in broad daylight.

How many times, most wicked of women, did you cherish your stepson in deceitful embraces while pretending to be his mother? How many times did you act with harmless drinks so that he might safely receive death from your hand? Feigning thirst, and perhaps the time and necessity of drinking, you contrived to offer death more swiftly. You acquired a reputation for mercy by complying with the wishes of your stepson. How many times did you occupy a mother’s place in order to display a stepmother more safely?

It is customary, guardians of liberty, in a marital union, to regard the child of one as a common pledge, since the affection that the father has gained passes to the son. When wives die, the foresight of men, seeking partners in their cares for raising their offspring, thus finds stepmothers.

Often, however, a mother approaches under this name, all the more cautious toward another’s offspring because she more earnestly wishes to overcome the tragic name. Security protects the mother who gave birth, as does the sacred bond of her name; even her anger is believed to be merciful.

We rightly reject, unfortunate woman, your flatteries, by which you clothe your inward malice in a disguise. I blush, most holy judges, to sustain for long through accusation one already condemned by her own merits. The judgment is not uncertain merely because I delay it through effort.

Would that she might be driven from the light by carefully devised tortures and, cut by slow wounds, remain a survivor of her own body! May the guilty soul be torn from its own dwelling not all at once. Purity is restored to affection whenever you cleanse the eyes of the community through the punishment of the guilty.

## DICTIO XVI

Against the man who demanded the marriage of a Vestal Virgin as the reward for a victory.

### CONTROVERSY THREE

Do you believe, judges, that through this man lamentations are mixed with victories and that the taste of triumph is spoiled by the reward? Do you think the gods are offended by the outcome of events and that the divine powers which aided the vows are brought to repentance?

Here is a most wicked man who orders us to groan because he conquered the enemies of our country; who, after completing the battles, while demanding the price of his labor, commends both the enemies and the wars; who considers the support of his labor exhausted unless he receives what is offered to angry heavenly beings, so that his city may lose what it is believed to have acquired through him.

He trusts that the genius of a warrior is not held by painted tablets and images, nor does he require it to be preserved through the ages in bronze. He thinks that the only joys are those to which a gift of adultery gives rise.

If you offered yourself to dangers for this purpose, so that you are ashamed to have the thing you demand named in return for your sweat, we cannot owe to prostitutes what we conquered. You did not wage wars for love, since after the enemy you engage in battle with shame in the middle of the city. You drove away the enemy without purpose, since in triumph you perform their functions.

We possessed a free condition of honor while we were exposed to dangers. The happiness of brave men by which we are joined to the miseries of those subjected must be avoided.

For, lights of the senate, why do we think that this man was brought to monstrous vows through the successive stages of his crimes? Through how many steps did a practiced crime reach the point where it purchased vices with praises?

We believed that, while living his life in tents and training his body for the insignia of strength through harsh campaigns, he was bound by civic love, so that through his military service neither the burning of the city nor the violation of sacred virgins would take possession of us. This man bought, through so many wounds, the power to prevent another from enjoying the fruit of crimes.

What do I owe you, most cruel of men? It is shown by the fact that through your benefits I, the victor, groan over the destruction of those whom we overcame.

Tell me, guardians of liberty, whom we had as the one who possessed our spirits amid the clash of trumpets, while the harvest of iron threatened destruction with the neighing of horses. I believe it was so that the free necks of fathers would not be bound by the rigidity of chains; so that the inviolate modesty of the mothers of the city would not perish in the city’s destruction; so that vowed virginity dedicated to sacred worship would not be carried off by the fire of a plunderer; so that chaste maidens would not become a price for an insulting enemy; so that, once freed from human condition, force would not seize their bodies and chastity, finally reduced to submission, would not serve an enemy’s lust.

I ask you, magnanimous hero—[Note: “hero,” according to an old manuscript preserved by Schott]—what evil you drove away from your country, if, while the favor of the gods added the deaths of the enemies to your blows, you desired as victor the very things I feared.

I ask whether you sought the heavenly powers as allies in that crisis. If you did, now that you have passed through the dangers, do you threaten their priests with what is owed as an offering? If you did not bring pious vows to the battle, what do I owe you, whom general prosperity accompanied and freed without their prayers? If you understand, you owe much to the divine powers if they listened to your entreaty; more if they gave victory to one who did not ask.

I suppose that, departing from battle, you venerated the shrines in the foremost place and offered thanks there, whence you intend to snatch spoils with hands set apart for the festival. I fear that, with no temple consumed by a torch, favorable chance may lead a Vestal Virgin away captive.

## DICTIO XVII

Against the man who withheld food from his aged father. Delivered to Arator.

### CONTROVERSY FOUR

I do not know, judges, whether a punishment can be found that satisfies the crimes of the accused. For the moment, the power of speech is lacking, when the novelty of the crime surpasses the accuser.

This is the son who, although he could have supplied food to his very old father, refused it, adding this to his crimes so that, while his father remained alive, he might be a parricide.

Do you think you escaped the punishment owed for not having inflicted death upon your father? By sparing him, you made yourself less innocent. [Note: Schott reads “more guilty” (nocentior).] You could have concluded the torments you inflicted with your father’s final end if you had offered a healing hand to his throat. The first invention of your evils is this: neither to remove the death of your own creator, as a pious son should, nor to inflict it, as a cruel one would.

What is this, ingenious inventor of refined danger? Between the two paths, having followed neither, you nourish yourself on the proclaimed decay of your father. Under your management the father lived all the more unhappily because he did not attain death through your management.

No one, most holy judges, doubts that the evils of this world, once death has been called in, are buried, and that death is a common wish for those placed amid adversity. What puts an end to bitterness must necessarily be desired.

I ask: with what beasts should the man be compared who, through his own management, inflicts harshness without end? Whose deceit, while his hand refrains from striking the author of light, has produced things that ought to be exchanged for death?

The father of this man was already crushed beneath the burden of years. The ravaging of age had already overthrown the traces of former strength through the old man’s trembling limbs. Through the bites of long duration, his form was already tending toward wrinkles that revealed the human condition. Yet he had reached maturity not without hope of support, since his older offspring was already smiling upon him.

With greater confidence he scattered what had been gathered for his sustenance, although we know that he had always placed his stores in the cheerful security of his pledge. He thought it safe to consider his property, since his son survived; he thought that this could suffice for his cold old age, because, restored in the years of his lineage’s greener time, he was not perishing. Then suddenly the excellent young man stripped his father of such security.

I would turn my words to him for a little while, venerable judges, but I fear that admonitions offered to ruined morals are wasted. Do we suppose, venerable judges, that anyone reaches such conduct through the teaching of some master? Nature’s instruction is sufficient for offspring, since the human law that teachers customarily instill in their breasts supplies what is required.

It is not accidental goodness to fulfill one’s obligations, nor can those endowed with reason lack what we see implanted in birds. In the opposite direction, we read that eagles are nourished by the service of their young. They repay, under a kind of strict equity, the benefit they received from their parents when, born featherless, they emerged from the covering of their eggs.

Birds do not think themselves free to deny what they have received. What sort of intelligence is it that, concerning devotion to their own kind, does not know how to imitate winged creatures? I pass over the many examples: wolves carry food to their parents in their hungry mouths, and the wild beast, unfed in its own entrails, runs to its creators with a mouth made rich.

Consider for yourselves the conscience of the accused and what punishment it deserves, since it has committed something unheard of. Vices multiply through impunity, and unless the judgment of judges came to the rescue, the force of sinning would spread through the whole body politic.

## DICTIO XVIII

Against the tyrant who, as a reward, gave a statue among brave men to a parricide. Delivered to Arator, Illustrious Man.

### CONTROVERSY FIVE

Although the likenesses of brave men are preserved in bronze destined to endure forever, and through these images they escape both death and burial; although through these arts the image of mortals passes into eternity and human skill conquers the narrow law of human nature, nevertheless neither did a parricide ever deserve the price of virtue nor did a tyrant pay it.

When has the gift of the innocent been elicited by a criminal or imposed by an oppressor of liberty? A statue, venerable magistrates, is the fruit of sweat and must be awarded by the judgment of the purest. Its fitting splendor must suit both parties: it must not disfigure the recipient if it comes from a worthy author, nor stain the giver if it is conferred upon one who deserves it.

If a free voice against a tyrant is permitted to detest vices, if faults may be pressed upon a guardian of crimes, I shall say what I think. Between two wicked men an honorable thing flew about, protected by neither, knowing neither from whom it should proceed nor to whom it should flow. Look to whose rights it has come: a matter long ago determined by lots and to be purchased by the votes of blood, so that the usurper of power may grant it and the slayer of his father receive it.

I do not know where to turn, venerable prince, caught among the abrupt precipices of your virtues. I do not know whether to accuse you because you are a tyrant or because you honor parricides with a reward. Both deserve crosses and should be driven from this present life in sacks.

Do you not think it enough that you have escaped the punishment you deserve, unless you also grant what is forbidden and he receives what he does not deserve? You presumed upon these things long ago through audacity, when the destroyer entered the citadel of justice and was raised to domination by those votes through which you conferred a statue upon another.

It is necessary, most exalted of men, to cherish all who have been what they were; and excesses are not corrected usefully except by those who have been corrected themselves. He is shameless who believes that the punisher of evil is a follower of crimes. The conscience of a judge is constrained by the necessity of secrecy, and it does not consider itself free to condemn in subjects what it did not hesitate to admit in itself.

Through what successes, or by what varied stages of growth, did you reach this sewer of crimes, so that, having attained the heights, you could sin so greatly whenever you wished, and invite the disgraceful to better positions by erecting statues to them?

You exchanged the taste of liberty for the gall of servitude; he turned the services owed to his father into swords. Consider how worthy of praise the things are that you have harmed. With the accuser’s mouth at rest, assess what a father and free birth deserve.

You bind necks that had been freed from the yoke to the wretched condition of servitude. In him the law of nature prevailed nothing. What you do to your country is what he did to his parent. In this you may perhaps be judged more cruel, because you dispense harsh commands under a kind of living death, and you do not provide an end, as with a healing hand, even to those for whom death is desirable. He, not allowing his father to remain in the world, tore life from the author of his own light with a deadly blow.

I do not know by what difference of crimes they are distinguished. For the moment, if it is permitted, they should be joined in punishment. If the swelling of some pride had raised you up against citizens, the injured community would mark you as guilty, and excessive elevation would proclaim you a deserter from private sweetness.

If he had looked upon his creator with a grim expression while his father remained alive, he would have possessed the merit of a parricide. Consider what is worthy of those who have reached the summit of crimes. Nothing remains that either the afflicted country or the slain father could regard as still outstanding.

Let us not, leading men, sharpen the committed crime through arguments. The bare names of the accused are sufficient and need no privilege of defense to protect them.

I shall add to the offense certain features that heighten the guilt, lest any matter seem to have been withdrawn from the action which, as I judge, you have discovered through your shrewd investigations.

The statue of the parricide is surrounded by the sides of brave men, and the image—which either literary care produced [Note: Schott reads “literary”] or the Field of Mars cast—is placed after this man’s image. If you believe them, those who have been raised through so many titles bear harshly that they are no different from the one who shed his father’s blood and that, if any strength remains to their souls, they lament their rewards, which they earned through the exertion of courage.

Where are honor, the efficacy of liberal study, and the gift of one who fights for his country, if the possessor of art displays bronze forms and the man who arranged his father’s funeral obtains the prize?

You must provide only punishments worthy of the merits, lest, if an unequal penalty condemns the accused, the direct praise of your judgment also be denied you. Let those whose lot in crime was almost equal be driven from life by one road.

## DICTIO XIX

Delivered to Ambrosius, against a gambler who gave as the price of play the field in which his parents had been buried.

### CONTROVERSY SIX
After, judges, the gambler’s shameful zeal had been reduced to the scantiness of his means, and lack of resources had enslaved his growing passion for play, even his parents’ tombs began to be taken away as a shameful stake. They began to await uncertain chances from the ashes, and to propose for ridicule the moments of contests arising from tears. Where are those who say that souls, once they have passed from the light, have nothing in common with the worshipers of this world, and that, after their separation from the age, they have been transferred to their own day? Behold, the elder generations of this man have nearly grown old beside the tombs they had acquired, and through the long passage of time even from those tombs they are already becoming ashes; yet, in the eyes of that most shameless reveler, they are still believed not to have lost the stakes of their purpose.

After the long courses of life, owing nothing to chance, the dead are ordered to await the outcome from dice; after the wealth that your parents had amassed through long frugality had been squandered; after the many weights of silver and gold that thrift, destined to produce an heir, had preserved within its measured limits: you, offspring worse than barrenness, honored the urns of the ancients by making them stakes at the gaming table.

If a lesser respect from later generations adorned the mausoleums of those who came before, the negligence would have to be punished, and punishment would await those judges who wish to correct their children’s character through the offenses of others. Instead of the fixed celebrations returning by the law of the seasons, instead of garlands and the gifts by which souls are nourished, you deemed it wrong for your parents’ tombs not to change masters.

You would not have been permitted to sell the final dwellings in exchange for the ransom of your pledge, taken away by enemies. I ask what necessity there is for me to see a stranger possessing your parents’ ashes; and nothing else is offered to me but a game. O miserable human condition, both when desires are denied and when they are granted more disastrously!

How often did those who begot you move God with anxious sighs, lest they pass from the use of this light—which is regarded as most ill-omened—without a legitimate heir? Born, instructed, and educated for this harvest, judges, he has reached it with a mind barren of shame, so that, after losing everything, he would not allow those who gave him his patrimony to possess their own right.

We condemn in this criminal the most disgraceful intention. For perhaps it happened that, through your fickleness, you sent the bones of your ancestors into the possession of honorable masters. Reverence for the dead is common to all, and universal humanity demands that those who have been committed to their final lot be honored with fitting religious care. Yet the final honors due to our ancestors are rendered with greater distinction, for reverence places them before our eyes in such a way that we believe the gods are honored whenever the commands of the dead are carried out.

We preserve everything they have ordered, not believing that what has been violated at their command can be touched with impunity. I cannot find a new kind of crime to explain it with novel language. For those to whom disobedience was sacrilege, what is it to have sold their final dwellings for games? Believe me, judges: imagine all this man’s ancestors standing before your eyes, awaiting the moment of vengeance. By appeasing them, the devotion that will endure among future generations toward parents may be established without stain.

## DICTIO XX

Against the man who placed a statue of Minerva in a brothel.

## CONTROVERSIA VII

[Col. 0295B]

We have always believed that the judgment of reverend judges concerning the confusion of sin was uncertain. The deliberation of the judge hesitated over the direction it should chiefly take where the fate of the offense was doubtful. For just as manifest vices demand a definition consonant with equity, so obscure ones suspend it.

When a crime is in the open, what hope remains in condemning it? Take this to heart, I beg you, and consider it with inward judgment: what sort of man is he who violated both the eyes of virginity and the secrets of a brothel? Sacrilegious in both respects, he neither reveres the vices to which he brought forward a hostile witness nor respects the blush of chastity, which he associates with what is unworthy.

I appeal to you, spectacle of the human race, who brought your frivolity to the point of erecting an image of Minerva through the rites of religion, while the outrage inflicted by the foulness of the place displays you as an enemy of integrity. The corruption made public cries out that you do not show reverence even toward Venus’s pollution.

Those who are provoked to transgress crime by their love of excess do not know the limits of sinning; those who have undertaken lofty crimes are ignorant of restraint in wrongdoing. While you mockingly unite Dione and Pallas—utterly different divinities, handed over to wandering opinions—through a single manufactured work of art, you have made your offense more bitter through your religion.

It is a deed deserving the greatest expiation: to mix discordant things and gather into one those whom, unless you provide them secrecy, you insult. Do you believe that a man can be found who holds neither side in this world’s double way of life—who is neither a friend to virtues nor proved faithful to vices?

Some people are accustomed to elevate themselves to contempt for good works by the protection of their faults; those who are strangers to the taste of praise rejoice in the fruit of license. But which of these paths has found you as its follower? You have raised hostile hands against the better order, yet you do not submit your neck sincerely even to the wicked.

I hate, distinguished men, judges who are indulgent toward their own morals. I condemn those who, through negligence of honorable actions, are dragged into uncertainty. Yet I detest still more those who, caught in both respects, offer a stable conscience to no one. For they promise an affection for decency at the time of repentance, although you see them showing loyalty to their sins.

If, most criminal of men, while you stood before Venus’s shrines, remembrance of Minerva had stirred you, your recollection, foolishly loving both powers, would have injured the ingenuity of your mind. You should have fled from the dwelling of the goddess whose adversary you retained in your thoughts. What honor is there in placing her statue where the goddess of modesty could have been violated merely by its presence?
