By failing to recognize, most ill-fated man, that you were advancing step by step toward the summit of accursed error, you nearly rekindled war among the inhabitants of heaven. Those eyes always see shameful things, hating embraces joined by a certain law of obscenity.

While, through your agency, a captive divinity occupies a brothel, you alone have shown that the power of the gods serves human lust, and that they are confined to the places assigned to them by mortals. How discordant will be the expense involved in burning the sacrifices! The offering to one divinity will inflict injury upon the other.

For while, through your foresight, a single couch has been occupied by the double power of the gods, and modesty and lust have met in one temple, neither will look with favor upon our devotion. Those whom you have mingled in one habitation we shall offend by separate sacrifices. What sort of gifts will these be, which must be carried in groups by both the unchaste and the virginal? One must be offended by cheerfulness, the other appeased by wantonness. Among the sacred branches and incense of the victims there will be a cause for conflict, and angry divinities will be produced by the very means through which they are soothed.

[Note: [Col. 0295D] Schot., *Submoveo*.] I shall remove from this sacrilegious man a lengthy account. Let him consume during his punishments the delays that the defendant will receive in the open court, since the disgracefulness of another’s deeds makes the narrator unattractive.

## DICTIO XXI

Against a certain father who, although he had not deigned to ransom his son captured by a pirate, nevertheless demanded that the son support him.

## CONTROVERSIA VIII

**Theme. Law.** Children shall support their parents or be imprisoned. A certain man had two sons, one frugal and one dissolute. Pirates captured both. They wrote to their father about the ransom. The father, having sold his property, went to seek the pirates. He was given the choice of which one he wished to ransom, because he had brought too little money. He chose to ransom the dissolute son, because he was ill; but when the son was returning, he died on the way. The frugal son escaped from the pirates. The father demands that he support him; the son objects.

An action has been brought against Quintilian. He defends the father; we defend the son. I ask you not to regard this as arrogance when you have read it.

### Preface

[Note: [Col. 0295D] “Is it lawful to speak against Quintilian?” Trebellius Pollio calls him the most acute declaimer of the Roman race in his *Postumius the Younger*. Ausonius, *On Professors*:

> Whether you wish to unfold fictitious disputes of the games,  
> Quintilian holds the doubtful palm.

This is Quintilian’s fifth declamation, **The Sick Man Ransomed**, to which Ennodius replies. The theme of the controversy, which is read in nearly the same words in Quintilian, and its opening—both of which were missing from the commonly circulated books—we have added from ancient copies.]

Is it lawful to speak against Quintilian except for the sake of truth? Or does eagerness make him forgetful of his own manner of speaking, when it assigns the words of justice? Urbanity suits deceivers: language adorned with the brush of falsehood assumes, in words alone worthy of praise, a foreign beauty.

Let equity be asserted, certainly, with the consolation of rhetorical art. I choose the display that defended probity will produce. Let simplicity, fortified by heavenly favor, advance against the most eloquent man. What we dare arises from confidence in our cause.

You, distinguished men, need only extend your kindness to us, while preserving the vigilance of your ears and minds, lest that lofty tragic style, prevailing through the power of speech, believe victory to be in its possession. What else is it to help us against his attacks than to lead justice back after its wanderings?

### Opening

I would rejoice, most distinguished judges, to have escaped the filth of prison and the chains of pirates, if, when I returned, my father had not taken the place of the pirate ship. He demands food from me, although he freed me neither with gold from my enemies nor with tears. He thinks that my return ought to benefit him, although he did not ransom me when he could.

In vain do you invoke the benefit of the law for food, since by your deeds you have dissolved the laws of nature. The law decrees that nourishment be provided to parents; this is not merely an oath expressed in a name. Let even the pirate say it, if you are a father.

When you often speak of my having been better than the one who died, you never show yourself to be better when you judge. Consider the path of the faults of my dead brother. He himself obeyed his father’s character more closely—the one who was preferred. As for me, the omen under which I spent my life driven among strangers by them was made clear when my father willingly abandoned me to the pirates.

He thinks he can bring powerful arguments against his offspring when he boasts that the guilty son, who was close to burial, deserved the greater gratitude. I ask you, judges, pronounce what I owe. In the meantime, it is clear that I was placed after even the ashes of the vicious son.

He is not ashamed to demand anything from me by parental authority, although he refused to be what is called a father. Would that the pirates’ chains had preserved my health for this purpose! By providing food that I do not owe, I would make my father a captive through shame, so that an unjust judge might lament the injustice of his own sentence.

Food provided by one from whom you have deserved no good drains you; the entrails of one who has no awareness of a benefit previously bestowed are hungry even in their fullness. I do not know what that man thinks remains of his hopes concerning his two sons: he returned one to the earth and allowed the other to remain under the perpetual domination of his captors.

Let him receive, if he is not ashamed, whatever my limbs, exhausted by punishments, have groaned. I do not know what the old man demands from one weakened by illness. Meanwhile, as I see it, we both have to be fed.

Why do you bring forward the smallness of your means? You wished to ransom one, and so sold your property that the price was insufficient for both. Who could set out my misfortune, who my misery? To whom, after the Cilicians, is even the liberty he is said to have regained subject?

Tell me, I beg you, judges: if we are pronounced debtors even in our own country, what have I escaped? My most revered father has added that I should grieve because they released my brother from his chains. As though nature demanded so much service from us that the joy of our brother’s rescue could compensate for my remaining behind.

We owe love to those united to us by flesh. Believe one who speaks plainly: a man who fears for himself cannot admit joy on behalf of another. For, in the manner of a corrupt court, he cries that the one from whom something is demanded is somehow the richer.

Crafted urbanity preserves such a device in petitions, using composed humility as a weapon, so that, through the fiction of proud abasement, it leaves no freedom to the person being asked. He testifies that he offered a sum reckoned for both, although it is clear that it was spent on one; he expects a double gratitude for a single benefit.

I do not know whether we should ask what he was thinking, since it is clear to everyone what he did. The pirate exhausted the defenses of your case when he gave us the choice. Let the father retain the tombs that alone he desired from his son—the son whom he ransomed only because he was going to die. For by preferring the sick man to the healthy, he declared that he abhorred the prospect of the latter’s living. I do not know what you demand from the survivor, possessing tears as your consolation—the tears you purchased.

### Narrative

Throughout my life, judges, I preserved the cultivation of honor, even at an age friendly to wrongdoing. I withheld expenditures from childish desires, so that maturity might have something with which to rejoice. Through the frugality of this conduct, we ensured that something remained for my father to offer for his dissolute son.

Why do you complain about the narrowness of the patrimony? If I had been equal to him in character, matters would have reached the point at which neither could have been freed. He is an unequal judge who wished another to benefit from what we had preserved through our own modesty.

As much as paternal severity asserts, our integrity was the cause of our long captivity. Healthy, dutiful, attentive to father and brother—does such a man not deserve to be restored to his country? And unless we had been captives together by the same lot, our return would have been sullied by suspicion.

We were equals in misfortune, but divided by our father’s affection. The fortunate youth, aided by his dissolute life, both exhausted a large part of our common property beforehand and benefited from what remained. Wretched me, forever captive to my father’s judgment!

In peace I rehearsed beforehand what I later endured; and while I kept to the path of righteousness, I learned, through the proof of frugality, how one should live among enemies. Thus, content with the food that savage people supplied, I lived amid the final consolations of habit, not through the humanity of my captor.

I ask what benefit that more frugal way of life preserved for me, if observance of a father’s equity deserves offense.

### Objection

What of the fact that the barbarian is said to have declared, “You brought the price of one”? Objections always receive the answer they deserve. You were not anxiously concerned by any auction. The gold you had brought you displayed before the eyes of your enemies before making your requests.

While everything was proceeding in this way, no one could doubt that it was enough for your desire to free one person. Yet as soon as you entered that place filled with the squalor of death, he knew what you would choose, even before the pirate granted you the option.

This hesitation did not arise from love. He showed nothing uncertain when, concerning his two sons, he announced through every sign of affection—as though he had come for one alone—that he had made his choice. After your departure they tightened the guard around me. Thanks to the gods, if he has protected my freedom even here, since I escaped.

Meanwhile your decision seems to have sent a message to the enemy: “Unless the one I leave behind is carefully guarded, he will escape.” Under divine guidance, our flight was placed before the eyes of the enemy and proved effective.

### Digression

Furthermore, since the father is rich in speech and has learned, through the length of his life, to present what he says, skilled at imposing necessity upon minds through hearing, he says to all who live in human society that food is common to everyone. He demands from one person what no one is permitted to deny, arguing generally that everything the earth produces is owed to all.

But when, for common use, grain-bearing fields and wine-producing vineyards poured forth their produce, the earth was not distributed individually among cultivators. No one among the enemy left a son in such a way that he could be believed to have preferred groans to acts of service.

I do not know, judges, after choosing tears, what he demands from the survivor. But he holds the fear of the law over us, and wishes the provision written concerning parents and children to be owed to him, although he has shown nothing of a parent.

He seeks our willingness while we are being compelled, and wishes us to offer to filial duty what he himself has confessed that even one wishing to excuse himself cannot deny to fear. Is there room for mercy where command is pressing? What cannot be withheld cannot be said to be granted through generosity. Clemency is not so called unless it is freely given. Whatever you lack the power not to give, count, if you give it, as a reciprocal gift.

Yet the repeated testimony of nature and the sacred name of the creator will oppose us, as though the use of life—bestowed by the gift of the heavenly powers—could be counted among the things granted by human beings. It is sacrilege to call the indulgence of the gods the offspring of mortals; the cruel father has testimony only from his own desire.

He also adds this to my burdens, when he demands consolation from the abandoned, saying that the state could have come to my aid if I had not returned. What else does this wish reveal except that the pirate should receive me again? If the sight of your unredeemed child is burdensome, at least you will possess my tomb without cost—something you are accustomed to purchase at great expense. My age indeed promises life, but the magnitude of the torments that I endured, more bitterly after your departure, promises death.

### Examples

Then you brought forward examples worthy of a father’s argument, but they were cheapened by your interpretation—as though gray age had supplied your desires with a model, rather than an imitation, of sacred institutions.

What burden of his father did the mighty shoulders of Aeneas feel? Or did he weigh down with his body the son whose bearer he himself had often been in deed? Do you want to know why he deserved rescue from the enemy? He was placed before his son’s eyes, yet did not wish to burden him, believing that the ruin of fallen Ilium would provide his burial.

And lest his aging limbs hold back his departing son, who was more worthy of life, he said that the fall of the city was sufficient for a tomb. That man wished to remain while his son escaped from the pirates; you returned to your country after abandoning yours.

Why do you recall the noble deeds of Scipio on behalf of his father? When he offered himself diligently for his parent, he gave everything, but did not exhaust all that he owed. The cause of good vows is always similar, and the efforts of benevolence are not different.

He declares what a father deserves from his son when he judges that the son will not come to the duties of nature unless compelled. The law threatens chains if I do not comply. What difference does that make? The long duration you arranged has shaped me for this familiarity with punishment, although enduring punishments for a long time does not make a person rebellious.

Yet I wonder whether my father has brought anything from the barbarians except what I escaped. There is nothing by which the pirates can be avoided if the same fate follows one into his homeland. As far as I can see, the adversity of native soil and foreign travel is one and the same; the bitterness is no different for returnees and captives.

Nevertheless, I find no difference, nor do I ask which chain most particularly binds my neck. I will encounter the bonds of rigid iron or pay tribute with my throat: the condition is the same. I shall carry meals while hungry to a man who is full—and, what is worse, to one who does not love me. With what disdain will he cast aside the food I offer? With what bitterness will he trample my devotion? He is a man whom I could not find merciful even while I was enduring the extremity of suffering.

He declares that my brother and I alike demanded ransom by letter, that we implored release with equal tears, and that, placed in a similar situation, we dictated our letters under the same fate. I do not deny it; I do not reject it. Let him win on this point.

Yet I demand to know what cause made it possible for what two had requested, and what was owed to two, to be received by one. For both of us you entered the seas, and, as you claim, under the guidance of filial devotion you crossed the dangers of the flowing element. Who would believe in a double affection in a man returning with one son?

Mercy is never praised unless it has been tested by danger. With what shame is affection proclaimed when its effect is absent? Does the secret of the heart always become truly known through the key of speech? Piety that is not also maintained silently through deeds is a spectacle.

Among all human beings, love will remain firm in an unshaken root if this boasting is valid. The law says: “Either let him support him or let him be imprisoned.” The father cries: “This nourishment is already owed to a parent, even if he does not ransom him.”

You armed yourself for these claims when you withdrew from the duty to which nature had subjected you. A windy defense achieves something, though shamefully denied to genuine purity. Believe me: when the law spoke of a parent, it did not remain silent about the redeemer. It urged, commanded, and compelled all the obligations of religious duty to be fulfilled adequately through their names.

My misfortune clouds your understanding of this matter. The ransom of a son, which consists in the care of kinship, could not consist in words of command. While you praise the “Ledaean pledges”—the children born to Leda—you accuse my impiety and my envy in the liberation of my brother.

You do not know that if an equal distribution between them had proceeded from your judgment, it would have produced error. For it would have condemned one to perpetual possession of the beauty of light, and the other to perpetual possession of darkness.

I am lying if your judgments concerning your sons were otherwise. What did you think would happen when the pirate, never intending to have one of them, released him, while retaining the other as though a father had handed him over and never intending to release him? Whatever I endured after your eyes left me in that savage land, I do not doubt that it proceeded from you.

All hope was destroyed for me after the redeemer departed from barbarian soil without me. How many ships sailing toward the inhuman shores did I not first inspect? Whatever my eyes could not follow as the vision faded, I grasped with my mind, since those who wait more eagerly see more keenly.

How often, before your arrival, whenever the pirate allowed us to look upon the air, did my father appear to me in unfamiliar persons? I saw in them the images that love paints for itself without the shame of lying. These visions long troubled and wounded my heart.

Alas, how often, when I refused the food that the pirate provided, did the barbarian support me with this consolation: “Fear nothing; sigh over nothing in this affliction. If your father is still alive, you are not far from the station of freedom.”

At last the fate I desired arrived. The pirate himself announced your arrival to me with joy. He was not far from the affection of perfect mercy, since he received the redeemer gladly.

We did not have inhuman masters, judges. There were men who could have been softened even by a plea. If tears had compensated for the lack of gold, he would have brought us both back at the same time. He testified that the father had not wished it to happen, since he had not pleaded for it at great cost.

Consider, I beg you, what he rightly demands from me, who did not aid me in my extremity even with a plea. You added that you are protected by the privileges of nature and that what you did against me may not be avenged.

But the man who places his defense in high rank does not possess the prerogative of innocence. Let the innocent shine in the light of the action. Without concealment, the man who judges his protection to lie in what precedes him confesses his crimes. No authority defends the guilty; among criminals, the sanctities of a name disappear.

### Epilogue

And this, most holy judges, I have argued after the custody of robbers through another labor of the heart, as though, even if I were a debtor, I were able to provide what is demanded. He does not consider bones stripped of flesh and soiled by the inhumanity of masters, nor does he look upon the secrets of nature exposed by executioners.

In my body, the torments brought into the light everything that is human; while the barbarian pressed me with torture and my father disdained to be present, the innermost parts of my body were laid bare. The atrocity exceeds all measure when, even in exacting debts, it does not first inquire into a person’s strength.

When you see in me the health of youth softened beneath the burden of suffering, when the strength of my age has been broken by the variety of repeated disasters, when I bear both the necessity of old age and the resentment of youth, you do not cease demanding from me what even the enemy would have forgiven in one exhausted.

You will receive a tribute from me, and still you assault me with the greatness of your name and the natural authority of a parent, while you disdain to show even to your own child the compassion you owe to every human being.

May the heavenly dispensation enrich your intention with this reward: that you may once again behold the votive funerals of your offspring, and that, burdened by the living presence, you may obtain the fullness of your desires from tombs.

## DICTIO XXII

[Col. 0301D]

## CONTROVERSIA IX. Preface

The distinguished young man, arranging in order the riches of his inventions, has indeed enriched them also with verbal abundance, and has expressed what he believed to belong to religion with a mouth worthy of reverence.

But let the devices of malicious arguments stand far away from the snares of opinion. We set the breast of our speech against Arator. Yet we do not cut off with an unfriendly sickle the vine-shoot emerging into the light of praise. Rather, by showing what path of words he ought to follow, we know that, if it should happen that he is preferred to us, we shall triumph more gloriously in him, because he drew from our resources whatever, with God increasing his gifts, he poured forth more abundantly from the riches of knowledge.

## THEME. LAW

After a city of enemies has been captured, the priests and Vestal virgins shall be released as free persons.

[Col. 0302A]

After the favorable outcomes of military combat, a law recited to resist the victorious cannot retain force amid triumphs and laurels. What have we accomplished with swords through a willingness to face death, if after the battles there is something we must fear?

Everything that until now threatened me lies lifeless before my eyes, and after the hostile encounter has been dispersed I do not know what terror the decrees of dead rulers bring against us. He does not know how to assess proven excellence who exults over armed men from the bridle of documents.

Let idle hearts be satisfied with such barriers. I scattered with the sword whatever was taking away my freedom. The only thing anyone can deny us is what we do not wish to have. I am content to have that as my limit, beyond which my desires have not called me to transgress.

The law grants me whatever I am strong enough to possess. Let those who deny something to leisure and the toga bear the consequences. Nature produced everything for me—whatever I extort while standing under arms. Our only written laws are these: to fear nothing.

I have asserted this to your ears as though the formula being brought against us were a good one. Yet the law, nurse of brave men, defender of liberty, bulwark of the fatherland, orders its heroes, after the battle, to turn a renewed attention to their reward; and, not content with successful deeds, by taking away the price of their toil it breaks their desire to fight.

Are commands good, then, when they stand in the way of our becoming good? Whatever removes the fruit of labor, most prudent judges, disciplines us through another’s power. Can enactments drawn up under an external legal claim have force? Or does it seem close to reason to cut off hope of future possession?

Why do you oppose religion to us in the persons of the priests? With God as my guide, I have obtained what you venerate in them. Since you desire, out of regard for him, that they escape the yoke of our servitude, know that they are held captive by his command.

He struggles against the gods who raises up anyone whom their judgment casts down. Those whom you hasten to rescue would never have been made slaves of men if they had deserved to be ministers of the heavenly powers.

Behold, I contend with you over the spirit of the law, as though I had no weapons to offer in reply. What justice do you think there is in that command which, in order to support the enemy, consigns to slavery allies who extend its dominion?

Take away the hope of booty, and you have taken away the wishes of battle. And if the spirit of the laureled victor is defrauded, everything he sought by despising life will return him to repentance.

Let the wise cease demanding such equity—not a law, I say, but a tyrannical inscription—which, under a false appearance of piety, is hateful to the gods, hostile to virtue, and fights against divine right and justice.

You do not know, most talkative of men, how just grief arises from the loss of the fruit of labor. This is what you are saying: “Whatever you acquired under the guidance of the gods, we are taking away.”

I saw the enemy city aging as though in a single fire, and the seats of the heavenly beings, deserted and stripped of divinity, thrown down. Do you think anything remained that ought not to belong to the victor?

Moreover, the constitution itself, frivolous and empty, is obscured by its own ambiguity. For it says that priests or Vestal virgins ought to enjoy freedom. I believe that it names those in whom the inhabitant of heaven has shown his dwelling, those whom heavenly favor has marked by its own light as greater than human beings.

It announces reverence for those whom they wish to be recognized as divine pontiffs. We saw the wretched people whom this law protects, waiting for aid amid the ashes of the fallen city with nothing but lamentation, and wandering among crowds oppressed by captivity, possessing no confidence in their appointed purpose.

There was no divine splendor on their faces, no cheerfulness that announced their office. Those whose innocent conscience provides a harbor amid the storms of the world do not know how to be disturbed by adversity. We saw those protected by the law’s ridiculous concession of mere names more terrified than the rest.

What place remains for merit if this sacred privilege survives only in the title? I believe that one thing is said and another is what a pontiff is.

[Col. 0303B]

I have often seen faces worn out by fasting, with weapons aimed at the throat, fall, and swords blunted against the unarmed lose their rigid nature. If you believe one who speaks of religious matters, no servant of the temples was one who needed human assistance amid every kind of danger.

The supreme judge knows how to clothe his possession in a new light. That heavenly mingling is not hidden; although it is clothed in the garment of human frailty, it shines forth.

Moreover, those who do not deserve to be dragged into service come ready to serve. One who is unworthy of this extremity does not rebel. Those whose minds are worthy of the heights come forward for service, and they expel the stubbornness of mortality—those whom it would be sacrilegious to constrain to dishonorable tasks.

These people of yours face dangers, if they do not deserve to be released. They cannot be taken away from men if we cannot perceive that they possess anything beyond human nature.

Help me, allies; help me, companions. With the assistance of truth, restrain the talkativeness of my opponent. The matter concerns something whose judgment by the heavenly powers we already know.

Let the undeserving be enslaved, so that we may have good high priests. Let them be instituted through those whom not a conciliatory tale, not an uncertain defense, but the very radiance of the supreme God declares to be his own.

## DICTIO XXIII

[Note: [Col. 0303D] **Against the disowned son.** It lacks a title in two ancient copies. In a third, which is more recent, it is entitled: “Invective against Orestes, who killed his mother Clytemnestra.” But whoever supplied this title was misled by the similarity of the subject. For Orestes killed his mother, not his father; this man killed his father and could not kill his mother. Therefore it is written without a specific name, “Against the disowned son.” There are many such pieces in Seneca, Libanius, and others, directed against those who disown or are disowned—*ἀποκηρύττοντας* (*those disowning*) or *ἀποκηρυττομένους* (*those being disowned*).]

Against the disowned son who, after killing his father, was also plotting against his mother.

## CONTROVERSIA X

After the disowned son, judges, avenged his father’s deed and his mother’s complicity with the sword, in execution of a just grief, he thinks he can unsettle the judges’ conviction of innocence and steal something toward acquittal from a manifest crime.

We do not know what fabricated words the criminal can devise in his defense. To refute him, we display the wound. The son, ruined by the persistence of his vice, after killing his father, attempts to extinguish his mother’s reputation. Grieving that we escaped the dagger, he pursues our reputation with a weapon, and we fear him all the more because of the modesty appropriate to our sex.

We show the path of the criminal: we show the breach made in our father. He, on the contrary, does not repent of his words. To prevent any support that seemed trustworthy to us from contributing to his sentence, he drew in our little one, who was ignorant of deceit, and overthrew him with a fabricated art of words, causing even him to perish who was thought to remain.

Why do you wish to veil naked justice with tricks? The hateful man could not spare, nor could he strike one whom you pretend he loved. Is there any need for arguments where the truth itself bears witness to his deed in his own voice? You destroyed every hope of defense when you carved up your mother’s limbs with the sword.

But although the advocate is handsome and well-groomed, we have no eyes with which to inspect these things.

## DICTIO XXIV

An extemporaneous piece, which Deuterius himself assigned.

## ETHICA I. THEME

> Diomedes, having traversed the sea, safe now on land,  
> Laments a shipwreck that was without water.  
> Though he had conquered varied storms while striving for her,  
> His wife had passed into union with another man.  
> The true cause of his complaints lies beneath a feigned name.  
> I beg you, calm companions, to hear his words.

[Note: [Col. 0303D] **Address.** We have noted that what the Greeks call *ethopoeia* (*ἠθοποιία*) the Latins in the age of Ennodius called *allocution*. Thus Priscian also says in his *Rhetorical Preliminary Exercises*: “An address is an imitation of speech adapted to characters and assumed persons, as in: ‘With what words could Andromache have spoken when Hector lay dead?’”—which is found in Libanius as: *τίνας ἂν εἴποι λόγους Ἀνδρομάχη κειμένῳ Ἕκτορι* (“What words might Andromache have spoken with Hector lying dead?”). In this way the Greeks presented the themes of ethical declamations. The Latins did so in approximately this form: “The words of Diomedes when he learned of his wife Aegiale’s adultery.”]

## ALLOCUTION
O divine powers, if, since you arrange everything, not all things fall within your control, then your authority is divided—or you are also the authors of evils. But if concern for any human being from [Col. 0304C] your number troubles you, grant me the happiness of returning, or else regret the error that you have brought to completion, ungrateful powers. If heaven is to be called the possession of the righteous, if on account of brief moments of joy gifts are prayed for on behalf of mortals, do not join vengeance to your benefactions. Why did we direct our vows toward such an outcome that, through the aid of heaven, adversity should be prepared from the opportunity for prosperity? Restore, I beg you, in your mercy, the misfortunes that you imposed; let the sea be restored, lest my fame perish in a shipwreck on land. After prosperity, the nearest evil is that whatever misfortunes follow should remain unknown. The disgrace that struck me in the face would not have touched me had I remained absent. My wife—shame upon it!—would not be believed lost unless I had returned to her: calamity, repudiated, has overturned my condition. The error of the fluid element was nearer to the station: I lost in my native land the harbor that I had often gained in the recesses of the vast whirlpool. Is this the desired home, at whose longing the forgetfulness of dangers was promised, when the present form of misfortune could be rendered unknown by hope of the joy to come? From what boundary of misery have beginnings ever arisen, or from dangers completed has a beginning ever emerged? Has what was once desired ever happened not to be loved? Or has escape from danger ever arrived in order to injure a person? Fortune has always struck me with the worst of new blows. If its change inclines toward something worse, it burns with a straightforward mode of harming, lest it grow insolent through succession.

I had as my wife a woman handed over to chastity in the light of nature, whose splendor of birth had increased through disciplined conduct, so that, defended by a double rampart, she would in no way be thought subject to the blows of crime, nor to soften the austerity of chastity by the disembowelment of obscenity. She never sought the adornment of yellow metal, nor imitated the snow of her body with the whiteness of precious stones; she possessed no aids to beauty. While she pleased, she knew that the rights of the marriage oath were not strengthened by artificial pursuits, nor that a husband bound to her could be held, when a married woman sought brilliance from another rather than from the one who descended from good character. Her free servitude in raising children remained, while she showed herself such a woman as deserved to be desired and never considered her husband absent. She had made her sex steadfast through firmness of mind, while those feminine weaknesses of judgment had drawn their substance from masculine authority. Already she resisted the lapses of her station, with instruction acting as medicine, and laughed at women’s excesses when transferred to other uses. In short, she perished as women of the sort commonly do who win tears from their husbands.

She was transferred from herself, as they say, by a Circean cup, and passed into the desire of an adulterer. But what shall we do, caught amid anxiety and uncertainty? Let hated navigation receive us as a remedy; let our weary hands once more contemplate the hempen bonds of the ropes; let the right hand cling to the helm, [Col. 0305C] so that through the rudder it may govern the laws of the restrained stern; let the star-bearing axis be restored to our sight; let the routes of our course be directed by the signs of night. Let it be a consolation to my eyes if the land of my marriage does not appear profaned. Let us flee the homeland in which our marriage was brought to such an outcome that we are ashamed to have lost it, while our vows dare not receive it back.

## DICTION XXV. The words of Thetis when she saw Achilles dead.

### ETHICAL EXERCISE II

The maternal deception sought by pious forethought has been intercepted. Fate found our Achilles and stole him away through another nature; nor did it help that cunning changed the sex which his origin had given him. He did not learn to be a woman through prolonged practice, and soft habit preserved the spirit of a brave man. Who could believe that the precaution was ineffective which both goddess and mother had devised? Immortality is no reward, since neither does a mother transmit it to her offspring, nor does it prevent through her that which steals a son away from his dangers. We are divine powers so that we may never be withdrawn from grief. What sort of condition is this, when from the inner chambers of our own entrails we produce what may serve death? Either let the power of the heavenly ones confer upon posterity what it possesses, or let it be granted to dear descendants, as the end of lamentation, to die. We are inferior to human beings, to whom we give birth as our likenesses; in this we are worse, subjected to the mockery of the Fates, because we do not know how to avert the deaths to which our children are pledged. You greatest of the gods, either withdraw our lineage from chance, or subject us in exchange for the granting of a benefit. Let it be permitted to endure death, if we cannot conquer it, for the sake of one dear to us.

Bereavement stands before my eyes, all the worse because I foresaw it in exchange for my own eternity. O lamentable happiness of the gods, when we are not granted the power to avert what, among adversities, cannot be unknown! I remember the anxiety of the past time, and recall my cares, over which I watched in vain. What did it avail that the body of my child was armed by the aid of the Stygian marsh, when we sought from the deep the thing that he ought to have taken from us? In the limbs of our offspring, whom the goddess held, there is a place for a wound. Why did the water not mingle with looser fingers, so that a higher wave might have excluded the blows of the gods entirely? What, too, did it help to choose the instruction of Chiron, who was to strengthen the slipperiness of youth through discipline? I believe that, through various paths of training, we discovered how war might please my son; under the greatest teacher it was arranged that the strength he acquired should not possess the counsels that followed. Who would wish a man hidden among women’s retreats to drink in the taste of battle, and then seek protection for his child from the very source through which he makes what he protects perish?

Already we were breaking hands hardened by spear-points to the handling of baskets, and the shoulders that had warmed the back of a stripped lion were enclosed by gold-studded or purple robes. It was no easy transition for our youth to imitate a girl after tasting glory; nor is something easily contrived which I did not command from the earliest beginnings of tender age. But why do I recall what is past, when the enormity of future calamity strikes my mind? I see the smoking destruction of Troy, and see it overthrown while its condition still stands. I see Hector’s bitter battles against the Greeks, who therefore grew in reputation so that, when he fell, the price of triumph might increase for my offspring. I recognize the body of one still destined to fight, dragged by chariots, and I see the advantages of my Achilles diminished by whatever is subtracted from the weight of the dead. I see what advances wrath perish through the shortening of its gain. But why should I, deprived of my child, feed on these praises? I shall cover the rest in silence, lest I be consumed by narration before the time of grief. Let our eternity possess consolation from silence, which it does not possess from nature.

## DICTION XXVI. The words of Menelaus when he saw Troy burned.

### ETHICAL EXERCISE III

Although the ravisher inflamed my grief with terrible fires, although we endured the torches of outrage, nevertheless the author of the immense crime, together with the whole community joined to him, grew old upon the deserved pyre. The insult is almost fortunate which deserves such vengeance, even if it comes with the greatest exertion. Who would refuse to accept a necessity that must be brought to completion by the conclusion of a triumph? The flavor of what follows removes the bitterness of what came before: what we grieved becomes sweet, because we regret that those who provoked our grief ever did so.

The shameful abduction of a woman became the origin of our increase. Our wife, separated from us, gave birth to empire, and from an adulterer’s embraces produced for us the homeland that we possess. Let those who mocked the unmarried man see him trampling the proud necks of enemies. We had a wife long trained in honorable conduct, ignorant of another’s companionship, who would not wish to desire what is forbidden. Habit did not drive her into vices; rather, compelled by the impulse of the criminal ravisher, she followed Paris with a captive will. [Col. 0307A] Her beauty never raised her conscience to this point, that she should believe herself loved; for, as we trust, those who remember that they are beautiful possess the most shameful morals.

Such vengeance suited one who had committed a great crime. He fell utterly who had taken for himself the position of a revered husband. Use such marriage rites, adulterer. With such insignia Alecto pursues you as your bridal attendant; and it is fitting both that we should be appeased in this way and that Paris should perish in this way. We have dictated the laws of marriage not with words but with swords, laying waste the crop of presumptions with the avenging sickle. Our having lost a marriage will benefit many for their preservation. Tell me, you who have received the name of wife anywhere: if vices creep in, whenever they do, will not both the name and the courage of Menelaus stand before you? Those who do not cultivate chastity will, unless I am mistaken, cultivate it from necessity; and equal discipline will be preserved everywhere, when both the willing and the compelled guard one and the same form.

## DICTION XXVII. The words of Juno when she saw Antaeus prove equal in strength to Hercules.

### ETHICAL EXERCISE IV

At last someone has been found who answered to our judgment, someone who, even while being overcome, would triumph over our enemy. Hercules’ strength will not lie defeated unless it has been crushed. The man whom we anticipated is proud even of his misfortunes. He stands great through his own strength, but he will be greatest through his fall. I do not know whether Hercules can prove his equal, or whether Antaeus can be overthrown by any means; but if adversity favors our enemy, we have reached the laurels. We know the future, but it is fitting for the gods above to speak as though to mortal human beings. Let Hercules consider what he ought to choose to do. He must be conquered when his enemy meets him; he must be conquered even when he lies prostrate. Let the man who played with poisons in his cradle, who pacified the forests of Erymanthus, who outran the hind in speed, have the choice of what follows: either, destined to perish, he will cast down his enemy, or, if he fears the contest, he will already be buried with his own rocks. The danger of Lerna, unless I am mistaken, will arise from the completion of the contest. Who would not believe that nothing remains for him to accomplish when he is seen spread upon the ground? But the purpose of our side will arise from his oppression, and the event that has happily completed the cause of increasing our strength on behalf of our enemy will supply the means.

## DICTION XXVIII. The words of Dido when she saw Aeneas departing.

[Note: [Col. 0307D] “Nor is your divine mother”—They called these passages “Virgilian loci” when Virgil’s verses were taken as the subject of declamations. Such is the metrical exercise that we saw in the old Pithoean manuscript, with this title and beginning by V. C. Coronatus:

**THEME, A VIRGILIAN PASSAGE.**

“I live indeed, and carry my life through every extremity.”

**V. C. CORONATUS**

“Harsh life is loosened by varied pain,

And, near to death, I go on living for grief;

Sick health remains: while winds torment our minds,

The breath of life departs. How many disasters after Pergamum

Did the plundering hand likewise see;

What griefs did it often endure, and again what ruins

Did Troy experience?” and what follows. For the errors of the faulty manuscript prevent further progress.]

“Nor is your divine mother [truly] the parent of your lineage.”

### ETHICAL EXERCISE V

Through the lesson of your cruelty, you have lost the testimony of your lineage, which you falsely claim by reputation. It is certain that Venus has no son who loves nothing: the order of things is that character announces ancestry, and that the deeds of a person follow the one through whom he came into the light. The goddess of Idalia does not recognize one who is ignorant of returning favors. It is not reputation but equality of conduct that reveals sons; if the conscience is different, the offspring called by that name is scarcely believable. Rather, the precipitous crags of Caucasian harshness gave birth to you, or a rocky womb brought you forth, after you were conceived in mountain recesses. And, lest that savage nature should be softened by nourishment, [Note: [Col. 0308D] “Snatching away the safety of Cytheris”—The words that follow show this to be the correct reading: “The ferocity that slaughters nourished you.” Barthius, *Adversaria*, p. 932.] [Note: [Col. 0308D] “Safety of Cytheris”—Perhaps so, in view of what follows.] Hyrcanian tigresses, snatching away the safety of Cytheris, supplied you with food: that ferocity which slaughters nourished you.

For what do I promise myself through dissimulation? Or what support do I gain by hoping for better things? He did not return with tears the tears that I poured out, tortured by love for him; his bloodstained mind did not console my groans with sighs of its own. In my grief, which has one unique remedy, he did not offer a companion sharing an equal grief, because it is almost the sole end of life to have found someone who shares it. [Note: [Col. 0308D] “He alone is the end in life”—V. C. Schottus most correctly reads *in anxietate*, “in anxiety.” The same, ibid.]

But I do not know what I shall say, what matter, I mean. Neither Juno’s kindly eye nor the gaze of the highest Thunderer will endure that I should be consumed by separation after so many expenditures, and that I should have advanced nothing through devotion except to deserve not to be loved. Alas, faith has been driven from all mortals, and what until now joined human beings to the gods has been expelled!

I, pitiable, took in a shipwrecked man, and subjected a queen to his power, remaining a captive while my lot of happiness endured. I made a fugitive commander play the master. Now, kindled by madness, I am tortured and groan at why my possessor should abandon me. [Note: [Col. 0308D] “I have suffered, pitiable, a shipwreck”—Read “I have suffered, pitiable, as one shipwrecked.” The same, ibid.]

So you depart, summoned by Apollo’s prophecies, and prefer the disaster of the Lycian oracle to the commands that are certain and already remain with you? Clearly this cruelty is arranged by heavenly authors, and the interpreter of the gods compels a man to such excesses that he flees shores devoted to him as though they were hostile soil; that through storms he betrays his safety, who flees the soil of affection.

Go. I shall no longer delay you. The road by which I am abandoned will have my vengeance; the sea in its fury will have its judgment. I shall hear the hoarse surges of the swelling storms. You will call upon Dido’s name amid dangers—she who both was a harbor and provided one. Or, certainly, what I fear: while I am avenged, you may die while I live, and I may learn the outcome of the voyage I desired after I have regained the use of the light. See the reward undeserved by crimes; I prefer to perish innocent before the guilty man.

He boasts that he was born from Venus’ seed, harsh and untamed,

And, denying it, praises the goddess’ lineage.

Venus therefore produced a fugitive bearing the name of Love,

And her clemency poured forth the poison of a raging heart.

# SONGS (C)

## BOOK ONE

## I. [Note: [Col. 0309C] The itinerary of Brigantio—Brigantio is a town in our Dauphiné, at the mouths of the Cottian Alps. Today they call it Briançon; it is *Brigantion*, *Brigantium* in Strabo and Ptolemy, and Ammianus Marcellinus likewise wrote it, although in Book XV of his *History* we read *Virgantia*. Ennodius therefore set out for it from Milan at the command of his bishop. Those traveling from Milan to Brigantio encounter rivers and other features that he describes.] THE ITINERARY OF THE FORTRESS OF BRIGANTIO

The higher Titan had climbed the star-bearing axis,

When, with his full lamp, he shone openly throughout the world.

The flame-bearing sun was drinking up the streams beneath burning Cancer,

When the reaper subdued his own crop with the sickle.

While, drinking from a spring, he is dried up, while the world pants,

Commanded to follow the Gallic regions on the journey,

I did not fear the torrid fields that conquer Syene.

Dust, flame, and thirst were the rewards of obedience.

[Note: [Col. 0310D] “Why, Muse, do you renew the radiance and the hot vapors for me?” Barthius reads this way in his *Observations on Statius’ Thebaid* I, p. 114, and says that in these words Ennodius expresses clear weather, light, day, and sun.]

Why, Muse, do you renew the radiance and the mighty heat for me?

It will be more to have overcome the freezing roads.

Whatever the plains heat, whatever the heights stiffen

With cold—tell of what I endured beneath the unregulated sky.

[Col. 0309B] The year’s war upon nature,

Which discord had made, brought summer and winter together in one day.

The bishop, fervent in authority, taught me to overcome white hoarfrost,

Clothed in mist—[Note: [Col. 0309C] “The bishop taught”—It is characteristic of Ennodius to put “poet” for “bishop,” as in “the poet of Cyprian, Ambrose, Laurence, and Eustorgius,” frequently. Thus in his own epitaph, and in that of Peter, bishop of Ticinum:

“Here is the Lord’s poet, because he lived in bodily purity;

He rejoices, mingled with the angelic assemblies.”]—a fiery authority.

A summer cloak had pressed upon my body beneath its burden;

I was naked, clothed in a thin covering.

When time fled from my eyes at its appointed hour,

For Phoebus’ lamp was the guide to the ice.

The horror of winter came to one praying for it,

And the warmth I sought gave no sign.

I pass over Matrona—[Note: [Col. 0309C] “I pass over Matrona”—The name of a lofty summit not far from Brigantio, on the side facing Gaul, today called Mont Genèvre. The *Jerusalem Itinerary*: “Station Ebredunum. From there the Cottian Alps begin; change of horses at Rame, 17 miles; station Brigantium, 17 miles. From there you ascend Matrona.” Ammianus Marcellinus writes: “In the Cottian Alps, whose beginning is at Segusio, a lofty ridge rises. From the summit of this Italian slope a plain extends for seven miles as far as a station called Mars; from there another, higher elevation, difficult to climb, reaches the summit of Matrona. Its name was given by the death of a noble woman. From there a road, indeed sloping but easier, extends to the fortress Virgantia.” Marcellinus places Matrona on this side of Brigantio with Ennodius. The author of the *Itinerary*, because he begins his journey in Gaul, places the section of Mount Genèvre after Brigantio, as I have said.]—I pass over the cliffs and the paths called impassable,

Pleasant at the entrance, difficult thereafter.

A painted appearance lured the wretched travelers;

Soon the trampled places gave birth to dreadful deaths.

The sacred antiquity of names deceives in nothing,

Since it wishes to call so many forms of death by their proper names.

A rocky path hung down beneath feet torn apart,

And, believe me, the track was not easy to see.

Why does the fame of the ancients wrap labyrinthine retreats

In words that the reader fears to repeat?

There the error of the craftsman stood deserving praise,

When Daedalus twisted the straight path by his ingenuity.

Here nature carries human beings over the summit of Olympus,

Where a dove can pass across and travel through the clear air.

Spare me, Pierian Muses, by keeping silent about the river-sea,

Lest speech restore what good fortune has driven away.

For the Duria, indeed, the Sessis, the torrent Stura, or the Orgus,

Surpass the violence of Ionian marble.

[Note: [Col. 0310C] “For the Doria, the Sēsis”—We have restored this verse by conjecture, since it was extremely corrupt even in the ancient manuscripts. Pliny, Book III, chapter 16, counts the Stura, Orgus, two Duriae, and the Sessis among the rivers that descend from the Alps into the Po on the left. They are still called by their ancient names, except that the Sessis is called the Sēsia and the Orgus the Orcus; from this it is clear that *Morgus* is not correctly read in Pliny.]

When sweet things follow upon varied dangers,

The outcome of events usually strengthens the heart.

[Col. 0310B] Forgetfulness does me no good amid doubtful grief;

I carry a heart drunk from the Lethean spring.

It is better to cleanse the thresholds of the saints while trembling,

To offer my tears to the martyrs.

Behold Saturninus, Crispinus, Daria, Maurus,

Eusebius, and Quintus prepare great joys.

Grant the merits of Octavius, Adventor; [Note: [Col. 0310C] “Restore, Solutor”—Octavius, Solutor, and Adventor, three martyrs of the Theban Legion, whose sacred relics are honored at Augusta Taurinorum. A sermon by Maximus, bishop of Turin, on them is extant.] restore, Solutor,

Lest a pure life fall beneath dark stains.

Let a mind conscious of righteousness sever hostile snares:

May what is fitting always please, and may what is fitting be permitted.

## II. DICTION [Note: [Col. 0310D] “A diction given to Deuterus, to be sent to Eugenetes”—Both are known from the letters. Deuterus the grammarian was discussed in Book I, Letter 19; Eugenetes the quaestor in Book IV, Letter 26. Deuterus therefore requests from Eugenetes a part of his little garden, and this poem was written by Ennodius in Deuterus’ name.] GIVEN TO DEUTERUS, A VERY ILLUSTRIOUS GRAMMARIAN, TO BE SENT IN HIS NAME TO EUGENETES, A VERY ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

Joys surpass my powers; a glad voice exults;

Prosperity does not fear the weakness of talent.

Sweet strands serve fortunate times:

Whatever the fortunate man has deserved will be a noble song.

May the voice of the just quaestor, the substance of laws, send us,

Like Phoebus, drums, plectra, and the lyre.

May the learned, holy crowd of the Camenae gather,

And offer what it speaks with eloquent thumb.

The swollen breasts of a prophetic bard could scarcely

Enumerate the forms of your virtues.

You are the glory of Italy, its most faithful hope of righteousness,

Its torch, trumpet of causes, our purple—farewell.

Rome, rich in eyes, called you its sun,

Receiving you in her lofty Quirinal embrace.

You will bring down the lynx with speech, and the lion with your voice;

By your honey the serpent will lower the weapons of its throat.

Tigresses deprived of their young would bring you gifts,

Which grief and wildness would give with trembling ear.

While the hand of fate tore you, almost fully reaped like a flower,

Christ struck down destruction.

Now the life of the blessed, restored to itself in better form, conquers,

And what comes from above is asserted by deeds.

Relying on these things, I did not draw out envoys or words of supplicants

By crafty arts disguised.

I myself, sending the words of a beggarly Thalia,

Beg you, in God’s manner, to grant me a gift.

A little garden, joined to a small portion,

Delays the firm hope that I may deserve to become its master.

Do not disdain to grant it to me, light of honors;

Thus, having obtained my wish, may you cultivate our ages.

Thus may the lofty power of the reigning man raise you high—[Note: [Col. 0311D] “Thus, of the reigning man”—Theoderic, whose quaestor he was.]—

Thus may golden destinies run according to your merits.

What Amphion of Dirce touched with his plectrum lived;

At that time nothing endowed with life could die.

The benefits of the Muses have never flowed for so many years;

Through affection, reconcile them to me as a reward.

## III. PREFACE [Note: [Col. 0311D] “To the grandsons of Proculus”—Proculus was a Ligurian poet, whom Sidonius numbers among the outstanding poets of his age, distinguished in both languages, in Book IX, Letter 15:

“Proculus, sprung from Ligurian soil and people,

Could always have sounded these things more powerfully

With melodious strokes,

Polishing every graceful poem,

So as to challenge Venetian Mantua in favor,

And himself, equal to Homeric glory,

Following Maro’s wheels with comparable art.”] SPOKEN TO THE GRANDSONS OF PROCULUS ON THE FIFTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF MAY

The earth, already pregnant, presses its breasts into an ear of grain,

Swollen with milk among the married clods.

The juice scattered through the grasses is drawn together for offspring,

Making solid progeny from drops.

The vine, clothed in jewels, stretches out its arms;

Look, a tendril grows green from the lap of the wood.

The vines, ordered through their growth now to destroy the forest,

Acquire wounds so that their fruits may increase.

[Col. 0311D] The joyful infancy of the world calls forth and seeks

The nurse whom the breeze of the warm sky has given.

[Col. 0312A] Rustic youth plays across the face of the fields,

Looking back at the sweet burden of harsh labor.

The year crawls forward in triumph through the murmurs of spring,

Bringing honey, broken open to speak, upon its lips.

While our feeling stammers songs amid events,

May a golden hand bring help to beginnings.

The reaper brings the ears more gently to the sickle

If he continues to comb the crop with rakes.

Now, teacher, receive the spring growth of Proculus;

Do not let immoderate heat scorch the tender shoots.

Let the laws be preserved; let the letter of the census run as it should.

Their grandfather surpassed these streams in Pindaric fashion,

He who sang learned songs with the Camenaean plectrum,

Whose Apollonian choirs left nothing unspoken.

May Phoebus soon summon him back, stronger in aid,

If Marsyas comes for another contest in art. [Note: [Col. 0311D] “If Marsyas comes”—That is, if Phoebus must again enter into a contest with Marsyas, may he wish to have Proculus as helper and companion.]

## IV. [Note: [Col. 0312D] “The epithalamium for Maximus”—We have seen several letters to Maximus in Books VII and VIII, including mention of his wedding, for which this epithalamium was written. Like nearly all Ennodius’ poems, it had been corrupted by ugly transpositions of verses; we have restored it to its proper order and polish. It consists of various meters, following the example of Claudian, who played with different measures in his poem for the marriage of Honorius and Maria. Sidonius, in his epithalamium for Polemius and Araneola, used only heroic verse; Paulinus used elegiacs in the epithalamium for Julianus Memor, bishop, son of F. and I, a most distinguished woman.] EPITHALAMIUM SPOKEN TO MAXIMUS, A VERY ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

### Preface

While the year, with its new sun, shapes tender ears of grain,

Nature, pregnant in the bridal chambers, sits intent on the coming birth. [Note: [Col. 0312D] “Nature in the bridal chamber”—That is, she is pregnant and soon attentive to the birth that is to come. Very elegant. Barthius, *Observations on Statius’ Achilleid* I, p. 1682.]

The world is painted with the varied distinction of flowers;

There is one appearance of earth: grace, adornment, love.

The strawberry trees grow together in life-giving moisture;

A concreted, fiery juice nourishes the seeds.

The earth, swollen by its generative husband, rises;

The parched forest grows green with luxuriant stripping.

The grass, nursing upon the turf, is pressed into a knot;

The arms of the vine give fingers gemmed with buds.

In the cultivation of things the bridal law joins the torches;

The breeze of heaven makes all shoots into a bridegroom.

Therefore with equal desire light, sky, rivers, Nereus,

Mountains, meadows, and wild creatures conceive their joys.

The world, Maximus, receives from you what blooms;

Your dowry accompanies natural power.

In you blood, wealth, genius, mind, and aspirations abound,

Supported foremost by the Muses’ brow.

Our age has given you as a memorial of faith,

Equal in bodily and inward purity.

A bright life gives you a bride surpassing you in merits;

When she surpasses you, thus the palm comes to you.

A harmonious flame smiles upon her snow-white lips;

She scatters white marks of modesty across her face.

May the spring of speech, in voice, mind, and plectrum, be present, I pray:

Art, nature, the Muse, and Phoebus, through whom eloquence swells.

[Col. 0312D] Nothing base should sound in the praises of the Maximi;

Phoebean words often wear down the lofty crown of the head.

[Col. 0313A] Venus, gracious, in the captive world, playing amid pleasant places

With the gifts of scattered flowers,

While she makes spring precious through the beauty

Of her shining star,

Scorned all the splendor of her golden robe;

She did not desire the display of foreign metal.

Richer in adornment, she stood with her clothing cast off,

Her hair scattered.

If wool, having drunk some noble poison by art,

Is superior through a counterfeit color,

Tell it—and the pebbles of the freezing sea—[Note: [Col. 0313D] “And the pebbles of the freezing sea”—The letters have merely been transposed in the reading *cedit algentis*, etc. But perhaps *sic et algentis*, “thus also the pebbles of the freezing sea,” is more correct. Barthius, *Adversaria*, p. 479.]—also yield;

She stands naked above them.

The gems of her breast had flashed rarely beneath an opening thread,

On her rosy nipples.

Driving away the envious covering from her limbs,

Another light appears.

Her body, revealed without a cloud,

Shone brightly when the prison was broken open:

And whatever the ill-protecting garment had kept hidden

Was revealed by art. [Note: [Col. 0314D] “It shone when the prison was broken open”—In old manuscripts and editions: “when the prison was broken.” Excellent: for she did not break the covering that enclosed it, etc. The same, ibid.]

The winged one returned with slackened bow,

Condemning his quiver to idleness,

Gladly carrying arrows moistened by no blood. [Note: [Col. 0314D] “Gladly carrying arrows moistened by no blood”—Cupid does not seem likely to be present gladly; Venus’ address also proves this. We should therefore read *lentus*, “slow,” so that, as though in sadness, a slow step may be ascribed to him. In the older editions this word is entirely omitted, and the final verse is made almost into a hexameter, which increases our suspicion of corruption. The same, ibid.]

Then, with floating weapons, he addressed his mother:

“We are defeated, mother; the rewards of our power are lost.

Now nowhere does Cythera resound; the tale of the Loves is mocked,

Nor does offspring suffice for the age that is being born.

Virginity, consuming many limbs with a new ardor,

Possesses them cold. Lofty vows subdue the flesh;

[Col. 0313C] The world scarcely remains under the slender name of its first condition;

The trembling young imitate the first age, their strength broken.

Rare, across the immense fields of the ages, behold,

Is the harvest of marriage. Through the flowers old age alone

Displays its white and famished, pallid hairs.

One faith in all things is not bent by any sweetness,

And if anything could lead tender morals astray,

It is trampled under evil commands. Everywhere

The mourning prohibition is preserved; it is a crime to name bridal chambers to the chaste.

You lie relaxed, unaware of so great a law,

Naked, looking back over your flowing limbs through your scattered hair.

Rise, come, and quickly shake off the sleep that obstructs you.

Nor should it be thought shameful that you possess a captive god,

Or that the law of chastity, or the ill-advised statute, should bind you.”

[Col. 0313D] At such words even the entrails of the sea would have burned.

The golden light gathers her loosened hair into a knot,

And, enclosing her natural beauty in a garment,

Changes her form. Then whatever jasper shines,

[Col. 0314A] Whatever emerald is green in value—[Note: [Col. 0313D] “An emerald fashioned as pasture”—*Pastura* is *νομή*. Just as *νομή* sometimes refers to the pastures themselves, as when *νομαὶ καὶ λειμῶνες* are joined, so here “pasture” means green grazing fields; likewise in Epigram 10: “The green rocks surpassing the grassy pasture.” Green is already the praise and value of the emerald. Pliny, Book XXXVIII, chapter 5: “We eagerly gaze upon green herbs and leaves; but upon emeralds all the more eagerly, since nothing at all compared with them shines greener.” Tertullian, *On the Judgment*: “And the huge emerald gleams green with grassy light.” Martianus Capella, Book I, on Jupiter: “The earth joined emerald, grass-green shoes, to his footprints with a wave of verdant brightness.”]—an emerald fashioned as pasture;

And the white stone, hidden in shells beneath a better guardian poison,

Comes forth to take light from a snow-white body.

A shining mantle tapers over her girded loins,

And a hard belt compresses her tender breasts.

She addresses her son: “Whom, my hope, are you trying to strike?

Whom are we pursuing? Where do you command us to go? After idleness,

A greater flame is fitting. Let peoples then learn to exalt the goddess

When she lies neglected. Let their fires, restored by double cares, show that the gods lose nothing through sleep.

Look, here is Maximus, as you see, the sole hope of the highest lineage;

Through long forgetfulness he mocks the sweet marriage torches.

He pursues a mother who is purer than heaven itself,

A woman whom we know surpasses womanhood in mind.

This man has subdued the boy; he receives the character of his grandfathers.

Alas, what shames us has remained unknown to him through a long age.

Let my lamp approach his hidden fibers:

Let him sigh, desire, run about, burn, and pray.”

She spoke; and, embracing her offspring with kindly nurturing,

She pressed soft kisses to his honeyed lips.

He flies, speeding through the clouds on a swift wind,

Joining all the elements in wanton passion.

When he stopped and saw the young man in the splendor of his appearance,

He said: “Are you, swollen with pride, scorning the son of Dione?

I have come here to honor Venus. The one who burns more slowly

Has a pyre that burns for a long time, and whatever wood

Is withdrawn from the fire will restore swift embers.”

He drew the arrow with which he had pierced all the gods.

Then the handsome bow struck its rounded curve:

Each arm drew in a different direction.

[Col. 0314C] Let the right hand of the winged one display the fate.

Soon he strikes, greeting the deed with a joyful cry:

“I, who always clung despised to your trembling

Entrails, fugitive one, offer this victim to my mother,

Whom you have not regarded for many years.

Look: again, having searched deeply the clay from which he may join a girl in marriage,

He sees her lofty star,

And, astonished, turns his eyes toward his mother;

Believing the girl to be his sister, he praises the noble theft.

But that boy strikes the tender girl with a lighter arrow,

And turns the whole force of his blow more powerfully upon the man.

After this, as he departs, he soothes their hearts with words:

‘May our wounds, young man, strengthen your powers.

For whoever is struck by my spear grows.

These things, believe me, make many descendants through warfare.

Be fortunate, and always carry my wounds with you.’”

[Col. 0314D] Now, aided by Pierian favor,

Noblemen, place me with a cheerful countenance.

May those who foster the slender poem throughout,

[Col. 0315A] By their learned kindness, sustain it.

Let the frost that now weighs upon my talent

Spread out again, warmed by the beauty of spring.

## V. THE ITINERARY OF THE PO

Cultivator of talent, fountain of speech, abundance of language,

May Castalian moisture come, with which Thracian Orpheus

May kindle shipwrecked hearts with an outpoured stream.

May it be present and join together the clefts of my parched heart.

Since I am about to speak of the waters of the Eridanus, unless I drench

My dry limbs with a broad stream of Pegasean liquid,

My burning words scarcely drip forth in their barren telling.

As I narrate the heaps of waters, furnish me with a stream.

How well does he unfold the waters for whom the river murmurs gently?

[Col. 0315B] It was the season of the year when the vine greens with tender grapes

And displays the gifts of autumn throughout the world.

When Lyaeus, wet with foreign rains,

Stretches the tunics of grapes in the prison of must,

With abundant rains, the bounds of its banks broken—[Note: [Col. 0315D] “The law of rocks subdued”—That is, with the embankments broken. The manuscripts vary: one reads *parcarum*, another *parumper*, a third *parum*. I think nothing should be changed; or, if anything is changed, *riparum* should be read from the traces of the third, that is, the Vatican copy, as in Epigram 133. For this is what Virgil means in Book II of the *Aeneid*:

“Not thus, when a foaming river bursts through broken embankments,

And overcomes the opposing dams with its flood.”]—the law of rocks subdued,

The Po had then, by chance, covered its fields with captives;

Its swollen ridges were singing with threatening foam.

The rooftops of the villas ran standing through the waves.

Then the sea preserved what it had seized, covered by the shore,

And, changing the lands, fortune remained with the cottages.

You might have seen forests ordered to abandon their position

And hurry toward devouring flames, with the Po as their guide.

Then I, drawn by fervent love for my sister,

Whose child the Fates had cut down with a cruel thumb,

And whose household they had made widowed although her husband remained—she who had always borne children for

[Col. 0315C] the city of Avernus—[Note: [Col. 0316D] “The city of Avernus”—All manuscripts perhaps read *urnis*, “urns,” so that he speaks of the sepulchral urns of Avernus, indicating that the sister had previously lost other children, all carried off by brief life and premature, bitter death.]—the city of Avernus,

Chose to expose my life in order to console her.

That greatest ruler of Ligurian rivers,

Sent beneath the yokes, groaned beneath the weight of the boat.

He swelled, then again released his threats and blasts,

And he who overcame the heavens was ordered to yield to me alone.

Thus piety subdues the elements; thus it restrains all things,

When compassion pleasing to God has possessed the mind.

Behold, again the sky, covered with wet clouds,

Drank up waters that would overwhelm every falling field.

The shipwrecked land did not see the face of heaven,

And dreadful darkness shone, bereft of stars.

A fish wandered, but was not captive in houses,

And the river’s flood lapped at food across their tables.

The sea vomited up the deepest inner rooms of human beings;

The watery seas enclosed the dusty fields.

Having endured the first dangers, I saw dangers return.

That triumphant novice in the contests of Nereus,

I bore my cold breast through the liquid waters,

[Col. 0316A] And with no dry eyes looked back upon the marble shores.

When suddenly the aged inhabitant saw the sea swallowed up,

He laughed and the remaining signs of the exposed terror.

Fields gleamed with mingled metal:

The Eridanus shone with bright sands.

The cheerful boatman immediately took me aboard his alder boat,

To whom the fortunate burden had long since granted a favorable omen.

Unskilled, he steered the rudder, safe from the weight,

And, with Christ as guide, carried me through festive shores.

## VI. Ennodius the Deacon’s Dictio on His Return from Rome

[Note: *Dictio on the return from the City.* Prose prefaces are placed before this poem and several others. Although they are sometimes longer, since they refer to the poems, we have thought it right to classify them with the poems. He describes his return from the City after the Palmary Synod and the *Apologeticus*.]

### Preface

Cheerfulness is always dear to a man returning to his native soil, while he confidently believes that he has escaped whatever fears an anxious mind produced for him during his wandering—as though they had been predetermined and arranged under heaven’s oppressive decree. A clear voice, therefore, is owed to joy, lest silent happiness take on the appearance of grief. For to whom can the secret of an exultant spirit be disclosed except when unlocked by the key of the mouth? The Mantuan poet even declared that returning swans play with their wings.

What shall I do, caught in the midst of a precipice, since I owe both fidelity in speech to my return and the necessity of silence to my purpose? Withdraw, I beg you, for a time, stern censor of duty; you have never mingled appropriately with joys. The most distinguished of the prophets, reducing their words to the rule of verse, sang their desires and prayers in song; their breasts, dedicated to divine converse, distributed the laws of the Church among peoples through the lyre.

Why should I, placed in the infancy of rank and merit, not strive to imitate the deeds of the greatest—especially since the semblance of narration strengthens the soldier of the altar for receiving the battles that arise against the faith? Nor shall I hesitate to say what is established by the present example. We have already learned amid what whirlwind the spear must be cast for love of the faith, nor has a mediocre struggle raised us to the price or titles of virtue.

I shall therefore gladly proclaim my joys in musical style; their fulfillment I promise, with God’s help, to announce in the greatest works of eloquence. The poisons of barking tongues will assail me, but through exercises of vocation and talent I shall gather together whatever the slanderer has hurled against the accused man’s merit. This is the practice of a well-disposed conscience: to join the bites of rivals to the profit of reputation and to hunt the gains of fame from envy.

Wickedly persistent tooth of jealousy, break yourself; and you who seek fuel for abuse from the place of glory, be silent. Say how profit can arise from merit if you count it boastfulness that we please through our toil. Labor is the friend of discipline and is joined to religion by a kind of kinship.

[Note: *Itinerary of the Po.* The name of the Po was added in place of a title, for it describes the voyage in which he was tossed about while the Po was in flood, when, as a duty, he went to visit his sister, recently bereaved of her only son.]

As damp cuttings, joined to foreign roots, bestow upon branches a nobility of fruit that the plantings producing them had long been unable to know, so a mind endowed with liberal training, pregnant with good care, rises toward the hope of a better offspring. The poisons of counsels prepared for human destruction are driven from the mind, and the moisture of lethal sap is removed whenever intellects submit themselves to occupations of this kind.

From here, as we move toward brighter things, the secrets of the divine books are revealed. While he opens their door when understanding knocks, he makes an unknown path accessible to peoples under his guidance: he leads the fastidious by the splendor of eloquence, the poorly educated by crafted Latinity, and, as they say, by artful rusticity. Who would not love and follow such a guide to salvation, who, mixing sweetness with what is necessary and severity with what is sweet, makes the doctrines of life lovable and compels unwilling people to desire them?

But let the honorable vows of the undertaking begun elsewhere be fulfilled. We are speaking among those who understand such matters: it is a work of virtue to contain joy; it belongs to diligent accomplishment to display a successful result through the laborious path of splendid diction—especially today, when a portion of my own being has entered the threshold of eloquence and, by rejoicing the father, grants him the eloquence that talent denies, since circumstance gives what nature did not provide.

Well done, young man of distinguished virtues, who in the hoary bloom of fruits display the number. You know how to drive away the ice of affliction and invite me to the springtime of speech. For while you devote to study what you owe, and I devote to joy what I owe, I think that we both make progress. It is similar to educating an unformed person and recalling one already idle to the fervor of declamation.

After hoary winters, after the losses of the frozen deep,

Whenever the sailor takes a tranquil course,

He grieves and despairs of favorable conditions on the treacherous sea,

And does not think that the face he sees belongs to salt water.

A light breeze whistles; he fears powerful storms

And judges the sea’s gentle threats to be real.

If the Zephyrs ruffle the sails hanging from the mast,

And the breeze plays with sweet obedience,

He swears that the wind-confused world is losing its laws

And believes that ancient Chaos has returned.

So joys raise up dangers amid peaceful circumstances;

There is no complete trust either in happiness or in uncertainty.

Not otherwise did Rome, having held me amid various perils,

Restore me to the embrace of the desired shore.

They soothe the venerable power of the sea with song,

The power whose hooked anchor bites its proper ground.

But the winds, about to make gentle sleep for the weary,

Disturb the mind of the sea-borne soldier.

[Col. 0317D] He subdues the ship’s gear, and shakes the oars and sails:

Thus the mind suffers shipwreck through suspicion.

May he come who pressed the blue waters with dry feet,

For he will be the happy harbor of salvation—

He who bound the waters, pouring out the rock into cups;

Who loosened stones and made waters solid;

Whom the mother, fertile without seed, brought forth for the ages,

Joining the burden of virginity to motherhood;

Who overcame death by the gift of his own death,

Giving life to the world, whom the tomb brought forth.

May he look upon me from high Olympus.

Then may I possess my homeland; then may I have the aid of a harbor.

Although loosened winds sweep the cloudy seas,

They strike the cracked stern, yet will harm it not.

Then I shall shake sweet drums with ordered strings

And paint our songs with new flowers.

To confess it, joyful speech is well expressed in words:

[Note: *Sad hearts do not contain the verse-speaker.* Sidonius to Lampridius: “You know well the joy of poets, whose talents are ensnared by griefs as little fish are caught in nets.” He therefore calls him *versiloquus*, not “crafty” or “versatile,” but a poet who fashions verses.]

Sad hearts do not contain the verse-speaker.

But let spring return; let the winter of fear now cease:

Bind garlands of foliage around your hair.

Let me sing what Ambrose the prophet was accustomed to utter beautifully,

While he fed the people with his mouth.

## VII. To Faustus: On His Poems

[Note: *To Faustus.* On the occasion of a poem he had received from Faustus, he extols his poetic ability with extraordinary praise. Moved, evidently, by Ennodius’s commendation, Petrus Crinitus and Lilius Giraldus placed this Faustus among the distinguished poets of the age. For, I believe, they had seen none of his poems, since none survive except the distich that Ennodius inserted in his epigrams concerning Ligurian wine:

> He who calls someone a drinker in the land of the Ligurians is mistaken.
>
> Does one who drinks Ligurian wine drink wine?

]

### Preface
