If I had not learned that the serenity of your conscience repudiates the itch of this evil, I would declare the abundance of your eloquence hateful to me. Let the thing allied to treachery withdraw from good deeds.

Yet I announce that your caution has harmed me. Until now you have withheld from the dryness of my little talent the rain that nourishes fruit. Good God! How I recognize in myself the unfamiliar resources of speech acquired from the riches of your mouth! Added to your richly furnished words, as I understand it, is the file of expertise, which smooths rusty tongues and dull minds.

You have a kind of fellowship with the Maker of humanity. He fashioned from nothing; you restore things to something better. I give thanks for the poem I have received, though I grieve over the benefit delayed. To the dishonor of the Muses, to whom no [Note: *Gluvidenus*, Book V, letter 8.] Gluvidenus is lacking, I added verses; and, prodigal toward paper destined to perish, I did not spare it. Read poems capable of stirring joy, and restrain, as they say, the astonishing ornaments of familiarity.

You kindle the innermost parts of a river, Faustus,

Whose flood feeds a great thirst for song.

Who could endure the heat of waters, and, drinking with a dry mouth,

Suck in flames akin to the flowing waters?

Your words give birth to vaporous heat from a spring;

From it the liver boils, and cups look ahead.

Whoever hastily approaches the river of talent

Must not think it uncertain that he drinks so as to thirst.

Noble water conceals a hidden flavor

And counts it a loss if I carry away less from it.

Let no slippery tongue, trusting in the Cecropian buskin,

Boast anything of the old men’s nobility.

Faustus composes new songs in the manner of the ancients,

Who by his art cuts his melody into limbs.

Learned to bring unworked words to the anvil,

Whatever verses he makes, he tests three and four times.

Hoary age tells how Maro animated with his fingers

The work he fashioned with his life-giving hand.

You give words a face and limbs through rhythm.

What nature gives to God, study gives to you.

If you turn your plectrum dexterously toward an aged corpse,

You make it primeval by building with the lyre.

If you imitate flowers frozen beneath the wagon of Boötes,

Soon the breeze whistles around Helice in springtime rhythms.

May snowy groves bloom with roses for you; may cold pour forth wine;

May Pallas, beneath her burning star, bring gifts.

May the fish you carry on the heavenly vault swim through it;

If you command it in verse, the stag will love the marble.

From the very middle of its jaws, from its glutted belly,

May you, powerful in speech, draw out the prey held in the lion’s mouth.

Now I know to what Castalian loves you have drawn me;

Your gifts are added to my faults.

My little boat is swept toward swollen storms,

About to endure the winter North Winds. A poor sailor,

Fashioning a cracked hull from thin bark,

Built it and gave it the uncelebrated name of “skiff.”

It is capable neither of sweeping the Aegean sea

Nor the shores of Phrixus, nor any waters with its harsh keel.

Aeolus it recognized; but, with good caution, it preferred

The calm bays of the deep whirlpool, where the South Wind serves,

Not where it seeks dominion. Whenever there,

With a slow rower, the breeze whistles and runs across the trembling vessel,

For while the sails tied to the highest [Note: *Nexa ceruchis.* In Greek, **κεροῦκος** (*keroukos*) means “horned.” Hence, because the ship’s yards resemble horns, they called them *ceruchi*, as did Lucan, Flaccus, Apuleius, and others. Some interpret the word as the ropes of the yards. Isidore, in the *Glosses*: “*Ceruchi*, the ropes of ships.”] yards ripple,

The winds that carry deaths grant me sleep.

Here I shall turn my vessel, entrusting my sails

To reliable winds—the course of my art and assistance.

Bend the route with your sails, Phoebus, and turn the rudder toward the shores.

Let the hooked anchor bite the cut-up ground.

Muse, head of the finest words,

Fashioning a grassy crown with ivy,

Which you may count among the poets

Cut out from the mass,

Bind around your hair.

The hull plows the immense sea;

The hand suited to the rudder does not know how to be guided

Toward whatever right-hand governance calls it through the waves,

A friend of art.

You proceed to Faustus, the balance of speech,

Whose mouth is able to equal the vast deep,

Whom the world itself venerates in the light,

The more dexterous one.

He holds the balance of ears among the Muses;

His blade cuts every wound

That lies hidden in the innermost marrow

Of sickly song.

If he wished my modest [Note: *My dithyrambs.* “My verses.” There is a double liberty in one word: a simple word is used for a compound, or rather a shortened expression for a complete one; *thyrambos* for *dithyrambos*, and a species for a genus—*dithyrambs* for any kind of poem. So again in epigram 108:

> Never through the long ages did the benefits of Castalia
>
> Flow to me in fruitful dithyrambs.

That is, I have never made any profit from my verses, as above, poem 2:

> Through all these years no benefits flowed to me from the Muses.

] dithyrambs

Hang in the mind by which he governs the whole world,

It is praise to hang them amid the trivial murmur

Of infants.

My light, Faustus,

My hope and salvation,

Receive gladly

The small gifts

Of my little letters.

May the supreme Christ

Thus preserve your bright

Offspring.

Extend your right hand

In honor of the nourishing Name.

To the Thunderer, the grateful

Grain offerings of the devout.

## VIII. To Olybrius: On His Eloquence

[Note: *To Olybrius.* This was said of Olybrius’s eloquence in connection with Book I, letter 9. Now, as an appendix, we shall rescue the memory of another Roman advocate who lived in the same age. He was Petilius Processius, V. S. (*vir spectabilis*), a togatus attached to the praetorian seat, whom an elegant epitaph teaches us to have died under the consulship of Probus the Younger—that is, in the year 513. We read it inscribed on a marble tomb in the basilica of blessed Paul in these words:]

> If love lives after death, if ancient gratitude
>
> Endures, driven into the mind’s hidden goodness,
>
> Receive, though mournful, your brother’s song,
>
> Lest a foreign tongue be harmful to your tombs.
>
> Nature, your mother, had depicted you with every art:
>
> In character, talent, body, mind, and faith.
>
> A pure cultivator of friendship, guardian of honor,
>
> You supported the wretched by eloquence or compassion.
>
> Hence we shall mourn you throughout all ages.
>
> What power you had as a young man and as an old man!
>
> Your mother, your brothers, and your beloved household
>
> Lament you together in grief with perpetual tears.
>
> HERE RESTS IN PEACE THE BLESSED PETILIUS PROCESSIUS,
>
> V. S., TOGATUS OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS PRAETORIAN PREFECTURE (INL. P. P.),
>
> WHO LIVED APPROXIMATELY THIRTY-EIGHT YEARS
>
> AND WAS BURIED ON THE FIRST DAY OF JULY,
>
> DURING THE CONSULSHIP OF PROBUS THE YOUNGER,
>
> ILLUSTRIOUS MAN.

### Preface

The flute does not sing whenever a rustic shepherd looks upon his country flock. Silent groves produce a frightening solitude; and fear is everywhere when no sound is heard to comfort the deserted place.

But if, in the whistling of breezes, the treetops imitate the appearance of tongues, and the pleasant shaking of the laughing leaves addresses a man, he will be thought to be among surrounding gatherings. Nor does he lament any hardship when nature herself speaks to him, in her secrets, through whatever means.

Then it is pleasant to bring the flute, companion of exile, to one’s lips and, scattering breath through the cracks of the tortoise-shell instrument, to compose from spirit and air a kind of ordered expression. Then the unformed and unskilled tongue addresses its own Palaemon; then it counts how many watches are needed to guard the folds; then it sighs over the many ambushes of wolves, sharpened by hunger, and whatever the breath has uttered falls into speech. He tries to comfort and soothe himself by this companionship.

If, while he is doing such things, some learned person should bring a talking lyre to the speaker, and urbane mockery should offer him its eloquent strings, unadorned simplicity is uncertain what to choose. The lyre’s touch, even with wandering fingers, produces a sweet sound that breaks the spirit; nevertheless he considers it wrong, if the charm of another’s playing is drawn away from its purpose, to learn not to love the ancestral skill. For while the unbridled breadth of rustic learning does not measure its limit, he understands that, through admiration for his superiors, he will lose even what he himself is capable of, since the mediocrity of paternal instruction, like something foreign, despises the inhabitant of the shepherd’s hut who does not know his own worth.

Not otherwise does your radiance of eloquence delight me, most eminent man, whom we must count among the greatest stars of the court; flame of talents, splendor of eloquence, wealth of diction. Through the trackless paths of the groves you delight me like a shepherd’s flute, which tells humble tales, while I fear your lyre and praise your plectra—those which, as I explained above, you join, urbane man, to my rustic fingers.

Remove, I beg you, the allure of polished speech that you employ to invite me. Let those bonds of conversation be absent which you use even among experts. Restrain the fingers of your words by which you are accustomed to compel resisting souls toward your desires. Let me either conceal my ignorance in silence or offer others, through a shrill reed, a trivial song. To converse with you is a work of ancient merit and new happiness.

But if, forgetting myself, I should attempt it, having acquired the sun’s chariot against my own advantage, I justly undergo the example of Phaethon. Since the subject has arisen and a warning has been added, the following poem shows what must be done.

Fame relates the deeds of the ancients, which it does not know how to destroy;

It always speaks of whatever has existed in the world.

While Titan scatters the offspring of light across the vault

And enriches the world with noble rays;

While damp reins restrain the vaporous four-horse chariot

And the shining flood sends daylight everywhere,

The sun bent the flowing reins with learned hands;

Well-known light carried an artful master.

But after he began, at Phaethon’s entreaty,

To entrust him with dominion without testing his strength,

The star perceived a degenerate driver in its first movements

And, once the horses were shaken loose, began to run.

Then the hoofed creature, breathing out the whole light from its nostrils,

Did not preserve the fixed periods of its law.

The splendor that gives light yielded to flame and burned what it illuminated;

What gives life to the earth produced destruction.

Then, while it shattered the Hyperborean crusts with its lamp,

The Tanais departed dry, drained of its waters.

Crystal melted, but the river’s course burned:

It dissolved stones and bound together the Eridanus.

So I, attempting to cross the rhetorical path,

Approach the sun’s chariot and authority.

I do not know what I shall expend upon the various regions of the sky;

I do not know what I shall hold; the heat overcomes everything.

The powerful court formed you smooth to the last detail

And commanded you to bring light to your ancestors.

You rival Phoebus: a fat victim smokes for you,

For whose sake the dwellers in heaven would desist from the thunderbolt.

But my poor gardens scarcely send me

The red vegetable rejected by the earthen bowl that received it.

I am, I confess, one whose words drip in the telling,

Words that reveal the thinness of a poor talent.

I sing no poems; nor, when I accompany the Muses,

Will the polished sound of my finger be granted to remain.

Whatever we used to say with Apollo’s plectrum, I have abandoned,

Forgetting the tongue that the strings gave me.

My rustic right hand wanders across delicate chords;

Barbarous plectra shatter sweet melodies.

Ah, how often Helicon flowed for me in glass-clear grass,

A stream that, smiling upon my lips, creates thirst!

Ah, how often I passed my days crowned with ivy,

Soothing the Aonian assembly with song!

But now, through forests, among the caves of wild beasts,

Resolved to conduct a rustic campaign,

I entrust great seeds to strong furrows,

So that darnel may fail to rob them of the germ of life.

Let milk-white words not expose my loosened mind,

Nor let me be called gentle in speech and talent.

Let my tongue not run across open fields,

Nor let me bring manly words on heavy trumpets.

Let my heart not be inflamed by the high-sounding buskin,

Nor let me be thought swollen in writings and manners.

Then the reader who seeks fame for me everywhere will find a harbor.

But steady modesty is proper to me if I remain silent.

You hold heaven; leave me quiet upon the earth,

For I know only the ground on which I have learned nothing well.

## IX. Dictio Delivered on the Birthday of the Holy and Most Blessed Pope Epiphanius, in the Thirtieth Year of His Priesthood

[Note: *On the birthday of Epiphanius.* When he was entering the thirtieth year of the chair, or episcopate, of Ticinum. Epiphanius’s thirtieth anniversary fell in the year 496. Thus, in that year, Ennodius delivered this panegyric.]

### Preface

I perceive what many people silently say in their minds, and with the attentive ear of my heart I understand the voice of their hearts. These silences cry out: what does a man of another profession seek from a theme? Why does one marked by titles of humility await, amid the clattering ranks of the common people, a voice of applause, which popular favor raises through the swelling bubbles of supporters?

They say that such things should once have been composed, when the flowers of adolescence and the remnants of childhood still bloomed in him, and the springtime of worldly license smiled; when it was fitting to be carried aloft by resounding acclamations, at the time when even the appearance of disguised pleasure could be enjoyed. Why does he now recite publicly, when public praise neither suits nor delights him?

Let them remember that I am performing the duty of my office, since it is clear that in a priest’s praises I feel what I ought to feel. Although I now render him modest praise at an unsuitable time, I shall nevertheless owe him the greatest praise hereafter, since in his ministry whatever ability I possess deserves to be expended.

I have also understood in my mind that if an account must be given for idle speech, no less must be given for idle silence. My silences would indeed have been idle if, while every kind of mind rejoiced around me, I alone had withheld words when I could give them.

For even in heavenly service it is fitting that hymns should be employed, and we believe that the Lord, who is beyond human nature, is soothed by the praises of human beings alone; he demands this by a special right from those whom he has endowed with a tongue. What should a bishop do, who by his own prayers brought it about that I should be able?

[Note: It is written in Isaiah, chapter 50, according to the edition of the Seventy interpreters:

**Κύριος δίδωσί μοι γλώσσαν παιδείας, τοῦ γνῶναι ἡνίκα δεῖ εἴπειν λόγον**

“The Lord gives me a tongue of instruction, so that I may know when it is necessary to speak a word.”

Tertullian followed this text in *Against Marcion* 4.29: “The Lord gives me a tongue of instruction, when I ought to utter a word.” Likewise in *Against Praxeas* 22: “The Lord gives me a tongue of instruction, to know when it is appropriate to speak a word.” Our Vulgate reading differs in the latter clause.]

For it is written: “The Lord gave me a tongue of learning, when it is appropriate to speak a word” (Isaiah 50:4). It is appropriate now, as I judge; and the door of the heart opens for the time of speaking.

But now I shall not open my mouth in poetic praise. Far from me be the sewer of poems, which, just as it does not praise what is true, so is not truly praised. Now lend favor to minds as I speak what is certain. If, because of the smallness of my talent, I do not say lesser things, I shall not invent greater things out of boastfulness.

The greatest virtue of speech among the ancient poets

Was this: if they knew how to deceive with learned words.

It was praise to compose a poem that lied in praise.

Then fraud was suited to the work; for, preserving what contains guilt,

They forbade, out of shame, the speaking of truth,

And everywhere faith despised the poem.

An art was pleasing that fault suited; for learned error

Dragged from certain tongues poems to be feared.

Law taught speech without law, when by art it vindicated

Whatever the laws forbid to be spoken. In deceptive song they fashioned foul gods

as restraints upon morality.

They said that Phoebus existed, and three times three sisters,

The Castalian water, and the various arts of Pallas.

Then they told of the laurel, tripods, the prophetic cauldron, drums, and plectrum;

Their understanding fled from the path of truth,

And an image deceived their wandering sight.

Now, faith, reject the tongue of the lyre that sings

With the mouth of the thumb. Rather, come now, Spirit, I pray,

By whose inexhaustible renewal each year revives

Whatever the earth creates, the sea generates, and the sky brings forth.

You who spread the seas, give solid substance to the fields,

Stir the rocks at your command; the terrible Caucasus fears you,

When, with obedient hearing, you subdue the strong hearts of servants;

You who see all things, whom all things tremble before:

Fountain, way, right hand, stone, calf, lion, morning star, lamb,

Door, hope, virtue, word, wisdom, prophet,

Sacrifice, shoot, shepherd, mountain, net, dove,

Flame, giant, eagle, bridegroom, patience, worm,

Exalted Son, Lord, God—Christ, all things.

Now I pray that he be present in my words—he who, entering the breast

Of the ancient prophet, in the time of Pharaoh’s reign,

Helped the prophet who was about to speak with a slender voice.

Then, I think, he himself was astonished, fully conscious of his mouth,

When he filled the ruler’s ears with accustomed murmuring,

By weight, voice, sound, meaning, integrity, and modesty.

You, holy one, counsel your servant; grant him to offer thanks,

Which it is a pleasure to owe. We all embrace

This holy day, on which he wished to bring his radiance to the earth

And more readily to enliven souls with his near rays.

At which the world rejoices, though they are not the world’s joys:

Do you see him, worshiping, lower his fearful countenance

In obedience to the prophet? The season of his birth feels

Festive, nor does it sadly despise the pupils admitted to it.

This day was the cause of life and of salvation for all,

Loosening the bonds of ancient guilt.

In this Christ bestowed honor, and yet in the Ausonian fields

Gave peoples one who would govern them with equal mind

And rule the nations with piety. The Author of Olympus,

Who had promised them a king of similar integrity,

Himself, as the right hand of God, grants laws from his shining throne.

He who is nearest heaven, whose mind is conscious of righteousness,

Will always be the one whom the just approve, whom public vows,

With the world as judge, choose. I confess, he contributed greatly

So that he might enjoy the bosom of an unpurchased see.

A free crowd made you its perpetual lord,

Worthy of praise for its service. Ah, how great was the fervor everywhere!

With the world applauding the holy man in tumult,

Everyone had the same mind, every crowd one voice.

Yet they competed with one another in their vows,

As though the reason were that they were engaged face to face

In war against a deadly enemy. Then the common people conquered

With their own blood, whenever they had promised to endure dangers.

So, when a tigress heavy with young circles Mount Niphates

In Caspian lands, or prepares her cubs for snatching prey,

She burns against those who are absent and commits mortal limbs

To savage spirits, seeking human death with bloodstained jaws.

One marveled at his old age in youthful years;

Another boasted of ancestors from an ancient stock.

The mind of one was scarcely content with blood:

It recalls a thousand honorable genealogies of a man’s virtues.

How many titles then stood enclosed within him!

Whenever they are conquered, the glory of character

Gives birth through long ages to a distinguished triumph for the defeated.

One raises to heaven in praise the chastity

That blooms more beautifully in a beautiful body,

And the figure smiling with pure light. That face

Certainly brought him distinction, though it had often been

The cause of danger to many. It is sufficiently beautiful to have remained chaste.

Such things are granted only from the summit of Olympus.

Thus, whenever the advantages of beauty come to holy minds,

Or increase in them, people then compete to conquer one another in war,

And the earth pours forth honor or gifts from the soul’s right hand;

One lives for oneself while perishing for another.

When the people recounted these things with many mouths,

There was one fixed judgment among all the crowds:

The assembly of priests and the court revered through the ages

Chose him, desired him, judged him worthy, received him, and loved him.

Behold another matter, new in speech and wondrous to all—

I have passed over what everyone fears and the whole world admires.

He was scarcely of his first age, when trembling feet

Trod the thresholds of light, when he was snatched from his mother’s breast

And a sweeter fluid was withdrawn from his tender mouth:

When the crafty mother, perhaps, poured the deceptive taste

Of herbs into his complaining little lips,

So that the child might not recognize his mother by taste.

Thus, milk being denied, he swallowed the substituted poison

Through an unaccustomed throat, in a laughable deception.

That was his age when the sign occurred.

For they say that his cradle shone with great light,

When such splendor gleamed in him

As the sky could then perform in obedience,

When, commanded to serve the man, the swift fire of Olympus

Raised its mortal limbs and walked in rapid descent,

Imitating the swift course of hoofed horses.

So the favorable flame then wandered around the boy,

Illuminated, venerated, looked up to, and surrounded him.

Then his fearful father spoke with lowered gaze:

“Supreme God, guardian of the holy summit of heaven,

Who make favorable omens that you behold with favorable light:

This child, from his earliest years, while he still crawls,

I dedicate to you, holy Father, before earthly ages

Bind him in their slippery nets of sin.

May they not do so; may he be, supreme God, a rich offering to you.”

He said this and shed the tears that joy brings forth.

Then he gladly sought Crispinus, whom no worthy eloquence

Can describe—even if one should now rise from Avernus—

Who could lead the forests from the rigid rocks of the Apennines

To the plectrum, while the rivers stood still.

He was more truly Elias; for who would leave Elisha

Upon earth, with the palm of a doubled gift?

He whom Paul nourished with pious milk,

Pressed from the breast, and whose right hand is full of evangelical breasts.

Hail, holy father; hail forever, ashes of Crispinus,

To whose authority returns whatever worthy thing

We admire in the wondrous doctrine of Christ.

You, as heir, possess well the wealth transmitted to you.

A considerable matter is shown by talents joined threefold.

It shows what Gaul, from the western parts of the world,

Sent as a suppliant captive crowd.

Savage hearts learned to bend when they saw you;

Armed with prayers, you overcame the king, great man.

Thus the tongue’s blow blunts fighting swords;

Thus a strong blade of words conquers iron.

For if reports speak truly, those who join the greatest things to small ones,

So does a steward await his lord after the fields have been subdued,

When, well softened by the curved tooth of the hoe,

He inscribes the fields and combs the face of the soil with plows,

So that the running vintage may foam at its full lips.

He inserts foreign plants into a strange plot;

The immigrant tree is joined by interwoven bonds;

The stocks are cut, and the shoot, harvested by the sickle, is grafted;

The wood is bitten by a tender opening;

A nobility not its own rises in a small shoot;

The branch grows rich through an unknown gift,

While the plantings, moistened beneath fresh bark, grow together.

Likewise he paints the backs of the Paestan roses;

The royal field is clothed in rustic purple.

[Note: *Lilies instead of the light of shining plaster.* Painters apply some color first to boards prepared for painting; they call this the “ground.” In rustic paintings applied to walls, the lime itself and the plaster serve as the ground. Thus, in the garden he imagines, Ennodius makes lilies serve in place of plaster and the ground of the painting, while the other flowers of different kinds and colors serve as the pigments.]

Lilies are spread in place of gleaming whitewash.

Then he paints violets, cytisus, colocasia, and marigolds,

Cinnamon, thyme, narcissus, balsam, and costus.

Then he plants again what the phoenix bears as its offspring.

The arriving lord orders this servant to recline;

He rises and himself serves the dishes at the table with his own hands.

Thus, cultivator of souls, in your thirty years

Your fields breathe roses; the soil, interrupted by no frosts,

Does not wither, but your teacher preserves it

In the fragrant turf of merits through perpetual spring.

Whenever your arbute trees dry up because dew has been withheld,

You pour in tears; you also heap up there a basket

Of unclean dung. Then it rises in splendid branches;

Then it surpasses the fruitful laws of birth given by God.

Receive now, right hand, our golden light of life,

The joys that make you bring forth a modest song.

When God has brought my prayers to fulfillment in their appointed order,

And the pliant vine planted by your right hand has shone,

After a hundred years I shall more powerfully repay what I owe you.

Behold, I have set down whatever song I now establish for you,

Under the strict law of the knot, Father—a law that joined

Diverse rhythms beneath a tightly woven form,

So that no deceptive syllable might alter it anywhere. I have spoken.

## X. Evening Hymn

[Note: *Evening hymn.* This is Prudentius’s hymn “at the lighting of the lamp.” Thus it is titled in the best manuscripts, hymn 6 of the *Cathemerinon*, which has the same subject—not, as it is commonly published, “At the lighting of the Paschal candle.” Hence they also called the office of evening prayers the *Lucernarium*, because it was performed in the evening and whenever it was customary to light lamps, namely at sunset. Saint Ambrose calls it the “hour of the lighting” in Book III *On Virgins*: “Certainly solemn prayers with thanksgiving are to be offered when we rise from sleep, when we go out, when we take food, when we have eaten, and at the hour of the lighting; finally, when we go to bed.”

As for the hymns that follow, although their style and character sufficiently reveal Ennodius as the author, they were absent from the manuscripts on which we relied. Since their restoration therefore remained conjectural, we have changed only a few things, and those clear and obvious.]

### Evening Hymn

The earth, covered now with a black cloak,

Receives the night,

So that living bodies may recover

Through sweet death.

The gentler image of death

Brings sleep’s tomb near,

While the mind grows warm in idleness,

Breathing hard beneath the heat of light.

Light, Christ, life, truth,

May the dark hours of sleep,

Prepared with gloomy shadows,

Not summon us to darkness.

May no night subject us to itself

Under the covering of black night,

Nor may heat, drunk with itself,

paint deceptive forms upon our bodies,

bringing a false charge of sin

to those ignorant of real guilt.

Through the gifts of rest,

Stand by as our ever-watchful guardian.

May the crafty enemy be far away:

May what harms us sleep.

May he who strives to gnaw with savage tooth

Those lying in their beds—

Bound in his limbs, may he grieve

To strike those whom you protect.

May the spirit, in flesh made wet,

Not perish, shipwrecked.

May chastity adorn the bed,

She who shines first among virtues;

May faith live in the breast,

Which blooms in perpetual light.

## XI. Second Hymn, for a Time of Sorrow

God, everlasting joy,

Christ, peace of the anxious heart,

And harbor of those who drift—

Whom not even a storm, if it sweeps

The depths with turbulent waves,

Can drive from the heart.

You who raise up those sunk in the sea,

You who raise up those weighed down by burdens,

You who are the guide of the shipwrecked prophet,

While he lives as the beast’s food,

While the sea does not know what it holds,

Tear the collector of tribute,

Safe food, from the savage throat.

Brought back by a dreadful oarsman,

Safe with the worst guardian,

The prophet, who had declared you God,

Then carried out your commands with greater strength.

He had lived sober amid unclean waters,

Through tombs upon the earth;

Living, he endured sepulchers;

Let the meal of the living be adorned.

He revealed the secrets of the whale,

A venerable witness of the innermost depths.

Thus we pray, God the King:

Snatch us, broken by sorrow, as food

From the belly of cares.

What kills lives in the marrow;

The depths of the entrails are disturbed;

In the fountain of flesh there is a heat

That overwhelms, burns, and afflicts.

But if you look upon us serenely,

Pressure will give birth to joy.

## XII. Third Hymn, on Saint Cyprian

The heart, tongue, understanding, and dignity

Of the prophet and martyr Cyprian

Proclaim themselves by enduring death.

Death gave a vital blow;

Light gleams, won by the sword.

He was radiant in speech

And rich in a single mouth,

Conquering with his eloquent speech

The torrent’s surging wave

And the arrows hurled from the horn.

The wealth of his venerable breast

He rightly returned to Christ.

Now he fulfills his former office:

The advocate pleads, prevails,

And moderates harshness in legal causes.

He makes the guilty blessed,

Breaking sins through song.

Neither flame, prison, nor chains

Can harm those whom he benefits.

Ordered to sacrifice victims,

He laughed at the gods who must be mourned.

[Col. 0328B] When danger soon pressed upon him,

He fled danger through death.

He shortened the delays

By the device of speaking,

He summoned the swords more gladly,

As death rushed on all the faster.

The proconsul [Note: [Col. 0327D] Proconsul Maximus] Galerius Maximus, who had succeeded Aspasius Paternus in the proconsulship of Africa. When Cyprian heard the sentence by which he was condemned to death, he replied only this: “Thanks be to God.” Moreover, as the deacon Pontius writes, with his eyes bound by his own hands, he tried to hasten the executioner’s delay. Ennodius refers to this when he says that Cyprian summoned the swords and caused the least possible delay by speaking.] Maximus could not be more savage,

While what he threatens is a gift;

Nor does gentler anger delay

Those who desire to see Christ.

XIII. HYMN IV. ON PENTECOST.

This too is a gift from above:

That tongue wages war with tongue.

[Col. 0328C] Who would not proclaim the rewards of the Thunderer

Through the gifts of that same One?

He who understands makes things happen by speaking;

Let him speak what is worthy of God.

Behold, the Spirit pours in

And once again equips their mouths.

He enters [Note: [Col. 0328D] “With clouded torpor.” Veternus is an adjective, used for veternosus (“torpor-ridden”) and vetustus (“ancient”): thus, in the panegyric, “consciences possessed by the torpor of error,” and in the poem To the Stepmother, “by the laws of ancient Erebus.”] breasts

Hollowed out by clouded torpor.

On this day among the apostles,

While the Word divides words,

He, all-powerful in the speech of the world,

Also gathered together the hearts of the world.

Let the Man be borne on the praises of the Most High:

He possesses the mouths of the nations.

Thracian, Gaul, and Indian are one.

[Col. 0328D] What wins by charm in Greece,

What fierce barbarian savagery does,

What the shrillness of Canopus roars,

What the Parthian tongue barks,

He has filled the breast of his guests.

The world runs toward salvation

By so many roads, though the world resists.

For sacred remission now,

In the likeness of Easter grace,

[Col. 0329A] Adorns the mystical crown

With a sevenfold gift.

The resources of abundance

Minister to the wealthy One.

Now sing with mind and voice:

Let this be our voice and mind before God.

XIV. HYMN V. ON SAINT STEPHEN.

What crown could you call more powerful than Stephen?

He is a martyr.

This is the man; this is the reward.

The fruit of labor is his name.

Let this brief praise be extensive;

Thus the illustrious are summoned forth.

Minister of death, behold,

[Col. 0329B] Bringing life forth from death.

What kills gives salvation.

Blessed beneath these blows,

He becomes everlasting through his death.

With blood he prepares the light;

He makes heaven a gift of the tomb,

So that triumph may drive away the enemy;

Like a palm, so he enters the contest.

He was the first to enter the way

Untrodden by any footsteps.

He surveyed the mysteries of heaven,

Hidden in the garment of flesh,

And cried, “Behold, the Son

Stands at the right hand of the Father.”

While the impious hurled stones,

[Col. 0329C] While a thousand engines of death were at work,

He alone conscious of goodness

Prayed, speaking in faith,

That heavenly wrath might not destroy

The guilty who did not know what they were doing.

He was innocent of madness;

Frenzy had brought the guilty man forward;

The struggle ran on through prayers:

The executioner groaned at the cross,

By which, as it grew, he had been subdued.

XV. HYMN VI. ON SAINT AMBROSE.

They proclaim Ambrose to heaven—

His name, his honor, and his conduct.

He owes nothing to eloquence;

All his endowment comes from his character.

The strong man, fortified by his own shield,

Does not desire one who helps him.

In the flesh, the flesh accomplishes nothing;

The queenly mind rules within the body.

He shattered every slippery temptation;

Thus he lived, not for himself,

But wholly for God his creator.

[Col. 0330A] Added here to the apostles,

He restored the faith that had been driven out.

He uttered the triumphs of the martyrs

With the laurels of a flourishing tongue.

With his mouth he snatched the prey

From the jaws of the savage serpent.

He who wages Christ’s wars,

Though unarmed, is feared by swords.

He lives buried and gives help,

Holding the helm of the Church.

Justina [Note: [Col. 0329D] “Justina lost her strength.”] the mother of Valentinian the younger Augustus, who, being an Arian, grievously persecuted Ambrose and the Church of Milan. Thus Gaudentius speaks of her in the preface to his work To Benivolus, formerly master of the records: “For she is the Jezebel of our age, the patroness and accomplice of Arian treachery; while persecuting the most blessed Ambrose, bishop of the Church of Milan, she also compelled you, who were at that time master of the records, believing that you had forgotten the saving faith, to compose writings against the Catholic Churches.”] lost her strength;

The punishment she inflicted on the prophet became his reward.

Remember the light of your seat;

Adorn future generations, holy one.

Supported by a noble patron,

[Col. 0330B] Let the leader of the serene height,

Though hidden in a cloud, not be afraid.

He who [Note: [Col. 0330D] “He is the shepherd of bishops.” This is the bishop of Milan, who by metropolitan right presides even today over many bishops, but formerly over many more. He therefore prays for Laurence, bishop of Milan.] is shepherd of bishops

Removes everything that is false.

He governs the flock of princes;

He is the teacher of teachers.

XVI. HYMN VII. ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD.

Now Christ has ascended the heavens.

He first slew death;

Buried, he drove death away;

Death collapsed at the assault of death.

Sing, ages, of what has happened:

The burial subdued Tartarus;

The slain One conquered the end.

[Col. 0330C] Pale death mourns from that moment

From which it had presumed to rejoice.

The devourer has been captured by food.

The robber of all has become prey.

Now the bound net is being dragged;

The chain lies fastened in its links.

The serpent brought forth its poisons;

The gentle One crushes its pride;

The Lamb disembowels the lion.

This is the greater display of power:

That you, Christ, take upon yourself our nature,

And, hidden in the garment of a servant,

Raise us up to triumph—

More than if, from your flashing throne,

You terrified the guilty with radiance.

[Col. 0330D] God is manifest through all things,

Removed from concealment by no veil;

But, so that he might raise the fallen,

He deigned to become what we are

And himself redeemed what was his by right.

He brought back the lost sheep

To the shepherd’s keeping.

Lift up the gates, angels:

[Col. 0331A] The dread judge enters,

Greater than the trophies of his enemies.

XVII. HYMN VIII. ON SAINT EUPHEMIA.

What tongue could, what style could express

The triumphs of so great a virgin?

Now learn strength of mind, you soft men;

Take her example, you sluggish ones:

A brave girl surpasses men.

Virtue is always ignorant of weakness,

And she knows no laws of sex;

Her mind was unbroken,

For once she had conceived Christ in her heart.

They release their breasts from perishable bonds,

Those in whose minds God has been hidden.

She endured powerful torments in her body;

[Col. 0331B] As pain weakened, love of the cross increased.

If you could learn to conquer a martyr,

Mad torturer, you would learn to spare.

Flames, scourges, executioners, wheels—

She for whom the cross must be followed fears none of them greatly.

When Priscus [Note: [Col. 0331D] Priscus] the proconsul of Asia, under whose authority Saint Euphemia the martyr was tortured at Chalcedon with the most savage punishments.]—more harmful than a source of poison—

Is said to have ordered her hurled headlong

Into furnaces crackling with fire,

(For thus, in a corrupt age,

They called the cruel judge of the holy virgin)—

While his attendants were eager

To consign the martyr to the furnace’s fuel,

A light more serene than the light of Olympus

Removed the work of those who desired evil,

While they at once pointed out the sword with a cry.

[Col. 0331C] “Send us hence to Tartarus, we pray;

For our hand does not violate the holy woman.”

His hot liver swells with gall;

Soon there are stones, pits, blows, and beasts.

A greater poison prepares its blandishments,

Against which the heroine bravely stood firm.

XVIII. HYMN IX. [Note: [Col. 0331D] On Saint Nazarius.] On the Milanese martyr, concerning whom there survives a sermon of Saint Ambrose containing many details very similar to those written in this hymn. But the fact that Saint Nazarius is said to have suffered under Nero was discovered after Ambrose’s death, since the priest Paulinus testifies in the Life of Saint Ambrose that it was still unknown in Ambrose’s time.] ON SAINT NAZARIUS.

The narrow periods of life,

Compressed within small limits,

Holy death grants room to grow;

It prepares boundaries that are eternal.

From the harvest of misfortunes he comes,

Through which the human race may rise.

In the good stock of Nazarius

[Col. 0332A] He added light from death.

Fortunate under the emperor Nero,

Having endured diverse evils,

He surveyed the world, chilled

By no oppressive fear in his heart.

But so that he might show the profane

By what path they could climb to heaven,

As a true teacher by his deeds

He gave examples, not words.

For that leader is strong

Who teaches war by his strength.

Whom do words draw into military service

If the commander himself abstains from action?

The windy exhortation of the tongue

Does not possess what conduct provides.

[Col. 0332B] But after he had scattered great seeds,

With the mattock writing upon the earth,

And poured them into the richest clods,

He soon sought Milan,

In which, by a noble triumph,

He repelled the ruin of the flesh.

He, lying slain by an undeserved death,

Soon, terrible in appearance, admonished the prophet [Note: [Col. 0331D] “He admonishes the prophet.”] Ambrose, the bishop who, as the same Paulinus relates, transferred the relics of Saint Nazarius, discovered in a garden, to the Basilica of the Apostles. Concerning this matter the verses of Ambrose himself are read in the Christian Monuments, to which he added the following inscription:

“Ambrose founded a temple and consecrated it to the Lord,

With an apostolic name, gift, and relics.

The temple is shaped as a cross, a temple of Christ’s victory.

The sacred triumphant image marks the place.

At the head of the temple is Nazarius of blessed life,

And the lofty floor rests upon the martyr’s remains.

Where the cross raised the sacred head beneath its curved vault,

That head is the temple and the house of Nazarius.

The victorious man who cherishes eternal rest through piety—

The cross was his palm, and the cross is also his embrace.”

There are also other verses indicating that the part of the basilica where the relics of Nazarius were buried had been decorated, by Serena, the wife of Stilicho, with Libyan marble, in fulfillment of a vow:

“Where the roofs rise in a hollow curve and return upward,

And the head of the consecrated cross bends in its arc,

Nazarius of spotless life, with limbs undefiled,

Is buried, rejoicing that this is the place of his tomb.

The pious Ambrose marked it with the image of Christ;

Faithful Serena polished it with Libyan marble,

So that she might happily enjoy the return of her husband Stilicho,

And of her brothers and her own children.”]

To add clear gifts once again,

Restored to the world.

XIX. HYMN X. ON SAINT MARY.

When I speak of the Virgin who bore a child,

What is worthy of praise in Mary?

Let the birth give, adorn, and demand

[Col. 0332C] What the closed door and the open door require;

Let she herself supply it.

Let the words be like a miracle.

Why should you seek an order, O mind?

Nature has lost everything.

This is salvation: that we are defeated.

When the virgin alone lived,

She conceived a son through her ear.

While the body marveled at the deed,

Her womb swelled with the Spirit.

What the tongue uttered was the seed;

The Word is enclosed in flesh.

From the mother he is wholly ours;

From the Father, God differing in nothing.

The offspring is whole in both—

She who gives birth and he who commands.

He is not greater than the servants,

Nor is he made less than the Creator.

The closed fountain receives the utterance;

The closed fountain brings forth limbs.

No narrower fissure yielded,

And the true offspring shines forth.

Tell me, mother and virgin, I pray:

Does anyone close a passage while emerging?

The inward parts are constricted by the child;

The child is the bond of chastity.

XX. HYMN XI. ON SAINT MARTIN.

When I speak of Martin’s deeds,

I pass over nothing worthy of praise.

[Col. 0333B] Virtue, divided among all,

Gathered together has made one man pre-eminent.

Through great labor he is a martyr,

His spirit victorious over the flesh.

This is close to triumph,

If inward battles are trampled down.

Though the body loses strength,

His fixed resolve remains crowned with laurels.

He raises up the enemy of the mind,

Who made the limbs his vows.

Here, knowing nothing of the fire of the spring,

He burned with the warmth of God.

He was joined to the waters by vapor,

Consecrated to Christ in his deeds.

With the garment in which he had covered a naked man,

[Col. 0333C] The king of heaven shone;

Through the filthy cloth he acquired

That with which the sphere of stars gleams.

What a just exchange!

The needy man repaid with a star;

The beggar prepared kingdoms.

Soon he touched the sacred life;

From the people he mocked the demons

And ordered the ashes to rise.

The dead came to life at his touch;

[Col. 0334A] He willingly endured the scourges

With which he wove his crown.

Compelled to become a bishop,

He assumed an office he had resisted,

Which holy faith fulfilled.

XXI. HYMN XII. [Note: [Col. 0333C] On Saint Dionysius.] The bishop of Milan, a most holy man, who was sent into exile by Constantius Augustus for the orthodox faith and there ended his life, as Saint Ambrose teaches in Letter 25 to the Vercellenses. [lacuna]] ON SAINT DIONYSIUS.

Christ gave Dionysius

As many victories as battles.

An exile is a citizen of the faithful;

He shares in the heavenly city.

Constantius, once a tyrant,

Drove the prophet from his place.

He did not yield to the storm;

Through dangers his faith grew.

Call this holy profession:

Punishment hands you over to prosperity;

Through evil you purchase what you desire.

Persist, torturer, assisting him:

This light is surrendered by denial.

O how blessed is adversity,

If exiles triumph in this way!

The confessor did not cease,

Fearless before the martyr.

Those whom scattered death afflicts

Fly toward the fulfillment of death.

Slow cooking destroys nothing;

It enters secretly into hidden places.

The funeral that gives life is sorrow;

The passage is swift healing.

[Col. 0334C] He laughed at the prince’s fury,

Running on while faith remained;

Fixed, he is led throughout the world,

Where the sun flashes more fiercely.

Denying us the opportunity to drink,

We take from you, O dread one,

As though it were ours, what you repay.

Send us the holy man, we ask,

So that you yourself may grant him to us.

BOOK TWO. EPIGRAMS.

I. EPITAPH OF A GOOD MAN.

[Col. 0333D]

Good in mind, shining in integrity, and [Note: [Col. 0333D] “Author of his name.” Φερώνυμος: “bearing a name truly,” a genuinely good man who corresponds to his name. He frequently uses such allusions, as in Epigram 11 on Honoratus and in Poem 3 on Maximus. Athalaric, in Book VIII, Letter 18 of the Variae, writes to the quaestor Felix: “You have taken your name from your character; preserve it so that you may always rejoice in the truth of your name. For since every name seems to have been imposed to declare the things themselves, it is exceedingly absurd to bear another’s name and to be called something that cannot be found in one’s character.”] the author of his name,

Is this how, tell me, grief lies in a narrow tomb?

The hope of an immense household is covered by a small tomb,

And lofty roofs are confined beneath little turf.

What is the honor in childhood? What do the thresholds of life provide?

[Col. 0334D] Death comes before the expected stages.

What does it profit him that he surpassed old age

In tender years and joined many funerals to his own?

Alas, the young man has died, he who concealed the sins of life

During the season when God gives life to the guilty.

Look: you perhaps fear the earliest years;

Age did not restrain the boy who surpassed it.

[Col. 0335A] Leaving an example to the earth, snatched up to the stars,

How well he shows the confessed the straight path!

He passed beyond twice ten winters and as many harvests,

Whom hostile fortune suddenly removed from our eyes.

II. EPITAPH OF HABUNDANTIUS, VIR ILLUSTRIS.

He never perishes through death, surviving in merit after the tomb;

Funerals do not contain his exalted soul.

Blood, honor, birth, integrity, steadfastness, and wealth

Destroy death through their many endowments.

The good man in the commonwealth does not feel the losses of the grave:

The Fates gather up the threads they had given to wretched men.

The hanging threads that bear the common people grow weary;

The strong threads fall to the lot of the noble.

The hoary ages renewed his venerable customs;

[Col. 0335B] And in turn he bore a pure heart as a temple.

III. ON THE EPIGRAMS MADE FOR THE BOOKCASES OF THE LORD FAUSTUS.

You fashioned harmonious poems for diverse books;

Let the lettering gladly receive what it bestows.

I do not know who could fail to praise such modesty, Faustus,

When you return whatever your reading has given you.

A mind always ignorant of righteousness loses what has been entrusted;

These lessons return people to honorable character.

Yet if you admit my words as right, I shall confess:

He who prevails by great things rightly drives away the little.

Let the prophets whom you depict in polished verse be praised;

Let the masculine tongue resound in rhetorical ornament. [Note: [Col. 0335D] “In rhetorical ornament.” Schema, σχῆμα, means a figure, adornment, or bearing. To speak “in rhetorical schemata” therefore means to adorn speech and to speak with the pomp customary to rhetors. “Oratorical schema” and “the schema and pomp of speech” occur in Book I, Letters 15 and 16. Thus “the schemata of the world” means the ornaments of the age in Book IX, Letter 9, and “the schema of human perfection” occurs in Poem 4. In this passage, however, the copyists had wrongly written stemmate (“by lineage”) for schemate, as they had also done in the hymn on Cyprian and Epigram 87.] 

As Paul taught Christ, both man and God,

May he rejoice in an eloquence that surpasses all.

Let Attic doctrines enrich Greek minds,

[Col. 0335C] And learned Greece marvel at our glory.

Let moral philosophy be told in concise language, natural philosophy in precise terms;

Let history, displaying events, point them out.

Let comic works be counted by the file, heroic works by applause;

Brilliant words suit your work.

No other person can do these things; but to speak of Faustus in sum

Will always be a game, if I speak what is well known.

IV. ON THE WAGON GIVEN BY THE BISHOP.

The supreme bishop bestows a noble gift upon you, Plaustrus.

He opens a path for great things and makes favorable omens.

V. [Note: [Col. 0335D] “Epitaph of Rustica.” This epitaph still survives at Milan, carved on a stone now inserted into the church of Saint Francis.] EPITAPH OF RUSTICA.

Rustica, pale fortune did not carry you away

From everlasting life, nor did death give you destruction.

[Col. 0335D] Purified, you walk through the heavenly realms without flesh;

Thus funerals ennoble the life of the chaste.

[Col. 0336A] What wonder that, widowed, your life stood sufficiently firm,

When love of your husband was rightly directed toward your child.

VI. EPITAPH OF MELISSA.

Whoever dies after overcoming the body survives:

[Note: [Col. 0336D] “Donat” seems to accord with the rules of metre. EDITOR.] Only sins impose the law of death upon man.

Nothing is lost to you, virgin: your pure mind has restored the flesh,

Which never lived in the service of the world.

Let funerals, tombs, and pyres—the wages of crimes—cease:

This passage from life to life is pleasing.

VII. THE BRONZE SERPENT ON THE CROSS.

Slayer of death, leader of life, plant of salvation,

Behold, now [Note: [Col. 0335D] “The serpent drives away poisons.” Prudentius, in the Enchiridion.] the prudent serpent, polished in bronze.

The Leader hung on the cross the serpent that restrains its poison. [Col. 0336D] With equal elegance and antithesis, Severian, bishop of Gabala, says that salvation, and “from the accursed one, blessing” (καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐπικαταράτου εὐλογίαν), flowed from that serpent, since it was a symbol of Christ’s cross, in Oration 2 of the ten published under Chrysostom’s name by Cardinal Sirietus. But Damascenus and Pope Hadrian, together with the Council of Paris, attribute to Severian this work, as I have said.] Behold, the serpent drives away poisons.

And what had already been, for the wretched,

The appearance of punishment and image of death,

[Col. 0336B] Is now certain salvation for me.

VIII. VERSES MADE AND WRITTEN IN THE BASILICA OF SAINT SIXTUS THE BISHOP, WHICH [Note: [Col. 0336D] “Laurence the bishop.”] Laurence, bishop of Milan, built.

The bishop, endowed with character, integrity, and modesty,

Adorned his gift with merits, and, joining the lights of life

To the value of the work, established these temples.

Fame does not scatter into uncertain retreats what has passed away;

Rather, the law of an ancient deed lives on, enlarged through the ages—

May kindly Sixtus receive this ancient deed as a gift from you, Laurence.

Thus the service remains which once came to the holy.

This man offered the temple; the one who comes consecrates it.

IX. ALSO IN THE BASILICA OF THE SAINTS, BECAUSE THE BUILDINGS THAT HAD PREVIOUSLY STOOD THERE HAD BURNED, AND THIS WAS MADE.

[Col. 0336C] The worthless roofs first yielded to blessed flames.

Thus splendor comes through loss; thus the summits, through flames,

Rise up to house God. If what is lost grows through fire,

If losses give adornment,

What will the restorer be like, enlarged by crackling ruins?

Laurence, waging your battles, conquer the fires.

The filthy earth would have lain hidden in a decaying retreat

If the ancient caves had retained their former appearance.

But after the powers above sent favorable flames,

The ashes drew these things toward a light worthy of worship.

Turn your pious eyes here, Father, who declare

That all things are to be cleansed by fire,

And instruct minds ignorant of what is right,

So that they may not falter through words.

X. [Note: [Col. 0336D] “In the house of Milan.” The house of the church, or the episcopal basilica, which Laurence himself had adorned with various objects.] IN THE HOUSE OF MILAN.

[Col. 0336D] To buildings, character has granted two things for all ages:

That they should shine with inlaid work, or with the merit of their master.

[Col. 0337A] Green rocks, [Note: [Col. 0337D] “Green rocks.” Lacedaemonian marble, green in color. Prudentius: “Which green Lacedaemon possesses.” Sidonius, in the Burgus:

“Marbles that bloom with grassy veins.”] imitating a grassy pasture,

Entice the eyes by a nobler deception.

Yet let art drive the work forward and nature govern its forms,

While it shapes the innards of the stones into images.

Let the teacher flood their whiteness from his rosy mouth;

Let him depict fitting limbs with scattered letters.

Gold, summit, ivory, panels, coffers, gems—

Human riches are not permitted to shine more brightly.

Chance plays, cautiously and without law, with what is valued.

Believe that it will be labor to remain constant in character.

XI. [Note: [Col. 0337D] “In the Basilica of the Apostles.” In all the books the title was “Verses in the same place,” which is false. We have therefore made another title from Poem 2, which has the same subject. Again, in the Vatican manuscript the first verse has only five feet, for the word antiquum is absent; in its place Fabri’s book has at the end lavacrum, in this form: “Behold the temple shines, which before the bath was filthy”; in the third copy, “before the ancient [building].”] IN THE BASILICA OF THE APOSTLES AT NOVARIA.

Behold, the ancient temple shines, which was previously filthy,

And new light has arranged its ancient face.

Who through religion destroyed the ancient sanctuary,

With the gods expelled, rightly possesses the true God.

[Col. 0337B] Gods to whom this place was open, leave the seats you occupied.

What Victor made, the victor everywhere possesses.

His successor added to its adornment through merit and deeds—

You who hence bear the name Honoratus.

To one who carries a clouded heart of viperine poison

It is not granted to make beautiful summits for God.

XII. ALSO IN THE HOUSE OF MILAN.

Behold from whose streams the narrow house has drunk,

And how it surpasses its halls with modest porticoes.

Constructed through the zeal of the supreme bishop, it gleams;

This place possesses its own day through Laurence.

Splendid buildings rise through wealth,

And what comes from the Lord knows no decline.

Rot, accompanied by age, will scarcely ever wear away

[Col. 0337C] The glory of its maker, who founded it well.

A story that will never be silent about great men preserves

What, overcoming time, carries the name to the stars.

XIII.

He was always the guardian of stern honor,

Terrible to the guilty and merciful to those who begged.

Vice never bent him; he was ever compassionate;

With a steadfast countenance, he rendered judgment everywhere.

He rebuked crimes by his expression and revived the contrite;

Your face, conscious of its secret, revealed you.

His mother poured him from her womb into the heavenly court,

Withdrawing him from her breasts and handing him over to the breasts.

Hoary ages marveled at the venerable prophet:

In his character he was already what he bears in office.

XIV.

He happily left the dwelling he had possessed for a long time,

[Col. 0337D] And the house, thus widowed for the Lord, grew.

[Col. 0338A] Having taken up the administration of the palace, he was carried away

And obtained what is sought at the price of the mind.

Now the place retains what it absorbed in a nourishing draught,

Guarding the prosperous deeds it once received.

At once, whoever succeeded as inhabitant and heir

Brought a fortunate foot into the place upon entering.

Learn what a partner contributes to a holy life,

If dedicated buildings return men purified.

XV.

Grant, almighty Father, we pray, through long ages,

Hope and assured forgiveness to your devout servants.

May the white threads of our merits not be darkened,

Nor may the palm prepared for my harvest be halted.

May he rise who, nourished in his mother’s womb,

Comes to the taste of life through your gifts.

You suffuse my heart even with a slight flavor;

[Col. 0338B] You make my tongue a witness of blood.

High trees grow leafy in shadowy luxury,

Which no farmer has touched with his sickles.

XVI.

Eloquence has stood as a sure index of nature,

For one who thirsts to seek the source of perfection.

Freedom is always opened up by honorable pursuits;

Nobility, not manufactured, lies hidden in pursuits.

The earth would have kept captive the metal in its veins,

Had its discoverer not brought forth what he calls into the open.

The pale investigator revealed the shining gold;

He who polishes it thus makes ingenuity his own.

Thus far, while surveying the Ionian sea with a small oar,

Turn my little boat toward harbor, Thalia.

XVII. ABOVE [Note: [Col. 0337D] “Above the royal door of the dining hall.” The largest central door, βασιλική; therefore he interprets postes and valvae. Thus they called the doors and royal entrances in basilicas. Gregory of Tours, Book IV, chapter 13: “While they were walking through the church, they approached the royal doors of the sacred building, which had then been opened.” Anastasius the Librarian, in his Life of Honorius: “He adorned with silver the royal doors at the entrance of the greater church, which are called central.” Likewise, in the Life of Conon: “Those who had been sent from the army to guard the closed royal doors of the basilica kept watch.” The Greeks call them βασιλικαί.] THE ROYAL DOOR OF THE DINING HALL IN THE HOUSE.

[Col. 0338C]

The sailor hangs gifts upon the doors of the bridge,

Carrying upon his own entrances what he has gained from the river.

The hunter places throwing weapons at the doors;

The vestibule is adorned with a soldier’s helmet.

Art, virtue, name, and origin are learned from the doors.

We are believed to be of God by the sign upon our forehead.

So, guide of the upright, open our devotion,

So that the character of the house may not conceal its Lord.

You who, satisfied, carry Latin dew in your breast,

Behold here the serpent waters of Helicon.

XVIII. ON A [Note: [Col. 0338D] “On a missorium.” On a platter or disk, as in Epigram 92. Isidore counts the missorium among serving vessels in Book XX of the Etymologies and thinks it named from a table, as though mensarium; I prefer to derive it from missus, “a serving,” as gustatorium comes from gustatio, “a tasting.” Isidore’s Glosses have “missorial platters.” Another old Glossary has “a missorial disk.” The Greeks use μισσώριον. Just as this missorium has a mounted warrior with Victory, and another below has an image of Ennodius himself, so Book IV of the Anthology describes a double μινσώριον: one “on which are the twelve signs of the zodiac,” another “having Aphrodite and the Cupids.” Idatius calls it an orbiculus when he writes of a golden missorium weighing five hundred pounds, which the patrician Aetius gave to Thorismund, king of the Goths, for his service against Attila. Since it had been plundered by the Goths, an old author of the Life of Dagobert, chapter 29, reports that two hundred thousand solidi were paid for it by Sisenand when it was sent to King Dagobert. Gregory of Tours, Book VII, chapter 5, also mentions another golden missorium belonging to King Chilperic. Aimoinus discusses both in Books III and IV. Flodoard the priest mentions two others, but silver ones, in the testament of Saint Remigius and Sonnatius, bishops of Rheims.] MISSORIUM, WHICH HAS AN ARMORED YOUNG MAN ON A HORSE, HOLDING VICTORY IN HIS HAND.

[Col. 0338D] Behold, his right hand holds the winged goddess of victory;

She has come, and on the return journey she has no weapons.

[Col. 0339A] Carrying a warlike burden, the horse threatens across its back;

The stranger, for whom terror smiles, rejoices in his skill.

Let the famous offspring in the Hyperborean fields learn

The genius of nature when he sees the images.

XIX. ON THE MARBLE LION THAT SENDS WATER IN THE HOUSE.

Behold the lion, its savagery laid aside, displaying gentleness:

From its mouth it pours water at the bidding of its breast.

Water flows from its muzzle; its tooth chews the cups of death;

The beast, losing its nature, refreshes us.

While savage throats pour forth glass-clear springs,

Cruel hearts are washed by life-giving waters.

XX. IN THE BAPTISTERY AT AGELLUM, WHERE MARTYRS ARE PAINTED WHOSE RELICS ARE BURIED THERE.

[Col. 0339B] The founder [Note: [Col. 0339C] “The founder Armenius.” To whom Letter 1 of Book II is addressed.] Armenius, who is worthy of heavenly honor,

Here produced a fountain of life-giving water.

Let us bear inward parts full of health-giving waters,

So that the one who drinks may not thirst after drinking once.

The painter gave life to bodies snatched from the tombs:

Seeing the living dead, let death depart to its tombs.

Yet this place embraces their limbs,

Whom the wall holds in its image and the devout mind holds in faithful belief.

XXI. ON SEVEN LITTLE DISHES HAVING BEASTS OR DIANA.

Diana, a stag, boar, tiger, lion, heifer, and leopard

Bring dishes to your tables, skillfully.

XXII. ON A COMPOSTILE HAVING SEVEN GAVATAE.

It keeps adjoining borders for diverse dishes,

While it encloses many courses by various pathways.

[Col. 0340A] What a joined row divides by fixed boundaries—

How well one belly is contained in silver!

XXIII. ON THE MAN WHO, TO RECONCILE A SON WITH HIS MOTHER, COMMITTED A THEFT.

[Note: [Col. 0340D] “Concerning the one who, as a son...” The six epigrams that follow are now being published for the first time.]

Who, I ask, has ever restrained crime through wrongdoing?

I embrace holy frauds that give rise to good,

While, through skillful increase, they break apart savage quarrels.

He who restores a son to his mother’s love through guilt—

It is clear that he will sow seeds of peace amid hatred.

In an inverted order, deceitful concord is a battle,

When the appearance of war falsely grants repose.

XXIV. ON THE MAN WHO WAS SAID TO BE THE SON OF A PROSTITUTE AND AN ASSELLION.

[Col. 0340B]

Gods, avert the threats that this dreadful birth announces.

The she-wolf, conceived by a filthy little ass,

Filled the unlawful husband’s bowels with offspring,

And the savage, lavish in violation of law, gave birth to a beast’s progeny.

What can a discordant mongrel do while breaking nature?

From what source can the offspring seek guidance—who could say?

His foolish father made him a thief;

His wicked mother, by degenerating from nobility, would have held him among those heights.

But, believe me, his parents recognize you as their own through your vices:

Tongue-tied, trembling, boasting, suited to fraud,

With an immense throat, swallowing whatever is everywhere.

Once he has opened jaws accustomed to human blood,

He does not turn his back on lowly bullocks.

XXV. ON A CAUCUS [Note: [Col. 0340D] “On a caucus.” Caucus is a kind of drinking vessel. Jerome, Book II Against Jovinianus, writes of Diogenes: “Once, while he had a wooden caucus for drinking, he saw a boy drinking from his cupped hand and is said to have dashed it to the ground, saying, ‘I did not know that nature had a cup.’” Spartianus, in the Life of Pescennius: “He was so strict that, when he saw certain soldiers drinking from a silver caucus during a campaign, he ordered all silver to be removed from military use, adding that they should use wooden vessels.” Trebellius Pollio likewise joins cavei and scyphi in the Letter of Valerian. But the strangeness of the word caused it to be corrupted in various ways. For in Spartianus and Pollio careos is printed, and in Jerome cavum; in Ennodius, Epigram 29, the title is “On Glaucus.” But the old books correctly read here and in that place, “On a Caucus.”] BELONGING TO SOMEONE, HAVING PASIPHAE AND THE BULL. WRITTEN IMPROMPTU.

Pasiphae, you will not leave the snowy bullock even in art,

[Col. 0341A] With arms spread around his neck, seeks his kisses as a suppliant,

And, more beautiful, in your counterfeit you mock real girls.

The white bull surpasses silver in the brightness of its color;

Love lives—the bull and the woman—without a real body.

XXVI. ON THE MAN WHO NEVER FED ANYONE EXCEPT AT HIS SON’S FUNERAL.

He who prepares sumptuous dishes amid weeping for his invited guests

Celebrates great annual solemnities through tears.

XXVII. OTHERWISE.

He never feeds such crowds while his house stands, believe me;

He who fills tombs for his children and tables for his friends.

XXVIII. OTHERWISE.

Wretched guests, demand many mournful lamentations:

As many banquets will come as there have been funerals.

XXIX. ALSO ON A CAUCUS [Note: [Col. 0341C] “Having Pasiphae.” Carved or engraved. This is surely what Pliny mocks in the preface to Book XXXIII: “It is pleasing to carve lusts on cups and to drink amid obscenities.”] HAVING PASIPHAE AND THE BULL.

The woman flatters, the bull feels, limbs move.

Art has supplied the forms; who has given them souls?

XXX. OTHERWISE.

And, fashioned, the bull preserves its rigid mind, wicked Venus,

So that, when lips approach, it may hold out its muzzle.

XXXI. OTHERWISE.

If you have souls, painter, with which you insert art,

Let a gentler spirit be enclosed in the bull’s mouth,

If strong hearts are not granted to the wretched girl.

Adjudication: `native-adjudication.md` records the source-specific disposition of the saved review. Material uncertainties in the transmitted Latin are marked in the text.

### XXXII. ON THE FACT THAT ENNODIUS THE CONSUL WAS CALLED “MESSALA” AS HIS COGNOMEN

[Note: Messala was consul in the year of Christ 506. In that consulship he entered a new cognomen for himself in the consular registers, so that he was called “Ennodius Messala.” In those centuries, therefore, they called “cognomen” what was placed before the actual name—that is, the final name. Thus Jerome writes that Caecilius Cyprianus and Gennadius that Sulpicius Severus had cognomina, which were placed first. The learned Panvinius held a different view: following the ancient Roman custom, already long obsolete, he thought the registers read “Messala Ennodius.” But in that case Ennodius would have been Messala’s proper name, not his cognomen. Messala, the son of Faustus and brother of Avienus, has been mentioned in the letters.]

[Col. 0341C]

I have joined the consul’s name to his genius in place of a lineage:

By giving light to the registers, I surpass the consular robes.

Why should your palm-embroidered robe alone blossom from purple dye?

Our purple has given you more than the red pigment that dyes [the robe].

[Note: Our purple: “Our name, inscribed in red pigment, in the registers.” From this color of writing, the consular registers were called “purple” by Martial and “purple-dyed” by Sidonius. “My name,” he says, “adorns Messala the consul no less than the palm-embroidered robe itself.”]

### XXXIII. ON AN ADVOCATE WHO SPOKE AGAINST HIMSELF

Shameless man, why do you confuse each thing with broken words?

Your buried tongue paints your character.

You accept, demand, presume, refuse, burn.

You make sad and flattering, strong and shifting things at once.

[Col. 0342A]

Anger, fear, fury, patience—all in a single moment—

you wear so many faces in an empty breast.

### XXXIV. VERSES WRITTEN FOR AGELLUS, WHEN THE SON OF ARMENIUS ANGELUS, AFTER DOING PENANCE, IS OFFERED TO CHRIST

[Note: The son of Armenius: Book II, letter 1.]

Jesus receives the one offered to him, the one to whom he has granted pardon.

After sins, souls are holocaust offerings to God.

Go on, boy: in good conscience surpass your tender years;

a pure life has aided the victorious pious.

### XXXV. ON A MAN WHO SPOKE AGAINST THE GAULS IN HIS OWN PRESENCE, THOUGH HE WAS A VENETIAN SLANDERER

[Note: The Transalpine Gauls are meant, since they were his own origin. The Veneti too are Cisalpine Gauls. “Venetian” is also a name for a color. Hence he calls badly dyed things “Venetians” and the little slaves of spotted earth so called, either because their complexion is darker than that of the Gauls.]

You mock the Gauls, badly dyed offspring of Venetians.

You have none of their brightness; your mind shows what your race is.

You despise the innocent children of spotted earth;

but the snow of the Rhône gives birth to children of integrity.

[Col. 0342B]

### XXXVI. EPIGRAM ON THE “SUBSCRIBED” BAPTISMAL CANDIDATE

[Note: On the subscribed candidate: Those who requested baptism were ordered to give their names in writing. Council of Carthage IV, canon 25. Ferrandus the deacon, in an as-yet unpublished letter to Fulgentius concerning an Ethiopian being baptized: “As the solemnity of Easter approaches, he is presented among the candidates, enrolled, and instructed.” Cyril, in the preface to his Catecheses, writes: “You entered; you were deemed worthy; your name was enrolled” (εἰσῆλθες, κατηξιώθης, ὄνομά σου ἐνεγράφη). Hence at that time they were called both “candidates” and “subscribed.”]

On the subscribed candidate.

Friend, whatever germ of nature the law has given you,

may the fountain of life-giving water grant to me.

### XXXVII. IN THE HOUSE BEFORE THE ORATORY

You purchase benefits from losses and joy from mourning,

if your faith in Christ is unwavering.

### XXXVIII. BEFORE THE OIL STORE

This is what fills the body with shining olive oil:

nothing more fitting belongs before holy doors.

[Col. 0342C]

### XXXIX. BEFORE THE GRANARY

The granaries are small, perhaps, but my mind is larger than they.

By not sparing my resources, I have earned wealth.

### XL. BEFORE THE STAIRS

May a figure come, with its witness opening the mind,

by which the vow is always revealed.

### XLI. BEFORE THE CELLAR

No hostile pressure constricts the storehouse of my mind:

what lies hidden in spacious chambers flows out in expenditure.

### XLII. BEFORE THE KITCHEN

[Col. 0343A]

The meals of my expansive kitchen do not give me lofty banquets,

nor does my stomach shake with the work of many cooks.

We serve a few dishes, surpassing their number in refinement;

the glory of the table does not damage health.

### XLIII. BEFORE THE WINE CELLAR

[Note: The wine cellar: Saint Augustine, Sermon 61 on Time: “There are many things which at one time or another we cannot bring out from the granary, wine cellar, or storeroom.” Isidore, in his Glosses: “Canava, a room behind the dining chamber.” Italians still call *canevari* wine stewards or those in charge of a wine cellar.]

The sober cellar preserves wine in heavily laden jars,

and strengthens bodies as they move forward in their proper steps.

Cups pour the flames of anger into many men;

warlike hearts grow gentle through our wine.

### XLIV. AT THE ENTRANCE OF THE GARDEN

Look, you who make your way through pleasant green spaces,

so that you may learn to prefer eloquence cultivated with care.

The shoot painted with the purple of speech smiles;

he who produces flowers in song has spring in winter.

Through the ice, warm words breathe out the west winds;

words drunk with brilliance have been steeped in shining purple.

In every matter the purple of speech reigns;

the water-snakes (*chelydri*) submit their necks to the command of the mouth.

When hearts grow young with rosy blood,

a letter displays their original freshness upon their chilled limbs.

Learned skill turns nature’s gifts toward obedience:

ages, appearances, measures, seasons, and forms.

### XLV. WITHIN THE GARDEN, ABOVE THE THRESHOLD

Let him praise the advantages of spacious gardens,

whose many cultivated acres satisfy hunger.

A generous endowment of small things surpasses extended wealth:

true nobility is what shines in modest circumstances.

Grace enters the enclosed space, leaving the open fields behind;

it has revealed what diligence can do in narrow quarters.

At the entrance a colonnade’s green shade is in bloom,

for the vine-bearing god himself poured out its genius.

Adorning great woven masses of leaves with clusters,

it will join coolness to the summer heat.

For lilies, laurel, and olives mingled with roses

have made the day itself desire its cultivation.

Garlands displaying foliage dear to triumph

have bestowed the golden earth's own affections.

Let the wealthy seek the rewards of a greater wish:

for us, this is enough—that we enjoy it without deceit.

### XLVI. ON THE GOLD CHAIN OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS WOMAN, WHICH IS ENCLOSED IN A SMALL CASE AND THEREFORE VERY THIN

[Note: On the gold chain of the illustrious woman: This means an illustrious woman, perhaps Firmina, whose ring he treated in epigram 97 and now whose little chain—that is, a gold chain resembling a fish, from which it received its name—he describes. Jerome describes such a chain in his letter 15 to Marcella. Anastasius frequently uses *murena* for *murenula*, in Gregory IV: “a chain on which thirteen hyacinth-colored gems hang”; likewise “a purple chain,” “a three-stranded chain,” and “a spun chain.”]

[Col. 0343D]

Breath-like lightness flits over the slender, slippery gold. [The corrupt wording permits no firmer subject.]

[Col. 0344A]

The bright metal scarcely touches her wearied limbs;

its weight has oppressed the treasure of the panting furnace. [The phrase is textually difficult.]

### XLVII. ANOTHER VERSION

The craftsman dissolves golden threads through mist;

pliant golden breezes play about his hands.

### XLVIII. ANOTHER VERSION

Here a breeze has brought together the limbs of precious metal.

The eyes fear, and cannot comprehend, what they have fashioned.

### XLIX. ANOTHER VERSION

It is nothing, yet I hold it: my right hand convinces the eye.

Air is compressed in the close interlacings of the fingers.

### L. ON THE MAN WHO SENT A FIG AS A GIFT TOGETHER WITH A TOKEN

[Col. 0344B]

Your right hand sends the condemned fruit of the tree.

[Note: The condemned fruit of the tree: This follows the opinion of those who believe that the tree forbidden to Adam was a fig tree, among them Theodoret in Question 28 on Genesis. He says that the token was sent along with the figs as a gesture of hospitality.]

These dreadful fruits first stripped the human being of his food,

[Note: They stripped the human being: There is no metrical license here, because the ancient grammarians teach that a syllable naturally short can become common when two consonants follow it in the next word, the first of which is S. Thus in Epigram 17, “Pande studium,” and in Virgil, “date tela, scandite muros.” Martial, Book VIII, epigram [reads]: “Pauca Jovem, / Nondum taxata, stulte, negata putas?” The best manuscripts read the verse in this way.]

and, serpent, after the deceit, you threaten nakedness as his lot.

Spare the gifts, I beg you; reserve misfortune and ruin.

Why do you think the fruit of the innocent can harm salvation?

Once the tree, fruitful in death, drove death away,

when life hung fixed upon its branches of triumph.

### LI. ON THE ADULTERER AND THE EFFEMINATE MAN

All ages are kept in Memphian woven cloth.

Laurentius never served Nero before this,

nor did the man who conquered the powerful flames with his body fear them.

### LII. ANOTHER VERSION

A man in face, a woman in bearing, yet in the leg both at once,

undoing nature's quarrels without distinction—

you are a hare, and you trample the neck of so great a lion.

### LIII. ANOTHER VERSION

Demand, little wife, the false beards of the crowd,

lest masculine lips diminish your profit.

### LIV. ANOTHER VERSION

Look at the portent created by mixed law:

of a common gender; yet it is better called an "all-thing."

### LV. ANOTHER VERSION

A constant deceit plays in ambiguous sex:

when it submits, it is woman; when it performs foul acts, it is man.

### LVI. IN THE BAPTISTERY OF MILAN

[Col. 0344D]

May he shine with a purer light than metal refined in fire,

he who arranges gifts worthy to be given to God.

Before the steaming furnaces of Laurentius,

[Col. 0345A]

Laurentius' life stood before steaming furnaces, to ennoble the gracious work.

Marbles, paintings, panels, and the lofty coffered ceiling—

he himself gave them to the church, shining in integrity.

Thus the builder adds character to the value of buildings,

as you carry Seric fleeces dyed with purple.

How the light of a guest accompanies the enclosed gems.

Whenever the snow of stone reddens more beautifully through art.

### LVII. ON JOVINIANUS, WHO, WEARING A CLOAK, CAME FORTH WITH A GOTHIC BEARD. IMPROMPTU

I marvel that a barbarian face should put on Roman dress,

and that nations should be distinguished in a small person.

### LVIII. ANOTHER VERSION

Night, the cloud over your face, darkens the Roman covering;

your face has overwhelmed your clothing beneath a dark veil.

[Col. 0345B]

### LIX. ANOTHER VERSION

Though ill groomed, you exalt your bearing in noble cloaks,

mixing discordant offspring in a hostile alliance.

### LX. IN THE BASILICA OF SAINT CALEMERUS, BISHOP AND MARTYR OF MILAN, WHEN IT WAS RESTORED

[Note: Saint Calemerus: Bishop and martyr of Milan, whose feast they celebrate on the day before the Kalends of August. *Calemerus*, like *Evemerus*, is the correct form: Greek Καλήμερος (“Fair-day”) and Εὐήμερος (“Auspicious-day”). Usage altered it into *Calimerus*, just as *Calocerus* arose from *Calocaerus*, Greek Καλόκαιρος (“Fair-season”).]

The roofs, freed from captivity, have deserved the light;

the face smiles, bearing no cloudy mark.

Here recently a gift almost of starry Olympus arrived,

brought by the ministry of the prophet Laurentius.

The building and the life of the man, whose form is now one,

are like the sun’s rays: similar in shape and color.

Well done, restorer of ancient things; proceed,

builder of new ones, illustrious in face and intellect.

[Col. 0345C]

Under your leadership the buildings reject their ancient form;
