a new genius stretches itself toward those about to fall.

### LXI. ON A CERTAIN OLD, FOOLISH ENEMY WHO FED WELL

You prepare lavish meals, but recoil from filth upon your tongue.

If you are absent as shepherd, you assemble the dishes.

Ambitious hunger, extravagant with an exhausted fortune,

assaults with its horns if the master is silent.

### LXII. ON THE MAN WHO DEVOURED THE RESOURCES OF THE POOR

Nourished on the entrails of the wretched and the poor man's blood,

why are the deaths of so many people your feasts?

Truffles, partridges, crane, thrush, dove, sea-urchin—

a thousand bodies do not fill your belly.

[Col. 0345D]

Unlucky for many, you are called fortunate for one alone,

because your belly will be heir to the wretched man.

### LXIII. ON THE SAME MAN

Polyphemus lived on human limbs,

and made flesh swollen with black blood his delight.

You reproduce the same madness, with the scene returned—

you, whom crowds of the weak supply with food.

### LXIV. ON THE MAN WHO FED HIS FRIENDS IN ORDER TO DRAW THEM TO HIMSELF

So that the serpent might plunge gods into death,

it offered food and bore deadly life as a gift.

Thus whoever sweetens my labors in a true paradise

suffers the snares of the banquet.

There departs the friend whom he held in his heart:

his dear throat goes as lodging to its master.

### LXV. ON THE CUNNING DEFENSOR

[Note: On the cunning Defensor: Epigram 76, “On the cunning man who was called Defensor.” Here *Defensor* is not ἔκδικος (“avenger” or civic defender), as when one says “defender of the city,” but the man’s proper name, as in Sulpicius Severus’ Defensor, who opposed Saint Martin, and in the ancient Notices, Defensor, first bishop of Angers.]

“Nescir s” is corrupt in the supplied text; the opening sense is uncertain. You withdraw from your wishes beneath a cloud of heart.

Though present, you are sought by the eyes in your face.

You know how to be visible to no one through evasions,

giving poisons with honey-sweet lips.

Swearing that you do not want what you do want,

you shake hearts with various cruel devices.

Skilled to surpass the Hydra in its coils and Prometheus in his forms,

so that the tale may not return to ancient times,

you stir up wars; you grow through plunder, Defensor, by what you have seized.

Proud booty runs toward your name.

[Col. 0346B]

### LXVI. PREFACE TO THE WHOLE POETIC WORK WHICH HE COMPOSED

While my anxious mind endures many surging waves

and I become the slave of the glassy sea,

while the stormy bearer of the returning wave,

the southwest wind, whirls me like captured spoils,

a Pierian warmth entered my mind; soon Apollo’s laurel

encircled my temples, which lacked a wreath.

Then green ivy clusters reddened upon my brow,

and I drank the gentle murmurs of Castalian honey.

At once, laying aside my withering cares,

I embraced praise, songs, and joy.

### LXVII. ON WHAT HE WROTE DURING THE VINTAGE SEASON

While our faithful servants store the must in jars

and play upon the press with fearless feet;

while they stain their feet with the rosy blood of Bacchus,

and the grape is torn, bearing its tender skins;

while he does not allow idle leisure to write poems on Nile papyrus,

[Note: Nile papyrus sheets: Sheets made from *biblos*, or papyrus. Aldhelm, On the Night-Raven: “I am written on Roman papyrus, but in a Greek voice.” Hence also the “Bibline letters” of Isaiah 18 among the Septuagint translators, where our author says “in vessels of papyrus.” They are called “Nile” sheets because papyrus grows in Egypt, in the marshes of the Nile. Pliny, Book XIII, chapter 11; Cassiodorus, Book XI, letter 38. Hence Martianus Capella also calls sheets “the collages of the Nile plant,” Book III.]

I have plowed the sheets, lest I be held by a tomb when I die.

Having confessed the drunken words of stumbling Thalia,

I am free of blame if she totters in her feet.

Let syllable and rhythm, the law of art, suit the sober [*jejunos*, literally “those fasting,” here contrasted with the drunken Muse]—

[Note: The syllable, rhythm: The printed and ancient texts have *remmus* incorrectly. Symphosius closes his riddles with a similar joke: “Among the mad it is necessary not to be sane. Reader, pardon the drunken Muse for having no wisdom.”]

No Muse is joined to Bromius.

### LXVIII. ON A CERTAIN GLUTTON WHO ATTACKED HIS WORK WITHOUT UNDERSTANDING IT

[Col. 0347A]

I do not know why, fool, you spare no sacred labor,

while observing your custom of leaping upon it with your teeth.

You go on chewing at me; but your belly knows no profit.

For you grasp winds in empty images.

The gorge of food receives nothing through broken, muttering cheeks,

nor does it overflow through chaste movements.

While you hunt the Phasian bird, fish, or udders,

feed your wet throats with foods cooked by fire.

I take pleasure in composing fasting words without a belch:

let the dishes of luxurious banquets satisfy you.

### LXIX. ON A TRIBUNE, A NOMINAL EUNUCH NAMED PEREGRINUS, WHO TRAVELED EVERYWHERE

[Col. 0347B]

A people, wealth, and life are asserted by witnesses, Tribune,

whenever we leave an ancient lodging.

You, whom wandering has carried through nations as they are surveyed,

are held by no house, however spacious, for a whole day.

Do you wish to be called wealthy, noble, handsome, and friendly,

sent by the heat of an unknown ocean?

Empty words fly about; no guarantor appears.

No reliable sign reveals your sex or homeland.

Beggar, old, timid, confused, breathless—

use these names, losing the truth.

### LXX. ON THE SAME MAN

You will be safe to speak falsely without a witness, Tribune:

the wind has a tongue empty of weight.

### LXXI. ANOTHER VERSION ON THE SAME MAN, BECAUSE HE NEVER STAYS ANYWHERE

The misfortunes of nature make Tribune unstable:

he flies away from here again unless bonds hold him.

Take up, poor man, a little ballast when the west wind comes;

no root is useful to your need.

### LXXII. ANOTHER VERSION ON THE SAME MAN

The eunuch begs a shameful livelihood at the crossroads:

he has no seed with which to make the earth bear.

The field keeps great shoots in its ploughed limbs,

and the harvest returns multiplied with offspring.

Cut in vain, he plows backs with the plow,

unless, splitting them, he scatters the wheat’s progeny.

### LXXIII. ON THE MAN WHO, THOUGH HE HIMSELF HAD GAULISH PARENTS, LOVED TO EAT GEESE

[Col. 0347D]

Here is a battle among birds, where the goose is slain by the Gaul:

the bird pays the penalty for its ancient betrayal.

[Note: Ancient betrayal: When the geese betrayed the Gauls besieging the Capitol by awakening the Romans with their cries.]

Once slaughtered, you profit shamelessly from that voice.

The one who gave life to the Romans dies.

### LXXIV. ON THE VARIETY OF CLERICS

He who knows the face of the sea and the number of grains of sand,

whom no woman can deceive even by swearing;

who knows the multitude of stars and observes lovers,

to whom Cynthia is known by her fixed horns—

he cannot retain the faces, names, and characters

which the clergy change in a very short time.

### LXXV. ON A BAD MAN WHO LOVED HORSES

The enemy of uprightness and needy of fairness rejoices in horses;

by excessive zeal he removes names from worthy horses,

presenting his backside against holy words.

But far removed from the beast is what the mind’s injustice judges:

the purpose of the race persists, which pedigrees establish.

### LXXVI. ON GALLIDUS, WHO WAS CALLED DEFENSOR

[Col. 0348B]

As a guest’s deceit, with its tricks, catches asps,

so beneath the appearance of play lies the image of death.

[Note: The provoked shadow: Seneca, On Anger, Book III, chapter 3: “Red color excites bulls; at a shadow the asp rises; a cloth provokes bears and lions; all things that are naturally wild and enraged are thrown into panic by empty objects.”]

A provoked shadow produces cunning plagues,

and war is waged with a flattering beginning.

Believe me, Defensor conducts battles no differently:

he accuses while laughing, he kills while calm.

### LXXVII. ON THE LIFE AND DEEDS OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP

[Note: The life of Saint Ambrose: The following twelve epigrams contain praises of twelve bishops of Milan, in the order in which they held the episcopal see, from Ambrose to Laurentius.]

Ambrose, a prophet in character and intellect,

put into practice, in merit and honor, what he taught.

His tongue shone, moist, with regal purple,

painting in its own spring the shoots he desired.

Wearing bright garlands around his noble brow,

he prepared a work distinguished by gems in his mouth.

By gesture, integrity, and modesty he instructed the peoples;

with a look he encouraged, rebuked, and admonished them.

As the duties of his voice demanded the final dangers,

so he pursued tender faults when he remained silent.

Girded with swords and protected by the weight of a shield,

he enclosed his breast in woven steel.

The sword has strength—the cutter and enemy of vices;

the viper does not touch the man’s scaly back.

### LXXVIII. ON SAINT SIMPLICIANUS, HIS SUCCESSOR AS BISHOP

When Ambrose left the duties of the bereaved people,

he transferred their care to you, Simplicianus.

The resources of the successor, the entrails of the despoiled kingdom,

grew through the merit of another age.

Just as a long-established ash tree, strengthened by kindly west winds,

is solidified by long repose so that it need not fear war,

so the fortunate recruit, called to gray beginnings,

did not, by degenerating, bend the ancient summit.

He feared nothing, his soul burning in frozen marrow.

The virtue of the bishop possesses the old age of a flower.

He who pressed earthly seas beneath an open roof,

touched the stars through his character and cultivation.

### LXXIX. ON THE BLESSED VENERIUS, HIS SUCCESSOR

[Col. 0349A]

Venerius, a youth, came to follow the form of chastity,

not serving his own name.

[Note: Serving his own name: Because he was “pure” although he was called Venerius. A similar case is mentioned in the epitaph of the girl Archontia: since her name seemed to suggest a certain military command, it was considered unsuitable for a virgin. Although this has little to do with Ennodius, I have inserted it here because of its elegance and because it concerns the Gauls, as it was copied by us a few years ago from a marble tablet excavated near the Mausoleum of Constantina at Rome. It reads as follows:]

EPITAPH OF REMUS AND ARCHONTIA, FULL BROTHER AND SISTER, GAULS BY NATION, WHO DIED ON THE SAME DAY AND WERE BURIED TOGETHER

This urn holds two siblings, different in sex,

whom bitter Lachesis drowned on a single day.

One was a boy whose face was marked by doubtful down,

to whom it was scarcely permitted to complete nine winters.

Nor did his distant sister, in her fifth triennial year,

I think, see the Tanarian waters at her funeral.

He was called Hemus, a name fabricated from Latin blood,

but drew his ancestors from the noble stock of the Gauls.

But this girl, Archontia, whose name echoed a Greek-born tongue,

bore a name unsuitable for a virgin choir.

DEPOSITED ON THE NONES OF NOVEMBER, IN THE CONSULSHIP OF DIOSCORUS, A MAN OF SENATORIAL RANK.

His strong limbs were withering under an aged judge;

age had deprived the present world of its boy.

After he climbed the lofty supports of the episcopal chair,

a tender old man explained doctrines to the peoples.

Golden patterns flowed from his wealthy tongue;

his eloquence restored the bright life of the sun.

When the belly of the Church had swollen with the seed of the word,

it did not lack nourishment from apostolic milk.

### LXXX. ON THE SUCCESSION OF THE VENERABLE MAROLUS

Marolus, who drank from the mouth of the outermost Tigris,

had seen the sun’s radiance in watery dwellings.

Labor had made him firm upon the proper axis of Syria;

he began his prophetic office with countless gifts.

Ever watchful, attentive, fasting, provident, ardent:

it was enough for his office that he maintained this way of life.

Whenever a tender mouth touched the taste of an honorable act,

what had been command passed over into affection.

The land once powerful, founded by blessed Fathers,

shines with noble births throughout the world.

### LXXXI. ON MARTINIANUS, A WORSHIPER OF GOD AND BISHOP

A mind of snowy milk, the evident appearance of a dove;

a serpent’s cunning—farewell, Martinianus.

While the slippery winds of the uncertain crowd demand you,

they find you fearful, lest you deserve to be elected.

He alone told the world, as judge, what was contrary to it;

to seize the kingdom, he did not deserve to conquer.

Immediately, led to the threshold of great honor,

as an exile he was admitted among the citizens of heaven.

Afterward he built two purer houses for the saints,

and ordered them to possess daylight with their light closed in.

### LXXXII. ON THE VENERABLE BISHOP GLYCERIUS

Flushed with red pigment and reddening through excellent deeds,

Glycerius follows with the face of a virgin.

While the bloody dew stains his pure form,

the painted face pleased simply upon his cheeks.

Wearing a gleaming brow with saffron-colored sprinkling,

he had tinged his joyful face with modest signs.

Having obtained the scepter, he bestowed what the witness-image declared;

the purple of his mind revealed his command.

[Col. 0350A]

The people possessed him, fortunate for scarcely any time,

but again he was sent to the service of the great.

[Note: The printed edition of Schott reads “Hence grandfather and people.” Perhaps the reading should be “The people possessed this man,” without *et*.]

### LXXXIII. ON SAINT LAZARUS, BISHOP

When Lazarus trampled underfoot the heights of the wicked world,

he came fiercely into the midst, summoned by voices.

His cheerful brow had painted him little as an enemy of vices,

striking down faults with the lights of his eyes.

Looking back, he wiped away the clouds of life’s falls;

he often devoted himself to the care of wounds.

The crime committed in hidden caves did not escape notice;

absent from crimes, he was everywhere their punisher.

He flourished serenely in peaceful light among the innocent,

like a mirror casting a face upon the guilty.

### LXXXIV. ON EUSEBIUS, FRIEND OF GOD, BISHOP

[Note: On Eusebius the bishop: His synodical letter to Leo the Great is extant; it was mentioned earlier when Crispinus, bishop of Ticinum, was discussed. Verses also survive which testify that Eusebius restored the church of Blessed Thecla at Milan after a fire; they once appeared inscribed in that church:

The ancient roofs rise again in restored temples;

those which the flame had burned have returned to their original form.

He who renewed Christ’s temples restored these things to their vows;

through Eusebius’ merits the destructive flame perished.]

Eusebius, a stranger, came to the country of the Ligurians,

drawn by friendship for an unknown people.

He was Greek, from the land upon which the Sun looks at his companion’s rising,

shaking waters from his fiery crown.

Gentle, composed, generous, pious, upright, bold,

so that one might believe he would never cause harm.

He wept, pitying poverty; he smiled upon the prosperous,

sharing joy and sadness with all.

Fame, announcing the man to the world that would speak of his work,

drew nations from their stations.

### LXXXV. ON GERONTIUS, BISHOP

After the Church’s seat had been obtained for you, Gerontius,

your predecessor did not fear death as he died.

When you restore it, its pale fortune returns and suffers death;

it lives after death through the disciple’s worth.

Joined to farmers, you cultivated the shoots of life,

and no serpent brought joyful nourishment from weeds.

He who gave to the public what the best law commands as food

purchased heaven with earthly fruits.

You pressed down the error of the mind by the law of labor;

you are carried by virtues, allowing no idleness.

### LXXXVI. ON THE VENERABLE BISHOP BENIGNUS

Bring forth the certain names that your mind has placed, Benignus;

everyone who calls you will bear witness to your merit.

While ancient faith recounts the man, it reveals his deeds;

he says nothing by chance, stunned by the pledge of his child.

The foreseeing vows of parents do not err about the future;

they turn their flattering words into true offspring.

Before his fathers, counting votes, he sat while the senate applauded;

that man raised his consecrated head above them.

But as a flower is cut down by a cruel plowshare,

hope, honor, and genius fell from the doorway.

### LXXXVII. ON THE MOST BLESSED MAN, BISHOP SENATOR

Look: Senator is here, surpassing consuls in the consular robe,

the throne, and the Gabine girdle.

Quick in intellect, careful of rounded speech,

the prize of virtues, the very form of chastity.

He brought into light the hidden mysteries of books,

closed to the prophet, in whatever arrangement he chose.

Sent to the revered secrets of the furthest world,

by diligent studies he repaired what had been torn apart.

Then the East, confessing itself conquered by an alien light,

stood still at the sight of another lamp.

### LXXXVIII. ON DOMNUS THEODORUS, BISHOP OF EVERY VIRTUE

You are the sure light to your people, the most trustworthy hope of affairs;

you, Theodore, are the strength of the apostolic prophet.

A heap of virtues, the luminous substance of truth,

shows what labor has accumulated through study.

Foreknowing, girded, strong, tranquil, friendly,

composed, simple—you are good and wise.

Always prophetic, you know hearts aware of what is to come.

When you lay it open, discovered evil pours forth.

He whom fierce men feared, trampling the world's heights,

loved you, scorning the harshness of your brow.

[The subject and object of the final couplet are compressed in the transmitted text; the address remains to Theodore.]

### LXXXIX

There remains the man whom the illustrious king may preserve through a long age . . .

[Note: There remains: Laurentius, still alive as bishop when Ennodius wrote this.]

### XC. TO DEUTERIUS

[Note: Guardian of the empire: I conjectured that this was written to Deuterius, partly because he usually calls Deuterius “teacher,” but especially because in ancient books it follows the address to Diomedes, which he wrote at Deuterius’ request.]

With your speaking thumb, animating the strings through measured numbers,

I have compelled the speaking threads to serve a song

under the blows of the plectrum, teacher.

Mighty Cyrrha of Phoebus, holy company of clear water,

you will always be for me: you who set closed hearts

upon far-off services and fill them with favourable divinity.

[The construction “pectorа clausa remotis / inseris officiis” is uncertain in the supplied text.]

I beg you, as one about to support an exact voice, receive it,

granting a reward for words extracted under your judgment.

### XCI. ON MARBLE IN MOSAIC WORK

[Note: On marble in mosaic work: Gregory of Tours, Book II of his History, chapter 16, says of the church that Bishop Namatius built in his city of Clermont: “Its walls around the altar are adorned with mosaic work from many kinds of marble.” From Ennodius’ words it is clear enough that *sarsorium opus* means work in which differently colored marble crusts are fitted together so as to create one body and, as it were, one painting. Cassiodorus skillfully describes this in Book I, letter 6: “Send us from the city the most expert marble workers, who may join what has been carefully divided and, binding it together with deceptive veins, may commendably imitate a natural face. Let art produce what surpasses nature; let the discolored crusts of marble be covered with the most pleasing variety of paintings.” Hence *sarsor*, a marble worker who practices this craft. In the Acts of Cirta concerning Numatius Felix, when sacred books were being sought under Diocletian: “And when they came to the house of Felix the mosaic worker, he produced five books.”]

[Col. 0352A]

By an ordered law imposed upon the mingled entrails of stones,

the craftsmen's efforts make a nature.

With their broken limbs made solid, the marbles have stiffened;

the genius of the parts is gathered into a crust.

He who could compose one form from varied fragments

has brought the stone into obedience.

### XCII. ON A DISH BEARING HIS OWN IMAGE

Among rich metals, the image of Ennodius is a treasure.

### XCIII. ON HIS OWN CUP

The wave gives birth to thirst, which the shining cup supplies.

### XCIV. ON THE HORSE HE RECEIVED FROM HUNISCUS

[Note: On the horse he received from Huniscus: Aurelianus used *Huniscus* in the same way as *Daciscus* in a letter preserved by Vopiscus. The nation of the Huns was always under arms and never without horses. Hence Sidonius, characteristically witty, says in his panegyric of Anthemius that other nations are carried on horses’ backs, but that the Huns live there:

Thus he always clings to the horse as though fixed to it;

another nation is borne upon the backs of hoofed horses,

but this one inhabits them; smooth bows and arrows are its delight.

I have transcribed the passage as it must be emended, because the printed text is full of numerous errors.]

[Col. 0352B]

War-bearing neighing steed, bred beneath a freezing sky,

carrying your dry breast through mid-Tanais;

grazing pale grass in frosty clearings,

whom valour has trained for itself by the law of your climate.

After nations have been subdued, after so many rivers of blood,

you have another master, but the labor remains the same.

Leave, I beg you, the trumpet; you are destined to endure blessed songs;

you are sent, a captive of peace, to services.

You have nothing to do with wars: the trumpet recommends death.

What good is it always to love deaths already experienced?

### XCV. EPITAPH OF SAINT VICTOR, BISHOP OF NOVARA

Victor in name, purpose, merits, and struggle,

you despise the lands oppressed by stained seed.

Master over the vices of the flesh, though exempt from the body,

with limbs subjected to you, you have subdued the slippery ages.

Tranquil, patient, reproving, provident, severe.

Here, returning ashes to the tombs, the spirit called to the heights,

shining, rejoices in the heavenly citadel.

It looks down compassionately from the brow of Olympus upon the tombs.

Therefore, looking back upon the conquered world’s funerals,

once freed from snares, you grant rewards to your limbs.

### XCVI. ON A CERTAIN ROMAN WHO WANTED TO BE A TEACHER

No study, an indicator of nature, has come to you;

no polished letter keeps company with your uncultivated tongue.

You could never be a pupil—tell me, how can you be a teacher?

### XCVII. ON A CERTAIN OLD WOMAN

[Col. 0353A]

While cold blood dies in a living body,

when the frost of years dries the nourishment of the vulva,

and blood, the useful guardian of seed, flees the groin,

why, shrivelled Galla, do you join yourself to a young husband?

Trust in the joined marriage bed will produce a pledge.

Accusing a child of living falsely in loose wrinkles,

pregnant, you give to feasts the offspring of your sewer.

The belly has brought forth what the husband joins to his lips.

### XCVIII. ON THE RING OF FIRMINA, AN ILLUSTRIOUS WOMAN

Nothing deceives though it imitates: what the right hand fashioned is real.

Motionless, by art the hare flees the standing Molossian hound.

Set among raging bears, golden frenzy laughs;

the lion, carried in hands, rages with gentler anger.

The design recognizes its mistress as the metal serves her.

She tames wild beasts while feeding the crowd of needy people.

### XCIX. ON ALBINUS

You see Albinus has given inscriptions after his tomb,

he who kills death by merits that live on.

Illustrious man, while you submit a master's laws to a prince,

that place has truly become a place of burial.

### C. ON A HUNTING DOG AND A LAMB

This clever little fellow here is called Cretius,

sharp-nosed, swift of step, fearsome in the mouth,

fearless, marking the tracks with his pressed muzzle,

wherever stag, doe, hare, wolf, or she-bear roams.

He finds the creature and catches the wary beast in its warm bed.

After so many battles, he is mocked by the lamb's flight;

the gentle creature by trickery outruns the winged Molossian.

### CI. ON LITTLE CUPS

[Note: On little cups: Just as the preceding poem describes a drinking cup engraved with the story of Pasiphae, so now it describes little cups engraved with Jupiter’s adulteries, and rightly chastises a custom harmful to modesty.]

While the craftsman well depicts in images so many of Jupiter's seductions,

so many living crimes, his right hand is vicious.

The value of silver is to preserve an ancient crime,

lest what Jupiter did by theft surpass what is pure.

Nothing is allowed to grow old: monuments of crimes rise again.

He who fashions ancient faults admonishes by examples.

### CII. ANOTHER

If the adulterous god then took on so many faces,

he first amused himself with false shapes.

What would that god not violate with a counterfeit body,

whose form rejoices in its own adultery?

### CIII. ON PASIPHAE AND THE MINOTAUR

Venus is not injured: nature's bonds hold firm.

The little cow, false work of Daedalus, ceases [to deceive].

The two-formed cow, alive by artifice, does not moo.

Nor do fabricated timbers give the heifer true intercourse.

Look: again a woman, a wife, is offered to a bull,

and the breasts of beasts pant with human flames.

A vast neck takes the yoke; the enclosure receives the neck's course,

as the withered creature sweated beneath a tightened leather strap.

[The syntax and imagery of the final couplet are uncertain in the supplied text.]

### CIV. ON DEUTERIUS THE GRAMMARIAN

[Col. 0354A]

In form, head, and face—in everything, teacher Deuterius—

that learned man is renowned for countless gifts.

His perfected genius has everywhere shaken the tongue awake.

What he does not know how to say, for that reason, displeases malicious men.

They boast that the teacher does not know the art of grammar;

this simplicity has better instructed him in character.

He did not touch the work of the orator or the stony heights of Tullius;

no one loves the lofty rhetorician.

For his pupils his face is enough; they behold the venerable

baldness that is silent, and eyes full of Phoebus.

### CV. ON THE BIRTHDAY OF THE CHILD ARATOR. IMPROMPTU

[Col. 0354B]

You rightly cultivate your own birthday, handsome Arator.

For if you did not cultivate it, you would never be Arator.

[Note: Schott reads “if perhaps.”]

### CVI. ON A CERTAIN MAN OF UNCERTAIN PURPOSE AND SHAMEFUL LIFE

Why do you chatter, two-formed magpie, deceitful in so many matters,

half-man, you who trouble shameful things with a trembling loin?

What purpose is yours; what sex has ever fallen to you?

What do you not claim falsely—to be man, woman, holy, profane?

### CVII. VERSES SENT TO AGNELLO, AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

Impromptu.

Whoever has stained a bright affection with defiling dye,

let him therefore bear a tongue

burned by the torches of Christ the Judge,

buried in his mouth.

Living by deceit that must be endured, he breaks every pressing bond,

and bears grudgingly whatever a more tranquil order requires.

Leave, I beg you, friend, at last the manners worthy of the crowd;

following the path of blood, preserve what you have been chosen for.

[The final word “depectus” is corrupt or otherwise uncertain in the supplied Latin; “what you have been chosen for” is a cautious gloss.]

**Ennodius to Agnellus.**
Before your diligence gave its command, the things entrusted to it remained intact. For I had been warned not to give these things to anyone either to read or to copy, and I opposed my hands to those who asked. Now, overcome by your affection, I have sent them. If you read them again, you will make my modesty stand in disgrace; if you copy them, in utter defeat.

### CVIII.

Love releases the bonds that another once tied:

The old law yields only to the law that follows it.

### CIX. On His Own Verses

[Col. 0354D]

Never, through long ages, have Castalian benefits flowed into me in fruitful dithyrambs.

As I scatter mournful songs from fasting lips,

why do you, new hope, stir me from the depths of Aonia?

But if you rejoice that the thread of the Fates has been changed,

now display Pegasus, bearer of hoofs, for me.

Let him carry his winged body across dewy meadows

without bending the tender crops beneath his steps;

lofty, strong, handsome, suited to swift strides—

if you bring him to me, Musa, you will soon please me.

[Col. 0355A] You are sent to ask a rich man for small gifts:

if you do not return rejoicing, tell me, Musa, farewell.

### CX. On the Castle of Bishop Honoratus

[Note: [Col. 0355D] “On the castle of Honoratus.” As Dictio 2 taught us, bishops were already then compelled to build castles because of the attacks of soldiers and brigands. Such, for example, was the castle of Nicetius, bishop of Trier, above the Moselle, which Fortunatus adorns in his verses, Book III; and Flodoard relates in many places which castles were founded by the bishops of Reims.]

The bishop’s fortress is the most trustworthy hope of life.

With a holy guardian, what harm could seek it?

Here the shield is a vow; Bellona, withdraw far from here.

What rests upon merits is burdened by no battles.

Here the founder strengthens the walls, the builder the defenses.

Let no one who hastens here in fear fear anything.

### CXI. On King Theoderic’s Garden

[Note: [Col. 0355D] “On the garden of King Theoderic,” for he was the only king of Italy in Ennodius’s time. In the fifth verse I have restored *scammate* in place of *stemmate*, following the traces of the manuscript.]

Mighty in war, your right hand is filled with famous triumphs,

wherever anything that fled obedience fell;

you who solidify lofty fame with scattered blood,

to whom the gentle ruler and the wielder of arms brought renown.

After you had reddened the broad battlefield,

you cultivate the fields, painting them with purple growth.

With your own purple you distribute fruit among the shrubs;

you give the plants fruit through your nobility.

The lowly turf boasts of its wealthy branch,

while it nurtures the bright seeds within the wood’s bite.

When one shoot has been cut down by iron, another flowers for you;

the naked dowry shines upon the married trees.

The grasses recognize their cultivator and, though mute, speak:

whatever the prince has touched has springtime even in the frost.

The earth, powerful in its bearing, shows for whom the tree has grown,

and here the lord reveals himself through his offspring and genius.

O serpent keeping watch over the fields of the Hesperides,

giving golden gifts to banqueters who have fasted.

[Note: [Col. 0355D] Schott gives *dant*, “they give.”]

[Col. 0355C] Who would pluck the offspring of the wood while its guardian’s poison stands watch?

Trust me: the grove is safe through death; no one enters it.

Here, O piety, you make common what you alone prepared.

With full entrails, hunger does not know how to depart.

### CXII. On a Certain Blind Glutton

From a hollowed-out eye-socket you carry a flowing wound in place of light,

displaying pestilential features and a buried face.

Your blind face is carried past countless companions,

who, seeing you, rightly grieve with their eyes.

You enrich your drunken, withering jaws with a stream,

and carry filthy lips around with thick dung.

Seek no kisses; suspend your dripping stench:

because of you I could wish to destroy what I see.

Who would think that foul flames grow together from the eyes?

[Col. 0355D] He sees nothing, yet keeps the straight path of crimes.

### CXIII. On His Old Horse

Our horse, supple under the aged reins,

now bears a young rider with gentle obedience.

Though very old, he lowers his soft back for the seated rider;

age makes him steady in his steps.

### CXIV. On the Child-Ploughman’s Whip

The learned mind joined in a whip things that encompass the world,

adorning the blows with wealth that makes them noble.

### CXV. Another Version

Whoever is beaten with the metals of silver and gold

mixes his greedy joys with weeping.

### CXVI. Another Version

Gold is enclosed by silver teeth;

let no one disdain to endure beautiful blows.

### CXVII. Epitaph of the Illustrious Lady Melissa

[Col. 0356B]

In blood, mind, wealth, beauty, virtue, and modesty,

I alone was the sort of woman one could desire.

I bore in my body only that portion of the world which the law permits,

adorning chastity with virtuous offspring.

Victorious, I held a brave husband through affection,

turning your laws, Severus, by my honey.

Those whom I bore I left united to a lofty lineage.

What is a vow among the holy, I achieved: I died before my husband.

Nothing has departed from me; I remain, surviving beyond the tomb:

death, which will never harm them, seeks the blessed.

And my name itself is sweet: because of my deeds I am called Melissa.

This name was rightly bestowed from my own character.

### CXVIII. On a Certain Fool Called Virgil

[Col. 0356C]

To such an extent has the fame of the ancient Maro declined

that our age should give you the name Virgil.

### CXIX. Another Version

If such a sacred name is given to a little fool,

the glory of the ancestors will become a reproach.

### CXX. Another Version

The foolish poet rejoices in a captive’s lineage.

[Note: [Col. 0355D] “The foolish poet rejoices in a captive’s lineage.” I think *raptivo* should be written instead of *captivo*. Barth, *Adversaria*, p. 1535.]

He is not Virgil, yet he is called so.

### CXXI. Another Version

Whenever, fool, you are called by a foreign name,

if you have any sense, take care lest you come.

[Note: [Col. 0356D] “Take care lest you come.” It should be read, “Take care lest you be sold,” that is, lest you be sold and led into slavery. The allusion is to the custom of the ancients, who imposed names at will upon purchased slaves. The long syllable, shortened here, does not invalidate this reading, since Arnulf of Lisieux noted this usage of Ennodius many centuries ago; and the writings of our Felix demonstrate it, though in this respect they are singularly unfortunate. The same author, in the same work.]

### CXXII. Another Version

[Col. 0356D]

Why do you falsely claim to be our Virgil, you worst of men?

[Note: [Col. 0356D] “You cannot be Maro, but you can be *moro*.” That faulty reading *moro* seems to require correction, with *baro* substituted; this more closely imitates the sound of the preceding word and is not disturbed by any contraction, while it denotes a stupid or dull-witted man, and so forth. The same author, in the same work, p. 1336.]

You cannot be Maro, but you can be *moro* (a fool).

### CXXIII. In a Bedroom, Above Books Set in Order

[Col. 0357A]

This is the path that prepares heavenly power,

the light of modesty, the food of the mind, the torch, remedy, and brightness.

Those who are stained by the dregs of the world do not know how to hold it.

The book stands open; whoever binds his neck with its strap is free.

This little hoe accompanies the vein of shining blood.

### CXXIV. Against Claudian, on the Mules

[Note: [Col. 0357D] “Against Claudian.” Claudian’s epigram on Gallic mules is twice as long as Ennodius’s, but the meaning of both is the same. Therefore *against* here signifies not opposition but imitation.]

Here behold one born of the swift torrent Rhodanus,

submitting its neck to the reins of your speech.

At spoken orders it flies, and at spoken orders it halts;

its will is captive to its ears.

They would not know bonds, if the luxuriance of their breed

were not destroyed by hearing, when their mouths are tightly bound by bits.

[Col. 0357B] When the cry pretends to be a goad, the cry is the reins;

their free limbs offer obedience to the tongue.

There is no need for reins, but the firm knot of speech

binds the hard muzzle of the chained beast.

### CXXV. On a Male Ass and a Mare

She is compelled to bring forth offspring from her own entrails

and to suckle the offspring of a wild species.

Nature’s conflicts, separated by a wide path.

### CXXVI. Another Version

A mother, poorly aware of what she was doing, produced an unknown offspring,

the deceits of nature through a more noble fraud.

### CXXVII. Another Version

The offspring joined unions that confused the distinction of species,

forced by a mixed law to produce a stock of intellect.

Here is a mule: two kinds of animal, but one body.

### CXXVIII. On His Journey by Night in Summer

The multitude of stars, not yet having lost its light

to the brightness of the sun, while mature night held sway,

poured down its ruddy, dew-moistened hair.

Cynthia, milky, shone through her saffron chariot,

undoing whatever her brother’s orbit had prescribed.

Silent brightness bloomed from the gift of night,

breaking the heat of Cancer’s season with cold;

when the painted face of the countryside called me,

wishing to reject the burdens of cares.

[Col. 0358A] I mounted a horse, such as Cyllarus could scarcely equal,

one who surpasses the heavenly breezes in gentle courses.

His rider runs motionless along the trackless ways,

flying while his feet move steadily in their appointed place.

### CXXIX. On the Litter of Viola, Wife of Bassus

How these wandering dwellings preserve their constant beauty!

Whatever valuables they possess is sent by their mistress.

For the golden metal glows with Viola’s light:

the owner scatters her rays everywhere.

### CXXX. Epitaph of Euphemia

She has overwhelmed the tombs and lives on after death through her deeds,

for she inserted nothing mortal into her character.

Earth embraces your limbs, Euphemia,

but how nobly your mind is joined to the snowy choirs!

Destruction has perished: then the harshest fate is enslaved,

when a life ignorant of evil overcomes death.

She was fruitful in marriage and, widowed in modesty,

made her daughter love God through her example.

### CXXXI. On a Sword in a Wooden Scabbard

[Note: [Col. 0357D] “On a sword in a stick.” The stick serves as a scabbard; some infantrymen in Gaul still use this kind of device when traveling. In the next epigram we have corrected the title, where *spathacinotus* was read. The proper form is *spatha cinctus*, “girt with a sword,” which the barbarians express in one word as *spathatus*, Greek σπαθᾶτος, “sword-bearing.”]

We use a sword enclosed through deception in a little wooden staff;

how well the death-dealing blade lies hidden beneath its wooden sheaths!

You carry protection; though you are held in terror by all,

what kills is peaceful obedience to us.

### CXXXII. On Boethius Girt with a Sword

The substance of rigid iron grows weak with you,

and steel is dissolved like flowing water.

An unwarlike hand softens swords, Boethius:

believe me, it was a sword a little while ago, but now it is a distaff.

The spear that you carry has changed into a thyrsus, you scoundrel.

Abandon the aid of Mars and remain constant in Venus.

### CXXXIII. On an Ivory *Stomatio*

[Note: [Col. 0358D] “On an ivory *stomatio*.” On the rattle. An old glossary gives *oscillum*, Greek στομάτιον. It was a kind of amusement, described vividly by Ausonius in the preface to his *Wedding Cento*: “It is like the toy which the Greeks called *stomation*: there are as many as fourteen rattles. By joining these little pivoting pieces in various ways, a thousand forms are represented: an elephant, a wild boar, a flying goose, a *mirmillo* in armor, a crouching hunter, and a barking dog; even a tower, a cup, and other marvelous figures of this sort, which one person varies more skillfully than another. But the arrangement of the experts is a marvel; that of the unskilled is ridiculous.” By this art, girls, as Ennodius says, enclosed a thousand objects in a small box, because with the few rattles taken from the box they fashioned countless things. The same idea is found in Petronius Arbiter’s silver mask, whose movable interlocking parts expressed different figures.]

The hearts of men, troubled by a light torment,

grow faint; it is permitted for maidens to play.

They shatter the elephant sent from the Marmaric fields;

scattered in fragments, the work is soon made solid again.

Through deception they learn to play with the punishment of the tender object.

For it is womanly to laugh by means of death’s gift.

They know how to enclose a thousand things in a narrow box;

all ivory here, woman, is the chest of your heart.

### CXXXIV. On a Bird Sitting and Crossing the Po upon the Foam

[Col. 0359A]

The Po, rising, had perhaps crossed the natural barriers of its banks

with its swollen whirlpool.

Forcing its flowing waters to harden into foam,

it carried scaly backs upon its powerful waves.

When the bird, trusting in the tender circle, then stood upon it,

giving its wings a rest, it safely pressed the waters.

For the water supplies its own alder-boat to the one who treads upon it,

while the little wet boat carries a dry bird.

### CXXXV. On the Tomb of the Emperor Majorian

When fortune, growing heavier, sought a tomb,

it brought its burden to your remains, Majorian.

Now look upon the unworthy masses of the pyramids [perhaps],

and leave cheap tombs to pious princes.

### CXXXVI. On a Padan Horse

All the horses born in lands of war,

and those whose bloody beds the current washes;

those that have subdued the icy depths of the Tanais,

whose powerful hooves trample the waters—

behold, here is the Padan horse, before whom, by a fair judgment,

let those whom the Aemonian climate nourishes yield.

He who traverses frosty pastures

comes unequal to both in merit and in beauty.

He walks gently, handsome in his noble limbs,

and delights the eye through his sweet obedience.

Let no tale now praise the offspring of Phasis,

[Col. 0359C] nor let foreign names carry lofty heads.

### CXXXVII. On a Drunken Praetorian Prefect’s Chief Official, Who Held the Vine-Branch

[Note: [Col. 0359D] “On the princeps of the praetorian prefecture.” That is, the chief official of the praetorian prefecture. The *princeps P. P.* was first among the officials of the praetorian seat. The *Notitia dignitatum* lists the staff of the praetorian prefect: the *princeps*, the *cornicularius*, the assistant, and so forth. In the same way, there were *principes* in the offices of the urban prefect, of the masters of both military branches, and of other dignities. All were sent from the school of the *agentes in rebus* to administer the offices. See Book 6, chapters c–d, of Theodosius, *On the Principes of the Agentes in Rebus*. The legal glosses give: Πρίγκιψ ὁ πρῶτος τῶν πολιτικῶν ταξεωτῶν, “the princeps, the first of the civil officials.” There was also a *princeps officii* under the emperor. King Theoderic, *Variae*, Book II, Letter 28: “to Stephanus, a man of the first rank, formerly chief official of our office.” Also on a Roman inscription: “Neritus, chief official of the emperor Claudius.” Their insignia, therefore, were a vine-branch or staff, like those of centurions. Hence Ennodius makes a joke about the drunken princeps Honoratus, whom he addresses in the following epigram and again in epigram 141.]

True honor gives the vine-branch, but the gifts of the vine

do not give wood to a fasting official.

### CXXXVIII. Another Version

As a princeps carries a scepter, so his right hand carries a vine;

may the goddess adorn her head with wine-skins as a crown.

### CXXXIX. Another Version

This dry vine-bearer embraces the mother of his mistress,

whose pressed breasts deny me wine.

### CXL. Another Version

[Col. 0359D]

Alas, how often, without fruit for my heated lips,

you have mocked me, reviving me with your bare name!

### CXLI. Ennodius to Honoratus, the Princeps

[Col. 0360A]

As a drinker, you obscure vice with the faults of lands;

you cannot be drunk while vomiting the wines of Liguria.

While wet Bacchus fills your burning breast,

our cups proclaim a powerful thirst.

### CXLII. On the Letter of Lord Ambrose Against Symmachus Concerning the Altar of Victory, When Symmachus Lost His Request for Its Worship; Composed Suddenly and Sent to Lord Faustus, Praetorian Prefect

[Note: [Col. 0360D] This is Letter 12 of Book II of Saint Ambrose’s letters, prefaced by the report of Symmachus, prefect of the city, which Ambrose refutes.]

Victory takes away the palm of eloquence from her friend.

She passes over to Ambrose: the goddess’s anger favors him more.

### CXLIII. Verses of Lord Faustus

[Col. 0360B] He who calls a drinker in the lands of Liguria is mistaken:

does the wine-drinker of Liguria drink any wine?

### CXLIV. Verses of Messala

Receive these little verses of ours, dearest Ennodius,

so that you may not cease to return our book to us.

Do not mar its appearance while you are unwilling above all to return

what you once promised us as well.

### CXLV. By Lord Ennodius

If you wished through your studies to reveal yourself to me as Messala,

there would be no lack of books that I could gladly give you.

An unjust mind takes away from a lover what it rejects too greatly.

A gift is not welcome when it flees the intellect.

### CXLVI. By Lord Ennodius

[Col. 0360C]

He who asks for a book of grammatical art concerning a poem composed—

[Note: [Col. 0360D] “Concerning a poem composed.” I think the older editions are better in reading *fracto*, “broken.” Barth, *Adversaria*, p. 405.]

who strives to have solid feet—

[Note: [Col. 0360D] “Strives to have solid feet.” The old manuscripts read *certat cavere pedes*, “strives to avoid feet.” I think *certat avere*, “strives to value,” should be written; that is, he wishes the feet of the poems to be solid and firm. The same author, in the same work.]

Would that, through our gift, certain joys concerning you,

young boy, might at some time come to the Muses!

[Note: [Col. 0360D] “Certain joys concerning you at some time, young boy.” I read *quondam neque gaudia certa*, “once, nor certain joys,” and so forth. The same author, in the same work.]

Unless I am mistaken, they avoid composing a limping verse,

or verses such as studies contemplate in dreams.

### CXLVII. On Honoratus

You desire a wife endowed with Flasconian Falernian,

her breast always filled with inexhaustible Lyaeus;

I, who worshipped Bacchus with wine-wet lips,

caressing the swollen god with wine I had belched,

am shut within the covering of a dry tomb, well aware of it;

yet I have a noble husband in heaven—well done!

whose blessed cups could never pass away.

If the Fates preserve that man as my husband, we both live for you.

### CXLVIII. Epitaph of Lady Dalmatia

[Col. 0361A]

Whenever a maiden is borne to the tomb, a funeral takes place.

There is one path of death: obedience to sin.

Rebellious nature was overcome by Dalmatia’s merits;

by an otherworldly nobility she holds heaven.

This is enough: to have trodden upon the world while in a worldly body,

and, having been taken from vice, to yield nothing to vices.

She surpassed the light of her lineage by the sun of modesty,

when her mind was joined to her purpose.

### CXLIX. On the Font of the Baptistery of Saint Stephen and the Water That Comes through the Columns

Look: beneath the roof, a serene rain falls without clouds,

and the clear face of heaven supplies water.

Streams flow forth over the sacred marble,

and behold, the stone gives birth to dew again.

For the dry portico pours out liquid springs,

and once more heavenly water comes to what has been born.

Holy water flows forth from heavenly recesses,

[Note: [Col. 0361B] “Of the poet Eustorgius.” He was bishop of Milan and succeeded Laurentius. A letter of King Theoderic to him survives under this title: “To Eustorgius, venerable man and bishop of Milan.” Now, so that I may add a marginal note in another hand rather than in my own words, I append an eight-line poem of similar subject concerning the fountain that Leo the Great constructed before the basilica of Saint Paul outside the Walls:

[Col. 0362B]

The water washes the stains of the flesh, but faith purer than the river

cleanses sins and purifies souls.

Whoever, suppliant, enters the venerable sanctuary of Paul

in accordance with his merits, wash your hands in the fountain.

Ancient neglect had destroyed the course of the waters,

which the pitcher now pours forth for you with full mouth.

The provident care of the shepherd Leo

gave these abundant streams to the sheep of Christ.]

drawn by the ministry of the poet Eustorgius.

### CL. Ennodius’s Apology for His Praises

Whoever marvels that I have exceeded the limits of duty in praising my friends

should recall how commanding affection always is, and that the force of love does not obey the laws of one’s purpose. Indeed, if he asks the reason for my action, he calls “devotion” what he had called excess.

So that eagles may be able to reveal offspring formed in their own likeness,

the life-giving inherent warmth breaks the tender egg.

Then the devoted, tireless father tears open the confined dwelling,

so that, through his efforts, those whom the womb produced may be born again.

At once the same judge summons Phoebus as witness to the lineage;

by probing with his light, he discovers the inner brightness.

In the same way a parent’s care exposes children born of a lofty lineage

to the rays of instruction.

See how steadily the tender ones receive the battles of flame,

overcoming lightning by their gaze.

### CLI. On Two Joined Houses

[Col. 0362B]

In twin houses a single pious glory shines,

and honor is joined together from what had been divided.

So that sacred uses should not be confused, whether at a distance or in the same place,

fortune gave the steadfast site a generous number.

One house, distinguished by a double building,

is joined together and shares the work it has well united.

## Appendix from Father Edmund Martène’s *New Treasury of Anecdotes*, Volume V, p. 61

### Ennodius’s Address on the Birthday of Laurentius, Bishop of Milan

(From the manuscript of Saint Remigius of Reims.) (C, G, S)

[Col. 0361C] It happens among human beings that as much as fame is diminished through boldness, no less is lost through fear. To write what is superfluous is vanity; to conceal what is necessary is contempt. Often the praise of a hidden teacher becomes the mother of blame. Affection sends forth an abundance of words; love suggests what talent denies. Let fear, hostile to a venerable purpose, withdraw. Glory is fleeting when the mind is subject to error. Without blame, a person is overcome by the immensity of the burden when, although unequal to carrying the load, he nevertheless comes forward devotedly. Joy without speech is withered, and it is an imitation of grief to conceal that you are rejoicing and, in the midst of happiness, to have no voice of gladness.

I am free to derive the beginnings of my speech from the season, and, if I can, to make my discourse bloom with the flower-filled infancy of the renewing year. Now, when the sap of the earth runs through the veins of drying shrubs into the grasses, and the womb of dry fuel, joined to moisture, swells; when the leafy hair of newly planted seed unfolds into gentle light upon the trees, and every interweaving of branches spreads out, while the natural ornaments of foliage are released from within their covering. When birdsong is attended by modulated sweetness, when the life of crops, buried in winter clods, is conceived—as though released from the barrier of frost and made pregnant by warmth. Now, in the white blossom, the farmer measures the hope of fruits, when the sunny beauty of the vineyards is woven together by the mutual arms of the vines, and before the time of ripeness cultivation shapes the fruit-bearing face, giving beauty with the taming sickle [Col. 0362D] and restraining sterile luxuriance with fruit-producing iron. When the violence of the deep whirlpool passes into a gentle hiss, and the fierceness of the winds, weakened by warmth, changes into delights for the sailor. When it is safe to loosen the little boat upon the sea and release the anchor from its biting hold. While the breaking of the storms that had so far terrified the sailors invites them onward and, across the watery expanses of the sea, permits the helmsman to sleep. When meadows, varied with jeweled color, grow rich with the resources of spring.

Gravity, modesty, chastity, and beauty have brought you to the highest pontifical office. Let these qualities establish praise in the place where it now belongs, since you possess what can be proclaimed about your character. Popular favor is driven by passing moments, and the unexamining crowd, carried away by enthusiasm, loves people it does not know. To one person you show that you are devout; to another, that you are strict; to another, that you are a distributor of a patrimony rightly acquired; to another, that you know how to preserve what has been rightly acquired. The entire community takes up this task: although each person might surpass another in the proposed praise, whether through comparison or conversation, nevertheless one would be surpassed by another in the proclamation of your superior title. [Col. 0363B] You did not know how to fear the cruelty of the plunderer; you rejected with the shield of steadfastness the poisons of flatteries, which are a more harmful weapon among the malicious.

[Note: [Col. 0363B] “To Venantius.” Perhaps the same Venantius to whom Ennodius addresses Letter 22 of Book V; see Sirmond’s note at that passage. The same Ennodius also mentions Venantius in Letter 9 of Book IV and calls him an illustrious man.]

### Ennodius to Venantius

Lord, I marvel at your restraint in speech, because he who has composed only a little produces nothing. Do you think that your knowledge can remain hidden under this pretext for your journey? Silence reveals incompetence, and an uncrafted conversation displays childishness. In the meantime, you were not previously lacking in grace, since you knew what diligence and the concern of one who loves require. You became conscious of good things after we sent you to obtain what are thought to be the greatest things. For the rest, farewell; receive the words of your admonisher, and, improved in yourself, make yourself known through assiduous writing.

### In the Year of the Lord 514–523

[Note: [Col. 0363C] The variants or notes that, after Labbe and Mansi, were copied into both margins of the page have for the most part been placed by us within parentheses in the text, and occasionally at the foot of the pages, preceded by an asterisk. Editor.]

## Pope Hormisdas

[Col. 0363]

### Notice

(From the *Book of the Pontiffs*.)

[Col. 0363B] [Note: [Col. 0363C] After Symmachus had been led from this life to eternal glory, with the entire Roman clergy in complete agreement and the schism removed, seven days after his death, on the seventh day before the Kalends of August, in the year of Christ 514, the twenty-fourth year of the emperor Anastasius and the twenty-second of King Theodoric, Hormisda, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, was created pope. When this became known throughout the world, Clovis [ [Col. 0363] King Childebert Clovis gives Saint Peter a golden crown] the most Christian king anticipated everyone’s obedience and surpassed them in service. For, at the suggestion of Remigius, he gave Blessed Peter a golden crown set with gems, which is commonly called a diadem; and for this deed he obtained from God the reward that the crown of the Frankish kingdom has endured to the present day.

During his pontificate the emperor Anastasius, a follower of Eutyches, plotted many measures for suppressing the Council of Chalcedon. Twice warned by the pope to see that the name of Acacius was expunged, in order to unite the Eastern Church with the Western, he not only failed to obey but began to persecute it with even greater fury [Col. 0363D]—especially once he had secured the favor of the Constantinopolitan populace by pretending to hold the orthodox faith, and had shaken off his fear of Vitalian, above all, who was in rebellion.

After perpetrating many crimes against the Church of God, he saw in a vision the figure of a man dressed in white addressing him in these words: “Behold, because of your perfidy I erase fourteen from you.” After these had been struck out in that book, he died on the third day with the crash of thunder.

Justin, a Catholic emperor who had been a keeper of cattle and swine, and a singular patron of the orthodox faith, was substituted by the senate and the entire army for Anastasius, defender of the Acephali. Then an anathema was proclaimed against all heretics; then the four ecumenical councils were approved; and all the events recorded in the acts of the council held at Constantinople under Hormisda, which are described below, took place.

When Hormisda was asked to confirm the decree of the council, after prior synodal consultation he replied that peace and communion requested by the Eastern Church were to be granted only if they completely erased and expunged the names of Acacius, Euphemius, and Macedonius, whom they had restored to the sacred registers.

To obtain this more quickly and easily, he sent a certain legation to Justin and to the bishop of Constantinople. With great care and exceptional diligence it was to ensure that the memory of the heretical emperors Zeno and Anastasius was condemned, that the formula of faith was secured by the bishops’ subscription, and finally that the name of Acacius and of the others whom they had restored to the sacred diptychs was plainly erased and utterly extinguished.

The matter succeeded according to the wish of the most holy pontiff. At this time the Easterners, who for approximately eighty years had separated themselves from the unity of the Church through schism, were received into communion with the Western Church [Col. 0364D]. This happened on the most holy feast of the Lord’s Resurrection, without any sedition or disturbance, and with such wonder, thanksgiving, and joy that scarcely any tongue can express it.

Baronius derived these things from Hormisda’s letters; from the notes on the letters and the councils that follow below you will learn more about the events carried out under Hormisda. Once the Catholic faith had been restored and freed from the bonds of schism, this further good resulted: it led the king and people of the Lazic realm, hitherto without knowledge of the true religion and divine law, to embrace the Christian faith.

Author of the *Miscellanies*, book XV. SEV. BINIUS.]

Hormisda was Campanian by birth, the son of Justus, from the city of Frusino (Frusione) [Col. 0364B] [Note: [Col. 0364D] Marcellinus in his *Chronicle* and the Vatican indices attest that he occupied the see for nine years and ten days, from the consulship of Cassiodorus to that of Maximus. Indeed, Anastasius himself contradicts himself here, placing Hormisda’s death and burial, and the accession of his successor John, under the consulship of Maximus. Therefore what Anastasius writes here about the duration of Hormisda’s pontificate is erroneous. SEV. BINIUS.], and sat for [Note: [Col. 0363D] Codex Luc. 490: 9.] eight years [Col. 0365A] and seventeen days.

He lived during the reigns of King Theodoric and the emperor Anastasius Augustus [Note: [Col. 0365C] Anastasius is mistaken, as is clear from what precedes above. SEV. BINIUS.], from the consulship of Senator to the consulship of Symmachus and Boethius.

He organized the clergy and instructed them in the psalms. He built a basilica in the Alban territory, on the estate [Note: [Col. 0365D] The same manuscript: Mefontis.] of Mesontis.

[Note: [Col. 0365C] For the pope’s first embassy to the emperor, see more in Baronius under the year 515, as well as the notes on Hormisda’s letters below. SEV. BINIUS.] At the same time, in accordance with the synod’s decision, he sent an embassy to Greece, displaying the apostolic see’s humanity (and reconciled the Greeks), because the Greeks were bound by the chain of anathema on account of Peter, bishop of Alexandria, and Acacius, bishop of Constantinople.

Under John, bishop of Constantinople, and with the counsel of King Theodoric (This pope went to King Theodoric at Ravenna and, on the king’s advice), he sent Ennodius, bishop of Ticinum, Fortunatus, bishop [Note: [Col. 0365D] The same manuscript: Catanensis.] of Catania, Venantius, a presbyter of the city of Rome [Col. 0365B], Vitalis, a deacon of the apostolic see, and [Note: [Col. 0365D] The same manuscript: Hilarium.] Hilary, a notary, to Anastasius Augustus. But they accomplished nothing.

[Note: [Col. 0365C] The second embassy, which he sent to the emperor in the year of Christ 517, the fourth of his pontificate. For more, see the notes on the letters. SEV. BINIUS.] He sent Ennodius [Note: [Col. 0365D] The same manuscript: “himself.”], bishop, and Peregrinus, bishop of Misenum (and Pollio, subdeacon of the city), carrying letters strengthening the faith and nineteen secret protests [*contestations*] [Note: [Col. 0365C] One of these survives below among Hormisda’s letters; it begins: “The first salvation is …,” etc. [Col. 0365D] Among other sacred statements he wrote this: “We wish to command, not to be commanded.” This letter is preserved below among Hormisda’s letters, after Letter 22; it begins: “Although something great ….” Near the end of this letter he says: “We can endure being insulted and annulled; we cannot be commanded.” This heretical emperor, very like Pharaoh, had cunningly pretended that he wished to obey the Roman pontiff in order to avoid Vitalian’s sword drawn against him and escape the scourges of God that pressed upon him; thus, merely in appearance, he bent his iron neck. But when he saw these dangers removed, he despised Moses together with God, and the pontiff together with Christ, with hardened obstinacy. What happened afterward in the East may be seen from the report of the archimandrites and monks of Second Syria, which is preserved below among Hormisda’s letters, after the twenty-second. SEV. BINIUS.]—the text of a written petition (and the petition by which they might return; if they refused to receive the letters, they were to scatter the protests throughout the cities).

In this petition Anastasius Augustus refused to agree, because he too had shared in the Eutychian heresy (he was in agreement with it). He therefore wanted to corrupt the envoys by means of a bribe [Note: [Col. 0365D] The manuscript adds: “but he could not.”]. But the envoys of the apostolic see, despising Anastasius Augustus, absolutely refused to accept money unless he effected satisfaction toward the apostolic see.

Then [Col. 0365C] the emperor, filled with fury, expelled them through a postern gate (a dangerous place) and put them aboard a dangerous ship (at the risk of death), together with soldiers and magistrates and prefects named Heliodorus and Demetrius [Col. 0366A]. The emperor Anastasius gave them this command: that they should enter no city.

But the envoys of the apostolic see secretly distributed the aforesaid nineteen letters concerning the faith throughout all the cities through the hands of monks and orthodox believers. Nevertheless, the bishops of the cities, who were Anastasius Augustus’s accomplices, out of fear that the letters might constitute a charge, all sent them to Constantinople.

Then Anastasius Augustus, filled with fury against Pope Hormisda, wrote among his other sacred statements: “We wish to command, not to be commanded.”

[Note: [Col. 0366C] Namely, in the year of Christ 518, after he had held the Eastern empire for twenty-seven years, three months, and twenty-nine days. What nightmares he suffered before his death I reported above from Zonaras. See Baronius, under the year 518, no. 16 and following. SEV. BINIUS.] At the same time, by divine will, the emperor Anastasius was struck by lightning (by a divine blow) and died.

Orthodox Justin therefore assumed the empire [Note: [Col. 0366C] By decree and decision of the synod of Constantinople, as is clear from the notes on that synod and from the letters written to Hormisda by Justin, John of Constantinople, and Justinian. SEV. BINIUS.] and sent his authority to Pope Hormisda of the apostolic see through Gratus, a man of illustrious rank [Note: [Col. 0366D] Codex Luc. 490: “hoping”], asking [Col. 0366B] the apostolic see that the peace of the churches be restored.

[Note: [Col. 0366C] Through this embassy the Easterners were received into union and communion with the Roman Church [Col. 0366D], after they had obeyed the command of the Roman pontiff, erased the names of Acacius, Euphemius, and Macedonius from the sacred diptychs, professed the Catholic faith in its entirety, and removed the memory of the heretical emperors Zeno and Anastasius from the list of emperors. Their names are nevertheless still found prefixed to various laws elsewhere in the Justinianic Code, because Tribonian, a pagan and impious man, compiled that same code, as we shall say below in the notes on the Life of Felix IV. This reconciliation of the Eastern Church with the Roman Church took place under the consulship of Justin, in the year of our Lord 519, the sixth year of Hormisda’s pontificate.]

Then Hormisda the bishop, with the counsel of King Theodoric, sent from the apostolic see Germanus [Note: [Col. 0366D] “Capuanus” is absent from the manuscript], bishop of Capua, John (bishop), and Blandus, presbyters, Felix and Dioscorus, deacons of the apostolic see, and Peter, a notary, furnished on every side with the faith and with the text of the penitential petition (together with the petition explaining how the Greeks were to return to communion with the apostolic see).

When they came near Constantinople, such grace of the faith shone upon them [Note: [Col. 0366D] In Codex Luc. 490, “upon them” is absent] that a very large multitude of orthodox monks and distinguished men came out to meet them. Among them Justin the emperor and Vitalian the consul (master of the soldiers) also came out together to the round fortress that leads (is said to extend) all the way to the city of Constantinople [Col. 0366C]. They entered together with Gratus, the Illustrious, and were received with glory by Justin the orthodox Augustus.

The entire clergy, together with John, bishop of Constantinople, therefore perceived [Note: [Col. 0366D] Codex Luc. 490: “understanding”] that they had been received with favor. Those who were Acacius’s accomplices, perceiving this as well, shut themselves inside the principal church called Hagia Sophia. After taking counsel, they sent word to the emperor, saying: “Unless an explanation is given us of why our bishop Acacius has been condemned (the bishop of our city), we will in no way consent to the apostolic see.”

This Pope Hormisda went to King Theodoric at Ravenna and, with his counsel, sent his authority to Justin; and with the bond of his signed document and the text of the petition, he restored unity with the apostolic see, condemning Peter and Acacius, as well as all heresies.

He found Manichaeans there too, whom, after examining them by means of beatings, he sent into exile. He burned their books before the doors of the Basilica of Constantine.

[Note: [Col. 0367C] By the authority of certain Vandal kings it had been established, as we saw above, that Catholics in Africa should not ordain other bishops in place of the dead. But Hilderic, son of Huneric, who took possession of the kingdom after the death of King Thrasamund in the ninth year of Hormisda’s pontificate, which is the year 522 of Christ, ordered (as Isidore testifies in his *Chronicle*) that the Catholic priests should be recalled from exile and the churches opened. He did this before he became king, lest he violate the religious obligation of the oath by which he had promised his predecessor Thrasamund, already dying, that he would open no churches to Catholics in his kingdom and restore none of their privileges. God wished to increase the most blessed pontiff by this blessing as well [Col. 0368C], so that after seeing the Eastern Church restored to Catholic communion, he might also see Africa—long afflicted by persecution and most recently trampled underfoot by King Thrasamund after all its bishops had been expelled—restored to its former splendor. Enriched by these and other gifts from God, he was finally called to the heavenly realms in the following year, ready to receive the crown of victory, as though, like the aged Simeon, he had already received the promise from the Lord that he would not see death before seeing Christ the Lord: namely, after the schism had been dissolved and the Eastern Church united with the Western, and the Western Church in Africa, once the tyrannical persecutor had been removed, had been restored to its former condition. SEV. BINIUS.]

During his pontificate the episcopate in Africa, after seventy-four years, was restored [Col. 0367B]—that is, reordained—after it had been exterminated by the heretics.

At the same time a royal gift arrived, with precious gems, from Clovis [Note: [Col. 0368D] This name is absent from chapter II, where the following is read: “At the same time a golden crown with the most precious gems arrived as a gift from the king of the Franks.” Correctly so.] the Christian king, for the apostle Blessed Peter.

During his episcopate many golden and silver vessels arrived from Greece, together with Gospels with golden covers, with precious gems weighing fifteen pounds; a golden paten with hyacinths, weighing twenty pounds, two silver patens, each weighing twenty-five pounds, a golden cup with gems, weighing eight pounds, a golden cup encircled by a diadem, weighing eight pounds, two gilded silver cups, each weighing five pounds, an amber-colored [*electrina*] bowl [Note: [Col. 0367C] Codex Luc. 490: *ylietina*.], weighing two pounds, two golden wax cases, weighing six pounds, and a small cloak [*palliolum*] of purple wool [Note: [Col. 0367D] The same manuscript: “a purple *olobyra*.”], with gold-covered panels, made from a *chlamys* or imperial robe [Note: [Col. 0367D] The same manuscript: “*suffictorium*.”], and a girdle [*succinctorium*] over the confession of the blessed apostle Peter [Col. 0367C].

All these things were offered by Justin Augustus [Note: [Col. 0367D] The same manuscript: “orthodox,”] in the pious fulfillment of his vows [Col. 0368A].

At the same time King Theodoric offered Blessed Peter the apostle two silver *cerostrata*, weighing [Note: [Col. 0367D] The manuscript adds: “each.”] seventy pounds.

At the same time Pope Hormisda made at Blessed Peter’s a beam, which he covered with silver; it weighed [Note: [Col. 0367D] Codex Luc. 490: 1,040.] one thousand and forty pounds.

He made in the Constantinian basilica a silver arch before the altar, weighing twenty pounds; and sixteen silver *canthara*, each weighing twelve pounds.

[Note: [Col. 0367D] In the same manuscript: “Likewise at Blessed Paul’s … six pounds”; everything is missing.] Likewise, at Blessed Paul’s he made two silver arches, each weighing twenty pounds; sixteen silver *canthara*, each weighing fifteen pounds; three silver *amae*, weighing three pounds; and six silver station cups with handles, each weighing six pounds.

[Note: [Col. 0368C] The same manuscript: “four.”] He held ordinations in the city of Rome during the month of December: twenty-one presbyters and fifty-five bishops in various places.

He too was buried [Col. 0368B] in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, on the eighth day before the Ides of August [Note: [Col. 0368D] Absent from the *v. c.* manuscript of Hardy, which we have used up to this point in reviewing the Lives of the Roman pontiffs.], in the consulship of Maximus. And the episcopate was vacant for seven days [Note: [Col. 0368D] The same manuscript: six.].

From the Hardy manuscript: After a council had likewise been held with Justin, the matter was discussed in the presence of all the illustrious men. Then the envoys of the apostolic see chose from among themselves the deacon Dioscorus to give an explanation. He then set forth for them the offenses of Acacius, so that all together, joining in the discussion with Justin, cried out, saying: “Acacius is condemned both now and forever.”

At the same time King Justin, having learned the truth, ordered that without any delay all the bishops who were in Justin’s kingdom should draw up petitions and return to communion with the apostolic see. This was also done, and they were reconciled from East to West, and peace ran throughout the Church.

The text of this petition is kept today in the archive of the Church.

[Col. 0367]

# Letters and Decrees of Pope Hormisda (C, S)

## First Letter of Pope Hormisda to Saint Remigius, Bishop of Rheims

After receiving congratulatory letters from him, Hormisda, on account of the excellence of his distinguished merits and the prerogative of his most noble see, delegated to him the vicariate of the apostolic see in Gaul.

[Col. 0367D]

[Col. 0368D] Hormisda to his most beloved brother Remigius.

Having received the communications of your fraternity, full of congratulations, in which the bodily safety supporting your spiritual duties made us rejoice through the evidence of your genuine salvation, we have recognized that it is fitting to disclose in words this very joy which we carry in our mind [Col. 0369A].

For you are providing evidence of a supreme pontiff when you both do things worthy of praise and do not delay in making them known. We have therefore assumed the prerogative of our judgment when we learned that you had accomplished what we urge others to undertake with the greatest determination: namely, that in provinces separated by such great distance you should take care to preserve both the vigor of the apostolic see and the rules of the Fathers.

Therefore, throughout the entire kingdom of our beloved spiritual son Louis (he had already died in the year 511), whom, with the help of heavenly grace, you recently converted, together with his whole people, through very many miracles accompanying the saving preaching—miracles comparable to those of the apostles—and consecrated through the gift of sacred baptism, we entrust our authority to you by this present instrument, without prejudice to the privileges which antiquity has decreed for metropolitans [Col. 0369B].

By sharing in this service we increase the dignity of your ministry and lighten our own vigils through the relief afforded by this administration. And although you do not need to be instructed about individual matters, since we have already proved that you preserve everything more keenly, it is nevertheless usually more welcome when a path is shown to those who are about to travel and the form of the assigned task is displayed to those who are about to labor.

We therefore command that the paternal rules and decrees defined by the most holy councils be observed by all. In these matters we display your vigilance; in them we show the care and exhortations of fraternal admonition.

When these regulations have been guarded with the reverence they deserve, no obstacle to holy observance leaves room for fault. There what is lawful and unlawful has been prescribed; there what is forbidden has been marked out, something to which no one should dare aspire; there what is permitted has been granted, which a mind seeking to please God ought to undertake [Col. 0369C].

Whenever the cause of religion requires a universal council, let all the brethren assemble when summoned by you. If the particular concern of any of them presses upon you, restrain disputes that have arisen among them, determining their controversies after examining them according to sacred law.

Whatever is established there for the faith and truth, prescribed by prudent administration, or confirmed by the authority of our person, must all be brought to our knowledge through a report furnished with testimony. In this way both our mind enjoys the love of the duty entrusted to us and yours enjoys the security of what has been received.

May God preserve you safe and sound, dearest brother. (In the year of the Lord 514.)

[Note: [Col. 0369D] Against the emperor Anastasius, who had expelled orthodox bishops, God raised Vitalian the Scythian, master of the cavalry. After occupying several provinces and advancing by plundering as far as Constantinople, he declared, as Marcellinus testifies in his *Chronicle*, that he was doing everything for the faith of the orthodox and for the restoration of Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople, whom the emperor had exiled.

Seeing that his affairs were desperate, Anastasius sought peace, swearing with the senate that he would recall the envoys, restore their episcopates to Macedonius and Flavian, hold a council at Heraclea, and summon the Roman pontiff to it.

Accordingly, when a council at Heraclea had been announced, on 25 December in the year of the Lord [Col. 0370D] 514 he sent a letter to the Roman pontiff, preserved below after Hormisda’s third letter, informing him about the future synod and asking him to attend in order to reconcile the Churches.

Knowing that this would be more easily obtained if the Roman pontiff possessed full authority to accomplish the matter, Vitalian and Anastasius sent Patricius, a man of the highest rank, as envoy to Pope Hormisda with this letter. Dorotheus, bishop of Thessalonica, added below his own letter, which has almost the same content.

What the pontiff replied is clear from the following three letters. SEV. BINIUS.]

## Letter of Anastasius to Pope Hormisda

He asks the pontiff to be willing to convene a council to settle the disputes that had arisen in the regions of Scythia. (C)

[Col. 0369D]

Victor Anastasius, pious, fortunate, illustrious, triumphant, [Col. 0370A] ever Augustus, to Hormisda, most holy and most religious archbishop and patriarch.

We do not think that it is unknown to Your Beatitude that divine Scripture, in its providence, has ordained what should be said and what should be kept silent according to the circumstances of the time. The completion of the period of silence has therefore granted us encouragement to speak.

For this reason we have judged it opportune to entrust to your hearing what is being stirred up among us under the appearance of religion. Previously, the harshness of those to whom responsibility for the episcopate which you now hold had been entrusted made us refrain from sending letters.

But now, as a pleasing opinion of you has spread, it has recalled to our memory the goodness of paternal affection, so that we may seek what our God and Savior taught the holy apostles in divine speech, and especially blessed Peter, in whom [Col. 0370B] he established the strength of his Church.

With these introductory words, therefore, we urge Your Apostolate to make itself a mediator in the matters that have arisen in the regions of Scythia, since we have also recognized that a council should be convened there, so that, once disputes have been cut off, the unity of the holy Church may be restored.

Everything we desire is granted to us if you remember us in your prayers and in frequent communications by letter.

Given on the day before the Ides of January at Constantinople, and received when Anthemios and Florentius, men of the highest rank, were consuls, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April through Patricius. (Given and received in the year of the Lord 515.)

## Letter II: Reply to the Emperor Anastasius
