He praises him for his concern for the Church’s peace and, once he has learned the reason why Anastasius desires the council to be convened, promises to give him a reply.

[Col. 0370C]

Hormisda, bishop, to Anastasius Augustus.

Thanks be to the heavenly power, which through the words of Your Piety has deigned to end a prolonged silence, offering such a beginning of conversation that we rejoice in the prosperity of Your Clemency and confidently hope that, with God’s gift, the holy Church can return to unity.

This was the work of heavenly clemency, and this was always the prayer of our predecessors, whom the events of history also show to have been ministers of paternal tradition and guardians of the right faith.

Peace is the beginning of all goodness. In relation to the worship of the Catholic faith, nothing is stronger and nothing ought to be considered more exalted than peace. It is therefore fitting to do and endure everything for it if one desires to be a credible disciple of the sacred Scriptures.

Christ our Lord is known to have proclaimed peace as the mother and nurse of all good things to his disciples, saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14).

With the religious care of your purpose, and with the Lord’s inspiration, you are providing for this peace when you consider the concord of the orthodox Church in reverence for blessed Peter the apostle, specially observing the divine commands.

This matter secures for your empire a greater defense from heavenly favor. Rightly offered worship to God grants an impregnable wall of defense to devoted minds.

Therefore we earnestly entreat almighty God, with prayers poured forth, that he who has granted you the zeal to seek peace among the Churches may himself, while preserving the Catholic faith, grant fulfillment to your desire in this matter.

Moreover, in the sacred communication sent to us, Your Piety deigned to mention a holy council. Concerning this matter we shall then be able to provide a fully developed answer, when he makes us clearly understand the reason for the assembly [Col. 0371B].

But now, since, by the favor of our Lord, the opportunity for conversation has been granted, we shall offer the appropriate duties of speech with due reverence.

Given on the day before the Nones of April (in the year of the Lord 515), in the consulship of Florentius, a man of the highest rank.

## Letter of Dorotheus, Bishop of Thessalonica, to Pope Hormisda

He praises the pontiff for caring about the Church’s unity and says that he desires the heretics to be condemned and the honor due to the Roman Church to be rendered. (C)

To the sacred, most blessed, and fellow-minister Pope Hormisda, Dorotheus, bishop of Thessalonica, sends greetings in the Lord.

[Col. 0371C] In one passage the most blessed Solomon, bringing forth all the wonders of the divine commandments, says: “As cold water is sweet to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a distant land” (Proverbs 25). And the sacred David, striking his spiritual lyre, sings: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim good things” (Romans 10), thus teaching us all.

What is so sweet to a man’s soul, or so invigorating to his bones, as to learn through beautiful news that the herald of true peace, and the champions of the right and never-erring faith, are taking charge of the holy Churches; that, as though from a certain citadel, they are gathering the dispersed into agreement with God; that they are hastening immediately to the primacy of your see, yielding to the supplications of a venerable brother; that the members of the Church, which Christ our God has entrusted to you [Col. 0371D], though previously despising concord, are coming to unity; that the earlier division and hatred have been destroyed by the decision (quietly) of your ordination alone; and that now every boundary of that holy Church is flowing together (or being fused, or standing together) into concord and fellowship?

We learned these things not long ago. But because we knew the ancient custom of the Church and had heard of your companionable and irreproachable manner, we hoped to learn firmer and clearer things from your letters.

But since it is understood that the winter season detained you from fulfilling these matters, it was fitting and proper, in a full and God-loving charity, to pass over even what was rough or scrupulous. I write [Col. 0372A] and address the blessed head of Your Holiness, declaring that we rejoice with the blessed see of the most sacred apostle Peter, because it is governed by a hand that has received not one who would seize honor, but one who would be seized by it; and—as the manifold tradition says, and as we believe the matter to be—one crowned, as with precious stones, with peace-making, championship of the right faith, humility (or humanity) of mind, and charity toward all.

For I want you, venerable father, to recognize everything: receiving from the ancient, holy, and venerable Fathers the affection of that blessed see, and preserving it as a paternal inheritance, I wish and hasten to add this, that a useful conclusion may come to this endeavor through the humanity of our Lord and God Jesus Christ, and through the intercessions of the most blessed [Col. 0372B] apostle Peter in all things and of the most wise Paul in everything.

Thus, let the honor justly due to their venerable see and to Your Beatitude be preserved and restored (or added), so that in our times it may receive the honor fitting to its rank after the primacy of the apostolic see; let every discord depart; and let all the Churches, by the Catholic will of you all and also of our Lord and God Jesus Christ, forever anathematize the impious Nestorius and Eutyches, those who preserve their doctrines, those who were or are their followers, and every heresy.

Let them hold the right and undefiled faith unshaken, like a sure and firm anchor, and now prepare peace, with no one hindering it—God forbid—especially since your venerable head, as we have learned, hates contentious men [Col. 0372C], for whom the separation of the priests of God disputing among themselves is both life and food. Since they are not quickly recognized by everyone, may such men be easily driven away from the apostolic Church, like wolves in sheep’s clothing.

I have now written these things to your blessed head through Patricius, a man of distinction, our common son, who surpasses custom in affection, is bound to that blessed see by charity, and desires every day to see that fitting and proper reverence is preserved for it.

Write, therefore, blessed one, in all things as one who is of one mind with us and desires even to offer his soul for the orthodox faith and the peace of the holy Churches, and desires that what is fitting for the venerable see of blessed Peter be preserved in all things. This will easily happen once all are ordered in unity and all hasten to you as to a secure harbor [Col. 0372D].

For divisions have always been accustomed to despise one another and fail to preserve what is fitting for order. I, and those who are with me, send many greetings in the Lord to the entire brotherhood attached to Your Holiness.

And in another hand: Pray that I may be saved in the Lord, most holy and blessed Fathers.

The letter of Dorotheus, bishop of the Church of Thessalonica, sent through Patricius, a man of the highest rank, was received under the date of the fifth day before the Kalends of April (in the year of the Lord 515), in the consulship of Florentius, a man of the highest rank.

## Letter III: To Dorotheus, Bishop of Thessalonica

He praises his piety and zeal for the Roman see.

To his most beloved brother Dorotheus, bishop: Hormisda, bishop.

[Col. 0373A] Wherever the commands of charity require preservation, even if something occurs that could move anyone’s spirit, nevertheless, so that the things we previously stated in the fellowship of concord may be preserved, it is necessary to pass over the matter calmly; for if something of this sort should arise through ignorance, it can certainly receive an excuse from that very simplicity.

Our God established his Church by his own ordinance, so that what is known to have been arranged by divine commands may in no way be passed over. You ought not to be ignorant of its knowledge or understanding.

For we are praised when we do good, and the adornment of words is then made complete when it properly joins together things that correspond to one another.

We have received your letter of affection through our son Patricius, a man of distinction, in which we hope to find a work complete and worthy of approval, so that there might be nothing that could separate it from the integrity of unity [Col. 0373B].

But since in that same letter you promise an affection that can specially urge us toward the matter we have mentioned, we pour out prayers to our Lord, asking that he, whose cause is also being handled, after removing or cutting off every scandal, may make his Church joined together under one agreement and in equal faith.

May he not allow anything to be found in his priests that seeks to please anyone through personal hatred, empty purposes, or men’s favor against God—which God forbid—and may he not permit them to deviate from the future hope by failing to despise all worldly things, according to the blessed apostle.

I exhort you for the sake of a common remedy; I invite you for the salvation of the faithful; I urge you for the sake of a universal medicine. For who would be content to see divided those whose unity he can celebrate? Therefore common labor is necessary, so that, preserving what we received from our Fathers, we may be able to stand with confidence before the divine judgment.

## Letter of Anastasius Augustus to Pope Hormisda

A council is to be convened at Heraclea to settle questions concerning the faith that had arisen in Scythia, and he asks the pontiff himself to attend it. (C)

Anastasius Augustus to Pope Hormisda.

Divine matters must be placed before all other business. With almighty God propitious, we trust that the commonwealth must both be preserved and improved.

Since, therefore, certain doubts about the orthodox religion appear to have arisen in the regions of Scythia, it has especially pleased Our Clemency that a venerable synod be held in the city of Heraclea in the province of Europe, so that, with minds in agreement and the whole truth examined, our true faith may become more clearly known to the entire world, and so that afterward there may be no doubt or discord.

Therefore may Your Holiness, together with whatever most reverend bishops you wish—those whom, from the Churches established under the care of their priesthood, you have judged capable and instructed in orthodox religion [Col. 0374A]—deign to come to the aforesaid city of Heraclea by the Kalends of July.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of January at Constantinople, in the consulship of Senator, a man of the highest rank. Received on the day before the Ides of May, in the consulship of Florentius, a man of the highest rank. (Given in the year of the Lord 514, received the following year.)

## Letter IV: To Anastasius Augustus, the Emperor

He commends the emperor’s zeal and promises to give his answer concerning the council through envoys.

Hormisda to Anastasius Augustus, through Severianus.

Your Clemency rightly trusts, as your glorious communications to me have indicated, that it will especially benefit your state if the cause of orthodox faith is placed before all other concerns. For this is the soundest concern of a ruler who has assumed the direction of affairs: to win for himself, through good works, the favor of Him who both grants and governs the whole empire. Therefore it is fitting that I too should beseech our Lord Jesus Christ, that He who has willed your Piety to consider the concord of His Church may deign to grant an effective outcome in this matter, so that in your times the whole world, endowed with orthodox faith, may rejoice.

[Note: He sent the four legates named in the heading of the following memorandum, not to hold a council, but only to discover with what intention he had asked that a synod be held: whether he was prepared, as he had promised, to profess the catholic faith, receive the letter of Saint Leo, and anathematize the heretics. This was so that the majesty of the Apostolic See might not be mocked by him while he abused pontifical authority, not to establish the catholic faith, but to confirm his rule and turn Vitalianus aside. The following memorandum and instruction report how they were to conduct themselves before the emperor. — Severus Binius.]

But concerning what you ordered to be done regarding the synodal assembly, I have instructed my brothers and fellow bishops, who will follow shortly, to report to Your Glory what ought to be done. Through their communication, if divine favor supports my prayers, you will be able to learn everything more appropriately. Given on 8 July [A.D. 515], in the consulship of Florentius.

## Memorandum given by Pope Hormisdas to the bishops Ennodius and Fortunatus, the presbyter Venantius, the deacon Vitalis, and the notary Hilarius, legates of the Apostolic See to Constantinople

[Col. 0374C]

With God’s help and the prayers of the apostles, when you come into the regions of Greece, receive the bishops with the veneration that is fitting, if they wish to meet you. And if they wish to arrange a separate gathering, do not reject it, lest laypeople judge that you are unwilling to have any concord with them. But if they wish to invite you to a banquet, decline with a courteous excuse, saying:

“Pray that we may first deserve to share that mystical table, and then this one will be more pleasing to us.”

As for provisions and whatever else they may wish to offer, except for transportation when circumstances require it, do not accept them. Excuse yourselves in this way, saying that nothing is lacking, and hoping also that they may attach their minds to you, where there are gifts and riches, charity and unity, and whatever is certainly appropriate to religious joy.

When, by God’s favor, you arrive at Constantinople under these arrangements, withdraw to the place appointed by the most merciful emperor. Before you see him, [Col. 0375A] do not give anyone permission to come to you except those whom his Piety sends. After you have seen the emperor, however, if any orthodox persons who are in our communion, or who are zealous for unity, wish to see you, receive them with every precaution. Through them you may perhaps discover what is being done.

When you are presented to the emperor, hand him the letters with this address:

“Your father sends you greetings. He daily begs God, and commends your reign to the intercession of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, praying that God, who has given you such a desire that you chose to have men sent and to consult for the welfare of His Church, may Himself also grant the fulfillment of your will.”

If, before receiving the documents, he wishes to learn the nature of the embassy, use these words:

“Order the writings to be received.”

If he says, “What do the documents contain?” answer:

“They contain greetings to Your Piety and give thanks to God because they know that you are concerned for the unity of the Church. Read them, and you will understand.”

Do not mention any matter at all unless the letters have first been received and reread. After the letters have been received and read, add:

“He has also sent a letter to your servant Vitalianus, who, having received permission from Your Piety—as he himself wrote—sent his men to your holy father the pope. But since it was right that he should first direct them to Your Clemency, he did this so that, by your command and arrangement, the writings we have brought might, with God’s favor, be conveyed to him.”

If the emperor asks for the letters sent by us to Vitalianus, answer as follows:

“Your holy father the pope did not command this of us, nor can we do anything without his order. Nevertheless, so that you may know the simplicity of the letters—for they contain nothing else but prayers addressed to Your Piety, asking you to devote your mind to the unity of the Church—let us have present the person in whose presence the letters delivered by us may be read.”

But if he says that he himself ought to read them, answer:

“You have already been informed that we were not ordered to do this by the holy pope.”

If he says, “Is this all that the letters contain? For other matters may also be conveyed through instructions,” then answer:

“Far be this from our conscience. It is not our custom. We have come for God’s cause, and we entrust ourselves to God. The embassy of the holy pope is straightforward, and his request itself is known to all: that the decrees of the Fathers not be corrupted, and that heretics be removed from the Churches. Our embassy contains nothing beyond this.”

If he says, “For this reason also I invited the holy pope to the synod, so that if anything is ambiguous it may be removed,” answer:

“We give thanks to God, and to Your Petition [variant: Piety], because we know that you possess this desire and intention: that the decrees established by the Fathers should be preserved by the whole Church. For true and holy unity can exist among the Churches of Christ only if, with God’s help, you choose to preserve what your predecessors Marcian and Leo safeguarded.”

If he says, “What are these things of which you speak?” answer:

“That the Council of Chalcedon and the letters of the holy pope Leo, written against the heretics Nestorius, Eutyches, and Dioscorus, may in no way be corrupted.”

If he says, “We have both received and maintain the Council of Chalcedon and the letters of Pope Leo,” immediately give thanks and kiss his breast, saying:

“Now we know that God is favorable to you, since you hasten to do such things. For this is the catholic faith; this is the faith preached by the apostles, without which no one can be orthodox. The whole body of priests must hold and preserve it by preaching.”

If he says, “The bishops are orthodox; they do not depart from the decrees of the Fathers,” answer:

“Then, if the decrees of the Fathers are preserved and nothing is corrupted of what was established at the holy Council of Chalcedon, what is the cause of such discord among the Churches of these regions? Or what causes the bishops of the East not to agree as one?”

If he says, “The bishops were at peace, and no discord existed among them. The predecessor of the holy pope stirred their minds by sending letters and brought them to the point of stirring up confusion,” answer:

“We have in our hands the letters sent by Symmachus of holy memory. If, apart from what Your Piety has said—that is, following the Council of Chalcedon and accepting the letters of Pope Leo—they contain nothing except an exhortation that these things be preserved, how is it true that confusion was generated through him? But if the letters contain what your father hopes for and Your Piety approves, what did he do? What, indeed, appears culpable in him?”

Add prayers and tears to this, entreating him:

“My lord emperor, consider God; place His future judgment before your eyes. The holy Fathers who established these things followed the faith of the blessed apostles, upon which the Church of Christ has been built.”

If the emperor says, “What do you wish me to do by this speech?” [Roman Edition: “to persecute him?”; variants: “by prosecution,” “by a settlement”], understand it thus:

“Here I am: communicate with me, since I receive the Council of Chalcedon and embrace the letters of Pope Leo. Now communicate with me.”

Answer:

“In what manner does Your Piety desire that communion with you be established? We do not avoid proclaiming Your Piety in this matter. We know that you fear God, and we rejoice that you regard it as pleasing to preserve the decrees of the Fathers. We therefore confidently ask that through you the Church may return to unity. Let all the bishops know your will, and that you preserve the Council of Chalcedon and the letters of Pope Leo, as well as the decrees of the Apostolic See.”

If he says that it is necessary to show in what manner these things should be done, again offer prayers with humility, saying:

“Your father has written generally to the bishops. Join your sacred letters to his, declaring that you uphold [variants: indicate or judge] what the Apostolic See preaches. Then those who are orthodox will not be separated from the unity of the Apostolic See, and those who oppose these things will be recognized. Once these matters have been arranged, your father is also prepared, if necessary, to lend his presence and, while preserving the decrees of the Fathers, to refuse nothing that is expedient for the integrity of the Church.”

If the emperor says, “Very well; meanwhile receive the bishop of our city,” again join prayers to your response, saying humbly:

“My lord emperor, with God’s help we have come to make peace, with your support and assistance, and to quiet the contention [variant: intention] in your city. The dispute concerns two persons. This matter has its proper order: first let the whole body of bishops be arranged; let there be one catholic communion; and then, in the next place, the case of these men—or of any others who are outside their Churches—can be examined more carefully.”

If the emperor says, “You mean Macedonius; I understand your subtlety. He is a heretic and cannot be recalled for any reason,” answer:

“We, my lord emperor, are not judging anyone personally. And if Your Piety considers the matter, we are speaking rather for the sake of your soul and reputation, so that there may be an examination and, if he is a heretic, the matter may be established by judgment, lest he be unjustly said to have been oppressed under the reputation of orthodoxy.”

If the emperor says, “What do you want? You now speak about the Council of Chalcedon, and then you will speak about the letters of Pope Leo. Here is the bishop of this city; he agrees to these things,” answer:

“If he preserves them in this way, they will be able to help him more in the examination of his case. And since you gave your servant Vitalianus, the master of the soldiers, permission of this kind—that, if he hoped for it from the most blessed pope, these persons might have their cases examined before him and that everything might be preserved intact in matters that could be disputed according to their place—”

If the emperor says, “Should my city be without a bishop? Do you approve that there be no bishop where I reside?” answer:

“We have already stated that the dispute in this city concerns two persons. As for what pertains to the canons, we have already explained it: to dissolve the canons is to commit irreligion. There are many remedies, many arrangements by which Your Piety need not remain without communion and the integrity of judicial procedure may be preserved.”

If he says, “What are these remedies?” answer:

“They are not newly invented by us. While the case of the other bishops is suspended, the person who agrees with Your Piety’s confession and with the decrees of the Apostolic See may, until the outcome of the investigation, hold the place of the priest of Constantinople, if, with God’s help, the bishops are willing to accommodate themselves to the Apostolic See. You have the text of the document issued in the archives of the Church, according to which they are to make their profession.”

If petitions have nevertheless been submitted against other catholic bishops, accept petitions especially against those who shamelessly anathematize the Council of Chalcedon and do not receive the letters of the holy pope Leo. Reserve the case, however, for the judgment of the Apostolic See, so that you may give them hope of a hearing while reserving for us the authority that is owed to us.

If the most serene emperor promises that he will do everything, provided only that we lend our presence, first send his sacred commitment to us by way of the bishops and through your letter—[Roman Edition: “or through”] one of your men carrying it through the provinces—together with the persons whom the emperor appoints. Thus it will become known to everyone that he preserves the Council of Chalcedon and the letters of the holy pope Leo. When these matters have proceeded in this way, send us written word, in Christ’s name, so that we may arrange our coming.

Furthermore, it is customary for all bishops to be presented to the emperor through the bishop of Constantinople. If their crafty arrangement discovers this device, wishing you to recognize the prescribed form of the embassy so that you may see the emperor together with Timothy, who now appears to govern the Church of Constantinople, act as follows: if, before you enter to the emperor, you learn that this has been arranged through certain persons, say, although you have not yet been presented:

“Your Piety’s father gave us these instructions and commands: that we should see Your Clemency without any of the bishops.”

Proceed in this way until he himself withdraws from this custom.

But if he absolutely refuses, or if it happens deceptively that you unexpectedly see Timothy before seeing the emperor, make this request:

“Let Your Piety order that a private audience be granted us, so that we may explain the matters for which we have been sent.”

If he says, “Speak; here he is before you,” answer:

“We are not committing an injury. But as far as the matters at issue are concerned, our embassy also includes his person, and he cannot be present during our representations.”

Under no circumstances make any allegation while he is present. Once he has gone out, produce the text of the delegation:

“Thus far the memorandum, or what they call the instruction. After it follow the statements concerning the individual cases, in this manner.”

## Chapters concerning the individual cases

[Col. 0378C]

That the Council of Chalcedon and the letters of the holy pope Leo be preserved. And that the most merciful emperor, agreeing to this, should send his sacred general letters to all the bishops, in which he declares that he both believes and upholds the matters stated above.

The bishops who agree must also proclaim these things in the Church, in the presence of the Christian people:

“That they embrace the holy faith of Chalcedon and the letters of the holy pope Leo, which he wrote against the heretics Nestorius, Eutyches, and Dioscorus, and also against their followers, Timothy Aelurus and Peter, and against those who are held liable in this same matter; likewise, that they anathematize Acacius, who was once bishop of the Church of Constantinople, and also Peter of Antioch, together with their associates.”

Writing these things in their own hand, in the presence of chosen and venerable men, they must act according to the text of the document that we issued through our notary.

Those deported into exile on ecclesiastical grounds are to be recalled for a hearing before the Apostolic See, so that judgment and a true examination may be conducted concerning them, while their cases are fully reserved for investigation.

If any persons who communicated with the Holy Apostolic See, preaching and following the catholic faith, have been driven out or are being held in exile, it is right that they be recalled before all else.

Furthermore, among the other matters that we entrusted to the legates, we instructed them that, if petitions should be presented against bishops who persecuted catholics, judgment concerning these men is to be reserved to the Apostolic See, so that the decrees of the venerable Fathers may be preserved in their regard and thereby edification may come to the whole Church.

## LETTER V. TO THE EMPEROR AUGUSTUS ANASTASIUS

It is unprecedented for the Roman pontiff to be summoned by the emperor to a council; nevertheless, he will go if the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon are not called into question.

### Bishop Hormisdas to Augustus Anastasius

Your Serenity rightly and beneficially exercises the care of principal judgment not only in administering the state but also in ennobling it through better institutions; and through your concern to restore unity you appease the Author of the venerable empire. For the protection of the Church is secure under a reigning ruler if, while the same rulers preside, its purity is not stained by the unwelcome mixture of the devil.

How can it be that the Church sends pure prayers to our God on behalf of rulers if the people have been fatally corrupted by unbelief? For just as, before all good things, perfect wisdom according to God is required in emperors, so supplication on their behalf ought to proceed from a sanctuary of pure hearts, with the fruitful faithfulness of souls. No material for triumphs, most exalted lord, can be more pleasing to you than the subjugation of unbelief.

We also confidently make this representation by virtue of the prerogative of the office entrusted to us: a man comes near to allowing his own splendor to be darkened by another’s cloud when, although he can remove darkness by God’s gift, he permits the shadows of error to remain among his subjects.

Therefore, since Your Gentleness has summoned the future synod by most sacred writings and has reminded us in those same pages—by God, as we believe, commanding you—that we ought to attend it, we rejoice, knowing that it belongs to upright minds to seek the teachers of the venerable Church. Only those whose lives are not self-controlled avoid an examination of conscience. Even with restrained speech, the man who desires to be confirmed or corrected through apostolic and undefiled faith and through competent preachers proclaims the splendor of good will.

Nevertheless, although no example of an earlier age exists in these matters, and although the character of an earlier precedent is recorded neither in books nor in memories, this does not concern us. By God’s favor, it is sweet for us, at the invitation of Your Piety, to begin better things and to impose upon ourselves an undertaking of such a distinguished work as we did not receive from our parents. We gladly embrace everything that contributes to the restoration of faith and the peace of the Churches, provided that the definition of our ancestors and the teaching of the holy Fathers remain unshaken at their roots; provided that Nestorius and his associates are anathematized—he who, emptying the divine sacraments of their nature, falsely claims that the blessed virgin Mary is the mother of a mere man, forgetting the angelic annunciation through which it was made known to the world that what would be born from her would be called holy, the Son of God.

Let the impious and most insulting honor paid to God by such men depart. For the divinity acted in the virgin’s womb in such a way that from her there proceeded the unity of flesh and human soul, an uncreated yet not confused union of substance; and if, in both natures, for love of our redemption, the person of Christ Jesus our Lord is one, the mystery being accomplished [lacuna] could have undergone death in nature [lacuna] and could by the power of heavenly sovereignty restore its weakness; or thus, for the unity of the person, both the Lord of majesty may be believed to have been crucified and the Son of Man to have descended from heaven.

The ignorance of Eutyches concerning all divine goods must likewise be rejected, together with the detestable name of him and his associates; they testified that God and our Lord Jesus Christ possessed only the appearance of flesh and did not possess the reality of our substance, not knowing of whom it was promised: “They shall see the one whom they pierced.” Thus both natures persist in one and the same person, so that Jesus Christ, one Son of God, appears to the hearts of the faithful as both God and man.

For what did the Lord’s presence accomplish during the forty days after the resurrection, when he lived and ate with human beings? Except that, in these matters, for the sake of those who would deny the reality of the flesh, he showed that the age of healing was greater than the age of the wound. Thus he said to the disciples:

“Why are you troubled in your hearts? Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24; John 20).

Nor would it have been a mystery that he entered while the doors were shut if he did not possess the integrity of a human body.

From this gift of the Word we could extend the preceding discourse at greater length, but we believe it sufficient to beseech Your Learned Clemency through our brief representations, hoping that, following the example of your venerable predecessors Marcian and Leo, you will strengthen the labor and care of the pastoral office also through the participation of imperial power.

With God’s favor, you will have a hope of victories that does not lie prostrate if, through a peaceful episcopal struggle against the devil’s assaults, you fortify yourself with the instruction necessary for combat. May the commemoration of Dioscorus, the associate of Eutyches; of Timothy and Peter, murderers, never revive in the memory of the holy Churches. May the definition of the Council of Chalcedon, which all must accept, be preserved, with God working through you.

Let Acacius, polluted by communion with Peter, the son of darkness, have as his associates those whom he chose; even amid his own transgressions, he did not allow himself to remain untainted by Peter of Antioch and his accomplices. Let the curses hurled against the pious doctrines of Pope Leo of holy memory cease; while he remains in his own teachings, they punish only those who utter them.

In these matters we call upon your imperial concern. By guarding them, Your Piety may be able to possess its titles and scepters, transferred after many years into another age. Receive our prayers, sent through our brothers and fellow bishops Ennodius and Fortunatus, as well as the presbyter Venantius, the deacon Vitalis, and the notary Hilarius, our sons, whose faith and zeal in the fear of God have shone brilliantly among us, and in our place lend a peaceful conscience to their supplications.

For we hope—and, trusting in God, we promise—that the efforts expended by you for true religion will not be without recompense and reward. Given on 11 August, in the consulship of Florentius, a man of illustrious rank.

[Note: This letter, together with certain subsequent letters, was written by the emperor Anastasius in A.D. 516, when, after issuing a profession of catholic faith, he pretended to be catholic, intending by this device to win the favor of the people and shake off fear of Vitalianus. He added to the respected legates of the Apostolic See Theopompus and Severianus, laymen with whom ecclesiastical matters were to be discussed. That Anastasius professed the catholic faith in these letters deceitfully and with the utmost cunning, and by the same art of deception approved the Council of Chalcedon, is clearly demonstrated by what has been written above concerning him and by what will be written below concerning the same man. The legates he sent were alien to the catholic religion and defenders of the Eutychian heresy; therefore they came especially to Rome in order, if possible, to win Hormisdas himself over to their side. But when Hormisdas learned these wholly unexpected facts, he ordered the legates to return to the emperor without having accomplished their mission, having by then become more fully informed about Anastasius’s treachery, long concealed beneath a covering of pious words. These matters are established below from Hormisdas’s letter to Avitus. — Severus Binius.]

## Letter of the Emperor Anastasius to Hormisdas, sent through legates of the Apostolic See

He professes the catholic faith; the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon are to be preserved; Acacius is not to be condemned for removing scandals; and peace is to be considered. (C)

### Copy of the sacred letter of Augustus Anastasius to Pope Hormisdas, through the bishops Ennodius and Fortunatus, the presbyter Venantius, the deacon Vitalis, and the notary Hilarius

We give thanks to almighty God because Your Holiness, instructed in heavenly disciplines, has sent, as we requested, the legates of the faith, the venerable bishops Ennodius and Fortunatus, and also the religious men Venantius the presbyter, Vitalis the deacon, and Hilarius the notary, such as the dignity of the matter required. By the clarity of ecclesiastical discourse they could meet the importance of the business; and, with God at work, carefully investigated everything pertaining to the right and true faith of Christians. They themselves declared these things as was fitting, and learned them from us as was proper: that there is one Church of God, everywhere strengthened by apostolic teachings.

Who, therefore, would dare to think otherwise than the truth itself teaches concerning the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, except by confessing that the Son is equal and consubstantial with the Father and that, for the sake of our salvation, according to the annunciation of the archangel, he assumed flesh from the virgin’s womb and became man? As the Apostle says, he took the form of a servant in order to receive the cross in the flesh for us.

Concerning him the blessed apostle Peter says to the Jews:

“You asked that a murderous man be released to you, but you killed the author of life.”

Concerning him we also read in the apostle Paul:

“He became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.”

For we confess that the blessed virgin Mary, the Mother of God, bore God our Savior for us in true flesh and with a rational and intelligent soul. He was homousios—consubstantial—with God the Father and the Holy Spirit before the ages; and at the end of time, because of our sins, we believe and affirm that he was begotten homousios—consubstantial—with us as well, just as the prophet David says:

“From my mother’s womb you are my God” (Psalm 21).

Our substance was nevertheless assumed without defect or confusion in such a way that the Son of God will come in that same flesh to judge the world, displaying to the eyes of all the marks of his wounds and nails, as it is written:

“They will see the one whom they pierced” (Revelation 1).

Together with all orthodox believers, we likewise shun and abhor the most impious Nestorius and Eutyches. We condemn and anathematize both their persons and their teachings, which are comparable to detestable sacrileges, since they either wished not to know the divine dispensation and the remedies for human weakness, or, having recognized them, blasphemed them.

From the beginning of our life, therefore, the supreme God has implanted in our minds such a disposition concerning the faith; and for this reason we believe that our empire is preserved. We are astonished that you wished to write anything to us concerning the most blessed Fathers who assembled at Chalcedon, since what they established is shown to have been confirmed by the multiple decrees of our predecessors.

No other synod has been held by which the arrangements made by that council were rendered invalid, nor has any law proceeded from us whose novelty would dissolve the decisions of that episcopal council—especially since the council itself declared that anyone who wished to teach or alter a faith other than that established at Nicaea by the 318 venerable Fathers ought to be anathematized. It also condemned those whom we have mentioned above, Nestorius and Eutyches, whom we likewise condemn.

For the divine letters sent to Alexandria bear witness to us in this matter, not once but many times. Through them we rebuked those people because they did not think the instruction in faith sent to them sufficient, while withdrawing from their anathema against the Council of Chalcedon and Leo, the bishop of venerable memory.

Therefore, even now we retain no small zeal and determination, so that we may draw these same people away from their unnecessary anathema and join them to the universal holy Church.

As for the one remaining issue, our will might perhaps have agreed with your request for the sake of the unity of the Churches, unless we believed that this would remove other scandals from the venerable Churches. Now consider carefully everything that must be done, because Our Clemency judges that it would be grave to expel living men from the venerable Church on account of the dead; and we know that what you write concerning this matter cannot be arranged without a great outpouring of human blood.

Nevertheless, hoping for everything from God, you will be able to accomplish matters better through a council than through those men who, because of their errors, travel through the provinces wishing discord to be hostile to the holy Gospels and the Churches.

Therefore take care that the unity of the Churches be pleasing to the heavenly Majesty. For if you rightly rebuke us, we do not know what obstructs us in the matters mentioned above. In every respect, however, you will be able to learn the purity of our will from the account of our legates.

We ask that Your Apostolate deign to pray for us. We will be able to recognize most clearly that you do this willingly if God, through your arrangements, deigns to grant us perfect unity among the Churches. For the voice of God commanded and granted this great blessing to those who love Him when it declared:

“My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14).

## Letter of the Emperor Anastasius to Pope Hormisdas

He sends Theopompus and Severianus, laymen, to the pontiff to offer greetings and establish peace. (C)

### Augustus Anastasius to Pope Hormisdas, through Theopompus and Severianus, men of illustrious rank

Everything conceived by benevolent minds is extended through sweet eagerness and commendable haste. Such minds do not think that rest can be granted them until they have brought what they desire to a most salutary outcome. Then a kind of rest comes to that very haste when the hope of their vows has been fulfilled.

We have experienced this in the present matter, waiting until heavenly favor might grant both a hearing to our petition and a serene fulfillment of your promise. Since the extreme length of the journey and the severity of winter beyond the usual custom made what we desired uncertain, we meanwhile restrained our desires within our hearts, seeking the divine benefits that, through their intervention, determine a good outcome.

Recognizing, therefore, that God granted us His first favor by allowing the embassy sent to us to return safely to Your Beatitude, we proceeded to a second step: we sent the promised embassy, through which both a recollection could be made of what we discussed at length with the most holy men and, with God as our guide, the clear light of both our petition and your grace might shine forth completely, granting the expected joys to the whole world.

To serve as a reminder and to render the honor of a greeting, we have sent to Your Holiness Theopompus, an illustrious man, count of the domestics, presiding over the school of our sacred palace, faithful to us both by his character and by his native attachment to our province, and also Severianus, a man of illustrious rank and count of our sacred consistory. By the testimony of their own voices they will confirm the contents of the letter and hasten the fulfillment we await, which we believe has also pleased the heavenly mercy.

Given on 16 July at Constantinople, in the consulship of Peter, a man of illustrious rank [A.D. 516].

## LETTER VI. TO AUGUSTUS ANASTASIUS

The emperor’s fraud has not yet been exposed. Hormisdas praises his efforts to establish peace and urges that the unity of the Churches finally be brought to fulfillment.

### Hormisdas to Augustus Anastasius, through Theopompus and Severianus
To keep your mind solicitous, most merciful emperor, you recall with eager ambition until the desired restoration of the hoped-for unity may come about. The desires of salvation are good, and praiseworthy is the intention that in this way commends itself to God. For it is a special mark of prudence when one impatiently seeks what one believes useful for oneself. If delayed treatment is harmful in bodily illnesses, how much more grievous is the late desire for faithful remedies in the salvation of the soul? We are instructed by spiritual teachings not to postpone until tomorrow what can be beneficial, as the wisest Solomon cries out: “Do not delay to turn to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day” (Ecclesiasticus 5). For just as the times of life are uncertain, so it is fitting that remedies for the soul be secure, so that the one whose Lord, when he comes, finds him doing what pleases him may enter into the joy of his Lord.

Therefore I confess that I was astonished that the promised embassy had been delayed for so long, since these things must be done so that the heavenly kingdoms may be seized. Nevertheless, the very impulse revealed by the address of your gentleness promises hope of heavenly mercy. For even the willing of what is good comes from above. I trust that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion. Therefore persist in the path you have begun, and, rejecting the slippery ways of those who err, plant your footsteps with us upon the solid rock.

By such agreement the holy Church grew, as the history of the apostolic acts testifies in these words: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4). For how can those whose hearts differ in their convictions be joined by bonds of grace? Grant, lord emperor, that the outcome of events prove the truth of your words. Human hearts are not known by speeches but by deeds. Even our father Abraham pleased God not by bare faith, but by works that commended his faith.

Therefore, whether in consideration of the stewardship entrusted to me or in view of the benevolence of your piety toward me, lord son, I exhort and entreat you: direct the zeal for peace that you display in your letters toward settling with us, with God’s help, those matters by which the Churches are troubled, because, according to the prophet: “Great peace have those who love your name, and there is no scandal for them” (Psalm 118). The matters that separate us from the unity we desire to restore are not unknown to your gentleness. Take care that the things you profess in praise may be completed by their effect. Follow with all your strength the discipline of the apostle whose communion you believe should be sought.

Reject altogether the contagion of the harmful, knowing that the impious have no portion with the devout, and that faith has no fellowship with faithlessness. It follows that whoever detests the leaders of error must hate their followers. Let what is condemned in the seed be held accursed in the flower. Offer this gift to God, I beg you; offer it for the sake of your times. For a long while now he has awaited this sacrifice from you in return for the many benefits Christ has bestowed upon you.

Why should one present prayers to the one who himself supplicates? You instruct the Senate of the city of Rome to exhort me to peace. I turn words of supplication to you not only together with them, but I also prostrate myself at your feet on behalf of the universal Church. Hear me as I discharge an embassy for Christ: do not allow the members of Christ to be torn apart by wicked dogs. Cut away what you see to be incurable, and heal what is sick. Why are healthy things shaken by being joined to the weak? Preserve the order that unity itself prescribes, and restore to the world the peace that you demand.

These things I request on the present occasion, and I shall again and repeatedly take care to entreat you, hoping that this persistence of mine will be pleasing both to God and to you also, since through continual petitions—which the Lord has taught us—our request will not be empty.

Given at Rome (in the year of our Lord 516).

## Letter of Anastasius to the Senate of the City of Rome, through Theopompus and Severianus, Most Illustrious Men

He urges the pope and the king to seek peace. (C)

**[Note: [Col. 0385D] In the Roman edition of the letters of the Roman pontiffs, these titles are expressed as follows: “Emperor Caesar Flavius Anastasius, illustrious pontiff, illustrious Germanicus, illustrious Alamannicus [Col. 0386D], illustrious Francicus, tribunician power for the twenty-fifth time, consul for the third time, pious, fortunate, victorious, and ever august triumphant ruler, father of his country,” with the consuls, etc.]**

Emperor Caesar Flavius Anastasius, pious, fortunate, victorious, ever august, illustrious Germanus, illustrious Francicus, illustrious Sarmaticus, father of his country, to the proconsuls, consuls, praetors, tribunes of the people, and his Senate, greetings.

“If you and your children are well, that is good; I and my army are well.” Whenever prosperity is sought for both public realms with favorable intention, not only exhortation but also petition is considered appropriate, so that, when two causes converge into one, an encouraged spirit may attain what is fortunate and beneficial to both parties.

For if Christ, our God and Lord, recalled us to himself both by his most gentle will and by a certain petition of his providential dispensation, and restored those whom he had redeemed with his own blood to liberty, granting salvation to mortals, it does not seem absurd to hope—both from the most glorious king and from the most blessed pope of the venerable city of Rome, the senators joined to the imperial petition—that, with God’s assent, things may advance jointly for us and for them. This means that they should not listen to the contrived speeches of fugitives, composed solely of lies, but that, once satisfaction has been received—which both the truth and the investigation of the envoys sent have disclosed—they should proceed with acceptable joy to God toward the desired peace.

It is beyond doubt that, throughout the long sequence of years, a large part of your commonwealth has vindicated its steadfastness. Therefore your most holy assembly ought, with diligent zeal and prudent labor, to strive both with the exalted king, to whom the power and responsibility of governing you have been entrusted, and with the venerable pope, to whom the capacity of interceding with God has been granted, so that they may deign to devote the goodness of their hearts to that cause in which the members of both commonwealths may be preserved in the health they hope for.

You will fulfill an ancient custom, well known to your deliberations, if, by discussing, hoping for, and requesting those things that serve the public good, you cause them, with God’s favor, to attain their effect. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of August (in the year of our Lord 516), at Chalcedon, in the consulship of Peter, most illustrious man.

## Reply of the Senate of the City of Rome to Anastasius Augustus, through Theopompus and Severianus, Most Illustrious Men

The pope has always been devoted to peace, which they acknowledge depends upon the condemnation of Acacius. (C)

[Col. 0386A]

If, unconquered emperor, devotion observed by rulers is always the first thing expected by those who supplicate, and obedience is won solely by the favor of masters, you will undoubtedly recognize with what rejoicing your Senate received the declarations of the sacred command—especially since the command of our lord, your son, the most invincible King Theodoric, who ordered obedience to your instructions, was added to them. We know that we are raised above all your benefits when you deem us worthy to be among those to whom commands should be given.

Accordingly, immediately, in our zeal to fulfill the sacred command, we believed that the most blessed pope Hormisdas should be entreated. It is insufficient merely to say of him that he anticipated the petitions of those who supplicate by his benevolence; for he also joined his prayers to ours, so that what you urge might be done. He supported his will with evangelical testimonies, showing that the world is burdened more by scandals than by the multitude of its sins, since the Lord’s voice says: “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matthew 18). He likewise showed that people ought to cut off the parts of those who cause scandal rather than, by failing to renounce scandals, be cast into eternal fire.

After this, by examples from divine Scripture, he demonstrated how good are the fruits of peace, saying that the apostle Paul, though full of the grace of God, found nothing better to desire for those whom he wished well than that the peace of God, which surpasses all excellence, might abound in their hearts. He also cited the Lord’s voice in the Gospel: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5). Returning again to that teacher of all the Scriptures, he showed how much greater charity is than faith itself—although by faith we presume upon the heavenly kingdoms and, by believing, are saved from the torments of sinners—adding this testimony: “Hope, faith, charity; but the greatest of all is charity” (1 Corinthians 13). That is, the Spirit, by the gift of divine grace, exalts charity above all virtues.

Since, therefore, we avoid scandals because of their punishment, pursue peace because of the good things of peace, and are urged toward charity by Christ, who is charity, what is it that restrains us from hastening with Catholic fervor? What is it that, in the person of the offending Acacius, prevents those who wish to see Christ? What is it that causes people to be free from their own error yet burdened by another’s?

Although these matters have been set forth at greater length in the venerable pope’s reply, we nevertheless thought it proper, in obedience to our duty, to add them here, lest we should seem not to have asked by concealing the answer we received when we made our petition. Therefore, most pious emperor, the Senate has added these words in its own name, prompted by the clemency of your serenity, so that you who have shown such a benevolent spirit in reconciling both commonwealths may likewise be recognized as pious in restoring unity to the Church.

For just as that peace of kingdoms is known to benefit their subjects, so this peace of religion benefits the ruler together with his people. Who would not think that the followers of faithless heresies have sinned more than the authors themselves? Who would not condemn those who, after the gallows of the cross, once again divide Christ’s members?

Would that this cause had begun when you assumed the kingship, so that emerging evils might more easily have been repressed than those already advanced. For who could doubt that the error might not have arisen if one had seen it corrected in your times?

Through Ennodius and Fortunatus, bishops; Venantius, presbyter; Vitalis, deacon; and Hilarus, notary.

**[Note: [Col. 0387D] In the Roman edition: Hilarianus.]**

## Letter, or Copy of the Report, of John, Bishop of Nicopolis, through Rufinus, His Deacon, to Hormisdas

He professes the Catholic faith and asks to be instructed about what should be avoided and what should be preserved. (C)

[Col. 0387B]

To my lord, in every respect most holy and most blessed father of fathers, fellow minister and chief of bishops, Hormisdas: John sends greetings in the Lord.

It has always been my concern to seek nothing more than to conduct a personal and familiar way of life free from worldly care and anxiety. But because “the judgments of God are a great abyss” (Psalm 35), as I know that your Beatitude also teaches, after our father and archbishop Alcyson was summoned by Christ to the heavenly dwellings, the holy synod and the clergy of pastors transferred their lot to me on account of good deeds, in the manner known to him who is Lord of what is possible.

I, however, referring all things to God, who makes the tongues of those who stammer eloquent, appropriately turn to your prayers, so that, according to the custom of your apostolic see, which has care for all the Churches, you may also deign to have care for the Nicopolitans, in keeping with your ancient spiritual disposition.

Since I ask that the Spirit be given to me for the opening of my mouth, as the Apostle taught (Ephesians 6), and since the Lord himself also commanded this, ask with me the giver of these gifts; seek together with one who seeks, and receive with your spiritual hand the one who knocks. If you do this, most holy father, I shall be able both to receive and to find, and, with Christ opening the way, to walk rightly through the word of truth.

Certain people, however, pretend to believe and follow with us the holy synods gathered at Nicaea, Constantinople, and Ephesus, in which the leaders were the bishops of holy memory, Celestine of your apostolic see and Cyril of Alexandria; and also the synod gathered at Chalcedon against the impious Eutyches, which confirmed all the truths mentioned above in orthodox judgment. Yet they dare to attack us, as though irrationally avoiding the bond of concord.

My resolve is to follow your teaching, just as my holy predecessor Alcyson did. I anathematize Dioscorus, Timothy called Aelurus, and Peter, the successor of these men; Acacius, who was mingled with them through Peter’s communion; and Peter, who disturbed the Church of Antioch. In all things I follow the synodical and apostolic letters written by Leo, the true bishop of the Roman Church.

I ask you to instruct me more fully and perfectly about what must be preserved, and by your authoritative letters to make known from what I must abstain. Thus, if perhaps I am still inexperienced and assigned to the order of readers, or if I have said or done anything inconsistent with your apostolic teachings, I may, being formed by your words, resist the machinations of heretics.

If you do this, most holy father, you will find the bishops of our holy synod made firmer, and you will strengthen the clergy and people of good works, making the holy Church of the Nicopolitans as one familiar to you. Receive with peace, as is fitting for you, the venerable deacon Rufinus, who has been sent for this most necessary purpose; and, granting him your confidence, deign to ensure his swift return to us bearing spiritual and apostolic decrees.

I, and those who are with me, salute in the Lord with the greatest affection all the fraternity in Christ, most holy father, of your Beatitude.

## Letter VII. To John, Bishop of Nicopolis

He praises his piety; he condemns Nestorius and Eutyches, and writes that he will indicate how those who return to the faith are to be received.

Hormisdas to John, bishop of Nicopolis, through Rufinus, deacon.

We rejoiced greatly in the Lord, dearest brother, when we received your letter, in which you profess that you have undertaken the priesthood by the grace of God. This is certain faith; this is secure hope without ambiguity: that the source of every good is believed to rest in the heavenly dispensation. Knowing this, dearest brother, you confess with a devout heart the grace of the benefits you have received from our God, although this too descends from the same source of mercy: that human humility should submit itself to its author.

For he says: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, except upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Numbers 11). Since you are shown to possess these qualities, you will shine more clearly as an example of this virtue to others also, since by God’s institution you have been brought to the point at which the Catholic Church may glory in you.

For, instructed by divine testimonies and formed, in accordance with the Apostle, by the teaching of the sacred Scriptures, you gave this auspicious sign of your ordination: that you agreed against those who deviate with the judgments of the apostolic see. You could not otherwise repay the giver of such great benefits than by displaying evident zeal for apostolic confession against his enemies.

It is clear that those who themselves profess consciousness and confidence in the faith nevertheless stand outside the religious fold. Their equality of holy communion with the devout is fruitless, even though it agrees with that of the devout, because without doubt whoever does not use the liberty he has deserved confesses that he has subjected himself to iniquities. Why should we glory in disciplines that we do not follow? He falsely calls himself a teacher who does not prove himself a disciple of his teachings.

But since now, in your confession, all things are the same as ours, and you have recovered the desire for your own liberty, wishing once again to be heirs together with us of the paternal inheritance, embrace the grace of the ancient tradition. Persist in the stability of that unshaken foundation, without changing your hearts with the times; for such change is usually the purpose of the inconstant. Therefore those who are well founded ought to cling firmly, since divine mercy knows how to foster such zeal, so that the firmness of your faith may bear fruit for you in the salvation of others, and so that the fervor of your zeal may kindle the hearts of others to recover their own good things. Thus it may also be believed that the holy apostle said of you: “Your zeal has stirred up very many” (2 Corinthians 9).

Therefore, with the impieties of Nestorius and Eutyches condemned according to the synodical decrees, and with their followers likewise accursed, let us say with rejoicing: “Come out from their midst and be separate, and do not touch what is unclean, says the Lord” (Leviticus 15). For how can anyone detest the authors of evil inventions if he does not shun their followers? Or how can anyone hate the origin who does not also curse the offspring? The reputation of teachers is proclaimed in their disciples, and as long as the root of badly sown seeds flourishes, cultivated by successive generations, so long will the memory of the authors not perish.

Let Acacius also be added to the condemned Eutyches: a disciple under Peter’s communion and mingled with the error of all the condemned. Your affection clearly expressed these men in your letter while asserting your faith.

For fuller instruction in your faith, we have appended below a brief statement indicating in what order those who return should be received into our communion. We hope in God, the giver of all good things, that the praiseworthy persistence of your devotion toward the faith may benefit not only the salvation of those who are joined to you by proximity, but also that of those to whom the swift report of your faith and devout will has reached.

We received in the love of Christ the deacon Rufinus, who brought us your letter. Commending him to the prayers of the apostles, we send him back in peace, urging you to have the letters sent by us to your affection and to the synod read again before the people. You should know that we have done this also in commendation of your faith.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Peter, most illustrious man.

## Synodical Letter, or Copy of the Report, of the Synod of Old Epirus to Pope Hormisdas

They request confirmation of John, elected bishop of Nicopolis, and wish to be instructed in the Catholic faith. (C)

[Col. 0389D]

To our lord, in every respect most holy and most blessed father of fathers, fellow minister and chief of bishops, Hormisdas: the synod of Old Epirus—John, Matthew, Constantine, Christodorus (Christophorus), Hilarus, Philip, Julian, and Chrysippus.

If we attempt to make use of worthy rewards, it is necessary to accomplish these things with many tears. For many of us were in Constantinople during the reign, when your most holy legates, the bishops Ennodius and Fortunatus, Venantius the presbyter, Vitalis the deacon, and Hilarus the notary, were staying there, steadfastly undertaking the contest of piety.

Our father and archbishop Alcyson, who has been numbered among the saints, was also with us. With every confidence, using petitions, he was found worthy in the presence of your Beatitude to share with us in communion with your apostolic see. But because he who holds power over all suddenly summoned him to himself, we, held back by unrestrained weeping, nevertheless reached our homeland, in no way tolerating error, by God’s grace, but everywhere following your decrees.

As we wept and lamented with those fellow ministers in the parish who had been restored with us, who could rightly guide Christ’s sheep from among the orthodox? He who consoles the humble consoled us also through your prayers, showing to the metropolitan city in every respect the most holy John. He had been raised in the Church without blame from childhood, indeed living in it commendably, so that no one in these times surpassed him; and in zeal for orthodoxy, in accordance with your apostolic admonitions, he yielded to absolutely no one.

By God’s providence, therefore, we ordained him bishop of the most holy Church of the Nicopolitans. We ask that, according to ancient custom, you too embrace him with your paternal affection, and that by God’s grace you become for us and for him invincible weapons through your admonitions and teachings. Incline your ear to us who supplicate, and discover the piety of concord according to the apostolic providence divinely inspired in you, so that, in the peace that is dear to him, all the most holy Churches may be joined together, weaving for you an unfading crown, and so that all may be embraced in Christ with complete piety and humility.

Kindly receive, as we request, the venerable deacon Rufinus, who has been sent for this most necessary purpose, and send him back to us speedily bearing your apostolic teachings.

And in another hand: Pray for me, most holy father of fathers, that I may remain safe.

**[Note: [Col. 0389] The same names of the sees occur here as in Letter 59, part 3 of the Council of Chalcedon; accordingly we have corrected several readings. Hardouin.]**

I, John, bishop, have again reported: Pray for me in the Lord, that I may remain safe, most holy and most blessed father of fathers.

I, Matthew, bishop of Butrotum, have reported.

I, Constantine, bishop of Hacnanopolis (Hadrianopolis), have reported: Pray for me in the Lord, that I may remain safe, most holy and most blessed father of fathers.

I, Christodorus (Christophorus), bishop of Anchiasmus, have reported.

I, Hilarius, bishop of Photice, have reported.

I, Philip, bishop of Phoenice, have reported.

I, Julian, bishop of Dodona, have reported.

I, Chrysippus, bishop of Congra, have reported.

## Letter VIII. To the Synod of Old Epirus

He condemns the followers of Eutyches’ errors and urges the bishops of Old Epirus to anathematize the heretics by name.

[Col. 0391A]

Hormisdas to the synod of Old Epirus.

Blessed be God, who joins together the members of his Church. Blessed be God, who, after they had been divided at the instigation of the evil one, makes them united in the same solidity that they formerly possessed. For although the enemy cried out for a long time in the manner of a partridge and gathered together those whom he had not begotten, as the prophet said, nevertheless he will be laid waste by abyssal confusion. The Lord’s sheep do not follow a stranger or listen to the voice of another shepherd.

Therefore we are not surprised that you have returned to the path of salvation, although we blame the delay more than anything in this restoration. Dearest brothers, we must use examples from our own household for the stability we seek. Timothy of Cherson, for example, was grievous when he learned and more grievous when he taught. A follower of Dioscorus and likewise the teacher of Peter, he exercised the violence of his recklessness against Proterius of blessed memory and exceeded every limit of cruelty. He carried out the slaughter of that religious man among the very altars, with his very jaws scarcely held back from that pious blood.

Then the universal Church, roused against the parricide in hatred, deprived the author of so great a crime not only of communion but also of the very Christian name; and the minds of all were struck with a new kind of astonishment at the audacity of such presumption.

At that time blessed Eugenius, holding the primacy of your parish, together with the holy synod subject to him, displayed a certain zeal by which he showed himself commended to God as a man of faith. Time cannot conceal the memory of this deed; rather, its great reputation among the orthodox multiplies from day to day.

To neglect the zeal of these men, so thoroughly approved, and not to love their judgments, is the same as committing an offense against the confession of our Lord himself. For us, now that your profession and letters have been received, it must be prayed that all the dogmas of the faith may be alike, with God joining his own people together, and that your will, by which you have revived our spirits, may remain in this confession.

But it is necessary, without regard to fear, to attack the madness of those who strive by a different faith. The more fiercely the error of unbelievers boils, the more our security commends itself if it resists. These matters must not be neglected through patience, since this evil, animated by the vice of perverse custom, has grown among many under a certain pretext of law, either because evil zeal joins together or because upright people withdraw.

To speak of the matter before us: Eutyches, as the inventor of a wicked heresy, is excluded even by those who love his doctrines. Among those very people he is so hated and shunned that they even hate mention of his name. Yet perverse ministers of religious institutions detest him as a true heretic, while by another path they embrace him as though he were a true orthodox believer.

For in the holy synod of Chalcedon, Dioscorus, sharing the same opinions, was condemned in the same manner. Since one judgment pursued [or “prosecuted”; Hardouin] both men, if anyone follows and loves one of them, let someone say how he can exempt himself from the judgment that condemned the designated persons, since those whom equality in transgression or impiety binds together are undoubtedly held by one bond of condemnation as well.

Timothy and Peter, their followers, men corrupted in mind and a certain plague of the Catholic name to be detested—their communion Acacius embraced in Peter—likewise deserved to undergo the same sentence. He considered so great an evil of little importance and never turned his purpose toward better things. He did not even abstain from those whom we detest in Antioch; there too, joined by communion to the transgressor Peter, he acted with hostility in Apamea and administered the Church of Tyre without the integrity that was required.

Therefore, dearest brothers, freeing ourselves from their entanglement and abandoning that kind of pestilential religion, let us preserve apostolic discipline and provide for our salvation with every diligence and concern. Let us avoid the errors of the wicked Nestorius with the same care with which we pursue the impious inventions of Eutyches.

For now, in particular, the religious doctrines of the faith are assailed by the diverse attacks of the men mentioned above, who weave their criminal arguments according to the circumstances of the time, seeking ways to insert the fraud of their impiety into the paths of the innocent.

Therefore, like skilled money-changers, prudently instructed, separating what is worthy of rejection from what is worthy of praise, you will be able to multiply the substance of the talent entrusted to you.

We have written these things, dearest brothers, under the impulse of complete charity, because we have first presumed upon the hope of your faith by God’s gift and then upon the profession of our brother John, who presides over you. In it he declared by name that all those whom the apostolic and universal Catholic Church condemns are accursed in his eyes.

You too ought clearly to have expressed these men in your letters. You should not think it sufficient, especially in the face of the many traps laid by cunning people, to include them under a general condemnation. They should be pursued and condemned individually and by name. Old wounds seek careful medicine, and nothing used for the integrity of the faith and the stability of religion is thought excessive.

Therefore we have sent a statement together with the letters. Insert your own signatures into it, so that your faith—attested by the writings sent through the deacon Rufinus—may become still more evident to us through the addition of this repetition.

Dated on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December (in the year of our Lord 516), in the consulship of Peter, most illustrious man.

## Letter IX. To John, Bishop of Nicopolis

Because the bishops of Old Epirus had not condemned the heretics by name in their letter, a statement is sent to which they must subscribe.

Hormisdas to John, bishop, through Pulio.

The sequence of your letter and your exposition of the faith, which agrees with the judgments of the apostolic see, have revived our spirits. We were not content with so much joy unless, through Pulio (Polio), subdeacon of the Roman Church, we could learn more fully what was being done among you. This was especially necessary because, in the report of the bishops living under the authority of your affection, not all that pertains to ecclesiastical decrees is clearly expressed, as it is in your own letter.

Therefore, both out of our concern and for their complete union with us, we have sent a statement **[Note: [Col. 0393D] We believe that this statement, which was attached to this letter, is the same one that was dated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April and is presented here to you from the Vatican manuscript. Severinus Binius.]** to which they must subscribe, since all the priests of your regions who have returned to communion with the apostolic see subscribed to the same profession.

This is the charity, this is the zeal for the common salvation that prompted us. I believe that your fraternity will gladly receive it, since, when the salvation of souls is at stake, you ought to devote your zeal and purpose to the matter, so that by taking the lead you may receive the fruit of such praise.

Send the aforementioned Pulio back to us speedily, with your affectionate reply, with God’s help, so that our desires may not remain suspended for long.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December (in the year of our Lord 516), in the consulship of Peter, most illustrious man.

## Rule of Faith

The first requirement for salvation is to preserve the rule of right faith and in no way deviate from the decrees of the Fathers. And because the sentence of our Lord Jesus Christ cannot be passed over—“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church,” etc.—the truth of these words is proved by events, because in the apostolic see religion has always been preserved undefiled.

Therefore, desiring in no way to be separated from this hope and faith, and following in all things the decrees of the Fathers, we anathematize all heretics, especially the heretic Nestorius, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, condemned at the Council of Ephesus by Pope Celestine of the city of Rome and by Saint Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria.

Together with him we anathematize Eutyches and Dioscorus of Alexandria, condemned in the holy synod of Chalcedon, which we follow and embrace. To these we add Timothy, the parricide, surnamed Aelurus; his disciple and follower Peter; and Acacius, who remained in fellowship with their communion, because whoever mingled himself with their communion deserved a similar sentence in condemnation.

We likewise condemn Peter of Antioch with his followers and all those mentioned above.

Therefore we receive and approve all the letters of Pope Leo, all those that he wrote concerning the Christian religion. Accordingly, as we said before, following the apostolic see in all things and proclaiming all its decrees, I hope that I may deserve to be in one communion with you—the communion proclaimed by the apostolic see—in which the solidity of the Christian religion is complete and true.

I also promise that those separated from communion with the Catholic Church, that is, those who do not consent to the apostolic see, are not to have their names recited among the sacred mysteries.

I have subscribed this profession of mine with my own hand and have presented it to you, Hormisdas, holy and venerable pope of the city of Rome.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April (in the year of our Lord 517), in the consulship of Agapitus, most illustrious man.

## Brief Statement through Pulio, the Subdeacon

What is to be done in the Church of Nicopolis.

With the help of God and the prayers of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, when you come to Nicopolis you must act as follows: after the bishop of Nicopolis has received our letter, he must gather the bishops whom he has in his parish and make them subscribe the statement attached to his letters.

If the aforementioned bishop says that it is burdensome to gather the bishops, he must send persons with you to each bishop, so that, in your presence, they may subscribe the aforesaid statement.

You must act with God’s mercy in such a way that the letters sent by us are read publicly. Or, if you see that the bishops are unwilling to do this because of fear, let them at least read these letters to their clergy. Leave this, however, to their own discretion. Bring back to us, with God’s mercy, the written subscriptions of the bishops and of that bishop—that is, John the metropolitan.

After this has been done, we do not want you to remain there any longer, because of the traps and cunning of the enemies.

Through John, his deacon.

## Letter of Avitus, Bishop of Vienne, to Pope Hormisdas

He congratulates him on the conversion of the provinces of Dardania and Illyricum and asks to be informed of the outcome of the embassy sent to Constantinople.

[Col. 0394C]

To the lord Hormisdas, most excellent in holy merits, most glorious in Christ, and most worthy of the apostolic see: Avitus.

While you see (printed as no. 87 in Sirmond’s edition of 1643) that the state of religion agrees with the full rules of the Catholic faith, so that your vigilant care of exhortation may instruct the flock entrusted to you through all the members of the universal Church, etc.

**(This letter may be read in volume 59, column 288, of our Patrology, among the works of Avitus, bishop of Vienne.)**

## Letter X. To Avitus, Bishop of Vienne

He praises his zeal for learning about the condition of the Eastern Church; he writes that, because of the faithlessness of the Greeks, nothing was accomplished by the legates, and that he intends to send another embassy to them. (C)

[Col. 0394D]

Hormisdas, bishop, to Avitus, bishop, and to all the bishops of the province of Vienne, or those residing under your diocese.

Whoever desires to be instructed, above all, in those matters that pertain to Catholic discipline clearly demonstrates what zeal he has for the divine commandments. For such concern cannot exist unless faith is unfeigned.
