[Col. 0395A] And therefore we rejoice in the Lord over the sincerity of your purpose, dearest brother, when we see you, according to the letter sent through the presbyter Alexius and the deacon Venantius, recalling the decrees of the apostolic see concerning the impious transgressors Eutyches and Nestorius, and inquiring whether our admonition has achieved anything against them—those by whom the Churches of the East are thrown into confusion. It is entirely fitting that the faithful should grieve over the falls of wretched people and take care that they themselves not be defiled by another’s contagion.

But do not suppose that we have neglected to ensure that suitable information would be conveyed to you if anything had been accomplished. Rather, we briefly clear ourselves of the silence that your affection finds painful. For the reason our admonition does not visit you more frequently is that we trust your conscience and the steadfastness of your faith. Concern must perhaps be expended on those who are uncertain; it is enough to point out what must be avoided to the perfect.

As for our legation, which we sent only once, not twice as you write, if a desired outcome had occurred, we would immediately and eagerly have shared with you what you desired; for we knew that this was both reasonable and suited to our purpose: that those whom we had made partners in our concern should join us in the joys of the restoration of unity. But as for the Greeks, they display their wishes for peace more with their lips than in their hearts, and they speak more of what is right than they do it. In words they boast that they wish to do what their deeds show they do not wish to do. They neglect what they professed and pursue what they condemned.

For how else can it be explained that, although through our brother and fellow bishop Ennodius they had promised that they would send priestly men [Col. 0395C] to confirm what the apostolic see had requested, promising also many things that we had sought for the correction of their perversity, they not only failed, according to their own decrees, to send religious men through whom a full account of that case could be supplied, but, as though a minor matter were being handled, sent laymen and men outside the ecclesiastical body—Theopompus, count of the domestics, and Severianus, count of the sacred consistory? They did not strive to free themselves from the mire in which they are held submerged; rather, they even believed that they could, God forbid, obscure with their own darkness the radiance of the Catholic faith.

This was the reason for our silence, as you too, with spiritual prudence revealing it to you, have seen. For what could I have indicated in letters sent to you about a matter whose obstinate preservation of perfidy I saw remaining unchanged? New developments call for the diligent investigation of an anxious report. Whoever says nothing about known matters declares clearly that the earlier state of affairs remains as it was.

Therefore, dearest brother, we exhort you in this present address, and through you, since the opportunity has arisen, we admonish throughout Gaul those whom the same faith as ours embraces: preserve the promised and God-beloved steadfastness of faith; avoid the society of transgressors; and present your steadfastness to Christ, as you promised, as a chaste virgin to one man. And take care lest, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so the minds of some should be corrupted from the simplicity and chastity [Col. 0396A] that is in Christ Jesus.

The flatteries of the wicked are deadly. Therefore you must remain vigilant, because the adversary of human salvation, like a roaring lion, prowls about seeking someone to devour; resist him, strong in faith. For this is the special characteristic of their father, cast down from the citadel of heaven, and of those who follow and love his footsteps: deprived of that light of truth, they rejoice that others too may be darkened by their own darkness. Although they know that they themselves will suffer the penalties of their perversity, they exult if they can join the wretched to their own condemnation.

For what else explains their attempt to attract those who live far away by the hope of ignorance, by frauds, and by various arts, when they are being abandoned by a large part of their neighbors—the Thracians, Dardanians, and Illyrians—who have learned their perversity, except that they wish by impious [Col. 0396B] contagion to stain in others as well the light that they themselves do not possess?

So that you may recognize the dispositions of those regions: many of the Thracians, although worn down by the assaults of persecutors, nevertheless remain in our communion, knowing that faith becomes more radiant through adversity. Dardania and Illyricum, neighboring Pannonia, requested from us—as we have already done wherever it was necessary—that bishops be appointed for them. They rejoice to separate themselves so completely from the communion of the lost that they seek remedies, provided only that they have nothing in common with transgressors.

The metropolitan of Epirus, that is, the bishop of Nicopolis, together with his synod, recently separated from the impious, came over to apostolic communion after making the profession that effected this. We judged that these matters should therefore be inserted in the present letter, so that, just as it is fitting for us to grieve over the lot of those who are perishing, so we may likewise rejoice over the salvation of those returning; and so that the faithful, being more fully instructed by them, may learn with what vigilance they must flee the poison of those whom they see avoided even by their own people with such just detestation.

And we, mindful of our stewardship, must necessarily summon them by the duty of a renewed legation. If they are not moved by concern for their salvation, by regard for God, or by consideration of reason, let them at least yield to those who knock insistently and persistently; and either, abandoning their errors, return to the right path, or, on account of their impenitent heart, be judged inexcusable by all, since, though so often admonished, they persist in the obstinacy of their perfidy.

Pray, and join your prayers and vows with ours before God, so that, through the help of his mercy, our action, laboring for the stability of the Catholic faith, may advance while you preserve yourselves immaculate [Col. 0396D] and undefiled from every association with transgressors; so that either we may join our minds and hearts with those who have been corrected, or may deserve to remain untouched by their poisons.

For since we know—as you too testify that your conscience is not unaware—that Eutyches and Nestorius were condemned by the authority of the apostolic, that is, Catholic, judgment, how can we be saved if in any respect we cling to their followers and successors, since Belial cannot have a share with our Christ?

We believe it belongs to your instruction that we make known to you, by reading the documents themselves, what was done among us concerning the Nicopolitans and Dardanians, and in what order they were received into communion. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Agapitus.

## LETTER XI. Sent to Anastasius Augustus through Ennodius of Pavia and Peregrinus, bishop of the Church of Misena in Campania, who were carrying out the commission of the second legation sent to Anastasius. The peace of the Church can be restored only after Acacius has been condemned.

Hormisdas to Anastasius Augustus, through the bishops Ennodius and Peregrinus.

When the legates of Your Clemency recently returned, I replied to your letters and commands—not indeed resolving everything fully, as the magnitude of the matter required, but nevertheless touching upon what was certain for the time. [Col. 0397B] Yet even if I had happened to set forth everything sufficiently, could I, while pleading the cause of faith before Your Clemency, have pressed you with repeated prayers and thereby been charged with importunity? Let those fear the accusation of such ingratitude who take care to devote their zeal to worldly affairs. He does not fulfill the work of the Gospel who thinks he may lawfully cease from its preaching. Pastors must keep the most vigilant watch, with their loins girded without relaxation.

Just as good admonition plainly bears sweet fruit, so it should not become burdensome. Besides, why should anyone call the frequent repetition of my request troublesome to Your Clemency, when through what is done as part of my office your rule is being served by the remedies of faith? For the concern that burdens me relieves you: it falls upon me, but will benefit you, although from different seed there is one fruit for both. For just as it is punishment neither to speak nor to do what is pleasing to God, so there is a sure reward both for the one who proclaims spiritual things and for the one who does not despise what he has heard.

Your Clemency did indeed offer, as it were, a pledge of your intention under the testimony of an imperial address, and bound yourself, so to speak, by a pledge of good will. But firmness must be added to what has been begun. Let the foundations already laid receive their full beauty. Let not the hands defending the Churches of God relax. The Israelite enemy intervenes as often as Moses does not lower his arms. The outcome commends the work, and the end commends the beginning. It is of no benefit to begin and then abandon the undertaking, because only perseverance gives faith salvation.

We bless God, whose zeal causes your piety to persecute the impious transgressors Nestorius and Eutyches, and those who profess their wicked and sacrilegious doctrines. Whoever condemns those who err proves that he hates their vices; whoever does not spare the transgressor leaves himself no place for deviation. The first degree of innocence is to hate what deserves condemnation. But it is the interest of truth, my lord son, and of Catholic discipline that you should also hate the followers and associates of those whose execrable leaders you judge. Crimes must be pursued not only in those who are condemned—that is, in the persons whose names are certain—but also in those who follow the condemned.

It is useless for someone to claim that he rejects many if he makes an exception for one of those judged worthy of detestation. For it is not the number of those who err but the character of their errors that is considered.

This is said lest Your Clemency easily think that the person of Acacius may be passed over. Is this not Acacius, polluted by the mire of the doctrine and communion of Peter, Dioscorus, and Eutyches, and immersed while joined to them? Does he not endure in his condemnation the punishment of the one whose companionship in communion he chose? Whoever hates each of these men individually on account of their impiety must necessarily hate Acacius in them, and must love no one among them in Acacius.

From him the leaven of wicked error spread throughout the Churches of the East. From there the pride of Alexandrian perfidy was nourished to such a degree that it does not submit, as you have written, to saving commands, although it serves the commands of the one whose authority it experiences as useful in the conduct of affairs. Such people must therefore be avoided with even greater detestation, because they assume what they ought to teach others, while they themselves have not yet been instructed; and, despising in these matters the admonitions of the ruler, in which they are almost commanded not to fear imperial authority, they forget their devotion to the detriment of their souls, when they ought to be obstinate for the sake of salvation.

Acacius’s communion joined with the perfidious has nourished these people in their ruined minds. He must therefore be regarded as occupying the place of an originator, since sin is more grievous when committed on the example of another. Nothing fosters vices more than imitation, when people suppose that what others also appear to embrace must not be disapproved.

Mortality is fragile and fleeting. Wicked thoughts scarcely perish even when they are suppressed. The harmful seed lies beneath error and does not fail; whoever joins agreement to wickedness opens a broad entrance for those who abandon themselves to it.

Would that, unconquered emperor, at the very beginnings of the apostolic severity the Eastern [Col. 0398C] Churches had avoided the wicked contagions of Acacius! That error would not have spread its harmful poisons among so many. Perhaps the necks of the Alexandrian Church, then also raised up, would have fallen, when they recognized their stricken perfidy in the condemnation of its imitator and saw that they themselves were displeasing in their accomplices.

But while errors badly nourished are fostered, and the useless agreement of the wicked is left uncorrected through misplaced leniency, the evil doctrines of their authors have multiplied through the impunity of their followers. If it pleases you, may you obtain from God with such efficacy that you condemn your own intention concerning another’s error. But it must be considered, most merciful emperor, whether it is enough before God for the one to whom the power to correct has been given merely to blame the errors. The remedy must not be delayed; let medical hands be applied to deep wounds.

Before Acacius, Alexandria alone was soiled by the filth of its perfidy. Consider how many regions the neglected correction has now polluted. How long, my lord son, will you allow the Church of God to mourn the division of its members? Let your benefits anticipate the sighs that will reach God. Take up the care of faith, and, raising the banner of salvation, rise up like another Hezekiah to remove errors from Israel. You may rightly equal the titles of the ancients by the praise of new works.

He destroyed the high places; you incline the pride of exalted impiety. He shattered the idols; you break the hardened hearts of unbelievers. He removed the memory of the bronze serpent; you pour out the poison of the present one. Set before God the righteous deeds he performed, and hope for the gifts he deserved. For the Lord is faithful, who repays each person according to his works (Matt. XVI). [Col. 0399A]

It is evident how great is the expectation of the faithful and how great the trembling of the perfidious. The former long to rejoice with the angels over those who have been received; the latter fear that, abandoned by those whom they had deceived, they will remain for the punishments prepared for them. The anxious hearts of all hang in suspense.

A legation sent to us from the farthest parts of Gaul, when our concern for the restoration of unity had accomplished something, followed the report and offered its support. Nor is the task difficult for Your Clemency. God knows how to assist the labors of his own people. It is customary for subjects to bow their necks before their rulers. The recent example of the religiously remembered Emperor Marcian offers a great and conspicuous sign. What did the common people or the populace do then? There is no need to revisit what is already known.

This perfidy has grown through the misguided and been lulled to sleep by the just. Imitate the integrity of his religious purpose, which you have equaled through your zeal for civil order. For these matters, and to support them with our tears and prayers, we have sent our brothers and fellow bishops Ennodius and Peregrinus in our place, also to offer an honorable greeting. We did this especially by placing the burden of a second legation upon the designated man, so that he who brought us the beginning of good hope might now, with God’s help, bring back its full result.

We beg you to heed the faithful admonitions of the one whose instructions we recently read that you welcomed with delight. Given on the third day before the Nones of April, in the consulship of Agapitus, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of our Lord 517).

## LETTER XII. Admonitory letter to Timothy, the heretical bishop of Constantinople, through the aforesaid legates. One must labor for the unity of the Church.

Hormisdas to Timothy, bishop of Constantinople.

[Col. 0399C] Your affection will not be surprised at the reason for my former silence if it considers all that preceded; nor will it be surprised at my present address if it weighs the power of charity. For we have learned from the teacher of the nations that charity endures all things (I Cor. XIII). Since charity, as the teaching itself declares, does not seek its own, am I improperly abusing my privilege by offering you what may rather benefit you?

I ought to await your liberation from association with those who err and then love you once you had been corrected; I ought to see you separated from those who must be condemned and thus embrace you in a written address. But if I desire your return, why should I delay calling upon you while you tarry? Why should there be no room for moderation when justice loses nothing? What benefits those who are struggling must be supplied, provided that they do not pollute us by the contagion of their association.

This is the reason for this letter: to exhort and admonish you, lest we allow our land to lie negligently barren. A diligent farmer does not permit an unfruitful tree to occupy the soil for long. He waits patiently—but does he continue indefinitely? When called to what brings salvation, do not delay. Whoever returns to innocence without delay is scarcely departing from it.

Be moved by the admonitions of the Fathers, and, following faithfully without stumbling or error in their footsteps, erase what came before through what is to come. It is now your task, sometimes by urging the peoples toward what is just, sometimes by pleading for the faith before the footsteps of rulers, to direct what is crooked and strengthen what is uncertain. You must labor greatly to ensure that diligent action in the present covers the causes of the past. Whoever contributes anything to the universal Church benefits his own soul. The matter stands thus: if you persist earnestly and tirelessly, the common cause will become beneficial to you. Given as above (in the year of our Lord 517).

## LETTER XIII. Admonitory letter sent through the second legation to all the heretical bishops of the East. The unity of the Catholic faith must be preserved.

Hormisdas to all the bishops established in the regions of the East.

Although the care of my admonition might require this, you ought, mindful of your own office, not negligently to omit what all are earnestly bound to preserve for the salvation of their souls, so that the discipline of the heavenly commandments might be shown to be present in you by your own purpose, not by the zeal of another. For although the one who obeys good counsels is not without praise, the person who anticipates what is right is so much more honored in wisdom than the one who follows instructions as teaching is more illustrious than learning.

Let each person remember to what calling he was called by the Lord and consider what is expected of him. It is wretched to fall short of the merit of one’s calling when what one bears in name is not displayed in action. We have achieved much if we fulfill what the things granted—or commanded—require. Whoever rejoices that he has been appointed to feed the sheep of the Lord’s flock should consider the judgment concerning the governance entrusted to him.

The most vigilant protection must be applied and the watch must be continuous. No place must be given to ravening wolves, and no one may be abandoned to chance, because neglect of the sheep’s error is the shepherds’ fault. The one who examines the accounts of the entrusted stewardship will come. It is indeed clear that justice belongs to all, and that no one has an unpunished license to sin. But who does not know that there are degrees of merit, and that just as rewards are not equal, so punishments are different? The blows multiply for those who know; few lashes, we read, are assigned to ignorance.

If this is so, as there is no doubt it is, one must consider what purpose is fitting in the person to whom the errors of others must also be attributed. The Holy Spirit cries out through the prophet: “O shepherds of Israel, do the shepherds feed themselves?” (Ezek. XXXIII). It is certain that more must be demanded from the one to whom more has been entrusted, and that we become more liable to account in proportion as we have been honored with more abundant grace.

The good Master, teaching light through obscurities and truth through the riddles of comparisons, did not accuse the servant of the talent entrusted to him of being unfaithful merely because he failed to increase it; rather, he condemned him as useless (Matt. XXV). Hence it is clear what fear should possess the one who has lost the Lord’s coin, if the man who preserved what he had received without diminution was blamed (Luke XIX).

Let no one be content with his own innocence, because before our God, who sees all things, we must also give an account through the constant preaching of the purpose entrusted to us concerning others. Teachers ought to possess abundant knowledge. The Christian faith does not love secrecy; whoever pours it only into the ear conceals it. The preaching of the word is entrusted to the apostles among all nations, and no one can keep silent about what has been entrusted to him without excuse.

What does it profit anyone to preserve reverence for the regulations of the Fathers if he patiently accepts that others shake them or treat them without honor? Whoever does not defend what he loves shows a weak affection. The sacred institutions are everywhere assailed by the perfidious, and wickedness, repeatedly revived after its excesses have been suppressed, rises again.

How, I ask, does the one who conceals such wickedness prove his devotion to God? Let us remember with what a multitude of Catholic priests we learned that those councils on which we rely were celebrated; how many were hindered neither by weakness nor delayed by burdensome old age. The distances across spacious regions seemed insignificant, and the labors themselves were joyful as a kind of consolation, while the wisdom directed by the spirit of holy assemblies allowed old age, though late, to receive what it should preserve.

And when the impious attack these things after perfidy has been condemned at its root, the one who knows that he has been commanded to speak remains silent: “Raise your voice, you who evangelize Jerusalem; raise it, do not fear” (Ps. XL). Did not the teacher of the nations, keeping this before his eyes, instruct his disciple so that he would not cease to evangelize at the proper time, admonishing him: “Pay attention to yourself and to your teaching; persist in them. For by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you” (II Thess. IV)?

Therefore, whether roused by prophetic goads or instructed by the norms of apostolic teaching, take up the care of salutary preaching. Love and defend the judgments approved by the devout and hostile to unbelievers. Returning to the rock upon which the Church was founded, acquit yourselves before the spirits of those Fathers whose venerable decrees are wickedly undermined, considering, when the Lord comes to that judgment which is awaited, what sort of person he was entrusted to the apostles as, what sort he was found to be through the doubt of certain tempters, and what sort he was promised to be by the announcing angel: whether it is better to be reproved by them or joined to their company; whether you will confess the Lord as he will be seen to be, or as he is denied by the impious.

Let nothing hold you back from salvation. Return to the road with swift steps. A fall does not burden one who has fallen, if he rises again. The Lord’s teaching of mercy is abundant. The bonds of error are harmful so long as they hold people fast. Justice hates the obstinate; mercy nurtures those who correct themselves. Given on the third day before the Nones of April, in the consulship of Agapitus, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of our Lord 517).

## LETTER XIV. Sent through the same second legation to the orthodox bishops of the East. He praises their steadfastness in the faith and writes that he has again sent legates from himself to Constantinople to establish peace.

[Col. 0401D]

Hormisdas to the orthodox bishops.

God is indeed the special consolation of the faithful, and those who have devoted themselves to him with all the zeal of their minds never fail amid any hardships. Nevertheless, I confess that I owe this wish to your purpose: just as I rejoice in the sincerity of your faith, so may I deserve to rejoice in the firmness of your steadfastness.

Therefore, looking upon you with inward sight, I rise ready with the desire to speak with you, so that a written address may both repay your love toward God and confirm your hope through exhortation on the page; and so that I may offer a joyful testimony of charity to those with whom I share holy communion. For it is not enough for my mind to be secure concerning you unless I also show that affection with which I embrace you. Indeed, whoever can fail to love those joined to God shows that he does not hate those separated from God's love merely on the basis of judgment.

Therefore I bless God as I consider the fervor of your faith amid varied storms and the adversities of tempests. I urge you also to glorify his piety concerning these matters with greater rejoicing. He tests the minds of his elect in order to make them more acceptable to himself; and although he knows them, he nevertheless proves them through certain difficulties, so that he may also show that justice is present in the gift he bestows.

Therefore it is fitting for you to persist steadfastly in your good purpose and not fail on the road that leads to the kingdoms of heaven. Whoever looks upon the Lord’s gifts as promises not to be undervalued can have regard for no danger. Consideration of present evils does not break a person unless forgetfulness of future goods prevails; for whoever loses the sweetness of the hope that is awaited excludes all the bitterness of labor.

What difficulty is equal to blessedness? What sufferings are worthy of the rewards—to speak of the future glory that will be revealed in us, as the Apostle announces (Rom. VIII)? Far be it from us that anything should separate us from the love of Christ. How great is the tribulation if it produces glory? What is thought to be adversity is the material of prosperity. While we are bent down, we are raised up. No one would receive future recompense unless he endured the necessities of the present.

See how greatly the earthly harvest of human beings rises through labor. How much more, then, must one labor to ensure that heavenly gifts do not perish? The life of the negligent is peaceful, but its substance is not rich in the fulfillment of hope: “The laborer is worthy to receive the fruit of his wage” (Luke X). If testing ceased to separate the good from the wicked, devotion would indiscriminately languish together with impiety.

The contest of the righteous is a spectacle most pleasing to the Lord. Nothing so wins heavenly grace for a person as the patient endurance of adversities. Who would admire soldiers under the security of peace?

[Note: [Col. 0401] The Roman edition reads: “What soldier merits [this] under the security of peace?”]

It is not difficult to plant secure footsteps on dry ground; nor does a calm sea display the skill of a helmsman. It is enough to advance fearlessly amid battles, not to slip amid slippery things, and to despise the waves in a storm.

[Col. 0402D] Let worldly temptation rage and exercise its movements, so long as those who are tested may appear clearly. Knowing these things, dearest brothers, hold fast to the steadfastness of your faith, and even, if they arise, love the dangers of spiritual warfare as contributing to your merits.

Announce what you honor, and share throughout the whole world the evangelical commands that you hold. In addition to your own rewards, let the correction of others also be credited to you. Among the other things by which the prophet, filled with the Spirit of God, wins divine grace for himself (Ps. L), and among those by which he seeks mercy for his preservation, he says that he will teach sinners the ways of the Lord and proclaims that through him the impious will be converted.

Blessed are those whose life, lived innocently, gives them a reward. Blessed are those through whom an example is also provided to others.

And we, insofar as it lies within us, do not cease either from concern or from labor, so that, imitating the humility that our Lord taught us, we may request what contributes to their salvation; so that, while the care of the stewardship entrusted to me is recognized, my duties may be approved.

For a second time we have sent our brothers and fellow bishops Ennodius and Peregrinus, bearing the commission of a legation, bringing forward explanations, exhortations, prayers, and tears, so that, separated from the contagion of the impious, they may come to the true faith by the same means as you, and by the means known to the apostolic see; or at least so that the world may recognize that we did not fail in preaching, but that they failed in their own salvation.

[Note: [Col. 0403D] The date is missing in the Roman edition.]

Given in the consulship of Agapitus, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of our Lord 517).

## LETTER XV.

[Note: [Col. 0403D] Possessor, an African bishop, was living in exile at Constantinople on account of the Catholic faith. There he issued a profession of the Catholic faith before the first legation. At this time he was staying at Constantinople with great benefit and advantage to all the Catholics. Baronius, year 517, no. 26. SEV. BINIUS.]

To Possessor, bishop. One must persevere in the Catholic faith.

[Col. 0403B]

Hormisdas to Possessor, bishop.

Having heard the excellent zeal of your charity and recognized the path of upright [Note: [Col. 0404D] The same edition adds: “faith.”] life that you defend without clamor, we give unceasing thanks to our God, so that you may persist in that disposition and be able to provide the others with an example to follow.

These are heavenly gifts; these are signs of divine recompense; these are the judgments of God, who did not wish you to be separated from the fellowship of Catholic priests. Therefore, dearest brother, we exhort you in this present address to persevere in the steadfastness in which you were chosen and to supply growth to your praiseworthy beginnings, because a good work—especially one pertaining to the teaching of the faith—unless it continually grows, seems to diminish.

And if worldly tribulation should occur, placing future rewards before your eyes, we advise you with apostolic admonition, saying: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us” (II Cor. X). We hope for better things, however, because God, who through the blessed Apostle said, “He did not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear” (Rom. VIII), will himself, in his mercy, as always rescue from the snares of the adversaries those whom he has chosen to be his own.

We received, through the return of our legates, the little book of your affection concerning the confession of the true faith, and in it we recognized the sincerity of your brotherhood, because you did not delay proclaiming under public testimony what you rightly believe. Given on the third day before the Nones of April, in the consulship of Agapitus, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of our Lord 517).

[Note: [Col. 0404D] With all these letters, the pontiff added a little book containing the confession of the Catholic faith, which we quoted above. By subscribing to it, anyone could prove that he was truly Catholic and could obtain Catholic communion with the Roman Church. SEV. BINIUS.]

## LETTER XVI. Sent to the people and monks of Constantinople through the same legates. One must abstain from association with heretics and persevere in the Catholic faith.

Hormisdas to the clergy, people, and orthodox monks residing at Constantinople.

[Col. 0404A] If the person who, following the evangelical commands, offers a cup of cold water receives the reward of a good purpose, with the Lord himself, who taught this, granting the recompense, does not the person who delays announcing the truth to so great a people of the faithful justly incur the penalty of condemnation?

For this reason, avoiding the threat of the heavenly commandment—what ought to be spoken must be spoken in matters pertaining to God, and must not be left unsaid—and also possessing concern for your salvation, I have undertaken the admonition that the present necessity requires. I solemnly charge all who care to preserve the Christian religion with an intact faith to turn away from and flee, with all the strength they can, those who avoid the holy Council of Chalcedon and the letters concerning the Catholic faith written by the blessed Leo.

For these are the very people who, polluted by the contagion of Eutyches and Dioscorus [Col. 0404B] of Alexandria—or rather by the wicked contagion of the Manichaeans—appear in words to wage battle against the decrees of the Fathers, but in their deeds openly rise against the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Remember, dearest ones, what was attempted when Basiliscus was occupying the imperial palace, and recall what was done or seen or heard in those times. Recall how criminal then was the presumption of Timothy, surnamed the Cat, how shameless and monstrous it was, and how great the fervor of your faith was shown throughout the whole world. The people of Constantinople then proved how purely believers ought to preserve the mysteries of Christianity.

Would that those efforts had passed away and that the present time did not now demand similar ones. For the same heretics again raise their wicked head from the depth in which they were submerged [Col. 0404C] and held fast. Therefore I ask, exhort, and admonish your affection: separate yourselves from their assemblies and communion. Remember your former zeal and show that the light and spark of spiritual fire live within you, lest the cunning of the lost rejoice that it has overcome in you the simple love of truth.

For the present necessity, and for the precaution that must be undertaken against the impious, it is enough to have said these things. I nevertheless hope that, if this admonition proves effective, it will be useful both to me and to you, since God will be glorified in your salvation and the fruit of our concern will appear. Given on the third day before the Nones of April, in the consulship of Agapitus, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of our Lord 517).

## LETTER XVII. To Ennodius and Peregrinus, bishops. He writes that he has learned from John of Nicopolis what the bishop of Thessalonica had attempted against him, and entrusts the same men through this letter with investigating the new case brought before the apostolic see.

[Col. 0404D]

Hormisdas to Ennodius and Peregrinus, bishops.

After your affection had departed, the deacon of Nicopolis, who also encountered you on the journey, came to Rome. We saw him without delay, considering whether there might perhaps be something that we ought to add to the instructions of the legation entrusted to you. The matter itself clearly shows that this was reasonably done.

For he presented us with a letter from his bishop John and another from the synod of the Church of Nicopolis subject to him. In these they complain that the bishop of Thessalonica had stirred up against them both executive and judicial authorities; that they were being severely afflicted by exactions and expenses because they had not, following ancient examples, sent a report to the bishop concerning their ordination.

For this reason they hoped that we would consider a remedy. They also consulted us about granting them permission to send a report, according to custom, to the designated bishop. We therefore discussed the matter and admonished the bishop of Nicopolis not to attempt anything of this kind if he wished to remain in communion with us, lest, if he sought confirmation from one who is alien to our communion, our communion too should suffer contagion through him.

We have instructed you about these matters so that you might know everything. What must be done concerning this matter, with God’s favor, is set out below. Given on the day before the Ides of April, in the consulship of Agapitus.

[Note: [Col. 0405D] The Roman edition adds: “concerning the matter.”]

## LETTER XVIII. To the same men. He prescribes what must be done in the case of Nicopolis with the bishop of Thessalonica.

Hormisdas to Ennodius and Peregrinus, bishops.

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, with the saints interceding and assisting: what should be done concerning the case of the Church of Nicopolis.

First, when, with God’s help, you arrive at Thessalonica, deliver to the bishop of Thessalonica the letters that we have sent in this matter, maintaining in his greeting the order that you know has been prescribed by us concerning those who are not in communion with the apostolic see, that is, with the Catholic Church. After delivering the letters, you must insist that he desist from harassing that Church, explaining that one who has returned to communion and to the body of the Church cannot have anything in common with those who have not yet returned; and that we do not revoke the privileges granted by our predecessors, provided that he himself does not abandon ecclesiastical institutions.

Certainly, let him return to unity, and we shall insist with him that all the privileges which his Church has obtained from the apostolic see be preserved inviolate. Tell him also openly that he shows himself an enemy of the faith if he persecutes those whom he sees returning to Catholic communion.

If, with God’s favor, you are able to settle the matter there, write to the bishop of Nicopolis and inform him of what your efforts have accomplished. But if he remains obstinate and refuses to cease his persecution, then, in accordance with the letters that we have sent to the most merciful emperor, prosecute the case of the Church of Nicopolis before the ruler in these terms:

“Alcyson, bishop of Nicopolis, made satisfaction to the Catholic Church; he was received and restored to communion. His successor, Bishop John, keeping both God before his eyes and his own salvation in mind, and following the good example of his predecessor, sent to the See of Blessed Peter the Apostle after condemning the heretics or transgressors, and he was received. The bishop of Thessalonica is now plotting against him and harassing him, wishing to exact from him conduct contrary to what he himself did.

“Therefore your father and all the orthodox ask that, by your commands, this harassment be removed from him, lest people think that he is suffering persecution because he has returned to communion with the apostolic see. Those who expect unity to be achieved through you will begin to think otherwise if they see your piety overlook this matter and receive it negligently.”

It seemed useful to us that the letters which we sent to the Thessalonian bishop concerning the Nicopolitan case should, in whatever order your prudence thinks best, be made public in various places, especially in the city of the Thessalonians. By this means, both the persecution of our people may cease and, if he corrects himself, we believe that his salvation may be advanced.

## LETTER XIX. TO ANASTASIUS AUGUSTUS

He commends John of Nicopolis to him.

Hormisdas to Anastasius Augustus, through the bishops Ennodius and Peregrinus.

When I consider the depths of your wisdom, most merciful emperor, I do not think that I shall displease you by taking thought for your own salvation. Neither divine admonitions nor human institutions teach that one who counsels what is good should be condemned by any reproach—especially since your piety also declares that it burns with zeal for unity and peace.

This matter compelled me, both because of my confidence in your conscience and because of the duty of administration entrusted to me, not to neglect the affair when it arose. John, my brother and fellow bishop, bishop of the city of Nicopolis, following the example of his predecessor, Alcyson of holy memory, sought communion with blessed Peter the Apostle together with his synod, after condemning those whom the Church detests.

He is now being worn down by grievous plots. I beg your gentleness: oppose those who are contriving injustice, remove the harassment, and support the man who has corrected himself, although pressure ought to have been applied to him so that he might correct himself. Those who have delayed will know that they will be guilty when they see that those who have already returned are being supported by you.

I confess, most merciful emperor, that I am astonished that the obstinacy of those who plot is moved neither by consideration of God nor by consideration of you. For those who hate in a person the pursuit of a good desire—by which they judge that they themselves are being assessed—persecute those who bring back the straying to the right path; and they deserve blame if they do not convert the wayward.

Give clear proof of your faith by considering how you may assist all who have been restored to unity, both by every duty and by every exhortation.

## LETTER XX. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF NICOPOLIS

He urges him to endure the hardships suffered for the faith with equanimity and therefore to confirm the provincial bishops in the unity of the faith.

Hormisdas to John, bishop of Nicopolis.

When our subdeacon Pulio returned, we received a letter expressing your affection. We rejoiced over your constancy in the faith and over the intention that you maintain concerning communion with the apostolic see; but we were saddened to hear that you are enduring certain hardships.

Yet these things cannot last long, because where God is worshiped purely, even if adversity occurs, it is changed into prosperity, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Hope does not disappoint” (Romans 5). The chief of the apostles, while walking across the sea in doubt, suffered distress (Matthew 14); yet, as soon as he called upon his Lord, he found him ready to extend his hand and not allow him to remain in danger.

Therefore, following the examples of our fathers and remaining firm in their faith, let us seek the help of him of whom it is written: “He does not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear” (1 Corinthians 10).

Accordingly, greeting your affection, we exhort you, as we said previously, to persevere in what has been begun well, because “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10). Do not cease frequently to relieve our concern by addressing us.

Confirm your parish priests also with suitable exhortation, because by doing this you will be able daily to multiply the talent entrusted to you. We are also considering the matter which your affection requests, so that our prayers may reach the most merciful emperor for the peace of all.

Only do not cease to support our desire and effort with appropriate prayers, since we ourselves have not been able to devote sufficient time to completing these matters with God as their author.

Given on the fifth day before the Nones of March, in the consulship of Agapitus, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of the Lord 517).

## LETTER XXI. TO THE SAME JOHN

[Col. 0407C]

Hormisdas to John, bishop of Nicopolis, together with his synod.

We would wish, dearest brothers, that you were free from every wave of hardship, that you might pass your life beneath the serenity of tranquility, and that, with the disturbance of your minds by worldly storms removed, you might serve our God … [lacuna] moved us, because what we do not wish to happen we must necessarily grieve when it has happened.

But the world abounds in troubles and temptations. This age in which we are pilgrims is everywhere exposed, like a great mass, to the storms of the winds. Thus the minds of the faithful are battered by the devil’s plots, and, as it is written, “all who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3).

Yet the hope promised by a just rewarder consoles us, because “blessed is the one who is not offended in the Lord” (Matthew 11). Let the fragile and passing assaults of this world not cast down God’s soldiers. He who stands beside the brave takes no pleasure in the cowardly.

Things that pass away are easily despised if those that will remain are kept in mind. The opportunity for testing must be embraced, because although the burdens of labor are hard, the rewards of virtue are greater. What reward will be fitting for one who proves unequal to the test?

Let us not be sluggish in matters of courage if we desire to reach the promises. Who would wait for a human voice on this matter, when the sentence of truth sounds in our ears every day: “Blessed are those who suffer for righteousness” (Matthew 5)?

But do not think, dearest brothers, that I have offered you only spiritual consolations for your strengthening, although these are great among the faithful. In providing remedies for your tribulation, I have not been idle insofar as human ability allowed. Through envoys sent to the ruler of the East and to the bishop of Thessalonica, I admonished him to cease his attacks upon you; and I added pages requesting that an appeal be made to the emperor.

These matters have been provided for as regards the present. But those that concern future hope should rather be considered by your minds.

I confess that I was greatly surprised that, amid the statements of your distress, this concern could find its way into your religious prudence: that you should ask me, under the guise of consolation, for permission to send firm letters directing the Thessalonian bishop. Would I become the author of something which, if I learned that it had been done without my knowledge, I would condemn? Far be such perversity from us.

Hear the apostolic voice, suitably applied to my own person: “If I rebuild what I destroyed, I show myself a transgressor” (Galatians 2). I beg you, do not return to the contagions that you scarcely escaped; do not allow the feet that were pulled away from the mud in which they were held to be immersed in it again through wrongdoing.

Allow the past to remain obliterated. “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9). Those who look back at what they are leaving are hindered from advancing along the journey they have undertaken.

Ecclesiastical discipline does not love those in whom the memory of that treachery remains. They must be entirely cut off from the erring, because those who return to what they rejected are considered so detestable that blessed Peter the Apostle (2 Peter 2) declared that it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them.

It is clear how steadfastly the faith once delivered must be guarded, if it is more tolerable to persist in error than to become entangled again in the pollutions from which one has fled.

Given on the day before the Ides of April, in the consulship of Agapitus, a man of illustrious rank.

## LETTER XXII. TO DOROTHEUS, BISHOP OF THESSALONICA

Hormisdas, bishop, to Dorotheus, bishop of Thessalonica.

John, my brother and fellow bishop, bishop of the city of Nicopolis, together with his synod, complains that he is being severely afflicted by various forms of harassment and loss because, having separated himself from the company of transgressors and having obtained communion with the apostolic see, he did not send to the Church of the Thessalonians the beginning of his ordination.

His neglect could have been culpable if there were one mystery of charity among all. But since many have separated themselves from the solidity of that rock which is Christ, who would not wish to be separated from the fellowship of those who err, so as to deserve to be joined with those who stand in the truth?

It was not custom, therefore, that was neglected, but contagion that was avoided. Who, then, could charge him with error when he recognizes that he prudently considered a salutary precaution?

As for us, we believed that you ought to have taken up this matter first, or at least that, after the example of others, you could have followed it. Is delay in the case of those who have fallen not enough, unless envy is also added, to increase the charge against you, even toward those who return to the way?

What else do those who persecute people fleeing to the altars of that very See of Peter hate—if it may be said without impiety—than the name itself which was given by the Lord to blessed Peter?

With what shame, I ask, do you desire the privileges of those people to remain with you when you do not observe their commands? And do you wish to have ecclesiastical authority confer upon you the reverence for the faith that you do not yourself display?

If you stood upon the same footsteps on which Catholics rely, you ought nevertheless to avoid persecuting your neighbor, knowing that, according to the teaching of our Lord and Savior whom we worship, the one who causes one of the least to stumble is liable to great sins (Mark 9).

Where, Lord, is the humility that you taught on the occasion of your disciples’ dispute about rank? You showed that the greatest is the one who strives to show himself little.

“Look down from heaven and see; visit this vine, which you planted as its cultivator” (Psalm 79). Give attention to the least in keeping your commandments, and to those exalted by ambition for honor.

Why do you desire recent things and abandon ancient ones, negligent in great matters and concerned with small ones? Is this not to tithe worthless things and to despise the precepts of the law?

Keep those things that accord with God, and those that come from human beings will easily follow. Rather, take up concern for your salvation and sigh because another has preceded you in truth, lest, if you persist in persecuting those who return to the members of the Church, you too should be joined with those whom the apostolic sentence explicitly condemns.

Given on the day before the Ides of April, in the consulship of Agapitus, a man of illustrious rank.

[Note: At this time the events occurred which Anastasius the Librarian records in the Life of Hormisdas, in these words: “Likewise, on the second occasion he sent Ennodius,” and so forth. After these events, the following letter indicates what massacres and injuries Severus of Antioch and the other Acephali inflicted upon the orthodox in Syria. Severus Binius.]

## LETTER OF ANASTASIUS TO HORMISDAS

He reproaches Hormisdas for excessive harshness. (C)

[Col. 0409C]

Anastasius Augustus to Pope Hormisdas.

Although silence is judged to be something great, it is nevertheless necessary, when we marvel at God’s mercy, to return continually to speech. And since no one is unaware that the beginning of the faith which our Lord and God, our Savior Jesus Christ, taught us excels in the forgiveness of sins, he himself cleansed all Adam’s sins through his own passion.

This was the work of his humility: to free the aforesaid man and all the brothers from slavery to sin, willingly assuming the person of a servant. For blessed Paul the Apostle taught us, writing to the Romans: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin” (Romans 5). From this, through a general arrangement—or through wondrous examples—it has in some way been made clear to all that particular examples ought to receive once and for all the commands of so great a law, and of one established by such pious goodness. [Note: The Roman edition adds “to receive.”] [Note: Another reading has “so great.”] [Note: Another reading has “by command.”] [Note: Another reading has “confirmed.”]

Thus the whole teaching which he delivered to his disciples rests upon this foundation. He drove away illnesses and the manifold kinds of suffering; by his own passion he loosened the knot of sin, as it is written; and, by his deeds and words, he instructed his disciples to perform similar things.

But if, as some strive to show, certain persons from among his apostles refused through disobedience to fulfill so pious a doctrine, we do not know where the teaching of the merciful Lord and great God could come to our aid.

We do not, however, believe for this reason that those who learned mercy should be thought merciless. Rather, for the present we restrain our request through silence, judging it unreasonable to extend the kindness of prayers to those who refuse to be asked and stubbornly reject them. We can endure being insulted and annulled; we cannot endure being commanded.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of July at Constantinople, in the consulship of Anastasius Augustus for the fourth time and Agapitus, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of the Lord 517).

## EXAMPLE OF THE PETITION OF THE MINOR ARCHIMANDRITES AND OTHER MONKS OF SECOND SYRIA

They write about what they suffer for the Catholic faith from the Eutychianists, whom the emperor had taken no care to restrain, and about how, having not been heard by the emperor, they appeal to the Roman pontiff as their common father.

[Col. 0410B]

To the most holy and most blessed patriarch of the whole world, Hormisdas, who occupies the See of the prince of the apostles, Peter: the prayer and supplication of the least archimandrites and other monks of the province of Second Syria.

The grace of Christ, the Savior of us all, has instructed us to flee to your blessedness as from winter and storm to a harbor of tranquility, and we no longer believe that we are held within the calamities surrounding us. For even if we suffer, we endure joyfully, knowing that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8).

Since Christ our God has appointed you and your holy angel as chief shepherd, teacher, and physician of souls, it is fitting to set forth the sufferings that have befallen us and to expose the merciless wolves who scatter Christ’s flock, so that, by the staff of your authority, he may drive them from among the sheep; by the word of teaching he may heal the soul; and by the medicines of prayer he may soothe it.

Who these men are, and who armed them against us, you have certainly heard, most blessed father: that Severus and Peter, who have never been counted among Christians, attack every day the holy Council of Chalcedon and our most holy father Leo with public anathema; who, making nothing of God’s judgment and trampling upon the canons to be revered as those of the holy Fathers, have bishops brought before the imperial power and have compelled us to mock the aforesaid holy synod, while afflicting us with immeasurable punishments.

As a result, some of them, unable to endure the wounds inflicted upon them, departed from this world, and a considerable number of our own people were killed. For when we were going to the monastery of the lord Simeon on account of the Church, the aforesaid polluted men lay in wait for us on the road. They attacked us and killed three hundred and fifty of our men; they wounded some; and they killed others who were able to flee to venerate the altars. They burned the monasteries, sending during the night a multitude of disorderly and hired men; and these pestilential people consumed all the ecclesiastical property of the poor in this manner.

The documents delivered to your blessedness concerning each matter will provide information through our venerable brothers John and Sergius, whom we had sent to Constantinople, hoping that vengeance would be taken for the crimes committed. But the emperor did not deem them worthy even of a word; indeed, he expelled them with great insult and threatened those who presented these matters.

From this we have learned, even if late, that such great wickedness and audacity against the Churches has been contrived by the instigation of that very man.

Therefore we implore you, most blessed father, beseeching and entreating you to rise up with fervor and zeal, to grieve justly over the mutilated body—for you are the head of all—and to vindicate the despised faith, the trampled canons, the blasphemed Fathers, and the synod attacked with such anathema.

God has given you the power and authority to bind and to loose. “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matthew 16).

Rise up, holy Fathers, and come to save us. Imitate our Lord, who came from heaven to earth to seek the wandering sheep. Look to Peter, the prince of the apostles, whose seat you adorn, and to Paul, the vessel of election, who went throughout the world and enlightened it. Great wounds require greater remedies.

When hirelings see wolves coming against the sheep, they abandon them to be scattered. But you are true shepherds and teachers, entrusted with care for the salvation of the sheep. The flock itself comes to meet you, recognizing its shepherd after being freed from the fiercest beasts and following the shepherd’s voice, as the Lord says: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10).

Therefore, most holy father, do not despise us, who are wounded every day by savage beasts.

For the complete knowledge of your holy angel, in this same petition, which has the force of a formal document, we anathematize all who have been cast out and excommunicated by your apostolic see. We name Nestorius, who was bishop of Constantinople; Eutyches; Dioscorus; Peter of Alexandria, surnamed Balbus; Peter called the Fuller, likewise of Antioch; and Acacius, who was bishop of Constantinople, and his communicants; and all who defend any one of those heretics.

## LETTER XXIII. TO THE ARCHIMANDRITES OF SYRIA

He consoles and exhorts them to persevere in the Catholic faith.

[Note: The following letters are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0415A]

Hormisdas, bishop, to the priests and archimandrites who are in Second Syria, and to the other orthodox living in whatever eastern region and remaining in communion with the Apostolic See.

After reading the letters of your affection, through which the madness of God’s enemies has been exposed and the stubborn fury of the unbelievers has been painfully revealed—those who, since they hate the Lord with the spirit of evil life, impiously persecute his members—as far as I have been able to understand from your steadfastness, I blessed the Lord, who preserves the faith of his soldiers amid adversities.

And again, considering the disturbance of the Churches and the burdens and labors of God’s servants, groaning with the prophet I cried out: “Arise, O Lord; judge your cause; remember your reproaches, those inflicted all day long by the foolish” (Psalm 72). I gladly add what follows in the same way: “Do not forget the voice of those who seek you; the pride of those who hate you has continually risen up against you.”

For just as we must preserve the firmness of the faith, so it is not fitting to distrust the justice of divine judgment. This labor of the Church is not new, brothers; yet, even while she is humbled by it, she is exalted, and through those things by which she seems to be impoverished, she is enriched.

It is the experience of God’s faithful that through the death of their bodies they gain the life of their souls. They lose what is fleeting, but purchase what is eternal; and while persecution makes a way for testing, the testing itself becomes the source of its worth.

Foolish men, raging in their blindness, do not understand that those whom they think they can separate from human society they are leading into the kingdom of God. Hence joy exists amid dangers and eagerness for suffering, for the giver of great rewards awaits the struggles of his own.

Who would not falter amid evils unless the opposing circumstances were consoled by rewards? That is the hope which does not allow us to grow weak in despair. The sweet taste of virtues shuts out the bitterness of afflictions.

Who would consider present things great while thinking upon those that are to come? Who would refuse death if he understood the recompense of the future?

Stand firm, my beloved, and, preserving your faith unshaken with steadfast judgment, bear the fruit of the praise of endurance, in which salvation lies, and of the reward of good works. Great are the things to which we unworthy people are called.

Let weakness not delay you, because the rewarder is faithful and a powerful helper. Let us not be deceived by hope in what is most pleasing, nor choose pleasant things or prefer what is easy. Our Lord did not promise us luxuries or flatteries; he promised rewards, not idleness. Praise and laziness do not belong together.

What room will there be for recompense if there is no concern for virtue? The gate is narrow, but the royal dwellings are broad; entry is granted to few, but to those who are approved.

Are these not the first words addressed to those whom he taught: “They will persecute you, and in their synagogues they will scourge you”?

“Through endurance,” as it is written, “let us possess our souls,” lest through lack of endurance we grieve after losing them.

Our Lord was the first to ascend the cross, and the teacher of his own endurance. He went up in his own form as an example to those whom he was to help. He himself, standing between virtues and labors, bears the yoke amid the poisons of the mad, so that, in accordance with the fury of persecution, he himself may also provide the crowns of the eternal kingdom.

Consider what was the end of the Maccabees: for the steadfast, struggle is followed by a record of praise. With what honor are Judas and that band of brothers acclaimed in death? In whose mouths is the people that was consumed remembered? All these powers, which existed for the defense of the law as likenesses and shadows of things to come, were deemed worthy of so many examples. We have seen them in our fathers, touched them, and tested them, so that we might know whom we should follow.

What does not fit the subject? What is contrary to the truth? What is not owed to the Redeemer? In these matters we gladly share these teachings with you.

For the wisest Solomon says somewhere: “Blessed is the one who proclaims a word to the hearing of one who obeys.” It is therefore a joy to speak with those who are willing and to urge toward the right path those who do not resist.

We possess the pledge of your faith: the steadfastness acknowledged in your letters, by which, having separated yourselves from the corruption of transgressors, you return to the doctrines and commandments of the Apostolic See. You entered the way of truth late, but blessed be God, who does not forget forever. He chastens and heals, and does not permit the sheep of his united flock to be torn apart by the attacks of plotting wolves.

Through blended severity, he overlooks neither the safety nor the salvation of his own.

But what wonder is it if that crafty, blood-stained, ravenous beast disturbed the sheep when the one and true shepherd had been abandoned and the sheep had been scattered? Those who abandon their own safety throw themselves into the dangers by which they are torn apart.

Therefore, even now, stand firm with steady steps upon the road of the fathers, to which you have returned. The mercy of God can reckon the correction of others also to your reward if, through you, they are guided toward the straight path.

But tear yourselves completely away from the mire in which the heretics are swallowed and held fast. Shake off the uncleanness of the dust that has clung to you, and condemn by a devout renunciation all who have deviated from the Apostolic doctrines.

“There is no fellowship between darkness and light.” Nor do those who walk along straight roads join their own footsteps to those who turn aside into error.

The bond of faith must be held fast, and the corruption arising from unbelieving communion must be rejected, because, according to the Apostle, “the one who joins himself to the Lord is one spirit; likewise, the one who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body.”

Virtues love one another’s fellowship, while impiety plunges those who cling to it into the abyss together with itself.

The doctrines of the Fathers are before our eyes, in our mouths, and in our very hands; we are commanded to preserve them. The venerable synods closely surround them for their preservation.

It would be a lengthy matter to reveal everything in detail: the matters of the Council of Chalcedon, in which the reverence of all is contained, and also the definitions issued by the most revered Leo from the very heart of the Apostles. We ought both to know and to preserve them.

In these things lies the reverence of the faith; in these are the bulwarks of truth; in these Christ is known; in these the hope of our redemption and the foundation of our faith are preserved.

This is the foundation of which we read in the Apostle, upon which anyone deceives himself if he attempts to build wood, hay, or straw, destined to be consumed by fire.

In these matters the poisons of Eutyches and Nestorius were destroyed by the synods. Although they contend with one another through opposing arguments concerning the lordly economy of the saving mystery, they agree in a kind of equality of sacrilege: unequal in their opinions, but united in impiety.

One of them, unwilling that the virgin Mary be the Mother of God, divides what is united in our Lord. The other, insofar as he confuses what is proper to the united natures, as well as what is true, extinguishes the mystery of our redemption. One impiously joins to this the religion of Photinus, another the folly of Manes, through an ungodly kinship.

Against these, beloved brothers, remedies were prepared in advance. Claim them by the power of reason, since you see the heretics fighting through impiety to overthrow them.

Let truth not be hesitant in its teaching. With what zeal ought salvation to be loved when you see deadly destruction embraced with such affection? Let us be ashamed to explain the laws of truth sluggishly when errors are defended so stubbornly.

The synodal decrees mentioned above pursue the originators of these evil inventions with just condemnations. But we also remind you likewise to avoid their followers. The Apostolic See recognized them as like their teachers and joined them to those already condemned: Timothy the parricide; Dioscorus; Peter of Alexandria; Acacius of Constantinople together with his followers; likewise Peter of Antioch, similar to the aforementioned man both in error and in name; and Severus of the same place, no less so in his poison; Xenaias of Hierapolis; Cyrus of Edessa; and Peter of Apamea.

They are to be condemned not only for their own destruction but equally for the destruction of others. For, while they ceaselessly roll themselves in the filth of their own opinions, they have polluted others through their teaching—those who followed them in evil. I exhort you with a general and saving command.

Therefore, reject everything brought forward from any writings whatsoever that is contrary to the canons of the Fathers. Let no one renew you with unsuitable commands or more recent definitions.

If such people are worldly and unable to govern the Churches, it is because it is more appropriate for them to be taught than to teach. For it is unlawful to offer foreign libations upon venerable altars, since God, in the sacred ordinances, clearly prescribed for the pious the limits of knowledge and honor, and distinguished the ministry between the Levites and his own people.

The authority of human beings is one thing; the services of priests are another. He who brought foreign fire into the divine sanctuary, polluting the sacred things, provoked the Lord rather than appeasing him.

Who is able to acquire for himself authority to command through foreign decrees? It is not a matter of doubt that one who offers the honor that is owed is punished in the temple solely for attempting to perform the ministry.

Uzziah remained in reverence and service; if, warned by the example of such a great rebuke, he had feared the sacred ordinances rather than daring to violate them, he would have ruled better. But, since the persistent transgressor did not withdraw even when the guardians of the temple opposed him, he was struck with the abomination of leprosy before the altars, lost the royal ministry, and invaded the priest’s service.

Let them know, therefore, that those things are not acceptable to God which are seized from his own commandments by the presumptuous, since, to display the judgment, he preserved one man for the punishment of such great disorder, while swift fire consumed others.

Therefore, whatever things have been received under some form of religious observance cannot possess authority when they are worn down by so many authoritative testimonies.

The Apostle Paul cries out: “Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you anything contrary to what we preached, let him be accursed.” He was not satisfied to say this once; he repeated the sound command: “As we said before, and now I say again, if anyone preaches to you anything contrary to what you received, let him be accursed.”

For he preserves the decision previously issued by the guardianship of the faith if anyone follows Apostolic teaching. This, then, is the concern that remains for us.

Indeed, in the double service of this embassy, we have brought forward whatever was humble in our petitions, whatever was reasonable in our defenses, and whatever was sound in our commands.

But is the way of righteousness therefore to be neglected? Since unbelief loves its own errors with madness, it is impossible to join oneself to the stumbling of those who fall without suffering our own corruption. Let those who turn aside from their own impieties perish without our corruption, even when their error is not scourged.

And with another hand:

May God preserve you in health, beloved children.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of February, after the consulship of Agapitus, a most illustrious man.

Hormisdas, bishop, to the priests, deacons, and archimandrites of Second Syria, and to the other orthodox living in whatever eastern region and remaining in communion with the apostolic see.

[Note: From an old Vatican manuscript, printed in the Roman edition of 1591 as Letter 21 and thereafter in other editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0415D] From another Latin version it is read in Hardouin.]

Having read the letter of Your Love, in which the madness of the enemies of God has been exposed and the obstinate fury of the unbelievers has been sorrowfully set forth—those who, hating the Lord with a revived spirit, wickedly persecute his members—I blessed God for the recognition of your steadfastness, since he preserves the faith of his soldiers amid adversity. But again, considering the upheaval of the Churches [Col. 0416B] and the troubles and labors of God’s servants, with the prophet’s help I cried out: “Arise, O Lord; judge your cause. Remember the reproaches directed against you all day long by the foolish” (Psalm 72), gladly adding what follows as well: “Do not forget the voice of those who seek you; the pride of those who hate you has continually risen up to you.” For just as we ought to preserve the firmness of faith, so it is not fitting to distrust the equity of divine judgment.

This is not a new labor for the Church, brothers; and yet, while she is humbled, she is raised up, and through the very things by which she is believed to be worn down, losses are avoided. It is customary for God’s faithful that, through the deaths of their bodies, they gain the lives of their souls: they lose what is perishable, but purchase what is eternal; and while persecution opens the way for testing, testing becomes the cause of merit. Fools, raging in blindness, do not know that those whom they think they can remove from human society they are bringing to the kingdoms of God. Hence, amid the very dangers, there are joys and an eagerness for suffering; for he who bestows great rewards awaits the struggles of his own.

For who would not be broken by misfortunes unless adversity were consoled by the promise of rewards? That hope does not allow one to fail in despair: the sweet savor of the virtues excludes the bitterness of tribulations. For who would value present things greatly [another reading: regard them as great], knowing how to esteem what is to come? Who would refuse the losses of this life if he considers what must be received?

Persevere, dearest to me, and, preserving the unshaken faith with steadfast courage, claim the praise of perseverance, in which lie the salvation and the crown of good people [Col. 0416D]. Great are the things to which we, though unworthy, are called. Let not weakness hold you back, because he who calls is a faithful rewarder and a strong helper. Let us not be deceived by the hope of prosperity or softness; let us not propose easy things. Our Lord has not promised us delights or flattering ease: he promised rewards, not leisure. Praise is not well joined to repose. What place will there be for recompense if there is no concern for virtue? The gate is narrow, but the kingdoms are spacious; the entrance is for the few, but for those who have been tested.

Are these not the words that preceded those whom he taught: “They will persecute you, and in the synagogues they will scourge you” (Matthew 15)? Let us possess our souls through patience, as it is written, lest through impatience we grieve that we have lost them [Col. 0418A].

Our Lord was the first to ascend the cross, and the teacher of patience itself, shaping by his example those whom he was to assist with his help. He himself holds the balance between virtues and labors, standing against the poisons of the enraged, so that, in proportion to the fury of the persecution, he may bestow on them the crowns of eternal rule.

Recall the steadfast praises that ancient history follows through the deaths of the Maccabees: how Judas and that final phalanx of the faithful are commemorated with the honor of death; with what steadfast voice the people consumed on the mountain are celebrated; and how all these forms and shadows of the future, offered for the preservation of the law of virtue, deserved such great examples. In the Fathers we have seen, touched, and tested whom we should follow. What should not be rendered to the cause that must not be denied to the truth? What is not owed to the Redeemer? [Col. 0418B]

We have gladly shared these doctrines with you. For the wisest Solomon says: “Blessed is he who proclaims the word in the ear of one who obeys” (Ecclesiasticus 25). It is indeed a joy to address those who are willing and to encourage those who do not resist toward the right path.

For we hold as a pledge of your faith, under the testimony of your letters, the steadfastness by which, separated from the contagion of transgressors, you return to the doctrines and commands of the apostolic see—entering the way of truth late, indeed; but blessed be God, who does not forget forever, who corrects and heals, and does not continually allow the sheep of his flock to be torn apart by the rapacity of lurking wolves. Through the measured strictness of discipline, he neither neglects the correction of his own nor their salvation.

But what wonder if a cunning, bloodthirsty, and rapacious enemy has disturbed sheep scattered after abandoning that one true shepherd? Those who forsake his protection expose themselves to dangers by which they may be torn apart. Therefore, now at least, stand firmly with solid steps on the way of the Fathers to which you have returned. The mercy of God will be able to credit to your reward the correction of others as well, if they are led by you to what is right.

But withdraw yourselves completely from the filth in which heretics are held submerged; shake off the impurity of the dust clinging to you; and condemn with religious abhorrence, as a whole, all who deviate from the apostolic doctrines. “There is no fellowship between darkness and light” (1 Corinthians 6); nor do those who walk along straight roads join their footsteps to the error of those who go astray.

The bond of faith must be held, and the contagion of faithless association avoided; for, according to the Apostle, “just as the one who clings to the Lord is one spirit, so the one who clings to a prostitute becomes one body” (ibid.). Virtues love their companions; and impiety, together with those who cling to it, plunges them into the depths. The doctrines of the Fathers, which we command to be guarded, are before us, in our eyes, in our mouths, and in our very hands; venerable councils constrain us daily to preserve them.

It would be lengthy to recount everything individually. We must know and defend the Council of Chalcedon, in which the reverence of all is contained, as well as the pronouncements of the venerable Leo, formulated from the very heart of the apostles. In these is the standard of faith; in these the fortress of truth; in these Christ is recognized; in these the hope and cause of our redemption are preserved.

This is what we read in the Apostle (1 Corinthians 5) as the foundation upon which anyone deceives himself who attempts to build above it wood, hay, or stubble destined to be consumed by fire [Col. 0420A]. In these councils the poisons of Eutyches and Nestorius were destroyed. For while, in disputes opposed to one another, they strive against the saving mystery of the Lord’s dispensation, they agree in a certain sacrilegious equality: differing in their judgments but united in impiety. One of them, unwilling that blessed Mary should be the Mother of God, divides in our Lord the things that have been united; the other, while confusing the proper and distinct features of the natures that belong together, extinguishes the mystery of our redemption. One touched the sect of Photinus, the other the madness of Manes, with an impious contagion.

Against these, dearest brothers, defend the remedies already provided with that courage of mind by which you see heretics fighting in their impiety for the overthrow of these things [Col. 0420B]. Let the assertion of truth not be sluggish. With what zeal ought salvation to be loved, when you see deadly perdition loved in this way? Let it shame us to assert the laws of truth sluggishly when errors are defended with such obstinacy.

The authors of the evil inventions mentioned above are pursued by the synodal decrees with just condemnations.
