But we also admonish you to avoid their followers, whom the apostolic see has recognized as equal to their authors and has joined them to the condemned [another reading: has condemned them]: Timothy the parricide, Dioscorus and Peter of Alexandria, Acacius of Constantinople together with his followers, and Peter of Antioch, similar to the aforesaid in error as well as in name. Likewise Severus of the same place; Xenaia [Xenea], also of Hierapolis; Cyrus of Elada [or: Edessa] [Note: [Col. 0419D] Facundus, p. 105, mentions this Cyrus and makes him a Nestorian. Ennodius also mentions him, Distinction 6; Victor of Tunnuna and Evagrius, book III, chapter 31.]; and Peter of Apamea—not merely to be condemned for their own sake, but also for the condemnation of others. For while they continually envelop themselves in the filth of their opinions, they also polluted others by teaching what they had wrongly grasped.

I warn you with the salutary force of a general command: reject whatever is produced against the rules of the Fathers from any commentaries whatsoever. Let no one move you with incongruous precepts or novel institutions. For if they are worldly, they cannot hold Churches, because it is more fitting for them to learn than to teach.

It is sacrilegious to bring foreign offerings to holy altars, because God prescribed definite boundaries for religious observances even at the very beginnings of his worship; he divided the office between the Levites and his people. One authority belongs to human beings, another ministry to priests (Luke 10). The one who introduced an alien fire into the divine sanctuaries as a violator of sacred things provoked the Lord rather than appeased him.

Who could assume for himself the authority to command in institutions belonging to another, when it is beyond doubt that the one offering the due honor was punished solely for his presumption of office? If Uzziah had remained within the reverence and administration proper to a king (2 Chronicles 26), he would have been better restrained by fearing rather than undertaking such things, after being warned by an example of such destruction and by religious institutions. But, while the obstinate violator did not desist even when the temple ministers forbade him, he was struck by the abomination of leprosy itself and lost the altars and offices of the kingdom while invading the ministry of the priest.

Let them therefore know that what presumptuous people undertake from God’s commands is not accepted by God, since he preserved one punishment as a vivid sign of disgrace [or: of great deformity], while a swift flame consumed others. And if some things are covered by some appearance of religion, they cannot possess force when they resist such authorities.

The Apostle Paul cries out: “Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be anathema” (Galatians 1). Nor is it enough that he said this once; he repeats the salutary command: “As we said before, and now I say again: if anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be anathema” [Col. 0422B].

Therefore, let whoever follows apostolic discipline preserve the sentence delivered for the safeguarding of the faith. Indeed, we have not lacked concern; for in the twofold service of our legation we have brought whatever was humble in our entreaties, whatever was reasonable in our pleadings, and whatever was salutary in our commands. But is the way of justice therefore to be neglected? Since unbelief loves its own errors with the obstinacy of faithlessness, those falling away must not be joined to the stumble of those who fall. Without our contagion, let those perish who do not turn away from their impieties even when their error has been chastised.

And in another hand: May God preserve you in health, dearest sons.

Issued on the fourth day before the Ides of February [10 February], in the year of Christ 518, after the consulship of Agapitus, the most illustrious man.

[Note: The collector of the decretal letters, following Surius, assigned the following letters to the second consulship of Agapitus and to the year of the Lord 541. If this were true, Hormisdas would have had to administer the pontificate for more than twenty years, whereas, according to the common judgment of all writers, he held the apostolic see for no more than nine years. Therefore I judged that I would do the reader a considerable service by placing these letters of Hormisdas, dated under the consulship of Agapitus, after the preceding letters marked with the same consular notation. [Col. 0422D] Sev. Binius. Binius was mistaken when he thought that the collector of the decretals had erred by wishing to refer these letters to the year 521, in which Valerius and Justinian were the ordinary consuls, while Agapitus was extraordinary consul, as the collector himself notes. Thus there was an error in the edition when, instead of 521, 541 was placed in the margin, says R. C.]

## Letter XXIV. To John, Bishop of Tarragona

He approves that he has gladly heard of his arrival in Italy, approves the letters he sent to the Spaniards concerning ecclesiastical institutions, and entrusts him with his own representation.

[Col. 0421C]

To his dearest brother John, Hormisdas.

Your Love did what was consonant with charity and faith by informing us in a letter of your arrival in Italy and by showing what depth of religious devotion is in you [Col. 0421D]. Would that the joys of your presence had come to us for the satisfaction of a fuller affection, so that we might rejoice in enjoying both your conversation and your presence, which we have already embraced through your letters.

Nevertheless, dearest brother, you have shown with what affection you venerate the Christian faith, since you desire to preserve without any further transgression the things that pertain to the rules of the Fathers [Col. 0422C] and to catholic commands. You hope that, by extending the general regulations established for the Churches of Spain, we may sanction what is done either too negligently or too irreligiously, in a manner suited to ecclesiastical discipline [Note: [Col. 0422D] “We may judge.” “We embraced the opportunity offered by this desired request.”]. We have embraced this request, taking advantage of the opportunity opened by your desire.

For what is sweeter to you than to speak with the faithful? Or what is more fitting [or: more blessed] for God than to recall those who have gone astray from error? Therefore, greeting the love by which we are joined, we signify through Cassian, your deacon, that we have sent general regulations in which we have either appropriately decreed what ought to be observed according to the canons or sufficiently instructed you concerning the precautions that ought to be taken regarding those who come from the Greek clergy.

The order and explanation of the matter itself will also teach you abundantly through ecclesiastical decrees, so that, recognizing both the transgression of the impious and the care of the apostolic see, which keeps watch for the rules of the Fathers, you may show that you detest [or: regard as detestable] the associations of the condemned and love those who are faithful.

And because, through your Love’s communication, the providential ordering [another reading in Hardouin: prudence] of this course has been disclosed to us, we reward your solicitude. While preserving the privileges established for metropolitans, we delegate to you the representation of the apostolic see to this extent: after examining these matters, see that either what pertains to the canons or what has recently been commanded by us is observed; and disclose to us in your report whatever concerning ecclesiastical cases may come to your notice.

It will be the task of your zeal and solicitude to show yourself in the matters entrusted to you in such a way that you imitate the faith and integrity of the one whose care you undertake [Col. 0423B].

Issued on the fourth day before the Nones of April [2 April], under the consulship of Agapitus, the most illustrious man [or: in the manuscript code, in the Spanish Era 555, in the year of Christ 517].

## Letter XXV. To All the Bishops of Spain

I. On ordaining priests according to the statutes of the canons.  
II. That no payment be accepted for a bishopric.  
III. On holding a council every year.

To his dearest brothers, all the bishops established throughout Spain, Hormisdas.

Blessed is the Trinity, our God, who, by his mercy, having spread the tranquility of his peace throughout all parts of the Roman state, has also granted us a way of demonstrating charity toward one another, so that those who are joined by the firmness of faith may also be united by the desired joy of conversation. Thus, more easily, while through the ministry of letters we reach you, we may also stir your hearts to religious worship by apostolic admonitions; and, while we return the pledge of our love as a kind of debt, we may show our complete devotion toward God.

Let us therefore join together, dearest brothers, in constant and humble prayers, and, beseeching our Lord with tears of mouth and heart, let us ask him in continual supplication that, both in institution and in conduct, we may cling to the one whose members we desire to be. Let us never turn aside by a wandering path from that way which is Christ, lest we be justly abandoned by him whom we wickedly abandon.

This can come to pass for us through the help of heavenly favor if we preserve the apostolic doctrines and the commands of the Fathers [Col. 0423D]. For our Lord says: “Whoever loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14).

Although these words could suffice as a general statement, whether to make us avoid errors or preserve catholic decrees, nevertheless, since it has been reported to us through the communication of our brother and fellow bishop John that certain things are being presumed against the reverence due to the canons, I judged that they must be proclaimed in general regulations, avoiding the danger threatening teachers because of silence and pierced by the prophetic voice that says: “Speak, do not be silent” (Isaiah 18).

### I. On Ordaining Priests

When priests are ordained, consider what has been prescribed and defined by the Fathers. For just as Christ is the head of the Church and priests are Christ’s vicars, so there ought to be conspicuous care in choosing them. Those who must preside over people requiring correction ought to be irreproachable; nor should anything be lacking in the character of one in whom the whole substance and dignity of religious discipline resides.

Let each person estimate the value of the Lord’s flock, so that he may know what merit is fitting for the one who appoints its shepherd. This will happen if the rank of the priesthood is not transferred indiscriminately to laymen by some kind of sudden leap. The person to whom the governance of the Church is entrusted must demonstrate his life through a lengthy period of testing.

We do not deny that there are among laymen ways of life pleasing to God, but faithful institutions seek soldiers who have been tested. Everyone must first learn before teaching, and must offer others an example of religious conduct from himself rather than receive one from them [Col. 0424A].

The one who must pray for the people ought to be an example of correction to the people. Religious worship should be handed down through long observance, so that it may shine forth; and the person who is to be educated through clerical service should serve in it, so that, brought to the highest venerable ranks, he may show what fruit humility produces.

It was neither insignificant nor meaningless that, even among the ancients, no one except men of Levitical descent was admitted to the holy altars, lest, with merit disregarded, someone unfit should approach sacred worship either through payment or presumption. At that time, descent from families supplied the privilege of admission to the institutions of worship; now instruction takes the place of lineage. What birth was for them, formation is for us. Nature gave them to the tabernacle; discipline brings us forth for the altars.

Nor do we merely prohibit the consecration of laymen; no one from among the penitents either should presume, as a profane violator, to aspire to such a rank [Col. 0424C]. Let pardon be enough for the one who seeks it. With what conscience can a guilty man absolve another when he knows that he has confessed his own sins before the people as witnesses? Who, having seen someone lying prostrate shortly before, would venerate him as a bishop? Bearing [another reading: carrying] the stain of a pitiable crime, he does not possess the clear dignity of the priesthood.

### II. That No Payment Be Accepted for a Bishopric

We add this also to what has been said above: no one should purchase for a price the blessing believed to be divine, given through the laying on of hands. For it ought to be kept before our eyes that Simon, wishing to buy the Holy Spirit with money, was struck by the Apostle’s condemnation (Acts 8). After that, who does not consider worthless what is sold?

The election should preserve such reverence for those being ordained priests that, amid the grave murmuring of the people, the judgment may be believed to be divine. For God is there where there is simple agreement without wickedness.

Nor do we omit this part of our concern and admonition: no one should consider himself free from guilt if, although he himself is free from the purchase, he has initiated a priest through the mystical blessing and nevertheless, whether willingly or under compulsion, has consented to the will of another purchaser. What does it profit him not to be polluted by his own error if he gives his consent to one who is erring? Without doubt, both the person who has his own sin and the person who follows another’s sin act against the commandments. The mind resists desire in vain if it does not also resist fear.

With God’s help, provision will more easily be made against these things if the privileges established by the holy Fathers for metropolitans remain in force; if metropolitans preserve their proper order in their dioceses with the reverence that is fitting; if the election of a bishop is neither bought with payments nor sought through acts of subservience, but if these matters are fixed in hearts just as they are read in the Scriptures.

If there are no seeds of buying and selling in the churches, there will be no fuel for discord; but, with charity reigning, people will live under that peace which God promised and bestowed upon us [Col. 0425A].

### III. On Holding a Council Every Year

For this reason the Fathers, moved by the Providence through which the Holy Spirit has deigned to pierce the hearts of his worshipers, taught that councils ought to be held twice a year in each diocese. Thus, assembled together according to the doctrines of salutary instruction, they might meet freely to deliberate on ecclesiastical matters; and, if everything stands according to their hope, they might praise God with united voices, since he grants what is desired.

It is difficult for anyone’s heart to become so hardened by evil thoughts that he allows blameworthy things to be done by him when he knows that he must undergo the judgment of the council. Let them always have their loins girded for this journey, knowing that an account of their actions must be rendered. Let fear restrain them from unlawful things, and shame those whom fear cannot restrain.

It is known that the holy canons established that a council should be held twice a year; and, if possible, the prescribed rule ought inviolably to be observed. But if either the needs of the times or emerging circumstances do not permit this to be fulfilled, we command that they meet at least once—although this is not sufficient—without any excuse.

These things, dearest brothers, and others contained in the rules of the Fathers, let us meditate upon with unwearied reflection on our lips and in our hearts. As it is written, let us recount them to our children, so that they may meditate upon them in their hearts, sitting in the house, walking on the road, sleeping and rising (Deuteronomy 6); for blessed is the one who meditates on the Lord’s law day and night (Psalm 1).

The teacher of the nations also established this, following his disciple, when he admonished him: “Meditate on these things; devote yourself to them” (1 Thessalonians 3). And, adding the full instruction, he says: “Pay attention to yourself and to the teaching.” For if we devote ourselves without interruption to instruction in the faith, we are separated from vices, since devoted care for divine work leaves no room for human error.

Issued on the fourth day before the Nones of April [2 April], under the consulship of Agapitus, the most illustrious man [in the year of the Lord 517].

## Letter XXVI. To Sallustius

[Note: Bishop of Seville: thus the manuscript code of Justinian.]

Sallustius is appointed vicar of the apostolic see throughout the provinces of Baetica and Lusitania.

[Col. 0425D]

To his dearest [or: most beloved] brother Sallustius, Hormisdas.

Having received the conversations of your brotherly affection with complete and welcome joy—conversations that gladdened us by the report of your twofold well-being, since they stated that you were sound in body and supported by spiritual duties—we judged it fitting to disclose the joy that we carry in our minds [Note: The Roman edition reads, “to express.”].

For you have produced the proof of a good bishop, since you both do what deserves proclamation and do not delay in urging others to do it. We have taken the privilege of judgment from our own election, since we have learned that you willingly embrace [another reading: perform] what we command to others.

We pray to the divine clemency [another reading: divine benefits], and we have transmitted to all the instruments of ecclesiastical peace. You received our wishes with faithful understanding and immediately fulfilled them through your devotion to duty, making known to all the brothers what you had recognized, through heavenly grace, would benefit everyone.

Since so many merits of pious solicitude and labor support you, it now certainly pleases us to entrust to you matters that properly belong to our care, so that, among provinces separated by such great distance, you may both represent us and safeguard the rules of the Fathers [Col. 0426B].

Therefore, with this present authority, we entrust our representation to you throughout the provinces of Baetica and Lusitania, without prejudice to the privileges that antiquity has decreed for metropolitan bishops. By sharing in this ministry, we increase your dignity and lighten our own watchfulness through this arrangement.

Although you do not need to be instructed about each matter, since we have already found that you observe everything with great caution, nevertheless it is usually more pleasing when the path is shown again and the task entrusted is set out more fully.

We therefore command that the paternal rules and decrees defined by the holy councils be observed by all. In these matters we extend your vigilance; in these matters we extend your care through fraternal exhortation. If you guard these things with the reverence they deserve, they leave no place for guilt or obstacle to holy observance.

There the lawful and unlawful have been prescribed; there is the prohibition to which no one should dare aspire; there is what has been permitted and what a mind pleasing to God ought to undertake.

Whenever the cause of universal religion requires it, let all the brothers, summoned by you, come together in council. If any of them is troubled by the dispute of a particular matter [another reading: intention], restrain the quarrels that have arisen among them, determining the conflicts after examining them according to the sacred laws.

Whatever you prescribe to them for the faith and for the ancient constitutions, whether by prudent arrangement or by the authority of our person you establish [another reading: confirm], let all of it reach our knowledge through the testimony of an informed report, so that our spirit may enjoy the loving service bestowed and yours may enjoy the security of having received it [Note: “May your spirit willingly devote itself to duties given in charity and, through the security of this decree, enjoy what it has received.”].

May God preserve you in safety, dearest brother.

## Letter of the Emperor Justin to Hormisdas

He announces that he has been elected emperor. (C)

[Col. 0426D]

Justin Augustus to Hormisdas, pope.

Although God’s benefits should be proclaimed to many, it is especially fitting that they be announced to the supreme pontiffs. Therefore, through these [Note: [Col. 0425D] The Roman edition adds “sacred.”] letters we declare to Your Holiness that, first through the favor of the inseparable Trinity, then through the support of the most eminent nobles of our sacred palace and of the most holy senate, and likewise through the election of the most steadfast army, we were elected and confirmed to the imperial power, although unwilling and refusing it [Col. 0427A].

We therefore ask you to entreat the divine power in your holy prayers, so that the beginnings of our rule may be strengthened. For it is fitting both that we hope for this and that you fulfill it.

Issued on the Kalends of August [1 August], at Constantinople, under the consulship of Magnus, the most illustrious man [in the year of the Lord 518].

## Letter XXVII. To Justin

While he reigns, he hopes that the peace of the Church will be restored.

Hormisdas to Justin Augustus.

In acknowledgment of the beginnings of your venerable reign, most glorious son, the catholic Church sends her congratulations as a gift. Through them she trusts that, after such weariness caused by discord, she will find the rest of peace. There is no doubt that you have reached the summit of affairs through heavenly providence for this reason: so that in your time the injury inflicted upon religion in the eastern regions may be wiped away [Col. 0427B].

[Note: [Col. 0427D] After Emperor Justin, in the preceding letter, following the ancient custom of orthodox emperors, had sent the Roman pontiff—whom he revered as a father—a letter concerning his election, with the intention openly to profess that the willing adherence of the faithful peoples could be won by no power stronger than communion with the chief bishop of the whole Church, Pontiff Hormisdas replied that he had performed what all orthodox emperors are rightly bound to perform. From this you see that it was anciently observed that the Roman pontiff should be informed concerning an emperor-elect, and that the consecration and confirmation of the elected emperor should be requested. SEV. BINIUS.]

You have returned to the blessed Apostle Peter the first fruits due from your empire. We have received them with devotion for this reason: because we believe that through you the harmony of the Churches will soon come without doubt.

May God, who has granted your pious mind the desire to address us, himself bring about, as we wish, the fulfillment of your sincere devotion to his religion. You have told us that the burden of imperial power was imposed upon you unwillingly and against your refusal. By this it is clear that you were elected by heavenly judgment, according to the Apostle’s saying: “There is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been ordained by God” (Romans 13).

It remains that, elected by God, as we also believe, you extend the consolation of your hands to the Church, which you see laboring [Col. 0427C]. Let those who resist her peace cease; let those who attempt, in the guise of shepherds, to scatter Christ’s flock be silenced. Their correction strengthens the power of your rule, because where God is revered, adversity has no effect.

We have not failed to send this letter of congratulation through Alexander, the most illustrious man, hoping, with the help of our God, that through our son Gratus, the most illustrious man, we shall provide Your Clemency with a response concerning each matter pertaining to the unity of the Church [in the Roman edition: to Gratus; in the year of the Lord 518].

## Letter of Justin to Hormisdas

At the request of the Council of Constantinople, Justin asks through Count Gratus that the pontiff deign to send legates to Constantinople to reconcile the Eastern Church to peace and receive those who have fallen. (C)

[Col. 0427D]

Justin Augustus to Hormisdas, pope.

John, the most blessed man, bishop of this royal city, and the other religious bishops found here from various places and cities, have informed Our Serenity that, for the harmony of those who cultivate the true and orthodox faith and for the unity of its venerable Churches, they have prepared letters to be presented to Your Holiness. They earnestly requested that we also send our letter to you concerning this matter.

Since we are always lovers of unity, we have gladly embraced their requests and judged that these divine letters should be sent to Your Blessedness. Through them, may Your Holiness deign to assist the wishes of the most reverend bishops mentioned above and, on behalf of us and the commonwealth—whose governance has been entrusted from heaven to our piety—to appease the heavenly Majesty by your prayers.

And so that the rights of peace, unity, and harmony belonging to Your Holiness may be more fully revealed, may you arrange for certain most religious priests who embrace and desire peace to come to our most sacred retinue. For this purpose we have sent Gratus, the most illustrious man, count of our sacred consistory and master of the bureau of records and memoranda, whose distinguished reputation has long been known to us.

Issued on the seventh day before the Ides of September [7 September], at Constantinople, under the consulship of Magnus, the most illustrious man [in the year of the Lord 518].

## Letter XXVIII. Reply to Justin Augustus

He commends his concern for restoring peace, urges him to persevere in what he has begun, and says that the name of Acacius must be abolished.

Hormisdas to Justin Augustus.

We have testified with reciprocal devotion to the joy that we derived from the beginning of your reign—a joy already deservedly powerful among us—which you doubled by your preceding address. Even then we foresaw what you have now signified through the inspiration of heavenly grace concerning your devotion to ecclesiastical unity [Col. 0428C].

Therefore, most clement emperor, you already possess glory from such a desire, but lasting perfection is awaited. These are the strongest foundations of your rule: at the very beginning of your kingdom, they place the worship of God above all things by holy disposition.

Hold fast, therefore, to this care of pious solicitude, and, as you have begun, persevere for the peace of the catholics. For our God, who has granted you this disposition, has also chosen those through whom he may bring it to fulfillment.

We also gladly embrace the wishes and prayers of the bishops that have been poured out to us. Yet, reminded by consideration of their position, they desire what the repeated exhortation of the apostolic see formerly did not fail to urge them to follow. And since we have learned that Your Clemency wishes this, and that they too are asking for it, neither your piety nor theirs avoids knowledge of the matter which, like a hidden cause, has until now divided the peace of the Churches through contentious obstinacy.

What they ought to do is contained both in our letters and in the text of the petition that we sent. If, with the help of our God and Your Clemency, they receive and follow these instructions, it will be possible to reach the harmony that we desire with the greatest ardor [Col. 0429A].

Moreover, our son Gratus, the most illustrious man, count of the sacred consistory and master of the bureau of records and memoranda, has shown in himself the judgment of Your Clemency through the maturity of his representation. When he reports it, the reason for his delay will be better explained to Your Clemency [in the year of the Lord 518].

## Copy of the Report of John, Bishop of Constantinople, Sent through Gratus

To obtain communion with the Roman Church, he sends a petition in which he professes the catholic faith, states that the pontiff’s name has been entered by him in the diptychs, and says that legates are to be sent through whom peace may be established. (C)

To the lord, most holy brother and fellow minister, Hormisdas, in every respect a lover of God: John sends greeting in the Lord.

[Col. 0429B] I salute Your Holiness, dearest brother in Christ, and in saluting you I proclaim that the right faith has been preserved and the charity of brotherhood has been strengthened. God alone, who is powerful, willed this to be brought about through the devotion of Christians and of the most pious emperors.

Therefore deign, in brotherly love of God, to write to us apostolically and to receive our replies fraternally. For I, holding the teaching of the most holy apostles according to the tradition of the holy Fathers for an inscrutable reason, likewise offer honor to the consubstantial and in every respect holy Trinity, just as the assembly of 318 promulgated at Nicaea, the gathering of 150 confirmed at Constantinople, the assembly of 200 confirmed at Ephesus, and the gathering of 630 Fathers confirmed at Chalcedon.

Preserving this faith, then, by the grace [Col. 0429C] of God until my final breath, I embrace with spiritual affection both Your Holiness and the orthodox Churches from my heart, thinking with you as one in truth, and hoping with you that on that day we shall be saved through this faith, by the good will of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. For all glory is owed to the consubstantial Trinity, now and throughout the ages of ages.

I and those who are with me in the Lord send every brother in Christ who is with Your Holiness our warmest greetings. We have written only to provide satisfaction, so that both the venerable name of holy memory, Leo, formerly archbishop of the city of Rome, might be entered in the sacred diptychs at the time of the consecration, for the sake of concord, and your blessed name likewise proclaimed in the diptychs.

But so that Your Holiness may be satisfied in every respect (since we embrace your peace and care for the unity of the holy Churches of God), we ask you to send peaceful men, worthy of your apostolic see, who may offer satisfaction and receive our satisfaction, so that in this matter also Christ our God may be glorified, He who through you has preserved this peace for the world.

Received on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January [20 December] (in the year of the Lord 518), after the consulship of Agapitus.

## Letter XXIX. Response to John, Bishop of Constantinople

He commends John the bishop and rejoices that he has embraced the Council of Chalcedon and the letters of the blessed Leo. He promises to admit him to communion with the Church if he expunges the name of Acacius from the sacred diptychs.

[Col. 0430A]

Hormisdas to John, bishop of Constantinople.

Your charity has conveyed spiritual joy through the letters you sent, teaching us that, with the help of our God, your pastors have received the discipline of the Catholic religion in its proper order. Who could doubt that these are gifts of heavenly mercy? Who could doubt that they should be added to the trophies of the venerable emperor? Who could doubt that for him a greater triumph is gained from this peace than from any battles?

The glory of this labor knows no setting, because wherever God is rightly worshiped, the wickedness of adversaries never increases. We have gratefully received your confession of faith, through which you affirm the holy synods. Among these, by the restoration of all their decrees, you have proclaimed the Council of Chalcedon, and, wishing to be numbered among Catholics, you assert that the name of the holy pope Leo is written in the diptychs.

These things are worthy of praise if their effect is followed by perfection. For to receive the Council of Chalcedon, to follow the letters of the holy Leo, and still to defend the name of Acacius is to maintain mutually contradictory positions. Who, while condemning Dioscorus and Eutyches, could show Acacius to be innocent? Who, while avoiding Timothy and Peter of Alexandria, and the other Peter of Antioch, and their followers—as we have said—would not abhor Acacius, who followed their communion?

From your charity, indeed, we expect better things with the help of almighty God, possessing the hope of an excellent promise, as the letters you sent us show. I think with you in truth and defend that truth itself, hoping that at the judgment you may be able to be saved through it.

After this, what remains except that you should follow without hesitation the judgments of the apostolic see, whose faith you say you embrace? Therefore show the Eastern provinces, through yourself, the example which they should follow, so that the praise of all who have been corrected may be credited to your labors.

Since, then, you make such great declarations and indicate that you embrace the faith of the blessed apostle Peter, rightly believing that our salvation can stand in it, send us a libellus signed by your charity, whose contents are appended below, so that we may have, as we pray, one communion without fear of conscience.

For our son, the most illustrious man Gratus, we also render unceasing thanks to our God. His faith and right belief have stirred our affection toward him. Truly he is worthy to undertake responsibility for so great an action and to bring the commands of the greatest emperor to us.

## Letter of Justinian Sent to Hormisdas through the Same Gratus, the Emperor’s Legate

For the peace and unity of the Eastern Church, he asks the pontiff to send legates if he is unwilling to come to Constantinople himself. (C)

Justinian, a count, to Pope Hormisdas.

The desirable time which we earnestly desired, when divine clemency, looking upon the sufferings of the human race, deigned to grant it, has arrived: a time when all Catholics and the faithful perfected in God can commend themselves to His majesty.

For this reason I have sent these letters to Your Apostolate, now that free permission has been granted me by heavenly favor. Our lord, the invincible emperor, always embracing orthodox religion with the most ardent faith and desiring to restore the holy Churches to concord, as soon as he obtained the imperial insignia by heavenly judgment, announced to the priests here that the Churches should be united according to the apostolic rules. A large part of the matter has indeed been settled, with God as its author.

Only concerning the name of Acacius does it remain for Your Blessedness to hear the agreement. For this reason our lord, the most serene emperor, has sent to Your Holiness the eminent man Gratus, my like-minded friend, with imperial documents, so that Your Holiness may deign by every means to come to Constantinople to settle the remaining matters of concord.

But we await your arrival [Col. 0431B] without any delay. If some delay should perhaps hold you back—which ought not to happen—hasten in the meantime to send suitable priests, because the whole world, having turned toward unity on our side, cannot endure delay.

Hasten, therefore, most holy lord, lest, in your absence, the matters which ought to be arranged while you preside [lacuna]. We know what the letters of Your Blessedness and of your predecessors, sent to the East, contain concerning this same matter. But so that nothing may be omitted, because of the cause so often mentioned, the invincible emperor has also entrusted the religious undertaking to your son, the eminent man Gratus, with the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ.

## Letter XXX. To Caesarius of Arles

He reports that the bishops of Dardania and Illyricum have returned to communion with the apostolic see after condemning the Eutychian heresy, and concerning the legation sent to the East.

[Col. 0431C]

Hormisdas to his beloved brother Caesarius, and to those who are under your direction.

It is right that those who rejoice in Catholic communion should rejoice with us over any concord that arises in the Church, so that, just as we share one agreement in faith, so also our rejoicing in prosperity may be undivided.

You know how the detestable Eutychian heresy has spread through the Eastern Churches; how often the general synod has extinguished the poison of that superstition; and how often its followers have spurned the salutary admonitions of the apostolic see. As though ashamed to extend their hands to the truth or obey the preaching of the apostolic see, they nevertheless persisted in this obstinacy.

Pride always brings danger to salvation; through pride its inventor, the devil, was deprived of angelic power. On their account your fraternity has often grieved with us, remembering the apostolic reading which declares: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (1 Cor. 12).

But the Lord, who wills all people to be saved and to come to knowledge of the truth, is now enlightening the minds of many and instilling in them a desire for communion with the apostolic see, so that what they formerly proclaimed with determination they now condemn by a profession of correction.

We therefore receive their return without the sting of suspicion, because, while confessing their sin without any veil of excuse, they show a manifest desire for correction.

Accordingly, almost all the bishops both of Dardania and of Illyricum, so as not to be condemned for their former error, are requesting communion with blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. Through letters and legations which they have sent, they confirm that they obey the rules of the apostolic see. Only those whose faith burns can understand how much we ought to rejoice over them.

You should therefore know that they now also anathematize Nestorius, who divides the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ and thereby attempts to assert two sons. Eutyches, who denied the reality of the flesh and did not proclaim two natures in one person, attempting by this means to introduce into the Churches of Christ the Manichaean fantasy, as he supposed, is likewise condemned.

To these is added Dioscorus of Alexandria, who, consenting to the aforesaid wickedness, became a participant in its condemnation at the holy Council of Chalcedon and, finding fruits equal to the evil seeds, fell into the pit he had prepared for the faithful.

Their successors were Timothy Aelurus and Peter. Their wickedness everywhere agreed with itself; they did not abandon their lying teachers in anything, but surpassed them in every depravity. These men were approved as the general source of injury. Their hands were stained by the shedding of priestly blood, and their violence brought about the death of innocent people.

Throughout the world they bear the marks of eternal condemnation fixed upon them by Catholics. The orthodox not only deprived them of communion but also stripped them of the name “Christians.”

As for Peter of Antioch and his associates, to avoid producing a lengthy discussion, it is enough to say this: Peter and his companions differed in no respect from the doctrine of those who had been condemned.

Acacius once condemned them, and by doing so had turned the mouths of all Christians toward his praises. By attacking those who defended the Eutychian heresy, he had appeared most pleasing to those who honored the faith. But the plotter, through his customary treacherous deceits, begrudged him because he was being deceived [the text is uncertain]. For afterward, desiring to have these men as his accomplices and turning his weapons against Catholics, he found his lot among those whom he had wished to have as partners.

It is too long, given the brevity of a letter, to run through everything. Therefore we have sent a portion of the entire matter for your instruction, judging that so important a matter could not remain unknown to you, especially since it had been reported to your regions through the letters of our predecessors.

We have also taken care to inform your fraternity about what has recently occurred, so that through the ignorance of the faithful the aforesaid men—[the] lost [or: ruined]—might not find a place anywhere by stealth; rather, it should be made unmistakably known that those who strive to defend such things must be excluded from the fellowship of sacred communion.

Therefore, wherever faith is at stake, let everything connected with the favor of this world be rejected. Natural affection must not be placed before heavenly matters, so that the Lord’s command may be fulfilled: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10).

As for the other matters which, in the cause of religion, we again hope at the present time from the regions of the East, trusting in divine gifts, we have sent legates. Beseech the Lord Jesus Christ [printed *supplicate*; perhaps *supplicato*], that He who in His goodness granted a prosperous beginning may deign to grant a corresponding outcome.

We have sent to your charity Urbanus, a defender of the apostolic see, who is also suited to this undertaking. Through him we wish to learn the desired news concerning the appropriate response to the causes and outcomes of all these matters.

May God keep you safe and sound, dearest brothers.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of September [8 September], in the consulship of the most illustrious man Florentius.

## Observation of P. Antonius Pagi on the Year of Christ 515, no. 3 (C)

The letters of Hormisdas written to Caesarius, bishop of Arles, should be assigned to the year of Christ 515. In them Hormisdas teaches that the bishops of Dardania and Illyricum had returned to communion with the apostolic see, and indicates that he had sent legates to the East.

That letter is said to have been issued on the sixth day before the Ides of September, in the consulship of Florentius, a *vir clarissimus*. Baronius and the collectors of the councils, supposing that the year of Christ 518 was marked by the consulship of Magnus and Florentius, referred these letters to that year.

In fact, in that year Magnus alone entered upon the consulship. Therefore these letters, which have connections with certain letters issued in the following years, must be assigned entirely to the year 515 and restored to their proper order in a new edition of the Councils.

[Note: [Col. 0433D] The pontiff Hormisdas wrote this letter together with the following nine concerning the peace and unity of the Eastern Church in the year of the Lord 519. He arranged for them to be conveyed to the apostolic see by a legation consisting of Germanus and John, bishops; Blandus, a presbyter; and Felix and Dioscorus, deacons. He gave them the following memorandum of matters to be carried out. SEV. BINIUS.]

## Letter XXXI. To Justinian Augustus

He indicates that legates are being sent to achieve peace and to condemn Acacius.

Hormisdas, bishop, to Justinian Augustus.

Having received the sequence of your letters, powerful through the support of religion, with the most desirable joy of devotion, we gave thanks to the Divinity, because you have shown that what we might have urged could easily be done by you.

For this reason, [Col. 0433C] because you voluntarily desire praiseworthy things, the ancestral line of your family has worthily reached the summit of imperial power. Therefore persevere and devote yourselves earnestly with religious vigor, so that, just as your family merited the height of empire through the beginning of its good will, you may possess eternal triumphs through the perfection of your work.

See with what desire the world, long deluded, exults at the joys of peace [printed *exhortet*; corrected *exsultet*]. Look upon the minds of all people, lifted by the sure hope of rest through the anticipation of your benefaction. There is no reason for doubt to intrude; there is no reason for ambiguity to arise, since you testify—and we know this well—that the vows of a religious ruler are approaching the concord of the Churches.

Therefore, giving thanks for such great magnanimity, we earnestly beseech you, with all the insistence we can command, that the name of Acacius, together with his followers, which wholly obstructs the joy of the united Church, be removed according to the order of condemnation.

We have sent legates appropriate to the character of the matter. In their presence, the beginning of joy which you have given may be fulfilled according to what is contained in the instructions (in the year of the Lord 517).

## Memorandum Received by the Legates of the Apostolic See

He gives instructions to the legates.

When, with God’s favor, you have entered the Eastern regions, if any bishops meet you and wish to offer a libellus signed by themselves, whose contents you have received, accept it and grant them a share in holy communion.

If, however, those whom you meet do not wish to make the profession in the manner stated above, treat them indeed with priestly affection; but neither share a table with them nor presume to accept food from them, except transportation, if necessity requires it, and hospitality, so that they do not think themselves wholly rejected with contempt.

When, with God’s help, you arrive at Constantinople, withdraw to the lodging which the emperor provides. Do not allow anyone to approach you first for a greeting, except those whom the emperor himself sends to you or whom you know to belong to our communion, until you have seen the emperor himself.

When you have been presented to him, greet him and offer our letters, explaining that we have received great joy concerning his empire and rejoice exceedingly that almighty God has raised him up for this purpose, in accordance with his sacred letters: namely, so that, according to the provisions established by the bishops of the apostolic see, and with God as author and his kingdom lending its support, the peace and unity of the Churches desired in these times may arise.

If he urges you to visit the bishop of Constantinople, tell him that you have fixed requirements, which have often also been made known by them, concerning the profession that must be made by all bishops who embrace Catholic communion.

If the bishop of Constantinople is ready to fulfill these requirements, we gladly meet him. But if he despises following the exhortation of the apostolic see, why should our greeting serve as an occasion for contention, when our instructions contain no cause for disputation or conflict?

If the emperor wishes you to explain what you require the bishop to do, show him the form of the libellus which you carry.

If, while agreeing to the anathema of Acacius, he says that his successors should be recited because some of them—namely Euphemius and Macedonius—were driven into exile for defending the Council of Chalcedon, you shall explain that you can remove nothing from the form of the libellus, in which the followers of the condemned are included equally.

But if you cannot turn them away from this position, at least agree to this: once Acacius has been specifically anathematized in the libellus which we gave you, let there be silence concerning the names of his predecessors, after their names have been erased from the inscription of the diptychs.

When this has been done, receive the bishop of Constantinople into your communion.

As for the libellus of either the bishop of Constantinople or the others whom, God willing, you may happen to receive, first arrange for it to be read publicly in the presence of the people. If this cannot be done, let it at least be read in the secretarium in the presence of clerics and archimandrites.

If all these things have been completed by God’s will, ask the emperor—or, according to the alternative reading, let the emperor be asked—to make known, through sacred letters sent by the metropolitan bishops and accompanied by letters from the bishop of Constantinople, that the bishop of Constantinople, with his own agreement, has been received into the unity of communion after making the profession which the apostolic see prescribed. Let him also exhort those bishops through these letters to make similar professions.

If the emperor creates any difficulty in this matter, the bishop of Constantinople must make known what he himself has done by sending commands to his diocesan bishops or to the other metropolitans, in the presence of those whom you likewise have sent. You must demand this from him by every means, so that, as testimony of this act travels everywhere, it cannot remain unknown even to all those who are situated far away.

## Letter XXXII. To Justin Augustus

He warns that those who, after accepting the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon, refuse to condemn Acacius are to be avoided; and he commends the legates sent for the peace and union of the Eastern Church.

[Col. 0435B]

Hormisdas to Justin Augustus.

It is evident that the fame of Your Glory has been extended so far through the grace of the Divinity, and that, with the support of the merit of your life, you have become so honorably known to the world through the report of men of the highest distinction, that it is rather believed that the summit of imperial power has been conferred upon you than that anyone says you are recognized through the empire.

It is certain that, through such an advancement of yours, a further accumulation of honor has been added to your former splendor. But just as you once held the primacy in character, so, when the greatness that cannot endure concealment has carried you through the mouths of nations, the fragrance of your good reputation has also reached us, as the Scriptures mystically speak, through the testimony of your graciousness.

Indeed, when the judgment of prudent men had widely disseminated reports of your religious life, we could not remain unaware of whatever had been proclaimed about you by the testimony of the world. For just as moderate praise cannot claim immense commendations for itself, so everything adorned with the admiration of goodness is carried among the people to be proclaimed without end.

Greatness rightly claims the testimonies of fame, because wonderful things do not know how to remain hidden. For this reason public laws entrusted you with imperial power and honors [Roman edition: *adoreas*, “honors”]. Since the distinction of your merits became the common desire, no arbiter of affairs could be so unjust as to judge that you had received the titles of an illustrious ruler [the printed text is corrupt: *p ssim ... arches inclytae*], when it cannot be denied that you had deservedly earned the summit of empire, since the world recognized your probity.

Yet it is little, even though by the judgment of all you have received the rights of ruling as a reward. More remarkable is that empires receive you, strengthened by the praise of humanity, in such a way that their judgments appear divine.

There is no doubt that those whom the proofs of sincere faith surround are brought by the venerable predestination of the Divinity to the ornaments of such great power. We may truly say that the words of the prophetic Spirit apply to you: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jer. 1).

To this glory, through the incomprehensible ordering of heavenly majesty, the service of nature brought you forth into the world; the probity of your past life formed you under the guardianship of faith; and divine clemency elevated you to imperial power. This was so that at last, when the dividers of the Lord’s body had been restrained by the execution of your faith, the concord of the Churches might cut down the devil’s obstacles and the whole world might rejoice in union.

This office is specially entrusted from heaven to your religion, your faith, and your serenity: to you we see both the ability to do all things and the permission to complete them granted. Therefore, as you have begun to do, apply yourself to the task entrusted to you, which you see has been imposed upon you by heavenly Providence.

And truly it was fitting that peace should be made through a prince, since the reverence owed to the Divinity demands it. Offer to our God the offerings of the imperial power you have received, so that through you the fruit of peace may be brought to completion.

Without doubt, whatever has been granted to your soul by such an act is judged by you to have been bestowed upon the world. Great and immeasurable is the matter for which you have been called by the judgment of the Divinity, venerable emperor.

Behold, the prayers of those who desire peace are extended. For a long period of time the indivisible communion of the Churches has mourned its severance. Brotherhood lies torn apart in lamentation, while opinion concerning the teaching of the Fathers is divided.

Gird your loins, therefore, with the strength of faith. Consider what king the Divinity wishes you to serve and how great is the matter whose fulfillment He is arranging through you.

Christ our Lord founded the venerable body of the Church through His own Passion; He has determined to unite it to Your Glory through your deeds. No way exists by which the grace of heavenly majesty may shine more brightly around you than if, through your service, the body of the Church formed by the redemption of the Lord’s blood is restored.

This calamity is indeed of very ancient origin, but because of its enormity its pain is most recent; and the groaning is all the more powerful in Christian hearts because it has been prolonged through the ages.

You must see how intensely the madness of the ancient enemy grows every day and, although the matter was once settled by a definitive judgment, how he creates delay in peace. Since both the Council of Chalcedon and the decrees of the blessed pope Leo are pleasing to us, do not cease striving to bring the disputants back to charity.

They follow what is set down in the aforesaid doctrines and do not withdraw from their adherents, whom they know to have been condemned by the aforesaid authority. They still hold in their embrace the name of Acacius, whom they see to have been deservedly subjected to condemnation by the judgment of the apostolic see.

Who does not understand that they speak hypocritically when they say: “We follow the teachings of the holy Fathers, but we do not love their actions”? “We cherish, venerate, and embrace what was established by the holy Council of Chalcedon and what is contained in the letter of the blessed Leo, but we offer our allegiance to Acacius, who followed the communion of the condemned.”

But why speak at length about matters already judged, when we ought only to exhort them, once the hypocrisy expressed above has been removed, to desire peace in complete purity?

In you lies the whole cause of my entreaty, excellent emperor. Resist such things and such people through the living charity of religious action. It rests with you that, just as you desired ecclesiastical concord during your private life, so you may bring it to completion during your reign.

Nothing could add more to the fullness of your grace than the fact that it has been divinely granted to you that what you have always wished to happen may be brought to its conclusion through you. Nor is the manifestation of divine grace toward you a small one, since you are given the power to do what you have always desired.

Therefore, since you see that the title of so great a cause has been reserved for you, remove whatever ambiguity is believed to remain, so that our joys may be complete.

We, having received the letters of your imperial authority through the most illustrious man Gratus, whose moderation we found suited to the office of legate, sent men appropriate to the magnitude of the cause: [Note: [Col. 0437D] At this point the name of Dioscorus the deacon is missing. It is found explicitly in the following letters, although not in this order. In those letters, immediately after the names of the bishops who were legates, both legate-deacons are named, and Blandus the presbyter is mentioned last. It may therefore be said, on the authority of this letter, that the sequence of names was reversed through a scribal error, so that the deacons appear before the presbyter. SEV. BINIUS.]

Germanus and John, bishops, and Blandus, a presbyter, as well as Felix, a deacon. Through them, if Your Serenity’s favor smiles upon us as we expect, the universal prayers for the unity of the Churches may be confirmed according to the instructions (in the year of the Lord 519).

## Letter XXXIII. To Euphemia Augusta

[Note: [Col. 0438D] Euphemia, the wife of the emperor Justin, a woman distinguished for piety, was formerly called Lupicina. When Justin became emperor, he wished, out of piety, to have his wife called by the name of Euphemia, the illustrious martyr in whose basilica the Council of Chalcedon had been celebrated, before he honored her with the title of Augusta. Zonaras and Cedrenus, in their accounts of Justin. SEV. BINIUS.]

He urges the Augusta to restore peace to the Church.

[Col. 0437B]

Hormisdas to Euphemia Augusta.

The peace of the Churches is now being arranged by heavenly ordinance, since God chose you for imperial power, having always known that the disposition of your religion was unimpaired.

For just as, in private life, you always worshiped God according to right doctrine, so that you might think about religious concord, many things have indeed been accomplished from the very beginning of your imperial rule which promise us hope of complete correction.

Therefore, because we rejoice that love of the faith burns within you, we give thanks to God and daily entreat the blessed apostle Peter on your behalf, so that he may intercede for your prayers before the Lord and bring the course of your good will to completion.

There is no doubt that you are assisted by divine help, since you obey the heavenly commands with such devotion to religion. For this reason, because the purpose of your marriage is known to be holy, we confidently send these letters to Your Clemency, so that through you the piety of your husband may be stirred more strongly toward accomplishing peace in the Church.

You have undertaken a great work; a great cause has been entrusted to you. Through you also Christ wishes to recall to the covenants of the Church peoples whom He wished to redeem from death through Himself.

A great opportunity for praise has also been prepared for your sex, if, through your earnest efforts, Christ joins together the members of His Church that had been divided.

Nor is her glory greater—the glory of the woman who searched for the wood of human salvation and found the one cross which the whole world venerates [Note: Helena, the mother of Constantine, found the cross of Christ.]. Indeed, you will surpass her merits, because through her the Church found its sign, while through you it will have its remedy.

Let the religious clemency of your husband therefore act, so that our brothers and fellow bishops may deign to affirm their faith under the terms of the libellus which we sent previously, so that the correction already begun may be complete. For every confession in the worship of God is useless if it lacks the fullness of faith.

What we asked the others to do has already, as is established, been accomplished by many priests. And a just unity in communion cannot exist if it has not been preserved in the act of returning (in the year of the Lord 519).

## Letter XXXIV. To John, Bishop of Constantinople

Acacius must be condemned, and a profession of faith must be issued into the hands of the legates.

Hormisdas to John, bishop of Constantinople.

We have indeed given, under ecclesiastical freedom, an appropriate response to your letters. We have clearly expressed what we congratulated you for in them, which had been passed over in silence.

Although repeated legations and the long duration of your experience in the Church have by now poured all this into your understanding, it is nevertheless useful to lay our counsel open more broadly by repeating the argument. Faith’s firmness is discussed well when the desire to establish peace is expressed in simple words.

We have always desired that your wishes—by which you attest that you are hastening toward ecclesiastical concord—should be shared by those regions; and we have not been content with the ambition of prayers alone, but have also employed entreaties.

What we say is strengthened by the testimony both of you and of the world, since, for the restoration of Catholic unity, we submit our authority with integrity. May divine mercy incline its ear to our prayers, so that you may follow what you believe ought to be requested and love what has been offered.

For us there is one concern in this matter and one guardianship: to desire peace in such a way that the religion and the decrees of the venerable Fathers are preserved. Since things that do not differ in harmonious belief ought to remain established through similar observance, this is only just.

But why do we delay any longer? You yourself know what the cause of unity demands; you yourself know by what road you must come to the fellowship of the blessed apostle Peter.

You have as the guide of your journey the gathering held at Chalcedon for the sake of religion, which you already assert that you follow. As you have also testified that you embrace it, the doctrine of the blessed Leo will accompany you as you return.

If these things please you, let the defense of the condemned Acacius not please you. This is what holds back the hopes of good zeal from perfection.

If those decrees were established by the gathering of the venerable Fathers against the enemies of God and His law, so that whoever followed those enemies in communion would already then incur the sentence of condemnation against himself, then what we now consistently carry out is not new. Rather, we preserve judgments made at that time according to the just constitution of the Fathers.

Therefore, brother, we exhort you and, with the mercy of our God assisting us, strike your mind, so that by condemning Acacius and his followers, you may separate yourself from every contagion of heretics and be nourished together with us by participation in the Lord’s body.

If you proclaim everything together with us, why do you not condemn everything together with us? You embrace with us the things we venerate only if you shrink with us from the things we detest.

Complete peace knows no distance, and the true worship of the one God cannot exist except in unity of confession.

Therefore, greeting you with the affection of brotherly charity, we announce that your request has been fulfilled by sending, as you hoped, the most religious men Germanus and John, bishops, [Note: [Col. 0439D] It is clear from the preceding Letter XXXII that the names of the legate-deacons are placed here before the name of the presbyter, as I stated above in the notes to that letter. SEV. BINIUS.]

Felix the deacon, Dioscorus the deacon, and Blandus the presbyter. You will clearly recognize, if you consider it, what instructions they have received before their statements.

They will receive your peace under the profession which we have often set forth in writing. Therefore, dearest brother, complete our joy and send through them to us the proclamation of your right faith, so that through you an example may be given to all (in the year of the Lord 519).

## Letter XXXV. To the Same

Since he now professes the Catholic faith, he should think especially about establishing the peace for which he himself sent legates.

Hormisdas to John, bishop of Constantinople.

We have understood what your charity conveyed in the letters you sent, and we rejoice that the signs of your faith have reached our conscience. We desire that our God may deign to grant full effect to your intention, which we wish to be right, concerning ecclesiastical peace. We have taken up its hope in our mind from the heavenly majesty, because we judge that divine Providence chose the most serene emperor for this purpose: so that through him the restoration of the Churches, desired for so many years, might come about.

Therefore, although the matters that must be done for the unity of the faith cannot remain unknown to your charity, we have nevertheless sent the legates whom the character of the cause required, so that, through their exhortations, both what we signified long ago and what we have recently repeated may, with our Lord as author, reach fulfillment.

## Letter XXXVI. To the Archdeacon and Clergy of Constantinople

The Catholics having been freed from the harassment of the heretics, legates are sent to confirm the peace.

Hormisdas to Theodosius, archdeacon of Constantinople, and to all the Catholics likewise.

We duly offer thanks to the mercy of God, [Col. 0439D] which did not allow your faith to labor for long; and indeed the time has been presented in which the Catholic Church may recover her faithful soldiers. For what greater joy can possess your mind than the recalled removal of evils? Offset the hardships of affliction with present joys, because our God, who has been the remedy, did not wish your charity to be crushed by adversity, but tested by it. For if you balance the evils of the past with the present recompense—which is undoubtedly divine—who doubts that you will obtain greater rewards than adversity could have caused you harm? And although our concern for the condition of the Catholic faith has never ceased, nevertheless, stimulated by the sacred communications of the most serene prince, we have taken care to send legates, through whose service, with God as author, we do not doubt that what we have often commanded will be brought to effect. Therefore strive earnestly and appropriately, so that you may offer this chief gift of your liberation to the Catholic Church, so that, when all that has hitherto caused harm has been driven away, we may rejoice together in the one communion we have always desired and be able without ceasing to render praises to our God.

## LETTER XXXVII. TO JUSTINIAN, COUNT OF THE DOMESTICI, LATER SUCCESSOR OF JUSTIN

He hopes that through his efforts the Church will attain peace, and announces that he has received the gifts sent by him.

Hormisdas to Justinian, illustrious man.

[Col. 0440B] We have received the letter of Your Magnitude, full of love for the holy faith, in which you announce that an opportunity has divinely arisen for us to exercise among you the firmness of apostolic preaching. Therefore we continually give thanks to our Lord, who has granted you both the time and the courage for such distinguished remedies. We ourselves have recognized that these things were being arranged from above, after the divine Majesty bestowed the empire upon him who shows himself appointed to establish peace among the Churches. It remains, therefore, that all the bishops of the Eastern party testify, according to the tenor of the libellus, that they have reached the effect of correction.

The venerable path of concord is open; the remedies of the desired healing are known [*notata*]. Let the priests who desire Catholic peace not refuse the Catholic profession; for the error must not merely be corrected in part, but uprooted from its foundations. Persist, therefore, as you have begun, so that your reward before God—which begins with the commencement of a good work—may attain its fulfillment through completion.

The communications you sent to us testify that your mind is such that you need little exhortation to reach the fullness of your good purpose. Nevertheless, the account [*ratio*; variant: *oratio*, “prayer”] that has given our hope grounds for confidence kindles our desire still more; and we long more eagerly for the joys to be fulfilled which we now judge, by divine arrangement, to be imminent. For this reason we daily and humbly implore the blessed apostle Peter that God may grant you, through whom the Church already hopes that her holy members will be restored, both a swift accomplishment and lasting salvation.

We, complying with your wishes, [Col. 0440D] have sent men to consolidate concord under the ordering of the apostolic disposition. It is your responsibility to ensure that, just as we did not wish to fail your good intention, so you cause them to report to us the desired result. Your gift has been received by the venerable shrines; you will make it still more acceptable to the blessed apostle Peter if through you they receive the Church’s desired unity.

*(In the year of the Lord 519.)*

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO CELER AND PATRICIUS, MOST ILLUSTRIOUS COURTIERS

They are asked to assist the legates in the cause of peace.

Hormisdas to Celer and Patricius, jointly.

Although, out of consideration for our position, we cannot remain silent about the cause of the Catholic faith, nevertheless the most serene prince has greatly stimulated our zeal in this matter by communications specifically directed to us, and at his wish we have sent legates. Since such a cause, concerning the children of the Church, ought to be supported by assistance, we greet you with the respect and honor appropriate to you and ask that you support before the mind of the most serene prince the representations of those who have been sent on behalf of ecclesiastical peace. Your Excellency will receive no small recompense for this labor, since you will enable us to render thanks to almighty God for your deeds.

*(In the year of the Lord 519.)*

## LETTER XXXIX. TO THE PRAETORIAN PREFECT OF THESSALONICA

The same as in the preceding letter.

[Col. 0441B] Hormisdas to the praetorian prefect of Thessalonica and the other illustrious men, jointly.

Although our concern for the ecclesiastical cause has never ceased, nevertheless, more readily stimulated by the sacred communications of the most serene emperor, we have sent legates with the favor of heavenly mercy, through whose service the good things we anticipate from the prince’s mind may be accomplished. Therefore, greeting Your Grandeur with the respect and honor due to you, we ask that you lend your efforts toward the restoration of the faith and not permit the wishes of the faithful, long delayed for so many years, to be postponed. For there is no doubt that Your Excellency will gain the fruit of such great praise if, through you, with the mercy of our God at work, the things desired by all good people come to pass.

*(In the year of the Lord 519.)*

## LETTER XL. TO ANASTASIA AND PALMATIA, MOST ILLUSTRIOUS SENATORIAL WOMEN, WHO STOOD UNSHAKEN FOR THE CATHOLIC FAITH DURING THE PERSECUTION OF ANASTASIUS

The same as in the preceding letter.

[Col. 0441C]

Hormisdas to Anastasia and Palmatia, jointly.

The zeal of a good will is always accompanied by the effect of divine prosperity. Through the providence of our God, an opportunity of time has been offered in which you ought to strive in return for the reward of your faith. Trusting first in heavenly mercy and then in the conscience of the most merciful prince, we have sent legates on behalf of the Catholic religion. Through them we greet Your Grandeur with the service of due veneration, asking that you not refuse your labor and assistance toward the restoration of ecclesiastical concord, so that, when those whom the authority of the apostolic See has condemned have been rejected and removed, and the Christian people have returned to the one communion—which is the right one—you may have the blessed apostle Peter, for whose faith we strive, as an aid through your deeds.

*(In the year of the Lord 519.)*

## EXAMPLE OF THE SECOND REPORT OF GERMANUS AND JOHN, BISHOPS; FELIX AND DIOSCORUS, DEACONS; AND BLANDUS, PRESBYTER

How honorably they were received at Scampis.

*(C)*

We reported to Your Beatitude in another letter the order in which, with God’s help, we arrived at the city of Aulon, how we were received by the bishop of that city, what was done, what reply they gave, and how he promised to make a libellus with his metropolitan. We have not allowed ourselves, through your prayers, to remain silent about what took place in the city of Scampis.

Before we entered that city, the venerable bishop Troilus, with his clergy and people, came out to meet us. We report to your apostolate how God was blessed on that very day and what celebration followed through his goodness. In our presence, and in the presence of his clergy and the noblemen of the city, he signed and handed over the libellus. We received it, and in the presence of all the clergy and people it was read aloud in due order by your servant Peter, notary of the holy Roman Church. The assembly was in the basilica of Saint Peter.

We confess to Your Beatitude that we have scarcely seen such devotion, such praises to God, such tears, and such joy among any other people. Almost all the men and women received us with candles, and the soldiers with crosses, throughout the city. Masses were celebrated; no name burdened by religious condemnation was recited, except only that of Your Beatitude. Our venerable bishop Germanus celebrated Mass. They promised that thereafter no names would be recited except those whom the apostolic See had received.

May the merciful God preserve in you the many things that have been accomplished through us. We composed this letter thirty miles from Lignidum, hoping to reach that same city on that day with God’s help. Since the bishop of Scampis came to us in this manner, we hope that the bishop of Lignidum will do likewise. If this happens, we shall write back when the opportunity arises.

While we were staying at Scampis, after Mass, at the evening meal, Stephen [Col. 0442C] and Leontius, most illustrious men, sent by the emperor, came to meet us, still unaware that we were in the regions of Greece, because such orders had been given to Count Stephen that they should cross into the regions of Italy to meet us. This Stephen is said to be related to your son, the master of the soldiers Vitalianus.

They announced to us that the senator Patricius had been proscribed and sent into exile. We cannot say for what reason, except insofar as the matter has reached us, because it is not easy to deliberate about such affairs. It is also said that the representatives of the Church of Thessalonica are being held, among whom, they say, letters were found; for what reason, we do not know. Philumenus, Demetrius, Magistrianus, and other persons whose names we do not know are being held with them.

These are the things we heard, as we have stated. Regarding the ecclesiastical cause, however, favorable news is being announced by God’s mercy. We have been wholly unable to understand for what reason the physician Cosmas came to Italy, except that he is being vigorously sought. You ought to be concerned to learn for what reason he came there.

## THIRD REPORT OF THE ABOVE-NAMED LEGATES

They have reached Lignidum, and everything has been carried out according to its instructions.

*(C)*

In another letter we informed Your Beatitude about the city of Scampis and the venerable bishop Troilus: how he gave the libellus and what celebration was held in that city. By God’s mercy we came to Lignidum, [Col. 0443A] and the venerable bishop Theodoret, a distinguished man of that city, likewise gave a libellus. The libellus was read aloud in the Church, and everything was done according to your ordinance.

Pray to God; hope from his apostles, the most blessed Peter and Paul, that God, who through your prayers granted such beginnings, may likewise bring about favorable continuations, so that the times of your crown may always be proclaimed through the correction of the Churches.

We sent this letter to your apostolate on the Nones of March.

## EXAMPLE OF THE REPORT OF ANDREAS, BISHOP OF PRAEVALITANA

It describes the simulation of the bishops in the synod of New Epirus, and what was done at Scampis and Lignidum upon the arrival of the legates.

*(C)*

[Col. 0443B] To my ever-lord, most blessed, and to the father whom, with intimate veneration, I honor as seated on the apostolic See and equal in angelic merit, father of fathers, Pope Hormisdas: Andreas.

Commending myself most humbly to your most pious footsteps, I report concerning the synod of New Epirus that they pretended to anathematize certain persons among themselves. They used this device only to trap their own mouth in its wickedness. The divine Trinity resisted them through your holy prayers; and when they had been caught in their wickedness, we were never able to persuade the archbishop to turn toward the way of truth and toward your commands.

But now, when the most blessed and holy lords—the bishops and deacons sent by your holy crown—arrived, the bishop of Scampis, the most blessed man Troilus, went out to meet them with every expression of joy and with lights. After presenting the libellus according to your command, they were immediately received into the peace of Christ, and they celebrated Mass with the bishop in the city of Scampis. When the people of Lignidum saw what the people of Scampis had done, they followed in the same way.

While we were composing this letter, Magistrianus arrived from the city of Constantinople. He announced that, by God’s favor and through your holy prayers, the people of Constantinople had anathematized Acacius and celebrated Easter in peace. May your intercession with God labor for what follows, so that we may be found to be, in the fullest sense, servants of the apostolic See.

I have sent to Your Piety, attached, the letters which the above-mentioned most blessed bishops sent to my humility.

Received on the day stated above.

[Col. 0443D]

*Note: [Col. 0443D] “Letter or libellus.”*

## EXAMPLE OF THE LIBELLUS OF JOHN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE

He professes the Catholic faith. He detests all heretics, especially Acacius.

*(C)*

To my lord in all things most holy and most blessed brother and fellow minister, Hormisdas: John, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord.

When the letters of Your Holiness were delivered to me, most beloved brother in Christ, through Gratus, the illustrious count, and now through Germanus and John, most reverend bishops, Felix and Dioscorus, most holy deacons, and Blandus, presbyter, I rejoiced in the spiritual charity of Your Holiness: namely, that you seek the unity of the most holy Churches of God according to the ancient tradition of the Fathers, and that you hasten, in your heart, to drive back the lacerators of Christ’s rational flock [variant: “to strike them through love”].

Know with certainty, therefore, most holy father in all things, that, as I wrote to you, agreeing with you in the truth, I too reject all the heretics repudiated by you, since I love peace. For I accept that the most holy Churches of God—that is, the Church of the elder Rome, yours, and of this new Rome—are one, the See of the apostle Peter; and I define that the See of this imperial city is one with it.
