I assent to all the acts of those four holy synods, namely, Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon, concerning the confirmation of the faith and the condition of the Church, and I allow no hesitation about what was rightly judged. But those who attempt, or have exerted themselves [variant: “have been torn apart”; alternative reading: *nisos*], to disturb even a single apex of their decisions, I know to have fallen away from the holy universal and apostolic Church of God. Using your rightly spoken words with evident appropriateness, I say this in the present writing:

The first salvation is to preserve the rule of right faith and in no way to deviate from the tradition of the Fathers; for the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ cannot be set aside, when he says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16). The truth of these words is demonstrated by the effects of events, because inviolate Catholic religion has always been preserved in the apostolic See.

Therefore, desiring not to fall away from this faith and following in all things the decrees of the Fathers, we anathematize all heresies, but especially Nestorius the heretic, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, condemned at the Council of Ephesus by the blessed Pope Celestine of the city of Rome and by the venerable Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria. Together with him we anathematize Eutyches and Dioscorus, bishop of the city of Alexandria, condemned in the holy Synod of Chalcedon, which we venerate, follow, and embrace. Following the holy Synod of Nicaea, it proclaimed the apostolic faith.

Together with these we anathematize Timothy, the parricide surnamed Aelurus, and likewise condemn his disciple and follower in all things, Peter of Alexandria. In the same way we anathematize Acacius, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, their accomplice and follower, as well as those who persist in their communion and participation. For whoever embraces communion with them receives a similar judgment with them in condemnation.

In the same way, condemning Peter of Antioch, we anathematize him together with his followers and with all his associates [variant: “with all the persons named above”]. Therefore we approve and embrace all the letters of the blessed Leo, Pope of the city of Rome, which he wrote concerning the right faith.

Accordingly, as we have said, following the apostolic See in all things, we proclaim everything decreed by it. For this reason I hope that I shall be with you in the one communion which the apostolic See proclaims, in which there is the undiminished integrity and perfect solidity of the Christian religion.

We promise that in the time to come the names of those separated from communion with the Catholic Church—that is, of all who do not agree with the apostolic See in every respect—are not to be recited among the sacred mysteries. But if I should attempt to doubt in any respect the profession I have made, I confess that, by my own condemnation, I am the associate of those whom I have condemned.

I have subscribed this profession with my own hand and sent it in writing to you, holy and most blessed brother and pope of great Rome, Hormisdas, through the above-written Germanus and John, venerable bishops; Felix and Dioscorus, deacons; and Blandus, presbyter.

And in another hand:

John, by the mercy of God bishop of Constantinople, of New Rome, consenting to this profession of mine, have subscribed all the above, sound in the Lord.

Given in the month of March, on the 27th [or 28th] day, in the twelfth indiction, [Col. 0445B] under the consulship of our lord Justin, emperor Augustus, and Heraclius [Eutharicus], most illustrious man, in the year 557 of the era; with the consent of our lord Justin, emperor Augustus, Eutharicus, most illustrious man, being consul.

*(In the year of the Lord 519.)*

## REPORT OF THE BISHOPS GERMANUS AND JOHN; THE DEACONS FELIX AND DIOSCORUS; AND THE PRESBYTER BLANDUS

How honorably they were received by the emperor; how the libellus was subscribed by Bishop John [the Roman edition adds: “the libellus”], Acacius and the other followers were condemned, and peace was restored to the Church.

*(C)*

We are not surprised that everything has turned out favorably for us through the prayers of your apostolate, knowing that your prayer works even more powerfully for us than our ministry. The entire course of the ecclesiastical affair proceeded in such a way [Col. 0445C] that it cannot be doubted that the miracle of blessed Peter was manifested in every detail.

First, we found such fervor for religion in the very men who hold office that Vitalianus, Pompeius, and Justinian came to meet us ten thousand paces away and did not consider it beneath them to rejoice at our arrival with thanksgiving to you. Next, there was such devotion even among the people that the greater part of the population awaited our arrival with candles and with praises of you.

Under this solemn celebration, therefore, we arrived safely and joyfully at Constantinople on the second day of the week of the Great Week. On the following day we were presented to the most pious prince, and were so relieved by his affection that, even if nothing else had preceded it, the favor of the most pious prince alone would have sufficed for our consolation. But greater things followed through your prayers.

For on that day, in the presence of the entire senate, four bishops were also present, whom John, bishop of Constantinople, had sent to defend his party. We showed them the libellus of the apostolic See and proved that everything in it was right and canonical. Finally, on the fifth day, that is, on the Lord’s Supper, the bishop came to the palace in the general assembly and, after the libellus had been read aloud, subscribed it with the greatest devotion in agreement with it.

Who could explain how great the joy of the prince and senate was there, what tears the joys produced, or what acclamations the favor of the entire assembly and clergy raised either in praise of the prince or of your See? These things cannot be explained in a report; [Col. 0446A] we leave to your reflection and to the bearer what we are unable to express.

We proceeded from the palace to the church with the greatest solemnity, so that a solemn celebration might also strengthen the concord of faith and minds [the Roman edition adds: “the communion”]. It can scarcely be believed what the weeping of those who rejoiced was, or how immense and overflowing was the multitude of the people. The crowd itself will marvel at its own joy. Nor could there be any doubt that a heavenly hand had been present, which bestowed such unity upon the world.

We report that, in our presence, the name of Acacius the transgressor, who had been anathematized, was erased from the ecclesiastical diptychs, as were the names of the other bishops who had followed him in communion. The names of Anastasius and Zeno were likewise removed from the recitation at the altar.

Through your prayers, peace has been restored to the minds of Christians: one soul of the whole Church, one joy. The enemy of the human race alone mourns, struck down by the victory of your prayer.

Pray that a similar happiness may also illuminate the Church of Antioch, concerning whose bishop the negotiations still appear uncertain, because the people’s various wishes have not produced agreement about the choice of a person. Nevertheless, we believe that, through the prayers of Your Beatitude, a worthy appointment there too will quickly emerge, so that the peace begun in your times may be directed throughout the whole world, and the Church, with all her members perfectly joined to her head as formerly, may be united in every region by those who come together in the apostolic communion and faith.

## REPORT OF THE DEACON DIOSCORUS THROUGH THE SUBDEACON PULLIO[N]

He announces what took place at Thessalonica and Constantinople.

*(C)*

[Col. 0446C]

The ineffable mercy of almighty God and his goodness, which he mercifully pours out upon the human race, cannot be measured by human strength or explained in words. It is enough simply to admire his counsels with devout minds and to know that all good things depend solely upon the remedies of his grace.

This is a daily proof. Yet I venture boldly to say, my most blessed lord pope, that the present cause surpasses all those of the past, and that God has reserved it for your times and merits. What was done at Aulon, what followed at Scampis, and what occurred at Lignidum, I reported in an earlier communication.

We reached Thessalonica. What disputes we had with the bishop of Thessalonica, what was said and also decided, you will learn from the living account of this bearer. Nevertheless, I shall not delay in reporting what ought not to be passed over in silence.

After many disputes, the aforesaid bishop, overcome by reason, wished to subscribe the libellus. But since all the bishops established under his ordination were not present, he agreed and promised the following: after the holy days, when one of us had been sent from the See of the city of Constantinople and the bishops established in his diocese had been assembled, they would subscribe the libellus. With God’s help, we believe that this will be completed.

These things were decided at Thessalonica. Commended to your prayers, we reached the city of Constantinople on the second day of the authentic week. Ten thousand paces from the aforesaid city, distinguished and magnificent men came to meet us, among them the master of the soldiers Vitalianus, Pompeius, Justinian, and other senators. All were burning with zeal for the Catholic faith and with a desire for the restoration of peace.

What more is there to say? We entered the city amid the almost universal joy of all. On the following day, which was the third day of the week, we were presented to the sight of the most pious prince. The entire senate was present, and in that assembly were also four bishops whom the bishop of Constantinople had sent on his own behalf.

We presented the letters of Your Beatitude, which the most merciful prince received with great reverence. The matters that needed to be made known before the examination of the case were stated, and immediately the case began.

The most merciful emperor urged us, saying: “Behold the bishop of this city, and in a peaceful manner render an account to one another.”

We replied in turn: “Why should we go to the bishop to engage in disputes? Our lord, the most blessed pope Hormisdas, who sent us, did not command us to dispute. Rather, we have in our hands the libellus which all the bishops who wished to be reconciled to the apostolic See composed. If Your Piety orders it, let it be read. If there is anything in it that is unknown or not believed to be true, let them say so; then we shall show that nothing outside ecclesiastical judgment has been written in that libellus. Or, if they can prove that it is inconsistent with Catholic religion, then it is our responsibility to establish the contrary.”

The libellus was read in the presence of the prince and the senate. We immediately added: “Let the four bishops present here on behalf of the bishop of Constantinople say whether the things written in the libellus are in no way contained in the ecclesiastical acts.”

They replied that everything was true.

After this we added: “Lord emperor, the bishops have both removed a great labor from us and done what was appropriate for themselves by speaking the truth.”

Immediately the most merciful emperor said to the bishops who were present: “And if these things are true, why do you not do them?” Similarly, some members of the senatorial order said: “We are laymen. You say that these things are true: do them, and we shall follow.”

On the fourth day, the bishop of Constantinople received the libellus from us in the palace. At first he seemed to try to make it a letter rather than a libellus. But after not many disputes, he agreed to write a brief preface and then append the libellus as Your Beatitude had dictated. He made a subscription corresponding to the libellus, and likewise dated it. We sent copies of it, both Greek and Latin, to your apostolate.

After the libellus had been completed, the name of Acacius was erased from the diptychs, and likewise those of Phravita, Euphemius, Macedonius, and Timothy. We report that this was done not only in the one church in which the bishop resides, but throughout all the churches, with great care and with God’s help. The names of Zeno and Anastasius were likewise erased from the diptychs.

The bishops of the various cities, as many as were found, likewise presented libelli. We report that the matter was guarded with great caution, so that no bishop would communicate with us who had not first submitted a libellus. In the same way all the archimandrites did so. We report that we also had disputes with the archimandrites, who said: “It is enough that our archbishop has done it; we follow his action.” What more is there to say? After many disputes, they too, overcome by reason, submitted libelli in every respect.

After all this, with God’s help, we proceeded into the church. You can see, by considering the action itself, what joys of unity took place, how God was blessed, and what praises were offered to the blessed apostle Peter and to you; my tongue cannot explain it.

Nothing happened according to the expectations of the enemies: no sedition, no shedding of blood, no tumult—things which the enemies had previously predicted as though to frighten us. The clergy of Constantinople themselves, astonished and giving thanks to God, say that they do not remember that at any time such a multitude of people communicated together.

After these things had been completed, the most merciful emperor also appended his letter to Your Beatitude, explaining the order of events, and likewise the most reverend man John, bishop of the city of Constantinople. Know also that general sacred decrees have been issued, and we believe that, by God’s favor and through your holy prayers, they will very soon be sent throughout all the provinces.

These things were done at Constantinople, and now the matter of the Church of Antioch is under discussion. It is still laboring because a suitable person has not yet been chosen. Therefore let Your Beatitude pray more earnestly, so that God, who, entreated by your prayers, restored the Church of Constantinople to the apostolic See, may himself grant a worthy person to be ordained at Antioch and continually unite the Churches.

Write back to the bishop of Constantinople. If it seems good to Your Beatitude, mention the condemnations of Severus and of those whom you named in the letter you wrote to Second Syria through the monks John and Sergius; let him include this very point when writing back to the emperor. If you do so, it seems to me that it will be necessary.

[Col. 0447D]

*Note: [Col. 0447D] “The emperor’s sacred letter.”*

## LETTER OF JUSTIN TO HORMISDAS

John, bishop, has embraced the Catholic faith and anathematized the heretics; the name of Acacius, together with the names of the other schismatics, has been erased from the sacred registers.

*(C)*

Victor Justin, pious, fortunate, renowned, triumphant, ever Augustus, to Hormisdas, most holy [variant: “most sacred”] and most blessed archbishop and patriarch of the venerable city of Rome.

Know, most religious father, that what we had long sought with the greatest efforts has been accomplished and made manifest to us, even before those whom you sent arrived: namely, that John, the most blessed bishop of your [variant: “our”] new Rome, together with his clergy, agrees with you, differing in no ambiguity and divided by no discord. Know that he has subscribed the libellus which you indicated was to be offered, a libellus consistent with the council of the most holy Fathers.

All hasten eagerly to receive the wishes both of you and of the See of Constantinople, illumined by the flashing brightness of truth. All gladly hasten along the clear path; they follow the most holy decrees of the Fathers and the most approved laws. With the councils of some who firmly held the right path confirmed, and with those who wandered uncertainly corrected, the matter is brought together in this: that they too may worship the unity of the undivided Trinity through the unity of their minds.

It has been denied that, henceforth, during the divine mysteries, remembrance is to be made [according to the tenor of the libellus mentioned above] of Acacius the transgressor, formerly bishop of this royal city, or of the other priests who either first acted against the apostolic decrees or became successors in error and were not corrected by repentance until their final day.

And since all our regions must be admonished [variant: “the religious duty of all our regions must be admonished”] to imitate the example of the royal city, we have decided that imperial commands should be sent everywhere. So ardently do we burn with religious duty, so zealously do we seek the peace of the Catholic faith, that our commonwealth may receive heavenly peace as its reward and that my subjects may be reconciled through heavenly protection.

For what could be found more pleasing, more just, or more illustrious than that those whom the same kingdom contains and whom the worship of the same faith illumines should not contend in diversity, but, with their minds gathered into unity, venerate institutions established not by human thought but by the wisdom of the divine Spirit?

Let Your Religious Holiness therefore pray that what is being procured through vigilant zeal for the concord of the Churches of the Catholic faith may, with the assistance of the divine gift, be preserved through unbroken perpetuity.

[Col. 0449C] Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of May at Constantinople.

[Col. 0449D]

*Note: In the year of the Lord 519, while the legates were still at Constantinople.*

## EXAMPLE OF THE REPORT OF THE BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE TO HORMISDAS

He announces that peace has been established in the Church and therefore urges him to rejoice greatly.

*(C)*

To my lord in all things holy and beloved of God, brother and fellow minister, Hormisdas: John sends greetings in the Lord.

When God works his own wonders among his people, then one ought confidently to proclaim what is contained in the divine writings in the words of Scripture itself: “Who can speak of the powers of the Lord, or make all his praises heard at all times?” (Psalm 105).

Behold, he has raised up such a pious prince for the Roman commonwealth as the Catholic Church had long needed and the whole human race desired to see. Therefore he has inclined toward him from heaven the horn [variant: “crown”] of grace, so that mercy might be abundantly poured upon his sacred head. Throughout the whole time of his proclamation, they glorified God, the ruler of all, with a loud voice, because he adorned such a ruler with such a crown through my hands.

This great emperor first displayed the palm of his struggles by conquering the enemy. Then, in accordance with the merit of his virtue, he wisely secured the union of the most holy Churches. As the third good of his reign, he joined together what had been scattered and wisely established the peace of the world.

Therefore, giving thanks in all things to the great God who governs all things with wisdom, I have announced peace to you, the son of peace, in every respect most beloved of God, so that you may leap for that joy in which David, according to the Law, figuratively exulted at the restoration of the ark of God (2 Samuel 8), while the apostles truly rejoiced through grace.

Rejoice, therefore, in the Lord with a joy appropriate to your holiness, and write what befits your kindly mind, man of God. For what had been divided has been joined; what had been dispersed has been gathered; what had been far apart has been united with one another. And, as I ought to say—and as I wrote long ago—clearly understanding that both Churches, that of the elder Rome and that of the new Rome, are one, and rightly defining that the See of both is one, I recognize their undivided union and the concordant confirmation of us both with complete integrity of judgment.

Therefore I ask God always to preserve it inseparable through the prayers of the holy apostles and through the prayers of Your Holiness, by which you entreat that the most merciful and most Christian prince Justin, and his most pious wife, our daughter Euphemia, may be granted to us and to the whole world in peace for many years, most blessed brother in all things.

We rejoiced, therefore, at the presence of your most reverend bishops and clergy, and we give thanks because, in accordance with our request, you sent such peaceful men, worthy of your apostolic See, who preserve the rule of the Fathers without confusion and guard the undivided faith. Embracing their mind in all things, we have accomplished through them everything necessary for the satisfaction of Your Holiness.

I, together with my people, offer abundant greetings in Christ to all the fraternity that is with Your Holiness.

[Col. 0450D]

*Note: In the year of the Lord 519. Refer here to John’s report presented above.*

## EXAMPLE OF THE LETTER OF JUSTINIAN TO HORMISDAS

He congratulates him on the overthrow of perfidy and the establishment of peace. Since the Church now enjoys peace, prayers are to be poured out to God for the emperor.

*(C)*

To my most holy lord Hormisdas, first archbishop and pope of the city of Rome: Justinian, count, sends greetings.

[Col. 0450D]

Your venerable Holiness’s promulgation of the rules, which continually entreats Christ God for the peace of the Churches and the concord of the people, has approved whatever is now to be carried out through its most blessed priests; through the favor of the Godhead all things have been brought to fulfillment, while the discord of certain persons has had no power at all. Therefore, strengthened by your sacred prayers and commands in the faith of the orthodox, we humbly ask that you deign to offer to the eternal King your accustomed and efficacious prayers for our most holy Augustus, the protector of the entire faith, for his commonwealth, and also for us, the guardians of your commands; and that you faithfully visit us with your life-giving replies (in the year of our Lord 519).

## Copy of the Letter of Pompeius to Hormisdas

He congratulates the pontiff on the overthrow of perfidy and the peace established in the Eastern Church. (C)

### [Col. 0451A]

To my most blessed lord and apostolic father, Hormisdas, archbishop of the universal Church: Pompeius.

The mercy of almighty God, moved by the holy prayers of your blessedness, has deigned to grant us a prince of such great faith that, through the most religious merits of his clemency, the restoration of ecclesiastical peace—which all the faithful desired—may rightly be considered to have been bestowed. In the accession of this king, the Holy Spirit’s action has established the firmest foundations of his rule, possessing as much strength of unconquerable stability as the excellence of his deed is judged to be unique and admirable.

### [Col. 0451B]

Therefore, greeting the venerable blessedness of your pontificate with the respect of a reciprocal address, we ask that you deign to pray more and more for the prosperity of our most merciful and unconquerable lord and prince, so that the ineffable mercy of almighty God may preserve by the assistance of his grace the gifts that he has granted—and among which the fruit of your cultivation also flourishes. May the intercessory support of your pontifical holiness assist us also, your sons, joined to you by spiritual affection, whose concern has always been especially touched by this work (in the year of our Lord 519).

## Copy of the Letter of Juliana Anicia to Hormisdas

She announces that, through the arrival of the legates, all the dissensions of the Church have been settled; they must not be permitted to depart until peace has been firmly established. (C)

### [Col. 0451C]

To the most blessed lord and father, Hormisdas: Juliana Anicia.

Through the prayers of your blessedness, and through the arrival of the legates of the principal apostolic see, the errors of the heretics having been struck down, we have gathered together into the unity of the Catholic faith, at the maternal breasts of the Church, on the day of the holy Resurrection. Therefore, addressing your holiness with a pen of reverence, we admonish you to instruct the most reverend men sent by you not to depart in any way before those things which they have properly arranged, as you have foreseen, have been firmly established; so that, with all remnants of the former error cut away, the unity strengthened by the expenditures of your blessedness may be brought to lasting fulfillment (in the year of our Lord 519).

## Copy of the Letter of Anastasia to Hormisdas

She asks him to pour out prayers to God for the safety of the most pious emperor. (C)

### [Col. 0451D]

To the holy and most blessed father of fathers, Hormisdas, archbishop of the universal Church: Anastasia.

We rightly confess that the grace of divine light has shone upon us, since we know from the written testimony of this page that the reverence owed to your apostolate is held in the holy memory of our heart. For, most blessed lord and father worthy of apostolic honor, we trust with true hope that the propitiation of heavenly mercy rests upon pontifical intercession. The ever-watchful vigils of your prayers, and the faith of the most victorious prince, always shining with Catholic splendor, have restored to the sacrosanct Churches the long-awaited harmony of peace.

### [Col. 0452A]

In all his triumphs he rightly rejoices that he has carried the unconquered standard most firmly. Therefore, may the unimpaired holiness of your fatherhood persist in offering vows and prayers to almighty God, without interruption, for the safety and prosperity of our aforementioned lord Augustus, so that he may deign to preserve for the advancement of future blessedness the ineffable grace of such great blessings which he himself inspired in the pious heart of the emperor. May prayer also be graciously offered by your pontificate for your wedded son, and for me, your particular worshipper, together with the offspring whom the Lord has deigned to grant us; through its support, may the protection of divine favor mercifully shine upon us (in the year of our Lord 519).

## Copy of the Letter of Theodoritus, Bishop of Lignidum, to Pope Hormisdas

He congratulates the pontiff on the union of the Churches. (C)

### [Col. 0452B]

To the holy, blessed, renowned, and venerable apostolic father Hormisdas, pope of the city of Rome: your humble servant, Theodoritus.

I know that such great presumption does not belong to my smallness, nor that I should send these little pages, small in expression, to your pious and holy apostolate. But because, in keeping with the innate humanity of your character, you are accustomed, with a pious and propitiatory spirit, to protect everything by the will of the Divinity, you have made the bright day, filled with every kind of festivity, available to the whole world; and through your prayers worthy of proclamation you have recalled it to its former state of truth [unity], and have consented that all should agree or be brought under one rule through your praiseworthy and venerable merits.

### [Col. 0452C]

Therefore, although overwhelmed by my sins and oppressed by them on every side, revived from hell itself [F. from those hells], when your servant, the religious man Pullio [Pollio], returned to your religious footsteps, I took the liberty of presenting myself through him, and also through these small and insignificant sheets, before your praiseworthy and venerable footsteps. With all my strength I invoke divine favor, and with a clear voice I sing together with everyone:

“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II).

He, in his incomprehensible mercy, has illumined and freed everything through your wondrous works; through your prayers worthy of God he has granted to the whole world a bright day filled with every kind of festivity; he has rescued it from every iniquity, loosed every knot of bondage,

### [Col. 0452D]

and opened every path. Offering this expression of congratulation, filled with devotion, to your apostolate, I beg you, holy, blessed, apostolic father, to deign to remember my tearful insignificance in your pious prayers. Received on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Eutharicus, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of our Lord 519).

## Letter XLI. To Germanus and the Other Legates

He wishes to be informed about their safety and their activities.

Hormisdas to Germanus and [added: John], bishops; Felix and Dioscorus, deacons; and Blandus, presbyter.

### [Col. 0453A]

The diversity of reports has long made us anxious about your prosperity and about the character of the undertaking you have accepted, especially since during so long a period we have been unable to learn anything certain through a reply from your belovedness.

Nevertheless, when the opportunity of a bearer was found, we preferred to communicate these matters. Therefore, greeting you with the help of almighty God, know that we are safe; and we desire to hear the same about you. But so that you may be able to inform our understanding more fully about everything that has been done, tell us by what persons and in what places you were received—as we believe—favorably, and where, or under what celebration of the Lord’s Resurrection, your belovedness spent the day. Also explain in every respect, in your prompt replies, what you have done thereafter, so that you may relieve your [F. our] concern regarding your prosperity and that of your actions,

### [Col. 0453B]

and so that, with the help of our God, we may add anything lacking to the instruction you received. Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Eutharicus, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of our Lord 519).

## Letter XLII. To the Same Legates

He grieves that they have not written; he says that he has sent Paulinus to the emperor.

Hormisdas to the persons named above.

### [Col. 0453B]

Our mind has been made anxious by prolonged expectation, especially since, having been sent to so great a prince, you ought to have made us informed with all speed. For we believed that we could receive your letter before the day of the Lord’s Ascension. Therefore, we desire to learn both the signs of your safety and the progress of the cause which, with the help of our God, you undertook to carry through.

We have taken care to send Paulinus, defender of the Roman Church,

### [Col. 0453C]

with these present letters, directing letters both to the prince and to each person to whom it was appropriate. Therefore, we pray to our God with fitting prayers that he himself may preserve your safety through his favor and deign to grant the cause the outcome we desire. For nothing greater can be inscribed among the titles of a good emperor than that the Greek Church, present and future, may deserve to proclaim him the author of peace. Given on the third day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Eutharicus, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of our Lord 519).

## Letter XLIII. To the Same Legates

He wants to be informed about what they are doing; he commends Stephanus.

### [Col. 0453D]

Hormisdas to our legates named above.

It is necessary for us to consider either the condition of the undertaking entrusted to you or the absence of your belovedness; and on these matters our concern does not allow us to omit any opportunity for writing. Previously, through Magistrianus, who returned to the service of the patrician Symmachus, we sent a letter to your belovedness, urging you not to omit informing us about everything that has been done or is being done in the ecclesiastical cause. You ought also to do this for the disclosure of our concern.

For it is our prayer that almighty God may deign to grant your labor the desired outcome. Assist Stephanus the merchant, through whom our words are delivered to you,

### [Col. 0454A]

with appropriate support wherever circumstances require, because you remember that he has always belonged to us. Given on the same day (in the year of our Lord 519).

[Note: This letter and the five following it were written after peace had been announced, in the year of our Lord 519.]

## Letter XLIV. To Justin Augustus

He congratulates him that, through his efforts, peace prevails at Constantinople; he urges him to arrange for the same to be done at Antioch and Alexandria.

Hormisdas, bishop, to Justin Augustus.

### [Col. 0454A]

After reading the pages of your clemency announcing the restoration of harmony in the faith, the mind of the whole Church, rejoicing, burst forth into a hymn of divine praise, in which it is sung:

“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II).

Therefore, in the confidence of this hymn, anticipate glory and happiness worthy of the merits of the faithful. For it was not merely human consensus that raised you, a prince pleasing to God, to the summit of imperial power; divine favor had fashioned you beforehand for itself. For he entrusted to you the rule of the East so that you might become the instrument of his works.

### [Col. 0454B]

Therefore, make this prophetic saying rightly applicable to you:

“You shall appoint them princes over all the earth; they shall remember your name, Lord, throughout every generation and age” (Psalm XLIV).

Since it is your purpose to preserve Christian peace, who could doubt that you have been loved [chosen] by Christ? These are the first foundations of your rule: to appease God by justice and to claim the aid of the highest Majesty, while you suppress his adversaries as your own enemies. These truly are the greatest foundations of the commonwealth, this its solid and unconquerable strength. For that which is surrounded by the firmness of divine grace cannot be penetrated by human blows.

### [Col. 0454C]

Prophetic Scripture bears witness to this, for it says:

“I have chosen David, my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him. For my hand shall assist him, and my arm shall strengthen him” (Psalm LXXXVIII).

But in vain does he seek weapons, in vain does he seek forces for himself, whom heavenly grace has abandoned. For it is truly written:

“Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain” (Psalm CXXVI).

You will indeed wage war, most excellent prince, protected by divine assistance, and you will subject the necks of the fiercest nations to the yoke of your commonwealth. But no victory can be greater than that you overthrow the enemy of the human race after he has sought supports for so long a time.

### [Col. 0454D]

The nature of other wars is distinguished by nations, bounded by regions, and stained with blood; this victory embraces the whole human race in its palm. You will carry this triumph into every region. And what is closest to divine mercy is that those who shortly before were raging under the leadership of the devil are now conquered, without the shedding of blood, for the attainment of their own salvation.

Therefore, the triumph of this Christian victory will endure throughout the ages. For what has been founded upon the eternal stability of faith cannot be erased by the stain of time. The fame of your deeds will remain far and wide; and, as the divine words declare:

“Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the earth” (Psalm XVIII).

In other wars you protect fields, cities, towns, and, most importantly, the liberty of those subjected—things which, when compared with mortal uses, must be dissolved by a similar mortality. In this struggle life itself is defended, and, in a manner of speaking, the battle is fought for the citadel of eternal blessedness.

### [Col. 0455A]

For this reason, the continuing preparation for so great a work requires your clemency’s attention. Make sure that the most savage enemy finds no place at all from which he may rise again. Strip him of every defense; and if any trace of him remains anywhere, cleanse it all with the remedy of the elements [reading uncertain]. Let every seed of wickedness be uprooted from the ground; let the stock opposed to God be cut back to the living root, lest its poisonous root, insufficiently suppressed—which God forbid—spread its shoots more widely again.

Why do we say this? Because the correction of the Alexandrian and Antiochene Churches, and of the others, still remains, and must in no way be neglected. If your clemency applies its care to this, there is hope that, by the same author through whom we believe all good things begin, they will quickly be completed with his assistance.

### [Col. 0455B]

We also commend to you the legates sent from the apostolic see, and entrust them to your faith and religious devotion. May your piety dismiss them only after everything has been completed, so that, through divine and your own benefits, they may bring back to the apostolic see full joy over the peace of all the Churches. We have transmitted these writings through Paulinus, defender of the Roman Church and servant of your piety, to be presented to you. Given on the seventh day before the Ides of July, in the consulship of Eutharicus, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of our Lord 519).

## Letter XLV. To John, Bishop of Constantinople

He praises John for having returned to the unity of the Church; he urges him to secure the union of the Alexandrian and Antiochene Churches, and commends the legates to him.

### [Col. 0455C]

Hormisdas to John, bishop of Constantinople.

As I consider the writings of your belovedness, in which you have professed that you share one faith with the see of the blessed apostle Peter, I am moved to exclaim with prophetic freedom:

“Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!” (Psalm XXXII).

For it makes no difference how far apart we are divided by the distances of place, since now, by God’s authority, we are joined together in the one dwelling-place of faith. Now, through divine mercy, the members of Christ once scattered have gathered into the likeness of one body; the Lord’s inheritance, seized by the most wicked robbers and announced by prophetic voices, is restored.

### [Col. 0455D]

And truly, upon the faith of this rock—that is, upon the firmness of the prince of the apostles—the foundations of the Eastern Church are made solid. Since your letters report that this has happened, it is timely to say:

“How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!” (Romans X).

Therefore, we give thanks to the most excellent Trinity, which has granted that the rulers of the Church and of the commonwealth should agree in Christ. Indeed, the salvation of affairs is present whenever one mind joins priests and princes in the truth of the Catholic faith. This is the firm bond of peace; this is the fellowship sent down from heaven. For it is not lawful for subjects to think differently about what they see their superiors agreeing upon.

### [Col. 0456A]

Is there any doubt that divine providence has arranged all these things? First, that a prince was chosen who, when he saw that he had received rule over human beings, did not forget that he was subject to God. Then, that he gave his Church such a bishop in your brotherhood—one who would undoubtedly enter with our see, that is, the apostolic see, into a sure and lasting harmony of faith.

For when you willingly accepted from us the little book of faith, and were eager for restoration in Christ, you are known to us never to have been alienated from the divine predestination. Therefore, dearest brother, attend to the benefits of our God as they proceed of their own accord. Gather together more fully the members of the flock once scattered, and guard them once gathered.

Remember that you have now been mercifully appointed ruler of the ship assigned by Christ. Consider the spirits of diabolical obstinacy, troubling the calm of the voyage and its care. Nor are you unaware of the waves of uncertain storm, which you must foresee with a watchful mind and counterbalance with your reason raised toward God.

### [Col. 0456B]

Let no negligence in the undertaking entrusted to you wrench the helm of the Lord’s ship from your hands. Keep constantly before your fixed gaze the one sign of the right course, so that you may more confidently despise the disturbances caused by the devil’s blasts and arrive peacefully at the promised harbor.

This is the Christian training ground of struggle; for such a soldiering of Christ the palm of eternal life is set forth. As you rightly consider these things, the protection of the commander will not be lacking to his soldier. And the more the ambushes of the enemies multiply, the more the grace of the supreme ruler makes the poisons of the adversary material for his mercy, as the word of apostolic truth affirmed, saying:

“Where iniquity abounded, grace abounded still more” (Romans V).

Only cling to divine and perfectly right teachings. By fostering ecclesiastical harmony, and as though marked by the sign of a peaceful will, you will prove yourself a disciple of him who said:

“I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John XIV).

### [Col. 0456C]

Also urge our son, the most merciful prince Justin, divinely provided for the Christian age, though he is already willingly tending toward what is right, to complete what he deigned to promise in his royal letters. Let him restrain by the authority of religion and the moderated power of the empire the devil’s deceit, by sending edicts to those whom misguided error still leads away from the breasts of the mother Church. Let him regard it as his greatest victory over the common enemy of all humanity if, with the help of divine favor, he suppresses the poisons of the ancient serpent.

Do not cease to be concerned also about the condition of the Antiochene and Alexandrian Churches, and repeatedly entreat the most merciful prince to restore peace in them as well through a religious ordering, so that he may add the fullness of perfection to his good beginnings. For a good work is begun in vain if completion does not follow it in its entirety.

### [Col. 0456D]

We also commend the legates sent from the apostolic see. May your belovedness arrange for them to return to us in such a way that they can bring us full joy concerning the peace restored to all the Churches. Given on the seventh day before the Ides of July (in the year of our Lord 519), in the consulship of Eutharicus, a man of illustrious rank.

## Letter XLVI. To Justinian

He commends him for having assisted Justin in restoring peace to the Church and urges him to bring it to perfect completion.

### [Col. 0457A]

Hormisdas to the illustrious man Justinian.

We bless the ineffable assistance of the Divinity, because we have learned that the desire of all concerning the peace of the Churches has been fulfilled in tranquillity. This indeed did not happen contrary to our expectation, since, relying upon the piety of the most religious Augustus, we had always held hope for peace, and it was our prayer that what we believed should be done under a Christian prince might be accomplished in the matter of union.

Therefore, the glorious emperor will receive from this cause the titles of triumphs—not titles into which forgetfulness of mortality may intrude, but titles which the grace of the Divinity will confirm throughout perpetuity. Nor will the reward of heavenly recompense be lacking for you, who assisted the undertaking of the good prince and, through fitting service, caused the horror of separation to be excluded.

Blessed be the Lord our God, who has visited and effected the redemption of his people (Luke I).

### [Col. 0457B]

Now, since it is certain that this duty has been imposed upon you by the providence of the Divinity, gird up your loins, as he says, and pursue with the strength of peaceful exhortation those from whom you do not see peace being acknowledged—especially since the glory of your grace is diminished if anything in this matter remains incomplete.

Survey everything with the faith by which you live, and with the diligence in which you excel, confront every assault by which you see the reverence of the Christian religion troubled, so that we may rightly say with rejoicing concerning your perseverance:

“All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Psalm XXI).

### [Col. 0457C]

Since these things are so, you who began the tranquillity of the Catholic Church ought to secure its completion. The favor of our Savior, who inspired you to begin this work, will not be absent from its perfection. Given in the consulship stated above (in the year of our Lord 519).

[Note: After this letter, in the Avellana Collection, there follows another letter, which Ballerini published from the same collection in *The Works of Saint Leo*, volume III, page 166.]

### [Col. 0457D]

Hormisdas.

Whenever it has been necessary to send writings to our lord son, the most merciful prince, we could not pass over your Excellency in silence. Therefore, after first offering the honor of a greeting, we commend those who have been sent on official business, asking that, with our lord as author, they may quickly reach the place to which they were sent [read: *ad destinata*] under your direction, so that the most sacred and religious emperor may learn without delay the glory of his merits.

## Letter XLVII. To Pompeius

He praises Pompeius for having shown himself devoted to peace; he urges him to labor so that complete tranquillity may be restored to the Church.

Hormisdas to Pompeius.

We confess that the mind of our devotion has been so filled with the joy of harmony that we believe no words are sufficient to match the purity of your faith.

### [Col. 0458A]

You will certainly pass into posterity with a great remembrance of felicity, because it is clear that you were firmly bound by concern in the making of peace. You have merit before the Divinity, to whose religion you pay your devotion. You have indeed carried out the desire of all, but your own vows have likewise been fulfilled; and while you have prepared a reward for your souls, the whole community rejoices that a benefit has been bestowed upon it.

Therefore, greeting you with the honor that is due, we exhort and ask that, with the vigor by which you began the Church’s tranquillity, you secure its completion. Wherever you see traces of any contention remaining, take every measure to pursue them. Be present for the fullest tranquillity of the Churches of God; persist in the labor which, through the gift of your faith, you have taken care to offer to the Lord.

### [Col. 0458B]

For you cause us to demand the fullness of the work from you with greater confidence, since we rejoice that you laid the votive foundations of the desired and most sweet union. Given in the consulship stated above (in the year of our Lord 519).

## Letter XLVIII. To Juliana Anicia

The same as in the preceding letter.

Hormisdas to Juliana Anicia.

After receiving the letters of your Excellency, we render thanks to our God for the restoration of the Catholic faith. We pray that, in accordance with his religious devotion, he may deign to preserve for a long time the zeal which he has granted to your mind, so that, just as your person is ennobled by the stream of imperial blood, your conscience may likewise shine with the light of good merits.

Therefore, greeting you with suitable respect and honor, we ask that you remain in the purpose with which you began and take care that the endeavor of so great a cause reaches fulfillment, lest any seed of this evil remain in the future, from which at some later opportunity any enemy of the faith might again grow strong (in the year of our Lord 519).

## Letter XLIX. To Anastasia

The same as in the preceding letter.

### [Col. 0458C]

Hormisdas to Anastasia.

After our God strengthened the members of his Church returning to their former peace, you had long desired struggles [the text is lacunose: “you had long desired struggles …”]. Rejoicing that this has come to pass, we also unceasingly beseech the divine clemency that, just as it has gladly received these first fruits of the reign, so it may always assist the faith of the good prince with every favor of prosperity and preserve both him and all of you in the sacred love of religion, so that you, whose faith has cast off the error of the most pernicious dissension, may flourish on earth in such a way that the reward of eternal salvation follows. Therefore, join your vows to ours and implore with all your strength from God that all the Churches may follow the example of this correction, so that the devil may not rejoice that anything remains to him, whom our harmony almost entirely celebrates as having been driven out (in the year of our Lord 519).

## Letter L. To Gratus

He greets Gratus and asks to be informed about his well-being.

### [Col. 0459A]

[Note: In the Avellana Collection, Vatican Codex 4061, this title is expressed as follows: “To Gratus, a man of rank: Hormisdas.”]

Hormisdas to Gratus, a man of sublime rank.

The silence of your Excellency saddened us, because amid whatever occupations you may have had, you ought not to have been forgetful of us. Therefore, lest we appear to incur in ourselves what we criticize in you, it was necessary to undertake the work of this present letter, through which we honorably greet your nobility and ask you not to cease informing our concern about the good state of your prosperity. For, with the favor of our God, we desire to learn of the blessings of your safety by whatever indications may be available.

## Letter LI. To All the Bishops of Spain

He sends the profession of John, bishop of Constantinople, on account of Eastern bishops [clerics] who may seek their communion.

### [Col. 0459B]

Hormisdas to his dearest brothers, all the bishops established throughout Spain.

Among the matters which our brother and fellow bishop John, with zeal for ecclesiastical benefit, has brought to our attention, he also advised, out of devotion to the Catholic faith and reverence for the apostolic see, in what manner holy communion should be granted to those coming from the Greek clergy—namely, because of the case of Acacius, condemned by our predecessors for communion with heretics. Those who do not separate themselves from his contagion are to be excluded from our communion.

I praise the purpose of a man burning with such zeal for the faith and for the apostolic institutions, so that he would not allow anyone, even through ignorance, to be plunged into the mire of another’s error. This is a concern worthy of the faithful: that they should always keep watch with vigilant zeal and preserve themselves blameless from every perversity. For this is the innocence of faith, that it takes precautions so that it cannot err even by chance [variant: “so that it may be able to foresee or avoid errors”].

### [Col. 0459C]

Therefore, satisfying both the praiseworthy desires of the aforesaid man and our own duty, as is fitting, and taking whatever documents were drawn from the archives of the Church, we sent them to your council for the instruction of all, so that, learning more fully from them what was done, you might separate yourselves from every communion [contagion] of those in error.

For the sentence pronounced against the impious transgressors, by God’s inspiration, was not a matter of personal hatred. In this matter, indeed, we never ceased preaching: we both entreated the prince and admonished priests and peoples that, once the transgressors had been absolved, they should turn to the right faith through love of God and fear of judgment. But pitiable obstinacy had brought them to the point that the deadly poisons could in no way be overcome, and that the evil seeds, with roots fixed toward worse things, should put forth shoots.

### [Col. 0459D]

Therefore, dearest brothers, instructed in every appropriate respect, preserve yourselves and the Church of God, pierced by the apostle’s exhortation (Acts XX). We have sent a little book, under which, if anyone from among the Eastern clergy should request your communion, he may be admitted to it. By the same rule, it is already established that many have been received from the regions of Thrace and Scythia, Illyricum, and Old Epirus, as well as from Syria, rejoicing to flock to what is right and to have turned away from what is deviant.

Therefore, we command you, lest anything be concealed, that every care and every concern remain vigilant, and that no place now be left for ignorance, nor anyone make use of an excuse based on former simplicity [variant: former simplicities]. For one who knowingly sins requires confession. It is necessary that the person who is shown to have persisted on a perverse path should ascribe the error to himself. Boniface, notary of the holy Roman Church, delivers copies of the little book issued from the archives.

### [Col. 0460A]

The first means of salvation is to preserve the rule of right faith and in no way deviate from the ordinances of the Fathers. And because the sentence of our Lord Jesus Christ cannot be passed over, when he says:

“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew XVI), etc.,

the things that have been said are proved by the results of events, because in the apostolic see Catholic religion has always been preserved without stain.

Desiring in no way to be separated from this hope and faith, and following the ordinances of the Fathers, we anathematize all heresies, and especially Nestorius the heretic, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, condemned at the Council of Ephesus by the blessed Coelestine, pope of the city of Rome, and by the venerable Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria.

Likewise, we anathematize Eutyches and Dioscorus of Alexandria, condemned in the holy synod of Chalcedon, which we follow and embrace and which, following the holy Council of Nicaea, proclaimed the apostolic faith.

### [Col. 0460B]

We detest Timothy, the parricide, surnamed Aelurus; we also condemn his disciple and follower in all things, Peter of Alexandria. We likewise anathematize Acacius of Constantinople, formerly bishop, condemned by the apostolic see, his accomplice and follower, and those who have remained in their communion or association. Since Acacius mingled himself with the communion of those persons, he deserved to have a sentence of condemnation like theirs.

We condemn Peter of Antioch as well, together with his followers and all those mentioned above. But we receive and approve all the letters of the blessed pope Leo which he wrote concerning the Christian religion. As we have said, we follow the apostolic see in all things and proclaim all its ordinances.

### [Col. 0460C]

And in every respect I hope that I may deserve to be in one communion with you—the communion which the apostolic see proclaims—in which there is the complete and true solidity and perfection of the Christian religion. I promise that in the time to come I shall not recite among the sacred mysteries the names of those separated from communion with the Catholic Church, that is, those who do not consent to the apostolic see.

But if I should in any respect attempt to deviate from my profession, I declare by this [variant: “my”] sentence that I am an accomplice of those whom I have condemned.

I have subscribed this profession with my own hand and sent it to you, Hormisdas, holy and venerable pope of the city of Rome.

## Letter LII. To Germanus and the Other Legates

He warns them to act with the emperor and his wife so that all the Churches, especially Alexandria and Antioch, may be recalled to communion with the apostolic see.

### [Col. 0461A]

Hormisdas to Germanus and John, bishops; Felix and Dioscorus, deacons; and Blandus, presbyter.

Concerning the matters included in the report of your belovedness about what has been done, we give thanks to our God, who has deigned to assist your labor. We exhort you to press upon the most merciful prince and his most pious Augusta, his wife, with the appropriate offices of duty, and, with the help of our Christ, to act in accordance with everything arranged under ecclesiastical observance, so that all the Churches situated in every part of the world may be recalled to communion with the apostolic see.

### [Col. 0461B]

As for the Alexandrian and Antiochene Churches, labor so that they may be joined to our faith under a reasonable observance, because the completion of so great a matter obtains the grace of divine favor both for the most merciful prince and for you. Given in the consulship of Eutharicus, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of our Lord 519).

## Letter LIII. To Dioscorus the Deacon

He asks him to consider how those who had condemned the Council of Chalcedon in writing and wished to return to the Church should be received. He commends to him the bishops Thomas, Nicostratus, and John.

Hormisdas to Dioscorus, deacon.

We congratulate you on the outcome of the work which, with the help of almighty God, you undertook, insofar as it has been accomplished [Col. 0461C]. We also indicate that you must consider how those who condemned the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon in writing are to be recalled. Perhaps such men should be regarded not as schismatics but rather as heretics. Or is the case of those who condemned it in speeches the same as that of those convicted of having condemned it in writing? For our son, the illustrious and devout Albinus, appears to be raising a question on this distinction. Consider, therefore, whether those who wrote against the Council of Chalcedon should be received merely through that general statement, or whether something more should be added.

With the assistance of our God’s consolation, strive concerning the Churches of Alexandria and Antioch, so that, when everything has been properly arranged, they may be joined to Catholic communion. The prolonged difficulties of our brothers and fellow bishops Thomas and Nicostratus also distress us [Col. 0461D], and we wonder why bishops seem to be laboring for the right faith before a Catholic ruler. Your charity must relieve their desires by acting so that, when they obtain what they seek, their sorrow may be turned into joy.

John, bishop of Nicopolis, wrote to us through the deacon Ammonius that certain malicious persons are trying to raise a charge against him before the emperor. We commend him to your affection and urge you to make every effort so that the surreptitious action of his enemies cannot harm his peace.

We did not wish to receive the deacon Ammonius, who was coming to us, into communion with the apostolic see until, after consultation with the deacon Sergius, we had investigated what ought to be arranged [Col. 0462A]. Our deliberation concerning the aforesaid deacon found it acceptable that he should be joined to Catholic communion through the testimony of a written statement. We therefore declare that, when the statement had been solemnly presented, he was admitted as one offering himself to our communion.

Given in the consulship mentioned above (A.D. 519).

## LETTER LIV. TO THE SAME

He praises his concern for consolidating peace. He says that he will write to the emperor so that he may arrange for him to be placed over the Church of Alexandria. He commends Thomas and others to him and urges him to leave nothing improperly arranged because of haste to return.

Hormisdas to Dioscorus, deacon.

We congratulate you on the outcome of the work which, with the help of almighty God, you undertook, insofar as it has been accomplished [Col. 0462B]. We declare to all the peoples of Italy that the things accomplished through you, with God as their author, were pleasing [Note: [Col. 0461] We supplied the words enclosed in parentheses from the Roman edition; through carelessness they were omitted in Labbe.] (and we continually render thanks to our God), who has enabled you to recognize that you were assigned not out of hatred, but rather because of the greatness of the cause.

Therefore, since divine mercy has assisted our humble and pure purpose through you, we must deliberately consider the reward and recompense for your diligence and exertions. For in the coming period we intend to write to our lord and son, the emperor, that he ought to ordain you bishop of Alexandria. It is right that the Church in which you especially served from the earliest beginnings of your life should be corrected by your teaching and moderation. We were displeased that the most exalted emperor was attempting to appoint your charity over the Church of Antioch [Col. 0462C]. It is better for you to receive the dignity of so great a priesthood in your own homeland, so that you may teach the peoples of Egypt, than, having been born in another part of the world, to seem to wander among Syrians, new and unknown people.

The prolonged difficulties of our brothers and fellow bishops Thomas and Nicostratus also distress us, and we wonder why bishops seem to be laboring for the right faith before a Catholic ruler. Your charity must relieve their desires by acting so that, when they obtain what they seek, their sorrow may be turned into joy.

John, bishop of Nicopolis, wrote to us through the deacon Ammonius that certain malicious persons are trying to raise a charge against him before the emperor. We commend him to your affection and urge you to make every effort so that the surreptitious action of his enemies cannot harm his peace [Col. 0462D].

We did not wish to receive the deacon Ammonius, who was coming to us, into communion with the apostolic see until, after consultation with the deacon Sergius, we had investigated what ought to be arranged. Our deliberation concerning the aforesaid deacon found it acceptable that he should be joined to Catholic communion through the testimony of a written statement. We therefore declare that, when the statement had been solemnly presented, he was admitted as one offering himself to our communion.

We commend Paulinus, defender of the Roman Church, and urge you to leave nothing improperly arranged because of the haste of your return. Everything is better arranged over a longer period with the help of our God, and it is more pleasing that the condition of all the Churches should be set in order through delay [Col. 0463A] than that something should remain incomplete through haste, thereby generating renewed labor for us and bringing difficulty to our arrangements.

Given in the consulship mentioned above (A.D. 519).

## LETTER LV. TO THOMAS AND NICOSTRATUS

He says that he is concerned for their welfare. He says that he has commended them by letter to John and Dioscorus.

Hormisdas to the bishops Thomas and Nicostratus.

Do not suppose that our mind is idle or negligent concerning your affair, for we think about your hardship no differently than about our own. When Mena, the notary of our Church, informed us, we learned that your charity is still enduring the burdens of these difficulties [Col. 0463B]. Therefore, in these adversities, may almighty God deign to provide a remedy. We have both sent a letter to our brother and fellow bishop John and instructed our most beloved son, the deacon Dioscorus, by our letters to inform our lord and son, the emperor Justin, of the necessity and cause of our affection, and to act insistently so that our lord may deign to grant an appropriate outcome to your desires.

Your Fraternity must speak with the deacon Dioscorus about this, because he must strive to advance your purpose, whether out of consideration for Catholic communion or in view of our exhortation.

Given in the consulship indicated above (A.D. 519).

## LETTER LVI. TO JOHN AND DIOSCORUS, THE LEGATES

He is distressed that Thomas and Nicostratus were not received at Constantinople with the honor appropriate to them.

[Col. 0463C]

Hormisdas to John, bishop, and Dioscorus, deacon.

We have learned that our brothers and fellow bishops Thomas and Nicostratus were not received at Constantinople as we desired and as they themselves had always hoped. For not only are the places due to them said to have been taken away, but we have also learned that they were suspended from communion. We believe that your Fraternity and affection can judge how bitterly this affects our mind.

Therefore, the greater the diligence you see the magnitude of the case to require, the greater the effectiveness you must provide without delay. Act so that we do not appear to have been treated with greater contempt—though they had been with us—since, contrary to the common desire [Col. 0463D], an improper burden of anxiety has been imposed upon them, to such an extent that nothing is said to have been arranged concerning their possessions, which are said to have been seized by our brother and fellow bishop John, nor are our letters, which we sent through them, said to have been received.

We desire you to act concerning all these matters with such urgency that your charity may quickly write back to us about the outcome of this case.

Given in the consulship indicated above (A.D. 519).

## LETTER LVII. TO JUSTIN, AUGUSTUS

He asks that he arrange for Elias, Thomas, and Nicostratus to be restored to their sees.

Hormisdas to Justin, Augustus.

The ecclesiastical crown of concord and the desired tranquillity of a peaceful world respond, in a universal proclamation, to the glorious labors of your clemency. This makes us sparing and restrained in offering thanks with words. Yet we must not remain silent about the fact that we continually pour out prayers to our Lord for your welfare, since boundless affection can be contained in our vows, while judgment can be finite in our proclamation.

Among these benefits of your piety, however, one [read: a single] concern does not leave us—indeed it affects us deeply [Col. 0464A]: that Elias, Thomas, and Nicostratus, my brothers and fellow bishops, who were the first to follow the ecclesiastical concord with eager devotion, are not only deprived of the great reward of their initiative, but are also accompanied by the misery of a harmful example [Col. 0464B].

Therefore, with tears mingled with our prayers, we beseech your clemency not to allow the intolerable rejection of the aforesaid men to disturb our joys—those joys which you grant us daily through the conversion of heretics. For it is not merely the cause of the persons themselves that concerns us, although the glory of a good deed and of merit might suffice for them as well; rather, it is that the decrees of the venerable canons are being despised, and that their rejection touches the apostolic see with no small injury.

Nor should the sincerity of your Christianity, by which you extend great protection to ancient decrees and confirm the primacy of the apostolic see through the reverence newly shown to its acts, leave to posterity an unresolved and unassailable question in this one matter.

## LETTER LVIII. TO EUPHEMIA, AUGUSTA

He says that he continually pours out prayers to God for the welfare of Euphemia and her husband. He commends Thomas and others.

[Col. 0464C]

Hormisdas to Euphemia, Augusta.

Our praying and offering vows to our God for your safety, together with the uninterrupted assembly of Catholic bishops, is prompted not by your pursuit of intercession, but by your devoted and steadfast purpose in ecclesiastical reconciliation. For who would hold himself separate from a heretical conspiracy? Who would use other principles in his supplication for rulers, except that life may be prolonged for you and for your most serene prince, your husband, and that divine grace may draw nearer to an increase of prosperity?

You consecrated the beginnings of your fortunate reign by punishing the execrations of error and drove out the discord that was friendly to the devil through a peaceful resolve. Therefore it is now fitting for you to persist in your praiseworthy beginnings and to spread perfect healing throughout the world [Col. 0464D]. For when a greater number of the flock is offered to Christ, it confidently demands a greater reward.

Among these concerns, let it be your care that Satan, long since struck down, inflict no wound, but that the unity of communion be a great support for obtaining justice. For we ask that, concerning our venerable brothers and fellow bishops Elias, Thomas, and Nicostratus, what the authority of the most sacred canons dictates may be fulfilled through your decision.

Let them not appear, as though they were the authors of some evil, to have been the only ones punished amid the common joy because they hastened first to the unity of the apostolic see, and let justice not appear to have yielded to personal hatred in a praiseworthy deed. Therefore join your prayers to ours before the most clement Augustus [Col. 0465A], so that hostile evasion may not take away the fruit which the rule of the Fathers commands to be granted and preserved for them.

## LETTER LIX. TO JUSTINIAN

He praises Justinian’s zeal for ecclesiastical peace and commends to him the bishops Elias, Thomas, and Nicostratus.

Hormisdas to Justinian, illustrious man.

We approve your zeal for ecclesiastical peace and for the errors condemned in heretical contention by the actual results of your actions. Without doubt, a great and immeasurable reward for this work awaits you. Therefore, whatever we have judged necessary for the stability of the canons and for the reverence of the apostolic see, we immediately entrust to your greatness with confident boldness, since multiple examples testify that you receive such expected causes with great joy [Col. 0465B].

Accordingly, setting aside lengthy introductory circumlocutions, we turn the words of this present page to the matter itself. The Church grieves and cannot enjoy the joy granted at the great beginning of the desired unity because of the affliction involved in one case. We earnestly beseech you to remove this anxiety from us through your benefits.

For we are distressed both by the present sorrow and by the occasion thus prepared for future conflicts, through which the rule of the venerable Fathers is neglected and the authority of the apostolic see is thought capable of being despised. For although, through the divine favor of the most clement prince and also through your joint efforts, only those are believed to be bishops and rightly to govern the Churches who consent to return to our communion after their errors have been condemned, our brothers and fellow bishops Elias, Thomas, and Nicostratus—who gave a good beginning to the cause even under a hostile emperor—have not only gained no advancement from their good endeavors, but cannot even retain the offices of dignity conferred upon them by the Lord [Col. 0465C]. Exiled from the flocks entrusted to them, they are compelled to undergo the sufferings of the condemned.

Therefore we ask and entreat you by the mercy of God to extend to their just cause the highest protection and the devoted support of your proven vigor. Follow the footsteps of the most pious prince, so that at last he may restore them to their Churches, both out of regard for piety and in contemplation of justice. For their enemies assert, to their insult, that the desired fellowship of our communion has displeased them.

## LETTER LX. TO GERMANUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

The same matters as in the preceding letter.

Hormisdas to Germanus, most illustrious man.

Since you are vigilant with a praiseworthy purpose for ecclesiastical peace and burn with such fervor for the faith, thanksgiving alone is not sufficient. You are not moved by the distinction of human praise, but are inflamed by the expectation of divine recompense. Therefore we perform what we chiefly owe, and daily beseech our God, for whose causes you labor, on behalf of your safety. We ask that your zeal in every aspect of your devotion to ecclesiastical unity may burn in such a way that no opportunity for good service remains where the protection of your defense does not stand by the rules of the Fathers [Col. 0466A].

Above all, however, the cause of our brothers and fellow bishops Elias, Thomas, and Nicostratus moves us. They first followed the concord that was necessary for the world [sic]; struck by the deprivation of their Churches, they are also oppressed by contempt for the venerable canons. Their glory in reconciliation has become a difficult matter, as though they themselves had resisted with the more stubborn mind and, while others returned to the unity of the apostolic see, had themselves torn the members of the Churches apart.

You ought to judge how harsh this is for us and how unworthy of the times of the most clement emperor, and at last to provide a remedy by which both their labors and our sorrow may be removed through a welcome consolation.

[Note: [Col. 0466B] In the Avellana Collection, another letter—first published by the Ballerini in the works of St. Leo, vol. III, p. 167—is added after this letter.]

### Justin, Augustus, to Hormisdas

We received the illustrious bishop R. with grateful feeling, not only because of the honor owed to priests, but also because of our affection for your holiness. For whoever has been approved by your judgment is also judged by us to be most highly approved.

A decision concerning the assistance and favor to be extended to the holy Churches will be made more opportunely when the legates whom we are known to have recently sent to the magnificent king Thrasamund return, if God is favorable, and bring us his response. May your Beatitude deign to ask the highest protection for us through your tireless prayers.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December at Constantinople, under the perpetual Augustus Justin. Received on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Rusticus.

## LETTER LXI. TO ELIAS, THOMAS, AND NICOSTRATUS

He indicates that he has written to the emperor and others on their behalf.

Hormisdas to Elias, Thomas, and Nicostratus, bishops.

It is unnecessary to establish in words, before those who approve mutual affection, how greatly our mind is wearied by sharing in your sorrow. May he who knowingly searches our mind and observes your labors turn our grief into joy through your prosperity.

But so that we may never cease on behalf of your case through a most just plea and gracious intercession, know that we have sent letters both to the most clement prince and to the most excellent Augusta, and also to our sons, the illustrious and magnificent men Justinian and Germanus. These letters specifically set out your case. We entrusted them to the eminent man Eulogius with instructions to leave it first to your decision whether you wish to present them yourselves, or whether they should instead be delivered by him, the bearer, both to the prince and to the other persons mentioned above.

## LETTER LXII. TO THE LEGATES

Concerning what he had heard by report about the actions of the Eutychians at Thessalonica, and the need to compel Dorotheus and Aristides to come to Rome.

[Col. 0467A]

Hormisdas to Germanus and John, bishops; Felix and Dioscorus, deacons; and Blandus, presbyter.

While the joys of ecclesiastical prosperity were lifting us up and we were daily gathering almost the full fruit of your labor, suddenly a hostile report, which had unexpectedly arisen, threw us into confusion. Although we suspect that the sequence of this report is uncertain because you have not yet given us an account, we believe that, given the magnitude of the matter itself, it must not be kept silent.

It has therefore been reported that our brother and fellow bishop John, when he approached Thessalonica merely to receive the statements that were being promised, was so shaken by the irrational revolt of the populace that, after the man who had offered hospitality to him on his arrival was first killed [Col. 0467B], John himself was also slaughtered in a similar massacre and escaped only barely, rescued by the reverence owed to the most holy font. The beginning of this revolt is said to have arisen through a contrivance of deceitful questioning narrated by the presbyter Aristides.

But if these things are established, we do not complain about the people. It will be within the power of the venerable prince to cut away, by whatever censure he orders, the injury done to his own time and to a Catholic priest.

For our part, however, we desire that you fulfill this matter with vigilant care, God being favorable. We do not wish anyone either to be converted without an account being rendered or to profess the right path of faith in such a way that the prince may impose something upon him without a remedy of instruction.

Therefore carry this out through the presentation of your petition: the bishop of Thessalonica, who under the pretext of questioning is attempting to dissipate ecclesiastical peace by prolonging the matter [Col. 0467C], since, having been sent by the prince to the city, he did not wish to receive it from you, should receive instruction from the apostolic see. Whatever he considers doubtful, let him come here and learn from our present inquiry. In this way he can prove that he maintains the safeguard of the Catholic profession, rather than maliciously defending deliberately conceived conflicts.

Let him know that we are ready both to instruct those who inquire properly and, under the guidance of knowledge, to recall those who err to the straight path of faith. For if a doubter does not wish to test the instruction placed before him, and again does not accept in simplicity of heart what is commanded for the sake of peace and religion, it is clear with what mind he resists either the commands of our God or the examples of the orthodox prince.

Let the whole activity of your petition therefore be directed to this part, since he cannot be saved by any other means, and the case of the incited people is better calmed under this moderation. At the same time, let the most clement prince order the presbyter Aristides to come to us, because, as we have said, we desire all those whose ecclesiastical peace is divided by uncertainty to experience together the medicine of Catholic knowledge through communion with us, once the sickness of harmful error has been driven away [Col. 0467D].

Furthermore, as soon as the present letter reaches you, you must send someone from among you to us with a report containing everything. In this way you must relieve our anxiety concerning what has been done or is being done. Add Datarius to your letter, so that the tardiness of the bearer cannot be attributed to you [Col. 0468A].

Given on the third day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of Eutharicus, illustrious man (A.D. 519).

## REPORT OF BISHOP GERMANUS, THE DEACONS FELIX AND DIOSCORUS, AND THE PRESBYTER BLANDUS

What was done at Thessalonica by Dorotheus against Bishop John. (C)

[Col. 0468A]

Great is the mercy of God, and unsearchable are his judgments; he leaves nothing hidden, so that each person’s conscience may be tested.
