Dorotheus, bishop of Thessalonica, did not appear to be a new man, nor was he made what he now is only recently; rather, he showed himself to be the man whom his former reputation truly proclaimed. Always entangled in his evil desires, he used the opportunity to carry out the crime that he had always been conceiving against the Catholic faith.

In another letter [Col. 0468B] we informed your Beatitude in what order we were unable to receive the statements while passing through Thessalonica. It had nevertheless been decided, after the ordination of the holy Church of Constantinople, that one of us should be sent to him. The aforesaid man hoped for this, so that one of us, after receiving the statements, might celebrate Mass with him, as though he thereby had testimony that he was joined in general to the unity of the apostolic see.

Although it happened late, it did happen: we sent the venerable John, bishop, to him, and by common agreement the presbyter Epiphanius was sent with him. Germanus, the venerable and illustrious bishop, was with them, as was Licinius, count of the Schola, by order of the most clement emperor.

Licinius, however, had previously been sent to Thessalonica for another reason. When a synod was convened from the parish of the Church of Thessalonica, he was found there, awaiting, according to the promise, one of us. They wished to prepare and sign the statements in his presence. This was done: the aforesaid man signed the statements, then came to Constantinople and reported what had happened.

The apocrisiarius of Dorotheus said to us: “Order someone to be sent to receive the statements.” As we said, it was decided that the venerable Bishop John should go, so that he might have testimony to their signatures. We asked the most pious emperor that Count Licinius should go with him, and this too was done.

When they reached the city, Dorotheus was informed by Count Licinius that our men were present. Dorotheus sent the presbyter Aristides with two other bishops, whom he knew to be the only opponents of the affair, to meet our men [Col. 0468C]. With them they wished to begin a dispute about the statements, saying: “There are chapters that must be corrected.”

Our men replied that it was not within their power to do this: “If you wish to do so, thanks be to God; if you do not wish to do so, we have come, we have greeted you, and we have made the journey.”

After these words they departed. On the following day they met again and spoke in the same way. Before they had even made their proposal in words, no dispute had arisen there and no insult had followed. Suddenly the mad crowd rushed upon them. The bishops killed two boys, struck the bishop’s head in two places, and shattered his lower back. Unless the mercy of God and the protection of the basilica of Saint Mark had snatched them from their hands [Col. 0469A], they would have perished there. They were nevertheless freed, as is said, because the public authorities arrived and were able to rescue them.

Dorotheus’s malice fabricated these events and their embellishments. Two days before our men reached Thessalonica, he baptized more than two thousand people [Note: [Col. 0469D] “Grains” is less satisfactory, as is clear from the following index.] and distributed such a quantity of the sacraments among the people that it could sustain them for some time, indicating to the people that the true faith was being changed. How could these things not have roused the people? Whom did they not invite to revolt?

After this, in front of the people, he tore up the very statement that he had made with the bishops, saying: “I will never do this until my death, nor will I consent to those who do it.”

They also killed a venerable Catholic man, John, who had received us when we arrived at his house. He had always been separated from the communion of Dorotheus because of the Council of Chalcedon. They inflicted upon him the kind of death inflicted by those who killed the holy Proterius.

These events reached the most clement emperor, and almost the entire city is in Catholic mourning because of such crimes as have occurred. His sacred Clemency promises to avenge them and to summon Dorotheus, for we protested to his piety, saying: “The most blessed pope cannot in any way receive Dorotheus among the bishops or into the communion of the apostolic see. Conversely, those who wish to receive him into their communion must know that, by ecclesiastical authority, they will be held guilty.”

We hastened to report these matters to your Beatitude, so that nothing taking place in these regions might remain unknown to you.

Received on the fourth day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Eutharicus (A.D. 519).

## LETTER LXIII. TO THE LEGATES

He grieves that John was killed; he orders that, once Dorotheus has been removed from the episcopate, another person—except Aristides—be appointed in his place. Thomas and Nicostratus are to be restored to their Churches. The Scythian monks are to be detained at Rome until the legates’ arrival.

Hormisdas to Germanus and John, bishops, and Blandus, presbyter.

The death of John, a Catholic, whom you report to have been killed by the madness of the heretic Dorotheus, has afflicted us severely. We have learned that Dorotheus himself was summoned to Constantinople by order of the prince. You must press our lord and son, the most clement prince, concerning him, so that he may not return again to that city [Col. 0469D]. Rather, after laying aside the honor of the episcopate, which he never exercised well, he must be banished far from that place and Church, or certainly be sent here to the city under suitable escort.

You must also be vigilant in this matter: Aristides, the instigator and accomplice of all the evil, must not be appointed in his place through any kind of surreptitious action. For it benefits no one to change the person if the same pattern of wickedness remains. You must choose such a man that the entire Catholic assembly may rejoice in your judgment.

With these matters observed, your affection must devote its greatest attention to the persons of our brothers and fellow bishops Thomas and Nicostratus [Col. 0470A]. For what benefit is there in restoring a Church if we see foreign priests in its body—men whom you know were received into our communion cautiously and reasonably? Therefore this matter deeply distresses us, if those who follow the preaching of the apostolic see neglect those who have been received in its faith and agreement.

Accordingly, as we have urged, press the most serene prince strongly concerning their communion and their place. On this same matter we have sent letters to our lord and son, the most clement prince, and to our son Justinian, an illustrious man, urging him to deal with them, together with your charity, insofar as concerns their reception into their Churches. We suspect that you have not forgotten this point of our admonition [Col. 0470B].

We explained how, once the usurpers had been excluded, those of whom we speak should return to their own Churches, so that the others may be appointed elsewhere, if indeed they are of the right faith.

Concerning the persons of the Scythian monks, the illustrious man Justinian wrote to us; we have sent copies of his letters to your Fraternity. Because they were unwilling to await the arrival of your affection and said that they could not endure the delays of these proceedings, they attempted to leave the city secretly. We shall therefore have them guarded more carefully, wishing to learn what they have said against you, so that, when you return, God being favorable, their error may be corrected by reasonable exhortations.

Given on the third day before the Nones of December, in the consulship of Eutharicus, illustrious man (A.D. 519).

## LETTER LXIV. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF MELICITANA [MILITANA]  
[Note: [Col. 0470D] At the point where he congratulates him, he subscribes to the communion of the Church of Constantinople.]

That the Church of Constantinople has returned to communion with the apostolic see.

[Col. 0470C]

Hormisdas to John, bishop of Melicitana [Note: [Col. 0469D] Perhaps Malacitana, in Spain. The following letter is also addressed to Spanish bishops. HARDUINUS.] (Nilecopolitana).

We do not wish our vows to remain unknown to your charity, lest one who shared our anxiety be deprived of the fruit of our joys. Therefore, with the Lord’s favor, we inform you through our address that the Church of Constantinople has returned to our communion and that the sequence of all the commands we gave to our legates has been completed.

So that perfect joy from this matter might reach your affection more fully, we have also thought it right to send copies of the statement of John, our brother and fellow priest, bishop of Constantinople, and of the sacred letters of Justin, the most clement prince of the East [Col. 0470D]. We also indicate that many bishops throughout the East have acted in the same way.

It remains for us to ask the Divinity through suitable prayers to grant that we may also rejoice in the restoration of the other Churches. You will take care to convey to the priests near your Fraternity the matters we have considered it proper to report, so that they too may not cease to give thanks with us for the effect of so great a deed through the benefits of heavenly mercy [Col. 0471A].

May God keep you safe, dearest brother.

## LETTER LXV. TO THE BISHOPS OF SPAIN  
(OF THE PROVINCE OF BAETICA)

He congratulates them on the peace of the Eastern Church.

To all the dearest brothers, the bishops established throughout the province of Baetica, Bishop Hormisdas.

[Note: [Col. 0471D] The letter of Pope Marcellinus is almost the same.]

What is as sweet to one who is anxious as learning from you those things that I desire? What is as consistent with religious institutions as priests preserving among themselves the peace which, in the exercise of their office, they must announce to others?

I received with complete joy your letter in which you reported, with the desired affection existing among you, the concord and peace of the Churches. Whatever I could exhort, whatever I could advise, was voluntarily brought to me. May God confirm what he has accomplished in us (Psalm 67), and may he himself who gave the commands concerning what must be done for the salvation of souls carry them out, in the piety by which he redeemed us.

In response to such good news, we too return the service of religious messengers. Whatever we previously reported in letters sent concerning the Easterners whom, through the help of our God, we recalled to the body and unity of the Church, we shall share with you again, when appropriate, in renewed reports [Col. 0471B].

Soon after our return, in accordance with our edict, an embassy was sent by the Easterners. It hoped for definite answers and consulted on definite matters. But we shall summarize what had to be said, sending you instead the replies that we gave, in order to inform you. Thus neither opinion nor error may claim anything for itself over the longer expanse of lands, when it is sufficient to hold to the truth itself as the basis of the facts [Col. 0471C].

As for the contents of your letter, it would indeed have been proper to set out your desires more fully, so that, after everything had been considered, a response appropriate to the matter could be given. But since you mentioned in the same letter the ancient privileges and the statutes of the Fathers, we have replied on this point to our brother and fellow bishop Sallustius, indicating briefly to you as well what was explained to him at greater length: namely, that privileges granted to us—or by us [the wording is uncertain]—must not be torn away, and that nothing is so consistent with the faith as preserving, in their honor, the decrees established by the Fathers.

May God keep you safe, dearest brothers (A.D. 519).

## REPORT OF DIOSCORUS, DEACON

Paul ordained bishop of Antioch. The Scythian monks caused disturbances, saying that one of the Trinity had been crucified. (C)

[Col. 0471D]

It is true that there are no joys that are especially spiritual from which tribulation can be wholly separated. We rejoice in the unity of the Church of Constantinople, which has been achieved with the Apostolic See; daily we are glad that statements of satisfaction from various bishops are presented to us. A minor scandal occurred in the city of Ephesus, where the Council of Chalcedon was despised and insulted. The most merciful emperor has been called upon to correct this, and he hopes, with God’s help, that it will be done [Col. 0472A]. Now, although after labors and after many efforts, the Church of Antioch has been set in order; a certain presbyter named Paul of the Church of Constantinople was chosen, whom they wished and attempted to ordain here, having found him most suitable for this honor by the emperor’s testimony. I, mindful of your command, objected, saying: “Our most blessed lord the pope has ordered that, according to ancient custom, he be ordained bishop there.” This obtained what you had commanded. Pray that God, through the prayers of the apostle Peter, may also grant that the city itself receive the chosen priest in peace.

And because these things are being done, and the Church is daily making progress in them, the ancient enemy has stirred up the monks from Scythia, who belong to the household of the master of soldiers Vitalianus and are opposed to the wishes of all Christians. Their unrest [Col. 0472B] has caused no small delays to the unity of the Churches, and especially to the ordination of the aforesaid Church of Antioch. Among these monks is Leontius, who says that he is related to the master of soldiers. They are hastening to Rome, hoping that certain propositions will be confirmed by Your Blessedness. Among them is one in which they wish to say that one of the Trinity was crucified. This has been stated neither in the holy councils, nor in the letters of the holy pope Leo, nor in ecclesiastical usage. If this is permitted, it seems to me that no small dissensions and scandals will arise among the Churches.

The emperor Anastasius hastened with great determination to impose this upon the Catholics; the disciples of Eutyches also proposed it at the Council of Chalcedon. For whenever the Fathers discussed God’s Son, our Lord [Col. 0472C] Jesus Christ, they called the Son of God the Word, consubstantial with the Father, *homoousion*—“of one substance”—with the Father. This formula—“one of the Trinity was crucified”—was never introduced by the Fathers into the councils, because it plainly could not in the least accord with the Catholic faith. If the intention of this expression is examined carefully, it becomes clear to how many heresies it opens the way and what evils might be introduced by it into ecclesiastical debates. Since it would be lengthy to explain this in the present letter, we pass it over.

Therefore it seems to me sound, useful, and appropriate to the peace of the Churches that no other response be given than this: “The holy Council of Chalcedon is sufficient, and it contains the other councils as well. The letters of Pope Leo, which the council confirmed, are sufficient. We neither wish nor ought to introduce novelty into the Church.”

There is also this crafty statement in their proposal [Col. 0472D]: “We have accepted the Council of Chalcedon; what we hope is that you will order us to explain it, because it is not sufficient in the form in which it has been explained against the Nestorian heresy.” They say this not as though they did not understand it, but as they attempt, through subtlety, to lead us to debate the Council of Chalcedon. If this is done, it is shown to be doubtful and unsound, and it is laid open to the error of all heretics.

If, after the Council of Chalcedon, after the letters of Pope Leo, and after the statements that the bishops have given and continue to give, by which they have satisfied the Apostolic See, something new is again added, it seems to me that everything already accomplished is thereby destroyed.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of June, at Constantinople.

### STATEMENT OF GERMANUS AND JOHN, BISHOPS; FELIX AND DIOSCORUS, DEACONS; AND BLANDUS, PRESBYTER

The same matters as above. (C)

[Col. 0473A]

Your Blessedness has already learned through other letters, sent by your servant Pollio, with what order and caution, by God’s mercy, we entered into communion with the Church of Constantinople. Likewise, in other letters, not once but twice, we took care to indicate what things men hostile to religion were attempting to signify, so that nothing done or contemplated should be hidden from Your Blessedness.

With God’s help, everything that has been arranged in the Church of Constantinople stands with us. The spiritual joys that Catholics celebrated and continue to celebrate do not waver. The matter of the ordination of the Church of Antioch [Col. 0473B] caused us not only labor but great tribulation, because men hastening to impede the general unity created various obstacles in various ways.

Our proposal concerned ordaining a priest in the aforesaid Church from among those who had withdrawn from the anathema. They did not place the future judgment before their eyes, openly saying: “All who were in communion with the Apostolic See are Nestorians,” and, still more, that those who now appear to have been restored to communion with the Apostolic See should not be believed.

After many afflictions, and after the conflicts had been prolonged by the Fathers for nearly three months, the most pious emperor, by his own authority, chose a presbyter named Paul from the Church of Constantinople to become bishop in the Church of Antioch. Among other things, he gave this testimony [Col. 0473C] concerning him: that, when stationed in Antioch for two years, he had resisted the heretic Severus with no ordinary steadfastness. All the Catholics expressed similar agreement. The emperor also promised that he would report all these matters concerning the aforesaid man to Your Blessedness.

The monks from Scythia were, however, the instigators and associates of these tribulations and an impediment to the unity of the Churches. They subsequently failed here—departed from here—having been designated by everyone as thinking of nothing peaceful. They ran to Your Blessedness, hoping to insinuate themselves and, through letters from your see, to have their purpose confirmed.

These men accuse bishops from their own province, among them Paternus, bishop of the city of Tomi. They submitted petitions, and, compelled by the command of the most pious emperor and of the lord Vitalianus, master of soldiers, we repeatedly came together for the hearing of the case [Col. 0473D], not because we wished to occupy ourselves with these matters—for Your Blessedness’s instructions were before our eyes, in which you commanded us to attend only to the case for which we had come and not to become involved in other matters—but because we hoped that their purpose might be pacified, and so we undertook this.

After we had labored for a long time and they accepted no reason, making no progress in the position we were maintaining, the most merciful emperor, at a public assembly in which we too were present, restored the aforesaid bishop Paternus and the magnificent man Vitalianus to favor. He also ordered Paternus’s accusers to supplicate their bishop.

When the monks likewise were sought for reconciliation, they slipped away in flight and preferred to leave the city [Col. 0474A] rather than attain reconciliation.

The aforesaid monks, coming to Italy, intend to propose several propositions, among them one concerning “one of the Trinity crucified.” They hope that this will be confirmed by the authority of Your Blessedness, as we indicated in other letters and now state again, so that no novelty may be written by the Apostolic See. For we declared both before the emperor and before the senate: “Apart from the four councils, and apart from the letters of Pope Leo, we neither state nor admit anything that is not contained in the aforesaid councils; and we do not accept anything that was not written by Pope Leo. For if our lord should wish to write any kind of novelty, this beginning would be worse than the error committed through Eutyches.”

It ought to be enough for the Church that for sixty years it has endured from Eutyches until now [Col. 0474B]. We have written what seemed right to us; it is in your power to deliberate what God has commanded you. For they strive to assert these things, wishing to satisfy themselves in this manner, so that we may profess and say that one of the Trinity suffered—something that neither the Fathers nor the councils said.

We have explained these matters one by one so that their subtlety may not boast over our simplicity on account of these new purposes of theirs.

They insinuated themselves with the magnificent man Vitalianus so that he might both exact such things on such pretexts and bring against us whatever obstacles he could. The whole Church mourns with us at his change.

Therefore we ask that, with your customary caution and with the vigilance our lord ordinarily displays, you consider how those who have departed from us in this manner and have been separated from our communion are to be suspended [Col. 0474C], what answer should be given them, and how their propositions should be rejected, because the entire Catholic Church of Constantinople abhors them.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of July, at Constantinople.

### STATEMENT OF THE LEGATES TO POPE HORMISDAS

They request that the relics of Saint Lawrence and the sacred relics of the apostles be granted to Justinian, who wished to place them in the Basilica of the Apostles. (C)

Your son, the magnificent man Justinian, acting in ways consistent with his faith, has established a basilica of the holy Apostles in which he desires that the relics of the blessed martyr Lawrence also be present. Through our humble agency he hopes that you will promptly grant the relics of the aforesaid saints [Col. 0474D].

The aforesaid man’s request was made according to the custom of the Greeks, and we explained to him the custom of the Apostolic See. He accepted the reasoning. Since such is the fervor of his faith that he deserves whatever he asks from the Apostolic See, and since he is such a man that he hopes thereby to increase both the salvation of his soul and the effectiveness of his faith, it is fitting not to deny requests of this kind.

Therefore, if it seems right to Your Blessedness, order that the sacred relics of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul be generously granted to him according to custom; and, if it can be done, that the relics themselves be deposited at the second cataract. It is yours to deliberate.

He also asks, if possible, for something from the chains of the holy apostles and from the gridiron of the blessed martyr Lawrence. These are the desires [Col. 0475A] of the aforesaid man; his faith has been stirred by them.

For this reason he sent the distinguished man Eulogius, *magistrianus*, to your city, judging that he would be satisfied if he might receive relics from that very source from which the relics of the apostles have been bestowed throughout the world. You do well to entrust an ecclesiastical matter of such importance, under solemn appeal to God, to such a man, whose sincerity and integrity concerning the Catholic religion are known to everyone.

They wished to have silver reliquary boxes made and sent here, but afterward they decided that he should also receive this from your see as a blessing. We nevertheless suggest that individual reliquary boxes should be made for the relics of each individual apostle.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of July, at Constantinople.

### COPY OF JUSTINIAN’S LETTER TO HORMISDAS

The dissensions stirred up by the Scythian monks are to be suppressed by him. He desires relics of the apostles. (C)

[Col. 0475B]

To the holy lord, most blessed in merits and apostolic lord, Father Pope Hormisdas, Justinian, illustrious man.

By the favor of the Divinity, which has always established the Catholic Church through the growth of faith, the unity of the holy Churches has come about through the teaching and authority of your apostolate.

But since we have learned that certain men called monks, in whom there is more zeal for discord than for the charity and peace of God, wish to disturb certain matters and have set out from here on their journey to your angelic presence, may Your Blessedness, having learned from the present writings the cause of their envy, deign to receive them as they deserve and drive them far from you. Their empty words, as they hasten to introduce novelties into the Church—novelties known to be contained neither in the four venerable councils nor in the letters of the holy Pope Leo—appear to be stirring up disturbances everywhere [Col. 0475C].

Therefore may Your Blessedness also deign to send your angelic representative to us from the most reverend bishops and deacons whom your apostolate has sent, and order that the monks themselves, struck by fitting correction, be expelled, as stated above.

Accordingly, we ask that you hasten greatly to send such letters to us through the same bearer, as was said above. Their names are Achilles, John, Leontius, and Mauritius (Maxentius).

This is the principal cause of our anxiety: lest the unity that your labor and prayer have achieved be scattered by restless men. We hope in the Lord God that, if anything still dissents from the peace of the whole world, this too may, through your prayers, be joined to the communion of the Apostolic See.

Relying upon the benevolence of Your Blessedness, we earnestly ask your fatherly love to deign generously to illuminate and adorn both us and the basilica of the holy apostles, built here in our residence under the name of the aforesaid venerable apostles, with relics of the holy apostles. For we recognize that you can bestow upon us no greater benefit or gift, most blessed lord and father, than the fulfillment of this request of ours.

When the aforesaid *agentes in rebus* suddenly set out on the journey, we also sent two silk cloaks for the adornment of the altar of the holy apostles. As you receive them, command that we be continually remembered in your most effective prayers.

### COPY OF JUSTINIAN’S LETTER TO POPE HORMISDAS THROUGH THE BROTHER OF PROEMPTOR

He asks that, once the matter of the monks has been settled, he send John and Leontius back to him. (C)

Whatever is more cautious, whatever is firmer, we desire to be done for the holy faith and the concord of the sacred Churches. Therefore our most glorious brother Vitalianus also wrote to Your Blessedness through Paulinus, an eminent man and defender of your Church, and we have likewise indicated through the same man that Your Blessedness ought to accomplish those things which grant peace and concord to the holy Churches [Col. 0476B].

Nevertheless, we have sent with letters from our most pious emperor a man who can bring you a more certain response concerning these matters. For the extent of the dispute that has arisen in our regions can also be explained to Your Holiness by the aforementioned religious defender.

Therefore we ask that, if possible, after giving an exceedingly swift response and satisfying the religious monks, you send John and Leontius back to us. For unless this dispute is resolved by your prayers and diligence, we fear that the peace of the holy Churches may not be achieved.

Knowing, then, that both reward and danger in this matter are reserved for you, deal with it carefully, and send us through the aforementioned religious monks, if possible [Col. 0476C], a most firm response before our legate reaches Your Blessedness. For upon this alone our entire concern depends.

### COPY OF JUSTINIAN’S LETTER TO HORMISDAS

Whether it should be said that one of the Trinity was crucified. (C)

So that the fullest perfection of faith may come to us through the teaching of Your Blessedness, we have sent Eulogius, a vigorous *agens in rebus*, again, along with other matters, also for this purpose. Through him we earnestly ask that in every respect we be confirmed in the confession of the Catholic faith by a careful and most cautious response from your apostolate.

For after the unity of the Catholic Church had once been granted by divine mercy, some assert that Christ, the Son of God, our Lord, crucified in the flesh for our salvation [Col. 0476D], ought to be proclaimed as “one of the Trinity.” If this is to be accepted, may your reverence, with paternal foresight, deign in a most cautious rescript to inform us what we ought to follow and what we ought to avoid in this matter. For the words appear to produce dissension, whereas the understanding among all Catholics is shown to be one.

Therefore, holy and venerable Father, take upon yourself once again the labor you have undertaken, following also in this matter your predecessors, whose memory you embrace and whose fellowship you adorn through your pontificate; hasten to make us free and secure concerning this intention.

For we believe that what is Catholic is whatever your religious response makes known to us. Since it has been said that the Scythian monks have come to your see on this matter in defense of the tradition of the Fathers and the order of the rules, give them a response and, fearing nothing, order them to be sent back to us with your letters. Also order that copies of these letters be given to the aforementioned vigorous man Eulogius.

We ask you to arrange all these matters with special caution so that no opportunity may be given to falsehood or intrigue. For we embrace the Catholic faith with the utmost longing and ask, through your teaching, that you grant unity to the whole world.

### LETTER LXVI. TO JUSTINIAN

The Scythian monks will not leave Rome before the arrival of the legates. He sends the sacred relics of the apostles.

Hormisdas to Justinian, illustrious man.

We know that Your Magnificence’s spirit is so vigorous in religious devotion that you wish a benefit from us for the perfection of the peace of the Church to be demanded from you rather than requested, judging that what your excellence offers at the desire of the whole community advances your merits. Therefore we too presumptuously ask this of you as something that we know will be beneficial to your merits. And so, lord son, greeting you with all charity, we hope that you will devote yourself to the work which, with the Lord’s help, you have begun, remembering the divine testimony: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X).

Moreover, we had wished the monks whom you indicated in your letters had come to Rome to return immediately to their own country. But because, calling upon the testimony of divine power, they said that they might suffer danger to their lives from ambushes prepared along the route if they wished to return to Constantinople [Col. 0477C], we did not permit them to be expelled by force.

Therefore we found it necessary, when our legates arrived, to investigate what cause had truly stirred up the disagreement among them.

As for the sacred relics of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, since you requested them with such religious devotion, we have sent them through the bearer of this letter with all reverence. We pray through their intercessions that the offering and desires of your mind may be acceptable to the grace of the Divinity.

We therefore ask that, both concerning what is being done for concord and concerning your safety and well-being, you send joy to our concern by the running page of your letters.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of September, in the consulship of Eutharicus, illustrious man (A.D. 519).

### LETTER LXVII. TO THE SAME

The Scythian monks will not leave Rome before the arrival of the legates.

[Col. 0477D]

Hormisdas to Justinian, illustrious man.

We have received, through our son Eulogius, illustrious man, the letters of Your Highness. As he returns, we discharge the duty of greeting and inform you that the Scythian monks have presented many allegations which we cannot leave unexamined. But, with God’s help, let us hasten the arrival of our legates. For this reason we believe that they should be kept in the City, from which they themselves do not dissent by their own arrangement.

Nevertheless, we trust that Your Greatness will retain what they wrote to us in letters sent at an earlier time. When, with the returning legates, we have been suitably instructed concerning their allegations, if our investigation discovers anything deserving of censure, it will be necessary for us to maintain ecclesiastical discipline toward them.

Furthermore, Victor, who is said to hold the office of deacon and whose faith these same monks vehemently accuse, or others who perhaps advance perverse questions, should, at the arrangement of our lord son, the most merciful emperor, be sent to the City at your suggestion [Col. 0478A], so that we may be able to learn all the allegations over which they are contending.

### STATEMENT OF DIOSCORUS THE DEACON TO POPE HORMISDAS

He declares that he has no association with heretics. The deacon Victor professed the Catholic faith. The Scythian monks condemned the Council of Chalcedon. He sets forth his faith and submits it to the judgment of the pontiff. (C)

[Col. 0478B]

Through Eulogius [Note: [Col. 0477D] The manuscript of the Avellana Collection reads: “illustrious man.”] we received the letters of Your Blessedness, in which you indicated the position of the Scythian monks and how it had seemed appropriate to your apostolate to delegate the matter to the bishop of Constantinople, so that he might hear the case between them and those whom they were attacking.

I had not been displeased by this, for where conscience, with God’s help, is troubled by no fear, one ought to withdraw from no one; rather, one ought to hasten all the more so that what is true may be made manifest to everyone through examination.

You indicated that they had given you a formal declaration that no heretics should be joined to me. I do not know whom they call heretics, unless perhaps those who accept the Council of Chalcedon, whom I call Catholics [Col. 0478C].

Victor is said to be a deacon. Before we entered Constantinople, certain men with him had a dispute concerning “one of the Trinity crucified,” concerning a composite Christ, and concerning other propositions while we were stationed here [Note: [Col. 0478D] The Roman edition reads: “while we were stationed hereafter.”]. They submitted a written statement against him both to us and to the bishop of Constantinople.

We met in the bishop’s house so that we might learn the dispute that had arisen among them. The aforesaid bishop produced the Council of Chalcedon. He read before everyone all that had been established in that council, saying: “Let nothing else be said to me besides these things. Whoever follows these things can be among the Catholics.”

Victor replied: “Likewise I accept the letters of Pope Leo and the synodal letters of Saint Cyril that are cited in the Council of Chalcedon [Col. 0478D]. I subscribe to these with my own hand and confirm by oath that I accept them and preach nothing besides them. If I should ever be found preaching anything outside them, I ask for no mercy concerning me.”

The Scythians, on the other hand, began to say: “Let ‘one of the Trinity’ be added.”

We, on the contrary, said: “What has not been defined in the four councils, nor in the letters of the blessed Pope Leo, we can neither say nor add.”

This statement displeased them. But whether Victor said these things sincerely or deceitfully, who can know except the one who knows hearts? We heard these words; it belongs to God to judge the mind.

Afterward, without us, the magnificent man Vitalianus, master of soldiers, summoned the aforesaid Victor between himself and the bishop of Constantinople. They spoke with him; what they decided among themselves we do not know. Afterward Victor neither came to us nor was the case stated.

Nevertheless, Your Blessedness should know that these Scythians call all who accept the Council of Chalcedon Nestorians. They say: “The council against Nestorius is not sufficient, and the council must be accepted in the manner in which they themselves have explained it.” What sort of men these are, what purposes they have, and what they wish to introduce into the Catholic faith has, with God’s help, been made clear to all Catholics. The matter does not need my labor, since God, in his mercy, has brought it into the light.

I have not kept silent or concealed what I learned from the Fathers and what the Catholic Church has always preserved. There is one God, of whom Moses speaks, saying: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI). And in another passage he says: “The Lord alone guided them.”

We believe the Trinity to be of one substance, just as I have stated that there is one divinity; there are three persons, because we neither speak of several gods, believing that there is one God—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—nor do we deny three persons, lest we appear to follow the teaching of Sabellius.

It is true that the person of the Son, that is, the Word of God, is consubstantial with the Father, and that this same one became flesh; this same one dwelt in Mary’s womb; this same one assumed human nature without sin; the Son of God himself became man and was born of the virgin Mary. For this reason we call and believe her to be the Mother of God, because the unity of divinity and humanity, which began when the angel Gabriel announced to Mary, saying, “Hail, Mary, full of grace; the Holy Spirit will come upon you” (Luke I), and so forth, was not divided in the womb, nor in birth, nor in nourishment, nor in the Passion, nor in the tomb, nor in the resurrection, nor in heaven.

For there is one Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, not divided in persons, not separated in natures, and not different in power. It is the same one who endured suffering. For all who either divide him, as Nestorius did, or deny him, as Eutyches did, or believe the incarnation less fully, as Apollinaris did, or introduce a phantom, as Manes did, have been cut off from the Catholic faith: men who work iniquity and enemies of the apostles’ teaching.

These things I learned and heard from our elders. If, perhaps, I do not know what we ought to follow beyond these things, it is necessary for me to follow whatever Your Blessedness explains [Col. 0479D].

As for Maxentius, who, under the title of abbot, said that he had a congregation, if he is asked either with which monks he lived, or in which monastery, or under which abbot he became a monk, he cannot say. Likewise, if I wished to speak about Achilles, I would be doing something pointless: it is enough for him always to remain hidden because of his conscience, condemned by all Catholics.

Given on the Ides of October, in the consulship of Eutharicus (A.D. 519). Received on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Rusticus, illustrious man (A.D. 520).

### LETTER OF JUSTINUS TO HORMISDAS

He reports that petitions containing questions about the faith were presented to him and that Dioscorus did not approve them. He will send someone to the pontiff to settle the questions. (C)

[Col. 0480A]

Justinus Augustus to Pope Hormisdas.

How earnestly we are striving to gather the most sacred Churches into concord, we made known publicly long ago. At the beginning of our reign we also judged it necessary to admonish Your Holiness to send trustworthy men, so that through their intervention some remedy might be found for these matters.

Before those who had been sent arrived, we prepared everything so that the matters requiring arrangement in this most flourishing city might be settled more easily.

But since petitions were presented to our divinity from various Eastern provinces, setting forth certain arguments concerning the Catholic faith and declaring the secrets of their minds—things which they affirm to be established among them concerning the indivisible Trinity, and which they show that they firmly intend to receive—after these had been reread, Dioscorus asserted that some matters had been inserted in an unsuitable order [Col. 0480B].

We therefore rightly decided to disclose to you what we had been taught. Not long afterward, someone will be sent by us to inform Your Blessedness more certainly about everything, to make known to you the supplications presented to us, and to bring back your pious response, by which unsuitable doubts may finally be cut away.

Secure, therefore, in our council, deign to appease the supreme Divinity for us through your anxious prayers.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, at Constantinople, in the consulship of Vitalianus and Rusticus (A.D. 520).

### REPORT OF JOHN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE

That the approaching day of the Lord’s Passion is rightly celebrated on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May. (C)

[Col. 0480C]

To the lord beloved by God in every respect, and to the most holy brother and fellow minister Hormisdas, greetings in the Lord.

We judge that you have been satisfied by these actions with the reverence due to you, dearest brother, considering how we hold you among ourselves with a pure heart and spiritual charity, and how in every respect we regard you as worthy of veneration. We obey the Lord’s voice, which plainly cries: “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do the same for them” (Matt. VII), and we embrace the apostolic teaching that says: “In showing honor, take the lead with one another” (Rom. XII).

We hasten to demonstrate these things by our actions, maintaining an indissoluble bond of spiritual charity for the union [variant: “gathering together”] of the holy Churches, so that, with the holy and consubstantial Trinity assisting us, we may not waver either under the blows of hostile spirits or through the fluctuations caused by the evil prince, the enemy of truth, and through the intercession of the glorious and true Mother of God Mary [Col. 0480D].

Through these means, most holy lord, we especially pray that the state of our holy Churches and of yours may remain immovable, and that we may likewise preserve the inseparable unity of the faith. For God is able to grant the palm of victory without struggle to those who hope in him.

We report that the reckoning of the approaching day of the Lord’s Passion, which is contained in your letters, is correct according to the Easter annals preserved among us [Col. 0481A]—although we already knew this earlier and have now investigated it more carefully. Without doubt, we hope to celebrate the festival of the world safely on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, which is properly the nineteenth day of the coming month of April.

Pray, therefore, and may your holy mind deign not to have any forgetfulness concerning our remembrance. I and my people also greet very warmly all the brotherhood that is with Your Holiness in Christ.

In another hand: “Safe in the Lord, pray for us, beloved and most holy brother of God.”

Given at Constantinople, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Vitalianus and Rusticus, most illustrious men (A.D. 520).

[Note: [Col. 0481] We supplied from the Roman edition the words enclosed in brackets, which are omitted in Labbe.]

### STATEMENT OF BISHOP GERMANUS, FELIX AND DIOSCORUS THE DEACONS, AND BLANDUS THE PRESBYTER

Dorotheus was taken to Heraclea, and the emperor did not permit him to be brought to Rome; but it is unknown by whom he was released from there. Concerning the Eastern Church’s agreement with Rome on the date of Easter. (C)

[Col. 0481B]

We received the revered greetings of your apostolate through your sons Leo and Eulogius with the joy we desired. The former’s initial instruction reproached us for not having reported what happened at Thessalonica. But long before his arrival, when the opportunity arose, we took care to make known everything we had learned either from the reports of those arriving, from the writings of those who had conveyed the information—copies of which we have added below—or from the account of the most pious emperor.

A promise of punishment followed, to such an extent that Dorotheus, bishop of Thessalonica, was taken to the city of Heraclea, until [Col. 0481C] the case reached its conclusion.

Meanwhile, in accordance with what you had commanded, we took care to make your apostolic authority known to the emperor, so that the aforesaid Dorotheus might be sent to Rome together with Aristides to receive instruction in Catholic purity.

He replied that the case was not one for which they should be delegated to Rome for a hearing, since there they could more freely defend themselves without the controversy of accusers.

But suddenly, while these things were taking place, he was released from the city of Heraclea, where, as far as we know, he was being held. For what reason, by what means or condition, or through whose agency, we do not know.

Concerning the day of Easter, may Your Blessedness know that the judgment of the Easterners agrees with the Apostolic See: the festival is expected to be celebrated on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, as will also be clear from the report of John, bishop of Constantinople [Col. 0481D].

It remains for us, with the aid of Your Blessedness’s prayers, to be presented as quickly as we desire at your feet.

### REGISTER SENT BY JOHN, BISHOP, OR BY EPIPHANIUS THE PRESBYTER, FROM THESSALONICA

The crimes of the Thessalonians are recounted. (C)

If, on account of our sins, these bishops who have been brought here should enter Constantinople, let us not say merely that they will in every way see the emperor, but that they will also be restored to their own places. For they have brought so much money with them that they could blind not men but angels. If, therefore—which God forbid—they enter, they will tell as many falsehoods in our absence as the devil can devise. For if they attempted many things here in our presence and were confounded while the Lord stood with us, what will they do in our absence? Therefore, so that their wickedness may be dispersed, command that, if proceedings concerning our sins are undertaken, we be present, so that it may be clear among men that we have been unjustly put to death and that they are laboring through the protection of money. For we can convict them in every respect before the senate, proving that they are complete heretics; only then can their deceit be exposed.

It should also be said: If they are not heretics, how, two weeks before we arrived, did all the bishops jointly decree that no one should celebrate the mysteries outside the city? Yet they brought everyone here, both so that a crowd might be assembled for the future sedition and so that they might be instructed according to their errors. After they learned and publicly announced that we had arrived, they declared that they must hurry with the children, lest, when persecution came, the pagan infants should die; and then, as though for another Easter, they baptized so many that they surpassed the customary festival.

It should also be said: If they are not heretics, how did they prepare so many sacraments that they could distribute them all in full baskets, lest, as they said, when persecution was imminent, they should be unable to receive communion?

Again, if they are not heretics, why were they later accused in the official records by Candidus, a high-ranking man, deputy of the master of the praetorian armies, before the prefects’ court?

And if they recognized that an imminent danger was approaching, why did they wish once more to come to the aid of the little ones, as though they were to be condemned, and, again though refuted, perform so many baptisms that they truly displayed themselves to everyone as heretics? At this the sufficiently powerful and distinguished authority of the prefects was gravely indignant.

Again, if they are not heretics, when we were hiding in the baptistery, how did they hold counsel through the night and, pretending that they wished to free us from danger, decide to put us on a ship, so that on that pretext we might be thrown headlong into the sea? When we replied through the deacons Demetrius and Andrew: “Everyone knows that we are among you. How can we sail by night? But if you have truly taken counsel for our safety, tomorrow command five or six senators who fear danger to their property or their lives, together with the masters of the armies and the deputy Candidus the count, to be summoned secretly. Let them themselves learn where we are being transferred, and we shall do what they order. But if you act alone and secretly, we shall not do this,” then, finding that their plan had not succeeded, they remained silent for the moment; and on the following day they again stirred up a popular sedition. From this we escaped only with difficulty, by God’s will.

## REPORT OF DIOSCORUS THE DEACON TO POPE HORMISDAS

Epiphanius appointed in place of John of Constantinople. (C)

It would have been desirable and in accord with our wish to announce what had happened previously—namely, that John, bishop of the Church of Constantinople, was still alive and that a confession had been issued in a written document. There is no doubt that his merits were pleasing to God, since among the Catholics and communicants of the apostolic see he was granted to depart from this life to another.

A certain presbyter named Epiphanius, formerly his syncellus, succeeded him in his place. His beginnings appear good: he speaks reasonably and promises that he will observe the rules of the Fathers and will not destroy the peace and ordered unity, but rather increase them. These are the things he promises. What he will actually be able to accomplish, however, we do not yet know.

We sent this letter on the fourth day after his ordination, having found an opportunity to do so. We have not yet entered into communion with him—not as though we were resisting, but because we have not yet been invited by him.

It remains that the prayer of your Beatitude should persist, so that, with the help of divine grace, he may emerge as such a man that through him we may rejoice in perfect unity.

Received on the seventh day before the Ides of April, in the consulship of Rusticus, a man of illustrious rank (A.D. 520).

## REPORT OF THE CONSTANTINOPOLITAN SYNOD CONCERNING THE ORDINATION OF BISHOP EPIPHANIUS

It indicates that Epiphanius was elected bishop. (C)

To our holy and most blessed father of fathers, archbishop and patriarch Hormisdas, Theophilus, Basiliscus, Isaiah, Anastasius, Paternus, Martianus, and the rest: the holy synod assembled in the city of Constantinople.

Reflecting, insofar as human beings are permitted to understand, upon the innumerable and unfathomable wisdom of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, we rightly marvel at his immense love, and with a loud voice cry out: “Who can speak of the mighty acts of the Lord? Who can make all his praises heard?” (Psalm 105). For behold, by the good will of the holy Trinity, which is of one essence, and through the intercession of the glorious Virgin Mary, as well as through the zeal and vigilance of the most Christian and most faithful emperor and the most devout empress, those members which had formerly been divided have, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, been restored to perfect unity and charity. And just as Moses and Aaron were called leaders of God’s true worship of Israel, so now we too, rejoicing, cry out: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored. He has become my helper and protector for salvation” (Exodus 15). We have been taught to think and proclaim these things with confidence.

Considering also the love and God-pleasing life of your Beatitude, as well as the peace of the holy Churches of God, both of elder Rome and of the new Rome, through the reverend legates sent by you—peace of which we ourselves are shown to have become participants—we customarily render thanks to the good Shepherd and ruler of all, Christ our God.

For after the death of holy memory, the former archbishop and patriarch of the city of Constantinople, God—who founded his own holy Church incorruptibly upon the rock of right faith and decreed that the gates of hell should not prevail against it (Matthew 16)—gave us the holy shepherd and patriarch Epiphanius, flourishing in virtues, in correction, and in the meditation of the divine Scriptures, holding the right faith, and exercising a fatherly concern for orphans. And what more shall I say? He surpasses every source of praise.

Since he abounds in these virtues, he is rightly recognized as having wisely and honorably discharged the immense cares of the Church entrusted to him, keeping in mind what was reported by the author of the sacred song: “My mouth shall speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart shall be understanding” (Psalm 88).

Therefore, in accordance with the right and approved judgment of our most faithful and most Christian ruler, the most devout empress, and the most glorious leaders of the commonwealth, and also with the testimony of all of us who live in this city, the judgment of Paul, that admirable teacher of the common Church, has not been frustrated in him—the judgment in which he declares that a bishop must be irreproachable (1 Timothy 3). Thus we see that our pontiff is crowned on every side with virtues.

Accordingly, fulfilling ecclesiastical law and rendering to your apostolate the duty owed in greeting, we hope that your charity will deign to preserve toward us an even greater bond of love and fatherly affection, and that you will act with the wise governance and humility befitting a Christian, and with the gentleness that contributes to the salvation of the rational flock entrusted to you. Consider it a common gain that, through you and your brother and fellow minister—our lord and patriarch—the peace of the Churches throughout the world has been secured. For a brother spiritually helped by his brother is an impregnable wall and a fortified city, as is received from the divine Scriptures.

For [Note: [Col. 0483D] Roman edition: “if there are intercessions”], if through the intercessions of your Beatitude general tranquillity is restored to the Churches of the orthodox, then glory will be rendered with joy to God on high, the Savior of all, through the angels; peace will be confirmed on earth; and the good will of our common Lord and Savior Jesus Christ will be established among his faithful servants.

The most holy bishop John of the city of Claudiopolis, our fellow minister, will therefore add to our supplications what has been left unsaid, together with Heraclianus, the most reverend presbyter of the Holy Greater Church and fellow resident of the aforesaid most holy archbishop and patriarch Epiphanius, and Constantine, the most reverend deacon of the same holy church. They are known to have given proof of their right faith and good will formerly to those who had been sent from your apostolic see. They will also be shown worthy of your holiness, of the administration [F. “the administration of peace and the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, our God, and the union of the holy Churches”], and of grace. We hope that, rejoicing in the Lord and announcing the desired peace, you will deign to have them return to us swiftly, instructed by your God-loving corrections.

We, and those who are with us, warmly greet all our brethren in Christ (A.D. 519).

## SIGNATURES

Theophilus, by the mercy of God bishop of the city of Heraclea, metropolitan, signing in the synodical documents: I greet you in the Lord, my lord.

Basiliscus, by the mercy of God bishop and metropolitan of the people of Zicinum [Note: [Col. 0485D] Read “of the people of Cyzicus.” Thus in the manuscripts Quiriacus often appears for Cyriacus. HARD.], as above.

Stephen, by the mercy of God bishop and metropolitan of the people of Nicomedia, as above.

John, by the mercy of God bishop of the city of Claudiopolis in the province of Isauria, as above.

Paternus, by the mercy of God bishop and metropolitan of the province of Scythia, as above.

Martianus, by the mercy of God bishop and metropolitan of the city of Chalcedon, as above.

Patricius, by the mercy of God bishop and metropolitan of the city of Eudoxiopolis, as above.

Polydeucius, by the mercy of God bishop and metropolitan of the city of Antioch, as above.

Eulogius, by the mercy of God bishop and metropolitan of the city of Melitene, as above.

Stephen, by the mercy of God bishop of the city of Philomedium [Note: [Col. 0486D] Alternatively, Philomelium], in the province of Pisidia, as above.

Christodorus, by the mercy of God bishop of the city of Methymna, as above.

Palmantius, the least, bishop of the city of Oenoanda in the province of Lycia, as above.

John, by the mercy of God bishop of the city of Attaleia, as above.

## LETTER OF JUSTINIAN TO HORMISDAS

Elijah cannot be restored to his church while the man who had been appointed in his place is alive. Thomas and Nicostratus will be restored to their own sees once peace has been secured. (C)

Justinian Augustus to Pope Hormisdas.

Since it is our intention, most religious father, that our counsels should agree with one another in every matter, we believe that the matter of the most reverend bishop Elijah should also be settled in accordance with what your legates have advised, since this has been seen to be the more expedient course amid the various considerations on both sides.

For at present the favor of everyone protects the bishop of the city of Caesarea. Because of his excellent institutions, not only do the inhabitants strongly believe that he should be retained, but almost the whole East undoubtedly venerates him. The man who previously held the same priesthood complains that he was removed unjustly.

It has therefore seemed appropriate that we should neither oppose the wishes of countless multitudes nor remove from his see a man distinguished for integrity who has shown himself worthy of it; nor should we entirely deprive the former occupant of hope that he may again recover the place from which he firmly maintains that he was deprived without cause. Rather, let us deal with this doubtful matter more moderately, so that, for the time being, this same most reverend bishop Elijah may remain in peace. But after his successor has died, then and only then may he return to the see, since he has ceased to employ beforehand all the measures which the most sacred regulations prescribe for obtaining permission to return, including the consent both of your apostolic see and of this most flourishing city, as well as of the other parties concerned.

As for Thomas and Nicostratus, the most religious bishops, everything will be brought to completion after the remaining matters have also been joined to you, and likewise after we have determined, with heavenly assistance, what ought to be established for the unity of the venerable Churches, in accordance with the order of the most sacred regulations.

Since, therefore, it was fitting that we should declare our decision to your holiness, so that this too might reveal the desire to which we devote all our efforts—to restrain and moderate controversies and to prolong the desired harmony among all—we have decided to send this letter as well, especially urging that, for the preservation of the commonwealth, the heavenly power be entreated through your prayers.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of June, at Constantinople, in the consulship of Vitalianus and Rusticus (A.D. 519).

## LETTER OF JUSTIN TO HORMISDAS

Through the diligence of the legates, peace has been restored at Constantinople and in other cities. Greater moderation should be shown in condemning the names of bishops. (C)

[Col. 0486C]

Justin Augustus to Pope Hormisdas, through the legates Germanus and John, bishops; Felix and Dioscorus, deacons; and Blandus, presbyter.

The greatest thanks are due to you because you do not hesitate to devote eager effort to gathering and uniting the venerable Churches. Yet your complete prudence shines forth especially in this, that you choose men who can serve the wishes of your holiness with a willing, sincere, and undivided spirit.

The most reverend bishop Germanus, as well as Felix, Dioscorus, and Blandus, most religious men, have shown themselves so attentive through their diligence and have conducted themselves with such wisdom that, insofar as their office is concerned, once everything had been fully settled and carefully completed, no further matter of dispute would remain.

But since human frailty is such that it desires to be treated with greater leniency and to have clear answers given to its questions, especially when some matter has been referred to an immense multitude of people, it has happened that in this most flourishing city everything ordered concerning the religious question and the celebration of unity with the apostolic see during the time of John of most religious memory, when he held the priesthood of this royal city, has, with God’s favor, been preserved unchanged. Moreover, your arrangement has been approved and accepted in many other cities.

The remaining matters, however, require a certain more merciful moderation concerning the names of the bishops—not of those specifically listed in the letter which your holiness is known to have sent us, but of others whose memory is cherished by the greatest cities and who are known to have flourished as survivors.

Accordingly, the legates of your holiness had no permission to depart from the terms of their instructions, with which they were sent. The entire conclusion of the affair now depends solely upon your judgment, so that the one who initiated the first beginnings of the matter should also be the one to conclude the peace. These matters, and certain others, will be explained more openly by our legate, who will be sent shortly.

For the present, as the most religious men are returning, we have thought it appropriate both to appeal to your reverence and to remind you to use your prayers on behalf of our rule and for the preservation of the commonwealth.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of July, at Constantinople, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Vitalianus and Rusticus (A.D. 519).

## LETTER OF THE AUGUSTA EUPHEMIA TO HORMISDAS

She commends herself and her husband to the prayers of the most holy pontiff. (C)

Euphemia Augusta to Pope Hormisdas.

We received the letter of your Beatitude with a grateful and joyful heart. For who would not gladly receive the words of one whom not only the authority of the apostolic see celebrates, but whose integrity of life and diligent zeal for right faith also commend? We therefore ask and urge that my name, and especially that of our most serene husband, may never be absent from your prayers, but that the heavenly protection may be entreated through your prayers both for the two of us and for the commonwealth.

## LETTER OF CELER TO HORMISDAS

Through the work of the legates, everyone at Constantinople is living peacefully; he hopes that the same will soon occur in the other cities. (C)

To the most blessed lord and apostolic father Hormisdas, Celer, illustrious man.

We are granted the greatest cause for rejoicing whenever an opportunity arises to write to your apostolate. Now, therefore, as the most blessed bishop Germanus and the most reverend men who were sent by you to unite the holy Churches are returning, we considered it necessary to pay our respects to your holiness and report that the aforesaid men indeed took pains so that your will might be fully accomplished.

But since the whole body was ill, the head—which was judged necessary first—has meanwhile been healed by the medicine you supplied; and the disagreement that existed between the venerable Roman and Constantinopolitan Churches has been buried through the intervention of unity, while other important members have likewise been cleansed and joined by the grace of the same Divinity.

We all also entertain this hope: that the grace of God, which has always remained and remains with your see, may provide you with such an inspiration of goodness that, through your gentleness and administration, the rest of the body, which is still considered ill—as we said above—may, having received unity through your medicine, be joined together.

We particularly beseech your pontificate to command that prayers be offered for us with the kindly spirit of a father.

## LETTER OF JULIANA TO HORMISDAS

She greets the pontiff. (C)

To the most blessed and most approved pontiff of the apostolic see, Pope Hormisdas, father, Juliana Anicia.

We first offer the customary services of greeting to your Beatitude, praying that God may cause this letter to be read by your venerable eyes, and may deign, for the strengthening of his Church, to support your life with salutary increase, so that, through your vigilance, the condition of the Church may be defended against hostile and rabid dogs.

For, venerable father, the care you show for the integrity of our faith is fitting for the vicars of the glorious apostle Peter, to whom the Lord entrusted the office of feeding the sheep. Let your holy concern for us therefore know that we hold more firmly the immovable steadfastness of right faith, for the preservation of whose sanctity we have resisted until now.

As for the fact that your apostolate has commanded care to be taken for so great a matter of piety, insofar as our strength allowed, we have not ceased to admonish our opponents in a spirit of gentleness, and, with God’s grace cooperating with us, [lacuna] the remainder is missing.

## LETTER 68. TO HIS LEGATES

He wishes to be informed about their safety and their activities.

Hormisdas to his legates.

Our concern for your safety and your activities so troubles us that, although we do not fail to urge you on frequent occasions, you should arrange for us to be informed about what is happening around you. For when, through the son of our illustrious and magnificent man, the patrician Agapitus, we sent words suited to your wishes, and now likewise believed that we should send consolation for your anxiety by dispatching the present letter, it is only necessary that you relieve us, at a suitable opportunity through the bearer, by addressing us concerning your activities and safety, as well as concerning the delay by which we greatly regret that you are being detained.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of July, in the consulship of the illustrious man Rusticus (A.D. 520).

## LETTER 69. TO THE SAME

Since he has not received their letters, he urges them to write.

[Col. 0488D]

Hormisdas to Bishop Germanus, the deacons Felix and Dioscorus, and the presbyter Blandus.

The prolonged silence of your charity, which grieves us through the absence of so much time, troubles our spirits, especially since the magnificent man, the patrician Symmachus, and the illustrious man Romanus, master of the armies, have promised us without delay the return to us of your beloved persons. We do not know whether the nature of the circumstances there, or some deception contrived under the guise of necessity, is actually detaining you.

Since we are continuously anxious and questioning nearly everyone from those regions, we receive diverse and conflicting reports. Therefore, since you are better able to discover, understand, and learn the causes of so great a delay, you ought to inform us of these matters, over which our spirit is distressed. Or, if there is a valid reason for the delay, as had been arranged, someone from your number ought to have been sent to us.

So that perhaps through cunning or some contrivance delay and obstacles may not be created for you, write to us quickly, so that, under a reasonable arrangement, we may petition our most clement emperor, our son, on behalf of your return.

Therefore inform us what is being done both concerning your persons and concerning the matter of the faith, on account of which you have been detained so long, and write back to us with the fullest account of everything. Once all the facts are known, with the favor of our God, let us consider how mercy may assist both your persons and the case itself, whose interests are at stake.

Given on the Ides of July, in the consulship of the illustrious man Rusticus (A.D. 520).

## REPORT OF POSSESSOR, BISHOP OF AFRICA, THROUGH HIS DEACON JUSTINUS

He consults the pontiff concerning the book of Bishop Faustus. (C)

To the most blessed, ineffably wondrous, and in the grace of Christ pre-eminent Pope Hormisdas, Possessor, bishop, eternal salvation in the Lord.

It is fitting and expedient to have recourse to the medicine of the head whenever the health of the members is at issue. For from whom should greater concern for those subject to him be expected, or from whom the stability of wavering faith more than from the president of that see whose first ruler heard Christ say: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16)?

I believe that your Beatitude is not unaware of the extent to which the Church suffers from plots in the city of Constantinople, and how, in the manner of an old disease, the wound seeks once more to burst into suppuration, although it is believed to have been covered by a scar.

Accordingly, when the minds of certain brothers were being scandalized by the book of a certain Faustus, a Gaul by nationality [Note: [Col. 0490D] The note is mistaken: he was indeed a Gaul by residence, but by nation a Briton, as he himself attests in several places.], bishop of the city of Riez [Note: [Col. 0490D] In the province of Narbonensis II.], a man who appears to have written eloquently about various matters, and more frequently about the grace of God, while others—as human intellectual interests tend to do—were referring them in the opposite direction, they believed that I should be consulted about this uncertainty.

I said that the things argued by interpreters according to the capacity of their own intellects are not to be accepted as canonical or observed as law in place of synodal decisions; but that we possess certain things, written in the Old or New Law and decreed by the general judgments of the Fathers, as the foundation of faith and the complete steadfastness of religion. The writings composed by various bishops, however, are ordinarily assessed according to their character, without prejudice to the faith.

But since these statements—as I perceived from their frequent requests—seemed more an excuse to them, either to comply with their request or to take the opportunity of rendering service to your apostolate, I presumed, through my deacon Justinus, to submit the little writings of my insignificance. In them I principally ask for the protection of your prayers, and I beg that, by consulting what your judgment is concerning the statements of the aforementioned author, they may learn this through the authoritative response of the apostolic see—especially since your sons, the masters of the armies Vitalianus and Justinian, also particularly desire to be instructed on this matter by a rescript from your Beatitude.

I also remember having previously sent for examination a book of treatises [variant: “a book to be examined”], containing explanations of the letters of the blessed apostle Paul, for which I did not deserve to receive a rescript of thanks. I therefore make the same request, that through a suitable response I may merit the privilege of your blessing.

Received on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of the illustrious man Rusticus.

[Note: [Col. 0489C] John Maxentius, a heretical and mendacious writer, was the first to deny that this letter belonged to Hormisdas; yet the very connection of the events, the character of the arguments and expressions, and finally the style itself plainly assign it to Hormisdas. We admit that John Cochlaeus, a man famous for his reputation and a most vigorous opponent of the heretics of our time, held the same opinion as Maxentius, but he fell into error through both mistake and good faith. For he thought that the apology of Maxentius, into which he had fallen, had been written by a Catholic, whereas it had been published by that most pestilential heretic. The learned man lacked the assistance of these letters of Hormisdas, recently published. Had he been furnished with them, he could have noticed the heretic’s fraud and deceit. See Baronius, year 520, number 22 and following; Possevinus, *Sacred Apparatus*, under “John Maxentius.” SEV. BINIUS.]

[Note: The audacious and shameless innovators who are followers of Jansenius recently undertook the defense of this most cunning heretic—who, to speak minimally, was stained with Eutychian soot—but with plainly unfortunate and fruitless success, as we shall show more fully elsewhere. The question is not whether the assertion “One of the Trinity suffered” can be tolerated, but in what sense, and by what deceitful arts of the flattering little fox, after the manner of the subtler heretics, John Maxentius stated and defended it with his Scythian monks. In this alone he properly earned the patronage of the Jansenists: in that, being injurious toward the apostolic see and the most shameless calumniator of Hormisdas, the Roman pontiff, he anticipated their insults against that same see and their calumnies against the supreme bishops of the Church.

Let us remain with the calumnies of John Maxentius and, so as not to wander farther afield, select one from among them. Hormisdas had said: “We shall make progress among those who oppose us through our own good qualities, if we are not entangled in the errors of others”—a statement more sound and truthful could not have been made. What did that utterly depraved sycophant say in response? “Cunningly,” he says, “you strive to conceal your perfidy,” and so forth. “He places before all eyes a perfidy entangled in Pelagian errors, because you confidently believe, in swollen pride, that among those who oppose you, you can make progress not by God’s gift but through your own good qualities,” and so forth.

You slander, shameless wretch, when with blasphemous mouth you rant that Christ’s vicar is a heretic and an enemy of the truth; and you magnificently outshine your excellent defenders. The holy pontiff Hormisdas opposes “own good qualities,” not to God’s gifts, but to the goods of others. The remaining matters do not allow the limits of this observation to be extended. For the learned man rightly warned that the writings of this heretic—whose greater cultivation makes him all the more dangerous—must be read by beginners with suspended step and sharp judgment, lest they stumble. PHILIP LABBE, S.J.]

## LETTER 70. TO BISHOP POSSESSOR

The Scythian monks, unwilling to condemn their errors, have been expelled from the city as heretics. The book of Faustus is not accepted by the Roman Church.

[Col. 0490C]

Hormisdas to Bishop Possessor.

Just as it accords with reason that those who are uncertain should consult, so it is right that those who have been consulted should answer, since the person who does not instruct the ignorant drives him into error. Nothing is more suitable for one devoted to religion than the investigation of truth [Roman edition: “inquiry”]. For the person who asks about the road on which he is walking avoids a wrong path more easily.

But before I undertake the task of answering the matters about which your charity inquires, I gladly confess that I have found in your letter the fervor of your faith. Kindled by its heat, you sigh that the revived perversity of unbelievers is flourishing in those regions. It is a most worthy grief, one that troubles hearts devoted to God. For among those who possess the spark of charity, no fall is beyond lamentation; the one spiritual desire is the unshaken salvation of all.

Yet the Church of God is neither ignorant of nor unaccustomed to storms of this kind. Although she remains unshaken under the governance of her ruler, she is nevertheless harassed by the various whirlwinds of rising waves. For from where comes the voice of the psalm-singing prophet, who, taking upon himself in the Spirit that moved him the person of the Church herself, says: “Often they have attacked me from my youth; yet they have not prevailed against me”? They shake her, but they will prevail in nothing. We are still on the threshing floor; the grains are mixed with the chaff; the good lament the company of the wicked, but the flame destined for what is unnecessary remains, and the granaries are already prepared for what has been proved.

Where in the world is this mixture absent? We ought to stand firmly in our fixed footsteps. “We shall make progress among those who oppose us through our own good qualities, if we are not entangled in the errors of others” [Note: [Col. 0491D] John Maxentius built a calumny upon these words of Hormisdas.]. For the person who, when pushed, is not moved proves the powerful strength of his virtue.

Where are there not the stings of various temptations? What subtle deceits, concealed by cunning, and what poisons serving their hatreds under the pretext of religion, have we endured for almost this entire year from certain Scythians who presented themselves as monks in appearance, not in truth; in profession, not in conduct? We strove to heal them of their inward wound through the restraint of healing patience, not failing to repeat the admonitions of blessed Paul: “Do not quarrel over words; for it is useful for nothing except the ruin of those who hear” (2 Timothy 2).

But when is the poison that has penetrated the vitals removed? When do hearts that have wrongly trusted themselves obey the ordinances of truth? When does pride, fortified by its own opinions, put on the humility of obedience? When do those accustomed to contention and devoted solely to conflicts, who love to seize upon religious matters only for disputation, consent to peace and obey the commandments?

Among them there has never been the charity commended by the new commandment, never the peace left by the Lord at his departure. Their one stubborn concern is to make reason obey them, not to believe; they despise ancient authorities and hunger for new questions; they think that the only right path of knowledge is whatever opinion they have formed with ease. They are so lifted up by swelling pride that they think the judgment of both worlds ought to bend to their decision. They do not count among the faithful those who follow their fathers’ tradition if they see that such people refuse to yield to their opinion. They are skilled at sowing accusations, composing the poisons of slander, hating the Church’s undivided body, preparing seditions, stirring up envy, and—rather than obedience, which holds primacy in the regular discipline of monasteries—loving the obstinacy of stubborn pride.

We could restrain them neither by admonitions, nor by gentleness, nor by authority.
