They even came forth into public assembly, shouting even around the statues of the emperors so as to disturb the peace; and unless the steadfastness of the faithful people had resisted, they would have stirred up among them, through the devil’s wicked seeds of weeds, dissension and discord (1 Timothy 3), through whom, with God’s help, dissension concerning their religion was driven away.

Only belatedly did we recognize that the Apostle had spoken prophetically when he said that in the last days perilous times would come, and that people would be lovers only of themselves, having the appearance of piety but denying its power; and that such people must therefore be avoided.

We have thought it appropriate to report these matters to your charity on this occasion, lest, if they should perhaps be brought there, you might be deceived by some simulation of words, not knowing how they had conducted themselves in the city of Rome.

As for those about whom you wrote that you had consulted concerning the statements of a certain Faustus, a Gallic bishop [Note: [Col. 0492D] Bishop of Riez in Gaul.], let them have this answer.

Neither he [Note: [Col. 0491D] “To be accepted” is lacking in the Roman edition.] nor anyone whom the examination of the Fathers does not accept can be received by the authority of the Catholic faith; nor can such a person generate ambiguity or cause prejudice to the religious. The ordinances established by the Fathers, which the faithful ought to follow, are fixed. Whether it is an interpretation, a proclamation, or a word composed for the edification of the people, if it agrees with right faith and sound doctrine, it is admitted; if it disagrees, it is abolished.

One foundation alone exists; apart from it, any structure that rises is weak [Col. 0492C]. Whoever builds upon it, whether with cheap or costly materials, must take this into account. He strays from the road who deviates from what the choice of the Fathers has shown. Yet diligence that investigates many matters is not thereby condemned; rather, it is the mind that turns away from the truth. Often instruction is provided concerning matters by which the very adversaries themselves may be convicted. Nor can one be blamed for knowing what one ought to avoid. Therefore those who read incongruous things do not incur guilt, but those who follow them do. If this were not so, that teacher of the nations would never have consented to announce to the faithful: “Test everything; hold fast to what is good” (I Thess. V).

It is not irrelevant, though worldly and not contrary to reason, to mix in an anecdote. It is said that a certain nobleman skilled in painting, wishing to depict a perfect horse with his brush, set a donkey before himself while painting [Col. 0492D] [Note: [Col. 0491D] Alternatively, “to be of use to him”], explaining that he did so not in order to imitate the shapeless animal, but so that he would not fall into the likeness of some misshapen outline.

It was not without foresight that the venerable wisdom of the Fathers defined for faithful authority what the Catholic dogmas were, and, with the Holy Spirit instructing it, established which books, even among the ancient ones, were to be received as authoritative. This was so that a reader, indulging his own opinion, might not assert what his pleasure had conceived rather than what accorded with the edification of the Church. Why, then, was there any need for those who bring accusations to extend their questions beyond the established boundaries of the Church, and to stir up controversies about things that have been stated as though they had not been stated, when the Christian faith is confined by a firm and unshaken limit—or course—through the canonical books, the synodal precepts, and the regular ordinances of the Fathers?

Nevertheless, concerning free choice and the grace of God, what the Roman—that is, Catholic—Church follows and asserts may be learned from the various books of blessed Augustine, especially those addressed to Hilary and Prosper. Yet the ecclesiastical archives contain explicit chapters on these matters. If you lack them and consider them necessary, we shall send them, although anyone who carefully considers the Apostle’s words clearly understands what he ought to follow. Given on the Ides of August.

## LETTER LXXI. TO EPIPHANIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE

He reports that Epiphanius, having been ordained bishop, neither wrote nor sent envoys.

### Hormisdas to Epiphanius, Bishop of Constantinople

For a long time, the beginnings of your dignity, since they had not been announced to us, kept us in suspense. Even amid the very joy of our common congratulation, we were greatly surprised that the former custom had been neglected, since, with the concord of the Churches restored by God’s favor, the fullness of fraternal peace demanded this duty—especially because it was claimed not by personal arrogance but by observance of the canonical rules.

It would indeed have been fitting, dearest brother, for you to have sent envoys to the apostolic see at the very beginning of your pontificate [Note: The bishop of Constantinople used to send envoys to Rome at the beginning of his episcopate], so that you might properly learn what affection is due to you and complete the form of the ancient custom [Col. 0493C]. But although, omitting these matters, you had judged that written communications alone would suffice for correspondence on the occasion, we, compelled meanwhile by grace—or, according to another reading, spurred on by grace—justly ended the silence of our expectation, returning words of mutual and reciprocal charity. For both our spirit, unable to endure the absence of love, and the welcome report of our envoys turned into kindly offices the silence which the circumstances had imposed and withheld. Through these services we now display the signs of our joy and, in a certain sense, fulfill the vows of private friendship.

We demand your embassy both on account of the favor with which we have for some time received it and in reliance upon the ancient constitutions, so that we may express more clearly both how much fruit of joy we derive from the honor of your pontificate and what thanks it is fitting to return to you for the services expended in promoting unity, as the report of our envoys has established in many ways [Col. 0493D].

## LETTER LXXII. TO THE SAME

He complains that Elias, Thomas, and Nicostratus have not been restored to their sees; it belongs to Epiphanius to ensure that this is carried out.

### Hormisdas to Epiphanius, Bishop of Constantinople

Your Fraternity ought, indeed, out of consideration for the divine judgment and in regard for our charity, after we had received our brothers and fellow bishops Elias, Thomas, and Nicostratus into communion with us, to admit them without delay to the divine mysteries [Note: The Roman edition adds “with you”], and, for the fullness of our peace, to recall them to their Churches, from which the error of discord had excluded them. Thus the unity that God, after the passage of many years, has restored to his Churches throughout the world would not be injured by any difference in our wills.

But since it has happened that so welcome a matter, and one so consonant with the venerable statutes of the Fathers, has until now been delayed by certain tardinesses—we also remember having written about this to your Fraternity’s predecessor—we exhort you not again to sadden by any cause of discordant minds the joy that we derive from the condemnation of the error of the former dissension. For no one seems to communicate with us with a mind wholly united if you separate from your fellowship those who communicate with us. Certainly those who delay fulfilling the commands of peace appear to receive peace in vain. Whatever delay you make in receiving them into communion detracts, in a certain sense, from our reconciliation.

It must also be provided, dearest brother, lest, if the concord of our Churches, finally granted from above, should take its beginning from such examples, both the venerable rule of religion and the authority of the apostolic see should—God forbid—appear diminished and more widely publicized throughout the East [Note: Alternatively, “absent: appear more widely publicized rather than restored”].

## REPORT OF EPIPHANIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE

Concerning his election. He professes the Catholic faith and agrees with the Roman Church on all matters. (C)

### To the most holy and blessed lord, brother, and fellow minister Hormisdas, Epiphanius, bishop, greetings in the Lord

God, who dwells on high and regards the lowly (Ps. CXII), and who abundantly provides all things for the salvation of human beings, in his goodness and mercy looked upon my insignificance. After the death of John, formerly archbishop and patriarch of holy memory, he deigned to confer upon me the priestly see of the holy Catholic Church of the royal city. This occurred by the decision and election of our most Christian and most just emperor Justin, and of the most devout empress, who shares with him in every divine endeavor. The consent of their followers also joined them: those of good conduct, those exalted above others in imperial honors, the priests and monks, and the most faithful people.

Therefore I deemed it necessary to place this first indication in my letter [Note: Alternatively, “to insert this”], in order to show what disposition I have toward your apostolic see. It is my earnest purpose, most blessed one, to be united with you, to embrace the divine dogmas that have been handed down from the blessed and holy disciples and apostles of God—especially from the chief of the apostles, Peter—to your holy see, and to consider nothing more precious than them.

For I do not ignore the constitutions of the holy Church as though I had come from elsewhere, but, by God’s will, nourished from infancy in the holy Catholic Church, I have obeyed its most holy priests and patriarchs throughout the years. For I have often presided over those who cast off their sins through the sacred and ineffable baptism, and I have taught the true faith of the Trinity of one essence, which, as I have stated, proceeds from the disciples of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ and is embraced by the whole assembly of priests and laypeople.

For I truly venerate and proclaim the holy, divine, God-given creed of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea, and I announce it to be the manifest judgment of Christian splendor. Likewise, I have learned, and have learned to teach others, that the venerable synod of the one hundred and fifty holy priests held in this royal city, the gathering of the two hundred God-loving Fathers held at Ephesus, and the synod of the six hundred and thirty most reverend Fathers and priests held at Chalcedon are one—or true—, harmonious, and joined to the holy councils mentioned above.

In these four holy and sacred synods the great mystery of piety has been proclaimed, and the salvation of all human beings has been established. I receive and embrace those who were or are of the same opinion, and I love to unite myself with them. But, on the other hand, I consider those who think or preach anything contrary to these synods, or who in former times attempted anything contrary to them, to be exiles from the assembly of the orthodox.

Likewise, I embrace and receive the orthodox and truly most religious letters of the venerable Pope Leo, written in defense of the right faith. Let your Blessedness’s holy fraternity therefore hold this conviction concerning me. I have made it manifest to you, and I proclaim it under my authority to the Churches, hastening in every respect to unite them, and myself with them, to your Blessedness by the bond of charity. These Churches must be united and inviolate, and must perpetually preserve themselves as one body of the common apostolic Church.

Command that it be considered how great my love is in every respect toward your venerable Fraternity. For those whom your apostolic see condemned and ordered not to be recited in the sacred diptychs, I also do not have named among the sacred mysteries. This is also known to the most reverend men sent by you: the most holy bishops Germanus and John [Note: The Roman edition omits “John” and has “bishop” in the singular]—the deacons Felix and Dioscorus, and the presbyter Blandus—who faithfully carried out what had been enjoined upon them by you.

Let your Holiness therefore pray both for me and for the priests subject to me, that we may be preserved perpetually while holding the right confession of God. Pray likewise for our most serene emperor and for the most Christian Augusta, since their welfare will be a common support for the holy Churches everywhere. With this intention held by you, it will no longer be possible for the holy Church of God to be torn apart, through the grace of the Holy Spirit and the intercessions of the holy and glorious virgin Mary, Mother of God.

We also, together with all who are with us, send abundant greetings in Christ to the entire fraternity that is with your Holiness.

In another hand: “Safe in the Lord, pray for us, most holy brother and lover of God.”

Received on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Rusticus, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of the Lord 520).

## COPY OF THE LETTER OF JUSTINIAN, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, TO POPE HORMISDAS

With Acacius condemned at Constantinople, peace prevails; peace with the Easterners should be established by whatever means; and concerning the most holy Trinity. (C)

With the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, he reigns in this world who founds his empire upon sacred religion, for he governs human affairs well when he has first pleased God in divine matters. We rejoice that this has occurred in our present times.

For your most merciful son, the emperor, having received the scepter through the gift of eternity, undertook to set forth the causes of the faith. By sending an embassy to your Holiness, we obtained the favor of the priests of the apostolic see, whose arrival greatly strengthened the harmony of the holy Churches, as was fitting, through your efforts [Col. 0496B].

After the name of Acacius, which represented the schism, had been utterly cut away, the desired unity arose in this royal city and in many other cities, in accordance with the tenor of the libelli that you sent. This unity, achieved through the greatest labors, ought to be venerated and must be preserved forever. Would anyone permit these things, which eternal majesty has properly arranged, to be reconsidered on any pretext?

But because the enemy of the human race frequently hastens to obstruct prosperous courses, a considerable part of the Easterners cannot be compelled by sword or fire to condemn the names of the bishops who died after Acacius [Note: Alternatively, “through exile”]. This difficulty delays general concord. Therefore let your Holiness, inspired from heaven, consider the circumstances of the times and affairs. Having condemned the authors of this error—Acacius of Constantinople, Peter and Timothy the Cat, Dioscorus of Alexandria, and Peter of Antioch—may you deign to bring the long-standing dispute to an end, leaving the question of the names of the others at rest.

In this way you may redeem from bloodshed the people whom our God has entrusted to our governance, and reconcile the people to our Lord not through persecutions and bloodshed but through priestly patience. Let us not, while wishing to win souls, destroy the bodies and souls of many.

For long-standing errors ought to be corrected through gentleness and mercy, especially since the predecessors of your Blessedness repeatedly wished to recall the bishops of our state to their communion, provided only that Acacius and the others mentioned above were kept silent. It is therefore not a difficult concession that your see has been persuaded to grant. We ask this all the more earnestly: may your Holiness, with the grace conceived from heaven, deign to consider what the Eastern bishops propose to discuss and to provide an agreement appropriate to their faith.

It seems to us that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, born of the virgin Mary, whom the chief of the apostles proclaims to have suffered in the flesh, is rightly said to reign as one of the Trinity with the Father and the Holy Spirit. For just as it seems ambiguous to say simply “one of the Trinity” without first naming our Lord Jesus Christ, so we do not doubt that his person is in the Trinity together with the persons of the Father and the Holy Spirit. For without the person of Christ, the Trinity can neither be religiously believed nor faithfully adored, just as Saint Augustine says: “One of the persons of the Trinity”; and elsewhere: “He alone in the Trinity received a body”; and again: “One of the three.”

We therefore ask you, most reverend one, greeting you with affection, to remember the future judgment and arrange the matter in such a way that no doubt remains for the future. When every scruple of discord has been removed, may the bonds of the desired peace be renewed throughout the world, and may the harmony of the venerable Churches flourish, with the members of the one body gathered back into their former condition.

That physician is rightly praised who hastens to heal old illnesses in such a way that new wounds do not arise from them. Let your apostolate therefore know in particular that, once these two points have been settled, all the priests of this state will gladly embrace your communion [Col. 0497B].

Received on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Rusticus, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of the Lord 520).

## REPORT OF EPIPHANIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE

He demonstrates the emperor’s and his wife’s eagerness, as well as his own, concerning the union of the Churches. The priests of Pontus and Asia, and especially of the East, who are unwilling to condemn the names of their bishops, are to be admitted into union. He sends the pontiff a chalice and other gifts. (C)

### To the most holy and blessed brother and fellow minister Hormisdas, holy in every respect, Epiphanius, bishop, greetings in the Lord

We believe that your Blessedness has already been satisfied by what has been done concerning how much eagerness we, together with our most devout and most Christian emperor and his most faithful wife, flourishing in every good quality, have shown toward the right and pure union of the holy Churches; and also concerning how, with the charity of God that was fitting for us, we received the holy bishops sent by you and honored the venerable clergy.

Nevertheless, we believed that if the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, our God, should present those same most reverend fellow ministers of ours unharmed to your sight, everything that has been stirred up would become manifest to you, most holy ones, and through them you would learn more clearly the labor that we have been able to endure.

By God’s grace and through the faithfulness of our princes, our Church of the city of Constantinople has been governed peacefully. The names that we learned to be impious in the judgment of your see have not been recited among the sacred mysteries; rather, the agreement of the four councils concerning the right faith is proclaimed, and this itself is made manifest to all through the recitation of the sacred diptychs.

Let them therefore announce to you that not a few priests are subject to us, and that a considerable multitude is subject under the ordination of bishops beneath them; this multitude embraces the good of the union now begun. Let your Holiness also know that you have been constituted both its leader and its initiator in this general good. Therefore your Blessedness must be strongly stirred by the incentives of praise to keep watch, lest what divine mercy has begun to arrange in your honor appear not to reach full completion, as the common unity requires [Col. 0498A].

Our most faithful and most devout princes, rejoicing in the unity and concord of the holy Churches of God, have more diligently sent petitions to your Blessedness. They received them from many holy priests, from both the province of Pontus and that of Asia, and especially from the East, among whom it appears difficult, indeed impossible, to remain silent about the names of their former priests. Their obstinacy is so great that they are prepared to endure every danger for this matter.

Therefore, considering all the necessary circumstances relating to the pursuit of peace and recognizing that through this sole path of humility we have found unity and salvation for all, may you, through those whom we have sent to you for this affair, question them as has been said, receive their satisfaction, and administer the matter with the peaceful governance that befits you.

For since each Church is one with the other, and each is undoubtedly good, the glory of common praise arising from what is accomplished through vigilance is gathered from both patriarchal sees, so that Christ, our true God, the Lord and creator of all, may be glorified as usual.

The most holy bishop John, who is laying aside many labors with us in the present struggle; Heraclianus, the most reverend presbyter of our holy greater church and our fellow resident; and Constantine, the most reverend deacon of that same greater church, earnestly entreat you concerning all these matters. Through them we have also sent our synodal letters according to the ecclesiastical laws of your Blessedness.

Our most devout emperor, demonstrating his zeal for the union of the holy Churches, has now sent to your Blessedness letters of peace concerning these matters and has forwarded the petitions presented to him by the people of Jerusalem and the East.

We, therefore, wishing to find an occasion for greeting, have written this letter to you. Through it we entreat you, setting before you, most holy ones, this divine saying: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI).

Behold, the Lord of all has entrusted us with a talent, so that it may be returned increased by the fruit of good work, and so that, through your praiseworthy administration, so many holy Churches, so many of their priests, and an innumerable multitude—now united to the holy Church but presently in danger and error—may be saved.

This will occur if the guidance of your Blessedness is delayed [reading uncertain; variant: “if the governance of your Blessedness is recalled”], especially for those who dwell in the holy places of Christ our God and cling everywhere to the holy Churches, so that their multitude ought not to be rejected. For, at the suggestion of these people, all persist so obstinately in the evil of their stubbornness that they would rather depart from life than abandon what they have contrived.

Thus, if God commands that these people be united through your Blessedness, may the merit of your praise be ascribed to you both in the present and in future times.

Let your Holiness pray both for our most devout and most Christian princes and for our insignificance and for universal union, so that, through the grace of the holy Trinity of one essence and the intercessions of our lady, the holy and glorious virgin and Mother of God Mary, everything may come together in undivided unity and the unshaken foundation of the Catholic faith may be confirmed in every respect, most holy brother.

As tokens of our charity in Christ our Lord, we have sent through the most reverend men gifts for the administration of divine worship and for your holy apostolic Church: a chalice surrounded with gems, a golden paten, another silver chalice, and two silk veils. We ask that your Blessedness receive them with that charity which we do not doubt you possess according to God.

We also, together with those who are with us, send abundant greetings in Christ to the entire fraternity that is with your Holiness.

Received on the day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Rusticus, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of the Lord 520).

## IMPERIAL LETTER OF JUSTIN AUGUSTUS

He announces that Bishop John, sent to negotiate the peace of the Church, will depart as soon as he has recovered. (C)

### Justin Augustus to Pope Hormisdas

When we dismissed the most blessed Bishop Germanus and those whom you had sent with him from this royal city, we gave them instructions of this kind: that we would subsequently make known to your apostolate, through the most reverend Bishop John, the points that pertained to the perfect unity of the Churches. These matters had nevertheless been explained while they themselves were present here.

But it happened that the aforesaid bishop John was detained by a long illness. Therefore, lest any unfavorable judgment enter your reverence—as though our promises were being brought to fulfillment less effectively through some voluntary negligence—we considered it necessary to explain the cause of the delay to you through Eulogius, a man of illustrious rank, tribune and notary, whom we have sent to the exalted king Theodoric concerning certain affairs.

We add this also: when the favorable majesty of the Lord and our God has wished to restore that most religious man John to his former health, we shall immediately send him to your Holiness, just as we once promised.

It remains for your Holiness to deign to obtain divine assistance for us through your prayers.

Given on the day before the Kalends of September at Constantinople. Received at Rome on the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Rusticus, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of the Lord 520).

## REPORT OF DOROTHEUS, BISHOP OF THESSALONICA

He refutes the charge brought against him. (C)

### To the most holy and blessed father and fellow minister Hormisdas, Dorotheus, greetings in the Lord

Our purpose and the chief object of our prayer, most blessed and thrice-blessed Father, is in every respect to write frequently to you, most holy ones, and to merit mutual correspondence; it is not fitting that I should ever be excluded from such joy.

Since I have clearly learned that certain people are disturbing your holy ears, and since I know without doubt that you are perfect in every respect and can hear nothing without judgment or give your mind wholly to anyone, I do not wish to appear any longer, through silence, to grant time to those who have indeed suffered no injury from us but have armed themselves against us without cause and needlessly.

Nevertheless, I make satisfaction to God and to your Holiness. On behalf of the most reverend Bishop John, who shortly before was sent by your venerable crown, I devoted myself to dangers, endured death, and know that I exposed my life for him. This is shown by the records, including those matters which, although I was absent, appear to have been examined with the greatest severity.

And what need is there for a lengthy speech, when our Lord God Jesus Christ can disclose and establish everything for you? When I learned that you had been summoned to the episcopate of the apostolic see, I judged it to be the common joy of the whole world. From that time, writing this very thing to you, I have omitted nothing, insofar as I was concerned, that pertained to your honor and satisfaction and to that of the apostolic see; nor do I now omit anything.

Shortly, with the Lord Jesus Christ’s assent, you will learn through venerable men that these things were devised by me from the beginning, and that when the Lord God granted the time, they were brought to completion.

I also, together with my people, send abundant greetings in Christ to the entire fraternity that is with your Holiness.

## LETTER LXXIII. TO DOROTHEUS, BISHOP OF THESSALONICA

He must come to Rome to receive Catholic doctrine and clear himself of the charge brought against him.

### Hormisdas to Dorotheus, Bishop of Thessalonica

Considering that the Church of your Fraternity, before the discord of former times, had long been joined to the apostolic see by the greatest charity, we believed that you had recently become the author of the restored peace. But since you delay even in following those whom you ought to have preceded, we lament not lightly the tardiness of your delayed correction.

You write that our ears have been disturbed by the atrocity of a certain crime. Would that this detestable report had traveled only as far as us, and had not announced to Christian minds throughout the whole world a deed so grievous and so execrable! Those who do not know you to be innocent may thus believe that you have likewise deviated from the path of Christianity.

In what part of the world does the ill repute of such savagery not both sadden the Catholic Churches and gladden the wicked hopes of heretics? We wish to show through your letters that it is foreign to the conscience of your charity. For what accords more with our desires than that bishops wishing to return to Catholic peace should always be proven innocent of cruelty and crimes?

We therefore await—if your Fraternity is not without the defenses of truth known to God—that you may both repel from yourself the ill repute of so great a crime and, in the reconciliation of the faith, at last follow the examples of those who have returned.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Rusticus, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of the Lord 520).

## LETTER LXXIV. TO JUSTIN AUGUSTUS

He acknowledges receipt of his letter and says that there has never been doubt concerning his faith and piety.

### Hormisdas to Justin Augustus

Blessed is the Trinity, our God, who has entrusted you with the reins of worldly empire, to whom veneration is due not only by right of kingship, but also because of the glorious modesty and integrity of your purpose.

We truly glorify God when we read the letters of your piety, in which, by excusing the delay of the embassy promised on account of the illness of the man who was to be sent, you have made clearer than light itself how much care you have for faith and honor. You show that supreme power is not sufficient for those who govern the highest level of dominion unless the adornments of character make their principate more precious.

May our God preserve his benefits toward you, most clement emperor, and, regarding your good deeds, grant you eternal rewards. Nor has any suspicion troubled us concerning delay in fulfilling the promise, nor do we believe that any change of plan has occurred. For it would be impious to doubt in any way the words of one whose faithfulness has been so clearly recognized in great affairs.

Therefore, as our son Eulogius, a distinguished man, tribune and notary, returns, we offer the service of the greeting that is owed. We continually beseech the great God in prayer that, having healed through your zeal the wounds inflicted by the faithless, he may, by extending your age through longer times, make the unity restored to the Church secure in every respect.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Rusticus, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of the Lord 520).

## LETTER OF JUSTIN TO HORMISDAS

He sends a gift to the pontiff and urges him, following the example of Anastasius, to show indulgence to the Asians and especially the Easterners who are unwilling to condemn the names of their bishops. He forwards the petitions presented by the same people for the union of the Churches. (C)

### Justin Augustus to Pope Hormisdas

[Note: Codex Lucensis 125 reads: “To the most sacred and blessed archbishop of the nourishing city of Rome and patriarch Hormisdas.” This heading was added by another hand of nearly the same antiquity; previously it stood as it does here in the text.]

We are known to have openly declared both the zeal with which we have always acted, and with which we now act, to reconcile the opinions of those who cultivate the Catholic faith, so that all may venerate the undivided Trinity with one mind. Now, for this very purpose, we voluntarily send to your Blessedness Gratus, an illustrious master of the record office [Note: The same codex reads “a distinguished master of the record office”], so that a remedy may finally be found for the various hesitations in the disputes [Note: The same codex reads “of contenders”]. At the same time, we receive with willing and submissive affection the most religious men whom your apostolic see has judged should be sent as intermediaries for unity.

Indeed, we looked upon them as though they were peace itself, viewing them with joyful eyes and embracing them with outstretched hands. We have also arranged with every effort that the venerable Church of Constantinople, as well as many other Churches, should accept the wishes of your see—not only in other matters but also in removing from the sacred diptychs the names whose removal you especially requested.

There were, however, certain cities and Churches, both Pontic and Asian, especially Eastern, whose clergy or peoples, though assailed by every threat and persuasion, were nevertheless in no way moved to remove and reject the names of bishops whose reputation flourished among them. They consider life harder than death if they condemn those dead whose lives they gloried in while they lived.

What, then, are we to do with such obstinacy? It obeys neither commands nor persuasion, and despises torments to such an extent that it judges it a grand and festive achievement if it abandons its religious resolve only after abandoning the body. It seems to us that we must act more gently and mercifully. If such a course is found in your Holiness alone, it will no longer be possible to find it elsewhere. For we have neither accepted a petition from persons eager for blood and punishments—an expression that is itself harsh—nor do we wish the desires for concord to remain unfinished through some small obstacle, but rather we seek to extend, by whatever means we can, the union of the members of the Church.

Which, then, will be more advantageous: for the sake of lesser matters, to have such great multitudes wholly added to us [Note: The same codex reads “separated from us”], or, by granting and remitting minor points, to secure the greater matters that must be sought by every reasonable means, so that what could not be obtained in every respect may at least be brought forward from the necessary parts [Note: In the same codex, the original hand reads this way; another hand of nearly the same antiquity corrects it to: “so that what could not be conceded after all, at least the greater matters may in every respect be secured,” and so forth]?

We therefore ask pardon concerning the names—not of Acacius, not of either Peter, not of Dioscorus or Timothy, whose names were contained in the letter sent to us by your Holiness—but concerning those whom episcopal reverence has honored in other cities. This request excludes the cities in which the libellus of your Blessedness has already been fully admitted, unless your benevolence should decide that this part also ought to be corrected more gently.

Nor is this matter without the judgment of the apostolic see, so that it should be called not a pardon but a deliberate and already considered decision [Note: The same codex reads: “nor is the matter without the judgment of the see,” and so forth]. Anastasius, of most religious memory, openly and clearly established the position of your Church when he wrote about this matter to our predecessor: it was sufficient for those seeking peace if the name of Acacius alone were kept silent.

Therefore he follows the earlier constitutions of your see who does not judge all memories of the dead worthy of contempt, so that it should not be considered unworthy or incongruous if your gentleness were proclaimed throughout every end of the earth as more gracious toward all—not only toward the dead but also toward the living.

We do not doubt that this will be so agreeable to you that the world will immediately be made more joyful by a peaceful response. Your Holiness also retains what we wrote earlier: that petitions have been sent to us from the East, containing their will and judgment, in which they show that they will remain steadfast and from which they consider that they cannot in any way withdraw.

Therefore, in accordance with our promises, we have rightly thought that this document should now be sent to you through the most reverend Bishop John, so that, once its contents have also been accepted by your see, it may help gather and unite the venerable Churches everywhere, and especially the Church of Jerusalem. All favor that Church as the mother of the Christian name, so that no one dares to separate himself from it.

It is therefore fitting that your Holiness should declare your favorable agreement also in a letter, so that, once it has become known and manifest to all that you too praise and steadfastly preserve the tenor of this document, the world may become more joyful.

Given on the Ides of September at Chalcedon, in the consulship of Rusticus, a man of illustrious rank. Received on the day before the Kalends of December, in the same consulship (in the year of the Lord 520).

## COPY OF THE PETITION

They ask that through his action they may be admitted to the unity of the Church. They profess the Catholic faith. (C)

### A prayer and supplication to the God-loving and most devout emperor, the Augustus and most Christian prince Justin, from the clergy, abbots, and landholders of the provinces of Syria—those of Jerusalem and Antioch, and of Second Syria
“Draw water with joy from the springs of salvation” (Isaiah 12), Isaiah the prophet, the herald, cries out [Note: The same manuscript has, “of the prophet Isaiah.”], plainly showing that the springs of salvation are the preachings of evangelical truth [Note: The same manuscript has, “the evangelical truths.”]. From these springs the blessed Apostles, their successors in order, and the wise teachers of the Church drew the saving water of faith and irrigated the whole holy Church of God. Founded upon the rock of the chief of the apostles, preserving a right and unwavering confession, she confidently cries out with him at every moment to the only-begotten Son of God, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16). [Note: The same manuscript inserts, “preserving [it] confidently.”]

Receiving this saving confession from the four holy synods [Col. 0503C], which have been honored by evangelical commandments, we have never, through the grace of Christ, deviated from the right doctrines handed down to us, as the testing of events bears witness and the steadfastness of our faith demonstrates in a time of necessity. Therefore, if, as Christians, we share in the reasoning of faith, most pious lord, and hasten toward common peace and unity, we make our faith—which we received from the beginning—manifest to your piety through this declaration of ours, so that it may be known that we join in the pursuit of peace and, with God’s help, do not depart from the right faith; rather, we equally abominate every heresy. We anathematize, with all our heart and boldly, not only the Eutychianists and Acephali, but also the Nestorians and those who worship a mere human being [Note: The same manuscript has, “hating.”].

We, most dear and most Christian lord emperor [Note: The same manuscript has, “most Christian”], as stated above, having been baptized from the beginning and believing in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit [Note: The same manuscript has, “one essence.”], worship the essence of God subsisting in three subsistences [Note: In the same manuscript an ancient hand corrects this thus; the earlier hand had written “substances”]. According to the creed of the holy Fathers, we believe in one God, the almighty Father, and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten God the Word [Note: The same manuscript has, “of God”], and likewise in one Holy Spirit. In accordance with this divine teaching [Note: That is, the creed or doctrine. HARD.], we understand and receive the definition promulgated by the holy Council of Chalcedon [Col. 0504A], confidently believing that the holy council proclaimed God the Word to be one substance or person—which is the same thing—in two natures, that is, in divinity and humanity, without division or confusion.

Our Lord Jesus Christ is one of the holy Trinity, which is of one essence. For if we accept, as stated, one God subsisting in three persons, and the Father was not incarnate, nor the Holy Spirit, then God the Word was incarnate and became man: one of the holy Trinity, which is of one essence, according to the distinctive property of sonship. Thus, believing according to the four aforementioned synods, we do not refuse to confess the second birth of God the Word according to the flesh [Note: In the same manuscript, “and the second” is absent].

Hence the holy Virgin who gave birth is properly believed to be the Mother of God [Note: The same manuscript has, “the holy Virgin, Mother of God,” etc.], since she bore from herself the Son, God the Word, who is by nature unchangeable, and made him man—he who is by nature and in truth of one essence with the Father. We confess the two natures in Christ as united in respect of essence or substance, as in one person or substance. After the union, we neither remove their difference or distinctive properties, nor have we been taught by the union to divide them into two persons or substances.

We know the same only-begotten Son of God both before his incarnation and afterward; the same both God and man; passible in the flesh, impassible in divinity; circumscribed in body, uncircumscribed in spirit; the same earthly and heavenly—he whom the world received as man but could not contain as God; mortal and immortal. Nowhere has the difference of his natures been taken away, nor do we divide their union in essence [Col. 0504B].

For this is the great mystery of true piety: that God the Word, one of the holy Trinity of one essence, became incarnate and man, and is known and worshiped in both natures, divinity and humanity, without division or confusion. He underwent neither conversion nor change, but preserves within himself the distinctive property of each nature in one person.

Therefore, receiving and preserving the aforementioned holy synods on account of this faith, we anathematize all who, at any time or in any manner, have written anything against them—especially John the Aegeote, who, like a Nestorian, spewed forth many blasphemies against the aforementioned holy Council of Chalcedon [Col. 0504D]. Likewise, we condemn Timothy, surnamed the Cat, as an Eutychianist, barking against that council together with his followers.

Thus we have always thought, with God’s help, and still think. Accordingly, we have offered this declaration to your piety and, as you deigned to command, have set out our own understanding and the manner in which we think concerning the sound faith: for certain heretics, while hastening to conceal their evil faith, attempt to disparage our freedom and right faith in Christ.

We therefore beseech your clemency to maintain complete vigilance in the uniting of the holy Churches, so that the unity which comes about with God’s help may thereafter enjoy peace and not be disturbed by any reasonable or unreasonable pretext. May the God of all fulfill your pious desire for his glory and for the good order of the commonwealth.

## LETTER 75. TO THE CONSTANTINOPOLITAN SYNOD

He congratulates Bishop Epiphanius on his election.

Hormisdas to the Constantinopolitan synod.

We rejoice, as your fraternity has reported to us, that our brother and fellow bishop Epiphanius has been raised, at Constantinople—most fortunate city, by God’s favor—to the office of the priestly ministry [Col. 0505B]. Reports are received with a certain added pleasure when the person who is loved is the one who has conveyed them; and the greater the authority of the messenger, the greater the joy that arises, since there is no reason to dispute his testimony.

Such was fitting, dearest ones; such affection toward a neighbor ought to be shown, so that through you the apostolic see might learn that he shines in character and holiness. He has so thoroughly imbued himself, as you also affirm, with every good discipline that there can be no stronger testimony to his merits than his being chosen to the honor of the priesthood.

What uncertainty could remain concerning a man in whom divine qualities have been anticipated and recognized under the test of an accomplished concord regarding his good character? Therefore you act holily, religiously, and piously when you willingly offer testimony to the truth and do not deny a reward to those who deserve it. To keep silent about the truth is the same error as to support falsehood; and it is the same injustice to withhold honor from pleasing character as to grant it to the unworthy.

It is certain, most beloved, that you share in the praises of the priest whom you commend, because what is praised in the one whom you chose from among yourselves is credited to the whole order of your fraternity. May almighty God, preserving the peace of his faith forever, strengthen with great firmness your election and ordination, which you religiously entrusted to be reported to the apostolic see through our brother and fellow bishop John, as well as our sons, the presbyter Heraclianus and the deacon Constantine. May he also scatter the struggles of all who disagree and restrain the hearts of those at variance. And just as the sign of peace was given under our brother and fellow bishop Epiphanius, so may we rejoice in its fulfillment.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Valerius, a man of illustrious rank (A.D. 521).

We have in our archives the proceedings in the case of Abundantius, bishop of Trajanopolis.

## LETTER 76. TO EPIPHANIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE

That he reached the priesthood by the proper course; that one must persevere in the union of the Church; and concerning the gifts received.

Hormisdas to Epiphanius, bishop of Constantinople.

We bless the Lord for the affection of fraternal charity, because we have learned not only from the report of the synod that you worthily attained the priesthood, but also confirm it by your deeds and character. The degree of your merit has so revealed itself to those who love you that we believed everything even before the testimony of our brothers and fellow bishops.

For what they promised you could accomplish, we see that you have fulfilled; and, as though the grace of peace had been preserved for your faith, so the divine hopes of unity have at last been extended. To their predestination has been added the designation of your charity by which you are now called; under this spirit of manifest concord it has come about that we say: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity” (Psalm 131).

Therefore, returning the duties of greeting in Christ our Lord, we urge you to continue the praiseworthy undertaking of your good work, according to the holy Gospel, which admonishes us: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10). Encourage the others, invite them by admonitions, gather them by kind words; for the multiplied returns of the entrusted talent are divine sacrifices.

Moreover, we received with the greatest gratitude the news that, through the good will of your charity, you honored our brother and fellow bishop John, as well as our sons, the presbyter Heraclianus and the deacon Constantine, who served as envoys. We do not think that anything could be sweeter. Although the aforesaid men, even if acting out of duty, would have praised you not merely on rational grounds, we are blessed in every way because the messenger reporting on a worthy matter proved himself worthy, so that you might have the clearest evidence of the envoys’ merits as an honor.

In the pope’s hand: We have received from your charity a gold cup set with jewels, a silver paten, another silver cup, and two veils intended for the service of the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Valerius, a man of illustrious rank (A.D. 521).

## EPISTLE OF EPIPHANIUS TO HORMISDAS

He reports that he sent to the emperor the petitions presented by the Easterners. (C)

To my lord, in every respect beloved of God, most holy brother and fellow minister, Hormisdas: Bishop Epiphanius, greeting in the Lord.

How great the zeal and what kind of desire the most pious and most Christian emperor has for the cherished and perfect union of all the Churches, he has shown not merely by his will but by deeds themselves, both while residing in this royal city and even before he attained the kingdom given him by God. He has made this especially manifest to your holiness through the efforts he has undertaken from the beginning of his reign until now, by which he strives with eager spirit to unite all the members of the Catholic Church into one body of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

And what need is there for lengthy words, when we can stand as true witnesses to the facts themselves? Your holiness also has evidence of this, which you have learned through written reports; what is now added confirms it. For certain religious priests from the regions of the Eastern territories, who are under his most powerful authority, presented petitions, explaining what they desired.

Because I did not wish this to remain unknown to your holiness, he wisely decided that what has now taken place should be reported to you in the present letter. Shortly afterward he will communicate this more clearly to them, so that, after the common counsel of all has preceded, the matters useful to the common good and irreproachable in every respect may be clarified through the corrections of the Catholic faith.

Therefore, judging it opportune to address your holiness in fraternal letters and with our dearest greetings, we ask you to deign to pray more earnestly and more urgently for our most pious prince to the Lord God of all.

I, together with my people, most warmly greet in Christ all the fraternity that is with your holiness.

In another hand: Safe in the Lord, pray for us, beloved of God and most holy father.

## REPORT OF EPIPHANIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE

He praises Paulinus’s diligence. (C)

To my lord, in every respect beloved of God, most holy brother and fellow minister, Hormisdas: Epiphanius, greeting in the Lord.

Paulinus, the defender of your see, who delivered your letter and displayed in himself the virtue of your holiness, spent time among us with joy and contributed his diligence to our common counsels and actions. But since it was not fitting to delay him for a longer period while he was hastening to you, we therefore address your holiness in return and commend the aforesaid man to your protection as one worthy of our love and as a faithful servant who has remained steadfast.

He will be a trustworthy narrator for us concerning what we have accomplished and the concern we bear for the holy Churches. For, through the prayers of your holiness, we look to the natural goodness of this matter with the most vigilant zeal; and, with God’s cooperation, the word of grace runs its course in many respects without any obstruction and brings our work and purpose to fulfillment.

But since certain difficulties have arisen, what is being undertaken here must rely upon governance and orderly arrangement and must be explained suitably, as your holiness knows above all. Those who have been chosen to feed God’s flocks must do and undertake everything for the glory of God, placing their hope of salvation in him. As it is written: “For those who love God, all things work together for good” (Romans 8).

We strive, most holy one, both to think and to act in accordance with what pleases you, as has been said.

I, together with my people, most warmly greet in Christ all the fraternity that is with your holiness.

## COPY OF THE LETTER OF JUSTINIAN, A MAN OF ILLUSTRIOUS RANK, TO HORMISDAS

He asks him to labor for the unity of the Churches and to respond to the matters he had written through his envoys. (C)

To the most blessed and apostolic father Hormisdas, pope of the city of Rome: Justinian.

You know from many letters how greatly we revere your blessedness, ever since your son, the most serene emperor, began to reign [Col. 0508A]. Now also, greeting your holiness with the modesty that is due, we earnestly ask that you labor through constant prayers and very frequent supplications for concord among your Churches [Note: The Roman edition has, “venerable Churches.”]. May your apostolate, through Eulogius, a man of illustrious rank, tribune and notary, deign to send us a complete and unambiguous reply both concerning the statement under dispute and concerning the names of the bishops who died under Acacius, just as we wrote after everything through your envoys. All the arrangements made in the presence of your envoys are, of course, to remain permanently and firmly in force.

For the religious man John, the bishop who is to come to Rome, is being detained by bodily illness. Nothing prevents concord from being anticipated even before his arrival [Col. 0508B], once religious doubt has been removed; nevertheless, with divine favor we shall soon send him, since he is already better. The matters that have fallen into ambiguity are neither difficult, nor is it expedient to prolong the cause of eternal life, lest something more uncertain arise through delay.

Therefore, may your holiness, mindful of the eternity above and of the fearsome judgment, hasten to entrust what has been committed to you to effective action, so that all may understand that you have rightly received the primacy of the apostolic see. Accordingly, command that what we write here in paternal affection [Note: Another reading has, “to our sons”] be fulfilled as quickly as possible. For you know how glorious it would be if the errors of so many years were utterly eradicated during your pontificate.

## COPY OF THE LETTER OF JUSTINIAN, CONSUL, TO HORMISDAS

We rightly confess that Christ the Lord is one in the Trinity and, in another sense, one from the Trinity. The names of condemned bishops should not be treated with excessive severity. (C)

To the blessed and holy father Hormisdas, bishop of the city of Rome: Justinian, consul [Note: This is how it is read in the Avellana Collection; earlier editions had “a man of illustrious rank.”].

Your blessedness is also witness to how great is our religious reverence and how solicitous we have always been for the uniting of the holy Churches. After our renowned lord the emperor began to reign, we sent letters through all who came to Italy, making the request appropriate to your apostolate. Now also, lest anything that ought to be done be omitted, the most reverend bishop John, the presbyter Heraclianus, and the deacon Constantius have been sent to this distinguished city and are proceeding happily to Rome [Col. 0508D], so that they may receive a complete reply concerning everything that your son, the most serene emperor, has written.

May your holiness therefore willingly receive these most religious men and, after offering prayers and appeasing the Divinity, arrange everything venerably, so that nothing further may remain in doubt.

It seems to us that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, born from the Virgin Mary, whom the chief of the apostles proclaims to have suffered in the flesh, is rightly said to be one in the Trinity, reigning with the Father and the Holy Spirit. We also devoutly believe that his person belongs within the Trinity and is one from the Trinity [Col. 0509A].

Concerning the names of the deceased bishops, make provision mercifully and as befits a peaceful father. For your predecessor, of blessed memory, wrote to the emperor Anastasius, so that, if only the name of Acacius were removed, we might have one communion.

Did not your see therefore urge you to imitate the blessed and most holy Leo, bishop of Rome? Just as he wrote to Leo, so should you, once every doubt has been removed, write complete and peaceful letters to the invincible emperor, your son, for the Church, so that before the tribunal of the coming judge you may share in the company of those whose see you rightly hold by priestly authority.

Let your apostolate therefore show that you have succeeded the apostle Peter, since the Lord will require from you, as from the chief shepherds, the salvation of all who can be saved once concord has been firmly established. For our part, once the chapters concerning which you received our letters have been concluded, we will no longer tolerate anyone stirring up a religious controversy in our commonwealth; nor is it fitting for your holiness to listen to those who contend over superfluous matters.

## LETTER 77. TO JUSTINIAN

He commends Justinian for the reverence shown to him; says that he awaits the promised embassy; and explains the mysteries of the most holy Trinity.

Hormisdas to Justinian, a man of illustrious rank.

By deigning to show how kindly your Highness feels toward me, you do something pleasing to God and consonant with a right conscience. Yet the benefits of this purpose are by no means small for us. A greater fruit of such goodness returns to us, for the honor shown to a bishop is not an empty distinction.

It is unquestionable that the honor shown to a minister is worship offered to the Lord, and that whoever honors the person of a priest will receive a greater reward from the one whom the priest serves. The Lord Jesus says that those who receive prophets with honor will receive their reward. For me, indeed, your favor is of great importance, but it is all the more precious because whatever favor you graciously show me, you display in the defense of the Churches.

But, to direct our words toward what your Highness desires: although both the most merciful emperor and you promise that an embassy will come, and although it is reasonable that we should await the arrival of those who are to be sent before addressing everything [Col. 0509D], nevertheless, because we welcome the zeal that you have shown concerning religion, it is not burdensome to anticipate the matter by saying that there is no need for the stability of your faith to be confused by the insolence of novel language—whether those speaking follow intention [or, “controversy”] rather than reason.

The holy Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is one God. Israel is commanded to worship this God, whose inseparable and undivided substance can neither be divided nor separated by sacrilegious distinction, while the distinctive property of each person is nevertheless preserved.

For the present, since we are considering the limits of an epistolary style, we believe that this is sufficient in a suitable brevity. More fully it will be discussed when the empire of the most merciful prince is flourishing, if, with God’s favor, it should fall to us to receive the promised embassy and, after all matters have been learned, to send back a reply with the help of our God for the instruction of all.

## LETTER OF JUSTINIAN, A MAN OF ILLUSTRIOUS RANK, TO HORMISDAS

He asks him to ensure that the envoys return as soon as possible after successfully completing their business [Note: This description of the letter’s subject is taken from the Roman edition and does not properly correspond to the letter itself. I would substitute: “He modestly complains that he has not yet received a suitable reply to the chapters proposed.”]. (C)

Your apostolate has carefully learned how ardent in faith the most serene emperor, your son, and we have been from the beginning. We have never ceased doing what pertained to the strengthening of divine religion. For this reason we recently sent the most reverend priests to Rome [Col. 0510B], so that a complete settlement might be reached concerning the chapters over which uncertainty had arisen.

But we do not know what difficulty has occurred, so that matters which appear to be of the slightest importance have not yet been brought to rest. Therefore, greeting your reverence, we ask that no opportunity be given for anyone to doubt your willingness. With the judgment of the heavenly Majesty before your eyes, may you deign to hasten in every way.

## LETTER 78. TO JUSTIN, AUGUSTUS

Nothing should be altered in order to avoid discord; and he writes to Epiphanius concerning those who may be admitted to communion.

Hormisdas to Justin, Augustus.

I know, venerable emperor, that your clemency is content solely with the consciousness of good work and that, in the arrangements you make for the unity of the Catholic Church, you do not need human praise—lest the glory of a great endeavor be cheapened by an unworthy reward.

For what human praise could be sufficient for one to whom it has fallen to have the kingdoms of the earth entrusted? Flattering words are dangerous in his case, since the humility offered to a ruler may arouse suspicion. Moreover, according to evangelical teaching, the one who expects praise as his recompense must necessarily lack the fruit of heavenly reward.

Therefore I do not doubt that I should refer to God all that your gentleness, endowed with every perfection of goodness, memorably accomplishes. You do not think of passing things or expect a reward from them for your deeds, but from him who is acknowledged to be the author of every good.

Nevertheless, I comply with the divine instructions that I obey, lest I conceal the benefits heaped upon your religious conscience, and lest my silence—which increases your glory—should, God forbid, become a fault for me.

I know concerning those ten whom the mercy of our Lord and Savior cleansed: nine were marked and condemned for ingratitude, while one returned testimony of faith and of the salvation he had received, offering thanks after he was healed.

I follow the examples I have learned, and what I proclaim through the office entrusted to me I present on the occasion of this written discourse. I give thanks as much as I can [Note: Another reading has, “more humbly.”], though I cannot give as much as I ought. Yet it consoles me that the world rejoices with me over your benefits [Col. 0511A], and that the members of the Church, so long torn apart, glory in being restored to their proper structure.

You have restored faith to the peoples and pursued error; the pride of the enemies of God’s Church has been humbled, and the humility of the faithful has been raised up. A great achievement has fallen to you, emperor; great benefits have joined you with your power. Understand what you deserve.

You have transferred to yourself no small part of that good work which our Lord Jesus Christ, as he ascended into heaven, bestowed. For through you the world has found the peace that he gave to his disciples. There is no doubt that the angels of heaven rejoice with you; for if, according to the evangelical testimony, there is joy among them over one sinner who is saved, what joy must there be for the people?

Hail, Hezekiah of the present age. For although there were good kings of Judah before him [Note: Another reading omits “good”] who did good things, none of them destroyed the high places. You too, destroyer of schisms and pride and restorer of ancient worship, may presume that your years will be lengthened in a likeness to his, since you imitate the examples of his deeds.

You undertake all these things, which contribute greatly to the increase of your glory, not urged by another’s exhortation or moved by any petitions. God alone is your counselor; no one seeks to insert himself into participation in so great a work. To you belongs the zeal for this action; to you belongs the result of the good action.

You, venerable emperor, have raised me, who mourned the wounds of the Church for so long, to hope for restored salvation. After such continual storms, when I had almost ceased from hope, you stirred me toward a new tranquility by voluntarily sending your pious letters. This too undoubtedly occurred through divine understanding: at the very beginning of your rule, you devoted yourself to the service of the faith to which you owed the empire, although I could not be the first to urge you to begin these things.

Now, provoked by such great benefits, I am compelled with greater confidence to pray that you not permit a deficiency in so good a work; that you not suspend the hands you raise to God before the work you have received is perfected.

I cannot deny that I ask these things for our Lord’s sake and out of affection for unity; but I confess that, because of your great gentleness, I also owe these efforts to your salvation. For it is written: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10).

Nor should the obstinacy of certain people make you slower in your purpose. It is harsh if the stubbornness of those who divide peace should prove more effective than the efforts of those who uphold unity.

Let wounds be loved when remedies are being provided for salvation; and let it be judged preferable . . . to be . . . with the dead than to cling to the living. Is it not just that those who are unmoved by example should submit to the authority of a religious prince?

Not every sick person accepts wholesome remedies, and the effort of healing is often unwelcome to those to whom it is applied. Nevertheless, necessity undertaken for salvation is welcome, and even those who are unwillingly cured remain indebted to the benefits afterward.

The cunning of those who introduce difficulties while striving to undermine what has been settled must be guarded against with the greatest care. Who could accept that we should be thought capable of being led by peace to what we could not be compelled to accept by the necessity of discord? And should it be judged right that a prince should follow the will of his subjects against their welfare, when subjects do not obey their prince’s authority for their own salvation?

Believe that the Church of God herself, venerable son, is pleading with me and with you to guard her without stain or wrinkle, as you know is pleasing to the Lord; let not that watchful eye see in her any blemish that it must reject. Love what, moved by God, you have chosen, and preserve undefiled that of which you have wished to become a part.

Previously this concern was mine alone; now your clemency has made it one cause for us both. Let no one say that I am harsher than my predecessors, nor let anyone’s exhortation be held authoritative merely on account of its sentence. What made me more diligent was not a devotion to obstinacy, but the scandals that followed.

Perhaps at the beginning there could have been room for leniency; but, as is well known, the errors grew worse through the accumulation of successive periods. Do not think lightly, most holy son, of what you have undertaken to heal, in which the holy Council of Chalcedon and the most religious decrees of the pope Leo, to be venerated among the saints, have had a place of honor.

Was not an army of enemies of God heard as though in battle against such foundations of the faith? The more fiercely these things were assailed, the stronger the defenses by which they must be fortified.

I ask you, most merciful emperor, not to compel me either to abandon [Roman edition: “destroy”] what was formerly well approved or to change it. For that voice continually murmurs in my ears: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9), since it is evident that repentance concerns evil works, not good ones.

Although we are pressed by these difficulties, nevertheless, out of consideration for your gentleness, and because of the plea of the venerable envoys—the bishop John, the presbyter Heraclianus, and the deacon Constantine—we were moved not to act inhumanely. Their argument held that remedies ought to be sought for those who were innocent or ignorant of the matter.

We have therefore sent a letter to our brother and fellow bishop Epiphanius, so that, mindful of the faith and mindful of religion, he may admit to the fellowship of his communion those whom he judges worthy of reception and, as is asserted, innocent and alien to the communion that we reject, while preserving the wording of the libellus that we have submitted.

For it is better, and more pleasing to God, that those who have been cut off should be joined to the ecclesiastical body with the faith preserved, than that those who have remained in the immaculate communion of blessed Peter should pass over to the ranks of the cut off.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Valerius, a man of illustrious rank (A.D. 521).

## LETTER 79. TO JUSTIN, AUGUSTUS

The mystery of divinity and incarnation is explained.

[Note: Codex Luc. 125 reads: “To the most glorious and most merciful son Justin, Augustus.”]

Hormisdas to Justin, Augustus.

Among the matters pertaining to the unity of the Church, for whose sake God chose Your Clemency’s imperial authority, you have set certain things down in writing. This too, venerable emperor, was added by your concern for the faith, to which you show yourselves devoted in many ways: namely, that the petitions of certain persons should be joined to a report of their humility, so that I might learn either what question had arisen or what answer, suitable to religious knowledge, should be given by me to remove the uncertainty of the consultation proposed. [Note: The same codex reads “of my humility.”]

I read everything with the diligence that was fitting. Although it might have sufficed for a complete answer if I had merely rewritten what had been defined by the ancients [or: by the authors], nevertheless, in order to reward the affection of your religious purpose, I judged that I should not withhold the service of my own discourse as well. For what did the paternal instruction omit when the poisons of Nestorius and Eutyches emerged? Nearly all their impieties, together with the inventors of such abominable doctrines, were compressed into one harmonious body by the synodical decrees; and once such dreadful seeds of unbelief had been cut away, no room remained either to believe that Christ our Lord existed without the reality of flesh, or to believe that the same Lord had not come forth from the undefiled fertility of His mother’s womb as both God and man. One of them, by denying the dispensation through which we were saved, rendered it void insofar as he could; the other, with an opposite opinion but similar impiety, excluded divine power from true humanity in the same Lord Jesus Christ. The former did not remember that Christ showed His flesh to be touched; the latter did not remember the Gospel’s statement that the Word became flesh (John 1), although the Lord’s voice ought continually to have resounded in his ears, when He said and taught:

> “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3).

These matters have often been contained in many earlier judgments. Yet Your Clemency, even though they have already been said, will not disdain to hear them repeated; nor are we ashamed to revisit what our predecessors proclaimed [or: preached]. For there can be no diversity of preaching where there is one form of truth; nor will it rightly be judged irrelevant if, in faith, we agree with those with whom we are in agreement, and harmonize with them in doctrine.

Let the synodical decrees and the constitutions of blessed Pope Leo, consonant with the sacred faith, be recalled to your pious and gentle ears. You will find in them the same things that you have reviewed [or: found] in ours. What, then, after that fountain of authoritative decisions for the faithful, should any investigator, however curious, seek further—provided that he preserves the boundary of faith? [Note: The same codex reads: “There is no need either for fuller exposition or for addition by the congregation, nor for a more perfect instruction,” and so forth.] Unless, perhaps, someone prefers to doubt rather than believe, to quarrel rather than understand, and to follow uncertainties rather than preserve decrees.

For if God is Trinity—that is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and God is one, as the Lawgiver expressly says, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy 6), then whoever holds otherwise must either divide the Godhead into many parts [or: divide it], or inflict suffering specifically upon the very essence of the Trinity. This would mean either introducing several gods in the profane manner of paganism, or transferring sensible suffering to a nature that is foreign to all suffering.

The holy Trinity is one. It is not multiplied by number or increased by addition; neither can it be comprehended by the understanding nor separated, by distinction, from what God is. Who, then, would attempt to introduce profane division into that secret and eternal, impenetrable substance, which no nature of visible or invisible beings has been able to investigate, and reduce the mysteries of the divine mystery to the reckoning of human custom?

Let us worship the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: the distinct yet undivided [or: indistinguishable] substance of the Trinity, incomprehensible and ineffable. [Dionysius reads “indistinct”; Hardouin.] Although reason admits number in the persons, unity does not admit separation of essence. Yet we must preserve what belongs properly to the divine nature and what belongs properly to each person: neither denying the singularity of divinity to the persons, nor transferring to the essence what properly belongs to the names.

Great is the holy and incomprehensible mystery of the Trinity: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, the undivided Trinity. Yet it is known that it belongs properly to the Father to beget the Son; properly to the Son of God to be born from the Father, equal to the Father; and properly to the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father and the Son under the one substance of the Godhead. [Note: In the same codex, the first hand had the passage approximately as follows: “It is also known that it belongs properly to the Holy Spirit; but it belongs properly to the Son of God, according to that which follows,” and so on. An ancient hand, nearly contemporary, revised the reading thus: “It is also known that it belongs properly to the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father and the Son under the one substance of the Godhead. It belongs properly also to the Son,” and so forth.]

It belongs properly also to the Son of God that, according to what is written, “In the last times the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1), He should be united within the womb of holy Mary, the Virgin and Mother of God, with both natures joined without any confusion; so that He who existed as Son of God before the ages should become son of man, and should be born in time according to human custom, being born without opening His mother’s womb and, by the power of His divinity, not destroying His mother’s virginity.

It was wholly fitting to God’s birth that He should preserve childbirth without corruption, who caused conception to occur without seed—preserving what He was from the Father and displaying what He received from His mother. For while He lay in a manger, He was seen in heaven; wrapped in cloths, He was worshiped by the Magi; born among animals, He was proclaimed by angels [Note: The same codex reads “announced”]. Scarcely beyond infancy, He announced mystical teaching without an instructor; amid the beginnings of childhood, He displayed heavenly signs of power.

He was the same God and man—not, as unbelievers say, through the introduction of a fourth person, but He Himself, the Son of God, God and man: power and weakness, humility and majesty, the redeemer and the one sold, placed upon the cross and bestowing the kingdoms of heaven. He shared in our weakness so that He could be put to death, yet He was Lord of innate power so that death could not consume Him. He was buried according to that by which He willed to be born as man, and according to that by which He was like the Father He rose again; suffering the wounds and saving the sick, one among the dead and the giver of life to those who die; descending to the underworld and not departing from the Father’s embrace. Therefore He soon took back the soul which, according to the common human condition, He had laid down, through His singular power and wondrous patience. [Note: The same codex reads “power.”]

That these things are so and ought to admit no doubt, the same Lord Jesus Christ instructed us by setting before us the example of two apostles: lest He be believed not to be God amid the sufferings of His body, or to be God alone and not man amid the works of wondrous power. By Peter’s faith He declared Christ our Lord to be God; by Thomas’s doubt He showed Him to be man.

For what purpose would He have wished His disciples to inquire whom men said He was, unless, when Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16), He wished to make known that this had not been revealed by flesh and blood, but by God the Father inspiring him, and that faith in the revealed truth had been made manifest through the testimony of that praised response?

Why, when the Lord appeared after the resurrection, was Thomas either absent from the others or alone in doubt, unless so that the world might believe what the doubting disciple examined [or: had examined]? By allowing Himself to be touched by one man’s hands, He made it possible for the whole company of the faithful to recognize what He was. [Note: The same codex reads “to examine.”] His doubt, therefore, was not introduced to condemn the disciple, but to provide instruction for posterity.

Does the episode signify anything else—or [variant: “look toward anything else”—] when the same Lord joined Himself to Cleopas and another disciple as they journeyed toward Emmaus and spoke about Him? Although they had learned of the Lord’s resurrection from the women who had first come to the tomb, He nevertheless wished, through their doubt, to provide firmness of belief for future ages. Beginning with Moses and all the prophets, He interpreted the Scriptures and showed that Christ had to suffer and thus enter into His glory, testifying in many ways through examples from the sacred Scriptures that human nature was present in Him through suffering and divine nature through glory. [Note: The same codex reads: “These things are suggested by many examples from the sacred Scriptures,” followed by a longer reading; “nor …”]

These things are said to your religious conscience, venerable emperor, as though they were unknown. For the faith itself, which you constantly affirm, gives you this gift: it pours into your understanding both affection for itself [Note: The same codex reads “and sends”] and knowledge, through which it may be asserted more diligently. The responsibility entrusted to me is so great that I too must not remain silent even among those who know, lest, as the Catholic preaching of the faith succeeds through the ages, what is unfailingly affirmed should be believed without faith.
