I could discuss at greater length what pertains to the divinity and humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, and how in Him the two natures exist without confusion, according to the definitions of the ancients, if we were debating those who dissent from these things. But since the synodical constitutions and the doctrines of blessed Pope Leo are in everyone’s hands, I have judged it more fitting to touch briefly upon a few matters than to unfold the whole of them.

Now it is enough to recognize and guard the propriety of each thing, and to consider the essence, so that it may be known what we ought to attribute to the person and what to the substance. Those who ignorantly [variant: “negligently”] fail to understand these things, or who deliberately conceal them through cunning impiety, while omitting what belongs properly to the Son, set snares for the unity [variant: “divinity”] of the Trinity. But if what has been stated is held fixed with firm roots and no one departs from the paternal tradition, every question is met steadfastly. Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Valerius, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of the Lord 521). [Note: The same codex reads “the eighth.”]

[Note: The following letters are printed in parallel in Migne.]  
[Note: From an old Vatican codex in the Roman edition of 1491, Epistle 77.]

## Letter LXXX. Hormisdas to Epiphanius

He delegates to him the office of representing the apostolic see in receiving the lapsed.

Hormisdas to Epiphanius, bishop of Constantinople.

I am filled with great joy because I have learned, concerning the peace of the Church and the most holy emperor and your affection, of the zeal you indicated in your letter and confirmed through the testimony of my legates. Clear evidence of heavenly mercy is manifested when earthly rulers join the cause of the faith to the administration of the state, and the leaders of the Churches, mindful of what belongs to their responsibility, carry out their duty.

After the storms of discord, the Christian religion needed such leaders, who, having calmed the disturbances through prudent administration, might restore the peace that had long been driven into exile after the storm had been dispelled. By extending examples of their purpose into future ages, they would unquestionably show that whatever their successors did in imitation of them and to God’s pleasure should be credited to them.

Let us bless God, dearest brother, that this has been granted in our days, and let us strive with all the strength of our prayers and labors so that what has been rightly corrected through the help of our God may, with His assistance, be completed in every respect. For it is to be hoped that the remaining members, which are still divided, will hasten toward the union of their own body and that the lesser will not disagree with the greater. Since your affection urges this through the zeal of Christian charity, you ought to follow what it prompts and embrace what it advises should be loved.

Since we are now undertaking a similar care for the faith, through religious patience we hope for an equal reward from the outcome of the good work. Difficulties must not be yielded to. Faith is not wearied by hardships; one does not reach the heights of heaven by an easy road; nor does anyone merit recompense without the exertion of labor. Therefore we are especially admonished lest, while doing good, we grow faint:

> “Blessed also are those who keep judgment and do justice at all times,”

as the Psalmist testifies (Psalm 105). For it is not the beginning of labor that customarily receives the reward, but its completion.

Therefore, assuming an equal zeal for vigilance, since we share one fellowship in communion and belief, just as we rejoice in the Lord concerning the Church of Constantinople, united to the apostolic see, so let us also care—as you affectionately urge—for the restoration of the remaining Churches. Let us first preserve our faith and integrity undefiled by every contamination.

For you know, most holy brother, what bonds preserve ecclesiastical concord, what protects us from the attacks of heretics, and through what means the authority of the canons is preserved. When these things have been guarded in their full strength with every care, remedies will be granted to those who hope for them.

The order of ecclesiastical regulations and the very form of justice require that reasonable medicine not be denied to those who hope for it kindly and faithfully. No one is so separated from humanity that heedless simplicity should not bend him away from the harshness of strict judgment.

But so that this may be carried out carefully, without complaint or any blemish of error, dearest brother, you must assume my person in this matter. You must know, as has been said, what should be done and what avoided in such cases, and you must provide for everything in such a way that you do not doubt that an account of this administration must be rendered to God. Yet those who have been joined to you in communion, or through you to the apostolic see, must make the matter known to us by letters from you; these letters must also include the contents of the petitions they present.

Thus we shall absolve the errors of Severus and his accomplices, or of others like them, and we shall not allow those who could have been healed to suffer loss. [Note: This manuscript adds “or Supplicius” for “Sulpicius of Sorensis”; but either reading is an absurd error.]

We believe that this has been specially entrusted to you, transferring our burdens to your diligence, because you have already produced no small demonstrations in resisting the heretics, and no doubt ought to be entertained concerning one who has been properly examined and found sound.

At the same time take up the remedies of healing, gird yourself with the authority of justice, and so soften your treatment of petitioners with humanity that you exclude from those for whom provision is being made for the restoration of the Church both those who persist in the contamination of heretics and those who pretend to innocence and agree with our people only in words. Ecclesiastical discipline must not be moderated toward such persons. For the benefits of mercy, granted because of the need of those for whom provision ought to be made, will not be good if they are indiscriminately shared by good and evil alike.

Since your affection also mentioned the people of Jerusalem in your letter, and since a certain profession from them has been brought to us, we judged it necessary either to review what was written or to answer what was appropriate. If they preserve the constitutions of the holy Fathers, if they venerate the foundations of the faith defined through them when the Holy Spirit moved them, they will not depart from them.

For either those constitutions are perfect, as they stand, and need no addition; or they are thoroughly sound and therefore must not be changed, since through them all the poisons of the heretics have been suppressed. Nor did the Council of Chalcedon omit anything useful that any diligence could have devised. It either made the doctrines of its predecessors clearer or confirmed them with repeated authority, undertaking a particular contest against Nestorius and Eutyches: the one separated the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ from the flesh and therefore avoided proclaiming holy Mary Mother of God; the other rejected the reality of the flesh in the Lord.

For our Lord Jesus Christ is the same Son of God and the same son of man, one person in two natures, of divinity and flesh. The natures were not confused in their union, nor was a fourth person added to the Trinity. Rather, the Son of God Himself emptied Himself and took the form of a servant (Philippians 1). Therefore we confess one and indivisible essence of the Trinity, while knowing that each person possesses its own proper character: one person of the Son of God together with the flesh assumed, and one person of the Holy Spirit. We designate the persons by their properties and, through the unity of essence, affirm the inseparable mystery of the Trinity.

For it cannot be doubted that the Word of God assumed human nature through the flesh within His mother’s womb, nor that, after the union of the natures had taken place in the womb, He was divided from Himself. For just as humanity was not born in Him without God, so on the cross the impassible divinity was not separated from the suffering of the flesh. The birth of the Virgin, her undefiled fertility, the singular resurrection from the dead, and the ascension into heaven all declare this.

If they preserve these things as they were defined by the Fathers, let them believe and not transgress what has been defined. Those who deviate from that path spread over themselves a cloud of doubt.

But to contentious people we must answer with the apostolic words:

> “We do not have such a custom, nor does the Church of God” (1 Corinthians 2).

These matters have been stated briefly because it is not proper to doubt things that have repeatedly been defined according to the faith, and because the defense offered to those already instructed is almost superfluous, especially since I have already touched upon this matter at some length in writing to our son, the most merciful emperor.

Since we have answered concerning the profession of the people of Jerusalem, we also thought it appropriate to add this for the sake of their salvation: if they desire the unity of communion with the apostolic Church, let them send to us through their own people the profession of their faith, written down in the form in which they presented it to our legates residing at Constantinople; or let them deliver it to your fraternity, written in the same form, as we have said, so that it may in every way be conveyed to us under your direction.

As for the Thessalonians, whose legates came to us under the direction of our most merciful and faithful son, the emperor, we wish you to know, lest we seem to have omitted anything, that—according to whatever our Lord Jesus Christ, inspiring us, has approved—the whole matter is to be examined under your direction, and, if they fulfill what is required, the necessary measures are to be arranged through our brother and fellow bishop, the venerable John, and also through our sons Heraclianus the presbyter and Constantinus the deacon, men worthy of ecclesiastical honor.

Having been content to write what pertained to the case, we rejoiced that in a man of our own order we had found equal merit and a religious purpose, together with instructions from the legation consonant with wisdom and character. For it is a wished-for and joyous thing that those who happen to share communion and office should be proved worthy by a just assessment.

And in another hand:

> “May God preserve you in health, most honorable brother.”

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Valerius, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of Christ 521).

The most holy archbishop said:

“Now let the most God-fearing notaries of our most holy Church make known to us any documents in their possession that concern the present case.”

When the documents had been produced by Cosmas, the most God-fearing deacon, notary, and archivist, Macarius, the most God-fearing deacon and notary, read both the petition submitted on behalf of the clergy of Theopolis and the report of the synod then assembled in the imperial city, addressed to John, the archbishop of that imperial city, now among the saints.

Calonymus, the most God-fearing deacon and notary, read from a codex the letter to John, the archbishop of Jerusalem, now of holy memory, and to Epiphanius, bishop of Tyre, of pious memory. He also read the letter sent by John himself, bishop of Jerusalem, and by his synod to holy John.

Stephen, the most God-fearing notary and deacon, read the report sent by Epiphanius, bishop of Tyre, and by the synod assembled under him.

Paul, the most God-fearing notary and deacon, read the report, together with the proceedings, sent by the bishops of Second Syria to the most holy John, archbishop of the imperial city. All these documents were entered into the record.

## Letter 80: Hormisdas to Epiphanius

Hormisdas to Epiphanius, bishop of Constantinople.

I have been filled with great joy because I learned, concerning the peace of the Church, the most holy emperor, and your affection, of such zeal as you indicated in your letters and as I learned through the report of my legates. From this there proceeds clear evidence of heavenly compassion: earthly kings join matters concerning the faith to the administration of the state, and the leaders of the Churches, mindful of what contributes to their own administration, fulfill their duty.

After the storms of discord, the Christian religion needed such leaders, who, once the tempests had been calmed through the most prudent administration, would restore the peace that had long been driven into exile after the winter had been expelled. By extending the examples of their purpose into future ages, they will plainly show that whatever later generations do to God’s pleasure in imitation of them is inscribed to their credit.

Let us bless God, brothers, that this has been permitted to occur in our days, and let us lean upon all the strength of our prayers and cares, so that what has been well begun through the cooperation of our God may, with His help in all things, be completed.

For there is hope that the remaining members, still divided, will hasten toward the harmony of their own body, and that the lesser will not disagree with the greater. Since your disposition urges me toward this through the zeal of Christian love, you ought to follow what it awakens and embrace what it advises should be loved.

As we now undertake a similar care for the faith, through pious endurance we hope for an equal reward in the outcome of the good work. For one must not yield to difficulties; faith is not worn down by rough things; nor does anyone rise to the heights of heaven by a downward path; nor is anyone judged worthy of recompense without the exercise of toil.

Therefore, lest we grow faint while doing good, let us be especially reminded. For blessed are those who guard judgment and do righteousness at every time, as the Psalmist testifies. The beginning of labor does not usually receive the reward of the prize; its completion does.

Therefore, taking up an equal zeal for vigilance, since those who share communion and faith possess one fellowship, just as we rejoice in the Lord concerning the Church of Constantinople united to the apostolic throne, so let us also care, as you earnestly advise, for the restoration of the others. Let us first preserve our faith and integrity undefiled by every stain.

For you know, most honorable brother, what bonds preserve ecclesiastical concord, what protects us from the plots of heretics, and through what means the authority of the canons is preserved. When these have been guarded in their proper strength with complete care, healing will be offered to those who hope for it.

The order of ecclesiastical canons and the form of justice itself require that reasonable treatment not be denied to those who hope for it willingly and faithfully. No one is so divided from human kindness that artless simplicity should not bend him away from the hardness of severity.

But so that this may be carried out safely and without complaint or any clouded error, beloved brother, you must take my place in this matter. Knowing, as has already been said, what should be done and what must be guarded against in such cases, you must provide for everything in such a way that you do not doubt that you will render an account to God for this administration.

You must also ensure that those who have been joined to you in communion, and through you to the apostolic throne, make the matter known to us by your letters, and that the contents of whatever petitions they present be included.

Thus Severus and those entangled with him, and others like them, will be released from error, and we shall not suffer the loss of those who may be healed.

We thought it right to impose this particularly upon you, transferring our burdens to your care, because you have already given substantial proofs while resisting the heretics, and there should be no doubt concerning one who has been properly shown to be approved.

At the same time take up the remedies of healing, gird yourself with the authority of justice, and so soften your treatment of petitioners with humanity that you exclude from the provisions being made for the restoration of the Church those who persist in the contamination of heretics, or those who claim innocence and agree with our people only in words. It is not beneficial to temper ecclesiastical severity toward such persons.

For the good things of mercy, gathered because of the need of those for whom provision ought to be made, will not remain good if they become indiscriminately common to the good and the evil.

Since your affection also thought it right to mention the people of Jerusalem in your letters, and since some confession from them has been brought to us, we considered it necessary both to read what had been written and to answer what was appropriate.

If they preserve the constitutions of the holy Fathers, if they venerate the foundations of that faith, and if they do not depart from what was defined through the Fathers when the Holy Spirit moved them, then they will not depart from them.

For either these things are perfect, as they stand, and need no addition, or they are soundly established and therefore must not be altered, since through them all the poisons of the heretics have been swallowed up.

Nor did the Council of Chalcedon omit anything useful that any diligence could have devised. It either made the doctrines of its predecessors more clearly manifest or confirmed them by repeating them with authority. It undertook a particular contest against Nestorius and Eutyches: the former separated the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ from the flesh and therefore avoided proclaiming holy Mary as Mother of God; the latter denied the truth of the flesh in the Lord.

For our Lord Jesus Christ is this Son of God, the same man, one person in two natures, divinity and flesh; the natures were not confused in the union. He was not a fourth person added to the Trinity; rather, the Son of God Himself emptied Himself and took the form of a servant.

Therefore we confess one and indivisible essence of the Trinity, and we know that the proper distinction likewise belongs to the persons. We confess one person of the Father, one of the Son of God together with the flesh assumed, and one of the Holy Spirit. By indicating the persons through their properties, and by confessing through the unity of essence the inseparable mystery of the Trinity, we preserve both truths.

For it is impossible to doubt that the Word of God assumed human nature through the flesh in His mother’s womb, and that after the union of the natures had taken place in the womb He was not divided from Himself.

Just as humanity was not born in Him without God, so on the cross the impassible divinity was not separated from the suffering of the flesh. The Virgin’s birth, her undefiled fertility, the extraordinary resurrection from the dead, and the ascension into heaven demonstrate this.

If they preserve these things as they were defined by the Fathers, let them believe and not transgress what has been defined. Those who deviate from that path pour over themselves a cloud of doubt.

But we must answer contentious people with the apostolic saying:

> “We do not have such a custom, nor does the Church of God.”

These matters have been stated briefly because it is not proper to doubt things concerning the faith that have often been defined, and because the defense offered to those already prepared is entirely superfluous, especially since we have already indicated many things on this matter to the most glorious and merciful emperor, our son.

Since we have answered concerning the confession of the people of Jerusalem, we thought it fitting to add this for the sake of their salvation: if they long for union with the catholic Church, let them send to us through their own people the form of their confession, written down, which they presented to our legates residing at Constantinople; or let them give it to your fraternity. It must nevertheless be written in the same form, as I have said, and conveyed to us in every way under your administration.

As for the Thessalonians, whose legates came to us through the arrangement of our most faithful and illustrious son, the emperor, we wish you to know, lest we seem to have omitted anything, that, according to whatever pleased our Lord Jesus Christ when He inspired us, the whole matter is to be examined by your deliberation, and, if they fulfill what is required, arranged accordingly.

Through our brother and fellow bishop, the most reverend John, and through our sons Heraclianus the presbyter and Constantinus the deacon, men worthy of ecclesiastical honor, we were content to reply in writing concerning what pertained to the matter. We rejoiced that in a man of our order we had found equal worth and a pious purpose, together with instructions from the legation consonant with wisdom and conduct.

For it is a wished-for and joyous thing that those who happen to be fellow heirs of communion and office should be proved worthy by a just assessment.

And in another hand:

> “May God preserve you in health, most honorable brother.”

The most holy archbishop said:

“Now let the most God-fearing notaries of our most holy Church make known to us any documents in their possession that concern the present case.”

When the documents had been produced by Cosmas, the most God-fearing deacon, notary, and archivist, Macarius, the most God-fearing deacon and notary, read the petition submitted on behalf of the clergy of Theopolis and the report of the synod then residing in the imperial city, both addressed to John, the archbishop who had been appointed, among the saints, to that same imperial city.

Calonymus, the most God-fearing deacon and notary, read from a codex the letter to John, the archbishop appointed to Jerusalem, of holy memory, and to Epiphanius, bishop appointed to Tyre, of God-loving memory. He also read the letter sent by John, the bishop of Jerusalem, and by the synod under him, to holy John.

Stephen, the most God-fearing notary and deacon, read the report sent by Epiphanius, bishop of Tyre, and by the synod under him.

Paul, the most God-fearing notary and deacon, read the report, together with the proceedings, sent by the bishops of Second Syria to John, the archbishop appointed to the imperial city, among the saints. All these documents were entered into the record.

## Letter of the Emperor Justin to Hormisdas

He indicates that Paul of Antioch, accused of certain matters, had resigned the episcopate.

Justin Augustus to Pope Hormisdas.

So that what happened concerning Paul, a most reverend man, may become known to Your Apostolate: he is said, although holding the priesthood of the city of Antioch, to have conducted himself in many matters foreign to religious bishops, so that he was accused by the betrayal of his own clergy, by the inhabitants of the said city, and by many others who frequently brought accusations—not only before the legates of Your Holiness who are stationed in this royal city, whom we likewise believe should be retained, but also after their departure.

Fearing, in addition, that the testimony of his bad conscience, once an inquiry had been held, might demand a more serious form of conclusion, he presented petitions of refusal so that he might be permitted to withdraw from the episcopal office he had undertaken, as has been said.

Since it has always been close to our heart that the bishops of cities should be held in the common love of all those whose souls they have received to govern, and since Paul, the most reverend man, voluntarily resigned his priesthood, as we have mentioned, we judged that the present letter should be sent so that the matter might be opened to you and that he might deign, through his own prayers, to obtain heavenly protection for us.

Given on the Kalends of May at Constantinople, in the consulship of Justinian and Valerius, men of illustrious rank (in the year of the Lord 521).

## Report of Epiphanius, Bishop of Constantinople

The same matters as in the preceding letter.

To the most holy and blessed lord, brother and fellow minister, Hormisdas: Epiphanius, bishop.

We desire to write more frequently to Your Beatitude and to enjoy the affection of fraternal charity. But now, wishing that what has happened should not remain unknown to Your Holiness, we have used the present writing.

For Antioch, the greatest city in the first Eastern diocese, was surrounded for a long period by many disturbances. On the pretext that Paul, beloved of God, held the episcopate of that city, and because, as some said, many inhabitants of the city were separating themselves from the Catholic Church, they made repeated appeals to our most peaceful and faithful prince, asking that an investigation be made public into the matters brought forward as accusations.

These matters began some time ago, as was not unknown to the legates beloved of God whom Your Holiness sent, when they were staying in the royal city, since they learned everything concerning them.

Accordingly, Paul, beloved of God, thinking that this would benefit him, chose through his own petitions to abandon the said city and the episcopate, showing that he preferred universal quiet and withdrawal from the accusations.

We know that he made all these matters known to our prince, beloved of Christ, and to Your Reverence. But now, what is more precious to all of us, and what we desire most, is that you should speedily send us good news concerning those legates beloved of God whom the most loving prince and we have sent to Your Beatitude: they are announcing peace pleasing to God and proclaiming the unity of the holy Churches, adorned with every beauty.

May you, blessed and most holy brother, deign to send them to us quickly, so that, as we have often written, the heavenly gain of the present case may belong to those who have brought about its good correction.

We and those who are with us salute the whole fraternity that is with Your Beatitude in Christ, for many years.

[Note: From Labbe’s Appendix, volume IV.]

## Letter LXXXI. To Remigius, Bishop of Reims

[Note: See the following note.]

### Observation of P. Antonio Pagi on the year of Christ 514, no. 5

Hincmar, in the Life of Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims, after narrating the Gothic war and the embassy sent by the emperor Anastasius to Gaul, discusses the vicariate, or primacy, of this bishop throughout the kingdom of Clovis, king of the Franks. Hincmar himself was the first to retrieve this account from the archives of his Church, and he attributes its origin to Hormisdas, who assumed the Roman pontificate in this year. But since it is certain that Clovis did not live into the time of Hormisdas, some learned men took this as a basis for judging the story fabricated, and various writings consequently appeared here and there. Sirmond rejected the letter of Hormisdas to Remigius from the Gallican councils and took no account of it.

He delegates his authority to him in the kingdom of Clovis, the Frankish king recently converted to the faith.

To his most beloved brother Remigius: Hormisdas.

Having received the communications of your fraternity with full fraternal rejoicing, by which you gladdened us through the indication of your genuine salvation, strengthened by bodily health together with spiritual duties, we recognized that it was fitting to reveal in words the joy we carry in our mind.

For you display the proofs of a supreme pontiff when you do what deserves proclamation and do not delay in making it known. We therefore take precedence from the judgment of our own election, since we have learned that you have done what we most earnestly command others to do: in provinces separated by such great distance, you should strive to apply both the vigor of the apostolic see and the safeguard of the Fathers’ regulations.

Accordingly, in the kingdom of our beloved and spiritual son Clovis, whom, with heavenly grace assisting, you recently converted to the faith together with his entire people, through a multitude of miracles accompanying your life-giving preaching, and whom you consecrated through the gift of holy baptism, we entrust our authority to you by the present decree, without prejudice to the privileges that antiquity granted to metropolitans.

By sharing in this ministry, we increase the dignity of your zeal and lighten the watchfulness required of us by the same administration. Although you do not need instruction about individual matters, since we have already proved that you preserve everything with exceptional care, it is nevertheless more pleasing when a path is shown to those who will travel it and the form of the task imposed is made clear to those who will labor.

We therefore command that the paternal regulations and the decrees defined by the most holy councils be observed by all. In these we display your vigilance; in these, your care and the admonitions of fraternal exhortation. When these are guarded with the reverence they deserve, no obstacle to holy observance leaves room for guilt. There what is permitted and forbidden has been prescribed; there what is prohibited is set out, to which no one may dare aspire; there what is granted is specified, which should be undertaken in a manner pleasing to God.

Whenever the cause of the whole religion demands a council, let all the brothers assemble when summoned by you. If the particular concern of any of them gives rise to disputes, restrain the quarrels that have arisen among them, settling the controversies after examining them according to sacred law.

Whatever is there established for the sake of faith and truth, commanded through prudent administration, or confirmed by the authority of our person, let all of it reach our knowledge through an informed report bearing testimony. Thus both our spirit will enjoy the charity of the office entrusted to us and yours will enjoy the security of what you have received.

May God preserve you safe, dearest brother.

[Note: Ballerini found the following two letters, not yet published in the collection of Avellana contained in Vatican Codex 4961, and published them in the dissertation prefixed to volume III of the works of Saint Leo the Great, page CLXVI and following. They are therefore transferred here.]

Hormisdas.

Whenever it is necessary for writings to be sent to the lord son, the most merciful prince, we cannot pass over Your Magnificence in silence. Therefore, after first offering the honor of a respectful greeting, we commend those who have been sent on official business, asking that, with the Lord’s help, they may quickly reach their destination under your direction, so that the most sacred and religious emperor may learn without delay the glory of his merits.

Justin Augustus to Hormisdas.

We received the illustrious bishop R. with a grateful spirit, not only because of the honor owed to priests, but also because of our affection for Your Holiness. For whoever has been approved by your judgment is also judged by us to be thoroughly approved.

A decision concerning the assistance and favor that should be offered to the holy Churches will be made more opportunely when the legates whom we recently sent to the mighty king Thrasamund have returned and, with the Divinity favorable, brought us his reply.

May Your Beatitude deign to ask heavenly protection for us through unceasing prayers.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December at Constantinople, under our lord Justin, perpetual Augustus—supply “in the consulship,” that is, in the year 519—received on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Rusticus, that is, in the year 520.

## Decrees of Pope Hormisdas Taken from Gratian

### First Decree

A man confined in a monastery to perform penance is not to be ordained a presbyter.

If a man who voluntarily seeks penance cannot be ordained bishop or presbyter, even if he performs that penance perfectly, so that, if he should have been ordained through ignorance and is afterward proved to have undertaken penance, he must be deposed—then with what conscience is a man who is unwillingly sent to a monastery to perform penance permitted to attain the priesthood? Such a man must certainly be called nothing other than a penitent.

Let no one bring against me any such objections contrary to the authority of the apostolic see or contrary to the constitutions of the three hundred and eighteen bishops and the remaining canons. For whatever is said against their definition, in which we believe the Holy Spirit spoke, I do not doubt that accepting it would be not only rash but dangerous (Distinct. 50, “If the one who…”).

### Second Decree

Secret marriages may not be celebrated.

No member of the faithful, whatever his condition, is to marry secretly. Rather, after receiving the priest’s blessing, he is to marry publicly in the Lord (30, question 5, “No member of the faithful”).

### Third Decree

Palea. The same, to Bishop Eusebius.

Your Holiness, venerable brother, asked us concerning an adulterous [or, according to the variant, adult] son whose father wishes him to marry, whether the father can do so without the will of the adult son. We answer: if the son does not consent in any way, it cannot be done.

But if the son is not yet an adult, so that his will cannot yet be discerned, the father may give him in marriage to whomever he wishes; and when the son reaches full age, he must entirely observe and fulfill the arrangement.

We command that this, sanctioned by us, be observed by all worshipers of the orthodox faith (31, question 2, “Your Holiness”).

### Fourth Decree

An altar is not to be erected in a consecrated church without the bishop’s permission.

No presbyter shall erect another altar in a consecrated church [Col. 0526C], except one that has been consecrated by the bishop of the place—or with his permission—so that there may be a distinction between what is sacred and what is not sacred; nor shall he pretend that a dedication has occurred when it has not. If he does so, he shall be degraded if he is a cleric; but if he is a layman, he shall be anathematized.

[Note: [Col. 0525] In my manuscript codex Burchard, Book III, chapter 18, reads thus, and, in my judgment, better: “or has been consecrated with his permission.” —Mansi.]

## FROM THE TEACHING OF POPE HORMISDAS, CHAPTER IV

Burchard, Book IV, chapter 57.

If anyone baptizes or performs any divine office recklessly, although he has not been ordained [variant: “has been ordained”], he shall be expelled from the Church and shall never be ordained.

[Note: [Col. 0525D]]

## PHILIPPE LABBE, S.J.,’S OBSERVATION

It has always seemed absolutely certain to learned men up to the present that Pope Gelasius, the supreme pontiff, wrote in a Roman synod of seventy bishops a decree or notice concerning the sacred and apocryphal books. To pass over countless ancient manuscript codices of the highest distinction, Pope Nicholas I himself mentions it in Letter 42, sent to all the bishops of Gaul, in these words:

“Saint Gelasius, pope, most holy and eloquent in his decrees, agrees with this most blessed Pope Leo, saying: ‘We decree that the decretal letters which the most blessed popes, at various times, issued from the city of Rome in response to consultations concerning various Fathers are to be received with reverence,’” and so forth.

Many years afterward, Gratian included it in his *Concord of Discordant Canons*, Part I, Distinction 15, chapter “The Holy Roman Church.” Yet there were some who, on the basis of certain manuscript codices—especially the Jurensian codex from the monastery of Saint Eugendus, or, as I may call it in ordinary speech, Saint Claude, and the ancient Urgellian codex of excellent quality, as Stephen Baluzius, who saw it, can testify to me—wanted to attribute it to Pope Hormisdas, who governed the Roman Church third after Gelasius.

See what our Chiffletius published at Dijon—when this fourth volume of ours was hastening toward the press—in the notes on Vigilius Tapsensis, p. 149, beginning as follows:

> Here begins the decretal issued in the city of Rome by Pope Hormisdas.
>
> Concerning what the universal Catholic Church receives regarding the divine Scriptures, and what after this it ought to avoid.
>
> **Titles**
>
> I. Concerning the order of the canonical books of the Old and New Testament. [Col. 0528A] II. Concerning the number of apostolic sees. III. Concerning the constitutions of the holy councils. IV. Concerning the writings of the holy Fathers that are received. V. Concerning the writings of the apocrypha that are not to be received. VI. The order concerning the Old Testament which the holy …  
>
> There is no need to repeat these matters here, since they have been published above. If any variant readings of significance occur that differ from ours, they will not be omitted in the notes to Gelasius’s decree. (See our *Patrologia*, vol. LIX, col. 166.)

[Col. 0527]

# APPENDIX TO THE LETTERS OF HORMISDAS

## Collector’s Notice

[Col. 0527B]

Since the distinguished Labbe, following a commendable policy, judged that spurious letters falsely attributed to pontiffs should also be added to the genuine papal letters in his collection, I likewise proposed to publish any spurious papal letters that I happened to encounter. Readers will therefore judge fairly and favorably if they find here a letter of Pope Hormisdas, which plainly bears the characteristic marks of a forgery, since it praises Pope John, who was certainly later than Hormisdas.

It was taken from the *Penitential* of Bishop Halitgar of Cambrai, compiled more than nine hundred years ago and published by Canisius in *Veterum Lectionum*, vol. II, part 2, p. 143, Basnage edition.

[Note: [Col. 0527D] Jacobus Petit published this same letter, written in nearly the same words—with the exception of a few variant readings—in volume I of the *Penitential of Theodore of Canterbury*, among excerpts of canons taken from the ancient collection of the Herovallian codex. There, Petit reports that it bears this heading: “Letter of Pope Hormisdas to all the provinces,” although Petit himself admits that the heading was added by a later hand. It is also worth observing that Gratian’s canons 29 and 58 of Distinction 50 were taken from this apocryphal letter. Moreover, the letter as printed by Petit contains at the beginning certain passages lacking in the Canisian version; for it begins: “If any deacon or presbyter, after receiving the Levitical blessing, is found incontinent with his wife, let him be expelled as incontinent. Behold, most manifestly …”]

## HERE BEGINS THE LETTER OF POPE HORMISDAS TO ALL THE PROVINCES

Behold, it is most manifestly established that this agrees with the titles of the ancient Fathers transmitted by Pope John, with the judgments of the three hundred and eighteen bishops, and also with the canons of the Gallican council. [Col. 0527C]

Clerics caught in adultery, whether they have confessed it themselves or have been convicted by others, cannot return to their rank. And because perhaps there are some who, through excessive compassion, are not at all pleased with the severity of the holy Fathers stated above, let them know that they are criticizing or condemning the judgments of the three hundred and eighteen bishops and of those who established the remaining canons.

Perhaps, however, their compassion is greater than that of the aforementioned 318 bishops, their mercy greater than that of holy John, the apostolic pope, and their charity greater than that of the other priests who, by examples or remedies, determined this in their ecclesiastical definitions. Therefore, let them either readily consent to their commands; or, if they do not, let them recognize that they are opposed to and enemies of all of them.

What kind of hostile kindness is it to stroke criminals and leave their wounds untreated until the day of judgment? Even if you see them performing the most severe penance for many years, we must both consider their salvation and preserve the ordinances of the canons. But when in some of them there appears neither the contrition of humility nor perseverance in prayer or lamentation, and they do not imitate blessed David, who said, “Every night I wash my bed; I water my couch with my tears” (Psalm 6), nor this: “I ate ashes like bread, and mingled my drink with weeping” (Psalm 10), and when we do not see them devoting themselves to fasting or reading, we can recognize how negligently, how lukewarmly, and with what hostile security of soul they would remain if they were restored to their former rank, believing that God had forgiven them without worthy penance, just as they see the priests have forgiven them. [Col. 0528B]

I speak truly: those very people whom we seem to forgive through dangerous and false mercy, when they come to be condemned before the tribunal of Christ for such great sins, will bring accusations against us, saying that, either because we feared the harshness of their speech or gladly accepted their false flatteries and dangerous praises, we permitted them, by granting them useless forgiveness, to remain in their sins—or even to increase those sins. Nor will they remember what is written in the Old Testament: “Because of one sinner, the wrath of God raged against all.”

O piety! O mercy! To spare one person and bring everyone into danger through a bad example!

Saint Cyprian, the most holy martyr, does not advise this when he says: “He who strokes a sinner with flattering words supplies fuel for sin.” He does not destroy the offenses of that person, but, like an inexperienced physician, fosters them again: he touches with a sparing hand the swollen recesses of wounds and, while preserving the hidden poison in their deepest cavities, makes it worse. Thus Saint John, bishop of Constantinople, also rebukes such conduct, saying: “He is an inexperienced physician who lays a scar over putrefaction that has not been digested.”

Therefore, consider carefully whether it is possible or right for us to disregard the canons of such and so many priests as we have mentioned above, and presume to observe or do anything different from what they established—especially when we have neglected the holy decrees of those three hundred and eighteen bishops, who ordered councils to be held throughout all the Churches. In disregarding them, we despise not only those men, but also, as was said above, the Africans and all the others who, under their direction, established something throughout the world by ecclesiastical discipline, thereby sinning against our own souls. [Col. 0528D]

I do not dare to expose myself to this danger, since my merits are not such that I should presume to take upon myself the sins of others. Nor do I possess such eloquence that I could plead before the tribunal of Christ against so many and such holy priests who established the canons. Let each person see how he intends to think and observe, and how he will be able to give an account on the day of judgment.

As far as God deigns to give me strength, I wish to strive to obey their commands, because I desire to have peace with such men, in whatever way that may be possible, not quarrels. This also must be carefully considered: if, according to what is written, those clerics who return to their own wives are to be suspended from office completely. And likewise of husbands in second marriages? Although they are doing something lawful, they nevertheless cannot be ordained as clerics; or, if they have been ordained, they must be deposed.

Saint Faustus, bishop, said of them in his letter: “The consecrated person loses grace when he wishes to exercise the office of a husband.” Since these things are so, with what conscience can anyone say that a man who has committed adultery may return again to his rank?

At this point, if someone should say, “Then you deny the mercy of God, who said, ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live’; and also, ‘Will not he who falls rise again?’; and again, ‘On whatever day the sinner is converted, all his iniquities shall be consigned to oblivion’?”—we both can and must answer these words freely.

Far be it from us even lightly to doubt these statements. For we firmly believe that whoever performs penance until the end of his life will not only receive forgiveness but will also attain eternal rewards. Nevertheless, because of ecclesiastical discipline and the institutions of the ancient Fathers, far be it from us to presume either to criticize or to scrutinize them.

Although we believe that, after blessed penance, a person comes to eternal life, we know from the commands of so many Fathers that he ought not to return to the clerical rank. Indeed, the canons state that no penitent may ever be ordained as a cleric.

If a person who voluntarily seeks penance cannot be ordained bishop or presbyter, even when he has performed that penance perfectly—and if, although he was ordained through ignorance, he is later found to have undertaken penance, he must be deposed—then a man who is unwillingly sent to a monastery to perform penance is certainly to be called a penitent. With what conscience, therefore, may he be permitted to attain the priesthood?

Let no one bring against me any argument contrary to the authority of the apostolic see, or contrary to the commands of the three hundred and eighteen bishops, or contrary to the ordinances of the remaining canons. For I have no doubt that to accept anything said against their definition—of those in whom we believe the Holy Spirit spoke—is not only rash but also dangerous. [Col. 0529C]

I greatly fear and tremble at the condemnation deserved by that priest because of his foolish indulgence: because he neither corrected his sons with due severity nor wished to strike them [variant: “to beat them”] or excommunicate them, the sons themselves were killed on one day, thirty thousand of the people were slain, the ark of the covenant was captured, and he himself, falling backward with his neck broken, died; his name was erased from the book of life, and so forth.

By contrast, Phinehas, moved by zeal for God, killed two adulterers together and thereby freed the entire people from God’s wrath.

I do not say this so that, as he did, the priests of the Lord should now avenge matters through bodily death; rather, I say that it is better for each person, for a short time while he lives in this world, to endure shame or disgrace than afterward to arrive at eternal punishments. It is much more beneficial for him, for the sake of the example of others, to live apart from honor and perform penance for as long as he lives, thereby acquiring a remedy for himself on the day of necessity.

Whoever wishes to burden my humble self in this matter, I do not propose to give any other answer than what the canons mentioned above appear to contain.

[Col. 0529]

# LETTERS OF POPE JOHN (C, G)*

[Note: [Col. 0529D] Many considerations demonstrate that this letter and the following one are spurious.]

## FIRST LETTER OF POPE JOHN I TO ZACHARIAS, ARCHBISHOP

### Concerning the Accusation of Bishops

John, bishop of the city of Rome, to Zacharias, archbishop, greetings.

[Col. 0530A]

Your affection, dearest brother, requires from us a precept of the apostolic see (Zacharias, Letter 1) in which the decrees of the Fathers concur, and which we believe it is not lawful to deny either to you or to any priest who lives and believes rightly. Although, on account of your merit (Innocent, Letter 2) and the dignity of the priesthood, in which you are especially distinguished, you know all the rules of ecclesiastical life and teaching [variant: “you are thoroughly acquainted with them”], nevertheless, because you have earnestly requested the norm and authority of the Roman Church, we have taken care to reply briefly to your written request [variant: “we have not refused”].

For it is unjust rashly to judge the hidden matters of another’s heart (Prosper, Saying 21), and it is a sin to condemn on suspicion someone whose works appear to be nothing but good. Therefore, the sheep entrusted to their shepherd ought not to rebuke him unless he has strayed from the true faith, and they can in no way accuse him. For the deeds of shepherds are not to be struck by the sword of the mouth, even though they may appear rightly subject to correction.

We say this because we have found in your writings that certain bishops in your regions were accused by their own sheep—some on suspicion, others for a definite reason—and that for this reason some were stripped of their possessions, while others were driven from their own sees. You should know that such men cannot be summoned either to a provincial synod or to a general council, nor can they be judged in any matter, until everything taken from them has been restored to their lawful authority. [Col. 0530B]

First, therefore, everything must be restored to them according to law; the Churches taken from them must be returned with all their privileges; and afterward they must be granted not a short period of time, but as much time as they appear to have been stripped or expelled, before they are summoned to a synod and heard by all the bishops of their province.

For a man who has been stripped or expelled can neither be summoned to trial nor judged [Ivo, *Decretals*, Book IV], since there is no privilege by which one who has already been stripped bare can be stripped again. Hence it was decreed in ancient times:

“Let all possessions, everything taken from him, and all his revenues be restored to the original possessor before the case is joined” [variant: “before the case is constituted”].

[Note: [Col. 0530D] I think *perceptos* should be read, rather than *praeceptor*, as the Justinian Code has it.]

Elsewhere it is written:

“He who has suffered violence shall receive back everything as it was, and shall securely retain what he possesses” [variant: “what he possessed”].

Elsewhere, in the synodal decrees of the Fathers and in the edicts of kings, the following ordinance is found:

“All things are to be restored immediately to bishops who have been stripped or expelled, by order of the pontiffs, and everything is to be completely recalled to their authority [variant: “ownership”] from which they departed—whatever the lapse of time, or whether they are known to have lost Church property, private property, or their possessions through fraud, captivity, the power of the great, or any other unjust causes—before their accusation or their lawful summons [variant: “convocation”] to a synod,” and so forth.

There is also a decree in the ancient statutes of the Church [Ivo, *Decretals*, Book IV] that whoever invades another’s property shall not go unpunished, but shall restore everything with increase. Hence it is written in the Gospel:

“If I have defrauded anyone, I restore fourfold” (Luke 19).

The laws of the world also provide:

“He who takes away another’s property shall restore to the person whose property was seized elevenfold what was taken.” [Col. 0530D]

And in the divine law it is written:

“Cursed is everyone who moves his neighbor’s boundary marker.” And all the people shall say, “Amen” (Deuteronomy 27).

Such actions, therefore, must not be presumed without punishment, nor carried out without condemnation. But you, dearest brother, take care not to transgress these things, and teach the other bishops—both those entrusted to your care and the rest—to uphold them firmly, because they cannot transgress the apostolic statutes without grave danger to the rank of the transgressor.

But do not believe hostile accusers, or those who come forward from an enemy’s gift [variant: “house”], or those who live with enemies; nor should angry men who desire to harm be trusted, lest those who have been injured wish to take revenge. Such persons too must be rejected, not approved.

Hold fast to these things, dearest brother, and always avoid what is forbidden. Strive to fulfill what was rightly said to Jesus son of Sirach:

“Fight for the truth unto death, and the Lord your God will fight for you always” (Ecclesiasticus 4).

For this reason the holy Church has been entrusted to you and to us: so that we may labor for everyone and not neglect to bring aid to all. For “while a strong man armed guards his courtyard, all that he possesses is at peace” (Luke 11).

Therefore, since such great necessity presses, it is especially necessary, by your apostolic authority, to restrain hostile bishops and raise up the oppressed, so that, with the Lord’s help, we ourselves may deserve to offer sacrifice unharmed and joyfully at all times, without serious difficulty.

The friendly character of the work I have undertaken also compels me to return to you (Ennodius, *Apology for the Same Symmachus*), since until now I have wished to devote myself to better matters through sermons [variant: “I have wished to recount better works”], while this poisoned necessity demands such a response. The dwelling of the heavenly command either joins us or separates us. It does not matter what distances divide us, if they are held together by the key of the heavenly dwelling. Such men will not be able to harm you if you do not delay in bringing one another assistance. [Col. 0531B]

It is an unheard-of form of sacrilege when a rival, marked out by the honor of a pretended religion, disguises himself. He dishonors the reverence due to a venerable name when he claims to be an assistant in matters which he boasts have been committed to God. It is an insult, as though he were present as a lofty support, in accordance with the Apostle’s words:

“Who are you to judge another’s servant?” (Romans 14).

Why do they deceive inexperienced ears and make the appearance of vengeance seem heavier than the guilt? If they hate, let them correct their excesses [variant: “cleanse them”]. Why, then, do they condemn crimes more freely than they avoid them? Everyone who attacks the Fathers or does not fear to disparage them is surely his own assailant.

There is nothing in which you cannot overcome the weapons of your enemies, with the Lord’s help, if, according to the voice of truth, you have toward one another the love that the Lord commanded (John 13). [Col. 0531C]

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, during the consulships of the most distinguished men Maximus [in the year of the Lord 523] and Olybrius [526].

[Note: [Col. 0531D] This consular date is erroneous, as will be evident from what we say below. I think it should be referred to the consulship of Maximus without a colleague, which fell in the year of the Lord 523. —Severinus Binius.]

[Note: [Col. 0531D] Pope John, having been banished from the city by order of Theoderic, wrote this letter from the prison in which, not long afterward, he expired, consumed by filth and hunger. He urges the bishops of Italy to defend the Catholic faith against the Arians and to restore to Catholic worship, by sacred rites, the churches usurped by them.]

## LETTER II TO THE BISHOPS OF ITALY

### Concerning King Theoderic; the Defense of the Catholic Faith against the Arians; and the Consecration of Their Churches by Sacred Rites and Their Reconciliation to Divine Worship

John, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Italy.

I have very often learned by experience that your holy zeal for the Christian religion grows and expands through glorious increase, and that the true faith—which consoles and strengthens not only me but all the priests of the Lord—is recognized and extended in your minds and works through your priestly ministry (Saint Leo, Letter 70).

[Col. 0531D]

Therefore, brothers, I exhort and admonish you to arm yourselves against Arian perfidy—which has been condemned not once but often in the past, and which is now reviving in certain places—with the sword of the Holy Spirit, so that, with divine grace assisting us, we may crush and eradicate it so completely that its root may not be found in the future.

Wherever you find churches belonging to the Arians, consecrate them as Catholic churches without delay through divine prayers and works. For when we were at Constantinople, both for the Catholic religion and for the cause and affairs of King Theoderic, and when the most pious and most Christian Justin, the orthodox emperor, advised and urged us while also eradicating the Arians, we consecrated as Catholic, with the Lord’s help, whatever churches belonging to them we were able to find in those regions. [Note: Gregory of Tours has nearly the same account in chapter 40 of the book *On the Glory of the Martyrs*.]

And although the aforesaid King Theoderic, inwardly touched by and outwardly enveloped in their pestilence, threatens to destroy us and our whole region [variant: “your region”] and consume it with sword and fire, do not therefore fail. Rather, work manfully in the Lord’s field, and, according to the voice of Truth:

“Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can cast both soul and body into Gehenna” (Matthew 10:28).

The outstanding Apostle to the Gentiles says:

“For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord, and ourselves as your servants through Jesus. For God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ himself shone in our hearts for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ Jesus.

“But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the excellence of the power may be God’s and not yours. In everything we suffer affliction, but we are not crushed; we are perplexed, but not destitute; we suffer persecution, but are not forsaken; we are cast down, but do not perish. We always carry in our bodies the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies. For we who live are always being handed over to death because of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our mortal flesh. Therefore death works in us, but life in you.

“Having the same spirit of faith, as it is written: ‘I believed, and therefore I spoke,’ we also believe, and therefore speak, knowing that he who raised Jesus will also raise us with Jesus and place us with you. For everything is for your sake, so that grace, abounding through many acts of thanksgiving [variant: “through many people in thanksgiving”], may abound to the glory of God.

“Therefore we do not fail. Although our outward man is being corrupted, yet our inward man is renewed day by day. For this momentary and light affliction of ours is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure, while we look not at the things that are seen but at the things that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:5–18). [Col. 0532C]

“For we know that if our earthly dwelling, this habitation, is dissolved, we have an edifice from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this we groan, desiring to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling, if indeed we are found clothed and not naked. For we who are in this tent groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be stripped but clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. Now the one who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the pledge of the Spirit.

“Therefore, always confident and knowing that while we are in this body we are away from the Lord—for we walk by faith and not by sight—we are confident, and we have the good will rather to be away from the body and present with the Lord. And therefore we strive, whether absent or present, to please him. For we must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive the things done in the body, whether good or evil.

“Knowing, therefore, the fear of the Lord, we persuade people; but to God we are manifest, and I hope that we are also manifest to your consciences. We do not commend ourselves to you again, but give you an occasion to glory on our behalf, so that you may have something to say to those who glory in appearance and not in heart. For whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are sober, it is for you.

“For the love of Christ urges us, judging this: that if one died for all, then all have died; and he died for all, so that those who live may no longer live for themselves but for him who died and rose again for them. Therefore, from now on we know no one according to the flesh. And even if we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him so. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new.

“But all things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation: namely, that God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not counting their offenses against them, and placing in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore, we act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God. He who knew no sin he made sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:1–21).

“And as helpers we exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For he says: ‘In an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.’ Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.

“Giving no one any occasion for offense, so that our ministry may not be blamed, but in everything let us present ourselves as God’s ministers: in great patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distresses, in blows, in prisons, in seditions, in labors, in vigils, in fasts, in purity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God, through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left; through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers yet truthful, as unknown yet known; as dying, and behold, we live; as chastised yet not killed; as sorrowful yet always rejoicing; as poor yet enriching many; as having nothing yet possessing everything” (2 Corinthians 6:1–10).

“Finally, brothers, rejoice; be perfected; exhort one another; be at peace, so that the God of peace and love may always be with you. Amen” (2 Corinthians 13:11, 13).

[Note: [Col. 0533B] This is erroneous and corrupt. If, as the *Roman Martyrology* states, the same John is recorded as having died on 27 May in the year of the Lord 526, during the consulship of Olybrius, it cannot in any way be maintained that he wrote this letter on the third day before the Ides of June in the same year and under the same consulship of Olybrius.]

Given on the third day before the Ides of June, during the consulships of the most distinguished men Maximus [Note: [Col. 0534B] The consulship of Maximus has been added here and must therefore be deleted. Each of the two men held the consulship in different years: Maximus in the year of Christ 523, Olybrius in 526. Moreover, it cannot be admitted that this letter was given on the third day before the Ides of June during the consulship of Maximus. At that time John was not yet pontiff, for he began to occupy the see in August of that same year. It must therefore be said that this letter was written during the consulship of Olybrius without a colleague, in the year of the Lord 526. Hence it is clear why I said above that the preceding letter should be referred to the consulship of Maximus without a colleague.] and Olybrius [Note: [Col. 0534B] This date too is erroneous, since John died on 27 May in the year 526.].

[Col. 0534B]

## AT THE SAME TIME: TRIFOLIUS, PRESBYTER

[Col. 0533]

## NOTICE

(From Cave.)

[Col. 0533C]

Trifolius, a presbyter by rank—but who can tell us from what place?—was prominent in the year 520. Faustus, a Roman senator and praetorian prefect, had asked him whether anything concerning the teaching of the Scythian monks could be found in the writings of the Fathers. Trifolius replied to Faustus by letter, in which he argues from the decrees of the four general councils against John the Scythian and his monks, who had recently arrived at Rome. Labbe recovered this letter, mutilated at the end, from the Sirmond papers and published it in *Councils*, vol. IV, p. 1590.

[Col. 0533]

# LETTER OF TRIFOLIUS THE PRESBYTER TO THE BLESSED FAUSTUS THE SENATOR, AGAINST JOHN THE SCYTHIAN MONK (C, S)

[Note: [Col. 0533] He appears to be the Faustus to whom, as praetorian prefect, several letters are extant in Cassiodorus, *Variae*, Book IV.]

## PHILIPPE LABBE, S.J.,’S OBSERVATION

[Col. 0533D]

Whoever has carefully considered the report of Dioscorus the deacon, sent from Constantinople to Pope Hormisdas at Rome, concerning the Scythian monks who affirmed that one of the Trinity had suffered and been crucified; the subsequent petition of Bishops Germanus and John; and the sixty-six letters of Pope Hormisdas, together with many others written afterward by him on the same matter—such a person will undoubtedly read without reluctance the hitherto unpublished letter of Trifolius the presbyter on the same subject, addressed to Faustus the senator. I found it lying hidden among the papers of our Sirmond, and now present it to you, reader, so that you may form a more certain judgment concerning this entire controversy.

You were pleased to inform me that Scythian monks had arrived from Constantinople who preach that one of the Trinity was crucified, hoping that I might find something of this kind in the teaching of the Fathers. This doctrine arose from the source of Arius and is consistent with all heresies. See: whatever the four councils placed in their definition of the faith—that is, Nicaea, Constantinople, the First Council of Ephesus, and Chalcedon—and whatever appears in the letters of the holy Fathers that the four holy councils wished to have authority in matters of faith—namely, the letter of Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, to Bishop Epictetus; one letter of Cyril to Nestorius and another to John of Antioch; and the letters of Pope Leo—if anyone wishes to add to, subtract from, or interpret otherwise than the Fathers set forth in the writings mentioned above or in their conciliar definition, whoever he may be, he is a heretic.

For the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three persons, one God: voice, word, and breath. The voice is the Father, the word the Son, and the breath the Holy Spirit. The person of the Father and the person of the Holy Spirit are without flesh; but the person of the Son, who was always with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is in the Trinity, that is, the Word of God. God entered the womb of the Virgin Mary and assumed from her the nature of flesh, not a person.

Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ has two natures and one person, the Word—that is, the Son of God, God immortal, invisible, and impassible. The flesh of this Word is mortal, visible, and passible. The Father is not the Father of the Trinity, but of the Son; the Son is not the Son of the Trinity, but of the Father; and the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Trinity, but from the Father and the Son.

There are not three gods, nor three fathers, nor three sons, nor three Holy Spirits. Those who say that one of the Trinity suffered—if they are not Arians—should say from which three one suffered: from three fathers, or from three sons, or from three Holy Spirits, or certainly from three gods, as Arius says.

There is one God, creator, impassible and immortal. But there is another created god, passible and mortal; or, as Sabellius says, since he denies that there are three persons and thinks that they are merely spoken of, he therefore said that one person of the Trinity, the Father, was incarnate and suffered.

Apollinaris, however, denies that Christ had a soul and an intellect and says that God took the place of his soul and intellect. Therefore he says that one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh. If one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh, the flesh remained impassible. Those who say that the Son, one of the Trinity, suffered worship two or three sons, of whom one suffered while two remain impassible.

But if the Son is of the Trinity, he is neither of the Father according to deity nor of his mother according to the flesh; rather, he is of the Trinity, and the Trinity becomes four, as Nestorius says: Mary’s son was associated with the Son of God and became common to the Trinity, and one of the Trinity suffered.

Arius divides one God into two gods. Nestorius, by adding another son according to the flesh to the Trinity, makes four persons. Eutyches mixes together the two natures of the one Son of God, like a baker mixing flour and water: afterward there is neither flour nor water, but a third thing, bread. In the same way Eutyches mixes the natures of God and man, so that afterward there is neither God nor man, neither Father nor Son nor Holy Spirit, but that one who is of the Trinity.

How do such men claim to follow the Council of Chalcedon while preaching what that council did not accept? For in the fourth session of the Council of Chalcedon, at the end, the judges questioned the archimandrites Carosus and Dorotheus as follows:

“Eutyches said that the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was not of our substance. What do you confess concerning this?”

Dorotheus the archimandrite said: “We have been baptized in the name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, confessing our Savior Jesus Christ, who descended and was incarnate from the holy Virgin Mary, assumed humanity, and was crucified: one of the Trinity suffered.”

For saying such things, the aforesaid archimandrites received condemnation together with the Eutychian and all heretics. “In the letter,” they say, “of Proclus it is written: ‘One of the Trinity suffered.’ If heretics have falsified the letters of the Fathers Athanasius, Cyril, and Leo, which were reread and confirmed by the universal holy councils, how much more likely are they to have falsified the letters of Proclus, which were not included in the definition of even one council?”

Heretics always try, by wrongly interpreting the sayings of the Fathers, to confirm their own heresies, as Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, says to John of Antioch, among other things:

“But when some of those who habitually pervert what is right change my words into whatever pleases them, let your holiness not marvel at this, knowing that all heretics gather from the divinely inspired Scriptures opportunities for their error.”

And shortly afterward:

“Since, moreover, we add that certain persons, corrupting the letter of our renowned father Athanasius addressed to the most blessed Epictetus, though it was sound, published it in such a form that many might thereby be harmed…”

Likewise Pope Leo writes to the emperor Marcian (*Epistle* 75), among other things:

“Since, moreover, the crafty wickedness of certain heretics is said to have falsified my letter, which I sent to Flavian of blessed memory, in order to disturb the simplicity of our people, so that, by changing certain words or syllables, it might assert that I accepted the error of Nestorius…”

If anything is found in the sayings of the holy Fathers that does not agree with the holy letters or with the definition of the Council of Chalcedon, it is clear that it has been falsified by heretics. Iniquity is always spoken, and never yields.

What does it mean to say that one of the Trinity suffered, except to point out that another of the Trinity was impassible, as Arius teaches? Or what does it mean to say that one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh, except to point out that another was impassible, as Nestorius teaches?

The Roman Apostolic See, concerning the faith of the Council of Chalcedon, has never permitted a single syllable or a single letter to be added or removed. See that no one deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit.

The faith set forth above by the council is itself the faith that agrees with the Gospel and the apostles, as the Savior says: “Thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise again according to the Scriptures” (Luke 24:46). The apostle Peter says: “Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same thought” (1 Peter 4:1). The apostle Paul says: “We preach Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 1:19). And again he says: “Whoever preaches to you anything other than what we preached, let him be anathema.”

[The remainder appears to be missing in the manuscript.]

## Observation of Father Antonio Pagi on the Year of Christ 533, no. 4

Since the proposition “One of the Trinity suffered in the flesh” can be drawn out into various meanings, which Lupus discusses in his notes on the Council of Ephesus—and since so many tragedies arose on account of it—Trifolius the presbyter, in his letter to the senator Faustus, understood it in an entirely erroneous sense and said: “This doctrine arose from the source of Arius and is consistent with all heresies,” and so forth.

Yet this error should be excused in the presbyter, who, when questioned by the senator Faustus in a letter about this proposition, had not been more accurately informed concerning the faith and doctrine of the Scythian monks, but only concerning the disturbances stirred up by them in Constantinople and Rome. He therefore easily persuaded himself that they asserted the proposition in a heretical sense, especially since they had the envoys of Hormisdas, the Roman pontiff, as their opponents, as well as the pontiff himself.

Moreover, the Scythian monks’ proposition was not reported faithfully to Trifolius, as is clear from the beginning of his letter. For Faustus the senator asked him what he thought of the proposition “One of the Trinity was crucified,” whereas the proposition of the Scythian monks was: “One of the Trinity was crucified in the flesh.”

Natalis Alexander resolves all Trifolius’s difficulties in *Dissertation 1 of the Sixth-Century History of the Church*.

# In the Year of Our Lord 525. Elpis, Wife of Boethius

## Hymns in Honor of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul (C, G, S)*

### Hymn I

Splendid light of eternity, you watered

The golden day with blessed fires,

The day that crowns the princes of the apostles

And opens a free path to the guilty toward the stars.

Teacher of the world and gatekeeper of heaven,

Parents and arbiters of Rome and of the nations,

One victorious through the death of the sword,

The other through the death of the Cross,

They possess the senate of life, crowned with laurel.

O happy Rome, consecrated

By the glorious blood of two princes:

Purpled by their blood, you alone surpass

All other beauties of the world.

To the Trinity be everlasting glory,

Honor, power, and rejoicing,

In the unity that governs all things,

Throughout all the ages of ages. Amen.

### Hymn II

Blessed shepherd Peter, mercifully receive

The voices of those who pray,

And by the word entrusted to you

Release the bonds of sins—

You to whom power was given

To open heaven to the earth

And to close what has been opened.

Excellent teacher Paul, instruct our ways

And draw our hearts with you to heaven.

While veiled Faith beholds the midday,

Let Charity alone reign like the sun.

To the Trinity be everlasting glory,

Honor, power, and rejoicing,

In the unity that governs all things,

Throughout all the ages of eternity. Amen.

# In the Years of Our Lord 475–525. Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, Senator

## General Prolegomena

### Preface of Henricus Loritus Glareanus to the Works of the Divine Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, Addressed to the Magnificent D. Antonius Fugger, Counselor to the Most Invincible Emperors, the Brothers Charles and Ferdinand

When I wished to write a preface to this most celebrated and learned author, noble D. Antonius, many things occurred to me that I had to weigh even before taking the author himself into my hands and examine, as they say, with lynx-like eyes. For I know that for several years now many have spoken ill of him and have judged him unworthy to be numbered among the classical writers. Some dislike his diction, saying that his phrasing is harsh and his style unlike that of others. Others criticize his learning as too proletarian, and find certain things ambiguous and scarcely worthy of learned ears.

It certainly seems difficult to answer all these objections. Whenever we have sometimes sought the judgment of very learned men concerning him, good heavens, how often that saying of Horace came to mind:

> Three guests of mine seem almost to disagree,  
> Asking for things greatly different to suit their varied tastes.

Lorenzo Valla, a very acute judge of the Latin language, did not hesitate to call Boethius the last of the learned men—a judgment, as I see it, excessively inclined toward reproaching that man. I think that Valla was assailed in his own lifetime by unjust judges, who considered Boethius great for no other reason than that he came closest to the sophistry in which they themselves excelled. The common saying is true: “Each person approves as much as he thinks he understands.”

There is also this reason why this author, while other excellent authors were almost in exile, remained in the hands of the barbarians: he teaches with such diligence that his excessive painstaking in instruction is almost tedious to a somewhat fastidious reader. This is especially true in his philosophical and mathematical works.

Yet in his musical works the difficulty of the subject overcame that diligence, so that the works remained untouched for many years, until the arrival of the never sufficiently praised Franchinus of Lodi, who did great service in elucidating them. Indeed, a few years ago many who professed music did not hesitate to say openly that no one could understand Boethius’ *Music*. A certain eminent music teacher in Cologne, when I was studying philosophy there thirty years ago, made this objection to me.

He held this opinion because, apart from the practice of songs, he possessed nothing else relating to the dignity of that discipline. Men of this sort sometimes judge authors with greater arrogance, by heaven, than men who are exceptionally learned. Sadly, this does not happen only in this field of knowledge, but everywhere, especially in our own age.

But let me return to the author himself. He wrote many works, of which the abbot Trithemius gives a full account. Of those that survive today, I consider the logical and mathematical works the chief. They do not differ in phrasing or diverge in style, so that one can clearly see that they all came from a single workshop—learned, cultivated, and utterly faithful to sound doctrine.

We leave his logical works unexamined and untouched, since many have reported various things about them.
