His mathematical works, however, which he left to us, seem worthy of every encomium and are exceedingly deserving of praise. Among them, his two learned books on arithmetic rightly hold the first place. They are an entirely complete work as far as theory is concerned; nothing can be taken away from them or added to them. In every respect they are smooth and perfectly rounded.

Although Georgius Valla, in that portentous volume of his *On Things to Be Avoided and Desired*, appears—if the gods approve—to have added something memorable from Martianus Capella. Yet although this same Georgius possessed all his more recondite knowledge of arithmetic from this author, he did not once wish to name him with proper recognition.

I say the same concerning the musical works. There he had Guillielmi, Bryennii, and I know not what other authors, not especially famous. Boethius had no place in his deserved catalogue, although whatever solid learning Georgius Valla published in music he owed to Boethius; the rest is empty compilation, touching neither heaven nor earth, though seeking both, with a subtlety more entertaining than necessary, as Pliny reported concerning the music of the stars.

Whatever our author produced in arithmetic and music is entirely solid, examined, and founded upon the innermost principles of mathematics. It will remain unshaken throughout the ages:

> As though it were hard flint or stood like Marpesian rock.

The fifth book on music, however, does not seem to me complete, although I know that the excellent Julius Martianus Rota, who recently prefaced this author, thought otherwise. On most matters concerning this author I agree with him.

There is considerable doubt concerning only two works, and the matter has not yet been fully settled in my mind, however much I struggle with it, move every stone, and alter, turn over, and reconsider every argument, not knowing

> By what knot I may hold Proteus, who changes his shape,

as the same Horace says.

For if the work *On the Two Natures of Christ Our Savior*, and likewise the work *On the Most Holy Trinity*, are his, as their titles indicate, and if their style does not contradict this, how did it happen that in the work *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, which is thought to be his last, Christ is not mentioned even once, although there were so many opportunities?

That excellent man was in prison, uncertain of his life. A savage tyrant threatened him, and he was treating the difficult subject of divine providence. Throughout the work he complained about the wickedness of this age, the instability of fortune, and the rule of evil men in this world. Surely Christ was not present in these matters even to be named once by so learned, honored, and pious a man?

Christ, I say—the example of all patience, who suffered far greater injuries from his enemies; God, Lord, and Creator fastened to the cross by his creature—was he not, I ask, to be named in this work, which they wish to be regarded as so splendid?

To speak frankly about what I think, although I know what great hostility this opinion may bring upon me, and that I am saying something more dangerous than moving Camarina—yet I must say what lies in my mind: the work seems to me more philosophical than Christian. It is not unworthy to be read by a Christian, but it is unworthy to be believed to have been written by one who, having received the name of Christ in holy baptism, professed him in the aforesaid writings, and who, though not cast into prison on account of that profession—for other causes of his imprisonment are reported—yet did not mention Christ even once.

I will not enlarge upon the matter as its importance might warrant. It is enough to have indicated to the reader what chiefly moves me.

As for the style, whether it agrees with Boethius’ other prefaces, let others judge. To many—and I can easily say that I am one of them—the prose and the poetry seem not to belong to the same man. The poetry possesses far greater grace than that barren prose. Anyone who considers this carefully will see that my opinion is not rash.

But what are we to say about the judgment of so many learned men before us? Who ever doubted the matter? Did they all fail to see? I do not say so. What then? They did not think about it, I say. If they had thought, judged, and examined the matter, they could have assessed it better than we can; but it did not occur to them, because their thoughts were occupied elsewhere.

In the same way, in our own age no man of moderately learned judgment will consider those highly learned and polished books of rhetoric *Ad Herennium* to be Cicero’s, but rather the work of some other learned man of that period, which then flourished with the greatest talents. Yet Lorenzo Valla and Angelo Poliziano, lights of Roman eloquence and men of exceptionally exact judgment, everywhere cite them as Cicero’s.

“You say they had no critical sense?” They certainly had one. But they did not think about the matter. Otherwise, from the difference of style and many other arguments, they could easily have concluded that the books were not Cicero’s, although learned, pure, and finished, and although the long-standing opinion of men protests otherwise. However much Georgius Valla, Antonius Mancinellus, and certain others struggled to persuade people of this, they achieved only that among the more learned they might be called either fools or stubborn men.

But let us return to that *Consolation of Philosophy*. If Philosophy rightly calls the Muses little prostitutes, as the sophists chatter, because they bring no solid consolation and no remedy to the afflicted soul, but Philosophy herself is the true medicine, why should we, to whom Christ has given the true faith, not in turn laugh at that barren philosophy and order it to depart from here—καὶ εἰς Κόρακας, “go to the crows”—since it has lied to so many philosophers about happiness in this world, deceiving men all the more powerfully as an adulterous matron deceives more powerfully than a little prostitute?

This philosophy, fabricated from some unknown beginning, is said to have come to the aid of the ailing Boethius. For philosophy has no more firmness than the Muses, which, as the critics think, are little prostitutes: an elegant invention for a pagan, but ridiculous for a Christian.

If you ask whom I think to be the author of this work, I could not easily say. Yet we gather from no slight conjecture that it was composed by some not unlearned person—or rather by several learned persons—who undertook this kind of lamentation out of affection for that excellent man, as a funeral consolation for one unjustly slain.

For we should hardly think Boethius so stupid, while held in prison, that he would so inopportunely wish to recall the tyrant’s injury. But enough concerning this work.

Whoever published a book on scholastic discipline under this author’s name seems to have been exceedingly shameless; more foolish still were those who believed it to be Boethius’ work.

Whether he began his geometry when he was young, as some have thought, and abandoned it because occupied with another study, or whether, as an old man, he failed to complete it after the books on arithmetic and music, I cannot say. It is certain that it did not reach us complete.

But now something must be said about the printer and the correction of the work.

Joannes Waldner of Zurich, a man who deserved the greatest gratitude for his services both to the best Latin and Greek authors and to the management of his own affairs, began printing the works of Boethius at his press several years ago. Prevented by death, he could not complete so pious a task. Nevertheless, he gave the opportunity to our great friend Henricus Petri, who was no less deserving in the cause of good letters and continues daily to deserve well of it.

Petri successfully completed the work that the Fates’ envy had interrupted, obtaining assistance both from living scholars and from silent teachers—that is, men of exceptional judgment and ancient manuscripts.

D. Sebastian Münster contributed to this edition, a man born for such honorable tasks, with tireless care and diligence. By the gift of Almighty God, an extremely ancient codex also came into our possession. It had belonged to the reverend father and lord in Christ, D. Joannes Kern, abbot of the monastery of Saint George in the Hercynian Forest.

Because of his love for sacred letters and the best authors, he did not hesitate to send this codex many miles. From it many passages in the musical works have been restored.

There was also the codex of D. Bonifacius Amorbachius, from his library, scarcely surpassed in learning by any other in all Germany. Nor was my own codex lacking, marked in many places.

I wanted the reader to know this, so that he would not think the work had been hastily thrown together, as happens in our age through the efforts of men more intent on hunting money than on seeking solid glory.

We have therefore wished this work, magnificent D. Antonius, to come into the light under the protection of your name. It is clear that you have deserved so well of honorable disciplines, and no less of their professors, that it would scarcely be possible in this age to call anyone else, with greater justice and greater merit, the Maecenas of our century.

Besides many other excellent men, two highly learned men and our closest friends gave me the fullest testimony to this: D. Otmarus Luscinius, now happily dead, and D. Christophorus Seld, advocate of the republic of Augsburg. Both were loved, assisted, and advanced by you.

May your kindness regard my boldness favorably.

Freiburg im Breisgau, 1 March 1546.

## Dedicatory Epistle

### Julius Martianus Rota to Georgius Cornelius, Designated Bishop of Treviso, Greetings

The first course has always been, in every field, to bring forth something new; the second, when one cannot attain that, to improve what has been drawn from others. Since I wished, Bishop Cornelius, to accomplish both for you, I began examining various libraries, hoping to achieve both aims.

The first, however, I was entirely unable to accomplish. For although many know that Severinus published books on Aristotle’s *Physical Lectures*, I have not yet been able to find them.

The second I think I have achieved abundantly, for we have made his commentaries far better than they had previously appeared in print. In many places they needed to be stabilized because of faulty transcription, and in others repaired because they had collapsed through long antiquity.

Let no one think that we undertook this task without reason. Boethius was not only a man of great eloquence and singular learning; he was also possessed by an extraordinary desire to help many people. Therefore, since as consul he could not keep the barbarians from Italy by arms, he did not hesitate to drive barbarism from Europe through learning.

For he was the first to give Aristotle, the master of dialectic and of both branches of philosophy—that is, of human happiness—to Latin, and to explain him. In this he not only equaled the distinction of Lucius Sulla but greatly surpassed it.

Cornelius Sulla, relying on wealth and power, carried to Rome the books of Aristotle that had been discovered at Athens. Manlius Severinus, relying on eloquence and learning, translated those same books from Greek into the Roman language and, through lucid explanations, made them accessible to every moderately educated person, although previously they had been so obscure that scarcely a few could understand them.

This usefulness greatly benefited not only the people of that age but, flowing down to posterity, has reached us even now.

When I noticed this excellent disposition of his mind while reading, I wished to gather into one place certain matters relevant to knowing him, both to return some measure of thanks to him, though he is dead, if I could, and to offer you, as you press more eagerly along the path of wisdom, a crown woven from many flowers.

For I do not think you would find it unwelcome to know him as though by sight, through whom you advance more and more each day and whose works delight you extraordinarily as you read them.

Yet, in doing this, I ask no one to think that I shall imitate many men of our time. Some exaggerate everything; others invent certain things as though they could not be refuted. I undertake to do neither now, although I understand very well that it is not easy to describe even the deeds of one’s own age, much less those of someone who died a thousand years ago—especially when there is such silence concerning his writings and those of the succeeding age that they did not even commit public matters to writing.

Therefore, let no one expect more from us than can be learned from his books or those of others, or at least grasped by evident conjecture.

You, most noble Georgius, read these materials, whatever they may be, gathered into a single work, with the willing disposition you customarily show toward all my works. Receive at last the complete history of Boethius, which long ago you carried away before it had been sufficiently polished.

Anicius Severinus Boethius, a Roman illustrious both for the nobility of his ancestors and for the gifts of his mind, lived in an age when Italy was held under barbarian oppression. For he was born not many years after Rome had been captured by Alaric. He flourished in the time of King Theodoric. This Theodoric, sent by Zeno with immense forces, had claimed for himself the Italy he had snatched from Odovacer, and, having established the seat of his kingdom at Ravenna, administered everything according to his pleasure. Seeing this, Boethius devoted his mind to honorable disciplines, understanding that this alone remained to him which was worthy of a free man.

Since, then, he had been educated in Greek and Latin literature from adolescence, he first translated certain works of Euclid, and translated them in such a way that he added from his own resources both methods of measurement and certain other matters, and taught how to establish a square equal to a circle—something that had not yet been discovered in Aristotle’s time. Later he rendered arithmetic, following Nicomachus not as a translator but using his own judgment, into Latin words. From this he gathered music, an intricate and perplexing discipline, from the best authorities, in which work he displayed both the resources of Aristoxenus and the judgment of Pythagoras.

There survives a letter of King Theodoric to Boethius which affirms that Boethius had rendered Ptolemy’s *Syntaxis* and Archimedes’ *Mechanics* into Latin. Yet I would believe that these were merely preliminary exercises toward what so great a man was considering in his mind. For he had resolved to illuminate philosophy in Latin literature—not Stoicism, as Varro did, nor the Academic school, as Cicero did, but that philosophy introduced by Aristotle, which had obscured the others and had been celebrated for so long an age by so many men of outstanding genius. He himself indicates this in these words:

> “I shall translate into Roman style the whole of Aristotle’s work, whatever may come into my hands, and write out in Latin prose the commentaries on all of it, so that if anything has been written by Aristotle concerning the subtlety of logical art, the gravity of moral knowledge, or the acuity of natural truth, I may translate it all in an ordered manner, and illuminate it with a certain light of exposition.”

Accordingly, he explained Porphyry, whom Victorinus Afer had translated in abridged form, and soon afterward, having himself translated the same work, he illuminated it anew with fresh expositions.

He had begun work on the *Categories* when, behold, he was made consul at Rome. He himself expresses this in his own words:

> “Although the cares of the consular office prevent us from devoting all our leisure and complete labor to these studies, it nevertheless seems to belong to some care for the commonwealth to instruct citizens in the doctrine of a matter worked out by night. Nor shall I deserve ill of my fellow citizens if, when the ancient virtue of men has transferred the empire of the other cities to this one commonwealth, I at least train the character of our state in the arts of Greek wisdom, insofar as anything remains to be done. For this too is not outside the office of a consul, since it has always been the Roman custom to honor more and more by imitation whatever is most beautiful and praiseworthy anywhere among the nations.”

These words also prove false the statement handed down by certain writers that Boethius wrote everything—not merely most things—while in exile.

He attained the consulship while still young through the favor of the leading men of the state. For they had taken responsibility for raising him, left fatherless as a boy, knowing both that he was descended from the ancient family of Manlius Torquatus and that they recognized in him the new character of his great-grandfather Anicius.

In Boethius’ first consulship, Odovacer, king of the Huns and of Italy, gained possession of Phaeba after the leader of the Rugians had been defeated and captured, as Cassiodorus relates. Cassiodorus mentions Boethius himself among the consuls only twice, once together with Symmachus.

Boethius not only attained this dignity himself but also saw his two sons, which had never happened before, made consuls at the same time: Patricius and Hypatius. In that year, in the senate-house, Boethius praised Theodoric, who had then been summoned to Rome for the first time, in the name of the Senate and People of Rome, with great eloquence; and in the circus, positioned between the two consuls, he presented a triumphal banquet to the multitude.

In his final consulship he had his father-in-law Symmachus as colleague. He administered the office with him in such a way that he placed the common good before private friendships. It happened that the royal agents desired the wealth of Paulinus, a former consul. Boethius openly defended the man. When Cyprianus falsely accused Albinus, Boethius demonstrated that the consular man was innocent.

A bitter famine was pressing upon Campania, and the tyrant’s agents had imposed an even more bitter compulsory purchase. The consul did not allow it to be exacted. He also repeatedly drove Triguilla, the superintendent of the royal household, away from acts of injustice, and restrained Conigastus, who was attacking the fortunes of every good man.

As a result of these actions he incurred the king’s indignation and was driven into exile by the denunciations of wicked men. The substance of the accusation was this: that he had prevented the senate from accusing someone of treason; and that he had sent a letter to the Emperor Anastasius concerning the recovery of liberty.

Three men of corrupt character appeared as informers: Gaudentius and Opilio, who at that time had been condemned to exile for countless frauds, and Basilius, who had formerly been removed from the administration of the royal household and was deeply burdened with debt.

Severinus would easily have cleared himself of the charges brought against him if Theodoric had given him the opportunity to confront and refute the informers in person. But Theodoric either did not wish, in his anger, to lose the opportunity for vengeance that had been offered to him, or, being wicked, did not wish to dissolve the calumny he himself had stirred up.

Thus, in his absence, Boethius—a man innocent and advanced in years—was exiled through the conspiracy of evil men and was not retained in his homeland by the good. He withdrew to Ticinum, a city situated in Insubria and assigned to him by the tyrant. As soon as he arrived there, so that he might also make his innocence known to posterity, he composed that most beautiful volume, *The Consolation*, imitating Cicero.

For just as Cicero, in order to lessen his daughter’s loss, demonstrates, while discussing the immortality of souls, that Tullia survives, so Severinus discusses the false and the true good and providence, and declares that everything happens to mortals by the divine will. In that work, however, Cicero did not touch upon poetry. Boethius combines both kinds of discourse, prose and verse, and combines them in such a way that he easily shows everyone that he never lacked talent for anything he might attempt.

But what is more difficult than natural philosophy? What is more thorny than dialectic? Yet he traversed both disciplines in his own prose in such a way that he made even the most hidden matters accessible to anyone. Nor did he pursue in his discourse one selected argument only; rather, entering the innermost sanctuaries of philosophy, he was the first to open to Latin readers **[Col. 0545]** those matters that Aristotle, its leading authority, had deliberately concealed in many places.

In this work he consulted the best authorities—Theophrastus, I mean, Eudemus, Andronicus, Aspasius, Herminus, Alexander, Syrianus, Porphyry, and Themistius—judging among their opinions as an impartial arbiter.

This is attested by his exposition of Aristotle’s book *On Interpretation*, completed in two books for the first part and six for the second. In the third book, when he says that he had written more adequately elsewhere, in his physical works, about the three modes of contingent things, he leaves it to be suspected that he had also worked out natural philosophy. Yet his commentaries on that subject are lacking to this day, although they were recently carried away from Tarvisium, as were those which he promised on the *Analytics* and the *Topics*.

For he himself cites these works, and declares that he composed seven books on Cicero’s *Topics*: a varied, difficult, learned work, which no one before Victorinus had attempted, and which he had attempted in vain. He undertook to render Plato’s dialogues into Latin; Cassiodorus asserts that he completed them. I would wonder how he could have accomplished so much unless I knew that those divine commentaries on Aristotle’s *On Interpretation* had been completed by him within two years—a period that scarcely seems sufficient even to read through so many commentators, much less to examine, judge, select, and adapt their generally conflicting opinions.

For among the Peripatetics there is scarcely any celebrated writer who did not write on this book. It is both exceedingly necessary and full of learning, but very obscure because of the acuteness of its doctrines and the brevity of its language. Boethius was composing these commentaries at the time when Theodoric, having crossed the Alps, defeated Clovis, his father-in-law and king of the Franks, in a great battle.

Moreover, Severinus was occupied not only in translating and explaining Aristotle; he also produced many works himself, as it were bringing them into being. Among these are those four most beautiful books *On Topical Differences*, by which he separates dialectical topics from rhetorical ones; and an equal number of other books on each of the two kinds of syllogism, as well as individual books on division and definition.

For the work entitled *An Introduction to Categorical Syllogisms* bears an embellished title: it is either, as he himself calls it, an abridgment of Aristotle’s book *On Interpretation*, or at any rate the same as the first book on categorical syllogisms.

The work *On Scholastic Discipline* also falsely claims not merely its title but its style and its invention. Boethius would have written otherwise if he had wished to write on that subject. But let us pass it by and bring forward instead something concerning the *Hebdomads*.

The *Hebdomads* are works divided into seven parts, just as works are divided into ten books as *decades*, and into nine as *enneads*. Varro was the first to give the title *Hebdomads*, and then Boethius himself. From these come the little book *On the Good of Substance* and another *On Unity and the One*. The remaining works were either not published because, as he seems to indicate, he had composed them only for himself, or they did not reach us.

Boethius composed the *Hebdomads* while young, as he also did the work *On Two Natures and One Person of Christ*. His own words lead me to think this. The writer of the letter says:

> “When the bishop, as though he did not wish to pass over a matter of very great necessity, stated that Christ consists of two natures and that Catholics believe equally in two [natures], I was struck by the novelty of the statement and pondered all the questions in my mind.”

This decree had been issued at the Council of Chalcedon, and Leo, the Roman bishop, had gone there. When his letter, sent to Rome, was later read in the presence of many people—after the Acephali had attempted to revive the dogma already condemned—and when they no longer understood sufficiently what had been decreed, it gave Boethius the occasion to compose that book against Nestorius, who joined two persons to two natures, and against Eutyches, who defended one nature and one person.

Therefore, if one counts the years from the Emperor Leo, who fostered the opinions of Nestorius and Eutyches, rejected under Marcian, down to Justin, one finds just short of fifty years. Subtracting these years from the life of Boethius, only the earliest period of his youth remains.

Let everyone accept this as he pleases. But I would certainly insist that one must not accept the claim that Boethius, overtaken by death, failed to complete his *Music*. For some object that the titles of the works still missing nevertheless survive. This rather draws us toward the contrary opinion, since we think it absurd to wish to give a name to works not yet written.

If Severinus left anything unfinished, I would judge that it was theology. He had illuminated philosophy sufficiently and more than sufficiently; therefore divine matters remained. He had already made considerable progress by following Augustine, as he himself says in writing to Symmachus concerning the Trinity:

> “You must examine whether the seeds of reason coming into us from the writings of blessed Augustine have produced any fruits.”

From this we may also conjecture why Theodoric killed Severinus and Symmachus only in the ninth year: perhaps because, as an old man, he had fallen into the opinion of Arius and had become so hostile to Catholics that he wished to destroy their churches in Italy if Justin did not restore the Arians in Asia.

Boethius and Symmachus, however, were always defenders of sound doctrine, and especially so at that time. Therefore the tyrant ordered them, after they had been thrown into prison, to be slaughtered.

The inhabitants of Ticinum have always consistently maintained that, according to what they received from their ancestors, when the royal executioner had inflicted the fatal wound, Severinus supported his torn-apart head with both hands. When asked whom he thought had struck him, he answered, “The impious.” Then, having come to a nearby church, he received the sacred rites on bended knees before the altar and died shortly afterward.

After his death he received divine honors from our people, because he had endured death on behalf of the Catholics against the perfidy of Arius.

Some write that he had first been summoned to Ravenna and placed in charge of the royal praetorium, and afterward killed together with several senators. This seems more appropriately to fit Symmachus. For a tower built of brick and stone is still pointed out at Ticinum as Boethius’ prison, and his tomb is visited in the church of blessed Augustine, at the point where the ascent into the sanctuary of the temple begins. The following epitaph is engraved there:

> Most renowned in Maeonian and Latin speech, and he who  
> was once consul here, I perished, sent into exile.  
> And because death seized me, integrity raised me to the heavens;  
> behold, now my fame flourishes greatly, and my work lives.

Another epitaph is also circulated, with which his tomb had formerly been adorned before it was placed there by Liutprand, king of the Lombards. Since it contains in a few words much that pertains to his life, we have appended it:

**[Col. 0547]**

> Behold, Boethius is here, great in heaven and known  
> throughout the whole world, a man wondrous to behold.  
> Denounced to the unjust King Theodoric,  
> he spent his old age in exile at Ticinum.  
> In that city, consoling his sorrow, he gave forth a little book;  
> after being struck by the sword, he departed from the world.

This was the end of the most illustrious man, who excelled greatly in eloquence, integrity, and learning: the last of all those descended from the ancient Romans to consecrate anything to literary monuments, and the first of all who began to illuminate Aristotelian discipline in Latin literature. He possessed such authority among posterity that there is scarcely any appeal from his judgments.

By his death we lost a great possession, and also the concord of Plato and Aristotle, which many later men attempted in vain. Boethius, the most skilled student of both philosophies, had promised to provide that concord, and, unless the wicked had taken his life, he alone would have been able to accomplish it.

Yet divine vengeance followed shortly afterward. When Theodoric was dining and a fish’s head was brought before him, the king seemed to see in it the face of Symmachus, grasping its lower lip with his teeth and repeatedly threatening him with fierce eyes. Terrified by the sight, the tyrant fell ill, and as soon as he confessed that he had seen what he had seen, he died.

His own people spread the report that he had died from a stroke of blood. But when Amalasuntha, who knew the truth of the matter, succeeded to the kingdom, she rescinded her father’s acts and decrees, which had been contrary to law and justice, and restored the property of Severinus and Symmachus, which had been confiscated into the treasury, to their children. This was a few years before Belisarius, sent by Justinian, expelled all the Goths from Italy.

There were, moreover, many men named Boethius. The first was a Stoic, whom Diogenes mentions in his *Life of Zeno*; the second was an Epicurean, whom Plutarch introduces in the *Convivial Discussions*; the third was a Cretan, a student of Aristotle and a former consul celebrated by Galen.

Besides these, there were other men who were both philosophers and Peripatetics: one was this very Boethius, a Roman patrician, about whom enough has already been said; the other was a Greek and more ancient, whom this Boethius himself, as well as Ammonius and Simplicius, recognize as an interpreter of Aristotle.

There were likewise two men named Symmachus, both highly esteemed in literature. The first lived in the time of Gratian and Valentinian; the second in the time of Zeno and Anastasius. The letters of the former are circulated, and he is frequently mentioned in Macrobius’ *Saturnalia*. Nothing by the latter survives; but, to pass over the testimony of Boethius, Priscian of Caesarea, writing on weights, praises him in such a way that he seems to have attained the highest points of every discipline.

# PART ONE OF THE WORKS. PHILOSOPHICAL WORKS.

## THE FIVE BOOKS OF THE CONSOLATION OF PHILOSOPHY

*(From the edition prepared for the use of the Dauphin.)*

## PROLEGOMENA

**[Col. 0547]**

### Dedicatory Letter

**Peter Callyus to the Most Serene Dauphin**

Whatever Louis the Great, your august father, undertakes, Most Serene Dauphin, is great—whether he rules peoples, conquers enemies, or benefits both sides by granting them peace. But your character and education are the greatest of royal achievements. You, like a noble mirror, reflect back the royal gifts of both mind and body that you have received from him, so that nothing is lacking in you that could belong to imperial majesty.

Your education, which that king began with his wisest counsels and strengthened with the most distinguished men, he completes with such a magnificent apparatus of books that, through an indescribable bond, as much as a son surpasses a father, so much does the father surpass all other kings through the son.

Behold, by his continuing command, Severinus Boethius shines among the ancient authors and presents himself to you, with a better claim and therefore with greater hope of the richest fruits.

Boethius presents himself to you as by far the most deserving of all authors of this kind. Those others were foreigners, entirely unfamiliar with French institutions, and needed a herald who, after proclaiming their worth, might gain them some standing at court. He, long ago received with the highest honors by Philip the Fair, king of the Gauls and a prince most devoted to literature and men of letters, is almost a member of the household and knows courtly customs as well as he is known by courtiers.

Those others are profane and commended by no piety except whatever they may happen to have received from recent interpreters. He is sacred and shines with the splendor of a Christian martyr more brightly than with the purple of a Roman patrician.

Those others, confined to one kind of discourse, possess either prose without verse or verse without prose. He is thoroughly skilled in both kinds of speech: as an eloquent orator he persuades, and as a graceful poet he delights.

Those others, inspired by gentler Muses, if they do not wound the mind with their opinions, at least reveal it as wounded—though they cannot heal it. He, instructed by the sterner discipline of philosophy, exposes disturbances and the causes of errors and vices in such a way that he seems able to contribute greatly to the mind’s health.

If that author, Most Serene Dauphin, finds easy access to you, he will hope to produce a greater increase of learning and virtue not only in you but also in all the young men to whom, as from the head to the limbs, the form of your royal education is transmitted.

It is certainly a great thing for you to possess perfect mastery of geography, chronology, and both profane and sacred history, enriched with outstanding Latin. But it is far greater to receive an increase of that philosophical knowledge of yourself and of God which you possess by nature and which Boethius here offers. For those earlier disciplines serve this later one just as servants serve their mistress.

Through this instruction a prince rises above peoples all the higher insofar as, conscious of himself and understanding his Creator, he despises the riches, honors, and enticements of pleasure with which a royal throne is usually surrounded, and forms humbler opinions of himself and loftier opinions of the divine majesty.

The liberal arts truly impressed upon your royal mind were not to be omitted. Yet the knowledge of human and divine nature inspired by Boethius seems altogether necessary to you. Even scepters are not free from the miseries to which that philosophical remedy of the Roman consul can usefully be applied.

Although your august lineage and outstanding education have raised you so high that this golden book could not afterward be of great use to you, your great dignity as Dauphin nevertheless seems to demand that you arrange for the book to be read to you—partly for other reasons, but chiefly so that Boethius may be restored by your royal example to the French academies, from which he has long been exiled with an injustice equal to that once suffered from the Roman walls.

It is surely disgraceful to the most Christian kingdom that this sacred teacher should be placed below Virgil, Cicero, Aristotle, and the other enemies of the Christian religion—and all the more so because he was not only the most serious authority and teacher in understanding but also in expression, and enriched our Christian schools with abundant resources from every branch of learning.

He taught grammar, after banishing barbarism, the wholesome uses of fables; he adorned rhetoric with the choicest words and the truest opinions; and he cultivated philosophy, freed from obscurity, in such a way that anyone who is willing to obey it can pass the whole of life without distress.

Permit, therefore, Most Serene Dauphin, a man at once noble, learned, and holy to enter the royal household, to be numbered among your other authors, and to be proposed for your hearing among those works with which you happily occupy yourself in literature.

Here you will observe holiness joined with learning, and both joined with nobility, in such a way that whatever you encounter there may contribute greatly both to the enlargement of your knowledge and to the attainment of the eternal crown toward which all kings ought to strive, and may be in no way unworthy of your august origin.

Caen, on the Kalends of November, in the year of Our Lord 1679.

**[Col. 0549]**

## PREFACE

**[Col. 0549A]**

Among the many works of our Boethius, the most outstanding and celebrated is the one entitled *The Consolation of Philosophy*. But the commentaries on this work that have so far been published were so imperfect that it is not without reason that new ones have been ordered for the use of the Most Serene Dauphin. I shall say a few preliminary words about the ancient and the more recent commentaries.

### I

The ancient—or rather, less recent—commentaries on the *Consolation of Philosophy* are imperfect. For which should one commend? Those attributed to Saint Thomas? Or those belonging to Raymond Palasin of Albi, called Valdericus? Or those of Jodocus Badius Ascensius? Or those of Johannes Bernartius of Belgium? Or those of Theodore Sitzman of Thuringia? Or those of René Vallin of Nantes? I have been unable to see more, even after the most careful search. But all these works are either ridiculous or wholly unsuitable for revealing Boethius’ thoughts.

First, the commentaries on this *Consolation of Philosophy* attributed to Saint Thomas are ridiculous. To omit innumerable examples, who could restrain laughter on reading these words in Book I, Prose 1?

> “Elea,” he says, “is a city of Greece in which Aristotle studied; hence his studies are called Eleatic. The Academy, however, was a city or village in which Plato studied; hence his studies are called Academic.”

Or consider these words in Book II, Metre 5, on the phrase “to mix with Tyrian poison”:

> “Tyre,” he says, “is a poisonous worm, in whose blood purple dye is dipped.”

Or these in Book III, Prose 8:

> “Alcibiades,” he says, “was a most beautiful woman. When certain disciples of Aristotle saw her, they brought her to Aristotle so that he might see her. When he had seen her, he said: ‘If human beings had lynx-like eyes, so that they could penetrate whatever obstructs their sight, then, once the entrails had been inspected, the body that appears most beautiful would be seen to be most foul.’”

Or these in the same book, Metre 8, on the words “rough sea-urchins”:

> “The sea-urchin,” he says, “is a small fish half a foot long which, by clinging on, seems to hold back a ship.”

Here *ἐχενηὶς*—in Latin *remora*—is confused with *echinus*.

I would be endless if I attempted to enumerate all the errors of this work—more a fabrication than a commentary—in grammar, poetry, history, and Boethius’ own thought. I therefore do not believe this work to be by Saint Thomas.

This work, however, appears to be by a certain Thomas, English by nation, Welsh by birth, and a Dominican by religious order. The *Summa of Logic* is also attributed to him, although it is commonly printed under the name of Saint Thomas Aquinas. Since that Thomas was said to be English and a Dominican, he may, because of the same religious order and a certain similarity of names, have been called first “Angelicus” and later “Saint Thomas” through the error of printers.

Hence this commentator cites Alanus in Book II, Metre 1, although Alanus flourished only in the fourteenth century, whereas Saint Thomas lived until the year 1274. Hence I think that this Thomas spoke English in Book I, Prose 4, where he says:

> “Compulsory purchase is an arrangement concerning a portion of something to be given from a thing bought or sold, and it is commonly called *UNGELT*.”

Although perhaps, through a printer’s error, the language has been corrupted; in French we say *monopole*. I do not know, either, how Saint Thomas could have said, at the end of Book I, Metre 2, “this Marquardus.”

And lest you think that I am inventing these things recklessly, you may consult both Vallinus and Ascensius, who likewise deny that Saint Thomas was the author of these commentaries. Ascensius says in the preface to these books of Boethius:

> “Nevertheless, I would not immediately believe them to belong to Saint Thomas, since they neither bear the scent of his phrasing, nor attain that remarkable abundance which he displays in his other works, nor agree with the period. For they sometimes cite the little works of Alanus, whom experts in these matters report to have died several years after Saint Thomas himself.”

Next, the commentaries of Raymond Palasin of Albi, called Valdericus, are chiefly concerned with three matters:

1. Very brief interpretations of certain more obscure names, written in the margin of the book.

2. A rather lengthy astronomical exposition explaining the movements of Hesperus, sometimes following the setting sun and sometimes preceding it in rising:

> “For understanding these matters,” he says on Metre 5 of Book I, “it is necessary to ‘archimedeize’—that is, to construct figures, whose inventor was Archimedes. Let it be noted what a circle is, what its center is, what its area is, and what its circumference is.”

Excellent annotations indeed!

3. Questions, which he calls “Cratonian,” concerning the fifth book:

> “Among them,” he says, “the following principal question is widely debated: namely, whether, when divine providence exists, human beings possess free will.”

Here that interpreter seems not to have grasped Boethius’ opinions in his mind.

**[Col. 0552A]**

For this reason, of these three parts, the first seems to us insufficient, the second excessive, and the third an obstacle to perceiving Boethius’ thought.

Afterward Ascensius, as he himself boasts in the preface mentioned above, taught the rules and varieties of the poems; he also recited the fables and histories more carefully; and he revealed the excellence of Latin, whether preserved or neglected, lamenting that he nowhere had been able to find Greek words with sufficient certainty.

Yet although this interpreter is greatly pleased with himself, he is poorly regarded by others. Theodore Sitzman, who will be mentioned immediately, says:

> “Jodocus Badius Ascensius did not refrain from defiling this and other excellent authors with refuse and mere chattering—whether I should say shamelessly or thoughtlessly.”

Even if this fault of Ascensius were not established, the same Ascensius nevertheless did not go beyond the limits of grammar, beyond which something more is required for an accurate understanding of these books.

Next comes Johannes Bernartius, who, after marking a few passages in the prose and even fewer in this verse discourse of Boethius, seems to have undertaken to illuminate and adorn himself in such a way that, whenever he first finds even the slightest opportunity to bring forward something he remembers saying, he heaps it together, whether or not it contributes to the subject. He seems intent on displaying his own learning rather than explaining the author’s thought.

The aforementioned Sitzman says:

> “He would have handed this book down to us much more polished, if he had been permitted to do so. But, carried off by premature death, he fell under the jurisdiction of Libitina and left unfinished the fabric he had begun.”

Theodore Sitzman himself follows. He is wholly occupied with composing variant readings, so that whenever he believes one reading explains Boethius’ thoughts better, he advises that it be retained after the others have been struck out.

> “Yet,” he says of himself, “I often sprinkle these with certain other materials, either drawn from philology, to which I had hitherto been wholly devoted; or from the storehouse of jurisprudence and politics; or from that whole realm of disciplines that serve the study of wisdom. I did this for no other reason,” he adds, “than to be useful sometimes and entertaining at other times in a gratifying exchange—in other words, to mix the useful with the pleasant.”

Let the fair-minded reader judge whether this interpreter has discharged his pledge. For my part, I think first that the Boethian text he edited required eyes more perceptive than his; and second, that this interpreter, imitating other interpreters of ancient books, wrote not so much for the sake of others as for his own sake.

Hence he cited other writers, whether orators or poets who had spoken in Boethius’ manner, in such a way that, after undertaking to explain one author, he presents several others for us to interpret without explaining any of them—a man of happy memory.

Finally, in our judgment Vallinus deserved better of Boethius than all the others. He corrected the text, which was very often corrupt. Therefore, as he says of himself:

> “We consulted the best manuscripts and established the text for the most part according to their agreement.”

These were two manuscripts written by hand at Saint Victor; two from the Thuana Library, both very ancient; one from the royal library; and also two of my own, though more recent. There was also a Greek manuscript of the same books, from the same royal library, which Maximus Planudes translated into Greek.

Among printed editions there was the Florentine edition of 1513 and any other excellent one. Moreover, Vallinus attempted to illuminate in his notes certain passages of this little work that he considered more obscure.

For this reason, the *Commentaries of Various Authors on this Consolation of Philosophy*, printed at Leiden nine years ago, consist of the notes of Johannes Bernartius, Theodore Sitzman, and René Vallinus like cement without lime.

Vallinus himself, however, omitting every interpretation of the words and silently passing over Boethius’ method of argument, supplied notes so rare and so brief that his work, otherwise useful, cannot suffice for a complete understanding of this work.

These, then, are the ancient—or rather, less recent—commentaries on the *Consolation of Philosophy*.

### II

The faults of the aforesaid commentaries on the *Consolation of Philosophy* were most perceptively noticed by a man outstanding in nation, learning, and every kind of virtue: Charles de Sainte-Maure, Duke of Montausier, tutor of the Most Serene Dauphin. Because of his exceptional prudence in advising princes, he was distressed that the deeds of that extremely wise courtier—whose counsels King Theodoric followed for as long as he lived a life worthy of an excellent ruler—lay hidden beneath obscure words.

The same matter was also understood by the most illustrious prince of the Church, Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet, Bishop of Condom and tutor of the same Most Serene Dauphin. Because of his extraordinary wisdom in divine mysteries, he grieved that the thoughts of that most wise theologian, who taught how human freedom is reconciled with divine providence, remained hidden and unknown under a compressed style of argument.

The distinguished man Pierre-Daniel Huet, once a student of our academy at Caen, also perceived this. The same Most Serene Prince makes use of his services in the study of literature and wisdom. Huet, in his incredible learning in every discipline, lamented that the elegant sayings of this outstanding orator and poet—within whom, as in the last heir of the Romans, the rich remains of purer Latin were preserved—were despised because they were mixed among the obscure authors of his barbarous age.

Those illustrious lights of our France, then, complained of the unjust fate of Boethius and of this *Consolation of Philosophy* when we were ordered to prepare these books of Boethius, with a translation and notes, for the use of the Most Serene Dauphin.

Whether our present labor will seem better or worse than those earlier works, we cannot foresee. But we have tried, with all the diligence we could, to observe the following rules prescribed for us, as a lasting monument of singular piety toward God, reverence toward the king, and love of literature.

#### 1

We used the reading established by René Vallinus after consultation of the sounder books, except for a few words which, as we noted there, we judged ought to be changed because we had been compelled by the strongest conjectures.

Since it matters little for a reader to know the errors of the ancients, we thought that, once a new and correct reading had been proposed, the old and false one could be omitted. We did so all the more willingly because, since scarcely any passage of this work had not at some time been corrupted, the variant readings would have had to be repeated to the point of tedium.

Nevertheless, so that we might not fail even in this duty, at the end of our work we have reported Vallinus’ variant readings, adapted to the numbering of this book.

#### 2

We have supplied two kinds of summaries, so that the reader may perceive, as though in a single act of thought, what the whole work and each of its parts contain.

The first is an outline of the entire work. There, by shaping certain arguments and moving the reader’s mind more effectively, we have attempted to demonstrate Boethius’ thoughts more clearly.

The second is a summary of each chapter, in which we have briefly embraced not only what is to be said but also the order in which it is to be said.

#### 3

Although these headings, “Metre” and “Prose,” were introduced by more recent interpolators of these books and added merely to aid memory—and although all the ancient books and the excellent Florentine edition lack them, as the aforementioned Vallinus observed—we nevertheless decided not to omit them.

They are now so much in use that whenever Boethius *On the Consolation of Philosophy* is cited—and it is cited very often—these headings are also named.

Vallinus himself discovered through experience what harm can result from neglecting these labels. With his edition, we are able to use the headings, though not without great expenditure of time, to establish the authenticity of references to Boethius. For this reason his edition is despised.

**[Col. 0554C]**

#### 4

Before undertaking their exposition and annotation, we first identified the kinds of verse used here by Boethius and set out their rules. Some of these metres are less familiar, especially to beginners, for whose benefit we also avoided the Greek expressions by which these verses are usually designated, since those expressions are more obscure.

These verses are of many kinds, and there is no point in counting them individually. But the poems composed of these verses are reduced to twenty-six kinds.

### 5.

We have appended a continuous interpretation for the metrical discourse, but an interrupted one for the prose; following the practice of those who before us, by command of Louis the Great, wrote on poets or Latin orators for the use of His Most Serene Highness the Dauphin, so that young men devoting themselves to letters may lack nothing that can contribute to greater progress in the liberal arts. [Col. 0554D]

### 6.

We have added our notes—not indeed longer ones, lest we seem to display empty erudition, nor shorter ones, lest other commentaries should have to be sought for our commentaries—but notes adapted to the use of the young. For this was the one thing desired by those most learned men to whose care the education of His Most Serene Highness the Dauphin was entrusted. Thus, while laboring for the prince’s education, they also labored to form the rest of the young, for the greatest advantage of the republic of letters and the glory of the French kingdom.

### 7.

We thought it worthwhile to place this entire work, furnished with interpretation and notes, between two indexes. [Col. 0555A] The first contains the principal subjects occurring throughout the work as explained; the second contains the words found in these five books of *The Consolation of Philosophy*. There we have taken care to print in different characters those words that seemed to us barbarous, or at least less Latin, so that the reader might be warned of this defect in Latinity, while our commentaries would not nevertheless be swollen with frequent notices of this kind. If this undertaking of ours should stimulate more learned men to complete the task, and, by adducing authority, to establish some of these words, that will be no unwelcome reward for our boldness. We do not know everything; we are always most ready to be taught. [Col. 0556A]

Finally, we judged that none of all these matters should be taken up before we had set forth, following the model of the other writings of His Most Serene Highness the Dauphin: first, the life of Boethius; second, the testimonies of various authors concerning both Boethius and his writings; third, a general conception of the books of *The Consolation of Philosophy*; fourth, an assessment of these books. For every one of these writers customarily prefaces his work with such material concerning its author, except that we have no example of a general conception of the work. Nevertheless, we hope that even this addition will prove to be of no small usefulness.

[Col. 0555]

## THE LIFE OF ANICIUS MANLIUS SEVERINUS BOETHIUS

### I.

[Col. 0555B]

Boethius was born at Rome [Note: [Col. 0555D] *Consolation of Philosophy*, book I, p. 5: “The most ancient law of your city.”], around the year of the Lord 475, a contemporary of John the Supreme Pontiff; the emperor Justin; and the ecclesiastical teachers Fulgentius, Ennodius, and Cassiodorus. We do not know his mother’s name or family. His father, however, was Anicius Manlius Flavius Boethius, himself a man of consular rank and the son of that Boethius who, while serving as prefect of the praetorium, was killed during the reign of Valentinian, at the same time that Aetius the patrician, a most vigorous commander and one who had always shared in his labors as in his victories, was killed by the hand of that same emperor. [Note: [Col. 0555D] Cassiodorus, *Chronicle*, under the consulship of Aetius and Studius, A.D. 454.]

### II.

This author, of whom we are now speaking, is called Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius [Col. 0555C] [Note: [Col. 0555D] This is how the books of *The Consolation of Philosophy* are inscribed.], with the praenomen placed after the name and cognomen. For it was customary among the ancient Romans for the same man sometimes to be given three kinds of appellation, which were called praenomen, nomen, and cognomen. [Note: [Col. 0555D] Valerius Maximus, or Probus, in the little book *On the Praenomen*.]

The praenomen, as the word itself indicates, is an appellation ordinarily placed before the name of the clan; these are the names that among us are called personal names, such as Louis. The nomen is the appellation of the clan, such as Hectorides; the cognomen is the appellation of the family within that clan, such as Bourbonides.

Just as the praenomen was often formerly placed before the nomen, and the nomen before the cognomen, so, not infrequently, with the order reversed as today, the nomen and cognomen were placed first and the praenomen after them. [Note: [Col. 0555D] For example, Flavius Vespasianus and Flavius Sabinus, brothers, in Suetonius.]

Thus our author is called Anicius by the name of his clan, since he was descended from the most ancient and noble clan of the Anicii. [Note: [Col. 0555D] St. Jerome, letter to Demetrias: “A family of illustrious blood, in which there is either no one or scarcely anyone who has not deserved the consulship.”] He is called Manlius Severinus by the name of his family, because he was descended from the Manlii Severini—unless there were two families, one, namely the Manlii, through his father, and the other, the Severini, through his mother; or unless it was one and the same family, known by the additional cognomen Severinus, because of that severity by which Titus Manlius, who introduced the cognomen Torquatus into the family after taking a torque from a Gaulish commander whom he had killed, ordered his son to be beheaded. [Note: [Col. 0556D] Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, line 824: “And behold the savage Torquatus with his axe.”] He had killed the Tusculan commander in single combat after that commander had challenged him contrary to orders.

He is called Boetius by his personal name—or, as some write it, Boethius, or, as others have it, Boethus—from the assistance that was given by the first person to whom this praenomen was assigned. For in Greek βοηθός means “helper.” Accordingly, several men in former times were given this praenomen, as may be seen in Laertius [Note: [Col. 0556D] In the *Life of Zeno.], Plutarch [Note: [Col. 0556D] In the *Table-Talk*.], and our author himself [Note: [Col. 0556D] Commentary on Porphyry.].

### III.

Since our Boethius had lost his father when he was at least twelve years old [Note: [Col. 0556D] That is, after the year A.D. 487, since his father was consul in that very year.], he was entrusted to the care of friends and relatives. [Note: [Col. 0556D] *Consolation of Philosophy* II, Prose 3: “The care of eminent men took you in when you had been left desolate by your father.”] He first studied at Rome and afterward at Athens [Note: [Col. 0556D] Cassiodorus, *Variae* I, letter 45: “You entered the schools of Athens though placed far away.”], where he made such progress in grammar, philosophy, and the mathematical disciplines that he translated into Latin not only several works of Euclid, Nicomachus, Pythagoras, Ptolemy, and Archimedes, but also works of Aristotle himself. [Note: [Col. 0556D] St. Antoninus, citing Sigebertus, *History*, part 2, title 11, chapter 15.] Had fate permitted, he would likewise have translated the remaining works of that philosopher and reconciled Aristotle with his teacher Plato.

Nor was that most learned man occupied merely with expounding the works of other authors; he himself conceived many works and brought what he had conceived to a successful completion. Witness is this admirable work, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, in which, imitating Cicero disputing on the immortality of souls in order to alleviate his longing for his daughter, he surpassed Cicero in this respect: whereas Cicero at that time did not employ verse, Boethius so interweaves both forms of discourse that whatever learning might be expected from grammar or rhetoric shines forth there in a wonderful manner. [Col. 0556D–0557A]

Witness also Boethius’s *Logic*, in which, besides the ancient opinions of Porphyry and Aristotle, he set forth his own doctrine concerning the Categories, division, definition, and syllogisms—a doctrine capable of greatly advancing the method of sound reasoning. Witness that work divided into seven parts, entitled, after the example of Varro, the *Hebdomads*, in which, insofar as it survives, he teaches much about what is good and what is one, after the manner of mathematicians, by setting forth certain propositions. Witness the five books *On Music*, in which he was so skilled that he is regarded as the inventor of the musical instrument commonly called the *chiterinus*. [Note: [Col. 0557D] In the *Supplement to the Chronicle*.] Witness that remarkable invention of two clocks, known and desired even by foreign kings. One of them [Note: [Col. 0557D] Cassiodorus, *Variae* I, letter 45.] was regulated by water flowing at a measured rate; the other [Note: [Col. 0557D] Ibid.] was distinguished by the captured illumination of the immense sun.

Boethius also rendered the greatest service to theologians. He wrote both on the mystery of the most holy Trinity, to Symmachus and to John, a deacon of the Roman Church, and on the Incarnation. His work on the Trinity was written [Note: [Col. 0557D] The Magdeburg Centuriators, century 6, chapter 10, and before them St. Antoninus, *History*, part 2, title 11, chapter 15, from Vincentius.] because he feared that Christians might suspect him of having withdrawn from the synod convened against the heretics, lest, on account of his eloquence, the task of conducting the case should be entrusted to him. His work on the Incarnation was written [Note: [Col. 0557D] Thus Boethius himself speaks in *On the Two Natures and One Person of Christ*.] so that the errors of Nestorius and Eutyches, the extreme and mutually opposed positions, might be removed.

### IV.

But the more learned Boethius was, the more diligently he cultivated virtue, fulfilling with the greatest care his duty toward God and human beings. What his thoughts were concerning the divine majesty is evident even from what he brought forth under the inspiration of Philosophy in that golden little work, *The Consolation of Philosophy* [Note: [Col. 0557D] Especially at the beginning of book III.]. For he taught nothing there that he himself had not done, nor could he then display such power with such ease unless he had practiced it through continuous piety from his earliest years. His exceptional benevolence toward all human beings, especially the unfortunate, is also made clear by the fact that, at grave risk to his own safety, he protected the senate and all the people with both the greatest eloquence and an authority exposed to danger. [Note: [Col. 0557D] *Consolation of Philosophy* I, Prose 4: “Then, amid grave dealings with the wicked,” etc.] It is likewise clear from the fact that he was generous toward the poor. [Note: [Col. 0557D] The Magdeburg Centuriators, from Procopius, book I *On the Gothic War*, etc., century 6, chapter 10.]

### V

[Col. 0558A]

Because of these outstanding qualities of character, Festus, the chief of the senate, dedicated his daughter Helpes, a foster-child of Sicily, to Boethius and joined her to him in a stable marriage. [Note: [Col. 0557D] *Consolation of Philosophy* II, Prose 3: “With such splendor of your fathers-in-law.”] Helpes, says Vallinus [Note: [Col. 0558D] In the *Life of Boethius*. Lilius Gregorius Gyraldus says the same in *History of the Poets*, dialogue 5.], far surpassed the advantages of her body and fortune by the gifts of her character. For she wrote highly polished verse, and a most agreeable genius attended her husband as he wrote.

He desired children by her, although some say that Boethius had by her two sons, Patricius and Hypatius. They add that Boethius commemorated this beloved wife in the following final poem:

> I was called Helpes, a foster-child of Sicilian land,  
> whom love of my husband drove far from my homeland.  
> Without him, the day is sad, the night anxious, the hour tearful;  
> not only flesh, but one spirit, we were.  
>   
> My light has not been extinguished: with such a husband remaining,  
> I shall survive as the greater part of a soul.  
> Now I rest as a stranger in the sacred porticoes,  
> having borne witness to the throne of the eternal Judge.  
>   
> Let no hand violate my tomb, unless perhaps my husband  
> should wish once more to join these limbs to his own,  
> so that, companion of both marriage-chamber and tomb, I may not be torn away even by death,  
> and each man’s ashes may bind together the partners of life.

But these verses do not bear the fragrance of Boethius’s elegant poetry—at least not for the most part.

Because of the same ornaments of learning and virtue [Note: [Col. 0558D] *Consolation of Philosophy* I, Prose 4: “Your father-in-law also, the holy Symmachus.”], Symmachus, likewise chief of the senate, after Helpes’s death gave his daughter Rusticiana in marriage to the same Boethius. By her he had, among other children, two sons, one called Symmachus after his grandfather and the other Boethius after his father. While still boys, they were made consuls. [Note: [Col. 0558D] Ibid., book II, Prose 3: “You saw your two sons at once advanced from your household to the consulship, amid the attendance of the fathers and the rejoicing of the people.”] Hence their father calls these sons [Col. 0558C] [Note: [Col. 0558D] Ibid., Prose 4.] “men of consular rank”; for in boys already of that age there shines a likeness of their paternal or ancestral genius.

### VI.

To the singular learning and virtue of Boethius we must also credit the fact that he was adorned with the highest dignities from adolescence onward. First, while still a young man [Note: [Col. 0558D] *Consolation of Philosophy* II, Prose 3: “I pass over the dignities assumed in youth and denied to old men.”], he was placed among the senators and fathers and became a patrician. Then, at approximately the thirty-fifth year of his life, he became consul. [Note: [Col. 0558D] Ennodius, book VIII, letter 1.] Finally, when more advanced in age, he became master of the offices. [Note: [Col. 0558D] *Consolation of Philosophy* III, Prose 4: “When you held office together with Decoratus.”]

He accepted and exercised these dignities only through the common support of all good men. [Note: [Col. 0558D] Ibid., book I, Prose 4: “No office was bestowed upon me except through the common support of all good men.”] Hence he always opposed the unjust designs of all the wicked. Hence he repeatedly restrained Conigastus, a tax-collector who was attacking the fortunes of unfortunate citizens. [Note: [Col. 0558D] Ibid.] Hence he recalled Triguilla, prefect of the royal household, from an injury already begun and already carried out. [Col. 0559C] [Note: [Col. 0559D] *Consolation of Philosophy* I, Prose 4.] Hence, by contending on behalf of Campania, he secured the prevention of an unjust compulsory purchase. [Note: [Col. 0559D] Ibid.] Hence he protected Paulinus, a man of consular rank, Albinus, and many others, both commoners and patricians, not without great danger to himself. [Note: [Col. 0559D] Ibid.]

### VII.

For this reason Boethius aroused such hostility against himself, especially among the wicked, that he was accused before Theoderic for the very qualities on account of which he should have been praised. Theoderic, driven by an immoderate love both of supreme authority and of the Arian religion, resolved to destroy Boethius.

Because of the qualities of character mentioned above, Boethius aroused the most serious hostility, especially among the wicked. [Note: [Col. 0559D] Ibid.: “Then there arose grave and implacable disagreements with the wicked.”] Certain courtiers [Note: [Col. 0559D] Ibid.: “The dogs of the palace.”], believing that the greater their authority, the more grievously they were injured by Boethius—whom they always found opposing their unjust schemes—pursued Boethius with the greatest hatred. Hence three wicked informers, Gaudentius, Opilio, and Basilius, accused Boethius before King Theoderic, either on their own advice or that of equally ruined men. The first two had been condemned to exile for countless frauds; the third had been removed from royal service and was deeply in debt. [Note: [Col. 0559D] Ibid.: “By whose accusations we were struck down.”]

Boethius was accused for the very reason on account of which he should have been praised. Because he had sought to protect not only commoners but also patricians, they alleged that he was guilty of treason and had stood on the side of the senate against the king. [Note: [Col. 0559D] Ibid.: “They falsely claimed that I had wished the senate to be safe.”] But because he excelled in every branch of learning, especially mathematics—a fate characteristic of ignorant ages—they falsely asserted that he had polluted his mind with magical arts, or, as our people say, with sorcery. [Note: [Col. 0559D] Ibid.: “They falsely claimed that I had polluted my conscience with sacrilege.”]

Finally, Theoderic, partly for his own reasons and partly on account of the Arian religion, readily seized the opportunity offered by the informers to destroy Boethius. That Arian prince had learned that the excellent emperor Justin treated not only the peoples subject to him with paternal affection, but also ordered all heretics infected with the Arian disease—except at least the Goths—to leave Constantinople and the entire East. [Note: [Col. 0559D] Sabellicus, book II, *Ennead* 8.] Fearing that, once the Catholic religion had been affirmed, the Romans, becoming more devoted to Justin, might expel both the Roman people and himself as an Arian, Theoderic arranged for Boethius, whom he suspected, to be punished as a warning to the rest.

Accordingly, on the very day on which King Theoderic had ordered Opilio and Gaudentius—unless they left the city of Ravenna within the prescribed time—to be driven into exile with marks branded on their foreheads, these same wicked informers were recalled into royal favor and sent by the king himself to Rome to accuse Boethius in his absence. [Note: [Col. 0559D–0560C] *Consolation of Philosophy* I, Prose 4: “When the royal judgment had decreed that Opilio and Gaudentius, on account of their countless and manifold frauds, should go into exile, and when, refusing to obey, they defended themselves by taking refuge in sacred buildings, and this became known to the king, he ordered that, unless they departed from the city of Ravenna by the appointed day, they should be expelled with marks branded on their foreheads.… Yet on that very day, when those same men brought accusations, the accusation against me was received.”]

The senate accepted the unjust accusation and by its decree condemned its innocent, unsuspecting, and undefended patron both to death and to proscription. [Note: [Col. 0559D] Ibid.: “Shall I call it a crime to have desired the safety of that order? He had made it a crime by his decrees against me.” “Because of our excessive devotion to the senate, we are condemned to death and proscription.”] Theoderic, fearing the emperor Justin and all good men, judged that these punishments should at least for a time be commuted to exile.

### VIII.

Thus, around the year 522 of the restored salvation, and therefore around the forty-seventh year of his life, Boethius was sent into exile under the reign of Theoderic. [Note: [Col. 0560D] This may be inferred from an ancient marble statue of Boethius, discussed below.] He was banished to the territory of Milan, or, as others hold, to Ticinum.

The duration of his exile seems to be inferable from the first poem of *The Consolation of Philosophy* [Note: [Col. 0560D] *Consolation of Philosophy* I, Meter 1, lines 9ff.:

> For untimely old age, hastened by misfortunes, came upon me unawares,  
> and grief commanded my years to bear its own age;  
> untimely gray hairs poured over my head.]

For Boethius himself says there that his old age, which he calls unexpected, had come upon him hastened by misfortunes, and that untimely gray hair had spread over his head. But unexpected old age and untimely gray hair do not befall a man before his fiftieth year.

Whatever the place and time of Boethius’s exile may finally have been, his exile was not a flight or a harbor from punishment, but punishment itself. [Col. 0560C] For a narrow place of residence was assigned to him; [Note: [Col. 0560D] Ibid., Prose 4: “The harshness of Fortune raging against us is sufficiently apparent in itself.”] there it was forbidden him even to see his relatives, friends, household companions, or books. [Note: [Col. 0560D] Ibid.: “Does the very appearance of the place move you not at all?” “Is this a library?”]

There Boethius, intending to demonstrate to posterity the integrity of his life and conduct [Note: [Col. 0560D] Ibid.: “I have committed the sequence and truth of this matter to writing and memory, so that it may not remain hidden from posterity.”], and intending to drive away his sad thoughts by the pleasing contemplation both of his own mind and of God himself, conceived this admirable work, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, and committed it to writing.

But while that illustrious man was occupied with this most holy task, another edict of the emperor Justin appeared. It attacked all Arians, not even excepting the Goths, and ordered that all heretical bishops be removed from their sees and that their churches be consecrated according to the rite of the Roman religion. Theoderic learned of this from the Arians who had fled to him. Therefore he sent ambassadors to Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0561D] Sabellicus, book II, *Ennead* 8.]—John the Tuscan, a Roman bishop, and the bishop of Ravenna; Agapetus and Patricius, Roman consuls; and Theodore and Importunus, senators and men of the highest distinction—and ordered them to demand from Justin that the Arian bishops and priests who had been removed from their positions be restored. If this were not done, Rome and all Italy would soon be filled with slaughter and even fires directed against the orthodox. [Note: [Col. 0561D] Sabellicus, ibid.; Paul the Deacon, book XV, chapter 5.]

When the ambassadors lingered on the journey longer than expected, Theoderic, impelled by the fury of his wickedness, put to death by the sword Symmachus and Boethius, former consuls and Catholic men. [Note: [Col. 0561D] Sabellicus, ibid.; Paul the Deacon, book XV, chapter 5.]

[Col. 0561B] He then imprisoned Pope John, who had returned from the embassy, together with his companions at Ravenna, and killed them by stench, thirst, and starvation, because the orthodox emperor had received him honorably and presented him with gifts. But the impious king also found an end of life worthy of his deeds. [Note: [Col. 0562D] Paul the Deacon, book XV; Procopius, book I *On the Gothic War*; Pomponius Laetus, etc.] From the time when he unjustly killed Symmachus, Boethius, John the Tuscan, bishop of Rome, and others, he fell into the deepest anguish of mind, so that when fish were served at table he imagined that they were the heads of the men he had murdered. Finally, on the ninetieth day after the death of Pope John, he died a sudden death.

### IX.

The manner in which Boethius was killed is not entirely certain. But at Ticinum a brick tower is shown as Boethius’s prison. The inhabitants of Ticinum, instructed by their ancestors, assert that Theoderic sent a tribune and an executioner there: the former to warn Boethius that, if he wished to remain alive, he should reveal whatever conspiracy existed; the latter to kill him if he refused to disclose it. [Note: [Col. 0562D] Julius Martianus Rota, in the *Life of Boethius*.]

They add that, when Boethius said that he was conscious of no action against the king, the executioner severed Boethius’s neck so completely that Boethius himself held up the severed neck with both hands. Then, when asked whom he supposed had struck him, he replied, “The wicked.” Afterward he went to a nearby church, received the sacred rites on bended knees before the altars, and finally breathed his last, destined to attain eternal glory.

For this reason Boethius was counted among the holy martyrs, and his memory is celebrated every year at Ticinum on the tenth day before the Kalends of November. [Note: [Col. 0562D] Ibid.] Likewise, at Ravenna the memory of Symmachus is celebrated on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, because both men met death for the faith against the Arians.

For this reason also his tomb, still visited at Ticinum in the church dedicated to St. Augustine, was adorned with several epitaphs. Formerly it bore these verses:

> Behold, Boethus is here, great in heaven and visible  
> to all the world, a remarkable man to be honored.  
>   
> Accused before the unjust King Theoderic,  
> he spent his old age in exile at Ticinum.  
>   
> In that city, consoling himself in sorrow, he produced a little book;  
> struck by the sword, he departed from the midst of men.

Now it bears these:

> Most renowned in the Maeonian and Latin tongues, and I who  
> was consul, here I perished, sent into exile.  
>   
> And because death seized me, my goodness raised me to the heavens;  
> behold, now my fame flourishes greatly, and my work lives.

[Col. 0562B] Boethius is therefore distinguished among his own by his ancestors, learning, virtues, wives, children, dignities, enemies, and death.

1. His ancestors were Anicii and Manlii, men so eminent among the ancient and noble Romans that they had few equals and certainly no superiors.

2. His learning was exceptional. As the last of all the ancient Romans to consecrate something to the monuments of literature, he was also the first of all to begin illuminating Aristotelian doctrine in the Latin language. Among posterity, moreover, he possessed such authority that scarcely any appeal is made from his judgment.

3. His virtue was peaceful in calm times; it shone in darkness; though driven from his place, it nevertheless remained and clung to his homeland; it always shone by its own light and was never dimmed by the stains of others.

4. His wives were worthy of their fathers, Festus and Symmachus, patricians greater than any praise. One of them imitated him in writing verse; the other made her husband a father through beautiful offspring.

5. His two sons, heirs of their father’s and grandfather’s virtue, were advanced together from their father’s house to the senate-house as consuls, amid an assembled senate and rejoicing peoples. There, while they sat in the curule chairs, their father, an orator of royal praise, earned glory for his genius and eloquence.

6. You might believe that dignities were innate in this family, for Boethius himself possessed from adolescence offices that were denied even to old men.

7. His enemies were wicked men alone—a great proof of exceptional virtue.

8. Finally, Boethius, loving God above all, shed his blood for the religion of his ancestors, around A.D. 525, in the fiftieth year of his life.

[Col. 0561]

## TESTIMONIES OF VARIOUS AUTHORS CONCERNING BOETHIUS AND HIS WRITINGS, CONTINUED IN AN UNBROKEN SUCCESSION OF AGES FROM BOETHIUS’S OWN LIFETIME DOWN TO OUR OWN TIMES

[Col. 0561D] Although the love of literature was not the same in all the ages that flowed from Boethius down to us, and although for that reason the memory of learned men was often interrupted, nevertheless, by a singular privilege of God, it came about that each of these ages has its own testimonies concerning the merits of Boethius. We shall select the principal ones.

## THE FIFTH CENTURY, THAT IS, FROM THE BIRTH AND FAME OF BOETHIUS TO A.D. 500

[Col. 0563A]

Priscian the Grammarian, a Caesarean by birth, a man highly skilled not only in grammar and rhetoric but also in philosophy and mathematics, says in his book *On Weights and Measures*: “Boethius attained the summit of integrity and of all the sciences.”

## THE SIXTH CENTURY, THAT IS, FROM A.D. 500 TO A.D. 600

Ennodius—or, as some read it, Evodius—bishop of Ticinum, a man highly distinguished both in his concise and in his prose style, writes to Boethius in the thirteenth letter of the seventh book of his letters:

> You, most accomplished of men, deign to praise my virtues, though industry made you ancient in your boyhood, without prejudice to your age. Through diligence you fill everything that is demanded of you; from the beginning of life, continual reading is your play, and another man’s labor is your delight. In your hands the doubled fire shines brightly, the fire by which the ancients gleamed as by a torch. For what scarcely happened to older men at the end of life abounds in you at its threshold.
