The same bishop, in the first letter of the eighth book of his letters, writes to the same Boethius after he had become consul:

> Full of the highest hope, for whom I desire success, I aspire to the care of an epistolary office. For it is fitting that this preface should be offered to your fasces, and that, among the purples of an owner whose light grows, I should not refrain from whatever conversation I may offer. Is love recognized only through the benefits of learning, and should it not be thought permissible for the desires of an unpolished man to come into the open? Vows are more simply made known when they are concealed by no artifice of expertise. Therefore, what we are in our hearts, we are with these lips. We cannot change the bitterness of our innermost thoughts by words that sweeten them. The modest praiser is the one whose mind suggests what must be said in the arrangement of flattery.

> Therefore let us give thanks to almighty God, who, while preserving in you the ancient good qualities of your family, multiplies new ones, and—what is more—makes those worthy of the summit of dignity worthy also of its heights. This glory is indeed restored to your ancestry, but what is clearer is that it has been obtained through the merit of your person.

> It may have been customary for the ancients to purchase the height of curule office by the sweat of the field and to shine with the light of honors through contempt for the light of day. But another kind of virtue is sought after Rome has become the reward of the victorious. Our candidate, after an evident contest, gains his deserved triumph though he has never seen war. He claims his laurels by judgment and did not think it necessary to engage with armed men.

> He shone between the swords of Cicero and Demosthenes and, as though born amid the very peace of the arts, gathered the sharp points of both their purposes. Let no one fear a discord between Attic perfection and Roman perfection, or doubt that the principal goods of nations can meet in fellowship. You alone embrace both, and you enclose, as an eager possessor of the greatest things, whatever, distributed among individuals, could have been sufficient.

> While imitating the eloquence of the ancients, you surpass it. While seeking the form of speech, you bestow it upon the most learned. I have before me a letter of yours whose revered composition bears witness to this. Would that what is sent by you were as frequent as it is pleasing!

> Perhaps you will be told: “It was fitting to praise a relative laboring for the common advancement,” because what seems to confer the palm upon one person alone is not truly personal. Indeed, a share in the curule office has come to me; but, if you allow me, I am more uplifted by the genius and studies of one who has been exalted.

> Sometimes these things have been added by circumstances; those others have fallen solely to virtue. A man almost destitute is brought to the staff of consular support, one who boasts only of his parents. In you both are stored: Latin learning and the vein of purple.

## II.

Cassiodorus, who joined understanding of sacred things with knowledge of secular matters, and joined both with the greatest holiness, sent several letters to Boethius in the name of King Theoderic, whose chancellor he was. One is the forty-fifth letter of the first book of Cassiodorus’s letters, and it is worded as follows:

> King Theoderic to Boethius, illustrious man and patrician:

[Col. 0564B] Things requested by neighboring kings as a matter of presumption are not to be despised, since small things often prove more capable of providing benefits than great riches can obtain. For frequently what weapons cannot accomplish, amusements of sweetness impose. Let us therefore act for the commonwealth, even when we seem to be playing. For this reason we seek pleasurable things: so that through them we may accomplish serious purposes.

Accordingly, the lord of the Burgundians earnestly requested that we send him a clock regulated by water flowing through a calibrated mechanism, and distinguished by the captured illumination of the immense sun, together with the masters of such things. Thus, by enjoying pleasures obtained from us, what is ordinary for us may appear to them a miracle. With good reason, indeed, they wish to look upon what they marvel at in the reports of their envoys.

[Col. 0564C] We have learned that you, nourished on much erudition, know this so well that you have drunk at the very source of the disciplines those arts which ordinary people, who practice them, do not know. Thus, though far away, you entered the schools of Athens; thus you mingled the toga with the choruses of the pallium-clad Greeks, so that you made the doctrines of the Greeks into Roman learning.

For through your translations Pythagoras the musician and Ptolemy the astronomer are read by Italians. Nicomachus the arithmetician and Euclid the geometer are heard by the Ausonians. Plato the theologian and Aristotle the logician debate in a Quirinal voice; and you have rendered Archimedes the mechanician Latin for the Sicilians. [Col. 0564D] Whatever disciplines or arts fertile Greece produced through individual men, Rome has received, through you alone as its author, in its native language.

You have made those men famous through such brilliance of expression and conspicuous through such precision of language that they themselves might have preferred your work, had they learned both languages. You entered the aforesaid art, born from the noble disciplines, through the fourfold gates of mathematics. You recognized it, seated in the innermost chambers of nature, by the light of your heart, with the books of its authors inviting you. Its purpose is to know difficult things, to display the wonders of practice, and to undertake to show what makes people marvel that it has happened. In a marvelous way, by transforming natural things, it deprives fact of credibility when it displays the vision before their eyes.

It makes waters rise from the depths and fall headlong; it makes fire run under weights; it makes organs resound with rough voices; and it fills pipes with foreign blasts so that they can sing by the art of music. [Col. 0565A] Through it we see the defenses of cities already tottering suddenly rise with such firmness that the one found helpless in strength becomes superior through the assistance of engines. Soaked structures are dried in seawater; hard things are dissolved by ingenious arrangement; metals bellow; the cranes of Diomedes trumpet in bronze; a bronze serpent hisses; artificial birds chirp; and things that do not know their own voice are shown to emit from bronze the sweetness of song.

We report only a little about an art to which it is permitted to imitate the heavens. In Archimedes’ sphere it made [the mechanism—object omitted in the source] move in accordance with the sun; it fashioned by human ingenuity a second zodiacal circle. It showed the moon, capable of being restored after its eclipse, through the illumination of art; and it rolled about with incomprehensible mobility a small machine pregnant with the world, a portable heaven, a compendium of things, a mirror of nature, fashioned in the likeness of the ether.

[Col. 0565B] Thus, although we may know the course of the stars, our deceived eyes nevertheless do not see them moving forward. There is a stationary passage among them: what you know by true reasoning to run swiftly, you do not observe to move. How remarkable that a human being should do what it may itself be marvelous even to have understood!

Therefore, since you are adorned with praiseworthy knowledge of such things, send us the aforesaid clocks at public expense and without loss to yourself. First, let there be one in which a pointer, the indicator of day, customarily shows the hours by a small shadow. Thus a fixed and small ray accomplishes what the sun’s so marvellous magnitude traverses, and matches the sun’s flight while itself never knows motion. The stars would envy such things if they could feel, and perhaps deflect their course lest they be subjected to such mockery. [Col. 0565C] Where is the singular wonder of hours coming from light, if shadow too shows them? Where is the praiseworthy unceasing revolution, if metals also accomplish this, though they remain fixed in a perpetual position? O inestimable power of art, which, while it says that it is playing, prevails in disclosing nature’s secrets. Let there be a second, in which the hour is recognized apart from the sun’s rays, dividing the nights into parts. So that it might owe nothing to the stars, it turned the scheme of heaven instead to the flow of waters; by their motions it displays what revolves in heaven. Art, conceived in bold presumption, grants to the elements what the condition of their origin denied. All learning and all the labor of the wise seek out nature’s power, in order that they may be able only to know it. Mechanism alone attempts to imitate it from opposites and—if it is permissible to say—strives in certain respects even to surpass it. [Col. 0565D] For it is known to have made Daedalus fly; to have made an iron Cupid hang in Diana’s temple without any fastening; today it makes the mute sing, the insensible live, and the immobile move. The mechanician, if it is permissible to say, is almost nature’s partner: revealing what is hidden, changing what is manifest, playing with miracles; imitating so beautifully that what is unquestionably constructed is judged to be reality. These things, since we have learned that you have studied them with especial care, you will hasten to send us as soon as possible: the aforesaid clocks. In this way make yourself known in that part of the world where you could not otherwise reach. Let foreign peoples learn through you that we possess nobles such as those who are read as authors. How often will those who see them refuse to believe? How often will they think this truth a playful dream? [Col. 0566A] And when they have recovered from their astonishment, they will not dare to call themselves our equals, knowing that wise men among us have conceived such things.

Another letter of the same Cassiodorus is the fortieth of Book Two, and runs as follows:

**King Theoderic to Boethius the patrician.**

When the king of the Franks, attracted by the fame of our banquet, earnestly requested a cithara-player from us, we promised that the request would be fulfilled for the single reason that we knew you to be skilled in musical learning. For it belongs to you to choose a learned man who can reach that discipline, placed as it is in a difficult position. What is superior to music, which modulates the structure of heaven with resonant sweetness and, through the power of its art, comprehends everywhere the harmony dispersed throughout nature?

And shortly afterward:

But since we have made a pleasurable digression—for it is always agreeable to converse about learning with experts—let your wisdom choose at the present time the best cithara-player whom, as we said, we requested from you. You will thereby do something of Orpheus’ kind, taming savage hearts among foreign peoples with sweet sound. And as much gratitude as is shown to us will be returned to you through our equitable compensation, since you both obey our command and accomplish what can bring you distinction.

The same Cassiodorus speaks of this same Boethius at the end of the book on Dialectic in these words:

“I have judged it fitting to summarize briefly whose labor brought these matters into Latin eloquence, so that their authors may not lose their glory and the truth of the matter may become fully known to us. The patrician Boethius translated the *Isagoge*, leaving two commentaries on it. The same patrician Boethius translated the *Categories*, and himself composed its commentaries in three books. The aforementioned patrician Boethius translated the *Peri hermeneias* into Latin and treated its commentaries himself in two extremely detailed discussions . . . The aforementioned patrician Boethius treated hypothetical syllogisms with the greatest clarity,” and so forth.

## III.

Procopius of Caesarea in Palestine, a rhetorician and sophist, wrote three books on the Gothic War among his various histories. In the first of these, what he wrote in Greek about Boethius is rendered into Latin as follows:

Symmachus and his son-in-law Boethius, both patricians, sprung from the illustrious blood of their ancestors, were leaders of the Roman senate and had been consuls. They devoted themselves to philosophy and justice more than other mortals, and supported many needy people—both Romans and foreigners—with their resources.

Having risen to immense glory, they aroused against themselves the worst men, who were envious of them. Persuaded by these informers, King Theoderic killed the highly distinguished men, as though they were plotting revolution, and confiscated all their property.

But a few days later, when the servants had placed before him, as he dined, the head of an enormous fish, Theoderic seemed to see in it the head of the recently slain Symmachus. Its teeth appeared to be fixed in its lower lip, while its eyes gazed fiercely and furiously, seeming to threaten him greatly. Terrified by the novelty of the omen and trembling and shuddering beyond measure, he hastened to his bedchamber. There, repeatedly ordering that a great quantity of garments be piled upon him, he found some relief.

Then, after explaining to the physician Elpidius everything that had happened, he lamented the crime he had committed against Symmachus and Boethius. Finally, having lamented this, he was overwhelmed by immense grief at the calamity he had suffered and died not long afterward. This was the first and last example of injustice that he exercised against his subjects, because he had proceeded against such great men without thoroughly investigating the case, contrary to his usual practice.

The same author, speaking in the third book of the aforementioned history about Boethius’ surviving wife, says:

“Thus all that remained for Rusticiana, once the wife of Boethius and daughter of Symmachus, for life and as an addition to her misery was that, dressed in servile and rustic clothing, she who had distributed her resources to the needy should beg from her enemies for bread and the other necessities of life. Going around the houses and knocking at the doors, she humbly begged that food be given to her,” with no disgrace whatsoever attaching to her on that account.

Indeed, the Goths had conspired to kill Rusticiana, accusing her of having distributed money to the commanders of the Roman army and of having overturned Theoderic’s statues, thereby avenging the slaughter of her father Symmachus and her husband Boethius. Totila, however, did not permit her to suffer any injury, but preserved her and all the others from insult.

## THE SEVENTH CENTURY, THAT IS, FROM THE YEAR 600 TO THE YEAR 700

Bede, called “the Venerable” because of the holiness of his life and the gravity of his character, esteemed Boethius and his teaching so highly that he wrote commentaries on Boethius’ book *On the Trinity*. This author frequently praises Boethius in many places, with honor and respect.

## THE EIGHTH CENTURY, THAT IS, FROM THE YEAR 700 TO THE YEAR 800

[Col. 0567C]

Paul the Deacon, who at the request of Adelburga, daughter of King Desiderius, added much to the history of Eutropius, says in the seventh book of this continuation, after stating that Pope John, Theodore, Importunus, and Agapitus, men of consular rank, together with another Agapitus, a patrician, had been delayed on their journey as envoys to Justin:

“Theoderic, driven on by the madness of his wickedness, slaughtered with the sword Symmachus, former consul and patrician, and Boethius the elder, former consul—Catholic men.”

## THE NINTH CENTURY, THAT IS, FROM THE YEAR 800 TO THE YEAR 900

### I.

Ado, archbishop of Vienne, who composed a brief chronicle extending from the origin of the world to his own time, says, speaking of Pope John:

“When he had returned and reached Ravenna, Theoderic, moved by envy because Justin, the defender of Catholic piety, had received him honorably, killed him together with his companions through the affliction of imprisonment. At that time the same Theoderic killed Symmachus and Boethius, men of consular rank, on account of their Catholic piety.”

### II.

Anastasius, keeper and restorer of the apostolic library, and for that reason called the Librarian, writes the following about Boethius in his *History of the Popes*, under John I:

“At the same time, when the persons mentioned above—that is, Pope John, together with the senators Theodore, former consul; Importunus, former consul; and Agapitus, former consul (Agapitus the patrician having died at Thessalonica)—had been stationed at Constantinople, the heretical king Theoderic seized two distinguished senators and former consuls, Symmachus and Boethius, and killed them, piercing them with the sword.”

## THE TENTH CENTURY, THAT IS, FROM THE YEAR 900 TO THE YEAR 1000

Since Boethius’ bones had lain neglected for many centuries and were insufficiently honored because of the passage of time, the Emperor Otto III ordered them to be enclosed in marble. An epitaph was inscribed, composed by Gerbert, archbishop of Ravenna, formerly the emperor’s teacher; after being made supreme pontiff, he was called Sylvester II. Like Boethius, he was falsely regarded by the ignorant as a magician because of his exceptional knowledge of hidden matters. He expressed that epitaph in the following verses:

While powerful Rome declares its laws throughout the world,

[Col. 0568B] You, father and light of your fatherland, Severinus Boethius,

As consul, guide the reins of affairs,

You pour light into learning and do not yield

To the intellects of the Greeks; but divine reason restrains

The empire of the world. When the sword of the Goths raged,

Roman freedom perished; you, consul and exile,

Leave illustrious titles through a glorious death.

Now Otto the Third, glory of the empire,

Who surpasses the highest arts, judges you worthy of his court;

And he establishes eternal memorials of your labor,

Adorning with honorable distinctions one who has deserved so well.

## THE ELEVENTH CENTURY, THAT IS, FROM THE YEAR 1000 TO THE YEAR 1100

### I.

Sigebert, a monk of Gembloux of the Order of Saint Benedict, who holds no insignificant place among historians in his work *On Illustrious Writers*, doubts whether Boethius should be ranked with, or preferred to, philosophers both secular and ecclesiastical.

“Boethius,” he says in chapter 37, “a man of consular rank, should be ranked with, or preferred to, philosophers both secular and ecclesiastical, since he leaves us uncertain whether he was more illustrious among secular or among ecclesiastical writers.

“Secular writers praise him because he translated the *Isagoge*, the *Peri hermeneias*, and the *Categories* from Greek into Latin and explained them; because he explained Cicero’s *Topics*; because he wrote the *Ante-Predicaments*, books on topical differences, on knowledge of dialectic and rhetoric, on the distinction of rhetorical topics, on the common predication of power and possibility, on categorical and hypothetical syllogisms, and many other works; and because he wrote arithmetic and music in Latin.

[Col. 0568D] “We ecclesiastical writers praise him because he wrote a book *On the Holy Trinity*; because, exiled by Theoderic, king of the Goths and Italians, for wishing to defend the freedom of the Roman city, he wrote the book *The Consolation of Philosophy*. He was killed by that same King Theoderic.”

### II.

Honorius of Autun, a priest of the Church, says in his *Chronicle*:

“Boethius, patrician or consul, wrote a book *On the Holy Trinity* and another *On Consolation*, and translated the quadrivium from Greek—that is, arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy. He explained dialectic. He was killed at Milan by Theoderic, king of the Goths.”

## THE TWELFTH CENTURY, THAT IS, FROM THE YEAR 1100 TO THE YEAR 1200

### I.

John of Salisbury, an Englishman by nationality and bishop of Chartres, who among his other works wrote the *Policraticus*, or *On the Frivolities of Courtiers and the Footprints of Philosophers*, highly commends Boethius’ book *The Consolation of Philosophy* in the same work, Book Seven, chapter fifteen.

“If you do not believe me,” he says, “let the book *The Consolation of Philosophy* be read more attentively, and it will be clear that these things lead in the opposite direction. Although that book does not explicitly express the incarnate Word, nevertheless among those who rely on reason it possesses no slight authority, since it prepares suitable remedies for restraining every pain of an ulcerated mind.

“Neither Jew nor Greek, under the pretext of religion, should reject the use of this medicine, since among the wise in faith and among those who foolishly reject faith, the skillfully prepared medicine of living reason is so beneficial that no religion dares detest what it combines—unless one is devoid of reason. It is profound in its judgments without difficulty, distinguished in its words without frivolity, a forceful orator, and an effective demonstrator. Toward what ought to be followed it now glides forward by persuasion, now drives one onward as though with the spur of necessity.”

### II.

To this may be added the author of the book *On the Spirit and the Soul*, which is attributed among the works of Saint Augustine—if Vincent’s conjecture in the *Speculum historiale* and that of Abbot Trithemius are correct, for they assert that this author was Hugh of Saint Victor, who flourished in the year 1130.

This author, whoever he may be, not only thought it worthy of honor to reproduce Boethius’ thoughts and words, saying in chapter eleven, “The mind now inserts its head among the highest things, now sinks down into the lowest,” and other words found in meter 4 of Book Five of *The Consolation of Philosophy*, but in chapter thirty-seven also employs Boethius’ authority:

“Boethius,” he says, “states that understanding belongs exclusively to God and to very few human beings.”

## THE THIRTEENTH CENTURY, THAT IS, FROM THE YEAR 1200 TO THE YEAR 1300

Saint Thomas, greater than all our praise, commends Boethius’ merits in a remarkable manner—not, indeed, in commentaries of his own on the books of *The Consolation of Philosophy*, since, as we have proved, these are not genuinely works of Saint Thomas, but through his frequent praise of this author, by which he ranks Boethius with the supreme Doctors of the Church and employs his authority to establish the truth.

Thus, in Part I, Question 10, Article 1, he explains in detail the definition of eternity, which he says was set forth by Boethius, placing it above the others:

“Eternity is the complete and perfect possession, all at once, of interminable life, as is found in Book V of *The Consolation*, prose 2, near the beginning.”

Likewise, in Question 29 of the same part, in the *Sed contra* argument, he gives the definition of person, which he says is Boethius’ from the book *On the Two Natures*, and explains it in detail:

“Person is an individual substance of a rational nature.”

And similarly in the other matters.

## THE FOURTEENTH CENTURY, THAT IS, FROM THE YEAR 1300 TO THE YEAR 1400

### I.

Philip the Fair, king of the Franks, as Peter Bertius reports in his preface to the books of Boethius’ *Consolation*, valued these books of *The Consolation of Philosophy* so highly that, although he himself understood Latin, he nevertheless regarded it as a favor that John of Meung, a poet learned according to the standards of that age, had translated them into French and dedicated them to him. A copy of this work is still preserved today in Paris, in the library of the Augustinians.

### II.

Maximus Planudes, a Constantinopolitan monk, paid no attention to the proud custom of the Greeks, who ordinarily do not render Latin books into Greek. He valued Boethius’ books *On the Consolation of Philosophy* so highly that he translated them into Greek. This copy is preserved in the king’s library.

## THE FIFTEENTH CENTURY, THAT IS, FROM THE YEAR 1400 TO THE YEAR 1500

### I.

Lorenzo Valla, a Roman patrician and himself a most learned man, not only says that Boethius speaks Latin, as Julius Scaliger reports, but also calls Boethius “the last of the learned,” in the preface to his own books on dialectic.

“Nor,” he says, “does Boethius, the last of the learned, think otherwise; he is, as it seems to me, more Platonic than Aristotelian. In one place he promised that he would teach that these authors differ little from one another.”

### II.

[Col. 0570C] Saint Antoninus, archbishop of Florence and a member of the Order of Preachers, wrote most honorably about Boethius in Part Two of his *History*, title 11, chapter 2, section 4:

“When King Theoderic of the Goths was oppressing the commonwealth in Italy in earlier times, Boethius, a most distinguished senator and, as will be said below, a lover of the commonwealth because of his wisdom, often opposed the king on behalf of justice. Since he was held in great esteem by everyone both because of the nobility of his birth and because of his eloquence, he was feared even by the king himself.

“Therefore, as is believed, certain people were suborned to accuse him of treason. They said that, after betraying the Roman state, he had summoned Prince Anastasius to Italy so that he might free the commonwealth from Theoderic’s hands. On this pretext, he exiled him, together with certain other Roman nobles, to Pavia, where, placed in prison, he wrote the book *The Consolation of Philosophy*. There he was finally killed by him.”

And in chapter 15, citing Sigebert, he says:

“At that time the patrician Symmachus distinguished the Roman commonwealth, and with him his son-in-law Boethius, a man of consular rank, conspicuous in both languages and in the learning of all the liberal arts, almost all of which he translated from Greek into Latin eloquence.”

### III.

James Philip Bergomensis, of the Order of Augustinian Hermits, says in his *Supplement to the Chronicle*, under the year of Christ 500:

“Boethius Anicius Manlius Severinus, a most Christian man distinguished by consular rank, and a most celebrated poet and philosopher, was at that time most distinguished at Rome as the son-in-law of the patrician Symmachus. Some call him Manlius, because they report that he descended from Manlius Torquatus.

“Since he was truly Catholic and often refused, even when repeatedly asked, to obey the Arians, he himself was ordered by King Theoderic, under the pretext of an alleged desire for freedom, to go into exile at Ticinum after his father-in-law. Later, at the instigation of the heretics, he was condemned to perpetual imprisonment.

“While enduring this calamity, and being highly learned in mathematics, he invented and carved the *chiterinum*—a stringed instrument—for the first time, to refresh his spirit. In modern times it is regarded as a celebrated musical instrument.

“While confined in the same place, he also produced, for the great benefit of many, extraordinarily distinguished and innumerable little works, as it were; and the works that have come into our hands are these.

“And afterward:

“This excellent and holy man, when King Theoderic could not bend him entirely to his own judgment, was stirred by the fury of the Arians and, after the long squalor of imprisonment, ordered to be killed at Pavia for the Catholic faith, under the Emperor Justin the Elder Augustus, in the year of Our Lord 520. His body is still buried there in the church of Saint Augustine. Some say that for this reason he was entered in the catalogue of the saints and called Saint Severinus.”

### IV.

Hermolaus Barbarus, a Venetian patrician, archbishop and patriarch of Aquileia, says in the preface he delivered when he began publicly to lecture on Aristotle’s books:

“Those who think that this entrance is open to no one who has never entered those schools of philosophy are greatly mistaken, since neither Marcus Varro, Brutus, Plancius, Chalcidius, nor Boethius entered such schools; nor did Alexander, Themistius, Porphyry, Iamblichus, or Simplicius, although they were most eminent philosophers and most devoted interpreters of Aristotle.”

### V.

Angelo Poliziano, who was distinguished both as a poet and as an orator and published many works in both Greek and Latin, speaks of Boethius in chapter 1 of his *Miscellanies* as follows:

“Who is sharper than Boethius in dialectic? Who more subtle in mathematics? Who richer in philosophy? Who more sublime in theology? The younger philosophers, whom I consider by far the most perceptive of all, valued him so highly that he deserved to have Thomas Aquinas, that holy man, and that great teacher of Thomas—good heavens, what men!—as his interpreters.”

“Indeed,” says Vallinus, “this refers to what Saint Thomas wrote on Boethius’ books *On the Trinity* and *On the Hebdomads*; for the commentaries on Boethius’ books *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, commonly attributed to Saint Thomas, are not by this most holy doctor.”

## THE SIXTEENTH CENTURY, THAT IS, FROM THE YEAR 1500 TO THE YEAR 1600

### I.

John Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, says in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*:

“Boethius Manlius Severinus, ordinary consul at Rome, philosopher, orator, and distinguished poet, learned in the divine Scriptures and the most learned man of his time in secular letters, was the son-in-law of the patrician Symmachus.

“He was abundantly steeped in Greek and Latin eloquence, since he translated into Latin many volumes both of Aristotle and of other philosophers from the Attic language. He was subtle in intellect, quick in understanding, and Catholic; in speech inferior to Cicero in no respect. It is established that he had the friendship of Saint Benedict and that, on Mount Cassino, he dined at the table of Tertullus, the father of the monk Placidus and a senator.

“He wrote many distinguished volumes, of which I have found the following:

“To his father-in-law Symmachus, patrician of the city of Rome, one book *On the Holy Trinity*, beginning: ‘After a very long investigation,’ etc.

“One book *On the Unity of the Trinity*, beginning: ‘I ask whether the Father and the Son,’ etc.

“One book *On the Two Natures in Christ*, beginning: ‘You have indeed anxiously,’ etc.

“One book *On the Faith*, to John the Deacon, beginning: ‘I have learned the Christian faith.’

“One book *On Unity and the One*, beginning: ‘Unity is that by which,’ etc.

“Two books *On Porphyry’s Isagoge*, beginning: ‘In the season of the wintry year,’ etc.

“One book on the second edition of the same work, beginning: ‘This second [edition],’ etc.

“Two books on Aristotle’s *Categories*, beginning: ‘These matters having been completed,’ etc.

“One book on the *Peri hermeneias* of the same author, beginning: ‘The books are indeed great,’ etc.

“Six books on the second edition of the same work, beginning: ‘Alexander in,’ etc.

“One book *On Divisions*, beginning: ‘How great a number of students,’ etc.

“One book *On Definitions*, beginning: ‘Of speaking and arguing,’ etc.

“One book, an introduction to categorical syllogisms, beginning: ‘Many ancient philosophers,’ etc.

“Six books on Cicero’s *Topics*, beginning: ‘At your exhortation,’ etc.

“Four books *On Topical Differences*, beginning: ‘Every method of reasoning,’ etc.

“Two books *On the Categorical Syllogism*, beginning: ‘The ancient Greeks wrote much,’ etc.

“Two books *On the Hypothetical Syllogism*, beginning: ‘Since in all matters,’ etc.

“One book *On the Hebdomads*, beginning: ‘You ask that from the hebdomads,’ etc.

“Two books *On Arithmetic*, beginning: ‘Among all the ancient,’ etc.

“Five books *On Music*, beginning: ‘The apprehension of all things,’ etc.

“Five books *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, beginning: ‘Songs once,’ etc.

“Three books on Euclid’s geometry, beginning: ‘But you, my Patrician,’ etc.

“One book *On the Discipline of Students*, as some believe, beginning: ‘Your,’ etc. This book is unworthy of being attributed to so great a man, and learned people do not attribute it to Boethius.

“One book *On Rhetorical Topics*.

“One book *On the Predication of Power*.

“One book of letters to various persons.

“He is also said to have written some other works, but they did not come to my notice. He died in the same year as the patrician Symmachus and Pope John, under the Emperor Anastasius, having been slain in prison at Ravenna by order of King Theoderic after a lengthy exile, in the year of Our Lord 524, in the second indiction. He is said to have been entered in the catalogue of the saints under the name Severinus.”

### II.

[Col. 0573A]

Julius Caesar Scaliger, a man of the highest renown in the republic of letters, very frequently praises Boethius, as in his *Hypercriticus*:

“Boethius Severinus’ intellect, learning, art, and wisdom easily challenge all authors, whether Greek or Latin. Because of the barbarism of the age, his prose is found in a worse condition; but the things he chose to play with in poetry are truly divine. Nothing is more polished, nothing more weighty. The density of his judgments did not remove their charm, nor did his sharpness remove their brightness. I certainly judge that few can be compared with him. Valla teaches that he speaks Latin; but Boethius teaches Valla to think well.”

Thus the same Scaliger sings of Boethius in *The Gods*:

You may enumerate the mighty seeds of his divine mind:

Add to these the senate, eloquence, and ancestral halls.

[Col. 0573B] It is not enough: add the heavens, and Boethius will have begun

To be a part of them; yet you still do not grasp his full gifts.

### III.

Lilius Gregorius Gyraldus, also very well known among learned men, likewise extols Boethius with the highest praises, in his *History of the Poets*, dialogue 5:

“But let us bring forward other men of this age, among whom was Boethius Anicius Manlius Severinus, a Roman patrician and former consul, whom most of our people place in the catalogue of martyrs.

“He and Symmachus, himself a patrician and, as almost everyone reports, Boethius’ father-in-law, were first exiled to Ticinum and then killed by Theoderic, king of the Goths, because they seemed to wish to restore the Roman people to freedom.

“As you know, Boethius was exceptionally learned in every discipline, as can be clearly established for you from his works. But, as far as the present subject is concerned, he displayed marvelous facility in composing verse. It would be superfluous to gather more about him, since his volumes are known to everyone. His intellect was certainly celebrated in extraordinary fashion by his murderer, King Theoderic, for those arts that lie beyond letters.”

### IV.

The Magdeburg Centuriators, century 6, chapter 10, *On Bishops and Doctors*, say:

“Boethius Anius Manlius Severinus, patrician and consul, was a man most learned in Greek and Latin. He left to posterity many books written in philosophy and other disciplines, both in prose and in verse.”

### V.

[Col. 0574A]

Justus Lipsius, who is honored by all learned and good men both for his outstanding learning and especially for his frank integrity of spirit, not only praises Boethius in his civil learning and other works, but, writing to his kinsman Janus Bernartius about *The Consolation*, which Bernartius had illuminated and emended, produced these Phaleucian verses:

Behold that Boethius, who boasts

That he is foremost among the wise,

Who published this work, excessively learned

And sufficiently eloquent,

Judged good by all good men.

Yet it possessed darkness,

Whether from the age or from his own talent;

That Bernartius, flower of my

[Col. 0574B] Belgians, drove away,

Holding forth a bright torch of his own.

Follow it, whoever, a lover

Of learning and wisdom, longs

Not merely to hear, but to be.

## THE SEVENTEENTH CENTURY, THAT IS, FROM THE YEAR 1600 TO OUR OWN AGE, 1779

I would be excessively lengthy if I wished to review and enumerate everything said in praise of Boethius during our own century. For there is no historiographer or theologian who has not spoken of that most illustrious author in elaborate and honorable terms.

If you wish, consult Baronius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, volume VII, under the year 522; Don Pietro of Saint Romuald, *Chronological Treasury*, volume II, under the year 510; and all the other historians. See the Reverend Father Caussin in the book entitled *La Cour sainte*, where, in presenting the ideal of a man whom he calls a “man of state,” he discusses at length Boethius’ nobility, learning, counsels, and death.

Read also, if you wish, Gerardus Johannes Vossius, *On Latin Poets*, chapter 5:

“In the period when Zeno and afterward Anastasius ruled in the East, and Odoacer and then Theoderic ruled in Italy, Anicius Manlius Boethius Severinus flourished, a man most learned in Latin and Greek and outstanding in every kind of discipline. Rome, from the time of Varro, had possessed no one more learned.

“How much he was able to accomplish in verse is shown by the five books *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, which he wrote in exile at Ticinum. That age, or even the one immediately preceding it, possessed nothing more graceful in poetry.”

[Col. 0573]

# OUTLINE OF BOETHIUS’ BOOKS *ON THE CONSOLATION OF PHILOSOPHY*

[Col. 0573D] This work, small in bulk but immense in learning, is a sequence of arguments known by the natural light of reason. Through these arguments the human mind, aroused by adverse circumstances, is so raised by attention to the first cause and the ultimate end that, once stripped of prejudices, it becomes more capable of attaining truth and cultivating virtue.

For this reason the work is entitled *The Consolation of Philosophy* and is divided into three parts. The first contains Boethius’ affliction; the second, the consolation of Philosophy; the third, arguments that seem opposed to the force of that consolation, together with their replies.

# BOETHIUS’ AFFLICTION

[Col. 0574D]

## BOOK I

Boethius, conscious of his own misery and therefore unable to endure it, seeks opposing thoughts on every side by which his grief might, if not be driven away, at least be diminished. Hence he turns his mind (Prose 1) to the Muses, formerly familiar to him and guardians of song. But he receives and drives away their remedies as new provocations of sadness; and through the help of philosophical reflection Boethius realizes that he is immersed in the greatest ignorance of all things—not only (Meter 2) in unawareness, but also (Prose 2) in inactivity.

Then, as the light of Philosophy gradually increases (Meter 3), he first recognizes Philosophy herself (Prose 3); next, both ancient and more recent philosophers, attacked by similar misfortunes but not overcome by them (Meter 4). Nevertheless, led by an old prejudice, he does not cease to complain to Philosophy about his exile (Prose 4), alleging only that human beings seem to be released from divine laws and, as though by an inverted order, to receive punishments and rewards (Meter 5).

# THE CONSOLATION OF PHILOSOPHY

After Philosophy has warned him that:

1. exile and Boethius’ adverse fortune are improperly called by those names (Prose 5);
2. Boethius’ mind cannot yet be treated with stronger remedies (Meter 6);
3. she will henceforth make use of the knowledge that Boethius possesses both of himself and of God, although it is obscured by disturbances (Prose 6 and Meter 7);

the same Philosophy sets forth three classes of arguments for consoling Boethius, of which she says that the first is of lesser weight, the second of greater weight, and the third of the greatest weight.

“First,” she says, “the person who has entrusted himself to the power of a mistress whom he knows to be as fickle as she is alluring, and to be no less often the parent of evil than of good, ought not to complain with her about the evil inflicted upon him, especially if he has received more good than evil from her. For a master and mistress may exercise their rights over a slave without any injury to the slave; nor may a slave who could have been treated badly complain when he is treated well.

## Book II

“But you, O Boethius, entrusted yourself to the discretion of Fortune, whom you knew to be naturally as changeable as she is alluring, mistress of good and evil, and from whom you received more good than evil. For under Fortune’s guidance you received, as a boy, an excellent education; as a young man, the highest honors; as a mature man, an excellent father-in-law, an excellent wife, and excellent children; and—what is most important—always an excellent disposition. From these things you could learn that, with equal prudence, both the highest and the lowest conditions of human life are to be avoided.”

“Second,” she says, “there is no just reason for complaining about the loss of things which are so far from being good that they are rather evils belonging to the human mind. For it is good—and therefore a cause rather for gratitude than complaint—to be deprived of evils.”

“But what you have lost, O Severinus—namely, riches [Col. 0575D] and the other things of that kind which you call goods—are rather evils of the mind than goods, and rather causes of misery than of happiness. For this reason [Metro 5] the age of our ancestors was happier: they were less enslaved than we are by desire for these things. For this reason [Prosa 6] power, when it has found a seat in an evil magistrate, produces countless slaughterings, as is especially clear from the example [Metro 6] of Nero. For this reason [Prosa 7] fame itself, by which every good man seems to be guided as though by a second life, [Metro 7] ultimately doubles death when it finally collapses. For this reason [Prosa 8] Fortune, which is commonly called prosperous, wrapping the mind in darkness, leads it both into error and into vice; whereas Fortune, which is commonly regarded as adverse, frees it from these things, [Col. 0576A] so that it may be aroused to truth, virtue, and even [Metro 8] divine love.”

## Book III

“But unless you grant that these things are evils, you must admit that in them there is only false happiness [Prosa 1 and Metro 1], which must be driven away before you can enjoy true happiness. Hence—”

“Third,” she says, “the man who has lost only those things in which happiness is believed, through a false assumption, to consist does not even complain justly, since he is thereby made all the more fit to attain true happiness. For he is thereby all the more free from the miseries that are the sole cause of complaint.”

“But you, O Manlius, having lost only those things in which happiness is believed, through a false assumption, to consist, are thereby all the more fit to attain true happiness.

“First, you have lost only those things in which happiness is believed, through a false assumption, to exist. For generally speaking, such is every created good [Prosa 2], to which the innate idea of the highest good within us is wrongly attached [Metro 2]. Such are [Prosa 3 and Metro 3] riches. Such are [Prosa 4 and Metro 4] offices. Such is [Prosa 5 and Metro 5] power. Such is [Prosa 6 and Metro 6] glory. Such is [Prosa 7 and Metro 7] bodily pleasure. Such are [Prosa 8 and Metro 8] all perishable goods.

“Moreover, you are for that reason better fitted [Prosa 9] to attain true happiness—namely, the true conception of the highest good—provided that God assists you; for this reason he must be invoked [Metro 9]. There is indeed [Prosa 10] a highest good, namely God, to whom every human being ought to devote himself in thought [Metro 10], as [Prosa 11] [Col. 0576C] to the final end of all things. To teach this to man [Metro 11], let him meditate more attentively upon his own mind. Through this meditation he will learn that all things have been made by God, are governed by God, and must be referred to God. Through this thought [Metro 12] we are happy; and we are unhappy only when, upon looking at perishable things, this same thought is either destroyed or at least obscured.”

## Arguments Opposed to the Consolation of Philosophy, with Their Responses

The more ancient prejudices are, the more difficult they are to cast off. Therefore, since Boethius has been disturbed by the foregoing arguments, he has several objections available against that philosophical teaching; but his Philosophy is not without answers.

## Book IV

### I

“If God,” says Boethius, “governed the world, neither virtue would be without reward nor vice without its appropriate punishment; yet we experience the contrary.”

“Neither is virtue without rewards,” replies Philosophy, “nor vice without its own punishments. First [Metro 1], the good, by cleaving to God in thought, are in their true homeland, from which the wicked are exiles. Second [Prosa 2], the good are powerful and the wicked powerless, especially because the former govern themselves while the latter obey their disturbances [Metro 2]. Third [Prosa 3], the good are transformed in mind into gods, while the wicked become [Metro 3] beasts. Hence the wicked [Prosa 4] are most miserable, and for that reason [Metro 4] deserve pity.”

### II

“Let the good have their happiness and the wicked their misery,” says Boethius. “But if God governs the world, why are the good affected by disadvantages and the wicked by advantages?”

“Many answers may be given,” says Philosophy. “First, even if the genuine cause of so great an arrangement were unknown to man [Ibid.], he ought nevertheless not to doubt that everything is rightly done [Metro 5]. A man may wonder at this, just as the common people wonder at celestial phenomena. Further, these reversals [Prosa 6] belong no less to divine providence than to fate. Therefore, just as [Metro 6] other things move in a certain cycle, so [Prosa 7] Fortune—even adverse Fortune—since it arises from God, must be referred to God, so that [Metro 7] man may enjoy what he desires only after enduring his labors.”

## Book V

### III

“Since God,” says Boethius, “provides for everything, nothing can be unforeseen. If God governs the world, there will be no chance in the world; yet experience teaches something contrary.”

“There will be no chance for God,” replies Philosophy [Ibid.], “but there will be chance for human beings. Thus two ships, carried along by the steady currents of two rivers, may each by its own chance encounter the other [Metro 1].”

### IV

“If divine providence is posited,” Boethius insists [Prosa 2], “human freedom will not stand, although every human being is conscious of possessing it.”

“Just as freedom stands in each individual mind,” Philosophy replies [Ibid.], “so human freedom will stand in its own right. At least God [Metro 2], whose nature it is to see all things, knows the manner in which human freedom can be reconciled with divine providence.”

### V

“How,” asks Boethius [Prosa 3], “can divine providence, since it is utterly certain, be reconciled with human freedom, which is free from necessity? [Metro 3] Is it because, as in other matters, so here the human mind neither knows everything nor is ignorant of everything, and therefore seeks to advance from what is known toward what is unknown?”

“This harmony [Prosa 4],” Philosophy replies, “seems difficult for the reason that divine foreknowledge, infinitely surpassing human foreknowledge, cannot be grasped by the human mind. Thus, whatever the Stoics may think [Metro 4], there are several modes of knowing in the same human being, some of which so transcend others that what we can understand we cannot for that reason imagine.

“Therefore [Prosa 5] [Col. 0578B], just as our understanding ought not to be denied on account of the weakness of our imagination, so divine foreknowledge of free future events ought not to be denied on account of the weakness of human understanding. Nor, I say, should human understanding be denied on that account; it seems to have been given to man [Metro 5] above other living creatures so that he might be raised toward the sight of heaven. [Prosa 6] God, therefore, being eternal, knows free future events as though they were present, without impairing human freedom.”

## Censure of Boethius’s Books *On the Consolation of Philosophy*

These books have had their opponents. Some complain that certain things were added to the work; others, that certain things were omitted. We shall now attempt to answer both groups.

### I

Henricus Glareanus, whom some support, believes, in his Preface to the works of Boethius, that the prose discourse of this work was not written by Boethius because it is more barbarous. From this he not only expresses doubt but denies that anything in the work is genuinely the offspring of Boethius.

To this I reply, first, that the prose and the metrical discourse of this work belong to the same author; second, that this author is Boethius; and finally, that Boethius was not without reason both a philosophical orator and a poet, speaking sometimes barbarously and sometimes in Latin [Col. 0577D].

First, the prose and metrical discourse of the *Consolation of Philosophy* belong to the same author. For if either form of discourse is removed, no connection remains. Consider, without going into further examples, how the final verse of the first poem,

> He who fell was not standing on a firm step,

cannot be connected without the intervening prose with the first verse of the second poem,

> Alas, how deeply plunged into a precipitous abyss

> is the dull mind!

Consider also how widely separated, without the intervening verses, are these final words of the first prose section and the opening words of the second:

> Philosophy lamented in these verses the disturbance of our mind; but, she says, it is time for medicine, not complaint, and so forth.

Furthermore, the author is Boethius, since all the writers whom we mentioned above list the five books of the *Consolation of Philosophy* among Boethius’s genuine works. No other argument would prove that the *Aeneid* is a genuine work of Virgil.

Finally, Boethius was not without reason in mixing barbarous words with Latin throughout this work. Since he wished to fulfill the role of a philosophical orator, he chose words adapted to the understanding of the barbarous common people of his time, so that his philosophical thought might be more easily grasped by the minds of his listeners. For in philosophy, as Tully excellently observes, things are considered, not words weighed.

But while sustaining the role of a poet, he wished to speak in the language, as they say, of the gods: not only so that the minds of those same listeners, wearied by weightier propositions, might be refreshed—for this reason Boethius, imitating Plato and several other ancients, wrote his books in disputation and dialogue—but also so that he might rescue the Latin language, already growing old in his rougher age and hastening toward destruction, as it were from the jaws of death. Since, as consul, he could not prevent the barbarians from invading Italy by force of arms, he tried at least, as a teacher, to drive barbarism from Europe through his verses.

For this reason the barbarism mentioned above sometimes appears in his other works as well, both philosophical and theological. Yet his verses are polished, elegant, and almost divine—as Glareanus himself admits.

### II

Petrus Bertius, whom I also see to have many supporters, believes, in his Preface to these books of Boethius, that Boethius did not complete the whole work of the *Consolation of Philosophy* as he had intended. He also thinks Boethius had planned to add, from Christian doctrine, material by which the human mind might be raised to consideration of eternal life.

For, he says, “It is not likely that a Christian, with death before his eyes, would have passed over that part, or that the man who wrote about the Holy Trinity in prison would not have sought consolation in adversity from the teaching of Christ and from the doctrine of things to be believed and hoped for, explained in the sacred books.” He adds that Boethius repeatedly promised, began, and hastened to complete greater works, and to open the road by which the mind might be raised to its homeland.

Boethius’s piety was indeed so great that no one can doubt that this most holy man thought of Christ in prosperity as well as in adversity. But whoever embraces in his mind the conception of this work that we have proposed will certainly acknowledge that the work is complete. For it has been brought as far as natural light—or philosophy, which, to use Tertullian’s expression, is “naturally Christian mind”—could reach.

Therefore, although throughout the whole work there were many opportunities for citing sacred Scripture, Boethius did so only once, using these words of Wisdom:

> He orders all things sweetly.

Boethius could therefore have said, speaking of his philosophical *Consolation*, what Justus Lipsius later said of his *On Constancy*:

“If I intended to act as a theologian, I have gone astray; if as a philosopher, why do they blame me? For, they say, we draw from pools which, although they are fed by the purest fountain of the divine Scriptures—do they summon me here? But I testify from my heart and answer that I know no other way of salvation than this, which leads along that one direct path. Yet I judge that human letters can also contribute some relaxation, indeed some assistance, toward traversing it.

“I know that Augustine’s counsel is to gather what has been written by philosophers ‘and claim it for our use, having taken it away from those unjust possessors.’ This I wished to follow, and I have sinned. I confess that I would have sinned if I had corrupted this pure and mystical liquor of our religion with some ancient and foul dregs. But, on the contrary, I have applied myself to the task and have attempted to cleanse and illuminate doctrine that was in itself sordid and insufficiently pure with this new sun.

“But for what good purpose would this not be good? In battle, we know that cavalrymen and infantry soldiers perform the principal service. Do you therefore reject the archers and slingers? In building a house, architects receive the greatest praise and have the greatest usefulness. Will you therefore dismiss the laborers and assistants? Think the same here. Those divine Scriptures produce true strength, true virtue, and solid constancy; yet do not utterly despise human wisdom. I mean the wisdom that does not exalt itself but quietly serves and ministers.

“We transport stones, cement, and lime from that old and long-collapsed building of philosophy. Do not begrudge the architect this little profit, and allow this material at least to be laid beneath the foundations. ‘But surely the sacred things are better, and one ought not to abstain from words?’ I admit that they are better; but add also that they are weightier. I measure my muscles, limbs, and abilities: why should I allow a burden to be placed upon me that I am not strong enough to carry?

“I leave those great and lofty matters to theologians—that is, to great and lofty men, of whom this age has produced many. My little boat will hug the shore. I shall act as a philosopher, but a Christian.”

Whatever Lipsius intended, our Boethius, in this *Consolation of Philosophy*, seeks remedies suitable not only for his own illnesses but also for those of other human beings—namely, their disturbances.

Arguments that could have been drawn from sacred doctrine and from the examples both of Christ and of the holy Fathers might have helped Christians, or perhaps Jews, but certainly not pagans. The philosophical arguments he uses, however, are founded upon the natural light implanted in all human beings and can therefore be of the greatest use to all human beings in curing the diseases of their disturbances.

Nor should anyone be troubled by the fact that Boethius repeatedly promised, began, and hastened to complete greater works. For since the natural light mentioned above is nothing other than a conception divinely impressed upon the human mind, or a thought by which God—being no less the teacher than the principle and end of the human mind—teaches that mind the way of eternal salvation; and since that mind’s attention is a kind of question or prayer by which the mind, God’s pupil, seeks greater instruction and asks its teacher God—who is most ready to enlighten it more fully—for it.

For as our attention to this first truth increases, the natural light mentioned above can grow in such a way that it may, to some extent, open the way by which the mind may be led back to its homeland. Nevertheless, as the Christian religion teaches, we cannot successfully travel this road unless Christ—who is the way, the truth, and the life—shows it to us, goes before us, and assists us.

## A. M. Sev. Boethius, *On the Consolation of Philosophy* (C)

# Book I

## 1. Meter

### Note: What Is Called Elegiac Meter

An elegy is a poem consisting of two alternating kinds of verse. The first is the heroic hexameter, which has a spondee in the sixth foot, a dactyl in the fifth, and either a spondee or a dactyl indiscriminately in the remaining four feet. The second is the elegiac pentameter, which has an anapest in the fifth and fourth positions, a spondee in the third, and either a spondee or a dactyl indiscriminately in the first two positions.

### Argument

Boethius, observing the contrast first between his earlier and present verses; second, between his prosperous and adverse fortunes; third, between the flourishing and declining periods of his life; and fourth, between the approach and withdrawal of his death, proves from the instability of his circumstances to his friends that the condition of his affairs had not been happy.

### Note

“I who once completed poems while my studies were flourishing—alas, now afflicted, I am compelled to undertake sorrowful verses. Behold, the torn Muses dictate to me what must be written, and the weeping elegies wet my face with genuine tears. No fear could induce even these Muses not to accompany me on my journey.

“These same Muses, who were once the glory of my fortunate and vigorous youth, now console the adverse fortune of a sorrowful old man. For hastened old age came upon me unexpectedly through hardships, and grief caused its own age to exist within me. Premature gray hairs are scattered over my head, and my skin, with my limbs exhausted, trembles in wrinkles.

“That death of human beings is fortunate which does not thrust itself into flourishing times, but comes often implored by the afflicted. Alas, how far inexorable death withdraws from suffering human beings, and how cruelly it refuses to close tearful eyes!

“When Fortune, rashly trusted because of her fickle favor, was smiling upon me, it was not far from happening that a sorrowful day would end my life. But now, since adverse Fortune has turned her deceitful face away, my cruel soul prolongs my unpleasant days. O friends, why did you so often say that I was happy? He who fell was not standing on a firm step.”

### Note 1: *Carmina*—“Poems”

*Carmen* is derived from *canere*, “to sing,” just as, according to Vossius, *germen* is derived from *genimen*; so *carmen* may derive from *canimen*, with *n* changed into *r*, as happens in several other words.

Hence *carmen* is a compact discourse composed of several verses, which poets are said to sing. Thus Virgil, beginning the *Aeneid*, says, “I sing of arms and the man.” A *carmen* is therefore called a somewhat longer work of a poet, such as an epigram. Thus Catullus’s epigrams are entitled *carmina*. The same is true of an ode: thus Horace’s odes are called books of poems. It is also true of any poem: thus Lucretius calls Book I a *carmen*:

> Recall what shines clearly in each poem of the first book.

But a single verse is not ordinarily called a *carmen*, unless perhaps, because it contains a complete thought, it seems comparable to a poem. Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* III.287, sings:

> I fasten them to the facing doorposts and mark the matter with an inscription:

> Aeneas [set up] these arms taken from the victorious Danaans.

### Note 2: *Modos*—“Measures”

“Verses.” For *modus* generally means moderation, beyond or short of which what is right does not exist, as Horace teaches:

> There is a measure in things; there are, finally, fixed limits,

> beyond or short of which the right cannot stand.

Hence *moderatus* means the same as “temperate,” *modestus* means “observing measure,” and *commodum* means “in accordance with measure.”

If moderation must be preserved somewhere, it must especially be preserved in what is received by the ears, whose judgment, according to Tully, is exceedingly proud. Hence music and poetry, which are said to be related at least in being perceived by the same sense of hearing, employ certain measures.

Tully says in *On the Orator* I: “Rhythms, voices, and measures.” Horace likewise says:

> Seek themes with a lighter plectrum;

> To be fitted to the measures of the lyre;

> To lessen great things with small measures;

> Knowing sweet measures and the lyre;

and in *The Art of Poetry*:

> Greater license has been added to rhythms and measures.

Therefore, one who composes verses is said, in the case of Virgil, Ovid, Horace, and others, to “measure” or “modulate.” Similarly Cicero, in *On the Nature of the Gods*, says that flutes “sing in measured fashion” and strings “sound rhythmically.”

Just as *carmen* is used only of a complete poem, so *modus* seems to be used only of the verses that are parts of this work. Thus Boethius, having opposed these words to one another in the first two verses—“I completed” and “I am compelled to begin,” “while study flourished” and “mournful”—now, continuing the antitheses, also sets “poems” and “sorrowful measures” against each other. In this way he teaches the reader what sort of man he was in his affliction and how greatly he had changed from Boethius—or himself—in his flourishing condition.

### Note 3: *Camenae*—“Muses”

The Muses are called *Camenae*, not, as some say, from pleasant song, but, like *carmen*, from *canere*, “to sing,” so that they were originally called *Carmenae.” This is because poems or songs are produced as though the Muses inspire them, or because, as Festus says, the Muses sing the praises of the ancients. For this reason one should write *Camenae*, not *Camaenae*.

These Muses are now described as torn because, sharing Boethius’s lot, they seemed to flourish when he flourished and to suffer when he was afflicted, appearing ragged and torn. For it was an ancient custom of the afflicted to tear their clothing. Thus in Job 1:20:

> Then Job arose and tore his garments;

and in 1 Samuel 4:12:

> A man of Benjamin came from the battle line to Shiloh that day, with his garment torn and dust upon his head.

Virgil likewise writes, *Aeneid* XII.609:

> They lower their spirits; Latinus goes with torn clothing,

> stunned by his wife’s fate and the ruin of his city.

These Muses are finally said to dictate to Boethius what he must write because poets imagine that nothing proceeds from them, whether by speech or writing, except what they have learned while the Muses inspire them. Consequently they do not ordinarily undertake a great poem without first invoking those same Muses.

Thus Homer says in *Iliad* II:

> Tell me now, Muses, who inhabit the heavenly dwellings; for you are goddesses, and you are present and know everything. We have received only hearsay, and know nothing.

Horace likewise says, *Satires* I.5:

> Muse, I ask you to remember;

and Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.641:

> Open Helicon now, goddesses, and stir the songs . . .

> For you, divine ones, remember and can recall;

> only a faint breath of rumor reaches us.

### Note 4: *Elegi*—“Elegies”

“Mournful or pitiable verses.” For *elegus*, from which *elegia* is derived, is a poem of alternating hexameter and pentameter verses, especially expressing sadness. Hence Horace writes in *The Art of Poetry*:

> Complaint was first enclosed in unequal joined verses;

> Later the expression of a completed wish was also enclosed.

> But what author sent forth the brief elegies,

> Grammarians dispute, and the case remains undecided.

He likewise says, *Odes* I.33:

> Do not grieve, Albius, too much in memory

> of harsh Glycera, nor sing pitiable

> elegies.

Ovid likewise writes at the beginning of *Fasti* II:

> Now for the first time, Elegy, you proceed with larger sails;

> recently, I remember, you were a small work.

These verses are called elegies especially because they were used at funerals. For *elegos* means “weeping,” from **ἀπὸ τοῦ ἒ ἒ λέγειν**, “from saying ‘eh, eh,’” the cry of mourners according to Aristophanes.

Therefore Ovid says in *The Art of Love* III, elegy 1:

> Release your mournful hair, elegy:

> Alas, your name is now all too true.

Just as the tears of elegies are now called genuine by Boethius, since they arise from sadness, which is ordinarily the subject matter of elegies, and the elegies are said to wet the face, as Virgil writes in *Aeneid* VI.699:

> Saying this, he simultaneously washed his face with abundant tears.

### Note 5: *Has saltem*—“At least These”

“Muses.” For among all the goods by which a human being can be affected—whether external, such as wealth, honor, friends, children, and parents; or internal, whether bodily, such as strength, beauty, and health, or mental, such as knowledge and virtue—only the goods of the mind are not exposed to the attacks of enemies.

For this reason Ovid writes in *Tristia* III, elegy 7:

> Fortune gives whatever she wishes and snatches it away;

> suddenly he is an Irus who was just now a Croesus.

> Why should I recount each thing? Nothing mortal do we possess

> except the goods of the heart and intellect.

> Behold, although I lack my homeland, and you and my house

> have been taken away—things that could be taken from me—

> nevertheless I accompany and enjoy my own intellect;

> Caesar could have no authority over this.

Boethius experienced this. Under Theoderic’s action, he lost not only his wealth, offices, and good health, but also was abandoned by his friends, who, overcome by fear of the emperor—who did not hesitate even to destroy Rome—fled. Therefore Boethius was accompanied in his exile only by the goods of the mind, namely knowledge and virtue. But since it was not fitting for a most modest man to speak openly of his virtue, he mentioned the Muses and remembered at least knowledge as his companion.

Thus Ovid writes in *Tristia* IV, elegy 1:

> The Muse also raises me, as I seek the places in Pontus to which I have been commanded to go;

> she alone remained the companion of my flight.

> Alone she fears neither ambushes nor the soldier’s sword,

> neither the sea nor winds, nor barbarism.

I shall not omit what grammarians teach: that *saltem* arose from captives who ask nothing else of the victor except their safety.

## The Poem

> I once completed poems while study flourished;

> alas, mournful, I am compelled to begin sorrowful measures.

> [Col. 0582A] Behold, the torn Muses dictate to me what must be written,

> and weeping elegies wet my face with genuine tears.

> [5] No terror could overcome even these Muses,

> so that they would not follow as companions on our journey.

> [Col. 0583A]

### Note 7: *Gloria*—“Glory”

Honor, good reputation, and glory differ from one another in such a way that honor is a genus under which, first, good reputation and, second, glory fall. Therefore, just as honor is generally a good estimation of another person’s virtue manifested by some sign, so is glory. But honor can belong to one person; good reputation only to a multitude; and glory consists also in the favorable estimation of distinguished people.

Hence, according to Scaliger, *gloria* is said as though it were *glosia*, just as *ara*, *lares*, and *arena* are said as though they were *asa*, *lases*, and *asena*. *Glosia* arises from Greek **γλῶσσα**, “tongue,” because glory is extensive fame concerning someone’s virtue and merits.

Thus Ennius says of himself:

> I fly alive through the mouths of men.

Virgil imitates him in *Aeneid* XII.235:

> Fame will follow, and alive he will be carried through men’s mouths.

Fame is considered great for no other reason than that it wanders through the minds and mouths of distinguished people. Referring to this, Tully says in *For Marcellus*:

> Glory is the illustrious and widely disseminated fame of the merits of many great men, whether toward their fellow citizens, their country, or the whole human race.

But the question here is whether that great fame of Boethius belonged to his knowledge or to his virtue. Those who believe it belonged to Boethius’s virtue think that one should read *solatur*, “he consoles,” since otherwise the syntax would not stand—as though Boethius, praising the past and saying that he had been sustained in old age by the consolation that during his youth he had been endowed both with virtue and with glory, the reward of virtue.

We, however, arguing on behalf of knowledge, believe that this glory belonged to the Muses mentioned in the final verse. Therefore we think one should read, as all ancient manuscripts read, *solantur*, “they console”—as though Boethius himself were saying: “The Muses, through whom, while I flourished as a young man, I obtained glory, now console me, an afflicted old man.”

Certainly, since the human mind cannot be powerfully affected by several thoughts at the same time, when it carefully devotes itself to a pleasant thought it often does not seem to be affected by a sorrowful thought, as though unaware of it. Thus those who are tormented by the stings of conscience after committing a crime soothe this sad thought as though with a consolation through games, conversation, or some other activity. Likewise, a father afflicted by the unexpected death of his beloved son may, through the demanding labor of hunting, wipe away his grief as though with a consolation, so that he seems unaware of it.

Ovid sings in *Tristia* IV, elegy 1:

> I was an exile, and my repose was sought, not fame,

> so that my mind would not remain continually intent upon its own evils.

> This is why even a miner bound in chains sings,

> softening his heavy labor with an unaccustomed rhythm.

> The man who leans forward, bent over the muddy sand,

> also sings as he carries his slow boat against the current.

> And he who pulls the slow oars equally to his breast

> turns his arms in rhythm through the beaten water.

> When the weary shepherd has leaned upon his staff and sat upon a rock,

> he soothes the sheep with a song upon his reed.

> The maidservant who sings while at the same time drawing out the allotted wool

> deceives herself and lightens her labor.

> They say that sorrowful Achilles, after the Lyrnessian woman was taken away,

> lessened his cares with the Aeolian lyre.

> And when Orpheus was grieving after losing his wife twice,

> he drew forests and hard rocks by singing.

Thus the Muse relieves Boethius.

Three things remain to be observed here. First, the force of the caesura in the words *felicis olim*, “once fortunate.” A caesura is nothing other than the syllable remaining from the preceding scansion, with which the subsequent scansion begins. It can lengthen a syllable that would otherwise be short, since, as the beginning of the following word, it must be raised in pronunciation so that it can support the remaining syllables of that word. Examples are familiar, such as Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.64:

> Eagerly examining the breathing entrails at their breasts.

Second, one must observe the distinction that some establish among *juventus*, *juventas*, and *juventa*. They say that *juventus* is a multitude of young people, *juventas* a goddess, and *juventa* an age. But these distinctions do not hold consistently, for Sallust called an age *juventus*.

Finally, one must observe Boethius’s age. Although he calls himself old here, when he wrote this he had not yet reached his fiftieth year. Therefore he adds that he had grown old not so much through a series of years as through a series of hardships.

### Note 9: *Venit . . . senectus*—“Old Age Came”

Boethius gives the reason why he called himself old. Old age, which according to Tully may be defined as the setting of life, occurs because the fibers from which the solid parts of a living body are composed become slowed, and those solid parts reach such hardness that they not only cease to grow but cannot even be nourished.

Hence gray hair, wrinkles, and trembling arise. Gray hair arises from old age because the fluid from which hairs are formed, being less vigorously moved, assumes the shape of rounded particles. For this reason snow, eggs, paper, and even ink turned into foam become white; for this reason linen cloth exposed to dew and sunlight becomes bright. Thus, if the same material of the hair recovers its former movement and changes this shape, grayness is shed, as has sometimes happened to those whose hair had turned gray through illness.

Wrinkles likewise arise from old age because the fibers of the skin, previously stretched by movement, become delayed and settle one upon another in such a way that, imitating furrows, they seem to plow the face. Finally, old people commonly tremble because of the lack of vital spirits diffused from the brain through the nerves.

There are two kinds of old age: natural and violent. The first comes through years; the second through a long succession of hardships. Hence Ovid writes in *Ex Ponto* I, elegy 5:

> Now a harsher age is scattered over me with gray hair,

> and now an old man’s wrinkle plows my face . . .

> I admit that years do this; but there is another cause as well:

> anxiety of mind and unceasing labor . . .

> An immense succession of hardships also weakens me:

> before my time I am compelled to be old.

But Boethius is not complaining here of old age caused by years. For such old age does not begin before the fiftieth year, which Boethius had not yet reached when he wrote this. Rather, he is speaking only of his old age caused by hardship. He therefore calls it, first, hastened by misfortunes, because his hardships were the causes of that old age; second, unexpected, because it arrived before its time; and third, an age of grief, because although the age of old people ordinarily brings grief, grief brought Boethius old age.

Hence Boethius’s gray hair is called untimely, because it arose through exile, imprisonment, and his other calamities. Scaliger, in *Exercises* 312 on Cardan, similarly relates that someone suddenly seized by fear of death became gray within the space of a single night.

Moreover, since gray hair, wrinkles, and trembling are companions no less of old age caused by hardship than of old age caused by years, they are mentioned in verses 11 and 12 as effects of an exhausted body.

For *effetus* first denotes any parent that has produced offspring; then a parent who, exhausted by frequent childbirth, has finally ceased to give birth; and finally any thing which, with its strength drained, has become so feeble that it can produce nothing. Thus Virgil writes in *Georgics* I.81:

> To scatter filthy ash over exhausted fields.

## The Poem

> The glory of a once fortunate and vigorous youth

> now consoles my sorrowful fate as an old man.

> For hastened by misfortunes, unexpected old age has come,

> and grief has ordered its own age to be present.

> Untimely gray hairs pour down from my head,

> and the loose skin trembles over my exhausted body.

> [Col. 0585A]

### Note 13: *Mors hominum felix*—“The Fortunate Death of Human Beings”

Since speech is the interpreter of thought, human speech ought to be of the same character as thought. For Christ truly says in Matthew 12:34:

> The mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart.

Thus Dido, according to the different thoughts with which she is affected by Aeneas, speaks differently, saying at one moment that he was born from the gods and at another that he was born from wild beasts:

> I believe indeed—and my belief is not vain—that he is of the race of the gods . . .

> Nor was a goddess your mother, nor was Dardanus your ancestor,

> faithless man; rather, savage rocks gave you birth— [text continues]

The Caucasus and the Hyrcanian tigresses fastened upon their udders. Since Boethius, therefore, had not yet consulted Philosophy, he speaks under the guidance not of understanding but of prejudice. I say that he does not speak under the guidance of understanding: for in prosperous fortune he would have said, with Cicero, that death threatens daily because of uncertain circumstances and, because of the brevity of life, is never far away; in adversity, however, that this same death compensates for delay by the eternity of the better life into which it introduces us. But Boethius speaks under the prompting of prejudice—namely, pleasure and distress, by which the human mind is affected in prosperity and adversity. For the person affected by pleasure regards as happy that death which does not intrude upon his sweet years; whereas the person afflicted by mental distress regards the death that comes when often summoned as so happy that it is all the more cruel insofar as, deaf—as it were—it allows life to be prolonged. Hence Boethius concludes that death was not even happy for him under these conditions: in prosperity it hastened forward, while in adversity it was unwilling to take his life and lingered. This will become sufficiently clear when certain words that follow are examined.

15. “With a deaf ear.” A person is called deaf when, because the ear is obstructed, he does not hear. Since the ear is especially obstructed by things that have entered it, a deaf person—*surdus*, or, as the ancients said, *sordus*—seems to be so called by contraction, as though from *sordidus*, “dirty.” But when the term is transferred from this usage to the mind alone, one is also said to be deaf in mind who, impeded by some contrary emotion, does not hear the person entreating him. Thus Statius, *Silvae* II:

> And you hate the lyre and turn away with a deaf ear.

Death, however, is represented by poets as a kind of person who, according to its various dispositions, can hear those who call upon it or fail to hear them.

16. “To close the eyes.” The importance of the eyes in preserving human life is so great that people commonly say that life resides in the movement of the eyes, and death in their repose. Hence the person who enjoys the light perceived by the eyes is considered to be living, while the person who lacks it is considered dead. Thus *Aeneid* IV, line 450:

> Then indeed the unhappy Dido, terrified by the Fates,  
> Begs for death: she is weary of looking upon the vault of heaven,  
> So that she may carry through what she has begun and leave the light …

17. “Faithless Fortune.” That is, Fortune in whom one can place no trust. Since Fortune is irrational, blind, brutish, and rolling like a round stone, as the philosophers maintain, she immediately casts down those whom she has raised up. Hence, in Horace, *Odes* I.35, Fortune is said

> Either to raise a mortal body from the lowest station,  
> Or to overturn proud triumphs  
> Into funerals.
