18. “The hour had plunged my head.” Time is called by poets the cause of things; hence one time is favorable because it helps, and another adverse because it harms. An hour is a certain portion of time; because it almost plunges Boethius into ruin, it is therefore called “sad.”

20. “Ungodly life.” An ungodly person is one who behaves badly toward God, toward parents, or toward those who stand in the place of parents. Hence a certain plant is called “ungodly” because, when it grows, it strangles its parent shoots. The life that Boethius had hitherto tried to cherish as a kind of parent now seems to behave badly toward him in this respect: by postponing its departure, it prolongs Boethius’s sufferings. Thus Quintilian, in the Preface to Book VI of the *Institutio Oratoria*, calls longevity “ungodly.”

21. “Friends.” Boethius addresses his friends, since they had previously called Boethius happy and can now, by the outcome itself, be convicted of their error. The notion of happiness and misery is implanted in human minds; hence we naturally flee misery and pursue happiness. Since both this notion and this inclination are gifts of God, who enlightens and moves us, each thought is, in itself, so right and of one kind in all human beings that it becomes unjust and multiple only through the perverse will of a human being who applies it wrongly. Thus, according to the varying force of their disturbances, one person thinks the rich happy, another the powerful, and another those endowed with other created goods. Accordingly, while Boethius was flourishing, some of his friends had called him blessed because he abounded in wealth; the others because he held office. But now, by the outcome, all are convicted that Boethius ought not to have been called happy for those reasons. A fall is certainly an indication of instability, and present misery proves that there was no past happiness—since, if the fear of losing prosperity is itself a kind of misery, no human prosperity can be considered happiness unless it shares in constancy, of which the person himself is conscious. But Boethius’s much-vaunted prosperity was not constant, since he was cast down from his position; and from this it is evident that he who fell was able to fall.

6. Happy is the death of human beings, which neither intrudes upon their sweet years  
nor, though often summoned, comes to those in misery.

[15] 7. Alas! How deafly does it turn away from the wretched,  
and how cruelly does it refuse to close their weeping eyes!  
While faithless Fortune favored me with fleeting goods,  
[Col. 0586A] the sad hour had almost plunged my head into ruin.

Now, because the clouds have changed their deceptive face,  
[20] ungodly life prolongs its unwelcome delays.

8. Why did you so often proclaim me happy, my friends?  
The man who has fallen was not standing on a stable foundation.

9. PROSE I

[Col. 0587A]

ARGUMENT.—Philosophy is described as approaching Boethius, lying on his couch, after driving away the poetic Muses, in order to lament the great disturbance of his mind.

While I was silently reflecting upon these matters within myself [Note: “I considered.”], and with the aid of a stylus [Note: “By the function of a stylus.” A *stylus* is a pointed instrument with which the ancients scratched letters into wax. Boethius says that he used it like a pen to write the verses mentioned above, which he calls a tearful lament because they are elegiacs; for elegiacs are mournful verses.] I was marking down a tearful lament [Note: “With the aid of a pen.”], the stylus having served this purpose, [Note: “She stood beside me.”] a woman of an exceedingly venerable appearance seemed to me to have stood above my head. [Note: “My crown,” that is, the top of my head.]

[Note: “She stood beside me.” It is customary not only among poets but also among orators to set before themselves first, and then before their hearers, for consideration through some sensible object what cannot be perceived by the senses, so that a truth which at first seems concealed may, once discovered, please all the more because of the difficulty of finding it. Hence, St. Jerome says in his commentary on Matthew 18, it is customary among the Syrians, and especially the Palestinians, to join parables to all their discourse, so that what hearers cannot retain through a simple precept may be retained through likenesses and examples. Hence the symbols common among authors, made by things, words, paintings, or images of things. Nothing more learned can be said on this matter than what the most distinguished Huet, having collected examples from every quarter, says in his little work *On the Origin of the Romans*, which you may consult if you wish.

But philosophy, since it consists in a certain activity of the mind, cannot be perceived by the senses. Boethius therefore judged that it should be set before himself first, and then before us, through some sensible object. Here are presented concerning Philosophy: (1) her origin, (2) her nature, (3) her subject matter, (4) her expressions, (5) her forms, and (6) her use.

I. The origin of philosophy is presented in this: a woman appeared to Boethius standing above his head. Since philosophy is nothing other than natural light diffused somewhat more broadly, it arises from God, from whom natural light comes. Thus Cicero says in *Tusculan Disputations* I: “Philosophy, the mother of all the arts, is a gift and invention of the gods.” Philosophy therefore ought to have been seen only in a lofty place and above the head, as though fallen from heaven. Hence Philosophy also appears exceedingly venerable or worthy of honor. For we judge venerable or worthy of honor that which we consider to surpass others in origin, age, wisdom, virtue, or any other dignity. “Philosophy,” says Cicero, “contains the discipline of virtue, duty, and right living; whoever professes it appears to sustain a most weighty role.”]

10. [Note: “With burning eyes.”]

II. The nature of philosophy is presented here. For the nature of philosophy consists in this: it is clear and distinct knowledge by which the human mind, avoiding haste and prejudice—through which people are commonly deceived—forms a true and certain judgment about the subjects under consideration. “All knowledge and practice concerning the best things,” says Cicero, *On the Orator* III, “is called philosophy.” Since Philosophy is now said to have burning and penetrating eyes, it is understood that her knowledge is clear and distinct. Since she is said to have penetrating eyes beyond the ordinary capacity of human beings, it is understood that haste and prejudice—by which people are accustomed to be led into error—are avoided by her. Since she is described as having a vivid color and inexhaustible vigor, it is understood that philosophy generates true and certain judgment and is, as it were, its parent. But since, although full of age, she is said to possess inexhaustible vigor, it is understood that philosophy is strengthened by continuous meditation, so that she gains strength as she proceeds.

A grammarian may observe several points here. First, the construction of the words “of venerable appearance, with burning eyes.” Although Valla says that it is unusual for both of these cases to occur in a single expression, the usage is nevertheless not faulty, since Pliny, according to Valla himself, speaks in this way; and Cicero says: “Lentulus, a young man of exceptional promise and outstanding virtue.” See the *New Method*. Next, the noun *valentia*, “capacity,” which Boethius also uses in Book III, Prose 9, and Book IV, Prose 2, does not seem to be very common among Latin writers. It has the same meaning as *potentia*, “power.” Hence some, on the authority of Solinus, chapter 2, derive the interpretation of the name of the city of Rome from it:

> There are some who wish it to appear that the name of Rome first arose from Evander, when he encountered there a settlement that the Latin youth had earlier called *Valentia*, “Power”; and, preserving the meaning of the name previously imposed, they called it in Greek *Rhōmē* and in Latin *Valentia*.

She had burning eyes, penetrating beyond the ordinary capacity of human beings, [Note: “Seeing beyond the common powers of human beings.”] and a vivid color, together with inexhaustible vigor, although she was so full of age [Note: “Ancient.”] that she could in no way be believed to belong to our time.

[Note: “Her stature was of uncertain proportion.”]

III. The subject matter of philosophy is presented. Philosophy first concerns the human being himself, considering the mind and body from which the human being is constituted; for the notion of the human being seems to be prior to all others. Therefore the woman mentioned above now reduced herself to the common measure of human beings. Next, once the human body is known, philosophy concerns the remaining bodies, including the heavens, insofar as knowledge of these bodies contributes to preserving human life. Hence the same woman now seemed to strike the heavens with the crown of her head. Finally, having come especially to know the human mind, philosophy concerns the most perfect mind of all, God. God teaches us inwardly in such a way that, so long as he is not recognized as supremely truthful, the first rule of truth remains unknown. Hence, when this woman raised her head higher, she penetrated even the heavens. But since God cannot be perceived by the senses in the way human beings are ordinarily said to perceive things, the same woman, while contemplating God, eluded the gaze of those who looked at her.

[Note: “Her height was of various proportions.”]

Her stature was of uncertain proportion. For at one moment she confined herself to the common measure of human beings [Note: “She was contained within it.”], while at another she seemed to strike the heavens with the crown of her head. When she raised her head higher, she penetrated even the heavens and eluded the gaze of those who looked at her. [Note: “She escaped the sight.”]

[The numeral (5) enclosed in parentheses represents the lines of the Delphin edition, for easier and more useful consultation of the alphabetical index. —Editor.]

11. [Note: “They were garments.”]

IV. The expressions of philosophy are presented here with remarkable artistry. First, philosophical expressions are the garments of philosophy itself, because words are the coverings and wrappings of thoughts, while philosophy, as knowledge, is a certain kind of thought. Second, philosophical expressions are made with the finest threads, delicate workmanship, and indissoluble material, because these terms are humble, adapted to understanding rather than display, and joined together by an indivisible bond. Since philosophers themselves discovered most of them, philosophy is therefore said to have woven them with her own hands; and because of this, a certain darkness of neglected antiquity commonly covers their appearance, as it covers smoky images. For this reason Boethius, whose outstanding Latinity shines forth in his verses, did not hesitate to use in his prose certain barbarous expressions employed only among philosophers.

Her garments were made with the finest threads, delicate workmanship, and indissoluble material [Note: “Indivisible.”]; as I later learned from her own account, she herself had woven them with her own hands. A certain darkness of neglected antiquity had covered their appearance, as it commonly covers smoky images. [Note: “At their extreme edge.”]

V. The forms of philosophy are now presented. “Philosophy,” says our Boethius in the Preface to Porphyry, “is a genus; its species are two: one called *theoretical* [Greek: θεωρητική, *theōrētikē*], the other *practical* [Greek: πρακτική, *praktikē*], that is, speculative and active.” The former species, marked by the letter Θ, is occupied with the pure contemplation of truth; the latter, marked by the letter Π, with the practice of virtue, as St. Augustine teaches in *The City of God* VIII.4, where he says that Socrates excelled in active philosophy, while Pythagoras applied himself more intensely, with whatever powers of understanding he possessed, to contemplation. Plato is therefore praised for perfecting philosophy by joining the two together.

[Col. 0589C] Theory was written at the top and practice at the lower edge. In Aristotle’s judgment, the contemplative excels the active; yet there are steps by which one may ascend from one to the other and descend again, because the practice of virtue cannot exist without contemplation of truth, nor ought contemplation of truth to exist without the practice of virtue.

Finally, the hands of certain violent people—those who philosophized under the influence of haste or prejudice and devoted themselves neither to considering truth nor to practicing virtue—tore apart the philosophical expressions and carried away whatever fragments each could seize. Romans 1:

> Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools.

At the lower edge of these garments, the letter Π was woven, while at the top the letter Θ was woven. Between the two letters, certain steps appeared, arranged like a staircase, by which there was an ascent from the lower element to the higher one. Yet the hands of certain violent people had torn the same garment, and each had carried away the fragments he could seize.

[Col. 0590A]

12. [Note: “She carried books in her right hand and a scepter in her left.”]

VI. Finally, the use of philosophy is presented. Philosophy is useful both for undertaking the other disciplines and for governing minds; this is signified by the books and the scepter.

First, philosophy is useful for undertaking the other disciplines, insofar as it prescribes on the one hand the laws for avoiding error and on the other those for discovering truth. Hence Cicero often says: “Philosophy is the mother of all the arts,” the creator and, as it were, parent of every honorable art. “Without the discipline of the philosophers,” he continues, “we cannot discern the genus and species of anything, explain it by definition, divide it into parts, judge what is true and what is false, discern consequences, recognize contradictions, or distinguish ambiguities.” This function of philosophy is signified by the books. A *libellus*, “little book,” is derived from *liber*, “book.” According to Isidore, Book VI, chapter 12, *liber* is the inner layer of bark adhering to the wood, on which the ancients wrote. Hence Pliny, Book XIII, chapter 11, says that people first wrote on palm leaves and later on the books—the bark—of certain trees. Cassiodorus likewise indicates this in Book XI of the *Variae*, letter 38, where he discusses paper. From this it came about that *liber* and *libellus* came to signify the things contained in what was written in them.

Next, philosophy is useful for governing minds. Minds are governed when their disturbances have been calmed and the truth has been disclosed—matters to which philosophy devotes itself. Hence, as will be said later, Plato taught that states would then be happy when either philosophers ruled or rulers philosophized. This second function of philosophy is signified by the scepter, for the scepter is a sign of authority. Thus Lucretius, Book V:

> Therefore, when kings had been killed, the ancient majesty  
> Of the thrones lay overthrown, and the proud scepters lay fallen.

Since the right hand is more agile than the left, and philosophy is consequently readier for teaching than for governing, she carried the books in her right hand and the scepter in her left.

She carried the books in her right hand and the scepter in her left. [Note: “When she saw the poetic Muses.”]

The Muses are said to be certain virgins who, under Phoebus as their leader, work through songs. For Boethius they are of two kinds: poetic and philosophical. The former judge under the influence of disturbance; the latter under the influence of clear and distinct knowledge.

The poetic Muses are those who, blinded by disturbances, approve and express whatever belongs to disturbance. Hence, according to the various kinds of disturbances or of things capable of arousing them, these Muses are commonly numbered as nine. For this reason Plato, in Book X of *The Republic*, thinks that they should be expelled from his state. “Plato rightly drives the poets out of the state he imagined,” says Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* II, “when he sought the best morals and the best constitution of a republic.” Agreeing with him, St. Augustine says in *The City of God* II.14 that the palm should rather be awarded to Plato, who, when rationally forming an image of what a state ought to be, judged that poets, as enemies of the state, should be expelled from the city. A person who pursues either truth or virtue ought to strip off old disturbances rather than put on new ones.

Hence these Muses are now said to be assisting at Boethius’s couch and dictating words to his tears, because Boethius now seems overwhelmed by disturbance and to utter nothing except what disturbance dictates. Hence the same Muses are said to be looked upon by Philosophy with stern eyes, because truth, which philosophy seeks to discover, is obstructed by the disturbances to which these Muses indulge. “There is an ancient quarrel,” says Plato in Book X of *The Republic*, “between philosophy and poetry.”

For this reason the Muses themselves are now called “little theatrical harlots” and “Sirens sweet even unto destruction,” because by their flatteries, fictitious matters, and songs they lead people into error and vice. For some, Sirens are harlots who reduce deceived sailors to utter poverty; for others they are sea monsters partly resembling women, who by the sweetness of their voices lull passing ships to sleep and devour them when asleep. Hence Ovid, *The Art of Love* III:

> The Sirens were sea monsters who, with melodious voice,  
> Detained every ship that came within their reach.

Therefore the same Muses are said to nourish Boethius’s pains with additional sweet poisons, to kill the harvest of reason with the thorns of the emotions, and to accustom minds to sickness rather than free them from it.

[Col. 0591B] The philosophical Muses, however, are those who, stripped of disturbances, judge as they know clearly and distinctly; hence they are never deceived. Plato praises them in Book X of *The Republic* as a divine kind and admits them into his state. After the poetic Muses have been driven away, they will teach Boethius.

When she saw the poetic Muses [Note: “Guardians of song”] assisting at my couch [Note: “Bed”] and dictating words to my tears, she was for a little while agitated and her eyes were inflamed with a stern light [Note: “Eyes”]. “Who,” she said, “allowed these theatrical harlots to approach this sick man? They not only offer no remedies for his pains, but even nourish them with sweet poisons. For these are the ones who kill the fertile harvest of reason with the fruitless thorns of the emotions [Note: “Barren” and “fruitless”; “rich in fruit”], and accustom the minds of human beings to sickness rather than free them from it.”

13. [Note: “But if some profane person.”]

The word *profanus* is applied both to a place and to a person. First, a profane place is one situated, as it were, far from a shrine and therefore not sacred. Thus, in *Aeneid* XII, line 778:

> And you, best of Earth, hold the sword:  
> If I have always honored your sacred rites,  
> Which the descendants of Aeneas made profane in war.

Second, a profane person is one who, as though far from the shrine, has not been initiated into sacred rites. Thus, in *Aeneid* VI, line 258:

> “Away, away, you profane,”  
> The prophetess cries, “and keep away from the entire grove.”

Philosophy therefore now calls that person profane who, uneducated in philosophical precepts, is alien to philosophy itself. Thus Horace, excluding uneducated people and those alien to the Muses from his poems as profane people from sacred rites, sings in *Odes* III.1:

> I hate the profane crowd and keep it away.  
> Keep silence: as priest of the Muses,  
> I sing songs never before heard  
> To virgins and boys.

Philosophy therefore uses a mode of speaking that the Greeks call *aposiopēsis* [Greek: ἀποσιώπησις], and Cicero calls “reticence.” By it speech is so abbreviated that it is scarcely apparent what the speaker would have said. She seems to speak as follows: “If, O poetic Muses, you had drawn some person ignorant of philosophy, as is your custom, away from reason into obedience to disturbance, I would consider that less troubling; for none of our labor would be harmed by such a person. But Boethius, thoroughly versed in every branch of philosophy …” The rest is left unspoken. Thus Juvenal:

> Whoever that first ancestor of yours was,  
> He was either a shepherd or something I do not wish to say.

So too Virgil in his well-known verse:

> Whom I … but it is better to calm the agitated waves.

But if your flatteries had dragged away some profane person [Note: “An outsider and common person.”], as you are accustomed to do, I would consider it less troubling; for nothing of our labor [Note: “Work”] would be harmed in such a person.

14. [Note: “This man, however, nurtured in Eleatic and Academic studies.”]

Dialectical and Platonic studies. Dialectical studies are called Eleatic because dialectic is said to have been invented by Zeno, who, since he was born at Elea, is called the Eleatic. Elea, according to Strabo, Book VI, was a city of Lucania founded by the Phocaeans and the birthplace of the Pythagoreans Parmenides and Zeno.

Platonic studies are called Academic because Plato first taught philosophy in the Academy. The Academy was a wooded place outside and near Athens, formerly called *Hecademia* [Greek: ἑκαδημία], after the hero Hecademus. Hence Horace, *Epistles* II.2:

> So that I might distinguish the straight from the crooked  
> And seek the truth among the groves of Hecademus.

Boethius, however, was exceedingly well trained in dialectical and Platonic doctrines. In dialectics, because he translated Aristotle’s dialectical books—Aristotle having, in Cicero’s judgment, *On the Orator* I, said much more and much better than all other teachers about the method of reasoning—and illustrated them with commentaries. In Platonic studies, because as the work proceeds it will become clear that Boethius correctly understood the opinions of the Platonists and was most devoted to them.

This man, however, nurtured in Eleatic and Academic studies [Note: “Dialectical and Platonic studies.”]—but rather go away, Sirens [Note: “Sirens sweet even unto destruction.”].

The Sirens, in Greek [Greek: Σειρῆνες], from which the name is written both with *ei* and with a long *i*, are of two kinds: terrestrial and marine. The terrestrial Sirens, a kind of insect, are called by natural philosophers [Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ σείρεσθαι], “from being drawn together,” because these little creatures lie curved with their membrane contracted. Pliny discusses them in Book XI, chapter 16; but they are not at issue here.

The marine Sirens are said to be so called either [Greek: ἀπὸ τῆς σειρᾶς], “from a bond,” or [Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ σύρειν], “from deceiving,” because by their song they bind and deceive unwary newcomers. They are said to be the daughters of the river Achelous and Calliope, resembling virgins above and fish below. Three are counted: Parthenope, Leucosia, and Ligeia. One sings with her voice, another with pipes, and the third with the lyre; all possess such sweetness of song that they destroy sailors, having lulled them into shipwreck. Ovid, *The Art of Love* III:

> The Sirens were sea monsters who, with melodious voice,  
> Detained every ship that came within their reach.

Hence anything that corrupts the minds of human beings is called a Siren, as in Horace, *Satires* II.3, where “pernicious idleness” is called a Siren to be avoided.

Thus the poetic Muses, the parents—or at least the nurses—of disturbances, are now called Sirens sweet even unto destruction or ruin. Hence these same Muses are ordered to depart and make way for the philosophical Muses, though not before they have been severely rebuked by Philosophy herself and have displayed their sorrow. Therefore that chorus is said to have been rebuked—*increpari* means to be reproved by severe words or other signs—and to have cast its sorrowful face down upon the ground.

At last that chorus departed and sadly crossed the threshold. For we cannot be imbued with the best teachings of philosophy until we have ordered those Muses, and similar causes opposed to the discovery of truth, to be gone. Although those disturbances often persist even after these causes have been removed, Philosophy therefore lamented the disturbance of Boethius’s mind in the following way.

“Sirens sweet even unto destruction, and leave him to be cared for and healed by my Muses.”

At this, the rebuked chorus [Note: “The rebuked crowd”] cast its sorrowful face down upon the ground, and, confessing its shame by its blush, sadly crossed the threshold. But I, whose sight was clouded and obscured by tears so that I could not discern who this woman of such commanding authority was, was struck dumb. With my eyes fixed upon the ground, I silently began to await what she would do next. Then she approached more closely, sat down at the end of my couch, and, looking upon my face weighed down by grief and cast toward the ground by sorrow, lamented in the following verses the disturbance of my mind.

16. METER II

[Note: This meter is generally called lyric, from the lyre, since it is suited to the lyre or strings; specifically it is called Alcmanian, after its inventor. It is a poem consisting of one kind of verse, each line being composed of the final four feet of a heroic verse, with one syllable remaining after the second foot.]

ARGUMENT.—Philosophy is about to describe the disturbance of Boethius’s mind and compares with it his former knowledge of heaven and of all nature, which is now contrasted with his apparent ignorance of everything.

[Col. 0593A]

Alas, how greatly the human mind, plunged into a rapid and deep sea of disturbances, is dulled, and, having neglected its own light, strives to rush into outer darkness, when harmful anxiety, swollen with earthly impulses, grows to its utmost extent! Once, when unimpeded beneath the open heavens, Boethius was accustomed to ascend in thought to the celestial regions. He gazed upon the rays of the purple sun, contemplated the form of the cold moon, and skillfully kept in mind all the stars, however many of them have wandering revolutions and turn through different circuits. Moreover, he used to inquire into and explain the causes by which the roaring winds disturb the level surface of the sea; likewise, what spirit turns the stable heavens, or why a star that is about to fall into the evening waters rises conspicuously from the purple east; what governs the calm days of spring so that it adorns the earth with purple flowers; and what causes autumn, abundantly fertile, to pour wine from swollen clusters. He was accustomed to investigate and relate the various causes of hidden nature.

That Boethius, once knowledgeable about heaven and earth, now lies stupid, his mental light weakened, as though bound by heavy bonds around his neck and, because of the weight of the bonds, holding his face downward. Alas, he is compelled to look upon the earth, the parent of so great a stupor.

[Note: The following notes comment on the preceding verses.]

1. “The mind plunged into a precipitous depth.” The mind afflicted by its disturbances, especially by excessive anxiety about perishable things, is immersed by them as though in a sea that is both deep and precipitous. It is deep because that affection is fixed in the mind with the deepest roots; it is precipitous because the same affection, stirred up like a kind of fury, drags the mind headlong into error and vice.

2. “It is dulled.” Properly, a sword whose edge has been blunted is said to be *hebes*, “dull”; by metaphor, anything whose movement has become sluggish is so called. Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* V, line 395:

> But the blood, chilled by delaying old age,  
> Grows dull, and the exhausted powers in the body grow cold.

So too Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I: “Just as those who look at the declining sun with keen eyes lose their sight altogether, so the edge of the mind, when it looks upon itself, sometimes becomes dull.” The more the human mind is overwhelmed by disturbances, the less it can contemplate truth; and thus it grows dull. Hence St. Gregory, Preface 2 to the *Commentary on Ezekiel*: “The more the mind busies itself with earthly things, the less it sees what is heavenly.”

2. “Having left its proper light.” A certain light has been implanted in our mind by God himself, the author of our mind. By this light the mind can recognize itself as stripped of errors and vices and can perceive itself joined to the divine mind. But those who obey their disturbances do not wish to enjoy this light.

3. “To go into outer darkness.” Although some knowledge is implanted—or rather innate—in our mind, the mind is nevertheless finite and subject to disturbances. It therefore lies under two kinds of darkness: internal and external.

Internal darkness consists in ignorance of things that we neither can nor ought to know. Of this darkness it is commonly said:

> Not to know certain things is a great part of wisdom.

External darkness, however, is ignorance of things that we can and ought to know but do not know because we are blinded by disturbances. Thus some people, living in complete ignorance of themselves and of God, apply to created things the thoughts they ought to direct solely toward God.

As we are blinded by other disturbances, so especially are we blinded by excessive anxiety about perishable things. Hence the human mind is now said to go into outer darkness whenever such anxiety grows without measure. Since the human mind, through that ignorance, falls into error, through error into vice, and through vice into eternal punishment, our author, writing this passage, may have had in mind what is reported in Matthew 22: “Bind him hand and foot and cast him into outer darkness.” There St. Gregory says: “Inner darkness is blindness of heart; outer darkness is the night of eternal damnation.”

4. “Increased by earthly blasts.” That is, by pleasure and by the esteem of the people among whom we live; by these, as by blasts upon a fire, our disturbance is nourished. Since the human mind is first joined to the body and then to those things or persons through which that first union seems to be maintained, this anxiety about perishable things arises through the activity of the body and grows stronger through the activity both of things and of persons.

Things act upon us through contact; persons act through their judgment concerning these things, which they demonstrate by their example. But as this anxiety grows, the virtue of the mind diminishes. Hence Christ, the divine teacher, refutes this anxiety with many arguments in Matthew 6, in order to commend the supreme providence of God. Hence St. Paul says in Philippians 4: “Be anxious about nothing.” Hence St. Peter says in the First Epistle, chapter 5: “Cast all your anxiety upon God, because he cares for you.” Once these things are stated, it is not surprising that this anxiety is called harmful here.

6. “Here once.” Boethius. Philosophy has proceeded from the indefinite question, which the Greeks call *thesis* [Greek: θέσις], to a definite issue, which they call *hypothesis* [Greek: ὑπόθεσις]. She commends the knowledge of natural things that Boethius once possessed, and is immediately about to speak of his present ignorance of those same things.

Boethius’s former knowledge, as it is now described, was extensive, both of heaven and of earth. First, as one knowledgeable about heaven, Boethius knew the sun, moon, and stars; the winds, which arise from the stars as effects from causes; and the Spirit of the Universe, by which, as by their very cause, the stars are moved.

Then, as one knowledgeable about the earth, the same Boethius knew the various seasons of the year—first spring, then autumn—and the various causes of nature. Hence Boethius is now said to be free beneath the open heavens, insofar as his mind, as though it had shaken off the yoke of the body and made for itself a path through the hidden regions of the ether, not only reaches but even traverses heaven in thought. Therefore the words are added: “Accustomed to enter the ethereal passages.” All these matters must be explained separately.

### 8. “He discerned the lights of the rosy sun.”

I. Boethius knew the sun; and no better witness to this knowledge, or to that of the things that follow, can be found than Boethius himself, speaking about himself under the persona of Philosophy. “The sun,” says Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I, “was so called either because it alone among all the heavenly bodies is so great, or because, when it has risen and the other heavenly bodies have been obscured, it alone appears.” Therefore, whoever has thoroughly understood the nature of this heavenly body may be regarded as highly accomplished in the contemplation of celestial matters.

### 9. “He watched the stars of the cold moon.”

II. Boethius knew the moon, as he himself also attests. “The moon,” says Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, “was named from shining; for she is Lucina. Thus, just as among the Greeks they invoke Diana, and Diana as the bringer of light, so among our people they invoke Lucina in childbirth—she who is likewise Diana.” That is to say, just as the sun appears to shine alone by day, so the moon appears to shine alone by night; hence she is called *noctiluca*, “night-shining.” Her study therefore greatly advances Boethius’s knowledge of astronomy.

But why does Philosophy here call them “the stars of the moon,” since the moon is one, whereas a *sidus* appears to be a constellation composed of several stars, such as Aries, Andromeda, and so forth? I answer that *sidus* is also used of every body distinguished from the common multitude of other things by its bright appearance. Thus it is elegantly said, “and the earth has its stars.” For *sidus* is derived from Greek εἶδος, “form” or “appearance,” with the spiritus changed into ς—a change that is not unusual. Why, however, is the moon called “cold”? Because the moon presides over the night, which, in the absence of the sun, is colder than the neighboring day.

### 10. “And whatever star, bent through various orbits, performs wandering circuits.”

III. Boethius, as he himself also testifies, likewise knew the stars—not merely in respect of their quality, which would already be significant, but, more importantly, in respect of their quantity.

The stars are of two kinds: non-wandering and wandering. The non-wandering stars, commonly called “fixed,” are bright heavenly bodies that seem, as far as the judgment of the senses can determine, always to preserve the same distance from one another. These stars are innumerable; hence in Genesis XV: “Count the stars, if you can.” Saint Augustine likewise says in *The City of God* XVI, chapter 23: “Nor should it be believed that all of them can be seen; for the more sharply anyone looks, the more he sees.” Indeed, all philosophers admit that the Milky Way contains an innumerable multitude of stars of this kind. Boethius therefore could not have had this multitude fully under observation.

The wandering stars, commonly called planets, are opaque heavenly bodies that at one time approach and at another recede from one another. For this reason the sun, being a bright heavenly body, is not counted among them by more recent philosophers. Some of these planets are larger and plainly visible to everyone: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury, and the moon. Boethius could have included these in his reckoning. Others are smaller and observed only with the greatest difficulty, such as those near Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, which are called the satellites of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars; the printed connecting words (*qui propter a dicuntur*) are corrupt or uncertain.

Indeed, to speak with Seneca, many others pass in secret, never coming before human eyes; for God has not made everything known to human eyes.

That Philosophy is speaking here only of the planets, and of the larger ones among them, is evident from her saying that these stars exercise “wandering circuits”: by returning, they depart from the path they first took; and they are said to be bent through various orbits, since each of the planets we observe has its own circuit.

Finally, “victorious” means the same as “having attained one’s desire.” Thus, according to Servius, Virgil is to be understood in *Georgics* III, verse 8:

> The way must be attempted by which I too may be able  
> To raise myself from the ground and, victorious, fly  
> Upon the lips of men.

> Alas, how deeply plunged into a precipitous abyss  
> The mind grows dull, and, having abandoned its own light,  
> Turns toward external darkness;  
> Whenever, swollen by earthly blasts,  
> The harmful care grows without limit!  
>
> Once free beneath the open sky,  
> Accustomed to travel the ethereal paths,  
> It discerned the lights of the rosy sun,  
> It watched the stars of the cold moon,  
> And whatever star, bent through various orbits, performs wandering circuits,  
> He, victorious, held it comprehended in numbers.

### 13. “Whence the resounding breezes…”

IV. Boethius also declares that he knew the causes of the winds. A wind, generally speaking, is the movement of air flowing here and there. Hence Scaliger, in *On Causes*, in the cited place, chapter 67, and many others derive *ventus* from *veniendi*, “coming,” because coming is movement, while wind is the movement of air.

A wind, however, is of two kinds, according to the two ways in which air can flow here and there. One kind of wind is produced by a collapsing cloud, just as we see wind raised by the fall of a tree, a tower, or some other large body—namely, because of the circular motion of moving bodies, without which no movement can occur in the world. In this way storms often arise on land, but more frequently at sea.

Another kind of wind is produced by vapors rarefied through the air by the sun, as we see wind produced in an apple, in green wood, and in the common vessel called an *aeolipile* when these are brought near fire.

Boethius, then, having understood the heavenly bodies, and especially the sun, understood the causes of such winds. For when the sun sets things in motion, it sometimes causes either a cloud to collapse or vapor to be rarefied through the air. Since this happens more frequently at sea than on land, because there is a greater abundance either of threatening clouds or of rising vapors, the “resounding breezes” are now said to trouble the waters of the sea.

The sea is called both *aequor* and *pontus*. It is called *aequor* because the surface of the water, its weight being everywhere evenly balanced, is perfectly level. Hence Cicero, *Academic Questions* II: “What appears so level,” he says, “as the sea?” For this reason poets also call it *aequor*. It is called *pontus*, if we accept the view of some, from the Euxine; unless the Euxine itself is called *Pontus* because the whole sea is called *pontus*, perhaps from Greek πόνος, “labor,” since it is full of labor.

Virgil, *Eclogues* IX, verse 57:

> And now the whole sea lies silent beneath you,  
> And behold, all the breezes have fallen  
> With the murmuring of the wind.

And *Eclogues* VI, verse 35:

> Then to harden the ground and confine Nereus  
> Within the sea.

These passages show how ingeniously the winds are said to trouble or disturb the waters of the sea, since *aequor* properly denotes not so much the sea as its level surface, which is disturbed by the blowing winds.

### 15. “What spirit turns the stable sphere?”

V. Boethius adds that he knew the Spirit of the Universe, whom Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, Virgil, and many other ancient authors recognized. This spirit is nothing other than a certain subtler body which, diffused through the other bodies, moves them according to the laws of motion established by God himself.

Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, verse 724:

> In the beginning, Spirit within sustains the heaven,  
> The earth, the watery plains, the shining globe of the moon,  
> And the stars of Titan. Diffused through its limbs,  
> Mind stirs the whole mass and mingles with the great body.  
> From it come the race of humans and beasts, the lives of birds,  
> And the monsters that the sea bears beneath its marble surface.  
> Their seeds possess a fiery vigor and heavenly origin;  
> Their earthly bodies do not delay them  
> Or dull their limbs and mortal members.  
> Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice,  
> Nor look back upon the air, shut away in darkness  
> And in a blind prison.

Philosophy now teaches that this spirit turns the stable sphere and is the cause not only of the rising and setting of the heavenly bodies but also of the redness of their rising.

First, it turns the stable sphere because it revolves the heavens. Since the heavens, as judged by the senses, always possess the same magnitude, shape, and motion, they are called “stable.” For the same reason the earth, the sea, and the air are called stable bodies, although there is in them a great succession of forms.

Next, the spirit is the cause of the rising and setting of the heavenly bodies. For just as a ship is carried away by the water that surrounds it, so the heavenly bodies—especially opaque ones such as the planets and comets—can be turned by the spirit that surrounds them.

Poets, when describing the rising and setting of the stars, imagine them both emerging from the waters and returning to the waters after completing their course. Thus they say:

> Where the sun rises from the eastern waves;  
> Where the horses of the sun lift themselves from the deep  
> Of the sea;  
> Leaving her saffron bed, Aurora;  
> Night rushes from the Ocean;  
> The sun, both when he rises and when he sinks into the waves.

They call the waters into which the heavenly bodies sink “Hesperian,” after the star called Hesperus. “The lowest of the five wandering stars,” says Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, “and the one nearest the earth, is Venus, which in Greek is called Φωσφόρος and in Latin Lucifer when it precedes the sun; but when it follows, Hesperus.”

Hence Virgil, *Eclogues* X, verse 77:

> Go home, my well-fed goats; Hesperus has come—go home.

Finally, the same spirit can cause the rising of the stars to be red by thickening or thinning the clouds, through which, as the light is variously modified, different colors can be displayed.

### 18. “Why a star, about to fall into the Hesperian waters, rises with a ruddy dawn; what tempers the tranquil hours of spring.”

VI. Boethius adds that he knew the spring season. Spring, says Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, is so called because at that time the shrubs begin to grow green and the season of the year begins to turn—unless one accepts the Ionic form βῆρ.

This season is known to everyone, and here it is commended both for its proper character and for its effects. Its proper character consists in this, that spring is a calm season, since at that time the sun makes the days equal to the nights. Hence the phrase:

> What tempers the peaceful hours of spring.

It is commended also for its effects, namely, the flowers with which that moderate season adorns the earth. Since they reproduce the colors of roses, they are called “rosy,” as Virgil elegantly explains in *Georgics* II, verse 123:

> Spring comes to the leaves of the groves, spring to the fruitful woods;  
> In spring the earth swells, and calls for its generative seeds.

> And whatever star, bent through various orbits, performs wandering circuits,  
> He, victorious, held it comprehended in numbers.  
>
> Whence the resounding breezes trouble the waters of the sea;  
> What spirit turns the stable sphere;  
> Or why a star, about to fall into the Hesperian waters,  
> Rises with a ruddy dawn;  
> What tempers the peaceful hours of spring,  
> To adorn the earth with rosy flowers.

### 20. “What has made autumn…”

VII. Boethius concludes that he likewise knew autumn. Autumn—or, as some prefer to write it, *auctumnus*—is called by some, according to Festus, by this name because at that time human resources are especially increased, when the fruits of the fields have been gathered. Hence Virgil, *Georgics* II, verses 520–522:

> The pigs, happy with acorns, return; the woods give their berries,  
> And autumn sets forth various fruits; high upon the sunny rocks  
> The gentle vintage ripens.

For this reason Philosophy now says that autumn, “fertile in a full year,” flows abundantly with swelling grapes. “Full” here means “filled,” just as in Virgil, *Georgics* II, verses 4–6:

> Come here, Father Lenaeus; here everything is full  
> Of your gifts; for you, with grape-laden autumn,  
> The field blooms, and the vintage foams from brimming vats.

“Flow abundantly” likewise means “to abound,” as Seneca speaks of “the gifts of flowing fortune.”

### 22. “To investigate.”

To examine closely, to inquire into thoroughly. For whoever investigates the causes of nature in depth ought to inspect everything like a hunting dog. Hence, says Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I, “the natural philosopher is an observer and hunter of nature.”

### 23. “To render the various causes of nature.”

The word *natura* is derived from *nascor*, “to be born,” just as Greek φύσις is derived from φύω, “to grow” or “to bring forth.” Therefore, in the category of efficient cause, nature is the cause from which things—especially sensible things—are born. In the category of form, however, nature is the inherent form of each body by which it is distinguished from other bodies.

In this way the differing opinions of philosophers can be reconciled. Cicero says in *On the Nature of the Gods* II:

> Some think that nature is a certain force without reason, bringing about the necessary movements in bodies; others, however, think that it is a force possessing reason and order… There are also those who call everything by the name of nature, such as Epicurus, who divides the nature of all existing things into bodies and void, and the properties that befall these.

Nature, considered as a cause, is of two kinds: first, God, whose skill, as the same orator says in that work, “no art, no hand, and no craftsman could equal by imitation”; and second, a certain divinely moved body. For this is “a force without reason bringing about the necessary movements in the other bodies.”

Nature, considered as form, is each individual body—and, if one wishes to follow Epicurus, the atoms and the void.

Whatever the case may be, the subject here is only nature considered as form. This nature is obscure, but it has its causes. Just as natural philosophers labor to investigate them, Boethius investigated and discovered them.

Nature is obscure because it must be grasped not only by general but also by particular thought. Since it depends upon almost infinitely many accompanying circumstances, it is exceedingly difficult to attain. Nevertheless, nature has its own causes, for nothing happens without its cause.

Natural philosophers devote themselves to investigating these causes so that they may obtain for themselves a certain happiness by which they are distinguished from other human beings:

> Happy is he who has been able to understand the causes of things.

Boethius had thoroughly examined these causes, since he had been accustomed to investigate heaven and earth and to render the various causes of hidden nature. But alas!

### 24. “Now he lies…”

The human mind is situated between God, by whom it was created and is preserved, and the body, of which it is the form. The more it obeys either God or the moving body, the more knowledgeable or ignorant it becomes.

For the body, as Wisdom IX says, “which is corrupted, weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling depresses the sense that thinks upon many things.” God, however, as John I says, “enlightens every human being who comes into this world.”

Thus perturbation is rightly said now to render the light of the mind exhausted and, like heavy chains, to depress the face toward the earth. But Boethius is said to have his neck pressed by chains—[the construction is uncertain in the supplied text: *supple secundum*]—as in Virgil: “His mouth and shoulders like a god.”

> What has made autumn, fertile in a full year,  
> Flow abundantly with swelling grapes,  
> While he was accustomed to investigate  
> The various causes of hidden nature.  
>
> Now he lies with the light of his mind exhausted,  
> His neck pressed beneath heavy chains,  
> Carrying his face bowed down beneath the weight,  
> And, alas, is compelled to look upon the senseless earth.

## PROSE II

### Argument

Philosophy assumes the role of a physician. After considering Boethius more attentively, she questions him; but when he remains silent, she concludes that he is suffering from lethargy. In order to cure him, she wipes with her garment his eyes, dimmed by the cloud of mortal affairs.

### “Now is the time for medicine.”

Just as the body has its diseases, so the mind has its diseases; and therefore each has its own medicine. Hence Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* III:

> Why is medicine for the mind not as desired, cultivated, welcome, and approved as medicine for the body?

Philosophy, since she is concerned with thought, practices the medicine of the mind, while observing the procedures ordinarily observed by physicians of the body. Physicians:

1. First, examine the sick attentively. “Before a careful physician attempts to apply medicine to a sick person,” says Cicero, *On the Orator* II, “he must know not only the disease that he wishes to cure, but also the habits of the healthy person and the nature of the body.”

2. They address the sick, so that by questioning and interrogating them they may draw out what they were unable to learn through their own reflection, both about the disease and about the habits of the healthy person and the nature of the body.

3. Especially when the sick are silent, they lay a hand upon them, so that, with touch as judge, the foregoing matters may be recognized more clearly. For once the cause of the disease has been discovered, physicians think that the cure has also been discovered.

4. They console the sick, asserting either that there is no disease or that its cure is easy. “Physicians,” says Cicero, *On Divination* II, “although they often understand that patients will die of a disease, never tell the sick that they will die of it.”

And so Philosophy now behaves toward Boethius.

> “Now is the time,” says Philosophy, “for medicine, not for reproach; it is a time for medicine, not for complaint.”

### “Then, fixing all her eyes upon me…”

1. Philosophy considers Boethius more attentively, so that, after applying her attention, she may learn not only the disease of Boethius, which she wishes to cure, but also the habits of the healthy person and the nature of the mind. Attention of mind is so proper to philosophy that by means of it rashness and prejudice—its most hostile enemies in the discovery of truth—are avoided.

The mind is said to direct all its eyes toward something when it thinks about it in such a way that no strength remains for thinking about anything else. Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, verse 100:

> You possess what you sought with your whole mind.

> Then, fixing all her eyes upon me—

### 24. “Are you that man?”

II. Philosophy addresses Boethius so that, whatever she appears unable to discover through attentive reflection concerning the condition of his mind, she may draw from Boethius himself by questioning and interrogation.

First, Philosophy questions Boethius about the former condition of his mind, instructed in philosophy. She compares its beginning, progress, and perfection most aptly with a human being who, before reaching manhood, is first nourished with milk and afterward with more substantial food. [Editorial note: “First a boy; then a youth; afterward a man and philosopher.”]

> Once nourished by our milk and raised on our food,  
> You had grown into the strength of a manly spirit.

Saint Paul likewise describes comparable stages of Christian life. In 1 Corinthians III he says:

> As infants in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able to bear it.

And in Hebrews V:

> You have become people who need milk, not solid food.

Referring to this, Saint Peter, 1 Peter II, says:

> Like newborn infants, desire the rational milk without deceit, so that by it you may grow into salvation.

The milk of Philosophy is her principles, which become known through the mind’s attention alone. Her more substantial food consists of the conclusions inferred from such principles with a greater degree of labor.

Next, Philosophy questions Boethius about the present condition of his mind. He is said to have fallen, overcome by perturbations, for no other reason than that, having cast aside his philosophical weapons, he refused to use them. Those weapons are the precepts of philosophy.

Boethius does not answer Philosophy’s questions—not because of shame, which, as Horace testifies, sometimes prevents a child from speaking, but because of stupefaction. Stupefaction is a kind of hardness of mind that, even when aroused, feels nothing; it therefore obstructs both thought and speech, which is the sign of thought.

Thus Boethius, overcome by stupefaction, is said not merely to be silent but entirely speechless and mute. A person is “silent” when, though possessing a tongue, he does not use it; “speechless” when, having lost the use of his tongue, he can at least stammer; and “mute” when he cannot speak at all. Thus Cicero spoke of a “mute forum,” a “speechless senate house,” and a “silent state.”

Virgil, speaking of stupefaction, sings of bulls in *Georgics* III, verse 520:

> Neither the shade of lofty groves, nor soft meadows,  
> Nor the stream that has rolled over rocks and seeks the plain,  
> Purified like amber, can move their minds;  
> But their flanks are loosened, and stupor weighs upon their inert eyes.

> Are you that man, she said, who once, nourished by our milk,  
> Raised on our food,  
> Grew into the strength of a manly spirit?  
> Yet we had supplied you with such weapons  
> That, had you not first cast them aside,  
> They would have protected you with unconquerable firmness.  
> Do you recognize me? Why are you silent?  
> Have you fallen silent from shame or from stupefaction?  
> I should prefer shame; but, as I see, stupefaction has overcome you.

When she saw that I was not merely silent but completely speechless and mute—

### “She laid her hand upon my breast.”

III. Philosophy lays her hand upon Boethius so that she may perceive the cause of his illness more clearly.

Just as physicians, after examining the heart, learn whether the body is healthy or unhealthy, because the movement of the heart is the cause of the body’s other conditions, so Philosophy, having learned a person’s will, perceives whether the mind’s thought is sound or corrupt, because the will is the cause of all other thoughts, whether praiseworthy or blameworthy. We cannot therefore fall into error or vice before we have willed to do so.

For this reason Philosophy is now said to lay her hand upon his breast. The breast signifies the will, as in Cicero:

> A friend is loved wholeheartedly.

> She gently laid her hand upon my breast and—

### 25. “There is no danger.”

IV. Philosophy consoles Boethius so that, having conceived hope of recovery, he may more willingly use the remedies that she will afterward prescribe.

Philosophy therefore says:

1. First, that there is no danger. Since our mind is immortal, it is exposed to no dangers except those of error and vice. Here, however, only a kind of forgetfulness is noticed, and this is not yet a sign of impending error or vice.

2. She says that Boethius’s mind generally suffers from lethargy. Lethargy is a violent compression of the brain, from which torpor, an almost irresistible need for sleep, forgetfulness of all things, and mental failure arise. Hence physicians treat those afflicted by this disease by striking, pricking, burning, and tormenting them in other ways until, once the brain has been relaxed, wakefulness, attention, and memory are restored.

The mind is therefore said, by a certain analogy, to suffer from lethargy when it appears to have forgotten things it previously knew. This is called the common disease of deluded minds, since minds never err unless, having forgotten the first principles of truth, they judge rashly and with prejudice.

3. Specifically, she says that Boethius’s mind has forgotten itself. Cicero says in *Tusculan Disputations* I:

> It is the greatest of all things for the mind to see the mind itself.

Cicero also explains the force of Apollo’s command that each person should know himself. He does not mean that we should know our limbs, stature, or physical shape; for we are not bodies, and when he speaks to you, he is not addressing your body. When he says “know yourself,” he means “know your mind.” The body is like a vessel or receptacle of the mind; whatever is done by your mind is done by you. To know the mind, unless this were divine, would not be the command of a particularly elevated mind, so that the ability to know oneself may be reckoned as something attributed to God.

It follows that the human mind cannot philosophize before it knows itself. Since Boethius’s mind has forgotten itself, it is rightly said to suffer specifically from lethargy.

4. Finally, Boethius’s mind has forgotten itself only for a little while, since the notion of itself implanted in the mind beforehand remains. At the first admonition of Philosophy, the same mind will therefore remember itself.

> “There is no danger,” she said. “He suffers from lethargy, the common disease of deluded minds. He has forgotten himself for a little while, but he will easily remember, provided that he knew us before.”

Finally, Philosophy, now intending to cure Boethius, wiped and dried his eyes, which were dimmed by the cloud of mortal affairs and overflowing with tears, using her garment gathered into a fold. These actions, continuing the foregoing symbol of Philosophy, are to be understood not so much of the body as of the mind.

First, Boethius’s eyes were dimmed by the cloud of mortal affairs because his mind appeared obscured by perturbations arising from perishable things—for example, by love or desire.

Next, the same eyes were overflowing with tears because his mind was afflicted with sadness on account of lost perishable things, tears being the signs of sadness.

Moreover, Philosophy wiped and dried Boethius’s eyes with her garment gathered into a fold. She wiped and dried them because she stripped the mind of its principal perturbations, from which the preceding darkness and sadness arose. The garment gathered into a fold means words joined together in philosophical discourse. Through use, thoughts become so closely joined to the words by which they are ordinarily signified that we very often cannot recall the thoughts unless the words are brought back to memory. It has already been said above that the garments of Philosophy are philosophical expressions.

> “So that he may be able,” she said, “let us for a little while wipe his eyes,  
> Dimmed by the cloud of mortal affairs.”

Having said this, she dried my eyes, which were overflowing with tears, with her garment gathered into a fold.

## 26. METER III

*The poem consists of two alternating kinds of verse: the first a heroic hexameter, the second a tetrameter whose four feet imitate the first four feet of the heroic verse, though with a more frequent dactyl.*

### Argument

Boethius sings that, with Philosophy assisting him, he was illuminated just as the earth recovers its former light when the clouds have been driven away by the wind.

> “Then,” says Boethius, “the darkness departed from me, the gloom having been dispersed, and the former light returned to my eyes. It was as when the stars are enveloped by the swift Corus, the west wind, and the sky is covered with clouds fertile in rain; the sun is hidden, and night rushes down from the heights upon the earth. If Boreas, sent from his Thracian cave, lashes this earth and opens the hidden light, the sun appears, and, released with sudden brightness, strikes the astonished eyes with his radiance.”

### “Then the darkness, the night having been dispelled, left me…”

1. Boethius’s mind, darkened by perturbations, had lost its former light, just as the eyes of the body are enveloped in darkness when night approaches. But scarcely had Philosophy appeared, like a new star, when Boethius’s mind, its perturbations calmed, began to see again with its former light, as it had been accustomed to do.

### “As when…”

3. This is an outstanding comparison, transferring an image from the body to the mind, from an unlike thing to a like one. Here the earth represents the mind; the sun, Philosophy; the clouds, perturbations; the winds, the spirits that give birth to perturbations; and the alternating night and day represent alternating ignorance and understanding.

### “The stars are massed together…”

The verb *glomerare* is derived from *glomus*, “a ball of thread.” Since a ball is formed when thread is wound around thread, the stars are now said to be “massed together” because they are enveloped by surrounding clouds. One must not suppose that Boethius thought the stars could be moved by winds in such a way that, when they approached one another, some kind of cluster of stars would be formed.

Virgil expresses something much like this in *Georgics* I, verse 323:

> And the clouds, gathered from on high, mass together  
> A foul storm with black rains.

### “By Corus…”

Corus, or Caurus, is a wind that blows from the summer sunset. Thus this wind runs contrary to the movement by which the air is driven from east to west. Clouds, compressed by opposing movements from either side, are thereby forced to release abundant rain unless they are otherwise dispersed.

Virgil, *Aeneid* V, verse 125:

> Which, once submerged and beaten by swelling waves,  
> The winter Cori conceal when they hide the stars.

### “And the pole stood beneath rain-bearing clouds…”

Rain-bearing showers are so called because they are contained within a cloud as within their own material. For *nimbus*, like *nubes*, generally denotes that which covers or conceals. Hence Isidore says in book XIX, chapter 31:

> A *nimbus* is a transverse band sewn from gold onto the linen worn on women’s foreheads.

From this Plautus spoke of a “cloud-bedecked prostitute.”

A cloud, which is nothing other than a dark vapor suspended high in the weight of the surrounding air, can be carried downward in two ways. According to the different manner of its descent, it can have different effects. Either the cloud descends whole or in fragments. If it descends whole, it can produce lightning, thunderbolts, thunder, and especially storms. If it descends in fragments, it usually takes three forms: snow, rain, and hail. The shaggy globules of a cloud, when falling, either preserve or change their form. If they preserve it, it snows; if they change it, they either merely melt, in which case it rains, or harden after melting, in which case hail falls.

### “The pole stood…”

The sky was covered. Thus Virgil, *Eclogues* VII, verse 54:

> The junipers stand, and the bristling chestnut trees.

And *Aeneid* VI, verse 300, speaking of Charon, whose eyes seemed covered with flame:

> His unkempt gray hair lies down; his eyes stand forth in flame.

And *Aeneid* XII, verse 407, speaking of the sky covered with dust:

> Now they see the sky  
> Standing beneath the dust.

Hence the next verse adds: “The sun lies hidden.”

### “And before the stars came into the sky…”

Night, especially among poets, is of two kinds. One arises when the sun has set and the other stars shine forth, for which reason they are said to rise. Virgil speaks of this night in *Aeneid* II, verse 250:

> Meanwhile the sky turns, and night rushes from the Ocean,  
> Enveloping both earth and the heavens in great shadow.

The other kind arises even before sunset, while the sun and the other stars are hidden. Virgil speaks of it in *Aeneid* I, verse 94:

> Suddenly the clouds snatch sky and daylight  
> From the eyes of the Trojans; black night settles upon the sea.

This is the kind of night now under discussion. Hence it is said to be poured from above upon the earth before the stars come into the sky—that is, before they customarily shine forth after the sun has set.

### “Boreas…”

Boreas is a wind blowing from the summer sunrise. Therefore it moves in the same direction by which the air is carried around from east to west. From this, everything commonly said about this wind can be inferred.

First, this wind blows opposite Corus, since Corus blows from the summer sunset; hence our author now mentions both winds.

Second, Boreas is violent because it travels westward together with the air. Since every violent wind is cold, Virgil sings in *Eclogues* VII, verse 51:

> Here we care as much for the cold of Boreas  
> As the wolf cares for numbers or the rushing rivers for their banks.

This may perhaps explain the interpretation of its name: Greek βορέας seems to derive from βοάω, “I shout,” and ῥέω, “I flow,” because that wind, being especially violent, rushes with a roar.

Third, this wind brings clear weather, because, moving together with the air, it disperses the clouds that have been gathered—the material of rain. Hence Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VI:

> I possess a power suited to me, by which I drive away  
> The gloomy clouds, shake the straits,  
> And overturn the knotty oaks.

Hence Boreas is now also said to unlock the closed day—that is, to drive away the clouds by which night has been produced even before sunset.

### “Sent forth from its cave…”

Boreas, or any other wind of the world distinct from a storm, is very suitably said to be sent forth from a cave, as in *Aeneid* I, verse 64:

> But the almighty Father had shut them away in dark caves.

For just as the wind in apples, chestnuts, green wood, and even in the bronze sphere called an *aeolipile* arises, when fire sets them in motion, from certain cave-like places—namely, vapors rushing out through an opening as they become rarefied—so the aforesaid wind of the world is accustomed to blow from the earth, mountains, and clouds that surround it, as though from certain great caves, when the sun causes vapors to flow through places where resistance is weakest as they become rarefied.

Hence Virgil, *Aeneid* I, verse 55:

> He came to Aeolia, the homeland of storms,  
> A place fertile in raging south winds. Here Aeolus, king,  
> In his vast cave confines the struggling winds  
> And the resounding storms beneath his authority,  
> And restrains them with chains and imprisonment.  
> They, indignant, roar around their mountain prison  
> With a great murmur.

### “Thracian…”

That is, Thracian. Either Boreas, sharing the name of this wind, was a Thracian, or this wind seemed to blow from Thrace when considered in relation to the place where Boethius was writing.

Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* XII, verse 365:

> As when the breath of Thracian Boreas resounds  
> Across the deep Aegean and the wave follows  
> To the shores, wherever the winds have pressed upon them,  
> The clouds flee from the sky.

For Greek ἠδωνοί, “Edonians,” is, according to Strabo, a Thracian people.

Moreover, *reserare* means the same as “to open.” To unlock is the opposite of locking, just as *claudo* and *recludo*, “to close” and “to open,” and *velo* and *revelo*, “to cover” and “to uncover,” are opposites. Locks are the things whose removal opens doors, according to Varro; or, according to Festus, they are wooden bars placed across doors.

Ovid, book VI of the *Amores*:

> Shake the lock from the door.

Hence Virgil, *Aeneid* XII, verse 584:

> Some order that the city be unlocked  
> And the gates be thrown open.

> Then the darkness, the night having been dispelled, left me,  
> And former vigor returned to my eyes,  
> As when the stars are massed together by swift Corus,  
> And the pole stands beneath rain-bearing clouds;  
> The sun lies hidden, and before the stars come into the sky,  
> Night is poured down upon the earth.  
> If Boreas, sent from his Thracian cave,  
> Should lash it and unlock the closed day,

### 9. “Phoebus…”

Phoebus, or Apollo, is said to be the son of Jupiter and Latona, born together with Diana on the island of Delos. He is the inventor of medicine and so skilled in divination, singing, and versification that he was regarded as the god of these arts.

Among poets, as here, he often signifies the sun, as the interpretation of his name itself shows: Greek φοῖβος is Latin *splendidus*, “bright.” Hence he is said to “flash forth” and to “dart forth suddenly with light.”

He is said to flash forth insofar as he shines; for *mico* is derived from *mica*, “a glittering grain of sand.” He is said to dart forth suddenly with light insofar as the sun emits a continuous beam all the way to the earth.

Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII, verse 524:

> For suddenly a flash, shaken from the heavens—

### “The wondering eyes…”

Wonder belongs only to the mind, since wonder consists in a certain thought of the mind. Yet, because the eyes are fixed by this affection of the mind, they too are said to wonder.

“Eyes are exceedingly expressive,” says Cicero; “they speak according to the state of the mind.”

Claudian, poem 24, verse 69:

> Measure with astonished eyes  
> How much you have benefited, how great a city you have saved.

> Phoebus flashes forth, suddenly darting forth with light,  
> And strikes the wondering eyes with his rays.

## 30. PROSE III
**ARGUMENT.**—Boethius, having at last recognized Philosophy as his nurse, learns from her through questioning that ancient as well as more recent philosophers were harassed by ignorant and wicked men.

In Socrates, I say, before Plato’s time wisdom was badly received. For Socrates, whose wisdom was so great that he became Plato’s teacher, while the Epicureans and Stoics boasted that they stood on his side, was condemned to death on account of his wisdom.

First, Socrates, born about the year 3600 from the creation of the world and therefore flourishing before Plato’s time, was exceedingly wise. He drew philosophy away from hidden things and from nature itself, which was wrapped in obscurity, so that it might inquire into virtues and vices, arguing that matters above us had nothing to do with us. He encouraged his hearers to live honorably not only by word but also by example. Throughout his whole life he preserved such evenness that, whether in prosperity or adversity, he always displayed the same countenance—neither more cheerful nor more disturbed.

Next, Socrates was Plato’s teacher. Hence Cicero, *On the Orator* III, says: “Socrates, whose genius and varied conversations Plato handed down to immortality in his writings, left behind not a single letter.”

Later Socrates was accused of holding wrong opinions about the gods and was condemned to death, most unjustly. For, according to Cicero himself, *On the Orator* I, he was the wisest of all and lived with the greatest holiness. Therefore the people mourned his death so deeply that they punished his accusers, some with death and others with exile, and erected a bronze statue to Socrates himself.

Nevertheless, he died with Philosophy standing beside him. For, as Cicero says in the same place, he rejected Lysias’ most elegant speech, which he might have used in court on his own behalf, and in the capital trial he spoke for himself in such a way that he seemed not a suppliant or defendant but a teacher or master of the judges. By this he earned victory over death. For, in Cicero’s judgment, that death—which was owed to nature and was paid above all for his country and for truth—brings either a better condition than that of life or certainly one no worse.

Finally, the Epicureans and Stoics divided among themselves the teaching of Socrates, which, because it reached certain people through his death like money, is therefore called his inheritance. The Epicureans philosophize under Epicurus’ leadership, the Stoics under Zeno’s. For there are two principal schools among the ancient philosophers, from which the others arose: the Ionic, whose founder is said to have been Thales of Miletus, and the Italic, whose head was Pythagoras. The Ionic school produced two celebrated families, the Academics and the Peripatetics; the Italic likewise produced two, the Stoics and the Epicureans. These, as Saint Augustine says, *City of God* VIII.7, “placed the judgment of truth in the senses of the body and thought that everything learned should be measured by their untrustworthy and deceptive standards”; and therefore, having experienced philosophy resisting and opposing them, they tore apart the philosophical garment—that is, the expressions by which they covered themselves—and, pretending to be true philosophers, departed.] did not his teacher Socrates earn, with me standing beside him, the victory of an unjust death? From this he concluded that the sun was not a god but a burning lamp; and for this reason he was driven into exile, or rather departed voluntarily. In Zeno too, before Plato’s time, wisdom was badly received. Zeno, likewise older than Socrates, suffered many tortures for his wisdom; but what these were, and who inflicted them, is uncertain. It is more probable that, while attempting to restore his native Elea to freedom, he was tortured at the command of the tyrant Nearchus, bit off his tongue amid the torments, and spat it into the face of the Cyprian king who questioned him. “We have learned,” says Cicero, “that Anaxarchus, Democritus, was tortured by a Cyprian tyrant, and that Zeno of Elea was killed under torture”—namely, by the tyrant Nearchus. Thus wisdom was harassed among the ancient philosophers.

II. The same wisdom was also harassed among more recent philosophers. Julius Canius—or, as Lipsius prefers, Canus—was born in the same century as Seneca and was an outstanding philosopher. Seneca the philosopher, a contemporary of Saint Paul, flourished in the first century after Christ. 36 Although their [Note: [Col. 0609B] **“A numerous army.”**] army of fools is larger than that of philosophers, according to Ecclesiastes I, “The perverse are difficult to correct, and the number of fools is infinite,” it must nevertheless be despised, because it is governed by no leader but is carried here and there, rashly and randomly, by error alone [Note: [Col. 0609A] **“Raging like Bacchus.”**]. Philosophers avoid rashness and prejudice in order to discover truth; this is difficult and therefore belongs to few. Fools, however, slip through rashness and prejudice first into error and then into vices. Since this can happen in almost infinitely many ways, it is both easy and common to many.

But multitude does not acquit folly, nor are fools less blameworthy because they are more numerous. That crowd of fools is therefore to be despised: it is governed by no leader but is carried about by error, raging madly, and is consequently occupied with plundering useless little burdens.

First, it is to be despised because virtue, the inseparable companion of true wisdom, is always and alone free; even when bodies have been captured by weapons and bound by chains, virtue retains its own right and the unpunished liberty of all things.

Second, it is governed by no leader. In this the followers of vice and virtue differ: the latter are held by fixed laws, the former by none; virtue can exist in only one way, whereas vice can exist in infinitely many ways. There must therefore be one standard.

Third, it is carried away by raging error—that is, by error driving it into madness. A person is called *lymphatus* when, as though driven by the Nymphs, guardians of the waters, he has been seized and carried into frenzy. Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* VII, verse 377:

> Maddened, she rages wildly through the immense city.

Fourth, it is occupied with useless little burdens. Following its own disturbances, it places all its cares and thoughts upon perishable things, which, like a useless weight, oppress the mind so that they do not allow it to cultivate truth and virtue.

Wisdom, by contrast, governed by reason as by a guide, rejects perishable things and devotes itself to truth and virtue, so that it not only flashes forth like a star but is also safe, like an impregnable tower, from all the weapons of folly.] whose [Note: [Col. 0609A] **“Fighting against us.”**] army, if at any time it forms its battle line against us and presses upon us with greater force, our leader [Note: [Col. 0609A] **“Reason.”**] draws her forces back into the citadel; while they are occupied with plundering useless [Note: [Col. 0610A] **“Loads.”**] little burdens. **ARGUMENT.**—A person who is free from fear and hope, says Philosophy, is not moved either by the dangers of sea, earth, and sky or by the fury of tyrants. Enslaved by hope and fear, such a person lies oppressed.

[Note: [Col. 0610A] Whoever, having ordered his life, calmly despised imperious death, and steadily regarded prosperous and adverse Fortune alike, was able to preserve an unconquered countenance: neither the fury and terror of the sea, tossing its highest and lowest waves, nor Mount Vesuvius, when, with its passage opened, it unsteadily sends out smoking flames, nor the path of blazing lightning, which is accustomed to strike lofty buildings, will trouble him. Why do the wretched so marvel at savage tyrants, raging with empty fury? Desire nothing and fear nothing; then you will disarm the fury of the unrestrained and powerless tyrant. But whoever trembles in fear or lives in hope, since he is neither steadfast nor master of himself, has laid down his shield and, thrown from his position, fastens the chains by which he may be carried away.]

[Note: [Col. 0609D]

**1. “Serene.”** *Serenus* is said to derive from the Greek ξηρός (*xērós*), meaning “dry.” Hence from *serum* comes *sereo*, and from it *serescere*, “to become dry.” Thus Lucretius, Book I:

> Finally, garments hung upon the wave-battered shore  
> become damp; when spread out in the sun,  
> they dry again.

Therefore clouds that, dissolving into breezes, allow the earth to dry are called *serenae* by Virgil, *Georgics* I: “The wind drives the clear skies.” Hence a brow freed from wrinkles was called serene by Martial and others. From the brow the word was finally transferred to the mind, insofar as the mind is free from the disturbances by which it is usually troubled. It is understood in this sense here and is commonly so understood by Latin authors. Lucretius, Book II:

> Who lead a tranquil age and a serene life.
