**1. “In life.”** That is, in life or existence. *Aevum* is said to derive from the Greek ἀιών (*aiōn*), itself understood as ἀεὶ ὄν, “always existing.” But a living thing is not considered to exist except insofar as it is affected by its life. Hence, according to the different kinds of life, one *aevum* is perpetual, belonging to minds; another is limited to a definite time. Here the life of a human being is meant, just as Horace calls a human being “short-lived,” and Virgil says of bees, *Georgics* IV, verse 206:

> Therefore, although a narrow limit of life  
> receives them, nor does a seventh summer  
> lead them farther.

A human life is said to be ordered when it is governed according to the will of God, which is the first rule of conduct; from this arises the highest tranquillity of spirit.

**2. “Fate.”** That is, death. *Fatum* seems to derive from *for*, “to speak,” as though it meant God’s will, decree, command, and utterance. For what else is fate, asks Minucius Felix in *Octavius*, than what God has spoken concerning each of us? Since it has therefore been established by the divine will that all human beings must die, as Hebrews IX teaches, death may also be called fate by Christians—as it is here. Whoever entrusts himself to God’s judgment and neither begs to live nor fears to die seems to place fate, or death, beneath his feet. “Free yourself,” says Seneca, *Letter* 80, “first from fear of death; it first imposes a yoke upon us, and then fear of poverty.” Thus Virgil, *Georgics* II, verse 490:

> Happy is he who has been able to know the causes of things  
> and has placed beneath his feet all fears  
> and inexorable fate,  
> and the roar of greedy Acheron.

**3. “Gazing uprightly upon both Fortunes.”** Among the pagans, Fortune was a divinity from which they thought everything proceeded whose cause they did not know. “Fortune,” says Cicero, *Academica* I, “produces many unforeseen things for us because of the obscurity and ignorance of their causes.” Hence they proclaimed her to be rolling like a globe-shaped stone, since the revolutions of a sphere follow one another no more swiftly than events whose causes we do not know. They therefore made her twofold: favorable Fortune, from which at least external goods proceed, and adverse Fortune, from which contrary evils arise, since, when the cause is unknown, we often pass from one state to the other.

Once that false divinity has been rejected, prosperous and adverse circumstances are meant here. The person who cultivates virtue regards them uprightly, so that he is neither depressed by the weight of adversity nor lifted up by the wind of prosperity. This is read from his countenance: since it becomes neither sadder in adversity nor more cheerful in prosperity, it remains unconquered. I cannot omit Horace’s words, *Odes* III.3, although they are familiar to everyone:

> The just and steadfast man,  
> whom neither the zeal of citizens commanding evil,  
> nor the face of an threatening tyrant  
> shakes in his firm mind, nor the South Wind,  
> the turbulent master of the restless Adriatic,  
> nor the great hand of thunder-bearing Jupiter.  
> If the world, shattered, should fall,  
> its ruins will strike him undismayed.]**

Whoever, serene in an ordered life,

38 has placed proud Fate beneath his feet

and, gazing uprightly upon both Fortunes,

[Col. 0611A] [Note: [Col. 0611B]

**5. “Neither the fury nor the threats of the sea will move him.”** I. The sea, especially when agitated and disturbed by winds, is so terrible that it seems capable of striking fear even into the bravest men. Hence Horace, *Odes* I.3:

> He had oak and triple bronze  
> around his breast who first entrusted  
> a fragile boat to the savage sea,  
> and was not afraid of the rushing South Wind  
> battling with the north winds,  
> nor of the gloomy Hyades, nor of the rage of the South Wind.

Hence the sea’s “fury and threats” are mentioned: its fury because it is swept here and there like a rabid or frenzied dog; its threats because its towering waves threaten death. Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* I, verse 166:

> On either side vast cliffs and twin crags  
> threaten heaven.

Whoever has placed fate beneath his feet is not moved by these dangers of the sea, because they are nothing other than omens of death, which he despises. We have already explained why the sea is called *pontus* in Meter 2, verse 14.

**8. “Vesuvius.”** II. The earth too, especially that which sends out fires from its own depths, is terrible; nevertheless, for the reason already given, the person who has placed fate beneath his feet does not fear it. Such is Vesuvius. Vesuvius, also called Vesevus, is a mountain of Campania near Nola, from whose summit fires frequently erupt; it is especially notorious because of Pliny’s death. They say that this celebrated author, who had gone there in his eagerness to investigate the fire, was killed by the smoke and flames emitted from it. Virgil mentions this mountain in *Georgics* II, verse 224, where he praises its fertility:

> Such is the rich land that Capua plows,  
> and the region near Vesuvius’ ridge.

The fires of Vesuvius are “smoke-producing” because they arise from a terrestrial exhalation. As long as this is confined and compressed within the earth, it is smoke; but when it finds a freer path through the air, it catches fire, and immediately, because its parts adhere more closely, resumes its original swollen form. Hence, as the Conimbricenses say, *Meteorology*, treatise 12, chapter 3, a cloud was once seen to rise from that mountain resembling and taking the form of a pine tree. These fires do not flash forth, however, unless the chimneys have been broken open, or an exit has been made for them. If the exhalation—the material of subterranean fire—had found a ready-made path, it would have passed into the air rather than into fire. Since this happens intermittently, the mountain is therefore now called “wandering.”**

**10. “The path of lightning.”** III. The sky, especially when lightning flashes and thunder roars, is exceedingly terrible, since it seems to threaten immediate death. [Col. 0612A] Hence those who are tormented by the goads—or rather the Furies—of a bad conscience chiefly fear lightning, and thus the omens of lightning, flashes, and thunder. Such was Gaius Caesar Caligula, who, as Suetonius says, although he so utterly despised the gods, would close his eyes and cover his head at the slightest thunder and lightning, but at more violent phenomena would leap from his bed and hide beneath it. So too, according to Juvenal, *Satire* V.13, every wicked person is terrified by lightning:

> These are the men who tremble and grow pale at every flash  
> when it thunders, lifeless at the first murmur of the sky,  
> as though the fire fell upon the earth not by chance  
> or through the fury of the winds, but as an angry judge.

Lightning and the lightning-flash agree not only in origin but also in nature. They agree in origin because, in Varro’s view, *On the Latin Language* IV, both words derive from *fulgor*, “brightness.” They agree in nature because both are an ignited exhalation. They differ, however, in that the lightning-flash perishes almost as soon as it is born, whereas the thunderbolt is not extinguished before it reaches the earth. It resembles the stars which, as Virgil says, *Georgics* I, verse 365:

> When a wind threatens, you will see  
> them rushing down from heaven through the darkness of night,  
> leaving long trails of flame glowing behind them.

Therefore the poem speaks of “the path of blazing lightning” and says that the thunderbolt is accustomed to strike lofty towers. The ignited exhalation, driven out from the clouds, is either emitted through the sides of the clouds or through the lower part of the cloud beneath it. In the first case, the path of the lightning is oblique, so that it encounters elevated rather than low objects. In the second, just as leather placed beneath a table makes the leather easier to pierce, so a lofty body beneath a cloud makes the part of the cloud corresponding to it more fragile and thus prepares a path by which it may be struck when the lightning descends.

Yet lightning cannot inflict an evil more serious than death upon the person under discussion, and he does not fear death; therefore he is not moved by lightning. Seneca, *Thyestes*, verse 347:

> He is king who has laid aside his fears …  
> Him the falling path  
> of slanting lightning will not shake …  
> He who, placed in a secure position,  
> sees everything beneath him  
> and willingly meets his fate:  
> he does not complain to die.

**11. “Why the savage tyrants?”** Finally, the person who is terrified neither by the fury of marine waves, nor by the fires of subterranean flames, nor by the blows of Jupiter’s lightning, fears tyrants still less, since their power to harm seems weaker.

Among the ancients, *tyrant* meant the same as king or prince. The word may perhaps have been derived from towers or lofty buildings, in which kings usually dwell. Hence Horace contrasts the cottages of the poor with the towers of kings, *Odes* I.4:

> Pale death knocks with equal foot  
> at the cottages of the poor  
> and the towers of kings; O fortunate Sextus.

Virgil likewise speaks of a tyrant, *Aeneid* VII, verse 266:

> It will be part of my peace to have touched the tyrant’s right hand.

Among more recent authors, however, a tyrant is called only that ruler who abuses his supreme power. In this sense Virgil says, *Aeneid* IX, verse 365:

> They are united by either the cruel hatred  
> or the sharp fear of the tyrant.

]

Yet he does not fear tyrants of this kind who, endowed with greatness and strength of spirit, neither hope nor fear anything from created things. “For,” says Cicero in *De Officiis* III, “it is characteristic of these virtues to fear nothing, to despise all human things, and to regard nothing that can happen to a human being as intolerable.” From this the same orator concludes that courage is contempt for pains and hardships. Therefore, in the eyes of great-souled men, savage tyrants are raging without strength.

Thus he was able to maintain an unconquered countenance:

[5] Not him will the fury and threats of the sea,

when it stirs up the surge and overturns it from its depths,

nor, whenever its chimneys have burst,

the wandering Vesuvius, twisting its smoke-belching fires,

[Col. 0612A] nor the path of the blazing thunderbolt,

which is accustomed to strike the lofty towers,

[10] move him.

40 Why do wretched men so greatly admire savage tyrants

raging without strength?

[Col. 0613A] [Note: [Col. 0613B]

13. “Neither hope for anything nor fear anything.”] This is Plato’s maxim, which the Stoics subsequently adopted for themselves and which all orators and poets alike approved with one accord. For Plato says in the *Philebus* that the man who has chosen a life of understanding and wisdom ought in no way to rejoice or grieve. Seneca the Stoic says in *On the Happy Life*, chapter 5: “He may be called happy who neither desires nor fears, by the benefit of reason.” Cicero, in verse 11, and Virgil, in verse 2, have been cited in this meter; to them may be added [Col. 0613C] Martial, book X, epigram 47:

“Be willing to be what you are, and prefer nothing else;

neither fear nor desire the final day.”

Indeed, when the mind has been freed from hope and fear of perishable things, it is thereby freed from the body, the source of errors and vices; and from there it is joined to God, the principle of truth and virtue. Hence it disarms anger, whose only power is either to take away the good you desire or to inflict the evil you fear; and whoever is angry with you is powerless—either because he follows wherever anger and desire carry him (for such a person is also called *impotens*, “powerless,” by Cicero), or because he is unable to do harm.

15. “Whoever is frightened or desires.”] On the contrary, whoever is affected by fear or hope of perishable things is: first, not steadfast, because his mind is ready to depart from the first principle of truth and virtue either through punishment or through reward; second, not his own master, because he is a slave—not so much to masters as to his own desires or fears; third, he has thrown away his shield, because the greatness and strength of spirit that he has cast aside are the strength and protection of the spirit itself; fourth, he has been moved from his position, like a soldier outside his own ranks, because the tranquility of mind from which he has withdrawn is the proper seat of that same mind; fifth, he fastens a chain by which he can be dragged, because he has conceived hope and fear—through which, as through the other disturbances, the human mind is swept away—and has endeavored to nourish what he has conceived.

Nor does anything else here seem worthy of annotation, except perhaps the interpretation and use of the word “shield,” verse 17. We do not appear to find any difference, either in origin or in usage, among *clypeus*, *clupeus*, *clipeus*, *clypeum*, *clupeum*, and *clipeum*. As to its origin, *clypeum*—and the same may be said of the others—is called, according to Salmasius, by metathesis (*κατὰ μετάθεσιν*), from *κύκλιον*, “made circular” or “given an oval form,” because that is the shape of this object. In usage, however, a *clypeus* or *clypeum* is a round woven shield, which, for display, is decorated with engraved images, and in battle covers the soldier’s left side. Hence, transferred from the body to the mind, the word now signifies, as has been said, greatness and strength of spirit.]

Neither hope for anything nor fear anything;

you will disarm the anger of the powerless man:

[15] 41 But whoever, trembling, is afraid or desires

because he is unsteady and not his own master,

has thrown away his shield, has been moved from his position,

and fastens a chain by which he can be dragged.

42 PROSE IV.

ARGUMENT.—Boethius, questioned by Philosophy about his understanding of the foregoing matters and about his own wound, recalls first the place, bearing, and countenance with which he had until recently been accustomed to receive Philosophy; then, the precepts that he had received from Philosophy and had diligently carried out; and he reports the unjust causes of his exile.

[Note: [Col. 0614B] “Do you understand these things?”] I. Boethius is questioned by Philosophy about his understanding of the foregoing matters. Since, according to Cicero, *Academica* I, “nothing is more disgraceful than for assertion and approval to precede knowledge,” Boethius ought not to have passed judgment on the foregoing matters before he had grasped them after they had entered his mind. Hence Philosophy asks Boethius whether he is merely a listener to these things, like an ass to a lyre—*ὄνος λύρας*, “an ass of the lyre.”

Indeed, such and so notorious is the stupidity of an ass that this expression was very often proverbial among Greeks and Latins for signifying a person’s ignorance. Thus one says *ὄνος ἐν πιθήκοις*, “an ass among monkeys,” and *ὄνος ἐν μελίτταις*, “an ass among bees,” of a stupid person among the clever or a sluggish person among the industrious. Likewise, *ὄνου κεφαλὴν μὴ πλύνειν νίτρῳ*, “do not wash an ass’s head with soda,” when one is forbidden to waste effort teaching the uneducated. Horace says similarly in book I of the *Satires*, satire 1:

“Unhappy man, you would be wasting your effort—as if someone

were teaching a little donkey in a field to run under the bridle.”

Likewise, *ὄνος πρὸς αὐλόν*, “an ass to a flute”; *ὄνος λύρας*, “an ass to a lyre,” with “listener” understood; or, as others read it, *ὄνος πρὸς λύραν*, “an ass to a lyre.” The former reading belongs not only to our author but also to Varro himself, in the satire entitled *The Testament*, quoted by Gellius, book III, chapter 16: “If there should be freeborn children, let them be disinherited asses of the lyre” (*ὄνοι λύρας*). Either expression is used to signify a person who, although he receives words with open ears, does not grasp their meaning.

Furthermore, Boethius is questioned about the cause of his weeping and tears: “Why do you weep? Why do you pour yourself out in tears?” This is called his wound, which Philosophy, acting as physician, must uncover; for an illness is not cured when its cause has not been declared and understood. Hence Philosophy urges Boethius to speak with these words of Homer, *Ἐξαύδα μὴ κεῦθε νόῳ*, “Speak out and do not conceal it in your mind.”

[Col. 0614D] “Do you understand,” she said [Note: [Col. 0613A] Philosophy.], “these things, and do they sink into your mind? Are you an *ὄνος λύρας*?” [Note: [Col. 0614A] An ass of the lyre.] “Why do you weep? Why do you pour yourself out in tears?” [Note: [Col. 0614A] Speak, and do not conceal it in your mind.] *Ἐξαύδα μὴ κεῦθε νόῳ.* If you expect the service of a physician, you must uncover the wound.

43 Then [Note: [Col. 0614A] Boethius.] I, gathering courage: [Note: [Col. 0614A] I reply.] “Does the harshness of Fortune raging against us still require an admonition, or does it not sufficiently reveal itself of its own accord? Does not the very appearance of the place [Col. 0614A] [Note: [Col. 0614D] The appearance of the place.] move you?”

II. Boethius recalls the circumstances with which he had received Philosophy previously and with which he receives her now, so that from the contrast between the two conditions the harshness of Fortune raging against him may be recognized by Philosophy herself. The nature and appearance of these circumstances, with which Boethius had been equipped, are set forth.

First are the circumstances of Boethius’s place, bearing, and countenance. Previously, the place had been a library, or place of books, whose walls, as will be said below, were adorned with ivory and glass—such as the houses of the wealthy used to be, as Horace testifies in book II of the *Odes*, ode 18. Now the place is a squalid and gloomy prison. Previously the bearing was good; now it is an unfavorable condition of body and mind. The countenance—which, like the mind, is a kind of silent speech of the rest of the body—was previously cheerful and is now sad.

[Col. 0615B] Next, the nature of Philosophy is disclosed by that ancient definition of philosophy: “the knowledge of divine and human things.” For, says Cicero in book I of *De Oratore*, “the philosopher is one who knows the nature and causes of all divine and human things.” Yet authors do not interpret these terms in a single way. In our judgment, “divine things” here are minds, while “human things” are bodies. Since every mind is either God or like God, it can not improperly be called a divine thing; similarly, since every body is either human or like a human body, it can also be called a human thing. Philosophy as a whole is concerned with knowledge of mind and body and of the ways in which these two things can be affected.

Finally, three branches of Philosophy with which Boethius is said to have been equipped are enumerated: physics, which searches out the secrets of nature—that is, seeks very deeply, even in its fissures, as Festus interprets this word; astronomy, which traces the paths of the stars with a rod—that is, with a staff by which, after certain figures have been drawn, the various parts of the earth and sky are brought before the eyes; and ethics, or moral philosophy, which forms our character and the whole order of our life according to the model of the heavenly order—that is, according to the divine will, which, just as it is the first cause of all things, is also the first rule of human actions.

Hence the prophet-king says, Psalm 142: “Teach me to do your will, for you are my God.” Hence Saint Paul says in Acts 9: “Lord, what do you want me to do?” Hence also our author, in the final meter of book II: “O happy race of humankind, if love, by which heaven is governed, should govern your minds.”

[Col. 0615A] “Is this the appearance of the place that moves you? Is this the library which you yourself had chosen as the most secure seat for you among our household gods?” [Note: [Col. 0615A] In our house.] “In it, often sitting with me, you used to discuss the knowledge of divine and human things? Was your bearing like this, and your countenance like this, when you and I searched out the secrets of nature? when you described for me the paths of the stars with your rod? when you shaped our morals and the whole order of our life according to the model of the heavenly order?” [Note: [Col. 0615A] Physics.] [Note: [Col. 0615A] Astronomy.] [Col. 0616A] [Note: [Col. 0615C] Moral philosophy.]

44 [Note: [Col. 0615C] “Are these the rewards?”] III. Boethius recalls the precepts of Philosophy, whose usefulness in administering the commonwealth in the best possible manner is so great that Boethius, together with Philosophy herself, seems justly to lament his misfortunes: “Are these,” he says, “the rewards we receive for obeying you?”

The usefulness of philosophical precepts in governing the commonwealth in the best possible manner is supreme, because virtue rests upon them as upon its principles, and because they are the seed both of present and of future happiness. Hence Plato, in book V of *The Republic*, with Philosophy herself prompting him, says that commonwealths would be happy if either lovers of wisdom governed them—insofar as philosophers enter public office—or if their rulers happened to study wisdom—insofar as those who entered public office become philosophers.

Hence that same man, Plato, in the sixth dialogue of *The Republic*, speaking through his own character, declared that Philosophy had warned the wise of the necessity of undertaking the administration of the commonwealth, lest, when the reins of cities were left to wicked and disgraceful citizens, they should bring ruin upon the good and destruction upon the state. For just as the best rulers lead their subjects toward virtue by their precepts and examples, so bad rulers lead them toward vice, at least by their example.

“For this is certainly so,” says Lipsius in the preface to the *Politica*: “we who are ruled are bound by a certain close chain to the one who rules. When he leads toward virtue, we follow; toward vices, we incline. When he acts well and happily, we flourish; when he acts badly, we stumble or fall with him. And as light or darkness comes from the sun upon the world beneath it, so from the ruler comes much that is wrong or right among his subjects.” That Caesar spoke both boldly and truthfully:

“All these things follow the movements of the great.”

Few of the human race live for themselves. Hence Boethius himself, following this authority, desired to transfer into public administration what he had learned from Philosophy amid secluded leisure, that is, without being hindered by the conversations and interruptions of other people, progressing, as they say, from theory to practice.

[Col. 0615D] “Are these the rewards we receive for obeying you? Yet you established this judgment through Plato’s voice: that commonwealths would be happy if either lovers of wisdom governed them, or if their rulers happened to study wisdom.” [Col. 0616A] [Note: [Col. 0616A] If philosophers governed them, or kings became philosophers.] “Through the voice of that same man you warned the wise that undertaking the administration of the commonwealth was necessary, lest, when the reins of cities were left to wicked and disgraceful citizens, they should bring ruin upon the good and destruction upon the state. Following this authority, I desired to transfer into public administration what I had learned from you during secluded leisure.” [Note: [Col. 0616A] By study.]

[Note: [Col. 0616B] “You to me.”] IV. Boethius adds that he diligently carried out the precepts of Philosophy and that he entered public office solely for that purpose. Vallinus advises that *magisteriatum* should be written here, because Boethius was *magister officiorum*, an office commonly called *magisteriatus*, and because the things that Boethius soon lists as having been nobly accomplished by him were done while he held that office.

But however this may be, we think that nothing should be changed here, because this general manner of speaking is better suited to prove that Boethius had always been most devoted to philosophical precepts, so that he reached not even a single office except under the impulse of the common pursuit of the good. To leave no room for doubt concerning this, he adds an oath, a solemn affirmation: “You and God are my witnesses.” Saint Paul swears similarly in Romans 1 and Philippians 1: “God is my witness.” Nisus swears likewise in *Aeneid* IX, verse 428:

“O Rutulians, all my treachery is mine: he neither dared nor was able—

I call this heaven and the conscious stars to witness.”

Finally, God is most appropriately said to have implanted Philosophy in the minds of the wise. For Philosophy consists in knowledge and love of the best things. Just as God, in creating matter, impressed upon it form and motion in such a way that whatever subsequently accrues to this matter in form and motion is nothing other than a certain mode, or, as they say, determination, of the prior form and motion, so in creating the human mind God impressed upon it a conception and inclination toward being, or toward God himself, in such a way that whatever afterward arises in that mind as conception and inclination—at least with respect to the best things—is nothing other than a certain mode, or, as they say, determination, of the prior conception and inclination.

Hence Lucretius, book V:

“For if, as the very majesty of the known universe demands,

it must be said: that god was he, god, illustrious Memmius,

who first discovered the way of life that is now called wisdom,

and who by his art brought life out of such great waves

and such great darkness and placed it in so tranquil

and so clear a light.”

[Col. 0616D] “You and the God who implanted you in the minds of the wise” [Col. 0617A] [Note: [Col. 0617A] You are witnesses.] “are my witnesses that I entered no public office except through the common pursuit of the good of all.” [Note: [Col. 0617A] Administration of public office.]

45 [Note: [Col. 0617B] “Then with the wicked.”] Since Boethius, devoted to philosophical precepts, entered public office only through the common pursuit of the good of all, he consequently had serious and irreconcilable disagreements with the wicked. Hence the different thoughts of Boethius and the wicked; hence, in defending justice, he always rejected the hostility of the powerful. This is freedom of conscience; for conscience here is nothing other than a mind conscious of, and convicted by, truth and goodness. Such is the freedom of this conscience that it is safe from all human injuries.

Hence there were many benefits that Boethius conferred upon his fellow citizens; these must be discussed separately.

[Col. 0617A] “Then there were serious [Note: [Col. 0617A] Implacable.] and irreconcilable disagreements with the wicked; and, as freedom of conscience demands, while defending justice, I always rejected the hostility [Note: [Col. 0617A] Enmity.] of the powerful.”

[Note: [Col. 0617B] “How often I opposed Conigastus.”] Boethius’s first service to his fellow citizens. Conigastus, or, as Cassiodorus writes, Cunigastus, was a powerful man at the court of King Theoderic. This is evident from the fact that, according to Cassiodorus, book VIII, letter 28, King Athalaric wrote to him and called him illustrious.

Conigastus, however, abusing the authority that he possessed with Theoderic, attacked the property of every weak person. Boethius, in accordance with his virtue, repeatedly checked him by confronting him in his capacity as *magister officiorum*. For it was the duty of this office to judge provincial governors and, after receiving the complaints of provincials, to report concerning them to the ruler at whose court he served.

“How often have I confronted Conigastus as he attacked the property of every weak person!” [Note: [Col. 0617A] Confronting him.]

[Note: [Col. 0617C] “How often I cast down Triguilla.”] Boethius’s second service, greater than the first by as much as Triguilla was no less wicked than Conigastus and was more powerful than he. For Triguilla was prefect of Theoderic’s royal household.

“How often have I cast down Triguilla, appointed over the royal household” [Note: [Col. 0617A] Commonly, superintendent of the royal household.] “from an injury already undertaken and fully carried out!”

46 “How often [Note: [Col. 0617C] The unpunished greed of the barbarians.] have I protected the wretched, whom the unpunished greed of the barbarians was harassing with countless accusations, by placing my authority between them and danger!” [Col. 0618A] [Note: [Col. 0618A] Of the Goths.] “I have never been dragged from justice into injustice by anyone. I have grieved over the destruction of the property of provincials through both private plunder and public [Note: [Col. 0618A] Unjust taxes.] imposts, no less than those who suffered it.”

This was Boethius’s third service, greater than the preceding ones because it is more difficult to resist a multitude than the evil plans of a single wicked man.

In ancient times, a barbarian was called anyone belonging to another people, because, being a foreigner, he seemed not so much to pronounce the ordinary manner of speech as to confuse it by muttering. Hence some conjecture that the word *barbarus* belongs to the group of words that are called *πεποιημένα*, “made” or artificial, because they appear to imitate the thing signified—for example, *balare*, “to bleat”; *boare*, “to bellow”; and *hinnire*, “to neigh.” Others derive its origin from the Arabic *barbar*, “I murmur.”

Hence among the Greeks all who were not Greeks were called barbarians, just as among the Latins all who were not Latins were so called. Thus Horace says in *Epodes* IX:

“With the lyre’s music mingled with the sounding pipes—

for this one, a Dorian song; for those, a barbarian one?”

Because those foreigners, being different in their customs, commonly exercised their cruelty against citizens, it could have happened through usage that *barbarus* came to mean “cruel.” Here the barbarians are at once foreigners and cruel men, since they are understood to be Goths, whose unpunished greed continually harassed the citizens unless Boethius’s efforts restrained it.

Those citizens are called provincials because they lived under alien laws and were also tributary, or subject to taxation. Properly speaking, a province was a region distant from the Roman people, conquered by arms or brought under their power by some other means, which they placed under the administration of a magistrate. The word *provincia* is therefore understood as meaning a region to be conquered—or rather, already conquered—at a distance.

For this reason, among the Romans some were allies, others provincials: the allies lived under their own laws, while provincials lived under foreign laws. Hence Cicero rightly distinguishes them in *Against Verres* VI and in the *Manilian Speech*: “A grave and dangerous war,” he says, “for your tributaries and allies.”

Boethius protected these provincials with such greatness of spirit that he allowed no one to inflict any injury upon them. “No one,” he says, “has ever dragged me from justice into injustice.” If, despite his diligence, it happened that the property of the provincials was ruined, both by private plunder—such as that of Conigastus and Triguilla—and by public imposts—such as those imposed by Theoderic himself, who, according to Cassiodorus, *Variae* V, letter 39, hastened to exact more for his own advantage—Boethius grieved no less than those who suffered it. He was like Job, who, in chapter 29, was a father to the poor and most diligently investigated a case he did not know; he broke the jaws of the wicked and snatched the prey from his teeth.

Finally, a tax (*vectigal*) was so called because it was paid from transportation (*vectura*). It was a tribute that provincials paid to the Romans for commerce, lands, forests, and also salt. There were therefore four kinds of taxes: the *portorium* or customs duty, tithes, the *scriptura* or pasture tax, and the revenues of the saltworks.

47 “When, during a time of bitter famine, a grave and inexplicable [Note: [Col. 0618C] An imposed compulsory purchase.] compulsory purchase [Col. 0618A] [Note: [Col. 0618A] Commonly, a monopoly.] had been imposed, and seemed likely to ruin the province of Campania through scarcity, I undertook a struggle against the prefect of the praetorium [Note: [Col. 0618A] Commonly, captain of the guards.] for the sake of the common good; I contended before King Theoderic, who investigated the matter [Note: [Col. 0618A] Theoderic.], and I prevailed so that the compulsory purchase would not be exacted.”

Boethius’s fourth service was greater than the preceding ones because he then had to fight not only against certain private individuals but also against the prefect of the praetorium and against the ruler himself, without whose authority this compulsory purchase did not take place.

Among the Romans, *coemptio* was a particular form of marriage by which each spouse purchased the property of the other, so that each became the heir of the other. “By the ingenuity of the jurists,” says Cicero in *Pro Murena*, “old men were devised for carrying out coemptions, for the purpose of abolishing sacred rites.”

Hence *coemptio* also came to mean the commercial arrangement by which provincials, even against their will, were compelled to supply grain to a city or army at a low or nonexistent price. Thus, according to Suidas, the burden that Justinian imposed upon the inhabitants of Bithynia, Phrygia, and Thrace—requiring them to transport grain to Byzantium under extremely harsh conditions—was called *coemptio*, in Greek *συνωνή*.

It could again have happened that the commercial arrangement by which all commodities, once purchased by one person, could be sold only by one person was called *coemptio*, commonly “monopoly.”

It is clear that *coemptio* here does not mean the purchase of spouses. But it is not equally clear, says Sitzmann, whether the provincials were compelled to purchase provisions from the treasury, or whether they were forced to sell them to the treasury at market prices. Yet because this compulsory purchase was imposed during a time of bitter famine; because it is called grave and inexplicable; because the province of Campania seemed likely to be ruined by scarcity; and because the common good was harmed by it, we think that both meanings are signified by this compulsory purchase: that the provincials were compelled to sell the aforesaid provisions to the treasury at a lower price and to buy the same provisions from the treasury at a higher price.

Hence Boethius undertook the contest against the prefect of the praetorium, contended before King Theoderic, who investigated the case, and prevailed so that the compulsory purchase would not be exacted.

But why Campania? Why the prefect of the praetorium?

Campania was the most fertile region of Italy. Florus describes it after Pliny in book I, chapter 16:

“Of all regions, not only of Italy but of the whole world, the most beautiful tract is that of Campania. Nothing is softer than its climate; indeed, it blooms with flowers twice each year. Nothing is more productive than its soil; therefore it is said to be the scene of a contest between Liber and Ceres. Nothing is more hospitable than its sea; here are the noble harbors of Caieta, Misenus, and Baiae, warm with springs; Lake Lucrinus and Lake Avernus, certain resting places of the sea. Here are the mountains clothed with vines—Gaurus, Falernus, Massicus—and Vesuvius, the most beautiful of all, imitating the fire of Aetna. Along the sea are the cities of Formiae, Cumae, Puteoli, Neapolis, Herculaneum, Pompeii, and Capua itself, the capital of cities, once counted among the three greatest together with Rome and Carthage.”

The prefect of the praetorium, says Rosinus, was the officer who commanded the soldiers whom the emperors had selected for their own protection.

Among the Romans, after the expulsion of the kings, those who gave advice to the senate were called consuls, while those who judged were called judges; they were also called praetors because they went before the people. But as the power of the Roman people grew, the magistracies multiplied, so that those who governed in the city were called consuls, while those who commanded in the army were called praetors. From *praetor* comes *praetorium*.

48 [Note: [Col. 0619C] A former consul.] “Paulinus, a former consul, whose wealth the Palatine dogs had already devoured in hope and ambition” [Note: [Col. 0619A] Courtiers more shameless than dogs.] “and whom they were greedily eyeing, I dragged from their gaping jaws. So that a former consul, Albinus, would not be seized by the penalty of a prejudged accusation [Note: [Col. 0619A] False.], I opposed myself to the hatred of the informer Cyprianus. Do I seem to have aggravated sufficiently great hostilities against myself?” [Col. 0620A] [Note: [Col. 0619A] Sharpened.]

Boethius’s fifth service ought to be preferred by so much over all those mentioned above as, among the Romans, allies were superior to provincials. For here Boethius benefited not only provincials but also allies, indeed even former consuls, Paulinus and Albinus, whom the Palatine dogs and the informer Cyprianus were attacking.

First, Paulinus, who was called Decius because he belonged to the family of the Decii, was consul in the year of Christ 498; hence he is now called a former consul. For, according to Cicero, a *consularis vir* is a man who was once consul.

Next, Albinus, who, because he belonged to the same family of the Decii, was also called Decius, was consul in the year of Christ 493; therefore he too is now called a former consul. Cyprianus, the brother of Opilio, who will be discussed shortly, hated Albinus; for this reason he accused him and was consequently called an informer. For *deferre* in court means “to accuse.”

Certain courtiers attacked Paulinus. They are now called the Palatine dogs. They are called Palatine because they lived in, or at least frequented, the palace or house of the ruler. The ruler’s house was called the palace because, from the time of Octavian Augustus, all the Roman emperors lived on the Palatine Hill.

They are called dogs either because, like dogs appointed to guard, they stand at the doors, or because, more shameless than dogs, they bite those by whom they have not been injured and, if not in reality, at least in hope and ambition, devour their wealth with open mouths.

Finally, Boethius rescued both former consuls from such great dangers. In this especially he carried out the precepts of Philosophy. Therefore he now rightly exaggerates his disagreements with the question:

[Col. 0620A] “Do I seem to have aggravated sufficiently great hostilities against myself?”

Here one should not read *exacervasse*, as many read it, since, as far as I know, this is not a Latin word. One should instead read *exacerbasse*, as Valdericus, Bernartius, and Sitzmann read it. Sitzmann says that in Rittershusius’s manuscripts *exacuisse* is found, a word that has the same meaning as *exacerbasse*, “to aggravate” or “sharpen.”

“But I ought to have been safer among the others” [Note: [Col. 0620A] Especially among those to whom I had given assistance.], “among those for whom, through love of justice, I had preserved nothing with the courtiers by which I might be safer” [Note: [Col. 0620B] A pleonasm, used by Plautus when he says: “to do still greater trifles”; “this is sweeter still”; by Valerius Maximus: “richer still in envy than in money”; by Cicero: “they prefer to be deserted by everyone rather than defended by you”; and by the author of the *Culex* attributed to Virgil:

“Who could be happier in a more desired age?”

Unless, however, *magis* is construed with *optato* rather than with *beatior*.] This demonstrates how diligently Boethius carried out the precepts of Philosophy.

49 [Note: [Col. 0620B] “By whom we were accused.”] V. Boethius reports the unjust causes of his exile. He recalls his exile in these words: “We were struck down.” One should not read *percussi*, as certain more recent writers do, but rather *perculsi*, as the older writers have it. Thus Cornelius Tacitus says in *Annals* XIV, section 57: “When Seneca had been struck down, it was easy to diminish the standing of Rufus Fenius.”

He then mentions the unjust causes of that exile, first on the part of the accusers, whom he now calls “informers.” For *deferre* in court is the same as “to accuse,” in a capital case, according to Cicero; and second, on the part of the charge, which either was not brought forward or, once brought forward, was in no way proved, as will subsequently be demonstrated.

[Col. 0620A] “But by what informers were we struck down?” [Note: [Col. 0620A] We were exiled.] [Note: [Col. 0620A] Namely, by unjust men, among whom—] [Note: [Col. 0620C] Concerning whom: Basilius.] “The first informer or accuser in a capital case, according to Cicero’s own judgment, must be genuine. Therefore, if he appears to have been moved by some prejudice, he must not be heard at all. Hence Cicero says in *Pro Murena*: ‘I do not want an accuser to bring power into the trial, nor any greater force, nor exceptional authority, nor excessive influence.’ Since, therefore, the judgment has already been prejudiced by the very disturbance, in a manner most contrary to the truth, whoever appears to accuse only under the impulse of some disturbance must, as a false informer or accuser, be rejected, and the penalty that would follow from such a charge must be regarded as unjust.”

Boethius’s informers were of this sort. Only three are listed: Basilius, Opilio, and Gaudentius. Basilius accused Boethius because he was driven by the necessity of debt; Opilio and Gaudentius accused him because of frauds for which they had been ordered into exile and in defense of which they sought refuge in sacred buildings.

Basilius is sometimes praised and sometimes blamed by Cassiodorus. He is praised in book II of the *Variae*, letter 10, which concerns his wife Agapita, called a distinguished woman, and in letter 11, where we read:

“Basilius, a distinguished man, reported in a written petition that his wife Agapita had been taken away from her own home by certain persons through the fault of seduction. And certainly, having been involved in these matters, she is shown to have lost sound judgment. For what could a respectable woman do who abandoned her husband when no faults were apparent?”

He is blamed in book IV of the *Variae*: in letter 22, where Theoderic himself says that Basilius and Praetextatus had long been polluted by the contagion of a sinister art; and in letter 23, where the same ruler writes that he had declared Basilius and Praetextatus to be entangled in magical arts.

If this Basilius was the same man who is now named by Boethius, he could have been expelled from royal service because of the charge of magic. Hence the necessity of debt by which he unjustly accused Boethius.

[Col. 0620A] “Basilius, formerly expelled from royal service, was compelled to accuse me” [Note: [Col. 0620A] Commonly, overwhelmed by debts.] “by the necessity of debt.”

[Note: [Col. 0621B] “Opilio.”] There was a father Opilio and a son Opilio. The elder, according to Sirmond, had been *comes sacrarum largitionum* under Odoacer. Theoderic’s words in Cassiodorus, *Variae* V, letter 41, seem to indicate this:

“Cyprianus boasts that his birth was not of the lowest rank. For his father, as you remember, was Opilio, a man who, although born in an age of decline, was nevertheless chosen for service among the Palatine guards. He could have risen much higher had loyalty not lain barren beneath an exceedingly eager expectation of reward.”

The younger Opilio, the brother of Cyprianus, was raised, like his father and brother, to the same high office of *comes sacrarum largitionum*, but after Boethius’s death, under Athalaric, in the year of Christ 528. Hence Athalaric himself says to Opilio in Cassiodorus, *Variae* VIII, letter 16, entitled “To Opilio, *comes sacrarum largitionum*”:

“We confidently entrust this to you, because we rejoice that it has so often been entrusted to your family. Your father held this office, and your brother also shone with the same distinction.”

This does not prevent this Opilio, the son, from having been condemned to exile by Theoderic because of his innumerable and manifold frauds, together with Gaudentius.

“Opilio, and” 50 [Note: [Col. 0621C] Gaudentius.] “Gaudentius, a man scarcely known except for his frauds and for this unjust accusation of Boethius—when the royal judgment had decreed that they should go into exile because of their innumerable and manifold frauds, and when they refused to obey it” [Note: [Col. 0621A] The ruler’s edict.] [Note: [Col. 0621C] In defense of sacred buildings.] “and defended themselves by taking refuge in sacred buildings”—

As among the pagans certain temples were asylums, so among Christians all temples have always been asylums: places so sacred that no one who had fled to them could be dragged from them to punishment. For *ἄσυλον* is so called as if it meant “a place where it is unlawful to strip or plunder.”

Some temples among the pagans were asylums. Virgil sings in *Aeneid* II, verse 761:

“And now, through the empty porticoes, in Juno’s asylum,

Phoenix and stern Ulysses, chosen as guards,

were guarding the spoils.”

Likewise in *Aeneid* VIII, verse 342:

“Here is the great grove that fierce Romulus called an asylum

and points out beneath the cool rock of the Lupercal.”

But among Christians all temples have always been asylums, as is clear from the Theodosian Code, book IX, title 47, *Concerning Those Who Flee to Churches*, and from canon 12 of the First Council of Toledo. Hence Cassiodorus, *Variae* II, letter 11, and book III, letter 47, mentions those who, conscious of their deed, believed that by fleeing within the precincts of a church they could avoid the vengeance prescribed by the laws—just as Opilio and Gaudentius did in the case now under discussion.

[Col. 0621A] “When they had protected themselves by the defense of sacred buildings as though in asylums” [Note: [Col. 0621A] Temples, as though they were asylums.], “and this became known to Theoderic, king of Italy” [Note: [Col. 0621D] It became known to the king.], “for after he had defeated and killed Odoacer, king of the Italians, he became king of Italy in the year of Christ 409”—

he ordered [Note: [Col. 0621A] He decreed.] that, unless they left the city of Ravenna before the appointed day [Note: [Col. 0621D] The city of Ravenna.]—

Ravenna is a city of Italy, on the shore of the Adriatic, which, because of the overflowing sea, receives a considerable quantity of marshy mud. Hence Silius, book VIII:

[Col. 0622A] “The marshy pools of Ravenna are slowly cut through.” From this city, it is said, arose several distinguished men, such as Cassiodorus [Col. 0622B] the senator; Saints Apollinaris, Vitalis, Gervasius, and Protasius; and also that Peter of Ravenna, most celebrated in sacred theology. In this city, moreover, Theoderic established the seat of his kingdom after Odoacer, and his successors, the Gothic kings, also occupied it. But Opilio and Gaudentius had arranged to remain in that same city in such a way that they were ordered to leave it under the punishment of the marks which Cicero calls *Thracian*.

They were driven from Ravenna (5). [Note: [Col. 0622B] “Marked on their foreheads.”] This punishment originally belonged to slaves; later it was imposed upon any convicted persons who were infamous and degraded. It was a punishment for slaves: for since masters considered that they possessed over slaves—regarded as human beings whom they might kill—the right of life and death, they therefore thought that they could inflict upon those same slaves whatever punishment they pleased. Hence Juvenal, Book V, Satire 14, verse 21:

> Then happy whenever someone, after calling for the torturer,  
> Is burned with a blazing iron because of two linen cloths.

And Martial, Book II, Epigram 29:

> And numerous plasters smear the star-marked forehead:  
> Do you not know who he is? Remove the spleens, and read the laws.

But the same punishment later belonged to convicted persons who were infamous and degraded. Seneca, Book III *On Anger*, chapter 3, says: “Various kinds of fetters, various punishments, mutilations of limbs, inscriptions on the forehead, and cages of savage beasts.” Among these, Cujacius, *Observations*, Book VII, chapter 13, lists false accusers. These people are said to be “marked with brands,” just as in Horace, “dressed in whatever way,” and in Virgil, “flowers inscribed with the names of kings,” understanding the Greek usage κατὰ—“according to,” “by,” and so forth.

From all this it is clear that Boethius’ informers ought not to have been heard as trustworthy. Hence he adds: “What can appear capable of being brought forward against this severity?” As if he were saying: Since such severe treatment was inflicted upon men of this kind after their vices had become known, no confidence ought to have been placed in those same accusers. Yet, says Boethius, on the very day on which they informed against us, the charge against our name was accepted as though it were entirely just. Did our pursuits deserve this? Certainly not, since we had always endeavored to cultivate truth and virtue. Did the prior condemnation make those accusers just? Not in the least. Indeed, since they had been condemned, they deserved at least this because of their own crime: that no confidence should be placed in them even when they spoke the truth. Therefore, if blind Fortune were not blind, she would have been ashamed—if not of the innocence accused, then at least of the accusers’ baseness. Thus, on the part of the accusers, this was an unjust cause of exile.

[Note: [Col. 0622A] “Branded persons.”]

They were driven out, branded on their foreheads. “What can appear capable of being brought forward against this severity?” Yet on the very day, through the same men who had informed against us, the charge against our name was accepted. What follows? Did our pursuits deserve this? Or did the prior condemnation make those accusers just? Did Fortune feel no shame—if not at the innocence accused, then at least at the accusers’ baseness? [Note: [Col. 0622A] “Infamy.”]

**51** [Note: [Col. 0622D] “But of what crime are we accused?”]

Next, the cause of the aforesaid exile is unjust with respect to the alleged crime, since the crime was either not alleged at all or was not proved. For the sum, or number, of the crimes charged against Boethius consists of the following:

1. That he wished the Senate to be safe.
2. That he hindered the informer of that same Senate.
3. That he composed letters for the restoration of the Roman republic.
4. That he polluted his conscience with sacrilege.

But all these things are either not crimes or have nothing to do with Boethius, as will subsequently be demonstrated.

“But of what crime,” you ask, “are we accused?” [Note: [Col. 0622A] “Are we accused?”]

[Col. 0623A] **Boethius’ first crime.** The Senate among the Romans was a council consisting of elders. Hence Cicero says in *Cato*: “If counsel, reason, and judgment had not existed in old men, our ancestors would not have called the highest council the Senate.” Among the Lacedaemonians, those who hold the highest magistracy are both what they are and are called elders. Therefore Ovid, in Book V of the *Fasti*, writes:

> Once great was the reverence shown to the white-haired head,  
> And an old man’s wrinkle possessed its proper worth.  
>   
> The young performed the work of Mars and waged spirited wars,  
> And stood guard for their gods.  
>   
> That old man, no longer useful for bearing arms,  
> Often aided his country by his counsel.  
>   
> Nor was the senate-house opened until the late years;  
> The Senate bears the gentle name of age.  
>   
> The elder gave laws to the people, and age was bounded  
> By fixed laws determining from whom honor should be sought.

Plutarch writes that Romulus created one hundred senators from the nobility and called their body the Senate on account of their age. This designation, at least in outward form, continued down to Boethius’ own time. Boethius’ first crime is said to have been that he wished this most distinguished order to remain safe—namely, when he defended and freed the innocent Senate, which had been accused of treason. Boethius does not deny that he did this: “I wished it,” he says, “and I shall never cease to wish it.” But he denies that it was a crime: “Shall I call it a sacrilege to have desired the safety of that order?” For although the Senate itself, by its decrees against Boethius, brought it about that anyone who judged according to disorder would consider it sacrilegious to have desired the safety of that order, Boethius nevertheless thought—believing that another person’s sin did not grant him permission to sin—that it would be sacrilege either to conceal the truth by remaining silent about the good things he knew in the Senate, or to admit falsehood by speaking the evil things that were being fabricated about the Senate. Socrates says very well in Plato, Book VI of the *Republic*: “One ought to hate falsehood and love truth.”

“We are said to have wished the Senate to be safe.”

**52** Do you seek the circumstances? [Note: [Col. 0623C] “The informer, so that he might not submit the documents by which he accused the Senate of treason, and so forth.”]

**Boethius’ second crime** was that he hindered the informer from submitting documents by which he might make the Senate guilty of treason. Yet this is so closely joined to the first crime that, if the first was not a crime—as it has been said not to be—this too cannot be a crime. Therefore, says Boethius, if we admit that we wished the Senate to be safe, the charge of having obstructed the informer will disappear.

But for this to be understood, it must be explained what *maiestas* is and what the crime of *maiestas* is. *Maiestas* is the highest honor with which the people are bound to honor the ruler, as the living image of God. “Be subject,” says Saint Peter, in his First Epistle, chapter 2, “to every human institution for the Lord’s sake: whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of those who do good; for this is the will of God . . . Fear God; honor the king.”

But since honor, of which *maiestas* is a part or species, belongs to the one who honors, while reverence concerns the honored ruler toward whom that *maiestas* is directed, the poets imagined *Maiestas* to be the daughter of Honor and Reverence. Hear Ovid, Book V of the *Fasti*:

> Until Honor and Reverence, graceful with tranquil expression,  
> Joined bodies to lawful marriage-beds,  
>   
> From them Maiestas was born, who governs the whole world;  
> And on the day she was brought forth, she was already great.  
>   
> Without delay she took her lofty seat in the midst of Olympus,  
> Golden and conspicuous against her purple breast.

The crime of *maiestas*, therefore, is said to be whatever is directed against the honor owed to rulers. Since the Roman imperial constitution had at one time been a government of the people, among jurists the crime of *maiestas* is whatever is committed against the Roman people or its security. Those who commit such a crime are called guilty of treason in Digest, Book 48, title 4, law 1, *Ad legem Iuliam maiestatis*. Although honor is the genus of *maiestas*, in ordinary speech, as Vives explains, honor and *maiestas* are distinguished in such a way that *maiestas* denotes the person whom we honor with supreme honor. Thus Cicero, Book II *On the Nature of the Gods*, says: “The difficulty of sustaining the office, because of weakness, does not at all apply to the majesty of the gods.” Likewise, when we Gauls speak of the king, we say, “His Majesty.”

In Boethius’ time the Roman Senate was accused of having plotted something against Theoderic, king of Italy, and against the honor owed to him. Boethius defended and freed it as innocent, and this is turned into a crime against him: “We are accused,” he says, “of having hindered the informer from submitting documents by which he could make the Senate guilty of treason.”

“What then do you think, O teacher?” [Note: [Col. 0623A] “Shall we deny it?”] “Shall we deny the crime, lest we bring shame upon you? But I wished it, and I shall never cease to wish it. Shall we admit it? Then the charge of having obstructed the informer will disappear. [Note: [Col. 0623A] “The alleged care.”] Shall I call it sacrilege to have desired the safety of that order?” [Note: [Col. 0624A] “The Senate.”] “He had indeed made this sacrilegious by his decrees against me. But folly, always lying to itself, cannot alter the merits of things. By a Socratic decree, I consider that it was not lawful for me either to conceal the truth [Col. 0624A] or to admit falsehood.”

**53** “But let the matter be as it may; I leave it to your judgment and that of the wise to assess. So that the sequence and truth of this affair might not remain hidden from posterity, I have also committed it to writing and to memory.” [Note: [Col. 0624A] “Regarding the letters falsely composed.”]

Boethius’ third crime consists in this: he is said to have composed letters in which he hoped for Roman liberty. But the informer’s own confession would have proved that these letters were written not by Boethius but by his enemies, if Boethius had been granted the opportunity to question the informers.

“Why should I speak of the letters falsely composed, by which I am accused of having hoped for Roman liberty? Their fraud would have been plainly exposed if we had been allowed to make use of the informers’ own confession, which has the greatest force in every legal proceeding. For what liberty remains to be hoped for? Would that any could remain! I would have answered in the words of Canius, who, when he was said to have been an accomplice with Gaius Caesar, son of Germanicus, in a conspiracy formed against him, said: ‘If I had known, you would not have known.’” (10)

[Note: [Col. 0624D] “Gaius Caesar, son of Germanicus.”] Germanicus, according to Suetonius in *Caligula*, was the son of Drusus and the younger Antonia. He possessed every virtue of body and mind, and it is sufficiently clear that no one had ever possessed virtues equal to his. Adopted by his uncle Tiberius, he held the quaestorship five years before the law allowed it and immediately afterward held the consulship. He was married to Agrippina, by whom he had nine children, among them Gaius Caesar. Because Gaius was raised among the soldiers in the dress of a common soldier, he acquired the name Caligula, a military nickname. This man, however, attacked nearly everyone of every age with no less envy and malice than arrogance and cruelty. Yet many did not lack the courage to attack him while he raged and rampaged. When one or two conspiracies had been discovered, while others hesitated because an opportunity was lacking, two men shared their plan and carried it out.

[Note: [Col. 0625B] “In this matter.”]

“In this matter, our grief did not so dull our understanding that we should complain that wicked men had criminally plotted against virtue. Rather, I am profoundly astonished that they achieved what they hoped for. To desire what is worse may perhaps have been our own defect.” [Note: [Col. 0625B] “Our deficiency.”] “But why we should desire what is good or better must be sought outside us, since, as we read in 2 Corinthians 3, we are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God. The reason why we should desire what is evil or worse, however, is within us, since, as weak beings, we are capable of sinning.”

“But that what every criminal has conceived should be accomplished against innocence, while God looks on, is like a portent.” [Note: [Col. 0625B] “While God looks on.”] Since God is supremely good, it seems worthy of wonder that good men should be oppressed by wicked men while God looks on. Hence this appears like something monstrous, as though contrary to the ordinary order of nature. [Note: [Col. 0625A] “And as though paradoxical.”]

**54** Hence, not without reason, [Note: [Col. 0625A] “Not undeservedly.”] “one of your familiars” [Note: [Col. 0625A] “O Philosophy.”] asked: “If indeed God exists,” he says, “where do evils come from? And where do good things come from, if he does not exist?” [Note: [Col. 0625A] “Since they cannot come from God.”] [Note: [Col. 0625A] “Since good things cannot exist without God.”]

But whoever may have been the author of this dilemma—“If God exists, where do evils come from? But if he does not exist, where do good things come from?”—the condition of the one who argues from the existence of good seems better than that of the one who denies that God exists on account of evil. For as many good things as there are, so many are the arguments for the existence of God; but no evil can establish that God does not exist.

“But it may be permitted”—that is, let it be lawful. For Festus says that *fas* is derived from *fari* (“to speak”), as though something spoken by the gods, or at least by the priests who serve the gods; just as *ius* comes from *iubeo* (“to command”), as though it were a command issued by a magistrate. Hence Virgil, *Georgics* I, verse 268:

> For the sacred rites and laws permit certain tasks  
> To be performed even on festival days.

Since nothing is more permitted than what has been commanded and spoken by God, *fas fuerit* therefore means “it may be permitted.”

[Note: [Col. 0625C] “Wicked men.”]

“Wicked men”—*nefarios*. As Asconius Pedianus says in his commentary on the Third Oration against Verres, *nefandum* means “not to be spoken”; *nefarium* means something that pollutes the sacred rites ordinarily celebrated with sacred meal. Therefore *nefarii* are sacrilegious men. But I would think that *nefarius* derives from the same origin as *nefandus*: an evil man is unworthy of being celebrated in speech. Thus someone is called *detestabilis* whom it is unlawful to invoke as a witness.

“Wicked men who seek the blood of all good men and of the entire Senate, and who wished to destroy us also, since they had seen us [Note: [Col. 0625D] “To defend the good and the Senate.”] defending the good and the Senate”—that is, defending the good and the Senate. Thus Terence says: “He wrongs me, if he wrongs anyone”; and the familiar expression is: “The heavens serve you.”

[Note: [Col. 0625D] “To destroy.”]

“They wished to destroy us”—not “to go destroyed,” since, grammatically speaking, these are supine substantive forms and therefore do not change gender according to the different gender of another substantive noun. Cicero says, for example, “Greece will be drenched in blood”; Livy says, “banditry will be removed.” No one, however, is ignorant of these constructions.

“But did we deserve the same from the fathers?” [Note: [Col. 0625D] “From the senators.”] Senators are called “fathers” both because of their age and because of their office, as Sallust teaches at the beginning of the *Catiline War*: “They were called fathers either because of their age or because of the similarity of their care.”

They were called fathers because of their age, since they were advanced in years like fathers. Thus, as we have already noted, senators were named from old age. They were called fathers because of their office, since, just as fathers care for their children, so they care for the republic. Festus says that at the beginning of the city’s foundation Romulus chose one hundred of them to distribute portions of land to the poorer citizens as though to children, and to divide money among them.

Observe how Boethius’ injury grows. It is a great injury that innocent Boethius should be hated by wicked men; greater still that he should actually be oppressed by them; greatest of all that he should be oppressed by men who, both by age and by office, were bound to protect him. But it is incomprehensible and ineffable that this should be done by those toward whom Boethius himself had rendered the greatest services by word and deed.

“Did we deserve this also from the fathers?” [Note: [Col. 0626A] “From the senators themselves.”]

“You remember, I think, since you yourself were always present to guide what I should say or do. You remember, I say—”

**55** [Note: [Col. 0626B] “Verona.”] Verona is a city of Venetia, founded by the Gauls under their leader Brennus. According to Justin, Book XX, it was first called Brenona and afterward Verona. Distinguished men arose from this city, such as Catullus and Julius Scaliger, and, as some hold, Pliny.

“You remember, I say, what happened at Verona when Theoderic, [Note: [Col. 0626B] “When the king.”] who was king of Italy, [Note: [Col. 0626A] “Theoderic.”] an eager promoter of general destruction, sought to transfer to the entire senatorial order the charge of treason brought against Albinus. [Note: [Col. 0626C] “The charge of treason against Albinus.”] The matter of the crime of treason was discussed in note 19 to this prose, and that of Albinus in note 10, as was also that of the Senate in note 20.]

“I defended the innocence of the entire Senate with what complete contempt for danger.” [Note: [Col. 0626C] “With what security regarding danger.”] Philosophers say that security is a sound and tranquil condition of mind that does not concern itself with impending evils. For just as one who uses care beyond measure is called *curiosus*, according to Varro, Book V *On the Latin Language*, so one who is without care is *securus*. Here, therefore, security means disregard or contempt of danger. Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* VII, verse 302:

> What did the Syrtes, or Scylla, or vast Charybdis profit me?  
> I am hidden in the desired channel of the Tiber,  
> Secure of the sea and of myself.

[Note: [Col. 0626A] “With contempt.”]

“You know that I speak these things truthfully and have never boasted of my own praise. For the secret of a conscience that approves itself diminishes, in a certain way, whenever someone displays his deed and receives the reward of reputation.” [Note: [Col. 0626C] “The secrecy of a conscience approving itself.”]

Conscience, in general, seems to be nothing other than the mind’s knowledge both of itself and of its own thought. Hence Cicero, *On Duties* III, says: “When a judgment must be delivered under oath, let him remember that he has God as his witness”—that is, as I understand it, his own mind. Thus, just as we are convicted by clear and distinct knowledge, so we are convicted by conscience. Quintilian therefore says in *Institutio oratoria* V: “Conscience is a thousand witnesses.” The meaning requires no interpreter.

Conscience is of two kinds: good and bad. “Conscience has great power in either direction,” says Cicero in the speech *For Milo*: “so that those who have committed nothing fear nothing, while those who have sinned think punishment is always before their eyes.” By a good conscience we are convicted of right actions; hence comes the most joyful recollection, which is now called “the secrecy of a conscience approving itself.” Yet this secrecy is diminished when a person shares his own praise, since it is then less secret. Therefore the Stoics teach: “Do not search for yourself outside yourself.” And Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* II, chapter 10, says: “The wise man places the fruit of virtue in conscience; the less perfect man places it in glory.”

Still more divinely, the Holy Spirit says in Proverbs 27: “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips.” Likewise in Matthew 6: “When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be honored by men.”

By a bad conscience we are convicted of evil deeds, and hence comes a sorrowful recollection. “Each person’s own crime drives him on and afflicts him with madness,” Cicero says in the speech *For Sextus Roscius*; “his evil thoughts and the conscience of his heart terrify him.”

“But you see what outcome has overtaken our innocence.” [Note: [Col. 0627A] “What the outcome and end of our integrity might be.”] [Note: [Col. 0627B] “What result might intervene.”]

For among its many meanings, *excipere* also means to intercept and seize. Thus Cicero writes in a letter to Atticus: “We were warned to take care lest we be intercepted by Caesar, since he was going to arrive at the same places toward which we were making our way, even more quickly than we could.” And Virgil, *Aeneid* X, verse 386:

> For Pallas, while he rages, intercepts  
> The unwary man rushing upon him,  
> Avenging the death of his companion,  
> And buries the sword in his swollen breast.

*Eventus*, according to Cicero, *On Old Age* I, is the outcome of some undertaking. Hence, in *On Oratory* II, he says: “First plans, then actions, afterward outcomes.” Whatever good or evil occurs by chance is therefore ordinarily called an outcome. The same orator says: “Those who know what has happened to others can easily foresee their own affairs from the outcomes of others.” Virgil, *Aeneid* X, verse 159:

> Here great Aeneas sits and ponders within himself  
> The varied outcomes of war.

And Ovid, *Letters from Pontus* II:

> For fear of a worse outcome is absent.

“You see what outcome has overtaken our innocence. In place of the rewards of true virtue, we suffer the penalties of a false crime.”

**56** “And what open confession of some more serious crime ever had judges so united in severity— [Note: [Col. 0627A] “Of some graver crime.”] [Note: [Col. 0627C] “Of an offense.”] a greater crime. For *facinus* is derived from *facio*, “I do”; hence it means some notable deed, whether good or evil. Sallust uses it in a good sense in the *Jugurthine War*: “He had performed many splendid military deeds.” Cicero uses it in a bad sense in *On Duties* III: “From this man no fraud or crime will be absent.” It is in this latter sense that it is now understood—

“—that not even one of them might be swayed either by the error of human understanding or by Fortune’s condition, uncertain for all mortals?” [Note: [Col. 0627D] “United in strictness.”]

Strictness properly belongs to a judge insofar as he relaxes nothing of the punishment, either through leniency or through feeling. Thus leniency and mercy are opposed to strictness, and one who remains firm in his judgment is said to persevere. Those who agree among themselves are considered united, appearing to possess a single mind. Since, according to Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I, the heart itself seemed to some people to be the mind, the terms *excordes*, *vecordes*, and *concordes*—“heartless,” “mad,” and “united in heart”—are derived from it. Thus Virgil, *Eclogue* IV, verse 46:

> Such ages the Parcae, united in purpose,  
> Spoke, as they spun them with the unchanging power of fate.

The author wishes to indicate here both the leniency and the mercy by which a judge’s strictness may be altered. Leniency is indicated by the error of human understanding, which, because of its innate weakness, inclines now this way, now that, like one who has lost his path. For error properly belongs to those who, ignorant of the road, turn aside from the appointed route. Hence Virgil, *Aeneid* V, verse 590:

> A thousand ways to conceal the trick,  
> By which he might mislead the unsuspecting signs,  
> And make the error irretrievable.

Mercy, however, is indicated by Fortune’s condition, which is uncertain for all mortals. For mercy is the feeling of a person who grieves over another’s misfortunes, such as those accidents to which he himself might be subject because of Fortune’s extreme instability.

“—so that not even one of them was swayed either by the human error of understanding or by Fortune’s condition, which is uncertain for all mortals?” [Note: [Col. 0627A] “So that not even one judge might depart from the common judgment of the rest, whether through human error or through mercy.”]

“If we were said to have wished to set fire to sacred buildings; if we were said to have slaughtered priests with an impious sword; if we were said to have plotted the death of all good men.” [Note: [Col. 0628B] “If we were said to have set fire to sacred buildings, and so forth.”]

“Yet a human judge would have punished us only after we had confessed or been convicted in his presence.” [Note: [Col. 0628B] “He would nevertheless have punished one who had confessed or been convicted in his presence.”]

A human judge delivers judgment only by the authority of God, whose representative he is. He must therefore deliver a judgment worthy of God. Just as God condemns no one unless he has been convicted, so a human being must likewise condemn no one unless he has been convicted. The accused is convicted either by his own confession or by other testimony to which he cannot reply. Since this cannot be done unless the accused is present, the accused must first be summoned, then questioned and heard. Yet this is denied to Boethius; so unjust is the punishment inflicted upon him.

**57** “Now, moved nearly five hundred miles from the city in which Boethius was condemned”— [Note: [Col. 0628C] “Nearly five hundred miles.”] Ticinum, where Boethius was imprisoned and held in confinement, was that far from the city in which he had been condemned. Ticinum is a city of Insubria, which later writers call Pavia; it takes its name from the river Ticino flowing past it—

“—and undefended, we are condemned to death and proscription by those judges by whom we are condemned, because of our excessive zeal for the Senate.” [Note: [Col. 0628A] “By those judges by whom we are condemned.”] [Note: [Col. 0628C] “To death and proscription.”]

Proscription is of two kinds, even in Cicero. One kind is the proscription of property, when goods are declared for sale by being listed on written notices. Thus Cicero, in *For Flaccus*, speaks of “proscriptions of estates.” The other kind is the proscription of persons, when they are sent into exile by written decree, so that their safety is not secure there. Thus Cicero, in *For Roscius*, says: “By the immortal gods, beware lest a new and much more cruel proscription appear to have been renewed through you.” Since Boethius here mentions death and proscription, he seems to be speaking of this latter kind. From this it is clear that Ennodius, in his *Panegyric of King Theoderic*, spoke more as an orator than truthfully when he said: “No one laments the hardships of proscription.”

“O men who deserved that none of you could be convicted of a similar crime!” [Note: [Col. 0628D] “O men deserving that no one could be convicted of a similar crime.”] As if he were saying: “O senators who are implicated in the sentence passed against us—for our speech now addresses you—men who deserved that none of you could be convicted of a similar crime, namely, of having shown excessive zeal for the Senate. Nothing could be more elegant for emphasizing, on the one hand, Boethius’ magnanimity and, on the other, the cowardice of all the senators.”

[Note: [Col. 0628A] “O our judges: none of you can be convicted of a similar crime; for even the informers themselves seem to think that no one was so guilty that they should strive to present it disguised as a fabricated sacrilegious crime.”]

“O men who deserved that none of you could be convicted of a similar crime! Even the men who informed against me recognized the dignity of the charge. In order to stain it by mingling it with some crime, they falsely alleged that, out of ambition for office, I had polluted my conscience with sacrilege.” [Note: [Col. 0629A] “By sacrilege undertaken for the sake of ambition for office.”]

Boethius’ fourth crime is sacrilege, but what this sacrilege consisted in is not entirely clear. The French interpreter of Boethius, de la Boucherie, thinks that the offense consisted in Boethius’ having fraudulently obtained the votes necessary for attaining office. The Latins call this crime *ambitus*, from going around and soliciting; the Greeks call it δημοκοπία, “demagogic solicitation.” It was punished by laws that had been enacted against it.

Others, such as Thomas and Ascensius, think that the offense was what we commonly call *sortilegium*, divination by lot. Pliny himself seems to use this term in Book XXVIII, chapter 4, to signify certain magical superstitions. Hence perhaps *sortilegio* should be read in place of *sacrilegio*. This opinion can be confirmed by the following arguments:

1. In Boethius’ own time, those who appeared to excel others by some art, as Boethius did, were often accused of magical art. Cassiodorus is a witness to this in Book IV of the *Variae*, letters 22 and 23, where the case of Basil and Praetextatus, accused of this crime, is entrusted to the judgment of five senators, “so that the innocent might not be oppressed and the guilty might not escape the laws.”
2. The arguments by which Boethius clears himself of such a crime do not have as much force against *democopia* as they have in favor of *sortilegium*, as will immediately be seen.
3. It is not so much the crime of *ambitus* as that of *sortilegium* that can be attributed to philosophy, since the former was said to belong even to the ignorant, whereas the latter belonged only to the learned.

Yet Boethius later says: “We shall appear to have been connected with magic because we have been imbued with your teachings and formed according to your principles.”

You may reply that the crime of *ambitus* is rightly called sacrilege because by it laws and the oath without which people once could not attain magistracies are violated. But the crime of magic is not so appropriately called sacrilege. I reply, first, that if *sortilegium* is to be read in place of *sacrilegium*, as it perhaps should, the difficulty disappears. Second, the laws and the oath by which we renounced evil spirits after initiation with lustral waters are violated by the crime of *sortilegium* no less than by *ambitus*. Hence Cassiodorus says in the aforesaid letter 22: “It is not permitted to practice magical arts in Christian times.”

Finally, *sacrilegus*, from which *sacrilegium* comes, means one who reads or steals sacred things—for *legere* can also mean “to steal.” Thus Virgil, *Eclogue* 9, verse 21:

> Or the songs that I secretly stole from you recently.

But whoever devotes himself to the aforesaid superstition steals the worship owed to God.

We must now examine the arguments by which Boethius clears himself of that crime.

**58** “But you, [Note: [Col. 0629D] “You implanted in us.”] who were implanted in us”— [Note: [Col. 0629A] “O Philosophy.”]

The first argument by which Boethius clears himself of the aforesaid crime is drawn from philosophy itself. Implanted in the human mind, philosophy separates it from perishable things and joins it to everlasting things—not to the most worthless of these, but to the one and first of them, namely God, whose likeness it possesses.
