Philosophy is implanted in the human mind, that is, in us, because it is wholly concerned with thought—namely, clear and distinct knowledge—and with judgment founded upon that knowledge. Thought is therefore rightly described as a quality implanted in the human mind.

This same philosophy separates the human mind from perishable things: that is, it drives every desire for mortal things from the seat of our soul, because it governs all the mind’s affections, and especially this desire for perishable things, which, according to Cicero, makes human beings blind, and which, according to the Apostle in 1 Timothy 6, is the root of all evils.

Philosophy joins the human mind to everlasting things, so that, since that part with which the human mind enters into fellowship through philosophy endures forever, love may be eternal, and therefore the undivided pleasure that accompanies that love may also be eternal.

But philosophy does not allow the human mind to cling so closely to created everlasting things, which we call evil spirits, that there could be room for sacrilege in its presence. For it daily instills in our ears and thoughts the Pythagorean saying ἕπου Θεῷ—“Follow God.” The same command is found in Deuteronomy 13: “Follow the Lord your God, fear him, keep his commandments, and obey his voice; you shall serve him and cling to him.”

Finally, since philosophy makes a human being like God—not in body, as Virgil expressed it, “like a god in face and shoulders,” since God is without a body, but in mind—it makes our mind, thinking in the likeness of God, refrain from error and vice. Philosophy therefore joins our mind to God, as to the first teacher of truth and virtue, so that it is not fitting for us to seek the aid of the most worthless spirits.

Those most worthless spirits are evil genii, through whose assistance certain ruined men are believed to perform marvelous deeds. This is taught not only by Christians, as sacred Scripture often shows, but also by the pagans themselves. Hence Virgil, *Eclogue* 8, verse 69:

> Songs can even draw the moon down from heaven;  
> By songs Circe changed the companions of Ulysses;  
> By singing the cold serpent is burst in the meadows.

Horace, *Epodes*, Ode 17:

> Or could I, as you yourself know,  
> Move waxen images,  
> And by my songs tear down the moon from heaven?  
> Could I raise the burned dead  
> And temper the potion of desire?

[Col. 0630D] Ovid and others give similar examples.

“You, implanted in us, drove every desire for mortal things from the seat of our soul, and under your eyes there could be no room for sacrilege. For you daily instilled in my ears and thoughts the Pythagorean saying [Note: [Col. 0629A] “Follow God.”] ἕπου Θεῷ. Nor was it fitting for me to seek the aid of the most worthless spirits, since you were forming me for such excellence that you made me like God.”

**59** [Note: [Col. 0630D] “Moreover, the inner chamber.”]

The second argument by which Boethius clears himself of the aforesaid crime is drawn from the outstanding virtue of his household, friends, and relatives, with whom Boethius had long maintained close relations. Since virtue and vice are so opposed that there can be no fellowship between them, if a man has close relations with virtuous household members, friends, and relatives, that man certainly ought not to be suspected of a crime that could neither have remained unknown nor gone unrebuked by those associates.

Since, therefore, the crime of *sortilegium*, being both more serious and more frequent and evident than the crime of *ambitus*, could not fail to be known and rebuked by the most holy members of Boethius’ household, if Boethius maintained the closest familiarity with virtuous members of his household, friends, and relatives, he certainly could not be guilty of *sortilegium*.

Boethius did maintain such relationships:

1. With virtuous members of his household. For, as it is said in Book II, Prose 3, he was most fortunate both in his wife’s modesty and in the distinction of his male offspring, so that he saw his two sons, both consuls, advancing from his house before an assembly of senators and amid the rejoicing of the people. Hence the phrase now used is “the innocent inner chamber of the house.”

An inner chamber is an interior place, called *penetral* from *penus*. Festus says that *penus* is the innermost place in the temple of Vesta, enclosed by coverings. Hence Virgil, *Georgics* I, verse 379:

> And more often he carried eggs out from the covered inner chambers.

An ant wearing away a narrow path. Secondly, with honorable friends: for there was always about him a company of the most upright friends. Thirdly, with honorable relations by marriage: for his father-in-law Symmachus was a holy man, and as worthy of reverence as Philosophy herself. How great that father-in-law Symmachus was may be gathered both from Cassiodorus, who says that King Theoderic wrote to him as a patrician, saying that permission to withdraw from the city should not be granted to the petitioner (*Var.* IV, Letter 6); and in Letter 22, that the same king wished that Symmachus, together with four other senators, should give judgment concerning the case of the aforesaid Basilius and Praetextatus; and in Letter 51, that the same king, writing again to Symmachus, said that Symmachus had adorned Rome with the beauty of its houses. It may also be gathered from Priscian of Caesarea, in *On Weights and Measures*, and from Ennodius, by whom Symmachus is said to have shone with every light of virtue and to have been capable of being presented to others as a model of virtue. Therefore Philosophy says below, Book II, Prose 4: “There flourishes unharmed the most precious ornament of the human race, Symmachus, your father-in-law.”

Moreover, the innocent inner chamber of the house, [Col. 0630A] the company of the most honorable friends, [Col. 0630A] and your father-in-law Symmachus, a holy man and as worthy of reverence as you yourself, all defend us from every suspicion of this crime. [Col. 0631A]

**60** But, oh outrage! They, in fact, [Col. 0631C] take the credibility of such a crime against me from you—[that is, on account of you, O Philosophy, they believe me guilty of so great a crime]. Thus Seneca says: “The mind scarcely gives credence to greater monstrosities than the truth”; and Virgil himself, *Aeneid* V, line 604:

> Here first Fortune, changed, renewed belief.

They take belief in so great a crime from you, [Col. 0631A] [you, O Philosophy, are the occasion of my accusation], and by this very fact we shall seem to have been accomplices in sorcery, [Col. 0631C] [because we have been imbued with your teachings]. Those who judge either through rashness or through prejudice commonly pronounce a reckless judgment about matters of which they themselves are ignorant. Thus Saint Jude expressed it in his Epistle: “Whatever things they do not know, they blaspheme.” So the ignorant common people attribute to evil spirits the unusual movements of those whom they call sorcerers or werewolves, although such movements are more often the result of a disordered brain or damaged imagination. Thus some have thought that the art of making gold comes from demons, as Delrio says, *Magical Investigations*, Book I. Thus Galen, speaking of himself in Book II, chapter 7, of *The Differences of Fevers*, and in chapter 10 of *The Faculties of Simple Medicines*, says that, because of his exceptional learning, he had been placed among those who drive away diseases with the aid of the arts of evil spirits. Thus Boethius, who—as King Theoderic says in Cassiodorus, *Variae* I, Letter 45—was “stuffed with much learning,” so that he had drunk from the very fountain of the disciplines the arts that the uneducated practice without understanding, seemed, because of his supreme learning, to have been an accomplice in this crime. Therefore, since no one can be said to be an accomplice in the crime of canvassing merely because he is exceedingly learned, whereas this is said of the crime of sorcery, it follows that Boethius was accused not of canvassing but of sorcery; yet unjustly, as is demonstrated above. Nevertheless, Boethius’s reputation among many people did not cease to decline.]

because we have been imbued with your teachings and formed according to your moral discipline. Thus it is not enough that your reverence has brought me no benefit, unless you are also voluntarily torn apart by my very injury.

(5) But here, too, a further burden is added to our misfortunes, [Col. 0632B] [namely, that many people judge not by clear and distinct knowledge—the first rule of true judgment—but are carried away by rashness and prejudice. Thus, because they pursue wealth with love and poverty with hatred, they hold a good opinion of the rich but a bad opinion of the poor. So Job’s friends, seeing him oppressed by calamities, judged him wicked. Hence it happens that a good reputation first of all deserts the unfortunate. Thus the common people judge only those things prudent which prosperity has commended.]

because the reputation of most people considers not the merits of things but the outcome brought by Fortune, and judges only those things [Col. 0632B] [to have been prudently undertaken] which prosperity has commended. [The common people customarily infer a man’s prudence from the outcome, so that, when they see that someone’s undertaking ended unhappily, they conclude that he began it badly and therefore imprudently. Ovid reproaches himself for precisely this, but immediately refutes it:]

> The outcome proves the deed; may he lack success,  
> Whoever thinks deeds should be judged by their outcome.

As a result, a good reputation [Col. 0632A] is the first thing of all to desert the unfortunate.

**61** Those rumors of the people now, [Col. 0632A] [about Boethius], and those many judgments so discordant, [Col. 0632A] [some of the common people condemning him, others defending him], I am reluctant to recall. This alone I shall say: the final burden of adverse Fortune is that, when some crime is fabricated against the wretched, they are believed to have deserved what they endure. [Those people had seen certain individuals justly punished for their crimes; therefore, led by this prejudice, they judge all whom they see afflicted because of an accusation to have deserved what they suffer. But this is rashness: since a human judge may participate in both injustice and justice, assent concerning the causes of misery must be restrained, lest one judge precipitously.]

And I, driven from all good things, stripped of my dignities, stained in reputation, have suffered punishment in return for a benefaction.

But I seem to see the criminal workshops, [Col. 0632C] [the houses of criminals]. A workshop—so called as though from *opificina*—is a part of a house in which work is done. Hence it differs from a storeroom, in which something is kept, and from a shop, in which work already completed is sold. We may therefore properly call the houses, or even the minds, of wicked men—within which the case against Boethius was fabricated with the utmost malice—“workshops.”]

of the most depraved criminals [Col. 0632A] overflowing with joy and delight. [Col. 0632D] [Just as a vessel is said to overflow or pour out because of an abundance of liquid, so a mind may be said to overflow because of an abundance of joy. “The spirit,” says Terence, “runs riot in luxury and wantonness.” What grows more broadly and abundantly is said by Virgil to overflow, *Georgics* II, lines 367–370:]

> Then, when they have risen, clasped by sturdy trunks,  
> The elms, bind up the branches; then lop the arms.  
> Before this they fear the iron; then at last  
> Exercise stern authority and restrain the streaming boughs.]

overflowing with joy and delight: [Col. 0632D] [overflowing with the most abandoned frauds and threatening harm]. For the impunity of the depraved breeds the frauds of similar men.] each of the most depraved [Col. 0633A] threatening new deceitful accusations. [Col. 0633A] [Intent upon it.] [Col. 0633B] [To cast down the good.] For, as it is said in Luke 23: “If they do these things in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?” If Boethius, endowed with such greatness and such virtue, is treated so badly, what may the other cultivators of virtue hope for?] casting down the good, and our [Col. 0633B] [with the terror of danger] prostrated by the same terror of danger. Danger is the same as peril. Just as *crinis* comes from the Greek *krinein* (κρίνειν), which properly means “to separate,” so *discrimen* comes from *diakrinein* (διακρίνειν), which also means “to separate” or “divide.” Hence we call hairs distinguished from one another *discriminated*. Claudian, *On the Marriage of Honorius*:

> With the bite of its many ivory teeth  
> It plows a many-forked parting.

Whatever peril someone is exposed to seems to separate him from the company of other people. Boethius, moreover, here briefly gathers up his calamities, their cause, and the evils that follow from them. His calamities are, first, that he has been driven from all good things; second, that he has been stripped of his dignities; third, that he has been stained in reputation. The cause of the calamities is the benefaction of Boethius himself—especially his service to the senate—for which he suffered punishment. The evils that follow are, first, that the guilty are carried by impunity not merely toward making false accusations but also toward daring, indeed accomplishing, every crime, while the innocent are deprived both of severity and of protection. Therefore one is moved to exclaim.]

the most disgraceful man is invited by impunity to dare a crime, and by rewards to accomplish it: [Col. 0633A] [the innocent] are deprived not only of safety but even of protection itself. Therefore I am moved to exclaim.

## 63. METER V

[Col. 0633C] [What Pindar calls Pindaric. It is a poem consisting of one kind of verse, each line generally containing a tetrameter composed of a spondee, an anapaest, a dactyl, and a spondee. But disregarding these rules, Boethius cares only that there be four feet.]

### Argument

Boethius, considering the most constant law by which God governs the alternating changes of the moon, Venus, the days, and the seasons, wonders that humanity alone seems released from law, so that, in a kind of inverted order, prosperity comes to the wicked and adversity to the good. Then he asks God at last to put an end to these things.

[Note: [Col. 0633C] O God, creator of the star-bearing heavens, who, seated upon an eternal throne, turn the heavens themselves with swift rotation and compel the stars to submit to your authority, so that at one time the moon, shining with a full disk and standing opposite the flames of her brother the sun, conceals the lesser stars; at another, with her disk covered and pale, she loses her light as she draws nearer to the sun. Thus Hesperus, who at the beginning of night seems to lead the procession of the cold stars, the same star as Lucifer, again changes his customary reins, pale at the rising of the sun.

You contract the day into a smaller space through the cold of winter, which strips the leaves; you divide the hours of night when warm summer has arrived. Your power so governs the changing year that the leaves which the northern wind removes are restored by the gentle west wind, and the crops which the constellation Arcturus saw sown are burned as ripened harvests by the other constellation, the Dog Star.

Nothing leaves free from the ancient law the work of its own creation. You, governing all things in a stable manner, disdain to restrain only the actions of human beings, as befits the wisest governor. Why does unstable Fortune alternate such great changes? Punishment owed to crime afflicts the innocent. But wicked morals sit upon the highest tribunal, and the guilty, in an unjust reversal, trample pious heads. Brilliant virtue lies hidden, buried in obscure darkness, and the pious person bears the infamy owed to the wicked. Perjuries do not harm the perjurers themselves; fraud concealed beneath a deceptive appearance harms them not. But when they choose to use their strength, they rejoice in subjecting to themselves great rulers whom countless nations fear.

O God, who govern the bonds of things, now look upon the suffering earth. We human beings, no insignificant portion of so great a work of yours, are tossed upon the storm of Fortune. Restrain, O governor, the violent storms of Fortune, and by the law with which you govern the vast heavens, make firm the steadfast earth.]

[Col. 0633C]

1. **“Of the star-bearing sphere.”** Heaven: for, as Cicero also judges, heaven is of two kinds. One is airy, in which clouds, rains, and winds are gathered; the other is star-bearing, which, being highest above our dwellings, surrounds and constrains everything, the outer boundary and limit of the world. Boethius now speaks of this second kind of heaven because he is about to discuss the laws observed both in lower bodies and in the stars. God himself established these laws from the first moment when he created these bodies; therefore God is now conceived as creator.

2. **“Who rests upon an everlasting throne.”** In general, a throne is a seat on which several people cannot sit together. “Thrones,” says Festus, “are seats on which not more than one person can sit individually”—as though *solium* meant something that accommodates only one. Specifically, a throne is a royal seat, commonly called *un trône*. Virgil often uses it in this sense, as in *Aeneid* VII, line 169:

> He commands, and seated in the middle of his ancestral throne,

God is now regarded as king; hence in line 27 he is rightly called “the ruler who restrains,” and in line 46, “Ruler, compress the rushing waves.” God’s kingdom differs from other kingdoms in this: the latter are subject to change, whereas God’s is eternal and unchangeable. Hence it is now called everlasting. This is also supported by the interpretation according to which *solium* means a solid seat, just as the earth, because it is solid, is called *solum*.

3. **“With swift rotation.”** *Turbo*, “a whirlwind” in French, comes from *turbare*, “to disturb,” because through a certain circular movement matter is so disturbed that what is above follows what is below, what is before follows what is behind, and the right follows the left. Thus a certain wind, which Lucretius calls *versabundus* and which whirls around bodies in its path, is called a *turbo*. Hence Virgil, *Aeneid* II, line 416:

> As once, when the opposing winds, their whirlwind broken,  
> Clash together.

Thus the spinning top, a familiar children’s toy, is also called *turbo* by Virgil. The circular movement of suspended yarn is likewise called *turbo* by Catullus. Whether heaven is believed solid or fluid, there is in it a continuous rotation of moving matter, and therefore a whirlwind.

4. **“And compel the stars to submit to law.”** Just as the first body moves only by God himself, by whom it was created, so that same body moves only according to the laws of motion which God himself established and preserves unchanged. Ovid expresses this excellently:

> Nothing is so sublime, extending above dangers,  
> That it is not subordinate and subject to God.

A moving body must therefore be moved by something else; an unmoved body does not move, and so forth—matters of this kind belong to philosophy. Hence Eternal Wisdom says in Proverbs 8: “When God prepared the heavens, I was present; when he enclosed the depths with fixed law and circuit; when he made firm the heavens above and balanced the springs of waters; when he surrounded the sea with its boundary and established a law for the waters, lest they pass beyond their limits,” and so on.

Since the stars are bodies, they not only come from God but are moved according to laws established and preserved by God himself. Thus God compels the stars to submit to law. Accordingly, God is now said to govern the alternating changes of the moon, Venus, the days, and the annual seasons, as will be explained below.

5. **“So that now, with full shining horn.”** First, the subject is the moon, whose changes consist in this: sometimes she is full, sometimes curved into horns. The moon is full, or “shining with a full horn,” when, with the earth between her and the sun, she stands diametrically opposite the sun and reflects the sunlight toward us from the middle of her disk—“meeting the flames of her brother in their entirety.” For the poets, Diana, who is also called Luna, and Apollo, who is also called Sol, are sister and brother, born in the same birth to Jupiter and Latona.

At that time the moon conceals the lesser stars, because the weaker light is obscured and overwhelmed by the greater. Although the stars for the most part exceed the moon in size, they are farther away and therefore diffuse less light to us than the moon. Thus Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, says that the moon is called as though *lucina*, because she alone shines at night. Hence the moon is also called the greater star, and the stars lesser stars, not only in sacred texts but commonly and among Latin authors. Horace, *Odes* I.12:

> The fame of Marcellus grows like a tree  
> In the hidden course of time; amid all the Julian stars  
> The star of Julius shines, as the moon among  
> The lesser fires.

The same moon is curved into horns, or pale with a dark horn, when, withdrawing from the place of full moon, she approaches the sun so that, waning toward conjunction and then waxing toward fullness, she returns. Therefore, nearer to Phoebus, she loses her light—not entirely, since half the moon is always illuminated by the sun, but the half turned toward us. Hence one could more accurately say that the moon loses the light of the sun.

10. **“And he who at the beginning of night.”** Second, the subject is Venus, whose changes consist in this: sometimes she follows the setting sun as Hesperus, and sometimes precedes the rising sun as Lucifer. For a clearer understanding of this star, the relevant teaching of grammarians, historians, poets, and philosophers must be set out.

Among grammarians, Hesperus, Hesperugo, Vesper, Vesperugo, Lucifer, and Phosphorus (Φωσφόρος)—the star both of evening and of morning—are all the star of Venus. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, says: “The lowest of the five wandering stars, and nearest to the earth, is Venus, which is called Phosphorus in Greek and Lucifer in Latin when it precedes the sun; when it follows, it is Hesperus.” Hence Martial, *Epigrams* VIII.21: “Phosphorus, restore the day.” And Virgil, *Eclogues* 10, line 77:

> Go home, my full-fed goats; Hesperus has come; go home.

Among historians, Hesperus was the brother of Atlas, a most accomplished astronomer, and equally devoted to astronomy. When he had climbed a very high mountain—perhaps the one named Atlas after his brother—in order to contemplate the stars more carefully, he was prevented from returning to his homeland, whether by death, illness, or some other accident. Hence the superstitious common people believed that he had been placed among the stars in heaven and consequently offered him divine honors. Thus there are two Hesperias: one Spain and the other Italy.

The first Hesperia is called after the star of the same name, because for the Greeks that kingdom, like the star, lies in the west. Horace speaks of it in *Odes* I.36:

> He who now, safe, has returned from the farthest Hesperia.

The second Hesperia is named after the aforementioned Hesperus, the brother of Atlas, who, expelled by his brother, occupied Italy and gave it a name taken either from himself or from his homeland. Virgil speaks of this in *Aeneid* I, line 534:

> There is a place which the Greeks call Hesperia by name.

Among poets, Hesperus is a star into which a human being was transformed—Venus according to some, the son of Aurora according to others. Since among those same poets the Sun rides in a four-horse chariot and the Moon in a two-horse chariot, Hesperus uses a single horse by himself, but alternates it so that in the morning he mounts a white horse and in the evening a dark one. Therefore Hesperus is now said to “change his customary reins again.”

Finally, among philosophers, Hesperus or Venus is a planet which, carried through the fluid heaven as straw is swept along through water, moves sometimes above and sometimes below the sun. Borrowing the sun’s light and reflecting it, it undergoes nearly the same changes of illumination as the moon. [Col. 0636A] Philosophers agree that this star sometimes precedes the rising sun and sometimes follows the setting sun, but they explain this differently according to the different systems of the universe, which there is no time to discuss.

It is therefore agreed by all that Hesperus follows the setting sun. Hence he is rightly said now to lead the cold stars at the beginning of night, or to lead the nocturnal stars, under whose rule the earth grows cold. It is likewise agreed that Lucifer, which is the same star as Hesperus, precedes the rising sun. Hence he is most aptly said to change his customary reins again at the rising of Phoebus, or the sun. Yet he is pale because of the greater light of the rising sun.]

> O creator of the star-bearing sphere,  
> Who rests upon an everlasting throne,  
> **64** You turn the heavens with swift rotation  
> And compel the stars to submit to law,  
> [5] So that now, shining with a full horn  
> And meeting the flames of her brother in their entirety,  
> The moon conceals the lesser stars;

14. **“You, through the cold of winter that lets the leaves fall.”** Third, the subject is the days, whose principal changes consist in this: they are shorter in winter and longer in summer. A day is the time during which the sun proceeds above our horizon from rising to setting. Night, opposed to day, is the time during which the same sun moves below our horizon from setting to rising.

Since the sun does not always circle the earth at an equal distance from the two poles, but sometimes approaches the south more closely and sometimes the north, following the circle called the zodiac, the day is therefore sometimes shorter and sometimes longer. It is shorter when the sun approaches the south, which happens from the autumnal equinox to the winter solstice—that is, from September 23 to December 22. This period is commonly called *bruma*, because of the shortness of the days, as Vossius says after Varro and Festus. It is cold because of the sun’s withdrawal and strips the trees of their leaves. Hence the phrase: “You, through the cold of winter that lets the leaves fall, shorten the light by a briefer duration.”

The day is longer when the sun approaches the north, which happens from the spring equinox to the summer solstice, namely from March 21 to June 22. At that time warm summer begins and the nights are therefore very short. Hence the poem says: “When hot summer has arrived, you divide the swift hours of night.” Thus Ovid, *Tristia* V.11:

> The solstice takes nothing from my nights,  
> Nor does winter make my days narrow.

Two points may be observed here. First, although the word *frondiflua* was not much used among ancient authors, it is nevertheless perfectly suited to express what Virgil described more fully in *Aeneid* VI, line 309:

> How many leaves in the woods, at the first cold of autumn,  
> Fall loosened to the ground.

Second, the hours of which either a shorter day or a shorter night is composed are called swift or ready because hours are of two kinds: some equal, others unequal among themselves. Equal hours are those which, in winter or summer, consist, as they say, always of sixty equal minutes. By this reckoning, we say that the sun circles the whole earth in twenty-four hours, returning from one point of heaven to the same point. Unequal hours, however, are those which, being only a twelfth part of either day or night, must grow and diminish as the days or nights lengthen and shorten.

18. **“Your power governs the changing year.”** Fourth, the subject is the seasons themselves, whose changes consist in this: just as spring restores the leaves that autumn removed, so summer ripens the crops whose seeds winter saw sown. The first two seasons are signified by the winds that commonly rule at those times: autumn by the north wind and spring by the west wind. The other two seasons are represented by heavenly signs: winter by Arcturus and summer by Sirius.

Boreas is called *ἀπὸ τῆς βοῆς* (“from the cry”), because it is turbulent and noisy. Among those who recognized only eight winds—one blowing from the south, one from the north, three from the east, and as many from the west—it was regarded as an easterly wind. Among those who posited twelve or more winds, it is northern. Because the sun approaches the north during summer, which is followed by autumn, this wind commonly blows during autumn. Thus the storms that then arise and the trees’ loss of leaves may be attributed to it. Hence Virgil, *Georgics* I, line 311:

> Why should I speak of autumn’s storms and stars?

Zephyrus is called as though from *ζωηφόρος* or *τὸ ζῆν φέρων*, “bringing life,” because plants revive, sprout, and flourish under it. Hence Pliny calls it “the generative breath of the world.” It is a wind blowing from the equinoctial west. “This,” says Pliny, *Natural History* XVIII.34, “begins spring and opens the earth, healthful with a slight chill.” It gives permission to prune vines, tend crops, plant trees, graft fruit trees, and care for olive trees; by its breath it exercises a nourishing influence. Therefore among the Latins it is called *favonius*, from *favere*, “to favor,” because it favors generation. Lucretius, *On the Nature of Things* III:

> The generative breeze of Favonius flourishes.

And Catullus, in the poem *On the Marriage of Peleus and Thetis*:

> Along whose riverbanks  
> The fertile breeze of warm Favonius produces flowers.

Arcturus, as though *ἄρκτου οὐρά*, “the bear’s tail,” is a star in the constellation Bootes, near the tail of the Great Bear. They observe that this star, at its rising, accompanies the rising sun from October onward, when the earth commonly warms the seeds placed in her bosom. Hence the poem says: “The seeds that Arcturus saw.” Thus Virgil, *Georgics* I, line 67:

> But if the earth is not fertile beneath Arcturus himself,  
> It will be enough to suspend it in a shallow furrow.

And at line 204:

> Moreover, for us the stars of Arcturus  
> And the days of the Kids must be observed.

Finally, Seirius—or, as others write, Sirius—is so called from *σείρω*, “I dry.” Hence the sun too, according to Suidas, is called *σεὶρ*. It is the brightest star in the mouth of the Great Dog, and at its rising accompanies the rising sun from July onward, when the ripe grain seems to dry out. Because this star appears in the mouth of the Great Dog, it is commonly called the Dog Star. But because the sun, whose rising it accompanies, then scorches the earth with its greater heat, this star is accused of producing such heat, and poets call Sirius “heat-bringing.” Thus our author says: “Sirius burns the tall crops.” So Virgil, *Georgics* IV, lines 425–428:

> Now swift Sirius burned the thirsty Indians  
> In heaven, and the fiery sun had drained  
> The middle region of the world; the grasses dried,  
> And the hollow rivers, their channels dry, were baked by the heated rays.

And *Aeneid* III, line 14:

> Then Sirius began to scorch the barren fields;  
> The grasses dried, and the sickly crop refused food.

Gassendi rightly observes, however, that the Dog Star is falsely accused of causing such heat—just as gray hair would falsely be accused of the death suffered in old age by the accusers of chaste Susanna. Indeed, the Dog Star is so far from being the cause of this heat that among peoples over whom it appears during our summer, the cold is actually more intense. Hence, says that same philosopher, those peoples could more justly accuse the Dog Star of their cold than we of our heat. If the heavenly power which the barbarians call “influence” really produced the effect commonly attributed to it, it would in fact produce it.]

> Now, pale with a dark horn,  
> Nearer to Phoebus, let her lights fail.  
> [10] **65** And he who at the beginning of night  
> Leads the cold rising of Hesperus,  
> Let him again change his customary reins,  
> Lucifer pale at Phoebus’s rising.

23. **“Nothing is released from the ancient law.”** The bodies mentioned above, by whose example judgment must be made concerning the rest, are so held within definite laws that we now see them behaving exactly as we read that they behaved among our ancestors. God governs all these things toward a definite end; or, as Wisdom 8 says, “He reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly.”

26. **“You alone reject the actions of human beings.”** The meaning is: although all other things are administered by divine providence so that each change corresponds to its proper alternation, human beings alone seem to have been abandoned by God, so that human affairs appear to be managed rashly and by chance. For prosperity ought to belong to the good and adversity to the wicked, yet adversity comes to the good and prosperity to the wicked. Hence some doubt divine providence. Claudian, *Against Rufinus* I, line 1:

> Often the thought has led my mind into doubt:  
> Do the gods above care for the earth, or is there no ruler,  
> And do mortal things flow by implanted chance?

[Col. 0638D] Hence our author: “For why does slippery Fortune turn about such great changes?” Fortune was discussed in Meter 1.

29. **“The harmful punishment owed to crime presses upon the innocent.”** Just as God, the supreme governor of all things, is infinitely just, so punishments are owed to each vice, by God’s determination. Because these punishments harm either body or mind, they are called harmful penalties. Such a penalty presses upon the innocent insofar as, subjected to the authority of the guilty, they suffer injustice from them, so that their virtue lies hidden, as it were, beneath the punishment owed to vice. Thus Claudian in the passage cited:

> But when I saw human affairs rolled in such great darkness,  
> And the guilty flourishing for a long time  
> While the pious were tormented, religion again  
> Fell, shaken to its foundations.

31. **“Perverse morals.”** Here the mode is named for the thing modified. It is not so much perverse morals themselves as the people affected by perverse morals who sit upon a lofty throne, adorned, naturally, with the highest dignities.]

> May gentle Zephyrus restore them, leafy;  
> And the seeds that Arcturus saw,  
> May Sirius burn the tall crops.  
> **68** Nothing released from the ancient law  
> Leaves the work of its proper station,  
> [25] Governing all things toward a definite end;  
> [Col. 0638A] You alone reject the actions of human beings  
> You refuse, O ruler, to restrain them by a fitting rule.  
> For why does slippery Fortune turn about  
> Such great changes? The harmful punishment  
> [30] Owed to crime presses upon the innocent.  
> **69** But wicked men sit upon a lofty  
> [Col. 0639A] [Col. 0639B]

32. **“And they trample sacred necks.”** Here likewise a part is placed for the whole: it is human beings who commit wrongdoing who trample holy people, rather than merely their necks. But this manner of speaking, like the preceding one, is especially common among poets.

33. **“In an unjust reversal.”** It seems unjust that the good are oppressed by the wicked. We call that a “turn” which we do or suffer by turns; hence *vicissim* (“in turn”) and *vicarius* (“substitute,” “deputy”).

34. **“Bright virtue lies hidden, buried in obscure darkness.”** It seems paradoxical that bright virtue should lie hidden in obscure darkness. These ideas can nevertheless be reconciled if virtue is obscure to other human beings but bright both to the mind of the person who practices it and to God, who infused virtue into that mind. Thus Cicero says, *For Sestius*: “Virtue is tranquil in the storm, and shines in darkness; driven from its place, it nevertheless remains and clings to its country, and shines by itself forever, never growing dull through the stains of others.”

[Col. 0639C] 35. **“And the just man bore the crime of the wicked.”** Here “crime” does not mean guilt, since guilt belongs only to the guilty, but rather infamy, which ought to follow guilt just as honor follows virtue. Thus Cicero, in *Against Verres*, says that an imperial reputation is overwhelmed by charges of avarice. In general, *crimen* is anything by which someone is distinguished or separated from others; hence *discrimen*. Since this infamy ought to belong to the wicked, it is now said to belong to the good. The poet adds the means by which the guilty commonly afflict others—perjury, fraud, and force—and says that these harm the guilty themselves not at all.

37. **“Perjuries do not harm.”** First, perjury is either swearing falsely or failing to do what one has sworn in accordance with one’s sincere intention. Hence, according to Cicero, in perjury faith and the oath are disregarded. According to the same author, *On the Laws* II, perjury has its own punishment: divine punishment is destruction, human punishment is disgrace. Yet, says Boethius, perjuries harm the guilty not at all—so unjust are the reversals of Fortune.

[Col. 0639D] 37. **“Fraud does not harm them.”** Second, fraud is deceitful flattery; hence it is now said to be “adorned with lying color.” Like a fox, a person tries to obtain by lying deeds or words what he cannot obtain by force. The ancients considered this worthy of greater hatred and therefore deserving of its own punishment. Nevertheless, says Boethius, the order of things seems so inverted that fraud does not harm the fraudulent themselves.

39. **“When it pleased them to use their strength.”** “Force,” says the Roman orator in *For Caecina*, “is that which compels us, under threat of danger, either to withdraw from somewhere or prevents us from approaching.” This is even more contrary to reason because, when the order of things is reversed, those to whom obedience is owed are also subjected to force, as the poem now says: “Whom countless peoples fear, they rejoice to subject—the highest kings.” Therefore this crime ought not to go unpunished, although the preceding guilty persons seem to suffer no harm.

42. **“O now look upon the wretched earth.”** The poet returns to God, with whom the poem began, and asks him to look upon the wretched earth inhabited by human beings, who endure things unworthy of them.

43. **“Who bind together the covenants of things.”** Namely, the changes of the natural causes and effects mentioned above.

44. **“Human beings, no insignificant portion of so great a work.”** A human being is indeed a part of the things created by God, since he could come neither from himself nor from nothing. Yet the human being is no insignificant part because he can think even of things that cannot themselves be thought.

45. **“We are shaken upon the sea of Fortune.”** Among poets as among orators, *salum* means the sea, since the sea contains much salty flavor. Hence *salacia* and *venilia* are commonly used by poets to signify the sea’s ebbings and flowings, by which the Ocean rises and falls twice each day. *Salacia* are the waves of the sea returning from the shore toward the open sea; *venilia* are the waves of the same sea coming from the deep toward the shore. The sea of Fortune is aptly named, both because other authors observe that, as from the sea, many good and bad things come from Fortune, though most inconsistently, and especially because our author is here experiencing the bitter reversals of Fortune.

46. **“Ruler, restrain the rushing waves.”** That is, the violent movements of Fortune, which is like a raging sea.

47. **“By the covenant with which you govern heaven, make the earth firm.”** Govern human beings so that, just as in heaven and in your other works each change corresponds to its proper alternation, so among human beings rewards may be given to virtues and punishments to vices.]

## 71. PROSE V

**Argument.**—Philosophy, partly disagreeing and partly agreeing with Boethius, reproves him for having called himself an exile and complained of adverse Fortune; but she praises him for having acted as well as he spoke, while meanwhile seeking a remedy for calming his disturbances.

When, after my continuous lament, I had [Note: “I had babbled foolishly.” Others read *delatravi* or *dilatravi*; but the word we use is so well suited to signify the thought Boethius now has concerning the matters mentioned above, and could so easily have been changed into the common readings because of similar pronunciation, that these seem to have obliterated it, as will be clear to an attentive reader. Festus says, of course, that *deblaterare* means “to speak foolishly,” for the Greeks call fools βλάκας (*blakas*). Hence, says Aulus Gellius, *blaterones* are men who fling themselves into words—troublesome talkers who, relying on no weight of subject matter, stream forth in moist and slipping words. The Normans call them *bavards*, “chatterers,” and not ineptly: for those who speak so precipitately, like infants, commonly sprinkle their cheeks and garments with flowing saliva.] babbled foolishly, [Note: “She with a calm expression.”] she—Philosophy, naturally, since she is the ruler of all things—[Note: “Philosophy.”] with a calm expression and unmoved by any of my complaints, [Note: Philosophy, of course, since she is the ruler of all things. Hence, according to Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* IV, the wise man or philosopher is one who, through moderation and constancy, is tranquil in mind and at peace with himself: neither wasting away through troubles, nor broken by fear, nor burning with desire as he thirsts for something, nor melting away in restless, frivolous exhilaration.] [Note: “When she had seen you sad and weeping.”] said:

“When I had seen you sad and weeping, I immediately recognized you as wretched, [Note: “I recognized you as wretched.”] [Note: *Miser*, as Cujas and many others hold, is derived from μισῶ (*misō*), “I hate,” because a wretched condition is hateful to everyone. Philosophy could have recognized Boethius’s wretched condition from the tears and sadness mentioned above, for these are the companions of misery.] and as an exile. [Note: “An exile.”] An exile—or, as the ancients read, *exsol*—is one who has been driven from his soil and lives apart from it. Hence they say that one should write *exsul*, not *exul*; but this is of little importance, since the letter *x* is composed of *c* and *s*.

“Philosophy recognized your exile not merely from your sadness and tears. These signify misery rather than exile in particular, since any other misery could be indicated by them; she recognized it from the very place in which you were weeping. Since that place was connected with Boethius, it could be left unmentioned by the author and easily understood by the reader.

“Yet since exile means deprivation of one’s homeland, and since a human being may be said to have one homeland of the body and another of the mind, exile can be understood not only of bodies expelled from their native soil but also of minds removed from heaven—or rather, from God. Thus, although Boethius in the poems mentioned above spoke only of the former exile, Philosophy takes the opportunity to speak of the latter as well. By pretending not to know, she intimates that his exile is not so distant: the human mind, whatever region of the earth it inhabits, is neither farther from nor nearer to its heavenly homeland because of that.

“Anaxagoras gave an excellent answer when asked whether he had no concern for his homeland. Pointing toward heaven, he said: ‘I have concern for my homeland, and indeed the greatest concern.’ Saint Paul most aptly reminds us in 2 Corinthians 5 that we have an eternal dwelling in heaven, a truth very familiar among Christians.

“Therefore no one is expelled from this homeland. You have not indeed been driven far from your homeland, for this is the distinction between the homeland of the body and that of the mind: even unwillingly, we can be expelled from the homeland of the body; but from the homeland of the mind—namely, from heaven, or rather from God—we withdraw only willingly. For toward it we strive; there we dwell through the affections of the mind, over which we have authority.

“Nevertheless, we sometimes stray from our heavenly homeland; and you have strayed insofar as our free will falls away from the divine will. The divine will, as it is the first cause of all things, is likewise the first rule of human actions. Therefore, if you prefer to be thought of as driven out, you drove yourself out—by your own will and consent, of which you are so much the master that no one could ever lawfully do this to you. So great is human freedom of mind that it cannot be contaminated by error or vice, by which we are barred from our heavenly homeland, unless it freely wills this itself.”

“I recognized you as an exile. But how distant that exile was, I did not know, unless your speech had betrayed it. Yet you have not been driven far from your homeland; you have strayed. But if you prefer to be thought driven out, you yourself rather drove yourself out. For no one could ever have been permitted to do that to you. [Note: “No one could have expelled you.”]

“If, then, you remember the homeland from which you originated—[Note: “Remember what homeland you come from.”]” The discourse begun concerning the heavenly homeland is continued. Boethius need only remember this homeland, since, whether instructed by God, by his own efforts, or even with the assistance of teachers, he had known for many years that heaven was his homeland. This notion, however, may have been obscured by his affections; hence he needed not so much to learn it for the first time as to remember it. [Note: “Remember the homeland from which you originated.”]

“Your homeland is not governed by the rule of the multitude, as Athens once was, but by that of this one.” [Note: “Your homeland is not ruled by the government of the multitude, as Athens once was, but by that of this one.”] [Note: “Not in the manner of the Athenians.”]

There are three modes of governing a homeland, or three forms of rule: monarchy, the government of the aristocracy, and popular government. For, as Cornelius Tacitus says in Book 11, “all nations and cities are ruled either by the people, by the leading men, or by individuals.” The Athenians first received their laws from the aristocrats and later from the people; hence they are said not only to have rejoiced in expelling deserving citizens but at times even to have compelled them to die.

But our heavenly homeland is governed neither by the people nor by aristocrats, but only by one ruler. As Homer says in the *Iliad*:

> There is one ruler,  
> one king.

> Let there be one master,  
> one ruler.

[Col. 0642C] Just as God alone is the creator of the human mind, so God alone is the governor of that mind. Therefore God is called in 1 Timothy 6, and elsewhere, “King of kings and Lord of lords.”

That supreme King rejoices in the multitude of his citizens. For this reason he created the human race and restored it, when lost, through the death of his only-begotten Son. Hence Christ says in John 10: “I have other sheep, which are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock and one shepherd.”

That same supreme King does not rejoice in the expulsion of citizens. For in 1 Timothy 2: “God our Savior wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” “As I live,” says the Lord God in Ezekiel 33, “I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live. Turn, turn from your evil ways; why will you die, house of Israel?”

Finally, to be ruled by the will of this highest King is perfect freedom; but this seems to require a somewhat longer interpretation.

“[Note: “There is one lord, one king.”] It is not governed, as Athens once was, by the rule of the multitude, but [Note: “There is one lord, one king.”] there is one lord, one king, who rejoices in the multitude of his citizens, not in their expulsion.” [Note: “To be guided by his reins and obey justice is perfect freedom.”]

Freedom, says Tully in *On Duties* I and in *Paradoxes* 5, “is the power to live as you wish”—not only externally, that is, with respect to bodily movements, but also internally, namely, with respect to the thoughts of the mind.

A human being can will, and therefore live, in two ways. First, by following the divine will, which, as the first cause, is likewise the first rule of our will. This is the highest freedom, which exists in us while we wish to be happy; it existed in Christ when, as a wayfarer, he fulfilled the commands of the eternal Father; and it will exist in all the blessed, who will love God by an eternal and happy necessity.

The second way is by turning aside from the divine will, that is, by sinning. This is the lowest freedom, which we would wish to exchange for the happy necessity of always loving God.

Since we can follow the divine will both by avoiding evil and by doing good, according to Psalm 36: “Turn away from evil and do good,” the highest freedom of a human being consists not only in turning away from evil, or being guided by God’s reins, but also in doing good, or obeying divine justice—namely, by observing the law of God, which commands what is honorable and prohibits its opposites. “The law of the Lord,” says Psalm 18, “is blameless, restoring the soul; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to the simple; the precepts of the Lord are right.” [Note: “To be guided by reins, that is, by authority.”] [Note: “By the laws.”]

“To be guided by its reins [Note: “By reins, that is, by authority.”] and to obey justice [Note: “The laws.”] is perfect freedom.

“Do you not know the most ancient law of your city?” [Note: “The most ancient law of your city.”] Philosophy uses the word *city* in a double sense, so that it can refer both to Rome and to heaven, from which Boethius originated. The laws of ancient Rome condemned no one to exile. Hence Cicero says in his speech *For Caecina*: “Exile is not a punishment but a refuge and harbor from punishment; for those who wish to escape some penalty or calamity turn there alone—that is, they change their dwelling and place. Therefore no law of ours will be found, as among other states, by which any wrongdoing has been punished with exile.”

The laws of the heavenly homeland much less condemn anyone to exile. Whoever wishes to remain within the boundaries of the heavenly kingdom and obey its supreme King will never be an exile there, since no one is barred from that kingdom except through a voluntary attachment to mortal and contrary things. Saint Augustine frequently speaks of the heavenly city in the book entitled *The City of God.”

“Do you not know the most ancient law of your city—[Note: “Of Rome and heaven.”] the law by which it was established that no one has the right to be an exile who prefers to establish his dwelling in it? For [Note: “Who is enclosed within its rampart and defense.”] whoever is enclosed within its rampart and defense has no fear of deserving to be an exile.”

A rampart is a wall of earth heaped along the edge of a ditch and strengthened with rows of stakes or posts. A defense, generally speaking, is any protection of a camp by which access is barred to the enemy. Here these terms are understood not only literally, insofar as they refer to the homeland of the body, but also metaphorically, insofar as they can refer to the heavenly homeland of the mind.

Since Boethius was a most Christian man, when he heard of the rampart of the heavenly city he could understand Christ crucified, and by its defense the grace Christ obtained for us by his death. Whoever is protected by this defense need not fear that he will deserve to be an exile from the heavenly homeland.

Saint Paul speaks in much the same way in Ephesians 6: “Be strong in the Lord and in the power of his might. Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.” [Note: “By its protection.”]

“But whoever ceases to wish to inhabit it likewise ceases to deserve it.” [Note: “Whoever ceases to wish to inhabit it also ceases to deserve it.”] For we inhabit and deserve the heavenly homeland only by a good will. “He possesses everything,” says Saint Augustine in Book 50 of his *Homilies*, Homily 8, “who has a good will. It alone can suffice, even if other things are absent. But if it alone is absent, whatever else one may possess is of no benefit. It alone suffices if it is present; all other things are useless if charity alone is absent.” [Note: “Therefore.”]

Having mentioned the two homelands and consequently the two exiles, and having established the distinction among all these matters, Philosophy, intending to answer all the complaints Boethius had made in Prose 4 of this book, now draws certain excellent conclusions.

“Therefore—[Note: “It is not so much the appearance of this place as your appearance that moves me.”]—I am not so much moved by the appearance of this place [Note: “Ticinum, where you say you are in exile.”] as by your appearance.”

I. Boethius had asked: “Does not the very appearance of this place move you?” Philosophy replies: “Not so much as your appearance,” in which, as in a mirror, the downfall of your mind can be seen. Philosophy is not as concerned with an earthly homeland as with the heavenly homeland, nor as concerned with the exile of the body as with that of the mind from its native soil.

“Nor do I seek the library’s [Note: “Nor the library in preference.”] walls adorned with ivory and glass [Note: “Nor the library in preference.”] so much as the dwelling of your mind. In it I placed not books but what gives books their value—the doctrines of my philosophy.” [Note: “Philosophical opinions.”]

II. Boethius had asked: “Is this the library which you yourself had chosen as the most secure seat for yourself in my household?” Philosophy replies: “I seek not so much the library as the adornments of your mind, namely, philosophical doctrines.”

In former times powerful men were accustomed to adorn their houses with gold, ivory, or at least glass, for the same purpose for which many now strive to have magnificent houses, prepare lavish banquets, and surround themselves with a large crowd of attendants: namely, to arouse in others admiration, honor, fear, and other such thoughts.

Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* I, verse 729:

> A din arises through the halls, and they roll their voices  
> through the spacious atria; lamps hang from golden ceilings,  
> burning, and torches overcome the night with their flames.

So too Horace, *Odes* II.18, distinguishes himself from the powerful:

> Neither ivory nor a golden  
> coffered ceiling shines in my house.

“And you, certainly—[Note: “Concerning your services to the common good.”]—have said too little about your services to the common good in proportion to the multitude of your achievements.” [Note: “By you.”]

III. Boethius had said that nothing except concern for the common good of all had impelled him toward public office. “You,” he says, “and God, who implanted you in the minds of the wise, are witnesses that I undertook no office except from concern for the common good of all.” Philosophy, in reply, not only acknowledges this but magnifies it: “You have spoken truly of your services to the common good, but in proportion to the multitude of your deeds you have said little about them.”

“You have recalled matters known to all concerning the honorableness or falsity of the charges brought against you.” [Note: “Of the things laid to your charge, whether honorable or false.”]

IV. Boethius had added that the charges brought against him were partly honorable and partly false. The honorable charge was that he had defended and freed an innocent Senate accused of treason: “They say,” he writes, “that I wished the Senate to be safe.” The false charge was that he practiced magical arts: “They falsely alleged,” he says, “that through ambition for office I had polluted my conscience with sacrilege.” Philosophy replies that no one is unaware of either the honorable or the false charges: “You have recalled matters known to all.”

“Concerning the crimes and frauds of the informers, you rightly thought it best to touch briefly upon them, since they are celebrated more fully and accurately by the speech of the people, who recognize everything.” [Note: “More concisely.”] [Note: “Of those who consider everything.”]

V. Boethius had said that he had been unjustly denounced by Basilius, Opilio, and Gaudentius. The first had been compelled to inform by financial necessity; the other two, condemned to exile for countless frauds, were defending themselves by taking refuge in sacred buildings. Philosophy replies that it was right to touch on these matters briefly, since the people, who recognize everything better and more fully, celebrate them in their speech.

For we communicate not only by words but also by nods, gestures, and other such accompaniments of human speech; even the silence of the people sometimes eloquently signifies more than much loquacity, although the people were not lacking in words about these matters.

“You also vehemently reproved the unjust action of the Senate.” [Note: “The Senate’s unjust deed.”]

VI. Boethius had remembered that the Senate had displayed such ingratitude that it issued decrees against him. “By its decrees against me,” he said, “it had made this outrage possible.” Philosophy replies and approves that Boethius had also vehemently reproved the Senate’s unjust action.

“You also grieved over the charge brought against us.” [Note: “The accusation against us.”]

VII. Boethius had complained that the very offense of which he was accused was being attributed to Philosophy herself: “They seek proof from you of so great a crime,” he said, “and by this very fact we will seem to have been accomplices in the offense, because we have been imbued with your teachings and formed by your character.” Philosophy, remembering Boethius’s affection toward her, approves the complaint: “You also grieved over the charge brought against us.”

“You also lamented the damage done to your reputation.” [Note: “The loss of your damaged reputation.”]

VIII. Boethius had added that he had undeservedly lost a good reputation among many people: “For,” he said, “the judgment of the majority looks not to the merits of things but to the outcome of Fortune.” Philosophy acknowledges that this too happened undeservedly.

“You lamented the injury done to your reputation.” [Note: “To your reputation.”]

IX. Boethius had complained especially of Fortune’s injustice, because she did not return rewards proportionate to merit: “I seem to see,” he said, “the wicked workshops of criminals overflowing with joy and gladness, while the innocent are deprived not only of security but even of defense itself.” Therefore Boethius asked God in carefully composed verse to rule the earth with the same peace with which he rules heaven. The Muse is now called “raging,” because she seems not even to spare God himself, saying in the fifth meter of this book:

> Governing all things toward a fixed end,  
> you alone refuse to restrain human actions  
> by a fitting measure, O ruler.

Philosophy will answer these complaints in what follows. But Boethius’s mind must first be stripped of certain prejudices. These prejudices arise from the emotions—for example, pain, anger, grief, and others—and some remedy must therefore be applied to them.

“Since,” says Philosophy, “a very great tumult of emotions has settled upon you, and pain, anger, and grief pull you in different directions, in your present state of mind you are not yet ready for stronger remedies.”

“Your last grief against Fortune has flared up, and you have complained that rewards are not weighed out according to merit. [Note: “It flared up.”] Finally, in the last part of the raging Muse, you offered prayers that, just as peace rules heaven, it might also rule the earth. But since a very great tumult of emotions has settled upon you, and pain, anger, and grief pull you in different directions, in your present state of mind stronger remedies have not yet touched you. [Note: “Move you.”]

“Therefore we shall use milder remedies for a while.” [Note: “We shall use gentler remedies.”]

This is an excellent comparison drawn from bodily conditions. Just as a swelling of the body occurs when fluids remain at some place and, hardening the body there, inflate it—and all the more as a greater quantity of fluids flows to that place and changes movement into rest—so a swelling of the mind occurs when emotions implanted there inflate the mind as though by hardening it, and all the more as a greater quantity of disturbances flows to the same place and remains there.

Thus, just as a bodily swelling is not removed until the affected part has been reduced to a certain softness by gentle remedies and the fluids mentioned above have been carried away by a stronger movement of the bodily substances involved, so the mind is not freed from such a mass of disturbances until, gradually softened by arguments as they increase, it drives away those affections through the greater power of holy thoughts. This is the work of a prudent physician.

“We shall for a little while use gentler remedies, so that what has hardened into a swelling through the influx of disturbances may become soft under a gentler touch and receive the force of a sharper medicine.”

## 77. METER VI

[Note: This meter is commonly said to have been named after its inventor, Glycon. It is a poem consisting of a single kind of verse, each line being a trimeter containing one spondee and two dactylic feet.]

**Argument.**—Continuing the discourse she has begun, Philosophy proves that Boethius’s mind cannot yet be treated with stronger remedies because particular times have been divinely prescribed for particular things—for the harvest, flowers, and grape-gathering.

[Note: When the heavenly sign of Cancer burns with destructive solar light, let the person who entrusted abundant seed to barren furrows, deceived by the promise of Ceres, the divine power of grain, make his way to the acorn-bearing oaks. Never should you enter a beautiful forest to gather violets when the field, disturbed by cruel north winds, has bristled with its harsh sound. Nor should you attempt in spring to tie or prune the vines with eager hand, if you wish to enjoy grapes; for Bacchus has bestowed these gifts in autumn rather than in spring. God marks out every moment, fitting its proper time to each gift, and does not allow the order he himself established to be disturbed. Therefore whatever abandons the prescribed order through inconsiderate haste does not achieve pleasant results.]

### 2. “When the constellation of Cancer burns.”

I. The example of the harvest proves that each thing has a time suited to it, so that, when crops fail, one may flee to acorns.

Cancer here is one of the twelve signs of the zodiac, which are usually expressed in these verses:

> Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo;  
> Libra, Scorpio, Archer, Goat, Water-Bearer, Pisces.

The sun is said to pass through one of these each month as it completes its annual course. Cancer occupies that part of the heavens which the sun reaches when it has moved northward at the end of June. It then gives us the longest day of summer, after which, proceeding no farther north, the sun begins to turn southward. Hence the circle which astronomers place as passing through the first degree of this sign is called the Tropic of Cancer, where the summer solstice occurs. Thus Manilius, Book 3:

> When Phoebus was with the constellation of Cancer,  
> it was the solstice, and he turned in the highest Olympus.

This constellation is now said to “burn” because the earth is then affected by the greatest movement or heat of heavenly fire. Thus Horace, *Epodes* 11:

> But if liberated bile burns within my breast.

It is also called “heavy with Phoebus’s rays,” because when the sun enters it the heat can scarcely be endured by the body; and also by the mind, because it is said immediately to bring sterility by scorching the crops.

Silius, Book 1:

> Libya, subjected to the summer-bearing Cancer, is tormented.

Anything generally is called “heavy” that can scarcely be endured, whether by body or mind; examples are readily available to everyone.

### 4. “He entrusted seed to the furrows.”

A furrow, *un sillon*—according to Varro’s judgment—is called *sulcus* from *sustollo*, “to lift up,” because the plowshare lifts up the earth; similarly *arvum* and *aratio* come from *aro*, “to plow.” A ridge, *le rayon sur lequel on sème*, is so called because the earth is extended or thrown up on both sides.

Whatever may be thought of these interpretations of the names, poets say that the farmer who sows “entrusts seed,” or the hope of the year, to the furrows or earth. Thus, if the seed disappears before the harvest through unfavorable weather, one may say that he has been deceived in Ceres’s promise.

So Virgil, *Georgics* II, verse 221:

> Before the daughters of Atlas have hidden themselves from you in the East,  
> and the Cretan star has withdrawn from the burning crown,  
> before you entrust the seed owed to the furrows,  
> before you hasten to commit the hope of the year to unwilling earth.  
> Many began before Maia’s setting,  
> but the expected crop deceived them with empty ears.

So Tibullus, Book 2, final elegy:

> The hope of the plowed furrows entrusts  
> seed which the field will return with great interest.

Thus, because of the excessive heat of burning Cancer, whoever has entrusted abundant seed to failing furrows—[Note: “Deceived in Ceres’s promise.”]—

> When Cancer’s constellation, heavy  
> with Phoebus’s rays, burns,  
> then whoever has entrusted abundant  
> seed to unyielding furrows,

### 5. “Deceived in Ceres’s promise.”

Ceres, in the poets, is the daughter of Saturn and Ops, by whom Jupiter is said to have fathered Proserpina. Pluto later carried off Ceres’s daughter; therefore Ceres, having lit torches on Mount Etna, traveled through the whole world in search of her daughter.

During that laborious journey she taught Triptolemus, son of the king of Eleusis, the method of sowing seed. He in turn traveled throughout the world and communicated the same art to other human beings.

For philosophers, however, if we believe Tully in Book 2 of *On the Nature of the Gods*, Ceres is nothing other than the earth itself. She is so called either from *gero*, “to bear,” with a change of letter, because she bears crops, or from “creating,” as the creator of crops. Whoever considers this more attentively will discover why the earth is called the daughter of Saturn and Ops, and why, made fertile by Jupiter, she is said to have borne Proserpina, later carried off by Pluto. But these matters do not belong to our present purpose.

### 6. “Let him go to the oaks.”

That is, to the acorn-bearing oaks, as to the earliest nurses of humankind. The oak is a tree known to everyone. It is said to have supplied food to certain peoples before crops were discovered. Hence Virgil, *Georgics* I, verse 159:

> And with the shaken oak you will soothe hunger in the forests.

Since the acorn, the fruit of this tree, does not ripen until after the harvest of grain, the two have been bound to different seasons, so that if the expected crop disappoints you, you may hope for food from the oaks, formerly rich in acorns. Thus, by the example of the harvest, it is proved that particular things have particular times, divinely prescribed.

### 7. “Never seek the purple forest.”

II. The example of flowers likewise proves that each thing has an appropriate time. The meaning is that flowers, which ordinarily grow spontaneously and are here understood by the violets mentioned, should not be sought in winter, when the north winds rage, in a purple forest. Something must therefore be said about the purple forest, violets, and the north winds.

“Purple” derives from *purpura*. Purple is a kind of shellfish whose liquid was formerly used to dye garments. Since the ancient purple dye has long since disappeared, the resulting ambiguity of the word has led *purpureus* to signify blackness—as when Cicero calls a darkening sea purple, Ovid calls black grapes purple, and Homer calls black death purple; whiteness—as when Horace calls swans purple and Ovid calls snow purple; redness—as when all poets call cheeks and blood purple; bluish color—as when Virgil says that purple shines beneath black violets; and finally any color, or any beauty that can arise from it. For beauty, according to Tully in *Tusculan Disputations* IV, is a fitting form of the limbs together with a certain pleasantness of color.

Thus Virgil, *Eclogue* 9, verse 40:

> Here is purple spring; here the earth pours forth  
> varied flowers around the streams; here the white poplar  
> hangs over the cave, and the pliant vines weave canopies.

We believe that the forest is called purple here in this last sense.

There are two kinds of violets, as may be gathered from Pliny, Book 21, chapter 6. Some grow naturally, others by cultivation. The latter grow in gardens; the former also in forests. The passage concerns those which, as the same Pliny says, grow spontaneously in sunny and lean places, purple and with a broader leaf.

Finally, the north wind is the wind which, according to Pliny, Book 2, chapter 47, blows between the north and the summer sunrise, opposite the northwest wind. This wind is frequent in winter; hence Pliny calls winter “northern,” and poets describe it as bristling with rigid north winds. “With savage north winds” therefore signifies that violets should not be sought in the forests during winter. Thus, by the example of flowers, it is proved that each thing has a time suited to it.

### 11. “Nor seek with eager hand.”

III. The example of the grape harvest proves that particular things have particular times. Since the grape harvest occurs in autumn, it is useless at this season to seek to strip or bind spring shoots. These words distinguish the duties of spring and autumn.

First, in spring some shoots are cut off and others merely tied. While the farmer performs either task, he is said to “strip” or “gather,” for he gathers leaves as well, as in *Georgics* I, verse 305:

> Yet then it is also time to gather the acorns of the oak,  
> the berries of the laurel, the olive, and the bloody myrtle.

And he gathers branches that he binds, as in the same work, verse 317:

> And the farmer would already gather the barley from its fragile stalk.

This is said to be done “with an eager hand.” When someone strongly desires to carry out some action with a particular part of the body, that part is metaphorically called “eager.” Thus Cicero calls ears eager: “Demosthenes,” he says in *On the Orator*, “does not always fill my ears; they are so eager and receptive, and always desire something immense and infinite.” Horace likewise calls hands eager, *Odes* IV.7:

> All the things you give with a friendly spirit  
> will escape the eager hands of your heir.

Whoever gathers the spring shoots desires to gather them so intensely that he seems afraid he might stop gathering.

Autumn, on the other hand, is suited to gathering grapes. Thus poets commonly describe it, as Lucretius does in Book 1:

> Besides, why do we see the rose in spring,  
> grain in the heat, and vines pour forth their yield in autumn,  
> if not because, when the fixed seeds of things  
> have come together in their proper season,  
> whatever is created comes forth?

Hence Bacchus is said to have bestowed his gifts in autumn rather than in spring. Since Bacchus is regarded as the inventor of wine, wine is his gift; and wine ordinarily flows from pressed grapes not in spring but in autumn. Thus the harvest, flowers, and grape gathering alike show that particular times have been divinely prescribed for particular things.

> Deceived in Ceres’s promise,  
> let him go to the oak trees.  
> Never seek the purple forest  
> to gather violets,  
> when the field, bristling  
> and shrieking under savage north winds,  
> has grown rough.  
> Nor seek with eager hand  
> to gather the spring shoots,  
> if you wish to enjoy grapes;  
> in autumn rather, Bacchus  
> has bestowed his gifts.

### 16. “God marks out the times, fitting them to their proper functions.”

God is the first cause not only of other things but also of all the modes by which those things are rightly ordered, so that nothing happens except according to laws established by the divine will. Hence Ecclesiastes 3: “Everything has its season, and all things under heaven pass through their appointed intervals: a time to be born and a time to die; a time to plant and a time to uproot what has been planted,” and so forth.

Therefore God does not permit the alternations that he has restrained by his own most constant will to be mixed or disturbed. Thus Phaedrus, Book 1, Fable 2:

> When Athens flourished under equal laws,  
> insolent liberty threw the city into confusion.

From this philosophers were able to derive certain principles on which they could base demonstrations concerning the subject matter of philosophy.

### 20. “Thus whatever abandons the established order by a headlong path…”

There is one kind of headlong movement in the body and another in the mind. Bodily precipitancy, says Saint Thomas, *Summa* II–II, question 53, article 3, consists in a body’s reaching the lowest place from a higher one through a certain impulse of its own motion or of something impelling it, descending without order through the intermediate stages.

Mental precipitancy, however, is an inconsiderate judgment concerning what is unknown. The internal rule of true and certain judgment is evidence. Without it, if a philosopher delivers a verdict, he will either err or expose himself to the danger of error. Therefore whoever abandons the established order by a headlong path will not have happy outcomes.

The passage concerns only this latter kind of precipitancy, not the former. Philosophy seeks remedies by which Boethius’s afflicted mind may be cured. It is afflicted by error, which cannot be healed except by the contrary truth. Since the first impediment to discovering truth, and consequently the first cause of error, is precipitancy, Philosophy rightly advises that one must not rush ahead but begin first with gentler remedies.

> Bacchus has bestowed his gifts.  
> God marks out the times,  
> fitting them to their proper functions,  
> and does not permit the alternations  
> he himself has restrained  
> to be mixed.  
> Thus whatever by a headlong path  
> abandons the established order  
> has no happy outcome.

## 82. PROSE VI

**Argument.**—Philosophy, questioning Boethius, compels him to admit that he partly knows, and partly does not know, both God and himself. She therefore declares that she will henceforth use that light to dispel the darkness of his mind, so that progress may be made from known things to unknown, and from what is most firmly believed to what is not yet believed.

First, then, do you permit me, by means of a few brief questions, to reach and test the state of your mind, so that I may understand what method of treatment is appropriate for you?

**[Note: “By certain little questions.”]**  
**[Note: “By questions.”]** I. Philosophy questions Boethius. For a person who asks questions—unless he is rash and utterly mad, as Cicero says—attends mentally to the conception he has of the matter proposed and expresses the judgment on that subject of which he himself is conscious; hence the hearer can draw further conclusions. Thus Socrates, who may rightly be called the father of philosophy, as Tully says in *De finibus* II, was accustomed, by questioning and interrogating, to elicit the opinions of those with whom he debated, so that, if anything seemed appropriate, he could respond to what they had said. Since this practice was not retained by later philosophers, Arcesilaus revived it and established that those who wished to hear him should not ask questions about him, but should themselves state what they thought; when they had done so, he would reply.

By this method Philosophy now approaches and tests Boethius’ state of mind, recalling him, so to speak, to the first notions that he can experience within himself. Through these notions he may both be freed from his former error and introduced into a new truth. This is the method of treatment; Boethius himself, however, agrees to it: “Ask me,” he says, “whatever you wish, in whatever manner you choose; I shall answer.”

“First, then, do you permit me, by means of a few brief questions, to reach and test the state of your mind, so that I may understand what method of treatment is appropriate for you?”

“Ask me,” I replied, “whatever you wish, in whatever manner you choose; I shall answer.”

**[Note: Philosophy says.]**  
**[Note: “Ask whatever pleases you,” Boethius says; “I shall answer you.”]**

Then she said:

**83**

**[Note: “Does this world act by rash…”]** II. Philosophy compels Boethius to admit that he knows God in part, at least from seeing the order by which this world is governed. It is as when we recall a friend previously known after hearing his voice or seeing his handwriting—not because the voice or writing itself introduces the notion of that friend, but because these associated things awaken and renew the friend’s former idea as though it had been asleep.

So we remember God, already known by the natural light, when we see this world and observe the order by which all bodies likewise are governed. Hence Boethius says: “I could in no way suppose that things so certain are moved by random chance. I know that God the Creator presides over his work.” Since such an evident notion is the best standard of truth, or of true and certain judgment, Boethius adds that there has never been a day that drove him from the truth of this opinion. Hence, a little earlier—namely, in meter 5, verse 25—Boethius sang:

> Governing all things toward a certain end,  
> You reject only the deeds of human beings  
> From the proper restraint of your rule.

Philosophy therefore, astonished that Boethius should suddenly utter such a remarkable expression, strongly wonders why, while holding these principles, he should plunge into the darkness of error or hesitate, like a sick man, to proceed toward the true judgment concerning God’s providence over all things, including human affairs:

“Ah! I am greatly astonished that, placed in so healthy an opinion—namely, that God governs all other things—you should be sick, either by denying or at least doubting that God administers human affairs by his supreme providence.”

Indeed, when two or more judgments are joined by a close connection to some prior judgment, which can therefore function as a principle, it is astonishing that a person of outstanding intelligence, such as Boethius was, should grant the prior judgment and then call the later ones into doubt.
