“For how,” asks Tully in *De natura deorum* II, “is it consistent that, when you look at a sign or a painted tablet, you know that artistic skill was employed; when from a distance you see a ship’s course, you do not doubt that it is moved by reason and art; or when you contemplate a sundial, whether marked out or made from water, you understand that the hours are shown by art and not by chance—yet you suppose that the world, which contains both these very arts, their practitioners, and everything else, is without counsel and reason? If someone were to carry into Scythia or Britain the sphere recently made by our friend Posidonius, whose individual revolutions produce in the sun, the moon, and the five wandering stars what is produced in the heavens each day and night, who in that barbarous land would doubt that the sphere had been made according to perfect reason? Yet these people doubt concerning the world, from which everything arises and comes to be, whether it itself was produced by chance, necessity, reason, or divine intelligence. We think that Archimedes accomplished more in imitating the revolutions of the sphere than nature did in producing them, although the latter is far more perfect in many respects than the former imitation,” and so forth.

“What,” says Salvianus in Book IV of *On the Government of God*, “is more insane than for someone, while not denying God as the Creator of all things, to deny him as their governor; and, while admitting that he is their maker, to say that he neglects what he has made?”

“Do you think,” she said, “that this world is driven by rash and random accidents, or do you believe that it possesses some governance of reason?”

“No,” I replied, “I could in no way suppose that things so certain are moved by random chance. I know that God the Creator presides over his work, and there has never been a day that has driven me from the truth of this opinion.”

“That is so,” she said, “for you sang this very thing a little earlier and lamented that human beings alone are excluded from divine care. As for the rest, you were not troubled by the thought that they were governed by reason. Yet I am greatly astonished that, placed in so healthy an opinion, you should be sick.”

**84**

“But let us investigate more deeply.”

**[Note: “Let us examine it thoroughly.”]**  
**[Note: “I conjecture that something is lacking.”]** III. Philosophy compels Boethius to admit that he is partly ignorant of God. Our mind stands midway between God and our body and is shaped by certain thoughts received both from God and from the body.

From God it receives the first conception of truth and the first desire for happiness, so that God is the first teacher and director of the human mind. From the body it receives both sensation and disturbances, by which the mind is sometimes so blinded that it is led by them into errors and vices, which are voluntary diseases of the human mind.

These disturbances therefore possess such power—“force,” as it is now called—that they can indeed move a person from his proper place by obscuring the thoughts mentioned above, but they cannot tear him away altogether or uproot the entire human being by completely extinguishing those thoughts. For as long as the human mind is preserved by God, by whom it was first created and formed, it will continue to be affected both by the natural light and by the natural appetite.

Thus Boethius does not doubt that God governs the world, while that light remains active; but he does not perceive by what rudders or means the world is governed, because disturbances introduce darkness. He knows from where all things have proceeded and answers that it is God, since the aforesaid natural light is shining; but he does not remember what the end of things is, or toward what the intention of all nature tends, because disturbance, and especially grief, has weakened his memory.

Thus something is lacking—namely, a clear and distinct knowledge of God insofar as God is the ultimate end of all things, human affairs included. That end is of the greatest importance in morality, since whatever virtue or vice exists in us arises from the good or bad end for the sake of which we act. Through this lack, therefore, as through a gap opened in a wall, the disease of disturbances has entered Boethius’ soul.

That disease of the soul is nothing other than error and vice, which arise from these darknesses, or ignorance.

**[Note: Concerning the term “force,” see Prose 1, note 3, column 587.]**

“I conjecture that something is lacking. But tell me: since you do not doubt that God governs the world, do you also perceive by what rudders or means it is governed?”

“I scarcely understand the meaning of your question,” I replied, “much less can I answer what you ask.”

“Have I not correctly judged,” she said, “that something is lacking through which, as though a gap had opened in a wall, the disease of disturbances has crept into your soul? But tell me: do you remember what the end of things is, and toward what the intention of all nature tends?”

“I had heard it,” I replied, “but grief has weakened my memory.”

“But how do you know from where all things have proceeded?”

“I know,” I replied, “and I answered that it is God.”

“And how can it happen that, once the beginning is known, you are ignorant of what the end of things is?”

“Yet these are the habits of disturbances. They possess such force that they can move a person from his proper place, but they cannot tear him away or uproot him altogether.”

**85**

“But I should also like you to answer this: do you remember that you are a human being?”

**[Note: “Do you remember that you are a human being?”]** IV. Philosophy adds that Boethius knows himself only in part and recalls him to this remembrance of himself, since a person must first and foremost be convinced concerning himself. Hence the command of Apollo, which urges each person to know himself.

Boethius readily acknowledges that he is a rational and mortal animal. This definition of the human being belongs both to ancient and to more recent philosophers; nevertheless, as may be observed, it appears to be rejected by our author—or rather by Philosophy herself, who is now addressing Boethius.

The definition can indeed be criticized not only because it is exceedingly obscure, as becomes clear to anyone who considers it, but also because, if animals are said to think—as the defenders of this definition themselves say, since they hold that animals perceive and therefore know, not merely inadequately but adequately, in their terminology—the definition will also apply to animals.

For a dog, for example, is, by the admission of these philosophers, a mortal animal. If, as they maintain, the same dog knows by perceiving, it cannot be denied that it participates in reason and should consequently be called rational. For reasoning is a mode of knowing, and indeed a less perfect one than clear and distinct perception. Therefore God, who perceives clearly and distinctly, is denied to reason discursively.

Accordingly, if a dog is said to know but not to reason, canine cognition, being thereby made more like divine cognition, will be more perfect than human cognition—if this is asserted in defense of the definition in question.

But the same definition of the human being appears to be rejected by our author—or rather by Philosophy herself, who is now speaking to Boethius. For after Philosophy had asked Boethius, “Do you know yourself to be anything else?” and Boethius had answered, “Nothing,” she said, “Now I know another and perhaps the greatest cause of your illness: you have ceased to know what you yourself are.”

“Do you remember that you are a human being?”

“Why should I not remember it?” I replied.

“Then can you state what a human being is?”

“Are you asking whether I know myself to be a rational and mortal animal?”

“I know it, and I confess that I am such.”

And she said:

“Do you know yourself to be anything else?”

“Nothing.”

“Now I know,” she said, “another and perhaps the greatest cause of your illness: you have ceased to know what you yourself are.”

**86**

V. Philosophy compels Boethius to admit that he is partly ignorant of himself. For, as Tully elegantly says in *Tusculan Disputations* I:

> It is indeed the greatest thing of all for the mind itself to see the mind; and surely this is the force of Apollo’s command, by which he urges each person to know himself. For I do not believe that he commands us to know our limbs, our stature, or our appearance. Nor are we bodies; and when I say this to you, I am not speaking to your body. When he says, “Know yourself,” he means, “Know your mind.” The body is, as it were, a vessel or some receptacle of the mind; whatever is done by your mind is done by you. To know the mind, therefore, unless it were something divine, would not be the command of a more penetrating mind, so that the ability to know itself may be regarded as something attributed to God.

Yet Boethius, occupied by certain prejudices and therefore failing to distinguish himself sufficiently from the condition of animals, did not seem to know his soul or mind adequately. Hence he fell into various errors, which Philosophy now undertakes to enumerate.

“You have ceased to know what you yourself are.”

**[Note: “I have found most fully both the explanation of your illness and the means of restoring your health.”]** VI. From the fact that Boethius has partly known and partly failed to know both God and himself, Philosophy draws first the causes of his illness and then the method of recovering his health. The causes of the disease are ignorance; the means of recovery are knowledge both of God and of oneself, as will now be explained.

“I have found most fully both the explanation of your illness and the means of restoring your health.”

**[Note: “Health.”]**

“For, first, because you are confused by forgetfulness of yourself, you grieved that you were an exile and stripped of your own goods.”

**[Note: “Because you are confused by forgetfulness of yourself.”]** Boethius, partly ignorant of his own mind and therefore as though forgetful of it, consequently grieved that he was both an exile and deprived of his own goods. For the person who knows his mind perfectly understands both the homeland of the mind—heaven, from which no one is exiled except by his own will—and the goods of that same mind, knowledge and virtue, which are inaccessible to its enemies. See Prose 4.

“Next, because, being likewise partly ignorant of God, you do not regard God as the ultimate end of all things, you therefore consider wicked and criminal men powerful and happy. Whoever remembers his own end and conceives of God as just will have no doubt that the prosperous fortune of the impious is an indication not of any happiness but rather of eternal misery.

“When the ultimate end of all things is ignored, the means by which God directs all things toward their ends must also be ignored. Whoever is ignorant of those means denies what is evident because he cannot comprehend what is obscure in his mind; and thus he denies the ruler of the world.

“Therefore it is now added: ‘Because you have forgotten by what rudders or means the world is governed, you suppose that these changes of fortune drift without a ruler.’ Yet ignorance both of the human mind and of God is the beginning of error and vice, just as clear and distinct knowledge of the human mind and of God is the beginning of truth and virtue. Hence those darknesses are now called causes not only of illness—that is, error—but also of destruction, namely, vice.”

“Because you are ignorant of what the end of things is, you consider wicked and criminal men powerful and happy. Because you have forgotten by what rudders or means the world is governed, you suppose that these changes of fortune drift without a ruler. These are great causes not only of illness but also of destruction.

“But thanks must be given to the author of your health, because nature has not yet entirely abandoned you.”

**[Note: “Thanks must be given.”]**  
**[Note: “God, the author of nature.”]**

**87**

Finally, because Boethius recognizes his own mind and especially God, the supreme governor of the world, he possesses the means of recovering health—or, less idiomatically in Latin, *sospitas*—as is best explained by the example of tinder.

“We possess the greatest tinder of your recovery: your true opinion concerning the governance of the world, because you believe that it is subject not to the rashness of chance but to divine reason.”

**[Note: “The beginning.”]** Philosophy explains this by the example of a spark. A fire-source is matter so suited to catching fire that, when one part of it has been ignited, the remaining parts are very easily kindled. Thus Virgil expressed it in *Aeneid* I, verse 178:

> First Achates struck a spark from the flint,  
> Then received the fire in leaves, and supplied  
> Dry fuel around it, and caught the flame in the tinder.

Since the human mind, once affected by some notion or light, can very easily advance not only toward more perfect knowledge—which is nothing other than the natural light spread somewhat farther—but also toward the cultivation of truth and virtue, in which the entire health of the human mind consists, a true judgment concerning the governance of the world, founded upon the natural light, is therefore the greatest spark of human health.

“Therefore fear nothing. From this very small spark of your mind, the life-giving warmth will shine upon you.”

**[Note: From this smallest light of your mind, truth and virtue, which are the first seeds of eternal life, will shine forth.]**  
**[Note: “It will arise.”]**

“But since it is not yet time for stronger remedies, I shall try for a little while to lessen it with gentle and moderate applications, so that, when the darkness of deceptive affections has been removed, you may be able to recognize the splendor of the true light.”

**[Note: “It is the nature of minds…”]** The condition both of body and of mind is not erased except by an opposite condition. Therefore, just as a true opinion does not leave our mind unless a false one takes its place, so, when a false opinion departs, the true one enters the mind.

There is a connection between disturbances and false opinions such that, just as false opinions arise from disturbances, disturbances arise from false opinions. Hence it is now said that the nature of minds is such that, whenever they cast off true opinions, they clothe themselves in or, as others read, are imbued with false opinions, from which the darkness of disturbances arises.

However disturbances arise, the human mind is overwhelmed by them, so that it is rightly said that the darkness of disturbances confuses the mind’s true insight.

“Such is the nature of minds that, whenever they have cast off true opinions, they are clothed in false ones, from which arises the darkness of disturbances; and this confuses that true insight.”

**[Note: “Of the mind.”]**

“When the darkness of disturbances has vanished, the true light will shine upon the mind. But just as with bodies, so with minds: moderate remedies must first be applied, and then stronger ones, as has already been said.”

**[Note: “These gentle remedies for a little while.”]**

“I shall try to weaken this darkness for a little while with gentle and moderate applications, so that, when the darkness of deceptive affections has been removed, you may be able to recognize the splendor of the true light.”

**88 METRE**

**[Note: This metre is called an Adonian after Adonis, son of the king of Cyprus. It is a poem consisting of one kind of verse, each line being a dimeter composed of a dactyl and a spondee. The human mind, if it is to attain truth, must first be formed by something like a sun, since it cannot itself be the source of its own light. Next, it must immediately become conscious of this formation; and the author of this formation informs it only by admonishing it. Finally, once convinced by the evident character of the formation itself, the mind must, by its own inclination and in agreement, proceed wherever the author of this light leads it. The form of truth consists in this agreement. Disturbances impede all these things, as will subsequently be shown by three examples. Philosophy therefore rightly concludes that, in order to attain truth, the mind must divest itself of such disturbances.]**

**VII**

**ARGUMENT.** As the light of the stars is hindered by clouds, the clarity of water by mud, and the course of a river by an opposing rock, so knowledge of the truth is obstructed by disturbances; these must therefore be driven away.

**[Note: Stars wrapped in black darkness cannot emit any light. If the south wind, turbulent and stirring the sea, disturbs the waves, water previously transparent and bright like light immediately becomes foul when the mud is dispersed through it and obstructs the sight. A river that flows down from lofty places is often halted by a rock opposing it, broken off from a mountain. Likewise, if you wish to behold the truth with evident knowledge and to follow, in judgment, the well-trodden road by a straight path, remove joy, remove fear, drive away hope, and do not let grief enter your mind. For when these disturbances rule the mind, the mind is darkened and held back as though by so many chains.]**

> Beneath dark clouds  
> The enclosed stars  
> Cannot pour forth  
> Any light.

**[Note: “Beneath dark clouds.”]** I. Thus, just as black clouds interposed between heaven and earth prevent the stars from sending their rays down to the earth—because those clouds are opaque bodies, whose nature is to reflect light—so disturbances, as though interposed between God and the human mind, prevent God, that Father of lights, from sending his rays down to the human mind; for the disturbances just mentioned, like opaque bodies, reflect back the heavenly light.

This may be related to Wisdom 9: “Even if someone is perfect among the children of men, if your wisdom is absent from him, he will be reckoned as nothing. . . . Send her from your holy heavens and from the throne of your majesty, that she may be with me and labour with me, so that I may know what is pleasing in your sight. . . . For what human being can know the counsel of God, or who can conceive what God wills? For the thoughts of mortals are timid, and our forethought uncertain; for the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things.”

**[5]**

> If the south wind,  
> Turbulent as it rolls the sea,  
> Should mingle the waves,  
> The water, once glasslike  
> And equal to the clear  
> Days,  
> Soon, when the mud  
> Has been stirred up, becomes foul  
> And obstructs the sight.

**[Note: “If the rolling sea.”]** II. Just as seawater, previously transparent like glass, is afterwards so dirtied by mud stirred up by winds that it becomes impervious to light and consequently conceals bodies immersed in it, so the human mind, previously penetrable by heavenly light, is obscured when disturbances are subsequently agitated, so that it sees itself flooded with no light and consequently fails to recognize what is familiar to it.

Nor is it without reason that seawater is preferred here to other waters, and the south wind to other winds. Since seawater is salty, it aids the direct passage of light more than fresh water and, other things being equal, is more transparent than any other water. Since the south wind blows from the south and is warmer, it seems to disturb seawater more when it stirs up the mud.

> And the river that wanders  
> Down from the lofty mountains,  
> Flowing downward,  
> Is often checked  
> By the barrier of a rock  
> Loosened from a cliff.

**[Note: “And the wandering one.”]** III. Just as a river rushing down from high mountains is checked by an opposing rock loosened from a mountain, so the human mind, inclined by a great natural impulse toward assent to truth, is held back by an opposing disturbance.

Here grammarians may observe the words *amnis*, *defluus*, *obex*, and *saxum*. First, according to Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, *amnis* is a river which goes around something, as though derived from Greek **ἀμφί** (*amphi*, “around”) and **νέω** (*neō*, “I flow”), or rather from *am*, “around,” and *no*, that is, *nato*, “I swim.” Perhaps for this reason Ocean, because it surrounds the whole world, is called a river by poets. Thus Tibullus, Book III, elegy 4:

> Now night, having traversed the ethereal world in her black chariot,  
> Had washed her wheels in the dark-blue stream.

Secondly, *defluus* means “flowing down” or “slipping down.” Yet I have been unable to find an earlier author who used this word, *defluus*; Virgil, *Georgics* III, verse 446, may have prompted it:

> And the ram is plunged in the whirlpool with dripping fleece,  
> And, cast into the favouring stream, floats downstream.

Thirdly, *obex* is so called from being placed in the way (*obicere*), because it is placed against doors. Hence poets more often write *objice*, and, with this spelling also altered, lengthen the first syllable, as in Virgil, *Georgics* IV, verse 422:

> Within, Proteus hides himself behind the barrier of a vast rock.

And Claudian, Book I of *The Rape of Proserpina*:

> Or because the wind, rushing among closed barriers . . .

Fourthly, *saxum* here means “mountain,” as in *Aeneid* II, verse 307:

> The shepherd, hearing the sound from the summit of the mountain.

> **[20]** You too, if you wish  
> With clear light  
> To discern the truth,  
> And by a straight route  
> To take the path:

Since the disturbances just mentioned are so great an impediment both to clear and distinct knowledge and to holding a true judgment, if you wish both to perceive truth by evident knowledge and, in judging, to follow where that evidence can rightly lead, strip your mind of prejudices in such a way that you pronounce no judgment led by joy, fear, hope, grief, or any other disturbance. For just as the mind that is to perceive is darkened by these affections as though by clouds, so the mind that is to judge rightly is restrained by them as though by reins. Accordingly Virgil, signifying that a mind darkened by these affections forgets even its own origin, sings in *Aeneid* VI, verse 733:

> Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice; nor do they look upon the air,  
> Shut up in darkness and a blind prison.

**[Note: “Drive away joys.”]** The disturbance consists in a certain movement of the mind arising from the body. Since that movement can occur in almost infinitely many ways, the number of disturbances cannot be fixed. Here, however, four classes of disturbance are listed, which is not new. Cicero often teaches that there are four disturbances: joy, desire, fear, and grief. He says that the first two arise from two supposed goods—joy from present goods and desire from future goods—while the latter two arise from two supposed evils—fear from future evils and grief from present evils.

Thus Horace, *Epistles* I.6:

> Whether he rejoices or grieves, desires or fears—what does it matter?

Saint Augustine, Saint Jerome, and many others after Virgil, in the passage cited shortly below, mention the same number. Certainly, just as the remaining winds can be signified by the four principal winds, so the remaining disturbances can be signified by the four principal disturbances. Someone, according to the testimony of the Coimbra commentators, expressed this as follows:

> Hope raises the fears that stand upon the lofty summit of the waves;  
> Then furious pleasure strikes the mind;  
> From another side comes grief. Like waves broken against waves,  
> They repeat their mighty cry. Hidden beneath pitch-black clouds,  
> Reason sends forth neither rays nor guides the sails.

> **[25]** Drive away joy,  
> Drive away fear,  
> Banish hope,  
> And let grief be absent.
>
> A cloudy mind  
> Is bound by reins  
> Whenever these things rule.

**[Note: “A cloudy mind.”]** The human mind, stirred by the disturbances mentioned above, either does not perceive the truth or, if it does perceive it, is prevented from assenting to the truth it has perceived. Therefore, for the sake of truth, the human mind must be freed from such disturbances, as from all other prejudices.

**BOOK TWO**

**91 PROSE I**

**ARGUMENT.** Philosophy, having declared that the cause of Boethius’ illness is his attachment to and longing for his former fortune, attempts, in the manner of a rhetorician, to persuade Boethius that he ought not to be distressed by Fortune’s instability. He knew that Fortune was naturally unstable, and he had proposed her to himself as a mistress whom he would follow wherever she wished to lead.

After this she was silent for a little while.

**[Note: Philosophy.]**

When she had gathered my attention through modest silence, she began as follows:

**[Note: “She gathered my attention.”]** Anyone who wishes not only to strip his mind of prejudices but also to form it through true disciplines must necessarily attend mentally, first to the causes of prejudices and then to the path by which truth is found. Through this attention, as though through a kind of prayer, we ask God, the author of light and truth, to furnish our mind with the benevolence by which he inclines toward us. Such attention of mind is commonly awakened not only by the silence of the listener but also by the silence of the speaker—a modest silence, as it is now called.

**92**

“If I have thoroughly learned the causes and character of your illness…”

**[Note: “The causes and condition of the illness.”]** That is, what produces the illness and the condition in which that illness lies, by which Boethius’ mind is afflicted.

**[Note: “You waste away from attachment to and longing for your former fortune.”]** Since it is already clear from what was said above that the cause of this illness is disturbance, it remains only to say what that disturbance is. It is most appropriately described as attachment to and longing for former fortune. Boethius, having hitherto experienced prosperous fortune, seems rashly to have believed it immutable. He is now held by such longing for it that, as the solid parts of a body are dispersed by fire, he appears to melt and dissolve; this is what it means to waste away.

“If I have thoroughly learned the causes and character of your illness, you are wasting away from attachment to and longing for your former fortune. It is only the alteration of that fortune, as you imagine it, that has overturned the condition of your mind.”

**[Note: “The various tricks of this monster.”]**  
**[Note: “The disguises of the prodigy.”]** I understand the many disguises of that prodigy.

If we believe Cicero, a *prodigy* is something that foretells the future. For, says Cicero in *De natura deorum* II, “predictions and foretellings of future events—what else do they declare except that things which are going to happen are displayed, shown, announced, and foretold to human beings?” From this, *omens*, *monsters*, *portents*, and *prodigies* receive their names.

Since Fortune is so unstable that she seems, as it were, to foretell prosperity by adversity and adversity by prosperity, she can here be called a prodigy.

A *fucus* is a kind of seaweed with which garments are dyed. Hence Horace, *Odes* III.5:

> Nor does the wool, dyed with the sea-purple,  
> Restore the colors that have been lost.

Since women especially used the color of that plant to counterfeit the color of the face, it may have happened that every falsehood came to be called a *fucus*, just as the counterfeit bee is called a *fucus*. Fortune’s deceptions are many, since, in order to deceive human beings, she changes herself into every form like Proteus. Philosophy can therefore rightly speak here of Fortune’s many disguises.

“I understand the many disguises of Fortune and her excessive familiarity with those whom she attempts to deceive.”

**[Note: “I know that Fortune is so familiarly flattering.”]** Some find this passage so obscure that, to make sense of it, they have thought that *exercet*—“she practices” or “exercises”—should be added, or at least *exercere*. We do not think anything should be added. It may be rendered as follows: “I understand Fortune’s disguises and her extremely flattering familiarity with those whom she attempts to deceive, until she…” The person who uses sweet but deceptive words is called flattering. No term could be more appropriate for Fortune, since, if not in words, then at least in actions, she is accustomed to use deceptions no less misleading than they are pleasant, so that she confounds with intolerable pain those whom she has abandoned unexpectedly.

“I understand Fortune’s disguises and her exceedingly flattering familiarity with those whom she attempts to deceive, until she overwhelms with intolerable pain those whom she has left unexpectedly.”

**[Note: “Unexpectedly.”]**

“If you recall her nature, her habits, and her deserts…”

**[Note: “Her nature, habits, and merit.”]** Philosophy is still speaking about Fortune in the manner of the pagans, as though about some divinity. Thus, as though she were speaking of a mind, she now attributes to Fortune a nature, habits, and deserts. The nature of this false divinity would be a thing capable of thought; its habits would be its manner of thinking; and its deserts would be the good or evil that comes from this divinity. For the person whom Fortune raises through prosperity she also casts down through adversity.

“If you recall her nature, her habits, and her deserts, you will recognize that you neither possessed anything beautiful in her nor lost anything beautiful. But, as I think, I shall not have to work very hard to recall these things to your memory.”

**93**

“For you used to attack even Fortune when she was present and flattering…”

**[Note: “With noble.”]**  
**[Note: “To attack or rebuke.”]**

“For you used to attack even Fortune when she was present and flattering with manly words, and you used to assail her with the judgments drawn from our sanctuary.”

That is, with philosophical judgments.

**[Note: “Drawn from our sanctuary.”]** The sanctuary is a sacred place to which no one except a priest is permitted to go. The word *adytum* is Greek, derived from the privative prefix **a-** and **δύω** (*dyō*), “I enter”; hence the pagans called the place from which oracles were delivered an **ἄδυτον** (*adyton*), an inaccessible sanctuary.

Virgil, *Aeneid* II, verse 114:

> In suspense, they sent Eurypylus to inquire  
> Of Phoebus’ oracle.

We send; and he reports these sad words from the inner sanctuary.

Since Philosophy is said to have her own temple and her own oracles, she must also have her own sanctuary from which she may deliver her pronouncements. Boethius used these pronouncements, while he enjoyed prosperity, in the manner of other orators, to attack Fortune when she was present and flattering.] [Note: [Col. 0659A] Philosophical.] You attacked her with arguments drawn from our sanctuary. But [Note: [Col. 0659C] Every sudden change, etc.] The human mind is joined by such a close bond, first with the human body and then with external things, that when these are changed, the mind is changed in its thinking as well. Thus, when the body is ill, the mind suffers; thus, not without a certain distress of spirit, we are torn away from our homeland, our friends, and our possessions. And this change is felt all the more strongly the more sudden it is. For, as Saint Gregory says in Homily 35, “The darts that are foreseen strike less severely; whatever happens unexpectedly does greater harm.”] Every sudden change of circumstances occurs not without a kind of agitation of the mind. Thus it happened that [Col. 0660A] you too withdrew for a short while (5) from your tranquility.

But [Note: [Col. 0659D] It is time.] Continuing the comparison that Philosophy employed above, Philosophy now advances from familiar bodies to an understanding of minds. Just as the organs of taste, after first taking in lighter and softer foods, are so prepared by use that they become capable of bearing heavier foods later, according to Martial, *Epigrams*, book V, epigram 77:

> Mithridates gained strength by often drinking poison,  
> lest savage toxins should be able to harm him.  
> You too, Cinna, have always taken such poor dinners  
> that you could never perish from hunger.

So the human mind, after first hearing lighter arguments, becomes more capable of grasping weightier arguments by which it may be freed from its errors. Therefore Philosophy, intending to set forth stronger arguments later, now begins with lighter ones, which she expounds partly in loose and partly in concise discourse. She calls these arguments lighter because of their persuasive and rhetorical sweetness. Persuasive, indeed: for persuasion—or *suada*—is the virtue of persuading, which the ancients called a goddess; hence the Greeks call it πειθώ (*peithō*), that is, “persuasion.” They are also rhetorically sweet because rhetors, being accustomed to speak at greater length in contrast with dialecticians, who speak more compactly, especially strive to please. Nor do they persuade unless they employ a clear and distinct conception, which we owe to philosophical teaching. Hence Tully says that without philosophy the eloquent man whom we seek cannot be produced. Hence Philosophy herself now asserts that persuasion proceeds along the straight road only when it does not abandon philosophical principles.

Finally, since Philosophy is about to present these rhetorical arguments in concise discourse, the philosophical household-servant of the Muses must necessarily sing their measures in accompaniment. Music is the art not only of singing but also of composing poetry. *Musica* is called so, like *museum*, from the Muses. But music is the household-servant of the philosophical hearth, because a *vernula*, or home-born slave, is a slave born from a slave; in this he differs from a slave who is not born but made subject to another’s authority. Music may therefore be called a slave born from the slave of philosophy, since music arose from the Muses, who serve philosophy as attendants. On the household gods, see book I, prose 3, note 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0659A] To the mind.] It is time for you to draw in and taste something soft and pleasant, which, once conveyed into your inward parts [Note: [Col. 0659A] Of the mind.], may clear a path for stronger draughts [Note: [Col. 0659A] Remedies.]. Let there therefore be the sweetness of rhetorical persuasion, which proceeds along the straight road only when it does not abandon our principles [Note: [Col. 0660A] Philosophical.]; and with it let music [Note: [Col. 0660A] The art of composing and singing poetry.], the home-born slave of our philosophical hearth [Note: [Col. 0660A] The slave of philosophy.], now sing lighter, now weightier [Note: [Col. 0660A] Let it sing poems.] measures. (10)

## 94

What, then, [Note: [Col. 0660C] O man.] O man, has cast you down into sadness and mourning?

[Note: [Col. 0660C] This manner of speaking belongs to a superior, or at least to one who indicates that he has no familiarity with the person whom he addresses. Thus Terence: “Good heavens,” he says, “you, man, are driving me mad.” So Peter in Luke 22: “O man, I am not”—“My friend, I am not.” Here Philosophy begins to present her little arguments rhetorically. If you attempt to reduce them to dialectical form, you may notice some repetitions; and this is not surprising. For it is well known what Zeno said: that rhetoric resembles the palm of the hand, while dialectic resembles the fist, because rhetors speak at greater length, whereas dialecticians speak more compactly. Seneca speaks in this way. Whatever the case, we note here two arguments of this kind in particular.]

[Note: [Col. 0660D] “I suppose something new.”] The first rhetorical argument may apparently be condensed as follows. Since the human mind, like the body, is not disturbed by old and familiar things, your mind, O Boethius, ought not to have been disturbed by Fortune’s event unless this event was new and unfamiliar. But nothing here is new or unfamiliar, since Fortune has always and everywhere been constant in her mutability, as you are now experiencing. Therefore, far from this Fortune’s event being a cause of such great sorrow for you, it ought rather to have been a cause of tranquility. For she has left you, and no one can ever be secure that she will not leave him; indeed, a prudent person, who looks ahead even to future events, ought to be certain that she will depart.

Here we need only add why Philosophy now calls Fortune “the blind deity’s ambiguous faces.” Among the ancients Fortune was, first, a deity, because they thought that, since the causes of many effects were unknown, those effects could arise only from Fortune, whom they therefore called a deity. Second, she was a blind deity, either because she recklessly bestowed evil upon the good and good upon the wicked, or because she generally made blind those whom she embraced. Third, she was a deity bearing ambiguous faces because, like a round stone—which is why she was imagined standing upon one—she was rolling and would transfer to disgrace those whom, shortly before, she had raised to glory with a kindly face, now with a severe one. Thus Horace sang of Gyges in *Odes* II.5:

> If you were to insert him into the chorus of girls,  
> he would wonderfully deceive the keen-sighted guests,  
> his distinction concealed by loosened hair  
> and an ambiguous face.]

[Note: [Col. 0660A] Perhaps.] I suppose you have seen something new and unfamiliar. Do you think Fortune has changed toward you? You are mistaken. These have always been her character and nature. Rather, amid her very mutability, she has preserved her own proper constancy. (5) Such was she when she was flattering you, when she played with you through the allurements of false happiness. You have discovered [Note: [Col. 0661B] Fortune’s varied forms.] the ambiguous faces of the blind deity. What she still conceals from others has become wholly known to you. If you approve of her [Note: [Col. 0661B] Fortune.], make use of her character [Note: [Col. 0661B] Of that same Fortune.] and do not complain. If you shudder at her faithlessness, despise and cast away the destructive creature at play. For what is now the cause of such great sorrow for you (10) ought to have been the cause of tranquility. She has left you, and no one can ever be secure that she will not leave him. Or do you consider a happiness that is destined to depart precious? Is the present Fortune dear to you, though she is not faithful to remaining and, when she departs, will bring sorrow?

[Col. 0661B] But if she can neither be retained at will nor, when fleeing, avoid making people wretched, what else is this fugitive thing but a sign of future calamity? Nor is it enough to look at what lies before one’s eyes. Wisdom measures the outcomes of things; and this same mutability in either direction makes neither Fortune’s threats to be feared nor her blandishments to be desired.

## 95

[Note: [Col. 0661D] “Finally, endure with an even mind,” etc.] The second rhetorical argument may apparently be expressed as follows. Whoever has voluntarily submitted himself to another’s yoke must patiently endure that person’s character; otherwise he will be unjust both to himself and to his master: unjust to his master if he wishes to prescribe for him the law of remaining and departing; unjust to himself if impatience aggravates the lot that he cannot alter. Thus sailors and sowers, because they have entrusted themselves and their possessions to the elements, do not sail according to their own command, nor do they reap according to it.

Since, therefore, O Boethius, you have voluntarily submitted yourself to Fortune’s yoke; since you have voluntarily chosen Fortune as your mistress; since you have entrusted yourself to Fortune to be governed, you must endure with an even mind whatever is done within Fortune’s domain and must obey the character of your mistress.

[Col. 0662B] A domain (*area*) is an empty place, as though it had dried up and could produce nothing. Thus the ground adjoining buildings, when it is vacant of buildings, is called an *area*. Likewise, the place designated for threshing grain is called an *area*. Philosophy may have called this world Fortune’s domain because, just as grain is turned about on a threshing-floor by the thresher, so in the world human beings are turned now this way, now that, by Fortune through prosperity or adversity.]

Finally, you must endure with an even mind whatever is done within Fortune’s [Note: [Col. 0661B] Kingdom.] domain, once you have submitted your neck to her yoke. But if you wished to prescribe a law of remaining and departing to her whom you voluntarily chose as your mistress, would you not be [Note: [Col. 0661B] Unjust.] unjust and aggravate by impatience a lot that you cannot alter?

If [Note: [Col. 0662B] You were sailing.] you entrusted your sails to the winds, you would advance not where your will directed but where the breezes drove you. If you entrusted seed to the fields, you would reckon years that were fertile with those that were barren. You have entrusted yourself to Fortune to be governed; you must obey the character of your mistress.

## 96

But you [Note: [Col. 0662C] Of the revolving wheel.] are trying to restrain Fortune’s revolving wheel’s momentum.

[Note: [Col. 0662C] The ancients represented Fortune not only as blind and like a madwoman but also as hanging from a rolling stone, because Fortune seemed to them to administer everything with reckless and blind force, giving adversity to the good and prosperity to the wicked, while, like a sphere, she wandered and rolled by a certain necessity of nature. Thus it was no less foolish to resist Fortune’s revolutions than those of the stars. Hence Baptista Mantuanus wrote:

> Trust in virtue: Fortune, more fleeting than the waves,  
> does not remain.]

But, most foolish of all mortals, if she begins to remain, she ceases to be Fortune.

## 97 — METER I

[Note: [Col. 0662C] What is called the iambic Hipponactean. It is a poem consisting of one kind of verse, each line consisting of six feet. The even-numbered feet generally contain iambs, and the odd-numbered feet spondees.]

[Col. 0662B]

### ARGUMENT

Fortune, like the Euripus, is unstable: she raises and casts down not only many people but even the same person within the space of a single hour.

[Note: [Col. 0662D] When Fortune has alternated these changes with an imperious hand, she is carried along like the overflowing Euripus. Cruel Fortune suddenly tramples kings who were to be feared, and immediately, deceitful, raises the humbled head of the subjugated man. She does not hear the afflicted; she is not moved by tears; and she laughs at the complaints that arise spontaneously from those whom she herself has cruelly caused to suffer. Thus Fortune plays; thus she tests her strength and displays the great marvel of her power, when, under her agency, the same person appears both wretched and blessed in the same hour.]

### 1. “She has altered the changes”

We call things that occur alternately *vicissitudes*; hence *vicissim* means “alternately.” Fortune, because of her innate inconstancy, changes everything by turns, now bringing prosperity, now adversity, to many people or to one. This is so frequent and familiar that the Latins call Fortune *vicem*, “a change” or “vicissitude.” Thus Cicero often says: “I must fear both my own lot and that of others”; “I deeply grieve both for my own lot and for yours.”

### 1. “With her proud right hand”

A part is put for the whole. Fortune is called proud by Horace and others because she seems, being higher than human beings, to rule them at will. Thus Seneca in *Medea*, line 205:

> Whoever has laid hands upon proud scepters.

### 2. “In the manner of the overflowing Euripus”

*Euripus* is a Greek word meaning a strait. There are two kinds. One is artificial, the other natural.

First, an artificial Euripus is a channel constructed with magnificent workmanship to convey water in the manner of a river. It differs from the similarly artificial Nile in that the Nile is larger, whereas the Euripus is smaller. Tully speaks of both in *On the Laws* II: “Who, when he sees these channels of water—which those people call Niles and Euripi—would not laugh?”

Second, the natural Euripus is the part of the sea between Aulis, a harbor of Boeotia, and the island of Euboea, mentioned by Strabo in book IX and by Pliny in book II. This sea does not surge like the Ocean but, seven times and more within the space of a day and night, rushes back with such force that it frustrates even the winds and ships under full sail. The water is driven headlong toward this place and is sent back on every side by the intervening islands. Hence it is now called “overflowing.”

From this it came about that Fortune, human thought, or anything else highly liable to change was called unstable like the Euripus.

Continuing in verse the proof of Fortune’s inconstancy that she had begun in prose, Philosophy now shows the same inconstancy even among kings.]

> When with her proud right hand she has altered the changes,  
> she is carried along in the manner of the overflowing Euripus;

[Col. 0663A]

### 3. “She tramples kings”

Fortune sometimes strips even kings and emperors of their authority and power. Thus, as Aelian says, when the Lacedaemonians were masters of the Thebans, they were later so completely subdued by them that the Thebans not only reached the Peloponnese but also crossed the Eurotas and ravaged the land of the Lacedaemonians. Likewise, according to Ammianus Marcellinus, Dionysius, once the terror of nations, became the head of a school of letters at Corinth.

### 4. “She raises the face of the defeated”

The same Fortune sometimes raises the defeated. Thus Amyntas of Macedon, according to the Aelian mentioned above, after being defeated by the neighboring and bordering barbarians and losing his kingdom, resolved in his heart to abandon the entire region, provided only that he could preserve his life safe and unharmed. While he was anxiously occupied with this thought, someone brought him a saying of Hellopidas. He therefore seized that place, gathered soldiers, and recovered his power.

Similarly, according to the same author, Dion, son of Hipparinus, after being sent into exile by Dionysius, defeated him again with two thousand soldiers. Thus he caused the author of his own misfortune to be thrust into the condition in which Dion himself had previously stood.

This vicissitude of Fortune seems such a great evil that Megaera, in Seneca’s *Thyestes*, line 33, invokes it among other calamities:

> Let the uncertain and violent household of Fortune  
> stagger among uncertain kings.  
> Let the wretched become powerful and the powerful wretched,  
> and let chance continually carry the kingdom on its waves.

### 5. “She does not hear the wretched”

Philosophers, following Cicero, maintain that Fortune is insane, blind, and brutish.

### 6. “She laughs voluntarily at the groans that she, cruel, has caused”

It is harsh to laugh at one who has been made wretched from being blessed; such a person ought rather to provoke your compassion than your laughter. It is harsher still to laugh at one whose misery you have unjustly caused; for such a crime ought rather to make you repent. But it is harshest of all to do this spontaneously. Necessity, by which we sometimes laugh even unwillingly, could lessen the cruelty of such laughter. Since Fortune, however, laughs spontaneously at the wretched whom she herself has unjustly made so, she is rightly now called harsh.

[Col. 0664B]

### 7. “Thus she plays”

A person is said to play when he runs recklessly here and there. The verb derives from the Lydians, who, under the leadership of Tyrrhenus, migrated from Asia into Etruria and introduced those extraordinary movements that were later called games, whether circus or theatrical. Hence *ludiones* or *ludii*—namely, adolescent boys dressed in elegant tunics and additionally armed with helmet, sword, and shield—used to proceed in circus and theatrical processions as leaders of the spectacle, like the Salii. Ovid mentions them in *The Art of Love* I:

> While an Etruscan flute-player provides the rough rhythm,  
> the dancer strikes the level ground three times with his foot.

For this reason Horace calls war a game of Mars in *Odes* I.2:

> Alas, too long sated with the game,  
> you who delight in shouting and in gleaming helmets,  
> and in the fierce, blood-stained face  
> of the Moorish infantryman against the enemy.

Therefore, since Fortune not only laughs, as has already been said, but also runs recklessly now here, now there, like Mars, now bringing prosperity and now adversity, she is most appropriately said to play.

Thus the same Horace called Fortune’s advance and retreat a game in *Odes* II.1:

> The civil disturbance under Metellus the consul,  
> the causes and vices and patterns of war,  
> Fortune’s game, and the grave friendships  
> and arms of princes.

Likewise Virgil sang in *Aeneid* XI.426:

> She revisited many in turn,  
> played with them, and then restored Fortune  
> once more to solid ground.

Thus she proves her strength. The comparison stated above is continued: those who play test their strength by competing.

### 8. “A portent”

A work so remarkable that it seems worthy of being pointed out with the finger as something marvelous.

### 9. “Struck down and blessed in a single hour”

This is surely the greatest proof of light and unstable Fortune. Some think that “hour” here means “day”; but the shorter the span of time indicated by an hour, the more clearly it reveals the meaning of Philosophy’s words.]

## 100 — PROSE II

[Col. 0664A]

### ARGUMENT

Fortune, claiming that wealth and honors belong to her jurisdiction, proves by the example of heaven, earth, and sea that she could, without injuring anyone, give and take these things at will from Croesus and others, and likewise from Boethius.

I should like, then, to speak a few words with you [Note: [Col. 0664D] In Fortune’s words.]

[Note: [Col. 0664D] Philosophy introduces Fortune speaking. For, as Cicero says in *On Invention* I, “In all things, likeness is the mother of satiety.” Therefore, to counter satiety by variety, Philosophy next employs the manner of speaking that rhetors call *conformation*, which occurs when an absent person is imagined as though present. And certainly, since it seems unjust for anyone to be condemned unheard, Fortune is now appropriately introduced to defend her case against Boethius, who has complained bitterly about Fortune herself. Philosophy wishes Boethius, with her presiding, to consider Fortune’s words more attentively, lest, moved either by haste or prejudice, he pass an unjust judgment upon Fortune.

Fortune’s speech may be condensed as follows. “If it is unjust for you to complain about the deity from whom you received not only no injury but whatever good you possessed, then those complaints with which you daily assail me are utterly unjust and wrongful. For I have not only done you no injury by taking away wealth and honors, since they were mine; whatever good you possessed—namely, wealth and honors—you owe entirely to me, as their mistress. Just as day is owed to heaven, from which comes night; fertility to earth, from which comes barrenness; tranquility to the sea, from which come storms; and good things to Jupiter himself, from whom evil things come. Thus I received Croesus, and likewise the king of the Persians, without doing either of them any injury. Consider, therefore, whether justice demands this.”]

Philosophy acts here through Fortune’s own words. [Col. 0665A] Consider, then, whether [Note: [Col. 0665B] Whether it is just.] justice demands it.

What, [Note: [Col. 0665C] O man.] O man [Note: [Col. 0665C] Fortune will say.], are you prosecuting me as a defendant with daily [Note: [Col. 0665C] Some write *quotidianis* instead of *cotidianis*, according to the different interpretation of the word. If *quotidianum* is derived from *quot*, meaning “each” or “every,” as Cornutus maintains in Cassiodorus—just as one says *quot calendis*, “every Kalends,” *quot mensibus*, “every month,” and *quot annis*, “every year”—then *quotidianum* is correctly written. But if it is derived from *continens dies*, “a continuous day,” as Marius Victorinus thinks in book I, it should be written *cotidianum*.] complaints? What injury have we done you? What goods of yours have we taken away?

[Note: [Col. 0665C] Before any judge.] Since no one can be a judge in his own case, Fortune rightly appeals to a judge; but preferably to any judge, so that there may be no suspicion of prior occupation.]

Contend before any judge with me concerning the possession [Note: [Col. 0665C] Possession here means the right of possessing.] of wealth and honors. And [Note: [Col. 0665D] If any mortal’s.] if you can show that any of these things is the property of any mortal, I will readily concede that what you demand back was once yours.

[Note: [Col. 0665D] Destitute of all possessions.] II. Fortune argues that the goods which Boethius complains he has lost are hers. The good of the mind consists chiefly in thought, especially thought of which the human being is master; and Fortune has no power over such good. When nature brought you forth from your mother’s womb, I received you naked and destitute of all things, without resources. Thus Tully says in *For Cornelius*: “If I have not been able to satisfy all my friends by returning thanks for my safety, I shall certainly satisfy them by proclaiming and acknowledging it.” He says the same elsewhere.]

[Note: [Col. 0666C] As though you had used what belonged to another.] The goods of the mind, as we have already said, are ours; the rest belong to others and, if Fortune so wills, are subject to her commands.]

You have no right to complain, as though you had utterly lost what was yours. Why, then, do you groan? We have inflicted no violence upon you. [Col. 0665B] (10)

Wealth, honors, and other such things belong to my jurisdiction. The servants recognize their mistress: they come with me, and when I depart, they depart. I would confidently affirm that, if the things whose loss you lament had been yours, you could not have lost them in any way.

This is our power; this is the continual game we play. We turn our wheel in a revolving circle; we delight in changing the lowest things into the highest and the highest into the lowest. Climb up, if you wish, but on this condition: that, when the rules of my game demand it, you do not consider descending an injury. Did you not know [Note: [Col. 0667A] My habit of playing.] my character?

[Note: [Col. 0667B] You did not know Croesus.] Croesus, the last king of Lydia and the richest of men, was defeated by Cyrus, king of the Persians. When he rebelled again and was defeated again, he was condemned to the flames and cried out from the pyre, “Solon, Solon, Solon.” When Cyrus asked who this Solon was, Croesus replied: “Solon, a very wise man, once warned me that no one is happy in this life; I am now experiencing the truth of his warning.” Then Cyrus, reflecting upon Fortune’s variability, saw that the fire he had ordered extinguished was suppressed by heaven’s assistance. Ausonius expressed the event in his book *On the Game of the Seven Sages*:

> With a great cry he calls Solon three times.

Did you not know that Croesus, king of the Lydians, shortly before formidable to Cyrus and soon afterward pitiable, was handed over to the flames of the pyre and saved by a rain sent from heaven?

## 105 — ARGUMENT

The greater, Fortune says, the increase of wealth and honors, the more a person seems to be in need, because his desire for those things grows along with them.

[Note: [Col. 0668A] However great an abundance may bring forth so many riches, pouring them out with a hand that never stops—so many as the sea, stirred by violent winds, rolls along as sands, or as the many stars shine in heaven, brought forth by star-bearing nights—human beings nevertheless do not therefore cease miserably to complain. Even if God, generous with the greatest wealth, willingly grants the prayers of human beings and adorns those who desire honors with illustrious dignities, previously acquired goods are nonetheless held cheap. Indeed, cruel desire, consuming what has been gained, opens deep chasms. What reins can now restrain thoughtless greed within a fixed boundary, since the passion for possessing, heaped up with great gifts, grows more and more? Whoever, fearful and sighing, considers himself poor never lives as a rich man.]

[Note: [Col. 0666D] 1. “The sea.” Specifically, the Euxine Sea; generally, the sea, a word very frequent among poets. See Meter 2 of book I, line 14.]

2. **Sands.** No one is unaware of what sand is; but some write *arena*, others *harena*, according to the twofold interpretation of this name. For either this word derives from *arendo* (“to be dry”), because sand is dry and absorbent—as Horace often calls sand *arentes* (“dry”); in that case it is written *arena*—or it derives from *haerendo* (“to cling”), because, absorbing water, it remains behind when the other liquid substance in which it had grown soft has been driven off; in that case it is written *harena*, as it is read in ancient books.

> If the Pontus, stirred by swift blasts,  
> tosses as many sands,

[Col. 0669A] [Col. 0669B]

3. **“Brought forth by star-bearing nights.”** Night is regarded by poets as the mother of the stars, as in Tibullus, Book II, elegy 1:

> Play: now night joins the horses, and the tawny stars  
> follow the chariot of their mother in wanton chorus.

For this reason the stars are now said to be “brought forth” or “produced by star-bearing nights,” that is, by nights bearing stars.

6. **“With abundance from a full horn.”** The horn of plenty, Greek *κέρας Ἀμαλθείας* (*keras Amaltheias*), signifies the highest abundance. Diodorus writes that Hammon, while traveling near the Ceraunian Mountains, fell in love with a maiden whom he saw there, exceedingly beautiful in form, named Amalthea, and had by her a daughter distinguished in appearance and bodily strength. He appointed Amalthea over a neighboring region, which, because it resembled an ox’s horn, was called the western horn. Since that region was rich in vineyards and other fruit-bearing trees, it came about that every field abundant in crops, every table furnished with various delicacies, every book filled with many kinds of learning, every letter producing great benefit, and every man endowed with manifold virtue was called a “horn of plenty.” Horace uses the expression frequently, for example, *Odes* I.17:

> The gods protect me: my piety toward the gods  
> and the Muse are dear to me. Hence for you abundance  
> will flow to the full,  
> from the beneficent, wealth-bearing horn of the countryside.

8. **“To weep complaints.”** “A new expression,” says Sitzmanus, “which one would not easily find among other authors.” A neuter verb is used actively, with a noun of kindred meaning added. But there is nothing new here: a neuter verb can always govern an accusative of kindred meaning, as in *vivere vitam* (“to live a life”), *gaudere gaudium* (“to rejoice a joy”), *ludere ludum* (“to play a game”), *servire servitutem* (“to serve a service”), and *peccare peccata* (“to sin sins”). Indeed, whenever these nouns are suppressed, they ought to be understood as though expressed.

12. **“What has already been acquired now seems worthless.”** So great is the human mind’s love for the body joined to it that the mind desires not only riches and dignities—by which, as though by so many fortifications, the mutual union of body and mind seems capable of being preserved—but also frequently asks God, in words expressing this thought, for such things. Thus it was a virtue, and one especially pleasing to God, that Solomon, when such goods were offered to him as a choice, rejected them and asked God for wisdom, 1 Kings 3. For this reason also the Lord Christ restrains that desire with many arguments in Matthew 6. “Throughout the whole Gospel,” interpreters say, “no affection of the soul is attacked and uprooted by Christ with such earnestness and by so many engines of argument.”

Yet that love—and therefore a person’s favorable estimation of riches and dignities—concerns only goods not yet possessed. After a person has tested them and learned that these goods increase rather than lessen his miseries, he despises what he possesses and, changing the object of his esteem and love, pursues with similar desire what he does not yet possess: what has already been acquired now seems worthless. Juvenal:

> Meanwhile, while the purse grows full of money,  
> the love of money grows as much as the money itself grows.

For this reason avarice, now called savage rapacity, is said, like some insatiable monster, to devour what has been acquired and open deep chasms. For this reason also no reins can restrain headlong desire within a definite limit: the thirst for possession, growing as gifts are received, burns ever more fiercely.

19. **“He never lives as a rich man.”** From what has been said, Fortune infers that those who are commonly regarded as rich do not truly live as rich men—for here *agere*, as in Terence, means “to live.” Such a rich man, she says, besides believing himself needy, both laments the wealth he has lost and fears that he may lose what he currently possesses: trembling and groaning. Claudian had previously expressed this in Book I of *Against Rufinus*, line 196:

> Why do you rush on, madman? You may possess both oceans;  
> Lydia may open her golden springs for you;  
> the throne of Croesus and the tiara of Cyrus may be joined for you;  
> you will never be rich, never be satisfied with gain:  
> whoever desires is always poor.

Indeed, since, as Varro says in Book IV of *On the Latin Language*, “rich” derives from *divus* (“divine”), only that man is rich who, like a god, seems to need nothing, either for others or for himself.

> Or as many stars, brought forth by star-bearing nights,  
> shine in the sky;
>
> [5] so much wealth may he pour forth, nor withdraw his hand,  
> with abundance from a full horn:
>
> 106 Yet the human race will not therefore cease  
> to weep its wretched complaints.
>
> Although God willingly receives prayers,  
> [10] lavish of much gold,  
> and adorns the eager with distinguished honors,  
> what has already been acquired now seems worthless:
>
> but savage rapacity, devouring what has been sought,  
> opens deep chasms.
>
> [15] What reins can now restrain headlong desire  
> within a definite limit,  
> when, rather, flowing in upon abundant gifts,  
> the thirst for possession burns?
>
> [Col. 0670A]
>
> 107 He never lives as a rich man who, trembling and groaning,  
> [20] believes himself needy.

108 **PROSE III**

**Argument.** Philosophy, having acknowledged that everything said thus far, whether in unbound or in metrical speech, was only a slight remedy for grief, recalls the blessings which Boethius, with Fortune as guide, received from his guardians, the people, his wife, and his children—as a boy, a young man, a husband, and a father—and shows that, because of Fortune’s changeability, the fact that they have departed may equally be evidence that this misery too will depart.

[Col. 0670B] **“With these words.”** If, then, Fortune were to speak with you in her own defence in these words, what indeed would you say against them? You would not utter a word. *Hiscere* is derived from *hiare*; properly, *hiare* is to emit breath with the mouth open, and thus *hiscere* properly describes one who opens his mouth, lips parted, in order to speak. Hence Cicero, *Philippics* V: “Would you dare to reply to these things, or even to open your mouth at all?” And Vergil, *Aeneid* III.313:

> He filled the place with shouting; scarcely do I address a few words  
> to the raging man, and, troubled, open my mouth in broken speech.

The reading is *hisceres*, not *haberes*. If you have anything by which you may justly support your complaint, you ought to bring it forward; we shall grant you leave to speak.

Then I [**Boethius**] said:

“What Fortune has introduced and expressed, whether in prose or in verse, has, if it is not true, at least some appearance of truth. Thus Horace in *The Art of Poetry*:

> Sometimes a tale is impressive in its passages  
> and properly characterized.

And Ovid:

> You give impressive names  
> to your guilt, Medea; but consider how great  
> a crime you are undertaking.

For *speciosus* (“impressive,” “plausible”) derives from *species* (“appearance”), and *species* from the ancient verb *specio*, “I see”; hence *aspicio*, *inspicio*, and so forth. Accordingly, *species* among the Latins, as with the Greeks *ἰδέα* (*idea*), means nothing other than a conception. Thus whatever is presented through another’s obscure or confused conception is said to be presented under a borrowed appearance. Philosophers say in this way that evil is loved under the appearance of good. Likewise, Fortune’s words are now said to be covered with the honeyed sweetness of rhetoric and poetry, so that, being pleasant through their sound, gesture, expression, and other accompanying features, they delight only while they are heard; immediately afterward they must be driven from memory by the more grievous sensation of sorrow, for the deeper perception belongs to misfortunes, and the sorrow implanted in the soul weighs more heavily.”

“Those things,” said Philosophy, “are indeed impressive, and covered with the honeyed sweetness of rhetoric and poetry; they delight only while they are heard. But the perception of misfortunes is deeper for the wretched. Therefore, when these words cease to sound in their ears, the sorrow implanted in their souls weighs them down.”

109 And Philosophy said:

“Indeed.”

I. Philosophy admits that whatever has been said thus far, whether in prose or in verse, is no remedy, or only a slight remedy, for grief: “These are not yet remedies for your illness,” she says, “but still only certain applications for pain that stubbornly resists treatment. When the proper time comes, I shall apply remedies that penetrate into the depths.”

Here, first, a remedy is a substance opposed to disease which drives the disease away. For this reason *remedium* derives from *re*, meaning “against,” and *mederi*, “to heal.” Cicero likewise says that none of the remedies applied to wounds causes as much pain as those that are beneficial. The term *remedy* is also transferred from bodies to minds, which likewise are healed by opposites.

Second, something is called *contumax* (“stubborn”) when, having contracted a kind of swelling either of mind or of body, it is more difficult to disperse and, when stirred, advances with greater force. Just as *audax* derives from *audeo* (“to dare”) and *tenax* from *teneo* (“to hold”), so *contumax* derives from *contumeo* (“to swell”). From the same source comes *contumelia* (“insult”), since this is an injury proceeding from a mind puffed up and swollen with arrogance.

Third, that is called a *fomentum* (“soothing application”) which, gently moving the cause of pain, seems to nourish and soften the swelling. Here Philosophy fulfills her promise: she had promised that she would first apply milder remedies to Boethius and afterward more severe ones. Therefore, she says, “when the proper time comes, I shall apply remedies that penetrate into the depths.”

“Nevertheless, lest you wish to be considered miserable, have you forgotten the number and measure of your happiness?”

II. Philosophy enumerates the blessings which Boethius appears to have received, as though with Fortune as his guide, giving their number and measure—or, as people say, their quantity and quality: namely, how many and what kind they were.

“First, Boethius is said to have been fortunate as a boy through the care of his guardians.”

[Note: “With his father dead.”]

[Note: “Bereft of a parent.”]

The Boethius under discussion had a different grandfather and a different father. His grandfather, while serving as prefect of the praetorium, was killed innocently in the Palace by the emperor Valentinian together with the patrician Aetius in the year of Christ 455. Cassiodorus says in his *Chronicle*: “In the consulship of Aetius and Studius, Aetius the patrician was killed in the Palace by the hand of the emperor Valentinian; Boethius, prefect of the praetorium, was killed while his friends stood around him.” His father died while Boethius was still a boy. Hence our Boethius is called “bereft of a parent.” Yet, raised through the care of such friends, the boy Boethius was sent to Athens to acquire knowledge of all the disciplines.

“Bereft of a parent, the care of the greatest men took you in; then you were chosen into affinity with the leading men of the state, which is the most precious kind of relationship: you began to be dear before you became a relative.”

Boethius is next said to have been fortunate through his fathers-in-law, namely Festus and Symmachus, the leading men of the state. Festus and Symmachus were indeed leaders of the Roman state. “For,” says Ennodius in his *Didactic Exhortation*, “the patricians Festus and Symmachus, the substance of every discipline and enduring embodiment of wisdom, do not withdraw from the most sacred city. In them lies the noble leadership of the senate; to see them is to be educated.”

They were likewise Boethius’ fathers-in-law, since he had married Elpis, the daughter of Festus, and, after her death, Rusticiana, the daughter of Symmachus. The former of these wives is said to have been celebrated not only for her virtue but also for her literary distinction, and above all for her love of the Muses. Boethius was therefore fortunate in such fathers-in-law, since it is a form of happiness to be honored by the most honored men. “The greatest and most delightful praise,” says Cicero in his speech *For Murena*, “is that which proceeds from those who themselves have lived in honor.”

Boethius was especially honored by these distinguished men because he was first loved by them and then selected into their family—dear before he was related. Who, then, would not proclaim Boethius supremely fortunate, given such splendid fathers-in-law?

“Bereft of a parent, the care of the greatest men took you in; then you were selected into the family of the leading men of the state, which is the most precious kind of relationship, and began to be dear before you became a relative.”

110 “Who would not call you supremely fortunate, with such distinguished fathers-in-law, both through the modesty of your wife—”

Boethius is also said to have been fortunate through his wife, because each of his wives, Elpis namely and Rusticiana, was endowed with the highest virtue; this is signified especially by *pudor* (“modesty” or “moral reserve”). For, as Cicero says in Book II of *On Ends*, modesty is the governor of desire.

Since Philosophy had spoken of Boethius’ fathers-in-law in the plural but now mentions only one wife in the singular, I believe that here she refers to only one of his wives, namely Rusticiana, who alone was still alive when these things were written.

“—and also through the blessing of male offspring.”

Moreover, Boethius is recalled as fortunate through his children, especially through male offspring. For Boethius’ sons, if not Patricius and Hypatius, at least Symmachus and Boethius, became consuls. For this reason Philosophy calls them consuls here and “consular children” below. She now adds that the memory of the day on which Boethius saw two sons simultaneously elevated from his household to the consulship, amid the attendance of the senators and the enthusiasm of the people; on which he, as an orator of royal praise, earned glory for his intellect and eloquence; and on which he satisfied the expectation of the surrounding crowd with triumphal generosity—this memory cannot be erased by any magnitude of evils pressing upon him.

“Did she also proclaim you fortunate through the advantage of male offspring?”

“I pass over common matters, for I am willing to pass them over.”

Boethius, before he saw his sons become consuls, was himself, while still a young man, a patrician and perhaps also a consul. That dignity was rarely conferred before a person’s thirtieth year; hence he is now signified as fortunate even through the people’s votes.

“Let us add to the singular height of your happiness the dignities acquired in youth and denied to old men. If any fruit of mortal affairs possesses any weight of blessedness, could the memory of that day be erased by any magnitude of evils pressing upon it, when you saw your two sons simultaneously elevated from your home to the consulship, amid the attendance of the senators and the enthusiasm of the people; when, with them seated on curule chairs in the senate, you, as an orator of royal praise, earned glory for your intellect and eloquence?”

Curule may designate both persons entitled to have an image set up and the seats on which they sat in a chariot. These seats seem to be called *curules* from the chariot (*currus*), just as carved ivory is sometimes called *ebur* (“ivory”). Thus Horace, *Epistles* I.6:

> That troublesome man will give the fasces to anyone  
> and snatch away the curule ivory from whomever he wishes.

And Ovid, *Letters from Pontus* IV.9:

> I should recognize also the figures fashioned on the curule seat,  
> and the whole carved work of Numidian ivory.

111 The *circus*, Greek *κύκλος* (*kyklos*), is generally every enclosure, circuit, orb, or circle. Cicero in his *Aratea* writes:

> You have seen the great Milky Way creeping round,  
> marked by excessive whiteness.

Here it is the oval place in which, on the authority of Tarquinius Priscus, the Romans held games; hence those games were called circensian from the place. Custom required every newly elected consul to stage such games at lavish expense, otherwise he seemed neither pleasing to the people nor able fittingly to sustain the character of so great a magistracy.

“When, in the circus, seated between your two sons as consuls, you satisfied the expectation of the surrounding crowd with triumphal generosity.”

“‘In the circus’—that is, between your sons. Among the Romans,” says Lipsius, “the middle position is first; the next is the right. Among consuls, however, preference was given not to the one who had been consul more often, but to the one who had first been consul. Therefore Boethius ought to have sat in the middle, not only as their father but also as a consul.”

“You gave Fortune, as I think, words to repeat, while she caressed you, while she cherished you as her darling.”

“You took away a gift which she had never granted to any private citizen. For no one, not even an emperor, attained such happiness as to see two sons, not yet advanced to the customary age, adorned with the dignity of the consulship in the same year, as Boethius saw. Rome did indeed see, in the same year—namely 395—Olybrius and Probinus, the two sons of Probus, colleagues in the consulship; but they had already ceased to be boys. Thus we may exclaim with Claudian, *Carmen* I, line 72:

> What god could be the author of so great a gift to both?

“Do you therefore wish to reckon with Fortune?”

To reckon is, generally, to use a little stone; specifically, it is the familiar token used by those who calculate. Hence Pliny the Younger says in Book II, Letter 14: “In choosing conditions, one must cast the reckoning stone.” Juvenal, Satire 9:

> Let the reckoning stone be cast; let the boys  
> be present with the tablet.

When it is said that someone “reckons with Fortune,” this means that, having compared the good and evil received from Fortune, he calculates—on his fingers, joints, pebbles, or any other signs—which total is greater.

[Note: “To reckon with Fortune—to review the accounts with Fortune.”]

Philosophy indicates that Boethius’ present adversity is far less than his former prosperity, as though she were saying: Fortune, prosperous from your earliest years, is now beginning to be adverse; and even this adversity is not inflicted by actions but merely by an envious glance—not seriously, but only by lightly touching you. Indeed, if anything seems intolerable, it will soon vanish. Therefore, if you consider the number and measure of your joys and sorrows, you still cannot deny that you are happy.

[Note: “Now she has first looked upon you with an envious eye.”]

“Now she has for the first time struck you with an envious eye. If you consider the number and measure of your joys and sorrows, you still cannot deny that you are happy. But if you do not consider yourself fortunate for this reason—that the things which then seemed joyful have departed—there is no reason for you to think yourself miserable, since the things now believed sorrowful are passing away.”

112 *Scaena*, Greek *σκηνή* (*skēnē*), “a shelter,” first meant a chamber made, naturally or artificially, from the mutually overhanging branches and foliage of trees, where especially in spring shepherds sang songs in varied melodies. Thus Vergil, *Aeneid* I.166:

> On either side huge cliffs, and twin crags threaten the sky;  
> beneath their summit the waters lie broadly quiet,  
> while above a stage gleams with waving woods,  
> and a dark grove hangs over it with bristling shade.

It then meant the concealed part of a theatre where actors customarily lay hidden behind curtains or other coverings; finally, a brief but complete theatrical action, in which the same person often plays different characters, now sad, now happy. Human life may therefore be called a stage: swift time itself often dissolves a person, and in human life sorrows succeed joys, as in the world night succeeds day, the south wind the west wind, and storm calm. The following poem treats this subject.

“Have you now suddenly entered this theater of life as a stranger? Do you think that anything in human affairs possesses stability, when swift time itself often dissolves the human being? For although there is rarely any reliability of permanence in things governed by chance, the final day of life is nevertheless also a kind of death of Fortune, even of Fortune that remains constant. What difference, then, do you think it makes? Do you abandon her by dying, or does she flee from you?”

113 **METER III**

[Note: A poem consisting of two alternating kinds of verse. The first is Sapphic, composed of a trochee, a spondee, a dactyl, and two trochees; the second is Glyconic, usually composed of a spondee and two dactyls.]

**Argument.** Philosophy proves, by the alternation of day and night, the west wind and the south wind, and the calm and storm of the sea, that nothing generated is constant.

[Col. 0674B]

[Note: “When the sun, carried in a four-horse chariot, first begins to spread daylight through the heavens, the nocturnal stars, subdued by the sun’s pressing fires, grow pale, their brightness contracted. When the forest has been reddened with roses by the gently warming breath of the west wind of spring, if the misty south wind blows wildly, its adornment must immediately depart from the rose bushes.
