Often the sea shines with tranquil calm when its waves are at rest; and often the north wind raises violent storms, disturbing the sea. If, therefore, an unchanging form is rare throughout the whole circle of the earth; if the world undergoes such great changes, go now and trust in the fragile riches of mortals; trust in fleeting goods. It has been decreed and established by God’s everlasting law that nothing generated should persist unchanged.”]

> When Phoebus, from the pole, with his rose-colored four-horse chariot  
> begins to spread light across the heavens,
>
> the star, its bright face dulled by the pressing flames,  
> grows pale;

[Col. 0675A]
>
> [5] 114 When the grove, by the breath of the warming west wind,  
> has reddened with roses of spring,
>
> let the misty south wind blow wildly:  
> now let beauty depart from the thorns.
>
> Often, in tranquil calm, the sea radiates  
> [10] with unmoving waves;
>
> 115 Often the north wind stirs boiling storms  
> across the overturned sea.
>
> If an unchanging form is rare in the world,  
> if it varies through such great alternations,
>
> [15] trust in the fleeting fortunes of human beings;  
> trust in fugitive goods.
>
> It is established, and fixed by eternal law,  
> that nothing generated remains constant.

[Col. 0674D]

1. **The Pole (*Polo*).** *Polus*, Greek *πόλος*, generally means every circuit, for it is said to derive *ἀπὸ τοῦ πολεῖν*, “from *polein*,” meaning “to turn.” Specifically, however, it means the heavens, because the heavens turn. Therefore the unmoving extremity of the axis could be called a pole by astronomers only *κατ` ἀντίφρασιν* (“by antiphrasis”).

1. **Phoebus (*Phoebus*).** The sun. On Phoebus, see Book I, Meter 3, verse 9. Moreover, Lucretius, Book V: > While the sun brings light into the heavens with his rosy torch.

[Col. 0675B]

1. **“With a rose-colored four-horse chariot” (*Roseis quodrigis*, as printed).** The sun is imagined by poets to travel in a four-horse chariot, drawn by four horses: *Pyrois*, *Eous*, *Aethon*, and *Phlegon*. These names signify fire, light, heat, and flame, the four chief effects of the sun; they also signify the four principal hours of the day. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II.153:

> Meanwhile the winged Pyroeis, Eous, and Aethon,  
> the horses of the sun, and fourth, Phlegon, fill the air  
> with their fire-bearing neighing and strike the barriers with their feet.

The rising sun is therefore said, on the one hand, to spread the day with its greater light and, on the other, to drive away the lesser stars that ruled through the night. The sun is consequently said to spread light, while the star, its brightness dulled by the sun’s pressing flames, grows pale. This is the alternation of night and day, with which the passage begins.

5. **“Of Zephyrus” (*Zephyri*).** The second alternation treated here is that of the winds, namely Zephyrus and Auster. The latter succeeds the former in such a way that what arises from the earlier wind perishes when the later one blows.

[Col. 0675C]

Zephyrus is the wind blowing from the equinoctial west. It is therefore mild and warm and is said for that reason to fertilize the earth. Hence among the Greeks it is called *ζέφυρος*, as though *ζοηφόρος* (“life-bearing”; the printed form stands for the usual *ζωηφόρος*); among the Latins it is called *favonius*, as though “the spirit that fosters the birth of the world,” from *fovere*, “to warm,” as Pliny says in Book XVI, chapter 25. Vergil, *Georgics* II.330:

> The kindly earth gives birth, and the warm breezes of Zephyrus  
> loosen the fields and open their bosoms.

For this reason the grove is now said to have been reddened with spring roses by the breath of warm Zephyrus.

Auster, however, is the wind blowing from the south. Hence, among peoples whose sea lies to the south, Auster is called the “transmarine” wind. This wind is considered both damp and hot. First, it is considered damp because it gathers the moisture which the north wind scatters. Thus Vergil calls it “damp,” Horace “wet,” Ovid “watery,” Claudian “soaked,” Saint Augustine “the cupbearer of rains,” and Boethius “misty.” Second, it is considered hot because it blows from the south.

[Col. 0675D]

Whether through its moisture, its heat, or both, this wind is said to harm animals, plants, and especially flowers. Hence Vergil, *Georgics* I.444:

> Known to trees and crops, and hostile to the flocks.

And *Eclogues* II.38:

> Alas, what have I wished for myself in my misery? In my madness  
> I have let the south wind upon the flowers  
> and wild boars into the clear springs.

The south wind is especially harmful to roses. Hence Statius, *Silvae* III.3:

> The budding roses are the first to die beneath the south winds.

For this reason Auster is here said to blow “madly,” that is, in a mad fashion; and when this same wind blows, beauty is said to depart from the thorns—that is, the rose perishes. The rose, queen of flowers, is both the offspring and the beauty of thorns. Accordingly, Antonius Hallaeus, once an ornament of our University of Normandy, sang of the rose with his customary elegance:

[Col. 0676B]

> Yet remember your origin,  
> O beautiful rose: an ugly thorn created you.

9. **“Often in tranquil calm” (*Saepe tranquillo*).** The third alternation introduced here as an example is that of the calm and storm of the sea. First the calm of the sea is described.

First, it is described as “in tranquil serenity,” or “with serene calm”—for grammarians treat *tranquillum* and *serenum* as substantive nouns—because a calm sea is free of winds.

Second, it is described as having “unmoving waves,” because, in the absence of winds, the sea, moved only by its ordinary motion, is not thrown into disorder.

Third, it is described as radiating with rays reflected by the sea. Depending on the manner in which it reflects rays, especially solar rays, the sea appears to share at one time in light, at another in color, and indeed in various colors. Thus Cicero says in the *Academica*: “That sea which now, when the west wind begins to rise, appears purple, seemed blue to us, yellow in the morning; and what now, because it shines in the sun, grows white and glitters, is unlike the neighboring mainland.”

[Col. 0676C]

Light falling upon calm or quiet waves is reflected by them in much the same way as by a mirror. Thus, like a mirror, still water can both strike the eyes and reproduce faces opposite it, according to the different manner in which the light reflected from these bodies affects the eyes. Here, however, only the radiation is at issue, since it can be diffused farther than the other effect of a mirror. Thus the calm of the sea is described.

[Col. 0676A]

11. **“Often with boiling storms” (*Saepe ferventeis*).** Next the storm of this same sea is treated: its violent motion, by which the sea is stirred by the winds, especially by the north wind. Aquilo, called *boreas* by the Greeks, is the wind blowing from the summer sunrise. It is a stronger wind, perhaps because it is carried by the same motion by which air ordinarily travels from east to west. Hence, according to Festus, it is called *Aquilo* because it is borne with the most violent flight, like an eagle; and, in Saint Augustine’s judgment, it is the broom of the lands.

The antithesis between the calm and storm of the sea may be noted: through the repetition of the word, *Aquilo* is opposed to the calm; boiling storms to the serene condition; and the overturned sea to the unmoving waves.

[Col. 0676D]

13. **“The world is constant” (*Constat mundo*).** Thus Pliny the Younger says, “Reverence is established for magistrates.” And Vergil, *Aeneid* V.748:

> What judgment now remains fixed in your mind?

15. **“Trust in fortunes” (*Crede fortunis*).** This is a witty and elegant dissimulation, which the supplied text calls *ὲιρωιείαν* (a corrupt spelling of *εἰρωνεία*, *eirōneia*). Philosophy says something other than she thinks and thereby withdraws still more from fleeting goods, the more she appears to attribute trustworthiness to them. Thus Seneca in *Medea*, line 221:

> Trust in kingdoms, when fickle chance  
> carries great riches here and there.

17. **“It is established, and fixed by eternal law” (*Constat, aeterna positumque lege est*).** A law is the honorable will of a ruler commanding and forbidding contrary things. Accordingly, there can be as many kinds of laws as there are kinds of rulers’ wills. Such will is twofold, divine and human; therefore law is also twofold, divine and human. Human law is not under discussion here.

[Col. 0677B]

Divine law, according to the three ways in which it can be considered, is again of three kinds: eternal, natural, and what is commonly called positive law.

Eternal law is the divine will insofar as, like God, whose will it is, it has existed from all eternity. Cicero speaks of this law in Book II of *On the Laws*: “I see this to have been the opinion of the wisest: that law was not devised by human intelligence, nor some decree of peoples, but something eternal which would govern the whole universe with the wisdom of commanding and forbidding.”

116 Natural law is the same divine will insofar as it is made known to human beings through an implanted and innate form. The same Tully speaks of this in Book I of *On the Laws*: “Law is reason implanted in nature, which commands what ought to be done and forbids the contrary.”

The law commonly called positive law is the same will of God insofar as it becomes known through a sign by which it is manifested. For Christians this law is of two kinds, the old and the new.

[Col. 0677C]

Since nothing occurs except through the will of the eternal God, nothing occurs except through eternal law. Among philosophers, however, some things that occur are said to be created and others generated. Those things are created whose only cause is external—namely, *res*, things or entities. Those things are generated which, in addition to an external cause, possess some matter—namely, *modi*, modes or modifications. Things or entities persist, but modes change. It is established and fixed by eternal law that nothing generated remains constant. Hence Seneca, *Hercules on Oeta*, line 1099:

> Whatever has been born will be able to die.

117 **PROSE IV**

[Col. 0677A]

**Argument.** Philosophy, once again setting forth Boethius’ father-in-law, wife, and children, as well as his mind—all of which Boethius still possesses—proves that he ought to be considered more fortunate than unfortunate.

Then I, Boethius [Note: [Col. 0677A] Boethius.], said: “You recall true things, O Philosophy [Note: [Col. 0677C] The nurturer of all the virtues. For since philosophy is clear and distinct knowledge of those things that pertain to the best ordering of life and morals, and since evidence is the standard of true and certain judgment, philosophy, like a most wise mother, leads her hearers and pupils first to judge well and then to live honorably. Hence, in Cicero’s judgment, philosophy is the mother of all beneficent and blessed things; it is the cultivation of the mind, which uproots vices; it contains the discipline of virtue, duty, and right living.], nurse of all the virtues, and I cannot deny [Note: [Col. 0677D] *Infitiari.* Or, as others prefer, *inficiare*, according to the differing interpretation of the word. It means the same as “to deny.” For *inficior* seems to arise from *in-* and *facio*, as though I were denying that I had done something; in that case it should be written with *c*, *inficior*. Or rather it may arise from *in-* and *fateor*, as though it meant “I do not confess.” For the Latins sometimes said *infiteor*, just as they still say *confiteor*; in that case it should be written with *t*, *infitior*. I would prefer the latter.] the exceedingly rapid course of my prosperity. But this is what sears a person more intensely when he recalls it [Note: [Col. 0677D] “Afflicts one who remembers more severely.” *Recolere* is said to derive from *colere*, which properly means “to plough.” But since the earth is turned over by ploughing, the verb was transferred to signify the thought by which our mind is, as it were, stirred. Hence the *cultus* of parents, which consists chiefly in thought: we are said to honor them because we venerate them especially in our minds. Hence also *recolere* means to think through repeated meditation, to recall, to remember. Examples occur everywhere. *Coquere* means the same as *angere*, or even *cogere*. The likeness is taken from bodies: just as bodies that are cooked or compressed normally become more tightly packed as their parts approach one another and are reduced to narrower spaces, so the mind appears to be constricted by its own sad reflection, so that it becomes less capable of thinking about other matters and can no longer extend itself further in thought.] [Note: [Col. 0677A] “One who remembers.”] [Note: [Col. 0677A] “Afflicts.”]. For in every adversity of fortune the most wretched kind of misfortune is to have been happy. 118 [Note: [Col. 0678B] “The kind of misfortune is to have been happy.”] Not in reality—for what has passed is no longer present and therefore, being as it were nothing, cannot actually afflict you—but in thought. For just as we are refreshed by the memory of past evils—“This remembrance of former things will one day bring joy,” as Virgil says—because by them we are reminded of some power, diligence, or other good quality of our own, so we are afflicted by the memory of past goods, because by it we are convicted of our weakness: for just as it pleases a person to have been able to do something, so it displeases the glory-seeking person not to be able to do it.”

“But,” she said [Note: [Col. 0677B] Philosophy.], “you are paying the penalty of a false opinion [Note: [Col. 0678C] “The punishment of a false opinion.”] and cannot rightly attribute that punishment to circumstances. For the memory of past prosperity is indeed a punishment or suffering of the mind, since, as has been said, the mind is afflicted by that memory. But that punishment arises from a false opinion, because the mind, driven on by precipitancy and prejudice, falsely judged that former prosperity to possess the character of some stable good. Therefore you cannot justly charge circumstances with that punishment: no one errs except willingly.” [Note: [Col. 0678C] “You are paying the penalty of a false opinion.”]

“For if this empty name of accidental happiness [Note: [Col. 0678A] “This empty name of accidental happiness.”] moves you, although you abound in many and very great things, you may consider them with me. Therefore, if what you possessed as the most precious thing in the whole inventory of your fortune [Note: [Col. 0678A] “Among all the goods of your fortune.”] has, by divine providence, remained so far safe and untouched, can you, while retaining the better things [Note: [Col. 0678C] “Can you, while retaining the better things, justly complain of misfortune?”]—but let us suppose,” said Philosophy, “that what is accidental is true happiness—when you retain the greater part of the goods that you think ought to be credited to fortune, can you, being happy rather than unhappy, justly complain of misfortune?” *Caussari*, or, as many now write it, *causari*, properly means nothing other than to seek or allege the cause of some effect. Thus Virgil, *Eclogue* 9, line 56:

> By pleading causes, you prolong our loves.

“Boethius, therefore, who has hitherto complained about adverse fortune, and who seems to have sought from it the causes of such great inconstancy, is not improperly said now to be ‘complaining,’ although he complains unjustly, as Philosophy will now show by enumerating the better goods that remain to him—namely, his father-in-law, wife, children, and even his own mind.”]

“Can you, while retaining the better things, rightly complain of misfortune?” [Note: [Col. 0678A] “To accuse calamity.”]

“And yet,” she continued, “there remains unharmed that most precious glory of the human race, your father-in-law Symmachus. I. Philosophy commends Symmachus, Boethius’ father-in-law. There were several men named Symmachus; if you wish, you may read their genealogy in Jacob Sirmond’s notes on Book VII of Ennodius’ letters. Here, however, the reference is to Symmachus, who was consul without a colleague under Odoacer in the year of Christ 485, and who was selected by King Theoderic, among others, as judge in the case of Basilius and Praetextatus, who were accused of magical arts, as Cassiodorus reports, *Variarum* Book IV, Letter 22. This Symmachus had two daughters: Galla, about whom, besides Fulgentius, Gregory the Great speaks in *Dialogues* IV.13, and Rusticiana, the wife of Boethius, by whom another Symmachus was born. That latter Symmachus was Boethius’ father’s colleague in the consulship and the grandson of the Symmachus just mentioned. Nor was that outstanding man so secure from personal injury as Boethius seemed to think, on account of the favor and influence that he appeared to enjoy with Theoderic. For that unstable king, inflamed by the wicked accusations of informers, ordered Symmachus, Boethius’ father-in-law, to be killed together with his son-in-law Boethius, according to Procopius, Book I, *On the Gothic War*.”]

“Your father-in-law Symmachus—a man whom you would willingly purchase at the price of your life [Note: [Col. 0678A] “Willingly.”], wholly formed by wisdom and virtues, [Note: [Col. 0678B] “Fearing no injuries to himself.”] secure regarding his own injuries—laments your injuries.” 119

“Your wife lives [Note: [Col. 0679C] “The wife lives.”], a woman modest in character, outstanding in the shamefastness of her chastity, and, to sum up all her virtues briefly, like her father. [Note: [Col. 0679B] Rusticiana.] II. Philosophy praises Boethius’ wife, namely Rusticiana, daughter of Symmachus. Boethius had two wives in succession: the first was Elpis, daughter of Festus, a most learned woman, who died without children; the other was Rusticiana, daughter of Symmachus, modest in character and pre-eminent in the modesty of her chastity—indeed, in a word, like her father Symmachus. She lives, I say, and preserves her life solely for you, although she hates this life; and I might even concede that your happiness is diminished by one thing: she wastes away from longing for you, in tears and sorrow.”

“Your children—what shall I say of them? [Note: [Col. 0679C] “What shall I say of the children?”] III. Philosophy celebrates Boethius’ children, remembering both their dignity and the talent with which they were endowed. She does indeed remember the dignity with which they were equipped, namely, the consulship; for among the Latins a man who was once consul is called *consularis*. Philosophy now calls Boethius’ children “consular,” although they were still boys. She also remembers their talent, which was so great even in these boys that in them there shone a specimen either of their father Boethius’ own talent or of their grandfather Symmachus’. Finally, the expression “for boys of that age” is a manner of speaking familiar even to Cicero. Thus he says in Book VI of his *Letters*, Letter 20: “Thus we have lived, and we have now reached such an age that we ought to bear bravely all that happens to us through no fault of our own.”]

“What shall I say of your consular children [Note: [Col. 0679B] “Who have already been consuls.”], in whom, though they are still boys of that age, there already shines a specimen either of their father’s [Note: [Col. 0679B] Boethius.] or of their grandfather’s [Note: [Col. 0679B] Symmachus.] talent?”

“From what has been said Philosophy concludes that Boethius is still happy, as though she were saying: whoever possesses those things that no one doubts to be dearer than life may be considered happy; for happy is the person who enjoys the highest good, and that seems to be what is dearer than life itself, since mortals are especially concerned to preserve life, as the highest good. But you, Boethius, possess things that no one doubts to be dearer than life—namely, a father-in-law, wife, and children, all outstanding in every virtue. I would believe that these words, ‘O happy are you, if you knew your blessings,’ were not spoken without recollection of Virgil, *Aeneid* II, line 458:

> O farmers, far too fortunate, if only they knew their blessings!

“When the chief concern of mortals is to preserve life, happy are you, if you know your blessings, since you still possess those things that no one doubts to be dearer than life. Therefore dry your tears. Fortune has not yet become wholly hostile [Note: [Col. 0679B] “The anchors.”], nor has a storm [Note: [Col. 0680B] “The storm.”] of excessive violence fallen upon you.”

“This is an allegory very common in Cicero himself. When a storm is mentioned, the attack of raging fortune is to be understood, since human beings seem to be overwhelmed by both. When strong anchors are mentioned, the most steadfast relatives are intended, since from both of these there may be present consolation for the present and hope for the future. Therefore, just as, while the anchors remain, sailors retain hope of swimming to safety, so, while the relatives mentioned above remain, Boethius may hope for better fortune.”]

“When tenacious anchors cling, which do not allow either present consolation or hope for the future to be absent, the storm has not overwhelmed you. And may they cling, I pray; while they remain, whatever happens, we shall swim to safety.” [Note: [Col. 0680B] “I, Boethius.”] “But you see how much distinction has been taken away from our adornments [Note: [Col. 0680C] Namely, with our wealth and dignities lost.].”

“And we have made some progress,” she said [Note: [Col. 0680B] Philosophy.], “in consoling you. [Note: [Col. 0680C] “We have advanced somewhat.” *Promovere* sometimes means the same as *proficere*, “to make progress,” as in Terence, *Hecyra*: “I shall leave here; I accomplish little by remaining.”—if you are not yet entirely displeased with your whole lot. [Note: [Col. 0680B] “If you are not yet weary of your entire condition.”] *Pudet* and *piget* differ: the former seems to signify shame, the latter rather distress at a harmful circumstance. Hence Cicero, *Pro Domo*: “I am not only distressed by my folly, but also ashamed of it.”] But I cannot endure your softness [Note: [Col. 0680C] “Luxuries.” *Deliciae* mean softness of spirit. They seem to be so called because the mind is attracted by them, from *de* and *lacio*, “I draw”: hence *lactat*, *illectat*, *delectat*, *oblectat*, *allicit*, *illicit*, *elicit*. Thus Lucretius, Book V:

> Which might lure them into fraud and hold them bound.

“Since the mind is attracted by any disturbance, but especially by love and pleasure, every disturbance, and particularly love and pleasure, is therefore called *deliciae*. Hence *deliciae* may be understood either positively or negatively. Just as bodily softness consists in the body’s being easily turned in any direction, so a mind is called delicate when it is subject to contrary affections and can easily be bent in every direction. Boethius seems to be such a person, since he complains so mournfully and anxiously that something is absent from his happiness.]”

“I cannot endure your softness [Note: [Col. 0680B] “The softness of your mind.”], when you complain so mournfully and anxiously that something is absent from your happiness. For who possesses happiness so perfectly composed [Note: [Col. 0680B] “Perfect.”] that he does not in some respect quarrel [Note: [Col. 0681A] “Dispute.” *Rixa* is a quarrel, dispute, or contention between two or more people, one of whom demands something that the other refuses to return. Thus, unless divine light shines upon them, there are perpetual quarrels among all human beings: human beings and their condition oppose each other like separate parties, so that a person seems to demand from his condition something that the condition refuses to give back. No one is happy in every respect.] with the character of his condition?”

“Anxiety is the condition of human goods [Note: [Col. 0681B] “The condition of human goods is an anxious matter.”], and one that either never comes to completion in its entirety or never remains perpetual.” [Note: [Col. 0681A] “Bitter.” *Anxium* is what presses upon someone with sorrowful concern. It is said to derive from *ango*, from the Greek ἄγκω, “I strangle, constrict,” first the throat and then the mind. Hence *angustus* and *angustia*, when someone is oppressed by such difficulties that he does not know where to turn. The condition of human goods presses upon the mind with sorrowful concern: for because this human condition is either never complete or never lasting, it always leaves room either for seeking the acquisition of absent goods or for fearing the loss of present ones. Hence anxiety of mind, as Philosophy will subsequently confirm with many examples.]

121 [Note: [Col. 0681B] “His wealth overflows.”]

“His wealth overflows, but his degenerate blood is a source of shame.” [Note: [Col. 0681A] “One man abounds in wealth, but is ashamed of his low birth.”]

“This is the first example, concerning the rich—those whose wealth is said to overflow because they abound in riches. *Census*, derived from *censere*, signifies wealth. Thus Claudian, *Poem* 17, line 231:

> And let them heap up treasuries with the assessed wealth of men.

“*Exuberare* means ‘to abound,’ as though something were flowing beyond the udders. Thus Virgil, *Georgics* I, line 191:

> But if the luxuriance of leaves overflows the shade.

“And *Georgics* II, line 516:

> Nor is there rest, whether the year overflows with fruits,  
> or with the offspring of herds.

“Such rich people consider themselves unhappy because those to whom they are related by blood are not noble; but degenerate blood is a disgrace.”]

“He is made known by nobility [Note: [Col. 0681C] “Nobility makes him known.”].” [Note: [Col. 0681C] The second example concerns noblemen. Here Philosophy seems to press the force of the word when she says, “nobility makes him known.” For *nobilis* is said from *notus*, “known,” just as *mobilis* is said from *motus*, “moved,” so that a noble person is one known through the distinction of his name. Yet these noblemen too may find their poverty a punishment. Enclosed by the narrowness of his household resources, a certain nobleman might prefer to be unknown. Poverty is very properly called “the narrowness of household resources”: just as a rich man, surrounded by palaces, fields, vineyards, money, herds, and people subject to him, seems so enlarged in authority and power that he readily considers himself invincible, according to Proverbs VIII: “The substance of the rich is his strong city”; so a poor man, as though crushed beneath his hut, little field, small vine, and burden of children, is constricted. Hence Horace, *Odes* III.2, calls poverty “narrow”:

> Let a boy, strong in harsh warfare,  
> learn to endure narrow poverty, my friend.]

“This man is noble, but oppressed by poverty; enclosed by the narrowness of his household resources, he would prefer to be unknown.” [Note: [Col. 0682A] “Another is noble but oppressed by poverty.”]

“He is surrounded by both [Note: [Col. 0681D] “He is surrounded by both.”].” [Note: [Col. 0681D] The third example concerns those who are both rich and noble, but who consider themselves unhappy because they lead a life without marriage. They lament a celibate life; a life without marriage is called *caelebs*, perhaps because it resembles the heavenly.]

“He, overflowing with both, laments a celibate life.” [Note: [Col. 0682A] “The third, both rich and noble, grieves that he lacks a spouse.”]

“He is happy in marriage [Note: [Col. 0682B] “He who is happy in marriage.”].” [Note: [Col. 0682B] The fourth example concerns the man who is happy in his wife. This is well signified by the marriage just mentioned. Although marriage involves both spouses, it is nevertheless more properly spoken of with reference to the wife than to the husband, because when the bride was led to her husband she married, or veiled her face, with the *flammeum*. Hence *nupta*, *connubium*, and so forth. Great, moreover, is the husband’s happiness when he has an excellent wife; it is a heavenly gift. Proverbs XIX says: “House and riches are given by parents, but a prudent wife is especially from the Lord.” Yet this happiness is often disturbed by childlessness: childless, he nourishes wealth for another’s heir. Seneca, *Hippolytus*, line 1248:

> O sad calamity of childlessness in broken years!

“An heir, from *heres*, ‘master,’ as though he were the master of the goods, is of two kinds among the jurists: namely, one’s own and an external heir. One’s own heirs, as stated in the *Institutes* II.19.2, are so called because they are household heirs and are regarded as masters in a certain sense even while their father lives—for example, a son, daughter, grandson or granddaughter through a son, and the other descendants. External heirs, here called alien heirs, are, says Vinnius, all the others who are not one’s own and domestic heirs. But just as a man who loves himself and his own rejoices in his own heirs, so he is distressed by external or alien heirs. Ecclesiastes IV says: ‘I considered and found another vanity under the sun. There is one alone, and he has no second—not a son, not a brother—and yet he does not cease laboring; his eyes are not satisfied with riches, nor does he reflect, saying, “For whom do I labor and defraud my soul of good things?” This too is vanity and a most grievous affliction.’”]

“He who is happy in marriage, but childless, prepares wealth for another’s heir.” 122 [Note: [Col. 0682C] “Another rejoices in offspring.”]

“This is the fifth example, concerning the man who rejoices in the birth of children. Since a human being, created in the image of God, desires eternity but cannot attain it on earth, it follows that each parent rejoices when a child is born, as though a great part of the parent were one day to succeed to the parent’s place. John XVI says: ‘A woman does not remember her anguish because of her joy that a human being has been born into the world.’ But just as parents are filled with great joy by children who are born and who cultivate virtue, so they are affected by equal sorrow if they see those children indulge in vices. A parent grieves and weeps over the sins of a son or daughter. Proverbs X says: ‘A wise son makes his father glad, but a foolish son is the sorrow of his mother.’ The reason is that children seem to be the sounder and more enduring part of their parents; therefore parents wish their children to be better than themselves.”]

“Another, rejoicing in offspring, weeps sadly over the sins of his son or daughter.” [Note: [Col. 0682A] “Vices.”]

“For this reason no one easily agrees with the condition of his fortune, since each person possesses something that the inexperienced do not know and the experienced dread. Add that the more fortunate a person is, the more delicate his sensibility is; and unless everything is present at his command [Note: [Col. 0682D] “At his will.” *Nutus*, derived from *nuere* or *movere*, properly signifies bodily movement. Thus, by moving our head or eyes, we are said to assent, dissent, or reject. Since this bodily movement customarily indicates our will, the sign came to be understood for the thing signified, and *nutus* came to signify not only human but also divine will. Hence *numen* itself denotes the will of God, as in Virgil, *Aeneid* XI, line 336:

> By the divine will I am driven into flames and arms.

“And line 777:

> These things do not happen without the will of the gods.] and is available to him [Note: [Col. 0683B] “Everything is present according to his choice.”] and is available to him [Note: [Col. 0683B] “Is at hand.”].” Since what is requested is more often obtained, usage has established that *suppetere* means the same as “to be present,” as though something had been obtained by asking. Hence *suppetiae*, which those endangered by adversity seek when they desire them to be available to them.]

“Every person unaccustomed to adversity [Note: [Col. 0683B] “Unaccustomed to any adversity.”] is overthrown by the smallest adversities.” *Insolens* means almost “not accustomed”; one is *solens* when one does what one is wholly engaged in, as though one were occupied with this one and only business. Therefore a person unaccustomed to adversity is one who has not been trained by adversity. Such a person, as is now added, is overthrown by the smallest adversities, because a mind unaccustomed to these disturbances is upset by the least thing. For just as passion does not arise from what is familiar, so it arises from what is unfamiliar, as the philosophers say. So very slight are the things that take away from the sum of happiness even of the most fortunate. In arithmetic, a sum is a whole formed by adding several smaller amounts, or that from which a smaller amount remains after subtraction. Thus here the sum of happiness means nothing other than the height or fullness of happiness—*le comble du bonheur*.]

“So very slight are the things that take away from the most fortunate the sum of their happiness.” 123 [Note: [Col. 0683C] “How many.”]

“How many people do you suppose there are [Note: [Col. 0683B] “You do not doubt.”] who would consider themselves almost equal to heaven [Note: [Col. 0683B] “Happy.”] if even the smallest portion of the remnants of your fortune came to them? This very place, which you call exile, is a homeland to those who inhabit it. Nothing, therefore, is miserable unless you think there is misery in it [Note: [Col. 0683B] “That there is something miserable in it.”]. Conversely, every condition is happy if it is endured with equanimity [Note: [Col. 0683C] “A happy lot.”]. A happy person is one whose mind is so constant in reflection that, like a balance steadied by equal weights, it is neither raised by prosperity nor depressed by adversity. But such a person is rare on earth; for who is so happy that, after having surrendered to impatience [Note: [Col. 0683D] “Has surrendered to impatience.”], he does not wish to change his condition? Cicero speaks similarly in *On Friendship*: ‘And finally he gives up; he allows himself to be conquered.’ Since a person ordinarily defends himself especially with his hands, once it is understood that he has yielded his hands, he is understood to have been defeated.]

“What person is so happy that, after having surrendered to impatience [Note: [Col. 0684B] “Has thought himself unable to endure.”], he does not wish to change his condition?” [Note: [Col. 0683D] “Does not desire to change his state.”] Like a sick person who cannot endure any position and turns himself in every direction.]

“Human happiness is sprinkled with how many bitter things [Note: [Col. 0683D] We have already observed that the human mind, as it lies midway between God and the human body, insofar as it is the work of God and the form of this body, is moved both by God and by the human body. From this, we think, arise the bitterness and sweetness of human happiness: sweetness from God who moves it, bitterness from the body. Since a human being, so long as he continues to exist, is affected by both causes, nothing is sweet to a human being unless it is joined with bitterness. Therefore of every bodily pleasure it may be said what Lucretius said of love in Book IV:

> Fine clothing, feasts, and food, games,  
> frequent cups, perfumes, garlands, wreaths are prepared:  
> in vain, since from the very fountain of delights  
> something bitter rises, which torments amid the flowers.

“Indeed, sweetness itself is bitter in this respect: against the will of the person who seems to experience it, it departs irreversibly and cannot be retained at will so as to prevent its departure, as is said here.] How many bitter things are mixed into the sweetness of human happiness! Even if it seems pleasant to the person enjoying it, it cannot be retained so that it may not depart whenever it wishes.” 124 [Note: [Col. 0684B] “It is clear, therefore.”]

“It is therefore clear how wretched is the happiness of mortal things: it neither endures perpetually among the equanimous nor wholly delights the anxious.”

“From the foregoing examples Philosophy concludes what she undertook to prove at note 18: that present human happiness is neither so complete that it wholly delights those who are anxious, nor so lasting that it endures forever even among the equanimous. Now, returning to the point from which she had digressed, Philosophy will consider Boethius’ own mind.”

“IV. Philosophy commends the mind of Boethius. First she says that mortals vainly seek outside themselves—in friends, wife, children, and, in a word, in the body—the happiness that they possess within themselves, namely, in the mind. Then she adds that mortals are confused by error and ignorance, since they seek outside themselves the happiness they possess within. Here it should be noted that error and ignorance differ in various respects, including this: every error arises from ignorance, so that there can be ignorance without error, but not error without ignorance. She then promises to show Boethius the hinge of supreme happiness, that is, the thing on which supreme happiness chiefly turns. Since a hinge is the point on which a door turns, usage has made the point on which any matter turns be called its *cardo*. Virgil, *Aeneid* I, line 676:

> It will not cease amid so great a hinge of affairs.]”

“What, then, O mortals, do you seek outside yourselves for the happiness placed within you [Note: [Col. 0684B] “Within your mind.”]? Error and ignorance confuse you. I shall briefly show you the hinge of supreme happiness.” [Note: [Col. 0684B] “O Boethius.”] 125

“Is there anything more precious to you than yourself [Note: [Col. 0684D] “Is there anything more precious to you than your mind?”]?”

“You will say, ‘Nothing.’” [Note: [Col. 0684D] “Nothing.”] “For whatever I know by the natural light to have been divinely made is either my mind or the body commonly called matter. But my mind is more precious than the body or matter itself, because it thinks about this matter, which cannot think about the mind, and by its own choice repeatedly turns it this way and that through thought.”

“Therefore, if you are master of yourself [Note: [Col. 0685B] “Of your own mind.”], you will possess [Note: [Col. 0685C] “It will be in your power.”] what you will never wish to lose. [Note: [Col. 0685C] As your knowledge of your mind, and therefore of your origin, increases, so too will your love of your mind and origin increase; for external goods are loved less in proportion as they are understood more.] For your mind, and consequently your thought, are so subject to your authority that inconstant fortune can do nothing to them. Fortune can indeed place before you the happiness that she flaunts as something desirable; but she cannot deceive you by persuasion unless you are willing. You will not be willing until, forgetful of your mind and its origin, you have been blinded, as it were, by the appearance of perishable goods.”

“And so that you may recognize this, Philosophy, by presenting the human mind and external goods, proves by certain arguments that true happiness lies in the mind rather than in the other goods. To understand these arguments, it should be noted that among moral philosophers the highest good is of two kinds: one in the category of thing, the other in the category of mode. The former is the supremely perfect thing; hence it is nothing other than God. Therefore the prophet-king, Psalm 143, after describing the mighty, whose sons are ‘like young plants in their youth,’ whose daughters are ‘adorned and embellished like the form of a temple,’ whose storehouses are full and overflowing from one thing to another, whose sheep are fertile and abundant in their pastures, whose oxen are fat, and whose streets have neither breach in the wall nor passage nor cry, and whom they called blessed, adds: ‘Blessed is the people whose Lord is their God.’

“The latter, which is otherwise called happiness or blessedness, seems to me capable of being defined as the thought of a mind constantly clinging to God. Whatever is recognized by the natural light as belonging to happiness can belong only to this thought, as we have proved more fully elsewhere. Here, however, the discussion is not about the former but only about the latter highest good, since it is said to be the mode of a nature living according to reason—that is, of the human mind.”]

“And so that you may recognize that blessedness cannot consist in these accidental things, reason as follows. If blessedness is the highest good of a rational nature [Note: [Col. 0685B] “Of a nature endowed with reason.”], that is not the highest good which can in any way be taken away, since what cannot be taken away is superior. It is evident that the instability of fortune cannot aspire to the attainment of happiness. [Note: [Col. 0685B] “Inconstancy of fortune cannot be happiness.”]

“First, an argument may be proposed in this way. Whatever good can be taken away—that is, can be lost against the will of its possessor—is not the highest good, not even in the category of mode, since within that category what cannot be taken away is better. But every good of fortune can be taken away, for this is why fortune is unstable. The good of the mind, however, such as virtue, cannot be taken away—that is, cannot be lost against the will of its possessor.”

“Furthermore [Note: [Col. 0685B] “Moreover.”], whoever is carried along by this mortal happiness [Note: [Col. 0685B] “Who is affected by this happiness.”] either knows or does not know that it is mutable. If he does not know, what kind of happy lot can there be in the blindness of ignorance? If he knows, he must fear that he may lose what he does not doubt can be lost; and continuous fear does not permit happiness. Or, even if he has lost it, does he think it should be disregarded [Note: [Col. 0686B] “Even if.”]? Even so, that good is exceedingly slight which can be lost and yet endured with equanimity.” 126

“Third, since you are the very person who, through many demonstrations, I know has been convinced and inwardly persuaded that human minds are in no way mortal, and since it is clear that accidental happiness ends with the death of the body, there can be no doubt that, if this death can take away blessedness [Note: [Col. 0686B] “Death.”], the entire race of mortals falls into misery at the end of death. If we know that many have sought the fruit of blessedness not only through death but also through pains and punishments, how can this present life make people happy, when, once it has passed, it does not make them wretched?”

“Third, an argument may be arranged as follows. Any happiness that can be ended by death is happiness in name only, since true happiness, like the human mind itself, whose happiness it is and which, as an innate conviction and through many demonstrations, is known to be immortal, must be immortal. But the happiness of fortune, since it belongs to the body, can be ended by death. Hence many have sought the fruit of another blessedness not only through death but also through pains and punishments, especially because this present life is rashly believed to be happiness. For if this life is true happiness, death, which is the deprivation of this happy life, must be regarded as true misery.” 127

**METER IV**

[Note: [Col. 0686D] A poem consisting of two kinds of alternating verses. The first, after its first foot—which may be an iamb, a spondee, or even an anapest—has two iambs followed by a remaining syllable and is Anacreontic. The second is Pherecratian, consisting of a spondee, a dactyl, and a spondee. An exception is the eighth verse, whose first foot is an anapest.]

## Argument

Philosophy, using the example of buildings—which do not last forever—teaches that, with equal prudence, both the highest and the lowest conditions of life must be avoided if a person is to live calmly and safely: buildings raised too high are battered by winds, while those placed too low are swallowed by sand.

### [Note: Col. 0686B]

Whoever wishes to establish a safe and lasting house, and strives for one that is stable and not scattered by the gusts of roaring Eurus, and to scorn the overflowing sea as though it threatened ruin with its waves, let him likewise avoid both the summit of a lofty mountain and the thirsty sands. Violent Auster assails that summit with all his force; but those loose sands refuse to bear a suspended burden. Thus, avoiding the uncertain outcome of a condition that seems pleasant, remember to establish a stable house upon low-lying rock. Then, although the wind roars, disturbing the seas with shipwrecks, you, hidden behind the protection of a steadfast embankment, will be happy; and, scorning the storms of heaven, you will lead a tranquil life.

### [Note: Col. 0686D]

1. “A lasting dwelling.” A house destined to endure for many years; for among Latin authors, especially poets, sedes means “house.” Perenne, “lasting,” is said of something enduring for many years; hence perennare means the same as “to persist for a long time.” Hence Anna Perenna, to whom the ancients offered prayers so that they might live and continue prosperously, according to Ovid, *Fasti* III.

Whoever wishes to establish a lasting dwelling,

[Col. 0687A] [Note: Col. 0687B]

2. “Cautious.” Safe; for cautus derives from cavere, “to beware.” According to Varro’s judgment, cavere derives from cavus, “hollow,” because, Pontanus says, those ancient peoples who held Latium even before the Aborigines mostly lived in caves, which were so called from being hollowed out. In them they protected themselves from heat and cold, as well as from many other inconveniences, and more cautiously guarded themselves and their possessions. Hence the jurists use cavere, cautio, and cautor of those by whom wealth is made safe and secure. Since a prudent person, as though looking ahead through his thoughts, protects himself and his possessions, he is therefore commonly called cautus or catus.

Horace, *Art of Poetry*:

“Should I suppose that everyone will see my faults, while I, secure and beyond hope of pardon, remain cautious? In the end I avoided blame.”

And *Odes* I.10:

“Eloquent Mercury, grandson of Atlas, who by speech fashioned the savage ways of newly formed humanity, shrewd, and with the decorum of the palaestra—”

3. “Stable.” Unmoved and firm in its own foundations. Since a body, once given rest, remains at rest forever until moved from its repose by something else, a house established on foundations can fall in only two ways: first, through the sensible motion of bodies striking against it, such as wind; second, through its own weight, when the foundations on which the house seemed to rest give way. Hence mention is now made of winds, waves of the sea, the summit of a mountain, and thirsty sands.

4. “By the gusts of Eurus.” Aulus Gellius says that Eurus is the wind coming from the eastern, that is, equinoctial, region. In Latin it is called Subsolanus. It is properly called noisy here: since it blows with greater force, following the usual course of the air flowing from east to west, it consequently produces a tremendous sound. Thus Virgil, *Georgics* II.441:

“Which the spirited Eurus continually breaks and carries away.”

6. “The sea.” Pontus generally means any sea, but specifically the Euxine Sea. Perhaps the two are connected because both are full of toil: for πόνος (*ponos*) means “toil” and may have been the origin of πόντος (*pontos*), whatever the truth may be.

7. “The summit of a lofty mountain.” Cacumen, “summit,” is used of both trees and mountains, because the various parts of such bodies converge upward into a single point. It is now called the summit of a lofty mountain because the higher a mountain is, the more it is driven by the winds mentioned above; consequently, a house founded there would be more exposed to collapse.

8. “Let him avoid the thirsty sands.” That is, sands capable of absorbing water. For when air, or any other body that must yield space to the entering water because it is heavier, is displaced among these sands, buildings placed upon them—being far heavier than the water itself—will immediately collapse when their foundations give way. Lucretius, *De rerum natura* II, called sand “thirsty”:

“It washed the thirsty sand of the curving shore.”

9. “Violent Auster presses upon it.” Auster attacks the summit of the mountain. Auster is the wind blowing from the southern quarter of the sky. Since Auster more often rises upward from the earth, just as the opposing Boreas moves conversely from the heights toward the earth, Auster, following a straight course as far as it can, often seems to strike the highest mountain peaks. It is therefore called violent here, from *proterere*, “to crush,” because it is accustomed to crush higher bodies placed in its way.

Seneca, *Agamemnon* 90:

“Inserted into the very clouds, the tower’s head is lashed by rainy Auster; scattering dense shadows, the ancient grove sees its strong oaks broken.”

11. “These loose sands refuse to bear a hanging weight.” These sands, separated from one another, cannot support a weight placed upon them. Just as a balance has two pans, moving alternately so that, if one is depressed by a heavier weight, the other must be raised, so on earth, in the water, and in the air we breathe, bodies support one another through balanced weights: if one becomes heavier, it inclines downward while the other is depressed. This could be demonstrated by innumerable examples. Buildings placed upon sand, however, are much heavier than the fluid by which the sands are softened.

Christ the Lord used the same example in Matthew 7: “Everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house upon sand. The rain fell, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they struck that house; it fell, and its fall was great.”

13. “Fleeing the dangerous lot of a pleasant dwelling.” In other words, whoever wishes to avoid the uncertain outcome of a condition that seems pleasant. Cicero says in *On Divination* II that *sors* means nearly the same as casting lots, throwing knucklebones, or rolling dice—things in which rashness and chance, not reason and deliberation, prevail. Hence those who foretold the future by drawing lots with a child’s hands were called *sortilegi*. Anything uncertain, capable of turning toward one side or the opposite, also came to be called *sors*. Such is a pleasant dwelling, which Philosophy therefore calls dangerous here.

15. “Remember, firmly, to fix your house upon low rock.” Place your house upon low-lying rock: upon rock, so that it may rest on a firm foundation; low, so that it may be less exposed to storms.

17. “Although the wind roars, mingling the waters with destruction.” The wind roars when, like thunder, it raises a great noise. It mingles the waters with destruction when, causing shipwreck, it throws down ships and other bodies placed upon the sea.

Cautious to establish a dwelling,

128 stable, and not to be overthrown  
by the noisy gusts of Eurus,  
and unafraid to scorn the sea  
threatening with its waves;

let him avoid the summit  
of a lofty mountain  
and the thirsty sands.

That violent Auster

[10] [Col. 0688A] presses upon it  
with all his strength;

129 these loose sands  
refuse to bear  
the suspended weight.

Fleeing the dangerous lot  
of a pleasant dwelling,  
remember, firmly,  
to fix your house  
upon low rock.

Although the wind roars,  
mingling the waters with destruction,

[Col. 0689A] [Note: Col. 0689B]

19. “Hidden.” Concealed, as in Virgil, *Georgics* I.441:

“When, concealed in a cloud, he has variegated the rising dawn with spots.”

20. “Happy in the strength.” Robur signifies any physical strength. Since the wild oak appears the strongest of all trees, it is therefore called *robur*.

20. “In the quiet strength of the rampart.” A *vallum* is a wall of earth heaped along the edge of a ditch and fortified with closely set stakes or poles. Thus a rampart has two parts: the embankment, or earth, and the stakes or poles. Hence the rampart is “quiet” or steadfast.

21. “You will lead a tranquil life, laughing serenely at the anger of heaven.” You will lead a peaceful life while scorning the violence of the sky. *Aevum* means “life,” as in Virgil, *Georgics* IV.206:

“Therefore, although a narrow limit of life should receive them.”

And *ira*, because unusual bodily movement commonly accompanies anger, often signifies violent movements not only of human beings but also of animals, and even of lifeless bodies.

Christ likewise used this example in the aforementioned chapter 7 of Matthew: “Everyone who hears my words and does them will be likened to a wise man who built his house upon rock. The rain fell, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they struck that house; yet it did not fall, because it had been founded upon rock.”

Mingling the waters with destruction,

you, hidden in quiet,

[20] happy in the strength  
of the steadfast rampart,

130 will lead a tranquil life,  
laughing at the anger of heaven.

131 **Prose V**

## Argument

Philosophy, now employing stronger arguments, proves that wealth in general—and money, jewels, fields, clothing, servants, and other things of this kind in particular—even if they are substantial possessions, are not goods of the human mind but rather evils: the more eagerly the mind enjoys them, the less happy it is.

Since the nourishment of my arguments is now descending into you, I think stronger arguments must be used. [Note: Col. 0689B] “They enter the mind.” [Note: Col. 0689C] “Come.” The word *age* is commonly said to be an adverb, but it seems to us to be the imperative of *ago*, “I do,” just as *fac* is the imperative of *facio*, “I make.” Therefore, if we address only one person, we say *age*; if several, *agite*. With this word we exhort a listener to think, speak, or act.

To think, as in Virgil, *Georgics* III.42:

“Without you the mind begins nothing lofty; come, break through its sluggish delays.”

To speak, as in *Aeneid* VI.343:

“Tell me, come: for never before has a deceiver been discovered by me.”

To act, as in *Georgics* I.63:

“Come, then: from the first months of the year let strong bulls immediately turn over the rich soil.”

[Note: Col. 0689D] “For if now—” [Note: Col. 0689D] “Perishable.” *Caducum*, “falling,” derives from *cadere*, “to fall,” and therefore signifies what has either fallen, is falling, or is about to fall. Thus Virgil uses it in *Aeneid* VI.481 of something fallen:

“And the Dardan descendants fallen in war.”

In *Georgics* I.368, of something falling:

“Often to see the light straw and the falling leaves flying about.”

And in *Aeneid* X.622, of something about to fall:

“If delay and time are requested for the young man whose present death is imminent.”

Thus, “if the perishable and fleeting gifts of Fortune were not—” [Note: Col. 0690B] “Fleeting.” *Fluxa*, “transitory.” Saint Ambrose uses this word, but I have not been able to find it in the Latin authors whom they call classical.

[Note: Col. 0689B] If the fleeting gifts of Fortune were not such, what is there in them that could ever become yours, or that, once examined and considered, would not grow shabby? [Note: Col. 0690B] “Do riches possess value by nature—yours or their own?”

I. Philosophy proves generally that wealth is not a good of the human mind—not only because every good of Fortune, such as wealth, lies outside the mind and becomes shabbier when examined more closely, as she has already said, but also because no wealth is precious. We therefore call something precious when it occupies a place in our estimation; for by this estimation we determine the price we are willing to pay in order to obtain it. Hence it is called precious.

Something may occupy a place in our estimation in two ways, corresponding to the two ways in which the ideas composing that estimation, as it were its material—for estimation is a judgment—may exist. First, because of its own nature: when the ideas in question are so clear and distinct that they contain nothing beyond what they have received from the things presented to thought, which are their causes. Second, because of your nature, human beings: when those ideas contain, beyond what they derive from the objects presented to thought, the prejudice of the person making the judgment.

Philosophy therefore asks very appropriately whether riches are precious by your nature or by their own. She then takes it as established that riches are not precious by their own nature and consequently do not belong among goods, and proves through the following enumeration of money, jewels, fields, clothing, and servants that they cannot even be counted among things precious by your nature.

Do riches possess value by nature—yours [Note: Col. 0690B] “O human beings”—or their own?

132 What, then, of them [Note: Col. 0690B] “Precious.” is more precious, [Note: Col. 0690D] “Gold, or the mass of accumulated money?”

II. Philosophy, intending to discuss specifically certain kinds of wealth—namely money, jewels, fields, clothing, and servants—begins with money. She says that money cannot be considered precious because, if it is distributed according to her argument, it ceases to be possessed by the act of giving and impoverishes the giver; while, if it is accumulated through avarice, it deprives others of it and becomes, in this respect, thinner than the thinnest of all things, the voice, which fills the hearing of many people equally in its entirety. This is not surprising, since voice, being a sound, consists in a certain vibration of the air, which, because it is fluid, can be moved in every direction by a single speaking person. Money, however, is a coin first made of bronze and later of gold or silver, by which, under established laws, goods can be exchanged for easier commerce. Although several bodies can be moved simultaneously, the same body cannot be contained in several places at once.

Gold, then—or the mass of accumulated money? Yet these things shine more brightly when poured out than when hoarded: avarice always makes people hateful, while generosity makes them renowned. If what is transferred to another cannot remain with anyone, then money is precious when, transferred to others, it ceases to be possessed through the practice of giving. But if the same amount is heaped up by one person as exists throughout the world, it will deprive everyone else of it.

The whole of a voice fills the hearing of many people equally; but your riches cannot pass to many unless they are broken up. Once that has happened, they must make the people whom they leave behind poor. O narrow and impoverished riches, which many people are not permitted to possess whole, and which cannot come to anyone without impoverishing the rest!

133 [Note: Col. 0691C] “Does the radiance of jewels attract the eyes?”

III. Philosophy says that jewels ought not to be precious to the human mind, because the light by which jewels shine belongs not to human beings but only to those bodies’ own properties. Since those bodies are lifeless, they are placed so far beneath the excellence of the human mind that they in no way deserve human admiration.

A jewel is a stone that, shining through like glass, transmits light because it was melted before it became stone. Hence, if some metal or other opaque body is poured into a still-molten jewel, the jewel is colored and becomes less able to transmit light. Thus jewels, whether transparent or reflective, possess their own radiance, by which the eyes are moved and the mind itself is first prompted to look at jewels, then to admire them, and sometimes even to love them—until, freed from every prejudice, it recognizes that this is nothing more than motion, inferior not only to the mind itself, by which it is considered, but also far below the life of bodies, which consists in perpetual and continuous motion.

Does the radiance of jewels attract the eyes? But if there is anything remarkable in this splendor, it is the jewels’ light, not humanity’s. I am greatly astonished that human beings admire them so intensely. For what is without the motion of life and the structure of limbs that can rightly seem beautiful to an animate and rational nature? Although such things, as works of the Creator and in their lowest distinct rank, derive some degree of beauty, they were nevertheless placed beneath your excellence and did not in any way deserve your admiration.

[Note: Col. 0691D] “Or does the beauty of fields delight you?”

IV. Philosophy adds that fields, too, ought not to be precious to the aforementioned mind. Since a field is a territory that, when carefully cultivated, produces crops, a field could be considered precious to the mind only because of its size—inasmuch as it is bounded by very distant limits—or because of its shape—inasmuch as it is free from irregular elevations, as though leveled like a cylinder—or because of its motion, inasmuch as it is not merely fertile but also productive. “For a well-cultivated field,” Cicero says, “nothing can be more abundant in usefulness or more beautiful in appearance.”

Yet in none of these ways can a field be precious to the human mind. Not because of its size: the moon, the sun, the stars, and the heavens—although they do not themselves seem precious to the mind—are portions of the most beautiful work and are larger than any field. Nor because of its flat shape: the sea, which nevertheless is not held in such esteem, when calm and serene, with its waters balanced at an equal level, is flatter not only than a field but than any other flat body. “For what seems so flat,” Cicero says in *Academica* II, “as the sea?” It is therefore also called *aequor*, “level expanse,” by poets. Nor, finally, because of its motion, whether it is flowering or productive, since the flowers and fruits of fields lie outside the human being. Even if some part of them enters the human body as nourishment, it must be so small that, if one tries to burden nature with more than it can contain, what is added either becomes unpleasant or harmful.

Lucretius, *De rerum natura* V:

“If anyone governs life by true reason, great riches for a human being are to live sparingly and with an even mind; for there is never a shortage of little.”

Does the beauty of fields delight you? Why should it not? [Note: Col. 0691B] “Boethius says this.” It is a beautiful portion of a work of surpassing beauty. So once we rejoice in the appearance of a calm sea; so we admire the heavens, the stars, the sun, and the moon. Does any of these things touch you? [Note: Col. 0691B] “Philosophy says this.” Do you dare to glory in the splendor of any such thing? Or are you yourself adorned with spring flowers? Does your abundance swell into summer fruits? Why are you carried away by empty pleasures? Why do you embrace external goods as though they were yours? Fortune will never make yours what the nature of things has made foreign to you.

The fruits of the earth are undoubtedly intended as food for living creatures. But if you wish to fill the need that nature considers sufficient, why seek the abundance of Fortune? Nature is content with few and very small things. If you try to burden its fullness with excess, what you add will either become unpleasant or harmful.

134 But now— [Note: Col. 0692C] “Is it beautiful to shine in varied garments?”

V. Philosophy proves that clothing, too, ought not to be precious to our mind, because the pleasing appearance of garments belongs not to our mind but either to the nature of the material or to the skill of the artisan. Indeed, even the most beautiful garment cannot free you from the smallest fever.

Lucretius, *De rerum natura* II:

“Nor do hot fevers leave the body any sooner if you strut in woven fabrics adorned with pictures and in reddening purple than if you must lie down in a common garment.”

Do you think it beautiful to shine in varied clothing? If its appearance is pleasing to the sight, I shall admire either the nature of the material or the skill of the artisan.

[Note: Col. 0692D] “Or does a long line of servants—”

VI. Philosophy likewise demonstrates that a crowd of servants ought not to be precious to the aforementioned mind, because these servants are either wicked or good. If wicked, they are not merely unprecious to their master but rather a destructive burden upon the household and intensely hostile to their master, since divine law obliges him both to restrain the servant from vice and to advance him toward virtue. Hebrews 13: “For they keep watch as those who will have to give an account for your souls.”

If they are good, how can another person’s goodness be counted among your possessions? Philosophy therefore rightly concludes that a person is not happy because he abounds in money, jewels, fields, clothing, and servants.

Horace, *Odes* IV.9:

“You would not rightly call the man who possesses much happy; more rightly that name belongs to him who wisely uses the gifts of the gods, knows how to endure hard poverty, fears disgrace more than death, and is not afraid to die for dear friends or for his country.”

Or does a long line of servants make you happy? If they are vicious in character, they are a destructive burden upon the household [Note: Col. 0692B] “A burden,” and intensely hostile to their master. But if they are good, how can another person’s goodness be counted among your possessions? From all this it is clearly shown that none of those things which you count among your goods is your own good.

If none of them contains a beauty worth desiring, why should you grieve when they are lost or rejoice when they are retained? But if they are beautiful by nature, what difference does that make to you? For even in themselves they are separated from your possessions. [Note: Col. 0693A] “Separated.” *Sequestratus* is said to derive from *sequester*, an arbiter between two parties, standing midway between them and judging without prejudice toward either side. Thus in *Aeneid* XI.133:

“They made a pact for twice six days, with peace as arbiter.”

Yet this word *sequestratus*, used by Arnobius in *Against the Nations* V and by Cassiodorus in *Variae* I.3, does not seem to belong to purer Latin.

[Note: Col. 0693B] “Separated.” They would have pleased you if they had been detached from you. They are not precious because they have entered your wealth; rather, because they seemed precious, you preferred to number them among your riches.

135 But what is it that you desire with so great a commotion over Fortune? [Note: Col. 0693B] “By frequently calling upon your Fortune and pursuing it with such eagerness.” [Note: Col. 0693B] “You seek abundance to drive away need.” Everyone who is affected by an excessively intense pursuit of the things mentioned above puts forward this single pretext. Each person, conscious of his own weakness, thinks that, surrounded by money, jewels, fields, clothing, and servants as though by so many bodyguards, he can be freed from every injury inflicted by enemies. But he is deceived:

“I suppose you seek to drive away need by acquiring abundance.” Yet this turns against you. [Note: Col. 0693C] “For more supports are necessary.” An *adminiculum* is an aid that is at hand or readily available. Since the aforementioned goods are exposed to continual corruption, the more we possess, the more aids must be at hand for preserving them.

For more supports are necessary to protect the variety of precious [Note: Col. 0693C] “Furnishings.” *Supellex* properly means the decoration of a hall, such as tapestries, seats, linens, vessels, and other household implements. The word apparently arises from the fact that these objects, wrapped in skins, were carried by soldiers and perhaps also by envoys for their own use. Here, however, the variety of furnishings means the multitude of the external goods mentioned above, the name of a part being transferred to the whole.

And it is true that those who possess very much need very many things, whereas those who measure their abundance by nature’s needs require very little. [Note: Col. 0693B] “Those who require them.” [Note: Col. 0693C] “Not by the superfluity of ambition.”

We pursue the acquisition of these riches not only for protection, as has been said, but also out of ambition, thinking that we shall arouse a greater estimation of ourselves in the minds of others the more numerous and greater such goods we enjoy. This is evident from the fact that, if we thought no one would ever see us, we would not be so eager for jewels, clothing, or any similar goods.

Is there, then, no proper and innate good of your own, so that you seek your goods in external and detached things? [Note: Col. 0693D] “Thus the order of things has been reversed.”

My mind is the form of my body, but it was created by God and for God. Therefore, as a participant standing between God its Creator and the body, it is shaped by both through concepts, and by both is drawn toward their respective sides. But alas! Although it ought to devote itself exclusively to loving God, under the unhappy weight both of its own weakness and of disorder it is driven first toward the body and then toward the other things that serve the body. In this respect, human beings—rightly called rational animals because of their divine reason—seem to do wrong both to God and to themselves.

[Col. 0694B] “In the first place, a human being is—”

Thus the order of things has been reversed [Col. 0694A] so that— [Note: Col. 0694B] “An animal divine by virtue of reason.”

For, as no one is unaware, a human being consists of mind and body joined together. The mind is reason; the body is often called an animal. But by the mind a human being resembles God, as is established in Genesis 1: “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” namely, insofar as our mind is a thinking thing like God. Hence human beings are called in 2 Peter 1 “partakers of the divine nature.” Therefore a human being is now called an animal divine by merit—or by the title—of reason.

Cicero says in *On the Universe*: “Human beings are, as it were, of the same clan as the immortal gods; they are called of divine stock and hold primacy over all living creatures.”

Next, the same human being is more foolish than the other created things, since— [Col. 0694C] “For this reason—” a human being, an animal divine by virtue of reason, seems to shine to himself only through the possession of lifeless furnishings.

136 And— [Note: Col. 0694C] “Other things are content with what belongs to them.”

For lifeless bodies, plants, and the animals themselves remain within the limits divinely prescribed for them, so that they are not held by desire for money, jewels, fields, clothing, or servants. Moreover, the same human being seems to do wrong to God:

Other things are content with what belongs to them; but you, human beings, whose minds resemble God, seek the ornaments of an excellent nature from the lowest things and do not understand how great an injury you inflict upon your Creator.

[Note: Col. 0694C] “He wished the human race, etc.”

Since God, whose wisdom is infinite, is wiser than even the wisest human being, the person who dares to place his own judgment before God’s does wrong to God. He thrusts beneath the lowest things the dignity that God wished to raise above all earthly things.

Such is the condition of the human being who yearns for the aforementioned goods. Good exists in perfection, so that whatever is good for someone seems more perfect than that person himself, since it can perfect him; and nothing can be perfected except by something more perfect. Therefore, since something is considered precious, as said above, when it occupies a place in our estimation, and since this estimation ought to increase only as the perfection of the thing considered increases, whatever appears good to someone must necessarily appear more precious to that person. Thus the human being absorbed by the greatest desire for servants, clothing, fields, jewels, money, and other such utterly base things judges these things to be more precious and more perfect than his own mind and consequently wrongs his Creator through that false judgment.

He wished the human race to surpass all earthly things; but you thrust your dignity beneath the lowest things. For if everyone’s good is more precious than the person whose good it is, when you judge the basest things to be your goods, you subject yourselves to those same things in your own estimation. [Note: Col. 0694D] “This does not unjustly befall him.” This false judgment is neither without some cause nor without some effect: it arises from the voluntary ignorance of the human mind, and that ignorance increases as the judgment and the disturbances accompanying it increase.

This does not unjustly befall him. [Note: Col. 0694B] “It happens.”

[Note: Col. 0694D] “For human nature, etc.”

A human being differs from the other animals in this: a human being can think, whereas the other animals cannot. Thus, that the other animals are ignorant of themselves belongs to their nature; but when a human being is ignorant of himself, this is his fault, insofar as, following rashness and prejudice, he refuses to turn his mind’s attention toward his own mind. Hence, by the just judgment of God, he is reduced beneath the beasts.

David says in Psalm 31: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding”—that is, lest, forgetful of himself, like a beast he be carried wherever the body drags him.

The condition of human nature is that it surpasses other things only when it knows itself; yet it is reduced beneath the beasts if it ceases to know itself. For the other animals’ ignorance of themselves belongs to nature; in human beings it is a fault.

137 [Note: Col. 0695B] “How widely this error of yours extends.”

This error, or false judgment, consists in a human being’s believing that his mind can be adorned with foreign ornaments—money, fields, jewels, and so forth. The things applied to it are praised, but what lies beneath them, covered and veiled, nevertheless remains in its own ugliness. Think of corpses buried in beautiful tombs, or dung covered with snow. This error extends widely not only because of the many people infected by it, but also because of the various movements both of mind and body that it causes. Consequently, through this error, a human being wrongs not only God, as has been proved, but also himself.

How widely, then, does this error of yours extend—you who think that something can be adorned with foreign ornaments? Yet this cannot happen. For if anything shines because of things applied to it, the things applied are praised; but what is covered and veiled by them nevertheless remains in its own ugliness.

[Note: Col. 0695C] “But I deny that something which harms its possessor is a good.”

This reasoning of Philosophy requires no interpretation. “What harms its possessor,” she says, “cannot be the possessor’s good”; for a good ought to help, not harm. Yet the aforementioned riches harm their possessors, among other reasons especially because every thoroughly wicked person, and therefore all the more avid for what belongs to others, considers himself alone worthy to possess whatever gold and jewels exist anywhere. Blinded by his own disorder, and especially by avarice, he therefore strives to acquire wealth by every lawful and unlawful means.

Plautus, *Captivi*, Act II, Scene 2:

“I hate gold: it has persuaded many people to do many wrong things.”

I deny that something which harms its possessor is a good. Am I lying? “Not at all,” you will say. Yet riches have very often harmed those who possess them, since every thoroughly wicked person, and therefore all the more avid for what belongs to others, considers himself alone worthy to possess whatever gold and jewels exist anywhere.

You, then— [Note: Col. 0695D] “Who now carry a staff, etc.”— Philosophy alludes to these verses of Juvenal, *Satires* 18, Book IV, verse 19:

“Though you carry only a few small vessels of pure silver, when you travel by night you will fear the sword and the staff, and you will tremble at the shadow of a reed stirred by the moon. The traveler without baggage will sing in the face of the robber.”

A robber is now called someone who blocks the roads and takes travelers’ possessions, often their lives as well. In earlier times a robber was a hired soldier or bodyguard, so called as though from *latero*, because he attended the side of his prince. Since such men abused their authority with kings and did not hesitate to attack travelers and take their money, all who block the roads came to be called robbers.

You, who now anxiously fear the long staff and the sword—if you had entered the path of this life as a traveler without baggage, you would sing in the face of the robber. O splendid happiness of mortal wealth: once you have obtained it, you cease to be secure!

138 **Meter V**

[Note: Col. 0695D] A poem consisting of one kind of verse, each line comprising three feet and one syllable left over. The third foot is always an anapest; the first and second may indifferently be a spondee or anapest.

## Argument

Philosophy, distinguishing between ancient and modern times, says that the age of our ancestors was happier for this reason: they were held by a lesser desire than we are for food, clothing, gold, and royal power.

### [Note: Col. 0695B]

The first age of ancient humanity was exceedingly happy, content with its fertile fields and not ruined by idle indulgence; after long fasts, it was accustomed to feed on the readily available acorn. These people did not know how to mix wine—the gift of Liber or Bacchus—with flowing honey, nor how to stain the white wool of the Serian peoples with Tyrian purple dye. Grass gave them healthful sleep; a clear river gave them drink; a tall pine gave them shade.

No human being had yet cleft the deep sea in a ship, nor had a foreign traveler, seeking wealth from every direction, gazed upon shores previously unknown. Then the cruel horns of war were silent, and blood shed through bitter enmity had not stained the dreadful weapons. For why would hostile anger have attempted to handle iron in those earliest times, when those first human beings recognized that cruel blows would be inflicted without any compensation for the blood shed?

Would that our age might now return to that ancient manner of life! But among us a burning desire for perishable goods boils more fiercely than the flames of Etna. Alas, who was the first of all to unearth the weight of hidden gold and the jewels born to be concealed—both of them costly dangers?

### [Note: Col. 0696B]

1. “The earlier age.” Philosophy distinguishes between ancient and modern times. Poets recognize four ages of the world: the golden, silver, bronze, and iron ages. For just as iron degenerates from bronze, bronze from silver, and silver from gold, so descendants degenerate from the virtue of their ancestors. Thus Horace, *Odes* III.6:

“What has ruinous time not diminished? The age of our parents, worse than that of our grandfathers, produced us, more wicked, soon to give—”

A more degenerate offspring.
