Here, however, the subject is the Golden Age, which is therefore called “the earlier age.” Most of what is now being said about that age was said by Virgil in Books I and III of the *Georgics*, by Tibullus in Book I, Elegy 3, by Lucretius in Book V, by Horace in Epode 16, by Ovid in Book I of the *Metamorphoses*, by Juvenal in Satire 6, and others.

**2. Content with faithful fields.** — II. Philosophy, about to discuss the food and drink of that Golden, or earlier, age, begins with the very source of such sustenance: the faithful fields, with which those ancient people were content. A field (*arvum*), says Festus, is land not yet sown; “faithful” is what answers one’s hopes and does not disappoint its owner’s expectation. Yet in that Golden Age the fields, neither plowed nor sown, supplied precisely this.

Lucretius, Book V:

> Nor was there yet any sturdy driver of the curved plow;  
> No one knew how to work the fields with iron,  
> Nor to bury young saplings in the ground, nor to cut away  
> The ancient branches from the tall trees with pruning-hooks.  
>   
> Whatever the sun and rains had given, whatever the earth had produced  
> Of its own accord, that gift sufficiently satisfied their hearts.

Ovid, Book I of the *Metamorphoses*, line 109:

> Soon, too, the earth, untilled, bore crops.

**3. Nor destroyed by idle luxury.** — Here “luxury” is the vice of a disordered mind, which, being drawn apart by its various thoughts as though into opposing directions, seems to dissolve like a liquid vanishing through motion. For just as *fluxus* comes from *fluo*, “to flow,” so *luxus* comes from *luo*, “to dissolve”; hence *luxuries*. Thus, in Terence, a young man is said to be “ruined by luxury.”

That luxury is rightly called “idle”: for *iners*, literally “without art,” generally signifies anything devoid of movement, as in Ovid, “nothing but an inert weight.” Such mental dissipation first impedes thought and then the proper movements of the human body itself.

> Happy beyond measure was the earlier age,  
> Content with faithful fields,  
> Nor ruined by idle luxury;  
> It used to relieve its late fasts with an easily obtained acorn.

**5. To break their fasts with acorns.** — III. In praising the food of that earlier age, Philosophy briefly notes the differences observable between our manner of eating and that of antiquity. Some concern the food itself; others, the manner in which it was obtained.

First, our food is usually elaborate and prepared by art; the food of antiquity was simple and supplied by nature herself. Next, our food is taken frequently, often without hunger urging us; ancient food was taken only after fasting—indeed, after a late fast, one maintained until almost the final hour. Finally, our food usually consists of meat, fish, and the finest kinds of terrestrial produce; ancient food consisted of acorns, the commonest and least distinguished of fruits. This can be confirmed by many other testimonies of both orators and poets.

Virgil, *Georgics* I, line 8:

> And he changed the Chaonian acorn for the nourishing ear of grain.

And line 159:

> And, shaking the oak in the forests, you will relieve your hunger.

Lucretius, Book V:

> Among the acorn-bearing oaks they cared for their bodies . . .  
>   
> But loathing of the acorn began.

Ovid, Book I of the *Metamorphoses*, fable 3, line 103:

> Content with foods produced without compulsion,  
> They gathered the fruits of the arbutus and the mountain strawberries,  
> The cornel-cherries, and the blackberries clinging to the hard brambles,  
> And the acorns that had fallen from Jupiter’s spreading tree.

Hence the first human beings were called **βαλανοφάγοι καὶ ὑδροπόται**, “acorn-eaters and water-drinkers.” Hence, too, an ancient common proverb said **ἅλις δρυός**, “an oak is enough.”

**6. They did not know Bacchus’s gifts.** — IV. Philosophy recalls the drink of that Golden Age, which, as it will say in the eleventh verse, was water—“the slippery river for drinking.” It therefore first states that those ancient people knew neither wine, the gifts of Bacchus, nor mulled wine, wine mixed with honey.

Wine is called the gift of Bacchus because Dionysus, said to be the inventor of wine, was called Bacchus, or **ἴακχος**, from **ἰαχή**, “a shout,” perhaps because wine first stimulates drinkers to speak and then even to shout. Horace, *Epistles* I.5:

> What does drunkenness not accomplish? It reveals what is hidden;  
> It bids hopes be fulfilled; it thrusts the unarmed into battle;  
> It removes a burden from troubled minds; it teaches skills.  
>   
> Whom have fertile cups not made eloquent?

Mulled wine (*mulsum*) is a drink made by mixing wine and honey; among the Greeks it is called **οἰνόμελι** and **μελίκρατον**. Just as water—the earlier drink of humanity—was mixed with newly discovered wine, according to Virgil, *Georgics* I, line 9:

> And he mixed the waters of Achelous with the discovered grapes,

so, as the appetite of gluttons increased, honey was mixed into the same wine, either for pleasure or even to prolong life. That drink is said to soothe the empty veins by its gentleness; hence it may have been called *mulsum* from *mulcere*, “to soothe.”

Thus Catius, in Horace, reproves Aufidius—not because he mixed honey with Falernian wine, but because he mixed it with harsh Falernian:

> Aufidius was mixing honey with strong Falernian wine,  
>   
> Improperly, since nothing but something gentle should be committed  
> To empty veins; you would better bathe the breast with gentle mulled wine.

Hence also Asinius Pollio, who lived beyond his hundredth year, when Augustus, his guest, asked him by what means he had preserved such vigor of body and mind, replied: “Mulled wine within, oil without.”

**8. Nor the shining fleeces of the Seres.** — V. Philosophy passes to the earliest clothing of humanity, which it has indicated by naming their beds and tents: the beds were grasses, and grass gave healthful sleep; the tents were trees—the very tall pine provided shade. It therefore first said that these ancient people did not know silk garments or the purple dye with which such garments were colored.

The Seres, then, are the people whom Orosius, Book III, chapter 23, places between the two rivers Hydaspes and Indus. Among them, it is said, there are certain trees laden with an exceptionally fine wool. This is supported by the testimony of many highly authoritative writers, such as Virgil, *Georgics* II, line 121:

> And the Seres comb their delicate fleeces from the leaves.

Seneca, in the *Octavia*, line 667:

> Nor does she embroider with a Maeonian needlework  
> What the Ser, exposed to Phoebus’s eastern breezes,  
> Gathers from eastern trees.

Claudian, poem 1, line 179:

> Which the Seres shear from the trunk with its soft thread.

There is, however, a serious dispute concerning the origin of this kind of wool: whether it comes from trees or rather from worms living there. The latter seems more probable: among those peoples the bombyces, as with us, draw thread from a gravid belly.

Antonius Hallaeus, a great ornament of our university, elegantly described that wrinkled and filthy worm in these verses:

> Its mother is putrefaction; its leafy nurse supplies  
> Food, while the mulberry is stained with Thysbean blood.  
>   
> When, shut within its hidden prison, it has fed its hungry  
> Gullet, and now, sated, swells throughout its body,  
>   
> It gradually empties its entrails and shapes from them  
> A soft wool; then, by wondrous methods, it spins the filth  
>   
> Into fine threads and, gathering them into a smooth ball,  
> Rolls them together in a rounded coil.  
>   
> But when, having completed its noble task,  
> It lies there like a lifeless thing, as though enclosed  
> In a precious urn, it is soon restored to the light;  
>   
> It puts on wings and is now a bird—and a worm,  
> Neither one nor the other, and finally a monster.

Purple, with which silk garments are dyed, is called Tyrian poison. It is “poison” because it is a liquid extracted from a shell, which enters wool like poison entering the viscera and veins and stains it from within. It is “Tyrian” because the Phoenician city of Tyre was famous for fishing the murex, the shell mentioned above.

Virgil, *Georgics* II, line 465:

> Nor is the white wool dyed with Assyrian poison.

**13. Had not yet cut through the high seas.** — VI. Philosophy recalls gold, which is obtained chiefly through commerce. Commerce, however, is conducted mainly by means of the obedient sea, which is now under discussion.

Thus Lucretius, Book V:

> Not yet did a single day send thousands of men  
> Led beneath standards to destruction; nor did the troubled waters  
> Of the sea dash ships against rocks and men.

Thus Tibullus, Book I, Elegy 5:

> Not yet had the pine scorned the dark-blue waves  
> And opened its breast to the winds.  
>   
> Nor had the wandering sailor, seeking shortcuts through unknown lands,  
> Pressed his ship with foreign merchandise.

Thus Ovid, Book I of the *Metamorphoses*:

> Not yet had the pine, cut from its native mountains  
> To visit a foreign world, descended into the liquid waves;  
>   
> And mortals knew no shores beyond their own.

Three words here require particular notice: *alta*, *mercibus*, and *hospes*.

The “high” parts of the sea signify the deep sea, farther removed from land. Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* I, line 38:

> Scarcely had they joyfully spread their sails  
> Out of sight of Sicilian land into the deep.

And *Aeneid* II, line 203:

> But look: twin serpents from Tenedos through the tranquil deep.

*Merx*, or, as the ancients said, *mercis*, derives from *mercari*, “to trade,” and therefore signifies a saleable object, especially what we call movable property—*du meuble*—of the kind commonly bought and sold at fairs after being collected from various places.

For this reason the deity whom ancient superstition believed to preside over profit and over the buying and selling of such things was called Mercury. Perhaps for no other reason was he depicted holding a wand in his left hand and a moneybag in his right, since merchants customarily set out equipped with these things.

Finally, *hospes*, or, as the earliest Latin writers said, *hostis*, is the person whom we now call a foreigner, in French *un hôte*.

> To break their fasts with acorns.  
>   
> They did not know Bacchus’s gifts,  
> Nor how to mix them with liquid honey;  
>   
> Nor to mingle the shining fleeces of the Seres  
> With Tyrian poison.  
>   
> Grass gave them healthful sleep,  
> And the slippery river gave them drink;  
> The very tall pine gave them shade.  
>   
> The ship had not yet cut through the high seas,  
> Nor had the stranger, with merchandise gathered from every direction,  
> Seen shores previously unknown.

**16. Then the savage war-trumpets were silent.**

> Then savage war-trumpets were silent,  
> Nor had blood, shed in bitter hatreds,  
> Stained dreadful weapons.  
> For why would hostile fury first  
> Wish to move any weapons,  
> When it saw savage wounds  
> And no rewards of blood?

VII. Philosophy is discussing kingship, for the sake of acquiring or enlarging which trumpets are sounded, arms are taken up, and much blood is shed.

*Classica*, therefore—almost *calassica*, from the ancient *calo*, “I call,” says Isidore, Book XVIII, chapter 4—are horns made for summoning people. In the same way, *classis*, derived from the same root, signifies a multitude of people who are accustomed to be summoned by some signal, whether at sea, on land, at home, or in military service. Hence our schools, too, because they are gatherings of summoned pupils, are commonly called classes.

Here, however, *classica* are military signals, as in Virgil, *Georgics* II, line 538:

> Golden Saturn was living this life upon earth;  
> Nor had they yet heard the war-trumpets being inflated,  
> Nor swords, laid upon hard anvils, ringing.

*Cruor* is blood—not merely blood rushing from the heart, as some maintain, since all blood that leaves the heart rushes, but blood poured outside the veins and then becoming still and cold. For *cruor* is said to derive from **κρύος**, “cold”; hence **κρυερός**, “cold.”

Because such blood commonly inspires horror, it is now said that blood is poured only amid bitter hatreds, and that weapons stained with it become dreadful. Thus, too, no one would first have wished to move arms for the sake of shedding blood unless some reward for shedding it seemed to exist—something that, as is now stated, was absent in that earlier Golden Age.

Ovid, Book I of the *Metamorphoses*:

> There was no helmet, no sword; without military service,  
> Peaceful peoples passed their gentle leisure.

As Lucretius sings, Book V:

> Thus sad discord gave birth to one conflict after another,  
> Something horrible to human peoples in war,  
> And day by day added increase to the terrors of battle.

**23. Would that our times might return, etc.** — The earlier age was indeed moderate in food, clothing, gold, and kingship; but our age appears to observe no restraint in desiring any of these things. Hence we lead a less happy life, and Philosophy’s wish is entirely just.

**25. The burning love of possessing glows more fiercely than the fires of Etna.** — The human mind loves itself and its own perfection; yet, conscious of its weakness, it naturally loves not only its own body but also external things. It therefore seems to form with these things a kind of society, of which it regards itself as no insignificant part.

For this reason it strives either to preserve such things, if it possesses them, or to acquire them, if it lacks them. If it happens to be deprived of possession or hope of any such thing, it suffers as though a part of its society had been removed, more or less according as that part was considered more or less valuable.

This love is not improperly said to be fiercer than the fires of Etna. Etna is a mountain in Sicily, commonly called Mount Gibel, perpetually famous for its fire and frequently celebrated by poets.

Virgil, *Georgics* I, line 472:

> We have seen Etna billowing after its furnaces burst,  
> Rolling forth globes of flame and molten rocks.

That disturbance, however, which is no less perpetual than the fire of Etna, produces far more numerous and more serious calamities.

Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII, line 324:

> Golden ages, as they say, existed beneath that king;  
> Thus he ruled his peoples in tranquil peace,  
> Until gradually a worse and darker age arrived,  
> And the madness of war and the love of possession succeeded.

Ovid, Book I of the *Metamorphoses*, line 128:

> At once every kind of wickedness burst forth  
> Into an age of worse substance: shame, truth, and faith fled,  
> And in their place came frauds, deceits, ambushes, violence,  
> And the criminal love of possession.

**27. Who was that first man?** — An elegant expression for indicating the force of the disturbance mentioned above.

Thus Tibullus, Book I, Elegy 10:

> Who was the first to bring forth the dreadful swords?

Thus Horace, *Odes* I.3:

> He had oak and triple bronze  
> Around his breast who first entrusted a fragile boat  
> To the savage sea,  
> And was not afraid of the precipitous southwest wind  
> Struggling with the north winds,  
> Nor of the gloomy Hyades, nor of the rage of the south wind.

**28. Who dug up the hidden weights of gold.** — Gold is rightly designated by its weight, not only because it is the heaviest of all metals but also because it is the most precious of all. Gold is also rightly called “hidden,” especially in relation to its discoverer, who is now under discussion, since gold is formed enclosed within the bowels of the earth.

**29. And the gems wishing to lie concealed.** — Gems, being without thought, have neither will nor appetite. But if one considers more attentively the origin and nature of gems, one might believe that they wish to lie concealed.

First, gems seem to wish to lie concealed by their origin: they arise in hidden places, namely in water and in earth, where they first melt like glass and then, hardened into brittleness, become translucent.

Second, those same gems seem to wish to lie concealed by their nature: they either shine through transmitted light or gleam by reflected light. If they shine through, then, because they resemble the air we breathe, they are less noticeable. If they gleam by reflection, they so dazzle the sharpness of the eyes that they cannot be viewed from every direction with fixed eyes.

**30. Precious dangers.** — Gold and gems are indeed precious, at least because of the judgment human beings have formed about them. Yet they are dangers—not only while they lie hidden in their native place, from which they cannot be extracted without great danger to the miner, but also after people have dug them out and either possess or pursue them. For they often bring death both to body and mind.

Virgil, *Aeneid* III, line 57:

> What do you not compel mortal hearts to do,  
> Accursed hunger for gold?

> And the gems wishing to lie concealed—  
> Does he dig up precious dangers?

## PROSE VI

**Argument.** — Philosophy, considering power from the standpoint of the powerful person, the subject, and power’s own property, observes that power: first, in a wicked magistrate, is a cause of blame, while in a good magistrate it is not a greater cause of praise; second, is effective only upon bodies, so that the powerful person can be harmed no less than he can harm; third, can neither drive away vices nor remove weakness. From these considerations she concludes that power is counted among goods only through an abuse of the name.

**On dignities and power.** — Dignities and power, or authority, are joined here because they differ only in name. “Dignity,” says Cicero in Book II of *De inventione*, “is an honorable authority belonging to someone who is worthy of esteem, honor, and reverence.”

Indeed, *dignitas* derives from *dignus*, “worthy.” *Dignus*, or, as the ancients wrote it, *dicnus*, comes from the Greek noun **δίκη**, “right” or “justice,” so that the worthy person is one whom it is just to obey.

Since one human being is equal to another, it cannot be just for one human being to obey another unless God, the creator and ruler of all people, commands it. Thus every dignity comes from God, so that subjects are bound to obey kings and magistrates who command, as persons representing God’s authority.

John 19: “You could have no authority against me unless it had been given you from above.”

The Apostle says in Romans 13: “Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities; for there is no authority except from God, and those authorities that exist have been ordained by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists the ordinance of God; and those who resist will bring condemnation upon themselves,” and so forth.

Dignity, therefore, or power, is a kind of form. For that reason it can be considered from the standpoint of the powerful person, of the subject, and of its own property—which philosophers speaking less correctly in Latin call its “formal effect.” From these three perspectives Philosophy will subsequently show that not only wealth, which she has already discussed, but also power itself does not have the character of a good in such a way that whoever lacks it must therefore be regarded as unhappy.

> But what shall I say about dignities and power,  
> Which you, ignorant of true dignity and authority,  
> Raise to the heavens by praising them  
> And make equal to the sky?

**146. If these should fall to the most wicked man.** — I. Philosophy is discussing the powerful man, or, as philosophers say, the subject of power. The newly powerful man is either wicked or good.

If he is wicked, so far is he from becoming better through the addition of power that, like a most violent fire or a rushing torrent, he instead produces great destruction, abusing his authority. The Roman kings and consuls bear witness to this.

If he is good, his goodness is not praised because of his power; rather, his power is praised because of his goodness.

To understand what is now being said about the Roman kings and consuls, something must be said about authority and its various forms among the Romans.

*Imperium*, which among the Greeks is **πολιτεία**, is, according to Lipsius, *Politics* II, chapter 1, “a definite order of commanding and obeying.” There are, he says, three forms of government: monarchy, aristocracy, and popular government. They are mixed with one another, I admit, and are weakened or strengthened, but always in such a way that one part inclines and outweighs the others, from which the government properly takes its name.

Monarchy is the authority of one person, who is therefore called a king or prince. Aristocracy is the authority of several people who, because they seem to excel the rest in virtue, obtain magistracies by election. Popular government, finally, is the authority of several people who obtain magistracies solely by lot.

The Romans experienced all these forms of government. First they had kings. The last, says Florus, Book I, chapter 7, was Tarquinius, who received the surname Superbus, “the Proud,” from his character. He preferred to seize the ancestral kingdom, which Servius held, rather than wait for it; and, having sent assassins against Servius, he administered the power acquired by crime no better than he had acquired it.

Next they had consuls. For, says the same author in chapter 9, under the leadership and authority of Brutus and Collatinus, to whom the dying matron had entrusted the task of avenging her, the Roman people, stirred as though by a divine impulse to vindicate the honor of liberty and chastity, suddenly deposed the king, plundered his property, consecrated his land to their own Mars, and transferred authority to those same champions of their liberty, though with a change of law and name.

For they decided that an annual office should replace a perpetual one, and that two men should replace one, lest power be corrupted by isolation or duration. They called them consuls instead of kings, so that they might remember that they owed counsel to their fellow citizens.

Finally, just as the form of Roman government had earlier changed from kings to consuls, so, according to Livy, it was again changed from consuls to decemvirs. As the pride of the consuls increased—or rather, as the fierceness of the Roman people, which had originated among shepherds, had not yet been subdued—the decemvirs eventually succeeded the consuls. Because they acted tyrannically in many respects, they were condemned, and their power was abolished in the third year after it had been introduced into the republic.

If these should fall to any utterly wicked man, what would be more voracious than the flames Etna spews forth? What flood would produce such devastation?

Certainly, as I think you remember, your ancestors wished to abolish the consular government, which had been the beginning of liberty, because of the consuls’ arrogance—those who, for that same arrogance, had earlier removed the name of kingship from the state.

But if honors are ever—something exceedingly rare—bestowed upon good men, what else in them pleases us except the goodness of those who use them? Thus honor comes not to virtues from dignity, but to dignities from virtue.

**147. What, then, is this splendid power?** — II. Philosophy discusses subjects, or the matter upon which the power mentioned above can be exercised; this is usually called by philosophers the object of power.

That matter subject to power is not absolutely subject to the powerful person, nor is it so substantial that power should therefore be greatly valued.

It is not, I say, absolutely subject to the powerful person. Since all human beings were created by the same cause and for the same purpose, they are equal. Apart from the divine will by which some rule over others, it would be no less absurd for one human being to claim authority over others than to see one mouse exercising dominion over another mouse.

Nor is this subject matter so substantial. Although a subject consists of mind and body, just as the powerful person does, the powerful person exercises his power only upon the body, namely through word or deed. In the same way, a human being is subject to a powerful person only in body.

As Christ taught in Luke 12: “Do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do.”

Power over the human body is not of such great importance, partly because nothing is weaker than the human body, and partly because what a superior can do to the body of an inferior may itself become material for virtue in the inferior; yet the inferior may also inflict injury upon the body of the superior.

> What, then, is this desirable and splendid power of yours?  
> Do you not consider, O earthly animals, those over whom you seem to preside?  
> For if you saw one mouse claiming for itself right and power over the others,  
> How greatly would you laugh!

First, nothing can be found weaker than the human body. A fly, a tiny creature, can bring death to the human body, either by stinging—as bees do, and especially hornets, commonly called *frelons* by the French—

Virgil, *Georgics* IV, line 236:

> Their anger exceeds all bounds, and, wounded, they breathe poison  
> Into their bites; they leave their hidden stings behind,  
> Fastened in the veins, and place their lives within the wound.

—or by entering the internal organs, as Spanish flies do. Cicero, *Letters* IX.21, says: “Gaius is said to have taken Spanish flies when accused by Lucius Crassus.”

Two words here may be noted: *expetibilis* and *muscularum*, for their Latin authority is unknown to me. I would use *desiderabilis* and *muscarum*. You may judge.

> But if you consider the body, can you find anything weaker than a human being,  
> Whom often even the bites of flies, however small,  
> Or their entry as they crawl into hidden places, can kill?

What right can anyone exercise over another except over the body—and what lies below the body, namely fortune? Can you ever command a free mind? Can you remove from its settled condition a mind firmly united by sound reason?

**148. When a certain free man, etc.** — Next, the torments that a superior inflicts upon the body of an inferior can become material for virtue. This happened to the philosopher Anaxarchus, a follower of Democritus, whom Philosophy now mentions.

For Anaxarchus, as Cicero says in *Tusculan Disputations* II, when he had fallen into the hands of Nicocreon, king of Cyprus, neither begged to be spared any kind of punishment nor refused any. He was thrown into a stone mortar and beaten there with iron hammers. “Pound away,” he said, “pound the sack of Anaxarchus; you are not pounding Anaxarchus.” When the tyrant threatened to cut out his tongue, he bit off his tongue with his teeth and spat it in the tyrant’s face.

> When a tyrant thought that he would force a certain free man by tortures  
> To betray those who knew of the conspiracy formed against him,  
> The man bit through and cut off his tongue  
> And threw it into the mouth of the raging tyrant.  
> Thus the torments which the tyrant thought would provide material for cruelty  
> The wise man made into material for virtue.

**Note:** Some say Zeno; others, Anaxarchus.

**What, then, is there that one person can do to another, etc.?** — Finally, what a superior can do to the body of an inferior, the inferior can often do to the body of the superior. There are many examples of this. Philosophy recalls Busiris and Regulus.

Busiris, born to Neptune by Libya, the daughter of Epaphus, was an exceedingly cruel tyrant of Egypt. He sacrificed his guests to Jupiter, sparing not even the prophet from whom he had received this advice. But when he prepared the same ambush for Hercules, Hercules killed him at the very altar, together with his son Amphidamas, the herald Chalbes, and the attendants.

Virgil, *Georgics* III, line 5:

> Who does not know the harsh Eurystheus  
> Or the altars of the infamous Busiris?

Claudian, poem 3, line 254:

> O gentle horses of Diomedes! The altars  
> Of Busiris were kinder!

The same author, poem 18, line 159:

> Thus for many years, beside a dry river,  
> Busiris first instructed the altars he had invented  
> With the blood of the guest whose slaughter,  
> He had been told, would appease the thunderer;  
> And he fell as the victim of the savage rite  
> He himself had prescribed.

Regulus was a consul who, as Pliny says, celebrated a triumph after defeating the Sallentines and was the first Roman commander to transport a fleet into Africa. He was killed by the Carthaginians—whom Philosophy here calls the Phoenicians—whom he had defeated, after his eyelids had been cut off.

> What can anyone do to another  
> That he cannot himself endure from another?

We understand Busiris, who was accustomed to kill his guests, to have been slaughtered by Hercules, his guest. Regulus had thrown many captured Carthaginians into chains during the war, but soon offered his own hands to the chains of those he had defeated.

Can you suppose that man’s power to be anything, who cannot prevent another from doing to him what he himself can do to another?

**149. Moreover, etc.** — III. Having considered the subject and object, Philosophy turns to the formal effect of power, as philosophers call it.

Her reasoning can be reduced as follows: Whatever is good by its nature makes its possessor good and therefore drives away the contrary evil from him. For the nature of each thing produces its proper effect, does not mingle with the effects of contrary things, and spontaneously drives away what is opposed to it. Thus courage makes a person courageous, speed makes one swift, music makes a musician, medicine makes a physician, and rhetoric makes an orator.

But neither power, which is now under discussion, nor any of Fortune’s gifts makes its possessor good or drives away the contrary evil from him. It is beyond doubt that the worst men commonly exercise dignities, and that all Fortune’s gifts come more abundantly to the most wicked.

**Moreover.** — If dignities and powers themselves contained some natural and proper good, they would never come to the worst men. For opposites do not normally associate with one another; nature rejects the joining of contraries.

Thus, since it is beyond doubt that the worst men commonly exercise dignities, it is also clear that those things are not good by their nature which allow themselves to cling to the worst men. The same can be judged of all Fortune’s gifts, which come more abundantly to the most wicked.

I also think this should be considered: no one doubts that a person is courageous when one sees courage in him; and whenever speed is present, it is clear that the person is swift. Thus music makes musicians, medicine makes physicians, and rhetoric makes orators. For the nature of each thing produces its proper effect, does not mingle with the effects of contrary things, and spontaneously drives away what is opposed to it.

**Yet neither wealth, etc.** — Indeed, the aforesaid goods of Fortune do not even seem to provide the very thing whose appearance and name they especially bear. Wealth does not make a person wealthy, power does not make a person powerful, and dignity does not make a person worthy.

Wealth does not make a person wealthy because it cannot extinguish insatiable greed. As wealth increases, greed increases with it, so that abundance produces poverty.

Power does not make a person powerful because, although it calls someone powerful, it does not make him master of himself, since vicious desires often hold him bound in unbreakable chains.

Finally, dignity does not make a person worthy. When conferred upon wicked men, it not only fails to make them worthy but rather exposes and displays their unworthiness.

Juvenal, Satire 8, line 140:

> Every vice of the soul bears a more conspicuous mark of guilt  
> The greater the person’s rank who commits it.

Yet wealth cannot extinguish insatiable greed; nor can power make a person master of himself when vicious desires hold him bound in unbreakable chains; and dignity conferred upon wicked men not only fails to make them worthy but rather exposes and displays their unworthiness.

**Why does this happen?** — IV. From what has been said, Philosophy concludes that people wrongly bestow upon these things both their particular and their general names:

> You rejoice, O human beings, to call things by false names,  
> Though their actual effects easily refute those names.

**First,** the things mentioned above are wrongly designated by their particular names, since what are called wealth, power, and dignity ought rather to be marked by contrary names, as has been said.

Therefore neither that wealth, nor that power, nor this dignity can rightly be so called.

**Finally,** the same conclusion may be drawn about Fortune as a whole, in which nothing desirable and nothing of innate goodness is present. These things do not always attach themselves to the good, nor do they make good those to whom they are attached, as has also been said.

> Thus neither that wealth, nor that power, nor this dignity  
> Can rightly be called by those names.  
>   
> And in Fortune as a whole there is nothing to be desired,  
> Nothing of innate goodness,  
> Since it does not always accompany the good  
> And does not make good those whom it accompanies.

## METRE VI

**Note:** It is called Sapphic after the woman who invented it. The poem consists of one kind of verse, each line containing five feet: a trochee, a spondee, a dactyl, and two trochees.

**Argument.** — Philosophy says that Nero’s power was so great that he ruled peoples spread from east to west and from north to south. Yet he descended to such wickedness that, after Rome had been set on fire, he killed several senators, his brother, and his own mother. So ruinous is it for a wicked man to become powerful.

> We know what great slaughter Nero caused. When Rome had been set ablaze,  
> Senators had been killed, and his brother murdered,  
> He was once a savage man stained with the blood of his own mother,  
> Whom he himself killed.  
>   
> As he surveyed his mother’s cold corpse with his eyes,  
> He did not wet his cheeks with any tears;  
> Nor was he ashamed to act as censor of the majesty he had destroyed.  
>   
> Nevertheless, this tyrant governed the nations  
> That the rising and setting sun behold,  
> The nations pressed by the seven northern stars with their cold,  
> And those which the powerful south wind burns with dry heat,  
> Scorching their burning sands more and more.  
>   
> Could lofty power transform the madness of deranged Nero?  
> O miserable condition of humanity,  
> When unjust authority is joined with savage cruelty!

**1. We know.** — No one is unaware of this; as Horace says in *Satires* I.7:

> It is known to all who have sore eyes and to all barbers.

[Col. 0706B] 1. “What great ruins he caused.” — Nero. He ruled the Romans in approximately the fifty-seventh year after the birth of Christ. For as long as he followed the counsels of Seneca, whose instruction had formed him, he was regarded as an excellent emperor. But after removing his teacher, he fell into every kind of disgrace and dishonor: forgetful of his dignity, he committed unheard-of acts of infamy and gave proof of luxury, greed, and cruelty. First, he appeared on the stage not merely as a tragedian but also as a lyre-player. Then he never wore any garment twice; he is said never to have traveled [Col. 0706C] with fewer than a thousand carriages, whose mule-shoes were made of silver; he fished with a golden net whose ropes were knotted with purple and scarlet. Moreover, coveting everyone’s wealth, he alone wished to be seen as rich. Finally, he transferred the blame and punishment for Rome—which he had ordered to be burned—to the Christians, whose leaders, the apostles Peter and Paul, he punished with death. Indeed, he killed his teacher Seneca, his aunt Antonia, his brother Britannicus, his wife Octavia, his mother Agrippina, and at last himself—a deed worthy of such great cruelty. See Suetonius, book VI. The principal crimes of this tyrant will be set out below.

2. “The city.” — A city is a settlement enclosed by a wall. It is so called, they say, from *orbis* (“circle”), because those intending to found a city were accustomed, in hope of future fertility, to yoke together a bull and a cow and mark out with a plow the furrow within which they would build the city. But because among all settlements enclosed by walls Rome once held the foremost place, Rome was therefore called *the city* κατ’ ἐξοχήν, “by way of eminence,” in Quintilian’s judgment. Virgil, *Eclogue* I, verse 20:

[Col. 0706D]

“I thought that city which they call Rome, Meliboeus,

Fool that I was, to be like this one of ours, where we shepherds

Often drive the tender offspring of our sheep . . .

Yet it has raised its head above other cities

As cypresses usually rise above pliant viburnums.”

2. “Set aflame.” — A part is taken for the whole: for Rome was not entirely consumed by fire, but only that part of the city which appeared disfigured by disreputable buildings; Nero set it alight as a spectacle, so that he might reproduce the burning of Troy. “For six days,” says Suetonius, book VI, “and seven nights, the disaster raged, with the common people driven into shelters at monuments and tombs. Then, besides an immense number of apartment blocks, the houses of ancient generals burned, still adorned with spoils taken from enemies; as did the temples of the gods, vowed and dedicated by kings and later during the Punic and Gallic wars; and everything worth seeing and memorable that had survived from antiquity.”

2. “And the senators having been slain.” — “For,” says Suetonius, “a comet, which is commonly thought to portend the destruction of the highest authorities, had begun to rise on successive nights. Alarmed by this, and having learned from the astrologer Babylonus that kings customarily expiated such omens by some illustrious slaughter and diverted them from themselves onto the heads of the nobles, he destined the nobility to destruction. It is established that some were killed together with their tutors and book-carriers at a single dinner, while others were forbidden to seek their daily food. Thereafter no selection or limit was observed in killing: whoever he pleased, for whatever reason, and so on.”

“We know what great ruins he caused—

152 When Rome had been set aflame and the senators slain—”

[Col. 0707A] [Note: [Col. 0707B]

3. “With his brother killed.” — Namely Britannicus, whom Claudius had fathered by Messalina, just as he had received Nero from Agrippina. Nero attacked him with poison, says Suetonius, moved no less by rivalry over his voice—which was more pleasant—than by fear that his father’s memory might someday prevail in the people’s favor. When Britannicus collapsed at the first taste, Nero pretended before the banqueters that he had been seized, as usual, by an epileptic fit; on the following day he hastily gave him a commoner’s funeral amid the heaviest rain.

4. “With his mother’s blood poured out.” — Nero was greatly distressed by his mother, who investigated and reproved his words and actions too harshly. Suetonius says that, terrified by her threats and violence, he resolved to destroy her. When he had tried poison and found that she was protected by antidotes, he prepared a ceiling which, by means of a loosened mechanism, would fall upon her while she slept. When several other attempts also failed to answer his wishes, he killed his mother with a dagger. Hence the verses:

“Who denies that Nero came from Aeneas’ great lineage?

The one removed his mother; the other removed his father.”

5. “Roaming over the corpse and the frozen face with his gaze.” — “Still more atrocious acts are added to the preceding ones,” says Suetonius, “on authorities that are not uncertain: Nero, it is said, hurried to view the corpse of his murdered mother, handled her limbs, condemned some and praised others, and, when thirst arose, drank.” Hence he is now called “the censor of extinguished beauty,” because, just as a censor used to assess each person’s property, Nero did not hesitate to inspect the individual parts of his mother’s body and pass judgment on each one. He did not weep—which is astonishing. The consciousness of guilt that he confessed tormented him as though with the lashes of the Furies and their blazing torches; and the same consciousness, when it caused the thirst mentioned above, ought to have compelled him to shed tears. But, I suppose, the voice of conscience was then scarcely audible to him because of the greater force of his agitation.

8. “Yet this man, etc.” — That most wicked Nero, nevertheless, since he was emperor of the Romans, ruled peoples from east to west and from north to south. The Roman Empire had, of course, spread far and wide and reached the four principal regions of the world: east, west, north, and south. Hence Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, verse 781:

“Behold, my son, under whose auspices that illustrious Rome—

Her empire over the earth, her spirit equal to Olympus—

Will arise . . .

This is the man, this is he whom you so often hear promised to you,

Augustus Caesar, offspring of the gods: he will found again a golden

Age in Latium, over the fields once ruled by Saturn;

He will extend his empire beyond the Garamantes and Indians;

A land lies beyond the stars, beyond the paths of the year and the sun,

Where Atlas, bearer of heaven, turns upon his shoulder

The axis fitted with burning stars.”

Here the four regions of the world are most appropriately indicated: east and west by Phoebus, who comes from the farthest east and sinks his rays beneath the waves. Thus Virgil, *Georgics* I, verse 438:

“The sun, too, both when rising and when he sinks into the waves,

Will give signs; the surest signs will follow the sun.”

North and south are indicated by the Seven Plow-Oxen and by the south wind scorching the sands; for the Seven Plow-Oxen are the northern constellation commonly called the Great Bear. Since it consists of seven principal stars, it seems to represent a wagon, the oxen drawing it, and the ox-driver leading them. Oxen were formerly called *teriones* because they wear down the soil, or *terriones* because they plow the earth, or *striones* because they make a furrow. The South Wind is the wind blowing from the south, and is therefore said to be accompanied by great heat.

14. “Could elevated power at last prevail?” — This is proved especially by Nero’s example: possessing power does not make its possessor better. This is the present teaching of Philosophy. If there was ever among human beings a power that could make its possessor better, it was Nero’s power, since he ruled the whole world by his authority. Yet this power, however great it was, could not transform the madness of insane Nero. “Rage” properly means a dog’s bite, by which a dog, violently rushing here and there, attacks everything in its path. So Nero was the cruellest of all tyrants.

[Col. 0708D] 16. “Alas, grievous is the human lot.” — Virgil says similarly in *Aeneid* VII, verse 293:

“Alas, hated race, and fates opposed to our own,

The fates of the Phrygians!”

This is most aptly said as: “Woe is me, ruined man! For pity’s sake, gods and men!”

16. “Whenever an unjust sword is added to cruel poison.” — Whenever unjust power is found joined with a cruel will; for here the sign is taken for the thing signified. Thus it is commonly said as a proverb: “Turn aside the sharp sword”; or, “Do not give a sword to a boy,” to show that power must not be entrusted to those who would use it to harm others.]

“He who once, savage, killed his brother,

Was drenched in his mother’s poured-out blood.”

[5] 153 “Roaming over the body, cold to behold,

He did not stain his face with tears, but was able

To be censor of extinguished beauty.

Yet with his scepter he ruled peoples—

Those whom Phoebus sees, coming from the farthest east,

As he sinks his rays beneath the waves;

Those whom the seven cold Plow-Oxen press;

Those whom the violent South Wind, with its dry heat,

Scorches, baking the blazing sands again and again.

154 Could elevated power at last prevail

[15] [Col. 0708A] Over the rage of insane Nero?

Alas, grievous is the human lot, whenever an unjust

Sword is added to cruel poison!”

155 PROSE VII.

[Col. 0708A]

ARGUMENT. — When Boethius declares how he himself attained public offices, Philosophy replies that the fame by which every excellent magistrate appears to be guided is negligible, since it is confined within narrow limits of place and time—especially for one conscious of his exile and his own immortality.

Then I [Note: [Col. 0708A] Boethius], [Col. 0708D] said, “You yourself know.” I. Boethius testifies that Philosophy, being conscious of all the thoughts Boethius had entertained concerning the way in which he himself attained public offices, says that he had wished for an opportunity to undertake public duties, not from ambition but so that silent virtue should not grow old. [Col. 0709B] “Ambition” and “candidacy for office” (*ambitus*) arise from the same origin: *ambi*, “around,” and *itio* or *itus*, from the verb *eo*, “I go.” For this reason the terms are first applied to bodies and later, by a certain likeness, to minds. *Ambitus* or ambition in bodies is a space of two and a half feet, by which neighboring buildings are separated from one another to allow passage around them. In minds, however, it is a certain circuit of thoughts, and then of words and actions, directed toward attaining honor. “This is ambition,” says Tertullian, *On the Apparel of Women*, chapter 4, “and its name is to be interpreted as arising from desire surrounding the mind, directed toward the hope of glory.” Boethius says that this ambition never ruled him. But since virtue is concerned especially with a good thought, which other people do not see, yet which it is sometimes fitting for others to know—Matthew V: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven”—Boethius therefore thought that he should desire an opportunity for action, so that silent virtue should not grow old.]

“You yourself know,” I said, “that ambition for mortal things exercised very little dominion over us. But [Col. 0709A] we desired an opportunity for undertaking public duties, so that [Note: [Col. 0709B] “So that not.”] virtue should not grow old in silence.” And she [Note: [Col. 0709B] Philosophy]:

156 “Yet [Note: [Col. 0709C] ‘This is the one thing,’ etc.] II. But those same minds are not yet endowed with perfect virtue, for Matthew VI says: “Take care not to perform your righteousness before men in order to be seen by them; otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.” Hence the Apostle says in Galatians I: “If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a servant of Christ.”] “This is the one thing,” [Note: [Col. 0709B] “She says.”] “that can attract minds distinguished by nature but not yet [Note: [Col. 0709B] “Endowed with the perfection of virtue.”] brought to the final stage of virtue’s perfection: namely, the desire for glory and the reputation of the best services rendered to the state. “What of the fact that the customs and institutions of different nations disagree among themselves, so that what is judged worthy of praise among some is judged worthy of punishment among others? 158 But” [Note: [Col. 0711C] “How many,” etc.] “IV. Philosophy adds that the foregoing fame ought to be considered worthless because of the narrow limits of the time for which it can endure. For either writers will be lacking, by whose repeated stirring of the brains and minds of men [the reading is uncertain] the impressions of your merits may be renewed, or they will be present. If writers are lacking, oblivion will erase you, just as it erased many men who were most renowned in their own times. Thus the merits of the Romans lay as though buried, according to Sallust in the *War against Catiline*, because the wisest men were chiefly occupied with affairs; no one exercised his intellect without bodily action; and every excellent man preferred doing rather than speaking, and preferred having his good deeds praised by others rather than recounting the deeds of others himself. Thus the virtue of brave men who lived before Agamemnon remains hidden, because they lacked writers and poets, in Horace’s judgment, *Odes* IV.9:

“Many brave men lived before Agamemnon;

[Col. 0712C] But if writers are present, since their books often perish either through the injury of time or through the negligence of the writers themselves, it still cannot be certain for you that your fame will remain perpetual through their service. But suppose the books survive, and the memory of the writers survives as well, so that you can say of your merits what Ovid sang of his poems in *Metamorphoses* XV:

“Now I have completed a work that neither Jupiter’s anger nor fires,

Neither the sword nor devouring age,

Will be able to destroy.”

Nevertheless, even if your fame were as old as the world itself, it would be too short-lived for you to act on its behalf—especially if the duration of that fame is compared with the eternity for which the human mind is destined to endure. For if the briefest delay of a single moment, compared with ten thousand years, is a small duration, then certainly the entire duration not only of an old man’s life but also of the world itself, compared with eternity, is a minimal—or rather, no—duration. For between the earlier durations, since both are finite, there is some relationship; but between the latter two, of which one is infinite, there is no proportion—what is now called a share or fraction. Thus Curtius speaks: “The reward,” he says, “will be ten talents for the one who first reaches the summit. He who comes next will receive one less, and the same proportion will be maintained for ten men.” The word “interminable,” which Boethius uses more than once, seems less Latin. Cicero would say “unbounded,” as in *On the Nature of the Gods* I: “If you could see the immeasurable and unbounded extent of the regions in every direction.”]

“How many men most renowned in their own times has oblivion erased for lack of writers! But if you draw it out by comparing it with the infinite stretches of eternity,” [Note: [Col. 0711C] “If you extend it by comparison.”] “what do you have that could make you rejoice in the long duration of your name? But this very number of years, and any multiple of it, cannot even be compared with an unbounded duration.” [Note: [Col. 0712B] “Infinite.”] “For between finite things there can be some relation to one another, but between the infinite and the finite there can never be any comparison. Thus fame of however long a duration, if considered alongside inexhaustible eternity, appears not small but entirely nothing.” [Note: [Col. 0712B] “However long.”] “Yet unless you are seeking popular applause and empty rumors” [Note: [Col. 0712C] “To stir them up.”] “you do not know how to act rightly; abandoning the excellence of conscience and virtue, you demand rewards from the idle chatter of others. He added that he would now discover whether the man was a philosopher, provided that he bore the insults inflicted upon him gently and patiently. The man briefly assumed an attitude of patience; then, having received the insult, he said, as though mocking him, ‘Do you now at last understand that I am a philosopher?’”

159 “Then the other, with excessive sharpness, replied, ‘I understood it—if you had kept silent.’” [Note: [Col. 0712D] “If you had kept silent.”] Cicero says something similar in *For Archias*: “Philosophers write books on despising glory, inscribe their own names on them, and in that very matter in which they disdain proclamation and renown, they wish themselves to be proclaimed and named.”

159 “But what does fame, after the body has been dissolved by final death, have to do with eminent men” [Note: [Col. 0713A] “Distinguished.”] “—for these are the men under discussion—who pursue glory through virtue? What, I ask, does it matter to them? For if, as” [Note: [Col. 0713B] “Our arguments forbid us to believe.”] “Indeed, there are many arguments by which Philosophy proves that the human mind is immortal, and therefore that the whole human being does not die. We present one drawn from the very nature of the mind. Every thing or substance whose only cause is external is enduring and perpetual, since God, from whom it comes, continues the mode of action with which that substance was created. Thus we believe that spirits, both evil and good, will be perpetual; thus matter itself, commonly called prime matter, is regarded by all as perpetual. The human mind, however, is of this kind. It is indeed a substance, because it does not inhere in another thing but underlies its own qualities; and it has no cause other than an external efficient cause and end, since it does not depend upon matter. The human mind is so conscious of this immortality of its own that it always desires it. Yet what it ought to attribute only to itself, it ascribes through a certain rash assumption even to perishable things with which it thinks it has some connection. Thus parents hope for a kind of immortal life in their children, authors in their writings, and everyone in increasingly magnificent tombs. Hence Tully says in *On Old Age*: ‘The soul of every excellent person strives most earnestly toward immortal glory.’”

“if our arguments forbid us to believe that human beings wholly die, then there is no glory at all, since the one to whom it is said to belong no longer exists. But if the mind, conscious of its own thoughts” [Note: [Col. 0713B] “Of its thoughts.”] “once freed from its earthly prison, freely seeks heaven, will it not despise every earthly concern, since, enjoying heaven, it rejoices to have been released from earthly things?”

161 METER [Note: [Col. 0713C] “A poem consisting of two alternating kinds of verse, the first having six iambic feet and the second likewise having four iambic feet, with spondees more often in the odd-numbered positions and iambs in the even-numbered positions.] VII.

ARGUMENT. — Repeating in measured speech what she had just said in prose, Philosophy proves by examples that fame, which during life can be only slight, ends with death. Thus, for those who regard this fame as a second life, a double death must be endured.

[Col. 0714A] [Note: [Col. 0714A]

Whoever, with a heedless mind, strives only after glory [Col. 0714B] and considers it the highest good should consider [Col. 0715B] on the one hand the vast expanses of heaven and on the other the narrow position of the earth. Surely he will then be ashamed of scattered rumor, which cannot occupy even the earth’s small circumference. Alas, why do arrogant men strive in vain to free their bodies from the servitude of death? Even if fame, dispersed everywhere through distant nations, spreads its wings through the languages of all those peoples, and a great family shines with illustrious honors, death nevertheless scorns this highest glory, encloses humble and exalted heads alike in the same tomb, and makes the lowest equal to the highest. Where do the bones of faithful Fabricius now lie? What is Brutus now, or stern Cato? Their slight remembrance records their empty name in a few letters. But since we recognize these beautiful names, is it not permissible for us, from this fact, to know that the people whose names these are have perished? You therefore lie utterly unknown, and fame does not make you known. But if you think that your life is prolonged further by human esteem, since a later age will eventually snatch away this esteem from you as well, then a second death awaits you.]

[Col. 0713C]

1. “With a headlong mind.” — Or, “with rashness.” Rashness is an inconsiderate judgment concerning what is unknown: it is the first origin of error and therefore of vice.

1. “Strives after.” — Properly, to strive after something describes a body transferred from one neighborhood to another; but by a certain likeness it is also said of the mind, insofar as the mind inclines toward something by its own will.

2. “And considers glory the highest.” — That is, the highest good. Since everything that is sought possesses some appearance of goodness, it is necessary that whatever is sought above all else should possess the appearance of the highest good. But mortal glory cannot appear to be the highest good except to those who are rash and are led to judgment by an obscure or confused conception—namely, to those who, moved by the innate notion by which we all wish to be happy, cling through a false assumption to a human being rather than solely to God.

3. “Let him behold the far-reaching regions of the ether.” — So great is the magnitude of the ether, or heaven, diffused in every direction that we cannot grasp it in imagination. Hence certain philosophers call heaven not infinite but indefinite: that is, spread more widely than our mind can define by imagining it. Thus, when heaven is considered more attentively, a person can be convicted of his own weakness, especially if he compares with heaven, as though with something immeasurable, the tiny earth, of which heaven is the smallest portion, or rather—

4. “The narrow position of the earth.” — Just as the entire globe of earth and water, compared with heaven, has the status of a point, as we have said, so the inhabited portion of the earth in which a particular person’s merits can be known and praised by human beings is, when compared with the rest of the earth where that same person can neither be known nor praised, a tiny point within that point. Therefore this person will be ashamed of his expanded name, which nevertheless cannot fill the brief circumference. Thus Alexander the Great was ashamed that, among the worlds he thought innumerable, he had not conquered even one.

7. “To lift their proud necks from the mortal yoke.” — To acquire for their names on earth an immortality of reputation; for, as has been said, those who seek to gain fame among posterity are possessed by this desire.

9. “Let fame, traveling through the peoples, unfold its tongues.” — Poets imagine Fame as having the nature of a person, equipped with wings and carried swiftly through even the most remote places, and as rousing peoples to speech with her loosened mouth and tongue. Virgil, *Aeneid* I, verse 461:

“Wars already spread by fame throughout the whole world.”

11. “Let it shine with illustrious titles.” — A title is the same as an honor. It derives from the Greek τιτὸς, “honor,” from τὸ τίειν, “to honor”; hence τιμή, “honor.” Thus genealogical trees, images, and any other signs of honors are commonly called titles. Claudian, poem 26, verse 144:

“And the common trophy marks the twofold titles.”

[Col. 0714D] 12. “Death scorns lofty glory, etc.” — For it is appointed for human beings to die once, Hebrews IX. Horace, *Odes* I.28:

“But one night awaits them all,

And the path of death must be trodden once.

The Furies give others as grim spectacles to Mars;

The sea is destruction to greedy sailors.

Funerals of old and young are heaped together:

Savage Proserpina spares no head.”

And in the same book, ode 4:

“Pale Death strikes with equal foot the cottages

Of the poor and the towers

Of kings, blessed Sextus.”

Our Malherbe rendered this successfully in book VI:

“Death has severities like no others:

One may plead with her in vain.

Cruel as she is, she stops her ears,

And leaves us crying.

The poor man in his hut, where thatch covers him,

Is subject to her laws;

And the guard who watches at the barriers of the Louvre

Cannot defend our kings from her.”

] “Whoever with a heedless mind seeks glory alone

And believes it the highest good,

Let him behold the far-reaching regions of the ether,

162 And the narrow position of the earth:

[5] “He will be ashamed of an expanded name

That cannot fill a brief circumference.

Why, O proud men, do you desire in vain

To lift your necks from the mortal yoke?

Although fame, traveling through distant peoples,

[10] Spread abroad, may unfold its tongues,

And a great house shine with illustrious titles,

Death scorns lofty glory,

Envelops humble and exalted heads alike,

And makes the lowest equal to the highest.

[15] [Col. 0715A] [Note: [Col. 0715B]

15. “Faithful Fabricius.” — Fabricius, a Roman consul, was renowned among very many people, both orators and poets, especially for his fidelity; he is therefore rightly called “faithful.” First, because when Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, tested him with great gifts and even promised him a fourth part of his kingdom, he could not induce him to abandon his country. Then, because Fabricius arranged for Timochares, a physician who was bringing poison to his own king Pyrrhus in hope of a reward, to be returned to his master. The king, astonished by this, said that Fabricius could more easily be turned away from honesty than the sun from its course. Hence Claudian, poem 26, verse 130:

“And Fabricius’ heart, inaccessible to every fault,

Unconquered by gifts or arms.”

16. “What of Brutus?” — Lucius Brutus, so called because of the stupidity he pretended out of fear of Tarquinius. After the Tarquins were expelled because of the violation of Lucretia, he asserted liberty for the Romans together with Collatinus. Hence the Roman people transferred authority to those same defenders of their liberty, though they changed both the law and the name. They decided that authority should be annual rather than perpetual, and twofold rather than singular, lest power be corrupted by isolation or duration; and they called their rulers consuls instead of kings, so that they might remember that they ought to consult for the welfare of their fellow citizens. Claudian frequently speaks of this Brutus, as in poem 22, verse 322:

“Let Stilicho be the avenger in the purple, and Brutus the discoverer.

Through the first consul Brutus, liberty was restored to the people

By the official rods; he expelled servitude by those very rods;

Brutus established the sublime office.”

16. “Stern Cato.” — Just as Brutus received his surname from feigned stupidity, so Cato received his from genuine wisdom. For *catus*, from which comes *Cato*, means “wise.” Ausonius: “wise in laws and powerful in speech.” For this reason several men were called Catos because of their wisdom. Juvenal, *Satire* 2, verse 40:

“The third Cato fell from heaven.”

There were, however, two outstanding men who received this surname and whom Philosophy could have had in mind here: namely, the Elder and the Younger. Both, though at different times, arose from the obscure Tusculan family of the Porcii. Cato the Elder, called the Censor, flourished in the year 570 from the founding of the City and lived to the extreme limit of old age. Cato the Younger, called the Praetorian, lived during the very period of the Caesarian war. Of him Lucan wrote shamelessly:

“The victorious cause pleased the gods, but the defeated cause pleased Cato.”

And Horace, *Odes* II.1:

[Col. 0716C]

“Already I seem to hear great commanders,

Soiled with dust not dishonorable,

And all the earth subdued

Except the fierce spirit of Cato.”

17. “The survivor marks, etc.” — When a person has died, his corpse remains; once it has decayed, the surviving name is written down in a few letters, at least by those endowed with a good memory, but without any awareness or benefit belonging to the dead. Therefore it is not undeservedly called empty.

## 19. “But that we recognize distinguished names,” etc.

When we see these names inscribed upon splendid tombs, they are evidence that those whose names they are no longer exist; for the inscription reads: “HERE LIES.” There is only one tomb of Christ upon which it was permissible to write: “HE DOES NOT LIE HERE” (Matthew 28).

## 23. “But if you suppose,” etc.

If you think that some life still persists in that surviving name, since even that name must at last perish when oblivion has been introduced, you will suffer a second death. Thus Sulpicius of Carthage wrote concerning Virgil’s *Aeneid*, which is said to have been destined by its author for the flames:

> Unhappy Pergamum nearly fell by a double fire,  
> and Troy was almost consumed upon another pyre.

> 163 Where now do the faithful bones of Fabricius lie?  
> What of Brutus, or stern Cato?  
>   
> 164 A faint surviving fame marks  
> an empty name in a few letters.  
>   
> But although we know the distinguished names,  
> [20] is it granted us to know that those men have been consumed?  
>   
> You therefore lie utterly unknown,  
> nor does fame make you known.  
>   
> But if you think that the breath  
> of a mortal name prolongs life,  
> [25] when a late day shall snatch even this from you,  
> a second death already awaits you.

## 165. PROSE VIII

[Col. 0716A]

### Argument

“Adverse fortune,” says Philosophy, “surpasses prosperous fortune in this respect: prosperous fortune, enveloping the mind in darkness, leads it both into error and into vice; adverse fortune, on the other hand, stripping the mind of prejudices, leads it by the hand, as it were, both to truth and to virtue.”

But lest you think that I am waging an implacable war against Fortune by declaiming against her, she sometimes deserves well of human beings—namely, when she reveals herself, uncovers her face, and openly declares her character. To “deserve” (*mereri*) is to do something for which a reward or punishment ought to be rendered. Hence the meal following lunch but preceding dinner is called *merenda*, because it is owed for hired laborers’ work; and one punished for some crime is said to “pay penalties,” as though rendering a debt. Thus Cicero, *On the Laws* III: “Vicious rulers deserve badly of the commonwealth.” Perhaps you do not yet understand what I am saying. It is remarkable what I want to say, and for that reason I can scarcely explain my thought in words. For I believe that adverse fortune benefits human beings more than prosperous fortune.

A human being, as has often been said, consists of mind and body, of which the former is far nobler than the latter. Therefore, what benefits the mind is preferable to that which benefits the other; and what benefits the other, provided it does not harm the mind, benefits the body alone. Now adverse fortune benefits the mind; prosperous fortune, if it does not harm the mind, benefits the body alone. This must subsequently be proved. Prosperous fortune, by the obscure and confused conception with which it informs the mind, first leads it into error, so that it judges perishable goods to possess the character of the highest good; then into vice, so that, despising God, it clings exclusively to those same goods.

Prosperous fortune, always flattering under the appearance of happiness, lies when she seems gentle; but adverse fortune is always truthful when she displays her instability by her changes. The former deceives; the latter instructs. The former binds the minds of those who enjoy her with the lie of apparent goods; the latter releases them through knowledge of fragile happiness. Thus you may see the former as swollen, shifting, and always ignorant of herself; the latter as sober, restrained, and made wise by the exercise of adversity. Finally, prosperous fortune draws those who have strayed from the true good onward by her flatteries; adverse fortune often pulls those returning back to true goods with a hooked staff (*pedo*, a staff or bent walking-stick). Adverse fortune, by the conception which it either finds or makes evident, first leads the mind to truth, so that it judges God alone to possess the character of the highest good; then to virtue, so that, setting all else aside, it loves God alone. Thus Proverbs 29 says: “The rod and correction give wisdom; but a child left to his own will brings shame upon his mother.”

Do you think it should be counted among the least of benefits that this harsh, this dreadful fortune has revealed to you the minds of your faithful friends, has distinguished for you the certain faces of your companions from the uncertain, and, when she departed, took away her own adherents but left yours? At what price would you have purchased this, had you remained unharmed and, as you seemed to yourself, fortunate? Stop now seeking the wealth you have lost: you have found the most precious kind of riches—friends.

Among external goods friends hold the foremost place; and that which reveals to you minds otherwise concealed is rightly considered the most precious even of external goods, since it distinguishes true friends from false. Adverse fortune does this: while fortune smiles, false friends are present together with true ones; when it is angry, false friends depart while true friends remain. Ovid’s well-known lines say:

> So long as you are fortunate, you will count many friends;  
> if the times become cloudy, you will be alone.

## 167. METRE VIII

### Note on the metre

This is called the Glyconic metre. It is a poem consisting of one kind of verse, each line being composed of one spondee and two dactyls. Taking his cue from the final words of the preceding prose, in which Philosophy indicated that Boethius’s friends had been tested by adverse fortune and remained with him, the author urges Boethius to contemplate love and its effects.

Love, like every human affection, may be considered in two ways. First, as philosophers say, inadequately: insofar as it is a certain state of the body—for example, a movement of the blood, the spirits, and the other parts of the human body, naturally instituted for preserving social relations. Second, as the same philosophers say, adequately: insofar as, in addition to the aforesaid bodily state, it exists in the human will as the will adheres to something that is, as it were, another part of the society of which the human being himself is the remaining part.

Hence, according to the three kinds of opinion that a human being may have concerning that part—valuing it as greater than, equal to, or less than himself—love is of three kinds: filial devotion, friendship, and love in the strict sense. In bodies there is love only insofar as love is a bodily state. In God there is love only insofar as it is a state of mind. In a human being love is present insofar as it is a state both of body and of mind.

The present passage deals first with bodily love, which is not so much love as an image of love; second, with human love; and third, with divine love.

### Argument

Having advanced from the image of love to true love, first human and then divine, Philosophy shows that the world, the elements, heaven, the sea, peoples, spouses, and companions are held together by love. Hence she concludes that human beings would be happy if they were governed by divine love.

### Note

To Love is due the fact that the world continually changes its harmonious cycles; that the opposing elements maintain eternal peace among themselves; that the sun carries forth its brilliant light in a golden chariot; that the moon rules the darkness which Hesperus has brought on; and that the sea, greedy for waters, restrains its waves within their prescribed boundary, lest, once spread abroad, they be permitted to extend more widely over the lands.

Love, ruling heaven, sea, and earth, joins this sequence of things. When love ceases, the things that now agree will immediately disagree and will attempt to destroy the structure which they now steadily set in motion through their splendid movements. Love keeps peoples joined to one another in uncorrupted peace; love confirms the marriage covenant with chaste flames; and love finally renders to faithful friends what is their due. O happy human beings, if the same love of God by which heaven is governed should govern your minds!

### Note on the poem

#### 1. “Because the world with steadfast faith,” etc.

The image of love observable in bodies is under discussion. To it may be attributed, first, the fact that the world—which is nothing other than the universe of bodies, agreeing in matter but differing in form—remains harmonious in its variety; second, the fact that the elements—which are nothing other than the bodies first formed, from which all other things consist—maintain an everlasting compact, both within and outside the bodies called “mixtures” because they consist of the elements; and third, the fact that heaven contains the stars in their appointed times and the sea its waves in their proper places. We have already spoken of Phoebus and Hesperus.

> Because the world with steadfast faith  
> changes its harmonious cycles,  
>   
> 168 because opposing seeds  
> maintain an everlasting compact,  
>   
> [5] because Phoebus carries the rosy day  
> forward in a golden chariot,  
>   
> so that Phoebe may rule during the nights  
> which Hesperus has brought on,  
>   
> so that the sea, greedy for waters,  
> [10] may restrain its waves within a fixed limit,  
>   
> lest it be permitted to the wandering lands  
> to extend their broad boundaries,  
>   
> love binds this sequence of things,  
> ruling lands and sea  
>   
> [15] and exercising command over heaven.  
>   
> If love should loosen its reins,  
> whatever now loves another  
> would wage continuous war,  
>   
> and would strive to dissolve the structure  
> which they now impel in allied fidelity  
> [20] through their beautiful movements.  
>   
> Here love also holds peoples  
> joined by a holy covenant;  
>   
> here love binds the sacred bond of marriage  
> [25] with chaste affections;  
>   
> here it dictates to faithful companions  
> the rights that belong to them.  
>   
> 169 O happy race of human beings,  
> if the love by which heaven is governed  
> [30] should govern your minds!

#### 22. “Here love holds peoples,” etc.

Human love is under discussion. It is of many kinds, but Philosophy now mentions only three: first, the love that exists among peoples, by which peoples are maintained in lasting peace; second, the love that exists between spouses, by which the sacred marriage covenant is confirmed; and third, the love that exists among friends, by which one friend, as another self to his friend, is moved to benefit him in thought, word, and deed—for these are the rights of companions.

#### 28. “O happy race of human beings,” etc.

Divine love is under discussion. By it not only heaven but also all bodies are governed, so that they do not depart even by a finger’s breadth from the divine will. The human mind alone is such that, because it has been loved by God in such a way that it shares in freedom, it can depart from the first rule of willing and acting, the divine will.

Therefore Philosophy’s one desire ought to be that the human mind, having despised its own will and its own love, conform itself to the will and love of God. Thus, imitating holy men and submitting itself in voice and thought, it may say with the prophet-king: “Teach me to do your will”; and with the Apostle: “Lord, what do you want me to do?”

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0719]

## 170. PROSE I

[Col. 0719B]

### Argument

Advancing again from lighter arguments to stronger ones, Philosophy tells Boethius—already moved and prepared by the preceding arguments to grasp greater matters—that, beginning with what is more familiar, she will lead him to true happiness.

She had now finished her song, when the sweetness of the poem had fixed me, eager to hear and still sitting in astonishment with my ears pricked up. Therefore, shortly afterward, I said:

“O highest consolation of weary souls, how greatly you have refreshed me, whether by the weight of your thoughts or even by the delight of your singing! So much so that I no longer think myself unequal to Fortune’s blows. Thus I do not merely dread the remedies that you said a little earlier were somewhat sharper; rather, I earnestly desire to hear them.”

### Note

#### I. “The song,” etc.

Boethius is said to have been moved by the force of the preceding philosophical arguments both in body and in mind. In body, because the song, sweet as honey-wine, had fixed him in astonishment, with his ears still pricked up—that is, with both the rest of his body and his ears motionless, so that he might listen more easily. This manner of speaking has been transferred from dogs, hares, and other animals whose ears move spontaneously to human beings, whose ears do not move in that way. Those animals, in order to receive sound more effectively, are accustomed both to stop and to raise their ears.

He is said to have been moved in mind also, because his mind, either through the weight of the thoughts or through the pleasure of the singing, had been so restored that he no longer considered himself unequal to Fortune’s blows. Consequently, he not only does not dread the remedies which Philosophy said above were sharper, but eagerly begs to hear them.

### II. “I perceived,” etc.

171 Then she said:

“I perceived this when you silently and attentively seized upon our words, and I have either awaited this disposition of your mind—or, more truly, I myself have brought it about. For such are the things that remain: when first tasted, they bite, but once received within, they become sweet.”

### Note

Boethius is said to have been prepared by the preceding arguments and by Philosophy herself. He is prepared by the preceding arguments because prejudices are gradually removed by them—prejudices that would make what is about to be said unpleasant, just as even the sweetest food displeases a palate in poor condition. The things that remain are of this kind: when first tasted, they bite, but once received within, they become sweet.

He is prepared by Philosophy herself because philosophical knowledge, being clear and distinct, is the principle from which every legitimate judgment and desire arises.

172 “But since you say that you are eager to hear,” she continued, “with what ardor would you burn if you recognized where we are undertaking to lead you.”

“Where?” I asked.

### III. “To true happiness,” etc.

Philosophy promises that she will lead Boethius to happiness. Since the present discussion concerns the formation of moral character, and since the best formation of character depends especially upon its end, Philosophy undertakes to discuss happiness, which is the end of rightly formed character. The notion of this happiness is implanted in human minds; therefore Philosophy adds:

“To true happiness,” she said, “which your mind also dreams of, but which it cannot contemplate because its sight is occupied by images.”

The mind is said to dream when, with the external organs of sense asleep, it is stirred by impressions impressed upon the brain and recalled by the spirits, according to the following lines of Claudian:

> All the desires that are turned over by the waking senses  
> friendly rest returns to the sleeping breast.  
>   
> When the hunter, exhausted, lays his limbs upon the bed,  
> his mind nevertheless returns to the forests and its familiar haunts.

Thus, just as there is often something false in human dreams, so there is always something true.
