There is often something false in them because the dreaming mind frequently attributes to external bodies something that does not belong to them. Yet there is always something true in those same dreams—for example, the fact that the dreamer is thinking.

Therefore, just as a human being does not dream except on the basis of forms previously received from the body, so the mind—which desires no particular good except under the guidance of the notion of happiness divinely implanted in it from birth—is not wrongly said to dream of this happiness. Accordingly, just as in sleep that implanted notion of happiness is so obscured by alien images that the happiness itself is not clearly and distinctly perceived by the mind in which it is implanted, so the mind, inclined by a false assumption toward riches or anything else different from God as its highest good and ultimate end, pursues it.

[The preceding editorial note ends with the inherited sentence fragment: “Therefore it must be sought …”]

Then I said:

“Please do so, and demonstrate without delay what that true happiness is.”

“I shall gladly do so for your sake,” she replied, “but I shall first try to indicate and shape in words the cause that is more familiar to you, so that, once you have grasped it, you may recognize a likeness of true happiness when you turn the eyes of your mind in the opposite direction.”

### IV. “The cause more familiar to you,” etc.

Philosophy warns that she must begin with what is more familiar. In every method, progress is made from what is more familiar to what is less known, so that by means of this evident notion we may be led both to investigate and to distinguish what is being sought from what is not in question.

## 173. METRE I

### Note on the metre

This is called the Phalecian metre. It is a poem consisting of one kind of verse, each line being composed of three dactyls and one pyrrhic. Accordingly, attention may be paid to the fourth verse, in which, contrary to common usage, the final syllable of the name *Ceres* is contracted, as in *miles*, *seges*, and *pedes*.

### Argument

By the example of bodies—namely, a field, the palate, and the air, all alternately affected for better and worse—Philosophy proves that the human mind must first be stripped of false opinions before it can be clothed with the true conception of goods.

### Note

Whoever wishes to sow an uncultivated field first clears the ground of shrubs and cuts away with the sickle the thorns and fern, so that Ceres may emerge afresh, laden with grain. Honey, the work of bees, seems much sweeter if the palate has first been steeped in an unpleasant flavor. The stars shine more pleasantly when the south wind ceases to make rainy crashes. After the star that brings back the light has driven away the night, the beautiful day leads forth the sun’s ruddy horses. Thus you too, O Boethius, who formerly directed your mind toward counterfeit goods, should at last begin to withdraw your mind from their tyranny; then true goods will enter your mind, at least in conception.

### Notes on the poem

#### 1. “Whoever wishes to sow a field,” etc.

Philosophy uses the example of a field, which cannot become fruitful until it has been cultivated by removing the shrubs.

#### 1. “Uncultivated” (*ingenuum*)

*Ingenuus* is formed from the preposition *in* and the verb *geno*, which Varro, Lucretius, and many others used for *gigno*, “to beget.” Thus *ingenuus* seems to mean the same as “inborn.” Likewise, *ingenium* is often used for the nature of a thing, as in Virgil, *Georgics* II, line 177: “Now the place is suited to the natures of the fields.” Lucretius similarly calls springs *ingenuus*, or native. A human being is called *ingenuus* when, free from the yoke of slavery from his first origin, he is born free.

Likewise, a field may be called *ingenuus* when, sown with no plants, it is so free that it seems suitable for receiving any seed, just as I would believe it was from its first origin. In the same way, a palate upon which no flavors have previously made an impression is called *ingenua* by Martial, *Epigrams* VI, 11:

> My palate, Marcus, is no less unspoiled for me.

#### 2. “It frees the fields”

Festus says that we call a field *arvum* when it has not yet been sown. In an unsown field, fern, brambles, and shrubs customarily grow—“fern, brambles, and every kind of undergrowth”—and these must therefore be cut away.

#### 4. “So that Ceres may go forth heavy with new grain”

This means that the earth should be fertile. For Ceres is the earth, since, as everyone knows, she is regarded as the discoverer and nourisher of grain. Virgil, *Georgics* I, line 147:

> Ceres first taught mortals to turn the earth with iron,  
> when the sacred forests were already failing in acorns and fruit,  
> and Dodona denied them food.

#### 5. “The work of the bees is all the sweeter”

Philosophy uses the example of the palate, or of any other organ of taste, to which sweetness is more pleasing because it has tasted bitterness. This signifies that truth becomes more welcome once error has been driven away.

The work of the bees is honey; bees, according to Virgil, gather flowing honey. It is called not only *apum* but also *apium*, since the former is contracted from the latter, just as *Quiritium* and *Quiritum*, *loquentium* and *loquentum* are used. But “all the sweeter” is a manner of speaking which grammarians call pleonasm. Thus Plautus said *magis majores nugas agere*, “to make much greater nonsense.”

#### 6. “If an unpleasant flavor first assails the mouth”

This is a form of expression called by the Greeks ὑπαλλαγή (*hypallagē*), “interchange,” by which, because of the mutual relationship of parts, what is normally said of one is sometimes said of the other as well. Thus Virgil said *dare classibus austros*, “to give the south winds to the fleets”; someone else might have said *dare classes austris*, “to give the fleets to the south winds.”

There is such a relationship between flavor and the mouth that, just as flavor penetrates the parts of the mouth and, as it were, divides them, so those same parts of the mouth, admitting the flavor, divide it. Or, to speak with the philosophers, if the organs of taste are modified by foods, foods are likewise modified by the organs of taste.

Finally, honey is best described as sweeter after bitter things, just as in music a concord that follows a brief discord seems more pleasing. The unpleasant movement inflicts a kind of wound upon the sensory organ, and that wound is repaired when another, pleasing movement follows.

#### 7. “The stars shine more pleasantly,” etc.

Philosophy uses the example of the air, insofar as it undergoes alternating contrary changes of two kinds. First, insofar as clear weather follows rain: the south wind, the same as the *Auster*, blows from the south, and because it drives clouds toward water that is about to fall, it is said to produce rainy or rain-bearing sounds.

When the falling rain obstructs the light, making it weaker and striking the eyes intermittently, it disturbs the eyes’ natural balance. Therefore the light, returning when the south wind ceases, restores the disturbed condition of the eyes, so that the same light appears more pleasing.

Second, the air undergoes change insofar as day succeeds night. Here Lucifer is the morning star, which is called Venus. Cicero says in *On the Nature of the Gods* II:

> The innermost of the five wandering stars, and the star nearest the earth, is Venus. In Greek it is called Φωσφόρος (*Phōsphoros*), and in Latin Lucifer when it precedes the sun; when it follows, it is Hesperus.

Virgil, *Eclogue* VIII, line 17:

> Rise, Lucifer, and, coming before the day, lead on the nourishing light.

The sun, moreover, the parent of day, is imagined by poets as riding in a four-horse chariot. Day, as preceding the sun, is now imagined as leading those horses.

> Whoever wishes to sow an uncultivated field  
> first frees the fields from shrubs,  
> cuts away the brambles and fern with the sickle,  
> so that Ceres may go forth heavy with new grain.  
>   
> 174 The work of the bees is all the sweeter  
> if an unpleasant flavor first assails the mouth.  
>   
> The stars shine more pleasantly when the south wind  
> ceases to produce rain-bearing sounds.  
>   
> When Lucifer has driven away the darkness,  
> [10] the beautiful day leads forth its rosy horses.  
>   
> 175 You too, who formerly looked upon false goods,  
> begin to draw your neck back from the yoke;  
> thereafter true goods will enter your mind.

### Notes

#### 11. “You too”

Since fields do not produce abundant fruits unless they are first cleared of shrubs; since honey is sweeter after a bitter flavor; since the stars shine more pleasantly when winds and rains have ceased; and since day does not arise until darkness has been driven away, you too, O Boethius, will be able to attain the truth about the good only after laying aside your prejudices. But this truth will be more welcome to you because it follows error. Therefore:

#### 12. “Begin to draw your neck back from the yoke”

The mind, like the body, has a certain captivity. But the mind differs from the body in this respect: the body can be held by certain bonds against its will, whereas the mind cannot be so held against the will of the human being to whom it belongs. Philosophy therefore appropriately urges Boethius to begin to draw his neck back from the yoke. That yoke belongs to the mind.

The human mind may be understood as being held by bonds in two ways. First, with respect to its conception, insofar as that conception is obscure or confused; second, with respect to its will, insofar as, led by ignorance, it falls into error or vice. The latter kind of bond is not yet under discussion, but only the former. Since the mind shares in thought in such a way that it cannot be stripped of an obscure conception without being clothed with a clear one, Philosophy now says that, if Boethius ceases to look upon these false goods, his mind will behold the true ones.

## 176. PROSE II

### Argument

Having proposed the notion of the highest good, Philosophy shows that human beings in general are deceived by a false assumption when they devote themselves exclusively to any created good.

Having fixed her gaze for a little while, and as though received into the august seat of her own mind, she began:

> All the care of mortals, exercised by the labor of pursuits of many kinds, proceeds indeed by different paths, but nevertheless strives to reach one end: happiness.

[Note: [Col. 0723D] **Having fixed her gaze.** Just as eyes turned now here, now there signify inconstancy, so fixed eyes signify the constant thought of a mind attending to something.]

[Note: [Col. 0723D] **Into the august seat.** Since Philosophy is a kind of queen, an august or royal seat befits her. Yet Philosophy, considered as a philosopher—or, as they say, in the concrete—appears to consist both of body and of mind. As long as the mind, carried away by the body, thinks according to the body’s persuasion, it wanders, or at least is exposed to the danger of wandering, since it is led by rashness or prejudice. Therefore, if the philosophical mind wishes to think in the best manner, it must return to itself, as though the body had been dismissed with an order to be quiet, and meditate more attentively upon its own thoughts.]

[Note: [Col. 0723B] **Royal.**]

[Note: [Col. 0724B] **All the care of mortals, etc.** This is the proposition which Philosophy now undertakes to prove: namely, that all human beings strive toward happiness, but by different paths. To carry this out, she first sets forth the notion of the highest good.]

[Note: [Col. 0723B] **By a different path.**]

[Note: [Col. 0724B] **That is, the good.** In general, “good” is called that which appears to make one happy; for, as Ulpian judges, *bonum* (“good”) is derived from *beare* (“to make happy”). Hence the ancients used *benus* instead of *bonus*, from which *bene* (“well”) and *bellus* (“pretty,” “beautiful”) remained in usage. But among philosophers that which appears to make one happy is of two kinds: one is called a thing, the other a mode. The former is called objective happiness, the latter formal happiness. Philosophy defines both here. The former is defined as follows: “the good which, once obtained, makes it impossible for anyone to desire anything further”; and this she calls the highest good, namely, in the category of the thing itself. The latter is defined as follows: “a state perfected by the gathering together of all goods”; and this she calls happiness. The former, for us, is God; the latter is the thought of a mind constantly adhering to God. But more on these matters later.]

> This, then, is the good which, once obtained, makes it impossible for anyone to desire anything further. It is indeed the highest of all goods, containing all goods within itself. If anything were lacking from it, it could not be the highest good, since something external would remain that could be desired. It is therefore clear that happiness is a state perfected by the gathering together of all goods.

177

[Note: [Col. 0724C] **Mortals pursue this by different routes.** Philosophy next proves that human beings strive toward happiness by different paths because they apply the innate notion of the highest good incorrectly.]

> As we have said, all mortals endeavor to attain this by different routes.

[Note: [Col. 0724A] **In various ways.**]

[Note: [Col. 0724C] **For the notion of the highest good is implanted in human minds, etc.** Just as God created the human mind for his own sake, so from its very origin he implanted in that mind not only the notion but also the desire for the highest good, which is nothing other than God himself.]

> For the desire for the true good is naturally implanted in human minds, but wandering error leads them away toward false goods.

[Note: [Col. 0724B] **Implanted.**]

[Note: [Col. 0724C] **Wandering error leads them away toward false goods.** As long as the human mind hears God as its teacher and follows him as its guide, it is free both from error and from vice. But scarcely has that same mind been released from the divine law when the associated body, unable to endure being commanded, arouses within the mind several disturbances. From these arise first the mind’s obscurity and confusion, and then its manifold error. That error is called “wandering,” not only because it is the thought of a mind deviating from the true standard of judgment, but also because it causes the appetite, the companion of the preceding judgment, to deviate from its own law as well. Hence it is said to lead away toward false goods—through a false assumption, namely. This must now be proved with respect to wealth, honors, power, glory, and pleasures, considered first separately and afterward comparatively.]

I. The discussion concerns wealth. Those who gape after it seem to reason as follows: “The highest good is to need nothing”—a most true proposition; “but those who abound in wealth need nothing”—a most false assumption. Indeed, the wealthier a person is, the more he needs.

> Some, believing that the highest good is to need nothing, labor to acquire wealth.

[Note: [Col. 0725B] **Others judge that the good which is most worthy of veneration, etc.** II. The discussion concerns dignities or honors. Those who pursue them seem to reason as follows: “The highest good is most worthy of veneration”—a true proposition; “but a person is worthy of veneration only if he is honored with public office”—a false assumption. For public office itself is not honored unless it is joined with virtue.]

> Others, judging that the good which is most worthy of veneration is such, strive, once they have obtained honors, to be revered by their fellow citizens.

[Note: [Col. 0725B] **Worthy of honor.**]

[Note: [Col. 0725C] **There are those who place the highest good in supreme power, etc.** III. The discussion concerns power. Those who desire it seem to reason as follows: “Supreme power is the inseparable companion of the highest good”—a true proposition; “but a person possesses supreme power only by ruling or by attaching himself to rulers”—a false assumption, since kings themselves are not powerful unless they rule their own disturbances.]

> There are those who locate the highest good in supreme power. These wish either to rule themselves or to strive to attach themselves to rulers.

178

[Note: [Col. 0725C] **But to those for whom renown seems the highest good, etc.** IV. The discussion concerns fame. Those who desire it seem to reason as follows: “It belongs to the highest good to be renowned”—which is true; “but a person cannot be renowned except through the arts of war or peace”—which is false, since these arts are often the material of vices.]

> But for those to whom renown seems some supreme good, the aim is to spread a glorious name through the arts of war or peace.

[Note: [Col. 0725C] **Many measure the fruit of the good by joy, etc.** V. The discussion concerns pleasures. Those who indulge in them truly propose that the highest good cannot exist without joy, but they falsely assume that this joy can be received from perishable things. Thus the discussion of perishable goods has been completed separately.]

> But most measure the fruit of the good by joy and gladness; they consider it the height of happiness to overflow with pleasure.

[Note: [Col. 0725D] **There are also those who exchange the ends of these, etc.** VI. The discussion concerns all the foregoing goods in comparison with one another. A person attaches himself now to more, now to fewer, now to these, now to those, according to the different assumption he makes. This seems to us most evident from the very connection of the discourse.]

> There are also those who exchange the ends and causes of these with one another: for example, those who desire wealth on account of power and pleasures, or those who seek power either for the sake of money or to advance their name.

[Note: [Col. 0725B] **From the goods mentioned above.**]

[Note: [Col. 0725D] **In these lies the direction of human actions and desires.** The sum—or whatever constitutes human desire and effort—is involved in these matters. For just as human action follows human desire, so human desire follows the mind’s aforementioned assumption and proposition. We act externally only according to what we inwardly will; nor do we will anything except what we have judged preferable; nor do we judge anything except what has appeared so, whether obscurely or clearly. Philosophy confirms this first with daily examples and then with examples from antiquity, such as Epicurus.]

> In these and other such things lies the direction of human actions and desires: for example, nobility and popular favor, which seem to acquire a certain renown; a wife and children, who are sought for the sake of pleasure. Friendship, however—which is the most sacred kind of good—is counted not among the possessions of fortune but among the virtues. Everything else is assumed either for the sake of power or for pleasure.

[Note: [Col. 0725B] **The sum.**]

> It is now easy to see that bodily goods too are referred to the higher goods. Strength and size seem to provide vigor; beauty and speed, renown; health, pleasure.

[Note: [Col. 0726B] **To make one vigorous.**]

[Note: [Col. 0726B] **It is evident to everyone.**]

> It is clear that in all these things only happiness is desired. For whatever each person seeks above all else, he judges to be the highest good. But we have defined the highest good as happiness. Therefore each person judges the state he desires above all else to be happiness. You have before your eyes, then, almost the complete form of human happiness: wealth, honors, power, glory, and pleasures.

179

[Note: [Col. 0726C] **Epicurus, considering these alone, etc.** Epicurus was a sufficiently well-known philosopher. In physics he taught that bodies are composed of atoms and the void; in ethics he held that the highest good consists in pleasure, reasoning approximately as follows: since there are no goods other than wealth, honors, power, glory, and pleasures, whichever good among these surpasses the others ought to be considered the highest. But pleasure surpasses all the others, since all the others are sought only because they seem to bring pleasure to the mind. Hence pleasure-seekers have customarily been called Epicureans.]

> Considering these things alone, Epicurus consequently determined for himself that the highest good was pleasure, since all the other things seem to bring pleasure to the mind. But I return to the pursuits of human beings. Their minds, although their memory is obscured, nevertheless seek again the highest good, but, like a drunk person, do not know by what route to return home.

[Note: [Col. 0726B] **Obscured.**]

[Note: [Col. 0726C] **Like a drunk person.** This is an especially apt comparison for explaining the reasoning of each person who clings to a perishable good. A drunk person has, first, some idea of his house, which he received from the house itself before he left to drink wine. Second, always remembering this idea, he prefers his own house to all others even when buried in wine; hence he strives to seek it again. Third, because wine disturbs his memory, he does not know the road by which he might return. Fourth, as darkness gradually increases, he clings motionless to someone else’s buildings as though they were his own.

So too the human mind has, first, an idea of its own origin and end—namely, God—which it received from its own Creator before it withdrew from him to drink in bodily pleasures. Second, never wholly forgetful of this idea, it judges its Creator preferable to all other things, even while indulging in bodily pleasures; hence it desires to return to him. Third, because the body obstructs its apprehension of duty, it does not know the way by which it may return to God. Fourth, as the darkness gradually increases, it clings motionless to external and perishable things as though they were its origin and therefore its end. Thus, like a drunk person, the human mind does not err except through a rash assumption.]

[Note: [Col. 0726D] **Do those who seek to need nothing, then, seem to err, etc.?** Philosophy finally examines separately the foregoing propositions concerning wealth, honors, power, glory, and pleasures, and proves them to be true. From this she concludes that these people err here only in their assumption. The verb *sequestrari* (“to be separated”) was discussed above.]

> Do those who strive to need nothing, then, seem to be in error? Yet there is nothing else that can perfect happiness as well as an abundant state of all goods, needing nothing external but sufficient unto itself.

[Col. 0727A]

> But do those who judge that whatever is best is also most worthy of reverential honor go astray?

[Note: [Col. 0727B] **In judging—that is, they err.**]

> Not at all. For that which almost all mortals strive to attain is surely not worthless and contemptible. Is power not to be counted among goods? What, then? Is that to be judged weak and without force which is plainly superior to all things? Or is renown to be held for nothing?

[Note: [Col. 0727B] **Denied.**]

> But it cannot be denied that whatever is most excellent must also appear most renowned. Why say that happiness is not anxious or sorrowful, nor subject to pains and troubles, when even in the smallest matters people seek what gives them pleasure to possess and enjoy?

180

[Col. 0727B]

> These, then, are the things which human beings wish to obtain. For this reason they desire wealth, dignities, kingdoms, glory, and pleasures: they believe that through these will come sufficiency, reverence, power, renown, and joy.

[Col. 0728A]

> Therefore that which human beings seek through such diverse pursuits is a good. How great is the force of nature in this matter

[Note: [Col. 0727B] **Affections.**]

[Note: [Col. 0727C] **The force of nature.** Namely, the idea naturally implanted in human minds, in which each person sees contained what is asserted by the foregoing propositions.]

[Note: [Col. 0727C] **Is easily demonstrated.** At least from the consequences—or, as philosophers say, *a posteriori*.]

[Note: [Col. 0727C] **Although opinions are varied and conflicting.** Namely, the foregoing assumptions.]

> is easily demonstrated, since, although their opinions are varied and conflicting, they nevertheless agree in choosing the end of the good.

[Note: [Col. 0727C] **They agree in choosing the end of the good.** Because of the aforementioned idea of the highest good, implanted in each person, on account of which the foregoing propositions are formed. As has often been said, in other things as in human beings, the end must return to the beginning.]

[Note: [Col. 0727B] **In the highest good.**]

181. **METER II**

[Note: [Col. 0727C] **What is called Pindaric.** This is a poem consisting of one kind of verse, each line having four feet, but arranged with such freedom that each foot may now be a spondee, now a dactyl, now an anapest, and now a trochee.]

**ARGUMENT.**—Although you drive out the natural disposition of lions, birds, and plants, it returns, like the sun returning from setting to rising, joining the end to the beginning.

[Note: [Col. 0727B]]

> I delight to sing skilfully upon slow strings how many inclinations of things powerful Nature turns, and by what laws provident Nature preserves the vast universe and, binding all things together, holds them fast with an indissoluble bond.
>
> Although African lions wear splendid chains, seize the food extended by their master’s hands, and fear the master himself, terrible as he is, accustomed as they are to receiving blows from him: nevertheless, if blood—especially blood shed by blows—stains their dreadful faces, their spirits, long idle, return; and the lions, remembering themselves, release their necks with a mighty roar, their bonds broken. The master himself, first torn apart by their cruel jaws, satisfies their savage fury.
>
> If a bird, accustomed to sing in chatter high in the trees, is shut into a cage as into a prison, although a kindly human being supplies it there with honey-sweetened drink and abundant food for amusement, nevertheless, if the same bird, leaping about in its narrow dwelling, sees the pleasant shadows of the forests, it tramples the scattered food beneath its feet, sadly seeks only the forests again, and murmurs of those same forests in a sweet twitter.
>
> A branch once bent downward toward the earth by strong force, as soon as the hand that bent it relaxes its grip, looks toward heaven with its tip raised upright.
>
> The sun sinks into the evening waters; but again, by a hidden path, it turns its chariot toward the customary east. All things seek their own return, and everything takes pleasure in its own recurrence. The order prescribed for each thing is not preserved unless it joins its end to its beginning and forms a stable circle of itself.

[Note: [Col. 0727C]]

**1. Reins.** Reins properly refer to horses, since with these instruments we guide and direct them according to our will. Because horses are turned here and there by reins, the word came to be used sometimes of the laws by which other things are governed, and sometimes of the inclinations of things themselves, by which those things are turned as though by reins. Thus Cicero says in *On Friendship*: “It is most advantageous to have the reins of friendship as loose as possible, so that you may draw them tight or slacken them whenever you wish.” Virgil likewise says in *Aeneid* XII, line 498:

> He arouses a dreadful slaughter, savage without distinction,  
> And releases all the reins of anger.

**2. Powerful Nature.** Since *natura* (“nature”) is said to derive from *nasci* (“to be born”), it is equivalent to “principle.” Therefore, just as “principle,” so also “nature,” is of many kinds. Here it is God, from whom the first inclinations of all things arise, as from the first principle. Thus Cicero says in *On the Nature of the Gods* II: “Nature is that which contains the whole universe and protects it.” Lucretius likewise says in Book I:

> Finally, unless the creative nature of things  
> Had accustomed itself to drive all things into their smallest parts.

**2. By what laws.** Just as bodies have laws for movement, so minds have laws for thought. These laws were established by the Creator, from whom these things first receive the capacity both to move and to think. Therefore, just as God is unchanging, so these laws are firm. They are consequently worthy of being considered as the proper subject matter of philosophical meditation and proposed by Philosophy to her students, whether in measured or in ordinary discourse.

In this skilful song, Philosophy employs four kinds of arguments to prove what she has proposed: the first is drawn from lions, the second from birds, the third from plants, and the fourth from the sun itself.

**7. African lions.** I. In order to prove that there is a perpetual cycle by which every thing returns to its principle, Philosophy argues from lions, which she calls Punic or African because, like the people, the lions of Africa are accustomed to be fiercer. Virgil says in *Aeneid* I, line 306:

> And now the Punic people perform the commands,  
> And lay aside their fierce hearts, when God wills it.

Seneca says in *Hippolytus*, line 347:

> The Punic lions shake their necks  
> When love has moved them; then the forest groans  
> With savage roaring.

It is as though he were saying: just as fierce lions, tamed by chains, food, and blows, immediately upon perceiving the blood that has been drawn—especially by their eyes and nostrils—roar as though forgetful of their captivity but mindful of their former nature, break their bonds, and tear apart the very man who subdued them, so a human being, mindful of his origin, strives to return to his principle.

Martial likewise says in Epigram 75 of Book II that a tame lion, stirred by the blood of wild beasts and gladiators poured out in the arena of the amphitheater, attacked children and pitifully tore them apart in the sight of everyone:

> The lion, accustomed to endure the blows of a heedless master  
> And gently to suffer a hand thrust into his jaws,  
> Unlearned peace, his savagery suddenly returning—  
> A savagery that ought not to have existed even on the Libyan ridges.  
> For he, savage and ill-fated, killed with frenzied tooth  
> Two boys from the tender band  
> That was renewing the bloodstained ground with rakes.  
> The Martial arena had seen no greater crime.

> How many reins of things powerful Nature turns,  
> By what laws provident Nature preserves  
> The immeasurable universe  
> And, binding each thing together, holds it fast  
> With an unbreakable bond—  
> This I delight to bring forth in skilful song  
> Upon slow strings.

182

> Although the Punic lions wear splendid chains  
> And seize the food given by human hands,  
> And fear their savage master,  
> Accustomed as they are to enduring his blows,

[Col. 0729A] [Note: [Col. 0729B]]

**12. The spirits once idle return.** These are, of course, those minute bodies which are the more subtle part of the blood and which, having entered the brain, pass into the nerves arising from it, like wind into musical instruments. These minute bodies are called *animi* and *spiritus* (“spirits” or “breaths”) because of a certain likeness they bear to wind and its motion. Virgil says in *Georgics* I, lines 415 ff.:

> I do not indeed believe that divine intelligence  
> Or a greater knowledge of things by fate  
> Has been granted to them;  
> But when storm and the changeable moisture of the sky  
> Have altered their courses, and humid Jupiter with southern winds  
> Condenses what was lately rare and loosens what was dense,  
> The forms of their spirits are changed, and their breasts conceive  
> One motion now, another when the wind drives the clouds.  
> Hence comes that chorus of birds in the fields,  
> The joyful herds, and the crows exulting in their throats.

Thus those spirits in domesticated lions, because of chains, food, and blows, are diverted from their customary course in such a way that they appear idle and almost motionless. But when the color or odor—or both—of freshly shed blood opens the paths hitherto obstructed, these spirits rush through the opening provided and follow the course prescribed for them by nature. They stir the lion by a motion unusual but no less natural. Hence the lions roar, break their bonds, and tear apart their master, so that he is said to imbue their anger. As Virgil says in *Aeneid* VII, line 541:

> The goddess, powerful to accomplish her promise,  
> When she has steeped war in blood  
> And committed the dead to the first battle.

**17. The bird that sings.** II. Philosophy argues from birds on the basis of the foregoing end. Although birds shut in cages are nourished there with the greatest human care, they seek the forests by every means available to them. The bird here—so called from *ala*, “wing”—is a bird that uses wings, one accustomed to rise to the highest places and therefore less readily than others to adopt alien ways.

**18. It is shut in the cavern of a cage.** In general, a cage is any hollow and dark place. Here, however, cages are prisons in which we customarily confine birds, called in ordinary speech *des cages*. Philosophy wished to oppose the cavern of the cage, where the bird is confined, to the high branches in which the bird is accustomed to chatter, so that she might more clearly indicate how far the bird’s present condition is removed from its natural state.

[Col. 0730B]

**22. Leaping about in the narrow dwelling.** I say “in the dwelling,” not “out of the dwelling”; otherwise it would not be said to trample the food scattered beneath its feet, nor to murmur sadly about the forests, but rather to have left the food behind joyfully and to be present in the forests. The cage and the other bodies surrounding the confined bird alter the channels through which the *animi* or spirits ordinarily spread, so that these spirits appear idle. But when the fresh color, sound, or odor of the shady woodland has diffused as far as the brain and either condensed what was rare or relaxed what was dense, then, with the channels changed, the courses of the spirits are altered, so that the wings are stirred to leap, the feet to trample the food, and hunger to murmur about the forests.

Ovid says in Book II of *Letters from Pontus*, Elegy 4:

> Although the daughters of Pandion are well shut in their cage,  
> Each strives to return to her own forests.

**27. The branch bent by strong force.** III. Philosophy argues from plants on the basis of the foregoing end. Plants possess that force which philosophers call elastic force, *vertu de ressort* (“spring force”). It consists in this: when a compressed or stretched body is released, it rebounds back and forth toward the point where there is less resistance. This force is found not only in certain metals but also in many plants. Therefore, if a branch of this kind, standing upright with its tip directed toward heaven, is bent toward the earth by the greater force of a hand, then, once given the opportunity to return, it springs back toward heaven.

**31. Phoebus falls into the western waters, etc.** IV. Philosophy argues from the sun for this reason. Poets imagine that the sun, when setting, sinks into the watery sea, so that, cleansed of the dust and other impurities it has gathered during the day, it may rise purer in the morning. The western or evening waters are called *Hesperian* from Hesperus, the star that first appears to us after sunset. Phoebus is the name of the sun, from the Greek *φοῖβος* (*phoibos*), “bright,” as we have often said.

**32. By a hidden path.** The route by which the sun returns from west to east is unknown to all human beings, since other people regard those standing opposite them as antipodes. The sun does not appear simultaneously to these and to those people; but poets in particular pretend both that the setting sun plunges into the waters and that the rising sun emerges from those same waters.

**33. He turns his chariot toward the customary east.** For these same poets imagine the sun being carried in a chariot whose parts are an axle, wheels, and horses. Ovid says in *Metamorphoses* II, lines 63 ff.:

> The first part of the road is steep, and the horses scarcely  
> Struggle up it, fresh in the morning; at mid-heaven it is highest . . .  
> The final road slopes downward and requires sure control.  
> Then even Tethys, who receives me in the waters beneath,  
> Is accustomed to fear that I may be carried headlong.

> If blood should stain their dreadful faces,  
> Their spirits, once idle, return;  
> With a heavy roar they remember themselves;  
> They free their necks, their bonds loosened,  
> And the master, first torn apart by their blood-stained tooth,  
> Steeps their savage fury [in blood].

183

> The bird that sings chattering in the lofty branches  
> Is shut in the cavern of a cage.  
> Though kindly human care, in playful service,  
> Should provide it with cups smeared with honey  
> And abundant food,

[Col. 0730A]

> Nevertheless, if, leaping about in its narrow dwelling,  
> It should see the pleasant shadows of the groves,  
> It tramples the food scattered beneath its feet,  
> Sadly seeks only the forests,  
> And murmurs of the forests in a sweet voice.

184

> A branch once bent by strong force  
> Bends its lowered tip.  
> If the hand that bends it releases it,  
> It looks toward heaven with its tip upright.
>
> Phoebus falls into the Hesperian waters;  
> But by a hidden path he turns again  
> His accustomed chariot toward the east.

[Col. 0731A] [Note: [Col. 0731C]]

**34. Each thing seeks its own return, etc.** Each thing endeavors to return to the state from which it departed, and seems to rejoice when that state has been recovered. Thus animals appear to seek their former habits, plants their former positions, and the sun itself its former place, recovering it as far as lies within its power. Horace says in *Epistles* I.10:

> Though you drive out nature with a pitchfork, it will always return.

**38. And has formed a stable circle of itself.** So that there may be one circuit for each thing returning to its principle. Thus in Ecclesiastes I:

> The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place;  
> There, rising again, it circles toward the south  
> And turns toward the north.  
> The spirit, traversing everything in a circuit, proceeds  
> And returns to its circles.  
> All rivers enter the sea, yet the sea does not overflow;  
> To the place from which the rivers issue, they return,  
> So that they may flow again.

From all these examples Philosophy leaves it to be concluded that human beings, born from God as from their principle, will form a certain circle of themselves and, like the other things, return to God as their end.

185

> Each thing seeks its own return,  
> And each rejoices in its own return.  
> No order assigned to anything remains,  
> Unless it joins its origin to its end  
> And forms a stable circle of itself.

186. **PROSE III**

**ARGUMENT.**—Philosophy now undertakes to prove specifically what she has hitherto proved generally: that wealth, dignities, kingship, glory, and pleasures are not the highest good. She begins with wealth, demonstrating in both ordinary and metrical discourse that, in these matters, the proposition is true but the assumption false, because wealth is accompanied by anxiety, fear, and other disturbances.

You too, O [Note: [Col. 0731D] Earthly animals.] human beings devoted to earthly things, [Note: [Col. 0731B] Human beings.] earthly animals, [Note: [Col. 0731D] With a faint image.] with a faint image—an innate form or idea, obscured by the impressions of the body with which it is associated—[Note: [Col. 0732B] Though obscure in thought.] although with a faint image, [Note: [Col. 0731D] You dream of your origin.] nevertheless dream obscurely, like those dreaming, of your origin, God, as we have already explained; [Note: [Col. 0732B] You think.] and [Note: [Col. 0731D] Your true end.] foresee that true end of yours, the end of blessedness—[Note: [Col. 0731D] Although with no very perceptive, yet with some sort of thought.] namely, by means of the aforesaid obscure form or idea, [Col. 0732B] which, because we are immediately conscious that it exists within us, is rightly called thought—although with no very perceptive [Col. 0731B] yet with some sort of thought; and toward it [Note: [Col. 0732C] Natural inclination leads toward the true good.] because our mind is divinely formed by the aforesaid image, in which it naturally perceives certain attributes to be comprehended, that same mind naturally forms, by judging, true propositions about the highest good; and, because of the connection between judgment and the desire for the good, natural inclination follows them. 187 And [Note: [Col. 0732C] The same source leads astray through manifold error.] namely, while that same mind, convinced by the aforesaid propositions, is deflected by prejudices, so that through false assumptions it forms its judgment and inclination concerning something to which the properties previously conceived of the highest good do not belong—as must be proved separately in each case, namely concerning riches, offices, kingship, glory, and pleasures—and first of all concerning riches—[Note: [Col. 0732C] The first question is addressed to you yourself, who shortly before were overflowing with riches.] from that same source manifold error leads you astray.

Consider, then, whether by the things through which people think they will acquire blessedness they can reach the appointed end. For if money, honors, and other things of that sort bring something which seems to lack none of the goods, let us too confess that some people become happy through acquiring them. But if they cannot accomplish what they promise and lack many goods, is it not [Note: [Col. 0732B] Clearly.] plainly evident that a false appearance of blessedness is detected in them? [Note: [Col. 0732C] I first question you yourself, who shortly before were overflowing with riches.] Boethius, before he came into disrepute with Theoderic, was exceedingly rich; hence, having had the experience, he knows how a person is affected by riches that have been lost, are about to be lost, and are still present, and can therefore answer Philosophy’s question that the rich are free neither from anxiety of mind, nor from fear, nor from many other emotions.]

First, then, I ask you yourself, who shortly before were overflowing with riches. [Note: [Col. 0732D] Among those riches, etc.] “Among all those abundant resources, did anxiety, arising from some injury, never confuse your mind?” (10)

“But I cannot remember,” I replied, “ever having been so free in spirit that something did not always trouble me.” [Note: [Col. 0732B] Tormented.] “Was it not because something you did not want to be absent was absent, or something you did not want to be present was present?”

“That is so,” I replied.

“Then you desired the presence of the latter and the absence of the former?”

“I confess it,” I replied.

“But everyone needs what he desires,” she said.

“I need it,” I replied.

“Now, is someone who needs something altogether self-sufficient?”

“Not at all,” I replied.

“Then, although filled with riches, you endured this insufficiency?” she said.

“Why should I not?” I replied.

“Therefore riches cannot make someone who needs nothing and is sufficient unto himself; yet that was what they seemed to promise.” 188 [Note: [Col. 0733B] II. The same Philosophy argues from fear, from which the rich are never free, approximately as follows. Wherever there is fear, there is no blessedness, because to fear is an evil, whereas blessedness expels every evil. Yet fear is always present among the rich, at least lest they themselves be unwillingly despoiled by the more powerful; for money is daily taken from its unwilling owner by force or fraud, as lawsuits prove and Boethius himself experienced. Hence riches are so far from being able to suffice that they instead make people dependent on another's protection.] But [Note: [Col. 0733B] I think this too deserves the greatest consideration.] this too, I think, deserves the greatest consideration: that money has nothing by its own nature which prevents it from being taken away against the will of those who possess it.

“I admit it,” I replied.

“Why would you not admit it, when someone more powerful can daily seize it from you against your will? For what else gives rise to legal complaints, unless money is recovered—taken away either by force or by fraud—from unwilling owners?”

“That is so,” I replied.

“Then each person will need external assistance, obtained by request, to protect his money.”

“Who could deny it?” I replied.

“Yet he would not need it unless he possessed money that he could lose.”

“That cannot be doubted,” I replied.

“Then the matter has fallen into the opposite position: riches, which were thought capable of making people self-sufficient, instead make them dependent on another’s protection.” [Col. 0733B] [Note: [Col. 0733C] But what limit is there, etc.] 189 Philosophy argues from several other emotions as well, which riches cannot prevent but more often arouse and increase; the argument can be condensed as follows. Where hunger, thirst, cold, and other such conditions inconvenient to the mind are present, there is no blessedness, since the good is opposed to these evils. Yet among the rich, no less than among the poor, there are hunger, thirst, cold, and other such conditions. Although riches can postpone them, they cannot remove them altogether.]

“But what means are there by which need can be driven away through riches? Can the rich not grow hungry? Can they not become thirsty? Do the limbs of the wealthy not feel winter’s cold? But,” you will say, “the wealthy possess the means by which they can satisfy hunger and dispel thirst and cold.”

“But in this way,” [Note: [Col. 0733C] This word more often signifies an action, but it is also found used in the opposite sense among the best authors. Asinius, in a letter of Cicero: ‘I consoled myself over the things I feared.’] need can indeed be consoled by riches, but it cannot be removed entirely. For if this [Note: [Col. 0733B] Need.] gaping need, always asking for something, is not filled by riches, it necessarily remains as something that can be filled.

“I say nothing of the fact that [Note: [Col. 0733C] Nature requires very little; avarice, nothing is enough.] nature [Col. 0733D] here means the body, while avarice means the desiring mind. Very little can suffice for the body: a very small amount of food can expel hunger, a very small amount of drink thirst, and a very small amount of warmth cold. But nothing is enough for the desiring mind, for, as Juvenal says,

> The love of money grows as the money itself grows.”

Thus, nature is satisfied with very little, while nothing is sufficient for avarice. 189 Therefore, if riches can neither remove need nor fail to create need of their own, [Note: [Col. 0733D] What is it that makes you believe they provide, etc.] why, O human beings, do you think that riches can suffice for you as the highest good? You rightly propose that the highest good is that which can suffice; but you falsely assume that riches can suffice.

“What, then, makes you believe that they provide sufficiency?”

## 190 METER III

[Note: [Col. 0733D] A poem consisting of two alternating kinds of verse, the first comprising six feet, iambic in character though with the iamb predominant; the second an elegiac pentameter.]

**ARGUMENT.**—The abundance of money, gems, and fields, says Philosophy, neither frees people who are alive from their cares nor consoles those who are dead.

[Note: [Col. 0733B]

Even if a rich man, greedy for gold flowing in a stream, gathers riches that will not satisfy him; even if he burdens his neck with the pearls of the Red Sea; even if he cultivates rich fields with countless oxen, these riches, just as they torment the living with their biting anxieties, so, being unstable, do not accompany the dead.]

[Note: [Col. 0733D]

1. “The rich man amid a flowing torrent of gold.” I. Money is under discussion. This first verse has been composed with such care that its legitimate meaning can be understood in two ways. First, *dives auri* can rightly be understood as “rich in gold,” just as Virgil says “rich in flocks,” and Horace “rich in many things.” In the second place, it can reasonably be understood as “amid a flowing torrent of gold,” with a certain river of gold imagined, just as the Pactolus and Tagus are said to flow with gold. For *gurges*, named from its sound, signifies a deep place into which water or some other similar liquid flows and rolls with a murmuring sound. Thus the uppermost end of the throat is commonly called the *gurgulio*; hence a man born for his belly who indulges in gluttony is called by Cicero himself “a torrent and abyss of his patrimony.” The sea and a river likewise signify the word *gurges* among poets. Virgil, *Aeneid* I, verse 122:

> Rare swimmers appear in the vast deep.]

Although, amid a flowing torrent of gold,

[Col. 0734B] the greedy rich man compels riches that will never satisfy him,

he burdens his neck with pearls from the Red Sea,

191 and splits rich fields with a hundred oxen,

[5] [Col. 0735A] [Note: [Col. 0735B]

5. “Nor does biting care,” etc. Philosophy says: although the rich man abounds in money, gems, and rich fields, he will not therefore be happy. For either he will live on while still alive, or he will die when life is over. If he lives, he will be tormented by care-producing anxieties, whether concerning the preservation of his old riches or the acquisition of new ones. But if he dies, whatever consolation he might have hoped for from his riches will not accompany him. For riches, serving a transient life, depart when life departs, passing to an heir whom they will affect with similar anxieties. If affection for that heir touches you, the riches must become for you a new cause of grief. You therefore falsely assume that the blessedness which you naturally recognize and desire is to be found in riches. Let us see whether the judgment is better concerning kingship.]

Nor does biting care abandon the survivor,

nor do fleeting riches accompany the dead.

## 192 PROSE IV

**ARGUMENT.**—The honor that follows offices, says Philosophy, depends so greatly on popular opinion that it is shown neither everywhere nor always to magistrates. Thus, by an equally false assumption, you will believe that the highest good—which you naturally recognize and love—is found in offices.

“But offices,” [Note: [Col. 0735C] Offices make the person who receives them honorable and worthy of reverence.] Boethius objects to Philosophy, “make the person to whom they come honorable and worthy of reverence.”

Philosophy replies that offices make a magistrate honorable and worthy of reverence not so much by their own nature as by popular opinion; hence it follows that magistrates are not honored everywhere or always. [Note: [Col. 0735B] Boethius objects.] Offices make the person to whom they come honorable and worthy of reverence.

“I. Philosophy replies that offices do not by their own nature make a person honorable and worthy of reverence. Since honor and reverence are inwardly a thought, but outwardly the best mark of another person’s merit, they accompany virtue in such a way that whatever makes a person honorable and worthy of reverence by its own nature, if it is not virtue itself, ought to implant virtue in people’s minds and thereby drive away vices. But offices, or magistracies, are not like this. They tend rather to illuminate wickedness than to dispel it, which is why we are often indignant that they have fallen to the worst of men, just as Catullus resented Nonius and Boethius himself resented Decoratus holding office.”

“Do you think offices have the power [Note: [Col. 0735B] Philosophy replies.] to implant virtues in the minds of those who exercise them and drive away vices?”

“Certainly not.” [Note: [Col. 0736A] Certainly not.]

“Yet they usually do not drive away wickedness but rather illuminate it, which makes us indignant that they have often fallen to the worst men: [Note: [Col. 0735D] Hence Catullus.] the famous poet, who was so biting in his verses that he did not even spare Caesar, did not hesitate to attack Nonius with abuse—Nonius sitting in the curule chair, as we would now say, and Catullus alluding to his cognomen—in *Poem* 53:

> What is it, Catullus, what makes you delay dying?  
> The scrofulous Nonius sits in the curule chair;  
> Vatinius commits perjury through his consulship.  
> What is it, Catullus, what makes you delay dying?”

[Note: [Col. 0735D] Many here think that Boethius was unaware that *struma* was Nonius's cognomen. Joseph Scaliger, commenting on the aforesaid verses of Catullus, says: “Boethius is mistaken, who thinks *struma* is not Nonius's cognomen but an insult.” Hence Sitzmann says here: “One should note at this point our Boethius's lack of historical knowledge (ἀνιστορησία), in thinking that *struma* was not Nonius's cognomen.” Bernartius likewise says: “Let us see whether that very great man has not drunk a drop from the river Lethe.” Murmellius holds the same opinion. But, with due respect to such great men, Boethius ought not here to be accused either of ignorance or error. For although *struma* was Nonius's cognomen, Catullus could still have called Nonius *struma* by way of insult. A cognomen taken from some defect either of body or mind can be used as an insult, especially against those on whom it was first bestowed: thus the cognomen may be thrown as an insult at the first man called Servius from a slave (*servus*), “a slave”; Spurius from an illegitimate child (*spurius*), “a bastard”; or Brutus from dullness (*brutus*), “a fool.” Indeed, among the ancient Romans you will never find such a cognomen joined to the name of a person against whom invective is directed except as an insult. Thus Marrucinus, the cognomen bestowed on Asinius, brother of Asinius Pollio, is, in Scaliger's judgment, thrown at that Asinius by Catullus as an insult, *Poem* 12:

> Marrucinus, Asinius, with your left hand
> you make poor use in jest and wine.

Likewise Superbus, Tarquinius's cognomen, is used by Propertius as an insult against Tarquinius, book III, elegy 10:

> What good is it now, Tarquinius, that your axes are broken,
> when a proud life brands you with a similar name?

Now *struma* was Nonius's cognomen, and it was given to him first; it was drawn from a bodily defect, namely scrofula, in French *des écrouelles*. Add that Catullus seems to have alluded all the more to the scrofula from which that cognomen arose because, in the aforesaid poem, he joins to the praetor Nonius the consul Vatinius, whom his enemy Cicero repeatedly designates as *struma* or “a scrofulous swelling” because he suffered from scrofula. In *For Sestius*: “They heal the state who cut out some pestilence like a scrofulous swelling”; in *Against Vatinius*: “at last the scrofulous swellings have departed from the shameless ivory”; and elsewhere: “We have a swollen orator.” This concerning Nonius.]

Thus Catullus calls Nonius a “scrofulous man,” [Note: [Col. 0736A] Although he calls Nonius, sitting in the curule chair, a scrofulous man.] even though he was sitting in the curule chair. Do you see how much disgrace offices add to wicked men? Yet their unworthiness would be less evident if they did not become distinguished through honors.

“Could you, too, when faced with so many dangers, have been brought to the point of thinking that you should hold office with Decoratus?” [Note: [Col. 0736D] With Decoratus.] Decoratus is the man to whom Theoderic writes in Cassiodorus, *Variae* V, letter 31, instructing him to compel certain people to pay money that had been demanded, if it should in fact be established that they were debtors. He served as assistant to the *magister officiorum* in judging cases and is therefore called there, in the customary language of the office, “devoted one” and “your devotion.” This does not prevent him from now rightly being called a most worthless buffoon and informer. He was a buffoon because, following powerful men, he sought food or some other advantage for himself through his jests; Juvenal says:

> He plays the mime,  
> such a fluent buffoon as Catullus’s urbane one.

He was an informer because he secretly accused others by bringing charges against them. Domitian ordered such men to be punished. “The emperor,” this ruler said according to Suetonius, “who does not punish informers, encourages them.” Boethius therefore, having been convinced that offices do not make people better, could not, even under threat of danger, be induced to hold office with that Decoratus.]

“Could you have thought of holding office with Decoratus, when you saw in him the mind of a most worthless [Note: [Col. 0736B] A buffoon, who obviously tries in every way to provoke laughter.] buffoon and informer?”

“For we cannot judge those worthy of reverence on account of their honors whom we judge unworthy of the honors themselves. But if you saw someone endowed with wisdom, could you consider him unworthy either of reverence or of the wisdom with which he is endowed?”

“Not at all. [Col. 0737A] For there is an inherent dignity in virtue, which it immediately transfers to those with whom it is joined.”

194 [Note: [Col. 0737C] Because popular honors cannot accomplish this.] II. Philosophy also intimates that the honor of offices depends on popular opinion; hence it is now called popular, that is, conferred by the people. Honor and reverence, as we have already noted, are inwardly a thought, but outwardly the best mark of another person’s merit. Whether it is that thought or that mark, it belongs to the person who honors and cannot make the person honored honorable and worthy of reverence. Only virtue can make the person honored honorable; therefore only virtue is the proper beauty of dignity.]

“Since popular honors cannot accomplish this,” [Note: [Col. 0737B] Conferred by the people.] it is clear that they do not possess the proper beauty of dignity. This point deserves even greater notice: for if a person is more abject the more people despise him, then, since dignity cannot make those whom it displays to many worthy of reverence, [Note: [Col. 0737C] Dignity makes the wicked more contemptible.] dignity instead makes the wicked more contemptible. [Note: [Col. 0737B] The same.] But not without penalty: the wicked return an equivalent service to the dignities which they stain by their contamination.

[Note: [Col. 0737D] “And so that you may recognize,” etc. III. Philosophy says that if offices made a person honorable and worthy of reverence by their own nature rather than by popular opinion, then, just as fire is hot always and everywhere on earth, so whoever held offices would always and everywhere be honorable. But this is not the case. First, those who hold offices are not honorable everywhere: if someone who had held several consulships happened to come among barbarian nations, he would not thereby seem honorable to them, but only to those who, by some prejudice, considered the consulship worthy of honor. Second, those adorned with offices do not always seem honorable. Among the same peoples, offices that are highly esteemed at one time are held in little regard at another: hence—]

“And so that you may recognize that true reverence cannot be attained through these shadowy dignities: if someone who had held several consulships happened to come among barbarian nations, would honor make him worthy of reverence in the eyes of the barbarians?” [Note: [Col. 0737B] Certainly not.]

“Yet if this were a natural property of offices, they would nowhere in the world depart from their function, just as fire everywhere on earth never ceases to be hot. But since it is not their own power, but the deceptive opinion of human beings, that attaches this to them, they immediately vanish when they come among people who do not judge them to be dignities. But that is among foreign nations. Among those, however, among whom they originated, do they persist forever?” [Note: [Col. 0738B] Certainly not.]

195 But [Note: [Col. 0738B] The praetorship was once a great power; now it is an empty name. Roman praetors, as the jurists teach, at first, by the law of their magistracy, merely published edicts stating in what matters and in what manner they would administer justice. As time passed, without opposition from the people, they also assumed the power to establish law by edict. But eventually they merely provided circus and theatrical games at their own expense; hence the dignity of praetor was then an empty name and a burdensome load. Similarly—] the praetorship, once a great power, is now an empty name and a burdensome load upon the senatorial census. [Note: [Col. 0738B] Burden.]

[Note: [Col. 0738C] If someone had managed the grain supply of the people, etc. The prefect of the grain supply was once so important among the Romans that Augustus himself retained the prefecture of the grain supply, which he had accepted from the people, for as long as he lived—or at least shortly before his death appointed C. Turrianus as his substitute. Turrianus was among the first to swear allegiance to Tiberius, as though the prefecture were among the chief magistracies. But in Boethius’s time the prefect of the grain supply had no authority except supervision and disciplinary power over the city’s bakers and sausage merchants, as can be gathered from the formula of this prefecture reported by Cassiodorus, *Variae* VI, formula 18. Therefore those who by their assumption believe that the highest good lies in offices, or magistracies, are mistaken.] “If someone once managed the grain supply of the people, he was considered important; now, what is more contemptible than that prefecture?” For, as we said shortly before, what possesses no beauty of its own now receives splendor from the opinion of those who use it and now loses it.

“If, then, offices cannot make people worthy of reverence; if they readily become sullied by the contamination of the wicked; if they cease to shine when times change; and if they become cheap in the estimation of nations, what beauty desirable in itself do they possess, much less what do they bestow on others?”

## 196 METER IV

[Note: [Col. 0738D] A poem consisting of two alternating kinds of verse, the first Phalaecian, with five feet—namely, a spondee, a dactyl, and three trochees; the second Archilochian, with two dactyls and an equal number of trochees.]

[Col. 0738B] **ARGUMENT.**—By the example of wretched Nero conferring offices, Philosophy confirms that offices can make no one happy.

[Note: [Col. 0738B]

Even if Nero adorned himself, proud in Tyrian purple and bright gems, nevertheless that emperor of raging luxury lived hated by everyone. Yet that same criminal emperor once bestowed dishonorable curule chairs on venerable senators. Who, then, could believe that those offices, which unhappy men confer, bring happiness?]

[Note: [Col. 0738D]

1. “Proud in Tyrian purple.” *Ostrum* (“purple”) is derived from *ostreum*. *Ostreum*, in Greek ὄστρεον (*ostreon*), generally signifies every kind of animal that lies hidden enclosed in a shell. But among these shellfish, says Pliny, there is one from whose cut shell a liquid is collected that is desired for dyeing clothing; this is properly called *ostrum*. Hence *ostrum* denotes not only the shell but also the purple color made from the secretion of that shellfish, and even garments dyed with that color. Tyre, a city of Phoenicia, was especially famous for fishing this shellfish; hence *ostrum* is called Tyrian from the city and Phoenician from the province. Purple, moreover, is of two kinds, red and violet. Virgil, *Georgics* II, verse 506:

> So that the gem may drink and sleep in Sarian purple.

And *Georgics* III, verse 17:

> I, victorious, and conspicuous in Tyrian purple.

And *Aeneid* I, verse 643:

> Garments worked by art and splendid purple.]

Although, proud in Tyrian purple,

[Col. 0739A] [Note: [Col. 0739B]

2. “He adorned himself.” *Comere* means “to adorn,” generally the body, but specifically the hair. It is derived from the Greek κοσμεῖν (*kosmein*), “to adorn,” whence *comtus*, “adorned,” and *coma*, hair carefully dressed. The expression is appropriately applied to Nero, who, as Suetonius says, was so shameful in his grooming and dress that he always wore his hair arranged in tiers, and during his journey through Achaea let it fall down behind his crown. He usually appeared in public wearing a woman’s tunic, with a scarf tied around his neck, ungirded and barefoot.]

he adorned himself with bright gems,

197 nevertheless Nero, raging in luxury, flourished though hated by everyone.

[5] Yet once the wicked man gave dishonorable curule chairs to venerable senators.

Who, then, could think those honors happy,

which unhappy men bestow?

[Note: [Col. 0739B]

2. “With snowy gems.” That is, with the most precious jewels. [Col. 0739C] For if, as Suetonius says of him, he never wore any garment twice; if he went fishing with a golden net whose cords were knotted with purple and scarlet; if he is reported never to have traveled with fewer than a thousand carriages, fitted with silver mule-shoes; if he thought that the only fruit of riches and money was lavish expenditure, then it is certainly believable that he was weighed down with gems and pearls, of which, according to the same Suetonius, he scattered a thousand each day among the people.]

3. “Nevertheless, he flourished hated by everyone.” This is evident not only from the curses and insults that he endured with some patience while alive, but also from the fact that his death produced such public joy that the people, wearing caps of liberty, ran throughout the entire city.

4. “Nero, of raging luxury.” Nero’s luxury was extreme, as we have already said, but his cruelty was no less so. He began parricides and murders with Claudius. He attacked Britannicus with poison, motivated no less by rivalry over Britannicus’s more pleasing voice than by fear that his father’s memory might one day prevail in the favor of the people. He killed his mother, aunt, wives, and closest associates.

5 and 6. “He gave curule chairs to the senators.” The curule chair was an elaborately carved ivory seat placed on the chariot in which the more distinguished magistrates were accustomed to be conveyed to the senate-house, and upon which those magistrates sat. Hence *curule ivory*, *curule chair*, and *curule*, often used substantivally as now, signify a senator’s higher dignity. Horace, *Epistles* I, letter 6:

> He will give the fasces to anyone and, troublesome brother or father,  
> will snatch away the curule ivory from whomever he wishes.

Ovid, *Letters from Pontus* IV, elegy 9:

> I would also recognize the figures fashioned on the curule chair,  
> and the whole sculpted work of the Numidian tooth.

Lucan, book III:

> The praetor is present, and the curule chairs give way from the empty place.

[Col. 0740B] Nero bestowed these senatorial dignities on those who pleased him most, alleging that no ruler had known what was permitted to him. But these dignities, conferred by the will of a most worthless emperor rather than on the basis of merit, were themselves dishonorable to the magistrates.

7 and 8. “Who could think happy those honors which unhappy men bestow?” What is now called *happy* is something capable of bringing blessedness. Thus Horace calls the countryside and fields “happy,” Catullus calls advantages “happy,” Ovid calls land “happy,” and Statius calls riches “happy.” Yet magistracies, which Philosophy now calls honors, are not such things—especially if unhappy men bestow them. A cause gives nothing unless it contains something of the effect in itself in some manner. Therefore anyone who, through a rash assumption, attributes to magistracies or offices the property of the highest good that he naturally conceives and loves is mistaken. Let us see whether the judgment concerning kingship is better.]

## 198 PROSE V

**ARGUMENT.**—Kingships, says Philosophy, and intimacy with kings, since they are neither perpetual, nor boundless, [Col. 0740A] nor secure, cannot provide the power that, led by a natural conception, you naturally desire.

[Note: [Col. 0740B] Whether kingdoms and familiarity with kings.] Among all forms of government, the most eminent and powerful is that which is called a principate or kingdom, since the others belong to several persons, whereas this belongs to one alone; and concentrated force is greater than force dispersed through itself. Therefore, if the power of the highest good, which is naturally recognized and desired, can rightly be attributed to any human government, it can most of all be attributed to a kingdom and to those who in some measure share in the kingdom. But this does not belong either to a kingdom or to those who share in it, because in no respect—

Can kingdoms, then, and familiarity with kings [Note: [Col. 0740C] Can make a person powerful.] make a person powerful? That is, in the way in which, guided by our natural conception of the highest good, we both judge and desire power: for this power must be perpetual, boundless, and secure. Perpetual, so that it may not at some time fail and be changed by weakness; boundless, so that, circumscribed by limits, it may not be overcome or impeded by greater or equal powers; and finally secure, so that it may not fear becoming subject to those over whom it rules when circumstances change. Yet this does not belong either to a kingdom or to those who share in a kingdom, as must be proved separately.

Can they make a person powerful? Why not [Note: [Col. 0740A] Someone may say.], when their prosperity endures forever? Yet antiquity is full of examples [Note: [Col. 0740C] The past is full of examples; the present age is full [Col. 0740D] of them also.]—and the present age likewise—of men who have exchanged prosperity for calamity.

I. That a kingdom is not perpetual is demonstrated by examples both ancient and recent. By ancient examples, certainly: Diomedes, king of Thrace, while cruelly feeding his horses human flesh at the city of Tyrida, was himself thrown by Hercules to those very horses to be devoured. Agis, king of the Lacedaemonians, who had waged the bloodiest wars against the Athenians, was finally killed by his own fellow citizens in prison. Perses, king of the Macedonians, was defeated by Aemilius, led to Rome, and died in prison. Croesus, king of the Lydians, was reduced to slavery by Cyrus, and so forth.

By more recent examples, namely those that occurred around the time of Boethius: Alaric, king of the Tolosans, was killed by the Franks; Syagrius, king of the Romans, by Clovis; and others by others. “Thus indeed,” says Vallinus here, “God permits mortals to be treated; offended by the character of rulers and peoples, he afflicts cities, brings provinces to ruin, and overturns kingdoms.”

Antiquity is full of examples [Note: [Col. 0740A] Says Philosophy.], and the present age too [Note: [Col. 0740A] Of those men.], of men who have exchanged prosperity for calamity. O splendid power, which is found not even to be sufficiently effective for preserving itself!

[Note: [Col. 0740D] The power responsible for happiness.] But if this power of kingdoms is the cause of happiness [Note: [Col. 0740A] That is, the cause. Thus Plautus said that a thing has an *auctor*, although Servius prefers to say *auctrix*. Valerius Probus seems to resolve this dispute: “If,” he says, “*auctor* is derived from the verb *augeo* [‘I increase’], it makes *auctrix*; but if it does not come from the verb, and signifies a leader—a noun not derived from the verb—then it makes *auctor* even in the feminine gender, as Virgil has it in the person of Juno: *Auctor ego audendi princeps* [‘I am the author, the foremost leader, of daring’]. Not ‘she who increases,’ for then he would have said *auctrix*.” There are, of course, three views concerning the origin of the word *auctor*. Some think that it comes from the Greek αὐτός, so that *autor* means the same as αὐτοῦργος, “one who acts on his own”; others derive it from the unused supine of the verb *aveo*, “to desire,” so that *autor* is said from *autum*, just as *cautor* comes from *cautum* and *fautor* from *fautum.” On this account, an *autor* is one who desires and wishes something to be done, whether by himself or by another. Finally, others think it comes from *augere*, “to increase,” so that at first *auctor* referred to one who advanced a matter begun by another, and afterward also to one who began and advised it. The older inscriptions support this last view, since they write *auctor*, not *autor*. Whatever the case may be, royal power cannot be the author, or effective cause, of happiness, since it is contained within definite limits.]

Is not power the cause of happiness [Note: [Col. 0740A] The cause.]? If it is deficient in any respect, does it not diminish happiness and bring misery?

II. Human kingship is not boundless [Note: [Col. 0741C] However widely, etc.], for although a king, even a very great one, rules many nations, he does not rule more numerous nations still. Therefore, if you measure happiness by dominion, there is more misery than happiness in such a king.

Although human dominions may be extended widely [Note: [Col. 0741A] May be spread abroad.], it is necessary that more nations be left over whom no king rules. In whatever direction power ceases to make people happy, impotence enters in its place and makes them miserable. In this way, therefore, kings must necessarily contain a greater portion of misery.

III. That human kingship is not secure is sufficiently proved by the well-known story of Dionysius the Tyrant [Note: [Col. 0741A] Dionysius, king of Sicily.], who, having experienced the dangers of his own condition, represented the fear of the sword hanging over Damocles’ head [Note: [Col. 0741A] Damocles, one of his flatterers.]. For, as Cicero says in the fifth book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, when one of his flatterers, Damocles, mentioned in conversation his resources, wealth, majesty, dominion, abundance of possessions, and magnificence of his royal buildings, and denied that anyone had ever been happier:

“Would you like, then, Damocles, since this life pleases you, to taste it yourself and experience my fortune?” When he said that he desired this, Dionysius ordered the man to be placed upon a golden couch spread with a beautiful woven cover embroidered with magnificent workmanship. He adorned several sideboards with chased silver and gold. Then he ordered selected boys of extraordinary beauty to stand beside the table and, watching him attentively at his nod, to serve him. Perfumes and garlands were present; fragrances were burned; tables were covered with the choicest delicacies. Damocles thought himself fortunate.

In the midst of this splendid arrangement, Dionysius ordered a shining sword, suspended from the ceiling by a horsehair, to be lowered so that it hung over the neck of the happy man. Thus Damocles neither looked at those beautiful attendants nor at the silver full of artistic workmanship, nor did he stretch out his hand toward the table. The garlands themselves were already slipping from him. Finally he begged the tyrant to allow him to leave, since he no longer wished to be happy.

Does it not seem that Dionysius sufficiently demonstrated that nothing is happy for one over whom some terror is always hanging? With this in mind Horace sings in Book III, Ode 1:

> For him above whose impious neck  
> The drawn sword hangs, neither Sicilian feasts  
> Shall prepare a sweet flavor,  
> Nor the songs of birds and the lyre  
> Restore sleep.

That assumption, therefore, is false by which you judge the highest good to lie in kingship. But familiarity with kings does not make one happier.

What shall I say about the friends of kings, when I show that kingdoms themselves are filled with such weakness? Those whom royal power sometimes leaves unharmed and sometimes overthrows—what power can they possess?

For what shall I say about the friends of kings? [Note: [Col. 0742B] “What shall I say about the friends of kings,” etc.] The friends of kings cannot possess greater power, and therefore greater happiness, than those whose friends they are—namely, the kings—whose power, as we have proved, is weak. Indeed, they possess much less. For either royal power remains unharmed, or it falls. If it falls, the friends of the kings are dragged into the same ruin with them. If it stands, it often overthrows those very friends. Seneca bears witness, and Papinian bears witness.

Nero, says Suetonius, compelled Seneca, his tutor, to die, although he had repeatedly sworn most solemnly, when Seneca asked leave to retire and surrendered his property, that he was needlessly suspected and would perish before he harmed him. For after one of the centurions, says Tacitus, had announced Seneca’s final necessity, he said that, after the deaths of his mother and brother, nothing remained except the death of his tutor and teacher. After this, Seneca and his wife opened the veins of their arms with the same stroke of the blade. Since Seneca’s aged body, weakened by scanty nourishment, offered a slow escape to the blood, he also severed the veins of his legs and behind his knees.

Nero compelled Seneca, his friend and teacher, to choose the manner of his own death.

[Note: [Col. 0742C] Papinian under Antoninus.] Papinian was so skilled in law that he is said to have surpassed all Roman jurists both before and after him. Besides succeeding Scaevola, whose student he had been, in the advocacy of the imperial treasury, he was related to the emperor Severus through Severus’s second wife, and was so intimate and friendly with him that, when Severus was dying, he entrusted his sons to Papinian.

But Antoninus, surnamed Caracalla, who held the Roman empire after Severus, is said to have ordered the aforementioned Papinian, after murdering his brother Geta, to wash away the crime in the senate and before the people. Papinian refused, arguing that parricide could more easily be committed than concealed, and that accusing an innocent murdered man constituted another kind of parricide. This so enraged Antoninus against Papinian that he ordered him to be killed by the soldiers. Whether the deed was carried out with a sword or with an axe—the punishment with the latter being considered more severe and more disgraceful—is uncertain. He is not said to have been killed by Antoninus himself, but merely to have been delivered by Antoninus to the soldiers’ swords.

Papinian, for a long time powerful among the courtiers, Antoninus exposed to the soldiers’ swords. Yet both wished to renounce their power [Note: [Col. 0742A] Among those courtiers.], for Seneca even attempted to hand over his wealth to Nero and withdraw into retirement.
