But while the collapsing mass [Note: [Col. 0742D] A huge burden both of wealth and of power, which, collapsing, overthrew Seneca and Papinian in its own ruin.] itself drags them down [Note: [Col. 0742A] Of wealth and power.], neither achieved what he wished. What kind of power, then, is this, which those who possess it fear; which, even when you wish to possess it, does not leave you safe; and which, when you wish to lay it down, you cannot escape?

Are friends a safeguard [Note: [Col. 0743A] In name only.], when it is not virtue but fortune that wins them? Yet the man whom prosperity has made your friend [Note: [Col. 0743A] For you.], misfortune will make your enemy.

For, because he is intimate with you, he knows the means by which he can harm you; but you do not consider how you can avoid his treachery. So false is the assumption by which you think that kingship and familiarity with kings have the character of the highest good.

What plague is more effective for doing harm than an intimate enemy?

## 202. METER V

[Note: [Col. 0743C] What is called Parthenic. This is a poem consisting of one kind of verse, each line being a trimeter with an anapaest before the third foot, followed by a remaining syllable; the first and second feet are either spondees or anapaests without distinction.]

**ARGUMENT.**—“The ruler of the world,” says Philosophy, “is not powerful unless he rules his own disturbances.”

[Note: [Col. 0743A] Whoever wishes to be considered powerful must subdue his rebellious impulses and must not, once overcome, submit himself to pleasure under shameful commands. For although distant India may fear your dominion, and farthest Thule, the last island of the Roman empire, may obey you, nevertheless you will not be powerful so long as you cannot drive away ruinous desire and repel wretched complaints.]

[Note: [Col. 0743C] 1. “Whoever wishes to be powerful.” To be considered powerful in the chief part of oneself, namely, the mind.

2. “Let him subdue his fierce impulses.” In its primary meaning, *animus* is wind, just like the Greek word ἄνεμος, from which it seems to derive. Therefore, just as wind, insofar as it differs from a storm, is nothing other than a thin vapor of water moving here and there wherever there is less resistance, so in its primary meaning *animus* is nothing other than a subtler vapor of blood that is about to leave the brain through the nerves wherever an opening is provided. Thus Virgil, *Georgics* I, verse 420:

> The forms of the spirits change, and breasts conceive  
> Now one kind of motion, now another,  
> While the wind drives the clouds.

And in *Georgics* IV, verse 86:

> These movements of the spirit and these great contests  
> Will be brought to rest by the casting of a little dust.

Thus, too, power is now said to consist in the subduing of the impulses, since our mind can do nothing to our body except through those spirits. But because these same spirits, striving to enter a well-trodden path in ordered formation, can be governed and, as it were, tamed with greater difficulty, like wild beasts, they are here called “fierce.” Their control is therefore a greater proof of strength and power.

3. “Nor submit his necks to the reins, overcome by desire.” The comparison is taken from captives, who customarily carry their necks bound with chains. Accordingly, “necks” here refers both to mind and body, overcome by desire or evil inclination. For *libido* generally means an evil inclination, as though the mind, swerving from the straight path through an evil wish, were slipping away. “Whatever is desired wrongly is desire,” says Saint Augustine, Book IV of the *Hypognosticon*.

5. “The Indian land.” India is so called from the river Indus. It is a vast region of land bounding Asia on the east; therefore it is here taken for the east.

6. “Let it tremble at your laws.” *Jus*, as Sanctius teaches, in its primary meaning signifies vegetables or porridge. But because equal portions were given to each person at banquets, *jus* was transferred to signify what belongs to each person. From this, the society established among human beings for returning to each person what is his is called forensic law, so that a person is said to be summoned “to law.” Since rulers, especially those appointed by God, exist so that the peoples may each possess what is their own, the will and edict of rulers is therefore called *jus*, and by analogy other laws are called *jura*. Hence *jura* here means the commands of every powerful person.

7. “Let farthest Thule serve.” Thule is the last of the lands once known to the Romans, and the most northerly toward the west; hence it here signifies the west. It is commonly said to be Iceland. Virgil speaks of this region in *Georgics* I, verse 29:

> Or do you come as god of the boundless sea,  
> And sailors worship your divinity alone,  
> While farthest Thule serves you?

8. “Drive away the dark cares.” “Dark care” now means the desire mentioned above. Desire is indeed care, because a mind wounded especially by desire is consumed by it; hence Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, verse 1:

> But the queen, long wounded by heavy care,  
> Nourishes the wound in her veins and is consumed by a hidden fire.

Yet this same desire is dark or harmful care, for among the ancients whiteness signified good and blackness an evil omen. Thus the appearance of an Ethiopian was believed to foretell misfortune. Hence melancholy, notorious for its many harmful effects, is called *atrabilis*—“black bile.” The desire mentioned above is harmful not only to the body but also to the mind.

9. “Drive away the wretched complaints.” Complaints are now called wretched both from their cause and from their effect, because arising from miseries they produce new miseries.

10. “The inability to do this is not power.” The mind is powerful only insofar as it is master of itself and governs its disturbances. Unless kings and the friends of kings accomplish this, they falsely claim to be happy. Glory follows.]

> Whoever wishes to be powerful,  
> Let him subdue his fierce impulses,  
> And let him not submit his neck,  
> Overcome by desire, to shameful reins.
>
> [5] For although the Indian land, far away,  
> Trembles at your laws,  
> And farthest Thule serves you,  
> Yet to drive away dark cares  
> And repel wretched complaints—
>
> [10] To be unable to do this is not power.

## 204. PROSE VI

[Col. 0745A]

**ARGUMENT.**—Philosophy adds that neither false nor true glory, whether founded upon one’s own merits or upon those of others, is to be regarded as the highest good.

[Note: [Col. 0745B] Glory.] Glory is honor spread abroad with praise for another person's merits. First, glory is honor—namely, a judgment expressing another person’s excellence. “The highest and perfect glory,” says Cicero in Book II of *On Duties*, “consists of these three things: if the multitude loves us, if it trusts us, and if, with a certain admiration, it thinks us worthy of honor.” Accordingly, in Meter 1, verse 7, of the first book, we said that honor is a kind of glory; see there.

Next, glory is honor joined with praise. For “glory,” says Cicero in Book III of the *Tusculan Disputations*, “is the unanimous and uncorrupted voice of those who judge well concerning distinguished virtue.” In this respect glory differs from honor in the simple sense, which is not always joined with such praise.

Finally, the honor called glory must be spread abroad with praise, so that it has reached even the leading men. In this respect glory differs from reputation, which may belong only to the common people. Thus one kind of glory is false, being discordant with a person’s merits; another is true, being in agreement with the merits—whether one’s own or external—of the person praised. Yet neither false nor true glory, whether founded upon your own merits or upon those of others, has the character of the highest good, as must be proved separately.]

But how often glory is deceptive [Note: [Col. 0745C] How often it is deceptive.]—how disgraceful it is!

I. False glory is under discussion. Since it is discordant with merits, it is so far from possessing the character of the highest good that it is rather an error and therefore an evil. Thus, not unjustly, the tragic poet Euripides, held in the highest honor by Archelaus, king of the Macedonians, cried out in the *Andromache*:

[Note: [Col. 0745B] Euripides in the *Andromache*.] “O glory, glory, you have made the life of thousands of mortals who had no merit great” [Note: [Col. 0745B] “O glory, glory, you have made the life of thousands of mortals who had no merit great.”]:

> Ὦ δόξα, δόξα, μυρίοισι δὴ βροτῶν,  
> οὐδὲν γεγῶσι, βίοτον ὤγκωσας μέγαν.

That is:

> O glory, glory, you have magnified the life  
> Of countless mortals who possessed no merit.

For many have often acquired a great name through the false opinions of the crowd. What more disgraceful thing can be imagined? Those who are falsely praised must necessarily blush at their own praises.

II. True glory founded upon one’s own merits is under discussion [Note: [Col. 0745D] If it is also founded upon merits.]. It does not therefore possess the character of the highest good, because, being outside the person honored, it adds nothing good to the mind or conscience of the wise person. Yet the wise person, being skilled in understanding his own mind, considers nothing good for himself except what is in his own mind and of which that mind is conscious.

Even if it has been acquired through merits, what has it added to the conscience of the wise person, who measures his good not by popular rumor [Note: [Col. 0745B] Of the crowd.], but by the truth of conscience?

But if it seems good to the wise person himself to have his name extended [Note: [Col. 0745D] If extending one’s name seems beautiful.], let us grant what nevertheless is not the case, says Philosophy: that it seems good to the wise person both to be praised externally and to be esteemed internally by the peoples. According to the law of opposites, it will then be necessary that not being praised and not being highly esteemed by the peoples be evil for the same wise person. Therefore, since, as has been said, there are far more people who do not know that wise person than there are people who recognize him as praiseworthy and honorable, the same wise person will possess more evil than the highest good.

But if extending one’s name seems beautiful, it follows that failing to extend it must be judged disgraceful [Note: [Col. 0745B] It is judged disgraceful.]. Yet, as I argued shortly before, there must be more nations to which the reputation of one person cannot reach. Thus the person whom you consider glorious will appear inglorious over the greater part of the earth [Note: [Col. 0745B] Dishonored.].

Among all this, I consider popular favor [Note: [Col. 0746B] Of the crowd.] not even worthy of mention, since it arises from no judgment and never endures securely.

III. How empty and worthless is the name of nobility [Note: [Col. 0746C] The futile name of nobility.]! True glory founded upon the merits of others—namely, upon descent—is under discussion. This is commonly called nobility and is now defined as a kind of praise deriving from the merits of one’s ancestors. But it is an empty and futile name unless you imitate the virtue of those whose blood you share.

Juvenal, Satire 8, verse 19:

> Although ancient waxen images adorn  
> The atria on every side,  
> Virtue alone, and virtue only, is nobility.
>
> Be a Paulus, a Cossus, or a Drusus in character;  
> Place these men before the images of your ancestors.  
> Let them precede the rods when you are consul.  
> You owe me first the goods of the spirit:  
> You deserve to be held holy and steadfast in justice  
> By your deeds and words.

Who does not see that nobility is a light and futile name [Note: [Col. 0746B] Light.], if it is taken as distinction? It is external to the person. Nobility seems to be a certain praise deriving from the merits of one’s ancestors. But if distinction is produced by public praise, those who are praised must be distinguished. Therefore, if you possess no distinction of your own, another person’s distinction does not make you illustrious.

If there is anything good in nobility, I think it is only this: that the nobles seem bound by an obligation imposed upon them not to degenerate from the virtue of their ancestors.

## 206. METER VI

[Note: [Col. 0746C] A poem consisting of two alternating kinds of verse. The first, the Alcmanic, has three feet of heroic verse with a remaining final syllable, though it is not composed entirely of spondees. The second, the Pherecratean, likewise has three feet, namely a spondee or an anapaest, a dactyl, and a spondee.]

**ARGUMENT.**—“Whoever cultivates virtue,” says Philosophy, “is the non-degenerate offspring of God, the noblest parent, and is truly noble.”

[Note: [Col. 0746] The whole human race arises on earth from the same beginning. For there is one parent of all things, God, and one governs all things. He gave the sun its splendor and the moon the appearance of waxing and waning. He also gave human beings to the earth and the stars to the sky. He enclosed in human bodies minds born from a lofty place. All people therefore have noble seed. Why do you boast of your origin and of your mortal ancestors? If you consider your beginning and your creator, God, no one degenerates before he withdraws from his God as his origin by sinning.]

> The whole human race on earth  
> Rises from a common origin.

[Note: [Col. 0746D] 1. “The whole race of human beings.” A human being is not merely corporeal, like an animal, nor merely incorporeal, like a good or evil spirit. Rather, the human being is a marvelous composition of soul and body joined together. This composition arises on earth, where the divinely infused mind is joined to the body, prepared as a kind of lodging; and it arises from a similar source, since the same beginning belongs not only to the mind and body themselves but also to their mutual union.

The beginning of both the human body and the human mind is the same, namely God. Since both this and that are things, and since a thing cannot be created except by God, it is necessarily the case that the same God is the beginning of the human mind and body. But God is also the beginning of the mutual union of the mind and body, since neither body acts upon mind nor mind upon body except by God’s granting it. Philosophy will now state all these points specifically, after having first said generally that everything comes from God.]

> For there is one father of all things,  
> One supplies all things.

[Note: [Col. 0747B] 3. “There is one father of all things.” I. In general, everything comes from God in such a way that God is the father of all things. For “father” means not only a producing cause but also a preserving cause; and God is the producing and preserving cause of all things.

Hence God is called Father by Christians, Jews, and even pagans. Christians say in prayer, “Our Father who art in heaven,” Matthew 6. To the Jews it is said in Deuteronomy 32: “Is he not your Father, who possessed you, made you, and created you?” Finally, Horace says: “Father and guardian of the human race”; and Virgil says: “The Father himself willed that the way of cultivation should not be easy.”

5. “He gave Phoebus his rays.” The sun is called Phoebus by poets because of its appearance and brightness; for φοῖβος is an adjective meaning “shining,” “bright,” or “pure.” God gave the sun its rays. Although the sun seems to derive the fact that it shines in one way or another from bodies placed before it, it nevertheless derives from God alone the fact that it shines.

Two kinds of effects can plainly be observed in the world: certain general effects and others—as philosophers barbarously call them—particular effects. A general cause must be sought for the former, and a particular cause for the latter. Thus, if one asks why a listener is moved when I speak, one must give not a general but a particular cause: the air extended from my mouth to his ears is moved by my lungs, tongue, teeth, and lips in such a way that the listener’s ears are moved by the same process.

But if one asks why, when the listener’s brain has been moved, thoughts arise in the same listener’s mind, one must give a general rather than a particular cause. Likewise, if one asks why the rainbow draws a thousand various colors from the opposing sun, the particular cause given is falling rain. But if one asks why the sun sends forth rays, the general cause—namely, God the all-good—is rightly given. Thus God—

6. “He also gave the moon horns.” Since the moon is an opaque body, it reflects light received from the sun in such a way that it appears now to wax, now to wane, now to disappear, and now to be full; or, as Pliny says, now curved into horns, now divided into equal portions, now hollowed into a circle, spotted and yet suddenly shining brightly with an immense full disk, and then suddenly nothing.

Virgil, *Aeneid* III, verse 645:

> Now the moon’s third horns are filled with light.

But the fact that this opaque body reflects light in this way, being a general effect, must be referred to God as its general cause.

7. “He gave human beings to the earth.” II. Specifically, the human being arises from God as from a father, first with respect to the body, which God formed from the earth and placed upon the earth—Genesis 1: “The Lord God formed man from the clay of the earth”—just as he formed the stars from the heavens and placed them in the heavens. Genesis 1 says: “And God made two great lights, the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars.”

Hence Psalm 113: “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord, but the earth he has given to the children of men.” Cicero himself, in Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*, says: “Human beings, raised from the earth, were established as cultivators of the earth.”

[Col. 0748B] 9. “He enclosed the remembering minds in their limbs.” III. The human being also arises from God as from a father with respect to the mind, since, because it has no external cause except this one, according to the judgment of philosophers it is created; and creation belongs to God alone. Hence Philosophy now says that minds are sought from a lofty seat.

Nor are the human body and mind merely created by God: they are also mutually joined by God as by a general cause. For if one asks why the human mind is joined to the human body at some time and for some duration, no other general cause can be given except the will of God, who made all things whatsoever he willed in heaven and on earth, Psalm 113. Hence, according to philosophical reasoning, God enclosed minds in limbs.

Lactantius, Book I of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 21, says: “This little body with which we are clothed is the receptacle of the human being. For the human being himself can neither be touched, nor seen, nor grasped, because he lies hidden within that which is seen.”

Claudian, Book I of *The Rape of Proserpine*, verse 55, introduces Lachesis speaking thus:

> O greatest ruler of night,  
> Powerful over shadows, for whom our threads labor,  
> Who grant both the end and the seeds to all things,  
> And repay the changes of birth with alternating death;  
> Who rule life and death—for whatever matter  
> The mother of all things produces,  
> Is created by your gift,  
> Is owed to you,  
> And through the fixed winding paths of time  
> Souls are again sent into bodily limbs.

11. “He brings forth all mortals as noble offspring.” Since *germen* means both the effect of what precedes and the cause of the body that follows, I see that this passage has two possible interpretations.

The first is that of Theodore Sitzmann, who thinks that *germen* signifies offspring. He says that “noble offspring” is an apposition, so that God—who is discussed in the preceding verses—is said to bring forth all mortals, who are themselves noble offspring. This may be confirmed by the fact that *germen*, as if from *genimen*, means that which is generated from seed.

The second interpretation belongs to others, who think that *germen* here signifies a beginning. They say that the construction is what grammarians call one of a nominative and a verb, so that the noble origin of mortals is signified. This too may be confirmed by the fact that *germen*, as if from *gerimen*, means that which bears offspring.

But whatever the truth may be concerning these two interpretations of the noun, the latter opinion seems to us both more properly concluded from what has been said and more suitable to establish as the starting point for what immediately follows.

Philosophy seems to have said: Since all human beings arise from God not only with respect to their body and mind but also with respect to the mutual union of these parts, all human beings arise from the noblest parent. Therefore, despising earthly lineage and ancestors, all human beings are of the highest nobility unless they abandon their proper origin through vices.

Those are therefore deceived by a false assumption who think that the nobility which they naturally know and desire as the highest good exists solely in the succession of noble mortal ancestors. The pleasures of the body remain.]

> He gave Phoebus his rays,  
> And he gave the moon her horns.
>
> He also gave human beings to the earth,  
> And the stars to the heavens.
>
> He enclosed minds in limbs  
> Sought from a lofty seat.
>
> [Col. 0748A] 208 A noble seed  
> Brings forth all mortals.
>
> Why do you make such a clamor about lineage and ancestors?
> If you look to your beginnings  
> And to God your creator,
>
> No degenerate person exists,  
> Unless, cherishing things worse through vice,  
> He abandons  
> His proper origin.

## 209. PROSE VII

[Col. 0749A]

**ARGUMENT.**—“The pleasures of the body,” says Philosophy, “because they have consequences that bring regret, cannot possess the character of the highest good.”

[Note: [Col. 0749B] What is to be said about bodily pleasures.] Pleasure is a thought by which the mind, conscious of it, is suffused with a certain delight. For, says Tully in *De Finibus* II, “in the usage of all Latin speakers, pleasure is said to exist when that which moves some sense is perceived as delight.” Since, therefore, our mind, both as God’s effect and as the form of our body, can have a pleasant thought in two ways—first, from God himself, by whom and for whom it was created; then from the body, with which it is joined—pleasure is of two kinds. One is pleasure of the soul, which is not under discussion here; the other is bodily pleasure, in which, as Philosophy seems to prove, the character of the highest good does not reside. Bodily pleasure is either prohibited by law or it is not. If it is prohibited by law, it is so surrounded both by preceding desires and by subsequent pains that it contains more bitterness than pleasantness intermixed. But if it is permitted by law, its fruits—children—are often so hostile to their parents that the person without children seems fortunate in his misfortune. All these matters will now be explained separately.]

But what shall I say about bodily pleasures, [Note: [Col. 0749C] Their desirability.] I. The subject is illicit bodily pleasure, for which future desire is conceived. For, says Tully in *De Officiis* I, “the power and nature of minds is twofold. One part lies in desire, which in Greek is ὁρμή (*hormē*), and which drags a person this way and that. The other lies in reason, which teaches and explains what must be done and what must be avoided.” [Col. 0749D] The desire for illicit pleasure, however, contains more evil than good, because it is full of anxiety—namely, that thought by which the mind, as though compressed, is distressed—as its satiety is accompanied by remorse. For remorse, derived from *poenitere*, “to repent,” is the thought of a mind grieving over what has been done by its own counsel and will. This sad thought is the inseparable companion of illicit pleasure, because God then warns a person of the sin committed. Nor are the fruits of remorse for this pleasure confined to the mind; they spread also into the body. Hence come diseases, pains, deaths, and other things of that kind.] The desire [Note: [Col. 0749B] Desire.] for them is indeed full of [Note: [Col. 0749B] Distress.] anxiety, but their satiety is full of remorse. [Note: [Col. 0749B] Use.] How many [Note: [Col. 0749B] Pleasures.] diseases and how intolerable pains do those pleasures usually bring back to the bodies of those who enjoy them, as a kind of fruit of wickedness! What pleasure their movement contains, I do not know. But whoever wishes to recall his lusts will understand that the outcomes of pleasures are sad.

210 If these pleasures can make people blessed, [Note: [Col. 0749B] To demonstrate.] there is no reason why beasts should not be called blessed as well. [Note: [Col. 0749D] There is no reason why beasts should not be blessed.] Moreover, being blessed seems so proper to human beings that no one thinks happiness consists in what can also belong to beasts. But to be occupied with the things from which bodily pleasures arise is common to human beings and beasts, since all the movements of beasts seem directed toward satisfying the body. For that reason this is now called [Col. 0750B] a hollow, because, just as a hollow contains water, so the body is nothing other than a very large vessel containing whatever liquid belongs to it. Unless you say that *lacuna* here means “need,” as in Tully, *In Verrem* IV, “that they might fill the hollow of their household estate.”] there is no reason why beasts, too, should not be called blessed, since all their activity hastens to fill the bodily [Note: [Col. 0749B] Need.] hollow.

[Note: [Col. 0750B] The most honorable pleasure of marriage, etc.] II. The subject is licit bodily pleasure, namely, that of marriage. This is called most honorable insofar as it is undertaken by divine will, which is the first rule of morals. For it belongs to the duty of virtue, says St. Augustine in *The City of God* XIX, chapter 1, “both to live for one’s country and to beget children for one’s country”; neither can be done without bodily pleasure. Yet this pleasure is also often sorrowful, since children are not rarely the torturers of their parents—not, perhaps, with respect to the body, as they say Oedipus, during a revolt among the Phocians, unknowingly killed his father Laius, king of Thebes, who was attempting to suppress the disturbance; but at least with respect to the mind, insofar as parents are tortured on account of their children by perpetual anxieties, by which they seem to be bitten as by certain dogs. Hence their condition is now called “biting.” Thus Plutarch says:

“From a child born, sorrow for the father lasts forever.” ]

The pleasure of a wife and the joy of children would indeed be most honorable, but [Note: [Col. 0749B] Experience of natural things proves this too strongly.] nature has spoken too truly in saying that I know not whom has found children to be torturers. Whatever their condition, it is so biting that there is no need to remind you either that you have experienced it at other times or that you are anxious now. In this matter [Note: [Col. 0750C] I approve the judgment of my Euripides.] I approve the judgment of my Euripides, who, although a poet, was nevertheless a philosopher—according to Tully, a disciple of Anaxagoras. Therefore Philosophy not unreasonably now calls him her own and approves the opinion he sets forth in *Andromache*: namely, that the person without children is fortunate in his misfortune, because, he says, “to have children is sweet to those without experience, but bitter to those who have experienced it.”] I approve the judgment of my [Note: [Col. 0750B] Philosopher.] Euripides, who said that the person without children is fortunate in his misfortune.

211 METER [Note: [Col. 0750D] What is called Anacreontic. It is a poem consisting of one kind of verse, each line being a trimeter with an iamb before the third foot, followed by an extra syllable; it has first an anapest and then an iamb.] VII.

ARGUMENT.—All pleasure, says Philosophy, is like a bee: those whom it feeds with honey, it stings with its barb.

[Note: [Col. 0750B] Every pleasure achieves this: it pricks with stings those who indulge in it, and, like departing bees, after it has sent forth its pleasant honey it flies away and tears with a very tenacious tooth the breasts it has touched.] [Note: [Col. 0750D] This is a most beautiful allegory, in which likeness is joined with metaphor. For pleasures are said to resemble bees, and words proper to bees are transferred to pleasures, just as Cicero in *Pro Murena* says that the instability of the elections is greater than that of the Euripus. Pleasures, I say, are said to resemble bees in this respect: just as bees do, pleasures bring both delight and sadness to the same person. Words proper to bees—namely, “stings,” “flying,” “pleasant honey,” and “tenacious bite”—are transferred to pleasures. Above all, observe the words “strikes the wounded hearts.” By these, both the manner in which a sting pierces bodies and the manner in which bodily pleasure pricks the mind seem excellently signified. For just as a bee, by continuous movement, pierces the flesh, so pleasure, by continuous thought, seems to lacerate the mind with repeated blows. Thus the former may be regarded as movement of the body, and the latter as thought of the mind. Therefore anyone is deceived who, through rashness and prejudice, assumes that the highest good resides in bodily pleasure.]

Every pleasure has this quality:

It drives those who enjoy it with stings,

And, like flying bees,

When it has poured forth pleasant honey,

[5] It flees, and with a bite

Too tenacious strikes the wounded hearts.

212 PROSE VIII.

[Col. 0751A]

ARGUMENT.—Philosophy, summarily repeating her preceding doctrine concerning wealth, rank, power, glory, and pleasure, says that these are so entangled with evils and so exposed to the weapons of their adversaries that they cannot possess the character of the highest good.

There is therefore no doubt that these roads to happiness [Note: [Col. 0751B] Those who go astray.] are certain byways, and that they cannot lead anyone to the place to which they promise to lead. How entangled with evils they are I shall show very briefly. What then? Will you try to gather money? But you will take it away from someone who has it. Do you wish to shine with offices of rank? You will plead with the giver of them; and you who desire to surpass others in honor will become base through the humility of petitioning. Do you desire power? Exposed to the plots of your subjects, you will lie beneath dangers. Do you seek glory? But, dragged through every hardship, you will cease to be secure. Do you lead a life of pleasure? But who would not despise and reject being the slave of the body, a thing most base and fragile? [Note: [Col. 0751B] What the body is like.] Now, those who parade the goods of the body—how slight and fragile a possession they rely upon! Will you surpass elephants in bulk or bulls in strength? Will you outstrip tigers in speed? Look upon the extent, firmness, and swiftness of the heavens, and cease at last to admire things that are worthless. Indeed, the heavens ought to be admired not so much for these qualities as for the reason by which they are governed. And the splendor of beauty—how swift it is, how fleeting, more fleeting than the changing of spring flowers! If, as Aristotle says, people used eyes like those of Lynceus, [Note: [Col. 0751B] The book of Aristotle now seems to be lost.] that is, eyes sharper than those of Lynceus, [Note: [Col. 0751C] With Lyncean eyes.]—the proverb is thought to have arisen from the claim that Lynceus was the first to discover mines of copper, silver, and gold. Hence they invented the story that Lynceus was so keen-sighted that he could penetrate the earth itself with the sharpness of his eyes and see what was happening among the dead below. “Who is so keen-sighted,” says Tully, “that amid such darkness he never stumbles and never falls into error?” Horace, *Epistles* I.1:

“You could not strain your eye as far as Lynceus,

Yet do not therefore disdain to have a bleary eye anointed.” ]

If people had Lyncean eyes, so that their sight could pierce obstacles, would not [Note: [Col. 0751D] The most beautiful body of Alcibiades.] Alcibiades’ body, most beautiful on its surface, appear most ugly when its internal organs had been inspected? Alcibiades was not a most beautiful woman, as Thomas the Englishman, author of commentaries on Boethius, says, but an Athenian commander, outstanding in intellect and very beautiful in body, who first devoted himself to vices and then, under Socrates’ instruction, to virtues. [Note: [Col. 0752B] That you appear beautiful, namely.] Therefore your appearing beautiful is due not to your nature but to [Note: [Col. 0751D] The weakness of the eyes.] the weakness of the eyes that look upon you. For if the eyes were so penetrating that the internal organs were also visible through them, the body, because it has a greater multitude of deformed than beautiful parts, would be considered deformed rather than beautiful. This would be all the more certain because beauty arises only from complete perfection, whereas deformity arises from even the slightest defect.] But estimate bodily goods as highly as you wish, provided you know that whatever you admire can be [Note: [Col. 0752C] By the spark of a three-day fever.] dissolved by the spark of a three-day fever. For whatever the body’s size, strength, agility, or beauty may be, all these vanish when the body has been shaken by fever and heat for three days. So true is it that the character of the highest good—which human beings naturally know and desire—does not reside in any of the goods mentioned above, to which people, led by a false assumption, cling.] From all this it is possible to draw the following conclusion: things that can neither provide the goods they promise nor, through the gathering of all goods, constitute perfection cannot lead to happiness as paths, nor do they themselves make people blessed.

214 METER [Note: [Col. 0752C] A poem consisting of two alternating kinds of verse. The first, the Asclepiad, contains a spondee, a dactyl with a syllable, and two further dactyls; the second is iambic, with four feet, most often spondees in the odd places and iambs in the even places.] VIII.

[Col. 0752B]

ARGUMENT.—People err, sings Philosophy, when, seeking earthly things on land, aquatic things in water, and flying things in air, each in its proper place, they look for happiness where it cannot arise, as though ignorant of the proper abode of the highest good.

[Note: [Col. 0752B] Alas, what ignorance turns you unhappy people away from the straight path and leads you astray! You do not seek gold in a green tree, nor gather pearls from a vine. You do not hide nets in high mountains in order to add fish to your feasts. Nor do you enter the Tyrrhenian Sea if you wish to hunt roebuck. Indeed, people know the hidden recesses of the sea concealed beneath the waters; they know which water is richer in white pearls, or which is richer in red-purple dye; they know which seas excel in tender fish or in shell-covered sea urchins. Yet blind people do not resent their ignorance of where the good they desire is hidden; and what has passed beyond the starry heavens they seek while entangled in earthly things. What misfortune worthy of foolish minds should I pray for? Let them pursue wealth and honors everywhere; and when they have amassed false goods with great labor, then let them recognize the true goods.] [Note: [Col. 0752C] 1 and 2. Ignorance leads those astray from the path.] People indeed err through rash assumption, thinking, as has often been said, that the highest good resides in wealth, bodily pleasures, and other things of that kind. But the cause of this error is ignorance. For just as, especially in philosophy, clear and distinct knowledge is the rule of truth, so that if we follow it we shall never err, so ignorance is the beginning of error, and we never err except because we are ignorant.

3. You do not seek gold in a green tree.] Gold is customarily produced in the bowels of the earth, not in trees, especially green ones, since neither can the seed of gold be brought there nor, once brought there, be formed.

4. Nor do you gather pearls from a vine.] Pearls are customarily found on land or in water, not in plants, for the reason given above concerning gold.

5. You do not hide snares in high mountains, etc.] People do not fish in the air or hunt boars in the sea. These things are so foreign to all human thought that they are used proverbially to signify, says Erasmus, those who seek something perversely where it cannot even be hoped for—for example, if someone seeks a tranquil life in public office, happiness in pleasures, or prosperity in wealth. Thus Libanus the slave, in Plautus’ *Asinaria*, when ordered by his master Demaenetus to defraud his master’s wife of money, indicating that there was no way to take anything from a woman of the greatest stinginess, says: “Order me, as one task, to fish in the air and hunt with a javelin in the middle of the sea.”]

Alas, what ignorance leads unhappy people

Astray from the path!

You do not seek gold in a green tree,

Nor gather pearls from a vine;

[5] You do not hide snares in high mountains,

[Col. 0753A] [Note: [Col. 0753B]

8. Tyrrhenian waters.] The Tyrrhenian Sea is that part of the Mediterranean which washes the southern side of Italy, just as the Adriatic Gulf washes the northern side. Hence the former is called the Upper Sea and the latter the Lower Sea. Virgil speaks of it in *Aeneid* I, verse 71:

“An enemy people sails the Tyrrhenian sea.”]

[Note: [Col. 0753B] 11 and 12. Richer in pearls or in red-purple dye.] Valla says that it is unusual for two cases, although each may be governed separately by the same word, to be joined simultaneously with it, as here *gemmis* and *purpurae* are joined with *feracior*, “richer in pearls and purple.” Yet this is not faulty, because in the syntax called figurative, words are joined not so much according to their forms as according to their meanings. Thus Cicero says, “I bought it for a hundred gold pieces and more.” Purple properly means a kind of shellfish whose liquid was once used to dye clothing. Pliny, *Natural History* IX.36, says that this liquid shone with the color of a dark rose; hence it is now called red. Nevertheless, blue, violet, and every beautiful color are often called purple. Thus waves, violets, and flowers generally are called purple, as has already been said.]

[Col. 0753D] 13 and 14. Which shores excel in tender fish or rough sea urchins.] Just as, in Virgil’s words, not every land bears everything, so not every shore produces every fish. In one place tender fish are plentiful; elsewhere shell-covered fish come more readily. An *echinus* generally is an animal armed on all sides with rough hairs. Hence, by a certain resemblance, the spiny covering of a chestnut, and also a certain rough architectural work, are called an *echinus*. But the animal called an *echinus* is of two kinds, terrestrial and marine. The terrestrial echinus sometimes takes on the appearance of a ball, with its head and feet drawn in, so that its front and rear cannot be distinguished. The marine echinus, according to Aristotle himself, is customarily served as food. Thomas the Englishman wrongly calls this fish a remora, which is called *echeneis*, evidently deceived by the similarity of the words. Horace is more accurate in *Satires* II.4:

“But not every sea is fertile in noble shellfish.

The Baian murex is better than the Lucrine oyster;

Oysters arise at Circeii, sea urchins at Misenum;

Tarentum boasts of its soft, widely opened shellfish.”]

17. He has gone beyond the starry pole.] For he is God.

18. They seek it, sunk into the earth.] The mind, depressed from its highest dwelling and as though sunk into the earth amid perishable things, as Tully says, thinks through a false assumption that the highest good resides there.

19. What curse should I utter?] To curse is to pray for some evil upon someone’s head. Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, verse 628:

“Shore against shore, wave against wave

I curse; arms against arms: let them fight, and their descendants too.”]

20. Let them pursue wealth and honors.] Let them plead by going around. For *ambio* is said from *ambe*, “around,” and *eo*, “I go,” because the Romans went about everywhere seeking the votes of the people, or even of the judges. This is the evil that Philosophy prays upon the heads of foolish people. But because it is unfitting for Philosophy, that teacher of virtues, to curse evil except for the sake of some good that may arise from it, she adds:

21. And when they have acquired false things, then let them recognize the true goods.] This is evidently by the example of Solomon, who, after devoting himself impiously to all the goods mentioned above, finally returned to God, exclaiming, “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.” We interpret *gravi mole* as “with great labor.” For, as I think I have already noted, *moles* is first used of bodies that, because of the rest inherent in their many parts, can be moved only with difficulty. Hence *moles* is not inappropriately derived from the Greek μοκλένω, “I move aside with levers.” From this a great stone is called *molaris*; and *moliri* likewise means to move something by gathering one’s strength. Then, by a certain resemblance, *moles* is used of every difficult undertaking, as in Virgil, *Aeneid* I, verse 37:

“So great a labor was it to found the Roman people.”]

So that you may enrich your banquets with fish.

215 Nor, if you wish to pursue roebuck,

Do you seek the Tyrrhenian waters.

Even the recesses of the sea,

Hidden beneath the waves,

[10] They know:

Which water is richer in snowy pearls,

Or which in red-purple dye;

And which shores, with tender fish

Or rough sea urchins,

[15] Are superior.

216 But where the good they desire may lie hidden,

Blind people endure not knowing,

And what has passed beyond the starry pole

They seek, sunk into the earth.

What misfortune worthy of foolish minds should I pray for?

[20] Let them pursue wealth and honors,

And when with great labor they have acquired false goods,

Then let them recognize the true goods.

217 PROSE IX.

ARGUMENT.—Philosophy now uses a transition by which she seems both to recall what has been said and to anticipate what is to be said. She adds that abundance, power, reverence, fame, and pleasure are properties of the highest good so inseparable—being different modes of one and the same thing—that whoever, by assumption, attributes one or another of them to different things is deceived through rashness or prejudice.

[Note: [Col. 0754D] Thus far.] I. Philosophy now uses a transition, whose use is frequent and useful among orators and poets. Thus Tully says: “Since I have spoken about the kind of war, I shall now say a little about its magnitude.” Likewise Virgil, *Georgics* II, verse 1:

“Thus far the cultivation of fields and the stars of heaven;

Now I shall sing of you, Bacchus, and with you

The woodland shrubs and the offspring of the slowly growing olive.” ]

Thus far it has been enough to display the appearance of false happiness. If you [Note: [Col. 0754D] Clearly.] look at it perspicuously—Is this a Latin word? I would say “clearly” or “evidently.”] look at it clearly, the next task is to show what true happiness is. But I see, I said, [Note: [Col. 0755C] Boethius speaking.] that sufficiency cannot come from wealth, power from kingdoms, reverence from offices, fame from glory, or joy from pleasures. Have you also discovered the reasons why this is so? [Note: [Col. 0755C] Philosophy speaking.] I seem to glimpse them through a narrow opening, [Note: [Col. 0755D] Boethius speaking.] but I would rather learn them more openly from you. [Note: [Col. 0755D] Addressed to Philosophy.] The reasoning is very plain. [Note: [Col. 0755D] Philosophy speaking.] [Note: [Col. 0755D] What is simple, etc.] II. Philosophy proposes that abundance, power, and the rest of this kind are modes of the highest good, not parts, as they are commonly thought to be. Therefore, to understand what follows, one must note the distinction between a part and a mode. They differ in this: a part can be clearly and distinctly conceived through its own separate idea, whereas a mode cannot. Thus mind and body are parts of a human being, because mind without body and body without mind can each be clearly and distinctly conceived through its own idea. Likewise, shape, rest, and motion are modes of body, because none of them can be clearly and distinctly conceived without conceiving body. Similarly, understanding and will, neither of which can be clearly and distinctly conceived without conceiving mind, are modes of mind. Now the goods mentioned above, which people falsely attribute to created things, cannot be clearly and distinctly conceived without conceiving some higher thing, namely God, as Philosophy proves separately and so evidently that no other interpretation seems necessary.] For whatever is simple and undivided by nature, human error separates and transfers from the true and perfect to the false and imperfect. Do you think that what needs nothing can need power? Not at all, I said. [Note: [Col. 0755D] Boethius speaking.]

218 You are right, [Note: [Col. 0755D] Philosophy speaking.] for if anything is weaker in strength [Note: [Col. 0755D] In power.] than something else, it must need external assistance for its support. That is so, I said. Therefore sufficiency and power have one and the same nature. So it seems. But do you think that what is of this kind [Col. 0755B] should be despised, or, on the contrary, that it is most worthy of the reverence of all things? That, I said, cannot even be doubted. Let us therefore add reverence to sufficiency and power, so that we judge these three to be one. Let us add it, if we wish to acknowledge the truth. What then? she said. Do you think this obscure and ignoble, or most renowned for universal fame? Consider whether what has been granted to need nothing, to be most powerful, and to be most worthy of honor can lack the renown that it cannot provide for itself, and thereby seem in some respect more abject. I cannot, I said, fail to confess that, just as it is what it is, so it is also most renowned. It follows, then, that we must confess that fame differs in no way from the preceding three. It follows, I said. Therefore, what needs nothing external, can do everything by its own powers, is renowned and worthy of reverence—is it not also evidently most joyful? But how any sorrow could steal upon such a thing, [Note: [Col. 0756C] No sadness seems able to exist in something of this kind.] I said, I cannot even imagine. Therefore, if the preceding qualities remain, we must confess that it is full of joy. Indeed, by the same reasoning it is necessary [Note: [Col. 0756D] That all these are one thing affected in several ways.] to conclude that the names sufficiency, power, fame, reverence, and pleasure are different, but that their substance in no way differs. It is necessary, I said.

This one thing, then, simple by nature, [Note: [Col. 0756D] By judging wrongly.] human perversity divides. While it tries to obtain a part of a thing that has no parts, it attains neither a portion—which does not exist—nor the thing itself, which it least seeks. How so? I asked. Whoever seeks wealth, she said, in fleeing poverty cares nothing for power. He prefers to be poor and obscure, and even deprives himself of many natural pleasures lest he lose the money he has acquired. But in this way he does not even attain sufficiency, since strength abandons him, hardship torments him, lowliness casts him down, and obscurity conceals him. Whoever desires power alone squanders wealth, despises pleasures, and cares nothing for honor or glory that lacks power. But you see how much is lacking to him as well. It happens that at some point he is in need of necessities and is bitten by anxieties; and when he cannot drive these away, he ceases to be powerful—the very thing he most desired. The same reasoning can be applied to honors, glory, and pleasures.

For since each of these is the same as the others, [Note: [Col. 0756D] One thing existing in several modes.] whoever seeks one of them without the rest does not even grasp what he desires. What then? I asked. If someone should wish to attain all of them simultaneously, would he be seeking the sum of happiness? But would he find it in these things, which we have shown unable to provide what they promise? No, I said. Happiness, then, must in no way be sought in those things that are each separately believed to provide one of the objects of desire. I admit it, I said; and nothing truer can be said.

You have, then, she said, both the form of false happiness and its causes. Now turn the gaze of your mind in the opposite direction, [Note: [Col. 0756D] Consider the contrary.] for there you will immediately see the true happiness we promised. Indeed, I said, this is clear even to a blind man, and you showed it shortly before when you attempted to reveal the causes of false happiness. For, if I am not mistaken, true and perfect happiness is that which makes a person sufficient, powerful, reverend, renowned, and joyful. And so that you may know that I have understood it inwardly, [Note: [Col. 0756D] By the mind’s own attention.] I recognize without ambiguity that whatever can truly provide one of these qualities—since they are all the same—provides complete happiness. O pupil, happy in this opinion, if only you add the following, she said. What is that? I asked. Do you think that anything among these mortal and perishable things can bring about such a condition? I do not think so, I said; and you have shown this in such a way that nothing more need be desired. These things, then, seem to give mortals either images of the true good or certain imperfect goods; but they cannot confer the true and perfect good. I agree, I said. Since you have recognized which is the true happiness and which things falsely profess happiness, it remains for you to recognize from where you can seek this true happiness. I have been eagerly awaiting that for a long time, I said.

But since, [Note: [Col. 0757B] As Plato, our teacher, approves in the *Timaeus*.] *Timaeus* included among his poems this Pythagorean precept: “Having first prayed to the divine powers, then begin your work.” Hence Plato says in the book entitled *Timaeus*: “All who possess even the smallest portion of sound mind, whenever they undertake anything, whether small or great, are always accustomed to invoke God.” Nothing better can be said, done, or thought. As Plato, our teacher, approves in the *Timaeus*, divine aid ought to be implored even in the smallest matters, what do you think must now be done so that we may deserve to find the abode of that highest good? We must invoke the Father of all things, I said; if he is passed over, no beginning can rightly be established. Quite right, she said; and at once she sang in this manner.

220 METER [Note: [Col. 0757B] What is called heroic. A poem consisting of one kind of verse, each line being a hexameter containing a spondee in the sixth place, a dactyl in the fifth, and, in the remaining four places, either spondees or dactyls without distinction.] IX.

ARGUMENT.—Philosophy prays to the Creator of the world that, just as he, unmoved, first moves every body in general and then in particular, so he may deign to illuminate the human mind after dispersing its darkness and to form it according to a clear conception of the highest good.

[Note: [Col. 0757B] O Creator of heaven and earth, who rules the world by an immutable law, who commands time to flow from the world’s first age, and, constantly unmoved, makes all things move; whom external causes did not induce to form the structure of moving matter, but rather the form of the highest good implanted in you, free from envy—you bring forth all things from the highest model, holding in your mind a splendid world, yourself most splendid, and forming that world according to a similar image, commanding it to perfect its parts in perfection. You reconcile the elements in such ways that cold things agree with hot and dry things with liquid, lest purer fire depart upward or gravity carry the depressed earth downward. Joining the soul, intermediate between insensible minds and sensible bodies, and making it move all things, you distribute it among compatible limbs. The soul, divided like a liquid body into tiny parts, after completing a double circuit, moves again through its own body, about to return into itself; it encircles the lowest soul and turns the heavens in a uniform form. You bring forth lesser souls and lives in a similar manner; adapting the higher ones to light bodies, you scatter them through heaven and earth. By a gentle law you make these souls, turned toward you, return to you, like fire returning to the place from which it came. Grant, Father, grant that our mind may rise to your royal throne; grant that it may seek the origin of the good; grant that, once the light has been revealed, it may fix the clear gaze of the mind upon you. Drive away the cloud and heaviness of the earthly structure, and flash forth with your radiance. For you are serenity; you are tranquil rest for the good; and our conception of you is the end: that you are the beginning, the sustainer, the guide, the way, and the goal.]

[Note: [Col. 0757C] 1. O.] This is a prayer entirely worthy both of Philosophy and of the subject to be treated. It is indeed a prayer: namely, the thought of a mind rightly desiring and asking something from God. Hence the elements which St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* I–II, question 83, article 17, proves to belong to prayer—namely, the intellect’s ascent to God, thanksgiving, and petition—are observed here. For the interjection “O,” expressing both wonder and invocation, signifies the first; the enumeration of created things and the ways in which they are governed signifies the second; and the requested light signifies the third. This prayer is also entirely worthy of Philosophy. Since Philosophy is natural light, shining as darkness gradually recedes, nothing else is now requested than some increase of Philosophy. Finally, this same prayer is entirely worthy of the subject now being treated. Just as it is fitting for the mind to ask for a conception of its end, so it is fitting to ask the Creator of the world for this conception, since he is both the first cause and the first teacher of that same mind. “Do not think,” says St. Augustine in his commentary on John, “that any human being learns anything from another human being. We can admonish through the sound of our voice; but if there is not one within who teaches, our sound is empty.”]

2. Sower of earth and heaven.] Philosophy prays to the Creator of the world. A sower, or planter, is first one who, having prepared the seed or matter of the effect, is the author of that effect. In this sense, according to Tully, *De Natura Deorum* II, the world itself is the sower and planter of all things; then the word signifies any author. God, however, is the first author of heaven and earth. Virgil, *Aeneid* I, verse 258:

“He, the father of men and gods, smiling upon him.”

But because God is the creator of the world, the world is governed by laws established by God. Hence he is now said to “govern the world by everlasting reason.”

2 and 3. You command time to proceed from eternity.] Among philosophers, eternity, age, and time differ. They are called certain kinds of duration—or, as they say in French, *durée*—which is nothing other than the persistence of an existing thing. Eternity is the existence of a thing without beginning or end, namely, God. An age is the existence of a thing without end but not without beginning, namely, a created thing such as mind and body, which have no cause except an external one. For these, once created by God at some point, will persist eternally. Time is the duration of a thing that exists neither without a beginning nor without an end: namely, bodily forms, such as the form of an animal, the form of a plant, and the form of inanimate bodies. For just as these forms once began when their opposites were driven away, so at some point they will vanish when driven away by contrary forms. Now the world’s matter scarcely came into existence possessing an age, since it was endowed with certain forms destined to endure for a certain period according to laws established by the divine will. Therefore God commands time to proceed from an age.

3. “And, remaining steadfast, you grant all things motion.”] For God, unmoved, moves all things. First, everything that is moved must necessarily be moved by God. For since motion is nothing other than a body touching, with its extremity, the extremity of something larger, all things derive from him the fact that they are moved, from whom they derive the fact that they are bounded by extremities and touch extremities larger than their own. But they can possess this only from him by whom they are created and likewise preserved—and such is God alone. Further, by moving all things God himself remains unmoved, since God is the most perfect mind. Malachi 3: “I am the Lord, and I do not change”; James 1: “With whom there is no change, nor shadow of turning.”

[Col. 0758D] 4. “No external causes impelled.”] Philosophers commonly recognize four causes: namely, the final, efficient, material, and formal causes. The first two are called external, while the latter two are called internal. Bodies that they call physical—such as heaven and earth—have both internal and external causes; created minds do not have internal causes, but they do have external ones. God, however, has neither internal nor external causes. Hence he could not have been impelled to create the world either by a final or by an efficient cause; or

5. “The work of fluctuating matter.”] The world is rightly called fluctuating matter. “Matter,” because the world is an extended thing in every direction, which is what matter is. “Fluctuating,” because heaven, earth, and the other bodies of which the world consists are driven by perpetual motions, if not in every respect, at least with respect to many of their parts.

5 and 6. “But the implanted form of the highest good.”] Although God’s nature is simple and uniform—not only insofar as it is without parts, like every other mind, but also insofar as it is not affected even by successive thoughts—nevertheless the human mind, being incapable of comprehending God, thinks of God as though he were affected by certain thoughts and consequently by forms, namely, an idea and a will. Thus there is no cause of fluctuating matter other than God’s idea and will. These possess not only the character of a final and efficient cause, but also that of an exemplary cause.

Saint Thomas, *Summa theologiae*, I, q. 15, a. 1: “The world,” he says, “was not made by chance, but was made by God through an intellect acting; hence it is necessary that there be in the divine mind a form according to whose likeness the world was made, and in this consists the nature of an idea … God, according to his essence, is the likeness of all things; hence an idea in God is nothing other than God’s essence.”

Since external causes did not impel God to create the world, but rather the implanted form of the highest good—that is, God’s infinite wisdom and will—God is rightly called free from envy. For, with the effect taken in place of the cause, envy is nothing other than jealousy; and one is rightly said to be free from envy who has no one whom he could envy. But God, being the highest good, from whom and for whom the world was made, has no one whom he could envy, since nothing better than the highest good can be conceived.

Hence also God “leads all things from above according to an exemplar,” namely, the divine idea and will; and since this is God, nothing can be superior to it. Hence God carries the world in his mind and forms it according to a similar image.

Saint Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 46: “Each thing was created according to its own proper reasons. Where, then, should these reasons be thought to exist, if not in the very mind of the Creator? For he did not behold anything placed outside himself, according to which he might establish what he was establishing; to think this would be sacrilegious.”

Some think that *similique in imagine* should be read here because of the meter. But several witnesses omit the word *in*. With it removed, the meaning is more correctly that the idea is the means by which God forms the world, and the verse will scan as in Virgil, *Georgics* I, line 281:

“Three times they tried to place Ossa upon Pelion.”

] O you who govern the world by perpetual reason,

Sower of earth and heaven, who command time

221 to go forth from eternity, and, remaining steadfast, grant all things motion;

Whom no external causes impelled to fashion

[5] the work of fluctuating matter, but rather the implanted

[Col. 0758B] form of the highest good, free from envy: you lead all things from above

according to an exemplar, yourself most beautiful, the beautiful one,

[Col. 0759A] [Note: [Col. 0759C]

9. “And, commanding the perfected parts to complete the perfect whole.”] [Col. 0759D] For just as the world was first formed by divine wisdom and divine will, so, by that same divine wisdom and will, the perfected world appears to complete its perfected parts, with certain laws of bodies divinely established being preserved. Thus, because matter was set in motion in a circular course from the beginning with respect to certain of its parts, and because certain laws of motion were preserved, there could first arise the elements, then a certain general soul of the universe, and afterward certain particular corporeal souls. All these will be discussed below.

10. “You bind the elements with numbers.”] I. The subject here is the elements. The bodies that first arise from fluctuating matter are called elements, because the remaining bodies, which are consequently called mixtures, are composed from these as their underlying constituents. These elements are fitted to one another both in number and in qualities or properties, so that cold things correspond with hot, hard things with liquid, and light things are not separated from heavy by some empty chasm.

Here Philosophy appears to refer to the qualities that philosophers commonly recognize in the elements, and which they call, less correctly in Latin, “alterative” and “motive” qualities. The alterative qualities, they say, are heat and cold, dryness and moisture, signified by these words: “that cold things may correspond with flames, dry things with liquids.” The motive qualities are lightness and heaviness. Their effects would rightly be feared here, unless the elements were confined by God in certain places in a remarkable way, especially according to the commonly accepted Peripatetic view.

For if, as the Peripatetics maintain, these four elements—fire, air, water, and earth—are affected either by appetite, inclination, or natural quality in such a way that air and fire tend upward by their lightness, while water and earth tend downward by their heaviness, what prevents these four elements, however thoroughly mixed, from eventually being freed from one another and being confined, if not by some intervening empty chasm, at least each in its own place—unless God continually performs a kind of miracle? Thus water and oil, however thoroughly mixed, free themselves from one another, so that the water lies below while the oil rises above. Hence Philosophy rightly adds: “Lest purer fire fly away, or weights draw down submerged earth.”

13. “You, joining together the middle soul of triple nature, and so forth.”] II. The subject is the Spirit of the Universe, which, once the laws of nature themselves have been established, must arise immediately after the production of the elements of the world.

We have said more about this spirit in the *Physics*. It is rightly called here: (1) a soul; (2) the middle of triple nature; (3) the mover of all things; (4) connected by God; (5) resolved through harmonious members; (6) traversing in sections; first through the greater, then through the lesser vortices of the world; and finally returning to its own beginning. By this example it is shown that a human being, who proceeded from God as from a beginning, must be recalled to God as to an end by completing a certain circuit. Once all these matters have been explained, this part of the work undertaken will not be, as it seems to Vallinus, the most difficult.

First, that Spirit of the Universe is recognized not only by sacred authors—Ecclesiastes 1: “The spirit, traversing all things in a circuit, proceeds and returns to its circles”—but also by profane authors, such as Plato, Aristotle, and many others. I shall cite Virgil alone, who sings in *Aeneid* VI, lines 724ff.:

“First, heaven and earth, and the liquid plains,  
and the shining orb of the moon and the Titanian stars,  
the spirit within nourishes; and, poured through the limbs,  
the mind moves the whole mass and mingles with the great body.  
From it come the race of men and beasts, the lives of flying creatures,  
and the monsters that the sea bears beneath its marble surface.  
They possess a fiery vigor and a heavenly origin  
in their seeds, insofar as harmful bodies do not weigh them down  
and earthly limbs and dying members do not dull them.  
Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice; nor do they look upon  
the air, shut away in darkness and a blind prison.”

Next, the same spirit is rightly called a soul. For since *anima* is said to derive from *animus*, and *animus* from Greek ἄνεμος (*anemos*), “wind,” and since wind is in some sense the hidden cause of many motions, usage has established that the innate and hidden principle of perpetual and continuous motion should be called a soul. The spirit in question exists not only in plants and beasts, but also in the human being himself; without that spirit serving it, the mind cannot move the hands and feet at will.

Furthermore, this soul is called “the middle of triple nature”—not because it consists of three innate elements, as those philosophers whom their profession calls “Chemists,” or others who are called “Cartesians” after their leader, might suppose—for they hold that the world has three elements—but rather because this soul is one of three things that we can know by the natural light, and is indeed the middle one. It lies between the insensible mind and the sensible body: like a sensible body, it is extended in every direction and capable of shape, rest, and motion; like an insensible mind, it eludes sensation and is the source of many effects. For this reason Virgil above calls it both “spirit” and “mind.”

It could be called “the soul that is the middle of triple nature,” just as in Book II, prose 3, someone is called “the middle one of two consuls,” and by Cicero “the middle one of two brothers,” and by Horace “the middle one of war and peace.” This soul could also undergo the enumeration of triple nature as a part, just as Capua was included among the number of the three greatest cities, although it itself was a part of that number. Florus, cited above on page 47, says: “Capua was once counted among the three greatest cities, Rome and Carthage.”

Moreover, this soul is said to move all things—not because all bodies are moved by this soul, for many bodies are solid and therefore their parts remain at rest, but because no bodies are moved unless this soul moves them. Thus in John 1 all things are said to have been made through God—not because all things were made by God at the same time, but because whatever has been made was made by God alone.

Just as we see certain sensible bodies moved by other sensible bodies—for example, a stick by a hand—so we infer that these sensible things are moved by insensible things—for example, that a hand is moved by spirits—proceeding from what is known to what is less known, until we have discovered some first body that is moved by God himself, in accordance with the philosophers’ maxim: “Whatever body is moved must be moved by another.”

Add that the same soul is said to be connected by God. Since a body moves only through contact, this soul could not move unless it were connected with the body it moves. It is connected by God, by whom it was first made and is moved according to the laws of nature that God himself established.

Indeed, this soul is divinely resolved through harmonious members—resolved, I say, through members. For that soul is an exceedingly fluid body, whose parts, as they move, are resolved into different places and enter the various members of the body they inform. These members are harmonious, or mutually fitting, both with one another and with the soul itself, by which they are to be moved. Thus the smaller members are first moved by the soul, and afterward the larger members are moved both by the smaller ones and by the soul itself. In this way salt, worn away by the sea, and a ship, worn away by both, gradually crumble.

Indeed, the aforesaid soul travels in sections, joining the end to the beginning of its motion, so that it appears to roll its motion into a circle, *en faire comme un peloton de fil*—“to make it like a ball of thread.” For *glomus* in French is *un peloton de fil*, “a ball of thread.” This soul is indeed divided into sections, because, being liquid like water, air, and fire itself, it is a mass of many little bodies which, as they move, are separated from one another.

But the soul itself moves in a circuit through the body in which it is found. For, generally speaking, every body continues its motion in the direction in which there is less resistance. Thus the sap of a tree rises toward the highest point of the tree rather than escaping through the thinner bark. Since the same soul meets resistance from different bodies on every side, it is easier for it to circulate within its own body than to leave that body.

Ecclesiastes 1: “The Holy Spirit,” it says, “traversing all things, proceeds in a circuit, and returns to its circles.” Hence, as it is now said, this soul moves so as to return into itself.

This soul, however, considered with respect to the machine that it informs, is of two kinds: one greater soul, which circulates through the greater vortex of the world, and another lesser soul, which, spread through the lesser vortex of that same world, circulates within it. Among the lesser souls there is one around which heaven revolves like a wheel around an axle. Philosophy now calls it the “deep mind.” It is called a mind, as Virgil himself called it a mind, because, like a mind, it is the insensible principle of motion; and it is called deep because it occupies the position of the center. In a sphere, however, no part is deeper than the center.

Perhaps the machine that is now signified as being informed by that deep mind is the earth. Although it cannot be proved by any demonstration that the earth is the center of the world, the earth can nevertheless be called the center of the vortex in which we live. Thus the greater soul causes heaven to revolve around the earth in a similar image. For at least the air, which is often called “heaven” both by sacred and profane authors, circles the earth, and it is sufficiently probable that the air is set in motion by no other body than this spirit. It also appears to revolve in a constant pattern. Although clouds, rains, and winds are driven about in this air, or heaven, the circuit of this heaven around the earth is nevertheless constant and uniform, as is its blue color, which is nothing other than light modified by the vapors and exhalations it encounters. But if that deep soul is not the earth, it will be one of the lesser souls about which Philosophy herself is now going to speak.]”

Carrying the world in its mind and forming it according to a similar image,

222 and commanding the perfected parts to complete the perfect whole.

[10] You bind the elements with numbers, so that cold things correspond with flames,

dry things with liquids; lest purer fire

[Col. 0760A] fly away, or weights draw down submerged earth.

223 You, joining together the middle soul of triple nature that moves all things,

resolve it through harmonious members;

[15] and when, divided, it has rolled its motion into two circles,

it moves so as to return into itself, and the deep mind

[Col. 0761A] [Note: [Col. 0762C]

18. “With equal causes you advance souls and lesser lives.”] III. Philosophy treats separately of corporeal souls, which she calls: (1) lesser souls and lives; (2) advanced by God through equal causes; (3) fitted to light chariots; (4) scattered through heaven and earth; and (5) returning, turned toward heaven.

The subject here is only corporeal souls, since they resemble the spirit just discussed or are a portion of it. For just as the Spirit of the Universe is introduced as an example, so these souls are introduced so that, having come to know them, the human mind may return through its thoughts to God, from whom it proceeded.

Next, these are called “lesser souls and lives” because, enclosed in lesser machines, they complete lesser circuits, as in plants, beasts, and the human being himself. There is, however, this distinction: in the human being, besides this corporeal spirit, there is a mind, or thinking thing, which that spirit serves. Consequently, because that corporeal spirit serves the principal form, it loses in the human being the name and dignity of soul, and therefore it is said that in the human being there is only one soul, and that soul is endowed with reason.

Virgil, *Georgics* IV, lines 220ff.:

“They have said that the bees possess a portion of the divine mind  
and draughts of ether, for God passes through  
all lands, the tracts of the sea, and the deep heaven.  
From this, sheep, herds, men, and every kind of beast  
draw for themselves their slender lives as they are born.”

[Col. 0763B] Next, these lesser souls come into being through the same causes as the aforesaid Spirit of the Universe: namely, from the same fluctuating matter and from God himself, with the same laws of nature being preserved.

Furthermore, these same souls are said to be fitted to light chariots—that is, to the bodies in which they are enclosed, and which they themselves appear to move and govern, as a driver is accustomed to move and govern a chariot. For the soul of a plant, for example, differs from the soul of a beast, and the soul of a beast again differs according to the different kinds of beasts. Thus the souls of bees, about which Virgil was just speaking, may be said to be fitted to light chariots.

[Col. 0763C] Moreover, the aforesaid souls are scattered through heaven and earth. For, besides the possibility that a similar spirit may also occur in the starry heaven and carry out the aforesaid circuits through the body in which it is enclosed, these lesser souls exist in beasts, some of which live on the earth and others in the aerial heaven.

Finally, these souls return, turned toward heaven. For, being subject to the general law of moving bodies that is now called beneficent—namely, that they tend in the direction in which there is less resistance—they strive toward heaven, where there is likewise less resistance. They are like fire returning upward. There is, indeed, the greatest similarity between these souls and fire; hence Virgil calls the aforesaid spirit “fiery vigor.”

Since heaven is regarded as the highest dwelling place of God—Matthew 5: “You shall not swear by heaven, because it is the throne of God”—God is therefore now said to cause these souls, turned toward him, to return to him. For this reason they are now introduced as an example.]

It travels in a circuit and turns heaven according to a similar image.

225 You advance souls with equal causes, and lesser lives,

[Col. 0762A] fitting them, exalted, to light chariots,

[20] and scatter them through heaven and earth; by a beneficent law

you make them, turned toward you, return in fire.

[Col. 0763A] [Note: [Col. 0763C]

22. “Grant, Father.”] God is called this not only by Christians but also by pagans, as we have already noted. This is Philosophy’s petition, for whose sake she prefaced the foregoing material. She asks God to free the mind from the darknesses arising from the body, for Wisdom 9 says: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things”; and thereafter to shape it by knowledge of the highest good and by love of that good.

26. “For you make it serene.”] “Making minds serene”: just as a clear sky is imagined to drive away clouds, so God drives away the darknesses of the mind.

27. “You are tranquil rest for the devout.”] Giving tranquil thoughts to those who, with God’s help, fulfill their duty toward God.

27. “The end is to behold you.”] The human mind was created by God for this end: that it should think, and consequently know, God. John 17: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God.”

28. “Beginning.”] It is no less necessary for our mind to know its beginning than to know itself, so that, not forgetful of the first benefit received from its creator, it may devote itself and all that belongs to it to that same creator.

God is the beginning of our mind in such a way that, although the mind might doubt whether God were the beginning of bodies, nevertheless, conscious of its own frailty, it is always convinced that it was created by no one other than God himself. Hence God says in Revelation 1: “I am alpha and omega, the beginning and the end”—α and ω, “the beginning and the end.”

“Driver.”] God preserves our mind. Since preservation is nothing other than continued production, God, by preserving our mind, appears to carry or convey it. Hebrews 1 says that God is “carrying all things by the word of his power.”

“Guide.”] For God not only creates and preserves the human mind, but also, from its origin, furnishes it with certain thoughts, namely, understanding and inclination. If the mind follows these while disregarding the body’s impulse, it will never go astray.

“Path.”] The mind’s path is one thing considered in the category of form, and another considered in the category of efficient cause. In the first sense, it is the thought by which the mind, withdrawing from perishable things, approaches God. Thus Proverbs 4 says: “The path of the just is like shining light, and it grows until the perfect day.” In the second sense, it is God himself, the author of right thought. Thus Christ says in John 14: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”

“Limit.”] A limit is that beyond which a thing, being bounded, does not extend. Thus, among blind nations, a rough and shapeless stone beyond which a field bounded by that stone did not extend was called the god Terminus.
