God, however, is that toward which the human mind ought to extend itself through thought, but beyond which that same mind cannot proceed in thought. John 6: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.”

Just as all these things are rightly said of God, as has already been explained, so they could also appropriately be said of the knowledge of God implanted in our mind, which is indicated by the words “to behold you.”

First, that implanted knowledge of God is rightly called the end, because we were made by God for this end: that we should think of God himself. Second, the same knowledge is rightly called the beginning, because just as every good work of ours arises from our good thought, so every good thought of ours arises from the knowledge of God itself, as from a beginning. As the common saying has it: “No desire arises for what is unknown.”

Third, this same knowledge of God is rightly called driver, guide, and path, because it appears to carry, move, and lead our thoughts and all our words and deeds toward God. Finally, this knowledge of God in us is rightly called the limit, since, in comparison with the perfect knowledge of God that we hope to enjoy after death, we shall rest as though at the limit of our life. John 17: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.”]

226 Grant, Father, that the mind may climb to the august seat;

grant that it may survey the fountain of the good; grant that, once the light is found,

it may fix the mind’s clear gaze upon you.

[25] Scatter the clouds and burdens of the earthly mass,

and flash forth in your splendor: for you are serenity,

you are tranquil rest for the devout; to behold you is the end,

227 the beginning, the driver, the guide, the path, and the limit all at once.

228 PROSE X.

ARGUMENT.—Philosophy demonstrates that there is a highest good, and that this quality belongs to God alone, being indistinct from himself, in such a way that he neither received it from anyone nor shares it with anyone. From this she concludes that the one who enjoys the highest good is, on the one hand, God by participation and, on the other, a participant in power, reverence, splendor, and pleasure.

[Note: [Col. 0764A] Once both the imperfect and the perfect good have been recognized, that thing which is supremely good must be demonstrated.]

Since, then, you have seen what the form of imperfect good is, and what also is the form of perfect good, I now think it must be demonstrated where this perfection of happiness is established. In this inquiry, I believe the first question is whether such a good as you defined shortly before can exist in the realm of things, lest an empty image of thought deceive us concerning the truth of the subject matter.

[Note: [Col. 0764B] Empty.]

[Note: [Col. 0764D] That it does exist cannot be denied.]

### I

Philosophy demonstrates that there is some supreme good [Col. 0765C]: since it is established from what has been said that the supreme good is the same as the perfect good, if something perfect exists, it is necessary that some supreme good exist. Now that something perfect exists is proved by this demonstration.

An imperfect thing cannot exist in any genus unless something perfect exists in that same genus. For that imperfect thing is neither called, nor thought of, nor is anything except by comparison with this perfect thing, whose diminution it is said and thought to be, and from which it took its beginning. But in the genus of good there exists something imperfect [Col. 0765D]—namely, that which is fragile and perishable, which has been discussed up to this point.

But that this [perfect good] exists and is, as it were, a certain source of all goods cannot be denied. For everything that is called imperfect is said to be imperfect through a diminution of the perfect. Hence, if anything imperfect appears to exist in any genus, it is necessary that something perfect also exist in that genus [Col. 0765A]. Indeed, once perfection has been removed, it cannot even be imagined from what that which is called imperfect could have arisen. Nature did not take its beginning from diminished and incomplete things [Note: [Col. 0765C] Imperfect], but, proceeding from things whole and complete, falls away into these extreme and [Note: [Col. 0765C] Weak] exhausted conditions.

And if, as we showed shortly before, there is a certain imperfect happiness belonging to fragile good, there can be no doubt that some solid and perfect happiness exists [Note: [Col. 0765C] Happiness].

“It has been concluded,” I said, “most firmly and most truly.” [Note: [Col. 0765C] I, Boethius.]

### 229

[Note: [Col. 0765D] Where it dwells.]

### II

Philosophy demonstrates that this quality of the supreme good belongs to God: since the first principle of all things must possess the nature or quality of the supreme good; otherwise there would be something better, more perfect, prior, and older than it, and thus it would not be the first principle. But God is the first principle of all things, as the common conception of human minds proves. Since this conception can be neither from nothing nor of nothing, if that conception is present in all human minds—as each person, being conscious of it, experiences that it truly is—then it is necessary that God exist, the first principle of all things, from whom and by whom that common conception of human minds exists.

“Consider,” she said, “where it dwells.” [Note: [Col. 0765C] Philosophy says in what thing that happiness is present.]

The common conception of human minds proves that God, the first principle of all things, is good. [Note: [Col. 0765C] The notion of God implanted in all human minds.] For since nothing better than God can be conceived, who would doubt that that than which nothing is better is good?

Reason demonstrates God to be good in such a way [Col. 0765B] that it also proves perfect good to be in him. For if he were not such, he could not be the first principle of all things: there would be something more excellent than he, possessing perfect good, which would appear to be prior and older than he. For it has become clear that all perfect things are prior to things that are less complete [Note: [Col. 0765C] Imperfect]. Therefore, to prevent reason from proceeding to infinity, it must be acknowledged that the supreme God is completely filled with supreme and perfect good.

But we have established that perfect good constitutes true blessedness. Therefore, true blessedness must be established in the supreme God.

“I accept this,” I said [Note: [Col. 0766C] I, Boethius], “and there is no way in which it can be contradicted.”

“But I ask you,” she said [Note: [Col. 0766C] Philosophy], “to observe how sacredly [Col. 0766A] and inviolably you establish that the supreme God is most full of the supreme good.” [Note: [Col. 0766C] That God possesses the nature of the supreme good.]

“How?” I said. [Note: [Col. 0765D] Lest you think otherwise of this Father of all things.]

### III

Philosophy demonstrates that this nature or quality of the supreme good is indistinguishable from God himself: since philosophy may judge only on the basis of concepts that it joins or separates from one another in judging, it cannot judge the nature of the supreme good to be distinct from God unless it can clearly and distinctly conceive both the supreme good and God separately, each by its own concept, so that it can truly conceive that the supreme good is not God and that God is not the supreme good.

For this reason philosophy judges that our mind is distinct from our body: from this it would follow that the nature of the supreme good which God possessed had been received from outside, and thus that there was some cause of God which had joined God and the nature of the supreme good to each other—just as the human mind, by which the body is given form, is received from outside and recognizes some cause of itself that has joined the mind and body together.

But philosophy cannot clearly and distinctly conceive the supreme good and God separately, each by its own concept, since the supreme good is conceived in the same way as God: namely, as that than which nothing more excellent, better, or prior can be established [Col. 0766D].

“Do not presume,” she said [Note: [Col. 0766C] Philosophy], “that this Father of all things either received from outside the supreme good with which he is said to be filled, or possesses it naturally in such a way that you imagine the substance of the possessing God and the possessed blessedness to be different. For if you suppose that it was received from outside, you might consider the giver to be more excellent than the recipient.

### 230

But we rightly acknowledge him to be the most excellent of all things. If, however, it is naturally present in him but different in essence, then, since we are speaking of God as the ruler of all things, let whoever can imagine it say who joined these two different things together.

Finally, whatever is different from any thing is not that from which it is understood to be different [Col. 0766B]. Therefore, that which by its nature is different from the supreme good is not the supreme good. But it is impious to think this of God, than whom nothing more excellent can be established.

For the nature of no thing can be better than its own principle. Therefore, I would conclude with the truest reasoning that whatever is the principle of all things is also, in the substance of itself, supreme good [Note: [Col. 0766C] In virtue of its own essence.]

“Most correctly,” I said.

“But it has been granted,” she said, “that the supreme good is blessedness.”

“So it is,” I said.

“Then,” she said, “it is necessary to confess that God is blessedness itself.”

“I cannot,” I said, “oppose the propositions previously established, and I see that this conclusion follows from them.” [Note: [Col. 0766C] To contradict.]

[Note: [Col. 0766D] See whether this also follows from it.]

### IV

Philosophy demonstrates that the aforementioned nature or quality of the supreme good cannot be shared with anything else by God—or, which is the same thing, that there cannot be two supreme goods. For from what has already been said, whatever possesses the nature of the supreme good, or is the supreme good, must be perfect. But it is impossible for there to be two things that are absolutely perfect, since absolutely perfect can neither be said, nor thought, nor exist except of that which lacks nothing; and if there were two supreme goods, each would lack the other [Col. 0767C].

“See whether this too,” she said, “may confirm more firmly the same conclusion: that two supreme goods which are distinct from each other cannot exist. For it is clear that goods which differ are not one another; therefore neither can be perfect, since each lacks the other. But what is not perfect plainly is not supreme. Therefore, in no way can things that are supreme goods be different.

“We have established, however, that both blessedness and God are the supreme good. Therefore, blessedness itself must be supreme, and that supreme blessedness must be divinity.”

“Nothing,” I said, “more true in fact, more firmly established by reasoning, or more worthy of God could be concluded.”

### 231

“Upon this,” she said, “then, just as geometers customarily infer something after propositions have been demonstrated…” [Note: [Col. 0767C] Certain *porisms* (πορίσματα).]

### V

Philosophy, following the manner of geometry, draws certain inferences from what has been demonstrated. The Greeks call them *porisms* (πορίσματα), and in Latin they are called *consectaria*, or also *corollaries*—certain things added beyond what was required; in Norman, “le repiquet” [Note: [Col. 0767C] Consequences.]—and so I too shall give you something like a corollary.

[Col. 0767B] [Note: [Col. 0767C] For since, etc.]

The first consequence is that human beings become gods through the attainment of blessedness. This is inferred as follows.

There is a God by nature; there is a God by participation. [Col. 0767D] God by nature is a supremely perfect being. Since, according to what has been said, there cannot be more than one supremely perfect being, God by nature is so uniquely one that he cannot be multiple.

A mind endowed with a thought very similar to the divine is called a god by participation. Thus in Psalm 81: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.” Likewise 2 Peter 1: “So that through these you may become partakers of the divine nature.” In this way the blessed become gods, because they are endowed with a thought very similar to the divine; by that thought they become gods by participation, just as a person becomes just by acquiring justice, and wise by acquiring wisdom.

“Since human beings become blessed through the attainment of blessedness, and blessedness is divinity itself, it is evident that they become blessed through the attainment of divinity. Just as people become just through acquiring justice and wise through acquiring wisdom, so, by the same reasoning, those who acquire divinity become gods.

“Everyone who is blessed, therefore, is a god; but by nature there is only one, whereas by participation nothing prevents there from being very many.”

“This,” I said, “is beautiful and precious, whether you prefer to call it a *porism* (πόρισμα) or a corollary.” [Note: [Col. 0767C] Consequence.]

[Note: [Col. 0767D] But this also, etc.]

The second consequence is that the human being who is blessed through the attainment of God, and therefore is a god by participation, is filled with riches, power, glory, and pleasure. This is inferred as follows.

If riches, power, and things of that kind were certain parts of the supreme good, they could be separated from the supreme good in such a way that the supreme good could exist without them. For just as parts or members can each be conceived separately by its own idea, so they can be separated from one another and preserved separately, as is evident in the case of mind and body, which are parts of a human being.

Moreover, if the things mentioned above belonged to the category of attributes without which the thing to which they belong can exist—as a body can exist without rest—the supreme good could also exist without the things mentioned above. It would therefore not follow that one who enjoyed the supreme good thereby enjoyed those things.

But the things mentioned are neither parts of the supreme good nor attributes without which the supreme good can exist, since, according to what has been said, the supreme good has neither parts nor any attribute that it could lack; otherwise it would not be absolutely perfect. Therefore, whoever enjoys the supreme good must also enjoy pleasure, glory, and everything of that kind.

Indeed, we seek neither riches nor anything similar except because they seem to possess the nature of the supreme good, or of blessedness.

“But nothing,” she said, “is more beautiful than this conclusion, which reason shows must be attached to what has been said.”

“What is it?” I said.

“Although blessedness seems to contain many things, do all these things join together as one body of blessedness through a certain diversity of parts, or is there something among them that completes the substance of blessedness, while the other things are referred to it?” [Note: [Col. 0768C] Whether all these things are one and the same, or whether one thing has several modes of being.]

“I should like you,” I said, “to make this clear by recalling the things themselves.”

“Do we not judge blessedness to be a good?”

“And a supreme good,” I said.

“You may add this to all the others. For the same sufficiency is supreme, and the same supreme power, honor, glory, and pleasure are also judged to be blessedness.

“What follows, then? Are all these things—goodness, sufficiency, power, and the rest—parts of blessedness, as it were, or are they all referred to goodness as to their summit?”

“I understand what you are proposing for investigation,” I said, “but I desire to hear what conclusion you reach.”

“Understand the distinction in this way. If all these things were parts of blessedness, they would also be distinct from one another. For it is the nature of parts to compose one body out of different elements. But all these things have been shown to be the same.”

### 232

“Therefore they are not parts, at all. Otherwise blessedness would appear to be composed of one part, which cannot happen.”

“That is not doubtful,” I said, “but I await what remains.”

“It is evident that the other things are referred to goodness. Sufficiency is sought for this reason: because it is judged to be good; power for this reason: because it too is believed to be good. The same may be conjectured concerning honor, glory, and pleasure.

“Goodness, therefore, is the sum and cause of everything desired. For that which retains no good in itself, either in reality or by resemblance, cannot be desired in any way. Conversely, whatever is desired by a human being is either actually good or at least appears to be good. Hence, philosophers say that neither good, insofar as it is good, is hated, nor evil, insofar as it is evil, loved.” [Note: [Col. 0768D] Things that are not good by nature.]

“Things that are not good by nature are nevertheless desired if they appear to be good, as though they were genuine goods. It follows that goodness is rightly considered the summit, pivot, and cause of everything desired.”

[Note: [Col. 0768D] Whatever is desired for the sake of something, etc.]

This is the axiom that philosophers usually express as follows: “That because of which each thing is such is itself more such.” Although this may perhaps fail in other kinds of causes, it is established in the category of the end, in which it is being used here.

“Whatever is the cause for which something is desired appears to be desired above all. Thus, if someone wishes to ride for the sake of health, he desires not so much the motion of riding as the result, namely health.

“Since everything is sought for the sake of good, it is not those things rather than good itself that everyone desires [Col. 0769A]. We have granted that blessedness is that for the sake of which the other things are desired; therefore blessedness alone is sought in this way as well.

“From this it clearly appears that good and blessedness have one and the same substance.” [Note: [Col. 0769B] Clearly.]

“I see no reason why anyone could disagree.”

“But we have shown that God and true blessedness are one and the same.”

“So it is,” I said.

“Then we may safely conclude that the substance of God too is situated in good itself, and nowhere else.” [Note: [Col. 0769B] Certainly.]

### 233

### METRUM X

[Note: [Col. 0769B] A poem consisting of two alternating kinds of verse. The first, the Phalaecian, has a spondee, a dactyl, and three trochees; the second, the Sapphic, has a trochee, a spondee, a dactyl, and two trochees—except that, in place of the Sapphic, whose alternation belonged in the second verse, the Phalaecian is repeated. It would have been very easy to correct this, but perhaps the author neglected it because both verses are hendecasyllabic.]

### ARGUMENT

Philosophy invites human beings blinded by disturbances to the previously described conception of the supreme good, since this conception is not only free from darkness but surpasses the light of the sun itself and is the source of peaceful rest.

[Note: [Col. 0769B]]

Come here, all of you deceived, whom deceitful desire,

taking possession of earthly minds, binds with cruel chains.

Here shall be rest from your labors; here a harbor remaining

in tranquil peace; this one refuge lies open to the wretched.

Neither the Tagus with its golden sands, nor the Hermus with its

shining bank, nor the Indus, near the region of heat,

with its white and green gems, illuminates minds;

rather, they wrap them more deeply in their own darkness.

The earth nourished in its lowest caves these bodies

that delight and stir the spirits. But the light

by which heaven is governed and lives guards the mind

against dark falls; therefore whoever is able to perceive this light

will deny that the rays of the sun are equally pure.

[Note: [Col. 0769B]]

“Here”: toward the previously mentioned conception of the supreme good.

[Col. 0769C] **1. “Come all together, captives.”** “Together” may be understood as joined either with the verb “come,” so that the meaning is “assemble,” or with the participle “captives,” so that the meaning is “deceived in the same way.” For a captive is generally one who is in another’s power, whence *captivus*; more specifically, it is one who, obeying his body, is led along by his disturbances. Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, line 194:

> Forgetful of kingdoms and captivated by shameful desire.

Hence desire, which is rightly called deceitful, is said to bind earthly minds with wicked chains. Desire, I say, which is nothing other than the mind’s thought obeying bodily movements, is rightly called deceitful because, drawing the mind away from God, who is the first truth and the first goodness, it leads it into error and vice.

The same desire binds minds with wicked chains because it prevents the mind from attaining the supreme good, which it naturally knows and desires. The minds inhabited—or, as our author more often says, dulled—by desire are earthly because they obey an earthly body. 1 Corinthians 15: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so also are the heavenly.”

**4. “Here shall be for you, etc.”** The evident conception of the supreme good, as the principle both of truth and of virtue, will free the mind from the storms of errors and vices; hence it will be rest, harbor, and asylum.

**7. “The Tagus with golden sands.”** The Tagus is a river of Lusitania which, rising among the Celtiberians, divides Lusitania and, beyond Ulyssipona—Lisbon—bursts into the Ocean. It is said to roll golden sands, just like the Pactolus and the Hermus; hence this verse:

> The Tagus, the Pactolus, and the Hermus are gold-bearing rivers.

Juvenal:

> What the Tagus and the Pactolus roll with their ruddy sand.

**8. “Or the Hermus.”** The Hermus is a river of Asia Minor [Col. 0770B], rising near Dorylaum, a city of Phrygia. Joined to the Pactolus, it waters the plains of Smyrna and finally flows into the Phocaean Gulf. It too is said to carry golden sands; hence Virgil, *Georgics* II, line 137:

> Nor the beautiful Ganges, nor the Hermus turbid with gold.

**9. “Or the Indus.”** The Indus is a river of the East which, marking India off on the west, gave it its name. This river—or at least the land to which it gave its name—abounds in gems [Col. 0770C]. Accordingly, Claudian, wishing to signify a garment woven with gems, sings in poem 8, line 584:

> The Indus roughens  
> the coverings with stone.

Some gems are white, others green, others blue, and others of another color, according to the varying modification of light. Hence the Indus is here said to mingle green stones with white ones. Lucretius, Book II:

> Sometimes, through a certain sensation, it comes about that he seems  
> to mingle green emeralds among blue ones.

**11. “They illuminate the vision.”** That is, the vision of the mind.

**11. “And make them blinder.”** He seems to allude to eyes that are overwhelmed by the excessive brilliance of gold, gems, or another shining or reflecting body, and that are sometimes blinded by an induced darkness. For although gold and gems appear to shine brightly before the eyes because of their great brilliance, they nevertheless do not illuminate the mind’s vision. Rather, by introducing the darkness of disturbances, they blind the mind so completely that they seem to bury it in the dark bowels of the earth from which these bodies were extracted, insofar as the mind, captivated by love of them, thinks of nothing but earth.

**15. “Splendor.”** The supreme good, or God, who in Hebrews 1 is called “the splendor of glory,” and in Wisdom 7 “the brightness of eternal light.”

**15. “By which heaven is governed and lives.”** For God not only creates bodies but also all minds, preserves them, and governs them. More specifically, heaven lives and is governed by motion, of which God is so truly the author that this motion neither begins nor continues except according to laws established by God himself.

**16. “Avoids the dark ruin of the soul.”** Since the mind is immortal, it has no ruin with respect to its substance, but only with respect to its mode—namely, thought. The mind’s thought is a ruin when the mind, departing from the proper standard of judging and choosing, falls into error and vice. There is no vice of the mind without error, and no error without obscurity. Therefore the mind’s ruin is so dark that God, the eternal Light, is said to stand far from it and consequently to avoid it. Thus God causes those whom he illuminates also to avoid such ruin [Col. 0771C].

Here come all together, captives,

[Col. 0770A] whom deceitful desire binds

with wicked chains, inhabiting earthly minds.

### 234

Here shall be for you rest from your labors;

here a harbor remaining in peaceful quiet;

this one refuge lies open to the wretched.

Whatever the Tagus gives with golden sands,

or the Hermus with its shining bank,

or the Indus, near the hot region,

mingling green stones with white ones,

does not illuminate the mind’s vision;

rather, it makes minds blinder

and buries them in their own darkness.

Whatever delights and stirs the minds,

the earth has nourished in its lowest caves.

[15] **235** The splendor by which heaven is governed and lives

avoids the dark ruins of the soul.

[Col. 0771A] [Note: [Col. 0771C]]

**17. “Whoever is able to perceive this light.”** God, who is the supreme good.

**18. “Will deny the bright rays of Phoebus.”** Brightness is the color most like light. Hence both bodies and minds are said to be endowed with greater brightness in proportion as they are suffused with greater light. Thus a star, writing, and thought itself are described by Horace, Cicero, and Ovid as sometimes more and sometimes less bright. However luminous the solar rays may appear, they nevertheless do not shine as much as God, who, according to 1 Timothy 6, “dwells in inaccessible light.”

Whoever is able to perceive this light

will deny the bright rays of Phoebus.

### 236

### PROSA XI

### ARGUMENT

After Philosophy has proposed that there is one good which all things desire, each in its own way, she concludes that the good is the end of all things.

“I agree,” I said. “For all things stand fast, bound together by the firmest arguments.”

Then she said: “How much will you value it if you recognize what the good itself is?” [Note: [Col. 0771C] The simple good under discussion here is supreme; it is enough to have said this once for the whole chapter.]

“Infinitely,” I said, “since I shall then also come to recognize God, who is good.”

“But I shall make this clear by the truest reasoning,” she said [Col. 0772B], “provided that what was concluded shortly before remains in force.” [Note: [Col. 0772B] These things will stand.]

“They will remain,” I said.

“Did we not show,” she said [Note: [Col. 0771C] We showed this in Prose 9 of this book], “that the things desired by many are not therefore true and perfect goods, because they would be distinct from one another and thus would not be good?” [Note: [Col. 0771C] They are not goods because they would differ from one another.]

### I

Philosophy proposes that good—by which term she understands the supreme good—is one, in approximately the following way. Since no intermediate can be conceived between one and many, it is necessary that the supreme good be either one or multiple. But the supreme good cannot be multiple. For this reason it was proved that riches, power, and things of that kind do not possess the nature of the supreme good: they are many [Col. 0771D].

“And since things that differ from one another, with each lacking the other, cannot provide a full and absolute good, true good comes into being when they are gathered into one form and efficacy, so that what is sufficiency is also power, honor, glory, and pleasure. Unless all things are one and the same, they possess nothing by which they might be numbered among desirable things.” [Col. 0772A]

“It has been demonstrated,” I said, “and there can be no doubt about it.”

“What, then, when they differ, are not good, but when they begin to be one, become good—does it not happen that they become good through attaining unity?”

“So it seems,” I said.

“But do you grant that everything which is good is good through participation in the good, or do you deny it?”

“I grant it.” [Note: [Col. 0772B] That which is good is affected by goodness.]

“Then you must likewise grant that one and good are the same.”

### 237

[Note: [Col. 0771D] Things have the same substance when their natural effect is not different.]

We do not judge of a cause except through its effect. Therefore, when we do not see different effects, we have no argument by which to judge that these are different things.

“For their substance is the same when their natural effect is not different.”

“I cannot deny it,” I said.

[Note: [Col. 0771D] Do you know, then, everything that exists?]

### II

Philosophy proposes that all things desire the supreme good, each in its own way, as follows. Since one and good are the same in substance, whatever desires one must necessarily desire good also.

But all things desire one, since they desire to exist, as can be seen in animals, plants, and inanimate bodies. These propositions are stated so clearly that they require no explanation from us.

I point out only that two kinds of desire must here be distinguished: one voluntary, the other natural. Voluntary desire is the will itself of the knowing mind. We are conscious of it because the very author of our mind and will teaches us, so that no human being could receive from anyone a greater understanding of it. Such is the desire by which we wish to be blessed; such also is the desire by which, as Philosophy now says, the human mind sometimes embraces death when compelled by causes that nature fears, or occasionally restrains the work of generation.

But Philosophy says that she is not now treating of these voluntary movements of the knowing soul.

Natural desire, on the other hand, is an instinct divinely impressed upon even an unconscious thing for its own preservation. First, this desire is called instinct, for it is an impulse; and every impulse is rightly called instinct. The term *instinctus* is derived from *instigare*, “to incite,” and that which incites also presses and urges.

Next, this desire belongs even to an unconscious thing, since it operates in inanimate bodies, in which there can be no cognition. Furthermore, this desire is divinely impressed, just as voluntary desire is, for God moves all things.

Finally, this desire is directed toward the preservation of the thing. For divine providence, as it is said here, gave things created by it this greatest reason for remaining: that, as far as they can, they naturally desire to remain.

Through this desire, as through a principle of nature, animals love to remain. By the same desire they always seek the work of generation, through which alone the continuity of mortal things endures. Through this desire we digest food that we have taken without thought. By it we breathe in sleep without knowing it. Finally, through this desire all things that exist naturally seek stability and continued existence and avoid destruction.

Thus in a sheep, when it sees a wolf, the spirits ordinarily flowing from the brain through the nerves turn toward those parts of the sheep that are designed for flight. In an ant, however, when it sees grain, those same spirits are driven toward the parts of the ant arranged for grasping it.

“Do you know, then,” she said, “that everything that exists remains and subsists as long as it is one, but perishes and is dissolved as soon as it ceases to be one?”

“How so?”

“In animals,” she said, “when soul and body come together and remain united, the result is called an animal. But when this unity is dissolved by the separation of the two, it is clear that the animal perishes and is no longer an animal.

“The body itself, too, when it remains in one form through the conjunction of its members, is seen to be a human form. But when the body’s parts, distributed and separated, destroy its unity, it ceases to be what it was.

“Proceeding through the other cases in the same way, it will doubtless become clear that each thing subsists while it is one, but perishes when it ceases to be one.”

“After considering many things,” I said, “I find that nothing else is the case.”

“Is there anything, then,” she said, “that, insofar as it acts naturally, would abandon its desire to subsist and desire to come to destruction and corruption?” [Note: [Col. 0773C] With its desire for self-preservation driven away.]

“If I consider animals,” I said, “which possess some nature of willing and refusing, I find nothing that, without any external force or violence compelling it [Note: [Col. 0773C] Without any force or violence from external causes], would cast aside its intention of remaining and hasten willingly toward destruction. For every animal labors to protect its life, while it avoids death and destruction.”

### 238

“But what I should say about herbs and trees, and about wholly inanimate things, I am entirely unsure.”

“There is no reason for you to doubt this,” she said, “when you observe herbs and trees. First, they grow in places suited to them, where, as far as their nature permits, they cannot quickly wither and perish.

“Some grow in fields, others in mountains; some are borne by marshes, others cling to rocks; some have fertile soil, while for others barren sands are fruitful. If someone tries to transplant them elsewhere, they wither. Nature gives each what is suitable, and strives to ensure that they do not perish while they are able to remain.

“What shall I say of the fact that all of them, as though their mouths were sunk into the earth, draw nourishment through their roots and spread strength and bark through their pith? What shall I say of the fact that whatever is softest, such as the pith, is always hidden in the innermost place, while outside it is covered with a certain firmness of wood? The outermost bark is placed against the harshness of the weather as a defender, as though it were capable of resisting more strongly [Note: [Col. 0773C] Resisting more strongly.]

“Moreover, how great is nature’s diligence in ensuring that all things reproduce by multiplying their seed! Who does not know that all these structures are not only devices for remaining for a time but also, generically speaking, devices for remaining as though forever?

“Do not even those things that are believed to be inanimate desire what belongs to them, each in the same manner? Why does lightness carry flames upward, while weight presses earth downward, unless because these places and motions suit each of them? Moreover, whatever is in accord with each thing preserves it, just as things hostile to it destroy it.

“Things that are hard, such as stones, cling most tenaciously to their parts and resist so that they are not easily dissolved. Things that are fluid [239; Col. 0774A], such as air and water, readily yield to things that divide them, but quickly flow back into the things from which they have been cut off. Fire, however, avoids every division.

“Nor are we now treating of the voluntary movements of the knowing soul, but of natural purpose. This is like the fact that we digest food we have taken without thought and breathe in sleep without knowing it [Note: [Col. 0773C] We breathe].

“For even in animals the love of remaining comes not from the soul’s acts of will, but from principles of nature. The will often embraces death when compelled by causes that nature fears; conversely, the work of generation, through which alone the continuity of mortal things endures and which nature always desires, is sometimes restrained by the will.

“So greatly does this love of itself [Note: [Col. 0774C] Love toward itself] proceed not from animal movement [Col. 0774B], but from natural purpose. Providence gave things created by it this greatest reason for remaining: that, as far as they can, they naturally desire to remain. Therefore there is no reason for you to doubt in any way that all things which exist naturally seek stability and continued existence and avoid destruction.”

“I confess,” I said [Note: [Col. 0774C] I now perceive so clearly the things about which I was previously uncertain that I can no longer doubt them], “that I now see without doubt what a little while ago seemed uncertain.”

“But whatever desires to subsist and remain,” she said, “desires to be one, since, once this has been removed, nothing could continue even to exist.”

“That is true,” I said.

“Therefore all things desire one.”

I agreed.

“But we have shown that this very one is what is good.”

“That is so.”

“Therefore all things seek good. You may describe it in this way: the good itself is that which is desired by all.”

[Note: [Col. 0773D] Nothing is truer.]

“For the natural desire mentioned above either comes from nothing or comes from some supreme ruler, to whom it must therefore be referred as to its first principle and ultimate end. But it is impossible for this desire to come from nothing, since nothing can be the cause of anything.”

“Nothing more true can be conceived,” I said.

“For either all things are referred to nothing, and, deprived of one summit, as it were, they will drift without a ruler; or, if there is something toward which all things hasten, that will be the supreme good of all.”

And she said: “I rejoice greatly, my pupil, for you have clearly fixed in your mind the mark of manifest truth.” [Note: [Col. 0773D] Of intermediate truth.] [Note: [Col. 0774D] “Of manifest truth,” as Servius interprets it. Virgil, *Aeneid* II, line 533:

> Here Priam, although already held in the midst of death.

[Note: [Col. 0774C] Manifest.]

“But this has become clear to you: what you said shortly before that you did not know.”

“What?” I said.

### 240

“What is the end of all things?” she said. [Note: [Col. 0774D] The end of all things.]

### III

Philosophy concludes that the end of all things is good, and indeed the supreme good, because that which is desired by all things is the end of all things. But, according to what has been said, the supreme good is desired by all things.

“That, then,” she said, “is the end of all things. For it is plainly that which is desired by all. Since we have concluded that it is good, we must confess that the end of all things is good.”

241 **METER** [Note: [Col. 0775A] What is called iambic. A poem consisting of one kind of verse, each line having six feet, often a spondee in the odd positions and an iamb in the even positions.] XI.

[Col. 0775A]

**ARGUMENT.**—Philosophy says that the Philosopher should consider his mind more attentively, for it possesses an innate light which, when instructed by a teacher, can also be the principle of the highest truth.

[Note: [Col. 0775A] Whoever seeks truth with profound attention, and wishes not to be deceived by wandering errors, should turn the light of his inward vision back toward his own mind; and, turning, should arrange the long sequence of his thoughts into a circle, and teach his mind that it possesses hidden in its own treasures everything it seeks outside itself. Then what the black darkness of error has long concealed will shine more brightly than the sun itself. For although the body is a mechanism that produces forgetfulness, it has not driven every light from the mind. Certainly the seed of truth remains within, spread abroad when the teacher acts. For how would you answer correctly when questioned, by your own resources, unless the spark of truth implanted in the depths of the mind were alive? And if Plato’s Muse speaks truth—that each person learns what he remembers after having previously forgotten it—]

[Note: [Col. 0775A]

**1. Whoever.**—The Philosopher; for, considering the interpretation of the name, a philosopher is one who pursues truth with his whole mind, devoted to wisdom. As Tully says in *Tusculan Disputations* V, when Leon had admired Pythagoras’ talent and eloquence, he asked him in what art he placed his greatest confidence. Pythagoras replied that he knew no art, but that he was a philosopher … that there are certain rare people who, regarding everything else as nothing, gaze attentively upon the nature of things; these he calls “devoted to wisdom,” which is what “philosophers” means.

**1. With a profound mind.**—“Profound” is said first of a body whose bottom limits its dimension; thus we speak of a deep sea. Then, by a certain likeness, it is said of the mind itself, whose thought penetrates deeply. Thus Quintilian calls a plan “profound” in *Declamation* 2.

[Col. 0775C] **1. Pursues truth.**—Truth, or the true, is of two kinds: the thing itself and the mode. A true thing exists outside; the true mode exists within the mind. Hence the latter true, or truth, can be defined as the thought of a mind that perceives or judges correctly. The present passage concerns this latter kind of truth; hence it will immediately say, at verse 6, “that the mind possesses it hidden in its own treasures.”

**3. Let him turn back into himself, etc.**—Let him inspect his own mind. For, in matters that are to be known by natural light, the human mind can possess no true and certain judgment—what is now called the truth to be investigated—unless it is preceded and guided by evidence, which is nothing other than clear and distinct cognition. Yet this evidence cannot be possessed before the mind has known itself; hence the saying, “Know yourself,” about which we have already spoken.

**4. And bend the long movements into a circle, etc.**—Let him have a thought of thought, and a third thought of that second thought, and so on, so that a kind of circle of thoughts is formed. For only in this way can haste and prejudice, the two impediments to discovering truth, be avoided.

**5. And teach the mind.**—Properly speaking, only God teaches the mind, since the mind, created and preserved by him, is first formed by him. Nevertheless, through frequent meditation, the human mind, thinking its own thoughts more attentively, is also considered to teach the mind itself, because, with the mind as it were questioning God and God answering it, natural light is spread abroad in such a way that what was previously hidden is perceived once the darkness has been dispelled. Among other things, our mind is taught by this attentive meditation on its thoughts that it possesses within itself the treasure which it had tried to find outside itself. Hence it adds:

**5 and 6. To possess hidden in its own treasures whatever it undertakes outside itself.**—*Molior* (“undertake, contrive”) is derived from *moles* (“mass, burden”); *moles* perhaps comes from Greek μοχλεῖν, “to move with levers.” Therefore, whatever we do with greater force, whether of body or of mind, is said to be undertaken or contrived by us. Thus, with the body, we contrive a journey; with the mind, ambushes; with both, we are said to undertake a fortress.

The mind is therefore understood to undertake truth outside itself when, disregarding its own thoughts, it considers more attentively the matter subjected to those thoughts. This is not in itself a fault, since our thought, being not nothing, depends upon external things as an effect depends upon its cause; nor is it faulty, in order to know an effect, to consider its cause. But since there can be more in the cause than in the effect, while there is nothing in the effect that is not in the cause, the human mind, when discovering truth, will first contemplate its own thoughts rather than the matter subjected to thought. Thus, within itself, or in its own treasures, it will recognize that it possesses what it had tried to find outside itself. In this way it will discover evidence, or clear and distinct thought; and, once this has been discovered, it will not only drive away the black cloud—that is, ignorance, the cause of error—but will also avoid error itself. Indeed—

**9. The body, bringing a mass of forgetfulness, has not driven all light from the mind.**—A human being is neither mind alone nor body alone, but a composition of mind and body acting upon one another. Hence the body, by its action upon the mind, does not extinguish the mind’s innate light, but casts a veil over it. I say “does not extinguish it”: for just as God, the author of this natural light, is utterly constant, so that light, as long as the mind endures, will endure forever. But the body casts a veil over it. For “the corruptible body weighs down the soul,” and “the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things,” as it says in *Wisdom* IX. Hence the body is now called—

**10. Bringing a mass that produces forgetfulness.**—There are two ways of explaining this proposition: one Platonic and false, the other philosophical and true. The Platonists thought that all human minds had been created before they were joined to bodies and had been furnished with every kind of learning; but, because of some crime of their own, had been sent into bodies and, in that unhappy exchange, had forgotten everything, as though they had drunk a cup of forgetfulness. Thus the body is said to be the cause of forgetfulness, while the mind itself is said thereafter to learn by remembering. But this opinion is false, since the human mind was not created before the form of its body.

Philosophers, at least those who are not led by prejudices, however, think that the human mind, standing midway between God, whose effect it is, and the body, whose form it is, is from the very beginning immediately formed by God with the best cognitions and affections concerning the highest good; but that it is so disturbed by contrary thoughts arising from the body that these cognitions and affections are either driven away or at least obscured. Nevertheless—

**11. The seed of truth remains within.**—A seed is that from which something comes into being when it is implanted. Therefore the seed of truth, existing within or inside our mind, is nothing other than a thought from which a true judgment arises by implantation. That thought is a notion, since a true judgment arises only from notions that precede it. Accordingly, if, despite the body’s force, some notion or idea always remains in our mind, then the seed of truth certainly remains within. Some such notion always remains—at least the one we received divinely from our origin, from and concerning that which exists, namely God. Hence a true judgment is aroused when instruction stirs it, insofar as, through the teacher’s admonition, that natural light is spread somewhat farther, like a fire stirred by a breeze. Seneca, *Letter* 94: “For the mind carries within it the seeds of all honorable things, which are aroused by admonition, just as a spark, aided by a gentle breath, unfolds its fire.”]

Whoever with profound mind pursues the truth,

and desires not to be deceived by any wandering,

let him turn within himself the light of inward vision,

[Col. 0776A] 242 and, bending them, force his long movements into a circle,

[5] and teach the mind that whatever it undertakes outside itself

it possesses hidden in its own treasures.

What the black cloud of error long ago concealed

will shine more clearly than Phoebus himself.

For the body, bringing a mass of forgetfulness,

[10] has not driven all light from the mind,

Certainly the seed of truth remains within,

[Col. 0777A] [Note: [Col. 0777C]

**13. Why, when questioned, etc.**—Why would all who have not devoted themselves to letters, when questioned about what are commonly called axioms—for example, whether the whole is greater than its part, or whether one should do to another what one does not wish done to oneself—answer correctly? Thus Socrates and Plato are said to have questioned boys about mathematics, and the boys, like experts, answered them.

**14. Unless submerged, etc.**—Unless there were present in the mind some notion that served as the spark and material of this true and right judgment. Since there is no notion or idea of colors in the mind of one born blind, you will teach such a blind person about colors in vain and question him in vain; he will never form a true and correct judgment about them. For this reason logicians teach that every method always proceeds from what is better known to what is less known.

**15. Plato’s Muse.**—Philosophy does not approve Plato’s opinion insofar as he taught that human minds were created before they were joined to bodies, since this does not seem capable of being known by natural light. But it does approve the idea that philosophical cognition arises from innate cognition in such a way that philosophy is nothing other than a mode of the innate, or the innate modified—just as free desire for riches is nothing other than a mode of necessary desire directed toward the good in general. Therefore—]

What is aroused when instruction stirs it:

for why, when questioned, do you spontaneously judge rightly,

unless a spark lived submerged in your deep heart?

[15] 244 And if Plato’s Muse proclaims the truth,

that what each person learns, having forgotten it,

he remembers.

245 **PROSE XII.**

**ARGUMENT.**—Using Boethius’ preliminary notion, Philosophy teaches Boethius, as though he were remembering, that God governs the world with such goodness and power that all things, apart from sin—which is nothing—turn of their own accord toward God by a kind of circuit; nor is there anything that either wishes or is able to resist this highest good.

Then I said, [Note: [Col. 0777D] “I strongly agree with Plato.”] The opinion of Plato mentioned above concerning recollection involves two points. The first is that human minds were created before they were joined to bodies and were furnished with knowledge of all things, as Aristotle says in *On Generation* II. The second is that these same minds, because of their association with the body, forgot their former learning, until, by their own labor and that of their teachers, they learned and, as it were, remembered their ancient education.

The first opinion was also accepted by certain Christians, such as Origen; but it is refuted both by Letter 1 of Leo to Turibius, bishop of Astorga, and by the First Council of Braga, chapter 6. The second, however, could be approved by Boethius insofar as the human mind, in every method, always proceeds from what is better known to what is less known, so that every notion considered new is a mode of some prior notion, just as every new desire is always a mode of an earlier desire. Indeed, since thought is the very life of the human mind, and since the mind could not have been created except as a participant in life, it seems to follow that the human mind, from its first origin, was affected by the thoughts mentioned above—namely, the general notion and desire of the highest good.] “I strongly agree with Plato,” I said, [Note: [Col. 0778B] Referring to verse 15 of the preceding meter.] for you now recall these things to me a second time. [Note: [Col. 0778C] “You recall their memory.” That is, you recall the memory of these things; for only under this rule are the words of recollection said by grammarians to govern the genitive.] First, I lost the memory of them through bodily contact, and afterward, when weighed down by the burden of sorrow. Then she said: If you look back at what was granted above, it will not be far from the case that you remember what you recently confessed you did not know. “What?” I said. “By what means,” she replied, “the world is governed.” “I remember,” I said, “that I confessed my ignorance; but although I can already see what you are bringing forward, I nevertheless desire to hear it more clearly from you. A little earlier,” she said, “you thought it entirely beyond doubt that this world is governed by God.” “Even now,” I replied, “I do not think otherwise, nor shall I ever think it doubtful; and I shall briefly explain the reasons by which I reach this conclusion.”

[Note: [Col. 0778C] **This world.**—Boethius proves by the following argument that the world is governed by God. Since the union of contraries must be either nonexistent, brief, or at least irregular, if the world is, as it truly is, an enduring and ordered union of contraries, it is necessary that the world be governed by God, by whom those contraries are joined, the joined things are held together, and the things held together are assigned their several functions.]

This world, composed of parts so diverse and contrary, would never have come together into one form unless there were one who joined such different things. Yet the very diversity of the natures, discordant and opposed to one another, would separate and tear apart what had been joined unless there were one who held together what he had bound. Nor would the order of nature proceed so reliably, nor would it unfold movements so well arranged in place, time, agency, extension, and quality, unless there were one who, himself remaining unchanged, arranged these varieties of change. Whatever this is, by which created things remain and are moved, I call God by the name familiar to all.

Then she said: Since you think this way, I believe that little labor remains for you before, having attained happiness, you safely revisit your homeland; but let us examine what we have proposed. [Note: [Col. 0778D] “Is it not in blessedness?”] **II.** Using Boethius’ preliminary notion, Philosophy teaches Boethius that goodness is like the rudder and steering mechanism by which the machinery of the world is governed. Her argument appears to be as follows. Since the highest good, being self-sufficient, needs no external assistance in undertaking anything, and since God is the highest good, God, needing no external help, must accomplish by himself alone—and therefore through his goodness—whatever he accomplishes. If, then, the world is governed by God, as you admit it is, the world must be governed by divine goodness.]

“Did we not count self-sufficiency among blessedness, and concede that God is blessedness itself?” “Indeed we did.” “Then,” she said, “in governing the world he will need no external supports; otherwise, if he needed something, he would not possess complete self-sufficiency.” “That,” I said, “must be so.” [Col. 0779A] “Therefore he arranges all things by himself alone.” “It cannot be denied.” “But God has been shown to be goodness itself.” “I remember.” “Therefore he arranges all things through goodness, since he governs all things by himself, whom we have conceded to be good; and this goodness is like a rudder and steering mechanism by which the machinery of the world is kept stable and incorruptible.” “I strongly agree,” I said, “and, though only by a slight suspicion, I anticipated that you would say this a little earlier.” “I believe so,” she replied, “for by now, as I think, you are guiding the eyes of your mind more attentively toward the sight of truth; but what I shall say is no less clear to behold.” [Note: [Col. 0779C] “Of the mind.”] “What?” I said.

247 [Note: [Col. 0779C] **Since God governs all things with the rudder of goodness.**—From the preceding proposition Philosophy infers that all things are governed willingly and spontaneously, because whatever is governed by the highest good, or by goodness, is governed willingly and spontaneously, since all things hasten toward the good by natural intention. “Since,” she said, “God is rightly believed to govern all things with the rudder of goodness, and since all things, as I have taught, hasten toward the good by natural intention, can there be any doubt that they are governed willingly and spontaneously, and that, as though in agreement and harmony with their ruler, they turn of their own accord toward the will of the one who arranges them?” “It must be so,” I said; “nor would the government be blessed if it were the yoke of those who resist rather than the salvation of those who obey. Therefore there is nothing that, while preserving its nature, attempts to oppose God.” “Nothing,” I said. [Note: [Col. 0779C] **What if it should attempt it?**] “Indeed, since the highest good is all-powerful, and since all things are governed by the highest good, all things are also governed by supreme power. Hence the passage in *Wisdom* VIII: “She reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly.” Philosophy has now recalled these words; and this is the only explicit authority from sacred Scripture that she uses in the whole work. Nor is this surprising, since Philosophy relies solely upon natural light. Yet these words from *Wisdom* please Boethius, so that at last the foolishness that loudly barks may be ashamed of itself—for foolishness, unlike wisdom, does not reach mightily from end to end and order all things sweetly, whatever it may boast.]

“What if it should attempt it?” she said. “Would it finally accomplish anything against him whom we have rightly conceded, by virtue of his blessedness, to be all-powerful?” “Absolutely nothing,” I replied. “Then there is nothing that either wishes or is able to oppose this highest good.” “I do not think so.” “Then there is a highest good that governs all things mightily and orders them sweetly.” [Note: [Col. 0779C] As it is said in *Wisdom* VIII.] Then I said: “How much I am delighted not only by the summit of arguments that has been established, but much more by these very words [Note: [Col. 0780C] As being words of sacred Scripture.] which you use, so that at last the loudly barking foolishness may be ashamed of itself.” “You have heard in the myths,” she said, “of the Giants who challenged heaven.” [Note: [Col. 0779D] **Giants.**—The Giants are said to have been men born from an angered earth for the destruction of the gods. 250 **METER** [Note: [Col. 0781C] What is called glyconic. A poem consisting of one kind of verse, each line having a spondee and two dactyls.] XII.

**ARGUMENT.**—“As soon as you possess knowledge of the highest good, you are happy,” says Philosophy, “but, when you look toward the earth, you unhappily lose it. Thus Orpheus, turning his eyes toward the underworld, lost his wife whom he had won by his song.”

[Note: [Col. 0782B]

He is happy who has been able to see the luminous fountain of goodness; likewise happy is he who has been able to free himself from the bonds of the weighty body. Long ago Orpheus, the Thracian poet, lamenting the death of his wife, first compelled trees to run while moved by his mournful song, and rivers to stand motionless; then, by the same song, he joined the hind’s fearless flank to savage lions, and the hare did not fear the sight of the dog. At that point, when the flame of love burned more fiercely and consumed the innermost parts of the poet’s heart, and the songs that had conquered everything could not soothe their author, he, lamenting the cruelty of the gods, entered the halls of the underworld.

There, fitting his songs to the gently sounding strings of his lyre, he brought forth with groaning whatever he had drunk from the excellent springs of divine Calliope, his mother, and whatever unrestrained grief and love that doubled his grief supplied. Stirring the entrance to the underworld, he asked in sweet prayer for pardon from its lords. Then Cerberus, the three-headed doorkeeper, astonished by the unheard-of song, stood spellbound. The goddesses who avenge crimes and shake the guilty with fear grew sad and wet with tears. The rushing wheel no longer seized Ixion’s head, and Tantalus, exhausted by prolonged thirst, scorned the waters. The vulture, satisfied by the song, did not tear at Tityus’ liver.

Finally the lord of the underworld, moved by pity, said: “We are overcome. We give the husband the wife whom he has won by his song; but let the condition restrict the gift: he must not be permitted to turn his eyes after he has left the underworld.” Who could impose a law upon lovers? Love itself is the greater law. Alas! Not far from the boundaries of the shades, Orpheus scarcely looked back at his wife Eurydice when he lost her, dead. This story concerns you, whoever wish to raise your mind toward God, the highest light. For whoever, weakening, turns his eyes toward the caves below, loses, while he looks toward the underworld, whatever excellence of thought he possesses.]

[Note: [Col. 0781C]

**1 and 2. Happy is he who has been able to see the clear fountain of goodness.**—That is, God. First, God is the fountain of goodness, since, according to what has been said, God is the highest good. Second, that fountain of goodness, God, is luminous, or emits light; for God is known only by the light which God himself gives to the knowing mind. Finally, the person endowed with knowledge of God is happy, because that knowledge is either happiness itself or at least the source of every thought in which happiness can exist. Happiness is the thought of a mind constantly adhering to God, or to the highest good. Hence—

**3 and 4. Happy is he who has been able to loosen the bonds of the weighty earth.** [Col. 0781D]—That is, of the human body. First, the human body is earth, since it was made from earth as its matter: “Why is earth and ashes proud?” (*Ecclesiasticus* X). Second, this body is heavy, since by its weight it presses the mind downward: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul” (*Wisdom* IX). Moreover, this body has bonds by which it constrains the mind, namely, the disturbances of the passions: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” (Romans VII). Finally, no one is happy before he has loosened these bonds, since the aforesaid thought of God, in which happiness consists, is impeded by these bonds as by so many opposing forces: “The earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (*Wisdom* IX).

**6. Thracian poet.**—Orpheus of Thrace. He, the son of Apollo and Calliope, played the lyre that he had received either from his father Apollo or from Mercury so sweetly that his song was said to move forests and rocks, halt the course of rivers, and make wild beasts gentler. He had Eurydice as his wife. When she fled through trackless places from Aristæus, who was inflamed by love for her, she was wounded by a serpent’s bite and died. Her husband bore this with the greatest grief and went down to the underworld. By his song he so charmed the lords of the underworld that they restored his wife to him, on the condition that Orpheus should not look at her before they had returned to the upper world. When, overcome by excessive love, Orpheus failed to observe this condition, Eurydice died again and returned to the underworld.

This story is now described elegantly, but it had first been described by Virgil in *Georgics* IV, verse 454 and following. Here Orpheus is said by his songs to have conquered first bodies and then minds. He conquered bodies both inanimate—whose rest he changed into movement and movement into rest—and animate, namely wild beasts, to which he inspired gentleness instead of savagery and courage instead of fear. He conquered the minds of the underworld.]

**16. Nor did the melodies that had subdued everything soothe their master.**—That is: the songs that had conquered everything did not conquer Orpheus himself, the author of those songs, either because his grief was greater or because, as philosophers say, “passion does not arise from what is customary.” We do not perceive any body except insofar as it moves the sensory organ, or rather certain parts of that organ. Bodies that are less frequently presented to the senses can produce a change in that organ; but those that are constantly present to the senses have, from their first contact, changed the relevant parts of the organ in every way they could, leaving only the resistant parts, through which we do not perceive. Hence we do not perceive the natural heat of our heart, the weight of our body, or even the familiar weight of our clothing.]

the clear fountain of goodness;

happy is he who has been able to loosen

the bonds of the weighty earth.

**18 and 19. Lamenting the pitiless gods, he entered the halls below.**—Poets posit two classes of gods, namely the gods above and those below. If they find the former inexorable, they flee to the latter. Virgil, *Aeneid* VII, verse 312:

“If I cannot bend the gods above, I shall move Acheron.”

Thus this poet has imagined the matter. But, for a fuller understanding of what follows, one must know how poets describe the underworld.

Virgil describes it in *Aeneid* VI, verse 273, as follows. First, before the entrance and at the very threshold of the underworld lie Grief and Care, avengers; Disease, Old Age, Fear, Hunger, Poverty, Death, Toil, Sleep, the brother of Death, the evil pleasures of the mind, War, the Furies, and Discord dwell there. Second, in the middle of the same vestibule, a great and shady elm spreads its branches and foliage, beneath which are empty dreams. Third, at the gates of the same place stand Centaurs, the two-formed Scyllas, Briareus equipped with a hundred hands, the Lernaean Hydra, the fire-breathing Chimera, the Gorgons, the Harpies, and the shade of three-bodied Geryon. Fourth, from there the road begins toward the river Acheron, which pours its sands into Cocytus. The ferryman Charon guards these waters—a cruel old man still—who transports the buried and leaves the unburied behind. Fifth, across the river is a three-headed dog called Cerberus, as though from Greek κρεαβόρος, “flesh-eating.” Sixth, everywhere appear those who suffer punishments worthy of their crimes: Tityus, who, because he had attempted violence against Latona, was killed by Apollo’s arrows and is eternally gnawed by a vulture as his tissues grow again; Ixion, who, because he attempted the chastity of Juno, is bound to a wheel and turned forever; Pirithous, who, because he wished to carry Proserpina away from the underworld, is consumed both by fear of an overhanging rock and by hunger in the midst of a banquet; Sisyphus, infamous for brigandage, who rolls a huge stone, and so forth.]

**20. Gently sounding.**—Something is said to sound gently, just as Virgil in *Aeneid* IX, verse 125, speaks of something sounding hoarsely. The omitted object is understood according to a manner of expression customary among authors, especially poets; it is called an ellipsis.

**22. From the excellent springs of the goddess mother.**—Calliope, who is regarded as, first, a goddess; second, Orpheus’ mother; and third, queen of the Muses, to whom the Castalian springs are sacred.

**24. Unrestrained grief.**—That which makes the mind unrestrained; thus Cicero in *Tusculan Disputations* V calls joy “unrestrained.”

**26. Stirring Taenara.**—The entrance to the underworld. For Taenarus, or Taenarum—whence the plural *Taenara*—is a certain promontory of the Peloponnese that divides the Messenian Gulf from the Laconian Gulf. Not only a city and a gulf, but also a cave said in myth to provide an entrance to the underworld, bears this name. Hence Virgil, speaking of Orpheus in *Georgics* IV, verse 467 and following, sings:

“Even the Taenarian jaws, the lofty gates of Dis,

and the grove dark with black terror,

he entered, and approached the shades and the dread king,

and hearts that knew not how to be softened by human prayers.”

[Col. 0784C] **28. Lords of the shades.**—The rulers of the underworld, either because there is no light there or because they rule over the minds of the dead, which are often called shades.

**29. Threefold doorkeeper.**—Cerberus, the dog who, as Apuleius says in *Metamorphoses* VI, “equipped with an enormous threefold and sufficiently large head, always keeping watch before the threshold and the black halls of Proserpina, guards the empty house of Dis.”

**32. Goddesses who avenge crimes.**—Commonly called the Eumenides, by ἀντίφρασις (“antiphrasis”), because they are not at all benevolent; for εὐμενής means “benevolent.” In the same way the Fates are so called because they spare no one.

**33. Now wet with mournful tears.**—The power of Orpheus’ songs is so great that the Eumenides, who know not how to be moved, are stirred by such profound pity that many tears seem to pour from them. Thus Ixion’s wheel is halted; thus Tantalus, forgetting hunger and thirst, no longer cares to pluck the apples or drink the waters; [Col. 0784D] thus the vulture does not tear at Tityus’ liver.

**34. The head of Ixion.**—We have already spoken of Ixion’s punishment. Ovid writes:

“Ixion rolls, and follows and flees himself.”

**36. With thirst.**—For *siti*, “by thirst,” just as *mare* is used for *mari*, “by the sea.” The poet says *mare*. I doubt whether anyone else knowledgeable in Latin has used *site*, although *vespere* and *vesperi*, *tempore* and *tempori*, *luce* and *luci*, *igne* and *igni* are read in the ablative.男人天堂
37. **Tantalus.** Tantalus, grandfather of Agamemnon and Menelaus—who are therefore called Tantalids—is said to have set before the gods his son, torn limb from limb, to be eaten. With fruits and water placed before him but inaccessible, he is tortured by perpetual hunger and thirst.

40. **Judge of the shades.** Pluto. For Saturn, with his wife Ops, had three sons—Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto—among whom the rule of the world was divided: Jupiter received dominion of the sky, Neptune of the sea, and Pluto of the underworld.

44. **Let the law restrain the gifts.** The prince of darkness grants nothing pleasurable except under conditions that either cannot or ought not to be fulfilled. Thus, in Matthew 4, he shows Christ all the kingdoms of the world and their glory and says: “All these things I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me.”

52. **This story concerns you.** A story is an invented example designed to persuade people of a truth. Therefore, according to Varro, theology among the ancients was of two kinds: one physical and the other fabulous. The former persuaded people of what was to be believed about the gods through natural effects; the latter through fictitious ones. Indeed, the more obscure and difficult to discover the truth that is concealed beneath these coverings, the more pleasing the discovery, and the more ardently the mind clings to it. [Col. 0786B] Hence, in sacred Scripture, there are frequent parables resembling apologues; hence Horace, *Satires* I.1:

> Thirsting, Tantalus reaches for the fleeing rivers  
> At his lips. Why do you laugh? With the name changed,  
> The story is told about you: with sacks heaped everywhere,  
> You fall asleep, gaping at them, and as though forced  
> To spare the sacred things, or as though delighted  
> With painted panels.

Thus, just as Orpheus, while looking back at the underworld, loses his wife, whom he had won and through whom he seemed happy, so, through rash contemplation of transitory things, the very thought of the supreme good is either extinguished or obscured as though it had been extinguished.
