## 256 PROSE I

[Col. 0785C]

**ARGUMENT.**—Philosophy teaches Boethius, who wonders that, while God governs the world, not only do evils exist and go unpunished, but virtue is deprived of rewards and trampled beneath the feet of criminals, that neither vices are without punishment nor virtue without reward.

When Philosophy had sung this gently and sweetly, preserving the dignity of her countenance and the gravity of her expression—[Note: Since a human being, when intending to signify his thoughts, speaks not only with his tongue but also with his eyes, forehead, nod, gesture, and other such means, so that, according to the various ways in which all these are employed, he both expresses different thoughts of his own and awakens different thoughts in another who is listening, Philosophy therefore, having assumed human form, persuades more successfully through these appropriate signs. In this she differs from the poetic Muses, whom she earlier called “little harlots,” sweet even unto destruction; since they speak with another expression, they also stir different thoughts in their hearers.] then I, not yet having entirely forgotten [Note: inwardly] my implanted grief, interrupted [Note: broke off] the speech of one who was preparing to say something further.

257 “Ah,” I said, “Philosophy, precursor of the true light”—[Note: Since Philosophy is clear and distinct knowledge, and therefore not subject to error, she herself is the true light. But because, for one who gives attention, she is the source of the light of light, that same Philosophy is called the precursor of the true light. Unless you say that the true light here means the light which the mind hopes one day to enjoy after the bonds of the body have been broken; for this light is preceded by philosophical light.]—“whose discourse up to now has poured forth [Note: clear and certain] things that, through divine [Note: speculation—a word that seems less Latin] contemplation, and through your unanswerable arguments, have plainly become evident. You have spoken of things which, although recently forgotten by me because of the pain of my misfortune, were not previously altogether unknown to me.

“But this itself is perhaps the greatest [Note: Just as a person is filled with the greatest joy when, from certain premises that have been established, he unexpectedly draws conclusions that he already knows from elsewhere to be entirely true, so a person is saddened when he cannot reconcile with his own principles what experience proves. The former arises from the light we love; the latter from the darkness we hate.] cause of our grief: that, although there is a good ruler of the universe, either evils can exist at all or they can pass unpunished. Surely you understand how worthy of wonder this alone is. But another, greater matter is added: while wickedness rules and flourishes, virtue not only lacks rewards but is also trampled beneath the feet of criminals and pays the penalties due to crimes in their place. That such things should happen [Note: under the reign of one who knows everything] in the kingdom of the God who knows everything, can do everything, but wills only what is good—no one can sufficiently wonder at or complain of.”

Then she [Note: Philosophy] said: “It would be a matter of infinite [Note: supreme] astonishment—and more horrible than all monsters—if, as you suppose, in the perfectly ordered household of so great a master, cheap vessels were cherished while precious ones grew dirty. [Note: But that is not how it is. Virtue is never without its reward, nor vice without its punishment, as is clear from what has been said.] But that is not how it is.

258 “For if what was concluded a little earlier is preserved unshaken, you will recognize, with God himself as the author of the doctrine concerning whose kingdom we are speaking [Note: God teaches a person when, with the mind stripped of prejudices, the thoughts of the mind itself alone are considered with greater attention; and just as God alone is then questioned, so he alone answers the questioning mind], that the good are always powerful, while the wicked are always rejected and weak; that vices are never without punishment, nor virtues without reward; that good fortune comes to the good, and misfortune always to the wicked; and many other things of this kind, which, when your complaints have been lulled to rest, will strengthen you with firm solidity.

“And since, while I was showing you earlier, you saw the form of true happiness and recognized where it is situated, after I have gone through everything that I think it necessary to set forth beforehand, I shall show you the road that will lead you home. [Note: Once a person knows his ultimate end, nothing remains except to know the means by which he can reach such an end. Matthew 6: ‘Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness.’ Since Philosophy has now taught the ultimate end of the human being, the structure of her undertaking requires that she discuss the means of attaining this end. This is now called the road that leads one home; hence she promises wings.] [Note: to the heavenly homeland] I shall also attach wings to your mind, by which it may lift itself on high, so that, once disturbance has been driven away, [Note: safe and unharmed: one is called *sospes* when one has the strength to go and return anywhere] you may safely return to your homeland under my guidance, along my path, in my vehicles. [Note: Philosophical knowledge is rightly called a guide, a path, and a vehicle, by which a person may safely return to God, from whom he came. It is a guide because, with it—being innate—as a leader, the mind is guided toward judgment. It is a path because things clearly and distinctly comprehended in it are to be judged accordingly. It is a vehicle because, bound as it were by it, the mind is carried along so that it is not in its power to think otherwise. For this reason the same Philosophy now sings.]”

## 259 METER I

[Note: A poem composed of two kinds of alternating verses: the first has the four opening feet of a dactylic heroic line; the second has four feet likewise, often spondees in the odd-numbered places and iambs in the even-numbered places.]

**ARGUMENT.**—“With my help,” says Philosophy, “the human mind, transcending all created things, reaches God; and, once he is known, turning back toward the earth, it sees here even kings living in exile.”

[Note: For I possess swift wings that ascend to the lofty regions of heaven. Once the ready mind has joined them to itself, hating the earth, it despises it; it transcends the sphere of the vast air; it sees the clouds behind it; and it passes beyond the summit of the fire that burns through the swift motion of the ether, until it rises to the star-bearing spheres and joins its course with the sun as it travels, or accompanies the path of old, cold Saturn, or becomes like a soldier of bright Mars, or retraces the orbit of whatever star marks the sparkling night. After it has had enough of seeing the bodies below, it leaves this highest heaven and treads upon the vaulted regions of the swiftest ether, becoming a participant in the august light that is to be revered. Here the King of kings holds his scepter and governs the government of the world; immovable, he guides the moving chariot, the splendid ruler of things. If your journey brings you back here, you will say: “This is the homeland that, now forgetful, you seek; I remember it—this is my homeland. From here I arose; here I shall rest.” From this seat, if you wish to turn your eyes toward the darkness of the earth that you abandoned, you will see tyrants, whom afflicted peoples fear as hostile to them, expelled from this homeland and living in exile.]

[Col. 0788B]

1. **I have swift wings.** Wings are the parts of birds by which birds, carried through the air, return to their proper places. Hence, by a certain similarity, wings are attributed to arrows, ships, and other such bodies that move more directly when their weights are balanced, as it were. Thus clear and distinct concepts are called philosophical wings, because by means of them Philosophy, as though balanced, returns more directly from earth to heaven, from which she arose.

**Swift.** *Volucer* is derived from flight. Therefore, just as flight is a rapid movement, so *volucer* means “swift” or “quick.” Thus Cicero, *For Plancus*: “Nothing is so swift as slander: nothing is more easily uttered, nothing more certainly received, nothing more widely scattered.” Virgil, *Aeneid* V.242:

> It fled to earth swifter than the south wind  
> And the winged arrow, and hid itself in the deep harbor.

Since, therefore, the thoughts of the aforesaid Philosophy are so swift that, compared with them, even the swiftest bodily movement is extremely slow, they are rightly called “swift wings.”

2. **The heights of the sky.** “The heights of the sky” is used here in the same way as Virgil’s “vaults of heaven,” Horace’s “sharp points of war,” and Lucretius’s “open spaces of heaven,” “clear spaces of heaven,” and “hidden regions of earth,” with places or spaces being understood. Philosophical wings, however, stronger in this respect than all birds’ wings, reach all the way to the highest summit of heaven, insofar as that summit is understood by Philosophy.

> What does it profit you  
> To have attempted the airy heights  
> And traversed in mind the rounded sky?

3. **The swift mind puts them on.** The human mind is indeed swift, because in the moment when, as though snatched outside itself, it reaches the earth, the seas, and heaven itself, however distant, it returns to itself and contemplates the thought implanted within it. Thus, in this circling movement, not even the mind itself is able to distinguish its beginning, progress, and end. In this respect the human mind seems to imitate the divine, so that the ancients concluded from it that the human mind both arose from God and is immortal like God. The same mind puts on philosophical wings by knowing clearly and distinctly.

4. **Hating the earth, it despises it.** The metaphorical expression continues: just as birds withdraw from the earth by flying, so the mind equipped with philosophical wings is understood to despise the earth in hatred of it. Nor is this without reason; for the more the mind clings to the earth, the more it is enveloped in dense darkness [Col. 0789B] and the less capable it is of contemplating God, its creator.

I have, indeed, swift wings

That ascend the heights of heaven.

When the swift mind puts them on,

260 Hating the earth, it despises it.

[5] [Col. 0789A] [Col. 0789B]

5. **It passes beyond the sphere of the boundless air.** The air is indeed defined by its own limits. But because it is so diffused that its extent is represented in our mind no more distinctly than the extent of any other body, however much larger, it is regarded by us, when we imagine it, as boundless. Our mind, however, which can conceive more than it can imagine, thinks of the air surrounding the earth on every side as spread out in a sphere, and proposes something beyond it for further consideration. Thus the same mind leaves behind, as it were, the clouds that are suspended in the air, just as ships are supported in water, with their weights balanced on either side.

8. **It passes beyond the summit of the fire.** If Philosophy acknowledges fire here, this fire certainly differs greatly from the fire which the Peripatetics commonly say exists in the concavity of the moon for the sake of the order and goodness of the universe. For this Peripatetic element is not affected by heat because it is rarefied; or, if it becomes hot, it does not do so through motion; or, if it is heated by motion, it receives this from itself rather than from another moving body. Yet Philosophy’s fire derives heat from the swift motion of the ether. Therefore this fire is perhaps nothing other than a part of the ether, which Cicero, in *On the Nature of the Gods*, calls “the ultimate blaze”; it is thin, transparent, and suffused with uniform heat. Having considered the summit of the ether, the mind mentioned above rises higher and contemplates first the planets below the sun, then the sun itself, afterward the planets above the sun, then the fixed stars, and finally God himself, as is stated below.

9. **Until it rises to the star-bearing dwellings.** I. The human mind contemplates the planets below the sun, such as the Moon, Venus, Mercury, and any other planets that may be there. Since these occupy the lowest parts of the starry heaven and are nearer to earth, they could be signified by the named “star-bearing dwellings.” No one is unaware that astronomers call the positions of the stars “dwellings.”

> What does it profit you  
> To have attempted the airy heights  
> And traversed in mind the rounded sky?

10. **And joins its paths with Phoebus.** II. The same mind contemplates the sun. The sun is often called Phoebus because of its appearance and brilliance; for the adjective *phoibos* (φοῖβος) means “splendid.” The sun’s path is twofold: one is daily, completed from sunrise to sunset in the space of twenty-four hours; the other is annual, which, according to Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, is completed in 365 days, with approximately a quarter of a day added. When the mind contemplates both paths of the sun, it is said to join its own paths with the solar paths.

11. **It accompanies the path of the cold old man.** III. The mind, about to contemplate the planets above the sun, first looks at Saturn and follows its course. To astronomers Saturn is the highest of all the planets; to poets it is called the “cold old man.” “Old,” because it is imagined to be the most ancient of the gods and to move with a slow step resembling that of an old man; “cold,” because, being the highest of all the planets, it affects the earth with the least heat. Hence Cicero says: “The highest star, Saturn, cools.” Finally, Saturn’s path consists in completing its circuit in thirty years.

12. **A soldier of the shining star.** Next the mind itself contemplates Mars, the other planet above the sun, and is therefore called its soldier. Mars was an ancient god of war; those whom he has as companions are called his soldiers. Mars is called the shining star because it shines more brightly than Saturn. Hence Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II: “The highest star, Saturn, cools; the middle one, Mars, burns.”

13. **Or whatever, and so forth.** IV. The mind contemplates the fixed stars, with which the glittering night is depicted, and completes their circuits by circling around them in thought as well.

15. **When it has contemplated enough.** That is, when the things mentioned above have been sufficiently considered. Thus Cicero, *To Quintus Frater*: “The speech of men has been exhausted,” as if he were saying: “People have now ceased speaking about that matter.” Likewise Virgil, *Georgics* II.397:

> There is also another labor in tending the vines,  
> For which one can never have enough of labor.

16. **It leaves the outermost pole, and so forth.** V. Having considered all the stars, and even the swift ether by which the stars are carried, as ships are carried by water, the mind rises to consider the heaven called the empyrean. This is called the chief dwelling of God and, because the other heavens are in motion, is commonly said to be unmoving. Hence our most learned Antonius Hallaeus, in an epigram whose subject is this:

> But alone the highest mass of the empyrean heaven,  
> The holy dwelling of God and the gods, free from rotation,  
> Stands firm, never disturbed by unsettling motion;  
> For fitting reason requires that the unmoving seat  
> Of those who enjoy deep peace and are at rest should rest in high tranquility.

God, now called the Lord of kings, in accordance with Revelation 19: “King of kings and Lord of those who reign,” and the brilliant judge of things—whom Seneca, in *Hercules Furens* 204, calls “the great ruler of Olympus and judge of the world”—is here said to hold the scepter, guide the reins of the universe, and steadily direct the swift chariot. For although God is everywhere, acting everywhere, nevertheless, since he acts in this heaven in a special manner, he also appears to exist in this heaven in a special manner. Psalm 148: “His praise and glory are above heaven and earth.” Indeed, Aristotle himself, in *On the World*, says: “God has received the highest and first seat of the universe.” This is the homeland of our mind, to such an extent that even kings themselves, insofar as they dwell on earth, may be regarded as exiles, as is said here.

19. **Scepter.** By the very origin of the word, a scepter is a royal staff or rod. Hence, with the sign put in place of the thing signified, “scepter” means the authority of a human being; from this it is transferred to God because of a certain similarity in ruling.

The boundless air’s sphere he passes beyond,

And sees the clouds behind him;

And the fire that grows hot

Through the swift motion of the ether

He passes beyond its summit,

Until he rises to the star-bearing dwellings,

[10] 261 And joins his paths with Phoebus,

Or accompanies the path of the cold old man,

A soldier of the shining star,

[Col. 0790A] Or, wherever the glittering night is depicted,

Retraces the circle of the star,

[15] And when he has had enough of exhaustion,

Leaves the outermost pole,

And presses upon the back of the swift ether,

Master of the light that must be revered.

262 Here the lord of kings holds the scepter,

[20] [Col. 0791A] [Col. 0791C]

20. **The reins of the universe.** The comparison is taken from horses, which we turn here and there at will with reins. For God so governs all things that everything moves wherever he wishes.

21. **The swift chariot.** The author seems specifically to understand the whole sphere of the mobile heaven; in general, however, the entire bodily universe may be called a “swift chariot.” Since that universe is a mass so compact that there is nothing empty within it, no movement occurs in the universe without a circuit of moved matter also taking place there.

29 and 30. **The grim tyrants.** *Torvus*, derived from *torquere* (“to twist”), describes one who signifies an inward movement of fury by a distorted expression, or rather by twisted eyes, so that he is terrifying to those who look upon him. Hence the bull is especially considered grim, because that animal frequently assumes this appearance. Virgil, *Georgics* III: “The finest form of a grim cow.”

Moreover, since an exile—whether, as some write, *exsol*—is so called as though driven from his soil or homeland, and since tyrants living on earth have been driven from their soil, or rather from heaven, their homeland, they may therefore be seen as exiles. Hebrews 13: “Here we have no lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come.”

He governs the reins of the universe,

And steadily guides the swift chariot,

The brilliant judge of things.

If the road brings you back here,

To the place you now seek in forgetfulness,

[25] You will say: “I remember; this homeland is mine.

I arose from here; here I shall halt my step.”

But if it pleases you

To look upon the night you left behind on earth,

263 You will see the grim tyrants

Whom wretched peoples fear.

[30] You will see them living in exile.

## 264 PROSE II

**ARGUMENT.**—From what has already been said, Philosophy demonstrates that the good are powerful and the wicked powerless.

Then I—“Papae!” [Note: [Col. 0791D] “Papae.” Or, as Plautus says, “babae,” is the interjection of someone suddenly receiving something marvelous; for, as we conjecture, these may be the first words that children, being ignorant of everything and therefore admiring everything, are accustomed to utter.] “Papae,” I say—“how great are your promises!” [Note: [Col. 0792C] “How great.”] [Col. 0791B] And I do not doubt that you can accomplish it; only, do not delay the one whom you have aroused. [Note: [Col. 0792C] “Delay.”] [Note: [Col. 0792C] “First, therefore, etc.” Philosophy sets forth what she must prove in this discourse: namely, that the good are powerful and the wicked powerless. She will prove this by three kinds of argument, which we shall try to condense.]

“First, therefore,” she said, “you may recognize that power is always present in the good, while the wicked are deserted by every strength; one of these propositions is demonstrated from the other. For since good and evil are opposites, if it has been established that good is powerful, the weakness of evil is clear; but if the frailty of evil becomes evident, the firmness of good is known. Yet, so that confidence in our position may be the greater, I shall proceed by either route, confirming the proposition now from this side, now from that.”

[Note: [Col. 0792C] “There are two, etc.” I. First kind of argument. Whoever obtains what he wants is powerful; whoever wants something but does not obtain it is powerless. The human result by which someone is judged powerful or not powerful necessarily involves will and ability: both are present in the first person, but only one in the second. Now the good person obtains what he wants, while the wicked person does not obtain what he wants. Both desire their happiness, but the good person obtains it, whereas the wicked person does not; for just as a person is called good only through the attainment of the highest good, so he is called wicked only through deprivation of that same good.]

“There are two things on which the outcome of all human actions depends: will, namely, and ability. If either is lacking, nothing can be carried out. For when will is lacking, no one even undertakes what he does not want; but if ability is absent, the will is futile. Hence, if you see someone wanting to obtain something which he decidedly does not obtain, you cannot doubt that he lacked the power to obtain what he wanted.” [Note: [Col. 0792C] “Ability.”]

“Evidently so,” I said, “and it cannot be denied in any way.”

“But when you see someone having accomplished what he wanted, will you doubt that he was also able?”

“Not at all.”

“Whatever someone can do, he is strong in that respect; whatever he cannot do, he must be considered weak in that respect.”

265 “I admit it,” I said. “Do you remember, then,” she said, “that in the preceding arguments it was established that the whole aim of the human will, driven by various pursuits, hastens toward happiness?”

“I remember; that too was demonstrated.”

“Do you also remember that happiness itself is the good, and that in seeking happiness everyone desires the good?”

“I certainly remember it, since I hold it fixed in my memory.”

“Therefore all human beings, good and wicked alike, strive with undivided purpose to reach the good?”

“So it follows,” I said.

“But it is certain that people become good through attaining the good.”

“Certain.”

“Therefore the good attain what they desire?”

“So it seems.”

“But if the wicked attained the good they desire, they could not remain wicked.”

“That is so.”

“Since, then, both seek the good, but the good attain it whereas the wicked do not, there can be no doubt that the good are powerful, while those who are wicked are weak.”

“Whoever doubts this,” I said, “can consider neither the nature of things nor the consequence of the arguments.”

[Note: [Col. 0792D] “Again, if there are two, etc.” II. Second kind of argument. Of two beings whom the Author of nature himself has appointed to tend toward some goal, if one, obeying its function, tends toward that goal, while the other, abandoning its function, either lingers or turns elsewhere, the former must be regarded as powerful and the latter as powerless. For power is nothing other than that impulse received from the Author of nature; it belongs to power to reach where God calls, and to weakness not to reach it. Thus, of two people whom the Author of nature himself has appointed to walk on their feet, if one fulfills his function and walks, while the other, abandoning his function, either rests or walks relying only on his hands, the former must be regarded as powerful and the latter as weak.]

“Again,” she said, “if there are two beings for whom nature has set the same goal, and one of them performs and completes that very task in accordance with its natural function, while the other cannot perform that natural function and, in another way contrary to nature, does not actually fulfill its purpose but imitates one who does fulfill it, which of these do you judge to be the stronger?” [Note: [Col. 0793C] “Stronger.”]

“Although I can infer what you mean,” I said, “I nevertheless wish to hear it more plainly.” [Note: [Col. 0793C] “I grasp this by conjecture.”] [Note: [Col. 0793C] “More clearly.”]

“Will you deny that the motion of walking is natural to human beings?”

“Not at all.”

“And do you doubt that the natural function of this activity belongs to the feet?”

“Not even that.”

“If, therefore, one person who is able to walk on his feet walks, while another, lacking this natural function of the feet, tries to walk by relying on his hands, which of them can rightly be considered stronger?”

“Continue with the rest,” I said; “for no one doubts that the one powerful in his natural function is stronger than the one unable to perform the same function.” [Note: [Col. 0793C] “Doubts.”]

266 “But the highest good,” she said, “which is set before wicked and good alike, the good seek by the natural function of virtue, whereas the wicked try to attain that same good through various desires, which are not the natural function of attaining the good. Do you think otherwise?”

“Not at all,” I said. [Note: [Col. 0793C] “Indeed.”] “For the consequence too is clear. From what I had conceded, it necessarily follows that the good are powerful, while the wicked are weak.”

“You anticipate me correctly,” she said; “and, as physicians are accustomed to hope, this is a sign of a nature already aroused and resisting.”

[Note: [Col. 0793D] “But since I see you, etc.” III. Third kind of argument. If you consider the goal toward which their purpose is directed, the weakness of both the good and the wicked will become evident, but that of the wicked will be greater. The weakness of both will be evident because, since both aspire to the highest good, neither can reach it unless purpose leads, guides, or almost compels them, with the great and nearly unconquerable assistance of the leading nature—or rather of God—which they received from God so that, through it, they might attain God himself. But the greater the assistance required for advancing, the less strength they seem to have for advancing. The greater weakness of the wicked will be evident for this reason: of two travelers, the stronger is the one who, walking onward, reaches the place beyond which it is not permitted to proceed; the weaker is the one who, turning aside from the place he intends to reach, does not even reach the place toward which his error seemed to be leading him. Thus the good, since they approach the final end, though compelled by God, are stronger; whereas the wicked, straying from the final end despite their implanted inclination, do not even attain those goods for which they yearn night and day, and are therefore weaker. This will become increasingly evident to anyone who attends to the causes of such error: for the wicked depart from what their implanted inclination seems to carry them toward either through ignorance, disturbance, or knowledge and will.]

“But since I see that you are exceptionally ready to understand,” she said, [Note: [Col. 0794C] “Many.”] “I shall heap up many arguments. Consider, then, how great is the weakness of vicious people, who cannot even reach the goal toward which their natural inclination leads and almost compels them. And what if they were abandoned by the assistance of that leading nature, so great and almost unconquerable? Consider, moreover, how great is the impotence of wicked people. They do not seek trivial or playful rewards, which they are unable to attain and possess; rather, they fail in the very sum and summit of things, and the wretched do not achieve the result in that which alone they labor at day and night. In this respect the strength of the good stands out. For just as you would consider someone exceedingly powerful at walking if, proceeding on foot, he could reach the place beyond which no further passage lay open to walking, so you must necessarily judge someone exceedingly powerful who grasps the end of desirable things, beyond which nothing exists. From this it follows, conversely, that the same wicked people, the same people, appear to be deserted by every strength.” [Note: [Col. 0794C] “Conversely.”]

267 “Why, then, do they pursue vices after abandoning virtue? Is it through ignorance?” [Note: [Col. 0794D] “Through ignorance?”] “Either of the true good, from which they depart, or of the counterfeit good toward which they approach? But ignorance, being nothing, is weaker than nothing. Or do they know what ought to be pursued? But what is more enfeebled than the blindness of ignorance?” [Note: [Col. 0794C] “What is weaker?”] “Or does desire hurl them headlong across the path?” [Note: [Col. 0794D] “Does desire hurl them across the path?”] “That is, is it disturbance? But this is a great indication of a weaker mind, since, overcome by the motions of the bodily servant, it obeys them.”

“Desire hurls them headlong across the path; and thus, through lack of self-control, they are weak, since they cannot struggle against vice.” [Note: [Col. 0794C] “Resist.”]

“Or do they knowingly and willingly abandon the good and turn aside to vices?” [Note: [Col. 0794D] “Do they knowingly and willingly abandon the good and turn aside to vices?”]

“But in that case they cease not only to be powerful but to exist altogether—not, indeed, with respect to their matter, for those wicked people always consist of mind and body, two things joined together, but with respect to their mode of existence. For since God is no less the final end of the human mind than he is its first cause, the human mind is said to exist according to its proper mode only if it tends toward God both in knowledge and in voluntary inclination; but the wicked do not tend toward God in this way.”

“Do they knowingly and willingly abandon the good and turn aside to vices?”

“But in that case they cease not only to be powerful but to exist altogether. For those who abandon the common end of all things likewise cease to exist. This may perhaps seem strange to someone: that we should say that the wicked, who comprise the greater part of humanity, do not exist. But this is how the matter stands. I do not deny that those who are wicked are wicked; but I deny that they exist purely and simply. Just as you may call a corpse a dead human being, but cannot call it simply a human being, so I may grant that vicious people are wicked, but I cannot confess that they exist absolutely. For whatever retains and preserves order preserves nature; but whatever falls away from it abandons even that existence which is grounded in its own nature.” [Note: [Col. 0795B] “To the extent that it can.”]

“But,” you will say, “the wicked can do things.” Nor would I deny this; but their power descends not from strength but from weakness. For they can do evils which they would be altogether unable to do if they could remain within the effective power of the good. This very ability demonstrates more clearly that they can do nothing.

[Note: [Col. 0795C] “For if evil is nothing, etc.” The weakness of the wicked stated above can be confirmed from the nature of evil itself, from God’s power, and from human desire. First, from the nature of evil itself: whoever can do nothing must be regarded not as powerful but rather as powerless; but the wicked can do nothing, since the evil which they are said to be able to do is, according to what has been said, nothing. Second, from God’s power: whatever possesses power belongs to God, since God is the highest good, which has already been proved to be omnipotent. But the ability to do evil, which belongs to the wicked, does not belong to God; otherwise he would not be the highest good. Therefore there is no power in evil, and consequently none in a wicked person insofar as he is wicked. Third, from human desire: whatever has the character of power has the character of good, and therefore can be desired and referred to the highest good, for whose sake all things are desired. But the ability to commit crime, in which alone the wicked person can glory, has no character of good; consequently it cannot be desired or referred to the highest good, as is clear to anyone who considers the matter. All this is confirmed by Plato’s authority; in the Gorgias and Alcibiades he seems to have taught most of what has been said in this discourse.]

“For if, as we gathered a little earlier, evil is nothing, it is clear that, although the wicked can do things, they can do nothing.”

“It is clear.”

“And so that you may understand what the force of this power is, we defined a little earlier that nothing is more powerful than the highest good.”

“So it is,” I said.

“But the highest good cannot do evil.”

“Not at all.”

“Is there, then, anyone who thinks that human beings can do everything?”

“No one, unless he is insane.”

“Yet these same people can do evil.”

“If only they could not!”

“Since, then, only the powerful in good can do everything, while those powerful in evil cannot do everything, it is evident that those who can do evil possess less power.”

“To this must be added that we showed that every power must be counted among desirable things, and that everything desirable is referred to the good, as to a kind of summit of its nature. But [Note: [Col. 0795B] “The power of sinning.”] the ability to commit crime cannot be referred to the good. Therefore it is not desirable. Yet every power is desirable. It is therefore clear that the ability of the wicked is not power. From all this the power of the good and the undeniable weakness of the wicked become evident.”

“And it is clear that this is truly Plato’s view [Note: [Col. 0795B] “In the Gorgias and the first Alcibiades; from these Boethius seems to have drawn these grounds of argument.”]: only the wise can do what they desire, whereas the wicked can indeed do whatever they please, but cannot accomplish what they desire.” They do whatever happens to please them because they think that, through the things in which they take delight, they will attain the good they desire; but they do not attain it, since disgrace does not lead to happiness. [Note: [Col. 0795B] “Which the wicked nevertheless seek even by sinning.”]

269 **METER II**

[Note: [Col. 0795D] A poem composed of two alternating kinds of verse. The first consists of four trochees, with a spondee sometimes substituted; the second consists of three feet, namely a spondee or an anapaest, a dactyl, and a spondee.]

**ARGUMENT.**—Confirming by an example the weakness of the wicked stated above, Philosophy shows that tyrants, terrifying in their seat, clothing, arms, face, and emotional state, are oppressed by as many masters as they have disturbances.

[Note: [Col. 0796B]

Those rulers whom you see sitting high upon the summit of the royal seat, splendid in shining purple, surrounded by cruel arms, threatening with harsh expression, driven by the fury of their hearts—if someone strips these arrogant men of the coverings of their empty adornment, he will immediately perceive that these rulers are inwardly oppressed by tenacious bonds. On one side desire agitates their breasts with insatiable diseases; on the other, disordered anger lashes their minds, stirring up tumults. Now grief breaks the defeated; now uncertain hope torments the same men. Since, then, as you see, one ruler is subjected to so many tyrannical passions, himself harassed by unjust masters, he does not do what he wishes.]

[Note: [Col. 0795D]

“1 and 2. ‘The kings whom you see.’” In proving further that the wicked are weak, Philosophy also shows that rulers commonly regarded as exceedingly powerful are powerless in this respect: overcome by their own disturbances, they become subject to them. She therefore first praises the power of those rulers and then enumerates their disturbances.

“2. ‘Upon the summit of the throne.’” The power of kings is first praised: (1) by their seat, the summit of the throne; (2) by their garments, distinguished by purple; (3) by their arms, or attendants, surrounded by grim arms; (4) by their face, threatening with a grim expression; (5) by the disposition of their mind, panting with the madness of their hearts. Nothing here seems to require explanation, since we have already explained the throne, purple, and grim expression.

“11. ‘For from here desire turns.’” Next the principal disturbances are enumerated, to which the conquered kings are obedient: desire, anger, grief, and hope, from the eleventh verse through the seventeenth.

First, desire, or unbridled craving, is named. Since, according to Cicero, *On Oratory* I, we are taught that it is through the authority and command of the laws that we keep our desires subdued and restrain all cravings, a ruler who believes himself bound by no laws is especially subject to desire. This craving is now said to ‘turn hearts with greedy poisons,’ because just as poison is a substance which, having entered the body and been carried through the circulating blood, spreads in such a way as to extinguish life, so the disturbance described above, infused into the mind, eventually drives away good will, the chief life of that same mind.

Second, anger is named, or, in Cicero’s words, the desire to punish one who seems to have injured someone wrongfully. Since this disturbance arises from the belief that one has been despised, and since a ruler, the greater he is, can the more easily imagine that he is being despised, he is therefore more often subject to anger. This anger of the king will raise all the greater waves in its turbulence as his authority is greater.

Third, grief, or sorrow, is named. This disturbance is a kind of tearful suffering arising from evils which cannot be driven away. It therefore seems greater in a ruler because, conscious of his authority, he readily believes that no evils ought to befall him which he cannot repel.

Fourth, hope, or expectation of good, is named, because a king surrounded by wealth and subjects thinks that he can do everything and is therefore easily affected by hope.]

The kings whom you see sitting high,

Upon the summit of the throne,

Resplendent in shining purple,

Surrounded by grim arms,

[5] Threatening with a grim face,

Panting with the madness of their hearts—

If someone strips the proud

Of the coverings of empty adornment,

He will immediately see them inwardly

[10] Bearing tight chains as masters.

270 For from here desire turns

[Col. 0797A] [Note: [Col. 0797C]

“17 and 18. ‘When you see one head bearing so many tyrants.’” When you see one ruler subjected to so many disturbances, as though to an equal number of tyrants.

“19. ‘He himself.’” Some may think that *ipsum* should be read, since it seems to refer to the previously mentioned *caput*, ‘head.’ But this is a syllepsis, a combination of sense rather than of words, as in Terence: ‘Where is the crime that destroyed me?’; in Cicero: ‘two unwelcome prodigies, whom poverty …’; in Horace: ‘so that he might give the fatal monster to chains, which, seeking a more noble death, …’]

Greedily turning hearts with poisons;

From here anger lashes the mind,

Raising turbulent waves;

[15] Either grief wears down the captives,

Or slippery hope torments them.

Therefore, when you see one head

Bearing so many tyrants,

He himself, a lord pressed by unjust powers,

[20] Does not do what he desires.

271 **PROSE III**

**ARGUMENT.**—Philosophy adds that the good are affected by rewards and the wicked by punishments inwardly, so that the good are transformed into gods and the wicked into beasts.

“Do you see, then,” [Note: [Col. 0798B] “O Boethius.”] “in what filth [Note: [Col. 0798B] “Mud.”] crimes wallow, and with what light virtue shines? It is evident in this that rewards are never absent from the good, nor punishments from crimes.”

[Note: [Col. 0797D] “For of things which are done, etc.” I. The good are affected by rewards. Since a reward is called an honor bestowed upon those who first and foremost have accomplished something outstanding—hence Scaliger and many others derive *praemium*, ‘reward,’ as though from *prae* and *emo*, ‘I take beforehand’—that for the sake of which each thing is done may rightly be regarded as the reward of that thing. It is, after all, the honor bestowed upon the doer and victor. Thus, for one running in a race, the crown for which he runs is the reward, just as Saint Paul says in 1 Corinthians 9: ‘Those who run in a race all run, but one receives the prize.’ Now good people attain that for the sake of which all human beings, good and wicked alike, act: namely, happiness, or the highest good. Otherwise they would not be good, since no one who lacks the good is good.]

“For of things which are done, that for the sake of which each thing is done may rightly be regarded as the reward of that thing; just as, for the runner in the stadium, the crown for which he runs lies before him as the reward. But we have shown that happiness is the very good for the sake of which everything is done. Therefore the good itself is set before human actions as their common reward.”

[Note: [Col. 0798B] “Rightly.”]

[Note: [Col. 0798C] “But this cannot be separated from the good, etc.” II. The reward by which the good are affected is inherent in them. Whatever reward exists in a person’s thought can be believed to be inherent in that person, since thought is a quality inherent in the mind. But the reward by which the good are affected exists in thought; otherwise it would not be considered a good reward, since no one judges a person who possesses the good to be deprived of a reward. Hence, however fiercely the wicked rage, just as they did not bestow this reward, so they cannot take away the reward of the good, which can be lost only through the evil will of its possessor.]

“But this cannot be separated from the good. For someone who lacks the good will no longer rightly be called good; therefore virtuous conduct does not abandon its rewards. However fiercely the wicked may rage, the crown will not fall from the wise person or wither. The wickedness of another does not seize the distinctive honor belonging to good minds. If he rejoiced in something received from outside, someone else—or even the one who had bestowed it—could take it away. But since each person’s virtue bestows it upon him, he will lack his reward only when he has ceased to be good. Finally, since every reward is desired because it is believed to be good, who would judge someone who possesses the good to be deprived of a reward?” [Note: [Col. 0798B] “A participant in the good.”]

[Note: [Col. 0798C] “But what reward, etc.” III. The good are transformed into gods. Whoever is happy must properly be called a god—not by nature, but by that union through which his mind, not merely by knowing but also by willing, becomes one thing with God, as was inferred above in the manner of a corollary. Now all good people, insofar as they are inwardly affected by reward, as we have proved, are happy, or united in thought with the highest good.]

“But what reward?”

“The most beautiful and greatest of all. Remember that corollary [Note: [Col. 0798B] “Inference.”] which I recently made especially prominent, and draw the conclusion as follows. Since the good itself is happiness, it is clear that all good people become happy simply by being good. But those who are happy must properly be called gods. Therefore the reward of the good—one which no day can wear away, no power diminish, and no wickedness darken [Note: [Col. 0798B] “Will obscure.”—]is to become gods.”

“Since this is so,” [Note: [Col. 0798D] “Concerning the inseparable punishment of the wicked as well, etc.”] “the wicked, conversely, are affected inwardly by punishments in such a way that they are transformed into beasts. For, as Cicero says, opposites have opposite consequences. Good and evil are opposed antecedents, while reward and punishment are opposed consequences; that is, they stand opposed to one another on contrary fronts. Therefore, just as reward belongs to the good, so punishment belongs to the wicked. Moreover, just as the reward of the good, inherent in good minds, exists in their thought, so the punishment of the wicked, inherent in wicked minds, likewise exists in their thought—namely, in conscience. ‘Great is the power of conscience in both directions,’ says Cicero in *Pro Milone*, ‘so that those who have done nothing wrong do not fear, while those who have sinned think punishment is always before their eyes.’ Saint Ambrose says in *On Duties* I: ‘The wicked person is punishment to himself, while the just person is grace to himself, so that the recompense of either good or evil deeds is paid from within.’ Finally, just as the good person becomes a god through good thought, so the wicked person becomes a beast through evil thought.

“The human mind stands midway between God, its creator, and the body, its companion. According to the character of its thought—good or evil—it forms, through a certain relationship, something unified either with God or with the body. Since there is so great a resemblance between the human body and the body of a beast that the former differs from the latter only through the mind by which it is formed, a human being therefore becomes a beast by reason of his evil thought. This is what the prophet-king forbids in Psalm 31: ‘Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding.’”

“A wise person cannot doubt the inseparable punishment of the wicked. For since good and evil, and likewise punishment and reward, stand opposed to each other on contrary fronts, whatever we see occurring in the reward of the good must necessarily correspond in the opposite way to the punishment of the wicked. Therefore, just as virtue itself becomes the reward of the good, so wickedness is the punishment of the wicked. Moreover, whoever is affected by punishment cannot doubt that he has been affected by evil. If, then, the wicked wish to assess themselves, can those be thought free from punishment whom the uttermost wickedness of all evils not only affects but deeply infects?” [Note: [Col. 0799B] “To judge themselves.”]

“Consider, on the contrary, what punishment accompanies the wicked in opposition to the good. For you learned a little earlier that everything that exists is one, and that the one itself is good. Consequently, everything that exists appears also to be good. In this way, whatever falls away from the good ceases to exist; hence the wicked cease to be what they had been. That they were human beings is still displayed by the remaining appearance of the human body. Therefore, having been turned into wickedness, they have also lost human nature. But since only virtue can raise someone above human beings, wickedness must necessarily thrust below the dignity of humanity those whom it has cast down from the human condition. Thus it happens that, when you see someone transformed by vices, you cannot regard him as a human being.”

273 [Note: [Col. 0799C] “Avarice burns, etc.”] Thus the miser resembles a wolf, because the wolf is an exceedingly voracious animal; hence prostitutes, being rapacious like wolves, are called *lupae*, ‘she-wolves,’ according to Isidore. The fierce and restless or agitated person resembles a dog, than which nothing is more shameless. The plotter resembles a little fox, the most cunning of beasts, which uses cunning to preserve its life. The person subject to anger resembles a lion, which Ovid calls irascible, because, as Lucretius says in Book III, “there is more heat in it.” The fearful person resembles deer, no animal being more timid; hence formerly a fearful man who trusted more in flight than in strength was called *cervinus*, “deer-like,” because, according to Lucretius in Book III, “there is more cold in deer.” The sluggish and stupid person resembles an ass, the slowest of animals. The fickle and inconstant person resembles birds, which flit here and there. The lustful person resembles swine, which, as Festus says, are the filthiest of all domesticated animals and possess the most ardent lust, so that an insult to women has been derived from this when they are said to *subare* and *surire*, “to be in heat.”]

[Note: [Col. 0799B] “The miser to the wolf.”] “Is he ablaze with avarice, a violent despoiler of other people’s wealth? You would call him like a wolf.” [Note: [Col. 0799B] “The quarrelsome person to the dog.”] “Is he fierce and restless, exercising his tongue in quarrels? You will compare him to a dog.” [Note: [Col. 0799B] “The plotter to the fox.”] “Does the plotter delight in stealing through hidden frauds? Let him be made equal to little foxes.” [Note: [Col. 0799B] “The angry person to the lion.”] “Does the intemperate man in anger roar? Let him be thought to carry the spirit of a lion.”

[5] [Note: [Col. 0799B] “The cowardly person to the deer.”] “Does the fearful and fleeing person dread things that need not be feared? Let him be considered like deer.” [Note: [Col. 0799B] “The sluggish person to the ass.”] “Is he sluggish and stupid, numb with torpor?” [Note: [Col. 0799D] “He lives an ass.” This is a sufficiently familiar manner of speaking, called ellipsis, in which some unexpressed particle must be understood. Here *secundum*, ‘as,’ is understood, as when one says, ‘He lies for the greater part; otherwise he is prudent,’ and similarly in other cases.] “He lives as an ass.” [Note: [Col. 0799B] “The flighty person to the bird.”] “Does the fickle and inconstant person change his pursuits? He differs in no way from birds.” [Note: [Col. 0799C] “The pleasure-seeker resembles a pig.”] “Is he immersed in filthy and unclean lusts? He is held by the sordid pleasure of a sow.”

Thus it happens that whoever, having abandoned virtue, has ceased to be a human being, cannot pass into the divine condition and is therefore transformed into a beast. [Col. 0800B]

274 **METER III**

[Note: [Col. 0799D] This is called Glyconic: a poem consisting of one kind of verse, each line composed of a trochee and two dactyls. It differs in this respect from another Glyconic poem, of which we have already spoken, in which a spondee precedes two dactyls. You will not understand this poem until you recall what poets commonly say both about Circe and about Ulysses. They say that Circe, daughter of the Sun and the nymph Perse, was highly skilled in magic. She married the king of the Sarmatians; after killing him with poisons, she fled to Italy, to a mountain which, because it is surrounded by certain marshes, appears to have the form of an island, and which was later called Circaean after its inhabitant. Here the cruel enchantress was said to transform human beings into beasts by offering certain cups and uttering certain words: some into lions, some into wolves, some into tigers, some into swine, and others into other beasts. Our celebrated Antonius Hallaeus elegantly expressed this from Homer:

“Those from whom the wanton goddess had taken human features

And to whom she had given those of beasts. Here is one bent into a wolf’s limbs,

Who howls and is afraid of himself; another grows into a lion,

Yet harmless in tooth and claw, or into a bear with blackening fur,

While another, a spotted tiger, ranges through spacious halls.”

Ulysses, on the other hand, was born on Mount Neritus in Ithaca, to Laertes—or, as some prefer, to Sisyphus—as his father, and to Anticlea as his mother. Homer represents him as a man endowed with great eloquence and no less experience, shrewd in counsel, excellent in war, and most patient of hardship. After Troy was captured, he boarded a ship to return to his homeland; but after various wanderings, which are not at issue here, he was carried by the winds to Mount Circaeum, where Circe transformed his scouts into swine. He himself, however, after taking the herb called *moly*, which Mercury had taught him about, preserved his form unharmed. The aforementioned Hallaeus described this as follows in continuation:

“When the new company entered together, not forgetful of

The Colchian art, the enchantress offers enchanted cups

To the astonished guests; and, with words suited to changing forms,

She murmurs the spells of the Titan’s daughter. In order, she strikes them all

[Col. 0801B] With the tip of her portent-bearing wand;

Without delay they fall upon the ground, and, preparing to mourn,

See themselves grunting hoarsely like swine and their hides bristling

Already with dense hairs; and, lying beneath the holm oak,

They chew the shaken-down acorns instead of Ceres’ gift.

Only Ulysses remains beneath a human appearance …

And blunts the hidden power of the rare plant,

Which the gods call *moly*: God had given the hero

A safeguard against these arts—God who crosses the air

On his feet and serves both highest and lowest Jove.”]

**III**

**ARGUMENT.**—“The vices of the wicked,” says Philosophy, “are more powerful than Circe’s spells. They do not, like those spells, transform bodies into boars, lions, wolves, tigers, or swine; they attack the mind itself.”

[Note: [Col. 0800B]

The ship in which Ulysses, the leader, was carried with his companions, after various wanderings at sea, was driven by the winds to an island where Circe, a beautiful goddess born from the Sun, lived and offered enchanted cups to newly arrived strangers. When Circe, powerful in herbs, had transformed them into various shapes, one assumed the face of a boar; another, made into an African lion, grew teeth and claws; one, counted among wolves, howled while trying to mourn; another, like an Indian tiger, roamed around the houses, though gentle. Although Mercury, the winged god of Arcadia, [Col. 0801B] took pity on Ulysses, tossed about by various misfortunes, and freed him from the poison of his hostess, nevertheless the rowers of that same leader had already swallowed the evil potions; already turned into swine, they had exchanged bread, Ceres’ gift, for acorns, and, having lost speech and bodily form, nothing of them remained intact. Only one mind survived, grieving over the monstrous transformations which it itself endured. O right hand of Circe, weaker than this! O herbs of the enchantress, ineffectual! Although they can change the body, they cannot change the mind. This is the power of perverse habits implanted in human beings and enclosed in the mind as in a hidden citadel: savage poisons that draw a human being away from himself more effectively, since they penetrate the mind and, while sparing the body, afflict the mind with a grievous wound.]

[Note: [Col. 0801B]

“1. ‘The sails of the Neritian leader.’” The ships of Ulysses, who is called Neritian after Mount Neritus, where he was born; and he is called “leader” because, under that title, he went to the Trojan War and rendered the Greeks extremely valuable service—although, if we believe Ajax in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XIII, verse 25:

“These deeds he performs without a witness; only night is aware of them.”

“2. ‘Wandering ships upon the sea.’” Ulysses wandered at sea for ten years.

“3. ‘The East Wind drove him ashore.’” Properly speaking, the East Wind is the wind blowing from the spring or equinoctial sunrise; but here it seems to be taken for any stronger wind. Unless one says that Ulysses sailed from east to west, intending to reach Circe’s infamous shore; for, approaching Mount Circaeum from the monstrous Laestrygonians, he departed from Formiae. Formiae, however, above Caieta, is an ancient promontory farther east than the ancient promontory of Circe, which lies below Tarracina.

“3. ‘Of the island.’” This refers to Mount Circaeum, which has something of the form of an island. Virgil, *Aeneid* III, verse 386: ‘And the island of Circe, Aeaea.’ And *Aeneid* VII, verse 10.”]

The nearest shores of Circe’s land are skirted.

5. “Born from the seed of the Sun.” Circe, daughter of the Sun. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XIV, line 10: “Circe, born of the Sun”; and line 33:

> Here I am, though I am a goddess, though I am the daughter of the radiant Sun;  
> I can accomplish so much by song, and so much also by herbs,  
> I vow that I shall be yours.”

Virgil, *Aeneid* VII, line 11:

> Rich in inaccessible groves, where the daughter of the Sun  
> resounds continually with song.

7. “Cups touched by song.” In the briefest terms, the wand, incantation, and herb are signified by which Circe used to transform men into beasts. Virgil, *Eclogues* 8:

> By her spells Circe changed the companions of Ulysses.

And *Aeneid* VII, line 19:

> Those whom the savage goddess Circe had clothed, by means of powerful herbs,  
> with the faces and backs of wild beasts.

10. “This man the form of a boar,” etc. Of her new guests, one is changed into a boar, another into a lion, this one into a wolf, that one into a tiger. But the lion is called Marmaric and the tiger Indian because Marmarica, a region of Africa toward Egypt, is accustomed to produce powerful lions, whereas India produces tigers. Ovid also recalls these forms, *Metamorphoses* XIV, line 260:

> A thousand wolves, and bears mingled with wolves, and lionesses,  
> by their encounter caused fear; but there was nothing to fear,  
> nor anything that would inflict a wound upon our bodies.  
> Indeed, they moved their gentle tails through the air  
> and accompanied our steps, fawning upon us, until  
> the maidservants received them.

18. “The winged deity of Arcadia.” Mercury, so called from *merces* (“merchandise”), because he is believed to preside over profit and over things bought and sold. Hence he is usually painted holding a wand in his left hand and a money-pouch in his right. Mercury is now called a deity because, as the son of Jupiter and Maia, he was believed, like a kind of divinity, to preside not only over unjust as well as just profit, but also over eloquence. Hence he is regarded as the messenger of the gods, insofar as minds become known through eloquent speech. But he is called a winged deity because he is imagined to bear wings both on his feet and on his head, since speech, over which he presides, is carried swiftly through the air.

He is also called the winged deity of Arcadia because the Arcadians derived their origin and name from Arcas, the son of Jupiter and Callisto; Mercury, however, was born in Arcadia. Hence Virgil addresses the Arcadians in *Aeneid* VIII, line 138:

> Mercury is your father, whom radiant Maia  
> bore, conceived upon the icy summit of Cyllene.

Finally, Mercury had given Ulysses, tossed about by various misfortunes, an herb by whose aid he was freed from Circe’s treacherous cups. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XIV, line 296:

> The peace-bringing Cyllenian had given him a white flower,  
> which the gods call *moly*; it is held by a black root.  
> Safe through it, and with the heavenly instructions as well, he enters  
> the house of Circe; and when she attempts, with her treacherous cup,  
> to stroke his hair with her wand, he repels her and, drawing his sword,  
> terrifies her as she trembles.

21. “Yet now the wicked rowers,” etc. A rower, from *remus* (“oar”), is one who propels a ship through the water with an oar. Such were those soldiers of Ulysses, since they were carried in the same ship as Ulysses and moved it—for the ship remained intact, carrying him and his companions. These soldiers or companions of Ulysses had been sent ahead by their leader to reconnoiter Circe. Before Ulysses himself arrived, they had already drunk the cup and been changed into swine, and had turned bread, or grain-food, into acorns. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XIV, line 281:

> We received the sacred cups given by her right hand,  
> and, thirsty, drank them down with our parched mouths.  
> The dread goddess touched the tops of our hair with her wand,  
> and—I am ashamed, but I shall tell it—I began to bristle with hair,  
> and no longer able to speak, I uttered a hoarse  
> grunt instead of words, and fell forward upon the ground,  
> my whole face to the earth. I felt my mouth hardening  
> into a broad snout, my neck swelling with folds,  
> and with that part by which the cups had just been taken  
> I left my tracks.

27. “The mind alone,” etc. Circe, like the Sun of whom she was the daughter, could, by the force of the herbs, words, and wand that she used, change bodies, but not minds, since just as minds are created by God alone and preserved by him, so they can be changed by God alone. Except that a certain divinely implanted power belongs to that same mind—namely, the will, mistress of itself—which, when it obeys the passions, seems indeed to spare the body, but withdraws the mind from God in such a way that it appears to depress that mind to the lowest condition of beasts.

> Now they had turned their grain-food
