279. **PROSE IV**

**ARGUMENT.**—Philosophy, intending to confirm still further the misery of the wicked, shows that they are more miserable because they accomplish what they desire for a longer time, live unpunished, and inflict injury upon others.

Then I said: “I confess, and I see that it is not unjustly said, that the vicious, although they preserve the appearance of a human body, are nevertheless changed into beasts in the quality of their souls. But I would not have those whose savage and criminal minds rage through the destruction of the good possess this very power.”

“They do not possess it,” she replied, “as will be shown in its proper place. Yet if that very thing which they are believed to possess were taken away from them, the punishment of criminal people would be relieved to a considerable extent.”

I. Philosophy proves that the wicked are more miserable because they accomplish what they desire. For to wish for a crime is great misery; to be able to commit it is greater; to accomplish it is greatest of all. These are forms of falling away, and they increase in proportion as one withdraws more and more from God, or from the supreme good. Therefore, if the wicked not only wish and are able to commit a crime, but actually accomplish it, they will thereby be more miserable. Yet in accomplishing what they desire, the wicked accomplish a crime; for since they are wicked, they attempt to accomplish nothing except evil, and therefore crime.

For if the following may perhaps seem incredible to anyone, it is necessary that the wicked are more wretched when they have accomplished what they desire than if they had been unable to fulfill their desires. For if it is miserable to have wished for wrongdoing, it is more miserable to have been able to do so, without which the effect of the miserable will would have languished. Thus, since each person has his own misery, those whom you see wishing for, being able to commit, and accomplishing a crime must necessarily be oppressed by a threefold misfortune.

“I agree,” I said, “but I fervently wish that they might quickly be rid of this misfortune, deprived of the ability to perpetrate crime and ignorant of wrongdoing.”

“They will be rid of it,” she replied, “sooner than you perhaps wish, or than they themselves imagine they will be.”

For within the very short limits of life there is nothing so slow that an immortal soul would regard waiting for it as long. Their great hopes and lofty structure of crimes is often destroyed by a sudden and unexpected end, which indeed sets a limit to their misery.

280. **“For if wickedness makes them miserable,” etc.**

II. The same philosophy proves that the wicked are more miserable because, living longer lives, they accomplish what they desire for a longer time. For just as misery makes a person miserable, so happiness makes a person happy; and just as someone is happier the longer his happiness lasts, so someone is more miserable the longer his misery lasts. Both acquire such strength as they proceed that the older either becomes, the more difficult it is for it to be destroyed by its opposite. But the longer the wicked, by living longer, accomplish what they desire, the longer their misery lasts, since, as we have said, accomplishing a crime is the greatest misery. Therefore they would be utterly wretched if death at least did not bring their wickedness to an end. Although death is not the boundary of the misery of each one of them, it is nevertheless the end of the crimes they accomplish.

For if wickedness makes people miserable, the longer a wicked person lives, the more miserable he must be. I would judge them utterly unhappy if death at least did not bring their wickedness to an end. For if we have drawn a true conclusion concerning the misfortune of wickedness, it is clear that the misery which is established as eternal is infinite.

Then I said: “The inference is indeed remarkable and difficult to accept, but I recognize that it agrees exceedingly well with what was granted earlier.”

“You judge rightly,” she replied. “But whoever considers it difficult to accept the conclusion ought either to show that something previously granted is false, or to demonstrate that the comparison of the propositions does not produce a valid necessary conclusion. Otherwise, once the premises have been granted, there is absolutely nothing about which one can complain in the inference.”

“For this also which I shall say,” etc.

III. Philosophy proves that the wicked are more miserable because they live unpunished—not only because punishments restrain the guilty and keep the innocent from crimes, but also because, just as misery increases through the addition of evil, so happiness increases through the addition of good. For just as good is happiness, so evil is misery, as has been said. Therefore, whenever something evil happens to a miserable person, he is thereby more miserable, just as whenever something good happens to a happy person, he is thereby happier.

But something evil happens to the wicked person because he lives unpunished. Since being punished and not being punished are opposites, and since being punished is something good even for the wicked, it necessarily follows that not being punished is something evil for that same wicked person, although great punishments of souls remain after the body has been put to death.

“For this too that I shall say may seem no less astonishing, but it is equally necessary from the premises.”

“What is it?” I asked.

“The wicked are happier when they undergo punishment than if no punishment of justice restrains them.”

“I am not now arguing,” she continued, “the point that may occur to anyone’s mind: that punishment reforms wicked conduct and leads people back to the right path through fear of punishment, while also providing an example to others to avoid what must be condemned. I consider the wicked more unfortunate when they are unpunished in another way, even when no account is taken of correction and no regard is paid to example.”

“And what other way is there?” I asked.

“Did we not grant that the good are happy and the wicked miserable?”

“That is so.”

“If, then, something good is added to someone’s misery, is he not happier than the person whose misery is pure and solitary, without any admixture of good?”

“So it seems,” I said.

“What if another evil were attached to that same miserable person, who is deprived of every good except those things through which he is miserable? Would he not be judged much more unhappy than the person whose misfortune is relieved by participation in some good?”

“Certainly,” I said.

“Therefore, when the wicked are punished, something good is attached to them—namely, punishment itself, which is good by reason of justice. But when they lack punishment, something further evil is present in them: impunity itself, which you have admitted to be evil by reason of its injustice.”

“I cannot deny it.”

“Therefore the wicked are much more unfortunate when granted unjust impunity than when punished by just retribution. But it is clear that the punishment of the wicked is just, whereas their escape unpunished is unjust.”

“Who could deny that?”

“But no one will deny this either,” she said: “that everything just is good, and, conversely, that what is unjust is clearly evil.”

Then I said: “These conclusions follow from what was established earlier. But I ask you: do you leave no punishments of souls remaining after the body has been put to death?”

“Very great ones,” she replied—“some, I think, are exercised with penal severity, others with purifying clemency. Vallinus says: ‘Here Boethius acknowledges the wicked—not merely as a Christian but also as a Catholic—that some are condemned to eternal punishments, while others, for their sins, are long tortured by suffering and purified for a long time by fire.’ The Magdeburg Centuriators also acknowledge this, century 6, chapter 4, as something conceived by Boethius. Unless, however, Philosophy, who is now speaking, wished here to express the views of the Platonists, or even of the Pythagoreans, according to whom certain souls, because their crimes could not be washed away by any purification, were subjected to eternal punishments; while others, whose crimes were lesser, either, after completing all purification, enjoyed the eternal pleasures of Elysium, or, partly purified, were thrust from Elysium into new bodies, even those of beasts. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, line 739:

> Therefore they are disciplined by punishments and pay the penalties  
> of their former wrongs: some are stretched out empty,  
> suspended in the winds; for others, beneath the vast abyss,  
> the stain of guilt is washed away or burned by fire.  
> Each of us suffers his own spirit. From there we are sent  
> through spacious Elysium, and a few possess the joyful fields.”

“I think that some are exercised by penal severity, others by purifying clemency. But it is not my present purpose to discuss these matters. Up to this point we have acted so that you would recognize that the power of the wicked, which seemed to you most deplorable, is no power at all; that those whose impunity you lamented never lack the punishments of their wickedness; that the license whose speedy end you prayed for is not long-lasting; that it would be more unfortunate if it lasted longer, and most unfortunate if it were eternal; and, finally, that the wicked are more miserable when dismissed through unjust impunity than when punished by just retribution. It follows from this judgment that they are then oppressed by more severe punishments when they are believed to be unpunished.”

When I considered your arguments, I said, I thought nothing could be said more truly.

282. **“But if we turn to human judgments,” etc.**

Our mind stands midway between God and the human body, being both an effect of God and the form of the human body. From each it suffers: it must be enlightened by God and darkened by the body. Therefore the same mind is not yet capable of delivering a true and certain judgment concerning proposed matters until, having rejected the movements of the body itself, it has questioned God alone as teacher and attentively understood him answering within.

For Saint Augustine says most excellently in *On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis* I, chapter 5: “The beginning of the intellectual creature is eternal wisdom; and this beginning, remaining unchangeably in itself, never ceases, through the hidden inspiration of its calling, to speak to the creature whose beginning it is, so that it may turn back to that from which it is. Otherwise it could not be formed and perfected.”

The same holy teacher says everywhere in *Confessions* X, chapter 26: “Truth, you preside over all who consult you and at the same time answer all who consult you, even when they consult you about different things. You answer clearly, but not everyone hears clearly.” For who, says that same most holy father in *On the Immortality of the Soul*, chapter 10, “when examining himself properly, has not discovered that he understood something more sincerely in proportion as he was able to remove and withdraw the attention of his mind from bodily senses?” Yet most people judge through haste and prejudice rather than according to these laws.

But if I return to human judgments, who is there to whom these things would seem not merely unworthy of belief, but at least unworthy of hearing?

“So it is,” she replied. “For eyes accustomed to darkness cannot raise themselves to the light of transparent truth. They are like bats and owls, whose eyes, because they possess more mobile fibers and membranes, can be illuminated by the slightest light of night but are overwhelmed by the greater brilliance of day. Therefore they are accustomed to fly only in the evening and at night, from which they take their names. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV, tale 12:

> And now the day had ended, and the time was approaching  
> that you could call neither darkness nor light,  
> but the boundary of uncertain night adjoining the light . . .  
> They inhabit not the forests and hate the light;  
> they fly by night and take their name from the late evening.”

“They are like birds whose sight night illuminates but day blinds. For while they look not upon the order of things but upon their own passions, they think either license or impunity for crimes to be happiness. But consider what the eternal law decrees: If you have conformed your soul to better things, you have no need of a judge to bestow a reward; you yourself have joined yourself to what is superior. If you have turned your zeal toward worse things, do not seek an avenger outside yourself; you yourself have thrust yourself into lower things. It is as though, alternately, you looked at filthy earth and at the sky: while everything external remained unchanged, by the very act of seeing you would seem now to be among mud, now among the stars.”

“But the common people do not consider these things.”

“What follows, then? Should we not approach those whom we have shown to be like beasts? What if someone, having completely lost his sight, also forgot ever having possessed the power of sight and believed that he lacked nothing for human perfection? Would we regard seeing people as equally blind?”

283. **“For they will not even accept this,” etc.**

IV. Philosophy proves that the wicked are more miserable because they inflict injury upon others. For since every wicked person is miserable, and since anyone deserving punishment is wicked, the more someone deserves punishment, the more wicked and therefore the more miserable he must be considered. Thus a judge who believes that inflicting injury is worse than suffering it determines that punishment should be inflicted not upon the person who suffered the injury but upon the person who committed it. Hence Christ says in Matthew 5: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution.” Referring to this, Saint Chrysostom says that no one is harmed except by himself.

But the wicked are more deserving of punishment because they have inflicted injury upon another; for it is in the interest of the commonwealth that the wicked be punished. From all this it follows that the wicked—those sick in soul—are worthy not of hatred but rather of pity, just as those sick in body are.

“For they will not even accept what rests upon equally strong foundations of reasoning: that those who inflict injury are more unfortunate than those who suffer it.”

“I should like to hear these very arguments,” I said.

“Do you deny that every wicked person is deserving of punishment?”

“Not at all.”

“That those who are wicked are unfortunate is clear in many ways.”

“That is so.”

“Then you do not doubt that those deserving punishment are miserable?”

“I agree.”

“If you were sitting as judge,” she said, “whom would you think ought to receive punishment: the person who had committed the injury, or the person who had suffered it?”

“I do not doubt,” I replied, “that I would satisfy the person who had suffered it by punishing the pain-causer.”

“Then the person who inflicted the injury would seem to you more miserable than the person who received it.”

“That follows.”

“On this and other grounds resting upon the same root—namely, that moral disgrace makes people miserable by its own nature—it is evident that an injury inflicted upon anyone is the misery not of the recipient but of the person who inflicts it.”

“But now,” she said, “advocates act contrary to this. On behalf of those who have suffered something grave and bitter, they try to arouse the pity of judges, although more just pity is owed to those who commit the injury. The latter ought to be led before the court not by angry but by favorably disposed and compassionate accusers, just as sick people are led to a physician, so that the diseases of guilt may be cut away by punishment. In this way the work of defenders would either become entirely useless, or, if they preferred to benefit people, it would be turned into the role of accusers.

“The wicked themselves, if they were permitted in some way to glimpse the virtue that remains through some small opening, and if they could see that they would lay aside the filth of their vices through the torments of punishment, would say that these torments were not torments in view of the compensation of attaining goodness. They would reject the services of defenders and surrender themselves entirely to accusers and judges. Thus among the wise no place at all is left for hatred. Who but the most foolish would hate the good? To hate the wicked, however, is without reason. For if, just as bodily weakness is a kind of illness, viciousness is likewise a sort of sickness of souls, and if we judge the bodily sick wholly undeserving of hatred but rather deserving of pity, then much more are those to be pitied, not persecuted, whose minds are oppressed by wickedness more grievously than by any illness.”

285. **METER IV**

A poem composed of two alternating kinds of verse. The first is a Phalaecian, containing a spondee, a dactyl, and two trochees; hence in the fifth verse one should read *apri*, not *aper*. The second is an elegiac pentameter, discussed above.

**ARGUMENT.**—Since death threatens, whether coming of its own accord or hastened by wild beasts and other human beings, Philosophy says that it is better to love the good and pity the wicked than to hate anyone or attack anyone with weapons.

“What benefit is there in stirring up such great movements of hatred and hastening death by your own hands? If you seek death, it approaches of its own accord and does not hold back its swift horses. Human beings, of course, kill one another with the sword, whom the serpent, lion, tiger, bear, and boar kill with their teeth. Do they therefore organize unjust armies, prepare cruel weapons, and desire to fall beneath returning weapons because their characters differ and disagree among themselves? This is not a sufficiently just reason for savagery. Do you wish to return a fitting recompense for a fitting merit? Love the good, as justice requires, and pity the wicked.”

1. “Such great movements.” Just as bodily disturbances are conceived through movements, so those disturbances, once conceived, produce various movements of the same body. Yet no disturbance produces movements as great as hatred does. For those who are stirred by hatred break out against the friends, possessions, reputation, and finally the very life of their adversaries.

2. “To stir up fate with one’s hand.” Properly, a person is said to “stir up” something when he moves a body from its place, as though, by moving it from its own ground, he leaves the neighboring object from which it departs without its own ground, so that the object itself departs. Hence, by a certain resemblance, we say that we stir the mind when we attempt to move it from its position by hope, fear, or any other means. Thus those who fight a duel, because they appear to move death toward themselves as though it had been driven from its own seat, are said to stir up death with their own hands. Seneca sings similarly in *Hercules Furens*, line 867:

> What good does it do to hasten harsh fate?  
> All this wandering crowd throughout the broad lands  
> will go to the shades and spread its sails  
> upon sluggish Cocytus.

3. “If you seek death,” etc. Philosophy seems next to set forth the causes of death. The cause of death is twofold. One is internal, or natural: the composition of the elements of which a human being consists. This is indicated by the words “it approaches of its own accord.” The other is external, and this in turn is divided into two kinds. Death is caused either by wild beasts—such as the serpent, lion, tiger, bear, and boar—or by other human beings, who, as though indignant that death hastened by the foregoing causes is taking too long, summon it by turning their weapons against one another.

> What benefit is there in stirring up such great movements  
> and stirring up fate with your own hand?  
> If you seek death, it approaches of its own accord;  
> it does not hold back its swift horses.

5. “Boars.” We read this with Vallinus as *apri*, not *aper*, because the first syllable of *aper* is always short; otherwise *apri* would not have a common first syllable. The first syllables of *matris* and *fratris* are likewise not common, since *mater* and *frater* lengthen their first syllables.

10. “There is not a sufficiently just reason for savagery.” Another person’s thoughts, opposed to your own thoughts, cannot give you any right to kill another human being, since human life is so completely under the supreme power of God alone that neither a judge nor the king himself may lawfully kill a human being, except insofar as the king acts as God’s representative. For, as God says in Genesis 9, “the human being was made in the image of God.”

11. “Do you wish to return a fitting recompense for merits?” By thinking of returning like for like, or compensating thoughts with thoughts.

12. “Love the good according to justice.” Since love can be compensated only by love, justice requires that we love those good people by whom we are loved. Yet it does not follow that hatred should be repaid with hatred.

12. “Pity the wicked.” Nothing is more consistent with reason than to pity the miserable. All the wicked, however, are miserable, both for the reasons stated above and especially because, by sinning, they fall away. For, if we believe Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, *miser* (“wretched”) is derived from *minus* (“less”), as being one for whom, when there is need, there is less than nothing; or, as Cujacius prefers, from the Greek μῦσος (*mysos*, “crime”).

286.

> Those whom the serpent, lion, tiger, bear, and boar  
> attack with their teeth, nevertheless attack one another with the sword.  
> Do their characters differ and disagree so greatly  
> that they wage unjust battle-lines and savage wars,  
> and wish to perish beneath weapons turned against one another?  
> There is not a sufficiently just reason for such savagery.  
> Do you wish to return a fitting recompense for merits?  
> Love the good according to justice, and pity the wicked.

287. **PROSE V**

**ARGUMENT.**—Because it seemed to Boethius astonishing, in the manner of a wise man, that although God governs the world, adversity comes to the good and prosperity to the wicked, Philosophy warns him that he ought not therefore to doubt that everything is rightly ordered merely because he does not know the reason for so great an arrangement.

“Here,” I said, “I see what happiness or misery is established in the very merits of the good and the wicked. But in this popular and ordinary fortune I perceive that there is also some good or evil.”

I. Boethius, as it seemed to him, wonders in the manner of a wise man that adversity comes to the good and prosperity to the wicked, for two reasons. First, the people would more readily trust wise leaders and observe their instructions more faithfully if they saw the happiness of wise leaders being infused into the people along with wisdom. Second, punishments seem to have been established only for the wicked. Here punishments mean imprisonment and chains. Chains—or, as others read, *lex*—are a punishment because to be weighed down by bonds is a punishment. Prison is also counted by Lucretius among the various kinds of punishment, book III:

> But fear of punishments in life for distinguished crimes  
> is itself distinguished, and the punishment of wickedness:  
> prison and the dreadful descent from the rock,  
> blows, executioners, the stake, pitch, the blade, torches.

For no wise person would prefer to be an exile, poor, and dishonored rather than powerful in resources, revered for honor, strong in authority, and flourishing in his own city. For the function of wisdom is treated more clearly and conspicuously when the happiness of rulers is, in a way, poured out upon the peoples they govern—especially since prison, chains, and the other legal torments of punishment ought rather to fall upon harmful citizens, for whose sake they were established. Therefore I am exceedingly astonished that these things are reversed: that the punishments of crimes oppress the good, while the wicked seize the rewards of virtue. I desire to learn from you what reason there can be for so unjust a confusion.

288. **“For I would be less astonished,” etc.**

II. Boethius is even more astonished that adversity comes to the good and prosperity to the wicked because God, infinitely wise, good, and powerful, governs the world. God cannot be accused either of ignorance, by which he would not know these reversals; of malice, by which he would wish them; or of impotence, by which, although knowing and willing, he would be unable to change them. David was astonished at this also, Psalm 72: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps had nearly slipped, because I was jealous of the wicked when I saw the peace of sinners.” Jeremiah was astonished at it too, chapter 12: “Why is the way of the wicked prosperous? Why is it well with all who transgress and act unjustly?”

“For I would be less astonished if I believed that everything was mixed together by chance events. But now God, the ruler, increases my bewilderment: although he often grants pleasant things to the good and harsh things to the wicked, and conversely grants hard things to the good and desired things to the wicked, unless the reason is discovered, what seems to distinguish this from chance events?”

III. Philosophy replies that this astonishment, like the others, arises from ignorance of the cause. But this ignorance is not a valid argument from which one may conclude either that God is not the good ruler of the world or that everything is not rightly ordered, as Philosophy will subsequently prove.

“It is not surprising,” she said, “if anything whose order is unknown is believed to be reckless and confused. But although you do not know the reason for so great an arrangement, nevertheless, since a good ruler governs the world, do not doubt that everything is rightly done.”

289. **METER V**

A poem that may be said to consist of two alternating kinds of tetrameter verse. The first begins with a trochee, the second with a spondee. After the first foot, however, each has a spondee, iamb, or dactyl together with the remaining syllable, which they call the caesura, and ends with a dactyl and a spondee. The twentieth verse is excepted, since its first foot is an iamb and its second a tribrach.

**ARGUMENT.**—For this reason, says Philosophy, the common people marvel at celestial phenomena but do not marvel at earthly ones, because they know the causes of the latter and do not know those of the former.

“If someone does not know that the stars of the Bear turn near the highest pole, he will greatly marvel at the law of the lofty heaven, by which Bootes, although he has a more rapid rising, drives his chariot slowly and never lowers his tardy fires into the sea. If the circle of the full moon grows pale, defiled by the boundaries of dark night, and if the lesser stars that the moon had veiled with her shining face are revealed when that face is darkened, this common error disturbs the peoples, who therefore weary their cymbals with repeated blows. No one marvels that the winds of the west strike the sea-shores with turbulent waves, nor that a heap of snow hardened by cold melts in the fierce heat of the sun, for here the causes are easily understood; there, hidden causes disturb every mind with wonder. The fickle common crowd marvels at whatever occurs rarely and suddenly. Let the dark error of the ignorant crowd depart; surely these things will cease to appear marvelous.”

1. “Arcturus.” *Arcturus* is said to derive from ἄρκτος (*arktos*, “bear”) and οὐρά (*oura*, “tail”), as though “the bear’s tail.” It is the star nearest the pole among all the stars composing the Great Bear; hence it is often called the pole-star. Since the Arctic Pole, named from this Bear, always appears to us above our horizon, this star, as though fearing the antipodes, never sets. Hence Virgil, *Georgics* I, line 246:

> The Bears, fearing to be dipped into the ocean.

This is attributed to Juno’s hatred, according to the poets’ fiction: she was distressed that the Great Bear had been admitted into heaven and asked Tethys not to allow the adulteress to bathe in her waters.

The same star is also called Arctophylax and Bootes, the latter being mentioned in the third verse. Arctophylax means “guardian of the Bear,” or, as Ovid says, “guardian of the Erymanthian Bear,” because he seems to guard the Bear whom he always accompanies. Bootes means “herdsman,” because he clings to the stars that represent oxen and a wagon, like a kind of herdsman. Hence Propertius says that Bootes turns the oxen and wagons. Juvenal, satire 5, line 22:

> Or at that time when  
> the sluggish wagons of Bootes turn coldly around him.

That constellation, therefore, given these three names, is rightly said to “slip by the highest hinge,” near which it is situated; hence it sinks its tardy late fires into the sea, while from another perspective it unfolds its rapid risings.

First, that star slips by the highest hinge because it turns toward the northern pole, which always appears to us and in which, as in the other hinge of the world, the celestial sphere is imagined to turn. Next, the same star sinks its tardy late fires into the sea because, never descending below our horizon, it never sets. Finally, the same star unfolds rapid risings because, once it has been hidden by the sun’s greater light, it emerges as soon as the solar light, obstructed by the earth, has diminished. The person who does not know this cause marvels at the phenomena described above.

7. “May the horns of the full moon grow pale.” The moon, also called Phoebe because she shines through the night, is an opaque celestial body that reflects solar light in such a way that it displays now an angular, now a rounded form of brightness. It sometimes happens that the earth lies between the sun and the full moon—that is, the moon shining with rounded brightness—in such a way that, darkened by earthly shadows, the moon immediately loses its rounded radiance, and the stars that had previously been hidden by the moon’s greater light begin to gleam forth.

The ancients, who falsely and superstitiously believed that the moon on the one hand suffered this eclipse through incantations and on the other was freed from it by the ringing of bronze or cymbals, fled to the bronze instruments of aid for the moon, as Tibullus calls them. The same Tibullus says:

> He tries by song to draw the moon down from her chariot,  
> and he would succeed if the struck bronze instruments did not resound.

Juvenal, satire 6, book II, line 440:

> You might say that so many basins at once, so many bells,  
> are being struck. Now no one tires either the trumpets or the bronze.

One moon can come to the aid of another in distress. No one is unfamiliar with that well-known line of Virgil, *Eclogue* 8, verse 69:

[Col. 0812C] “Songs can even draw down the moon from heaven.”

All these matters, which Philosophy elegantly describes in the six verses just mentioned, are objects of popular wonder because the common people do not know their cause.

### 13. “No one wonders,” etc.

After Philosophy had brought forward certain things which people commonly wonder at because they do not know their causes, she now reports the contrary things, which those same people do not wonder at because they know their causes. First, people do not wonder that the Corus, or Caurus—the wind blowing from the summer sunset—strikes the shores with roaring waves, because they know that this wind is a body in motion, and that a body in motion naturally strikes bodies in its path. Nor, in the second place, do those same people wonder that the mass of snow, hardened by cold, melts beneath the sun’s burning heat, because they know that the motionless particles of hard snow can be moved by the moving particles of the sun’s heat.

### 19 and 20. “What the rare age brings forth and marvels at sudden things.”

The ignorant populace marvels at whatever happens both rarely and suddenly. Wonder is, of course, a sudden agitation of the mind, which observes with particular attention things that appear new and impressive. Hence the cause of this disturbance is something both rare and sudden. Rare, certainly; for, as barbarians say, “passion is not produced by familiar things.” Sudden, however, because, as Saint Gregory rightly says, “darts that are foreseen strike less forcefully.”

“But,” says the grammarian, “by what right is the populace here said to wonder at *rara* and *subitis*, with the cases altered? Does the conjunction require matching cases?”

“It does,” I reply, “require matching cases; but it is not uncommon for the meanings alone to be joined, with the construction of the words disregarded. Thus Cicero said: ‘I bought [it] for a hundred gold pieces and more.’ Although here the usual construction is not actually altered, a suppressed verb must be understood, as though it were said: ‘he marvels at things that are rare, and he marvels at sudden things.’ For just as Tully said, in Book II *On Ends*, ‘We Varrones are astonished,’ so Horace sang in Book I of the *Satires*, Satire 4:

> The splendor of silver captivates him; Albius marvels at bronze.

### 21. “Let ignorance yield.”

The ignorant; although everyone here reads *inscitiae*, we have nevertheless thought that, with the final syllable deleted—a form which the ignorance of copyists could easily have introduced—one should read *insciti*, that is, “of the ignorant populace.” For the rules of this poem cannot permit *inscitiae*, whose second syllable is lengthened in Horace, Book II of the *Satires*, Satire 2:

[Col. 0813C]

> Either wickedness or ignorance of crafty law [has affected] him.

> If anyone does not know how the stars of Arcturus  
> Glide near the highest pole,  
> Why slow Bootes guides the Wain  
> And sinks its late fires into the sea,  
> [5] While it displays its rising too swiftly,  
> He will marvel at the law of the lofty heavens.  
>   
> 290 The horns of the full moon grow pale,  
> Stained by the dark marks of night,  
> And Phoebe, whose shining face had covered  
> The stars in confusion, reveals them:  
> [10] A common error agitates the peoples,  
> And they weary the air with repeated blows.  
>   
> No one wonders that the breezes of the Corus  
> Strike the shore with roaring waves,  
> [15] Nor that the hard mass of snow,  
> Frozen by cold, melts in Phoebus’ burning heat.  
> Here it is easy to see the causes;  
> There, hidden, they trouble men’s hearts—  
> Everything that the rare age brings forth  
> [20] The fickle populace marvels at when it is sudden.  
> Let the cloudy error of ignorance yield;  
> Surely let wondrous things cease to appear wondrous.

## 292 PROSE VI

[Col. 0813A]

### ARGUMENT

Philosophy, having indicated the subject that is to be treated next and the manner in which it will be discussed, sets forth definitions both of divine Providence and of fate. From these she demonstrates that the matter is so subject to Providence that it belongs no less to divine Providence than to fate that good people are now afflicted with sad circumstances and wicked people with circumstances they desire.

“So it is,” I said. “But since it is your task to unfold the causes of hidden things and explain reasons veiled in darkness, I ask you [Note: [Col. 0813B] ‘That you state your opinion on this matter.’] to decide the question here and, since this marvel troubles me most of all, [Note: [Col. 0813B] ‘That you explain it.’] expound it.”

Then she, smiling slightly, said: “You summon me to a matter of the greatest importance among all matters under inquiry, one for which scarcely anything can be sufficiently exact, even when all resources have been exhausted. [Note: [Col. 0813B] ‘It can be said that nothing is sufficiently precise.’] For the subject is such that, when one doubt has been cut off, countless others grow up like the heads of a hydra. [Note: [Col. 0814B] ‘A serpent with several heads.’] Nor will there be any end unless someone restrains them with the keenest fire of the mind. [Col. 0813B] [Note: [Col. 0813C] ‘For in this inquiry concerning the simplicity of Providence,’ etc.] I. Philosophy indicates the subject she is about to treat, in which, when one doubt has been cut off, innumerable others arise. Such matters are divine Providence, fate, and the reconciliation of human freedom with divine foreknowledge. The hydra, whose likeness Philosophy now employs, had fifty heads, or, according to others, a hundred; when one was cut off, two grew back, until Hercules, cutting off each head, applied fire to the wound. This Lernian beast will be discussed below, in meter 7 of this book, verse 22.]

“For here questions commonly arise concerning the simplicity of Providence, the sequence of fate, sudden events, divine knowledge and predestination, and freedom of choice. You yourself can judge how great a burden these matters involve. But since knowing these things too is part of your healing, although confined within a narrow limit of time, we shall nevertheless try to touch upon something of them. [Note: [Col. 0814B] ‘To touch upon it lightly.’] If the pleasures of musical verse delight you, you must postpone that pleasure for a little while, until I weave together in orderly sequence the arguments connected with one another.”

“As you wish,” I replied.

### 293 [Note: [Col. 0813C] “Then, as though beginning from another starting point.”]

#### II

Philosophy indicates the manner in which the discussion will proceed. Since God is no less the first cause than the ultimate end of all things, Philosophy may draw arguments for proving her position from God under both kinds of cause. The arguments set forth up to this point have been taken from God as the end; those that follow will be taken from God as the first efficient cause. Hence Philosophy begins:

“Whatever is created, preserved, and affected in any way is created, preserved, and modified by God as by the first cause. For since it is done always in the same and simple manner, it must be done by one simple mind—namely, God. Thus the divine mind establishes a multiplicity of ways in which things are to be carried out. When this manner is viewed in the purity of the divine intelligence, it is called Providence; but when it is referred to the things which God moves and arranges, the ancients called it fate.”

Whether *puritas* is a Latin word is disputed. Some say that it is; others deny it. Scioppius, in his *Observations on Vossius*, attempting to restore to this expression its rightful place in Latin, says:

“But if Vossius agrees that *impuritas* is Latin on the authority of Cicero, then, by his own judgment, *puritas* ought by no means to appear barbarous . . . . In my judgment, therefore, Vossius may now be secure in mind. Although he has not found the word *puritas* in the surviving books of the ancient authors—for it is well established that the greater part of them has perished, and with it countless Latin words have been lost—nevertheless, since we read *impuritas* in Cicero, he has no reason to cast himself, and with him other very learned men, into the crowd of the barbarous vulgar. Yet although Cicero said *infinitas* and *infirmatio*, and Terence *infortunium*, it does not follow that *finitas*, *firmatio*, and *fortunium* are Latin words.”

Then, as though beginning from another starting point, she spoke as follows:

“The generation of all things, the entire development of mutable natures, and whatever is moved in any manner receive their causes, order, and forms from the stability of the divine mind. This mind, established in the citadel of its simplicity, determines a multiplicity of ways in which things are to be carried out. When this manner is viewed in the purity of the divine intelligence, it is called Providence; but when it is referred to the things which it moves and arranges, it was called fate by the ancients. The difference between these two will easily become clear if one perceives the force of each with the mind.”

[Note: [Col. 0814C] “For Providence,” etc.]

#### III

Philosophy offers a definition of divine Providence:

“It is,” she says, “that very divine reason established in the supreme ruler of all things, which orders everything.”

Because this definition is defended by all theologians, it appears to require a more careful explanation.

It is therefore called, first, “reason.” Since *ratio* is derived from *reor*, and since *reor* means the same as “I think” or “I consider,” every act of thought is rightly called *ratio*. Hence, I believe, it happened that for Tully *ratio* also means mind, intelligence, counsel, judgment, argumentation, purpose, and other things of that kind. Every Providence, however, is a kind of thought, since it is a certain quality implanted in the mind, of which the mind itself is immediately conscious. Providence, therefore, is reason.

But since thought is of two kinds—namely, conception and will—theologians dispute whether Providence is conception alone, will alone, or conception and will together. The last view appears to me to have more supporters, although those same theologians dispute among themselves which of these two thoughts is primary in Providence itself. Hence divine Providence is defined by Ludovico Vives as “the will of God governing all things by counsel.”

It is called, secondly, “divine.” For Providence can be spoken of with respect to every mind, whether divine or created. Indeed, since Providence, according to Tully, is that by which something future is seen before it has happened, and since nothing is future for the divine mind, whereas many things are future for created minds, Providence could more properly and correctly be said of other minds than of the divine mind. Here, however, we are concerned only with divine Providence; hence it ought to have been called the divine reason, or the thought of the divine mind.

It is called, thirdly, “established in the supreme ruler of all things,” because divine Providence is an attribute of God insofar as God is the supreme ruler of all things. For it belongs to the supreme ruler to provide for everything. Wisdom 6 says: “He has equal care for all”; and chapter 8: “She reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly.”

It is called, fourthly, “that which orders everything,” because it belongs to a provident mind to place the matter subject to it in its proper order and place, according to the end it has proposed for itself. Hence divine Providence is defined by Saint Thomas as “the reason of the order of things toward their end.”

For Providence is that very divine reason [Col. 0815A] established in the supreme ruler of all things, which orders everything.

### 294 [Note: [Col. 0815C] “But fate is inherent,” etc.]

#### IV

Philosophy adds a definition of fate:

“Fate,” she says, “is an arrangement inherent in moving things, by which Providence joins each thing to its proper order.”

We shall also try to interpret this more clearly.

First, in the interpretation of the word, fate is nothing other than a sign of the divine will, or a divine utterance. For, according to Varro’s judgment, what the Fates decreed for one at birth is called *fatum* from *fari*, “to speak.” In this sense Saint Augustine, Book V of *The City of God*, chapter 9, says that there is fate among Christians:

“For we cannot deny,” he says, “that it is written in the Holy Scriptures: ‘God spoke once’ . . . . What is meant by ‘he spoke once’ is that he spoke immutably—that is, unchangeably—just as he knows unchangeably all things that are future and all things that he himself will do.”

Lucan, in Book 9, says:

> The godhead needs no uttered words;  
> The author spoke once to those being born  
> Whatever it is permitted to know.

Next, fate is an arrangement because it is the created thing itself—namely, a body or mind—affected at its proper time, place, or in any other manner. For this is the command and utterance of God willing it.

Moreover, this arrangement is inherent in moving things. Fate is merely the mode of a created thing, since such a thing can neither come into being, nor be preserved, nor be affected in any way except by the divine will, of which that arrangement is the sign.

Furthermore, through this arrangement inherent in moving things, divine Providence joins each thing to its proper order. For, says Quintus Curtius, “I would believe that, by an eternal constitution and through a connection of hidden causes determined long beforehand, each thing proceeds through its own order under an unchangeable law.”

In a single word, fate is the very mode of being acted upon and acting by which a moving thing is affected by the immovable God with the greatest wisdom. This will become clearer to anyone who considers the distinctions between Providence and fate that follow, which Philosophy will present as consequences, so to speak, of the two definitions given above.

But fate is an arrangement inherent in moving things, by which Providence joins each thing to its proper order.

For Providence embraces all things together—though they are diverse and though they are infinite—whereas fate sorts individual things into motion, distributed among places, forms, and times. Thus, when this exposition of temporal order is united in the vision of the divine mind, it is Providence; but when that same unity is ordered and unfolded through time, it is called fate.

Although these are different, one nevertheless depends upon the other. The fatal order proceeds from the simplicity of Providence. For just as an artisan, perceiving in his mind the form of the thing to be made, brings about the work’s result and leads through temporal stages what he had foreseen simply and immediately, so God, through Providence, arranges individually and firmly the things to be made; but through fate he administers in diverse and temporal ways the very things he has arranged.

### 295 [Note: [Col. 0816C] “Whether, therefore, through things serving,” etc.]

Although it is established that fate is a mode of a moving thing, and further that this mode comes from God as from the first cause, it may nevertheless be questioned whether fate comes immediately from God or through certain other things that serve him. Hence Philosophy briefly touches upon certain philosophical opinions on this subject, without preferring any of them to the others. For although God uses both good and evil spirits, the spirit of the universe, the elements, heavenly bodies, and other such things to exercise some form of fate, none of these things is used by God generally to move all the other created things, or to produce every form of fate.

“Whether, therefore, fate is exercised through certain divine spirits serving Providence, or through the soul, or through all of nature serving it, or through the motions of the heavenly stars, or through angelic power, or through the various cunning of demons, or whether the fatal sequence is woven through some of these or through all of them, this much is certainly clear: Providence is the immovable and simple form of things to be done; fate, however, is the moving connection and temporal order of what divine simplicity has arranged to be done.”

[Note: [Col. 0816D] “From this it follows,” etc.]

From what has been said Philosophy concludes that divine Providence extends more widely than fate. Whatever is subject to fate is also subject to Providence, but whatever is subject to Providence is not necessarily subject to fate—not because any created thing could be modified without God modifying it, but because not every created thing is equally mutable. Since fate is an arrangement inherent in moving things, certain created things are said to be more or less subject to fate according as, moving farther from or nearer to the first mind, they are more or less liable to change. Philosophy explains this by the example of several orbits revolving around the same unmoved axis, arranged in such a way that the nearer they are to the axis, the lesser is the motion by which they are driven, and the farther away, the greater.

Thus everything subject to fate is also subject to Providence, and fate itself is subject to Providence. But certain things placed under Providence surpass the sequence of fate. These are things fixed in stability, close to the primal divinity, which transcend the order of fatal mutability.

For just as, among circles revolving around the same axis, the innermost approaches the simplicity of the center and becomes, as it were, a kind of axis for the others situated outside it, around which they revolve; while the outermost, rotating through a greater circumference, unfolds through wider spaces in proportion as it departs from the indivisible unity of the central point; but if anything connects and unites itself with the center, it is compressed into simplicity and ceases to spread and flow away—so, in like manner, whatever departs farther from the first mind becomes more entangled in the bonds of fate, and something is freer from fate in proportion as it approaches that axis of things more closely.

But if it clings to the firmness of the heavenly mind, being without motion, it also transcends the necessity of fate.

[Note: [Col. 0817C] “Therefore, as reasoning is related to understanding,” etc.]

For just as reasoning arises from understanding or intelligence—which is nothing other than clear and distinct knowledge, and which is the standard both of true and certain judgments and of true and certain reasoning; just as, while the matter remains the same, diverse bodies are produced—for example, crop, wheat, bread, blood, and flesh; just as time, the duration of a thing existing with a beginning and an end, proceeds from eternity, the duration of a thing existing without beginning and without end; and just as a circle moves from an unmoved center—so the moving sequence of fate is subject to the immovable Providence of God.

### 296 [Note: [Col. 0817C] “Therefore, as it is related to intelligence,” etc.]

Thus, as reasoning is related to understanding; what is generated to what exists; time to eternity; and a circle to the center point, so the moving sequence of fate is related to the stable simplicity of Providence.

That sequence moves heaven and the stars, tempers the elements with one another, and transforms them through alternating change. The same sequence renews all things that are born and die through corresponding progressions of offspring and seeds. It also binds the actions and fortunes of human beings in an indissoluble connection of causes. Since these proceed from the beginnings of immovable Providence, the fortunes themselves must also be unchangeable.

For things are governed in the best manner when the simplicity remaining in the divine mind brings forth an undeviating order of causes, and this order restrains mutable things, which would otherwise flow along at random, by its own unchangeability.

Hence, although to you, who are quite unable to contemplate this order, everything may appear confused and disordered, nevertheless its proper mode directs and arranges everything toward the good. For there is nothing—even among the wicked themselves—that is done for the sake of evil. As has been demonstrated most fully, a perverse error turns them away while they seek the good, [Note: [Col. 0817C] “Far from it that,”] rather than the order proceeding from the axis of the highest good turning anyone aside from its own beginning.

[Note: [Col. 0817D] “But what kind of,” you will say, “can any be,” etc.]

#### IV

From the principles already stated Philosophy infers that it belongs no less to Providence than to fate that adverse circumstances befall the good and favorable circumstances the wicked. This is so either because those whom people judge good or wicked are not such in God’s judgment, or because the constitution of minds, like that of bodies, varies.

First, since human beings are ignorant, whereas God knows the thoughts of all people perfectly, it can happen that human and divine judgments differ concerning good and wicked people: those whom God approves may be disapproved by human beings, and those whom human beings approve may be disapproved by God. Thus, at the time when Job’s friends were condemning him, God was acquitting Job. Indeed, human judgments on this matter are contrary to one another, and some consider people worthy of reward whom others consider worthy of punishment.

Next, the constitution of minds differs—at least insofar as they are considered in relation to the bodies with which they are joined—in such a way that some are weaker than their bodies, some stronger, and some, as it were, equal in balanced strength. Through God’s providence, favorable or adverse circumstances befall all of them according as these things contribute to removing vices or promoting virtues. This is as unknown to human beings as the innermost constitution of souls.

“But what confusion,” you will say, “could be more unjust than that both adverse and favorable circumstances befall the good, and that both desirable and hateful things befall the wicked? Do human beings live with such integrity of mind that those whom they judge good or wicked must necessarily be as they believe them to be?”

Yet human judgments here fight against one another, and some consider people worthy of reward whom others consider worthy of punishment.

But let us grant that someone might distinguish the good from the wicked. Could he then perceive the innermost constitution of souls, as one commonly speaks of the constitution of bodies? It is no less a marvel to someone who does not know why sweet things suit some healthy bodies, while bitter things suit others, or why some sick people are helped by mild remedies and others by harsh ones. A physician, however, who recognizes the condition and temperament of health and illness, is not at all surprised by this.

What else does the health of souls appear to be than uprightness? What else is illness than vices? And who else is the preserver of the good and the remover of evil than God, the ruler and physician of minds? When, from the high watchtower of Providence, [Note: [Col. 0818C] “This means here a place from which watchmen see farther.”] he looks down, he recognizes what suits each person and applies what he knows to be suitable.

Hence arises that remarkable wonder of the fatal order: when what ignorant people marvel at is carried out by one who knows. To touch briefly upon what human reason can say concerning the divine depth, [Note: [Col. 0818C] “Concerning the incomprehensible God.”] what you think just and most attentive to equity appears otherwise to the all-knowing Providence.

Our friend Lucan, skilled in Philosophy, reminded us that “the victorious cause pleased the gods, but the defeated cause pleased Cato.”

Therefore, whatever you see happening contrary to expectation is, in the order of things, proceeding rightly; but to your opinion it appears as perverse confusion. [Note: [Col. 0818C] “Everything is indeed done rightly, but you judge wrongly concerning its outcome.”]

But suppose someone is so well-formed in character that divine and human judgment agree concerning him. He may nevertheless be weak in the powers of his soul. If adversity were to befall him, he might cease to cultivate innocence, through which he had been unable to retain his good fortune. Wise dispensation therefore spares one whom adversity might make worse, so that it does not force someone to undergo hardship when hardship is unsuitable for him.

There is another person complete in every virtue, holy, and close to God. Providence judges it wrong that he should be touched by any adversity, so much so that it does not even allow him to be shaken by bodily illnesses.

### 298 [Note: [Col. 0819D] “For as someone superior even to me says.”]

“According to Ascensius, Hermes Trismegistus is believed—although pagan religion fabulously represents him as having become a god—to have said the following. The Greek words, *andros hierou*, etc., ought to be rendered as follows: ‘The virtues build up the body of a holy man.’ Although, according to the Apostle, 2 Corinthians 12, ‘virtue is perfected in weakness,’ bodily health, wealth, and other advantages of this kind nevertheless often contribute to the cultivation of virtue. Thus, when God declared Job to be a just man and one who worshiped God, the evil spirit replied that this was not surprising, since everything was prosperous for him. [Note: ‘Book of Job.’]”

For, as someone who is perhaps superior even to me says:

> Ἀνδρὸς ἱεροῦ σῶμα δυνάμεις οἰκοδομοῦσι.

“The virtues build up the body of a holy man.”

It often happens that the supreme administration of affairs is entrusted to good people, so that abundant wickedness may be restrained. [Note: [Col. 0819C] “Having run rampant.”] To others Providence distributes a mixture of circumstances according to the quality of their souls. It wounds some, lest they grow wanton through prolonged prosperity; [Note: [Col. 0819C] “Afflicts.”] it allows others to be harassed by harsh experiences, so that the virtues of their souls may be strengthened through the practice and exercise of patience. Some fear more than they ought what they are able to bear; others despise more than they ought what they are unable to bear. Providence leads these people into sad circumstances as a test of themselves. Some have obtained a venerable name among later generations by the price of a glorious death. [Note: [Col. 0819C] “They attained renown among posterity through a distinguished death.”] Others, unconquerable by punishments, have set before the rest an example that virtue is invincible by adversity.

There can be no doubt that these things happen rightly and orderly and for the good of those to whom they appear to happen. For the fact that sad and desirable things alike befall the wicked also proceeds from the same causes.

No one wonders at their sad circumstances, since everyone considers them to have deserved ill. Their punishments both deter others from crimes and correct those upon whom they are inflicted. Their prosperity, however, speaks loudly to good people about how they ought to judge such happiness, which they see often serving the wicked.

I believe that the following too is arranged for a reason: perhaps someone has a nature so headstrong and unreasonable that poverty in his household might drive him more readily into crime. Providence cures this illness with the remedy of money granted to him. Seeing his conscience stained by disgrace and comparing himself with his fortune, he may perhaps fear that what he enjoys possessing will be painful to lose. He will therefore change his ways and, while fearing to lose his fortune, abandon his wickedness.

### 299

Prosperity obtained undeservedly has hurled others into the ruin they deserved. To some, the right of inflicting punishment has been granted, so that it might be an exercise for the good and a cause of punishment for the wicked.

For just as there is no agreement between the good and the wicked, so the wicked themselves cannot agree with one another. Why should they? Each disagrees with the others because of the vices tearing at their consciences, and they often do things which, once they have done them, they decide ought not to have been done.

From this supreme Providence has often brought forth a remarkable wonder: that the wicked should make the wicked good. While some see themselves suffering injustice at the hands of the worst people, they return to the fruitfulness of virtue, burning with hatred of the guilty and striving to be unlike those whom they hate.

There is only one divine power to which even evils are good, since by using them appropriately it draws forth the effect of some good.

[Note: [Col. 0819D] “For there is a certain order,” etc.]

For just as all created things have one principle and one end, so they must have one order, one Providence. Since this Providence is infinite, we can neither grasp it with our minds nor explain it in words. Homer expresses this very well, *Iliad* 12:

> Ἀργαλέον δ` ἐμὲ ταῦτα θεὸν ὡς πάντ` ἀγορεύειν.

That is:

> “It is difficult for me, as a god, to speak of all these things.”

A certain order embraces everything, so that whatever has departed from the order assigned to it falls back into another order, lest anything be left to chance in the kingdom of Providence.

[Note: [Col. 0820C] “But it is difficult for me, as a god, to speak of all these things.”]

For it is not permitted to a human being either to comprehend by intelligence or to explain in speech all the mechanisms of the divine work. It is enough to have perceived this much: God, the author of all natures, also arranges everything while directing it toward the good. As he hastens to preserve the things he has brought forth in his own likeness, he drives out every evil from the boundaries of his commonwealth through the fatal sequence of necessity. [Note: [Col. 0820C] “Expels.”]

Thus, if you consider Providence as the one who orders everything, you will judge that nothing of what is believed to abound on earth exists anywhere at all.

But I see that you have long been burdened by the weight of the question and wearied by the length of the reasoning, and that you are awaiting some sweetness of song. Receive, then, [Note: [Col. 0820C] “A cup.”] a draught which, once refreshed by it, will enable you to press on more firmly to what follows.

## 300 METER VI

[Note: [Col. 0820D] Some call this “spondaic.” It is a poem consisting of one kind of verse, each line of which is a tetrameter that most often has a dactyl in the third position and a spondee in the fourth; in other places, besides these feet, it also has an anapest.]

[Col. 0820C]

### ARGUMENT

Philosophy is about to confirm divine Providence by examples. “This,” she says, “is the law established by divine authority: once peace has been made among the stars, the elements, the seasons of the year, and all living bodies, they repeat their perpetual circuits, returning to that from which they proceeded, the principle of every good.”

[Note: [Col. 0820C]

If you wish to perceive the Providence of the supreme God, consider with an attentive and pure mind the heights of the lofty heavens. Here the stars preserve the ancient harmony of things under a fixed covenant. The sun, carried along by splendid flame, does not obstruct the moon’s cold course. Nor does the Bear, which revolves around the highest pole of the universe, although it has never been washed from one side in the western ocean while seeing the other stars washed there, strive to bathe its own fires in that same sea. Always, in alternating but orderly succession, the evening star announces the darkness of night, and that same star, as the morning star, brings back the life-giving light.

Thus reciprocal love restores perpetual motions; thus discordant war has been banished from the star-bearing regions. This harmony governs the elements by just laws, so that moist things yield alternately to dry things, and cold things enter into peace with hot things; suspended fire flies upward, and weighty earth remains below through its own gravity.

By these laws the year, parent of flowers, sends forth fragrances in the mild season of spring; hot summer cooks the harvest; autumn returns laden with fruits; falling rain sprinkles winter. This balance nourishes and produces every body that lives and acts in the world; but the same balance removes and conceals that living body, destroying it with final death.

Meanwhile God, the supreme creator of all things, sits and governs all things as though with reins, arranging them. He himself is ruler, lord, principle, origin, law, and wise moderator of what is just. Whatever he grants to be stirred by motion, he restrains and strengthens while it is in motion. For unless God, preventing straight courses, were to promote circular revolutions again, the things that now cohere in a firm sequence would be torn away from their principle and perish.

This is the common striving of all things: everything strives to be held by the end of the good. For the things God has created cannot continue in any other way unless, through love turned back again, a certain circuit of causes is produced.]

[Note: [Col. 0820D]

### 1. “The laws of the thunderer.”

Divine Providence. For since, according to what has been said, Providence is the divine reason established in the supreme ruler of all things, which orders everything, it is not improperly called the divine right or divine law. Moreover, God is the thunderer. Since the particular causes of lightning, thunder, and the thunderbolt are not commonly known, these effects have become customarily attributed to God alone, so that poets especially, when they name the one who flashes, thunders, and hurls lightning, intend God to be understood.]

> If you wish to know the laws of the lofty thunderer,

[Col. 0821A]

[Note: [Col. 0821C]

### 2. “To discern with a pure and attentive mind.”

To know clearly and distinctly, with the mind stripped of every prejudice, divine Providence. According to Philosophy, the proofs of this Providence are the laws of nature themselves, which we see being observed, first in the stars, then in the elements, afterward in the seasons of the year, and finally in all living bodies. Philosophy will speak of these separately.]

### 5. “The stars preserve peace.”

#### I

The laws of the Providence mentioned above are observed in the stars—namely, in the sun, moon, Bear, Lucifer, and the other stars. Although the sun is so luminous a body that it may be considered fire, in accordance with the words of Ecclesiasticus 43, “The sun burns up the mountains, breathing forth fiery rays,” while the moon is so opaque a body that, unless it shines with borrowed light, it ought to be considered cold rather than hot, nevertheless the sun moves in such a way that it does not impede the moon’s course.

Similarly, the Bear, near the pole to which it gave its name, moves around that same pole in such a way that it never sets when the other stars set. Venus likewise, which alternately foretells night and day—Lucifer in the morning and Vesper in the evening—most consistently alternates its turns, with no obstruction from the other stars.

So true is it that the stars observe the laws prescribed by Providence. But Lucifer was discussed in meter 5 of Book I, the Bear in meter 5 of Book IV, and the stars which, when they set, are said by poets to sink into the ocean have been discussed in many places.

### 19. “This harmony,” etc.

#### II

The same laws of Providence are observed in the elements. An element is called a divisible body formed in such a way that other things are composed from it. Commonly four elements are admitted: fire, air, water, and earth. These are said to contend with one another both through the qualities called altering qualities and through those called motive qualities.

The altering qualities, they say, are heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. The motive qualities are lightness and heaviness.

Here the subject is only the harmony of such elements, whether considered with respect to the altering qualities, expressed as “let moist things yield to dry things, and let cold things join faith with flames,” or with respect to the motive qualities, expressed as “let hanging fire rise on high, and let the heavy regions of earth sink down under their weight.”

25. “By the same causes, etc.”] III. By these same laws of Providence the four seasons of the year—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—follow one another. Spring, with its mild warmth, sends forth flowers and fragrances. Summer, with its heat, dries the crops. Autumn, heavy with fruit, returns; and finally winter, named from the rains—or from *ἀπὸ τοῦ ὕειν*, “to rain”—waters the fields with downpours. All these things are most clearly set forth here.

30. “This harmony, etc.”] IV. By these same laws of divine Providence living bodies are first nourished after being formed in the womb; then they come forth into the air; and finally, when the course of life has been completed, they die. This is indeed marvelous when considered generally, but far more marvelous when considered in detail.

34. “Meanwhile he sits, etc.”] V. Philosophy teaches that these changes of bodies arise from God’s providence. Hence, according to Philosophy, God is called creator, governor, king, lord, source, origin, law, and wise arbiter, so that by these names she may illuminate and awaken the idea or notion of God implanted within us but obscured by disturbances and, as it were, lulled to sleep. For through this idea—or rather, with God himself as teacher—we shall at last come to recognize that God alone is properly the cause of the movements described above, which we marvel at, whether in the stars, the elements, or other bodies of this kind, just as the author of the book *The Search for Truth* demonstrated no less piously than learnedly. Hence the same Philosophy now teaches that not only the rest but also the motion of bodies, indeed even the ways in which bodies move, proceed from God’s providence itself:

“He checks what he draws back, and makes firm what wanders”: behold rest.

“And spurs things onward in motion”: behold motion itself.

“Calling back straight courses, he forces bent paths again into circles”: behold the modes of motion.

And lest you should suppose that God entrusted this office to some nature, form, qualities, accidents, or other such things, Philosophy adds that, unless God himself supplied these things, the stable order that now holds everything together would fall apart, severed from its source.]

Behold the summits of the highest heaven.

304 PROSE VII.

ARGUMENT.—Thus, says Philosophy, every fortune, whether prosperous or adverse, since it arises from God’s providence, is referred back to God himself and is therefore good; it is evil only through the fault of those who misuse it. Thus prosperity ought to reward the good and adversity to exercise them; whereas adversity should punish the wicked and prosperity correct them.

“Do you now see, then, what follows from all these things that we have said?”

“What?” I replied.

[Note: [Col. 0824C] Both kinds of fortune, namely prosperous and adverse, are good.]

“All fortune,” she replied, “is entirely good.”

“And how,” I said, “can that be?”

“Consider: since every fortune is either pleasant or harsh, and since it is brought about either to reward or exercise the good, or to punish or correct the wicked, every fortune is good if it is established to be either just or useful.”

“Your reasoning is certainly too true,” I replied, “and, if I consider the Providence or fate that you taught a little earlier, it rests upon firm foundations. But, if you please, let us number it among those things that you shortly before called [Note: [Col. 0823D] ‘incredible’] incredible and, as Cicero calls them, paradoxical.”

For the common people, judging hastily and prejudicially, regard as incredible what appears most true and certain to wise people judging with clear and distinct understanding. Philosophers offer many examples of this, concerning light, colors, and other such things. Thus ordinary speech uses the expression, and frequently, that some people have bad fortune. Accordingly, Philosophy, using the language of the common people, proves that every fortune is good and that none is evil except through the fault of those who misuse it.

“Therefore,” she said, “shall we follow the language of the common people for a little while, so that we may not seem to have withdrawn too far from ordinary human usage?”

“As you wish,” I replied.

305 [Note: [Col. 0824C] “Is not the good, etc.”] I. Philosophy proves to the common people, by what is called an *ad hominem* argument, that all fortune is good. Since usefulness is a kind of good, and since even the common people are accustomed to regard one thing as honorable, another as pleasant, and another as useful, whatever is useful must necessarily be regarded even by the common people as good. But both kinds of fortune are useful, since one or the other exercises or corrects.

Every fortune, of course, belongs either to the good or to the wicked; and each of these kinds is in turn usually regarded as either adverse or prosperous.

1. If this fortune is adverse to the good—that is, to those who cultivate virtue—it benefits them, either by freeing them from past sins, preserving them from future sins, or advancing them toward greater virtue.

2. If this same fortune is prosperous for the good, then even in the opinion of the common people it is excellent, not only because it is the reward of past virtue but also because it provides material for future virtue.

3. If fortune is adverse to the wicked, it is the just punishment of past vices and a restraint upon future ones.

4. If fortune is prosperous for the wicked, it is evil only through their fault; for—

“Do you not, then, think that what benefits someone is good?”

“That is so,” I replied.

“Whatever either exercises or corrects benefits.”

“I admit it,” I replied.

“Then it is good.”

“Why should it not be?”

“But this fortune belongs to those who, established in virtue, wage war against adversity, or, turning away from vices, take up the path of virtue.”

“I cannot deny it,” I replied.

“What of pleasant fortune, which is given as a reward to the good? Does the common people decide that it is bad?”

“Not at all. It judges it to be as good as it truly is, and therefore also to be the best.”

“What of the remaining kind, which, though harsh, restrains the wicked by just punishment? Does the people think that it is good?”

“On the contrary,” I replied, “it judges it to be the most wretched of all things that can be imagined.”

“See, then, whether, by following the opinion of the people, we have not produced something very [Note: [Col. 0824C] ‘incredible’] unexpected.”

“What?” I replied.

“For from what has been granted,” she said, “it follows that for those who are either in possession of virtue, advancing toward it, or attaining it, every fortune, whatever it may be, is good; whereas for those who remain in wickedness every fortune is the worst.”

“That is true,” I replied, “although no one would dare admit it.”

“Therefore,” she said, “a wise man ought not to take it badly whenever he is brought into the contest of fortune, just as it is unbecoming for a brave man to be indignant whenever the tumult of war breaks out. For difficulty itself is material for the one to increase glory and for the other to strengthen wisdom. From this also virtue is so called, because, relying upon its own strength, it is not overcome by adversity.

“For you who are advancing in virtue have not come in order to overflow with pleasures and grow weak in delight. You engage in too fierce a battle with every fortune lest either sadness oppress you or pleasure corrupt you. Hold firmly to the middle ground, where virtue resides, with all your strength. Whatever remains below or advances beyond it possesses contempt for felicity but no reward for labor.”

306 [Note: [Col. 0825B] “It lies in your hands, etc.”] II. Philosophy shows that no fortune is evil except through the fault of those who misuse it, because things that are good and lie outside a person’s will may be judged good or bad according to that person’s good or bad will. For the will is especially considered in matters of character.

But fortune, whether prosperous or adverse, is, as is clear from what has been said, a good existing outside the human will. Fortune, therefore, is good in such a way that it is never bad except through the evil will or fault of those who misuse it. Since the wicked, insofar as they persist in their wickedness, always misuse their prosperous fortune, Philosophy concludes that all fortune of the wicked is the worst; whereas the fortune of the good is always good. For every fortune that appears harsh to the good either exercises or corrects them, or else punishes them. Nor do these good people reach eternal happiness except through the fortune that appears harsh to them. Thus—

“For it lies in your hands what kind of fortune you prefer to fashion for yourselves. Every fortune that seems harsh, unless it either exercises or corrects, punishes.”

307 METRE [Note: [Col. 0825C] This is called Sapphic. It is a poem consisting of one kind of verse, each line containing a trochee, a spondee, a dactyl, and two trochees. The poem nevertheless closes with an Adonic verse, which consists of a dactyl and a spondee and is customarily placed after every third Sapphic verse.] VII.

ARGUMENT.—Philosophy proves by the examples of Agamemnon, Ulysses, and Hercules that human beings do not enjoy what they desire until after they have endured many labors.

[Note: [Col. 0825B]

Agamemnon, son of Atreus, after campaigning for ten years against the Trojans, destroyed Troy and avenged the abduction by Paris of the wife of his brother Menelaus. But before that, when Agamemnon wished to set sail with the Greek ships and to purchase the winds—since they were denied to him because he had killed a hind sacred to Diana—he laid aside his paternal devotion and, acting as priest himself, sorrowfully slaughtered his wretched daughter Iphigenia.

Ulysses, king of Ithaca, grieved over the loss of his companions, whom the savage Polyphemus, dwelling in a great cavern, sent down into his enormous belly. Yet this same Polyphemus, blinded in the face and driven mad, restored joy to Ulysses in place of his sorrowful tears.

Troublesome labors distinguish Hercules. He conquered the proud Centaurs, stripped the hide from the savage lion, and pierced the Stymphalian birds with unavoidable arrows. He took the apples from the watchful serpent while carrying golden metal in his hand. He led away the three-headed Cerberus in three chains. He is said, as victor, to have offered the savage Diomedes to be devoured by his own savage horses.

With the same Hercules victorious, the serpent with many heads fell, its poison destroyed by flames. The river Achelous, disfigured in face because its horn had been torn away, hid its shameful countenance within its banks. That same Hercules killed Antaeus in the fields of Libya. Cacus, killed by Hercules, restrained the anger of his opponent Evander. The boar marked with its foam the shoulders of Hercules, which the lofty heavens were destined to press. Finally, Hercules’ last labor consists in the fact that he carried the heavens on his motionless neck; hence he earned the heavens once more, as the reward especially of his final labor. Therefore, come, noble men: since a great example shows you the lofty path, why do you, in your laziness, turn your backs and flee? Conquered earth grants heaven.]

[Note: [Col. 0825D]

1. “Wars waged for twice five years, etc.”] I. Philosophy proves by the example of Agamemnon that a person does not enjoy what he desires until after undertaking and enduring many labors. Paris, son of Priam, king of the Trojans, having fitted out a fleet and set out for Greece, came to Menelaus, king of Sparta, and carried off his wife Helen. Agamemnon, son of Atreus and brother of the aforementioned Menelaus, took this crime bitterly.
