He summoned the leaders of Greece, crossed the sea to Phrygia, besieged Troy, and, after a ten-year war, captured it by deceit and devastated it with sword and fire.

But when the same Agamemnon, intending to besiege Troy, had reached the harbor of Aulis in Boeotia and was reviewing his army there, he unknowingly killed a hind sacred to Diana. Diana, angered by this, sent a plague and suppressed the winds. They consulted an oracle, which replied that the gods would not be reconciled until Iphigenia, Agamemnon’s own daughter, had been sacrificed. The father obeyed and, acting as the priest himself, slaughtered his daughter. Thus, after many calamities and many labors, he finally obtained the fruits of his undertakings.

Virgil, *Aeneid* II.108:

Often the Danaans, with Troy left behind, wished

To contrive their flight and depart, exhausted by the long war—

And would that they had done so! Often harsh winter

Blocked the sea and terrified the south wind as they went.

Especially when the horse, already standing,

Constructed of maple timbers, made the whole sky resound with thunder.

In suspense, we send Eurypylus to inquire of Phoebus’ oracles,

And he brings back these sorrowful words from the shrine:

“You have appeased the winds with blood and a slaughtered virgin,

When first you Danaans came to the Trojan shores.”

8. “The Ithacan wept for his lost companions.”] II. The same Philosophy proves by the example of Ulysses that a person is not filled with joy until after having been afflicted with sorrow. Ulysses, king of Ithaca and the islands of Dulichium, whom we have already discussed in the third metre of this book, was carried to Sicily amid his other misfortunes and entered the cave of a certain Cyclops together with his companions.

That Cyclops, called Polyphemus, was said to be the son of Neptune. He possessed an enormous body but only one eye, which he had in his forehead. He had already devoured some of Ulysses’ companions and was about to kill the rest in the same manner when Ulysses, fearing for himself no less than for his surviving companions, intoxicated Polyphemus and, after plunging him into deep sleep, blinded him with a club or a charred stake. Then he bound his companions and himself beneath the fleeces of rams. Finally, they all escaped from the cave together with the flock and experienced as much joy as they had conceived sorrow from the death of their companions and the danger to themselves.

13. “Harsh labors celebrate Hercules.”] III. By the example of Hercules, Philosophy proves that heaven is not obtained until many earthly labors have been overcome. Hercules was the son of Jupiter and Alcmena, and was so hated by Juno that, through her agency, he was constantly exposed to new dangers. As others have done, Philosophy now recounts the twelve labors of Hercules, but in a different kind and order.

14. “He subdued the Centaurs, etc.”] Hercules’ first labor. The Centaurs were a people of Thessaly living near Mount Pelion. Because they were the first to tame horses and fight from horseback, other peoples imagined them as monsters who were partly human and partly horse; hence they were also called Hippocentaurs, and for that reason they are now called proud. Hercules attacked and killed them because they had rushed toward the cave of Pholus, who had received Hercules as a guest, as though intending to do him harm.]

Wars waged for twice five years,

The avenger, son of Atreus, by the ruin of Phrygia

Avenged the marriage-bed of his lost brother.

While he desires to set sail with the Greek fleet

[5] And purchases the winds with blood,

He strips away his fatherhood and, sorrowfully acting as priest,

Binds the wretched throat of his daughter.

308 The Ithacan wept for his lost companions,

Whom the savage Polyphemus, reclining in a vast cavern,

[10] Buried in his monstrous belly.

Yet, raging with a blinded face,

He repaid his sorrowful tears with joy.

Harsh labors celebrate Hercules;

He subdued the proud Centaurs,

[15] [Col. 0827A] [Note: [Col. 0827B]

15. “He took the spoils from the savage lion.”] Hercules’ second labor. In the Nemean forest there was a lion of extraordinary size, impenetrable by either iron or bronze. Hence they said that it had fallen from heaven. Hercules pursued it and killed it by the strength of his bare hands. He dressed himself in the hide of the slain animal, which no weapon could pierce, and wore it for as long as he lived.

[Col. 0827C] 16. “He pierced the birds with sure arrows.”] Hercules’ third labor. The Stymphalian birds, so called from the city, mountain, or lake of Stymphalus, were said to be of such great size that they overshadowed the rays of the sun, and of such rapacity that they devastated all Arcadia. Hercules, as Diodorus Siculus says in Book IV, drove them away by constructing a bronze rattle and producing a great noise with it; or rather, as Catullus explains in his verses, he pierced them with his arrows. Lucretius speaks of these birds in Book V:

“Those birds of Arcadia, dwelling at Stymphalus,

To be feared for their hooked claws.”

17. “He snatched the apples from the watching dragon, etc.”] Hercules’ fourth labor. The Hesperides were the daughters of Hesperus, who was the brother of Atlas—namely, Aegle, Arethusa, and Hesperethusa. They are said to have inhabited gardens near the Mauritanian town of Lixus, gardens rich in golden trees and guarded by a watchful dragon. Hercules killed the dragon and carried the apples away to his stepfather Eurystheus. Venus is said to have received from that garden of the Hesperides the golden apples by scattering which Hippomenes defeated Atalanta in the race.

“His left [hand] heavier”: understand the omitted noun in this phrase, just as Virgil says in *Aeneid* I.593, “in face and shoulders like a god.”

19. “He dragged Cerberus with a threefold chain.”] Hercules’ fifth labor. Pirithous, son of Ixion, after the death of his wife Hippodamia, made an agreement with Theseus that neither would marry any woman except one born from Jupiter. Theseus then carried off Helen. Pirithous, however, planning to carry off Proserpina, the wife of Pluto, descended to the underworld accompanied by Theseus and Hercules.

But Pirithous was killed by Cerberus at the first assault. When Theseus tried to help him, he himself fell alive into the power of Dis and was bound by him, until Hercules restrained the three-headed Cerberus, bound with a threefold chain. We discussed Cerberus in the twelfth metre of Book III.

20. “The victor is said to have placed the merciless lord, etc.”] Hercules’ sixth labor. Diomedes, king of Thrace, was so sparing of barley, says Apuleius in Book VII of the *Metamorphoses*, that he satisfied the hunger of his ravenous horses by supplying them with human bodies. Hence Ovid:

“Does the image of savage Diomedes not come to mind,

That wild man who fed his horses human flesh?”

But Hercules threw this tyrant to the same horses to be devoured.

22. “The Hydra perished, its poison consumed by fire.”] Hercules’ seventh labor. The Hydra was a serpent living not only on land but also in water; hence its name derives from *ὕδωρ*, “water.” It lived in the marsh of Lerna between Mycenae and Argos, and therefore is called the Lernaean plague. It had seven heads, or, according to others, fifty; when some of them were cut off, others were reborn in double number. [Col. 0828C] Hercules finally killed the beast by applying fire to each of its wounds.

23. “The river Achelous, disfigured in face.”] Hercules’ eighth labor. Achelous, son of Oceanus and Tethys, fought with Hercules for Deianira, daughter of Oeneus, king of Calydon. But Achelous, unequal in strength, first changed himself into a serpent and then into a bull. Hercules cut off the bull’s horn, which was given to the companion of Fortune, Copia. Thus Achelous, disfigured by the loss of one horn, concealed himself in the river that bears his name.

There is no need to remind me that here *turpatus* must be pronounced with a lengthened final syllable because of the metrical caesura; poets provide innumerable examples of this.

25. “He struck down Antaeus on the Libyan sands.”] Hercules’ ninth labor. Antaeus, son of Neptune and Earth, possessed such a great body that he grew to forty cubits in height. When he engaged Hercules, whenever his limbs failed him he was restored each time by touching the earth. Hercules noticed this and killed him by holding him aloft in the air.

26. “Cacus satisfied the anger of Evander.”] Hercules’ tenth labor. Cacus, son of Vulcan, harassed Latium everywhere with his robberies and spared not even Hercules. For he dragged Hercules’ cattle by their tails into his cave, thereby reversing their tracks. But Hercules, alerted by the lowing of the cattle, recovered them and killed Cacus, avenging the wrong done to Evander, whose guest Cacus had been—or, as others maintain, his slave.

28. “The bristling one marked his shoulders with foam.”] Hercules’ eleventh labor. The Erymanthian boar in Arcadia devastated the entire region because it was of immense size. Hercules brought it to Eurystheus. But since the boar was not then killed by Hercules, it is said merely to have marked Hercules’ shoulders with foam—shoulders that the high vault of heaven was destined to press, since Hercules is said to have carried the sky upon his shoulders.

29. “The final labor of heaven, with the neck unbent.”] Hercules’ twelfth labor. Atlas, king of Mauritania, is said to have supported the heavens on his shoulders. In order to free him from so great a burden, Hercules placed his own shoulders beneath the heavens. Through this final labor above all he earned heaven and was transferred into the company of the gods, becoming, as some think, the star of Mars.

Moreover, descriptions of all these labors of Hercules occur so frequently among the poets that we have thought it unnecessary to cite the poems that various poets wrote on the subject. Yet we must not omit here what the most learned Huet recently published about Hercules in his splendid book *Demonstration of the Gospel*, proposition 4 on the Book of Joshua, no. 13:

“It is the widespread opinion of learned men that there were several Hercules, and that the deeds of all of them were combined by the Greeks into one Theban Hercules; or rather, that the name Hercules was bestowed upon all men distinguished for their courage. Diodorus recognizes three: the Egyptian, the Cretan, and the Theban. Arrian, in Book II of *The Expedition of Alexander*, recognizes three: the Egyptian, the Tyrian, and the Greek; to these he adds an Indian Hercules in *The Indian Affairs*, on the authority of Megasthenes. Others regard the most ancient Hercules as Phoenician, the second as Egyptian, and the last and most recent as Theban. Some acknowledge two Egyptians; Herodotus, two Greeks, one a god and the other a hero; Cicero, six; others, twelve; and some, many more. I maintain that there was only one, and that he was Joshua, for you can see that what is attributed to the others can all suitably be referred to Joshua.”]

309 He took the spoils from the savage lion,

And pierced the birds with sure arrows;

He snatched the apples from the watching dragon,

His left hand made heavier by golden metal;

He dragged Cerberus with a threefold chain.

[20] The victor is said to have offered

The merciless master as food to his savage team.

310 The Hydra perished, its poison consumed by fire;

[Col. 0828A] The river Achelous, disfigured in face,

Dipped his shameful features into the banks.

[25] He struck down Antaeus on the Libyan sands;

Cacus satisfied the anger of Evander;

And the bristling one marked with foam

The shoulders that the high vault of heaven was destined to press.

The final labor: with neck unbent,

[30] He bore heaven upon it, and once again earned

[Col. 0829A] [Note: [Col. 0830A]

32. “Where.”] No place is designated here. Otherwise it would have been necessary to say “to which he leads,” but rather the cause is indicated for which brave men must proceed, just as Cicero said: “Once someone has sworn falsely, he ought not afterward to be trusted.”

33. “The way of example leads.”] This refers to Agamemnon, Ulysses, and Hercules, whose labors teach us that the path of vice is easy but its end bitter, whereas the path of virtue is difficult but its outcome sweet.

Seneca, *Hercules on Oeta*, line 1983:

“Never is glorious virtue carried

To the Stygian shades. Live bravely,

Nor will cruel fate drag you

Through the Lethean rivers. But when

The spent day brings your final hours to an end,

Glory will open a path to the heavens.”

34. “You turn your backs.”] The image is taken from soldiers, for whom it is shameful to turn their backs in battle when great rewards have been proposed and noble commanders are leading the way. Likewise, it is shameful for the human mind, when eternal life has been set before it and many holy men have shown the example, to turn away from God and turn toward other things. Hence the addition: “The earth once conquered grants the stars,” as though it were said: the mind that has conquered the body without wavering will cling to God forever. Matthew 11: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.”]

He earned heaven as the reward of his final labor.

311 Go now, brave men, where the lofty path

Of the great example leads. Why, in your idleness,

[Col. 0830A] Do you turn your backs? Once earth is conquered,

[35] It grants the stars.

BOOK FIVE.

[Col. 0829]

312 PROSE ONE.

[Col. 0829C]

ARGUMENT.—Because nothing can be unexpected to Providence, and because an accident is an unexpected event, Boethius objects that, once divine Providence is posited, no accident could exist. Philosophy answers that the question concerning accident is a matter of terminology: depending on the different use of the word, accident may both be denied and affirmed.

[Note: [Col. 0829D] Philosophy] had spoken and was turning the course of her speech toward other matters to be treated.

[Note: [Col. 0829D] “To treat and resolve certain other matters.”] For what must now be said about accident does not belong to the present undertaking except as a kind of appendix or addition, and, as they say, only accidentally. Therefore Philosophy will immediately say that although these matters are very useful to know, they nevertheless depart for a while from the path of her subject.]

Then I said: “Your exhortation is certainly reasonable and altogether worthy of your authority. But I am discovering in fact that the question concerning Providence which you recently said was entangled in many complications is indeed so.”

“For I am asking whether you think that anything at all exists as accident, and what accident is.”

313 Then she said: “I am hastening to fulfill the promise I made to you and to open a path by which [Note: [Col. 0829D] ‘You may return to your homeland.’] you may return to your homeland.

[Note: [Col. 0829D] “You may be led back to your homeland.”] Servius says that authors use this expression, and that in the question *quo* they either add or remove a preposition. Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* I.6:

“Driven from his homeland by fate, he came to Italy

And the Lavinian shores.”]

Although these matters are very useful to know, they are nevertheless somewhat removed from the path of our subject; and there is a danger that, wearied by [Note: [Col. 0829D] “Extraneous questions.”] digressions, you may not have enough strength to complete the straight road.”

“Do not fear that at all,” I replied. “For it will be a kind of rest to me to recognize the things in which I take the greatest delight. At the same time, when [Note: [Col. 0830D] ‘Every side of the argument.’] every side of your discussion has been established with unquestionable confidence, nothing concerning what follows will be uncertain.”

[Note: [Col. 0830D] “Every comprehensive survey of your question.”] By “every side” we mean, as we commonly say, the antecedents, accompanying circumstances, and consequences—the whole aspect of the question. “The things we consider,” says the author of *The Search for Truth*, “never appear entirely evident to us until the understanding has examined all their sides and all their relations.”]

Then she said: [Note: [Col. 0830D] “I shall comply.”] “I shall comply with your wishes,” and at once began as follows.

[Note: [Col. 0830D] “She began.”]

[Note: [Col. 0830D] “If someone defines an event, etc.”] Philosophy next explains the various uses of the word *accident* and teaches in what way accident should be rejected and admitted. The word *casus* is derived from *cadere*, “to fall,” in the sense in which “to fall” means the same as “to happen.” Therefore, in general, accident is nothing other than an event.

That event, however, can be said to arise in two ways: first, without any connection of causes; and then, through some connection of causes. If accident is said to be an event produced by a random movement and by no connection of causes, then certainly accident is nothing but an empty word. Since nothing cannot be the cause of anything, every event must necessarily have some cause, at least an external one.

But if accident is said to be an event produced through some connection of causes, yet apart from the awareness and intention of the agent, a distinction must be made. For this cause, apart from whose awareness and intention the event is said to occur, is either the first cause, namely God, or a secondary cause, namely a human being.

If the cause is the first, there is no accident at all, since no event is produced apart from God’s awareness and will. The concurrence and convergence of causes—what we now call their coming together—is produced by that order which proceeds through an unavoidable connection. Descending from the source of Providence, it arranges all things in their proper places and times.

But if the aforesaid cause is secondary, accident may be admitted, because an event often occurs apart from the awareness and intention of a human being. For example, if someone digging the earth in order to cultivate a field discovers a quantity of buried gold. Although there was some cause that buried the gold, and although there is also some cause by which the cultivation of the ground revealed the gold, nevertheless, because the gold is discovered by the farmer contrary to his awareness and intention, that event is called an accident.

From this follows the definition of accident: “An unexpected event arising from convergent causes in things undertaken for some purpose.” Since animals, plants, and inanimate bodies do not properly possess awareness and intention apart from which an event could occur, they therefore have no accident.]

[Note: [Col. 0830D] “But if.”]

“If someone,” she said, “defines as accident an event produced by a random movement and by no connection of causes, I affirm that there is no accident at all and declare it to be an utterly empty word, [Col. 0831A] signifying no underlying thing.

“For, with God ordering everything into its proper arrangement, what room can there be for randomness? The proposition that nothing comes into existence from nothing is true; no one among the ancients ever [Note: [Col. 0831B] “Contradicted it.”] opposed it, although they did not apply it to the operative principle—that is, to the efficient cause—but only to the material subject, the thing that is modified, as though they had laid down as a foundation that a mode or manner could not arise from nothing.

“But if something arises from no causes, it will appear to have arisen from nothing. If this cannot happen, then neither can an accident of the kind we defined a little earlier be possible.

“What, then?” I asked. “Is there nothing that can rightly be called an accident or a chance occurrence? Or is there something, although it escapes the common people, to which these terms apply?”

“My Aristotle,” she replied, “defined this in his *Physics* by a brief explanation close to the truth.”

“In what way?” I asked.

“Whenever something is undertaken for the sake of some purpose, but something other than what was intended occurs for certain reasons, it is called an accident. For example, if someone digging the earth for the sake of cultivating a field discovers a quantity of buried gold.

“This is therefore believed to have happened by chance, but it did not arise from nothing. For it has proper causes, whose unforeseen and unexpected convergence appears to have produced the accident. If the cultivator had not dug the earth, and if the person who deposited the money had not buried it in that place, the gold would not have been found.

“These, then, are the causes of the chance gain [Note: [Col. 0832B] ‘Profit or advantage.’] that arises from causes meeting and converging with one another, not from the intention of the person acting. For neither the person who buried the gold nor the one who cultivated the field intended that the money should be found. But, as I said, the one buried it, the other happened to dig there, and the two actions met and converged.

“It is therefore permissible to define accident as an unexpected event arising from convergent causes in things undertaken for some purpose. The convergence and meeting of causes, however, are produced by that order which proceeds through an unavoidable connection and, descending from the source of Providence, arranges all things in their proper places and times.”

### 315. METER

[Note: This is called elegy. Elegy is a poem consisting of two alternating kinds of verse, the first hexameter and the second pentameter, as stated in Book I, Meter 1.]

**From the crags of Achaemenian rock.** From the Persian mountain. For Achaemenia is Persia, or at least a part of Persia so called after Achaemenes, who, according to Herodotus, *Histories* I.4, was the first Persian king, from whom all the kings down to Darius descended. Hence Horace, *Odes* II.12: “Or you, who possessed the wealthy Achaemenes”—that is, the king of the Persians—and III.1: “Achaemenian perfume,” that is, Persian unguent. Here, however, some take Achaemenia to be Armenia, while that mountain is Mount Taurus. Sallust, a most reliable author, asserts—as is read in the fragments of his *Histories*—that the Tigris and Euphrates rise from a single spring in Armenia; flowing in different directions, they divide farther apart, leaving between them a space of many thousands, while the land enclosed by them is called Mesopotamia.]

**FIRST.**

**ARGUMENT.**—As Philosophy says: just as the meeting of ships carried along by the steady currents of two rivers may be fortuitous, so chance is governed by the fixed laws of divine Providence.

[Note:

Just as the Tigris and Euphrates flow forth as though from the same source, from the crags of the Persian mountain, where the Parthian warrior, fleeing in battle, drives reversed arrows into the breasts of his pursuers, and immediately those two rivers separate as their waters divide: if they meet and are again brought together into a single course, then whatever the water of either river carries along will come together; thus ships and tree trunks swept along by the river will converge, and the mingled waters will confuse their chance waves. Yet their uncertain movements are governed by the sloping land itself and by the fleeting course of the flowing river. Likewise, chance, which appears to occur without a guide and as though the reins had been loosened, is governed as if it had accepted the bridle; and the same thing occurs under the rule of God’s providence.]

[Note:

**1. “Where he turns against the pursuers,” etc.**—Here the Parthians are meant, namely those peoples who, originating among the Scythians, extended their empire as far as those regions of Asia watered by the Tigris and Euphrates. These peoples were especially formidable because of their arrows, which, while fleeing, they turned back against their pursuers, hurling them, as they turned themselves about, into the breasts of their enemies; then, suddenly turning their horses, they renewed the battle. Hence Virgil, *Georgics* III.31:

“Trusting in flight, the Parthian, with arrows turned.”

**3. “The Tigris and Euphrates.”**—The Tigris is so called from its swiftness, because its name in the Persian language is cognate with “arrow.” It is a river that rises in Armenia, if not from the same spring, as the aforementioned Sallust says, at least from the same mountain from which the Euphrates rises. It then flows into the Euphrates, watering Mesopotamia with its waves, and together with it reaches the Persian Gulf. Virgil speaks of this river in *Eclogue* I.62:

“Before, an exile, having traversed the lands of both,

The Parthian will drink the Arar, or Germany the Tigris.”

The Euphrates, however, is so called because of the joy it brings to the inhabitants by fertilizing their fields with its flooding. It is another river that likewise rises from the aforementioned mountains of Armenia. Like the Nile in Egypt, it fertilizes Mesopotamia by overflowing and, joined by the waters of the Tigris, flows into the Persian Gulf. Virgil speaks of it, signifying the war of the Parthians, whose boundary was the Euphrates, in *Georgics* I.509:

“From here the Euphrates moves; from there Germany brings war.”

Nor can I omit what Quintus Curtius says in Book V about both rivers: “These rivers,” he says, “flow from the mountains of Armenia, and thereafter, by a great division of their waters, pursue the course they have begun. They traverse 2,500 stades, marking an immense interval around the mountains of Armenia. When they begin to cut through the lands of Media and the Gordyaeans, they gradually draw closer together; and the farther they flow, the narrower the intervening space of land becomes. They are nearest to one another at the place which the inhabitants call Mesopotamia. For they enclose Media on both sides. Through the territory of the Babylonians they burst forth into the Red Sea.”]

> From the crags of Achaemenian rock, where fleeing battle  
> Drives its arrows into the breasts of the pursuers,  
> The Tigris and Euphrates spring from a single source,  
> And soon, separated, part their waters.

[5]

[Note:

**6. “The water of the ford.”**—A ford is water that, where its banks are not far apart, can be crossed on foot, on horseback, or at least in a small boat more easily than the sea. Hence some think *vadum* derives from *vadere*, “to go,” or from the Greek βάδος, “a place through which one goes.” In French we say *le gué*, *passer à gué*; the lower Normans say *le grand et le petit vé*. That alternating ford, or river, therefore, since it flows according to the laws of nature themselves, moves in so familiar and certain a course that it can be foreseen and intended by human beings; nevertheless, the vessels, logs, and other bodies of this kind, carried along while surrounded by such waters, meet by a fortuitous or unexpected occurrence.

**9. “The slopes of the land.”**—These may be understood as places. This, moreover, is the divinely established law of a moving body: a body in motion proceeds where it encounters less resistance; sloping places offer less resistance.

**11. “With the reins loosened.”**—The comparison is drawn from horses which, when the reins are loosened, run rashly here and there.

**12. “Chance.”**—That is, accident: the cause is taken for the effect. For among the ancients *fors* means a cause that brings something about at random. Hence Virgil, *Aeneid* II.94:

“And if chance had carried me anywhere.”

**12. “Accepts the bridle.”**—The comparison with horses that are governed by bridles is continued. Virgil, *Georgics* III.182:

“The first labor of the horse is to behold the courage and arms  
Of the warriors, to endure the trumpets, and, groaning under the strain,  
To carry the wheel, and in the stable hear the bridles resounding.”

Hence anything that is governed is commonly said to “accept the bridle,” as in Virgil, *Aeneid* XI.567:

“Today I shall tear up the city, the cause of war, and the very kingdom of Latinus,  
Unless they confess that they will accept the bridle and obey as conquered;  
I shall lay its smoking roofs level with the ground.”

**12. “It moves by that very law.”**—Namely, divine Providence, which, as has already been said, reaches powerfully from end to end and orders all things gently.]

> If they meet and are again recalled into one course,  
> What the water of the alternating ford carries along will converge;  
> Ships will meet, and tree trunks torn away by the river,  
> And the mingled water will entangle its chance patterns.  
> Yet these wandering accidents the slopes of the land themselves,  
> [10] And the flowing course of the descending current, govern.  
> Thus what seems to flow with loosened reins,  
> Chance accepts the bridle and moves by that very law.

### 318. PROSE II

**ARGUMENT.**—Philosophy teaches Boethius, who is questioning whether human freedom must be denied on account of what has been said, that every mind possesses freedom, and she explains its various kinds.

“I understand,” I said, “and I agree that it is as you say. But [Note: “In this chain of causes linked together,” etc.] Boethius seems to assume the role of those who could not reconcile human freedom with divine Providence, believing that one of these two alternatives must be necessary: either God does not foresee the future, or human beings possess no freedom. Cicero and many other ancients held this view. But since every human being is conscious of his own freedom more clearly than of divine Providence, Cicero and certain of those ancient thinkers, affirming human freedom, denied divine Providence. ‘Cicero,’ says Saint Augustine, *City of God* V.9, ‘as a great and learned man, and one who considered human life with the greatest and most expert care, chose free choice of the will from these two alternatives. To confirm it, he denied foreknowledge of future events; and thus, while wishing to make human beings free, he made them sacrilegious. The religious mind, however, chooses and confesses both, and confirms both by the faith of its piety.’

“Therefore, so that what Philosophy will henceforth propose on this subject may be understood more clearly, after setting forth a definition of freedom itself, we shall defend that same freedom under Philosophy’s guidance and explain its various kinds.

“I. Freedom in general may be defined as follows: a mind which, guided by cognition, can act upon itself by willing.

“It is called, first, ‘a mind,’ because freedom is a certain mode of the mind. A mode of the mind, however, since, like other modes, it cannot be conceived through its own separate idea, cannot be known without mention of the mind. Thus we do not know figure, rest, and motion without mention of the body. Philosophers say that modes are better known concretely than abstractly.

“It is called, secondly, ‘which can act upon itself,’ or, as some say, move and determine itself. The Greeks, using words derived from common intelligence and experience, most aptly call a free mind αὐτοκίνητος, ‘self-moving,’ and αὐτοκρατής, ‘ruling itself.’

“Saint Augustine used this notion of freedom, among other places, especially at the beginning of Book III of *On Free Choice of the Will*, where he discusses, as here, the agreement of free choice with divine Providence: ‘If the movement by which the will turns this way and that were not voluntary and placed within our power, a person could neither be praised when he turns toward higher things nor blamed when he twists toward lower things, as though toward a kind of hinge of the will. Nor should he be admonished at all to neglect these things and desire to attain eternal realities, or to refuse to live badly and instead wish to live well.’

“It is called, thirdly, ‘by willing.’ For, as Saint Augustine says in Book II of the *Retractions*, chapter 1, ‘we say that only that is within our power which happens when we will it; and first and above all, this is willing itself.’ Therefore all philosophers teach that the seat of freedom is the will. Hence they recognize two kinds of free acts: one they call elicited, which is willing itself; the other they call commanded, which is the body’s obedience to the mind’s command.

“It is called, fourthly, ‘guided by cognition,’ because, as the same philosophers say, the will does not move toward what is unknown: there is no desire for the unknown.

“But for a mind endowed with this general freedom to act and move itself, it is not necessary that it be placed, as it were, midway and indifferent between two contraries or even between contradictories. For theologians teach that this general freedom is found even where there is no such indifference. Thus Saint Thomas, *On the Power of God*, question 10, article 2, reply to objection 5, following Saint Augustine, teaches that God freely loves himself, and that the Holy Spirit proceeds freely from the Father and the Son, although not contingently. Yet no one would say that God is indifferent toward loving himself, or that the Father and Son are indifferent toward producing the Holy Spirit.

“Furthermore, Saint Thomas, *Sentences* III, distinction 18, question 1, article 2, reply to objection 5, seems to recognize this freedom in Christ the Lord: ‘Even if Christ’s free choice were determined toward one specific thing, such as loving God—which he cannot fail to do—he would not thereby lose freedom or the character of praise or merit, because he tends toward it not under compulsion but willingly, and thus is master of his act.’

“From this it follows that the power to sin does not belong to the nature of this freedom, since God and Christ, in whom there was no power to sin, nevertheless possess this freedom.

“It also follows that God, moving our mind toward himself as the highest good—whether while our mind is joined to our body or while it is separated from that same body—increases rather than removes this general freedom of our mind. For, as Saint Augustine says in Book III of *On Free Choice of the Will*, chapter 3: ‘Our will would not be a will unless it were in our power. But because it is in our power, it is free for us. For what we do not have in our power is not free for us, nor can what we have in our power fail to be.’

“Although a mind endowed with this general freedom is therefore not indifferent, this does not prevent freedom, in us who live this mortal life, from being a capacity for either alternative, or indifference. Hence among us there are two kinds of freedom: the freedom of contradiction, by which we can act or not act; and the freedom of contrariety, by which we can do this or that, as philosophers explain more fully. ‘We must confess,’ says Saint Augustine, *On Grace and Free Choice*, chapter 1, ‘that we possess free choice both for doing evil and for doing good.’”

“In this chain of causes linked together, is there any freedom of our own choice,” I asked, “or does a fatal chain also constrain the movements of human minds?”

“There is,” she replied. [Note: “There is freedom of our own choice.”]

### 319

[Note: “For there will be no rational nature without freedom of choice belonging to it.”]

**II.** Once the foregoing definition of freedom has been posited, the same freedom can easily be defended, under Philosophy’s guidance, as follows: since freedom is nothing other than a mind which, guided by cognition, can act upon itself by willing, every mind which, guided by cognition, acts upon itself by willing must necessarily possess freedom. But every mind is so constituted. For every mind not only knows and, by judging, distinguishes what should be avoided and what should be desired; it also seeks what it judges should be desired and avoids what it believes should be avoided, as everyone experiences within himself.”

“For there will be no rational nature without freedom of choice belonging to it. For whatever can naturally use reason possesses judgment by which it distinguishes each thing. By itself, therefore, it recognizes what should be avoided or desired. Whatever someone judges should be desired, he seeks; and whatever he considers should be avoided, he avoids. Therefore, wherever reason exists, there also exists the freedom to will and not to will.” [Note: “But I do not maintain that this is equal in everyone.”]

**III.** Having established a distinction between the divine, angelic, and human mind, Philosophy teaches that freedom differs in these minds. Concerning the divine and angelic mind, which Philosophy now calls the higher and divine substances, she appears to reason as follows: the mind which, guided by cognition, can act upon itself by willing more effectively should be considered freer, since freedom consists in this power. But the higher minds mentioned above—namely, God and the angel—can act upon themselves by willing more effectively under the guidance of cognition. For in every mind four things may be considered: perception, judgment, choice, and execution. These are so interconnected that there can be neither execution without choice, nor choice without judgment, nor judgment without perception. Therefore, as perception varies, the other elements vary as well. In the higher and divine substances, however, judgment is more penetrating, the will incorrupt, and the power to attain what is desired more effective than in other beings.

As for the human mind, four states may be distinguished in it; and according as these are higher or lower, they possess greater or lesser freedom.

The first state is that of the mind separated from the body, which preserves itself in contemplation of the divine mind; this mind is most free, because, guided by the most excellent cognition, it can act upon itself most fully by willing and loving God.

The second state is that of the mind joined to a body which obeys it at its command, as was the mind of the first parent before he sinned. For this mind descended to the body. This freedom of the human mind is not indeed as great as that of the blessed minds, but it is nevertheless greater than that of the remaining states, since Adam, endowed with greater cognition, could act upon himself more effectively by willing.

The third state is that of a mind afflicted by disturbances but not consenting to them, such as the mind of Saint Paul when he says in Romans 7: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members. Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.” This freedom of the human mind joined to earthly limbs is less than in the preceding state but greater than in the following, because the mind, not yet conquered, grows weary.

The fourth and final state is that of a mind obedient to disturbances. Its freedom is so slight that it seems rather to have the character of slavery. “The extreme of freedom,” says Philosophy, “is slavery, when minds devoted to vices have fallen from possession of their own reason.”

“But I do not maintain that this is equal in everyone. For in the higher and divine substances there is ready both penetrating judgment, incorrupt will, and effective power to attain what is desired. Human souls, however, must be freer when they preserve themselves in contemplation of the divine mind [Note: “Contemplation.”], less free when they descend into bodies, and still less free when they are bound to earthly limbs. The extreme is slavery, when, devoted to vices, they have fallen from possession of their own reason.”

### 321

[Note: “For when they turn their eyes,” etc.] The reader should attend to the admirable reasoning of the foregoing rather than expect me to explain it.]

For when they have cast their eyes down from the light of supreme truth toward lower and dark things, they immediately grow dim under the cloud of ignorance and are disturbed by pernicious emotions. By approaching and consenting to these, they strengthen the slavery they have brought upon themselves, and in a certain sense become captives of their own freedom. Yet the One who, from eternity, foresees all things, sees them with the gaze of Providence and disposes each thing, predestined according to its own merits. [Note: “God, in his providence.”] [Note: “He sees and hears everything.”] [Note: Πάντ’ ἐφορᾷ καὶ πάντ’ ἐπακούει. That is, “He sees everything and hears everything,” as Homer says of the sun in *Iliad* III.] Πάντ’ ἐφορᾷ καὶ πάντ’ ἐπακούει. (He sees all things and hears all things.)

### 322. METER

[Note: This is called by some Archilochian meter. It is a poem consisting of one kind of verse, each line of which has four final feet of heroic verse.]

**II.**

**ARGUMENT.**—What Homer says of the sun, says Philosophy, belongs to God alone: to see everything.

[Note: Homer, the poet of sweet eloquence, sings of the sun shining with pure light. Nevertheless, the sun cannot penetrate the innermost depths of earth or sea, because the splendor of its rays is weak. It is not so with God, the creator of the great world. Not even the densest mass of earth resists him, since from on high he sees everything; dark night with its gloomy shadows does not obstruct his sight. With one act of the mind he sees present, past, and future. Since God alone therefore sees everything, you may call God the true sun.]

[Note:

**2. “Homer.”**—Homer was the most celebrated poet, said to have been so called because, being blind, he needed a guide. Although his date is uncertain, he lived many years before Romulus. The Colophonians claim him as their own, the Chians vindicate him as theirs, the Salaminians claim him back, and the Smyrnaeans insist that he was theirs; hence they dedicated a shrine to him in their city. Whatever may be said about his homeland, he was so eloquent a poet that Alexander the Great is said to have been especially fortunate because he found in Homer a herald of his excellence. Homer often praises the sun and its light, but Philosophy seems to have taken the occasion for these verses from *Iliad* III. Hence the final words of the preceding prose are drawn, where Homer sings, addressing the sun:

> Ἥλιος θ’ ὃς πάντ’ ἐφορᾷς καὶ πάντ’ ἐπακούεις.
>
> “Sun, who see everything and hear everything.”

It is as though Homer had thought that the sun, like a kind of divinity, sees and hears everything. Pliny, Book XI, chapter 6: “The sun,” he says, “lends its light even to the other stars; splendid and pre-eminent, it looks upon everything and also hears everything. I see that this pleased Homer, the prince of literature, in the sun alone.”

**3. “Yet although,” etc.**—Although Homer says that the sun possesses such great light that it sees everything, the sun is nevertheless possessed of light so weak that, when its rays are diminished both by earth and by sea, it cannot illuminate—and therefore cannot see—the innermost depths either of earth or of sea. To see these things belongs to God alone, by whom all these things were created and are preserved.

**6. “Creator of the great world.”**—God, who truly is the creator not only of the human being, who is called the little world, but also of all the rest, whose collective structure is called the great world.

**7. “Seeing all things from on high.”**—If God derived the concept he has of created things from the created things themselves, since such things are far inferior to God, he would be said to observe them from below. Since God needs no outside assistance either for willing or for knowing, and possesses the concept of these things from himself, he is rightly said to observe them from on high.

**10. “What is, what has been, and what will come.”**—The present, past, and future. Since God’s cognition is infinite, it cannot be confined by any distinctions of present, past, or future time. Moreover, because God’s cognition is infinite, it cannot be multiple; therefore God sees all things in a single act of the mind.

**12. “Because he alone sees everything,” etc.**—Philosophy seems to have had in mind both the Homeric statement mentioned above and these words of Cicero, *On Divination* I and *On the Nature of the Gods* II: “The sun,” he says, “was so called either because it alone among all the heavenly bodies is so great, or because, when it rises and the other stars have been obscured, it alone appears.” Philosophy may therefore have reasoned as follows: whoever sees everything, and sees it alone, may, in Homer’s and Cicero’s judgment, be called the true sun. But God sees everything, and sees it alone. Therefore, in the judgment of such great men, God may be called the true sun.]

> Homer, with honey-flowing speech,  
> Sings Phoebus bright with pure light;  
> Yet he cannot pierce the innermost depths of earth  
> Or of the sea with the feeble light  
> [5] Of his rays.  
> Thus it is not with the creator of the great world:  
> For him, seeing all things from on high,  
> No mass of earth offers resistance;  
> No night with dark clouds obstructs him.  
> [10] What is, what has been, and what will come,  
> He sees in a single act of the mind.  
> Since he alone sees everything,  
> You may call him the true sun.

### 324. PROSE III

**ARGUMENT.**—Having learned about divine Providence and human freedom, Boethius shows that their agreement is difficult: first in general, then specifically, both from the side of Providence itself, which cannot be uncertain, and from the side of freedom itself, which appears to be free from necessity.

Then I [Note: Boethius] said: “See, I am confused again by a more difficult ambiguity.” [Note: “By a more difficult ambiguity.”]

Ambiguity lies in the fact that, when several possible paths have been proposed, it is uncertain which one should be taken. For *ambiguum* is derived from *ambigo*, “I go around”; and *ambigo* from *ambe*, “around,” and *ago*, “I drive,” as though someone who is uncertain were driven around. Hence ambiguity is first used of bodies which, acted upon by equal forces on either side, are moved neither in this direction rather than that nor in that rather than this; secondly, it is used of minds which, impelled by equally balanced arguments on both sides, do not assent to one part of a question rather than the other. The more Boethius understands Philosophy’s argument, however, the more his mind appears uncertain, with the weight of the arguments balanced, concerning divine Providence and human freedom—subjects on which Philosophy has so far spoken and which appear to conflict in such a way that one destroys the other. Hence Boethius presents arguments by which he believes the agreement of divine Providence and human freedom can be destroyed.

“What is this ambiguity?” she said. “I already conjecture what is troubling you.”

“I am excessively,” I replied, “confounded by a more difficult ambiguity.” [Note: “Divine foreknowledge and human freedom seem to contradict each other.”] “For it appears excessively opposed and contradictory that God foreknows everything and that there is any freedom of choice.”

[Note: “For if God sees everything,” etc.]

**I.** The foregoing agreement is shown in general to be impossible. For, as has already been said—and as daily experience confirms, a fact known even to Cicero and the other pagans—the freedom of the wayfarer is a capacity for either alternative. Since whatever is necessary is such that it cannot exist at all, or cannot exist in any way other than the way in which it does exist, is not free for a human being; and therefore there is no human freedom concerning it.

But, given divine Providence, everything a person does, says, and thinks will be such that it cannot be otherwise. For since divine Providence is cognition not only of all past and present things but also of future things, if these things can either fail to exist or exist in a way other than that in which they do exist, divine Providence will not be evident foreknowledge, firm and incapable of error, but rather obscure, uncertain, and liable to error—which it is impious to think of God.

“For if God sees all things,” she said, “and can in no way be deceived, what Providence has foreseen as future must necessarily occur. Therefore, if from eternity he foreknows not only the things human beings have done but also their plans and wills, there will be no freedom of choice. For no other act, nor any will at all, will be able to exist except the one that divine Providence, incapable of error, has foreseen.”

### 325

“For if things can be turned aside in a direction different from that in which they were foreseen, there will no longer be firm foreknowledge of the future, but rather an uncertain opinion—something I judge impious to believe about God.”

[Note: “Nor do I approve the argument,” etc.] Boethius raises against himself the response that some customarily give in order to defend the foregoing agreement: namely, that it is not divine Providence which is the cause of future events, but future events which are the cause of divine Providence. From this it follows that divine Providence, rather than the future event, is necessary. But Boethius refutes this response, first because it does not solve the difficulty, and then because it is backward to make future events the cause of divine Providence.]

“Nor do I approve the argument by which some believe they can dissolve this knot of the question. For they say [Note: ‘Something is not future because God foresaw it; rather, God foresaw it because it was future.’] that something will not happen because Providence has foreseen that it will happen; rather, since something is going to happen, it cannot be hidden from divine Providence, and in this way necessity slips back to the opposite side. For it is not necessary that what is foreseen must occur; rather, it is necessary that what is going to occur be foreseen.”

[Note: “As though,” etc.] “First,” he says, “this response does not solve the difficulty, since the question is not which is the cause of the other—whether Providence is the cause of the future event or the future event of Providence. For whichever of the two is necessary, the necessity of the other follows as well. Just as from the fact that I truly know you to be sitting, it necessarily follows that you are truly sitting; or from the fact that a wooden mass is equal to a measuring rod, it necessarily follows that the measuring rod is equal to that wooden mass, even though the measuring rod may be called the cause of this equality, or your sitting the cause of that judgment.” [Note: “But this does not solve the matter.”]

“As though it were being disputed which is the cause of what: whether foreknowledge is the cause of the necessity of future events, or the necessity of future events is the cause of Providence.” [Note: “Let us nevertheless attempt to prove the point itself.”]

“But let us try to demonstrate that, whatever the order of causes may be, the outcome of foreknown things is necessary, even if foreknowledge does not appear to impose the necessity of occurring upon future things.

“For if someone is sitting, the opinion that judges him to be sitting must be true; and conversely, if an opinion is true concerning someone because he is sitting, he must be sitting. In both cases, therefore, there is necessity: in the one, the necessity of sitting; in the other, the necessity of truth. Yet a person does not sit because the opinion is true; rather, the opinion is true because it has been preceded by someone’s sitting. Thus, although the cause of truth proceeds from one side, there is nevertheless a common necessity in both.”

### 326

“We must reason similarly about Providence and future events. For even if things are foreseen because they are future, and do not occur because they are foreseen, nevertheless it is necessary either that God foresee what is going to happen or that what he has foreseen occur. This alone is sufficient to destroy freedom of choice.” [Note: “Now how backward it is,” etc.]

“Further, it is backward or perverse—since the order of things has been reversed—to make future events the cause of divine Providence. For since every cause is prior to its effect, it is backward to make something that exists only from a certain point in time the cause of something that exists from all eternity. This would be the case if a future event were the cause of divine Providence. For things that once happened—for example, the walls of Rome—although they were previously future, would be causes of divine Providence, which is eternal.”

“Now how perverse it is,” she said, [Note: “Perverse.”] “to call the outcome of temporal things the cause of eternal foreknowledge! What else is it to suppose that God foresees future things because they are going to happen than to think that things which happened long ago are the cause of that supreme Providence? Furthermore, just as, when I know that something exists, it is necessary that it exist, so when I know that something will happen, it is necessary that it will happen. Thus the outcome of a foreknown thing cannot be avoided.

“Finally—[Note: ‘If anyone should think something otherwise,’ etc.]—

**II.** The foregoing agreement is shown specifically, from the side of divine Providence itself, to be impossible. For the quality of mind that philosophers call knowledge must be not only evident but also true and certain, at least with respect to the judgment attached to it, so that it is neither false like an error nor uncertain like an opinion. Since divine Providence is knowledge—and knowledge in a more excellent sense than any human cognition—divine Providence must therefore be not only evident but also true and certain. But of things that would be future through human freedom there could be no evident, true, and certain Providence, since such knowledge exists only concerning things that are necessary.”

“If someone believes something otherwise than the matter stands,” [Note: “Not in the same way.”] “that is not merely not knowledge; it is a deceptive opinion, far removed from the truth of knowledge. Therefore, if something is going to happen in such a way that its outcome is not certain and necessary, how can it be foreknown that it will happen? For just as knowledge itself is unmixed with falsity [Note: “It is free from error.”], so what is conceived by knowledge cannot be otherwise than it is conceived. The reason knowledge is free from falsehood is that it is necessary for each thing to be as knowledge comprehends it to be.

“What, then? How does God foreknow these uncertain future events? For if he judges that things will inevitably happen which can also fail to happen, he is deceived—which it is not only impious to think but even impious to utter. But if he determines that they will be future just as they are, while recognizing that they can equally occur or fail to occur, what kind of foreknowledge is this, which comprehends nothing certain and nothing stable?”

### 327

“Or what does this differ from divination?” [Note: “How does this differ from divination?”] “And certainly, if divine Providence concerned these free future events—that is, things which can equally fail to happen or happen—the same opinion would be like that ridiculous prophecy of Tiresias: ‘Whatever I say will either happen or not happen.’”

Tiresias was a Theban prophet who is said to have been blinded by Juno after offending her, and to have been granted the power of prophecy by Jupiter out of pity. Horace, *Satires* II.5:

> “To you also, Tiresias, when I ask beyond what has been recounted,  
> Tell me by what arts and means I may recover my lost possessions …  
> O you who never deceive anyone, you see that,  
> Guided by you, I return home naked and destitute …”

This prophet, like others, spoke ambiguously and was accustomed to say: “Whatever I say will either happen or not happen,” meaning that his statements would either prove true or not, while leading others to understand that his statements would always prove true, whether he affirmed or denied them. Horace, in the passage cited above:

> “O son of Laertes, whatever I say will either happen or not.”

For great Apollo grants me prophetic power. That ridiculous prophecy of Tiresias?

[Note: [Col. 0841C] In Horace, Book II of the *Satires*, Satire 5.]

“Whatever I say will either happen or not happen.”

[Note: [Col. 0841C] How would divine providence be greater than human opinion?]

How, moreover, would divine providence surpass human opinion if, like human beings, it judged uncertain those things whose outcome is uncertain? But if, in that supremely certain source of all things, nothing can be uncertain, then certain is the outcome of those things which he has firmly foreknown as future.

Therefore there is no freedom in human deliberations and actions: the divine mind, seeing everything without error or falsehood, binds and constrains them to one determined outcome.

[Note: [Col. 0842C] Once this has been admitted.]

### III

It is proved specifically, from the standpoint of human freedom itself, that the foregoing harmony cannot stand: for where there is no power toward either alternative, there is no freedom belonging to a human being on the journey through life. The Church wisely condemned this proposition:

“For merit and demerit in the state of fallen nature, freedom from necessity is not required in a human being; freedom from coercion is sufficient.”

It is also rightly said that, once this power has been removed:

1. There would be neither virtue nor vice, and therefore neither reward nor punishment.

2. God would be the author of all vices.

3. There would be no basis either for hope or for prayer, and thus the one means of intercourse between human beings and God—namely, hoping and praying—would be taken away.

4. Finally, the human race, severed and separated from its source, would waste away.

But once divine providence is posited, there will be no power in a human being on the journey through life toward either alternative. For divine providence, as has been said, since it is evident, true, and certain knowledge, concerns only necessary things—things, as philosophers say, determined toward one outcome.

[Note: [Col. 0842D] The power toward either alternative.]

[Note: [Col. 0841C] If you grant this, namely, that there is no freedom in human beings themselves.]

Once this has been admitted, it is clear how great a collapse of human affairs follows.

For rewards and punishments are proposed in vain to the good and the wicked, since no one has deserved them through a free and voluntary movement of the mind. And what is now judged most just—either punishing the wicked or rewarding the good—will appear most unjust, because it is not their own will that sends them toward one alternative or the other, but the certain necessity of the future that compels them.

[Note: [Col. 0841C] Toward either alternative.]

Thus neither vices nor virtues will amount to anything; rather, there will be a mixed and indiscriminate confusion of all merits.

[Note: [Col. 0842C] A confused disorder.]

And—nothing more criminal can be imagined—since the whole order of things proceeds from providence and human deliberations can accomplish nothing, it follows that our vices too must be attributed to the author of all good things.

[Note: [Col. 0842C] God.]

There is therefore no basis either for hoping for anything or for praying.

[Note: [Col. 0842C] Asking.]

For what could anyone hope for, or even pray for, when an unbending sequence joins together everything that ought to be desired?

[Note: [Col. 0842C] Unchangeable.]

Thus the one means of intercourse between human beings and God—namely, hoping and praying—will be taken away.

[Note: [Col. 0842C] Asking.]

For by the price of proper humility we merit, in return, the immeasurable grace of God.

[Note: [Col. 0842C] By rightly abasing ourselves, we merit God’s grace, whose value cannot be sufficiently estimated.]

This alone seems to be the means by which human beings can converse with God and, even before they obtain what they ask, be joined to that inaccessible light through the very act of supplication. But if, once the necessity of future events has been admitted, prayer is believed to possess no power, what will remain by which we can be connected with and cling to that supreme ruler of all things?

[Note: [Col. 0842C] God.]

Therefore it will be necessary for the human race, as you sang a little earlier,

[Note: [Col. 0842D] Namely, in Book IV, metre 6, line 43, where Philosophy was speaking.]

to be severed and separated from its source and to waste away.

[Note: [Col. 0842C] Separated from its source, it perishes.]

## 329. METRE III

[Note: [Col. 0843B] This may be called Pindaric. It is a poem consisting of a single kind of line, each of which seems to be a tetrameter governed by no fixed rules. Sometimes it consists of the four final feet of a heroic line; sometimes it replaces these with anapaests. Nevertheless, the poem closes with an Adonic line, containing a dactyl and a spondee.]

### Argument

[Col. 0843A]

“Whence,” sings Boethius, “do divine foreknowledge and human freedom, which stand separately, seem to struggle when joined together?” The reason is that, in this matter as in others, the human mind neither knows everything nor knows nothing; it attempts to advance from things known toward things unknown.

[Note: [Col. 0843A] What discordant cause dissolves the harmony of things? What power places so great a conflict between these two true realities—divine providence and human freedom—that, although each exists separately, both seem unable to exist together? Is there some discord among things that are true? Do certainties always agree with one another? There is discord, and these things do not always seem to agree in the human mind, since the mind, oppressed by the body that blinds it, cannot perceive, in the splendor of its extinguished light, even the smallest connections among familiar things.

But why is this same mind inflamed with such zeal to discover the hidden signs of truth? Does it know what it anxiously desires to know? No: for who strives to know what is already known to him? But if it does not know, what does it seek in its ignorance? For who desires what he does not know? Or who could pursue things unknown? How could anyone find, or recognize the form he has found, while ignorant of it?

When the human mind looked upon the supreme mind, did it not itself know things both individually and generally? Now, however, veiled by the darkness of the body, although it is not wholly forgetful of itself, it knows other things not individually but generally.

Whoever therefore investigates the truth is affected neither wholly by ignorance nor wholly by knowledge. For he neither knows everything nor is he altogether ignorant of everything; rather, he consults the supreme reality of which he retains a memory, recognizing those things that he knows by divine gift, so that, by knowing, he may add to the things he remembers those things that he has forgotten.]

### 1. “What discordant cause?”

I. Boethius, having compared divine foreknowledge with human freedom, wonders why each appears separately to be established by firm arguments, but, when joined together, to destroy the other. He therefore seeks the cause of so great a mystery. This cause is called “discordant” because it seems to dissolve an agreement made—or at least needing to be made—between divine foreknowledge and human freedom.

### 2. “What God?”

Since an effect does not exist without its cause, the discord between divine providence and human freedom, of which Boethius is already conscious, must have some cause. Since that cause is unknown, it is questioned whether it might be some god. Thus the ancients spoke of a *deus ex machina*, a god appearing unexpectedly. Cicero says in Book I of *On the Nature of the Gods*:

“Because you do not see how nature could accomplish anything without some mind, when tragic poets cannot work out the conclusion of their plot, you take refuge in a god; yet you would certainly not need his assistance if you could see the vast and boundless magnitude of the regions extending in every direction.”

Cicero seems to have taken this from Plato’s *Cratylus*, where Plato says:

“Unless, of course, like writers of tragedies, whenever they are stuck, they take refuge in machines, raising up gods.”

### 3. “Two true things”

Namely, divine providence and human freedom. For just as it is true that God foreknows everything, so it is also true that human beings possess freedom of choice. Yet the one seems to conflict with the other so completely that, although they stand separately, together they seem to destroy each other.

### 6. “Is there none?”

As though the question were, “Is there not any?” For this is a form of question in which the questioner appears nevertheless to request that what he asks be granted to him. Thus Terence says: “Did I not say that this would happen?” So Boethius is saying: “Does no discord occur even among things that are true? Do all truths always agree with one another in such a way that neither conflicts with the other?”

Certainly they do not always agree in that way. This is elegantly expressed by the particle *sed* (“but”) that immediately follows. If the light implanted in our mind were infinite, then those things that, standing separately, are true to our mind because they are clearly and distinctly known would also seem true to that same mind when joined together, since nothing is hidden from infinite light. Thus, for God, things that are true separately are also true together.

But because the light of our mind is confined within its own very narrow limits, it can happen that things clearly and distinctly known by our mind—and therefore true to it separately—are nevertheless unknown to that same mind together, and therefore are not true to it in combination. Yet none of the things clearly and distinctly known should on that account be denied. Clear things must not be denied because the mind cannot grasp obscure things.

Saint Augustine, Book II of *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 14:

“Is what is clear to be denied because what is hidden cannot be comprehended? Are we therefore to say that what we plainly see to be so is not so, merely because we cannot discover why it is so?”

### 8. “But the mind, overwhelmed by blind limbs…”

Apart from the fact that our mind is finite, the light implanted in the human mind is so darkened by the body with which the mind is joined—according to the saying of the sacred text, Wisdom 9: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks upon many things”—that the same mind cannot recognize even the tenuous connections among things, upon which the judgment of truth depends.

How, then, will that same mind comprehend the lofty connections between divine providence and human freedom?

“We judge with difficulty,” the Wise Man continues in the passage just cited, “the things that are on earth, and we discover with labor the things that are before us; but the things that are in heaven, who can investigate?”

Here is Boethius’ question. In order to solve it, he first establishes that our mind does not know everything; then that it is not altogether ignorant of everything either, so that it may pass from what is known to what is unknown.

### 11. “But why does it burn with such love?”

II. Boethius proves that the human mind does not know everything. Since desire is only for what one does not possess, if the human mind anxiously desires to know something, then certainly it does not possess a conception of what it desires to know; and therefore it certainly does not know it. Experience, moreover, proves that the human mind anxiously desires to discover the hidden signs of truth. Therefore it does not know those signs.

### 14. “To know what is known”

The quantity of the word *nota* may be observed here. Its final syllable, otherwise short, is long by position, as they say, because it is followed by two consonant letters. Although these two consonants are each separated from the preceding vowel by the boundary between words, they nevertheless do not cease to lengthen that vowel. Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* IX, line 37:

“Quickly bring iron, give weapons, climb the walls.”

The same phenomenon occurs very frequently in Catullus and Martial. I think this is why the ancient poets more carefully avoided the collision of an otherwise short vowel with several such consonants, even when all those consonants occurred in the following word—especially if the sound of both letters was distinctly perceived by the ears, whose judgment is most exacting:

“all things they grasp, all things they reject, all things they write,”

and so forth.]

What discordant cause dissolves

the covenants of things?

## 330

What god sets such great wars

between two true things,

so that what separately stand firm

refuse, when mixed, to be joined?

Is there no discord among truths,

and do certainties always cohere?

But the mind, overwhelmed by blind limbs,

cannot recognize, in the fire

of the light pressed down,

the tenuous connections of things.

## 331

But why does it burn with such love

to discover the hidden signs of truth?

Does it know what it anxiously desires to know?

But who labors to know what is known?

[Note: [Col. 0845B] “But if it does not know”—etc.]

But if it does not know, what does it seek blindly?

For who would desire anything in ignorance?

Or who could pursue things unknown?

Or how could anyone find them,

or, having found them, recognize their form

while ignorant of them?

### 15. “But if it does not know…”

III. Boethius proves that the human mind is not ignorant of everything. Apart from the fact that the human mind desires to know the truth, as has already been said, no one desires what he does not know; there is no desire for what is wholly unknown.

Furthermore, Boethius says, no one can pursue what he does not know, since the investigation itself, being the mind’s first thought, is a kind of knowledge or perception. And even if someone ignorant could inquire, he could not find what he sought. How could he find it? Nothing is found except through conception; and just as color gives no conception of itself to a blind person, so a thing wholly unknown gives no conception of itself to a mind that is ignorant of it.

Finally, even if an ignorant person could both inquire into and find what was unknown, he could not recognize it and distinguish it from other things.

“Who, being ignorant, could recognize a form that he had found?”

Plato argues in the person of Socrates in the *Meno* as follows. Let us suppose, he says, that a runaway slave is being sought by another slave who has no knowledge whatsoever of the fugitive, while the master of both commands the search. The searching slave will seek in vain. For even if he comes upon the runaway slave whom he is seeking, he will not know that he has found him and therefore will not be able to recognize or distinguish him from the others.

### 20. “When it saw the supreme mind…”

Many think that in the remainder of this poem Boethius follows Plato’s view. As is clear from Plato’s *Meno* and many other works, Plato believed that human minds, before being joined to bodies, had been created and divinely endowed with perfect knowledge of everything; but that they lost this knowledge through their association with the body, so that only through great labor could they recover the memory of what they had previously known.

I do not deny that this interpretation of Boethius may be admitted. Yet what Boethius now says can also be understood even if that Platonic doctrine is rejected.

Suppose the state of innocence in which we believe Adam was created. In that state the human mind perceived the higher mind in a special way—namely, God. Hence it knew the greater part of the things to be known not only generally but also individually. It knew both the whole and the particulars.

Adam’s descendants, however, as punishment for the first sin of their ancestor, are so affected by disturbances that their minds, although not yet entirely forgetful of themselves, know many things only generally and not individually. They retain the whole while losing the particulars. For insofar as the mind is formed by the conception of God—or of that which is—it knows everything generally; but insofar as it is hindered by its bodily companion, it does not perceive many things individually.

### 25. “He seeks truth”

“Philosopher”: for philosophy, according to the meaning of the name, is the pursuit of wisdom, or the investigation of truth.

### 26. “He possesses neither state”

According to Cicero, *On Invention* II, a state or habit consists in some perfect and stable completion of the mind or body. Thus “habit,” in general, insofar as it may be said both of thought and of the privation opposed to thought, can be understood as a mode of completion within its own category.

In this sense the mind is now said to possess neither state: the human mind exists neither in complete knowledge of all things nor in complete ignorance of all things.

### 26–27. “He neither knows nor is wholly ignorant of everything”

This is directed against the Academics and the Dogmatists. The Academics—namely, the disciples of Plato, so called from the Academy, the Athenian philosophical school—believed that nothing could be known evidently by human beings and that, consequently, no true and certain judgment could be made by them. This view was also held by the Pyrrhonists, whom the Greeks called *skeptikous* (σκεπτικοὺς), “contemplators.”

The Dogmatists, on the contrary, as they are called, believe that everything can be known by human beings with such evidence that there is no room for doubt concerning any subject.

### 28. “Remembering the whole, which she retains, she consults it”

Namely, the implanted and innate conception of God.

First, the human mind, always retaining this conception, remembers it, since this conception cannot be extinguished and endures as long as the human mind itself—that is, forever.

Second, this same conception is rightly called the whole or summit of the other things that can be known by the human mind. For the conception of mind, the conception of body, the conception of a thing, indeed the conception of being in general, as logicians speak, is nothing other than this innate conception of God, whether taken simply or in a modified form.

Finally, the human mind first consults this general conception, so that whatever is clearly and distinctly contained in it may first be recognized before judgment is passed. That conception is therefore the first standard of true and certain judgment, as is proved more fully elsewhere.

Indeed, by repeatedly attending to and examining this conception, the human mind becomes more learned, and seems to remember what it has forgotten—whether through the first parent or, as Vallinus thinks here, through each human being at the moment of creation.

Things that have been forgotten are also said in a passive sense by Virgil, *Eclogue* IX, line 53:

“Now forgotten by me are so many songs…”

But if it does not know, what does it seek blindly?

For who would desire anything in ignorance?

Or who could pursue things unknown?

Or how could anyone find them,

or, having found them, recognize their form

while ignorant of them?
