When the mind saw the higher mind,

did it likewise know both the whole and the particulars?

Now, enclosed in the cloud of its limbs,

it is not wholly forgetful of itself,

and retains the whole while losing the particulars.

Therefore whoever seeks the truth

possesses neither state:

he neither knows,

nor is he wholly ignorant of everything.

## 333

But, retaining and remembering the whole,

he consults it, recalling what he has seen on high,

so that he may add to what he has preserved

the portions he has forgotten.

## 334. PROSE IV

### Argument

Philosophy explains that the harmony between divine providence and human freedom has seemed difficult both to the ancients and to more recent thinkers because divine foreknowledge, infinitely surpassing human knowledge, cannot be grasped by the human mind. After explaining the arguments that troubled Boethius, she proves that whatever is known is comprehended not according to the power of the thing itself but rather according to the capacity of the knower.

Then she said:

“This is an ancient complaint concerning providence,

[Note: [Col. 0846B] Philosophy.]

and Marcus Tullius himself…”

### I

Philosophy recalls the ancient thinkers to whom the harmony between divine providence and human freedom seemed difficult. Among them Marcus Tullius Cicero was especially prominent. By denying divine providence on the one hand and affirming human freedom on the other, while wishing to make human beings free, he made them sacrilegious as well, says Saint Augustine in *The City of God* V, chapter 9.

Cicero’s argument is the same one Boethius used above: once human freedom is posited—as experience proves it must be—divine providence cannot be an evident, true, and certain knowledge of future things, or else it cannot exist at all.

And Marcus Tullius,

[Note: [Col. 0846B] Book II of *On Divination*, where he attempts to abolish the divination that his brother Quintus had defended.]

when he discussed divination, treated a matter that had been vigorously debated, and one that you yourself had long and earnestly investigated, but that none of you had yet succeeded in resolving with sufficient care and firmness.

[Note: [Col. 0847D] The cause of this obscurity.]

### II

Philosophy says that the reason why ancient and recent thinkers have been unable to reconcile divine providence with human freedom is that their minds are too weak to perceive divine foreknowledge. Hence, judging rashly and prejudicially, they deny divine providence—something Philosophy promises to demonstrate after answering the arguments that previously troubled Boethius.

The cause of this obscurity is that the movement of human reasoning cannot be brought near to the simplicity of divine foreknowledge. If that simplicity could be conceived in any way, nothing at all uncertain would remain.

[Note: [Col. 0847C] Doubtful.]

I shall attempt to reveal and explain this, however, only after I have first examined the matters that have troubled you.

[Note: [Col. 0847C] Explained.]

## 335. “For I ask…”

### III

Philosophy answers the arguments that Boethius used above, approximately as follows.

If, once human freedom is posited, divine providence can be not only evident but also true and certain knowledge of future things, then divine providence will certainly be rightly reconciled with human freedom, since all the preceding opposing arguments are contained in the contrary proposition, as will be clear to anyone who pays attention.

But the matter is in fact as follows. Since the conception of present things and the foreknowledge of those same things as future are the same mode of thought, differing only in time—and God is not subject to time—then, just as knowledge of present things can be evident, true, and certain, so foreknowledge of future free things can be evident, true, and certain, without imposing any necessity upon them.

“For I ask why you think less effective the argument of those who resolve the difficulty by judging that foreknowledge is not the cause of necessity for future things and therefore that nothing prevents freedom of choice. Do you derive the argument for the necessity of future things from anywhere other than the fact that things foreknown cannot fail to happen?

If, therefore, foreknowledge adds no necessity to future things—which you yourself admitted a little earlier—what is it that compels voluntary outcomes to a fixed result?

Let us assume, for the sake of argument, that there is no foreknowledge. Insofar as this is concerned, are things that happen by choice compelled by necessity? Certainly not.

Let us assume again that foreknowledge exists but imposes no necessity upon things. Then, I think, the same complete and absolute freedom of the will will remain.

But, you will say, although foreknowledge is not the necessity by which future things come to pass, it is nevertheless a sign that they will necessarily come to pass.

In this way, then, even if foreknowledge had not existed, it would still be established that future outcomes are necessary. For every sign merely shows what something is; it does not bring about what it signifies.

Therefore it must first be demonstrated that nothing happens except by necessity, so that foreknowledge may appear to be a sign of this necessity. Otherwise, if necessity does not exist, foreknowledge cannot be a sign of something that does not exist.

It is evident, moreover, that a proof supported by firm reasoning must be drawn not from signs or arguments imported from outside, but from causes that are congruent and necessary.

But how can it happen that those things do not come to pass which are foreseen as future?

As though we believed that the things which providence foreknows as future will not occur, rather than holding that, although they do occur, they possessed no necessity by their own nature in order to occur. This can easily be understood from the following.

While many things are taking place, we observe them before our eyes—for example, the actions of charioteers as they guide and turn their teams.

[Note: [Col. 0847C] In chariot races.]

And so with other matters. Does any necessity compel these things to happen in this way? Certainly not. The product of an art would be useless if everything moved under compulsion.

Therefore, just as things lack necessity of existence when they are taking place, so they will be future without necessity before they take place. There are therefore certain things that will happen whose outcomes are free from every necessity.”

No one, I think, will deny that things now taking place were going to happen before they took place. These things, therefore, even when foreknown, have free outcomes. For just as knowledge of present things imposes no necessity upon things that are taking place, so foreknowledge of future things imposes no necessity upon things that are going to happen.

But you object that it is precisely this that is in doubt: whether there can be foreknowledge of things that do not have necessary outcomes.

[Note: [Col. 0848C] To conflict.]

For these things seem incompatible. You think that if they are foreseen, necessity follows; and that if necessity is absent, they cannot be foreknown, since nothing can be comprehended by knowledge unless it is certain.

If things whose outcomes are uncertain are foreseen as though they were certain, you think this must be the obscurity of opinion, not the truth of knowledge.

[Note: [Col. 0848C] Obscurity.]

You believe that judging things otherwise than they are is incompatible with the integrity of knowledge.

[Note: [Col. 0848D] The cause of this error.]

### IV

Philosophy shows that the cause of the foregoing error lies in this: since knowledge requires both a knowing mind and an object to be known, the opponents of divine providence interpret divine foreknowledge according to the nature of the object known, although it must instead be interpreted according to the nature of the knowing mind. Philosophy first proves this through several examples and then through reasoning.

The cause of this error is that each person thinks that everything he knows is known solely through the power and nature of the things themselves. But the whole matter is the opposite.

[Note: [Col. 0848C] Whatever is known is known not according to the mode of the thing known but rather according to the mode of the knower.]

Everything that is known is comprehended not according to its own power but rather according to the capacity of those who know.

To make this clear through a brief example, the same roundness of a body is apprehended differently by sight and by touch.

[Note: [Col. 0849C] A round body is perceived as absent by sight and only as present by touch.]

Sight, remaining at a distance, observes the whole at once by casting out its rays; touch, however, in contact and joined with the sphere, comprehends its roundness piecemeal by moving around its circumference.

[Note: [Col. 0849C] “Differently by sense, etc.” These examples are, specifically, sense; sense in general; imagination; reason; and intelligence. They must be understood from the side of the knower: although they concern the same subject matter—for example, the same round body—they differ. Clearly, the human mind, which can be informed only by another, knows in two general ways: by God, whose effect it is, and by the body, of which it is the form. Informed by God, the human mind is again said to know in two ways: by initial and by continued attention. Initial attention is called intelligence; continued attention is called reason, so that reason is nothing other than innate conception extended a little further. Informed by the body itself, the human mind can likewise know in two ways. First, insofar as it perceives when moved only by the brain, of which it is the form—as when, in sleep, a hunter’s mind thinks of woods and coverts; this is called imagination. Second, insofar as it perceives when moved also by other bodies, both internal and external; this is called sense. Sense is either internal, such as hunger and thirst, or external: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. All these modes of knowing are so ordered that, the fewer causes on which they depend, the more perfect they are, since they come closer to divine wisdom. Thus taste is more perfect than touch; smell than taste; hearing than smell; sight than hearing; imagination than sense; reason than imagination; and intelligence than reason. Thus the examples prove that the mode of knowing is determined according to the nature of the knower.]

The human being himself is contemplated differently by sense, differently by imagination, differently by reason, and differently by intelligence.

Sense perceives the figure constituted in matter. Imagination judges the figure alone, without matter. Reason surpasses this as well and considers, in a universal way, the form that exists in individual things.

## 337

[Note: [Col. 0849C] Intelligence is a higher mode of knowing.]

The eye of intelligence is higher still.

For, rising beyond the scope of the universe, it contemplates that simple form itself with the pure gaze of the mind.

Here this must be considered above all: the higher power of comprehension embraces the lower, whereas the lower in no way rises to the higher.

Sense cannot accomplish anything apart from matter; imagination does not contemplate universal forms; reason does not grasp the simple form. But intelligence, as though looking down from above, judges everything that lies beneath it once the form has been conceived—and does so in the manner in which it comprehends the form itself, which could not be known by anything else.

It knows the whole domain of reason, the figure of imagination, and material sensible things, without using reason, imagination, or the senses, but by that single stroke of the mind which, so to speak, sees everything formally.

Reason too, when it considers something universal, comprehends what is imaginable or perceptible without using imagination or the senses. For it defines the universal concept of its conception in this way: “A human being is a two-footed rational animal.”

No one is unaware that this universal conception also concerns an imaginable and perceptible thing. Yet it considers that thing not through imagination or sense but through rational conception.

Imagination too, although it took its beginning from the senses, from seeing and forming figures, nevertheless illuminates all sensible things in the absence of sense, judging them not through a sensory but through an imaginative mode.

Do you see, then, how in knowing all things the powers of cognition use their own capacity rather than the nature of the things known?

### 338

[Note: [Col. 0850C] Nor is this unjust.]

This is proved by reasoning as well. For the mode of a thing, since it is not distinguished from the thing modified, must be understood according to the nature of the modified thing rather than according to the nature of some other thing that modifies it.

Now conception, no less than judgment, is a mode of the very mind that knows and judges.

And certainly this is not unjust:

[Note: [Col. 0849C] Not without reason.]

since every judgment is an act of the one who judges, each person must carry out his own activity not through another’s power but through his own.

## 339. METRE IV

[Note: [Col. 0850C] This is called Glyconic. It is a poem consisting of one kind of line, each of which generally contains one spondee and two dactyls. “Generally” is said because the number of syllables may remain the same while their stated quantities are sometimes disregarded.]

### Argument

Although, says Philosophy, the Stoics believed that the human mind perceives nothing except what is formed in it by bodies, the mind is nevertheless formed by a more effective principle and perceives insensible things without the service of bodies, and sensible things with the bodies themselves serving it.

[Note: [Col. 0849C] The Athenian Stoa once produced philosophers who were insufficiently learned. They believed that all sensations and conceptions, arising from external bodies, were impressed upon minds—just as the ancients used to impress letters with a swift-moving pen upon smooth paper bearing no previous characters.

But if our mind develops nothing through its own thought, and merely submits to impressions from bodies, suffering only their influence and reflecting useless images of the objects presented to it like a mirror, why is the universal knowledge of all things so clear in human minds? How are individual things known? How are known things divided? How are divided things recombined? How does the mind alternately ascend from the lowest things to the highest and descend from the highest to the lowest? How, arranging itself within itself, does the mind refute error by truth?

The cause of all these things is much more effective and powerful than the human mind, which, like matter, passively receives impressed forms. Yet the impression made upon the living body comes first, arousing and moving the powers of the mind—just as light strikes the eyes or a voice sounds in the ears. Then the power of the mind, once moved, compares the forms implanted in itself with such movements or adventitious forms and joins the two together.]

### 1. “The Stoa”

Namely, the Athenian Stoa. At Athens there was a certain colonnade in which some people used to gather to discuss every kind of subject. In the same way, Caen, Bayeux, and other smaller cities each have their own place where many people customarily gather to hear and discuss new matters.

Zeno, the most famous of the ancient philosophers, found this opportunity and began teaching philosophy there. His disciples were called Stoics from that place: for *stoa* (στοά) means “colonnade” in Greek.

Philosophy now calls these men “exceedingly obscure old men”: old men because they cultivated virtue above all, believing that the happy life consisted entirely in it, like the wisest elders; obscure because they went astray here, since error arises from obscurity.

Because these same Stoics devoted themselves especially to dialectic—of which their Zeno is said to have been the principal inventor—Philosophy, having now set out their error, refutes them with arguments drawn from dialectic and then explains what ought to be thought.

Once the Stoa produced

men excessively obscure,

### 3. “Who [held] that sensations and images, etc.”

### I

Philosophy sets out the error of the Stoics. It consists in their believing that not only the senses but also all conceptions—which Philosophy here calls “images,” and which the Stoics themselves, according to Cicero in the *Topics*, called *ennoiai kai prolepseis* (ἐννοίαι καὶ προλήψεις, “conceptions and preconceptions”)—are impressed upon minds even by external bodies, just as letters are impressed upon paper by a moving pen.

Hence, says Saint Augustine in *The City of God* VIII, chapter 7, the Stoics placed the criterion of truth in the bodily senses and judged that everything learned must be measured by their untrustworthy and deceptive rules.

## 10. “But if the mind is vigorous through its own powers, etc.”

### II

Philosophy refutes this error of the Stoics with arguments drawn from dialectic, which they studied with the greatest devotion. For dialectic deals not only with conception, both universal and particular, but also with division, definition, method, and the very standard of truth; none of these things could exist if the human mind referred all its conceptions to impressions received from bodies.

First, there would be no universal conception—that is, no conception which surveys all things—for a universal conception is not acquired through the senses. Whatever is perceived by the senses is confined to a definite time and place and is therefore particular.

Second, there would likewise be no particular conception, by which the mind apprehends individual things. For, apart from the fact that the human mind cannot apprehend itself as an individual while dependent upon the body, the particular triangle or circle believed to be perceived through touch and sight is not truly a triangle or circle. A particular triangle consists only of three lines meeting one another in such a way that they form three angles equal to two right angles; a circle consists only of one line drawn around a single point in such a way that all its parts are equally distant from that point. Yet every sensible triangle or circle, as we can observe through refined optical instruments, or, as they are called, microscopes, consists of almost infinitely many lines, some projecting beyond and others intruding within the foregoing particular notion of a triangle or circle.

Third, there would be no division, by which the mind divides what it has apprehended, since division occurs only when the mind separates things that appear conjoined to the senses—or, as the logicians say, by abstraction.

Fourth, there would be no definition, by which the mind gathers together what it has divided. For, says Crassotius, *Posterior Analytics*, book II, chapter 1, article 1:

> If all the parts of a mechanical clock are taken apart and, after their separation, each is presented for inspection, this seems to provide something like an example of division and logical partition. But if you apprehend all those parts clearly and distinctly, each in its proper place and order within the whole, then this seems to provide an example of definition.

It follows that a power which cannot divide what it has apprehended cannot also gather together what it has divided—that is, cannot define.

Fifth, there would be no method, which, like a mountain and a valley, sometimes ascends from subordinate species to the highest genus and sometimes descends from the highest genus to subordinate species, arranging each in its proper order. For, as has already been said, neither genus, species, nor their order is perceived by the senses.

Sixth and finally, there would be no standard of truth by which the mind could refute what is false. The Greek term for the standard of truth is *κριτήριον* (*kritērion*), that which, as a guide that neither deceives nor is deceived, persuades the human mind to form a judgment as true and free from every doubt. But the senses under discussion cannot be such a standard, since we are often deceived by them. Therefore, the Stoics, believing that every conception arises from the senses, rejected every standard of truth as well. Saint Augustine noted this in the aforementioned book VIII of *The City of God*, chapter 7, where he also says:

> When they say that no one but the wise is beautiful, by what bodily senses did they see this beauty? With what eyes of flesh did they behold the form and splendor of wisdom?

[Col. 0852C] Philosophy indicates this standard of truth when she says that the mind “refers itself to itself.” There are two kinds of such a standard of truth: one external, belonging to the category of the efficient cause—namely, God, who, being infinitely wise and good, can neither be deceived nor deceive; and the other internal, belonging to the category of form—namely, evidence, that is, a clear and distinct conception. If we follow this, we shall never err, since we have been taught by God himself, our teacher.

Thus, when our mind refers itself to itself, let it attend inwardly to this evidence of its own, or to its clear and distinct conception. As long as it does not know things clearly and distinctly—or evidently—in matters unrelated to the mysteries of faith, let it suspend assent, lest it rush headlong if it proceeds rashly, as Cicero says. “For,” says that same orator, “it is disgraceful for assertion and assent to precede knowledge and apprehension.” But once that same mind has clearly and distinctly perceived its clear and distinct conception, then, having removed all doubt, let it pronounce judgment, certain that it is taught inwardly not by human beings but by God himself:

> “If you have understood,” says Saint Augustine in *On John* XL, “it has also been said to your heart. Understanding is God’s gift.”

It should be noted that the following words are found in chapter 11 of *On the Spirit and the Soul*, a work commonly listed among the writings of Saint Augustine:

> “Now the mind inserts its head among the highest things; now it falls into the lowest; now, bringing itself into itself, it refutes false things by means of true ones.”

Together with the errors of transcription *decidit* (“falls”), *infimis* (“among the lowest”), and *inferens* (“applying”), these words lead the scholars of Louvain, among many other arguments, to conclude very convincingly that this book is not the work of Saint Augustine but of someone much more recent, perhaps Hugh of Saint Victor, since in chapter 33 of the same book Boethius is mentioned.

### 340. “Who believe that senses and images”

Who believe that senses and images  
Are impressed upon minds  
By outer bodies,  
As once, with a swift stylus,  
It is customary to fix letters  
Upon the surface of a page  
That bears no marks.

### [10]

But if the mind, vigorous through its own powers,  
Explains nothing through its own movements,  
But merely lies passive,  
Subject to the marks of bodies,  
And, taking the place of a mirror,  
Returns empty images of things,  
From where does this conception,  
Which surveys all things, arise in minds?  
What power apprehends individual things,  
Or divides what it has apprehended?  
What power gathers together what it has divided,  
And, reading the path in either direction,  
Now inserts its head among the highest things,  
Now sinks down into the lowest,  
Then, referring itself to itself,  

[The supplied source ends this passage here.]

### [Note: Col. 0853C]

**26. “This is rather the efficient cause, etc.”** — III. Philosophy explains what must be held. First, unless the human mind were informed by God, who is no less its teacher than its creator, it could apprehend nothing, either universally or individually; it could not divide, define, or arrange things in order, nor would it possess any standard of truth. For all these things are either an innate conception of God, who is, or some mode of such a conception. Therefore, this is by far the more powerful efficient cause.

Next, since the mind is the form of the body, it is also affected in sensation when the body is moved. For, according to Saint Augustine, *On the Quantity of the Soul*, chapter 25, sensation is “a passion of the body that does not remain hidden from the soul.” Thus a bodily affection precedes, stirring the living body. Here it should be observed that the word “passion” is not entirely idiomatic Latin, but no more suitable term is available for expressing this thought of Philosophy.

Thus light is nothing other than the movement of the eye when moved by the sun or by some other similar body. When the eye has been moved, the nerve extending from it as far as the brain is moved; consequently the brain too is moved, and when it is moved, the mind—especially united with the brain—is so moved that it not only senses but also sees. In the same way, sound moves the ears.

Finally, when the mind compares this adventitious idea with the prior innate idea, it judges with such freedom that it can not only join things that agree and separate things that disagree, but also suspend every assent.

Does it refute false things by means of truths?

### 342. “This is rather the efficient cause”

This is rather the efficient cause,  
Far more powerful  
Than that which merely suffers  
Marks stamped upon matter.

Yet there first comes the stimulus  
That rouses and moves  
The powers of the soul:  
An affection in the living body.

When light strikes the eyes  
Or sound resounds in the ears,  
Then the mind’s awakened vigor,  
Calling forth the forms  
It holds within,  
Applies them to the external marks  
And mingles the images  
With the forms stored within.

## 343. PROSE V

### ARGUMENT

“Therefore,” says Philosophy, “just as imagination is not to be denied on account of the weakness of sensation; nor reasoning on account of the weakness of imagination; nor human understanding on account of the weakness of reasoning: so divine foreknowledge of free future events is not to be denied on account of the weakness of human understanding.”

If, then, in the perception of bodies, although qualities presented from without [Note: Externally.] affect the instruments [Note: Organs.] of the senses, and a bodily affection precedes the vigor of the active mind, calling forth within itself the mind’s act and awakening forms meanwhile at rest within—if, I say, in the perception of bodies the soul is not marked by an affection [Note: The soul is not marked by an affection.] such as that by which a body joined to the soul is marked, namely by shape, rest, and motion—although the body is affected by these, the mind is not thereby affected—but by its own power judges the affection undergone by the body (yet this does not prevent the mind from being said to suffer in sensation, on Aristotle’s own authority, insofar as the body’s suffering does not remain hidden from the mind, as Saint Augustine teaches), how much more must those things that are free from every bodily affection [Note: Free from the commerce of bodies], in distinguishing, not follow objects presented externally, but carry out the activity of their own mind? [Note: In this way different kinds of cognition belong to different things.]

In this way, therefore, multiple kinds of cognition have been assigned to different and distinct substances.

### [Note: Col. 0853D] “Sensation”

We define sensation differently from our author, but this has no bearing on the present purpose. First, sensation seems to us to be defined as Saint Augustine defines it: “a passion of the body that does not remain hidden from the soul.” Accordingly, sensation may be understood in two ways, as the philosophers say: inadequately, insofar as it is a passion of the body; in this sense sensation is also found in beasts; and adequately, insofar as it is “a passion of the body that does not remain hidden from the soul.” In this sense sensation belongs to the human being alone, since the human being alone consists of body and mind.

Second, our author places sensation, in the proper sense, even in beasts, but with this distinction: in shellfish there is sensation without imagination; in mobile beasts there is also imagination without reason; whereas in the human being there are sensation, imagination, and reason, but without understanding, which he calls divine in kind.

But, I ask, if sensation exists in shellfish, why should imagination not exist in them as well, since sensation and imagination differ only in this: sensation is completed through each creature’s own organ, while imagination is completed through the common organ, namely the brain—and the brain is also found in shellfish?

If imagination exists in other beasts, for example in a fox, why should reason not exist in them? For they perform many actions which, if some cognition is necessary for them, require not only that which is called sensation and imagination, but certainly also reason—that is, the progress of the cognizing being from known things to unknown ones.

Finally, if reason exists in the human being, as it truly does, why should understanding not exist in the same being, since reason does not exist without judgment, nor judgment without understanding?

Unless, however, by the understanding she has named, Philosophy intends a conception received from no one and infinite to be understood. For this understanding belongs to God alone.

Third, we have noted these matters all the more freely because they contribute nothing to Philosophy’s present demonstration. Whether beasts properly have sensation or not, it is enough for observing the distinction and order stated above that one human being has sensation.

Likewise, although the human being is affected by understanding, divine understanding, being infinite, so surpasses human understanding that things which cannot be grasped by human understanding are rightly comprehended by divine understanding.

Sensation alone, deprived of every other kind of cognition, was assigned to creatures without movement, such as sea-shells and whatever other creatures feed while clinging to rocks. Imagination, however, was assigned to mobile beasts, in which there seems already to be some impulse toward fleeing or seeking. Reason belongs to the human race alone, just as understanding belongs to the divine alone. Hence that cognition excels the others which by its own nature apprehends not only what is proper to itself but also the subject matter of the other cognitions. [Note: It apprehends both its own proper matter and the matter subject to the other cognitions.]

### 344. [Note: Col. 0855C]

**“What, then, if reasoning, etc.”** — Philosophy finally proceeds to the comparison for which the lengthy preliminaries were intended, a comparison which is called one of proportion. Her meaning is this: as sensation, considered in relation to its subject matter, is related to imagination considered in relation to its subject matter; or as imagination, considered in relation to its subject matter, is related to reason considered in relation to its subject matter; so reason, considered in relation to its subject matter, is related to understanding considered in relation to its subject matter. Therefore, just as imagination is not to be denied because of the weakness of sensation, nor reasoning because of the weakness of imagination, so divine understanding—or foreknowledge—of free future events is not to be denied because of the weakness of reasoning or of human understanding.

### 344. “What, then, if sensation and imagination oppose reasoning”

What, then, if sensation and imagination resist reasoning, saying that the universal is nothing, although reason thinks it beholds it? For whatever is sensible or imaginable cannot be universal. Must we therefore conclude either that reason’s judgment is true and that nothing is sensible, or—since it is evident to reason that many things are subject to sensation and imagination—that reason’s conception is empty when it considers as something universal what is sensible and particular?

Suppose, in reply, that reason answers that it does indeed perceive both what is sensible and what is imaginable under the aspect of universality, whereas those faculties cannot aspire to knowledge of universality, since their conception cannot exceed bodily shapes. In the knowledge of things, then, we ought rather to trust the firmer and more perfect judgment.

In such a dispute, should we, who possess the power both of reasoning and of imagining and sensing, not rather support the cause of reason?

The case is similar when human reason does not believe that divine understanding can behold future events unless it beholds them in the same way that human reason does. For you argue as follows: If events do not appear to have certain and necessary outcomes, they cannot be foreknown as certain to occur. Therefore, there is no foreknowledge of such things; or, if we believe that there is foreknowledge even of them, nothing will occur except by necessity.

If, then, just as we participate in reason, we could possess the judgment of the divine mind—as we judged that imagination and sensation ought to yield to reason—so we would rightly consider it just that human reason should submit to the divine mind.

### [Note: Col. 0855D]

**“Therefore, let us raise ourselves, if we can, to the summit of that supreme understanding, etc.”** — Let us strive to approach divine understanding. For since the harmony between divine providence and human freedom mentioned above is perfectly comprehended by this divine understanding, the closer we come to the divine manner of understanding, the more clearly this harmony will become known to us. But we cannot approach God except by directing diligent attention toward God himself. Even the structure of our own body seems to encourage us to do this, since—

Therefore, let us raise ourselves, if we can, to the summit of that supreme understanding. There reason will see what it cannot behold within itself. It will see how even those things that do not have certain outcomes can nevertheless be seen with a certain and determinate foreknowledge, and how this is not opinion but rather the unbounded simplicity of supreme knowledge.

## 346. METER V

### [Note: Col. 0855D]

This is called the Archilochian meter: a poem consisting of a single kind of verse, each line being a heptameter. It contains first the four initial feet of the heroic meter, followed by three trochees.

### ARGUMENT FROM CICERO, *ON THE LAWS*, BOOK I

“Nature,” says Philosophy, “cast the other living creatures down toward feeding, but raised human beings alone upright and stirred them to behold, as it were, their kinship with heaven and their former dwelling-place.”

### [Note: Col. 0855C]

How many living creatures roam the earth endowed with different shapes! Some have long bodies; serpents crawl through the dust by the strength of their breasts and draw out a continuous furrow. Others, wandering on light wings, beat the air and cross great stretches of the fluid atmosphere in prolonged flight. Others delight in walking upon the earth, whether they cross green fields with their steps or enter the forests.

Although all these living creatures, as you see, differ from one another in many ways, they agree in this: their faces, inclined toward the earth, weigh down and dull their senses.

The human race alone raises its lofty head higher, stands lightly with its body upright, and scorns the earth. This bodily form warns you—unless, buried in the earth, you foolishly rave—that, since you direct your face toward heaven and raise your brow, you should also lift your mind on high, lest your mind lie oppressed below, lower than the body that stands upright.

### [Note: Col. 0855D]

**1. “How variously, etc.”** — Many orators and poets have said that human beings alone walk upright, while the other animals proceed with their faces turned downward. You have heard Cicero; now hear Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book I, fable 2:

> While the other animals look down toward the earth,  
> He gave the human being an uplifted face  
> And commanded him to look upon heaven  
> And raise his countenance toward the stars.

A distinction nevertheless seems necessary between the position of the body and the position of the face, both in human beings and in the other animals. The human being is upright, while the other animals are prone in body. But the faces—and therefore the gaze—of both human beings and the other animals (except, at least, that fish called *οὐρανοσκόπος*—“sky-gazer,” because, having its eyes on the upper part of its body, it looks toward heaven as though unwillingly) are directed not upward but more or less toward the horizon. Hence the structure of the brain differs in all animals.

This seems to be the distinction observed here. The passage does not say that beasts see the earth and human beings heaven with their eyes turned downward or upward; it says only that the other animals stand with their bodies prone, while human beings stand upright. This is sufficient for the human mind to be aroused by the distinctive structure of its body to contemplate God.

The beasts enumerated here are: (1) serpents, (2) birds, and (3) walkers, which either traverse fields or enter forests. There is nothing further about them that requires noteworthy comment.

**5. “In the fluid flight of the long ether.”** — This is a transposition of words, which grammarians call hyperbaton, since one ought to say “fluid ether” and “long flight.” Compare Virgil: “They went, obscure, beneath the solitary night”; “May he hurl the accursed spear”; “To grant southern winds to the fleets.”

### 346–347

In shapes of many kinds the animals traverse the earth:

For some have bodies stretched out long, and sweep the dust,

And, driven onward by the force of their breasts, draw out

A continuous furrow.

There are others whose winged lightness wanders and beats the winds,

### [5] 347

And swims through the long expanses of the fluid ether in flight;

Others rejoice to press their tracks upon the ground with their steps,

Whether to cross green fields or enter forests.

### [Note: Col. 0857B]

**9. “The prone face can weigh down and blunt the senses.”** — The senses are active only through the spirits diffused from the heart to the brain and from the brain through the nerves to the other parts of the body. These spirits, however, flow less freely into a face turned downward than into a head held upright.

**12. “The bodily form admonishes.”** — If bodies in general can serve as examples of minds, as they certainly can, then the human body ought to be a particularly significant example for the mind with which it is joined. Just as the human body, in accordance with the laws governing light bodies, tends straight toward heaven, so the human mind should aspire through thought toward God. There is another explanation as well, namely—

**14. “Lest, weighed down, it sink, etc.”** — Lest the human mind, overcome by the disturbances of the body, whose mistress it ought to be, become the body’s slave. Compare Philippians 3: “Their glory is in their shame, who set their minds on earthly things.”

Though you may see that all these creatures differ in varied forms,  
Their prone faces can nevertheless weigh down and blunt their senses.

The human race alone raises its lofty summit higher,  
And, light of body, stands upright and scorns the earth.

This bodily form, unless you are foolishly deluded by the earth, warns you:  
Since with upright face you seek heaven and raise your brow,  
Lift your mind also on high, lest, weighed down, it sink below,  
And the mind sit lower than the body raised more loftily.

## 348. PROSE VI

### ARGUMENT

Philosophy finally concludes that divine cognition, like the cognition of God who knows, is wholly simultaneous, so that, just as the conception of present things does no harm to human freedom, so divine foreknowledge of free future events does not harm human freedom.

Since, as was shown a little earlier, everything that is known is known not from its own nature but from the nature of those who comprehend it, let us now consider, so far as is lawful for philosophers, what the state of the divine substance is, so that we may also recognize what its knowledge is like.

[Note: It is the common judgment that God is eternal.]

For eternity is clearly and distinctly comprehended in the clear and distinct notion of God, which all human beings possess as divinely implanted—not otherwise than as three angles are understood to be comprehended in the idea of a triangle. Therefore, just as all human beings judge that a triangle consists of three angles, so all judge that God is eternal.

[Note: “Of the living.”]

That God, then, is eternal is the common judgment of all living beings. Let us therefore consider what eternity is.

[Note: Once eternity is known, both the divine nature and the divine knowledge must necessarily be known.]

For this will disclose to us alike the divine nature and its knowledge.

[Note: Eternity is the complete and simultaneous possession of an interminable life.]

This definition of eternity is accepted by Saint Thomas and the other theologians; therefore it seems that it should be explained point by point.

It is called, first, “possession,” because eternity is God’s proper perfection. In other words, the term “possession” is transferred from bodies to minds. The possession of bodies consists in this: we are so much their masters that we can place our feet upon them and establish a seat in them. For *possidere*—“to possess”—seems to be derived from *potens*, or *potis*, or even *pos sedere*, “to be able to sit upon”; just as *pos* has remained in *compos* and *impos* in place of *potis* or *potens*. Therefore, possession may most appropriately be called, in the case of minds, the indivisible perfection of the mind; eternity, however, is the indivisible perfection of God, since a supremely perfect thing cannot be conceived except as eternal.

Saint Thomas, *Summa theologica*, I, q. 10, a. 1, ad 6: “That which is possessed,” he says, “is held firmly and peacefully.” Thus, in order to designate the immutability and unfailingness of eternity, Boethius used the term “possession.”

It is called, second, “of life.” For just as eternity is a certain mode, so eternity must be the eternity of something. Nothing can more properly be called the eternity of than life, since life distinguishes not only animate bodies from inanimate ones, but also minds from bodies, and even minds from other minds. The life of which eternity is, as it were, the mode seems to be nothing other than thought, since eternity can belong only to a mind, whose living is thinking.

Hence Aristotle says in Book XII of the *Metaphysics*, chapter 7: “The thought of the mind is life.” Therefore, as Saint Thomas says in the same place, I, q. 18, a. 3, having shown that God is intelligent, he concludes that God possesses the most perfect and everlasting life, because his intellect is most perfect and always in act.

It is called, third, “wholly simultaneous,” because the life whose mode eternity is said to be possesses no succession. In this it differs from time, which is called the duration of a thing that, just as it began to exist, will also cease to exist, such as the form of a horse. For the divisions of time—namely, the present, the past, and the future—are never simultaneous but succeed one another.

It is called, fourth, “interminable,” because eternity belongs to a life bounded neither by a beginning nor by an end. In this too it differs from the *aeon*, which is called the duration of a thing that indeed had a beginning but will never have an end, such as my mind. For the *aeon* is bounded by at least one limit, namely, the beginning from which it began.

It is called, fifth, “perfect,” because, since eternity is the mode of a mind and therefore of a perfect life, it too must be perfect. Accordingly, it must acknowledge no cause of itself. In this respect eternity will differ even from the world, if, as Aristotle imagined, the world had existed from eternity.

From all these points, in which Philosophy is said to locate the nature of eternity, there is one that Philosophy especially explains: namely, that eternity is wholly simultaneous. She says that the other durations—the *aeon* and time—imitate this property of eternity as far as they can, so that, if they cannot possess that abiding presence, they may at least seem to possess it.

[Note: The infinite.]

Eternity, then, is the complete and simultaneous possession of an interminable and perfect life.

[Note: This becomes clearer by comparison.]

This is made clearer by comparison with temporal things.

[Note: It is evident.]

For whatever lives in time proceeds from the past, through the present, into the future; and nothing constituted in time can embrace the whole span of its life simultaneously. It has not yet grasped tomorrow, while it has already lost yesterday. Even in today’s life you live no longer than in that moving, transitory moment.

[Note: Fleeting.]

Whatever, therefore, is subject to the condition of time—even if, as Aristotle judged of the world in *On the Heavens*, Book I, it never began to exist, never ceases to exist, and its life extends along with the infinity of time—still cannot rightly be considered eternal. For it does not comprehend and embrace the whole span of its life simultaneously, however infinite that span may be; rather, it does not yet possess the future, while it no longer possesses the past.

Whatever, therefore, comprehends and possesses the fullness of an interminable life in its entirety and simultaneously, so that nothing of the future is absent from it and nothing of the past has flowed away, is rightly declared to be eternal. It must also necessarily be ever present to itself, self-contained, and have the infinity of moving time present to it.

Hence some are mistaken who, when they hear that Plato held that this world neither had a beginning in time nor would have an end, suppose that the created world thereby becomes coeternal with its creator. It is one thing to be led through an interminable life, which Plato attributes to the world; it is another thing to possess, all at once, the entire presence of an interminable life, which is plainly proper to the divine mind.

Nor should God appear older than created things by the quantity of time, but rather by the simplicity of his nature. For the infinite movement of temporal things imitates this abiding state of an immovable life, which is wholly simultaneous. Since that movement cannot reproduce or equal it, it falls from immobility into motion and declines from the simplicity of presence into the infinite quantity of the future and the past. And since it cannot possess the entire fullness of its life simultaneously, by the very fact that it never ceases to exist in some manner, it seems in some measure to imitate what it cannot fulfill or express, binding itself to whatever sort of presence belongs to this small and swiftly flying moment.

[Note: Which is wholly simultaneous.]

Because this moment bears a certain image of that abiding presence, it grants to whatever things it touches the appearance of being. Since it could not remain, it undertook the infinite journey of time. Thus it happened that it continued its life by proceeding onward, although it could not embrace its fullness by remaining.

Therefore, if we wish to assign names worthy of things, following Plato we should call God eternal, but the world everlasting.

[Note: “Since, then,” and so forth.]

From what has been said, Philosophy seems to reason as follows. Since judgment concerning a notion must be made according to the nature of the mind that knows, and since God, who knows free future events—the matters now under discussion—is by nature eternal, that is, always thinking and always living without any distinction between present, past, and future, God’s notion must accordingly be conceived as eternal, or wholly simultaneous, so that it relates to free future events in the same way as it relates to present things.

It follows that God’s notion should more properly be called not foreknowledge, as though of the future, but knowledge of an ever-unfailing present moment. Hence it is called not *prevision* but rather *providence*, because, established above the lowest things, it surveys all things as though from the lofty summit of reality.

Now, the notion of present things imposes no necessity upon them. For the sight by which you perceive present things adds no necessity to them. Similarly, if God, ignorant of future things, did not know them except when they were present, this notion of God would impose no necessity upon them. The difference would be the same as that which we now observe between the rising of the sun and my speaking: the former occurs necessarily, the latter freely.

Therefore, just as necessity cannot be inferred from the notion of present things, so from divine foreknowledge of free future things it cannot be inferred that they are necessary except conditionally. And just as the notion of present things—even when a human being is acting freely and possesses unimpaired power to choose either alternative—is evident, true, and certain knowledge, so divine foreknowledge of future things—even though the human being who will one day act retains unimpaired power to choose either alternative—is likewise evident, true, and certain knowledge.

This is all the more so because, although my speech is the cause of the notion by which you now know that I am speaking, no thing, whether present or future, is the cause of the divine knowledge or foreknowledge. God has obtained the power to comprehend all things and to behold their presence not from the outcome of future events but from his own simplicity.

[Note: “As it is now said.”]

Since, then, every judgment comprehends the things subject to it according to the nature of the mind that judges, and since God always possesses an eternal and present state, his knowledge too, having surpassed every movement of time, remains in the simplicity of its presence. Embracing the infinite spans of past and future, it considers all things in its simple cognition as though they were already happening.

Therefore, if you wish to weigh the presence by which he distinguishes all things, you will more properly judge it to be not foreknowledge, as though of the future, but knowledge of an ever-unfailing present moment. Hence it is called not *prevision* but rather Providence, because, established above the lowest things, it surveys all things as though from the lofty summit of reality.

Why, then, do you demand that those things which are illuminated by the divine light should become necessary, when human beings do not even make necessary the things they see? Does your perception add any necessity to the things you see as present? Not at all.

[Note: Comparison.]

Now, if there is a proper comparison between the divine present and the human present, just as you see certain things with your temporal present, so he sees all things with his eternal present.

[Note: God.]

Therefore this divine foreknowledge does not alter the nature or property of things, but sees them present to itself in the very condition in which they will one day occur in time. Nor does it confuse the judgments concerning things: with one intuition of his mind it recognizes things that will come to be necessarily no less than things that will come to be non-necessarily.

[Note: He knows both what will necessarily come to be and what will not necessarily come to be.]

Just as you see a person walking on the earth and the sun rising in the sky at the same time, and although both are seen simultaneously, nevertheless distinguish between them and judge one to be voluntary and the other necessary:

[Note: You distinguish them.]

[Note: The person walking.]

[Note: The sun rising.]

So the divine intuition, looking down upon all things, does not disturb their quality: in itself they are present, but in relation to the condition of time they are future.

It follows that this is not opinion but knowledge grounded rather in truth, since it knows that something will exist while also knowing that the same thing lacks the necessity of existing.

[Note: Certain knowledge.]

If you say that what God sees will occur cannot fail to occur, and that what cannot fail to occur happens necessarily, and thus bind me to the term “necessity,” I shall admit that the matter is one of the most solid truth, but one accessible scarcely to anyone except a contemplator trained in divine matters.

[Note: It is indeed a matter of the truest reality, but accessible only to the mind accustomed to contemplating divine things.]

For I shall reply that the same future event, when referred to the divine notion, is necessary; but when considered in its own nature, it appears wholly free and unrestricted.

There are two kinds of necessity. One is simple necessity, as in the proposition that all human beings must be mortal. The other is conditional necessity, as in the proposition that, if you know someone to be walking, that person must be walking. For whatever anyone knows cannot be otherwise than it is known to be. But this condition does not at all entail that simple necessity.

[Note: Necessity.]

For it is not its own nature that makes this necessity, but the addition of the condition. No necessity compels someone who is walking voluntarily to walk, although, while he is walking, it is necessary that he be walking.

[Note: The person walking.]

[Note: While he is walking.]

In the same way, if Providence sees something as present, it must be, although it possesses no necessity in its nature. Now God beholds as present those future things that proceed from free choice. These things, therefore, become necessary in relation to the divine intuition through the condition of the divine notion; but when considered in themselves, they do not cease to possess the absolute freedom of their nature.

[Note: They are not deprived of the absolute freedom of their nature.]

Everything, then, that God foreknows as future will undoubtedly occur, but some of these things proceed from free choice. Although they occur, they do not thereby lose their proper nature; before they came to be, they could also have failed to occur.

What, then, does it matter that they are not necessary, since, on account of the condition of divine knowledge, they occur in every respect as though by necessity? It matters precisely as in the examples I proposed a little earlier: the rising sun and the walking person cannot, while they are occurring, fail to occur; nevertheless, one of them was necessary to exist even before it occurred, whereas the other was not.

So too, things that God possesses as present undoubtedly exist; but one derives its existence from the necessity of things, while the other derives its existence from the power of those who bring it about.

[Note: Not without good reason.]

We therefore rightly said that these things, if referred to divine knowledge, are necessary; but if considered in themselves, they are free from the bonds of necessity. Just as everything that is evident to the senses, if referred to reason, is universal, but if considered in itself, is singular.

“But if it lies within my power to change my intention,” you will say, “I shall nullify Providence if I happen to change what it foreknows.”

I shall reply that you can indeed turn aside your intention; but since Providence’s present truth sees both that you can do so and whether you will do it and in what direction you will turn, you cannot evade divine foreknowledge—just as you cannot escape the gaze of a present eye, even though you may turn by free choice toward various actions.

“What, then?” you will say. “Will divine knowledge be changed by my disposition, so that, when I now will this and now that, it too seems to alternate its acts of knowing?”

Not at all. For the divine intuition anticipates every future event and turns it back and recalls it to the presence of its own knowledge. It does not, as you suppose, alternate between foreknowing this now and that later; rather, remaining itself unmoved, it anticipates and embraces all your changes in a single act.

God has obtained the power to comprehend all things and to behold their presence not from the outcome of future events but from his own simplicity.

[Note: From the outcome.]

This also resolves the point you raised shortly before: that it would be unworthy if our future actions were said to furnish the cause of God’s knowledge. For the power of this knowledge, embracing all things through its present notion, itself establishes a measure for all things, while owing nothing to what comes later.

[Note: Owes it nothing as received.]

Since this is so, the freedom of choice remains unimpaired for mortals. Nor are laws unjust in proposing rewards and punishments when wills have been released from every necessity. God also remains above all things as their foreknowing spectator, and the eternal present of his vision always coincides with the future quality of our actions, distributing rewards to the good and punishments to the wicked.

Hope and prayers are not placed in God in vain; when they are righteous, they cannot be ineffective. Therefore turn away from vices, cultivate virtues, raise your spirit toward upright hopes, and extend humble prayers into the heights.

[Note: “A great necessity of uprightness has been imposed upon you,” and so forth.]

For, as Saint Basil says in the *Shorter Rules*, response 2, the mind becomes inert and gives itself over to an excessive ease of idleness because it does not believe that God is present, searching hearts and reins. For if it believed this, it would certainly do what is said: “I kept the Lord always before my eyes, for he is at my right hand, that I may not be shaken” . . . .

“For who,” he says in response 29, “being subject to another’s authority, would ever dare in the sight of his prince to do anything that does not please him?”

[Note: “A great necessity of uprightness has been imposed upon you,” if you do not wish to dissemble, since you act before the eyes of a judge who sees all things.]

## VARIOUS READINGS

*(From the recension of Renato Vallini.)* The first number indicates the page number printed in bold type; the second indicates the line number.

[Col. 0863]

[Col. 0863A] 4, 2, “They console.” Thus all the old manuscripts; “he consoles” is incorrect. 11, 1, “and indissoluble.” Two Victorine manuscripts read “indissoluble”; the first is from the library of Saint Victor in Paris. 11, 9, “they had taken away.” The second Victorine manuscript reads “he had taken away.” 14, 1, “nourished.” Here, although the books vary, we have retained “nourished” rather than “reared,” since we often find the former used by the ancients in the same sense as here: in Velleius Paterculus, Book II, where Tiberius is described as “nourished in the disciplines of heavenly instruction”; and in Apuleius, “a maiden nourished in every delight.” Pliny the Younger had earlier spoken of people “nourished by the sea.” 14, 2, “go away instead.” The first Thuaneus manuscript, from the library of a most distinguished man, reads “go away.” 14, 5, “It had grown dark, lest.” “It may grow dark and not” is not an implausible reading. 17, 2, “increased.” The Florentine edition reads “done.” 18, 6, “among the numbered items.” That is, “he held in ready money”; this reading is found in all the manuscripts. [Readings: 14,1: *innutritum* / *enutritum*, both “nourished/reared,” with different prefixes. 14,5: *Caligarat, ne*, “it had grown dark, lest”; *Caligaret nec*, “it might grow dark, and not.”]

[Col. 0863B] 24, 3, *prius*, “earlier” (adverb). All the manuscripts except the Florentine read *prior*, “earlier” (adjective). 31, 1, “had occupied his attention.” The Florentine alone reads “had occupied.” 32, 2, “nor the burden.” The Regius manuscript, which comes from the Royal Library, reads “lest the burden.” 32, 5, “And as though something new.” Thus the second Victorine and the Florentine; the others read “of something new.” In the same place, “I would shudder.” The Regius manuscript and the second Victorine read “thus I would shudder.” 38, 6, “stirring up the heat.” The first Thuaneus, the Regius, and both Victorine manuscripts read “agitating the heat,” but incorrectly and contrary to the meter. 40, 1, “savage tyrants.” The first Thuaneus and both Victorine manuscripts have “cruel tyrants”; likewise incorrectly. 42, 3, “You must uncover the wound.” Thus the first Thuaneus, the Regius, the Florentine, and both Victorine manuscripts. 44, 5, “they might inflict.” The first Thuaneus, the Regius, and the Florentine manuscript have “they might carry.” 45, 2, “of the more powerful.” The Florentine has “of the powerful.” [Readings: 38,6: *excitantis* / *exagitantis*, “stirring” / “agitating”; 40,1: *feros* / *saevos*, “savage” / “cruel.”]

[Col. 0863C] In the same place, 4, *Triguillam* (Triguilla, accusative). The second Victorine manuscript has *Trigguillam*; this may perhaps be the person whom Ennodius, in Letter 21 of Book IX, calls *Trigguam* (Triggua), influential with Theoderic. In the same place, 5, “and what had been perpetrated.” The Regius and the second Victorine have “and what had been perpetrated”; but the first Victorine very properly reads “and what had already been commanded.” 48, 1, “of the Palatine.” The first Thuaneus and both Victorine manuscripts read “of the Palatine” in the feminine. 49, 1, “among whom Basil, formerly.” So all the books. In the same place, 9, “of baseness.” The first Thuaneus and both Victorine manuscripts read “baseness”; the Florentine, “of usefulness”—incorrectly. [Readings: 45,5: *perpetrataque* / *et perpetrata*, both “and things perpetrated,” with the conjunction differently placed; *imperataque jam*, “and things already commanded.” 48,1: *Palatini* / *Palatinae*, masculine/neuter versus feminine forms of “Palatine.” 50,4: *ut ni* / *uti ni*, both “so that if not.” 50,6: *eodem die*, “on the same day”; *eo die* / *in eo die*, “on that day,” without/with the preposition. 50,9: *vilitatis*, “of baseness”; *viltas*, “baseness” (the supplied contracted/corrupt spelling); *utilitatis*, “of usefulness.”]

[Readings: 286,1: *apri*, “of a boar,” versus *aper*, “boar” (nominative). 296,9: *proficiscantur* / *proficiscatur*, “may they set out” / “may he set out.”]

[Col. 0867D] In the same place, 10, “even the things themselves unchangeable.” The second Victorine reads “even the thing itself unchangeable.” In the same place, 19, *suo quemquam*, “his own ... anyone” (*quemquam*, accusative). Both Thuaneus manuscripts, the Regius, and the second Victorine read *suo quoquam*, “by any of his own ...” (*quoquam*, ablative); correctly. 297, 3, “he will have judged.” The second Victorine reads “they judged.” In the same place, 15, “looks back upon.” The second Victorine and the Regius read “looked back upon.” 298, 2, “to be carried out.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts and the first Victorine read “to be ruled.” In the same place, 5, “allows to be agitated.” “Allows” is absent from all the manuscripts; incorrectly. In the same place, 22, “looking to conscience.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts, the Regius, and both Victorine manuscripts read “expecting conscience.” 299, 1, “past happiness.” The second Victorine reads “increased happiness.” In the same place, 2, *ut exercitii*, “as/of exercise ...” (genitive fragment). The first Thuaneus reads *ut exercitium*, “as an exercise” (nominative/accusative). In the same place, 5, “and those who disagree.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts, the Regius, and both Victorine manuscripts read “each who disagrees”; incorrectly.

[Col. 0868A] In the same place, 13, *ab assignata*, “from the assigned ...” (feminine ablative). The Regius reads *a signati*, “from/of the marked ...” (irregular case construction), perhaps *ab assignati*, “from/of the assigned ...” (likewise a fragment with mismatched case); correctly [in the editor’s judgment]. In the same place, “had departed.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts, the second Victorine, and the Florentine read “had died.” In the same place, 16, “of divine work.” The Regius and the first Victorine read “of divine labor.” 301, 9, *tingere flammas*, “to dip/dye flames.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts and the Regius read *tinguere flammas*, the same meaning with an alternative verb form. 303, 7, “may be able to endure.” The second Victorine reads “are able to endure.” 304, 3, “who?” he says. The first Thuaneus and the first Victorine read “And who?” he says. 305, 19, “for confirming wisdom.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts, the Regius, and the second Victorine read “for shaping wisdom.” In the same place, 24, “but whatever.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts and the Regius read “whatever or,” correctly. 306, 2, “unless he either trains or corrects, he punishes.” Thus all the books, including Planudes. The Victorine manuscripts, fuller by one verb, read “unless he either trains or corrects or condemns, he punishes”; but incorrectly.

[Col. 0868B] 314, 4, “therefore by chance.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts, the Regius, and both Victorine manuscripts read “therefore by chance” with the ablative form. In the same place, 7, “in that place.” The Regius reads “in that place”; the second Thuaneus, “in that place.” In the same place, 11, “which he overwhelmed.” The Regius and the second Victorine read “which he overwhelmed” with the neuter relative. 316, 5, “may agree.” The second Thuaneus, the Regius, and the second Victorine read “will agree.” 319, 3, “and which distinguishes.” Both the Thuaneus and Victorine manuscripts read “and what distinguishes.” 320, 2, “in which reason exists.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts, the Regius, and both Victorine manuscripts read “in those very beings in which reason exists.” In the same place, 9, “they fell.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts, the Regius, and the second Victorine read “they may have fallen”; the Florentine, “they fell.” 321, 2, “of ignorance.” The Regius and the second Victorine read “of unawareness.” 323, 5, “what they are, what they have been, and what may come, in one.” So both Thuaneus manuscripts, both Victorine manuscripts, and the Florentine; correctly. Everyone can see that all the other editions have transposed the words. [Readings: 314,4: *hoc igitur fortuito* / *hoc igitur fortuitu*, “this therefore by chance,” alternative forms. 314,7: *eo loci*, *eo loco*, *in eo loco*, “in that place,” genitive construction / ablative / prepositional construction. 314,11: *quo ille obruit*, “where/by which he overwhelmed”; *quod ille obruit*, “what he overwhelmed.” 320,9: *ceciderunt* / *cecidere*, “they fell,” alternative perfect endings; *ceciderint*, “they may have fallen.”]

[Col. 0868C] 325, 1, “if matters are directed elsewhere.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts, the Regius, and both Victorine manuscripts read “if elsewhere,” correctly. In the same place, 12, “but we.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts and the second Victorine read “and not.” The Regius reads “and now.” 326, 12, “and the things themselves.” The Regius and the second Victorine read “than the things themselves,” correctly. 327, 2, *humana opinione*, “by human opinion.” The reading *humanae opinione* changes the adjective to a form not agreeing with *opinione*; perhaps *humanae opinioni*, “to human opinion.” 328, 2, “let anyone hope.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts, the Regius, the second Victorine, and the Florentine read “let each one hope.” 331, 5, “but if he does not know.” The second Thuaneus reads “or if he does not know.” 335, 10, “occur by choice.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts, the Regius, and the second Victorine read “come by choice.” 336, 9, “which are uncertain.” The second Thuaneus reads “by which they are uncertain”; not implausibly. In the same place, 10, *opinionis constat id*, “that belongs to opinion, it is established ...” [fragment]. Both Thuaneus manuscripts, the Regius, and the second Victorine read *opinionis id*, “that of opinion,” omitting *constat*, “it is established.” 337, 10, “of imagination.” The second Victorine reads “of an image.” In the same place, 15, “thus he defines.” The second Thuaneus and the Regius read “thus he defined.”

[Col. 0868D] In the same place, 18, “not by imagination.” The second Thuaneus reads “not in imagination.” In the same place, “but rational.” The second Thuaneus reads “but reasonable.” 340, 21, “settles down.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts and the first Victorine read “departs.” 344, 7, “a certain universal.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts and the first Victorine read “something universal.” In the same place, “let him consider.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts read “he considers.” 345, 5, “there is no foreknowledge.” The second Thuaneus reads “that there is no foreknowledge.” In the same place, 7, “we could have.” The second Victorine reads “we may have.” 348, 7, “he will have revealed.” Both Victorine manuscripts read “he reveals”; both Thuaneus manuscripts read “he revealed.” 349, 16, “presence.” Vallinus corrected this on the basis of the agreement of all the old manuscripts. 350, 24, “necessary rather than non-necessary.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts, the Regius, and the second Victorine read “necessarily rather than non-necessarily.” [Readings: 337: *rationali* / *rationabili*, “rational” / “reasonable,” distinct adjective formations. 350,24: *necessaria, quam non necessaria*, “necessary rather than non-necessary” (adjectives); *necessarie quam non necessarie*, “necessarily rather than non-necessarily” (adverbs).]

[Col. 0869A] 331, 11, “someone walking.” The first Thuaneus reads “some human being walking.” In the same place, 15, “walking voluntarily.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts, the Regius, and the second Victorine read “walking by will.” In the same place, “yet he.” The first Victorine and the Regius read “then he.” In the same place, 24, “which earlier.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts read “which earlier” with the alternative relative. In the same place, 27, “I proposed.” The first Thuaneus reads “I placed.” 352, 5, “you ... divine foreknowledge” [fragment]. The second Thuaneus and the Regius read “you ... divine presence” [fragment]. [Readings: 331,24 [number as supplied]: *quae prius*, “which things earlier”; *qua prius*, “by which way earlier.”]

[Col. 0870A] In the same place, 8, “now I would like that.” Both Thuaneus manuscripts and the second Victorine read “now I would like something else.” In the same place, 16, “the force of knowledge.” The second Thuaneus reads “his knowledge.” In the same place, “embracing all things.” The Regius reads “seeing all things or embracing them.” In the same place, “owes to the later things.” The second Thuaneus reads “he gave to the later things.” In the same place, 23, “are right.” The first Thuaneus reads “are received.” In the same place, 26, “prescribed.” The second Victorine reads “implanted.” [Readings: 352,26: *indicta*, “prescribed/announced”; *indita*, “implanted/bestowed.”]

# Appendix to the Books of *The Consolation of Philosophy*

[Col. 0869]

## Various Literary Monuments Prefixed to the Books of *The Consolation* in the Glarean Edition

### Johannes Murmellius of Roermond to Rudolph Langius, Canon of the Church of Münster: Greetings

[Col. 0869B]

At last, Rudolph Langius, most humane, eloquent, and devout of all the men I know, I bring to light for the use of students my commentaries on Boethius Severinus’s *The Consolation of Philosophy*, a work especially fruitful, and I dedicate them to your illustrious name—not because I trust that any splendor could be added to it by my trifles, but so that, protected by the safeguard of your outstanding authority, as if fortified by Ajax’s shield, they may come before the eyes of men with greater security and may not fear the tongues of critics, naturally sharpened on the whetstone of envy—as someone elegantly says—and more harmful than the bite of asps.

Boethius is truly worthy, if I speak frankly, of being assigned a commentator far [Col. 0869C] better than I. Yet I am so far from thinking that this edition of the commentaries has satisfied so great a writer that even in this form I wish most earnestly to stimulate more learned men to assist the studies of students. As for the commentaries on him that have been published up to now, there is no need to say anything: if they pleased learned men, I would gladly have abstained from the labor of writing and from the danger of submitting myself to human judgment—for I am excessively burdened by daily elementary lectures and by the responsibilities of directing a school.

Nevertheless, I trust that my work will win the approval of the candid reader, not merely because I have brought light to obscure matters, but also because I have restored to their proper places the Greek passages that were missing. These were sent to me last year by Johannes Caesarius from Italy—most learned in both languages and an outstanding professor of philosophy and medicine—[Col. 0869D] and by Johannes Aedicollius from Deventer, a master of the liberal arts, uncertain whether more learned or more humane. I have also removed quite a number of errors, both from the prose and from the verses.

In this matter your industry and manifold learning once helped me considerably. Concerning your immense praises, I think it better to remain silent than to say too little—just as Sallust says of Carthage—since time urges me to hasten elsewhere. I have placed certain materials before our own, which, I hope, the diligent reader will by no means disdain. Farewell, [Col. 0870B] and love me, as you do. At Alkmaar, on the third day before the Nones of April, in the year 1514 from the birth of Christ our Savior.

### Johannes Caesarius of Jülich in a Letter to Murmellius

What you write, that you are preparing commentaries on Boethius’s five books *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, is certainly nothing more pleasant for me to hear. For I have long desired precisely this: that commentaries of this kind should be published by some learned man, properly trained in good letters—such a man as I both judge and know you to be—commentaries worthy of so great an author and suited to so great a subject.

### Nicolaus Crescius of Florence, Cistercian Monk, to Antonio Lanfredini, Illustrious Citizen of Florence

Many things, Antonio Lanfredini, are found both in philosophy [Col. 0870C] and in theology that are obscurely expressed and difficult to understand. Yet those celebrated questions concerning fate, the blessed life, divine foreknowledge, and Providence especially lead most readers, through their ambiguous meaning, astray toward a worse interpretation.

Although some have discussed and illuminated these matters so carefully and fully that no room for doubt seems to have been left, no one has treated them more carefully, seriously, or clearly than Severinus Boethius, who, in my judgment, was the most learned man of his entire age. Although he wrote a good deal in many branches of learning, he wished in this book, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, and in those which he entitled *On the Trinity* and *On the Two Natures of Christ*, to test honorably how far he had advanced in sacred letters.

[Col. 0870D]

But this book had already been so corrupted by the neglect of the ages that no brilliance of its author and scarcely any polish could be recognized. When, in recent years, it called for restoration, it was afflicted with many more wounds. For the printers brought it into people’s hands mutilated, disordered, and greatly altered from itself, together with commentaries falsely attributed to Saint Thomas Aquinas.

I was therefore asked to correct this very book of Boethius and, as far as I could, restore it to its original integrity. I did this all the more willingly because the subject under discussion is certainly one [Col. 0871A] that most befits a religious man. In this work Boethius employed a style of expression that seems no less ornate than serious and is especially suited to philosophy. It is also varied, and therefore pleasing: now he argues with the utmost gravity in prose, now he plays more elegantly in meter.

We therefore dedicate to you, Lanfredini, most distinguished man, this work, corrected by our care and diligence, whatever its quality may be—not because I think its reading can add much to your learning, but so that, set in the format of a handbook under your patronage, it may go forth into the public more honorably and safely. From it, the difference between that earlier book and this one of ours may readily be judged. If you approve it, I shall consider that I have satisfied everyone. Farewell.

## Lecture of Jacob of Bologna on Boethius Severinus

[Col. 0871B]

Most distinguished men, I had resolved this year to refrain from a preface, lest I always remain fixed in the same track. For, as Cicero says, persistence produces distaste and satiety. But you partly compelled me to change my plan by your excessive devotion and affection for me—for every year you honor me with your most distinguished presence and most honorable attendance—and partly did so through the magnificence and generosity of our illustrious and magnificent senate, which recently judged that I should be granted a more substantial salary and, in addition, adorned me with a more honorable title by assigning me as colleague to a man of great learning and humanity.

Mindful, therefore, of such great services—for, as Menander says, earth produces nothing worse than an ungrateful person—and recalling that Amyclae perished through silence, and that, as Ausonius says, no one pleased by remaining silent, I am compelled and driven to recite something new before you, something that at least by its very variety may charm and delight your ears.

[Col. 0871C]

Why have you knitted your brows? Is it because I promised that I should recite? If I recite, the precedent is not mine. But the very learned men of old regularly did this. I call it new because no one before me has woven it together. Thus the learned will have things they can readily recognize, and the unlearned things they can learn and admire.

Today, therefore, I shall speak about the almost innumerable errors by which nearly all of us are deceived—not only the ignorant and the irreligious, which would be less painful to endure, but also, and this exacerbates my sorrow, the learned and, so to speak, the priests of the Muses.

But when I have irritated the diseases and ulcers, listener, expect the medicine. So let everyone be favorable and attend with an impartial mind. For, as Jerome says, blessed is the one who speaks into the ears of a listener.

[Col. 0871D]

All human care and striving seeks to reach one state of tranquility, though by different paths. One person therefore commits himself entirely to Fortune, saying that she bends and turns human affairs according to her will. He watches and venerates her as a saving divinity, supreme and omnipotent. At first enticed by the flatteries and seductions of this deceitful and changeable goddess, when at last he sees her blowing against him and hostile, he complains, sighs, and groans, calling her slippery, inconstant, blind, and wandering, and sparing her no reproach.
