He is a fool—or, not to call him insane—who wants there to be nothing hard inside the olive or outside the nut. Since he has dared to entrust his life and hope to her—the ancients and [Col. 0872A] our forefathers imagined her, because of her mobility, as sitting upon a ball, and Ausonius wisely and wittily said that she stood upon a little wheel because she could not remain in one place—if you have given yourself to Fortune to govern, you must obey the character of your mistress.

Another person longs to gather resources and pile up riches, and devotes himself wholly to them, believing that through them solid happiness and every advantage and profit for mortals are brought in, in accordance with the following lines:

> For if some accident has fastened you to your bed, you have someone who  
> will sit beside you, prepare soothing remedies, and ask the physician to  
> revive you and restore you to your children and dear relatives.

He also frequently has this on his lips:

> Clearly, a wife with a dowry, loyalty and friends,  
> noble birth and beauty, Queen Money gives,  
> and Persuasion and Venus adorn the well-funded man.

[Col. 0872B]

This man also thinks that heaven and the gods can be bought with gold, moved by this verse of Tertullian:

> It is not permitted to know the gods for free.

And by this couplet of Petronius:

> I speak grandly: with money at hand, ask for whatever you wish,  
> and it will come; the chest possesses even Jupiter when he is shut inside.

But if, on reconsideration, you examine the matter, you will find nothing more wicked, nothing more pernicious, and nothing that harasses and unsettles the human race more than wealth and money. Yet if you first wish to build up wealth, you will have to take it away from someone who possesses it. Hence Flaccus called riches “increased by wrongdoing.” Jerome likewise says: “A rich man is either unjust or the heir of an unjust man.”

Money is therefore harmful and useless when it is dishonorable; and the old saying is: “Ill-gotten gains are ill-spent.” Wealth is also pernicious because through it people are enervated and softened, diseases and illnesses grow, and shame, laws, rights, towers, citadels, fortifications, and the most heavily defended towns are stormed. For money, as Cicero says, “knows all the roads.”

[Col. 0872C]

That Cynic Diogenes used to say that the path of virtue was so narrow, difficult, and rough that barely even naked people could cross and traverse it, much less those encumbered by any burden and stuffed with gold. Lucretius likewise left it written that the dead, naked and destitute, enter the underworld. From this Ausonius wittily played in the following poem upon the meeting of Diogenes and Croesus among the dead:

> Diogenes the Cynic saw your likeness,  
> O Croesus, richest of kings, among the shades.  
> He stopped, and, shaken by a laugh  
> louder than usual, said: “Of what use to you now  
> are your riches, O richest king of kings, when you are  
> [Col. 0872D] as solitary as I, and even poorer than I?  
> For whatever I possessed I carry with me, whereas you, Croesus,  
> carry nothing with you from all those riches.”

Another person strives to move through the stages of public office and creeps toward honors, so that afterward he may appear conspicuous, illustrious, and venerable, adorned with the official rods. For, as Cicero says, whatever excels commands a proper reverence; and triple applause raises and inflates this gaping man. Lifted up by popular favor, he thinks that he is scratching the sky. Sweet glory follows him, the companion of public offices and labors, and the nourishment of every generous spirit. For we are all drawn by the desire for praise, and every good man is especially fattened by glory. It is pleasant to be pointed out with a finger and to hear, “This is he.”

[Col. 0873A]

But since such dignities depend upon the judgment of the profane multitude, they seem for that reason less desirable. For, as Annaeus Seneca advises:

> Avoid whatever pleases the crowd.

How wicked and perverse the examination and judgment of the people are may be recognized, to pass over other examples, from the single case of Cato and Vatinius. For that Cato, a living image of the virtues, suffered defeat when he was a candidate for the praetorship. Vatinius, however, a frivolous and worthless man, attained it, to the astonishment and admiration of the very populace that had done this.

Envy usually accompanies this splendor. For, as Aemilius Probus says, “It is a common fault in great and free states that envy accompanies glory, and that people gladly disparage those whom they see rising higher.”

[Col. 0873B]

Euripides shows how deceptive, shameful, and empty glory is in *Andromache*, exclaiming in this sense:

> O glory, glory, you are nothing other than a great inflation of the ears.

Many people, after laboring manfully in this dust because they desired this glory and splendor, have finally received exile, imprisonment, or death as their reward.

Another person boasts of his family line and nobility and swells with pride when he gazes in the atrium upon the smoky images of his ancestors, of whom he himself possesses nothing similar except the color, as I may say with Cicero. He frequently looks up to and admires these images, and displays them as though the titles and inscriptions of his great-grandfathers could somehow conceal and dignify him if he were degenerate and sordid.

The opposite, however, usually happens: through these memorials a man’s wickedness and worthlessness become increasingly conspicuous. [Col. 0873C] “Not everyone can be a patrician,” as Cicero says. But he is worthy of every commendation who has shone before his descendants through his own virtue. For if nobility is a certain praise arising from the merits of one’s parents, then, by Hercules, it is someone else’s. It is miserable, as that famous saying has it, to rest upon another’s reputation. Hence Boethius said gravely:

> Why do you make such a din about family and ancestors?  
> If you look to our beginnings  
> and to God our creator,  
> no one is degenerate,  
> unless, cherishing worse things through his vices,  
> he abandons his own origin.

[Col. 0873D]

Another person places the highest good in supreme power. He either desires to rule or clings to rulers, having been reminded that kingship comes from God by this Homeric saying:

> Nor should you, Polides [the supplied *Polide*, a corrupt name], wish to contend with a king,  
> to whom dignity has been granted by Jupiter himself,  
> such as has never been granted to anyone else.

Therefore, so that he may excel and command, leaving nothing unattempted and nothing undared, he hastens wickedly toward his desire by right and wrong alike, appropriating these words of Euripides:

> If justice must be violated, let it be violated for the sake of sovereignty;  
> in all other matters, observe piety.

For kings are close to the immortal gods, as Caesar says. Cicero also calls the royal name sacred. But you earthly human beings, do you not consider over what sort of things you seem to preside? If, among mice, you saw one claiming authority and power for himself,

> could you, my friends, admitted to the spectacle, restrain your laughter?

If, however, the human body is weighed in the balance, what is weaker or more fragile than it, since so very often it dissolves and perishes within an hour or a moment? How anxious and wretched is the condition of tyrants and princes—that king revealed, who, before placing the diadem upon his head, considered it and said: “O cloth more noble than happy! If anyone were to look inside it and see how many dangers and miseries it is filled with, he would not pick it up even if it were lying on the ground.” And there was that Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, who expressed the fears and dangers of kings and princes by that sword suspended by a slender thread and made familiar on the lips of many.

Antiquity teems with countless examples, and our own age is full of men who have exchanged royal and princely happiness for calamity. The most wretched kind of misfortune, however, is to have been happy; hence Horace said:

> Flee greatness, though beneath a poor roof  
> You may outlive kings and the friends of kings.

What should I say about the companions of kings and princes? Did not Tiberius order Sejanus, who had always been closest and most intimate to him, to be dragged by a hook and torn to pieces? Did not Domitius Nero also drive Seneca, his teacher, to death? Did not Antonius expose Papinianus, long powerful among courtiers, to the swords of soldiers? For this reason the same Flaccus elegantly said:

> Sweet to the inexperienced is the favor of a powerful friend;  
> The experienced man fears it.

Another, judging renown the highest good, hastens to extend his glorious name and longs above all to become famous in military affairs, remembering Cicero’s words:

> Military valor surpasses all other things. It won this name for the Roman people; it won eternal glory for this city. It compelled the whole world to submit to this empire, and everything within the city is protected and guarded by military valor.

Such a man therefore considers the inglorious and nameless fit to be counted among the beasts, especially since it is possible to become famous either in peace or in war, as that author says. Yet many of the most celebrated men of their own time have perished in obscure deaths, having found no historians for their deeds. What of the fact that writings and monuments waste away and perish with time? Hence the saying:

> We marvel that men have perished; monuments decay.  
> Death comes even to stones and names.

Add to this that if human beings die wholly—which is nevertheless far removed from our institutions and laws—there is no renown or glory, since the person himself no longer exists. But if a mind conscious of righteousness, released from its earthly prison, seeks heaven in freedom, will it not despise every earthly concern? And, enjoying heaven, will it not rejoice that it has been freed from these things? Hence the saying:

> He did not live badly who passed unnoticed in dying and in being born.

And the Vergilian poet says:

> …the fairest things first  
> Your gods and your character shall bestow.

Another measures the good by joy and delight. He considers it the height of happiness to overflow with pleasure, toward which nature inclines us—or rather drives us headlong. Whatever is according to nature, says Aristotle, comes pleasantly; and all animals pursue the pleasure that accords with nature. This man therefore asserts that the gods are everlasting for this reason: they continuously and uninterruptedly enjoy pleasure in security. He gladly adopts the saying of Persius:

> Let us pluck the sweet things: what belongs to us  
> What you live is yours; you will become ash, shades, and a tale.

But if human beings considered pleasures as they pass away, and recognized that only regret for what they had done remains, they would avoid and flee them more than sailors flee the seductive Sirens and the harsh Symplegades. Who would not willingly despise and cast off servitude to the body, a thing utterly base and fragile?

Antisthenes the Socratic used to say: “I would rather go mad than be entertained.” Diogenes also said: “If you were not drunk, you would obey Socrates; and either devote yourselves to continence throughout all your lives or end your lives by hanging.” Cato likewise, in a certain speech, deters human beings from pleasure in these words: “If through pleasure you do anything wickedly, the pleasure will quickly pass away, but that wicked deed will always remain with you.”

Another, thinking bodily form and dignity the greatest goods, says: “This is the dowry that wins people over and attracts and invites the gods,” unaware and forgetful of what happened to Hippolytus, Bellerophon, Hyacinthus, Hylas, and others of that kind, for whom beauty proved costly and harmful. Add to this that the radiance of beauty is rapid and fleeting, more fugitive than the changing flowers of spring. Hence Sallust called the glory of beauty transitory and fragile; and Calpurnius said:

> The gift of beauty is brief, nor does it lend itself to you through the years.

For this reason that Etruscan, Spurinna, won no ordinary praise among posterity: when his striking appearance attracted the eyes of many married women, he disfigured his own face with many dishonorable wounds and ugly scars, so that he might preserve the true beauty of his soul.

But if, as Aristotle says, human beings had Lyncean eyes, so that their sight could pass through obstacles and penetrate within, would not the body of Alcibiades, beautiful on the surface, appear utterly foul when viewed from within? For something appears beautiful not by its own nature, but because of the weakness of the eyes that look upon it.

Another, placing true peace of soul and tranquility of mind in virtue, advances toward it with great strides and complete force, believing that everything resides in the person who possesses virtue, mindful of this hymn:

> Virtue, best of all hunts, you are for all mortal beings.  
> Such a noble fruit you cast into their breasts,  
> A fruit that endures forever.  
> You are better than gold.

This man therefore wishes to grow pale over nocturnal pages. He is spurred on by the example of Zeno, who, when he had consulted Apollo about how he might live best, received the answer: “If he were of the same color as the dead”—that is, if he were to devote himself with great diligence to reading the books of the ancients.

But since the arts and disciplines are various, one person pursues grammar. As Fabius says, grammar is divided into two parts: the knowledge of speaking correctly and the explanation of poets. Setting aside and neglecting what pertains to solid benefit, this person, fussy and refined, wants to know trivial and playful matters—for example, whether one should say *quoties* or *quotiens*; *conjunx* or *conjux*; and whether *amicei*, in the plural, should be written with *e* and *i*, as Nigidius held; and whether in the plural *vireis* and *omneis* should take an *e*, as Terentianus asserts; along with other matters of that sort which a careful reader will notice in Plautus. Yet I would certainly not count these as matters of great importance, as I say with Livy.

Some are occupied with letters and syllables; “Seek the meanings,” says Jerome. One person pursues dialectic, merely running through certain sophisms, riddles, and traps that are labyrinthine and Menandrian, and always occupied with the question of what is true and what is false. While doing this, he becomes as much farther removed from knowledge of the truth as that Simonides was driven away from knowledge of God. When Simonides was compelled by the tyrant Hiero to investigate and inquire what God was like, he first asked for one day, then two, and afterward requested that the time be doubled. When the tyrant wondered at this, the philosopher replied: “The longer I consider it, the more obscure the matter seems.”

One turns toward rhetoric, calling it the queen of all things. He says that it brought savage, rustic, and wandering people together, enticed them into the discipline of civic obedience, and ruled and bent the law courts, gymnasia, colonnades, and theaters at Athens as well as at Rome according to its will. Yet, using himself as the worst teacher, as the saying goes, and observing none of the universal principles and rules of rhetoric, this man wants to be called an orator.

Although one ought above all to use clear and lucid words, he employs, with greater ostentation in his writing and with more *σοφιστεία* (*sophisteia*), that is, pretension, than with actual work, words long obsolete, antiquated, and completely buried. He wishes to be called an affected imitator and an antiquarian, a display of learning rather than its true possessor. To him applies that witty definition of an orator:

> An orator is a bad man unskilled in speaking.

For a perfect orator is still wanting.

Another—“to set my sails,” as it were, toward mathematics, that is, toward the higher disciplines—strives after astrology. He judges that person perfectly blessed and happy beyond his desires who thoroughly understands the courses of the stars and constellations, the pathways of heaven, the settings and risings of the signs, and the eclipses of the sun and moon. With Hercules and Atlas having discharged their service and now wearied, this man wants to support heaven upon his own head. Thus, says Ovid, one seeks heaven, perhaps admiring Anaxagoras, who predicted that a stone would fall from the sun.

But since there are countless stars that have not yet come into the knowledge of mortals, the astrologer is often deceived and abandoned by his art. For this reason Diogenes, when he saw someone discoursing on the nature and power of the sun and persuading everyone of his claims, said: “When did you come down from heaven?”

If I wished to recount the remaining errors of human life in the other disciplines, I might perhaps be called a third Cato, an eighth wise man, and a ninth teacher of morals; I would be mocked, and would produce satiety in myself but weariness and nausea in you. I shall therefore withdraw my foot from this subject and turn briefly to medicine, which I promised to discuss.

Above all, most distinguished listeners, it is necessary to establish this: nothing happens with God without reason, as Jerome says. God, who is supreme reason, fashioned human beings for this purpose: that, with reason as their teacher and guide, they might live a heavenly life on earth. If they abandon this, they will plunge headlong into ruin. Hence Persius wisely said:

> Reason has granted you nothing: stretch out a finger—you sin.

The holy Jerome likewise said that the senses of our body are like horses running without a driver, while the soul and reason, like a charioteer, hold back the reins of those running horses.

Whoever therefore walks under the guidance of reason will first of all trample upon fortune—which among the wise possesses no divine power—and subject fate beneath his feet. He will scorn riches and wealth, regarding them as material for intemperance and wickedness, the seedbed of every crime. He will desire the barrel and wallet of Diogenes, living according to nature, which is content with few and very small things.

He will likewise fear ambitious titles and useless offices as enticing plotters, fortified by the consciousness of good conduct. Rejoicing in the goods that are within himself, despising external things and not valuing them at a penny, he will be content with virtue alone. As Horace says:

> Virtue, ignorant of sordid rejection,  
> Shines with unstained honors;  
> It neither lays down nor assumes the axes  
> At the will of popular favor.

And Claudian:

> Virtue itself is its own reward, and alone, secure  
> In the wide realm of fortune, shines; nor is it demanded  
> By any rods, nor does it seek to grow famous  
> Through the applause of the crowd, needing nothing external,  
> Needing no praise.

He will laugh at glory as an empty thing, comparable to a bubble suddenly swelling, and at nobility as something belonging to another. Contemplating the heavenly lineage and starry origin of humanity, he will repeat what Anaxagoras said, looking up at heaven: “That is my homeland.”

He will avoid the power and intimacies of princes, in accordance with Lucan:

> Let the man who wishes to be righteous leave the court;  
> Virtue and supreme power do not come together.

He will turn away from pleasure as from a seductive enemy, which secretly drains away all one’s strength through its sweet enticements. Pleasure is like a leech that will not release the skin until it is full of blood. He will despise beauty, which fades through disease and age and can be cut off and vanish in a moment.

And since true virtue consists in fleeing vice, he will therefore apply himself and devote himself to grammar, dialectic, rhetoric, astrology, and the other mathematical disciplines with this intention: that through these easier steps there may be an approach to philosophy—philosophy, I say, the teacher of all virtues. For philosophy urges and compels a person to investigate the secrets of nature, and, shaping and conforming him to heavenly morals, makes him a god from a human being.

Since philosophy is a kind of meditation on death, through it alone, says Diogenes, the soul is separated from the body. When one sees, hears, smells, or tastes, the body is present. The same Diogenes said: “When we do not meditate with the mind, the end of life must be awaited as something grievous; for the soul is afflicted with sorrow when it has lost its pleasures. But when we have practiced the best meditation, life is sweet and death is in no way troublesome.”

But so that I may once and for all confirm my words by some deed and in reality—for I hate a person whose philosophical maxim is accompanied by idle work—I have decided, most distinguished listeners, to lecture publicly on Boethius’ philosophy on feast days, so that at last this almost divine and heavenly work may emerge from neglect and squalor, polished and cleansed, into the light—on feast days, I say.

For, as Macrobius says, if no religious scruple forbids leading water through a stream during sacred ceremonies, and if divine and human law permit sheep to be immersed in a health-giving river, why should it not be considered an act of religious reverence to dedicate the sacred study of letters on sacred days?

Whoever, therefore, reads this work of Boethius—or, better still, hears it, since the living voice nourishes more fully, as they say—will be taught pleasantly and happily to live according to reason. Having trampled down and erased every passion of the mind, and rehearsing for death, he will afterward, when death truly comes, not merely fail to fear it but, rejoicing like Socrates, will go to meet it and receive it with an undaunted heart and cheerful face. I have spoken.

# John Murmellius’s Preface to Boethius Severinus’s Work on the Consolation of Philosophy

Since I am about to explain the five books of Boethius on the *Consolation of Philosophy*, I must first set forth certain preliminary matters by which the minds of students may appropriately be prepared for what is to be treated. They are these: the life of Boethius, the title of the work, the quality of its style, the author’s intention, the number of the books, the usefulness of the work, and the branch of philosophy to which it belongs.

## I. The Life of Severinus Boethius

The life of Boethius is as follows. Severinus Boethius was a Roman, descended from the most noble family of the Torquati. From childhood he surpassed the distinction of his lineage through honorable studies and through the nobility of his virtues and learning. Since he knew Greek no less than Latin, and had joined the whole of philosophy with the arts of oratory and poetry, he judged that he had been born not for himself alone but for human society. He therefore undertook the administration of public affairs and, through the highest offices, became consul, a most devoted cultivator of justice in every matter and its outstanding defender.

Thus he won the goodwill of good men and aroused against himself the hatred of wicked men. His wife was a woman of the noblest birth, distinguished both for modesty and chastity: Rusticiana, daughter of Symmachus, a senator and former consul. By her he had children. He also had two sons who displayed the promise of their father’s and grandfather’s genius; the father himself once saw them, honored with the consulship, being carried from the house amid the eager rejoicing of the senators and the people.

Reliable authorities report that Boethius was a friend of the holy Benedict and that, on Monte Cassino, he reclined at table with Tertullus, the Roman senator and father of the monk Placidus. But after he had flourished for many years in both wealth and honors, and the wickedness of evil men could no longer endure the incredible splendor of his virtues, he was surrounded by the unjust accusations of the worst informers and driven into exile at Ticinum by Theodoric, king of the Goths.

There, so that he might not waste away in inactive idleness and the weariness of grief, he composed this divine work of philosophical consolation. Finally, when the tyrant’s madness grew more savage, he was put to death together with his father-in-law Symmachus, in the year 524 after Christ’s birth—either because he was suspected of aspiring to freedom or because he had attacked the Arians, whose stain had polluted King Theodoric.

Theodoric died as punishment for his cruelty, either of apoplexy or, as Agnellus maintains, from a discharge of the bowels, on the ninety-eighth day after, by his order, Pope John and several Roman consuls and senators had died in prison from the torment of hunger at Ravenna, and in the thirty-eighth year after he had gained control of Italy.

Nevertheless, Procopius, at the beginning of his account of the Italian war against the Goths, relates that while Theodoric was dining after having killed Boethius and Symmachus, a fish’s head was served to him, and he saw in it the terrifying face of Symmachus, who, biting down upon his lower lip, threatened him with grim eyes. Struck with terror, the king fell into the illness in which he confessed his wickedness: namely, that at the suggestion of ruined men he had killed the holy bishop and other distinguished Romans, as well as the outstanding men Symmachus and Boethius. Immediately after this confession, he breathed his last.

A similar and more certain testimony to the sudden death inflicted upon King Theodoric as punishment for his injustice is offered by Gregory, holy doctor of the Church, in the *Dialogues*. He writes that on the day Theodoric died at Ravenna, a solitary man of great virtue living in the wilderness on the island of Lipara told a certain noble Goth that he had seen the soul of King Theodoric being carried off to be plunged into Vulcan’s cauldron by Pope John of Rome and Symmachus, whom he had killed at that time.

The king’s daughter was Amalasuntha, whom Cassiodorus, a most authoritative writer, counts among the foremost and rarest of women. Thoroughly instructed in Greek and Latin letters and skilled in many languages, she was, he says, a marvel to behold and to hear speaking. After her father Theodoric’s death, she restored to the sons of Boethius and Symmachus the paternal property that had been confiscated into the treasury.

Several years later, when Totila, king of the Goths, had captured Rome, Rusticiana, once the wife of Boethius, was accused by the Goths of having ordered the statues of King Theodoric to be broken and destroyed in vengeance for her husband Boethius and her father Symmachus, whom Theodoric had caused to be killed. The charge concerning the statues was thought to be true, but just grief excused the woman, since it was established that those great men had been unjustly killed. For this reason Totila acquitted her and protected her from the attack of the Goths.

## II. The Works of Boethius Now Extant

Two commentaries on Porphyry’s *Isagoge*, the first and the second.

Two books of commentaries on Aristotle’s *Categories*.

A first edition of his book *On Interpretation*, and a second edition divided into six books.

One book *On Division*.

One book *On Definitions*.

An *Introduction to Categorical Syllogisms*.

Six books of commentaries on Cicero’s *Topics*.

Four books *On Topical Differences*.

Two books *On the Categorical Syllogism*.

Two books *On the Hypothetical Syllogism*.

Two books *On the Trinity*.

One book *On the Hebdomads*.

One book *On Unity and the One*.

One book *On Two Natures and One Person of Christ*.

Two books *On Arithmetic*.

Five books *On Music*.

Two books *On Geometry*, translated from Euclid.

And this divine work, *On the Consolation of Philosophy*.

He also wrote other works, both in verse and in prose, which are now lost. Moreover, the book commonly entitled Boethius’ *On the Discipline of the Schools* is not his, but belongs to some barbarian or other. Besides many other indications that expose this, its style plainly shows that it is entirely foreign to Boethius’ learning and elegance. I am not unaware that Baptista Pius of Bologna thinks otherwise, but we shall easily refute him elsewhere.

Our Boethius also translated into Latin several books of Aristotle and some dialogues of Plato, and promised that he would write a reconciliation of the two philosophers. Whether he fulfilled this promise, we do not know. At the present time no translation of Boethius survives, as Leonardo Aretino correctly attests in the fourth book of his *Letters*, except those of Porphyry, the *Categories*, and the books *περὶ ἑρμηνεῖας* (*On Interpretation*). If you read them carefully, you will see that this great man translated those books without any foolishness. The text is polished and clear and corresponds to the Greek.

Leonardo himself, in the fifth volume of his letters, rightly calls Boethius a most learned man. It has pleased me to append here certain honorable testimonies about his excellence from other writers.

### Baptista Mantuanus

Baptista Mantuanus, in his *Apologeticus*, calls Boethius “a most grave and holy man, most skilled in every science, and an outstanding investigator and discoverer of truth.”

### Angelo Poliziano

Angelo Poliziano, in his *Miscellanies*, says:

“For who,” he asks, “is sharper than Boethius in dialectic, subtler in mathematics, richer in philosophy, or more sublime in theology? The younger philosophers, whom I consider by far the most perceptive of all, have held him in such esteem that he deserved to have as interpreters Thomas Aquinas, that holy man and great teacher of Thomas—good God, what men!—and that there is scarcely any appeal from his judgment.”

### Platina

Platina, in his *Life of Pope Hormisdas*, recorded the following in his literary monuments:

“Theodoric first sends Boethius and Symmachus into exile, and afterward into prison, on suspicion that they had aspired to freedom. In this calamity Boethius wrote many works that are still read. He also translated most of Aristotle and commented upon them. He was considered highly learned in mathematics, as his *Music* and *Arithmetic* demonstrate. Finally, he was killed together with the senator Symmachus by order of Theodoric. Some, however, write that Boethius suffered so great a calamity because he attacked the Arians, toward whom Theodoric had inclined. The former opinion seems more credible to me.”

### Raphael Volaterranus, in the *Anthropology*

“Boethius, during the reign of Zeno, was condemned to exile by King Theodoric on suspicion of aspiring to freedom. Then, handed over to custody, he wrote several works. At last he was killed together with his father-in-law, the senator Symmachus, and other distinguished men. His statues were afterward restored by Amalasuntha, and his patrimony was returned intact to his heirs. He was the one man among all who was both extremely learned and without genius in writing.”

### Matteo Palmieri of Florence, in the *Chronicles*

“Boethius, a senator, was condemned to exile by Theodoric on suspicion of aspiring to freedom and was soon afterward thrust into prison, where he composed several works.”

The same writer adds shortly afterward:

“Boethius, recalled from exile some time earlier and made prefect of the praetorium, was killed by order of Theodoric together with the senator Symmachus and other distinguished men.”

### Marcus Antonius Sabellicus, *Enneads*, Book VIII, Chapter II

“Boethius’ writings endure for a long time, and his varied genius ranged through every part of philosophy so abundantly and elegantly that one cannot tell whether he was the last of those who spoke Latin or the first to undertake to restore declining eloquence to its former integrity. He wrote some things on divine subjects, but much more on mathematics. Commentaries on dialectic survive, and a poem also survives. Since the two kinds of writing differ from one another, it may rightly be doubted which was more natural to him. In all his works he is so chaste and elegant that he can compete with any of the ancients.”

In Cassiodorus’ books of *Various Letters*, several learned and especially honorable letters of Theodoric, king of the Goths, to Boethius are preserved. I thought one of them should especially be copied here:

> “To Boethius, illustrious man and patrician, Theodoric the king sends greetings.
>
> “Requests made by neighboring kings for the sake of showing their confidence should not be rejected, since small things often have more power to provide pleasure than great riches have to obtain it. Frequently, what arms cannot accomplish is achieved by agreeable amusements. Let it therefore be for the commonwealth, even when we seem to be playing. For this reason we seek pleasurable things: so that through them we may accomplish serious purposes.
>
> “The lord of the Burgundians has therefore earnestly requested us to send him, together with masters of such matters, a clock regulated by water flowing through a calibrated device, and another distinguished by the measured illumination of the immense sun, so that, by enjoying the pleasures he has obtained, he may regard what is daily for us as a miracle for himself. It is only right that they should wish to see what they marvel at in the reports of their ambassadors.
>
> “We have learned that you, richly furnished with learning, know these things so well that, although the unlearned commonly practice those arts, you have drunk at the very fountain of the disciplines. For you entered the schools of Athens while far away; you mingled the toga with the choruses of the cloak-wearing philosophers, so that you made the doctrines of the Greeks into Roman learning.
>
> “You learned with what depth speculative knowledge is considered together with its parts, and by what method practical knowledge is acquired with its divisions, bringing before Roman senators whatever the Cecropids had made singular for the world. Through your translations, the musical Pythagoras and the astronomer Ptolemy are read as Italians. Nicomachus the arithmetician and Euclid the geometer are heard as Ausonians. Plato the theologian and Aristotle the logician debate in the Quirinal tongue. You even made Archimedes the mechanic Sicilian into a Latin, and whatever disciplines or arts fertile Greece produced through individual men, Rome received in its native language through you alone.
>
> “You rendered those authors illustrious with such brilliance of expression and conspicuous with such precision of language that they themselves might have preferred your work, if they had known both languages more fully. You entered the aforementioned art, born from noble disciplines, through the fourfold gates of mathematics. While it sat within the innermost chambers of nature, you came to know it by the light of your heart, invited by the books of its authors.
>
> “Its purpose is to learn difficult things and to display marvels. It endeavors to show what makes people astonished that they have discovered it, and, by transforming the properties of nature in a marvelous way, it takes credibility away from what has happened, even while displaying the sight before the eyes. It makes waters rise suddenly from the depths and fall headlong, makes fire move by weights, makes organs resound with unfamiliar voices, and fills pipes with foreign blasts so that by art they may sing as if possessing a soul.
>
> “Through it we see the defenses of cities already tottering suddenly rise with such strength that the one found helpless in his own power becomes superior through the aid of machines. Wet structures are dried in seawater. Hard things, once ingeniously arranged, are dissolved. Metals bellow. Diomedes sounds more heavily in bronze; a bronze serpent hisses; artificial birds twitter; and things that do not know how to possess a voice of their own are proved to emit the sweetness of song.
>
> “We say little about an art to which it is permitted to imitate heaven. It made the sun move in the sphere of Archimedes. It constructed another zodiacal circle through human ingenuity. It showed the moon, which can be restored after its eclipse, by the illumination of art; and it caused a small machine, pregnant with the world—a portable heaven, a summary of things, a mirror of nature—to revolve with an imperceptible motion, displaying the appearance of the ether.
>
> “Thus, although we know the courses of the stars, our deceived eyes do not see them advance. There is in them a motion that seems stationary; though by true calculation you know how swiftly it runs, you do not perceive it to move. What could be more marvelous for a human being than to make even what he has been able to understand?
>
> “Therefore, since your celebrated knowledge of such things adorns you, hasten to send us the aforementioned water-clocks at public expense and without loss to yourself, so that you may make yourself known in that part of the world to which you could not otherwise have reached. Through you let foreign peoples recognize that we possess such noble men as the authors record.
>
> “How often will they refuse to believe what they have seen? How often will they think this truth a playful dream? And when they have recovered from their astonishment, they will not dare call themselves our equals, since they will know that wise men among us conceived such things.
>
> “Farewell.”

## III. The Title of the Work

The title of the work appears in most copies as follows:

> *The Five Books on the Consolation of Philosophy of Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, a most illustrious and distinguished man of consular rank.*

Anicius, Manlius, Torquatus, and Severinus are names drawn from Boethius’ family and lineage. The Anician family was extremely noble at Rome, as the holy Jerome also testifies in his letter to Demetrias in these words:

> “Surely I must now recall the celebrated names of the Probii and Olibrii, and the lineage of the illustrious blood of the Anicii, among whom either no one or scarcely anyone will be found who did not deserve the consulship.”

The poet Prudentius, in the second book against Symmachus, sang in this manner:

> For the noble Anicius is said, before all others,  
> To have adorned the head of the City;  
> Thus illustrious Rome boasts herself.

It seems to me that this family of the Anicii derived its origin from the Manlian clan, whose founder was Manlius Capitolinus. The surname Torquatus was added from the valor of Titus Manlius, who, when military tribune under the dictator Sulpicius, killed a Gaulish challenger and placed around his own neck the torque stripped from the Gaul’s neck.

From the same man the surname Severinus was transmitted to his descendants. He was so severe that, during the Latin War, he struck his own son with the axe because the son had fought against his father’s command, although he had defeated the enemy. Hence Virgil’s words:

> Behold the savage Torquatus  
> And the axe.

Cicero shows in Book I of *On the Ends* that this severity was characteristic, and almost innate, of this family. It is therefore ridiculous that ignorant people say Boethius was called Severinus because he opposed King Theodoric.

Still more ridiculous is the claim that Boethius received his name from eating beef, since more learned men think that he was called Boethius after an ancient philosopher whose name was Boetius. If this is so, the name should be written with aspirated *th*. It is interpreted as βοηθός (*boēthos*), “supporter,” “helper,” or “assistant.”

As for the fact that this work is entitled *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, one should know that distinguished authors often invent forms and create descriptions of persons; for this reason the Greeks call it προσωπογραφία (*prosōpographia*), “character portrayal.” Thus Prodicus, as Xenophon reports, makes Virtue and Pleasure contend with each other before Hercules. Ennius, according to Fabius, presents Death and Life contending in a satire.

## IV. The Quality of the Style

To make the quality of the style clear, Boethius in these books uses both verse and prose, so that the reader’s weariness may be relieved by a pleasant alternation. Before Boethius, others did this, especially Petronius Arbiter and Martianus Capella.

He makes beautiful use of poetry before prose. For, according to Strabo, poetic adornment itself first came forward before all else and, once approved, gave pleasure. Later Cadmus, Pherecydes, and Hecataeus released speech from meter.

Moreover, Boethius’ mind was deeply disturbed: in elegies he laments the changeability of fortune and reveals the distress of his soul, thereby preparing a very suitable place for Philosophy to be introduced in prose as a consolation.

One should know that there are two kinds of discourse: metrical and prose. In this work he used various kinds of meter, which will be presented in their proper places. Prose discourse is called *prosa*, because it is straightforward and not turned back according to a fixed number. For the ancients called *prosum* “straight.” Fabius says:

> We learn verses by heart more easily than prose discourse.

Some wish *prosa* to be so called because it is poured forth, or because it proceeds and extends more broadly, with no fixed limit prescribed for it.

The style is moderate and more philosophical than oratorical. It is not embellished or ornamented, but is such as cannot displease an investigator of truth.

## V. The Author’s Intention
Having indicated the style of this work, let us now examine the author’s intention and, as the Greeks say, its *skopos* (σκόπος, aim). Just as M. T. Cicero, withdrawn from senatorial and forensic affairs amid the disturbances of war, devoted himself entirely to philosophical [Col. 0884C] studies and to writing books by which he might benefit posterity, so Boethius, exiled and thrown into prison, since he could no longer benefit mankind by wise counsel and action, summoned philosophy as a consoler and composed this divine work in the form of a dialogue. He did so both to endure his own adversities with a more even mind and, by exposing Fortune’s instability and revealing the highest good, to provide for posterity.

### VI. The Number of the Books

The work is divided into five volumes, evidently in imitation of Cicero, who composed five books *On the Ends of Good and Evil* and an equal number of books of *Tusculan Disputations*, with a not altogether dissimilar subject—unless I am mistaken.

In the first of these, Boethius explains the causes of Philosophy’s lamentation and of his own distress. In the second, [Col. 0884D] Philosophy wisely applies certain gentler remedies to Boethius and tenderly consoles him, teaching that the goods of Fortune are not to be counted among our goods. The third book contains sharper remedies; after rejecting the appearance of false happiness, it displays true blessedness. The subject of the fourth is that all wicked men are unhappy and powerless, while the good, by contrast, are happy and possessors of all their desires. Finally, in the fifth, he discusses with the greatest acuteness chance, human free will, and divine providence.

### VII. The Usefulness of the Work

Moreover, no one can doubt that the usefulness of these volumes can easily be understood from what has already been said, since they must be exceedingly beneficial: through them we learn to distinguish true goods from false, and, rejecting the most deceptive gifts of Fortune, to attain solid and everlasting blessedness by living well and honorably.

### VIII. To Which Part of Philosophy This Work Belongs

It remains for us to say to which branch of philosophy this work belongs. Philosophy is commonly divided into three parts: moral, natural, and rational. The first disciplines the soul, the second investigates the nature of things, and the third examines the properties and structure of words. [Col. 0886A] Philosophy is also divided into contemplative and active philosophy. The latter concerns itself with the practice of virtues, while the former concerns itself with the contemplation of truth.

This work, then—unless I am mistaken—belongs principally to active and moral philosophy. For its chief concern is to lead the human soul, cleansed of disturbances and cultivated in the virtues, to the contemplation of the highest good. In the final book, however, the discussion rises to a loftier level and in a certain way touches upon metaphysics and theology. But enough of this; now, with the Holy Spirit’s aid, let us begin the exposition of the first poem.

[Col. 0885]

## COMMENTARIES OF JOHN MURMELLIUS AND RUDOLF AGRICOLA ON THE BOOKS OF THE CONSOLATION OF PHILOSOPHY

[Note: [Col. 0885D] In these commentaries, whenever the reader finds no name attached, he should understand that they are to be attributed to John Murmellius.]

## BOOK ONE

### ON THE FIRST METER

[Col. 0885B]

In this first volume Boethius is about to set forth, in lamentation, the causes of his distress; appropriately, he breaks into elegiac verses, in which we chiefly find the expression of weeping and mourning. Hence the name given to them: *elegos* (ἔλεγος), for this means “mourning.” Thus the practice arose of composing epitaphs and dirges chiefly in verses of this kind. In the earliest times, indeed, people poured nothing but their laments into elegies. Later, other subjects also began to be written in this verse. Hence Horace:

> In verses joined in unequal measure, lament first,

> Then the thought of a fulfilled desire was also enclosed.

And Terentianus:

> These they called elegies, because such a close

[Col. 0885C]

> Is, as they say, more suited to mournful measures.

On their invention Horace says:

> Yet who first sent forth the slender elegies—

> Grammarians dispute, and the case still awaits a judge.

Terentianus likewise:

> They question which author first fashioned the pentameter;

> Some do not hesitate to say Callinus.

The pentameter is attached to the hexameter in such a way that one scarcely finds it separated from it. In one author alone, as far as I remember—Martianus Capella, in the ninth book—I have read a poem composed entirely of pentameters. Our Boethius, however, in the third book of this work, placed the pentameter after an iambic six-foot line.

So much for the kind of poem. Let us now explain what he intends by it. Boethius, cast down from the most exalted position of wealth and honors, laments the change in Fortune with a deeply troubled mind and sets forth the profound grief he has conceived from it. He grieves that a life which had almost been lost amid prosperous circumstances is now prolonged, amid adversity, into increasing misery and pain, when death is preferred to life.

**Poems**] Lyric odes and verses of joy. The word should not simply be taken as referring to any poems whatsoever, but to lyric compositions written in a cheerful spirit, just as Horace wrote four books of *Odes*.

[Col. 0886B]

**In bloom**] Flourishing through fortunate leisure and peace of mind.

**I completed**] I composed, I brought to completion.

**Mournful**] Sorrowing, grief-stricken. Ovid, in Book V of the *Tristia*:

> As our condition is mournful, so is the poem mournful,

> Written in keeping with its subject;

> Whole and joyful, I once played with joyful and youthful things;

> Yet now I regret having composed them.

Something is also called mournful when it deserves to be mourned. Horace, in the *Odes*:

> He died mourned by many good men,

> By none more mourned than by you, Virgil.

**Mournful measures**] Sad and elegiac verses.

**To begin**] To commence.

**Behold**] Whenever *behold* occurs, something necessarily follows that either causes fear or amazement. This is especially characteristic of Cicero in unexpected circumstances, a usage that Virgil carefully both read and transferred. So says Asconius. Boethius therefore uses the adverb appropriately here, signifying the sudden and remarkable change both in Fortune and in his studies.

**Torn**] Disturbed and sorrowful, as though their garments had been torn apart by grief of mind. For poets introduce the Muses as women assisting them.

**Dictate**] They suggest, and tell me what I should receive and write down. Sappho, in Ovid:

> But the daughters of Pegasus dictate their sweetest songs to me.

To dictate is to say something which another person takes down in writing. Hieronymus: “For we do not dictate with the same elegance with which we write.” It also means “to suggest.” Fabius: “For us, it is both safest to follow several authors, and reason seems in this way to dictate.”

**Muses**] The Muses.

**True**] Not feigned, but proceeding from the pain of the heart.

**Water**] They moisten. Seneca, in the *Octavia*:

> And she drenches her face with mournful tears.

Virgil, in Book VI:

> As he spoke, he likewise drenched his face with abundant tears.

The same author, in Book IX:

> And he drenched his face and cheeks with tears.

[Col. 0887A]

**These**] The Muses.

**At least**] As though he said: “Although everything else has deserted me, the Muses could not be drawn away from me by any terror.” Thus Ovid, in Book IV of the *Tristia*:

> The Muse, too, lightens my burden as I go to the shores of Pontus,

> She alone remained the companion of my exile.

> Alone she fears neither ambushes nor the soldier’s sword,

> Neither the sea nor the winds nor the barbarian land.

He adds not long afterward:

> Rightly, therefore, I venerate the goddesses who relieve my sufferings,

> My anxious companions in exile from Helicon,

> Who have deigned partly by sea and partly by land

> To follow my footsteps, whether by ship or on foot.

**Glory**] Let the plural nominative *Muses* be repeated, so that the construction is: “Muses, once the glory of my happy and flourishing youth, now console the fate of a sorrowful old man.” That is, the Muses, who were formerly no small ornament and distinction to me when I was flourishing both in youth and in the happy successes of Fortune, now bring consolation to me, disturbed and afflicted by adversity and growing old through grief before my proper time.

M. Tullius, in his speech *For Archias*:

> For the other pursuits, he says, belong neither to every season nor to every age nor to every place. These studies nourish youth, delight old age, adorn prosperity, and provide refuge and solace in adversity; they delight us at home, do not hinder us abroad, spend the night with us, travel with us, and accompany us in the country.

**The fate of a sorrowful old man**] Lorenzo Valla, who alone among all scholars rendered outstanding service to the Latin language, finds this expression of Boethius scarcely tolerable because the participle is missing. In my judgment, however, it can easily be supplied—say, *made*—so that the sense is: “The Muses now console my fate, since through Fortune’s injustice I have been made a sorrowful old man.” This is what he adds next.

**Unexpected**] That is, unexpected old age, which secretly came upon me sooner than I had imagined.

**Came in haste**] That is, introduced quickly and hurriedly.

**Through evils**] That is, because of evils and the adversities of Fortune. This is a seventh-case construction. Erasmus, the singular glory of our age, gives the proverb: “Evils hasten old age,” derived from the Homeric line:

> For suddenly men grow old through cares and troubles.

Ovid, in Book I of the *Epistles from Pontus*:

> An immense succession of labors weakens me also;

> Before my time I am compelled to be an old man.

[Col. 0887D]

**His age**] His old age. For just as youth belongs to joy, so old age is the age of sorrow.

**Untimely**] Born before the proper time.

**Crown**] Through the crown of the head, on the head.

**Gray hairs**] Gray hair. Valerius Maximus, Book II: “Puberty was restoring its honor to gray hairs.”

**Exhausted**] Drained of strength and weakened by the pain of the mind.

**Happy death of men**] A disturbed man depends entirely upon Fortune and, apart from her success, prefers death to life.

**Happy death of men**] Supply “is.” “Happy,” he says, “are those men for whom life remains as long as Fortune remains, and ends together with her departure.” When Antisthenes the Cynic was asked what among human beings was happiest, he replied: “To die happily.”

**Sweet things**] Things that belong to Fortune.

**Inserts**] Sends in, inflicts.

**Sorrowful**] By sorrowful, that is, sad, people. Maximinianus, a poet not wholly contemptible:

> O how harshly the condition of life presses upon the wretched.

> Nor is death subject to human command.

> It is sweet for the wretched to die, but the desired death withdraws;

> But when a man is sad, it comes headlong.

Incidentally, in these verses one should note the second syllable of *condition*, which has been lengthened by poetic license. I am surprised that certain little scholars, on the basis of a slight suspicion, attribute to Gallus, the poet Virgil’s friend, the elegies that belong to Maximinianus. But I shall discuss this more fully elsewhere.

[Col. 0888A]

**Alas, alas, how deaf**] *Alas* is an interjection of grief, as the most authoritative grammarians teach. *Eheu* is not a Latin expression, since an interjection alone among the parts of speech is never compounded; rather, one must say *heu heu*, by doubling it. Tibullus:

> Alas, alas, I see girls rejoicing in wealth.

The same author:

> He is iron-hearted, alas, alas, whoever remains in the city.

The form *heheu* is also found, according to Perottus. The verse may also correctly be read: “Alas, how deaf.” Servius, in his commentary on the second book of the *Aeneid*: “*Heu* is now one syllable, but sometimes two are made for the sake of the meter, as in:

> Alas, how lean is my bull to me in the rich field.”

**Turns away**] Death rejects and shuns those wretched people who call upon it.

**And tearful eyes**] Arrange the words as follows: “And savage death refuses”—that is, does not allow—“the wretched,” supply, “to close their tearful eyes.” Or in this way: “Savage death refuses tearful people”—that is, people weeping because of the calamity of this life—“the closing of their eyes,” that is, to die.

He alludes to the custom of the ancients, by which the eyes of the dead were usually closed by their relatives. In the Book of Tobit, in the final chapter, we read:

> After the death of his mother, Tobiah departed from Nineveh with his wife, his sons, and his sons’ sons, and returned to his in-laws. He found them unharmed in a good old age, cared for them, and himself closed their eyes; and he himself received all the inheritance of the house of Raguel.

Valerius Maximus, concerning the woman Assana:

> She summoned the hands of her daughters to perform the final duty of closing the eyes.

Silius Italicus, in Book IX:

> And at the end of my labors,

> With this right hand, I pray, close my eyes.

Ovid, in Book III of the *Tristia*:

> I shall give no instructions, nor, amid the final cry,

> Will a loving hand close my falling eyes.

**Light**] Changeable, fleeting, perishable.

**Faithless**] Untrustworthy, inconstant.

**Would favor**] “Is lacking to me.”

**For fleeting goods**] This is a seventh-case construction.

**Almost a sorrowful head**] That is, I was almost dead.

**Cloudy**] Dark and adverse. Thus Ovid:

> If your times should be cloudy, you will be alone.

**Unwelcome**] Unpleasant; supply “to me.”

**Cruel life**] Cruel toward me, wretched as I am and longing to die. Publius the Writer of Mimes:

> O life, long for the wretched, brief for the fortunate.

[Col. 0889A]

Seneca, in the *Hercules Oetaeus*:

> He who was equal to the gods, for whom

> Day and Fortune were alike, possesses death’s turns,

> When life is slowly dragged out amid groans.

The same author, in the same work:

> Death follows the fortunate; it flees the wretched.

**Why did you call me happy?**] In these verses he shows that no one should be called happy whose condition Fortune can change. True happiness, for it is genuine, has no end.

**Why**] For what reason, to what end, why. With a certain indignation of spirit, he turns his speech toward his friends.

**You boasted**] You proclaimed it insolently and with a kind of proud display.

**He who has fallen**] This is a most truthful statement, and it can easily be demonstrated from its opposite: whoever stands on a stable footing cannot fall.

## ON THE FIRST PROSE

In this prose passage, as though in a preface, he discloses the argument of the entire work. He introduces Philosophy as having appeared to him in a very beautiful description, although she was less recognizable because of his mental disturbances; having dismissed the lesser Muses, she undertook to care for and heal his sick mind with her own more serious remedies.

It should be understood that this work is composed as a dialogue between Philosophy, by whom right reason is understood, and Boethius, a man afflicted by the adversities of Fortune and subject to various disturbances. A dialogue, as Laertius holds, is composed of question and answer concerning a matter that touches either philosophy or the affairs of the state, with appropriate and fitting expression of the characters assumed and careful arrangement of the words.

**These things**] The things already described in the elegies.

**Silent**] Keeping silence.

**I would ponder**] I would meditate upon.

**Lamentable**] Suited to tears.

**The duty of the stylus**] Writing, the tracing of letters.

**I would depict**] I would describe.

**Above the crown of the head**] Above the head.

**Woman**] Philosophy is appropriately introduced as a woman, since the word is feminine in gender and denotes a form or figure. In the same way, Virtue and Pleasure are represented as women, not men, by the sophist Prodicus. According to Servius in his commentary on Book IX of the *Aeneid*, both a maiden and a married woman may be called *mulier*. His words are:

> Usage has established that we call unmarried women virgins and married women wives. Among our ancestors, however, *virgo* and *mulier* were used indiscriminately, for either word signified only the female sex.

**Reverent**] Venerable. Whatever is endowed with wisdom is especially worthy of reverence and honor.

**Burning**] Possessing fiery force and penetrating power.

**Power**] Capacity. *Valentia* means power, strength, or force. Titinnius:

> Wisdom steers and turns the ship; not brute force.

**Perceptive**] Keen. A perceptive person is one who can discern things through the sharpness of sight and inspect them completely. [Col. 0890A] Philosophy’s eyes are fiery and more perceptive than ordinary human power, because the study of wisdom penetrates the innermost things with the eyes of the intellect and investigates matters entirely unknown to the common crowd by searching out their hidden causes.

**With a vivid color**] With a natural appearance that displays health and strength. Since Philosophy is perfectly constituted, she is said to have a vivid color and extraordinary beauty.

**Unexhausted**] Infinite, never failing.

**Age**] Lifetime.

**Full**] Abundant.

**Of our age**] Of our era. Although, he says, Philosophy was so ancient that she was believed to have flourished long before our age, she nevertheless possessed inexhaustible and wholly undiminished vigor. For wisdom never grows old and never loses its power. The more you have attained through devotion to it, the more you will discover remains to be learned.

In the earliest ages, philosophers existed among the Hebrews, Egyptians, Greeks, Latins, and other peoples. One generation succeeded another, yet they were never able to exhaust the power of philosophy or reach the end of learning. Jerome, writing to Nepotian:

> Let Wisdom, my Abishag, embrace me now; let her, who never grows old, rest in my bosom.

(1 Kings 1.) She is undefiled, perpetually virginal, and incorruptible; like Mary, she gives birth every day and is always in labor.

**Of ambiguous stature**] “The woman,” he says, “who appeared to me had a stature of ambiguous determination,” that is, she possessed a stature that no one could easily identify with certainty. He then gives the reason:

“For at one moment she restrained herself to the ordinary measure of human beings,” that is, she did not exceed ordinary human stature. This is said with reference to those branches of philosophy that deal with matters of which the human intellect is capable and which human understanding can attain through definite reasoning. Such are the three branches of rational philosophy—grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric—as well as the mathematical disciplines apart from astronomy, most of physics, and the whole of moral philosophy.

**But now she seemed to strike heaven with the crown of her highest head**] This appears to refer to astronomy and to that part of physics which deals with heaven and the world.

**When she had raised her head higher**] By these words he signifies the first philosophy, whose speculation concerns divine matters and the highest causes, which the mortal intellect cannot easily comprehend. As the philosopher says:

> For just as the eyes of bats are related to the light of day, so the intellect of our souls is related to those things that by nature are most manifest of all.

**Of those looking back**] Turning their sight backward.

**Her garments were made of the finest threads**] By the garments understand the philosophers’ treatises, discussions, and precepts concerning divine and human affairs. By the finest threads, simple expressions and the elements of arguments. By the delicate workmanship, understand the skillful art of reasoning called dialectic. By the indissoluble material, understand the coherence of true propositions, premises, and conclusions, by which philosophical arguments hold together.

This material is indissoluble. For if you dissolve it and seize upon a fragment of an argument conducted on either side, you may perhaps believe and affirm what is false as though it were true. This happened to many others, but especially to Aristippus. When he heard Socrates discussing bodily pleasure, he abandoned the truth and seized upon falsehood—that is, those arguments that appeared to demonstrate that bodily pleasure is the highest good.

[Col. 0891B]

**As I later learned from the same person who revealed it**] This is a parenthesis.

**As**] Just as.

**Later**] Subsequently.

**The same**] Philosophy.

**Revealing**] Indicating. This will become apparent in the third prose passage of this book.

**With her own hands**] With philosophical thoughts and expressions. Philosophy’s hands are meditations and expressions concerning divine and human matters, by which Philosophy’s garment is woven—that is, the disputation in which falsehood is rejected and truth approved is constructed.

**Whose**] Of the garments.

**Appearance**] Form.

**As she usually does with smoky images**] This is a parenthesis.

**Smoky**] Covered with smoke. Seneca:

> An atrium full of smoky ancestral images does not make a man noble.

**Usually**] Supply: “the obscurity of neglected antiquity is accustomed to cover.”

**Darkness**] Obscurity.

**Had covered**] Had concealed. These words signify that the study of philosophy had long lain neglected in darkness.

**Of these**] Of the garments.

**At the extreme edge**] At the lowest extremity.

**Π**] This represents *praktikē* (Πρακτικὴ), that is, active philosophy.

**At the upper edge**] Supply “margin.”

**Θ**] This signifies *theōrētikē* (θεωρητικὴ), that is, contemplative philosophy. There are two branches of philosophy, contemplative and active, because human beings are born principally for two things: action and contemplation. Aristotle, in the second book of the *First Philosophy*:

> For the end of contemplative philosophy is truth, while the end of active philosophy is action.

**Between the two letters**] Between Π and Θ.

**Marked**] Designated, indicated.

**By which**] By these steps.

**From the lower**] From the element Π.

**To the higher element**] To Θ. This is taken from Platonic doctrine, as are a hundred other things in Boethius. The Platonists teach that the human soul reaches divine understanding by three steps: first through civic virtues, second through purificatory virtues, and third through the soul once it has been purified.

[Col. 0892A]

**Yet the same garment**] The philosophical disputation cohering in complete truth.

**Of certain violent men**] Epicureans and Stoics, who, as will be said in the third prose passage of this book, attacked the power of philosophy after Socrates’ death. Since they could not comprehend it in its entirety, they tore its garment apart and each took away whatever fragments he could. Lactantius, in Book VII of *On the Divine Reward*, explains why philosophers were unable to comprehend truth in its entirety, although they grasped it piecemeal.

**Little books**] By these he signifies contemplation, which he rightly places in the right hand, since contemplative philosophy is far superior to active philosophy, as Aristotle teaches in the second book of the *First Philosophy*.

[Col. 0892B]

**Scepter**] Understand by this the administration of the state and political government.

**When**] After.

**Dictating**] Suggesting.

**For a little while**] For a short time. It was not fitting for Philosophy to remain angry for long, as Horace says:

> Anger is a brief madness; rule your mind.

**For a little while**] *Paulisper*, *parumper*, *tantisper*, *quantisper*, and similar compounds are figures, as Priscian says, and signify a measure of time. They are explained as follows: *paulisper*, for a little while; *tantisper*, for that amount of time. Pomponius, in the *Dotata*:

> Can I persuade you to withdraw from me for a little while—only for as long as is sufficient?

**Glaring**] Terrible.

[Col. 0892C]

**Eyes**] Eyes. Ovid:

> Now I am dying; close your dear eyes with your hand.

**These theatrical little prostitutes**] The poetic Muses, accustomed to prostitute themselves on stages and in theaters for the sake of profit. *Scena* has a diphthong by usage rather than by reason: in Greek, *skēnē* (σκηνὴ) means a tent, deception, or tabernacle. The word is applied to that part of a theater extending from one of its horns to the other in the form of a semicircle. There, on structures built with two or more levels, actors recited poetic plays. Hence *scenicus*, “theatrical.” Thus Philosophy now calls the Muses theatrical little prostitutes, as an insult.

This passage gave many less learned people an opportunity to attack poets, because they failed to notice that there are two kinds of poets. One kind Philosophy rightly rejects and expels; the other she gladly embraces and recognizes as her own. The former is frivolous, affectedly Greek, filled with mere trifles, and directed only toward the pleasure of the ears. Of this kind are the common versifiers who submit to the disturbances of the mind and compose erotic and immodest songs. Their life and their verses alike are foreign to philosophy and, as Flaccus rightly says, “empty trifles and melodious nonsense.”

Of this kind of poetry Cato said in his poem *On Morals*:

> The honor of the poetic art was absent if someone devoted himself to it or attached himself to banquets; he was called a prowler.

And the blessed Jerome, writing to Damasus concerning the prodigal son:

> The food of demons, he says, is the poetry of poets, worldly wisdom, and the pomp of the rhetoricians’ words.

All these things delight everyone through their own sweetness; and while they captivate the ears with verses flowing in a sweet modulation, they also penetrate the soul and bind the innermost parts of the heart. But once they have been read through with the greatest zeal and labor, they give their readers nothing except empty sound and noise. There is no fullness of truth and no nourishment of justice to be found there; those devoted to them remain hungry for truth and lacking in virtues.

Thus far Jerome.

The other kind of poetry is serious, philosophical, and holy. Drawing the precepts of right living from the innermost sanctuaries of philosophy, it sternly deters people from vices and diligently urges them toward virtues. It is worthy of the highest honor, as sacred and wholly friendly to Philosophy, who in this work calls Euripides and Lucan her associates.

Baptista Mantuanus, in a letter to John Francis Pico:

> Obscene and immodest poems are, in my judgment, among true poems what fornicating prostitutes are among respectable matrons. For I do not consider a poem true, and capable of passing every test, unless it is serious, chaste, and holy—as Horace suggests when he says:

> The writings of Socrates will be able to show you the truth.

**Among fruitless thorns**] This is a metaphor drawn from agriculture.

**Profane**] Not initiated into our sacred rites.

**As is customary among the common people**] This is a parenthesis.

**In this**] In this matter, namely, in attacking the profane.

**Our labor**] Our efforts.

**This man**] Boethius.

[Col. 0893C]

**Eleatic studies**] Dialectical studies. Elea was a city of Greece in the Aeolian region, where Zeno, the inventor of dialectic, was born. Hence “Eleatic studies” means dialectical studies. Atticus the Platonist, in the book he wrote against those who possess Aristotelian learning but do not dare to profess Platonism. But Zeno and all those of the Eleatic school devoted themselves solely to logic.

**Academic**] Platonic. The Academy was a wooded place a thousand paces from Athens, made famous by Plato’s school. Hence “Academics” were those who followed his sect.

**Nourished**] Raised, fattened, cultivated. Here supply something such as: “Your flatteries attempt to disparage us,” or something similar. This is the figure *aposiiōpēsis* (ἀποσιώπησις), highly suitable to Philosophy in her great anger. Cicero calls it reticence; Celsus, withholding speech; some call it interruption, others cutting-off. Thus, when an angry god speaks in Virgil:

> Whom I—but it is better to calm the stirred waves.

The missing word is “punish,” or something similar.

**But go away**] She gravely rebukes and expels the Muses who serve the disturbances of the mind.

**Sirens**] In Greek it is written *Seirēn* (Σειρὴν). Those who write it with *y* are therefore mistaken. It is derived not from *syrō*, “I drag,” but either from *seiō*, or—what is more widely accepted—from *seira*, “a chain.”

The story of the Sirens is well known. Poets say that they lured sailors to destruction by the sweetness of their song. Ovid:

> The Sirens were monsters of the sea, who with melodious voice

> Detained whatever ships drew near.

[Col. 0894A]

Martial elegantly calls the Sirens “the cheerful punishment of sailors” and “cruel joy.” Dino, the father of Clitarchus, says that in India the Sirens are birds, and that those whom their song soothes they tear apart once they have been laid down in sleep. Poets tell of three Sirens, one singing with her voice, another with pipes, and the third with the lyre. In truth, however, they are believed to have been prostitutes who, because they reduced passersby to poverty, were imagined to cause shipwrecks.

**Sweet even unto destruction**] This resembles the proverbs “deadly mulled wine,” “a honey-smeared sword,” and “honeyed poison,” which are said of something so pleasant that it is at the same time harmful.

**My Muses**] Philosophical, serious, and holy poems. Observe, diligent reader, that Philosophy too has her Muses. Let the ignorant theologians therefore be silent: although they are utterly alien to the Muses, they recklessly call those who study them heretics.

**That chorus**] Of the immodest Muses, who arouse depraved passions.

**She cast down her face**] Thus Virgil, in Book III of the *Aeneid*:

> She cast down her face and spoke in a lowered voice.

**Toward the ground**] Toward the earth.

**More sorrowful**] Very sorrowful, or more sorrowful than before. For he had been sorrowful from the beginning, hence:

> The torn Muses dictate what must be written.

**So imperious**] Someone imperious is one who commands too harshly, is severe, and behaves almost as a display of authority.

**Authority**] Authority is a kind of dignity formed from the good qualities of mind and body. By both her presence and her speech, it causes others to show her reverence and to follow her example.

**At the far end of my little bed**] He has represented the custom of physicians sitting beside a sick person.

## ON THE SECOND METER

This poem is called Alcmanian, dactylic, tetrameter, and hypercatalectic. It is called Alcmanian after its inventor, Alcman (Ἀλκμὰν), a lyric poet from Laconia or Messenia, the inventor of amatory poetry, who wrote in the Doric language. Papinius, in the *Silvae*, writes of him:

> Covered over, and sung by harsh Amyclaean Alcman.

The error of those who pronounce “Alcman” with three syllables is therefore ridiculous. It is called dactylic from its principal foot; tetrameter from the number of its feet; and hypercatalectic because one syllable remains after the first two feet in the middle. It consists of a heroic penthemimeral caesura, together with a dactyl and a spondee.

It resembles the verse that Terentianus quotes, taken from a shortened line of Virgil:

> But the queen, wounded by grievous care.

There is a similar line in a hymn-writer:

> O how gloriously you flash with light.

Philosophy is indignant that such ignorance of truth should arise in mortal minds from their disturbances that, abandoning the light of contemplation of heavenly things and setting aside meditation on the most honorable arts, they are carried with their whole desire toward earthly matters.

**Alas, how deeply submerged in a precipitous abyss**] Arrange it as follows: “Alas, how great”—that is, how deeply—“the mind is submerged,” that is, overwhelmed, “in a precipitous abyss,” the depth of disturbances from which it is not easy to emerge. Or thus: “Submerged,” that is, immersed, “in a precipitous abyss,” that is, an abyss into which one falls headlong.

[Col. 0895A]

**How, I say, it is dulled**] It is blunted and forgetful of true wisdom.

**And having abandoned its own light**] That is, having abandoned the use of reason and the twofold contemplation of truth.

**It strives**] That is, it contends and endeavors.

**To go**] To be carried.

**Into external darkness**] Into earthly and bodily matters, whose allurements darken the spirit through their contamination.

**Whenever**] Whenever.

**Care**] Desire for external things.

**Harmful**] Harmful to the understanding and delaying it.

**Stirred up**] Aroused.

**By earthly blasts**] By accidental events and the allurements of riches.

[Col. 0895B]

**It grows**] It increases.

**Without measure**] Beyond all measure.

It should be understood that the inner human being—that is, the spirit—is by its own nature carried, through the grace of God, toward the contemplation of heavenly things. Yet because of its contamination by the earthly body and its desire for temporal things, it is affected by various disturbances and held back from its proper task. “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26). Above all, therefore, a person must strive to dispel the clouds of corrupt affections, so that spiritual light may shine forth and desire may continually be subjected to right reason. This is what Philosophy now undertakes for Boethius’s consolation.

*Precipitous* is compounded from *prae* and *caput*. Properly, someone is called *praeceps* who falls or is sent downward in such a way that the head goes first. Hence a place situated higher up is also called *praeceps*, because a person can easily be thrown down from it; and, conversely, something deep is called *praeceps*, because something can be thrown into it. Virgil, in Book XI:

> Some, driven by the crushing collapse, are rolled

> Into precipitous pits.

Understand the expression “in a precipitous abyss” in this way. *Praeceps* also means hasty, ill-considered, or reckless. But enough of this for now.

**Care driven by earthly blasts**] This is expressed with truly elegant metaphor. Since care is like a fire burning the heart, it is rightly said to be driven and stirred by earthly blasts. For, as the poet says:

> Fire is nourished by wind, but quenched by water;

> A gentle breeze feeds the flames, while a stronger wind puts them out.

[Col. 0895D]

**Here, once free beneath the open sky**] He particularly expresses his profound indignation at Boethius’s altered mind and shows from what height of condition he has been cast down.

**Here**] Boethius.

**Once free**] When he had not yet been subject to the passions of the mind.

**Accustomed**] Used.

**To go**] To be carried through contemplation into the ethereal paths—that is, into the movements of the heavenly bodies—and, with the sky open and accessible to the intellect, to behold the lights of the rosy sun, that is, the red, beautiful, and shining sun. Virgil, in Book XI:

> Unless rosy Phoebus, already tired in the Iberian waters,

> Dips his horses and brings back night as day declines.

**He beheld**] He gazed upon.

[Col. 0896A]

**Stars**] Lights.

**Of the cold moon**] She presides over cold and moist nights. The sun is so called either because alone among all the heavenly bodies it is so great, or because, when it has risen and everything else has been darkened, it alone appears. The moon is named from shining. She is likewise called Lucina. Cicero is the authority for this in Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*.

And victorious] That is, having attained his wish, he had comprehended in numbers the whole of that stellar system which—whatever it may be, that is, which, bent and moved through the various orbits posited by astronomers—performs wandering revolutions, that is, erratic motions. Besides those stars said to be fixed in the eighth heaven, whose number is unknown to astronomers, there are seven others, not in the eighth heaven like those, but each in one of the seven lower heavens: Saturn in the seventh, Jupiter in the sixth, Mars in the fifth, the Sun in the fourth, Venus in the third, Mercury in the second, and the Moon in the first. These stars are called planets, that is, “wanderers” (for in Greek πλανάομαι means “I wander”; hence πλάνη, “error”; πλάνης, πλάνητος, *planēs*, “planet”; and πλανήτης, “wandering,” “wanderer”), both because they are carried along in their course and because, moving contrary to the motion of the heavens, they revolve eastward from the west. Pliny, in book two, chapter six, of his *Natural History*, says that these seven stars are called wandering from their motion, although nothing wanders less than they do. Hence Cicero’s verses also survive:

> Which, in word and in the Greeks’ false expressions, wander,  
> Yet in truth are carried along by a fixed course and distance.

The same author says in book two of *On the Nature of the Gods*: “Most remarkable, however, are the motions of those five stars which are falsely called wandering. For nothing wanders which throughout all eternity preserves its progress and regress, together with its other motions, constant and orderly.”
