Moreover, the Sun, midway among the planets, moves with the greatest magnitude and power; it is the ruler not only of times and lands but also of the stars themselves and of heaven. It supplies light to all things and removes darkness; it hides the other stars; it regulates the alternation of the seasons and the ever-renewed year in accordance with nature; it dispels the sadness of heaven and even clears the clouds from the human mind; and it lends its own light to the other stars as well. The Moon follows its annual course in monthly intervals; her very faint light is produced by her nearest approach to the Sun, while each successive withdrawal makes it fullest. Not only are her appearance and form changed, both by increasing and by returning to her beginnings through waning, but her position also changes, being at one time northern and at another southern.

The star of Saturn, called Φαίνων (“Shining”) by the Greeks, is farthest from the earth and completes its course in approximately thirty years. Below it, and nearer to the earth, moves the star of Jupiter, called Φαέθων (“Radiant”); it completes the same circuit of the twelve signs in twelve years. Next below this is Πυρόεις (“Fiery”), the star called that of Mars; it traverses the same orbit in twenty-four months—six days fewer, according to Cicero—than the upper planets. Below it, with the Sun interposed, is the star of Venus, called Φωσφόρος (“Light-bringer”) in Greek and *Lucifer* in Latin when it precedes the Sun; when it follows, it is called Ἕσπερος (“Hesperus”), in Latin *vesper* (“evening star”). It completes its course in a year, traversing the breadth and length of the zodiacal circle; it never moves farther from the Sun than the interval of two signs, whether preceding or following him.

Next is the star of Mercury, nearest to the Moon. It is called Στίλβων (“Gleaming”) by the Greeks; in approximately one year it traverses the zodiacal circle, and it never moves farther from the Sun than the interval of one sign, whether it goes before or follows him.

Of these seven planets Lucan writes elegantly in book nine of the *Pharsalia*:

> The stars that alone govern the flight of Olympus  
> And meet the pole—each with its different power—  
> By the law of the universe a different primary power was assigned to them.  
> The Sun divides the seasons of the year,  
> Changes day into night, and with his powerful rays  
> Forbids the stars to move, restraining their wandering courses by his station.  
> The Moon, in her appointed alternations, mingles Tethys with the earth.  
> To Saturn fell the cold ice and the snowy zone;  
> Mars has winds and uncertain lightning.  
> Beneath Jupiter there is mildness and air never troubled.  
> Venus possesses the seeds of all things that bear fruit;  
> The Cyllenian is arbiter of the boundless sea.

Per varios orbes] Understand “various circles.” Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, and Venus each have three circles, together with an epicycle, through which, according to the teaching of astronomers, they move in various ways; Mercury has five circles and an epicycle. An epicycle is a small circle along whose circumference the planetary body is carried.

The word *orbit* (*orbis*) is ambiguous, as Macrobius testifies. Sometimes it signifies a circle. Cicero writes: “Among the flames there shone forth a circle of the most brilliant radiance, which you, having received the term from the Greeks, call the Milky Circle.” Sometimes it means a sphere. The same author writes: “Everything is joined together for you by nine circles, or rather spheres.” Sometimes *orbit* is taken for a return and revolution from one place to the same place after a circuit has been completed. The same author writes: “Those round and spherical bodies, animated by divine minds, complete their circles and orbits with marvelous speed.” Virgil:

> The farmer’s labor returns, having been carried around in a circuit.

Sometimes the word means a table of circular shape. Juvenal:

> Unless it supports broad circular tables,  
> A great mass of ivory.

Quin etiam causas] The order is: “Moreover, he was accustomed to investigate causes and to provide the various causes of hidden nature.”

Unde] That is, “for what reasons.”

Sonora flamina] That is, “the sonorous blasts of the winds.”

Sollicitent] Let them disturb, agitate, and stir.

[Col. 0897D] Aequora] Even and level surfaces before the blasts of the winds.

Ponti] Of the sea. Wind is moving and agitated air, as can be demonstrated by a small hand-fan. Wind is understood as nothing other than a wave of air, which—as Clement says—is compressed and constrained, as though from certain lofty mountains, by God’s ordering, and is forced out and expressed into winds to stir the waves and moderate the heat. It receives different names according to the different regions of heaven.

Quis spiritus volvat] That is, “what breath turns around.”

Orbem] The world, that is, heaven.

Stabilem] Constant in perpetual continuity and in the most certain observance of excellent order. The heavenly spheres, as some think, are moved by their own substantial forms. But, as others appear to judge more correctly, intelligences—also called spirits—who divinely attend the heavens, turn them around. The Platonists believed that God was mingled with the entire world and implanted in all its parts, and that he caused so great a mass to revolve. Following their opinion, the poet sang:

> In the beginning, heaven, earth, the liquid plains,  
> The shining globe of the Moon, and the Titanian stars—  
> An inward spirit nourishes them, and Mind, infused through all their limbs,  
> Moves the whole mass and mingles with its great body.

And Manilius, in book one of the *Astronomicon*:

> This work, constructed in the body of the immeasurable universe,  
> And the diverse limbs of nature, formed in different shapes—  
> Air, fire, earth, and the lying sea—  
> The divine power of the soul governs; and God, in sacred movement,  
> Breathes together and guides it by silent reason,  
> Distributing many covenants throughout all its parts,  
> So that one may make and bear the powers of another,  
> And the whole may remain related through its various forms.

Vel cur sidus surgat ab ortu rutilo, casurum in undas Hesperias] The sense is: Boethius, accustomed to investigate and explain natural causes, asks why the stars rise in the east and set in the west, and, according to popular belief, plunge down into the Ocean at their setting. The cause of this is the circular motion of the first, moving heaven, which carries all the stars—both wandering and fixed—with it from east to west, and again from west to east.

In undas Hesperias] Into the western Ocean. From *Hesperus* comes *hesperius*, “western”; *Hesperia*, at the extreme western end, means Spain, although *Hesperia* taken simply means Italy.

Quis temperet placidas horas veris] That is, “the hours of springtime.”

Ut] Supply “so that.”

Ornet roseis] “May adorn the earth with purple flowers.”

Deus] Indeed, the Sun accomplishes this through his service: when he has climbed toward the upper regions, he tempers spring; when he reaches the highest point of heaven, he kindles the summer heats; descending again in autumn, he restores mildness. When he returns to the lower circle, he leaves us the severity of winter’s cold from heaven’s icy structure.

Pleno] Abounding in various crops.

Gravidis] Swollen with vine-liquid, that is, wine.

Rimari] To inquire into and investigate.

Effeto] Weakened and deprived of strength.

Lumine] In intellect.

Pressus colla] Having the neck bent downward.

[Col. 0898D] Gravibus catenis] By desires for earthly things.

Declivem] Prone and inclined toward the ground.

Pondere] By earthly anxiety.

Stolidam] Making one foolish. Thus the satirical poet also exclaims:

> O souls bent toward the earth and empty of heavenly things!

## IN PROSE II

In this prose Boethius relates what Philosophy attempted to do for him after the lamentable song had ended, and how she first addressed him, languishing, in gentle speech; then, drawing her robe into a wrinkle, dried his eyes, which were streaming with tears.

Luminibus] With his eyes.

Atqui] “But”; this is an expression frequently used by Boethius.

[Col. 0899A] Talia contuleramus arma] Valerius Maximus, book three: “There is also that vigorous and steadfast warfare of the soul, rich in letters—the venerable priestess of learning, Philosophy—which, once received into the breast of human beings, drives away dishonorable and useless passion, establishes the whole person in the stronghold of solid virtue, and makes him more powerful against fear and pain.” Antisthenes the Cynic said that virtue is a weapon that cannot be taken away.

Nisi prior abjecisses] Virtue and philosophy do not abandon a person unless the person first casts them away by voluntary sin.

Pudore] Shame is fear of just reproach. Astonishment, however, is a certain alienation of the senses.

Lethargum] *Lethargus*, Greek λήθαργος, is sluggishness and an almost unconquerable need for sleep, accompanied by mental alienation; it differs from phrenitis not in location but in material. Phrenitis is produced by blood or yellow bile; lethargy by wetter and colder phlegm, which dissolves the brain. In this disease forgetfulness of everything occurs.

## IN METER III

The poem is two-membered and two-stanzaed, consisting of one heroic verse and one Alcmanian verse, dactylic and tetrameter, acatalectic; it is composed of four dactyls, though it sometimes admits a spondee except in the fourth position. Here Boethius shows that, once her wiping had cleared his eyes, he gladly recognized Philosophy as his nurse. This is entirely correctly said. No one can behold philosophy itself—that is, wisdom, by which the intellect contemplates truth—unless the darkness of disturbances has first been driven away and the eyes of the soul cleansed.

Tunc] When Philosophy wiped my eyes with her garment.

Discussa] Scattered and dispersed.

Nocte] By ignorance of the truth and the darkness of depraved affections.

Tenebrae] The soul’s blindness and the darkening of the mind.

Luminibus] With the eyes of the soul.

Rediit] Was restored and returned.

Vigor] The power and capacity to know the truth.

Ut cum praecipiti] With a very elegant and fitting comparison he shows that his former power of understanding was restored, just as, when the air has been darkened by clouds, if the north wind blows and the clouds are driven away, the serenity of the air and the Sun’s light are immediately restored.

Ut] Just as.

Cum] When.

Praecipiti] Rapid.

Glomerantur] Are wrapped together, covered over, and, as it were, gathered into a mass.

Coro] By the west wind blowing against the north wind.

Polus] Heaven.

Stetit] The past tense appears to have been used for the present.

Sol latet] The Sun does not appear.

Nondum coelo venientibus astris] That is, before the proper time of night.

Desuper] From above.

[Col. 0900A] Nox] The darkness of night.

Hanc] This night.

Thraicio ex antro] Because the north wind seems to the Italians to be sent out from the caves of Thrace. *Thracius*, *Thraicius*, and *Threicius* are used with the same meaning. Lucan:

> As great as the north wind from pine-bearing Ossa when it is Thracian.

Boethius, in book three of this work:

> The grieving Thracian poet.

Horace, in book one of the *Odes*:

> If sweeter than Thracian Orpheus.

Reseret] May open and uncover.

Diem] The light of day.

Emicat] Appears.

Subito] Suddenly.

[Col. 0900B] Vibratus] Moved and agitated.

Ferit] Strikes.

Mirantes oculos] That is, the eyes of people marveling at the sudden clear sky.

I am brief in explaining this poem, since it seemed not inappropriate to append here a letter of Augustine Dathus, in which the same passage is explained no less learnedly than elegantly, under his name—for, with the candor that is mine, I do not wish to claim another’s work as my own:

> Lest, if one day the flock of birds should come to reclaim  
> Its feathers, the little crow, stripped of its stolen colors,  
> Should provoke laughter.

This, then, is his letter.

### Augustine Dathus to Bernardino, greetings

You desire, Bernardine, as you yourself say, an explanation of those verses which Severinus Boethius composed in his book *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, not long after the beginning of the work, when he says: “Then, when the night had been dispelled, the darkness left me.” And the rest of the poem follows.

I praise you and your talent, and I strongly approve, Bernardine, of your delight in reading Severinus. He was one of our own, a man of singular learning and unskilled in no discipline. He not only thoroughly mastered the Latin language but also greatly enriched it. This is shown by his many other books, and especially by the one entitled *On the Consolation of Philosophy*. In that work he certainly reveals the full power and praise of philosophy, since, through her agency, the darkness of ignorance is driven away and the splendor and brightness of truth shines forth. For when a human being, blinded by the darkness of disturbances, is entangled in great errors, philosophy herself approaches and he comes, in a sense, to his senses and returns to the dignity of human nature.

There are two stages of true wisdom. The first removes obstacles; the second introduces knowledge of truth, than which no nourishment is sweeter to a human being. Well, therefore, does the man who previously wandered in the deepest darkness of ignorance, when the shining light of philosophy—which professes the pursuit of wisdom—appears, say what is contained in the poem under discussion:

> Then, when the night had been dispelled, the darkness left me,  
> And the former vigor returned to my eyes.

The first stage of wisdom is the removal of obstacles; hence the words: “Then, when the night had been dispelled, the darkness left me”—that is, when the obscurity had been removed, the darkness, which is the blindness of ignorance and the gloom of the mind, left me.

The second stage of wisdom is introduced when he adds:

> And the former vigor returned to my eyes.

“Eyes” here means the keenness of the soul and mind. “Vigor” is knowledge of truth, through which the soul grows strong; indeed, it is not merely strengthened but nourished, enlarged, and fortified with the greatest power. For no food is sweeter to the soul than knowledge of truth.

What belongs to the soul, and is hidden and invisible, is explained by a visible and most beautiful likeness:

> As when the stars are gathered beneath the rushing west wind.

For the stars are massed together by the constriction of clouds, especially when the western wind blows. This is the wind which Gellius calls *caurus* and which the Greeks usually call *argestes*; it blows against the north and, as some report, is also called *iapix*. Some winds drive clouds, while others push them away:

> And heaven stood beneath rain-laden showers;  
> The Sun is hidden.

The pole is a part of heaven and is commonly used for heaven, especially for that region which turns near the Arctic or Antarctic pole. Heaven is not said to stand because it is always driven by the swiftest motion; but human beings do not feel or perceive that motion except through the course of the stars, whose movement is easily seen. Thus, when the stars are hidden, clouds intervene, and rains pour down upon the earth, heaven appears to stand still, the Sun to be concealed, and—even before the stars come into heaven—day, which the Sun’s presence produces, to be taken away, while night is poured down upon the earth from above. Something similar is found in Virgil:

> Suddenly the clouds take away both heaven and daylight.

The Sun signifies the light of reason and the clarity of understanding. The rain-laden west wind signifies the assault of hostile fortune and its fiercest weapons. The cloud, which spreads black night over everything, signifies a heavier disturbance and sickness of soul, which, by covering it with a certain darkness, obscures the light and reason of the mind itself.

> If the Thracian north wind, sent from the north, should scourge it.

For the north wind—which the Greeks so call and the Latins call *aquilo*—when it blows, dissolves the clouds and, beating them apart, disperses them; thus it unlocks the day that had been shut in. Some read *antro Thraicio* (“from a Thracian cave”), because winds, formed in the caves and hollow caverns of that region, blow forth from them with greater force and drive away the clouds. Others prefer to read *ab arcto* (“from the north”). The north is the northern region, as in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*:

> He swam out toward the icy Bears.

For the Greeks call the east ἀνατολή (“rising”), the west δύσις (“setting”), the south μεσημβρία (“midday”), and the north ἄρκτος (“Bear,” or north).

Thus, when the clouds have been rejected and driven away by the north wind:

> Phoebus flashes forth, his light suddenly brandished,  
> And strikes with his rays the eyes that marvel.

Phoebus is the same as the Sun, just as the Moon is called Phoebe. The Sun is the source of light, as Cicero says, and he flashes forth suddenly not only when, with dawn preceding him, he fills all lands with light, but also when, after the clouds withdraw, he suddenly spreads abroad and fills the entire world with his radiance.

“Brandished” (*vibratus*) means “quivering,” and both “brandished” and “striking the eyes” are metaphors taken from a weapon, especially a shining sword, both of whose characteristic actions are to be brandished and to strike. Thus not only a sword but also the keenness of the eyes is called an *edge*. Our own vision, however, is overwhelmed by the light of the Sun placed before it, so that those who gaze at the Sun too long lose the light of their eyes and are completely overcome by the more powerful brightness.

But, to return to the subject, the author’s entire intention in this poem concerns the twofold stage of wisdom: first, that the obstacles—which are the disturbances of the soul and the darts of striking fortune—should be removed; then that the clear knowledge of truth should follow, which philosophy and the pursuit of wisdom introduce. Philosophy is the knowledge of all things, both divine and human; she is the light of truth and therefore the guide of life, the pursuer of virtues, and the expeller of vices.

Our soul is compared with heaven, which at one time grows dark with clouds and at another shines in clear weather. In the same way, our soul is sometimes confused by disturbances and entangled in great errors, and at other times shines with pure and lucid knowledge of truth. From these contrary conditions arise the contrary states of misery and happiness.

If you ask what it means for “the former vigor to return to the eyes,” it would not be unreasonable to interpret it according to Plato’s view. Plato asserts that the soul is divine, eternal, and perfect in its knowledge of all things, but that it is confused and made forgetful by the prison of the body and the confinement of the flesh; through study and exercise, however, it recovers its former knowledge.

Or, if that interpretation is not approved, Severinus may mean a man who had formerly been engaged in the studies of philosophy and therefore illumined by the light of truth, but who, through disturbance and grief of soul, had forgotten his former clarity and, returning again to the studies of philosophy, recovered his former knowledge of truth. Which is more probable I leave to your judgment. In my opinion, however, both interpretations can rightly be accepted, and both display the chief benefit of philosophizing.

We acknowledge that the soul is divine, and in this we agree with Plato. But we understand “divine” to mean created by God and infused into the body; we deny that it has always existed, though we do not deny that it will always exist.

Finally, to summarize briefly all that has been said, know that this poem is divided into two parts. In the first, Boethius declares the effect of the approach of philosophy; in the second, he reveals the same effect by means of a comparison. The effect of philosophy’s arrival is twofold: to drive away the darkness of ignorance and to introduce the light of truth.

Of the first he says: “Then, when philosophy intervened, the darkness—that is, the darkness of ignorance—left me, the night having been dispelled and the obscurity removed.” Of the second he says: “And the former vigor returned,” that is, certain knowledge of truth returned, recovered by the eyes of the mind.

Then the comparison is added. Our soul is compared with heaven. Heaven is sometimes darkened by clouds and sometimes shines in clear weather. So our soul is sometimes entangled and confused by disturbances and errors, and sometimes shines with knowledge of truth.

“AS,” that is, “just as,” when the stars are gathered together—“rushing,” that is, rapidly—beneath the *CORUS*, the wind blowing from the west; and the *POLE*, that is, heaven in this region, stood still, or appeared to stand still. The course of the stars most clearly reveals the motion of heaven, so that when the stars are hidden heaven seems to stand still.

“BENEATH RAIN-LADEN SHOWERS,” that is, beneath more violent rains.

“THE SUN IS HIDDEN,” concealed, before the stars come into heaven; this usually happens after sunset.

“NIGHT,” that is, the darkness of night, is poured down and sent upon the earth from above; night settles upon the lands before its proper time.

“But,” by contrast, if the north wind is sent from the north, from the northern region, or from a Thracian cave, since winds issue from hollow caverns:

“LET IT SCOURGE,” namely, heaven and the clouds; and “LET IT UNLOCK,” let it open the day that had been closed—namely, the clarity of day, shut in by the darkness of the clouds.

“PHOEBUS,” the Sun.

“FLASHES FORTH,” shines brightly; “BRANDISHED,” quivering; “SUDDENLY,” with sudden light and radiance; “STRIKES,” beats; “MARVELING,” gazing; “EYES,” with the rays of his own brilliant light.

Let it be enough to have touched briefly on these matters. Farewell, devote yourself to your studies, and take great delight in exercises of this kind.

## IN PROSE III

Boethius now relates how, after his former vigor had been restored, he addressed the Philosophy he had recognized, and how she answered him with the greatest kindness. She teaches that it has always been the case that the wicked hate those devoted to virtue and wisdom; therefore he ought to rejoice rather than grieve if, because of the dissimilarity of character, he displeases every worst person, and, fortified by the bulwark of wisdom, is attacked in vain by the weapons of the profane multitude.

Haud aliter] In no other way than the sight of the Sun is restored when clear weather returns.

Hausi] I looked upon.

Medicantis] Bringing a remedy to the darkness of the eyes.

Diduxi] I opened. *Diducere* means either “to divide” or “to open”; *deducere* means “to lead downward.” Beware of reading *deduxi* here unless you understand Boethius to have been lying on the higher part of the couch and to have lowered—that is, led downward—his eyes toward Philosophy, who was seated at the lower end of the same couch.

Ab adolescentia] That age is suitable for beginning the studies of philosophy.

O omnium magistra virtutum] Cicero, in book five of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “O Philosophy, guide of life, investigator of virtue and expeller of vices, what could not only we but the whole life of human beings have been without you? You founded cities; you summoned scattered human beings into the fellowship of life; you first joined them together in dwellings, then in marriages, and afterward in the communion of letters and speech. You were the inventor of laws and the teacher of morals and discipline. We flee to you; from you we seek aid. To you we surrender ourselves, as formerly in great part, so now entirely and wholly.” Thus far Cicero.

Super cardine] From heaven.

An] Supply “therefore”: “therefore have you come into these solitudes of our exile?”

Quoque] Also.

Rea agiteris] You are accused. To prosecute someone as guilty is to accuse him; to carry the case of the guilty person through to its end is to condemn him.

Illa] Philosophy.

Alumne] “Boethius, whom I nourished.”

Sarcinam] A burden.

Partirer] I would share it, or rather willingly take upon myself a part of it.

Quam mei nominis invidia sustulisti] For the wicked both hated and accused Boethius because he was a philosopher and a cultivator of justice.

Scilicet] That is, “Certainly not.”

Censes] “Do you really think so?” These words must be read as a question.

Lacessitam] Challenged and attacked.

Nostri Platonis] The foremost of philosophers, whom you too imitate above all in this work. Plato of Athens was the most distinguished of the pagan philosophers, a disciple of Socrates and teacher of Aristotle. His life was recorded by Diogenes Laertius, and later by Guarinus of Verona and Marsilio Ficino.

Plato himself also endured great dangers because he was a philosopher. On this subject Marcus Tullius writes in his speech *For Gaius Rabirius*: “We have learned that Plato, easily the most learned man in all Greece, was involved in the greatest dangers and ambushes through the injustice of Dionysius, the tyrant of Sicily, to whom he had entrusted himself.” Cicero also records that Callisthenes, a learned man and companion of Alexander the Great, was killed by Alexander; and that Demetrius—distinguished both for the republic of Athens, which he had organized most excellently, and for his learning—who was called Phalereus, was deprived of life in the same place, in the Egyptian kingdom, by an asp applied to his body. Thus far Cicero.

Certamen certavimus] An elegant expression, like Lucilius’s:

> We fought a great fight.

Eodem] With Plato.

Superstite] While he was still alive.

Socrates] This celebrated Athenian philosopher was the son of Sophroniscus, a marble-worker, and Phanarete, a midwife. He treated moral philosophy extensively.

At one time, when he mocked Anytus, a wealthy and factious Athenian, for his foolishness, the comic poet Aristophanes—a learned man, certainly, but a person of poor character—accepted a large sum of money from Anytus and wrote a comedy against Socrates entitled Νεφέλαι, “Clouds” or “Nebulae.” Among other accusations, he invented the charge that Socrates worshiped clouds, disparaged the religious observances of the Athenians, and so instructed the minds of the young that they could piously and dutifully lay violent hands upon their parents.

When this matter, through the accusations of Anytus, Lycon, and Meletus—as Plato writes in the *Apology for Socrates*—had stirred the entire people against Socrates, he was condemned to death in a kind of fury and anger. He fearlessly drank the cup of hemlock publicly provided for him. He was so far from seeking revenge that he always maintained that the person who commits an injustice is more wretched than the person who suffers it.

The Athenian people soon mourned his death so deeply that they punished his accusers either with death or exile and dedicated a bronze statue to Socrates himself. In Greek his name is written Σωκράτης; hence the first syllable must always be long.

Therefore, in passing, we warn the diligent reader to correct the verse in our book of *Moral Letters*, printed in the tenth letter as follows:

> Socrates is dead, and Plato too is dead.

We wrote that it should instead be read:

> Isocrates is dead, and Plato too is dead.

For we imitated Cato the Elder in Cicero, where he mentions both Isocrates and Plato, each of whom lived to an advanced age.

In the same letter one incorrectly reads:

> With a strong hand he loosens in the world,

instead of “he rages.” Likewise, in the second letter, *quamvis parum* (“although little”) should read *quamque parum* (“however little”). But this is not the place for these matters; let us therefore pass them over and return to our subject.

Promeruit victoriam injustae mortis me astante] For, having established the immortality of souls through philosophical arguments, he drank the poison fearlessly and conquered an unjust death; by his innocence he turned his unjust condemnation back upon his accusers, who were justly condemned.

Cujus haereditatem cum deinceps Epicureum vulgus ac Stoicum, caeterique] Socrates deserves great praise because he is said to have possessed the true inheritance of philosophy, from which most of his disciples seized only fragments for themselves.

Socrates was the first of all philosophers to discuss life and morals, but he did so with a remarkable kind of irony, arguing each matter vehemently in both directions. Thus his individual disciples, whose intellectual capacities were as diverse as human natures are, seized from these discussions not what he himself thought but what seemed most congenial to them. Hence arose the various and differing philosophical schools.

Socrates sometimes discussed bodily pleasure, arguing both for and against it. Those whose character inclined more strongly in that direction therefore took from his arguments not what he asserted but what pleased them more, and declared the agreeable movement of the senses—that is, pleasure—to be the highest good. Zeno of Citium and the Stoics who arose from him, however, placed happiness in virtue alone. Others held other views, as Beroaldus learnedly explains in the little work he composed on happiness.

Epicureum vulgus] Epicurus was an Athenian philosopher who despised dialectic and declared bodily pleasure to be the highest good. His followers were therefore called Epicureans. He rightly says “the Epicurean multitude,” because they are very numerous. Thus Lactantius, in book seventeen of *On False Wisdom*: “The teaching of Epicurus has always been much more popular than that of the others—not because it offers anything true, but because it attracts many to the popular name of pleasure. No one is not inclined toward vices.”

[Col. 0905D] Stoicum] The Stoics took their name from the Athenian Stoa, or Portico, in which Zeno of Citium—so called from Citium, a city of Cyprus—taught. For στοά in Greek means in Latin *porticus*, “portico,” *fornix*, “vault,” or *testudo*, “covered colonnade.” Hence στωϊκός, with the small letter changed into the capital, gives *Stoicus*, “Stoic.”

Pro sua parte] According to their own strength.

Quisquis] Figuratively, supply “should attempt.”

Raptum ire] To begin to seize.

Molirentur] They might attempt and strive.

Reclamantem] Refusing, resisting, and shouting out against them.

Vestem] Philosophy—the philosophical argument held together by solid truth—which was discussed above in the first prose.

Disciderunt] This is because philosophy was divided into many sects.

Panniculis] Little scraps and fragments.

Nostri habitus] That is, of our garment.

Vestigia] Traces and signs.

Imprudentia] The foolishness that is always opposed to philosophy.

Nonnullos eorum] For example, the Cyrenaics, Epicureans, and others of that kind.

Profanae] Unlearned and uninitiated into the sacred rites of philosophy.

Errore] By the false opinion that pleasure is the highest good and that the world is not governed by divine providence.

Pervertit] Corrupted and alienated from the truth.

Quod si nec Anaxagorae fugam] He proves by examples that philosophers have always been hated and detested by the unlearned multitude.

Anaxagorae] This distinguished philosopher was by origin from Clazomenae. At Athens he was accused of impiety for saying that the Sun was a glowing and thoroughly fiery mass, and, according to some reports, escaped judgment by flight. Others, however, say that he came to trial and was released through the compassion of the judges.

He later departed for Lampsacus and died there. When the leading citizens asked whether he wished anything to be done, they say that he ordered the boys to be permitted each year to play during the month in which he had died, and that this custom has been preserved ever since. The authority is Laertius.

Zenonis] Laertius reports that there were eight men named Zeno. Two of them were distinguished philosophers: the first, whom we have mentioned, Zeno of Citium, founder of the Stoic school; the other—the one now under discussion—Zeno of Elea, inventor of dialectic, as we said above.

When this Zeno wished to overthrow and defeat the tyrant Nearchus or Diomedon—or, as others report, Phalaris—he was captured. When his accomplices were being sought, he declared that all his friends were involved in the conspiracy. Then, after indicating that he wished to whisper something into the tyrant’s ear, he seized it with his teeth and did not release it until he had torn away the ear and left the tyrant’s head mutilated.

Valerius Maximus assigns examples of endurance to two Zenons. Laertius and others assign them to one Zeno of Elea. Cicero, in book two of the *Tusculan Disputations*, writes: “Let Zeno of Elea be brought forward, who endured everything rather than reveal the accomplices of the plot to destroy the tyranny.” The same author, in book three of *On the Nature of the Gods*: “We have learned that Anaxarchus the Democritean was tortured to death by a tyrant of Cyprus, and that Zeno of Elea was killed under torture.”

Tertullian, in the *Apologeticus*, writes: “When Zeno of Elea was asked by Dionysius what benefit philosophy provided, he replied, ‘Contempt of death.’ Exposed to the tyrant’s merciless lashes, he maintained his opinion even unto death.”

In Suidas it is written as follows: “Zeno, son of Teleutagoras, an Eleatic, was a follower and contemporary of Pythagoras and Democritus—for he flourished in the seventy-eighth Olympiad—and was a pupil of Xenophanes. When he attempted to free Elea, his homeland, from the tyranny of Nearchus or, as others say, Diomedon, he was captured and ordered to reveal his accomplices. He bit off his own tongue and spat it into the tyrant’s face. Finally, thrown into a mortar, he died after being crushed by repeated blows.”

Peregrina] Foreign and external.

At] “But,” or at least. This particle must be read three times here, instead of the *aut* (“or”) which the unlearned read. Repeated in this way, it gives greater force to the speech.

Canios] Proper names expressed in the plural have greater force in discourse. For they signify not only those who bear the names but also others who were like them.

Canius was a poet from Gades, of gentle and pleasant eloquence. Martial writes of him in book one of the *Epigrams*:

> Gades rejoice in their jocose Canius.

Some report that Livy of Padua, a serious and distinguished historian, reproached him for delighting in the love of many women, in these words:

> You cannot share our philosophy while you are shared by so many. For Tityus does not love Latona with that liver which many vultures tear apart so extensively.

To him Canius replied:

> Whenever I labor, I rise again more cautiously; if I am oppressed a little, I draw breath again more vigorously. The alternations of night make the days more bearable. But perpetual darkness is like hell. Thus the first lilies, delicate in the seasons of spring sunlight, luxuriate in changing variety—now in the joy of the east wind, now of the south wind, now of the west wind—until the thunderous south wind, pressing upon them in a single blast, brings about their setting. Thus Mars, with his snares broken, reclines as a guest of the gods at the heavenly table, while the uxorious Mulciber is kept far off from his own thief. Thus many threads bind less tightly than a single chain. So may philosophy be a consolation to me—and to you.

They say, then, that Canius replied jokingly to Livy in this manner. But let us now return to what concerns the subject undertaken.

Canius, because he dissented from the behavior of wicked men, was accused by Gaius Caesar, son of Germanicus, of having been privy to a conspiracy formed against him. To him he replied:

> If I had known, you would not have known.

Nevertheless, he was cruelly put to death by him. More about this same man in the next prose section.

### “But Senecas”

Marcus Annaeus Seneca of Córdoba came to Rome as an outstanding declaimer, although his works did not survive for posterity. He was immediately made a knight, attained honors, and had children whom he had fathered in Spain by his wife Elbia: Lucius Annaeus Seneca, Junius Annaeus Gallio, and Annaeus Mela. Seneca became at once a philosopher, declaimer, and distinguished poet. He died under Nero, after opening his veins. More will be said about him below. Whether he was the same man who wrote the surviving tragedies remains unsettled among the most learned scholars, although I am not unaware of what Sidonius Apollinaris left written on this subject.

### “But Soranos”

Valerius Soranus was a highly renowned poet. He was the first to write truthfully about the supreme God, and for that reason is believed to have been crucified by impious hands.

### “Very ancient”

Excessively old.

### “Uncelebrated”

Uncommon, not celebrated.

### “Into disaster”

Into ruin.

### “In this sea of life”

That is, in this sea. A very elegant metaphor indeed. For what else is this age but a stormy sea? Saint Ambrose, in his letter to Constantius:

> You have undertaken the office of priesthood, and, seated in the Church’s vessel, you steer the ship against the waves. Hold the rudder of faith, so that the storms of this age may not be able to disturb you. It is indeed a great and spacious sea, but do not be afraid, because he himself founded her upon the seas and prepared her upon the rivers. Therefore, not without reason, amid so many straits of the world, the Church of the Lord, built as it were upon the apostolic rock, remains immovable and perseveres upon an unshaken foundation against the assaults of the raging sea. She is washed by the waves but not shaken.

The sea is called *salum* from the taste of salt. Virgil:

> And through the waves, with the sea rising above them.

### “Of whom”

Of the worst men.

### “Numerous”

Frequent.

### “Rashly”

Without consideration, without counsel, without prudence.

### “Everywhere”

Now here, now there, with no definite end in view.

### “With frenzy raging”

With madness tormenting.

### “With frenzy”

“I torment with madness.” Vale, Sta. Flaccus:

> He had driven the city mad.

Hence those who are called *lymphati* or *lymphatici* are frenzied, insane, and bacchant-like people who have contracted the disorder from water; that disorder consists in running about here and there.

### “Who”

The army of the worst men.

### “Battle line”

The military order and formation prepared for fighting.

### “Arranging”

Drawing up, forming.

### “Our leader”

Right reason; for it is the leader of philosophers.

### “Its forces”

Its army, composed of virtues and branches of knowledge.

### “Into the citadel”

Into the intellect of the soul, which the Platonists place in the brain as in a citadel. He maintains the metaphor beautifully.

### “Collects”

Gathers, assembles.

### “Those men”

The worst enemies of philosophers.

### “Useless little bundles”

External and bodily goods.

### “But”

Yet.

### “From above”

From the citadel of contemplation.

### “The most worthless things”

The goods of the body and of fortune, which, compared with the goods of the soul, are utterly base.

### “Unconcerned”

Having no care, despising them. *Securus* means calm, tranquil, one who is without care, as though set apart from care. Sometimes it means “one who despises.” Maro:

> Unconcerned about the loves  
> of his sister.

### “Rampart”

The fortification of virtues.

### “To which”

To which rampart.

### “Raging”

Advancing while acting savagely.

### “To approach”

To come near, to approach.

### “May not be permitted”

That is, may not be allowed. Valerius Maximus:

> The exercise of a sound mind admits no assault from a more sorrowful fortune.

## ON THE FOURTH METRE

When I was twenty years old and had begun, driven by what Horace calls “bold poverty,” to teach the liberal arts—not unsuccessfully, in the populous and exceedingly splendid Saxon city called Münster—through the good offices of Johann Grovius of Münster, a thoroughly learned man, especially educated in all the liberal disciplines, a most highly praised teacher, and one worthy either of a longer life or of a less pitiable kind of death, several pages of Rudolph Agricola the Frisian came into my hands. They contained autograph commentaries, except for the final poem, on the succeeding part of this first book. Agricola was at once the most learned and the most eloquent of men. He had once written these commentaries at Groningen at the request of Lambert of Groningen, a physician endowed with extraordinary learning and experience, when—as I learned familiarly from his own account—he had begun in his homeland an explanation of the books *On the Consolation of Philosophy* and had reached this poem:

> Whoever, with his age composed and serene...

Thus the most learned Agricola took this as his starting point, intending to treat the remainder at a more suitable time, if other occupations and an untimely death had allowed it.

He wrote rather more on Boethius than came into my possession. The same Lambert whom I have just mentioned had received those writings for me and had promised to lend them so that I might copy them out for myself and for students. He would certainly have lent them very willingly, had not his sudden departure from this life prevented it.

Since what has been transcribed seems to me of such a character that students of Boethius ought by all means to read it, I cannot fail to append it here. I do so lest a credulous reader attribute to me any glory arising from another man’s labor, and lest the most spotless pearl remain any longer hidden without honor in my gem case. In some places I shall add my own observations, whatever their quality, and only briefly sketched, lest excessive length produce weariness and nausea in a delicate reader.

### “Whoever, with his age composed”

The metre is an hendecasyllable, that is, a verse of eleven syllables. It is a Phalaecian, named after its author Phalaecus, a pentameter consisting of a spondee, a dactyl, and three trochees.

Its meaning depends upon what Philosophy had previously said in the person of the wise man: that he is safe and defended by a fortification of virtues which no force or injury inflicted by foolish or wicked men can breach. He therefore adds:

Whoever has rightly composed his soul and despised the accidents of human affairs can thereafter be disturbed in spirit or moved in mind by nothing: neither dangers of the sea, earthquakes or fires, whirlwinds or disturbances of the air, nor even human savagery or violence. He neglects everything and considers it nothing.

By contrast, whoever does not possess a composed and steadfast spirit, but fears or desires something, because he is not his own master but depends upon fear of another’s evil or hope of another’s good, has thrown away his shield—that is, the defense of his virtue. Driven from the place where he stood and which he ought to have defended, he fastens a chain by which he may be dragged; that is, he provides a way by which harm may be done to him. For, according to the Stoic doctrine, no one is harmed except by himself.

Others may indeed harm our possessions—that is, our wealth, honors, reputation, and other things of this kind—but they cannot harm us, that is, our mind, which is the finest part of us.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Whoever”

That is, “anyone.” Words of this kind, when doubled, signify the same thing as when joined with the particle *-cunque*. Thus Terence in the *Eunuch*:

> However great you are,

that is, “as great as you may be”; and in the same comedy:

> Wherever he is,

that is, “wherever he may be.”

**AGRICOLA**

### “Composed”

*Componere* sometimes means to arrange or establish rightly, as here; and Virgil says in the first book of the *Aeneid*:

> And at last, composed in peaceful calm, he rests.

Sometimes it means to pacify. Virgil in the *Eclogues*:

> It is not ours to settle such great quarrels among you.

Sometimes it means to compare. The same poet in the *Eclogues*:

> Thus I used to compare great things with small.

Sometimes it means to join together. Persius:

> Right and wrong composed in the mind.

We likewise say *componere librum*, “to compose a book,” and *componere ignem*, “to bank a fire.”

**AGRICOLA**

### “Serene”

It is derived from *serere*, “to sow,” as though referring to a time suited to sowing. For *serenum* properly describes the weather, just as *amoenum* means what is suited to being loved, *egenum* comes from *egere*, “to lack,” and *plenum* from *plere*, an obsolete verb.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Age”

It comes from the Greek αἰών (*aiōn*), which in Latin means *saeculum*, “an age.” Some hold that it is a period of fifty years, others of one hundred. Here it is understood by synecdoche as the life we live.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Fate”

It is so called because God *fatus est* it—that is, spoke it, meaning that he commanded it to happen.

**AGRICOLA**

### “He gave beneath the feet”

It should be read *dedit*, not *egit*, as most books have it. Otherwise the verse will not stand, since its third foot must be a trochee; if it is *egit* rather than *dedit*, it becomes an iamb.

Boethius ought to have said *sub pedes dedit*, “he placed beneath the feet,” not *pedibus*, because of the nature of the preposition joined to a verb signifying motion toward a place. It should therefore be read figuratively, so that *sub* and *dedit* form one expression, with *pedibus* inserted by the figure called *tmesis* in Latin; thus it is *sub pedibus dedit*, that is, *subdidit pedibus*, “he subjected it to the feet.”

**AGRICOLA**

### “Fortune”

*Fortuna* comes from *fors*, which itself comes from *ferre*, “to bear,” because fortune bears—that is, drives and governs—human affairs.

We use *fortuna* in the singular either for a goddess, as antiquity believed, or for chance, by which human affairs are rolled about in unstable and uncertain ways. In the plural, however, *fortunae* means the goods of fortune, especially divine gifts.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Countenance”

*Vultus* differs from *facies*. *Facies* is the natural appearance implanted in each thing. *Vultus* is changed by joy or sadness, just as the will is; for *vultus* derives from the verb *velle*, “to wish.”

*Facies* comes from *facere*, “to make,” because a thing is so made. We speak not only of the face of a human being but also of the face of an animal or a place—that is, its form or shape. *Vultus* belongs to human beings alone.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Pontus”

Among poets it is generally taken by synecdoche for the sea. Properly, it is a certain part of the sea situated beyond Constantinople, which sailors today call the Sea of Leo; from it the neighboring peoples are called Pontic.

The name is Greek, *pontus*, supposedly derived from “laborious,” because it is always agitated by storms; for in Greek πόνος (*ponos*) means “labor.”

**AGRICOLA**

### “Heat”

*Aestus*, from which *aestas*, “summer,” is derived, means heat. Hence Latin authors also call the movement of the sea produced by ebb and flow *aestus*, because the sea appears to boil and seethe. Pliny therefore called an estuary *aestuarium*, a place into which the sea’s tide pours.

I would also believe that the word for what we now barbarously call a *stufa*, following the sound of the German language, has been corrupted and distorted from *aestuarium*. Pliny called it a *caldarium*. Where we bathe, the proper term is *balneum*.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Furnace”

It comes from the Greek καίομαι (*kaiomai*), “I burn.” Martial called it *fumarium* in Latin. Here it is taken metaphorically for the cavern or hollow through which Vesuvius emits flames.

Vesuvius is a mountain in Campania, not far from Naples, always burning. Sometimes it is stirred and swells with such heat that all the neighboring regions are shaken by immense earthquakes and the fields are covered with ashes.

There is also another mountain of immense height in the Alps, called *Vesulus*, not *Vesevus*, as some ignorant writers say.

**AGRICOLA**

### “High”

It comes from *cello*, an obsolete verb, from which *percello*, *excello*, and *antecello* are derived.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Tower”

It is said to be called *turris*, as though from *terris*, “to terrify,” because it terrifies enemies.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Thunderbolt”

Just as *fulgur*, “lightning,” is derived from *fulgere*, “to shine.”

**AGRICOLA**

### “Tyrants”

In Greek it means “ruler.” Hence Virgil wrote in Book VII of the *Aeneid*:

> It will be a part of my peace to have touched the tyrant’s right hand.

But because the Greeks always desired to be free and without kings, the name *tyrant* came to be regarded among them—and consequently among everyone—as something detestable.

**AGRICOLA**

### “You will disarm”

For *exarmabis*, “you will disarm.” Priscian generally seems to take the subjunctive as an indicative in passages of this kind, although perhaps it is more correctly interpreted as “you will be able to disarm” or “it is possible for you to disarm.”

**AGRICOLA**

### “Powerless”

*Impotens* is generally used in a bad sense. It does not mean the same as weak or feeble, but rather one who is not master of himself, as people commonly are when placed in great fortune.

Thus Pliny says in his letters:

> I know how uncontrolled love always is.

We likewise say *impatient of love* and *impatient of anger*, not because someone does not suffer them, but because he does not suffer them properly.

**AGRICOLA**

### “He threw away his shield and was moved from his place”

This is a periphrasis, that is, a circumlocution for a deserter who abandons the position assigned to him in the battle line by his commander.

According to the discipline of ancient warfare, it was not permitted to leave one’s position except for the purpose of striking the enemy, saving a fellow citizen, or recovering a weapon. By saying “he threw away his shield,” he alludes to the Greek word for deserter, ῥίψασπις (*rhipsaspis*), that is, “thrower-away of the shield.”

**AGRICOLA**

The metre which Agricola and many others call Phalaecian is more commonly called *Palaecian*, with the diphthong *ae*. Some call it *Phalecine*, others *Phalcutic*. But one must be very careful not to call it *falencium* with an *n*, as ignorant people do.

### “Serene”

Free from the clouds of disturbances, just as, at the end of this poem, the mind is called cloudy when covered by depraved affections. Ovid:

> Poems arise, drawn from a serene mind.

Marsilio Ficino, in Book 12 of Plotinus *On Happiness*:

> The good man is always serene; his state is tranquil and his disposition self-sufficient. Provided that he is truly good, none of the things called evils disturbs him at all.

### “Fate”

What fate is is explained below, in Book IV. Here, however, understand by *fate* the things that come from fate.

He seems to have imitated Virgil’s words in Book II of the *Georgics*:

> Happy is he who has been able to learn the causes of things,
>
> and has placed beneath his feet all fears and inexorable fate,
>
> together with the roar of greedy Acheron.

And these words of Seneca the tragedian, in the *Hercules Oetaeus*:

> Whoever has placed rapacious fates beneath his feet,
>
> and his vessel beneath the final light,
>
> will not offer captive arms to chains,
>
> nor will he come to the noble litter of pomp.

Likewise these elegant verses of the same author, in the tragedy entitled *Thyestes*:

> He is king who has laid aside fears,
>
> and the evils of a dreadful heart;
>
> whom neither uncontrolled ambition,
>
> nor never-stable popular favor,
>
> moves—the favor of the rushing crowd;
>
> whom nothing that the setting sun digs up,
>
> nor whatever the golden Tagus
>
> carries down in its bright channel,
>
> nor whatever the burning threshing floor
>
> of Libya grinds beneath its harvests,
>
> will disturb;
>
> whom neither the falling path
>
> of the slanting thunderbolt,
>
> nor the east wind carrying off the sea,
>
> nor the swelling of windy Adriatic,
>
> swift upon the savage strait,
>
> will shake;
>
> whom neither a soldier’s spear
>
> nor drawn steel has subdued;
>
> who, established in a secure place,
>
> sees everything beneath him,
>
> and willingly meets his fate,
>
> nor complains of dying.

### “He did”

It is entirely satisfactory to agree with Agricola that *dedit*, “he gave,” should be restored, so that the verse may scan.

### “Both fortunes”

Both prosperous and adverse fortune.

### “Gazing upon”

Looking upon, observing.

### “Upright”

Unbent. Cleobulus:

> While prosperous fortune smiles, do not become proud; when adversity roars, do not be broken. Learn to endure the changes of fortune bravely.

Periander:

> In prosperity be moderate; in adversity be prudent.

### “Unconquered”

Steadfast, not yielding to the changes of fortune.

### “Frenzy will not shake him, etc.”

Horace says similarly in Book III of the *Odes*:

> The just man, firm in his purpose,
>
> is not shaken in his steadfast mind
>
> by the ardor of citizens commanding wicked things,
>
> nor by the face of an urgent tyrant;
>
> nor by the turbulent leader
>
> of restless Adriatic,
>
> nor by the great hand of thunder-bearing Jupiter.
>
> If the world, shattered, should fall upon him,
>
> its ruins will strike him without fear.

### “Stirring up”

This should be read *excitantis*, as Rudolphus Langius quite correctly holds, not *exagitantis*, as it is commonly read in corrupted copies contrary to the metre.

### “Vesuvius”

This mountain is near Naples, in Campania. Having changed its former name, it is called *Summa*. It once erupted, as Pliny reports in his letters, and as Suetonius and Eusebius record. Under the emperor Titus it emitted such a fire that it burned the neighboring regions and cities together with their inhabitants.

Saint Jerome writes in one of his letters:

> For neither fires, nor the land of Vulcan, nor Vesuvius and Olympus, blaze with such heat that youthful marrow, filled with wine and inflamed by banquets, could rival them.

It is also called *Vesuvius*, whence *Vesuvian*. Papinius:

> The Vesuvian summit and the fiery winter
>
> of the dreadful mountain did not so completely empty
>
> the trembling cities of their inhabitants.

### “High lands”

Horace:

> More often the huge pine is shaken by the winds,
>
> and lofty towers fall with heavier ruin,
>
> while lightning strikes the highest mountains.

### “Savage tyrants”

This should be read *feros*, “savage,” not *saevos*, “fierce,” as Rudolphus Langius replied twelve years ago, when I consulted him, that he had read it in a certain copy.

### “He threw away his shield”

Philostratus, Book II, reports that Apollonius spoke as follows to his companion Damis:

> If, persuaded by your arguments, I accepted money of this kind, would you not call me greedy and contemptuous of philosophy, and even worse than soldiers who throw away their shields in battle? For a man who throws away his shield can be given another no worse than the first, as Archilochus says; but how can philosophy be recovered by one who has once despised or cast it away?

Horace says in his *Epistles*:

> He has lost his arms and abandoned the place of virtue who
>
> is always eager for and overwhelmed by the accumulation of wealth.

This is a metaphor taken from military affairs. For it was considered especially disgraceful for a soldier either to abandon his place in the battle line or to allow his weapons to be taken from him while he was still alive.

## ON THE FOURTH PROSE

### “Do you perceive?” he said

Here Boethius, proceeding in a certain order toward the consolation of his misfortunes, explains and laments his own situation and shows how unjust and grievous an adversity of fortune he is suffering, since he has been condemned most unjustly.

That this was indeed the case is gathered from every aspect of the matter: first from his own person, then from the persons of the accusers, afterward from the charges falsely or unjustly brought against him; next from the persons of the judges and the senate; further from the manner of the trial; then from the false charge fabricated against him, whether of magic or of the worship of the gods.

Finally, by way of an epilogue, he shows not only that these charges were gravely fabricated against him, but also that they were believed by the ignorant and accepted as true, and that similar danger thereafter threatened all good men because of what had happened to him. Each part will be discussed in its proper place.

First, then, Philosophy, in order to draw out Boethius’ complaint and elicit from him the cause of his grief, asks him, in the customary manner of dialogues, whether he understands what she herself said above, and also urges him to state clearly what he is suffering.

Boethius then begins by saying that words are unnecessary, since she can easily perceive from the appearance of the place—that is, the prison in which he was—the cause of his grief. This has happened to him all the more indignantly because he had entered public administration as though at Philosophy’s command and had endeavored to conduct everything in it according to justice and goodness, fearing no one’s hatred.

He therefore says that he had always opposed Conigastus, Tergulla, and the other barbarians, so that they might not everywhere oppress the weaker according to their own pleasure. He likewise says that he defended Campania from destruction, when, during a time of famine, the prefect of the praetorium wanted to purchase all the grain.

In the same way, he says that he defended Paulinus and Albinus, men of consular rank, from the injustice of their accusers. By these actions, because of his love of justice, he stirred up against himself the hatred of wicked men.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Do you perceive?”

*Sentire* properly means to perceive something through one of the five senses. It is generally transferred to the perception of every kind of knowledge. Thus Juvenal says:

> What I cannot show, but only perceive,

that is, “only understand.”

Sometimes it means “to judge.” Persius:

> What do you think of Jupiter?

That is, “What is your judgment?” Juvenal:

> What do you suppose all people think, Calvinus,
>
> about your recent crime?

**AGRICOLA**

### “Slip into”

He speaks elegantly; there is a double metaphor. Both “words slip in” and “slip into the mind” are metaphorical expressions, since literally it is a bodily object that slips.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Ἄρα εἶ ὄνος πρὸς λύραν”

This is a Greek proverb commonly used among them of people whose uneducated minds are poorly suited to understanding what is said. It means:

> Are you an ass before a lyre?

**AGRICOLA**

### “Why do you weep?”

That is, “Why are you sad?” or “Why do you laugh?” This is said by *ellipsis*, that is, by omitting or lacking the preposition *propter*, so that the full expression would be *propter quid fles?*, “on account of what do you weep?”

**AGRICOLA**

### “You flow with tears”

Similarly, our Jerome said of Livy:

> Flowing with the milky river of eloquence.

Horace speaks differently of wine in his *Epistles*:

> Which, remaining with rich hope,
>
> flows into my veins and my spirit.

And in the same work:

> Although many a tear flows for him.

Again, in the same work:

> For you trust that poetic honey flows.

Thus one may apparently say: *mano lacrymis*, “I flow with tears”; *manant mihi lacrymae*, “tears flow for me”; and *mano lacrymas*, “I flow tears.”

**AGRICOLA**

### “Ἐξομολόγησαί τε σὲ λυπεῖ”

That is:

> Confess what is troubling you.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Labor”

Terence seems to explain most conveniently the distinction between *opus* and *opera* in the *Heautontimorumenos*:

> If you spend any labor on making the work...

Thus *opera* is labor, while *opus* is the product and completion of the labor—that is, its result.

Horace in the first book of the *Epistles*:

> And diligently bring hatred upon your little books
>
> through vehement labor, as a servant.

Virgil in the first book of the *Aeneid*:

> The interrupted work hangs unfinished.

**AGRICOLA**

### “You expect”

*Exspectare* sometimes means “to desire.” Cicero, in a letter to Curio:

> You have stirred up such expectation of yourself that you must be able to satisfy it.

Sometimes it means “to attend to.” Ovid, in Book III of the *Metamorphoses*:

> The final day must always be awaited
>
> by a human being.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Wound”

That is, something caused by violence and still recent. Virgil in Book XII:

> No one boasted to Aeneas of his wound.

An *ulcus* is a sore that has become putrid through age; a wound turns into an *ulcus* through long duration, as Seneca correctly explained in his consolation to Marcia:

> For wounds too are easily healed while they are fresh with blood.

He adds:

> When they have become corrupted and turned into a malignant sore, they are cured with greater difficulty.

What we commonly call an *ulcus*, which the Greeks call an *apostema*, is called in Latin a *furunculus*. Pliny in his letters seems to have called it a *clavus*, “a boil.” He says:

> A malignant, incurable boil will be born for him.

It is still called *clavus* in French.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Strength”

In the singular, *vis* also signifies strength. Sallust in the *Catiline*:

> With great strength of mind and body.

It also signifies violence. Martial in Book VI:

> I am not accused of violence, murder, or poison.

In the plural, *vires* signifies strength alone. Cornelius Tacitus, however, used the genitive *vis* in his book *On the Causes of Corrupted Eloquence*, *magnae vis*, “of great strength,” by which he seems to show that the singular can be declined through all its cases.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Stands out”

Here it is used for “appears,” although *eminere* properly means to project above other things. It derives from *e-* and *manere*, “to remain.” Virgil in the first book of the *Aeneid*:

> Advancing, she towers above all the goddesses.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Of the raging one”

*Saevire* sometimes means “to be cruel.” Juvenal:

> Accustomed to rage against the chorus and the court with whips.

Sometimes it means “not to tolerate a ruler.” Livy in Book XXI:

> If ever the beasts should rage.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Harshness”

That which is *asperum*, “harsh,” is so called because it is without hope, just as *prosperum*, “prosperous,” is what turns out *pro spe*, “according to hope.” Both words derive from *sperare*, “to hope.”

**AGRICOLA**

### “Is this...?”

As Servius says in his commentary on Donatus, the ancients used *hicce*, *haecce*, and *hocce*. From this, with *e* changed into *i*, *hiccine* is used for *hicne*.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Library”

A repository of books. In Greek, βίβλιον (*biblion*) means “book,” and θήκη (*thēkē*) means “repository.” Therefore the books of both Testaments ought not to be called *Biblia*, *Bibliae*, since that word is neither Greek nor Latin, but *Biblia*, *-orum*, from the word *biblion*.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Seat”

Properly, we call the place in which someone sits a *sedes*. Sallust in the *Catiline*:

> They wandered under Aeneas as their leader, uncertain of their settlements.

Virgil in the first book of the *Aeneid*:

> Where the fates reveal peaceful seats.

The object on which we sit is more correctly called a *sella*, “chair.” Virgil in Book IV:

> The throne and the robe, the insignia of our rule.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Household gods”

A *lar* is a household god, also called a *penates*, either because they preside over the pantry (*penus*) or because they are worshiped deep within the house.

Virgil in Book IV of the *Aeneid*:

> And the household gods scattered by fraternal slaughter.

Plautus in the *Aulularia*:

> I am the household Lar of this family.

Juvenal:

> The Galli do not dare to let a crest grow
>
> for the household gods.

Here it is also taken by synecdoche for “house.” Horace in the first book of the *Epistles*:

> Rejoicing in his wicked companions and his secure home.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Appearance”

Not properly clothing, as it is commonly understood, but the whole outward form of a person into which he has composed himself. Pliny in his letters:

> Composed in the appearance of a student.

Hence Terence says in the *Eunuch*:

> If a woman is somewhat more substantial, they call her a boxer,

that is, somewhat more corpulent.

Cicero in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*:

> If such power exists in forming the mind in those things which are produced in the body.

**AGRICOLA**

### “I might search out”

That is, “as though I were carefully searching through cracks.”

**AGRICOLA**

### “Star”

Some wish it to be written with Greek *y*. I believe it is Latin, derived from *sidere*, “to settle,” because it is firmly seated in the heavens.

*Stella* and *sidus* differ. *Stella* is said to be like a drop (*stilla*), a single individual heavenly light. Virgil in the first book of the *Georgics*:

> Where the cold star of Saturn withdraws.

But *sidus* is sometimes used for a star. Lucan in Book I:

> And the salutary star
>
> of Venus grows dim.

Sometimes it means a constellation composed of many stars, such as the constellation of Aries, Taurus, and the others. Virgil in the *Eclogues*:

> Let us turn the sheep of the Ethiopians beneath the constellation of Cancer.

*Astrum* is Greek and means “constellation,” just as ἀστήρ (*astēr*) means “star.”

**AGRICOLA**

### “Radius”

I think it is used for what we call a compass, by analogy with the spokes of a wheel, which we also call *radii*. Virgil in the *Eclogues*:

> He described with a compass the whole world for the nations.

Cicero:

> I shall raise the old man for you from the dust and the compass.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Pattern”

It derives from *eximere*, “to take out,” because something is taken from it. An *exemplar* is the thing according to whose likeness something is made. An *exemplum*, however, is the likeness itself that is reproduced.

**AGRICOLA**

### “That they would be blessed, etc.”

This statement of Plato, celebrated by everyone, is gathered from the book entitled the *First Alcibiades*. *Fore*, *confore*, and *affore* always have future meaning. Horace in the first book of the *Satires*:

> Nor should he say that henceforth he will be
>
> so accommodating.

*Forem*, “I would be,” has the same meaning as *essem*, “I were.”

**AGRICOLA**

### “Public”

That is, *populicas*, “belonging to the people”; this is what we call public.

**AGRICOLA**

### “To be devoted to”

It means “to favor,” and is sometimes joined with the dative. Horace in the first book of the *Epistles*:

> Lest you offend through excessive devotion to us.

That is, “through favor.”

Sometimes it means “to endeavor.” Terence in the *Eunuch*:

> While I endeavor to restore your sister to you.

There it is joined with the accusative.

Sometimes it means “to study” or “to learn.” Cicero in Book V of *On the Ends of Good and Evil*:

> Or that very thing which he studies to do, he may do more elegantly.

Thus it is used indifferently with both the accusative and the dative.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Authority”

*Autoritas* properly means the more honorable or dignified opinion held about someone, through which he can easily persuade or dissuade others. It is related to *auctor*, “author,” whose origin different writers explain in various ways.

Some say it should be written with *c*, from *augeo*, “to increase,” although this scarcely suits the nature of the noun. Others derive it from the Greek αὐτόν, meaning “itself,” but this seems too remote a derivation. Others derive it from elsewhere.

To me it seems that it should be written without *c*. Just as *faveo* has the perfect participle *fautum*, so *aveo*, “to desire,” would have *autum*, though the form has fallen out of use. From this, *autor* seems to descend, since an author is one who desires a thing to be done—that is, wishes it.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Magistrate”

*Magistratus* and *magisterium* differ. *Magistratus* means authority; *magisterium* means an art or craft.

Among the ancients, *conscius* and *conscientia* generally had a bad meaning. Juvenal:

> Who is loved now except the guilty?

Horace in the first book of the *Epistles*:

> To have no guilty awareness and to grow pale at no fault.

Sallust in the *Jugurtha*:

> Lest anyone turn modesty into guilt.

By contrast, Virgil says:

> Virtue conscious of itself;

and Quintilian, speaking of a mother’s disgrace:

> The heedless simplicity of a good conscience.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Weak”

As though “without a staff,” that is, without support or strength.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Calumnies”

Priscian says that *calumnia* derives from the old verb *calvo*, “I deceive.” It signifies sometimes a false accusation and sometimes the harassment of someone in lawsuits through fraud and frustration.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Barbarians”

The Greeks used to divide the whole human race into barbarians and Greeks. Later, the Italians too were removed from the category of barbarians because of their refinement and learning.

Christian writers commonly now use “barbarians” for pagans.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Tributes”

A *vectigal* is a tax, so called because it is paid on goods that are transported. Usage established the word first for every kind of tax and then for every kind of census or revenue. Hence land from which revenues are collected is called *vectigalis*, “tax-bearing.”

**AGRICOLA**

### “Campania”

The name is derived from the city of Capua; a citizen is called *Campanus*. Hence *Campania* means everything that was once under the authority of Capua.

A *province* is a region conquered by the Romans which, after its own princes or magistrates had been removed, was governed under Roman magistrates and laws. Thus Suetonius says in his *Life of Tiberius*:

> He also reduced his kingdom to the form of a province.

It is called *provincia* as though from *porro victa*, “thoroughly conquered.”

**AGRICOLA**

### “Of the praetorium”

In a military camp, *praetorium* means the place where the commander pitched his tent; hence, in cities, it means the place where a praetor or chief magistrate publicly resided.

The prefect of the praetorium was the man who occupied the praetorium in the emperor’s place and was in command of the soldiers.

We call a man *consularis* if he had been consul. At Rome two consuls were always elected for each year. They presided over the senate, that is, the public council; anyone who belonged to it was called a senator.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Palatine dogs”

He calls the greedy ministers of the palace “Palatine dogs.”

**AGRICOLA**

### “Ambition”

Here he uses the word in its proper sense, which is expressed by its etymology, not in the way it is commonly understood by Latin speakers.

*Ambitio* means desire for office, because those who sought honors and magistracies went around among the citizens, visiting and canvassing them and asking for their support. Hence *ambitus* means what the common people today call simony.

Here he used the word because the men were going around among the judges and buying judgments.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Courtiers”

Properly, we call those who live in the halls of princes *aulici*; today, in barbarous usage, they are called *curiales*.

Virgil in Book II of the *Georgics*:

> They enter the halls and thresholds of kings.

For *curia* comes from *cura*, “care,” and means the place where a public council is held.

**AGRICOLA**

### “Are you an ass before a lyre?”

This is how it is read in a copy which the very learned Johann Caesarius lent me. It means:

> Are you an ass before a lyre?

In the margin of that copy the following is written:

> ἢ πρὸς λύραν ὄνος τελεῖς,

that is:

> Are you an ass before a lyre?

In a letter sent to me by Aedicollius, the phrase is:

> Ἀν εἶ ὄνος λύρας?

Supply *ἀκροάτης*, “listener”: “Are you an ass listening to a lyre?”

Rudolphus Agricola wrote the Greek in Latin letters, perhaps because the person for whose use he was writing did not know Greek.

The words are:

> Ἄρα εἶ ὄνος πρὸς λύραν,

that is:

> Are you an ass before a lyre?

This proverb is used of those who are dull-witted, thick-eared, and entirely lacking in judgment, so that they understand little of what is said.

Saint Jerome, in his letter to Marcella:

> For a lyre sings uselessly to an ass.

The same author, against Vigilantius:

> Although I shall act foolishly if I seek a teacher of teachers and try to impose a limit upon one who does not know how to speak and cannot remain silent.

The Greek proverb is:

> Ὄνος λύρας.

Lucian, *On Those Who Serve for Pay*:

> What business has an ass with a lyre?

> ἐξαύδα, μὴ κεῦθε νόῳ.

In Caesarius’ little book these Greek words occur, and they are interpreted as:

> Speak out; do not hide it in your mind.

The letter which Aedicollius sent me has:

> Ἐξηγέου ἐμοὶ, ἐν μὲν ἀδήλῳ τίθεσθαι οὐ πείθω,

which may be interpreted:

> Explain it to me; I do not advise placing it among uncertain things.

Rudolphus read the following Greek:

> Ἐξομολόγησαι, τί σε λυπεῖ,

that is:

> Confess what is troubling you.

**Library**—in Greek, βιβλιοθήκη (*bibliothēkē*), a repository of books. [Col. 0919A] For βίβλος (*biblos*) means papyrus, reed, codex, book, or silk. Some write it with υ, especially Theodore Gaza. There is also Βύβλος, a city of Phoenicia, which is always written with υ. Most assert that the distinction is that βίβλος, meaning a book or codex, is written with ι, through the change of one variable-length vowel into another, as Isaacius testifies in his interpretation of Lycophron. By diminutive formation, in the neuter gender, βιβλίον (*biblion*) means a volume or little book. θήκη (*thēkē*) in Latin means *theca*, sheath, tomb, coffin, or repository. M. Tullius, in Book XIII of the *Letters to Friends*: “My slave Dionysius, who had charge of my library, worth many thousands of coins, fled when he had stolen many books and thought that he would not get away with it unpunished.” In Latin it is called *libraria*, a name also used for a place where books for sale are stored. Aulus [Col. 0919B] Gellius, in Book V, chapter 4, of the *Attic Nights*: “By chance, at the *Sigillaria*, I and the poet L. Paulus, the most learned man of his generation, were sitting in a bookshop.”

**According to the model of the heavenly order**—For just as heavenly things are directed by the most certain order, remain constant in perpetual regularity, and are preserved in the highest harmony, so in a human being the body must be subjected to the rule of the mind, the appetites governed by right reason, and in everything convenience, order, proportion, and harmony must be carefully observed.

**That states would be blessed**—Valerius Maximus, in Book VII: “A judgment bound to Plato’s words, but surpassing them in meaning: he declared that the world would at last be happy when either the wise began to rule or rulers began to become wise.” Julius Capitolinus [Col. 0919C], in the *Life of Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher*, Roman emperor: “Plato’s judgment was always on his lips: cities flourish if either philosophers rule or emperors philosophize.” Prudentius, in his speech against the orator Symmachus:

> Surely some very learned man would rightly say:
>
> “The commonwealth would then be sufficiently fortunate,
>
> if either kings were wise or the wise were kings.”

**With the mouth of that same man**—There exists a letter of Plato to Archytas of Tarentum, which Marsilius Ficino interpreted in the following way:

> Plato wishes Archytas of Tarentum well.
>
> The companions of Archippus and Philonides came to us, bringing the letter you had given them and reporting what was appropriate concerning your affairs. They conducted the public business of the city without difficulty. It was not particularly burdensome. But they reported that you were greatly troubled because you could not free yourself from the public duties of the city. It is clear to nearly everyone that the sweetest kind of life is to attend to one’s own affairs, especially if one has chosen to undertake matters such as those you have chosen. But you must also consider that none of us is born for himself alone: part of our origin belongs to our country, part to our parents, and part to our friends. Moreover, many things occur to us according to the changing times, and our life is occupied by them. Since your country itself calls you to govern the state, it would perhaps be absurd not to obey, especially when it also happens that access to public office is left open to wicked men, who approach public affairs without any regard for what is best in the state. [Col. 0919D]
>
> [Col. 0920A]
>
> Enough about these matters for now. At present we are caring for Checrates, and we shall continue to do so in the future, both for your sake and for that of his father Phrynion, and also on account of the young man himself.

**By whom they were brought forward**—He gathers the seriousness of the case from the unworthiness of the accusers. Basil, after being dismissed from the king’s household, was compelled by poverty to accuse him. Opilio and Gaudentius, although ordered into exile on account of their crimes and afterward protected themselves by the shelter of sacred places, were again ordered by the king to leave the city of Ravenna by a fixed day, or else their foreheads would be branded. Yet on that very day on which the king had issued this order, when the accusers were declaring that they were accusing Boethius, he himself was made the defendant, and they were heard. What, then, could have happened more disgracefully [Col. 0920B] than that Boethius had not deserved to be accused and those men were unworthy to accuse him? **AGRICOLA.**

**Brought forward**—*Deferre* properly means “to bring” or “carry.” Virgil, in Book IV of the *Aeneid*:

> The same impious rumor  
> carried word to the frenzied woman  
> that the fleet was being armed.

Then, through customary usage, the verb was twisted into a worse meaning, so that it signifies accusing someone and secretly charging him. Juvenal:

> The Stoic informer killed Boreas, his friend.

**Struck**—It would be better to read *perculsi*, “shaken” or “stricken.” Thus Cornelius Tacitus: “When Seneca had been stricken, it was easy to diminish Senio Rufus.” **AGRICOLA.**

**Service**—*Servitium* and *ministerium* differ. *Servitium*, like *servitus*, signifies a condition of life in which someone loses his freedom. [Col. 0920C] Tibullus:

> Here I see slavery prepared for me, and a mistress;
>
> farewell now to that ancestral freedom of mine.

*Ministerium*, however, means every service that is provided either for pay or under any other condition. **AGRICOLA.**

**Another’s debt**—Among the ancients, *aes alienum* was called a debt. Hence Horace, in Book II of the *Epistles*:

> I am poor in my own money.

As if he had said: “I have little money—that is, cash—but I have no *aes alienum*, that is, I am indebted to no one.” **AGRICOLA.**

**Frauds**—Sometimes *fraus* means malicious deceit, that is, deception. Virgil, in Book VI:

> and fraud attached to the client.

Sometimes it means an offense, as here. Pliny, in Book I of the *Natural History*: “It was no offense to anyone, in whatever way he might be able, to worship the gods.” [Col. 0920D] **AGRICOLA.**
