**Censure**—Properly, this signifies the office held by a censor. There were two censors at Rome, who were in charge of the census of the people—that is, of counting the Roman citizens—and of assessing each person’s census, that is, his wealth, as well as of public morals. Hence they were also called “guardians of morals.” Thus Juvenal:

> Censure pardons the ravens and harasses the doves.

There, however, the word is used by synecdoche for the censors; here likewise, by synecdoche, it means the censor’s investigation or judgment. **AGRICOLA.**

**Buildings**—*Aedes* in the singular is used for a sacred building. Thus the ancients said *aedes Vestae*, “the temple of Vesta,” and *aedes Concordiae*, “the temple of Concord.” [Col. 0921A] In the plural, however, it is used only when it signifies a house; and only the houses of noblemen are called *aedes*. I believe both expressions arose because temples and the houses of nobles are elevated, that is, high. **AGRICOLA.**

**In the city of Ravenna**—This is contrary to the rule of our grammarians, who teach that in an apposition the more general term must always come first. Here, however, *urbe*, “city,” which is the more general term, follows. **AGRICOLA.**

**Marked on their foreheads with brands**—This is a Greek figure of speech. It would nevertheless have been expressed more correctly and significantly if he had said *frontibus notis insigniti*, “marked with brands on their foreheads.” For *nota*, since it signifies the instrument of the verb *insigniti*, “marked,” ought properly to be joined with it in the ablative. Moreover, *insignitus frontem*, “marked as to the forehead,” just as *albus pedem*, “white as to the foot,” and *flavus comam*, “yellow as to the hair,” would have been more customary and intelligible. **AGRICOLA.**

[Col. 0921B] **Severity**—*Severus* is interpreted as though it meant “following the truth,” whose proper opposite is indulgence. Hence elsewhere too he praises judges as severe, just as he praises them as holy. Horace:

> I shall entrust the fountain of Libo’s Forum
>
> to the sober, and I shall forbid singing to the severe.

*Astrui*, “to be joined,” comes from *ad* and *struo*. **AGRICOLA.**

**Undertaken**—It would have been more suitable to say *accepta*, “accepted.” For informers properly *undertake*—that is, take on or sustain—an accusation; a judge is more correctly said to accept it. **AGRICOLA.**

**Arts**—*Artes* is sometimes understood as morals. Juvenal:

> When, he says, there is no place in the city
>
> for honorable arts.

Sometimes it means branches of learning, as in Juvenal:

[Col. 0921C]

> dividing the art of Theodorus.

And Terence:

> Whatever happens to fall, correct it by skill.

Sometimes it means cunning or deceit. Ovid, in Book I of the *Art of Love*:

> Then simplicity, now exceedingly rare in our age,
>
> opens minds, while God drives out deceit.

**Was Fortune then ashamed of nothing?**—“Was Fortune ashamed of no matter whatsoever?” *Nihil puduit* is a Greek-style expression. Thus, as Priscian testifies, Terence in the *Adelphoe*, following Greek usage, said:

> whom nothing shames at all.

And again:

> Alas for me, are you not ashamed of this?

**If not**—Supply: “if Fortune was not ashamed.” **Of my innocence**—Supply: “of my innocence.”

[Col. 0921D] **But of the baseness of the accusers**—This is the correct reading found in corrected copies; supply: “she would have been ashamed of it.”

**Baseness**—Wickedness and impurity. “Of the accusers,” that is, of those who accused me.

**But of what crime are we accused?**—Here he demonstrates the disgracefulness of the condemnation from the charges brought against him by the accusers up to this point. This extends to the words, “But let it be granted that wicked men …” He therefore sets forth two charges. One was that he was said to have prevented a messenger from carrying to the king a letter containing the information that the senate was taking a position against the king, so that on this account the senate might be charged with treason against the king’s majesty. The second charge was that he was said to have written letters containing the claim that he was attempting [Col. 0922A] to restore the Roman people to freedom. He answers each in order.

First he admits the charge, but says that he acted rightly. He denies the second. Thus he diminishes and disdains the charge brought against him. “What sort of crime,” he says, “is being brought against me, if you wish to know its substance—that is, the whole matter summed up in a few words? This is our crime: we are said to have wished the senate not to be condemned. If you wish to know how we did this, we are said to have prevented the man who was going to the king from carrying to the king the documents and proofs by which he was attempting to show that the senate had violated the king’s majesty.”

The Philosopher therefore asks Philosophy what she commands: whether he ought to deny this in order to remain safe and avoid bringing any [Col. 0922B] disgrace upon Philosophy in his own person. But he says that he wished to do this and always wishes to do so. If, on the other hand, he admits it, the informer will now accomplish what he intended and cannot be prevented from prosecuting him.

He then adds that it was right that he had wished the senate to be safe. Although the senate, by its decrees—that is, its enactments—had deserved so badly of him that he should no longer, with good reason, wish for its safety, nevertheless the senate’s folly, by which it had ruled badly concerning him, could not alter the merits of the matter: that is, it could not make what was rightly done become wrong because of its own unjust judgment. Moreover, from the customary bonds of fellowship, he thought it impermissible for him to say anything other than what the facts were.

Nevertheless, whether these things were rightly or wrongly done, other learned and wise men must judge, because he left behind a written account of the matter, [Col. 0922C] namely, the speech in which he composed his defense. Then, at “For concerning the forged material,” he answers the second charge, saying that there is no need to say anything about the forged letters in which he was said to have wished to restore Rome to freedom; this could easily have been inferred from the accusers’ own words, if the accusers had been permitted to be heard against him.

He then says that he did not do this, because Rome was already so oppressed that no further hope of freedom could be entertained. And if there had been any hope of freedom, he would have kept it so secret that it ought by no means to have come to the king’s knowledge. Thus Canius, whom he mentioned above and who was also killed by Gaius Caesar Caligula, replied to Caesar when Caesar said that Canius had been an accomplice in a conspiracy against him: [Col. 0922D] “If I had known, you would not have known”—that is, “I would have handled the matter so prudently that you could not have discovered it.”

After this comes: **“In which matter we are accused.”** *Arguere* sometimes means “to rebuke,” as here, and in Virgil, Book XI:

> Charge me with cowardice,
>
> you, Draucus.

Sometimes it means “to prove,” as in Juvenal:

> because the soft window-bars in the ear
>
> will have proved it, although I myself deny it.

Hence Cicero defined *argumentum* as “a probable invention devised to produce belief.” Ovid, in Book I of the *Metamorphoses*:

> We offer proofs of the origin from which we were born.

**Substance**—*Summa* means the collection of a complex [Col. 0923A] or numerous matter into a single beginning or head, under which all the remaining elements are contained. Cornelius Tacitus: “Flaccus entrusted him with the chief command.” We likewise speak of the totals of money or accounts, that is, the sum collected. Juvenal:

> The third had a larger sum than that one,
>
> which the corner of the broad chest could scarcely contain.

**Senate**—We call it the public council, which our unlearned people call the consulship. The consulship is the office of the consul, just as the praetorship is the office held by a praetor. What the common people call a “consultation” is the senate, said to derive its name from old age, as Sallust says in the *Catiline*: “Those chosen, whose bodies were weakened by years but whose minds were strong in wisdom, deliberated concerning the republic.”

They call someone “guilty of treason” when he is accused of having attempted something tending to the destruction of the state [Col. 0923B] or the ruler, or even something of conspicuous disgrace. Hence the expressions “injured majesty” and “guilty of injured majesty”; and by omission of the word *laesae*, “injured,” one says simply “guilty of treason,” since the meaning is sufficiently understood.

*Reus* seems to derive from *reor*, “I suppose,” because we suppose—that is, suspect—that he did what is alleged against him. Properly, the term denotes one who has been summoned before the court. Ovid, in Book II of the *Art of Love*:

> not merely so that you may protect frightened defendants.

We also sometimes call someone *reus* who is already bound or indebted. Hence a person who has obtained what he vowed and is obliged to pay his vow is called *reus voti*, “liable under a vow.” Jurists also call two persons *rei promittendi*, “jointly liable promisers,” when each has bound himself by making a promise. **AGRICOLA.**

**To have prevented**—*Impedire* and *expedire* derive from binding [Col. 0923C] and unbinding the feet; afterward they came to mean “to loose” and “to bind.” Horace, in Book I of the *Odes*:

> Now it is fitting to bind the hair with green myrtle.

Then *impedire* means “to restrain” or “to resist,” as here. Cicero, in Book I of *On Duties*: “Use your own judgment about the matters themselves; for I am preventing nothing.” **AGRICOLA.**

**Will cease**—*Cessare* sometimes means to be idle. Persius:

> But if you are idle and fix the sun upon your skin.

Thus Horace: “Damas the idler,” that is, Damas the idle, sluggish, delaying man. Sometimes it means “to stop” or “to make an end,” as in this passage. Ovid, in Book I of the *Art of Love*:

> Thus the gambler, lest he lose, does not cease to lose.

It is a frequentative formed from *cedo*, because an idler yields to his work. **AGRICOLA.**

[Col. 0923D] **Order**—*Ordo* is the definite arrangement of things by which it is established what comes first, what second, and what follows afterward. Horace:

> This will be the virtue and beauty of arrangement.

There were three orders among the Roman people: the plebeian, the patrician—that is, the senatorial—and the equestrian, which stood between the plebeians and the patricians. Those of the equestrian order are what unlearned people today call soldiers. For *miles*, “soldier,” means everyone who earns pay in war. Therefore he says “of that order,” that is, the senatorial order.

**Impious**—*Fas* and *nefas*, like *damnas* and *inficias*, are indeclinable. We say *inficias eo*, “I deny” or “I reject,” and jurists say: “Let Titius be bound as my heir to pay Teius one hundred,” that is, “let him be obligated.” *Fas* and *nefas* are derived from *for*, “to speak.” Hence Virgil, in Book I of the *Aeneid*, used the following for both:

> But hope that the gods remember what may and may not be spoken.

[Col. 0924A] *Fas* is what we do with God’s authority or according to natural equity, just as *ius* is what is done by human command.

**Merits**—He used the word metaphorically for “price” or “payment.”

**By the Socratic judgment**—Because at Athens it was customary for an accused citizen to estimate the penalty he believed he deserved, and the judges allowed the accused to do so, Socrates said that he deserved to be publicly provided with meals at the city’s expense. He did not wish, since he knew that he had done nothing deserving of punishment, to estimate or declare himself deserving of any penalty, although by doing so he might have softened the judges’ anger. The judges, angered by this free reply as though he despised them, condemned him to death. [Col. 0924B]

**By a decree**—That is, what in Greek is called δόγμα (*dogma*), which unlearned people take to mean “doctrine.” Among the Greeks, however, anything established by the people is called *dogma*, just as among us one speaks of a decree of the people or a decree of the ruler.

**Sequence**—*Series* may derive from *sero*, “to sow,” as though it meant an order of things extending from the first seed, that is, from the origin. Statius, in Book I of the *Thebaid*:

> A long sequence reaching back.

**With the pen**—This comes from the Greek στῦλος (*stylos*), “column,” and the similar Latin *stylus* is understood as writing. Hence Cicero, in Book I of *On the Orator*, called the pen “the finest craftsman of eloquence.” The ancients used to write on wax tablets. Ovid, in Book I of the *Art of Love*:

[Col. 0924C]

> Let your wax first be the confidant of your mind.

**For remembrance**—That is, for the remembrance of posterity.

**Letters**—*Littera*, “letter,” in the singular is used by orators for the individual figure or character with which we write, such as *a*, *b*, or *c*. It means a letter or epistle only in the plural. Therefore Cicero always says “one, two, or three letters.” Poets, however, because of metrical necessity, use the singular for an epistle. Ovid, in the *Epistles*:

> The letter you are reading came from the abducted Briseis.

**Concerns**—Properly, this means “to apply” or “attach,” from *ad* and *teneo*. Plautus, in *The Two Captives*:

> Now he applies the knives.

[Col. 0924D] Sometimes it means “what is necessary,” as here. Quintilian, in Book XII of the *Institutes*: “What need is there after so many years …?”

**To use**—*Utor* is joined with the accusative. Quintilian, in Book I of the *Institutes*: “That speech must be used.” This is an older usage; it is more customary for it to be joined with the ablative. Juvenal:

> You use, amid the crowd,
>
> what has been left beneath the covering.

**It would have been permitted**—Properly, *licere* is said of what is not forbidden by law. Persius:

> Why should it not be permitted to me, when my will has commanded whatever it wishes?

It is also taken to mean “to be able.” Virgil, in Book IV of the *Aeneid*:

> Was it not permitted to lead, without guilt,
>
> a life deprived of marriage, like a wild creature?

[Col. 0925A] So also here.

**To be hoped for**—*Sperare* properly means to have an expectation of some future good, as here. Virgil, in Book IV of the *Aeneid*:

> I indeed hope that, if the divine powers can do anything,
>
> he will drain punishment among the middle rocks.

Sometimes it means to expect whatever is going to happen. Virgil, in Book I of the *Aeneid*:

> But hope that the gods remember what may and may not be spoken.

Terence, in the *Heautontimorumenos*:

> We have one hope: that we shall be hungry enough.

**Gaius**—*Caius* and *Cnaeus*, like *curculio*, which means “worm,” are written with *c* but pronounced with *g*. **AGRICOLA.**

[Col. 0925B] **Caesar**—This is not a title of dignity but the name of a Roman family from which Julius Caesar originated. He was the first to suppress Roman liberty. Hence all the emperors who followed him adopted this name as a title of legitimate succession. Up to Nero, the emperors were connected with this family either by kinship or adoption; after Nero, the others assumed the name merely by usurpation. **AGRICOLA.**

**Of Germanicus**—This Germanicus, the son of Drusus Nero, fathered this Gaius and Agrippina, Nero’s mother, as well as other children whom it is unnecessary to enumerate. This Gaius was surnamed Caligula, a name derived from the military *caliga*, which the common people call an *ocrea*, because he was raised in a military camp. For what we commonly call a *caliga* is what the ancients called *braca*, whence [Col. 0925C] Gaul was called *bracata*. What we call *braca*, the ancients called a *femorale* or *subligar*.

The verbs *inquit* and *inquam* are used only in speech when we represent the very people to whom we attribute the words as speaking. For one should not properly say, “He says that he is occupied and cannot come,” but rather: “He says, ‘I am occupied and cannot come.’” The speaker must always use the same words that the person whom we introduce would have used. Juvenal:

> “Nothing has been accomplished,” he says, “unless with Punic soldiers
>
> we break the gates and plant the standard in the middle Subura.”

And elsewhere:

> “When,” he says, “there is no place in the city
>
> for honorable arts.”

**AGRICOLA.**

[Col. 0925D] **But of what crime**—The order is: “But you ask for the substance of the crime of which we are accused.”

**But I wished it, and I shall never cease to wish it**—Supply: “that the senate should be safe.”

**By the Socratic judgment**—By the judgment of Socrates, whose words on this subject in Plato’s *Theaetetus* are: “It seems utterly impious to me to admit what is false and refute what is true.”

**In whatever manner**—In whatever way.

**I also committed it to writing and remembrance with my pen**—I do not think that this little book of Boethius now survives.

**In which matter**—Here he demonstrates the disgracefulness of his fortune from the judges by whom he was condemned. Since, however, there are two kinds of judges of all things, God and human beings, he first complains about divine judgment and then about human judgment, that is, the judgment of the senate.

He says: “Although [Col. 0926A] the pain of adversity has greatly occupied and disturbed my mind, I am not yet so deprived of reason that I should take it ill that wicked accusers attempted an abominable act against me, since wishing for worse things is almost a consequence of the defect and weakness of human nature. But I consider this more worthy of wonder: that wicked men can accomplish what they wish against the good while God, without whose permission nothing can happen, sees it. For it is like a prodigy—that is, incredible—that he should wish to permit this,” just as a certain philosopher said: “If there is a God, how can there be any evil? If there is no God, where do good things come from?”

After this, at “But it would have been permissible,” he shows from the judgment of the senate that he was disgracefully condemned by it. First he does so from the person of the senate, which he had saved at the risk of his own life when it was accused before the king; [Col. 0926B] then from the procedure of the trial, because he was not heard in his absence and was condemned without an examination of the case.

He says: “Although it may have pleased God that those who hated all good men should also wish me, who was defending good men and the senate, to perish, nevertheless we did not deserve this from the senate, so that it should itself wish such a thing. For when King Theoderic at Verona wished to transfer to the senate the charge of which Albinus had been accused, you know, Philosophy, at what great risk to myself I defended the senate. Yet in return for that service I was condemned by the senate through a false judgment.”

Then, at “And of what crime at any time,” he gathers the disgracefulness of the judgment from the manner in which it was conducted, saying: “Even when judging the most obvious crimes, judges never agree so completely that none of them is moved to pity—either because all human beings are inclined [Col. 0926C] to err and to do what they ought not, or because fortune is common to all and no one knows what may happen to him personally.

“Even if I had wished to commit crimes of the greatest magnitude, I ought nevertheless to have been punished only after confessing or being convicted. Now, without my defense having been heard, although I was five hundred thousand paces from the city, namely in prison at Pavia, I was condemned to death.”

He therefore exclaims: “O deserving fathers!”—that is, “O senate!”—so that no one could be convicted of a similar crime. This is what he means: “The senate deserved that no one should defend it, because on account of the crime that I wished to defend it, I was convicted and condemned by it.”

Then follows: **“The disgracefulness of whose accusation.” AGRICOLA.**

**Thus**—Today almost all unlearned people use this as an adverb of affirmation, which is wholly incorrect; it signifies similarity instead. Virgil, in Book XI:

> Bitias and mighty Pandarus did not find me so.

He says *ita*, “thus,” that is, “in such a manner.” **AGRICOLA.**

**Blunted**—He spoke metaphorically, for properly the word is used of iron or anything else suitable for cutting. **AGRICOLA.**

**Against virtue**—By synecdoche he used an accident for its subject, that is, “against good men.” **AGRICOLA.**

**Undertaken with difficulty**—*Moliri* means to attempt something with great effort, that is, difficulty. Virgil, in Book IV of the *Aeneid*:

> And does he himself not undertake the labor
>
> on the strength of his own praise?

**To have accomplished**—*Facere* and *efficere* clearly differ. We often do many things without producing an effect; but *efficere* means to attain something by what one does. Thus a physician [Col. 0927A] often does everything necessary to heal a sick person, but nevertheless does not heal him. If he succeeds in making him healthy, however, he unquestionably heals him. **AGRICOLA.**

**Worse things**—*Deterior*, “worse,” comes from the verb *detero*, “to wear away.” Hence we call *detritio* “wickedness,” and *detrimentum* “injury” or “damage.” **AGRICOLA.**

**Prodigy**—*Monstrum* comes from *monstrare*, “to show,” because the ancients thought that whenever prodigies occurred, some great evil or impending disaster was shown by them. Likewise *ostentum* comes from *ostendere*, “to display,” because it shows that something will happen; *portentum* comes from *protendere*, “to extend forward,” because it announces something; and *prodigium* comes from *procul agere*, “to drive away,” because monstrous births, if human, were accustomed to be carried away into deserted places [Col. 0927B] and forests, while those of other animals were buried alive. **AGRICOLA.**

**One of your companions**—This saying is attributed to Carneades, a particularly distinguished author of the New Academy. **AGRICOLA.**

**Companions**—*Familia* is derived from *famulatus*, “service,” and *familiaris* originally meant “a slave.” Usage later established *familia* as a term for kinship, hence *paterfamilias*, *materfamilias*, and *filiusfamilias*. **AGRICOLA.**

**If indeed**—Here it must be read as two separate words. Sometimes they are joined and pronounced with a single accent, in which case they mean “certainly.” Pliny, in Book I of the *Natural History*: “If indeed they change color.” **AGRICOLA.**

**Let them seek it with blood**—This is said by antonomasia, that is, [Col. 0927C] “they desire destruction.” **AGRICOLA.**

**They seek**—*Peto* sometimes means “I demand,” as in Horace, Book II of the *Epistles*:

> What he eagerly sought, he left behind when the time was ripe.

Sometimes it means “to go toward,” as in Valerius, Book II: “Seeking the countryside, he reported it on his return to the city.” Sometimes it means “to beg,” and is joined with the accusative while a preposition intervenes with the ablative. Quintilian, in *The Infamy of a Mother*: “I ask this of you, O state, with my final prayers.” We also say *peto illum ferro*, “I attack him with the sword,” and *peto lapidibus*, “I attack him with stones,” that is, “I throw at him” or “inflict violence upon him.” Virgil, in the *Eclogues*:

> Galatea attacks me with an apple,

that is, “throws an apple at me.” **AGRICOLA.**

**Fathers**—The senate was called the “fathers.” Sallust: “They called them fathers either because of their age or because of the similarity of their concern.” [Col. 0927D] **AGRICOLA.**

**Present**—Someone who is physically present is called *praesens*; the word is also used figuratively of something effective. Virgil, in the *Eclogues*:

> Nor elsewhere recognize the gods as so present.

Quintilian, in *Poison Poured Out*: “I prepare a present poison,” that is, one that corrupts suddenly and immediately. **AGRICOLA.**

**At Verona**—Verona is a town of Transpadane Italy through which the river Athesis flows. It is situated at the foot of the Vindelician Alps. **AGRICOLA.**

**What he was going to say**—This means “something.” The accent must be transferred to the preceding word, as with *que*, *ve*, and *ne*, which we attach to other words.

**Destruction**—*Exitium* derives figuratively from *exeundo*, “going out,” just as *initium* derives from *ineundo*, “going in.” It is used for disaster or ruin because an ending—that is, death—is the greatest disaster for each person. [Col. 0928A] **AGRICOLA.**

**Security**—That is, neglect or contempt. For *securus* means “without care.”

**To bring forth**—Here it means “to bring out.” Juvenal:

> Bring forth your head, Galla.

Sometimes it means “to postpone.” Plautus, in *The Two Captives*:

> When, after postponing their affairs, men go to the country,

that is, “after delaying their business or lawsuits.” It also means “to carry far away.” Virgil, in Book I of the *Aeneid*:

> He extends his power over the Garamantes and Indians.

[Col. 0928B] **To have boasted**—Here *jactare* means to mention something arrogantly or boastfully. Quintilian, in *The Infamy of a Mother*: “A large part of the will is boastfulness.” Sometimes, metaphorically, it means to make a great verbal din. Virgil, in Book X of the *Aeneid*:

> Now you rise too late with complaints
>
> and raise unjust and empty quarrels.

Properly, however, it means frequently to throw. Ovid, in Book II of the *Art of Love*:

> and shake out the torches that have been thrown.

**By displaying**—*Ostentare*, like *jactare*, means “to display,” but *jactare* is more especially done with words, while *ostentare* is done with things.

**Crime**—*Facinus* derives from *facere*, “to do,” and now, through the force of usage, is understood in a bad sense. Among the ancients it could be used in either sense, good or bad. Sallust, in the *Catiline*:

> who seeks a reputation for some glorious deed
>
> or honorable art.

[Col. 0928C] **To be strangled**—*Jugulare* properly means to cut through the throat. The *jugulus* is that part near the neck formed by the bones that define the chest, because those bones resemble a *jugum*, either a mountain ridge or the yoke placed upon oxen for plowing. **AGRICOLA.**

**Death**—The common run of grammarians says that the nominative of this word is not found. Cicero nevertheless says in his speech *For Milo*: “But what death can be unjust for an assassin and a robber?” Likewise *prex*, “prayer,” is also found in the nominative, as the grammarian Phocas said. *Nex* and *mors* differ just as *necare* and *mori* differ: *nex* is death inflicted by violence, whereas *mors* is any kind of human death. **AGRICOLA.**

**Five hundred thousand paces**—The Latins measure journeys in thousands of paces, just as the Greeks use stadia and the Gauls leagues. [Col. 0928D] Five thousand paces constitute the same distance as what the Germans call a mile, the Egyptians a parasang, and the Persians a schoenus. **AGRICOLA.**

**More favorably**—That is, more carefully or with a greater inclination. The word comes from *propendere*, “to hang forward,” as with a balance: whichever side bears more weight hangs lower. Thus we too are said to lean toward, and to be inclined toward, what we pursue with greater zeal. **AGRICOLA.**

**For proscription**—The term *proscriptio* arose from the civil wars. During civil conflicts such as those between Marius and Sulla, Caesar and Pompey, and the others, the victors displayed on tablets the names of those who belonged to the opposing party, [Col. 0929A] offering rewards to anyone who killed one of them and confiscating their property. Later, usage established that those banished into exile were called *proscripti*, “proscribed.” **AGRICOLA.**

**Against virtue**—Against men endowed with virtue.

**One of your companions**—One of the philosophers.

**If indeed**—If.

**Blood**—The shedding of blood.

**To defend the good**—To defend good men.

**What**—Something.

**To have boasted of it in no praise of mine**—Although these things are true, he says that he never boasted of them. M. Tullius, in Book I of *On Duties*: “It is also disgraceful to praise oneself, especially falsely, and, amid the laughter of one’s listeners, to imitate the boastful soldier.” [Col. 0929B] Saint Cyprian, to Donatus: “Boastfulness in one’s own praises is hateful.” Pliny, to Pompeius Saturninus: “For if even the praises of others are usually received with ears that are not wholly impartial, how difficult it is to ensure that speech about oneself or one’s own affairs does not seem tiresome!”

**For he diminishes**—The order is: “Whoever— that is, anyone—diminishes in some way the secrecy of a conscience that approves itself,” that is, that is pleased with itself through virtue and good deeds, “whenever, by displaying a deed, he receives payment for it,” that is, the reward of fame.

Cicero, in the *Tusculan Disputations*: “Even if you are in the eyes of the multitude, I would not wish you to stand by its judgment, nor to think the same thing beautiful because it thinks so. You must use your own judgment. If you please yourself by approving what is right, then you will have conquered not only yourself—which I instructed you to do shortly before—but everyone and everything. [Col. 0929C] Set this before you: greatness of spirit, and a kind of exaltation of the soul, which rises highest in despising and disdaining suffering, is the single most beautiful thing of all, and it is more beautiful if it is free from the crowd and does not seek applause, but delights only in itself.

“Indeed, everything that is done without self-advertisement and without the people as witness seems more praiseworthy to me—not because all good deeds should be hidden, for they all wish to be brought into the light, but because no theater is greater for virtue than conscience.”

Pliny, to Saturninus: “Furthermore, we remember how much more generously the fruit of uprightness is placed in conscience than in reputation. Glory ought to follow, not be sought; and if by chance it does not follow, what deserved glory is not for that reason less beautiful.”

[Col. 0929D] Those who adorn their good deeds with words are thought to have done them not because they had done them, but in order to have them praised. Thus what would have been magnificent when reported by another person fades away when reported by the one who performed it. For when people cannot destroy the deed itself, they attack its boastful presentation. Thus, if you have done things that ought to remain unmentioned, the deed itself [sentence incomplete]; if you do not keep silent about things that deserve praise, you yourself are blamed.

Macrobius, in the *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*: “The consciousness of distinguished deeds itself is the greatest reward of virtue.” The same author, in the same work: “The wise man places the fruit of virtue in conscience; the less perfect person places it in glory.” Saint Ambrose, in a certain letter: “For a wealthy conscience abounds in its own witness.”

**In exchange for the rewards of true virtue, [the penalty] of a false crime**—This is a fine antithesis.

[Col. 0930A] **And of what crime ever**—Here *et* is a particle suited to an interrogative. Thus Virgil, in the *Eclogues*:

> And what was the great reason that you wished to see Rome?

**Of a similar crime**—That he had shown an especially strong devotion to the senate and had wished it to be safe.

### “The indignity of his accusation”

He now shows the greater indignity of his situation: although it was evident that these charges were not such as either accusers could bring forward with any appearance of credibility or judges could condemn under any color of justice. He also says that the charge was brought against him on the basis of his principal distinction: because he was a philosopher, they accused him of being a magician. For philosophers in ancient times were often burdened with this suspicion. Thus Apuleius of Madaura was accused of magic, and books of his defense still survive; Apollonius of Tyana and Menippus were also regarded as magicians, and even wished to appear so, although each was a philosopher. He therefore says that, out of a desire to obtain the consulship and magistracies in the city, his accusers charged him with having dealings with demons. He demonstrates the falsity of this from his studies: since he was devoted to philosophy, which commanded him to serve God and not the gods, it is unlikely that he would join himself to the worst spirits or employ their assistance. He then refutes the same charge from the modesty of his household, the integrity of his friends, and his kinship with Symmachus, whose daughter he had as his wife—people who could not have associated with him if his life had been so criminal. AGRICOLA.

### “Commistione”

*Commistio* must be written with an *s*, not an *x*. If *mixeo* existed in the indicative, we could say *mixtum*; but now, from *misceo*, how could the form be *mixtum*? AGRICOLA.

### “Fuscarent”

*Fuscus* is a color such as appears on bodies from exposure to the sun. Virgil, in the *Bucolics*:

> What then, if Amyntas is dark?

Ovid, in the second book of *The Art of Love*:

> Bodies will be darkened in the field.

*Ater* is the color of coals and garments; hence we say *atramentum*, “ink,” and call those who have changed their clothing for mourning *atrati*. *Niger* is that dark color tending from red or brightness toward black; hence we speak of dark wines and dark blood. Virgil used *nigrantem nimbum*, “a blackening cloud,” in the first book of the *Aeneid*. Authors, however, often confuse these terms. AGRICOLA.

### “Sacrilegio”

*Sacrilegium* was originally derived from *legere*, that is, “to steal” sacred things; afterward it came to mean violence committed against sacred things. Thus Seneca, in his letter to Serenus, said: “Nothing in nature is so sacred that it does not find a sacrilegious violator.” Boethius then seems to extend this name to every profanation of sacred things. For all incantations and rites for summoning spirits were called sacred. Boethius, shrinking from this name, preferred to call it *sacrilegium*: this is what we properly call magic, by which human beings produce marvelous things exceeding every order or power of nature—that is, what the uneducated call necromancy. In Greek it is called *νεκρομαντεία* (*nekromanteia*), or more commonly *νεκρομαντεῖον* (*nekromanteion*). It consisted solely in practicing divination from the souls of the dead by means of the incantations of the person summoning them. AGRICOLA.

### “Polluisse”

*Polluo* is said to derive from *porro* and *luo*, that is, “I cleanse completely,” meaning “I stain.” AGRICOLA.

### “Insita”

That is, “inserted” or “implanted,” from *insero*. AGRICOLA.

### “Instillabas”

*Stilla* means “a drop”; hence *stillicidium* is the place where raindrops fall from roofs. From this comes *instillo*, “I instill.” AGRICOLA.

### “Pythagoricum”

Pythagoras was born on the island of Samos. He lived in that part of Italy which was once called Magna Graecia, around Tarentum and Croton. When he was asked whether he was *σοφός* (*sophos*), that is, “wise,” he replied that he was not, but rather *φιλόσοφος* (*philosophos*), that is, “a lover of wisdom.” Since before his time those endowed with more distinguished learning were called “wise men,” afterward they began to be called “philosophers,” and from Pythagoras arose the school that was called Italian philosophy. AGRICOLA.

### “Θεῷ, ἀλλ᾽ οὐ θεοῖς”

That is, “to God and not to the gods.” AGRICOLA.

### “Conveniebant”

Here *convenire* means “to be suitable” or “to be fitting”; sometimes it means “to agree.” Horace:

> And in every respect his way of life disagrees,

that is, “is at variance.” Ovid, in the first book of *The Art of Love*:

> Let it be agreed between us that we do not ask any woman beforehand.

Hence we say, “We have agreed about this matter,” and, “We shall come to an agreement about this matter.” It also means “to assemble,” which is its proper meaning. Sallust:

> After Catiline saw that those whom he had summoned had assembled.

One also says, “I *conveni* him at the forum,” that is, “I addressed him.” AGRICOLA.

### “Penetral”

The inner part of a house is called *penetral*, from “penetrating.” Virgil, in the second book of the *Aeneid*:

> The inner chambers of Priam and the ancient kings appear.

Boethius aptly spoke of “the innocent inner chamber of the household,” since crimes are usually hidden away and removed from human sight. AGRICOLA.

### “Coetus”

It is derived from *coire*, that is, “to come together.” AGRICOLA.

### “Socer”

A *socer* is the father of one’s wife or husband, just as a *socrus* is the mother. A man who has your daughter in marriage is called your *gener*, “son-in-law”; a woman who has your son is called your *nurus*, “daughter-in-law.” AGRICOLA.

### “Affines”

He used this in an improper sense, meaning “connected” or “related.” In ordinary usage, *affinis* refers to someone who is not our blood relative but is joined by marriage to our relatives. AGRICOLA.

### “Instituti”

That is, “arranged,” “accustomed,” or “formed.” Quintilian, in the first book of the *Institutio oratoria*:

> Before we form their manners, we form their palate.

Sometimes *instituere* means “to teach.” Juvenal:

> And the better locust trained the neighboring inexperienced ones.

It is also used for proposing or intending, as in Cicero, in the third book *De oratore*: “As I was intending, brother Quintus,” that is, “as I wished or was preparing.” AGRICOLA.

### “Lacereris”

This is said figuratively by metaphor, meaning “you are attacked” or “you are criticized.” AGRICOLA.

### “Cujus dignitatem”

Although Rudolph Agricola, otherwise a very acute judge, seems to read *indignitatem*, I would nevertheless prefer to read *dignitatem*, as almost all the copies do. For there was great dignity and honor in the accusation for which Boethius was prosecuted—namely, his excessive devotion to the senate—but the informers attempted to stain and blacken it with the false charge of magic. In addition to the authority of the manuscripts, this reading is supported by what follows immediately in the prose:

> You have recalled to everyone the honesty or falsity of the charges brought against you.

### “Ἔπου θεῷ”

“Follow God.” This Greek reading occurs in the copy lent to me by Caesarius and in a letter written to me by John Aedicollius. It is also found in the second *Chiliad* of Erasmus’ *Adagia* and in Politian’s *Praelectio Homerica*. It is attributed to Pythagoras, who, in Marsilio Ficino’s translation, says in his *Symbols*:

> Above all, restrain your tongue, imitating God.

Rudolph Agricola appears to set the following Greek words here:

> Θεῷ ἀλλ᾽ οὐ θεοῖς

that is, “serve God and not the gods” (with “serve” or “one ought to serve” understood).

### “Consimilem Deo faceres”

Seneca, in his letter to Lucilius 48:

> For this is what philosophy promises me: that it will make me equal to God.

### “Ultro”

“Moreover” or “in addition.”

### “At vero hoc etiam”

He now shows the severity of his calamity from what commonly happens to all good people. He says, therefore, that it is not merely undeserved that he has endured all the grievous things he has enumerated; what remains to complete his misfortunes is that he should appear to deserve to suffer these things, and that, after losing everything, he should also lose the good name of his integrity and reputation. The ignorant crowd believes only those things to have been done wisely and prudently which turn out successfully and prosperously. Since, therefore, all his affairs have gone against him in an unhappy manner, he will be thought worthy of these things and to have deserved them.

Later, where he says, “But I seem to see,” he speaks thus because now our innocence has been conquered and oppressed by the wicked. It will happen that all the criminals against whom he had resisted will rejoice, and will bring similar accusations against good men when they see that they can do everything with impunity. Good men, meanwhile, will not dare to resist them, seeing that they are not only exposed to dangers but also deprived of the means of defense. He therefore cries out: “O star-bearing one,” and so forth. AGRICOLA.

### “Cumulus”

That is, “a completion” or “an addition.” Properly, *cumulus* means a heap or mass of things piled together. AGRICOLA.

### “Merita”

That is, “force” or “value.” AGRICOLA.

### “Provisa”

He says this as though the things had been done prudently and properly. According to the philosophers, whatever is done rightly is done prudently; conversely, whatever is done prudently is also done rightly. AGRICOLA.

### “Rumores”

*Rumor* is derived from *ruere*, “to rush,” as though it were the roar of a crowd, resembling the sound produced by the collapse of things. It means the same as *fama*, “reputation,” but *fama*—because it derives from the Greek *φήμι* (*phemi*), which among us means “to speak”—signifies speaking something more certainly and consistently. *Rumor* conveys something more uncertain. AGRICOLA.

### “Affingitur”

Some read *affigitur*, which is indeed metaphorical but nevertheless more suitable. AGRICOLA.

### “Perferunt”

Juvenal:

> And carrying far the resounding

> Ionian sea—

that is, “she endured.” Sometimes it means “to bring,” as in Cicero: “I gave letters to be delivered to you.” AGRICOLA.

### “Officinas”

An *officina*, derived from *officium*, is a place in which craftsmen perform their tasks—that is, practice their arts. AGRICOLA.

### “Fluitantes”

That is, “moving about,” “trembling,” or “rejoicing exuberantly.” Cicero calls unrestrained joy “leaping” or “exulting joy,” meaning that it continually moves and trembles, as is customary among the joyful. AGRICOLA.

### “Perditissimum”

Those are called *perditi* who are not merely or tolerably wicked, and of whom there is no longer any hope of goodness. The Greeks, and sometimes Cicero when he uses the word, call such people *ἀσώτους* (*asotous*), “profligates.” AGRICOLA.

### “Insontes”

*Insons* is derived from *sons*, a word still used today, although the ancients used it more frequently. Festus Pompeius attests to this: he says that *sonticus* means “just,” quoting Naevius:

> The cause for which you destroy the woman must be serious.

Festus would have spoken more correctly had he said “grave” or “harmful.” I think *sons* was said of one from whom a sound proceeds—that is, one who is the subject of human report and speech. AGRICOLA.

### “Cumulus accedit”

“An addition of heaps” is proverbially said of great evils and calamities, just as “a heap” or “pile” of good things is said of great wealth. Cicero also commonly uses such expressions as *cumulare officiis*, “to heap up services,” *cumulatissime satisfacere*, “to satisfy most abundantly,” and *cumulus meritorum*, “a heap of merits.”

## INTO THE FIFTH METER

### “O stelliferi”

In this poem Boethius laments the condition of human nature. God has bound everything in nature to a fixed law and arranged all things so that they cannot err or sin. To human beings alone he gave freedom, so that they could do good and evil, and allowed them frequently to misuse this freedom, with the result that the wicked oppress the better.

The meter is anapaestic and Pindaric. It is called anapaestic from the foot, since the anapest is its proper foot, although it also admits the spondee and dactyl. It is called Pindaric from Pindar, its author.

He therefore says: “O God, who, dwelling in heaven, turn it in swift motion and cause the stars always to preserve their order; who cause the full moon, standing opposite the sun, to hide the other stars with her light, and, when she again draws near the sun, to lose her light. You also cause Hesperus sometimes to shine after sunset and sometimes, under the changed name Lucifer, to precede the rising sun. Moreover, in winter you make the days short and in summer the nights short.

“Nor does your power merely compel heaven to maintain its order; it also governs the earth in a similar fashion, so that leaves falling in autumn are reborn in spring, and what is sown in winter ripens in summer. Yet although you direct these things in so fixed a course, you permit human affairs alone to go astray. For if this were not so, whence would come such power of Fortune that she now inflicts unjust punishments on the innocent and, conversely, raises up the wicked? Virtue is neglected and despised, while evil crimes do not harm the wicked. Indeed, whenever Fortune wishes, even the most powerful kings are subjected and crushed.

“Therefore, O God, govern human affairs as well—human affairs, which are not an insignificant part of the world—and send to earth the order that exists in heaven.” AGRICOLA.

### “Conditor”

*Condere* sometimes means “to make,” as here, and in Virgil’s *Bucolics*:

> May Pallas herself inhabit the cities she founded.

Sometimes it means “to hide,” as is said below:

> May she hide the lesser stars together.

Properly, however, it means “to heap together” or “to collect.” Horace, in the first book of the *Odes*:

> If he has stored him in his own granary,

and again in the first book of the *Epistles*:

> I store and arrange what I shall soon be able to bring forth. AGRICOLA.

### “Orbis”

This is what is round on every side; we also call it a globe. Hence, because of its roundness, we call the world an *orbis*, that is, what is called a sphere. AGRICOLA.

### “Nixus”

That is, “supported” or “resting upon.” Quintilian, in *The Marian Soldier*:

> Let him seek life resting on one knee.

AGRICOLA.

### “Solio”

A *solium* is a royal seat or throne. Thus Seneca, in *On Tranquility of Mind*, speaking of the mutability of Fortune, says: “There is only a moment between a throne—that is, kingship—and another’s knees—that is, captivity.” The ancients also called a certain vessel in a bathhouse a *solium*: it was filled with water, and bathers sat in it and washed themselves. AGRICOLA.

### “Coelum”

Some thought it was so called as though from *caelatum*, “engraved,” because of the various figures of the stars; hence the world also seems to have been named from its adornment. Likewise among the Greeks *κόσμος* (*kosmos*), “world,” is derived from “adornment.” Others derive *coelum* from the Greek *κοῖλον* (*koilon*), “hollow.”

If the first derivation is accepted, it must be written with the diphthong *ae*; if the second, with *oe*. But the popular explanation that *coelum* is like *casa ἡλίου*, “the house of the sun,” is foolish, like many sayings of the uneducated. AGRICOLA.

### “Turbine”

That is, “with force” or “in a rush,” from *turbare*, “to disturb.” Hence Virgil, in the first book of the *Aeneid*:

> And they blow over the lands with a whirlwind.

A *turbo* is also called what the Greeks call *τρόχος* (*trochos*), and from that borrowed name we call it a *trochus*, from *τρέχω* (*trecho*), “I run,” for the same reason: it runs with a whirlwind, that is, with force. *Turbon* was also the proper name of a certain gladiator. AGRICOLA.

### “Legem”

*Lex* is said to derive from *legere*, “to read,” because it was read aloud before the people. Then the consul asked whether they wished or ordered it to be done in that way; if the people assented, it became a law. If a tribune of the plebs did the same thing, it was likewise a decree, called a *plebiscitum*. Here *lex* is used metaphorically and figuratively for a fixed order. AGRICOLA.

### “Pleno cornu”

That is, “with the horns filled,” which occurs at the full moon. When the moon stands opposite the sun, the part turned toward us is entirely illuminated by the sun. The moon does not possess light from itself but receives it from the sun, just as polished vessels reflect the light they receive. Thus, illuminated by the sun, the moon returns its light. When she again approaches the sun, the parts turned away from us receive the light; because of her roundness, the visible light gradually seems to contract into horns. AGRICOLA.

### “Flammis”

*Flamma* is said to derive from *flagro*, “I burn.” AGRICOLA.

### “Fratris”

That is, “of the sun.” For the myths say that Latona, impregnated by Jupiter, gave birth to Phoebus—that is, the sun, from *φοιβέω* (*phoibeo*), “I burn”—and Diana. AGRICOLA.

### “Luna”

She seems to have been named from *lucere*, “to shine,” because she shines among the heavenly bodies. In the same way, they say that the sun was named because he shines alone and hides all the stars with his light. AGRICOLA.

### “Lumina perdat”

This is so only in relation to our sight. The moon is never more fully illuminated, nor does she receive light more broadly, than when she is closest to the sun. For it is clear from mathematical reasoning that when a less luminous body is brought near a more luminous one, the closer it comes, the more of its surface is illuminated. AGRICOLA.

### “Agit”

*Agere* has several meanings. It can mean “to be busy” or “to do something.” Horace, in the first book of the *Epistles*:

> What is the high one doing for me?

Sometimes it means “to lead” or “to drive.” Virgil, in the *Bucolics*:

> Drive the well-fed sheep along.

Horace, in the second book of the *Epistles*:

> The inexperienced man fears to drive a ship.

Sometimes it means “to bring an action in court.” Hence in civil law we speak of *actiones*, “actions,” and of an *actor*, the person who prosecutes the defendant. It is also said of an actor that he *agit*, that is, “recites” or “performs.” Hence Cicero uses *actio* for delivery. *Agere animam* means “to die”; thus Cicero, in *Pro Milo*:

> Whom he had left while breathing out his life.

We also say *agere gratias*, “to give thanks,” which the uneducated express as *regratiari*. AGRICOLA.

### “Algentes”

*Algere* is Greek, but among the Greeks it means “to suffer pain,” whereas among us it means “to be cold.” Horace, in *The Art of Poetry*:

> The boy endured much, did much, sweated and shivered.

AGRICOLA.

### “Hesperus et Lucifer”

They are the same star, called Venus. In Greek it is called *ἕσπερος* (*hesperos*), from the evening; we have changed the aspiration into *v* and call it *vespera*, “evening,” because it shines and sets after the sun. *Lucifer*, however, is the name it bears in the morning, when it precedes the rising sun and, as though its guide, carries the light before it. AGRICOLA.

### “Ortus”

Since various names for the rising and setting of the stars are found among authors, this passage seems to require that we explain the matter briefly and as clearly as possible.

First, we must understand that there are two kinds of rising and setting of the stars: some are called “cosmic,” others “solar.” A cosmic rising occurs whenever a star, as the revolving heavens turn, begins to rise above the earth so that it can be seen by us, unless the sun prevents it. Conversely, setting occurs when the star is again hidden beneath the earth in the west, removed from our sight. These risings and settings happen daily to all stars because of the complete revolution of the heavens.

Solar risings and settings are as follows. Whenever the sun is joined to a star within fifteen degrees—or, as we commonly say, fifteen divisions—of a sign, he conceals it with the magnitude of his light so that it cannot be seen. The star is then said to be “under the rays.” After the sun has advanced beyond fifteen degrees, or, according to Pliny, eleven degrees, the star begins to emerge from the rays and appear in the morning before the rising sun; this is called the morning rising.

When the sun has advanced until he is 180 degrees from the star, he is said to be opposite it. Afterward, when the star begins to rise fifteen degrees after the sun has set, this is called the evening rising.

Again, when the sun approaches the star and begins to come within fifteen degrees of it, this is called the evening setting, because the star sets shortly after the sun. Finally, when the sun again begins to approach the fifteen degrees nearest the opposition, because at that point the star is last seen setting as the sun rises, this is called the morning setting.

In the case of Venus and Mercury, it would be more accurate to call the evening risings and morning settings “emergences” and “concealments,” because these two stars always follow and cling to the sun. When they begin in the morning to emerge from the rays and appear, they are said to rise with a morning rising. When they return to the sun in the morning and seem to be concealed, they are said to set with a morning setting. Similarly, when they emerge in the evening, they are said to rise, and when they return beneath the rays, to set.

This is what Boethius means here by saying that Venus rises in the evening: she begins to appear after the sun has set. Observe this explanation carefully, since learned writers frequently mention the matter and rarely explain it with sufficient precision. AGRICOLA.

### “Habenas”

*Habenae* is derived from *habere*, “to hold” or “to restrain,” because horses are checked and held by them. Here the word is used figuratively for order or course. AGRICOLA.

### “Frondifluae”

Because leaves flow or fall from trees. AGRICOLA.

### “Brumae”

*Bruma* is derived from brevity, since it is the shortest day of the entire year, just as the solstice is the longest day. Pliny is the authority for this. AGRICOLA.

### “Aestas”

It is derived from *aestus*, “heat.” AGRICOLA.

### “Agiles”

Properly, we call those *agiles* who are busy doing something. Horace, in the first book of the *Epistles*:

> Now I become active and move amid civic waves.

Here it means “swift.” AGRICOLA.

### “Horas”

*Hora* is Greek. AGRICOLA.

### “Boreas”

This is a wind between the north and the summer rising of the sun, called in Latin *Aquilo*. AGRICOLA.

### “Zephyrus”

This is what we call *Favonius* in Latin; it blows from the equinoctial west. AGRICOLA.

### “Arcturus”

In Greek, this means “the bear’s tail.” It is a constellation whose morning rising occurs in November, when farmers sow. AGRICOLA.

### “Semina et segetes”

These differ because *semina* are the seeds scattered in the fields by sowing, whereas *segetes* are what grow in the fields from the seeds. Persius:

> Another crop is still in the grass.

AGRICOLA.

### “Sirius”

This is the star we call the Dog Star. It rises in the morning in July, when the crops ripen. AGRICOLA.

### “Stationis”

A *statio* was the place in a camp assigned to each soldier, whether for keeping watch or for defense. Quintilian, in *The Marian Soldier*:

> The soldier is led away from his assigned station.

The word also means a place in which a person or thing stands. Virgil, in the second book of the *Aeneid*:

> Now only a bay, and an unsafe anchorage for ships.

AGRICOLA.

### “Omnia certo fine, etc.”

The uneducated, whose productions are always full, commonly criticize Boethius here, as though he had not thought correctly or worthily of a Christian. Since Boethius says, “You alone reject the acts of human beings,” they interpret him as saying that God has placed human affairs outside his care and does not govern human actions by his providence.

But Boethius does not say this. He merely laments that, while everything else is governed in proper order and does not err or sin, human beings alone have been given the power to act well or badly. This is not difficult to see from what he says at the end of the poem: “And the heaven which you govern,” and so forth. Its meaning is no different from what we pray every day: “Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.” AGRICOLA.

### “Gubernas”

*Guberno* is said to derive from the Greek *κυβερνάω* (*kybernao*), which has the same meaning. AGRICOLA.

### “Respuis”

That is, “you refuse,” “despise,” or “reject”; it is a rather low metaphor. AGRICOLA.

### “Lubricum”

It is derived from *luere*, “to wash.” Hence *delubra* are called temples, because things that are *luta*, that is, wet, are slippery. AGRICOLA.

### “Noxia”

It is derived from *nocere*, “to harm.” AGRICOLA.

### “Poena”

It is derived from *punio*, just as *moenia*, “walls,” comes from *munio*. AGRICOLA.

### “Resident”

Used for *sedent*, “they sit,” for metrical reasons. AGRICOLA.

### “Celso”

*Celsus* is derived from the ancient verb *cello*, from which *excello* and *excelsus* also come. But *procello* means “struck down.” Something is called *celsus* because it is *cellatur*, that is, “driven high,” like a spear or missile that has been thrown. AGRICOLA.

### “Justus”

*Justus* is derived from *jus*, “law,” because a just person does what the law prescribes. *Jus* is derived from *jubere*, “to command,” because something is ordered by the command of a higher authority.

*Sanctus* is derived from *sancire*, “to ratify” or “to make inviolable,” because what is sacred may not be violated. We use the word in two ways. We call something sacred when it is untouched by vices. Juvenal:

> An outstanding and holy man.

Sometimes we use it of something to which violence may not be done. Thus we speak of sacred envoys, and Virgil says:

> And the sacred senate.

Juvenal also says:

> Nothing else is sacred or safe from sexual violence.

AGRICOLA.

### “Nil”

It is derived by syncope from *nihil*, just as *mi* comes from *mihi* and *prendo* from *prehendo*. AGRICOLA.

### “Compta colore”

This metaphor seems to have been made by Boethius with insufficient care. Although *comere*, “to adorn,” can properly be used metaphorically, it is not suitable to say that something is adorned with color. The metaphors therefore conflict or disagree with one another. It would have been coherent if he had said “dyed with color,” since both expressions would still have been metaphorical. As it stands, “adorned with color” is no more appropriate than “colored with a comb.”

He attempted to imitate the expression Virgil used:

> And arm the iron with poison.

But that is more restrained. We can appropriately say that a serpent is armed with poison; but one would speak imprudently in saying that something is “adorned” with color. Theophrastus rightly prescribed that metaphor should be modest. AGRICOLA.

### “Sed cum libuit, etc.”

Most people read these three verses as saying that the guilty rejoice in subjecting the highest kings, producing what seems to be a cold and absurd meaning. It will therefore be more correct to read them so that Fortune rejoices in subjecting the highest kings whenever she wishes to use her power, and to write *gaudet*, “she rejoices,” not *gaudent*, “they rejoice.” For Boethius is displaying Fortune’s twofold power: first he shows what she can accomplish by deceit; here he shows what she can accomplish by force, namely, that she can crush the highest kings. AGRICOLA.

### “Vilis”

That is, “despised” or “easily obtained.” Thus we call grain *vile* when it is sold cheaply. Horace:

> The price of friends is low to the good when something is lacking.

AGRICOLA.

### “Salo”

The open sea is called *salum*, from *sal*, “salt.” AGRICOLA.

### “Immensum”

From *metior*, “I measure,” whose participle is *mensum*. AGRICOLA.

Some call the meter of this poem Pindaric, others Archilochian. It is anapaestic, dimeter, and acatalectic. It resembles:

> Avoid Venus’ shrine, discerning girl.

And this passage of Seneca:

> Now rarely the languid stars gleam  
> In the sloping heavens; night, overcome,  
> Draws together her wandering fires. When light returns,  
> She gathers the shining host of Phosphorus.

### “Totis fratris”

This verse should be read as follows:

> With all the flames of the brother, and facing them.

For a trochee has no place in it. AGRICOLA.

### “Hesperus”

Poets and astronomers say different things about Lucifer and Hesperus. The poets assert that on the same day on which Lucifer appears before the rising sun, he follows the setting sun. Some astronomers deny that this can happen on the same day. They admit that Lucifer sometimes precedes the sun in the morning and sometimes follows it after sunset, but on different days. Perhaps the poets were deceived because they saw Lucifer in the morning but Mercury after the sun had set.

Cinna, in the *Smyrna*:

> The morning star saw you weeping,  
> And the same Hesperus saw you weeping shortly afterward.

Horace:

> You always urge, in mournful strains,  
> Your lost Mystes; nor, when evening rises,  
> Do your loves fall away from you,  
> Nor when the swift sun flees.

Virgil, of roses:

> The bright morning star saw this one just being born;  
> Returning late, Hesperus saw it aged.

Manilius, in the first book of the *Astronomica*:

> Nor would Lucifer shine in the morning hours,  
> Had Hesperus not given light to the sunken heavens.

Seneca, in *Hippolytus*:

> Like the herald of the first darkness,  
> The messenger of night, Hesperus,  
> Just washed in the waters; then, with darkness  
> Driven back, that same star is Lucifer.

### “Hominum solos respuis actus”

He speaks as a human being of deeply disturbed mind—not because he truly thinks this, since he is very far from the opinion of the Epicureans, but in order to preserve the propriety of his character and make room for the reproach addressed to Philosophy.

It seems to me that he carefully imitated the tragedian Seneca, whose following verses in *Hippolytus* are very elegant:

> O great parent of the gods, Nature,  
> And you, ruler of the fiery heavens,  
> Who swiftly scatter the stars through the universe  
> And drive along the wandering courses of the constellations,  
> Turning the poles on your rapid axis:  
> Why do you take such care  
> To keep the everlasting paths of the lofty ether in motion,  
> So that now the cold of hoary winter  
> Lays bare the forests,  
> And now the shadows return to the trees,  
> While now the summer’s lion’s neck  
> Cooks Ceres with great heat,  
> And the year moderates its own powers?  
>   
> But why does the same power that governs so much,  
> Beneath which the weights of the vast world,  
> Balanced, pursue their appointed orbits,  
> Remain so unconcerned about human beings—  
> Not anxious to help the good  
> Or to harm the wicked?  
>   
> Fortune governs human affairs without order,  
> And scatters gifts with blind hand,  
> Cherishing the worse.  
> Savage desire conquers the holy.  
> Deceit reigns in the lofty palace.  
> The people delight to hand over the fasces to the base;  
> They honor and hate the same men.  
> Sad virtue has borne perverse rewards for uprightness; evil poverty follows the chaste,  
> While the adulterer, powerful through vice, reigns.

Thus far Seneca.

### “Crimen iniqui”

This verse is monometer, like the following verse of Seneca:

> The adulterer reigns.

### “Mendaci colore”

That is, “with a false pretext” or “false covering.” Take care not to read *mendacii*, “of falsehood.”

## INTO THE FIFTH PROSE

### “Haec ubi continuato”

After Boethius has related his complaints and shown in what respect consolation must be applied to him, Philosophy now begins to undertake the consolation. Everything from this point to the end of the first book is the preface to the consolation.

Accordingly, following the rule of a preface, she first wins over her hearer by reproving his error—his belief that he is in exile—and by this means strengthens his sad and grieving spirit. Then, in the passage beginning “And you indeed concerning your contribution to the common good,” she briefly recalls all the complaints and causes of sorrow that he had previously set forth. By this confession and acknowledgment of the injuries he has suffered, she also makes Boethius well-disposed.

Next, in the passage beginning “But since many,” she makes him teachable by showing the order of the matters to be discussed, and then adds the poem that follows, which concerns the same subject. Finally, she prepares him for the arguments and teachings of the consolation that follow by investigating Boethius’ mind on certain matters. Once he has granted these points, Philosophy’s approach to consoling him will be easier and more secure. This belongs partly to the task of making him teachable, which is appropriate to a preface, and partly to making him attentive.

Moreover, as the author of his restoration to health, by showing that he can be healed she also shows the method by which this can be done. Boethius therefore says that Philosophy, after hearing his complaints, replied that as soon as she saw him weeping, she understood that he was in exile—but that this exile was not exile from a place or from the prison in which he was confined. Rather, it was exile from the true and correct judgment of his own mind.

For, as the Stoics believed, the whole world is the homeland of a good man, and its one Lord and King is God. No one can be expelled from it except the person who expels himself through an error of mind. AGRICOLA.

### “Latravi”

That is, “I spoke with a cry.” It is a metaphor transferred from the irrational to the rational, since barking properly belongs to dogs. AGRICOLA.

### “Placido”

*Placidus* is used of what pleases, as in Ovid’s *Heroides*:

> It is virtue to abstain from pleasing possessions.

Virgil, in the first book of the *Aeneid*:

> At last he rests, composed in tranquil peace.

It is also used of something that is calm, as here, and in Virgil’s *Bucolics*:

> How calm the sea would stand in the winds.

That is, “quiet,” “peaceful,” and “undisturbed.” AGRICOLA.

### “Questibus”

*Questus* sometimes means “complaint,” as here, and is derived from *queror*, “I complain.” Sometimes it means “profit,” in which case it is derived from *quaero*, “I seek,” and is written with the diphthong *ae*. Cicero, in the *Paradoxa*:

> But if, through greed for money, you think no profit dishonorable.

AGRICOLA.

### “Ilico”

That is, “immediately.” AGRICOLA.

### “Exsulem”

*Exsul* is said as though from *extra solum*, “outside one’s soil,” just as *extorris* means someone who is outside his own land. AGRICOLA.

### “Prodidisset”

*Prodere* sometimes means “to make public,” as when we say *memoriae proditum est*, “it has been handed down to memory.” Sometimes it means “to hand over treacherously,” as when we say that a town has been betrayed. AGRICOLA.

### “Procul”

As though from *porro ab oculis*, “far from the eyes,” hence “far away.” AGRICOLA.

### “Patria”

The word is derived from paternal habitation and is used relatively: “This is my homeland; that is your homeland.” It is not properly said that someone is “the lord of many homelands,” but rather “of many regions,” “provinces,” or—using the term most common among the ancients—“lands.” Thus they spoke of the land of Italy and the land of Attica.

When Virgil says, in the first book of the *Aeneid*:

> What barbarous homeland permits such customs?

“Your” must be understood. Likewise, when we call someone “lord” or “slave,” saying “O lord” or “O slave,” we always understand “my.” AGRICOLA.

### “Enim”

Neither Cicero nor anyone after him places *enim* at the beginning of a speech. In Terence, however, it is found at the beginning of the *Andria*:

> For indeed it contains a sufficiently tested example of self-restraint.

This entire thought of Boethius is taken from Socrates, who, when asked what country he belonged to, replied that he was a citizen of the world. AGRICOLA.

### “Quae non uti Atheniensium, etc.”

He says that the world is not governed by the will of a multitude, as Athens once was. There are three forms of government. Some states are governed by the rule of one person, which is called kingship; others by the power of a few, which we call aristocratic government; others by the will of the people, which is called popular government. The last is generally the most turbulent and seditious.

The Greek written here is as follows: “But of these, one”—*kyrios*, that is, “lord”—“is”—*estin*, that is, “is”; “one”—*basileus*, that is, “king.” AGRICOLA.

### “Frequentia civium”

That is, “a multitude.” We also speak of people as *frequentes* when many have assembled. Sallust, in *The Catiline*:

> Because they had not yet assembled in large numbers.

We also speak of places as *frequentia* when many people gather there. Livy, in book 32:

> He occupies the least frequented places of the city.

AGRICOLA.

### “Cujus agi frenis, etc.”

The thought is taken from Cicero’s *Pro Cluentio*, where he says:

> We are servants of the laws so that we may be free.

AGRICOLA.

### “An ignoras, etc.”

The common people do not understand this passage. At Rome there was a law that whoever lived there, even if he had been expelled from his own homeland into exile, would nevertheless not be considered an exile while he was at Rome, because they wanted Rome to be the common dwelling place of the entire world. Boethius now applies this analogy to his earlier statement that he was born from the world. AGRICOLA.

### “Exsulare”

This is a noun of the type *exsularis*, like *insularis*. AGRICOLA.

### “At quisquis”

The thought is that no one can be expelled into exile from the state of the wise person unless he wishes to be. Therefore, as soon as someone begins not to wish to dwell in that state, he also begins not to dwell there and becomes an exile. For it is solely by the will that we remain subject to God, and by which we withdraw from his rule. AGRICOLA.

### “Itaque non tamen, etc.”

Philosophy says this: “Although I see you here in prison and outside your homeland, I do not for that reason think you an exile. Rather, I think you one because you have departed from the constancy and tranquility of your mind.” AGRICOLA.

Ebore ac vitro] It was the custom of the ancients to adorn their libraries most carefully with images of distinguished men and commanders of every kind, made of ivory and glass. Ivory is the elephant’s tooth, of which a pair grows on either side of its mouth, sometimes reaching ten feet in length; some call it the elephant’s horn. AGRICOLA.

Sententias] We sometimes call *sententia* a brief saying that makes a general pronouncement concerning something relevant to human life, such as: “Everyone is such as the friends he enjoys”; “The miser lacks as much what he possesses as what he does not possess.” Sometimes we call every thought or determination of our mind a *sententia*. Thus Virgil:

> Now what judgment, father, sworn, has changed you?

At other times we call the meaning or thought of the words we speak a *sententia*; it is so called from *sentire*, “to feel,” because in this way we feel—that is, judge. AGRICOLA.

Et tu quidem] Philosophy briefly repeats Boethius’ complaint and recalls its particulars; and, as we said earlier, she wins his goodwill by acknowledging as true what is plainly evident in the text. AGRICOLA.

In commune bonum] That is, for the public benefit. AGRICOLA.

[Col. 0942A] Pauca] There is this difference between *paucum* and *parvum*: *paucum* relates chiefly to number, while *parvum* refers to quantity. Thus two giants are few people, but not small ones; conversely, a thousand pygmies are small, but not few. AGRICOLA.

Honestate] Because many things were being charged against him which it would have been shameful for Boethius to deny—for example, that he had wished the senate to remain unharmed, along with other matters of the same kind. AGRICOLA.

Strictim] That is, briefly; from *stringere*, “to tighten” or “to bind together.” AGRICOLA.

Vulgi] *Vulgus* is found in both the masculine and neuter genders. Virgil, in Book II of the *Aeneid*:

> Hence to scatter ambiguous voices  
> among the people.

Horace, in the *Odes*:

[Col. 0942B]

> I hate the profane crowd and keep it at a distance.

AGRICOLA.

Damna] I think *damnum* is derived from *dare*, “to give,” that is, “to expend,” just as *scamnum* comes from *scandere*, “to climb.” It should therefore be written without *p*, like *scamnum*, *somnus*, and *temno*; and, to state the matter once for all, the letter *p* never occurs between *m* and *n* in Latin words. The *m* itself, as Quintilian testifies in Book I of the *Institutio Oratoria*, should in Latin pronunciation be sounded almost as though it were the letter *n*. AGRICOLA.

Postremo adversus, etc.] Boethius did this in the poem:

> O creator of the star-bearing universe.

AGRICOLA.

Incanduit] That is, “burned up” or “burst into flame.” Properly, *candere* means “to be white” and almost to give off a gleam. Virgil, in Book I of the *Aeneid*:

> He poured it between the horns of the gleaming cow.

Horace, in the *Odes*:

> Apollo the prophet, clothed in a cloud  
> that covered his gleaming shoulders.

The word was then extended metaphorically, so that things which have been set on fire are called *candentia*, “glowing.” Horace:

> He would say that the bellies of his grandsons  
> ought to be burned with a glowing blade.

Hence, just as we speak of anger “burning,” so we speak of *excandescere* and *incandescere*, “to grow hot” or “to flare up.” AGRICOLA.

Musae] That is, “of poetry.” By synecdoche, he has put the cause for the effect. AGRICOLA.

Pax] *Pax* is said to derive from the old verb *pago*, whence also come *compages* and *pactum*, whose perfect form was *pegi*. Hence it seems that *impigo, impegi* should be said, rather than *impingo*, which would require *impigi* with a short middle syllable, just as *pepigi*, from which it is compounded, has it. AGRICOLA.

Vota] Sometimes *votum* means what is promised to God for the purpose of obtaining or entreating something; sometimes it means a desire or prayers. Thus we say that something has happened “according to one’s wish,” and here he says *vota*, that is, “you have offered prayers.” AGRICOLA.

Sed quoniam plurimus] Here Philosophy makes him receptive, showing in what order she intends to discuss matters relevant to Boethius’ consolation. She wishes first—in this, the second book—to employ gentler remedies, so as to prepare him, as it were, to receive sharper remedies later. *Plurimus* means “very abundant”; this usage arises more from ordinary human speech than from the inherent force or true signification of the word. AGRICOLA.

Affectuum] *Affectus* is what the Greeks call πάθος (*pathos*), which our people today, ignorant of Cicero and the other Latin-speaking authors, call “passion of the soul.” It is a certain greater movement of the soul that eventually comes to an end; for if it persists, it loses the name *affectus* and is called a habit. Thus anger is an affection, whereas irascibility is a settled disposition. Cicero, however, calls *affectio* every agitation not only of the soul but also of the body—what our dialecticians call a disposition. In the same way, what they call a habit would more properly be called a custom, practice, or habituation: thus a trembling caused by fear is an affection, whereas a trembling left by old age or illness is a habit.

AGRICOLA.

Incubuit] This is said metaphorically, meaning “attacked” or “invaded”; properly, it means “to lie upon something.” Virgil:

> And it settled upon the whole.

AGRICOLA.

Uti nunc mentis] This is expressed in that figure of speech by which we say, “I am of a cheerful mind.” Ovidius:

> And you will be of a better countenance.

That form of expression has a pleasing and not inelegant grace. AGRICOLA.

Nondum te validiora, etc.] Many and far-reaching metaphors are joined together here, and the speech almost turns into an allegory. AGRICOLA.

Non quidem pulsus es, sed aberrasti] He speaks according to the Stoic view, who say that a wise man cannot be expelled from his state unless, overcome by depraved desires, he himself strays from it. Cicero, in the *Paradoxa*:

> The wise man’s spirit is fortified as though by walls—by greatness of judgment, endurance of human affairs, contemplation of fortune, and finally all the virtues. Who, then, could overcome and storm it, when he cannot even be expelled from the state?

Ἀλλὰ εἷς βασιλεὺς ἔστιν, εἷς κοίρανος] These words occur in a copy which the most learned Caesarius lent me. They are interpreted as follows: “But there is one king, one lord.” In the same margin they are also written in this form: Ἀλλὰ εἷς κοίρανός ἔστιν, εἷς βασιλεύς—“But there is one lord, one king.” In the letter of Aedicollius they appear somewhat differently: Εἷς κοίρανος ἔστω, εἷς βασιλεύς—“Let there be one lord, one king.” Agricola, however, reads them in this manner: εἷς κύριός ἐστιν, εἷς βασιλεύς—“There is one lord, one king.”

[Col. 0943D] This is taken from Homer, who says in the second rhapsody of the *Iliad*:

> Οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη, εἷς κοίρανος ἔστω,  
> Εἷς βασιλεύς

That is:

> The rule of many is not good; let there be one lord,  
> one king.

As Philip Beroaldus prefers, this may be rendered in one line:

> It is not fitting that many should rule; let one prince command,  
> one king.

We may also render it:

> The rule of many is not good; let there be one lord,  
> one king.

Tuae civitatis] The state of the wise. Cicero, in Book III of *De Finibus*, reports the following concerning the Stoics: “They believe that the world is ruled by the divine will, and that it is, as it were, the common city and state of human beings and gods, and that each of us is a part of that world.” The same author, in the *Paradoxa*: “Death is terrible to those whose whole existence is extinguished with life, but not to those whose glory cannot die. Exile is terrible to those whose place of habitation is, as it were, confined within boundaries, but not to those who say that the whole world is one city.” Again, in the *Tusculan Disputations*: “Thus Teucer’s saying may be adapted to every circumstance: ‘Wherever one is well, there is one’s fatherland.’” When Socrates was asked of what country he was, he replied, “Of the world.” For he considered himself an inhabitant and citizen of the entire world.

Prosper, the learned Christian poet:

> I do not fear exile; the world is one home for all.

Saint Ambrose, in his sixth letter: “Wherever the wise man goes, he is everywhere a citizen; everywhere he understands that everything is his; nowhere does he regard himself as a foreigner or a guest.” Theophrastus used to say that the learned man, among all people, alone is neither a foreigner in foreign places nor without friends. There is an old proverb: “Every land is a fatherland,” by which we are reminded that a wise and good man is happy wherever in the world he lives. Ovid, in the *Fasti*:

> Every soil is a fatherland to the brave, as the sea is to fishes.

Papinius, in the *Thebaid*:

> Every soil is native to a human being.

Ei jus exsulare non esse] That is, that it is not permitted him to be an exile, or to endure exile. In my judgment, *exsulare* here is a verb, although Agricola thinks otherwise. It may also be explained as *jus exsulare*, that is, “the right of going into exile,” just as Horace says:

> It is time for you to depart;

that is, “it is time for departing.”

INTO METER VI

Cum Phoebi radiis] This poem depends upon what precedes.
