Since Philosophy has said that she wishes first to soften Boethius’ troubles and pains with gentler remedies, so that afterward he may become more receptive to sharper medicines, in this poem she shows, as though by a general principle, that everything should be done in its proper season. If we hurry before the proper time, or attempt something outside its season, we shall labor in vain and without result.

The meter is Glyconic, named after its author Glycon: a trimeter, consisting of three feet—a spondee and two dactyls. He says that anyone who wishes to sow in summer, when everything is burning with heat, will hope in vain for a harvest; likewise, in winter one must not gather violets, nor in spring collect grapes. God has assigned every thing its proper seasons, and whoever does not follow them will not bring his undertakings to a happy conclusion. AGRICOLA.

Cum Phoebi radiis grave, etc.] The whole expression is a periphrasis—that is, a circumlocution—for summer. AGRICOLA.

Cancri] Cancer is a sign of the zodiac in which the sun reaches its summer solstice, at which time summer is hottest. AGRICOLA.

Negantibus] *Negare* is used both of refusing in words, as in Terence’s *Eunuchus*:

> He says, “I say”; he denies, “I deny”—

and of failing to comply in action. Lucan, in Book I:

> And to stand for long  
> was denied to the highest.

AGRICOLA.

Sulcis] A *sulcus* is the elongated hollow left in the fields between the earth thrown aside on either side by the plow. AGRICOLA.

Credidit] Properly, *credere* means to place trust in someone. Hence we sometimes use it of entrusting or handing something over to another, such as money or a secret: for we generally entrust nothing to someone whose good faith we do not trust. AGRICOLA.

Quernas] This is the proper possessive form from *quercus*, “oak”; not *quercinas*, as the common people barbarously say. The *quercus* is an acorn-bearing tree unknown in our regions; what we call *quercus* is properly *robur*. AGRICOLA.

Purpureum nemus] Boethius used this adjective without sufficient consideration. He is describing winter, during which he says that one should not go to a purple grove to gather violets. Yet at that time a grove is never purple, since there are then no flowers. Thus he seems to have said “purple grove” rather carelessly, unless he was alluding to the Greek property of the word. The Greeks say πορφύρεον, that is, *porro φυρόμενον*, “thoroughly mixed and agitated.” Hence he may have called the grove “purple” as being troubled and disturbed by the winds of winter. AGRICOLA.

Nemus] It is said to derive from the Greek νέμω, “to pasture.” The ancients pastured herds in groves, as is still done in many regions. AGRICOLA.

Lecturus] Properly, *lego* means “I gather”; hence we also say that we “read” letters, because by gathering and joining them we form words, and from words we form sentences. AGRICOLA.

Inhorruit] That is, “was shaken” or “was roughened.” Properly, *horrere* means to be shaken by fear or cold. Juvenal:

> Is it merely madness to squander a hundred thousand,  
> and not return a cloak to a trembling slave?

AGRICOLA.

Vernos] *Ver*, “spring,” like many Latin words, is derived from the Greek ἦρ, with a letter prefixed; just as the Greeks say ἴς, while we say *vis*. AGRICOLA.

Palmites] The branches of vines are called *palmites*, because, as though by feeling their way, they cling to the supports by which they are sustained. AGRICOLA.

Autumno] I think *autumnus* was so called because it is the source of all the labors undertaken in cultivating the earth throughout the year, since autumn brings back the fruit of those labors. AGRICOLA.

Bacchus] This is a Greek name signifying the god of wine; in Latin he is called Father Liber. AGRICOLA.

Tempora] *Tempus* seems to be derived from *tendere*, “to stretch,” because it stretches through everything and embraces all things. AGRICOLA.

Aptans] That is, “fitting” or “adapting.” It is said to derive from the old verb *apo, apis, apere*, meaning “I join together,” whence also *apiscor*, from which *adipiscor* is formed, just as *facio* gives *faciscor*, and yet *proficiscor*. From this also comes *apex*, which, according to Festus Pompeius, was a woolen thread with which the flamen bound his head, keeping his hair from spreading loose. AGRICOLA.

Officiis] Sometimes *officium* means merit or service. Cicero, in Book I of the *Letters*: “By every service, or rather by every expression of devotion, I satisfy all others in their dealings with you.” Hence *officiosus* is also used in this sense. At other times it means what someone does according to his profession: the physician’s duty is to heal, the builder’s to construct, and the good man’s to act rightly. Cicero therefore entitled a book *On Duties*, because he discusses there the duties of a good man. AGRICOLA.

Praecipiti] This is derived from *prae* and *caput*, “head.” A person is said to be thrown headlong when he is cast from a height so that his head goes first and his feet follow. The term is then also applied to a place that rises directly and perpendicularly upward, rather than sloping gradually and gently. AGRICOLA.

Via] As Varro says, it is derived from *vehere*, “to carry,” as though *veha*, because things are carried along it, just as *iter* comes from *ire*, “to go.” AGRICOLA.

INTO PROSE VI

Primum igitur] Here Philosophy prepares Boethius’ mind, through a series of questions, to receive more effectively what she is about to offer for his consolation. Just as geometers propose certain assumptions which, once granted, enable them to demonstrate from them what they wish to their opponent, so Philosophy proceeds here.

There are two principal considerations by which it can be shown that we should not be distressed by whatever adversity befalls us. The first is that God governs the world by his providence; therefore it is certain that nothing is done by him in the world except for the good. Whatever, then, is sent to us by him is good, and we ought not to grieve because of it, whatever it may be.

The second is that human beings have been endowed with an immortal soul, made to attain eternal blessedness. No one, therefore, ought to grieve because of any adversity, since adversities are brief, and through them the way to blessedness is opened to us.

Boethius had to grant both of these points, not only because he was a Christian, but also because of the philosophical school he followed, the Old Academy founded by Plato. The Epicureans denied both providence and the immortality of the soul, as did almost all the ancient natural philosophers, whose view Lucretius has explained at length in his poem. The Stoics affirmed God’s providence governing the world, but denied the immortality of souls. If, therefore, Philosophy had been disputing with them, one or both of these propositions would first have had to be established, lest the argument proceed from unacknowledged premises. In the present case it was enough to remind the believing Boethius of them.

Boethius quickly grants the first point. Regarding the second, Philosophy tries to draw it out through many questions, preserving the propriety of Boethius’ character: he is sad and disturbed in mind and, because of his grief, cannot understand what Philosophy is saying. He gives no definite answer, especially since Philosophy does not openly propose the point but wishes to elicit it through other questions.

She divides this second point into two assumptions. From the immortality of the soul, joined to the fact that the world is governed by providence, it follows that God is the soul’s end—that is, blessedness, for which it has been ordered by God.

Philosophy therefore first asks Boethius whether he believes that the world is governed by divine reason. Boethius readily admits this, just as he had already sung in the preceding poem. Philosophy then asks whether he knows by what governing instruments the world is ruled. He replies that he scarcely understands what she is saying and therefore cannot easily answer her questions. Philosophy accordingly adds that it is not surprising if, in such ignorance or error, certain disturbances have invaded his mind.

Strictly speaking, however, this later question is superfluous after the earlier one, and Boethius does not seem to have carefully distinguished the nature of these questions. For if it is granted that the world is not governed by random accidents but by divine reason, what need was there to ask afterward by what governing instruments it is ruled, when the earlier confession has already established that the world is governed by divine reason—that is, by providence?

The first question should rather have been whether he believed that any God exists, since some entirely denied this. Others, such as Epicurus and his followers, said that God exists but is idle and does not care for human affairs. Both groups therefore held that the world is governed by chance. Once Boethius had granted that God exists, it would still have been necessary to ask whether he believed that the world is governed by God’s providence. No one has ever been found who, while believing that God the creator presides over the world, also thought that affairs are driven by chance; rather, he believed that everything is governed by providence. AGRICOLA.

Sed dic mihi, meministi, etc.] Here Philosophy attempts to elicit the second assumption: that human beings were made to attain blessedness. She therefore asks whether Boethius remembers what the end of things is. Boethius says that he has forgotten what it is.

Philosophy again attempts to draw it out through another question, asking whether he knows what the beginning of all things is. He replies that it is God, as he said shortly before. Philosophy therefore says that it is strange that, while he knows the beginning of all things, he does not know their end.

This is because, if he knows that God is the beginning of all things, he ought to know that God made all things to be good, since the goodness of each thing is its blessedness. Therefore God willed everything to be blessed, insofar as the nature of each thing was capable of blessedness, as Plato says.

Then, in the passage beginning “But this also,” she asks a third question concerning the immortality of the soul. She asks whether Boethius remembers that he is human, and then whether he knows what a human being is. Boethius answers, following Porphyry, that a human being is a mortal rational animal, although it would have been more correct to define a human being as an animal composed of a body and a rational, immortal soul.

Since Boethius has forgotten that he consists of an immortal soul, it is not surprising that he is disturbed by these brief adversities. Philosophy therefore says that this is even the principal cause of his trouble: he has forgotten himself and ceased to know himself.

[Col. 0948A] She gathers these three assumptions in her customary manner, beginning with the last. Because he has forgotten himself—that is, because he does not know that he is destined for immortal blessedness—he laments as though he were an exile and deprived of his own goods. This cannot be, since nothing mortal can be either good or evil to what is immortal.

Next, because he does not know the end of things, he is deceived into thinking those people happy whose crimes prosper. He ought instead to regard them as the most wretched, since the gravest punishments for their crimes await them.

Finally, because he thinks that there is no providence governing the world, he supposes that everything occurs by uncertain chance and accident. These errors are sufficiently powerful to overthrow and destroy the mind entirely. AGRICOLA.

Pateris] *Patior* sometimes means “I permit,” as here, and as in Cicero against Catiline: “I will not permit it; I will not endure it; I will not allow it.” Sometimes it means “to be afflicted.” Juvenal:

> When they begin to suffer pain in the side  
> together with a fever that keeps one awake.

AGRICOLA.

Statum] *Status* sometimes denotes the posture of a body standing upright, as when we speak of standing, sitting, and reclining; sometimes it means a condition. Virgil:

> What is the condition of ancient Latium?

AGRICOLA.

Curationis] Properly, *curare* means to apply care. Since the physician’s chief care is directed toward curing the sick, *curare* also means “to heal.” Sometimes, however, it does not mean to heal, but to attend to the patient’s health; thus a physician is said to care for a patient even when the patient is not healed. Horace, in Book II of the *Epistles*, nevertheless says:

[Col. 0948C]

> You would avoid being treated  
> by a root or herb that accomplishes nothing.

A person may therefore be treated with a root that accomplishes nothing, but in no way healed. AGRICOLA.

Arbitratu] That is, by will or judgment. The ancients used *arbitrari* to mean “to inspect” or “to learn”; hence one who speaks alone with someone is said to speak “with the arbiters removed.” An *arbiter* is also called a judge. AGRICOLA.

Ullum] Some wish *ullus* to be derived from *unus*. AGRICOLA.

Conditore] *Condere* sometimes means “to make,” as here and above:

> O creator of the star-bearing universe.

Sometimes it means “to store up.” Horace, in Book I of the *Odes*:

> If he has stored him in his own granary.

[Col. 0948D] At other times it means “to hide.” Virgil, in the *Bucolics*:

> I have often seen [—] turn into a wolf and hide himself in these woods.

AGRICOLA.

Exsortes] *Exsors* is derived from *ex* and *sors*, as though “outside one’s lot,” that is, one’s share; it denotes someone wholly deprived of a thing. AGRICOLA.

Papae] This is an interjection expressing astonishment or admiration, derived from the Greek Βαβαί. AGRICOLA.

Sententia locatus] The metaphor “to be placed in an opinion” seems cold and sluggish. It would have been more correct to say *utcunque* or “having placed an opinion in him”; still better and more modest would have been: “Why, possessing so wholesome an opinion,” or “being supported, endowed, or strengthened by such an opinion, should he be sick?” AGRICOLA.

[Col. 0949A] Conjecto] That is, “I suspect.” Hence interpreters of dreams and similar matters are called *conjectores*, because they infer future events from suspicions. AGRICOLA.

Ambigis] *Ambigere* is derived from *am*, meaning “around” in compounds, and *ago*, with the letter *b* inserted between them. AGRICOLA.

Num inquit, etc.] The meaning is: “I did not doubt that there was some error in you which was allowing this pain caused by adversity to enter your mind.” AGRICOLA.

Hiante valli robore] The comparison is drawn from fortifications. When part of a rampart is missing so that it gapes—that is, is open—it gives enemies access to the defenses. AGRICOLA.

Morbus] Here the word is used metaphorically. I think it is derived from *mors*, “death,” because illness leads to death. AGRICOLA.

Exstirpare] This is derived from *stirps*, which in the masculine gender means “root,” as though “to tear out by the roots.” AGRICOLA.

Vel maximam] Here *vel* is not used disjunctively but has almost the force of “even.” Thus Propertius:

> In a single night anyone may even become a god.

AGRICOLA.

Reconciliandae sospitatis] This is a harsh metaphor, used instead of “restoring” or “recovering.” Properly, people who have become enemies after being friends are *reconciled* when they return to friendship. The word *concilium*, “assembly,” derives from *concio*, “a gathering of people”; hence *conciliare* means to bring people into agreement.

Cicero severely censures in his *Tiro* a somewhat more restrained but not entirely dissimilar metaphor, when Tiro had said *valetudini fideliter serviendo*, “by faithfully serving health.” AGRICOLA.

Nequam] That is, “not belonging to anyone,” meaning a person who is worthless and of no value. Its opposite is someone called *frugi*, who provides some good fruit and usefulness from himself. Thus Plautus called a counterfeit coin *nummus nequam*, “a worthless coin.” AGRICOLA.

Vices] That is, changes and alternations. AGRICOLA.

[Note: [Col. 0949D] Agricola’s commentaries end here; from this point onward Murmellius alone will comment. EDIT.]

The remaining works of Rudolph Agricola which he is said to have written on Boethius have not come into my hands. Would that they had! For just as I would gladly share these with you, so too would I have shared those. For the rest, courteous reader, I ask you to be content for the time being with these writings of ours, whatever their quality, until you have obtained better ones.

Sed sospitatis auctori grates] He makes Boethius attentive and well disposed at the same time, saying that there is no reason entirely to despair of his recovery, but that thanks should be given to God because the elements of restored health remain.

Sospitatis] Safety; soundness.

Auctori] To God.

Grates] We should supply “let us give thanks.”

Sed quoniam firmioribus] He shows by what means Boethius’ health can be restored.

Tempus uti] This is a figurative expression for *tempus utendi*, “a time for using.” Thus Horace in the *Epistles*:

> It is time for you to depart.

Propertius:

> Now is the time to depart.

Hanc] The darkness of the disturbances.

Fomentis] Remedies. Philosophy promises Boethius two kinds of remedies. First, gentle and moderate remedies to remove the darkness of the disturbances, which prevents the mind from contemplating truth. Then sharper and stronger remedies, so that, once he has perceived the appearance of false happiness, he may be able to behold the form of true blessedness.

INTO METER VII

This poem is Adonic, consisting of a dactyl and a spondee. Philosophy teaches through three very beautiful comparisons that the human mind can be so obscured by the darkness of disturbances and so bound by the chains of the passions that, once reduced to servitude, it is sometimes utterly unable to perceive the truth.

It should be understood that there are four principal disturbances of the soul, also called affections, and by younger writers passions. Two arise from an opinion of good—joy and hope; two from an opinion of evil—pain and fear.

Joy, also called exultant pleasure—that is, joy raised beyond measure—is an affection of the soul arising from an opinion of some great present good and not obeying reason.

Hope, also called desire, is an affection of the soul arising from an opinion of some future good and not obeying reason.

Pain, or distress, is an affection of the soul arising from an opinion of some great present evil and not obeying reason.

Fear is a disturbance of the soul arising from an opinion of some great impending evil, contrary to right reason.

The great poet has embraced these disturbances in a few words in Book VI of the *Aeneid*:

> They fear and desire him, grieve and rejoice, nor look back  
> upon the air, shut away in darkness and a blind prison.

[Col. 0950C] Every vice arises from these. Hence Francesco Filelfo, in the *Satires*:

> A disturbed mind dares every disgrace and crime.

We must therefore make every effort above all to eradicate these disturbances, or at least to subject them to the rule of reason, so that we may attain blessedness.

Saint Ambrose, in Book II of the *Letters*: “The wise man rises up as a victor, having subdued and triumphed over lust, fear, cowardice, melancholy, and the other vices, until he expels them from possession of his mind, drives them beyond all their boundaries and limits, and keeps them at bay.”

Giovanni Boccaccio, in the *Bucolics*:

> O Damon, Damon, how greatly each person has blessed himself  
> who has been able to calm the mind’s raging swellings.

Baptista Mantuanus:

[Col. 0950D]

> It is a difficult thing to conquer others; the greater victory  
> is to compose the storms of one’s own mind,  
> to subdue fears, and defeat the swellings  
> of joys, and to place hope beneath a heavy yoke.

Seven years ago we too played at this theme in the *Moral Eclogues*:

> By mighty wars subdue your spirits;  
> let anger be restrained  
> by the bond of peace;  
> let gnawing care remain far away,  
> and let depraved desire be kept at bay.  
>   
> Let no one boast of capturing cities  
> in shining armor;  
> let no one admire famous triumphs  
> with which tyrants so often swell.  
>   
> Whoever has driven away exultant joy  
> with a tranquil mind,  
> and conquered harsh sorrows,  
> panting hopes,  
> and fearful dread in his heart—  
>   
> he alone has deserved the laurel crown,  
> he alone the purple,  
> triumphing peacefully.  
> to whom true pleasure grants  
> a seat nearest to the blessed.

And in Book IV of the *Elegies*:

> The splendid gifts of fortune do not make a king,  
> nor the purple garment, nor a noble house.  
> He is a king who governs himself,  
> restraining with the reins of right reason  
> the harmful desires of his mind.  
>   
> One is not rightly judged brave  
> who, excessively bold,  
> engages in grim wars with a terrible body.  
>   
> Brave is the devout and noble mind,  
> endowed with the exceptional gift of virtue,  
> conscious of exalted justice,  
> which subdues depraved affections  
> under the proper governance  
> and vigorously conquers bodily allurements.  
>   
> At its command seductive pleasure flees,  
> and pain, restless hope, and fear  
> take flight.

Volvens] Agitating; driving into turbulence.

Turbidus auster] A turbulent wind; a species is put for the genus.

[Col. 0951B] Aestum] The movement of the sea.

Vitrea] Transparent.

Par] Similar.

[Col. 0952A] Visibus obstat] It does not allow sight to pass through.

Defluus] Flowing downward.

Resistit] Delays; holds back.

Obice] By an obstruction.

Saxi soluti rupe] Loosened from the rock.

Lumine] By sight.

Cernere] To see.

Verum] Truth.

Carpere callem] To go. Thus Ovid:

> If a wheel is lacking, travel the road on foot.

Nubila] Obscured; disturbed.

Ubi] In which mind.

Haec] These disturbances, concerning which Filelfo writes in the *Satires*:

> One fears, another desires; here pain rages, there pleasure.

And we, in Book I of the *Elegies*:

[Col. 0952B]

> Gnawing cares exhaust languishing hearts—  
> here hope, there fear, joy and pain.

Regnant] They rule; they dominate.

BOOK TWO

[Col. 0951]

INTO PROSE I

In the preceding volume the causes of Boethius’ complaint, pain, and distress were set forth. Having examined them thoroughly, Philosophy, the highly skilled physician of languishing minds, now supplies in this book the remedies she promised above—remedies that are gentler, so that in the following volume she may apply sharper ones more effectively.

The entire discussion now aims to show that the goods of fortune should by no means be counted among our goods.

[Col. 0951C] Post haec] After the immediately preceding poem had been sung.

Ubi] After; when.

Modesta] Moderate; restrained.

Collegit] Restored; strengthened.

Exorsa est] She began to speak.

Habitum] Affection; discourse.

Tabescis] You are wasting away.

Pervertit] Disturbs; throws into confusion.

Illius prodigii] Of that monstrous fortune.

Fucos] Deceptions; frauds. Terence, in the *Eunuchus*:

> A deception has been contrived for the woman through the opening in the roof.

Quos eludere nititur] Giovanni Campano:

> Fortune lends a hand to those to whom she intends to do harm:  
> she smiles to entice them, extends her hand to seize them.

Seneca:

[Col. 0951D]

> When Fortune flatters, she comes to capture her victim.

Incessere] To attack; to assail. Gellius: “When he assailed me with insults.”

Adyto] An *adyton* is a more secluded place in a temple, to which access was permitted only to the priest. Virgil:

> And from the sanctuary he brings back these sorrowful words.

Here understand it as Philosophy’s inner sanctuary, since she is sacred and worthy of veneration like a divinity.

Verum omnis subita mutatio rerum, non sine quodam quasi conflictu contingit animorum] This is a beautiful and most truthful observation, and it agrees with the following saying of Seneca:

> Every unforeseen event causes greater harm.

And with another saying of the same author:

> Every evil is grievous when it lies before the eyes unseen.

Conflictu] Agitation; torment.

[Col. 0952B] Tempus haurire] For *tempus hauriendi*, “a time for drinking in.” Thus Horace in the *Epistles*:

> It is time for you to depart.

Propertius:

> Now is the time to depart.

Suadela] The power and ability to persuade.

Nostra instituta] The precepts of Philosophy.

Musica] Poetry, which Terence also calls “music.”

[Col. 0952C] Haec natura] Namely, that it is changeable.

In ipsa sui mutabilitate constantiam] Ovid, in the *Tristia*:

> With uncertain steps changeable Fortune wanders,  
> and remains fixed and tenacious in no place.  
>   
> Now she remains cheerful, now assumes a bitter expression,  
> and is constant only in her fickleness.

Ambiguos vultus] Uncertain faces—now cheerful, now sorrowful.

Caeci numinis] Fortune, whom the ancients imagined as a blind goddess. Pliny, in Book II, chapter 7 of the *Natural History*: “Throughout the whole world, in every place and at every hour, Fortune alone is invoked by human voices and alone named; she alone is accused, alone prosecuted, alone contemplated, alone praised, alone criticized, and amid insults alone worshiped. She is changeable and, in the opinion of many, even blind; wandering, fickle, uncertain, variable, and the patron of the undeserving. To her all things are charged, to her all things are credited, and in the whole accounting of mortals she alone fills both pages.”

M. Tullius, in the *Laelius*: “For Fortune herself is not only blind, but usually makes blind those whom she has embraced.”

Francesco Petrarch, in the *Bucolics*:

> Blind Fortune turns loyalty; fate turns all things.

According to Cebes of Thebes, Fortune seems to stand upon a certain round stone; she is not only blind but also insane and deaf. She wanders through every land, taking resources from some and giving them to others; then immediately taking back from those same people what she had given, and bestowing it arbitrarily and unstably upon others.

Pacuvius:

[Col. 0953A]

> Philosophers say that Fortune is insane and brutish,  
> and declare that she is rolling like a rounded stone.  
>   
> They hold that Fortune falls wherever chance  
> has pushed the stone.  
>   
> They call her blind because she sees nothing  
> toward which she should direct herself.  
>   
> They say she is insane because she is savage,  
> uncertain, and unstable;  
>   
> brutish because she cannot distinguish  
> the worthy from the unworthy.

Apuleius, in Book VII of *The Golden Ass*: “It occurred to me that the men of ancient and venerable learning had not without reason imagined and pronounced Fortune blind and completely without eyes, since she always bestows her riches upon the wicked and undeserving and never chooses any mortal by judgment; indeed, she most often dwells with those whom she ought to flee if she saw them from a distance. And what is most extreme of all, she assigns us contradictory, even opposing reputations, so that the bad man glories in the reputation of a good man, while the most innocent person is punished by the mouths of the guilty.”

An vero tu pretiosam] He shows that true happiness does not consist in the goods of Fortune, because she is exceedingly unstable and, by departing, brings far more sorrow than joy she brought with her on arrival.

Nec manendi fida] Valerius Maximus, Book VI: “Those things called human strength and wealth are excessively fleeting and fragile, suited to children. They flow in suddenly and suddenly disperse; they stand rooted firmly in no place and in no person, but, driven here and there by Fortune’s most uncertain breath, plunge those whom they have raised on high, abandoned by an unexpected reversal, miserably into the depths of disaster. Therefore they ought neither to be considered nor called goods, since by the longing they arouse for themselves they double the bitterness of the evils inflicted.”

Allatura moerorem] Baptista Mantuanus, in the first *Parthenice*:

> Sad, hoped-for, proud— … [fragmentary; syntax uncertain]

Now present, she makes him grieve over what has been lost.

“Wisdom measures the outcome of things”] This is a memorable maxim, to which the following passage of Terence in the *Adelphoe* corresponds:

> That is wisdom: not merely to see what lies  
> Before one’s feet, but also to foresee  
> What is still to come.

“In either circumstance”] Either in adversity or in prosperity.

“Nor are Fortune’s threats to be feared”] Seneca the tragedian:

> Let no one trust too greatly in prosperity;  
> Let no one despair of better things after a fall.  
> She mixes these with those, and forbids Clotho  
> To let Fortune stand still; she turns every fate.  
> No one has had the gods so favorable  
> That he could promise himself tomorrow.

[Col. 0953D]

> God whirls our affairs, driven onward by a swift  
> Whirlwind.

Baptista Mantuanus, in the first *Parthenice*:

> This too sometimes consoles embittered minds:  
> Fortune permits nothing to endure, but alternates  
> Her changes; like the wind, she now presses upon the prow,  
> Now the gentle breeze murmurs from the stern.

“Finally, with an even mind”] Philosophy offers Boethius another argument, by which she shows that he ought not to complain about Fortune, as follows: Whoever has once entrusted himself to Fortune’s dominion must necessarily bear it with an even mind. Since you accepted wealth and offices from her, you subjected yourself to Fortune; therefore bear patiently if you are compelled to lay down what was entrusted to you on the condition that it could not remain with you forever.

“Within Fortune’s threshing-floor”] Within the place where Fortune rules. The metaphor seems to be taken from the threshing-floor where, in former times, threshing was carried out by oxen bearing the yoke. Although some read *aleam* (“the die”) not inelegantly, the former reading is more acceptable to me.

“If you were to entrust your sails to the winds”] He proves by highly appropriate comparisons that what we cannot change must be endured, not blamed.

“Turning”] Either turning itself around, or revolving.

“You try”] This should be read interrogatively, and with indignation.

## INTO THE FIRST METER

In this iambic poem, which is called *skázon* (σκάζον), that is, “limping,” he says, in confirmation of what precedes, that Fortune never pleases him more than when, within one and the same hour, she has seen some exceedingly powerful person become exceedingly wretched. This poem resembles the following passage of Persius:

> Nor have I bathed my lips in the horseman’s spring.

“This”] Fortune.

“When”] After she has.

“Has changed”] Has altered.

“Changes”] Alterations of circumstances and conditions.

“Boiling over”] Overflowing beyond measure. There is an old proverb, *tyche Euripos* (τύχη Εὔριπος), “Fortune is the Euripus,” meaning changeable, revolving, or tidal; the metaphor is drawn from the extraordinary rapidity with which the sea of Euripus alternately flows in one direction and then the other. Euripus is the part of the sea between Phocis, a region of Boeotia, and the island of Euboea, mentioned by Pliny in Book II. He says:

> Yet certain places have a nature peculiar to themselves, such as the Euripus of Tauromenium, and more often that of Euboea, which reverses its flow seven times by day and by night, with so rapid a change that, as Pomponius Mela reports, it carries along with it winds and even ships under full sail. Nor has the cause of this astonishing phenomenon yet been adequately investigated by writers, although Livy, in Book VIII of the Second Punic War, thinks that it is swept along by certain winds blowing there.

Seneca, in the *Hercules Oetaeus*:

> The unstable Euripus bends its wandering waves,  
> And bends them back seven times, returning as many times,  
> While Titan sinks his weary light into Ocean.

Cicero, *For Plancius*:

> What strait, what Euripus do you suppose to have such movements, such great and varied agitations, changes, and waves as the elections have disturbances and tides?

It is also known from Suetonius, Tacitus, Seneca, and others that the ancients made temporary artificial lakes called Euripi, in which they staged naval battles; they also called them Niles.

“Some time ago”] A little earlier.

“Dreadful”] To be feared because of its power.

“Overthrows”] Brings to ruin.

“Raises”] Lifts upward and elevates.

“Hard”] Inexorable.

“Proves”] Shows.

“Portent”] A prodigy or miracle.

“Is seen”] Appears.

[Col. 0955A]

“Laid low”] Cast down, wretched.

## INTO THE SECOND PROSE

Here Fortune is introduced as sternly reproaching Boethius because he grieves over what he has lost as though he had lost goods belonging to him personally. If he had possessed them as his own, he could never have lost them. Fortune therefore claims for herself wealth, honors, and other things of that kind, and says that they come and depart together with her. And, to make Boethius’s complaints seem less justified, she promises that whatever she has taken away will be acknowledged as his, and that she will immediately concede this if he can demonstrate that any of those things is truly the property of any mortal. Afterwards she admits that her inconstancy is her strength, and that she is treated most unjustly if she is prevented from exercising it. Finally, by various examples, she shows that it has always been her right to turn her wheel in its revolving circle and to direct it according to her own will.

“To agitate”] To handle or discuss.

“What, you man?”] The words of Fortune against Boethius.

“You bring a charge against me”] You accuse me. To bring someone to trial means to accuse him; to carry the matter through means to condemn him.

“What”] Something.

“Naked of all things”] We are born naked and die naked. Pliny, in the preface to Book VII of the *Natural History*:

> Man alone is born naked and cast naked upon the naked earth, on his birthday, immediately to cries and wailing.

Lucretius:

> Then, like a sailor thrown upon the cruel waves,  
> The infant lies naked upon the ground,  
> A helpless child, deprived of every aid to life,  
> When nature first brings him forth from his mother’s womb  
> By labor into the shores of light.  
> She fills the place with mournful cries, as is fitting  
> For one who must pass through so many evils in life.

[Col. 0955C]

“Prone”] Inclined or disposed.

“Subject to me”] Under my dominion.

“Abundance”] Plenty.

“Give thanks”] Be grateful in spirit.

“Or am I alone?”] She argues separately that each person is always permitted to exercise his natural right. Since it is her own right to turn her revolving wheel in continual rotation, she complains and indignantly protests that mortals, driven by insatiable desire, demand constancy and an unbroken continuity of prosperity from her, although inconstancy and change are natural to her.

“To compose”] To put together, close, or finish.

“Countenance”] Appearance or face. This is a sufficiently bold metaphor, transferring a human feature to an inanimate and very serious object.

[Col. 0955D]

“To crown”] To adorn.

“To confuse”] To disturb.

“Spread out”] Arranged or composed.

“Surface”] A level place or even surface.

“Unfulfilled”] Insatiable or inexhaustible.

“Will bind”] This must be pronounced interrogatively and with an expressive countenance, as though she were saying, “She will certainly never be able to bind it.”

“This is our power”] Namely, that we preserve no constancy.

“Continuous”] Without interruption.

“Wheel”] An image of Fortune. Some of the ancients represented her with a horn of plenty and a rudder, as though she bestowed riches and governed human affairs. Virgil agreed with this view when he called Fortune omnipotent; so did the historian who wrote: “But in truth Fortune rules everything.” Others cleverly imagined her standing upon a certain rounded stone. Others attach to her a revolving and turning wheel with four human figures: the first already ascending, the second holding the summit, the third descending again, and the fourth crushed down at the bottom of the wheel. Above them is this verse:

> I shall reign; I reign; I have reigned; I am without a kingdom.

“By her revolving circle”] With rapid rotation. Baptista Mantuanus, in the *Epigrams to Falco*, has these verses:

> Trust in virtue: Fortune, more fleeting than the waves,  
> Does not remain, and knows no fixed dwelling.  
> While she feigns joy, she plots to overturn her wheel;  
> Laughing, she prepares ambushes and destruction.

It should be observed in passing that ignorant pedants wrongly take *orbis* here to mean the world, whereas the sense is this: while Fortune feigns joy, and while she appears gracious, she plans secretly and contrary to human expectation to turn her wheel, which has a circular shape.

“From the lowest to the highest”] Seneca the tragedian:

> A brief hour changes the lowest into the highest.

There survives a rather pleasing poem by some unknown author on Fortune, which I thought should especially be inserted here:

> O powerful Fortune! How changeable you are,  
> How much ruthless authority you claim for yourself!  
> You overthrow the deserving and choose the wicked.  
> Nor can you keep faith with your gifts.  
> Fortune raises the undeserving with honors;  
> Fortune afflicts the innocent with disasters.  
> She burdens just men with poverty  
> And blesses the unworthy with riches.  
> She carries off the young and preserves the old,  
> Dividing the seasons by unjust judgment.  
> What she takes from the deserving, she transfers to the wicked.  
> She makes no distinction and judges rightly none.  
> Inconstant, fragile, faithless, slippery,  
> She does not continually cherish those whom she exalts,  
> Nor continually crush those whom she has deserted.

Ausonius:

> Fortune never remains in the same condition.  
> She is always moving, varying, and changing her turns;  
> She overturns the highest into the lowest and raises what has fallen.

“By that law”] On that condition.

“So that not”] That not.

“To descend”] Understand: that descending is an injustice.

“Croesus”] Croesus was the exceedingly wealthy king of Lydia. After he had been captured by Cyrus, king of the Persians, he was shackled and placed by Cyrus upon a huge pile of wood that had been constructed, so that he might be burned alive. While Croesus stood upon the pyre, they say that he remembered what Solon had told him by divine inspiration: that no living person should be called happy. When Cyrus heard this, they say that he repented, recognizing that he too was a human being, since he was about to hand over alive to the fire a man whom he had once regarded as no inferior to himself. Moreover, fearing punishment on that account and reflecting that nothing in human affairs is stable, he ordered the fire, which had already been kindled, to be extinguished as quickly as possible. When the men summoned to extinguish it could not do so, Croesus is said to have invoked Apollo and to have been saved when a great quantity of rain poured down from heaven. For a fuller account, see Herodotus, Book I.

“Paulum Persi”] That famous Perses, king of the Macedonians, who possessed more gold than courage. After being defeated and conquered in war by the Romans, he surrendered himself to Gnaeus Octavius, asking to be taken to the general Paulus Aemilius. Aemilius came to meet him with his friends, rose to his feet, and, as the historians relate, wept, reflecting on Fortune’s changes, which had dragged a king from the highest summit of dignity into ruin. Perses was then led in triumph with his sons and died in prison, consumed by grief—or, according to others, exhausted by sleeplessness and constant wakefulness. In the form *Persi*, because of *homoioteleuton* (ὁμοιοτέλευτον), he omitted the letter *s*, which is generally treated as a sibilant, not merely for reasons of necessity but also of euphony. Thus Sallust writes *a principio Urbis ad bellum Persi Macedonicum* (“from the beginning of the City to the Macedonian war of Perses”) instead of *Persis*. The *s* is also omitted from the genitive of the third declension. Virgil, in Book I of the *Aeneid*:

[Col. 0957B]

> The Trojan remnants of the Danaans and of fierce Achilles.

“Of tragedies”] Tragedy is the representation of heroic fortune in adversity. Sadness and frequent lamentation belong to it. Therefore, when King Archelaus asked Euripides to write a tragedy about him, Euripides refused and prayed that nothing proper to tragedy might happen to Archelaus, thereby showing that tragedy is nothing other than a representation of misery.

“Was he not still a young man—‘two jars, one of evils and the other of blessings’ (δύο τοὺς πίθους, τὸν μὲν ἕνα κακῶν, τὸν δὲ ἕτερον ἀγαθῶν)?” The Greek text, sent to me by Johannes Aedicollius from a very old manuscript, is rendered as follows in Latin: “Two jars, one indeed of evils, but the other of blessings.” In our Caesarian book there is this second reading, *οὐ μειράκιον ὢν ἔτι δύο πίθους, τὸν μὲν ἕνα κακῶν, τὸν δὲ ἕτερον ἀγαθῶν*:

> Not yet being a young man, two jars, one indeed of evils, but the other of blessings.

This may be interpreted literally as follows: “Not yet being a young man, even two jars, one indeed of evils, but the other of blessings.” It should be observed that *non* is used in place of *nonne* (“is it not?”), and that the sentence demands an affirmative answer. This is taken from the final book of Homer’s *Iliad*, where the following appears, translated by Lorenzo Valla:

> For there are two jars standing on Jupiter’s threshold, full of gifts which he has appointed to be given to us: one of evils, the other of blessings. From these Jupiter gives a man now evils, now blessings. The man to whom he gives evils he exposes to injury, so that he may live in misery. Yet he lives, honored neither by gods nor by men.

Nicolaus Valla rendered Homer’s verses into Latin as follows:

> They say that, besides, two vessels stand at Jupiter’s threshold,  
> From which the god himself dispenses either lot.  
> Wretched is he to whom the bitter lot of fate falls;  
> Alas, how many groans and how hard a destiny he shall see!  
> He will endure destruction and spend his whole life  
> Mixed with dark sorrows; men and gods alike will pursue him with hatred.

[Col. 0957D]

Socrates, in Plato’s second book *On the Republic*, seriously rejects this Homeric view, saying that we ought not to admit that Jupiter is a distributor of good and evil for us. Here Philosophy is speaking not in her own person but in the person of Fortune; nor does she say that the matter is actually so, but reports that the young Boethius learned it from Homer.

“What?”] Supply: “What will you say?”

“Of hoping for better things”] In accordance with the tragedian’s maxim:

> Let no one despair of better things after a fall.

## INTO THE SECOND METER

In this poem, whose first verse is Asclepiadic and whose second is Pherecratean, Fortune, at last deeply offended by the unjust habits of mortals, inveighs against the insatiable greed of those who, the more they have amassed, desire far more.

“How many”] Either “how many” or “how great.” It is better, however, to take it as “how many.” Silius Italicus, Book XV:

> How many things the god himself has produced for joyful uses.

Claudian, *On Human Affairs*:

> Souls gather, as many as the savage south wind  
> Strips from the trees—the leaves.

Terentianus:

> Likewise, how many Greeks I was able to know.

“Swift”] Impetuous.

“Sea”] The ocean.

“Turns”] Repeatedly changes.

[Col. 0958B]

“Brought forth”] Given to the light.

“Plenty”] They imagine her to be the goddess of fertility, whose horn the Naiads consecrated after Hercules had torn it from Achelous, who had changed himself into the form of a bull, and after they had filled it with the first fruits of every kind. Thus Ovid, on Achelous:

> While his savage right hand held the hard horn,  
> He broke it and tore it from his mutilated brow.  
> The Naiads filled it with fruit and fragrant flowers  
> And consecrated it; and rich Plenty is the owner  
> Of my horn.

Lucian, *On Those Who Serve for Wages*:

> You will possess the horn of Plenty and milk a hen dry.

Horace:

> Blessed Plenty with her full horn.

The same poet:

> Rich Plenty poured forth the golden harvest  
> Of Italy from her full horn.

“Therefore”] On account of that abundance of wealth.

[Col. 0958C]

“Prodigal”] Generous. It is now taken in a favorable sense. Yet he seems secretly to allude to the habits of a prodigal person, who often gives money beyond measure to the undeserving. Claudian:

> Generous with praise, but not prodigal of gold.

“Nothing already acquired seems sufficient”] That is, things which, while they were being desired, seemed great to the greedy, are regarded as nothing once they have come into their possession; they always gape thirstily after what lies farther ahead.

“What reins?”] As though he were saying, “None.”

“Can restrain”] Can hold back.

“The thirst for possessing”] Ecclesiastes, Chapter V:

> The miser will not be filled with money,  
> And he who loves riches will gain no profit from them.

Juvenal:

> The love of money grows as money itself grows.

Prudentius:

> For the hunger for gold becomes greater through the gold acquired.

Horace:

> Care follows wealth as it grows,  
> And hunger for more.

Saint Ambrose, in the third book of his letters to Simplicianus:

> Who is rich before God except the peaceful and moderate spirit, which is never corrupted? Does he not seem rich to you who possesses peace of mind and the tranquillity of repose, so that he desires nothing, is shaken by no storms of passions, does not disdain old things and seek new ones, and, by always desiring, becomes needy amid the greatest riches?

The same author, in the same book, to the same person:

> But the foolish man does not possess even what he thinks he has. Do you suppose that he possesses anything who, lying day and night upon his treasure, is tortured by greedy and wretched anxiety? He is truly needy; and although he seems rich to others, he is poor to himself—he does not use what he has, but continues to seize some things and desire others. Where there is no limit to desire, what profit is there in riches? No one is rich who cannot take away with him what he possesses here. For what is left here, and so forth.

The same author shortly afterwards:

> An ancient history describes two neighbors, King Ahab and the poor Naboth (1 Kings 21). Which of these do we believe was poorer, and which richer? One, furnished with the royal support of wealth, insatiable and unfilled by his possessions, desired the poor man’s small vineyard. The other, looking upon the imperial treasures—“the richly golden fortunes of kings” (βασιλέων τὰς πολυχρύσους τύχας)—was content with his own vine. Does he not seem richer, more truly a king, who had enough for himself and governed his desires so that he desired nothing belonging to another? But the other was utterly destitute: his own gold seemed worthless to him, while another man’s vine seemed supremely precious.

The same author, in the tenth book of his letters:

> The more each person acquires, the more he thirsts, and, as though seized by a kind of intoxication, he burns with his desires.

The same author, in his book *On Naboth*:

> O rich man, you do not know how poor you are, how needy you seem to yourself, although you call yourself rich. The more you have, the more you demand; and whatever you acquire, you still remain in need. Greed is inflamed by profit, not extinguished. Desire has steps of a sort: the more it climbs, the more eagerly it hastens toward higher things, and thus a heavy fall awaits the one who is about to slip.

A little later he adds:

> Who seems poor to you, then: the one who is content with his own, or the one who desires what belongs to another? The latter is certainly poor in his disposition. A rich disposition does not know want, while abundant wealth cannot fill a greedy heart. Therefore the rich man is greedy.

To express envy of possessions and complaint of poverty, someone added to Ambrose’s book, which we have just mentioned, an epigram not unworthy of being included here:

> The rich man who possesses everything desires to have still more;  
> Great abundance, in fact, makes men poor.  
> Few care where they may obtain things, but they must possess them,  
> Even through crime and wickedness; the poor man lies everywhere.  
> Father Ambrose bears witness to this in Naboth’s shadow,  
> Who fell for his land at the king’s command.

We too added, several years ago, when we undertook to explain the same work to our students, this modest imitation of a poem:

[Col. 0959D]

> The human mind, not treasure or a chest, should be considered rich;  
> He for whom nothing is ever enough is always needy and greedy.  
> As a swollen dropsy grows while indulging its thirst,  
> So love of wealth increases as riches are heaped up.  
> Mad desire treats divine law and human justice as nothing  
> And thinks that whatever it wishes is permitted by its blind mind.  
> So that you may recognize the greedy man as poor amid riches, reader,  
> Now read this work of the divine Ambrose.

“Acts”] Lives.

“Needy”] Horace:

> Poor amid great riches.

Periander:

> It is better for one who does not use good things to die than to live in need.

## INTO THE THIRD PROSE

Above, Fortune spoke to Boethius in this way: “What if you had received a more abundant share of good things?” Philosophy now reviews all the things with which Fortune had adorned him, and says that he complains less justly, since he cannot yet deny that he is happy when calculation proves that he has received and retained more good things than bad.

“Were you to speak”] You would speak. *Hisco* means “I speak softly,” or “I open my mouth to speak.” Plautus:

> He does not even dare to open his mouth.

Accius:

> I fear that the captive will speak more than is permitted.

“Sweetness of music”] Poetic delight.

“Then”] At that time.

“When”] Whenever.

“Deeper”] More profound.

“Grief”] Sadness.

“Defiant”] Rebellious or disobedient.

[Col. 0960B]

“Fomentations”] Soothing remedies, which the Greeks call *malágmata* (μαλάγματα).

“Penetrate”] Enter deeply.

“Desolate”] Bereft.

“Parent”] Father.

“That”] Namely, that someone was dear before he became a close relation.

“Dear”] Loved because of his outstanding character.

“Closest”] A relative by marriage. The sense is: You were dear to the leading men of the state because of your devotion to virtue before you became their close relation through marriage.

“Of your fathers-in-law”] Symmachus and his wife, or even her brothers or sons. Virgil, in Book II of the *Aeneid*:

> Unhappy Andromache, while the kingdom still endured,  
> Often used to go without escort  
> To her fathers-in-law, and dragged the boy Astyanax  
> To his grandfather.

In the Book of Tobit:

> After the death of his mother, Tobias departed from Nineveh with his wife, his sons, and his grandsons, and returned to his fathers-in-law.

*Socer* (“father-in-law”) is a relational noun: it refers to the son-in-law. Hence Ovid:

> No guest is safe from his guest,  
> Nor father-in-law from his son-in-law.

“Of your wife”] Of your wife Rusticiana.

“Fruit”] Use accompanied by a certain pleasure.

“Of light”] Of day.

“However great”] However large.

“Impending”] Threatening.

“Evils”] Adversities.

“Consuls”] Among the Romans there were once annual laws that forbade anyone to enter the consulship before his forty-third year. Yet, as Cicero says in his fifth book, in earlier times Rulli, Decii, Corvini, and many others, and in more recent memory Scipio Africanus and Titus Flaminius, became consuls while still very young and accomplished such great deeds that they increased the power and adorned the name of the Roman people. No one, therefore, should wonder that after the collapse of the empire, when barbarians already held Italy and most Roman laws had been abolished, Boethius’s two sons, almost still boys, became consuls together, chiefly through Fortune’s support, because of the merits of their father’s virtue and wisdom. This occurred by order of Theodoric, king of the Goths, who for a long time had been well disposed toward good men.

“Curule”] These were ivory chairs used by the higher magistrates, who were accustomed to be carried in a chariot to the senate-house as a mark of honor.

[Col. 0961A]

“Those seated upon them”] We say *insideo sellae* (“I sit in a chair”) and *insideo sellam* (“I sit upon a chair”), though the latter is rarer.

“Royal praise”] The praise of King Theodoric.

“In the circus”] The Circus at Rome was a very spacious place capable of holding a crowd and suitable for viewing spectacles. In it, aediles and consuls scattered gifts—which were called *missilia*—among the people in order to win their favor more effectively.

“Of the two”] Of your two sons.

“Middle”] In former times the middle position was an honored place, and it still is among some people. Hence Ovid, speaking of an elder man, in Book V of the *Fasti*:

> He went among the young men in the middle,  
> Without their resenting it, and even ahead  
> If there was only one companion.

There is a noteworthy passage in Spartianus concerning Hadrian. When Hadrian saw his slave walking between two senators, he sent someone to strike him in the face and say: “Do not walk among those whose slave you may still be.”

“With triumphal generosity”] With a magnificent and consular distribution of gifts.

“You deceived Fortune with words”] You deceived Fortune with flattering words. As is universally known, to “give words” means to deceive with empty words and promises. Martial:

> To whom you yourself gave nothing, he gave you words.

“To be her darling”] We call someone another person’s *deliciae* (“darling”) when he is that person’s favorite. Virgil, in the *Eclogues*:

> The shepherd Corydon burned for beautiful Alexis,  
> The darling of his master.

“Private citizen”] A private citizen is one who does not hold public office or a principate.

“To set down the counter”] To calculate or reckon. For calculations are usually made with counters; hence Martial’s word *calculator*.

“With a livid eye”] Until now, he says, Fortune favored you; only now has she begun to oppose you. By “with a livid eye,” however, he seems to allude to women who fascinate people by their gaze and kill those upon whom they gaze too long, especially with angry eyes, because their evil does greater harm to tender youth. Fortune, therefore, he says, who until now had cherished you like an indulgent mother, her darling, has now for the first time fascinated you in the manner of an African or Illyrian woman.

“Struck”] Injured, corrupted, or harmed.

“Livid”] Not at all bright, pestilential, and emitting livid vapors.

“Upon this stage of life”] He uses the elegant metaphor of calling life a stage, since life resembles a drama of the kind usually performed on the stage by actors. Seneca, Letter 77:

> As is a play, so is life. It matters not how long it is, but how well it has been acted.

Moria, in Erasmus’s *Praise of Folly*:

> Moreover, what else is the whole life of mortals than a kind of play, in which people come forward, concealed beneath different masks, and each performs his own part until the stage manager leads him off the stage? Yet he often orders the same man to appear again in different costume, so that the one who has just played a purple-clad king may now wear the rags of a little servant. Everything is indeed a shadow, but the play is conducted in no other way.

Cicero, in *Cato the Elder*:

> In this we are wise: that we follow nature, our best guide, as though she were a god, and obey her. Since the other acts of life have been properly assigned, it is not likely that the final act was neglected as though by an incompetent poet.

The same author, in the same work:

> What pleasures of the body can be compared with the rewards of authority? Those who have used these splendidly seem to me to have completed the drama of life, and not to have collapsed in the final act like untrained actors.

Again, in the same work:

> Nor is the play to be performed merely so that the actor may please. Whatever act he is in, let him be approved. Nor should the wise man wait until the applause.

Likewise, near the end of the same dialogue:

> Old age is the completion of life, as of a play, and we ought to escape its weariness, especially when satiety has been added.

[Col. 0962B]

“Sudden”] Unexpected.

“Guest”] A stranger or foreigner.

“Any stability in human affairs?”] He argues from the greater to the lesser. The human being himself cannot escape corruption, since he is often dissolved by sudden death. Much less, therefore, is there constancy in human affairs. Horace, in the *Art of Poetry*:

> We and all that belongs to us are owed to death.

“Swift hour”] There is an old proverb of Varro: “Man is a bubble.” Faustus:

> Mortal bodies are subject to a fixed destiny,  
> And all their times, flowing rapidly, rush headlong away.  
> So quickly does the human race perish within an hour,  
> As a swollen bubble melts in the rainwater.

“What is man?” asks Seneca. “Any vessel that has been shaken, any fragile object tossed about. What is man? A very weak and fragile body, naked by nature, unarmed, dependent upon another’s aid, exposed to every insult of Fortune, unable to bear cold or labor, composed of weak and fluid elements. Its smell and taste, fatigue and wakefulness, moisture and food—without which it cannot live—are deadly to it. Wherever it moves, it immediately becomes conscious of its weakness, diseased and rotten through the slightest causes and injuries.”

Therefore the wisest of poets rightly sang:

> Such indeed is the race of men as the race of leaves.

“Fortune’s gifts”] The good things bestowed by Fortune. Valerius Maximus, Book VI:

> Exceedingly perishable and fragile, and fit for children’s sandals, are those things called human strength and wealth. They flow in suddenly and suddenly dissipate; they stand rooted firmly neither in any place nor in any person, but, driven here and there by Fortune’s most uncertain breath, they plunge those whom they have raised aloft, abandoned by an unforeseen reversal, miserably into the depths of disaster. Therefore those things ought neither to be considered nor called good which, by making us desire them, double the bitterness of the evils inflicted upon us.

“Yet the final day of life is a kind of death even for Fortune that remains”] Prosper writes in his *Epigrams*:

> When the unjust man rejoices, rich in earthly wealth,  
> He does not know that he is wretched and lacks true goods.  
> For what is there that, within a single moment of time,  
> The condition of the world cannot take away,  
> Even if, while adversities cease, everything remains,  
> Since by the law of death he must nevertheless become needy?

## INTO THE THIRD METER

[Col. 0963A]

This poem is two-membered, consisting of a Sapphic and a Glyconic verse. It clearly shows not only that there is no constancy in human affairs, as has already been said, but also that almost nothing in this world is unchanging, since everything that has been born must at some time perish.

“Phoebus”] The sun.

“Rose-colored”] Red.

“Blunted”] For the greater light obscures the lesser. Hence Ovid:

> Behold, at her bright rising Aurora has opened  
> Her purple doors; and her halls, full of roses,  
> Are revealed. The stars disperse, and Lucifer drives  
> Their host before him and is the last to leave  
> His station in the sky.

“Flames”] The splendors of the sun.

[Col. 0963B]

“Pressing upon”] Darkening the stars.

“May blow”] “If” is missing.

“Insane”] Unhealthily; a noun used adverbially.

“Cloudy south wind”] This is the wind blowing from the south, cloudy and damp. The Greeks call it *notos* (νότος), from *notis* (νότις), meaning moisture or dampness. In Latin it is called *auster*, either because it flattens and dulls the ears, or *hauster*, from drawing up water. Cornelius Celsus, in Book II, Chapter I of *Medicine*, says of it:

> The south wind dulls the ears, slows the senses, causes headaches, loosens the bowels, and makes the whole body dull, damp, and languid.

Horace, in the *Satires*:

> Nor does harmful ambition destroy me, nor the leaden south wind.

Ovid, in Book VII of the *Metamorphoses*:

> The death-bearing south winds breathed with hot blasts.

“Beauty”] The beauty and adornment of roses.

[Col. 0963C]

“In tranquil clearness”] In tranquil serenity.

“Unmoved”] Not stirred.

“Aquilo”] This is a wind named from the violent flight of an eagle. It is northern and extremely cold; the Greeks call it *boréan* (βορέαν), the accusative form of “Boreas.”

“Boiling”] Seething.

“Turned”] Overturned, ruined, or agitated.

“Surface”] The level expanse of the waters. *Aequor* (“surface”) is clearly derived from equality or evenness.

“If the world rarely retains its own form”] He argues from the greater to the lesser. The world seems more likely to possess constancy and an unbroken continuity than mortal affairs, which are subject to Fortune and change. Yet, as has been gathered from particular examples, the world does not always retain the same appearance and unbroken constancy. It is therefore much less surprising if human affairs undergo the variety and reversals of chance.

“Believe”] This is irony, as though he were saying, “You certainly should not believe it.” Thus the poet:

> Go now and mock virtue with your proud words.

And Horace:

> Go now and compose melodious verses to yourself.

“With good things”] This is an iamb. For, as Terentianus teaches, the Glyconic verse, like the Phalaecian, admits an iamb or a trochee in place of a spondee. Septimus:

> And he carries into the city  
> The panting flocks of Panope.

The same poet:

> The old gatherers of purple,  
> Within, where the seed has been planted.

Horace, in the *Odes*:

> Fire upon the Trojan houses.

Catullus:

> We are under Diana’s protection,  
> Pure girls and boys.

The same poet:

> Measuring the year’s journey,  
> May you fill the rustic  
> House of the farmer with fruits.

“Is eternal”] This is a beautiful and entirely true conclusion, by which he shows that everything born is liable to corruption. Aristotle, in the first book *On the Heavens and the World*:

> What has been generated and what is corruptible necessarily follow one another.

Seneca, Letter 88:

> For one to whom birth has been granted, death remains.

The same author elsewhere:

> It is a useful law that commands us to be born and to die.

[Col. 0964B]

“Is established”] Certain and firm—namely, so that nothing generated is established, that is, endures and remains forever. Maximianus:

> All things return to their origins  
> And seek again their mother.

Baptista Mantuanus:

> Water, earth, and air perish; moist ether perishes,  
> Fire dies; and whatever these four create perishes.

## INTO THE FOURTH PROSE

In the preceding prose, Philosophy showed how greatly Boethius had been endowed and enriched with Fortune’s goods; by recounting them, she easily proved that Fortune had bestowed more upon him than she had taken away. Now she teaches that such great goods still remain to him that, if there is any happiness in Fortune’s possessions, he does not yet appear to have lost it. Then, speaking familiarly, she reproves the man for being too deeply disturbed in spirit over the loss of part of his goods, since no mortal is fortunate in every respect. Afterwards she teaches that true happiness does not at all consist in Fortune’s goods. Therefore one who seeks blessedness has no reason to grieve over losing things that cannot truly make him blessed.

“Remembering”] Recalling and going over in his mind.

“Boils”] Torments. Ennius:

> Or lighten the care  
> That now torments you.

“To have been happy is the most wretched kind of misfortune”] Plautus, in the *Rudens*:

> It is a miserable and most dreadful word:  
> To have possessed, and to possess nothing.

Maximianus:

[Col. 0964D]

> The memory of former goods is sufficiently harsh for the wretched,  
> And those who fall from the highest summit plunge more heavily.

“Therefore, if”] He begins to recall the goods that still remain to Boethius.

“By divine favor”] From God.

“But”] Yet.

“Safe”] Unharmed.

“Symmachus, your father-in-law”] This passage clearly shows that Boethius had been sent into exile considerably earlier than his father-in-law Symmachus was arrested and thrown into chains, at the time when he composed this divine work. Symmachus was a most eloquent man, adorned with the highest virtues. After Boethius had lost his father, Symmachus, because of the young man’s exceptional intellect and excellent character, gave him his daughter Rusticiana in marriage. Several writings of our Boethius addressed to this Symmachus still survive.

A notable error of many people must be corrected: they think that this Symmachus wrote the letters that survive—short and elegant letters, but composed by an impious enemy of Christians. There was another Symmachus, an orator and prefect of the city of Rome, to whom those letters and the speech to the emperor Valentinian belong. In that speech he tried to persuade the emperor to restore the altar of Victory; the Christian poet Prudentius and Saint Ambrose replied to him, Ambrose in a speech and Prudentius in two poetic books. Boethius’s father-in-law, however, flourished many years later, in the time of Justin the Elder. He was a most Christian man and, according to the testimony of Pope Saint Gregory, a saint. Whoever wishes to judge correctly about this matter must agree with me.

[Col. 0965B]

“Which”] The most precious glory of the human race.

“Not sluggish”] Active and eager.

“Made from the virtues of wisdom”] The opposite is Cicero’s statement in his speech *For Cluentius*: “And he was wholly made of fraud and falsehood.”

“His”] His injuries.

“Secure”] Having no concern.

“Wife”] Rusticiana, Symmachus’s daughter.

“Surpassing in the modesty of chastity”] Jerome, *Against Jovinianus*:

> It is the saying of a most learned man that chastity must above all be preserved; once it is lost, every virtue collapses. In this lies the preeminence of women’s virtues. It commends a poor woman, exalts a rich woman, redeems an unattractive woman, and adorns a beautiful one. It benefits her ancestors, whose blood she does not corrupt with secret offspring; it benefits her children, who need not be ashamed of their mother or doubt their father; and above all it benefits herself, whom it protects from the dishonor of an outsider’s body.

“Or”] Also.

“Through longing for you”] Because she longs for you. Things that are absent are missed.

“What”] For what reason, or for what purpose.

“Children”] Your sons.

**Consulares**] Those who were consuls, as stated above.

**Quorum**] Your sons.

**Specimen**] Properly, something displayed to a buyer from merchandise for sale, so that he may judge the other goods by it—for example, a piece of cloth, a little grain, or a taste of wine [Col. 0965D].

**Ingenii paterni**] Of Boethian talent.

**Aviti**] Of Symmachian ancestry.

**Ut**] Inasmuch as.

**In pueris id aetatis**] That is, boys of that age; this is a figurative expression. *Id aetatis*, like *id genus* attached figuratively to any case, means “at that age” or “of that age.” Plautus in the *Asinaria*:

> Nor was he ashamed, at his age, to contrive his swindles.

Livy:

> When Scipio asked him who he was, what his nationality was, and why he was in the camp at his age, he replied that he was a Numidian, whom his countrymen called Massius.

**O te si tua bona cognoscas felicem**] “O” is now an interjection expressing wonder, and this imitates Virgil’s line in the second book of the *Georgics* [Col. 0966A]:

> O farmers, too fortunate, if only they knew their blessings.

**Quae vita nemo dubitat esse cariora**] “Things which no one doubts are dearer than life”: Symmachus, his father-in-law, his wife, and his children.

**Ad unum omnis**] Everyone, without exception. Livy:

> The Roman consul, having caught them in the Algidus, killed them all to the last man.

**Nimium**] Beyond measure.

**Valida**] Violent.

**Quando**] Since.

**Tenaces ancorae**] He remains beautifully within the metaphor, taken from sailors struggling amid a storm. In Greek, anchor is called ἄγκυρα (*ankyra*). There is an old proverb: “The anchor of the house,” meaning a refuge for the family. Whatever we lean upon and whose support gives us confidence is called an anchor, by a metaphor taken from ships: when ships are secured by anchors, they rest as though defended from the waves. Euripides in the *Hecuba*, speaking of Polydorus:

> He who alone now remains as the anchor of our race.

**Utcunque**] In whatever way.

**Enatabimus**] We shall escape the danger of death. He continues the metaphor.

**Promovimus**] We have advanced.

**Ferre**] To endure.

**Quis est enim**] This is an entirely true statement, elegantly expressed as a question. It agrees with the saying found in the rhetorician Hermogenes: “A human life free from trouble cannot be found.” Seneca: “No fortune is so good that you could complain about nothing in it.” The same author, in *On Anger*, book III: “No one’s fortune is so compliant that it answers favorably everywhere to one who attempts many things.” Horace:

> Nothing is blessed  
> In every respect.

Erasmus, translating from the Greek:

> No mortal is fortunate in every respect.

The same author expressed the same thought thus:

> No one lives fortunate in every way.

Euripides:

> Since among all the affairs of mortals  
> Nothing is continually and everywhere prosperous.

Pliny, book VII: “No mortal is happy.” The same author in the same book: “No mortal is wise in possession of all good things.” Maharbal to Hannibal in Livy: “The gods have not granted everything to the same man. You know how to conquer, Hannibal; you do not know how to use victory.” Ulysses in Homer, translated by Philelphus:

[Col. 0966D]

> God does not grant everything to one man, so that he may be  
> Handsome and wise at once, eloquent and rich in praise.  
> The man deprived of beauty God, in his reverence, adorns  
> With strength of eloquence, so that others may marvel at him,  
> Captivated by the sweetness of his pleasing tongue.  
>   
> This man speaks with confidence and gentle modesty,  
> And as he moves among the assembly he stands out; those in whatever city you pass through  
> Regard him, as he speaks, like a god.  
>   
> But another, whose beauty makes him like the gods  
> When seen up close, is utterly deprived  
> Of the grace of eloquence.

Claudian in the *Panegyric on Stilicho*:

> For ever since the earth first began to be cultivated  
> No mortal man has been granted an unalloyed lot of blessings:  
> Whom reputation adorns, his character disgraces;  
> Whom a nobler mind adorns, his body abandons;  
> That man is distinguished in war, but vice mars his peace;  
> Happy in public affairs, but less so in private life.  
> Each is ennobled by separate gifts: one by comely form,  
> Another by strength in arms, another by severity, another by piety,  
> Another by legal skill, another by offspring, another by a chaste marriage-bed.

**Rixetur**] Let him quarrel, disagree, or differ.

**Huic census**] He shows that in this life no one receives complete happiness.

**Degener sanguis**] Ignoble ancestry.

**Utroque**] By both wealth and nobility of birth.

**Vitam caelibem**] A life without a wife. Horace in the first book of the *Epistles*:

> The marriage-bed is in the palace;  
> He says that nothing comes before it, nothing is better than a celibate life.  
> If it is not so, he swears that only married men live well.

**Inexpertus**] Untried.

**Adde quod felicissimi**] He shows that the more accustomed mortals are to success, the less able they are to endure adversity.

[Col. 0967B]

**Ad nutum**] According to one’s inclination and will.

**Insolens**] Unaccustomed.

**Prosternitur**] Is cast down.

**Adeo**] To such an extent.

**Per exigua**] Very slight.

**Summam**] Perfection.

**Coelo proximos**] Fortunate beyond measure. To be near heaven, or in heaven, or to touch heaven with one’s finger, means to be extraordinarily fortunate and glorious. Marcus Tullius: “Bibulus is in heaven—I do not know why, but he is praised in that way.” The same author: “Our leading men think they touch heaven with their finger if there are no bearded men in the fishponds who come to their hand.”

**Adeo nihil est miserum, nisi cum putes**] Thus Menander:

> You have suffered nothing especially terrible  
> Unless you imagine it so for yourself.

**Aequanimitate**] Patience. Plautus:

> In misfortune, if you use a good spirit, it helps.

Horace:

> But whatever it is wrong to correct  
> Is made lighter by patience.

**Dederit manus**] Has submitted. The expression is transferred from those captured in war who offer their hands to the victor to be bound.

**Quam multis amaritudinibus humanae felicitatis dulcedo respersa est**] Plautus in the *Amphitryon*:

> Such is the condition of every human life;  
> Such is the will of the gods: sorrow follows pleasure as its companion.  
> Indeed, when something good has occurred, some inconvenience and evil  
> Immediately follow.

Plato, from the same source, considers sweetness and bitterness, pleasure and pain, to flow down from the same summit. Apuleius, in the fourth book of the *Florida*: “But it is certainly a true saying that they utter: Nothing so prosperous has been divinely granted to man that some difficulty has not also been mixed with it, so that even in the greatest joy some small complaint lies hidden, through a kind of union of honey and gall. Where there is an udder, there is also a lump.” Ovidius:

> So completely is no pleasure pure,  
> And something troubling intervenes amid joys.

Solomon, Proverbs XIII: “Laughter shall be mingled with sorrow, and mourning shall occupy the end of joy.” Lucretius, book IV of *On the Nature of Things*:

> Banquets, games,  
> Frequent cups, perfumes, garlands, and wreaths are prepared  
> In vain, since from the very midst of the fountain of delights  
> Something bitter rises, which troubles them amid the flowers.

**Extra**] In external things, that is, things placed outside you.

**Intra vos**] In your minds. Cicero in the *Paradoxa*: “No one can fail to be supremely happy who is wholly self-sufficient and places everything in himself alone.”

**Inscitia**] Ignorance. Persius:

> So that feeble ignorance may restrain forbidden actions.

**Cardinem summa felicitate tibi**] That upon which the greatest and true happiness turns and depends.

**Cardo**] As though it were the heart of a door, the thing on which it turns. Virgil:

> The hinge creaked on the bronze doors.

It is sometimes taken to mean an opportunity. The same author:

> The hinge of affairs will not delay so long.

We also say that something “turns upon” the hinge on which the whole matter depends.

[Col. 0968B]

**Si tui compos fueris**] A person is master of himself when, with his emotions brought under control, he subjects his appetites to right reason.

**Si beatitudo**] He argues that the highest good is not placed in things dependent on fortune, as follows: Whatever other good is more excellent is not the highest good. There is, however, a good more excellent than success dependent on fortune—namely, that which cannot be taken away. Therefore success dependent on fortune is not the highest good. It follows that it cannot bestow happiness either, since happiness is nothing other than the highest good of a nature living according to reason.

**Ad haec**] He adds another argument to this effect: The highest good cannot be something that is understood in no way. But when the goods of fortune are understood, they are recognized as deceptive and fleeting; hence arises a continual fear of losing them, and such fear cannot coexist with happiness. If, on the other hand, they are not understood, happiness is again excluded, for blindness caused by ignorance is far removed from it, whereas happiness consists above all in the contemplation of true goods.

[Col. 0968C]

**Et quoniam tu idem es**] He adds to the preceding arguments another reason by which he demonstrates most clearly that happiness and fortune are not joined together. “That,” he says, “cannot be the highest good of a human being which can be separated from him. Yet by the death of the body, fortune’s happiness is separated from the immortal human soul. Therefore either this is not the highest good of a human being, or we must admit that the entire race of mortals sinks into misery at death’s end.” But that this is not so is demonstrated by the glorious deeds of many who, boldly resisting tyrants for the name of Christ, acquired happiness through sufferings and punishments. Therefore true happiness cannot consist in the successes dependent on the fortune of this life.

**Permultis demonstrationibus**] Not merely Platonic demonstrations, but Christian ones as well.

**Haec**] Death.

**Multos**] Understand not Stoics or Cynics, but rather Christian martyrs.

**Doloribus**] Baptista Mantuanus:

> It is better to endure few things and, through brief punishments, obtain  
> Eternal joys, than, while we vainly strive to retain  
> The fleeting goods we embrace, to waste our labor  
> And finally descend to the infernal rivers.

The same author elsewhere:

[Col. 0969A]

> If the human race possessed wisdom and were not so wholly captured  
> By sloth and enticed by pleasures, and if it cared for its body  
> Only through the fleeting years of life, rather than for falling kingdoms,  
> Mud, and houses destined to collapse; if it were not ashamed  
> Of a cheap lodging that gathers into its bosom all the refuse  
> Of heaven and sea, where grim stars rain down misfortunes  
> And continual deaths with hostile light—

## INTO METRE IV

The poem is two-membered and two-stanzaed; its first line is an Anacreontic iambic dimeter, acatalectic, consisting of three feet and a syllable, resembling the following line of Prudentius:

> Remember, worshiper of God.

The second line is Pherecratian, consisting of a spondee or an anapest, a dactyl, and a spondee.

He teaches that it is safest not to yearn excessively for external goods. For if fortune seems to bestow great prosperity, on departing it will also bring the greatest pains. He therefore advises avoiding excessive prominence, since it is exposed to envy, just as mountain peaks are harassed by perpetual winds. The squalor of poverty must likewise be avoided, since it cannot bear the burden of lofty virtue and is therefore compared with thirsty sands. The middle condition, then, indicated by the lowly rock, is best and must be embraced above all. For, as Aristotle states in book IV of the *Politics*, there are three classes of people in every state: the rich, the poor, and those of moderate means. The best are those of moderate means, because the middle is always best. He also writes that citizens of moderate means are more secure, since they neither suffer plots nor practice fraud as the others do; consequently, they live without danger.
