In the same book he says: “The closer anything comes to the middle, the better it is; the farther it departs from the middle, the worse it is.”

Horace, *Odes* II:

> You will live more rightly, Licinius, neither always  
> Pressing toward the open sea, nor, while cautiously fearing storms,  
> Keeping too close to the treacherous shore.  
>   
> Whoever loves the golden mean  
> Avoids safely the squalor of a decayed roof,  
> And, sober, avoids the palace  
> That invites envy.  
>   
> The great pine is more often shaken by winds,  
> Lofty towers fall with a heavier crash,  
> And lightning strikes the highest  
> Mountains.

Ovid, in the third book of the *Tristia*:

> If you believe anything of a friend instructed by experience,  
> Live for yourself, and flee far from great names.  
> Live for yourself as much as you can, and let your life be free  
> Of public splendor; the savage lightning comes from a splendid height.

[Col. 0969D] The same author not long afterward:

> Believe me: he who has concealed himself well has lived well, and each person  
> Should remain within the limits of his own fortune.

**Quisquis**] Whoever.

**Perennem**] Perpetual, lasting, enduring.

**Ponere**] To build.

**Sedem**] A dwelling, a place of habitation.

**Euri**] East winds.

**Pontum**] Sea.

**Bibulas arenas**] Dry sands capable of absorbing moisture. In the Gospel according to Matthew (Matthew VII), Christ, the Savior of the human race, says:

> Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house upon rock. The rain fell, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they beat upon that house, and it did not fall, because it had been founded upon rock. And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house upon sand. The rain fell, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they beat upon that house; it fell, and its ruin was great.

Juvencus explained the same subject in these splendid verses:

> Whoever devotes both ears and deeds to my warnings,  
> I shall compare to the man who lays foundations on solid rocks,  
> Upon which, properly balanced, walls will rise.  
> That house will remain unharmed by rains and winds  
> And will overcome the threats of torrents with its firm strength,  
> Since it clings to the rock’s immovable foundation.  
>   
> But whoever merely hears my commands  
> And proceeds far away from them on slippery paths,  
> I shall make like the foolish man who supports  
> The foundations of his house upon sand. As soon as winds  
> And rain, poured out in streams, begin to bear down upon it,  
> The whole mass collapses beneath its overturned weight,  
> And ruin follows with the heavy destruction of the roof.

There is a Greek proverb: εἰς ψάμμον οἰκοδομεῖς, “You are building on sand.” It is used when someone undertakes a useless enterprise, because its foundations have not first been properly laid.

**Illud**] The summit of a high mountain.

**Protervus**] Very grim and terrifying.

**Auster**] The south wind.

**Urget**] Harasses, shakes. Ovid:

> Envy attacks what is highest; the winds blow upon the loftiest things.

Seneca in the *Phaedra*:

> Peaks brought close to the heavenly abodes  
> Receive the harsh south winds,  
> The threats of raging Boreas,  
> And rain-bearing Corus.  
>   
> A moist valley rarely suffers the stroke of lightning.

[Col. 0970C]

**Hae**] The sands.

**Pendulum**] Hanging.

**Ferre**] To endure.

**Periculosam sortem**] A condition full of dangers.

**Amoenae sedis**] A pleasant dwelling on the summit of the mountain.

**Figere**] To establish, to build.

**Tonet**] Resounds violently and terribly.

**Ruinis**] Overthrows.

**Robore**] Strength.

**Duces**] You lead.

**Serenus**] Composed with a peaceful mind.

**Aevum**] The time of life.

**Ridens**] Treating as insignificant.

[Col. 0970D]

**Iras**] Storms of the air.

## INTO PROSE V

Thus far Philosophy has argued that the goods of fortune do not remain permanently with one and the same person. For even if they do not abandon someone during life, they are nevertheless separated from him by the necessity of death. Now, however, she argues that even if these goods are firm and stable, they still cannot be called a human being’s own goods, nor can they be compared with human dignity, which is far superior to all the riches of fortune.

**Rationum**] Arguments.

**Fomenta**] Remedies, medicines. Properly, *fomenta* are applications of warm or moist substances to injured parts of the body for the sake of healing. A *fomes* is a splinter knocked from a tree while it is being cut. It also means any dry material in which fire is easily kindled. Metaphorically, we call anything a *fomes* that kindles and incites us to do something.

[Col. 0971A]

**Validioribus**] More effective arguments.

**Age**] Here an adverb used to attract attention: “Now.”

**Earum**] Of those riches.

**Potius**] Better, more excellent.

**Aurumne**] “Is it gold,” he asks, “which is called *aurum* from *aura*, that is, from its brightness?”

**An vis**] That is, a quantity of money.

**Congestae**] Heaped up.

**Atqui**] But.

**Hae**] This money.

[Col. 0971B]

**Nitent melius effundendo**] They shine more brightly when they are distributed.

**Quam coacervando**] Than when they are accumulated.

**Siquidem avaritia semper odiosos, claros largitas efficit**] This is a magnificent statement, worthy of the gravity of philosophy: greed always makes people hated, while generosity makes them renowned.

**Et vox quidem tota**] He shows that the nature of the voice is superior to riches, since a whole and undiminished voice fills the hearing of many simultaneously, whereas riches cannot pass to many unless they are diminished and divided. Our Boethius, in book I of *On Music*, chapter 14:

> Let us now discuss the manner of hearing. Something of the following sort customarily occurs in voices, like what happens when a stone thrown from a distance sinks into a marsh or still water. First it gathers a wave into a very small circle; then it spreads circles of waves into larger circles, continuing until the exhausted motion ceases to produce waves. Each later and larger wave is spread with a weaker force. If something should obstruct the growing waves, the motion immediately turns back and, as though returning to the center from which it began, forms itself into circles through the same waves. Thus, when struck air produces sound, it strikes the air nearest to it and in a certain way stirs up a rounded wave of air. It therefore spreads out and strikes the hearing of all those standing around at the same time. The voice is fainter for the person standing farther away, because a weaker wave of the struck air reaches him.

**An gemmarum fulgor**] As above with gold, he now treats of gems and shows that they possess nothing that human beings ought either to admire or desire.

[Col. 0971D]

**Gemmarum est lux illa, non hominum**] Thus Saint Ambrose in *On Naboth*: “I do not deny that these stones possess a certain grace of brilliance, but it is still the brilliance of stones.”

**An vos agrorum pulchritudo**] He likewise teaches that the beauty of fields is by no means proper to human beings.

**Quidni?**] “Why not?” Boethius replies.

**Pulcherrimi operis**] Of the world.

**Pulchra portio**] A beautiful part.

**Facie**] In appearance, form, or aspect.

**Vernis floribus**] Saint Ambrose, in book III of *The Six Days of Creation*:

> What should I describe for you? Purple violets, white lilies, glowing roses, fields painted now with golden, now with various, now with yellow flowers—so that you cannot tell whether the beauty of the flowers or the power of their fragrance gives greater pleasure. The eyes feast upon the delightful spectacle; fragrance is spread far and wide, and we are filled by its sweetness.

**Ubertas**] Fertility.

**Animantium**] Living creatures, animals.

**Alimentis**] Nourishment.

**Quod naturae satis est**] This is a parenthesis.

**Quod**] To fill a need.

**Paucis enim minimisque natura contenta est**] This is a celebrated maxim. The comic poet Sextus Turpilius:

> Certainly, the more completely each person was content,  
> The more fortunate a life he led,  
> As those philosophers say: anything is enough.

The philosopher Seneca, letter IV:

> What nature desires is readily obtained and costs little once acquired; it is for superfluities that we sweat. Those are the things that wear out the toga, make us grow old beneath a tent, and drive us onto foreign shores. What is enough is close at hand. Whoever lives comfortably with poverty is rich.

Lucan, book IV of the *Pharsalia*:

> O extravagant luxury of possessions,  
> Never content with modest preparation,  
> And ambitious hunger for foods sought by land and sea,  
> And the glory of a sumptuous table.  
> Learn how little is enough to prolong life,  
> And how much nature requires. Noble Bacchus, spread  
> By an unknown consul, does not make the sick man rise.

The same author shortly afterward:

> A river and grain are enough for the people.

That is, bread and water. Euripides, quoted by Aulus Gellius:

> For what else is useful to mortals besides those two things alone—  
> The gift of Ceres and the cup of water, which are present  
> And can nourish us, though our appetite is never satisfied?

Luxury, however, consists in the pursuit of all other dishes. Cicero in book V of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “The day would fail me if I wished to defend the cause of poverty. The matter is obvious, and nature herself reminds us daily how few, how small, and how cheap are the things we need.” Saint Ambrose in book X of his *Letters*: “The law of nature is rich enough for everyone who can quickly find what is sufficient. But for desires, every abundance of riches is poverty.” Jerome in *Against Jovinianus*: “Nature’s needs are quickly satisfied; cold and hunger can be driven away with simple clothing and food. Hence the Apostle also says: ‘Having food and clothing, with these we are content.’” Prudentius in the *Psychomachia*:

> Complete peace is to desire nothing beyond what necessary use requires,  
> So that simple food and a single garment may cover  
> And moderately restore the weakened limbs,  
> Without extending beyond nature’s fulfilled measure.

**Jam vero pulchrum**] He teaches that the beauty of clothing also does not belong to human beings, but is proper either to the material or to the workmanship, although the old saying remains: εἰματα ἀνὴρ, “clothes make the man,” and the common proverb says, “Dress makes the man; let the one who has clothing put it on.”

**An vero te**] He proves that happiness does not consist in a long retinue of servants.

**Sarcina**] Properly, a bundle of utensils and things needed for personal use, such as a pack that someone might carry on a journey. Hence soldiers who intend to move camp are said to gather their packs, and those who move to another house to arrange their baggage. Metaphorically, however, we use *sarcina* for a useless burden. Aurelius: “And one day I would lay down this burden of the body.” Ambrose: “For what else is sin than a burden?”

[Col. 0973A]

**Ex quibus omnibus**] By induction from the particular points stated above, he draws a universal conclusion.

**Quid id tua refert**] “What does that have to do with you?” As reported by Laertius in the *Life of Solon*, some say that Croesus, after adorning himself most elaborately with every kind of ornament and sitting on a lofty throne, asked Solon whether he had ever seen a more beautiful spectacle. Solon replied that he had seen domestic cocks, pheasants, and peacocks, since they are clothed by nature with their own native colouring and extraordinary beauty.

[Col. 0973B]

**Sequestrata**] Separated, set apart.

**Quid autem tanto**] He rebukes mortals who yearn so intensely for the goods of fortune, and shows that through the greatest labors they obtain want instead of the sufficiency for which they strive day and night.

**Adminiculis**] Supports, aids.

**Permultis indigere eos**] Ecclesiastes, chapter V: “Where there are many possessions, there are many who consume them.” Aulus Gellius, book VIII: “It is certainly true what wise men have said after observing the use of things: the person who possesses much has many needs, and great want arises not from great poverty but from great abundance. For many things are required to preserve the many things one possesses.” In Xenophon’s *Cyropaedia*, book VIII, Pheraulas says:

> “Do you really think, Saca, that I now live more pleasantly because I possess more? Do you not know that I eat, drink, and sleep no more pleasantly than when I was poor? But since these possessions of mine are so numerous, my only gain is that I must guard more things and give more things to others; and the more I attend to, the more business I have. Now many servants ask me for food, many for drink, many for clothing, and others need physicians. Someone also comes to report that sheep have been devoured by wolves, that oxen have fallen over a precipice, or that disease has attacked the flocks. Thus I seem to myself more troubled because I now possess more than formerly, when I had little.”

**Itane autem nullum est proprium vobis**] These words are extremely beautiful through to the end and should always be kept in mind.

[Col. 0973D]

**Merito**] By merit.

**Haud immerito**] Deservedly, justly.

**Tum**] Then.

**Cum se cognoscit**] The ancient saying is γνῶθι σεαυτόν, “Know yourself.” Saint Ambrose, in the final book of the *Hexaemeron*: “Now, since you see elephants subjected to you and lions placed beneath your power, know yourself, O human being.” This saying—which they report as belonging to Apollo of Delphi, but which belongs to holy Solomon, who says, “Unless you know that you are beautiful among women”—had already been written much earlier by Moses in Deuteronomy: “Pay attention to yourself, O human being.” “Pay attention to yourself,” says the Law. And the prophet says: “Unless you know yourself.”

**Ego vero nego illud**] He introduces a syllogism to show that riches are not good. It is as follows: Whatever harms its possessor is not good. Riches, however, often harm their possessor. Therefore they are not good. Experience demonstrates the minor premise every day, as does the authority of Juvenal. Valerius Maximus also left us the following, written with great elegance, in book VII:

> Socrates, a kind of earthly oracle of human wisdom, thought that nothing more should be asked from the immortal gods than that they grant good things, because only they know what is useful to each person. We, however, generally seek in our prayers what it would have been better not to obtain. For the human mind, wrapped in the densest darkness, is unable to see: into how vast an error are you scattering your blind prayers? You desire riches, which have been the ruin of many. You crave honors, which have destroyed very many. You turn over kingdoms in your mind, whose ends are often seen to be miserable. You reach out your hands toward splendid marriages, yet these, just as they sometimes illuminate households, sometimes overthrow them completely. Therefore cease foolishly yearning for future causes of your misfortunes as though they were the happiest things, and entrust yourself wholly to the will of heaven, since those who readily bestow good things can also choose them most wisely.

Juvenal, satire X:

> But for many, money amassed in excessive quantities  
> Chokes them with anxiety, and wealth surpassing every estate,  
> As much greater than a dolphin as a British whale is.

**Cum pessimus quisque**] The order is: “When every basest person, more greedy for borrowed money—that is, another’s money—thinks himself alone worthy to possess whatever gold and gems exist anywhere.”

**Contum**] A spear. A *contus* is a stake or spear, longer and harder than usual, suitable for striking. Virgil:

> Accustomed to defend the walls with a long spear.

It also means a pole with iron at its end, which sailors use to investigate places suitable for ships. The same author:

> He suddenly poles the raft.

**Pertimescis**] You fear greatly. The proverbial expression δειλὸς πλοῦτος means “timid riches.” For in every matter the rich person is more fearful than the poor. He fortifies his house more cautiously through fear of thieves. He fears storms because of the grain he has in the fields and the merchandise he has at sea. He fears friends, lest he be compelled to give something to those who ask; he fears enemies, lest they do him harm. He insults people more timidly, fearing a penalty. He does and says everything more cautiously, fearing accusation, which is especially often contrived against the rich, since they have something that can be taken away. If war threatens, the rich man is tormented above all. Finally, he is not free even from superstition, lest some unfriendly deity inflict damage. The learned Erasmus gives these observations in the first *Chiliad* of his *Adages*.

**Vacuus viator**] This entire passage is taken from Juvenal, whose verses are:

> Although you carry a few vessels of pure silver,  
> Once you have begun your journey by night, you will fear  
> Sword and spear, and tremble at the shadow  
> Of a reed moved by the moon.  
> The traveler who is empty-handed will sing before the robber.

**O praeclara**] “O splendid [thing]!” This is irony. He mocks riches, which are fleeting and drag along with them a great burden of cares, in accordance with the saying:

[Col. 0975A]

> As money grows, care follows it,  
> And hunger for more.

## INTO METRE V

The poem is one-membered, anapestic, parthenian, dimeter, and catalectic. In the first and second divisions it admits an anapest and also a spondee; in the third it admits only an anapest, after which one syllable remains. It resembles the following:

> Flee the shrine of Venus, maiden.

He praises the customs of the earliest age, which poets called golden because of its excellence of morals and virtues, and he does so in condemnation of human greed, which can never be satisfied.

**Prior**] The first age, described in the first book of the *Metamorphoses*. Virgil in the *Georgics*, and Tibullus.

**Aetas**] The noun must be supplied.

[Col. 0975B]

**Fidelibus arvis**] Fields that faithfully and with increase return the seed entrusted to them.

**Facili**] Easily obtainable.

**Sera**] Long-lasting and continuing into the evening.

**Solvere**] To break.

**Glande**] Before the discovery of grain, mortals fed on acorns. Hence Ovid:

> Content with food produced without compulsion,  
> They gathered arbute fruit and mountain strawberries,  
> Cornelian cherries and blackberries clinging  
> To hard brambles, and acorns fallen  
> From broad-branched Jupiter’s tree.

**Bacchica munera**] Wines.

**Norat**] Had learned, knew, was skilled in.

**Confundere**] To mix.

**Melle**] A kind of drink made from wine and honey is called *mulsum* in Latin and μελίκρατον (*melikraton*) in Greek.

**Lucida**] Bright, white.

**Serum**] These peoples are of Scythian Asia, concerning whom the poet writes in the *Georgics*:

> The Seres comb their delicate fleeces from the leaves.

Solinus: “The Seres, with the leaves flooded by the sprinkling of water, comb the wool from the trees by means of the liquid, and tame the tender height of the down with moisture for use. This is silk, admitted into public use at the cost of strictness, and which the desire for luxury first persuaded women, and now also men, to display upon their bodies rather than use for clothing. The Seres themselves are gentle and extremely peaceful among themselves, but they avoid the gatherings of other mortals to such a degree that they reject commercial contact with other nations. Merchants first cross their river; on its banks, without any linguistic exchange through an interpreter, they judge the prices of the goods deposited there with their eyes, hand over their own goods, and do not purchase ours.” Thus far Solinus.

The nominative singular of this word is *Ser*. Sidonius:

> The Assyrian has gems, the Seres wool, and the Sabaean incense.

Ausonius:

> Now the silk-clad Seres merchant flies across the sea.

The silkworm itself is also called *ser*, as Pausanias records.

**Tyrio veneno**] Purple, purple dye. Tyre is a city of Phoenicia where the finest purple is produced. *Venenum* is used for the color because it permeates clothing as poison permeates the body. For what the Latins call *venenum*, the Greeks call φάρμακον (*pharmakon*). Virgil:

[Col. 0976A]

> Nor is the white wool dyed with Assyrian poison.

**Somnos salubres**] Sleep that preserves health. He alludes to medicinal herbs. *Salubris* may also be read. Virgil:

> And gentle sleep beneath the tree.

**Lubricus**] Flowing, shifting.

**Alta**] Deep. Tibullus:

> Not yet had the pine scorned the blue waves  
> Or offered its open bosom to the winds;  
> Nor had the wandering sailor, seeking shortcuts  
> Through unknown lands, pressed his ship  
> With foreign merchandise.

**Undique**] From every side.

**Lectis**] Gathered.

**Nova littora viderat hospes**] Ovid:

> Mortals knew no shores except their own.

**Tunc**] In the golden age.

[Col. 0976B]

**Classica saeva**] Trumpets by which savage soldiers are roused for battle.

**Tacebant**] Did not resound. According to Servius, *classicum* signifies both the trumpet itself and its sound. Virgil:

> Nor had they yet heard the trumpets blown, nor yet  
> The swords clatter upon the hard anvils.

**Horrida**] Terrible, producing horror. Tibullus:

> There were no battle lines, no anger, no wars, no swords;  
> No savage smith had forged them by his cruel craft.

**Quid enim**] Why, for what reason.

**Utinam**] He wishes that the ancient customs and that former integrity of life among mortals might be restored.

**Aetna**] Mount Etna, whose fire burns perpetually in Sicily; Virgil discusses it in book II, and Claudian writes much about it.

**Amor habendi**] Greed. Ovid:

[Col. 0976C]

> And the criminal love of possession.

**Heu primus quis fuit ille**] He curses the inventor of gold, just as Tibullus curses the inventor of weapons:

> Who was the first to bring forth those dreadful swords?  
> How savage—and truly made of iron—he must have been!

**Auri tecti**] Gold hidden in the caverns of the earth, which can be extracted only through the greatest labors. For its discovery, if desired, see Lucretius. Ovid:

> We dig up solid gold from the earth in place of grain.  
> The soldier possesses wealth discovered through bloodshed.

Plautus:

> I hate gold: it has often persuaded many people to do wrong.

Tibullus:

> Many evils often lie hidden beneath gold.

Propertius:

> Everyone worships gold, now that piety has been conquered;  
> Faith is driven out by gold, and laws are for sale.  
> Gold is followed by law, and soon modesty exists without law.

Phocylides, translated by Aldus Manutius:

> Avarice is the mother of every evil. Gold and silver are ever a deceit to human beings. O gold, chief of evils,  
> Destroyer of worth, diminishing everything! Would that you were not  
> A lovable harm to mortals. For on your account there are  
> Battles, plundering, and slaughter; sons become enemies to their parents,  
> And brothers to their brothers.

Diodorus Siculus, book VI, records the following about the Balearic islands: “They do not use gold or silver, and prohibit these metals from being brought to the island, claiming that long ago Hercules conquered Geryon, son of Chrysaor, who was exceedingly rich in gold and silver. They believe that, by being without gold and silver, they will easily escape all the snares of life.”

As Solinus reports, the town of Barbitae lies 135,000 paces from Susa. There all mortals, out of hatred for gold, purchase this kind of metal and throw it into the depths of the earth, lest, polluted by its use, they corrupt justice through greed.

Silius Italicus, book I:

> But God conceals the causes of crimes. The greedy Astur  
> Is plunged into the deepest entrails of the wounded earth  
> And returns unfortunate, the color of the gold he has dug up.

Pliny, book XXXIII, chapter I of the *Natural History*: “Would that gold could be entirely banished from life—that accursed hunger for gold, as the most famous authors have called it, condemned with reproaches by all the best men and discovered for the destruction of life.”

**Latere volentes**] Hidden in the caverns of the earth, into whose entrails, as Pliny testifies, we descend, seeking riches in the dwelling place of the dead. “Precious dangers” is an appositional phrase: he adds this to what came before, meaning that these are indeed precious things, but also causes of danger, on account of which very many mortals often place themselves at risk. Ovid:

> But the journey has been made into the entrails of the earth,  
> And the riches it had concealed and brought near  
> To the Stygian shades are dug out—incitements to evil.

Pliny, book II, chapter 65: “We penetrate into the entrails of the earth, mining veins of gold and silver and ores of bronze and lead. We also seek gems and certain small stones, driving shafts deep into the ground and extracting the earth’s entrails so that a gem may be worn upon a finger. How many hands are worn down so that one finger may shine!”

Having thus far taught that riches are not to be desired by human beings, he now shows, through the most beautiful and truthful arguments, that honors and power possess nothing either worth desiring or capable of conferring true happiness.

[Col. 0977C]

**Inscii**] Ignorant.

**Coelo exaequatis**] Compared and judged equal to the highest things.

**Quae incendia**] “What conflagrations?”—as though he were saying: none.

**Eructantibus**] Bursting forth.

**Slaughter:** Calamities, devastations.

**He will have given:** He will have inflicted.

**As:** Just as.

**Consular authority:** He shows that no stability inheres in the dignities of this age, since the condition of the Roman state was often changed. At first Rome was under kings, the seventh of whom was Tarquinius—given the surname *Superbus* (“the Proud”) from his character—who was driven from the kingdom when the lust of his sons had been added to his arrogance. When one of them had violated Lucretia, a most distinguished woman, the Roman people, with Brutus and Collatinus as leaders and instigators, suddenly deprived the king of power and transferred authority to those same champions of their liberty; they called them consuls instead of kings, so that they might remember that they ought to consult for the welfare of their fellow citizens. Later, however, the Romans wished to abolish consular authority as well, and, with the consulship entirely removed, entrusted the chief power at one time to a dictator, at another to the decemvirs, and at another to the tribunes of the plebs.

**Which is very rare:** This is a parenthesis. It is very rare for honors to be conferred upon upright men. For, as we read in Sallust’s *Catiline*: “There is no distinction between the good and the wicked; ambition possesses all the rewards of virtue.”

**But what is this power of yours?:** He mocks the power of mortals as ineffectual and feeble.

**Among the mice:** He seems to allude to the Homeric poem entitled the *Batrachomyomachia*, in which Homer describes the battle between frogs and mice and makes Troxartes their king.

**How much:** To the greatest possible extent.

**More feeble than man:** It is proverbial to call a human being *fictilis*, that is, soft, weak, and fragile. The expression is derived from earthen vessels, which are easily shattered. Homer:

> Nothing on earth that nurtures is weaker than man.

**Men whom:** This expression deserves notice, for the antecedent and the relative disagree in number. Thus, earlier in the prose of this book, in the fifth prose: “Or does the force of accumulated money”—he expressed the antecedent in the singular. Then he added in the plural: “Yet these shine.” Catullus likewise, to pass over others for now:

> Then let no woman any longer trust a man who swears,  
> Nor let any woman hope that a man’s words are faithful—  
> Men who, when their eager spirit longs to obtain something,  
> Fear nothing to swear, and spare no promise.

**Where, then, could anyone?:** He shows that tyrants have no authority over the freedom of the mind, and that they can rage only against the body. He confirms this by a memorable example from a certain philosopher.

**Whereby:** By what means, in what manner, or with what instrument.

**You will command:** Someone will command.

**A certain free man:** He seems to mean Anaxarchus, an Abderite by origin and a philosopher by profession, who had Nicocreon, the tyrant of Cyprus, as an enemy. When Alexander the Great once asked him at a banquet what he thought of the dinner, Anaxarchus is said to have replied, looking at Nicocreon: “Everything is magnificently prepared, O king; but the head of some satrap ought by now to have been served.” When Nicocreon heard this, he was enraged. After the king’s death, Anaxarchus was being transported by ship and, against his will, put in at Cyprus. Nicocreon had him arrested, threw him into a hollow rock, and ordered him to be beaten with iron mallets. Unconcerned about his punishment, Anaxarchus is said to have repeatedly uttered the famous saying: “Beat, beat Anaxarchus’s vessel; for you are not grinding Anaxarchus.” When Nicocreon ordered his tongue to be cut out, tradition says that Anaxarchus bit it off and spat it into his face. Yet this story is more correctly attributed to Zeno of Elea—of whom enough was said in the first commentary—because a conspiracy is mentioned here, and that does not concern Anaxarchus. Eusebius also records the following in Book X of his *Preparation for the Gospel*: “Zeno of Elea, when he was attempting to overthrow a tyranny, is said to have bitten off his tongue with his teeth and spat it into the tyrant’s face while being tortured by the tyrant to disclose his accomplices.”

**But what is it, etc.:** He argues that the power of mortals is extremely small, since they cannot prevent the force that they inflict upon others from being inflicted upon themselves in turn by others.

**From another:** There is an old saying in Seneca: “Expect from another what you have done to another.”

**Busiris:** Busiris was king of Egypt. He sacrificed the strangers who had come under his protection, and Hercules killed him when Busiris also wished to kill Hercules. Virgil:

> Who does not know either harsh Eurystheus  
> Or the altars of infamous Busiris?

**Regulus:** Marcus Atilius Regulus, a Roman consul, triumphed after defeating the Salentines and was the first of the Roman commanders to transport a fleet to Africa. He captured sixty-three longships that had been damaged by Hamilcar, as well as two hundred towns and two hundred thousand people. During his absence, public funds were provided for his wife and children because of their poverty. Later he was captured through the strategy of Xanthippus, a Spartan mercenary, and sent to prison. He was dispatched to Rome as an envoy to negotiate an exchange of prisoners, after swearing that, if he did not obtain the exchange, he would return. In the senate he argued against the proposal; he rejected his wife and children and returned to Carthage, where he was thrown into a wooden chest with nails driven inward and punished by sleeplessness and pain.

**In addition to this:** Moreover. He proves by another argument that dignities and powers contain no natural or intrinsic good, since they generally fall to the worst people.

**Nature rejects:** That is, it does not allow opposites to be joined. Saint Cyprian, *Against Novatian*: “Bitterness cannot cohere and be joined with sweetness, darkness with light, rain with clear weather, war with peace, sterility with fertility, drought with springs, storm with calm.” Franciscus Philelphus, in the *Satyres*:

> Light rejects all darkness,  
> Nor does virtue allow vice to grow together with it;  
> Reason always scorns folly. Opposites can never  
> Stand equally in the same place.

**And this indeed concerning all things:** He shows that the gifts of Fortune cannot rightly be called good, since they are generally attached to evils and cannot make good those to whom they are joined. This passage also recalls, like many other passages in Boethius, Plato’s teaching, in which Socrates says in the *Gorgias*: “There is pleasure, in whose presence we rejoice; but the good is that in whose presence we are good. Indeed, we ourselves are good, and whatever else is good, because of some virtue that is present.”

## IN METER VI

This poem is Sapphic. Through the example of Nero, Philosophy teaches that dignities and power, when joined to wicked men, not only fail to correct their character but bring them greater savagery and depravity.

**We know:** We understand.

**He will have given:** He will have inflicted upon men.

[Col. 0979D]

**Ruins:** Slaughters. In these verses he designates Nero, by far the most cruel of all mortals. He was born to Domitius Ahenobarbus and Agrippina, the daughter of Germanicus. When she later married Claudius Caesar, Nero was adopted by him. Nero was once a name of praise, as Suetonius shows in his account of Tiberius: “Among his surnames he also assumed Nero, which in the Sabine language signifies strong and vigorous.” Now, however, Nero is the name of the utmost cruelty. He became so inflamed by madness that he killed a very large part of the senate, nearly destroyed the equestrian order, and did not even refrain from parricide: without hesitation he struck down his mother, brother, sister, wife, and the rest of his relatives and kinsmen. His recklessness in impiety toward God increased this mass of crimes. For he was the first at Rome to inflict punishments and deaths upon Christians, ordered them to be tortured by the same persecution throughout all the provinces, and attempted to eradicate their very name. He killed the most blessed apostles of Christ—Peter by crucifixion and Paul by the sword.

**When the city had been burned:** Consumed by fire. Nero, as Tranquillus writes, openly set fire to the city, supposedly offended by the ugliness of the old buildings and the narrowness and winding course of the streets. The disaster raged for six days and seven nights, and the populace was driven to take refuge among monuments and tombs. Then, besides an immense number of apartment buildings, the houses of ancient commanders—still adorned with the spoils of war—burned, as did temples of the gods that had been vowed and dedicated by kings and later during the Punic and Gallic wars, and everything ancient that had survived as worth seeing and memorable. From the Maecenatian tower Nero watched the fire and rejoiced in its beauty, as he said; dressed for the stage, he sang the *Sack of Ilium*. Eutropius and Eusebius report that Nero set fire to Rome so that he might behold a spectacle resembling the image of Troy burning after its capture.

**And the senators having been killed:** With the senators murdered. For he killed many senators, openly indicating that he would spare none of the rest, that he would eventually abolish that order from the state, and that he would entrust the provinces and armies to Roman knights and freedmen.

**His brother:** Britannicus, the son of Claudius and Messalina. He was therefore his brother by adoption, since, as we have said, Nero was adopted by Claudius, not his natural brother.

[Col. 0980C]

**Having been killed:** Removed by poison. Read Suetonius on this subject.

**His mother:** Because Nero’s mother Agrippina was harsh and threatening, and because she investigated and criticized his words and actions too severely, Nero tried to kill her in various ways. First he attempted poison, but when he realized that she was protected by antidotes, he prepared a mechanism by which a ceiling might be loosened and fall upon her at night while she slept. When this plan was insufficiently concealed by those involved, he devised a collapsible ship by which she might perish either in a shipwreck or through the collapse of its cabin. Thus, pretending reconciliation, he summoned her to Baiae with an extremely pleasant letter, so that they might celebrate the festival of the Quinquatria together. He arranged with the captains that the small vessel in which she had arrived should be broken as if by an accidental collision. He prolonged the banquet, and when she wished to return to Bauli, he offered her the cleverly contrived vessel in place of the damaged ship. When his mother had swum ashore from it, the most impious of sons ordered soldiers to kill her. Some authors write that, not content with this unspeakable crime, he hurried to see the body of the murdered woman, handled her limbs, condemned some parts, praised others, and, when thirst arose, drank. Tranquillus and Cornelius Tacitus give a fuller account of these events.

**He did not stain:** He did not drench.

**Censor:** Arbiter, judge.

**Of beauty:** Of bodily beauty.

**Of the extinguished:** Of the dead.

**Gathering the rays:** Setting. By this he signifies the nations of the whole world, throughout its four regions.

**Phoebus:** The sun.

[Col. 0981A]

**The Triones:** In the ancient language, *triones* meant ploughing oxen. The seven stars are arranged in that part of the sky so as to seem to form a wagon with oxen; they are also called the Septentriones, and they gave their name to that region, the north. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I:

> Scythia, and the seven Triones,  
> Were invaded by the terrifying north wind.

**Notus:** The south wind.

**In the dry heat:** In the warmth. It should be understood, according to Macrobius, that the south wind is cold at its origin, as the north wind is among us; but because it travels to us through the flame of the torrid zone, it is mixed with fire and becomes hot. Thus it begins cold but arrives warm.

**Surely?:** Is it possible?

**Lofty power:** Outstanding power.

[Col. 0981B]

**To change:** To alter. Here this verb lengthens its final syllable because two consonants occur at the beginning of the following word, although over-clever grammarians deny that this can happen, since they have never carefully read Juvenal, Prudentius, or this author.

**Rage:** Inflamed savagery.

**Alas, grievous fate:** A beautiful exclamation, and no less true. “Alas,” he says, “what a harsh and intolerable condition it is when an unjust sword—that is, unjust power—and unjust rule are added to savage poison—that is, to a monstrous and brutal character and the most corrupt morals.” Seneca: “Thunderbolt is he in whom anger dwells together with power.” Aristotle, *Politics* I: “For just as man, when perfected, is the best of all animals, so, when separated from law and justice, he is the worst of all animals. Injustice armed is the most savage.” Lactantius, *On Justice*, chapter 11: “What Caucasus, what India, what Hyrcania has ever nourished beasts so savage and bloodthirsty? For the fury of all wild animals rages only until the belly is satisfied, and when hunger has been appeased, it immediately becomes quiet. But that true beast, at whose single command

> dark blood is poured everywhere, cruel mourning everywhere,  
> fear everywhere, and the image of death in abundance—

no one can adequately describe the savagery of so great a monster: though reclining in one place, it rages throughout the whole world with iron teeth, and not only scatters human limbs but crushes the bones themselves and reduces them to ashes, so that no place of burial remains.” Baptista Mantuanus, in the second *Parthenice*:

> No virtue is safe beneath an unworthy prince;  
> Beneath an incestuous king there is no glory for the chaste.

## IN PROSE VII

Thus far it has been argued that true happiness consists neither in riches nor in dignities and power. Now he demonstrates, by the finest and most truthful arguments, how empty and ineffectual glory is—the glory pursued with the greatest eagerness by nearly everyone. To approach the subject more suitably, Boethius himself speaks in turn and admits that he was not so much captivated by ambition for mortal things as inflamed by the desire to spread his reputation and acquire glory.

**Then:** An adverb of sequence.

**Least:** *Minimum* and *minime* differ: *minimum* is an adverb of quantity, whereas *minime* is an adverb of negation.

[Col. 0982A]

**Ambition:** Desire.

**In carrying out:** In administering.

**So that not:** So that he might not. Horace, *Satires*:

> So that the enemy might not rush upon empty Rome.

**Silent:** Unknown. Claudian:

> Virtue joined to a mighty deed is greater and more useful;  
> virtue hidden in darkness is worthless: for what will it profit,  
> Submerged in obscurity, like a ship without a helmsman,  
> A lyre that is silent, or a bow that is not bent?

**To the final hand:** To complete fulfillment. “To put on the final hand” means to finish something in all its parts. The metaphor is taken from craftsmen: they first shape a rough outline of the work, which they call the first hand; then they form it more precisely; finally, with the greatest care, they polish it, and this they call the final, highest, or ultimate hand.

[Col. 0982B]

**The desire for glory, of course:** Marcus Tullius, *For Archias*: “We are all drawn by the pursuit of praise, and the best of us are most strongly led by glory. Those very philosophers, even in the books they write on despising glory, inscribe their own names in the very work in which they despise renown and distinction; they wish to be praised and named.” The same author, in the same speech: “For no virtue desires any other reward for its labors and dangers apart from this praise and glory. If this were taken away, judges, what is there that would make us engage in such great labors during this very brief span and short course of life?” Cicero speaks impiously, as a man without true religion and wisdom, since he lacked hope of eternal life and contempt for empty glory.

[Col. 0982C]

**The whole circuit of the earth:** From the narrow confines of the entire dwelling-place of mortals, he very clearly shows how slight the dissemination of fame is and how futile the effort to extend one’s name.

**As you have learned from astronomical demonstrations:** This is a parenthesis. Astronomers demonstrate that, in relation to the firmament, the earth occupies the place of a point. Wherever we may be situated on the surface of the earth and observe the stars from different locations, neither their apparent sizes nor their distances from one another seem to vary. Hence it is established, on the basis of sense perception, that they are equally distant from the earth. The earth, therefore, is the center of the sphere and consequently performs the function of a point. The same applies to the earth when compared with the sphere of the sun, as is also shown by other indications. Bodies placed at the centers of circular instruments cast shadows, and these shadows move far away in the direction in which the sun itself, shining, is carried by its primary motion. From the regularity of the shadow’s movement, which we discern by the senses, it is inferred that the sun moves regularly around the center of the instruments; therefore the centers of such instruments regularly occupy the position of the center of the universe, around which the primary motion occurs. Since the earth’s thickness introduces no variation into these matters, the proposed conclusion appears sound. Moreover, the horizon conceals half the sky from an eye located upon it and allows half to be seen. This is proper to no flat surface except one passing through the center of a sphere. Otherwise the situation would be different if the earth had any considerable size in relation to the heavens.

[Col. 0983A]

Marcus Tullius, *Tusculan Disputations* I: “For mathematicians teach that the earth, situated in the middle of the universe, occupies the place of a point in relation to the whole compass of the heavens; they call it the *kentron* (κέντρον), or center.” Seneca: “The place we inhabit is a point, and less than a point.” Read Pliny, *Natural History* II, chapter 70, whose title is “What Portion of the Earth Is Inhabited.”

**A point:** Macrobius records the following in his *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*: “Geometers said that a point is something which, because of its incomprehensible smallness, cannot be divided into parts, nor is it itself a part of anything; it is said to be merely a mark. Physicists taught that the earth occupies the status of a point in relation to the size of the circle through which the sun revolves.”

[Col. 0983B]

**Ptolemy:** This astronomer was Egyptian by birth. He studied at Alexandria and became distinguished in the liberal arts and in Greek letters during the reign of the emperor Antoninus, as he himself demonstrates in his *Great Composition*. In the science of astronomy he yielded to none of his predecessors. He was the first among the Greeks to explain the entire structure of the heavens with greater care and to display more clearly the instruments invented by Hipparchus. He published that great composition which is called the *Almagest*, as well as a work in four treatises. He wrote a *Centiloquy* on matters relating to the practical prediction of celestial phenomena, consisting of one hundred maxims, which the Greeks call *karpoi* (κάρποι), because they say these are the fruit and practical test of predictions. He also composed three books on music and wrote on geography, in the manner of an astronomer. [Col. 0983C] Among his principal commentators from the non-Greek peoples are Haly and Albumazer; among the Greeks, Tappus and Theon. He himself composed a Greek four-line epitaph for his tomb, which someone translated as follows:

> Although I know that I was created mortal by fate,  
> Yet while I examine the paths of the stars in the heavens,  
> I stand far from the earth beneath my feet, and sit beside  
> The Thunderer as a god; I feed upon ambrosia.

**Be inhabited:** Be dwelt in.

**By thirst:** By dryness.

**Vast:** Desolate.

**Region:** A small district.

**By boundaries:** By limits.

**Confined:** Restrained, constricted.

**Add:** He shows that, because of the diversity and distance of nations, fame cannot be spread very far.

[Col. 0983D]

**By reason:** By means, or in this way.

**Distant:** Different. There is a Greek proverb, “Law and region” (Νόμος καὶ χώρα), meaning that every people has its own laws and institutions of life.

**As he himself indicates in a certain passage:** In Cicero’s *Dream of Scipio*, Africanus says to his grandson: “From these cultivated and familiar lands, could your name—or that of any one of us—cross beyond this Caucasus, which you see, or swim across that Ganges?”

**Caucasus:** Caucasus is a mountain of Scythia, called, as Pliny says in Book VI, almost as though from *graucasus*, meaning white with snow. Caucasus is an extremely lofty mountain, also extremely rugged and inhospitable, separating India from Scythia on the borders of Assyria.

[Col. 0984A]

**The Parthians:** These peoples live in Greater Asia near the Medes, Hyrcanians, Arians, and other neighboring nations of that kind. They were exiles from the Scythians, for in the Scythian language *Parthi* means “exiles.” At first they were obscure among the eastern peoples; later, through their valor, they advanced to the highest glory. They fight while advancing on horseback or while retreating; they often also feign flight, so that they may have pursuers less cautious about wounds. Read more about them in Justin, Book XLI, and in Plutarch’s *Life of Crassus*.

**In those regions:** To those living in that place. “Of those regions” is a figurative expression, like the expression given above, “to children of that age.”

[Col. 0984B]

**Fearful:** To be feared. *Formidolosus* ordinarily means timid, as in Terence: “Am I fearful?”—that is, “Am I someone who is afraid?” It can also mean one who inspires fear in others. Sallust: “Good men are more suspect to kings than bad men, and another’s virtue is always fearful to them.”

**Of the Roman name:** Of the Roman man. This is a paranomasia, called in Latin *agnominatio*, or wordplay through related names. He draws his argument from what is called the argument from the greater: it may be explained as follows. It seems more likely that the name of the Roman state than that of any individual Roman could advance beyond the Caucasus; but since even that name cannot do so, neither can the individual’s.

**What of the fact that different nations:** He proves from the discrepancy of the customs and institutions followed by different nations that it is not useful to extend anyone’s name among many peoples, since what is judged worthy of praise among one people may be judged worthy of punishment among another.

**Customs and institutions disagree:** On this subject, read Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* VI, chapter 8; Valerius Maximus II; Jerome, *Against Jovinianus*; Bessarion IV, *Against the Calumniator of Plato*, chapter 3; Philippus Beroaldus in his proverbial oration; and our Erasmus in his explanation of the proverb “Law and region.” For now, it is enough that I have pointed these works out to students of such matters, since I am hurrying on to other subjects.

**That glorious one:** This is a mockery of empty glory.

**But how many very famous men:** He argues that glory is ineffectual, both because writings are lacking and because those writings are unstable and by no means lasting.

**Poor in writings:** The praises and achievements of many peoples, especially the Germans, lie hidden and unknown because in those ancient times writers who might hand down glorious deeds in literary monuments were lacking, when character had not yet been softened and gradually corrupted by foreign luxuries. Even now Pliny’s books on the German wars are missing, as are doubtless many other writings once composed, of which not even the titles have reached us.

**But you, etc.:** He argues most eloquently that fame, however long it may last, cannot in any way be compared with eternity, since it eventually admits an end.

**Which:** Time.

[Col. 0985A]

**You should consider thoroughly:** You should weigh it intellectually and turn it over in your mind.

**Ten thousand years:** Ten thousand years. To over-clever scholars, some expressions seem insufficiently grammatical, although they are not merely grammatical but also highly elegant and used by the best-established writers. This is an example: “ten thousand years,” by apposition. Thus in Latin we say: “This merchant owes ten thousand gold pieces.” Jerome, who uses this type of expression abundantly elsewhere, wrote in *Against Jovinianus*: “It is one thing to owe ten thousand talents, another to owe a farthing.” Florus: “When more than ten thousand men had immediately gathered, they were not content merely to escape; they already wished to take vengeance as well.” The same author: “Two thousand were chosen from the very flower of the equestrian order and the senate, to be ordered to die.” Here “men” or “persons” must be understood, so that people may cease criticizing the expression found in Sacred Scripture: “Twelve thousand were sealed.”

[Col. 0985B]

**And however manifold it may be:** And however greatly that number may be multiplied, as in a thousand times a thousand thousands of years, or more or fewer.

**Comparison:** Comparison, proportion. Aristotle, *On the Heavens and the World* I: “There is no proportion of the finite to the infinite.”

**However much:** Here it is an adverb.

**Extended:** Long.

**Unexhausted:** Infinite, without end.

**But unless you:** He rebukes the folly of mortals, who are generally so disposed that they pursue human praise and the celebrity of fame more than purity of conscience and the true security of virtue. For, as it has been most rightly said, “Many respect fame; few respect conscience.”

**To popular breezes:** To the favor and applause of the people, which wise men, according to Donatus, do not seek. *Aura* signifies brightness. Horace:

> May your breeze not delay husbands.

The word is used for air, the condition of the winds, breath, inspiration, or favor. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI:

> Now too greatly you rejoice in popular breezes.

Jerome: “The disciple of Christ ought to surpass the philosopher of the world, that creature of glory and purchasable slave of popular favor and rumors.”

**Little conversations:** Little rumors. *Sermunculus* means a small conversation, just as *rumusculus* means a small rumor. Jerome, *To Nepotianus*: “Beware of hunting after the little rumors of men, lest you exchange God’s displeasure for the praise of the people.” The same author, *To Paulinus*: “Flee little rumors, little glories, and flattering flatterers as enemies.”

**Listen:** Hear and understand.

**In such frivolity:** In vanity. It is also read as *levitatem* (“frivolity”), which I prefer, so that it may stand in opposition to this kind of proud vanity.

**How amusingly:** How pleasantly, wittily, and humorously.

**He mocked:** He joked.

**He had attacked:** It is also read *adorsus*, a form that I likewise find in Ambrose and Jerome.

**He had endured:** He would have suffered.

**For a little while:** For a short time.

[Col. 0986A]

**Anger:** Through anger.

**He:** The false philosopher’s mocker is also being tested.

**If you had kept silent:** Solomon, in Proverbs: “He who restrains his words is learned and prudent, and the man of disciplined spirit is educated. Even a fool, if he keeps silent, will be considered wise; and if he holds his lips closed, intelligent.” Diogenes said to a philosopher who was arguing something too contentiously: “Wretched man, you are corrupting by philosophizing in words what is best and most important in the life of a philosopher.” Thales: “Not using many words is a sign of a prudent mind.” Solomon, Proverbs X: “In much speaking sin will not be lacking. He who restrains his lips is most prudent.” Ecclesiastes: “The fool multiplies words.” Seneca: “Always maintain a balance between speech and silence. He who does not know how to be silent does not know how to speak.” Macrobius, *Saturnalia* VII: “Since an orator is proved only by speaking, a philosopher philosophizes no less by remaining silent at the proper time than by speaking.” Valerius Maximus VII: “How praiseworthy was the reply of Xenocrates, when he listened in complete silence to the abusive speech of certain men, and one of them asked why he alone restrained his tongue: ‘Because,’ he said, ‘I have sometimes regretted speaking, but never keeping silent.’ If you wish, read the beautiful saying of Maro on this subject in Donatus’s *Life of Virgil*.”

**But what is this?:** He shows that glory benefits the dead nothing. Hence someone aptly said:

> After the ashes, glory comes too late.

**Which:** That human beings die wholly, in body and soul.

**Our arguments:** Philosophical arguments.

[Col. 0986C]

**Forbid:** Do not permit.

**Earthly prison:** The body, which is like a prison, tomb, or bond of the soul.

**Released:** Set free.

## IN METER VII

This poem is *dicolon distrophon*. Its first verse is Archilochian, iambic, senary, and acatalectic; its second is iambic dimeter and likewise acatalectic. Through it Philosophy urges mortals to despise empty glory. This glory will easily appear the vainest of all things if, after contemplating the narrowness of the lands, they look up at the immense expanse of heaven.

**Headlong:** Hasty, unconsidered, rash.

**Highest:** The highest good, the supreme thing, the end of goods.

[Col. 0986D]

**Of the ether:** Of heaven.

**May behold:** May contemplate.

**Regions:** Areas, districts.

**Narrow:** Tight, confined. Africanus, in Cicero’s *Dream of Scipio*, from which this poem seems largely to have been taken, together with the prose already explained: “All the earth that you inhabit, narrowed at the poles and broader at the sides, is a small island surrounded by that sea which on earth you call Atlantic, Great, or Ocean; yet you see how small it is despite such a great name.” Hence Petrarch, *Africa* II:

> Confined within narrow boundaries, the world  
> Is a small island in its situation, which Ocean  
> Encloses with curving folds. Do you see how small it is  
> Despite its great name?

[Col. 0987A]

**To fill the brief space:** The order is: “He will be ashamed”—understand “the man who has contemplated the narrowness of the earth and the immeasurable spaces of heaven”—“of a magnified name,” that is, a name extended and enlarged, yet unable to fill the brief circuit, meaning the narrow habitation, of the earth. Scipio, in Cicero’s *On the Republic* VI: “Indeed, the earth itself seemed so small to me that I was ashamed of our empire, by which we touch, as it were, only a point of it.” In the same work the grandfather addresses the same grandson: “Therefore, if you wish to look upward and contemplate this place and eternal home, do not give yourself over to the talk of the crowd, nor place your hope in human rewards for your accomplishments. Virtue itself must draw you by its attractions toward true honor. Let others see what they say about you—but say it they will. For all that speech is confined within the narrow limits of these regions which you see; it has never been lasting concerning anyone, and is overwhelmed by the death of all things and extinguished by the forgetfulness of posterity.”

**What:** To what purpose.

**O:** An exclamation of wonder, or of pity and grief at the error of mortals. The order is: “O, why do the proud vainly strive to lift their necks from the mortal yoke?” That is: “Why do proud and arrogant men vainly attempt to make themselves immortal by spreading their name?”

**To lift their necks from the yoke:** He alludes to oxen resisting the yoke but unable to throw it off, according to the saying:

> The bull does not love the yokes, yet what he hates he bears.

**Mortal yoke:** The condition of mortality to which they are subject.

**Although:** Although, even though.

[Col. 0987C]

**Passing:** Transient.

**May explain:** May interpret.

**House:** Nation, family, or lineage.

**Death scorns lofty glory:** Seneca, Letter 91: “Ash makes all equal; we are born unequal, we die equal.” The same author, Letter 99: “Amid such upheaval of human affairs, nothing is certain for anyone except death.” Horace, *Odes*:

> Pale death knocks with equal foot at the huts of the poor  
> And the towers of kings.

Lucretius:

> Scipio, the thunderbolt of war and the ruin of Carthage,  
> Gave his bones to the earth just as though he had been the lowest servant.

> Add the discoverers of learning and delights;  
> Add the companions of the Muses.

The same author:

> Then many other kings and men powerful in affairs  
> Fell—men who had ruled over great nations.

The same author:

> What great evil does such desire for life impose upon us?  
> A certain end of life awaits mortals,  
> And death cannot be avoided; we must meet it.

**Faithful Fabricius:** This was a Roman consul, called faithful because he thought faith must be kept even with an enemy and that nothing should be done by fraud or ambush. When, to use Marcus Tullius’s words, King Pyrrhus had made war upon the Roman people and when there was a contest for dominion with a noble and powerful king, a deserter came from Pyrrhus’s camp to Fabricius and promised that, if Fabricius offered him a reward, he would return secretly to Pyrrhus’s camp, just as he had come secretly, and kill him with poison. Fabricius arranged for the man to be returned to Pyrrhus, and the senate praised his action. On this subject see also Valerius Maximus, Aulus Gellius, and Plutarch’s *Life of Pyrrhus*.

**They lie:** It is also read *manent*, “remain.”

**What is Brutus now?:** Supply “what is he now?” Junius Brutus, the first Roman consul, liberated the city after expelling the kings. Because his sons had conspired with the Aquilii and Vitellii to restore the Tarquins to the city, he had them beaten with rods and struck with the axe. Later he engaged in single combat with Arruns, the son of Tarquinius; both killed each other with mutual wounds. Marcus Brutus, a praetorian man distinguished both by learning and by courage, killed Julius Caesar in order to restore liberty; later defeated in battle by Octavian, he took his own life.

[Col. 0988B]

**Rigid:** Severe, inflexible.

**Cato:** There were many Catos at Rome, but two were distinguished above the rest: Marcus Porcius Cato the Censor and the Stoic Cato, who, after taking his own life at Utica, was called Cato of Utica. Both were renowned for justice, severity, and the utmost gravity of character.

**What:** To what purpose.

**Honorable names:** Beautiful names.

**We know:** We know and retain.

**Surely?:** Is it possible?

**Consumed:** Dead.

**You lie:** Supply “you men lie after death.”

**Completely:** Entirely.

**Unknown:** Without renown.

[Col. 0988C]

**To be dragged:** To be prolonged.

**Breeze:** Splendor.

**Of a mortal name:** Subject to death and corruption. Ausonius:

> We marvel that men have perished; monuments decay;  
> Death comes even to stones and names.

**When:** When.

**A late day:** A time that will eventually come.

**This:** The name.

**A second death:** The death by which the name is extinguished, just as life is extinguished by the first death. In Petrarch, *Africa* II, Africanus addresses Scipio in this way:

> Quickly will pass the things you think will remain.  
> Only virtue can remain, unaware of setting.  
> It makes a path to the gods above; proceed by it, brave men,  
> Nor let backs wearied by heavy toil yield.

[Col. 0988D]

> But if false glory delights your wandering mind,  
> Look at what you desire: time will pass, this body  
> Will fall, and its limbs will yield to an unworthy tomb.  
> Soon the monument too will collapse, and the title cut in marble  
> Will perish; here, my son, you will suffer a second death.

## IN PROSE VIII

Thus far Philosophy has exposed Fortune’s inconstancy, fraud, and treachery, and has shown that there is no true good in her gifts. Now she says that adverse Fortune benefits human beings more than prosperous Fortune does: prosperity, by its flatteries, deceitfully draws those whom it has enticed away from the true good, whereas adversity generally leads those who are wandering back toward the pursuit of true happiness, dragging them back as if with a hook.

**Inexorable:** Something that cannot be settled by any prayers.

[Col. 0989A]

**Is:** Happens, occurs.

**That one:** Fortune.

**Then:** At that time.

**When:** When.

**I desire:** I long for.

**And for that reason:** And on that account.

**That one:** Prosperous Fortune. He offers arguments by which he proves the truth of what he has said.

**This:** Adverse Fortune. Seneca the Tragedian:

> It is permissible to prefer bad fortune to good.

**Windy:** Inconstant. Horace:

> At Rome I love Tibur; at windy Tibur, Rome.

**Flowing:** Luxuriant, overflowing, wandering. Ovid:

> Minds generally grow luxuriant in prosperous circumstances,  
> Nor is it easy to endure advantages with an even mind.

[Col. 0989B]

**And always ignorant of itself:** For men lifted up by the successes of Fortune become excessively proud and in no way know themselves.

**Sober:** Self-controlled.

**Girded:** Restrained, not overflowing.

**Through the exercise of adversity:** Baptista Mantuanus, *Silvae* II:

> Virtue, shaken by adverse circumstances,  
> Grows, and, tormented by long ... [The supplied source ends here.]

[It] takes on [a sheen] through rubbing, and with its surface more thoroughly cleansed,

it gleams white.

**From the true good.** Saint Ambrose, in *On Intercession*: “The abundance of prosperity is a great enticement to wrongdoing. It makes people complacent and inflated, and instills forgetfulness of their creator.” The mime-writer says:

> Fortune makes foolish the one whom she favors too greatly.

**[Col. 0989C]** Baptista Mantuanus, in the first book of the *Parthenice*:

> Leisure commonly enervates secure minds  
> and casts shadows over souls, so that dust, once compacted  
> by a watery rain, can no longer be carried away by the light East Winds.  
> So adversity weighs down rebellious senses,  
> compels them to obey God, drives out hidden diseases,  
> and calms the burning passions in the breast.  
> As entrails preserved with sprinkled salt  
> are protected from corruption and decay,  
> so minds are strengthened by hardship, and cast away  
> every cause of corruption; harsh fortune provides a safe road,  
> and by this road leads to the starry citadels.

**Of faithful friends.** Ennius:

> A true friend is recognized in uncertain circumstances.

Hence we have played upon this verse:

> In uncertain circumstances, a faithful friend is recognized.

Ovid:

> Just as gold is tested in the fire,  
> so faithfulness must be examined in difficult times.

**[Col. 0989D]** **Their own.** Their companions; for those who follow fortune are not true friends, but companions and associates of fortune.

**Unharmed.** Not yet injured, not yet stripped of your possessions.

**Cease.** This is a fine conclusion, drawing its ornament from opposites.

**You have found friends.** Now, when fortune has become hostile, you recognize your true friends. The proof of true friendship is not abandoning a friend in adversity.

## INTO METRE VIII

The poem is Glyconic, similar to the sixth poem of the first book. It teaches that all things are joined by love and that the harmony of the whole world consists in love; by love, too, peoples are united in treaty, and spouses and friends are brought together. Franciscus Philelphus, in the *Satires*:

> Harmony binds everything with an everlasting bond.  
> Whatever love joins endures throughout the ages.

Claudian, addressed to Honorius:

> Neither watchmen nor surrounding spears  
> guard as love does; nor can you compel anyone to be loved.  
> Mutual trust and simple affection grant this.  
> Do you not see how the world itself, most beautiful of works,  
> binds itself together through love? How the elements, joined  
> for ages without force, harmonize among themselves—  
> the sun content with its central boundary,  
> the sea content with its shore,  
> the air which perpetually surrounds and carries the earth,  
> neither weighed down by its burden nor yielding?

As Plato teaches in the *Timaeus*, the world embraces itself in harmonious friendship and coheres so suitably that it cannot in any way be dissolved except by the same power by which it was bound together. In Latin, *mundus* (“world”) is named from purity; *caelum* (“heaven”) from carving; in Greek, from adornment: **κόσμος** (*kosmos*). C. Pliny, in Book Two: “What the Greeks called *kosmos*, using the word for ornament, we likewise call *mundus*, from perfect and complete elegance. We have unquestionably called the heavens *caelum* from the idea of carving, as Marcus Varro interprets it.”

**With stable faith.** With perpetual constancy.

**Changes.** Exchanges.

**Seeds.** The elements. Pliny, Book Two, chapter five:

> I do not see that there is any doubt that there are four elements: fire at the highest point, from which come the eyes of so many shining stars; next, spirit, which Greeks and Romans alike call by the same name, air—vital, permeating all things, and thoroughly interwoven with them. By its force the earth, suspended together with the fourth element, water, is balanced in the middle of space. Thus, through the mutual embrace of differences, a bond is produced, and light things are restrained by weights from flying away. Conversely, heavy things are suspended so that they do not fall, while light things rise upward. Thus, each thing, striving equally in opposite directions, remains in place by its own force, bound within the restless circuit of the world itself. Since that circuit is always running back into itself, the earth stands at the lowest and central point of the whole, suspended and balanced upon an inverted axis. Thus the earth alone is immovable, while the revolving universe moves around it; and it is joined to everything, while everything rests upon it.

**Things at odds.** Opposites.

**Perpetual treaty.** Perpetual peace. Ovid:

> He bound things separated in place with harmonious peace.

Manilius, *Astronomica*, Book One:

> This work, constructed from the vast body of the universe,  
> contains the various members of nature, formed  
> from air, fire, earth, and the lying sea.  
> A divine power of spirit governs it; God harmonizes it  
> through a sacred movement and directs it by silent reason.  
> He distributes many covenants throughout all its parts,  
> so that one may produce and sustain the powers of another,  
> and so that the whole may remain related through varied forms.

The same author, Book Three:

> The Fates govern the universe; everything stands under a fixed law,  
> and long ages are marked out by appointed courses.

**Phoebus.** The sun.

**Rose-colored.** Beautiful, shining, ruddy.

**Golden.** Bright, clear, illustrious.

**Which.** The nights.

**When Hesperus has led them.** Hesperus is the leader of night, for it goes before it, following the setting of the sun in the evening.

**[Col. 0991A]** **Phoebe.** The moon.

**Greedy.** Desirous and voracious.

**May restrain.** May hold back.

**Wandering.** Passing beyond the prescribed limit.

**To stretch.** To extend.

**Sequence.** Connection, continuous progression.

**Sea.** The ocean.

**Ruling.** Exercising authority.

**Here.** Love.

**Should have relaxed the reins.** Should have abandoned governance and restraint. The metaphor is taken from those who restrain horses with reins.

**Immediately.** At once, without delay.

**With companionable faith.** With mutual harmony.

**They urge on.** They set in motion.

**Let them compete.** Let them strive eagerly against one another.

**To dissolve.** To destroy, corrupt.

**The structure.** The body of the world.

**Here.** Love.

**[Col. 0992A]** **Holy.** Just, lovers of peace, confirmed by the blood of Christ; or holy in the sense of being joined by sacred acts and oaths that have been sworn.

**And.** Also.

**Of marriage.** Of matrimony.

**Sacred.** A sacrament.

**With chaste loves.** With modest amorous affections.

**Love is threefold.** Base love pursues bodily pleasure alone and is therefore the passion of brute animals. Noble love looks to a noble mind, ready for the duties of virtue. Intermediate love cherishes both bodily and spiritual beauty.

**Dictates.** Prescribes, suggests.

**To faithful companions.** To true friends.

**O happy race of humankind.** Supply: “You would be happy if the love by which heaven is governed governed your minds,” that is, the minds of human beings. “You humans,” he says, “would be happy if there were as much concord among you through love as there is among heavenly things.” But, as the poet says:

> By the law of the gods, discord troubles the lowest throng of things;  
> the highest things maintain peace.

# BOOK THREE

## INTO THE FIRST PROSE

In the second book Philosophy clearly exposed the deceptive character of fortune and demonstrated that her gifts are not true goods. In this third book she describes the form of false happiness and then introduces the beauty of true blessedness, which is its opposite. She clearly shows **[Col. 0991C]** where true blessedness consists, what the one highest good is, and that God, blessedness, and the highest good are not different. Furthermore, she teaches that the person who has attained blessedness has simultaneously attained sufficiency, reverence, power, renown, and joy. She also shows that although these names differ in sound—sufficiency, reverence, power, renown, and joy—their force is nevertheless one and the same. From this the error of human beings becomes plainly evident: treating these things as different, they regard one of them as desirable above the others. They place their happiness in different things, although it can by no means be found there. Some think they will attain blessedness through wealth, others through offices, others through kingdoms, many through glory, and very many through pleasure; but they are deceived, since wealth cannot provide sufficiency, office reverence, kingdoms power, glory immortality of name, or pleasure genuine joy. Thus, **[Col. 0991D]** although people hold entirely different opinions and mortals stray from the true good while seeking happiness, they nevertheless all agree and concur in desiring the highest good. It follows that God is the one end of all things, since blessedness and the highest good, and God, are different names but one reality. In this way Boethius is reminded of what he had earlier confessed that he did not know—namely, what the end of all things is.

**Greedy.** Desirous.

**Astonished.** Wondering.

**[Col. 0992B]** **Sweetness.** Pleasantness, soothing, delight; from *mulcere*, “to soothe.” Saint Cyprian, *To Donatus*: “Let religious sweetness charm the ear.” Sidonius Apollinaris also used this expression in his letters.

**Had fixed.** Had rendered attentive.

**Of the weary and exhausted.** Of those worn down by cares and pains.

**[Col. 0992C]** **Solace.** A comforter.

**You have revived.** You have refreshed.

**So greatly.** To such an extent.

**Unequal.** Unable to resist.

**I do not shrink back.** I am not afraid.

**I earnestly demand.** I eagerly seek.

**I perceived.** “I recognized that, eager to hear, you were urgently demanding sharper remedies.”

**Condition.** Affection, disposition.

**What remains.** The remedies that remain.

**You would burn.** You would be on fire.

**Whither?** Where, for what purpose?

**Dreams.** Imagines and conjectures as if in a dream.

**[Col. 0992D]** **Toward images.** Toward representations of happiness.

**That very thing.** True happiness.

**Without hesitation.** Without delay.

**Specimen.** Example, form, demonstration.

## INTO THE FIRST METRE

The poem is ithyphallic, dactylic, tetrameter, catalectic-free, consisting of three dactyls and a pyrrhic. It is scanned as follows:

> Who sows the fertile field.

Terentianus calls this type of metre Phaliscian, saying:

> We have read such Phaliscian verses.

By four elegant comparisons he proves that the appearance of false blessedness must first be represented in words, so that afterward the form of true blessedness may be more readily recognized.

**Who should sow.** “First,” he says, “harmful weeds and shrubs must be uprooted before seeds can be entrusted to the earth.” Faustus Andrelinus:

> The worst weed must be pulled by the anxious farmer,  
> lest the lone crop perish through abundant corruption.

Saint Jerome: “Unless a thorny field has first been cleared by the labor of its cultivator, it does not nourish the seeds cast into it but suffocates them.”

**To sow.** To fill with seeds.

**Fertile.** Productive.

**Fruits.** Shrubs occupy a position between trees and herbs. They are smaller than trees, but unlike herbs they do not wither in winter.

**Fern.** Fern is a commonly known plant, especially harmful to grain. Horace:

> Fern, fit to be burned, grows up in neglected fields.

**Ceres.** The crop. Here he has permissibly shortened the final syllable, as Horace does in the *Art of Poetry* with *palus*, which is naturally long. Virgil:

> Golden Ceres gazes in vain from lofty Olympus.

Perhaps Boethius left *seges* written in the text, since it is easy to slip from one word into the other. The order is: “Let a new Ceres go forth,” that is, let it grow heavy, that is, full of grain. Ceres is called the goddess of crops, as though from *geres*, with the first letter changed.

**The labor of bees.** Honey.

**More.** More greatly.

**Bitter taste.** Bitterness. Thus Jerome: “The bitterness of preceding pain commends more strongly the joys that are to follow.” Claudian:

> Unexpected joys always increase  
> the sorrows that preceded them in turn;  
> the harshness of the sea commends the tranquil harbor.

**Let it eat.** Let it bite, torment.

**Stars.** The stars.

**When.** After.

**Notus.** The South Wind.

**Rain-bearing.** Bringing rain.

**When.** After.

**Rose-colored.** Reddish because of the dawn.

**Drives.** Brings forth.

**Gazing.** Looking upon.

**Yoke.** Servitude.

**To draw back.** To withdraw.

**[Col. 0993D]** **True.** Supply: “good.”

**Will have undergone.** They will undergo.

## INTO THE SECOND PROSE

He teaches that all mortals naturally seek the highest good and pursue blessedness, but that they are shamefully led away from it by various errors along different paths, since they suppose they will attain happiness through wealth, offices, kingdoms, glory, and pleasures—something that cannot happen at all.

**Then.** Next.

**With fixed gaze.** It expresses the gesture of someone contemplating something with the deepest concentration.

**With fixed gaze.** With his eyes lowered and directed toward the same place. Virgil:

> He stood and fixed his eyes upon the kingdoms of Libya.

**Of mortals.** Of human beings.

**Of manifold pursuits.** Terence:

> As many people, so many opinions;  
> each has his own way of life.

Persius:

> A thousand types of human beings, and each has  
> a different desire regarding things; no one lives by a single wish.

Horace, in the *Satires*:

> Castor delights in horses, while Pollux, born from the same egg,  
> delights in boxing: as many heads as live, so many thousands  
> of pursuits exist.

He composed the first of all his odes on this idea: that different people are led by different pursuits, and that different things appeal to different people. Euripides, in the *Crowned Hippolytus*:

> Different things please different people.

Homer, in the *Odyssey*:

> For different things smile upon and please different people.

Pliny the Younger: “Human judgments are various, and human desires are various.” Our friend Hermannus Buschius Pasiphilus:

> Human beings’ pursuits are not alike, nor is their will one;  
> each continually enjoys the fulfillment of his own wish.

**But nevertheless everyone strives to reach one end, blessedness.** Saint Aurelius Augustine, *City of God*, Book Ten, chapter one:

> Everyone who can use reason in any way is agreed on this: all human beings wish to be blessed. But while human weakness investigates who the blessed are and how they become so, many serious controversies have arisen, in which philosophers have worn out their studies and leisure.

Thus Augustine. When I was young and sufficiently bold, I once expressed this passage in verses in the fourth book of my *Moral Elegies*. I am pleased to include them here:

> Noble Moderson, who by our sweet companionship  
> are accustomed to forge learned words with me,  
> you see how we all strive toward one end  
> by paths of life and counsel that are very different.  
>   
> One pants after riches, poor amid piled-up gold,  
> and thinks that nothing is more beautiful than wealth.  
> Another, ambitious, seeks great honors for himself  
> and rejoices everywhere to be revered.  
>   
> Some think that splendid power is the good,  
> and delight in ruling countless men.  
> These wish either to be kings or to be added to kings,  
> and seek with every prayer to have the greatest power.  
>
