> Some are delighted by deferred glory and renown;  
> they make their name famous by any art.  
> Deceptive pleasure ensnares most people,  
> who eagerly pursue delicacies.  
>   
> Part of humanity flourishes in those for whom wisdom is dear,  
> who take delight in the knowledge of things.  
> Some pursue what is honorable as though it were the goal,  
> although for them the shadow of goodness scarcely appears.  
>   
> For while they strive to seem prudent and just by themselves,  
> they perish, bursting with pride and swelling arrogance.  
> Surely no one here can rightly be called happy.  
> The highest good remains in the citadel of heaven.  
>   
> That is eternal peace, as I understand it,  
> or God himself, overflowing with goodness.  
> Let us strive together toward it by the steps of justice.  
> Whoever enjoys such a good desires nothing else.

**That.** That is the end of blessedness.

**Who?** Someone.

**Having obtained.** Having acquired.

**Would be absent.** Would be lacking.

**It is clear.** It is established and evident.

**The state of blessedness.** He gives the following definition of blessedness: “Blessedness is a state made perfect by the aggregation of all goods.” Speusippus, in his *Definitions of Plato*, gives formulations that correspond well to this: “Blessedness is a good accumulated from all goods; a power sufficient in itself for living well; perfection according to virtue; sufficient provision for life.” *Beatitudo* and *beatitas* are used with the same meaning. Cicero, however, regarded both words as altogether harsh, though usage could soften them. Augustine, *City of God*, Book Five, chapter one: “It is established that happiness is the fullness of all desirable things.” From these words the following definition is derived: “Happiness is the fullness of all desirable things.” Philippus Beroaldus:

> Happiness is a great matter, desired by the most honorable person at every hour and by every wish. The wishes of all mortals aim at it; it is the sum of desirable things; our desires end in happiness. Whoever possesses happiness lacks absolutely nothing. Some people are found who do not desire kingdoms, but no one exists who rejects happiness. No one fails to wish to be happy; no one fails to agree that happiness is the highest of goods.

Cicero, *On the Ends*, Book Five: “For we are all inflamed by the desire to live happily.” Saint Augustine, *City of God*, Book Four, chapter 23: “Happiness is preferable to kingship. No one doubts that it would be easy to find someone afraid to become king; but no one is found who does not wish to be happy.”

**Naturally implanted.** Implanted by nature or innate from nature. Nature, as Cicero says in Book Three of the *Tusculan Disputations*, gave us little sparks, which we quickly extinguish through bad habits and corrupt opinions, so that the light of nature appears nowhere. Seeds of virtue are innate in our minds; if they were permitted to grow, nature itself would lead us to a blessed life. But as soon as we have been born and received into the light, we immediately become involved in every kind of depravity and the greatest perversity of opinions, so that we seem almost to have sucked error in with our nurse’s milk.

**Some of whom.** He sets out the various pursuits of mortals in seeking the highest good.

**May abound.** May be plentiful.

**Having obtained.** Having acquired. He uses a past participle from a deponent verb with passive meaning.

**To cling to those who rule.** Seneca, in *Hercules on Oeta*:

> This man wishes to be close to the king himself,  
> renowned and moving through the lofty cities.

**Renown.** Fame of name, nobility of reputation. Pliny, Book Eight of the *Letters*: “One person thinks one thing, another another; I consider that person happiest who enjoys the expectation of a good and lasting reputation and, certain of posterity, lives with future glory.”

**To extend.** To advance, spread.

**But very many.** They go in a crowd on foot in this direction, learned and unlearned alike, eagerly pursuing pleasure. On the ends of goods, see Aristotle, *Ethics*, Book One; Cicero, *On the Ends of Good and Evil*; Augustine, *City of God*, Book Ten; and Philippus Beroaldus, his little work *On Happiness*.

**[Col. 0996A]** **There are also some.** The meaning is: some people seek what they seek from these things not for its own sake but for the sake of something else. Thus some desire wealth for power or pleasure, while others desire power for money or brilliance of reputation. Ovid:

> Wealth grew, and the mad desire for wealth grew with it;  
> though they possess very much, they seek more.  
> They strive to seek things in order to consume them,  
> and, once consumed, to seek them again;  
> these very things become nourishment for their vices.

**There are.** Supply: “some.”

**Of these.** Of these goods.

**One or the other.** One of the two.

**In these.** In wealth, offices, power, glory, and pleasure.

**And in other such things.** In the remaining things of this kind, such as nobility and popular favor, marriage and children, as well as friends and possessions, which can readily be referred to the categories mentioned above.

**Of wishes.** Of desires, choices, and aspirations.

**Nobility and popular favor.** Supply: “are.” He could have placed these in the ablative, but preferred the nominative because of the relative pronoun that follows in the same case.

**Popular favor.** The favor of the people.

**Children.** Offspring.

**But as for friends.** As Aristotle teaches in Book Eight of the *Ethics*: “There are three kinds of friendship: honorable, useful, and pleasant. Friendships based on utility and pleasure are not friendships in themselves but accidentally, and they can easily be dissolved. The friendship of good people, however, is a perfect friendship between those who resemble one another in integrity and virtue; it is lasting and permanent. This is friendship in the fullest sense and the best friendship.”

The same author, in Book Two of the *Great Morals*: “The most constant, stable, and honorable friendship found among good people is that which exists because of virtue and is good in itself. Virtue is unchangeable, and the friendship formed through it is most constant. But the friendship that arises from advantage is not stable, since it slips away when the advantage does; the same is true of friendship formed for pleasure. The friendship of the best people, then, is stirred up by virtue; the friendship of many others arises from advantage or pleasure, and from the burdens that arise from such relationships.”

**Or of power.** Useful friendship is assumed for the sake of power or wealth; pleasant friendship for the sake of enjoyment.

**Now, the goods of the body.** He shows how bodily goods are referred to the higher categories. The Academics—that is, the Platonists—and the Peripatetics—that is, the Aristotelians—taught that there are three kinds of goods through which happiness is perfected. First are goods of the mind, such as virtues and learning. Second are bodily goods, such as health, strength, size, beauty, speed, and soundness of the senses. Third are external goods, attributed to fortune, such as wealth, honors, power, authority, and glory.

**To provide.** To confer.

**Strength.** Power.

**Beauty.** Bodily beauty is the harmony of the parts together with a certain pleasantness of color, as Aurelius Augustine teaches in the final book of the *City of God*.

**Renown.** A distinguished abundance of reputation.

**Health.** Bodily soundness.

**Above the others.** Before the other goods.

**Epicurus.** An Athenian philosopher, Epicurus placed the highest good not—as Aristippus did—in bodily pleasure, but in the mind’s freedom from pain. On this subject, read Diogenes Laërtius.

**Growing dim.** Failing, and as though covered by mist and darkness.

**Do these people, then, seem to be in error?** He shows that people are not mistaken in their desire for the good, but in acquiring it, since they seek it where they can least find it.

**But.** Yet.

**They slip.** They err.

**Not at all.** In no way.

**Among goods.** Among the goods.

**To be set apart.** To be segregated. A *sequester* is someone to whom several parties have entrusted the same disputed matter. As Gellius explains, the word is so called because both parties place their trust in the person chosen. He stands between two disputants, and something is deposited with him. Hence *sequestro*, “I deposit with a sequestrator”; from this comes the expression “a sequestered thing.” It sometimes means “I separate,” “set aside,” or “segregate.” Saint Jerome: “What you ask is that I separate various psalms for you in order.”

**Sufficiency.** According to Speusippus, sufficiency is the perfect possession of goods, a condition in which each person becomes master of himself.

## INTO METRE II

The poem is anapaestic, similar to:

> O creator of the star-bearing universe,

through which the power of nature is displayed by many highly appropriate comparisons, and it is shown that nothing can entirely forget its own nature. Hence he proves that the origin of humankind is heavenly and proceeds from the highest good, and that the human being cannot rest unless he has returned to it. The order is as follows:

**It pleases.** Supply: “me.”

**To bring forth.** To bring into the light and express clearly.

**With flexible strings.** With pliant lyre-strings.

**Melodious.** That is, with resonant song.

**[Col. 0997D]** **What reins.** That is, what restraints or governing measures of things.

**Mighty nature may bend.** That is, may direct; something is omitted.

**By what laws.** That is, by what conditions and agreements.

**May watch over the immense universe and, binding it, may hold it tight.** That is, may connect it.

**Each by an unloosable bond.** That is, by an indissoluble fastening. Properly, a rein is the restraint of a horse, by which the horse is held—that is, restrained.

**Nature.** It is so called from the fact that it causes something to be born. Some have said that nature is God, from whom all things were created. Seneca, Book Four of *On Benefits*: “For what else is nature than God, and divine reason implanted in the whole world and in its parts?” The word is sometimes understood as natural power, and as the reproductive organs of both males and females. *Nature* is also taken to mean form or essence. Philosophers define nature in this way: “Nature is the principle and cause of movement and rest in that in which it is primarily, intrinsically, and not accidentally.” It is also defined thus: “Nature is a power implanted in things, producing like things from like things.”

**Although the Punic lions.** By the example of lions he demonstrates the great force of nature.

**Punic.** Libyan, Marmarican.

**A harsh master.** A cruel and whip-wielding trainer.

**To endure.** To suffer.

**Rough.** Terrible.

**Faces.** The faces of lions.

**Resting.** Lurking, at rest, sluggish.

**Inactive.** One who sits, resting, sluggish, idle. Virgil, Book Six:

> Who will break the leisure of his country  
> and call its inactive men to arms—Tullus.

**Long ago.** For a long time.

**Spirits.** The impulse of wildness, the natural effects of a tendency toward savagery.

**With a roar.** With a growl.

**Loud.** Terrible, great.

**They remember.** They are mindful.

**Their own.** Their own nature.

**They loosen.** They free.

**From their bonds.** From their fetters.

**Torn.** Mangled.

**Tamer.** Trainer.

**[Col. 0998C]** **The mangled tamer incites their furious rage.** He provides the beginning of savagery to the wild lions. Martial, Book Two:

> A lion accustomed to endure blows from a careless trainer  
> and, gentle, to endure a hand inserted into its mouth  
> suddenly forgot peace when its savagery returned—  
> a savagery no greater than it ought to have possessed  
> on the Libyan mountains.

**What she sings.** By the example of a little bird shut up in a cage, she proves that the power of nature is very great.

**On the branches.** Supply: “in.”

**Bird.** A bird.

**Cage.** A *cavea* is an underground pit covered above. It is used as a refuge for wild animals. Martial:

> Let the boar not leave his cage badly fed.

*Caveae* are also enclosures made of wood, ivory, or another material in which we keep little birds. Ovid, Book One of *Letters from Pontus*:

> Although the birds born in Pontus are securely shut in their cage,  
> each strives to return to its own woods.  
> Bulls seek the accustomed leaps, lions their accustomed caves—  
> their wildness does not prevent them.

**To this one.** To the bird.

**Rich food.** Abundant nourishment. *Dapes* are magnificent and sumptuous banquets. Martial:

> It is indeed elegant and furnished with splendid feasts.

*Dapes* may refer to the food of human beings or to the nourishment of animals, both beasts and humans. But Boethius has rightly used *dapes* here, in order to magnify the matter greatly. Many people provide their little birds with food prepared with such care that they seem to be serving not birds but the most delicate human beings. Nevertheless, if given the opportunity, those birds—such is the force of nature—would prefer to fly away into the woods.

**In a narrow enclosure.** In a cramped cage.

**[Col. 0999A]** **Mournful.** Sad, because, being confined, it cannot fly away.

**To the woods.** Toward the woods, and from longing for the woods.

**Strong.** He confirms what he has said through the natural force of a rod.

**Once.** At some time.

**Bent.** Moved, curved.

**Downward.** Inclined.

**Bends.** Allows itself to be bent.

**This.** The rod.

**Straight.** Upright, as before it was bent. Horace says similarly in the *Epistles*:

> Though you drive out nature with a pitchfork, it will always return.

The metaphor is apparently taken from branches, which are bent contrary to the position nature gave them. When the force is removed, they bend back in the direction they had previously taken.

**[Col. 0999B]** **Falls.** Sets. He adds the example of the sun, which travels from rising to setting and then, hidden from us, returns eastward through the lower hemisphere.

**Into the western waters.** Into the western ocean. He speaks like the poets, according to popular belief.

**They return.** He concludes with a universal statement that all things return to their natural origin, and that each delights in its own return, as that poet said:

> All things return to their origins and seek their mother.

Since the human mind was created by the highest good, it cannot be made blessed unless it is reconciled by divine grace and brought back into that good through that good itself.

**Unless it has joined its origin to its end.** Unless it has attained the natural end proper to its origin.

**[Col. 0999C]** **Its own.** Its own nature.

**Sphere.** Circuit.

## INTO THE THIRD PROSE

Thus far he has explained that all human beings naturally seek the highest good, although they do not all agree where it is situated: some place it in office, others in power, others in renown, and others in pleasure and joy. Now he argues that the highest good and true blessedness are found in none of these things. First, he teaches with clear arguments that wealth does not make a person blessed.

**You also, earthly beings.** He has just given the example of the sun, which the Platonists, together with the heavens, called celestial living beings. Continuing his speech, he adds:

**[Col. 0999D]** **You too, human beings, earthly animals, dream.** That is, you see as if in a dream.

**Your origin.** That is, God the creator and the highest good.

**Although.** Although.

**With a faint image.** With slight knowledge.

**You look toward.** You look toward from afar.

**For that reason.** Because you perceive the highest good by however slight a form of knowledge, though not with penetrating insight.

**By attainment.** By acquisition.

**Clearly.** Manifestly, evidently.

**Appearance.** Outward form.

**First.** He argues that wealth does not confer blessedness because it provides neither the perfect state formed by the gathering of all goods nor the true sufficiency it appears to promise to any mortal.

**You were abounding.** You had plenty.

**Confounded.** Disturbed.

**So that something would always trouble you.** So that you would always be disturbed by something. Saint Ambrose, Book Six of the *Hexaemeron*: “As banquets stretch the belly, so riches fill the mind with cares and anxieties.”

**Of that one.** Of what was absent.

**Of this one.** Of what was present.

**Everywhere and entirely.** *Usquequaque* means “entirely,” “everywhere,” “continually,” or “always,” as though in every place or at every time. Cicero, to Trebatius: “One ought to be wise in every circumstance.”

**Why not?** Why not?

**But this too.** He proves that money can easily be taken away from unwilling owners.

**Stronger.** More powerful.

**Forensic complaints.** Complaints made in a judicial forum; supply: “there are.”

**Unless.** Supply: “because money seized from unwilling or unwillingly dispossessed owners is reclaimed either by force—that is, violence—or by fraud and malicious deception.”

**Then he will be in need.** The satirist:

> Miserable is the guardianship of a great fortune.

Strabo, Book Nine: “Since wealth is envied, guarding it is burdensome, even if it has been assigned and consecrated to some deity.”

**[Col. 1000C]** **But what limit?** He shows that wealth does not remove need, but merely consoles and somewhat relieves it.

**To console.** To relieve. *Consolor* is a common verb; we say, “I console you.” Cicero, Book Five of the *Letters to Friends*: “Although I, who wish to console you, must myself be consoled.”

**I say nothing of what concerns nature.** This is a most beautiful thought. Seneca: “The mind should rather be awakened from sleep, shaken, and reminded that nature has established very little for us. No one is born rich; each person, when ordered into the light, is required to be content with milk and a cloth.” The same author: “Nature desires bread and water.” Moreover, no one is poor among those things within which each person has confined his desire, and each person may contend with Jupiter himself concerning happiness. It has pleased me to append here some verses of the poet Claudian against the miser Rufinus, no less useful than brilliant:

> Where are you rushing, madman? You may possess both oceans,  
> you may loosen the golden springs of Lydia for yourself;  
> let the throne of Cyrus and the tiara of Croesus be joined to you—  
> you will never be rich, never satisfied by gain.  
>   
> Whoever desires is always in want. Fabricius, content with what is honorable and small,  
> despised the gifts of kings;  
> and the consul Serranus sweated at his heavy plow,  
> while a narrow cottage held the warlike Curii.  
>   
> This poverty is less cramped for me; these dwellings are greater  
> than your lofty rooftops. For you, luxury seeks empty  
> and harmful foods; for me, the earth gives feasts without purchase.  
> Your fleeces absorb Tyrian dyes,  
> and your embroidered garments are saturated with purple.  
>   
> Here flowers shine, and the living delight of the meadow  
> is varied by its own artistry; there, shining supports rise  
> upon beds. Here soft grass spreads itself,  
> not to tear away sleep troubled by cares.  
> A crowd of greeters makes your cheerful halls resound.  
>   
> Here are the songs of birds and the murmur of a flowing stream.  
> One lives better on little. Nature has granted  
> that all should be blessed, if anyone knows how to use it.  
> If these things were known, we would enjoy a simple way of life:  
> trumpets would not roar, nor the creaking ash advance;  
> the wind would not batter ships, nor siege engines the walls.

**There is nothing sufficient for greed.** Aristotle, Book One of the *Politics*: “All who pursue money increase their wealth without limit.” Ecclesiastes: “The miser will not be filled with money, and whoever loves riches will obtain no fruit from them.” Seneca: “The miser lacks what he possesses no less than what he does not possess.” Solomon, *Proverbs*, chapter 13: “There is one who is as though rich, though he has nothing; and one who is as though poor, though he possesses many riches.” Saint Ambrose, Book One of *On Intercession*: “Greed has no limit; it is not satisfied by plundering but is stimulated by it. The more it has sought, the more needy it becomes.” Seneca: “What are the greatest riches? Not desiring riches. Who possesses the most? The one who desires the least.”

## INTO METRE III

The poem is a *dicolon*, consisting of an iambic senarius and an elegiac pentameter. In it he censures the insatiable desire of mortals, teaching that wealth satisfies neither the miser while he lives nor accompanies him once he is dead.

**Flowing.** Abundant.

**A torrent of gold.** A gold-bearing river, such as the Pactolus and Hermus in Lydia, the Tagus in Lusitania, and the Durius in Spain. Horace, in the *Epodes*:

> You may be rich in cattle and abundant land,  
> and may the Pactolus flow for you.

**Not destined to fill.** Not destined to satisfy his mind.

**Berries.** Gems, precious stones. A *bacca* is the fruit of the laurel, olive, cornel, myrtle, and similar trees. By analogy, the word is used for a precious stone; thus we speak of the “berries” of amber or coral. Horace, in the *Epodes*:

> Nor may she be a married woman who walks about  
> weighed down by rounder berries.

Hence *baccula*, “a small berry.”

**Of the red shore.** The shore of the Erythraean Sea. The Red Sea is said to extend from the Persian Gulf toward Arabia. Nearchus and Onesicritus, companions of Alexander the Great, reported that the popular belief that the sea’s waters were red somewhere was foolish; they themselves believed that the sea had received its name from King Erythras, whose tomb—marked with the letters of his people—they had seen on an island not far from the mainland. Others assert that the water appears red although it is not, either because the seabed is reddish and, when lightly disturbed, produces that color among the waves, or because the reflection of clay-colored mountains reddens the calm surface of the sea. It is established that many precious stones and shells are found there. Tibullus:

> And whatever gems the dark-skinned Indian gathers  
> from the Red Sea’s shore, close to the eastern waters.

The same author:

> Or what shell is found on the Erythraean shore,  
> or what wool, dyed with Sidonian purple, gives pleasure?

**With a hundred oxen.** With one hundred oxen. He uses a definite number for an indefinite amount.

**Let it cut.** Let it plow with the plow.

**Rich.** Fat, fertile.

**Gnawing care.** A heart continually burning and, as it were, consuming by bites. Hence someone says:

[Col. 1002A] Gnawing cares consume languid hearts. And another says: “The traveler who is empty-handed and naked does not fear the robber’s ambush. The poor man sleeps safely from nocturnal thieves, even if he does not secure his doors; but the rich man’s wealth always imagines the robber’s arrival and, through unceasing anxiety, takes away his sleep at night.” Claudian:

“Foul, sleepless cares, clasping the breast of their mother Avarice,  
Come in a long procession.”

“Defunctum”] Dead. Propertius:

“You will carry no wealth to the waters of Acheron.  
Naked, foolishly you will travel in the underworld’s boat.”

Saint Ambrose, in the final book of the *Hexaemeron*: “We are all born naked, and we die naked. There is no distinction among the corpses of the dead, except perhaps that the bodies of the rich, swollen with luxury, stink more heavily.” Ludovicus Bigus:

“The wealthy man takes nothing with him when he dies, nor does the needy man;  
In death we are those who will leave behind more or less.”

[Col. 1002B] “The rich man’s delusion, the miser’s, raises itself without limit,  
And he has no place where he may settle with a peaceful mind.” The same:

“We brought nothing here, nor can we take anything away.  
The king, dying, leaves behind his cities; the needy, his trifles.  
Nature asks little; whoever has lived in accordance with her  
Can never be needy here.”

## INTO PROSE IV

Just as he has now shown that riches do not confer true sufficiency, so he argues that offices and dignities do not make those who receive them honorable and worthy of reverence. Often, when bestowed upon wicked men, they make them more contemptible, since they expose to many people vices that had previously been unknown.

“Dignities”] Magistracies and honors. *Dignitas* properly signifies an honor conferred upon someone because of merit, expenditure, [Col. 1002C] or obligation. Gellius: “Whose dignity can be increased neither by praise nor diminished by detraction.” It is sometimes understood as the administration and honor of magistracies. Cicero: “So that in all matters you may commend yourself to him, insofar as your trustworthiness and dignity permit.” It is sometimes used for manly beauty. The same author, in the first book of *On Duties*: “There are two kinds of beauty: one feminine, which we call loveliness; the other masculine, which we call dignity.”

“Reddunt”] It should be read as a question.

“Num”] “Surely?” or “Can it be that?”—as though he were saying, “By no means.”

“Atqui”] But.

“Illustrare”] To make notable, to ennoble.

“Nequitiam”] Wickedness.

“Indignemur”] Let us endure it with pain and indignation.

[Col. 1002D] “Catullus”] This poet, a Veronese by birth, wrote many most graceful poems, some of which are lost while others survive. Ovid said of him:

“Mantua rejoices in Virgil, Verona in Catullus.”

And Martial:

“Verona loves the syllables of her learned poet.”

“Licet”] Although.

“In Curuli”] On an ivory chair. The *sella curulis* was made of ivory and was used by the higher magistrates in a chariot. Horace, in the *Epistles*:

“To whomever he wishes, this troublesome man will give the fasces  
And snatch away the curule ivory.”

For senators who had held a curule magistracy—that is, a higher office—were accustomed, as a mark of honor, to be conveyed into the senate-house in a chariot containing an ivory seat on which they sat.

“Nonium”] Nonius Struma was a Roman, noble by birth but notorious for luxury and idleness. Catullian verses survive against him and Vatinius:

“What is this, Catullus? Why do you delay dying?  
Struma Nonius sits in the curule chair.  
Vatinius commits perjury through his consulship.  
What is this, Catullus? Why do you delay dying?”

The poet is speaking indignantly to himself because such great dignities have been conferred by the people upon utterly unworthy men. It should be noted, however, that thirteen years ago Rudolphus Langius, canon of Münster, a man highly distinguished by birth, learning, and virtues, pointed out to me, then a young man, that Catullus does not call this Nonius “Struma” as though he were marking him with that name as a kind of insulting epithet, as Boethius’s words might suggest. Rather, *Struma* was the cognomen of Nonius and of his family. This is also shown by Pliny’s words in Book XXXVII of the *Natural History*, where, writing about the extremely precious opal, he says: “Indeed, even today there exists a gem of this kind on account of which the senator Nonius was proscribed by Antonius—Nonius, son of Struma Nonius, whom the poet Catullus could not bear to see dishonorably seated in the curule chair, and grandfather of Servilius Novianus, whom we saw as consul.”

*Struma* is the name of a disease, namely a swelling in which certain formations, like glands, arise beneath the skin, congealed from pus and blood. Those who suffer from this defect are called *strumosi*, and the part of the body affected by it is called *strumosa*.

“Cum Decorato”] During Boethius’s time, Decoratus was a most wicked buffoon [Col. 1003C] and informer. Boethius refused to hold office with him.

“Putares”] You would wish. According to Acron, *puto* is used to mean “I wish.” Horace, in the *Satires*:

“So that you may regard them as essential”—that is, “so that you may wish it.”

“For dignity is inherent in virtue.” Horace:

“Virtue, which knows not the disgrace of rejection,  
Shines with honors unstained.”

“Dignity makes the wicked more contemptible rather”] Seneca: “Among the unworthy, dignity is a place of disgrace.” Claudian:

“Monstrous honor rages against its author.”

An old proverb says: “A monkey is a monkey, even if it wears golden insignia.”

“But not with impunity”] He means that although dignities make wicked men more contemptible, they do not do so with impunity, [Col. 1003D] that is, not without harm to themselves; for by contact with those men they are in turn stained. Saint Jerome, in his consolatory letter to Pammachius: “Although illustrious honor becomes cheap in a crowd, and among good men the dignity itself becomes more unworthy because many unworthy men possess it.” Hence Cicero said brilliantly of Caesar: “When he wished to adorn certain men, he did not make them honorable; rather, he corrupted the ornaments themselves.” Cicero, in the second *Philippic*, about Mark Antony: “For in a most disgraceful man the insignia of dignity were growing dull.”

“Umbratiles”] Empty, resembling shadows.

“If someone possesses many offices”] He reasons elegantly that dignities do not make anyone worthy of reverence everywhere, nor is this their natural function. Whatever is natural to a thing belongs to it everywhere. But making someone worthy of reverence does not belong everywhere to dignities; therefore it is not natural to them. He demonstrates the proposition—which many call the major premise—by an example, or an imperfect induction that can easily be completed. Heat is naturally present in wood everywhere; therefore whatever is natural to a thing is nowhere absent from it. He proves the assumption, commonly called the minor premise, to be true in this way: If someone has repeatedly held the consulship at Rome and should happen to come among barbarian nations where he is unknown, he will by no means seem worthy of reverence to the barbarians, who neither know the man nor have admired his dignities.

“Quoquo”] Wherever.

“But this”] Supply “happens,” “occurs,” or something similar.

[Col. 1004B] “Among those people, however”] He argues that dignities do not remain permanently even among the people among whom they originated, and he proves this clearly by examples.

“Prefecture”] Romulus chose one man and placed him in charge of urban affairs, as Dionysius says. It is sufficiently clear that this man was the Prefect of the City. Much later, in the time of the Caesars, the prefecture claimed such authority for itself that it heard all criminal cases in the city. Finally, when the Caesars were absent from Rome, the prefect ruled like another Caesar and deliberated on all matters relating to the city. In Boethius’s time, however, when Theoderic, king of the Goths, ruled Italy, the prefecture was nothing but an empty title and a burdensome charge upon the senatorial census, since senators were compelled to maintain the Prefect of the City at their own expense. He was prefect in name only and retained none of his ancient authority.

“Now that prefecture”] Some say that the prefecture of the grain supply began in the fifteenth year after the expulsion of the kings, during the consulship of Appius Claudius Sabinus and Publius Servilius Priscus. It is more truly established, however, that it began in the eighteenth year, during the consulship of Titus Sicinius and Publius Minucius, when there was an extreme scarcity of grain and Publius Valerius and Lucius Geganius were sent to Sicily to transport grain. Others maintain that Lucius Minucius was the first prefect of the grain supply. It is sufficiently clear that this magistracy was created only because of a shortage of grain.

“Proprii decoris”] Of personal beauty.

“Nunc”] Sometimes.

“If, therefore, they make people worthy of reverence”] In a brief conclusion he repeats what has already been said and concludes that dignities contain nothing desirable in the way of beauty.

## INTO METER IV

The poem is a *dicolon*, whose first verse is a Phalaecian hendecasyllable and whose second is an Alcmanian—or, as others prefer, an Archilochian tetrameter acatalectic—composed of two dactyls and an equal number of trochees. It teaches by Nero’s example that dignities often adhere to the most corrupt morals and that honors, when granted by wretched men, can confer happiness upon no one.

“In Tyrian purple”] In Tyrian purple. *Ostrum* means purple. Virgil, in the *Georgics*:

“So that the gem may drink and sleep in Sarian purple.”

“Comeret”] Would adorn.

“Snow-white”] Bright white.

“Vigebat”] Was living.

[Col. 1005A] “Vim”] That is, he exercised violence.

“Nero of raging luxury”] Saint Augustine, in Book V, chapter 19, of *The City of God*: “But the man who despises glory and is greedy for domination surpasses beasts, whether in the vices of cruelty or of luxury. There have been many such Romans. For although they abandoned concern for reputation, they did not cease desiring domination. History reports that there were many of them. But Nero Caesar was the first to attain the summit, and as it were the citadel, of this vice: his luxury was so great that no manly quality was thought to be feared from him; his cruelty was so great that, had it not been known, he would have been thought incapable of anything gentle.”

“Wicked”] The most criminal Nero.

“Reverend”] Worthy of reverence.

“Fathers”] Senators.

[Col. 1005B] “Indecorous”] Dishonorable and shameful because of the extreme wickedness of the man who bestowed them. Virgil:

“Why do you fail, dishonorable ones, at the very threshold?”

The nominative singular is *indecor*, or *indecoris*. Accius:

“Whose life is dishonorable,  
It is not fitting for him to flee a shameful death.”

“Curule offices”] Dignities.

“Who are those men?”] The first foot of this verse is an iamb. He uses a dialectical argument drawn from the place of efficient cause: those who bestow honors and bring dignities into being are generally wretched because of the flood of their vices. Therefore dignities are neither happy in themselves nor do they make those who receive them happy.

## INTO PROSE V

[Col. 1005C] Up to this point he has argued that neither true sufficiency can be obtained through money nor true reverence through dignities. Now he argues that true power does not consist even in kingdoms or in intimacy with kings.

“Why not?”] Why not?

“When”] Since; and it is ironic, as the following words readily show.

“They have exchanged happiness for calamity”] They have become wretched from being happy and fortunate.

“O splendid power!”] This is irony, for he mocks the extremely feeble power of this age, which cannot even preserve itself.

“But if this power of kingdoms is the source of happiness”] He argues sharply from contraries and concludes that kings possess more powerlessness than power, and [Col. 1005D] a greater share of misery than of happiness.

“Having experienced the lot”] The order is: “The tyrant, having experienced the dangers of his lot, imitated”—that is, signified, fashioned, or represented—“the fear of kingship by the terror of a sword hanging above the head,” that is, above the head of the flatterer. This should be understood of Dionysius, the tyrant of Syracuse. As Eusebius reports in the *Preparation for the Gospel*, historians of Sicily say that Dionysius was so suspicious even of his most beloved wife that he spread boards across the bedroom floor so that a louder noise would be made when she approached him. He also required her to come naked, so that she could carry nothing secretly, and blocked the very entrance with a ditch, so that, whether by leaps, long strides, or going up and down, she could not conceal any weapon.

With how many and how great evils, then, must the mind of a man have been filled when he was suspicious even of his wife? He certainly seems to me very like those who climb lofty precipices: before they seek still higher places, they are already exhausted, yet, when they look down upon the chasm and depth, they do not dare descend.

Having undertaken tyranny as though it were a divine thing, he learned its dangers and, while persisting in his resolve, saw countless dangers increasing day by day. He had no doubt that death threatened him because of them, since everyone was armed against him—not in body, perhaps, but certainly in mind. Dionysius himself indicated that this was so.

For when a certain man praised the life of tyrants to him as though it were happy, Dionysius is said to have invited him to a banquet prepared with royal magnificence. He then suspended a sharp sword by a very slender thread above the head of the seated man. After the guest suddenly looked up at it, he did not dare rise because of fear of the tyrant, nor could he drink or eat. Struck by the danger, with his neck and eyes directed toward the hanging sword, he awaited death.

When Dionysius saw this, he said: “Do you understand how happy our life is? Such it is, unless we wish to flatter ourselves. Although we have an abundance of all things, because of the frequency of dangers and the fear hanging over us we can enjoy none of them. We resemble those who are often deceived by ugly prostitutes who, richly adorned with clothing and gold and concealing the ugliness of their faces with cosmetics, draw young men caught by these traps toward themselves like fish on a hook.

“This misfortune weighs upon us, who seem happy to many; and just as many people are compelled by torture to reveal the secrets of their minds, so at times, overcome by the distress of this life, we utter the truest expressions of our misery. For tyrants are certainly like those animals that are fattened, to which an abundance of food and drink is offered for no other purpose than their destruction.”

Horace, Book II of the *Odes*:

“For him above whose impious neck  
A drawn sword hangs, the Sicilian feasts  
Will not prepare a sweet flavor,  
Nor the songs of birds and the lyre  
Restore sleep.”

“Above the head”] Above the head of Democles or Damocles, the flatterer, about whom Cicero speaks at greater length in the last book of the *Tusculan Disputations*.

“Do you think that man powerful?”] The question has more force than if he had simply presented the argument.

“Bodyguard”] Attendant.

“Surrounds”] Encloses.

“He who terrifies others fears more himself”] Seneca, in the *Oedipus*:

“He who rules a scepter with harsh authority  
Fears those who fear him; fear returns upon its author.”

Laberius, the writer of mimes:

“He whom many fear must fear many.”

Claudian:

“He who terrifies others fears much more; this lot suits tyrants.  
Let them envy the illustrious and slaughter the brave; [lacuna]  
Let them live armed with swords and surrounded by poisons,  
Practice uncertain arts, and threaten in trembling.”

Saint Jerome: “There is an ancient saying: Each person hates the one he fears; and whoever hates someone desires his death.” Marcus Tullius, in the second book of *On Duties*: “Of all things, nothing is more suitable for preserving and maintaining power than being loved, nor anything more alien than being feared.” Ennius expresses it splendidly:

“Whom they fear, they hate; and whoever hates another  
Thinks it expedient that he perish.”

And shortly afterward: “For those who wish to be feared must necessarily themselves fear the very people by whom they are feared.”

What do we suppose was the state of mind of that earlier Dionysius, and by what torment of fear was he accustomed to be afflicted, when, fearing razors, he singed his hair for himself with a glowing coal? What do we suppose was the state of mind of Alexander of Pherae, who, as we read, lived in such a way that, although he loved his wife Thebe deeply, nevertheless, when he came from dinner to her bedroom, he ordered a barbarian—and one, as the account says, marked with Thracian tattoos—to go before him with a drawn sword. He also sent ahead some of his bodyguards to search the woman’s chests and inspect her clothing, lest any weapon be concealed there.

O miserable man, who thought a tattooed barbarian more faithful than his wife! Nor was he deceived in this belief. For he himself was killed by her because she suspected him of keeping a mistress.

“For why should I speak of the households of kings?”] He argues from what appears to be the stronger case: intimacy with kings makes no one powerful, since kings themselves are so weak.

“Nero [and] Seneca”] Suetonius, on Nero: “He compelled his teacher Seneca to die, although, when Seneca often requested permission to withdraw and surrendered his property, Nero had solemnly sworn that he was needlessly suspected and that he would die before harming him.”

“Papinian”] He was a pupil of Cervidius Scaevola and contributed to the *Pandects* thirty-seven books of questions, nineteen of answers, two of definitions, one on adultery, and one on the aedilician law. He was regarded as the keenest of all the founders of jurisprudence, and they call him the sanctuary of legal history and the treasury of legal learning. Students of law who had made progress were sometimes called Papinianists after him.

He was a friend of the emperor Severus, having been his fellow student, and was also related to him through Severus’s second wife. He succeeded him as administrator of the imperial treasury. Finally, when Severus was dying, he entrusted his sons to no one more than to Papinian. Papinian was Prefect of the City and had more power at court than he wished. After repeatedly trying in vain to lay down this dangerous power, he was at last handed over by Antonius Caracalla, the son of Severus, to the soldiers’ swords and struck with an axe because he refused to excuse the emperor’s parricide.

“Antonius”] Aurelius Antoninus Bassianus Caracalla, son of Severus, succeeded his father in the empire. He was called Bassianus after his maternal grandfather. He received the name Caracalla from a garment that he gave to the people, hanging down to their ankles, as Spartianus reports. He ordered his brother Geta and many other distinguished men to be killed. Papinian, however, was struck with an axe in his presence and killed by the soldiers. After this had been done, Caracalla said to the executioner: “You ought to have carried out my order with a sword.”

“The very mass”] The excessive magnitude of dignity and power, and therefore its harmful magnitude.

“Which”] As though he were saying: none.

“Are friends a protection?”] It has already been said that useful friendship is sometimes sought for the sake of power. He now briefly shows that the friends of fortune are very easily estranged and that no plague is more effective for causing harm than an intimate enemy.

“But whom happiness”] This is a very familiar maxim, often sung by Ovid, whose verses from the first book of the *Tristia* are on the lips of nearly all educated people:

“As long as you are fortunate, you will count many friends;  
When the times grow cloudy, you will be alone.”

The same author, in the second book of the *Epistles from Pontus*:

“No one is loved except the man whose fortune is favorable;  
As soon as it thunders, it drives away all those nearest to it.

“Behold me, once defended by not a few friends,  
While a favorable breeze blew upon my sails:  
When the sea swelled like a wild beast beneath the stormy wind,  
I was left amid the waters in my shattered ship.”

Saint Jerome: “A friendship that can come to an end was never true.”

“But what plague?”] As though he were saying: none. Saint Jerome: “It is easier to guard against an avowed enemy than to endure a hidden enemy under the name of a friend; under the name of a friend, the ambushes of an enemy are discovered.” The same author: “For a flattering sycophant is an enemy.” Solon, according to Laertius, gave this advice: “Observe each person carefully, lest they perhaps conceal hatred in their hearts while addressing you with a flattering and smiling face, and lest a double, black tongue speak from their mind.”

When Diogenes was asked what beast bites most dangerously, he replied: “Among wild beasts, the slanderer; among the tamer, the flatterer.” Marcus [Col. 1008C] Tullius, in the *Laelius*, said that no plague in friendships is greater than flattery, blandishments, and sycophancy.

## INTO METER V

The poem is of the same form as the fifth poem of Book II. Philosophy teaches us here that true power can fall to no one unless, having driven away disturbances, he rules his own mind and, having removed vices, successfully attains through unconquered courage the kingdom of virtue—which alone is stable and entirely free.

Seneca, to Lucilius: “If you wish to subject everything to yourself, subject yourself to reason. Reason will make many kings of you. From it you will learn what you ought to undertake and how.”

In Livy, Scipio says to Masinissa: “Believe me, the danger to our age is not so great from armed enemies as from the pleasures surrounding us on every side. Whoever has conquered them by temperance has won for himself a victory like the one we achieved by conquering Syphax.”

Solomon, Proverbs, chapter XVI: “He who is patient is better than the strong man, and he who rules his spirit than one who captures cities.”

Horace, Book II of the *Odes*:

“You will rule more broadly by mastering  
Your greedy spirit than if you joined Libya  
To distant Gades, and both Carthaginians  
Served one master.”

Valerius Maximus, Book IV: “For it is much, much more difficult to overcome oneself than an enemy—to catch the man fleeing adversity in hasty flight or the man rushing toward prosperity with uncontrolled joy.”

Baptista Mantuanus:

“He is worthier who conquers himself than he who conquers  
The strongest cities; virtue cannot rise higher.”

[Col. 1009A] Seneca the tragedian, in the *Thyestes*:

“What madness drives you  
To shed one another’s blood  
And assail the scepter with crime?  
Do not covet citadels,  
Wherever the kingdom may lie.  
Wealth does not make a king,  
Nor the color of Tyrian clothing,  
Nor the mark of a royal brow,  
Nor beams shining with gold.  
He is king who has laid aside fears  
And the evils of his cruel heart.”

And after several lines he adds:

“A good mind possesses the kingdoms.”

And again:

“He is king who fears nothing;  
Each person grants this kingdom to himself.”

“Spirits”] The emotions of the mind.

“Fierce”] Immoderate and not obedient to right reason.

[Col. 1009B] “Subdues”] Soothes and subjects to the authority of right reason.

“By lust”] By immoderate desire. According to Aurelius, in Book XIII of *The City of God*, *libido* is a general term for every desire. For example, there is the desire for revenge, which is called *libido ulciscendi*. There is the desire to possess money, which is avarice. There is the desire to conquer by any means, which is obstinacy. There is the desire for boasting, which is called ostentation.

The same author, in Book XIX of the same work: “It is happier to be enslaved to a man than to lust, which, apart from other things, devastates the hearts of mortals with its most savage domination—the lust for domination itself.”

“With shameful reins”] Into the most disgraceful slavery. Macrobius, Book I of the *Saturnalia*: “One serves lust, another avarice, another ambition; all serve hope, all serve fear.” And certainly no slavery is more disgraceful than voluntary slavery.

Saint Ambrose, in the second book of his *Letters*: “For a fool, even to command is slavery, and, what is worse, although he presides over a few, he serves many masters, and harsher ones. He serves his own passions; he serves his desires, whose domination he can flee neither by night nor by day, because he has masters within himself and suffers intolerable servitude within himself. For there is a twofold slavery: one of the body, the other of the soul. The masters of the body are human beings; the masters of the soul are wickednesses and passions, from which the wise man is rescued by the freedom of his mind, so that he may escape their slavery.”

Sidonius Apollinaris, Book II of his *Letters*: “For it cannot be said how much misery the life of those happy people—if indeed they should be called that—endures hour by hour in this life, those who, like Sulla, arrogate this name to themselves. They have gone beyond the common law of right and wrong and regard supreme power as supreme happiness. They are sufficiently miserable in this very respect: they scarcely understand that they are subject to the most restless servitude. For just as kings rule human beings, so the desire to rule governs kings.”

“Let him submit”] Let him subject himself.

“Although”] Even though. Claudian, to Honorius:

“Although you may rule widely over the distant Indians,  
Although the Mede, the gentle Arab, and the Seres adore you,  
If you fear, if you desire what is wrong, if anger drives you,  
You will endure the yoke of slavery and bear  
Another’s unjust laws. Then you will possess everything by right  
When you can be king of yourself.”

“Your laws”] Your power, your rule.

“Let it tremble”] Let it fear.

[Col. 1010A] “Let it serve”] Supply “you.”

“Distant Thule”] This is a half-line from Virgil’s *Georgics*, Book I:

“May distant Thule serve you.”

According to Servius, Thule is an island in the Ocean, between the northern and western regions, beyond Britain and the Orkneys. It is the last island in the Ocean, where, when the sun is in Cancer, there are said to be continuous days without nights. It should be written with *u* after the *th*, as Georgius Merula, Christophorus Landinus, and Antonius Mancinellus attest, although it is commonly written *Thyle* with a Greek upsilon. In Greek it is written Θουλή (*Thoulē*).

“Dark”] Harmful. Alexander Hegius, once my teacher in the very well-attended school of the noble city of Deventer:

[Col. 1010B]

“It happens that the human mind is anxious with unceasing cares,  
Nor can it fail to remember its own misery.  
If you wish to calm it, abandon the fuel of care;  
Desire nothing beyond what is fair, and you will be free.”

The same author:

“Your highest freedom, Christ, is to carry out your commands;  
No one is freeborn unless he serves you, Jesus.  
No one reigns unless he is your faithful servant, Jesus.”

## INTO PROSE VI

He teaches how deceptive and empty glory is, which most mortals pursue with such zeal, and that no one can become happy through the renown of his name. Aurelius defines glory in Book V, chapter 12, of *The City of God*, in these words: “Glory is the judgment of people who think well of other people.” In the same book, chapter 19: “For the person who possesses virtues, it is a great virtue to despise glory.” The author of *Rhetoric for Herennius* defines it as follows: “Glory is frequent fame concerning someone, accompanied by praise.” Marcus Tullius, in his speech for Marcus Marcellus, gave it this definition: “Glory is illustrious and widespread fame for services rendered, whether among one’s fellow citizens, toward one’s country, or among the entire human race.”

“Shameful”] Dishonorable and disgraceful.

“Not without reason”] Justly.

“The tragedian”] Euripides, who introduces Andromache crying out as follows:

Ὠ δόξα, δόξα μυρίοισι δὴ βροτῶν  
Οὐδὲν γεγῶσι βίοτον ὤγκωσας μέγαν.

That is, according to the translation of Antonius Codrus Urceus:

“O glory, glory, you have swollen the worthless life  
Of countless mortals into something great!”

There are, however, some who read and interpret these lines somewhat differently:

“O glory, glory, for ten thousand human beings,  
Nothing but a great swelling or a great inflation.”

But since we who now live near the shores of the German and British Oceans lack copies of Greek poets, apart from very few, we refer diligent students to Euripides himself and to teachers of the Greek language.

“By which”] By the removal of his great name through the false opinions of the crowd.

“What?”] As though he were saying: nothing.

“Let them blush”] Let them be ashamed and affected by modesty and disgrace. Symmachus, in his *Letters*: “As true praise adorns, so false praise chastises.”

“Whom”] Praises.

“What?”] As though he were saying: nothing.

[Col. 1011A] “They have added”] They have contributed.

“Not by popular rumor”] Not by the empty proclamation of the people,

“Who, foolishly serving fame,  
Often bestow honors upon the unworthy.”

“But measures it by the truth of conscience”] Rather, he defines and determines his own good by the truth of his conscience. Content with this, he does not seek popular applause. Seneca, to his Lucilius: “Consider yourself within; do not trust others concerning what sort of person you are.” Persius:

“Live with yourself, and you will know how scant your household goods are.”

That is: measure yourself by your own possessions and weigh yourself by your own good or evil qualities. Horace:

“It is right for each person to measure himself by his own standard and foot.”

We are warned by this not to judge our true worth by the praises of flatterers or by the opinion of the crowd, but by our own genuine gifts and the virtues of our mind. Franciscus Philelphus, Satire V:

“Rejoice in your own good, and, scorning the fleeting  
Applause of the crowd, remember to depend upon yourself.”

Ludovicus Bigus:

“O supremely happy is the man who searches himself to the depths  
And wishes to trust no judgment except his own.  
He does not allow his integrity to depend  
On an unstable breeze, but wishes to be good to God alone.”

“But if this very thing”] He draws the argument from contraries, similar to the argument he previously brought forward concerning power and powerlessness, or rather from opposites according to affirmation and negation. If, he says, extending one’s name is thought beautiful and honorable, then not extending it must be judged shameful and dishonorable. Opposites correspond to opposites. But there are far more nations among whom anyone’s name is unknown than there are nations among whom it is known. Therefore the man who is thought glorious should rather be judged inglorious.

“As”] In the manner in which.

“A little earlier”] In Prose VII of Book II.

“I have discussed”] I have argued.

“Among these matters”] For two reasons he shows that popular glory is not worthy even of remembrance: it does not arise from true judgment but from a judgment that is excessively corrupt—that of an unlearned, foolish, and, so to speak, many-willed multitude, which often praises the harmful and blames the innocent and never remains consistent, but is shifted this way and that by the slightest impulse.

Michael Fernus, to Sabinus:

“Alas! How empty is this hope and glory of fame:  
For fame we die, learned Sabinus, through hunger.  
Let the glory of virtue stand throughout the whole world;  
Live rightly before God; all else will be smoke.”

[Col. 1011D] “Now how empty it is”] He argues that nobility of birth does not confer true and proper distinction, which virtue alone supplies, in accordance with the saying of the satirist:

“Nobility is virtue alone and virtue only.”

There are three kinds of nobility: nobility from birth, nobility from virtue, and nobility from both. There is also a nobility—or rather a notoriety—arising from vices, since some people become known through crimes and the most shameful deeds.

Joannes Campanus: “The nobility that is adorned by its own proper virtue is preeminent, joined as it is with the splendor, dignity, glory, and antiquity of one’s ancestors.”

“Distinction”] Brightness and the splendor of a name.

“Alien”] Not one’s own, since the people who are illustrious—parents or ancestors, for example—are those who are praised for their virtues and distinguished deeds; it is not the descendant who, born from their line, does not imitate their virtues.

“For it seems”] He defines nobility of birth in this way: “Nobility is a certain praise arising from the merits of one’s parents.”

“Alien distinction”] Joannes Campanus: “To rely upon the praises of others is nothing other than being unable to produce one’s own.” Seneca: “What is more foolish than for someone to take pleasure in himself because of something he did not do?” The same author: “A hall filled with smoky ancestral portraits does not make a person noble. No one lived for our glory, nor is what existed before us ours. The mind makes a person noble, since from any condition it is permitted to rise above fortune.”

“But if there is anything”] He shows for whom nobility of birth may be useful. [Col. 1012B] Baptista Mantuanus:

“It is certainly something great, as I seem to see, to have been born from distinguished parents. Young men who possess some natural ability commonly imitate the dignity of their ancestors, lest they seem degenerate, and strive toward the glory of their paternal praises. Thus the name of Philip stirred Alexander; the glory of the elder Africanus stirred the younger Scipio; the fame of Julius Caesar stirred Octavian; and Pyrrhus, descendant of Achilles, was made bold by the image of his father.”

Faustus Andrelinus:

“There is something in the splendor of illustrious and great ancestors;  
For posterity, eager to emulate, has in it a spur.  
As a young hound, when it sees a bear approaching,  
Moves its emulous heart toward its father’s strength,  
So that no one may be degenerate from such great deeds:  
Great-hearted minds are stirred by vigorous actions.”

## INTO METER VI

The poem is a *dicolon*. Its second verse is called an Alcmanian dactylic trimeter hypercatalectic, consisting of three feet of a heroic verse and one syllable, though it is not composed entirely of spondees. The other is a Pherecratean, composed of a spondee or an anapest, a dactyl, and a spondee.

It teaches that one and the same person is the father of all, from whom the whole human race has a common origin. Therefore no one is degenerate except the person who, disfigured by vices, falls away from that most beautiful, best, and greatest parent.

Saint Jerome: “Before God, the only freedom is not to serve sins; before God, the highest nobility is to be illustrious in virtues.”

“From a similar origin”] From a common origin.

“For one is the source of all things”] The prophet Malachi, chapter II: “Have we not all one father? Has not one God created us all?”

Lactantius, Book V of *On Justice*, chapter 15: “For God, who generates human beings and inspires them, wished them all to be equal, that is, alike. He established the same condition of life for all; he generated all for wisdom; he promised immortality to all, for no one is excluded from his heavenly gifts. Just as he distributes his one light equally to all, sends springs to all, supplies food, and grants the sweetest rest of sleep, so he bestows equity and virtue upon all. No one is a slave before him, and no one is a master. For if he is the same father of all, by equal right we are all free. No one is poor before God except the person who lacks justice; no one is rich except the person full of virtues; no one is eminent except the person who is good and innocent; no one is most illustrious except the person who has generously performed works of mercy; and no one is most perfect except the person who has fulfilled every degree of virtue.”

Pindar, as Eusebius reports in Book XIII of the *Preparation for the Gospel*: “There is one race of human beings, and all come from one mother. We have one father, the supreme and best creator and craftsman, who assigns different stations to each according to merit.”

“One supplies everything”] Take care not to read it, against the meter, as “one who supplies everything.”

“Closed”] Enclosed.

“Members”] Bodies.

“Lofty seat”] From heaven.

“Produces”] Brings forth.

“Noble offspring”] Noble origin, distinguished lineage.

“Boasts”] Displays or vaunts. He is addressing people who glory in the nobility of their birth.

[Col. 1013B] “Your beginnings”] Your origin and that of all other mortals.

“Look”] Consider, O Boethius. Unlearned people corrupted this passage by reading *spectetis*—“you should look”—which damages the meter, instead of *spectes*—“you should look.” This seems to have arisen from the word *vestra*, “your.” They feared that the construction would otherwise be grammatically unsuitable, not noticing that *spectes* refers to Boethius alone, whereas *vestra primordia*, “your beginnings,” refers to Boethius and other human beings.

“Ni”] Unless.

“Cherishing”] Embracing.

“Worse”] Evil; a comparative used in place of the positive.

“By vices”] This is the seventh case and must be construed with *deserat*, “abandons,” so that the order is: “Let him abandon his proper origin through vices,” that is, “Let him become degenerate from his proper origin through vices.”

## INTO PROSE VII

[Col. 1013C]

He says that pleasures not only fail to bring happiness but also cause many illnesses and diseases.

“Of which”] Of pleasures.

“Appetentia”] Appetite or desire.

### Anxiety

“Anxiety”: solicitude. Giovanni Pico della Mirandola: “For what is there desirable in the pleasures of the world, which, while they are sought, weary us; when acquired, make us foolish; when lost, torture us?” Bigus:

> What desirable thing do the joys of the present life possess?  
> If someone seeks them by sea or land, they weary him;  
> Once obtained, they dull the heart, and when lost, they cruelly torment it.

Horace:

> Reject pleasures; pleasure purchased with pain is harmful.

Saint Jerome: “Lust, once past, always leaves behind its own regret”—that is, repentance. There is a Greek proverb: “Sorrow is the sister of pleasure.”

### “How many diseases”

Annaeus Seneca, the most severe censor of vices, inveighing against the pleasures of gluttons, wrote almost divinely as follows:

> Hence comes pallor, and the trembling of nerves drenched in wine, and a wasting more pitiable from indigestion than from hunger. Hence uncertain feet, slipping beneath one, and the staggering that is always characteristic of drunkenness itself. Hence moisture admitted beneath the skin, and the distended belly, while it wrongly becomes accustomed to taking in more than it could. Hence the suffusion of dark-yellow bile, the discolored face, the wasting of tissues rotting within themselves, the twisted fingers with their joints stiffening, the torpor of nerves lying without sensation, or the continuous throbbing of bodies quivering without pause. Why should I speak of the dizziness of the head, the torments of the eyes and ears, the wormlike agonies of the fevered brain, and all the organs through which we are relieved, afflicted as they are with internal ulcers? Besides these there are innumerable kinds of fever: some advancing in sudden attacks, others creeping on with a subtle pestilence, others coming with horror and violent shaking of the limbs. Why should I mention the countless other diseases—the punishments of luxury?

### “But that they are sad”

Everyone knows that sorrow follows pleasure, but this is especially true of the lustful; for, as the philosopher testifies, every animal is sad after intercourse. Seneca to Lucilius: “Above all, eradicate pleasures; count them among the cheapest things, which embrace us after the manner of robbers in order to strangle us.” According to Valerius Maximus, Aristotle’s most useful precept was that we should contemplate pleasures as they depart; by displaying them in this way, he diminished them, presenting them to our minds as exhausted and full of regret, so that they would not be eagerly sought again.

### “If these can make men happy”

“If,” he says, “bodily pleasures brought happiness, then even animals would be happy, since they share them with us. But it is utterly unworthy to attribute the highest good to animals. Therefore bodily pleasures—which, according to the philosopher in Book III of the *Moral Works*, are bestial and savage—can in no way make anyone happy.”

### “Why not?”

Why not?

### “The bodily receptacle”

The belly. *Lacuna* comes from *lacus*, “a lake,” and signifies a collection of water. Servius: “Lacunae are hollows in which collected water customarily stands.” Virgil:

> From there the hollow pools sweat with warm moisture.

By metaphor it is used for the belly or abdomen, where food and drink are heaped together. Some copies read *lasciviam*, “wantonness,” and the sense is quite clear.

### “Most honorable indeed”

Above he said that wives and children are sought for the sake of pleasure, by which words he indicated that marriage is pursued for the sake of pleasure. Now he says that this pleasure would be the most honorable, if it too did not bring with it an excessive amount of anxiety and sorrow.

### “By nature”

Against nature.

### “I do not know who has found children to be torturers”

Baptista Mantuanus:

> Often a father raises in his own offspring a savage enemy,  
> And, unknowingly, plays with his own destroyer.  
> Often mothers feed themselves on tears, while hoping for joys,  
> And nourish the future reproaches of their own family.

### “Biting”

Full of cares and anxiety.

### “Whatever the condition”

Even if it is a good one.

### “At another time”

At another time; understand that it was necessary to admonish you.

### “You have experienced”

Since you have children, you know from experience how much anxiety is required to raise them.

### “Anxious”

Sad and troubled. For now more should not be added to your anxiety, but rather something should be taken away from it.

### “My Euripides”

The learned poet and most accomplished master of philosophy.

### “Who said that the man without children was happy through his misfortune”

For the man who lacks children, although he seems unfortunate because he preserves his wealth for someone else and increases it for an heir, is nevertheless happy through that misfortune because he receives none of the trouble that comes from children, as most others do, and fears no reproach from them. Sophocles, in the *Antigone*, translated by Erasmus:

> Whoever sows useless children,  
> What else would you say he creates for himself  
> Than pains and laughter for the malicious?

Once Solon and Thales of Miletus met, and a discussion arose about marriage and children. Solon approved both beyond measure and wondered that Thales was the sort of man who had never devoted himself to procreation. Thales then devised a story not unworthy of remembrance. He suborned a man who was to say that he had arrived at Miletus from Athens during those very days. Asked about the condition of the city, this man was to say that everything there was flourishing, except that, shortly before his departure, one grievous misfortune had occurred: the only son of a most distinguished man, whose father was said to be abroad, a young man of outstanding character, had died. The entire city, he was to say, had accompanied the funeral in profound mourning.

Then, when asked the father’s name, he was to say that it had slipped his memory, though, if prompted, he could easily recall it. The next day, therefore, while the two men were walking according to custom through the crowded marketplace, the accomplice presented himself at the appointed moment. At the first mention of the funeral, Solon’s spirit was shaken. As the story progressed, and the visitor came to the point at which he withheld only the father’s name—while everything else plainly announced the son’s death to Solon—he finally supplied Solon’s own name, as though in a state of madness, and affirmed that he himself was the father.

Overcome by the magnitude of his grief, Solon forgot both his own person and the place. He threw himself to the ground, tore at his hair and beard with alternating hands, and filled the entire marketplace with howling, bellowing, and lamentation. The whole crowd, shocked by the ugliness of the affair, immediately turned toward him alone.

Thales, aware of this empty struggle, allowed the visitor for some time to rage in that insane and womanish lamentation. At last, gently raising the man from the ground, he said: “Take heart, Solon; your son is alive. But I wanted you not to be unaware to what madness love of children drives parents, and how sensible those are who, when they can honorably do so, escape these bonds of the heart.”

## Into Meter VII

The poem is Anacreontic: a catalectic dimeter consisting of an anapest, two iambs, and a syllable. It sometimes has a spondee in place of an iamb, as can be seen in the first verse, which can nevertheless be correctly read, with the words transposed:

> All pleasure has this.

Some call this meter anapaestic because its first foot is an anapest. I would rather call it iambic, however, since it can admit either an iamb or a spondee in its first division, as in Prudentius:

> Come, supreme Father.

It signifies that pains, disgust, and anxiety are companions of pleasure.

### “With goads”

With barbs.

### “It afflicts”

It affects, pierces.

### “Those enjoying”

Those who enjoy pleasure.

### “Equal”

Similar.

### “When”

After.

### “It flees”

It departs with the utmost speed.

### “Clinging”

Bringing lasting pain.

### “It strikes”

It beats, injures.

### “Struck”

Touched. Solon: “Flee pleasure, for in the end it gives birth to pain itself.” Plato very often inflamed the young toward a happy life in this way:

> Observe the contrary nature of virtue and pleasure. The momentary sweetness of pleasure is followed by sudden regret and perpetual pain; but brief labors undertaken for virtue are followed by eternal pleasure.

Claudian, to Stilicho:

> Nor did luxurious pleasure deceive you with its pleasing face,  
> That exceedingly sweet evil which, always devoted  
> To the body’s commands, dulls the senses with darkness  
> And softens the limbs more fiercely with Circe’s herbs.  
> Pleasant indeed in appearance, but inwardly  
> Nothing is more hideous: with painted cheeks  
> And clothed in treacherous allurements,  
> It binds grim water-snakes about itself.

It entangles many people on the hooks of pleasure. Baptista Mantuanus:

> Let treacherous pleasure deceive no one.  
> Always entering beneath a flattering appearance,  
> It presents the juices of nard, perfumes,  
> And honey-sweet flavors, and applauds with a friendly face.  
> But nothing is without deceit: poisons lie hidden beneath the honey.  
> Once you have unwittingly drunk them, it suddenly flees,  
> Rejoicing in its deception, while the wound remains fixed beneath the breast.

Giovanni Francesco Pico, in a vow for the health of his wife:

> O wretched race of mortals, for whom sad things  
> Follow upon joyful ones, and cups flow  
> Stained with bitter gall from the rim of a honeyed vessel.  
> For whatever has delighted the present moment  
> With sweet affection, once lost we lament;  
> And the wounded mind pours forth words in bitter grief  
> And renews the wound within the breast.

We too once wrote in Book III of the *Moral Elegies*:

> How brief, how mingled with pain is lust!  
> It flees away swiftly, but pain remains forever.

And shortly afterward:

> Why does this flatter you so much? Why does it seem sweet,  
> When little honey contains savage bitterness?  
> Satiety follows, disgust follows, sorrow,  
> And anxiety; the greatest punishment awaits the guilt.  
> Immediately those things flee which gently affect the senses  
> For a brief time and cannot remain.  
> The conscious mind itself gnaws at its wretched ways  
> And cannot be healed unless its author brings aid.

Likewise:

> Anxiety, its companion, tears away joy.

## Into Prose VIII

In this prose passage Philosophy first briefly repeats what she discussed above, saying that pleasures, glory, kingdoms, dignities, and riches neither lead to happiness as though they were paths to it nor make people happy. Then she teaches that bodily goods are especially fragile and should not be highly valued by prudent people.

### “These paths”

The paths which the common people foolishly imagine to lead to happiness.

### “Why, then?”

This is an interrogative particle, meaning “Why not?” It is also comic, as Acron testifies. Horace, Book I of the *Satires*:

> Military service is preferable—why not? They engage  
> In battle within the space of an hour.

The sense is: “Why should I not show as briefly as possible how many evils these paths contain?” It may also be taken simply as a sort of preparation for the question that follows; this too is frequent among comic poets and in ordinary speech.

### “Of soliciting”

Of canvassing for and seeking magistracies.

### “You might spend”

You might live.

### “Service of the body”

Seneca to Lucilius: “I am greater and born for greater things than to be a slave to my body. Indeed, I regard the body as nothing other than a weight, a punishment, and a chain placed around my freedom.”

### “Now indeed”

He passes neatly to bodily goods, which can easily be referred back to what was said above.

### “Display”

They exhibit them and wish, as though happier than others, to be preferred to others.

### “Surely?”

Surely? Is it possible?

### “Elephants”

According to Pliny, the elephant is the largest of terrestrial animals and the one closest to human intelligence. Tamed elephants serve in war, carry towers filled with armed men against the enemy, and bring to completion a large part of the wars in the East. They overthrow battle lines and crush armed men. They are born in Africa beyond the Syrtic deserts, in Mauretania, in Ethiopia, and among the Troglodytes; but the largest are in India. The Africans fear them and dare not look upon them, for the Indian elephants are larger. Read Pliny, Book VIII of the *Natural History*.

### “Bulls”

A bull is an ox reserved for breeding. The word is also used of any robust ox. Virgil:

> Come, then: let the strong bulls at once  
> Turn the rich soil of the earth  
> From the first months of the year.

### “Tigers”

The Hyrcanians and Indians produce the tiger, an animal of terrifying and celebrated speed, especially when it is captured. Its entire litter—which is always numerous—is carried off by an ambusher on a horse of the greatest possible speed and is repeatedly transferred to a fresh horse. But when the mother finds her den empty—for the males do not care for the offspring—she rushes headlong, tracking the scent.

As the pursuer approaches with a roar, he throws down one of the cubs. She picks it up in her mouth and, driven onward even more swiftly by its weight, returns; then she catches him again, and this continues until he has returned to the ship and her frustrated fury rages uselessly on the shore. This is from Pliny. More about the same matter from other authors will be given below.

### “Look upon”

Consider.

### “Extent”

Breadth.

### “Strength”

Firmness.

### “Speed”

Swiftness.

### “By these”

By extent, firmness, and speed.

### “By its own nature”

By the divine spirit.

### “But the splendor of form”

He shows that bodily beauty is exceedingly fleeting and changes with great speed.

### “As much as”

To the extent that.

### “Swift”

Passing quickly. Domitian, in Suetonius: “You should know that nothing is more pleasing than beauty, nor anything more short-lived.” Ovid, Book II of the *Art of Love*:

> Add the gifts of intelligence to the advantages of the body.  
> Beauty is a fragile good; as it approaches old age,  
> It becomes less, and is diminished by the passage of time.  
> Neither violets nor lilies bloom forever;  
> The rose stiffens, its thorn left behind when the flower is gone.  
> And for you, handsome man, gray hairs will soon come,  
> And wrinkles will soon come, which will dry out your body.  
> Now cultivate a mind that will endure, and build up your character.  
> The mind alone remains to the final funeral pyres.  
> Nor should you lightly neglect to cultivate your breast  
> With the liberal arts and to learn two languages.

Again the same author:

> So beware of trusting your deceptive appearance.  
> Whoever you are, possess something greater than the body.

Isaiah, chapter XL: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field.” Human beauty is rightly compared with a flower, since it almost grows green and withers in the same instant. Marcus Varro: “The man whom you saw handsome in youth, you see deformed in old age.” Apuleius, in *The God of Socrates*, wishing to signify that nothing is shorter-lived than beauty, says: “He is handsome; wait a little, and he will not be.”

Calpurnius, in the *Bucolics*:

> The gift of beauty is brief, nor does it accommodate itself to the years.

Seneca, in the *Hippolytus*:

> Beauty is an uncertain good for mortals,  
> A brief gift of a little time.

### “As you slip swiftly with rapid foot”

Again the same author:

> As the glow that shines upon tender cheeks  
> Is snatched away in a moment, and every day  
> Takes something from the beautiful body.

> Beauty is a fleeting thing: what wise man  
> Would trust in a fragile good?

The same author—or, as some think, another Seneca—in the *Octavia*:

> Only the goods of mind and sound character,  
> Subject to no one, remain forever.  
> Every day plucks away some flower of beauty.

Sallust: “For the glory of riches and beauty is fleeting and fragile; virtue is regarded as illustrious and eternal.”

Saint Ambrose, in Book III of the *Hexaemeron*:

> Earlier the rose had risen, mingled with tender flowers and without thorns; the most beautiful flower was blooming without any deceit. Later the thorn enclosed the loveliness of the flower, as though presenting a mirror of human life, which often pricks the sweetness of its enjoyment with the neighboring goads of cares. For the elegance of our life has been fenced about and obstructed by certain anxieties, so that sadness has been joined to grace. Therefore, whenever someone rejoices either in the sweetness of reason or in the success of a more prosperous course, he ought to remember the fault through which, while we were flourishing in the delights of paradise, the thorns of the mind and the brambles of the spirit were assigned to us by the sentence of condemnation. Therefore, O man, even if you shine with the splendor of nobility, the height of power, or the brilliance of virtue, always look down upon what lies beneath you; you are always producing thorns, and enduring grace does not remain. In a short time, once the flower of life has run its course, everyone withers.

Aristotle of Stagira, son of Nicomachus the physician, pupil of Plato, and teacher of Alexander the Great, wrote a great deal not only with vigor but also with elegance, against the opinion of certain philosophers who, in the vulgar manner, philosophized sordidly.

### “With Lyncean eyes”

With extremely sharp and penetrating eyes. Some think that “Lyncean eyes” are called sharp after the lynxes, which, as Pliny testifies in Book XXXII, chapter 8, of the *Natural History*, see more clearly than all quadrupeds. Others think instead that the expression derives from Lynceus, one of the Argonauts, who possessed an exceptionally sharp gaze and who, according to the stories—and as Jerome relates—was said to see through a wall.
