According to historians, Lynceus observed the last moon and the first moon on the same day in the sign of Aries—something that only a few mortals have seen. From this arose the story of Lynceus’s sight, as Pliny explains. Horace says of him:

> Lynceus alone will pass through the clouds.

Horace mentions him in the *Epistles* and says in the *Satires*:

> Nor should you contemplate the finest features of the body  
> With Lyncean eyes.

Lynceus is frequently mentioned by learned writers, especially Cicero, Apuleius, and Seneca. Plato too mentions him in one of his letters. Aristotle, in Book I of *On Generation and Corruption*: “For things that would be mixed to one possessing weak sight would not be mixed to one who sees sharply, as one possessing a Lyncean eye.”

Aristophanes, in *Plutus*:

> I shall make you see more sharply than Lynceus himself.

Lucian, in *Hermotimus*: “But you are more penetrating for us than even Lynceus, since, as it seems, you see through the breast itself what lies within.”

Some report that Lynceus was the first to discover mines of copper, silver, and gold; hence the popular story that he could also see what lay beneath the earth. Apollonius, in the *Argonautica*, writes that Lynceus was so penetrating in sight that he could even pierce the earth itself with his gaze and see what was happening among the dead.

Erasmus, a most learned and equally eloquent man, translated his verses as follows:

> But Lynceus possessed a marvelous sharpness of vision,  
> If the report is true which praises the man  
> As having easily seen what lay hidden beneath the deep earth.

Eusebius, Book VIII, chapter 5, of the *Preparation for the Gospel*:

> Moreover, you would be far from the truth if you considered any wicked person happy, even if he were richer than Croesus, keener of sight than Lynceus, stronger in body than that Crotonian Milo, more handsome than Ganymede, and abounding in all other bodily and external goods. For the man who has subjected his mind to the domination of many masters and to the worst passions—desire, pain, fear, folly, and ignorance—can in no way be happy and blessed, even if he is commonly called happy. For if you are willing to raise the eyes of your mind a little and consider true goodness, insofar as this is possible for a human being, you will pursue with great laughter all the things you now appear to admire. For whenever better things are hidden, evils intruding into their place are praised. But when good things are brought into the open, then the things contrary to them display their shame more clearly than in daylight. Therefore, if you conceive that divine good in your mind, you will not readily place among goods any of the things you have mentioned as being found among the vicious. Their most precious treasures are indeed the mines of silver and gold, which customarily come forth from the worst part of the earth. For there is a very great difference between the sterility of metal-bearing soil and the fertility of earth without metals. The nature of silver and gold is far removed from the goodness of crops, without which we cannot live—as is especially clear in the high price of grain. For when necessity demands a brief supply of food, people rightly judge all treasures in comparison with it and willingly throw them all away. But when the necessities of life flow to us in abundance, and we abound in nature’s goods, we cannot be content; instead, we gape after silver and gold and, as though blinded in the eyes, are driven here and there by our earthly burden because of greed, while for the sake of money we are continually harassed by war.

> We also desire magnificent clothing, which is nothing other than the praise of the weaver’s art and the flower of sheep, as certain poets have said. But whoever is so desirous of glory that he wishes to be praised even by the wicked must necessarily be wicked himself, since each thing delights in what resembles it. He will seek good health of the ears once he has learned that no small diseases of the mind arise from hearing. Let the man who lifts his neck on the strength of his body place the most savage beasts before his eyes. Thus he will understand that it is most shameful for a human being to boast of the strength of wild animals.

> No one who possesses a sound mind can boast of bodily beauty, since it is extinguished so quickly that it seems to have withered before it has even flowered—especially when he sees that even lifeless works of art, painted, molded, or woven, can possess considerable beauty. None of these things has ever been counted among goods by God. Why do I say by God, when even knowledgeable people who philosophize correctly neither judge nor call these perishable things goods?

Thus far Eusebius.

### “Alcibiades”

Alcibiades of Athens was not only a renowned commander but also extremely eloquent in speech, as Demosthenes and Theophrastus relate. As Probus says, he was by far the most handsome man of his age, suited to every undertaking, full of plans, a supreme commander by land and sea, and possessed of such great charm of face and speech that no one could resist him in debate. He was rich; when circumstances demanded it, he was industrious, enduring, generous, magnificent no less in his life than in his table, approachable, agreeable, and exceptionally skillful in adapting himself to circumstances.

Yet as soon as he relaxed, he was found to be so luxurious, dissolute, lustful, and intemperate that everyone marveled that one man could contain so great a difference and such a contrary nature. Thucydides reports much about him. You can find his life in Plutarch and in Aemilius Probus, whom I have just cited.

Marsilio Ficino, in his commentary, has Diotima address Socrates among other things as follows: “If nature had given you Lyncean eyes, my Socrates, so that you could penetrate whatever came before your sight, the outwardly most beautiful body of your Alcibiades would appear to you utterly deformed.”

### “A three-day fever”

A fever lasting three days. It should be known, as Servius testifies, that fever, although it is named from heat, can also be cold. By diminutive formation it is called *febricula*, “a little fever.”

### “To be dissolved”

To be corrupted. Saint Ambrose, in Book III of the *Hexaemeron*:

> Today you see a strong young man, flourishing in the vigor of youth, with a pleasing appearance and lovely complexion. The next day he meets you changed in face and mouth; he who the day before appeared to you most elegant and beautiful now appears pitiable, weakened and dissolved by the infirmity of some illness.

Saint Bernard, in his little book *On the Formation of Character*:

> What kind of beauty is this, which a slight fever and wrinkled old age so completely dissolve that it seems never to have existed?

## Into Meter VIII

The poem is twofold in form: one verse is Asclepiadic and choriambic, the other iambic dimeter. He says that mortals know very well where they should seek other things, but are utterly ignorant where they can obtain happiness.

### “This ignorance”

How great. Some copies read *quanti*, “how great,” or *quantum*, “how much,” or *mis­eros*, “wretched,” or *devio tramite*, “by a wandering path.”

### “Roe-deer”

Wild goats. *Caprea* means a wild goat. Martial:

> You will see a roe-deer hanging from the summit of a cliff;  
> You may expect it to fall, but it deceives the dogs.

### “Tyrrhenian waters”

The Tuscan Sea. The Etruscans were called Tyrrhenians after King Tyrrhenus, with whom they once migrated from Lydia to Italy.

### “Recesses”

Spaces.

### “Snowy”

White as snow.

### “More fertile”

More productive.

### “Tender fish”

A soft kind of fish.

### “Rough sea-urchins”

He uses an appropriate epithet, for the sea-urchin is a little fish belonging to the crab family and possessing spines that it uses in place of feet. Martial:

> Although this sea-urchin may prick fingers  
> With the needle of its shell,  
> Once it has shed its shell it will be soft.

Juvenal:

> And he would say, “the shore of Chios, seen only once.”

Horace, in the *Satires*:

> But not every sea is fertile in noble shellfish;  
> The Lucrine *peloris* is better than the Baian purple shell;  
> Oysters arise at Circeii, sea-urchins at Misenum;  
> Soft Tarentum boasts of its broad scallops.

There is an old proverb, “Rougher than a sea-urchin,” spoken of an unmanageable person with unpleasant manners. It should also be known that there is a land urchin, covered with spines on every side.

### “Where?”

In what place, where.

### “Not to know”

Understand: “themselves not to know.”

### “Endure”

Suffer.

### “The star-bearing pole”

This is an anastrophe. Ludovicus Bigus:

> No one lives content; rather, he desires better things.  
> The more excellent the things, the more he attains them.  
> Since our nature is carried toward the highest good,  
> The mind cannot quench its thirst in the sea.  
> It must fly upward, free, beyond the heavenly heights,  
> If it wishes to satisfy itself with a full throat.  
> The spirit, born for the solace of the heavenly court,  
> Will never be at rest in an earthly dwelling.

Foolishly, therefore, mortals, sunk in desire for earthly things, seek on earth what has been placed above the star-bearing heaven.

### “Let them seek”

Let them desire by seeking. According to Nonius, *ambire* sometimes means to seek by ambitious striving. Saint Jerome: “Riches that will not follow after a man’s death are loved. The honor of the fasces, which will fade through a successor, is sought.”

### “When”

After.

### “False”

The deceptive goods of this age.

### “With a heavy burden”

With the greatest difficulty and the greatest labors.

### “They have prepared”

They have acquired.

### “Then”

Then, afterward. True goods, so that they may attain happiness, from which false goods divert and draw minds away. For, as Lactantius testifies, just as one reaches true good through deceptive evils, so one reaches true evil through deceptive goods.

## Into Prose IX

Thus far Philosophy has shown Boethius the form of false happiness. Now she gives the reasons why the highest good cannot be found in the things mortals desire, and says that the greatest error of human beings arises from the fact that, through their own perversity, they have divided what by its nature is simple and indivisible and tolerates no division. For true happiness, which the foolish crowd separates into parts, embraces everything at once: sufficiency, power, reverence, renown, and joy. No one can ever obtain any one of these without the others.

### “Thus far”

Up to this point.

### “Of the false”

Of the false thing.

### “Clearly”

Sharply, acutely.

### “Thereafter”

Then, step by step.

### “Like a little fissure”

A beautiful metaphor.

### “I would prefer”

I prefer; *malim* is used for *malo*, “I prefer,” just as *velim* is used for *volo*, “I wish.”

### “But indeed”

He clearly shows where the error arose, and gradually establishes by certain arguments that sufficiency, power, reverence, renown, and joy are one and the same in nature.

### “To need renown”

Understand: “to seem to need renown.”

### “More contemptibly”

More despicably.

### “Divides”

Divides into parts.

### “Of the thing”

Of true happiness.

### “Which he least desires”

Above it was said that everyone desires the highest good and true happiness. How, then, does he now say that someone least desires the thing itself? To resolve this difficulty, lest it perhaps trouble anyone, it should be observed that human beings possess two kinds of desire.

The first is natural, confused, and disordered. Through it all mortals are carried toward the highest good, as was said above, and desire true happiness. The second is rational, discriminating, and ordered. Through it only a few are directed by divine grace toward the highest good: namely, those who know where and how it must be sought, and who, relying on faith, hope, and charity, press forward by the right path in order finally to attain it.

Therefore explain “which he least desires” as meaning “which he desires and seeks with the nearest, direct, and ordered appetite,” and in the manner and by the path in which that highest good must be investigated.

### “He who seeks riches”

He clearly teaches how mortals, foolishly straying from the right path, try to acquire one particular part—while neglecting the others—of a thing that has no parts.

### “To possess power alone”

To possess power alone.

### “Squanders”

Scatters, wastes, pours out.

### “May be bitten”

May be saddened.

### “The highest perfection”

The complete and integral reality.

### “In the opposite direction”

Into the contrary part of the mind.

### “This”

True happiness.

### “Or”

Even.

### “Transparent”

Open. That is called transparent which is accessible to sight.

### “That is true”

This is a definition of happiness, differing in words from the one given above but agreeing with it in substance.

### “As”

Just as.

### “In the *Timaeus*”

In that most distinguished dialogue. Timaeus of Locri was a Pythagorean philosopher, outstanding in nobility and wealth. He held the highest magistracies and honors and successfully climbed to the loftiest heights of all philosophy. Plato gave his beautiful book its title from him. In it Socrates addresses Timaeus as follows:

> It is therefore your task, Timaeus, after invoking the gods according to custom, to begin the discussion.

Timaeus replies in this way:

> You give sound advice, Socrates. For since all who possess reason in any degree customarily invoke God at the beginning of every work, whether great or small, how much more fitting is it for us—who are about to discuss the universe, whether it came into being or is ungenerated—to invoke divine aid, unless we are completely foolish?

Saint Augustine, Book II of the *Academics*: “Above all, divine assistance must be sought with every devotion and piety.” Plato, in his letter to the relatives and friends of Dion: “In all matters, both in speaking and in thinking, one must always begin from the gods.”

### “Properly”

Correctly, well.

### “Has been composed”

Has sung.

## Into Meter IX

He now appropriately uses heroic verse, since he is invoking God, the creator, preserver, and best, greatest, most beautiful, and most powerful Father of all things—or, to say it all at once, the inexpressible one. He begins with an exclamation, which possesses the greatest force of wonder. We commonly use such an exclamation when we wish to signify that someone’s praises and merits are so great that we cannot attain them adequately in any words.

This poem, moreover, most beautiful and learned, has been drawn with marvelous ingenuity almost entirely from Plato’s *Timaeus*.

### “O”

An interjection expressing wonder at the immeasurable, infinite, and incomprehensible majesty of God.

### “By perpetual design”

By eternal disposition, everlasting providence.

### “Sower”

Creator.

### “You command time to proceed from eternity”

That is, after eternity you command time to flow as its image. There are three things: eternity, the age, and time. The first belongs to God alone, who has neither beginning nor end, but is himself the beginning and end of all things. The second is attributed to the angels, who have a beginning but lack an end; some have thought that it should also be attributed to all enduring things. The third—namely, time—was established in the final place for things subject both to generation and to corruption, although the term is also transferred to other things.

Giovanni Francesco Pico, in his first hymn:

> Then time first flowed from distant eternity,  
> Drifting from the motion of the never-ceasing heavens.

Timaeus in Plato:

> When that father who had generated this everlasting image of the gods saw that it moved and lived, he rejoiced in his work. Led by this joy, he conceived the plan of making his work still more like its original model. Therefore, just as that living being is eternal, so he determined to make this universe eternal insofar as possible. That living being’s nature is eternal, but this cannot wholly belong to a generated work. For this reason he resolved to fashion a moving image of the age. While ordering the heavens, he made a certain eternal image of the eternity that remains in unity but flows in number; this we call time. He then commanded the days and nights, months and years—which did not exist before the heavens—to come into being when the world was born. All these are parts of time.

This is Timaeus.

Now let us see what time is. According to Speusippus, Plato defined time in the following way: “Time is the motion of the sun, the measure of its progression.” According to Plutarch, in the *Opinions of the Philosophers*, Pythagoras said that time is the sphere of the outermost encompassing sphere; Plato, that it is a moving likeness of the age, or the interval of the world’s motion; Eratosthenes, the sun’s course; Plato, that the essence of time is the motion of heaven; and most of the Stoics, that it is motion itself.

Macrobius, Book I of the *Saturnalia*: “Time is a definite dimension derived from the revolution of heaven.” Aristotle, Book IV of the *Physics*: “Time is the number of motion according to what is earlier and later.” This definition is customarily explained as follows: time is the numbered number of local motion itself—not of just any motion, but of the first mover—according to the prior and posterior parts of succession.

Rudolf Agricola of Friesland, a man of extraordinarily acute intellect and singular learning, says in Book I of the *Dialectics*: “Time is customarily defined as the number of motion according to what is earlier and later.” We shall say more plainly that it is the space derived from the revolution of heaven and the sun by which we measure the agitation and succession of all things.

This is Agricola.

Saint Aurelius Augustine, by far the most learned of all mortals, confesses in Book XI of the *Confessions* that he does not know what time is, although he sees that it is a kind of distension. In the same book, rejecting among other things the Platonic and Aristotelian definitions of time, he says:

> Let no one therefore tell me that the motions of heavenly bodies are times. For when, at someone’s request, the sun once stood still so that the victorious Joshua might complete the battle, the sun stood still, but time moved on.

### “Stable”

Marsilio Ficino, Book III of the *Theology*: “God moves and acts upon all things through himself, while he himself is stable through himself.” Baptista Mantuanus, in Book III of the *Calamities*:

> Let him see the Father alone and worship him reverently,  
> Who sits stable and moves all things by a single nod.

Saint Augustine, Book I of the *Confessions*:

> But you, Lord, who always live and in whom nothing dies, since you are before the beginnings of the ages and before everything that can even be called ‘before,’ you are God and Lord of all that you have created. With you the immutable origins of all mutable things remain, and the eternal reasons of all irrational and temporal things live.

The Psalmist: “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same.” Saint James the Apostle: “With whom there is no change or shadow of alteration.” And he himself says through the prophet Malachi: “I am the Lord, and I do not change.”

### External Causes

That is, causes situated outside the divine mind [Col. 1025A], since there were none, nor could God be moved by anything else. Aristotle posited four causes by which everything comes to be: first, that which is the principle of motion; second, that out of which something is made, which he calls matter; third, the rationale and form by which each thing is formed; fourth, the end for whose sake each thing is produced. Plato adds a fifth, the exemplar, which he calls *εἰδέα* (*idea*); that is, the model toward which the craftsman looks when he produces what he has purposed. God, however, possesses within himself the exemplars of all things. He created the world from nothing, aroused by no external causes, but according to an internal exemplar and because of his supreme goodness. And this is what he adds below.

### Truly

But.

[Col. 1025B]

### Form

Idea, exemplar.

### Implanted in the Supreme Good

Internal, situated within.

### Free from Envy

Without envy. Philo Judaeus, writing according to Moses’ account of the creation of the world, says that God, the maker of all things, is good and envies none of the things that exist, and that for this reason he established the world. The Platonic Timaeus says:

“Let us state for what reason the author of all things brought generation and this universe into being. He was good. But no good being is ever touched by envy concerning anything. Therefore, since envy was entirely foreign to him, he wished everything to become as much like himself as possible.”

And shortly afterward:

“He constituted the whole world so that it might be the most beautiful and best work of nature.”

### You Bring Forth

You produce.

[Col. 1025C]

### From the Heavenly Exemplar

From the eternal idea. Ideas are certain primary, eternal forms contained in the divine intelligence, as Augustine says in his book *Eighty-Three Questions*: although they themselves neither arise nor perish, everything that can arise and perish is nevertheless said to be formed according to them, as is everything that arises and perishes. These ideas exist in the divine mind and may be called exemplars, according to Thomas, who says that they are “the principles of the making of things”; whereas the rational principles are regarded as the principles of knowing. For God himself perfectly knows his essence in every way in which it can be known—not only as it exists in him, but also as it can be participated in by created things through a certain likeness. Whatever has been created, however, possesses its own form, by which it participates in the likeness [Col. 1025D] of the divine essence.

### The Beautiful One Himself, Most Beautiful

The Platonic Timaeus says:

“Since the world is the most beautiful of all generated things, and its author is the best of all causes, there can be no doubt that he followed an eternal exemplar. Thus generated, it was brought into being according to that which can be comprehended by reason and wisdom alone and which remains immutable.”

### Commanding the Perfected [World]

The order is: “And you command the perfect world to be completed,” that is, to have its parts complete and perfect. The same Timaeus says:

“The world received each of those four things as a complete whole. For its maker composed it from all fire, air, water, and earth in such a way that he left no part or power of any of them outside it. He did this for the following reasons: first, so that this whole living creature might be as perfect as possible, being made from perfect parts; second, so that it might be one, since nothing had been left outside from which another could be generated; finally, so that no disease or old age might affect it.”

### You Bind the Elements with Numbers

The same Timaeus says:

“Since the world was destined to be bodily, visible, and tangible, and nothing can be seen without fire, nothing touched without solidity, and nothing solid without earth, at the beginning of this work God first created fire and earth. But two things alone cannot suitably cohere without some third thing, and they require some intermediate bond. The most fitting and beautiful bond is that which makes both itself and the things it binds together as unified as possible. Proportion and the ratio of reciprocal comparison achieve this most fully. For whenever, in three numbers, masses, or powers, the middle term is to the last as the first is to the middle—and conversely, as the last is to the middle, so the middle is to the first—then what is in the middle becomes both first and last, and the last and first become middle terms. Necessity therefore requires that all things bound together in this way be identical in relation to one another. Once they have become so related, all become one.

“If the body of the universe had needed breadth but no depth, one intermediate term would have sufficed, both for binding it to itself and for joining its extremities. But since the world required solidity, and solids are always joined not by one but by two intermediates, God placed air and water between fire [Col. 1026C] and earth, and compared them with one another, as far as possible, in such a way that fire is to air as air is to water, and air is to water as water is proportionately related to earth. From this conjunction the world was constituted so that it could be seen and touched. Therefore the body of the world was formed from four such things, joined by the proportion I have described. Through it the world embraces itself in harmonious friendship and coheres so suitably that it cannot be dissolved in any way except by the same one by whom it was bound together.”

Our Severinus, *On Music*, book I, chapter 2:

“How could the different and contrary powers of the four elements come together in one body and structure, unless some harmony joined them? Yet this entire diversity produces both the variety of seasons [Col. 1026D] and of fruits, while nevertheless forming the single body of the year. Therefore, if you mentally and intellectually tear apart any of those things that provide such variety to the world, everything perishes and, so to speak, retains nothing harmonious. Just as in the grave strings there is a proper degree of depth, so that the gravity does not descend into silence, and in the high strings a proper degree of sharpness is maintained, lest the strings, stretched too far, break through the thinness of the sound, but the whole remains mutually consonant and fitting—so too in the music of the world we see that nothing can be so excessive that it dissolves another through its own excess. Rather, whatever it is either produces its own fruits or helps others to produce theirs. Winter contracts, spring loosens, summer scorches, autumn ripens; and the seasons in turn either bring forth their own fruits [Col. 1027A] or assist others in bringing them forth.”

On the connection of the elements through numbers, read much that is truly delightful in Macrobius’ first book of the *Commentaries* he composed on the *Dream of Scipio*.

### With Numbers

With the quaternary number of the elements and the ternary number of the intervals. For the four elements are most suitably joined by three intervals: the first from earth to water, the second from water to air, and the third from air to fire.

### Cold Things with Flames

Cold things with hot things.

### Dry

Arid.

### Liquid

Moist.

### Purer

More unmixed.

### Let It Fly Out

Beyond the prescribed place because of excessive weight.

### Let Them Draw Down

Let them depress.

[Col. 1027B]

### You, Joining the Middle of Threefold Nature

The order is: “You, joining the middle soul that moves all things, which is of a threefold nature, release it,” that is, expand it; supply “it,” and repeat “middle” through the corresponding clauses.

### Of Threefold Nature

Because, as Plato held, God fashioned the nature of the world-soul from three kinds of things—being, sameness, and otherness—mixing them so exactly that, in its essence, the other was everywhere present, while in its sameness the other and essence were likewise present; and again, in its otherness, essence and sameness lay concealed. Or it is called “of threefold nature” because the world-soul, joining lofty causes to their lowest effects, remains in itself, descends toward effects, and rises toward causes.

### Middle

As Plato maintains, God established the soul in the middle [Col. 1027C] of things and extended it from there throughout the whole, while drawing part of it beyond the world, so that, in caring for the world, it might turn toward God. Thus the soul is the middle degree of things and joins all degrees, both higher and lower, into one, since it rises toward the upper regions and descends toward the lower.

The Timaeus in Plato says:

“From that substance which is indivisible and always the same and alike, and from that which again becomes divided around bodies, he mixed a third kind of substance in the middle. This third kind was to partake both of the nature of the same and of the nature of the other, and by means of these he constituted it in the middle between indivisible substance and that which is divided around bodies. Having taken these three, he blended them all into one form.”

[Col. 1027D]

### Moving All Things

Virgil, *Aeneid*, book VI:

> “And mind, infused throughout its limbs,  
> Moves the whole mass and mingles with the mighty body.”

### Through Harmonious Members

Through the parts of the world joined and made consonant by a certain harmony. The Platonic Timaeus says:

“After the entire constitution of the soul had been completed according to the mind of that creator, he immediately fashioned within it everything bodily, fitting the middle to the middle and joining it by an appropriate modulation. Extending from the middle through everything to the boundaries of heaven, and spread around it externally, then turning back upon itself, it gave the whole of time the divine beginning of an everlasting and wise life. The body of heaven was made visible [Col. 1028A], but the soul escaped the sight of the eyes; endowed with reason and harmony, it was produced by its universal author, the best of all things that eternally exist and belong to understanding, as itself the best of all generated things.”

### Which

The soul of the world.

### Divided

Divided into two parts, referring to motion.

### He Rolled Together

He set in circular motion.

### Into Two Orbits

Into twin circles, namely, the fixed sphere, which does not wander, and the orbits of the wandering planets. The world-soul advanced in such perfection that it nearly fulfilled its own idea. Its division lengthwise shows that the soul’s proper motion is naturally straight, namely, toward sensation and the nature of growth or motion. It is likewise divided into two in order to show [Col. 1028B] that the soul has a twofold straight motion, namely, toward sensing and toward moving, and that from the soul into bodies there is likewise a double motion, namely, uniform and multiform. It intersects the two lines in order to represent the soul; then it bends them into a circle, indicating that the nature of the soul, naturally more inclined toward straight motion, is through the gift of intelligence from God completely adapted to circular motion—by two circles, I mean, the fixed sphere and, beyond the fixed sphere, the orbits of the wandering planets. The revolution of the fixed sphere properly represents the nature of identity and intelligence. The manifold windings of the planets properly represent the nature of otherness and of the soul’s lower parts.

### Into Itself

Into itself.

[Col. 1028C]

### It Moves

It is moved.

### Mind

Deep intelligence. For the soul’s revolution accompanies the orbit of intelligence. If the soul is completely abandoned by intelligence, its motion immediately becomes straight, both in perception and in action. But its returning upon itself and rolling together similar circuits through other things comes from a higher intellect, which, while remaining in itself and suddenly turning toward its cause, bestows intelligence upon the soul. Through this intelligence, as though extending a hand, it restrains the soul, naturally wandering by its own nature, and bends its restless motion—which is naturally more inclined toward a straight line outside itself—into an orbit midway between straight motion and rest. Hence the soul:

> “It moves, destined to return into itself, and circles  
> The deep mind, turning heaven with a similar image.”

[Col. 1028D]

### You Advance Souls from Like Causes

Plato says that the rational soul of human beings was formed by God from the same kinds of things, mixed in the same vessel, from which the world-soul had been formed. The vessel signifies the idea of rational life itself; but he adds that it was made from the remnants of the earlier mixture, signifying that individual lives are inferior to universal life. Then God assigns souls—that is, the individual orders of souls—to individual stars. He also supplies vehicles, namely ethereal bodies. He teaches the fated laws as well, when he infuses souls with the patterns of ideas, through which souls, at some point turning back upon themselves, may recognize the rational principles of things.

The words of Plato’s *Timaeus*, translated by Marsilio Ficino, are these [Col. 1029A]:

“After saying this, he again poured the remnants of the earlier mixture into the same vessel in which he had blended and tempered the soul of the whole world, mixing them in a certain similar manner, though not equally perfect, but deficient from the first in the second and third degree. Finally, after constituting the universe, he distributed an equal number of souls among the stars, assigning one to each; and, placing them upon them as though upon vehicles, he showed them the nature of the universe and proclaimed the fated laws.”

### Souls

Supply: of human beings.

### From Like Causes

By a similar method and from causes and kinds of things identical with those from which the world-soul was made.

### Lesser Lives

More ignoble souls, such as those of brute animals and plants.

### You Advance

You produce.

[Col. 1029B]

### Light

Swiftly moving.

### Lofty

More excellent souls.

### Chariots

Vehicles. For, as Plato held, God placed bodies beneath souls as vehicles.

### You Sow

You sow; this is said according to the Platonic view, which held that God scattered different spirits into the earth, the moon, and the other instruments of time, as though he had sown them.

### Benign Laws

So that human beings might overcome the violent passions aroused in the soul through its conjunction with the body and live justly.

### To the Returning One

Making him return, bringing him back. Those who return are properly called people who have escaped great dangers.

### With Fire

With love. Marsilio the Platonist, *Commentary*, discourse IV, chapter 6:

“Eternal love, by which the soul is always moved toward God, causes it always to rejoice in God as though in a new spectacle. This love is always kindled in the soul by the same goodness of God, which also makes the lover blessed. In brief, then, we shall praise three benefits of love: that, restoring us from our former division into wholeness, it brings us back to heaven; that it places each person in his own dwelling and makes all tranquil in that distribution; and that, when all tedium has been expelled, it continually kindles in the soul, through a certain ardor of its own, an almost new delight, making the soul blessed through a gentle and sweet enjoyment.”

At this point, before proceeding to discuss other matters, I wish to warn the reader that Boethius’ philosophy in this poem imitates Plato not only carefully but also cautiously. Plato’s opinions concerning the world-soul and the other souls—those of human beings, animals, and trees—are not accepted in every respect by Christian people, although we have expounded nearly every point of Platonic doctrine in Latin with no little diligence. Moreover, that the heavenly spheres possess souls is acknowledged not only by the Platonists but also by all the Peripatetics. Aristotle teaches this in book II of *On the Heavens*, again in books V and VIII of the *Physics*, in book II of *On the Soul*, and in book XI of the *Metaphysics*; Theophrastus, Aristotle’s disciple, teaches it in his *On the Heavens*. Avicenna and Algazel strongly confirmed it.

Augustine Aurelius, in the book entitled *Enchiridion*, and Thomas Aquinas, in book II of *Against the Gentiles*, state that, as far as Christian doctrine is concerned, it makes no difference whether heavenly bodies have souls or do not [Col. 1030A] have them. Paulus Cortesius, *Book of Sentences*, book II, distinction 4:

“Following Plato as their leader, many have wished the stars to be living beings. The Stoics, however, hold that the stars possess divine power and mind. Anaxagoras was prosecuted by the Athenians because he had said that the sun was a glowing stone, neither a god nor a living being. Among our own writers, Origen, following Plato, considered the stars living beings; Jerome also seems to follow him gradually and hesitantly. Saint Augustine, acting as an arbiter in an uncertain matter, does not assent to either opinion when he cannot pursue a middle position. But Apollo of the Christians, Saint Thomas, binds the whole question more learnedly by reason. For, by examining the operations of the soul, he proves that no operation appropriate to a soul belongs to heavenly bodies except understanding and motion. [Col. 1030B] He says that the soul is joined to bodies not as their form but through the application of its power, as a driver is attached to something that moves, just as a bottle moves when it is pushed downhill by the force of one’s feet.”

### Give, Father

Thus Martianus Capella addresses the sun:

> “Grant, Father, that the mind may ascend into the heavenly company.”

### August Seat

A sacred, divine seat, filled with the majesty of the supreme good. Properly speaking, according to Servius, *augustum* is a roof consecrated by augury. By extension, *augustum* means noble, as though full of majesty. Virgil, *Georgics*, book IV:

> “If ever you leave honey in its august seat  
> And in its guarded storehouses.”

Servius reads it this way. Some others read *angustam* (“narrow”), and some also read it that way in this passage, so that it means a narrow seat, reached only by a narrow and constricted path. But in my judgment it should be read with *u*: *augustam*.

### Earthly Mass

Bodily contamination.

### Mists and Weights

Disturbances arising in the soul from the body’s heaviness.

### With Your Splendor

With your internal, ineffable, and incomprehensible light.

### You

Supply: are.

### Serene

Serenity.

### To Behold You

Contemplation of you; supply: is.

### End

The supreme good. In the Gospel of John, chapter XV, Jesus Christ says to the Father:

> “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.”

Thomas Aquinas, the glory of theologians, in book III of *Against the Gentiles* [Col. 1030D]:

“The highest and perfect happiness of an intellectual nature consists in the vision of God.”

### Beginning

John in the *Apocalypse*, chapter I:

> “I am the alpha and the omega, the beginning and the end, says the Lord God, who is, who was, and who is to come, the Almighty.”

God is the beginning, middle, and end of all things: beginning, insofar as he produces them; middle, insofar as he draws what he has produced back to himself; and end, insofar as he perfects those who return.

### Conveyer

One who advances toward happiness.

### Guide

A guide along the narrow path.

### Path

A truly narrow way, along which few travel.

### Boundary

The end of all things.

## Into Prose X

[Col. 1031A]

Thus far Philosophy has shown Boethius the form of perfect and imperfect happiness. Now she carefully and incisively discusses where true happiness—or blessedness, or the supreme good—consists, showing that it is in God, is wholly identical with him, and is signified by various expressions as one and the same substance. Finally, she concludes that God’s substance too is situated in the good itself.

### Where

Where. In Boethius you will frequently find *quo* used for *ubi*, that is, “in what place.”

### Some Good of This Kind

The supreme good, perfected by the gathering together of all goods.

### Empty

Void, ineffectual, futile.

### Image

Form.

### Indeed

That is.

[Col. 1031B]

### For Everything

He concludes with the greatest firmness and truth that the supreme good exists.

### Exhausted

Worn out in strength and [lacuna]a and weakened.

### Where

Where.

### Common Conception

Boethius, *On the Hebdomads*, chapter 1:

“A common conception of the mind is a proposition that everyone approves when he hears it.”

### Lest This One of All Things

He clearly proves that God and the supreme good are one and the same substance.

### Most Excellent

Most outstanding.

### Whoever Can Imagine It

That is, no one can imagine it.

### Finally, That from Any

The same as just now; he now proves it by a new argument.

### Geometers

Professors of geometry, which is the science of measuring correctly.

[Col. 1031C]

### Porisms

Corollaries. Georgius Valla, *On Things to Be Sought and Avoided*, book II:

“A porism is also what appears from things demonstrated, even though the theorem itself was not proposed to us; hence it received its name, as though it were a certain gain arising from a scientific demonstration. In Latin it is called a corollary; in Greek it is written *πόρισμα* (*porisma*).”

### Corollary

A corollary, as Marcus Varro explains in book I of *On the Latin Language*, signifies something added beyond what was owed, as a kind of increase. The ancients used the word in this way; Plautus used it for what was added above the proper measure or weight. The word *corollarium* derives from *corollae*, garlands, because these were customarily given on stage when the actors had pleased the audience. Hence Pliny also calls the crowns themselves *corollaria* [Col. 1031D]. Suetonius says:

“Therefore, at other people’s spectacles and games too, he frequently and lavishly offered corollaries and prizes from his own resources.”

Seneca, *On Benefits*, book VI:

“To sellers of even the most contemptible crafts we added something beyond the established amount if their work seemed especially diligent to us; and we sprinkled a corollary upon the pilot, the craftsman dealing in the cheapest wares, and the laborer who hired himself out by the day.”

### To Become Gods

Saint Augustine, *City of God*, book IX, chapter 23:

“But Scripture also calls human beings gods among the people of God. ‘I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’ (Psalm 81).”

Jerome, in his sermon *On the Nativity of the Lord*:

> “God became man so that man might become God.”

### With Much

He teaches that the good completes the substance of blessedness and that everything which happiness seems to contain is referred to it as to a summit.

### Substance

Essence, rational principle.

### With Delight

With pleasure. Franciscus Philelphus, in his address to the men of Pavia, calls pleasure *jucunditas*, delight, since it benefits both mind and sense.

### Therefore, the Sum of All Things Desired

Aristotle, *Moral Works*:

“Every art, every science, every action, and likewise every choice, appears to seek some good. Therefore the ancients rightly said that the good itself is that which all things seek.”

Dionysius, chapter 4 of *On the Divine Names*:

“All things,” he says, “desire the good and the best.”

## Into Meter X

[Col. 1032B]

The poem is composed of alternating Phalaecian and Sapphic verses, except for the second verse, which is Phalaecian. It could be changed into a Sapphic verse by transforming one word:

> “Whom deceit binds with heavy chains,”

as from the fourth verse, by changing the order of the words, one could make a Phalaecian:

> “Here rest will be for you after labors.”

But our Boethius first sang three consecutive Phalaecians and then added a Sapphic, equal to the hendecasyllable in the number of syllables and proportion of metrical times.

After Philosophy has shown that the supreme good and blessedness have the same substance as God, she now eagerly invites and exhorts mortals to strive together toward this true happiness, abandoning the earthly and deceptive pursuit of worthless goods [Col. 1032C], which blind the mind rather than enlighten it, bind rather than release it, and provoke desires rather than satisfy them.

### Captives

Saint Jerome, in his consolatory letter to a sick friend:

“You judge those to be free—or alienated from their proper character—whom barbarous pleasures have bound. They do not possess a chain, but savage luxury holds them in bonds with its ferocious bite. They have fallen into the snares of savage pleasures like birds captured by the deceit of bird-catching; the more they try to escape, the more they entangle themselves in countless bonds and plunge into deeper recesses.”

Saint Ambrose, *Letters*, book II:

“Let us renounce luxury and delights, which bind us with certain chains of desire. For delights do no good to a fool.”

Marsilio the Platonist:

“Moderate youth makes old age easy; immoderate youth makes it difficult. Whoever obeys the lusts of the body undoubtedly serves insane tyrannies.”

### Earthly

Buried beneath desires for earthly things.

### Blunting

Dulling, making dull and sluggish. In book VII of the *Ethics*, Aristotle proves from this that pleasure is not the supreme good, since, he says, pleasures impede prudence; and the greater they are, the more they cloud the mind, as is clear in sexual matters, that is, in things pertaining to Venus. For while engaged in the service of Venus, no one can perceive anything clearly with the mind.

### Here

In the supreme good. In Greek, *ἄσυλον* (*asylum*) is an inviolate temple granted by the law of consecration, from the privative prefix *a-* and *συλάω* (*sulaō*), “I seize, plunder, or violate”; or, as Servius explains, it is called *asylum* as though *ἄσυρον* (*asyron*), because no one could be forcibly dragged from it. Those who fled there were safe and could not be removed. The Athenians first constructed such a place; Romulus later did so.

Saint Augustine, *City of God*, book I:

“Romulus and Remus are said to have established an asylum, so that whoever fled there would be free from every injury, seeking thereby to increase the population needed for founding the city.”

So, by a beautiful metaphor, he calls the place of blessedness an asylum. He does not say that it is open to the wretched because the wretched can enter it; rather, one must understand that otherwise they would be and remain wretched unless, to escape misery, they took refuge in the asylum of true happiness.

### Tagus

A gold-bearing river of Lusitania.

### Hermus

A gold-bearing river of Lydia. Virgil:

> “Or Hermus, turbid with gold.”

[Col. 1033B]

### Shining

Gleaming with golden sands.

### Indus

The greatest river of India, abundant in various gems.

### In the Hot Region

In the eastern region, where the sun rises.

### They Illuminate

They enlighten.

### Sight

The power of the mind’s vision.

### Blind

Blinded by perverse desire.

### Into Their Own Darkness

Their own proper darkness; for metals and gems generally lie hidden in the dark caverns of the earth.

### Prevails

Has power.

### Avoids

Does not admit.

### Dark Ruins

Disturbances, errors, and falls into wickedness through ignorance or lack of judgment.

[Col. 1033C]

### To Mark

To see.

### This Light

The radiance of the supreme good.

### He Will Deny the Bright Rays of Phoebus

That is, he will say that, compared with it, the sun possesses no light.

## Into Prose XI

Thus far Philosophy has argued that the supreme good exists and where it consists. She will now teach what the good is, concluding that nothing is good unless it is also one. For when the principle of unity has been removed, whatever exists ceases to be good.

### Of the Infinite

Supply: I shall consider.

### Through Participation in the Good

The Platonic Socrates, in the *Gorgias*:

“Pleasure is that in whose presence we rejoice; the good is that in whose presence we are good. Indeed, both we and whatever else is good are good because of a certain virtue that is present.”

### By a Similar Argument

Because, as has been granted, things that are good become good both through attaining unity and through participation in the good. Whatever things naturally have the same disposition possess the same substance. Unity and goodness, however, naturally have the same disposition. Therefore unity and goodness have the same substance.

### Do You Know, Then

He teaches that each thing subsists so long as it is one; but when it ceases to be one, it perishes. This serves to show that all things desire unity by natural inclination, and since unity is the same as the good, that the good is sought by all. Thus Boethius recalls to mind what he had shortly before confessed he did not know: that the good is the end of all things.

[Col. 1034A]

### Everything That Exists Remains and Subsists as Long as It Is One

There is an excellent and golden little book by our Boethius on unity and the one. If you possess it, diligent reader, read it carefully and repeatedly in order to understand this passage thoroughly. From it we have also chosen to append the following, so that our labor may benefit even those who lack an abundant library:

“Unity is that by which each thing is said to be one. Whether it is simple or composite, spiritual or corporeal, a thing is one through unity; nor can it be one except through unity, just as it cannot be white except through whiteness, nor quantified except through quantity. It is not only one through unity, but whatever a thing is, it remains so as long as unity is within it. When it ceases to be one, it ceases to be what it is.

“Hence this follows: whatever exists exists because it is one. This is shown as follows. All being in created things comes from form; but no being comes from form unless form is united with matter. Being exists only from the conjunction of form and matter. Hence philosophers say, in describing it: being is the existence of form in matter. When form is united with matter, something one is necessarily constituted from the conjunction of the two; and in this constitution that one thing remains only so long as unity holds form together with matter. But the destruction of a thing is nothing other than the separation of form from matter. Separation and union are opposites; therefore, if a thing is destroyed by separation, it is plainly preserved in its being only through the unity opposed to separation.”

Saint Aurelius Augustine, *On the Order of Things*, book II:

“For a stone to be a stone, all its parts and its entire nature have been consolidated into one. What of a tree? Would it not cease to be a tree if it were not one? What of the limbs, organs, and everything else that constitutes any living creature? Certainly, if they suffer separation from unity, the animal will no longer exist. What else do all things strive to be than one?”

Saint Bernard, *To Eugenius*, book II:

“Where there is unity, there is perfection. The remaining numbers do not possess perfection but division, since they depart from unity.”

### Yet There Is No Reason Concerning This

He removes from Boethius the scruple of doubt, showing even more clearly concerning plants and inanimate things what he had confessed concerning animals.

### For Some Indeed Are in the Fields

Maro, *Georgics*, book II:

> “Nor can you make all lands bear everything:  
> Willows grow beside rivers, others in thick marshes;  
> Sterile ash trees on rocky mountains.  
> Shores rejoice in myrtles; finally,  
> Bacchus loves open hills, and yew trees the north wind and cold.”

Ovid, *Art of Love*, book I:

> “Nor does the same earth produce everything:  
> One region suits vines, another olives; here grain flourishes well.”

### As Though They Had Plunged Their Mouths into the Earth, They Draw Nourishment from the Roots

Aristotle, *On the Soul*, book II:

“What the mouth and head are in an animal, the root is in a tree.”

### Everything Most Noble

It is also read: “everything softest.”

### It Protects

It is protected. He used a deponent verb passively.

### But How Great, Indeed

He teaches that nature takes the greatest care that, since individual things cannot persist, species may at least be preserved and continue unharmed through the multiplication of things by means of seeds [Col. 1035A]. According to Aristotle in book II of *On the Soul*, the most natural and primary function of the vegetative soul is to generate something like itself in all living things—provided they are complete, not mutilated in their members, not deformed, and not spontaneously generated. It is appropriate for an animal to generate an animal like itself and for a plant to generate a plant like itself. Thus they always persist according to their likeness, since the individual things themselves cannot remain numerically identical, and they attain, insofar as is granted to them, assimilation to the divine nature and condition. All things desire this, and for its sake everything that exists in nature acts.

### By Genera

According to each genus.

[Col. 1035B]

### Nor Do We Now

He says that he has not been discussing the voluntary motions of the knowing soul, but natural inclination.

### But One and the Same

A definition of the good taken from book I of Aristotle’s *Moral Works*, as reported above.

### By One

By unity.

### Summit

The top.

### For You Have Fixed in Your Mind the Mark of the Middle Truth

A most elegant allusion or metaphor taken from archers, who achieve their aim only when they have struck the target.

### Mark

The target, that is, the sign set up in the middle so that arrows may be shot at it.

### Mind

Not an arrow, but the conjecture and thought of the soul.

## Into Meter XI

[Col. 1035C]

This is a type of iambic poem called *scazon*, that is, “limping.” It has a spondee in the sixth position. It resembles the following verse of Persius:

> “Nor have I wetted my lips at the horse’s spring.”

Before Philosophy reached the point at which she showed Boethius that the end of all things is the good, she used a rather lengthy argument, like someone who finally obtains gold buried in the deepest veins of the earth only after great labor. She now teaches that truth, wrapped in obscure digressions or more often submerged beneath false opinions, can be grasped only by exact contemplation of the mind. She also wishes it not to be sought in vain among external things, but diligently investigated within the innermost treasures of the soul, once obstacles have been removed. [Col. 1035D] For the seeds both of virtues and of the sciences are implanted in our souls.

### With a Deep Mind

With the deepest contemplation.

### He Searches Out

He investigates.

### Truth

The truth.

### From There

This is the correct reading, not *ille*, as it is commonly read.

### From There

From the investigation of truth.

### Inner Sight

Intellect.

### Long Motions

Acts of the soul extending lengthwise.

### Into a Circle

Into a circle.

### Bending

Curving.

### Turned Back

Turned back toward itself.

### Treasures

Powers, namely memory and intellect.

### A Short While Ago

A little earlier.

[Col. 1036A]

### Dark

Obscure.

### Covered

Veiled.

### It Will Shine

It will appear clearly and flash forth distinctly.

### More Perceptively

More clearly.

### Phoebus

The sun.

### For It Has Not Driven All Light from the Mind

It is a Platonic doctrine that souls descending from heaven absorb forgetfulness of divine things, of which they had been conscious in heaven, some more and others less. Therefore on earth they do not learn but remember what they had previously known there. Hence what is called *learning* among the Latins is called “repeated cognition” among the Greeks, because when we learn truths, we recognize again what we knew naturally before the influx of matter, upon entering the body, intoxicated the souls. Thus Plato says in the dialogue on virtue, entitled *Meno*, in which Meno converses with Socrates:

“To seek and to learn is recollection.”

And Jerome testifies that philosophers say that acts of learning are acts of recollection. Saint Aurelius Augustine rejects and refutes this opinion of Plato in book XII, chapter 15, of *On the Trinity*.

### Forgetful Mass

The weight of disturbances and forgetfulness—not of things someone knew in another life, for it is utterly foolish to suppose that a human being had another life before birth, but of those things that the soul would naturally be capable of knowing if it were not infused into and joined with the body.

The *Book of Wisdom*, chapter IX, says:

> “For a corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things.”

[Col. 1036C]

**Haeret**] It is present.

**Profecto**] Certainly.

**Semen**] A certain beginning and germ by which a human being is naturally suited to apprehend truth and acquire knowledge.

**Introrsum**] Toward the interior, inwardly, within.

**Quod**] The seed.

**Excitatur**] A metaphor taken from fire, which is kindled by being fanned in the fuel.

**Ventilante**] Moving, stirring. *Ventilo* means “to move so as to catch the wind.” To winnow grain is to cleanse it. To fan the face is to cool it with a breeze; Juvenal also speaks of fanning gold with sweat-covered fingers.

**Doctrina**] Through the activity of a teacher.

**Cur**] Why.

[Col. 1036D]

**Rogati**] Questioned. Marcus Tullius, in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, writes: “He possesses memory first, and an infinite memory of innumerable things. Plato wishes this to be recollection of a former life. For in the book entitled *Meno*, Socrates questions a certain boy about geometry concerning the measurement of a square. The boy answers him like a child, and yet the questions are so easy that, by answering them gradually, he reaches the point as though he had learned geometry. From this Socrates seeks to establish that learning is nothing other than recollection. He explains this passage much more precisely in the conversation he held on the very day on which he departed from life. For he teaches that anyone who appears entirely ignorant of everything, if he answers a skillful questioner, shows that he is not then learning those things but recognizing them through recollection. Nor could it in any way happen that, from childhood onward, we possessed notions of so many and such important things, implanted and, as it were, stamped upon our minds—what they call *ennoiai* (ἐννοίαι)—unless the mind had flourished in knowledge of things before it entered the body.”

**Recta**] True.

**Censetis**] You think; you maintain.

**Ni**] Unless.

**Mersus**] Implanted.

**Alto corde**] In the depths of the mind.

**Fomes**] The seed and beginning of knowledge.

**Si Platonis musa personat verum**] He rightly expresses doubt in a matter full of ambiguity as to whether Plato spoke truth or falsehood. Plato is called a “Muse” because he employed the highest and most extraordinary eloquence, for which reason Xenophon too was surnamed the Attic Muse. Or, by Plato’s Muse, understand a poem composed according to Plato’s teaching and imbued with his opinion.

**Immemor**] Forgetful.

## IN PROSE XII

This final prose passage of the third volume contains an account of by what governing principles the world is governed—something Boethius himself had previously not understood. Hence he supposed that the good were subjected to punishments, while the wicked were invited to crime by rewards. Philosophy now teaches that the world is governed by divine goodness, and that the one who is the supreme good, because he is God, is the cause of no evil and cannot even be capable of it. Therefore evil is nothing other than a defection from good; and he who can do all things cannot do evil. It follows that the wicked do not flourish at all, but are rather miserable and unhappy, as will be discussed more fully in the next volume.

**Vehementer**] Very greatly.

**Horum**] That our learning is recollection, and that the light of the mind has been obscured by the darkness of the body.

**Commemoras**] You remind me. This expression deserves notice.

**Corporea contagione**] Through the conjunction of body with soul.

**Mole**] Heaviness.

**Quin**] So that.

**Dudum**] A little earlier.

**Inscitiam**] Ignorance.

**Accedam**] I shall agree.

**Divelleret**] Would tear apart.

[Col. 1037D]

**Sospes**] Safe, unharmed.

**Revisas**] You revisit.

**Alioquin**] Unless this is so.

**Vigilantius**] More attentively.

**Diducis**] You open up; you explain.

**Cum Deus inquit**] He teaches that all things are arranged by God gently and most fittingly, since they voluntarily obey and submit themselves to divine goodness.

**Detrectantium jugum**] A metaphor taken from oxen. Hence the poet:

> The bull does not love the yoke, though he hates it and bears it.

**Deo contraire**] To oppose God’s will.

**Jure beatitudinis**] Which, like all the other things, also includes supreme power.

[Col. 1038A]

**Fortiter**] Powerfully.

**Suaviter**] In an orderly way, harmonizing good things most fittingly.

**Lacessentes**] Challenging to battle.

**Coelum**] The celestial gods.

When they attempted to drive the gods from heaven, they were destroyed by Jupiter’s thunderbolts. Macrobius, in the first book of the *Saturnalia*, says: “What else should the Giants be thought to have been than a certain impious race of human beings, denying the gods, and therefore imagined to have wished to expel the gods from their heavenly seat?” Their feet ended in coils of dragons; this signifies that they thought nothing upright and nothing heavenly, since the course and progress of their whole life plunged into the underworld.

**Collidamus**] Let us bring together forcefully; let us clash sharply.

**Arbitratu**] By judgment; by decision.

**Malum igitur**] He concludes by this reasoning that evil is nothing: whatever is something, the omnipotent God can do. But the omnipotent God cannot do evil. Therefore evil is nothing. Saint Augustine, in the eleventh book of *The City of God*, chapter 9: “For there is no nature of evil; evil has received its name from the loss of good.”

**Labyrinthum inexplicabilem**] An insoluble and impenetrable difficulty, from which no one can easily extricate himself. A labyrinth is a place so entangled with winding paths that, once one has entered it, no exit is apparent. Here the word is used metaphorically.

**Orbem**] Circle.

**Munusculum**] A small gift; a corollary.

**Dudum**] A little earlier.

**Exegimus**] We have completed. Ovid:

> And now I have completed the work.

**De ea**] Of the divine substance.

**Parmenides**] This man was an Eleatic and, according to Suidas, a disciple of Anaxagoras; according to Diogenes, a disciple of Xenophanes. Plato mentions him and wrote a dialogue under his name, calling it *Parmenides*, or *On Ideas*. He expressed natural philosophy in verse, as did Empedocles and Hesiod, and said that it was twofold: one kind consisting in truth, the other in opinion. He flourished in the sixty-eighth Olympiad. His Greek verse is:

> Πάντοθεν ἐν κύκλοισι φέρεις ἐναλίγκιον ὄγκον.

That is: “On every side, in circles, you carry a similar mass.” But the statement added in printed editions—“He turns the movable universe of things while preserving himself unmoved”—is not by Boethius, but a gloss by someone unknown, first added in the margin and later inserted into Boethius’s words.

Iamblichus the Platonist explains Parmenides’ statement in this way: “Everything exists from God in such a manner that nothing, however small, is ever abandoned by God. For divine unity flourishes everywhere, through which each thing subsists and is wonderfully revolved by a perpetual and inward circle toward God himself, from whom and in whom all things are. Otherwise they would suddenly collapse into nothingness.”

**Cum Platone sanciente didiceris**] Plato’s *Timaeus*: “Arguments seem to have a certain kinship with the things they express. Therefore, when one discusses a firm and stable thing apprehensible by the mind, the arguments too must be firm, similarly unchangeable, and, so far as possible, altogether impregnable. But when one discusses the likeness of the firm and stable thing itself, probable arguments are sufficient—arguments related to the former arguments as a likeness is related to its model. Indeed, what essence is in relation to generation, truth is in relation to its end.”

## IN METER XII

[Col. 1039B]

The meter is Glyconic, similar to the sixth meter of the first volume. Philosophy urges Boethius to persevere in contemplating the excellence of the supreme good, lest, overcome by a wrongful desire, he relapse into longing for earthly things. For, as someone has said not inelegantly, when a person is fixed in mind upon God, he is tickled by passions and rolls down from heaven to earth.

To demonstrate this, the story of Orpheus is introduced most charmingly. It is reported at length by Diodorus Siculus and most elegantly by Virgil in the final book of the *Georgics* and by Naso in the tenth book of the *Metamorphoses*. Some interpret it as follows: Orpheus had a wife, Eurydice, who, while fleeing Aristaeus through places adorned with grasses and flowers, stepped on a hidden serpent. Killed by its poisonous bite, she descended to the underworld.

Eurydice is the human soul. She is called Eurydice, “having broad judgment,” because she is rational. She marries Orpheus when she is joined to the body, and is loved by Aristaeus, that is, by “the best.” But she becomes ensnared by bodily pleasures. For the flowers and grasses are the beauties of the earth. She flees through them from the Good, which is God, and is killed by the serpent—that is, by sin—which lies hidden among those pleasures, and is plunged into the underworld.

Yet Orpheus is granted permission to recall her from the underworld by the sound of his lyre—that is, by the excellent ordering of actions, which is the greatest harmony and from which virtue arises—meaning to free her from vices, but on the condition that he not look back, that is, that he not relapse into vices.

Since that murder seemed incapable of being removed by water, fumigations, or the passage of days, Jupiter purified him. But Ixion showed little gratitude for this and dared to challenge Juno to adultery. The goddess, after consulting Jupiter, sent a cloud. Ixion embraced it in place of Juno, and fathered the Centaurs. Condemned among the dead, he is carried around by the perpetual turning of a wheel. Tibullus:

for *cognomine*, as Servius attests; and Ovid in the *Fasti*:

for *bimestri*. The same author, in the fifth book of the *Tristia*:

**Tantalus**] He ruled Smyrna in Phrygia or, as others report, Mount Sipylus. In the underworld, as Homer sings, he suffers perpetual thirst while waters lap at his mouth. Not everyone gives the same account of the cause of his punishment. Some say that he is paying the penalty because he served his son Pelops to the gods as a feast. Others report that the golden watchdog of Jupiter’s temple in Crete, stolen by Pandareus of Miletus, came to Tantalus; when Tantalus denied it to Mercury, who demanded its return, he was afflicted with this punishment. The dog was golden and breathing. As Asclepiades relates from a myth, Tantalus was punished because he had revealed the gods’ secrets to mortals. Ovid:

> Tantalus seeks water in the water and grasps at fleeing fruit;  
> His garrulous tongue brought this upon him.

Euripides says that he was tortured while suspended in the air from a balancing stone. Some say that he was placed beneath Mount Sipylus in Lydia. Petronius holds that Tantalus represents misers, whose wealth is of no use to them and who lie upon their stored-up money with dry throats. His verses, quoted by Fulgentius, are:

> The wretched Tantalus neither drinks amid the waters  
> Nor plucks the exposed fruit,  
> Whom his own desires oppress.  
> Such is the appearance of the wealthy man:  
> He possesses everything far and wide,  
> Yet with dry mouth digests his hunger.

**Tityi**] According to Pherecydes, Tityus was the son of Jupiter and Elara, whom Orchomenus fathered. He is nevertheless called a son of Earth because, when his pregnant mother Elara hid in a cavern of the earth out of fear of Juno, she gave birth to the child there. Strabo indicates in Boeotia a cave called Elara after this event. Others think that he is called a son of Earth because myths represent savage and monstrous beings of the human race—of which sort Tityus was—as born from the earth; Callimachus likewise calls all especially terrible beasts an offspring of Earth.

In the underworld he is stretched over nine acres and feeds vultures, according to Homer, because he attempted violence against Latona; or, as Euphorion sings, because he violated Diana. For this reason Pindar relates that he was killed by the arrows of Apollo and Diana.

**Vultur**] Homer sings of two vultures fastened upon Tityus; Ovid and Claudian of one. Seneca likewise writes in *Hercules Furens*:

> Tityus offers eternal banquets to the bird.

The ancient theologians, as Macrobius reports in his commentary on the *Dream of Scipio*, wished the vulture tearing at the immortal liver to signify nothing other than the torments of conscience subject to crime: the vulture searches out the innermost organs and tears at the very vital parts by constantly reminding the criminal of the deed committed, and, if his anxieties ever attempt to rest, rouses them again, clinging as though to regenerating sinews and sparing him no compassion. Under this law, no guilty person acquits himself when he is his own judge, nor can he escape his own verdict.

Those tortured by banquets placed before their faces, wasting away from hunger and starvation, represent those whom an ever-greater desire to acquire possessions prevents from seeing the abundance already present, and who suffer the evils of poverty amid plenty because they do not know how to look upon what they have acquired while still longing for what they lack.

Those hanging stretched upon the rays of wheels represent people who foresee nothing through counsel, regulate nothing through reason, accomplish nothing through the virtues, and entrust themselves and all their actions to fortune, being continually whirled about by accidents and chance.

To roll a huge stone represents those who wear out their lives in ineffective and laborious efforts. The dark rock, always about to fall and resembling one already falling, hangs over the heads of those who pursue lofty powers and an ill-fated tyranny. They will never live without fear and, forcing the subjected populace to hate them while fearing them, always seem to encounter the destruction they deserve. This is Macrobius.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1043]

## IN PROSE I

[Col. 1043A]

In the first volume Boethius had said: “Yet I seem to see the impious workshops of criminals overflowing with joy and delight; every utterly depraved person threatening us with new frauds and accusations; the good lying prostrate, struck down by fear of our peril; every shameful person encouraged to dare a crime by impunity and to accomplish it by rewards; while the innocent are deprived not only of security but even of defense itself.” Therefore he wishes to exclaim:

> O creator of the star-bearing universe.

In this poem, since his mind was excessively disturbed, he adds, among other things:

> The deserved penalty for crime  
> Presses upon the innocent who have done no wrong.

> But perverse conduct sits upon a lofty throne,  
> And the guilty trample upon sacred necks  
> In an unjust reversal.

And other lines to the same effect.

In this book, therefore, Philosophy—as she digs out the root of the disease completely—strongly rebukes and refutes Boethius’s opinion. She teaches that the good, possessing virtue, are always powerful, whereas the wicked are always abject and weak; that vices are never without punishment, nor virtues without reward; and that happiness comes to the good, while misfortune always comes to the wicked.

On these matters, read Plato’s *Gorgias*; Saint Gregory’s *Moralia*; chapter five of the eighth book of Eusebius of Caesarea’s *Preparation for the Gospel*; chapter 23 of Lactantius Firmianus’s *On Justice*; Saint Jerome’s consolatory letter to the exiled virgin; another of the same author to a sick friend; and again the one entitled *To Oceanus*; Book V of Baptista Mantuanus’s *On Patience*; and other works of this kind.

## IN METER I

The poem is a two-line, two-stanza form, consisting of an Alcmanic dactylic tetrameter acatalectic in one line and an Archilochian iambic dimeter acatalectic in the other. It depends upon what the preceding prose said: “I shall also attach wings to your mind, by which it may raise itself on high.” Philosophy now says that no one can attain true blessedness unless, lifted up by the wings of virtues and scorning all earthly things, he transcends the heavens and joins himself to the supreme good through contemplation.

**Pennae volucres**] The powers of the mind, to be raised through the contemplation of truth.

**Celsa**] The high regions.

**Poli**] The heavens.

**Quas**] The wings.

**Qui**] Fire.

**Agili motu**] Because of its exceedingly swift rotation.

**Aetheris**] Of heaven.

[Col. 1044A]

**Verticem**] The summit.

**In astriferas domos**] Into the spheres of the planets.

**Phoebo**] The sun.

**Conjungat vias**] May approach and attach itself.

**Aut comitetur**] The order is: “Or until the mind itself, as a soldier”—that is, as servant and companion—“may accompany” the path of the shining star, that is, Jupiter, whose brightness, according to Marcus Tullius, is favorable and health-giving to the human race; and “may accompany the journey of the cold old man,” that is, may join itself to Saturn, the highest of the planets. Among the ancients Saturn was depicted as an old man, gray-haired, with a long beard, bent, gloomy, pale, and with his head covered. In his right hand he held a sickle; in the same hand was an image of a serpent biting its own tail; in his left he held his infant son to his mouth, about to devour him. Virgil, in the *Georgics*:

> Where the cold star of Saturn retreats.

[Col. 1044C]

**Recurrat**] Let it return; let it revisit. It says *recurrat* because the soul is heavenly in origin; therefore, through contemplation, let it return to its homeland, although some read *percurrat*, “let it traverse.” By “the circle of the star” he means the star-bearing heaven, which is also called the firmament.

**Ubi**] After.

> For which there is never enough of what has been exhausted.

The unlearned therefore incorrectly read *exhaustum*.

> Therefore the living force of the mind prevailed, and far beyond  
> It proceeded outside the flaming walls of the world,

[Col. 1044D]

Saint Jerome, in *Against Jovinianus*, drawing on Theophrastus: “The wise person can never be alone; he has with him all who are and all who have ever been good, and he carries his free spirit wherever he wishes. What he cannot do with his body, he embraces in thought; and if there is a lack of human companionship, he speaks with God. He will never be less alone than when he is alone.”

Rudolph Agricola, in the *Protrepticus*: “What greater or more certain divinity of philosophy can there be than one closed within no boundaries and contained by no space? For the sacred spirit of a human being proceeds freely, released and constrained by no limits; it wanders wherever the nature of things permits, and traverses not only lands and seas but the stars themselves and the related heavens. Nothing too subtle resists it: it comprehends, surpasses, and penetrates everything.”

## IN PROSE II

Philosophy offers very beautiful and very firm arguments by which she proves that the good and those endowed with virtue are always powerful, whereas the wicked are weak and deprived of all the powers of true strength.

**Nam cum bonum malumque contraria sint**] According to Cicero, in Book V of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “Contraries have contrary consequences.”

**Veramque illam Platonis**] This statement occurs in Plato’s *Gorgias*, where Socrates says to Polus:

[Col. 1045C]

> “I maintain, Polus, that both orators and tyrants possess the least power in cities, just as I said a little earlier. For they do nothing, so to speak, of what they wish to do; yet they do what seems best to them in their own opinion.”

## IN METER II

The poem is a two-line, two-stanza form, consisting in one line of an Alcmanic trochaic dimeter catalectic and in the other of a Pherecratian. It teaches that tyrants, although they commonly appear and are judged to be powerful, are nevertheless not powerful at all, since they are continually oppressed by the gravest slavery to their desires.

Diogenes the Cynic rightly said that slaves serve their masters, but the wicked serve their desires. According to the Evangelist John: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8).

Saint Augustine, in Book IV of *The City of God*, chapter 3: “The rule of the wicked harms the rulers themselves more, for they ravage their own souls with the greater license of their crimes.” A little later he adds: “Therefore the good person, even if he is a slave, is free; but the wicked person, even if he reigns, is a slave—not merely of one man but, what is more serious, of as many masters as he has vices.”

**Septos**] Surrounded; crowded together.

**Tristibus**] Causing sadness.

**Torvo**] Terrifying.

**Rabie**] Fierceness.

**Intus**] Within their conscience.

**Hinc**] On the one hand.

**Versat**] Agitates.

**Avidis venenis**] Alluring passions.

[Col. 1046A]

**Hinc**] On the other hand.

**Flagellat**] Beats; shakes. The order is: “Turbulent anger, raising waves, lashes the mind.”

**Fluctus**] Movements and agitations of the soul.

**Turbida**] Turbulent.

**Tollens**] Raising; stirring up.

**Captos**] Overcome by the force of sadness.

**Lubrica**] Unstable, changeable, yielding to fear.

**Ergo**] The order is: “Therefore, oppressed by unjust masters, he does not do what he desires, since you see one man bearing so many tyrants.”

**Unum caput**] One wicked man.

**Tot tyrannos**] So many vices ruling him.

**Ferre**] To endure.

**Non facit quod optat**] He does not accomplish what he wishes, and thus is shown to be neither free nor powerful.

## IN PROSE III

He argues sharply and clearly that rewards never fail the good, nor punishments fail their crimes; and he teaches that mortals, through the splendor of the virtues, attain such excellence that they can suffer neither harm nor obscurity from the wicked—and, what is far greater, become gods. Conversely, through the infection of crimes they degenerate so far from the dignity of human nature that they are transformed into beasts.

**In stadio**] In the racecourse. The Greek word *stadion* (στάδιον, or στάδιος) means in Latin “racecourse”; it is a place where horses and human beings run and athletes compete. It is said to derive from *apo tēs stadios* (ἀπὸ τῆς στάδιος), that is, “from standing,” because Hercules stopped after covering the distance in a single breath. A stadium contains one-eighth of a thousand paces.

Saint Jerome: “This life is a stadium for mortals. Here we contend so that elsewhere we may be crowned.”

Saint Ambrose, in the first book of *The Duties*, chapter 16: “Why do you demand here what is owed elsewhere? Why do you hastily demand the crown before you have conquered? Why do you wish to wipe away the dust, why do you desire rest, why do you long to feast before the contest is concluded?
