The people are still watching; the athletes are still in the arena, and you already ask for leisure?

“But perhaps you say: ‘Why do the impious rejoice? Why do they live in luxury? Why do they not labor together with me?’ Because those who have not enrolled for the crown are not held to the labor of the contest. Those who have not entered the stadium do not bathe themselves in oil or smear themselves with dust. Let those whom glory awaits also await hardship: the anointed usually watch rather than compete; they do not usually endure the heat, dust, and rains.

“Let the athletes say to them as well: ‘Come, labor with us.’ But the spectators will answer: ‘Meanwhile we judge you here; you, however, will claim the glory of the crown without us—if you win.’

“Those, therefore, who have placed their efforts in indulgence, luxury, plunder, profits, and honors are spectators more than fighters. They possess the gain of labor but not the fruit of virtue. By cunning they foster leisure and by wickedness heap up piles of riches, but they will pay the penalty of their wickedness, even if the payment is delayed.”

[Col. 1046D]

**Neque enim bonus ultra jure vocabitur, qui careat bono**] This is the statement of the Platonist Socrates in the *Gorgias*: “That is good,” he says, “in whose presence we are good. We ourselves, and all other things that are good, are truly good because of a certain virtue that is present.”

Marcus Tullius agrees with the Socratic and Platonic view in Book V of the *Tusculan Disputations*, in these words: “We wish all good people always to be happy. Whom I call good is clear: we call those men good who are equipped and adorned with every virtue. Let us see who should be called happy. I consider those happy who possess good without any accompanying evil. There is no other meaning attached to this word when we call someone happy than the fullness of good gathered together after all evils have been removed.” Thus far Cicero.

But Lorenzo Valla, otherwise a very learned man and one of sharp intellect and judgment, driven by an excessive desire to quibble, attacks our Boethius too rashly and foolishly in the third book of *On the True and the False Good*. There he claims that Boethius erred in the word “good,” because it signifies both virtue and happiness, and that he wrongly inferred: “Whoever is good possesses good.”

But, if I may say so with due indulgence, Valla himself falls into a shameful error when, attacking Boethius, he writes that virtue and vice are actions, whereas happiness and unhappiness are qualities, and that these things are far removed from one another even in their effects. For, contrary to his fancy, virtue and vice are not actions but qualities; and, what is more, they belong to the same category of quality as happiness and unhappiness—namely, the category that Aristotle calls habit and disposition.

But lest anyone fall into error, it must be observed that happiness is twofold. One kind is begun happiness, which a human being attains in this life through the pursuit of the virtues by God’s grace; this we say belongs to the first species of quality. The other is perfect happiness, complete in every respect, which no one possesses before death and which is of the same substance as the supreme good and its God, as was proved above. Because of its infinity, we judge that it should be placed under no category.

Therefore Boethius rightly said that one who lacks good cannot properly be called good—that is, whoever is good possesses good, whether one understands this as virtue or as happiness. It is not perfect happiness, but begun happiness, which does not differ from virtue but is, in reality, the same thing.

The prophet also testifies to this:

> Blessed is the man to whom the Lord imputes no sin,  
> And in whose spirit there is no deceit.  
> (Psalm 31)

Saint Ambrose likewise writes in the second book of *The Duties*: “It is certain that virtue alone is the sole and supreme good, and that it alone is sufficient for the fruit of a happy life. Life is made happy not by external or bodily goods but by virtue alone, through which eternal life is acquired.”

In the same book he adds: “Where one virtue exists, the others are present as well.” I have added this lest some foolish and impious person suppose that vices, which make human beings miserable, are joined to virtue.

Socrates, in Plato:

> “Therefore it is altogether necessary, Callicles,” he says, “that the temperate man, since, as we have said, he is just, brave, and pious, be perfectly good. The good man acts well and honorably in whatever he does. The one who acts well is happy and blessed; but the wicked person who acts badly is miserable.”

[Col. 1047D]

**Quare probos mores sua praemia non relinquunt**] Saint Ambrose, in the first book of *The Duties*: “Therefore the impious person is himself his own punishment, while the just person is himself his own grace. For each receives from himself the reward of his good or bad deeds.” Silius Italicus, in Book XIII:

> Virtue itself is the most beautiful reward for itself.

**Evenit igitur**] Giovanni Francesco Pico, in his commentary on the second heroic hymn: “People are said to be transformed into brute animals when their passions, through an excessive inclination of the will and the neglect of reason’s use, lead them to this result. Thus the angry man is said to be transformed into a lion, the crafty man into a fox, and the lustful man into a boar.”

Hence among the Pythagoreans and Platonists there are accounts of human transformations into brutes, which Severinus also indicated neatly in his notes. Antonius Codrus, in his first discourse:

“Just as a rational and good soul gives form to a human being and makes him a participant in divinity, so an irrational and wicked soul gives him the form of an animal and transforms the human being who departs from what is right into a beast. The body, therefore, as I show you, does not make the human being; the soul does.

“Hence Plato, rightly, as I believe, used to say: οὐκ ἔστιν ἄνθρωπος τὸ ὁρώμενον—that is, ‘A human being is not what is seen.’ Therefore you do not see Codrus, but Codrus’s face, hands, and limbs. Thus the violent robber of other people’s wealth makes himself a wolf. The one who lays ambushes and practices fraud carries a cunning fox beneath his hollow chest. The lustful man, immersed in filthy pleasures, has transformed himself into a goat or a boar. The one who exercises his tongue by biting this person and that is a dog.

“Thus we say that a human being is changed into other beasts when, having abandoned reason, he assumes an irrational appetite.”

## IN METER III
The poem is Glyconic, similar to the sixth poem of the first book; but in this one the first foot is generally a trochee, except in the last verse, where a spondee occupies the first metrical position [Col. 1048C]. If anyone reads it as *Mentis ulcere saeviunt*, assigning a trochee to the first position throughout, that position is nevertheless common to a spondee, a trochee, and an iamb, as we have also explained above; anyone who has carefully read Catullus, Horace, Seneca the tragedian, Terence, and, among more recent writers, Marullus, will readily agree with us. Philosophy says, however, that the vices of the soul are much more pestilential than Circe’s magic spells and poisons, which are traditionally said to have harmed bodies only, not minds. The vices, on the contrary, bring the most dreadful destruction upon souls.

**“Of the Neritian leader”** — Ulysses. Neritus, as Strabo explains in Book X, is a wooded mountain on the island of Ithaca, which Ulysses ruled; he is therefore called the Neritian leader. Ovid writes:

> In place of the Neritian leader, learned poets, write of my misfortunes;

[Col. 1048D]

> For I have suffered more misfortunes than the Neritian leader.

**“On the sea”** — On the ocean, across the sea.

**“Ships”** — Vessels.

**“In which”** — On which island.

**“The goddess”** — Circe. As Homer writes, she was the daughter of the Sun by Perse, daughter of Oceanus; the sister of Aeëtes, king of Colchis; and highly skilled in magical knowledge. She lived on the island of Aeaea, in an elevated place around which bears and lions wandered. By mixing enchantments into their food and drink she had turned them from human beings into wild beasts; nevertheless, they did not rage against human beings but fawned upon them like dogs. She turned Ulysses’ companions into swine, except for Eurylochus, who suspected that there was a trap in the house and did not enter. Let Homer, *Odyssey* X; Virgil, *Aeneid* [Col. 1049A] VII; Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XIV; and Diodorus Siculus, Book V, be consulted.

**“Born from the Sun’s seed”** — Either “the daughter of the Sun,” as Homer says, and Virgil follows him:

> Where the daughter of the Sun, rich in song, continually resounds through inaccessible groves;

and Ovid:

> She had come into the woods, and the daughter of the Sun into those same woods.

Or, as Diodorus prefers, she was the granddaughter of the Sun through her father and his great-granddaughter through her mother Hecate.

**“By song”** — By enchantment. Virgil writes:

> By spells Circe changed the companions of Ulysses.

**“Whom”** — Her guests.

**“When”** — After.

**“Into various forms”** — Into different shapes of wild beasts.

**“Changed”** — Transformed.

[Col. 1049B]

**“Powerful in herbs”** — Powerful through herbs.

**“Marmaric”** — From the region of Africa where lions are especially numerous.

**“He grows in tooth and claws”** — After being transformed into a lion, he acquired larger teeth and claws.

**“Added above”** — The unlearned read this incorrectly as *nuper additus*, “recently added”; the proper reading is *superadditus*, “added above.”

**“He howls”** — This word is placed with its first syllable lengthened, whereas Virgil contracts it:

> And the great lions’ forms to howl.

**“Indian tigress”** — Thus Juvenal in Satire XV:

> The Indian tigress makes peace with the raging tigress.

Pomponius Mela, Book III, writes: “The forests also produce other dreadful animals, and, in particular, tigers—the fierce race of beasts of Hyrcania—which are so swift that they can overtake even a mounted rider who has gone far away, not merely once but repeatedly, returning each time at a run to the place from which they began. The reason is this: when the rider has seized their cubs and begun to carry them away swiftly, in order to frustrate the rage of the pursuing animals he cunningly leaves one of the cubs behind. They take up the abandoned cub and carry it back to their den, then return again and again and do the same thing, until the ravisher has escaped farther than they dare to pursue him.”

The blessed Ambrose, in Book VI of the *Hexaemeron*, reports that when a tigress finds the den empty of her stolen offspring, she immediately follows the robber’s tracks. But although he is riding a swift horse, he sees that the beast can overtake him by speed and that he has no means of escape. He therefore resorts to this stratagem: when he sees that she has come near, he throws down a glass ball. [Col. 1049D] The tigress is deceived by her own reflection and thinks that it is her cub; she checks her charge, wishing to gather up her offspring. Again, after pausing over the empty image, she throws herself with all her strength upon the rider; driven on by the spur of anger, she presses close upon the fugitive. He again delays his pursuer by throwing down a glass ball. Yet memory of the deception does not exclude the mother’s devotion. She turns over the empty image and sits down as though she were going to nurse her cub. Thus, deceived by the zeal of her maternal affection, she loses both her vengeance and her offspring.

**“Gentle”** — Inflicting violence upon no one. In accordance with Homer’s thought, Ovid writes:

> A thousand wolves, mingled with wolves, and bears and lionesses,  
> At their meeting caused fear, but none was to be feared.  
> Nor was there any wound or injury to our bodies;  
> Indeed, they moved their friendly tails through the air,

[Col. 1050A]

> And, fawning, accompanied our footsteps.

**“Although”** — Even though.

**“Divine power”** — Power.

**“The Arcadian winged creature”** — Mercury, born on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia, whom the poets represent as winged.

**“The leader”** — Ulysses.

**“Will have released”** — Will have liberated.

**“From the plague”** — From destruction, that is, from transformation into a swine.

**“Of the guest”** — Of Circe. For, according to Homer, Ulysses was saved from transformation into a wild beast both by Mercury’s advice and through his assistance. Hence Ovid, imitating Homer, writes:

> The peace-bringing Cyllenian had given him a white flower;  
> The gods call it *moly*, held by a black root.  
> Safe through it, and at the same time instructed by heavenly warnings,  
> He enters the house of Circe.

[Col. 1050B]

**“Rowers”** — Ulysses’ companions.

**“Evil”** — Harmful, magical, destructive.

**“They had drawn”** — They had drunk.

**“Cereal food”** — Bread.

**“Acorn”** — The food of swine.

**“They had changed”** — They had transformed.

**“In voice”** — In speech.

**“In body”** — The word *and* is omitted.

**“Nothing”** — Understand: “nothing except the mind.”

**“Moreover”** — In addition.

**“Monsters”** — Transformations. Virgil writes:

> Lest the pious spirits of the dead should suffer such monsters.

**“Light”** — Of little effect.

**“Hand”** — Power.

**“Although”** — Even though.

[Col. 1050C]

**“Hearts”** — Minds.

**“These poisons”** — The vices.

**“More powerfully”** — More effectively than Circe’s poisons.

**“For itself”** — For him himself. This is an incorrect construction adopted for the sake of the meter.

**“Dreadful”** — Pestilential.

**“Deep within”** — Inside the soul.

**“By the wound of the mind”** — For this certainly harms a human being most of all. The blessed Ambrose, in Book V of the *Letters*, writes: “No pain is greater than that which wounds the conscience with the sword of sin; nor is there any heavier burden than the load of sins and the weight of crimes. It weighs down the soul and bends it to the earth, so that it cannot rise. Heavy, my son—very heavy are the weights of sins.” The same author, in Book I of *On Duties*, writes: “You see the sinner’s banquet; question his conscience. Does it not stink more terribly than all tombs? You look upon his happiness and marvel at the health of his body and the abundance of his children and possessions. Look within at the ulcers and the sorrow of his living soul and heart.” Again, in Book III of *On Duties*: “What punishment is heavier than the inward wound of conscience?”

Lodovicus Bigus writes:

> Briefly the destructive pleasure  
> Of wickedness passes, but it wounds the bones, the marrow,  
> The mind and soul alike.

The same author writes:

> Ah, miserable men, we are deceived: no crime exists merely outwardly;  
> It reigns in the midst of the breast.  
> A deadly wound gapes open, yet no medicine is prepared,  
> Nor do we hasten to a physician.  
> If our limbs hurt, we travel over land and sea,  
> Yet no one cares for the failing soul.

When we too were very young, we played thus in our moral elegies on a matter hardly suited to play:

> You see the splendid banquets of a magnificent king,  
> The attending boys, the golden vessels.  
> If only it were permitted to see his mind,  
> You would behold ulcers dirtier than mud,  
> Countless plagues and many monsters,  
> More to be fled than the hound of Hell.

## In Prose IV

In this prose Severinus first admits that the vicious, although they retain the appearance of the human body, are nevertheless transformed into wild beasts in the quality of their souls. Yet he says that it seems especially astonishing and unworthy that people cast down into such degradation can rage to the destruction of the good and carry out their evil desires. Philosophy counters this with thoroughly truthful arguments and discusses two propositions far removed from popular opinion, though no less true. The first is that the wicked become much more miserable when they have satisfied their lust than when they have been unable to carry out what they wrongly desired. The second is that the wicked are less miserable when they are paying the penalties for their crimes—even if no correction or regard for example is involved—than when they escape punishment for a time with impunity and are restrained by no penalty of justice.

**“At a suitable place”** — In the sixth prose of this book.

**“Therefore much more unhappy”** — Socrates in Plato’s *Gorgias*: “According to my opinion, Polus, the person who commits injustice and is unjust is altogether more miserable than others; but he is more miserable if he never pays the penalty for his injustices, and less miserable if he does pay it and receives the punishment imposed by gods and human beings.” The blessed Augustine, in Book XII, chapter 3, of *The City of God*, writes: “Although the vicious nature is in punishment, apart from the fact that it is nature, there is also this good in it: that it is not unpunished. For this is just, and everything just is undoubtedly good.”

## In Meter IV

The poem is a two-membered, two-stanza composition: one verse consists of an hendecasyllable, the other of an elegiac pentameter. In it Philosophy condemns the savage conduct of human beings. Although they are exposed to very many dangers, they nevertheless hasten toward death by waging wars and rage against one another in mutual slaughter, even though the good ought rightly to be loved and the wicked pitied rather than pursued.

**“Fate”** — Death.

**“With the sword”** — With a weapon. Let the elegy of Tibullus be consulted, whose opening is:

> Who was the first to bring forth dreadful swords?

**“Have pity”** — Show mercy. *Miseresco* is derived from *misereo*, which among the ancients was a personal verb. Ennius, in Book V of the *Annals*, writes:

> They compelled the weeping enemies to have pity.

## In Prose V

Up to this point he has argued that all wicked people are miserable and degenerate into wild beasts in the quality of their souls, while the good become blessed and attain the condition of gods. Yet Severinus is not thereby comforted in every respect. Remembering his former dignity and still grieving over his exile and the insult he received—although it has already been proved that the goods of fortune are not genuine goods—he nevertheless says that no wise person lives who would not prefer the goods of fortune to the calamities and punishments that, as he laments, are inflicted everywhere upon those endowed with virtue by the most wicked of men: chains, prisons, squalor, and beatings, which have been established by the prescriptions of the laws against destructive criminals. Yet the wicked escape with impunity, while the innocent are punished. Astonished at the cause of this confusion, Boethius asks Philosophy to explain it.

## In Meter V

By examples she gathers that astonishment arises from ignorance of causes; once these causes have been received and thoroughly understood, astonishment is removed and knowledge takes its place. The poem is a two-membered, two-stanza composition. Nevertheless, Nicolaus Perottus, otherwise a very learned man, insufficiently considering the metrical structure, reported that this poem was dactylic, an Alcmanian tetrameter hypercatalectic, such as the verse in the first book:

> Alas, how plunged into a precipitous depth.

This poem differs from that one—so far as the first verse is concerned—in that here the first metrical position is always a trochee, whereas there it is not a trochee but a spondee or dactyl. The first verse of this poem therefore seems to be mixed from the Sapphic and Alcmanian forms, consisting of a first trochee, a second spondee or dactyl, and a spondee or trochee. The second verse is an Alcaic tetrameter, iambic, consisting of an iambic penthemimeres, a dactyl, and a spondee; it differs from Horace’s verse only in the final foot:

> You see how the lofty mountain stands white beneath the snow.

For in Horace’s verse the foot is a dactyl, whereas here it is a spondee corresponding to it in temporal quantity. What if we say that the second verse is also composed of a half-Alcaic and an Alcmanian? But no one should find this surprising if our Severinus, highly skilled in the musical art, uses new verses by right of his own authority, verses not found among other Latin poets, since it is clear that he carefully observed the proportions of temporal values and sang these verses with exceptionally sweet musical modulation.

**“On the hinge”** — For *on the hinge*; this is antiptosis, since one case is used in place of another. Thus Virgil writes:

> And mingles himself with his great body,

where *body* is used for *to the body*.

**“Let him pass over”** — Let him omit.

**“Boötes”** — Arctophylax, “the Bear-keeper.” Boötes rises on the third day before the Ides of February, as Ovid teaches in the *Fasti*. Arctophylax means “guardian of the Bear”; he is also called Boötes. Manilius writes:

> Behind shines Arctophylax, also called Boötes.

[Col. 1052D]

Cicero, in *On the Nature of the Gods*, cites a verse of Aratus in this form:

> Arctophylax, commonly said to be Boötes,

> Who shakes the Bear before him, attached as though to a wagon-pole.

He is also called Arcturus, as the grammarian Lactantius teaches. Servius, however, writes that Arcturus is properly a star in the constellation Boötes, whose rising and setting produce very severe storms. Boötes itself neither rises nor sets like the other constellations. But because it is near the wagon, which revolves around the pole, it seems to set at the point of its turning and to rise when it lifts itself. According to Hyginus, the arctic circle encloses its left hand, so that it seems neither to set nor to rise. It is positioned from the arctic circle to the summer circle, inclined lengthwise with its right foot resting upon the summer circle. A circle passing through both poles divides its shoulders and chest from the rest of its body and touches Aries and Libra. It sets with Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, and Leo. It is therefore said to set late because, standing more upright, it reaches the earth from its feet more slowly. Yet when rising it appears earlier than Libra. Hence poets call it sometimes slow and sometimes sluggish. Its setting consumes the time of four signs of the zodiac, as we have said.

**“May they grow pale”** — The words *if* or *why* are omitted.

**“May they grow pale”** — May they be darkened by an eclipse.

**“Covered”** — Darkened.

**“By the barriers”** — By obstruction.

**“Of opaque night”** — Of the earth, which causes darkness. A lunar eclipse occurs through the interposition of the earth between the sun and the moon.

**“And each”** — And what follows.

[Col. 1053B]

**“With shining face”** — With bright countenance.

**“Had covered”** — Had hidden, concealed, or darkened. For nature dictates that a greater light obscure smaller ones.

**“Confused”** — Suffering an eclipse.

**“May uncover”** — May permit it to shine.

**“And weary the air with repeated blows”** — For, as Pliny writes in Book II, chapter 12: “Great men, among whom were Stesichorus and Pindar, believed that the moon suffered an eclipse and something like death through incantations; therefore, lest the moon suffer this, they came to its aid with discordant clamor.” Hence Juvenal, in his sixth satire, writes of a noisy woman:

> Now let no one weary the trumpets and bronze instruments:  
> A single woman will be able to aid the suffering moon.

According to Plutarch, Aganice, daughter of Agetor of Thessaly, because she understood the times of full-moon eclipses and could foresee when the moon would be intercepted by the earth’s shadow, unsettled women’s minds and persuaded them that she could draw down the moon.

**“Of Corus”** — Of the winds.

**“Roaring”** — Resounding heavily.

**“To strike”** — To beat.

**“To be dissolved”** — To be loosened, liquefied.

**“Lying hidden”** — The causes are to be understood.

**“Of ignorance”** — Of lack of knowledge. It should be noted that in the scansion of the verse, through synizesis, a four-syllable word has been made three-syllabled, so that the later *i* functions as a consonant, as in Seneca the tragedian’s Sapphic verse:

> Everything fears wealth and chance.

## In Prose VI

In this prose Philosophy gives the causes of what Boethius mentioned above and said seemed extraordinarily astonishing unless its rationale were discovered. She says that all these things derive their course from the providence of the divine intelligence, or from fate, and teaches what difference there is between God’s providence and fate.

**“Your office”** — Your duty.

**“To unfold”** — To examine, investigate.

**“Veiled”** — Covered over.

**“With darkness”** — With the darkness of ignorance.

**“I ask”** — I entreat. He asks that the causes of the matters at which he is astonished be explained.

**“Exhausted”** — Of exhaustion.

**“Of the Hydra”** — In Latin it is called *excetra*. Simonides sings that it had ninety heads, Alcaeus fifty; if one was cut off, two grew back in its place. Hercules overcame it with the help of Iolaus, who, at Hercules’ command, immediately burned the severed head by applying flames to it, as Hesiod reports. Ovid’s Deianira refers to it:

> And the serpent that overflowed with fertile wounds,  
> Fertile and rich in losses drawn from its own destruction.

Seneca the tragedian writes:

> What numberless evil of the savage monster of Lerna  
> Did he not finally conquer with fire and teach to die?

Some write that the Hydra existed in the marsh of Argos at Lerna, vomiting forth waters that devastated the neighboring cities; when one channel was blocked, many others burst forth. Hercules, seeing this, burned the places themselves and thus blocked the watercourses. Socrates in Plato’s *Euthydemus* says: “I am much weaker than Hercules, who was unable to fight at once against the sophistic Hydra, from which, because of its wisdom, many heads sprang up in place of a single head of speech that had been cut off; and also against a certain sophist called the Crab, who had come from the sea and, as I suppose, had recently arrived by ship. When Hercules was being troubled on the left by him and sharply bitten by his words, he called upon the assistance of his nephew Iolaus, who came to his aid with the greatest zeal.”

**“With the fire of the mind”** — With the vigor of the intellect.

**“In this”** — In this subject.

**“On the simplicity of providence”** — He lists five questions, extremely obscure and never adequately explained, that pertain to the subject under discussion.

[Col. 1054C]

**“But since this too”** — Philosophy promises that she will explain the causes of the matter requested.

**“Shut in”** — You and I, surrounded.

**“The generation of all things”** — An equally acute and delightful discussion of divine providence and fate.

**“With stability”** — With constancy and immutability.

**“Obtains”** — Acquires.

**“This”** — The divine mind.

**“In the citadel”** — At the summit.

**“To be managed”** — To be administered and brought about.

**“Determines”** — Prescribes.

**“By purity”** — By simplicity.

**“Is perceived”** — Is considered.

**“Which”** — Providence and fate.

[Col. 1054D]

**“For providence”** — He first describes providence and then fate.

**“But fate, inhering”** — According to the Stoic Chrysippus, fate is an eternal and unalterable sequence of things, a chain that rolls itself onward and intertwines itself through eternal orders of succession, from which it is fitted and connected. Anyone wishing to know more about fate should read Marcus Tullius Cicero; the Platonist Marsilio Ficino; Landino’s commentary on the sixth book of the *Aeneid*; Gellius, Book VI; and Eusebius, Book VI of *Preparation for the Gospel*.

**“For providence”** — He shows the difference between providence and fate.

**“Although these are different, one nevertheless depends upon the other”** — He teaches how the things that he had just considered different participate in one another.

**“But certain things”** — He says that although certain things are subject to divine providence, they nevertheless surpass the fatal sequence.

**“For just as the spheres”** — By the beautiful comparison of the spheres he teaches that some things are entangled in greater bonds of fate, others in lesser ones, while some rise above fatal necessity.

**“Outermost”** — The outermost sphere.

**“To it”** — To the point.

**“Is compelled”** — Is constrained.

**“By so much”** — Understand: “the more.”

**“Therefore, just as”** — A graphic comparison. “Just as,” he says, “reasoning is related to understanding, becoming to being, time to eternity, and the circle to the central point, so the mobile sequence of fate is related to the stable and immobile simplicity of providence.”

**“That sequence”** — He shows how far the force of fate extends.

**“Unalterable”** — Unavoidable.

**“About to fluctuate”** — About to waver or drift.

**“From which it follows”** — A very beautiful conclusion, and one entirely worthy of Philosophy.

**“But what, you will say”** — He responds to the tacit objection that he introduces in Boethius’ words and shows that God judges in a manner very different from mortals, and that God’s judgments are a profound abyss, inaccessible to our senses and thoughts.

**“Surely”** — Is it not so?

**“They live”** — They dwell.

[Col. 1055C]

**“They have judged”** — They have considered.

**“As”** — Just as.

**“Temper”** — A balanced constitution.

**“Is it really unlike”** — He offers a very beautiful comparison.

**“From the one who knows”** — From God.

**“Those who are ignorant”** — Human beings.

**“I shall touch upon”** — I shall gather together and briefly summarize.

**“Of the just”** — Of justice, imitating Virgil.

**Lucan** — Marcus Annaeus Lucan was Spanish by nationality and from Corduba by birth. He wrote a work on the war between Caesar and Pompey entitled *Pharsalia*, ten books of *Saturnalia* and *Silvae*, the tragedy *Medea*, which he did not complete, *On the Burning of Troy* with the calamity of Priam, *Orpheus*, several other plays, and letters. He corrected the first three books of the *Pharsalia* with his wife Argentaria, but left the remaining books unfinished and uncorrected because of his premature death, ordered by Nero. His verses in Book I of the *Pharsalia* are:

> Nor can Caesar now bear anyone before him,  
> Nor Pompey anyone equal to himself. Who should more justly take up arms  
> It is impious to know; each defends himself with a great judge.  
> The victorious cause pleased the gods, but the defeated pleased Cato.

Marcus Tullius, in his speech *For Quintus Ligarius*, writes: “The cause was nevertheless doubtful, because there was something on either side that could be approved. Now the one must certainly be judged better, since even the gods helped it.”

[Col. 1055D]

**“Our intimate”** — True poets belong to the household of Philosophy. Hence Horace says:

[Col. 1056A]

> Wisdom is both the beginning and the source of writing well.

**“Beyond hope”** — Beyond your hope and expectation.

**“But let there be someone”** — He shows the various and different modes of divine dispensation.

**“Someone superior even to me”** — A Greek theologian, and therefore superior to Philosophy. For the unlearned, who say *excellentior me* meaning “superior through me,” are plainly ridiculous. He then appended the following Greek verse of a theologian whom I do not doubt was eminent among Christians:

> Ἀνδρὸς ἱεροῦ σῶμα δυνάμεις οἰκοδομοῦσι.

In this it should be observed that the *ε* in *ἱεροῦ* is lengthened because of the following liquid, just as in Homer and Persius the first syllable of *μέλος* is read as long, although some alter the *ε* to *η*, reading *ἱηροῦ*. A literal interpretation in Latin is: “The powers built the body of the sacred man.” The verse may be rendered:

> The powers built the body of the sacred man.

**“Mixed”** — Partly prosperous and partly adverse.

**“Lest they luxuriate in prolonged happiness”** — For, as Ovid says:

> Minds commonly grow luxuriant in favorable circumstances,  
> Nor is it easy to endure prosperity with a balanced mind.

**“He permits others to be troubled by hardships”** — Baptista Mantuanus, in Book II of the *Silvae*, writes:

> Virtue shaken by adverse circumstances  
> Grows and, tortured for a long time,  
> Takes strength from the friction; with a more polished face  
> It shines more brightly.  
>  
> Renowned honors shun leisure.  
> Labor leads the noble to triumphs.  
> Sweat shows an open road  
> To distinguished crowns.

**“By afflictions”** — By adversities.

[Col. 1056C]

**“By reproaches”** — By vices.

**“Of exercise”** — Understand: “for the sake of exercise.”

**“For just as with the good and the wicked”** — He beautifully says that the wicked not only disagree with the good but also have no harmony among themselves. They disagree with themselves because their vices tear apart their conscience.

> Ἀργαλέον δ` ἐμέ ταῦτα θεῶν ὡς πάντ` ἀγορεύειν.

This is a heroic Greek verse, if I am not mistaken, by Homer. Literally translated, it means: “It is difficult for me to explain in speech how God governs all things and arranges them by his providence.” The verse may be rendered in Latin as:

> It is difficult for me to say all these things of the gods in this way.

**“Producer”** — Originator, creator.

**“With a draught”** — A metaphor taken from travelers who, refreshed by taking a draught of wine, continue on the journey they have begun.

## In Meter VI

This poem is of the same kind as the fifth poem of the first book. Through it Philosophy proves what she said shortly before: namely, that God, the ruler of all things, banishes all evils beyond the boundaries of his commonwealth, keeps everything within its proper duty, and restrains with the best order all things that would otherwise drift along through rash movements. See above, in the final poem of the second book, the treatment of almost the same subject.

**“High”** — Most exalted.

**“Laws”** — Power.

**“Of the thunderer”** — Of God.

[Col. 1057A]

**“Pure”** — Cleansed of disturbances and vices.

**“Skilled”** — Ingenious, perceptive, using sharp contemplation.

**“To perceive”** — To see.

**“Summits”** — Lofty regions.

**“There”** — In heaven.

**“The ancient peace”** — The ancient harmony.

**“Of Phoebe”** — Of the moon.

**“Axis”** — Chariot, vehicle.

**“At the highest point”** — At the northern pole, of which the poet writes:

> This pole is always lofty for us, but the black Styx  
> And the spirits below see that one beneath their feet.

**“Swift courses”** — Rapid movements.

**“The Bear”** — In Greek, Ἄρκτος. Hyginus writes that the figure of the Bear is formed by stars and does not set. He says: “They deny that the wife of Oceanus allows it to enter the sea, although the other stars reach their setting, because Tethys is Juno’s nurse, and Callisto had lain with her as a rival.” Ovid teaches the same in Book II of the *Metamorphoses*. The true reason it does not set is that, since the arctic pole is above us, it is always visible to us. Thus Virgil writes:

> The Bears, fearing to dip their fires in the sea of Oceanus.

**“To dip its fires in Oceanus”** — To set.

**“Star-bearing”** — Heavenly.

**“In alternation”** — By turns.

**“May sink”** — May incline downward and be depressed.

**“For the same reasons”** — From the same harmony of the universe.

**“Breathes”** — Sends forth by breathing.

**“Flower-bearing”** — Bearing flowers.

**“The year”** — Here the year is equally divided into four parts, according to the poetic line:

> And a year equal in its different seasons.

These are spring, summer, autumn, and winter. As Macrobius says in Book VII: “Spring, the maker of all things, made warm and moist; summer is dry and hot; autumn dry and cold; winter equally moist and cold.”

[Col. 1057C]

**“In fruits”** — Ovid, in Book I of *The Remedy of Love*, writes:

> Autumn gives fruits; summer is beautiful with harvests.  
> Spring supplies flowers; winter is lightened by fire.

**“Heavy”** — Full, abundant.

**“Flowing downward”** — Flowing toward the lower regions.

**“This balance”** — Moderation and harmony.

**“Breathes life”** — Lives.

**“The same”** — The same balance.

[Col. 1057D]

**“Hides”** — Conceals.

**“By death”** — By setting, by death.

**“Sinking”** — Overwhelming.

**“Creator”** — Maker.

**“Of the just”** — Of justice.

**“Drives on”** — Commands, compels.

**“To go”** — To move.

**“Brings to a halt”** — Commands to stand.

**“Drawing back”** — Calling back to itself.

**“Wandering”** — Mobile.

**“Makes firm”** — Stabilizes.

**“Movements”** — Motions.

**“Again”** — Once more.

**“Into curved circles”** — Into circular movements, which are far more perfect than straight ones.

[Col. 1058A]

**“Separated”** — Divided.

**“From its own source”** — From God, its source.

**“Will dissolve”** — Will be dissolved.

**“In no other way”** — In no different manner.

**“May flow back”** — May return.

**“Causes”** — Toward the first cause.

**“Being”** — Essence. Thus he also sang above, in Book III:

> Each thing seeks its own proper return,  
> And each rejoices in its own return;  
> No order handed down remains for anything,  
> Except what joins the beginning to the end  
> And makes its own circle stable.

Marsilio Ficino, in his *Commentary*, second discourse, chapter 1, writes: “The Pythagorean philosophers wished the Trinity to be the measure of all things. I think the reason is that God governs things by the number three, and things themselves are also completed by the number three. Hence Virgil’s line:

> God delights in an odd number.

For that highest creator first creates each thing individually, second receives it, and third perfects it. Each thing first flows forth from that everlasting source when it is born; then flows back into the same source when it seeks its origin again; finally, it is perfected after it has returned to its beginning.”

## In Prose VII

From what he discussed above with great learning, both concerning divine providence and concerning the fatal sequence, he draws a beautiful and no less true inference: although popular opinion sees things differently, all fortune is good, since it is either just or useful. Therefore a wise man ought not to take it hard if he is brought into conflict with fortune, so that his tested virtue may shine more and more brightly.

**“Which”** — How.

**“Supported”** — Established, sustained, upheld.

**“Unanticipated”** — Incredible, removed from popular opinion.

**“Shortly before”** — In the fourth and sixth prose sections of this book.

**“Which”** — Why, in what way.

**“As”** — How, just as.

**“Do you not therefore consider it good?”** — This is a syllogism in the first mode of the third figure: whatever benefits is good; fortune, whether exercising or correcting, benefits. Therefore it is good.

**“This”** — Fortune, which either exercises or corrects.

[Col. 1058D]

**“Unanticipated”** — Incredible and contrary to the opinion of the wise.

**“Therefore, he says”** — From what has already been said he infers that the wise man should not grieve at all when compelled to struggle against harsh fortune; for virtue is thereby both tested and made more conspicuous. Hence Ovidius writes:

> Virtue, which lies hidden and remains unknown in favorable circumstances,  
> Appears and is proved by misfortunes.

Silius Italicus, in Book IV, writes of the Romans:

> It is a joy to pass through dangers  
> To honor and to establish with the right hand a memorable name,  
> Such as fortune has never granted in favorable circumstances.

Again, in the same work:

> Adversity tests men, and through harshness  
> Fearless virtue strives up a hard slope toward praise.

[Col. 1059A]

**“Proper to glory”** — Faustus Andrelinus writes:

> Brave hearts overcoming difficult misfortunes  
> Possess names renowned for everlasting praise.

**“Virtue is called”** — He shows the origin of the name *virtue*: it is called so because, relying upon its own strength, it is not overcome by adversity. Marcus Cicero, in Book II of the *Tusculan Disputations*, writes: “For *virtue* is derived from *man* (*vir*). Manliness is especially fortitude, whose two greatest functions are contempt for death and pain. We must therefore use these qualities if we wish to possess virtue—or rather, if we wish to be men—since virtue has borrowed its name from men.” Lactantius, in *On the Workmanship of God*, writes: “He is called *man* because there is greater strength in him than in a woman. From this virtue also received its name.”

## In Meter VII

By the examples of three very brave men she shows that the road to virtue and glory lies only through difficulties and steep places. The struggle must therefore not be avoided, nor labor refused, since through it the material of virtue and wisdom is supplied to us, in accordance with the poetic verses:

> Whoever, for the love of virtue,  
> Has overcome harsh misfortunes  
> Will win for himself praise and honor.  
> But whoever follows idle sloth and luxury,  
> While, through an unwary mind, he flees the labors before him,  
> Passes a shameful and miserable life, poor in every respect.

**“Twice five”** — Ten.

**“The avenger”** — The avenger, the ravisher of Helen.

**“The son of Atreus”** — Agamemnon, son of Atreus. Horace writes in the *Epistles*:

> Nestor hastens to settle the disputes  
> Between the son of Peleus and the son of Atreus.

**“Phrygian”** — Trojan.

**“By ruins”** — By destruction.

[Col. 1059C]

**“Of his brother Menelaus”** — Of Menelaus, his brother.

**“The lost marriage-bed”** — Helen, the stolen wife, by far the most beautiful of women.

**“He atoned for”** — He purged. Virgil writes:

> And they shall atone for the guilt by the death of the wretched.

The meaning is that Agamemnon, by the avenging war and destruction of Troy, purged the abduction of Helen perpetrated by the lustful Paris. Crimes are purged and removed by vengeance.

**“He”** — Agamemnon. As he was setting out for the Trojan War and waiting at Aulis for the other leaders of Greece, he inadvertently killed a hind belonging to Diana. The goddess became angry and raised such a storm at sea that the Greek fleet could not depart. When they also began to suffer from plague, Calchas was consulted; he replied that Diana’s anger had to be appeased by Agamemnon’s blood. Finally, therefore, Iphigenia was brought forward with Agamemnon’s consent and sacrificed. Virgil, in Book II of the *Aeneid*, writes:

> You appeased the winds with blood and with the slaughter of a maiden,  
> When first you Greeks came to the shores of Ilium.

Others report that Diana secretly removed Iphigenia from the priest and substituted a hind in her place.

**“For the Greek fleet”** — For the ships of the Greeks.

**“He redeemed”** — He purchased.

**“The winds”** — Understand: favorable winds.

**“With blood”** — With the blood of his daughter.

**“He stripped off”** — He laid aside.

**“His father”** — His paternal affection. Thus Ovid writes:

> After public necessity  
> And the king conquered the father, and Iphigenia, about to give  
> Her chaste blood, stood before the altar amid weeping attendants.

**“He made a covenant”** — Having made a covenant, he fell upon and sacrificed her.

**“Of the daughter”** — Of Iphigenia.

**“The Ithacan”** — Ulysses.

**“Companions”** — Associates. Propertius writes:

> Gradually Ulysses mourned the loss of his companion.

**“Savage”** — Brutal, excessively remote from humanity.

**“He submerged”** — He swallowed up, concealed.

**“Polyphemus”** — He was the son of Neptune by Thoosa, daughter of Phorcys. When Ulysses arrived in Sicily with twelve companions, carrying three jars of excellent wine, he was astonished at the size and appearance of a man who had a single eye in his forehead and who alone was lifting a stone that twenty yoke of oxen could scarcely have moved. Ulysses asked him what kind of people they were and what their customs were, and earnestly begged, by Jupiter, to be allowed to depart safely. But Polyphemus replied arrogantly that he did not fear Jupiter. Seizing two of Ulysses’ companions, he devoured them with savage brutality; at dawn the next day he consumed two more, and did the same again in the evening.

Therefore, fearing for himself and the rest, Ulysses offered Polyphemus the jar of excellent wine he had brought and begged him to spare him and the others. The Cyclops promised to do so if Ulysses would offer him wine again. After the third cup was offered, Polyphemus, his mind overcome, stretched out his enormous body in the middle of the cave to sleep. Ulysses, seeing him buried in wine and sleep, thrust a weapon into his eye and blinded him. But when the Cyclops, eventually roused, was forced to open the entrance of the cave for his flocks, he removed the enormous stone; nevertheless, he felt the animals as they came out, touching them with his hands. When Ulysses and his companions noticed this, they escaped the Cyclops by putting on the animals’ skins. Read Homer, *Odyssey* IX.

**“Hercules”** — Hercules was the son of Jupiter and Alcmena. In strength and courage he surpassed all other human beings beyond what can be believed. His various exploits are related by Diodorus Siculus, Ovid, Seneca the tragedian, Nicolaus Perottus in the *Cornucopia*, and others.

**“Hard labors”** — The labors of Hercules are proverbial; Erasmus discusses them at length in the third chiliad of the *Adages*, proverb 1.

**“Centaurs”** — These were Thessalians who were human in their front parts and horses in their rear parts. Hercules wished to drive them from Mount Pelion, but he himself did not wish to initiate an unjust war. When he was received as a guest by Pholus, he therefore arranged for a jar of excellent wine to be brought out. Attracted by its smell, the Centaurs attempted to seize the wine. Hercules, finding his opportunity, either killed them all or drove them away.

**“Spoil”** — The hide that he used as a shield.

**“For the lion”** — This was a huge and monstrous lion that could not be subdued by weapons. Hercules watched the entrance of its cave, seized it as it emerged, and strangled it.

**“He fixed”** — He pierced.

**“Certain”** — Unavoidable.

**“The birds”** — The Stymphalian birds. Claudian writes:

[Col. 1061A]

> Alone, girded with the Amazonian bow, the Stymphalian birds.

Appetis. Hercules shot at the Stymphalian birds among the very clouds, and, having killed them, brought them down. They were waterfowl in the Stymphalian marsh of Arcadia, of such enormous size that they were said to obscure the rays of the sun.

Poma] Hercules carried off the golden apples from the gardens of the Hesperides after killing the dragon that guarded them, keeping watch over them day and night.

Cernenti] To the one who is keeping watch.

Laeva] With the left hand.

Cerberum] When Hercules heard that Pirithous had been destroyed by Cerberus, the infernal dog, and that Theseus was being held among the dead, he hastened there. After capturing Cerberus and binding him with a triple chain—for he had three heads—he liberated Theseus. [Col. 1061B]

Victor immitem] He killed Diomedes, king of Thrace, who fed his horses on the flesh of strangers, and threw him to be devoured by his horses.

Hydra] We have spoken of this above; and Claudian writes:

> It did not help Antaeus to fall, nor the Hydra to grow.

Fronte] When Hercules and Achelous were fighting over Deianira, and Achelous was changing himself into various forms, he finally transformed himself unsuccessfully into a bull. Defeated and deprived of one horn, Achelous, overcome by shame, threw himself into his own river. Statius writes in the fourth book of the *Thebaid*:

> And the river, its face disfigured by Hercules’ wrestling,  
> Still scarcely dared to raise its truncated brow  
> From the depths of the waters, and, its head submerged in a green cavern,  
> Mourns; the banks grow sick with the dust they breathe.

Antaeum] He was a son of Neptune, begotten from the earth, and grew to a height of sixty cubits, according to Pherecydes. This long seemed fabulous, until his enormous bones, brought to Olympia, made it credible by their extraordinary size. Plutarch says that the Roman commander Sertorius, having opened a tomb near the town of Tingena in Libya which the inhabitants repeatedly declared to be the tomb of Antaeus, found a human corpse of unusual size. Antaeus, as the stories relate, when thrown down, received strength from the earth, his mother, and indeed received greater strength each time. Once Hercules had learned this, he kept Antaeus away from the earth and subdued him while holding him aloft. Lucan elegantly describes this contest in the fourth book of the *Pharsalia*.

Cacus] According to the myth, he was a son of Vulcan, vomiting fire and smoke from his mouth and ravaging everything nearby. According to the philologists and historians, however, the truth is that he was Evander’s most wicked slave and a thief. Some say that, after seizing a kingdom in the region around the Vulturnus and Campania, he was overcome by Hercules, who happened to be present at the time, while Cacus was also attempting to appropriate the territories that had been granted under the jurisdiction of Evander, king of the Arcadians. Virgil treats of him in Book Eight.

Setiger] The boar. Hercules captured the Erymanthian boar alive by a stratagem, as Polyaenus relates. He says:

> The Erymanthian boar was roaming in a certain valley covered with snow. When Hercules noticed this from the brow of the valley, where the snow lay deepest, he attacked the beast by throwing stones. Thus provoked, while it tried to rush upon Hercules, it fell into the deep snow and was easily captured by him. He carried it on his back to Mycenae and released it in the middle of the assembly, to the great alarm of everyone—and especially of Eurystheus, who is said to have thrown himself into a bronze vessel, as Apollonius sings. [Col. 1062B]

Ultimus coelum] Hercules is said to have supported the heavens on his shoulders in place of Atlas. Claudian writes:

> The greatest Atlas shuddered at you  
> When, with the pole imposed upon you, you were weighed down.

Hercules went to Atlas after learning from Nereus that he could not obtain the apples of the Hesperides without Atlas’s help. But while Atlas was assisting Hercules, Hercules himself took up the heavens. When Atlas did not seem likely to return, Hercules deceived him by a stratagem. He persuaded Atlas to resume the heavens for a little while, so that Hercules might prepare a cushion for himself against the burden. Then, having seized the apples that lay on the ground, he immediately departed victorious.

Pretium] Reward.

# BOOK FIVE

## IN PROSE I

[Col. 1061]

In the preceding volume Philosophy argued that only the good are powerful, whereas all the wicked are weak, and that evil is nothing, since the providence of the greatest and best king, together with the chain of fated necessity, directs everything toward the good, as toward its end. Hence it follows that—as seemed incorrectly to Boethius—evil never befalls the good, since adversity is especially material for the exercise of virtue, in accordance with Ovid’s words:

> Virtue exercised amid adversity  
> Has, in grievous times, material for praise.

But since it was stated above that fate proceeds from the beginnings of immovable providence, and that the very connections of fate must therefore also be immovable, the question arises how human freedom of choice can stand together with the inevitable necessity of divine providence and fate. It also seems futile to believe that chance is anything, since nothing can happen that has not merited God’s providential regard. Accordingly, this entire book discusses chance and human free will. First, however, chance is explained as follows: chance is an unforeseen outcome arising from converging causes in matters undertaken for another purpose.

Sed quod tu dudum de Providentia dixisti, re experior] This is how it is read in the ancient manuscripts. The meaning is: “But I experience in fact”—that is, I learn through experience to be true—what you said earlier about Providence, namely, that it is such a subject that, once one difficulty has been cut off, countless others grow up, like the heads of the Hydra. In other copies, with certain additions, the passage reads: “But what you said earlier about Providence—that it is a question entangled with many others—I learn by experience.”

Haec] Whether chance exists, and what it is.

Tramite] By a method, a concise path.

Decerno] I determine; I establish.

[Col. 1063A] Nihil ex nihilo existere] This is to be understood naturally and through particular causes. For God, the universal cause of all things, created the world from nothing.

De operante principio] Concerning the efficient cause.

Rationum] Of forms.

In Physicis] In Book Two of the *Physics*.

## IN METER I

In this elegiac poem, Philosophy teaches, by means of a beautiful comparison, that chance does not arise from nothing, even though it does not proceed from the intention of the agent. For just as, when the courses of two rivers join, boats and logs, which had previously been received by the waters in different channels, are necessarily brought together by the rivers flowing at last into a single channel, although this occurs contrary to their expectation and intention, so chance, although it does not arise from the mind of the agent, nevertheless has its own particular causes. [Col. 1063B]

Rupis Achemeniae] Of the Armenian or Parthian mountain. Porphyry wished Achaemenes to have been a king of the Parthians, and Herodotus wrote that the kings of Persia descended from the lineage of the Achaemenids. Hence *Achaemenian* may mean Persian, Parthian, or Armenian. Lucan writes:

> He allowed the Achaemenian to run far across the plains.

Scopulis] On projecting rocks.

Ubi] The order is: “Where the fleeing battle fixes its arrows in the breasts of those pursuing.” The meaning is: From the mountain of Greater Armenia, to which Parthia is joined—the Parthians, according to Trogus, do not know how to fight at close quarters in battle or to storm besieged cities. They therefore fight either by riding forward or by turning their backs; they often pretend to flee so that they may expose to their arrows those pursuing them incautiously. Most often, in the very heat of battle, they abandon the fighting and shortly afterward renew the battle from their flight. Hence the poet writes:

> Trusting in flight, and with arrows turned backward?

“From one and the same source the Tigris and Euphrates arise.”

Pugna fugax] The Parthian people fighting by flight.

Tigris] It received this name from its swiftness and course. For *Tigris* means “arrow” in the language of the Medes, as Solinus and others report, and Dionysius calls it the swiftest of all rivers. Others, however, wish it to have been named after the animal, the tiger. Saint Jerome writes: “The Tigris is a river issuing from Paradise, according to the testimony of Scripture, and flowing toward the Assyrians; after many windings, as Josephus holds, it empties into the Red Sea.” It is called by this name because of its speed, like a beast running with extraordinary rapidity. According to Francisco Pico, this name forms the genitives *Tigrios*, *Tigritos*, and *Tigridos*, and in Attic Greek Τίγρεως.

Euphrates] It took its name from the fact that it brought good things. Jerome writes of it: “The Euphrates is the river of Mesopotamia, rising in Paradise.” Sallust, a most reliable authority, asserts that the sources of both the Tigris and the Euphrates are shown in Armenia. From this we understand that Paradise and its rivers must be interpreted differently. Diodorus Siculus writes in Book Three:

> After the Nile and the Ganges, the most famous rivers of all Asia, the Euphrates and the Tigris have their sources in the mountains of Armenia. They are separated from one another by fifteen hundred stades; carried through Media and the country of the Paraetaceni, they descend into Mesopotamia, which they surround on every side and from which the region received its name. Then, flowing through Babylonia, they are carried into the Red Sea. [Col. 1064A]

Strabo writes in Book Two of the *Geography*:

> Amanus grows greatly both in breadth and height and is divided into many branches. Its southern part is Taurus, which separates Armenia from Mesopotamia. From here flow the Tigris and Euphrates, which surround Mesopotamia and join one another among the Babylonians. They then discharge into the Persian Gulf. The Euphrates is the greater of the two and traverses more territory in a winding channel. Its sources are in the northern part of Taurus. It flows westward through Armenia, which is called Greater Armenia, as far as Lesser Armenia, which it leaves on its right, while it has Lisana on its left. Then, turning south, it joins the borders of Cappadocia, which it leaves on the right, and the borders of Commagene on the left. Again, leaving Sicinsina and also Sophene of Greater Armenia on the left, it advances into Syria; then, taking another bend, it reaches the Babylonians and the Persian Gulf. The Tigris, carried from the same mountain to Seleucia, approaches the Euphrates and there forms Mesopotamia; then it enters the same gulf. The sources of the Euphrates and the Tigris are separated by two thousand and fifty stades.

Thus far Strabo. [Col. 1064B]

Uno fonte] From the sources of one and the same Armenian mountain, which, according to Strabo, is called Taurus.

Abjunctis] Separated.

Quos tamen] The order is: “Whom wandering chance the slopes”—that is, the declivities of the earth—“cover,” and “whom the descending course of the flowing current governs.”

## IN PROSE II

[Col. 1064C]

At this point Boethius raises the question whether there is any human freedom of choice, or whether the movements of souls themselves are also constrained by fated necessity. Philosophy replies that every rational nature possesses freedom of choice, but that it is greater in the higher and divine substances; next come human souls, which, although they do not possess an equal freedom, come nearest to them when they preserve themselves in contemplation of divinity. They are less free when they descend into bodies, and still less free when they are bound to earthly limbs. It must be observed, however, that all this is stated according to Plato’s opinion, as though souls existed before they were joined to bodies. She says that the most extreme slavery belongs to those souls which, enslaved to crimes, have lost their proper freedom.

Inscitiae] Of ignorance.

[Col. 1064D] Caligant] They are darkened; they grow dim.

Πάντ᾽ ἐφορᾷ καὶ πάντ᾽ ἐπακούει] “He sees everything and hears everything.” This is the second part of a Homeric verse from Book Three of the *Iliad*:

> He sees everything, and hears everything.

## IN METER II

This poem is of the same kind as the penultimate poem of the fourth volume. In it Philosophy prefers the perspicacity of divine providence to the brightness of the sun. Homer writes of this:

> The sun, who sees all things and hears all things most greatly.

For although the sun shines forth with extraordinary brilliance, it cannot penetrate the innermost parts of the earth. The immeasurable light of providence, however, not only looks upon all things but also perceives their most hidden depths. Neither the darkness of night nor the mass of the earth can obstruct it. [Col. 1065A]

Phoebum] The sun.

Melliflui] Flowing with honey.

Canit] He praises in song, both elsewhere and in Book Three of the *Iliad*, as was also said shortly before: “And you, sun, who see and hear everything.” See Pliny, Book Two of the *Natural History*, chapter 6.

Perrumpere] To penetrate.

Cuncta tuenti] Looking upon all things. The ancient Sibyl, in the work of Justin the philosopher and martyr, translated by Francisco Pico, says:

> For there is one God, alone unbegotten, immense,  
> Seeing everything, invisible, the ruler,  
> Whom mortal flesh can never comprehend.

## IN PROSE III

[Col. 1065B]

In this prose Boethius, hesitating, discusses human free will and God’s foreknowledge. He cannot see how the two can stand together without one obstructing the other. Once the necessity of divine foreknowledge is admitted, everything seems to be bound and held by an unbending chain. If this were so, human beings would hope or pray in vain for things that, being entangled in the laws of future necessity, could not be changed or turned in another direction.

Aut quid hoc refert vaticinio illo ridiculo Tiresiae] The meaning is: “Or what difference does this make”—as though he said, “This is no different from that ridiculous prophecy of Tiresias,” which appears in Horace, Book Two of the *Satires*:

> O son of Laertes, whatever I say will either happen or not happen;  
> For great Apollo grants me the power to prophesy.

[Col. 1065C]

Tiresias of Thebes, when he happened to strike two snakes that were mating, was changed into a woman and is said to have remained in that sex for seven years. When he struck the same snakes again, he returned to his former sex. So that no one may think this entirely fabulous, let him also read Pliny in Book Seven of the *Natural History*, and Saint Augustine’s work *On the Marriages of the Old and New Law*, both of whom assert that this happened to certain people. Moreover, when Jupiter and Juno were disputing whether the pleasure of intercourse was greater for the male or the female, Tiresias was chosen as judge and affirmed that the female pleasure was greater. Juno, angered by this judgment, blinded him. Jupiter, however, in compensation for the loss of his eyes,

> Granted him knowledge of the future and lightened his punishment with honor. [Col. 1065D]

Callimachus and Propertius say that Tiresias was blinded because he had seen Pallas bathing naked in the waters. Hence the proverb Τυφλότερος Τιρεσίου, “Blinder than Tiresias,” applied to someone who is extraordinarily blind.

Uti paulo ante cantabas] In the sixth poem of Book Four.

## IN METER IV

This poem is of the same kind as the preceding one. In it Severinus, filled with wonder, is astonished and seeks the reason why two propositions—one concerning divine foreknowledge, the other concerning our freedom of choice—are accepted as true when considered separately and in isolation, but seem entirely incompatible when joined together.

Carptim] Separately.

[Col. 1066A] Jugari] To be joined; united.

Sed mens] He attributes our inability to perceive the truth of things to the ignorance of our mind.

Obruta] Buried; overwhelmed.

Caecis membris] With the body, which brings darkness and forgetfulness upon the mind.

Luminis] Of the intellect.

Igne] With vigor.

Tenues nexus] Subtle connections.

Sed cur] This is Platonic. In Plato’s dialogue on virtue, entitled *Meno*, Socrates leads Meno, the pupil of Aristippus and Gorgias, to the conclusion that it is impossible for us to learn anything by inquiry; or, if we attain and learn something through inquiry, we must have known it previously. To learn it, therefore, is nothing other than to remember and recall it to memory. “By what path,” Meno asks, “will you investigate, Socrates, something of whose nature you are entirely ignorant? How will you propose what you do not know and inquire into it? Or even if you should come upon it, by what sign will you recognize that it is what you did not know?” Socrates replies: “I understand what you mean, Meno. But do you notice how contentious an argument you have brought forward? You claim that a person investigates neither what he knows nor what he does not know. If he knows it, he has no need of inquiry; but neither does he investigate what he does not know, for he does not know what he is seeking.” Accordingly, he finally concludes that by inquiry we can learn nothing except what we knew previously, and in the same way.

Mentem altam] The divine mind.

[Col. 1066C] Cerneret] He would contemplate.

Summam] A universal proposition.

Singula] Particulars.

Neutro est habitu] Although Boethius is more Platonic than Aristotelian, he nevertheless presents himself as a middle position between the two philosophers and once promised to demonstrate their agreement. Whether he fulfilled that promise, God knows. Aristotle’s view is that there is no contradiction in knowing what one is learning in one respect and not knowing it in another. There is nothing absurd, for example, in knowing in a universal way what one is learning particularly and properly. But if one knows it in precisely the same way and to the same extent as one learns it, that is incongruous. Thus one knows universally what one does not know particularly, and one learns particularly what one knows universally.

[Col. 1066D] Consulit] He calls into consultation; he consults.

Alte] In the divine mind.

Visa] Perceived; seen clearly.

Retractans] Recalling.

Oblitas] Given over to oblivion. He uses the passive form. Thus Virgil writes:

> Now forgotten by me are so many songs.

Addere partes] An Adonic verse, added at the end of the other verses of the poem.

## IN PROSE IV

Philosophy dissolves the objections that the hesitant Severinus has raised, and unties the knots of the objections one by one, showing that God’s foreknowledge and human freedom of choice can stand together. Saint Jerome writes in the thirty-second chapter of *Against Jovinianus*:

> God created us with free choice, and we are not drawn toward virtues or vices by necessity. Otherwise, where there is necessity, there is neither condemnation nor crown. Just as God is perfect in good works—for “it is not of him that wills, nor of him that runs, but of God who shows mercy and assists” [Romans 9]—so that we may be able to reach the finish, so in evil deeds and sins our seeds are incentives, and the devil brings them to completion. When he sees us building hay, wood, and straw upon the foundation of Christ [1 Corinthians 3], he sets fire beneath them. [Col. 1067A]

Quod ita demum] Boethius suspected that providence deprived us of free choice and reaches this conclusion by the following reasoning: Whatever is going to happen is either necessarily future or contingently future. If it is necessary, freedom of choice perishes. If it is contingent, how can there be foreknowledge, since there is no knowledge of contingents, but rather conjecture? Philosophy therefore first begins by showing that foreknowledge does not impose necessity upon future things; then she proves that God’s foreknowledge of contingent and uncertain things can nevertheless be certain. [Col. 1067B]

Quaero enim] At this point Philosophy in some way defends the reasoning that Boethius above rejected entirely: things do not happen because God foresaw them; rather, God foresaw them because they are going to happen. This reasoning is sound insofar as it frees free choice from necessity, but false insofar as it makes future events the cause of foreknowledge.

Quae quia praescientiam] The meaning is: “I ask you, Severinus, why you think the reasoning offered by those resolving the problem is less effective. Is it because you do not think that foreknowledge is the cause of necessity in future things? But consider this: if you believe that future events are necessary, from where do you derive the cause of that necessity except from foreknowledge? If, therefore, I show you that this divine foreknowledge does not impose necessity upon future things—which you yourself admitted shortly before—there will be no reason for you to think that free choice is impeded.” [Col. 1067C]

Quantum ad hoc attinet] That is, with respect to this conclusion, which says that foreknowledge is the cause of the necessity of future events.

Sed praescientia, inquies] She responds to an unspoken question. Severinus might have objected as follows: “Granted that future events do not derive their necessity from foreknowledge, foreknowledge is nevertheless a sign that they will necessarily occur.” Philosophy replies in this way: Even if there were no foreknowledge, the necessary outcome of the future would be evident in the same manner. The reason is that a sign does not bring about the thing of which it is a sign; it merely shows what the thing is. For example, ivy hung before an inn indicates that wine is for sale; it does not cause the wine to be offered for sale.

Quasi vero] The meaning is: “We are not concerned with whether the things foreknown will occur, but with whether, by their own nature, they are subject to some necessity of occurring.”

Sed hoc, inquies] Philosophy resolves the difficulty that Severinus had proposed above in these words: “If something is going to happen in such a way that its outcome is not certain and necessary, how can it be foreknown as going to happen?”

Cujus erroris causa] Philosophy now undertakes to remove another of Boethius’ difficulties: whether there can be foreknowledge of uncertain things, since knowledge comprehends nothing except what is certain. Accordingly, if uncertain things are foreseen as certain, he thinks that this is not foreknowledge but the darkness of opinion. In dissolving these objections, Philosophy says that the cause of the error is our belief that everything known is comprehended by its own nature, rather than through the power or capacity of the knower; this is false. For if cognition followed the nature of the thing known, rather than the capacity of the knower, all things would be known by everyone in one and the same way, and there would be no distinction at all between divine and human intelligence. Who does not see how false that is?

Ille] The sight; the visual faculty.

[Col. 1068B] Eminus] From a distance.

Jactis] Sent forth. Here he follows Plato’s opinion, to which Aristotle objects. A most shameless crowd of theologians has dared to receive Aristotle into heaven against the judgment of the ancient and equally learned theologians. But this will be treated more suitably elsewhere. The Stoics say that the causes of seeing are the emission of rays from the eyes toward things capable of being seen, together with the simultaneous focusing of the air. Democritus and Epicurus think that vision occurs through images inserted into the visual faculty, with certain rays emitted from the eyes returning to and being inserted into them again as soon as they strike the object placed before them. Aristotle, a man of exceptionally keen intellect but inferior to Plato, holds that vision occurs when the forms of the visible object are received within the eyes. Empedocles mingled rays with images and called this combination “the rays of the image.” Hipparchus maintains that perception is conveyed to the visual faculty by means extending from each eye toward the outlines of bodies, as though the upper surfaces of bodies were being felt by the approach of the hands. Plato thinks that sight occurs through co-radiation: light emitted from the eyes flows for some distance through the air related to it, while light brought forth from bodies encounters it, disperses the intervening air, and, making it receptive, strengthens it together with the visual fire. This is called Platonic co-radiation. [Col. 1068C]

Hic] Touch.

Orbi] To a round body.

Intelligentia] An incorporeal intellect, separate from matter. By examples he shows that in knowing, everything makes use rather of its own faculty than of the things that are known. [Col. 1068D]

## IN METER V

In this Glyconic poem Philosophy sharply attacks the Stoics, the sowers of the error just mentioned—namely, the belief that things are comprehended by their own nature rather than through the faculty of those who know them—and refutes their opinion. They maintained that cognition is completed solely by likenesses of external bodies impressed upon the mind. If that were true, the mind would suffer passively from external things. Yet all who philosophize correctly admit that the intellect is active and that, when the mind understands, it acts rather than suffers.

[Col. 1069A] Porticus] He means the Stoics, whom we discussed in the first commentary.

Obscuros] From whose obscure and tangled words the meaning can scarcely be gathered.

Qui] The Stoics.

Sensus] Sensations.

E corporibus extimis] From external things. He has lengthened the word freely, although it ought to be shortened. He seems, however, to have imitated the ancients, who said *corpus* and *corpor*, like *decus* and *decor*, *algus* and *algor*, *frigus* and *frigor*.

Ut] Just as.

Quondam] At some time; formerly.

Aequore] On a flat surface, plane, or level expanse.

Notis] The first syllable is contracted; that is, by the signs which bodies impress from outside.

[Col. 1069B] In vicem] In likeness; correspondingly.

Notio] Cognition.

Quae vis] Power; capacity. It must be understood that there are three kinds of intellection. The first is called the apprehension of simple things. This is what he means by “She surveys individual things”: that is, she understands each thing individually and separately, and in its simplicity. The second is composition or division, which gives rise to “Or does she divide what she has known? Does she gather together what she has divided?” The third is reasoning, by which we attain, from things known, things that had been unknown. Hence he says, “Then, turning back upon herself, she refutes falsehoods by truths.”

Legens] Passing over; running through.

Alternum iter] Sometimes ascending from the lowest things to the highest, sometimes descending from the highest to the lowest.

Desidit] “She descends,” that is, the middle external stages.

[Col. 1069C] Tum] Then; thereafter.

Referens] Bringing back, and, as it were, gathering the reasoning into a circle.

Praecedit] Here, as he often does, he expresses Plato, who thought that the forms of things were implanted in the soul from the beginning. But because of its contact with the earthly body, the soul becomes drowsy and weighed down, and does not act unless it is awakened by the impression of external sensations. Once awakened by the form impressed by the external sense, it is summoned forth; and only when the internal form is joined with the form received from outside does it finally understand.

## IN PROSE V

From what was discussed above—namely, that cognition follows not the nature of the thing known but the power and capacity of the knower—it is shown that God can foreknow future events of uncertain outcome as certain, although the human mind can in no way comprehend this. For if cognition follows the nature of the knower, we must hold that different substances have different capacities for knowing, one of which excels another. Thus the more perfect capacity contains within itself the lower capacities, while the less perfect cannot rise to the level of the more excellent. Neither sense nor imagination rises to the judgment of reason, and reason cannot comprehend the mode of divine intelligence, which is far more complete and embraces future events, uncertain to us, in the most certain foreknowledge.

## IN METER VI

This poem is an Archilochian dactylic composition consisting of a four-foot dactylic bucolic line—that is, three dactyls or spondees, or alternating forms—and a fourth foot that ends a portion of the sentence with a dactyl, followed by three trochees. Philosophy recalls the dignity and excellence of human nature and reminds human beings, from the posture and stature bestowed by fortune, to love and contemplate heavenly things. Of all living creatures, human beings alone look down upon the earth and, lifting their faces, look up toward heaven. [Col. 1070A]

Alia extento] Such as snakes and creeping animals.

Enatet] It flies out; this is a very familiar metaphor.

Transmittere] To cross over. The ancients used *tramitto* for *transmitto*.

Prona] Inclined toward the earth. Ovid writes:

> While the other animals look downward toward the earth,  
> He gave the human being an elevated face and commanded him  
> To look upon heaven and raise his countenance erect toward the stars.

[Col. 1070B]

Marcus Tullius Cicero writes in Book One of *On the Laws*:

> Countless arts were discovered under the instruction of nature, and reason, imitating nature, skillfully acquired the things necessary for life. Nature not only adorned human beings with the swiftness of the mind but also assigned the senses to them as attendants, and gave the body a form suited and adapted to human intelligence. For while she had cast the other living creatures down toward their food, she raised the human being alone and awakened him to the sight of heaven, as though of his former kinship and dwelling-place. Then she shaped the appearance of his face in such a way that it expressed, deep within it, the hidden places of the mind.

Silius Italicus writes in Book Fifteen:

> Do you not see how God has raised the lofty faces  
> Of human beings toward the stars and fashioned their elevated features,  
> While he has scattered cattle, the race of birds, and the forms of beasts  
> Indifferent and obscene, face down upon their bellies?  
> If the human race, born for praise, receives the gifts of the gods,  
> Happy is the human race born for praise. [Col. 1070C]

Lactantius writes in Book Two of *On the Origin of Error*, also in chapter two:

> It is therefore pleasing, as though established upon some lofty watchtower from which all people could hear, to proclaim that saying of Persius:
>
> “O souls bent toward the earth and empty of heavenly things! Look instead upon heaven, to the sight of which the true God, the maker, has raised you. He gave you an elevated face, yet you bend toward the earth; you press down your lofty minds, which were raised with your bodies toward their father, toward lower things, as though you regretted not having been born four-footed. It is not fitting for a heavenly creature to associate with earthly creatures and with things that incline toward the earth. Why, deprived of heavenly benefits, do you willingly fall prostrate toward the earth? Miserably you roll upon the ground when you seek below what you ought to have sought on high?”

Saint Ambrose writes in Book Six of the *Hexaemeron*:

> Beware, O human being, of bending yourself in the manner of cattle; beware lest you bend yourself toward the belly not so much in body as in desire. Look at the form of your body and assume the appearance appropriate to lofty vigor. If only animals feed with their faces toward the ground, why do you yourself lie down while eating, when nature has not laid you low? Why do you delight in what is an insult to nature? Why, intent upon food by night and by day, do you graze upon earthly things in the manner of cattle? Why, devoted to bodily pleasures, do you dishonor yourself while serving the belly and its appetites? Why do you deprive yourself of the intellect that the Creator bestowed upon you? Why do you compare yourself with beasts of burden, from which God wished you to be separated, saying, “Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding”? Or, if the appetite of a horse and its intemperance delight you, and if neighing after females is pleasurable, then let it also delight you to have your jaws held by a bit and restrained by a bridle.
