Alternatively, divide the proportion maintained between the given terms, and place what remains as the middle term. For 40 is four times 10. If you divide the quadruple, you obtain the double, namely 20; for 20 is twice 10. If you place this in the middle, it will produce a geometric mean.

You will find the harmonic mean as follows. Multiply the difference of the terms by the lesser term; then add the terms together, and alongside the number produced by their sum place the number produced from the difference and the lesser term. Having found its breadth (that is, the quotient), add it to the lesser term and place the result as the middle term. Thus, 10 and 40 make 30; if you multiply this by 10, the lesser number, you must obtain 300. Place this 300 alongside the number produced by adding the two terms, namely 50. For 50 times 6 makes 300, and the breadth is found to be 6. If you add this to the lesser term, the result is 16; and this number, placed between 10 and 40, will preserve the harmonic proportion and mean.

## CHAPTER LI. On the three means that are contrary to the harmonic and geometric means

These are the means discovered and approved by the ancients. We have treated them at greater length and with greater clarity because they are found especially often in the writings of the ancients, and because their usefulness extends to almost every aspect of their learning. We pass over the remaining means more briefly because they are not of much assistance in our studies, but serve chiefly to complete the number ten. Nevertheless, so that they may not remain hidden or unknown to anyone, we shall set them forth. They appear to be contrary to the means described above, from which they derive their origin. For these too have been constructed from them.

There is a fourth mean, which appears to be opposed to the harmonic mean. In it, when three terms are given, the proportion of the greatest term to the smallest is the same as that of the difference between the lesser terms to the difference between the greater terms. Thus, take 3, 5, 6. Six is twice three. The lesser terms are 5 and 3, while the greater terms in this arrangement are 6 and 5. The difference between the lesser terms, namely between 5 and 3, is 2; the difference between the greater terms, namely between 5 and 6, is 1. The comparison of 2 with 1 gives a double proportion. Therefore, as the greatest term is to the smallest, so the difference of the lesser terms is to the difference of the greater terms.

It is clear that this mean is opposed, and in a certain sense contrary, to the harmonic mean, because in the latter the difference of the greater terms is to the difference of the lesser terms as the greatest term is to the smallest. Here the order is reversed.

A property of this mean is that the product of the greatest term and the middle term is twice the product of the middle and the smallest. For six times five is 30, while five times three is 15.

Two other means, the fifth and sixth, are contrary to the geometric mean and appear to be opposed to it.

The fifth mean occurs when, in three terms, the proportion of the middle term to the lesser is the same as the proportion of their difference to the difference between the middle and the greater. In the arrangement 2, 4, 5, four is twice two; the difference between four and two is 2, while the difference between four and the greater term, five, is 1. Two is twice one.

Its opposition to the geometric mean lies in this proportion: in the geometric mean, as the greater term is to the lesser, so the difference of the greater terms is to the difference of the lesser terms. Here the reverse is true: as the lesser terms are related to one another, so the difference of the lesser terms is compared with the difference of the greater terms.

This arrangement also has the property that the product of the greater term and the mean is twice the product of the two extremes. For five times four is 20, while five times two is 10, and 20 is twice 10.

The sixth mean occurs when, in three given terms, the proportion of the greater term to the middle is the same as that of the difference between the lesser terms to the difference between the greatest terms. In the arrangement 1, 4, 6, the greatest term is to the middle in a sesquialteral proportion, while the difference of the lesser terms, namely of 1 and 4, is 3, and the difference of the greater terms, namely of 4 and 6, is 2. Three compared with two produces a sesquialteral proportion.

This mean is contrary to the geometric mean in the same way as the fifth, because the proportion of the differences is reversed from the lesser terms to the greater.

## CHAPTER LII. On the four means added by later writers to complete the number ten

These, then, are the six means. Three of them remained current from Pythagoras through Plato and Aristotle. Later writers added the three others discussed above in their commentaries. A subsequent age, as we have said, added four further means in order to complete the number ten. They are not found so readily in the books of the ancients. Let us set them out as briefly as possible.

The first of these, but the seventh in order, is formed as follows: in three terms, the proportion of the greatest term to the last is the same as that of the difference between the greatest and smallest terms to the difference between the lesser terms. Take the arrangement 6, 8, 9. Nine is in a sesquialteral proportion to six, and their difference is 3. The difference between the lesser terms, namely between 8 and 6, is 2; compared with the preceding 3, it produces a sesquialteral proportion.

The second among these four, but the eighth in order, occurs when, in three terms, the proportion of the extremes to one another is the same as that of their difference to the difference between the greater terms. Thus, take 6, 7, 9. Nine is in a sesquialteral proportion to 6, and their difference is 3. Compared with the difference between the greater terms, namely between 7 and 9, which is 2, this gives a sesquialteral proportion.

The third among these four, but the ninth in order, occurs when the proportion maintained by the middle term to the smallest is retained in the comparison of the difference between the extremes with the difference between the lesser terms. Thus, take 4, 6, 7. Six is in a sesquialteral proportion to 4, and their difference is 2. The difference between 7 and 4 is 3; when this is compared with the preceding 2, the two are joined in a sesquialteral proportion.

The fourth, which is tenth in order, is considered in three terms when the middle term is compared with the smallest in the same proportion in which the difference of the extremes is related to the difference of the greater terms. Thus, take 3, 5, 8. The middle term 5 is superbipartient in relation to 3. The difference of the extremes, namely of 8 and 3, is 5; compared with the difference between the greater terms, namely between 5 and 8, which is 3, it too is found to be superbipartient.

## CHAPTER LIII. The arrangement of the ten means

Let us therefore arrange all the means in order, so that their several forms may be understood as easily as possible.

## CHAPTER LIV. On the greatest and perfect consonance, which extends through three intervals

It remains to discuss the greatest and most perfect harmony. Since it is constituted by three intervals, it possesses great force both in the harmonies of musical composition and in the examination of natural questions. Nothing more perfect than this mean can be found: extending through three intervals, it possesses the nature and substance of a most perfect body.

In this way we have shown that a cube, thickened in three dimensions, is also a complete harmony. This harmony is found when two terms are given that themselves increase through three dimensions—length, breadth, and depth—and two corresponding middle terms are established, themselves marked by three intervals. They may be produced either from equal quantities by equal quantities equally, from unequal quantities to unequal quantities equally, from unequal quantities to equal quantities equally, or in any other manner. Thus, while they preserve a harmonic proportion, they may nevertheless be related in another way so as to produce an arithmetic mean; and the geometric mean, which lies between the two, cannot be absent.

For if there are four terms, and the first is to the second as the third is to the fourth, with the proportional relation preserved, a geometric mean is expressed. The product of the extremes will be equal to the product obtained by multiplying the two means together.

Again, if the greatest of the four terms has to the term next to it the same difference as the term next to the greatest has to the smallest, such a proportion is presented in an arithmetic consideration. The sum of the extremes will be twice the mean.

But if the third term exceeds the fourth by the same amount by which the first exceeds the second, such a proportion and mean will be recognized as harmonic. The product of the sum of the extremes and the mean is twice the product formed by the two extremes.

Let the following be an example of this arrangement: 6, 8, 9, 12. There is no doubt that all these quantities are solid numbers. Six arises from one times two times three, while 12 arises from two times two times three. Their means are represented by 8, which is one times two times four, and 9, which is one times three times three. All the terms are therefore related to one another and marked by the dimensions of three intervals.

A geometric proportion is found among them if we compare 12 with 8 or 9 with 6. Each comparison is sesquialteral, and the product of the extremes is the same as that of the means. For twelve times six equals eight times nine. This, then, is a geometric proportion.

It is arithmetic if 12 is compared with 9 and 9 with 6. In both cases the difference is 3, and the sum of the extremes is twice the middle term. For if you add 6 and 12, you obtain 18, which is twice the middle term, 9.

We have thus observed the geometric and arithmetic means. The harmonic mean is also found here if we compare 12 with 8 and again 8 with 6. The amount by which 8 surpasses 6, namely one third, is the same as the part of 12 by which 8 is surpassed. For the 4 by which 8 is exceeded by 12 is one third of 12. If you add the extremes, 6 and 12, and multiply them by the middle term 8, the result is 144. If the extremes are multiplied by one another, 6 times 12 gives 72, and 144 is twice that number.

Here too we find all the musical consonances. For 8 compared with 6, and 9 with 12, produce a sesquitertial proportion and together form the diatessaron consonance. Six compared with 9, or 8 with 12, produces a sesquialteral proportion and the diapente consonance. Twelve compared with 6 produces a double proportion and sounds the diapason consonance. But 8 and 9, considered as the middle terms in relation to one another, form the epogdous, which in musical composition is called a tone and is the common measure of all musical sounds. This is the smallest of all the sounds.

Hence it is clear that the difference between the diatessaron and diapente consonances is a tone, just as the sole difference between the sesquitertial and sesquialteral proportions is the epogdous. We have appended below an illustration of this arrangement.

## ANICIUS MANLIUS SEVERINUS BOETHIUS, FIVE BOOKS ON MUSIC. (C)

The remarks noted in the margin of Glarean’s edition opposite the text have been transcribed by us at the foot of our columns.

# BOOK ONE

## CHAPTER ONE. That music is naturally joined to us, and either improves or corrupts our character

The perception of all the senses is present in certain living beings so spontaneously and naturally that an animal cannot be conceived without it. Yet knowledge and firm apprehension of those same senses are not equally acquired through the investigation of the mind. The use of sensation to perceive sensible things requires no labor. But what the nature of the senses themselves is, according to which we act, and what the property of sensible things may be, cannot be obvious or explainable to everyone unless suitable inquiry has guided the person through contemplation of the truth.

Sight is present in all mortals. Whether it is produced by images coming before the sight, or by rays emitted toward sensible objects, is indeed a matter of dispute among the learned; the common crowd passes over even the question itself. Again, when someone looks at a triangle or a square, he readily recognizes what is presented to the eyes. But he must seek from a mathematician what the nature of a triangle or square is.

[Note: [Col. 1167] “The same also.”]

The same may be said of the other senses, and especially of the judgment of the ears. Their power apprehends sounds in such a way that it not only judges them and recognizes their differences, but is often delighted when the melodies are sweet and well joined, while it is distressed when they strike the sense in a scattered and incoherent manner.

[Note: [Col. 1167] “Sensible things.”]

Thus, although there are four disciplines of mathematics, while the others labor toward the investigation of truth, music is joined not only to speculation but also to moral character.

[Note: [Col. 1167] “It is not read: ‘is.’”]

Nothing is so proper to humanity as being relaxed by sweet melodies and tightened by contrary ones.

[Note: [Col. 1167] “Humanity.”]

This applies not only to individuals, or to particular pursuits and ages, but spreads through all studies. Infants and young people, and even the old, are naturally joined by a kind of spontaneous feeling to musical melodies, so that there is absolutely no age separated from the delight of sweet song.

Hence it may also be understood that Plato did not speak idly when he said that the soul of the world had been joined together through musical harmony. For when, from what is joined and fittingly adjusted within us, we receive what is joined and fittingly adjusted in sounds, and take delight in it, we recognize that we ourselves too are composed according to the same likeness.

[Note: [Col. 1167] “It is not read: ‘from.’”]

Similarity is friendly; dissimilarity is hateful and contrary.

[Note: [Col. 1167] “It is not read: ‘indeed.’”]

Hence changes in character also chiefly arise. A wanton mind either delights in more wanton melodies or, often hearing the same melodies, is quickly softened and broken. Again, a harsher or more impetuous mind either rejoices in more vigorous melodies or is made harsher by them.

This is why musical modes have been designated by the names of peoples, such as the Lydian and Phrygian modes. Each mode is called by the name of the people whose character it resembles, since a people delights in modes through their likeness to its character. Soft things cannot be joined to hard things, nor hard things to softer things, or delight in them. As has been said, similarity produces love and delight.

Therefore Plato considers it especially necessary to take care that nothing be changed in music that has been well ordered morally. He says that no corruption of character in a republic is so great as the gradual alteration of a modest and disciplined music. The minds of those who hear it immediately suffer the same change and gradually withdraw, retaining no trace of what is honorable and upright, if something immodest enters their minds through wanton modes, or something savage and monstrous through harsher ones.

No path to the mind is more open than that through the ears. When rhythms and modes have descended through them into the mind, there can be no doubt that they affect and shape the mind in the same manner in which they themselves are constituted.

[Note: [Col. 1169] “They affect.”]

This can also be understood among peoples. The Getae, who are harsher, delight in harsher modes. Those who are gentler prefer moderate ones, although in our time this is almost nowhere to be found. The entire wanton and soft human race, however, is held by theatrical and stage melodies.

Music was modest and disciplined when it was performed with simpler instruments. But once it was treated in a varied and confused manner, it lost its measure of gravity and virtue, nearly slipping into disgrace, and preserves scarcely any trace of its former character. Hence Plato commands that boys should not be trained in every mode, but rather in strong and simple ones.

Above all, this must be retained: if something were altered in any way through the smallest changes, it would scarcely be noticed at first, but later would make a great difference and descend through the ears even into the mind. Plato therefore considers music to be a great safeguard of the republic when it is morally ordered and modestly joined to it—modest and simple, manly rather than effeminate, savage, or various.

The Lacedaemonians preserved this with the greatest care. Among them Taletas the Cretan,

[Note: [Col. 1169] “Gortynian.”]

summoned at great expense, instructed the boys in the discipline of musical art. This was an ancient custom and long remained so.

[Note: [Col. 1169] “Custom.”]

But when Timotheus of Miletus added one string beyond those previously devised and made the music more elaborate, they expelled him from Lacedaemon. A judgment was rendered concerning him. Since this judgment is noteworthy, I have appended it in the very Greek words, in the language of the Spartans, who change the letter S into R.

“Since Timotheus of Miletus, coming to our city, dishonored the ancient song, and, turning away from playing the lyre with seven strings, introduced polyphony and corrupted the hearing of the young by his many-stringed instrument and by the novelty of his melody; since, instead of clothing the Muse in what was simple and ordered, he clothed her in what was ignoble and varied, constructing the arrangement of the melody upon the chromatic genus and making a contrary exchange in place of the enharmonic; and since, having also improperly arranged the treatment of the myth at the contest of Eleusinian Demeter—for he did not teach the young the eleven birth-pangs of Semele—may it be resolved by the kings and the ephors to censure Timotheus, and so forth.”

That judgment contains the following meaning: the Spartans were angry with Timotheus of Miletus because, by making the music more elaborate, he impeded the minds of the boys whom he had undertaken to educate and hindered them from the modesty of virtue; and because he had changed the harmony he had received as modest into the chromatic genus, which is softer.

So great was their concern for music that they believed it could possess the mind as well. For it is commonly known how often a song has restrained anger and how many remarkable effects it has produced either in bodily or in mental conditions.

Who does not know that Pythagoras made a drunken youth of Tauromenium, inflamed by the sound of the Phrygian mode, milder and master of himself by having a spondaic melody sung in accompaniment? When a prostitute was shut up in a rival’s house and the youth, raging, wanted to burn the house, Pythagoras was observing the courses of the stars, as was his nightly custom. When he realized that the youth had been incited by the sound of the Phrygian mode and would not desist from his deed despite the many admonitions of his friends, he ordered the mode to be changed, and thus tempered the young man’s raging spirit into a state of complete calm.

[Note: [Col. 1169] “The word ‘to’ is not present.”]

Marcus Tullius recalls this in the book he composed about his counsels, although in a different form and in these words:

“But, to compare the smallest things with the greatest by some resemblance, when drunken young men, incited—as often happens—even by the sound of pipes, were breaking down the doors of a chaste woman, Pythagoras is said to have advised the flute-player to perform a spondaic melody. When she had done so, the slowness of the modes and the gravity of the performance calmed their raging insolence.”

To collect briefly similar examples: Terpander and Arion of Methymna rescued the Lesbians and Ionians from serious illnesses by the aid of song. Ismenias the Theban is said to have removed all the suffering of many Boeotians afflicted by the torments of sciatica by melodies.

Empedocles too, when someone attacked his guest in a rage with a sword because that man had condemned his father by an accusation, is said to have changed the mode of his singing and thus tempered the young man’s anger.

[Note: [Col. 1169] “Those devoted to its studies.”]

So widely was the power of musical art known among the students of ancient philosophy that the Pythagoreans, when they were relieving themselves of the cares of the day in sleep, used certain songs so that gentle and peaceful slumber might come upon them. When they awoke, they cleansed the stupor and confusion of sleep with other modes. They knew, of course, that the entire structure of our soul and body is joined together by musical harmony.

For as the condition of the body is, so the pulses of the heart are also stimulated in their movements. Democritus is said to have handed this knowledge on to the physician Hippocrates when Hippocrates visited him in custody for the purpose of treating him, since all Democritus’s fellow citizens believed him to be insane.

But why have I related these things? Because there can be no doubt that the condition of our soul and body seems to be composed in a certain way according to the same proportions by which a later discussion will show harmonic melodies to be joined and united.

This is why even infants are delighted by sweet song. Something harsh and unfeeling suspends them from the pleasure of hearing. Surely every age and every sex experiences this. Although their activities are distributed among their several forms, they are nevertheless united by one delight in music.

What happens when mourners give their very lament a melody in their weeping? This is especially characteristic of women: the cause of weeping becomes sweeter when accompanied by a kind of song. In ancient times it was also customary for the sound of the flute to precede funeral laments.

Papinius Statius bears witness in this verse:

> The deep horn bellows with its curved mouth,  
> while the flute is accustomed to lead forth the tender ghosts.

And someone who cannot sing sweetly nevertheless sings something to himself—not because what he sings gives him pleasure through any particular excellence, but because people delight in the innate sweetness that the singer somehow brings forth from his mind.

Is it not also clear that the minds of those fighting in war are inflamed by the music of trumpets? If that is credible, then it is also possible for someone to be brought from a peaceful state of mind into fury and anger. There is no doubt that a more restrained mode can bind the anger of a disturbed mind or restrain excessive desire.

What of the fact that, when someone receives a song more willingly with his ears and mind, he is also involuntarily led to make his body imitate the movement of the song he has heard, and that the mind itself, remembering what melody it has heard, takes something of it for itself?

From all this it is plainly and undoubtedly evident that music is naturally joined to us in such a way that we cannot be without it even if we wish to be. Therefore the power of the mind must be directed toward retaining by knowledge what has been implanted by nature.

For just as, in the case of sight, it is not enough for educated people to observe colors and shapes unless they also investigate their properties, so it is not enough to delight in musical songs unless one also learns by what proportion of voices they are joined to one another.

## CHAPTER II. That there are three kinds of music, in which the power of music is described

At the beginning of a discussion of music, it seems necessary first to say how many kinds of music we know to have been recognized by its students. There are three. The first is worldly or cosmic music; the second is human music; the third is the music established in certain instruments, such as the lyre or flutes, and in the other instruments that serve song.

The cosmic kind is to be perceived especially in the heavens themselves, in the structure of the elements, and in the variation of the seasons. How could the mechanism of the heavens, moving with such speed, travel in silent and soundless motion? Even if that sound does not reach our ears—which must happen for many reasons—such exceedingly rapid motion of such enormous bodies cannot produce no sound at all, especially since the courses of the stars are joined together with such harmony that nothing can be understood as equally well ordered or so perfectly mixed.

Some bodies are carried higher, others lower, and all revolve with equal impetus, so that a measured order of courses is produced through unequal differences. Therefore this heavenly rotation cannot be without a measured order of melody.

Again, how could the diversity and contrary powers of the four elements come together into one body and structure unless some harmony joined them? Yet this whole diversity both produces the variation of the seasons and gives rise to different fruits, while still forming one body, the year. If you tear apart in mind and thought any of the things that provide such variety to the world, everything perishes and, so to speak, retains nothing consonant.

Just as in grave strings there is a proper degree of depth, so that their gravity does not descend into complete silence, and in high strings a proper degree of sharpness is preserved, lest the strings, stretched too far, break because of the thinness of their sound, but everything remains mutually consistent and fitting, so too in the music of the world we see that nothing can be so excessive that it dissolves something else through its own excess.

Whatever it may be, it either produces its own fruits or helps other things to produce theirs. Winter contracts, spring loosens, summer scorches, autumn ripens; and the seasons in turn either bring forth their own fruits or assist others in bringing them forth. These matters must be discussed more carefully later.

Anyone who descends into himself understands human music. What else could mingle the incorporeal vitality of reason with the body except a certain fitting adjustment and, as it were, a tempering that produces one consonance from high and low voices? What else could join together the parts of the soul, which, as Aristotle holds, is composed of a rational and an irrational part? What else could mix the elements of the body or hold its parts together in a measured adjustment? I shall speak of this later as well.

The third kind is said to reside in certain instruments. It is produced either by tension, as in strings; by breath, as in flutes and instruments moved by water; or by percussion, as in those instruments in which a hollow bronze rod is struck and different sounds are produced from it.

This work should therefore first discuss the music of instruments. That is enough for a preface. We must now discuss the elements of music themselves.

## CHAPTER III. On voices and the elements of music
Consonance, which governs every musical modulation, cannot occur apart from sound. Sound, however, is not produced apart from some impulse and percussion. An impulse and percussion, in turn, cannot exist in any way unless motion has preceded them. For if everything were immobile, [Col. 1173A] one thing could not come together with another, so that one might be pushed by the other. But with everything standing still and lacking motion, no sound could necessarily be produced. Therefore sound is defined as follows: “An uninterrupted percussion of air extending to the hearing.”

Some motions are swifter, others slower; and of these motions some are rarer, others denser. For if someone looks at continuous motion, he must necessarily apprehend either speed or slowness. If, on the other hand, someone moves his hand, he will move it either with frequent motion or with rare motion. And if the motion is slow and rarer, low sounds must necessarily be produced by the very slowness and rarity of the striking. But if the motions are swift and dense, the sounds must necessarily be rendered high. For this reason the same string, if it is stretched more tightly, sounds high; if it is slackened, low. When [Col. 1173B] it is tighter, it produces a swifter impulse and returns more quickly, striking the air more frequently and densely. But what is looser emits relaxed and slow impulses, and, rare because of the very weakness of its striking, does not tremble for long.

Nor should one suppose that whenever a string is struck only one sound is produced, or that there is only one percussion in it; rather, the air is struck as many times as the trembling string strikes it. But because the sounds’ speeds are joined together, no interval is perceived by the ears. A single sound—whether low or high—strikes the sense, although each consists of many sounds: the low sound of slower and rarer ones, the high of [Note: [Col. 1173] swifter] swift and dense ones. It is as though someone carefully [Note: [Col. 1173] adorns] decorated a cone, which they call a spinning top, and drew upon it one stripe of red or another color, then turned it with whatever speed he could; the entire cone would appear stained red—not because the whole of it was actually so, but because the speed of the red stripe would encompass the uncolored parts and prevent them from appearing. But more will be said about this later.

Since, then, high voices are stimulated by denser and swifter motions, while low voices are stimulated by slower and rarer ones, it is clear that by adding motions, height is intensified from lowness, while by removing motions, lowness is extended from height. For height consists of more motions than lowness. But wherever plurality produces a difference, it must necessarily consist in some numerical relation. Every small number, moreover, is related to plurality as one number is compared with another. Of things compared according to number, some are equal to one another and some unequal. [Col. 1175D] Therefore sounds too are partly equal and partly separated by inequality. But among voices that differ in no inequality whatsoever, there is no consonance at all; for consonance is the harmonious agreement of unlike voices brought together into one.

## CHAPTER IV. On the kinds of inequalities

Unequal quantities preserve the measures of inequality among themselves in five ways. For one number either exceeds another by a multiple, by a part, by several parts, by a multiple and a part, or by a multiple and several parts.

The first kind of inequality is called multiple. It occurs when the greater number contains the lesser number wholly, either twice, three times, four times, and so on, with nothing lacking and nothing exceeding. It is called double, triple, quadruple, and so forth, and proceeds in this order to infinity. 

The second kind of inequality is called superparticular, that is, when the greater number contains the lesser number wholly and also one of its parts—either half, as three compared with two, which is called the sesquialterate ratio; or a third, as four compared with three, which is called sesquitertian. In the same way, in subsequent numbers some part contained by the greater numbers is added above the lesser numbers.

The third kind of inequality occurs whenever the greater number contains the lesser wholly and, in addition, several of its parts. [Col. 1174B] If it contains two parts above it, the ratio is called superbipartient, as five compared with three. If it contains three parts above it, it is called supertripartient, as seven compared with four. The same correspondence may also be found in the remaining cases. [Note: [Col. 1173] It is not.]

The fourth kind of inequality is compounded from the multiple and the superparticular, namely when the greater number contains the lesser either twice, three times, or any number of times, and also one of its parts. If it contains it twice and also half of it, it is called double sesquialterate, as five compared with two. If the lesser is contained twice and a third of it is added, it is called double sesquitertian, as seven compared with three. If it is contained three times and half of it is added, it is called triple sesquialterate, as seven compared with two. In the same way, the names of multiplicity and superparticularity vary in the remaining cases.

The fifth kind of inequality is called multiple-superpartient, when the greater number contains the lesser wholly more than once and also more than one of its parts. If the greater number contains the lesser twice and two of its parts in addition, it is called double superbipartient, as eight compared with three; and again triple superbipartient, as eleven compared with three. We have explained these matters briefly and concisely here because we have treated them more fully in the books we wrote on the *Fundamentals of Arithmetic*.

## CHAPTER V. Which kinds of inequality are suited to consonances

Of these kinds of inequality, then, let us leave aside the last two, [Col. 1174D] since they are compounded from the preceding ones. [Note: [Col. 1173] Let us proceed.] The first three must be examined. Multiplicity, therefore, appears to possess the greater authority in relation to consonances, and superparticularity comes next. Superpartient inequality, however, is separated from harmonic concord, as seems to some authorities apart from Ptolemy.

## CHAPTER VI. Why multiplicity and superparticularity are assigned to consonances

Those things are rightly judged consonant with comparison that are simple by nature. And since lowness and height consist in quantity, those things will seem especially to preserve the nature of concord that can preserve the character of discrete quantity. For one kind of quantity is discrete and another continuous. Discrete quantity is finite at the minimum, but proceeds toward infinity through greater magnitudes. In it the unit is both minimal and finite. Plurality, however, increases to infinity, as with number, which, although it begins from the finite unit, has no end in its growth.

Continuous quantity, on the other hand, is finite as a whole but is diminished through infinitude. For a line, which is continuous, is divided by infinitely many successive partitions, although its total may be two feet or some other definite measure. Therefore number always grows toward infinity, whereas continuous quantity diminishes toward infinity.

Multiplicity, then, since it has no end to its growth, most of all preserves the nature of number. Superparticularity, [Col. 1175B] because it diminishes the lesser number toward infinity, preserves the property of continuous quantity. It diminishes the lesser number because it always contains it together with either half, third, fourth, or fifth of it. For the part named from the greater number is always smaller. Since a third is named from three, and a fourth from four, and since four exceeds three, a fourth is found to be smaller than a third.

Superpartient inequality, however, already departs in some way from simplicity. For it has two, three, or four additional parts, and, departing from simplicity, overflows toward a certain plurality of parts. Multiplicity, by contrast, always contains wholeness. For the double contains the whole lesser number twice; the triple likewise contains the whole lesser number three times; and so on. Superparticularity [Col. 1175C] preserves nothing whole, but exceeds by either a half, a third, a fourth, or a fifth. Yet it operates through division into individual and simple parts.

Superpartient inequality, however, neither preserves the whole nor subtracts individual parts. [Note: [Col. 1175] individual] And [Note: [Col. 1175] for this reason] for this reason, according to the Pythagoreans, it is least of all applied to musical consonances. Ptolemy nevertheless places this ratio among the consonances, as I shall show later.

## CHAPTER VII. Which ratios are suited to which musical consonances

It must nevertheless be understood that all musical consonances consist either in the double, triple, quadruple, sesquialterate, or sesquitertian ratio. The ratio that is sesquitertian in numbers is called the diatessaron in sounds. That which is sesquialterate in numbers is called the diapente in voices. That which is double in ratios is called the diapason among consonances. The triple is the diapente together with the diapason. The quadruple is the bisdiapason. Let this, for now, be stated universally and without distinction. Later the whole account of the ratios will become clear.

## CHAPTER VIII. What sound, interval, and concord are

Sound is a modulation of the voice, *emmeles*, that is, suited to melody, at a single pitch. We do not now wish to define sound in general, but the sound that in Greek is called *phthongos* (φθόγγος), a word derived from the similarity of *phthengesthai* (φθέγγεσθαι), “to speak.”

An interval is the distance between a high and a low sound. Consonance is a mixture of high and low sound that reaches the ears pleasantly and uniformly. Dissonance is the harsh and unpleasant impact of two sounds mixed with one another as they come to the ear. For since they do not wish to mix with one another, and each strives in some way to arrive intact, while each obstructs the other, both are conveyed unpleasantly to the sense.

## CHAPTER IX. That judgment must not be entrusted entirely to the senses, but reason must be trusted more fully; concerning the fallibility of the senses

We make these statements, however, in such a way that we do not assign every judgment to the senses, although the whole beginning of this art is taken from the sense of hearing. For if there were no hearing, no discussion of voices would have arisen at all. Hearing nevertheless occupies, in a certain way, the place of a beginning and almost of an admonition. The final perfection [Note: [Col. 1175] concerning] and power of recognition, therefore, reside in reason, which, holding to fixed rules, [Note: [Col. 1175] ever by any means] never slips into error.

What more need be said about the error of the senses, when neither is the power of perception the same in everyone, nor is it always equal in the same person? It is useless for anyone to entrust to variable judgment what he seeks to investigate truthfully. For this reason the Pythagoreans are said to follow a middle path. They do not entrust every judgment to the ears, yet they do investigate certain matters through the ears alone. They measure consonances themselves by the ear. But the intervals by which consonances differ from one another they entrust not to the ears, whose judgments are dull, but to rules and reason, so that the sense may be like an obedient servant, while reason is the judge and commander.

Although almost all the activities of the arts, and of life itself, have been brought forth through the occasion provided by the senses, there is nevertheless no certain judgment or apprehension of truth in them if the authority of reason withdraws. For the sense is equally corrupted by the greatest and the smallest things. It cannot perceive the smallest because of the minuteness of the sensible objects, and it is often confused by larger ones. Thus with voices: if they are very small, hearing captures them with difficulty; if they are very great, it becomes deafened by the force of the sound itself.

## CHAPTER X. How Pythagoras investigated the ratios of consonances

This, then, was the chief reason why Pythagoras, abandoning the judgment of the ears, turned to the authority of rules. Trusting neither human ears, which are altered partly by nature, partly by external accidents, and partly by the changes of age, nor instruments, to which great variation and instability often give rise—for if one examines strings, a more humid air might blunt their vibration, a drier air might dry them out, the thickness of a string might make the sound lower, a finer string might sharpen it, or some other circumstance might alter the state of their former constancy—he considered all these matters untrustworthy and of little value. He long wrestled with the question of how he might learn the properties of consonances [Col. 1177A] by a firm and constant method. [Note: [Col. 1177] might combine.]

Meanwhile, passing by divine prompting near the workshops of craftsmen, he heard the hammers [Note: [Col. 1177] distinctly heard] striking and making one kind of concord resound from different sounds. Astonished, then, that he had come upon what he had long sought, he approached the work. After long consideration, he supposed that the difference in sounds was produced by the strength of the strikers. To investigate this more clearly, he ordered that the hammers [Note: [Col. 1177] be changed] be exchanged among themselves. But the character of the sounds did not depend on the men’s arms; it followed the hammers when they were exchanged.

When he noticed this, he examined the weight of the hammers. There happened to be five hammers, and those that corresponded with one another according to the diapason consonance were found to have double the weight. He also found that the same hammer which was double another was sesquitertian in relation to a third, to which it sounded a diatessaron. [Col. 1177B] In relation to another hammer, with which it was joined by the diapente consonance, he found the same hammer to be sesquialterate. The two hammers to which the upper double had proved to be sesquitertian and sesquialterate [Col. 1177C] [Col. 1178A] were weighed and found to preserve a sesquioctave ratio to each other. The fifth was rejected because it was dissonant with all the others.

Since before Pythagoras musical consonances were called partly diapason, partly diapente, and partly diatessaron—the smallest consonance—Pythagoras was the first to discover in this way by what ratio this string of sounds was joined together.

To make what has been said clearer, let there be, for example, four weights of hammers, represented by the numbers written below: 12, 9, 8, and 6. The hammers whose weights were 12 and 6 sounded the diapason consonance in the double ratio. [Note: [Col. 1177] concord.] The hammer of twelve weights and the hammer of nine weights, and the hammer of eight weights and the hammer of six weights, were joined according to the epitritic ratio in the diatessaron consonance. [Col. 1178B] The weights nine and six, and twelve and eight, produced the diapente consonance. Nine and eight resounded a tone in the sesquioctave ratio.

This final figure is also found at the very end of the *Arithmetic* [Col. 1178C].

## CHAPTER XI. The various methods by which Pythagoras measured the ratios of consonances

[Col. 1177C]

After returning home, he examined the matter by various tests, to determine whether the entire principle of symphonies consisted in these ratios. At one time he attached equal weights to strings and judged their consonances by the ear; at another, he restored doubleness and halving in the lengths of reeds and applied the other ratios, gaining the most reliable assurance through different experiments. Often, according to the capacities of the measures, he placed cups of equal weight in bowls; often he struck the bowls themselves, made with different weights, with a rod of bronze or iron, and rejoiced that he had found no difference.

Led on by this, he also undertook to examine the length and thickness of strings. Thus he discovered the rule of which we shall speak later. It took its name from the thing itself—not [Note: [Col. 1177] because it is wooden] because it is a straightedge by which we measure the dimensions of strings and sound, but because it is a fixed and firm kind of inspection of this sort, so that it does not mislead any investigator with doubtful judgment.

## CHAPTER XII. On the division of voices and their explanation

But enough of this. Let us now gather together the differences among voices. [Col. 1178C] Every voice is either *continuous* (συνεχής), that is, continuous, or *diastematic* (διαστηματική), which is said to be suspended with an interval.

A continuous voice is so called because when speaking or reading speech aloud, we run through the words. The voice then hastens not to remain fixed on high and low sounds, but to pass through the words as quickly as possible; the momentum of continuous voice serves to unfold meanings and express speech.

A diastematic voice is one that we suspend in singing, in which we serve not words so much as melodic patterns. The voice itself is slower, and through the variations that it modulates it creates an interval—not of silence, [Col. 1178D] but rather of suspended and slow song.

To these, according to Albinus, a third difference is added, which can include intermediate voices. We read the poems of heroes neither in a continuous rush, as prose, nor in the more suspended and slower manner of voice used for a song.

## CHAPTER XIII. That human nature has bounded the infinity of voices

The continuous voice, and likewise the voice with which we run through a melody, are naturally infinite. For when considered in itself, no limit is imposed either on unfolding speech or on raising high pitches and relaxing low ones; but human nature has established a proper limit for both.

The human breath has set a boundary for continuous voice, beyond which you cannot in any way proceed. Each person speaks continuously only as far as his natural breath allows. Again, human nature sets a boundary for diastematic voice, determining their high and low pitches. Each person can raise the pitch or lower the lowness only as far as the natural range of his voice permits.

## CHAPTER XIV. What the manner of hearing is

Let us now discuss the manner of hearing. Something occurs in voices similar to what happens when a stone thrown from a distance sinks into a marsh or into still water. First it gathers a wave into a very small circle; then it scatters globes of waves into larger circles, continuing until the motion, exhausted by producing waves, comes to rest. The later and larger wave is always spread out with a weaker impulse.

If something obstructs the growing waves, that motion immediately returns and, as though toward the center from which it had begun, becomes rounded into the same waves. Thus, when struck air produces sound, it strikes the air nearest to it and in a certain way stirs up a circular wave of air. The wave therefore spreads out and simultaneously strikes the hearing of everyone standing around. The voice is fainter for the person standing farther away, because the wave of struck air reaches him with less force.

## CHAPTER XV. On the order of theorems, that is, investigations

With these matters established, it seems necessary to say into how many kinds every melody is woven, the kinds considered by the discipline of harmonic invention. They are the diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic. These can be explained only after we first discuss the tetrachords and how the increasing number of strings reached the plurality that exists now. This will be done if we first recall the ratios in which musical symphonies are combined.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the consonances of ratios, and on the tone and semitone

[Col. 1179C]

The diapason [Note: [Col. 1179] symphony] is a consonance that occurs in the double ratio, as in 1 and 2. The diapente consists of the numbers 2 and 3. The diatessaron consists in the ratio 3:4. The tone is enclosed by the sesquioctave ratio, but is not yet a consonance, as in 8 and 9.

The diapason together with the diapente is gathered in a triple comparison, as 2, 4, and 6. The bisdiapason is completed by a quadruple comparison, as 2, 4, and 8. The diatessaron and diapente together complete one diapason, as 2, 3, and 4. [Col. 1179D] [Col. 1180A]

For if one voice is twice as high or low as another, the diapason consonance will result. If one voice is in a sesquialterate, sesquitertian, or sesquioctave ratio to another, the higher or lower voice will produce the consonance of a diapente, diatessaron, or tone. Likewise, if a diapason, such as 2 and 4, and a diapente, such as 4 and 6, are joined, they produce the triple ratio and create the symphony that is the diapason together with the diapente.

If two diapasons are produced, such as 2 to 4 and 4 to 8, a quadruple consonance results, namely the bisdiapason. If a sesquialterate and a sesquitertian ratio—that is, a diapente and a diatessaron—are joined, such as 2 to 3 and 3 to 4, a double, that is, a diapason, is naturally produced. For 4 to 3 preserves a sesquitertian ratio; 3 is joined to 2 by a sesquialterate comparison; and the same 4, when set against 2, is joined to it by a double comparison.

The sesquitertian ratio, therefore, creates the diatessaron, and the sesquialterate ratio creates the diapente consonance. The double produces the diapason symphony. Thus the diatessaron and diapente join together into one diapason consonance.

Again, a tone cannot be divided into equal parts; the reason will become clear later. For now it is enough to know that a tone is never divided into two equal parts. To demonstrate this most easily, let the sesquioctave ratio be 8 and 9. No natural middle number falls between them. If we multiply them by two, 8 becomes 16 and 9 becomes 18. Between 16 and 18, however, one natural number occurs, namely 17. Let them therefore be arranged in order: 16, 17, 18. [Col. 1181C]

When 16 and 18 are compared, they retain the sesquioctave ratio and therefore constitute a tone. But the middle number 17 does not divide this ratio into equal parts. Compared with 16, it contains 16 wholly and one-sixteenth of it, namely one unit. But if 18, the third number, is compared with it, that is, with 17, it contains it wholly and one-seventeenth of it. Thus it does not exceed the lesser and fall short of the greater by the same parts. The smaller part is one-seventeenth; the larger is one-sixteenth. Both are called semitones—not because semitones are exactly equal halves, but because *semi* is ordinarily said of something that does not reach complete wholeness. One of these is called the greater semitone and the other the lesser. [Col. 1181D]

## CHAPTER XVII. In which prime numbers the semitone consists

I shall now explain more clearly what constitutes a whole semitone and in which prime numbers it consists. What was said about the division of the tone was not intended to show the kinds of semitones, but rather to establish that a tone cannot be separated into two equal parts.

The diatessaron, which is a consonance, consists in four voices but three intervals. It consists of two tones and a less-than-whole semitone. Let the following arrangement be given: 192, 216, 243, 256. If 192 is compared with 256, the sesquitertian ratio results, and it sounds the diatessaron consonance.

But if 216 is compared with 192, the sesquioctave ratio is present. Their difference is 24, which is an eighth part of 192; therefore this is a tone. Again, if 243 is compared with 216, there is another sesquioctave ratio. For their difference is 27, which is proved to be an eighth part of 216.

There remains the comparison of 256 and 243, whose difference is 13. Multiplied by eight, this does not appear to equal half of 243. It is therefore not a semitone, but less than a semitone. It would rightly be judged a whole semitone if their difference, 13, multiplied by eight, could equal half of the number 243. The true lesser semitone is therefore the comparison of 243 to 256. [Col. 1182B]

## CHAPTER XVIII. That the diatessaron stands apart from the diapente by a tone

Again, the diapente consonance consists of five voices and four intervals: three tones and a lesser semitone. Let the same number, 192, be posited, and let its sesquialterate be taken, which produces a diapente consonance with it. Let that number therefore be 288.

Let the numbers previously discovered above—192, 216, 243, and 256—be placed between them, so that the arrangement is formed as follows: 192, 216, 243, 256, 288. [Col. 1182D]

In the preceding arrangement, 192 and 256 were shown to contain two tones and a semitone. There remains, therefore, the comparison of 256 and 288, which is sesquioctave, that is, a tone; their difference is 32, which is an eighth part of 256. Thus the diapente consonance has been shown to consist of three tones and a semitone. [Note: [Col. 1181] to consist.]

Previously, the diatessaron consonance extended from the number 192 to 256. Now the diapente extends from the same 192 to 288. The diapente therefore exceeds the diatessaron consonance by the ratio contained between 256 and 288, and this is a tone. The diatessaron symphony, therefore, is exceeded by the diapente by a tone.

## CHAPTER XIX. That the diapason is joined from five tones and two semitones

The diapason consonance consists of five tones and two semitones, which nevertheless do not complete one tone. For it has been shown that the diapason consists of a diapente and a diatessaron; the diatessaron has been proved to consist of two tones and a semitone; and the diapente, joined with three tones and a semitone, produces five tones. But since those two semitones were not complete halves, their combination does not reach full completion. It exceeds a half but falls short of wholeness.

The diapason therefore consists, according to this account, of five tones and two semitones. Just as these do not reach a complete tone, so they extend beyond a complete semitone. What the explanation of these matters is, and how the musical consonances themselves are found, will be explained more clearly later.

Meanwhile, the present discussion must be received with moderate [Note: [Col. 1183] credulity] confidence. Firm certainty should be accepted only when each matter has become clear through its own [Note: [Col. 1183] proper] demonstration.

With these matters arranged, let us briefly discuss the strings of the *cithara*, their names, the way in which they were added, and the reasons for their names. Once these matters have first come to our knowledge, it will be easy to embrace the science that follows.

## CHAPTER XX. On the addition of strings and their names

[Col. 1183C]

Nicomachus reports that music was originally simple, so much so that it consisted entirely of four strings. This continued until Orpheus. The first and fourth strings sounded the diapason consonance; the middle strings, both with one another and with the outer strings, sounded the diapente, diatessaron, and tone. Nothing among them was dissonant, in imitation, as it were, of the music of the world, which consists of four elements. Mercury is said to have invented this four-stringed instrument.

Afterward Chorebus, son of Athys and king of the Lydians, added a fifth string. Hyagnis the Phrygian added a sixth. A seventh string was added by Terpander of Lesbos, in accordance, naturally, with the likeness of the seven planets.

Among these strings, the lowest was called *hypate*, as though “greater” and “more honored.” Hence they also call Jupiter *Hypatos*. They give the consul the same name because of the excellence of his rank. The string was attributed to Saturn because of the slowness of its motion and the lowness of its sound.

*Parhypate* was the second, as though placed and positioned beside the *hypate*. *Lichanos* was the third because *lichanos* means “finger,” which we call the index finger. The Greek calls it *lichanon*, from licking. Since, in singing to the string that was third from the *hypate*, the index finger—which is the *lichanos*—was found to be used, the string itself was therefore also called *lichanos*.

The fourth is called *mese*, because among seven it is always in the middle. The fifth is *paramese*, as though placed beside the middle. The seventh is called *nete*, as though *neate*, that is, “lowest.” Between the *nete* and the *paramese* is the sixth, called *paranete*, as though placed beside the *nete*.

The *paramese*, because it is third from the *nete*, is also called by the name *trite*, that is, “third,” so that the arrangement is as follows: [Col. 1184C]

To these, Lichaon of Samos added an eighth string and fitted a middle string between the *paramese*, which is also called *trite*, and the *paranete*, so that it itself would be third from the *nete*. The *paramese* alone retained its name, [Note: [Col. 1183] alone] since it was placed after the middle string. The *trite*, however, lost its name after a string third from the *nete* had been placed between it and the *paranete*—a string that could properly receive the name *trite*. Thus, following Lichaon’s addition, the eight-stringed instrument was arranged as follows: [Col. 1184D] [Col. 1185A]

In the two arrangements given above, the seven-stringed and eight-stringed instruments, the seven-stringed instrument is called *synemmenon*, meaning “joined,” while the eight-stringed instrument is called *diezeugmenon*, meaning “disjoined.”

In the seven-stringed instrument there is one tetrachord: *hypate, parhypate, lichanos,* and *mese*. Another runs from *mese* through *paramese, paranete,* and *nete*, since we count the *mese* string a second time; therefore two tetrachords are joined through the *mese*.

In the eight-stringed instrument, because there are eight strings, the upper four—*hypate, parhypate, lichanos,* and *mese*—complete one tetrachord. From there, a separate and complete tetrachord begins with *paramese*, proceeds through *trite* and *paranete*, and ends at *nete*. This separation is called *diezeuxis* [Note: [Col. 1185] diazeuxis]. The tone is the distance between *mese* and *paramese*. [Col. 1185B]

Thus *mese* retained only its name. It is not middle in position, because in the eight-stringed instrument there are always two middle strings, while one single middle string cannot be found.

Prophrastus the Periote added one string on the lower side, in order to make the whole instrument nine-stringed. Since it was added above the *hypate*, it was called *hyperhypate*. When the cithara had only nine strings, it was called *hyperhypate*. Now, after other strings have been added above it, it is called *lichanos hypaton*. Since it came to the index finger in this order and arrangement, it was called *lichanos*. This will become clear later. For now, the arrangement of the nine-stringed instrument is as follows: [Col. 1185C]

Hestiaeus of Colophon fitted a tenth string onto the lower part, while Timotheus of Miletus [Col. 1185D] added an eleventh. Since these were added above the hypate and parhypate, they were called hypate hypaton, as if “the greatest of the great” and “the gravest of the grave,” or “the highest of the high.” The first among the eleven was therefore called hypate hypaton. The second was parhypate hypaton, because it was placed beside hypate hypaton. The third, which had formerly been called parhypate in the enneachord, was named lichanos hypaton. The fourth retained the ancient name hypate. The fifth was parhypate. The sixth, retaining its ancient designation, was lichanos. The seventh was mese. The eighth was paramese. The ninth was trite. The tenth was paranete. The eleventh was nete.

Thus one tetrachord consists of hypate hypaton, parhypate hypaton, lichanos hypaton, and hypate. [Col. 1186A] Another consists of hypate, parhypate, lichanos, and mese; these are joined together. The third consists of paramese, trite, paranete, and nete. But since between the upper tetrachord—hypate hypaton, parhypate hypaton, lichanos hypaton, hypate meson—and the lowest, which is paramese, trite, paranete, nete, there is, by its position, a middle tetrachord consisting of hypate, parhypate, lichanos, and mese, this entire middle tetrachord was called meson, as though “of the middle notes.” With this addition it is called hypate meson, parhypate meson, lichanos meson, mese.

Since, however, between this meson tetrachord and the lower one, that of the netes, there is a separation—namely, between mese and paramese—the entire lower tetrachord of the separated notes, that is, the diezeugmenon, was so called, with the following additions: paramese diezeugmenon, trite diezeugmenon, paranete diezeugmenon, nete diezeugmenon. Thus the arrangement is as follows: [Col. 1186C]

Here, therefore, there is a separation between paramese and mese, and for this reason this tetrachord was called diezeugmenon. But if paramese is removed, so that there are mese, trite, paranete, and nete, then the three tetrachords will be joined together—that is, synemmena—and the final tetrachord will be called synemmenon, as follows: [Col. 1186D] [Col. 1187A]

But since in this or in the preceding arrangement of the hendecachord mese, which is so called because of its middle placement, approaches nete and lies far from the lowest hypates, without retaining its proper position in the intervals, another tetrachord was added above nete diezeugmenon. Since this tetrachord exceeded in pitch the netes placed above it, the whole tetrachord was called hyperboleon, as follows: [Col. 1187B] [Col. 1187C]

But since once again mese was not in the middle position, but lay nearer to the hypates, one string was therefore added above hypate hypaton. This is called proslambanomenos; by some it is called prosmelodos. It is separated from hypate hypaton by a whole tone. Proslambanomenos itself—that is, proslambanomenos—is an octave from mese, sounding with it in the consonance of the diapason. It likewise sounds a diatessaron with lichanos hypaton, [Col. 1187D] that is, a fourth; lichanos hypaton in turn sounds a diapente consonance with mese, and is a fifth from it.

Again, mese is separated from paramese by a tone; and this same mese makes with nete diezeugmenon the fifth consonance, the diapente. Nete diezeugmenon makes with nete hyperboleon a fourth, the diatessaron consonance. Proslambanomenos with nete hyperboleon produces the bisdiapason consonance, as follows: [Col. 1188A] [Col. 1188B]

## CHAPTER XXI. On the kinds of melodies

These matters having been settled, we must speak of the kinds of melodies. There are three: diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic. The diatonic is somewhat harder and more natural. The chromatic, already departing from that natural tension [Note: [Col. 1187] “Departing.”] and falling into something softer, is so called because it is like a change of color. The enharmonic is most excellently and appropriately joined.

Since there are five tetrachords—hypaton, meson, synemmenon, diezeugmenon, and hyperboleon—in all of these, in the diatonic kind, the voice proceeds through a semitone, a tone, and a tone within one tetrachord. Again, in another tetrachord it proceeds through a semitone, a tone, and a tone, and so forth. It is therefore called diatonic, as though it proceeded “through a tone and through a tone.”

The chromatic, which is called “color,” is sung as if it were the first alteration from this kind of tension: through a semitone, a semitone, and three semitones. For the entire diatessaron consonance consists of two tones and a semitone, though not a full one. The name chromatic was adopted from surfaces which, when changed, pass into another color.

The enharmonic, which is more closely fitted together, is sung in all the tetrachords through a diesis, a diesis, and an incomposite ditone. [Note: [Col. 1187] “Ditone.”] A diesis is half a semitone. Thus the arrangement of the three kinds, extending through all the tetrachords, is as follows: [Col. 1189B]

## CHAPTER XXII. On the order and names of the strings in the three kinds

The order must now be set out of all the strings that vary according to the three kinds, or that are arranged in differing orders.

The first is proslambanomenos, also called prosmelodos; the second is hypate hypaton; the third, parhypate hypaton; the fourth is universally called lichanos. But if it is fitted to the diatonic kind [Note: [Col. 1189] “Fitted.”], it is called lichanos hypaton diatonos. If it belongs to the chromatic kind, it is called diatonos chromaticae, or lichanos hypaton chromaticae. If it belongs to the enharmonic kind, it is called lichanos hypaton enharmonios, or diatonos hypaton enharmonios.

After this comes hypate meson, then parhypate meson, and here lichanos meson simply. In the diatonic kind [Note: [Col. 1189] “In the diatonic.”], it is diatonos meson. In the chromatic, lichanos meson chromaticae, or diatonos meson chromaticae. In the enharmonic, diatonos meson enharmonios, or lichanos meson enharmonios. These are followed by mese.

After this come two tetrachords, partly synemmenon and partly diezeugmenon. The synemmenon is that which is placed after mese, namely trite synemmenon. Next comes lichanos synemmenon, which in the diatonic kind [Note: [Col. 1189] “In the diatonic.”] is likewise diatonos synemmenon. In the chromatic it is either diatonos synemmenon chromaticae or lichanos synemmenon chromaticae. In the enharmonic it is either diatonos synemmenon enharmonios or lichanos synemmenon enharmonios. After these comes nete synemmenon.

But if the synemmenon tetrachord is not added to the string mese, and the tetrachord is diezeugmenon, [Col. 1190B] then after mese comes paramese. Next is trite diezeugmenon, followed by lichanos diezeugmenon, which in the diatonic kind is diatonos diezeugmenon. In the chromatic it is either diatonos diezeugmenon chromaticae or lichanos diezeugmenon chromaticae. In the enharmonic it is either diatonos diezeugmenon enharmonios or lichanos diezeugmenon enharmonios. The same note is also called paranete, with the addition of either diatonic, chromatic, or enharmonic.

Above these are nete diezeugmenon, trite hyperboleon, paranete hyperboleon, and nete hyperboleon. Paranete hyperboleon is likewise called, in the diatonic kind, diatonos hyperboleon; in the chromatic, chromaticae hyperboleon; and in the enharmonic, enharmonios hyperboleon. The last of these is nete hyperboleon.

The arrangement is therefore of the following kind, so that it contains the disposition of the three kinds [Col. 1190C], in which you will observe both the similarity and the difference of the names. If the strings that are alike in all respects are combined with those that are unlike, all twenty-eight will be included together. This is shown by the following arrangement:

## CHAPTER XXIII. What the proportions are between the notes in each kind

In this way the division according to the characteristics of the kinds has been made through the individual tetrachords, so that all five tetrachords of the diatonic kind are divided by two tones and a semitone. In this kind the tone is called incomposite [Col. 1190C], because it is set down whole and no other interval is joined to it. The individual intervals, however, contain whole tones.

In the chromatic kind the division is made by a semitone, a semitone, and an incomposite trihemitone. We called this trihemitone incomposite because it is placed within a single interval. [Note: [Col. 1189] “For it can.”] In the diatonic kind, however, it may be called a trihemitone consisting of a semitone and a tone; but it is not incomposite, for it is completed by two intervals. The same is true in the enharmonic kind.

The enharmonic consists of a diesis, a diesis, and an incomposite ditone. [Note: [Col. 1191] “Diatonic.”] We call it incomposite for the same reason: it is placed within a single interval.

## CHAPTER XXIV. What synaphe is

When the tetrachords have been arranged and established in this way, there is synaphe among them. We may render this word in Latin as “joining”: it occurs whenever a single shared boundary-note continues and joins two tetrachords, as in this tetrachord: [Note: [Col. 1191] “Here therefore.”]

This, then, is one tetrachord: hypate hypaton, parhypate hypaton, lichanos hypaton, hypate meson. [Note: [Col. 1191] “Of the tetrachords.”] Another is hypate meson, parhypate meson, lichanos meson, mese. In both tetrachords hypate meson is counted. In the upper tetrachord it is the highest note, but in the later one it is the lowest.

This joining is one and the same string, hypate meson, joining the two tetrachords, just as the same hypate meson joined the hypaton and meson tetrachords in the preceding arrangement [Col. 1191D]. Synaphe, therefore, which is called “joining,” is the middle note of two tetrachords: the highest of the upper one and the lowest of the later one.

## CHAPTER XXV. What diezeuxis is

Diezeuxis is the term for what may be called “separation,” whenever two tetrachords are divided by an interval of a tone, as in these two tetrachords.

[Col. 1192A] [Col. 1192B]

It is therefore clear that there are two tetrachords, since there are eight strings. But diezeuxis—that is, separation—lies between mese and paramese, which differ from one another by a full tone. These matters will be explained more clearly when a later treatise undertakes to expound each point more carefully.

But for anyone who examines the matter attentively, there are found to be five, and no more, tetrachords: hypaton, meson, synemmenon, diezeugmenon, and hyperboleon.

## CHAPTER XXVI. The names by which Albinus called the strings

Albinus translated their names into Latin in this way: he called the hypates “principals,” the mesae “middles,” the synemmenae “joined,” the diezeugmenae “separated,” and the hyperboleae “exceeding.” [Col. 1192C] But we must not linger over another person’s work.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Which strings correspond to which heavenly bodies

For the present, however, something should be added concerning the upper tetrachords: from hypate meson to mese there is, as it were, a model of the order and separation of the heavens. Hypate meson was assigned to Saturn; parhypate was made similar to the circle of Jupiter; lichanos meson was assigned to Mars; the Sun obtained mese; Venus possesses trite synemmenon; Mercury rules paranete synemmenon; and nete represents the lunar circle.

Marcus Tullius, however, gives the order in reverse. For in Book VI of *The Republic* he says:

> Nature has arranged it so that the outermost bodies sound gravely on one side and acutely on the other. For this reason that highest course of the star-bearing heaven, whose revolution is swifter, is moved by an acute and elevated sound, while this lunar and lowest sphere is moved by the gravest sound.

Tullius places the earth as a kind of silence, since it remains motionless and fixed in the lowest position. After this, the body nearest to silence gives the moon the gravest sound. Thus the moon is proslambanomenos, Mercury hypate hypaton, Venus parhypate hypaton, the Sun lichanos hypaton, Mars hypate meson, [Col. 1193A] Jupiter parhypate meson, Saturn lichanos meson, and the outermost heaven mese.

Which of these are immobile, which wholly mobile, and which remain both immobile and mobile will be more appropriately explained when we discuss the regular division of the monochord.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. What the nature of consonances is

Although the sense of hearing also judges consonance, reason weighs it. Whenever two strings, one lower than the other, are tuned and struck together, producing a sound blended in some way and pleasing, and when two notes seem to combine and coalesce into one, then what is called consonance occurs.

But when, struck together, each seeks to proceed on its own and they do not blend into a pleasing sound at the ear, a single sound composed of two, then what is called dissonance occurs.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Where consonances are found

In these comparisons of low and high pitch, those consonances necessarily occur which are commensurable with one another—that is, which can have a common measure. Thus, in multiple ratios, in the double ratio, the part that measures the two terms is their difference: between two and four, two measures both; between two and six, which is triple, two measures both; between nine and eight, the same unit measures both.

Again, among superparticular ratios, if the ratio is sesquialter—such as four to six—two is the measure of both, being their difference. If the ratio is sesquitertian, as when eight is compared with six, the same two measures both.

This does not occur in the other kinds of inequalities mentioned above, such as the superpartient. If we compare five with three, the difference between them, two, measures neither. Compared once with three, it is smaller; doubled, it exceeds three. Likewise, compared twice with five, it is smaller; on the third comparison it surpasses it.

For this reason this first kind of inequality is separated from the nature of consonance—still more because there are many similarities among the ratios that form consonances, whereas in those others there are scarcely any. This can be shown as follows: the double is nothing other than twice the simple; the triple nothing other than three times the simple; the quadruple is likewise four times the simple. The sesquialter is twice a half; the sesquitertian is three times a third. Such relations are not easily found in the other kinds of inequality.

## CHAPTER XXX. How Plato says that consonances arise

Plato [Note: [Col. 1193] “However.”] says that consonance is produced in the ear in the following way. The higher sound, he says, must be swifter. When it has preceded the lower sound, it enters the ear rapidly; and, having struck the farthest part of the same body, it returns through a repeated motion as though thrown back. But now it is slower, and not as swift as when it ran forth at the first impulse; consequently it is also lower.

When, therefore, on returning in a lower form, it encounters for the first time a sound coming toward it that resembles the low sound, it mingles with it and, as Plato says, forms one consonance. [Note: [Col. 1193] “As Plato says, it is not found.”]

## CHAPTER XXXI. What Nicomachus thinks against Plato

Nicomachus does not consider this account truthful. He does not think that consonance is produced by similar things, but rather by dissimilar things coming together into one and the same consonance. If a lower sound is mingled with a lower sound, it produces no consonance, because the harmony of singing is not produced by similarity but by dissimilarity.

Although this dissimilarity separates the individual notes, it is joined together in their mixture. Nicomachus instead thinks consonance arises in the following way. There is not merely one impulse that sends out a single form of sound; rather, once struck, a string repeatedly drives the air and produces many sounds. But because the speed of the striking is such [Note: [Col. 1193] “So that one sound embraces another by reason of the interval.”] that one sound in some way embraces another, the interval is not perceived, and the sound reaches the ears as though it were one.

If, therefore, the strikes of the low sounds are commensurable with the strikes of the high sounds, as in the ratios mentioned above, there is no doubt that this very commensurability blends them together and produces one consonance of the notes.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Which consonance ought to precede the others

Among all the consonances we have mentioned, a judgment must be made, both for the ear and for reason, as to which should be considered the better. The ear is affected by sounds, and the eye by sights, in the same way that the mind’s judgment is affected by numbers or continuous quantity.

Given a number or a line, nothing is easier than for the eye or the mind to apprehend its double. After the apprehension of the double comes that of the half; after the half, that of the triple; after the triple, that of the third part. Since the representation of the double is easier, Nicomachus considers the diapason the best consonance. After this comes the diapente, which holds the middle position; then the diapente together with the diapason, which is the triple. [Note: [Col. 1193] “And the remaining consonances.”] He judges the remaining consonances according to the same order and pattern.

Ptolemy does not proceed in the same way. I shall explain his entire position later.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. How the foregoing statements should be understood

[Col. 1194D]

Let us now briefly and summarily attend to all the matters that will subsequently require more careful explanation, so that for the moment these things may accustom the reader’s mind to them on the surface, while in a later treatment he descends to the inner knowledge.

It was customary among the Pythagoreans that, whenever something was said by the teacher Pythagoras, no one dared to demand reasons for it; the teacher’s authority served as the reason. This continued [Note: [Col. 1193] “As long as.”] until the learner’s mind, strengthened by firmer instruction, could itself discover the same account of things without a teacher. In the same way, we now commend what we propose to the reader’s trust, asking him to accept that the diapason rests on the double ratio, the diapente on the sesquialter, the diatessaron on the sesquitertian, the diapente together with the diapason on the triple ratio, and the bisdiapason on the quadruple ratio. [Note: [Col. 1195] “Afterward reason will explain it more carefully.”]

Later, reason will explain this more carefully, as well as the ways in which musical consonances are apprehended by the judgment of the ears. A fuller treatment will also expound everything said above: that the tone makes the sesquioctave ratio and cannot be divided into two equal parts, just as no ratio of the same kind—that is, no superparticular ratio—can be so divided; that the diatessaron consonance consists of two tones and a semitone; that there are two semitones, a greater and a lesser; that the diapente contains three tones and a lesser semitone; and that the diapason is completed by five tones and two lesser semitones, never reaching six tones in any way.

I shall establish all these matters later, both by numerical reasoning and by the judgment of the ears. For the present, this is enough.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. What a musician is

We must now observe that every art and every discipline naturally possesses a more honorable rational understanding than the practical skill exercised by the hands and by the work of the artisan. It is far greater and higher to know what one is doing than merely to accomplish the thing one knows how to do. Bodily craftsmanship serves like a slave; reason, like a mistress, commands. Unless the hands produce what reason prescribes, the work is done in vain.

How much more excellent, then, is musical knowledge in the understanding of reason than in the mere execution and performance of the work—by as much, plainly, as the mind surpasses the body! The body, deprived of reason, lives in servitude, whereas reason commands and leads toward what is right. Unless the work obeys its command, it will falter because it lacks reason.

Thus rational contemplation does not require practical execution, whereas the work of the hands is nothing unless it is guided by reason. The glory and merit of reason can also be understood from the fact that other, so to speak, bodily craftsmen have received their names not from a discipline but rather from the instruments themselves.
