Thus a citharoedus is named from the cithara, a tibicen from the tibia, [Note: [Col. 1195] “A flute-player.”] and others likewise from the names of their instruments.

A musician, however, is one who, after considering reason, assumes the knowledge of singing not as the servant of practical work but as the commander of contemplation. We see the same thing in the work of buildings and wars, and in the corresponding use of the term: buildings are named, or triumphs are conducted, after those by whose command and reasoning they were organized, not after those whose labor and service completed them.

There are therefore three kinds of people concerned with the art of music. One kind works with instruments; another composes songs; the third judges the work of instruments and songs.

Those who devote themselves entirely to instruments and spend all their labor there—such as citharoedi and those who demonstrate skill on the organ and other musical instruments—are separated from understanding the science of music. As has been said, they serve; they contribute nothing by reason and are wholly without contemplative understanding.

The second kind consists of poets who practice music. They are carried toward song not so much by contemplation and reason as by a kind of natural instinct. For this reason this kind, too, must be separated from music.

The third kind possesses expertise in judging, so that it can assess rhythms, melodies, and their songs. Since this is wholly grounded in reason and contemplation, it is properly assigned to music. A musician is one who possesses the ability, according to the proposed and appropriate principles of contemplation and reason, to judge modes and rhythms, kinds of melodies, combinations, and all the matters that will be explained later, as well as the songs of poets.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 1195]

## CHAPTER I. Preface

[Col. 1195D]

The preceding volume set out everything that I have now proposed to explain more carefully. Therefore, before I come to the matters that must be fully demonstrated by their proper arguments, I shall first set forth a few preliminary points, so that the listener’s mind, made more diligent by study, may be prepared to receive what is to be said.

## CHAPTER II. What Pythagoras established philosophy to be

Pythagoras was the first of all to call the pursuit of wisdom “philosophy.” He defined it as the knowledge and discipline of that which could properly and truly be said to exist. He thought that those things existed which neither increased by extension nor diminished by diminution, nor were altered by any accidents. These are forms, magnitudes, qualities, relations, and other things which, contemplated in themselves, are immutable, but which, when joined to bodies, are transformed and altered through their connection with a mutable thing in many kinds of variation.

## CHAPTER III. On the differences of quantity and the discipline assigned to each

According to Pythagoras, all quantity is either continuous or discrete. Continuous quantity is called magnitude; discrete quantity is called multitude. Their properties are almost entirely different and contrary.

Multitude begins with a finite quantity and proceeds by increasing into the infinite, so that no end to its growth is encountered. It is bounded at the minimum but unbounded at the maximum. Its principle is the unit, than which nothing is smaller. It increases through numbers and extends into infinity; no number sets a limit by which it can cease increasing.

Magnitude, on the other hand, receives a finite quantity according to its measure, but decreases into infinity. If there is a line one foot long, or of any other measure, it can be divided into two equal parts; its half can be divided into a half, and that half again into another half, so that no limit is ever imposed on the division of the magnitude.

Thus magnitude is bounded with respect to greater size, but becomes infinite when it begins to decrease. Number, by contrast, is finite with respect to lesser size, but begins to be infinite when it increases.

Although these things are infinite in this way, philosophy nevertheless treats them as though they were finite things, and within infinite things discovers something bounded to which it may rightly apply the acuity of its own contemplation.

Some magnitudes are immobile, such as the earth, a square, a triangle, or a circle. Others are mobile, such as the sphere of the universe and everything that revolves within it at a fixed speed.

Among discrete quantities, some exist in themselves, such as three, four, and the other numbers; others exist in relation to something else, such as the double and the triple, and the other things that arise from comparison.

Geometry holds the contemplation of immobile magnitude. Astronomy pursues the science of mobile magnitude. Arithmetic governs discrete quantity considered in itself. Music is acknowledged to possess expertise in discrete quantity related to something else.

## CHAPTER IV. On the differences of related quantity

We have sufficiently discussed discrete quantity considered in itself, which belongs to arithmetic. Related quantity has three simple kinds: the multiple, the superparticular, and the superpartient.

When the multiple is combined with the superparticular and the superpartient, two further kinds arise from them: the multiple-superparticular and the multiple-superpartient.

The rule for all these is as follows. If you wish to compare the unit with all the natural numbers, the order of multiples will be formed. Two compared with one is double; three compared with the same is triple; four is quadruple; and so on in the same manner, as the following arrangement shows.

If you seek a superparticular ratio, compare a natural number with the one immediately preceding it, after subtracting one: thus three is sesquialter in relation to two; four to three is sesquitertian; five to four is sesquiquartan; and so forth, as the following arrangement demonstrates. [Col. 1198B]

You will find the superpartients in the following way. Arrange the natural numbers beginning with three. If you omit one, you will recognize a superbipartient ratio; if you omit two, a supertripartient; if you omit three, a superquadripartient; and the same applies to the rest.

A diligent reader, attending to this order, will also contemplate the ratios compounded from the multiple and the superparticular, and from the multiple and the superpartient. But all these matters have been treated more conveniently in the works on arithmetic.

## CHAPTER V. Why multiplicity takes precedence

In these matters it must be considered that the multiple kind of inequality appears to be much older than the other two. The arrangement of the natural numbers is compared, in the multiples, with the unit, which is first. The superparticular, however, is not formed by comparison with the unit, but by comparison of the numbers arranged after the unit: three with two, four with three, and so on in this manner.

The formation of the superpartients lies much farther back. It is not compared with consecutive numbers but with numbers separated by gaps, and not always by equal gaps: now one number is omitted, now two, now three, now four, and so the sequence grows into infinity.

Moreover, multiplicity begins from the unit, superparticularity from two, and the superpartient ratio from three. But enough of this. We must now set forth certain propositions, which the Greeks call *axiomata*, and only when we treat the demonstration of each individual matter shall we understand what they appear to concern. [Note: [Col. 1199] “We understand.”]

## CHAPTER VI. What square numbers are, and the study of them

A square number is one that has grown through a twofold dimension into equality: two times two, three times three, four times four, five times five, six times six. Their arrangement is as follows: [Col. 1199B]

The natural number arranged above is therefore the side of the squares described below. For the squares that follow one another in the order below are naturally consecutive, such as 4, 9, 16, and the others.

If, therefore, I subtract a continuous smaller square from a continuous larger square, the remainder will be equal to what is formed by joining the sides of the two squares. Thus, if I subtract four from nine, five remain; these five are formed from two and three, the sides of the two squares, joined together.

Likewise, if I subtract nine from the number written under sixteen, seven remain; this is formed by joining three and four, which are the sides of the aforementioned squares. The same applies in other cases.

But if the squares are not consecutive and one square has been passed over between them, what is formed by joining the two sides is half of the remainder. Thus, if we subtract the square four from sixteen, twelve remain; half of twelve is the number produced by joining the sides of the two squares. Their sides are two and four, which together make six.

The same method applies in other cases. But if two squares are omitted, what is formed by joining the two sides will be one third of the remainder. Thus, if I subtract four from twenty-five, with two squares omitted between them, twenty-one remain. Their sides are two and five, which make seven; seven is one third of twenty-one.

The rule is therefore that if three squares are omitted [Note: [Col. 1199] “Are.”], the number formed by joining the two sides will be one fourth of what remains when the smaller is subtracted from the larger. If four are passed over, it will be one fifth; and the number of the parts will always exceed by one the number of the omitted squares.

## CHAPTER VII. That every inequality proceeds from equality, and its demonstration
Just as unity is the principle of plurality and number, so equality is the principle of proportions. For by three rules—as stated in the *Arithmetica*—we produce multiple proportions from equality; from reversed multiples we generate superparticular relationships; and from reversed superparticular relationships we form superpartient comparisons.

Let three units be posited, or three twos, or three threes, or any number of equal terms. Let the first be equal to the first term in the next order; the second to the first and second; and the third to the first, two second terms, and the third. As the number thus advances, the first multiple proportion becomes double, as the following description indicates [Col. 1200B]. For the unit placed in the second order is equal to the first unit arranged above it. Likewise, two is equal to the first and second units. Likewise, four is equal to the first unit, two second units, and the third unit; thus the arrangement is 1, 2, 4, a double proportion.

If the same is done with these, a triple comparison will be produced; from the triple, a quadruple; from the quadruple, a quintuple; and thereafter the generation of such relationships proceeds in the same manner.

Again, by these same three rules, superparticular proportions are produced [Note: [Col. 1199] “Will be produced” (*fient*)], as we show by one example [Col. 1200C]. Let us now reverse the order and arrange the larger number first: 4, 2, 1. Let the first be equal to the first, that is, 4; the second to the first and second, that is, 6; and the third to the first, two second terms, and the third, that is, 9. When these have been arranged, a sesquialterous proportion is indicated. If the same is done with triples, a sesquitertian proportion results; with quadruples, a sesquiquartan proportion; and similarly, with corresponding names on either side, proportionality arises from multiplicity. From superparticularity, however, a superpartient relationship is derived in reverse order [Col. 1200D].

Let a sesquialterous comparison be arranged in reverse: 9, 6, 4. Let the first be equal to the first, that is, 9; the second to the first and second, that is, 15; and the third to the first, two second terms, and the third, that is, 25. Let them be arranged in order as follows. Thus a superbipartient relationship has been produced from reversed sesquialterous relationships [Col. 1201A]. If an attentive investigator applies himself to this inquiry, he will produce a supertripartient relationship from reversed sesquitertian relationships; and, with the corresponding names likewise adjusted, he will marvel that all the species of superpartient relationships are generated from superparticularity.

From unreversed superparticular relationships, remaining in the form in which they were produced from multiplicity, multiple superparticular relationships must be created. From superpartient relationships remaining in the form in which they arose from superparticular relationships, no others but multiple superpartient relationships will be produced. Enough on this subject for now, since the matter has been discussed more fully in the books of the *Arithmetica*.

## CHAPTER VIII. The rule for finding any number of continuous superparticular proportions

[Col. 1201B]

It often happens that a student of music seeks three, four, or any number of equal superparticular proportions. But so that no error arising from chance or ignorance may obstruct those who attempt this, by this rule we shall derive any number of equal proportions from multiplicity. Every multiple, counted from unity, precedes as many superparticular relationships—named in the contrary direction—as the number by which it has departed from unity [Note: [Col. 1201] Has departed.].

Thus the double precedes sesquialterous relationships, the triple sesquitertian relationships, the quadruple sesquiquartan relationships, and so forth in this manner.

Let the following be an arrangement of doubles [Col. 1201C].

In the preceding arrangement the first multiple, two, has beside it a three which can form a sesquialterous proportion. Three, however, has no other number that can be its sesquialter, since it lacks a half. Again, four is the second double; it precedes two sesquialters, six and nine, the latter of which lacks a half. Therefore no sesquialterous relationship corresponds to it; and the same applies in the other cases.

Triples likewise generate sesquitertian relationships in the same manner. Let there be a similar arrangement of triples [Col. 1201D].

In the preceding arrangement we see that sesquitertian proportions arise in such a way that the first triple [Note: [Col. 1201] The ternary.] precedes one sesquitertian, the second two, and the third three [Col. 1202A]; and the third part is always closed by a natural limit in the final number.

If you establish quadruples in the same manner, you will find sesquiquartan relationships; if quintuples, sesquiquintan relationships. Thereafter, each multiple [Note: [Col. 1201] Multiples by denomination.] precedes as many superparticular relationships as the number of places by which it has itself departed from unity.

We shall present only one arrangement of quadruples, so that in it, as in the others, the diligent reader may exercise his intellectual acuity.

This inquiry appears to have been devised for the following purpose: whenever someone wishes to investigate four, five, or any number of sesquialterous, sesquitertian, sesquioctaval, or other proportions, he should not fall into error by trying to fit such proportions to a first number that cannot precede and follow as many terms as are proposed [Col. 1202B]. Instead, he should arrange the multiples and observe how many superparticular relationships are required. He should then attend to the multiple that has departed from unity by the number of places in question, as in the preceding arrangements.

Thus, if he should seek three sesquialters [Note: [Col. 1201] Sesquialterous proportions.], he should not begin his investigation with four. For since this is the second double, it precedes only two and cannot accommodate a third; instead, he should try to place halves beginning with eight [Col. 1202C]. Since this is the third, it will produce the three sesquialterous proportions he seeks. The same applies in the other cases.

There is also another way of increasing proportions, as follows. The roots of proportions are called the smallest proportions in the same comparisons. Let a natural number multiplied by unity be arranged. The smallest proportions are, for example, in the sesquialterous relationship, 3 to 2; in the sesquitertian, 4 to 3; in the sesquiquartan, 5 to 4; and so forth without limit—indeed, all the proportions that precede one another by unity.

Suppose, then, that it is proposed to produce two sesquialterous proportions in continuous comparison [Col. 1202D]. I take the sesquialterous root and arrange it as 2 and 3. I multiply two by two, producing 4. Likewise, I increase three by two, producing 6. Again, I multiply three by itself, producing 9. These are arranged as follows. Thus we find the two proposed sesquialterous proportions: 6 to 4 and 9 to 6.

Now suppose that it is proposed to find three. I arrange the same numbers that I previously proposed for finding two sesquialterous relationships [Note: [Col. 1201] In seeking them], together with the sesquialterous proportions themselves [Col. 1203A]. I multiply four by two, producing eight. Again, I multiply six by two, producing 12. Again, I multiply nine by two, producing 18. Again, I multiply nine by three, producing 27. Let these be arranged as follows.

The same procedure applies in other cases, so that [Note: [Col. 1203] Which] if you wish to extend sesquitertian proportions, place the roots of the sesquitertians, namely four and three, compared with one another [Col. 1203B]. If you arrange the roots of the sesquiquartans, you will likewise extend as many sesquiquartan proportions as you wish [Note: [Col. 1203] Extend] by the same multiplication. The following sequence will show how useful these considerations are.

## CHAPTER IX. On the proportion of numbers measured by other numbers

If the difference between two numbers measures them exactly, the numbers measured by their own difference are in the same proportion as the numbers according to which their difference measures them.

Let the numbers be 50 and 55. These are compared with one another in a sesquidecimal relationship, and their difference is five, which is a tenth part of 50. Five therefore measures 50 ten times, but 55 eleven times [Col. 1203C]. Thus, according to the numbers 10 and 11, the proper difference of 55 and 50—that is, five—measures them, and 11 to 10 forms a sesquidecimal comparison.

The numbers whose own difference has measured them exactly [Note: [Col. 1203] Exactly] are therefore in the same proportion as the numbers according to which their own difference has measured them.

But if a difference measures the numbers of which it is the difference in such a way that the plurality of the numbers exceeds that same measure, and the excess is the same in both, and the measure of the difference is smaller than the plurality of the numbers, the numbers will have a greater proportion to one another if what remains after the measurement is subtracted from both than they had when they were whole and their own difference measured them [Col. 1203D].

Let the two numbers be 53 and 58, and let their difference, five, measure them [Note: [Col. 1203] Measured them]. Five measures 53 ten times, up to 50, but leaves three. Again, the same five measures 58 eleven times, up to 55, and once again leaves three. Let three therefore be removed from both; the results are 50 and 55, which are arranged as follows.

It is therefore clear that 50 and 55 have a greater proportion to one another than 53 and 58. In smaller numbers a greater proportion is always found, as we shall demonstrate shortly [Col. 1204A].

But if that measurement by the difference exceeds the plurality of the numbers, and exceeds both numbers by the same numerical amount, the numbers measured above, with the addition of the sum by which the difference exceeds both, will have smaller proportions than they had previously, when their own difference measured them.

Let the numbers be 48 and 53, whose difference is five. Let five measure 48: ten times five produces 50. Thus 50 exceeds 48 by two. Let the same five measure 53 eleven times: the result is 55, which likewise exceeds 53 by two. Let two be added to both and let them be arranged as follows [Col. 1204B].

The proportions of 50 to 55, with the addition of the two by which the difference measuring them exceeds them, are therefore smaller than those of 48 and 53, which were measured by the same difference of five, although that difference exceeded them.

Greater and smaller proportions are understood in this way. One-half is greater than one-third; one-third is greater than one-fourth; one-fourth is greater than one-fifth; and so forth in the same manner. Hence a sesquialterous proportion is greater than a sesquitertian, and a sesquitertian surpasses a sesquiquartan. The same applies in other cases.

From this it follows that among larger numbers the superparticular proportion always appears smaller, and among smaller numbers greater. This is evident in the natural numbers. Let the natural numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 be arranged [Col. 1204C]. Two is double in relation to one; three is sesquialterous in relation to two; and four is sesquitertian in relation to three. The larger numbers are three and four [Note: [Col. 1203] Three and four]; the smaller are two and one. Thus the smaller proportion is contained in the larger numbers, and the greater proportion in the smaller numbers.

From this it is evident that if an equal plurality is added to numbers containing a superparticular proportion, the proportion before the equal increase will be greater than after an equal plurality has been added to them.

## CHAPTER X. What multiple proportions arise when multiple and superparticular proportions are multiplied [Note: [Col. 1203] “Multiplied” (*multiplicatis*)]

This too should not be omitted: as will be demonstrated shortly [Col. 1204D], if a multiple interval is multiplied by two, what arises from that multiplication will also be multiple. If, however, what is produced by such multiplication is not multiple, then that which has been multiplied by two is not multiple.

Likewise, if a superparticular proportion is multiplied by two, the result is neither superparticular [Note: [Col. 1203] Or] nor multiple [Note: [Col. 1203] Or]. But if what arises from such multiplication is neither multiple nor superparticular, then that which has been multiplied by two is either superparticular or of another kind, but not multiple.

## CHAPTER XI. Which superparticular proportions produce which multiples

[Col. 1205A]

To this we must add that the first two superparticular proportions together produce the first multiple proportion: thus the sesquialter and the sesquitertian, when joined, create a double. Let the numbers be 2, 3, 4 [Note: [Col. 1205] Three in relation to two]. Three is sesquialterous in relation to two; four is sesquitertian in relation to three; and four in relation to two is double.

Again, the first multiple added to the first superparticular produces the second multiple. Let the numbers be 2, 4, 6. Four is double in relation to two, and is therefore the first multiple. Six is sesquialterous in relation to four, and is the first superparticular. Six is triple in relation to two, and is therefore the second multiple.

If you add the triple to the sesquitertian, a quadruple is produced; if the quadruple to the sesquiquartan, a quintuple. In this manner, by joining multiple and superparticular proportions, multiple proportions are produced without limit [Col. 1205B].

## CHAPTER XII. On the arithmetic, geometric, and harmonic means

Since we have already stated what had to be treated for the time being concerning proportions, we must now speak of means. A proportion is a certain comparison of two terms with one another; by “terms” I mean the sums of numbers. Proportionality is a collection of equal proportions.

Proportionality properly consists of three smallest terms, although it often consists of more, such as four or six terms. When the first term retains the same proportion to the second that the second retains to the third, this is called proportionality. Among three terms, the middle term is the second [Col. 1205C].

The proportions joining the middle term form a threefold division. Either the difference of the smaller term from the middle is equal to the difference of the middle from the largest, but the proportion is not equal, as in the numbers 1, 2, 3. Between one and two, and between two and three, the difference is one; but the proportion is not equal. Two is double one, while three is sesquialterous in relation to two.

Or the proportion in both cases is equal, though the differences are not equal, as in the numbers 1, 2, 4. Two is double one, just as four is double two. But the difference between four and two is two, while that between two and one is one.

There is a third kind of mean, which consists neither of the same proportions nor of the same differences. Rather, as the largest term is related to the smallest, so the difference of the larger terms is related to the difference of the smaller terms, as in the numbers 3, 4, 6 [Col. 1205D]. Six is double three; the difference between six and four is two, while that between four and three is one. But two compared with one is again double. Thus, as the largest term in the numbers is related to the smallest, so the difference of the larger terms is related to the difference of the smaller terms.

The mean in which the differences are equal is therefore called arithmetic; that in which the proportions are equal is called geometric; and that which we described third is called harmonic [Col. 1206A]. We shall provide examples of these below.

We are not unaware that there are also other means of proportions, which we discussed in the *Arithmetica*; but for the present discussion these are sufficient. Among these three means, proportionality is properly and especially called geometric, because it is entirely composed of equal proportions. Nevertheless, we shall use the term indiscriminately, also calling the others proportionalities.

## CHAPTER XIII. On continuous and disjunct means

[Col. 1206B]

Among these, one proportionality is continuous and another disjunct. The continuous is as we arranged it above [Note: [Col. 1205] It consists of three terms.]. For one and the same middle number is placed now after the greater term and now before the smaller term.

Whenever there are two middle terms, the proportionality is called disjunct, as in the geometric proportion 1, 2, 3, 6. For as two is to one, so six is to three; and this is called disjunct proportionality. From this it may be understood that continuous proportionality is found in three—the smallest number of terms—whereas disjunct proportionality is found in four [Col. 1206C].

Continuous proportionality can also exist in four and more terms, provided it is arranged in this way: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Here, however, there will not be two proportions but more, always one fewer than the number of terms established.

## CHAPTER XIV. Why the means described above have been so named

One of these means is called arithmetic because there is an equal difference between the terms according to number. The second is called geometric because the quality of the proportion is similar. The harmonic is so called because it is arranged in such a way that equality of proportions is observed in the differences and the terms [Col. 1206D].

These matters have been discussed more fully in the *Arithmetica*. Here, however, we have merely reviewed them in order to recall them.

## CHAPTER XV. How the means described above arise from equality

We must briefly explain how these proportionalities are generated from equality [Note: [Col. 1205] Are produced]. For it was stated that in number unity has the same force that equality has in proportions; and just as unity is the head of numbers, so equality is the principle of proportions.

The arithmetic mean therefore arises from equality in this way. When three equal terms have been posited, there are two ways in which this proportionality can be produced. Let the first be equal to the first; the second to the first and second; and the third to the first, second, and third. This is shown by the following example.

Let there be three units. Let the first be equal to the first, that is, one. Let the second be equal to the first and second, that is, two. Let the third be equal to the first, second, and third, that is, three. The arrangement will therefore be as follows [Col. 1207A] [Note: [Col. 1207] This].

Again, let three twos be established in equality: 2, 2, 2. Let the first be equal to the first, that is, 2. Let the second be equal to the first and second, that is, 4. Let the third be equal to the first, second, and third, that is, 6. The arrangement will be as follows [Note: [Col. 1207] Again, the same with three].

In these examples we must observe that when unity is established as the principle of equality, unity is also the difference between the numbers, and the numbers themselves leave no number between them. If two maintains the equality, two is the difference, and one number is always interposed between the terms. If three is likewise the difference, two naturally constituted numbers are interposed between the terms [Col. 1207B]; and so forth in the same manner.

There is also another way of producing arithmetic proportionality. Let three equal terms be posited, and let the first be equal to the first and second; the second to the first and two second terms; and the third to the first, two second terms, and the third. Thus, if there are three units, let the first be equal to the first and second [Note: [Col. 1207] First], that is, to two. Let the second be equal to the first and two second terms, that is, to three. Let the third be equal to the first, two second terms, and the third, that is, to four [Col. 1207C].

Here unity constitutes the difference between the terms. Between two and one, and between three and two, there is a difference of one. No natural number is interposed. For after one comes two, and after two comes three, naturally constituted.

Let the same be done again with twos. Let there be three twos, and let the first be equal to the first and second, that is, four; the second to the first and two second terms, that is, six; and the third to the first, two second terms, and the third, that is, eight.

Here too two constitutes the difference between the terms, with one natural number interposed between them [Col. 1207D]. For five is naturally interposed between 4 and 6, and seven is placed between 6 and 8.

If three is the principle of equality, the difference will be three. For example, let three terms be arranged below according to the preceding rules [Note: [Col. 1207] Three numbers]. In these, therefore, three is the difference, and two numbers are interposed—that is, always one fewer than the difference between the numbers [Col. 1208A]. The same is evident in the case of four and five, and the diligent reader will discover for himself, by the same rules, the cases that we omit for the sake of brevity.

We showed how geometric proportionality can be found arising from equality when we were demonstrating how all inequality flows from equality [Note: [Col. 1207] We shall show that it flows forth]. Since it is not tedious, it should now be repeated briefly. Let three equal terms be established. Let the first be equal to the first; the second to the first and second; and the third to the first, two second terms, and the third [Note: [Col. 1207] Third]. Let the same be done continuously, and thus geometric proportionality will take its beginning from equality.

We have discussed the properties of these proportions with the greatest care in the *Arithmetica*. If a reader approaches these matters equipped with that knowledge, he will not be troubled by any uncertainty or error [Col. 1208B].

The harmonic mean, which must now be treated somewhat more fully, is generated in this way. If we are concerned to form doubles, let three equal terms be posited. Let the first be equal to the first and two second terms; the second to two first terms and two second terms; and the third to one first term, twice the second, and three times the third.

Thus, let the terms be units. Let the first be equal to the first and two second terms, that is, three. Let the second be equal to two first terms and two second terms, that is, four. Let the third be equal to the first, two second terms, and three third terms, that is, six [Col. 1208C].

If equality is constructed in twos or in threes [Note: [Col. 1207] Is established], the same kind of mean appears, with the terms and differences separated from one another by a double interval, as the following arrangements indicate.

If a triple proportion is to be made at the extremes, let three equal terms be established. The first is to be made from the first and second; the second from the first and two second terms; and the third from the first, two second terms, and three third terms, as the following description shows.

Since we have entered upon a discussion of the harmonic mean, I do not think that matters which can be stated about it more fully should be silently passed over. Let harmonic proportionality be arranged, and in it let the differences among the terms in the preceding arrangement be set out in order [Col. 1209A].

Do you see, then, how four to three produces the *diatessaron* consonance—“the fourth”—six to four agrees in the *diapente*—“the fifth”—and six to three joins in the *diapason* symphony—“the octave”? Their differences likewise establish the same consonance again [Col. 1209B].

Two is double in relation to one, constituting the *diapason* consonance. If the extreme terms are multiplied together and the middle term likewise increases by multiplication with itself [Note: [Col. 1209] By multiplication], the numbers compared will preserve the relationship and concord of a tone. Three times six produces 18, while four times four produces 16 [Note: [Col. 1209] Produce]. But 18 exceeds 16 by an eighth part.

Again, if the smallest term multiplies itself, it produces 9. If the larger term increases by multiplication with itself, it produces 36; these, compared with one another, preserve a quadruple consonance, that is, a double *diapason*.

If we examine this more carefully, the whole operation consists in multiplying the differences or terms by one another [Col. 1209C]. If the smallest term is multiplied by the middle, the result is 12 [Note: [Col. 1209] They produce]. If the smallest term is multiplied by the largest, the result is 18. If the middle term is increased by the numerical quantity of the largest [Note: [Col. 1209] For], the result is 24. Again, if the smallest term increases by itself, the result is 9 [Note: [Col. 1209] And in the same way]. Likewise, if the middle term does so, the result is 16. Six, which is the largest, if it multiplies itself, produces 36.

Let these therefore be arranged in order: 36, 24, 18, 16, 12, 9 [Col. 1209D].

The *diatessaron* consonance—the fourth—is sounded by 24 to 18 and by 12 to 9. The *diapente*—the fifth—is sounded by 18 to 12, by 24 to 16, and by 36 to 24. The triple proportion, which is the *diapason* and *diapente*—the octave and fifth—is 36 to 12. The quadruple proportion, which is the double *diapason*—the double octave—is 36 to 9. The *epogdous*, the tone or eighth-part proportion, is preserved in the comparison of 18 to 16.

## CHAPTER XVI. How the means described above are successively placed between two terms

[Col. 1210A]

Two terms are often given and proposed, so that an arithmetic, geometric, or harmonic mean may be placed between them. We have also discussed these matters in the *Arithmetica*, but we shall now explain them briefly.

If an arithmetic mean is sought, the difference between the given terms must be observed, divided, and added to the smaller term [Note: [Col. 1209] And this]. Let the terms placed at opposite ends be 10 and 40 [Note: [Col. 1209] Between 40 and 10], and let their mean according to arithmetic proportionality be sought. I first consider their difference, which is 30. I divide this, producing 15, and add it to the smaller term, namely 10 [Note: [Col. 1209] The ten], producing 25. If this is placed between 10 and 40, the arithmetic proportionality is formed as follows: 10, 25, 40 [Col. 1210C].

Let us likewise place a geometric mean between the same terms. I multiply the extremes by their own numerical values: 10 times 40 produces 400. I take the square root of this, producing 20 [Note: [Col. 1209] Twenty]. For twenty times twenty produces 400. If I place 20 between 10 and 40 [Note: [Col. 1209] We place it], the geometric mean is formed as follows: 10, 20, 40.

If we seek a harmonic mean, we join the extremes to one another, so that 10 and 40 produce 50. Let us multiply their difference, which is 30, by the smaller term, namely 10 [Note: [Col. 1209] We multiply], so that thirty times ten produces 300. If this is divided according to 50, the result is 6. When this is added to the smaller term, the result is 16. If we place this number as the mean between 10 and 40, harmonic proportionality is obtained: 10, 16, 40 [Col. 1210D].

## CHAPTER XVII. On the pattern of consonances according to Nicomachus

Enough on these matters [Note: [Col. 1209] Concerning these]. It now seems appropriate to add how the Pythagoreans prove that musical consonances are found in the proportions mentioned above. Ptolemy does not appear to agree with them in this matter [Note: [Col. 1209] Agreeing], as we shall discuss shortly.

The first and most agreeable consonance must be established as that whose nature the more evident sense apprehends. For whatever something is in itself, such is it also perceived by the senses. If, therefore, the consonance that consists in doubleness is more familiar to everyone, there is no doubt that the *diapason*—the octave—is the first of all consonances and rightly surpasses the others, since it precedes them in intelligibility.

According to the Pythagoreans, the remaining consonances necessarily occupy the order established by the increases of multiplicity and the decreases of superparticular relationships. For it has been shown that multiple inequality surpasses superparticular proportions in priority and rank.

Let the natural numbers from unity to four therefore be arranged: 1, 2, 3, 4. Two compared with one produces a double proportion and yields the *diapason* consonance, which is the greatest and, by its simplicity, the most familiar [Col. 1211A].

If three is compared with one, it will sound the concord of the *diapason* and *diapente*—the octave and fifth. Four compared with one maintains a quadruple proportion, producing the symphony of the double *diapason*. If three is compared with two, the result is the *diapente*. If four is compared with three, it supplies the *diatessaron* consonance—the fourth [Note: [Col. 1211] Consonance]. This is the order of all of them when compared with one another [Col. 1211B].

For the remaining comparison—if we compare four with two—falls into the double proportion that two held when compared with one [Note: [Col. 1211] And]. Thus the sounds are farthest apart in the double *diapason*, when they depart from one another by a quadruple measure of interval.

The interval is smallest when the higher exceeds the lower by a third part of the lower, and thereafter the order of consonances is established. It can neither extend beyond the quadruple nor be compressed within the third part.

According to Nicomachus, then, this is the order of the consonances: first the *diapason* (octave); second the *diapason* and *diapente* (octave and fifth); third the double *diapason* (double octave); fourth the *diapente* (fifth); fifth the *diatessaron* (fourth).

## CHAPTER XVIII. The view of Eubulides and Hippasus concerning the order of the consonances

Eubulides and Hippasus, however, establish another order of consonances. They say that the increases of multiplicity correspond in due order to the decreases of superparticularity [Col. 1211C]. Thus there can be no double without a half, nor a triple without a third part.

Since there is a double, therefore, the *diapason* consonance is produced from it. Since there is a half, from it, as if by contrary division, a sesquialterous proportion is produced, that is, the *diapente*.

When these are joined—the *diapason* and the *diapente*—a triple is produced, containing both symphonies. But again, the third part of the triple is divided by contrary division, and from it the *diatessaron* symphony arises.

When the triple and the sesquitertian are joined, they produce a quadruple proportional comparison. Hence the *diapason* and *diapente*, which together form one consonance, and the *diatessaron*, one consonance [Note: [Col. 1211] Consonance], are joined into a single whole; because it consists in the quadruple, it receives the name double *diapason* [Col. 1211D].

According to these thinkers, the order is therefore: *diapason* (octave), *diapente* (fifth), *diapason* and *diapente* (octave and fifth), *diatessaron* (fourth), double *diapason* (double octave).

## CHAPTER XIX. Nicomachus’s view of which consonances are assigned to which

[Col. 1212A]

But Nicomachus does not judge the contrary arrangement to be the same. Rather, just as unity in arithmetic was the principle of increase and decrease, so also the diapason symphony is the principle of the remaining consonances; these, however, can be established in relation to it by contrary division. This will be easier to understand if it is first anticipated in numbers. Let unity therefore be established, and let two parts flow from it, one of multiplication and the other of division. Let the following be the scheme: [formula not supplied] [Col. 1212B] And the progression continues in this manner to infinity. For two is double unity. Its contrary part shows one-half of that same unity. Three is triple, and its contrary part is a third. Four is quadruple, and its part is a fourth, with its contrary. Thus, in simple unity, there is the principle of increase and decrease.

Let us now apply the same principle to the consonances. The diapason, which is double, occupies the place of the principle; the remaining consonances are arranged in contrary division as follows. [Col. 1212C] The sesquialter is opposed to the triple, and the sesquiter­tian to the quadruple; this will be proved by the following argument. The first sesquialter is the same as the first principal triple, namely, that of unity. For three is the first triple in relation to unity. It is also the first sesquialter when compared with two. Again, in relation to the difference which it has from two—and whose natural position is proved to be sesquialter—the same three is triple. Since, therefore, the sesquialter is rightly opposed to the triple, the diapente consonance is reasonably judged to be opposed to the consonance of diapente and diapason.

Again, the quadruple holds the contrary division of the sesquiter­tian. For what is the first quadruple is found also to be the first sesquiter­tian, in this way. Four is the first quadruple in relation to unity, and the first sesquiter­tian when compared with three. Again, in relation to the difference which it has between itself and three, it becomes quadruple. [Col. 1212D] Hence the sesquiter­tian proportion, which is the diatessaron, is divided in opposition to the quadruple proportion, which is the bis diapason.

But since the double has no opposed proportion, and is itself not the sesquialter of anything, nor is there any number to which two—the first double—can be joined by a superparticular proportion, this form of contrary proportion exceeds it. And therefore, according to Nicomachus, the diapason occupies the position of the principle in the following manner: [Col. 1213A]

Nevertheless, he says, although the matter stands thus, it is better that all multiple proportions precede the consonances and the superparticular proportions follow, just as we described shortly before.

Since, then, a consonance is a measured blending of two voices, while a sound is the fall of a modulated voice, produced with a single tension, and is itself the smallest particle of modulation; and since every sound is constituted by an impulse, while every impulse arises from motion; and since some motions are equal and others unequal, and among the unequal some are greatly unequal, others less unequal, and others moderately unequal—[Col. 1213B] from equality arises equality of sounds. From inequality, however, those inequalities which are separated by a moderate interval arise as manifest, primary, and simpler proportions, namely, the multiple and superparticular proportions: the double, triple, quadruple, sesquialter, and sesquiter­tian consonances. From those inequalities which occur in the remaining proportions—whether in many forms, or less clearly, or at a great distance from one another—dissonances arise. No concord of sounds is produced.

## CHAPTER XX. What must be prefaced in order to demonstrate the diapason in the multiple genus

[Col. 1213C]

With this distinction established, it will be demonstrated that the diapason consonance, which is the finest of all, is found in the multiple genus of inequality and in the relation of doubleness. First, however, we must demonstrate how the diapason consonance can be recognized in the multiple genus.

We must first address a brief point, the prior understanding of which will make the demonstration easier: whenever one subtracts from a superparticular proportion the continuous superparticular proportion belonging to it—that is, the smaller one—the remainder is less than half of the proportion that was subtracted, as in the sesquialter and sesquiter­tian proportions.

Since the sesquialter is the greater, let us subtract the sesquiter­tian from the sesquialter. The sesquioctave proportion remains, but when doubled it does not produce a complete sesquiter­tian proportion; [Col. 1213D] rather, the interval is smaller, namely that found in the semitone. If a doubled sesquioctave relation is not equal to the complete sesquiter­tian, a single sesquioctave is not the full half of the sesquiter­tian proportion. Likewise, if one subtracts the sesquiquart from the sesquiter­tian, what remains does not constitute half of the sesquiquart; and the same is true in the other cases.

## CHAPTER XXI. Demonstration by impossibility that the diapason belongs to the multiple genus

Let us now return to the diapason consonance. [Col. 1214A] If it does not belong to the multiple genus of inequality, it will fall into the superparticular genus of inequality. Let the diapason consonance therefore be a superparticular proportion. Let its continuous consonance, namely the diapente, be subtracted from it; the diatessaron remains.

Twice the diatessaron is therefore less than one diapente, and the diatessaron itself does not fill half of the diapente consonance, which is impossible. For it will be shown that twice the diatessaron exceeds the diapente consonance by a tone and a semitone. Therefore the diapason cannot be placed in the superparticular genus of inequality. [Col. 1214B]

## CHAPTER XXII. Demonstration by impossibility that the diapente, diatessaron, and tone belong to the superparticular genus

[Col. 1214C]

It remains, then, to demonstrate that the diapente, the diatessaron, and the tone must be placed in the superparticular genus. Although this was already made sufficiently clear in the first proof, by which we showed that the diapason should not be placed in the superparticular genus, let us nevertheless treat the matter separately and more carefully.

If someone denies that these relations should be placed in the superparticular genus, he will admit that they must be located in the multiple genus. For it was explained above, as I believe, why they cannot be placed in the superpartient or in the other mixed genera.

Let them therefore, if possible, be placed in the multiple genus. Since the diatessaron consonance is smaller and the diapente greater, let the diatessaron be assigned to the double proportion and the diapente to the triple proportion of multiplicity. For it is plausible that, just as the diatessaron is a consonance continuous with the diapente, so, if the diatessaron is established in the double, the diapente should be placed in the multiple proportion continuous with the double, namely the triple. The tone, however, since it is placed after the diatessaron in musical relations, should evidently be placed in the proportion that is smaller than the double. But this cannot be found in the multiple genus. It remains, therefore, that it fall into the superparticular relation.

Let the proportion of the tone therefore be the first, namely the sesquialter. For if we subtract the double from the triple, the remainder is the sesquialter. If, then, the diatessaron is double and the diapente triple, [Col. 1215A] when the diatessaron is subtracted from the diapente, the remaining tone is produced. There can be no doubt, therefore, that the tone must be established in the sesquialter proportion.

But two sesquialter proportions exceed the double, as anyone instructed in arithmetic can gather for himself. Thus two tones will exceed the diatessaron, which is incongruous: for the diatessaron exceeds two tones by the interval of a semitone. It is therefore impossible for the diapente and diatessaron not to be placed in the superparticular genus of inequality.

If someone should also insist that the tone belongs to the multiple genus, since the tone is smaller than the diatessaron, and the diatessaron is smaller than the diapente, let the diapente be placed in the quadruple, the diatessaron in the triple, and the tone in the double. But the diapente [Col. 1215B] consists of the diatessaron and the tone. According to this arrangement, therefore, the quadruple would consist of the triple and the double, which cannot happen.

Again, let the diatessaron be established in the triple and the diapente in the quadruple. If we subtract the triple from the quadruple, the sesquiter­tian remains. Again, if you subtract the diatessaron from the diapente consonance, the remaining tone is produced. According to this arrangement, therefore, the tone will consist in the sesquiter­tian proportion. But three sesquiter­tians are less than one triple. Thus three tones will in no way complete one diatessaron, which is utterly false. For two tones and a semitone complete the diatessaron consonance.

From this it is demonstrated that the diatessaron consonance is not multiple. I say, moreover, that the diapente consonance also cannot be placed in the multiple genus. [Col. 1215C] For if it is placed there, since the smaller continuous proportion belonging to it is the diatessaron, the diapente cannot be located in the smallest multiple proportion, namely the double, so that there might be a place where the diatessaron consonance could be fitted. But the diatessaron consonance does not belong to the multiple genus. Therefore the diapente cannot be fitted into any greater multiple relation than the double, which is the smallest.

If, then, the diapente is placed in the smallest multiple relation, namely the double, while the smaller diatessaron cannot be fitted into the multiple genus—for nothing is smaller than the double—let the diatessaron be sesquialter and the tone sesquiter­tian, since it will be placed in the continuous proportion. But two sesquiter­tians are greater than one sesquialter. Thus two tones would exceed one diatessaron consonance, which cannot occur in any way.

From this it is proved that the diapente [Col. 1215D] and diatessaron cannot be placed in the multiple genus. They will therefore rightly be placed in the superparticular genus of inequality.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Demonstration that the diapente and diatessaron are placed in the greatest superparticular proportions

This too must necessarily be added: if the diapente and diatessaron hold superparticular proportions, they are placed in the greatest superparticular proportions. These are the sesquialter and sesquiter­tian.

This will be established as follows. [Col. 1216A] If the diapente and diatessaron consonances were placed in proportions smaller than the sesquialter or sesquiter­tian, there is no doubt that, just as any other superparticular proportions joined together apart from the sesquialter and sesquiter­tian do not produce one double, so the diapente and diatessaron could in no way complete one diapason.

Since it has been shown that the diapason exists in the double proportion, and since the double proportion is composed of the sesquialter and sesquiter­tian, while the diapason is joined from the diatessaron and diapente, there is no doubt that, if we establish the whole diapason in the double, the diapente and diatessaron must be located in the sesquialter and sesquiter­tian proportions. Otherwise, the joined diapente and diatessaron could not complete the diapason, which consists in the double proportion, unless they stood in these two proportions, namely the sesquialter and sesquiter­tian. For other superparticular proportions could in no way combine to form the double. [Col. 1216B]

## CHAPTER XXIV. The diapente is in the sesquialter, the diatessaron in the sesquiter­tian, and the tone in the sesquioctave

I say, moreover, that properly the diapente consists in the sesquialter proportion and the diatessaron in the sesquiter­tian proportion. Since, of the two proportions—the sesquialter and the sesquiter­tian—the sesquialter is greater and the sesquiter­tian smaller, and since among the consonances the diapente is greater and the diatessaron smaller, it is evident that the greater proportion must be fitted to the greater consonance and the smaller to the smaller. [Col. 1216C] The diapente, therefore, must be located in the sesquialter, and the diatessaron in the sesquiter­tian proportion.

If we subtract the diatessaron consonance from the diapente, the interval that remains is called the tone. If we subtract the sesquiter­tian from the sesquialter proportion, the sesquioctave proportion remains. Thus the tone must be established in the sesquioctave relation. [Col. 1216D]

## CHAPTER XXV. The diapason and diapente are in the triple proportion, and the bis diapason in the quadruple

Since it has been demonstrated that the diapason is double, the diapente sesquialter, and that the double joined with the sesquialter produces the triple proportion, it is also evident from this [Col. 1215] that the diapente and diapason are established in the triple proportion.

But if one joins the sesquiter­tian relation to the triple proportion, it produces the quadruple. Therefore, if the diatessaron symphony is joined to the consonances of diapente and diapason, a quadruple interval of voices is produced—the interval which we showed above to be the bis diapason. [Col. 1216D]

## CHAPTER XXVI. According to the Pythagoreans, the diatessaron and diapason do not form a consonance

[Col. 1217A]

The careful reader should recognize in these matters that consonances placed upon consonances produce certain other consonances. For the diapente and diatessaron, when joined, create the diapason, as has been said. If the diapente symphony is again joined to this—that is, to the diapason—a consonance is produced which is named from both terms, namely the diapason and diapente. If the diatessaron is added to this, the bis diapason is produced, which holds the quadruple proportion.

What, then, if we join the diatessaron and diapason consonances? Will they produce any consonance according to the Pythagoreans? By no means. For it immediately falls into the superpartient genus of inequality, and preserves neither the order of multiplicity nor the simplicity of the superparticular genus.

Let numbers be established, then, by which we may demonstrate this more easily. Let there be three, whose double, namely six, consists in the diapason proportion. Let the sesquiter­tian, which we have said is the diatessaron, be fitted to it, producing eight. For eight holds the diatessaron proportion to six, while eight compared with three contains it twice. But it is not multiple, since it also contains some parts of it, and not simple ones. For it exceeds it by two units, which are two-thirds of three, the first and smallest term that we establish.

Let the terms therefore be 3, 6, 8. [Col. 1217C] This is also the relation that falls between two successive consonances: it is neither an integral double, so as to produce the diapason consonance, nor a triple, so as to produce the diapason-and-diapente symphony. If a tone is added to it, however, it immediately produces the triple mode of proportion.

Since the diapason and diapente joined together produce the triple, while the diatessaron and tone combine to form the diapente consonance, if the diapason consonance is added to the diatessaron, the result is dissonant, since no natural multiple proportion can be understood between the double and the triple. If I add a tone to it, however, the result is diapason, diatessaron, and tone, which will differ in no respect from diapason and diapente. For the diatessaron and tone constitute the diapente.

Let the diapason, then, be 3 and 6; the diatessaron 6 and 8; the tone 8 and 9; the diapente 6 and 9; and the diapason and diapente [Col. 1218A] 3 and 9. Thus the triple proportion will be represented as follows: 3, 6, 8, 9.

Although Nicomachus has said much about these matters, we have nevertheless proved, with as much brevity as we could, partly by bringing forward the very claims made by the Pythagoreans and partly by reasoning from certain consequences of those claims, that when the diapason consonance is added to the diatessaron, no consonance can be formed from them. What Ptolemy thinks about these matters I shall add later. But enough of this; we must now consider the semitones. [Col. 1218B]

## CHAPTER XXVII. The smallest numbers in which the semitone consists

The intervals called semitones seem to be so called not because they are truly halves of tones, but because they are incomplete tones. The character of the interval which we now call a semitone, but which among the ancients was called a *limma* or *diesis*, is as follows.

When two sesquioctave relations, which are tones, are subtracted from the sesquiter­tian proportion, which is the diatessaron, the interval that remains is called the semitone. Let us therefore seek two tones described in continuous arrangement. Since, as has been said, these consist in the sesquioctave proportion, and since we cannot employ two continuous sesquioctave proportions unless the multiple from which they can be derived is found, let unity be the first term [Col. 1218C] and let eight be its first eightfold.

From this I can derive one sesquioctave. But since we seek two, let eight times eight be taken, producing 64. This will be the second eightfold, from which we can derive two sesquioctave proportions. For eight, which is the eighth part of 64 units, added to it produces the whole sum 72; and when its corresponding eighth, namely nine, is similarly added to 72, the result is 81. These two continuous tones will therefore be written in their principal arrangement as 64, 72, 81. [Col. 1218D]

Let us now seek the sesquiter­tian of 64 units. Since 64 is shown not to possess a third part, let all these numbers be multiplied by three; they will then acquire a third part, while all will remain in the same proportion in which they were before the multiplier three was applied.

Let three times 64 therefore be taken, namely 192. Its third, 64, added to it produces 256. This will therefore be the sesquiter­tian proportion holding the diatessaron consonance. [Col. 1219A]

Let us now place the two sesquioctave proportions, containing two intervening numbers, in measured order against 192. Let three times 72 be taken, namely 216. Again, let three times 81 be taken, namely 243. These are placed between the two terms written above in the following way: 192, 216, 243, 256.

In this arrangement of proportions, the first number in relation to the last constitutes the diatessaron consonance. The first in relation to the second, and the second in relation to the third, constitute two tones. The interval remaining from 243 to 256 is therefore established as the form of the smallest semitone. [Col. 1219B]

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Demonstrations that 243 to 256 is not half a tone

I therefore affirm that the distance from 243 to 256 is not the full measure of half a tone. For the difference between 243 and 256 consists of only 13 units. These thirteen are less than an eighteenth of the smaller number, but more than a nineteenth. If thirteen is multiplied by eighteen, the result is 234, which in no way equals 243; if it is multiplied by nineteen, the result exceeds it, whereas every semitone—if it truly occupies half an integral tone—ought to be located between a sixteenth and a seventeenth.

This will be demonstrated later. For now, it will be clear that such a semitone interval, doubled, cannot complete one tone. Let us arrange two successive proportions of the same kind as 256 is to 243, according to the rule described above. Let 256 and 243 be multiplied by themselves; let the greatest term be 65,536. Let 243 likewise be compounded by its own number, and let the smallest term be 59,049. Again, let 256 be compounded with 243. The result will be 62,208. Let this be placed in the middle as follows:

65,536; 62,208; 59,049.

Thus 256 and 243 are in the same proportion as 65,536 is to 62,208, and likewise as 62,208 is to 59,049. [Col. 1219D]

But the greatest of these terms, 65,536, in relation to the smallest, 59,049, does not produce one complete tone. If the proportion of the first to the second, which is equal to the proportion of the second to the third, were proved to be a complete semitone, two halves joined together would necessarily produce one tone. Since, however, the proportion of the extreme terms is not sesquioctave, it is evident that these two intervals should not properly be regarded as halves of tones.

For whatever is half of something, when doubled produces that of which it is called the half. If a doubled fraction cannot complete it, the fraction is less than half. If it exceeds and goes beyond it, it is more than half. [Col. 1220A]

Moreover, it will be proved that 65,536 does not make a sesquioctave proportion when compared with 59,049, if an eighth part of 59,049 is added to it according to the rules described in arithmetic. Since that eighth part does not consist in an integer, we leave its calculation to the diligence of the readers.

It is therefore clear that the proportion established between 256 and 243 is not a complete half of a tone. Accordingly, what is truly called a semitone is a part of a tone smaller than half. [Col. 1220B]

[Note: Addition by Henricus Glareanus: “I would have drawn the whole interval of the tone. But the smallest term, namely 59,049, does not have the preceding sesquioctave, since it is itself the fifth sesquioctave of the fifth eightfold. You will discover this in the little figure drawn above.”]

## CHAPTER XXIX. The smallest numbers in which the greater part of a tone consists

The remaining part, which is the greater, is called *apotome* by the Greeks; by us it may be called a “cutting.” [Col. 1220C] Nature dictates that whenever something is cut so that it is not divided into equal parts, by however much the smaller part is less than half, by that same amount the greater part exceeds and surpasses half.

Therefore, by as much as the smaller semitone is less than a complete half-tone, by so much the apotome exceeds and surpasses the complete half-tone.

Since we have shown that the semitone principally consists in 256 and 243, let us now establish the interval called the apotome in the smallest numbers in which it can consist. If 243 could receive an eighth when a sesquioctave number was compared with it, then the relation of 256 to the sesquioctave sum, compared in the smallest numbers, would necessarily reveal the apotome. But since it is shown that 243 lacks an eighth, let both numbers be multiplied by eight.

Eight times 243 produces 1,944. If its own eighth, namely 243, is added to it, the result is 2,187. Again, let 256 be multiplied by eight, producing 2,048. Let this be placed in the middle of the terms written above. [Col. 1221A]

The third term therefore retains the proportion of a tone to the first. The second in relation to the first gives the smaller semitone. The apotome is the third in relation to the second. Thus the proportion of the apotome appears to consist in these same smallest terms, while the interval of the semitone is contained in the smallest numbers, 256 and 243.

The reason that 1,944 and 2,048 are in the same proportion as 243 to 256 is that 256 and 243 have been multiplied by eight. For if one number multiplies any two numbers, the numbers produced by that multiplication will be in the same proportion as the numbers which the first number multiplied.

## CHAPTER XXX. The proportions in which the diapente and diapason consist, and that the diapason does not consist of six tones

[Col. 1221B]

Since we have discussed the diatessaron consonance at greater length, let us speak more briefly, and almost entirely in pure numbers, about the diapason and diapente consonances.

The diapente consists of three tones and a semitone, that is, of the diatessaron and a tone. Let the numbers contained in the description above be arranged: 192, 216, 243, 256. [Col. 1221C] In this arrangement, the first term in relation to the second, and the second in relation to the third, retain the proportions of tones. The third in relation to the fourth gives the smaller semitone, as was shown above.

If an eighth of 256 is added to the number whose eighth it is, the result is 288. When compared with 192, these produce the sesquialter interval of proportion. [Col. 1221D] Accordingly, there are three tones when the first is compared with the second, the second with the third, and the fifth with the fourth. The comparison of the third term with the fourth holds the smaller semitone.

If, then, the diatessaron consists of two tones and a smaller semitone, while the diapente consists of three tones and a smaller semitone, and if the diatessaron and diapente together appear to produce one diapason, there will be five tones and two smaller semitone intervals, which do not appear to complete one tone.

The diapason consonance therefore does not consist of six tones, as Aristoxenus judges; this is also clearly evident when the numbers are arranged.

Let six tones be arranged in order, established in sesquioctave proportions. Six sesquioctave proportions are generated from the sixth eightfold. Let the sixfold eightfolds therefore be arranged as follows: [Col. 1222A]

From this last number, let six tones established in the sesquioctave proportion be placed in the following arrangement, with the eighth parts of the terms added beside the terms themselves. Let the description be as follows: [formula not supplied] [Col. 1222B]

The rationale of this arrangement is as follows. The continuous line, which is called the boundary, contains eightfold numbers. From the sixth eightfold, sesquioctave proportions are derived. Wherever we have written eighth parts, these are the eighth parts of the numbers beside which they stand. When these are added to the numbers beside which they stand, they create the succeeding numbers, as in the first case, which is 262,144. Its eighth is 32,768; when these are joined together, they produce the succeeding number, 294,912. The same will be found in the other cases. [Col. 1222C]

If the last number, 531,441, were double the first number, 262,144, the diapason would rightly appear to consist of six tones. But if we seek the double of the smallest number, namely the first, it will be less than the greatest and highest number. The double of 262,144 is 524,288, which bears the diapason consonance to it. This, then, is less than the number that contains the sixth tone, namely 531,441.

The diapason consonance is therefore smaller than six tones. The amount by which the six tones exceed the diapason consonance I call the comma, which consists, in the smallest numbers, of 524,288 and 531,441. [Col. 1222D]

What Aristoxenus thinks about these matters—he who assigned all judgment to the ears—I shall mention elsewhere. For now, in order to avoid weariness, I shall compress the sequence of the book. [Col. 1223]

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1223]

## CHAPTER I. Against Aristoxenus: a superparticular proportion cannot be divided into equal halves, and therefore neither can a tone

[Col. 1223A]

In the preceding book it was demonstrated that the diatessaron consonance is joined from two tones and a semitone, and that the diapente consists of three tones and a semitone. But, when considered separately, those semitones cannot produce a complete half-tone, and therefore the diapason in no way reaches six tones.

Since Aristoxenus the musician, entrusting everything to the judgment of the ears, does not believe that these semitones are, according to the Pythagoreans, narrower than half a tone, but believes that, just as they are called semitones, so they are halves of tones, we must discuss them again briefly. First, however, we must demonstrate that no superparticular relation in a known number can be divided into a complete equal half.

Between two numbers containing a superparticular proportion—whether they are principal numbers, whose difference is one, or subsequent numbers—no middle number can be placed such that the proportion which the smallest holds to the middle is held by the middle to the extreme, as in a geometric proportion. Rather, the middle number can produce equal differences, so that there is an equality according to the arithmetic mean; or, when placed between the same terms, it can produce the harmonic mean; or it can produce any of the other means that we discussed in arithmetic.

If this is demonstrated, then it will also be impossible for the sesquioctave proportion, which is the tone, to be distinguished in half, since every sesquioctave consists in the superparticular genus of inequality. This will be shown more effectively by induction.

If, after examining each proportion individually—namely, the superparticular proportions—not one is found which, with a middle term inserted, can be divided into equal proportions, there is no doubt that a superparticular relation cannot be divided equally.

If something appears to sing consonantly to the ears when a small voice separated from another by two tones and a complete semitone is compared with it, nature shows that this is not consonant. But since the senses cannot grasp everything that is smallest, they cannot distinguish this difference, which goes beyond consonance. It will nevertheless be detected if such a small interval increases very frequently through the same errors. For what is not clearly seen in something small becomes perceptible when it has begun to grow large through composition and combination.

From what proportion, then, should we begin? [Col. 1224A] Or shall we shorten the question by beginning with the matter under inquiry? That matter is whether the tone can be divided into two equal parts. We must now examine the tone and demonstrate how it cannot be divided into two equal parts. If someone transfers this demonstration to the remaining superparticular relations, it will similarly be demonstrated that a superparticular proportion cannot be separated into equal parts in a known and integral number.

The first numbers containing a tone are 8 and 9. But since these naturally follow one another in such a way that no middle number lies between them, let us multiply them by two, the smallest multiplier possible. They become 16 and 18; between them there naturally falls the number 17. Thus 18 in relation to 16 is a tone.

But 18, compared with 16, has the same tone as 10 and 8 compared with 10 and 7, together with its seventeenth part. A seventeenth part is naturally smaller than a sixteenth. The proportion contained between 16 and 17 is therefore greater than that between 17 and 18. Let them be arranged as follows: let A be 16, C 17, and B 18.

An integral half-tone can therefore in no way fall between C and B. For the proportion C–B is smaller than the proportion C–A. The exact half must therefore be placed toward the greater part. Let the half be D.

Since the proportion D–B, which is a complete half-tone, is greater than the proportion C–B, which is the smaller part of the tone, while the proportion A–C, which is the greater part, is greater than the proportion A–D, which is half a tone; and since A–C is the sesquisixteenth, while C–B is the sesquiseventeenth, there is no doubt that a complete half lies between the sesquisixteenth and the sesquiseventeenth.

But this cannot in any way be found in an integral number. [Col. 1225B]

Since 17 compared with 16 holds a supersesquisixteenth proportion, let us seek a sixteenth of the same 17. It will be one unit and a sixteenth of a unit. If we add this to the same number 17, the result is 18 and a sixteenth.

If 18 and a sixteenth are compared with 16, they appear rightly to exceed the measure of a tone, since only the number 18 in relation to it preserves the sesquioctave proportion. Hence, since the supersesquisixteenth proportion, doubled, exceeds a tone, it is not a complete half-tone. For whatever, when doubled, exceeds something is seen to be more than half of that thing which it exceeds.

Therefore the supersesquisixteenth is not half a tone. Consequently, no proportion greater than the sesquisixteenth can be half a tone, since the sesquisixteenth itself is greater than a complete half-tone.

But since the sesquiseventeenth proportion continuously follows the sesquisixteenth, let us see whether, when doubled, it fails to complete a tone. The term 18 holds a sesquiseventeenth part in relation to 17. If we compare another number with 18 in the same proportion, the result will be 19 and a seventeenth part.

If, however, we compare with the term 17 a number placed in the sesquioctave proportion, the result will be 19 and an eighth part. An eighth part is greater than a seventeenth part. The proportion of the numbers 17 and 19 plus an eighth is therefore greater than that contained between 17 and 19 plus a seventeenth, which represents two sesquiseventeenth proportions.

Thus two sesquiseventeenths do not appear to complete one tone. The sesquiseventeenth is therefore not half a tone, since what does not complete the whole when doubled does not contain half. For a half, when doubled, is always equal to the thing of which it is half. [Col. 1226A]

[Col. 1227A]
