Now, if we arrange those numbers that remain after two tones have been subtracted from the sesquitertian proportion, we can consider in them whether the proportion remaining after the two tones should be regarded as the equivalent of an integral semitone. If this is found to be so, it is likewise proved that the diatessaron consonance is joined together from two tones and an integral semitone.

The first term above was therefore 192. To this, 256 held the sesquitertian proportion. But 216 produces a tone in relation to the first term. In turn, 243 occupies the place of a tone in relation to 216. What remains, then, from the whole proportion of the diatessaron is the ratio consisting in the units 243 and 256.

If this is proved to be half an integral tone, there can be no doubt that the diatessaron consists of two tones and a semitone [Note: [Col. 1227D] To consist.]. Since it has been demonstrated that half a tone lies between the sesquisextadecima and sesquiseptimadecima proportions, this proportion too must be measured by that comparison.

So that we may not proceed farther than necessary, I take an eighteenth part of 243; this amounts to 13½. If I add this to 243, the result is 256½. It is therefore evident that the smaller proportion is that of 256 to 243, in the ratio sesquioctavadecima.

But if half a tone is greater in the sesquisextadecima proportion and smaller in the sesquiseptimadecima proportion, while the sesquioctavadecima is smaller than the sesquiseptimadecima ratio, then the comparison of 256 to 243—which is what remains from the diatessaron after two tones have been subtracted—is smaller than the sesquioctavadecima. There is no doubt, therefore, that the ratio of these two numbers is very considerably smaller than a semitone.

## CHAPTER III. Demonstrations against Aristoxenus that the diatessaron consonance does not consist of two tones and a semitone, nor the diapason of six tones.

[Col. 1227D]

But if—as Aristoxenus says—the diatessaron consonance is joined from two tones and a semitone, two diatessaron consonances must necessarily produce five tones; and the diapente and diatessaron, joined together just as they form one diapason, must likewise be equal in continuous proportion to six tones.

Since a little earlier we arranged six tones, whose smallest number was 262,144, while the final number, placed at the sixth tone, was 531,441, and the fifth tone was represented by 472,392, let them be arranged as follows:

[Col. 1228A] [Col. 1228B]

Let us now speak of the smaller numbers—that is, of the five tones. If, then, the diatessaron consisted of two tones and a semitone, and twice the diatessaron consisted of five tones, when I raised a diatessaron from 262,144 and lowered another diatessaron from 472,392, the same number ought to be found between the two elevations or descents.

This occurs as follows. From the number 262,144 I raise a diatessaron, that is, a sesquitertian proportion; it results in 349,525⅓. Again, from 472,392 I lower a sesquitertian proportion, which results in 354,294. Let us arrange these proportions as follows, with the first number A, the second B, the third C, and the fourth D.

[Col. 1228D]

Since the term A is separated from the term D by five tones, and since, in Aristoxenus’ view, the diatessaron is joined from two tones and a semitone, with one diatessaron placed between A and B and another between C and B, the terms B and C ought not to be different but one and the same, so that the five tones may appear to consist integrally of two diatessaron consonances.

But since there is a difference of 4,768⅓, it is proved that the diatessaron is by no means joined from two tones and a semitone.

## CHAPTER IV. That the diapason consonance is exceeded by six tones by a comma, and what the smallest number of the comma is.

But if we seek to express this difference [Note: [Col. 1229A] Not found in the text.] in whole numbers: since adding one third to the two-thirds part makes a complete unit, and that third is half of the same two-thirds, if I add to the whole difference its half, namely 2,384⅓, the total will be 7,153. This previously represented the proportion of the comma.

For the comma is that by which six tones exceed the diapason consonance; it is contained in the first 7,153 units.

For just as we added half of the difference itself so that it would increase to 7,153, so let us also add their proper halves to all the terms A, B, C, and D. The same proportion stated above will then apply to all of them, and the difference between five tones and twice the diatessaron will be the same as the difference between six tones and the diapason consonance—namely, 7,153 units.

Hence it follows that five tones exceed twice the diatessaron, and six tones exceed one diapason, by a comma. This is found in the first 7,153 units. The following diagram will make this clear:

## CHAPTER V. How Philolaus divides the tone.

[Col. 1229A]

Philolaus the Pythagorean attempted to divide the tone in another way, establishing the beginning of the tone from the number that first produces a cube from the first odd number—which was held in the highest honor among the Pythagoreans.

Since the number three is the first odd number, three times three produces 9, and if this is multiplied by three, 27 necessarily results. This is a tone distant from the number 24, preserving the same difference of three. For three is an eighth part of the sum 24. When this is added to the same sum, it produces the first cube from three, namely 27.

From this Philolaus forms two parts: one greater than a half, which he calls the apotome; and the other smaller than a half, which he again calls the diesis, later called by his successors the lesser semitone.

He calls their difference the comma, and judges the first diesis to consist of 13 units, because this is the difference observed between 256 and 243. The same number, 13, consists of nine, three, and one: the unit occupies the place of the point; three, that of the first odd line; and nine, that of the square of the first odd number.

For these reasons, since he assigns 13 to the diesis, which is called a semitone, he establishes the remaining part of the number 27, consisting of 14 units, as the apotome [Note: [Col. 1231] Apotome.]. But since one unit makes the difference between 13 and 14, he judges that a unit should be placed in the position of the comma. He locates the whole tone in 27 units, because the difference between 216 and 243—which are a tone apart—is 27.

## CHAPTER VI. That the tone consists of two semitones and a comma.

[Col. 1231C]

From these points it easily appears that the tone consists of two lesser semitones and a comma. For if the whole tone consists of an apotome and a semitone, while the semitone differs from the apotome by a comma, the apotome is nothing other than a lesser semitone and a comma. If, therefore, someone removes two lesser semitones from the tone, the comma remains.

## CHAPTER VII. Demonstration that a tone exceeds two semitones by a comma.

[Col. 1231D]

This will also be proved in the following way. If the diapason consists of five tones and two lesser semitones, and six tones exceed the diapason consonance by one comma, then, when the five tones are removed from both intervals, what remains of the diapason will be two lesser semitones, while what remains of the six tones will be one tone. This tone exceeds the two remaining semitones by a comma.

If, therefore, a comma is added to those same two semitones, they will equal the tone. Thus it is established that one tone is equal to two lesser semitones and a comma, which is found in the first 7,153 units.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the smaller intervals of the semitone.

[Col. 1232B]

Philolaus therefore encloses these and smaller intervals within the following definitions. “The diesis,” he says, “is the interval by which the sesquitertian proportion is greater than two tones. The comma is the interval by which the sesquioctava proportion is greater than two dieses, that is, two lesser semitones. The schisma is half a comma. The diaschisma is half a diesis, that is, of a lesser semitone.”

From these statements it follows that the tone is principally divided into a lesser semitone and an apotome. It is also divided into two semitones and a comma; consequently it is divided into four diaschismata and a comma.

An integral half-tone, which is a semitone, consists of two diaschismata [Note: [Col. 1231] Not found in the text.], namely one lesser semitone, and a schisma, which is half a comma. For since the whole tone is joined from two lesser semitones and a comma, anyone wishing to divide it completely will produce one lesser semitone and half a comma.

But one lesser semitone is divided into two diaschismata, while half a comma is one schisma. It was therefore correctly said that an integral half-tone can be divided into two diaschismata and one schisma.

Thus an integral semitone appears to differ from a lesser semitone by one schisma; the apotome, however, differs from the lesser semitone by two schismata. For it differs by a comma, and two schismata make one comma.

## CHAPTER IX. On obtaining the parts of the tone through consonances.

[Col. 1233A]

But enough of this. It now seems necessary to explain how, through musical consonances, we can at one time extend and at another lower the intervals that have been prescribed.

This should be done lineally, with the lines that we draw being understood in place of vocal sounds. Let the reasoning itself now demonstrate the matter.

Suppose that the interval of a tone is to be obtained through a consonance, toward the acute and the grave. Let the sound be B. From this I raise another sound, separated from B by the interval of a diapente, to the sound C. From C I lower a diatessaron consonance to D. Since a tone makes the difference between the diapente and the diatessaron, the interval D–B is found to be a tone.

We shall modulate toward the lower part of the tone as follows. From B I raise a diatessaron to F, and from F I lower a diapente to K. K–B will be a tone.

The attentive reader will therefore observe that the tone has been produced toward the acute part in D–B, and toward the grave part in K–B.

[Col. 1233D]

Suppose that a lesser part of the tone is to be obtained through a consonance, toward the acute and the grave. The lesser part of the tone is the interval by which the diatessaron consonance exceeds two tones.

Let the sound be A. From A I raise a diatessaron to B. Again, from B I raise a diatessaron to C; from C I lower a diapente to D. Thus B–D is a tone.

Again, from D I raise a diatessaron to E. From E I again lower a diapente to F. Thus D–F is a tone. There are therefore two tones, B–D and D–F. And A–B was an integral diatessaron. Thus F–A will be the lesser part of the tone, which is called a semitone.

[Col. 1234A]

Toward the grave part, the procedure is as follows. Let the sound be A. I raise two tones through a consonance to G; from G I lower a diatessaron to K. Thus K–A will be the lesser part of the semitone, as was required.

[Col. 1234B]

If, therefore, we subtract a diatessaron from three tones, the apotome remains. Let the three tones be A–B, B–C, and C–D; let the diatessaron A–E be subtracted from them. Thus E–C will be the lesser semitone; E–D will therefore be the apotome.

[Col. 1234C]

We shall obtain this apotome conveniently as follows. First, toward the acute part, I raise three tones from A to B; from B I lower a diatessaron consonance, producing C. C–A is the remaining apotome.

[Col. 1234D]

If we wish to produce the same interval toward the grave sound, it is done as follows. Let the sound be A. I raise the lesser semitone A–D, then lower from D the tone D–E. Thus E–A is the apotome we seek.

Suppose that a comma is to be obtained toward the acute part. Let the sound be A. I raise the apotome A–B, then lower the lesser semitone B–C. Since the lesser semitone is smaller than the apotome by a comma, C–A will be the comma.

[Col. 1235B]

Again, toward the grave part, I proceed as follows. From sound A I raise the lesser semitone A–D; from D I lower the apotome D–E. Thus C–A will be the comma.

## CHAPTER X. The rule for obtaining the semitone.

[Col. 1235C]

All these consonances must properly be known to the mind and ears. For they are gathered in vain through reasoning and learning unless they have become thoroughly familiar through use and practice.

But, so that what we have undertaken in musical instruction may for the moment be judged not by the ears—which belongs to those already advanced in music—but by reasoning, we shall give one example of finding an interval that seems somewhat more difficult: namely, the lesser semitone, so that it may be discovered in the proper order in both directions, toward the acute and toward the grave.

Let the diatessaron be A–B. It is therefore necessary to bring a consonant lesser semitone around A–B toward both the lower and the higher part.

I therefore raise a diatessaron B–C. Again, I lower a diapente C–D. Thus B–D is a tone: for the diatessaron consonance is exceeded by the diapente consonance by a tone, and the interval C–B is exceeded by the interval C–D by the interval B–D.

Again, I raise a diatessaron D–E and lower a diapente E–F. Thus D–F is a tone. But D–B was a tone. Therefore A–F is the lesser semitone remaining from the diatessaron A–B after the two tones F–D and B–D have been subtracted.

Again, I lower a diatessaron A–G and raise a diapente G–H. Thus A–H is a tone. But A–F was a semitone. Thus F–H is an apotome.

Again, I lower a diatessaron H–K and raise a diapente K–L. Thus H–L is a tone. But H–A was a tone. Therefore L–B is the lesser semitone. But B–D was a tone. Therefore I–D is an apotome.

Again, I raise a diatessaron F–M. Therefore B–M is a semitone. I lower a diatessaron L–N; therefore N–A is a semitone.

Thus, through consonances, the diatessaron, two semitones, and the whole interval have been obtained around A–B: B–M toward the acute, and N–A toward the grave. M–N is smaller than the diapente.

For it consists of five semitones and a doubled apotome—that is, of two tones and three lesser semitones—and two semitones cannot complete one tone.

[Col. 1236B]

A comma therefore remains, and the whole interval M–N is smaller than the diapente consonance by one comma. The attentive reader will understand this very easily [Note: [Col. 1235] Understands.].

[Col. 1236C]

But since we have said a little about the nature of the comma, we must not avoid showing in what proportion the comma itself is contained. The comma is the smallest interval that hearing can comprehend. We must therefore state of how many commas the lesser and greater semitones each appear to consist, and likewise of how many commas the tone itself is joined.

Let us begin with an appropriate starting point.

## CHAPTER XI. Demonstration that Archytas’ superparticular proportion cannot be divided equally, and its refutation.

[Col. 1236D]

A superparticular proportion cannot be divided equally by inserting a proportional mean number. This will be firmly demonstrated later. For the demonstration that Archytas offers is excessively weak.

It is as follows. “Let A–B,” he says, “be a superparticular proportion. I take the smallest numbers C–E in the same proportion. Since C–E are the smallest in the same proportion, and since they are superparticular, the number E exceeds the number C by one of its own parts. Let this be D.

“I say that D will not be a number but a unit. For if D is a number and E is one of its parts, D will measure the number E [Note: [Col. 1237] Measures.]. Consequently, it will also measure E as a number. Thus it will likewise measure C. Therefore the number D will measure both C and E, which is impossible.

“For the numbers that are smallest in the same proportion are relatively prime to one another, and retain only their difference, namely one unit [Note: [Col. 1237] By one unit.]. D is therefore a unit; consequently, the number E exceeds the number C by one unit. Hence no intermediate number will occur that can divide this proportion equally [Note: [Col. 1237] Does not possess.].

“Thus no intermediate number can be placed between those that hold the same proportion, which could divide that proportion equally.”

According to Archytas’ reasoning, therefore, no intermediate term falls within a superparticular proportion that divides it equally, because the smallest numbers in the same proportion differ only by one unit.

Yet why should the smallest numbers in a multiple proportion not likewise have this same difference of one unit? We see that there are multiple proportions besides those situated at the roots, among which an intermediate term capable of dividing the same proportion equally can be fitted.

Anyone who has carefully examined our arithmeticians will understand this more easily. It must be added, however, that this occurs as Archytas thinks only in the superparticular proportion. It must not be asserted universally.

Let us now turn to what follows [Note: [Col. 1237] Not found in the text.].

## CHAPTER XII. In what proportion the comma lies, and that it is greater than 75 to 74 but smaller than 74 to 73.

[Col. 1237D]

First, I say that the numbers containing the comma retain among themselves a greater proportion than 75 to 74, but a smaller one than 74 to 73.

This will be demonstrated as follows. First, we must recall that six tones exceed the diapason by a comma.

Let A be 262,144; let B contain the diapason consonance in relation to it, established in the duple proportion, namely 524,288; and let C stand six tones distant from A, namely 531,441. All these figures must be gathered from the arrangement of the tones in the second book.

The proportion of the comma is therefore contained between B and C. I subtract the number B from the number C, leaving D, which consists of 7,153 units [Note: [Col. 1237] Which.].

This number D is smaller than a seventy-third part of B, but greater than a seventy-fourth part. For if I multiply the same number D, which is 7,153, seventy-three times, I obtain the number E, consisting of 522,169 units [Note: [Col. 1237] It becomes.]. If I multiply it seventy-four times, the number F becomes 529,322. E, which has been increased by seventy-three, is smaller than the number B, whereas F, which has been increased by seventy-four, is greater than B.

It was therefore correctly said that D is smaller than a seventy-third part of B, but greater than a seventy-fourth. Consequently, the number C exceeds the number B by a part of B that is smaller than a seventy-third, but greater than a seventy-fourth [Note: [Col. 1237] Smaller.].

The proportion of C to B is therefore greater than 75 to 74 but smaller than 74 to 73. In the former, the unit is a seventy-fourth of the smaller number; in the latter, the same unit is a seventy-third.

[Col. 1238C]

The same point must be explained in another way. Let us first assume that, if a proportion is increased equally by the proper difference of the numbers that compose it, the smaller proportion will be contained between the numbers produced after the addition than between the earlier numbers, which had previously stood apart by a certain proportion.

Thus, if 2—their difference—is added to 6 and 4, they become 8 and 6. But between 6 and 4 there is a sesquialteran proportion, whereas between 8 and 6 there is a sesquitertian proportion. The sesquitertian proportion is smaller than the sesquialteran.

With this established, let the numbers described above that contained the proportion of the comma be arranged: 531,441, designated A, and 524,288, designated B. Their difference is C, 7,153.

The number C does not measure the number A seventy-five times [Note: [Col. 1237] Not found in the text.]. If, therefore, you multiply C seventy-five times, the result will be D, namely 536,475. Thus D exceeds A by the number E, namely 5,034.

Again, if the number C measures and is multiplied by B seventy-four times [Note: [Col. 1237] And multiplies.], the resulting number F is 529,322. F is greater than B by the same number E, namely 5,034.

Therefore D exceeds A by E, while B is exceeded by F by the same E. If we add E to A, D results; if we add E to B, F results. But D has been increased seventy-five times by multiplying C, whereas F has grown by multiplying C seventy-four times. Therefore D and F retain between themselves the proportion of 75 to 74.

But D and F are A and B with the same E added to them. The proportion between A and B must therefore be greater than that between D and F. For A and B, after the addition of E, became D and F. The proportion between D and F is therefore smaller than that between A and B.

But the proportion between D and F is the same as that between 75 and 74. Therefore the proportion between A and B is greater than that between 75 and 74.

[Note: [Col. 1239] Alternatively.] A and B contain the comma. The proportion of the comma is therefore greater than that of 75 to 74.

[Col. 1239C]

Since we have shown that the proportion of the comma is greater than that represented by the comparison of 75 with 74, we must now show how the numbers containing the interval of the comma retain a smaller proportion among themselves than that represented by the comparison of 74 with 73.

This will be demonstrated as follows [Note: [Col. 1239] It will be demonstrated.]. First, we must recall what we said in the second book when discussing the measurement of a difference. If we subtract from any proportion the difference between the numbers that contain it, the numbers that remain will possess a greater proportion than the numbers that existed before the reduction of the difference.

Let the numbers be 8 and 6. I subtract their proper difference, namely 2, and they become 6 and 4. But the former contain a sesquitertian proportion, while the latter contain a sesquialteran proportion. The sesquialteran proportion is greater than the sesquitertian.

Let A and B therefore be the same numbers described above, whose difference is C. I multiply the difference C seventy-four times, obtaining F, namely 529,322. Compared with A, it is smaller by the number G, namely 2,119.

Again, I multiply C seventy-three times, producing K, namely 522,169. Compared with B, it too is smaller by the same G, namely 2,119.

After G has been subtracted from A and B, they become F and K. The proportion between A and B is therefore smaller than that between F and K. But F and K retain the proportion of 74 to 73, since they were produced by multiplying C. Therefore the proportion between A and B, the numbers containing the comma, is smaller than that of 74 to 73.

A little earlier it was shown that this same proportion of the comma is greater than 75 to 74. It has therefore been shown that the numbers containing the comma have a proportion greater than 75 to 74 but smaller than 74 to 73, as was required.

[Col. 1239A] [Note: [Col. 1239A] The following two notes appear at the foot of columns 1239 and 1240, but the callout figures (+ and *) have not been printed in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 1239] Smaller proportion: 74 to 73.]

[Note: [Col. 1239] Greater: 75 to 74.]

## CHAPTER XIII. That the lesser semitone is greater than 20 to 19, but smaller than 19½ to 18½.

[Col. 1240C]

If this kind of investigation is applied to the lesser semitone, we shall likewise find its proportion very easily. It is contained between 256 and 243.

Let A therefore be 256, B 243, and their difference C, 13. I say that A retains a smaller proportion in relation to B than 19½ to 18½.

Let C measure 19½ times; the result is 253½, designated D. Compared with A, this is exceeded by A by the same amount, namely 2½. Let this difference be F, namely 2½.

Again, let the same difference C measure B eighteen and a half times; the result is 249½, designated E. Compared with B, E is likewise exceeded by the same F, namely 2½.

D is therefore smaller than A by the difference F, and E is likewise smaller than B by the same difference. After F has been subtracted from A and B, they become D and E. D and E therefore retain a greater proportion between themselves than A and B.

But D and E retain between themselves the same proportion as 19½ to 18½. A therefore retains a smaller proportion in relation to B than 19 [lacuna]½ to 18½, as was required.

[Note: [Col. 1241A] The following two notes appear at the foot of columns 1241 and 1242, but their callout figures (+) have not been printed in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 1241] Greater elsewhere.]

[Note: [Col. 1241] Smaller elsewhere.]

[Col. 1241A] [Col. 1241B]

Nevertheless, the same proportion of 256 to 243 appears to be greater than that contained by 20 and 19.

Let A, B, and C be the same as those described above. Let the difference C measure the term A twenty times; the result is 260, designated D [Note: [Col. 1241] Let it be.]. Compared with A, D exceeds it by the same amount, namely 4; let this be F.

Again, let the same C measure B nineteen times; the result is 247, designated E. Compared with B, E exceeds it by the same F.

D therefore exceeds A, and E exceeds B, by the same F. If F is added to A and B, they become D and E. The proportion between A and B is therefore greater than that between D and E.

But D and E were produced by multiplying C twenty times and nineteen times respectively. Therefore the proportion between A and B—which contains the semitone—is greater than that of 20 to 19.

It has therefore been demonstrated that the lesser semitone has a proportion greater than 20 to 19, but smaller than 19½ to 18½.

Let us now compare this lesser semitone with the comma, which is the smallest interval, lying at the limit of hearing and the final proportion.

## CHAPTER XIV. That the lesser semitone is greater than three commas but smaller than four.

[Col. 1241D]

We therefore propose to demonstrate that the lesser semitone is greater than three commas but smaller than four. This can be recognized very easily from the following.

Let three numbers be arranged so that they contain among themselves the proportion of the diapason and that called the proportion of six tones.

Let A be 262,144. Let five continuous tones be raised to B, which is 472,392; let the diapason consonance be referred to C, which is 524,288; and let six tones be raised to D, which is 531,441.

With these arranged and established, it is clear that a comma is constituted between C and D, and that their difference is 7,153; let this be K.

Let two tones be lowered from B to E, which is 373,248. Again, from E I raise a diatessaron to F, which is 497,664.

Since there are two tones between E and B, and a diatessaron between E and F, the lesser semitone is found between B and F.

For when two tones are subtracted from the diatessaron consonance, the lesser semitone remains—the one I stated to consist in the first numbers 256 and 243. If you multiply these same numbers 1,944 times, you will obtain the numbers B and F. They must contain the same proportion as the numbers mentioned above, since both have grown through multiplication by one and the same number, namely 1,944.

Again, from F I raise a diatessaron to G, which is 663,552. From the same G I again lower two tones to P, producing 524,288. P must necessarily exhibit the same sound as the number C, for it has proceeded to its equality by the following method.

The diapason consonance A–C, which consists of five tones and two lesser semitones, is exceeded by six tones by a comma. From the same term A, therefore, the number P has receded by five tones and two semitones, as follows.

From A to B there are, of course, five tones. From B to F there is a lesser semitone. F and P likewise contain the same lesser semitone. Thus from A to P there are five tones and two lesser semitones. P and C are therefore correctly written with the same number.

But since there is a lesser semitone between F and C, let us see what their difference is, so that we may compare it with the comma. Their difference is 26,624; let this be M.

Thus K is the difference of the comma, while M is that of the lesser semitone. If we increase K by three times, the number will be 21,459; let this be L. If we multiply the same K four times, the result will be 28,612; let this be N.

M is therefore greater than L, but smaller than N. N grew through the comma multiplied four times, L through it multiplied three times, while M represents the difference of the lesser semitone.

It was therefore correctly said that the lesser semitone is smaller than four commas but greater than three.

[Col. 1243]

## CHAPTER XV. That the apotome is greater than four commas but smaller than five, and the tone greater than eight but smaller than nine.

[Col. 1243A]

By the same method we can also find how many commas the greater semitone—which, as stated above, is called the apotome—contains.

Let A be 262,144. Let B be five tones distant from it, namely 472,392. Let D be six tones distant from A, namely 531,441. There is therefore a tone between B and D.

B is separated from C by a lesser semitone; let C be 497,664. The proportion of the apotome therefore remains between C and D. Since B–D is a tone, if B–C, the lesser semitone, is subtracted from it, C–D remains greater; we stated above that this is the apotome.

The difference between D and C is therefore 33,777; let this be E. The difference of the comma was 7,153; let this be F.

If I multiply F, that is, the comma, five times, I obtain 35,765; let this be G. If I multiply the same F four times, the number K is 28,612.

G is therefore greater than E, while K is smaller. G has been increased five times by the comma, K four times, while E is the difference of the apotome.

It was therefore correctly said that the apotome is smaller than five commas but greater than four. From this it is proved that the tone is greater than eight commas but smaller than nine. For if the lesser semitone is greater than three commas but smaller than four, and the apotome is greater than four commas but smaller than five, then the lesser semitone joined to the greater semitone, which is the apotome, will be greater than eight commas but smaller than nine.

But the apotome and the lesser semitone together make one tone. The tone is therefore greater than eight commas but smaller than nine.

[Col. 1243C]

## CHAPTER XVI. Demonstration by numbers of the foregoing statements.

[Col. 1244A]

Although it has been demonstrated by this reasoning how the tone compares with the commas, we should nevertheless not grow weary, as though through laziness, of allowing the tone itself to show independently its comparison with the commas.

Let A be 262,144; B, five tones distant from it, 472,392; C, containing the diapason consonance in relation to A, namely 524,288 [Note: [Col. 1243] Not found in the text.]; and D, differing from A by six complete tones, 531,441 [Note: [Col. 1243] 441.].

D is therefore separated from C by a comma, since six tones exceed the diapason consonance. Let this be E, 7,153.

D is separated from B by a complete tone—six tones from five tones. Let this be F, 59,049 [Note: [Col. 1243] F 59049.].

If, therefore, I increase E nine times, I obtain H, 64,377. If eight times, the result is 57,224; let this be G.

Compared with F, H is greater, while G is smaller; F is the difference of the tone. H represents the comma multiplied nine times, G the comma multiplied eight times.

The tone has therefore been shown to be smaller than nine commas, but greater than eight commas.

[Col. 1244C]

Although it has thus been shown by this reasoning how the tone compares with the commas, nevertheless, the fact that the greater semitone differs from the lesser semitone by a comma will also be proved independently by the following numbers.

Let A be 497,664. Let B be the number separated from it by a lesser semitone, the number already described above [Col. 1245A] as 524,288. The apotome is separated from A by the number consisting of 531,441 units; let this be C [Note: [Col. 1245D] Here.].

Since A–B is the lesser semitone and A–C the greater, the difference between B and C must be sought. It is 7,153; let this be D. But this number previously represented the comma. The comma therefore makes the difference between the greater and lesser semitone.

[Col. 1245B]

Again, I propose to demonstrate that a tone is greater than two lesser semitones by only one comma.

Let A be 472,392. From this let a tone be raised to 531,441; let this be D. From A let a lesser semitone be raised, namely B, and let B be 497,664. Again, from B let another lesser semitone be raised, namely C, and let C be 524,288.

Since A–D is a tone, while A–C contains two lesser semitones, let us see what difference is established between the numbers C and D. It is E, namely 7,153 units.

It has therefore been demonstrated that a tone is greater than two lesser semitones by a comma.

[Col. 1246B]

Since everything that we promised to prove has now been demonstrated by its proper method, what remains for musical instruction is the division of the regular monochord. Because this matter requires a longer treatment, we have decided to transfer its discussion to the latter commentary.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1245]

## CHAPTER ONE. That the differences of sounds consist in quantity.

[Col. 1245C]

Although we arranged everything that would have to be demonstrated in the treatment of the preceding book, I do not regret once again briefly recalling the same matters to memory, presenting them with some variation in treatment, so that, when they have returned to our memory, we may proceed to the division of the rule, toward which the whole intention is directed.

If there were rest in all things, no sound would strike the ear. This would happen because, when all movements had ceased, no things would set one another into vibration. Therefore, for there to be a voice, vibration is required. But for there to be vibration, motion must precede it. Thus, for there to be a voice, motion is necessary.

Every motion, however, contains both speed and slowness. If, therefore, the motion in striking is slow, the sound becomes lower. For just as slowness is close to stillness, so low pitch is adjacent to silence. Swift motion, on the other hand, produces a high sound.

Moreover, a sound that is low falls toward the middle by intensification, whereas a high sound falls toward the middle by relaxation. Hence every sound appears to be composed, as it were, of certain parts. Every combination of parts, however, is joined according to some proportion. The combination of sounds, therefore, is constituted by proportions.

Proportions are principally considered in numbers; and a simple numerical proportion is found either among multiples, or among superparticular, or among superpartient proportions. According to multiple and superparticular proportions, consonant or dissonant sounds are heard. Consonant sounds are those which, struck together, join with one another in a pleasant and blended sound; dissonant sounds are those which, struck together, do not produce a pleasant or blended sound.

Having stated these matters, let us say a little about proportions.

## CHAPTER II. Different investigations of intervals

If a multiple interval is multiplied by two, the interval produced by this multiplication is multiple. Let the multiple interval be B–C, with B a multiple of C; and let B be to D as C is to B. Since B is a multiple of C, the term C measures B, either twice, or three times, or subsequently; and C is to B as B is to D. Therefore, the term B measures D. Consequently, since C measures B, it will also measure D. D is therefore a multiple of C, and the interval C–D has been produced by composing, joining to itself, and multiplying by two the interval B–C.

The same is proved numerically. Let B be double C, as two is to one, and let C be to B as B is to D. D will therefore be four. B is a multiple of C—that is, two is a multiple of one. D is a multiple of B—that is, four is a multiple of two. Therefore D, four, is a multiple of C, one. Four is quadruple one, and it is the interval B–C, multiplied by two from its half.

[Col. 1247A]

If an interval, multiplied by two, produces a multiple interval, the original interval itself will also be multiple. Let the interval be B–C; let C be to B as B is to D; and let D be a multiple of C. I say that B is a multiple of C.

Since D is a multiple of C, C will measure D, and it will also measure B. It has been shown that, if terms are proportionally arranged, when the first is compared with the last, if the first measures the last, it also measures the middle.

**[Note: [Col. 1247] If the numbers are proportional.]**

C therefore measures B. Thus B is a multiple of C.

The same may again be shown with numbers. Let C be one, and D, produced from the doubled proportion, while B–C is four and is a multiple of C. It is quadruple. Since four is generated from the doubled proportion of B–C, the proportion B–C will be half of it; therefore the proportion B–C is double. But double is a multiple proportion; therefore the proportion B–C is multiple.

[Col. 1247C]

In a superparticular interval, neither one nor several proportional numbers will intervene as a mean. Let B–C be a superparticular proportion, and let D, F, and G be the least numbers in that same proportion. Since D, F, and G are least in the same proportion, they are the first terms of the same proportion.

**[Note: [Col. 1247] Alone.]**

Accordingly, one will measure them. Let G therefore be subtracted from D–F, and let D remain. This, then, is the common measure of both; it will therefore be one.

Consequently, no number can fall between F–D and G that is smaller than F–D but greater than G. For only one unit lies between them; and however many numbers intervene proportionally between the least terms of the same proportion in superparticular proportions,

**[Note: [Col. 1247] That intervene.]**

the same number will also intervene between the other terms of that proportion. But no number can intervene between F–D and G, the least terms of the same proportion. Therefore no number can fall proportionally between B and C.

Numerically, let the superparticular proportion be sesquialter—these are 10 and 15—while the least terms in the same proportion are 2 and 3. I subtract 2 from 3; the remaining unit

**[Note: [Col. 1247] The same unit that measures both.]**

measures both. Therefore no number will exist between two and three that is greater than two but less than three. Otherwise the unit would be divided, which is impossible.

Therefore, not even between 10 and 15 will one find a number that bears to 10 the proportion that 15 bears to it.

[Col. 1248B]

If an interval that is not multiple is multiplied by two, what results from this multiplication is neither multiple nor superparticular.

**[Note: [Col. 1247] Not in the old manuscript.]**

Let the non-multiple interval be B–C, and let C be to B as B is to D. I say that D is neither a multiple nor a superparticular of C.

Suppose first, if possible, that D is a multiple of C. Since it is known that, when an interval is multiplied by two and a multiple interval is produced, the interval that has been multiplied is itself multiple, B–C would therefore be multiple, contrary to the assumption.

Thus D will not be a multiple of C, nor will it be superparticular. For no proportional mean term intervenes in a superparticular proportion. But between D and C a proportional term has been placed, namely B: C is to B as B is to D. Therefore it is impossible for D to be either a multiple or a superparticular of C, as was to be demonstrated.

Numerically, let a non-multiple interval be 6 to 6, and let 4 be to 6 as 6 is to some other number. That number will be 9, which is neither a multiple nor a superparticular of 4.

[Col. 1248D]

If an interval is multiplied by two and what is produced by that multiplication does not become multiple, the original interval itself will also not be multiple. Let the interval be B–C; let C be to B as B is to D; and let D not be a multiple of C. I say that B also will not be a multiple of C.

For if B were a multiple of C, D would also be a multiple of C. But it is not; therefore B is not a multiple of C.

[Col. 1249B]

A double interval is joined from the two greatest superparticular proportions, the sesquialter and the sesquitertian. Let A be sesquialter of B, and B sesquitertian of C. I say that A is double C.

Since A is sesquialter of B, A contains all of B and its half. Therefore two A are equal to three B.

Again, since B is sesquitertian of C,

**[Note: [Col. 1249] Therefore B contains all of it.]**

B contains C and its third part. Therefore three B are equal to four C. But three B were equal to two A. Therefore two A are equal to four C; hence one A is equal to two C. Thus A is double C.

Numerically, let 12 be sesquialter of 8, and 8 sesquitertian of 6; therefore 12 is double 6.

[Col. 1249C]

From a double interval and a sesquialter interval, a triple interval arises. Let A be double B, and B sesquialter C. I say that A is triple C.

Since A is double B, A is equal to two B. Again, since B is sesquialter of C, B contains all of C and its half. Therefore two B are equal to three C. But two B were equal to one A; therefore one A is equal to three C. Thus A is triple C.

Numerically, let 6 be double 3, and 3 sesquialter of 2. Therefore 6 is triple 2.

[Col. 1250A]

If a sesquitertian interval is subtracted from a sesquialter interval, the remainder will be sesquioctave. Let A be sesquialter of B, while C is sesquitertian of B. I say that A is sesquioctave of C.

Since A is sesquialter of B, A contains B and its half. Therefore eight A are equal to twelve B.

Again, since C is sesquitertian of B, C contains B and its third. Therefore nine C are equal to twelve B. Twelve B were equal to eight A; therefore eight A are equal to nine C. Thus A is equal to C and an eighth of C. A is therefore sesquioctave of C.

Numerically, let the sesquialter interval be 9 to 6, and the sesquitertian interval 8 to 6. Thus 9 to 8 is a sesquioctave proportion.

[Col. 1250C]

Six sesquioctave proportions are greater than one double interval. Let A be a number, B its sesquioctave, C the sesquioctave of B, D the sesquioctave of C, F the sesquioctave of D, G the sesquioctave of F, and K the sesquioctave of G.

**[Note: [Col. 1249] “Of this one, moreover.”]**

Let this be done according to the method described in the *Arithmetic*, and let the numbers be A, B, C, D, F, G, K. Let A be 262,144; its sesquioctave, B, 294,912; its sesquioctave, C, 331,776; its sesquioctave, D, 373,248; its sesquioctave, F, 419,904; its sesquioctave, G, 472,392; and its sesquioctave, K, 531,441.

And K, 531,441, is more than double A, 262,144.

**[Note: [Col. 1249] “A, two hundred sixty-two thousand one hundred forty-four.” But Glarean does not approve this reading.]**

Therefore six sesquioctave proportions are greater than one double interval.

[Col. 1251A]

## CHAPTER III. The naming of musical notes by Greek and Latin letters

[Col. 1251B]

Since it remains for us to divide the string according to the consonances mentioned above, and since this division will provide the necessary sounds in the three genera of song, we must meanwhile add the musical notes, so that, when we have marked the divided line with these same little signs, each one’s name may easily be recognized.

The ancient musicians, for economy of writing, so that it would not always be necessary to write out complete names, devised certain little signs by which the names of the strings could be indicated, and divided them according to genera and modes. At the same time they sought this advantage from their brevity: whenever a musician wished to write down a melody, he could place these signs for the sounds above a verse extended by the rhythmic composition of its meter. Thus they wonderfully ensured that not only the words of the songs, expressed through letters, but also the melody itself, marked by these signs, would endure in memory and for posterity.

Of all these modes, however, let us provisionally arrange one, the Lydian, together with its signs, through the three genera; we defer doing the same for the remaining modes to another time.

If at any point I describe the arrangement by naming the Greek letters, let no reader be disturbed by the novelty. For this entire notation is composed from Greek letters, diminished in various ways and also bent.

**[Note: [Col. 1251] Not found.]**

We shall take care not to alter anything from the authority of antiquity. The earlier and upper signs will therefore belong to the diction, that is, to the words; the second and lower signs will belong to the percussion.

Parhypate hypaton, “the subordinate principal of the principals”: an incomplete Β and an inverted Γ.

Hypaton enharmonios, “the enharmonic of the principals”: an inverted V and an inverted Γ,

**[Col. 1252A]**

with a stroke extending backward.

**[Note: [Col. 1251] “The principal of the principals.”]**

Parhypate meson, “the subordinate principal of the middle”: Ρ and an inverted C.

Meson enharmonios, “the enharmonic of the middle”: the Greek Π and an inverted C.

Meson chromaticae, “the chromatic of the middle”: the Greek Π with a stroke, and an inverted Π with a stroke through its middle.

## CHAPTER IV. Division of the regular monochord in the diatonic genus

[Col. 1253A]

But now it is time to come to the division of the regular monochord. Concerning this, the following must first be stated: whether the division to be drawn is established in the measurement of the string, in numbers, or in their proportion, a greater space of the string and a greater quantity of numbers will produce lower sounds. But if the length of the string is shorter, and the numerical quantity likewise smaller, higher sounds must necessarily be produced.

From this comparison it follows that, by however much one string is longer or marked by more numbers, and another shorter or marked by fewer numbers, the former is found proportionally lower and the latter higher.

Nor should the reader be troubled by the fact that, when we were ascending, we often marked spaces of proportions with larger numbers, but, when descending, with smaller ones, since ascent produces high pitch and descent produces low pitch. There we were marking only the spaces of the proportions, without attending to the properties of low or high pitch; hence we often ascended toward high pitch with larger numbers and descended toward low pitch with smaller ones.

Here, however, where we shall measure the spaces of the strings and the sounds, it is necessary to follow the nature of things: to the greater length of the strings, from which low pitch arises, we must assign greater numbers, and to the lesser length, from which high pitch arises, smaller numbers.

Let the taut string be A–B, and let a ruler equal to it be divided according to the proposed divisions, so that, when the ruler is placed beside the string, the same divisions that we previously assigned on the ruler may be marked on the length of the string. We shall now divide as though we were dividing the string itself, not the ruler.

Let A–B be divided into four parts by the three points C, D, and E. The whole A–B will therefore be double each of D–B and A–D; individually, A–D and D–B are double each of A–C, C–D, D–E, and E–B.

Thus A–B will be the lowest, namely proslambanomenos,

[Col. 1254A]

while D–B will be mese. For it is half of the whole; and just as A–B is double B–D in spatial extent, so B–D is double A–B in pitch. For, as stated above, the order of spatial extent and pitch is always reversed. A string is proportionally higher in pitch the smaller it is in spatial extent. Therefore E–B will also be higher.

Nete hyperboleon, E–B, is half of D–B in quantity but double it in pitch. Again, since E–B is one quarter of A–B in spatial extent, it will be quadruple it in pitch.

Thus, as stated, nete hyperboleon will be double mese in pitch, and mese double proslambanomenos. Nete hyperboleon will be quadruple proslambanomenos in pitch. Therefore proslambanomenos and mese will form a diapason consonance; mese and nete hyperboleon, a diapason; and proslambanomenos and nete hyperboleon, a double diapason.

Again, since A–C, C–D, D–E, and E–B are equal parts, A–B consists of four such parts, while C–B consists of three. A–B is therefore sesquitertian of C–B.

Again, since C–B consists of three equal parts while D–B consists of two, C–B is sesquialter of D–B.

Again, since C–B consists of three equal parts, each equal to one E–B, C–B is triple E–B. Therefore C–B is lychanos hypaton diatonos.

Proslambanomenos and lychanos hypaton diatonos will therefore form a diatessaron consonance. The same lychanos hypaton diatonos will form a diapente consonance with mese. And the same lychanos diatonos will form a diapason-and-diapente consonance with nete hyperboleon.

Again, if I subtract a ninth part from the whole A–B, namely A–F, eight parts, F–B, will remain. F–B will therefore be hypate hypaton, to which A–B—that is, proslambanomenos—bears a sesquioctave proportion, in music a tone.

[Col. 1255A–B]

The greater the spatial extent, the greater the low pitch; where it is smaller, there is the greater high pitch. Since A–B exceeds E–B fourfold in spatial extent, proslambanomenos will rightly be fourfold lower in pitch, while C–B will be fourfold higher. And since A–B is sesquioctave in spatial extent to F–B, it is surpassed by F–B by a tone; F–B will therefore be hypate hypaton.

Again, A–B is sesquitertian to C–B in spatial extent; therefore C–B will be lychanos hypaton diatonos. And C–B will surpass A–B itself in pitch by a diatessaron consonance.

Moreover, A–B is double D–B in spatial extent; therefore D–B will be double A–B in pitch. Thus C–B will constitute nete hyperboleon, as the learned reader will readily perceive upon closer examination.

The preceding diagram, which contains the lower signs, belongs to the diagram in which we placed little signs beside the strings, since it would have taken too long to write out their names.

Likewise, if A–B is divided by three cuts, the third part will be A–G.

**[Note: [Col. 1255] “Which …”]**

Thus two equal parts will be G–B. A–B, proslambanomenos, will therefore form with G–B, hypate meson, a diapente consonance in the sesquialter proportion. C–B to G–B will be sesquioctave

**[Note: [Col. 1255] “Sesquioctave.”]**

and will contain a tone; and this follows in due order. For lychanos hypaton diatonos, that is C–B,

[Col. 1255D]

contains a tone in relation to hypate meson, that is G–B.

Again, A–B, proslambanomenos, has a diatessaron consonance with C–B, lychanos hypaton diatonos; while A–B, proslambanomenos, has a diapente consonance with G–B, hypate meson.

Likewise, C–B, lychanos hypaton diatonos, has a diapente consonance with D–B, mese; while G–B, hypate meson, has a diatessaron consonance with D–B, mese.

But lychanos hypaton, that is C–B, in relation to the mode of the whole string, from A to LL—this A, proslambanomenos, I divide as 9216, taking half toward O, so that the whole A is double in comparison with hypate meson, that is G–B, and will be separated from it by a tone.

If I take one quarter of C–B, it will be C–K. Therefore C–B bears a sesquitertian proportion to K–B,

**[Note: [Col. 1255] “Will possess.”]**

while K–B will be separated from D–B by a sesquioctave proportion. K–B will therefore be lychanos diatonos meson; and C–B, that is lychanos hypaton diatonos, will contain a diatessaron consonance in relation to K–B, that is lychanos diatonon meson.

Again, if I take a ninth part of D–B, it will be D–L. Therefore L–B will be paramese.

If I take a quarter of D–B, it will be D–M. Therefore M–B will be nete synemmenon.

If I take a third of D–B, it will be D–N. Therefore N–B will be nete diezeugmenon.

If K–B is divided into two equal parts, it will be K–X, and X–B will be paranete hyperboleon.

[Col. 1256C]

## CHAPTER V. Division of the monochord’s netes hyperboleon through the three genera

The description of the diatonic genus has now been completed, namely in the simpler and principal mode that we call Lydian. It is not now necessary to discuss the modes. But so that the mixed description may proceed through the three genera, and a suitable abundance of numbers may be assigned to all of them in order to preserve the proportions of the tones and dieses, a number has been devised capable of fulfilling all these requirements: the greatest number, assigned to proslambanomenos, is 9216, and the smallest 2304.

The proportions of the remaining sounds will be constructed between these numbers. We proceed, of course, from the lower end, and indicate all the names of the strings not only by names but also by letters placed beside them.

**[Note: [Col. 1255] “Placed beside.”]**

Since the division must be made through three genera, however, and the number of strings exceeds the number of letters, when the letters run out we double them again in this fashion: when we have reached Z, we write the remaining strings as double A, namely AA; double B, namely BB; and double C, namely CC.

Let the first and greatest number, occupying the place of proslambanomenos, be 9216. Let this be O. Let O be double LL. Therefore A will be proslambanomenos, O mese, and LL nete hyperboleon.

A will therefore have 9216, while O will have half of this, 4608, so that mese and proslambanomenos may form a diapason consonance. LL will be half of mese, so that proslambanomenos will be quadruple nete hyperboleon and will form a double-diapason consonance with it; LL will therefore be 2304.

If I subtract an eighth from 2304,

**[Note: [Col. 1257] “I raise [or remove].”]**

namely 288, and add it to the same number, I obtain 2592. NN will therefore be 2592, and it will be paranete hyperboleon, separated from nete hyperboleon by a tone.

Again, from NN, that is 2592, I subtract its eighth, 324, and add it to the number of which it is the eighth. The result will be 2916. I thus obtain FF, trite hyperboleon diatonos, in the diatonic genus: 2916, separated by a whole tone from paranete hyperboleon,

**[Note: [Col. 1257] “They are not read.”]**

but by a ditone from nete hyperboleon. The same FF will be trite hyperboleon chromatica in the chromatic genus. In the enharmonic genus, however, it will be paranete hyperboleon enharmonios. The reason for this will be more easily recognized when we have described the three first tetrachords of the three genera, beginning from nete hyperboleon.

Since, if two sesquioctaves are subtracted from A in a sesquitertian proportion, a lesser semitone remains, I take one third of LL, that is, of nete hyperboleon, namely 768. I add this to the same number, obtaining 3072. DD will therefore be 3072, containing a lesser semitone in relation to trite hyperboleon.

For since nete diezeugmenon contains a diatessaron consonance in relation to nete hyperboleon, while trite hyperboleon diatonos is separated from nete hyperboleon by a ditone,

**[Note: [Col. 1257] “From nete hyperboleon.”]**

the space remaining between nete diezeugmenon and trite hyperboleon is a lesser semitone.

[Col. 1257D]

Since, then, we have completed the diatonic tetrachord of hyperboleon, the chromatic and enharmonic tetrachords must now be supplied as follows.

Since paranete hyperboleon is separated from nete hyperboleon by a tone in the diatonic genus, by three semitones in the chromatic genus, and by two tones in the enharmonic genus, if we take the distance between paranete hyperboleon and nete hyperboleon in the diatonic genus and add half of it to paranete hyperboleon of the diatonic genus, we shall have a number separated from nete hyperboleon by three semitones; this will be paranete hyperboleon in the chromatic genus.

I therefore subtract 2304, nete hyperboleon, from 2592, paranete hyperboleon of the diatonic genus. The remainder is 288. I divide this, obtaining 144; I add it to 2592, paranete hyperboleon of the diatonic genus, and obtain 2736. This will be paranete hyperboleon chromatica.

Again, since trite hyperboleon, whether diatonic or chromatic, is separated from nete hyperboleon by two tones, and in the enharmonic genus paranete hyperboleon is separated from nete hyperboleon by two tones,

**[Col. 1258B]**

**[Note: [Col. 1257] Not found.]**

the paranete hyperboleon that is trite hyperboleon in the diatonic or chromatic genus will be the paranete hyperboleon of the enharmonic genus.

But since trite hyperboleon of the diatonic and chromatic genera preserve a lesser semitone in relation to nete diezeugmenon, while the enharmonic tetrachord consists of two whole tones, a diesis, and a diesis—which are half-spaces of the lesser semitone—I take the distance between nete diezeugmenon and paranete hyperboleon enharmonios.

Since nete diezeugmenon is 3072 and paranete hyperboleon enharmonios 2916, their distance is 156. I take half of this, namely 78. I add it to 2916 and obtain 2994. This will be EE, trite hyperboleon enharmonios.

The tetrachord of hyperboleon has therefore been described according to the three genera.

## CHAPTER VI. Explanation of the description set out above

Three tetrachords have therefore been described for us in this manner. Every tetrachord retains a diatessaron consonance.

Thus nete hyperboleon and nete diezeugmenon, in the three genera—that is, diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic—contain a diatessaron symphony.

The diatessaron consonance consists of two tones and a lesser semitone. In the tetrachords mentioned above this has been divided among the three genera as follows.

In the diatonic genus, the first, paranete hyperboleon, namely 2592, has a tone as its distance from nete hyperboleon, namely 2304; we marked this with the sign “To.” Again, trite hyperboleon of the diatonic genus, namely 2916, has a further difference from paranete hyperboleon of the diatonic genus, namely 2592, which we marked with a similar sign [lacuna]T.

Nete diezeugmenon, namely 3072, bears a semitone in relation to trite hyperboleon, namely 2916, and we marked it with the sign “To.” Thus the entire space between nete diezeugmenon and nete hyperboleon consists of two tones and a semitone.

[Col. 1260A]

But the same two tones and semitone have been divided in the chromatic genus as follows.

The second genus, chromatic, has been described in this way: paranete hyperboleon chromatica, namely 2736, compared with nete hyperboleon, namely 2304, contains the space between paranete hyperboleon of the diatonic genus and nete hyperboleon, which is one tone—that is, two semitones, major and minor. The space between paranete hyperboleon of the diatonic genus and nete hyperboleon was again divided in this way; for it is half a tone, though not an exact half, because, as was shown at great length above, a tone cannot be divided into two equal parts.

We shall therefore mark this space of three semitones, that is, a tone and a semitone, in this way: To To To.

Again, paranete hyperboleon chromatica and trite hyperboleon retain a portion of a tone, namely the semitone that remained from the two tones contained between trite hyperboleon diatonica and nete hyperboleon.

After four semitones have been subtracted, the remainder of the entire tetrachord is a semitone, contained between nete diezeugmenon and trite hyperboleon.

This tetrachord, therefore, also consists of two tones and a semitone, divided into one space of three semitones and two spaces of two semitones. Three spaces are thus contained by four strings.

In the enharmonic genus, the manner of understanding it is especially easy. For paranete hyperboleon enharmonios, namely 2916, is separated from nete hyperboleon, namely 2304, by two whole tones, which we shall mark in this way: To To.

The remainder of the entire tetrachord, consisting of two tones and a semitone,

[Col. 1260C]

is therefore one semitone, contained between nete diezeugmenon and paranete hyperboleon enharmonion. This we divided into two dieses in trite hyperboleon enharmonion. We marked the intervening middle space, and the space of the diesis, in this way.

Thus the tetrachord of hyperboleon has been described for us. Having completed it, let us proceed to the tetrachord of diezeugmenon. There is no need to linger over the same explanations in the remaining cases, since an example for them too may be taken from this description.

## CHAPTER VII. Division of the monochord’s netes diezeugmenon through the three genera
Therefore, if I take half of *nete diezeugmenon*, which is 3072, it will be 1536. Added to the former, this makes 4608, which is *mese*, designated by the letter O. But if from *nete diezeugmenon*, that is, DD—namely 3072—I subtract a third, the result will be 1024. Joined to the former, this makes 4096, which will be called *paramese*, marked below with the letter X.

Thus *nete diezeugmenon*, namely 3072, will form a diapente consonance with *mese*, namely 4608, since it stands in the sesquialteral ratio. The same *nete diezeugmenon*, namely 3072, retains a diatessaron consonance with *paramese*, namely 4096, which is related to it in the sesquitertial proportion.

If, therefore, from *nete diezeugmenon*, 3072, I subtract an eighth, namely 384, and add it to the former, the result will be 3456. This will be *paranete diezeugmenon diatonos*, marked with the two letters CC [Note: [Col. 1261] “Diatonos,” with the two letters CC.], and it will stand a tone above *nete diezeugmenon*. From this, if I again subtract an eighth, namely 432 from 3456, and add it to the same, the result will be 3888. This will be *trite diezeugmenon diatonos*, marked with the letter Y.

But since *nete diezeugmenon* held a sesquitertial proportion with *paramese*, while *trite diezeugmenon diatonos* is two tones distant from *nete diezeugmenon*, a semitone will be contained between *trite diezeugmenon* and *paramese*.

Thus the diatonic genus is completed in this tetrachord and pentachord in such a way that the tetrachord from *nete diezeugmenon* to *paramese* has the diatessaron consonance, while the pentachord from *nete diezeugmenon* to *mese* has the diapente consonance.

We shall construct the enharmonic and chromatic genera as follows. I take the distance between *nete diezeugmenon* and *paranete diezeugmenon diatoni*, namely 3072 and 3456. Their difference is 384; I divide this, obtaining 192. If I take this and add it to *paranete diezeugmenon diatonos*, namely 3456, the result will be 3648. This will be *paranete diezeugmenon chromatica*, marked with the doubled letter BB [Note: [Col. 1261] “Distant from *nete*.”], standing a tone and a semitone above *nete diezeugmenon*, that is, three semitones, and containing the remaining semitone up to *trite diezeugmenon*, previously diatonic but now chromatic, namely 3888.

The remaining semitone of that tone which was divided between *paranete diezeugmenon diatonos* and *trite diezeugmenon diatonos* is now found between *paranete diezeugmenon chromatica* and *trite diezeugmenon chromatica*. Let the other remaining semitone of the tetrachord lie between *trite diezeugmenon chromatica* and *paramese*. This is the semitone left over from the diatessaron consonance between *nete diezeugmenon* and *paramese*, after subtracting the two tones contained by *nete diezeugmenon chromatica* and *trite diezeugmenon chromatica*.

What is *trite diezeugmenon diatonica* in the diatonic genus is called *trite diezeugmenon chromatica* in the chromatic genus. In the enharmonic genus it is called *paranete diezeugmenon enharmonios*, since it is a full two tones distant from *nete diezeugmenon*; it is marked AA. No string lies between *nete diezeugmenon* and *paranete diezeugmenon enharmonion*, and therefore it is called *paranete*.

We divide the semitone between *paranete diezeugmenon enharmonion* and *paramese*, namely between AA and X, in this way, so that it becomes two dieses. I take the difference between *paranete diezeugmenon enharmonia* and *paramese*, namely between 3888 and 4096; it is 208. I divide this and obtain 104. I add this to 3888, making 3992. This will be *trite diezeugmenon enharmonios*, marked with the letter Z.

I have appended below a description of this tetrachord in the three genera, and have joined to it the tetrachord of the *hyperboleon* arranged above, so that there might be one description of both and the complete form of the arrangement might gradually emerge. [Col. 1262C] [Col. 1262D] [Col. 1263A]

## CHAPTER VIII. Division of the monochord of the *netae synemmenon* according to the three genera

The preceding description shows how the two tetrachords that are joined to one another but separated from *mese* are positioned in the three genera. [Col. 1263B] We must now come to another tetrachord, called *synemmenon*, which is joined to *mese*.

For since we have stated that there is a diapente consonance between *nete diezeugmenon* and *mese*, and since a diapente consonance consists of three tones and a semitone, there are three tones in this pentachord. One is between *nete diezeugmenon* and *paranete diezeugmenon diatonos*. Another is between *paranete diezeugmenon diatonos* [Note: [Col. 1263] “Diatoni.”] and *trite diezeugmenon diatonos*. The third is between *paramese* and *mese*. The remaining semitone lies between *trite diezeugmenon diatoni* and *paramese*, since the tetrachord from *nete diezeugmenon* to *paramese* is separated from *mese* by the tone between *paramese* and *mese*.

If, from the pentachord extending from *nete diezeugmenon* [Col. 1263D] to *mese*, we remove one tone—namely, the tone contained between *nete diezeugmenon* and *paranete diezeugmenon diatonon*—we shall be able to join another tetrachord to *mese*, so that it becomes *synemmenon*, which is joined in the following manner. [Note: [Col. 1263] Not found.]

Since *paranete diezeugmenon diatoni*, which is CC, has the numerical value 3456, a third of this added to it will produce *mese*. This number, therefore, marked with the letters CC in the *diezeugmenon* tetrachord, stood a tone above *nete diezeugmenon* in the diatonic genus and was called *paranete diezeugmenon diatonos*. In the *synemmenon* tetrachord, that is, among the joined strings, it is *nete synemmenon*, established in the three genera and marked with the letter Y.

If an eighth, namely 432, is subtracted from it and added to it, the result will be 3888, which is *paranete synemmenon*, marked with the letter T [Note: [Col. 1263] Not read.]. Let an eighth of this be taken, namely 486. If this amount is added to the number of which it is an eighth, the result will be 4374, which is *trite synemmenon diatonos*, namely E.

But since *nete synemmenon* bears to *mese*, that is, 3456 to 4608, the sesquitertial proportion, which is the diatessaron, while *trite synemmenon* bears to *nete synemmenon*, that is, 4374 to 3456, the proportion of two tones, there remains between *trite synemmenon diatoni* and *mese* the proportion of a semitone. Thus this tetrachord is joined to *mese*, and for that reason is called *synemmenon*, as though continuous and joined.

The proportion of the diatonic genus is therefore established in this way. The chromatic division is as follows. I take the difference between *nete synemmenon* and *paranete synemmenon diatonici*, namely between 3456 and 3888. It is 432. If I divide this so that a semitone may result, the result is 216. I add this to 3888, so that three semitones may result; the result will be 4104, which is *paranete synemmenon chromatica*, with the letter S placed above it.

From this, namely from *paranete synemmenon chromatica*, to *trite synemmenon*, formerly diatonic but now chromatic [the text reads “chronic”], there is a semitone. From *trite synemmenon chromatica* to *mese* there is another semitone.

But since from *nete synemmenon* to *trite synemmenon*, whether diatonic or chromatic, there are two tones, what is *trite synemmenon diatonos* or *chromatica* in the diatonic or chromatic genera is *paranete synemmenon enharmonios* in the enharmonic genus. It has the value 4374 and is designated R, A; from it to *mese* there is a semitone.

I divide this into two dieses as follows. I take the difference between *paranete synemmenon enharmonii* and *mese*, namely between 4374 and 4608 [Note: [Col. 1263] “It is.”]. The result is 234. I divide this and obtain 117. I add this to *paranete synemmenon enharmonios*, namely 4374, making 4491. This is marked with the letter P and is *trite synemmenon enharmonios*.

Thus the semitone contained between *paranete synemmenon enharmonion* and *mese*, namely between 4374 and 4608, is divided by *trite synemmenon enharmonion* [Note: [Col. 1263] “It.”], namely by the one whose value is 4491. Accordingly, the procedure for this tetrachord too is clear.

Now, however, a description must be made, joined with the other tetrachords, namely those of the *hyperboleon* and *diezeugmenon*, so that the description may gradually proceed in a properly ordered manner. [Note: [Col. 1263] Not read.] [Col. 1265]

## CHAPTER IX. Division of the monochord of the *mesae* according to the three genera

From what has been stated, I do not think that more labor is needed in the remaining cases. The other tetrachords, those of the *mesae* and the *hypatae*, must be constructed according to this model.

First, we shall describe the meson tetrachord of the diatonic genus in the following order. I take a third of *mese*, which is O, 4608; it is 1536. I join this to the same number, making 6144. This is *hypate meson*, marked II, containing a diatessaron consonance to *mese*. It is divided into two tones and a semitone as follows.

I take an eighth of *mese*, namely 4608, which is 576. I add this to the same number, making 5184. This is *lychanos meson diatonos*, namely M. From this, an eighth is again taken [Note: [Col. 1265] “Again.”] [Note: [Col. 1265] “Let it be taken.”], namely 648. I add this to the same number [Col. 1265B], making 5832. This is *parhypate meson diatonos*, marked I, standing a tone above *lychanos meson diatonon* and two tones below *mese*.

There remains, therefore, a semitone between *hypate meson diatonon* [Col. 1266A] and *parhypate meson diatonon*, namely between 6164 and 5832. [The number 6164 appears to be an obvious numerical error for 6144.]

We divide this same tetrachord, between *mese* and *hypate meson*, in the chromatic genus as follows. I take the difference between *mese* and *lychanos meson diatonon*, namely between 4608 and 5184; it is 576. I divide this in half, obtaining 288. I add this to the larger number, namely 5184, making 5472. This becomes *lychanos meson chromatice*, marked N.

There remain two semitones: one between *lychanos meson chromatica* and *parhypate meson chromatica*, namely between 5472 and 5832; and another between *parhypate meson chromatica* and *hypate meson*, namely between 5832 and 6144.

We divide the enharmonic genus as follows. Since what was *parhypate meson diatonos*, or what was *parhypate meson chromatice*, stood two tones below *mese* and had the numerical value 5832, in the enharmonic genus it will be *lychanos meson enharmonios*, marked with the letter L, likewise standing two tones below *mese*.

The remaining semitone between *lychanos meson enharmonion* and *hypate meson*, namely between 5832 and 6144, is divided into two dieses as follows. I subtract the difference between 5832 and 6144; it is 312. I divide this in half, obtaining 156. I add this to 5832, making 5888. This is *parhypate meson enharmonios*, marked K.

There are two dieses: one between *lychanos meson enharmonion* and *parhypate meson enharmonion*, namely between 5832 and 5988 [the text earlier gives 5888]; and another between *parhypate meson enharmonion* and *hypate meson*, namely between 5988 and 6144. [The numerical sequence is internally inconsistent; the preceding calculation gives 5888.]

Thus the meson tetrachord has been divided. It should be placed in the description so that it is joined to the tetrachords described above. [Col. 1268A]

## CHAPTER X. Division of the monochord of the *hypatae* according to the three genera, and the arrangement of the complete description

Now the *hypaton* tetrachord must be divided according to the three genera. I take *hypate meson*, namely 6144, and half of it, namely 3072. If I add this to the same number, the result will be 9216, which is *proslambanomenos*, preserving a diapente consonance with *hypate meson*.

But of *hypate meson* itself [Note: [Col. 1267] 6144], if I subtract a third, namely 2048, and add the remainder to the same number, the result will be 8192. This is *hypate hypaton*, marked B.

Thus *hypate meson* has a diapente consonance with *proslambanomenos*, and a diatessaron with *hypate hypaton*.

From *hypate meson*, therefore, namely 6144, let an eighth be subtracted; the result is 768. If this is added to the same number, the result will be 6912. This is *lychanos hypaton diatonos*, standing in the proportion of a tone to *hypate meson*.

Again, let an eighth be subtracted from 6912; the result is 864. If this is joined to the same number, the result will be 7776. This is *parhypate hypaton diatonos*, marked C, standing a tone above *lychanos hypaton diatonon* and two tones below *hypate meson*.

There remains, therefore, a semitone between *parhypate hypaton diatonon* and *hypate hypaton*, namely between 7776 and 8192. Such is the tetrachord of the diatonic genus.

We divide the chromatic genus as follows. I take the difference between *hypate meson* and *lychanos hypaton diatonos*, namely between 6144 and 6912; it is 768. I divide this in half, so that two semitones may be produced; the result is 384. I add this to 6912, so that three semitones may result; the result is 7296. This will be *lychanos hypaton chromatice*, marked F, three semitones distant from *hypate meson*.

There remain two semitones: one between *lychanos hypaton chromaticen* and *parhypate hypaton chromaticen*, namely between 7296 and 7776; and another between *parhypate hypaton chromatice* and *hypate hypaton*, namely between 7776 and 8192.

The enharmonic genus remains, and its division follows the preceding model. Since *parhypate hypaton diatonos* or *parhypate hypaton chromatice*, marked with the value 7776, is two tones distant from *hypate meson*, in the enharmonic genus the same will be *lychanos hypaton enharmonios*, standing two full tones below *hypate meson* [Col. 1269B] [Note: [Col. 1269] “Is distant.”].

There remains, therefore, from the diatessaron consonance, a semitone between *lychanos hypaton enharmonion* and *hypate hypaton*, namely between 7776 and [Note: [Col. 1269] Not read.] 8192. We divide this into two dieses as follows.

I take the difference between *lychanos hypaton enharmonios* and *hypate hypaton*, namely between 7776 and 8192; it is 416. I take half of this, namely 208. I add this to 7776, making 7984, which is *parhypate hypaton enharmonios*, marked D [Note: [Col. 1269] 9084. The note’s number conflicts with the main text’s 7984.].

There are therefore two dieses: one between *lychanos hypaton enharmonion* and *parhypate hypaton enharmonion*, namely between 7776 and 7984; and another between *parhypate hypaton enharmonion* and *hypate hypaton*, namely between 7984 and 8192.

The final tone is contained between *proslambanomenos* and *hypate hypaton*, namely between 9216 and 8192.

Thus the *hypaton* tetrachord has been divided according to the three genera: diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic. If the tetrachords of the *hyperboleon*, *diezeugmenon*, *synemmenon*, and *meson* are joined to the preceding ones, there results a complete and perfect description of the monochord, divided throughout according to its regular system.
