## CHAPTER XI. Explanation of the arrangement described above

In the form given above, the *proslambanomenos* has a diapason consonance with *mese*, and *mese* with *nete hyperboleon*. The *proslambanomenos* has a double-diapason with *nete hyperboleon*.

The *hypate hypaton* preserves a diatessaron consonance with *hypate meson*; *hypate meson* with *mese*; *mese* with *nete synemmenon*; *paramese* with *nete diezeugmenon*; and *nete diezeugmenon* with *nete hyperboleon*. [Col. 1273B]

This arrangement enables us to count complete tetrachords by means of these consonances. [Note: [Col. 1273] Not found.] To make the whole order of the strings in this form clearer [Note: [Col. 1273] “May be seen.”], only five tetrachords are marked according to the three genera.

The first and lowest is the *hypaton*, whose beginning is *hypate hypaton* and whose endpoint is *hypate meson*. The second is the *meson*, beginning with *hypate meson* and ending with *mese*. The third is the *synemmenon*, beginning with *mese* and ending with *nete synemmenon*. The fourth is the *diezeugmenon*, beginning with *paramese* and ending with *nete diezeugmenon* [Note: [Col. 1273] “Beginning.”]. The fifth is the *hyperboleon*, beginning with *nete diezeugmenon* and ending with *nete hyperboleon*.

## CHAPTER XII. Fixed and movable notes

Of all these notes, some are entirely immovable, some entirely movable, and some are neither entirely immovable nor entirely movable.

The entirely immovable notes are *proslambanomenos*, *hypate hypaton*, *hypate meson*, *mese*, *nete synemmenon*, *paramese*, *nete diezeugmenon*, and *nete hyperboleon*. They are so called because they are the same in all three genera, changing neither their names nor their positions, whether they form pentachords or tetrachords.

They form pentachords, for example, *proslambanomenos* to *hypate meson*, and *mese* to *nete diezeugmenon*. They form tetrachords, for example, *hypate hypaton* to *hypate meson*, and *hypate meson* to *mese*.

The movable notes are those that change according to the individual genera, such as the *paranete* and *lychanos* of the diatonic and chromatic genera, and the *trite* and *parhypate* of the enharmonic genus.

For *paranete hyperboleon diatonos* is one thing, *paranete hyperboleon chromatica* another, and *paranete hyperboleon enharmonios* another; likewise *trite diatonos* and *trite chromatice* are distinct from *trite enharmonios* [Note: [Col. 1273] “*Paranete hyperboleon enharmonios* is one thing; *trite diatonos* and *trite chromatice* another.”].

*Paranete diezeugmenon diatonos* and *paranete diezeugmenon chromatica* are likewise different. Nor is *trite diezeugmenon enharmonios* the same as those in the other genera. Neither are *paranete synemmenon diatonos* and *paranete synemmenon chromatica* the same [Note: [Col. 1273] “And *paranete synemmenon enharmonios*.”], nor is *trite synemmenon enharmonios* the same as the *trite* in the other genera.

*Lychanos meson diatonos* and *lychanos meson chromatice* also differ [Note: [Col. 1273] “And *lychanos meson enharmonios*.”], and *parhypate meson enharmonios* resembles no *parhypate* of the other genera. Nor do *lychanos hypaton diatonos* and *lychanos hypaton chromatice* retain the same positions and numerical values [Col. 1274B] [Note: [Col. 1273] “And *lychanos hypaton enharmonios*.”]. For *parhypate hypaton enharmonios* is found to be unlike the *parhypates* of the other genera.

Those notes are not entirely immovable or movable which remain the same in two genera, namely the chromatic and diatonic, but change in the enharmonic genus.

This can be observed as follows. *Trite hyperboleon diatonos* and *trite hyperboleon chromatice* are described identically in the form above [Note: [Col. 1273] “With the same [values].”], with the same numerical value, 2829. But when we examine the enharmonic genus, we find another *trite*, namely 2916. Thus the note that was common to two genera is changed in the third.

The same occurs in the *diezeugmenon* tetrachord. *Trite diezeugmenon diatonos* and *trite diezeugmenon chromatica* are the same and agree with one another, but *trite diezeugmenon enharmonios* differs from the preceding one [Col. 1274C] [Note: [Col. 1273] “From the preceding ones.”]. The same is true in the *synemmenon*. *Trite synemmenon diatonos* and *trite synemmenon chromatice* are the same, but *trite synemmenon enharmonios* is different.

Likewise, *parhypate meson diatonos* and *parhypate meson chromatica* are marked identically. But in the enharmonic genus, just as the *trite* was different above, so here the *parhypate* beside *hypate meson* is found to differ, although it has a different force and pitch from the others.

Again, *parhypate hypaton diatonos* and *parhypate hypaton chromatica* are the same, but it is not the same when sought in the enharmonic genus.

To make this incomplete mutability of these notes clearer, let us return to the *hyperboleon* tetrachord. The note that is *trite hyperboleon* in the diatonic and chromatic genera changes in the enharmonic genus and becomes *paranete*. Likewise, what was called *trite diezeugmenon* in the diatonic or chromatic genus is called *paranete* in the enharmonic genus. What was *trite synemmenon* in the chromatic or diatonic genus passes into *paranete* in the enharmonic genus.

What appeared as *parhypate meson* in the chromatic or diatonic genus is found as *lychanos meson* in the enharmonic genus. What was called *parhypate hypaton*, whether in the diatonic or chromatic genus, is called *lychanos hypaton* in the enharmonic genus.

The immovable notes, therefore, are *proslambanomenos*, *hypate hypaton*, *hypate meson*, *mese*, *nete synemmenon*, *paramese*, *nete diezeugmenon*, and *nete hyperboleon*. The movable notes are those which we call *lychanos*, *paranete*, diatonic, chromatic, or enharmonic [Note: [Col. 1275] “Which we call.”].

Those that are neither entirely movable nor entirely immovable are the notes which we call *parhypatae* and *tritae* in the diatonic or chromatic genera, but *lychanos* or *paranetae* in the enharmonic genus.

## CHAPTER XIII. The types of consonances

We must now discuss the types of the primary consonances. The primary consonances are the diapason, diapente, and diatessaron.

A type is a particular arrangement possessing its own form in each genus, established within the terms of each proportion that produces a consonance. Thus, in the diatonic genus, if we place the *diezeugmenon* tetrachord between the *hyperboleon* tetrachord and *mese* [Note: [Col. 1275] “And *meson*.”], after removing the *synemmenon* tetrachord, there will be fifteen strings. But if *proslambanomenos* is removed from these, there will be fourteen.

Let these be arranged as follows:

- A: *hypate hypaton*
- B: *parhypate hypaton*
- C: *lychanos hypaton*
- D: *hypate meson*
- E: *parhypate meson*
- F: *lychanos meson*
- G: *mese*
- H: *paramese*
- I: *trite diezeugmenon*
- K: *paranete diezeugmenon*
- L: *nete diezeugmenon*
- M: *trite hyperboleon*
- N: *paranete hyperboleon*
- O: *nete hyperboleon*

From *hypate* to *paramese* there is a diapason consonance. From *mese* to *hypate meson* there is a diatessaron, and from the same *mese* to *lychanos hypaton* there is a diapente.

The diapason will therefore consist of eight strings, the diatessaron of four, and the diapente of five. Consequently, the diatessaron will have three types, the diapente four, and the diapason seven. There will always be one fewer type than there are notes.

Beginning with *mese*, the diatessaron consonance has three types, as follows. One type is from G to D; the second from F to C; the third from E to B. The types of the diatessaron extend no farther than this.

This is because, up to this point, each type contains two strings of the same diatessaron: G–D contains E and F [Note: [Col. 1275] Not found.]; F–C contains E and D; and E–B contains C and D [Note: [Col. 1275] Not found.]. If I add the diatessaron D–A to these, it will not be different from G–D, for it will contain only one string of the G–D consonance, namely D alone. Thus it exceeds the G–D consonance, and for that reason the diatessaron is said to have three types. The same principle applies to the other consonances.

The diapente has four types, as follows: one is H–D; another G–C; another F–B; and another E–A.

The diapason consonance has seven types, as follows: the first is O–G; the second N–F; the third M–E; the fourth L–D; the fifth K–C; the sixth I–B; and the seventh H–A.

It is clear from what has been said that the diatessaron consonance occurs only once among the immovable and fixed notes. For if I begin with *hypate hypaton*, it is A–D, that is, from *hypate hypaton* to *hypate meson*, the first in the sequence. The others end on movable notes, namely B–E and C–F. For *parhypate hypaton* and *parhypate meson*, as well as *lychanos hypaton* and *lychanos meson*, have been shown to be movable [Note: [Col. 1275] Not read.].

If, again, we begin the diatessaron consonance from *hypate meson*, the type ending on fixed notes will be G–D, the first, namely from *hypate meson* to *mese*. The others, E–H and F–I, do not. For *parhypate meson*, *lychanos meson*, and *trite diezeugmenon* are not shown to be immovable.

Again, if *paramese* receives the diatessaron as its starting point, there will likewise be a type enclosed by fixed notes, namely H–L, from *paramese* to *nete diezeugmenon*, which is the first [Note: [Col. 1275] Not read.]. The others, I–M and K–N, end on movable notes. For we have stated that *trite diezeugmenon*, *paranete diezeugmenon*, *trite hyperboleon*, and *paranete hyperboleon* are movable notes.

The diapente consonance, however, has only two types enclosed by fixed notes. If we begin with *hypate meson*, one is D–H, namely from *hypate meson* to *paramese*, and this is the first. The other is G–L, namely from *mese* to *nete diezeugmenon*, and this is the fourth. The remaining ones, E–I and F–K, are not enclosed by fixed notes. For *parhypate*, *lychanos*, *trite*, and *paranete* are shown to be unstable.

The same reasoning applies if the types of this consonance are considered from *nete diezeugmenon* toward the lower register, that is, toward *mese*, for they will be enclosed by the same immovable notes mentioned above. Whether we lead the consonances downward from *hypate meson*, from *mese*, from *paramese*, or even from *nete hyperboleon* [Note: [Col. 1275] “Toward.”], there can be no destruction [Note: [Col. 1275] “Distinction.”] of the two that are enclosed by fixed notes.

The diapason consonance, whether its sequence is taken from *hypate hypaton* to *paramese*, or from *nete hyperboleon* to *mese*, has only three types enclosed by immovable notes.

Beginning from *hypate hypaton*, one is A–H, the first, from *hypate hypaton* to *paramese*. The second is D–L, the fourth, from *hypate meson* to *nete diezeugmenon*. Then there is G–O, the seventh, namely from *mese* to *nete hyperboleon*.

The outer notes of the remaining types are in no way established by immovable notes [Note: [Col. 1275] Not read.]. For *parhypate*, *lychanos*, *trite*, and *paranete*, as was also said above, are not immovable.

Likewise, if we begin from *nete hyperboleon*, the sequence of the types is formed through the same notes, and the following description makes the understanding of all these matters clearer [Note: [Col. 1275] “Will make [it] more familiar.”]. [Col. 1277A]

## CHAPTER XIV. The beginnings of the modes, in which the arrangement of the notes according to each mode and its notes is set out

From the types of the diapason consonance arise what are called modes, which are also called *tropes* or *tones*.

The *tropes* are arrangements of the entire series of notes, differing either in gravity or in pitch. An arrangement is a complete body, as it were, of a melody, consisting of a conjunction of consonances, such as a diapason, a diapason and diapente [Note: [Col. 1277] “Diapente.”] and diatessaron, or a double diapason.

A diapason arrangement is from *proslambanomenos* to *mese*, with the other intermediate notes included; or again from *mese* to *nete hyperboleon*, with the intervening notes; or from *hypate meson* to *nete diezeugmenon*, together with the notes enclosed between the outer notes.

A diapason-and-diapente arrangement is that which extends from *proslambanomenos* to *nete synemmenon*, together with the intervening notes. A double-diapason arrangement is considered from *proslambanomenos* to *nete hyperboleon*, together with the notes placed in the middle.

If someone makes these arrangements entirely higher or lowers them entirely, according to the types of the diapason consonance mentioned above, he will produce seven modes. Their names are: *hypodorius*, *hypophrygius*, *hypolydius*, *dorius*, *phrygius*, *lydius*, and *mixolydius*. Their order proceeds as follows.

Let there be an arrangement of notes in the diatonic genus from *proslambanomenos* to *nete hyperboleon*, and let this be the *hypodorius* mode. If someone raises *proslambanomenos* by a tone and lowers *hypate hypaton* by the same tone, while making all the remaining notes higher, the entire sequence will become higher than it was before it received the raising of the tone.

Thus the entire arrangement, having been made higher, will be the *hypophrygius* mode. If, in the *hypophrygius*, the notes again receive a raising by a tone, the *hypolydius* melody will arise. But if someone raises the *hypolydius* by a semitone, he will produce the *dorius*. In the other cases too, the progression in raising and heightening is similar.

So that the principle may be grasped not only intellectually [Note: [Col. 1277] “Of the understanding.”], but that its form may also be recognized by the eyes, a description handed down by the ancient musicians must be supplied. But since among the ancient musicians each note was marked by different symbols in each mode, a description of the symbols should first be provided, so that, once these have been understood in themselves, the examination of the descriptions of the modes may be easy. [Col. 1279]

## CHAPTER XV. A description containing the order and differences of the modes

The preceding description contains the names of the strings written beside them, together with the symbols placed next to them, and the addition of the names indicates which belongs to each mode, whether *lydius*, *phrygius*, or *dorius*. [Col. 1280A]

But since we have said that these modes are found in the types of the diapason consonance, let us describe them in the diatonic genus alone, so that their order, falling under the eye, may not delay understanding. [Col. 1281]

## CHAPTER XVI. The description of the modes arranged above

[Col. 1281A]

We had previously said that there were seven modes, but there should seem to be nothing incongruous in the fact that an eighth has been added above them. We shall explain the reason for this addition a little later. For now, it must be considered that these small pages, which are distinguished from one another by the straight arrangement of the lines, sometimes contain musical notes and sometimes do not, as in the mode written “hypermixolydian.” The first small page is marked by the letter ω, the third by Φ. The second is without a note [Note: [Col. 1281] “N tulis” (uncertain reading).]. Thus, in this interval between the notes, a tone is shown to intervene [Col. 1282A]. But the fact that a straight line drawn in regular order, rather than a small page, separates Φ, the mark of the third page, from γ, that of the fourth, declares that they differ by a semitone. This is proved as follows: if ω is the proslambanomenos, Φ the hypate hypaton, and γ the parhypate hypaton, there must be a tonal distance between the proslambanomenos, which is ω, and the hypate hypaton, which is Φ; while between the hypate hypaton, which is Φ, and the parhypate hypaton, which is γ, there must be a semitone difference [Note: [Col. 1281] Thus.]. This must now be observed as a rule in all cases: if a whole page has separated the notes, we should know that the distance between them is a tone [Col. 1283A]. If a line, rather than a page, distinguishes the notes, we should not fail to recognize that their distance is a semitone.

With these points established, if two orders constituting a double-octave consonance are compared with one another, so that it may be recognized which order is lower, then, if the proslambanomenos [Note: [Col. 1283] Not legible.] is lower, or if any other note in the same position is marked as lower than the corresponding note of the same kind, the entire order must likewise be lower. This is more readily determined, however, from the middle note, which is the mese. For of two orders forming a double-octave consonance, whichever has the lower mese will also have the lower entire order [Note: [Col. 1283] Order.]. For all the other notes, compared individually with their counterparts, will likewise be found to be lower. Thus, if one middle note appears a tone higher or lower than another middle note, all the strings, provided they belong to the same kind, will likewise appear, when compared individually with one another, to be a tone higher or lower [Col. 1283B].

If, however, among four middle notes the first maintains a fourth with the fourth, while the first differs from the second by a tone, and the second likewise differs from the third by a tone, the third will form a semitone difference with the fourth. Let there be four middle notes, A, B, C, and D; and let A, compared with D, maintain with it the sesquitertian ratio, which is the fourth. Let A also be a tone distant from B, and B a tone distant from C. It follows that C maintains a semitone distance from D [Col. 1283C]. The same applies if there are five middle notes. For if the first is distant from the fifth by the sesquialteral ratio [Note: [Col. 1283] “Destiterit,” for “disteterit,” perhaps.], and the first from the second, the second from the third, and the fourth from the fifth are each distant by tones [Note: [Col. 1283] “Destiterint,” for “disteterint,” perhaps.], the third will form a semitone difference with the fourth.

Likewise, whichever middle notes approach the proslambanomenos of the other modes produce lower modes. Those which approach the netes produce higher ones [Note: [Col. 1283] Whichever.]. Since, therefore, in the modes described on the preceding page, the first proslambanomeni occupy the reader’s left-hand side [Col. 1283D], while the reader’s right-hand side is closed by the extreme netes, the mode called hypermixolydian will be higher than all the modes, and the hypodorian will be lower than all of them [Note: [Col. 1283] Mode.]. Beginning with the lowest, hypodorian, we shall indicate the difference that the others have among themselves.

In the hypodorian mode, the mese ω is a tone distant from the mese in the hypophrygian mode [Note: [Col. 1283] Is distant.]. This will readily be seen if one compares the hypophrygian mese, which is φ, with the hypophrygian ω, which is the hypodorian mese but, in the hypophrygian, the lychanos meson. For φ and ω differ by a tone, as the intervening page demonstrates [Col. 1284A].

Likewise, the hypolydian mese differs by a tone from the hypophrygian mese. For C, which is the hypolydian mese, is a tone distant from φ, which is the hypolydian lychanos meson but, in the hypophrygian, the mese.

Again, the hypolydian mese, C, is a semitone distant from the Dorian mese. This may be recognized from the fact that the upward-moving order of the hypolydian mese and the upward-moving order of the Dorian mese are distinguished by a single line, not by a page. Consequently, the hypodorian mese is separated from the Dorian mese by the consonance of a complete fourth. This is proved as follows: the ω which is mese in Hypodorian is the same ω which is hypate meson in Dorian; and in every mode or genus the hypate meson differs from the mese by the consonance of a fourth.

Likewise, the Dorian mese, which is π, is a tone distant from the Phrygian mese, that is, M. For what is the mese in Dorian, π, is the lychanos meson in Phrygian.

Again, the Phrygian mese, M, is a tone distant from the Lydian mese, that is, I. For what is the M mese in Phrygian is the lychanos meson in Lydian.

Again, the Lydian mese is a semitone distant from the Mixolydian mese, that is, Η. For, if the straight Lydian order containing the mese is compared with the straight Mixolydian order containing the mese, they are separated not by a small page but by a line [Note: [Col. 1283] “Is.”]. The mese Η, which is the Mixolydian mese, likewise differs by a tone from the hypermixolydian mese, that is, Γ, because Η, which is the mese in Mixolydian, is the lychanos meson in hypermixolydian.

Hence the Dorian mese is separated from the Mixolydian mese by the consonance of a fourth [Col. 1284C]. This is proved as follows: the π which is the Dorian mese, that is [Note: [Col. 1283] “N.”], is the same as the π which is the Mixolydian hypate meson [Note: [Col. 1283] “N.”]; the hypate meson maintains the consonance of a fourth with the mese of every mode.

Likewise, the Dorian mese, that is [Note: [Col. 1283] “N.”], π, maintains with the hypermixolydian mese, which is r, the consonance of a fifth. For the Dorian mese, that is, π, is the lychanos hypaton in the hypermixolydian order; and the lychanos hypaton, when compared in the diatonic kind with the mese of any mode, is separated from it by the consonance of a fifth.

The reason why the eighth mode, hypermixolydian, has been added is now clear [Note: [Col. 1283] Hence.]. Let this be a double-octave consonance.

## CHAPTER XVII. The rationale of the foregoing arrangement of the modes

[Col. 1284D]

The octave consonance therefore extends from A to H, for it is contained by eight notes. We call A–H the first species of the octave; B–I the second; C–K the third; D–L the fourth; E–M the fifth; F–N the sixth; and G–O the seventh. H–P consequently remains outside; it was added so that the entire order might be completed, and this is the eighth mode, which Ptolemy appended above.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How musical consonances can be judged with certainty by the ear

[Col. 1285A]

In order that the account of consonances may be gathered with certainty, this can be accomplished by a very brief and simple instrument [Note: [Col. 1285] Therefore.]. Let there be a carefully stretched rule, A–D, upon which two semicircles—which the Greeks call *magadai*—are placed, so that a line drawn from the curvature at E to the point B produces right angles around itself; and likewise a line drawn from the curvature at F to the point C produces right angles around itself. Let these be equally polished on all sides for the same purposes, and let other equal semicircles be prepared for them. Over these, let an evenly tensioned string be stretched, namely A–E–F–D.

If, therefore, I wish to discover what the consonance of a fourth is [Note: [Col. 1285] Not legible.], I shall proceed as follows: from point E, where the string touches the semicircle, to point F, where on the other side the string again joins the other semicircle, I divide the space E–F into seven parts, and place the point K at the fourth of the seven parts. Thus E–K has to K–F the sesquitertian ratio. If I place a semicircle at K equal to the upper ones, and strike E–K and K–F alternately with a plectrum, they will sound the interval of a fourth. But if I strike both portions, E–K and K–F, together, I recognize the consonance of a fourth [Col. 1286A].

If we wish to produce a fifth, I divide the entire string—that is, the space from E to F—into five parts, assigning three to one ratio and two to the other; and, after placing the semicircle in this way, I assess consonances and dissonances according to the method stated above. Likewise, if I wish to test the consonance of an octave, I cut the whole into three parts and distribute them into one and two; then, striking these together or alternately, I recognize which sounds consonantly and which dissonantly [Note: [Col. 1285] Which.].

The tripla, which arises from mixed consonances, is produced as follows: if we divide the whole into four parts [Note: [Col. 1285] “Patiamur,” perhaps corrupt.], and divide the entire length of the string into three and one, then a semicircle placed at the three-part division will produce the dissonance and consonance of the triple ratio [Col. 1286B].

[Col. 1286]

[Col. 1285C]

After the division of the regular monochord, I think that we should add the matters on which the ancient teachers of music disagree in their opinions, and that a careful judgment should be made concerning all of them; what is lacking in the proposed work must be supplied by an arrangement of moderate learning [Note: [Col. 1285] “Dispensation,” that is, arrangement.].

For there can also be another division in which only a single string is not employed to divide the proportions once they have been established [Note: [Col. 1285] “Dividatur,” let it be divided.]. Instead, an eight-stringed instrument of this kind may be made [Note: [Col. 1285] So that.], or one with more strings, so that the entire account of the proportions, as it were, may be set before the eyes and seen.

## CHAPTER I. The power of harmonics, its instruments of judgment, and the extent to which the senses should be trusted

But we shall speak of these matters a little later. For now, we must say what the power of harmonics is. Since we began to discuss it, we have filled four books. We have deferred expressing its nature and power to the sequence of this fifth volume [Note: [Col. 1285] “Vimque,” its power.].

Harmonics is the faculty that weighs the differences between high and low sounds by sense and reason [Col. 1286C]. Sense and reason are, as it were, certain instruments of the harmonic faculty.

Sense notices something confused and something nearly like the object it senses. Reason, however, judges completeness and pursues the differences individually [Note: [Col. 1285] But.]. Thus sense discovers things that are confused and close to the truth, but receives completeness through reason. Reason itself discovers completeness, but receives through sense a confused likeness that is close to probability [Note: [Col. 1285] Not legible.].

For sense conceives nothing in its entirety, but approaches only what is near. Reason, however, judges—for example, if someone draws a circle by hand, the eye may perhaps judge that circle to be a true circle. Reason, however, understands in no way that it is what it imitates.

This happens because sense turns toward matter, and the form is apprehended in matter; but forms in matter are fluid and imperfect [Note: [Col. 1285] “Nec,” and not.], neither determinate nor polished to the utmost degree [Note: [Col. 1285] “Atque,” and.], as matter itself is. Therefore confusion also follows sense [Note: [Col. 1285] Sense.]. But mind and reason, because they are not detained by matter, contemplate the forms they foresee apart from their association with the subject. For this reason completeness and truth accompany them; rather, they correct or complete what is erroneous or deficient in sense [Note: [Col. 1285] “Potiusque quod in sensu aut peccatur”: rather, what is faulty in sense.].

Perhaps what sense recognizes not completely but confusedly, and with less than the truth, like an unskilled assessor, involves only a small error in each individual case [Col. 1287A]. But when these errors are collected, they are multiplied into a sum and therefore produce a great difference [Note: [Col. 1287] Greatest.].

For if sense judges that two little sounds are a tone apart when they are not, and then supposes that a third is a tone distant from one of them when there is no complete and true tonal distance; if it judges a tonal difference between the third and the fourth, and is likewise mistaken about this so that there is no tonal difference; and if, finally, it supposes that a fifth is a semitone distant from the fourth, without judging the matter truly or completely—in each individual case the error may perhaps seem small.

But what sense left over in the first tone, together with what was mistaken in the second and third tones and in the fourth semitone, gathered and collected into one, will bring it about that the first sound does not contain a consonance of a fifth with the fifth sound, although this ought to happen if sense had judged three tones and a semitone completely [Col. 1287B]. What was insufficiently perceived in each individual tone is clearly revealed as a consonance when collected together.

And so that it may be clear that sense collects confused impressions but in no way rises to the completeness of reason, let us consider the following. Given a line, it is not difficult for sense to find one that is greater, smaller [Note: [Col. 1287] Or.], or different. But if a measure is proposed and it is required to find one so much greater or so much smaller, the first conception of sense will not accomplish this; it requires the skillful discovery of reason.

Or, again, if it is proposed to double a given line or cut it in half, this may perhaps be accomplished somewhat more difficultly than finding one that is confusedly greater or smaller; nevertheless, it can be established by the discovery of sense. But if it is ordered that a line triple the proposed one be made, or that a third part be cut from it, or that a quadruple be established, or a fourth part cut off, would this not be impossible for sense unless the completeness of reason were added? This is because, as the procedure advances, room for reason increases while what is available to sense decreases.

For if someone is ordered to remove an eighth part of a proposed line, or compelled to give its eightfold, he must first take half of the whole [Note: [Col. 1287] Half.], then half of the half, so that it becomes a fourth, and then half of the fourth [Note: [Col. 1287] Not legible.], so that it becomes an eighth. Conversely, he must take double the whole, then double the double, so that it becomes fourfold, and then double the quadruple, so that it becomes eightfold. Thus, in such a great multiplicity of operations, sense accomplishes nothing. Its entire judgment is sudden and situated on the surface; it does not set out completeness and exact pursuit.

For this reason, the entire judgment should not be entrusted to the sense of the ears; reason must also be supplied to guide and regulate erring sense, so that sense, slipping and failing, may lean upon it as upon a staff [Col. 1287D]. For just as individual arts have certain instruments by which they shape something partly in a confused way, such as a small cutting tool [Note: [Col. 1287] Calepinus: *Asciacum*. With c after s, it is a carpenter’s tool used for cutting off and carving. Its diminutive is *asciola*. I suspect that the text is corrupt here.], and partly discover what is complete, such as a compass, so the harmonic faculty also has two parts of judgment: one by which sense apprehends the differences of the sounds presented to it, and another by which it considers the character and measure of those differences.

## CHAPTER II. What the harmonic rule is, and what Pythagoreans, Aristoxenus, or Ptolemy said the aim of harmonics was

[Col. 1288A]

An instrument of this kind, in which differences of sounds are investigated by applying the method of reason, is called the harmonic rule. In this matter there was disagreement among the opinions of many learned men [Note: [Col. 1287] The same place; many things.].

Some who placed the greatest trust in Pythagorean disciplines said that the aim of harmonics was that everything should follow what agrees with reason. Sense, they said, gives in some way the seeds of knowledge, while reason perfects them.

Aristoxenus, on the contrary, said that reason was an attendant and secondary element, while everything was determined by the judgment of sense and should conform to its modulation and agreement [Note: [Col. 1287] “Tendendum,” to be pursued.].

Ptolemy, however, defines the aim of harmonics in a certain way: namely, that nothing should be contrary to either the ears or reason [Col. 1288B]. According to Ptolemy, the harmonic practitioner seems to aim at this: that reason should also weigh what sense judges, and that reason should discover proportions in such a way that sense does not protest; the whole aim of harmonics consists in the agreement of these two.

In this respect he especially criticizes Aristoxenus and the Pythagoreans: Aristoxenus, because he trusts nothing to reason but everything to the senses; and the Pythagoreans, because they give little weight to the senses while devoting the greatest attention to the proportions of reason [Note: [Col. 1287] Because.].

## CHAPTER III. Where Aristoxenus, the Pythagoreans, and Ptolemy placed the basis of low and high pitch

Since everyone agrees that sound is a striking of the air [Col. 1288C], Aristoxenus and the Pythagoreans nevertheless established the difference between low and high pitch in different ways.

Aristoxenus judged that differences among sounds according to low and high pitch consisted in quality [Note: [Col. 1287] “Arbitrabatur,” he judged.]; the Pythagoreans, however, placed them in quantity.

Ptolemy appears closer to the Pythagoreans, because he too considers low and high pitch to be constituted not in quality but in quantity. For denser and finer bodies produce high pitch, while rarer and larger bodies produce low pitch—without our saying anything at present about the manner of tension and relaxation.

Yet even when something is relaxed, it becomes, as it were, rarer and thicker [Note: [Col. 1287] Something.]; when it is tightened, it becomes denser and is made finer and thinner.

## CHAPTER IV. Ptolemy’s view of the differences among sounds

[Col. 1288D]

Having settled these matters [Note: [Col. 1287] Not legible.], Ptolemy divides the differences among sounds as follows [Note: [Col. 1287] “Divisit,” divided.]. Some sounds are unisonous, others non-unisonous. Unisonous sounds are those in which there is one sound, whether low or high. Non-unisonous sounds are those in which one is lower and the other higher.

Among the latter, some are such that their difference is joined by a common boundary. Their difference is not discrete, but proceeds continuously from low to high, so that it appears continuous. Others are non-unisonous sounds whose difference is distinguished by an intervening silence.

For sounds to be joined by a common boundary, this happens as follows. Just as, when a rainbow is seen in the clouds, the colors are close to one another, so that there is no fixed boundary when one is separated from another [Note: [Col. 1289] “Disgregatur,” is separated.], but, for example, the color departs from red toward pale yellow through continuous change and turns into the following color, without any definite intermediate color intervening to distinguish the two, so it also commonly happens with sounds.

If someone strikes a string and twists it while striking it, the result is that at the beginning of the stroke the sound is lower, but while it is being twisted the sound becomes higher; thus the sounds of the low and high notes become continuous.

## CHAPTER V. Which sounds are suitable for enharmonic music

Since some non-unisonous sounds are continuous and others discrete [Col. 1289B], continuous sounds are those whose difference is joined by a common boundary, with no designated position occupied by the high or low sound. Discrete sounds, however, have their own positions, like unmixed colors whose difference is visible as established in its own place.

Continuous non-unisonous sounds are separated from the harmonic faculty. They are unlike one another and do not produce a single unified sound. Discrete sounds, however, are subject to the art of harmonics. For the difference between sounds that are distant and unlike one another can be detected; those which, when joined, can produce a melody are called ἐμμελεῖς (*emmeleîs*, suitable for melody), while those with which no melody can be produced are called ἐκμελεῖς (*ekmeleîs*, unsuitable for melody).

## CHAPTER VI. What number of proportions the Pythagoreans establish

[Col. 1289C]

Sounds that are consonant are those which, when joined, produce mixed and pleasing sounds; dissonant sounds are those which do not. This, then, is Ptolemy’s judgment concerning the difference among sounds.

We must now explain how he differs from the other musicians in establishing consonances. The Pythagoreans consider the consonances of the fifth and fourth simple, and from these join one octave consonance. They also recognize the fifth together with the octave, and the double octave: the former in the triple ratio [Note: [Col. 1289] “Triplici,” triple.], the latter in the quadruple ratio.

They do not consider the octave together with the fourth a consonance, because it does not fall under a comparison that is either superparticular or multiple, but under a multiple-superpartient comparison. The ratio of the sounds is eight to three. For if one places four between these numbers, the terms become 8, 4, 3. Of these, 8 to 4 produces the consonance of an octave; 4 to 3, that of a fourth; while 8 to 3 is constituted in a multiple-superpartient ratio [Col. 1289D].

What a multiple-superpartient comparison is must be learned from the arithmetic books and from what we set out in the second book of this work. The Pythagoreans place consonances in multiple and superparticular ratios, as was stated in the same second and fourth books. But they exclude consonance from superpartient and multiple-superpartient ratios.

The ways in which the Pythagoreans join the octave in the double ratio, the fourth in the sesquitertian ratio, and the fifth in the sesquialteral ratio must be sought in the fourth book of the second book of this work on Music [Col. 1290A] [Note: [Col. 1289] “Conjungunt,” they join.].

## CHAPTER VII. What Ptolemy criticizes in the Pythagoreans concerning the number of proportions

Ptolemy criticizes the Pythagoreans and, in several ways, the entire demonstration that we set out in the preceding books. In particular, he criticizes the fact that they join the fourth and fifth by the sesquialteral and sesquitertian ratios, while, although the remaining superparticular ratios belong to the same genus, they apply no consonances to them at all [Col. 1290B].

## CHAPTER VIII. Ptolemy’s demonstration of the consonance of the octave and fourth

He proves that a certain symphony is produced from the octave and fourth as follows. Since the consonance of the octave produces such a conjunction of sounds that the string appears to be one and the same—and the Pythagoreans also agree on this—if any consonance is added to it, the octave remains whole and unbroken [Note: [Col. 1289] Not legible.]. The added consonance is joined to the octave as to a single string.

Let the octave consonance be contained between the hypate meson and the nete diezeugmenon [Col. 1290C]. These two agree with one another so completely in sound that one voice, as though from a single string rather than a mixture of two, strikes the hearing.

Whatever consonance we join to this octave consonance remains intact, because the two are joined as though to one small voice and one string. If the hypate meson and the nete diezeugmenon are each joined upward by a fourth, then, if the nete diezeugmenon is joined to the nete hyperboleon and the hypate meson to the mese [Note: [Col. 1289] “As it is joined.”], each will be consonant with each: the mese with the nete diezeugmenon, and the same mese with the hypate meson. Likewise, the nete hyperboleon will be consonant with the nete diezeugmenon and with the hypate meson.

Again, if the two fourths are relaxed toward their lower side [Note: [Col. 1289] “Utrisque,” both.], then, while retaining a fourth consonance with the hypate meson, there will be the hypate hypaton; and toward the nete diezeugmenon, the paramesē [Note: [Col. 1289] “Mesen,” mese.]. The hypate hypaton will also be consonant with the hypate meson and with the nete diezeugmenon; and the paramesē with the nete diezeugmenon and with the hypate meson [Note: [Col. 1289] “A nete,” from the nete.].

This occurs in such a way that the lower note retains a fourth consonance with the note nearest to it, but with the more distant note a fourth and octave: thus the hypate hypaton has a fourth with the hypate meson, but a fourth and octave with the nete diezeugmenon. Likewise, the nete hyperboleon, which is higher, has a fourth consonance with the nete diezeugmenon nearest to it, but a fourth and octave with the hypate meson [Col. 1291A].

## CHAPTER IX. The particular character of the octave consonance

He maintains that this occurs because the octave is almost a single small voice and is a consonance that in a certain way produces one sound. Just as, in the number ten, whatever is added within it is preserved whole and unaltered [Note: [Col. 1291] “Inviolatusque,” and unbroken.], whereas this does not at all happen in other cases, so it occurs in this consonance.

For if you add two to three, you immediately produce five, and the form of the number has been changed. But if you add the same two to ten, you produce twelve, and the binary number, joined to ten, is preserved. The same applies to three and the other numbers.

Thus the octave symphony preserves whatever other consonance it receives; it neither changes it nor turns a consonance into a dissonance. For just as the fifth symphony, joined to the octave consonance in the triple ratio, preserves the consonance of the octave and fifth, so the fourth, being a consonance, when joined to the octave produces another consonance. According to Ptolemy, the addition is that of another consonance [Note: [Col. 1291] “Ejus quae,” namely, that which is.], and it is the octave and fourth, constituted in a multiple-superpartient ratio [Col. 1292A].

This is the double-superbipartient ratio, namely eight to three; for eight contains three twice, together with two parts of it, that is, two units.

## CHAPTER X. The ways in which Ptolemy establishes consonances

Ptolemy thus judges the Pythagorean position. We must now begin from the point at which he investigates the proportions and numbers of consonances.

“Sounds,” he says, “are either unisonous or non-unisonous. Of non-unisonous sounds, some are aequisonous [Note: [Col. 1291] Others are consonant.], some emmelic, some dissonant, and some ecmelic.

“Unisonous sounds are those which, when struck individually, produce one and the same sound. Aequisonous sounds are those which, when struck together, produce from two sounds one sound that is in some way simple, as in the octave and the doubled octave, which is the double octave [Col. 1292B].

“Consonant sounds are those which produce a compound and mixed, yet still pleasing, sound, as in the fifth and fourth. Emmelic sounds are those which are not consonant but can nevertheless be correctly fitted to a melody, such as those that join consonances. Dissonant sounds are those which do not mix their sounds and strike the sense unpleasantly. Ecmelic sounds are those which are not admitted into the joining of consonances; we shall discuss them a little later in the division of the tetrachords.”

Since aequisonous sounds are closest to unisonous ones, the inequality of numbers that is nearest to equal numbers must necessarily be assigned to them. The ratio nearest to equality is the double ratio [Col. 1292C]. For it is both the first species of multiplicity and the case in which the greater number surpasses the lesser by an amount equal to the lesser itself: two surpasses one by one, which is equal to that same unit. The double ratio is therefore rightly applied to aequisonous sounds, that is, to the octave. The double octave is assigned twice the double ratio, that is, the quadruple ratio.

The ratios that divide the double ratio, the first and greatest ratio, must be applied to those consonances that divide the octave, the aequisonous consonance [Note: [Col. 1291] “Aequisonantiam,” aequisonous consonance.]. Hence the fifth is joined to the sesquialteral comparison and the fourth to the sesquitertian comparison.

Consonances joined to aequisonous sounds produce other consonances: the fifth and octave in the triple ratio, and the fourth and octave in the ratio of eight to three.

Emmelic sounds are those that divide the fifth and fourth, such as the tone and the other ratios, which we shall discuss a little later in the division of the tetrachords—their simple parts [Col. 1292D].

## CHAPTER XI. Which sounds are aequisonous, which consonant, and which emmelic

Aequisonous sounds are the octave and double octave, because through their adjustment and mixture one sound, in a certain sense simple, is produced.

The consonances are, first, among the superparticular ratios, the sesquialteral and sesquitertian ratios, that is, the fifth and fourth; also the octave and fifth, and the octave and fourth. These are compound and joined, formed from aequisonous and consonant intervals [Col. 1293A] [Note: [Col. 1293] “The remaining sounds are emmelic.”].

The remaining intervals may be placed among the emmelic ones, such as the tone, which is the difference between the fourth and fifth. In a certain way, the aequisonous intervals are joined from consonances—for example, the octave from the fourth and fifth. Consonances, in turn, are formed from those sounds called emmelic, such as the same fifth and fourth from tones and the other ratios to be discussed later.

How the ratio of all these may be gathered must be taken from the passage that we described at the end of the fourth volume, where a number was stretched over semicircles [Note: [Col. 1293] “Nervus,” string.]. There the aequisonance—the octave and double octave—the simple consonances, the fifth and fourth, the compound consonances, the octave and fifth and the octave and fourth, and the emmelic sounds, such as those consisting in the difference of the tone, are all discovered [Col. 1293B].

## CHAPTER XII. How Aristoxenus considers the interval

What Aristoxenus thought about these matters must now be briefly disclosed [Note: [Col. 1293] “Ipse,” he himself.]. Since he established no treatment of the subject through reason but entrusted it to the judgment of the ears, he does not mark the sounds themselves with numbers in order to collect their proportions. Instead, he takes the difference between them, placing his investigation not in the sounds themselves but in what distinguishes them from one another.

He does this most imprudently, since he thinks he knows the difference between sounds whose magnitude and measure he does not establish.

He therefore proposes that the consonance of a fourth consists of two tones and a semitone, the fifth of three tones and a semitone, and the octave of six tones. The preceding books have demonstrated that this cannot be so [Col. 1293C–D].

## CHAPTER XIII. Description of an eight-stringed instrument showing that the octave consonance is less than six tones

Ptolemy teaches, through the division of a certain eight-stringed instrument [Col. 1294A], that the octave falls within six tones, as follows.

Let the eight strings, A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, be stretched. Let A–K be sesquioctave to B–L; B–L sesquioctave to C–M; C–M sesquioctave to D–N; D–N sesquioctave to E–X; E–X sesquioctave to F–O; and F–O sesquioctave to G–P. Thus there will be six tones.

Again, between F–O and G–P let the middle string H–R be stretched. Then A–K will be double H–R. If A–K and H–R are struck together, they will sound the aequisonance of the octave. But if someone strikes G–P, it will always be slightly higher than H–R.

Therefore the six tones exceed the octave consonance. For if A–K and G–P, when struck, sounded the octave, the octave consonance would consist of six tones. But if, while A–K and G–P are not consonant, A–K and H–R sound the octave, and H–R is higher than G–P, the octave consonance would exceed six tones [Col. 1294B].

Now, however, since H–R is found to be lower than G–P while A–K and H–R are consonant, there can be no doubt that six tones exceed the octave consonance. Thus, by sense as well, it can be established that the octave consonance falls within six tones [Note: [Col. 1293] “Intra,” within.]. In this way the error of Aristoxenus is refuted beyond doubt [Col. 1294C].

## CHAPTER XIV. The consonance of the fourth is contained in the tetrachord

We must now speak about the division of the tetrachords. The consonance of the fourth is formed by four strings; for this reason it is also called *diatessaron*. Therefore, in order that a tetrachord may be formed from two strings placed at either end and sounding together in the symphony of the fourth, two strings must necessarily be placed in the middle, producing three proportions both with one another and with the outer strings [Note: [Col. 1293] “Ac,” and.].

## CHAPTER XV. How Aristoxenus divides the tone, and the arrangement of his genera and division

[Col. 1294D]

Aristoxenus divides this fourth according to the genera in the following manner. He divides the tone into two parts and calls that a semitone. He divides it into three parts, calling the third part the diesis of the soft chromatic. He divides it into four parts, and calls the fourth part together with its own half—that is, with an eighth of the whole tone—the diesis of the hemiolic chromatic [Note: [Col. 1293] These words are not read.]. Again, he calls the fourth part alone the enharmonic diesis.

[Col. 1295A]

**GLAREANUS’S FIGURE**

Semitone — half a tone — semitone

[Col. 1295B]

**The division of all the intervals contained in the tone according to Aristoxenus**

**TO THE READER**
It was not possible to draw the minute divisions, dear reader, since Aristoxenus divides the tone into twelve parts. Thus the enharmonic diesis will contain three; the diesis of the soft chromatic four; finally, the semitone six; while the diesis of the hemiolic chromatic will contain four and a half. But if the interval is doubled, as Boethius does shortly afterward, all the intervals we have mentioned will have to be doubled, for the sake of more convenient numbers, as the learned reader will readily see. Farewell.

Since these things are so, and since according to him the division of the genera is twofold, one genus is softer and the other more intense. The softer is the enharmonic, while the more intense is the diatonic. Between these stands the chromatic, sharing in intensity and softness. Thus, according to this order, six differences of mixed genera arise: one of the enharmonic; three of the chromatic—that is, the soft chromatic, the hemiolic chromatic, and the thoniaean chromatic; and the remaining two of the diatonic, the soft and the intense.

The division of all these according to Aristoxenus is as follows. Since the fourth part of a tone has already been called the enharmonic diesis, and since Aristoxenus does not compare the notes themselves with one another but measures the difference and interval between the notes, and since according to him a tone consists of twelve units, its fourth part will therefore be an enharmonic diesis of three units. Since the diatessaron consonance is joined from two tones and a semitone, the whole diatessaron will consequently consist of twelve plus twelve plus six units.

But since it often happens that, if we wish to carry the divisions as far as the octaves, we fall not upon whole numbers but upon certain fractions, [Note: [Col. 1295] Not read.] the whole diatessaron consonance must therefore be made 60. The tone, then, is 24; the semitone, 12; the fourth part, which is called the enharmonic diesis, 6; and the eighth part, 3. When the eighth part is joined with the fourth—that is, six with three—to produce the diesis of the hemiolic chromatic, the result will be 9.

With these matters thus established, Aristoxenus seems to assign the following properties to the three genera—the enharmonic, chromatic, and diatonic—namely, that some are called dense and others not dense. Dense are those whose two lower proportions do not exceed in magnitude the one placed toward the higher note. [Note: [Col. 1295] “Qua.”] The non-dense, on the other hand, are those whose two proportions can exceed the remaining one. [Note: [Col. 1295] “Qua.”] The enharmonic and chromatic are dense, whereas the diatonic is not dense.

Thus the enharmonic, according to Aristoxenus, is divided as follows: 6, 6, 48. Between the low string and the one next above it is one fourth of a tone, which is called the enharmonic diesis, since the tone consists of 24 units. Likewise, the second interval, from the low string to the third, is the same fourth part of a tone. [Note: [Col. 1295] 6.] The remaining 48 of the 60 units belonging to the whole proportion are placed between the third string from the low and the highest, fourth string. The two proportions placed toward the low—namely 6 and 6—do not exceed the one placed toward the high, namely 48.

The soft chromatic makes the following division: 8, 8, 44. Thus 8 and 8 are thirds of tones; for the tone, as has been said, consists of 24 units, and a third part of a tone is called the diesis of the soft chromatic.

The hemiolic chromatic divides the diatessaron as follows: 9, 9, 42. [Note: [Col. 1295] “For.”] The diesis of the hemiolic chromatic is the eighth part of a tone together with the fourth part—that is, six plus three out of the 24.

Likewise, the division of the thoniaean chromatic according to Aristoxenus is as follows: 12, 12, 36. That is, each of the two intervals contains a semitone, with what remains placed in the last interval.

In all these cases, however, the two proportions nearest to the lower string do not exceed in magnitude the remaining one placed toward the high. [Note: [Col. 1295] “Magnitude.”] For, as has been said, these are dense genera. The dense genera are indeed the enharmonic and the chromatic.

The diatonic division itself is also twofold. The division of the soft diatonic is as follows: 12, 18, 30, so that 12 is a semitone, 18 is a semitone and a fourth part of a tone, [Note: [Col. 1295] 30.] while 32 is what remains. Of these, 18 and 12 make 30, and they are not exceeded by the remaining portion.

The division of the intense diatonic is such that it has a semitone and two whole tones: 12, 24, 24. Of these, 24 and 12—that is, 36—are not exceeded by the remaining part toward the high; rather, they exceed it.

Such, according to Aristoxenus, is the aforementioned division of the tetrachords, as is shown by the diagram appended below.

## GLAREANUS TO THE READER

We have, I hope, explained the entire matter of the hyperbolaeon tetrachord in such a way that the reader may readily understand what God wished me to work out. Much, however, must be presupposed from the preceding material, especially how the division of the genera is arranged; otherwise the labor will be useless.

The rest, dear reader, I leave for your consideration and attention. Farewell, and love me. I do, however, wish to warn you that, in applying the material, you have turned the lower strings toward the greater number, although this number does not belong to the strings but rather to the intervals. Therefore, where the nete diezeugmenon stood, the nete hyperboleon could appropriately have been placed. Nevertheless, believe that the error is slight. The names do not entirely impede the interpretation.

## CHAPTER XVI. How Archytas Divides the Tetrachords, and Their Description

[Col. 1297A]

Archytas, establishing everything [Note: [Col. 1297] Not read.] according to reason, not only [Note: [Col. 1297] “Sense.”] failed to observe the perception of the ears in the primary consonances, but also followed rational calculation above all in the division of the tetrachords. Yet he did so in such a way that he neither effectively accomplished what he was seeking nor made the account he proposed agree with perception.

He considers there to be three genera: enharmonic, chromatic, and diatonic. In all of them he establishes the same lowest and highest sounds, assigning 2016 to the lowest sounds in every genus and 1512 to the highest. Between these he places, in all three genera, the string nearest to the lowest—namely, the one that is 1944—so that the proportion between it and 2016 is one-and-one-twenty-seventh, that is, a sesquivicesima-septima proportion. [Note: [Col. 1297] “Sesquingesimam,” apparently an OCR corruption.]

Below the high string, and as the third from the lowest, he then places in the enharmonic genus the string that is 1890; 1944 is joined to it in a one-and-one-thirty-fifth proportion, that is, sesquitricesima quinta. The 1890 string is likewise placed in a one-and-one-fourth proportion, sesquiquarta, in relation to the highest, 1512.

In the diatonic genus he places as the third from the lowest, and the second from the highest, the string that is 1701. It is joined to 1944 by a one-and-one-seventh proportion, sesquiseptima. The 1701 string itself stands to the highest, 1512, in a one-and-one-eighth proportion, sesquioctava.

In the chromatic genus he places as the third from the lowest and the second from the highest the string which bears to 1701—the third from the lowest in the diatonic genus—[Note: [Col. 1297] “The same.”] the same proportion as 256 bears to 243. This string is 1792, and is the second from the highest. The second from the highest in the diatonic genus, namely 1701, bears to the second from the highest in the chromatic genus, namely 1762, the proportion which 243 bears to 257.

The appended diagram displays the form of these divine tetrachords according to Archytas’s account.
