## CHAPTER XVII. How Ptolemy Detects the Divisions of the Tetrachords of Aristoxenus and Archytas

[Col. 1299A]

Ptolemy criticizes both divisions of the tetrachords as follows. First, he criticizes Archytas because the second string from the highest in the chromatic genus, namely 1792, is placed in such a way that it forms no superparticular proportion either with the highest, 1512, or with the next lower, 1944, although Archytas assigned such importance to comparisons by superparticular proportions that he admitted them even in the account of consonances.

Next, he criticizes him because perception detects the first proportion from the lowest string in the chromatic genus as greater than Archytas made it. [Note: [Col. 1299] “Sensus esse.”] For in the chromatic genus Archytas made the distance from 1944 to 2016 a one-and-one-twenty-seventh proportion, [Note: [Col. 1299] “Sesquingesimam.”] whereas according to the customary modulation of the chromatic genus it ought to be a one-and-one-twenty-first proportion. [Note: [Col. 1299] “Sesquingesima.”]

Likewise, in the enharmonic genus, the proportion which Archytas retains as the first from the lowest in his division is such that it ought to be much smaller than it is found to be in the other genera. Yet he makes it equal to those of the other genera, placing the first proportions from the low in all three genera as one-and-one-twenty-seventh proportions. [Note: [Col. 1299] “Sesquingesimas.”]

He criticizes Aristoxenus because, in the soft chromatic and in the hemiolic chromatic, he placed as the first and second proportions from the low string proportions so close to one another that perception cannot distinguish the difference. For the first proportion in [Note: [Col. 1299] Not read.] the first division of the soft chromatic according to Aristoxenus is eight, while in the hemiolic chromatic it is nine. The difference between eight and nine is one unit. But a whole tone, according to the established calculation, consists of 24 units, each unit being one twenty-fourth.

Therefore the first proportions from the low in the soft chromatic and the hemiolic chromatic differ from one another by one twenty-fourth of a tone; because of the smallness of the difference, the hearing perceives it in no way.

He also criticizes Aristoxenus for making only two divisions of the diatonic genus, dividing it into the soft and the intense, although other species of the diatonic genus can also be found.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How He Says the Division of the Tetrachords Ought to Be Made

[Col. 1300B]

Ptolemy [Note: [Col. 1299] “For.”] divides the tetrachords according to a different principle. He establishes at the outset that, between two sounds placed at opposite ends, such intervals must be fitted as exceed one another by superparticular proportions, though unequal ones, since a superparticular proportion cannot be divided equally.

Next, he requires that every comparison made with the string that is lowest should be smaller in all three cases than the comparisons joined to the higher notes. But in those that we call dense, the arrangement must be such that the two proportions nearest the low are smaller than the proportion remaining toward the high. [Note: [Col. 1299] Not read.] But in the non-dense genera, as in the diatonic genera, nowhere a single [one].

# GEOMETRY

## PREFATORY LETTER

### NICOLAUS JUDECUS OF VENICE TO DONATUS CIVALELLUS, A RHETORICIAN, GREETINGS

When a few days ago, Donatus, most elegant cultivator of the Muses, I was reviewing some books of the divine Boethius on Geometry, consulting the Greek exemplar of Euclid—whose numerous theorems Boethius translated word for word into Latin—I noticed that the eminent geometer Euclid is read by our people with very great error and, in my opinion, is not expounded correctly enough. The former fault seems almost entirely to have arisen from the translator.

Whoever he was, in transferring the volumes from the barbarous Greek language, he rendered them into half-Latin. For he leaves certain words in their barbarous form just as they stand, although Latin possesses words of its own, and indeed excellent and thoroughly approved ones.

The quadrilateral figure which both Greeks and Romans call a rhombus, he calls by some, so to speak, exotic word *helmuaim*. And the related figure, which the Greeks call *rhombo den* [rhomboid], he calls a similar *helmuaim*. There are also other quadrilateral figures which the Greeks call trapezia and we call tables or little boards (*mensulae*).

[Col. 1301B]

Yet our translator, equally ignorant of both the Latin and the Greek term, does not hesitate to call them *helmuarifas*. But let these matters be considered trivial and not worthy of much attention.

This, certainly, if I am not mistaken, cannot be defended by any excuse: he both confuses and falsifies the definitions of things that we use as the principles of the entire science, and, with a kind of reckless boldness, substitutes definitions which Euclid never even imagined in place of those that belonged to him.

For immediately at the beginning of the work he concludes the definition of a line with these words: “A line is length without breadth, whose extremities are two points.” This definition cannot at all be accommodated to the line which the Greeks call a circumference, since that has no extremities, although some more recent writers, deceived by the faulty translation, try to defend this as Euclid’s genuine definition. They say that a circumference is indeed without extremities and boundaries in actuality, but that it recognizes boundaries and limits in potentiality, to use their expression. This is utterly ridiculous.

By the same example, I could define a line as length without breadth that lacks extremities. If you object and bring forward a finite straight line, I will reply that it is without boundaries in capacity and power, although in actuality it is not without them. Therefore either both definitions must be accepted—which could not be more absurd—or both must be rejected.

That the latter is the correct course will be evident if one notices how carelessly this excellent translator has joined together two definitions belonging to very different things into a single form, and has adopted them for the definition of one thing alone.

For when Euclid had defined a line as length without breadth, and since some lines were finite and bounded, he immediately declared what the ends and boundaries of a line were, saying: “The extremities of a line are points.” But our author of so ingenious a translation, by mixing and confusing two definitions, constructed a single body of definition and thought that it could be fitted and applied to the line alone.

For a complete definition of a line, therefore, nothing else need be added beyond what has been said: that a line is length without breadth. In this way it includes both lines that run in a curve and straight lines, and likewise both finite and infinite lines. The earlier definition, as is perfectly clear, admitted no infinite lines.

Now let us also show that this translator sometimes omits Euclid’s definitions—being, as he is, equally diligent in everything—and substitutes others in their place. We shall not have to investigate this at great length. Immediately after the definitions just given, he defines a straight line in these words: “A straight line is the shortest extension from one point to another, receiving both of them at its extremities.”

Euclid does not say this. Rather, he sums up the whole definition very briefly in the following way: “A straight line is one that lies evenly between its points.”

He is no less mistaken in the definition of a plane surface. For while Euclid defines it as follows—“A plane surface is one that lies evenly between its lines”—this man has invented a quite different definition: “A plane surface is an extension from one line to another, receiving them at its extremities.”

These and many other things of the same kind are partly translated ineptly and without learning, and partly altered and inverted. If you should at some point happen to read both texts carefully, you will very easily detect this for yourself.

I shall now begin to explain to you what I noted in Campanus’s exposition of the first book of the Elements. In this matter I ask and hope to obtain from all learned men who have leisure to read our work that they be moved less by the authority of the man than by reason itself and truth.

In Euclid’s first book of the Elements there are two theorems, one of which reciprocates with and returns to the other. Campanus demonstrates both by a reduction to the impossible. But so that you may understand more clearly where I am beginning, receive first the theorems themselves together with their demonstrations, just as Campanus read and constructed them. Afterwards you will hear briefly what he may have done wrong and what we think. The theorems are these.

### The longer side of every triangle is opposite the greater angle.

Let triangle ABC be such that angle A is greater than angle C. I say that side CB will be greater than side AB. For if it were equal, then by proposition 5 angle A would be equal to angle C, contrary to the hypothesis.

But if AB is greater, let it be cut down to equality with CB according to proposition 3. Let DB be equal to CB. Therefore, by proposition 5, angle DCB will be equal to angle BDC. But BDC is greater than angle BAC by proposition 16. Therefore BCD is greater than BAC; and consequently, all the more, the part ACB would be greater than the whole, which is impossible.

### The side opposite the greater angle of every triangle is the longer side.

Let triangle ABC be such that side BC is greater than side AB. I say that angle A will be greater than angle C; this is the converse of the preceding theorem.

For if it were equal, then by proposition 6 side AB would be equal to side BC, contrary to the hypothesis. But if C were greater, then by the preceding theorem side AB would be greater than side BC, again contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore the proposition is established.

[Col. 1303A]

Thus Campanus. But so that you may more easily perceive in what respect he seems to us to have thought less correctly, it is necessary to note and interweave a few matters from the field of dialectic.

In every question, as Aristotle maintains in the final books of the Analytics, there are two things: one is given and the other is sought. For example, if the question assumes that the heaven exists, what is asked is whether it is round.

Campanus, however, does not seem to have correctly resolved the proposed theorems into what is given and what is sought. In the first theorem he asks that the greater angle be given and then asks whether the greater side is situated opposite it. In the second, by contrast, he wishes the greater side to be given and asks whether it is opposite the greater angle. The procedure ought to be the reverse.

For anyone moderately trained in dialectic, in my view, can easily see that in the theorem which proposes that the longer side of every triangle corresponds oppositely to the greater angle, the longer side of the triangle ought to be given and posited, while it is asked and asserted whether it is placed opposite the greater angle. Conversely, in the theorem that reverses it, the greater angle should be granted, while the longer side is sought.

From this error another, far more serious one followed. Campanus established neither of the proposed theorems by an assertoric demonstration; rather, he showed both by a reduction to the impossible. In geometry this should be avoided as much as possible whenever it can be done, since demonstrations there are ordinarily drawn from what is prior and better known by nature, not merely to us—such as those called assertoric and direct demonstrations.

The origin and beginning of this error was as follows. Campanus gave the first theorem a predication contrary to nature. He posits the greater angle of the triangle and predicates the longer side of it, since in every question the subject term is what is given and the predicate what is sought.

But it is prior by nature for a triangle to have sides, and thereafter angles, since angles are understood to arise and be produced from the meeting of the sides. Whoever therefore makes the angle of the triangle the subject and predicates the side of it subjects what is accidental to the predication of that to which it belongs, and for that reason makes the predication backward and contrary to nature.

Aristotle regards this either as a predication that must be called “of the accidental,” or as not simply a predication but a predication accidentally. Wherever a predication contrary to nature is involved, it is difficult, or certainly impossible, to apply an assertoric demonstration.

For in such a demonstration it is necessary that the cause of both the greater extreme, which is predicated in the conclusion, and the lesser extreme, which is made the subject in the same conclusion, should be the middle term. But it is in no way possible to establish that what is accidental is the cause of that to which it is accidental.

Thus Campanus was compelled in the first theorem—having incompetently divided what was given and what was sought—to use a demonstration leading to the impossible. And because he considered the later theorem, which returned to the first, to be the principal one, he established it by no other argument than one leading to the impossible.

Thus Campanus applied no direct and assertoric demonstration to establish the theorems we have mentioned, although he ought to have done so, since a direct demonstration is superior to one leading to the impossible.

These, dear Donatus, are the matters which, so far as the proposed theorems are concerned, we have judged worthy of criticism in Campanus. But I know for certain that those who have not read Aristotle’s final Analytics with the greatest care will not fully and subtly understand what we have discussed briefly.

It remains, therefore, for us to demonstrate the theorems themselves, as we promised, though first translating them as they ought to have been translated. We shall resolve and separate the principal theorem into what is given and what is sought, as is proper, and we shall use an assertoric demonstration to establish it. The later theorem, which returns to the principal one and has a predication contrary to nature, we shall briefly collect by means of a demonstration leading to the impossible.

We now undertake the demonstrations themselves. Pay attention.

### The greater side of every triangle is extended under the greater angle.

Let triangle ABC have side AC greater than side AB. I assert that angle ABC, under which side AC is extended, is also greater than angle BCA, to which side AB corresponds on the opposite side.

Since side AC is greater than AB, let AD be constructed equal to AB, and let side BD be extended. Since, in triangle BDC, the exterior angle ADB is greater than the interior angle DCB opposite it, while angle ADB is equal to angle ABD because side AB was equal to side AD, angle ABD is therefore greater than angle ACB. Consequently, angle ABC will be much greater than angle ACB.

Therefore the greater side of every triangle is extended under the greater angle, which was to be demonstrated.

### In every triangle, a greater side is extended beneath a greater angle.

[Col. 1304D]

Let triangle ABC have angle ABC greater than angle BCA. I assert that side AC is also greater than side AB.

For if AC is not greater, then it will either be equal to AB or less than it. It is certainly not equal to AB, for then angle ABC would also be equal to angle ACB, whereas it was not. Therefore side AC is not equal to side AB.

Nor is AC less than AB, for then angle ABC would be less than angle ACB, whereas it was not. Since, therefore, side AC is neither equal to AB nor less than it, it must be greater than AB.

Therefore the greater side of every triangle is extended under the greater angle, which was to be demonstrated.

[Col. 1305A]

These, then, are demonstrations of this kind of theorem: both easy and entirely true, and especially well suited to the matter.

But before I let you go, I want you to hear of another error of this man—perhaps a somewhat lighter one, yet disgraceful and not to be neglected in a philosophical writer.

In the same first book of the Elements there is a problem of the following kind: to construct, on a given straight line and at a given point on it, a rectilinear angle equal to a given rectilinear angle. Campanus reads and derives it as follows.

### On a given straight line, at its endpoint, to construct an angle equal to any proposed angle.

Let the straight line FE be given, and let the lines BA contain the given angle, to which the base C is attached. At point F of line EF I am instructed to make an angle equal to the given angle. To line EF I join FD equal to line A; from FE I take FG equal to B; and from GE I take GH equal to C. On points F and G I describe two circles, DK and KH, according to the lengths of the two lines FD and GH; these intersect at point K, as was taught earlier. Drawing lines KF and KG, the two sides KF and FG of triangle KFG will be equal to the two sides A and B of triangle ABC, and base GK will be equal to base C. Therefore, by proposition 8, angle KFG will be equal to the angle contained by A and B, which was required.

[Col. 1305D]

At first sight this construction seems to have been made with sufficient skill and care. But if you read it closely and attentively, you will find that it ought not to be approved by a serious philosophical discipline.

Since art ought to imitate nature, and nature itself does not abound in superfluities, a person who piles up more elements in a construction than are necessary for the demonstration should not be judged to have constructed it artistically. Campanus, somehow, does not avoid this but runs directly into it.

What is the purpose of the designation of those two circles? What is the purpose of that laborious drawing of so many lines of the same measure? Could he not—and, indeed, ought he not—have taken the given angle contained by lines A and B, together with the attached base C, omitted that anxious and almost pedantic construction, and immediately, by taking three lines equal to the three given lines, constructed a triangle? That this could be done was abundantly clear from the preceding problem.

Therefore anyone who wishes to set out this problem more carefully and precisely will, in my opinion, demonstrate it as follows.

### On a given straight line and at a given point on it, to construct a rectilinear angle equal to a given rectilinear angle.

Let the straight line AB be given, and let point A be given on it. Let the rectilinear angle DCE also be given. It is therefore required to construct, on the given straight line AB and at the given point A, a rectilinear angle equal to the given rectilinear angle DCE.

Let the points D and E be taken, if desired, on the lines ED and CE, and let DE be extended. From the three straight lines AF, AG, and FG, construct lines equal respectively to the three given straight lines CD, CE, and DE. Let triangle AFG be constructed so that line AF itself is equal to CD, line AG itself equal to CE, and finally line FG itself equal to DE.

Since the two straight lines DC and CE are equal respectively to the two straight lines FA and AG, and base DE is equal to base FG, angle DCE will also be equal to angle FAG.

Therefore, on the given straight line AB and at the given point A, an angle FAG equal to the given rectilinear angle DCE has been constructed. This was what had to be done.

I would have added several other errors, much more serious ones, had I not remembered that I was writing a letter. Perhaps at some future time we shall read Euclid through together and note everything in which our people seem to depart from right reason.

For now I have written these few things to you, dear Donatus, so that they might remain with you as a token of the goodwill and respect with which I attended—and still attend—you when you served as rector of our Paduan academy of philosophers.

Farewell from the Paduan school of philosophy.

[Col. 1307]

# TWO BOOKS OF THE GEOMETRY OF EUCLID OF MEGARA, TRANSLATED BY ANICIUS MANLIUS SEVERINUS BOETHIUS: (G, S)*

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 1307A]

Since, most accomplished Patricius, exerciser in geometry, at your urging I have undertaken to expound and polish with a clearer approach Euclid’s obscurely presented account of the figures of the geometrical art, I think that first of all the nature of measure must be defined.

### On Measure

Measure is whatever is bounded by weight, capacity, length, height, breadth, or the mind. The beginning of measure is called a point. A point is that which has no part. A line is length without breadth, and the ends of a line are points.

### On the Kinds of Lines

A straight line is one that extends evenly between its points. A surface is that which is measured by length and breadth. The boundaries of a surface are lines.

[Col. 1307B]

A plane surface is one that is contained evenly by its straight lines.

### On the Kinds of Angles

A plane angle is the meeting of two lines in a plane, touching one another but not lying in a straight line, and enclosing a space between them.

[Col. 1307C]

When the lines containing an angle are straight lines, the angle is called a rectilinear angle.

[Col. 1307D]

[Col. 1308A]

When a straight line standing upon a straight line makes the angles on either side equal to one another, each of the equal angles is a right angle. A line standing upon a straight line is called perpendicular. An obtuse angle is greater than a right angle.

### On the Kinds of Figures

A figure is that which is contained by one or more boundaries.

A boundary is the end of anything.

A circle is a certain plane and enclosed figure contained by a single line, called the circumference. From a point placed within the figure, all the straight lines drawn to the circumference are equal to one another. This point is called the center of the circle.

[Col. 1308B]

The diameter of a circle is a certain straight line drawn through the center and bounded on each side by the circumference of the circle; it divides the circle into two equal parts.

A semicircle is a plane figure contained by a diameter and the circumference which the diameter cuts off.

[Col. 1308C]

Rectilinear figures are those contained by straight lines.

[Col. 1308D]

A trilateral figure is one contained by three straight lines.

A quadrilateral is one contained by four.

A finite mensural line is a line observed either for the sake of some measurement or as one of the boundaries.

A multilateral figure is one contained by more than four sides.

### On Triangles

An equilateral triangle is one contained by three equal sides. [Note: [Col. 1309D] The following three kinds of triangle are distinguished according to unequal sides.]

[Col. 1309B]

An isosceles triangle is one that has only two equal sides.

A scalene triangle is one that has three unequal sides.

[Col. 1309C]

Further, among trilateral figures, a right-angled triangle—that is, a rectangle-shaped triangle—is one that has one right angle. [Note: [Col. 1310D] The following three kinds of triangle are distinguished according to unequal angles.]

An amblygonium, which in Latin is called an obtuse-angled triangle, is one that has an obtuse angle.

An oxygonium, that is, an acute-angled triangle, is one in which all three angles are acute.

[Col. 1310A]

### On Quadrilaterals

Among quadrilateral figures, that which is both equilateral and rectangular is called a square.

[Col. 1310B]

A rectangle is rectangular but not equilateral.

A rhombus is equilateral but not rectangular.

[Col. 1310C]

A rhomboid is a figure that has opposite lines and angles equal, but is not contained by right angles or equal sides.

Apart from these, all quadrilateral figures are called trapezia, that is, tables or little boards.

[Col. 1310D]

Parallel lines, that is, alternating straight lines, are those which are placed in the same plane and, when extended in both directions, do not meet on either side.

### On the Postulates in Geometry

The postulates, which the ancients called petitions, are five.

The first postulates that a straight line may be drawn from any point to any point.

[Col. 1311A]

The second requires that a defined straight line be extended continuously in a straight direction.

The third commands that a circle be described from any center and with any radius.

[Col. 1311B]

The fourth requires that all right angles be equal to one another.

The fifth commands that, if a straight line falling upon two straight lines makes the two interior angles on the same side less than two right angles, the straight lines, when extended indefinitely, will meet on the side where the two interior angles are less than two right angles.

[Col. 1311C]

### On the Common Notions in Geometry

The common notions are what the Greeks call *koinai ennoiai* (κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι), “common conceptions”:

When spaces and intervals are equal to the same thing, they are equal to one another.

If equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal.

If equals are added to equals, the wholes are also equal.

Things that coincide with one another are equal.

[Col. 1311D]

Every rectangle is said to be contained by the two straight lines that enclose its right angle.

Of all the parallelogrammatic spaces situated around the same diameter, each one together with the two supplements is called a gnomon.

Circles whose diameters are equal are equal; those whose diameters are not equal are unequal.

A straight line is said to touch a circle when, touching the circle, it does not cut it on either side when extended.

[Col. 1312A]

Circles are said to touch one another when, touching each other, they do not intersect.

[Col. 1312B]

Straight lines in a circle are said to be equally distant from the center when the perpendiculars drawn from the center to them are equal to one another.

[Col. 1312C]

A line is said to be farther from the center when the perpendicular falling upon it is longer.

[Col. 1312D]

A segment of a circle is a figure contained by a straight line and the circumference of a circle.

In a segment of a circle, an angle is said to exist when some point is taken on the circumference of the segment and two straight lines are drawn from that same point to the endpoints of the line.

[Col. 1313A]

A circular angle is the angle contained by two lines drawn from the center. When the lines that are joined encompass some portion of the circumference, the angle is said to stand upon that portion.

[Col. 1313B]

A sector of a circle is a figure contained by two lines drawn from the center and by the circumference enclosed between them.

[Col. 1313C]

Similar segments of circles are those that contain equal angles, or in which the inscribed angles are equal to one another.

A figure is said to be inscribed within another when the sides of the inscribed figure touch the figure in which it is inscribed, at each of its angles, on the inner side.

[Col. 1313D]

A figure is said to be circumscribed around another whenever the circumscribed figure touches all the angles of the figure around which it is circumscribed with all its sides.

THE PROLOGUES END. THE DIAGRAMS BEGIN.

To construct an equilateral triangle upon a given finite straight line.

[Col. 1314A]

To place at a given point a straight line equal to a given straight line.

[Col. 1314B]

Given two unequal straight lines, to cut off from the greater a straight line equal to the lesser.

[Col. 1314C]

If two triangles have two sides equal, respectively, to two sides of another triangle, and the angle contained by the equal straight lines is equal to the corresponding angle, they will also have equal bases; the one triangle will be equal to the other, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles, each to each, namely those subtended by the equal sides.

[Col. 1315A]

The angles at the base of an isosceles triangle are equal to one another.

[Col. 1315B]

If two angles of a triangle are equal to one another, the sides subtended by the equal angles will also be equal to one another.

[Col. 1315C]

Upon the same straight line, and with the same two straight lines, two other straight lines equal respectively to them cannot in any way be constructed, at different points on the same side and having the same endpoints as the first straight lines.

[Col. 1315D]

In any two triangles whose two sides are equal to two sides of the other, and whose base is equal to the other base, the angles contained by the equal sides must be equal.

[Col. 1316A]

To divide a given finite straight line into two equal parts.

From a point lying on a given straight line, to erect a straight line at right angles.

[Col. 1316B]

If two triangles possess two sides equal to two sides of the other, respectively, and have their bases equal, they will also have equal angles, namely those contained by the equal straight lines.

[Col. 1316C]

From a given point not lying on a given infinite straight line, to draw a perpendicular straight line to it.

[Col. 1316D]

Whenever a straight line standing upon a straight line makes angles, it will either make two right angles or be equal to two right angles.

If two straight lines are drawn to a certain straight line and to a point on it, on opposite sides, and together make angles equal to two right angles, those lines must lie in a straight line with one another.

[Col. 1317A]

If two straight lines intersect one another, they will make the vertically opposite angles equal to one another.

[Col. 1317B]

In every triangle, when one side is produced, the exterior angle is greater than either of the interior and opposite angles.

[Col. 1317C]

In every triangle, the two angles taken together are in every respect less than two right angles.

[Col. 1317D]

In every triangle, the greater side is subtended by the greater angle.

[Col. 1318A]

In every triangle, the greater angle is subtended by the greater side.

In every triangle, two sides taken together are greater than the remaining side in every direction.

[Col. 1318B]

If, on any side of a triangle, two straight lines are drawn inward from the endpoints of the side and form an angle, the lines so drawn will be less than the other two sides of the triangle, but they will contain a greater angle.

[Col. 1318C]

Upon a given straight line and at a given point on it, to construct a rectilinear angle equal to a given rectilinear angle.

[Col. 1318D]

If two triangles have two angles equal, respectively, to two angles of the other, and one side is equal to one side—whether the side adjacent to the equal angles or the side subtended by one of the equal angles—the remaining sides will be equal to the remaining sides, respectively, and the remaining angle will be equal to the remaining angle.

[Col. 1319A]

If a straight transversal crossing two straight lines makes alternate angles equal, the straight lines must be parallel.

[Col. 1319B]

If a straight transversal crossing two straight lines makes the exterior angle equal to the interior angle opposite it, or makes the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles, the straight lines must be parallel.

[Col. 1319C]

Through a given point, to draw a straight line parallel to a given straight line.

In every triangle, the exterior angle is equal to the two interior and opposite angles, while the three interior angles of the triangle are equal to two right angles.

[Col. 1319D]

Lines that join equal and parallel straight lines on the same side of a straight line are themselves parallel and equal.

[Col. 1320A]

Of those spaces contained between one another, which are called parallelograms, the opposite sides and opposite angles are equal to one another, and their diagonal also divides them into two equal parts.

[Col. 1320B]

All parallelograms constructed on the same bases and between the same parallels are proved equal to one another.

[Col. 1320C]

All parallelograms constructed on equal bases and between the same parallels must be equal.

All triangles constructed on equal bases and between the same parallels are equal to one another.

[Col. 1320D]

Equal triangles constructed on the same base and on the same side must also lie between the same parallels.

[Col. 1321A]

Equal triangles constructed on equal, collinear bases and on the same sides must necessarily also lie between the same parallels.

[Col. 1321B]

If a parallelogram and a triangle are constructed on the same base and between the same parallels, the parallelogram must be double the triangle.

[Col. 1321C]

Along a given straight line, to construct a parallelogram equal to a given triangle and contained in a given rectilinear angle.

[Col. 1321D]

To place, within a given rectilinear angle, a parallelogram equal to a given rectilinear figure.

[Col. 1322A]

In every parallelogram, the parallelogram supplements situated about the same diagonal must be equal to one another.

[Col. 1322B]

To describe a square upon a given finite straight line.

[Col. 1322C]

In those triangles in which one angle is right, which we call right-angled triangles, the square described upon the side subtending the right angle is equal to the squares constructed upon the sides containing the right angle.

[Col. 1322D]

[Col. 1323A]

If the square described upon one side of a triangle is equal to the squares described upon the other two sides, the angle contained by those other two sides is a right angle.

[Col. 1323B]

FROM THE SECOND BOOK OF EUCLID THE MEGARIAN.

If there are two straight lines, one undivided and the other divided into any number of parts, the rectangle contained by the two straight lines will be equal to the rectangles contained by the undivided line and each of its divisions.

[Col. 1323C]

If a straight line is divided, the rectangle contained by the whole and one portion is equal to the rectangle contained by the two portions together with the square described upon the aforementioned portion.

If a straight line is divided in any way, the square described upon the whole is equal to the squares described upon each portion, together with twice the rectangle contained by those portions.

[Col. 1323D]

If a straight line is divided both equally and unequally, the rectangle contained by the unequal parts of the whole, together with the square described upon the segment between the two sections, is equal to the square described upon half the line.

[Col. 1324A]

If a straight line is divided both equally and unequally, the squares described upon the unequal portions of the whole are double the squares constructed upon the half and upon the segment between the two sections.

[Col. 1324B]

If a straight line is divided equally, and another straight line is joined to it in a straight direction, the rectangle contained by the whole together with the added line and by the added line, together with the square described upon the half, is equal to the square described upon the line composed of the added line and the half.

[Col. 1324C]

If a straight line is divided equally and a certain straight line is joined to it in a straight direction, the square described upon the whole together with the added line, and the square described upon the added line,

[Col. 1324D]

must, when the two squares are taken together, be double the square described upon the half and the square described upon the line composed of the half and the added line, those two squares likewise being taken together.

[Col. 1325A]

To divide a given straight line so that the rectangle contained by the whole and one portion is equal to the square constructed upon the remaining segment.

[Col. 1325B]

In a triangle that has an obtuse angle, the square on the side subtending the obtuse angle exceeds the squares on the sides containing the obtuse angle by twice the rectangle contained by one of the sides about the obtuse angle, upon which the produced perpendicular falls, and by the segment cut off outside the obtuse angle by the perpendicular.

[Col. 1325C]

To construct a square equal to a given rectilinear figure.

[Col. 1325D]

FROM THE THIRD BOOK OF EUCLID THE MEGARIAN.

If a line drawn through the center of a circle bisects a certain straight line not passing through the center, it cuts it at right angles. And if it cuts it at right angles, it divides it into two equal parts.

[Col. 1326A]

[Col. 1326B]

In equal circles, the angles standing upon equal circumferences are equal to one another, whether they are formed at the centers or at the circumferences.

To divide a given circumference into two equal parts.

[Col. 1326C]

In a circle, the angle in a semicircle is a right angle; the angle in the greater segment is less than a right angle; and the angle in the lesser segment is greater than a right angle. Thus the angle of the greater segment is greater than a right angle, while the angle of the lesser segment is less than a right angle.

[Col. 1326D]

[Col. 1327A]

If a straight line touches a circle, and from the point of contact a straight line is drawn cutting the circle, whatever angles it makes, the two angles situated in alternate segments of the circle are equal.

From this it is therefore clear that, if from a point two straight lines touch a circle and are equal to one another, it is appropriate to describe parts of circles upon the given straight lines.

Within a given circle, to fit a straight line equal to a given straight line that is not greater than the diameter.

[Col. 1327B]

[Col. 1327C]
