[Col. 1329A]

For everything that exists is established by the principle of numbers. And proportionally, circumferences are constituted one from another, exceeding one another according to their respective multiples and, by their alternating proportions, forming their limit.

[Col. 1329B]

## On Geometrical Figures

Since the foregoing investigations of figures were set forth by Euclid briefly and obscurely, and since we have translated them in a compressed manner, rendering word for word, it seems appropriate that certain matters should be repeated and reiterated, so that the reader’s mind may not be deterred by obscurity but may instead be delighted by the light of some example supplied by us. For certain things must be inserted by us into this work: they are highly necessary to this art, correspond to what was said above, and are suited to what follows. Whoever approaches their understanding equipped with the theorems of our arithmeticians is led to a more readily accessible comprehension.

It was therefore stated above that an equilateral triangle ought to be constructed upon a given finite straight line [Col. 1329C], but the statement was too involved; for this reason we have appended the outline of this example. Let the given finite straight line be A B. It is therefore necessary to construct an equilateral triangle upon A B. With center A and radius A B, let the circle B C E D be described. Again, with center B and radius A B, let the circle A C F D be described. From the point G, where the circles intersect, let straight lines be joined to the points A and B: the straight lines C A and C B. Since A is the center of the circle B C E D, A B is equal to A C. Again, since B is the center of the circle A C F D, B A is equal to B C. But A B has also been shown equal to C A and to A C. Therefore A B will be equal to B C. [Col. 1329D] Thus the three lines C A, A B, and B C are equal to one another; therefore triangle C A B is equilateral. It has consequently been constructed upon the given finite straight line A B, as was required.

[Col. 1330A]

It was stated above that at a given point one ought to place a straight line equal to a given straight line. To those inexperienced in this art, however, the statement is obscure and difficult. Therefore, as if introducing and entertaining the reader’s mind, we make clear the explanation of the following figure by setting out the labels of the letters and lines.

Let A be the given point and B C the given straight line. It is therefore necessary to place at point A a straight line equal to B C. Let the straight line A B be joined from point A to point B, and upon A B let the equilateral triangle D A B be constructed. Let the straight lines D A and D B be produced in a straight direction to A G and B M. With center B and radius B C, let the circle C F E be described; and again, with center D and radius D F, let the circle F K L be described.

Since B is the center of circle C F E [Col. 1330B], C B is equal to B F. Again, since D is the center of circle F L K, D L is equal to D F. D A is equal to D B, for triangle D A B is equilateral. Therefore the remaining segment A L is equal to the remaining segment B F. But B F has also been shown equal to B C. Thus B C is equal to A L. At the given point A, therefore, the line A L has been placed equal to the given straight line B C, as the accompanying diagram shows was required.

[Col. 1330C]

Third in order, Euclid stated above that, given two unequal straight lines, one should cut off from the greater a straight line equal to the lesser. But he did so very briefly, and for that reason obscurely and confusedly. We, however, so that the reader’s mind may be led, as though by certain steps, toward a clearer understanding, have appended the description in diagrammatic form.

Let two unequal straight lines be given.

[Col. 1331A]

Let them be A B and C D, and let A B be the greater. It is therefore necessary to cut off from the greater A B a line equal to the lesser C D. At point A, let A E be placed equal to C D. With center A and radius A E, let the circle E G F be described. Since A is the center of circle E G F, A E is equal to A G. But C D was equal to A E, and therefore C D is equal to A G. Thus, from the two given unequal straight lines A B and C D, the straight line A G, equal to the lesser C D, has been cut off from the greater A B, as was required.

[Col. 1331B]

Having been initiated by these concise introductions—which are nevertheless absolutely necessary for beginners in this art—the reader, if he should hesitate or shrink from any of the propositions given above, can by himself discover and construct similar descriptions of the figures without encountering any obstacle.

But now it is necessary to proceed to the account of the geometrical table adapted into Latin by Archytas, a by no means inferior author in this discipline, after first stating what the kinds of angles and lines are and saying a little about summits and extremities.

[Col. 1331D]

There are therefore three kinds of rational angles: right, obtuse, and acute. They have nine species: three of straight lines, three of straight lines and circumferences, and three of obtuse angles and circumferences.

A right angle is *orthigrammos*—that is, enclosed by straight lines—and is called in Latin *normalis*. Whenever a straight line standing upon another straight line makes equal angles, and a perpendicular line is joined, it produces a right-angled triangle.

An obtuse angle is greater than a normal angle, that is, it exceeds the position of a right angle, because if a triangle is constructed in accordance with this position, the perpendicular will lie outside the adjoining lines.

[Col. 1332A]

An acute angle, however, is narrower than a right angle. If from a straight line serving as a base a straight line is emitted according to its inclination, and another straight line is received in opposition with a similar restriction, it produces a triangle having the perpendicular within the three lines.

[Col. 1332B]

There are three kinds of lines: straight, circumferential, and winding.

A straight line is one whose points are arranged equally and which, being laid out evenly on a plane, does not converge. A circumferential line is one whose points are curved on both sides and, remaining at a distance from one another, do not converge; if those points meet, the figure should be called a circle, not a circumferential line. A winding line is multiform, like the lines of trees, rivers, and other features whose extremities end in the likeness of winding fields and of many things naturally formed in a similar straight alignment.

[Col. 1332C]

There are two kinds of summits: a summit and a plane summit. A summit, in geometrical terminology, is that which extends in length and breadth.

[Col. 1332D]

The boundaries of a summit are lines.

A plane summit is that which is bounded everywhere by equal straight lines.

Of all summits there are, in the twenty-second [text uncertain], two observations: the irregular and the level.

The irregular is that which is contained on every side by straight lines.

The level is that which, to lessen labor while preserving the rule of right angles, is drawn according to the extremities themselves.

There are two kinds of extremities: one preserved for straightness and the other for what is winding. Straightness is whatever is seen directed between two points, as though in the form of a line.

[Col. 1333A]

Winding, however, is whatever is curved according to the nature of places. For what in a field has been directed straight to the end by a reaper for the sake of his work is called straightness; whatever is written in imitation of this form is called a line.

There are two straight courses when they extend with intervening spaces, as roads generally proceed.

Anyone who approaches the study of this art must know what digits are, what articulated numbers are, what composite and non-composite numbers are, what multipliers are, and what divisors are, in order to understand the system that we are about to present.

The ancients used to call digits all the numbers below the first limit—that is, all those that we count from unity up to the sum of ten [Col. 1333B]:

1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9.

The articulated numbers, however, are all those arranged by tens and progressing to infinity. They are called composite, namely all the numbers from the first limit, ten, up to the second limit, twenty, and all the others that follow them in order, except the limits themselves. The non-composite numbers are all the digits, together with the limits.

Multipliers are therefore numbers that are turned by mutual multiplication of one another: sometimes the greater is the multiplier of the lesser, and sometimes the lesser is the multiplier of the greater. Sometimes, moreover, a number increasing by multiplication receives the increments of multiplication.

[Col. 1333C]

Divisors, on the other hand, are always constituted as numbers smaller than the greater numbers.

## On the Principle of the Abacus

The men of ancient wisdom, therefore, following the Pythagorean doctrine and being diligent investigators and observers of Platonic authority, established the entire summit of philosophy by the power of numbers. For who could recognize the harmonies of musical melodies without reckoning their numbers? Who, ignorant of the nature of numbers, could discern the heavenly bodies of the firmament, compacted of stars, or calculate the risings and settings of the constellations?

What need is there to speak of arithmetic and geometry, when, if the force of numbers disappears, it is not even apparent in the act of naming? Since enough has been said about this in the sections on arithmetic and music, let us return to what remains to be said.

The Pythagoreans, so that they might never be deceived in multiplication, division, or land-measurement, being ingenious and subtle in all things, devised for themselves a certain scheme. In honor of their teacher they called it the Pythagorean Table, because they had learned what they had drawn by observing their master demonstrate it. By later generations it was called the Abacus. Thus, what they had conceived in their lofty minds could be transferred into everyone’s knowledge more effectively if they displayed it as though by sight; and they formed it below with a remarkably ingenious arrangement.

[Col. 1334A]

They used the scheme of the description arranged above in the following manner. They had variously formed points or characters. Some of them wrote down signs of this kind, so that one such sign corresponded to unity:

1.

Another to two:

2.

A third to three:

3.

A fourth to four:

4.

A fifth was assigned to five:

5.

Another to six:

6.

A seventh corresponded to seven:

7.

Another to eight:

8.

And another was joined to nine:

9.

Others, in depicting this arrangement, adopted letters of the alphabet for themselves in such a way that the first letter represented unity, the second the number two, the third the number three, and the remaining letters, marked and inscribed in their natural order, represented the corresponding numbers. [Col. 1334C] They used to scatter these points in various ways, as though dust, in multiplication and division, so that if they placed the characters already mentioned beneath the natural order of the numbers, by joining them together, no numbers other than the digits would result.

They determined that, beneath the inscription 10, 20 should be assigned to the first number—that is, two, since unity, as has been stated in the arithmetic, is not a number but the source and origin of numbers—30 to three, 40 to four, and the others following in order according to their proper denominations.

Beneath the line marked with the number one hundred, they placed the same points, designating two as 200, three as 300, four as 400, and decreeing that the others should correspond to their fixed denominations. In the succeeding lines of the pages, doing the same thing, they were not obscured by any cloud of error.

[Col. 1334D]

It is also necessary to know and to examine carefully, in multiplication and division, on which page the digits and on which the articulated numbers are to be placed. For a single multiplier places tens of digits in the tens, and articulated numbers in the hundreds. The same single multiplier places hundreds of digits in the hundreds, and articulated numbers in the thousands. A multiplier of thousands places digits in the thousands and articulated numbers in the tens of thousands; a multiplier of hundreds of thousands places digits in the hundreds of thousands and articulated numbers in the thousands of thousands.

A multiplier of tens, multiplying by itself, places digits on the page marked C, and articulated numbers in the thousands. A multiplier of one hundred places digits in the thousands and articulated numbers in the tens; a multiplier of one thousand places digits in the tens and articulated numbers in the hundreds; and a multiplier of one hundred thousand will have thousands.

[Col. 1335A]

A multiplier of one hundred, likewise multiplying by itself, places digits in the tens and articulated numbers in the hundreds and thousands. Multiplying digits in the hundreds and articulated numbers in the tens of hundreds, and multiplying one hundred thousand, it will place digits in the tens of thousands *ῖ* and articulated numbers in the hundreds of thousands *ῖ*. Multiplying ten thousand, it will place digits in the thousands *ῖ* and articulated numbers in the tens of thousands *ῖ*. [The Greek letter ῖ is printed in the source.]

A thousand likewise multiplying itself places digits in the tens and articulated numbers in the hundreds. A multiplier of one hundred thousand places digits in the hundreds of thousands *ῖ* and articulated numbers in the thousands *ῖ*. Producing an increase of ten thousand, it will be recognized as having digits in ten thousand thousands and articulated numbers in the hundreds of thousands *ῖ*, though the reading is uncertain.

[Col. 1335B]

A multiplier of ten thousand, multiplying one hundred thousand, will be found to have digits in a thousand thousand thousands and articulated numbers likewise in the tens of thousands; increasing itself, it will have digits in the hundreds of thousands and articulated numbers in a thousand thousand. A multiplier of one hundred thousand, multiplying itself, likewise places digits in the tens of thousands and articulated numbers in the hundreds of thousands.

## Heading on Divisions

Once the reader’s mind has been introduced to divisions of whatever magnitude, it can readily understand them. We shall speak of these matters briefly and only in outline; if anything obscure should occur, we leave its investigation to the diligent exercise of readers.

If tens are proposed to be divided by themselves, or [Col. 1336A] hundreds, or higher numbers, the smaller numbers are to be subtracted from the greater as far as possible. A single divisor should divide tens, hundreds, thousands, or higher numbers by taking their difference; or a divisor of tens should divide the successive tens.

A composite number of tens together with a single number is to be divided by the second or third place, and thereafter, according to the denomination of the parts, the divisor will be either a ten or a simple or composite number.

If a careful investigator approaches the division of hundreds of thousands or higher numbers by a composite ten, he will understand that they can be divided by taking the difference and dividing by the first articulated numbers, or by applying the numbers in the second place, with the numbers to be divided increased by those placed beneath them.

A hundred composed with a single number, denoted by M, is understood to divide hundreds or thousands in this way. [Col. 1336B] Having taken one of the numbers to be divided, whatever remains is to be made equal to the divisor; whatever exceeds it is to be set aside and retained.

The single divisor—or, as some prefer, the marked divisor—is to be multiplied by the equalization of the greater numbers. The completed difference is to be placed beneath the digits, while the incomplete articulated number is to be placed before it and joined only after the whole has first been set aside. This difference also indicates whether something has perhaps been excluded and what remainder results from the numbers being divided.

Having offered this brief introduction, and lest anything stated obscurely be omitted on account of tedium, we entrust whatever is unclear to the diligence of the attentive reader. We hereby bring this book to an end and, as it were, turn ourselves toward what follows.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1335C]

In the treatment of the preceding volume, all the theorems of the geometrical art were stated, briefly though they were. But this book, in the manner of a collection of problems, will without hesitation resolve by explanation the intricacies of all questions concerning land-measurement. For the ancient surveyors were accustomed to make every square measurement half as long again or half as broad again. Whatever was greater in width they wished to call a *scamnum*, and whatever was greater in length they wished to call a *longum*, as the diagram below teaches.

## Heading on Measurements

The ancient land-measurers, therefore, extremely cautious observers, established twelve kinds of measurement, by which they could measure the areas of figures and fields whenever they wished. Their names are: the mile, the stadium, the *actus*, the ten-foot measure, which is also called the *pertica*; the pace, the step, the cubit, the foot, the half-foot, the palm, the ounce, and the digit.

It has been established that a mile has an extent of five thousand feet. A stadium is agreed to contain twenty-five feet.

The *actus* is divided in three ways: into the minimum, the square, and the doubled. The minimum *actus* extends only four feet in breadth and 120 feet in length.

[Col. 1336C]

The square *actus* is enclosed by 120 feet on every side. The doubled *actus* extends 240 feet. The ten-foot measure contains ten feet; the pace, five; the step, two and a half. The cubit is recognized as having one and a half feet. The foot has four palms; the half-foot, two; and the palm is completed by an extent of four digits.

We shall speak more fully of the ounce and digit measure when, in what follows, we discuss ounces, signs, and names. We shall explain it more clearly when we have treated the subtleties of the small divisions and minute parts. For now, we must return to the exposition of the following treatment, after first demonstrating what an extended foot, a contracted foot, and a square foot are.

[Col. 1336D]

An extended foot is said to be present when only a measurement of length is considered. A contracted foot is judged to be one in which length and breadth are considered. A square foot is understood to be present when a consideration of three dimensions is reckoned according to inequality. But now it is time to approach the subject we have undertaken.

## Heading on Measurement and the Three Dimensions

Although at the beginning of the preceding book we also explained what measurement signifies, it is nevertheless pleasing, in order to satisfy the investigators of this art, to define specially—following Julius Frontinus, the most provident examiner of the geometrical art—what measurement is.

[Col. 1337A]

Measurement is a finite length of several intervals that are equal to one another. The measuring investigation of the geometrical art is gathered through consideration of three dimensions: length, breadth, and thickness. To resolve the matter more clearly, it is recognized according to the straight, the plane, and the solid.

The straight is that which is measured only by length, such as the lines of porticoes, stadia, miles, the widths of rivers, and many other things directed in a long extension, as the depiction of the line below indicates.

A plane is what the Greeks call *epipedon* (ἐπίπεδον), but what we call contracted feet, because it is considered according to length and breadth. Examples are the level surfaces of fields and the areas of buildings without their roof-work, ceilings, floors, and similar features, as the diagram below demonstrates.

[Col. 1337B]

The solid is what the Greeks call *stereon* (στερεόν), but what we call square feet. It is shown to possess length, breadth, and thickness, as do buildings, pillars, pyramids, heaps of stones, and many other things, as the diagrams below indicate.

## Heading on Land-Measurements

But now it is time, as we promised, to touch upon the knowledge of questions concerning land-measurement by explaining them, and immediately to speak about the investigation of foot-measurement.

Concerning triangles, however, which, just as three naturally precedes four, ought to be placed before quadrilaterals, pentagons, and the rest, I judge that we must first speak.

## Heading on Triangles

[Col. 1337D]

There are six principal kinds of triangles: the equilateral (*isopleuron*), the isosceles, the scalene, the right-angled (*orthogonium*), the obtuse-angled (*amblygonium*), and the acute-angled (*oxygonium*). We shall explain the forms and measurements of all of them in what follows.

## Heading on the Equilateral Triangle

The equilateral triangle, *isopleurus*, which at nearly the beginning of the preceding book was called an equilateral triangle, is shown to have equal sides.

Let an equilateral triangle be given, each of whose sides measures thirty feet. Its *embadum*, that is, its area, is to be found in the following way. The sum of one side multiplied by itself produces the number 900. If 510 is subtracted from this [Col. 1338A], 390 remains; so many feet does the area of this equilateral triangle contain.

For its perpendicular is established as extending twenty-six feet. If this is multiplied by half of one side, namely fifteen, the product completes the area. Alternatively, if one third of one side is increased by three and by ten, 300 will result. If, however, the sum of one side is multiplied by the same three, it will produce ninety; these ninety, added to the preceding 300, will make 390, that is, the area of the aforementioned triangle. Let the diagram of the foregoing be made below.

[Col. 1338B]

So that the reader may not be hindered in such investigations by any cloud of error or ignorance, we shall append an illustrative demonstration of the same equilateral triangle—that is, of a figure with equal sides. Let there be, then, an equilateral triangle whose individual sides measure twenty-eight feet.

If one of them is increased by itself, the sum 784 will result [Col. 1338C]. If you add to this the number of one side, 812 will arise. By taking half of the foregoing sum, you will recognize the area of the aforementioned equilateral triangle, as the diagram below demonstrates.

To enable someone investigating the measurement of each side of this often-mentioned triangle and to state it, we shall provide a very clear demonstration of the method. Let it be proposed, then, that an area extends for 406 feet; let us determine how many feet in breadth each side comprises. Let the aforesaid area therefore be multiplied by eight, and the number 3248 results. If one is added to this, the total is 3249. If I take the square root of this total, it will be 57. If one is subtracted from this, 56 remain. If I investigate half of this, 28 results. Thus each side of the equilateral triangle extends for 28 feet.

The isosceles triangle, which Euclid, highly skilled in geometry, defined as having only two equal sides, is established second in the order of triangles. If its two sides extend by an odd number, namely 25 feet, its base is noted as having fourteen feet of space. We must therefore determine how many feet the perpendicular height of its area comprises. For if half the base, that is 7, is multiplied by itself, 49 results. But if you multiply the measure of one side by itself, that is, 25 by 25, you obtain 625; if you set aside 49 from this, 576 remain. If you take the square root of these, it will be 24: by so many feet the perpendicular of this triangle is understood to extend. Its area is found as follows. Once again half the base must be taken, that is 7; if you multiply these 7 by the perpendicular, namely by 24, you will produce 168. Such is the area of the aforesaid triangle in feet.

[Col. 1339B]

### On the scalene triangle

The scalene triangle, therefore, was defined by Euclid as having three unequal sides. We shall give clear numerical examples of its form. Let there be proposed a scalene triangle, which the Latins call a *cuneus* (“wedge”), whose shorter sloping side comprises 15 feet, while its base is noted as having a length of 25 feet. It remains to determine how many feet the perpendicular of this triangle extends and what its area is.

Let the length of the shorter side therefore be multiplied by itself: 225 results. Likewise, if the base is multiplied by itself, 625 is produced; when these are combined, 850 results. The length of the longer side, which has been set apart by itself, must now be multiplied by itself; that multiplication produces 400. If you subtract this 400 from the previously set-aside total, namely from 850, 450 remain. If you take half of this, you will obtain 225; if the total of the base, namely 25, is subtracted from it, 9 will remain. This is the number of feet contained in the smaller cut-off or removed portion of this triangle.

It remains to determine how many feet the perpendicular has. Let the shorter side therefore be multiplied by itself, as above: 25 results. Again, if the increased little sum of the smaller cut-off portion is multiplied by itself, it produces 81. If you subtract this from the side multiplied by itself, 144 remain. Its square root is recognized as 12; the perpendicular of this triangle is said to comprise so many feet.

The area is measured in the following way. Let the perpendicular, namely 12, be multiplied by the base, 25; 300 will result. Half of this measures the area of the aforesaid scalene triangle, as is shown in the figure below.

[Col. 1339D]

### On the right-angled triangle

In fourth place, naturally, Euclid inserts the right-angled triangle. It is marked by having one right angle and contains unequal sides. We consider it more difficult to understand by hearing alone, and more obscure than the others. For this reason we shall spend more time explaining it.

Let there now be a right-angled triangle whose perpendicular is marked by an even number, or extends for 8 feet. If its sides are unknown, Archytas prescribes that they be investigated in this way. Let half of the aforesaid perpendicular be taken, namely 4, and multiplied by itself; 16 will result. If one is subtracted from this, 15 appears. This is recognized as the number of feet in the base of the triangle. If one is added to the aforesaid total increased by the half of the perpendicular, there will be 17 feet in the hypotenuse. The area is likewise to be found from the same total, namely 16: let half of this total be multiplied by the perpendicular, and 64 will result, completing the calculation of the area, as the form below plainly demonstrates.

[Col. 1340D]

### On the same subject

Let us attempt to establish a clear and reliable description of this right-angled triangle by means of both an even and an odd number. Let an even number be assigned first to the perpendicular, namely 6. When half of it is multiplied by itself, 9 results. If, according to the rule of our instruction set out above, one is subtracted from this, the base of the triangle will be 8. Its half, namely 4, multiplied by the perpendicular, completes the area, as was stated above. The hypotenuse can likewise be determined from the perpendicular and the base.

We shall give an easy and evident example within the authority of our exposition. Let half of the perpendicular of this triangle be multiplied by itself, and let one be added to the total that results from this multiplication: this will be the length of the hypotenuse. If one is subtracted from the same total, it will be the base. Let a diagram of this matter be made.

[Col. 1340D]

Let us now establish a credible explanation of this right-angled triangle by means of an odd number. Let the perpendicular be marked with the odd number 3. If you multiply it by itself, you obtain 9; when one is subtracted, 8 remains. If half of this is taken, it is proved to be the length of the base of this right-angled triangle.

[Col. 1341A]

If you add one to this base, or to its half, namely 4, you will establish the hypotenuse of the triangle. Its area is found, as stated above, by multiplying the perpendicular by half the base, as can be seen in the picture below.

So that no obscurity may mislead the curious investigator of this discipline, I do not hesitate to discuss this same right-angled triangle again. There is another method for finding the perpendicular, base, and hypotenuse. Let the perpendicular extend for 5 feet. If you multiply it by itself, you obtain 25. Let a base measuring 12 feet be assigned; when it is likewise multiplied by itself, 144 results.

Those totals, 25 and 144, when joined, produce 169. It is clear that the square root of this is 13, namely the hypotenuse of the aforesaid triangle.

Finally, if you multiply the hypotenuse by itself, it returns the same total as that previously combined, namely 169. If from this you subtract the perpendicular multiplied by itself, 144 remains; its square root, namely 12, restores the base. From the hypotenuse multiplied by itself, if someone subtracts the base multiplied by itself—that is, 144 from 169—no more than 25 remains. Its square root, namely 5, establishes the perpendicular. The area is measured by multiplying half the base by the perpendicular.

It is also appropriate in this triangle to derive the length of the base from the perpendicular. Let the perpendicular above be 5; multiplied by itself, it gives 25. If one is subtracted from this, 24 results, and half of it forms the base. Again, if the same unit is added to the quantity of the base, the hypotenuse is obtained. If the base is multiplied by the perpendicular, the total advances to 60. Half of this completes the area.

### Again on the same subject

We shall also set before the reader another method for proceeding with this triangle, so that those who investigate it carefully may reach without doubt, by a repeated line of reasoning, the result they seek. Let there therefore be proposed a description of the same right-angled triangle, marked with the same quantities: a perpendicular of 8, a hypotenuse of 17, and a base of 15 feet.

We shall try to demonstrate how, from the square of the hypotenuse, the total length in feet of the perpendicular and the base may be found. Let the hypotenuse be multiplied by itself; the number 289 results. If four times the area is subtracted from this, 49 remain. If you seek the square root of these, you will find it to be 7. If this 7 is added to the combined perpendicular and base, 30 results, and half of this constitutes the length of the base. If, however, you subtract 23 from the combined total, namely 50, it is unquestionably proved that 8, the perpendicular, remains.

[Col. 1342A]

### The same subject again

Let us once more describe the form of the aforesaid right-angled triangle, using other numerical quantities, so that when someone is required to explain the doctrine of this triangle by either larger or smaller numbers, he may not fall into error. Let there be a right-angled triangle bounded by one even and two odd numbers: let 20 be assigned to the base, 15 to the perpendicular, and 25 to the hypotenuse.

The calculation of the area must be sought according to the rule of our instruction given above, namely by multiplying half the base by the entire perpendicular; for it contains 150 contracted feet of area.

The perpendicular and base are investigated in the following way. Let the hypotenuse be multiplied by itself; 625 results. If four areas are added to this, 1225 results. If you take its square root, namely 35, you will establish the combined totals of the base and perpendicular.

It is also necessary to know and investigate by what number the perpendicular and base differ from one another. Let us make this clear. If I subtract from the hypotenuse multiplied by itself the four areas that I added above, the total returns to 25. The fifth part of this contains the difference, namely 5. If I add this again to the two combined totals, namely 20 and 15, I will obtain 40; half of this completes the base.

If I subtract the same difference, namely 5, from the base, I establish the perpendicular, as can be seen in the figure below.

### On the circle inscribed in a right-angled triangle

We judged that what was approved by Archytas in this same right-angled triangle, and previously discovered by the most painstaking investigation of Euclid, should not be omitted. It often happens that a geometrician asks how many feet the diameter of a circle will comprise if the circle is inscribed in this right-angled triangle. So that no one, defeated by ignorance, may refuse to speak about it, we briefly explain the matter.

Let a circle therefore be inscribed so that it touches all the lines of the right-angled triangle. Once this has been done, let the perpendicular and base be added together. If from the combined total you subtract the length of the hypotenuse, you will obtain the diameter. For the perpendicular and base, joined together—12 and 8—give 20. If the hypotenuse, namely 15, is subtracted from this, the diameter is established as 5, as the figure made below shows.

[Col. 1343A]

### On the obtuse-angled triangle

The fifth in the order of triangles, the obtuse-angled triangle, was introduced by Euclid and is said to have an obtuse angle. We shall approach it by explaining it briefly and clearly. For if a diligent reader comes equipped with the instructions and formulas of our preceding exposition, he will not stumble here.

Let there now be an obtuse-angled triangle whose base is 18, whose larger hypotenuse is 10, whose smaller hypotenuse is 9, and whose perpendicular is marked by the number 4.

Let the base therefore be multiplied by half the perpendicular, that is, 18 by 2; 36 results, and this total fills out the plane of the area. But Archytas, employing reason in all things, established that the area of this obtuse-angled triangle could be found in another way. He thought that a smaller quantity, rather than this total, could be contained in the area, and therefore added that the perpendicular should be multiplied by itself and by 2, or by itself and by 8, with the products doubling one another. The quantity resulting from this multiplication, he held, constituted the area—not 36, but 32.

[Col. 1343C]

Whoever intends to draw the forms of this triangle on a plane should begin with the quantity of the base, in such a way that the endpoint produced by joining the smaller and larger hypotenuses exceeds the endpoint of the base by a small amount. Thus, if the base is measured as 20 feet, let the larger hypotenuse be marked as 11 and the smaller as 10. But we shall better demonstrate what we have explained numerically by presenting the form of an example.

### On the acute-angled triangle

[Col. 1343D]

It remains to speak of the acute-angled triangle, which Euclid, a geometer of no small ability, places sixth in the description of triangles and defines as having an acute angle. Let there therefore be an acute-angled triangle whose shorter side, namely the shorter hypotenuse, is bounded by 13 feet, while the longer is 15 and the base measures 14. Its perpendicular and area are calculated as follows.

Let the quantity of the shorter side be multiplied by itself; 169 results. Likewise, if the base is multiplied by itself, 196 results. If you join these totals, you obtain 365. Then let the length of the hypotenuse also be multiplied by itself, producing 225. If you subtract this from the total previously combined, 140 remain. Half of this is recognized as 70, which, distributed over the base, contains the base itself five times. The smaller cut-off portion controls this total; multiplied by itself, it produces 25. If you subtract this from the shorter side multiplied by itself, 144 remain. Its square root, which is 12, completes the total of the perpendicular.

Take care to investigate the area in this way: multiply half the base by the perpendicular, namely 7 by 12, and 84 will result. You should recognize that this total completes the floor-area of the triangle. Let such a figure therefore be drawn.

[Col. 1344B]

Since in the preceding discussion we have explained sufficiently to the investigation of diligent readers the measurement of triangular figures, it remains for us to pass briefly to the consideration of quadrilaterals and to treat them.

[Col. 1344C]

The calculation of squares is easier than the others, and let us begin first with the regular quadrilateral in the following way. Every quadrilateral regularly constituted forms its plane area by multiplying its width by its length, and unquestionably completes its measurement. Let there now be a quadrilateral marked by an even number, namely 8. If I multiply this width by its length, that is, by itself, I obtain 64, the area of the quadrilateral described below.

[Col. 1344D]

If you do the same with an odd number, the same method will hold without difficulty. This is the regular quadrilateral called by Euclid equilateral and rectangular, and similarly named by Nicomachus in his arithmetic works.

### On the oblong

The oblong is defined by Euclid as rectangular but not equilateral; Nicomachus calls it *heteromeres* (“having unequal parts”). Its length multiplied by its width demonstrates the area in feet, whether the dimensions are even or odd. Let there now be an oblong whose length is 8 feet and width 4, or whose length is 9 and width 6, 5, or 4 feet.

Let the width therefore be multiplied by the length, namely 4 by 8; 32 results. This is the area of the oblong, as these figures marked with even and odd numbers show.

[Col. 1345B]

### On the rhombus

To the parallelograms already mentioned we think that rhombi and rhomboid quadrilaterals should be added. Although they differ from the aforesaid parallelograms either in their angles or in their sides, they must nevertheless be counted among them.

Let there be a four-sided rhombus whose individual sides are marked as ten feet, while its diagonal—that is, the straight line across the angles—is counted as twelve. If 6 is multiplied by itself, 36 results. If this is subtracted from the base multiplied by itself, 64 remains. Its square root, namely 8, constitutes the perpendicular of this rhombus.

The diagonal multiplied by the perpendicular displays the area. Euclid defines this figure as having equal sides but neither equal nor right angles. Let a representation of this figure be made.

[Col. 1345D]

### On the rhomboid

Euclid proposed the rhomboid as having neither equal angles nor equal sides. We too shall open it up through a clearer approach by assigning numbers. Let there be a rhomboid whose first side is 8 feet, the second 4, the third 6, and the fourth 2. If you join the largest dimensions, which comprise the length, you obtain 14; half of this is 7. The smaller quantities, brought together, make 6, whose half is 3. If these halves, 7 and 3, are multiplied by each other, 21 results: these are the square feet of the area of this quadrilateral, as appears below.

[Col. 1346B]

We think it appropriate to add a right-angled trapezium, marked laterally by a double and a sesquialteral proportion of numbers. Let 15 be assigned to the upper side, 30 to the perpendicular, exceeding it twofold, and let a dimension maintaining a sesquialteral relation to this be assigned to the base. The area of this trapezium is to be established by these quantities in the following way.

Let the upper side be added to the base: 15, 45, and 60 produce the total. If half of this is multiplied by the perpendicular, it displays the extent of the area, as is clear in the figure written in the middle.

[Col. 1346C]

### On finding the diagonal

It often happens in the study of this art that one asks how long a diagonal line extends, that is, how many feet it comprises in these quadrilaterals. So that this may not be unknown, we shall provide the easiest and clearest example of the method.

Let there be a rectangular parallelogram with a length of 80 and an altitude of 60 feet. Its length multiplied by itself gives 6,400, while its width multiplied by itself gives 3,600. These quantities, 6,400 and 3,600, when combined, give 10,000. If I take the square root of this 10,000, I will obtain 100, that is, the diagonal of this rectangular parallelogram, as can be seen in the figure written below.

### On polygonal figures

[Col. 1347A]

Since we have spoken sufficiently and briefly about the principles of quadrilaterals, it remains for us to discuss pentagons, hexagons, and the other figures.

Every pentagon with equal sides displays the surface of its area by multiplying the length of one side by itself, multiplying the result by three, subtracting the same side again, and taking half of the resulting total. Let there now be a pentagon whose individual sides measure 6 feet. If I multiply 6 by itself, I obtain 36; multiplied by three, this gives 108. If I subtract from this the length of one side, namely 6, I obtain 102. If I take half of this, I complete the area of the pentagon described below.

[Col. 1347B]

### On the hexagon

The hexagon must next be discussed in its order. Let an hexagon be described, marked by 8 on each side. If I multiply this eight by itself, I obtain 64. This total, multiplied four times, produces 256. If to this 256 I add the quantity of one side, namely 8 multiplied twice, 272 appears. If you take half of this, you will obtain the area of this hexagon.

[Col. 1347D]

### On the heptagon

After this, in order to complete our discussion of the method of the following heptagon, it is necessary to insert it here in the third place, as the number seven naturally appears third in the order of odd numbers. Let there be a heptagon bounded by the quantity six. If you multiply the length of one side by itself, you obtain 36. This quantity, multiplied five times, yields 180. If you subtract from this the quantity six multiplied three times, 162 remain. Half of this, namely 81, gives the area of this heptagon in square feet.

[Col. 1348B]

### On the octagon

The octagon, established fourth in the natural order of even numbers, should naturally be taken as fourth in this discussion. Let there be an octagon whose individual sides measure 7 feet. If you multiply this natural quantity, namely 8, by itself, you obtain 64. If you multiply this by 6, you obtain 384. If from this you subtract four times the quantity of one side, no more than 352 remain. If half of this is taken, it is recognized as the area of the octagon.

[Col. 1348D]

### On the enneagon

Let an enneagon be bounded by individual sides of 6. If you multiply this six according to the rule of our instruction given above, you obtain 36. Multiplied seven times, this produces a total of 109 [text apparently corrupt]. If from this you subtract five times the quantity of one side, you obtain 79. If half of this is taken, it shows that the area of this enneagon contains 38½ square feet.

[Col. 1349A]

### On the decagon

[Col. 1349B]

It remains to speak of the calculation of the area of the decagon. Let a decagon be bounded on its sides by the number ten. If the quantity of one side, according to the rule of our instruction often mentioned above, is multiplied by itself, it produces 100. Multiplied eight times, this gives 800. If you take half of this, you will undoubtedly recognize that the area of this decagon is contained in 400 feet.

[Col. 1349C]

If you do the same for the hendecagon and the descriptions of the other many-sided figures, you will not stumble through any obstacle of error. Proceed in this manner: in the natural order, multiply the quantity of one side, naturally increase the quantity that arises from this multiplication, and naturally subtract the same side; then find the area by means of the halves.

[Col. 1349D]

### On the circle

Since we have discussed angular figures sufficiently for the learned reader, it remains briefly to explain the circumference of a sphere or circle. Let a circle be marked with a circumference of 44 feet, and let its diameter be described as extending for 14 feet. If this quantity is multiplied by itself, 196 results. Multiplying this by 11, you obtain 2156. The fourteenth part of this, namely 154, displays the area of this circle, as may be seen below.

There is another method for finding the area of this circle. Take half the circumferential quantity, namely 22, and multiply it by half the diameter, that is, by 7. The result of this multiplication displays the area.

[Col. 1350B]

### On the semicircle

With these brief beginnings concerning circular theorems, we have judged that we should speak next of the semicircle. Let a semicircle be written with a base of 28 and a radius of 14 feet. If its area is unknown, it may be found in the following way.

Let the length of the base be multiplied by the length of the radius; the result reaches 392, and this total produces 4211 when multiplied by ten [text apparently corrupt]. If the fourteenth part of this is taken, namely 312, the surface of the area is completed, as is shown below.

These statements about the measurement of plane figures will suffice for the present. It remains to treat, more briefly, the calculation of mountainous terrain. Let a mountain be marked as having a circumference of 300 feet around its summit, extending 800 feet from its foot to its top, while the foot of the same mountain is marked by a circumference of 1000 feet. Let it now be asked how many *jugera* are contained in this mountain.

The calculation must be begun in this way. Let the two circumferences, that of the foot and that of the summit, be joined, namely 1300. If the ascent, that is, 800, is multiplied by their half, namely 650, the space of this mountain will be proved to contain 520,000 feet. If you distribute this total over 28,800, you will establish that 18 *jugera* are contained in this mountain, with only 1,600 feet remaining.

[Col. 1351A]

But if the mountain has a circumference at its foot of 2500, a half-circumference of 1600, a circumference at its summit of 100, and an ascent of 500 feet, the *jugera* are to be found as follows. Let the totals of the three aforesaid circumferences be joined, and 4200 results. If the third part of this, namely 1400, is multiplied by the mountain’s ascent, that is, by 500, 700 results. Dividing this by the *jugera*, you will obtain 24, with no more than 200 feet remaining.

[Col. 1351C]

If the mountain is irregular, that is, unequal, with a circumference at its foot of 1400, a sloping summit of 200, an ascent on the right-hand side of 850, and a rise on the left side of 750 feet, its area in *jugera* is to be investigated as follows.

Take half of the two circumferences gathered together, namely 800, and half of the combined ascents, namely 800. When these halves are multiplied by each other, they produce 640, the measurement of the aforesaid mountain. From the number of feet you will easily find the total in *jugera*, according to what was stated above.

[Col. 1351D]

Since we have now discussed sufficiently, briefly and clearly, the methods of calculation belonging to all the investigations that had to be included in this art, it remains for us, as we promised, to speak of the uncia and the digit, of points and minutes, and of the other small units. We shall publish a remarkable diagram, necessary both for this art and for the other mathematical disciplines, which we learned under the preliminary instruction of Archytas.

### On the small units

[Col. 1352A]

The ancient geometricians, extremely subtle investigators and especially Pythagoreans, when they divided everything by definite systems of measurement and came at last to things that nature refused to divide and cut, distributed by ingenuity what was naturally indivisible, assigning written marks and corresponding names to it.

After they had divided fields by *actus*, by *perticae*, that is, by radii, by paces, by degrees, by cubits, by feet, by half-feet, and by palms, they had no palm by which to divide something smaller than a palm but larger than a digit. They therefore preferred to call it an *uncia*. In the second place they set down the digit; in the third, the *stater*, that is, the half-*uncia*; in the fourth, the quarter; in the fifth, the drachma; in the sixth, the scruple; in the seventh, the obol; in the eighth, the half-obol, which the Greeks call the *keration*; in the ninth, the carat; in the tenth, the point; in the eleventh, the minute; and in the twelfth, the moment.

After discovering these small units and publishing their names, they assigned to them multifarious marks. Since these marks were partly Greek and partly barbarous, they did not seem to us suitable for inclusion in Latin speech. Therefore, wishing not to wrap an obscure matter in obscure and unknown signs, we place in their stead, in order, the marks of the Latin alphabet, so that A corresponds to the *uncia* (inch), B to the digit, C to the stater, D to the quarter, E to the drachma, F to the scruple, G to the obol, H to the half-obol, I to the carat, K to the point, L to the minute, and M to the moment. Let the diagram of *unciae* (inches) that we mentioned be represented with these letters in the following way.

[Col. 1352C]
