## Boethius, Book on Geometry (C, G, S)*

Geometry is the discipline of immovable magnitude and the contemplative description of forms, through which the boundaries of each thing are customarily explained. It is also a visible lesson of the philosophers, which in Latin is called “the measurement of the earth.” Since Egypt is said to have first been divided according to the various forms of this discipline, out of necessity for marking the boundaries of the land that the river Nile used to flood during the season of inundation, the teachers of this discipline were formerly called surveyors.

But Varro, most skilled among the Latins, records that the reason for this name arose as follows, saying: “At first, measurements of lands, with boundaries established, provided the benefits of peace to wandering and quarrelling peoples. Then the circle of the entire year was divided according to the number of months. At that time the months themselves, because they measure the year, were also so called.” He also reports, with a plausible account, that the measurement of the globe of the earth was collected in this way. Thus it came about that the discipline itself received the name *geometry*, since it remained established through long ages.

### On the usefulness of geometry

The usefulness of geometry is threefold: for material resources, for health, and for the soul. For material resources, as in the case of mechanics and architects; for health, as in the case of physicians; for the soul, as in the case of philosophers.

If we pursue this art closely, diligently, and with a disciplined mind, it greatly clarifies our senses by what has been made evident in the divisions mentioned above. It also enables the mind to ascend to the heavens, to examine by investigative reasoning the whole of that celestial structure, and, through the elevated contemplation of the mind, to gather and recognize in part the maker of the world, who has concealed mysteries so great and so numerous.

For the world itself is said to have been gathered into a spherical roundness, so that it might enclose the various forms of things within the circuit of its circumference. Hence Seneca composed a book in agreement with the philosophers’ discussion, entitled *On the Form of the World*.

In geometry, certainly, we acknowledge that one part is useful for being held and applied in practical actions; indeed, we consider it beneficial in everything. Nor without reason did eminent men devote diligent effort to this science, since geometry is divided into numbers and the forms of numbers.

Knowledge of it is necessary not only to the orator but to everyone who has received even the first elements of education. It is extremely subtle in precision, highly useful for knowledge, and exceedingly pleasant as an exercise. It is very frequently sought in legal cases, because the ordering of geometry is fundamental.

Does geometry not also establish the subsequent from the prior in eloquence, and the uncertain from the certain? For this reason you will find many who, being likewise dialecticians and rhetoricians, enter upon this art. The dialectician uses the syllogism when the matter requires it; the most powerful grammarians, who are called *apodeixeis* in Greek, prove the same things. So too does the enthymeme, which is a rhetorical syllogism and which in Latin is interpreted as “a conception of the mind”; the art-writers commonly call it imperfect.

It too finally proves what form a circumference has, how many straight lines contain it, and by what methods it is bounded. It investigates whether the encircling line makes a circle, which is the greatest and most perfect of plane figures, and how many spaces it encompasses. If a square produces equal squares, a triangle produces triangles, and the figure with equal sides produces more than one with unequal sides, there are perhaps other matters that are more obscure; experience must also follow the work.

These are matters concerning planes. In mountains and hills, however, the point is clear even to the untrained, because it is understood from the course of the ground alone and from the movement of shadows, and because it is separated by the divergences of waters.

Now let us come to the letter of Julius Caesar, since it concerns the origin of this art. In this way the glory of its author will not perish, and the truth of the matter will come fully to our knowledge. Whoever wishes to read this letter attentively, having been introduced by certain summaries, will grasp the statements of the ancients more clearly and briefly.

### Rubric

The divine Julius Caesar, a most vigorous man and ruler of many peoples, trained the soldier through continuous warfare. For the purpose of increasing the state through the enterprises of greater wars, he entered the cities of distinguished men; he received peoples of nations who appealed to him; he killed tyrants with the sword; and after obtaining enemy territory, he destroyed the cities of the enemy and established new cities again, enlarging their citizens by giving them once more the name of a colony.

He made soldiers into colonists, some in Italy and others in certain provinces. These cities, which the divine Augustus, after assigning them, ordered for the army of the provinces because of the sudden clashes of war, were not merely to be surrounded with walls at last; difficult and rugged places were also to be sufficiently secured, since both that arrangement and the nature of the place constituted a strong defense. From the new dedication of the fields he called them agricultural colonies. These colonies were assigned to the victorious soldiers who had taken up arms for the sake of the time.

Therefore, so that we may not seem to have omitted anything but rather may follow their examples, it will often be necessary to look to the form of the land. Since the discourse showed that the heights of the mountains stood foremost, we laboriously left a line of signals constructed from stones along the ascent of the lofty summit. A fortified and distinguished measurement of the places remains, separately divided by the divergences of the waters; the division on both sides is very clear. In some places the course of the banks is preserved, so that, even if an enemy had wished to attack us, we could break through against them by assaulting them from the nearest bank.

Around the maritime region we judged that the boundaries should be straight, compacted from stones. We shall demonstrate the entire straight course of the boundaries, because all colonies established by the sea are bounded by the seashore. We arranged the fields of the valleys according to the ordinary law and called them intercisive fields. In the plain, however, we marked out the boundaries in straight lines.

There are usually many assigned fields whose boundary measurements, although different, nevertheless stand apart from one another by 100 feet, 150 feet, 240 feet, 300 feet, 361 feet, 420 feet, 480 feet, 600 feet, 700 feet, 840 feet, 962 feet, 1020 feet, 10,200 feet, 1340 feet, 10,600 feet, 10,700 feet, 10,800 feet, or 2200 feet; yet they remain within the long view by which we lay out the boundary with markers.

If a boundary is thick and narrow, and on the other side a long thick boundary is doubled, these two boundaries are called the great *decumanus* and *cardo*. They run together for many thousands of feet, and unless they end in the Alps, they divide the fields to right and left, containing straight lines between them.

You should make every measurement of this cultivation either longer or broader in the middle. Whatever is longer in width is a *scamnum*; whatever is longer in length is a *striga*.

[Col. 1355A]

There are estates of men who have rendered good service, and they have been assigned narrower dimensions in proportion to their fertility.

Lean and dry places are enclosed by a more extensive boundary. There are residual lands (*loca subsicciva*) that do not belong to the ordinary legal allotment; but if the possessors agree among themselves, let them possess them; if they do not agree, they remain under the authority [of the state].

Other, more fully developed lands belong to public law; likewise, if the possessors agree, they possess them.

The following, however, are public lands: those designated as public woods and public pastures of the Augustans, which cannot be alienated in that manner, and which are held for the protection either of public temples or of bathhouses. These lands are called *colliva*.

An *ager extraclusus* is land lying between the boundary line and the centuriae; it is called *extraclusus* because it is enclosed beyond the outer boundaries.

## On disputes

[Col. 1355B] There are two subjects of disputes: boundary and land. One of these includes whatever is disputed concerning the field. But since disputes marked out in these parts also have different conditions, they must, insofar as I have been able to understand them, be named individually.

There are fourteen kinds of disputes: concerning the placement of boundary markers; concerning the region; concerning the boundary; concerning the land; concerning ownership of a house; concerning possession; concerning alluvion; concerning territorial right; concerning residual lands; concerning public lands; concerning abandoned and excluded lands; concerning sacred and religious places; concerning the access of rainwater; and concerning roads.

A dispute arises between two or more neighbors. Between two, the question is whether the matter lies within the strict boundary of the others, without a rational basis [for the claim]; between several, it creates a three-way boundary, and in some places a four-way boundary, according to the neighboring possessions. While they do not understand this, they do not reach agreement, and the possessors themselves create various disputes among one another. Some litigate about the land, others about the boundary line, and others consider the estates. But the origin of the case must first be sought with careful attention. Because of inheritance, disputes of this kind arise from this opinion, and so litigation proceeds according to ordinary law. Nevertheless, the question of possession must first be settled in court; then the surveyor must be ordered to go to the places, so that, once the truth has been brought to light, this kind of litigation may be ended.

The following are kinds of disputes arising from a river—not disputes over occupied fields, but cases in which the force of the water has carried something away and there is no right of recovery. Such places must necessarily be protected by a bank, and anyone may construct and protect his own bank without damage to another. But if the torrent of a river should at some time flow with such violence that it changes its channel, it occupies the fields of many people beyond the bank and often even creates islands. Cassius Longinus, however, the most judicious authority and judge of the law, established this rule: whatever the water has carried away by gradually washing against the bank, the possessor must accept, since he must protect his own bank without damage to another. But if a greater force should flow and change its channel into another person’s boundaries, and an island should be formed where the waters meet, each person must acknowledge the extent of the greater river, and the person whose land it has promptly occupied will claim that island for himself, since it appears to have been taken not through the possessor’s negligence but through the violence of the storm.

A residual field, according to its own boundaries, [Col. 1356A] is entered in the records: we enter it in the emperor’s archive, and whatever has been granted or assigned by privilege to a colony—whether nearby or among other cities—we enter in the books of grants. Everything else belonging to the surveyors’ documentation for the colony’s land must bear the undersigned mark of the founder’s hand in the emperor’s archive.

There is a field similar in condition to a residual and excluded field, unassigned, which, if it has not been given to the republic, to the Roman people, to the colony itself within whose boundary it is enclosed, or if it does not belong to the Roman people, remains under the authority of the person who could assign it.

The following are signs of final boundaries in different regions—or names, villages, or possessions—testimonies concerning the land that must be divided between the two possessors.

In the mountains we find dry and rugged places marked by stones.

The principal boundary markers of the mountains are *agustei*—that is, round markers—some marked with letters in the likeness of a column; final chests (*archae finales*) in the portions of the *grumi*, that is, heaps of stones; trees set before them and left untouched by iron; a heap of masonry, that is, where stones collected from both sides form a boundary; and sacrificial stones, altars, in places where untouched trees seem to stand, at which place the ancients, wandering about, made sacrifice. Elsewhere military roads make the boundary, and are fortified by a marker. [Col. 1356C] Other right-hand features of the mountains—that is, banks running along the side of the mountain—make the boundary. Sometimes tombs make the boundary. Therefore the tombs must be followed, for where the outer boundaries meet, several convergences of fields are expected. All monuments, indeed, bear witness to their owners.

There are boundary markers called *cursory*, made in the form of an inscription; fixed places of streams; final cradles or “stepmothers,” constructed according to rules; and *scorpiones*, where two wedge-shaped boundaries join.

If, by chance, markers are found in level country, where fields have been laid out on the plain and assigned in *iugera*, there are also, among the ravaged rocks, trees set before them and left untouched, as I said above, for sacrificial purposes; elevations of earth formed in the likeness of a boundary; millstones; pits or landmarks; lakes; *legonati*; and *calaviones* constructed by craftsmen. At times there are square stones bearing inscriptions, [Col. 1356D] which indicate who owns the field and how much space they protect. Not every inscription has been placed on a title-stone, since in some places there are no inscribed stones, but stones have been set in the form of boundary markers, which we call *cursory*. The mountains themselves, moreover, wholly determine the places, while the boundary markers do not all contain one and the same measurement, at the command of Augustus Caesar, Balbus the surveyor, who distinguished and explained the measurements of all the provinces, and the boundaries of the places are established through the testimonies written above.

There are boundary markers to which no confidence should be given; these are called itinerant markers. All boundaries that divide private limits on the right and left must serve the public road, with the public road running between them. Such markers are not found in every place. In any event, a sign ought to be found beneath every boundary marker; whatever is found there must be observed and preserved as the sign belonging to that place, so that it may be directed from one marker to another, whether by night or from one mark to another. [The final wording is textually uncertain.]

For there are established customs and observances of the law: a sign has always been placed beneath all boundary markers. We find either ashes, or charcoal, or pottery, or bones, or glass, or a mass of iron, or bronze, or lime, or gypsum, or a clay vessel. These were also trampled down with certain fragments of stone and firmly secured with careful attention, so that they would stand more firmly. Thus they made such a sign between the owners whose boundaries were being established.

Boundary markers, however, are not found in every place; there are also many other innumerable testimonies. By reading the law carefully and understanding it, you will learn their significance. Whoever understands what he sees can remove disputes and contention concerning fields. Nevertheless, the surveyors who are to judge must possess prudence, as must those whom they call in as guarantors. In judging, the surveyor must act as a good and just man, unmoved by ambition or corruption, and must preserve his judgment according to the measurements and according to moral conduct. Truth must be guarded by every craftsman; those who set falsehoods against truths are excluded. Some sin through lack of prudence, others through lack of expertise. Thus, when what is generally added as true is altered in the course of a professional statement, craftsmen are compelled to make measurements unnecessarily through argumentative and conjectural dispute; but the craftsman who judges must be a reliable person.

## Names of the surveyors

[Col. 1357C] Hyginus, Marcus, by order of Caesar Nero.—Julius Frontinus, Junius, by order of Caesar Claudius.—Siculus.—Flaccus, Nypsus, Hyginus, Euclid, Cassius.—Agenius Balbus, by order of Caesar Tiberius.—Urbicus, the surveyor Longinus.—By order of the emperors Severus and Antoninus.—By order of the emperor Vespasian.—By order of the emperor Hadrian.—By order of the emperor Trajan.—By order of the emperor Augustus Caesar.—By order of the emperor Nero.—By order of the emperor Valentinian.—By order of the emperor Theodosius.—By order of the emperor Arcadius.—By order of the emperor Honorius.—By order of the emperor Constantine.

## Names of final stones and positions of boundary chests

*Orthogonius*: straight; it produces a right angle.  
*Isopleurus*: straight, set beneath.  
*Isosceles*. A lined boundary marker.  
*Exculenus*, or hexagonal. A cursory spatula.  
*Excultelatus*: with sides. A boundary marker set upside down.  
*Sumbus*, or trapezoidal. Also a cursory spatula.  
*Isosceles*. A four-way boundary marker.  
*Solus trigonus*: a triangle throws out another form. Also a four-way boundary marker.  
*Parallelogrammus pentagonus*. A hooked boundary marker. Hexagonal. A lined boundary marker, that is, a four-way boundary marker.  
*Septagenus*. Also a four-way boundary marker.  
*Sinagonus*. A stepmother.  
A boundary marker inscribed with a Greek letter. *Simmatus*.  
A boundary marker pointed at the top. *Centustatus*.  
A circular pyramid, also resembling a pointed form. *Trivortinus*.  
Also a pyramid resembling a truncated point. *Amicirculus*.  
A complete rhombus, *amblygineus*. *Varoberinus*.  
A square semicircle. *Trudeus*.  
An *agusteus* boundary marker. An Augustan boundary marker pointed at the top.  
A cursory boundary marker. A millstone.  
A boundary marker of the limit. A monument.  
A burial place with bones, a final marker. *Mauspleus*.  
A boundary marker in small bricks. A final chest.  
A four-way boundary marker. *Lippus*.  
A round boundary marker. *Kalasiones*.  
A boundary marker beneath which there is an angle. A four-way boundary marker.

You who wish to be a perfect geometrician, read all the matters listed below under their headings. First of all, you must know the art of arithmetic, which contains the causes and divisions of numbers, namely: what definition and division apply to even and odd numbers; what number is composite and what number is non-composite; what number is perfect and what number is imperfect; what number is divisible and what number is indivisible; what number is *particular* and what number is *superpartient*; what number is excessive and what number is diminished; what number is multiple and what number is submultiple; what number is solid and what number is spherical; how geometry was discovered; what geometry is; what its usefulness is; what the order of the preliminary statement is; what the principle of arrangement is; what belongs to disposition; what belongs to distribution; what belongs to description; what belongs to demonstration; what belongs to conclusion; what a straight line is; what the surface of a line is; what a *divitrica* line is; how many kinds of extremities there are; how many kinds of summits; how many kinds of angles; what a plane angle is; what an obtuse angle is; what a blunt angle is; what a right angle is; what an acute angle is; what kind of measure is divided; how far a *stadius* extends; what a *sitacus* is; what *climata* are; what a *centua* is; what a *leuca* is; what an *arrapennis* is; what a *iugerum* is; what a *centuria* is; what a point is; what a diameter is; what a parallelogram is; what a figure is; what a circle is; and into how many parts division is made.

If you know all these things completely, you understand the separation of places. For those who do not know the rule of this art put forward many false things in place of true ones.

**D. How was geometry discovered?**

**M.** The Egyptians say that geometry was discovered because of the need to establish the boundaries of land, which no one could mark out during the season of inundation.

**D. Where did the name geometry come from?**

**M.** Geometry was named from the measurement of the earth, through which the boundaries of each individual piece of land are ordinarily made clear.

**D. What is geometry?**

**M.** Geometry is the discipline of magnitude and figure, [Col. 1358D] which contemplates things according to magnitude.

**D. What is its purpose?**

**M.** Euclid’s purpose is twofold: it concerns the student and it concerns the nature of things. It concerns the student because he ought to begin with introductory matters, for the sake of ease, brevity, and the fact that this makes the questions free from difficulty. It concerns the nature of things because the physical sciences and the teaching of Timaeus, or of Plato, are known to demonstrate many geometrical matters.

**D. What is its usefulness?**

**M.** As we stated above, the usefulness of geometry is threefold: for practical ability, for health, and for the soul. It is useful for practical ability, as in the case of mechanics; for health, as in the case of physicians; and for the soul, as in the case of philosophers.

[Col. 1359A] **D. What is geometry’s order among the disciplines?**

**M.** In one respect it is subordinate to arithmetic; in another respect it is third.

**D. How is the inscription of the title to be understood?**

**M.** The title is a preliminary statement of the elements, which are the simpler figures; from these other figures are composed, and into these they are also resolved.

**D. Is it a proper book?**

**M.** This book is said to follow Euclid’s arrangement; in its demonstrations or discoveries, however, it is said for the most part to belong to others.

**D. Into how many parts is it divided?**

**M.** This book is divided into four parts: plane figures, arithmetic, rational and irrational lines, and solids.

[Col. 1359B] **D. What elements are present in geometrical demonstration?**

**M.** Proposition, arrangement, distribution, description, demonstration, and conclusion.

It remains for us to hand down a certain very profound discipline, one that, by reason, is especially concerned with the integrity of all nature and of all things. There is indeed great benefit in this science, if one does not fail to understand that goodness—defined, falling within knowledge, and always imitable and perceptible by the mind—is the first nature, perpetual in the beauty of its substance; whereas the boundless disgrace of evil, resting on no principles of its own but by nature always wandering away from every definition of principle, is as though formed from some sign impressed with the figure of the best form and is held back from that flood of error. For a mind serving as a kind of ruler, strengthened by pure intelligence, restrains excessive desire and the immoderate, unbridled fury of anger.

Nevertheless, what Nicomachus discussed at greater length concerning numbers, and what Varro set forth concerning measurements, we have gathered together with measured brevity. Whatever, because it had been passed over too rapidly, provided a narrower entrance to understanding, we have opened up by moderate additions, so that at times we might also use our own formulas and descriptions to make things evident. A sober reader can easily recognize how many vigils and how much toil this has cost us. By laboring with moderated goodness, we have gathered together these forms of inequality in a certain way; the reader himself will judge them, since we have contracted them from the abundance of Greek letters into the treasury of Roman language. If anything has shone forth from the teachings of wisdom, let it be approved through us by the judgment of the wisest.

You see, therefore, that the result of so great a labor awaits only your examination, reader, and that it does not venture forth into public ears unless it is supported by the assent of learned judgment. This should seem no surprise, since a work that pursues the discoveries of wisdom depends not on the author’s judgment but on that of another. Wisdom is the true knowledge and complete understanding of the causes of numbers and of their divisions. To anyone who despises this—that is, the path of wisdom—I declare that he cannot philosophize correctly.

This is arithmetic; for it is prior to everything, not only because God, the creator of this worldly structure, first possessed it as the model of his reasoning and established all things according to it, so that whatever was fashioned by rational design found harmony through the assigned order of number, but also because arithmetic is shown to be prior for this reason: whatever is prior by nature, when removed, takes away what is posterior at the same time. But if what is posterior perishes, nothing in the state of the prior substance is changed—just as an animal is prior to a human being. If you remove the animal, the nature of the human being is immediately destroyed as well. If you remove the human being, the animal does not perish. Properly speaking, however, the very nature of numbers preceded everything.

Whatever was constructed by the primordial nature of things appears to have been formed by the rational principle of numbers. This was the principal model in the mind of the creator. From it came the multitude of the four elements; from it, the cycles of time; from it, the motions of the stars and the revolution of the heavens. Properly speaking, the very nature of numbers established all the courses of the stars and the whole science of astronomy. Thus we calculate risings and settings; thus we observe the slowness and speed of wandering stars; thus we recognize eclipses and the moon’s manifold variations.

Since, as has been made clear, the use of arithmetic is prior, let us take the beginning of our discussion from it. The same point also appears in geometry and arithmetic. For if you remove numbers, how can we comprehend a triangle or a square, or anything else belonging to geometry, all of which are named according to numbers? This will be clear if we understand that all inequalities grew from beginnings, so that equality itself, possessing in some manner the power of mother and root, imbued all the species and orders of inequality.

Let us posit three pairs, or three triples, or three quadruples, or as many more as one wishes. What occurs in these three terms occurs likewise in the others. According to the order of our instruction, you may therefore first see multiples arise when they are reversed, and among these first doubles, then triples, then quadruples, and those that follow in the same order. Again, when multiples are reversed, superparticulars arise from them: from doubles, sesquialter numbers; from triples, sesquitertian numbers; from quadruples, sesquiquartan numbers; and the others in the same manner. From reversed superparticulars, superpartients must arise: from a sesquialter, a superbipartient; from a sesquitertian, a supertripartient; and from a sesquiquartan, a superquadripartient. When the earlier superparticulars are set in their proper order and not reversed, multiple superparticulars arise. When superpartients are set in their proper order, multiple superpartients are produced.

The three rules are these: first make the first number equal to the first; then make the first equal to the second; then make the second equal to the third; and make the first equal to two seconds and to the third. When you have made the terms equal, the doubles will arise from them. If you do the same with those doubles, triples are produced; from these, quadruples; and so, to infinity, you will unfold all the forms of multiple numbers.

Those whose parts extend farther than is proper are called excessive, such as 12 or 114. Compared with their whole, their parts produce a greater sum of parts: for twelve has one-half, 6; one-third, 4; one-fourth, 3; one-sixth, 2; and one-twelfth, 1. All this accumulation amounts to 16, and exceeds the total of the whole body. Again, one-half of 24 is 12; one-third, 8; one-fourth, 6; one-sixth, 4; one-eighth, 3; one-twelfth, 2; and one twenty-fourth, 1. Together these amount to 36. In this it is clear that the sum of the parts is greater and overflows beyond the proper whole.

On the other hand, a number whose combined parts are exceeded by the total quantity of the term, such as 8 or 14, is diminished. The number eight has one-half, 4; one-fourth, 2; and one-eighth, 1. Together these make 7, a sum smaller than the whole body. Again, fourteen has one-half, 7; one-seventh, 2; and one-fourteenth, 1. When these are collected together, the sum becomes 10, and is therefore less than the whole term.

But those numbers that are like the first—whose parts exceed them—appear as though someone had been born with many hands beyond the nature of things, or joined to a double body, or had seized something monstrous from nature in the multiplication of parts.

The smaller numbers are as though a necessary natural part had been removed, or as though one had been born with less than a complete eye, or had been shortened in some other limb and thereby suffered a loss from the natural fullness of the whole. Between these, as between equal immoderacies, lies the balanced measure of the number called perfect—a rival of virtue—which is directed neither by excessive increase nor weakened by contracted diminution. It maintains the mean: among its equal parts it neither advances through abundance nor lacks through poverty, as with 6 or 28.

The number six has one-half, 3; one-third, 2; and one-sixth, 1. When these are reduced to a single sum—3, 2, and 1—the whole body of the number is found equal to its parts. Twenty-eight has one-half, 14; one-fourth, 7; one-seventh, 4; one-fourteenth, 2; and one twenty-eighth, 1. Reduced to one sum, its parts equal the whole body, for joined together they produce 28.

There is also in these a great likeness between virtue and vice. You will find perfect numbers rarely, and they are easily counted, since they are few and are produced in a very regular order. But you will find excessive numbers infinite in number, scattered everywhere without order, and generated by no definite limit.

The perfect numbers within ten are 6; within one hundred, 28; within one thousand, 416; within ten thousand, 800 and 128. These numbers always end in the two even numbers 6 and 8, and the endings of the sums always occur alternately in these numbers. For first comes 6, then 28, and after these 496. The same six that was first comes after 800 and 128; the same eight that was second [comes thereafter].

There are five parts of greater inequality: one is called multiple, another superparticular, the third superpartient, the fourth multiple superparticular, and the fifth multiple superpartient. Opposed to these five greater parts are five other parts, each named by the same terms according to the lesser species, differing only by the prefix *sub-*.

They are called submultiple, subsuperparticular, subsuperpartient, submultiple-superparticular, and submultiple-superpartient. In the first part, when a number is multiplied, it is called multiple. In the second, it is called superparticular. In the third, superpartient; in the fourth, multiple superparticular; in the fifth, multiple superpartient. The smaller numbers, with one remaining in some part, extend through their parts according to the rule and quantity of the greater numbers.

## On even and odd numbers

The description that has been placed below was made in the following manner: however many evenly even numbers the number three multiplied in order, all the numbers produced from it were arranged in the first row. Again, those produced by the same multiplier, five, were placed in the second position. Then those produced by seven multiplying the others were placed in the third position; and we complete the same arrangement through the rest of the description.

The principle of the description arranged above is this: if you look at the width, where two terms have one middle term, and join the terms themselves, you will find them doubled by their proper middle term. Thirty-six and 20 make 56, whose middle is 28; and if you join 12, they make 150, of which 20 is found as their middle term. [The numerical example is corrupt in the supplied text.] But where there are two middle terms, the two extremities joined together become equal to the two middle terms, as when 12 and 36 are joined and make 48; if you apply their middle terms to one another—that is, 20 and 28—the result is the same.

On the other side of the width, the numbers produced in the same order have been marked, and the principle of the two widths differs in no respect. You will notice the same thing in the same order in the remaining numbers. This occurs according to the form of the evenly even number, in which, as has already been said above, this property exists.

Again, if you look at the length, where two terms have one middle term, what arises from multiplying the extremes also arises when the middle term receives the increase of its plurality. Twelve times 48 makes 576; but if their middle term, 24, is multiplied by itself, it produces the same 576. Again, if 24 is multiplied by 546, the result is 2304; and if their middle term, 48, is multiplied by itself, the same 2304 is produced. [The supplied text reads “546” in these places; the arithmetic appears corrupt.]

But where two terms enclose two middle terms, what occurs through multiplication of the extremes is likewise reproduced when the middle terms are multiplied by one another. Twelve times 546 produces 152; but if their two middle terms, 24 and 48, are multiplied by one another, they restore the same 152. [The numerical wording is uncertain.] This property is recognized as generated in imitation and kinship of the evenly even number, from which it derives by participation. On the other side of the length the same principle and arrangement is marked. From this it is clear that the whole number has been produced from the two preceding numbers, and retains their properties.

Since by nature and according to the proper succession of order we have placed the multiple form of inequality before all others and shown it to be the first species, although this may become clearer in the order of the later work, let us here also touch upon it and teach what we have proposed as plainly and briefly as possible.

Let there be an arrangement in which the natural sequence of consecutive numbers is set in order up to ten; in the second row let a double sequence be woven; in the third, a triple; in the fourth, a quadruple; and so on up to tenfold. In this way we shall recognize how the multiple species is primary in relation to the superparticular, the superpartient, and all the others. We shall also observe certain matters at once: matters most subtle in precision, most useful for knowledge, and highly pleasurable as an exercise.

If, then, the first two sides of the proposed formula, which form an angle from one to ten, and the ten numbers extending along them are considered, and the lower rows are compared with them—those that begin at 4 and place their terms up to twenty—the double, that is, the first species of multiplicity, is displayed. The first exceeds the first by one unit: two exceeds one. The second surpasses the second by two: four surpasses two. The third surpasses the third by three: six surpasses three. The fourth exceeds the fourth by the quantity four: eight exceeds four. The remaining numbers likewise surpass one another in succession by the plurality of the lesser number.

If the third angle is considered, beginning at nine and extending its length and width on either side through numbers of thirty, and if this too is compared with the first width and length, the triple species of multiplicity appears. The comparison is made through the figure of the letter X, and the numbers surpass one another according to the naturally established connection of parity: the first exceeds the first by two, as three exceeds one; the second exceeds the second by four, as six exceeds two; the third exceeds the third by six, as nine exceeds three; and the remaining numbers increase in the same manner. Nature itself has presented this to us, without our contriving anything beyond it, as appears in the very pattern of the arrangement.

If someone wishes to compare with the preceding figures the term of the fourth angle, marked by the number sixteen, and the length that ends in the forties, he will recognize, by comparison according to the form of the letter X, a fourfold multiplicity. These numbers have an ordered progression above themselves: the first exceeds the first by three, as four exceeds one; the second conquers the second by six, as eight exceeds two; the third passes beyond the third by nine, as twelve exceeds three; and the succeeding sums always leap forward by the addition of three.

If anyone looks at the lower angles, the same result will appear through all the species of multiplicity, arranged in an orderly sequence up to tenfold.

If anyone seeks superparticulars in this description, he will find them as follows. If he marks the second angle, whose beginning is the number four and above which lies the number two, and adapts to it the next sequence, the sesquialter proportion is revealed. The third of the second row is sesquialter in relation to it: three to two, or six to four, or nine to six, or twelve [Col. 1364A] to eight. The same combination may be made with the remaining numbers in the same series, and no difference of variation will intrude. The same excess of sums is found here as in the doubles. The first exceeds the first by one, as three exceeds two; the second exceeds the second by two; the third exceeds the third by three; and so forth.

If the fourth row is compared with the third—4 to 3—and the remaining numbers are followed in the same order, the sesquitertian comparison is obtained: 4 to 3, or 8 to 6, or 12 to 9. Do you see how the sesquitertian relation is preserved in all these? Moreover, if by doing the same thing you compare the following rows below them with one another, you will recognize all the species of superparticular without any difficulty.

The divine feature of this arrangement is that all the angular numbers are square numbers. A square number, to put it very briefly—though it will be explained more fully later—is one that is produced by multiplying two equal numbers. Thus, in this description, one multiplied by one is one, and by its power it is a square. Likewise, twice two is four, and three times three is nine; multiplication by themselves produces them at the beginnings.

Around them, those that lie around the angles are oblong numbers. I call oblong numbers those produced by multiplying numbers that exceed one another by one. Around 4 are 2 and 6. Two is produced from one and two, when you multiply one by two. The unit precedes the binary by one; 6 is produced from two and three, for twice three gives six. Six and twelve enclose nine; twelve is produced from three and four, for three times four makes twelve. Six is produced from two and three, for twice three makes six. All these are produced by sides that exceed one another by one.

For when 6 is born from two and three, three exceeds two by one, and all the others are of the same kind: they are produced by multiplying the terms of the first and second rows against one another, so that what is born from two oblong numbers set on opposite sides, and twice the middle square, is itself a square. Again, what is born from two squares placed on opposite sides and from one middle oblong number taken twice is itself likewise a square.

Of the angles of the whole description set around the angular squares, one angle has the first unit, while the opposite angle has the third; the angle on the other side has two units. The two angles of the angular squares make equal the quantity contained beneath them, equal to what is produced by one of those opposite angles. Many other useful and remarkable things could be examined in this description. For the sake of the restrained brevity proper to an introduction, however, we temporarily leave them unknown and now turn our purpose to what follows.

## End of the book on Geometry by Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius

If anyone should think that something more is required in this work, let him judge it with goodwill and fairness. We have corrected very many passages; in some places it seemed best to leave each person his own judgment and to change nothing rashly. Certainly, insofar as diligence, industry, and expense could accomplish it, nothing has been omitted by us.

# POPE HORMISDAS

**Notice.** 363

# LETTERS AND DECREES

**Letter I** *(to Saint Remigius).* — After receiving his congratulatory letter, he delegated to him, on account of the outstanding excellence of his merits and the prerogative of his most noble see, the office of prefect and vicar of the Apostolic See in Gaul. 367

Letter of Anastasius to Hormisdas. 369

**Letter II** *(to the Emperor Anastasius).* — He praises him for striving for the peace of the Church and writes that, once he has learned the reason why Anastasius wishes a council to be convened, he will give him a reply. 370

Letter of Dorotheus to Hormisdas. 371

**Letter III** *(to Dorotheus).* — He praises his piety and his devotion to the Roman See. 372

Letter of Anastasius Augustus to Hormisdas. 373

**Letter IV** *(to the Emperor Anastasius).* — He commends the emperor’s zeal; concerning the council, he promises that he will reply through legates. 374

**Brief memorandum** delivered by Pope Hormisdas to Ennodius and Fortunatus, bishops; Venantius, presbyter; Vitalis, deacon; and Hilary, notary—legates of the Apostolic See to Constantinople. 374

**Letter V** *(to the Emperor Anastasius).* — It is unprecedented for the Roman pontiff to be summoned by the emperor to a council; nevertheless, he will go, provided that the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon are not called into question. 379

[Column 1443] Letter of the Emperor Anastasius to Hormisdas. 381

Letter of the same to the same. 383

**Letter VI** *(to Anastasius Augustus).* — Before Anastasius’s fraud has yet been detected, he praises his efforts to establish peace and urges him finally to condemn the heresies so that the unity of the Church may take effect. *Ibid.*

Letter of Anastasius to the Senate of the City of Rome. 385

Reply of the Senate of the City of Rome to Anastasius Augustus. 386

Letter of John, bishop of Nicopolis, to Hormisdas. 387

**Letter VII** *(to Bishop John).* — He commends his religious devotion; he writes that Nestorius and Eutyches must be condemned and that he will indicate by a memorandum how those who return to the faith are to be received. 388

Synodical letter of the Synod of Old Epirus to Hormisdas. 389

**Letter VIII** *(to the Synod of Old Epirus).* — He condemns the followers of Eutyches’ errors and urges the bishops of Old Epirus to anathematize the heretics by name. 391

**Letter IX** *(to Bishop John).* — Since the bishops of Old Epirus had not condemned the heretics by name in their letter, a booklet is sent to which they must subscribe. 392

Rule of faith. 393

**Brief memorandum.** — What is to be done in the Church of Nicopolis. 394

Letter of Avitus, bishop of Vienne, to Hormisdas. 394

**Letter X** *(to Avitus, bishop of Vienne).* — He praises in him his eagerness to learn about the condition of the Eastern Church; but he writes that, because of the Greeks’ faithlessness, nothing was accomplished by the legates, and that he intends to send another embassy to them. 394

**Letter XI** *(to Anastasius Augustus).* — Peace cannot be restored to the Church unless Acacius is condemned. 397

**Letter XII** *(to Timothy, bishop of Constantinople).* — One must labor for the unity of the Church. 399

**Letter XIII** *(a memorandum to all the heretical bishops of the East).* — The unity of the Catholic faith must be preserved. 400

**Letter XIV** *(to the orthodox bishops of the East).* — He praises their steadfastness in the faith and writes that he has again sent legates to Constantinople to establish peace. 401

**Letter XV** *(to Bishop Possessor).* — One must persevere in the Catholic faith. 403

**Letter XVI** *(to the people and monks of Constantinople).* — They must abstain from association with heretics and persevere in the Catholic faith. *Ibid.*

**Letter XVII** *(to Ennius and Peregrinus, bishops).* — He writes that he has learned from John of Nicopolis what the bishop of Thessalonica attempted against him, and that he has entrusted to them by this letter the investigation of the new case brought before the Apostolic See. 404

**Letter XVIII** *(to the same).* — He prescribes what is to be done in the case of Nicopolis together with the bishop of Thessalonica. 405

**Letter XIX** *(to Anastasius Augustus).* — He commends John of Nicopolis to him. 406

**Letter XX** *(to Bishop John).* — Sufferings endured for the faith must be borne with equanimity; therefore he urges him to confirm the provincial bishops in the unity of the faith. 406

**Letter XXI** *(to the same John).* 407

**Letter XXII** *(to Dorotheus, bishop of Thessalonica).* 408
